## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and most diligently corrected; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions published during the last three centuries had been completed, and furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; augmented by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in which places of their works, commented on the several texts of the several books of Scripture. A most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if the following are taken into consideration: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of the works reprinted, the exceedingly convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection, which is single, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, but brought together for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Published by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# Flavius Lucius Dexter

> **Note:** The Chronicle published by Bivarius under the name of Dexter is unanimously declared spurious by the bibliographers of our age, who attribute it to a certain Jesuit of the sixteenth century. **Editor.**

[Col. 0009]

# Dedication Letter of the Editor Bivarius

To the Most Illustrious and Reverend Lord, Lord Gabriel de Treio, most distinguished Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church,

Brother Franciscus de Bivar, Procurator of Saint Bernard, sends greetings and offers his service.

It is evident to everyone that great gifts ought to be given to great men, whom lesser gifts do not suit; for the greater a person is, and the more eminent the position he occupies, the less he concerns himself with trifles. Just as one who looks down from a lofty tower must necessarily look down upon the things below, since he can scarcely discern them.

To you, therefore, Most Illustrious Prince, who sit at the lofty pole of heaven, having been made second among the moving intelligences by whose nod the entire Christian world is governed on every side, no gift so very small as this Chronicle will seem to many ought to have been offered. Nevertheless, if things are to be judged not by their size but by their worth, I shall never be persuaded to admit that Dexter’s Chronicle should be considered insignificant because it is very small in volume. When weighed on a just balance, it outweighs by its substance many enormous volumes that have hitherto been written on ecclesiastical matters.

I do not know whether it may rightly be called a splendid pearl, a large pearl, or a diamond, rather than a book—or whether someone might call it a little golden book, wrought by an unusual art of intellect. For what such deeply hidden riches of history have ever existed that were omitted by Dexter? He embraces, in a style as lucid as it is concise, the successions of the Roman pontiffs, the deeds of emperors, the eradication of heresies, the exact examination of councils, the writings of Doctors, the overthrow of kingdoms, and the transformations of monarchies that took place throughout the whole world from the birth of the Lord to the author’s death.

Nor is this all. The apostolic division, journeying, preaching, and conversion of the world itself; the marvelous and varied foundations of patriarchal and episcopal sees; the victories of martyrs; the triumphs of confessors; and countless matters of the same kind—he paints almost all of these on a single page with a light brush.

As for the glorification of his own country—for this country was Spain—he made it more illustrious than others by erecting in each city memorials to martyrs and distinguished men. In this respect Spain owes almost solely to Dexter the fact that it reclaimed for itself many eminent and most holy parents of its faith, whom time, the parent of oblivion, had torn from its crown, with great loss to its honor.

This gift, therefore, must by no means be considered of little worth, and for that reason it is not unworthy of Your Eminence. I also consider it fitting when I examine the correspondence between the gift and the recipient’s merits. For Jerome, famous in the world and devoted to the faith of Christ, called this author distinguished: he was noble by blood, had shone through illustrious offices of the praetorian prefecture, and had distinguished himself by his own deeds; moreover, he had become a renowned defender of the Christian faith both in writing and in action.

Everyone knows you, too, to be distinguished in the world, whether I bring before your eyes the lineage of your most famous nobility, or the archiepiscopal college at Salamanca, whose alumnus you were, or the public rectorship of the evening chair of jurisprudence, which, before my own eyes, you gloriously held in that illustrious academy.

Devoted thereafter to the faith of Christ, you were made one of the royal judges of the military religious orders, enrolled among the noble knights of Alcántara, and elected censor of the supreme tribunal of the faith throughout Spain. Finally, as your merits required, you were raised to the glory of the highest office. From there, wholly devoted to the faith in word and writing, you have never ceased to defend—or shall I say, to glorify—the Church. You accomplish both.

Dexter’s Chronicle is therefore owed to you on both counts: a Spaniard was to be given to a Spaniard, and a learned man to a learned man; a treasure was to be given to one who alone would be able to estimate its value according to its merits.

Dexter himself had a rightful claim to this, since long ago he consecrated his work to a cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, namely Jerome. Yet when I, having restored the work to new light by means of commentaries, consecrate it again to you, likewise a cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, I am greatly embarrassed to see how far I stand from both of you in the long interval between us. I therefore seem less suited to join this great man Dexter to Your Eminence, and I fear that a gift offered by an unworthy person may prove less welcome.

Nevertheless, your kindness gave me the courage to attempt it. Nor is the undertaking unusual, since nature itself joins great bodies by an indivisible measure—that is, by an indivisible surface. Such, in my judgment, is whatever labor I have expended in elucidating Dexter. I now offer it under Dexter’s own protection to you, seeking, as it were, a defender and protector for him, and therefore I have not feared to approach your feet.

For in you I find both a tower of defense against the waves of his adversaries, which you carry in arms, and moons fighting all around in ordered battle—as though it had been said of them: “The stars from heaven fought in their order against Sisera” (Judges 5:26).

Here I opportunely appropriate to myself that passage of Seneca, writing to Lucilius:

> “Moreover, that you allow my commentaries to be sent to you, I know to be a matter of indulgence, not judgment; and if it is a matter of judgment, indulgence has imposed it upon you. But whatever they may be, read them as though I were still seeking the truth, did not yet know it, and were seeking it obstinately. For I have made myself the possession of no one, I bear the name of no one, I trust the judgment of many great men, and I claim something for my own judgment as well. For they too have left us not things already discovered, but things still to be sought” (Seneca, Letter 45).

Farewell, Most Illustrious Prince.

From the house of Saint Bernard at Rome, 21 September 1624.

[Col. 0011]

# Letter to the Editor Bivarius

Gabriel, Cardinal Priest of the title of Saint Bartholomew on the Island of the Holy Roman Church, and so forth, sends greetings to the venerable man Brother Franciscus Bivarius, Procurator General of the Spanish Congregation of Saint Bernard.

You had previously done me a common favor when you gave me your handwritten commentaries on our very ancient Spaniard Flavius Dexter. Now, by saying that they are to be printed and made public, you confer upon me a public honor and a perpetual benefit, after I had earlier experienced with the greatest gratitude the favor of a gift lent for a short time.

What, then, do I not owe you, when I already professed myself your debtor? Yet I now discharge part of my debt by willingly and eagerly receiving your favor and offering the clearest sign of gratitude. For no mark of a miserly and ungrateful spirit is clearer than to reject, or to receive with a gloomy expression, benefits for which one does not hope to show gratitude.

You are now bringing to light Flavius Dexter, a Spaniard and distinguished writer on the history of our ancient homeland, previously buried beneath the darkness of silence and oblivion. You reveal to everyone a most limpid spring, previously hidden and inaccessible, and you exalt by a new proclamation and a clear voice, resounding from that ancient breast, the very ancient faith and religion of our people, illustrious through the glory of its holy martyrs, confessors, and virgins. You add new things to ancient ones and confirm the credibility of the ancient author by the authority of modern writers, becoming like the head of a household who brings forth from his treasure new things and old (Matthew 13).

You have therefore poured out your entire treasure; what remains for you? Why do you excuse the smallness of your gift? Are you speaking hyperbolically? Or contrary to your intention? I should rather think that, in the evangelical manner, after doing everything you can, you say: “We are unprofitable servants” (Luke 17).

The book of Flavius is small if one considers the volume itself, but great if one considers what it contains. In a small codex it contains great things. I find no idle word in it. It is quite unlike the verbose commentaries of philosophers and the writings of others, in which, after you have spent the longest time, you scarcely find anything that ought to remain in your mind.

We should not therefore despise a work that contains in a brief style a long sequence of ancient events, nor esteem those who, with a lengthy display of words, confuse everything rather than explain it—unless we wish to resemble the man who chose to take poison from a large, golden, beautiful spoon rather than suck honey from one that was tiny and made of humble material (Cyril, Book 7 Against Julian).

I considered Flavius’s book similar to a certain Phoenician ship mentioned by Xenophon. Its construction was exceedingly narrow, yet although it was filled with an immense variety and multitude of weapons, instruments, merchandise, and household goods of every kind, each item was so artfully placed and arranged in such skillful order that anyone could move about the ship without hindrance, see each object with his eyes amid so great a multitude of things, and have every article ready to hand and easily find it.

Everything in Flavian history is arranged in the same way: like a small ship full of diverse merchandise, it displays before the eyes all that it contains and holds, in every verse—not to say every word—in weighty abridgment what could have filled a longer history.

He wrote not to display his own wisdom, but to make Jerome, who lived in a distant part of the world, better informed about the religion of Spain. Therefore, since the book had to be entrusted to a long journey, he touched upon matters with a brief pen.

But lest anyone perhaps think that his elevated and concise style had incurred the poetic reproach, “While I strive to be brief, I become obscure” (Horace, *Art of Poetry*), you have not only brought into the light the pages previously folded away in lengthy silence and brevity of expression; you have also unfolded, adorned, and explained them. At the same time, you have embellished our homeland.

For it is certain that Spain was so distinguished by apostolic preaching that, according to Tertullian, all the boundaries of Spain received the faith (Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 7), and according to Cyprian, persevered rightly in it (Cyprian, Letter 68). Nevertheless, there are people who wish to slander, injure, ridicule, and stain our reputation.

Now, unless they wish to behave insolently and obstinately, they will see with a light brighter than that of Phoebus how greatly the Spaniards advanced from the beginning of the nascent Church; how many holy martyrs arose from that people; how often tyrants were not lacking; how many celebrated confessors flourished when, persecution having ceased, they were able freely to practice virtue; and how many virgins, having overcome their sex and achieved victory over flesh and world, presented themselves chaste to Christ, their most beloved bridegroom.

Flavius Lucius Dexter will therefore now blow favorably, whom you have brought out of the prison of oblivion—as Juno brought the winds from their caves—and whom you have lucidly and skillfully explained, confirming the truth of his history.

Nor should anyone think that renewing and adorning the writings of the ancient Church is of less benefit to the holy Catholic Church than publishing new books. If we love the truth, it is of greater benefit. For the ancients surpass the moderns in authority and excel them in trustworthiness. I do not know what authority holy antiquity claims for itself.

Consequently, unbelievers who oppose the Christian name, and heretics who do the greatest harm to the holy Church, are convicted by no other argument more effectively than by the authority and teaching of ancient writers. Those who bring such writers into the light may truly be said to bring forward the more powerful arms of the holy Church, like shields hanging in David’s tower.

In this history of Dexter, the firmness of faith in the martyrs shines forth most clearly, to the confusion of heretics who say that anyone may deny the faith he professes in order to escape danger to his life. The authority of holy bishops also shines forth, as does their skill in governing the Church, to confound those who deny episcopal dignity and rashly call it a new invention.

We read that at that time pilgrimage was already permitted, temples were being built, the sacrifice of the holy Mass was being celebrated, all the sacraments were being administered, images were being venerated, various miracles were occurring, and the holy Roman See was being honored, along with whatever other practices the innovators deny. Yet when they see that the primitive Church observed these things at that time, they are confounded and recognize that our Catholic Church agrees with the primitive Church.

For so many reasons, then, I owe you thanks— as many as the benefits I perceive to have arisen from your labor. I give thanks for the honor and benefit of the holy Church, as an unworthy minister of that same Church and a priest-cardinal; for the adornment and glory of Spain, as a man of that nation; and for the favor bestowed upon me, as a friend who is not ungrateful.

Farewell, and may the most holy Spirit of God fill you with all his divine gifts.

Given at Tivoli, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the year 1624.

[Col. 0013]

# Second Letter to the Editor Bivarius

[Col. 0013] To the Reverend Father Brother Franciscus Bivarius, Cistercian, a man of perfect integrity and a most esteemed friend.

In the countryside of Tivoli, amid the summer heat, I saw hurriedly and only superficially your continuous commentaries on the *Chronicle of Flavius Lucius Dexter*, sent to the Most Illustrious Cardinal de Treio.

At first sight I approved the subject of the work and called your undertaking laudable—if only it might prove successful—on the part of its elucidator. I earnestly desired to examine the whole work, but at the time I could not, being distracted by various minor occupations, even though the Most Illustrious Cardinal returned the codex within a few days.

Now I have read it as you left it, according to my wish, and I have read it gladly for more than one reason: because the subject was weighty; because it concerned the best teachers of our faith; and because it came from you, whom I have long regarded with a certain veneration and love.

I therefore gladly looked at it a second time and read it even more gladly. The subject itself, your writing, and your judgment drew me along. You have opportunely interwoven many things for the sake of faith, understanding, the commendation of history, and the veneration of the saints.

You have reclaimed the finest antiquities of Spain, illuminated foreign matters, and fully revived the buried memory of the best events. And if you have bound every distinguished nation to you by a great favor, Spain owes you more than all the others, since Dexter marked its affairs with greater care and fidelity because they were more familiar to him, and you at last elucidated them skillfully.

This universal history shows that your Western land produced every kind of saint, and by learned commentary you fully establish its credibility, however difficult it may be to believe. I have now fully approved your fortunate and commendable undertaking, since you firmly establish that Dexter really is this author and properly distinguish the deeds of the saints from apocryphal accounts.

I would dare promise that this history of yours will be welcome to everyone. It contains varied and every kind of color—as I might say in the words of an ancient and grave historian—gleaming and golden flowers; someone might most aptly call it a garden-bed fertile in every kind of herb.

Above all, it abounds in those flowers that glow as they sprout, those that bloom in purple, and those whose brilliance inclines most toward blackness and therefore shines most intensely. The stole of the hierarchs, sparkling through the holiness of life above the sun itself; the true and venerable purple of the martyrs, richly dyed and drenched with their blood; and, in addition, the blackening garment that brings light and is woven by divine power—these suit especially those who strive and aspire toward the angelic life.

From these things the Church of Christ, wholly surrounded and clothed in a golden adornment of virtues like a bride, presents and represents the most beautiful thing in the entire universe to the emperor of all kings (Nicephorus, dedication to the Emperor Andronicus).

Do not doubt, then, that your work will be approved by everyone. From this I would say that your latest and recent decision ought to be rejected. Everyone will condemn your desire for withdrawal and your retreat into solitude.

Are not even peaceful men like yourself in retreat amid the city, and in solitude amid the noise of the forum? Was it fitting, in the middle of life, to withdraw your hand from the pen and your mind from study, and did you choose to devote yourself to solitary leisure?

Take care, excellent man, lest you be said to have hidden your talent, and lest the stern collector tell you that you ought and were obliged to trade with it (Matthew 25), rather than idle away your time in shady valleys.

But where am I going? I fear offending your piety and disturbing, amid the greatest tranquility, one who is avoiding the tumult of the world.

Proceed, man of God; study for yourself and, if permitted, study for everyone. Father, write both for the honor of God and for our benefit.

Farewell, from across the Tiber, at Saint Peter’s on the Golden Mount, 17 January 1625.

Your most devoted,

**Brother Lucas Waddingus**

[Col. 0013]

# The Life of the Author

Collected from his own writings and those of others, by Brother Franciscus Bivarius.

[Col. 0013A] Barcelona, an illustrious city of Spain, boasts of being founded by the Carthaginian Hamilcar, the brother of Hannibal, as all the most serious authorities report; and Ausonius sang in a letter to Paulinus:

> “Barcelona, Carthaginian, wounds me.”

(Ausonius, Letter 24.)

It has its seat on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea, ruling over that region, flourishing no less in pleasantness than in wealth and strength [Col. 0014A]:

> “And the pleasant, wealthy seats of the Barcelonians,
>
> For there the harbor opens its safe arms.”

So says Festus Avienus.

It is made much more illustrious by the splendor of its great citizens. For it produced the holy virgin Eulalia [Col. 0015A], conspicuous for nobility and martyrdom; Philetus and Laeda, holy spouses and leaders of their senate, together with their sons and fifty-five companions, martyrs; many bishops notable for holiness and distinguished by the laurel of martyrdom; Etherius, a disciple of Saint James; two Severuses; and the outstanding confessor of Christ, Theodosius, successor of Etherius.

For the moment I pass over Saint Cucuphas the martyr, whom Africa indeed brought forth for the world, but Barcelona restored to Christ, as well as many others whose names are in the book of life.

To Barcelona’s adornment, these stars established in the noble firmament were joined by two other fellow citizens, father and son: Pacianus, I mean, and Dexter. Why should I call them stars, when Jerome attests that they were renowned for learning and dignity, and yet it was said to Daniel:

[Col. 0015B]

> “Those who instruct many in righteousness shall be like stars for everlasting eternities.”

Of Pacianus, Jerome says: “Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona, distinguished,” he says, “for chastity and eloquence, and illustrious both in life and in speech.” Of Dexter he says: “Dexter, the son of Pacianus, of whom I spoke above, distinguished in the world and devoted to the faith of Christ.”

Indeed, the fact that Saint Pacianus, while he was not yet a bishop, fathered Dexter by a lawful wife proves this, namely, that among his other qualities of mind and body, his chastity is commended by Jerome with singular praise.

“Pacianus,” he says, “distinguished for chastity and eloquence”—something that could not be said of an adulterer, however penitent.

The nobility of his lineage is indicated by Jerome’s words: “Distinguished in the world,” especially since they concern praises of Dexter while he was still young. They were spoken at the time when he was in his twenty-third year, as we shall soon see.

He was also related by blood to Paulus Orosius, as Dexter himself admits under the year of the Lord 417:

> “Paulus Orosius, son of Flavius Orosius, a blood relative of Pacianus my father and a citizen of Tarragona.”

The family of the Orosii was distinguished for nobility, since it possessed its own burial place at Rome in the basilica of Saint Eusebius. It was made illustrious and conspicuous not only at Tarragona and Rome, but also throughout Lusitania and throughout the world, as Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, writes under the years of the Lord 471 and 602.

Pacianus, the father, having been deprived of his wife—or perhaps separated from her, as was frequently the case in those times—and restored to the Church, wonderfully shepherded the sheep entrusted to him by word and example. He defended them from the attacks of raging wolves—I mean the Novatians and Arians [Col. 0015D]—not only by word but also by his writings. We still admire the remarkable eloquence of those writings together with their teaching, namely, in the letters sent to Symphorianus, in the *Paraenesis on Penance*, and in the short work *On Baptism*. Together with the Roman and universal Church, we venerate his holiness, for the Church reads his name in the catalogue of the saints on 9 March.

Flavius Lucius Dexter was born in the year from the Lord’s birth 368, as may be gathered from what he writes at the end of the Chronicle: that in the year of Christ 440 he was seventy-two years old.

But what progress would Dexter not have made under such a father? Jerome reveals in the prologue to his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* that Dexter exercised himself in his youth in humane letters, when, addressing him, [Col. 0016A] he specially calls Cicero “his own”:

> “What your Cicero,” he says, “who stood at the summit of eloquence, did not disdain to do in the *Brutus*, weaving a catalogue of the orators of the Latin language.”

Thus, while still young, Dexter was urging Jerome to undertake the very task: following Suetonius’s example, to gather the distinguished orators of the Christian faith and eminent Doctors of the Church into a brief catalogue, and to do among our own writers what Suetonius had done in enumerating the illustrious men of pagan letters.

The present Chronicle proclaims the man’s eloquence joined with piety. For he was so devoted to humane letters that he diligently applied himself to ecclesiastical history.

While he had not yet passed beyond the boundaries of adolescence, he became involved in military service. This kind of life was particularly dear at that time throughout the Roman Empire to the sons of noblemen, and especially in Spain, because the great glory of the world, Theodosius the Elder—truly “the Great” in all things—had from that region risen to the summit of imperial power in the year of Christ 379.

Under such a ruler, then, Dexter entered military service and made noble progress in it, being gradually elevated through the military honors. Thus at last he deserved to rise to the prefecture of the praetorium of the Eastern Empire, which was the highest office, since from the histories we know that many who were summoned to the imperial crown came from it.

It is reasonable to believe that he attached himself to the Emperor Theodosius when he was no more than eighteen years old, when Theodosius, in the tenth year of his reign, together with his son Arcadius, Caesar, and Valentinian Augustus, came down into Italy to defeat the tyrant Maximus; and that Dexter entered Rome with them and then departed with them for the East.

In truth, however, Dexter was so devoted to military affairs that from time to time he gave attention to letters when opportunity allowed. On his journey to the East he consulted and heard the most learned and holy men who were flourishing at that time: John Chrysostom at Constantinople, Epiphanius in Cyprus, Gregory at Neocaesarea, Cyril at Jerusalem, Ephrem at Edessa in Syria, another Gregory at Nissa, the brother of Basil—to pass over Sophronius and others.

Above all, he maintained a friendship with Jerome, as is clear from the second apology of the latter addressed to Rufinus, where he says:

> “When my friend Dexter, who administered the prefecture of the praetorium, etc.”

For this it was necessary that he meet him not once or twice but frequently, enjoy his familiar conversation in his retreat at Bethlehem, and repeatedly urge him by letters, while absent, toward various studies.

We have a distinguished proof of this in the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Since the Christian world seemed in that age to be greatly illuminated by the writings of so many and such great Doctors, beside whom the subtlety and eloquence of pagan philosophers and rhetoricians had grown worthless, Dexter was deeply distressed that pagans everywhere reproached Christians with rusticity, alleging that the Church had possessed no philosophers, no rhetoricians, and no Doctors, since it had been founded by people of rustic simplicity or taught chiefly by certain fishermen.

Therefore, confident in Jerome’s competence—for Jerome had read nearly all authors, ecclesiastical and secular, Greek and Latin—Dexter imposed upon him a task that he declared would be worth his effort: if Jerome would reduce the names and writings of all the Doctors who had illuminated the Church of God by their lives and writings, in the manner of a catalogue, to a single short volume of encomium.

Then, when pagans held up to us a catalogue of their own rhetoricians and poets, which Suetonius Tranquillus had composed in his book published *On Illustrious Grammarians*, Catholics could produce a catalogue of their own and rebuke for incompetence and ignorance the pagans whom unknowing antiquity revered.

O thought worthy of a Christian and learned man! O noble spirit! Is it surprising that he is called not only distinguished in the world but also—something rare in a secular man—devoted to the faith of Christ?

Indeed, we owe the enjoyment of the catalogue of the Doctors of the Church to Dexter, a man of distinguished virtue. For at his urging Saint Jerome [Col. 0017B] undertook that task. Without Jerome’s work, it would have been necessary for us to remain ignorant of countless ancient Doctors whose writings no longer exist.

Complying, therefore, with Dexter’s wishes, Jerome not only completed the desired catalogue but also dedicated the book itself to Dexter and prefixed to the book a letter, namely:

# Jerome to Dexter

You urge me, Dexter, to follow Tranquillus and arrange the ecclesiastical writers in order; and what he did in enumerating the illustrious men of pagan letters, I am to do among our own writers. That is, from the Passion of Christ to the fourteenth year of the Emperor Theodosius, I am to give you a brief account of all who have handed down anything concerning the Holy Scriptures for remembrance.

Among the Greeks, Hermippus the Peripatetic, Antigonus of Carystus, Satyrus the learned man, and Aristoxenus the Musician, by far the most learned of all, did the same thing. Among the Latins, Varro, Santra, Nepos, Hyginus, and—following whose example you wish to spur me—Tranquillus did so.

But my situation is not like theirs. For they, unfolding ancient histories and annals, were able, as it were, to weave a small crown for their little work from a vast meadow. What am I to do, since I follow no predecessor and possess myself, as the saying goes, as a very bad teacher?

Although Eusebius Pamphilus has been of the greatest assistance to us in the ten books of his *Ecclesiastical History*, and the volumes of the individuals about whom we are to write often testify to the ages of their authors.

Thus I pray the Lord Jesus Christ that what your Cicero, who stood at the summit of Roman eloquence, did not disdain to do in the *Brutus*, weaving a catalogue of orators of the Latin language, I may worthily accomplish, encouraged by your exhortation, in enumerating the writers of that Church.

If any of those who continue writing down to the present day have been omitted by me in this volume, they must blame themselves rather than me. For if they concealed their writings, how could I know what I had not read? And what may perhaps be known to others may have been unknown to me in this remote corner of the earth.

Certainly, once they have become famous through their writings, they will not sigh greatly at the loss caused by our silence.

Let Celsus, Porphyry, and Julian, those rabid dogs against Christ, learn this; let their followers learn it—those who think that the Church possessed no philosophers, no eloquent men, and no Doctors. Let them learn what great and what kind of men founded, built, and adorned it, and let them cease accusing our faith of rustic simplicity. Rather, let them acknowledge their own ignorance.

Thus far Jerome to Dexter.

At that time Dexter was in his twenty-third year. Although he had not yet passed beyond the limits of adolescence, he bore before him in spirit an old man in learning. Consequently, he had begun to compose his *Chronicle of Universal History* for the benefit of that same Jerome, in order to encourage him to arrange his catalogue of writers.

Yet because Dexter was occupied for a long time with military affairs and the service of the emperors, and detained by the immense variety of the events he recorded, he was unable to finish the work until many years later—namely, when, worn out by old age, he sought rest at home, having rejected foreign offices, in order to practice Christian philosophy.

This explains why Jerome mentions his book in his catalogue, which he completed in the year of the Lord 393, while Dexter nevertheless placed the final hand on his own work in the year of the Lord 430, after Jerome’s death, as is clear from the prologue.

It is also highly probable that Dexter’s history was not inserted into Jerome’s catalogue in the year when the catalogue was composed, but several years later, when Dexter’s work and his intention of dedicating it came to Jerome’s knowledge. In the same way, we shall say in its proper place that Jerome gradually inserted others as time passed, writers previously unknown to him.

As Dexter’s fame increased, he was finally raised by Arcadius, who had inherited the rule of the East from his father Theodosius by hereditary right, to the prefecture of the praetorium. No dignity in the whole empire was equal to this, since we know from histories that many men summoned to the imperial crown came from that office.

The precise year in which Dexter entered the prefecture of the praetorium is unknown. One thing, however, is clear: in the year of the Lord 403, when Saint Jerome gave his second apology to Rufinus, Dexter had already completed his prefecture, although in the year 393, when Jerome completed his catalogue of writers, Dexter had not yet risen to it.

For in that catalogue Jerome does not honor him with that title but uses his simple name: “Jerome to Dexter: You urge me, Dexter.” In the *Apology*, however, he says:

> “A decade ago, when my friend Dexter, who administered the prefecture of the praetorium, asked me to compose for him a catalogue of the authors of our religion ...”

I think he became prefect of the praetorium in the thirtieth year of his life. At thirty-three, having already completed his prefecture, he had met Jerome so often in familiar conversation and through letters that he deserved from him the title of friend.

Having successfully administered the affairs of the prefecture, and after spending many years in the service of the emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and the younger Theodosius, he at last returned to his homeland with their permission. Yet he was not granted the peaceful retirement he desired for long, for he was appointed to govern the city of Toledo and was consequently compelled to interrupt somewhat the studies he had begun. Even so, he did not entirely abandon them. As time permitted, he searched the ancient archives of Toledo—which he admits were of great benefit to him—and for a full two years endeavored to confer that service upon his homeland, so that an intimate and friendly relationship might be established between the people of Barcelona and Toledo. He himself bears witness to this in the *Chronicle*, saying:

> The closest relationship has been established between the Toletans and the Barcelonans, from the time when I, Dexter, governed that city for two years; and I confess that I found many things worthy of knowledge in its archives.

Returning home from there, he completed the *Universal History* in the year of Christ 430, at the age of sixty-two, and dedicated and sent it to St. Jerome. Jerome, however, had already obtained a better life among the blessed a few years earlier, although news of this had not yet reached Spain. For Idatius, a Spanish writer of that period, writes under the year 433:

> At that time, the report of those who related when St. Jerome died had not yet been published.

When Dexter subsequently learned of Jerome’s death, and the book could not reach his hands, since he was dead, Dexter gave it another dedicatee; he also enriched and expanded it in many places. For it is clear that he recorded Jerome’s death in it under the year of the Lord 426. Thus at last he dedicated the expanded *Chronicle* to his friend and kinsman Paulus Orosius, after putting the final hand to it in the year of Christ 440, in the current Caesarean era 478, and in the year 1191 from the founding of Rome, at the age of seventy-two, when extreme old age was already beginning, as he himself asserts at the end of the *Chronicle*.

He does not explain what caused him, although he subscribed it in the year 440, nevertheless to end the history in 430 and envelop the entire intervening decade in silence. I think, however, that in this also he wished to imitate Jerome, who likewise refrained from including the final decade in his *Chronicle*. “For,” he says, “I have reserved the remaining period of Gratian and Theodosius for the fuller style of history,” not because “I feared to speak and write truthfully about the living—for the fear of God drives out the fear of men—but because, while the barbarians are still raging in our lands, everything is uncertain.”

The same must be believed concerning Dexter, who saw with his own eyes the barbarian nations raging—namely the Alans, Vandals, Suebi, and Goths—and bringing Spain to ruin. Their history required a fuller style than a *Chronicle* could bear, and, while the barbarians were still raging in our lands, everything was uncertain. For although they had entered Spain from the year of Christ 409 and had divided the country among themselves, so that in Galicia the Suevian king Rechila, successor of Hermenericus, exercised dominion, while Theodoredus, third after Ataulf, ruled over the Goths and possessed many provinces of Spain, the Romans had not yet been completely expelled, and hope of recovering everything had not yet been abandoned. The final outcome of affairs, therefore, was still awaited for committal to history.

In that very year 440, according to Idatius, Asturius, commander of both military forces, was sent to Spain and slaughtered a multitude of Tarraconensians. In the following year a comet began to appear in December, foretelling the pestilence that followed and the scourges of the wars then present. Asturius was succeeded by Merobaudes, commander of both military forces, noble by birth and, on account of his eloquence—especially in the cultivation of poetry—comparable with the ancients. On both counts he was especially important to Dexter.

Finally, in the year 444, Sebastianus, commander of the army, having fled from Constantinople and come to Theodoredus, king of the Goths, entered Barcelona, which he had sought for himself, as an enemy, by whatever means he could. Meanwhile Dexter, no less wearied by the disasters of his homeland than by old age, and exhausted by his labors, was taken from this life. His continuator M. Maximus bears witness to this, saying:

> Caesarean era 482, but the year of the Lord Christ 444: Flavius Lucius Dexter, almost completely worn out by old age, died at Barcelona on the tenth day before the Kalends of July; a thoroughly learned, prudent, and pious man. He was certainly preferable to many others because he alone disclosed in a written *Chronicle* many matters that contribute to the glory of the universal Church for later generations, and because he labored more than the rest to clarify the affairs of Spain, his homeland.

He also flourished in poetry, as is shown by the epitaph that he placed upon the tomb of King Ataulf and had engraved in marble, part of which is still visible today at Barcelona. Vasaeus, Morales, Nonius, and Pujades copied it; Dexter himself places it at the end of the *Chronicle*.

Moreover, the *Chronicle* itself, which had lain hidden for many years, has been found in part—namely, from the birth of the Lord to the end—although it is clear from the Author’s prologue that it began with the creation of the world and continued to the year of the Lord 430. The earlier portion, from its beginning up to Christ’s birth, is still waging war with the bookworms in some dusty corner of a library. May God grant that it may one day see the light, for His greater glory.

[Col. 0019]

# SELECTED TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING FLAVIUS L. DEXTER

[Col. 0019D] **ST. JEROME**

In the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, almost at the end:

> Dexter, son of Pacianus, of whom I spoke above, famous in the world and devoted to the faith of Christ, is said to have composed for me a *Universal History*, which I have not yet read.

Concerning Pacianus he had said:

> Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona in the Pyrenean mountains, distinguished for chastity and eloquence, and for both his life and his speech, wrote various short works.

I omit here the dedicatory letter of that same book, which I set out above.

In the second *Apology against Rufinus*, chapter 6:

> About ten years ago, when my friend Dexter, who administered the prefecture of the praetorium, had asked me to compile for him a catalogue of the writers of our religion.

**SOPHRONIUS**, a Greek writer and contemporary of Jerome:

> Dexter, son of Pacianus, of whom I spoke above, illustrious in public life and devoted to the faith of Christ, is said to have composed for me a universal history, which I have not yet read.

[Col. 0021A] **M. MAXIMUS**, bishop of Zaragoza, continuator of Dexter; died in the year of the Lord 616.

His letter to Argebatus, bishop of Porto, is extant, as follows:

> To the holy and venerable lord Argebatus [variant: Argiovitus], bishop of Porto, M. Maximus sends greetings in the Lord.
>
> When we had been summoned to the royal city for a council by our glorious lord, King Flavius Gundemar, we often met one another. Since much conversation had arisen concerning the history of the kings, which I had published not long before, your holiness then informed me that you wished to have a continuation of the *Universal History* composed by Flavius L. Dexter—a request which you made of my humility with considerable modesty.
>
> Although, on account of your benevolence toward me and my respect for you, your holiness could have commanded me, you preferred to seek it from me by entreaty, as though you could command, or rather demand as a right of your own, what you ordered. We shall follow the sequence of time in our customary manner, by Caesarean eras and the years of Christ, rather than by the years of the City, the consuls, or the emperors.
>
> Would that I had carried out your command as diligently as I attempted to fulfill it willingly! For I extended the narrative of events from Caesarean era 469 to era 650—that is, from the year of Christ 431 to the year of Christ 612, shortly after the death of Flavius Gundemar.

In the *Chronicle*, under the year of the Lord 444, he discussed the death of Dexter. We have given his words in the Author’s Life.

**HELECA**, bishop of Zaragoza; lived in the year of the Lord 860.

[Col. 0021C] His additions to the *Chronicles* of Dexter and Maximus are extant. Among other things, speaking of his own time, when Spain was groaning under the yoke of the Saracens, he says:

> The Sacred Scriptures translated into Arabic are kept by Catholic priests and circulated with scholia, especially the New Testament, the Epistles of Paul, the Apocalypse of St. John, and the book *On the Lives of the Fathers*, as well as the Latin history of Flavius Lucius Dexter, M. Maximus, and others, the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, and the books of St. Augustine *On the City of God*, because the Latin language was already disappearing.

See with what honor the *Universal History* of Dexter was held in Spain at that time.

**EUTHRANDUS**, first a Toletan subdeacon, later a deacon of Pavia; lived in the year 960.

His letter concerning the continuation of the *Chronicles* of Dexter and Maximus is extant. It is mentioned in the *Bibliotheca Hispana* and accepted by Father Gabriel Vasquez, volume I, in part III of the works of Thomas Aquinas. It is as follows:

> To the holy Father Regimundus, bishop of Iliberis, Euthrandus, an unworthy servant, sends greetings.
>
> Most blessed Father and greatly revered lord, I was delighted that my *Antipodosis*, in which I now play in verse and now in prose, finally reached your hands. I was no less pleased that your holiness ordered me to search in the library of the monastery of Fulda, where I now live in exile, for the *Chronicle* of Dexter, which Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, continued at the request of Bishop Argenbatus [variant: Argiovitus], and, if I had leisure, to carry it down to our own times. For you say that you are suffering from an extreme scarcity of certain books.
>
> Among the barbarian Saracens there is no supply even of necessary things, much less an abundance of good books. I grieved over your situation, that you should be enduring life so harshly; but in such great difficulties let this console you: as a good shepherd, you are a comfort and aid to your sheep.
>
> I found the *Chronicle* you requested in this library, written on ancient parchment, and, as I was ordered, I added the sequence of years up to the present time—that is, to era 960.
>
> I congratulate myself that, when I traveled from Toledo—where I was a subdeacon under the most holy Toletan bishop Bonitus—to Italy, I carried some history books with me. In them a sequence of many bishops had been collected in order; I also found them in this library, brought from Spain, as I believe, at the command of St. Charlemagne. They say that the most holy Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, had presented them to him after he repented of his error concerning the Adoption of Christ.
>
> I have done what you commanded, most blessed Father. Whether my effort has answered your wish, you will see, since you gave the command. Farewell, and commend your exiled servant, himself an exile, to God.

Lest anyone take offense at this letter, I should point out that the Author confuses an era with a year, or treats them as the same thing, as Morales proves many men of his age did in his *Antiquities*. It is clear from this that Euthrandus extended his *Antipodosis* to the year of Christ 960, during the schism of Leo and Benedict. Moreover, Bonitus of Toledo, under whom he is said to have been a subdeacon, was the third of that name to occupy the Toletan see; according to Julian in the *Chronicle*, he was elected in the year of the Lord 946.

[Col. 0022C] **HUGO OF PORTO**, bishop, one of the authors of the Compostellan history; lived until the year of the Lord 1100.

In a very ancient manuscript codex on parchment, written in Gothic characters and preserved in the royal monastery of Santa Cruz at Coimbra, at the end of the history of Sampirus, bishop of Asturias, there is a letter written by Hugo, bishop of Porto, to Mauritius, archbishop of Braga. He responds to a question put to him by Mauritius: whether there had formerly been in that see any apostolic legates for all Spain. In it he reports verbatim a statement drawn from Dexter’s *Chronicle*, found under the year of the Lord 91, and asserts that Dexter dedicated his work to Orosius, as the codex we present states. It is worthwhile to give the entire letter, since it will be useful to us in many places. The most learned man and our friend, Gaspar Albarez de Losada, copied it from the autograph; through his gift we received it, sent from Lisbon.

**Letter of Hugo, bishop of Porto**

> To my lord Mauritius, archbishop of Braga, greetings.
>
> I find that St. Peter of Rates was the vicar of St. James in Spain while James went to Britain and other provinces, although I have no knowledge whatsoever of the authority by which he acted. There are also those who say that he continued in this office for as long as he lived.
>
> The authority for this vicariate, and for another entrusted by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, is Caledonius of Braga, in the Life of that same blessed Peter [that is, Peter of Braga]. This Life, together with the other acts of the Spanish saints, is in my possession in a very ancient parchment codex written at the command of Argiovitus, formerly bishop of this see [that is, the see of Porto]. It reads as follows:
>
> St. Peter, a citizen of Braga, also called Samuel, was raised up by St. James, the brother of John and son of Zebedee, and consecrated bishop of Braga. Sent by him, he converted there many of his own people who were scattered among the tribes, as well as gentiles. From there he departed and preached at Tui and Iria, and along the entire maritime coast as far as Cape Cinthius [that is, Cape Luna or the promontory of Lisbon], also called Ulysses.
>
> From among the disciples of his master whom he had brought with him, he appointed bishops at Porto, Eminium, Coimbra, and Lisbon, and others beyond Cape Nerium [today Cape Finisterre]. Following his example, he did not remain in one city alone but, driven by zeal for the faith, traveled through the inland regions on both sides of the Tagus, visiting the peoples entrusted to him. He spread the word of God at Egitania, Callentia, Mérida, Ambratia, and in other cities of the Vettones and Lusitanians. After crossing the Douro on his way to Pannonia, he returned to Braga Augusta.
>
> When scarcely fifteen months had passed, his master James had raised a little shrine at Zaragoza in honor of the Virgin Mother of God, installed Athanasius there, and departed for Braga. There he consecrated to the same Lady, together with Pius of Seville, Elpidius of Toledo, and other leading disciples of his, another little shrine in a certain crypt near the baths, beside a temple once dedicated by the Egyptians to Isis.
>
> From there, boarding a ship at Brigantium, he arrived in Britain, leaving at Braga St. Peter, his vicar and chief among the other bishops whom he had consecrated in Spain.
>
> Thus far, I believe, the account is from Caledonius. He adds:
>
> Concerning the first legation sent to Spain by blessed Clement, Dexter, son of Pacianus, writes as follows in his history addressed to Orosius, which I find copied in the same codex:
>
> Philip, surnamed Philotheus, who had earlier buried at Milan the bodies of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, his fellow citizens of Milan, was converted in the Laminitanean plain by blessed Paul the Apostle. He followed Paul and attached himself to Clement. Sent by Clement as a legate to Spain, he preached at Barcelona, Zaragoza, Valencia, Toledo, Seville, and many other cities. He came to Toledo under Aulus Cornelius Palma, a most distinguished man, or under the Toletan and Christian duumvir [the name M. Marcellus is missing], and there established the chief see of all Carpetania [more correctly, of Spain].
>
> Dexter and Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, say much about the other legations. From this let your Serenity see [lacuna].

The remainder was missing from the codex from which Losada extracted this passage, for, alas, approximately one hundred leaves had been cut away by some plagiarist to cover old women’s distaffs, as the roots of the leaves that remained plainly show.

**JULIAN PETRI**, archpriest of Toledo; in his *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 36; flourished about 1100.

As the continuous tradition handed down from apostolic times, supported also by the testimony of many ancients—Torquatus, Ctesiphon, Honoratus, Melantius, Dexter, M. Maximus, Isidore, Bede, and others—relates, in the year of the Lord 36 St. James the Apostle, son of Zebedee, came to Spain for a highly honorable purpose and visited all its cities. These things agree with what Dexter writes under the same year.

**HONORIUS OF AUTUN**, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, no. 132, under the year of the Lord 390; flourished in the year of the Lord 1120.

> Dexter, son of Pacianus, famous in the world and devoted to the faith of Christ, composed a universal history.

**RAPHAEL VOLATERRANUS**, book XV of the *Anthropology*, letter D:

> Dexter, son of Pacianus, the bishop, a most distinguished man and devoted to the faith of Christ, is said to have published a universal history. He was a native of Barcelona and prefect of the praetorium under the emperor Theodosius. Jerome, who bears witness to these facts, dedicated to him the book *On Illustrious Men*.

**CONRAD GESNER**, in the *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*:

> Dexter, son of Pacianus, famous in the world and devoted to the faith of Christ, composed for me a universal history, which I have not yet read. St. Jerome, in *On Illustrious Men and Ecclesiastical Writers*, appears to have dedicated it to this Dexter. Sophronius, a friend of Jerome who translated this book into Greek, indicates that this Dexter was prefect of the praetorium.

**ANTONIUS POSSEVINUS**, of the Society of Jesus, in the *Sacred Apparatus*, letter D:

He gives the same words as Gesner.

**JOANNES RIOCHE**, of the Order of Friars Minor of the Observance, in the *Compendium of Times*, book II, chapter 24, column 1:

> Dexter, son of Pacianus, wrote a universal history to Jerome.

[Col. 0024C] **CAESAR BARONIUS**, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, volume IV of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*.

Speaking of St. Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona, under the year of the Lord 388, he adds:

> To his son, distinguished by the prefecture of the praetorium, that same Jerome, as we shall say, wrote the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Under the year of the Lord 392:

> It is easy, he says, to enumerate one by one all the works of St. Jerome published up to this year, the fourteenth of the emperor Theodosius, if you read what he has at the end of his *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*. He wrote that work for Dexter, a distinguished man, whom he himself reports to have been honored with the prefecture of the praetorium in the *Apology against Rufinus*, when he says: “About ten years ago, when my friend Dexter, who administered the prefecture of the praetorium, had asked me to compile for him a catalogue of the writers of our religion, among the other interpreters . . .”
>
> That same Dexter had previously written a history to Jerome himself. Jerome bears witness to this in the following words: “Dexter, son of Pacianus, of whom I spoke above.” But it too was lost, to our own detriment.

Likewise, under the year of the Lord 395, volume V:

> We have also said that Dexter, prefect of the praetorium in the time of Theodosius, composed a work on the same subject.

**ABRAHAMUS BZOVIUS**, of the Order of Preachers, volume I of the *Ecclesiastical History*.

Under the year of the Lord 34 he cites Dexter’s words concerning the preaching of St. James the Apostle in Spain and concerning his disciples, for by the time he wrote, such a *Chronicle* had already come into his hands.

[Col. 0025A] I deliberately omit the numerous host of more recent authors who recognize Dexter’s *Chronicle*, lest I weary the readers. I shall nevertheless cite some of them in the following *Apology*.

[Col. 0025]

# APOLOGY FOR DEXTER’S CHRONICLE, TO THE READER

Through this warning at the very threshold, the reader is instructed to pass over everything that follows without stumbling.

§ 1. What and how many things prove that this entire History is genuinely the work of Dexter?

[Col. 0025A]

[Col. 0025B] What formerly happened with the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite also happened with the chronicles of L. Dexter of Barcelona. Those writings had long remained hidden and were finally discovered and brought to light, to the great benefit of the Catholic Church; likewise these chronicles, written twelve hundred years ago, were published to the world only after many centuries, also, as we hope, with immense benefit to ecclesiastical history.

Just as some people once opposed those writings because they asserted certain things contrary to everyone’s expectation, so certain scruples have likewise arisen concerning these chronicles. It will now be worthwhile to dispel them, lest a reader frightened by such objections deny so great an author the credibility he has rightly earned.

Would that Dexter had been granted another Theodore, such as Dionysius enjoyed! He would then more easily have received the honor he deserved from everyone. Yet even in the absence of such a man, if not through the authority of an elucidator, then at least through reason—which alone we presently wish to put to the test—we do not doubt that we shall attain our purpose. For there are many important considerations that prove precisely this, and these we must now discuss.

In the first place, no one denies that this *Chronicle* ought to possess an authority of great weight if it is established that its author is that Dexter who dedicated his *Universal History* to Jerome. For the most holy Doctor repeatedly praises him with great force and shows him considerable deference, as is clear from the Life of Dexter previously written by us.

Our entire case, therefore, turns on demonstrating that the present work is the legitimate product of his mind. Whatever may be said of other matters, those through whose good offices these chronicles came into our hands possess such authority and such sincere devotion to truth that no room for doubt about the matter itself remains.

They are the Reverend Fathers Thomas de Torralba and Hieronymus de la Higuera, priests of the Society of Jesus, distinguished for their learning. Thomas, while he was in Germany, encountered, by God’s providence, at Worms an exceedingly ancient manuscript on parchment in which the chronicles of Dexter and M. Maximus—so greatly desired by learned men—were written in Gothic script.

At that time the codex was perhaps in the possession of a learned citizen of Worms, who frankly acknowledged that he had received it from the celebrated library of the monks at Fulda and valued it highly because of the venerable history of antiquity contained in it. Those are mistaken who think that the codex was copied in the monastery of Fulda and still remains in its library, whereas Torralba asserted only that the autograph codex had belonged to the people of Fulda.

Since Father Thomas could obtain the original codex from its owner neither as a gift nor by purchase, he managed at least to secure a copy of it. He immediately sent the copy to Spain to Father Hieronymus de la Higuera, together with letters written at Worms in the year of the Lord 1594.

The letters themselves and the copy of the *Chronicle* sent from Germany were repeatedly seen and read by men entirely worthy of belief. I myself discussed the matter at Toledo with Father Francisco Portocarrero, a priest of the same Society. From him I heard that he had seen and read with his own eyes the *Chronicle* and Father Thomas de Torralba’s letter, had recognized Torralba’s hand and signature, and possessed copies of both. He gives the same testimony in the prologue to his book on the Life of St. Ildefonsus, which he printed at Madrid in the year of the Lord 1616.

The authority of so many witnesses removes every ambiguity, since they are undoubtedly beyond all exception: eminent in learning, distinguished in religion, outstanding in zeal for the truth, and such as could lend the weight of their authority to matters of greater importance, whose credibility might otherwise waver.

Moreover, the matter did not take place within private walls and then emerge into the light. From the very year 1594, when the *Chronicle* was sent from Germany to Father Hieronymus in Spain, he communicated it to the most eminent prelates, doctors, and princes throughout Spain, and they accepted it as genuine. It is therefore astonishing that anyone should be able to cast it into doubt.

Among others, it was examined by the most illustrious and most reverend lords: Don Sancho Dávila, successively bishop of Jaén, Sigüenza, and Plasencia, in the book of St. Vitalis, archpriest of Toledo and martyr, and in his work *On the Veneration of Relics*; Don Bertrand Ladron de Guevara, archbishop of Compostela, a man famous throughout Spain and Italy for his outstanding learning, in his book *On the Coming of St. James*; Don Prudentius de Sandoval, bishop of Tuy and Pamplona and royal historiographer, in his book on the Church of Tuy; and Don Alexius de Meneses, archbishop of Braga. Before him, Don Augustine of Jesus, bishop of the same see, had caused the material concerning his metropolitan church recorded in these chronicles to be separately preserved in the archiepiscopal archives. I could add countless others, whose judgments were certainly of great public weight, as their acts and writings testify.

Nevertheless, some remain doubtful because nothing had hitherto been heard of these chronicles in Spain and no ancient author cited them, although they ought to have been preserved in Spain rather than in Germany or other foreign provinces, since they were written and composed there, and ought to have been read and published by learned Spaniards.

I wish they would raise the same objection against many other ancient Spanish books that were discovered outside Spain and printed in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*. Let the *Chronicle* of Idatius serve as an example. It had disappeared from Spain, yet it was first discovered and printed in Germany by Heinrich Canisius, then in France by Joseph Scaliger, and finally in Paris in a much fuller form by Father Jacques Sirmond of the Society of Jesus.

I should note in passing something concerning this author. To establish confidence in his codex, he thought it sufficient to say:

> It has recently begun to circulate at Rome, from our ancient codex—which the person responsible for the Roman edition, because he had heard that it was in Paris, called “Parisian.” We would rather call it “Mettensian,” because we think that it was once copied at Metz; certainly it came to us from a monastery that was neither obscure nor insignificant.

How much greater authority, I ask, accompanies the publication of Dexter’s *Chronicle*, which we believe was copied not merely from a codex belonging to a city and monastery that were neither obscure nor insignificant, but for which we provide definite names and trustworthy witnesses concerning all these matters?

But, to return to the point: the fact that these chronicles are not currently found in Spain matters little, since during the time of the Saracen devastation it became known that Catholics had transferred their books to other places, so that they might be made safe from barbarian fury. We read something similar about St. Donatus in Ildefonsus’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: during the persecution of the Vandals, he brought a large supply of books to Spain by ship.

In the same way our codex was transferred, together with other books, to the regions of Germany. Clear evidence of this was found together with it—namely Euthrandus’s letter to Regimundus, bishop of Iliberis, at the end of which he writes:

> I congratulate myself that, when I traveled from Toledo, where I was a subdeacon under the most holy Toletan bishop Bonitus, to Italy—this occurred around the year of the Lord 940, at a time when most of Spain was groaning under the yoke of the Hagarenes—I carried some history books with me. I also found them in this library [he is speaking of Fulda], brought from Spain, as I believe, at the command of St. Charlemagne, and presented to him by the most holy Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo.

Julian Petri says the same in a letter to the abbot of Fulda:

> Many books were brought from here [from Toledo] to you by Gumesindus the archdeacon and Lupus Figueras the Mozarab, a leading man, ambassadors of Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo.

This letter, together with Julian’s *Chronicle*, was in the possession of Don Antonio Agustín, archbishop of Tarragona. He himself had received it at Pavia, as men of great authority testify. I myself examined a copy of it and of the *Chronicle* at Toledo in the library of the Count of Mora.

Let me meanwhile say nothing of the fact that the Saracens persecuted not only Christians but also their books, as St. Eulogius writes in the *Memorial*, when all books had to be hidden or sent abroad; and there is no doubt that many perished in the fury of the persecution.

Those who think that Dexter was never known or read by anyone before the aforementioned year 1594, when Father Torralba sent him to Spain, are even farther from the truth. For in the time of the Gothic kings M. Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, continued the *Chronicle* itself to the year of the Lord 612.

If St. Isidore mentions only Maximus in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, or *On Illustrious Men*, and not Dexter, the reason is that Dexter had already been inserted into that catalogue by St. Jerome, whereas Maximus had not.

Again, during the time of the Saracen devastation it was continued a second time, to the year of the Lord 960, by Euthrandus, a Toletan subdeacon. His short works and those of Maximus were copied together with Dexter from the Fulda codex and sent to Spain. Euthrandus has not yet been printed, however, because it had not reached the hands of the Reverend Father Joannes Calderón, who was publishing the remaining works at Zaragoza.

But does anyone perhaps still doubt these matters? I possess testimony closer to our own time that proves the same thing.

At Coimbra, in the library of the royal convent of Santa Cruz of the Canons Regular of St. Augustine, there is a very ancient parchment codex written in Gothic characters containing the *Chronicle* of Sampirus, bishop of Asturias. It also contains a letter of Hugo, bishop of Porto, one of the authors of the Compostellan history, written to Mauritius, bishop of Braga. In this letter Hugo states that Dexter’s *Chronicle*, written to Orosius and accompanied by Maximus’s continuation, is in his possession in a very ancient parchment manuscript. He also cites certain words from Dexter’s *Chronicle*. Among other things he says:

> Concerning the first legation sent to Spain by blessed Clement, Dexter, son of Pacianus, writes as follows in his history addressed to Orosius, which I find copied in the same codex, now in my possession:
>
> Philip, surnamed Philotheus, who had earlier buried at Milan the bodies of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, his fellow citizens of Milan, was converted in the Laminitanean plain by blessed Paul the Apostle. He followed Paul and attached himself to Clement, by whom he was sent as a legate to Spain. He preached at Barcelona, Zaragoza, Valencia, Toledo, Seville, and many other cities.

These words certainly stand verbatim in Dexter’s codex under the year of the Lord 91.

Authentic testimony to this fact is provided in a notarized instrument by Gaspar Albarez de Losada, apostolic notary and secretary of the royal archive of Portugal, called the Torre do Tombo, and reformer of royal patronages in that kingdom. It is dated the fourth day of March in the year 1622. I have often seen this testimony and kept it for some time; it was sent to Rome in support of the proper Office of St. Liberata, which the Church of Sigüenza earnestly requested from the Congregation of Sacred Rites.

It will not be difficult to visit the letter itself at Coimbra and read it in the original; we have reproduced a transcript of it among the author’s testimonies. Hugo of Porto flourished in the year 1100, as is proved from the Compostellan history. I do not see what probable answer can be made to this argument.

I shall add an author of the same century, Julian, archpriest of St. Justa at Toledo, who was present when that same city was recovered by Alfonso VI, king of Castile, in the year of the Lord 1065. His *Chronicle*, copied from a certain codex in the library of the most illustrious Don Antonio Agustín, is for the most part constructed from the chronicles of Dexter and Maximus, as we shall often prove in these commentaries. He specifically designates them by name when, under the year 36, he writes of St. James’s arrival in Spain. His words are:

> As the continuous tradition handed down from apostolic times relates, supported also by the testimony of many ancients—Torquatus, Ctesiphon, Honoratus, Melantius, Dexter, M. Maximus, Isidore, Bede, and others—in the year of the Lord 36 St. James the Apostle, son of Zebedee, came to Spain for a highly honorable purpose.

He undoubtedly borrowed the authors mentioned before Dexter from Dexter himself, who refers to the work of each of them.

To come closer still to our own time, men entirely worthy of belief assert that a copy of Dexter’s chronicles was in the possession of Don Peter Pecha, bishop of Jaén, two hundred years ago. By his gift the Hieronymite fathers of the monastery of Císla, near Toledo, possessed it for a long time. It remained there until, together with other codices, it was sold to a certain bookseller. Eventually Joannes de Vergara, a Toletan canon who died not many years ago, purchased it from him for ten ducats. The book disappeared when Vergara died.

Father Portocarrero asserts this emphatically, both in a statement made to me orally and in writing in the Life of St. Ildefonsus; so too does Escolanus in his *History of Valencia*, book II, chapter 1, decade 1; Losada in the aforementioned account; Carrillo in the Life of St. Valerius, bishop of Zaragoza; and others.

And why delay? Lord Laurentius de Padilla, archdeacon of Ronda and historiographer of the emperor Charles V, used Dexter’s *Chronicle* in many places in his work *On the Saints of Spain*. I think the same should be said of Fernando Pérez de Guzmán in his *Valerius of Histories*, since he mentions many saints whose homeland he plainly borrowed from Dexter.

For example, no one except Dexter had asserted that the holy martyrs Honorius, Eutychius, and Stephen died at Asta in Spain as witnesses to the faith. Padilla nevertheless asserts it; Morales and the other modern writers received it from him, and Baronius records them on November 21.

The same must be said of St. Faith, a virgin who suffered at Agen in Gaul. Before Padilla, everyone thought that she was from Gaul, and they did not know that she had as her companion in the struggle and crown St. Sabina, likewise a Spanish virgin. Both facts, however, were taken from Dexter. The same is found concerning other saints.

But let us freely grant that we lack all the arguments that establish the authority of Dexter’s *Omnimoda Historia*. The History itself, nevertheless, and the contents of it, sufficiently prove that it is genuine. The matters contained in it breathe the author’s sincerity and antiquity; they are full of gravity and clarity. Nothing is unworthy of remembrance, nothing commonplace; many things are exceedingly rare and hitherto unheard of. All these are indications of an author whose work had not yet been published. His style is filled with the purest eloquence, proportionate to the subject, as befitted a man of the most eloquent age, a Palatine official and noble citizen, a servant of the Roman emperors in the prefecture of the praetorium, a familiar associate of St. Jerome, and one whom Jerome praised with distinction.

From this an argument may also be drawn in favor of Maximus, Euthrandus, and Julianus: in proportion as they have fallen further away from antiquity, Latin purity and brilliance likewise decline in them. Maximus stands far below Dexter in eloquence, and the others still somewhat farther; and it is certain that Latin eloquence gradually declined in this manner, as anyone can easily judge by comparing authors of the two periods.

If such chronicles of different authors were spurious and forged, fabricated by some single impostor, it would have been impossible for him, occasionally forgetting himself, not to confuse the very degrees of eloquence belonging separately to the authors mentioned above. And if he possessed eloquence, it would have been impossible for him, throughout the whole of Maximus’s and Euthrandus’s Chronicle, to decline from it gradually with such persistent consistency. Many things are also reported in the present History of Dexter that could not have been known from elsewhere, as will be clearly demonstrated to anyone who examines our commentaries. For now, it is enough to bring forward two or three examples.

In the year of the Lord 57, it is asserted that certain disciples of St. James the Apostle were burned at Iliberri under the judge Alotus, a minister of Nero, for confessing the name of Christ Jesus. He is speaking of Saints Caecilius, Ctesiphon, Iscius, and others. The manner of their martyrdom—namely, that they were consummated by fire—was unknown to everyone; indeed, the martyrdom itself was disputed, since from the most ancient times they had been believed and celebrated as pontiffs and confessors.

You might perhaps say that this could have been learned from the leaden tablets of the Holy Mountain of Granada, which assert the same thing. But nothing could be further from the truth. Rather, by God’s providence it happened that Dexter came down from Germany into Spain before the treasure of the Holy Mountain was discovered and excavated. For Dexter had arrived in the year of Christ 1594, as is plainly proved by the letters of Father Torralba and by all the copies of the Chronicle that now exist; it also began to be published in that very year. The tablets of Granada, however, were found in the following year, 1595; they had lain hidden since the time of Nero.

One of them, found on March 22, contained these words:

> In the second year of the emperor Nero, on the Kalends of March, the chosen Iscius, a disciple of the Apostle James, suffered martyrdom in this place of Illipula, together with his disciples Turillus, Pannutius, Maronius, and Centulius, passing through the midst of the fire. They sought eternal life, and were burned alive, so that the stones were turned into lime. Their ashes lie in the caverns of this sacred mountain.

In the same month another bronze tablet was discovered, containing these words:

> The burned body of St. Mesiton the martyr. He suffered under the authority of the emperor Nero.

On April 10, the sacred ashes of St. Ctesiphon were found, together with a leaden tablet; and on the 30th of the same month, the relics of St. Caecilius, with his tablet.

Thus, by God’s marvelous providence, it happened that Dexter anticipated the discovery of those tablets and sacred relics, so that they might mutually confirm one another: Dexter might establish the credibility of the treasure of the Illipulitan mountain, and might now himself receive reciprocal confirmation from it.

Furthermore, under the year of the Lord 71, the author speaks of the arrival in Spain of St. Onesimus with St. Polyxena of Spain and St. Sara, her companion, who had been disciples of the Apostle Andrew in Achaia. Yet this account is found written nowhere in full, so that it could have been attributed to Dexter.

We do not deny that the Greek menologion, under September 23, according to Cardinal Sirlet’s translation, speaks of St. Polyxena, a disciple of St. Andrew, who returned to Spain with the virgin Rebecca. In the original Greek text itself there is also an account of the arrival of St. Onesimus with them, which Sirlet omitted, as we note in its proper place. Nevertheless, nothing that Dexter asserts here could have been derived from that source. If this history had been derived from it, there is no doubt that an impostor would have written that Onesimus went to Spain with Rebecca and Polyxena, as the Greeks assert there. But here Rebecca is not called Polyxena’s companion; Sara is. We are therefore compelled to affirm that this portion of our author’s history was not recently composed from the Greek menologion, or stolen from elsewhere, but was arranged by someone who preceded that menologion and received the account from older histories and testimonies.

Again, under the year of the Lord 255, the author speaks of that well-known Felix who, in the case of Basilides, bishop of Astorga, and Martial of Mérida, wrote to St. Cyprian. If his memory had been recorded by a modern author who wished to attribute it to an ancient one, he would certainly have called him, in accordance with the common opinion of writers, the bishop of Zaragoza, so as not to depart from the truth in an obvious matter. For Cyprian says of him:

> And as another Felix of Zaragoza, a cultivator of the faith and defender of the truth, signifies in his letter.

But our author does not call him a bishop; he calls him a presbyter. Nor does he say that he was from Zaragoza, but from Vallata Urbicua. This certainly could not have been written except by a very ancient author, since all modern writers unanimously assert the former. As we shall clearly demonstrate in its proper place, under the year of the Lord 255, that Felix was the presbyter of Vallata Urbicua among the Vaccaei, not far from the city of Astorga, and that he pleaded the cause of that Church in his letter to St. Cyprian. The claim that he was bishop of Zaragoza is entirely without foundation; with God’s help we shall establish this.

The same point can be clearly proved from the errors, defects, and redundancies of this codex. For who, writing a new Chronicle and passing it off as the work of a most learned author, would not take care not to alter what was commonly accepted, to attribute nothing incredible to him, and to bring it to light without mistakes or errors? Who would omit matters that were very well known and concerned the author’s own homeland? Who would repeat some things while leaving others truncated? Who would give the proper names of men known to Dexter in an uncertain form?

Yet our codex is full of errors and defects in all these respects. Many things are written here differently from the way more recent writers understand them, although there is nothing unreasonable, nothing unworthy of so great an author and of such antiquity—as our commentaries expressly defend. Let us, however, give examples of errors, and you, reader, I ask you to judge whether they could have been fabricated by some modern writer.

In this matter considerable credit must be given to the Reverend Father Calderón, who published this Chronicle in all its profusion of errors. No greater testimony could have been produced in Dexter’s favor; nothing could have proved such antiquity as the codex itself, left unpolished by any labor or correction.

Let us now draw arguments from it. Under the year of the Lord 34, the codex read as follows:

> At that time there flourished in Spain C. Oppius C. F. C. father centurion, who proclaims at Jerusalem that the dying Christ is the Son of God.

The words “C. Oppius C. F. C. father centurion,” exactly as they stand, can convey no meaning. Caius Oppius was not the son of Caius, nor was he a father who was a centurion; rather, he was a centurion, the son of Cornelius, who was likewise a centurion.
