Nor did the father-centurion proclaim the dying Christ; Caius Oppius himself did so. Therefore the words must necessarily be restored in this manner:

> C. Oppius cent. F. Corn. pariter centurio,

that is:

> Caius Oppius, a centurion, son of Cornelius, likewise a centurion, who proclaims the dying Christ, and so forth.

Other testimonies of Dexter necessarily compel us to believe this. Could this passage have been so shamefully corrupted deliberately? Certainly many copyists must have joined in producing such a deformation, with later writers turning the ignorance of their predecessors into something worse.

Let another, still more obvious, example be added. Under the year of Christ 300, we read in the existing codex of Dexter:

> At Seori in Cantabria, St. Centolla, a citizen of Toledo, daughter of the consul Lucius Rago Quintianus. C. Catania: under her father L. Quintianus, the most courageous virgin St. Agatha suffered, suffering together with the widow Helena in the persecution of Diocletian.

Nothing could be more corrupt than this passage, for as it stands it contains many absurdities: namely, that St. Agatha suffered in the persecution of Diocletian, although she had been crowned with martyrdom under Decius fifty years earlier; that St. Helena the widow suffered not in Spain but at Catania, and was St. Agatha’s companion in martyrdom, although, as all writers unanimously acknowledge, she was the companion of St. Centolla, a Spanish virgin; and that St. Centolla was not crowned with martyrdom. We may also note that the letter “C” at the end of the preceding clause conveys no meaning.

Nevertheless, the passage must be read so that the two parts form a single period, and so that the “C” is not a letter but a sign of parenthesis enclosing the whole phrase, “At Catania, under her father L. Quintianus, the most courageous virgin St. Agatha suffered.” Thus Helena is joined with Centolla, and both are said to have been crowned with martyrdom under Diocletian, whereas St. Agatha is not. The passage should therefore be read as follows:

> At Seori in Cantabria, St. Centolla, a citizen of Toledo, daughter of the consul L. Rago Quintianus (at Catania, under her father L. Quintianus, the most courageous virgin St. Agatha suffered), suffered together with the widow Helena in the persecution of Diocletian.

Its meaning is easy and clear.

Certainly such a great error could have been committed only by a most ignorant copyist, or by one who presumed excessively upon his own abilities. Observing that neighboring sentences began with the name of a city, he believed that this sentence too began with Catania, just as he read:

> At Tarragona, the crown of the holy martyrs. At Carthage, St. Concessa. In the city of Solium, St. Marcellus. At Seori, St. Centolla.

And countless similar examples occur. He therefore believed that one ought likewise to say, “At Catania St. Agatha suffered,” without noticing that the preceding sentence had been left incomplete.

Moreover, under the year 429 the bishop of Toledo is called Martin or Majorianus; and under the year 430 the bishop of Zaragoza is called Valerius or Valerianus. Here, as we have also shown in other passages of our commentaries, a variant reading arising from the corruption of copyists has been inserted into the text. The fact itself proves that some, ignorant of the true reading, wrote one form in the margin and another in the text, as we see happening in all ancient writers. Otherwise, how could the author have failed to know, at least by name, the most distinguished bishops of his own age and homeland? Or what more recent writer, given the power to invent, would attribute this to Dexter—unless he were insane and wished to turn everyone’s judgment against himself?

Furthermore, it is incredible that a later writer who wished to impose a recent work upon Dexter could have omitted St. Vincent the martyr and St. Eulalia of Barcelona. No martyr was more illustrious or better known than Vincent, and Eulalia came from Dexter’s own city. I say nothing of other better-known Spaniards who are absent from the codex. Certainly no sane person who had woven in more obscure martyrs would have rejected more famous ones.

It is therefore clear that these are not defects of the author but of the copyists. Such defects cannot belong in a modern work, but they can occur in a very ancient one, which over the course of a long period was transcribed from various exemplars, with many new defects introduced day by day, whether through the forgetfulness or haste of copyists.

No very famous martyr, as one ought to believe, was omitted by Dexter. Rather, the negligence of the scribes accounts for the omission of many. Their fault must likewise be blamed for the transpositions and repetitions of certain sentences, about which we have already spoken. When something once omitted had to be restored, it happened through error that what had first been restored in the margin was later inserted by another copyist in an inappropriate place.

I return to the preface, or dedicatory letter, which is read as having been written to Paulus Orosius. Who could be so dull as not to see that anyone wishing to forge Dexter’s Chronicle would in every way have attributed it to St. Jerome? Why, I ask, would Orosius have come to mind, and why would he have rejected Jerome, to whom he read that the Chronicle had been dedicated in Jerome’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*? And how could he have extended the Chronicle beyond the fourteenth year of the reign of Emperor Theodosius, when he read in that same Jerome that Jerome had written his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* in the fourteenth year of Theodosius?

The Chronicle of Dexter, however, extends many years beyond that point: from the year of Christ 393, which was the fourteenth year of Theodosius, to the consulship of Theodosius the Younger’s thirteenth year, that is, to the year of Christ 430. Certainly no one would depart even by a finger’s breadth from Jerome’s testimony, since almost nothing else concerning Dexter could be found in the commonly known authors, and that testimony would have to be followed as one follows a heavenly sign.

Since, therefore, the author departs very far from the proposed aim that any later writer would undoubtedly have followed, it follows that we must altogether deny that this work is a recent fabrication and restore it to its genuine author.

It is remarkable how much human judgments differ among themselves. From the same flowers some draw honey, while others draw gall and poison, as happens with bees and wasps. They make the very objection against us by which they seek to attack us.

They therefore think that the authority of this Chronicle is disproved because it was not written to Jerome, because it is full of errors, and because it contains certain things beyond everyone’s knowledge and expectation—as though these very features did not much more strongly prove the author’s antiquity and genuineness, as we have just been explaining.

For if, in an author who lived more than twelve hundred years ago and whose work had lain hidden for so many centuries, nothing at all were found except commonplace material; if his codex were nowhere erroneous and nowhere entangled in difficulties, who would not distrust its antiquity? Would he then have been so dull and indolent as to assert nothing distinctive? So pure that copyists could not stain him—something that was not even granted to the sacred books themselves?

Others bring forward more plausible objections, and it is now worthwhile to answer them.

## § II. That there is nothing capable of weakening the authority of this Chronicle

The objections that the detractors of this Chronicle have thus far devised against its genuineness—although various and numerous, in keeping with the diversity of their minds—we can, for the sake of clarity, reduce to three headings:

1. It is alleged that the work does not correspond to the author’s circumstances and qualities.
2. That it does not correspond to the title assigned to it by Dexter himself.
3. That the History itself contains many things unworthy of so great an author, and that some of them are much later than the author himself.

From all this they wish to prove that the work is spurious and forged.

But let them beware, I ask, lest the words of the Apostle Jude be applicable to them:

> These people blaspheme whatever they do not know; and whatever they know naturally, like irrational animals, by these things they are corrupted. Woe to them.

Nor is this surprising, since they are clouds without water, carried about by winds—menacing destruction and ruin, but dissolving after the thunder and lightning into winds and mere blasts; autumn trees, fruitless, twice dead, uprooted, because they did not produce the fruits promised by their pompous foliage; wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own confusions, since, while threatening a storm from afar, they immediately collapse into foam upon reaching the shore, with no little confusion of their own; wandering stars, for whom the storm of darkness has been reserved forever.

For although they could instruct many in justice and truth, like fixed stars, unto everlasting ages, and could attribute to their masters and authors every sort of little work, they continually stir up a storm like wandering stars; yet the storm of darkness has been reserved for them alone, while others remain in light and peace.

Concerning such men I could certainly say, with Jerome, to the calumniators of his Chronicle:

> I am not unaware that many will come who, with their customary appetite for attacking everything—a thing no one can avoid except one who writes nothing at all—will sink a double tooth into this volume. They will slander the chronology, alter the order, criticize the facts, toss the syllables about; and, as commonly happens, they will attribute the negligence of copyists to the authors.

Although I could repel them in accordance with my rights, telling them that if they dislike the work they need not read it, I prefer nevertheless to send them away appeased by briefly dissolving their objections one by one.

First, it is objected that the work does not correspond to its author. Dexter ought to have completed his Chronicle before the year of Theodosius—or the year 393 from the birth of the Lord—since St. Jerome mentions him in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, which was composed in that year, as is clear from the work itself. Yet the codex now published extends the History to the year of the Lord 430; indeed, at its conclusion it is said to have been written in the year 440, when the author’s life was beginning to decline into old age.

Moreover, it seems incredible that the work was dedicated to Orosius because it could not reach Jerome’s hands. This may perhaps have been inferred from the words of the holy Doctor himself:

> It is reported to me that he has composed a complete History, which I have not yet read.

Yet from the year 393, when Jerome said this, he lived on for another twenty-seven years, or even somewhat longer, since he died in the year of the Lord 420, according to the common opinion, or 426, as is asserted in Dexter. Who could believe that during so many years Dexter’s History did not reach Jerome’s hands?

It is further asserted that Dexter was prefect of the praetorium. Here, they say, two Dexters have been confused. The man who wrote the book did not hold that office; rather, it was the Dexter to whom Jerome dedicated *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. The former was a Spaniard, having been born at Barcelona; the latter was a Roman. Of the latter Jerome says in the preface:

> And so I pray the Lord Jesus Christ that what your Cicero, who stood upon the summit of Roman eloquence, did not disdain to do in his *Brutus*, weaving a catalogue of the orators of the Latin language, I may, encouraged by your exhortation, worthily accomplish in enumerating the writers of the Church.

Dexter is called Cicero’s man because both were Romans.

These matters, however, have an easy solution. Some maintain that when Jerome says he completed that book in the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius, he must be understood to mean Theodosius the Younger, whose fourteenth regnal year fell in the year of the Lord 415. From then until Jerome’s death not enough years elapsed to make it remarkable that a book written in Spain could not be sent to Jerome, who was living in Bethlehem, while he was still alive—especially in those calamitous times, when almost the whole world, and not merely the kingdom of Spain, was in the greatest confusion because of the incursions of the Alans, Vandals, Suebi, and Goths.

But let us grant that Jerome was speaking of Theodosius the Great and Elder, and that he truly completed his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* in the year of the Lord 393. Who does not see that, after once completing the catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, he could later have added others whom he had not yet learned about? Certainly he came to know, day by day and throughout the remainder of his life, some who had previously been unknown to him. Nor can it be denied that, as time passed, the writings and names of others who published their works after that year became known to him.

Once this is granted, we must likewise admit that he added newly discovered or newly published authors to his catalogue, since the same reasoning that had moved Jerome to write the catalogue would have compelled him to do so. That he added certain authors anew to the earlier catalogue is clearly demonstrated by the example of St. Gregory of Iliberri. He is indeed found inserted in it, yet he wrote his book *On the Faith against the Arians* at least twelve years later, since he dedicated it to Galla Placidia Augusta, the wife first of Ataulf, king of the Goths, and afterward of Constantius Caesar, by whom she bore Valentinian the Younger, in the year of the Lord 419.

Who, then, can prove that the same did not happen in Dexter’s case? Once the possibility has been established, the event itself is confirmed by Jerome’s catalogue and by the date of Dexter’s writing.

Besides, Jerome does not affirm from certain knowledge that Dexter had written to him a complete History, but reports it from others. For he says:

> It is reported to me that he has composed a complete History, which I have not yet read.

It was therefore easy, before the Chronicle had been completed, for someone reporting that Dexter was writing it for Jerome’s benefit to say that Jerome had taken note of Dexter’s book. Nevertheless, it need not have been completed in every respect at that time, nor published by the author, but may have appeared only many years later.

If anyone still resists, I will not continue to argue that Dexter was added to the catalogue after it had once been completed. But what if Dexter began his book as a young man, when he was twenty-two years old—the age he had reached in the fourteenth year of Theodosius the Elder—and gradually continued it as time allowed, finally completing it as an old man in the year of Christ 430?

Augustine certainly completed his books *On the Trinity* in old age, although he began them as a young man. One of the more recent writers spent thirty years on a very small volume of moral aphorisms. In Dexter’s case this is made more probable by the military office he held and by the secular affairs to which he had been devoted from his youth.

For the office of writer did not hold first place in Dexter’s life; military service and the prefecture did. He was chiefly occupied with these, and, for the refreshment of his mind, devoted himself from early youth to the study of ecclesiastical matters, granting them whatever time remained. Thus St. Jerome first calls him “Clarus in the world,” and afterward says that he devoted himself to the faith of Christ.

Dexter himself writes to Orosius that, in order to complete those studies in which he had spent a good part of his life, he had returned home, weary of public duties, and there completed his complete History up to the year of Christ 430 and dedicated it to Jerome.

Since he had begun his Chronicle in his youth, before the aforesaid year 393, or the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius, he could easily have been mentioned by Jerome in that very year, at least on the basis of a report. Nor should anyone suppose that such a work required little time to complete merely because it is small in volume. The matters contained in it demanded a long period of time from the author for their verification. It is the mark of rustic minds to assess things merely by their size, rather than by their value and excellence. You, reader, will learn from reading how highly this little book ought to be esteemed.

Finally, what is asserted about the multiplication of Dexters has been said entirely without basis, since there is no disagreement in name, time, or any other respect. The fact that Jerome, addressing Dexter, called Cicero “his own” refers not to his homeland but to his profession of eloquence, in which Dexter excelled and which, as the work shows, he imitated above all others. This is sufficiently indicated by Jerome’s addition:

> Your Cicero, who stood upon the summit of Roman eloquence.

The fact that, when speaking of the author of the Chronicle, Jerome did not call him prefect of the praetorium is not enough to allow us to assert that another man held that office. Even when dedicating to him the little work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Jerome did not add his official title, but simply wrote: “Jerome to Dexter.”

“You urge me, Dexter, to follow Tranquillus”—some believe Jerome did this when he said that Dexter was “Clarus in the world.” I think he used that expression because Dexter had not yet been honored by the emperor with that office, but was serving in other military posts.

A decade later, when Jerome composed his second *Apology against Rufinus*, he added the title to Dexter’s name, saying:

> Nearly ten years ago, when my friend Dexter, who administered the prefecture of the praetorium, asked me to compose a catalogue of the authors of our religion—

This was because Dexter had by then held that office. In the same way, a title was later added to Sophronius’s name when he translated the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* into Greek, as Erasmus notes in his annotations. It was afterward translated once more from Greek into Latin, and the title remained with the name, in these words:

> Jerome’s letter to Dexter, prefect of the praetorium, translated from Latin into Greek.

But let us proceed to other matters.

It is objected that the codex of the published Chronicle does not correspond to the title of the work composed by Dexter. That work, as is clear from Jerome, was called *Omnimoda Historia*; but this codex does not contain a complete History, only chiefly the affairs of Spain. Therefore it must belong to someone other than Dexter, whose History, since it is complete, ought to report the deeds of every nation. Hence it does not describe the succession of emperors and Roman pontiffs in the manner of a Chronicle, but mentions them confusedly and together.

If it is called complete because it embraces all events that occurred from the creation of the world up to the author’s own time—as the prologue of this work also asserts that Dexter completed it—how can the published Chronicle begin with the Nativity of the Savior? Furthermore, it was not transmitted by its discoverers in one uniform manner before it was printed. For the copy held by the bishop of Segorbe was much more abbreviated and differed in certain respects from the printed edition.

Anyone who denies that these Chronicles constitute a complete History has read very little in them. The author omitted almost nothing that happened anywhere in the world and concerned the splendor of the Church; and he incorporated into his account all who distinguished it in their own time by their writings or by notable deeds.

If he wrote more about Spanish affairs, this should not be counted as a fault in a Spanish author. For who, when composing a Chronicle, has not written more fully about the affairs of his own homeland and more briefly about those of foreign lands?

Eusebius of Caesarea, a Greek writer and the first author of an ecclesiastical Chronicle, recorded many things concerning the Greeks and few concerning the Latins. Thus, when Jerome translated him into Latin, he inserted many Roman matters, writing these words in his prologue:

> For it must be understood that I have partly performed the office both of translator and of writer, since I have rendered the Greek with the utmost fidelity and have added certain things that seemed to me to have been omitted, especially in Roman history, which Eusebius, the founder of this kind of book, seems to me not so much to have been ignorant of—for he was learned—as to have passed over briefly, since he was writing in Greek, matters that were less necessary to his own people.

Jerome also continued that Chronicle from the twentieth year of Constantine to the sixth consulship of Valens and the second of Valentinian, but wrote almost the whole of it concerning Roman history, as a Roman author.

In continuing the Chronicle, Jerome was followed by Prosper of Aquitaine and Victor of Tunnuna. They filled their pages with the affairs of Africa or Aquitaine, in which they had been born or educated. The same thing happened with Spanish authors. Hydatius of Lamego continued Eusebius’s Chronicle at the point where St. Jerome had ended it; nevertheless, he wrote so much about Spanish affairs that St. Isidore said of him in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 12:

> Hydatius, bishop of the province of Gallaecia, following the Chronicle of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, or of the presbyter Jerome, continues the history appended from the first year of Theodosius Augustus to the eighth year of the reign of Leo; in it he narrates chiefly the cruel wars of the barbarian peoples that were oppressing Spain.

What shall I say of John of Biclaro, afterward bishop of Gerunda? He promises to continue the aforesaid Prosper and Victor, and everything he subsequently writes concerns the Goths of Spain and their kings, Liuvigild and Reccared—especially Liuvigild, whose deeds he almost entirely touches upon in concise chronological form.

Marcellinus comes likewise continued Jerome’s Chronicle, and, being an Illyrian, devoted most of his account to the history of the Eastern Empire. This led him to say in his preface:

> I, however, have followed only the Eastern Empire, with a merely simple computation.

It is therefore unjustly objected to Dexter that he devoted special attention to recording the affairs of his homeland, when no fault is charged against the others who did the same. Indeed, it ought to be considered a great merit, and not lightly praised, that each of them gave us particular knowledge of his own affairs, and expanded upon what he knew best, where there was less danger of error, while also providing an account more useful and welcome to his own people—as Jerome said of Eusebius.

This is why, as we see in this codex, Dexter followed the succession of almost all the bishops of Barcelona, since he knew them better as the bishops of his homeland. He mentions them under their own years: St. Eusebius, the disciple of the Apostle James and founder of that see; St. Theodosius; Aulus Victor; Lucius; Fulta; both Severus the martyr; Avitus; Mademarius; St. Pacianus; Emila; and Lampadius, who flourished in his own time. Yet he does not observe this practice in other sees, except Toledo, whose bishops he enumerates all together because of the prerogative of its primacy.

In the succession of Roman pontiffs and emperors—this too was brought against him—he proceeds in such a way that he does not assign each one to the year in which he began his office, but gives the succession of many together, saying:

> Tiberius succeeds Augustus; Caius, Tiberius; Claudius, Caius; Nero, Claudius;

or:

> In the see of Peter, Calixtus succeeds Zephyrinus; Urban succeeds Calixtus; Pontian succeeds Urban.

He did this only up to the point reached by the Chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome, namely, the year of the Lord 380, since those authors had already treated the matter in its proper place. In what follows, however, he mentions the Roman emperors and pontiffs individually in their proper places, as can be seen in the codex.

What sort of argument is it to say that the surviving Chronicle begins with Christ the Lord rather than with the creation of the world, and therefore is not a complete History? It is as though the author’s defect could be inferred from the defect of the codex, which contained only half of his work.

If the work were forged, and the forger had chosen to write nothing about events before the birth of Christ, he would certainly not have said in the prologue that Dexter had composed a history from the creation of the world to his own time. He would instead have said that he had written a history from the birth of the Lord, since Jerome’s or any other writer’s authority in no way compelled us to make the former assertion. Jerome merely says:

> It is reported to me that he has composed a complete History.

Since the prologue makes this assertion, while the present codex lacks the history of the Old Testament, it plainly indicates that the first part of the Chronicle, containing the history from the creation of the world to the Nativity of the Lord, was omitted by the copyist, although it belonged to the author’s original. Or perhaps it was transcribed in another volume, which has hitherto escaped our notice.

Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that the extract of Dexter held by the bishop of Segorbe differed somewhat in the size of the volume and in the report of certain matters from the edition printed at Zaragoza. Before the work was printed, the whole and complete codex was not circulated to everyone. Rather, it was distributed in parts, according to the will and devotion of each person. Some shortened the Chronicle as they pleased because they did not see that everything contained in it served their purpose. In this way they introduced not a few errors, which others attribute to Dexter.

One such version was the extract copied by the bishop of Segorbe. Some people were especially displeased that it said St. Pacianus, the father of Dexter, succeeded St. Severus, bishop and martyr of Barcelona, who was crowned at the beginning of the persecution of Diocletian in the year of the Lord 285. Pacianus, however, flourished a hundred years later, namely in the year 384. If this were true, they said, this new Dexter would not even recognize his own father.

But they are suffering from an obvious confusion concerning St. Severus. There were two Barcelona bishops of that name, both martyrs: the first suffered at the hands of the pagans under Diocletian in the year of the Lord 285, while the second suffered at the hands of the Arians in the year 352. Dexter himself mentions both of them. His father followed the latter Severus in the see, and perhaps not immediately.

Nevertheless, that truncated transcription of Dexter’s codex was subject to many difficulties, which disappeared when the complete Chronicle was printed.

## The third head of the objections

The third head of the objections concerns the history itself. For, they say, there are many things in it alien to the truth, not a few incredible matters, and things beyond all human belief. To these I could first respond that Jerome attributes the reliability of the statements to the author himself when replying to the detractors of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*; and, furthermore, that this author was not modern, nor was the work included in the catalogue of canonical Scriptures, and therefore it is not surprising if it occasionally departs from the truth. Nor was he a modern writer, composing only what had by his time been accepted among the commonly read authors. Indeed, the antiquity of the author is plainly demonstrated by the fact that he writes certain things differently from the way they are now believed.

It does not therefore rightly follow from the fact that he may be mistaken in some matters that someone other than Dexter was the author of this *Chronicle*; it follows only that the book is not canonical, as I have said. In truth, however, the author asserts nothing incredible or improbable, however much certain loud objectors may resist. They raise many objections: concerning the letters of James and Paul to the Hebrews, which are said in this codex to have been written only to the Spaniards, and the letter of James son of Zebedee, contrary to the common judgment of the learned; concerning the Gospel centurions, who are reported to have been born in Spain; concerning the preaching and disciples of the same Saint James; concerning the Spanish Jews, who supposedly gave no assent at all to Christ’s death; and finally concerning six hundred other matters regarded as either false or incredible. To answer all these objections individually and fully belongs to our commentaries, where the foundations of each assertion are explained at sufficient length and the contrary arguments are blunted.

Nevertheless, the adversaries insist that some things found in these *Chronicles* are more recent than Dexter—for example, that mention is made of the feast of the Immaculate Conception under the year of the Lord 308, although it is plain to everyone, even to the bleary-eyed and barbers, that nowhere in the world was such a feast celebrated before the year 1100; and that the Augustinian order is mentioned, although until approximately that same century not even the name of the order, much less the Augustinian order, was in use. Finally, they add that the ingenuity of the modern forger is especially evident in this: although he inserted the names of many martyrs into these *Chronicles*, he deliberately admitted only those who are recorded in the ancient Church registers without the name of their city or province, assigning them to particular Spanish cities; and he likewise transferred from Africa to Spain certain martyrs who had received their crowns at Carthage.

Neither argument, however, proves the point intended. The fact that some things found in these writings may be more recent than Dexter does not immediately establish that the whole work is apocryphal. Since it passed through the hands of many people in different centuries, it is impossible that something was not added to the margin by someone for the sake of fuller explanation, and that this addition was subsequently introduced into the text itself by others, thereby producing some confusion. It is also suggested that even this material was added many years ago by Euthrandus, or Julian, or at least by some highly learned monk of Fulda: Father Torralba and Father Higuera testified that the autograph contains everything exactly as it now stands. They deserve particular credence here because none of the matters suspected of having been added appears to benefit their own order. For these matters do not belong to the disciplines of Augustine or Benedict; but we shall discuss the subject itself more fully in its proper place.

As for what is asserted about the feast of the Immaculate Conception, it has a quite different meaning from that commonly supposed. The meaning is that Saint James the Apostle instituted in Spain the feast of the Lord’s Incarnation, which is now rightly called the Conception of the Mother of God: namely, the conception by which she conceived God and man, Christ, in her chaste womb—not the conception by which the Virgin herself was conceived.

We are moved to assert this first because, although the mystery itself of the Blessed Virgin’s preservation from original contagion may perhaps have been recognized by the holy Apostles and the ancient doctors, as we have demonstrated in a special work defending the Fathers, nevertheless no feast was ever made of it until the time of Saint Anselm. Here, however, the subject is not so much the mystery of the Conception as the feast. Secondly, the name “Conception” until the time of Duns Scotus signified only the bodily union of those who beget, and the acts involved in it, as we have clearly proved in the work mentioned above. None of the ancients called the conception of the Virgin—that which arose from the union of her parents—immaculate; rather, they applied the term to the Virgin herself at the moment when she received her soul. Finally, the apostolic feast of which Dexter speaks in that passage was not concerned with the passive conception of the Virgin herself, but with the active conception.

We shall say many other things on the same subject in our commentaries on that passage, which you should consult under the year of the Lord 308, Commentary 1.

It is also wholly gratuitous to assert that all the holy martyrs found in the Roman martyrology without the name of their city or native place were deliberately interspersed in these *Chronicles*. For many more appear in those same registers, yet no mention is made of them in this work, as anyone can easily discover by reading the catalogue of saints appended to the topographical index of the Roman martyrology under the heading “Names of the saints whose place is not indicated by the martyrology,” and comparing them with the saints contained in these *Chronicles*.

And who would believe that someone was so anxious and careful to appropriate to his own homeland saints belonging to no particular—so to speak—diocese, while it is nevertheless clear that he failed to enumerate the well-known ones? Indeed, if someone in this age had been able to fabricate a *Chronicle* for Dexter, he would first have inserted into it the Spanish martyrs known throughout the world, rather than searching out foreign and unknown ones. Yet it is clear that this was not done.

But what is most important in this matter is that many of those mentioned here had not appeared in the registers of the Roman martyrology before the year 1584, when it was revised and enlarged at the command of Gregory XIII. The revisers borrowed them from the Greek menologion, where they too are found without the name of their own city.

This nevertheless provides no slight argument in favor of the present work. If those saints who were transferred from the Greek menologion into the Latin martyrology had been Greeks and had received their crowns in the cities of the East, there is no doubt that the Greeks would have identified each city by name. Since they did not do so, we must believe that this information had not reached them and that those martyrs received their crowns in regions exceedingly remote from the Greeks. And what cities, I ask, were more remote from the Greeks than those of Spain?

It is far more probable that the Greeks, conversely, learned of these martyrs from no other source than Dexter’s *Chronicles*, borrowed their names from him, and placed them in their ecclesiastical registers, while omitting the names of the cities in which Dexter reports them as having suffered—either because those names seemed barbarous to them, as the names of Spanish cities certainly were in ancient times, or because it made little difference to them whether they knew the names of those cities or not. Being exceedingly remote, they could know them only by name. Yet we see that in the case of their own martyrs they carefully ensured that the names of the regions and cities which they had ennobled by their sufferings were recorded in the menologion.

But why—one asks—if they suffered in the West, were their names, and those of the cities reddened by their blood, not found in the Latin martyrologies before they were sought and received from the Greek registers? The reason is readily supplied: Dexter remained hidden, and his work had not been sufficiently made available to the public when the martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, and the others which we now possess were published. Consequently, they could not borrow anything from him.

That no modern author took from the Greek or commonly used Latin martyrologies the saints mentioned in these *Chronicles* is sufficiently proved by the fact that in these *Chronicles* we find certain martyrs assigned to cities quite different from those named in the other works. For example, the Greeks and Latins say that Saint Aza and his companions received the crown of martyrdom in Isauria, a province of Asia, whereas Dexter places them in Gallaecia. Again, the Greeks and the Roman martyrology report that Saint Antonina suffered with Alexander the soldier at Constantinople, while Dexter places her at Olcades in Carpetania. Likewise, others say that Saints Quiricus and Julitta were crowned at Tarsus in Cilicia, whereas Dexter places them at Hippo in Carpetania. I say nothing for the moment of the others whose cities are concealed in silence by the Greeks, but whose acts and most ancient monuments repeatedly confirm in these commentaries that they were no other cities than those assigned by Dexter.

Who would be so witless as to alter recently the well-known cities of martyrs? But I return to Carthage. Certainly Spanish Carthage was not so obscure that during the Roman and Gothic periods it failed to give its name to the entire province of Carthage. In the most ancient councils, especially those of Toledo and Braga, frequent mention is made of the province of Carthage, which once included Toledo and Carpetania as well.

Once this is granted, it is plausible that some of the martyrs who are recorded in the ecclesiastical registers as having been crowned at Carthage actually suffered martyrdom in Spain, and not all in Africa. For how could it have happened that, although countless Christians fought the good fight throughout Spain, consecrating all its cities and towns with their blood, Carthage alone—one of the most illustrious cities of all—could boast of no martyr?

Examine carefully the entire sequence of the Roman martyrology, and among the countless martyrs said to have suffered at Carthage you will find none of whom it is specifically said that he suffered in Spain. Yet, to say nothing for the moment of the other agents of the persecutions in Spain, it is established that Galba was acclaimed at Spanish Carthage as emperor against Nero, although he had previously dealt with the Christians with extreme severity, so much so that on a column erected to Nero he declared that this had been done because the province had been cleansed of brigands and of those who inculcated a new superstition into the human race.

We must therefore believe that many of those reported as having been killed at Carthage were crowned in Spain, as we shall now see in Dexter. From all that we have treated at such length, it must finally be inferred that this codex, which we undertake to interpret, is the genuine offspring of Dexter of Barcelona, and that none of the objections brought against it has any weight whatsoever. Therefore, candid Reader, do not hesitate even slightly in reading it, I beg you, but proceed through it with an untroubled step.

## § III. With what diligence the elucidator had to labor in order to shed light on Dexter’s assertions

[Col. 0044A]

When the *Chronicle of Universal History* by L. Dexter first came into my hands, candid Reader, I perceived that a treasure of priceless riches lay concealed within it. I was thereby raised to such hope that, if I applied all my strength and study to excavating it, I would not depart wholly cheated of the reward of my labor.

At that time I was living in Madrid, the court of the Catholic King and my native city. There I was readily supplied with the company of men distinguished for great learning and with access to numerous libraries, through whose assistance and from whose resources I trusted that the burden of my undertaking could be lightened.

But while I was still standing at the threshold of the work, what difficulties, what phantoms to overcome, presented themselves to me! I had either to succumb, exhausted, or to fight manfully until I overcame them. Do you wish to know how many and of what kind?

The variety of matters contained in these *Chronicles* was immense. To unravel them, it was necessary to examine the whole history of antiquity, both human and divine, and to judge the authors and the matters themselves after first comparing them with one another: who, and in what matters, deserved to be heard above the others; what was more probable and what had to be rejected.

For this purpose we had to consult Livy, Suetonius, both Plinys, Plutarch, Dio, Tacitus, Philostratus, Capitolinus, Lampridius, Eutropius, Trebellius, Vopiscus, Martial, both Senecas, Silius, Lucan, Juvenal, and the other teachers of human history whom it would take too long to list. In the end, we had to compare with Dexter’s writings the lives, deeds, successions, and chronologies of the Roman emperors and of the barbarian peoples who fought against them.

Besides these matters, many things from the Old Testament had to be treated expressly, whether concerning the Books of Kings and Chronicles or the prophecies of the prophets. The New Testament, too, had to be examined in its entirety in order to elucidate its chronology: the Gospels, the apostolic Acts, and the letters and writings of the Apostles. For there is nothing that Dexter did not touch.

It was also necessary to consult all the Fathers, especially the earlier ones, both to draw out the true meaning of the sacred statements and to investigate matters belonging to ecclesiastical history. I mean Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Dionysius, Irenaeus, the other Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius, Origen, Tertullian, Cyprian, Basil, Gregory Nazianzen and Gregory of Nyssa, Chrysostom, Epiphanius, Pacian, Juvencus, Ambrose, Paulinus, Jerome, Augustine, and the rest whose writings survive.

What shall I say of the councils, all of which the necessity of the undertaking compelled me to read carefully, both for calculating the years and for bringing the truth to light? What of the acts of the holy martyrs, whose necessary materials I found not all assembled in the works of Lippomanus, Surius, Mombritius, Lipeloo, Velser, Haraeus, Sainctor, Villegas, Trugillo, and similar writers?

The martyrologies did not yet supply all the names, especially the Roman martyrology—whether the ancient one edited by Rosweyde or the modern one illuminated by Cardinal Baronius—and then those of Bede, Notker, Rabanus, Usuard, Ado, Molanus, Galesinius, Maurolycus, and their like. The Greek menologia had been abridged by Cardinal Sirleto; it was necessary to return to the Greek sources themselves. Even this was insufficient: one had to consult the most ancient manuscripts of the acts of the holy martyrs, as well as the old breviaries of different Churches.

Again, for the chronology of the years assigned in the margin to each statement, I had to undertake great labor, especially because Dexter often appeared to disagree with the calculations of others.

Even if these monsters could perhaps be overcome, four further obstacles arose, demanding the shoulders of an Atlas merely to support such a burden.

1. The novelty of many statements, which had entirely escaped our hearing. For example, that the Gospel centurions had been Spaniards; that Paul’s Letter to the Hebrews had been written to Spaniards converted from Judaism; that the region of Ophir was in Spain; and many matters of this kind, which will readily occur to anyone in the text.

2. The geography of the Spanish cities, which requires that they be recognized according to their ancient names and also compared without discrepancy with their newer names. No region of the whole world changed the names of its cities so often as Spain, since no region endured so many incursions and dominations by barbarians. First, as far as we know, it was conquered by the Phoenicians, then by the Carthaginians, again by the Romans, afterward by the Goths, and finally by the Moors; each of these peoples imposed names upon the cities in its own language.

3. Nor was it a matter of lesser weight to overcome the errors of the copyists, with which the codex teemed at every third line. Some interrupted the very sense and sometimes corrupted it. Who could enumerate the transpositions, duplications, and abbreviations of clauses? In this I find that what once happened to Saint Jerome when he was unfolding and translating Eusebius’s *Chronicle*—then much more recent than Dexter’s now is—has happened to me, so that I can say with him:

> In addition to the common difficulty which we have alleged in every interpretation—for my part, exposition—there is this particular difficulty: the history is manifold, containing barbarous names, unknown matters, inexplicable numbers, and strokes interwoven among both the matters and the numbers; so that it is almost more difficult to learn the order of reading than to arrive at an understanding of what is read.

4. Finally, there were the adverse judgments of various men who held different views concerning the genuineness of this work. Not everyone believed Dexter’s offspring genuine, but rather a fabrication—either composed in support of the Immaculate Conception of the Mother of God, because Dexter is thought at one point to say something about it, or produced to magnify the antiquity of the order of the hermits of Saint Augustine, because it occasionally mentions the monks of Augustine. A similar judgment is expressed concerning the continuation by M. Maximus, since we read in it much about the same hermits and about Benedictine monks.

This is indeed the established custom among mortals: each person elevates and exaggerates the authority of those who benefit his own interests, while treating as worthless those who might in any way hinder them. Only those who think that Dexter’s *Chronicle* harms their own opinions disparage it; conversely, many value it solely because it appears to support their views. Neither group fights for the truth of the *Chronicle*: each is led by his own inclination.

Once they had come to detest Dexter’s statements, they devised many contradictions which seemed to attack not only the author but also the work, and to weaken their own authority.

Who, I ask, would not have grown weary amid so many difficulties, hesitated, lost confidence, or abandoned the undertaking? Yet these monsters not only did not make me withdraw or despair; they did not even make me hesitate. Rather, they added spurs to my running. At their sight I put on greater strength and a spirit more courageous for so great a labor, rejecting all leisure until at last I had elucidated Dexter’s *Chronicle*. I judged that this would bring no contemptible glory not only to Spain but also to the universal Church of Christ, since many controversies in ecclesiastical history are supported by Dexter’s testimony, and no small number of matters omitted by others receive through him their supplement.

For this reason I searched out whatever I believed in Spain, Italy, or France might contribute to my undertaking, whether material belonging to humane letters among secular authors or material belonging to the more solid and divine disciplines among the holy Fathers and ecclesiastical doctors, councils, martyrologies, and collections of saints. I spared neither labor, rest, nor expense, always keeping before my eyes the need to approach the sources themselves whenever they were available, consult the older codices, and be moved neither by hatred nor by love, so that I might more easily attain the truth.

In Spain I visited the royal library of the Escorial, then that of Toledo belonging to the Holy Primate Church; and many libraries of monasteries of my own order, especially those of Nucales, Toledo, La Espina, Huerta, Salamanca, Alcalá, and others, which supplied the acts of the Spanish saints in various manuscripts.

At Madrid, the most illustrious master Egidius Gundisalvi Dávila, royal historiographer of Castile, out of his benevolence toward me, made available a generous supply of ancient breviaries formerly used in various Churches, especially those of Salamanca, Cuenca, Palencia, Astorga, and Toledo, printed according to the Roman custom by Cardinal Silíceo. For I also found, both at Toledo and at Rome, the more ancient breviary according to the order of Saint Isidore, commonly called the Mozarabic.

These works certainly supplied me with abundant material for constructing and embellishing the undertaking. When I reached Rome, I visited the Vatican library more than once and that of the Roman College very frequently. The library of my most illustrious and reverend lord, Cardinal Trejo, which is exceedingly rich because of the distinguished prince’s exceptional and universal learning, brought me much illumination.

The Anician Library of the Gregorian College, recently established for the monks of the entire order of our holy father Benedict, assisted me greatly through the writings of the Reverend Father and dearest friend Don Constantine Gaetano, whose works are sufficiently praised. It was also useful from time to time to visit the Vallicellian Library, enriched by the studies of Cardinal Baronius.

To omit other matters for the sake of brevity, the library of Saint Peter in Montorio contributed greatly. There, as though in my own house, through the kindness of its author, I devoted myself almost daily to my work, aided by the counsel and judgment of the Reverend Father Luke Wadding, lecturer in sacred theology and chief chronographer of the entire Seraphic Order. The library itself belongs to him, as do many varied works, some already published and others soon to be published, which bring him immense glory and honor.

All these works I did not hesitate to examine in order to elucidate the variety, antiquity, and novelty of Dexter’s history and to bring its chronology into agreement.

Spanish geography had to be sought from Ambrosius Morales, Florián de Ocampo, Resende, Nonius, Quevedo, Mariana, Zurita, Goes, Blanca, Beuther, and other authors on that subject; and with much greater precision from Ptolemy, Antoninus, Pomponius, Pliny, Strabo, Appian of Alexandria, Solinus, and their contemporaries. Nor could Ortelius, Mercator, Villanova, Moleto, Mill, Nebrissensis, Tarafa, Clusius, and the various histories of the different kingdoms be omitted, as will easily be confirmed by experience in these commentaries.

Our author sheds such great light on the affairs of his homeland by recording the cities of each martyr under its proper name; by introducing illustrious memories of the doctors and bishops who flourished throughout Spain in those ancient times; by showing from which of them the Catholic faith received its beginnings, progress, and growth; which cities were reddened by the blood of the principal martyrs; which were honored by the councils of great Fathers; and which errors and abuses were condemned and expelled there.

Thus all Spaniards may rightly rise up in applause of so great an author and, after first singing praises of thanks to Almighty God for the discovery of such a *Chronicle*, take for themselves, in meeting him, Cicero’s words from Book I of the *Academic Questions*, concerning Marcus Varro:

> Wandering and straying through our cities as though we were strangers and visitors, your books have led us home, as it were, so that at last we could recognize who and where we were. You have revealed the age of our homeland, the divisions of time; the laws of sacred things, the laws of priests; domestic and military discipline; the situation of regions and places; the names, duties, and causes of all divine and human affairs.

We have certainly found the same to have happened to us through Dexter’s benefaction. We inhabited the cities and towns of Spain as strangers and visitors, unaware of what notable events had once occurred in them. We did not know which distinguished predecessors, martyrs, bishops, or doctors those cities had produced in ancient times. Now, however, with Dexter as our guide, we shall henceforth recognize, revere, and celebrate them as great protectors, outstanding patrons, noble fellow citizens, and beloved brothers. Through their patronage, may it be granted us to unlock the immense treasures of God’s mercies, far more richly than before.

In correcting the text of Dexter’s reading, we also had to labor no less diligently, especially because the original codex itself was filled with countless errors, while the scribes who drew their copies from it, preserving those errors, introduced new ones. It was therefore difficult to restore the text to its former purity. Nevertheless, after comparing other copies, I removed many additions introduced later; and I corrected other readings which, from the text itself, clearly required correction and plainly revealed an error not of the author but of the copyist.

For example, under the year of the Lord 300, the following sentence had been written twice in exactly the same words:

> In the city of Mellaria in Spain, in Baetica, Saint Firmus the martyr, etc.

It extended for six lines, and therefore ought to have been written only once.

Moreover, under the year of the Lord 86, the memory of Saint Narcissus, bishop of Braga, killed at Gerunda, had been inserted, although, according to Dexter’s own testimony, he was killed nearly two hundred years later. Dexter writes of his martyrdom under the year 277, and therefore the earlier notice had to be removed.

Under the year 110 there was a discussion of the philosopher Porphyry and of the writers who opposed him, although this properly belonged to the year 310 and had necessarily to be restored there.

Proper names of cities and persons, wherever they had been corrupted, had to be corrected from other testimonies of the same author and from the readings of ancient writers who treated them. Other matters were easily corrected from what preceded and followed. Nevertheless, Dexter could not yet be restored to his original brilliance, chiefly because it is clear to us that certain things are missing from the surviving text—things which manifestly could not have been omitted by Dexter.

For who could persuade himself that Dexter passed over in silence the most illustrious martyrdom throughout the world of Saint Vincent the Deacon of Zaragoza? Who would believe that the memory of the holy virgin and martyr Eulalia of Barcelona, the protectress of Dexter’s own homeland, had been removed from these writings? Who would suspect that Marcellus of León, the centurion, and his twelve sons, so well known throughout Spain, had found no place in these *Chronicles*—especially when Dexter himself had read in Clement Prudentius the hymn in praise of the martyrs Emeterius and Chelidonius of Calahorra, sons of that same Saint Marcellus?

I say nothing for the moment of several others, such as Zoilus with his nineteen companions; Gerontius, bishop of Italica; Evasius of Casale; Hermogenes and Donatus; Lupus and Aurelia; Cyriacus and Paula; Sandalius of Córdoba; and Dalmatius of Gerunda, some of whom perhaps never came to Dexter’s notice.

And why proceed further? Certainly, readers will be able to discover by reading alone the labor we have devoted to illuminating these *Chronicles* and their incredible usefulness. Let them read, I beg, and recognize that Dexter has come forth publicly for the great benefit of the Church of God.

[Col. 0049]

# FLAVIUS LUCIUS DEXTER OF BARCELONA, *CHRONICLE OF UNIVERSAL HISTORY* (G)

## Together with the commentaries of Friar Francis Bivarius, in which the entire ecclesiastical history from the birth of Christ through the year 430 is examined with exact precision

[Note: [Col. 0049A]

A short work required a short title: *The Chronicle of Universal History of Flavius Lucius Dexter*, and so forth. The Author offers us a very small treasure if quantity is considered, but a great and precious one in quality. Once someone has grasped it, he will call it altogether an immense and priceless wealth. Things are not distinguished by their price, according to whether they are great or small, but by their virtue and excellence.

Since this *Chronicle* possesses such power, I judged it worthwhile to explain it in these commentaries. It was necessary for them to grow to such a size that I might bring to light, as best I could, what lay hidden in the work’s value. Yet I do not believe that I have been excessively prolix, nor that I have achieved everything in the most exact manner. It will be enough if I provide an opportunity for a wise person to bring light to the Author, supply what I have omitted, and correct what I may perhaps have expressed with insufficient success.

That will honor Dexter, greatly please me, and benefit the entire Christian world, especially Spain. But let us come to the matter itself.

Dexter chose a difficult style of writing when he wrote his *Chronicle*. It is much more difficult to touch upon great matters briefly than to explain the deeds of many people over many periods in a lengthy treatment. For this reason Jerome did not wish to write in the style of a *Chronicle* about the slaughters and invasions of the barbarians into the Roman Empire that occurred in his own time, since he judged that they should be reserved for writing in the broader style of history, as he declares in his prologue.

For this is the difference between chronicles and histories, according to Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine Scripture*, chapter 17: chronicles are images of histories and the briefest recollections of times—one might call them epitomes of the histories—whereas histories are developed and extended in a broader style.

Just as the deeds of many rulers, and the series and exploits of different kings, unfold over lengthy periods yet are depicted on very small tablets, so too they are set down in more compressed chronicles, while they are narrated in the broadest books of history.

For this reason Saint Jerome called this kind of writing “Chronological Canons” in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. In his account of Eusebius of Caesarea, when he lists his books, he enumerates fourth the *Universal History of the Chronological Canons*. Yet when he later lists his own works in the final chapter, he calls it simply the *Chronicle of Universal History*.

Since it is a *Chronicle of Universal History*, it necessarily follows the compression of canons, such as apostolic and conciliar canons, which contain great teaching in very few words. They are called canons because *kanon* is Greek for what is called *regula* in Latin, and, as Aristotle testifies, it belongs to the nature of a rule to be small or minimal.

Nearly all those who wrote chronicles among the ancients used approximately the same style: Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper the Elder and the Younger, Isidore of Seville and of Córdoba, Victor of Tunnuna, Idatius of Lamego, John of Gerunda, Marcellinus, the author of the Alexandrian *Chronicle*, Ado, Sigebert, and countless others whom I omit.

Among these, after Jerome and Eusebius, Dexter claims the first place, both in the ordering of time, the dignity of his writing, and the refinement of his style.

There is no contradiction between the fact that the title of this book is *Chronicle of Universal History* and that Jerome, when mentioning it, calls it simply *Universal History*: “He is said to have written for me a universal history.” For in that ancient period universal history was not written in a historical and expansive style, but in the manner of a chronicle. History embraced the deeds of only one kingdom, one region, or one distinguished man; and from many different histories, reduced to concise canons, a single universal history was woven, enjoying either the title *Chronicle* or *Universal History*, or both at once.

Indeed, in Jerome’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* there is no universal history written by any of the ancients that does not employ the style of a chronicle; nor is there any chronicle that is not called universal history.

Moreover, in Dexter himself we see that he called his work, which he entitled *Chronicle of Universal History*, simply *Universal History* in the dedicatory letter to Orosius, when he says: “Furthermore, the universal history which extends from the creation of the world to our own times, that is, to the year of Christ 430,” and so forth.

It is certainly regrettable that the earlier part of Dexter’s *Chronicle* has perished—or at least continues to struggle with moths and cockroaches—the part containing the historical canons from the creation of the world to the birth of Christ. Through it we would have learned many matters worth knowing, especially matters relating to Spain, which have until now remained unknown. This was why, in the Zaragoza edition, it was called the “Fragment of Dexter’s *Chronicle*.” We have refrained from that title, however, being content with the genuine one, especially since the work contains an entire history from the birth of the Lord up to the author’s own times.

## After [he came] from the East, etc.

How great was the dignity of the praetorian prefect, with which Dexter was invested, Cassiodorus explained in Book VI of the *Letters*, saying:

> No dignity is equal to the authority of the praetorian prefect.

That is, he held, as it were, the second place after Caesar and presided over the correction of public discipline. Thus we know that many men were raised from such a prefecture to the summit of imperial power, including Vespasian, Macrinus, Philip, and others.

In the time of Romulus, the praetorian prefect was called the man placed in charge of the *praetorium*, namely of the cohorts and praetorian soldiers who defended the emperor’s palace. According to Alciatus in his *Commentary on the Meaning of Words*, it was called the *praetorium* because the soldiers of the praetor kept watch there. Among the ancients, any commander of soldiers was called a *praetor*.

In those ancient times, the praetorian prefect sometimes went out to war against the enemy. But when Roman power increased, the offices were distinguished. Then the man who kept watch to protect the emperor’s safety was called the Prefect of the Watch, while the prefect who defended the empire against enemies was called the Praetorian Prefect.

Later the Master of the Soldiers was added, the man who was continually engaged with the enemy. His office differed from that of the praetorian prefect in that the authority of the masters of cavalry had been introduced by the laws of the Roman people, whereas that of the praetorian prefects depended upon the discretion of the emperors.

Some hold that among the ancient Frankish kings the praetorian prefects, or prefects of the palace, were those called masters of the household, or mayors of the palace, and that the duties of the two offices amounted to the same thing.

In Book I of Justinian’s *Code* there is a special title concerning the office of the Praetorian Prefect of the East, which Dexter administered. In law 2, the prefect is granted the power to establish general statutes that are not contrary to the imperial laws and that remain in force until they are repealed by the emperor.

But in order that the extent of his authority and the loftiness of his office may once be made clear, I shall insert here, for Dexter’s honor, the formula that the emperors gave to praetorian prefects when they ordered them to assume this dignity, as Cassiodorus sets it down in Book VI of the *Variae*, chapter 3. He wrote it at the time when he himself was invested with the same prefecture, as is evident from the prologue to those books of the *Variae* and from many letters in Books XI and XII.

## FORMULA OF THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT, OR TITLE OF HIS OFFICE, IN WHICH THE EMPEROR IS INTRODUCED SPEAKING TO THE PREFECT
If the origin of any office is praiseworthy, and if a good beginning can commend what follows, then the praetorian prefecture may boast of such an originator—one who was the wisest of the world and especially acceptable to the Divinity. For when Pharaoh, king of Egypt, was beset by the danger of a coming famine through unheard-of dreams, and no human counsel could reveal so great a vision, Joseph, that blessed man, was found: he both foretold the future truthfully and most wisely came to the aid of the endangered people. He was the first to consecrate the insignia of this dignity; he was the first reverently to ascend the *carpentum* [a ceremonial carriage], raised to this pinnacle of glory so that through wisdom he might confer upon peoples what the power of a ruler had been unable to provide. From that patriarch onward—and even now he is called the Father of the Empire—the herald’s voice continues to resound, instructing the judge not to allow himself to be unlike him. It was fitting that one to whom such authority could be entrusted should always be admonished in the same way.

For certain rights belong to this dignity in common with us: he produces distant persons before the court without limitation by prescription; he imposes heavy fines upon wrongdoers; he distributes the treasury at his own discretion; he grants travel permits with comparable authority; he confiscates ownerless property; he punishes the offenses of provincial judges; by a word he pronounces judgment. What has not been entrusted to one whose very speech is itself a judicial decision? He almost possesses the power to enact laws, since his authority can settle cases without appeal.

When he enters the Palace, he is frequently worshipfully saluted according to our custom; and this office seems to release him from the ordinary practice by which he could accuse others. In authority, therefore, no dignity is his equal. He judges everywhere in the place of the sacred authority. No soldier prescribes to him concerning the jurisdiction of his court, except, I believe, an official of the master of soldiers—so that Antiquity might yield something even to those who seemed to conduct the wars of the Republic. He also scourges the members of the curia, who are called by the laws the “Lesser Senate.”

In his office he retains a singular jurisdiction, and he is known to command persons of such rank and importance that even the judges of the provinces would not dare to disregard them in any respect. His office is plainly gifted, effective, equipped, and exceedingly strong in the firmness of its spirit: those who carry out his commands do so without delaying what has been ordered by any postponement. To men who have completed their military service he grants the rank of tribunes and notaries, and he makes his soldiers their equals; these, mingled among the leading men, attend upon us in our presence.

We gladly fulfill what he establishes, whose authority binds us in such a way that, without hesitation, we do what we recognize him to have decreed. This is not undeserved, since by his provision he sustains the Palace and, while we serve, procures our grain allowances; he also shows consideration even to the judges themselves. He fills the truthful ambassadors of foreign peoples with his instructions. Although other dignities have fixed titles, almost everything that is administered in our empire with balanced moderation is carried out through this one.

Finally, this most beautiful burden of all our cares—which may be prosperous for us and useful to the Republic—we fittingly place upon your shoulders from the [present] indiction onward. May you support it by the strength of your [intellect?] and strive to handle it with the utmost fidelity. The more this dignity is constrained by diverse anxieties, the more it triumphs in the highest praises. Therefore let such a light of glory shine upon your actions that it may gleam both in our Palace and in the farthest reaches of the provinces. Let prudence be equal to your authority, and let the fourfold virtue of a good conscience attend you.

Know that your tribunal has been made so lofty for this reason: once placed there, you should think of nothing low or contemptible. Consider what you ought to say when such persons receive your words. Let the public records contain such things that no one will be ashamed to say he has read them. A remarkable governor has no share in offenses, because unless he continually does something outstanding, he incurs blame even through inactivity. For if that holy originator mentioned above is recalled, it is, in an appropriate sense, a priesthood to exercise the dignity of the praetorian prefecture properly.

Thus far the formula of the dignity.

Before Dexter held this prefecture under Theodosius the Great, Cynegius had held it. He had rendered the Christian Republic the greatest service, was a man worthy of every praise, and was also of Spanish origin, as may be inferred from his burial. Idatius records the following about him in his Consular Fasti:

> In the consulship of Theodosius for the second time and Cynegius, Cynegius, prefect of the East, died at Constantinople during his consulship. He restored all the provinces, deceived by the decay of a long period, to their former condition; he penetrated as far as Egypt and overthrew the images of the Gentiles. Hence, amid the great lamentation of the entire population of the City, his body was escorted to the Apostles—that is, understand the Church of the Twelve Apostles at Constantinople—on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April. A year later his wife Achantia conveyed him overland to Spain.

Consider what predecessors Dexter had in the office of prefect of the East, men who came from his own homeland. But let us return to Dexter’s preface.

“After I returned home,” and so forth. Jerome praises Dexter as not merely illustrious in the world—a statement relating to his birth and prefecture—but also devoted to the faith of Christ. I believe this was said because of his writing of the Chronicle, in which he says that he spent a good part of his life, with the praise and admiration of men, although he was overcome by modesty and reserve [the transmitted reading is uncertain]. He had begun writing it many years earlier, while he was living in the East; but, wearied by public duties, he finally withdrew to his own house at Barcelona, where he completed it, already an old man and worn out by age.

Here I should advise readers that the importance of this Chronicle is commended in the present letter from three perspectives. If we consider its author, he was prefect of the praetorian prefecture of the Eastern Empire and held the second position after Caesar. We should therefore assume of so great a man that he would not have brought anything into the light under his own name unless it were true or highly probable. He cannot be believed to have devoted himself to fables or trifles, or to have wished deliberately to deceive; rather, he must have woven into his work nothing that was not pure, nothing that had not been tested and confirmed from every direction.

If we consider the time when it was composed, it should be judged to have emerged from his hands in an especially pure and refined form, since it was not prepared in one or two years but over at least forty whole years. For if Jerome included Dexter in his Catalogue in the year of Christ 393, when he brought him to completion at his own urging—as we have sufficiently explained in the Apology—it follows that it had been begun several years before 393, so that Jerome had learned of it at least through reports from friends. Since it was carried down to the year of the Lord 430, as is clear from the work itself and as Dexter admits in this letter, it must have been completed after forty years from its beginning.

In any event, the author’s own words make the matter clear when he says: “I turned my whole attention to those studies in which I spent a good part of my life.” He therefore delayed putting the final hand to this little work for so long in order eventually to become more certain about everything and to ensure that nothing immature would emerge from his workshop.

Finally, those to whom the Chronicle was dedicated—Jerome and Orosius—demonstrate that it was of great importance and possessed no ordinary authority. For nothing lacking in such qualities ought to have been dedicated to teachers of such stature, especially since they possessed outstanding judgment and critical discernment in this kind of writing. Jerome himself had written a Chronicle of Universal History, while Orosius, at the urging of Saint Augustine, had published his own *Hormesta* in a nearly chronological manner.

“Universal,” and so forth. He rightly calls it “Universal,” since he combines secular and ecclesiastical history in it. He carefully yet very briefly portrayed the triumphs of the martyrs, the foundations of episcopal sees, the successions of the Roman bishops, synodal assemblies, the succession of emperors, wars, seditions, disturbances, transfers of dominion, and noble or notable men of both social orders, along with countless matters of the same kind. Yet he is fuller and more expansive in explaining Spanish affairs, especially ecclesiastical ones, since he knew these more precisely than the others. Other writers of this kind did the same. Thus Eusebius touched only briefly upon Latin affairs, while he was extensive concerning Greek matters; Marcellinus almost entirely avoided the history of the Western Empire and devoted himself wholly to recording the developments of the Eastern Empire, whose foster son he was; Victor of Tunis followed chiefly African history; Idatius and Viclarensis followed Spanish history. In the end, each writer is drawn somewhat farther by love of his homeland than by interest in other regions. On this matter, consult what we left stated in section 2 of the *Apology*.

“From the foundation of the world,” and so forth. While I was staying at Toledo, I received from men fully worthy of trust the following information: Dexter’s codex, which had been kept for many years in the monastery of Cysla and which the Toledan canon Vergara had happened by chance to purchase from a bookseller, contained both parts of the Chronicle. It extended not merely from the birth of the Lord but from the foundation of the world down to Dexter’s own time. It had formerly belonged to Don Pedro Pecha, bishop of Jaén, and had been intended for the use of Don Lorenzo de Padilla, the imperial historiographer. But that codex was lost, to our own detriment as well.

The Fulda codex, a copy of which we possess, had likewise been stolen from the Fulda library—for it was found not at Fulda but at Worms—and lacked the first part of the Chronicle. Nevertheless, it contained this dedicatory letter, which necessarily ought to have been placed before the entire work. Apparently the copyist was content with a history beginning at the birth of the Lord and attached the displaced letter to it.

Furthermore, Dexter’s statement that he carried his Universal History down to the year of the Lord 430 and the thirteenth consulship of Theodosius the Younger is plainly supported by the truth. For it is established from the Fasti of Onuphrius and from Cardinal Baronius’s *Annals*, volume V, that the aforesaid consulship fell in the year 430 of the Lord, and that Valentinian, the third and also younger man, was his colleague. In that year the general Council of Ephesus was celebrated against Nestorius, and the great Aurelius Augustine exchanged this life for death.

Since Dexter does not mention Augustine’s death, it is reasonable to believe that he completed the Chronicle before 28 August of that same year, on which Saint Augustine died. His continuator, M. Maximus, supplied the deficiency by beginning his own Chronicle with Augustine’s death.

“To the holy presbyter Jerome,” and so forth. This is clear from Jerome’s own testimony in his book *On Illustrious Men*, which was dedicated to Dexter, through whose encouragement it had been produced:

> Dexter, son of Pacianus, whom I mentioned above, illustrious in the world and devoted to the faith of Christ, is said to have composed for me a Universal History, which I have not yet read.

He asserted this on the report of others, for Dexter had begun his work with the intention of dedicating it to Jerome, so that he might satisfy him through a book already dedicated to him. But when he completed the work and sent it to Bethlehem, the holy Doctor had already died in peace.

“To you, a Spanish man of Laletania,” and so forth. Bishop Hugo of Portugal agrees with this in his letter to Mauritius of Braga, which we included among the author’s commendations. Consider it fortunate for us that Dexter dedicated the book to Orosius a second time, for in order to do so he enlarged and enriched it in many places; and in this enlarged and enriched form we have been allowed to enjoy it.

The author spent another decade on this task, as is plainly inferred from what we read at the end: “When I was writing this, the year of Christ 440 was running,” and so forth. These words clearly show that they were written during a revision of the work, when he dedicated it again to Paul Orosius. The reason why he added nothing concerning events in the year 430, to which he had first extended his history, and why the enrichment was made not in the years covered but in the events themselves, has been explained by us in section 2 of the *Apology*.

He calls Orosius “Laletanian” because Tarragona belonged to the ancient region of Laletania, while Orosius was Tarraconensian. We know from the ancient authorities, however, that Laletania and the territory of Tarragona differed somewhat. Pliny, discussing the wines of Spain in Book XIV, chapter 6 of his *Natural History*, says:

> The wines of the Spains are distinguished by the abundance of those from Laletania, but by their excellence those from Tarragona.

More clearly, in Book III, chapter 3, he writes:

> The region of the Cossetani, the river Subi. The colony of Tarragona, the work of the Scipios, just as Carthage was the work of the Phoenicians. The region of the Ilergetes, the town of Subur, and the river Rubricatum, from which the Laletani derive their name.

Martial likewise says in Book I, in an epigram concerning the places of Spain, addressing his friend Lucian as he returned to Spain:

> You will revisit the sunny shores of Tarragona  
> and your own Laletania.

Ptolemy agrees: in the second map of Europe, chapter 6, he places Tarragona among the Cossetani and Barcelona among the Laletani. According to him, whatever land was watered by the river Rubricatum—commonly called the Llobregat—was called Laletania. Hence some also think that the name Catalonia derives from it; among them are Tarapha, Nebrissensis, and Carolus Stephanus.

“To the writer of histories,” and so forth. The history of Paul Orosius, which he dedicated to Saint Augustine, is in everyone’s hands and is universally praised. We shall say more about it with Dexter in its proper place below, where we shall discuss their friendship and kinship, in addition to what has been recorded in the author’s life.]

## DEXTER’S DEDICATORY LETTER

To the holy lord PAUL OROSIUS, presbyter of Tarragona, FLAVIUS L. DEXTER sends greetings.

After I returned home from the East, where, as you know, I was praetorian prefect, I began to grow exceedingly weary of public duties. I turned my whole attention to those studies in which I spent a good part of my life—if not with praise, at least without shame.
