I had dedicated to the holy presbyter Jerome a Universal History, which extended from the foundation of the world to our own times, that is, to the year of Christ 430 and the thirteenth consulship of Theodosius the Younger, though it was not yet sufficiently enriched. Since it could not reach the hands of the deceased Jerome, I now dedicate it, enlarged and enriched in many places, to you, a Spanish man of Laletania, an accomplished writer of histories, and one most devoted to me.

Farewell.

## THE CHRONICLE BEGINS

[Col. 0055] [Note: Col. 0055A]

### A.D. 1 — 1. “In the consulship of Lentulus and Messala,” and so forth

Since Dexter is going to write a Christian chronicle, he rightly begins from what is the starting point of the Christian reckoning of time—namely, from the birth of Christ according to the flesh. He carefully identifies it both by the consuls who presided over the Roman people and by the year elapsed since the foundation of the City. Saint Augustine declared this necessary in Book II, chapter 28 of *On Christian Doctrine*, saying: “Many things are often investigated by the names of the consuls; and ignorance of the consulship in which the Lord was born has compelled some people to err.”

This difficulty has often and powerfully strained the ingenuity of learned men. Some have thought that the Lord was born in the consulship of Augustus for the thirteenth time and Silvanus, as Epiphanius relates in *Panarion*, heresy 51; among more recent writers this view is embraced by Panuinus in Book II of his *Commentary on the Fasti* and by John Mariana in Book IV, chapter 1 of his *History of Spain*.

Others assert that he was born under the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus, a view defended by Severus in Book II of his *History*. Finally, some accept neither of these positions but hold that the Lord’s birth fell during the consulship of Lentulus and Messala. Cassiodorus was previously thought to have been the first to teach this in his *Chronicle*; he was later followed by Marianus Scotus, the distinguished chronicler, and by Cuspinianus in his notes on Cassiodorus. Cardinal Baronius also subscribed to this opinion in the *Apparatus* to his *Ecclesiastical Annals*, both because it appears more consonant with the Gospel of Luke and because the fact that Cassiodorus should be followed recommends it. Cassiodorus was a Roman, highly educated in every branch of letters, and especially versed in these matters, since he wrote not only a work on the consular Fasti but also a treatise on the computation of Easter, with great care and deliberation.

The greater conformity of this opinion with Luke’s Gospel is inferred from the following. According to the evangelist himself, in chapter 3 the Lord Christ came to baptism in the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius, being about thirty years old. That fifteenth year of Tiberius had Rubellius and Rufius as its two consuls. If, beginning from those consuls and that year of the emperor and counting upward through the thirty consulships in the Fasti found in Cassiodorus and Onuphrius, one arrives at the consulship of Cornelius Lentulus and Valerius Messala. It will therefore be certain that Christ’s birth occurred in that year, since exactly thirty consulships—neither more nor fewer—are found between those consuls and these.

We are speaking of the ordinary consuls, who were elected at the beginning of each year, not of the substitute consuls, who were appointed during the year in place of others and governed only for the part of the year that remained.

This may also be deduced from the reckoning of the Olympiads, which was especially important among the Greeks. According to Eusebius, in Book II, chapter 3 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, the fifteenth year of Tiberius was the fourth and final year of the 201st Olympiad. From that point up to and including the second year of the 194th Olympiad, when Lentulus and Messala entered upon the consulship, there are seven complete Olympiads. Since each Olympiad comprises four years, these amount to twenty-eight years. If two further years of the 194th Olympiad are added, they reach the thirty years we are seeking. Consequently, we shall assert that the Lord Christ was baptized at the beginning of the fourth year of the 201st Olympiad and was born at the end of the second year of the 194th Olympiad—namely, in the last month of the year and in its final days, that is, on 25 December, during the consulship of Lentulus and Messala.

The complete clarification of this truth must, however, be derived from the true meaning of the words of the holy Evangelist: “Jesus was beginning, being about thirty years old.” These words may mean either that he had almost completed thirty years, lacking only a little; or that he had merely begun his thirtieth year; or that he had completed thirty years and begun his thirty-first. In the first interpretation, the birth must be assigned to the consulship of Augustus for the thirteenth time and Silvanus; in the second, to the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus; and in the last, to the consulship of Lentulus and Messala. But since we shall examine Luke’s words exactly below, under the year of Christ 31, we refer the reader there so as not to repeat the discussion here. For the present, we affirm that the last interpretation is much more certain than the others.

Dexter’s assertion must therefore be judged remarkable, since he recorded the birth of the Lord Jesus under the consulship of Lentulus and Messala. Cassiodorus, whom Baronius praises and follows, ought rather to be confirmed from Dexter than Dexter from Cassiodorus, since Dexter preceded him by sixty years or more. Cassiodorus flourished in the year of the Lord 500, whereas Dexter wrote in 430. Dexter therefore becomes the first of all whose works survive to bring into the light the assertion that the Lord was born under Messala and Lentulus. He deserves no less praise than Cassiodorus and is supported by no less authority. The fact that he was Roman by upbringing and official service, highly educated in every branch of letters, and spent a good part of his life especially on these matters, should persuade us to follow him as well.

What thanks to God would Cardinal Baronius have given if he had been allowed to enjoy Dexter, who so brilliantly confirms the foundation of his chronology? Do not object that you read in Dexter that the Lord was born “in the consulship of Lentulus and Messalinus.” The cardinal himself admits in the *Apparatus*, under the heading “The Year in Which Christ Was Born,” that both names were used. Cassiodorus calls him Messala, as Dexter does; perhaps, because of his small stature, some began to call him Messalinus.

Twenty-seven years earlier, Messala had been consul with Augustus for the third time, in the year in which the memorable battle of Actium occurred. Whether he was one and the same man as Lentulus’s colleague, I have so far been unable to determine. Let what has been said about the consulship under which the Lord was born suffice.

When Dexter adds, “one year before the consulship of Augustus and Silvanus,” do not understand him to mean that the event occurred a full year before their Fasti. His meaning is that the Lord’s birth did not occur in the same year in which Augustus for the thirteenth time entered the consulship with Silvanus as his colleague, but in the preceding year, marked by the Fasti of Lentulus and Messala—namely, on 25 December, at the end of their consulship.

### A.U.C. 752

Thus far we have discussed under which consuls Christ was born. We must now investigate in what year after the foundation of the City this occurred. On this one point Baronius disagrees with Dexter. Baronius believes that the consulship of the aforementioned Lentulus and Messala fell in the 751st year of the City, whereas Dexter assigns it to the following year, 752.

The reckoning of these years, however, is not so consistent among all authorities that we can derive anything certain from it, since a major dispute still exists even among pagan writers concerning the assignment of the years from the foundation of the City. Ausonius, as Baronius himself notes, differs from Varro by at least twenty years. Baronius therefore wisely warns that Christians cannot safely and certainly count the years from the foundation of the City.

Nevertheless, I am surprised that so learned a man departed on this matter from the reckoning prescribed by the Catholic and Roman Church. For although the Roman Martyrology plainly states on 25 December that Christ was born in the 752nd year from the foundation of the City, Baronius insists that he was born in the preceding year, 751. We shall much more suitably follow Dexter’s opinion, which agrees with the ecclesiastical tables and which Orosius also supports, being of the same antiquity and authority as Dexter.

Certainly, if the matter is weighed precisely, those who assert the opposite will be shown to be laboring under an ambiguity. What is the reason? It is this: the years from the foundation of Rome must not be counted from the beginning of January, but from the month and day on which the City itself was founded—namely, the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, or 21 April, which is the same date. On that day the festival of Pales, goddess of shepherds, was customarily celebrated, as we learn from the most ancient authorities.

Ovid, treating of that festival in Book IV of the *Fasti*, wrote:

> The fitting day is chosen on which to mark the walls with the plow;  
> Pales was present for the sacred rites, and from this the work begins.

Dionysius of Halicarnassus taught the same. Messala Corvinus, in his book *On His Ancestry* addressed to Augustus, says: “They say that Romulus laid the foundations of the City on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May.”

The author of the *Chronology* prefixed to Livy’s history cites Tullius, Plutarch, and Solinus in support of the same opinion. Marlianus likewise asserts it in his book *On the Origin of the City of Rome*, as does Velcurio in his commentary on Book II of Livy:

> The natal day of Rome, on which its foundation began, is held to be the second day before the Kalends of May.

Finally, Propertius says in Book IV:

> It was a festival for the City, the Fathers declared, the Parilia;  
> This was the first day on which it began to possess walls.

It follows that the consulship of Lentulus and Messala included part of the 751st year from the foundation of the City and part of the 752nd. When they entered the consulship on 1 January, the 751st year of the City was running; but on 21 April the 752nd year from the foundation of Rome began. Since the Lord Christ was born not on the Kalends of January, at the beginning of the aforesaid consuls’ term, but at the end of the year—that is, on 25 December, under those same consuls—we must assert that this occurred in the 752nd year of Rome, as Dexter maintains.

Yet this does not depart from Varro’s reckoning, which places the consulship of Lentulus and Messala in the 751st year of the City. That statement must be understood of the beginning of their consulship, not of its end, by which time a new year of the City had already dawned.

It is enough to have made this point once; henceforth it will not be necessary to linger over the reckoning of the years from the foundation of the City. Once it is known that the Lord’s birth fell in the year 752, the corresponding year of the City can easily be assigned to any year of the Lord by adding the years of Rome that preceded the Lord’s birth to the Christian year in question. For example, if one asks which Roman year corresponds to the year of Christ 120, the answer is 871, which is obtained by combining the stated 120 years of the Lord with the 751 Roman years that preceded his birth. The same applies to the remaining years.

[Col. 0058A]

### 2. “With three shepherds,” and so forth

Here Dexter asserts two things: first, that the shepherds to whom the divine child was shown before all others were distinguished by holiness; second, concerning their number, that there were three—neither more nor fewer.

Anyone can readily persuade himself of the former by considering the splendid and singular benefit God bestowed upon them when, above all the people of the entire world, he made them participants in the joys of his birth. They were certainly not ungrateful for this; rather, they returned glorifying and praising God for everything they had heard and seen, just as had been told them. They had been worthy to hear from the angel, radiant with the glory of God:

> I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord.

For when he specifically said that he had been born “for you,” this seems equivalent to the angel’s saying more openly: “He has been born for you before all other mortals,” since you will be the first to see and worship him.

As for their number, Bede expressly agrees with Dexter. In Book 8 of *On the Holy Places* he says:

> To the east, at the Tower of Ader—that is, of the flock—one thousand paces from the city of Bethlehem, stands the Church of the Three Shepherds who were witnesses of the divine birth. It contains their memorials and bears witness both to the number three and to the holiness of the shepherds, in whose honor the church was built.

He confidently asserts both points, since the tradition received from the hands of his ancestors pronounced upon both matters at that place and time. Dexter was undoubtedly aware of this tradition; as one who had been prefect in the East, he writes that the Gospel shepherds were three and holy. It also seemed highly consistent with reason that only three shepherds should be the first among men to worship the Word of the Father made flesh through the agency of the Holy Spirit, so that they might become worshipers of the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity, as we shall likewise see in its proper place in the case of the three Magi.

For the number of the shepherds, see Cardinal Baronius under the year of the Lord 1 and Suárez, volume II, part 3 of the *Summa of Theology*, question 36, disputation 14, section 2.]

A.D. 1. A.U.C. 752. In the consulship of Lentulus and Messala, one year before the consulship of Augustus and Silvanus, Christ is born.

[Col. 0057] A.D. 1. A.U.C. 752. He is first revealed to three shepherds, who were holy.

[Col. 0057] [Note: Col. 0058C]

### A.D. 2 — 1. “Three suns,” and so forth

The ancients saw three suns on many occasions. There were at least five such instances, which Pliny, in Book II, chapter 31 of his *Natural History*, says occurred under the consulships of Spurius Postumius and Quintus Mucius; Quintus Marcius and Marcus Porcius; Marcus Antonius and Publius Dolabella; and Marcus Lepidus and Lucius Plancus. To these he adds a sixth appearance of three suns:

> Our own age also saw one under the emperor Claudius, during his consulship, with Cornelius Orfitus as his colleague.

This last occurrence fell in the year of the Lord 52, when Claudius and Orfitus were consuls. The event witnessed under Lepidus and Plancus inaugurated the Triumvirate, when Caesar joined Marcus Lepidus and Marcus Antonius to establish the Republic. It occurred forty years before the birth of Christ and in the year 712 from the foundation of the City, as Onuphrius proves in Book II of his *Commentary on the Fasti*.

But why discuss this? So that you may understand that Pliny was certainly not referring in that passage to the appearance of the three suns that occurred in Spain shortly after Christ’s birth. Some of the events he lists are much earlier: the event under Plancus and Lepidus was later than those preceding it, yet it occurred forty years before the Lord’s coming; while the event in his own time, under the consulship of Claudius and Orfitus, occurred fifty-two years afterward.

Julius Obsequens nevertheless discusses three suns seen in Spain around the time of the Lord’s Advent in chapter 128 of his *Book of Prodigies*. The Angelic Doctor likewise says, in part 3, question 36, article 3, response to the third argument:

> It is credible that in other parts of the world as well—not only in the East, where the star appeared to the Magi—some signs of Christ’s birth appeared, just as oil flowed at Rome and three suns appeared in Spain, gradually coalescing into one.

Certainly, among the other regions of the world, it was especially fitting that clear portents of the Lord’s birth should appear at Rome and in Spain, since faith in the newborn God was afterward destined to shine most brightly in both places. At Rome, an oil spring had previously appeared: oil suddenly burst forth in a tavern for charitable lodging across the Tiber and is said to have flowed for the space of one day, in the third year of the Triumvirate and thirty-seven years before Christ’s birth, as our Orosius testifies in Book VI, chapter 19, followed by Baronius. The three suns seen in Spain signified God newly born in the flesh, since according to Dexter’s testimony they appeared in the second year after his birth. Dexter deserves credence on this matter, especially because he devoted himself before all others to recording Spanish affairs and because no one contests him in this respect.

I should mention in passing that such a meteorological appearance could have occurred without a special miracle, although we believe that it took place at that time not without a profound mystical significance. The two suns standing beside the one in the middle are nothing other than images of the true sun situated between them; they appear in a cloud as in a mirror. For this reason the Greeks call them *paralleli* [“parallel suns”], that is, “images of the sun.”

The cloud must be clear, thin, regular, uniform, dense, polished, and shining like a mirror. Then the sunlight is strongly refracted in it, and the cloud presents itself to our sight like a perfect and intact mirror, showing not only the color of the light but also the form of the sun itself. Aristotle discussed this in Book III of the *Meteorologica*, and we have treated it with him in our *Physiological Disputations*.

Pliny adds that more than three have never been seen at once, evidently because the true sun has only two sides capable of serving the mirror. As for Dexter’s statement that the three were gathered into one, or Saint Thomas’s that they gradually came together into one, the point is to teach that the two standing beside the true Sun disappeared, while the true Sun itself nevertheless continued.

### 2. “Augustus adopts Tiberius,” and so forth

Cardinal Baronius thinks that Tiberius’s adoption occurred in the sixth year of Christ and is moved by the testimony of Valerius Paterculus. Dexter, however, contends that it occurred in this second year. He has Eusebius in the *Chronicle* in his favor, who writes under the present year of the Lord:

> In the year of the Lord 2, Augustus adopts Tiberius and Agrippa as sons.

Dexter seems to have borrowed these words from him.

Since Tiberius was not the son of Augustus Caesar but his stepson—namely, the son of Augustus’s wife Julia by another husband—and since Germanicus Caesar had the strongest claim to the scepter, Augustus, moved by the improper entreaties of his wife, adopted Tiberius as his son so that he might succeed to the empire upon Germanicus’s failure. It happened, however, that Germanicus Caesar, while administering the prefecture of the East, was deprived of life through Piso’s treachery, and Tiberius succeeded him.

Tiberius and Agrippa, therefore, adopted by Augustus as sons, were brought up in the Palace as his children. Agrippa’s fortune was different: Tiberius kept him confined in prison for many years, which apparently brought Agrippa death. The following clause is textually defective: Tiberius “was publicly reproached by Gaius, his grandson, [concerning] life and kingdom.” After Tiberius’s death, however, Agrippa was not only released from his chains but also elevated to the kingdom of the Jews by that same Gaius, who had already succeeded Tiberius in the empire. Josephus discusses this extensively in Book XVIII of the *Jewish Antiquities*.

### 3. “Judas the Galilean,” and so forth

Eusebius also attests this in his *Chronicle*:

> In the year of the Lord 2, Judas the Galilean urges the Jews to rebel, so that they should not consent to pay tribute to the Romans.

Other authors took the matter from him, such as Vincent of Beauvais in Book VI, chapter 96 of his *Historical Mirror*.

At the Jewish assembly where the Apostles were ordered to give an account, the exceedingly learned and holy Gamaliel, in Luke’s *Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 5, recalled this rebellion of Judas the Galilean. He had spoken of Theudas’s revolt and downfall and then said:

> After him Judas the Galilean arose in the days of the registration, and he drew the people after him; he too perished, and all who consented to him were scattered.

Moved by the census that Augustus demanded from the Jews, Judas stirred the people to rebellion. He preached that it was not lawful for the Israelite nation to pay tribute to anyone, but only to God.

Josephus describes the sequence of events in Book XVIII, chapter 1 of the *Jewish Antiquities*:

> There arose a certain Judas the Gaulanite, born in the town of Gamala, who, having joined to himself the Pharisee Sadoc, incited the peoples to rebellion, repeatedly declaring that the census was nothing other than an open declaration of slavery, and exhorting the entire nation to defend its liberty. The common people received these words eagerly, so that they were inflamed to attempt something; and it can scarcely be said how greatly these men disturbed the whole nation, while they mixed everything with murders and robberies—under the pretext, indeed, of defending public liberty, but in reality from a desire for private profit.

So Josephus writes. Yet he departed from the truth when he claimed that Theudas rebelled after Judas’s revolt. Baronius rightly points this out under the first year of the Lord, since the testimony of Gamaliel in Acts 5 clearly establishes the contrary—except that later, under the year of the Lord 34, Josephus attempted to defend himself after forgetting his earlier account.

Furthermore, concerning the year in which this revolt of Judas occurred, there is considerable dispute. Josephus, in the passage cited and in Book II of *The Jewish War*, chapter 7, asserts that it happened not under Herod’s reign, nor even under that of his son Archelaus, but after the deaths of both, at least nine years after Herod’s death. Yet he is greatly mistaken, since the Evangelist’s account makes it clear that it occurred “in the days of the enrollment.” The most celebrated enrollment at that time was the one conducted under Caesar Augustus and Quirinius, governor of Syria, when everyone went to be registered, each to his own city, so that each might pay his own assessment [Col. 0060C]. Judas seized this as the occasion for revolt.

Pagninus translates the phrase *in diebus professionis* as “in the days of the registration” (*in diebus descriptionis*), namely, that registration by which it came about that, at the command of one man, the whole world was registered. From this Baronius inferred, both in his *Apparatus* and in Volume I of his *Annals*, that Judas revolted in the first year of the Lord, because that registration of the world took place then. Dexter and Eusebius, however, assign the revolt to the second year; and this is more credible, both because of their authority and because Judas would necessarily have spent some time proclaiming the revolt and carrying out the many murders and acts of brigandage that Josephus related above.]

A.C. 2. A.R. 753. Three suns appeared in Spain, gathered together into one.

[Col. 0059] A.C. 2. A.R. 753. Augustus adopts Tiberius and Agrippa as sons.

A.C. 2. A.R. 753. Judas the Galilean urges the Jews to rebel against Rome.

[Col. 0059] [Note: [Col. 0060C]

A.C. 3.—1. Herod, etc. There was indeed an ancient controversy among the Doctors concerning the year of the Bethlehemite massacre of the infants. Some held that it occurred a year and a half after the birth of John, or, which is the same thing, after one year had elapsed from the birth of the Savior. This is the view followed by Nicephorus in Book I of his *History*, chapter 14. Others, however, maintained that it was carried out in the very first year of the Lord’s infancy. Many more recent writers claim to derive this view from Augustine, Chrysostom, and other Fathers, and Baronius and Suárez vigorously defend it.

The principal argument in their favor is that, after the adoration of the Magi, which occurred on the feast day of that same year, Matthew immediately says: “Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the Magi, was exceedingly angry, and sending, he killed all the boys,” etc. If this happened then, it seems to have occurred in that same year.

Dexter departs entirely from all these writers, assigning the slaughter of the Innocents to the third year of Christ. Baronius dares to brand this opinion as fictitious; I, however, am eager to show that it is so far from being a fiction that it either surpasses the others in probability or at least equals the most strongly established view.

Dexter’s assertion is supported by such authority and antiquity that it deserves an honorable place among prudent and judicious men. For, besides Dexter—whose authority alone would suffice to establish even more difficult matters—Epiphanius subscribed to the same opinion in the *Panarion*, Book I, heresy 30, when he teaches that the Magi came to Bethlehem to adore Christ two years after the Savior’s birth. Hippolytus of Thebes taught the same thing earlier in his *Chronicle*, as cited by Canisius in Volume III of *Ancient Readings*, in these words: “From Christ’s birth until the arrival of the Magi, two years elapsed.” Since the savage slaughter of the infants followed the return of the Magi, it follows, according to the view of Epiphanius and Hippolytus, that it occurred in the third year of the Lord.

Eusebius likewise holds this in his *Chronicle*, and Dexter undoubtedly followed him in this as in other matters. He says: “In the third year of Christ, when Herod had learned of Christ’s birth through the information supplied by the Magi, he ordered all the infants in Bethlehem to be killed.”

To these authorities I add the Angelic Doctor, whose opinion, by its own weight alone, can never be shaken. He clearly supports Dexter in *Summa Theologiae* III, question 37, article 6, reply to the third objection. There he observes that, if we follow the common opinion and say that the Magi completed their journey in the thirteen-day period between the Nativity and the Epiphany of the Lord, then we must consequently affirm that Herod slaughtered the children not immediately after the Magi’s departure, but two years later:

“Others say”—these are Saint Thomas’s words—“that the star first appeared when Christ was born, and that the Magi, immediately upon seeing the star, undertook their very long journey and completed it in thirteen days; and according to this, Herod killed the children not immediately after the Magi’s departure, but two years later.”

This also seems to be inferred, not insignificantly, from Matthew’s words, when in chapter 2 he reports that Herod killed all the boys “from two years old and under,” according to the time that he had carefully learned from the Magi. Why did he order the killing of boys two years old rather than those three years old or infants of some other age?

I see Matthew’s answer: Herod did this according to the time that he had learned from the Magi. Yet his statement can be understood in three ways. Either he means that the star appeared two years after Christ’s birth, while the Magi were living in the East, so that one would have to suppose that the child Jesus had already completed two years when the Magi, after adoring him, deceived Herod; or that they did not reach Jerusalem until two years after the star’s appearance; or, finally, that two years had elapsed from their arrival.

The first two interpretations are rightly rejected by everyone as lacking all reason and foundation. Therefore the third must be accepted, and it is the one we intend.

“But,” you say with Jansenius in the *Concordia Evangelica*, “the phrase ‘according to the time’ should not be joined to the expression ‘from two years old,’ so as to indicate that the time learned from the Magi was two years. Rather, it should be joined with the words ‘and under,’ so that the meaning is that the time learned from the Magi was considerably under two years. Thus Herod killed those children who were not more than two years old—not all those who had not yet completed two years, but those who had been born when the star arose in the East for the Magi.”

In this interpretation, the phrase “under the time that he had learned from the Magi” establishes the minimum limit, as the philosophers would say, while “two years old” sets the maximum. Consequently, one must admit that those children who had not yet exceeded twelve or thirteen days—for this was the time assigned by the Magi for the star’s appearance—were by no means killed.

Let the authors of this Commentary judge whether this is not rather a fiction. For, at the very least, it is so novel that it escaped all the Fathers of the Church and the ancient writers. Saint Thomas taught that their opinions could be reduced to only two, neither of which pleased Jansenius.

Indeed, even if other support for the common opinion were lacking, this consideration would suffice for devout people: according to the view we are attacking, many of the Bethlehemite children who had been born at the time of the massacre are said to have been deprived of the crown of martyrdom—namely, those who had not yet completed twelve days when the Magi arrived in Jerusalem, since they fell outside the minimum limit. Yet no one has ever thought that any of those children was spared because of his extreme youth.

On the contrary, this is denied not only by Catholic Doctors but even by pagans. For Macrobius, remembering the same massacre in Book II of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 4, explicitly states that all those under two years old were killed. Here are his words:

“When Augustus heard that among those whom Herod, king of the Jews, had ordered to be killed in Syria while they were under two years old, his own son had also been killed, he said, ‘It is better to be Herod’s pig than his son.’”

He was incidentally noting the Jewish abstention from pork and the superstitious cruelty of the man who murdered his own son. Yet when he says that they were killed “under two years old,” he excludes none of those who had not completed two years.

I shall ask the opponents again: if, according to their opinion, Christ was at most two or three months old at the time of the slaughter of the Innocents, why did Herod rage against children of two years? If they answer that he did this lest Christ be older than the Magi had said, they will then have to explain why he did not also order the newborn infants to be killed, even though they had not reached those two months of the Lord’s age. For he could likewise have feared that Christ had not yet been born when the Magi met him to adore the Lord.

Certainly, if he had been driven by fear, he ought rather to have fixed upon the period closest to that indicated by the Magi. It is clear, however, that newborn infants are less distant from the age of two months—which Christ is said to have reached at that time—than are those who had already approached two years.

It will therefore be better to affirm with Dexter that Herod killed the boys under two years old because this was the period that he had learned from the Magi, calculated from the rising of the star and the Lord’s birth. We shall demonstrate this without difficulty from another consideration, beginning with the feast of those same Innocent Martyrs, namely, 28 December.

There is no reason to suppose that the Church would celebrate their memory on any day other than that on which they suffered for Christ the Lord. Indeed, from the feast itself, almost as from an ecclesiastical tradition, we learn that the holy children were crowned with martyrdom on that day, as the author of the *Treasury of Preachers* asserts.

Once this is granted, we must first admit that their savage slaughter occurred at least one year and four days after the Lord’s birth. It could not have happened in that same year, after only four days had elapsed, since it followed the arrival of the Magi and even the Purification of the Virgin.

It also follows that when Matthew says, “Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the Magi, was exceedingly angry,” etc., the adverb “then” does not establish an immediate succession in time. Herod did not kill the children immediately after the Magi’s departure, as the day of their martyrdom proves. Rather, it indicates the continuation of the history and means the same as “afterward.”

Once this has been granted, there is nothing in the whole Gospel that compels us to assert that only one year intervened between Christ’s birth and the massacre of the infants, rather than two years and four days of the third year. Nor is there any reason not to retain the Evangelist’s words in their full force: namely, that the boys from two years old and under were killed because that much time had elapsed since the rising of the star, the time that Herod had learned from the Magi.

“But why,” you may ask, “did Herod refrain from killing the infants for so long?”

First, because he was not immediately informed of the Magi’s return or of the fact that they had deceived him, since they returned secretly rather than openly. Thus several months necessarily passed before Herod, at last overcome by weariness and despair, judged that he had been deceived and sent people to seek out the Magi and the child.

Here I am strongly attracted by an explanation that now occurs to me. When the angel warned Joseph in a dream to take the child and his mother into Egypt, he gave this as the reason for their departure: “For it will happen that Herod will seek the child in order to destroy him.”

Herod therefore sought the child first, to see whether he might seize and destroy him, before sending to kill all the children who were in Bethlehem and throughout its territory. Much deliberation was required before he could be led to such a massacre.

It is not believable that he resolved upon so cruel and general a slaughter without first sending once and again to search for the birth of the new King and to destroy him. Thus, when he was finally frustrated in his hope, found that there were many children there, and had equal reason to doubt in the case of all of them, since he could suspect none more than the others, he despaired of accomplishing his purpose in any other way and resolved to kill all the boys under two years old—not only in Bethlehem but also throughout its territory. Still unsatisfied, he killed his own son, who was also two years old.

Accordingly, it is not surprising if a considerable part of the time was consumed in the various searches for the child that preceded his decree of slaughter, especially since he could easily suppose that during the whole period of the child’s infancy no danger of rebellion threatened. The child had neither sufficient strength nor resources, and no multitude of confederates stood ready to support him. But when two years had elapsed, lest the matter be prolonged any further, he resolved to put the child to death.

I omit mentioning how many and how great occupations could have burdened the kingly office, and for many other days either entirely diverted him from that purpose or delayed him. These are Augustine’s words in Book II of *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 11.

Others add that Herod went to Rome during this interval. Josephus, however, contradicts them in Book XVI of the *Jewish Antiquities*, chapters 7, 8, and 9. Baronius contends that Josephus asserts Herod went to Rome only twice: once to accuse his sons before Caesar, in the 192nd Olympiad, which preceded Christ’s birth, and again much later.

Nevertheless, Saint Thomas, in the passage cited above, question 36, approves what many say: that Herod went to Rome during this period after being accused. Those who deny this rely only on a calculation of the years of Herod’s reign. They claim that such a journey cannot be reconciled with the first two years of the Lord. Yet Baronius himself judges in the *Apparatus of the Annals* that this calculation, as Josephus presents it, is fictitious; therefore it cannot harm our position.

We can also draw an argument from what the Church sings concerning Saint John’s going into the desert in his tender years, in the hymn:

“Desert caves, while still in tender years,

You sought, fleeing the throngs of citizens.”

Bernard said in his sermon *On His Privileges*: “Within the tenderness of his years, this blessed child was led into the wilderness.” The Evangelist Luke also sufficiently indicates this in chapter 1, when he says: “But the child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel.” Here he first says that he grew, and afterward that he was led into the wilderness.

From all this it clearly seems to follow that he was not taken into the wilderness immediately after he was born, but in his tender years, or “within the tenderness of his years”—which signifies at least his third year of life.

Saint Peter of Alexandria teaches in canon 3 of his rules, received by the Sixth Synod, that John the Baptist was taken into the wilderness by his parents so that he might be removed from Herod’s slaughter, which threatened him, if not on account of the Bethlehemite designation, at least because of the fame surrounding his conception and birth.

If John was in his third year at the time of the slaughter of the Innocents, it remains that Christ had completed two years and begun his third. Dexter therefore rightly notes that the massacre of the infants occurred in the third year of the Lord, since Christ had completed his second year and had begun his third by four days.]

A.C. 3. A.R. 754. Herod kills all the boys in the Bethlehemite region.

[Col. 0063] [Note: [Col. 0064A]

A.C. 6.—1. Herod, etc. Whoever carefully considers the bitterness of the sufferings and the multitude of illnesses and afflictions under which Herod died will be unable to deny that he paid God the penalty for his violated piety.

Josephus, in Book XVII of the *Jewish Antiquities*, chapter 8, counts ten illnesses: “The king’s disease became more severe, as the deity exacted punishment for his impiety.

“First, he was consumed by a slow fever, which was detected less by external touch than by the way it ravaged his internal organs.

“Second, he suffered from an intense voracity, requiring food to be supplied continually.

“Third, he was also afflicted by ulceration of the intestines;

“fourth, by colic pains;

“fifth, his feet swelled with a moist and transparent phlegm;

“sixth, so likewise did his groin;

“seventh, his private parts themselves putrefied and swarmed with worms;

“eighth, this was accompanied by a foul and no less troublesome priapism, not without the most grievous stench;

“ninth, on top of all this he suffered from contraction of the nerves;

“tenth, and from difficulty in breathing.”

Eusebius explains for what impiety he was paying the penalty in Book I of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 8, saying: “It is worthwhile to understand what recompense followed the cruel crime committed by Herod against Christ and the children of his age whom he killed, and in what manner Divine vengeance immediately afterward, without even the slightest delay, tormented him while he was still alive,” etc.

Herod therefore paid the penalty for his cruel massacre of the infants. Yet the authors do not agree in what year of Christ this occurred. Cardinal Baronius, following Josephus’s calculation of the years of Herod’s reign, thinks that it happened in the eighth year of the Lord, for that was the thirty-seventh year of Herod’s reign. But this is not very secure, since, as Baronius himself testifies in the *Apparatus*, that calculation is fictitious.

Indeed, since Eusebius—whose opinion Baronius embraces here—says that immediately after the slaughter of the infants, “without even the slightest delay,” Divine vengeance tormented Herod, his death could by no means be postponed until the eighth year of the Lord, especially according to Baronius’s view that the infants were killed in Christ’s first year.

I prefer to follow Eusebius, whom Dexter undoubtedly followed. For Eusebius says in his *Chronicle*: “In the sixth year of the Lord, Herod, struck down by disease and with worms swarming throughout his body, dies miserably and deservedly.” Dexter rightly omitted the phrase “with worms swarming throughout his body,” since Josephus, who records all Herod’s illnesses as we have seen, says only that his private parts were gnawed by worms.

2. Asinius Pollio, etc. This was the distinguished orator whose praises Seneca and Quintilian have lavishly celebrated. “In Asinius Pollio,” says the latter, “I find very great diligence, so great that it seems excessive to some; and sufficient judgment and spirit.” He was a friend of Augustus, taught at Rome in the time of Pompey the Great, and succeeded Thymagenes in the school. He wrote on the war of Caesar and Pompey, and was the first of all to give public readings of his writings at Rome.

Pliny, in Book XXXV, chapter 2, testifies of him that, by dedicating the first library at Rome, he made men’s talents a public possession through a new invention. But what sort of invention does he call new? “For,” he says, “not only are those whose immortal souls speak in those very places dedicated in libraries in gold, silver, or at least bronze; indeed, even things that do not exist are fashioned, and they give rise to desires for faces not handed down, as happened in Homer.”

According to Cassiodorus, Asinius’s consulship fell in the 747th year of the City, six years before Christ’s birth, and he had Gaius Martius as colleague. But because in his time Cicero had flourished as a new river of eloquence, while Asinius was so far removed from Cicero’s polish and charm that he might have seemed of an earlier age, his son Asinius Gallus, himself a man of consular rank, wrote a book comparing his father with Cicero, in which he preferred Pollio to Cicero. Against him Claudius Caesar published a defence of Cicero, as Suetonius relates in his *Claudius*; Caelius Rhodiginus also treats of it in his *Ancient Readings*.

Eusebius has this concerning Asinius in his *Chronicle*: “In the sixth year of the Lord, Asinius Pollio, orator and former consul, who had triumphed over the Dalmatians, dies in the eightieth year of his age at his Tusculan estate.” What he says about Pollio’s triumph over the Dalmatians does not conflict with Tiberius’s triumph, of which we must speak immediately. Asinius had celebrated a triumph over them long before, but Tiberius subdued their rebellion and subjected them again.]

A.C. 6. A.R. 757. Herod, struck down by disease and with worms swarming, perishes.

A.C. 6. A.R. 757. Asinius Pollio, a former consul and orator, dies at more than eighty years of age.

[Col. 0065] [Note: [Col. 0665B]

A.C. 9. Tiberius, etc. Eusebius uses almost the same words in his *Chronicle*: “In the ninth year of the Lord, Tiberius Caesar brings the Dalmatians and Sarmatians under Roman authority.”

The Dalmatians were among the last peoples whom Octavian Augustus subjected to the Roman Empire. Although they were brought into the provinces under the auspices of Augustus, the work was accomplished under the command of Tiberius Caesar, who had already been declared his successor. Plutarch, Suetonius, Dio, Florus, and the other Roman historians discuss this matter.

Dalmatia is a part of Illyricum, from which the great Jerome came; he was born in the town of Stridon. Pliny discusses it in Book IV, chapter 25. It is now under Venetian rule, and formerly, under Nero Caesar, it abounded in gold, so that one of its streams alone yielded fifty pounds each day, according to Pliny himself in Book XXXIII, chapter 4.

The region of the Sarmatians extended very widely, from the very borders of Germany and the river Vistula all the way to Hyrcania. It is now called Croatia. It was inhabited by extremely savage peoples, some of whom lived in the mountains and forests, while others used dwellings in the marshes.

Pliny writes in Book XXII, chapter 1, that, for the sake of appearance and as part of an established custom, they used to paint their bodies with the juices of certain herbs—a practice that in our own age was also customary among the peoples of America. He also says that they were generally nourished on a porridge made from raw millet flour mixed with horse’s milk or blood. Consult Strabo and Ptolemy concerning them.]

A.C. 9. A.R. 760. Tiberius Caesar subjects the Dalmatians and Sarmatians to the Romans.

[Col. 0065] [Note: [Col. 0065C]

A.C. 12. Christ, etc. No Christian may rightly doubt this point, since Saint Luke expressly asserts it in chapter 2: “When Jesus was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem,” etc. “And it came to pass that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers.”

Accordingly, an evident error has entered the annotation of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, since the eleventh year of the Lord is placed in the margin, although it is certain by the faith that this disputation occurred in his twelfth year.

I would mention in passing that the custom of depicting the Lord Christ at twelve years of age seated upon a teacher’s chair arose from popular devotion. At that time he did not present himself as a Teacher but as a Disputant. Dexter rightly observes that he does not say that Christ taught the Pharisees, but that he disputed in their midst.

The Evangelist says: “Listening to them and asking them questions,” and, during the discussion, giving answers at which they were astonished: “And all who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers.”

Thus he first approached by testing and questioning, which is the role of one who disputes. Then, when the teachers questioned him about difficult testimonies from the Law and the Prophets, he gave such marvelous answers while standing among them that he threw his listeners into amazement.

Hence Saint Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx and a disciple of Saint Bernard, said in his homily on this same history, which is included among Bernard’s works: “It is therefore fitting that after three days he is found in the temple in the midst of the teachers, first listening and asking questions, and then revealing the most sacred mysteries.”

This was given as a model of humility and reverence for boys and young men, so that among their elders they may be silent and listen, ask questions, and learn.]

A.C. 12. A.R. 763. The boy Christ disputes in the midst of the teachers.

[Col. 0065] [Note: [Col. 0066A]

YEAR 14. Augustus, etc. Thus Eusebius in his *Chronicle*: “In the fourteenth year of the Lord, Augustus, conducting a census at Rome with his son Tiberius, found 9,370,000 people.”

It was customary among the Romans to conduct a census every lustrum. Indeed, according to Varro, the word *lustrum* derives from *luere*, “to pay,” and denoted a period of five years, because every fifth year the taxes assigned by the censors were paid and tribute was collected from the citizens.

Pliny, in Book II, chapter 47, says that the beginning of the lustrum was the rising of the Dog Star in whatever intercalary year it occurred. Thus the lustrum did not complete five years; rather, the census was conducted at the beginning of every fifth year.

Accordingly, this census of which Dexter and Eusebius are now speaking was not the ordinary one conducted every fifth year for the collection of taxes, but a special and new census. For from the first year of Christ, when it is established that a census was conducted by Augustus under Quirinius, governor of Syria, three lustra—or three and a half intercalary years—had elapsed by this fourteenth year. Thus a census ought to have been conducted at the beginning of years 5, 9, and 13.

This census, therefore, falls outside the number of the others and is consequently worthy of special consideration—especially because it is said to have been conducted specifically at Rome, not throughout the whole world, and because there were found there as many human beings as Eusebius reports: 33,300,000, that is, thirty-three myriads and three hundred thousand people. This exceeds almost all credibility. Dexter wisely refrained from giving the number.]

A.C. 14. A.R. 765. Augustus conducts this census in the present year with his son Tiberius.

[Col. 0065] [Note: [Col. 0066C]

A.C. 15.—1. The eclipse, etc. Besides Dexter, Eusebius states in his *Chronicle* that both events occurred in this year, including the fact that Augustus died in the seventy-sixth year of his life. He died at Atella, now Nola, in Campania, and was then transferred from there to the Campus Martius of the city.

Some say that, when he was spending his final day, he boasted that he was leaving a marble city where he had found one of brick. For an account of Augustus’s deeds, one should consult Suetonius, Tacitus, Plutarch, Dio, and the other Roman historians.

2. Tiberius, etc. The printed Codex of Dexter, published at Zaragoza, corruptly read: “Tiberius Julius, son of the divine Augustus, our Lord Caesar Augustus Germanicus, and brother, third emperor.” It must plainly be read: “brother of Germanicus, third emperor.”

Onuphrius has in his *Fasti*: “Tiberius Julius, son of the divine Augustus, of the divine N. Caesar Augustus Germanicus, third emperor of the Roman people.” But he should explain what he means by the genitive expression “of the divine N. Caesar.” As for whether one should read “Germanicus” or “brother of Germanicus,” Dexter’s reading pleases me, since I do not see how he could have been called Germanicus unless perhaps in memory of the deceased Caesar.]

A.C. 15. A.R. 766. An eclipse of the sun. Augustus also dies at the age of seventy-six.

A.C. 15. A.R. 766. Tiberius Julius, son of the divine Augustus, our Lord Caesar Augustus, brother of Germanicus, third emperor.

[Col. 0067] [Note: [Col. 0067A]

A.C. 19.—Titus Livy, etc. This year became memorable through the deaths of two princes of belles-lettres. One of them celebrated Roman history in flowing and elegant prose; the other filled the world with golden verses sparkling with jewels of thought. Eusebius recorded the deaths of both in this very year, using almost precisely Dexter’s words, except that he names Tomi in Pontus as the place of Ovid’s death.]

A.C. 19. A.R. 770. Titus Livy, an outstanding historian, dies at Padua.

A.C. 19. A.R. 770. In the same year Ovid dies in exile in Pontus.

[Col. 0067] [Note: [Col. 0067A]

A.C. 23.—The theater, etc. Eusebius’s *Chronicle* also records this event. Pompey’s theater was a notable structure erected in the form of a semicircle and furnished with many tiers, from which the entire populace could watch the games from an elevated position.

The senators sat at the lowest tiers, in front of everyone else. The Roscian law had decreed that no one except men of the equestrian order might sit in the first fourteen tiers. The remaining common people filled the higher seats, among them the *decoctores*, that is, men who had squandered their patrimony, whether through fault or by accident.

Beneath the amphitheater was a cavea capable of holding forty thousand people. To adorn it, Pompey placed marvelous statues, most carefully fashioned by the skill of great artists. Among these, according to Pliny in Book VII, chapter 3, was the statue of Eutychis, who was carried from Tralles to the funeral pyre after bearing thirty children from twenty pregnancies.

In this year of the Lord 23, the theater was seized and devastated by fire, to the great grief of the Romans.

There was another theater, built by Marcus Scaurus. Its stage had three levels and rose to a height of 360 columns: for each stage, the lowest part was of marble and the middle part of glass, an unprecedented form of luxury even afterward. Between the columns stood three thousand bronze statues. The cavea could hold forty thousand people. It was the greatest work ever made by human hands—not merely as a temporary construction but with the intention of lasting forever. These are Pliny’s words.]

A.C. 23. A.R. 774. Pompey’s theater is seized and destroyed by fire.

[Col. 0067] [Note: [Col. 0067B]

A.C. 24.—Drusus, etc. This too is taken word for word from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius and Jerome.

Furthermore, in the preceding year Tiberius, his father, had made Drusus his associate in the government, after Drusus had held the consulship twice: once with Gaius Norbanus Flaccus as colleague, in the sixteenth year from Christ’s birth, and again six years later, namely in the twenty-second year of the Lord, with Tiberius himself as his colleague.

Ancient inscriptions give his name as follows:

DRUSUS JULIUS TI. AUG. F. DIVI. AUG. NEPOS. CAESAR.

A short time earlier Livia Augusta had given birth to another Drusus, whose death Ovid commemorated by sending a consolatory poem to his mother Livia.]

A.C. 24. A.R. 775. Drusus Caesar dies by poison.

[Col. 0067] [Note: [Col. 0067C]

A.C. 28.—Pontius Pilate, etc. Eusebius likewise says this in his *Chronicle*, as does Onuphrius in his *Fasti*, drawing on Josephus, who left it recorded in Book XVIII of the *Jewish Antiquities*, chapter 5, that in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar Pontius Pilate was sent to Judea to serve as procurator and governor, succeeding Valerius Gratus, who had spent eleven years in that office.

The twelfth year of Tiberius coincided with the twenty-eighth year of Christ, since Augustus died in his seventeenth year, and Tiberius succeeded him.

Dadraeus noted in the margin of Eusebius that Eusebius contradicted himself, since in his *Ecclesiastical History* he writes that Pilate was sent to Judea in the twelfth year of Tiberius, whereas in his *Chronicle* he assigns it to the thirteenth year.

Yet the two statements can easily be reconciled. Augustus did not die at the beginning of the seventeenth year of the Lord, from which point twelve years would intervene before the twenty-eighth; he died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September in the sixteenth year of the Lord. If one counts from that date, one finds thirteen years.

Thus the twenty-eighth year of Christ, with which we are presently concerned, coincided partly with Tiberius’s twelfth year and partly with his thirteenth. In which portion of that year Pilate was sent to Judea is not clear.

Dexter’s opinion is embraced not only by Eusebius in former times but also now by Cardinal Baronius. From this, reader, you may observe how much authority our author’s opinions possess, since he everywhere arrives at the more probable conclusion.]

A.C. 28. A.R. 779. Pontius Pilate, procurator of Judea, is sent by Tiberius into Judea.

[Col. 0067] [Note: [Col. 0068A]

A.C. 31.—He preaches to the peoples. A great controversy once arose among the Fathers concerning the year in which Christ’s preaching began, and recent interpreters of Sacred Scripture have not yet brought it to an end.

The source of the entire uncertainty was the passage in Luke 3: “And Jesus himself was beginning as if he were about thirty years old.” Since these words admit of three meanings, they have likewise produced three ways of understanding them.

The Evangelist may mean that, at the time when Christ hastened to John’s baptism, he had completed his twenty-ninth year and entered his thirtieth. The meaning would then be: “He was about thirty years old”—not that he had already completed thirty, but rather that he was beginning it.

Or he may mean that at that time Christ had nearly completed thirty years, so that the meaning of the words would be: “He was about thirty years old”—that is, he was approximately that age, not exactly thirty, but almost, because he was already beginning to complete the number.

Or, finally, he may mean that Christ had already completed thirty years and begun his thirty-first. In this interpretation the particle “about” (*quasi*) is not diminutive but affirmative, in the sense in which it must again be understood in John, when he speaks of the glory of the Divine Word: “as of the only-begotten from the Father”; that is, he possessed the glory proper and worthy to the only-begotten Son of the eternal Father.

So here also: “He was beginning as if he were thirty years old” would mean: he was then a man of mature age, as one who was thirty years old. In this way the word “beginning” does not determine the year of his age but the commencement of his new preaching office. The meaning would be: he was beginning to exercise his office while he was thirty years of age.

Neither of the first two interpretations lacks distinguished authorities. The first was embraced by Origen in Homily 1 on Ezekiel, by Saint Jerome on the same passage, by Tertullian *Against the Jews*, by Eusebius in Book I of his *History*, chapter 10, and by Lactantius in Book IV of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 10. The second was followed by Saint Epiphanius in the *Panarion*, heresy 51, and adopted by Cornelius Jansenius.

The third was taught by Chrysostom in Homily 10 on Matthew, chapter 3, by Bede in *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 45, and by the Greek Doctors generally. Among other ecclesiastical canons, they also established the rule, as Saint Martin of Braga reports in *On the Greek Canons*, chapter 20, that no one should be admitted to the priesthood before completing thirty years, because Christ the Lord was baptized at that age and began to teach.

Now observe again, candid reader, the skill of our Dexter, by which, in so ambiguous a matter, he chose the safer and truer path. “In the thirty-first year of his age,” he says, “Christ our Lord preaches to the peoples of the Jews.”

He therefore teaches the third opinion, supported and established by the stronger foundations. What are they, you ask? Stronger reasoning, greater antiquity, and—what is the chief point of all—ecclesiastical tradition.

I shall explain each in turn. It is a constant truth in the Church’s liturgical offices that Christ was initiated through baptism on 6 January, since on that day we sing: “Today the Church has been joined to the heavenly Bridegroom, because Christ washed her sins in the Jordan.” And in the hymn:

“Or by the mystical baptism,

The waters of the Jordan,

Once turned backward on the third—”

You are consecrated on this holy day. [Col. 0069A] On this point all the Fathers agree (with the sole exception of Epiphanius): Gregory of Nazianzus, Cyril, Chrysostom, Jerome, Augustine, Maximus, and Bernard, in their sermons on the Epiphany. Add to these Eucherius of Lyon, Isidore, *On the Offices of the Church*, chapter 26, Paulinus, and Eusebius, cited by Baronius under the thirty-first year of Christ.

From this, at the very least, the falsity of the second opinion follows: namely, the assertion that, when Christ was baptized by John, He had nearly completed thirty years—or, as Epiphanius says, had completed twenty-nine years and almost ten months. This position therefore cannot stand, for He completed His twenty-ninth year on the twenty-fifth of December, the day on which He was born; from that date until the sixth of January, when His baptism subsequently took place, only thirteen days intervene. Thus, when He was baptized, the Lord would have been merely twenty-nine years and thirteen days old.

Accordingly, the words “He was beginning to be about thirty years old” cannot mean “He was beginning to complete thirty.” For the completion of a year does not begin in the first days of the year, but only after at least six months have passed.

I am not unaware that Epiphanius said Christ was not baptized on this day, but on the sixth day before the Ides of November. Yet in this matter he must not be followed as the sole authority, any more than in what he says in the same place: that Christ was born on the sixth of January. In both points he departs from the Church’s common understanding. Christ therefore could not, at the time of His baptism, have been nearly completing His thirtieth year. One of two alternatives is necessary: either He had merely entered His thirtieth year thirteen days earlier, as the earlier Fathers held; or, as the later Fathers and Dexter maintain, He had completed thirty years and had begun His thirty-first year thirteen days before.

Antiquity, however, militates against the earlier opinion. For who was more ancient than Saint Ignatius, who saw the surviving mother of the Lord Christ, as we shall show under the forty-third year? Yet when he writes to the Trallians, he expressly acknowledges that the Lord had completed thirty years before His baptism. Here are his words, faithfully translated from the Greek: “After completing three decades of years, He was truly baptized by John.” “After completing,” he says, “three decades”: therefore He had already begun His thirty-first year.

Blessed Father Bernard speaks in the same way in Sermon 1 on the Epiphany: “When Christ,” he says, “had spent thirty years of time in the flesh, He came amid the crowds of His fellow countrymen to John’s baptism.”

Finally, concerning tradition, Bede writes the following about the Roman Church’s understanding in *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 45:

“The faith of the Church holds, if I am not mistaken, that the Lord lived in the flesh a little more than thirty-three years, until the time of His Passion. Indeed, the holy Roman and Apostolic Church testifies that it holds this faith by the very brief inscriptions customarily written annually on its Paschal candles.”

To this may be added what we read in its very ancient ritual book—where it is certain that it preserves what it received from the Apostles—under the heading “The Epiphany of the Lord”: “For, after completing the course of thirty years, Christ came to the Jordan to be baptized by John.” “After completing,” it says, not “after beginning.”

Nor should you object that the word “almost” has been added, since it is evident from this wording that the number is in no way diminished by the preceding expression, “after completing.” For how could He not yet have been thirty if He had already completed thirty? The word “almost” must therefore be taken affirmatively, as Baronius learnedly observed in his *Apparatus*. In that passage, and again below under the thirty-first year of Christ, he most vigorously embraces Dexter’s opinion and defends it against its opponents.

A.C. 31. A.R. 782. The Lord Christ preaches to the Jewish peoples.

[Col. 0069] [Note: [Col. 0069D]

A.C. 34.—1. Christ the Savior, etc. That the Savior’s trial and death under the governor Pontius Pilate occurred in the thirty-fourth year of His age, and not the thirty-third, necessarily follows from what has just been said. For if—as was amply proved there—the Lord Christ came to baptism when He was beginning His thirty-first year, it follows that He underwent death on the cross for us after beginning His thirty-fourth year, since four Paschal festivals intervened between His baptism and His saving death.

This is plainly evident from the Gospels and may be demonstrated as follows. Matthew, chapter 4, testifies that immediately after His baptism He withdrew into the wilderness for the fast of forty days. After stating that the dove descended upon the newly baptized Jesus and that the Father’s voice was heard, he adds: “Then Jesus was led into the wilderness.”

After overcoming the cunning enemy and defeating him three times, He went up to Jerusalem to celebrate Passover, as John, the beloved Apostle, teaches in chapter 2. There, having made something like a whip of cords, He drove the buyers and sellers from the Temple:

“And the Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem, and found in the Temple those who were selling oxen and sheep and doves, and the money-changers sitting; and when He had made something like a whip of cords, He drove them all out of the Temple.”

This was the first Passover, namely, in the thirty-first year.

At the second, He restored to health the sick man of thirty-eight years who lay at the Pool of Bethesda. John speaks of him in chapter 5:

“After these things there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is at Jerusalem a pool called Bethesda,” etc.

That this feast was Passover, and not Pentecost or the Feast of Tabernacles, is sufficiently clear from John’s own context. Saint Irenaeus teaches the same in book 2, chapter 10:

“After these things He went up again, the second time, to Jerusalem for the feast of Passover, when He healed the paralytic who had lain beside the pool for thirty-eight years.”

This Passover therefore fell in the Lord’s thirty-second year.

As the third Passover, that is, the Passover of Christ’s thirty-third year, approached, He fed five thousand men with only five barley loaves and two fish. At this point John notes that “the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near.”

Since, in addition to these three Passovers, it is certain from the divine Gospels that the Lord Christ suffered death on the Passover of another year, it necessarily follows that His death occurred at Passover in His thirty-fourth year, exactly as Dexter ingeniously asserts.

In this respect Baronius agrees with Dexter’s opinion. There is no doubt that Baronius would have valued Dexter’s *Universal History* highly if he had been able to obtain it and establish his own position by its authority. See, I ask you, how excellent a reckoner of Christ’s years Dexter was: everywhere he chose what is more probable and more consistent with historical reasoning, and what Baronius boasts of attaining through laborious effort and study, Dexter presented briefly and clearly.

2. Claudia Procula, the wife of Pilate, etc. That Pilate’s wife sent a message to her husband while he was seated on the tribunal, urging him to refrain from Christ’s execution and to decide nothing to His harm because many things had happened to her in a vision that night on His account, is recorded in Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 27:

“While he was sitting on the tribunal,” Matthew says, “his wife sent to him, saying: ‘Have nothing to do with that just man; for I have suffered many things today in a vision because of him.’”

That Pilate took his wife with him to Syria when he was made governor of that province is known not only from the Gospel but also from pagan writings. For although five years earlier—as Cornelius Tacitus writes in book 3 of the *Annals*, under the fourth consulship of Tiberius Caesar, which fell in the twenty-second year of Christ, as is clear from Onuphrius’s *Fasti*—Severus Caecina had proposed in a very weighty speech that wives should not accompany husbands departing for the provinces, the proposed law was nevertheless evaded through the intervention of Valerius Messalla, who demonstrated that it was more advantageous in every respect if wives followed their husbands. This was therefore ordered.

But how can what Dexter reports about Pilate’s wife stand—namely, that she was warned in a dream, believed in Christ, and obtained salvation? How was she warned in a dream when she admits that she suffered in a vision: “For I have suffered many things today in a vision”? And if she was terrified in a vision by a demon, how does it follow that she believed in Christ? What salvation did she obtain? That of the soul, or of the body?

As for the vision, we need not trouble ourselves over whether it should be said that she suffered “in a vision” or “in a dream.” It is certain that the event occurred at night, since she sent word about it in the morning to her husband, who was seated on the tribunal to judge Christ. Hence, where the Vulgate edition reads in the Gospel, “Today in a vision,” Saint Pagninus translates, “Today in a dream.” The word “today” therefore means “this night,” since dreams more frequently occur at that time.

Furthermore, many—I admit—have believed that she was terrified that night by the Lord’s saving death through the prior action of an evil demon. Having been led to regret what he had done, the demon feared that Christ’s death might perhaps become the cause of greater evils for him than His life itself. Among others, Rabanus Maurus taught this:

“The Devil, understanding that he would lose his spoils through Christ, wishes to free them through a woman.”

Baronius cites Saint Ignatius in support of this opinion, in his letter to Polycarp; yet I have been unable to find anything on this subject either in that letter or in any other of Ignatius’s writings.

However, eminent Fathers distinguished in holiness and doctrine judged that Pilate’s wife had not suffered that night through the deception of an evil demon, but through a vision and consolation granted by a merciful God, by which she was warned of her salvation and of the divinity of Jesus Christ.

Thus Chrysostom says:

“It is not Pilate who sees the dream, but his wife, because she was more worthy—or perhaps because he would not have spoken.”

As if he were saying: His wife was more worthy of divine illumination, and therefore Pilate did not receive it, but his wife did. God wished to confirm His innocence by that testimony. If He had warned Pilate about it in a dream, Pilate would not have wished to make the vision public; but through his wife it came about that, in the sight of the entire people, while her husband sat upon the tribunal, testimony to the Lord’s innocence was given. Therefore Chrysostom adds:

“For this reason God arranged that what the woman saw should be made manifest to all.”

Hilary likewise says in Canon 33:

“The vision in her signifies the Gentile people, which, already believing, calls the unbelieving people to faith in Christ, with whom it associated. Because she suffered much for Christ, she invites him to the same glory of future hope.”

Ambrose says similarly in book 10 on Luke, chapter 23:

“His wife warned him—but by whom was she moved? Grace shone in the night; divinity was manifest, yet he did not thereby restrain himself from the sacrilegious sentence.”

Augustine does not disagree, as cited by Saint Thomas in the *Catena Aurea*, when he teaches that, through God’s action, both spouses publicly bore witness for Christ. He cried out, “He has done nothing wrong”; she said, “Have nothing to do with that just man.” Jerome also testifies that this was a foreshadowing of the faith of the Gentile people.

I find this opinion—which Dexter also upholds—far more convincing. It is impossible to understand how, at the very moment when the devil was plotting the Lord Christ’s death, he could have desired so earnestly to prevent it by terrifying Pilate’s wife. On that very night he incited Judas and the Jews to lay hands upon Christ and remove Him from their midst, while Pilate’s wife was suffering many things in a vision.

If he had already regretted what he had done, why did he not restrain the hearts of the Jews from the hatred they had conceived against Christ? Or, what would have been easier, why did he not incite the crowd devoted to Christ to a revolt by which the innocent man might be rescued from death? He did none of these things, although, if regret for his deed had truly moved him, he would have left no stone unturned to bring that about.

Therefore, with Dexter, we assert that Pilate’s wife was warned in a dream, recognized the innocence and majesty of the Lord Christ, and believed in Him.

But what does it mean that she is not simply said to have seen something, but to have suffered many things in dreams? Nothing more consistent suggests itself than that Dexter’s account is to be understood: she was warned by the things she suffered to believe in Christ. Since she was a pagan woman, and any ordinary warning would not have been enough to induce her to believe, it was fitting that she should suffer the most bitter torments until, having been granted faith in Christ, she obtained salvation both of body and of soul.

Nor should it seem strange that Pilate’s wife adhered to Christ through faith, since, according to Luke, chapter 8, among the other women who ministered to Jesus from their possessions while He preached was Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward.

Finally, after investigating at length and anxiously the name of Pilate’s wife, to discover whether anyone besides Dexter had called her Procula, I eventually came upon the conclusion of the *Gospel of Nicodemus*, where the same point is confirmed in these words:

“While Pilate was considering what he should do concerning Jesus, his wife, named Procula, sent to him, saying: ‘Have nothing to do with that just man, for I have suffered many things today in dreams because of him.’ The Jews answered and said to Pilate: ‘Did we not tell you that he is a sorcerer? Behold, he has sent a dream to your wife.’”

Thus it is written there.

We do not deny that the *Gospel of Nicodemus* and the Gospel of Joseph are counted among the apocrypha. This, however, does not prevent them from being accepted in matters that do not conflict with divine doctrines. In this passage it offers nothing contrary to Matthew, especially concerning the name of Pilate’s wife, which Matthew does not state.

Accordingly, on this point it is accepted not only by Dexter but also by Vincent of Beauvais in book 7, chapter 41 of the *Speculum Historiale*, who supplied us with the words just cited.

Perhaps this Claudia Procula, Pilate’s wife, is the Claudia mentioned by Paul in 2 Timothy 4: “Eubulus greets you, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia.” The details agree: the name, the period, the religion, and the location. For this Epistle was written in the city, where it is plausible that Pilate’s wife remained when he was driven into exile at Lyon, and that she did not accompany him because of the difference in their religious observance.

3. The Lord Christ. Since the holy Evangelists have left all these matters sufficiently attested in their writings, there is no reason to linger over them. Only one point remains: Eusebius noted in his *Chronicle* that pagan authors also mentioned this great eclipse of the sun.

Hear Eusebius speaking:

“In other commentaries of the pagans I found the following written word for word: ‘An eclipse of the sun took place, and darkness covered the whole earth. Bithynia was shaken by an earthquake, and in the city of Nicaea many buildings collapsed.’”

He then adduces the testimony of Phlegon, a freedman of the emperor Hadrian and a historian:

“Phlegon also wrote about these events. He was an excellent reckoner of Olympiads, and in the fourteenth book he says: ‘In the fourth year of the 201st Olympiad—which was indeed the very year of human redemption—a great and remarkable eclipse of the sun took place, greater than any that had occurred before it. At the sixth hour of the day—which was when Christ ascended the cross—the day was changed into such a dark night that stars were seen in the sky; and an earthquake in Bithynia overturned many buildings in the city of Nicaea.’”

Moreover, the philosopher Apollophanes and Dionysius the Areopagite, who were then staying at Heliopolis for the sake of their studies, observed three things in that eclipse that occurred beyond the powers of nature.

First, it took place at the time of the full moon. Second, it proceeded from east to west, contrary to the customary course and the arrangement of nature. Third, for the space of three hours the moon covered the sun with the densest darkness.

Saint Dionysius himself offered testimony to this when he wrote letters both to Polycarp and to Apollophanes. Struck by these events and thrown into astonishment, he said: “Either the God of nature is suffering, or the mechanism of the world is being dissolved.” Apollophanes replied: “These, good Dionysius, are the transformations of divine things.”

Orosius was certainly unaware of Dionysius when, in book 7, chapter 4, he reports that the eclipse occurred differently, saying:

“It is evident that no cloud obstructed the light of the sun to such an extent that, on that same day, the moon—having traversed the entire region of the sky—was reported to have been very far from the sight of the sun.”

He must therefore be corrected by eyewitness testimony. Joseph Scaliger discusses Phlegon’s testimony more fully in his notes on Eusebius’s *Chronicle*.

4. The Centurion. If Dexter reports anything new and worthy of admiration in praise of Spain, these are surely the things he relates about the centurions mentioned in the Gospels. His view is that nearly all the centurions spoken of in the New Testament originated in Spain, especially those who displayed some notable example of piety and religious devotion.

Consider, first, the man who, when Christ was about to heal his servant in the city of Capernaum, moved by extraordinary faith and humility, said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my servant will be healed.”

Or consider the man who, at the Lord’s death, professed faith in Him with a loud voice and praised Him, saying: “Truly this was the Son of God.” Saint Luke testifies that he glorified God:

“When the centurion saw what had happened, he glorified God, saying: ‘Truly this man was righteous.’”

Finally, consider the man named Cornelius, a devout person who feared the Lord, whom God’s angel honored with his presence and who, according to Acts 10, was baptized by Peter, the leader of the Apostles.

Dexter testifies that all these men were Spaniards by birth, although at that time they were staying in Syria on military service.

However novel this may appear, it should not immediately be condemned as false, since this novelty does not arise from the novelty of the author—which could be considered a fault in an ancient matter—but from the injury of time, which conceals these very ancient writings. For in Dexter’s time these matters could hardly have been judged new, since they were widely circulated by word of mouth among everyone, or at least among the learned. This follows from his statement that the reputation of these men flourished in Spain in his own age.

Nor is this surprising, since the centurions mentioned above lived under the rule of the Roman emperors, whom Dexter himself and all Spain served. Since Spain in Dexter’s time remained under the same Roman rule as it had been under Christ and the centurions, and had not yet experienced a change of dominion, it is not surprising that the memory of distinguished men who had served under the same emperors remained bright and unharmed by the ravages of time.

To this is added Dexter’s authority, which was so great that he would dare to assert nothing unless it were supported by weighty evidence, especially when addressing the most learned and distinguished Jerome and Orosius, to whom he dedicated this work of universal history.
