If Dexter’s testimony deserves credence in any matter, it certainly deserves it in the history of soldiers and centurions who had flourished shortly before in the very places over which he later held supreme authority. It is established that Dexter had been governor of the imperial praetorium in the East, and that archives and records of military affairs were then available to him. From these he could easily learn the names, deeds, and national origins of the older centurions and soldiers who had hitherto served under the emperors in Syria.

Indeed, he himself later reports that he inserted much into this history from the *Jerusalem Annals*. It is therefore sufficiently plausible that he derived the account of these centurions from that source as well.

As for the homeland of the centurion who was present at the Lord’s Passion, we possess testimony consistent with Dexter from Julian, formerly archpriest of the Church of Saint Justa at Toledo, who flourished in the time of Alfonso VII, emperor of Spain, and compiled his deeds.

These manuscripts exist together with a chronicle extending from the birth of the Lord to Julian’s own times. They are preserved at Toledo by the most illustrious lord Francisco de Sandoval y Rojas, noble Count of Mora, who, out of his courtesy toward me and toward all men of letters, allowed me access to read Julian’s chronicle.

Under the year of the Lord 36, Julian writes that he learned the following from the most ancient records of the archive of Saint Justa:

“Many Gentiles who came to Jerusalem to pray at the holy Temple were Spaniards. They wished to see and speak with Jesus, desiring that He preach to the Gentiles of their own land, especially the Spanish centurion who was present at the Lord’s Passion and made the request. He later accompanied James.”

But let us show from another source that these same centurions originated in Spain.

Saint Luke provides a substantial basis for this assertion when, in Acts 10, speaking of Cornelius the centurion whom the Apostle Peter baptized, he notes that Cornelius commanded the Italian cohort:

“There was a certain man in Caesarea named Cornelius, a centurion of the cohort called Italian, devout and fearing God.”

What is the purpose of this statement? It is to infer that the soldiers of his cohort were Italians, since no one denies that cohorts took their names from the nations of their soldiers.

Yet it is perfectly clear from this that they were Spaniards, since Italica was a city of Spain, exceedingly famous throughout the world. It gave the world Trajan and Hadrian, and gave Rome the consul Silius. Ptolemy, Pomponius, and Strabo mention Italica, and its ruins still survive to this day not far from Hispalis, under the name Sevilla la Vieja.

Dio, in book 5 of his *Roman History*, gives abundant testimony to Italica’s extraordinary distinction among the other Roman legions. He also records that Augustus Caesar led this cohort into Judaea, that it did not depart from there until the time of Nero, and that it was then sent elsewhere, namely to Armenia, from which it was again returned to Syria.

Cardinal Baronius lacked Dexter’s present testimony—which he would gladly have accepted had he been given the opportunity. Guided instead by the word “Italian,” he conjectured that Cornelius and the soldiers of this cohort originated in the kingdom of Italy, as though the cohort had been called Italian because it came from Italy:

“There is no doubt that those soldiers belonged to the nation from which the cohort was named, namely, Italians. The centurion, bearing the Roman name Cornelius, is easily conjectured to have been Roman by birth. For the names of cohorts, like those of legions, were often derived from the provinces from which their soldiers had been levied.”

Thus far Baronius, under the year of Christ 41.

Yet that he was far from the truth is evident not only from Dexter’s authority but also from many other considerations that lead us toward the conclusion we intend. The principal one is that, according to the testimony of Dio at the place cited, the Italian legion stationed in Syria, or Palestine, was the one otherwise called the Sixth, because it was listed in that order among the Roman legions. Baronius himself likewise reports this from Dio.

That the Italian legion was Spanish and sixth, rather than first or second, becomes clear from the fact that—as Baronius himself admits—legions and cohorts were given surnames from the provinces from which they had been levied.

The Spanish province was sixth in the Roman order, as is evident from the division of the provinces made by the Romans, after which praetors were sent to govern them. Titus Livy, the distinguished historian of Roman affairs, says in book 35:

“It was decreed concerning the provinces that the first should be the foreign and urban province; the second, that of the Bruttians, who, as Ptolemy testifies, lived on the border of Italy beside the Tyrrhenian Sea; the third, the fleet that was to sail wherever the Senate should determine; the fourth, Sicily; the fifth, Sardinia; and the sixth, Further Spain.”

Let it therefore remain certain that the Italian cohort serving in Judaea and Syria was Spanish, since Dio says that it was the Sixth. The Sixth, according to Livy, came from Further Spain, in which region the city of Italica was situated. The Romans called that province “Further” because, in relation to Rome, it lay beyond the Ebro. No one can doubt that Italica, situated on the Baetis, lay beyond the Ebro.

Nor should anyone think that our cohort was placed sixth because it was inferior to the others in strength or esteem. It was sixth because its soldiers lived farther from Rome in both home and origin, and the provinces were listed according to their proximity to Rome.

Thus the first was that of the urban population and foreigners living in the city; the second, that of the Bruttians, who lived within continental Italy; the third, that of the naval fleet, namely those who embarked on ships along the coasts of Italy; the fourth, that of the Sicilians; the fifth, that of the Sardinians, who lived closer to the city—for Sicily is nearer to Rome than Sardinia; and finally the sixth, that of the Spaniards, who were situated farthest away.

Those cohorts, like the provinces, therefore preserved among themselves an order based on distance from the city. Otherwise, it is certain from Roman writers that the Spanish cohort was judged the strongest of all. Dio testifies that it was accustomed to be called not only the Sixth but also the “Iron” legion (*ferrata*).

The Roman army had ample experience that the Spaniards were more robust and stronger than the soldiers of other nations. Spain was conquered with greater difficulty and more slowly than all the other provinces of the world taken together, as Livy himself, the historian of Roman affairs, attests in book 28:

“Spain was the first of the provinces to be entered, but the last of all to be subdued, under the leadership and auspices of the emperor Augustus.”

And what glory did the Numantines and Saguntines not deserve? Who does not marvel at the strength of the Cantabrians? Silius Italicus says of them in book 3:

“The Cantabrian, unconquered before all others by winter, heat, and hunger, and bearing away the palm from every hardship,” etc.

The Roman emperors, after conquering Spain, also held Spanish soldiers in such high esteem that, because of their innate loyalty and courage, they assigned them to guard the most important provinces.

In the year 23 before Christ was born, Augustus selected the Calagurritans from Spain as his personal bodyguards. Ludovicus Nonius records this in his *Hispania*, chapter 81, and we read that Galba later did the same. Dio also reports that the Praetorian soldiers of Severus Pertinax were Spaniards and Italians. In Egypt likewise the imperial guard consisted of Spanish and Lusitanian cavalry, and the same was true in Arabia, according to the book entitled *The Notitia of the Provinces*. Morales noted this in book 10, chapter 33, so that we may readily believe the same concerning Judaea.

Nor does it harm our argument that the cohort was called “Italian” rather than “Italicensis,” which would seem to be its proper designation if it derived its name from Italica. The citizens of the city of Italica were accustomed to be called not only *Italicenses* but also *Italici*.

The Spanish poet Silius, who was especially dear to Domitian and was advanced to the consulship through his favor, provides more than sufficient evidence of this. Although he came from the city of Italica, he was called Silius Italicus, not Silius Italicensis.

Indeed, people from Italy are more frequently called *Itali* than *Italici*, as Virgil testifies in book 6 of the *Aeneid*:

“Those descendants who shall remain from the Italian race.”

And in book 3:

“And often to call upon Hesperia, often the Italian kingdoms.”

Horace likewise says in book 2 of the *Odes*, ode 7:

“By the ancestral gods and the Italian sky.”

Ovid says in book 4 of the *Fasti*:

“When Aeneas carried Troy into the Italian fields.”

And in book 5 of the *Tristia*, elegy 6:

“May he carry me into the Italian regions and to the favorable lands.”

The same usage appears in book 2 of *Letters from Pontus*, elegy 3, and in countless other authors. Thus one can see that the cohort was correctly called Italian because it originated from Italica, although the patronymic derived from the city of Italica is sometimes rendered *Italicensis*. In this form Dexter later calls Cornelius *Italicensis*, under the year of Christ 40.

Nor does it matter that the centurion of Caesarea was called Cornelius, a Roman name, for this does not prevent him from being a Spaniard. Spain was then under Roman rule, and Roman customs and names were in force there.

But the decisive point is the clear and explicit opinion of Saint Jerome in volume 1, in his letter to Lucinius, a native of Baetica, which begins:

“While I was not expecting it, your letter was suddenly delivered to me. The more unexpected it was, the more full of joy it proved, raising my resting soul, so that I immediately embraced in love the man whom I did not know by sight.”

Jerome admired Lucinius’s faith, since he was a man living at the farthest edge of Spain and of the world—that is, in Baetica, where Italica also stood—and yet sent gifts and letters from there to Jerome, who was living in the East.

Jerome then adds that Lucinius’s remarkable faith had long before been foreshadowed by Cornelius, the centurion of the Italian cohort, who was likewise born in that same province and brought to faith. In both men the saying of the Lord was fulfilled: “Many will come from the East and from the West and will recline with Abraham,” etc.

Jerome adds that the Apostle Paul desired this very thing intensely when he wrote to the Romans: “When I begin to travel to Spain, etc., I hope to see you in passing and to be escorted there by you.” By this desire Paul demonstrated what he sought from that province: the faith of the Spaniards, which shone in Cornelius and in Lucinius of Baetica.

Here are Jerome’s words:

“Truly now in you, O Lucinius of Baetica, the saying of the Lord has been fulfilled: ‘Many will come from the East and from the West and will recline in Abraham’s bosom.’ Cornelius, the centurion of the Italian cohort, already foreshadowed the faith of my Lucinius. The Apostle Paul, writing to the Romans, says: ‘When I begin to travel to Spain, I hope that, passing through, I shall see you and be escorted there by you.’ By such great storms he demonstrated what he sought from that province.”

Thus Jerome understood both matters to bear upon the same point: Cornelius’s faith and Paul’s desire.

In what respect, I ask, did Cornelius foreshadow Lucinius’s faith, unless it was because he originated from the same people from whom Lucinius later descended, and whom Paul desired to bring to faith? Otherwise, at the time of his conversion Cornelius was not at the farthest limits of the earth, so that the Lord’s saying might be fulfilled in him; he was living at Caesarea, not far from Jerusalem.

Jerome extensively praises Lucinius and his wife Theodora in the letter mentioned above and in the following one, which you may consult.

We therefore leave it sufficiently and more than sufficiently established that Cornelius the centurion mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, and his cohort, originated from the Spanish city of Italica.

But how can we infer that two other centurions, whose cohorts are not named, were Spaniards? From the fact that in Judaea there was one and the same cohort of Roman soldiers, who, under different centurions, were distributed among various cities of the land.

For, according to Dio, the only cohort stationed in Palestine was the Sixth, which was Italian and Iron. Nevertheless, some of its soldiers, with their centurion Cornelius, were at Caesarea; others were at Capernaum in Galilee with the centurion whose servant the Lord healed; and still others were at Jerusalem, where that centurion was stationed who, when Christ was dying, confessed with a loud cry that He was the Son of God.

We therefore rightly infer from the homeland of one centurion and his soldiers the ancestral homes of the other soldiers and centurions, since all belonged to one and the same cohort and were distributed throughout Judaea in order to provide more effectively for the peace of the entire province.

Spain may therefore rightly glory in its centurions.

But, O marvelous piety and devotion of these men! How free and open was their confession! How fearless and powerful their cry in obedience to faith! How worthily the Evangelists celebrate them with praises!

The Capernaum centurion considers himself unworthy of the Lord’s visitation:

“Lord,” he says, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”

Yet he presumed so greatly upon Christ that he believed, through a single word, that He could drive away every illness:

“Only say the word, and my servant will be healed.”

Indeed, he regarded all things as subject to Christ even more, and much more, than each servant or soldier was subject to his own master:

“For I too,” he says, “am a man placed under authority, and I say to this man, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

Why, then, Lord, should You, who are above all things, not be able by a mere command to drive the illness far from the boy?

It is no wonder that, when Jesus heard this—as Matthew notes in chapter 8—He marveled and said to those following Him:

“I have not found such faith in Israel.”

Who would not also marvel at the frank declaration of the Jerusalem centurion? When all the Jews were mocking the Lord, when even the disciples had fled, and when He had been fastened to the cross and reckoned among criminals, the centurion raised his voice before the entire people:

“Truly this was the Son of God.”

The holy angels also honored the piety, almsgiving, and other works of virtue of that Gentile centurion at Caesarea. These virtues were of such weight before God that through him the door to public preaching among the Gentiles was opened.

Let us now see what Dexter confidently asserts about these centurions. It will be useful to gather into a brief summary what he reports about them, scattered over many years, so that the reader may know at once who each of them was.

The centurion of Capernaum, named Gaius Cornelius, was by birth a Malacitan; his son was Gaius Oppius, also a centurion—namely, the man who lived at Jerusalem and glorified the dying Christ with a solemn confession. Thus Dexter, in this very year, 34, acknowledges, saying:

> “Cornelius, the centurion of Capernaum, master of the servant whom the Lord healed (and also father of Gaius Oppius the centurion), a Spaniard, flourishes remarkably in Spain.”

He had previously written concerning Gaius Oppius:

> “Gaius Oppius, a Spanish centurion, believes in Christ dying upon the cross.”

Saint James the Apostle, who had already arrived in Spain, baptized him there. Concerning him Dexter writes under the year 53:

> “The Malacitan centurion flourishes, whom Saint James baptizes there.”

And under the year 34:

> “At that time in Spain Gaius Oppius, the son of Cornelius, likewise a centurion, flourishes. He proclaims at Jerusalem that the dying Christ is the Son of God, amid the crashing of rocks striking against one another, while the day is covered in darkness. He was the first Spanish centurion from among the Gentiles to believe after Christ’s death. He was a Roman citizen, and, having been baptized by Saint Barnabas, became the third bishop of Milan. Truly an apostolic man, he was the first of all to report to the Spaniards, his own people, Christ’s death and the remarkable eclipse, to the astonishment of his hearers.”

As for Gaius Oppius, Dexter again states under the year 66 that he had two sons, Gaius and Demetrius, men renowned for holiness. Saint John, writing from Ephesus, addressed his Third Epistle to this Gaius. Demetrius he calls a hospitable man because, following the example of his father Gaius Oppius, he received and cared for travelers in his home.

Moreover, Dexter asserts under the year of the Lord 70 that Gaius Oppius later lived at Corinth, although he was Malacitan by origin, and that he generously received Saint Paul, when Paul was approaching Spain, into his house and entertained him there. He then visited Saint John, recently recalled from exile in Asia; he also accompanied John when he came to Spain, preached there, and returned again to Asia. Thereafter he presented himself as the companion of Saint Ignatius from Antioch all the way to Rome, where Ignatius was given to the beasts. Finally, when Oppius had again traveled through Milan toward Spain, he became bishop of that Church and was the third after Blessed Barnabas. There, renowned for his merits and good works and filled with labors undertaken for Christ, he departed to God, worn out by old age.

Let this be said only in summary and passing, so that we may possess at least some knowledge of the genealogy, birth, and deeds of these centurions; otherwise it would be difficult to grasp everything that the author relates about them in scattered passages.

As for the name Gaius Oppius—lest anyone be troubled by it—it is Roman and was used by citizens of the highest rank. Such were Spurius Oppius, surnamed Cornicen, and Marcus Oppius, both Decemvirs, as well as Lucius Oppius, called Salinator, whom Livy mentions in Books III and XXXV. There was also that celebrated Gaius Oppius who, during the consulship of Quintus Fabius and Titus Sempronius, in the year 541 from the founding of the City, proposed the Oppian Law concerning the adornment of married women. It was called after his name and provided:

> “No woman was to possess more than half an ounce of gold, wear a multicolored garment, or travel in a vehicle drawn by animals within the city or town, or within a thousand paces of it, except for the purpose of attending public religious rites.”

Would that our Spain had enacted such a law! But at Rome also, alas, it was later repealed by Lucius Valerius, tribune of the plebs, who vigorously defended the cause of the married women in a polished speech, despite everything that Marcus Porcius Cato had argued with all his strength before the Rostra in defense of that most sacred law. Livy himself reports this in Book XXXIV.

Concerning Cornelius the centurion residing at Caesarea, Dexter writes under the year of Christ 40:

> “Cornelius, the Italian centurion, while Peter was preaching, is filled with the Holy Spirit; and when the conversion of the Gentiles to faith in Christ had been solemnly announced at Jerusalem, Cornelius, having been baptized, flourishes.”

The rest will be treated in its proper places.

### 5. Pilate reported Christ’s death, etc.

That governors of provinces were accustomed to write to emperors about important events occurring in their provinces is established by a thousand incontrovertible examples. Several trustworthy authors testify that Pilate reported these matters to the emperor Tiberius, especially Tertullian in the *Apologeticus*, chapters 5 and 21; Eusebius, Book II of his *History*, chapter 2; Orosius, Book VII, chapter 4; and Gregory of Tours, Book I of his *History*, chapter 24.

Indeed, Saint Justin, that distinguished martyr of Christ and eminent philosopher, testifies in his *Apology*, which he presented in defense of the Christian religion to the emperor Antoninus, that in his own time there existed at Rome, in the archives of the state, records written in the public registers concerning Jesus of Nazareth, crucified at Jerusalem under Pilate. He says:

> “You can learn that these things happened from the Acts that were written under Pilate.”

But since Dexter adds that Pilate did not write to Tiberius about this matter in that year, why, I ask, does the author note that Pilate had decided to do so precisely then? Did he mean that only his intention seemed worthy of being recorded? I conjecture that Dexter intended to indicate that Pilate had decided not merely in his mind to have the Lord’s death committed to public writing, but that many matters—especially those concerning the Jews’ hatred and the Redeemer’s innocence—had also been recorded by the hand of public notaries at his command. Nevertheless, such public records were not sent to Rome, to the emperor Tiberius, until the year of the Lord 38.

Dexter does not explain what caused so long a delay. Yet anyone can readily understand that Pilate himself may have been restrained by the consciousness of his injustice, lest he appear to have condemned Christ to death most wickedly, since he had repeatedly allowed it to be declared publicly that Christ had done nothing deserving death. The Jews, too, may have opposed Pilate’s sending the records concerning Christ to Rome, since they had every reason to fear that their savage hatred would become known to the Senate and the emperors.

Pilate therefore resolved to send Tiberius an account of Christ’s death and miracles and now had these matters entered in the public registers. Nevertheless, for the reasons already stated, the action was not carried out for four years. If Cardinal Caesar Baronius had weighed these considerations—or if he had obtained Dexter—he would have differed less from Eusebius. He says:

> “In this report concerning Christ made by Pilate to Tiberius, we do not know for what reason Eusebius places it five years later, in the year in which Tiberius died on 16 March.”

But we believe that Pilate’s report was made immediately after Christ’s resurrection had become publicly known. Dexter agrees with Eusebius in this respect: he says that such a report by Pilate to Tiberius was made in the year 38, but adds that immediately after the Lord’s death and resurrection Pilate had decided to report it to the emperor, since it was customary for public records to be made at the time events occurred. He nevertheless delayed its completion for four years, whether through his own initiative or because of Jewish pressure.

I readily persuade myself that both considerations moved that wicked judge, especially since the character of the Jews is known to me from the Gospel. They strove with all their might, even contributing a vast sum of money to the soldiers, to prevent the publication of the Lord’s resurrection. Nor could they have been unaware that Pilate—as they saw was customary concerning other events—would immediately inform Tiberius about Christ’s miracles, preaching, death, and resurrection. Nothing had ever occurred throughout the world more illustrious or more worthy of fame. It was therefore necessary that the Jews should leave no stone unturned with Pilate to bury all the affairs of the God-man in dense silence: first, so that Christ’s name might not be spread throughout the Roman Empire; and second, so that their impiety, hatred, and malice might not be exposed.

Yet the man who, against the prompting of his conscience, could delay the report for four years could not finally conceal the truth. At last he reported it to the emperor, as we shall see in its proper place with Dexter under the year 38.

### 6. Saint Petronilla, etc.

No one denies that the Apostle Saint Peter, when he passed from catching fish to catching human beings at the Lord’s command, had a wife. This is clearly taught—leaving Jerome and Tertullian aside—by the very ancient martyr Ignatius, who writes to the Philadelphians:

> “I do not disparage those blessed men who were joined in marriage. For I desire to be found worthy of God in his kingdom at the footsteps of such men as Peter and some of the Apostles who were united in marriage.”

Marcus Marcellus Eugenius, a disciple of that same Apostle, also professes this at the place to be cited shortly.

Clement of Alexandria, in Book VII of his *Stromata*, reports from the tradition of his predecessors that Peter’s wife was crowned with martyrdom in his presence. Clement’s words are:

> “They certainly say that blessed Peter, when he saw his wife being led away to death, rejoiced because of her calling and because she was returning home”—that is, proceeding to the heavenly homeland, which is our home and from which we are exiles. “He encouraged and consoled her greatly, addressing her by her own name and saying: ‘Remember the Lord,’ namely, the things that he suffered for you; for in this way you will bear your torments with extraordinary courage.”

Consult Eusebius, Book III, chapters 24 and 30.

Some call Peter’s wife Concordia, others Mary; this is noted by Marcus Maximus and Heleca. Others call her Perpetua, as Molanus does under 4 November, on which day some celebrate her feast.

Everyone who mentions that holy Virgin agrees that Peter had a daughter by his wife, named Petronilla after her father. The authors of the martyrologies especially affirm this on the last day of May. The Roman Martyrology says:

> “At Rome, Saint Petronilla, daughter of Blessed Peter the Apostle. She rejected the marriage of Flaccus, a nobleman, and, having obtained a three-day postponement for deliberation, spent the interval in fasting and prayer. On the third day, immediately after receiving the sacrament of Christ, she gave up her spirit.”

These details have been briefly extracted from what the distinguished martyr of Christ Eugenius, archbishop of Toledo, committed to posterity in his writings concerning the life and death of Saint Petronilla. He was the disciple of his father and a familiar associate of the Virgin herself at Rome. Elsewhere he was called by his proper name, Marcus Marcellus; later, because of the distinction of his family—he belonged to the household and lineage of Nero, as we shall learn from Dexter in its proper place—he was called Eugenius, a name that in Latin means “noble.”

This man, so great and distinguished, and our patron, wrote a vivid account of the life and death of Saint Petronilla in response to inquiries from the holy martyrs Nereus and Achilleus, who were then exiled to the island of Pontia for confessing the Lord. Among the other matters he wrote to them, his account remains today in the acts of those martyrs preserved by Surius. Receive here the very words of Blessed Marcus Eugenius’s letter, which are set down here verbatim for remembrance and reverence of him, and because we must defend it elsewhere.

### Letter of Saint Marcus Marcellus Eugenius to the Holy Martyrs Nereus and Achilleus

Marcellus, servant of Christ, to the holy confessors Nereus and Achilleus.

After reading your letter, I was filled with joy because I understood that you remained steadfast in the faith and were fighting manfully for the truth. After many remarks concerning the Apostle Peter, he continues:

> “Since you carefully inquire about Petronilla, the daughter of the Apostle Peter, my Lord, and ask what the end of her life was, I shall record it briefly.
>
> “You know well that Petronilla became bedridden through the will of the Apostle Peter. I remember that you were present when many of his disciples were dining with him, and Titus said to him: ‘When everyone is healed by you, why do you allow Petronilla to lie bedridden with paralysis?’ Peter then replied: ‘It is beneficial for her in this way.’ Yet lest anyone think that by these words I intended to say that she could not be healed, he added: ‘I wish her to rise and minister to us.’ Immediately she rose up healed.
>
> “When her service was completed, the Apostle ordered her to return to her bed. After she had become perfect in the fear of God, not only was she herself healed, but through her prayers she obtained healing for many others.
>
> “Since she was of exceptional physical beauty, the count Flaccus came to her with his soldiers, intending to take her as his wife. Petronilla said to him: ‘Do you come to an unarmed girl with armed soldiers? If you wish to have me as your wife, arrange that respectable matrons and virgins come to me after three days, so that I may come with them together to your house.’
>
> “Having obtained a period of three days, the holy virgin devoted herself to fasting and prayer, with the holy virgin Felicula beside her, a woman perfected in the fear of God. On the third day Saint Nicomedes the presbyter came to her and celebrated the mysteries of Christ. When the most holy virgin had received Christ’s sacrament, she reclined upon her little bed and gave up her spirit.
>
> “The matrons and virgins whom Flaccus had sent to her celebrated her funeral rites.”

Thus far the most blessed Eugenius, later our primate, concerning the happy death of Saint Petronilla.

Yet in what he reports there are certain matters that seem to cast doubt upon what has hitherto been universally accepted concerning Blessed Petronilla—namely, that she was the daughter of the Prince of the Apostles. For how can Petronilla be called the daughter of Simon, when he had not yet acquired the name Peter at the time of her birth? The name Petronilla clearly seems to be derived from Peter. Moreover, the fact that she was born before he was enrolled among Christ’s Apostles is made evident by the circumstance that thereafter he nowhere used his wife, having professed continence along with the other Apostles who were married.

Here the difficulty becomes greater. She appears to have been a woman of many years when she was staying at Rome with her father. She had been with him not only for a considerable number of years at Jerusalem and Antioch, but, after he moved to Rome, she lived there for several years as a paralytic, as Saint Eugenius acknowledges. How, then, could Flaccus fall in love with a virgin of advanced age and wish to take her as his wife? Or how can it be believed that after so many years she retained such exceptional beauty as the letter describes?

Further, the Petronilla about whom Marcus Eugenius speaks, whose feast is celebrated in the Church, appears to have been a girl of the highest nobility. A man of such distinction, a count by office, accompanied by so many soldiers, wished to take her in marriage. Indeed, she did not plead poverty of fortune or lowliness of birth; rather, she demanded that many matrons and virgins accompany her so that she might be taken as the count’s wife. If she had been the daughter of a poor fisherman, none of this would seem likely to have happened to her; at the very least, she ought immediately to have pleaded her poverty in order to escape the marriage of so eminent a man.

These considerations caused the most illustrious Baronius to depart from the ancient path. He was led to suspect that she was not called the daughter of the Apostle Peter because she had been begotten by him from his wife, but because he had accepted her as a daughter through special devotion. In the same way, Peter calls Mark his son in his First Epistle when he says:

> “The Church that is in Babylon”—by which he means Rome—“greets you, and so does Mark, my son.”

Baronius rather believes that Petronilla was the daughter of a certain Petronius, a noble Roman citizen. For Petronilla is derived from Petronius, whereas from Petrus one would derive Petrilla, just as Drusilla comes from Drusus and Priscilla from Priscus.

I do not deny that this was ingeniously devised; nevertheless, there is no reason for us to depart from the ancients. If the objections are properly weighed against the touchstone, they do not compel us to invent new opinions.

As for the chronology, there is nothing surprising in a virgin who had not yet completed twenty-six years retaining the full bloom of her beauty. But from where is this age of Petronilla gathered? Clearly from what Dexter teaches here: namely, that she had lived only ten years in the very year of the Lord’s Passion. If eleven years are added to those ten—the years that elapsed from the year of Christ 34, when he suffered death on the cross for human beings, to the year 45, when, according to the Cardinal himself, Saint Peter founded the Roman see—or to 44, as may be inferred from Dexter, concerning which we shall speak in its proper place—then it follows that his daughter entered Rome with her father at the age of twenty-one.

To these we add another five years, during which she was afflicted by paralysis and, after being healed by the Apostle, exercised the grace of health that had been granted to her. It is therefore plainly established that she died at the age of twenty-six, an age at which she could have been sufficiently fresh and beautiful. This is so persuasive to me that I consider her to have been in the full bloom of youth at that time, even if she had reached thirty years when Flaccus sought her in marriage.

Nor does it trouble me that he was a count by office. First, before the time of Constantine, as Baronius himself learnedly explains in his notes on the Martyrology, *comes* was not a title of rank but denoted an assessor of judges. Second, there is nothing surprising if a man of the highest nobility did not disdain the marriage of an Apostle’s daughter, whom he saw held in great honor by the leading men among Christians. Marcus Marcellus Eugenius himself provides an example: although he belonged to the household and family of an emperor, he nevertheless repeatedly called Saint Peter his Lord, saying in the letter:

> “Concerning Petronilla, the daughter of the Apostle Peter, my Lord,” etc.

Clement too—to say nothing of the other Roman nobles—although himself born of consular and senatorial stock, revered the same Apostle as Lord and Teacher.

Why, then, would Flaccus, however noble and however pagan, not desire to take the daughter of so great a man in marriage, especially when he was overcome by a blind love of her beauty? We also believe that this was why Petronilla did not plead the great disparity between her own poverty and his position. Rather, she wisely refrained from an answer that she saw would not be accepted by a passionately enamored suitor. To drive him away more easily, she demanded a three-day postponement, which he could scarcely refuse.

She should be understood to have requested virgins and matrons of respectable character as companions in order to evade his vanity, while making a demand suited to that vanity. Nevertheless, it is a weak argument to say that she did not plead her poverty to the count because Eugenius does not report it. It may have happened that, when such considerations and many similar ones failed to change his mind, she finally resorted to the three-day postponement and the noise of the women accompanying her.

As for the name Petronilla, we admit that she was not marked by it from the womb in childhood. Either she received it at baptism, when her father was already enjoying the name Peter, or it was not the virgin’s proper name but an honorary surname bestowed upon her by her father’s disciples to indicate that she was Peter’s daughter. In the same way, Marcus Marcellus was marked by the name Eugenius, as other Christians were marked by other names.

It makes little difference whether she was called Petrilla or Petronilla, since it is otherwise established that she was the daughter not of Petronius but of Peter.

Nor is Baronius’s comparison with Mark similar. Mark is called “son” only once; elsewhere he is generally named without that designation, which indicates that the term was given to him merely as an expression of affection. Petronilla, however, is always and by everyone called the daughter of Saint Peter. This is no slight indication that she truly was his offspring.

Among the ancient writers, too, there was one who was not satisfied with the ambiguous designation “daughter” but called Petronilla Peter’s offspring. Wandelbert appears to have done this in his metrical Martyrology when he said, on the day before the Kalends of June:

> “Then, on the day before, Petronilla, sprung from Peter’s holy stock,  
> Shines forth, a radiant Virgin, adorned with Christ’s beauty.”

The tomb of the most holy Virgin was discovered under Pope Paul I of Rome, around the year of the Lord 758, with this inscription carved in marble:

> “To Aurea Petronilla, his most beloved daughter,”

as it seems, placed there by the Apostle himself. See P. Galesinus under 31 May.

### 7. On the twenty-seventh day of March, at dawn

There is no reason to linger here, since whatever Dexter says about the Lord’s resurrection is certain and consistent. Since his death occurred on 25 March, it follows that the resurrection is said to have occurred on the 27th, at dawn, after the places beneath the earth had first been stripped—those places where the ancient Fathers, although distinguished in holiness, were detained because of the bond of original sin. See what Baronius learnedly notes concerning the hour of the resurrection in Volume I.

### 8. Herod, etc.

Josephus relates in Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 9, that when Gaius, emperor of the Romans, had made Agrippa, the brother of Herodias, king from the status of a private citizen, Herodias herself—the mistress of Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, driven by envy of her brother’s good fortune—also desired the royal diadem. For the sake of this ambition she moved her lover to sail to Rome with a suitably splendid retinue, so that he too might be elevated to royal rank through Caesar’s favor.

Events did not turn out according to their wishes; indeed, they took a turn for the worse. For King Agrippa sent his freedman Fortunatus to Gaius with gifts and letters, accusing Herod of a double revolt from the Roman Empire: first, with Sejanus against the emperor Tiberius, and again with Artabanus the Parthian against Gaius himself. As evidence he offered the tetrarch’s preparations, since Herod allegedly possessed in his arsenals enough weapons to equip seventy thousand armed men.

Herod had almost reached Gaius when Fortunatus arrived in Rome. After reading the letters, the emperor became enraged. To obtain greater certainty, he asked Herod whether the reports he had heard concerning the quantity of his weapons were true. When Herod assented, the emperor considered the charge of rebellion sufficiently proven, deprived him of his tetrarchy, and punished him with exile. He also assigned the tetrarchy to Agrippa, his rival, thereby increasing the cause for resentment.

Finally, he spared Herodias, who was present and had accompanied her husband, because of the loyalty of her brother Agrippa. Yet how could the woman who had been the cause of so many evils, had incurred the indignation of the divine majesty, and had against her the blood of John the Baptist crying out, fail to pay a fitting penalty?

But, so that one might marvel all the more at God’s most profound providence, she herself rejected the pardon that the emperor had granted her and willingly embraced the exile and punishment she deserved. Thus she said to Gaius, who had pardoned her:

> “You, emperor, speak in a manner worthy of your majesty. But conjugal love prevents me from enjoying this indulgence. For I do not consider it right to abandon now, in adversity, the man whose companion I was in prosperity.”

But he, indignant—Josephus says—at such lofty courage in a woman, expelled her also along with Herod and bestowed her property upon Agrippa. Thus it came about that both of them departed from Judaea toward the western part of the world, condemned to perpetual exile.

Where they went, however, may rightly be questioned. Nicephorus, in Book I of his history, chapter 20, says that Herod lived in exile at Vienna. Josephus, in the passage cited above, says:

> “Herod, however, was condemned to perpetual exile at the city of Lugdunum,”

and on this authority it is commonly believed that he died at Lugdunum.

But Josephus himself, in Book II of *The Jewish War*, chapter 8, toward the end of the book, states that Herod fled to Spain with Herodias as his companion. He writes:

> “Driven to this by necessity, Herod came to Gaius, who severely rebuked him for his greed. He fled to Spain, for his accuser Agrippa had followed him; and Gaius Caesar added Herod’s tetrarchy to Agrippa’s. Thus Herod died in Spain, while his wife traveled there with him.”

From this Baronius thinks that Josephus contradicted himself in the two passages. In the first he says that Agrippa sent Fortunatus to Rome after Herod; in the second, he says that Agrippa himself went to Rome. In the first Herod was deprived of his rank on the charge of rebellion; in the second he was severely rebuked by Gaius for greed. Finally, in the first he was punished with exile at Lugdunum; in the second he fled to Spain and died there while traveling with Herodias.

But whatever may be said about the other matters—which I do not now discuss—there is no verbal contradiction in this author concerning the place of exile. For it was necessary that, after being driven from Rome, Herod should first go to Gaul, and there he could have remained for some time at Lugdunum. From there he could have proceeded to Spain; Josephus never denies this. Nowhere does he assert that Herod died at Lugdunum, but only that he was relegated to perpetual exile. It is therefore not unbelievable that he afterward fled toward Spain and died there while living as an exile. This is what Josephus admits in the later passage, and it is made completely clear by the testimony of other authors.

Hegesippus, a very ancient writer, asserts in Book II of his account of the destruction of Jerusalem, chapter 5, that Herod came to Spain, adding that he died consumed by grief. Josephus—another author, the son of Gorion—also says in Book V of his histories, chapter 46:

> “Tiberius Caesar, king of the Romans, transferred Herod to Spain, where he also died.”

Ribera cites these words in connection with Obadiah:

> “The exile of Jerusalem that is in Bosphorus.”

See how learnedly Dexter asserts that Herod entered Spain and died there unhappily. Yet there is one detail that we owe to Dexter alone, previously unknown to others: the name of the city in which he died, namely Ilerda, which we now call Lérida.

### 9. Herodias, however, etc.

A horrible but most just death for the woman who had wickedly raised her head against the just man. Nicephorus recounts it more fully in the passage cited above, except that in certain details he seems to differ from Dexter. Nicephorus asserts that the dancing girl was drowned in a river covered with ice; Dexter attributes this fate to her mother Herodias. Moreover, Nicephorus says that the girl was decapitated, whereas Dexter says that she was submerged.

Let us hear Callistus:

> “That frenzied, adulterous, and incestuous woman, who was regarded as Herod’s wife but was in reality Philip’s wife, after having prolonged her life and first seeing her dancing daughter carried off by a bitter fate, was reserved for the judgment and punishment of the age to come, where she would most swiftly drain the dregs of divine wrath and the cup of the Lord’s intolerable indignation.
>
> “The death of her daughter—for it deserves to be committed to memory—was as follows. She had to go somewhere in the winter and cross a river, the Sicoris, the river of Ilerda, now commonly called the Segre. Since the river was bound and sealed with ice, she crossed it on foot. But when the ice broke—and this did not happen without divine providence—she was immediately submerged up to the head. While her lower body moved playfully and lightly, she danced, not on land but upon the waves. Her guilty head, however, was frozen solid by the cold and ice, and then wounded and severed from the rest of her body, not by iron but by fragments of ice. Thus, upon the ice itself, she performed a deadly dance, and by that spectacle, displayed to all, recalled to the minds of the spectators the deeds she had committed.”

So far Callistus.

I freely acknowledge that, as this author describes it, the dancing girl’s fate displays a marvelous providence of God: he punished her by the head because she had sought to punish the Baptist by the head. Yet I greatly marvel at the statement that her head was severed not by iron but merely by fragments of ice. I do not doubt that this could have happened by a miracle, but I do doubt that it actually happened.

Nevertheless, in a doubtful matter I prefer to follow Dexter, whether the issue concerns the manner of death or the person who suffered it. First, Dexter lived many centuries before Nicephorus. Second, he was himself a Spaniard from Barcelona and reported events that occurred at Ilerda in his own province, not far from Barcelona. Nicephorus, by contrast, lived much later and was born and raised in Greece.

Nor do I find in Josephus that the dancing girl was also sent into exile, or that she accompanied her mother, so that she could have been drowned or decapitated at Ilerda. Who knows whether she remained in Galilee or Judaea after being married? It would also seem consistent with reason that the woman who had sinned more gravely in John’s death should be punished with a more severe penalty. No one is unaware, however, that the girl demanded the Baptist’s head only after being instructed by her adulterous mother.

But enough of these matters.

### 10. Gaius Cornelius, the centurion

Dexter had previously dealt with Gaius Oppius, who lived at Jerusalem. He now speaks of his father, Gaius Cornelius of Malaca, likewise a centurion but residing in the city of Capernaum. He says that this was the centurion whose praise is found in the Gospel—the man, I mean, whom the Lord praised in Luke 7, saying:

> “Amen I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.”

Two of the holy Evangelists, Matthew and Luke, relate the exceedingly moving story of how he approached Jesus, asking him to heal a servant who was in danger of death. When Jesus said, “I will come and heal him,” the centurion did not consent to his coming personally. He considered himself unworthy to receive so great a guest, and regarded Jesus as so powerful that by a mere word—which would be the easiest thing, if he wished—he could heal the sick man and drive away his illness. For all things, he thought, would obey Jesus even more readily than his own soldiers and servants obeyed him.

> “Lord,” he said, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof. But only say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I am absolutely certain that you are able to do this. And why should it seem surprising? I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me, and I say to this one, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it. How much more will everything obey you, who are subject to no one!”

When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those following him:

> “Amen I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.”

The Doctors, in interpreting the Gospel text, marvel at so many things in this one man that it would take too long to enumerate them all.

Chrysostom elegantly weighs the depth of his faith:

> “Consider the centurion’s faith. He did not say, ‘Come and heal him,’ because he believed that Christ was present everywhere.”

Later Chrysostom compares the centurion’s faith with that of the others:

> “Andrew believed, but only after John said, ‘Behold the Lamb of God.’ Peter believed, but only after Andrew preached to him. Philip believed, but only after reading the Scriptures. Nathanael believed, but first received a sign of Christ’s divinity—namely, that Christ had seen him beneath the fig tree, where Christ was not bodily present.”

Origen follows.

Jairus, a ruler of Israel, asking for his daughter, did not say, “Say the word,” but, “Come quickly.” Nicodemus, hearing of the sacrament of faith, said, “How can this happen?” Mary and Martha said, “Lord, Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died,” as though doubting that the power of God could be present everywhere.

By those words—“I have not found such great faith in Israel”—the Lord wished to imply all these things.

Ambrose adds:

> “If you read the passage in this way—‘I have found such great faith in no one in Israel’—the simple and easy meaning is that he was speaking only of those who were then living. But if, according to the Greeks, you read, ‘I have not found such great faith even in Israel,’ then he places this kind of faith above that of the Elect and those who saw God—namely, the patriarchs and prophets.”

Bede rightly cautions, however, that Christ is not speaking of all the patriarchs and prophets of former times, but of the people of the present age. The centurion’s faith is therefore preferred to theirs because they had been instructed by the teachings of the Law and the Prophets, whereas this man believed spontaneously, without anyone teaching him.

Besides faith, that man’s great humility [Col. 0085D] is commended by the words, “Lord, I am not worthy.” Concerning this passage Rabanus says: “Because of his conscience regarding his pagan way of life, he thought himself more burdened by the favor than helped by it; for although he possessed faith, he had not yet been anointed with the sacraments.” Augustine says in *Sermon 6 on the Words of the Lord on the Mount*: “By saying that he was unworthy, he made himself worthy—not that Christ the Word should enter the walls of his house, but his heart. Nor would he have said this with such great faith and humility unless he carried in his heart the one whom he feared would enter his house.” Ambrose says that, insofar as the mystery is concerned, the centurion saw that Christ was not yet able to penetrate the hearts of the Gentiles.

The centurion’s prudence, says Jerome, appears in this: that beyond the covering of the body he perceived the hidden Divinity; [Col. 0086A] and for that reason he conducted himself toward him with such reverence. Add that prudence was required in his first sending the Jewish elders to Jesus, and then his friends, when Jesus was already not far from the house, as Luke reports. Finally, he himself approached, asking that Jesus not enter his house—what Matthew wrote. Chrysostom’s explanation seems to me the easier reconciliation of the Evangelists:

> “That Matthew does not say that he spoke through friends,” Chrysostom says, “but through himself, is not at all contrary to this: it is reasonable to suppose that, after he had sent his friends, he himself came and said these things. If Luke did not say this, nor Matthew that, they do not contradict one another; rather, they complete what each had left unmentioned.”

The same Chrysostom notes the man’s wisdom, since he did not say, “Come here and heal him.” For he is not recorded as having explicitly requested the servant’s healing; he merely explained the illness, saying: “Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and is grievously tormented.” Explaining the reason for this, Chrysostom says: “For he knew that Christ was powerful enough to act, wise enough to understand, and merciful enough to hear; therefore he explained only the illness, while leaving the remedy of healing to his mercy.” Finally, observe his goodness—Chrysostom himself says this—for he was so solicitously concerned for the servant’s health that he hurried on his account.

Add that, although he was still a Gentile, he himself had built a synagogue for the Jews in his own city, Capernaum; and he loved them, at least as far as religion was concerned. The Jewish elders themselves bore witness to this before the Lord—“salvation even from enemies”—when, as Luke says, they came to Jesus and earnestly pleaded with him: “He is worthy that you should grant this to him, for he loves our nation, and he himself built the synagogue for us.”

This centurion, then, was a great man. Indeed, such a man was fitting to be the first of the Gentiles converted to faith through the preaching and miracles of Christ. Let no one suppose that I am attributing this dignity and glory to the centurion without the support of a very weighty authority, for I have Chrysostom, who says here concerning Matthew:

> “This centurion was the first-fruit of the Gentiles, in comparison with whose faith the faith of all the Jews was found to be unbelief.”

Some grant this distinction to the centurion Cornelius. But apart from the fact that this man too was of Spanish origin, since he was born at Italica, the matter has a very different meaning: namely, that he was the first sacrificial offering of the Gentiles to God after the door of faith had been opened to them—not that he was the first of the Gentiles to believe. That cannot stand, since the Magi who worshiped the infant Lord were earlier in faith than the centurion of Italica. We shall speak of these matters again in their proper place, in the year of the Lord 40.

Finally, this should be ascribed to our Capernaum centurion’s glory: that he gave the whole Church the model for receiving Christ into the houses of their bodies. From the most ancient custom, those who receive the sacred Eucharist have been accustomed to utter the centurion’s words, “Lord, I am not worthy,” and so forth. This custom is so ancient that Origen highly commended it, saying: “When you eat and drink the body and blood of the Lord, then the Lord enters beneath your roof; and you too, humbling yourself, should say: ‘Lord, I am not worthy,’” and so forth.

### “He flourishes greatly in Spain”

That he flourished greatly in Judaea, enjoying a reputation for virtue and piety before God and human beings—both the Jews and his own Gentiles—is clear from what has been said. Dexter adds that he also flourished in Spain, evidently because, having left military service, he returned to his homeland as a veteran soldier. Since he was a citizen of Malaga, as we established above, it follows that he shone there with a reputation for holiness. The remaining matters concerning his preaching and death [Col. 0087A] are written by Heleca in his additions to Dexter, in these words:

> “The memory of Saint Caius Cornelius the centurion is no less celebrated—he was that centurion whose servant Christ healed at Capernaum. Later he joined the apostles and was present at the death of Saint Stephen; he accompanied Peter and Paul when they came to Spain. At last, while preaching to the people of Scepsis, he died near Ida. He preaches in Spain. This man is entirely different from Cornelius, the centurion of the Italian cohort: that Cornelius was much younger, whereas this man was older. He lived as far as the time of Hadrian, to whom he was also dear, as Dexter teaches below under the year of Christ 66.”

### 11. “The holy Apostles of God”

Until now the Doctors have held differing opinions concerning the time of the Apostles’ division. Some think that it took place immediately after the Lord’s Passion; Theophanes leads them in his *Harmony of the Old and New Testament*. Some Spaniards readily embrace this view, since it allows them easily to defend the departure of Saint James for Spain as having taken place shortly after the Lord’s resurrection, even though it did not occur before the division of the other Apostles. Saint Clement of Rome seems to indicate this fairly clearly in his First Epistle to James, the brother of the Lord.

Others, moving to the opposite extreme, insist that the division was completed in the twelfth year after the same Passion. Among the most ancient authorities, Apollonius taught this through Eusebius, Book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 17; his words are:

> “He had received by tradition that the Savior had commanded his Apostles not to depart from Jerusalem for twelve years.”

Clement of Alexandria reports the same form of the command in Book VI of the *Stromata*: “After twelve years go out into the world, so that no one may say, ‘We did not hear.’” Bede follows this view in his *Martyrology*, and Usuard reports it through Molanus on 15 July.

Neither of these positions can stand with the truth. Against Theophanes’ claim stands Saint Luke in Acts 6, teaching that, after a great persecution against the Church arose following the death of the protomartyr Stephen, all were scattered except the Apostles. Since the martyr’s death occurred at the end of the year of human redemption, and the Apostles were not then scattered, it follows that their division did not occur immediately after the Lord’s Passion.

Against the statement of Apollonius and Clement stands the fact that Saint Mark closed his Gospel by asserting that, when he wrote it, the Apostles had gone forth and preached everywhere according to the Lord’s command, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed. It is certain and universally accepted that Mark the Evangelist wrote in the eleventh year after the Passion of Christ the Lord. Therefore the division of the Apostles could not have been postponed to the twelfth year, since in the eleventh they are found not only divided but also preaching throughout the whole world and performing many miracles.

Moreover, in the third year after his conversion Paul came to Jerusalem to visit his predecessors, the Apostles, as he himself acknowledges in Galatians 1; yet at that time he found there no one except Peter and James, the brother of the Lord. We shall discuss this matter below, in the year of Christ 38.

[Col. 0087D] Perhaps in order to avoid these difficulties, other authors, steering away from both extremes, chose a middle course. Among them was Melito, bishop of Sardica—or the author of the little work on the Dormition of the Virgin that appears in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers* under Melito’s name. He holds that the Apostles’ division fell in the second year [Col. 0088A] after Christ’s death.

This opinion displeased Bede so greatly that he did not hesitate to call it false:

> “It is clear,” he says, “that the man who wrote that book lied when, presenting a work on the death of the Virgin under the name of Melito, bishop of Asia, he says that in the second year after the Lord’s Ascension all the Apostles were divided throughout the world, each to preach in his own province.”

Bede confirms this by the testimony of Luke in Acts 8: “All were scattered except the Apostles.” If the Apostles were not scattered in that first persecution, then they were certainly not divided from one another throughout the whole period of that persecution, which lasted at least through the entire second year after Christ’s death.

Add that they had received the command to preach to the Jews before they were scattered throughout the world for the conversion of the Gentiles. Therefore they had first to devote themselves seriously to preaching in Jerusalem and in the other cities of the Jewish people.

From this arose another opinion of Genebrard, who in Book 3 of his *Chronology*, under the year of Christ 46, postponed the Apostles’ division to the seventh year after [Col. 0088B] Christ’s death. But he does not show why he chose the seventh year rather than the fifth or sixth. The solution of this difficulty depends upon what follows.

### 12. “On the last day of June,” etc.

There is no less disagreement concerning the day on which this sacred division of the whole world among the Apostles took place. Prochorus, Saint John’s disciple, asserts in his history that, among the other events occurring at this division, the first was the election and consecration of James the Less as bishop of Jerusalem.

This is not surprising, since that was the lot of this Apostle. According to Eusebius in his *Chronicle*, under the year 34, Saint James was consecrated on 27 December—a date followed by Rabanus in his *Martyrology*, as cited by Canisius in Volume 6 of the *Antiquae Lectiones*. It therefore follows that the division of the Apostles itself took place on that same day.

Nevertheless, nearly all the authors of Martyrologies assert that the division of the Apostles fell on 15 July: Bede, Ado, Usuard, and Molanus. So too does the Greek *Menologion*, in these words:

> “On 15 July, the feast of all the Apostles, when they were divided from one another; on this feast Chrysostom and the other Fathers delivered sermons.”

Peter of Equilinum, the bishop, also agrees, assigning it to that day. More importantly, the Roman Church formerly celebrated the same division in its ancient Breviary and Missal, singing the Epistle, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Romans 10), and the Gospel, “Go into all the world” (the last chapter of Matthew), as Equilinus notes in Book VI, chapter 99. Yet Dexter appears to differ considerably from both dates when he teaches that it occurred on the last day of June.

Both questions—of the day and of the year of the apostolic division—are easily resolved if we observe that the division, or allotment, of the provinces among the Apostles was not made and carried out on one and the same day. First, on the last day of June of the same year in which Christ died for us, the Apostles assembled together. Having received from him the command to travel throughout the whole world and preach the Gospel in every province of the earth, they cast lots among themselves for the provinces, so that each might know what burden of souls had been entrusted to him and might pray for their salvation without delay or interruption.

The allotment of the provinces, however, was not put into effect until the seventh year, as we shall soon say. For it was necessary first for all of them to devote themselves to the conversion of Jerusalem and the whole region of Judaea, to unite into one body and defend themselves against Jewish persecution, and to arrange the many things necessary for establishing the Catholic faith throughout the world—namely, matters concerning the celebration and administration of the sacraments and the governance of the whole Church.

Since so many and such great matters relating to the establishment of the Church could not be accomplished suddenly, but required first, as was proper, extensive discussion and mature judgment, Dexter correctly noted that “the divine allotment was made after deliberation.” Thus this apostolic council could not have been completed in one day or a few days, but necessarily occupied many.

Its memory came to be celebrated at Jerusalem and in the East on the day when it began, namely, 30 June, the last day of the month. The Greek *Menologion* bears witness to this, agreeing with Dexter, as follows:

> “On 30 June, the assembly of the twelve holy and blessed Apostles.”

Usuard, as cited by Molanus, also mentions this same feast and these words on that very day.

I would note incidentally that those are mistaken who thought that on this day the Greeks celebrated a feast of all the Apostles together, as though a single festive day were consecrated to all of them after the solemn celebrations previously held for their leaders, Peter and Paul. If that had been what the Greeks intended, they would not have said, “The assembly of the twelve Apostles,” but rather, “The feast of the Apostles.” For the word “assembly” signifies a council. They should also have observed that Saint Chrysostom preached his homily on the division of the Apostles to the people on this very day, as Molanus reports in his notes on the Ides of July, no. 3, in his *Usuard*.

What, then, was first done in this council was the division and allotment of the provinces, and this took place on the first day of the assembly. Afterwards, over many other days, they dealt with the Apostolic Constitutions and the canons concerning the sacraments. Then the consecration of James the Less—whose lot had assigned him the administration of Jerusalem—was celebrated on 27 December, the date assigned to it by Eusebius and Rabanus. Finally, when the Synagogue had been rejected and the door had been opened to the Gentiles, they separated from one another and departed, each to his own province.

This division of the Apostles from one another occurred on 15 July, according to the tradition preserved by the Church, which formerly used to celebrate this division on that day.

We shall show in its proper place, together with Dexter and Genebrard, that this division occurred in the seventh year after Christ’s death.

Someone may perhaps object: if they were not going to depart immediately, why did the Apostles divide the world so quickly? The scruple is easily removed by anyone who considers that the Apostles were not slow or lazy, but provident and exceedingly diligent. Besides, each of them had to be equipped and prepared for the work to which he had been called and to pray for his own sheep. In the meantime, many matters concerning particular provinces could arise—as I shall now say regarding Spain.

If this seems difficult to anyone, I shall ask him: if the Apostles were not supposed to be scattered into the world immediately after the Lord’s Passion, why, even before the coming of the Holy Spirit, did they cast lots and choose Matthias as an Apostle? While they were all living together, it seemed less necessary that there should be twelve rather than eleven. Whatever answer may be given to this question, I shall give the same answer to that objection.

Furthermore, it may be inferred that the division of the provinces took place shortly after the coming of the Holy Spirit, because no mention was made in it of Paul, to whom the conversion of the whole Gentile world was later entrusted. If he had been an Apostle at the time of the division, there is no doubt that he would have shared the allotment with the others.

Add that it is universally agreed that James was then appointed bishop of Jerusalem, when the provinces were allotted among all the Apostles; for Jerusalem itself fell by lot to James. This must have occurred before the death of Stephen, since Stephen exercised the diaconate under him, as Saint Ignatius testifies in his Epistle to the Trallians:

> “What are deacons except imitators of Christ, serving the bishop, just as Stephen served the most blessed James, Timothy and Titus served Paul, and Anacletus and Clement served Peter?”

He repeats the same statement in his Epistle to Heron. Indeed, Jerome says in his book *On Illustrious Men*, under James:

> “Immediately after the Lord’s Passion, he was ordained bishop of Jerusalem by the Apostles.”

### 13. “Forty-eight days”

I have restored this reading of Dexter, since the manuscript had corruptly read “thirty-eight days” after the coming of the Holy Spirit, when the apostolic assembly concerning the division of the world took place. For if, as is true and as Dexter states first, it was celebrated on the last day of June, not thirty-eight but forty-eight days intervened between that day and the coming of the Paraclete. Everyone knows that Christ’s death and the Pasch occurred that year on 25 March, and consequently Pentecost on 15 May, fifty days after the Pasch. From 15 May, when the Holy Spirit came, to 30 June, when the world was allotted among the Apostles, forty-eight days intervened.

### 14. “In the upper room of Zion,” etc.

Anselm appears to stand in the way of this, in his description of the Holy Land, recently printed by Canisius in Volume VI of the *Antiquae Lectiones*, where he says:

> “Forty paces from the place of Christ’s Ascension, the very ancient walls of a collapsing structure are still visible, at the place where the Apostles divided among themselves the provinces to which each was to go, and there composed the Creed.”

The allotment, therefore, was not made in the upper room of Zion but outside the city, at the place reported by Anselm.

This author, however, confuses the division of the provinces, which took place in the upper room, with the division of the Apostles from one another, which occurred at that place seven years later. He says that the basilica, or sacred site, had once been erected in memory of the most devout conversation that the Apostles held when at last they departed from one another.

The fact that they composed the Creed there, and not in the upper room of Zion—which was the house of Mary, the mother of John surnamed Mark—does not conflict with Dexter’s statements. Dexter was speaking not of the Creed but of the Apostolic Constitutions. How the twelve participated in the composition of the Creed, assigning individual articles of faith to individual Apostles, is discussed by Augustine in *Sermon 115 on Time*, Ambrose in *Sermon 38* toward the end, Rufinus in the work transmitted by Cyprian, and Venantius Fortunatus in his exposition of the same Creed.

### 15. “Spain fell by lot to Saint James, son of Zebedee,” etc.

It is not so certain which province of the world fell by divine lot to each Apostle, since we do not possess a certain ecclesiastical testimony on the matter. Nor is it the same thing for an Apostle to have preached the Gospel in one place or another and to have received that place as his allotted province. Each of them taught not merely one region of the world, but many, often extremely distant ones. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that each devoted himself especially to the conversion of the region entrusted to him.

Thus Dexter very appropriately asserted that Spain fell to James, son of Zebedee, although James preached in Judaea and throughout the entire journey to Spain. He assigned Asia to his brother John, although many maintain that John also taught the Parthians the faith, on the basis of the title of his First Canonical Epistle, which was formerly read as addressed to the Parthians. He assigned Ethiopia to Matthew, although Isidore testifies that Matthew also enlightened Macedonia with the word of God. He assigned India to Thomas, although the Roman *Martyrology* sings that Thomas preached to the Parthians, Medes, Persians, Hyrcanians, and Brahmans. He assigned Scythia to Philip, who nevertheless, according to the same testimony, reached Hierapolis in Asia.

What Dexter adds concerning Gaul in the case of Philip, Baronius considers an error of the writer—in Isidore’s book *On the Death of the Fathers*—who likewise assigns Gaul to Philip. Baronius argues that the text should read [Col. 0091A] “Galatia,” which is a part of Phrygia bordering on Scythia. I too once found this convincing. For although the Apostles later visited many various and remote regions, it does not seem credible that, in the allotment of the world, several regions lying at the greatest distance from one another should have been assigned simultaneously to one man.

Nevertheless, that book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* is truly by Saint Isidore, as we shall prove below; and the same matter is again asserted in the hymn of Saint James the Apostle found in the Gothic Breviary, which the entire Church of Spain once used. Therefore the authority of both sources ought to carry great weight with everyone, especially since it is supported by the testimony of the ancients.

In addition to those listed by Dexter, add Andrew, to whom Thrace and Achaea fell; Bartholomew, to whom Armenia and the other part of India, on Thomas’s side, were assigned; Simon, to whom Egypt fell; Thaddaeus, to whom Mesopotamia and Persia fell; and Matthias, whose particular harvest was Judaea. We may omit James the Less, who presided only over the city of Jerusalem, and also Peter, prince of the Apostles, who, although appointed shepherd of all, nevertheless preached first in Asia and then in the West.

Accordingly, the division reported by Peter of Equilinum in Book VI, chapter 99, is sufficiently consistent with reason: the world was divided into four regions, so that the East fell to Thomas and Bartholomew, both of whom preached in India; the South fell to Simon and Matthew, the former carrying the Gospel to Egypt and the latter to Ethiopia; the North fell to Philip and Thaddaeus, Scythia belonging to the former and Mesopotamia to the latter; and the West fell to Peter and James, whose provinces were Italy and Spain. The center of the world belonged to Matthias and James the Just, of whom the former undertook the instruction of Judaea and the latter that of the holy city.

Finally, the provinces of the Mediterranean belonged to John and Andrew, since the regions they taught—Asia Minor, Thrace, and Achaea—lie beside the Mediterranean Sea.

As for the noble provinces of Gaul and Britain, it should be said that they fell to James the Greater and Peter, whose concern was the conversion of the West. Hence Dexter later admits that James preached not only in Spain but also in Gaul and Britain, although not as earnestly as in Spain. Innocent, in his Epistle to Decentius, assigns the faith of Gaul to Peter.

Authors say that Simon the Cananaean also went to Britain for the sake of preaching, from Egypt and Africa, where he had been living: Dorotheus in his *Synopsis*, the Greek *Menologion*, and Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 40. No mention is made of Paul or Barnabas in the allotment of the world, because Paul had not yet been converted to the faith, and consequently neither had been enrolled in the apostolate.

Bede discusses the same division in his *Collectanea*; Saint Julian of Toledo in his commentary on Nahum, Volume II of the *Supplement to the Library of the Ancient Fathers*; Thomas of Cantimpré in Book II of *On Bees*, chapter 25; and the hymn of Saint James, which we shall reproduce below from the Gothic Breviary. Metellus, a monk of Tegernsee, treats it most elegantly in his *Quirinalia*, in Peter Canisius, Volume I of the *Antiquae Lectiones*. He was living in the year of the Lord 1060.

This author therefore describes the division of the Apostles according to the four regions of the world, as Equilinus had done, under the title: “How Persia, formerly devoted to paganism, once received the faith through the Apostles.” For the benefit of learned readers, I gladly append his words:

> Once the Lydian realms,  
> Persia with its princes and royal offspring,  
> Subdued in the primitive age of the Church,  
> Gave themselves to the faith.  
>   
> Through the vigorous deeds of the Apostles,  
> The whole world gladly received  
> The laws of the Lord from heaven.  
>   
> From the borders of India, where the Sun  
> Gives the day its beginning,  
> Thomas possessed those lands.  
>   
> As far as the Spaniards enclosed  
> Beneath the axis of the setting star,  
> James instructed them.  
>   
> From the perpetual cold of the Scythians,  
> Enduring for all ages,  
> Philip had carried [the faith].  
>   
> As far as the regions near Perusia,  
> The dark-skinned Ethiopians  
> Matthew sanctifies.  
>   
> The whole world had now learned  
> The teachings of salvation;  
> Abandoning barbarism,  
> It drank in the discipline of the Catholic religion.

This is what he says. He teaches that the preaching of the East ended with Thomas in India, that of the West with James in Spain, that of the North with Philip in Scythia, and that of the South with Matthew in Ethiopia.

### 16. “James, the brother of the Lord,” etc.

Anacletus, in his Epistle to the Bishops of Italy, states that James was consecrated bishop of Jerusalem by three of Christ’s Apostles: Peter, James the Greater, and John. From this arose the rule that a bishop should not be ordained except by three bishops, as may be seen in Gratian; in Clement of Alexandria, Book VI of the *Hypotyposeis*; and in Eusebius [Col. 0092B] Book II, chapter 1.

This should not be understood to mean that Saint James, the brother of the Lord, was then ordained bishop as though he had not already been ordained by Christ the Lord together with the other Apostles. Rather, the solemn ceremonies were then celebrated for the first time, as an example for the rest who were to be newly ordained, although the holy Apostles themselves often created bishops without the assistance of others, by the laying on of hands alone.

Eusebius and Rabanus, as we said above, handed down that James’s solemn institution took place on 27 December.

### 17. “The holy Virgin,” etc.

This was especially fitting to the majesty of the Mother of God. Dexter was careful not to say absolutely that she served as president of the apostolic college, for that office belonged to Peter, the vicar of Christ, and not to a woman. Rather, he says that she presided in that sacred assembly by her counsel in doubtful matters, by the light of her teaching in the mysteries of the faith—revealing many of its secrets, which she alone had experienced—and by the wondrous example of her life.

It is most consistent with reason to believe that they undertook no serious matter without her counsel and direction. It is certain, above all, that she was always present at the sacred assemblies. For concerning the first assembly of all, in which Matthias was elected an Apostle, we have an explicit statement in Acts 1, where Luke says of the Apostles:

> “All these were persevering with one accord in prayer, with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus.”

Her presence at the coming of the Holy Spirit is likewise clear from Acts 2:

> “When the days of Pentecost were completed, they were all together in the same place.”

There the word “all” signifies those of whom Luke had said that “all were persevering,” and so forth, together with Mary the mother of Jesus.

The remaining assemblies may be inferred from Acts 2, which says that “all who believed were together,” and from the following words in Acts 5:

> “They were all together with one accord; but none of the others dared join them.”

If none of the faithful was absent at that time, how could the mother of the Lord have been absent?

Moreover, the principal reason why the blessed Virgin’s life was prolonged after her Son’s death was that she might encourage the apostolic college by her presence and advance the beginnings of the nascent Church. Thus the blessed Ignatius, in his First Epistle to John, calls her the teacher of the new religion:

> “She is the teacher of our new religion and repentance.”

In the Litanies she is called “Queen of the Apostles”; indeed, the Fathers also call her “the illuminator of the Apostles.” Among them are Rupert of Deutz, the abbot; the Idiota in *On the Contemplation of the Virgin*, chapter 3; Antoninus, Part IV of the *Summa Theologica*, title 17; the blessed Bridget in *On the Excellence of the Virgin*, prayer 1; and, in addition to these, Augustine, in Sermon 6 on the Nativity, toward the end, calls her “the teacher of the nations.” See also Galatinus, Book VII of *On the Secrets*, chapters 4 and 12.

### 18. “The seven Apostles,” etc.

Luke reports in Acts 6 that the election of the first seven deacons in the Church took place this year.
