It arose from a complaint by the Greek disciples against the Hebrews, because their widows were being neglected in the daily ministry—that is, the Greek widows were not being supplied with daily food in the same way as the Hebrew widows.

The greater part of the disciples were Hebrews and the smaller part Greeks, although all were sons of Moses and of the circumcision: the former had been born in Judaea or Galilee, while the latter had been born in Greece, in the Dispersion.

That the issue concerned food is clear from the fact that, when the Apostles assembled the disciples—namely, those who were complaining—they said to them:

> “It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables.”

This was as though they had said: “Devoted to the preaching of the Gospel, we cannot also serve the tables, so that everything may be distributed equally to all without distinction between Hebrew and Greek.”

Therefore they ordered the disciples to choose from among themselves seven men of excellent reputation, to whom they might entrust the care of their widows, so that the Apostles would not be hindered in preaching.

They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte from Antioch. They set them before the Apostles, who prayed and laid their hands upon them—that is, they ordained them deacons by the laying on of hands.

All of them, therefore, were chosen from among the Greeks, as Dexter noted, and this is sufficiently clear from the context of the apostolic history, especially from the words:

> “Choose from among you seven men of good reputation.”

The Greek expression τὸ ἐξ ὑμῶν—“from among you”—refers to those whom the Apostles wished the disciples to appoint. These were Greeks, who had brought their case against the Hebrews before the Apostles.

### 19. “He flourishes at that time,” etc.

Above, Dexter had reported the conversion of this holy centurion. He now teaches that the centurion had gone to Spain, where he flourished with an uncommon reputation for holiness, being the first of all to announce to the Spaniards Christ’s death, which the general and wondrous eclipse had signaled and which they themselves had witnessed with astonishment.

### 20.

In place of the words “Caius Oppius the centurion, son of Cornelius, likewise a centurion,” the manuscript had most corruptly read: “Caius Oppius, son of Caius, father, centurion.” I have restored the word *likewise* in place of *father* and explained the meaning of the letters C. F. C.

### 21. “From among the Gentiles,” etc.

That he was the first of the Gentiles to believe after Christ’s death is clear from the Gospel:

> “When the centurion saw that he had expired while crying out in this way, he glorified God.”

This does not exclude the possibility that others had believed before Christ’s death, such as his father, Cornelius the centurion of Capernaum, and the Canaanite woman. We shall explain under the year of Christ 40 what is meant by the statement concerning Cornelius of Italica, that he was the first-fruits of the Gentile people, even though that event occurred six years later.

The holy Doctors wrote many laudatory statements in praise of this centurion. Jerome contrasts Arius—otherwise a Christian—with the confession of this Gentile:

> “From this it should be considered that, in the very scandal of the Passion, the centurion truly confesses the Son of God, while Arius preaches in the Church that he is a creature.”

Jerome adds:

> “The last now become first: the Gentile people confess, while blinded Judaea denies, lest the last error become worse than the first.”

Theophylact says:

> “Thus the order is reversed: the Jews kill, the disciples flee, and the Gentile confesses.”

And again:

> “Now what the Lord had said appears to have been fulfilled: ‘When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself.’ For, lifted up on the cross, he drew the thief and the centurion.”

Bede says:

> “The Gentiles who fear God glorify him with an open voice of confession; the Jews, merely beating their breasts, return home in silence. Hence the faith of the Church is rightly represented by the centurion, for while the Synagogue is silent, the Church affirms the Son of God.”

But enough on this subject.

### 22. “Who was a Roman citizen,” etc.

This does not mean that he was born at Rome, but that he was born in a city enjoying Roman privileges. Otherwise, being Spanish by origin, he was born at Malaga and had a Corinthian home, as the same Dexter testifies under the year of Christ 70.

### 23. “And having been baptized by the blessed Barnabas,” etc.

The meaning is not that Caius Oppius was baptized by the blessed Barnabas—although he remained attached to him as a disciple for some time. [Col. 0094B] He was regenerated in Christ by the waters of baptism at Malaga in Spain by James, son of Zebedee, as Dexter himself teaches under the year 52. There, although he is not called by his proper name but “the centurion of Malaga,” it is stated below, under the year 70, that he is the same as Caius Oppius.

For there it is asserted that the centurion of Malaga later became the third bishop of Milan, which is now said of Caius Oppius. The meaning, therefore, is: “And having been baptized”—that is, after he had been baptized—“he was made the third bishop of Milan by the blessed Barnabas.”

This is entirely true. The first bishop of Milan was Saint Barnabas the Apostle, as Hippolytus the Martyr reports in his book *On the Seventy-Two Disciples*, and Dorotheus in his *Synopsis*, and—most importantly—the Roman *Martyrology* on 25 September, where, concerning the second bishop of Milan, it says:

> “On the same day, Saint Anathalon, bishop, who, as a disciple of the blessed Apostle Barnabas, succeeded him as bishop of the Church of Milan.”

The Milanese Church records testify that Saint Caius, also a disciple of Barnabas, succeeded Anathalon as the third bishop after the blessed Barnabas. Baronius reproduces these records in his notes on 17 September. On that day the Roman *Martyrology* says of him:

> “At Milan, Saint Caius, bishop, a disciple of the blessed Apostle Barnabas, who baptized the holy Gervasius and Protasius, suffered much during the persecution of Nero, and rested in peace.”

Galesinus gives this account somewhat more precisely in his *Martyrology* on the same day. In his notes he asserts that he took the life of Saint Caius from the records of the Milanese Church preserved in the Ambrosian Basilica of the monks of the Cistercian order.

Cardinal Baronius, however, admits that he read a manuscript life of Caius, composed by Andrea Alciato, in the possession of Cardinal Alciato.

We shall treat the remaining matters together with Dexter in their proper places. For now it is enough to have established that Caius was the third bishop of Milan, which Dexter now asserts. The fact that the Milanese records have not hitherto recognized their Caius as the same centurion who believed in Christ dying on the cross should cause us no difficulty, since they do not deny it. We owe it to Dexter that he remembered both men.

### A. D. 34. A. R. 785

Christ the Savior of the World, accused, is brought before Pilate.

### A. D. 34. A. R. 785

Claudia Procula, Pilate’s wife, warned in a dream, believes in Christ and obtains salvation.

[Col. 0071] A. D. 34. A. R. 785

Christ our Lord, led to the cross and crucified on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, willingly undergoes death for the salvation of the whole human race, through the envy of the Jews.

A.D. 34. A.R. 785. An eclipse of the sun; and darkness covers the earth.

[Col. 0073] A.D. 34. A.R. 785. C. Oppius, a Spanish centurion, believes in Christ dying on the cross.

[Col. 0077] A.D. 34. A.R. 785. Pilate decides to write to Tiberius about Christ’s death and miracles.

[Col. 0079] A.D. 34. A.R. 785. Saint Petronilla, ten years old, flourishes as the daughter born from the marriage of Saint Peter the Apostle.

[Col. 0081] A.D. 34. A.R. 785. On the twenty-seventh day of March, before dawn, Christ, having conquered death and wondrously stripped the infernal regions, rises again from the dead, restored to life and victorious.

A.D. 34. A.R. 785. Herod Antipas, together with Herodias, his incestuous concubine, expelled from all Judea, goes first into exile in Gaul and then at Ilerda in Spain, where he dies miserably.

[Col. 0083] A.D. 34. A.R. 785. Herodias, while dancing upon the Sicoris, the river of Ilerda, which had frozen over with ice, is submerged and perishes miserably.

[Col. 0085] A.D. 34. A.R. 785. Caius Cornelius, the Capernaum centurion and master of the servant whom the Lord healed, and also the father of C. Oppius the Spanish centurion, flourishes wonderfully in Spain.

A.D. 34. A.R. 785. On the last day of June, the holy Apostles of God, approximately forty-eight days after the coming of the Holy Spirit, assemble in the upper room on Zion, which was the house of Mary, the mother of John surnamed Mark. After deliberation, by divine lot they divide among themselves the provinces of the world for the purpose of preaching. Spain falls to Saint James the son of Zebedee, Asia to John, Ethiopia to Matthew, India to Thomas, Scythia and Gaul to Philip. At this time the canons are issued and the apostolic constitutions composed, for the ordering of the Sacraments and of the whole Church.

[Col. 0091] A.D. 34. A.R. 785. James, the brother of the Lord, is made the first Bishop of Jerusalem. The Holy Virgin presides over the apostolic college through her counsel, the light of her teaching, and the wondrous example of her life; and they undertake nothing serious that they do not undertake by her counsel and direction.

[Col. 0093] A.D. 34. A.R. 785. The Apostles appoint seven apostolic deacons, all of them Greeks.

A.D. 34. A.R. 785. At this time in Spain C. Oppius, a centurion, the son of Cornelius, likewise a centurion, flourishes. At Jerusalem, amid the crashing of rocks striking against one another and the day being covered with darkness, he proclaims that Christ, dying, is the Son of God. Of the Gentiles, he was the first Christian centurion to believe after Christ’s death. He was a Roman citizen, and, after being baptized, was made the third Bishop of Milan by Blessed Barnabas: a truly apostolic man, who was the first of all to report to the Spaniards, his own people, Christ’s death and the astonishing eclipse, to the amazement of his hearers.

[Note: [Col. 0094D]]

### A.D. 35

**1. “Stephen having been stoned,” etc.** Since the death of the Lord Christ occurred while he was completing the thirty-fourth year of his age, and Stephen suffered martyrdom in that same year not long after the Lord’s Ascension, as the Roman Martyrology sings on December 26, how can what Dexter now reports stand—namely, that Stephen was stoned in the thirty-fifth year of Christ? We answer the matter easily: both statements are entirely true. For if we speak of the solar year, the deaths of Christ and Stephen occurred in precisely the same year: Christ’s on March 25, and Stephen’s on December 26. If, however, we speak of the years of the Lord Christ, he himself died while he was in his thirty-fourth year, whereas Stephen died on the second day of the thirty-fifth year, because, after the preceding birthday had completed thirty-four, he had begun his thirty-fifth year.

**2. “A great persecution,” etc.** Luke has the following concerning this in chapter 8 of Acts: “And on that day there arose a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the Apostles.” That this day of persecution was the martyrdom of Saint Stephen is shown by what follows immediately: “And devout men took care of Stephen” (that is, they buried him after embalming him with spices), “and made great lamentation over him.”

That Dexter numbers more than fifteen thousand fugitives, whereas Blessed Luke does not give the number of those scattered at this point, should not seem remarkable, since it can be inferred from what the holy Evangelist himself reports there. For at Peter’s first sermon, delivered on the very day of Pentecost before the entire multitude, “there were added,” he says, “about three thousand souls” to the faith on that day (Acts 2). At the second sermon preached by the chief of the Apostles, prompted by the power and integrity granted to the lame man, “many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand” (Acts 4).

In a similar proportion, not only through Peter’s preaching but also through that of the other Apostles, and not merely through the display of one miracle but through the many signs and wonders that the Apostles performed, the number of the faithful increased daily more and more. Thus, after first stating in chapter 5 that “many signs and wonders were done among the people by the hands of the Apostles,” Luke adds: “And the multitude of those who believed in the Lord increased still more, both men and women,” so greatly that they boldly and courageously brought out the sick into the streets and placed them on beds and pallets, so that when Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow some of them and they might be delivered from their illnesses.

Not only did many of the citizens of Jerusalem believe; a multitude also came from the neighboring cities, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits to Jerusalem, and all were healed. Who would say that all these people came without faith?

Finally, after the election of the deacons, Luke says in Acts 6: “The word of God increased, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem; and a great multitude of priests obeyed the faith.” No one, therefore, should find it incredible that, at the time of the first persecution, the number of believing men had risen to fifteen thousand. Since Luke tells us that all were driven from Jerusalem except the Apostles, Dexter was not wrong to report that more than fifteen thousand men were expelled from there.

**3. “Some to Asia.”** Since the sacred text tells us that all were scattered through the regions of Judea and Samaria, how can Dexter’s statement stand: “Some come to Asia, others to Europe”? The answer is that all first went into the regions of Judea or Samaria, as Luke teaches; afterward, however, it is clear that some went on to other places. For after the passage already cited he adds: “Therefore those who were scattered went about preaching the word of God.”

Where some of them reached is shown in chapter 11: “And those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch.” We also learn from the apostolic Acts themselves, in chapter 9, that Ananias the disciple who baptized Paul was established not in Judea or Samaria but in Damascus, a city of Syria.

It is also reasonable to believe that many of them returned to their native regions in order to preach the kingdom of God to their fellow citizens. Some had originated in Asia and others in Europe, since they had been converted from the day of Pentecost onward. On that day there were present at Peter’s preaching Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and inhabitants of Mesopotamia, Cappadocia, Pontus, and Asia Minor—all regions included within Greater Asia. Besides these, Roman newcomers were also present. By that name they called all Italians and those who used the Roman language, especially Spaniards, as Josephus himself testifies; Baronius quotes his words in volume 1, under the year of the Lord 72:

> “The clemency of the Romans granted to all not a small gift of their name, not only to individual men but also collectively to the greatest nations. Thus the ancient Spaniards, Tyrrhenians, and Sabines are called Romans.”

Augustine says the same in Psalm 58: “All have become Romans, and all are called Romans.”

That some are said to have come to Europe is supported by the considerable example of Mary Salome, the wife of Zebedee. Driven out in this very persecution, she withdrew into Italy and, exhausted by her journey at Verulae among the Hernici, died in peace, as the ancient records of the Church of Verulae relate, where her venerable body is reverently preserved. Cardinal Baronius uses this example in his notes on July 25 to explain the words, “They were all scattered through the regions of Judea and Samaria,” although we shall discuss the matter more fully in its proper place.

**4. “Of these, more than,” etc.** We know from the testimony cited in chapter 11 of Acts that the greater part of the fugitives traveled as far as Cyprus: “And those who had been scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus.” This is not surprising, since the Evangelist adds: “Now some of them were Cypriot men.”

That Blessed Barnabas was among those who went to Cyprus is established by the Roman Martyrology on June 11. From the same source it is also learned, on the following June 29, that Mary, the mother of John surnamed Mark, whose house was the apostolic upper room, fled there and found rest there.

That a large part of the fugitives sailed from Cyprus to Spain is made exceedingly probable by the fact that there was very frequent navigation from Asia through Cyprus to Spain. The Tyrians and Phoenicians had founded many considerable cities along the coast for the sake of conducting trade, as is reported by Quintus Curtius, book 5 on the deeds of Alexander, chapter 12; Strabo, book 3 of the *Geography*; Plutarch in the *Life of Scipio*; Solinus, *On the Wonders of the World*, chapter 34; Pomponius Mela; and others, who count among the Tyrian foundations in Spain Carthaea, Gades, Abdera, and Malaca, and, on the opposite African shore, Carthage, of which Spanish Carthage was a daughter. The disciples of the Apostles are said to have gone there.

It is highly consistent with reason that those seeking escape hired a ship in which they might flee to the most remote regions, and that they first found a merchant vessel available for hire and boarded it as it was departing for Spain. To this it may be added that many of the fugitives were natives of that region, as we shall soon show, and that others—especially Europeans—could readily have joined them.

That they landed at the harbor of Carthage in Spain was due to the renown of that most famous emporium, which even to this day is frequented by merchant ships and triremes. Livy once described the Carthaginian harbor in book 6, using these words:

> “Carthage is situated as follows. There is a bay of the sea, almost midway along the coast of Spain, most exposed to the southwest wind, extending five hundred paces inland and somewhat more than that in breadth. At the mouth of this bay, a small island lying offshore makes the harbor safe from every wind except the southwest. From the innermost part of the bay a peninsula projects—the very hill on which the city was founded—bounded by the sea on the east and south. On the west a lagoon closes it, extending somewhat toward the north, of uncertain depth; and when the sea rises or falls, a narrow ridge about two hundred and fifty paces wide joins the city to the mainland.”

**5. “Divided throughout Spain,” etc.** Nothing is more credible than what Dexter announces here: namely, that those who had fled and landed at the harbor of Carthage, divided among the various regions of Spain, announced to the Spaniards what they had seen with their own eyes concerning the death, resurrection, teaching, and miracles of the Lord Christ. They added that his most holy Mother was still alive, thereby inflaming in them the desire to see her.

No one should be surprised at the Spaniards’ pilgrimage to the Blessed Mother of God. At that time nothing was more customary among the faithful of all nations than, out of the greatest fervor of faith, to undertake a journey to Palestine and venerate the holy places of our redemption; this had always been customary in the Church. If the practice was later observed with such perseverance even when the charity of the faithful had grown cold, how much more must it have been observed in the time of the nascent Church, when the fervor of faith burned exceptionally in Christian hearts!

Who would not see that the desire to visit and converse with the Blessed Virgin, the Mother of the Redeemer himself, must have impelled Christians in a remarkable way to undertake that pilgrimage? Would you like me to offer some evidence of this? I cite the words of Saint Ignatius the Martyr, who says the following in a letter to the Apostle John:

> “There are also here many of our women who desire to see Mary Jesus and who wish to hurry daily from us to you, so that they may touch her and handle her breasts, which nourished the Lord Jesus, and ask Mary Jesus about certain more private matters. There is also Salome, the daughter whom you love, who spent a year and five months with her at Jerusalem. Some perhaps have informed you that this same Mother of God, abundant in every grace and fruitful in every virtue and grace, is cheerful in persecutions and afflictions, not complaining in poverty and need, gracious toward those who wrong her, rejoicing in troublesome circumstances, suffering with the wretched and afflicted and not slow to help them. Against the deadly conflicts of vices, she shines forth in the struggle of faith. She is the teacher of our new religion and repentance, and among the faithful the minister of every work of piety. She is devoted to the humble and humbles herself more devotedly before the devoted. She is wonderfully magnified by all, even while she is slandered by the scribes and Pharisees.”

[Col. 0097D] Moreover, many—namely, those who had traveled there, seen her, and spoken with her—report many things about her. Nevertheless, we do not dare to believe everything about everything, nor to relate it to you; but, as it has been told to us by trustworthy persons, “in Mary Jesus the nature of human nature is joined to angelic holiness.”

And such things stirred our inmost being and compelled us greatly to desire the sight of this—if it is lawful to say so—heavenly marvel and most sacred wonder. He added a second letter concerning the same matter, beginning as follows:

> “If it is permitted me with you, I wish to go up to the regions of Jerusalem and see the holy faithful who are there, especially Mary Jesus, whom they say is admired by all and desired by everyone. For who, if he is a friend of our faith and religion, would not delight in seeing and addressing her who gave birth from herself to the true God?”

What Ignatius reports caused the faithful to undertake pilgrimages even from the most distant provinces, so that they might behold with their own eyes, as far as possible, what they had heard with their ears. Who, if he were now granted the opportunity to speak with and see her alive, just as the most blessed Mother of God was then alive, would not make such a journey?

In favor of the pilgrimage that the Spaniards are said to have made to her, it may also be added that they had always been exceedingly eager to see great things and, for that reason, were willing to travel to the remotest regions of the world whenever necessary. The histories of the ancients provide us with many examples of this, showing that they undertook such journeys for lesser matters.

To give one example, Saint Jerome writes to Paulinus:

> “We read that certain noblemen came from the farthest borders of Spain to Livy, flowing with a milky fountain of eloquence; and those whom Rome had not drawn to contemplate herself were brought there by the fame of one man.”

After hearing of the fame of the great Antony, many Spaniards also penetrated the most remote deserts in order to see him, as Saint Athanasius records in his life:

> “He showed us a man hidden in almost another world and placed amid the immense solitudes of Africa and Spain.”

Again, was it not remarkable to see a man living upon a pillar? Theodoret likewise teaches in the life of Simeon Stylites that Spaniards had traveled there among others, saying:

> “There one may see a sea of men arriving from every direction and converging like rivers. Not only our own people come, but also Ishmaelites, Persians, their neighboring Armenians, Iberians, Homerites, and even more inland peoples. Many also come from those who inhabit the farthest West—namely, Spaniards, Britons, and Gauls, who lie between them; to speak of Italy would be superfluous.”

But enough of this.

**6. “Of these, the first,” etc.** Since the faithful driven out in this first persecution were the firstfruits of the faith in Spain, there is no doubt that Saint James chose Apostles from among them and that they joined him while he was preaching in Spain. Paul also taught that bishops should be selected from those who were older and more approved in the Church, when he wrote to Timothy:

> “The bishop must be blameless, not a novice, lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil.”

**7. “The Spaniards, especially the Jews,” etc.** Jews and Gentiles lived together in Spain. Anyone who knows how favorably disposed they were toward the Lord will readily believe that both groups, inflamed by the preaching or reports of the fugitives from Jerusalem concerning Christ’s miracles and teaching, desired to be more fully instructed in the matters just mentioned concerning him.

Dexter later reports, under the year 37, that the Spanish Jews who inhabited Carpetania—what we now call the kingdom of Toledo—received letters from the Jerusalem authorities seeking their agreement concerning Christ’s death. They not only refused to consent to his killing but also sent letters in reply dissuading the Jerusalem authorities from so great a crime.

I have learned that what Dexter teaches here was commonly said and accepted in that very kingdom of Toledo long before his *Chronicle* was discovered. This is not surprising, since we read that letters of this kind had been deposited in the public archives of the city of Toledo by royal authority under the great Alfonso VI, emperor of Spain.

Julian, archpriest of Saint Justa and the distinguished historian of that same Alfonso, offers important testimony to the antiquity of this tradition in his *Chronicle*, which the most illustrious Count of Mora kindly lent me in manuscript. Here are Julian’s words concerning the year of Christ 36 and the monuments of Saint James that exist at Toledo:

> “I found in the same archive of Saint Justa of Toledo two or three letters in Hebrew, Arabic, and Latin. One of them was from the Jews of Jerusalem to the Hebrew Spaniards, especially those of Toledo and Zamora, asking them to support the death of Christ the Savior. The Jews who had come from Jerusalem to Toledo had built there the most celebrated synagogue in all Spain and the world, unwilling to return to Jerusalem because they had heard that the Temple, once rebuilt, would again be destroyed. And they absolutely refused to consent to the killing of the most innocent Jesus. The Toledans sent a reply with their messengers to the Jerusalemites, refusing to consent to their requests. One of them was called Athanasius and another Joseph. Athanasius later came with Blessed James to Spain.”

The rest of Julian’s account we shall insert in its proper place.

Antonius Beuterus also relates this history in his *Chronicle of Aragon*, as does the no less diligent, learned, and distinguished Don Juan de Salazar in his *Apology for the Coming of Saint James*, chapter 10. There he cites another letter discovered a hundred years ago in the church of Metinaecampensis, in which the Jews of Jerusalem grant our Zamorans permission to interpret the books of Moses, although they were unworthy of such a favor, because, they say, “they did not subscribe to that decree concerning the death of the Transgressor”—that is, because in their written responses they did not consent to the decree concerning the Lord’s death. This letter is carefully preserved there.

All this agrees in every respect with Dexter’s words, which are as follows:

> “The Spanish Jews, especially the Carpetanians—that is, the Toledans—who, after receiving letters from the Jerusalem authorities seeking their agreement concerning Christ’s death, had detested those letters, are converted, gladly receiving the preaching of Saint James.”

This may be understood as having happened in several ways. Perhaps not all the judges of the council and elders of the people had consented to the sentence imposing death upon Christ. At least this is certain concerning Gamaliel, and it is reported concerning certain others in an image of that trial recently printed at Paris, if it is worthy of belief. It is also certain concerning Nicodemus, according to John’s testimony. For that reason, they may have thought it necessary to consult those living in Spain, so that, with their votes added, the death might be carried out.

This, however, must have occurred in the preceding year if a reply was to be awaited. Thus such letters did not issue from the final council held against the Lord, but from another council about which John says in chapter 7:

> “After this Jesus walked in Galilee, for he would not walk in Judea, because the Jews sought to kill him. Now the Jews’ feast of Tabernacles was near,”

a feast celebrated from September 15, at least six months and more before the Crucifixion.

Alternatively, if the letters had issued from the final council, they were not certain about the time of the death. The judge could have delayed it for a considerable period, and therefore they wished meanwhile to draw their absent brothers over to their opinion. Whether the decree of death was carried out before the messengers returned or not, the exchange of letters would have been more useful than harmful. If the decree had not been executed when the messengers returned, they would have had—as they believed—a multitude of new votes with which to confront the Judge more securely, while also claiming that the Jews living at such a distance were so hostile to him that they judged him worthy of death. If the sentence had already been carried out, at least they would have warned them in advance not to dissent from their judgment.

Their expectation nevertheless deceived them, as we have said. They could extract nothing less from the Spanish Jews than consent; rather, the Spanish Jews detested their envious purpose and designs and sent letters and messengers to them to say so.

Lest anyone be surprised on hearing that the Jerusalem Jews wrote to the Spaniards concerning Christ’s death, I shall add the testimony of Saint Justin the Martyr, who lived close to the time of the Apostles. In his book *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, he charges the Jew Trypho with having sent messengers not merely to Spain but throughout all the provinces of the world to forestall the preaching of the Apostles:

> “For no other nations,” he says, “are as guilty as you are of the iniquity committed against us and Christ himself. You have even become the authors of prejudice against that Just One and against us, who are called by his name. After you had led to the cross that one blameless and just man, by whose wounds healing comes to those who approach the Father through him, and after you had learned that he had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, just as the prophecies had foretold, you were so far from repenting and being moved to penitence for the evils you had committed that you even chose distinguished men from Jerusalem and sent them throughout the whole earth, saying that the sect and heresy of the Christians honored no divinity—that is, according to the Greek text, that they were atheists—and spreading such reports against us that all who do not know us repeat them. Thus you were not merely yourselves guilty of iniquity, but also made all other mortals everywhere so. And Isaiah rightly cries out: ‘Because of you my name is blasphemed among the Gentiles.’ You therefore diligently labored to ensure that darkness and injustice would be proclaimed throughout the entire world against the one blameless and just light sent by God to mortals.”

Thus far Justin. Oecumenius wrote similar things in his commentary on the final chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, citing ancient historians and stating that this had long before been foretold through Isaiah in chapter 18. He says:

> “Before Paul came to Rome, the Jews who were there had been warned not to admit the preaching of Christ; and not only they, but also all the Jews who were everywhere throughout the world. How is this clear? In the writings of the ancients we find that the priests, scribes, and elders who were in Jerusalem sent letters to the Jews who were everywhere, ordering them not to admit the teaching of Christ, which they calumniated as being alien to God—that is, as atheistic. This too seems to be signified by Isaiah’s prophecy, which says: ‘Woe to you, wings of ships, sending hostages beyond the rivers of Ethiopia into the sea, and papyrus letters upon the water.’ By these words the Prophet signifies that beyond the region of Ethiopia and to the farthest shores of the earth, the sound of the Jews’ wickedness was transmitted by ships as though they were flying things, and that their messengers, carrying papyrus letters, traveled upon the waters and sailed over the sea to every part of the world, calumniating the preaching of our Savior.”

For this reason, some say that many Gentiles came to believe that Christians were atheists. Those who branded the ancient Galicians with the charge of atheism may have had no other intention; indeed, those people themselves were among the first Spaniards to receive the faith of Christ through the preaching of the disciples of the Apostle Saint James.

Nor are there lacking those who contend that the prophecy of Isaiah just mentioned also refers to Spain. For it says that messengers were sent by the Jews to a terrible people, after whom there is no other; and this is fulfilled in Spain.

That the Jews everywhere took care to forestall the preaching of the Apostles was professed clearly enough by the Jews living at Rome when, in the final chapter of Acts, they said to Saint Paul:

> “As for this sect, we know that everywhere it is spoken against.”

Indeed, Saul in Acts 9 seems to have intended nothing else when:

> “He went to the high priest and asked him for letters to Damascus, to the synagogues, so that if he found any men or women belonging to this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.”

Without doubt he asked for this because other Jews, burning with zeal, were being sent into other regions.

How it came about that the Spaniards, and especially the Jews—as Dexter now asserts—sent messengers to the Apostles, asking that one of them come to them as soon as possible to instruct them more truly and fully concerning the matters just reported about Christ by the disciples driven from Jerusalem, we learn from the aforementioned Julian. Relating the letters he himself found at Toledo in the Archive of Saint Justa, he says:

> “The third letter, which existed only in Hebrew, was a reply. The Jerusalem Jews of priestly descent—Annas and Caiaphas, Joseph, and others—asked that, if the disciples of Christ came to Spain (for they said that James the son of Zebedee, his Apostle, was already coming), the Spaniards should in no way admit them, but should drive them from their cities as deceivers and vagabonds.”

I understand the report that James was coming to have arisen from the casting of lots and the division of the Apostles.

> “The Spaniards, however, sent Euphrasius and Indalecius, asking Peter and the other Apostles to send James immediately. When they came to Jerusalem, they gave their letters to Peter. After witnessing his miracles, they were converted and came with Blessed James. Since Christ had designated James for so honorable a mission, they gladly entrusted themselves to him. I translated these letters from Arabic into Spanish, and another Hebrew letter by order of the Most Serene Emperor Alfonso VI; I ordered them carefully deposited in the city archive of Toledo for preservation.”

Consider how greatly Satan envied the conversion of the Spaniards and how the members of his body, the Jerusalemite scribes and Pharisees, forestalled the Spanish Jews by defaming Christ’s Apostles, lest the Spaniards listen to them and submit to the faith when they came there. Yet by God’s great providence it came about that our people also sent messengers to the Apostles and asked for a teacher.

It should also be noted in passing how diligently the ancients worked to preserve and publish letters of this kind, which were translated in different ways for the various languages of Spain. First they were written in Hebrew; for the convenience of the Gentiles who, in Roman times, used Latin, they were translated into Latin; afterward they were translated into Arabic by those living under Arab rule; finally Julian translated them into Spanish for the convenience of the Catholics who had cast off the Moorish yoke.

I earnestly wish that the archives of Toledo might be searched, in case they should be found in one of them. They contain many monuments of antiquity written in Arabic, especially in the archive of the Holy Church, as the librarian himself assured me when I was there.

**8. “Then the Apostles,” etc.** In the printed edition the words “they recognized the disposition of the people of Spain to receive the faith of Christ” were missing. Yet the meaning of the sentence clearly requires these words or something similar. In place of the particle *Cognitamque* (“and having recognized it”), the reading *Cognitionemque* (“and the recognition”) had been printed, which could be retained neither grammatically nor in any meaningful sense.

**9. “And they had recognized it from those Gentiles,” etc.** Good heavens! Philip is the first of all to arrange for the Spaniards to be admitted to the grace of the Lord Christ! Is it surprising, then, that in later times Christ should place so many Philips over the Spaniards, men who would defend the Christian cause most fervently and strive to bring the remotest nations to knowledge of it?

We read this not only in Dexter but also in Julian, who says under the aforementioned year 36:

> “From the Archive of Saint Justa of Toledo we learn that many Gentiles who had come to Jerusalem to pray at the holy Temple were Spaniards. They wished to see and speak with Jesus, desiring that he preach to the Gentiles of their own land.”

Saint John relates that this event took place immediately after the resurrection of Lazarus and Christ’s triumphant entry into Jerusalem. He says:

> “Now there were certain Gentiles among those who had come up to worship on the feast day. These therefore came to Philip and asked him, saying: ‘Sir, we wish to see Jesus.’ Philip comes and tells Andrew”—either because Andrew was standing nearer to Christ and Philip wished him to disclose the Gentiles’ desire, or because, as Chrysostom thought, Philip had heard the words, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles,” and therefore, sharing the matter with his fellow disciple, referred it to the Teacher—“and Andrew and Philip tell Jesus. But Jesus answered them, saying: ‘The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.’”

[Col. 0102B] Augustine says here:

> “He saw that after his passion and resurrection the Gentiles throughout the world would believe.”

Thus, on the occasion of these Gentiles who wished to see him, he announces the future fullness of the Gentiles and promises that the hour of his glorification has already arrived.

Chrysostom, however, says:

> “Since he was thereafter going to send the disciples to the Gentiles, he sees the Gentiles leaping forward toward faith and shows that the time had come for him to go to the cross.”

After giving the comparison of the grain of wheat, which, if it dies, produces much fruit, he shows these Gentiles the sign from heaven that he had denied to the Jews. For the Gospel continues:

> “Now my soul is troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name.”

Then a voice came from heaven, saying:

> “I have both glorified it and will glorify it again.”

The crowd standing there and hearing it said that thunder had occurred. Others said:

> “An angel has spoken to him.”

Jesus answered and said:

> “This voice came not for my sake but for yours. Now is the judgment of the world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out. And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.”

Thus far the Gospel.

We should certainly value greatly the fact that the visit of the Spanish Gentiles brought such great joy to Christ, and that, on their account, the Father promised to glorify Christ again. He seems to have foretold in them the conversion of the remaining Gentiles, as though showing that the preaching of the Gospel among the Gentiles was first to begin with them.

Peter of Natalibus, in book 4, chapter 103, speaking of Saint Eutropius, Bishop of Xaintes, a martyr and disciple of the Apostles—whom he also says was the son of Xerxes, the celebrated king of the Persians and Babylonians—adds:

> “He was among those Gentiles who came to Philip so that they might see Jesus, as is said in John 12.”

But apart from the fact that this does not prevent the others from having been Spaniards, he undoubtedly took this from the Apocrypha. For we read his story very differently in the Breviary of Salamanca on the last day of April. There it is not said that Eutropius met Philip together with the Gentiles—an event that occurred near the Passion—but that he was present at the feeding of the five thousand in the wilderness of Tiberias, which had occurred in the preceding year, as we showed above under the year 34.

> “Having heard of the Savior’s fame for miracles, he sought him from city to city and through the various towns. When he saw him departing across the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias, together with innumerable crowds of people who followed him and saw the signs he performed, he caught up with him.”

The account adds that, after returning from there to his homeland—that is, Babylon—he rejoiced greatly when he saw the holy Apostles Simon and Jude preaching Christ’s death and resurrection, and was baptized together with his parents.

Moreover, the Evangelists never customarily concealed the rank of those who came to Christ, as we see in the case of Regulus, the centurion, and others. Since John does not say that any of the Gentiles who approached Philip was the son of a king, we should hardly believe that Eutropius was there, the son of the king of Babylon.

A.D. 35. A.R. 786. After Stephen the protomartyr was stoned to death, a great persecution arose in Jerusalem and the surrounding districts [Col. 0095]. More than fifteen thousand men who had believed in Christ through the preaching of the Apostles were driven out. Some came to Asia, others to Europe.

A.D. 35. A.R. 786. More than five hundred of these, transported by ship from Cyprus, reach the Carthaginian harbor of Hispania.

[Col. 0097] A.D. 35. A.R. 786. Scattered [variant: Divided] throughout Hispania, they proclaim the death and resurrection of Christ, and the life of Mary, to whom frequent pilgrimage was made from Hispania—especially after the conversion of Cornelius the centurion—and they fill the whole province on every side with wondrous and unheard-of reports.

A.D. 35. A.R. 786. From these, the first bishops and pastors of the cities are chosen by Blessed James; whether they were all Jews is uncertain.

A.D. 35. A.R. 786. The Hispani, especially the Jews, send envoys to the Apostles, asking that one of them come to them as soon as possible, someone who might teach them more truly and more fully about Christ concerning the matters just mentioned.

[Col. 0101] A.D. 35. A.R. 786. Then the Apostles recognized the remarkable disposition of the people of Hispania to receive the faith of Christ.

A.D. 35. A.R. 786. They had also learned this from those Gentiles who had come from Hispania for the purpose of prayer and had asked Philip to announce their arrival to Christ: a clear indication that the Gospel was first to be preached among the Gentiles to the Hispani.

[Col. 0103] [Note: [Col. 0103A]

A.D. 36.—1. Hispania the first, etc. The truth of this statement depends upon establishing the year in which the faith began to be proclaimed in Hispania; and this, in turn, depends upon the arrival of Saint James there. For if this is once established firmly and securely, no one will be able to deny that Hispania was the first province of the Gentile world upon which the light of the Gospel shone. For in those very years when [Col. 0103B] Saint James was preaching there, the other Apostles, dispersed throughout Judaea, Galilee, and Samaria, were occupied with the conversion of the Israelites. Yet no one should think that Hispania can contend with the Roman Church over universal primacy on this basis, or that it wishes to do so. Universal primacy does not follow from the antiquity of apostolic preaching; otherwise the Church of Jerusalem would enjoy it. Nor does it follow merely from the fact that such a Church was in some way established by Saint Peter; rather, it follows from his final will, confirmed by God’s authority, by which he willed that his see should perpetually endure as the Roman Church. Dexter is now concerned only with precedence in time regarding the reception of the faith. Two matters therefore need to be clarified here: namely, that Saint James traveled through Hispania and that he first arrived there in the year of Christ 36.

The most excellent and learned Constable of Castile, the first to debate this matter in a published book and to triumph successfully, employs the authority of Dexter for this purpose [Col. 0103C], among many other testimonies of the most weighty Doctors. He was later followed by all who clarified the same argument, namely, Don Juan de Salazar, Don Mauro de Castile, Don Bertrand de Guevara, archbishop of Compostela, Friar Francis of Jesus, and many others. Apart from Dexter, so many authors of such great renown acknowledge the arrival of Saint James in Hispania that they can scarcely be reduced to a number. Bartholomew Laurentius, prior of the Holy Church of Pilari, counted seventy. Don Juan de Salazar increased the number to 110, and Francis of Jesus to 148.

The principal witnesses, however, are four Supreme Pontiffs: Innocent II, Leo III, Callistus II, and Callistus III. Among the Fathers are Don Isidore, in his book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, chapter 71; Saint Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah*, book X, chapter 34; Saint Athanasius the Sinaite, in his book *On the Passions of the Martyrs*; Don Braulio, in his abridgement of the life of Saint Isidore and in his sermon on Saint Isidore, which exists together with the book of the *Etymologies* in the House of God, the Carthusian monastery near [Col. 0103D] Zaragoza; Saint Bede, in his *Collectanea*; Saint Notker, in his *Martyrology*, on 25 July; Don Julian, bishop of Toledo, in his commentary on Nahum, chapter 1; Walafrid Strabo, in his poem on the same Apostle; Venantius Fortunatus, in an epigram on the same; Otto, bishop of Freising, book III, chapter 15 of his *History of Emperor Frederick*; Don Antonio, part I of his history, title 6, chapter 7; Vincent of Beauvais, bishop, in the *Historical Mirror*, book VIII, chapters 6 and 7; Thomas of Cantimpré, book II of *On Bees*, chapter 25, whom we cited above; the first bishop of Chalon, in his *Spiritual Map of the World*, under the word “Compostella”; Saint Vincent Ferrer, in his sermon [Col. 0104A] on Saint James; Gotfried of Viterbo, *Chronicle*, part 14, chapter 7; Martin of Poland, in the thirty-fourth year of his *Chronicle*; Philip of Bergamo and Hermann Schedel, most renowned chroniclers, in the forty-third year; Beleth, in the *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, chapter 140; Durandus, together with him, book VII, chapter 17; Lyra, on Obadiah, at the words “The migration that is in Bosporus”; Alphonsus Tostado; Leonard of Udine; Dionysius the Carthusian; Peter of Natalibus; Gualbert Fabricius, in the third prologue of his *Chronicle of the Catholic King*; Thomas Bozius, volume I, book IV, chapter 1; Roderic Sánchez, bishop of Palencia, part I of his *History of Hispania*, chapter 4; Ambrosius Morales, book VI, chapter 7; Peter Canisius, *On the Mother of God*, at the passage; James Pamelius, in his notes on Tertullian’s *Against the Jews*, note 44; John of Bordallo and Louis Aux, in *The Defense and Foundation of the Church of El Pilar*; Peter Zenedo, in his *Collections of Canon Law*, 22, question 2, chapter “Blessed Paul”; James of Voragine, in the *Legend of Saint James*; Genebrard, book III of his *Chronology*, year 43; Francis Tarapha, *On the Kings of Hispania*; Villegas [Col. 0104B] Ribadeneira, in the *Flowers of the Saints*; Martin del Rio, book II of the *Magical Investigations*, question 26, section 4; Master Isella, book of the *Rule of the Order of Saint James*, chapter 3; Galesinus and Maurolicus, in their *Martyrologies*; and nearly innumerable others.

To these must be added the fact that the Fathers of the Council of Braga, held approximately in the year of Christ 400 and discovered not long ago in Lusitania in one of the principal archives of the Kingdom, taught the same thing; we shall shortly cite their words and give them in full in their proper place under the year of the Lord 400. There is also the privilege of King Ramiro of Hispania, which is found in Morales; and Don Athanasius, the first bishop of Zaragoza and beloved disciple of the Apostle himself, left this matter attested for us. His fragment of works, obtained from the archives of the kingdoms of Sardinia and Aragon, was later printed by the bishop of Tuy and Pamplona in his *History of Tuy*. Likewise, Saint Caledonius, bishop of Braga, in the life of Saint Peter of Rates; and Saints Braulio and Heleca, bishops of Zaragoza, in additions to the *Chronicle of Marcus Maximus and Lucius Dexter* [Col. 0104C]; Julian, archpriest of Saint Justa of Toledo, in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 36; and Hugh of Portugal, in a letter to Maurice of Braga, who flourished in the year of the Lord 1100.

Indeed, even if none of those mentioned had left this in writing, the Ecclesiastical Offices that have always been sung throughout the universal Church concerning this same Blessed Apostle would amply suffice as a tradition of this truth. For it is asserted in all the ancient Breviaries, especially in the Breviary called that of Saint Isidore the Mozarab; likewise in the ancient manuscript of Zaragoza and in the newly printed one; in the Breviaries of Toledo, Valencia, Calahorra, Lleida, Tarazona, Mondoñedo, Compostela, Huesca, Palencia, Salamanca, Astorga, Sigüenza, Milan, Benedictine, Cistercian, Carmelite, Franciscan, Dominican, Mercedarian, Aragonese, Hieronymite, and the ancient and reformed Roman Breviary. In these, tradition asserts that he is the patron of the Churches of Hispania.

And [Col. 0104D] what is especially noteworthy is that several Churches of Hispania recited the little Office of Blessed James every Thursday throughout the year, out of reverence for so great a Doctor of their own. This can be seen in the general rubrics of the Salamanca Breviary, in Note X, where the following is found:

“Our Church of Salamanca has, after God, a special devotion to the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and to Saint James the Apostle, the singular patron of our Hispania. Therefore, on Thursdays free from the feasts of other Saints, it has been accustomed to celebrate an abbreviated Office of Saint James.”

I found the same thing in the tenth general rule of the Astorga Breviary. In that Office, one of the Responsories was “He is present to us,” etc., in which the preaching of Saint James in Hispania is contained; we shall cite it shortly. An outstanding argument is also to be drawn from the foundation of the Church of the Column, or Pilar, at Zaragoza. For although all the other evidence were lacking, this alone would irrefutably establish the point at issue; but we shall discuss it below.

[Col. 0105A] Three principal objections are raised that seem to weaken the arrival of Blessed James in Hispania. First, his martyrdom, which occurred before the Apostles’ division; second, certain words of Pope Saint Innocent in his letter to Decentius, by which he seems to argue that none of the Apostles preached in Gaul and Hispania, but only those whom Peter sent there; third, a certain dispute said to have been held at Rome in the Lateran Council between Roderic, archbishop of Toledo, and the archbishop of Compostela, concerning the right of primacy over Hispania. For there the Toledan opposed the Compostelan, saying that if anything was being asserted about Saint James’s preaching in Hispania, it was not found in [Col. 0105B] approved authors but was merely a pious old women’s tale.

The Constable and those who later followed him have sufficiently shown that these matters do not constitute an obstacle. If I wished to add anything to their work, I would undoubtedly seem to be doing what had already been done. Nevertheless, I shall not hesitate to answer the objections briefly and perfunctorily, in their proper order.

The first objection must be met by distinguishing between speaking of the allotment of provinces among the Apostles and speaking of their separation from one another. The former preceded Saint James’s arrival in Hispania; the latter followed his return. Therefore, once the allotment had been made, nothing could prevent the Apostle from going to the province that had fallen to him by lot, even though the others did not immediately withdraw to their own provinces. Certainly, the brevity of Saint James’s apostleship urged him to travel, lest his allotment be in vain. For why would the Holy Spirit entrust Hispania to him by divine lot if he was not going to travel there? The other Apostles, however, had to remain longer in Judaea, to whom [Col. 0105C], evidently, a longer life was granted. I shall omit the fact that James was summoned by the Hispani, whereas the inhabitants of the other provinces did not summon the others.

Nor is it necessary to interpret Luke’s words, “all were scattered except the Apostles,” concerning the persecution that arose after Stephen’s death, in such a way that they would be true for the greater part, as some have devised. For Saint James did not come to Hispania in the year 35, but in the following year, 36, as we shall see; nor did he come as a fugitive from persecution, but as one sought and invited.

Second, nothing would be taken away from Innocent even if we said that he spoke out of ignorance of history. For if he alone was unaware of James’s arrival, four other Roman Pontiffs recognized it and left it attested in their writings: Innocent II, in the bull on the translation of Saint James, which is preserved with the signatures of the Cardinals; Leo III, in a letter on the same translation, beginning “Let your fraternity know”; Callistus II, in five books that he published on the miracles of the same Apostle; and Calixtus III, in the bull *Holy [Col. 0105D] Mother of God of the Column*, which is preserved at Zaragoza.

Nevertheless, out of reverence for so great a Father, we maintain that his words can be interpreted in a favorable sense: namely, that he may have wished to say that no one else could introduce a custom contrary to that of the Romans and of the Apostles while the Pontiff opposed it, since supreme apostolic authority remained in him alone. Or they may be understood to mean that none of the Apostles preached in Hispania or Gaul except those whom Peter sent; on this point we do not dispute, since James too was ultimately sent by him.

Third, it is clear that those manuscripts from the library of the Holy Church of Toledo, recently published by Loaysa together with the Gothic councils, are spurious, since they are filled with many falsehoods. For example, they assert that Alexander III succeeded Gelasius, although eight Roman Pontiffs intervened between the two. [Col. 0106A] They also say that Alexander himself imprisoned the antipope Burdinus, although it is certain that this was accomplished not by Alexander but by Callistus. Again, they state that Maurice’s schism arose while Paschal was alive and that Emperor Henry sent an army to Rome, although this occurred after Paschal’s death.

I shall omit the fact that the manuscripts themselves were found without an author and without the identification or signature of a notary or any other person—something that seemed necessary to establish the certainty of the case said to have been debated there. Moreover, the archbishop of Toledo himself wrote a special book on the primacy of the Church of Toledo and makes no mention of that dispute or of the judgment said in those manuscripts to have been obtained by him from Innocent III at that Lateran Council. Yet Roderic could have cited nothing in his book that would have established the primacy he sought equally well.

Again, although he gives an especially detailed account of all his journeys in his *History of Hispania*, he says not a single word about that dispute or about his attendance at the council. Indeed, [Col. 0106B] Peter of Mantua elegantly proves in his notes on Mariana’s history, while defending the Constable, that Roderic was not absent from Hispania throughout the entire period of the council’s celebration. He was detained by the death of King Alfonso VIII, which occurred in the very year indicated for the council, namely 1214, on 22 September, and also by the death of the queen, which occurred on 17 October of the following year. He was present at both events and took part in settling the disputes raised by the knights of Lara concerning the guardianship of the young king.

The archbishop Loaysa himself, who printed those manuscripts, added an antidote in the margin, saying: “Blessed James, son of Zebedee, came to Hispania and preached the Gospel of Christ there,” etc. Nor could Roderic himself have been ignorant of this truth, which was supported not only by the authority of so many writers but was also read in the Toledan Breviary, whether according to the institution of Don Isidore or according to Roman custom. For in the latter there is a Responsory that reads:

“Here is present for us the very joyful [Col. 0106C] day of the most excellent Apostle James, through whose most salutary preaching the whole people of Hispania began to recognize their Redeemer.”

The Isidorian hymn likewise reads:

“Then the great sons of thunder,

shining, obtained their glory through the prayer of their renowned mother;

John alone rules Asia with his right hand,

while his brother is placed on the left, Hispania.”

We shall give it in full below.

Let such absurdities therefore be dismissed, and let such manifest forgeries be recognized as such. But in what year of the Lord this occurred must now be examined.

2. Hispania the first. Julian, showing in his *Chronicle* with how great a weight of authority it is established that Saint James came to Hispania in this very year, says:

“As constant tradition, handed down from apostolic times to the present, and the testimonies of many ancient writers—Torquatus, Tisiphon, Honoratus, Melantius, Dexter, Marcus Maximus, Isidore, Bede, and others—relate, in the year of the Lord 36 Saint James, son of Zebedee, came to Hispania for a sufficiently honorable purpose. He visited all its cities; established his first see at Toledo; distinguished the metropolitan sees; and appointed the first bishops at Seville, Braga, Zaragoza, Barcelona, Tarragona, Cartagena, Asturias, and Toledo.”

Shortly afterward he also says that he found in the archive of Saint Justa of Toledo that James had been ordered to come to Hispania for this reason—namely, because of the embassy of the Hispani to the Apostles—and that he came two years after the Savior’s death, as has been said. Since that event occurred in the year 34, it follows that James came to us in the year 36.

Moreover, in a letter sent from the Church of the Column, which he found in the same archive, it is said that the Apostle remained in Hispania until the year 41, for nearly six years. From this [Col. 0107A] the proposed conclusion is manifest: between the year 36 and the year 41 there are precisely six years. Therefore, if he remained in Hispania for six years and departed from it in the year 41, he must have arrived there in the thirty-sixth year.

3. And its Gentile population, etc. Cardinal Baronius, in his notes on 25 July in the Roman Martyrology, thinks that the preaching of Saint James in Hispania should be understood to mean that he preached the Gospel there only to Jews and not to Gentiles. For, he says, the door had not yet been opened to them by the decree of the Apostles.

However, even if we granted that the Lord had forbidden the Apostles to preach to the Gentiles until the door was opened to them after the rejection of the Synagogue, this could in no way hinder Saint James. For that prohibition, if there was one, lasted only three years, according to Saint Ambrose, book VII on Luke, chapter 3. Saint James, however, came to Hispania in the third year after Christ’s death and remained there for six further years. During all that time he was free to preach to the Gentiles without [Col. 0107B] prohibition.

If the opening of the door is said to have occurred at the baptism of Cornelius the centurion, performed by Saint Peter after the heavenly vision shown to him of unclean animals that he was to kill and eat, as recorded in Acts 10—for Chrysostom, in Homily 22, said, “You see from where the beginning of the Gentiles arises,” and Ambrose, in Sermon 15, called Cornelius the first animal among those that Peter had been commanded to eat—then Cornelius’s baptism occurred in the year of the Lord 40, as we shall see. Since James did not leave Hispania until the following year, 41, it follows that he could have preached there to the Gentiles for at least two years.

Yet what we have said about the opening of the door of evangelical preaching to the Gentiles must not be taken too rigidly, as though the gate of salvation had then been entirely closed to them. This must never be asserted, since it would greatly detract from the supreme mercy and providence of God, who always willed all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

[Col. 0107C] Moreover, the prohibition given to the Disciples—“Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans,” Matthew 10—seems to have been removed by the command, “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them,” Matthew 28. Jerome noted this when he said, in his exposition of the former passage:

“This passage is not contrary to the command that is later given, ‘Go and teach all nations,’ because the one command was given before the resurrection and the other after the resurrection.”

Bede likewise noted this in his homily:

“For he who before his Passion had said, ‘Do not go into the way of the Gentiles,’ after rising from the dead says, ‘Go, teach all nations,’ as though he had said that from then on it was lawful for them to preach to the Gentiles.”

It is true, however, that they were commanded, according to Luke 24, to preach to every creature in such a way that they were to begin from Jerusalem; and that they were not to depart from Jerusalem until they had been clothed with power from on high through the descent of the Holy Spirit upon them, Acts 1. This had been fulfilled long before the baptism of Cornelius.

Saint James observed both requirements before leaving Jerusalem. He did not leave until he had been clothed with power from on high, and he began his preaching from Jerusalem. From there [Col. 0107D] he proceeded to Hispania, where he preached to Jews and Gentiles without distinction of persons, as he had been commanded, under the designation “every creature.”

But why should we dwell on these matters any further, when Daniel, chapter 9, foretold that the New Testament, or covenant, was to be proclaimed and confirmed to the Jews over the period of one week of years—namely, with Christ the Lord preaching to them for three and a half years and the Apostles, after his ascension, for an equal period? “He will confirm the covenant with many for one week,” he says, “and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering will cease.”

Theodoret explains this as follows:

“In this one week the New Testament [Col. 0108A] will be given to believers and will fill them with every power; and in the middle of that week sacrifice and libation will be taken away. That is, the sacrifice according to the Law will cease; the offering of the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world is the true sacrifice. If anyone also wishes to understand this, it will be learned from the Gospel of John. For when the Lord had preached for approximately three and a half years and had strengthened his holy disciples through teaching and miracles, then he suffered. And after the cross, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, and after the coming of the most holy Spirit, the holy Apostles, preaching and performing miracles in Jerusalem during the remaining time of the week, led many thousands of people to evangelical doctrine and bestowed the gift of the New Testament upon them, so that they might also obtain the grace of holy baptism. Then, when the Jews had dared those impious crimes against Saint Stephen, and the people had been scattered through the towns of Judaea, the holy Apostles, after remaining in Jerusalem for a short time, hastened to Samaria, Lydda, and Joppa, offering salutary decrees to all people. [Col. 0108B]

“Therefore,” God’s archangel said to blessed Daniel, “‘he will confirm the covenant with many for one week’—that is, counting together the time before the cross and the time during which the holy Apostles taught in Jerusalem after the Savior’s resurrection.”

Thus far Theodoret. Eusebius, book VIII of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, and Jerome, in his commentaries on this passage of Daniel, write in agreement with him. It is therefore perfectly clear that the Apostles remained with the Jews for the establishment of the New Testament for no more than two and a half years.

Even during that period, notwithstanding this, the Gospel could be preached to the Gentiles. We have an irrefutable example in Paul, who preached to the Gentiles before Cornelius’s baptism and before the vision shown to Peter. Luke gives testimony to this in Acts 9. After recounting Saint Paul’s conversion and stating beforehand that he grew increasingly strong and confounded the Jews, affirming that Jesus is the Christ, he adds that Paul [Col. 0108C] also spoke to the Gentiles and disputed with the Greeks.

That this occurred long before the centurion’s baptism is clear from the very context of Acts. For after the words just mentioned, the Evangelist relates that Paul then withdrew from Jerusalem to Tarsus; that Peter, as he passed through all the places, restored Aeneas, who was in Lydda and had been paralyzed for eight years; that he then raised Tabitha from the dead at Joppa; and that he remained there for many days with a certain Simon, a tanner. Only after all these events, which he had related in Acts 9, does he introduce the vision shown from heaven to Peter and Cornelius’s baptism in the following chapter, chapter 10. It necessarily follows that Paul preached to the Gentiles long before Cornelius was solemnly baptized.

An argument can also be drawn from the Samaritans, who were included in the same prohibition as the Gentiles, since the command concerning both was expressed in the same terms to the Apostles: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans.” Yet [Col. 0108D] before a year had elapsed after the Lord’s Passion, immediately after Stephen’s martyrdom, the word of God was preached in Samaria by the disciples scattered throughout it, especially by Philip the deacon. When the Apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them (Acts 8). Therefore Paul and James could rightly preach to the Gentiles before Cornelius’s conversion, no less than preaching had taken place among the Samaritans.

Consider, please, God’s providence in these two Apostles. In the same year, 36, in which James set out for Hispania, Paul was converted to the faith, as though he were destined to supplement James’s place and lot. Blessed Amadeus himself wrote that this had been divinely revealed to him by the command of an angel in his new *Apocalypse*. Both [Col. 0109A] preached to Jews and Gentiles, and both assumed responsibility for preaching in Hispania.

Would you like to see that the conversion of Hispania lay as close to Paul’s heart as to James’s? Listen to what he writes to the Romans:

“When I begin to set out for Hispania, I hope to see you in passing; and I hope to be escorted there by you, after I have first enjoyed your company in part.”

And again: “I shall travel through you to Hispania” (Romans 15).

What does “When I begin to set out for Hispania, I hope to see you in passing” mean, unless he was much more concerned about the Hispani than about the Romans? This seems entirely clear to me. His principal intention was not to go to Rome, since he promises to do that incidentally and by way of opportunity: “I hope,” he says, “to see you in passing,” that is, on the way. And as though he had not expressed his meaning clearly enough, he says again, “I hope to be escorted there by you”—that is, “You will be assistants in my principal undertaking.” He adds, “after I have first enjoyed your company in part.” What does that limitation “in part” signify? Precisely the same as “in passing.”

His principal intention, therefore, was Hispania [Col. 0109B], not Rome or Italy, since Italy was being nourished with the food of evangelical doctrine by Peter, the chief of the Apostles. Accordingly, Paul seems to have undertaken principally the province of James.

But no one should suppose that Paul promised merely to visit the Romans incidentally because he had already dealt seriously with them at some earlier time. He himself addresses this in chapter 1:

“I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often resolved to come to you but have been prevented until now, so that I might have some fruit among you as among the other Gentiles.”

And in chapter 15 he assigns the boundaries of his journeys, which he had completed up to that point, from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum. This did not yet reach Italy. He adds:

“For this reason I have been hindered many times from coming to you, and I have been prevented until now. But now, having no further place in these regions—that is, since I am free from their affairs—and having had for many years a desire to come to you, when I begin to set out for Hispania, [Col. 0109C] I hope to see you in passing.”

He had not yet come to Italy. Although he had greatly desired to do so for many years, he nevertheless says that he will go there only as an opportunity arising from his journey to Hispania. Theophylact entirely agrees. On the words in chapter 16, “All the Churches of God greet you,” he says: “He had not yet seen the city or the Romans.” But on chapter 15, concerning “When I begin to set out for Hispania,” he says:

“Lest the Romans also object, ‘Paul, you are now preparing this journey to us as something superfluous, since you are going elsewhere,’ he added, ‘and I hope to be escorted there by you.’ That is, when you have considered the necessity pressing me to visit the Hispani, you will be the first to send me to them. It is not because some unfavorable judgment concerning you has been formed in my mind that I shall pass you by, but because I am compelled to do so.”

Whatever may be said concerning the other Apostles who at that time remained in Judaea, it is nevertheless certain that James preached in Hispania to Gentiles as well as to Jews. Venantius Fortunatus asserted this in an epigram [Col. 0109D] on the same Apostle, which Pope Calixtus quotes:

“The servant of the Lord’s sound goes forth through the whole world;

here he teaches the Gentiles; there he rebukes the Jews;

and, making faith fruitful for God, he brings it to the ends of the earth.”

He said that he “brought faith to the ends of the earth” to express that James preached as far as the remotest shores of Hispania, where the end of the land and of the world lies. Julian likewise reports that the letter concerning the foundation of the House of the Column states that the Apostle remained in Hispania until the year 41 and, for nearly six years, with remarkable speed, preached to Jews and Gentiles.

Walafrid Strabo speaks particularly of the Gentiles in his poem on Saint James, printed by Henry Canisius in volume VI of the *Ancient Readings*:

“First he converted the peoples of Hispania by his teaching,

turning barbarian throngs through divine words—

those who had long worshiped ancient rites

and gloomy shrines, deceived by the fraud of the dreadful demon.”

It must therefore be said that the prohibition against preaching to the Gentiles, if there was such a prohibition, did not extend beyond the boundaries of Judaea. Or—and this interpretation is especially pleasing—it was said that the door had been opened to the Gentiles in Cornelius because from that first moment, so to speak, it was lawful for them to be preached to, although the Jews had previously to be addressed first. Alternatively, the Synagogue had already suffered rejection from its position as firstborn, and the Gentiles were being summoned in its place.

It is in this sense that Cornelius is called the first animal offered to God from among the Gentiles: that is, after the opening of the door and the rejection of the Synagogue.]

A.D. 36. A.R. 787. Hispania was the first of the provinces of the world, after Galilee, Judaea, and Samaria, in the western regions to embrace the faith of Christ; and its Gentile population was converted to the faith, the true firstfruits of the remaining Gentiles.

[Col. 0110] [Note: [Col. 0110A]

A.D. 37.—1. For James also, etc. The Acts of James [Col. 0110B] in Hispania are summarized here. It should not be understood that he completed all these things in the single year 37, but that from 36 through 41, inclusive, he traveled through all the cities of Hispania, established many Churches there, and consecrated bishops in them. Julian said that this was found under the year 36 on the basis of constant tradition and the testimonies of very weighty authors. He adds: “He visited all its cities, established his first see at Toledo, distinguished the metropolitan sees,” etc.

The Milanese Breviary of the ordination of Saint Ambrose likewise reports not that James passed through one or another of its cities but that he spread throughout all Hispania: “James the Greater,” it says, “after traveling through the whole of Hispania by preaching,” etc.

2. Peter of Braga, etc. All who have written about Hispania testify that this most holy martyr of Christ and first bishop of Braga was a disciple of the Apostle Saint James and was adorned by him with episcopal insignia in that same city. Vasaeus, in his *Chronicle*; Marinus Siculus, book V; Ambrosius Morales, book IX, chapter 8; Marieta [Col. 0110C], *On the Saints of Hispania*, part I, book I, chapter 21; Truxillo, in the *Treasury of Sermons*, on 26 April, the day on which he suffered martyrdom; and on the same day Sanctorus and Villegas treat of him in the *Flowers of the Saints*. In addition to these, Zianca does so in his *History of Saint Secundus*, book I, chapter 2.

What deserves still greater veneration is that the Fathers of the Council of Braga mentioned above likewise confess this. For they say:

“Concerning our father and the apostle of this region, Peter of Braga, whom James, the Lord’s kinsman, sent away to save souls,” etc.

Among all the other wonderful things that Saint James accomplished in Hispania, nothing is more worthy of such remembrance than the raising of this holy bishop, whom he restored to life—not after four days, like Lazarus, but after he had been dead for many centuries. This means approximately six hundred years, counting backward from the Babylonian captivity to Saint James’s arrival in Hispania: from the year 171 of the founding of the City, when the Jews were led captive into Hispania according to Mariana’s calculation [Col. 0110D], book I, chapter 7—or, as others prefer, from the year 149 to the year 788 of the same City, which falls in this thirty-seventh year of Christ.

This is so, if credence is to be given to a fragment of the works of Saint Athanasius I, bishop of Zaragoza, and fellow disciple of the same Peter under the instruction of the holy Apostle. The fragment was obtained from the archives of a library in Sardinia and also from another in the kingdom of Aragon, through the agency of Father Bartholomew of Olivenza, provincial of the Society of Jesus on the island of Sardinia. It was later printed by Saint Prudentius of Sandoval, bishop of Tuy, in his *History of that Church*. It has seemed worthwhile to insert it here verbatim. These are the words of Saint Athanasius, bishop of Zaragoza.

“I knew Saint Peter, the first bishop of Braga [Col. 0111A], whom Saint James, son of Zebedee, my master, raised up as an ancient prophet. He had come with the twelve tribes sent by Nabuchodonosor into Hispania, from Jerusalem, under Nabuzardan, or Pyrrhus, the governor of the Hispani. This prophet was called the younger Samuel or the elder Malachi because of the gravity of his character and the beauty of his countenance; he was the son of the prophet Uriah.

“Having become a bishop, he converted many of the Jews to the faith, saying that he had come with their ancestors and had preached to those who had been transported into exile; but he died twenty years after their arrival in Hispania.

“This apostolic man, having received from Saint James the apostolic institutions, the Gospel, and the order of the Mass, together with the celebration of the Sacraments, came to Braga. He wrote letters full of the apostolic spirit to the Churches in which he established bishops: for example, the bishop of Iria, the bishop of Amphilochia, the bishop of Eminium, and the bishop of Porto. There he installed Saint Basil, his fellow disciple, who succeeded him in the see of Braga after Peter was taken away by martyrdom; and he installed Epytatius at Tuy.

“These divine and wholly apostolic men did not remain always in one city, like the Apostles; rather, wherever [Col. 0111B] the Holy Spirit seized them, they were carried. Thus Epytatius preached not only in the diocese of Tuy but also in Ambracia, a city of Lusitania. They adorned their preaching with signs and with a variety of languages. Nor did they go alone to preach, but accompanied by many disciples, as Christ, Peter, James, and the other Apostles had done.”

Thus far the fragment of Athanasius.
