That it certainly deserves much credence is convincingly shown by the Life of St. Peter itself, written more than 1,350 years ago by Blessed Caledonius, likewise bishop of Braga, who died in the year of the Lord 260. There he reports everything that St. Athanasius says here, as the Portuguese bishop Hugo gives irrefragable testimony concerning this matter in the letter cited above by us among the author’s encomia; consult that letter. Certainly St. Anastasius Sinaita, perhaps because of this raising of St. Peter, asserted in his *Book on the Passions of the Martyrs* that, when St. James preached to the Spaniards, he performed among them miracles at which the astonished people marveled, so that he converted them to the acknowledgment of the faith of the exalted God [Col. 0111C].

Moreover, among the many things said here, as though surrounding the principal subject, there is nothing that is not supported by substantial foundations—whether the discussion concerns the migration to Spain of the twelve tribes carried out by Nebuchadnezzar, or Uriah, the father of St. Peter of Braga, or the apostolic Constitutions, the Gospel, and the order of the Mass handed down to him by Blessed James, or the foundation of the churches of Iria, Amphilochium, Eminium, and Porto; likewise Basil, his fellow disciple, and Epiphatius, his disciple, together with their preaching. We shall discuss the migration of the tribes shortly.

Jeremiah gives the history of the prophet Uriah in chapter 26:

> There was a man prophesying in the name of the Lord, Uriah son of Shemaiah, from Kiriath-jearim; and he prophesied against this city (namely, concerning the captivity of Jerusalem) and against this land, in accordance with all the words of Jeremiah. And King Jehoiakim, and all his mighty men and his princes, heard these words, and the king sought to kill him. When Uriah heard this, he was afraid, fled, and entered Egypt. King Jehoiakim sent men to Egypt, Elnathan son of Achbor, and men with him, and they brought Uriah out of Egypt and brought him to King Jehoiakim. He struck him with the sword and cast his corpse into the graves of the common people.

The migration which Uriah prophesied to this Jehoiakim, son of King Josiah, occurred, however, in the time of another Jehoiakim, his son and Josiah’s grandson, as is reported in the last chapter of 2 Kings and by the same Jeremiah in his final chapter. From this one may see that Uriah’s son was alive at the time of that migration.

There can be no doubt concerning the apostolic Constitutions and the order of the Mass which St. James is said to have handed down to Peter, since it was shown above [Col. 0112A] that they were composed by the apostles immediately after the coming of the Holy Spirit. Some person might perhaps question how the Lord James left the Gospel in Spain, since the Gospel of Matthew, the first of the four, was not written until the year 41, when James had already departed from there.

It occurred, however, through a great gift of God that in the year 1595, on Mount Ilipulitano in Granada—now called, because of the event, the Holy Mountain—not only were the sacred ashes and bones of the most distinguished disciples of St. James discovered, but also eighteen books written on bronze or lead tablets. Several of these are said to have been composed by the holy apostle, especially one entitled *On the Mass of the Apostles*, with its ceremonial, and another, *On Evangelical History*. From this one may see that the blessed apostle, in order to communicate the holy Gospel of Christ to his disciples, had no need of Matthew’s Gospel—especially since he had been present at the Lord’s more secret actions.

Furthermore, Julianus in his *Chronicle* states that the Mass, or Liturgy, which was formerly customarily recited in Spain and now exists in the Mozarabic Missal, was originally composed by St. James, enlarged by Melantius and Asturius, prelates of Toledo, and finally revised by St. Isidore. For this reason, out of reverence for so great an author, many prayers in the Canon are said by the priest in memory of the apostle St. James, although no other apostle is mentioned there. We shall return to these matters below [Col. 0112B].

As for those bishoprics founded by Lord Peter of Braga, it is established that they were all once subject to the metropolitan see of Braga, as may be seen in the division of bishoprics made by Constantine, in Lucas of Tuy’s *Chronicle*, in Ambrosius Morales, and in others. The see of Iria, today called Padrón, was transferred to Compostela; Amphilochium is Orense itself; Eminium is the same as Mondoñedo; and Porto retains its name. Since they all served under the see of Braga, it follows that they were founded by him; for no other disciple is recorded as having preached there [Col. 0112C]. We shall show in their proper places that Basil was Peter’s fellow disciple and successor in the see of Braga, and that Epiphatius was assigned by him to Tuy and was an apostle in Ambracia.

Finally, the fact that Peter was once called Samuel the Younger or Malachi the Elder refers to this: he was younger in age than that famous Samuel, but older than Malachi, who, according to Jerome, prophesied during the Babylonian captivity, in the days of Haggai and Zechariah. He acquired these surnames because of the integrity of his conduct.

### 3. The first temple, etc.

Nothing has been established by the testimony of more weighty authors, and nothing throughout Spain has been more sacred or more deeply revered in the minds of its people, than the story of the angelic foundation of the house of St. Mary of the Pillar in the city of Zaragoza, which Dexter reports in this place. Let us examine the foundations of that tradition.

Blessed Caledonius, bishop of Braga, certainly reported it in the *Life of St. Peter of Ratis*, preserved by Hugo, bishop of Portugal, when he says:

> After scarcely fifteen months had elapsed, his teacher James had raised a small shrine at Zaragoza in honor of the Virgin Mother of God;

and shortly afterward he adds that James erected another at Braga in memory of the same Virgin.

The tradition was also approved by Calixtus III of blessed memory in his bull dated at Rome on 23 September 1456, where, among other things, he says:

> The first church among all those under the title of Blessed Mary, in which the said Blessed Mary, before she was assumed into heaven, appeared to Blessed James the Greater upon a pillar.

And below:

> In that place innumerable miracles are performed daily by divine providence.

And again:

> The faithful of Christ, with great devotion and veneration, worship and honor the image of the same Blessed Mary and of her Son in a certain chapel of the same church [Col. 0113A]—which was built at the command of the said Blessed Mary by the said James and exists under the name of the Angelic Chamber of the Mother of God of the Pillar—and they do not cease to visit it with the greatest devotion.

It is especially noteworthy that this pontiff does not report the story as resting on the authority of other authors, but asserts it as something certain and known to him, since he was born in Spain, in the kingdom of Valencia, not far from Zaragoza.

Further weight is added by the very ancient office of the Mass formerly accustomed to be sung in that church. Its Introit was:

> As the Virgin Mother of God stood by, the angels sang praise, saying: Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you.

The Collect, or prayer, was as follows:

> Almighty and eternal God, who graciously permitted your most sacred Mother, while she was still living, to come among the choirs of angels upon a marble pillar sent down by you from on high, so that the basilica of the Pillar might be built in her honor by the protomartyr of the apostles, James, and his most holy disciples: grant, we beseech you, that through her merits and intercession what we ask with faithful mind may be obtained. You who live, etc.

The same is contained in the Offertory:

> Offertory. The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land, when, as the Blessed Virgin spoke at Zaragoza in the apostle’s ears, she sounded most sweetly, saying: Behold, James, the place marked out and assigned to my honor, in which, through your diligence, my church shall be preserved.

The canons of that church preserve the very history itself, which breathes a venerable antiquity both in the simplicity of its style and in the age of its characters and parchments, in a special secret cabinet of their library. It is written at the end of the later volume of the *Moralia* of St. Gregory, whose superscription is:

> In this chest are contained the *Moralia* of St. Gregory, miraculously discovered at Rome by Taio, bishop of Zaragoza.

Among other things, the *History of the Pillar* contains the following:

> Meanwhile, when the Holy Spirit revealed it, Blessed James the Greater, son of Zebedee, received a command from Christ to go to the regions of Spain to preach the word of God. Then, it says, the Blessed Virgin addressed him in these words: “See, son, fulfill the command of your Master, and in one of the cities of Spain where you convert the greater number to the faith, there build a church in my memory, as I shall show you.”  
> 
> When the apostle was praying, as was his custom, beside the bank of the Ebro at Zaragoza, at the very hour of midnight he heard the voices of angels singing: “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” The Blessed Virgin herself then addressed the apostle from the pillar in this manner: “Behold, James, my son, the place marked out and assigned to my name, in which, through your diligence, my church shall be built in my memory. In this place especially, through my prayers and reverence, the power of the Most High will perform signs and wonders for those who in their needs implore my help. This Pillar shall remain in this place until the end of the world, and those who worship Christ in this city shall never fail. Look, moreover, upon this Pillar on which I sit; for my Son and your Master sent it down from on high through the hands of angels,” etc.

It would be lengthy and extremely laborious to cite the words of every author who taught the same tradition [Col. 0113D]. Among them are Gualbertus Fabricius the Cistercian in his *Chronicle*; Marinaeus, book 5, chapter “On Sacred Buildings”; Vasaeus, years 37 and 44; Beuterus, part 1 of the *Chronicle of Spain*, chapter 25; Damianus a Goes, in the *Genealogy of the Kings of Spain*, volume 2 of *Hispania Illustrata*; Stephanus Garibay, in the *Compendium of Spanish History*, book 7, chapters 3 and 4; Morales, book 9, chapter 7; Romanus, book 1, chapter 3; Ludovicus de Estrada, abbot of Huerta, part 2 of the *Rosary*, folio 112; Canisius, book 5, *On the Mother of God*, chapters 21 and 23; Andreas Betendorpius, *On Apparitions of Spirits*, chapter 2, thesis 207; Thomas Bozius, volume 2, book 9, chapter 6, number 12; D. Laurentius Padilla, *First Century*; Gundisalvus Illescas, in the *Pontifical*; Loaysa, in his notes on the decree of Gundemar; Garibay, in his account of Alfonso, king of Navarre, chapter 7; Hieronymus Blancas, part 3, chapter 143; Prades, book 2, chapter 5, section 1; Zurita, book 1 [Col. 0114A] of the *Indian Affairs of Aragon*; Boniface, in the *History of Blessed Mary*, book 2, page 119; D. Maurus, book 1, chapter 23; Mendoza, *Quodlibet* 5; Ribadeneira, in the *Life of St. James*; and D. Martinus Garsia, bishop of Barcelona, sermons 90, 91, and 100. Also Martin del Rio, *Disquisitions on Magic*, book 2, question 26, section 4.

Special treatises on the foundation of the Angelic House of the Pillar were also published by Joannes Michael de Bordalbo, Ludovicus Aux, P. Zenedus in the *Collections of Canon Law*, 22.2, chapter “Blessed Paul,” Murillus, and others.

The tradition has been so received in the minds of Christians in Spain that Isella, in book 3, chapter 3 of his *Rule of the Military Order of St. James*, said:

> Particularly in the kingdom of Aragon, we regard it as scarcely less certain than an article of faith that James personally came to preach in this province and kingdom, and that he built the church of Our Lady of the Pillar.

Do you require royal diplomas? John II, king of Aragon, says the following in a privilege granted to that church at Zaragoza on 26 October 1459:

> Out of consideration and favor toward that church, which shines among the other churches of Spain with divine mysteries and miracles, many miraculous things are reported, as history testifies, concerning its institution and construction, and principally this remarkable fact: that it was constructed and built in the life of the Blessed and glorious Virgin herself and at her command by Blessed James the Greater, the apostle. At its head the Blessed Virgin herself commanded that the marble Pillar which she had received from heaven, and upon which she appeared to the same Blessed James, be fixed and placed.

His son as well, Lord Ferdinand the Catholic, king of Spain, in a similar privilege dated 12 April 1504 at Medina del Campo, says:

> We believe that no Catholic in the western world is unaware that near the city of Zaragoza there exists a sacred and most ancient building, or celebrated temple, dedicated to the most pure and immaculate Virgin Mother of God under the title of Blessed Mary of the Pillar, shining with countless and continual miracles. There, while she was still living in the flesh, that most gracious Virgin, taking pity on the Spanish people, who did not yet behold the light of orthodox faith, presented herself bodily in a wondrous manner to St. James and those standing around him upon a stone Column. From this there arose a saving light for all the peoples of Spain, hardened by the blind credulity of the pagans.  
> 
> It is said that, after the Column had been left in that place by the same immaculate Virgin, together with her white image above it, a very small chapel was built there by Blessed James and his followers. This was the first church in Spain to obtain that name. In time, however, as devotion increased and pious gifts provided support, the house itself, as befitted the palace of so great a Queen, was greatly enlarged and finally brought to the condition in which it exists today, etc.

Let there also be added the statute of the metropolitan see of Zaragoza, promulgated on 9 May 1471:

> Therefore, we, Peter Michael, vicar general for the most reverend Lord John, perpetual administrator of Zaragoza, with the counsel and consent of the entire Chapter, considering that he himself founded the first church of this city (he is speaking of St. James) and preached the word of God in this city by his presence, order and establish that the natal day of the same most glorious apostle, namely 25 July, be celebrated in the metropolitan church of Zaragoza for all time with the solemnity of six copes.  
> 
> Although in the other octaves the office of the Virgin is commonly omitted in order to increase the solemnity, in this octave of Blessed James we have not judged that it should be omitted, because of the memory of the apparition by which the most glorious Virgin, while still living, appeared to that apostle in this city.

The same archiepiscopal see exempted the Angelic House of the Pillar from the charitable subsidy customarily given by prelates for the possession of their dignity, assigning as its reason that it is established that the said church, in which the glorious Virgin Mother of God, while still living in the flesh, graciously appeared to the Blessed Apostle James upon a marble Pillar carried by angelic hands [Col. 0115A], etc.

Finally, with the same consideration, when the question of the right of precedence of this Church of the Column over the episcopal churches of the kingdom of Aragon was being considered at Zaragoza, judgment was rendered in its favor by the most illustrious Lord Justice of Aragon, D. Martin Bautista de la Nuza, and by the councillors of that kingdom, equally learned men: Joannes Clemente Romeu, Matthaeus Deza, Petrus Hieronymus Mendieta, Martin Jodini, and Michael Martini de Villari, in the year 1605. The grounds of this judgment were printed at Madrid by Ludovicus Sancius in the same year. Its principal cause was the following:

> For it possesses—through the most widely received tradition of all the churches, especially of those of this very extensive province, a tradition repeatedly approved by its pontiffs—the primacy among all the churches of the world in antiquity, excellence, and origin. Therefore Zaragoza may truly and rightfully glory in having been and in being the first place not only in Spain but in the whole world to possess and maintain the faith and altar of the Catholic faith: the church having been erected by the hands of angels at the command of the Most Sacred Queen, the Virgin Mother of God, while she was still living in the flesh, through the agency of Lord James the Greater, apostle of Christ and his cousin.

Add also the testimony of St. Braulio in his additions to Maximus, which we shall soon cite, together with that of Julianus, archpresbyter of St. Justa at Toledo.

For the present, it is enough to report the words of Aimo, who flourished in the year of the Lord 870. In book 1, chapter 6 of his *Translation of St. Vincent the Martyr*, after stating that the monk Audaldus transported the relics of the holy martyr as far as Zaragoza in the year 855, he adds:

> The aged bishop, astonished and greatly amazed, and judging that it was certainly the body of some holy martyr, ordered it to be taken away and reverently deposited in the church of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin (of the Pillar), which is the mother of the churches of that city. In that place, under Bishop Valerius, the same vigorous martyr and athlete had once held the distinguished office of archdeacon.

Here he clearly affirms that, by the privilege of its merits, that church was the cathedral in the time of St. Vincent and the mother of the other churches of the city [Col. 0115C], since it had been built by the apostle St. James.

But lest so noble a monument of antiquity perish, I am pleased to insert here a graceful epigram composed a thousand years ago by D. M. Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza:

> The first house dedicated to Mary was called the Pillar.  
> The gracious Mother herself entrusted it to James.  
>   
> When the sacred herald, preaching the seeds  
> Of the divine word, first scattered them here,  
> Traversing the Iberian towns in faith,  
> The Mother worthy of reverence, of man and God, stood here  
> And commanded that a house arise in the great city.  
>   
> Since it was to be the first, alone before all other shrines,  
> Peoples gathered from every direction would seek it.  
> O excellent house, blessed hall of the great heavenly beings,  
> Which the gracious Mother chose for herself!  
>   
> If anyone ever desires heaven upon earth,  
> Let him here offer vows and prayers to the Mother of God.  
> For here he will experience the Mother’s divine presence  
> And from here receive help in troubled affairs.  
>   
> Upon entering, fear and sudden reverence arise  
> For the Mother, for the place, and for the choirs of heaven [Col. 0115D].  
>   
> What wonder that this house, full of the divine power of the Mother,  
> Moves the earth? For she moves heaven.

The following hymn concerning the house of the Blessed Virgin of the Pillar is likewise by M. Maximus:

> O glory of Zaragoza,  
> And sweet protection,  
> Pillar of the Iberian people,  
> Temple of the immovable Column.  
>   
> You are said to surpass all  
> The sacred shrines of Iberia,  
> O wondrous Jerusalem,  
> House of the chaste Virgin.  
>   
> The Mother herself chose you  
> Before all chambers beneath the sun—  
> She who bore in her gracious womb  
> The Son of the Thunderer Most High.  
>   
> For she commands James the Apostle,  
> Her kinsman,  
> To build a shrine  
> That will endure through all ages.  
>   
> She showed herself joyful to him,  
> And on her birthday  
> The temple rites of the golden Conception  
> Endure [Al. “praises”].  
>   
> From this place James teaches the Spaniards  
> The day of the Conception,  
> And proclaims her, like the others,  
> Free from every stain.  
>   
> From this arose the custom  
> Of continually celebrating this day  
> Among the Iberian peoples,  
> A custom that endures to this day.  
>   
> From this also arose the practice  
> Of calling individual episcopal sees  
> “Jerusalems,” and from this house  
> The practice of using that name began.  
>   
> O great apparition  
> First made to James,  
> In the thirty-ninth year  
> Of the blessed Lord’s birth [Col. 0116B].

As for what is said here about the feast of the Conception, we refer the reader, so as not to burden this place, to the year 300, where we shall have to discuss that matter with Dexter. We likewise omit the fact that Maximus, in his *Chronicle*, attests to the same truth under the year of Christ 571. For now it is sufficient to have shown abundantly the tradition of the foundation of the Church of the Pillar, which is the subject here for the author. We shall discuss the nature of the apparition under the year 37.

### 4. Many miracles also, etc.

There is no justification for doubting that the holy Apostle performed many miracles in Spain by which he confirmed his preaching, since the Evangelist wrote concerning all the apostles:

> They went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.

There can be no doubt that those signs were the ones he had mentioned previously: “They will speak in new tongues, they will take up serpents,” etc.

The raising of the ancient prophet whom he appointed bishop of Braga was certainly an astonishing sign. Among the lead books discovered on the Holy Mountain of Granada, one is *On the Life, Journeys, and Miracles of St. James*, by St. Caecilius, his disciple; may God at some time bring it forth into the light.

Julianus too, speaking in his *Chronicle* under the year 36 about the monuments of Toledo, says:

> In the same archive of St. Justa there is a Latin history of the life of St. James, in which very great miracles are related.

Speaking of these, St. Notkerus says in his *Martyrology*, on 25 July:

> The same peoples are said to have been converted to the faith of Christ by his bodily presence, his teaching, and the efficacy of his signs.

Recall the testimony of Anastasius Sinaita which we cited above:

> He performed among them miracles at which the astonished people marveled, etc. [Col. 0116D]

### 5. Many Jews there also, etc.

Until now he had dealt with the conversion of the Gentiles; he now turns to the conversion of the Jews living in Spain.

It certainly seems impossible to deny that Jews had lived in Spain for many years before the preaching of Blessed James, since innumerable and highly authoritative writers acknowledge this, as is clear from what was said above. No one has yet called into question the fact that the apostle preached to Jews in Spain. Indeed, we know that some of their synagogues continued until the time of Ferdinand the Catholic, by whom they were finally expelled from Spain.

Besides those already cited there, Calixtus II taught this in his homily on St. James, saying:

> He went around villages, hamlets, and castles, entering the synagogues of the Jews and preaching the word of God.

The question raised by some is therefore: who were these Jews? From where, and when, did they come into Spain?

On this matter Florianus de Ocampo, Stephanus Garibay, and Joannes Mariana, in their Spanish chronicles, hold that the Jews were brought there by Pyrrhus, or Nabuzardan, commander of the fleet of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and that they were among those who had been led captive to Babylon at the time of the Babylonian captivity.

The authorities for Nebuchadnezzar’s journey to Spain are Megasthenes, book 4 of *Indian Affairs*; Josephus, book 10, chapter 11 of the *Jewish Antiquities*, and book *Against Apion*; and Strabo, book 15 of the *Geography*. They followed Megasthenes, who claimed—according to Josephus—that Nebuchadnezzar subdued a good part of Spain and—according to Strabo—reached as far as the Pillars of Hercules, as far as which he also brought Tearcon (I read: Tarracon). He then led that army from Spain into Thrace and the Pontus. No one denies that Nebuchadnezzar brought many Jews along in that army [Col. 0117B].

This was the most widely accepted assertion among the Spaniards, yet there is nothing so firmly established that those eager for novelties cannot find in it an occasion for doubt.

Among more recent writers, Alderete denied Nebuchadnezzar’s journey into Spain, in book 3, chapter 4 of *Spanish Antiquities: On the Languages of Spain*. Pineda rose against him in book 4, chapter 14 of *Solomonic Affairs*. Yet there was someone who defended Alderete against Pineda: Mantuanus, in his *Annotations on Mariana’s History*, while discussing chapter 7 of book 1 of that work, argued with all his strength that Megasthenes was a compiler of fictions, since he wrote incredible things about Indian affairs, as Pliny noted in book 6, chapter 17, and since even Strabo does not approve him.

Strabo says:

> Indeed, whoever has written about India has told many lies; among them Damaicus most of all, and Megasthenes next.

These are the men who report people lying on their ears, without mouths or nostrils, one-eyed, long-footed, and with fingers turned backward, etc. [Col. 0117C]

Moreover, those highly authoritative writers who recorded Nebuchadnezzar’s deeds, he says, do not mention this arrival in Spain: Berosus the Chaldean, cited by Josephus in book 1 *Against Apion*; Clement of Alexandria, book 1 of the *Stromata*; Tertullian, book *Against the Jews*; and Eusebius of Caesarea, book 9 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, following the assertions of Alexander Polyhistor and Alpheus.

It also matters that in Acts 2, among all the nations from which Jews had gathered at Jerusalem for the feast, Spain is not listed; nor does Philo, in *The Embassy to Gaius*, mention it in his catalogue of the provinces inhabited by Jews.

Finally, Nebuchadnezzar’s journey to Spain does not seem compatible with the divine oracles. Florianus, Mariana, and their associates assert that he besieged Tyre for thirteen years. Josephus taught this in book 10, chapter 13 of the *Antiquities*, from Philostratus, and in book 1 *Against Apion*, from the histories of the Phoenicians, where it is read that under King Ithobalus Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years [Col. 0117D].

When the Tyrians were freed from the siege with the aid of the Spaniards—many of whom had descended from the Tyrians themselves—it supposedly happened that Nebuchadnezzar, eager for vengeance against them, prepared an expedition and at that time took many Jews with him and brought them into Spain.

This, however, is shown to be impossible because the entire period of his life is most exactly reckoned in the sacred Scriptures, and no year can be assigned in which he could have turned aside to Spain.

In the eighth year of his reign, having made Jerusalem tributary, he brought King Jehoiakim with him to Babylon, according to 2 Kings 24:

> The king of Babylon took him in the eighth year of his reign; he also transferred Jehoiakim to Babylon.

Again, after nine years, Zedekiah, whom he had appointed king, rebelled against him. He besieged the city again and captured it after two years of siege—namely, in the eleventh year of Zedekiah’s reign, or of the captivity of Jerusalem, which was the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, as is expressly stated in 2 Kings 25, with verses 1, 2, and 8 taken together [Col. 0118A].

Since only nine years intervened between the first and second captivities of Jerusalem, it follows that Nebuchadnezzar could not have besieged Tyre during this period, since he is said to have spent thirteen full years in that siege.

He besieged Tyre, at the earliest, in the following year after the conquest of Jerusalem, namely, in the twentieth year of his reign. For in that same year of the second captivity, the eleventh year of the earlier captivity, the Lord threatened the destruction of Tyre through Ezekiel:

> And it came to pass in the eleventh year (namely, of the captivity of the prophet himself, who had been taken captive with Jehoiakim) that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Behold, I am bringing Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, against Tyre [Ezekiel 26], etc., because she had mocked the fall of Jerusalem.

He spent thirteen years in the siege of Tyre, so that the following words were rightly spoken by the Lord through Ezekiel, chapter 29:

> Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, made his army perform a great service against Tyre; every head was made bald and every shoulder stripped of hair.

Theodoretus comments:

> Prolonged residence commonly causes such things, since the heat often draws the skin apart in those parts that are exposed and uncovered on the body.

We now have thirty-three years of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, consisting of twenty and thirteen. Immediately afterward he went into Egypt and subjected it, just as God had promised him through the mouth of Ezekiel. After the words “every shoulder stripped of hair,” Ezekiel adds:

> Behold, I will give Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, the land of Egypt, and he shall take away its multitude.

Indeed, Josephus, book 10, chapter 2 of the *Antiquities*, states that he first invaded Coelesyria with great forces; after subduing it, he waged war against the Ammonites and Moabites; and after conquering them as well, he entered Egypt in hostility. Having killed the man who then reigned and appointed another king, he again carried the Jews found there away captive to Babylon.

Who would deny that he spent at least one year in conquering and traversing so many regions? Thus the thirty-fourth year of his reign would have been completed [Col. 0118C].

After two years had elapsed following the devastation of Egypt, Josephus says in book 4, chapter 12, Nebuchadnezzar saw the remarkable dream reported by Daniel in chapter 2:

> In the second year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, Nebuchadnezzar saw, etc.

Jerome, on the authority of the Hebrews, interprets the expression “in the second year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign” to mean the second year of his reign over all the barbarian nations—the Egyptians, Moabites, and others.

Another year must necessarily be added to allow time for the convocation of all the satraps, magistrates, judges, commanders, tyrants, prefects, and all the rulers of the provinces, so that they might assemble for the dedication of the statue that the king had erected, as described in Daniel 3. This makes thirty-five years of his reign.

After he had seen another vision concerning the fact that he would live among the beasts, deprived of his kingdom and of human society, which occurred after the completion of twelve months, as Daniel 4 relates, thirty-six years had passed.

Add to these the seven “times” that elapsed over him while he lived among the beasts, ate grass like an ox, and was finally restored to his kingdom and brought his life to its end. These amount to another seven years, according to the interpretation of Tertullian, book 1 *On Repentance*, and Josephus, book 10, chapter 12 of the *Antiquities*. Together they make forty-three years, which the same Josephus, in the following chapter, reports as the duration of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign.

Thus no time remained for him to travel to Spain with the Jews.

Let us also leave aside the fact that it is not easy to believe that the king of Babylonia carried away Jewish colonists to cultivate a recently conquered province; for it would have been appropriate to send there not rebellious captives, but wholly loyal subjects.

Such, in substance, is their argument.

Nevertheless, although these weapons seem extremely powerful to their authors, it will nevertheless be easy for us to shatter them all. The fact that Megasthenes is not to be trusted in everything does not prevent him from being accepted in matters that he himself witnessed and that involve neither impossibility nor anything monstrous. Hence Josephus, although he ridicules his marvels, does not reject Nebuchadnezzar’s journey to Spain. Let us grant, moreover, that Berossus, Tertullian, and Eusebius do not mention it; yet if they do not deny it, they can in no way obstruct us. We have already shown that Spaniards were present at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, among all the nations that are under heaven, and that the Evangelists designate them under the name “Roman sojourners.” Josephus the Jew, as cited by Baronius under the year of the Lord 72, no. 30, bears especially clear witness to this, saying:

> The clemency of the Romans granted to everyone a not inconsiderable gift in the use of their name, not only to individual men but also collectively to the greatest nations. Thus the ancient Spaniards, Tyrrhenians, and Sabines are called Romans.

And Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 48, says: “They all became Romans, and they are all called Romans.”

Finally, that chronological arrangement—or, as I might call it, that stitching together—of Nebuchadnezzar’s years and deeds is not so orderly and even that it cannot bear a thousand tears and cracks through which the Jews might have passed into Spain. Nine years intervened between the captivity of Jehoiachin and his people and the captivity of Zedekiah; during this period Nebuchadnezzar is said to have been occupied with no other undertaking. Why, with so much leisure, could he not have gone to Spain with the Jews, namely, exiling those who had been taken captive to Babylon with King Jehoiachin?

If you object that he had not yet besieged Tyre, out of hatred for which he is said to have set out because the Spaniards had aided it, I can readily answer that this rather supports our position. For when Josephus says in Book I Against Apion: “In the seventh year of his reign Nebuchadnezzar began to besiege Tyre,” this cannot be understood of the principal thirteen-year siege, which occurred after the captivity of Zedekiah. It therefore follows that he besieged Tyre twice: first in the seventh year of his reign, and again in the twentieth. During the first siege he was compelled to withdraw from there because of the auxiliary forces of the Spaniards, and then he proceeded to Jerusalem, in the eighth year of his reign. There, after defeating King Jehoiachin, the whole of Jerusalem was led away captive, as stated in 2 Kings 24.

In this passage I seem to see it indicated clearly enough that not all the Jews of Jerusalem were taken away to Babylon, but only seven or eight thousand, although the entire, innumerable multitude of the people is said to have been transferred into captivity, with nothing left except the poor of the land. Yet the place to which those many thousands were transferred is not specified; and thus room is left for the Spanish migration.

These are the words of the holy author when he treats of the first captivity:

> Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came to the city of Jerusalem to attack it; and he transferred all Jerusalem, and all the princes, and all the army’s mighty men—ten thousand—into captivity, together with every craftsman and smith. He also transferred Jehoiachin to Babylon, and all the strong men, seven thousand, and the craftsmen and smiths, one thousand—all the mighty men and warriors. The king of Babylon led them captive to Babylon.

When he first says that “all the army’s mighty men, ten thousand,” were transferred into captivity, why, when he enumerates the captives again, does he not say that ten thousand mighty men were taken away, as he had said previously, but only seven thousand, together with one thousand craftsmen? I do not see how this difficulty can be resolved unless we say that the ten thousand mighty men mentioned first were indeed transferred into captivity, but that the place to which they were taken is not specified. Later, however, those who were brought specifically to Babylon are identified. For if all the captives had been taken there, it would not have been seven thousand but ten thousand warriors who were said to have been transferred to Babylon.

It therefore remains that, of the ten thousand first mentioned, seven thousand mighty men were taken to Babylon, while the remainder—that is, three thousand—were expelled and transferred elsewhere, but not to Babylon. Indeed, of the entire multitude of the people who were led captive, apart from the seven thousand warriors and the one thousand craftsmen mentioned above, it is not said to what places they were transferred. Therefore many of them could have been taken to Spain.

Moreover, during that interval of thirteen years in which he later besieged Tyre, who cannot see that he could have gone to Spain with a large force of his peoples, while the siege had not yet been lifted, by way of the Mediterranean Sea? In this way he would not only restrain the Spaniards from again bringing aid to the Tyrians, as they had done during the earlier siege, but would also take vengeance upon them and send many Jews into their vast territories—especially so that such a great crowd of enemies would not remain within his own kingdom. He could prudently have feared rebellion if, while he himself was outside Babylon with all his forces for thirteen years, he had left so many thousands of Jewish captives in his kingdom and household.

I shall say nothing of the possibility that in subsequent years he might have sent Nebuzaradan, the commander of his army, with an army to Spain, even if he himself remained in Babylon; for whatever his ministers conquered would be said to have been accomplished by him.

Whatever may be said about the time when the Jews were transferred to Spain, it is certain in every respect that they were transferred there at some point. Besides the authors already cited, Julian taught this in his *Chronicle* under the year 36, saying:

> The Jews who had come from Jerusalem to Toledo built there the most celebrated synagogue in all Spain and the world, unwilling to return to Jerusalem because they had heard that, after the temple had been rebuilt, it would again be destroyed.

And farther on, under the year 66, speaking of the Apostle James, he says: “He preached to the twelve tribes established in Spain, as Sophronius teaches, and wrote the canonical epistle, as Isidore teaches.”

Saint Athanasius, the first bishop of Caesaraugusta, had lived long before Julian. We cited his fragment above; in treating of Saint Peter of Braga, he says:

> He had come with the twelve tribes sent by Nebuchadnezzar from Jerusalem into Spain, under the leadership of Nebuzaradan or Pyrrhus, the governor of the Spaniards.

[Col. 0120C] But when we possess divine testimony, why do we try to seek support elsewhere? “The migration of Jerusalem that is in the Bosphorus,” says Obadiah, “shall possess the cities of the South.” Where Jerome has the word *Bosphorus*, the Hebrew has *Sepharad*, which among all the Hebrews means Spain, as Rabbi Solomon and Lyra noted in that passage, and most learnedly Arias Montanus.

The fact that Jerome translates it as “Bosphorus” does not conflict with this. To say “the migration that is in the Bosphorus” is the same as saying “the migration that extends to the strait, or as far as the Bosphorus”—for “strait” and “Bosphorus” mean the same thing—namely, the migration that was carried as far as the Pillars of Hercules, which shall possess the cities of the South. Certainly, since he placed the Bosphorus as the limit of a great distance, the Pillars of Hercules should also be understood antonomastically.

Arias Montanus derives this from the fact that the Hebrews use only consonantal letters. The same consonants, however, form *Sepharad* and *Sperida*, namely S-P-R-D. No one is unaware that Spain was formerly called *Sperida* by the Greeks, or, with aspiration, *Hesperida*. Therefore what is *Sperida* among the Greeks must be called *Sepharad* among the Hebrews, namely Spain. It was indeed customary among Greeks, Hebrews, and Chaldeans for proper names to differ only in their vowels, while retaining the same consonants. An example is Mithridates: the Greeks call him *Mithridates*, the Chaldeans *Mathredat*, and the Hebrews *Mithridath*. Thus, in Obadiah’s time, one must say that the migration of Jerusalem already existed in *Sepharad* or *Sperida*, that is, in Spain.

There are also substantial conjectures based on the names of several towns that appear to have been given by Jews in Spain so that they might preserve the memory of their homeland: Maggedo, Ascalon, Jobbe, and Nobe—today Maqueda, Escalona, Jeppes, and Nobes—in the kingdom of Toledo. Indeed, Toledo itself is believed to have been named by them from the Hebrew *Toledoth*, meaning “tribes” or “generations,” because the division of Jewish families was observed especially carefully in that city. Thus Arias Montanus on Obadiah, and Mariana in the place cited.

If any disagreement remains among the authors, it concerns the claim of some that all the Jews brought into Spain came from the single tribe of Judah, which Arias Montanus vigorously maintains. His words on Obadiah are:

> It is the settled opinion of all the writers of that people that this entire multitude consisted of families of the Jews who had inhabited Jerusalem and the tribe of Judah, and not of the other tribes.

Others, however, maintain that they came from the twelve tribes. This is asserted by Saint Athanasius of Caesaraugusta and by the archdeacon Julian in the words cited above. Yet the two views can be reconciled if we say that the Jews taken away by Nebuzaradan belonged only to the tribe of Judah, since they had been taken from the captivity of Jerusalem; afterward, however, many from the other tribes joined them—refugees from the Assyrian captivity, under whose dominion the ten tribes of Israel had been led captive.

It is credible that they came to Spain when they received news of the prosperity of those already living there. These, Montanus says, were first settled in two places: one called Lucina, a very populous town in that province during those centuries, which we believe to be either Lucena or Sessa, formerly Lucentia; the other Toledo. Thereafter they inhabited Ascalon, Mageddon, and other towns.

But, so that we do not pass over anything in silence, what Obadiah foretold—that the Jews of that migration which is in the Bosphorus, or in Spain, would possess the cities of the South—was fulfilled in Saint James and his disciples, as Lyra interprets the passage. “This was fulfilled,” he says, “through the Apostle James and his disciples, who first preached the faith of Christ there and subjected the necks of the nations.” This is suggested by what the prophet adds: “And saviors shall ascend Mount Zion to judge the mountain of Esau, and the kingdom shall belong to the Lord.”

Rabbi Solomon reads: “And the kingdom shall belong to the Lord in Spain.” Farther on, under the year 68, we shall examine Isaiah’s notable prophecy, by which he predicted that Spain would be the first province of the Gentiles to be converted to the faith by the apostles. I say this out of affection for my reader.

### 6. “And especially he sends them the Canonical Epistle,” etc.

This statement caused many people no small scandal and perhaps led them to doubt the author of this *Chronicle*. “Who,” they ask, “could persuade himself that a man equally learned and serious was ignorant of what was obvious to anyone with eyes and a barber?” This is especially difficult to assert of Dexter, since he had an unusually close relationship with Saint Jerome, who stated in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*—under James—that the canonical epistle was written not by the son of Zebedee but by the son of Alphaeus. Before Jerome, Eusebius had made the same assertion in Book II, chapter 22, of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

This assertion is certainly confirmed by the common judgment of the Doctors of the Church, and no opening for doubt seems to remain, since the most sacred Council of Trent affirmed it in Session 14, chapter 1, *On the Institution of the Sacrament of Extreme Unction*, saying that it is indicated in Mark and, through James the apostle and brother of the Lord, commended and promulgated to the faithful—namely, in the words of this Epistle, chapter 5: “Is anyone among you sick?” etc. Epiphanius used the same manner of speaking in Book *Against John, Bishop of Jerusalem*.

Everyone knows that the Apostle James, called the brother of the Lord, was the son of Alphaeus. Paul designates him by this name when he says in Galatians 1: “I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord.” The reason for this title, Saint Ignatius says in his second letter to John the Apostle, is that they report him to have been like Jesus Christ in face, life, and manner of conduct, as though he had been his twin brother from the same womb: “They say, ‘I see him if I see Jesus himself,’ according to all the features of his body.”

Someone has nevertheless attempted to defend Dexter from this blemish by observing that he did not say that “our James” wrote that canonical epistle, but that he sent it to the Spaniards—which, he says, does not exclude its having been written by someone else.

But, to state my own view, there is no doubt that such authors became fearful precisely where there was no cause for fear. To make this clear, I shall attempt to demonstrate two things: first, that the Church has not yet defined that James the son of Alphaeus was the author of the canonical epistle, thereby leaving room for Dexter’s opinion; second, that Dexter’s position rests not on slight grounds but on many arguments of great weight.

The first point is made certain for me by all the catalogues of the canonical books of the Bible: that of Pope Gelasius, issued at the Roman Council and found in Distinction 15, chapter *Sancta Romana*; those of the Councils of Nicaea, Milevis, Laodicea, Carthage, Florence; and also that of the Council of Trent itself, found in Session 4. For nowhere do they say that the epistle was written by anyone other than “the Apostle James,” without adding any distinguishing title of the author. The Council of Trent uses the same wording in canons 1, 2, and 4 concerning the sacrament of Extreme Unction.

Since, however, chapter 1 of the aforementioned Session 14 says that the sacrament was promulgated through “James the apostle and brother of the Lord,” it must be certain that this does not define the author of the epistle as James the Lesser. The words “and brother of the Lord” do not substantially belong to the intended definition, which concerned the truth of that sacrament, established by the testimony of the Epistle of James, and which was disputed with the heretics. All theologians know that words spoken incidentally by councils do not possess the force of a definition when no prior deliberation and disputation concerning them has taken place; and that nothing can be defined without sufficient prior examination.

Two matters concerning this epistle have thus far been disputed and defined in the Church against the heretics: that it is canonical and that it was published by the Apostle James. Which James it was, however, has not yet been defined.

I say this for those who think that the title “brother of the Lord” belongs exclusively to James the son of Alphaeus. This, however, is not secure, since the chronicler Julian states that James the son of Zebedee was also once accustomed to be called by the same name. Indeed, a feast of his Translation was celebrated in Spain under that title on December 30.

Here are the words of this author when he discusses the matter under the year 66:

> His feast is held under the name of James the brother of the Lord, a name that also applies to James the Greater.

Nor is this surprising, since in the Gospel not only James the son of Alphaeus but also his brothers Simon and Thaddeus, and besides these James and John, the sons of Zebedee, are called the brothers of the Lord. Matthew 12, Mark 3, and Luke 8 teach that they were commonly so called, in these words:

> While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside.

Commenting on this passage, Jerome says against Helvidius:

> It remains that you understand them to have been called brothers by relationship.

And on Matthew he says:

> Some suppose that the brothers of the Lord were sons of Joseph by another wife, following the ravings of the apocrypha and inventing a certain little woman named Escha as his wife. We, however, understand the brothers of the Lord not as sons of Joseph but as the Savior’s cousins.

Bede likewise says:

> The brothers of the Lord are not, according to Helvidius, sons of the ever-virgin Mary; nor, according to certain others, are they to be considered sons of Joseph by another wife. Rather, they are to be understood as his relatives. Relying on the privilege of this blood relationship, the mother of the sons of Zebedee dared to ask the Lord that he grant her two sons, James and John, the two principal seats of the heavenly kingdom, as Matthew reports in chapter 20.

Paul does not stand in our way in his Epistle to the Galatians. There he does not say that James the Lesser was specially called “the brother of the Lord” among all the apostles, but that he was the brother of the Lord—which is entirely true. Ignatius merely says that he greatly desired to see James the Lesser because he was exceedingly like Christ in face. He does not say at all that this likeness was the reason for the title. He says similarly:

> I desire to see that venerable James, who is called the Just, whom they report to have been like Jesus Christ in face, etc.

Let us now examine the considerations supporting the contrary opinion, which Dexter follows here and which seem to me to carry considerable weight. Heleca, bishop of Caesaraugusta, taught this opinion—he flourished in learning and virtue around the year 800 of the Lord—in his additions to M. Maximus. Speaking of his own age, when Spain was oppressed by the wretched servitude of the Moors, he says:

> The Holy Scriptures translated into Arabic are held by Catholic priests and circulate with commentaries. In particular, the New Testament, the Gospel, the Epistles of Paul, and the Epistle of James the son of Zebedee, sent to the Spaniards, the Jews already converted from the Dispersion; the Epistles of Peter, Paul, and Jude, which were sent to all those converted from Judaism, but especially to the Spaniards gathered from the twelve tribes; the Apocalypse of Saint John; and the book *On the Lives of the Fathers*, etc.

King Alfonso of Spain, called the Wise, held the same belief and left it written in his book *The Treasury*, as Mariana reports in his treatise on Blessed James. More significantly, the Syrians expressly profess this in the Syriac edition of the New Testament published by Tremellius and Wastadius, where we read:

> We seal the three Epistles of James, Peter, and John. These are the men who bore witness to the revelation of our Lord, when he changed himself before their eyes on Mount Tabor.

Everyone knows that the James who witnessed the Lord’s Transfiguration was not the son of Alphaeus but the son of Zebedee, as Matthew teaches in chapter 17, and Mark and Luke in chapter 9.

Julian expressly acknowledges the same thing in his *Chronicle* under the year 66, in these words:

> When the twelve tribes had been established in Spain, as Sophronius teaches, he preached and wrote the canonical epistle, as Isidore and, before him, other celebrated Spanish writers teach. This was the common opinion of that age, as the Mass of Saint James, purged by Isidore, supplemented by Melantius, and enlarged by Saint Serrano Asturius, most clearly testifies, along with others.

If these things are so, no one can doubt that Dexter’s position carries great authority.

Let us now consider the individual points. Saint Isidore, in Book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, chapter 71, writes:

> James, son of Zebedee and brother of John, fourth in order—preceded in the catalogue of the apostles by Peter, Paul, and Andrew—wrote to the twelve tribes that are in the dispersion of the nations. He preached the Gospel to the peoples of the western regions of Spain and poured the light of preaching into the western part of the world.

Because this testimony is so explicit, it is customary to answer it in two ways. Baronius denies that the author of the book was Isidore of Seville. But this is wrong, since it is found in all the surviving ancient manuscripts of the works of this holy Doctor, and possesses the same antiquity as they do. Saint Ildefonsus, his disciple, recognizes it as a genuine work in his additions to Jerome’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he says:

> After his brother Leander, Isidore wrote works both distinguished and numerous, namely the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, etc.

Saint Braulio of Caesaraugusta, also a disciple of Isidore, enumerates the latter’s works in his abridgement of Isidore’s life, saying:

> One book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, in which he briefly recorded their deeds, their dignity, and also their deaths and burials.

Vincent of Beauvais, Saint Antoninus, Sigebert, Peter of Equilinum, Trithemius, Zurita, Morales, Lipomanus, Surius, and all who have thus far discussed the works of Saint Isidore agree with this.

Baronius himself uses the following argument in his notes for April 4 to prove that Saint Isidore was not the author of the *Collection of Decrees* attributed to him: Saints Ildefonsus and Braulio, his disciples, do not mention that work. It seems to me that the Cardinal himself would concede this point unless the author had so clearly professed the arrival of Saint James in Spain.

Therefore others, admitting the book but shaken by fear, say that the word *scripsit*—“he wrote”—must be excluded from Isidore’s statement, so that it would say only:

> To the twelve tribes that are in the dispersion of the nations he preached the Gospel to the peoples of the western regions of Spain.

But this too, I speak boldly, is done recklessly. For if, in every difficult statement of the Fathers, one were permitted to remove a word, we would have nothing certain or consistent throughout the writings of the holy Doctors, and the heretics would be given a reasonable basis for slander. Let those who do this now in the case of Isidore consider by what authority they act.

It would indeed be sufficient if some ancient manuscripts lacked that word; but this is not found. On the contrary, Peter of Fontiduena, a canon of Salamanca, compared eighteen very old manuscripts at the command of Philip II, Catholic King. If the word had been absent from any of them, he would undoubtedly have noted it; yet he did nothing of the kind. John Grial, who edited the work, and Loaysa, who also corrected it, likewise, when they judge that the word *scripsit* should be excluded, do not cite a single reading without it. They merely say: “We agree with those who consider the word *scripsit* foreign to the text.”

I, however, agree not with them but with the oldest manuscripts. To reassure those who have hitherto thought that the word should be removed, let them read chapter 77, where Isidore speaks of another James. If the holy Doctor had considered James the son of Alphaeus to be the author of the epistle, and not James the son of Zebedee, he would certainly have ascribed the epistle in that chapter to James the son of Alphaeus, as Jerome did in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Yet he did nothing less than this, although, had he held the contrary opinion, he would not have passed over a matter so worthy of note.

Here are his words:

> James the son of Alphaeus, called the Just, bishop of Jerusalem, son of the sister of the Mother of the Lord, and therefore also called the brother of the Lord; a man of light and worker of truth, and of such holiness that the people eagerly vied with one another to touch the hem of his garment.

Isidore then continues with his account of James’s martyrdom: how he was thrown from the pinnacle of the temple, and how, according to Josephus, many believed that Jerusalem was captured by Titus because of his death. But concerning the epistle he says not a word. It is therefore beyond doubt that Isidore agreed with Dexter.

This should not seem surprising, since in the Missal of Saint Isidore, within the very Canon of the Mass, James the son of Zebedee is expressly called the author of the canonical epistle—and this more than once. In it the priest is said to pray as follows:

> Recognizing Jesus, our most beloved brothers, who calls us to himself—he who, calling his most blessed Apostle James to himself while he was mending his nets in the boat, afterward admonishes and teaches us through his spiritual doctrines that, when we ask, we should not hesitate in faith—let us entreat that same Lord with complete devotion of mind and tears, so that our petition may obtain for us from God the fulfillment of what we have learned through the words of that Apostle.

And farther on:

> Let us pray. We are forewarned by your Apostle James that if any one of us lacks wisdom, he should ask it of you, who give generously to all and reproach no one, etc.

And again:

> May Christ God, the Son of God the Father, whom James followed with the full intention of his heart after leaving his father in the boat, make you cling continually to his footsteps. Amen. May he who, through this Apostle of his, converted the worshipers of demons to the faith grant you, by rejecting the vanities of this world, to love him in truth. Amen.

And in another prayer for Saint James the son of Zebedee, he says:

> May the teaching proclaimed by your Apostle James live in us, Lord Jesus—namely, the teaching that he preached and gave us, by which we are taught that blessed is the one who was able to bear the burden of temptation with equanimity.

Thus the whole Church of Spain, which once used this Missal and Breviary, and which still preserves them in Toledo, Seville, and Salamanca, professes without hesitation—not in a corner but in the church and in the very venerable sacrifice of the Mass—that its patron, James the son of Zebedee, taught us that if anyone lacks wisdom, he should ask for it, etc.; that we should not hesitate when asking in faith; and that blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life, etc. These are the very words of chapter 1 of the canonical epistle.

That this was the man whom Christ called to himself while he was mending nets in the boat is taught by Mark in chapter 1 and by Matthew in chapter 4.

Saint Clement, pope, is especially useful to this argument. When writing his second letter to James, the brother of the Lord and bishop of Jerusalem, he cites in confirmation of his teaching the words of chapter 4 of this epistle:

> Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you. Do not speak evil of one another, brothers. Whoever speaks evil of a brother or judges his brother speaks evil of the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. There is one lawgiver and judge, who is able to destroy and to save. But who are you to judge your neighbor?

He introduces so long a passage from the epistle when writing to him. If the epistle had belonged to that Apostle, there is no doubt that he would have prefaced it by saying that James had rightly written, “Humble yourselves,” etc. But he asserts nothing of the kind. Rather, he cites the saying as though it were sacred Scripture belonging to another and distant author.

There are also matters in the epistle itself that cannot suit James the Lesser but do suit James the Greater, especially its opening:

> James, servant of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, sends greetings to the twelve tribes that are in the dispersion.

I omit the fact that in chapter 4 the Apostle forbids wars: “From where do wars and quarrels arise among you?”—words that sufficiently suggest the warlike spirit of the Spaniards.

From this it follows that the author was the James who preached to the twelve tribes living in the dispersion. The apostles wrote to those who were inhabitants of the provinces assigned to their preaching, so that they might preserve in writing what they had taught them by word. As for regions that did not belong to their own provinces, none of the apostles took such care of them, lest he appear to put his sickle into another’s harvest. Each considered it sufficient to give an account of the sheep specially entrusted to him.

But the James who preached to the twelve tribes living in the dispersion was James the Greater, not James the Lesser, as will be evident from Sophronius, Dorotheus, and Isidore. Sophronius says in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> James, son of Zebedee, preached the Gospel to all the twelve tribes that were in the dispersion.

Dorotheus, in his *Synopsis*, title “On the Twelve Apostles,” chapter 3, says:

> James, son of Zebedee, the fisherman, preached to the twelve tribes living in the dispersion.

Isidore, in Book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, chapter [number omitted in the source], writes the same words that we cited above. Julian says the same in his *Chronicle* under the year 66.

But concerning James the son of Alphaeus, no one even hints at such a thing. Indeed, no one says that he preached anywhere except Jerusalem, where he dealt not with those in the dispersion but with the inhabitants. This is what Blessed Julian, archbishop of Toledo, intended in his commentary on Nahum, chapter 1, on the words “and the clouds are the dust of his feet,” when he used this expression of the other apostles:

> Peter brought him to Rome, John to Asia, Andrew to Achaea, James to Spain, etc.

Of James the son of Alphaeus he does not say that he brought the Lord here or there, but rather: “James the son of Alphaeus kept him in Jerusalem.” Namely, his own allotted portion was that city; whereas Spain fell by lot to James the son of Zebedee, where the dispersion of the twelve tribes existed, as we have already shown.

And why should I delay? Jerome himself admits that it is not so certain that the epistle is the work of James the Lesser; indeed, he says that it was published by someone else under his name. Nor should it seem surprising that Saint Jerome, who never reached Spain, did not know the epistle’s true author, since the testimony concerning him existed there, especially in the Mass of Saint James the son of Zebedee.

After I had written these things, the distinguished and highly learned John de Salazar, archdeacon of Úbeda in the holy Church of Jaén, gave me a copy of his apologetic treatise *On the Coming of Saint James*. I was especially pleased when I read that in chapter 6 he vigorously and learnedly defended the position that the epistle was written by Saint James the son of Zebedee. I refer my readers to him, and promise that in a single volume they will find everything they could desire concerning the arrival of Saint James in Spain. I have also found that Father Gaspar Sancius held the same opinion as a probable one in Treatise 3, chapter 12, *On the Preaching of Saint James*.

### 7. “Which was the first writing,” etc.

Since Saint James migrated to heaven through martyrdom before the other apostles or evangelists wrote, with Matthew alone excepted, it is only with Matthew that there can be a dispute concerning priority in the time of writing. Nevertheless, in its proper place we shall see that Matthew wrote in the year 41, while James wrote in the year 40.

When this epistle is compared with the other writings of the New Testament, it appears to be the first in chronological order. For this seems to have been the sole reason why it has until now held the first place among the other canonical epistles in the Church. This order is found not only in recently printed Bibles but also in ancient manuscripts, and even in the catalogue of books issued at the Council of Laodicea in the year of the Lord 364, where we read:

> Seven canonical epistles: one of James, two of Peter, three of John, and one of Jude.

It cannot be understood why it is placed before the Epistles of Peter except because it was written earlier. The four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, and the fourteen Epistles of Paul precede it because they are the more important parts of the New Testament, not because all of them were written before the seven canonical epistles.

Furthermore, the sacrament of Extreme Unction was promulgated in this epistle, chapter 5. It does not seem possible that the other sacred writers could have omitted it unless it had already been written down.

Finally, when this epistle was written, no heresy had yet arisen, since it attacks none of that period. We do not find this in the other epistles and Gospels. Therefore it contains only moral instruction and exhortation to every virtue, especially patience, prayer, mercy, faith joined to works, observance of the whole divine law, and moderation of the tongue. It argues against partiality, anger, lust, every form of desire, proud riches, and slander. Finally, it commends Extreme Unction and confession of sins, and discusses the communion of suffrages.

Cardinal Baronius objects under the year of Christ 63, no. 11, that Saint James dwells at length in this epistle on refuting the heresy of Simon, which had already arisen and which held that faith and hope without works were sufficient for salvation. He therefore argues that the epistle belonged to the son of Alphaeus and not to the son of Zebedee. This is not conclusive.

First, Simon had preached his errors at least one year before Saint James the son of Zebedee departed from Palestine—that is, in the year 35, shortly after the death of Saint Stephen—whereas James came to Spain in the year 36 and, as we have said, did not write the epistle until the year 40. Thus he had ample opportunity to write against that error.

Second, even if James admonished people that good works were necessary together with faith, it does not necessarily follow that he was there attacking a particular heresy, as though he could teach nothing except in opposition to heresies that had already arisen.

Certainly, when the other apostles attack heresies in their writings, they commonly identify their authors. Thus Paul says in 2 Timothy 2:

> Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have departed from the truth by saying that the resurrection has already taken place.

Peter says in his second epistle, chapter 2:

> Bold and self-willed, they are not afraid to introduce sects, blaspheming.

John says in his first epistle, chapter 2:

> Now many Antichrists have arisen; they went out from us, but they were not of us.

And Jude says:

> For certain ungodly men have slipped in, turning the grace of our God into licentiousness, etc.

Was James, then, the only one to spare the heretics, content simply to teach the truth opposed to their errors? Certainly not. Rather, since he does not identify them, we are taught that he was not arguing against heretics.

Moreover, Simon did not teach that faith and hope in God were sufficient for salvation. Rather, he taught of the hope and faith that people had in him and in his concubine Helen, arrogating to himself the dignity of Christ. Even if the other conclusion followed from this, we still do not know what he said about God, since heretics are not always consistent with themselves.

## 8. “Many disciples”

Authors hold differing opinions concerning the number of Saint James’s disciples. Some venture to say that he produced scarcely any fruit in Spain, and converted at most two or three disciples there—namely Athanasius and Theodore, and perhaps one other. Others extend the number to seven, specifically those who were afterward chosen by Peter as bishops and sent to Spain for the purpose of preaching: namely Torquatus and his companions. Some acknowledge nine, as does the Bishop of Equilinum, book VI, chapter 133, counting the first two together with the seven just mentioned. Finally, some enumerate twelve, adding to those already named three others whom James had converted to the faith at Jerusalem: Hermogenes and Philetus, previously devoted to magical arts, and Josias, who, having recently been baptized, was beheaded together with the Apostle. The author of this opinion is said to be Pope Calixtus II, in his book *On the Miracles of Saint James*. His words are as follows:

> “But it should be known that Blessed James had many disciples, but twelve special ones,” etc.

Here he appears to agree rather with Dexter, who says:

> “He brings many disciples with him to Spain, but twelve in particular.”

The meaning of these words, however, is not that he brought all of them into Spain—since he had plainly converted some of them before entering Spain, and this is not true—but that he led them into Spain, that is, across Spain from one of its provinces to another.

Dexter assigns the Apostle’s disciples who were in Spain. For he does not mention Philetus, Hermogenes, and Josias, whom James converted at Jerusalem after his departure from Spain. Since Dexter alone enumerates so many, no one ought to be considered so diligent in this matter; nevertheless, there is not one of them for whose apostolic connection with James as his disciple we lack serious testimony. Let us examine them individually.

### 1. Saint Peter

The first bishop of Braga, concerning whom enough has been said above. He was taken away by martyrdom in the year 45, on April 26, the day on which the Roman Martyrology, Usuard, and other authors commemorate him.

### 2. Saint Basil, second bishop of Braga

Saint Anastasius of Zaragoza recorded that he was James’s disciple. Speaking of Saint Peter of Braga, Anastasius says:

> “He appointed Saint Basil, his fellow disciple, to the see of Porto; and when Peter had been taken away by martyrdom, Basil succeeded him in the see of Braga.”

He suffered martyrdom for Christ in the year of the Lord 95, on May 23. On that day he is listed in the Roman Martyrology together with Saint Epitatius, bishop of Ambracia, whom we shall discuss below, in these words:

> “In Spain, the holy martyrs Epitatius the bishop and Basil.”

“Basil the bishop” is to be understood in the same way. Thus Equilinus teaches that the statement should be understood in his book II, at the end, number 148, where he says:

> “Epitatius and Basil, bishops, are renowned in Spain on May 23.”

An ancient manuscript martyrology of the Church of Plasencia in Spain, which glories in the teaching of Saint Epitatius, reads as follows:

> “Of the holy bishops of Spain, Epictetus and Basil: the former our bishop of Tui, and the latter the disciple of Peter, bishop of Braga.”

Prudentius de Sandoval, bishop of Pamplona, in his *History of Tui*, and Marieta, *On the Saints of Spain*, part I, book II, chapter 32, discuss Saint Basil as a disciple of Saint James.

### 3. Saint Pius, first bishop of Seville and martyr

That he was a disciple of the Apostle Saint James was taught more than five hundred years ago by the serious and learned Spanish historian Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1100, in the time of Alfonso VI, king of Spain. His book is preserved in the royal library of Saint Lawrence at the Escorial and in the library of the Church of Oviedo, where Ambrose de Morales read it. The aforesaid Sandoval, bishop of Pamplona, published it together with Pampyrus of Astorga and Sebastian of Salamanca, both bishops and very ancient writers.

Mariana likewise testifies to the same in book IV of his *History of Spain*, chapter 2, where he writes:

> “Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, who wrote his history nearly five hundred years ago, makes these men disciples of James: Calocerus, Basil, Pius, Chrysogonus, Theodore, Athanasius, and Maximus.”

Pius suffered martyrdom in the year of the Lord 60, on March 4. Caledonius of Braga also mentions him in his account preserved by Hugo of Portugal.

### 4. Saint Athanasius, first bishop of Zaragoza after the Apostle Saint James

Of all the Apostle’s disciples, Athanasius is the best known. He is recognized by Leo III, Calixtus II of Beauvais, and others when they write about Saint James; by the Breviaries of Córdoba and Évora and nearly all the ancient Breviaries of Spain; and by Pelagius of Oviedo, Vasaeus, Mariana, Marieta, and the other Spanish writers. He himself acknowledges this in the fragment quoted above concerning Saint Peter of Braga, saying:

> “James, son of Zebedee, my teacher,” etc.

M. Maximus wrote an epigram in his honor. It begins:

> Athanasius first becomes bishop in our city,  
> And an honored shepherd of the angelic house.

Further on it reads:

> Blessed in the piety of your spirit, old man, bishop and father,  
> You are James’s disciple and the glory of pontiffs.

More will be said about him in its proper places, under the years 42 and 50. We also discussed him above under the year 35, Commentary 2, where, on Julian’s testimony, we showed that he was sent with others to Jerusalem by the Jews of Spain concerning the death of Christ the Lord. See also the Caledonius and Hugo mentioned above.

### 5. Saint Theodore

Theodore succeeded Athanasius in the episcopate of Zaragoza. All those who discuss Saint Athanasius—including the Calixtus, Leo, and the others whom we have just cited—acknowledge Theodore as his disciple. The same is true of Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, and M. Maximus in the hymn that he composed concerning the first three bishops of Zaragoza. We shall give that hymn below, under the year 71. We shall speak of Theodore again under the years 50 and 71, in which he was crowned with martyrdom.

### 6. Saint Maximus

Maximus was a presbyter whom Pelagius of Oviedo also recognizes among Saint James’s disciples. He suffered martyrdom at Utica in Baetica with his companions Castus and Magnus, in the year 66, on September 4. Dexter discusses him again under that same year, 66.

### 7. Saint Chrysogonus

Chrysogonus, or Grisogonus, was a presbyter and a disciple of the same Apostle, as the same Pelagius of Oviedo acknowledges.

### 8. Saint Calocerus

Calocerus was the companion of Saint Apollinaris, the first bishop of Ravenna. When Apollinaris departed to evangelize the province of Emilia, Calocerus, a presbyter, governed the Church of Ravenna in the meantime. We read this in his *Life* as preserved by Equilinus, book VI, chapter 128.

Before this he had been a disciple of Saint James, as can be seen in the same Pelagius. That he later became bishop of Ravenna is established by the Roman Martyrology, under February 2, the day on which he departed to heaven.

The feast of Saint Apollinaris, bishop and martyr under the emperor Vespasian, is observed in the same Martyrology on July 23. Saint Marcian, his disciple, martyr, and fourth bishop of Ravenna, is commemorated on May 22. Jerome Rubeus writes in his *History of Ravenna*, book I of the second edition, that Marcian suffered martyrdom during the reign of the emperor Hadrian.

Since Hadrian began his reign in the year 118, while Calocerus succeeded Marcian in the episcopate, it follows that Calocerus must then have been more than one hundred years old, since he had been Saint James’s disciple in Spain from the year 38 or 40. This is not surprising, since at that very time Saint Simeon, bishop of Jerusalem, an old man of one hundred and twenty years, courageously endured the punishment of the cross.

We shall speak of Saint Calocerus again under the years 44 and 130, in which, specifically, he completed his course.

### 9–15. The remaining seven principal disciples

9. Caecilius;  
10. Thesiphon;  
11. Iscius;  
12. Torquatus;  
13. Secundus;  
14. Indalecius;  
15. Euphrasius.

These seven are the more famous disciples of Saint James, recognized by the supreme pontiffs Calixtus and Leo, and also by Primus, bishop of Chalon, in his *Spiritual Map of the World*, where he mentions Attacum, Abila, Almería, Eliberis, Iliturgis, and other places. They are also recognized by the Roman Breviary, which says:

> “Seven from their number were afterward ordained bishops by Blessed Peter and sent first into Spain.”

All the Churches of Spain have preserved and transmitted this tradition, received from their ancestors, continuously through the generations.

Their discipline under so great an Apostle is also proclaimed by the lead tablets discovered with the sacred ashes of the holy martyrs on the holy mountain of Granada. We shall have to discuss these again, and at length, below, where we shall see that after the death of their teacher they were ordained bishops by Saint Peter.

### 16–24. The other nine bishops

There remain nine other holy bishops:

16. Basil of Carthage Spartaria;  
17. Eugenius of Valencia;  
18. Agathodorus of Tarragona;  
19. Elpidius of Toledo;  
20. Aetherius of Barcelona;  
21. Capito of Lucus Augusti;  
22. Ephraem of Astorga;  
23. Nestor of Palencia;  
24. Arcadius of Juliobriga.

Saint Pius, bishop of Seville, whom we mentioned third, was their companion and inseparable associate. These ten suffered martyrdom under Nero, in the year of Christ 60, at Penniscola, a city of the kingdom of Valencia, as we shall say under that year together with Dexter.

That all of them were disciples of Saint James is clearly established by the testimony of Pelagius of Oviedo, who lists Basil and Pius among the Apostle’s disciples. Caledonius of Braga lists Pius and Elpidius, along with others. Likewise, the Church of Astorga, preserving a tradition received from its ancestors, holds that Saint Ephraem was a disciple of Blessed James and its first bishop.

It is established by the Greek Menologion, the Roman Martyrology, Usuard, Molanus, Galesinius, and others that all these bishops—ten in number—were companions of one another and received the crown of martyrdom together at the same place, on March 4. Therefore, without doubt, the same conclusion applies to all of them.

The aforesaid martyrologies do not assign their episcopal sees; this information must therefore be credited to Dexter. Since his account agrees with the others in so many names and in their order, place, and manner of death, it leaves no room for detractors to doubt.

A sufficiently effective argument also leads us to this conclusion. It was a custom carefully observed by the holy Apostles that, whenever they came to a province for the sake of preaching, or sent disciples to instruct it, they approached as soon as possible those cities that were the capitals of kingdoms. In this way the voice of the Gospel could reach everyone’s ears more quickly and easily; for once the ruler had been brought to the faith, the others would readily give their allegiance.

Thus Peter went to Rome and Antioch; Matthew to Nataaber, the royal city in which an Egyptian ruled; Andrew to Patras, the principal city of Achaea; and Bartholomew and Thomas brought the kings of their provinces to the faith, together with a vast multitude. I say nothing of Paul and John, whom we know to have traveled through the chief cities of the world.
