The same principle will easily be recognized in the disciples of the Apostles. Thus Dionysius went to Paris; Paul Sergius to Narbonne; Lazarus to Marseille; Julian to Le Mans; and so forth.

No one is unaware that the principal cities of the kingdoms of Spain were Toledo, Tarragona, Valencia, Seville, Barcelona, Lucus, and Astorga. We must therefore acknowledge that the Gospel was first preached and bishops established in these cities.

But the seven disciples whom Peter sent into Spain—Torquatus and his companions—were directed neither to any of these cities nor to the interior regions of Spain, but only to coastal Baetica: namely Acci, Urci, Iliturgi, Carteia, Hispalis, and Vergium. Secundus alone was an exception, for he preached at Abula, an inland city.

Why, then, did none of them become bishop of Toledo, Seville, or Barcelona? Nothing better suggests itself than that those principal cities had already been adorned with the bishops mentioned above. See what we shall say about these matters under the year 60.

## 9. “The Jews of Spain”

Enough has already been said about this matter under the year 35, Commentary 2. There we cited Julian’s repeated assertion that he had read these letters in the Hebrew language, in which they had been written, and also in Latin and Arabic, into which they had been translated by Christians during the time of the Romans and later by the Moors who subjected Spain to themselves.

Julian himself, in the time of King Alfonso VI, who freed Toledo from Arab tyranny, translated these same letters into the Spanish language at the king’s command and deposited them in the archives of Toledo, where they were to be preserved for perpetual remembrance.

The Romans called that part of Spain which we now call the kingdom of Toledo *Carpetania*. They also called the mountain ranges that we now call Puerto de Somosierra, Guadarrama, Fonfría, and Palomera the *Carpetanian Mountains*. These separated one Castile from another.

That this was the ancient name can be seen in Pliny, Strabo, Morales, Mariana, and others. Some call it *Carpentania*, but that form was less common among the ancients.

## 10. “They had cursed”

The reading was formerly “exhorting.” But unless an entire line is missing, no sentence can be formed with that word; with the other reading, however, the sense is readily established.

## 11. “The Blessed Virgin to James”

We have discussed this matter sufficiently and more than sufficiently above, in this same year 37, Commentary 1, number 3, under the words “the first temple.”

What is now added concerning the arrival of the Apostle Saint John with the Blessed Virgin is said by Julian to have been read by him in an ancient writing at Toledo. It is better, however, to hear Julian himself speaking in his *Chronicle* under the year 36:

> “I also translated from Latin into Spanish a certain letter brought here—to Toledo—from Saint Mary of the Pillar at Zaragoza. It relates how James was summoned from Ephesus by Blessed Peter and came to Spain to preach, setting out from Joppa through the Mediterranean in the year 36. He traveled throughout that entire region and put in at the port of Tarragona, where he began to teach.
>
> “Then, after sending many disciples and messengers to Peter, he came from there to Zaragoza. While he was praying at night, the Blessed Virgin appeared to him upon a pillar, accompanied by angels and heavenly citizens, bringing with her Saint John, who had been the Blessed Virgin’s inseparable companion during her life. She commanded that a church be erected there in her honor, and an altar upon that pillar. She promised that devotion to the Blessed Virgin and the anchor of the holy faith would always remain there unshaken, more than in the other cities of Spain.”

With respect to the year of this apparition, M. Maximus differs slightly from Dexter. Dexter teaches that it occurred in the year of the Lord 37, whereas Maximus assigns it to the year 39, in these words of the hymn quoted above:

> O great apparition  
> First made to James,  
> In the thirty-ninth year  
> Of the birth of the gracious Lord.

Greater credence should be given to Dexter, as the older authority: Dexter died in the year 444, whereas Maximus died in 616. Nevertheless, even if the apparition occurred in the year 37, the erection of the temple took place in the year 39, as we shall say shortly.

## 12. “The Blessed Virgin, with John as her inseparable companion”

Consult Saint Bonaventure, the Carthusian, and all those who piously meditate upon the practices of the Blessed Mother of God after the death of her Son. Certainly no one who has a proper understanding of the Virgin Mother of God’s love and faith toward her Son will dare to deny this.

She therefore sanctified the devout stations at the Holy Sepulchre and at the other places associated with our redemption, providing an example for all the orthodox to do likewise.

---

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

For Saint James the holy Apostle, son of Zebedee, after traveling through the cities of Spain and erecting many churches and creating bishops from among the newcomers, left Peter as the first bishop of Braga. At his command and in his presence, he also erected at Zaragoza a temple or oratory to the Blessed Virgin upon a pillar.

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

He also performs many miracles. By the power of his preaching, he brings the fierce hearts of the Spaniards under the gentle yoke of Christ.

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

Many Jews from the twelve tribes of the Dispersion, exiled from Babylonia, are converted there; James also preached to them at that time.

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

He sends them especially the canonical letter, which begins as follows:

> “James, servant of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes that are in the Dispersion: greetings.”

This was the first writing of the New Testament, worthy of so great an Apostle.

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

He also brings many disciples with him into Spain in apostolic fashion, twelve in particular: Basil, Pius, and Athanasius, bishops; Maximus and Chrysogonus, presbyters; Theodore, Caecilius, Thesiphon, Iscius, and Calocerus, lectors; Torquatus, exorcist; and Secundus, Indalecius, and Euphrasius, doorkeepers.

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

Of these, Basil succeeded Peter of Braga; Athanasius was the first bishop of Zaragoza; and Pius was bishop of Seville.

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

Saint James also created other bishops: another Basil, who was the first bishop of Carthage Spartaria; Eugenius of Valencia; Agathodorus of Tarragona; Elpidius of Toledo; Aetherius of Barcelona; Capito of Lucus; Ephraem of Astorga; Nestor of Palencia; and Arcadius of Juliobriga.

All these were refugees, and Saint James preached with remarkable speed in all these cities and in other places in Spain.

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

Afterward Calocerus departed for Italy, joined Apollinaris, bishop of Ravenna, and, having been made a presbyter by him, succeeded Marcian. He became bishop when more than one hundred years old, yet still vigorous.

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

Seven other bishops, created by Blessed Peter, are sent back to Spain.

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

The Jews of Spain, especially those of Carpetania—who had cursed the letters sent by the priests of Jerusalem requesting their agreement in the death of Christ—receive Saint James’s preaching most willingly and are converted.

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

The Blessed Virgin appears upon a pillar at Zaragoza to James as he pours out prayers; John the Theologian also comes in spirit.

### A.D. 37. A.U.C. 788

The Blessed Virgin, with John her Son’s inseparable companion, very frequently visits the holy places associated with the Passion and Resurrection of her Son.

## [Note: [Col. 0131D]]

### A.D. 38

#### 1. “Saul,” etc.

Paul’s arrival at Jerusalem in the third year after his conversion is recorded by Paul himself in his Letter to the Galatians, chapter 1:

> “Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and remained with him fifteen days.”

Cajetan and others teach in that passage that these three years are to be reckoned from his conversion. This is also established by the events that he carried out during that interval: first, he disputed with the Jews at Damascus; after some days, when he was escaping their plot, he was lowered over the city wall in a basket. He did not then come to Jerusalem to his predecessors, the Apostles, but went away to Arabia and returned again to Damascus. Then, after three years had been completed, he came to Jerusalem to see Peter.

The fact that he uses the same expression shortly afterward in the same account in the Letter to the Galatians also supports this interpretation. In chapter 2 he says:

> “Then, after fourteen years, I again went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus with me.”

Yet these fourteen years must necessarily be reckoned from his conversion, not from the event immediately preceding, since otherwise many more years would have to be counted. We would allow three or four years for his preaching at Damascus, his journey to Arabia, and his return to Damascus. To these would have to be added the three years after which he is said to have gone to Jerusalem.

Again, two additional years must be counted, which he completed when he went from there into the regions of Syria and Cilicia, where he himself admits, in Galatians 1, that he preached the word of God. No one will deny that he spent at least two years in this work.

If these eight years must be added to the fourteen of which he said, “Then, after fourteen years, I again went up to Jerusalem,” it follows that twenty-two years had elapsed from his conversion when he went up to Jerusalem for the second time.

This is altogether impossible, since by then Paul was already being held in chains at Rome.

You ask how I establish this? From the fact that his conversion occurred after the death of Stephen. Not, however, in the following year, which was A.D. 35; for in that case only thirty days would have intervened between December 26 of the year 34, when Stephen died, and January 25 of the following year, when Paul’s conversion would have occurred. This conflicts with what Luke writes in Acts 8 and 9 concerning Paul’s persecution, by which he devastated the Church, entering houses and dragging men and women into custody; concerning his obtaining letters from the chief priest; and concerning his journey to Damascus. None of these things could have been accomplished in thirty days.

It must therefore be asserted that his conversion occurred on January 25 of the year 36.

The Roman Martyrology does not contradict this assertion when it says that the event took place in the second year after the Lord’s Ascension. The Ascension occurred on May 5 of the year 34, and from that day until January 25 of the year 36, less than two full years had elapsed.

Now, if we add to the year 36 of Christ—which was the first year of Paul’s conversion—the twenty-two years he is said to have spent before his second arrival at Jerusalem, it follows that he did this in the year 58 of Christ.

This is wholly impossible, since that was the fourth year of Nero’s reign—Nero began his reign in the year of Christ 55—and Paul was then being held at Rome, as can be seen in Jerome’s book *On Illustrious Men*, in the section on Paul, and in Sophronius’s book *On the Four Evangelists*, in the section on Luke.

We may also omit the fact that this conflicts with what Paul himself says in Galatians 2: that at that time he visited Peter and John at Jerusalem, although Peter was then preaching in Italy and John in Asia.

Those three years, therefore, of which he says, “After three years I went to Jerusalem,” and those fourteen of which he later says, “Then, after fourteen years, I again went up to Jerusalem,” must always be reckoned from his conversion, as Dexter does here.

Cardinal Baronius holds the same opinion, although his view is unsatisfactory in assigning Paul’s arrival to the year 39. In particular, when discussing the year 39, number 4, he says:

> “This is the year counted as the third from Paul’s conversion.”

But if Paul was converted at the beginning of the year 36, as Baronius himself admits, that year was the first after his conversion; consequently, the year 37 was the second and the year 38 the third—not the year 39.

We shall discuss these matters again under the year 48.

I would note in passing that when Paul, already an Apostle of Christ, first came to Jerusalem, during the entire fifteen days that he remained there he saw none of the other Apostles except James, the brother of the Lord, and Peter, whose guest he was (Galatians 1). Since John was not there, it is necessary that the most blessed Virgin was also absent, for John was her inseparable companion.

But since the two of them appeared at the same time to James, who was preaching in Spain, and since we do not read that they were present elsewhere at that time, it seems reasonable to say that this did not occur so suddenly or in a moment of rapture that they did not spend several days with the Apostle in Spain.

What happened to them may be compared with what we read in Acts 8 concerning Philip the deacon. Although the Spirit of the Lord carried him away to Azotus from the road near Jerusalem on which he had baptized the eunuch of Candace, he was not immediately snatched away and restored to his former place; rather, as he passed through, he evangelized.

Thus we should believe that the Mother of God and John were indeed carried to Zaragoza by the ministry of angels, but remained there with James for several days before being brought back to Jerusalem.

#### 2. “Pilate,” etc.

This is borrowed from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, who under the same year 38 says:

> “When Pilate reported to Tiberius concerning the Christian doctrine, Tiberius referred the matter to the Senate, so that Christians might be received among the other religious observances. But when, after consultation with the senators, it had been decided that Christians should be expelled from the city, Tiberius threatened the accusers of Christians with death by an edict.”

Tertullian writes this in his *Apology*, chapters 5 and 21. It is also reported by Eusebius in book II, chapter 2 of his *Ecclesiastical History*; Nicephorus, book II, chapter 8; Rufinus, chapter 2; Orosius, book VII, chapter 4; Gregory of Tours, *History*, book I, chapter 24; Regino and Hermannus Contractus in their chronicles; the compiler of chronicles in his own work; Ado of Vienne; and others.

Cardinal Baronius thinks that Pilate’s report to Tiberius was made not in the year 38 but in the year 34, as can be seen in his work, number 230. He asks:

> “How could what had been done concerning Christ have remained concealed for so many years, when it had been public and evident to everyone?”

Nevertheless, since he cites no ancient authority on his side, whereas we have both Eusebius and Dexter, we believe that it occurred in the year 38.

Pilate could have delayed making the report because he feared the emperor’s displeasure, since, in pronouncing the sentence of death upon so great a man, he had not observed the requirements of the law; indeed, he had killed him unjustly. He delayed until he saw that the affairs of Christ and his miracles were being proclaimed throughout the entire world.

There exists a letter of Pilate concerning this matter to Caius, although the Cardinal himself disparages it; it is also found in Hegesippus. The letter encompasses the entire Gospel history with great clarity and seems rather to bear the stamp of a man thoroughly acquainted with the law of Christ than of a pagan.

I refer my reader to Baronius under the year of Christ 34, number 225. In this matter, however, I defer greatly to Hegesippus, and even more to Orosius, who in book VII, chapter 4, reports that Pilate wrote to Tiberius almost these very words:

> “Pilate,” he says, “reported to the emperor Tiberius concerning the Passion and Resurrection of Christ and the miracles that followed—those that had been openly performed either by Christ himself or by his disciples in his name—and concerning the fact that, as the faith of many grew rapidly, God was believed in.”

Certainly all these matters were extremely evident and, as such, had to be reported by Pilate.

Concerning Pilate’s death: in the year of the Lord 41, at Vienne in Gaul, where he was living in exile after being banished, he killed himself with his own hand, having previously fallen into many calamities by God’s just judgment. Eusebius discusses this in his *Chronicle*, citing Roman historians. Orosius, book VII, chapter 5, Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*, and Ado likewise in his *Chronicle*—he too was bishop of Vienne—report the same. Ado’s words are:

> “Pilate, who had pronounced the sentence of condemnation against Christ, was confined at Vienne in perpetual exile. There, oppressed by such great anguish inflicted by Caius the emperor, he pierced himself with his own hand and sought, by the speed of death, an end to his many sufferings.”

The family of the Pilates still exists at Rome, claiming to have received its ancestral nobility from the ancient Romans who bore that surname, among whom Pontius Pilate was one. The tomb of Claudius Pilate can be seen near Saint Augustine, with the following inscription:

> **To the most good and great God.**
>
> Dionysius Lunatius of Milan and a Roman citizen endowed this chapel and altar of Saints Cosmas and Damian so that two Masses might be celebrated each week for his soul, providing a perpetual endowment from a certain house located near the church of Saint Martinella.
>
> Claudius Pilate of Rome, his son-in-law, likewise endowed this chapel and altar, for the souls of their parents, with two hundred gold pieces from the Monte di Pietà, so that three Masses might also be celebrated each week.
>
> If these Masses are not celebrated, such donations are to revert to the hospital for the incurable.

#### 3. “The first of the entire world,” etc.

Calixtus III agrees with Dexter in the foundation bull of the Church of the Pillar, dated at Rome on September 23, 1456, where he calls it “the first among all churches under the name of Blessed Mary.”

There can be no doubt about this matter, since no church in the entire world erected under her name before that time can be produced.

Indeed, many contend that it was not merely the first of the churches dedicated to the Blessed Virgin, but absolutely the first church or temple of all Christendom. Loaysa, cited above, makes this assertion, as do the petitions and arguments of the judgment delivered at Zaragoza in favor of the canons of the Pillar in the year 1605 concerning the right of precedence in synods. There we read:

> “For, by the most widely received tradition of all the churches, especially of this most extensive province, repeatedly approved by its bishops, it holds among all the churches of the world the primacy of antiquity and excellence of origin.”

Vasaeus under the year 37, Garibay in chapter 7 of his account of King Alfonso of Navarre, Blancas on pages 5 and 143, Pujades, book II, chapter 5, section 1, Illescas, Canisius, and Morillus discuss this matter.

I would exclude from this general claim the upper room of Zion, which the Holy Spirit honored with his presence and which the Blessed Virgin, much earlier, frequented with the entire apostolic college as a holy place of prayer.

What Dexter adds concerning the bishops of Toledo, Seville, and Tarragona is highly probable, since churches of this kind were established from their origin under the patronage of the Blessed Virgin.

Caledonius discusses the church at Braga, consecrated by Saint James to the same Virgin, in his *Life of Saint Peter of Ratensis*, saying:

> “James came to Braga, where, together with Pius of Seville, Elpidius of Toledo, and others among his first disciples, he consecrated to the same Lady another small shrine in a certain crypt near the baths, beside a temple once dedicated by the Egyptians to Isis.”

Consult the letter of Hugo of Portugal preserved among Dexter’s *Eulogies*.

---

### A.D. 38. A.U.C. 789

After his conversion, Saul arrived at Jerusalem.

### A.D. 38. A.U.C. 789

Pilate reported concerning Christ to Tiberius, and Tiberius reported the matter to the Senate.

### A.D. 38. A.U.C. 789

The first shrine in the entire world was erected to the Blessed Virgin at Zaragoza. Later, the bishops of Tarragona, Seville, Toledo, and others dedicated sacred churches or oratories to the Virgin.

## [Note: [Col. 0134D]]

### A.D. 40

We proved above, under the year 34, that this man was originally from the Spanish city of Italica.

Saint Luke devotes the whole of Acts 10 to recounting his prayers and almsgiving, on account of which he deserved to receive an angelic vision and a visit from Peter. There Luke relates how, at the preaching of the Apostle, the Holy Spirit fell upon him and all his household before they had received the gift of baptism.

When the faithful who were of the circumcision and had come with Peter were astonished that the grace of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the Gentiles—for they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God—Peter then baptized Cornelius and his household.

Again, in chapter 11, Luke relates how Peter went up to Jerusalem and, when reproached about this matter by the faithful of the circumcision, declared that the door of the Gospel had now been opened to the Gentiles.

For this reason, when Cornelius was afterward chosen bishop of Caesarea, Peter elevated that see to such honor that it, rather than Jerusalem, became the metropolis of all Palestine.

Cardinal Baronius noted this in his notes on February 2 in the Roman Martyrology, on the basis of canon 7 of the Council of Nicaea and Jerome’s Letter 62 to Pammachius.

Saint Cornelius died on the aforesaid day, on which his feast is celebrated by the Latins; the Greeks commemorate him in the Menologion on September 13.

That his baptism occurred in the year of Christ 40 we learn from Dexter. Cardinal Baronius, however, rejects this and assigns it to the following year. He is influenced by the consideration that Peter healed Aeneas at Lydda in the year 40, raised Tabitha at Joppa, and finally, according to Luke in Acts 9, remained many days with Simon the tanner before going to Caesarea. It therefore appears that Cornelius’s baptism should have occurred in the year 41.

Nevertheless, this is not a conclusive argument, since the assumption on which it rests is not certain.

### A.D. 40. A.U.C. 791

Cornelius, a centurion from Italica, is filled with the Holy Spirit while Peter preaches. After the solemn conversion of the Gentiles to the faith of Christ has been announced at Jerusalem, Cornelius is duly baptized [alternative: “truly baptized”] and flourishes.

---

## [Note: [Col. 0135B]]

### A.D. 41

#### 1. “And, having left Theodore’s Church,” etc.

This means that he left it as its guardian and archpresbyter, not as its bishop, for Athanasius was the bishop, as we have already said. We shall give Saint Braulio’s epigram concerning him under the year of the Lord 50.

#### 2. “Where also the splendid [church]” etc.

This is the church that the faithful now venerate upon the Pillar. They believe that Saint James placed the church there with his own hands, since it possesses such great antiquity that it has no known beginning; the same is confirmed by continuous tradition.

#### 3. “James, with tears,” etc.

In the *History of the Church of the Pillar*, chapter 12, it is said:

> “After consecrating the aforesaid church and dismissing the Christians in peace, he returned to Judaea.”

That he departed from Spain in the year 41 is recorded in the letter sent from Zaragoza to Toledo, which Julian discusses in his *Chronicle* under the year 36, saying:

> “It is said there that the Apostle remained in Spain until the year 41, for nearly six years.”

This will be established by what follows, when we show below that he was taken from Jerusalem by martyrdom in the year of the Lord 42. For if he died in the year 42, it is necessary that he departed from Spain in the year 41.

### 4. He visited Gaul, etc.

This should be understood as having happened because by lot the farthest provinces of the whole West after Spain had fallen to him [Col. 0135D]. Therefore he also went to Gaul. From there, incidentally, he visited Britain [Col. 0136A], which is now called England. There he boarded a ship and, passing again through the straits of Cádiz into the Mediterranean Sea, made for Joppa, not far from Jerusalem; by this route he would spend much less time than if he had returned on foot overland.

As for what is asserted about Venice, it should not be understood as referring to the city that now bears that name and stands on the Adriatic Gulf, for at that time it had not yet been founded. Rather, *Venetiae* was the name of towns in eastern Gaul, as can be seen in Ptolemy and Pliny. Since these towns lay in the direction of England, it is readily understood that the Apostle visited them when he was traveling from Gaul toward England or Britain. Unless someone prefers to think that Dexter deliberately did not say “he visited Venice” but “the towns of the Veneti”—that is, those situated near the place where the exceedingly wealthy city of Venice was later built. For it is also an irrefutable testimony that the Veneti inhabited that region in ancient times, as Silius Italicus states in Book VIII, not far from the end:

> Nor does Aquileia rage with arms alongside the Veneti.

Here he places the Veneti near Aquileia, and not far from Ravenna, of which he had said two verses earlier:

> The sluggish waters of marshy Ravenna they cut through.

Perhaps in memory of this preaching of James, as soon as the Venetians had founded their city, they dedicated to that same Apostle, by vow, its most ancient church. There an inscription of this kind can still be read, carved into ancient marble in the Rialto district:

> The foundations of this church, erected by vow to the Apostle James, were laid in the year 421 of Christian salvation, on 25 March, under Zosimus, Roman pontiff, while Honorius was emperor.
>
> Its dedication was celebrated the following year on the same day by four bishops: Severianus of Padua, Hilary of Altinum, Jucundus of Treviso, and Epodius of Opitergium.
>
> At first, its administration was entrusted to the priest Felix.

### 5. James takes part, etc.

In the year of Christ the Lord 34, shortly after his Ascension, I showed in the commentary on that year, section 7, that the Apostles had drawn the provinces of the world among themselves by lot. For the following two years, at least, they remained together in Jerusalem, in accordance with Acts 8: “All were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the Apostles.” When Samaria had received the word of God in the second year through the preaching of Philip the Deacon, and the Apostles who were in Jerusalem had heard this—so Luke says—they sent Peter and John to them. When their mission there had been completed, they, having testified and spoken the word of God, returned to Jerusalem.

In the third year all the Apostles were scattered throughout the regions of Judea, Samaria, and Galilee to evangelize the Jews, before they went forth to preach to the Gentiles scattered throughout the entire world. The exceptions were James, who went to Spain; the other James; and Peter, who were found in Jerusalem that year by Paul, as he affirms in Galatians 1 [Col. 0136D]:

> Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and I remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other Apostles, except James, the brother of the Lord.

Above, in the year 38, I showed that these three years are to be counted from his conversion.

After the Gospel had been preached in Judea, and the synagogue had been rejected so that they might turn to the Gentiles and now receive their own provinces, they assembled in Jerusalem. Once the arrangements for preaching had been made and the creed had been composed, they were finally scattered throughout the whole world.

In what year this occurred is stated in more than one way. I reported the varying opinions of authors in the commentary on the year 34, section 7; but extremes must be avoided in this matter. The Apostles’ separation from one another should not be postponed until the twelfth year after the Lord’s Ascension—that is, to the year 46—as Apollonius did in Eusebius, Book V, chapter 17; Clement of Alexandria in Book VI of the *Stromata*; and Peter de Natalibus in Book VI, chapter 99. Nor should it be believed that it happened so quickly that it occurred in the second year after the Lord’s Ascension, as Melito of Sardis is said to have thought [Col. 0137B]—if the book *On the Passing of the Mother of God* is indeed his.

For in that case the Apostles would not have been granted time to preach in Judea before going to the Gentiles. Mark refutes this view: writing the Gospel in the eleventh year of Christ—or in the tenth, as Cardinal Baronius proves from Euthymius in his preface to Matthew and from others, in the year 45—he testifies that they had gone forth and preached everywhere.

Proceeding, therefore, along something of a middle path, Cardinal Baronius argues in the *Ecclesiastical Annals* that the Apostles’ departure took place in the year 44. Yet his opinion is struck down by the same argument. This was the eleventh year after the Ascension, which he himself admits occurred in the year 34; from 34 through 44 inclusive there are eleven years. But Mark is then writing not that the division had just taken place, but that the Apostles had already preached throughout the world and had performed many miracles. Several years must necessarily have been spent on their very long journeys and in preaching.

Dexter is much more satisfactory in assigning this event to the year 41, the seventh year after the Ascension, excluding the year of the Ascension. Genebrard embraces this opinion in Book III of his *Chronology*. In that same year—specifically, the seventh year of the episcopate of James the Less—Equilinus says in the *Life of James the Less*, Book IV, chapter 108, that all the Apostles assembled in Jerusalem.

Thus three years are granted to the Apostles, so that Mark could say of them that they had gone forth and preached everywhere, and so forth. Matthew offers a considerable conjecture in support of this. In that very year, 41, Eusebius of Caesarea says in his *Chronicle* that Matthew wrote the Gospel:

> In the year 41 Matthew first wrote the Gospel in Judea.

For just as, before the Apostles’ departure, they had to compose the creed, so that, once this token had been given, the faithful dispersed throughout the world might be distinguished from unbelievers by holding the same true faith—my point is the same concerning the Apostolic Constitutions and their canons—so it was also necessary first to compose some Gospel, by which all the disciples together might be instructed in the faith.

This Gospel was first composed in the year 41. Once that had been done, there seemed to be no further reason to wait before going throughout the world to preach. Indeed, that Matthew wrote Christ’s Gospel in the year 41, before the Apostles were dispersed throughout the world, is taught—as the learned Cardinal Baronius customarily does—from Eusebius’s *Chronicle* and other sources.

### 6. Some of the Apostles, etc.

Why not all of them? Because John remained the Blessed Virgin’s inseparable companion; James the Less was already living in his own province, namely Jerusalem; and Peter, as is known, was imprisoned there by Herod in the following year, 42, after the death of James the son of Zebedee. He mentions the other eight.

### 7. In the year 40 James wrote the Epistle, etc.

See what we said about it in the commentary on the year 37, sections 6 and 7. From this it is evident that it was written in Spain, where James was living in that year.

### 8. John the Theologian, etc.

When the Blessed Virgin was about to leave Jerusalem for a time and travel with John to Ephesus, it is not surprising that she was accompanied by the Blessed James and by those three persons, her exceptional devotees—Lazarus, Martha, and Mary. It would not have been fitting for so great a Lady to visit and traverse lands so far away with only one companion; nor would the love with which they cherished her have allowed it. The difficulty and labor, therefore, lie not in this, but in establishing that such a journey by the Virgin took place.

We have, however, the most weighty testimony of the Fathers of the great Council of Ephesus, whose authority no person of sound mind will reject. In their letter deposing Nestorius, found in Volume II of the Councils, chapter 27, under the heading “The Holy Synod to the Most Religious Clergy and People of Constantinople, greeting,” they say:

> No one has ever dared to resist his Creator and escaped divine vengeance. Therefore Nestorius also, the restorer of an impious heresy, having been installed in the city of Ephesus, which John the Theologian and the Holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, once inhabited, voluntarily alienating himself from the assembly of the holy Fathers and bishops, was condemned by the judgment of the holy synod and by the divine judgment of the holy Fathers after three citations, and was stripped of every priestly dignity.

That most impious man maintained that the Blessed Virgin should not be called *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, “Mother of God”), but *Christotokos* (Χριστοτόκος, “Mother of Christ”)—as though she had not borne the true God but merely a human being. By God’s providential arrangement, however, it happened that he was condemned in that city which the Mother of God herself had once inhabited, with the sacred council approving the judgment.

Theodore Peltanus noted this in the margin of the Council, and Cardinal Baronius, in his notes on 27 December in the Roman Martyrology, accepts the history. Among more recent writers, Arias also accepts it in his book *On Spiritual Progress*, where he discusses imitation of the Virgin.

Among the ancients, Bishop Heleca of Zaragoza says the following in his additions:

> A commemoration and feast day had been celebrated from the time of his entry into Spain in honor of Saint James, son of Zebedee. He does not say “is celebrated,” because he was living under Moorish rule. After James went to Spain, he accompanied the most holy Virgin to Ephesus, together with John, his brother; not before he came to Spain, but after returning from Spain. From there he returned to Jerusalem, and, preaching boldly and steadfastly, was struck down by the sword.

Here it should be noted that some have asserted that Saint James went to Ephesus before going to Spain. The first was apparently the Cabilonensis in his *Topography of the Martyrs of Christ*, under the heading “Ephesus,” where he says:

> Ephesus, a city of Asia Minor. Here James, son of Zebedee, began to preach after the Lord’s Ascension, and from here he departed for Spain.

Julian likewise reports in his *Chronicle* that he found in an ancient letter concerning the foundation of the Church of the Pillar that Saint James had been summoned from Ephesus by the Blessed Peter and had come to Spain [Col. 0139A] to preach. Heleca, however, maintains that Saint James went to Ephesus after returning from Spain, and not before.

But who knows whether the Apostle preached in Ephesus once or twice—first before his journey to Spain and again after his return, while accompanying the Blessed Virgin? For I read with admiration what is said of the Apostles:

> Who are these who fly like clouds? (Isaiah 60)

As for the journey of the Virgin and John, the martyr Saint Ignatius gives us testimony about it. While he was staying near Ephesus, he revealed, in two letters addressed to the Apostle John, his teacher, the intense desire with which he and the other disciples burned to see the Blessed Virgin.

In the first letter he says:

> Brother, we grieve deeply over your delay, for we need to be strengthened by your conversations and consolations. If your absence is prolonged, it will leave many of our people without support. Hasten, therefore, to come, because we believe this will be beneficial. There are also here many of our women who desire to see Mary, the mother of Jesus, and so forth.

He adds:

> These things have stirred our inmost hearts and compel us greatly to desire the sight—if it is permissible to say so—of this heavenly marvel and most sacred wonder.

He also wrote to the Blessed Virgin about this matter more than once, and received from her a very brief reply, in which, among other things, she said:

> I shall come together with John to see you and those who are with you.

There should be no doubt that she kept her promise and that the Blessed Virgin consoled Ignatius by her presence, as Dexter now asserts.

### A.D. 41. A.R. 792.

Having honorably fulfilled his mission and arranged the affairs of Spain with the greatest holiness, James left the Church called the Church of the Pillar in the care of Theodore. The Blessed Virgin had preserved, blessed, and consecrated it by her presence, and there she had left her splendid image. From that time onward the heavenly shrine was frequented by the devotion of the faithful. James returned to Jerusalem amid the tears of the Spaniards.

### A.D. 41. A.R. 792.

On his return James visited Gaul, Britain, and the towns of the Veneti. There he preached, and then returned to Jerusalem to consult the Blessed Virgin and Peter about matters of the greatest importance.

### A.D. 41. A.R. 792.

James took part in the departure of certain Apostles to preach—namely, Matthias, [Col. 0137] Thomas, Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Simon, Jude, and also Matthew—who, under God’s guidance, set out in this year. In that same year Matthew wrote the Gospel in Hebrew; in the year 40 James wrote the Epistle.

### A.D. 41. A.R. 792.

In this same year, to provide some indication of his apostolate, John the Theologian set out for Ephesus accompanied by the Blessed Virgin, and also accompanied by the Blessed James, who preached in Ephesus for a time. Lazarus, Martha, and Mary accompanied the Virgin, and there too the Blessed Virgin consoled Ignatius by her presence.

## Note

### A.D. 42

**1. “With John having returned from there,” etc.** Good God, how many opinions authors have devised in assigning the year of James’s death! Casanaeus, in Part 3 of the *Catalogue of the Glory of the World*, consideration 29, asserts that Christ’s Ascension occurred at the beginning of the following year, that is, in the year 35. Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*, assigns it to the year 36. Sabellicus, in Book I of the seventh *Aeneid*, assigns it to four years after the Ascension, namely, the year 37. Dadraeus, in his notes on Eusebius, following Vasaeus, postpones it to the year 43. Leo III, in his letter *On the Translation of Saint James*, says that James was beheaded “at the completion of the eleventh year from the Lord’s Passion”; consequently, he places the event in the year 44, a view also embraced by Ambrosius Morales, Book IX, chapter 7, and by Cardinal Baronius. Mantuanus, in his notes on Mariana’s history, Book IV, chapter 2, argues that James was martyred in the year 45. Finally, Franciscus Maurolicus, in his *Martyrology* under 25 July, teaches that James was crowned with martyrdom fourteen years after Christ’s death, that is, in the year 46.

Dexter differs from all of these, assigning the event to the year 42. Mariana likewise follows him in his Latin history *On the Affairs of Spain*, Book IV, chapter 2. I shall show that Dexter’s opinion is much more consistent with the teaching of the Acts of the Apostles, and altogether true.

I pass over Casanaeus and Sabellicus, who have no foundation whatsoever, and Eusebius, who is inconsistent with himself in this matter, since in Book II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 8, he places James’s death much later, as Dadraeus noted in the margin of the *Chronicle*.

The entire disagreement arose from differing interpretations of the historical context of chapters 11 and 12 of the Acts of the Apostles, especially these words:

> At that time King Herod stretched out his hands to afflict some of the Church. And he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.

Since the expression “at that time” is referred to the immediately preceding history, some argue that James’s martyrdom occurred at the time of the great famine that took place under Claudius and that caused the elders to send a collection to Jerusalem, by the hands of Barnabas and Saul, for the relief of the poor; for Luke had just discussed that famine. It occurred in the fourth year of the emperor Claudius, that is, in the year of Christ the Lord 46, since Claudius began his reign in the year 42 of Christ.

Others refer the expression to what the Evangelist had narrated somewhat earlier, and, according to the differing application, hold differing opinions about the year of the Apostle’s death. Still others reason from what is narrated later, as Mantuanus does. He weaves together a lengthy argument, maintaining that Herod’s withdrawal to Caesarea and his wretched death, when he expired consumed by worms, should be connected with James’s death and Peter’s imprisonment, because all these events are narrated successively by the Evangelist, without any indication of elapsed time.

It is established, however, from Josephus, Book XIX of the *Antiquities*, chapter 7; Book II of the *Jewish War*, chapter 10; and Eusebius, Book II of his *History*, chapter 9, that Herod died in the third year of the reign of Caesar Claudius, who began his rule in the year 42 of Christ. This would mean that Herod died in the year 45, and consequently that Peter was imprisoned and James killed in that same year.

Neither of these years, however—45 or 46—can be derived from the Evangelist’s context. The expression “At that time King Herod stretched out his hands,” etc. [Col. 0140B], undoubtedly refers to the matter immediately narrated. But that matter is not the famine as an accomplished event; it is merely the famine prophesied by Agabus as future.

Here are Luke’s words:

> In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them, named Agabus, rose and signified through the Spirit that a great famine was about to occur throughout the whole world, which happened under Claudius.

That is, it happened afterward, in its own time, namely in the fourth year of Claudius. He is not therefore speaking of a famine that already existed, but of one that was to come. Thus, at the time when this prophecy was pronounced, he does not say that the disciples immediately sent relief to the poor of Jerusalem—although they could have anticipated the future famine, whose certain arrival they knew—but that they proposed to send it:

> The disciples, Luke says, decided that each according to his means should send assistance to the brothers living in Judea.

And this they did—that is, afterward, at the proper time—sending it to the elders through the hands of Barnabas and Saul [Col. 0140C].

Then he adds:

> At that time King Herod stretched out his hands, etc.

At what time? Clearly, when the famine had been prophesied by Agabus and the disciples had proposed to send assistance to Jerusalem. It matters little, therefore, that the famine fell in the year of Christ 46, or the fourth year of Claudius; that fact does not establish the definite year of James’s death.

Again, Herod’s wretched death cannot at all serve to establish the desired year. It is not clear from the Evangelist, nor from any other source, that Herod died in the same year in which he imprisoned Peter and ordered the soldiers who had been guarding him—those held responsible for Peter’s escape—to be brought before him. Nor is it stated that Herod immediately went down to Caesarea, or that, after going there, he died in the same year. On the contrary, Luke indicates that he remained there for some time:

> After descending from Judea to Caesarea, he remained there.

What does “he remained there” mean? At the very least, this manner of speaking excludes a sudden death immediately after his arrival. If he had expired, consumed by worms, as soon as he reached Caesarea, he would certainly not be said to have remained there. Therefore he must have spent several years there [Col. 0140D].

This is especially so because he had a serious and important matter there with the Tyrians and Sidonians, and the time at which it was settled is not stated:

> He was angry with the Tyrians and Sidonians. But they came to him with one accord, and, having persuaded Blastus, who was over the king’s bedchamber, they sought peace, because their country was supplied with food by him. On the appointed day Herod, dressed in royal clothing, sat upon the tribunal and addressed them. The people shouted, “The voice of a god and not of a man”—that is, “It is God who speaks, not a man.” Immediately the angel of the Lord struck him because he had not given glory to God; and, consumed by worms, he expired.

Who does not see that the Tyrians and Sidonians must have been granted time to confer among themselves about approaching Herod, and afterward to travel to him while he was staying at Caesarea; to present their petition to Blastus; and finally for the king to appoint a day for the public address? After that period had elapsed, he was struck by the angel and, consumed by worms, was brought to his death by an agony that did not abate for five continuous days, as Josephus says in Book XIX of the *Antiquities*, chapter 7.

The calculation must therefore be sought elsewhere.

Amid such a diversity of opinions, many will find it difficult to understand why Dexter should be preferred to another authority. I, however, greatly wonder that the most learned men who have debated this matter preferred to turn aside through streams of conjecture rather than return to the very source: the lunar years derived from the cycle of epacts, where clear and limpid water may be drawn.

Once we have established the fixed day of Saint James’s triumphant death, which everyone admits occurred on 25 March, at the beginning of the days of Unleavened Bread, as the Evangelist also declares, we should seek the year in which the fourteenth or thirteenth lunar day of March fell on 25 March. In that year we should acknowledge that the Apostle was beheaded. Had they done this, there would have been no room for them to depart from Dexter’s opinion.

Everyone knows that James died on 25 March, because this is asserted in his Passion, as can be seen in Equilinus, Book VI, chapter 133, where he says:

> He completed his martyrdom on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, namely on the day of the Annunciation and of Christ’s Passion.

Callistus II, in his treatise *On the Three Solemnities of Saint James*, says:

> He was judged about the third hour, and about the ninth hour, like Christ, he suffered; on the same day and at the same hour on which the Master suffered, the disciple also suffered.

“On the same day,” he says—that is, 25 March.

That this also occurred at the beginning of the feast of Unleavened Bread is clear from Luke. Having first mentioned James’s death, which had pleased the Jews, he immediately adds that Peter was seized also. But at what time?

> Now it was the days of Unleavened Bread.

Leo III, in his letter *On the Translation of Saint James*, asserts:

> At the time of Unleavened Bread, the most blessed Apostle James was beheaded by order of Herod.

Since the Jews could not carry this out on the very day of Passover, it must be understood to have happened on the day immediately preceding Unleavened Bread, or Passover.

The year must now be sought in which the moon corresponds in such a way that the thirteenth or fourteenth lunar day of March falls on the aforesaid 25th. This must be determined from the cycle of epacts, which serves to establish the moon’s age. For greater clarity on the matter, I consider it necessary to insert it here.

The year of Saint James’s death must therefore be determined from this cycle in the following manner.

In the year of Christ the Lord’s death and of his age, 34, the fourteenth lunar day of March fell on the 25th, the day on which he was crucified; there is no disagreement about this. Since the epact corresponding to that day in the calendar is VI, it is necessary that, fourteen days earlier, the new moon of that year and month corresponded to epact XIX, which is located on 12 March.

From this it necessarily follows, against Casanaeus, that Saint James was not killed by the sword in the following year, Christ’s 35th. Its epact was I, corresponding to 30 March, and the fourteenth lunar day then fell on 12 April.

Nor did it happen in the year 36, as Eusebius taught, because its epact was XII, corresponding to 19 March, and the fourteenth lunar day fell on 1 April.

Nor in the year 37, because its epact was XXIII, corresponding to its new moon on 8 March. Consequently, the fourteenth lunar day fell on the 21st of that month, and 25 March would then have been the fourth day of Unleavened Bread, on which no one was permitted to be killed.

Nor in the year 38, because its epact was IV, corresponding to the new moon on 27 March; consequently, the fourteenth lunar day fell on 9 April.

Nor in the year 39, because its epact was XV, corresponding to the new moon on 16 March; the fourteenth lunar day then fell on the 29th of that month.

Nor in the year of Christ 40, because its epact was XXVI, corresponding to the new moon on 5 March; the fourteenth lunar day then fell on the 18th. Thus 25 March would have been the seventh and final day of Unleavened Bread, the most sacred of all.

Again, it could not have happened in the year of Christ 41, because its epact was VII, corresponding to the new moon on 24 March; thus the fourteenth lunar day fell on 6 April.

Nor in the year 43, as Vasaeus and Dadraeus maintain, because its epact was XXIX, corresponding to the new moon on 2 March. Consequently, the fourteenth lunar day fell on the 15th of that month, and therefore 25 March [Col. 0142D] would have followed Unleavened Bread by almost four days, contrary to Saint Luke.

Nor in the year 44, as Leo III seems to assert, because its epact was X, corresponding to the new moon on 21 March; thus the fourteenth lunar day fell on 3 April.

Nor in the year 45, as Mantuanus argues, because its epact was XXI, corresponding to the new moon on 10 March. The fourteenth lunar day then fell on the 24th of that month, and 25 March would have been the second day of Unleavened Bread and the principal day of Passover, on which no one was permitted to be killed.

Finally, nor in the year 46, as Maurolicus asserted, because its epact was II, corresponding to the new moon [Col. 0143A] on 29 March; the fourteenth lunar day then fell on 11 April.

I pass over the other years, about which there is no controversy, for it is established that James did not live beyond this point. The same reasoning would apply to the remaining years. In the year 47 the epact was XIII, and the fourteenth lunar day fell on the last day of March. In the year 48 the epact was XXIV, and the fourteenth lunar day fell on 20 March; thus the Apostle’s death would have fallen within the days of Unleavened Bread, which cannot be admitted. In the year 49 the epact was V, and the fourteenth lunar day fell on 8 April.

In the years mentioned above, therefore, the day of the holy Apostle’s martyrdom either falls far from the fourteenth lunar day of March, or lies within the seven days of Unleavened Bread, during which time it was not lawful to put a person to death, or else is postponed until after all seven days had passed. The Evangelist expressly contradicts this last possibility, for he teaches that Peter was seized after James’s death but before the end of Unleavened Bread.

Therefore, if all these difficulties disappear in the year of Christ 42 and everything we require is found there [Col. 0143B], we cannot possibly depart from Dexter’s opinion.

Consider, I beg you, the marvelous agreement of all the circumstances. The epact XVIII corresponds to the year of the Lord 42, and its new moon falls on 13 March. The fourteenth lunar day then falls on 26 March, only one day after the 25th, on which Saint James was beheaded. Thus James was killed on the 25th day of the month, which was the thirteenth lunar day.

On the following day, 26 March, the moon was fourteen days old; toward evening the days of Unleavened Bread began. Seeing that James’s death pleased the Jews, Herod then proceeded to seize Peter:

> It was the days of Unleavened Bread.

After he had seized him, he put him in prison, entrusting him to the custody of four squads of soldiers—that is, sixteen soldiers—intending to bring him out before the people after Passover.

Since Peter was captured after the solemnity of Unleavened Bread had begun, on its third or fourth day—namely, after the king had seen that James’s death pleased the Jews—Herod could not immediately put the prince of the Apostles to death. He therefore postponed his execution until 3 April, which was the twenty-second lunar day, only one day after the seven days of Unleavened Bread. By the Lord’s command in Exodus 12, those days extended through the twenty-first lunar day inclusively:

> In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the month at evening.

But when Herod was about to bring Peter out—after the Unleavened Bread had ended on 2 April, which was the twenty-first lunar day—that very night, before 3 April and the twenty-second lunar day on which he was to be put to death, Peter was sleeping, and so forth; and he was freed by the angel.

This assertion also has a connection with other facts, especially with Saint Peter’s Roman see, which was founded by him in the year of Christ 44, as we shall say in that year. This follows from the twenty-five years during which, according to the common assertion, the Apostle presided over the Roman Church. These twenty-five years lie between the year 68, in which he was removed from this life by the cross on 29 June, as we proved in its proper place, and the year 44, on 18 January, when that see was established.

Now observe the connection between the two assertions. In the same year in which James was beheaded, Peter also escaped from his chains, at the beginning of April; this is clear from Acts 12. The year of Peter’s liberation was therefore 42, since he spent a year and a half preaching from Jerusalem all the way to Rome. He should not be allotted more time for that journey, but neither should he be allotted less, since he followed Simon Magus as far as Rome, preaching against his deceptions, as can be seen in Sophronius’s commentary on the journeys of Peter and Paul, in Volume 7 of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, where he says:

> He was released by an angel and, on account of the treachery of Simon Magus, traveled through Syria. He then went also through Pontus, Asia, and Galatia, sowing the word of God everywhere, and reached Rome.

From the beginning of April in the year 42, when he was rescued from his chains, until 18 January in the year 44, when he entered Rome [Col. 0144A] and established his see there, there elapsed one year and nine months.

Finally, this agrees sufficiently with what Saint Luke records in Acts.

In the year 40 Peter baptized Cornelius the centurion, as we have already said, in Acts 10. Then Acts 11 says:

> The Apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. When Peter had gone up to Jerusalem—from Caesarea, where he had remained with the centurion for several days—those who were of the circumcision disputed with him, saying, “Why did you enter men who were uncircumcised and eat with them?”

Peter then began to explain to them the sequence of the vision of the sheet full of unclean animals let down from heaven, and how, while he was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word. These Gentiles, having been anointed, were speaking in tongues and magnifying God. He concluded:

> If, therefore, God gave them the same grace as he gave us, who was I that I could hinder God?

When they heard these things, they fell silent and glorified God, saying:

> Then God has also granted repentance to the Gentiles unto life.

This was the opening of the door of the Gospel to the Gentiles and its public proclamation in Jerusalem; there is no doubt that it occurred only a few days after the heavenly vision.

Luke then adds that, after Cornelius had believed at Caesarea, many Greek Gentiles also believed at Antioch through the preaching of those disciples who had been scattered during the persecution that arose after Stephen’s death:

> The report about them came to the ears of the Church that was in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas as far as Antioch. When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced, and a great multitude was added to the Lord. Barnabas then departed for Tarsus to seek Saul. When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the Church there and taught a great multitude, so that the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.

Since the opening of the Gospel to the Gentiles was publicly proclaimed in Jerusalem in the year of Christ 40, it seems quite consistent with reason that Barnabas spent one year—namely, the year 41—on his journey to Antioch and Tarsus and on his return, together with Saul’s journey from Tarsus to Antioch. The report of the Gentiles converted at Antioch by the disciples driven into exile during Stephen’s death must therefore be placed either at the beginning or at the end of the year 40, for the Evangelist immediately joins it to the conversion of Cornelius.

When Saul and Barnabas came to Antioch, they spent a whole year there. That year was the year 42 of Christ the Lord.

That Saint James was killed in this same year is sufficiently indicated by Luke when he says:

> In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them, named Agabus, rose and signified through the Spirit that a great famine was about to occur, and so forth.

There the expression “in those days” plainly refers to the time of the immediately preceding account—namely, to the year in which Barnabas and Saul spent time at Antioch and caused the disciples first to be called Christians. That was the year 42, as has been said.

Therefore, when Luke again adds, “At that time King Herod stretched out his hands,” etc., this must necessarily refer to the very year in which Barnabas and Saul remained at Antioch, because James’s death is said to have occurred at the same time as the famine foretold by Agabus. That famine occurred “in those days” in which the faithful were first called Christians, namely, in the year 42.

Finally, so that we may omit nothing worthy of note that might contribute to the glory of so great an Apostle, we observe that Anastasius of Sinai, in his book *On the Passions of the Martyrs*, teaches that, as regards the kind of death, Saint James was not merely beheaded but also subjected to multiple tortures:

> On this day, he says, Saint James the Apostle, brother of John son of Zebedee, suffered multiple martyrdoms; and this happened after he had gone to the West.

He does not, however, disclose where he obtained this information [Col. 0145A]. It is not incredible that this happened to him: before he was beheaded, he may also have been subjected to other tortures, which can indeed be inferred from the most wicked hostility with which the Pharisees pursued him. Nor is this contradicted by the Evangelist, for we often say that martyrs were beheaded even though they had endured many other kinds of torture before their beheading.

Perhaps someone will ask what was the reason that Herod inflicted punishment upon St. James above the other Apostles. For why did he not first commit St. Peter to prison, since he was the head of the entire apostolic college? There is no question concerning the other Apostles, because they had been scattered through their own provinces, with the exception of John and James the son of Alphaeus, who were still being detained at Jerusalem.

Certainly the cause was the great and astonishing miracles that James, son of Zebedee, had performed in those days. Philetus, speaking of them before Hermogenes the magician, his master, said: “I saw him casting demons out of possessed bodies and cleansing lepers; my friends also assert that they saw him raising the dead.” Thus it is read in the Ancient Lessons of the Breviaries of Astorga, Compostela, and other churches of Spain. There was also the remarkable conversion to Christ of both demoniacal magicians, which the very ancient Breviaries recount and which may be found in Peter, Bishop of Équilis, *Catalogue of the Saints*, book VI, chapter 133.

First, when Hermogenes had rendered Philetus immobile by demonic power, the Apostle freed him with his handkerchief. Then, when Hermogenes himself was oppressed by demons, he protected him with his staff amid the howling infernal phantoms in the air. To this was added the fact that a great multitude of Jews was converted to the faith through him:

> When an insurrection had been stirred up by the people, it was said that he ought to be brought out and heard according to the law.

These are the words of the Astorgan Breviary. When this had been done, and the Apostle had given them testimonies from the Prophets concerning the incarnation, Passion, and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord bestowed such grace that all who were present were converted and said with one voice: “We have sinned; tell us what we should do.” He answered them: “Men and brothers, do not despair; believe and be baptized, so that your sins may be blotted out.” And a great multitude of Jews in Jerusalem was baptized.

Here, then, is the reason for the Apostle’s beheading. When Abiathar, the high priest of that year, saw that the people had believed, he stirred up a riot among the crowd. Earlier it had been said that the Jews had offered money to Lysias and Theocritus, the centurions, so that they might arrest James. The account continues:

> It happened that Josias, one of the scribes, placed a rope around the Apostle’s neck and led him to the praetorium of King Herod, who immediately ordered him to be beheaded. As he was being led away, he saw a paralytic lying in the road and healed him. Then Josias was converted and asked forgiveness. But Abiathar said to him: “If you do not withdraw from James and curse the name of Jesus, you will be beheaded with him.” Josias replied: “Cursed are you, and blessed is the name of Jesus.” Then Abiathar ordered that his face be beaten with fists; and, without making any report about him to Herod, he ordered that he too should be beheaded. When they had arrived at the place of execution, James said to the executioner: “Before you kill us, have water brought for us.” A flask full of water was brought, and he baptized the man who had asked about the faith. After giving him the kiss of peace, he was beheaded with the Apostle and became a martyr.

Thus far the history of St. James.

Heleca speaks of Josias in his additions to M. Maximus, in these words:

> Josias is held in high esteem among the faithful of Spain because, together with his patron James—whose most sacred body is honorably venerated at Compostela—he suffered at Jerusalem for the faith of Christ.

He is speaking of the period when the Arabs ruled in Spain, and when Heleca himself was living.

As a conclusion to what we have said about so great an Apostle, I wish to quote that hymn which we have promised more than once and which is preserved in the Gothic Breviary of St. Isidore, as follows:

## Hymn

O Word of God, brought forth from the Father’s mouth,  
Creator of things and true beginning,  
Everlasting Author, light and source of light,  
Born from the womb of the glorious Virgin,  
Christ, you reveal yourself to us as Emmanuel.

King and priest, for whom the sacred stones—  
Four times three: onyx, agate,  
Shining beryl, sapphire, carbuncle,  
Amethyst, sardius, topaz,  
Emerald, jasper, hyacinth, chrysolite—  
Are appointed.

You, fittingly the sun, resplendent with the gems—the twelve hours, the finest pearls—  
Growing bright for the world now freed from darkness,  
And with the lampstand set above you,  
Shine in the lamps of the twice-six Apostles.

Peter goes to Rome, his brother to Achaia;  
Thomas to India, Levi to Macedonia;  
James to Jebus, and Zelotes to Egypt;  
Bartholomew to Lycaonia, Judas to Edessa;  
Matthias to Judea, and Philip to Gaul.

Then the great sons of thunder,  
Having attained their shining honors  
Through the prayer of their illustrious mother,  
Both received the insignia of the summit of life:

John alone governs Asia at the right,  
While his brother, placed at the left,  
Governs Spain.

The renowned Master, the harmless Creator,  
Assigns one to the right, in the bonds of peace;  
The other, drawn to the left, in judgment.  
The pledges twice chosen in diverse ways for the kingdom  
Hasten to glory from both poles.

Brought forth and glorious in reward,  
Chosen there and honored through martyrdom,  
He is called James of Zebedee, Christ’s apostle,  
Fulfilling the life of apostleship duly,  
And victorious, he seizes the marks of suffering.

For, covered with divine aid,  
He restrains the guilty wrath of the magicians’ demons  
And punishes the poison of his rivals.  
The threats of demons in their deceitful oracles  
Are unraveled, and the believing heart repents.

Once perplexed, he obediently lends his voice  
To one who asks for twin aids in sickness.  
By his desire he opens the gifts of faith;  
With the banner of peace he advances salvation,  
And, having wielded the sword, he secures himself in glory.

O truly worthy and holier Apostle,  
Illustrious radiant head of Spain,  
Our protector and native patron,  
Be our heavenly salvation by averting plague;  
Drive away entirely disease, ulcer, and famine.

Be favorably present, kindly benefactor, to the flock,  
And a gentle shepherd to clergy and people.  
Grant that we may enjoy the joy of heavenly riches;  
Having attained the kingdom, may we be clothed in glory;  
May we all escape Tartarus forever.

Grant this, we ask, O unique Power,  
Who alone fills the whole universe with glory.  
By your strength, be our mighty glory,  
Whose praise and mercy are eternal,  
And whose honor endures abundantly through the ages.

Amen.

### 2. He was present earlier in this year at the consecration, etc.

There can be no doubt that the most sacred house of Loreto, made supremely blessed by the birth of the Mother of God, the incarnation of the divine Word, and the residence there of both for many years, was consecrated by the holy Apostles. Horatius Tursellinus provides evidence for this in book I, chapter 1, of his *History of Loreto*, in these words:

> First of all, it is sufficiently established that it always possessed great renown and veneration among Christians; and that the Apostles themselves were the authors of this veneration. For it was they who duly consecrated the Virgin’s house, either to preserve its memory for posterity or to increase the Christian religion. From that time, therefore, the Apostles themselves honored it with immense reverence and wished it to be honored by others with equal devotion. The authority of the Apostles consequently prevailed among later generations; and succeeding ages vied with one another in celebrating the cradle of the heavenly Queen and the traces of the God who had been conceived, with the religion and worship that were fitting.

The *Flumensian Annals*, preserved by Jerome Angelita, report the same opinion. For the other matters concerning the divine little house, see Tursellinus in the same work.

### 3. The disciples, etc.

Vincent records the history of the Apostle’s Translation in *Speculum historiale*, book VIII, chapters 6 and 7; Antoninus, part II of his *History*, title 6, chapter 7; Équilis, book VI, chapter 133; and ancient manuscripts preserved in the Vatican Library and elsewhere, including those of my monastery at Nucale and of Mount Zion outside the walls of Toledo. In the archives of that same city there is also preserved a Hebrew letter concerning the matter, which Julian had rendered into Spanish. Morales, Zurita, Villegas, Mariana, Marieta, Vasaeus, and all who have written about Spanish affairs likewise relate it.

Most especially, however, Leo III does so in his treatise, or letter, on the Translation of St. James, which begins:

> Let your fraternity know, most beloved rectors of all Christendom, how the entire body of the blessed Apostle James was transferred to Spain. After the Lord’s Ascension, etc.

After recounting the martyrdom, he continues:

> The body of that most holy Apostle was taken up by his disciples during the night, out of fear of the Jews. With an angel of the Lord accompanying them, they reached Joppa on the seashore. While they were hesitating among themselves about what they ought to do, behold, at the command of the Mother of God, a ship appeared. Rejoicing, they entered it, carrying the fosterling of our Lord the Redeemer. With the sails raised and favorable winds blowing, they sailed with great calm over the waves of the sea, praising the mercy of the Lord the Savior, and reached the harbor of Iria. There, in their joy, they sang this Davidic verse: “In the sea is your way,” etc.
>
> Leaving the ship, they carried away and placed the most blessed body in a certain small estate called Liberandonus—later Campus Stellae, or Compostela—eight miles from the aforementioned city of Iria, where it is now venerated.

The Salmanticensian Breviary adds:

> They traveled by ship across the sea for six days without oars, the hand of the Lord guiding them. On the seventh day the little vessel rested on the shore between Ulla and Tare, at the place called Iria, between two streams; these places are called Bisria.

Équilis writes:

> Having taken the body from the ship, they placed it upon a great stone. This yielded to the body like soft wax and wonderfully adapted itself to the body in the form of a sarcophagus.

Morales, book IX, chapter 7, gives testimony to this and adds that the little ship was tied to a marble column on which these letters are still read: **NO. ORISES. D. S. P.** He believes that from this the place was called Iria Flavia, and later El Padrón, because among the Spaniards such stones, marking the boundaries of roads or different territories, are now called *padrones*.

What the disciples did afterward is related by Équilis, among others, in these words:

> The disciples therefore entered to the queen—truly Lupa in deed and name—and said to her that Christ had sent her the body of his Apostle, so that she might receive him dead whom she had not wished to receive alive. But the queen deceitfully sent them to the king of Spain, so that they might seek his consent concerning the matter. He seized them and shut them in prison; but while he was reclining at table, an angel of the Lord released them and allowed them to depart free. When the king heard this, he sent soldiers after them to kill them. But while the soldiers were crossing a bridge, the bridge broke and they were all submerged in the river.
>
> When the king heard this and feared for himself and his people, he peacefully recalled the Apostle’s disciples. Together with his people he received the faith of Christ from them and freely granted everything they had requested.
>
> When Lupa heard this, she was distressed. When the saints returned and informed her by letter of the king’s consent, she replied that they should yoke to a wagon her oxen, which she kept on a certain mountain, and carry the body of their Master wherever they wished to bury it.
>
> She did this deceitfully, because a huge dragon, breathing fire—which was believed to be through the art of demons—guarded the oxen. The bulls were untamed: they could neither be yoked to a vehicle nor, if yoked, refrain from running here and there and thus scattering the body.
>
> The disciples, unaware of the trick, climbed the mountain and, by the sign of the cross, split the enormous dragon that was breathing fire upon them through the middle of its belly. They yoked the bulls to the wagon, as gentle as lambs, and placed upon it the body of the Saint together with the stone upon which he had been laid.
>
> Without anyone guiding them, the oxen carried the body into the middle of Lupa’s palace. When she saw this, she believed and became a Christian, and granted everything they had requested. She dedicated the palace to the Saint’s body as a church and endowed it magnificently. There he rests, shining with innumerable and very great miracles.

Thus far Équilis, whom all the others agree with, except concerning the woman’s name. Some call her Luparia, others Lupa; among the Spaniards she is commonly called *la Reina Loba*, “the Wolf Queen,” and the steep mountain on which she held her fortress is called *El Pico Sacro*.

These matters must certainly be understood in such a way that she is not believed to have been a queen in the strict sense, but a *regula*, or a most noble woman, as the Salmanticensian Breviary calls her. At that time, under Roman rule, there was no king anywhere in Spain except the Roman Emperor. By “king” I likewise understand a petty ruler.

These accounts are supported not only by the authors cited but also by the ancient Breviaries of the churches of Spain. The Conchensian Breviary has these antiphons for the second nocturn at the Translation of St. James:

1. A place is requested from the king in which he may be buried; the bridge is dissolved by cement, and the crowd is scourged.

2. The enormous dragon is broken; the strong bulls are tamed; the savage matron is overcome, and the places are consecrated.

3. Having seen such great miracles, the matron is baptized; the idols are rejected, and a burial place is prepared.

In the Toledan Breviary of Roman observance there are two hymns containing the whole history of the Translation. I have thought it worthwhile to set them down here for the benefit of learned readers.

## Hymn at Vespers

The joyful day is here,  
On which blessed James  
Is given to the land of Spain,  
Its illustrious leader and patron.

He who, after Christ’s Passion,  
Was the first among the Apostles  
To suffer,  
Gave the sign of the journey to heaven.

His disciples, lifting his body  
In the middle of the night,  
Out of fear of the pagan people,  
Seek refuge at Joppa.

A ship prepared by God,  
The Lord of the seas,  
Is sent to them;  
His body is carried in it  
Across the long expanse of sea.

After seven days, entering the harbor  
Of Iria,  
They sing praises with great joy  
To the heavenly court  
In triumphant celebration.

There many miracles  
Are divinely displayed;  
The body, burning like a torch,  
Shines with heavenly brightness.

Glory to you, etc.

## Hymn at Matins

Rejoice, happy Spain,  
Exulting with joyful hearts;  
Celebrate in worthy songs of praise  
The solemn feast of your leader.

This is that magnificent soldier,  
Powerful in combat,  
The first among the company  
Of Apostles to be glorified with the palm.

After the sentence of death,  
Carried by ship to Iria,  
He gave you knowledge  
Of the kingdom of heaven.

So that you might reject idols  
With all their abominations,  
You were already made believing through faith,  
After seeing many miracles.

For the great dragon is broken,  
Struck by the disciples;  
At the sign of the Cross,  
The dreadful herd of oxen obeys.

The bridge is dissolved by cement;  
The crowds are submerged in the river.  
The savage matron is overcome  
When she receives the name of Christ.

The body is immediately placed in a tomb  
With various spices  
And carried to Compostela  
With psalms and heavenly hymns.

Buried there in a tomb,  
It shines with many wonders;  
By the nourishment of a virtuous life  
It guides and protects us.

Glory to you, etc.

The Roman Martyrology also speaks of the same Translation of the Apostle on 25 July, where these words are read:

> His sacred bones were transferred from Jerusalem to Spain and buried in the furthest parts of that country, in Galicia. They are venerated with the greatest renown among those peoples, as Christian crowds frequently go there for reasons of religion and devotion and piously honor them.

With regard to these words, Cardinal Baronius admits the sermons of Pope Calixtus on the Translation of St. James, as well as his letters on the same subject and his five books on the miracles of the holy Apostle; he also admits the letter of Pope Leo III concerning the Translation of St. James to Spain, made on the third day before the Kalends of January, and the letters of Pope Innocent II bearing the subscription of the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church.

See also Usuard on 25 July concerning the same Translation, as well as Molanus, Galesinius, Maurolicus, and the other authors of martyrologies; and above all St. Notker, in Henry Canisius, volume VI of *Lectiones antiquae*, whose words are these:

> The most sacred bones of this blessed Apostle were transferred to Spain and buried at its farthest limits, namely opposite the British Sea. They are honored with the greatest veneration among those peoples. And rightly so, because those peoples are said to have been converted to the faith of Christ by his bodily presence, his teaching, and the efficacy of his signs.

St. Jerome undoubtedly confesses the same when, in explaining Isaiah 34—“He himself cast the lot for them, and his hand divided it”—as referring to the casting of lots among the Apostles, he writes:

> He gave them their lots and divided them, so that one might go to the Indians, another to the Spains, another to Illyricum, and another to Greece; and each might rest in the province of his Gospel.

In this passage he acknowledges that one of the Apostles who preached in Spain rests there. This can apply neither to Peter nor to Paul nor to anyone other than James, to whom Spain fell by lot.

Concerning the place of St. James’s burial, Mantuanus correctly warns in his notes on Mariana’s *History* that Isidore’s *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers* should not be read as saying, “He was buried in Marmarica,” nor, as Morales and Mariana correct it, “in a marble ark,” but rather, “He was buried in Tamarica.” Marmarica is not a region of Spain but of Egypt, as may be seen in Ptolemy, Table 3 of Africa, chapter 5; today it is called the kingdom of Tunis. That part of Galicia where St. James was buried, however, is called Tamarica, after the very famous river Tamaris, which flows through that region, as Pliny, book IV, chapter 20, and Pomponius Mela, *On the Situation of the World*, book III, chapter 1, attest. From it the region is still called Trans-Tamara.

### 4. An altar over the sacred [body], etc.

We must now consider who those disciples were who carried the Apostle’s body to Spain. Those who had been appointed bishops by him or ordained priests and assigned to particular congregations did not accompany him to Jerusalem. Remaining in their own churches, they hurried to Iria Flavia when they heard the news of his body’s arrival.
