Among the principal men Dexter numbers Basil, Bishop of Carthage; Athanasius of Zaragoza; Elpidius of Toledo; and the priests Chrysogonus and Agathodorus.

It is also established that St. Peter of Braga hurried there, because he established the church and see of Iria, together with those of Tui, Ourense, Mondoñedo, and the other sees of Galicia subject to its metropolitan authority. We know this from a fragment of the works of St. Athanasius of Zaragoza, which we transcribed above under the year of the Lord 36. It is sufficiently plausible that St. Basil, the first bishop of Portugal, and St. Epitacius, the first bishop of Tui and his disciple, accompanied him.

The constant companions of the holy Apostle, however, were Torquatus and his companions. Concerning these seven, the Conchensian Breviary says in lesson 4 of the Translation of St. James that none of the seven aforementioned countrymen was lacking from his companionable fellowship, and that they had hastened with him to Jerusalem.

St. Braulio, in his additions to M. Maximus, adds Philetus and Hermogenes, whom James had converted to the faith at Jerusalem shortly before his martyrdom. His words are:

> Hermogenes and Philetus saw the holy Apostle dying at Jerusalem, and together with the other disciples accompanied his body by ship to Spain. After his landing at Iria Flavia, a city of Galicia, Hermogenes went to Italy and, preaching at Syracuse during Nero’s persecution, was killed with others.
>
> Philetus remained in Spain. Preaching through various cities, he saw St. Peter, Paul, Clement, and Philemon preaching there. Finally, during the same persecution, on 28 March, he was killed with other companions at Carthage, the old city.

The Roman Martyrology speaks of him on that day. In that passage Baronius confuses him with another Philetus, who is treated on the preceding day; and in the *Annals*, volume I, under the year 59, number 20, he again confuses them with Phygellus and Hermogenes, whom Paul reports in 2 Timothy 1 to have apostatized from the faith.

Braulio—or Heleca—in his additions further writes:

> There is also a tradition that when St. James came to Spain, Mary of Clopas, and Salome his mother, and a certain Mary Magdalene accompanied him courteously; and that they returned with him and came with the body. Both Clopas and Magdalene died in the town of Civitatis, commonly Ciudad Rodrigo, in Lusitania, on 10 April. Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, however, went to Gaul.
>
> Mary Salome, returning with James her son—that is, with his body—traveled through the regions of Germany, England, and Italy, where he preached. When she reached Verulam, worn out by age, she rested there on 24 May.

Here Heleca introduces another Mary Magdalene, distinct from the sister of Lazarus and Martha. Although this is not established for me, it is nevertheless not unbelievable that in the same little village, or castle, of Magdala there was another female disciple named Mary—a name, I say, sufficiently common at that time, as appears from the Gospel—who was also called Magdalene from her native place.

As for Mary of Clopas, his companion, the Roman Martyrology establishes that she died on 9 April, one day before the date assigned by Heleca. I have no doubt that a mistake has entered one of the two accounts, so that 10 was written in place of 9, or conversely.

After an altar had been erected over the sacred body of the Apostle on the estate of the petty ruler Luparia, his disciples began to celebrate the feast of his deposition. From that time it was observed every year in Spain, as M. Maximus clearly attested under the year of Christ 563, saying:

> From apostolic times down to the present, the feast of St. James the Apostle, son of Zebedee, has been celebrated with renown. He was the first of all the Apostles to preach in the western lands.

Heleca likewise writes in his additions:

> From the time when St. James, son of Zebedee, entered Spain, his memory and feast day were celebrated with renown.

This author was living in the year 830, when, after the devastation of Spain by the Moors—which had caused the tomb of St. James to pass into oblivion—it was found again by Theodemir, Bishop of Iria. Heavenly lights went before and pointed out the place around the year of Christ 830, under King Alfonso, surnamed the Chaste. When he received the news, Alfonso hurried there with great devotion of heart to venerate the Apostle’s remains, and donated to him three miles of land in every direction.

The Apostle then appeared as a protector to King Ramiro, Alfonso’s successor, before all who were present, in the battle of Clavijo. In that battle the infamous tribute of one hundred virgins, which was paid annually to the Saracen king, was abolished. In gratitude for this, the king and nobles granted the Apostle the privilege called *de los Votos*, issued at Calahorra on 22 May in the Era 872, which is the year of Christ 834.

Then, in the year 1045, the Apostle again became visibly present as an armed warrior and helped King Ferdinand, surnamed the Great, against Coimbra. Finally, King Alfonso, likewise called the Great and grandson of Ramiro, built a most magnificent temple for the Apostle. For its consecration, as recorded by Sampiro, Bishop in Asturias and an author of that period, Pope John VIII sent his legate Rainaldus with the king’s ambassadors Severus and Sydericus.

The dedication was celebrated on 6 May in the year of the Lord 863, in the presence of, and with the diploma subscribed by, John of Oca, Vincent of León, Gomellus of Astorga, Ermenegild of Oviedo, Dulcidius of Salamanca, Naustus of Coimbra, Argimirus of Lamego, Theodemir of Viseu, Gumaldus of Porto, James of Coria, Argimirus of Braga, Didacus of Tui, Egila of Ourense, Sisenandus of Iria, Ricaredus of Lugo, Theoderindus of Britonia, and Heleca of Zaragoza, bishops.

Thus report Rodrigo of Toledo, *History of Spain*, book V, chapter 17; Lucas of Tui; and Sampiro; and, from them, Morales, book IX, chapter 7.

From this it is clear that those are mistaken who think that this dedication and the discovery of the saint’s body took place under Charlemagne, through Turpin of Reims and sixty other bishops—a view that it is astonishing Baronius accepted in his notes on 25 July in the Roman Martyrology. For it is established that Charlemagne died in 814, as the epitaph of his tomb itself attests, whereas the Apostle’s body was discovered afterward, in the year 830. Documents concerning this event and the entire history are preserved in the archives of the church of Compostela. But enough of this.

---

**A.D. 42. A.R. 793.** When John returned with the Blessed Virgin—for as long as she lived, John never left her—St. James also returned. Preaching most vigorously to the Jews, he had earlier been present that year at the consecration of the sacred house of Nazareth, in which the Virgin conceived God, with several of the Apostles present. After recently returning to Jerusalem, he was beheaded by Herod and gloriously endured his noble martyrdom on 25 March.

**A.D. 42. A.R. 793.** The disciples of St. James, at God’s command and on the Virgin’s advice, placed their Master’s body aboard a ship at Joppa and reached the Galician city of Iria Flavia by a fortunate voyage.

**A.D. 42. A.R. 793.** They erected an altar over the sacred body and, according to sacred custom, Basil, Athanasius, Chrysogonus, Agathodorus, and Elpidius—who, upon receiving news that the body of their kinsman had been brought to Spain, immediately hurried to Iria—consecrated and dedicated it to the Apostle.

**[Note: Col. 0151C]**

**A.D. 43.—Buried was the body, etc.** Since St. James suffered martyrdom on 25 March in the year of the Lord 42, and since his body was taken up by the disciples during the night and carried to Spain by those who boarded the ship at Joppa in no more than seven days—as is clear from what was said above—it is necessary that he reached Iria Flavia on the third or fourth day of April in that same year.

The dispute with Luparia and the petty ruler lasted several months. In this matter, and in summoning Elpidius, Basil, Athanasius, and the remaining disciples who were scattered throughout Spain for the consecration of the apostolic altar and tomb, the rest of the year was consumed. For, according to tradition, the consecration took place on 30 December, by which time the year 43 had already begun from the Nativity of Christ.

Dexter therefore rightly assigns the departure of the seven disciples for Rome to the year 43. Indeed, I think they did not set out immediately, but only after the work of evangelical preaching and the guarding of the sacred body had been properly arranged over several months.

The bishops, the disciples of St. James, thought it appropriate—knowing that the prince of the Apostles had been released from prison and was about to leave the Eastern Church, descend into the West, and make for Rome—to send the aforesaid seven disciples to him as messengers, so that they might report to him the Translation of St. James’s body and the circumstances of the conversion of Spain.

Whether they preceded the Apostle to Rome and arrived there in the year 43, or followed him in the following year, it is certain from what we have said under the year 42 and from Eusebius’s testimony in the *Chronicle* that St. Peter came to Rome in the year 44 of the Lord. He established the Roman see, or chair, on 18 January, the day on which his feast is celebrated.

Thus it follows that they met him at Rome in that same year 44 and were ordained bishops by that Apostle. Relying upon his authority, they returned to Spain to preach in the cities of coastal Baetica, since the other regions already had their own preachers and bishops, as is plainly established from what was said above under the years 36 and 37.

There is therefore no doubt that Eysengrenius speaks without evidence in the *Chronicle of Speyer* when he states under the year 45 of Christ that Torquatus and his companions were ordained bishops at Rome. Nor should Baronius be followed when he assigns this ordination to the year 46 and, although he admits that Peter came to Rome in 44, without cause postpones the establishment of the chair to the following year, 45. For the establishment of the chair was nothing other than his arrival at Rome, since his authority did not depend upon taking possession of a particular place according to canonical procedure. In this matter the author of the *Treasury of Preachers*, in the *Life of St. Peter*, supports our view.

The day on which they landed in Spain and reached the city of Acci—now Guadix—and were delivered by a miracle seems to have been 15 May, because the memory of all of them is celebrated on that day, although they did not pass to the better life on the same day but on different days: Secundus on 2 May, Indalecius on 30 April, Thesiphon on 1 April, Caecilius on 1 February, Isicius on 1 March, and so forth.

The Roman Martyrology seems sufficiently to indicate this when it changes the designation “birthday,” used by Usuard for their day, removing the term *birthday*, which signifies the day of death, and calls it simply a feast day:

> In Spain, it says, the holy Torquatus, Thesiphon, and the others rested in different places throughout that province.

There seems to have been no other reason for this feast than their arrival in Spain and the beginning of the miraculous conversion of the Gentiles to the faith.

Bede recounts the history in the Martyrology on 15 May, in these words:

> When they had come to the city of Acci and were resting for a short time because of the labor of the journey, they sent the disciples into the city to purchase food. Immediately a crowd of pagans—who happened at that time to be celebrating a festival for their gods—pursued them as far as the river. There a bridge of marvelous size and strength, which had been built over the river, collapsed completely by God’s will, after the saints had crossed, with the entire crowd of pursuers.
>
> Terrified by this miracle, the others followed the example of a certain noblewoman of senatorial rank, Luparia, who, divinely inspired, received them kindly and believed; abandoning their idols, they believed in Christ the Lord.

Some might think that in this history the miracle of the collapsing bridge and the conversion of Luparia have been confused with what is narrated concerning the translation of Saint James to Galicia, in the presence of those same seven disciples, Torquatus and his companions. But the unquestionable authority of learned writers proves that the miracle of the bridge happened twice to the saints: once at Iria Flavia and a second time at Acci. Luparia of Acci, a woman of senatorial rank, was moreover the daughter of another Luparia, the ruler of Galicia, as Dexter shortly shows under the year 60.

Certainly, besides Bede (to omit more recent authors of Spanish history—Morales, Truxillo, Mariana, Marieta, Villegas, and countless others), Addo agrees in his Martyrology, as do Equilinus, book V, chapter 3, and very ancient manuscripts. I read one of these in the library of the monastery of Mount Zion outside the [Col. 0153A] walls of Toledo. It was written in ancient characters on parchment, and after the history of the broken bridge contained the following:

> When the greater part of the people saw this event, they were overcome by intense terror. Among them was a certain senator’s wife, illustrious for her possessions and adorned by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, most noble by birth, named Luparia. When she learned the reputation of those saints, she sent her messengers to them, through whom she begged those supreme princes to present themselves before her. As soon as she was granted the opportunity to see them—she whose inward heart had already been enriched by heavenly gifts—she boldly asked where those most holy old men came from and from what regions they had arrived. When they had been announced to her as men sent by the holy Apostles to preach the kingdom of God and proclaim the Gospel of Christ to Spain . . . while they were teaching her . . . she immediately acquired faith in the new holy doctrine. Asking for the gift of holy baptism, she was told that she should not receive what she requested before she had built a basilica at the baptistery which the saints had chosen. Having received this vision, she devoted herself continually to the work until she brought the entire structure of the basilica [Col. 0153B] to its summit and completed the roof of the temple she had begun. When the work was now finished and she had completed everything the saints had commanded her, they established a font according to custom, in which the holy woman was to be bathed with the water of saving purification. When the whole people, who had worshiped the empty superstition of idols, followed the holy example of this woman, they abandoned the temple of their ancient guilt and embraced the teaching of the holy old men with enlightened minds. From that time the polluted seat of the idols was abandoned; and there, consecrating altars to Saint John the Baptist, they built a church of Christ. As the faith grew, the people of God increased.

The historian is of such great antiquity that it is clear from what he writes at the end of his history that he lived scarcely later than the death of these saints. The ancient Breviaries of Spain support this account: the Toledo Breviary of Roman institution, the Cordoban, the Granadan, and the others.

But more authoritative and venerable than all these is the agreement of the Gothic Office of Saint Isidore. In the Preface [Col. 0153C] of the Mass (or *Latio*, as it is called there), we read:

> It is worthy and just that we should always give thanks to you, eternal and almighty God, whose glorious name the pliant doctors proclaim with trumpet blasts, and who rejoice in the privilege of preaching in particular places. Among their number we recognize these men, endowed with the grace of episcopal office and sent by the Apostles to our regions: namely Torquatus, Secundus, Indalecius, Thesiphontus, Euphrasius, Caecilius, and Iscius. Apostolic authority sends them to the Spaniards to hand on the faith of Catholic instruction. Their glorious prophecy, now approaching our cities, renews for us a celebration of joys that has been brought about through the advance of miracles.
>
> For when they had sent disciples into the neighborhood of this city and ordered them to purchase some food, their followers carried out the commands given to them. But behold, suddenly, when they saw men sacrificing to idols, and recognized the faithless people openly practicing their religion, a crowd of the impious pursued them at a furious run all the way to the river. But there an ancient bridge, built of massive construction, set a boundary for both sides. For just as, in the ancient history, Israel crossed the Red Sea and a path of salvation was extended to it, so now, when the blessed disciples were fleeing, the bridge itself, through the intervention of a sudden miracle, dissolved. It saved the people of the saints who were fleeing, but overwhelmed the persecutors, wholly faithless, in the river’s slippery waves.
>
> There the sea’s waters were divided for Israel’s crossing; here the structure of a huge mass was dissolved to save Christ’s servants. There the Egyptians were suffocated with their chariots; here the faithless were submerged beneath the stones. There the Israelites, when their enemies had been drowned in the depths, raised a song of praise to God; here the people who had been delivered, rejoicing with similar gladness, proclaimed a hymn to you together with the holy angels, saying: “Holy, Holy,” and so forth.

Then, before the Lord’s Prayer, he says:

> Behold, dearly beloved brothers, lift your eyes with me on high, praying especially to the Lord that, just as by the grace of faith he suddenly deigned to illumine the heart of blessed Luparia, so at this moment he may effectively deign to cleanse us from every stain of sin, while we proclaim to you from the earth and say: “Our Father,” and so forth.

I cannot restrain myself, although I may seem to repeat the same thing often, from presenting a hymn extracted from the Breviary of that same Saint Isidore. It is most elegant and embraces the whole account.

## Hymn of Saint Isidore on Saint Torquatus and his Companions

Now the white toga of the Roman city  
Proclaims the seven bishops in bright succession:  
Those sent to Hesperia, whom ancient tradition  
Assigns to the faith as sent by the Apostles.

These are heralds of radiant light:  
Torquatus, Thesiphontus, and also Iscius;  
Then Indalecius, and Caecilius,  
Joined with Euphrasius and Secundus.

Endowed with the lamp of the Gospel,  
They illumine the parched lands of the West,  
So that they burn with Catholic fires  
And harmful furnaces yield to their torches.

Acci lies close at hand for the men,  
Twelve stades distant from where they are staying.  
They send followers to seek food  
With which to restore their weary limbs.

There the disciples see the idols of the nations  
Being honored with empty rites.  
While the pagans sacrifice upon the mound  
With tears, they are immediately terrified by the impious deed.

Soon the insane, roaring crowd of attendants,  
When it recognized upon them the marks of faith,  
Drives them in rapid flight  
Along the difficult road as far as Flavius’s bridge.

But the bridge, stronger than solid masonry,  
Suddenly collapses and falls apart:  
Rescuing the righteous from the hands of their enemies,  
And crushing the enemies in the river’s whirlpool.

This is the first road of faith for the peoples.  
Among them the holy woman Luparia  
Approaches the saints, sees them, and implores them,  
Laying the saints’ instructions within her heart.

Then the handmaid of Christ, attentive to the service  
Of the saints, resolves to build a structure  
Where the waters of the baptistery might be opened  
And grace might cleanse everyone’s sins.

There the holy woman of God is immersed,  
And, washed in the bath of life, is reborn.  
At once the people hasten to the faith,  
And become numerous in Catholic doctrine.

Afterward the beloved fellowship of the bishops  
Hastens to divide itself among seven cities,  
So that, distributed among different places, they might pour forth doctrine  
And set the peoples aflame with scattered fires.

Through these men the swift grace of faith  
Shone forth, implanted in the lands of Hesperia.  
From that time, by various signs  
And the power of miracles, it urges people to believe.

Then, renowned for the fruits of righteousness,  
They bring their lives to an end with manifold increase,  
And are laid in tombs in their own cities.  
Thus one crown belongs to their scattered ashes.

Therefore, powerful throng, sevenfold yet one,  
Having prayed, we ask you from the depths of our hearts  
That through your prayers we may be carried,  
As a star in heaven, to fellowship with the angelic citizens.

Glory be to you, triune Lord, yet one,  
Father with the Begotten and the Paraclete,  
Who alone are the one and triune Lord,  
Holding the ages of ages in your mighty power. Amen.

Isidore thus played upon the names of Torquatus and his companions in the Capitula of the same feast:

> The bright and evident annual celebration of those seven bishops of yours is present, O Lord, returning with the passage of time. May Torquatus extend to us the ornaments of virtues; may Thesiphontus, who is from you, the fountain of life, satisfy us with the most abundant draught from the torrent of doctrine; may Iscius cleanse away the expiation of our sin; may Indalecius, the examiner, provide the spiritual nourishment of good works; may Secundus join us to the elect in the joy of your future coming; may Euphrasius strengthen the doctrines of the Catholic faith with the fourfold river of the Gospels; may Caecilius associate us with the assemblies of the angels.

**A.C. 43. A.R. 794.** After the body of the most sacred master had been buried, Torquatus, Thesiphontus, Caecilius, Iscius, Secundus, Indalecius, and Euphrasius set out for Rome.

[Col. 0155] [Note: [Col. 0155A]

**A.C. 44.—1. And by Blessed Peter, etc.** Many have thought that these men were ordained jointly by the holy Apostles Peter and Paul and sent to Spain, as the Palencian, Cordoban, and Granadan Breviaries state, as does Gregory VII in his letter to King Alfonso. But this could by no means have happened, since Paul had not yet gone up to Rome until the second year of Nero, according to Jerome’s testimony in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and in that year many of these bishops died after a long period of preaching.

Therefore the Roman Breviary, together with Baronius, volume I, year 46, section 2; Padilla, first century, chapter 19; Mariana and the Constable, in their treatise *On the Coming of Saint James*; Madera, book *On the Antiquity of Granada*, chapter 32; and Alderete, book II of *Spanish Antiquities*, chapter 12, affirm that they were sent and ordained by Peter alone, as Dexter now asserts.

When Isidore and the Martyrologies say that they were sent to Spain by the holy Apostles, this should be understood as meaning that they were first sent by James and afterward by Peter, or that the common designation does not invalidate the particular one.

[Col. 0155B] **2. Calocerus, etc.** We dealt with him under the year 37. Consult what was said there.

In the following year of the Lord, 45, the martyrdom of Saint Peter, the first bishop of Braga, occurred at Ratis, not far from Bracara Augusta. Dexter discusses him below under the years 66 and 110, where he says that he shone forth through many miracles.]

**A.C. 44. A.R. 795.** The bishops consecrated by Blessed Peter return to the southern regions of Spain, namely to coastal Baetica, to preach.

**A.C. 44. A.R. 795.** Calocerus, a disciple of Saint James, preaches throughout Carpetania.

[Note: [Col. 0155B]

**A.C. 48.—1. The Jerusalemites, etc.** These things are supported by the accounts reported by Dexter, by ancient manuscript codices, and by the old Breviaries of Spain, among which I read the Asturician and Palencian; also by Peter de Natalibus, book VI, chapter 124, concerning Magdalene; chapter 151, concerning Martha; chapter 152, concerning Marcella; and book I, chapter 72, concerning Lazarus; and book V, chapter 101, concerning Maximinus.

He adds Celidonius, or Cedonius, whom he says was the man blind from birth whom the Lord healed in John chapter IX; he discusses him in book V, chapter 102.

He differs only concerning Joseph of Arimathea. In book IV, chapter 2, he relates that Joseph was enclosed by the Jews within a wall so that he might perish from hunger and darkness, but was nourished with heavenly food and illumined by supernatural light until the destruction of Jerusalem; that at that time, when the wall was broken, he was released from it and presented himself to Titus; and that afterward he lived peacefully with the disciples until the day of his death.

Since, however, he produces no author for so remarkable an account, we agree rather with Dexter, who makes him Magdalene’s companion.

But in what year this expulsion of the saints took place may be questioned, since it is commonly said to have occurred after the martyrdom of Stephen, as may be seen in Cardinal Baronius under the year 35. Nevertheless, it should not be believed to have happened immediately, but only after fourteen years had elapsed from Christ’s Passion.

The aforementioned Bishop Equilinus relates it in book VI, chapter 124, in these words:

> After the Lord’s Ascension, therefore, in the fourteenth year after the stoning of Stephen and the dispersion of the disciples, the Jews seized Magdalene together with several Christians. Among them was blessed Maximinus, one of the seventy-two disciples, to whom Magdalene herself had been specially entrusted by Blessed Peter; also her brother Lazarus, her sister Martha, and Marcella, Martha’s maidservant; likewise blessed Cedonius, who had been blind from birth and whom the Lord had illumined; and many others. Placing all these people on a ship and exposing them to the open sea without oars or a pilot, so that they might perish in the sea, the Jews drove them away from the borders of Judea. Under God’s guidance they landed at Massilia.

This agrees with what he had said in book I, chapter 72, concerning blessed Lazarus: namely, that in the fourteenth year he was appointed bishop of Massilia.

Since Christ the Lord suffered in the thirty-fourth year of his age, it follows that, when the aforesaid fourteen years are added—the years that intervened between his Passion and the sending away and expulsion of these saints—the expulsion itself occurred in the year 48, as Dexter asserts.

From this we can clarify the question concerning the number of years lived by the most blessed Mother of God, a question that has often and greatly troubled authors.

Some, on the authority of Blessed Elizabeth, nun of Schönau—not the widow of the Landgrave, as Dom Antonius said in part III, title 19, chapter 11, but a member of the Order of Saint Benedict—who wrote this in book IV of her revelations, chapter 1, have said that Mary survived Christ by only one year and three months. Beletus, chapter 147 of *On Divine Offices*, and Equilinus, book VII, chapter 65, followed them.

This, however, does not agree with the truth, since Paul, who was present there, had not yet been converted to the faith in that year, 35, through 36, as we demonstrated above.

I pass over Equilinus’s argument, since it is very weak. He says:

> This is judged more truly from the fact that Dionysius says that all the Apostles were present at the Virgin’s dormition. That could not have happened if she had lived any longer after the Ascension, since the Apostle James, son of Zebedee, suffered martyrdom literally two years after the Lord’s Passion.

But Dionysius does not assert that all the Apostles were present there, as I shall now explain. And even if he had said so, he would have to be understood as speaking of those who were alive, or else as meaning that James had descended from heaven at that time with Christ the Lord. James himself did not die in that year, but much later, as we showed under the year 42.

On the other hand, others maintain that the Virgin survived until the eightieth or ninetieth year of her life, but without testimony; consequently they should not be heeded.

Some wish to place the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin twelve years after Christ’s Passion, because, they say, he had instructed the Apostles not to depart from Jerusalem for that length of time. But Bede calls this a falsehood, and we rejected it above under the year 34.

It seems to me most probable in this matter that one of two years should be assigned as the limit of the life of the Mother of God: either 63 or 73. Epiphanius embraces the latter, maintaining that she survived her Son for twenty-four years, namely until the year 58 of the Lord. For if twenty-four years are added to the year 34 of the Passion, the result is 58. Since, according to Epiphanius himself, the Blessed Virgin gave birth to the Lord in the fifteenth year of her age, it follows that she was taken up into heaven at the age of seventy-three, in the Son’s year 58.

The former date, however, is commonly accepted, since the faithful, in memory of the years of the life of our Lady, recite a crown of angelic prayers numbering sixty-three. I also deduce this from the present testimony of Dexter.

For the fact that Magdalene was expelled from Judea in the year 48 of the Lord, together with her brothers and companions, and not earlier, sufficiently suggests that in that same year the Blessed Virgin, whose inseparable companion Magdalene had been, was taken from the living into heaven. Indeed, from the splendid and public solemnity of the Virgin’s funeral, it is plausible that the Jews were inflamed with anger—as Melito of Sardis also asserts in his little book *On Her Passing*, if he is truly its author—and that they then seized Magdalene and her companions.

Because of the nobility of their blood, however, they were not put to death but sent into exile and exposed to the dangers of the sea. The year 48 of the Lord was the Virgin’s sixty-third year, if we accept, as Epiphanius teaches, that she gave birth at fifteen.

Eusebius also noted this very point in his *Chronicle* in these words:

> In the year 48 of the Lord, Mary the Virgin, mother of Jesus Christ, was taken up to the Son in heaven, as some write that this was revealed to them.

(Note the very ancient revelations concerning her.)

Furthermore, the year 63 is a climacteric year and, as it were, a natural limit of life, or at the least brings with it the greatest danger of death. Hence many men of the highest distinction died in that year of their age, among them Benedict, Bernard, and others.

Although the Most Blessed Virgin was not afflicted by illness, it is nevertheless sufficient that by its nature this is a climacteric year, so that we may believe that she died and was assumed in it.

There is likewise a significant indication of this in the fact that, according to this calculation of the years of the Mother of God, she is believed to have lived for as many years after her Son’s death as she had lived without him before the Incarnation: that is, fifteen years on each side, and thirty years in all. It is not without mystery that those fifteen years of her life after the Resurrection were granted to her without the presence of her Son, just as she had spent another fifteen years without him before, while still a virgin, she conceived him; thus the end corresponded to the beginning. In the middle of those thirty years she spent approximately the same number with that Son—namely, thirty-three.

Moreover, it is established from the sacred writings that after the end of the year 48, or at the beginning of the following year, certain Apostles were present in Jerusalem: Peter, John, James son of Alphaeus, Paul, Barnabas, and Titus, as well as Mark and Judas surnamed Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, as Luke says in Acts XV.

All these men were present in Jerusalem without any vehicle of clouds and without a miracle, for the purpose of holding the council at which the legal observances were prohibited.

Concerning Peter, indeed, we have in the very history of Magdalene, as told by Equilinus, that a certain ruler of Massilia, converted by Magdalene, departed from Rome with that Apostle and traveled with him to Jerusalem.

John was present in the Virgin’s household; James was in his Jerusalem see; Paul and Barnabas, taking Titus with them, were sent by the faithful concerning the legal observances; the others were companions of the Apostles.

Since miracles should not be admitted without necessity, it remains for us to acknowledge that the Blessed Virgin was assumed in the year when these men were in Jerusalem, without a miracle. For if she had been assumed after that year 48, while the Apostles were present, we would have to allow the miracle that Melito recounts: that the Apostles were carried on clouds and returned to the places where they had previously been. Yet Gelasius rejects this history as apocryphal in distinction 15, chapter *Sancta Romana*, and Bede rejects it in his work on the Acts of the Apostles.

I nevertheless see that Damascene relates it in his Sermon on the Dormition of the Mother of God, and that the Roman Breviary admits it in the feast of that event. But insofar as the account is true, it must be understood of the other Apostles—those, namely, who did not attend the council and at that time were far from Jerusalem.

That the council took place in the year 48, as Onuphrius asserts, or at least at the beginning of 49, after the Virgin’s passing, is clearly deduced from Paul’s words in Galatians II:

> Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also.

He says that he went up according to a revelation and conferred with them the Gospel that he preached among the Gentiles—namely, without imposing upon converts from the Gentiles an obligation to observe the legal ordinances.

That this was the reason for Paul and Barnabas’s journey to Jerusalem is shown by Luke in Acts XV, where he discusses that council. There Paul found three Apostles: Peter, John, and James. “When they recognized the grace that had been given to me,” Paul says, “James and Cephas”—that is, Peter—“and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, that we should go to the Gentiles”—namely, without imposing the burden of the legal ordinances—“and they to the circumcision” (Galatians II).

Since, therefore, this council, according to Paul, was held fourteen years after his conversion—for this is how, as we proved above, the words “then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem” must be understood—and since his conversion occurred at the beginning of the year 36 of the Lord, it follows that the council fell in the year 49, shortly after the Virgin’s Assumption. The Assumption itself therefore occurred in the year 48.

Perhaps Paul was summoned by revelation to go to Jerusalem for this reason, as he himself noted when he said, “I went up according to a revelation.” For a revelation was not necessary merely because of the council concerning the legal ordinances, since he and Barnabas were sent by the Jews and the brothers who were staying at Antioch (Acts XV).

I would incidentally observe that Cardinal Baronius did not correctly assign this council to the year 51, while at the same time maintaining that the fourteen years were to be counted from Paul’s conversion to the council and that he was converted in the year 36.

I see that the words “after fourteen years” can be taken to mean the same as “after fourteen years had been completed,” or “at the beginning of the fifteenth.” Nevertheless, even so the council could not have occurred in the year 51 but in 50, since nearly the whole year 36 of the conversion must be counted—for the conversion occurred at the beginning of that year—which Baronius does not do.

[Col. 0158B] Since we see that this interpretation agrees with many other truths, we take the word “after” in a sense that does not exclude the fourteenth year itself. The Apostle does not say “after fourteen complete years,” but “after fourteen years.” Therefore we more correctly say that the council was held in the year 49.

As for Paul, either he was not present at the Assumption, which occurred in the year 48, or the meaning of his words is this:

> After fourteen years, when I had come to Jerusalem, and so forth—

that is:

> When I came to Jerusalem and was present at the Virgin’s dormition, fourteen years after my conversion, but in the Lord’s year 49, I conferred with them the Gospel, and so forth.

There is one matter that seems to introduce considerable difficulty into this opinion: namely, Dionysius’s testimony in chapter 3 of *The Divine Names*, in which he appears to assert that not only the Apostles but also many of the disciples came together for the Virgin’s funeral, and among them Dionysius himself with Saint Hierotheus. For the Greeks assert in the Menologion, on October 4, that this man too was one of the Areopagite judges whom Paul converted to the faith at Athens.

That Saint Paul converted Dionysius to the faith after the council concerning the legal ordinances is clear from Luke. For in Acts XV, after the council had been completed in Jerusalem, Luke says that Paul and Barnabas departed for Antioch and brought the council’s decree to the church. After some days they separated from one another because of Mark: Paul did not want him to be their companion, whereas Barnabas did.

Then, in chapter XVI, Paul, taking Silas, went through Derbe and Lystra, where he converted Timothy and associated him with himself. He then passed through Phrygia, Galatia, and Mysia while preaching; and, at the request of the Macedonian who appeared to him in a vision, he went to Troas, Samothrace, Neapolis, and Philippi, a city of Macedonia. There he converted Lydia, the purple-seller, together with her household, and freed the pythonic slave-girl.

Nevertheless, after being sent to prison and beaten with many blows, he finally emerged free and went on through Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica, as chapter XVII relates, and then to Berea. Finally he reached Athens, where he was brought before the Areopagus. Taking as the theme of his speech the altar to the unknown god, he converted Dionysius the Areopagite.

Who could deny that the Apostle spent at least two or three years on so many and such extensive journeys and preaching missions? Many more years must be added for Dionysius and Hierotheus to become thoroughly learned in Paul’s school, as they clearly were at that time, according to chapter 3 of *The Divine Names*.

It will therefore ultimately follow that the Blessed Virgin did not depart to her Son in the year of the council concerning the legal ordinances, but much later.

Perhaps someone might evade the force of this argument by maintaining that the council was not held in the year 48 or 49, but perhaps much earlier. For the Acts of the Apostles do not establish the date, although they do show that it occurred long before Dionysius’s conversion. Nor does Paul in Galatians II say that he went to the council fourteen years after his conversion; he says that he went to confer with the Apostles the Gospel that he preached among the Gentiles, which could have happened without a council.

Once it is granted that the council was not held in the year 48 but earlier, room is left for the claim that Paul, preaching at Athens after the council, converted Dionysius and instructed him in the mysteries of the secrets of the faith, and that Dionysius finally came to the Virgin’s funeral in the year 48.

This escape, however, cannot be admitted. Many things prove that the council was not held before the year 48.

First, so many and such important affairs intervened before the council that it could by no means have been held before the year 48. For in Acts XII, after Peter’s release from imprisonment and Herod’s death, eaten by worms, the celebrated famine foretold by Agabus is mentioned; it occurred under Claudius (Acts XI). According to Eusebius and others, it happened in the fourth year of Claudius, which was the year 46 of Christ.

Claudius succeeded Augustus at the end of the year 42. At that time Paul and Barnabas were sent by the church of Antioch to Jerusalem to carry a collection and assistance to the brothers living in Judea. When this service had been completed, Luke says in chapter XII, they returned from Jerusalem to Antioch.

These events, therefore, took place in the year 46.

The Evangelist then relates in chapter XIII that, while they were staying at Antioch, they were set apart for the apostolic work among the Gentiles at the command of the Holy Spirit. They immediately went to Seleucia and from there sailed to Cyprus, where they preached at Salamis. After traveling through the whole island as far as Paphos, Paul struck Elymas the magician blind and converted Sergius Paulus the proconsul to the faith.

From there they sailed to Perga in Pamphylia and came to Antioch in Pisidia. After many Gentiles had been converted there, they said to the Jews:

> It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it, we turn to the Gentiles.

They departed again from there for Iconium. There, Luke says in chapter XIV, they remained for a long time, acting boldly in the Lord, who granted that signs and wonders be performed through their hands, and so forth.

But when they had finally been subjected to insults there and attacked with stones, they fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and to the whole surrounding region, and there they preached the Gospel.

At Lystra Paul healed a man lame from birth. Because of this, the Gentiles believed that he was Jupiter and Barnabas Mercury. But finally Paul was stoned and went to Derbe. After preaching Jesus there and teaching many people, they returned again to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch in Pisidia, appointing presbyters in each church. Passing through Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia; and, after preaching the word of the Lord at Perge, they went down to Attalia. From there they sailed to Antioch, from which they had departed.

After all these events, Luke says at the end of chapter XIV, they remained for no little time with the disciples. At last a dispute arose concerning the legal ordinances, and Paul and Barnabas were sent from Antioch to Jerusalem to the Apostles concerning this question.

The council is related throughout the following chapter, XV.

Consider, I ask, how much time intervened between the famine and the council; how long a journey they completed; and how, according to Luke, they remained for a long time at Iconium and for no little time at Antioch before the council was held. It is astonishing that all these events could have been accomplished in two or three years.

Since the famine that preceded all this occurred in the year 46 of Christ, it cannot be otherwise than that the council was postponed until the year 48 or 49.

Moreover, Paul’s own words in Galatians II provide an irrefutable proof of this matter. It is clear from the letter that when Paul went up to Jerusalem in the year 48 or 49 of Christ—that is, after fourteen years from his conversion—Barnabas was his companion:

> Then, he says, after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas.

But from Acts XV we learn plainly that immediately after the council Barnabas and Paul separated from one another:

> There arose a disagreement, so that they separated from one another. Barnabas, taking Mark, sailed to Cyprus; but Paul, choosing Silas, traveled through Syria and Cilicia.

That journey of Paul with Barnabas, therefore, could by no means have occurred after the apostolic council, but at the time when the council itself was held, and consequently in the year 48.

I pass over the fact that Paul’s words, “And I conferred with them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles”—that is, without the burden of the legal ordinances, as the Apostle argues throughout the Epistle in demonstrating to the Galatians—denote nothing other than that he brought the question of the legal ordinances before them. That question was certainly discussed in the council.

I also pass over the fact that Acts XV makes it clear that Paul returned from the council to Antioch, whereas from the Epistle we learn that Paul was there immediately after conferring his Gospel with the Apostles. For when Peter came to Antioch, Paul opposed him to his face concerning his pretense regarding the legal ordinances.

Thus, at last, one can see that the two testimonies correspond to one another in every respect and deal with precisely the same matter: the council occurred in the year that Paul records in Galatians II.

What, then, should be said regarding Dionysius? It remains for us to adopt the exposition and opinion of Hilduin, a most learned man, who, at the command of Charlemagne, arranged the history of Dionysius (which we have in Surius, volume V). He maintains that Blessed Dionysius, in the testimony cited from chapter 3 of *On the Divine Names*, is by no means speaking of the Virgin’s passing, nor asserting that he and Hierotheus were present at it; rather, he says that the two of them had at some time met with Peter and James son of Alphaeus, and with other disciples, in order to see the Lord’s tomb, out of reverence, gratitude, and devotion. Once this is granted, his testimony does us no harm, since we are investigating the passing of the Lady.

I admit that Metaphrastes, Damascene, Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, Nicephorus, and Glycas, among the ancients, are opposed to us; among more recent writers, Baronius in the year 48, and others who interpret Dionysius’s words as referring to the Virgin’s dormition. Nevertheless, with due respect for them, we cannot force ourselves into their interpretation. Nor is this surprising, since—Baronius excepted—they have plainly failed in explaining the same text of Dionysius, believing that it also establishes that Timothy, Paul’s beloved disciple and bishop of Ephesus, was present there, and that Dionysius dedicated his books to him; yet we shall demonstrate, God willing, in commentary 11 on the year of the Lord 100, that this is not true. Nor do Dionysius’s words favor them in any way if we weigh them exactly.

According to Marsilius’s new interpretation, which corresponds very closely to the Greek text, they are as follows:

> At some time we assembled with our God-filled hierarchs (“ours,” that is), both we and he himself [Hierotheus, whom he had mentioned], and many of our holy brothers, in order to see that body which received God, the author of life. There were also present James, the brother of the Lord, and Peter, the lofty and most exalted summit of the theologians. After the contemplation, therefore, it pleased all the hierarchs to praise, each according to his ability, the goodness of the divine power, infinitely mighty. Hierotheus, however, a theologian after those other sacred teachers there, as you know, surpassed them all: wholly transported, wholly beside himself.

If Dionysius had reported some of the hymns that were composed there, perhaps we could have grasped the true meaning of the place from them. Yet he entirely refrained from doing so. For lower down he says to Timothy:

> But for the present let us pass over the things mystically treated there, since they could not be expressed to many, and since they are known to you.

Therefore, we must rely solely on the words quoted above. Yet in them there is nothing that contributes to the interpretation of the Virgin’s passing, and everything can readily be referred to Christ’s tomb. For if he were speaking of the passing, he would not say that they had assembled at Jerusalem to see that body which had received God, the author of life; rather, he would say that they had assembled to attend her departure—she who had received the author of life—and not merely to see her, but to receive her final blessing; nor merely to see the body, but to see her alive before she departed to the Son.

If anyone wishes Dionysius to call the Virgin, while still possessed of life, a “body,” he will introduce an unusual manner of speaking, for which no usage among the learned can be found. But the Lord’s monument or tomb, which, according to the testimony of Matthew XXVII and Mark XV, had been hewn from rock, is most aptly called “the body which received God, the author of life.” And Christ is rightly called here the author of life, so that it might be expressly noted that he was free among the dead; while the one who received him dead was nevertheless the author of life.

Again, he indicates the same thing when he adds: “After the contemplation, therefore, it pleased all the hierarchs,” and so forth. The apostles and disciples, then, did nothing other than see and contemplate—something entirely appropriate to the Lord’s tomb, but wholly inappropriate to the Virgin’s body, which they not only saw but also committed to burial.

Add to this that, according to Dionysius, not all the apostles were present, but only two, Peter and James. On this point many are certainly mistaken, for Dionysius names only these two. Who, then, does not see that, if Paul too had been present there, Dionysius would also have named him, and that the disciple would have commemorated his teacher? Say the same regarding John, who held the first place in the Virgin’s passing and affairs, especially since Dionysius is numbering those great theologians who were present. John, however, had most rightly secured this designation for himself among the other apostles.

Moreover, if James and Peter were to be named before the others, this would have to be because they had done or said something special there; but no such thing is shown. It is simply said: “James and Peter were present.”

Nor should anyone suppose that, by the designation “hierarchs” in the words “At some time we assembled with our God-filled hierarchs,” Dionysius was referring only to the apostles. Rather, he was referring to all the bishops who were there, including James and Peter—that is, with them or among them. For afterward he numbers Hierotheus among the hierarchs, although he was not an apostle but the bishop of Athens, as the Greek Menologion states, and Usuardus, following it, under 4 October:

> After the contemplation, therefore, it pleased all the hierarchs to praise the divine goodness. But Hierotheus surpassed all the sacred teachers there, after those theologians.

If it pleased all the hierarchs to sing hymns, and Hierotheus also sang, then certainly he is numbered among the hierarchs. Therefore, the designation “hierarchs” was not used solely on account of the apostles, whom he nevertheless called “theologians” by a special title.

Nor is what Cardinal Baronius noted true—namely, that Timothy was also present there, to whom Dionysius dedicated his work. For the phrase “At some time we assembled” does not include both persons; it is a familiar manner of speaking used by Dionysius throughout the book, denoting only his own person, as the preceding words make clear. Moreover, he himself often exhorted Timothy to the same undertaking and said that he had sent him the book itself as something surpassing measure in excellence (he is speaking to Timothy). Hence he also says: “We assign this only to him,” and so forth; “But we, who are nearer to ourselves, shall set forth divine things according to the measure of our understanding,” and many other statements of this kind.

This seems to me to be the genuine meaning of Dionysius’s testimony. If, however, someone should decide to accept the authority of the learned writers who explain it as referring to the Virgin’s passing, he will consequently assert that the Blessed Virgin was assumed at the age of seventy-three, nine or ten years after the council of the apostles, and in the year 58 of Christ.

Yet this still seems difficult to me, since in the year 57, which was Nero’s second year (as Jerome testifies in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Paul), Paul arrived in Rome in chains, where he remained for a full two years in his rented lodging: Acts, last chapter. Thus, in the year 58 he could not have been present at Jerusalem. Especially since, once he had come to Rome, he never returned to the East, as he himself had foretold in Acts XX:

> Behold, I know that you will all see my face no more, among whom I have passed preaching the kingdom of God.

Peter, on the other hand, returned at least twice: once in the year 48, at the time of the council, and again on the occasion that Dionysius records here. But enough on these matters.

## 2. Verenice, etc.

She is commonly called Veronica. It is clear from the Acts of Saint Martial, preserved in Vincent of Beauvais’s *Historical Mirror* and in Saint Antoninus, part I of his *History*, title 6, chapter 25, § 2, that Veronica, together with her husband Amator, accompanied Saint Martial, the apostle of the Lemovices, into Gaul. His words are:

> He [Martial] came to Rome with the blessed apostle Peter and was sent by him into Gaul, having in his company Amator and his wife Veronica, who was a close and intimate friend of the Virgin Mary.

Saint Amator led a solitary life upon the rock that is now called Amator’s, and there he died. Veronica, however, followed Saint Martial as he preached in the territory of Bordeaux, and there grew old. But she ended her days at Rome, as Dexter asserts in this passage.

The Lord’s countenance, which he impressed with his own blood upon Veronica’s cloth, is preserved at Rome in Saint Peter’s, where I have often venerated it. Another [image]—for the cloth was folded double—is preserved in Spain, in the city of Jaén, with the greatest reverence.

Equilinus, book VI, chapter 151, reports from Ambrose that the woman with the issue of blood mentioned in Mark V and Luke VIII was Martha. This does not seem probable, however; for the Evangelist would not have concealed her name if she had been Martha.

More famous is the account of Eusebius: that the woman with the issue of blood was a citizen of Caesarea Philippi and, out of gratitude and in memory of the benefit received from Christ, placed a statue of him in her garden. At its feet she herself appeared to be touching the fringe of his garment. It then happened that the plants which grew beneath the statue and touched the Lord’s fringe acquired such power that women suffering from hemorrhage were healed by touching them. Equilinus further testifies that the apostate Julian removed this image and substituted one of himself in its place; yet that image was shattered by a stroke of lightning.

Regarding the face of the Lord Christ preserved at Rome, its miracles, antiquity, and other matters relating to it, there exists a manuscript in the archive of the Vatican basilica of Saint Peter. From it Bzovius transferred much material into the first volume of his *Ecclesiastical History*, which you may consult.

### A. C. 48. A. R. 799. [Col. 0157]

The Jews of Jerusalem, vehemently hostile to Blessed Lazarus, Magdalene, Martha, Marcella, Maximinus, Joseph of Arimathea, a noble decurion, and many others, place them aboard a ship without oars or sails and without a helmsman, and order them into exile. Carried divinely across the vast sea, they safely reach the harbor of Massilia.

### A. C. 48. A. R. 799. [Col. 0161]

Saint Verenice, a holy woman, came from Gaul to Rome; there, having left behind the divine countenance, famous for miracles, she departed to the Lord in the year 70. They say that Christ had healed her of an issue of blood.

> **[Note: [Col. 0162D]]**

## A. C. 50. A. R. 801.

### 1. Peter, etc. [Col. 0162D]

Regarding the arrival of the Apostle Peter in the Spanish provinces, all who have written about Spanish affairs agree: Ambrose; Morales, book IX, chapter 14; Pineda, part II of the *Monarchia*, chapter 28, § 4; Marieta, *On the Saints of Spain*, part I, book I, chapter 13; Alfonso Chacón, *On the Supreme Pontiffs*, under Peter; Romanus, book I of *The Christian Commonwealth*, chapter 3; Pujades, *History of Catalonia*, book IV, chapter 9; and others. Among foreign writers, the same is maintained by Onuphrius Panvinius in his *Ecclesiastical Chronicle*; Lipomanus and Surius; Haraeus and Lipelous in the *Life of Saint Peter*. All of them derive the account from Simeon Metaphrastes, in his narrative concerning the journeys of the apostles Peter and Paul, which Surius has in volume III.

Here are his explicit words:

> When he had not remained long among the Romans, and had regenerated many through holy baptism, established a church, and ordained Linus bishop, he came to Tarragona. After ordaining Epaphroditus bishop there, he came to Sirmium, a city of Spain. Having appointed Epaenetus bishop in that place, he proceeded to Carthage, a city of Africa. After appointing Crescent bishop there, he came into Egypt. Having ordained Rufus bishop at Thebes, which has seven gates, and Mark the Evangelist bishop at Alexandria, and so forth.

Observe the remarkable agreement between Metaphrastes and Dexter. Nor is this surprising, since Metaphrastes could have borrowed it from Dexter, who preceded him by many years, or both may have drawn from the same ancient tradition that then still existed.

### 2. Images, etc. [Col. 0163A]

It is accepted by ecclesiastical tradition that the use of sacred images in the Church originated with the holy Apostles. This matter was treated at length in the Second Council of Nicaea, which was the Seventh General Council. In its honor the Greeks celebrate an annual feast on the Sunday immediately following 11 October, as may be seen in Molanus’s *Usuardus* under that day.

In its fifth session the history is admitted of the image of the Savior sent by the Lord Christ to King Abgar of Edessa, although the letters concerning it are rejected by Gelasius among the apocrypha. As for the same sacred countenance, which is today held in great veneration in the convent of the nuns of Saint Sylvester in Rome, together with the head of Saint John the Baptist, the Greeks also celebrate a special feast on 17 August.

On this matter consult Baronius in his notes under 9 November, where he gathers much in its favor. Also call to mind the sacred countenance of Christ impressed upon Veronica’s cloth, and the images painted by Saint Luke, which are preserved here in Rome with the greatest devotion and reverence: at Saint Mary Major, in the basilicas of the Madonna del Popolo and of Peace, in the Via Lata, and elsewhere. From these examples, and from the dignity of his supreme apostolate, it is clear that Peter, if any apostle did so, introduced sacred images wherever he preached.

That the images he brought into the Spanish provinces were carried from Antioch can readily be inferred from the fact that at that time he was coming from Antioch, where, after the council concerning the legal observances held at Jerusalem in the year 49 or 48, he was rebuked by Paul, as Paul himself reports in Galatians II.

A significant testimony to this continues at Madrid in the sacred and miraculous image of the Blessed Virgin commonly called *de Atocha*. Many believe that it has been venerated there since the time of the Apostles. It was already famous more than five hundred years ago, in the time of Saint Isidore the Farmer; and since it is certain that it is older than the Moorish domination in Spain, while certain characters attached to it show that it bears the marks of the apostolic age, this is all the more notable.

Yet in such great antiquity no satisfactory explanation of its name can be assigned, except that it was formerly called “of Antioch” and that the word was gradually altered somewhat, becoming *de Atocha*. Thus we received it from Saint Peter, brought from Antioch.

The belief that it was named after a certain rural shrub called *atocha* in Spanish, as though it had appeared upon such a plant, is a popular and insignificant notion. It is nowhere read that the image appeared anywhere, and the name *Atocha* is more recent in the Spanish language than could have been the case if it were to give a Gothic image its name of at least such antiquity.

Some assert that a letter of Saint Ildephonsus exists in which he mentions this sacred image. So reports M. Gil González Dávila, royal historiographer, in his *History of Madrid*, and Father Morillo agrees with him in his *History of the Pilar*.

### 3. Epaenetus, etc. [Col. 0163D]

The other authors cited above, together with Metaphrastes, affirm that he held a bishopric in Spain. Metaphrastes says of Saint Peter:

> He came to Sirmium, a city of Spain, where he appointed Epaenetus bishop, and so forth.

Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that Dexter calls Epaenetus’s see not Sirmium but Sexifirmum. For that city is known by both names, and Dexter himself below, under the year 100, calls it Sirmium when he discusses the martyrs Maxima and Montanus.

It might be the place that Ptolemy, in his map of Baetica, calls Sex, perhaps the word having been truncated in the manuscript. Villanueva identifies it with Vélez-Málaga; Floriano, with Motril. Others prefer to think that it formerly existed on the Granada mountain, one of the Alpujarras, called Tregiliana.

Nor are there lacking those who think it was called Sexifirmum, as though it were *Saxifirmum*, “firm rock,” which we now call in Spanish *Piedrafita* or *Piedrahita*. Epaenetus will be mentioned again below under the year 64, in which he died in his own city.

### 4. Many accompanying him, etc. [Col. 0164A]

Let us set out Peter’s journey, so that Dexter and Metaphrastes may be illuminated, and so that it may readily be established which of the disciples was taken into Peter’s company and where each was left.

Peter, being in Rome from the year 44 through 47, brought many to the faith. Among them was the distinguished Marcus Marcellus, formerly a disciple of Simon Magus and afterward of Saint Peter, as he himself admits in his letter to Nereus and Achilleus concerning the death of Petronilla, preserved in Surius, volume III, under 12 May.

Born at Rome of the most noble senatorial blood, from the house and family of Nero, he was called by the faithful Eugenius for this reason: the name means “noble.”

While Peter was also living at Rome, he ordained as bishop Apollinaris, his disciple, whom he had brought with him from Antioch, and sent him to Ravenna. He was of Antiochene origin, as his Acts state; Mombritius relates them in volume I, Surius in volume IV, and Equilinus in book VI, chapter 128. His ordination and mission are discussed by the Roman Martyrology, Bede, Usuardus, and Ado under 23 July.

“When he had not remained long among the Romans,” says Metaphrastes—that is, only three or four years—and had ordained Linus bishop, his suffragan or co-bishop, so that in his absence he might care for the Roman Church, Peter left Rome in the year 47 or at the beginning of 48, traveling toward Jerusalem. His companions were Marcus Marcellus Eugenius, Epaphroditus, Epaenetus, Rufus, Crescent, and others.

It is clear that Epaenetus and Rufus had been living at Rome, for Paul greets them in writing to the Romans, chapter XVI, and calls Epaenetus “the first-fruit of Asia.” With these companions, Peter, passing through Ravenna, took Apollinaris with him and finally reached Jerusalem. There, in that year, he was present at the Assumption of the Virgin, and in the following year he took part in the council concerning the non-observance of the legal prescriptions by converts from the Gentiles.

The Apostles sent the council’s decree to Antioch through Judas, surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, whom Luke in Acts XV calls “leading men among the brethren.” They went down to Antioch, gathered the multitude, and delivered the letter. Judas and they themselves were prophets, and they consoled the brethren with much discourse. Then Silas attached himself to Paul; Judas, however, went away to Jerusalem and attached himself to Peter.

Peter again departed for Antioch, where Paul opposed him to his face. Barnabas, dissenting from Paul, took Mark with him and sailed to Cyprus, where Mark had been born. Paul, choosing Silas, traveled through Syria and Cilicia, instructing them to observe the Apostles’ commands. For the decretal letter of the council had been written to the brethren in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia who had been converted from the Gentiles.

Thus far from Acts of the Apostles, chapter XV, and from the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter II.

Peter should be thought to have spent some time in Antioch and Jerusalem, visiting the faithful. From there he sailed to Cyprus in the following year, namely 50, intending to depart for Spain. Barnabas joined him there with Mark, and from there, with his remaining companions Marcus Marcellus, Apollinaris, and Judas, he sailed to Spain. As I believe, he visited Rome along the way, then set sail from Tarragona, where, according to Metaphrastes, he appointed Epaphroditus bishop. Some, however, read *Tarracina* instead of *Tarragona*; Tarracina is a city of Italy.

The very learned Peter Galesinus, an Italian, nevertheless reads the passage in Metaphrastes in such a way that he affirms that the text has *Tarragona*, not *Tarracina*, and that Epaphroditus was appointed bishop of that Spanish city by the Apostle. This reading is particularly attractive, because the author is narrating Peter’s journey from Rome to Spain:

> “After he had left Rome,” he says, “and ordained Linus bishop there, he came to Tarragona, where he appointed Epaphroditus bishop; then he came to Sirmium, a city of Spain,” and so forth.

Certainly Tarracina does not lie on the route to Spain, but on the eastern side opposite Rome. Moreover, there is no record of Epaphroditus at Tarracina, so that we would be forced to make him bishop of that city.

By means of this reading we can also readily reconcile Metaphrastes with Dorotheus, who in his *Synopsis* reports him as bishop of Adera. Adera or Adeha was a city situated near Tarragona among the Ilercaones, as may be seen in Ptolemy.

It seems quite probable that Torquatus, Secundus, Caecilius, and the others whom Peter had ordained bishops at Rome met him there and accompanied him through Spain. At that time Calocerus, a disciple of Saint James, attached himself to Apollinaris, with whom he later lived at Ravenna, as may be seen in Equilinus, book VI, chapter 128, in these words:

> Meanwhile Calocerus the presbyter governed the Church of Ravenna.

Peter seems to have established some bishops and presbyters anew, although it is not known who they were, apart from Epaphroditus, whom he appointed bishop at Tarragona, and Epaenetus, whom he appointed at Sirmium or Sexifirmum.

When Peter departed from Spain and boarded a ship, he proceeded to Africa. There he appointed Crescent bishop among the Carthaginians, according to Metaphrastes. From the Second Epistle to Timothy, chapter IV, we learn that, while Paul was being held in chains at Rome, Crescent had gone from Rome to Galatia in the year 58. Yet Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 51, and Theodoret on this passage of Paul, together with the Roman Martyrology under 27 June and 29 December, insist that “Gaul” should be read instead, and it is certain that Crescent founded the Church of Vienne in Gaul.

Baronius maintains that he preached in both places in his notes under 24 June, and this is likewise asserted in the text of the Roman Martyrology under that day and in Usuardus.

Nevertheless, he [Crescent] first had to appoint a successor for himself at Carthage, where he had been the first bishop appointed by Saint Peter. From Africa Peter departed for Egypt. There, at Egyptian Thebes—for there is another Thebes in Asia near Corinth—he appointed Rufus bishop. Rufus later came to Spain and sat as bishop at Dertosa or Tortosa, as we shall say below under the years of Christ 100 and 112. Finally, at Alexandria he ordained Mark as bishop.

After completing this journey, he boarded a ship and returned to Rome, while Barnabas founded the Church of Milan, as Baronius asserts under the year 54.

### 5. He remains in Spain, etc. [Col. 0165D]

The Roman Martyrology, Bede, Usuardus, and Ado treat of Saint Quartus on 3 November, as do Equilinus, book X, chapter 16, and book VI, chapter 100. But among the others Peter Galesinus, on the same day, agrees with Dexter, saying:

> The birthday of Saint Quartus, who was one of the seventy-two disciples and bishop of Berytus; thence he went into Spain and, after the apostle James, transmitted to the Spaniards the teaching of the Christian religion.

Dexter, however, again treating of Saint Quartus under the year 105, says:

> Saint Quartus, a disciple of the apostles, travelled through Spain twice: once after James, and again after being left by Paul.

He was indeed with Paul at Corinth when Paul wrote the Epistle to the Romans, in which he greeted them in Quartus’s name: “Quartus the brother greets you.” But since Paul wrote that epistle at Corinth about the year of the Lord 54, more or less, it must be said that Saint Quartus left Spain for the East before that year, perhaps intending to bring Paul there at the Spaniards’ request, since they furnished strong reasons for his coming. A little earlier Paul had said to the Romans concerning this:

> When I begin my journey into Spain, I hope that I may be conducted there by you;

that is, as Theophylact comments:

> You yourselves, seeing the necessity that presses me to visit the Spaniards, will be the first to send me to them, since I am compelled to do so.

He remained with Paul until Paul sent him into Spain while Paul himself was held at Rome in chains; for in the Second Epistle written from Rome to Timothy, chapter IV, he says: “Luke alone is with me.” Thus Quartus was absent at that time. It is probable that he went to Spain to explain to the faithful why Paul was being detained in chains at Rome, and that the chains prevented his journey to them. (We shall say the same of Saint Secundus under the year 52.)

But there is no agreement among all writers as to which church he was bishop of. Hippolytus and Dorotheus, followed by Equilinus, make him bishop of Berytus, and Galesinus asserts this; yet Galesinus says in his Notes that others maintain that he was bishop of Nursia. According to Dexter, whom we follow more readily, he was bishop of Betyri in Spain, a town among the Vettones, formerly called Conciolum, which Ptolemy also places among the Vettones near Salamanca. It was first called Berela and afterwards, in Dexter’s age, Baetirus, by others Baetira. See Dexter under the year 105.

### 6. Lucius Seneca, etc. [Col. 0166B]

In place of *Sentica*, as it was formerly read in the manuscript, I have changed it to *Sentria*, a town of Lusitania now called Sintra. In its church dedicated to Saint Michael there still survives, on a very ancient stone, the epitaph of L. Seneca, common not only to him but also to his son L. Aelianus and his wife Casia Quintilia. Ambrosio Morales cites it in book IX, chapter 9, of his *History of Spain*, while treating the events of the year 55. It is as follows:

> L. AELIUS L. F. GAL. AELIANUS. H. S. E.
>
> L. AELIUS SEX. F. GAL. SENECA PATER. H. S. E.
>
> CASIA Q. F. QUINTILIA MATER. H. S. E.

That is:

> Lucius Aelius Aelianus, son of Lucius, of the Galerian tribe, lies here;
>
> Lucius Aelius Seneca, father, son of Sextus, of the Galerian tribe, lies here;
>
> Casia Quintilia, mother, daughter of Quintus, lies here.

Here it is especially to be noted that the marks *D. M. S.* or *D. M.* are not placed above the inscriptions; they signify “Sacred to the Manes” or “To the Manes,” whom the Gentiles believed to be gods of the dead. Since they occur in all Gentile epitaphs and are entirely absent here, this is a manifest sign that these were Christian persons—especially because there is no other Gentile mark there, and because many stones bore the inscription *Aug. Sacerdos*, “priest of Augustus,” or something similar.

### 7. At this time. [Col. 0166D]

We have treated of Saint Athanasius under the year 35, commentary 2; under 36, likewise commentary 2; and also under 42, commentary 2; in approximately those places Saint Theodore was discussed, and also under 41. Galesinus, on 15 May, says:

> By those same two, Athanasius and Theodore, who had never departed from Spain, the teaching of the Christian religion was propagated through many parts of that province.

What is said here concerning Saint Athanasius’s preaching throughout Celtiberia and Carpetania was elegantly sung by M. Maximus in this epigram, printed with his *Chronicle* at Zaragoza in 1619:

> Athanasius first becomes bishop in our city  
> (Caesaraugustan),  
> and the honored shepherd  
> of the angelic household.
>
> Through the Carpetanian lands he scatters holy seed,  
> and preaches among the Celtiberian peoples.
>
> Hail in the piety of your spirit, old man, bishop, and father;  
> you are of James’s disciples and the glory of bishops.
>
> Pray for the people entrusted to you, splendid shepherd;  
> you who are called the anchor of faith, be favorable.

Of Saint Theodore, his companion, he sang as follows:

> With equal zeal Saint Athanasius and loving Theodore  
> plant their footsteps in Spain.
>
> This man was its first presbyter and gladly taught  
> the sacred doctrines in Celtiberian soil.
>
And when Cynthius had completed forty circuits,  
his head wreathed with foliage, he ascends in glory to the stars.
>
> He is the companion of the other Theodore, to whom was given the care  
> of guarding the venerable tomb of his father.
>
> Hail in spirit, sacred Theodore, guardian of the Caesarean fold,  
> shining honor of religion.
>
> Diligently pray before God for us,  
> who, under your guidance, have tasted the ambrosia of faith.

Here M. Maximus distinguishes two Theodores: one, a disciple of Saint James, who lies buried beside the body of his father and master; the other, who was the first archpresbyter of Blessed Athanasius. Whether this latter was also a disciple of Saint James, or of Athanasius himself, is not sufficiently established, although the former seems probable to me.

By the words, “And when the Moon had completed fourteen circuits,” etc., he seems to indicate that this archpresbyter died in the fortieth year of his age, unless perhaps he means that, forty years after his preaching—on account of which “Saint Athanasius and loving Theodore plant their footsteps in Spain with equal zeal”—he exchanged life for death, which I judge more likely. By this reckoning, he must be said to have died in the year 76, since Spanish preaching began in the year 36.

Concerning the year and day of Saint Athanasius’s death, Maximus adds at the end of his epigram: “He died near Zaragoza in the year 59 and is venerated on the first day of November.” As to the manner of his death, Galesinus believed him to be a confessor, under 15 May in his Martyrology. Nor is that surprising, since his martyrdom rests only on the authority of M. Maximus, whose writings had not yet appeared when Galesinus wrote.

In a hymn concerning the first three bishops of Zaragoza, Maximus sings, among other things:

> First, holy Athanasius, I praise you,  
> and you, Theodore, in an outstanding song;  
> nor are you, Bishop Epitectus,  
> less worthy of our odes.
>
> The Iberian himself sees the third and the first  
> suffer bravely, etc.

That is, Athanasius and Epitectus. He says that the river Ebro saw each suffer bravely, because they were put to death as martyrs near Zaragoza on its bank.

Yet although he died there, his body was transferred to Compostela by his disciples, as he himself had provided in his first testament, choosing a tomb for himself beside the Apostle. This is asserted by Morales, book IX, chapter 7, of the *History of Spain*, and by Marieta, book I of *On the Saints of Spain*; and, more importantly, Leo III had taught it earlier in his letter *On the Translation of Saint James*. On this matter the Cordoban Breviary says:

> The other disciples Athanasius and Theodore (as is read in Blessed Leo’s letter) were buried beside the Apostle’s body, one at the right and the other at the left.

Callistus II and Vincent of Beauvais agree.

As to the places where Saints Athanasius and Theodore preached, Ptolemy’s *Geography*, book II, map 2 of Europe, chapter 6, shows that ancient Celtiberia did not encompass the whole of our kingdom of Aragon, but extended from the Ebro to the kingdom of Toledo, with part of the March, or Mancha, and the Alcarria. Carpetania, however, was what is now called New Castile, or the kingdom of Toledo; it is bounded on the north by the bank of the Duero, on the west and south by the mountains called the passes of Somosierra, Guadarrama, Fuenfría, and Palomera, and on the east borders Celtiberia.

### A. C. 50. A. R. 801. [Col. 0163]

Peter, as Christ’s vicar, came to the Spanish provinces and brought images from Antioch. He left Epaenetus as bishop of Sexifirmum in Baetica, accompanied by many: Marcus Marcellus Eugenius; Apollinaris of Ravenna, whom Calocerus joined on his return to Italy; Barnabas; and Judas. From there he proceeded to Africa and Egypt.

### A. C. 50. A. R. 801. [Col. 0165]

Saint Quartus remained in Spain and died in the year 76.

### A. C. 50. A. R. 801.

Lucius Seneca, a centurion and a true Christian, died at Sintra.

### A. C. 50. A. R. 801. [Col. 0167]

At this time Saint Athanasius, the first bishop of Zaragoza, Greek by nationality and a disciple of Saint James, one of those whom James had in Spain, preached throughout Celtiberia and performed wonders there. He and Theodorus traveled throughout Carpetania, preaching and teaching.

> **[Note: [Col. 0168A]]**

## A. C. 52.

### 1. Iscius, etc. [Col. 0168A]

In the years 44 and 50 he had discussed the preaching of certain disciples of Saint James—namely Calocerus, Athanasius, and Theodorus. Now and thereafter, up to the year 60, he designates the places in which Torquatus, Iscius, and their companions preached, with one exception: Saint Secundus, bishop of Abula, whom he does not mention here with the others.

He does not explain the reason. It seems to me, however, that the reason was that Saint Secundus was absent from Spain during these years, having become Saint Paul’s companion on his journeys. For in Acts XX, among the other disciples who accompanied Paul throughout Greece and as far as Jerusalem and Rome, Secundus is listed. Until now no one has acknowledged two disciples of the Apostles named Secundus, so that anyone might assert that this one was different from the other.

Furthermore, Saint Quartus, bishop of Spain, was also with Paul at that time, and it is probable that, having been requested by the Spaniards, he was going to bring Paul there with him. See what we said concerning Quartus under the year 50. We shall discuss Secundus again under the year 100.

Dexter says that Saint Iscius preached at Carteia near the strait, and at another Carteia not far from Carthage Spartaria.
