Whether one should read *Cartheia*, *Cartesia*, or *Cartesa* need not greatly concern us; in ancient names of places, considerable variation has occurred through the passage of time.

Equilinus, Molanus, and the Cordoban Breviary read *Carthesia*. The Roman Martyrology, however, reads *Carteia*, agreeing with Dexter under 15 May. This is the name most widely received among reliable authors: Titus Livy, books XXVIII and XLIII; Strabo, book III of the *Geography*; Pliny, book III, chapter 1; Hirtius, book I of *On the Spanish War*; Cassius Dio, book XLIII of the *Roman History*; Silius Italicus, in the *Punica*; and Ptolemy, book II of the *Geography*, chapter IV. Later writers followed them, though they read the name with aspiration as *Cartheia*.

Those who read *Carthesia* maintain that it was a city situated near Asturica, which is now the deserted place called Ventosa. So say Molanus and the Cordoban Breviary, followed by Mariana, book IV of his *History*, chapter 2.

They are entirely mistaken, however, concerning Spain, because among the ancient and reliable authors there is no city called Carthesia anywhere in the Asturicensis district. Moreover, Saint Iscius and his companions exercised their ministry of preaching in coastal Baetica, as we have already shown, and not in the inland provinces of Spain.

In addition, at that time Saint Ephraem, bishop of Asturica, appointed to that province by Saint James, was engaged in converting that region. It would therefore not have been necessary for Saint Iscius also to have been established as bishop in a city so near to it.

Therefore, there can be no doubt that Saint Iscius’s see was in Baetica. There is still disagreement among authors, however, about the location of his Carteia. Ptolemy places it in the Bastuli, near the Strait of Cádiz; Morales, in his *Antiquities*, fol. 81, maintains [Col. 0169A] that it was Algeciras; Mariana, book I, chapter 2, holds that it was Tarifa. Finally, others believe it was the place now called Cartaya.

Even among those who place Carteia near the strait there is a difference of opinion. Some think it stood on the side of the strait where the Mediterranean Sea begins, which is Ptolemy’s view; others place it on the side where the Ocean joins the strait. “That city is situated on the Ocean coast, where the sea first opens out from the narrow entrance,” says Livy in the passage cited and in book XLIII. In those passages he discusses the naval battles fought at Carteia, at the mouth of the narrows of the Strait of Cádiz, between Laelius the Roman and Hanno the Carthaginian; it was also in that place that Caesar and Pompey fought in triremes.

Certainly, if these matters are to be brought into some degree of agreement, we must say with Dexter that there was formerly not just one Carteia on the shores of Baetica, but two. One was the Carteia that Titus Livy places on the Ocean coast, on the outer side of the strait, where the Ocean first opens out from the narrow entrance—and here we disagree with Ptolemy. The other is the place now called Cartaya, [Col. 0169B] not far from New Carthage.

The ancients called the former Tartessus, as Pliny reports in book III, chapter 1—he too places it in the Atlantic Sea, that is, the Ocean: “From the Atlantic Sea, Carteia, called Tartessus by the Greeks”—and as Saint Jerome reports in book II of his *Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians*, in the preface.

We call the latter Cartaya. It is not directly on the seashore, but somewhat inland and separated from the sea. Thus the sense of Dexter’s words is that Saint Iscius preached at the Carteia near the strait, the city situated on the Ocean where it joins the Strait of Cádiz, and traveled along the entire coast of the inland sea—that is what he calls the sea lying between the mouths of the strait, and what Ptolemy calls the “inland sea” on his map of Baetica, when he says that Mount Calpe and the Pillar are in the inland sea. He also preached at Alone and at the other Carteia in the Mediterranean Sea, and so forth—that is, at the city situated on the Mediterranean side, although not on the shore itself, but near Carthage.

[Col. 0169C]

But where Alone, or Alo, was situated must now be considered. Ptolemy places it not in Hispania Baetica but in Tarraconensis, among the Contestani, not far from New Carthage, or Spartaria, in the Gulf of Ilici, that is, the Gulf of Elche. Arnoldus Milius thinks it was Ilice itself—now Elche—and that Pomponius Mela calls it Ilice.

Mela’s words in book II, chapter 6, are these: “The next gulf, the Ilicitan Gulf, contains Alone and Lucentia [now Lucena], whence it is named Ilice.” Certainly, since he distinguishes it from the city of Ilice and says that the gulf received its name from that city, the name seems, according to Mela, to have originated from Alone. I believe the text should be read exactly as follows: “The Ilicitan Gulf contains Alone and Lucentia, and Ilice, from which it takes its name.” That is, it also contains Ilice, from which it takes its name—namely, Ilicitanus. Since *Ilicem* is in the accusative, derived from the nominative *Ilici*, it cannot be read otherwise according to the rules of grammar. Nor is the gulf ever found called Ilice; it is called Ilicitanus.

Morales, in his *Spanish Antiquities*, fol. 7; Tarapha, in *On the Kings of Spain*; and Michael Villanova in his commentary on Ptolemy, maintain that it was Elche or Alicante. Nevertheless, since Alone and Ilice were different cities, it must absolutely be said that Ilice was Elche, while Alone was Alicante—as is sufficiently clear from the names themselves—and that Saint Iscius also sowed the seeds of evangelical preaching at Alicante.

### 2. The Temple of the Pillar

He does not assert that a part of the Lord’s Pillar was there, but only that certain people—that is, the common people—believed this. We discussed the temple of the Pillar under the year of Christ 37, comments 2 and 3.

### 3. The Centurion Flourishes, etc.

See what we discussed about him at length under the year of the Lord 34, comments 3, 6, and 8. This was Gaius Oppius himself, as we shall say under the year 70, comment 2.

### 4. Saint Torquatus, etc.

That he was a Roman and a very distinguished man is sufficiently indicated by the name Torquatus itself. Dio Cassius, book LIX, Cassiodorus, and Baronius write about the consulship of his father, Publius Nonius Asprenates, together with Marcus Aquilius Julianus, in the year of the Lord 40. The *Consular Fasti* of Onuphrius discuss Lucius Nonius Asprenates—I believe he was the son of Publius Nonius and the brother of Saint Torquatus—because he entered the consulship with [Col. 0170B] Arricinius Clemens in the year 96.

Saint Torquatus preached at Acci, that is, Guadix, and at Malaca, now Málaga, and as far as the mouth of the Strait of Gibraltar. No one disputes that Acci was Guadix. Ptolemy places it on his map of Tarraconensis, among the Bastetani, or Bassetani. He was also appointed bishop there.

A printing error therefore entered the old Cordoban Breviary, quoted by Alderete in book II, chapter 12, when it says: “Torquatus among the Gaditani, whom they then called Accii.” It should read *among the Guadixani*, not *Gaditani*. We shall discuss Saint Torquatus again below, under the year 66.

### 5. Saint Martial, etc.

The Roman Martyrology speaks of him on June 30, where Baronius reports that he was not only the founder of the see of Limoges but also of other sees. Since his bishopric was not far from Spain—he lived beyond the Pyrenees—it was easy for him to approach Spain itself.

It was certainly a very common practice among the early faithful of the Church to visit one another, so that they might consult one another about matters relating to the preaching of the Gospel. Many difficulties necessarily arose that required consultation, and they also encouraged one another through mutual conversation to face death for Christ.

Baronius likewise asserts in the *Annals*, under the year of the Lord 74, that Saint Martial established the peoples of Limoges, Toulouse, Bordeaux, Cahors, and Aquitaine. See his letters concerning these matters in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers.*

A. C. 52. A. R. 803. Iscius preaches at Carteia near the strait and travels along the entire coast of the inland sea; he also preaches at Alone and at the other Carteia in the Mediterranean Sea, not far from Carthage Spartaria.

A. C. 52. A. R. 803. The faithful frequently visit the Temple of the Pillar at Caesaraugusta—for some believe that a part of the Lord’s Pillar is there—and venerate it with the greatest devotion.

A. C. 52. A. R. 803. The Malacitan centurion flourishes; Saint James baptizes him there.

A. C. 52. A. R. 803. Saint Torquatus, a Roman by birth and the son of Publius Nonius Asprenates, a very distinguished man, is said to have preached at Acci, Málaga, and as far as the mouth of the strait.

A. C. 52. A. R. 803. Martial, apostle of the Limogians, the Cadurci, and the people of Toulouse, came to Spain and visited the faithful while preaching.

[Note: [Col. 0170C]]

A. C. 54.—1. Saint Indalecius, etc. Urci was formerly a not insignificant city among the Bastetani, according to Ptolemy’s map of Tarraconensis. Michael Villanova maintains that it was also called Aquila. It is now called Vera, near New Carthage and Muxacra. So says Ambrosius Morales in book VIII, chapter 50, and book X, chapter 32, although in the latter passage the author confuses Urci with Vergi, which were nevertheless different cities, as can be seen in Ptolemy.

Urci was in the Gulf of Ilici, near Lucena and Guadix; Vergi, however, was in the Gulf of Vergi, which received its name from that city and is now called Vera. Between the two lies the promontory of Caridemi, or Cabo de Gatas. Hence the Roman Martyrology says that Indalecius was bishop of Urci, while Tesiphon was bishop of Vergi.

Iliberri, or Iliberi, as others call it, was situated in the mountain district that we now call—after a slight alteration of the name—Elbira, or the Sierra de Elbira, two leagues from Granada, which succeeded it. So say Morales, book IX, chapter 13, and book X, chapter 32, as well as Tarapha and Villanova; Ptolemy also mentions it among the Turduli of Baetica.

In one of the books recently discovered near the Holy Mountain of Granada it is written that, when Saint James was staying near Hiberris, he taught his disciples for some time in a certain cave there. For this reason, it says, he called that place—previously called the Ilipolitan Mountain, after nearby Ilipa Magna, a town of no little importance—*Garnata*, which means “cave of instruction.” For in Hebrew *garah* means “to empty” or “to strip”; hence in Psalm 136, where we read *exinanivit* (“he emptied”), the original has *gariu*, that is, “emptiness”—and a cave is a kind of emptiness—and *nataalem* means “to teach.”

Likewise, in the Arabic language *gar* means “cave,” and *nata* means “instruction.” We, with only a slight corruption of the word, say not *Garnata* but *Granada*. We have adopted the pomegranate (*malum granatum*) in a much more corrupt form as the emblem of the kingdom of Granada, as though the name came from it, rather than from *gar* and *nata*, that is, “cave of instruction.” Bernardus Alderete learnedly noted this in his *Antiquities*, book II, chapter 24.

The Arab Rasis agrees with this account. In book III, chapter 13 of his *Destruction of Spain*, when discussing Granada, he says—according to the old Spanish translation of his work:

> “The Castle of Granada, which they call the Town of the Jews, is the oldest town there is in the territory of Elbira, and the Jews settled it.”

That is, Saint James’s disciples and the ancient Christians settled it. Baronius splendidly demonstrates that Christians were once likewise called Jews, in volume I of the *Annals*. Dion Cassius had already made this clear in express words, book XXXVII of his *Roman History*, year 691, saying:

> “Not only are the true Jews called Jews, but also other people”—he had previously been speaking about the true Jews—“who live according to their statutes, although they are foreigners. There is such a class of people among the Romans also. Although it has often been diminished, with countless persons removed by martyrdom, it nevertheless grew so greatly that it overcame the power of the laws.”

Caecilius was the first bishop of that city, and I shall now speak of him.

There was also another city of the same name in Spain, but far removed from it, situated among the Indigetes, at the foot of the Pyrenees and on the Mediterranean coast. Even today it retains the name Eliberis, being called Colibre; it was first called Eliberis and later Caucoliberis.

Carthage Spartaria was so called from the abundance of *spartum*—esparto grass—that grew in its territory. This name distinguished it not only from Carthage in Africa but also from another city of the same name in Spain, situated between Tarragona and Lérida among the Hercaones, which Ptolemy also mentions. It was called Old Carthage. Spartaria, however, was called New Carthage, and Ptolemy places it among the Contestani.

Saint Indalecius is also said to have preached at Eliocrota. This city was a bishop’s see even in the time of Constantine the Great. For in the division of the dioceses and assignment of all the sees then existing in Spain under five metropolitan bishops, Eliocrota was made subject to the see of Toledo, as can be seen in Lucas of Tuy when he discusses King Wamba, and in Ambrosius Morales, book X of his *History of Spain*, chapter 32.

At the Council of Iliberri, Bishop Successus of Eliocrota subscribed, as did Liberatus, his presbyter. [Col. 0172A] I have found nothing in the authors about the location of this place. If conjecture may be permitted, I would believe that it was Valladolid or stood in its territory. Constantine seems to place it there, not far from Segovia and Palencia, forming almost a triangle with them.

The dioceses of the metropolitan see of Toledo, arranged according to the Constantinian order, are:

1. New Carthage  
2. Oretum  
3. Castulo  
4. Mentesa  
5. Acci  
6. Basta  
7. Vergi  
8. Ilice  
9. Valencia  
10. Saetabis  
11. Valeria  
12. Dianium  
13. Segobriga  
14. Ercabria  
15. Seguntia  
16. Uxama  
17. Segovia  
18. Palencia  
19. Eliocrota

Among these, Carthage was placed first because of its dignity and merits. The next three, in the same order, were situated among the Oretani; the next ten, from Acci to Ercabica, were in Baetica, in approximately the order in which they are listed; the remainder were in Old Castile.

Since Eliocrota is assigned a position almost bordering on Segovia and Palencia, it does not appear that it could have been situated anywhere except in the territory of Valladolid. This is especially so because Valladolid seems to have been named from *Valle Aelicia*, or “Valley of Elius,” which is the first part of the name Eliocrota, or Aeliocrota.

To those who believe that Valladolid was formerly called Pintia, we reply that many other cities in Spain also had two names. Ptolemy, who listed Pintia, therefore omitted Eliocrota, although he did not suppress the name of another famous city. Let this, however, be regarded as conjecture. For I see that Antoninus Pius places Eliocrota twenty-five thousand paces from Carthage, on the road to Castulo. Consult Vasaeus, *Chronicle of Spain*, chapter 20. Nevertheless, it may have been another town of the same name.

### 2. Whom Clarus, etc.

In the printed text of Dexter there had entered an error whereby the reading was *Clarus and Clerus*, as though they were two persons, rather than one and the same Clerus, whom others call Clarus. Peter Equilinus discusses his martyrdom in book XII, chapter 130, no. 34. He says that Clerus suffered on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, that is, January 14. He makes him, however, the companion of Saint Euphrasius, not of Saint Indalecius, saying:

> “Euphrasius the bishop and Clerus the deacon suffered on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February.”

Nevertheless, since Euphrasius too preached throughout the territory of Carthage, Clerus could have been the companion of both and finally suffered martyrdom together with Euphrasius. I shall now discuss Euphrasius.

### 3. Euphrasius, etc.

His particular see was the distinguished city of Iliturgi, whose ruins can still be seen above Andújar, one league away, at the confluence of the Baetis, or Guadalquivir. It is now called Andújar el Viejo, for the new Andújar succeeded it. So says Ambrosius Morales in his *Antiquities*, under “Iliturgi,” fol. 57; he proves it splendidly from Pliny, who says the same in book VI, chapter 1.

Accordingly, Carolus Clusius, cited by Ortelius, is mistaken when he maintains that Iliturgi was Aldea del Río. Ptolemy also did not call it Ilurgi among the Turduli, since Iliturgi was only among the Contestani, where Cartagena also lies, as we likewise infer from Plutarch’s *Life of Scipio*. Villanova was also mistaken in identifying it with Lora and saying that Pliny called it Forum Julium.

The territory of Saint Euphrasius’s preaching extended from Iliturgi to Assotum, which Ptolemy and Pliny call Asso. It was above the Contestani, among the Bastetani, according to Ptolemy. As Dexter notes below, in the year of the Lord 100, in his time the name had begun to be pronounced in a somewhat corrupted form as Erotus.

Saint Euphrasius was killed on January 14, the day on which Usuard and the Roman Martyrology commemorate him. An error entered the Roman Martyrology when it says that he was killed in Africa, although Usuard and Equilinus refrain from naming the city and province of his martyrdom. This is correct, for the Euphrasius under discussion on that day had Clerus the deacon as his companion, as can be seen in Equilinus and as we have already said; but this Euphrasius was a disciple of Saint James, killed in Spain.

During that memorable disaster inflicted on Spain by the Moors, Christians carried his relics to Galicia in the year of the Lord 714, to a place called Valdeomao, where there is now the priory of the monastery of Saint Julian of Samos, of the order of Saint Benedict.

On the stone placed over Saint Euphrasius’s tomb are carved a staff, a mitre, a crown, and a palm. The first two signs indicate dignity, while the latter two indicate martyrdom. His head is reverently preserved in the monastery.

Moreover, in the year 1596, by order of Philip II, Catholic King, the blessed man’s tomb was opened on May 15. A portion of the holy remains was given to the king for the monastery of Saint Lawrence at the Escorial, and another portion to the city of Andújar, which desired the relics of its apostle. Therefore, the following inscription was placed on the stone as a testimony for posterity:

> “In this sacred tomb are contained the bones of the blessed Euphrasius. A portion of them, exhumed by royal command and at the humble request of Philip II, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June in the year 1596, left behind for posterity, through its wonderful fragrance, an unquestionable testimony concerning itself.”

### 4. Caecilius, etc.

All the Martyrologies, and all who discuss the seven disciples of Saint James, declare that he was the first bishop of Iliberri.

Recently, a considerable number of books were found under the name of Saint Caecilius, bishop and disciple of Saint James, on the Holy Mountain of Granada. They were written in characters on lead plates. Among them are:

- *On the Excellence and Miracles of Christ the Lord and His Mother, from the Incarnation of the Word to the Ascension*, book I;
- *On the Supreme Providence, Mercy, and Justice Which God Exercised in the Work of the Incarnation*, books II;
- *On the Angelic Nature*, book I;
- *On Punishment and Glory*, book I;
- *On the Life, Pilgrimage, and Miracles of Saint James*, book I.

Add to these the plainly miraculous commentaries that he composed on the prophecies of Saint John. They were found in the upper part of the uninhabitable tower of Turpiana in the year 1595. They were written not in Hebrew, Greek, or Latin, but in the common Spanish language that we now use after so many and such extensive changes in vocabulary.

Lest anyone suppose that this was the fraud of some impostor, the bishop of Granada, acting as an apostolic judge, received a formal legal deposition. In it prudent and learned men swore that, having seen the place—or tower—in which these commentaries were found, and having examined the antiquity of the characters and plates on which they were written, they were without doubt extremely ancient writings. At the very least, they surpassed by many hundreds of years the perfection, purity, and refinement of the language in which they were written—namely, the Spanish that we use now, at the time of their discovery.

Saint Caecilius therefore wrote in a language that did not yet exist. The claim made by some that this very language may already have been in use among the Spaniards at that time is asserted without foundation. For from royal privileges, ancient histories, and the old Spanish laws enacted in former times, it is clear that the farther any Spanish writing stands from our own, the harsher, more obscure, and less pure our language was. Consequently, the vernacular used by the Spaniards in Saint Caecilius’s time would have differed much more from the language we use today than the vernacular of two or three hundred years ago did. This is especially clear because experience shows that the language itself is constantly altered by continuous and new changes in vocabulary.

I shall give some of his words as an object of wonder and as an example. He interpreted the text of Saint John’s prophecy partly in prose and partly in meters of various kinds, beginning with this heroic line:

> “The age of light has begun.”

In his preface he says:

> “Then I translated it into the common Spanish language, and by this we did not corrupt either the phrasing or the secret manner, both of the Hebrew and of the Greek in which it was written. No one will understand its true meaning and commentary, made by the servants of God, except the one whom He wills, and at the appointed time and not before, so that the princes may be warned.”

Later, speaking about the doctrine of the Gospel, he adds:

> “Which belongs to us through the mercy of God.”

Finally, he signs himself:

> “Caecilius, bishop of Granada.”

What, then, must be said? Certainly, in him the promise of Christ the Lord recorded in the final chapter of Mark was fulfilled literally concerning those who would believe in Him: “They will speak in new tongues.” He not only promises that they will speak languages they had not previously known, but also new languages. What, however, is a new language if not one that did not previously exist? A language already in use among some people cannot be called new.

Whether anyone besides Caecilius spoke in new languages is not known to me, nor does this seem necessary for the truth of the promise. The same applies to what Christ said to His disciples in Matthew 9: “If you say to this mountain, ‘Move from here and throw yourself into the sea,’ it will happen”; and to what Paul says in 1 Corinthians 13: “If I have all faith, so that I can move mountains.” We read that this was fulfilled in one wonder-worker.

Certainly, those who received the Holy Spirit in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 10, are not said to have spoken in new languages, but merely in languages: “They were speaking in languages and magnifying God.” On Pentecost the apostles likewise are said to have spoken only in the languages of those who heard them: “We hear them speaking in our own languages the great works of God” (Acts 2).

Indeed, in Paul’s very extended discussion with the Corinthians—1 Corinthians 12, 13, and 14—about the gift of tongues, he never mentions new languages. Unless perhaps someone applies to new languages Paul’s statement in chapter 14: “The one who speaks in a language does not speak to men but to God.” Yet this does not seem necessary for interpreting the text.

Whatever may be said about the rest, this much is clear to us concerning Saint Caecilius: he prophesied at least in the Spanish language, long before it had been formed by the agreement of the Spaniards—a claim that certainly cannot be demonstrated concerning other vernacular languages.

There are nevertheless still some who object to this Caecilian interpretation of Saint John’s prophecy. They say it could not have been made by Saint Caecilius, since the Apocalypse, or prophecy, was revealed to the Apostle John and written by him in the fourteenth year of Domitian Caesar, which was the year of Christ 97, as Cardinal Baronius proves from Saint Jerome’s testimony under that year. But the blessed Caecilius had already suffered martyrdom forty years earlier, namely in the second year of Nero and the year of Christ 57.

These considerations are by no means obstacles to what has been said. To say nothing of Epiphanius of Salamis, Arethas, Andrew of Caesarea, and several other Greeks who asserted that John wrote the Apocalypse in the first year of Nero—that is, before Saint Caecilius’s death, as can be seen in Sixtus of Siena, book VII of the *Holy Library*—and to set aside the fact that it would have been no more difficult for the prophetic Spirit to teach Saint Caecilius about the future Apocalypse than about a future language and a new manner of writing, which leaves room for Caecilius’s commentary to have been composed before the Apocalypse was written, without any difficulty, especially since it is established that Saint Caecilius showed the prophecy or commentaries to none of his disciples, and at that time spoke to God alone, not to men, as Paul says—to set these matters aside, since they entirely weaken the objection, there can be no doubt that the prophecy commented on by Saint Caecilius was not the Apocalypse of Saint John but a very different one.

For in it are read several things about the future Muhammad, the destroyer of the world, and about the devastation of Spain under his followers. Since these were translated word for word by Saint Caecilius from a Hebrew text into the Spanish language, they produce a less polished form of expression.

The prophecy says:

> “When six centuries have passed since his Advent, because of the grave sins that will be committed, darkness will rise in the eastern regions and will spread through the western regions by furious ministers who will be raised up there. Thus the light of our Sun will be eclipsed, and the temple of the Master and his Faith”—that is, of Saint James—“will suffer grave persecutions.”

He supplied the following commentary in highly polished Spanish:

> “A shortened year, nearly six hundred after the Savior, a king will come from the eastern inhabitants, a demon-possessed prophet of falsehood, because of the sins and offenses of the peoples, by permission of the most high and almighty Lord.”

This occurred around the year 644, when Muhammad invaded Spain, according to Isidore’s *Chronicle*.

Later, speaking of his followers, who nevertheless devastated Spain in the year 714, he says:

> “Lord, many peoples will come from east to west, and they will approach the maritime cities of Spain. With his darkness he will obscure the light of the holy Church, and its high citadel will suffer from the sea of this persecution. They will reach and encompass many peoples, who will be beaten down and cast aside with contempt. There will be the endurance of the saints.”

See what Bernardus Alderete wrote about this matter, worthy of so great a man, in book II, chapter 19.

Who, however, does not see that this text does not occur in the Apocalypse of Saint John? When Saint John wrote such a prophecy, or whether it belonged to another Saint John, is unclear. It is clear nevertheless that not all the writings of the apostles survive in the catalogue of authentic books.

To say nothing of the fact that all the apostles, who were certainly disciples, instructed those absent by their writings, although only a few of their letters survive, Paul himself testifies, when writing to the Colossians in chapter 4, that he had written a letter to the Laodiceans; that letter has perished, or at least was not received into the canon. I mention this because of the letter cited by Sixtus of Siena.

Moreover, if we speak of prophecies, it is certain that many things were revealed to the holy apostles concerning future disasters of the Church, such as the statement in 2 Timothy 4: “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine,” and so forth.

Paul likewise testifies that other Apocalypses had been revealed to others, in 1 Corinthians 14, in these words: “When you come together, each one has a psalm, has a teaching, has an Apocalypse, has a language.”

Indeed, Saint Isidore, in the Mass office of Saints Torquatus, Caecilius, and their companions, calls them “our prophets”:

> “Let us celebrate with devoted minds this day, beloved brothers, on which the memory of our prophets is honored.”

He therefore acknowledges that they foretold certain things to us. What those things were, the books of the Holy Mountain tell us. We shall discuss Saint Caecilius again below, under the year of the Lord 57.

### 5. Tesiphon, etc.

The Martyrologies and writers unanimously assign Tesiphon the bishopric of Vergi; only Dexter assigns him to Vergilia, which, according to Ptolemy, appears to have been a very different city.

Vergi, according to everyone, was situated on the coast of the sea that was named the Gulf of Vergi after it. This gulf extends from Vergi as far as the Scombrarian Promontory, commonly called Cabo de Palos. Vergilia, however, is placed some distance inland, among the Bassetani, at the very boundary between Tarraconensis and Baetica in Spain.

Nevertheless, if what this author says is carefully considered, it can be reconciled with the other writers. He does not, as they think, place Vergi as a city different from Vergilia, but rather identifies it with Abdera. Although many believe Abdera to be ancient Vergi, it is altogether different from it.

Indeed, even today two towns stand on the coast of Baetica, close to one another and not far from Almería. One is called Verza and the other Adera. Ptolemy therefore called Vergilia what the others called Vergi, except that he did not know its latitude accurately; for *Vegilia* means the city of Vergi.

As Morales noted in his *Antiquities*, under “Iliturgi,” fol. 56, the word *Ili* means “city.” The evidence is the many Spanish cities marked by that word: Iliberri, Ilice, Iliturgi, Ilipa, Ilipula, Ilarcurris, Ilurbida, and Ilerda, which have the element *Ili* at the beginning of their compounds. Others have it at the end, such as Bilbilis, Hispalis, Sacilis, Orcelis, Arcialis, and similar names. I believe Vergilia belongs to this group, or rather *Vergili*, so that it is the same as *Vergi-Ili*, that is, “the city of Vergi.”

These cities, I say, demonstrate that *Ili* means “city” in the language of the ancient Spaniards, because it appears in the most common compounds. We are led to the same conclusion when we believe that *Briga* meant “city” in the ancient language of Spain, since we find it in the names of numerous cities, such as Augustabriga, Deobriga, Juliobriga, Talabriga, Caetobriga, Lacobriga, and so forth.

Therefore, when Dexter says that Saint Tesiphon preached in the Baetican city of Vergilia, he means the same thing as the Martyrologies when they use the name Vergi. This city is not Abdera, although it is near it, but Werza, whose principal city is now Almería. It seems to have taken the place of ancient Vergi, so that the citizens of Almería, succeeding to the rights of the ancient Vergitani’s nobility, might also assume devotion toward their patron Tesiphon and venerate him fervently as such.

Basta and Osca—now Baza and Huéscar—also owe to Tesiphon the first foundations of their religion and faith. They were situated in Baetica, or the kingdom of Granada, not far from one another, and were noble and ancient cities.

The peoples were formerly called Bastetani from Basta, or Bassetani from Bassa, as others read. That ancient Basta is modern Baza is learnedly demonstrated by Ambrosius Morales in book X of his *History of Spain*, chapter 32.

Regarding the location of Baetican Osca, Ptolemy is mistaken when he places it among the Turditani beyond the Strait of Cádiz, since it lies this side of Granada, near Baza. There is another city of the same name in Aragon, now called Huesca. From this city came the famous martyrs Lawrence and Vincent, celebrated throughout the world; but Dexter is now speaking of the Baetican city, which is Huéscar.

One of the books found on the Holy Mountain of Granada states that Saint Tesiphon and Saint Caecilius were brothers, natives of Arabia, and that Tesiphon was called Abenathar before his conversion.

The following books were found there under the name of Tesiphon:

- *The Foundation of the Church*, in two books, written in Arabic on five lead plates;
- *On the Essence of God*, book I;
- *On the Repentance of Saint Peter*, book I;
- *On the Prayer of Saint James*, book I.

It is also read on a lead plate that, in his epitaph, he wrote another book on the purity of life and the miracles of his teacher, Saint James.]

A. C. 54. A. R. 805. Saint Indalecius is regarded as exceedingly famous in those regions, preaching at Urci, Iliberri, Carthage Spartaria, and Eliocrota.

[Col. 0171]

A. C. 54. A. R. 805. Clarus [or Clerus] the deacon accompanies him. This deacon, together with many clerics, is cruelly thrown into the sea near Carthage Spartaria, not far from the city’s harbor.

A. C. 54. A. R. 805. Euphrasius preaches fervently at Iliturgi, not far from Carthage Spartaria, among the peoples called Contestani, as far as the city of Assotum, and travels throughout the entire territory of Carthage.

[Col. 0173]

A. C. 54. A. R. 805. Caecilius preaches at Iliberri and throughout the surrounding region. He displays himself as extraordinary and advances the peoples entrusted to him in the fear of God and in faith through his teaching.

[Col. 0175]

A. C. 54. A. R. 805. Tesiphon laid the first foundations of the Christian religion in the Baetican city of Vergilia, at Basta, at Osca, and in other cities.

[Note: [Col. 0176D]]

A. C. 57.—These men of Saint James. This testimony splendidly confirms and establishes what is written on the lead plates recently discovered on the Holy Mountain of Granada; in turn, Dexter’s testimony receives strength from those plates, so that neither permits the truth of the other to be called into question.

For in the year 1594 the present Chronicle of Dexter was discovered in Germany, and an extract from the original and very ancient manuscript of the library of the monastery of Fulda was sent to Spain. In the following year, namely 1595, the monuments of the Holy Mountain of Granada were discovered. It follows that the present statement of Dexter could not have been taken by some impostor from the Granada plates, which were still lying hidden beneath the earth, and inserted into Dexter.

Likewise, since one year before the discovery of the books of that mountain Dexter spoke to the Spaniards about the ancestry, place, and year of death of certain blessed disciples of Saint James, there is no room for doubting the truth of the plates, especially in those matters in which they agree with Dexter.

Indeed, by the great kindness of God and His singular providence, it was arranged that Dexter, who had lain hidden abroad for six hundred years, should finally return to his native land and open the way for what the Granada lead plates were to reveal in the following year concerning the martyrdom of the disciples of Saint James.

But let us see what the lead tablets say. On 22 March of the aforesaid year, 1595, a tablet of Saint Iscius was discovered, containing the following:

“In the second year of Nero’s reign, on the Kalends of March, Saint Iscius, chosen for this purpose, suffered martyrdom in this place of Ilipula, together with his disciples Turillus, Panuntius, Maronius, and Centulius, through the midst of fire, in which they were burned alive. Seeking eternal life, they passed over, so that the stones were turned into lime; their ashes lie in the caverns of this holy mountain. Let them be venerated here, as reason demands, in their memory.”

In that same month of March another tablet was found, likewise of lead, containing these words:

“The burned body of the martyr Saint Mesiton. He suffered under the authority of the Emperor Nero.”

Again, on the following 10 April, in the aforesaid year, this was discovered:

“In the second year of Nero’s reign, on the Kalends of April, Saint Tesiphon—before his conversion called Abenathar—disciple of the apostle Saint James, a man endowed with learning and holiness, suffered martyrdom in this place of Ilipula. On lead tablets he wrote that book called *The Foundation of the Church*. His disciples, Saints Maximus and Luparius, suffered with him; their ashes and the book are with the ashes of the holy martyrs in the caverns of this holy mountain. Let him be venerated in their memory.”

On the following 22 April, a book was found under this title:

“Book: *The Foundation of the Church*, written in the characters of Solomon.”

And on the 25th, another by the same author, with this inscription:

“Book concerning the Essence of God, which Saint Tesiphon, disciple of the apostle Saint James, wrote in his native language, Arabic, in the characters of Solomon; and another, called *The Foundation of the Church*, which lies in the caverns of this holy mountain. May God deliver these two books from the Emperor Nero. Here he brought his works to an end, writing of the miracles and integrity of life of his Master [lacuna] in the caverns of this holy mountain [lacuna].”

Finally, on the last day of April, a lead tablet written in Latin letters—though very ancient ones—was discovered, revealing the martyrdom of Saint Caecilius. It contained the following:

“In the second year of the reign of the Emperor Nero, on the Kalends of February, Saint Caecilius, disciple of Saint James, a man endowed with learning, languages, and holiness, suffered martyrdom in this place of Ilipula. He commented upon the prophecies of Saint John, which, together with other remains, have been placed in the upper part of the uninhabitable tower of Turpiana, as his disciples Saint Septentrius and Patritius told me; they suffered with him. Their ashes lie in the caverns of this holy mountain. Let them be venerated in their memory.”

Everything stated in the tablets was immediately found; together with them, the account of Saint Patritius was discovered, showing the remarkable degree of prophecy to which his master Caecilius had attained, and how long beforehand he had foretold his own death. Among other things, he said:

“And he warned me,” he says, “to keep his book hidden and place it somewhere where it could never come into the power of the Moors, until God should wish to reveal it. And I, better than I understood, shut it up in this place where it lies, praying God to preserve it.”

I have borrowed these things from the distinguished and most learned doctor Gregorio Lupi Madera, royal councillor, in his apologetic book *For the True Antiquity of the Sacred Mountain*; from Antonio de Cianca, Book I of *The Life of Saint Secundus*, chapter 16; and from the Reverend Alderete, Book II of the *Antiquities*, chapters 10 through 25.

Now let us compare Dexter with the tablets; their agreement is remarkable. First, the tablets testify that certain disciples of Saint James suffered martyrdom on Mount Ilipula, which lies beside the city of Granada. Dexter, however, asserts that they were killed while going to the Council of Iliberris; and we have already shown above, under the year 54, that Iliberris was situated near Granada and that Granada succeeded it.

Again, both accounts affirm that they were brought to completion through fire, wonderfully arranged by God so that those whom he had first made the torches of Spain should be consummated by fire. Saint Isidore gives them this honorific title in the Gothic Breviary, where, in the third morning prayer of their feast, it is said:

“These are, Lord, the seven torches set throughout the regions of Hesperia, sent from heaven to drive away the infidelity of night from that land.”

Likewise, the year 57 of Our Lord, in which Dexter teaches that they entered the heavenly kingdoms, was the second year of Nero; for he had taken up the reins of the empire in the year of Our Lord 55, as may be seen, among others, in Ambrosio Morales, Book IX of the *History*, chapter 6. Therefore, on the Kalends of April, when the last of these disciples of the Apostle, Saint Tesiphon, was burned for Christ, Nero had not yet completed the second year of his reign.

Finally, Dexter does not say that all seven principal disciples of Saint James were burned, but only some of them. The tablets identify three: Iscius, Caecilius, and Tesiphon. Indeed, what they add concerning their disciples—that Saints Maximus, Luparius, Mesiton, Septentrius, Patritius, Turillus, Panuntius, Maronius, and Centulius were burned together with them—Dexter had not concealed in silence. For he did not merely say of the disciples of Saint James, “Stripped of their possessions, they were crowned,” but added, “of their own possessions and of all the possessions of their followers.” That is, of their disciples, who were stripped together with their masters and, dying nobly with them for the faith of Christ, were crowned.

It is fitting here to append the inscription that Alderete composed for the new and magnificent church of the Sacred Mountain of Granada, since it embraces its entire history.

**To the Most Blessed Apostle James, Son of Thunder, Patron of Spain**

Who, at the command and under the auspices of Christ Jesus, God and our Savior, and of his Virgin Mother Mary,

brought the light of faith to all Spain and illumined it with his radiance;

dwelt for several days upon this sacred Mount of Ilipula;

and in its cave established a chair and observatory of evangelical doctrine;

and also, through his most holy disciples and scribes, confidants of mysteries, Caecilius and Tesiphon, brothers from Arabia,

and Iscius,

who with immense labor cleansed the peoples of Baetica from impious superstition;

who, having received pontifical miters and being kindled by fires—though rather heavenly ones—adorned them with the triumphal laurels of martyrdom;

and likewise to the illustrious disciples of these prelates:

Patritius, Mesiton,

Septentrius,

Turillus, Panuntius, Maronius, Centulius, Maximus, and Luparius,

who, in the second year of the Emperor Nero,

together with their teachers, were cast into blazing furnaces

and in these crypts gave illustrious testimony to the faith;

whose sacred and most pure ashes, buried in these caverns,

lay unknown for more than fifteen hundred years;

but were at last, in this age, discovered by divine providence;

and with them also the leaden books, enclosed in lead and stones,

not merely intact, but, miraculously, after so many centuries, of the most recent appearance;

written with the greatest refinement in the most ancient Arabic dialect and in the characters of Solomon;

filled with many great mysteries of our faith;

while their characters, the contests of the martyrs, and the time

are likewise recorded by leaden tablets found at the same time in these caverns;

on account of these and other most august and divine gifts, before which the human mind is astonished;

and for the temple of the priests, the altars, and the adornments of this sacred mountain and its cave,

Peter de Castro Quiñones, Archbishop of Granada,

offering less than what is owed for greater and more august things,

yet, filled with devotion, consecrates and dedicates this

to their praise, honor, rightful veneration, and memory.

In the year of Our Lord 1610.

### What kind of martyrdom carried off the disciples of Saint James?

Since only three of the seven disciples of Saint James completed their martyrdom by fire, let us see what happened to the other four.

Saint Torquatus survived for another sixteen years, until the year 66 of Christ, when he too was made a martyr, as we shall say in the same place.

Saint Secundus prolonged his life until the hundredth year of Our Lord; we shall speak of him there.

We discussed the death of Saint Euphrasius under the year 54, although it is not plainly established what kind of martyrdom carried him off. Nevertheless, since Equilinus, cited there, asserts that Saint Clarus the deacon suffered with him, and since, according to Dexter’s testimony, Clarus received the crown of martyrdom by being thrown into the sea not far from Carthage Spartaria, it follows that Euphrasius too was drowned. However the matter may stand—whether he ended his life by the sword or in water—it is certain that he was eventually buried at Iliturgi, or Andújar, then transferred from there to the Valley of Omao in Galicia, and finally that part of his sacred relics was restored to his see at Iliturgi.

He is celebrated in the Church of Jaén—now Jaén, in whose diocese Andújar lies—on 18 May, the day of the translation of his relics, since his feast of death is 14 January. See what we said about him above.

Saint Indalecius lay buried near Almería, having first been honored with a noble martyrdom, until, in the year 1084, through the agency of Sancho, the first king of that name of Aragon, his sacred body was solemnly transferred to the royal monastery of Saint John of Peña on the Thursday of Passion Week. The king named above, his son Peter, Infante of Aragon, and Saint Sancho, abbot of Peña, were present. Zurita recounts the history of this event in Part I of the *Annals of Aragon*, Book I, chapter 27.

The metropolitan see of Burgos celebrates Saint Indalecius’s feast on 30 April; the Church of Almería, on 23 March. It is therefore clear that one celebrates the feast of his death and the other that of his translation.

Formerly they were celebrated under the title and office of Confessors and Pontiffs, since we read nothing concerning their martyrdom either in the Roman Martyrology, in Usuard’s or Ado’s Martyrology, or in Bede, Saint Isidore, or Equilinus. But after—by God’s will—the sacred relics of our apostles were discovered near the Granada mountain and recognized by the authority of the Supreme Pontiff, all Spain thereafter venerates and celebrates them as martyrs.

This is attested by that book printed every year at Madrid, entitled *The Order for Reciting the Divine Office*. There, in the section concerning the saints of the Church of Compostela, we read:

15 May: Torquatus, bishop, and his fellow martyrs, double office.

But in the Church of Guadix:

15 May: Torquatus, bishop and martyr, double office of the first class, with octave.

In the Church of Granada:

1 February: Caecilius, bishop, martyr, and patron, double office of the first class.

And on 1 March:

Iscius, bishop, and his martyred disciples, double office of the second class.

And on 1 April:

Tesiphon, bishop, and his martyred disciples, double office of the second class.

In the Church of Burgos, on 30 April:

Indalecius, bishop and martyr, double office.

In the Church of Ávila, on 2 May:

Secundus, bishop and martyr, first class, with octave.

Finally, in the Church of Jaén, on 18 May:

Euphrasius, bishop and martyr, double office of the first class, with octave.

Moreover, testimony to the martyrdom of these disciples of Blessed James was given not only by Dexter and the lead tablets of Granada, but also many years ago by Gregory VII, Roman Pontiff, in a letter to King Alfonso, dated 19 March, in the twelfth indiction, where he says that seven bishops had been sent from the city of Rome by the apostles to instruct the peoples of Spain; that, after destroying idolatry, they founded Christianity and planted the faith, showed the order and office of divine worship, and dedicated churches with their blood, and so forth.

Cardinal Baronius also quotes these words in his notes on 15 May in the Roman Martyrology.

**A.D. 57. A.R. 808.** Some of these disciples of Saint James, while traveling to the Council of Iliberris under Alotus, Nero’s judge, were burned by the flames; stripped of their own possessions and of all those belonging to their followers, they died nobly and were crowned for the faith of Christ.

[Note: A.D. 60.—1. “Many,” etc. The fact that Nero’s persecution began in Spain in the year 57, or the second year of his reign, is amply confirmed by what we have just said concerning the martyrdom of Saints Caecilius, Tesiphon, and Iscius and their companions. That the persecution raged not merely in one place or another, or in one city, but throughout Spain, and that by its force such a slaughter of martyrs occurred, and so innumerable a multitude of Christians were removed from the midst of the living by martyrdom, that it was believed that the entire religion had everywhere been extinguished and utterly destroyed—this is attested by that stone, or marble column, which was erected at Clunia Colonia, that is, Coruña del Conde, by Nero’s ministers. It is cited by Aldus Manutius in his *Orthography*, by Ambrosio Morales, Book IX of the *History*, chapter 17, and by Baronius under the year 69 of Christ; and first by Cyril of Anchona.

**To Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus, Pontifex Maximus,**

**because he cleansed the province of robbers and of those who inculcated—or had inculcated—a new superstition upon the human race.**

Do not suppose that only this one monument was then erected under such an inscription, but that there were many; for Aldus likewise reports that another was found among the ruins of the town of Maramezar.

It is highly probable that, later, when the Catholic Church had suppressed and overcome idolatry, Christians broke all these monuments and adapted them to other uses, so that trophies erected against the Church might not remain. But by God’s highest providence it happened that some of them were eventually found, so that they might become witnesses to those most blessed martyrs who planted the faith of Christ in Spain with their blood, and who were seized in so immeasurably great a number that the impious believed the province had been completely cleansed of Christians. This is what the words “because he cleansed the province of those who had inculcated a new superstition upon the human race” indicate.

Cardinal Baronius rightly observed at this point:

“Consider from these things how exceedingly fierce Nero’s persecution was, so that it was believed that the Christian religion had been completely rooted out by him.”

And again:

“From these things, learned reader, you may also infer that the Church of Spain was flourishing exceedingly at this time, when the impious regarded it as some immense benefit conferred by Nero that he had purged that province of Christians.”

Dexter notes the cities that abounded in the greater number of martyrs, since they were then more populous, and consequently persecution burned more fiercely in them.

Euphrasius, a disciple of Saint James, fell as a martyr at Iliturgi, or Andújar—or was condemned to death there and sent into the sea near Carthage. At Iliberris were the three distinguished disciples of the same apostle, Caecilius, Tesiphon, and Iscius, together with the companions enumerated above.

Likewise, Saint Athanasius, the first bishop of that see and of the Church of the Virgin Mother of God of the Pillar, was crowned with martyrdom at Zaragoza. His martyrdom occurred in the year 59 of Christ, that is, the third year of Nero’s persecution. I take this from M. Maximus, who adds at the end of an epigram composed in his honor:

“He died near Zaragoza in the year 59. He is celebrated on 1 November.”

He is said to have died near Zaragoza because he was led out of the city to be struck with the sword. The same Maximus admits that he was taken away by martyrdom in a Sapphic hymn concerning the first three bishops of Zaragoza, where he says:

I praise you first, holy Athanasius,

and you, outstanding Theodore, in song;

no less worthy of our odes,

bishop Epitectus.

The Iberus himself sees the third and the first

suffer bravely; but the second

sowing bright seed through the Libyan regions,

in sacred Cyrene.

When he says that the first of the named bishops suffered bravely beside the Iberus, he means Athanasius, since he was killed near Zaragoza. We shall discuss Theodore and Epitectus in their proper places.

Concerning the martyrs who suffered at Tarragona at that time, I have nothing particular to say, although there can be no doubt that the persecutor’s savagery especially thirsted for and poured out Christian blood there, in so illustrious a city that much of Spain had taken the name “Tarraconensis” from it as a province, and where Saint Agathodorus had sown the seeds of the divine word.

I would say the same concerning the city of Seville, over which Saint Pius presided with distinction, himself also, together with Agathodorus, one of the first disciples of Saint James. But although the memory of the martyrs of Seville under Nero has been obliterated, this is not so with those of Italica, not far from Seville, who are believed to have been brought forth in the faith under the same bishop Pius.

I received the history of these illustrious martyrs from the account which Jeremias, Patriarch of Constantinople, translated from Greek into Latin in the year of Our Lord 1580, and gave, together with the relics of Saint Photina, the evangelical Samaritan woman, to the ambassador of the Emperor Rudolf III. Adam Dietrichstein, the emperor’s chamberlain, received it from him and, through Don Juan de Borja, ambassador of Philip II the Catholic King to the aforesaid Rudolf, sent it as a gift to the most serene Empress Maria, who was living at Madrid in the royal monastery of the Discalced Virgins.

In that history it is asserted that the Samaritan woman, whose name was Photina, had five sisters—Anatolia, Photis, Photide, Parasceve, and Cyriaca—and two sons: Joseph, who accompanied her in the ministry of the Gospel, and Victor, who was especially favored by Nero on account of his outstanding military skill, which had shone forth particularly in the war fought against the Avars in Scythia. For this reason the same emperor sent him to Spain as supreme and general commander of the army stationed at Italica.

The author recounts in the following words what miracles Victor performed at Italica and how he drew the Spanish commander Sebastian to the faith—like another Ananias leading a second Saul—together with a great multitude of citizens. I have thought it fitting to set them down verbatim, to revive the memory of such great deeds and for the benefit of Dexter, who writes here concerning the martyrs of Seville under Nero.

At the time when Nero, king of the Romans, had stirred up a great persecution against the Christians, Saint Photina was preaching the Gospel of Christ at Carthage in Africa together with her son Joseph, and with her was her elder son Victor, who had conducted himself most bravely in the war that the Romans had waged against the Avars, a most savage people of Scythia.

It happened that Victor was sent at that time by the king to Italica to assume the office of supreme commander of the army, with the additional duty of investigating and persecuting any Christians whom he might find there.

While he was staying there, another commander approached him, named Sebastian, and said:

“I know, commander, that you are a Christian and, together with your mother and your brother Joseph, a follower of Peter. I beg you to carry out the king’s command and will, lest you perhaps endanger your life.”

Victor replied:

“I ardently desire to fulfill the will of the superheavenly and immortal King. But what Nero has commanded me concerning the persecution of Christians I cannot hear without grief.”

Sebastian answered:

“I advise you as a dearest friend: if at this most favorable time you search out the Christians and put to death those brought in for examination, you will enjoy both exceptional royal favor and their riches. I would also advise you to send letters to your mother and brother, so that they may not speak so freely and publicly, zealously urging the Greeks to abandon their ancient religion; lest you too suffer with them the cruel and inglorious death which would undoubtedly be inflicted upon you. But if such cruelty delights you, it would be better to keep the matter secret and not make it public.”

Victor answered:

“May God never permit me to plot any evil against the Christians, to take away their riches, or to advise my mother or brother not to preach the power and divinity of Christ. Indeed, I too am his herald, and I glory in this no less than they glory in it.”

The commander said:

“I have certainly given you the advice most advantageous to you; you must decide for yourself.”

With these words, he suddenly lost his sight and, overcome by immense burning and pain in his eyes, fell to the ground and became speechless. Those present carried him home and laid him on a bed, where he lay silent for three full days.

When they had passed, he cried out loudly:

“There is one God of the Christians.”

Victor entered and said to him:

“Where has this sudden change come from?”

“Christ is calling me,” he replied, “most beloved Victor.”

Therefore, without delay, he was catechized and admitted to baptism, with which he also recovered his sight, and he gave thanks to God for such great gifts. When the Italicenses saw this miracle, they feared that something similar might happen to them if they persisted in their unbelief, and they were baptized.

When Nero eventually learned that Victor, general of the army at Italica, and Sebastian, likewise commander of that city, were preaching the teaching of Peter and Paul and bringing everyone to Christ, and that Photina, the mother of the same general, together with her son Joseph, had abandoned her ancestral sect and was sowing the same faith at Carthage, he was moved by intense anger. He sent soldiers to Italica to bring before him for punishment any Christians of either sex whom they could find.

Then the Lord appeared to all those gathered together, so that they might become more courageous in undertaking martyrdom for his love, and he said:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; and do not fear, for I am with you. Nero, however, will perish with his followers.”

And to Victor he said:

“From now on you shall be called Photinus—that is, ‘illustrious’—because many enlightened by you have come to the knowledge of me; and your word strengthened Sebastian to endure martyrdom. Blessed is the one who fights to the end.”

After saying these things, he was again received into heaven, and he revealed to Photina whatever she would have to endure.

The author continues by relating how Victor and his companions were brought to Rome and examined by Nero concerning the faith they held in Christ; and how his mother Photina, with her son Joseph and her five sisters—Anatolia, Photis, Photide, Parasceve, and Cyriaca—flew willingly to martyrdom and presented themselves before the emperor. They endured all the most grievous and innumerable torments with joyful courage.

First they were thrust into a most terrible prison; then they were placed for three full days in a burning furnace, from which they were extracted unharmed. They were given poison once and again; molten lead and resin were poured into Photina’s mouth and into the ears of the others without harming them; they were repeatedly beaten with ox-hide thongs; with iron combs they were suspended high by the head, their flesh torn away; and they were burned with unknown torches applied to the sides of the martyrs.

Finally, their eyes were torn out, and they were again taken to a prison swarming with venomous creatures, where they were expected to die miserably without food or medicine. But when they were suffused there with the light and vision of Christ, they were restored to their former health and given back the use of their eyes; they were refreshed by miraculous food for three months and an equal number of days. Again they were brought to a new contest, once more savagely mangled with scourges, and at last, after their skin had been stripped off, they were cut into pieces and, with their heads severed, received the most glorious palm of martyrdom.

Photina alone was excepted: she was thrown into an old cistern and then drawn out again; kneeling, she surrendered her undefiled spirit to God on 20 March, the day on which both Latins and Greeks celebrate her annual memorial.

I do not regret having said these things concerning the martyrs of Italica. Anyone who says that some of them were killed at Italica and others—that is, the nobler ones—suffered at Rome will not, in my judgment, depart from the truth. For it would not easily have been possible to bring the entire city to Rome; nor could it have happened otherwise than that many were brought there by the soldiers whom Nero had instructed—as we have said—to bring before him not only Victor and Sebastian but as many followers of Christ, whether men or women, as they could find there.

As for what Dexter adds concerning Nero’s persecution—that it burned not only in the cities of Seville, Iliturgi, Iliberris, Tarragona, and Zaragoza, but also in the provinces of Lusitania, Baetica, and Carpetania—the reason must be believed to be that more followers of evangelical truth, and consequently more martyrs, necessarily had to be found where more preachers of the divine word had shone forth.

In Lusitania there were Saints Peter and Basil, bishops of Braga and disciples of Saint James, and Saint Epitatius, bishop of Tui.

In Baetica there was Saint Pius of Seville, together with the seven others—Torquatus, Caecilius, Tesiphon, and their companions.

In Carpetania there were Saint Elpidius, bishop of Toledo, and Saint Athanasius of Zaragoza, together with Saint Theodore, archpriest, concerning whom Dexter had written above under the year 50:

“They travel throughout all Carpetania preaching and teaching.”

M. Maximus also sang of this in his epigram for Saint Athanasius:

“Throughout the regions of the Carpetanians he scatters the sacred seeds.”

Add to this that the people of Carpetania sent an embassy to Peter on behalf of sending the apostle James to Spain. From this alone it is credible that innumerable worshipers of Christ existed in that province in Nero’s time, whom the Church triumphant in heaven received among her own after they had been tested by persecution and redeemed with the laurel of martyrdom.

Finally, what else does the Nero column mentioned above, found at Clunia on the border of Carpetania, indicate except that so many Christians were killed there that, although they were almost innumerable, the province was nevertheless believed to have been cleansed of them?

### 2. At the same time, etc.

The Roman Martyrology commemorates these holy bishops and martyrs on 4 March, in the reading, with these words:

“At Chersonesus, the passion of the holy bishops Basil, Eugenius, Agathodorus, Elpidius, Capito, Ephraem, Nestor, and Arcadius.”

It does not, however, specify the locations of their sees or of their martyrdom. For although it says that they suffered at Chersonesus, the place of their martyrdom is not thereby sufficiently made clear. Ptolemy assigns seventeen Chersonesi, in Sicily, Sardinia, and Crete, in the Peloponnese, and elsewhere repeatedly. Thus one sees that not only Tauric, Cimbrian, and Thracian regions are so called, but almost any tract of land surrounded by the sea in the manner of an island.

For in Greek *Chersonesus*—or *Cherronesus*, as some pronounce it—means in Latin “near-island” or “peninsula.” It is not an island, since it is not entirely surrounded by the sea, although it falls only a little short of being so surrounded.

From Dexter alone we learn which cities these men governed, in what period they flourished, under whose instruction they were taught, and, finally, in what city they underwent martyrdom.

There is, near Valencia, a city called by ancient and modern writers *Peninsula* in Latin and, in a slightly more corrupt form, *Peñíscola* in Spanish. I find it called *Chersonesus* by Strabo in Book III of the *Geography*, situated above Valencia not far from ancient Saguntum, in the true location of our Peñíscola. Mariana, Book XII, chapter 17, recognizes both of its names. Speaking of the victories of King James, he says:

“Several other towns and fortresses in that region maintained their existence, and necessarily submitted to the king’s authority; above all, Peñíscola, which Ptolemy calls Cherronesus.”

He should have said “Strabo,” for Ptolemy does not mention it.

The same author, in Book XX, the final chapter, calls it *Peninsula*. Hieronymus Zurita was also speaking of the same James in Book I of *Indian Affairs Conducted by the Kings of Aragon* when he said:

“In the year 1225, on the Kalends of October, the king invaded the enemy’s territory and besieged Peñíscola, a town of the Ilergaones. Its situation is such that, being set upon a rock, it is almost surrounded by the sea; hence it acquired its common name.”

From this it appears that the Greeks also called it Cherronesus for that reason.

Bernardino Miedes, bishop of Albarracín, continually calls it *Peninsula*, as may be seen in a thousand passages of Book V.

Marinaeus Siculus, Book II of *Spanish Affairs*, speaking of Benedict XIII, who ended his days there, says:

“Having given this answer, he pushed the oars and withdrew to the Peninsula, that is, the little island called Peñíscola, near Valencia.”

From this you can see that no grounds for doubt concerning the place of martyrdom remain.

The Greeks also celebrate their feast in the *Menologion*, but on the seventh day of the same month, not the fourth as the Latins do. From them Galefinus transferred the following words into his Martyrology:

“7 March. In Greece, the holy bishops and martyrs Basil, Ephraem, Chariton, Eugenius, Aetherius, and the others, who, tortured in Chersonesus and finally drenched with blood, gave illustrious testimony to the Christian faith.”

It is characteristic of this author to preface the saints whom he borrows from the Greeks with the words “in Greece.” He thought that whenever the *Menologion* failed to assign a place or province, it thereby meant that the martyrdom had occurred in Greece. Since the *Menologion* itself does not assert this, however, the phrase is improperly added.

The Greeks frequently celebrate the feast of saints without assigning their city; this occurs especially with saints who lived at a considerable distance from the Greeks themselves. This one circumstance—particularly important for understanding this *Chronicle*—is why the sees of these ten holy bishops are not assigned in the *Menologion*, nor is the particular Chersonesus in which they were martyred specified.

For those who flourished within Greece, or throughout the East, always have the place of their see and death expressly stated, since these were easily known to the Greeks themselves. But in the case of those who died for the faith in distant regions, the place is very often omitted, since it was not known to them at all.

Because Spain was the limit of the ancient world and lay farther from the Greeks than other lands, it happened that the feasts of the Spanish saints were placed in the *Menologion* without a definite city or region. Yet if those saints had been Greek, the Greeks would by no means have omitted such information.

For this reason, when the Roman Martyrology speaks of them, it too omits their cities and provinces, since it borrowed their feasts and names from the Greek *Menologion*, which itself lacked them.

Why the memory of these saints perished in Spain, where they had flourished, is easy to explain: no one is unaware of the calamities and devastations that Spain often endured. But thanks be to God that, through Dexter’s return from oblivion, we may apply to him what Cicero said to Varro in Book I of the *Academica*:

“We, wandering and straying in our own city like strangers and guests, were led home by your books, so that at last we might learn who and where we were. You disclosed the age of our fatherland, the descriptions of times, the laws of sacred things, the offices of priests, domestic discipline, military discipline, the locations of regions, the names, duties, and causes of all divine and human things.”

And so that the citizens of Toledo, Seville, and the other cities may know which saints governed them and may honor their patrons, let them not be reluctant to observe with what reverence the Greeks have hitherto celebrated our martyrs in their *Menologion*.

The name of Saint Pius, bishop and martyr of Seville, is absent from the Roman Martyrology. Nevertheless, Pelagius of Oviedo and Hugh of Portugal mention him together with the other companions whose names we discussed above, and before them Saint Caledonius of Braga mentioned him in the *Life of Saint Peter of Rates*.

The statement that they were killed while assembling for the Council is sufficiently and clearly deduced from the fact that ten bishops were martyred together. It does not seem otherwise possible that men separated throughout all Spain could have been killed at the same time unless they had assembled for a Council.

The location of the Council also indicates the time of the most savage persecution. For this reason they withdrew to a very remote place, and to the Peninsula itself, where they could become more secure and attend to the peace and advancement of the afflicted Church of Spain. But by divine providence the crown of martyrdom found them precisely where they seemed for a time to be avoiding it.

I have suspected that Alotus, Nero’s judge under whom these holy martyrs suffered, was that Aulus surnamed Caecina, quaestor of Baetica under Nero, whom Cornelius Tacitus discusses, and after him Morales in Book IX of the *History*, chapters 17 and 20. He was one of the first who, at New Carthage, enthroned Galba against Nero.

It would have been easy for someone to read *Alotus* or *Aulotus* where the name was *Aulus* or *Aulon*.

Josephus, in his *Life*, speaks of Aliturus, who was dear to Nero; but he was Jewish by birth and an author of mimes, not a quaestor or judge, and it cannot be shown that he ever went to Spain.

Nevertheless, there certainly was another Alotus—or Halotus—one of the eunuchs of Claudius Caesar, who, at Agrippina’s urging, administered the poison to him so that Nero might rule. Tacitus mentions him in Book XIII of the *Annals*.

As a reward for this service, Alotus was sent to Spain and appointed quaestor at the beginning of Nero’s reign.

### 3. “Augustus, Tiberius, etc.”

Dexter runs through the succession of emperors, beginning with Octavian Augustus, in whose reign Christ the Lord was born, and continuing to Nero, who was reigning in those days. The name Caius was missing from the printed Zaragoza manuscript, but I restored it from the manuscripts. Augustus died in the sixteenth year of Christ, as Epiphanius testifies in the *Ancoratus*. Tiberius succeeded him and reigned twenty-two and a half years; he died in the year of the Lord 39. Caius Caligula succeeded him and completed almost four years in power, until he was killed in the year of Christ 43. After him Claudius Drusus Germanicus ruled the world for thirteen years and eight months, until his death in the year of the Lord 56. Claudius Nero then succeeded him and reigned until the year of the Lord 69, as we shall say in its proper place. Dio Cassius, Suetonius, Tacitus, and the other historians of the Roman emperors agree on these points; Cardinal Baronius followed them.

[Col. 0186C]

### 4. “An earthquake, etc.”

Know that this was borrowed from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, where we read: “In the year of the Lord 60, an earthquake occurred at Rome, and an eclipse of the sun.”

### 5. “Luparia was alive, etc.”

We demonstrated above that there were two women named Luparia, one Galician and the other Baetican, under the years 42 and 43. The holiness of the Baetican Luparia is attested splendidly by Saint Isidore in the hymn of Saint Torquatus and his companions in the Gothic Breviary, where she is repeatedly called holy:

> This is the first path of faith for the peoples;
>
> among them the holy woman Luparia,
>
> approaching the saints, sees them and entreats them,
>
> storing the saints’ admonitions in her heart.

And farther on:

> There the holy woman of God is washed;
>
> washed in the bath of life, she is reborn.

In the Mass of these same saints, the priest reads the following prayers before the Lord’s Prayer:

> Behold, dearly beloved brothers, raise your eyes with me on high, asking this special favor from the Lord: that he who was graciously pleased suddenly to illumine the heart of blessed Luparia with the grace of Christian faith may at this moment also graciously and effectively cleanse us from every stain of sin. Let us cry out to you from the earth and say:
>
> Our Father, etc.

[Col. 0186D]

### 6. “Regulus, etc.”

Consult what we noted from the ancient Breviaries of Spain and from Peter, bishop of Equilinum, concerning the conversion of this Regulus under the year of the Lord 42. Dexter now adds that he advanced so far in faith that, abandoning everything and withdrawing into solitude, he lived a holy life in a sacred grove.

[Col. 0187A]

### 7. “Saint Martial, etc.”

The emperor Domitian is said to have reached such cruelty and madness that he reproduced among Christians the ancient story of Laureolus, in order to provide the Roman people with extraordinary spectacles enacted in real life. The poets considered Laureolus a most wicked brigand; for that reason he was crucified and torn apart by a bear. This story was represented several times in spectacles at Rome, once indeed by Lentulus, whom Dexter will mention below under the year 86 and whom Juvenal also mentions:

> Swift Lentulus also performed Laureolus well:
>
> in my judgment, he was worthy of a real cross.

Thus what was represented only figuratively on the stage, Domitian enacted literally in the martyrs; and Nero had done the same before him, as we shall now see. Martial therefore mocks them, in order to please the pagans, in Epigram 9 before Book I:

> As Prometheus, banished to the Scythian cliff,
>
> fed an ever-present bird upon his snow-white [or: living] breast,
>
> so he exposed his naked breast to the Caledonian bear,
>
> Laureolus hanging upon no false cross.

As if he had said: “This new Laureolus reproduces the story of the ancient one; yet he does not hang upon a false cross, merely in representation, but has truly been fastened to a cross.”

Martial adds:

> His limbs lived, mangled, with their members dripping,
>
> [behold the slaughter of a martyr]
>
> and nowhere in his whole body was there a body whole.

He then imputes crimes to the martyr:

> In the end, that guilty man had suffered the punishment of death
>
> for murdering his father,
>
> or, guilty, had pierced his master’s throat with a sword;
>
> or, madman, had plundered temples of their hidden gold,
>
> or had set cruel torches beneath you, Rome.

[Col. 0187C]

Yet it is clear that the man in question had committed none of these acts; no definite crime is charged against him, but one or another of the following is alleged: parricide, the murder of his master, temple robbery, or finally the burning of the city of Rome. From this one point it becomes evident that the martyr of whom the poet speaks was one of those upon whom Nero fastened the charge of having burned the city—although he himself had set it on fire. This is what Martial means:

> He had set cruel torches beneath you, Rome.

Finally he adds:

> The criminal had surpassed the crimes of the ancient tale;
>
> in his case, what had been a story—that is, a representation—
>
> became punishment.

That is, it became reality. The celebrated memory of these holy martyrs is renewed every year in the Roman Martyrology on June 24, although not all of them were killed in the same manner. There we read:

> At Rome, the commemoration of very many holy martyrs who, under Nero, were falsely accused of having set the city on fire and were ordered by him to be savagely killed by different kinds of death. Some of them, covered with the skins of beasts, were exposed to be torn apart by dogs; others were fastened to crosses, etc.

[Col. 0187D]

See Tacitus, Book XV; Suetonius and Dio in their accounts of Nero. In the printed manuscript, *Furculos* appeared instead of *Laureolos*, but this was an error. Martial does not call the martyrs *Furculi* but *Laureoli*. The mistake could easily have arisen from one reading being confused with the other because of the similarity of their letters, and because it is certain that those who were crucified were also put upon a forked stake. Consult Calepinus on Laureolus and Baronius under the year 98.

Whether Martial mocked the same martyr or another in the following Epigram 18, he gave him the name Daedalus, saying:

> Daedalus, when you are thus torn by a bear at Lucanus,
>
> how you would wish now to have possessed your wings!

He alludes to those doves of Daedalus, the great astronomer, which he caused to fly through the air, balanced by precise weights, although they were made of bronze or wood. They nevertheless had no wings with which to escape.

A.D. 60. A.R. 811. Many in Spain, during Nero’s first persecution—which began here in the year 57—suffered atrociously at Hispalis, Iliturgi, Iliberri, Tarragona, Zaragoza, in Lusitania, Baetica, and Carpetania, after being deprived of all their possessions.

[Col. 0183]

A.D. 60. A.R. 811. At the same time, when the holy bishops and also the disciples of Saint James the Apostle had assembled in the city of Cherronensia near Valencia in Spain for the purpose of a council—Basil of Carthage Spartaria, his first disciple; Eugenius of Valencia; Pius of Hispalis; Agathodorus of Tarragona; Elpidius of Toledo; Aetherius of Barcelona; Capito of Lugo; Ephrem of Asturias; Nestor of Palencia; and Arcadius of Juliobriga—they were stripped of their possessions and killed under the same judge.

A.D. 60. A.R. 811. Augustus was succeeded by Tiberius, Tiberius by Caius, Caius by Claudius, and Claudius by Nero.

A.D. 60. A.R. 811. A violent earthquake occurred at Rome, followed by an eclipse of the sun.

A.D. 60. A.R. 811. Saint Luparia was alive: the Baetican daughter of the other, Galician Luparia.

A.D. 60. A.R. 811. Regulus, converted in Galicia, lived a holy life in a sacred grove.

[Col. 0187]

A.D. 60. A.R. 811. In Epigrams 7 and 8, Martial calls the martyrs who were crucified flying Laureoli and Daedali.

[Note: [Col. 0188A]]

### A.D. 61. “Nero, etc.”

Eusebius also records the violent deaths of both women in this year in his *Chronicle*, saying: “Nero kills his mother Agrippina and his father’s sister.” Read Suetonius or Dio concerning them.

[/Note]

A.D. 61. A.R. 812. Nero killed his mother Agrippina and his father’s sister.

[Note: [Col. 0188B]]

### A.D. 63. “Barnabas, etc.”
