In the readings of the Roman Breviary we read that Saint Barnabas suffered martyrdom in Cyprus around the seventh year of Nero. Since Nero began to reign in the year of the Lord 56, on October 13—the day on which Claudius died—it follows that Saint Barnabas’s martyrdom, after Nero had been reigning for seven years, fell in the year of the Lord 63. The feast of Saint James is also held to have occurred in this very year, according to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, which states: “In the year of the Lord 63, James, the brother of the Lord, was crushed by stones by the Jews.” Jerome, in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, reports that he was not only killed by stones but also thrown headlong from the pinnacle of the Temple and struck on the head with a fuller’s club or staff.

[/Note]

A.D. 63. A.R. 814. Barnabas was killed in Cyprus, and James the Less at Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 0188B]]

### A.D. 64.––1. “Before Nero’s table, etc.”

I believe this too was taken from Eusebius, whose very words these are.

[Col. 0188C]

### 2. “Epaenetus, etc.”

We dealt again with the same man, together with the Author, under the year of the Lord 30, number 3, where we showed from Metaphrastes that he was bishop of Sexifirmum, which Pliny mentions in Baetica, Book III, chapter 1. It was once a notable city on Mount Fregiliana, in one of the Granada Alpujarras, or—what may perhaps appeal more to others—Motril or Vélez-Málaga.

We now think that we should add that Dorotheus the abbot, whom Peter of Equilinum reports and follows in Book VI, chapter 100, believed that Epaenetus had been appointed bishop of the Carthaginians. If this is true, the matter might be understood as follows: he was first designated bishop of Sexifirmum by Peter; after the martyrdom of Saint Basil, bishop of Carthage Spartaria, which occurred in the year of the Lord 60, he was transferred to the see of Spanish Carthage; there he exchanged life for death after four years, namely in the year of the Lord 64.

There can be no doubt that African Carthage is meant here, for in those days Saint Crescens presided over it, as we demonstrated in the cited place under the year 50, number 3.

As for the holiness of the Lord Epaenetus, it is highly significant that Paul greets him among his first and chief disciples in Romans 16, declaring that he was greatly beloved by him—undoubtedly on account of his integrity—and that he was the first disciple of all Asia, as it were the foundation or gateway of the faith of the Asians:

> Greet Epaenetus, beloved by me, who is the firstfruits of Asia in Christ.

It is not clear by what death he died, whether peacefully or by the sword.

[Col. 0189A]

### 3. “Lucius Annaeus Seneca, etc.”

Dexter asserts nothing about Seneca beyond what those great champions of the Church in his own age, Jerome and Augustine, said. Jerome places Seneca among ecclesiastical writers, saying:

> I would not place him in the catalogue of the saints, were it not for those letters which are read by very many people as letters from Paul to Seneca and from Seneca to Paul.

Augustine, in Letter 53 to Macedonius, says:

> Seneca rightly says so—the Seneca who lived in the times of the apostles, and to whom certain letters to the Apostle Paul are also read ascribed.

Thus the letters exchanged between Seneca and Paul, which Augustine and Jerome, contemporaries of Dexter, recognized as letters, Dexter himself acknowledges here. Nor does he absolutely assert that Seneca was a Christian, but only that he was believed to have been a Christian and a disciple of Paul. Jerome inferred this from the same letters, to such an extent that for this sole reason he placed Seneca among Christian teachers.

Saint Linus too, in his little book on the martyrdoms of the Apostles Peter and Paul, himself an eyewitness, says:

> People from Caesar’s household came in crowds to him [that is, to Paul]. His tutor also was so closely bound to him in friendship that he could scarcely restrain himself from conversing with him; and when he was unable to speak with him face to face, he enjoyed the sweetness of his frequent letters, their extraordinary conversation, and their counsel, through letters sent and received.

Honorius of Autun includes these letters in his book *On the Luminaries of the Church*, saying:

> Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Cordoba, a disciple of the Stoic Pothinus and the uncle of the poet Lucan, wrote certain letters to the Apostle Paul, and the Apostle wrote certain replies.

Sixtus of Siena, in the *Bibliotheca Sancta*, records eight short letters sent by Seneca to Paul and six from Paul to Seneca. In some of them they speak as though they were inhabitants of the same city, as when Seneca says in the first:

> I believe, Paul, that you have been told what I discussed yesterday with our Lucillus about hypocrisy and other matters.

In others he sends a letter to one who is far away. One of these seems to be the letter which Dexter says he wrote to Paul while Paul was living in Spain:

> We are distressed by your excessive withdrawal. What is it, or what circumstances, that are keeping you there? If it is the Lord’s displeasure because you have withdrawn from the ancient rite and sect and have converted others anew, there will be an opportunity to ask that you consider this to have been done by reason, not by levity. Farewell.

That Seneca thought very highly of Christianity is shown by another letter, in which he says:

> I confess that I was favorably impressed while reading the letters that you sent to the Galatians, Corinthians, and Achaeans—that is, to all those of the same province in which Corinth is situated, for that province is called Achaia. Hence the title of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians says, “To the church of God which is at Corinth, with all the brothers who are throughout Achaia.” For the Holy Spirit in you and above you expresses exalted, sublime, and most venerable thoughts.

And shortly afterward:

> I confess that Augustus was deeply moved by your thoughts. When he had read the beginning of your letter, he said: “One might marvel that a man who has not been properly trained”—that is, without the disciplines of rhetoric—“could think in such a way.”

That Seneca finally, although secretly, surrendered to the faith is suggested by the last letter from Paul to Seneca, namely:

> Paul to Seneca. Greetings. What your wisdom has understood must be established as everlasting. Consider the observances of pagans and Israelites to be avoided. What you have nearly attained, communicate to the temporal king, to his household, and to all his trusted associates. Although your persuasion will be harsh and incomprehensible to them, since most of them are not at all moved by your insinuations, nevertheless the word of God, instilled into them, will produce in them a new person hastening toward God. Farewell, Seneca, dearest to us.

Observe how Paul commands him to proclaim to Nero and the Palatine household what he himself had believed.

Cardinal Baronius, under the year 66, argues that these letters are false because certain errors occur in the dates assigned to the consuls. But this should not be an obstacle, since false consular dates could easily have been inserted by ignorant people into genuine letters of Seneca and Paul. It is certain, however, that Paul never appended the names of the consuls to his letters, nor was it necessary for Seneca to do so in such short and familiar letters.

[Col. 0189D]

### 4. “Saint Paul, etc.”

What Paul had desired and promised so earnestly—namely, to visit Spain—he finally accomplished after being released from the chains that had prevented him from beginning the journey when he wrote his letter to the Romans from Corinth. Nothing else had stood in the way except imprisonment, and the same necessity, or an even greater one, demanded his arrival. Indeed, as we demonstrated above under the year of the Lord 36, the need for him to enter Spain was much greater than the need for him to enter Rome.

An innumerable company of holy teachers acknowledge his arrival in Spain. Among the Latins are Jerome, in chapter 11 of Isaiah, in his commentary on chapter 5 of Amos, in his commentary on Ephesians, and in Letter 28; Gregory the Great, Book XXXI of the *Moralia*, chapter 22 or 37; Isidore, in his book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, chapter 71; Bede in the Martyrology on March 22, where the Roman Martyrology makes the same assertion; Anselm on Romans 15; Usuard on December 12; Ado of Vienne in his *Chronicle* under the year 59; and Rupert, Book II on Isaiah, chapter 10.

Among the Greeks this was also the common opinion: Athanasius in his letter to Dracontius and in the *Synopsis*; Cyril in Catechesis 17; Epiphanius in Heresy 27; Hippolytus in his book *On the Twelve Apostles*, which is preserved in the library of Cardinal Sirlet; Sophronius in his sermon on the Nativity of the Apostle; Chrysostom in the preface to the Hebrews, in his *Homily on the Praises of Paul* 7, and in Homily 76 on Matthew; Theodoret on the final chapter of Second Timothy, on chapter 1 of Philippians, and on Psalm 116; Metaphrastes in the *Life of Saint Paul the Apostle*; and the *Menologion* on September 23.

There is also a certain tradition of the Churches of Spain and Gaul, which writers of both kingdoms vigorously defend. Among the Spaniards are Lucas of Tuy in his *Chronicle*; Abulensis on chapter 33 of Genesis and chapter 2 of Matthew; Morales, Book IX, chapter 2; Mariana, *History of Spain*, Book IV, chapter 3; Marieta; Villegas; and the others who have written about Spanish affairs or its saints. Trugillus discusses it at length in Volume II of the *Treasury of Sermons*.

Several churches also give this tradition authority in their divine offices, professing that the Apostle Paul visited them and appointed bishops for them. The church of Dertosa, or Tortosa in Catalonia, sings that it received Rufus as bishop from him—so Trugillus, Marieta, and others report—and that Rufus was the son of Simon of Cyrene, accompanying Paul when he went to Spain.

Narbonne makes the same claim concerning Sergius Paulus, as the Roman Martyrology asserts on March 22:

> At Narbonne in Gaul, the feast of blessed Paul, bishop and disciple of the apostles, who, tradition says, was Sergius Paulus the proconsul. Baptized by the blessed Apostle Paul, he was left at Narbonne when Paul was going to Spain and was there honored with episcopal dignity.

Usuard, on December 12, says:

> Whom the blessed Apostle Paul ordained and appointed bishop for that same city; and when he was going with the same Apostle to Spain to preach, he was left there.

Saint Anselm also supports this in his commentary on chapter 16 of the Epistle to the Romans. I have shown elsewhere, in my *Anselm Vindicated* in the matter of the Conception of the Virgin, that this work belongs to Anselm and not to Hervaeus. He says:

> Nor does the man who promises that he will go to Spain speak falsely; for he did go, as Jerome, Bede, and the other Doctors testify. Hence, as he passed through Narbonne, he is said to have left a certain disciple of his there, named Paul, as bishop. He therefore reached Spain, and by preaching he ran from the Red Sea to the Ocean, imitating the course of the sun from east to west, so that the earth would fail him before his eagerness to preach. Since, therefore, he was hastening to forestall the false apostles in Spain, he says: “When I begin to travel to Spain,” etc.

The same author says this in his commentary on chapter 2 of Galatians and on Second Timothy 4.

As for Paul of Narbonne, Ado says the same in his Martyrology, as may be seen in Mosander’s seventh volume of Surius, or in the additions to it, as Heribert Rosweyde notes.

Ado himself also asserts in his *Chronicle*, under the year 59, that on the same journey Paul left Trophimus at Arles and Crescens at Vienne as bishops.

Again, in the history of the holy martyrs Facundus and Primitivus, we read that, when questioned by a judge about their faith, they said that they had been taught Christianity by Paul, the Apostle of Christ. This could not have happened outside Spain, as Morales and Trugillus noted.

Most importantly, the citizens of Astigi—that is, Écija—preserve by transmission from their ancestors a tradition concerning their fellow citizens Probus and Xantippa, a most noble married couple, whom they say were converted by Paul in Spain. This is not surprising, since the same story was also known to the Greeks.

Simeon Metaphrastes gives the following account in the *Life of Saint Paul*:

> Now when he was in Spain, they say that something of this kind happened. A woman distinguished by birth, wealth, and learning, who had long ago heard the apostolic teaching, desired to behold with her own eyes the herald of truth and to be instructed by her own ears in the doctrines of true piety. When, therefore, by some divine inspiration, she decided to go to the marketplace, at the moment when the man whom she loved merely from report was passing through it, she is said to have seen him entering gently and calmly, possessing not only conduct filled with grace beyond that of others, but also a gracious manner of walking. She persuaded her husband, whose name was Probus—easily the leading man among those who lived there—to receive the stranger into their house.
>
> After he had been summoned and had come near them, a certain miracle is said to have occurred to the woman. When the eyes of her mind were opened, she saw upon the forehead of the guest who had been received golden letters saying: “Paul, herald of Christ.” Astonishment and fear seized her because of the unexpected vision. Filled with tears, she fell at the Apostle’s feet. After being instructed by him in catechesis, she first received baptism and was called Xantippa. Then her husband Probus, who was known to Nero, was baptized; afterward Philotheus the prefect, and then all who inhabited that region.

This golden story establishes not only Paul’s arrival in Spain but also the conversion to the faith of the holy and noble married couple Probus and Xantippa and of Philippus, surnamed Philotheus, whom the author mentions here.

Finally, evidence for this truth may be found in what we shall say below, together with Dexter, concerning the holy virgins Basilissa and Anastasia of Setabis [Xantiba], born in the kingdom of Valencia and converted there by Paul, and concerning Saint Polyxena.

Since we have such a cloud of witnesses asserting the matter, it can no longer reasonably be called into question—especially since the Apostle had enough time to undertake such a journey after he was released from imprisonment at Rome, and since he was not lacking in willingness. It is certain that from that time until his death he never withdrew to the East, as I shall now explain.

Two objections nevertheless appear at first sight to stand in the way, and it is necessary to resolve them here.

The first is that Pope Gelasius, in Question 22, chapter 2, *Beatus Paulus*—whom Saint Thomas is said to follow in lecture 3 on chapter 15 of Romans—denies that the Apostle went to Spain as he had promised.

These authors, however, deny only that Paul went there at the time he had promised, namely while passing through Rome—not while making a stay in Spain. The Pontiff intends to establish not a doubtful matter but a Catholic principle: namely, that a person who has no intention of deceiving does not lie even if he fails to fulfill what he promised, when, because God ordered matters otherwise, he was unable to fulfill his promise.

The heading of that canon is as follows:

> To confirm this, the blessed Apostle Paul should not therefore be believed to have deceived anyone—which God forbid—or to have contradicted himself, because, although he had promised that he would go to Spain, he was unable to fulfill what he had promised because, by divine arrangement, he was occupied with greater matters. Insofar as his own will was concerned, he declared what he truly wished to accomplish; but with respect to the hidden counsel of God, he was forestalled by the heavenly arrangement.

What is necessary for Gelasius’s argument is therefore only what we learn from the sacred Scriptures: that Paul did not fulfill his promise to set out for Spain as soon as possible and not to linger in Rome. This is what he had said to the Romans: “When I begin to travel to Spain, I hope that as I pass through I shall see you.” Yet divine providence arranged matters otherwise, for he was detained in chains at Rome for two years.

That alone supplies the case addressed by Gelasius: namely, how Paul did not lie. By this certain historical truth he proves that a person does not lie when, because he was unable, he failed to fulfill what he had promised.

It was not relevant to Gelasius to deny the Apostle’s arrival in Spain after his imprisonment, first because this was not a matter that had to be established by proving something at least historically uncertain, and also because it is not credible that Gelasius would have wished, without cause, to oppose so many and such great testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning Paul’s journey to Spain.

Say the same concerning Saint Thomas Aquinas: he denied only that Paul came to Spain at the time he himself had promised, not that the Apostle went there after his imprisonment. Clear evidence of this is found in the same work shortly afterward, in his commentary on Galatians 2, on the words “that I might not run, or had not run, in vain,” where he explicitly acknowledges Paul’s arrival in Spain, saying:

> He calls his preaching a race because of the speed of his teaching, since in a short time the Gospel was carried beforehand from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum and even to Spain.

You can therefore see that the earlier passage must necessarily be interpreted in Gelasius’s sense, lest Thomas contradict himself.

Let us now consider the second objection that may be raised against us. If evangelizing Spain was so deeply fixed in Paul’s mind, as we assert, how could it happen that during the entire two-year period in which he was held and detained at Rome he did not write a letter to those whom he so greatly desired to see? If he had always intended to travel to Spain as soon as he obtained his freedom, there is no doubt that he would have disclosed to them by letter his desire to travel to them.

Yet if the only point at issue is to concede Paul’s arrival in Spain—although this is not at all necessary, for he could have told the Spaniards who were staying at Rome in person, so that they themselves might write there concerning his intention and his daily desire to visit Spain; or perhaps he wrote a letter that was subsequently lost, as happened with the letter he sent to the Laodiceans—we nevertheless now possess a canonical letter addressed to the Spaniards, namely the one entitled *To the Hebrews*.

This will nevertheless appear harder to believe than Saint Paul’s arrival itself. I ask readers to wait patiently until the year of the Lord 66, where, together with Dexter, we shall discuss this matter expressly. In the meantime, I ask them not to mark the opinion at once with disapproval merely because of its novelty. In view of the foundations by which it is supported, it will, I hope, appear sufficiently plausible.

It will become clear from what is said there that Saint Timothy accompanied Paul when he went to Spain.

What Dexter adds concerning Philemon may be inferred from the fact that, when the Apostle wrote to him and commended Onesimus—whom he had begotten in the faith while in chains, but who had formerly been Philemon’s slave—he stated that he had wished to keep Onesimus with him because he was useful to him, yet he did not wish to do anything without Philemon’s consent.

When Philemon received this message, it is credible that he not only sent Onesimus back but also came personally to Paul. At that time Paul, released from his chains, was preparing to travel to Spain. Thus Philemon too may have gone with him, as did Luke, who was with the Apostle in chains and ministered to him (2 Timothy 4). The most authoritative writers likewise report that Luke remained with the Apostle until his death.

We shall see the same concerning Titus below, together with Dexter, under the year 220.

### 5. “Libysoca and Laminum, etc.”

Libysoca was once a not insignificant city, called *Forum-Augusta* by the Romans, as Morales testifies in Book IX of his *History*, chapter 33. Ptolemy places it among the Oretani, not far from Laminum, which, according to him, was at the edge of Carpetania and bordered on the Oretani. From it the district of Laminium received its name; it is now called Campo de Montiel.

Libysoca itself, reduced to an insignificant town near Alcaraz, is now called Lezuca. So say Morales, Charles Stephen, Ortelius, and all the authorities on geography.

Morales adds in Book IX, chapter 38, that a stone was found at Libysoca bearing the inscription:

> COLONIA LIBYSOSANORUM

He therefore believes that the city should not be called Libysoca but Libysosa, and that Pliny should be corrected, since he reads *Libysoca*. If this is so, Dexter and Ptolemy too must certainly be corrected, for all of them read *Libysoca*.

The river Anas, commonly called the Guadiana, rises in the district of Laminium, or Campo de Montiel. Dexter asserts that it was there that Paul led Philippus, surnamed Philotheus, to the faith, together with Probus and Xantippa, although they were citizens—as is believed—of Astigi and among the leading Romans. We learn from the same Dexter that they had come from Rome at that time and were converted to the faith of Christ at Laminium before reaching Astigi. We shall discuss this under the year 100.

### 6. “In this year, etc.”

The name of this martyr is absent from all the manuscripts that I have seen. Its loss is a great misfortune for the people of Pax, whether this was the city now called Badajoz, as Mariana argues in Book III of his *History*, chapter 25. He says that Augustus built it after conquering the Cantabri and called it Pax Augusta, declaring that peace had then been restored to the whole world, at the time when our Lord was born.

Vaseus in his *Chronicle of Spain*, Tarrapha in his *On the Spanish Kings*, and Molecius, whom Ortelius cites in his geographical map, follow this view.

Or whether, as Ambrosius Morales more plausibly argues in Book IX, chapter 32, it was Beja, a city of Lusitania—an opinion vigorously defended by Resendius in Book IV of his *Antiquities of Évora* and in a special letter to Vaseus concerning the colony of Pax, over which he disputed with him.

Varrerius and Ludovicus Nonius follow Resendius in chapter 33 of his *Spain*.

Whatever they may say, I find it much easier to agree with Dexter, who places Pax Augusta above the river Anas. This suits the city of Badajoz, but not Beja. Ptolemy also supports this, placing it among the Turdetani, that is, not in Lusitania but in ancient Baetica—a location that fits Beja in no way, but does fit Badajoz.

Finally, the name itself, together with the bishopric of Pax, has remained attached to the city of Badajoz, not Beja.

I add the irrefutable testimony of M. Maximus, which agrees with Dexter. In his *Chronicle*, under the year of the Lord 529, he says:

> Aprigius, bishop of Pax Augusta in Spain, not far from the city of Emerita Augusta, which Pax is situated beside the river Anas.

Behold, Maximus, an author of more than a thousand years’ antiquity, recognizes Pax Augusta as situated beside the river Anas, just as Dexter said. He adds that it lies not far from Emerita, which suits Badajoz, not Beja: Beja is almost thirty leagues from Emerita, whereas Badajoz is only six or eight leagues distant.

A.D. 64. A.R. 815. After Epaenetus had labored long and greatly in Spain, he finally rested a blessed death in his own city. It is uncertain whether he was a martyr.

[Col. 0189]

He is believed to have become a secret Christian and to have been Paul’s disciple; he also writes affectionately to Paul while Paul was staying in Spain.

### A.D. 66.––1. “Saint Paul of Narbonne, etc.”

We discussed him above under the year 64. As for his preaching in Spain, we have the testimony of Usuard, who affirms it. He says that Paul first appointed him—that is, designated him—as bishop of the people of Narbonne; that he then went with Paul to Spain for the purpose of preaching; and that finally he was left at Narbonne.

Here are Usuard’s words under December 12:

> At Narbonne, the feast of Saint Paul, bishop and confessor, whom the blessed Apostle Paul ordained and appointed bishop for that same city; and when he went with the same Apostle to Spain for the purpose of preaching, etc.

The Roman Martyrology identifies him as Sergius Paulus the proconsul whom Paul himself led to the faith in Acts 13, under March 22.

Peter, bishop of Equilinum, adds in Book I, chapter 60, that after becoming Paul’s disciple he followed him until his passion. After his own passion, the blessed Apostle appeared to him in a vision at Paphos and commanded him to go to the regions of Spain and Gaul to preach. Paul had indeed returned to the island of Paphos, where Sergius had been converted. Sergius faithfully fulfilled the command.

Peter goes on to describe his miracles and journeys in detail: how he was brought from Paphos to Rome with his deacons Rufus and Stephen; how he then went to Gaul and, after leading many to the faith by the power of miracles, traveled through Spain preaching.

[Col. 0194C]

You can therefore see that he not only traversed Spain with the Apostle while evangelizing, but later traveled through it again with the disciples Rufus and Stephen. When he subsequently returned to Narbonne, he ordained them bishops: Rufus he placed over the people of Avignon, while he designated Stephen as his successor. For, having been warned of his death by a threefold vision of the blessed Paul, he arranged the affairs of his church and, while praying in it, departed to the Lord.

Read Peter of Equilinum concerning these matters. He also asserts that Sergius consecrated the church of the blessed Apostle Paul at Rome.

Ambrosius Morales, Book IX, chapter 11, also adduces Vincent of Beauvais in the *Historical Mirror* and the Breviary of Tarragona as testimony to his preaching in Spain. In it that holy church affirms that he preached in its city.

Consult the testimony of Saint Anselm concerning the same Paul, which we cited above under the year of the Lord 64, number 41.

[/Note]

## 2. C. Oppius, etc.

See what we noted concerning him in the year of Christ 34, comments 3 and 8. As for what Dexter now asserts—that, worn out by old age, he remained dear to the emperor Hadrian after many years—it is not clear to whom this refers. For in this context it can be applied to Gaius Oppius, and also to his father, Cornelius of Capernaum. One might more easily think that he was speaking of Oppius, because from the death of Christ until the beginning of Hadrian’s reign, which commenced in the year of the Lord 119, eighty-five years intervened. Therefore, if Oppius—who, while serving as a centurion, professed Christ on the cross to be the Son of God—was at least thirty years old when he became dear to Hadrian, he would then have been ninety-five; his father, however, would have been considerably older, namely about 115, which one would not so readily believe.

To me Dexter seems to have been speaking of the father, both because Dexter indicates that his life had been prolonged almost miraculously to that age by the words “after many years” and “already worn out by old age”—for unless his age had been extraordinarily remarkable, he would not have emphasized it in this way—and also because Gaius Oppius was devoted to preaching and had been appointed bishop of Milan. His father, by contrast, did not abandon or change his military service, and therefore would more easily have been able to win the favor of a pagan emperor.

Lest anyone think the age of this holy centurion unique, I should point out that in that golden age several Fathers of the Church, by God’s gift, reached an extremely advanced old age. Thus Saint Dionysius the Areopagite was killed at the age of 120, as we shall show under the year 130 of the Lord. Saint Simeon, a kinsman of the Lord and bishop of Jerusalem, was crucified in the 120th year of his life. Concerning him Hegesippus, quoted by Eusebius in Book III, chapter 26, says:

> To the amazement of all who were present, and even of the judge himself, he, an old man of 120 years, endured the punishment of the cross bravely and steadfastly.

This has also been inserted into the Roman Martyrology under 18 February. Cardinal Baronius adds many others in Volume II of the *Annals*, under the year 109: namely, Saint Ignatius, who had seen the Lord in the flesh; Saint Quadratus, who had known persons healed by the Lord; both of whom lived into the time of Trajan; also Hermas, who lived until Antoninus Pius; and Polycarp, the disciple of blessed John the Apostle, who—something much more astonishing—reached the reigns of Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Verus, who began to rule in the year of the Lord 140. The Evangelist himself also lived to nearly a hundred years.

Therefore, one should not think that the centurion of Capernaum alone reached so great an age. Nevertheless, I would not take too literally what is asserted here concerning his relationship with Hadrian, as though he had never met him in friendship until Hadrian had risen to the imperial dignity. Rather, Hadrian had known him for many years previously, since he was a Spaniard and a soldier whom another Spanish soldier could easily have approached.

## 3. The holy women, etc.

The Greeks recount the wondrous contest of these holy women in the menologion, under 15 April, in these words:

> On the same day, the holy martyrs Basilissa and Anastasia, who, being distinguished at Rome by birth and wealth and disciples of the holy Apostles, took care to remove their relics by night after the Apostles had been crowned with martyrdom, were brought before the emperor Nero. They were therefore thrown into prison and brought out shortly afterward. When they confessed that they would remain steadfast in the confession of Christ, they were hung up, and after their breasts, hands, feet, and tongues had been cut off, they were beheaded.

From this one may see that the Greeks agree very closely with Dexter concerning their nobility, their martyrdom, and its cause—namely, that it arose from the care they had taken in burying the bodies of the Apostles Peter and Paul.

According to Galesinus, who on this day draws from the Greek *Horologion*, they were accused before Nero and handed over to prison. Then, after being brought out, when they remained steadfast in their resolve concerning the faith, “with their hands, feet, tongues, and finally their necks cut off, they obtained the palm of martyrdom.” He also adds that they flourished not only in nobility but in wealth.

The Roman Martyrology agrees with this, saying:

> At Rome, the holy Basilissa and Anastasia, noble women, who, being disciples of the Apostles and remaining steadfast in the confession of the faith, under the emperor Nero, with their tongues and feet cut off [“and hands” is omitted], were struck with the sword and obtained the crown of martyrdom.

What is said concerning their caring for the bodies of the Apostles does not conflict with the history of Plautilla, the disciple of Paul, who is represented on the bronze doors of the Apostles at Rome and described by Equilinus in his *Life of the Apostle*. On the journey itself to his martyrdom, the Apostle received her handkerchief, but returned it when, having been beheaded, he departed to heaven. I say that this does not conflict with the account, for the fact that Plautilla also cared for Paul’s body does not prevent Basilissa and Anastasia from having cared for it as well. They could all have done this together.

There is one detail that Dexter adds above the other authors: namely, that the women had been converted in the city of Setabis, among the Edetani, peoples of Hispania Tarraconensis—something the others omitted. It was customary for the Greeks to pass over the names of Spanish cities in silence, as we shall frequently see throughout this history. They were moved to do this because, since Hispania lay farther from them than the other provinces of the world, they knew less about its cities.

They also went astray in this respect, believing Basilissa and Anastasia to have originated in the city of Rome, having been led to that conclusion by seeing that they were very noble and had suffered at Rome. In this matter we are more inclined to agree with Dexter, who belonged to the same province as they did, namely Tarraconensis, and therefore knew the homeland of these holy women much better.

Setabis was a noble city not far from Valentia, which we now call Satiba or Xatiba. The Romans called it Augusta Valeria, according to Pliny, as noted by Taraffa in his book *On the Kings of Hispania*, Michael Villanovanus in his notes on Ptolemy, and Nonnius in his *Hispania*, chapter 68. All agree that it was Xativa, and Ambrosius Morales supports them in Book X, chapter 32.

Ptolemy places Setabis among the Contestani, whereas Dexter places it among the Edetani. It was easy for Ptolemy to be deceived, since the city lay on the border of the two provinces. Dexter, however, had more complete knowledge of the matter, having been born not far from Setabis—unless one should say that the boundaries of those provinces were not permanently fixed, which is not improbable.

## 4. Saint James, etc.

Julian, archpriest of Saint Justa at Toledo, mentions the work of Saint Torquatus in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 36, saying:

> As constant tradition, handed down from apostolic times to the present, is established by the testimonies of many of the ancients—Torquatus, Tesiphon, Honoratus, Melantius, Dexter, M. Maximus, Isidore, Bede, and others—in the year of the Lord 36 Saint James, son of Zebedee, for a most honorable reason, visited Hispania and traversed all its cities, establishing his first see at Toledo, etc.

At Monte Santo in Granada, together with the other books, the books of Saint Tesiphon were found, in which he dealt with Saint James. There was also found a book on the life, journeys, and miracles of that same Apostle, by Saint Caecilius. But the book of Saint Torquatus mentioned here has not, so far as I know, yet been found. Nevertheless, since Julian cites it—Julian having lived around the year 1080—there remains hope that it may one day be discovered, to the great benefit of the Christian commonwealth.

Concerning the miracles that the Lord is accustomed to perform at the tomb of Saint Torquatus and his companions, through their merits and intercession, the following is found in a very ancient manuscript on parchment preserved in the monastery of Mount Zion, of the order of Saint Bernard, outside the walls of Toledo:

> Whoever, being ill, comes with pious devotion to their sacred places and holy tombs is freed by the unconquerable help of the blessed Martyrs. For they drive demons from possessed bodies; by their prayer they restore to the blind the sight they have lost; and, truly, all who honor their intercession receive at once, obtained from heaven, whatever they confidently request there.

The most remarkable sign of all is that God deigned to work, not once or twice but every year, for a period of seven hundred years, upon an olive tree planted at the tomb of Saint Torquatus. Ado recounts this in his *Martyrology*, from which Equilinus copied it in Book V, chapter 3, in these words:

> In the city of Acci, at the tomb of Saint Torquatus, an olive tree, flowering by divine power beyond the course of nature on his feast day, becomes laden with ripe olives, whose oil cures illnesses.

From this source Morales, Trugillus, Alderete, Villegas, and all modern writers have taken the account.

I shall, however, provide an eyewitness to the matter: namely, the author of the history mentioned above, which is preserved at Mount Zion. His words are these:

> Nor should we cover with the cloak of silence those exceedingly glorious miracles of the Lord which, through the pious and faithful merits of the saints—Torquatus and his companions—he works on their anniversaries even to the present day. All of us know the things we relate, and the persecutors of the Church themselves and the worshipers of falsehood acknowledge their truth.
>
> In the same place, before the doors of the church [in the city of Acci, or Guadix], a small olive root was planted by the saints themselves. The Lord granted such an abundance of grace to it that, on the evening when the birthday of those holy men begins [14 May], it appears more covered with flowers than with leaves. In the morning [15 May], from those very flowers, the entire assembly that has come with pious devotion and venerates the saints’ protection—or the whole multitude of pagans, heretics, and followers of perverse doctrines who come together—gathers olives that are as perfectly formed and abundant, and as beautifully adorned, as those ripened at their proper seasons. Thus everyone, faithful or unbelieving, carries away as much as each is able to gather.
>
> Who could describe the abundance of this fruit? If it had been lawful to gather it all together, it could have filled a very large number of baskets of olives, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who received his martyrs and confessors, etc.

The continual miracle of the sacred olive tree continued until the year 714, when almost all Hispania came under the rule of the Moors. At that time the venerable body of Saint Torquatus was transferred to Galicia, to the small monastery of Saint Columba de Vande, a priory of the distinguished monastery of Cella Nova, of the order of Saint Benedict.

In the year of the Lord 1196, certain Portuguese attempted to steal the body and transport it to their own province. But by God’s providence it happened that, enveloped in a great fog, they discovered—when they thought they had completed a long journey—that they were still standing at the gates of the monastery of Cella Nova. At that very moment the bells, moved of their own accord, gave forth a great sound.

When this miracle and the theft were discovered, arrangements were made for a new and solemn transfer of the sacred relics from Vande to Cella Nova. At length the transfer was carried out with the most solemn rites by Jacinto, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and legate *a latere* of Alexander III, who, after being raised to the supreme dignity of the Apostolate, was called Celestine III.

Finally, in the year of the Lord 1601, the body was transferred by Michael, bishop of Ourense, into a silver casket elaborately fashioned at great expense and skill—for upon it are beautifully carved the miracles of the ruined bridge and of the olive tree of Acci—with many prelates and an innumerable multitude of the faithful in attendance.

At that time the heart of the same most holy bishop and martyr Torquatus was found sound and whole, through a great miracle of God. Moreover—and this is exceedingly remarkable—an arm has for many centuries been preserved whole and unharmed in the monastery of Saint Mary of La Vega, of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Palencia. It is entirely covered with flesh and has, between the fourth and fifth fingers of the hand, an open wound, said to have been caused by a lance. From this one may believe that he died after being wounded by lances.

It would be difficult to convey here in detail the fragrance of the holy arm or to recount the miracles God works through its intervention. It is enough to say that the peoples spread throughout the surrounding region, out of reverence for it, make a vow to God and Saint Torquatus and celebrate his feast day, abstaining from servile labor and flocking in crowds to kiss and venerate the holy relics of the arm.

## 5. Saint Crispinus, etc.

Almost all the Martyrologies—Roman, Ado’s, Usuard’s, and those of more recent authors—commemorate Saint Crispinus on 19 November, using nearly the same words.

The Roman Martyrology says:

> In the city of Astigi, the blessed Crispinus, bishop, who obtained the glory of martyrdom by being beheaded.

Ado gives a fuller account:

> Crispinus, bishop and martyr, suffered at the city of Astigi. When he was bishop of that city and preached Christ the Lord, he was seized by the pagans and urged to sacrifice to the gods. When he refused to offer sacrifice, he obtained the glory of martyrdom by being beheaded.

Peter, in Book X, chapter 84 of his *Catalogue of the Saints*, reports these very words of Ado. Thus one may see that, as I believe, he copied Ado, who was earlier than the others and was the first to insert these words into his Martyrology. It is therefore not surprising that the others added nothing to Ado’s wording.

But since Ado’s text was corruptly read as “the city of Astiagensis” instead of Astigi or Astigitana, the others inherited the error of the reading. That the correct form should be Astigitana is taught not only by Dexter but also—an irrefutable argument for the truth—by Saint Isidore in the hymn for Crispinus in the Mozarabic Breviary of Toledo:

> His buried body is placed within the tomb  
> And consigned to the city of Astigitana.

There were formerly two cities in Baetica with almost the same name. One was Astigi—this is Écija—and belonged to the Turdetani; the other was Astigis or Astiagis and belonged to the Turduli. Ptolemy discusses both in his map of Baetica, as does Nonnius in his *Hispania*. In chapter 18 Nonnius discusses Astigi, situated on the bank of the Singilis, now called the Genil; in chapter 27 he treats Astigi or Astiagi. He says that the former was called Augusta Firma by the Romans, and the latter Julia, so that we may believe one was named for Augustus Caesar and the other for Julius Caesar.

From the former comes the designation Assigitana; from the latter, Astiagensis.

Pomponius Mela, the Spanish geographer, writes in Book II, chapter 6, that the most distinguished cities of Baetica were formerly Astigi, Hispalis, and Corduba, among which he assigns first place to Astigi—that is, Écija. The other was not of equal distinction, nor is it today; for it is now called Ahama, according to Jacobus Moletius, whom Nonnius cites in chapter 27.

As for the blessed Crispinus, whom Isidore and Dexter make bishop of Astigi, Peter Galesinus is demonstrably in error when he assigns his martyrdom to the time of Diocletian. I do not know what led him to this conclusion, unless perhaps he confused the name with that of another martyr, Crispinus of Soissons, the brother of Crispinianus. According to the Roman Martyrology, Crispinus of Soissons suffered under the emperor Diocletian and the judge Rictiovarus on 25 October. Otherwise, as you see, none of the ancient writers even faintly suggests such a date. From Dexter, on the other hand, we learn that Crispinus flourished in apostolic times.

I suspect from his name, period, and place that this was the Crispus who was ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, whom Paul baptized with his own hands, as is said in 1 Corinthians 1. Saint Luke speaks of his conversion in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 10:

> Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with his entire household; and many of the Corinthians, hearing, believed.

We therefore have among Paul’s disciples a man named Crispus who could easily have accompanied the Apostle when he traveled to Hispania and could there have been appointed by him bishop of the city of Astigi. This is especially plausible since Hippolytus and Dorotheus, who wrote about the disciples of the Lord and the Apostles, assign definite cities to the episcopal jurisdiction of the others but assign none to Crispus. This leaves room for the belief that he was bishop of Astigi.

Nor should the difference in names between Crispus and Crispinus be judged substantial; the transition from one form to the other is easy in writing. But we leave the matter uncertain, and readily forgive Galesinus for calling him Crispinianus, as well as the printer of Saint Isidore’s Breviary, who, in the illuminated rubric of his feast, calls him bishop and confessor, although he ought to have written martyr, since the hymn that follows is an outstanding monument to his former purity and speaks at length of his martyrdom.

> Let us praise the illustrious martyr Crispinus [Breviary: *Christo*, “to Christ”],  
> Who washed his body in sacred blood.  
> Following [Alternative: frequently following] the one God under the threefold name,  
> He left [Alternative: leaving] the world and all its riches,  
> Becoming a companion of the angels in God’s kingdom.
>
> He did not regard the flatteries of this age,  
> But looked ahead to the Lord, ruler of the world.  
> Following him with great joy,  
> He hastened happily toward paradise  
> And swiftly repelled the unspeakable enemy.
>
> Christ placed his sign upon his forehead,  
> For from heaven he saw him worship him devoutly.  
> Whenever the serpent wished to attack,  
> He did not yield, but with eager spirit  
> Renounced the envious devil.
>
> The true grace of almighty God  
> Granted Crispinus such steadfastness  
> That prison, punishments, whips, and flames—  
> Neither thirst nor hunger—could defile his body,  
> Though these things were capable of violating his faith.
>
> As a joyful soldier looked toward heaven,  
> His prepared neck received the sword;  
> And, consecrated [Alternative: made delicate] by his shed blood,  
> His body, buried [Alternative: *humanum*, “human”] in a tomb, was laid to rest  
> And consigned to the city of Astigitana.
>
> To his body come the afflicted,  
> The lame, the deaf, the blind, and the lunatics;  
> Confessing Christ, they receive salvation  
> And obtain the healing of health.
>
> You, gracious, guiding martyr and intercessor,  
> Intercede more closely [Alternative: graciously] for our evils,  
> So that all our crimes may be washed away  
> And free our souls and every part of our bodies  
> From the snares of the pursuing enemy.
>
> Amen.

## 6. Not long afterward, etc.

Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, whom we mentioned above under the year 37, recognizes Maximus as a disciple of Saint James. The Roman Martyrology celebrates his feast, together with those of his companions Castus and Magnus, on 4 September, saying:

> On the same day, the holy martyrs Magnus, Castus, and Maximus.

Peter de Natalibus, in Book XI, the final chapter, number 237, says:

> Magnus, Castus, and Maximus receive the palms of martyrdom on the same day, namely, the day before the Nones of September, or 4 September.

Usuardus mentions two of them, saying:

> On that day, the holy Magnus and Castus.

But in his additions, as well as in the Roman Martyrology, Maximus is also included. Maximus is named last, not because he was less worthy, but perhaps because he was crowned with martyrdom after the others.

Dexter adds the time and place of their martyrdom: namely, that they suffered by Nero’s sword at the city of Utica, a not insignificant city of Baetica in Hispania.

Ammianus of Alexandria discusses this city when recounting the deeds of Viriathus. He writes that, after being defeated once by Pompey, Viriathus took refuge at Mount Venus, not far from the Lusitanian city of Évora; and that, when he advanced from there, he killed many Romans, captured certain standards, and forced the rest to flee. He also drove the Roman garrisons from the city of Utica and destroyed all the coastlands of the Bastetani, who were allies of the Romans.

Ambrosius Morales agrees with this in Book VII, chapter 49. Utica, therefore, was situated between Évora and the peoples of the Bastetani, adjoining Carthago Spartaria. I suspect that it was Úbeda.

## 7. In Hispania, etc.

Bede mentions the holy martyrs Marcus and Hadria in his Martyrology under 13 October, asserting that they suffered in Hispania. From him Morales took the account in Book X, chapter 28, adding Saint Faustinus the martyr; Marieta did likewise in Part I of *The Saints of Hispania*, Book IV, chapter 51, and Villegas in the first volume of his *Flower of the Saints*, at the end of the volume, where he discusses the saints of Hispania.

Peter de Natalibus, in Book XI, the final chapter, number 287, adds Saint Marcellus the martyr. He calls Hadria “Hadrian,” saying:

> Marcellus, Hadrian, and Marcus are crowned with martyrdom on the same day—that is, on the third day before the Ides of October, or 13 October.

They suffered at the very distinguished city of Castulo. Concerning the location of this city, our historians were long and greatly perplexed. At last Florianus de Ocampo, Ambrosius Morales in Volume II of his *History of Hispania*, under the entry “Castulo,” Juan de Mariana in *On the Affairs of Hispania*, and Ludovicus Nonnius in chapter 64 established that Castulo was situated where Cazlona now stands, three leagues from Baeza and one from Linares, in the Marianus pass or Sierra Morena, on the bank of the river Guadalimar, which shortly afterward flows into the Baetis.

The location agrees with that assigned to it by Ptolemy. It also seems to agree with what Dexter says, namely, that it was at the entrance to Baetica.

It is nevertheless very difficult to reconcile this with the assertion of the same author that Castulo was situated beside the Tagus, which flowed past that city. The Tagus, after all, waters not Baetica but Hispania Tarraconensis.

The difficulty is increased by the fact that, as Hieronymus Paulus, a particularly learned man, states in his book *On the Rivers of Hispania*, the Tagus has its sources in the very territory of Castulo:

> Bursting forth from the territory of Castulo and flowing into Carpetania, it almost surrounds the powerful and strong city of Toledo.

Silius Italicus seems to suggest the same thing in Book III of the *Punica*, when he writes:

> Castulo of Parnassus shines with its distinguished standards.

As Morales explains in the passage cited, this suggests that Castulo was founded by Phocaeans, Greek settlers in whose territory Mount Parnassus stands. Therefore they called their city Castulo in order to preserve the memory of their Castalian spring. It follows that, according to Silius, in the territory of Castulo there was a spring belonging to some notable river, and no river can be identified other than the Tagus.

I admit that, if Castulo was situated at the sources of the Tagus, it should in no way be said to have stood where Cazlona now is, but rather where Priego stands, in whose territory the Tagus rises. In that case it could be said to have been situated at the entrance to Baetica, because under Dexter the boundaries of Baetica included the whole region that we call La Mancha and joined Tarraconensis Hispania not far from Priego.

But if this seems difficult, and someone insists that Castulo was Cazlona—which is undoubtedly at the entrance to Baetica—then it will be necessary to say that the Guadalimar was also formerly called the Tagus, so that it may be true that the Tagus flowed past Castulo.

This, however, seems incredible to me. For the source of the Tagus is not there, so that Castulo could on that account be called Castalian or Parnassian; nor will anyone deny that, when the Tagus is mentioned without qualification, it signifies that principal river which flows into the Ocean at Lisbon.

I therefore prefer to agree with Dexter and Silius, distinguished geographers or historians born in Hispania, on whose testimony Castulo is believed to have existed beside the source of the Tagus. Among more recent authorities, the cited Hieronymus Paulus agrees with them; among the ancients, Titus Livy does so in Book XXVIII of the *Decades*. Describing one of Scipio’s journeys, he says:

> Setting out from Tarraco, he reached Castulo, and from there proceeded to the city of Baetula.

Castulo, therefore, was situated between Tarraco and Baetulo, or Baetula. As Morales proves in Book VI, chapter 15, and under the entry “Betulo” in his *Antiquities*, this city is either Úbeda or Baeza.

But if Castulo were Cazlona, it would not lie between Tarraco and Baetula, as the source of the Tagus does. Nor would Livy say that Scipio, having set out from Tarraco for Castulo, proceeded to the city of Baetula; he would have said that he returned, since Úbeda and Baeza lie not beyond Cazlona but on this side of it, between Tarraco and Cazlona.

There was another Baetulo in Hispania, not far from Barcelona. Morales says in Book IX, chapter 33, that it is now called Badalona, but it is not the city relevant to Livy’s account.

Speaking elsewhere of the nobility of Castulo, namely in Book XXIV, Livy says:

> Castulo, a strong and noble city of Hispania, so closely allied with the Carthaginians that Hannibal had a wife from there, defected to the Romans, etc.

## 8. Persius, etc.

These words are taken verbatim from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, except that Eusebius records the death of Persius in the year of the Lord 65, whereas Dexter places it in 66.

## 9. The baths, etc.

This too is taken from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, under the year of the Lord 65.

## 10. Nero, etc.

Eusebius says the following under the year 65:

> Nero, competing at Rome in the contest of the lyre players, surpasses everyone.

Under the year 67 he again discusses a similar contest of Nero, in which, after defeating all musicians and poets, he was crowned at the Olympic games. He again treats the same matter under the year 68. From this arose Nero’s hatred of Lucan, because Nero had been defeated by him in a poetic contest.

## 11. M. Annaeus, etc.

Annaeus Mela, the brother of Seneca, by Acilia, daughter of Acilius Lucanus, a distinguished orator, while living at Corduba, fathered M. Annaeus Lucan, a most eloquent orator—or, as some prefer, historian—because he sang historical truth rather than the fables of poets in the graceful rhythms of his poems.

Some say that Lucan was born at Luque, a town nine leagues distant from Corduba. But, as Ambrosius Morales observes in Book IX, chapter 10 of his *History*, there is no evidence by which this can be proved.

He was born on 2 November in the year of the Lord 39. While living at Rome, he married Polla Argentaria, a woman no less distinguished in poetry than in wealth and birth.

He was arrested in the Pisonian conspiracy, by which, after Nero’s removal, the empire was to be prepared for Calpurnius Piso—or, according to others, whom Cornelius Tacitus reports in Book XVI, for Seneca himself, with the military tribune Subrius Flavus acting as intermediary. Lucan was condemned to death and, being allowed to choose the manner of dying, opened a vein and died after letting out his blood. He was twenty-seven years old, in the year of the Lord 66, according to Eusebius and Morales, in agreement with Dexter.

Peter Crinitus is the authority for saying that, on the last day of April, Nero—remembering his friend and repentant of what he had done—erected a statue to Lucan with this inscription:

> TO M. ANNAEUS LUCAN,  
> OF CORDUBA,  
> POET,  
> WHOSE FAME WAS PRESERVED  
> BY THE FAVOR OF NERO.

Polla, the wife who loved her husband dearly, celebrated his birthday. To honor her, Statius Papinius composed a *Genethliacon* for Lucan near the end of Book II of the *Silvae*. It begins:

> Let the day that belongs to Lucan be thronged.

Among other lines, he says the following about Corduba:

> Happy—ah, too happy—the land,  
> Baetica, that with your oil-anointed olive-mills challenges  
> Tritonian Athens, fertile in such presses;  
> You may count Lucan among your lands:  
> This is more than giving Seneca to the world  
> Or begetting the eloquent Gallio.

The latter was, of course, the brother of Seneca and of Annaeus Mela, Lucan’s father, and a noble orator.

Martial also wrote three epigrams on Lucan’s birthday, found in Book VII, numbers 21, 22, and 23. In the first he addresses Polla:

> This is the day that, conscious of a great birth,  
> Gave Lucan to the people and to you, Polla.  
> Alas, cruel Nero, hateful beyond every shadow:  
> At least you should not have been permitted this.

In another, speaking of the day of Lucan’s birth, he says:

> This day deserved, when it gave you, Lucan, to the lands,  
> That the Baetis should be mingled with Castalian waters.

Finally, in the last epigram:

> Phoebus, come—but be as great as you were when, to one singing of wars,  
> You yourself gave the second plectrum of the Latin lyre.

Martial had also discussed Lucan and his native Corduba in Book I, epigram 61. Addressing Licinianus under the heading “From where do writers come?” he says:

> Eloquent Corduba speaks of two Senecas  
> And one Lucan.

Finally, to say everything, Eusebius records under the year of the Lord 66:

> M. Annaeus Lucan, the poet of Corduba, having been discovered in the Pisonian conspiracy, offered his arm to a physician to cut his veins.

He adds:

> Junius Annaeus Gallio, the brother of Seneca, an outstanding declaimer, killed himself with his own hand, while Nero postponed his death until he had brought him into his presence.

Under the year 70 he adds:

> L. Annaeus Mela, the brother of Seneca and Gallio, obtained from Nero the property of Lucan the poet, his son.

## 12. Helena, etc.

Eusebius recounts in Book II, chapter 11 of his *Ecclesiastical History*—and Josephus, earlier than him, in Book XX, chapter 2 of the *Jewish Antiquities*, as well as Nicephorus in Book II, chapter 11 of his *History*—that Helena, queen of the Adiabenians, traveled to Jerusalem under the reign of Claudius with her son Izates, out of devotion. During the famine mentioned in Acts 11, she supplied food to the saints and the poor. At that time she was also brought to the worship of the true God, although she had previously been an idolater.

It is not clear to everyone what religion she followed, since some believe that she adhered to Jewish rites, while others believe that she became a Christian. Baronius, under the year 66, does not dare to decide in either direction, for he saw that Josephus and Eusebius asserted that she was Jewish, whereas Orosius and Ado held her to have been Christian.

Dexter, however, resolves the question by asserting not only that she embraced the faith of Christ but also that this was known to him from the Jerusalem Annals, which had been available to him while he was prefect of the praetorian guard in the East.

Orosius, who makes the same assertion in Book VII, chapter 6, was a contemporary of Dexter and a most diligent writer. Ado, who followed him in his *Chronicle*, has likewise always been regarded as a distinguished historian.

Among those who assert that Helena was Jewish, Eusebius merely reports Josephus; he does not affirm the matter himself. Josephus, however, being an enemy of the Christian religion, invented this account to serve his own perfidy.

It is indeed extremely difficult to believe that a noble and pious queen would at that time have converted to the Law of Moses, when the Apostles were performing countless signs in Jerusalem and the synagogue was hated by everyone. Nor will I readily grant that Divine Providence permitted something that could so greatly confirm and reestablish the old Law. Rather, everyone knows that the conversion of kings was promised to the Church, not to the synagogue, and was very frequently foretold by the prophets.

The most pious queen died at Jerusalem, and her son built a noble mausoleum for her. Besides the authors already cited, Saint Jerome mentions it in Letter 27.

## 13. Saint Fronto, etc.

An error had crept into the printed book, so that instead of *Fronto of Périgueux*—that is, the bishop—the reading was *Pythagorean*, as though he were a philosopher.

The Martyrologies of Bede, the Roman Martyrology, Usuardus, and more recent writers discuss him on 25 October. Peter Equilinus gives his life in Book IX, chapter 109, and the Belvacensis in Book IX, chapters 43 and 44 of his *Historical Mirror*.

He was a disciple of Saint Peter the Apostle, who sent him as bishop to the people of Périgueux in Gaul, with the priest George as his companion. But when George died after three days of travel, Fronto returned to the Apostle, received his staff, and, placing it upon the body of the deceased, restored George to life.

As he approached his own city, he converted a great multitude of that people to Christ and became renowned for many signs and miracles, which Peter recounts in his *Catalogue of the Saints*. Peter adds that Fronto established 700 monks and, while overcome by sleep during the celebration of Mass, was present in spirit at the funeral of Saint Martha between the reading of the Epistle and the Gospel.

His feast was formerly celebrated in Hispania, as may be seen in the Breviary of Palencia.

There is one matter in which Dexter differs from the other writers: namely, the manner of Fronto’s death. The others make him a confessor, whereas Dexter makes him a martyr. They say that, renowned for many miracles, he died peacefully; Dexter, however, says that Saint Fronto of Périgueux suffered martyrdom.

What makes me accept Dexter’s judgment is that he himself called many others martyrs whom we had venerated as confessors—for example, the blessed Torquatus and his companions, disciples of Saint James, to omit Orientius and Patientia, the parents of Saint Laurence—and the truth of their martyrdom was eventually revealed, so that they are now venerated as martyrs.

I believe the same should be thought concerning Saint Fronto, especially since I see that Dexter, who records him as a martyr, lived many years earlier than the others who call him a confessor. The closer he was to the time of Saint Fronto, the more readily the truth could have been known to him.

Equilinus himself, although he calls Fronto a confessor, affirms that he suffered persecution from the prefect Squirius, who also subjected many monks and disciples of the blessed Fronto to martyrdom. It may therefore easily be believed that he also raged against the master himself.

The brother of the holy Pontiff, likewise called Fronto and himself descended from the most noble Roman family, rose as far as a third consulship. He entered upon it together with Trajan, who was also holding his third consulship, in the year of the Lord 102. This consulship is mentioned by Pliny the Younger in his *Panegyric of Trajan* and by Martial in Book XI, in the epigram in which he prays to the gods for Nerva Trajan, saying, under number 4:

> And you, Janus, who now bring the third names  
> Into the purple rolls for Nerva.

Martial certainly had a close relationship with Fronto, as is sufficiently shown by the epigram in Book I, number 55, dedicated to that same Fronto and entitled “To Fronto, on his wish for life”:

> If you wish, Fronto, briefly to know the wishes of your Marcus—  
> You who are the renowned glory of military service and the toga—  
> This is what he asks: to cultivate an estate of his own, though not a great one,  
> And to love unadorned leisure amid modest possessions, etc.

There is also one who makes Saint Fronto, bishop of Périgueux, a native of Hispania: Damianus à Goes, a knight and distinguished Portuguese historian, whose work is extant in Hispania.

## 14. He flourished, etc.

Martial mentions the nobility and wealth of Gaius Caesonius Maximus more than once, in Book VII, epigram 73, addressed to Maximus, where he recounts his three palaces:

> You have a house on the Esquiline, a house on Diana’s hill,  
> And your lofty residence stands in the Patrician quarter.  
> Here are Cybele’s double crossroads, there Vesta’s shrine;  
> From one side you look upon the new Jupiter, from the other the old.

In Book II he gives him two epigrams, teaching and warning him not to court Caesar’s favor like a slave, since he is a prince in his own house. The first concludes thus, under epigram number 18:

> Let a king, Maximus, have no king as his master.

The second, number 53, begins:

> Do you wish to become free? You are lying, Maximus; you do not wish to.

But if you wish it to be done, you can do it in this way, etc. But as I considered what may have prompted Dexter to mention C. Caeson(ius) Maximus in his Chronicle, the following occurred to me: he was treating the death of Seneca, whose one uniquely devoted friend was Caesonius, since, when Caligula sent Seneca into exile on Corsica, Caesonius voluntarily became an exile himself and accompanied him; and after Seneca’s death, because his friendship with Seneca was made a charge against him, he was compelled by Nero to undergo exile in Sicily. The former point is reported by Cornelius Tacitus in Book XVI, the latter by Martial in Book VII, in two epigrams addressed to a certain Ovidius. This Ovidius was intimate with Caesonius and, just as Caesonius had followed Seneca, had followed him. The first reads, under no. 44:

> This is that Maximus of yours, Ovidius, Caesonius,  
> whose face the living wax still preserves.  
> Nero condemned him; but you dared to condemn Nero,  
> and to follow the fate of an exile not your own.  
> You went as the great companion of an exile across Scylla’s waters,  
> though just now you had refused to go as companion to a consul.

And shortly afterward:

> The present crowd and the generations to come will hear this:  
> that you were to him what he was to his own Seneca.

In the second epigram, again addressing Ovidius, the intimate of Maximus Caesonius, he says under no. 45:

> Powerful friend of eloquent Seneca,  
> next to Gaius—or before Serenus—  
> this is that Maximus whom the fortunate page  
> greets repeatedly in its abundant writing.  
> Following him across the Sicilian waves,  
> Ovidius, whom no tongue should keep silent,  
> you spurned the wrath of your raging master.

Who that raging master was, he makes clear by adding:

> You clung as companion to Nero’s exile.

Caesonius was related by blood to the empress Caesonia, the wife of Gaius Caligula. Suetonius discusses her in *Caligula*, chapter 59; and Martial composed an epigram for her birthday in Book IX, beginning, “The first light shines upon the Palatine,” etc. Saint Ignatius speaks of another Fronto in his *Epistle to the Ephesians*: this man visited him in chains, [Col. 0204D] together with other Ephesian men.

### 15. Peter, who in Greek, etc.

This Peter, who was called *Megistos* in Greek, was one of the three soldiers whom the apostle Paul brought to the faith during the very journey to his martyrdom. Receive the account of this event from Peter of Equilium, Book VI, chapters 23 and 41:

> After these words Paul was led to the place of execution. When three soldiers—Longinus, Megistus, and Acestus—asked him who that king was whom he loved so greatly that he willingly underwent death for him, Paul announced Christ to them and converted them to the faith. When they asked how they could be saved, he instructed them to come in the morning to the place of his beheading, where, once the matter was known, they would be washed in the water of baptism and made coheirs of the eternal King.  
>   
> After this, when he himself was being led to execution with other soldiers sent by Nero to hasten Paul’s death, Paul met his disciple Plautilla at the Ostian gate. He asked her for the veil with which her head was covered, so that he might bind his eyes with it, and return it to her after he had been beheaded. When she had handed it to him, the executioners mocked her for giving him a costly veil, which the dead man could scarcely return to her.  
>   
> After the sacrifice had been completed, when the soldiers were returning, Plautilla displayed the veil stained with blood and told them that at that very hour Peter and Paul had entered the city, clothed in splendid garments and adorned with radiant crowns, and that Paul, in accordance with his promise, had returned the borrowed veil to her. By this miracle the three soldiers believed in the Lord still more firmly.  
>   
> In accordance with Paul’s instruction, on the following day they came to Paul’s tomb and found two disciples, Titus and Luke, praying; they saw Paul standing in their midst. When those disciples saw them, they fled in terror. As Paul immediately disappeared, the soldiers called after them that they were not pursuing them in order to capture them, but to receive baptism from them; they followed them and testified that they had seen Paul standing among them. When the disciples heard this, they returned and baptized them with joy. Two days later Nero detained them, and they were beheaded for confessing the name of Christ on the sixth day before the Nones of July—namely, on 2 July—the date recorded by Dexter.

Yet Dexter notes above all that one of these three noble soldiers was that same Caesonius Maximus whom he had said was flourishing; that is, the man who at baptism was called Peter by Luke and Titus. He is the one called *Megistos* in Greek, for *Megistos* means “Maximus” in Latin. We must therefore assert that he spent at most two years in exile in Sicily: he had been sent there in the year of the Lord 66 on account of Seneca’s death, and in the year 68, three days after Paul’s death, he died for Christ on 2 July. Read Usuard, Ado, and the Roman Martyrology on that day, [Col. 0205C] and there Cardinal Baronius, who maintains that the names of those three soldiers occur in ancient manuscripts; also read Saint Chrysostom, volume V, in his encomiastic oration on the leaders of the apostles.

### 16. Saint Paul, etc.

The author has now inserted this almost as a digression; otherwise, before mentioning Paul’s arrival in Spain, it ought to have been referred to the year of the Lord 60 or thereabouts, as will be evident from what follows. For this reason the author deliberately uses the past tense here when he says, “Saint Paul wrote the Epistle,” etc., whereas elsewhere, in matters occurring in their proper years, he customarily uses the present tense, saying: “Persius dies. Nero surpasses all others. Lucan perishes,” etc.

#### That Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews was written to the Hebrews of Spain

What we promised above to investigate and establish—in the year of the Lord 64—concerning the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews of Spain must now be presented. Since the matter is novel and, as far as I know, has not previously been examined by anyone, I have decided to investigate it now in detail for the benefit of learned readers. To begin, as they say, from the egg, let us first show that the Epistle to the Hebrews was not sent to those living in Jerusalem or Judaea, nor to any others settled in the East; and, again, that it was not sent to all Hebrews dispersed throughout the world. This leaves room for maintaining that it was sent to the Spanish synagogue—a most celebrated synagogue then existing there, as has been abundantly demonstrated with the strongest testimony in the commentary on the year of Christ 37, and earlier in commentary 2 on the year 35—namely, that of those Jews who had in no way consented to the Lord’s death and had not wished to return to Jerusalem, because among them there had persisted a prophecy concerning the destruction of the Temple erected by Zerubbabel.

That this Epistle was not addressed to all the Jews throughout the world is evident from the fact that interpreters generally infer from its having been written in Rome while Paul was in chains, on the basis of the words in chapter 10: “For you had compassion on those who were in bonds.” Theophylact explains: “You were also a source of consolation to others, and to me who was cast into chains.” Paul’s Greek text reads: “You had compassion on my chains.”

I, however, think that the Apostle wrote it immediately after being released from his chains, when he was preaching freely in Rome, but before he departed from there for any other place; consequently, it was the last in the sequence of his Epistles. Baronius also noted this in the year of the Lord 60, no. 42. I infer it not only from the place it occupies among all Paul’s Epistles, but also from the fact that the Second Epistle to Timothy was unquestionably at least the next-to-last, since in it he says: “I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand.” He summons Timothy from the East, where he was engaged in preaching, to come to him at Rome: “Make haste,” he says in chapter 4, “to come to me quickly,” and again, “Make haste to come before winter.”

In the Epistle to the Hebrews, however, at its conclusion, he says that he is eagerly awaiting the speedy arrival of that same Timothy whom he had summoned: “Know that my son Timothy has been released; with whom, if he comes sooner, I shall see you.” Therefore those who believe that the Second Epistle to Timothy was written after the Epistle to the Hebrews must be judged to think incorrectly. For if, when he wrote to the Hebrews, he was awaiting Timothy’s speedy arrival, he had already written to him to hasten to come to him; otherwise he could not say that Timothy would arrive quickly.

But why all this? Simply so that we may infer from it that Paul did not write this Epistle to Jews dispersed throughout the world, since he promises those to whom he writes that he will depart with Timothy, whose speedy arrival he was awaiting. It is certain that he could not have made such a promise to Jews scattered throughout the world, because in the aforementioned Epistle to Timothy he had already confessed both that the time of his departure was at hand and that he had completed his course. It cannot be believed that he would again traverse the whole world in order to visit Jews scattered everywhere. Therefore it is certain that he wrote not to all, but to some in a particular province. This will become still more certain from what follows.

Nor was it written to those living in Jerusalem or Palestine. The same argument proves this: if he was going to return there again, he had not truly said that he had already completed his course, since he would rather be beginning a new course. On one occasion he had described his great course to the Romans in these words, chapter 15: “So that from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum I have fully preached the Gospel of Christ.” Yet he would have completed an even greater course if he were now to travel from Rome all the way to Jerusalem, since Illyricum lies approximately halfway along the route between the two cities. Indeed, he could not then have claimed that he had even passed through the middle of his course, much less completed it.

But let us proceed to other matters. Timothy, whom Paul hoped to see in the East, was preaching the word of God everywhere, although he had been appointed specifically as bishop of the Ephesians; Paul himself had released him from his chains. But where do we obtain this? We know from chapter 20 and the following chapters of Acts that Timothy had accompanied the Apostle as far as Rome, and from the Epistle to the Philippians, which the two of them sent from Rome. At its beginning we read: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ,” etc. Later, indicating the place and circumstances of the writing, he says: “Thinking that they would arouse affliction for my chains.”

That Paul then sent Timothy from Rome to the East we learn again from chapter 2 of the same Epistle to the Philippians: “I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly.” For this reason, in the Epistle to the Hebrews he calls him “released,” when he says: “Know that our brother Timothy has been released; with whom, if he comes more quickly, I shall see you”—as if he were saying: “I hope that the one whom I first sent there will soon return.”

From this I also derive the following conclusion. Paul calls—or rather summons—Timothy from the East so that he might travel with him to those to whom he was writing. Therefore Paul himself was not planning to travel to the East; otherwise he would not summon Timothy from the East, but would himself go to him. Nor did he need Timothy’s companionship as though he had no other companion. Paul had many other disciples with him at Rome who could accompany him on his journey. He lists them when he writes to Timothy: “Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, and Claudia, and all the brethren greet you”; and earlier he had said that Luke was with him.

Furthermore, when he summons Timothy there, he orders him to bring with him all his belongings, which he had left at Troas: “Bring the cloak”—that is, a garment; Phoebadius, in volume V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* [volume XX of our *Patrologia*], interprets it as a hood—“which I left at Troas with Carpus, when you come; and the books, especially the parchments.” The transportation of his belongings, although it is evidence of a poor man in keeping with apostolic custom, plainly indicates that he was changing his residence.

Again, the words in the Epistle to the Hebrews—“Know that our brother Timothy has been released; with whom, if he comes more quickly, I shall see you”—could in no way have been addressed to the Jerusalem or Eastern Jews. Timothy was not unknown to them, so that the Apostle would need to say to them, “Know him.” Rather, he was as well known to them as Paul himself, since he had been the companion of his entire missionary journey, as the Acts of the Apostles and Paul’s own Epistles abundantly testify. He was therefore writing to others, to whom Timothy was unknown both by face and by reputation.

The meaning is: “Know that I have a disciple whom I greatly love on account of his integrity. Get to know him—that is, begin to become acquainted with him—and you will know him more fully when I see you with him, whom I hope will soon come from the East.” Nor could he have said “I shall see you” to Easterners, since, when he departed from them to be taken in chains to Rome, he is recorded in Acts, chapter 20, as having addressed them in these words:

> And now, behold, I know that you will all see my face no more, among whom I have gone about preaching the kingdom of God. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all; for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.

After much more in the same sense, Saint Luke adds:

> And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. And great weeping arose among them all, and falling upon Paul’s neck they kissed him, grieving most of all at the word which he had spoken, that they would see his face no more.

There Paul certainly testifies that he knows that all those among whom he had passed while preaching the kingdom of God would see his face no more. Therefore, if we are not to call the Apostle a liar, we must conclude that, while in Rome, he did not write to Eastern Hebrews that he would see them again, since these were the very people among whom he had passed, evangelizing the kingdom of God, from the time of his conversion until his Jerusalem imprisonment, from which he was brought to Rome after appealing to Caesar. We are consequently compelled to assert that he sent this Epistle to other Hebrews whom he had never seen.

Add to this that in such a long Epistle he never even lightly hints that he had previously addressed those to whom he writes, nor that he had ever seen them.
