If they were Eastern Hebrews—as is generally believed—with whom he had associated throughout the entire course of his life, not merely throughout his preaching; from whom he had suffered so many persecutions; and of whom he had brought so many, and so great a number, to the faith, it would be remarkable—indeed incredible—if he remembered none of these things. It would certainly overturn the Apostle’s constant epistolary practice. For he is never found to have written to people whom he had previously taught without recalling his preaching.

In the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 2, he says: “When I came to you, brethren, I did not come with superiority of speech.” In the Second, chapter 13: “Behold, this is the third time I am coming to you.” To the Galatians, chapter 1: “But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a Gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed.” To the Philippians, chapter 4: “What you have learned and received and heard and seen in me, do these things.” In the First Epistle to the Thessalonians, chapter 1: “Our Gospel did not come to you in word only, but also in power, as you know what sort of men we were among you for your sake.” In the Second, chapter 2: “Do you not remember that, when I was still with you, I used to tell you these things?”

I omit the Epistles written to particular disciples—Timothy, Titus, and Philemon—in which the same feature is found throughout. Would he then say nothing of this kind in this one Epistle to the Hebrews? Would he not at least have called them his sons or disciples? On the contrary, he speaks at one point of the teachers of these Hebrews, in chapter 13, as though they were quite different people, saying:

> Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; and, contemplating the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith.

If they had received any teaching from him, he would certainly not have remained silent when speaking of others. Indeed, Theodoret, commenting on these words, says that the Apostle is speaking among others of James the brother of John, who had already been killed. This strongly suggests that the Epistle was sent to the Spaniards, especially since Theodoret himself maintains that Paul preached the Gospel nowhere except in Spain after his Roman imprisonment, and that he returned from there to Rome and was beheaded. We shall give his words below.

Finally, it is especially necessary to consider that, if Paul were addressing Hebrews whom he had previously known, there is no doubt that he would have discussed something concerning circumcision. For he had been in continual disagreement with them over this matter, especially since the occasion was pressing: he was speaking of the abrogation of the ancient law in chapter 7, with the words, “For the law brought nothing to perfection.” Yet the Jews to whom he was speaking not only did not observe circumcision together with baptism—as it is clear that the Easterners had erred by doing—but had fallen into the opposite error, believing that baptism could be repeated whenever someone had sinned. The Apostle rebukes this error at length, beginning in chapter 5:

> You have become sluggish in hearing; for although by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you, etc.

In chapter 6, explaining in what respect they had become infants, he gives as the reason that they were returning again to baptism, which nevertheless belongs to the condition of children, and says:

> It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, etc.

Again, in chapter 10, he returns to the same point when he says:

> If we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there remains no sacrifice for sins, etc.

Jews who had embraced baptism with particular devotion could more easily fall into this error than those who wanted to combine circumcision with baptism, as though baptism alone were insufficient for the removal of sins. It is established from what was related above that the Spanish Jews hastened eagerly to baptism, whereas the Jerusalem and Eastern Jews wished to combine it with circumcision. Yet the Apostle attacks not the latter but the former error.

Because, however, this error had arisen from ignorance and from excessive enthusiasm for baptism, he does not rebuke them harshly, but admonishes them gently. For in chapter 6 he says: “But, beloved, we are confident of better things concerning you, and things nearer to salvation, although we speak in this way.”

From what has been said, we have established that the Epistle to the Hebrews was not written to all the Jews dispersed throughout the world, nor specifically to the Jerusalem or Eastern Jews. Let us now see whether it was sent to the Spaniards. This too must be deduced from what has already been said. We established, on the basis of the strong testimony of many authors, that at that time a most distinguished synagogue existed in the Carpetanian province of Spain. If we add to this the Apostle’s vehement desire, expressed to the Romans, to visit Spain; and the fact that everything treated in this Epistle corresponds especially well to those Hebrews—namely, that he had never known them and had never addressed them; that he was obliged and desired to visit them; that they said nothing about the necessity of circumcision; that they had received the faith from other apostles and disciples, not from Paul—namely, from Saints James, Peter, and their disciples, whom he calls their leaders, who spoke the word of God to them; and that after them he himself undertook the ministry of preaching among them, as one who was to take the place of the great James Boanerges—then the case becomes compelling.

He perhaps intimates this in chapter 2, when he says:

> Since the word, having first been spoken through the Lord by those who heard him, was confirmed to us by them.

“By us,” I say, who did not hear the Lord in mortal flesh, as James did, who began to proclaim salvation to you, and in whose place I was confirmed. We examined and demonstrated this point above, when discussing Paul’s arrival in Spain, and showed that it had been divinely revealed to Blessed Amadeus, as he himself writes in the eighth rapture of his *New Apocalypse*.

And when we see that the facts correspond to the truth, we find that what Dexter teaches—namely, that Paul came to Spain with Timothy—is precisely what the Apostle says in this Epistle: “With whom, if he comes more quickly, I shall see you.” Again, what Dexter had related earlier concerning Nero’s bitter persecution of the Spaniards, in which many were put to death as martyrs and still more were stripped of their possessions, is expressed word for word in the Epistle, chapter 10:

> Recall the former days, in which, after you had been enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings: sometimes being made a spectacle through reproaches and tribulations, and sometimes becoming companions of those who were treated in this way. For you had compassion on those in chains, and accepted with joy the plundering of your possessions.

At this point Theophylact says:

> Consider, therefore, how great and noble in character these men were, who for Christ’s sake despised both glory and wealth; then, after being subjected to insults and made a spectacle and object of ridicule, like men hissed and mocked in a theater, they endured the injuries inflicted by the insignificant and contemptible.

We do not read this of other Hebrews.

I pass over the fact—also attested by Dexter—that at this time the Spaniards were especially devoted to hospitality. Paul commends this virtue, which they had so excellently practiced, when he writes in chapter 6:

> For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love which you showed in his name, when you ministered to the saints and continue to minister, etc.

Then in chapter 13:

> Do not forget hospitality.

And below:

> Do not forget beneficence and communion.

Theophylact explains why he does not say, “Pursue hospitality,” but rather, “Do not forget it.” It could have happened that, having been deprived of their worldly goods, they received guests and strangers more sparingly and less frequently. He therefore exhorts them to continue the hospitality which they had previously begun.

Someone may object: If Paul had written to the Spaniards, he would certainly have suggested that he had long been girded for the journey to visit them, and that, had he not been hindered by chains, he would have met them much earlier. Yet this too is not absent from the Epistle. For the Apostle meant nothing else when he said at its conclusion:

> Pray for us. I urge you still more earnestly to do this, so that I may be restored to you more quickly.

It is just as if he had said: “Pray that the things which have kept me away from you and prevented me from coming to you may disappear. Thus I shall be restored to you more quickly; and you would certainly have had me already, had chains not intervened.”

If we ask jurists what “to restore” properly means, Alciatus answers in *De verborum significatione*: “To restore is to place back”—that is, to establish a thing in the condition in which it would have been if nothing had occurred against which restoration had to be made. Spiengelius agrees in his *Lexicon of Law*, under the word *restituere*. He deliberately did not say “to establish the thing in the condition in which it was,” but “in which it would have been,” because restoration consists not only in returning what was taken away, but also in compensating for the loss incurred; for the thing would have been in that condition if it had not been taken away or obstructed.

Now tell me, please, in what condition or place would Paul have been established when he wrote these words, if he were not being held in chains? If we follow his own words, it cannot be denied that he would have been in Spain: “When I begin my journey to Spain,” etc. Therefore he had been taken away chiefly from the Spaniards, not from the Easterners, whom he willingly left; nor from others, whoever they may have been, since he promised to go to no others. He therefore had to be restored to the Spaniards and not to anyone else, when he said, “so that I may be restored to you more quickly.”

To this add what he says to Timothy: “I have completed my course.” The Apostle himself explains this below by saying that the completion of his preaching was still lacking:

> But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear; and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion.

To fulfill the preaching means nothing other than reaching by preaching from the East to the end of the West; and no one doubts that this end was in Spain. For this reason he was strengthened by the Lord and delivered from the mouth of the lion—that is, he was freed from his chains.

He therefore writes to the Spaniards that he will come to them quickly, namely so that the preaching might be fulfilled in them through him. Finally, the following strongly supports this interpretation and leads me to believe that the Epistle was written to the Spanish Hebrews: I read in it that immediately after his imprisonment he would go to those to whom he was writing: “I shall see you more quickly.”

All the holy teachers who discuss Paul’s journey immediately after his imprisonment assert that he went nowhere except to Spain. From this you may see that he was addressing those people. Indeed, Chrysostom, who often places his arrival in Spain after his imprisonment, sometimes adds that he also visited there the Jews to whom he had written. Here are his words from Homily 76 on Matthew:

> After he had therefore spent two years in chains at Rome, he was finally released. Then he went to Spain and visited the Jews there as well. Perhaps he then returned to Rome, when he also suffered execution by Nero’s command.

Chrysostom was speaking of the Jews whom Paul had promised to visit, and he says that he visited them there—that is, in Spain. He therefore admits that he wrote this Epistle to them.

Theophylact gives the same testimony in the preface to the Epistle:

> He himself had already been detained in chains for two years. From there he was permitted to depart, as he himself testifies in the Second Epistle to Timothy, chapter 4: “At my first defense no one stood by me, and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion”—namely, Nero. Then, when he had come to Spain, he perhaps revisited the Jews. Theophylact had previously begun to speak of those Jews of whom Paul had said: “With Timothy, if he comes sooner, I shall see you.”

He adds that from there—Spain—Paul returned to Rome and was put to death by Nero. Thus they nowhere believe that Paul preached except in Spain, in accordance with his promise, and that there he visited the Hebrews as he had promised. From there he returned to Rome, where he was beheaded. Theodoret also writes this in his commentary on chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Philippians:

> For two years he first lived at Rome by himself, residing in his own hired lodging. But when he had departed from there for Spain, and had also delivered the divine Gospel to them, he returned; and then he was beheaded.

From these statements I construct a new argument. Paul promises the Hebrews that he will come quickly, and so quickly that, unless Timothy comes more quickly, he will depart for them without him. For that is the meaning of the words, “with whom, if he comes more quickly, I shall see you”: that is, “I shall see you with him, provided that he comes more quickly; otherwise”—as follows from the statement—“if he does not come more quickly, I shall depart without him.”

Why does he desire Timothy’s speedy arrival unless it is so that he may depart with him, since he was about to leave immediately for the Hebrews? Yet as soon as he is released from his chains, he hastens to Spain, according to Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Theodoret, among others. The Hebrews to whom he sent the Epistle must therefore have been there. For if they were elsewhere, Paul could not truthfully say that he was preparing to make his journey to them so quickly that, unless Timothy came more quickly, he would depart there without him, when in fact he would first have to travel to Spain, as is established.

But enough of this, etc.

### 17. Lucius Annaeus, etc.

Since Seneca and Lucan were killed at the same time, during the suppression of the Pisonian conspiracy, I do not know how Eusebius came to assign Seneca’s death to the year of the Lord 67, when, according to his own report, Lucan died in the year of the Lord 66. Dexter is therefore much more consistent in reporting that Seneca too was killed in the same year.

Ambrosius Morales agrees with them in Book IX, chapter 9, though he must be corrected slightly on one point: he says that Seneca died in March, whereas he ought to have said May. For Lucan, who fell first according to Eusebius and Dexter, died on the last day of April. It is therefore appropriate to say that Seneca died in the following month, May.

He was born at Córdoba to Seneca the Elder, a distinguished orator, and to Helbia, or Albina. His father’s declamations are extant among the works of the son, as Morales correctly asserts and proves. These parents had three sons: Annaeus Seneca the philosopher, Nero’s tutor; Junius Gallio; and Annaeus Mela, the father of Lucan.

Seneca married Pompeia Paulina, a woman of the highest nobility. When, by Nero’s command, she saw Seneca releasing his soul by cutting his veins, she too had her veins cut, so that she might accompany her beloved husband even in death. But by the emperor’s favor her life was spared.

Eusebius adds that Seneca died not only by the cutting of his veins—the manner of death he had chosen, with the emperor’s permission—but also by taking poison. When he had been removed from life, his own Zoilus was not lacking: I mean Xiphilinus, the abbreviator of Cassius Dio, who heaped many insults upon him. Above all, he criticized him for living differently from what he wrote: although he advised withdrawal from the city, he himself lived in the palace; although in his writings he defined wealth as something to be despised, he eagerly embraced it in practice. But Xiphilinus is heard by no one; therefore he alone speaks.

Saint Augustine, in Book VI of *The City of God*, chapter 11, records that Seneca openly rebuked the Jews, but, although Christians were already at that time the Jews’ most bitter enemies, dared to mention them on neither side, lest he either praise them contrary to the ancient custom of his homeland or condemn them contrary, perhaps, to his own inclination. This sufficiently suggests that he secretly adhered to the Christian faith. Dexter repeats the same point here; but we have treated the matter above, under the year of Christ 64.

### 18. In this same year Saint Matthias, etc.

Equilinus reports in Book III, chapter 149, that he was first overwhelmed with stones and finally struck on the head with an axe. Everyone reports that he was killed in Judaea. Since, as I shall now say, the Jerusalem war began in this very year and all Judaea was in turmoil, it was easy to kill Saint Matthias at that time.

His most sacred body is preserved at Rome in the church of Saint Mary Major, where an ancient image of him executed in mosaic can be seen with this inscription:

> ME TENET. ARA. PRIOR.

And so it truly is, for the sacred remains of his body lie beneath the high altar, in the apse constructed at the expense of Cardinal Pinelli from various beautiful marbles. His head, enclosed in a silver reliquary on the feast day of the same holy Apostle, is offered for veneration to the Christian people, who gather there in great crowds.

### 19. In this same year the Jerusalem war, etc.

Cardinal Baronius assigns the beginning of the Jerusalem war to the year 68, moved by the fact that, according to Josephus in Book XX of the *Antiquities*, chapter 19, and in Book II of the *Jewish War*, chapter 13, the war against the Jews began when they revolted from the Romans, in the twelfth year of Nero, in the month of May.

The Cardinal, however, follows a substantially different reckoning of Nero’s imperial years from ours. He maintains that Nero began to rule in the year of the Lord 56, whereas we place it in the year 55, following Dexter’s reckoning, which among others is adopted by Ambrosius Morales in Book IX, chapter 6. Indeed, we shall show below, under the year 68, that Baronius is not consistent with himself but ultimately comes over to our position.

If, therefore, we count the years of Nero’s reign from the year of the Lord 55, counting that year 55 inclusively as well, the result is—as Dexter asserts—that the Jerusalem war began in the year of the Lord 66, since this is the twelfth year of Nero designated by Josephus.

### 20. Amphitria, etc.

Usuard mentions the same Saint Liberatus on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January—the day on which Dexter records that he died—saying: “At Amphitrea, Saint Liberatus.” Peter of Equilium, bishop, also discusses him in Book XII, final chapter, no. 17, in these words:

> The confessor Liberatus and Bishop Gregory became illustrious at Amphitrea on the same day—that is, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January.

We shall discuss Saint Gregory below, together with Dexter, under the year 94.

As for the city Amphitria, or Amphitrea, when Dexter explains that in his own time it was called Fita, I have nothing to add except that, in the course of time, with F changed to H according to Spanish custom, we now call it Hita. The Romans called it Fita, or perhaps Fitriam, after removing the first syllable of the name Amphitria. The name seems Greek to me, and provides no slight indication that such a town was once founded by Greeks, as many others in Spain were.

Ptolemy names Alternia in Carpetania, not far from Caraca, or Guadalajara, where Hita now stands. Therefore the name appears to be corrupt in his text, so that we should now read Alternia [Col. 0212C] in place of Amphitria.

### 21. In this same year the holy apostles Peter, etc.

Those who postpone the apostles’ death to the year 69 or 70 of the Lord also postpone their return to the City to the aforementioned year 68, so that they might reach Rome at least one or two years before their death. Since Dexter maintains that they were killed in the year 68, he was obliged to assign the apostles’ return to the year 66.

And, in my opinion, this is closer to the truth. For, as even the authors of the opposing faction concede, the reason for bringing the apostles back to Rome was that the monstrous persecution which the most savage Nero had raised against the Christians came to their attention, while he wickedly shifted onto them the charge of the fire of Rome, which he himself had set.

According to the common judgment of the authors whom Cardinal Baronius cites and follows in his notes on 14 June in the Roman Martyrology, the burning of the city occurred in the year of the Lord 65; it began on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, that is, on 29 July. As soon as the apostles received news of the affliction of the Roman Church, therefore, although they were far from the City—Paul being in Spain, Peter in Britain or Africa—they immediately set out for Rome, lest they abandon their sheep in so great a tribulation.

For they were not hirelings who, seeing the wolf from a distance, fled, but shepherds who wished to rescue the sheep from the wolf’s jaws. Thus, in the year following the fire—namely, 66—they returned to Rome.

### 22. The memory of Saint Peter flourishes, etc.

We have discussed him at length above, under the year 37. As for what Dexter adds—that he was killed at Ratis, in the region of Ophir, which received this name from the descendants of Ophir who had arrived there—this compels us to discuss the precise location of the region of Ophir. Since this question is closely related to the one concerning the true location of Tarshish, it has seemed necessary to treat both together. Saint Jerome did the same when writing to Marcella in Letter 133, as did all who have hitherto written about Ophir or Tarshish.

## The places where Tarshish and Ophir existed are investigated in detail.

It is truly remarkable how much this question has tortured human ingenuity [Col. 0213B]. Josephus maintains that Tarshish is the same as Tarsus, the maritime city of Cilicia from which Paul originated; and therefore that everywhere in Sacred Scripture *Tarshish* should be rendered *Tarsus*. Rethicius of Augustodunum does not disagree with him in his commentary on the Song of Songs, chapter V, whom Saint Jerome cites in Letter 133; nor does the author of the Hebrew dictionary called *The Ark of Noah*, who says: “Perhaps it is preferable not to admit this meaning so readily, but to interpret it here and always as the city of Tarsus.”

The Septuagint translators usually render Tarshish as Carthage, the city of Africa. Thus, in Isaiah 23:1, where the Hebrew has, “Howl, ships of Tarshish,” they render it, “Ships of Carthage”; and in verse 6, for the Hebrew “Cross over to Tarshish,” they give, “Cross over to Carthage”; and in verse 10, where the Hebrew reads, “Daughter of Tarshish,” they say, “Daughter of Carthage”; and in verse 14, “Howl, ships of Tarshish,” they again render, “Ships of Carthage.” The same occurs often elsewhere. Yet they do not always do so, for sometimes they retain the word *Tarshish*, as may be seen in 3 Kings 10:22: “For the ships of Tarshish,” etc. [Col. 0213C] Likewise in Isaiah 66:19: “I will send survivors from them to the nations, to Tarshish,” etc. At other times they render it as Chalcedon, the maritime city situated opposite Constantinople, or Byzantium, as may be seen in Ezekiel 27. For where the Hebrew has, in verse 12, “The merchants of Tarshish were your merchants,” the Septuagint gives, “The merchants of Chalcedon were your merchants.”

The Vulgate likewise displays the same variety. At several points it translates *Tarshish* as “sea,” as in Isaiah 23: “Howl, ships of the sea”; “Cross over the seas”; and “Daughter of the sea,” although the Hebrew text has *Tarshish* in these places. Sometimes it renders it as Carthage, as in Ezekiel 27: “The Carthaginians were your merchants”; sometimes as sapphire, as in Ezekiel 10: “Like the appearance of a sapphire stone”; sometimes as hyacinth, as in Song of Songs 5: “His hands are full of hyacinths”; and sometimes as chrysolite—as in Exodus 28 and Ezekiel 28—for the stone called *Tarshish*. Finally, it often leaves the name itself untouched, as though it signified some region or city, for example in Psalm 47: “With a violent wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish,” [Col. 0213D] and in Jonah 1: “So that he might flee to Tarshish.”

It is therefore not surprising that, when Saint Jerome wrote to Marcella, he regarded the name as homonymous or equivocal, since it signified many things: a certain region of India, the stone called *Tarshish*, and, because of the resemblance of that stone, even the sea itself. In his commentary on Jonah 1 he agrees with Josephus, who believed that when the prophet is said to have gone to Tarshish, he went to Tarsus, the city of Cilicia. Yet Jerome admits that the first letter in the names is changed—namely, Θ into Τ—and adds: “As far as can be understood from the Book of Chronicles, a certain place in India is so called.” [Col. 0214A] He then reports that the Hebrews of his own time generally held that the sea was called *Tarshish*.

As for Ophir, Jerome himself says in Book V of his commentary on Isaiah 13: “Ophir is a place of India, where the finest gold is produced, just as we read in Genesis concerning the river Pishon, etc., which is believed to be the Ganges of India.” Theodoret agrees in his commentary on 3 Kings, question 31; so do Procopius in the same place, where Rabanus and Strabus appear in the *Ordinary Gloss*, as well as Nizetas, Abulensis, Lyra, Forerius, Adamus Ribera, and others. They disagree, however, when assigning the region, province, and site in which Ophir was located. Some wish it to have been in eastern India: among them, some think it was the island of Zophala, others Taprobane, others Pegu, and others, according to their preference, some entirely different place. More recent writers, however, contend that it was the Peruvian region of western India, both because the Hebrew letters of the name *Ophir* agree with those of *Peru*, and because of the immense quantity of gold and silver extracted from that region. Acosta discussed this at length in Book I, chapter 13; Barrerius in a special treatise on Ophir [Col. 0214B]; and Barradas in Book V, chapter 11, of his *Harmony of the Gospels*.

Again, some confuse Ophir with Tarshish, while others distinguish them. To the former, Divine Scripture appears to speak indiscriminately of both, as is evident from chapters 9 and 10 of 3 Kings, where it reports, without distinction, that Solomon’s and Hiram’s fleet sailed at one time to Tarshish and at another to Ophir. To the latter, they appear to be different regions, although one and the same fleet visited both.

What, then, should one think amid such disagreement? Here too, let everyone abound in his own opinion. My own opinion in this matter is strongly inclined to the view that Tarshish and Ophir, which are celebrated in Sacred Scripture and were frequented by Solomon’s fleet for the sake of gold and silver, were in Spain. More precisely, Ophir was in the district of Braga, as Dexter asserts here, while Tarshish was in Baetica, or Andalusia, where [Col. 0214C] ancient Tartessus was situated. The latter view was defended vigorously and at length by Goropius Beccanus in several books of his *Hispania*, especially the fifth and sixth. Ludovicus Nonnius follows him in chapter 12 of his *Hispania*. The same opinion was held by Joannes Baptista Suarez de Salazar in Book I, chapter 4, of his *Antiquities of Cádiz*; Pineda in Book IV, chapter 14, of *The Affairs of Solomon*; Ribera in his commentary on Jonah 1; Forerius on Isaiah 23: “Daughter of Tarshish, it is no longer a girdle for you”; Soto Major on Song of Songs 5, on the words “His hands are golden cylinders full of Tarshish”; and Thomas Bozius in Book XV, chapter 18, of *The Signs of the Church*. Bozius says that Solomon’s fleet customarily sailed around the coasts of Africa and made for Spain and the city of Tartessus, which they wish to be called Tarshish by Sacred Scripture.

Let us prove each point separately. First, it must be regarded as certain that Tarshish and Ophir were not altogether the same region. Jeremiah 10:9 plainly demonstrates this: “Silver beaten out of Tarshish is brought, and gold from Ophaz,” where the original [Col. 0214D] Hebrew has “and gold from Ophir.” From this it is clear that gold was customarily brought from a different place than silver; therefore there were two regions or provinces, not one and the same.

Again, Genesis 10 describes the distribution and renewal of the whole world after the universal Flood among the sons and grandsons of Noah. Each of them received a different province and gave it his own name, as may be gathered from the words: “These are the families of Noah according to their peoples and nations” (Genesis 10:32), together with the words, “according to their kindreds, languages, generations, lands, and nations” (ibid., verse 20). These words imply that the author described not only the generations of Noah’s sons and grandsons by their designated names, but also [Col. 0215A] their lands and peoples, although he did not report names for those lands different from the names of their founders. Among the names of the founders of various regions are Tarshish and Ophir: Tarshish as the grandson of Japheth, son of Noah; Ophir as Noah’s fifth-generation descendant, not from Japheth but from Shem.

A small difficulty now arises, for this testimony from Genesis seems to favor our opponents. The three sons of Noah occupied the three principal divisions of the world in such a way that Japheth received Europe with his sons. This is evident from Tubal, who inhabited Spain and Italy, and from Gomer, who inhabited Gaul. Ham, with his sons and grandsons, received Palestine, Egypt, and Africa; for, as Jerome testifies, Phut, Ham’s grandson, possessed Africa, while Canaan, his brother, and Cush, the father of both, possessed the province of the Canaanites, or Palestine. Finally, Shem, the eldest, occupied the eastern [Col. 0215B] part of Asia with his sons and descendants, as the very words of the same chapter demonstrate: “And their dwelling was from Mesha as one goes toward Sephar, the eastern mountain. These are the sons of Shem.”

Thus we learn from Isidore, Book IX, chapter 2, of the *Etymologies*, and from a very ancient anonymous author who wrote a *Chronicle of the World* in the thirteenth year of the reign of Alexander Severus and in the year 236 of Our Lord. His work survives in Henry Canisius, volume II of *Antiquae Lectiones*, together with the compiler of the *Chronographical History*, a contemporary of Charlemagne. In chapter 2 this author says:

“After the Flood, the lands of the three brothers, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, were divided. Shem, the firstborn, possessed the region from Persia and Bactria far away as India, and as far as Rhinocorura. Ham, the second, possessed the region from Rhinocorura as far as Gadira”—that is, as far as the Strait of Cádiz, but on the African side to the south. “Japheth, the third, possessed the region from Media as far as Jadira to the north”—that is, to the northern side of the strait, which begins at Spain. “Japheth has the river Tigris, which divides Media and [Col. 0215C] Babylonia; Shem has the Euphrates; and Ham has the Gihon, which is called the Nile.”

Here is a division of Europe, Asia, and Africa according to the three rivers of Paradise. Later, in chapter 8, the same Anonymous author says of Japheth’s descendants: “Tubal, from whom came the Italians; Elisa, from whom came the Sicilians; Tarshish, from whom came the Iberians; Cethim, from whom came the Romans, who are also the Latins.” Further on he says:

“These are the sons of Japheth: the Medes and Albanians, etc.; the Calabrians, Latins, Gauls, Aquitanians, Bastetani, Cerretani, Lusitanians, Vaccaei, Cluniacenses, etc. Those among them who know letters are the Iberians, Latins, Spaniards, Greeks, Medes, and Armenians. Their lands are Media, Albania, etc.; Galicia, Lusitania, Italy, Iberia, Greater Spain, etc.”

He distinguishes Iberia from Spain in this way: for him Iberia is the same as Baetica, while Greater Spain is the same as Tarraconensis, as the author himself explains in chapter 7, saying:

“The peoples who possess languages are the Hebrews, Assyrians, Chaldeans, etc.; Latins, Gauls, and Tarraconensian Spaniards.”

Elsewhere he consistently distinguishes Lusitania from these. For this reason he calls Tarraconensis [Col. 0215D] “Greater Spain,” since it is much larger than Baetica and Lusitania.

The question now arises concerning Ophir, who is numbered among the sons of Joktan, from the stock of Shem. It seems to follow that he lived in eastern India, for this is said of him and his brothers: “Joktan begot Elmodad, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab; all these were the sons of Joktan. And their dwelling was from Mesha as one goes toward Sephar, the eastern mountain.”

At the very least, however, it follows from this that Tarshish was part of Europe, since it is numbered among Japheth’s descendants: “The sons of Javan were Elishah and Tarshish,” while Javan was the son of Japheth.

But as for the proposed difficulty concerning Ophir, it is easily solved from the very words of our author. Dexter does not teach that Ophir himself inhabited the district of Braga, but that his descendants did. We therefore concede that Ophir chose for himself some region of eastern [Col. 0216A] Asia, although it is not specifically established that it was India. We add, however, that his descendants, moving their settlement from there, arrived in Lusitania and gave the region of Braga the name of their ancestor.

This should not be considered unprecedented, since many assert that the Moors of Africa came from India, as Strabo records in Book XVII: “There are some who say that the Moors are Indians who came down to this place with Hercules.” I also read that learned men hold that Ophir himself established colonies elsewhere besides India.

This seems sufficiently plausible to me for another reason: the line of Japheth spread from Spain, or the boundaries of Europe, throughout the western world and into America. It could therefore have happened that other descendants of Shem, to whom some part of all Asia had perhaps fallen, came to the Spains, which the descendants of Japheth had been unable to fill entirely, since they had inhabited not only Europe but also the half of the world that we call America.

I infer this from the blessing Noah gave to his younger son Japheth: “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in [Col. 0216B] the tents of Shem, and may Canaan be his servant.” To this must be added what the sacred author placed after listing Japheth’s generations: “From these the islands of the nations were divided in their lands, each according to his language, families, and nations.”

Noah therefore prophesied concerning Japheth that he would be so greatly enlarged that he would reach the provinces of Shem’s sons. This was fulfilled in the following way: Europe, which Japheth first received, passed through Spain and then filled America, until it reached the boundaries of the East, where Shem’s descendants lived. This was indeed an enlargement beyond that of his brothers, and an acquisition and division among his people of the islands of the nations, something not said of the others. For all America is full of islands, and America itself is also regarded as an island.

Thus among Japheth’s sons are numbered Tubal, who inhabited Spain; Gomer, whose name is still preserved by one of the Fortunate Islands; Magog, who gave his name to eastern Tartary; and Javan, whose name we recognize in two islands of the East, [Col. 0216C] namely Greater and Lesser Java. This, then, was Japheth’s enlargement, until he dwelt in the tents of Shem.

There is therefore nothing surprising if some of Shem’s descendants moved in the opposite direction, toward the West, since it was the region of Japheth, who had invaded their lands. This is sufficiently demonstrated by Lud, son of Shem, from whom Lydia, a distinguished part of Asia, received its name, as we learn from Isaiah 66, where the original has *Lud* in place of Lydia. Since it is established from what has been said that Lud, as a son of Shem, inhabited the East, it consequently follows that his descendants moved from East to West and founded the people of Lydia after the name of their ancestor. We believe that the same happened with the descendants of Ophir.

But let us derive the same conclusion from another source. I infer it from the fact that the Tyrian merchants visited the gold mines of Ophir and the silver mines of Tarshish in one and the same voyage. It follows that the two places were not far from each other. If Tarshish and Ophir had been in India, this voyage would have had to be made through the Red Sea [Col. 0216D], not through the Mediterranean, as it was in fact made. Since it was conducted through the Mediterranean, it had to proceed not eastward but westward, and therefore not to India but toward the boundaries of Europe.

Let us prove each point, since we leave nothing to the reader’s indulgence. In 3 Kings 10:11, we are told that the fleet of the Tyrian king regularly sailed to Ophir and brought gold from there. The text says: “The fleet of Hiram, which carried gold from Ophir, brought from Ophir a very great quantity of thyine wood and precious stones.” [Col. 0217A]” Again, in verse 22, the same fleet is said to have brought gold and silver from Tarshish. Solomon’s fleet accompanied it at that time in conducting the same commerce: “For the king’s fleet, together with the fleet of Hiram, went to Tarshish once every three years, bringing from there gold and silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.”

Again, in 3 Kings 9:26, both fleets are said to have sailed together to Ophir: “King Hiram sent in the fleet his servants, seamen who knew the sea, together with Solomon’s servants. They came to Ophir and brought from there to King Solomon four hundred and twenty talents of gold.”

Thus Hiram’s fleet, together with Solomon’s fleet, went to Ophir and Tarshish in the same voyage, as though they were provinces customarily visited together; consequently, they were not very far apart.

Nor should anyone suppose—as I once read in a certain author—that Solomon built two fleets, one of which sailed through the Red Sea to eastern Ophir, while the other sailed through the Mediterranean to western Tarshish. Let him read 3 Kings 22. There it is said that King Jehoshaphat built fleets on the sea to sail to Ophir for gold—intending, of course, to restore or repeat Solomon’s voyage—and that they were unable to sail because they were wrecked at Ezion-geber.

When this same history is related again in 2 Chronicles 20, the fleets which in the Book of Kings are said to have been prepared at Ezion-geber [Col. 0217B] for Ophir, but unable to sail because they were wrecked, are said to have been prepared for Tarshish. The text reads:

“After this Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, entered into an alliance with Ahaziah, king of Israel, whose works were most wicked. He became his partner in making ships to sail to Tarshish, and they built a fleet at Ezion-geber. Then Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying: ‘Because you have entered into an alliance with Ahaziah, the Lord has struck down your works’; and the ships were broken and could not sail to Tarshish.”

The same fleet is therefore said indiscriminately to have sailed to Ophir and Tarshish, as though the two places were not far apart. Hiram’s and Solomon’s fleets were thus both at Ezion-geber.

But here is the difficulty: 3 Kings 9:26 expressly states that Ezion-geber, and the fleet built by Hiram and Solomon, were on the shore of the Red Sea: “King Solomon also made a fleet at Ezion-geber, which is near Elath, on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom. Hiram sent his [Col. 0217C] servants, seamen, with Solomon’s servants.” From Ezion-geber, they had to sail through the Red Sea not westward but toward eastern India, whether they were bound for Tarshish or Ophir; for whichever of the two places they were heading, they sailed from Ezion-geber, as we have already shown.

However, if we can show that the Ezion-geber mentioned here was not situated on the Arabian Gulf, which by a special usage we call the Red Sea, but near the Mediterranean Sea, the testimony will not stand against us but in our favor. Many considerations prove this.

First, Solomon’s fleet made the same voyage that Hiram’s fleet and his servants had repeatedly made. For this reason Sacred Scripture calls Hiram’s servants seamen who knew the sea. The voyage was first regularly undertaken by the Tyrian king, and from there David undoubtedly obtained all the gold of Ophir that he left to his son for the expenses of the Lord’s Temple, as described in [Col. 0217D] 1 Chronicles 29.

But the Tyrians could not have made this voyage through the Red Sea; they necessarily made it through the Mediterranean, beside which Tyre itself lies. An important argument to this effect is supplied by 2 Chronicles 2, where Hiram is said to have written to Solomon:

“We will cut timber from Lebanon and bring it to you in rafts by sea to Joppa; and you shall transport it from there to Jerusalem.”

Since Joppa—now Jaffa—is on the Mediterranean, it follows that the Tyrian rafts were not on the Red Sea but on the Mediterranean.

Someone may say that 3 Kings 9 does not state that Hiram sent his ships, which were in the Mediterranean, with Solomon’s fleet, but only his seamen: “Hiram sent his servants, seamen who knew the sea, with Solomon’s servants.” This could have happened even if Solomon’s fleet was on the Red Sea.

But when the same history is related in [Col. 0218A] 2 Chronicles 8, Hiram is said to have sent his ships as well as his servants: “Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and to Elath, on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom. Hiram sent him ships by the hands of his servants, together with seamen who knew the sea; and they went with Solomon’s servants to Ophir.”

Let our opponents explain how Tyrian ships could have entered the Red Sea. Unless they were carried from sea to sea on wagons, or perhaps brought there by some other means, I cannot measure the route by which they traveled.

The same conclusion follows from 3 Kings 10: “The king’s fleet went with Hiram’s fleet by sea to Tarshish.” Here it is evident that not only Tyrian sailors accompanied Solomon’s fleet, but Hiram’s fleet itself did so. The word *fleet* signifies a number of ships.

Moreover, Strabo and Aristotle testify that the Tyrians and Phoenicians themselves carried great quantities of gold and silver from Tartessus in Spain and frequently conducted this voyage and commerce. Goropius and Nonnius, cited above, report their testimony. This is [Col. 0218B] not surprising, since the city of Cádiz was founded by Tyrians, as Pomponius Mela states in Book III, chapter 6:

“Cádiz bears, on one horn, a wealthy city of the same name, and on the other, a temple of Egyptian Hercules, distinguished for its religious antiquity and riches; the Tyrians founded them.”

Regarding the time of its foundation, he adds: “The number of years during which it has endured begins from the time of the fall of Troy.”

The anonymous author contemporary with Alexander Severus, whom we cited above, does not differ greatly from this account when he writes that Cádiz and the Balearic Islands were inhabited—chapter 8—by Canaanites and Jebusites at the time when they were expelled from their homes by Joshua son of Nun, who led the Israelite people into the Promised Land.

Strabo in Book III of his *Geography*, Mela himself in Book III, chapter 6, Solinus in chapter 34 of his *Marvels of the World*, and Dionysius of Alexandria in his *Description of the World* also report that not only Cádiz but Carthaea, Abdera, Málaga, and several other coastal cities of Spain were founded by Tyrians or Phoenicians. Their testimony is cited by Alderete in Book II, chapters 3 and 4, of his *Antiquities of Spain*; Tarapha in his book on the Kings of Spain; Pineda; and Nonnius.

[Col. 0218C] Indeed, what happened in our own age to the Portuguese in eastern India evidently also happened long ago to the Tyrians and Phoenicians: for the sake of their commerce they established trading stations and cities, especially in the region of Tartessus, where the sun’s bounty produced a greater abundance of gold and silver. Nonnius writes:

“Certainly, the fertility of the surrounding region, its unfailing abundance of gold and silver, and the unanimous judgment of writers concerning it make me agree with Goropius without reluctance. Above all, Strabo and Aristotle say that the Tyrians and Phoenicians themselves, who were sent with Solomon’s fleet, brought an immense quantity of silver from this neighboring region.”

Wherever the Tyrians had their trading stations, commercial cities, and gold mines, and from wherever they were accustomed to carry away gold and silver, there Solomon’s ships certainly sailed. We have seen, however, that the Tyrians sailed not to eastern India but to Spain.

The same conclusion is supported by what is said in Jonah 1 concerning Jonah’s flight to Tarshish: “Jonah arose to flee [Col. 0218D] to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish; he paid its fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish.”

Here is a ship sailing to Tarshish. But from where did it depart? Not from some port of the Arabian or Red Sea, but from the city of Joppa, which lies on the Mediterranean.

Some attempt to evade this testimony by claiming that *Tarshish* there does not designate a particular region but the sea itself. But if they are confronted with the consequence—that when Solomon’s fleet is said to have gone to Tarshish, this merely means that it went out to sea, so that the gold and silver it brought from Ophir, as well as the algum wood, peacocks, apes, and elephants’ teeth, would have been drawn not from some land but from the sea itself—they have no satisfactory answer.

Either, then, Tarshish denotes a particular region of the world in the history of Jonah as well, [Col. 0219A] or it denotes one nowhere in Sacred Scripture. The latter cannot be admitted. This is especially clear because, if anywhere Tarshish must signify not the sea itself but a certain region, it must do so in Jonah. There it is said not only that Jonah attempted to go to Tarshish, but that at Joppa he found a ship prepared to go to Tarshish. No one will say that this phrase signifies that the ship was going not to one province rather than another but merely to the sea. Who would say that a ship is going to the sea when it is already at sea? These points are therefore sufficiently clear.

There is one consideration that has deterred writers from our opinion: namely, that 3 Kings 9 and 2 Chronicles 8 expressly say that Solomon’s and Hiram’s fleets, which sailed to Tarshish, were built at Ezion-geber, near Elath, on the shore of the Red Sea. If the sacred text itself says that they were on the Red Sea, who would dare transfer them to the Mediterranean? This seems especially difficult because, as is evident [Col. 0219B] from Numbers 33, Ezion-geber was the thirty-second encampment of the Israelites in the desert and does not seem to have been on the shore of the Mediterranean but inland.

Yet I can construct an argument of the same kind from the testimony of the prophet Jonah, where the sacred text plainly states that the ship going to Tarshish departed from Joppa, the well-known port of the Mediterranean. Who, then, would dare assert the opposite and transfer the voyage to Tarshish to the Red Sea? At the very least, we possess a testimony of Sacred Scripture as clear as that of our opponents. Therefore, even if we had nothing else in our favor, this single testimony would make our opinion as probable as theirs is considered by them.

If, however, we investigate carefully what is more probable, we shall find many reasons supporting our position. Besides the arguments we shall immediately adduce, there are two considerations that prove that the testimony concerning Ezion-geber on the Red Sea does not [Col. 0219C] oppose us, and that it signifies not what our opponents think but what we maintain.

The first is that the province in which that port—whatever port it was called Ezion-geber—was located is determined in the same text, namely the land of Idumea. The text says in 3 Kings 9: “King Solomon also made a fleet at Ezion-geber, which is near Elath, on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Idumea”; and in 2 Chronicles 8: “which is in the land of Edom.”

Now the land of Edom, or Idumea, does not border the Red Sea, which we call the Arabian Sea because of its proximity to Arabia. Rather, it lies westward beside the Mediterranean, and to the north beside the land of Judea, the Promised Land. Anyone can see this clearly on the geographical map of Abraham Ortelius, included in his *Theatrum Orbis* under number 66. He writes:

“Judea is joined to Idumea on the west and south, though with uncertain boundaries.”

And again:

“The Idumeans inhabit the region from the emergence of Lake Serbonis [Col. 0219D] westward; their cities are Maresha, Rhinocorura, Gaza, Anthedon, Ashkelon, and Azotus.”

All these cities lie on the shore of the Mediterranean. Lake Serbonis is near Damietta, where the Nile flows into the Mediterranean through its eastern mouth, and Azotus is the port nearest to Joppa. Ortelius derived this information from Ptolemy, Josephus, and others.

Consider also Strabo’s words, which support the same conclusion:

“The western extremities of Judea, near Cassius, are held by the Idumeans, and the lake of Serbonis”—that is, the lake of Serbonis, or Damietta, which is beside the sea; plainly the Mediterranean.

You can therefore see how far that port, Ezion-geber, was from the sea called the Red Sea. Indeed, the same testimony proves that it was situated nearer the Mediterranean, since Idumea has been shown to lie not on the shore of the Red Sea but on that of the Mediterranean.

The thirty-second encampment of the Israelites called Ezion-geber belonged to an entirely different [Col. 0220A] region and, at the very least, could not have been on the shore of the Red Sea. After the Israelites had once withdrawn from that sea, they never again reached its shore. The place described here was far from the Red Sea. From there they first came to Kadesh, where Miriam, the sister of Moses, was buried.

Hear Moses’ words in Numbers 20 concerning the location of Kadesh:

“Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, saying: ‘You know all the labor that has overtaken us. Behold, we are stationed in the city of Kadesh, which is at the extreme limits of your territory. We beg you to allow us to pass through your land.’”

They were therefore already very near the Promised Land. They had reached Kadesh, which was at the extreme boundary of Edom, so that once they had crossed Idumea they might take possession of the desired land.

Observe, please, where the sacred text places the boundaries of Edom, so that you may infer how near the Israelites already were to the land of Canaan and how far from the Red Sea. In the same chapter of Numbers, it is later said that, when passage through Idumea was refused and they had moved their camp from Kadesh, “they came to Mount [Col. 0220B] Hor, which is at the borders of the land of Edom,” where Aaron died. Chapter 21 adds that there, on that mountain, they triumphed over the Canaanite who had come out against them.

See how close they were to the Promised Land of Canaan. As for the statement, “They set out from Mount Hor by the road leading to the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom,” this does not mean that they returned to that sea. It means that they did not set out directly from the borders of Edom. Since they had been forbidden to pass through Idumea, they were compelled to go around it, and in making that circuit they retreated for a short distance by the road leading toward the Red Sea. This is made clear by the encampments they occupied, listed in Numbers 33.

What, then, is the meaning of the explicit statement in 3 Kings 9 that Ezion-geber was the port of the ships of Tarshish on the shore of the Red Sea? The solution is not difficult. Indeed, this is the second of the two considerations I said worked in our favor. [Col. 0220C]

In Sacred Scripture, the name “Red Sea” is not always applied to the Arabian Gulf. Sometimes it signifies the Dead Sea, or Lake Asphaltites; sometimes it even signifies the Mediterranean itself, although more frequently it denotes the Arabian Gulf, which the Israelites crossed on dry ground.

Let us give examples of both meanings. In Exodus 23, when God defines the land that he promised to give Israel, who at that time were stationed at Mount Sinai, he says to Moses in verse 31:

“I will set your boundaries from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the river. I will deliver the inhabitants of the land into your hands,” etc.

Nothing is more certain than that in this passage the expression “Red Sea” does not signify the Red Sea in the ordinary sense—unless someone wishes to say that, immediately upon crossing the Red Sea, the Israelites had already set foot in the Promised Land. That assumption would overturn the entire history of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua, as well as a large part of the Psalms, in which nothing is asserted more frequently than their forty years of [Col. 0220D] wandering in the desert and their delay before entering the Promised Land.

Certainly, if the Red Sea were the boundary of the Promised Land, God would have promised at Mount Sinai what he had already given. But such statements are nonsense. God is therefore defining the length of the Promised Land from east to west when he says, “I will set your boundaries from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines.”

Since everyone agrees that the Sea of the Philistines is the Mediterranean, because the Philistines inhabited its shores, as may be seen in Strabo, Josephus, and others, it remains that by the name “Red Sea,” which is set opposite it to the east, God intends the Dead Sea. The Dead Sea lies east of the Mediterranean and is a definite boundary of the Promised Land.

In the original Hebrew, therefore, the word which the Vulgate here translates as “Red” is *Suph*, which properly signifies that which is an end or boundary. [Col. 0221A] There are countless examples of this meaning in Sacred Scripture.

Ecclesiastes 7:3 says: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, for in that house the end of all mankind is recalled.” And Ecclesiastes 12:13 says: “Let us all hear the conclusion of the discourse.” In both places, *Suph* is used for “end.”

Daniel 4:8 says: “Its appearance reached to the ends of the whole earth”; and Daniel 7:28: “Thus far is the end of the matter.” In both places the Hebrew word rendered “ends” and “end” is *Suph*.

2 Chronicles 20:16 says: “You will find them at the summit of the torrent,” that is, at its end; and there too we read *Suph*.

To summarize many points in a single statement: all the authors of dictionaries, whether Hebrew, Syriac, or even Chaldean—the Boderianus, Ferrerius, *The Ark of Noah*, and the others—teach that in all these languages the word *Suph* means nothing other than the end or boundary of a thing.

You can therefore see that the Sea of the Philistines and the Sea of *Suph*, which the Vulgate translates as “Red Sea,” signifying the Dead Sea, were the eastern and western boundaries of the length of the Promised Land. [Col. 0221B]

The words added in the definition of the land—“and from the desert to the river”—define its breadth: from the south, where the desert of Gaza lies, to the river, that is, the two sources of the Jordan. As we read in Jerome’s commentary on Matthew 16, these are called Jor and Dan; together they form the name Jordan and rise at the foot of Lebanon. The reference to Lebanon itself concerns the addition made by the king of Tyre, as we learn from 3 Kings 5.

Thus in 1 Kings 3 and often elsewhere the boundaries of all Israel are described as extending from Dan to Beersheba—that is, from the spring of Dan, the northern boundary of the Jordan, to Beersheba, which lay near Gaza, or the desert, the southern boundary.

The boundaries of the same land are again specified in Numbers 34. Its eastern boundary is called the most salt-laden sea, that is, the Dead Sea; its western boundary is the Great Sea, namely the Mediterranean. Its southern boundary is the desert near Edom, and its northern boundary is the great mountain, namely Lebanon.

From these points you will infer that the Sea of *Suph* is the same as the Salt Sea, or Dead Sea, and not the Red Sea that separates Egypt from Arabia.

A similar testimony occurs at the beginning of Deuteronomy: “These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the wilderness of the Arabah, opposite the Red Sea”; and in verse 5 there is added, “beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab.” At that time Moses was with the people—as is stated in Numbers 33:48 and 35:1—in the plains of Moab above the Jordan, opposite Jericho, after he had given an inheritance to the tribes of Reuben and Gad and to half the tribe of Manasseh in the lands beyond the Jordan that he had taken from the Moabites, Numbers 32. Thus Moses stood at the threshold of the promised land and is said to have been in the plains of Moab above the Jordan, opposite the Red Sea; yet the sea situated in the plains of Moab is the Dead Sea, whereas the Red Sea, or Arabian Sea, lay extremely far away. In Hebrew, this place likewise [Col. 0221D] reads *mare Suph*—that is, “boundary”—because it was the boundary of the promised land. Therefore *mare Suph*, which the Vulgate sometimes reads as “Red Sea,” often signifies the Dead Sea. It can also signify the Great Sea, or Mediterranean, as Jonah’s testimony proves beyond dispute. For where, in chapter 2, he is said to have cried from the belly of the whale, “The deep covered my head,” the original has, “The sea Suph covered my head.” Yet it is clear that at that time he was not covered by the waters of the Red Sea but by those of the Mediterranean, not far from the port of Joppa.

Let us now return from this to our purpose by what seems to me a very strong line of reasoning. Solomon’s and Hiram’s fleet, which sailed toward Tarshish and Ophir, was on the shore of the Sea Suph, 1 Kings 9. But Jonah’s ship, which departed from Joppa to go to Tarshish, was [Col. 0222A] also in the Sea Suph, since the Sea Suph had covered Jonah’s head. Therefore the sea mentioned in 1 Kings 9 was one and the same as that mentioned in Jonah chapters 1 and 2, and it was none other than the Mediterranean, since Joppa lies on it. Consequently, Jonah, fleeing westward to the furthest regions from the eastern city of Nineveh, was sailing westward; and Hiram and Solomon were sending their fleets westward across the Mediterranean.

The Mediterranean was called the Sea Suph, or “boundary,” most appropriately above all because it borders all lands and provinces. It is the boundary separating Europe, Africa, and Asia, as well as Palestine, Syria, Cilicia, Greece, Illyricum, Italy, Gaul, Spain, Libya, Egypt, Macedonia, Crete, Cyprus, Sicily, and other regions of lesser importance. Thus Goropius rightly wishes it to be called the Sea Suph because it divides all these lands from one another.

The opponents object that 1 Kings 10 proves that Solomon’s fleet spent three years in navigation; but if it were sailing to Spain, or westward, [Col. 0222B] it would not spend even one year. They further add that the ancient geographers make no mention of a Mediterranean port called Ezion-geber, situated near Elath. But both assumptions are false. For the sacred text nowhere asserts that the fleet customarily spent three years on a voyage; it says only that it was sent to Tarshish once every three years: “Once every three years it went to Tarshish” (1 Kings 10). Likewise, 2 Chronicles 9 says: “The king’s ships went to Tarshish once every three years.” That is, it was sent every third year, either because it transported gold and silver in such quantities that the work of three years’ labor by the craftsmen was represented in it; or because it seemed more convenient to carry in a single fleet what had been gathered in the gold and silver mines over three years; or for other reasons unknown to us. Whatever the truth may be, at the very least this alone is established: it was accustomed to go to Tarshish once every three years.

As for the objection concerning Ezion-geber, Beccanus Goropius successfully resolves it in book 5: in Hebrew, he says, the name is read *Gastion [Col. 0222C] Gabar*, which is near Eloth. *Gastion* means a fortress, monument, or citadel, and is the same as the fortress of Gabar, or Gabriae. Strabo, however, places it on the Mediterranean coast, while Ortelius places it near Lake Sirbonis, in the territory of Idumea; Ptolemy calls it Baeto Gabriae. Eloth, which the Syriac and Chaldean writers call Elus, is said by the same Ptolemy to be the penultimate city of Idumea. Thus one may see a remarkable harmony among all the details.

The Septuagint interpreters come very close to our position, as do all the Doctors of sacred Scripture belonging to the Greek Church, since all of them read “Carthage” in Greek where the text has Tarshish. They therefore acknowledge that ships customarily sailed to it not by the Red Sea but by the Mediterranean. Let us hear, above all, Theodoret, who says this concerning the prophecy of Jonah:

“From these considerations it is concluded that Jonah fled not to India but to Carthage.”

Adding the reason, he says:

“No one would sail to India by this sea, departing from Joppa, since [Col. 0222D] a vast continent lies between our sea and India—inhabited on one side and entirely deserted on the other—and in between stand many great mountains, beyond which lies the gulf of the Red Sea, where the Indian Sea joins it.”

We have so far seen that Tarshish and Ophir existed not in eastern India but in the western part of the world. But how do we know that Tarshish was in Spain rather than in Cilicia, at Tarsus, the city of the Apostle Paul, or, according to the Septuagint, in Africa, at Carthage? For the same Theodoret, in the passage cited above, says of Tarshish: “Carthage, the chief city of Libya,” and “Blessed Isaiah and the admirable Ezekiel call it” by that name.

Certainly that Tarshish was not Tarsus is sufficiently refuted by Saint Jerome in his letter to Marcella. This is evident both because Tarsus lies very near Palestine, whereas sacred Scripture [Col. 0223A] indicates that a great voyage was made to Tarshish, and because Tarsus never possessed such an abundance of gold and silver as was brought to Solomon and Hiram from Tarshish and Ophir. I say nothing of the peacocks, apes, and elephants brought from Tarshish and Ophir, none of which were found in Tarsus or anywhere in Cilicia.

Let Josephus therefore cease to be regarded as the discoverer of this Tarshish. He is also inconsistent with himself, since he places Tarshish at Tarsus but Ezion-geber in the Red Sea and Arabian Sea, *Jewish Antiquities*, book 8. Again, that Carthage, strictly speaking, was not Tarshish is demonstrated by the difference of the names and by the scarcity of gold there. But that Tarshish was the Spanish Tartessus is shown by the similarity of the names and by the abundance of gold and silver in the province.

Strabo, *Geography*, book 3, states that in Spain, between the two mouths of the river Tartessus—that is, the Baetis—there stood a town bearing that name. He also testifies to the incredible abundance of gold and silver produced in that province, saying:

“It has been discovered that nowhere in the world [Col. 0223B], up to the time of Tiberius, was gold, silver, or copper produced in such quantity or of such quality as in Spain.”

This is the sole testimony still needed to demonstrate our point.

Pausanias, in the *Eliaca*, agrees with Strabo. Stephanus of Byzantium, however, joined both matters together, saying:

“Tartessus, a city of Iberia, was named from the river that flows from a silver mountain”—that is, from the Baetis.

Claudian, book 1, *Against Rufinus*, wrote:

> Nor would the precious tempest of the Tagus  
> Have satisfied him with Tartessian sands.

Hence, amid the excessive and overflowing riches that Anacreon is said to have rejected, one of his sayings was that he did not wish to rule Tartessus for a hundred and fifty years. He was referring to Argantonius, the king of Tartessus, of whom Silius Italicus, book 3 of the *Punica*, wrote:

> Carthaea arms the descendants of Argantonius;  
> Their ancestral king was the richest man of the human age,  
> Having passed through three times ten times ten years of warfare.

[Col. 0223C] Cartheia truly was a city within the Tartessian dominion; indeed, some believed Cartheia itself to be Tartessus, as Mela noted in book 3, chapter 6, when discussing the Strait of Gibraltar. For the same reason, Gades itself is sometimes found called Tartessus, although the whole province came to bear the same name from the city of that name once situated at the mouth of the Baetis. Ovid seems to have spoken in this manner in *Metamorphoses* 15, when he wrote:

> The western Phoebus presided over the Tartessian shores.

And Ausonius:

> Tartessian Calpe had already laid the horses of the sun to rest,  
> And the distinguished Titan shrieked in the Iberian strait.

There was also such an abundance of Tartessian gold that Homer, according to Strabo, and Suidas placed there the kingdom of Pluto, the lake Avernus, and the Elysian fields. We may readily infer from Ezekiel 27 that Elisah was located there, when he says to Tyre, the lord of Tartessus: [Col. 0223D]

> Hyacinth and purple from the islands of Elisah  
> Became your covering.

For it is clear from Genesis 10 that Elisah and Tarshish, as brothers, founded cities together in the West, and that the whole Japhetic population of the West was called “the islands of the nations.” This is especially evident because nowhere was there more exquisite purple than in Tartessus. Hence Martial, concerning the Parthenian toga, wrote in book 8, epigram 27:

> Or did the Tartessian nourisher of Iberian herds,  
> The Baetis, wash you too in Hesperian water?

Now, however, Granada is famous. Baderianus states that the Hebrew word *Tarshish* corresponds in Chaldean to *Cheman Jama*, which, he says, is sometimes used for crimson and very often for hyacinth-blue, so that the statement is true of the lordship of Spanish Tartessus: “Hyacinth and purple are your covering.”

[Col. 0224A] Corduba also belongs among the richest Tartessian cities, as the same Martial reports in book 9, epigram 61:

> In Tartessian lands there is a most famous house,  
> Where wealthy Corduba delights in the tranquil Baetis.  
> There the fleeces grow pale with their native metal,  
> And living gold leaf stains the Hesperian sheep.

It would be tedious, not to say impossible, to enumerate the riches of Spain that are found scattered throughout the ancient authors. Pliny said:

“Almost the whole of Spain bristles with mines of lead, copper, silver, and gold.”

This led Catullus to say to someone, “Son of rabbit-filled Celtiberia,” calling Celtiberia a province of Spain “rabbit-filled” because it abounded in gold mines, as Textor explains in his *Cornucopia*.

Papinius, book 3 of the *Silvae*, wrote:

> Whatever Iberia casts up from her gold-bearing mines.

Elsewhere Pliny says:

“Asturia, Gallaecia, and Lusitania supply twenty thousand pounds of gold each year.”

[Col. 0224B] Silius, speaking of Spain and of Tartessus, wrote:

> But wicked Astur discloses the causes of the crime;  
> He plunges into the deepest entrails of the wounded earth  
> And returns, unhappy, the color of the gold he has excavated.

But why should we travel to foreign peoples when the canonical and sacred testimony of 1 Maccabees 8 provides us with this statement:

“Judas heard of the Romans, and of the things they had done in the land of Spain, and that they had brought under their power the mines of silver and gold that are there.”

Bernard, book 3 of *On Consideration*, chapter 1, says:

“Your people who often visit the land of the South go and return through the midst of them, or pass beside them; but what good they have yet done among them we have not heard. Perhaps we would have heard, if the salvation of the people had not been made cheap by the gold of Spain.”

When he says that the people’s salvation had been made cheap by the gold of Spain, he is not speaking of envoys who went to Spain but of those who traveled toward the South. Thus, there too, Spanish gold was called money because of its excellence.

If evidence of Solomon’s voyage in Spain [Col. 0224C] is desired, there are authors who assert that a Hebrew stone was discovered in the ruins of ancient Saguntum, namely an epitaph of Adoniram, a client of King Solomon, mentioned in 1 Kings 5:14, who crossed to Spain with the fleet and there ended his life. Morales reports this in *Antiquities*, under the heading “Saguntum,” folio 77.

If, finally, we ask which of the ancient Fathers bears witness to the matter itself, we have first the Anonymous author cited above, venerable on account of his antiquity, who expressly states that Tarshish existed in the Baetican province of Spain. We gave his words earlier.

We also have that great Athanasius of Sinai, who deserves even greater acceptance because, living at Sinai not far from the Red Sea, he ought to have defended Ezion-geber as that region’s port and Solomon’s voyage in its interest. Yet he does precisely the opposite and affirms that Spain was the true Tarshish. Here are his words in book 10 of the *Hexaemeron*, as he explains the words of Genesis 2, “and the serpent was,” and so forth: [Col. 0224D]

“In the third book of Kings we find that Solomon’s ship came every third year to Tarshish, which is Hesperia, a region of the West.”

I add Theodoret on Jonah. After first stating that in Isaiah and Ezekiel Tarshish signifies Carthage, the chief city of Libya, he adds:

“But the Libyans and Africans too occupy even now the western part of the world.”

This is because, as Mela says in book 3, chapter 6, the Phoenicians who crossed from Africa inhabited the Baetican city of Tartessus. It is as though he had said that Carthage is called Tarshish because the Tyrians—or, which is the same thing, the Phoenicians—its founders, having crossed from Africa, inhabited Tartessus, not because Carthage itself was the true Tartessus, or Tarshish. In the same sense the Septuagint interpreters called Carthage “Tarshish,” because it was inhabited by the Carthaginians and they ruled it.

[Col. 0225A] The same point is involved in Ezekiel 27:

“Carthaginians”—in Hebrew, *Tarshishians*—“were your merchants; with the multitude of all kinds of wealth, with silver, iron, tin, and lead, they filled your marketplaces.”

The Carthaginians brought these goods to Tyre from nowhere other than Tarshish in Spain.

Likewise, the statement in Psalm 44, “The daughters of Tyre in gifts will entreat your face; all the rich among the people,” was spoken of cities built by the Tyrians or subject to their dominion. No daughter of Tyre, however, was as rich as Tartessus; and of it, rather than of any other, it may be said that “in gifts it will entreat the face of the Church.”

Since the principal aim of the voyage was gold, silver, and gems, and since these were obtained especially from Tartessus, or Tarshish, it came about that the fleets of Tyre and Solomon were called “ships of Tarshish,” as the Psalm indicates:

“With a vehement wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish.”

The Mediterranean itself, across which they sailed, was likewise called Tarshish, as in Isaiah 23: “Howl, ships of the sea,” although it could most appropriately be rendered, “ships of Tarshish.”

[Col. 0225B] The statement in Psalm 71, “The kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts; the kings of Arabia,” Goropius learnedly believes to have been said with particular reference to Tartessus. It is as though the Psalmist were saying: From the West to the East, or—as he had said earlier—“He shall rule from sea to sea,” which Theodoret explains as “from the sea of Hesperia to the Indian Sea of the East,” the kings will obey Christ.

For the same reason, those gems brought from Tartessus acquired their name from the place Tarshish, as may be seen in Ezekiel 28, Exodus 28, and likewise Song of Songs 5.

Since Tarshish signifies Tartessus, or the region of Spain, it will be easy to understand Isaiah’s celebrated prophecy. In chapter 66, foretelling the preaching of the apostles and the conversion of the world, he says:

“I will set a sign among them, and I will send some of those who are saved from them to the nations, to the sea, to Africa, and Lydia, those who bend the bow; to Italy and Greece, to the distant islands, to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory.”

[Col. 0225C] Where the Vulgate reads “to the sea,” the original Hebrew text has “to Tarshish,” and the Septuagint preserves it as the proper name of a region. Thus Tarshish is the first of the provinces to which the apostles are sent. They were not sent to the sea itself to preach to the nations, but first to Tarshish, then to Africa and Lydia, and afterward to Italy and Greece.

This was a most beautiful and noble prediction of the preaching of Saint James the Apostle and of the conversion to the faith of Christ of ancient Tarshish, or the ancient province of Tarshish—for all Spain is so named from a part of it—before all the other provinces of the Gentiles. For one of those who had been saved is said to be sent first to Tarshish, and we have seen above, with Dextro, that this was fulfilled through the Apostle James.

This also greatly supports our argument. If an apostle was to be sent first of all to Tarshish among the Gentiles, Tarshish certainly cannot have been a place in India. No apostle was sent [Col. 0225D] to India first. We have sufficiently and more than sufficiently proved that Spain was the first province of the Gentiles converted to the faith through the preaching of Saint James and his disciples. Spain, therefore, is the true Tarshish of which sacred Scripture speaks.

Finally, Ausonius greatly supports the voyage to Ophir as one customarily made to Braga and its region. In his book *On Noble Cities*, while celebrating other cities with various praises, he says that Braga alone boasts of its gulf and riches:

> Rightly, after these, you will be remembered by me, Emerita, an Iberian name,  
> Past which the sea-like river glides;  
> [Col. 0226A] All Spain yields its fasces to Corduba,  
> For neither Tarraco, powerful in its citadel, rivals you,  
> Nor wealthy Braga, which boasts in the bosom of the sea.

But enough has been said about Tarshish and Ophir.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Paul of Narbonne, bishop, who came to Spain with Paul, preaches there.

C. Oppius, son of Saint [or “of S.”] the centurion, who after a long time, worn out by old age, became dear to the Emperor Hadrian, was a Christian in Spain and was renowned for his reputation for virtue.

[Col. 0195] A.D. 66; A.R. 817. The holy women, the virgins Basilissa and Anastasia of Spain, from the city of Setabis, in the Edetan territory, followed the Holy Apostle Paul. Caring for the bodies of both him and Peter, they received a glorious crown from Nero Caesar on this account.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Saint Torquatus, a disciple of James, wrote the lives of Saint James and his other disciples; afterward he too suffered martyrdom.

[Col. 0197] A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Saint Crispinus, bishop of Astigi in Baetica, suffers under Alotus.

[Col. 0199] A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Not long afterward, at Utica in Baetica, Maximus, a disciple of the divine James in Spain, suffers martyrdom with his companions Castus and Magnus.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. In the Spanish city of Castulo, on the river Tagus, which flows past that city at the entrance to Baetica, the holy martyrs Marcus and Hadria are killed for the name of Christ.

[Col. 0201] A.D. 66; A.R. 817. The satirical poet Persius of Volaterrae dies at the age of twenty-nine.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Baths built by Nero are called Neronian after him.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Nero, performing as a cithara player at Rome, surpasses everyone.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Marcus Annaeus Lucan, having opened a vein, dies in the bath.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Helena, queen of the Adiabenians, a Christian, flourishes at Jerusalem, having been converted through the preaching of the apostles. From the *Jerusalem Annals*.

[Col. 0203] A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Saint Fronto of Périgueux suffers martyrdom, the brother of the consul Fronto.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Gaius Caesonius Maximus was flourishing.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Peter, called *Megistos* in Greek, becomes a martyr on 2 July.

[Col. 0205] A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Saint Paul wrote the Epistle to the Hebrews converted in Spain.

[Col. 0211] A.D. 66; A.R. 817. Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Corduba, a man of consular rank and notably inclined toward the Christian religion, to which he secretly adhered, and who is celebrated for having exchanged letters with Paul, dies by the cutting of his veins on Nero’s orders.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. In this same year Saint Matthias is killed.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. In this same year the Jewish war begins.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. At Amphitria, a city of the Carpetani—now Fitia—Saint Liberatus, bishop of Hiberra, dies peacefully on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January.

A.D. 66; A.R. 817. In this same year the holy apostles Peter and Paul returned to Rome from their very long journeys.

[Col. 0213] A.D. 66; A.R. 817. The memory of Saint Peter of Rates, martyr and first bishop of Braga, flourishes. He was killed in the year 45 at the town of Rates among the Bracarenses, in the Ophirian region, which received this name from descendants of Ophir who arrived there.

[Col. 0225] [Note: [Col. 0226A]

A.D. 68.—Saints Peter and Paul, the chief apostles, and so forth. Authors of no slight authority disagree with Dextro both concerning the year and concerning the day of the passion of the two apostles. For Augustine, *Sermon* 28 *On the Saints*, Arator, book 2 *On the Acts of the Apostles*, and Prudentius, hymn 12, taught that they were not killed on the same day but that Paul was killed a full year after Peter. Prudentius says:

> One day, renewed after a full year had passed,  
> Saw both crowned with the glory of a proud death.

Yet I do not know what certain heretics of the age of Prudentius and Augustine intended by following this opinion. Nevertheless, those who were condemned in the Roman Council under Damasus are clearly identified, where we read:
