“Paul was crowned in the city of Rome under Caesar Nero, not on a different day, as the heretics falsely chatter, but on one and the same day with Peter.”

I would suppose that they asserted that Paul was killed on another day of the same month or of the following month, but not on the same day of the following year, as Augustine maintains. Whatever the truth concerning them, the opinion now received by the Church from the Fathers is harmonious: both were taken from this life in precisely the same year and on the same day. This was taught by Epiphanius, *Against Heresy* 27; Maximus, in his sermon on Saints Peter and Paul; Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle*; Metaphrastes; Eusebius; and others.

Authors have held different opinions concerning the year of Christ in which this occurred. Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*, places the apostles’ death in the year 70; Cassiodorus, in his own work, in 71. Their positions, however, are rejected by common reckoning. For it is established that Nero, who killed them, survived for approximately one year but did not reach A.D. 71 or 72, as would consequently have to be admitted.

The only question, therefore, concerns the years 68 or 69: which of them witnessed the suffering of the chief apostles? Cardinal Baronius, volume 1 of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, and in the notes to 29 July of the Roman Martyrology, argues that according to the more accurate calculation they suffered in the year 69. Dextro, as you see, places it in 68; his opinion pleases me much more. It had earlier pleased the learned Ambrosio de Morales, book 9 of *Spanish History*, chapter 19, whose judgment concerning the calculation of historical years was uncommon and whose diligence was exceptional.

I derive the same conclusion from Epiphanius, *Against Heresy* 27, who emphatically states that they were killed in the twelfth year of Nero. If one counts Nero’s reign from A.D. 55, as authors commonly do, his twelfth year falls in A.D. 68. Baronius argues that Nero assumed the reins of empire in A.D. 56. But even on this calculation, if the year 56 is taken inclusively, as it ought to be, the twelfth year of his reign still falls in the aforesaid year 68.

Certainly, a lapse of memory in a man—however learned—is not especially surprising. For in his notes on 24 June, when discussing those martyrs whom Nero killed after falsely charging them with the burning of Rome, he had taught our position. There he says:

“Such a dreadful burning of the city began on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August and lasted six days, in the consulship of Bassus and Frugi; this year is reckoned by more recent writers as A.D. 65. Their martyrdom occurred three years before the passion of the apostles.”

But if three years are added to the year 65, the result is not 69 but 68, the year in which he now admits that the apostles were put to death.

In support of his view he cites Metaphrastes, who reports Caius, an ancient theologian, Pope Zephyrinus, and Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, as holding the same opinion: that the apostles were killed in the thirty-sixth year after the Passion of the Lord. But if one counts thirty-six years inclusively from the year 34, one reaches 69. This could safely be said if it were known what they thought concerning the year of the Lord’s death. For many Fathers, and very weighty ones, believed that Christ endured the cross in the thirty-third year of his age—Origen, Tertullian, Jerome, Eusebius, and others whom we cited under the year of Christ 31. If these writers agree with them, then, since the year of death must be counted inclusively, they will acknowledge that the apostles were killed in the year 68, for there are that many years from 33 through 68.

If, however, they mean that the Lord was crucified in the thirty-fourth year of his age and that Peter and Paul were taken up by martyrdom after thirty-six years, then the event occurred in A.D. 69. But they kept their view of the year of the Lord’s death to themselves, and therefore it can neither harm nor support either side.

In the *Life of Saint Photina the Samaritan*—whom we mentioned above under the year 60—it is expressly stated that she was crowned with martyrdom by Nero in A.D. 69, on 20 March, the same year in which Nero himself was killed. Since it is universally agreed, including by the Greek author of Saint Photina’s martyrdom, that Nero died approximately one year after the apostles, it follows that the apostles were crowned with martyrdom in A.D. 68.

To summarize in a single statement the principal deeds of Peter: in A.D. 36, after he had gone down to Samaria with John, he established his see at Antioch. Seven years later—as Gregory states in the *Register*, book 6, letter 37 to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, as do the *Liber Pontificalis*, Eusebius, and others—namely, in A.D. 44, he founded the Roman see. We discussed this under that year itself with Dextro. Finally, after spending twenty-four years there, he suffered death for the Lord in A.D. 68.]

A.D. 68; A.R. 819. The holy chief apostles Peter and Paul die at Rome on the third day before the Kalends of July: one is crucified, the other beheaded with a sword.

[Col. 0227] [Note: [Col. 0227B]

A.D. 69.—1. The Ides of June, and so forth. Eusebius has the following in his *Chronicle*:

“When Nero was being summoned by the Senate, he fled from the Palace to the fourth milestone of the city, to the suburban estate of his freedman, and killed himself, in the thirty-second year of his age; and in him the entire family of Augustus came to an end.”

Since this happened on 10 June, his downfall could not have occurred until approximately one year after the death of the apostles, namely in A.D. 69.

2. “Linus succeeds Peter in the see,” and so forth. Some have said that Saint Linus was merely Peter’s co-bishop and assistant while Peter was still alive in the Roman see, but that he died before Peter’s death and therefore was not the supreme Pontiff. Metaphrastes taught this in his entry for 29 June, and Panvinus follows him.

Dextro, however, follows the stronger side, namely those who assert that Linus outlived Peter and succeeded him. These include Tertullian, book 3 of the *Poems against Marcion*; Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 3; Epiphanius, *Against Heresy* 27; Augustine, letter 161; and Cardinal Baronius together with the greater part of more recent writers.

When Linus was appointed in the place of Peter, the chief of the apostles, is also disputed. Baronius suspects that he began his pontificate on the very day of Saint Peter’s martyrdom. He was led to this by the statement under A.D. 80, no. 1:

“When it is not apparent for how many days the see of a Pontiff was vacant, we are compelled to count the years of the one appointed from the day following the death of his predecessor.”

But, as you see, this is not a secure or exact calculation. Since Equilinus says that Linus was killed under Nero, he must at the very least acknowledge that Linus was appointed before Nero’s death.

Dextro believes that Linus was appointed after Nero’s death, with considerable justification. For in the year during which Nero survived, such a savage persecution raged in the Roman Church that it is quite plausible that the clergy could not assemble to elect a new Pontiff. Once Nero had been removed and Christians had been given an opportunity to breathe again, they gathered together. Clement yielded to the nomination made by Peter in his favor—if indeed such a nomination had been made—and the matter of choosing a new Pontiff was discussed. At that time Linus was appointed to Peter’s see. We shall discuss the years of his pontificate below.]

A.D. 69; A.R. 820. On the fourth day before the Ides of June, Nero, the most criminal of men, killed himself with his own hands.

A.D. 69; A.R. 820. Linus succeeds Peter in the Roman Pontifical see.

[Note: [Col. 0228A]

A.D. 70.—1. Servius, and so forth. Servius Sulpicius Galba had governed Hither Spain for eight years. At first he conducted himself with the utmost severity toward Christians, in which Aulus Vitellius vigorously assisted him; afterward he became peaceful and benevolent. This was the reason that Julius Vindex, governor of Gallia Narbonensis, raised him against Nero as emperor, like an idol against an idol.

Nevertheless, although Galba initially resisted and later consented, Silvius Otho proclaimed him emperor at New Carthage shortly before Nero’s death. But what Nero did when he heard the news, hear from Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 42; the same words are also reported by the Beauvais author in book 9 of the *Mirror of History*, chapter 118:

“When he learned of the revolt of Gaul, he received it so slowly and sternly that he gave the impression of rejoicing, as though an opportunity had arisen to strip, by right of war, the wealthiest provinces. But when he learned that the Spanish provinces too had defected, his spirit collapsed, and for a long time he lay speechless, like a dead man.”

See how highly he valued sovereignty over the Spanish provinces.

After Nero was removed, Galba was again acclaimed emperor by the soldiers in Spain. He proceeded to Rome, where, after seven months and a few days, he was killed by Marcus Salvius Otho, who seized the empire from him. Otho had previously been quaestor of Lusitania under Nero and, as Morales relates in book 9 of *Spanish History*, had erected stones to Nero as a title and trophy of the region cleansed of brigands and of those who had inculcated the new religion.

After three months, Otho killed himself with his own hand. Aulus Vitellius succeeded him, and Spain submitted to Vitellius through Cluvius Rufus. Vitellius was then killed by Vespasian’s generals, after he had spent eight months in power.

This is how the Roman historians report the events, and from them Ambrosio de Morales, book 9 of *Spanish History*, and Cardinal Baronius, volume 1 of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, derived their accounts. They disagree, however, because Baronius believes that these events occurred as follows: Galba was killed on 16 January A.D. 71; Otho killed himself on 20 April; and Vitellius was killed on 3 October of the same year.

Morales, however, insists that the events occurred in A.D. 70, and Dextro embraces his view. Eusebius reports the matter in this way in his *Chronicle*:

“After Nero, Galba [ruled] in Hibernia”—that is, Spain—“and Vitellius was beheaded in the forum of the city of Rome. Otho died by his own hand at Bebriacum in the third month of his reign. Vitellius, killed by Vespasian’s generals in the eighth month of his rule, was thrown into the Tiber.”

But Eusebius is mistaken in assigning the year, since he postponed Nero’s death until A.D. 70.

2. “At Heraclea,” and so forth. There were formerly many cities of this name throughout the world. Ptolemy places one in Sicily, two in Syria, one in Media, one in Thrace, and another in Macedonia, which he calls Sintica; one near Lake Maeotis in the Tauric Chersonese; another among Pontus and Bithynia; and finally one in Asia Minor.

Strabo mentions the Heraclea of which Dextro is speaking in book 3 and asserts that it was situated near the Strait of Gibraltar, in that part of the mainland lying immediately east of the islands of Gades. Dextro agrees with this in other passages. Under A.D. 296 he says, “At Heraclea in Spain, near the Herculean Strait,” and under A.D. 300, “In the city of Heraclea, at Calpe in Spain.”

Joannes Mariana, book 16 of *Spanish History*, chapter 2, believes that it was Calpe itself, or Gibraltar, which is the same thing. He is mistaken, however, for, as you see from Strabo, it was situated farther inland, near Gades.

Aquila, a native of Pontus, was therefore sent to this city by the Apostle Paul for the purpose of preaching. He had been expelled from Rome with his wife Priscilla, or Prisca, along with the other Jews. He first came to Corinth, where he received Paul as a guest and employed him in his own trade of tentmaking. He then went to Ephesus, where he more carefully instructed the celebrated Alexandrian, Apollos, in the faith.

Hear Saint Luke in Acts 18:

“After this Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth. Finding a certain Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy, and Priscilla his wife—for Claudius had ordered all Jews to depart from Rome—he approached them. And because he was of the same trade, he stayed with them and worked. They were of the trade of tentmaking”—that is, those who prepared leather for making pavilions and tents, or for constructing awnings from painted and gilded hides, whom in Spain we commonly call *guadamacileros*. I derive this explanation from Bede and Chrysostom.

Luke continues:

“Paul, after remaining many days longer, took leave of the brothers and sailed for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. He came to Ephesus and left them there.”

A little later:

“Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus, powerful in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John. He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately,” and so forth.

They must certainly have been exceedingly learned in the faith, since they fully instructed so learned a man in the mysteries of the faith of Christ.

While these events were taking place at Ephesus, Paul wrote his First Epistle to the Corinthians, staying at Ephesus with Priscilla and Aquila; hence, at its conclusion, he sends greetings to the Corinthians in their name, saying: “Aquila and Priscilla greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the church in their house, with whom I am staying.” After Claudius had been removed from the scene and Nero was reigning, around the year of the Lord 58, they returned to Rome once more. For at that time Paul, writing from Corinth to the Romans and preparing to travel through them to Spain, says: “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their own necks for my life; to whom not only I give thanks, but all the churches of the Gentiles; and their domestic church.” On this passage Chrysostom, in the special homily which he wrote about Priscilla and Aquila, gathers together much in their praise from every source. It is likewise inferred from Paul’s Second Epistle to Timothy that they withdrew again from Rome to Asia. For, writing to Timothy and asking him to come to him quickly so that, now released from Nero’s chains, he might depart with him for Spain—as he wrote to the Hebrews—Paul orders him to greet them: “Greet Prisca and Aquila.” From this one may see how great was their concern for the Gospel, and how anxiously and diligently they often traveled back and forth from the West to the East and from the East to the West.

Moreover, there is no doubt that they returned to Rome again with Timothy, or shortly afterward; and that Aquila and Priscilla were sent by the Apostle to Spain. For, as Dexter asserts, Aquila preached there at Heraclea. Dorotheus writes the same in his Synopsis; indeed, he says that Aquila was appointed bishop of that same city—thus Baronius reports the passage from Dorotheus in his notes for 8 July in the Roman Martyrology—even though Dorotheus does not explain where that city of Heraclea was situated. Since one of the Heracleas lies in Bithynia, a province of Asia Minor, many were consequently misled into asserting that Aquila died in Asia Minor. But we shall discuss this with Dexter under the year of the Lord 95.

### 3. In Arabia Felix, etc.

That those Gospel Magi originated in Arabia Felix and went from there to Bethlehem to adore the Lord in the stable is taught by Justin in *Dialogue with Trypho*; Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, and book III *Against Marcion*; Cyprian, in his sermon *On the Star and the Magi*; Epiphanius in his *Epitome*. That they were kings—I mean petty kings—is written by Tertullian and Cyprian in the passages cited, by Chrysostom in Homily 6 on Matthew, Hilary in book IV *On the Trinity*, Basil in his homily *On the Human Generation of Christ*, and Idacius in his work addressed to Varimundus.

Chrysostom further adds—Equilinus reports this in book II, chapter 48—that these Magi, that is, wise men skilled also in the knowledge of the stars, derived their origin from Balaam and that, from his prophecy, “A star shall rise out of Jacob,” etc., they eventually came to know the new star announcing the birth of Christ. But how did this happen? Certain observers of secret things chose twelve from among them, and whenever one died, his son was substituted for him. Every year, after the harvests, they ascended a high mountain called Victorialis; remaining there for three days, they raised themselves in prayer to God, asking him to show the star foretold by Balaam, their father. Thus, successively, three at a time, all twelve performed the rite. When these three kings happened to be there on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, the newly created star appeared to them, indicated the king who had been born to the Jews, and invited them to adore him.

Equilinus further relates that, although from that time they became faithful, having abandoned all paganism, they did not receive baptism until, after the Apostles had been dispersed to preach, they were baptized by Saint Thomas the Apostle, who preached in India. Confirmed in the faith of Christ, they became his assistants in preaching. Such is Equilinus’s account.

Chrysostom’s words in Homily 2 of the *Imperfect Work on Matthew* are as follows:

“I have read in someone’s work that these Magi learned from the books of Balaam about the appearance of this star. I have also heard some people report a certain Scripture—and although it was not certain, that is, canonical, it nevertheless did not destroy the faith but rather delighted it—for there was a certain nation situated at the very beginning of the East, beside the Ocean, among whom a certain Scripture was said to be preserved, bearing the name of Seth, concerning the appearance of this star and the offering of such gifts to it. This tradition had been handed down through successive generations of learned men, fathers relating it to their sons. Therefore they chose twelve from among themselves,”

and the rest as reported by Equilinus. He adds:

“It appeared to them bearing within itself something like the form of a little child, and above it the likeness of a cross; it instructed them and commanded them to set out for Judaea. As they traveled, the star went before them for two years, and neither food nor drink failed in their bags.”

And a little later:

“When they had returned, they remained worshiping and glorifying God much more diligently than before; they preached to all their own people and instructed many. Finally, when the Apostle Thomas went into that province after the Lord’s resurrection, they were brought to him, baptized by him, and became assistants in his preaching.”

Thus far Chrysostom.

Certainly, if they were assistants to Saint Thomas in the Gospel, it is not surprising that Dexter extended their deaths to this seventieth year of Christ. Nevertheless, one of them would have had to live to the age of one hundred, and perhaps several years beyond; especially if what Equilinus likewise reports, and what the most ancient paintings indicate, were true: namely, that when they went to Bethlehem, the eldest, Gaspar, was sixty years old, the middle one, Balthasar, forty, and the youngest, Melchior, twenty. Yet I shall never be persuaded that any of them had then reached sixty, since they would not have possessed the strength necessary to complete so long a journey in only a few days.

As for their number, Saint Leo teaches in Sermon 1 and in Sermons 4 through 8 *On the Epiphany* that there were only three. Rupert and Bede follow him, although in their collections they call them by their names, as Equilinus likewise does in the passage cited. I do not, however, agree with Equilinus when he says that their Hebrew names were Appellius, Amerius, and Damascus; their Greek names, Galgalath, Malgalath, and Sarrachin; and their Latin names, Gaspar, Balthasar, and Melchior. At least the latter names are not Latin but Chaldaean, as is clear in the case of Balthasar from Daniel.

Maurolycus has the same names—Gaspar, Balthasar, and Melchior—in his *Martyrology*, as do many more recent writers. Tradition sufficiently confirms them, since many Christians assume these names for themselves at baptism in honor of the Magi. Equilinus, moreover, thinks that they died a natural death, whereas Dexter says that they died as martyrs. Here too we should stand by Dexter, as the more ancient and more diligent authority.

Nevertheless, it is worth reproducing Equilinus’s words, in which he describes the translation of the bodies of the three holy Magi in book IV, chapter 45:

“Eustorgius, a bishop of Greek nationality, was sent by the emperor of Constantinople as an envoy to the people of Milan. He became so pleasing to the citizens that, when he was returning from there and the see had become vacant, they elected him archbishop. But, without consulting the Emperor, he refused to consent to the election. Thus he returned to Constantinople and reported to the Emperor what had happened. The Emperor, however, received the news with the greatest pleasure and sent him back to Milan to be consecrated.

“Moreover, he granted Eustorgius, as a gift, the bodies of the three Magi, which had long before been buried in a great chest and brought from Persia to Constantinople. The saint transported them by ship as far as the port. When he had placed the chest containing the bodies upon a cart—at the gate, as it is said—and several pairs of oxen could not pull it with sufficient strength, by divine revelation two very poor heifers belonging to a devout woman drew the cart with the greatest ease. A wolf killed one of them on the journey.

“The holy Bishop then commanded the wolf to take the place of the heifer as far as Milan. Immediately, having laid aside all its ferocity, the wolf became tame, presented itself to the vehicle, and, yoked together with the remaining heifer, pulled the cart to Milan. There the bodies of the holy Magi rested in burial until the time of the Emperor Frederick, surnamed Barbarossa. At that time, when Milan had been destroyed, the chest was left there and the holy bodies were transferred to Cologne. There they are still venerated today amid the great gathering of the Christian people.”

Echius discusses these same translations in his homily *On Saint Thomas the Apostle*; among more recent writers, Illescas does so in part I of his *History of the Pontiffs*, Trugillus in his *Treasury of Preachers*, and others.

[Col. 0231D]

### 4. The Emperor, etc.

Morales, in book IX, relates with Dexter that Vespasian assumed the imperial power in this very seventieth year of Christ. He had been sent by Nero to Jerusalem and throughout Judaea, which, unable to endure the avarice of Festus Florus, had rebelled against the Romans. He then returned to Rome to seize the imperial power, leaving his son Titus with the army in Judaea, as Josephus and the other historians of Roman affairs relate.

All agree that Vespasian’s reign lasted nine years but did not complete ten. Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*, thinks that he ruled nine years, eleven months, and twenty-two days—namely, that he fell eight days short of completing ten years. Baronius thinks he fell short by only six days. Dexter assigns him only six months beyond nine years, unless there is a scribal error in the manuscript.

### 5. During these times, etc.

That is, under Vespasian, John wrote his Third Epistle to Gaius, which begins: “The Elder to the most beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth.” Since Dexter does not say that he wrote it in this very year of the Lord 79, the first year of Vespasian, but merely “during these times,” that is, while Vespasian was ruling, it remains uncertain whether the letter was sent at the beginning of his reign or later, up to the year of the Lord 79 or 80, when Vespasian died.

I have said this for a fuller explanation of the title “the Elder.” For in these times of Vespasian the Apostle was seventy-five years old—or seventy, if, as reason suggests, we suppose that he was enrolled among the Apostles at the age of twenty-five or twenty. He had already established the churches throughout all Asia, since he is said to have spent most of his time in Asia from the year 48, when the Virgin Mother of God was translated to heaven.

[Col. 0232B]

This Gaius, to whom the letter was written, was not that centurion Gaius surnamed Oppius, who confessed the dying Christ to be the Son of God, but his son, as Dexter’s words make clear: “Whose father later became bishop of Milan.” The author had stated under the year 34 of Christ that this man was the third bishop of that see after Saint Barnabas. Now, however, he calls him “the Malacitan centurion Gaius,” of whom he had likewise said under the year 52: “The Malacitan centurion flourishes, whom Saint James baptizes there.” A little later, under this seventieth year, he says: “Gaius, Corinthian by residence but Spanish by origin, etc., came from there to Milan, became bishop there, and died in the Lord.”

There is no contradiction in these statements. For it is one thing to be Malacitan, or Spanish by origin, and another to be Corinthian by residence: both could have been true at once. He could have been born at Málaga in Spain and have lived for some time at Corinth. Or perhaps he is called Malacitan not because he was born at Málaga, but because he derived his paternal ancestry from there; yet he could still be called and be Corinthian by residence. At Corinth he also generously received Paul for a time into his house and lodging. Paul himself, writing to the Romans while staying with him at Corinth, says in chapter 16: “Gaius, my host, greets you.”

This Gaius Oppius, therefore, so great and distinguished a man, is said by Dexter here to have had two sons: Gaius, to whom John writes, and Demetrius, whom John highly commends in the same letter, saying: “Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone and from the truth itself; and we also bear witness.” Of what does he speak? Clearly of that quality for which Gaius himself was now to be praised by the Apostle, and in which Diotrephes, a most foolish bishop, had failed.

Listen to the Apostle himself addressing Gaius:

“Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers, and especially for strangers, who have testified to your charity before the church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God; for they have gone out for his name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to receive such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth.”

Behold Gaius praised for hospitality. But what of Diotrephes?

“I would perhaps have written something to the church; but Diotrephes, who loves to hold the first place among them”—that is, whether bishop, intruder, or wicked man—“does not receive us. He himself does not welcome the brothers, and he prevents those who do welcome them and expels them from the church.”

Dexter says: “Diotrephes was preventing guests who were coming to Spain as pilgrims.”

John therefore sets Demetrius against him, saying:

“Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone and from the truth itself”—namely, that he was a hospitable man and willingly received traveling guests—“and we also bear witness,” since we saw this and he received us ourselves together with others.

[Col. 0233A]

As far as I can understand from John and Dexter, Gaius Oppius had so arranged his affairs that whatever he possessed at Málaga or Corinth was devoted to the support of faithful pilgrims. Thus his son Gaius at Málaga in Spain and Demetrius at Corinth in Asia were assigned by him to these responsibilities, while he himself had devoted himself to perpetual travel here and there to the holy places. Hence he is found now in Spain, now at Jerusalem, now at Corinth, now at Ephesus, now at Rome, and now at Milan.

For this reason Dexter says: “Pilgrimage to the holy places of Spain, undertaken by many people from various other regions of the world, and pilgrimage from Damascus to Saint Ananias, are also celebrated throughout the regions of Spain; just as they were from apostolic times, when the centurion Gaius Oppius supported pilgrims in Spain.”

When Dexter adds, “Gaius, Corinthian by residence but Spanish by origin, also generously received the Lord Paul, returning from there, into his house and lodging,” I do not understand him to be referring to the hospitality that Gaius showed Paul at Corinth, for Paul himself bears witness to this when he writes to the Romans: “Gaius, my host, greets you.” Rather, I understand him to mean the hospitality with which Gaius received Paul at Málaga when the Apostle was leaving Spain and hastening to Rome for martyrdom. For Dexter taught above, under the years 64 and 66, that Paul was then there.

It is highly plausible that Gaius accompanied Paul to Rome until Paul was beheaded. For that Gaius afterward migrated to Asia is indicated by our finding him shortly afterward in Asia visiting Saint John, indeed receiving in writing John’s Gospel after becoming the Apostle’s secretary when it was first dictated by him. This I learn from Athanasius, whose words in his *Synopsis* are as follows; Baronius also cites them under the year of the Lord 99:

“The Gospel according to John was preached by John the Apostle and Beloved One while he was on the island of Patmos, and afterward was published by him at Ephesus through Gaius, the beloved host of the Apostles, of whom Paul, writing to the Romans, says: ‘Gaius, my host, greets you.’”

Although others attribute this Gaius to Prochorus, we shall speak of that with Dexter under the year 94.

[Col. 0233C]

What Dexter adds about Gaius Oppius has hitherto been unheard of: “He visited John after John returned from exile, and accompanied John again as far as Rome, to Ignatius.”

Did John, then, also travel to Spain? That he did travel there, accompanied by Gaius Oppius, and that Gaius afterward escorted him back as far as Ephesus, is what we learn here from Dexter. His testimony deserves the highest consideration not only from me but from every learned man. Although we do not know where he obtained the information, there is no reason to doubt so great an author; ancient writers must have supplied him with a substantial foundation for this truth.

For my part, I am certain that Dexter needed no other evidence than the assertion that Gaius, a hospitable man, was the son of Gaius Oppius of Málaga. Given this alone—which was doubtless abundantly known to Dexter—the arrival of Saint John the Apostle in Spain follows clearly. For when John wrote to that Gaius in Spain, praising him for receiving pilgrims, he promised that he would soon visit him:

“Diotrephes does not receive us. Therefore, if I come, I will call attention to his works, which he does, babbling maliciously against us. And as though these things were not enough for him, he himself neither receives the brothers nor allows those who wish to receive them, and he expels them from the church.”

He adds:

“I had much to write to you, but I did not wish to write to you with ink and pen. I hope to see you shortly, and we shall speak mouth to mouth.”

The Apostle therefore promised that he would go to Spain, where Gaius lived, in order to rebuke Diotrephes and visit Gaius himself and his friends, to whom he had also sent greetings, saying: “Greet the friends by name.” Why, then, should we deny that he went there? At the very least, after his release from exile, nothing could have prevented the Apostle, especially since, like a true son of thunder, he never remained in one place for long.

Certainly those who think that John never withdrew his foot from Asia Minor—now called Anatolia—for the sake of preaching are mistaken and wander very far from the truth. For Metaphrastes, on 5 September in Lipomanus, states that he also went to Phrygia. Baronius likewise proves that he went to Parthia in his notes for 27 December, from the First Epistle of the same Apostle, which bore the ancient title *To the Parthians*. Indeed, the most ancient memories discovered there by the Fathers of the Society of Jesus declare that he penetrated even to India, as may be seen in their letters dated 1555.

No one should be surprised to hear that he also went to Spain, especially since very weighty conjectures support that journey. One such consideration is that his presence and arrival were ardently desired by Spain, since the Spanish were the children of his elder brother in the holy Gospel; hence there is no doubt that they were always especially dear to Saint John. There was also a considerable incentive to the journey: he had been visited by many of those who traveled from Spain to Asia on pilgrimage. Of them he had said: “I rejoiced greatly at the brothers who came, for they desired nothing so much from the Apostle as to bring him into his homeland.”

Furthermore, John himself had two precious and especially beloved pledges in Spain: the body of his brother and the sacred church of the Pillar, at whose consecration he himself had been present, carried by angelic hands together with the holy Mother of God. Would anyone suppose that he never at last visited, as his desire dictated, places which he had not seen for many years? And he who omitted nothing that he preached in words—and who preached and commended pilgrimages to holy places with such emphasis—would he alone have failed to fulfill this by his actions? Could Asia alone contain so great a light that it would be seen by no other regions? And how could so brilliant a lightning flash, the son of thunder, fail to illuminate the whole world from East to West, from Asia to Spain?

Indeed, Christ the Lord, who gave John the name “lightning,” or “son of thunder,” said of lightning in Matthew 24: “Lightning goes out from the East and appears even to the West.” What is the true East, if not Asia? And what, in the eyes of all the ancients, is the true West, if not Spain? Did not Ausonius sing of it:

> Thartesian Calpe had already yoked the horses of the Sun.

And Ovidius:

> Phoebus, setting, had presided over the Thartesian shores.

Thus you may believe, even on the basis of the argument supplied by the Lord Savior himself, that this lightning too went out from the East and appeared as far as the utmost West. Or was this one lightning alone confined to the East? Or what we saw James, his brother, do within a few years, since he too was a son of thunder and a most illustrious lightning flash of faith—could John not have done in the sixty-eight years which, according to Isidore, he survived after the Lord’s Passion?

Let whoever wishes believe it. I, for my part, more willingly agree with Dexter and profess that Saint John visited Spain; I affirm that he visited there the sacred relics of his most beloved brother and the church of the Virgin at Zaragoza. I affirm that he rejoiced greatly at the abundant success of Saint James’s disciples and at the veneration and frequent pilgrimage by which the house of the Mother of God of the Pillar was visited by the faithful flocking to it from every direction. There is no doubt that that house was left under his special care, since he himself had founded it as the first shrine in honor of so great a Mother, especially after the death of his brother Saint James.

But let us return once more to Gaius, after he had accompanied the Apostle on his return from Spain as far as Ephesus. We shall discuss the deeds of this same Saint John again with Dexter under the years 91 and 105.

[Col. 0235A]

### 6. And he accompanies Ignatius as far as Rome.

The printer had corrupted the reading and had printed *Iginius* instead of *Ignatius*. Iginius sat as bishop of Rome in the year 154, at least fifty years after the death of Gaius. Yet Gaius accompanied Saint Ignatius from Syria, as Dexter asserts, when Ignatius, condemned to the beasts under Trajan, was brought to Rome in chains. On this journey, writing letters to many people, Ignatius sometimes mentions Gaius Oppius, who accompanied him, under the name Oppius, and sometimes under both names, Gaius and Oppius.

I wish those who have hitherto believed that *Agathoppius* in the letters of Saint Ignatius was the simple name of one of his companions to observe this. It is in fact a compound name, meaning the same as “good Oppius,” for *agathos* means “good.” At that time it was customary to assign an additional name expressing piety to men of proven virtue. Thus Ignatius himself was called *Theophoros*, that is, “God-bearing”; Marcus Marcellus was called *Eugenius*, that is, “noble,” because he belonged to Nero’s family; and in the holy Scriptures Simon was surnamed Cephas or Peter, James and John were called Boanerges, Joseph was called Justus, and James the son of Alphaeus was called Oblias, that is, “holy,” to say nothing of others. So Gaius Oppius is now called *Agathos* by Ignatius, and in a single word *Agathoppius*, or, corruptly, *Agathoppus*.

But let us run through the letters.

First, in the seventh, which is addressed to the Tarsians, Ignatius says:

“Philo, your deacon, greets you. Agathoppius the deacon greets you, who follows me from Syria in Christ.”

When he says that Agathoppius follows him “from Syria,” he intends to indicate that Agathoppius accompanied him from Antioch—which is in Syria—all the way to Rome, where Ignatius was hastening to martyrdom. Thus, in his fourteenth letter, addressed to the Ephesians, he says: “Pray for the church of the Antiochians, which is in Syria, from which I am being led as a prisoner to Rome.”

Again, in the eighth letter, addressed to the Philippians, he says:

“Philo and Agathoppius the deacons greet you.”

In the ninth, addressed to the Philadelphians:

“Concerning Philo the deacon, a religious man from Cilicia, who now ministers to me in the word of the Lord together with Gaius, who is also Agathoppius, a man of very distinguished character, who follows me from Syria, I testify to you that they have renounced the world and chosen to seal their commitment with martyrdom.”

In some manuscripts the relative pronoun *who* is absent where it reads, “Gaius, who is also Agathoppius.” Nevertheless, its omission is clearly an error, because there is no doubt that Gaius and Agathoppius are one and the same person. For immediately afterward Ignatius uses the singular: “a man of very distinguished character, who follows me from Syria.” If they were different men, he would have used the plural. Moreover, just as he praises Philo and Agathoppius, he would also have praised Gaius with a special commendation, which he does not do.

Certainly, throughout all his letters Ignatius says that only two men were his companions: Philo and Agathoppius. This is clear in the seventh and eighth letters just cited, and in the twelfth, addressed to the Antiochians, where he again says:

“Philo and Agathoppius the deacons greet you, who follow me.”

In the tenth letter, addressed to the Smyrnaeans, he again names Gaius, whom he also calls Agathoppius, saying:

“You do well to receive Philo and Gaius, who is also Agathoppius, who follow me in the word of God, as ministers of God. They also give the greatest thanks to the Lord for you, because you refreshed them with every kindness.”

This evidently occurred when they passed through Smyrna with Ignatius, not by land—for the letter was written as an act of thanksgiving after they had departed from Smyrna.

By this time Gaius had been ordained a deacon, as I believe, from the time when he committed John’s Gospel to writing; for that was the ministry of a deacon. After John’s passing, Gaius joined his most beloved disciple Ignatius, primate of Antioch in Syria, whom he accompanied to Rome, burning with the desire for martyrdom. When this hope was frustrated, he attempted, now very old, to return to his homeland in Spain. He was detained at Milan, however, and chosen bishop of that city. There he completed his life in holiness and departed to God on 27 September, the day on which his annual memorial is celebrated among the people of Milan.

The Roman Martyrology praises him with this entry:

“At Milan, Saint Gaius, bishop, a disciple of the blessed Apostle Barnabas, who baptized Saints Gervasius and Protasius and, after suffering much during the persecution of Nero, rested in peace.”

He is discussed in the life of those same saints written by Philip Philotheus, which is found in Ambrose, in Surius, volume III, and in Mombricius, volume I.

“Gaius always gives birth to something new.” Behold how much he endured for the name of Christ in Nero’s persecution, and what sons he brought forth through baptism. Certainly, it would be difficult to find the achievements of a single man as numerous and magnificent as those we have attributed to Gaius. See what we said about him under the year of the Lord 34, Commentary 3.

Through ignorance of this Gaius Agathoppius, some pedant added to the Roman Martyrology, under 25 April, a feast of Philo and Agathopodus, deacons, although Agathoppius is entered under the name of Gaius on 27 September. He is found neither in Bede, nor in Ado, nor in Usuard, nor in the Greek menology; nor is there any mention of these men anywhere except in the letters of Saint Ignatius.

### 7. Pilgrimages to the holy places of Spain, etc.

At the very least, there is no doubt that even in that period Catholics came and made pilgrimages to the body of Saint James and to the most holy and first church of the Blessed Mary at Zaragoza. For, apart from the holy places of Jerusalem and the thresholds of the Apostles, no place in the entire world was ever holier. That the faithful were accustomed to make pilgrimages to the saints is made clear by John’s Third Epistle, which we cited. This is especially evident from the fact that Saint Cletus, pope and disciple of Peter, who assumed the governance of the Roman see in the year of the Lord 80, approved and commended pilgrimages to the saints in a special decree addressed to all Christian peoples. Many report this, among them Peter Equilinus; see book IV, chapter 44. This demonstrates that pilgrimage was already customary at that time, although it had been attacked by certain heretics.

Pilgrimage to Saint Ananias at Damascus, who was its bishop according to Dorotheus, is likewise shown to have begun in these times, since Lucilius Bassus, his executioner, was then raging against the rebellious Jews, as Josephus often relates in book VII *On the Jewish War*, especially chapters 26 and 29, where he says among other things:

“Three thousand Jews who had fled into the grove of Jardes were killed by Lucilius Bassus, the legate.”

An error has crept into the Roman Martyrology: instead of Lucilius it reads Licinius. But Licinius, who put many Christians to death, lived in the East in the time of Constantine the Great, as we learn from Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book I, chapter 44, and from Severus, book II of his *Sacred History*. Baronius notes this under 2 January, in his account of Saint Marcellinus the boy, who suffered at Tomis in Pontus under the Emperor Licinius.

The Greeks, in their menology—from which the Roman Martyrology, Bede, Ado, and others took their material—celebrate the feast of Saint Ananias on 1 October and recite his martyrdom. But the Roman Martyrology, under 25 January, has the following, as Dexter gives it:

“At Damascus, the feast of Saint Ananias, who baptized the Apostle. After preaching the Gospel at Damascus, Eleutheropolis, and elsewhere, he completed his martyrdom under the judge Lucilius—not Licinius—by being beaten and torn with sinews, and finally crushed by stones.”

These details were taken from the Greeks.

From there he wrote to Gaius the Spaniard, son of Gaius the Malacitan centurion and brother of Demetrius the hospitable man, whose father later became bishop of Milan. Diotrephes, however, prevented guests who came to Spain on pilgrimage. But this wicked bishop was deposed because of his crimes and pride.

[Col. 0235]

**A.C. 70. A.R. 821.** Pilgrimage to the holy places of Spain, undertaken by many people from various regions of the world, and pilgrimage from Damascus to Saint Ananias, who suffered under Lucilius Bassus, procurator of Judaea, on 25 January, are also celebrated throughout the regions of Spain. Such was the practice from apostolic times, when the centurion Gaius Oppius supported pilgrims in Spain. This Gaius, Corinthian by residence but Spanish by origin, also generously received the blessed Paul, returning from there, into his house and lodging. He visited John after John returned from exile to Spain. He accompanied John, and Ignatius as far as Rome. From there he came to Milan, became its bishop, and died in the Lord.

[Col. 0237]

[Note: [Col. 0237A]]

**A.C. 71.—1. At Jerusalem, etc.** What could be said by us here is better taken from Josephus, in the books which he wrote *On the Jewish War*, and from Hegesippus, in those which he wrote *On the Destruction of Jerusalem*.

As for the year of the destruction itself, Eusebius places it in the year 73 of the Lord, consistently with his reckoning of Vespasian’s years. Since Josephus makes clear that it occurred in the second year of Vespasian’s reign, and Eusebius thinks that Vespasian began to rule the world in the year 72 of Christ, it follows, according to his principles, that the destruction of Jerusalem fell in the year 73. Baronius, however, who maintains that Vespasian began to reign in the year 71, places the destruction in the year 72.

But the whole matter depends on the correct assignment of the year of Nero’s death. We dealt with this at length above and showed, together with Dexter, that Nero killed himself in the year of the Lord 69, while Vespasian began his reign in the year 70. From this it is clear that Dexter correctly states here that the destruction occurred in the year 71; Genebrardus likewise follows this view in book III of his *Chronology*.

As for the date, Josephus makes clear in book VII, chapters 10 and 17, that Jerusalem was captured by Titus on the sixth day before the Ides of September, but that the Temple was burned on the sixth day before the Ides of August. Therefore I think that in Dexter one should read “August” instead of “September,” or that something is missing from the text. The reading should be:

“Jerusalem was destroyed on the sixth day before the Ides of September, and the Temple was burned on the sixth day before the Ides of August.”

Josephus states that 1,100,000 Jews perished from famine and the sword during the siege; another 100,000 were publicly sold into slavery; and 600,000 were killed.

## 2. St. Onesimus, etc.

Paul relates in his Epistle to Philemon [Col. 0237C] that Onesimus had been Philemon’s slave, had fled from his master at Colossae to Rome, and had there visited Paul himself while he was in prison. Converted by him to the faith, Onesimus became so dear to Paul that he calls him now his son, now his brother, and even his own heart:

“I appeal to you for my son,” he says to Philemon, “whom I begot in my chains, Onesimus, who was once useless to you, but now useful both to me and to you, whom I have sent back to you. Receive him as my own heart. I had wished to retain him, so that he might minister to me in your place in the chains of the Gospel; but without your consent I wished to do nothing. Perhaps for this reason he departed from you for a time, so that you might receive him forever, no longer as a slave, but instead of a slave, as a most beloved brother—especially to me. So if you regard me as your partner, receive him as you would receive me. But if he has wronged you in anything, charge it to me. I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay it.”

Theophylact, in the prologue to his Commentary on this epistle, writes that Onesimus secretly took money from Philemon’s household and fled; and this, he says, is what Paul meant by: “But if he has wronged you in anything, charge it to me.” For, he adds, it was reasonable to suppose that Onesimus had already spent what he had taken when he fled.

From the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 4, it is clear that he was from that city. Paul says to the Colossians: “Everything concerning me Tychicus, the beloved brother, will make known to you, whom I have sent to you so that he may comfort your hearts, together with Onesimus, the beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you everything that is happening here.”

Observe the man’s fortunate progress. From slavery he is taken up into the ministry of the Gospel, and he immediately awakens Paul’s love to such an extent that Paul calls him his own heart. After Timothy’s martyrdom, he is appointed bishop of Ephesus, as the Roman Martyrology declares on 16 February. At that time he visited Ignatius, who was hastening to Rome for martyrdom, as Ignatius himself testifies in his Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 14. Praising Onesimus with extraordinary commendation, he calls him his teacher:

“I received your multitude in the name of the Lord, in Onesimus, our beloved teacher, and your bishop. I exhort you, according to Christ Jesus, to love him, and for all of you to be united in him in concord. Blessed indeed is God, who has granted you to possess such a bishop in Christ.”

Hence Nicephorus plainly erred in book 3, chapter 11, when he writes that Onesimus was put to death before Trajan’s reign, namely under Domitian. For it is certain from the Roman Martyrology, 2 February, that Ignatius himself—who suffered before Onesimus—underwent martyrdom under Trajan, in the eleventh year of that emperor, as Eusebius testifies in his Chronicle and Jerome in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* [Col. 0238B]. The very Acts of Onesimus, which Metaphrastes recorded, also say that he suffered under Trajan.

Moreover, without doubt an error has entered the Roman Martyrology where it says that the apostle Paul ordained Onesimus bishop of Ephesus after Timothy: “whom he also,” it says, “ordained bishop of Ephesus after Timothy.” This certainly cannot be true, because Paul did not outlive Timothy so as to ordain Onesimus as his successor. Rather, Timothy outlived Paul, since Timothy was killed at the beginning of Domitian’s reign, in the year of the Lord 83 or 84, as Metaphrastes testifies in his Acts, and as Baronius takes from him in volume 1 of the *Annals*. It is certain, however, that Timothy lived until his death in his own episcopate and was not promoted to another office.

Therefore the entire passage in the Roman Martyrology:

“The feast of the blessed Onesimus, about whom the apostle Paul writes to Philemon, whom he also ordained bishop of Ephesus after St. Timothy, bishop of Ephesus, and entrusted to him the word of preaching,”

should be rendered as we read it in Usuard:

“The feast of the blessed Onesimus, about whom the apostle Paul writes to Philemon. The same apostle, ordaining him bishop, entrusted to him the word of preaching.”

The meaning is that he entrusted the word of preaching to him without restriction to any particular church or city, but wherever among the nations, so that he might preserve in their purpose those whom Paul himself had brought to the faith. For this reason he ordained him bishop, so that he too might ordain bishops and presbyters wherever the need for preaching required it.

I am also displeased with Usuard’s statement that Paul left Onesimus, newly ordained, in the city of Ephesus. This cannot stand with the truth, since Onesimus was not converted to the faith while Paul was staying at Ephesus, but when Paul was in prison at Rome, as he himself writes to Philemon. Nor did he afterward travel any farther into the East, as Paul had prophetically testified to the Ephesians themselves in Acts 20:

“From Miletus,” Luke says, “he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the Church. When they had come to him and were all together, he said to them: ‘Now, behold, I know that you will all see my face no more, among whom I have passed preaching the kingdom of God.’”

Certainly, in the menologion of the Eastern Church—where the memory of this matter ought to have been preserved most tenaciously—it is nowhere asserted that Onesimus was left by the Apostle at Ephesus or ordained bishop of the Ephesians by him. It says only that Paul entrusted to him the word of preaching; and this is entirely true.

After Paul’s death, therefore, Onesimus traveled throughout the whole world, especially wherever the Apostle had sown the seeds of the divine word [Col. 0239A]. He spent sixteen years in this ministry, from the year 68, the year of Paul’s death, until 84, the year of Timothy’s death, when he himself was attached particularly to the Church of Ephesus and appointed in Timothy’s place.

You may see that, in the year of the Lord 71, descending from Achaia, he had a suitable time and place for traveling through Spain with the holy virgins Polyxena and Sara, according to Dexter’s account. This can be supported by Paul’s preaching in Spain—for wherever Paul was, Onesimus also preached—and by the companions he took with him. The Greek menologion for 23 September suggests that they went to Spain at this time. There we read the following, according to the translation of Cardinal Sirlet, preserved in volume 2 of Henry Canisius’s *Collection of Ancient Readings*:

“On the same day, the feast of the holy women Xantippa and Polyxena, who were descended from Spain under the reign of the Emperor Claudius. Xantippa heard the apostle Paul preaching the Gospel of Christ to the Spaniards, since he had been the author of faith and salvation to her husband Probus. Polyxena first heard the apostle Peter, then the apostle Philip, and finally the apostle Andrew, who baptized her. She had been abducted in Greece, where he was then present, by a certain man, but, with God’s help, she remained entirely undefiled. When she returned to Spain with a certain virgin named Rebecca, a Jewess by birth, she found Xantippa, her sister, shining with the splendor of her virtues. Thus, teaching many the faith of Christ, they rested in peace.”

As I have said, this comes from Sirlet’s menologion. Yet he did not translate the Greek text word for word, but paraphrased it; and in this passage not very successfully, for he omitted the arrival of Onesimus with them in Spain—a matter of great importance and one that confirms Dexter’s account exactly.

The Greek text, rendered word for word, reads as follows:

“On the same day, the feast of the holy women Xantippa and Polyxena, twin sisters. The choirs of angels receive the twin sisters Xantippa and Polyxena as their companions. They were from the region of the Spaniards under Claudius Caesar. Xantippa was the wife of Probus, a man who held rule over the region. She was instructed by the apostle Paul, who was traveling through that region; and afterward her husband also”—that is, he too was instructed by him.

“Polyxena was abducted by a wicked man, but by the grace of God she remained undefiled and was baptized by the apostle Andrew. When many came to believe through her, she took with her the apostle Onesimus and set out for her native Spain. After many voyages and innumerable escapes, she brought with her Rebecca, with whom she had been baptized, and found her uterine sister Xantippa. They passed the rest of their lives rightly, worked many miracles, and departed to the Lord.”

From this we can draw many noteworthy conclusions: namely, that Xantippa and Polyxena were twin sisters; that the former was given in marriage to St. Probus, while the latter remained a virgin; and again, that Xantippa alone was a disciple of St. Paul. For this reason Dexter mentioned only her earlier, when he was speaking of Paul’s preaching in Spain, as Metaphrastes also did. Now, however, when he writes of Onesimus’s preaching in Spain, he speaks only of Polyxena [Col. 0239D].

On one point alone he differs from the Greeks: he called Polyxena’s companion, whom she brought with her to Spain, Sara, whereas the Greek menologion calls her Rebecca. The transition from one name to the other was easy enough; nevertheless, I think Dexter should rather be followed, since he possessed greater knowledge of Spanish affairs than the Greeks.

Finally, when the menologion says that they flourished under Claudius, this must be understood of Claudius Nero, not Claudius Drusus Germanicus. For during the days of the latter, Paul—who instructed Xantippa in the faith—had not yet gone to Rome, much less to Spain; this did not happen until the time of Nero.

Since Xantippa and Polyxena were disciples of not one but many apostles, the Roman Martyrology speaks correctly and precisely when it says, on 23 September:

“In Spain, the holy women Xantippa and Polyxena, who were disciples of the apostles.”

Concerning the martyrdom of Onesimus, see Metaphrastes in Surius, volume 1, and Galesinus in his Martyrology.

## 3. St. Hierotheus, etc.

Whoever wishes fully to understand the spirit of this divine Teacher should read St. Dionysius, who was first his fellow disciple under the discipline of the apostle Paul and afterward his disciple, in the book he published on the divine names. Indeed, even the glory of so great a disciple would by itself have made Hierotheus sufficiently renowned, had everything else been lacking.

Metaphrastes, in Lanselius’s *Life of St. Dionysius*, says:

“Having received from the blessed Hierotheus the first exercises and disciplines of the faith, and having been instructed by him both in word and in life, he also received from him communion in the Holy Spirit.”

And Michael Singellus writes:

“He surrendered himself to the discipline of his teacher, Hierotheus, inspired by the divine Spirit, and was instructed in his teacher’s divine teachings.”

Indeed, from Dionysius’s testimony it is clear not only that Hierotheus surpassed the other teachers of the Church by a long interval after the apostles, but also that he deserved the name Hierotheus, which means “sacred God.” This is so because, through the deifying activity of God—for these are Dionysius’s words—by which each person becomes godlike according to his capacity, many gods are produced.

Having contemplated this marvelously, that common guide of ours and of our teacher—he is speaking of Paul, the teacher of both himself and Hierotheus—said under divine inspiration in his holy writings, 1 Corinthians 8:

“There are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth,” etc.

If, then, one becomes more or less godlike according to his greater or lesser approach to God’s deifying activity, how far, I ask, did he approach it, and how godlike did he become, who above all others deserved to claim for himself the name Hierotheus, or “Sacred God”?

Observe now how reverently Dionysius speaks of his teaching in chapter 3. Having stated beforehand that he was writing about the divine names and attributes of their authors, and seeing that Hierotheus had written about these matters earlier, he clears himself of the charge of working either superfluously or arrogantly, lest anyone think that he was laboring in vain:

“Perhaps we require a defense. For since our renowned teacher Hierotheus brought together the theological elements with extraordinary skill, someone may perhaps wonder why we have written theological works both elsewhere and here, as though those works were insufficient.”

He answers the objection as follows:

“If he had wished to arrange all theological matters in an orderly sequence—that is, not treating them merely in general and abstractly, without descending to particulars, which Aristotle teaches is characteristic of the highest wisdom—and if he had set out each heading of the whole of theology with particular explanations, we should never have fallen into such madness or ignorance as to suppose that we could penetrate theological mysteries more clearly or divinely than he, or that by saying the same things twice we should uselessly undertake a superfluous task. Nor would we have dared thereby to wrong our teacher and friend and claim for ourselves the most excellent understanding and exposition of him by whom, after St. Paul, we were instructed.

“Nevertheless, in his reverent exposition of divine matters, he presented to us certain summaries—that is, universal propositions—filled with remarkably lucid concision. In one statement he embraced many things, instructing us and the other teachers of inexperienced minds to explain and distinguish, according to our ability and in language suited to us, the luminous and concise mysteries flowing inwardly from his supremely intellectual power.”

A little later he adds:

“Indeed, we observed this most carefully: we never touched upon what that divine teacher had clearly expressed to us, lest we repeat, in order to explain the same point, what he had already set forth in his exposition of the divine words.”

For this reason, as an example of Hierotheus’s remarkable knowledge and of the way in which he generally spoke of the highest mysteries in the most universal terms, but sometimes, when he wished, adapted himself most eloquently to the capacity of each person, Dionysius relates the widely known story of the gathering of Hierotheus and himself with the apostles at Jerusalem. Some think that the gathering was held to celebrate the burial of the Blessed Virgin; we, however, established earlier, under the year of the Lord 48, that it concerned a visit to the Lord’s tomb:

“On one occasion,” he says, “we gathered with our God-filled hierarchs, both he and we together, and many of our holy brothers, to behold that body which had received the Prince and God of life. James, the brother of the Lord, and Peter, the lofty and most exalted summit of theologians, were also present.

“After the viewing, it pleased the hierarchs that each should praise, according to his ability, the infinitely powerful goodness. Hierotheus surpassed all the other sacred Doctors there, as you know, after the theologians—that is, the apostles—being wholly transported, wholly outside himself, and sharing in what he praised. Therefore, by all who heard and saw him, whether they knew him or not, he was judged to be possessed by God and a divine praiser.”

These words concern his highest and most universal teachings. Therefore Dionysius adds:

“But let us for the present pass over the things mystically treated there, since they cannot be expressed to many.”

Regarding the other method of teaching, adapted to each person’s capacity, in which Hierotheus also excelled wonderfully, he continues:

“Whenever it was necessary to make matters common to many, so that we might introduce as many as possible into our holy discipline, it was truly marvelous how far Hierotheus surpassed the great number of holy teachers in the sustained diligence of his instruction, the purity of his mind, the exactness of his care in explanation, and all the other qualities pertaining to sacred discourse. Therefore we would never dare to fix our gaze upon so great a sun.”

And shortly afterward:

“We descend to writing, daring to introduce nothing new, but discerning and explaining through smaller inquiries arranged point by point those things that the true Hierotheus—that is, a certain sacred God—had transmitted with lucid concision.”

Thus it seems that whatever Dionysius wrote had first been written by the blessed Hierotheus in a higher style and was afterward translated by Dionysius according to our capacity.

Fragments of Hierotheus himself survive in the same author, from his book *Theological Elements*, in which he discussed the good, light, beauty, love, ecstasy, zeal, and other matters. Speaking of the divinity and excellence of Christ, he says:

> The divinity of Jesus, which is the cause of all things, fills all things, and preserves the harmonious parts of the universe. It is neither part nor whole; yet again it is both part and whole, since it has comprehended within itself every part and every whole, and possesses and prepossesses them eminently.
>
> It is perfect in imperfect things, as the source of perfection; but in perfect things it is not perfect, since it precedes perfection in excellence and origin.
>
> Moreover, in things lacking form it is the formative form, as the principle of form; but in forms it is formless, as surpassing form.
>
> It is also essence, seated wholly beyond the contagion of essences, existing above essence, and completely detached from every essence; distinguishing all principles and boundaries, and placed above every principle and order.
>
> It is the measure of beings, and eternity, and above eternity, and before eternity. It is full in needy things, but overflowing in full things; ineffable and unutterable; above intellect, above life, above essence. It possesses a supernatural gift in a supernatural manner, and an superessential gift in a superessential manner.
>
> Therefore, when it came down to our nature in supreme goodness and truly assumed the substance of our flesh, and that supreme God was called man—may the things we now praise, which surpass understanding and speech, be propitious—then too the supernatural and superessential gift shone forth in these things.
>
> This was so not only because he communicated himself to us immutably and without confusion, suffering nothing in his overflowing fullness from his ineffable self-emptying, but also because—what is the newest of all new things—in our natural realities he was supernatural, in the things belonging to our essence he was above essence, containing all that is ours from what is ours, and excellently surpassing us above ourselves.

Nothing has been said by later teachers about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and the majesty of his divinity so concisely or so profoundly. In a very few words he destroyed all the later heresies of Nestorius, Eutyches, Valentinus, and Arius.

He also composed hymns of love, in which, undergoing divine things, he explains beyond human understanding the definition, species, union, and power of love. A noble fragment of these hymns survives. St. Dionysius, citing it in chapter 4 of *On the Divine Names*, says:

“This renowned teacher of ours, who instructed us in the sacred writings, expounded these matters with an extraordinary divine power in his hymns of love.”

The fragment is as follows:

> Whether we call love divine, angelic, intellectual, animal, or natural, let us understand it as a certain power that unifies and mingles; moving higher things toward the providence of lower things; again exhorting things of the same order toward mutual communion; and finally recalling lower things so that they may turn toward higher realities.
>
> Thus far we have arranged many loves proceeding from one love, and we have described what the concepts and powers of love are, both among worldly things and among things above the world. According to the intention of the discourse indicated, the orders and adornments of intelligible and intellectual loves preside over these worldly loves. Above them stand intelligible and divine loves in themselves, which we have celebrated, according to our ability, as truly beautiful.
>
> Now, taking them all up again into one, let us gather and assemble the concentrated love, the father of all loves.
>
> First, compressing the many into two universal powers of love, which the absolute cause of all love contains and governs, let us place them beside the beginning that surpasses all things, toward which the universal love of all things strives according to the nature of each.
>
> Come, then: gathering these together once more into one, let us say that there is one simple power, moving itself toward a certain unifying commixture, from the good itself to the furthest limit of the universe; and from that limit, again through all things, returning to the good, reflecting itself in a circle from itself, through itself, and in itself, and always gathering itself into itself in the same manner.

Thus far he wrote. Nothing else, alas, survives from all his writings. Yet thanks be to God that at least one claw of so great a lion has been preserved, so that from the claw we might recognize the lion.

By what steps do you think he ascended to so sublime a height of divine theology? Dionysius identifies three, and they are the most excellent: first, that he received much from the holy apostles; second, that he devoted himself to the frequent and constant study of the sacred writings; and third, that, accustomed to divine revelations, he immediately heard the divine truth teaching him.

“Our renowned teacher,” Dionysius says in chapter 1, “celebrated these matters wonderfully and beyond the measure of nature in the *Theological Elements*. He received them either from the holy theologians—that is, the apostles—or discerned them through the skillful investigation of the sacred writings, by frequent exercise and long study of them; or he perceived them through some more divine inspiration, learning divine things not merely intellectually but undergoing them, and, through a certain sympathy with them—if one may speak in this way—being perfected for their unteachable and secret union, and finally for their faith.”

Thus far concerning the teaching of Hierotheus.

As regards the history of his life, it is accepted by the common judgment of Spanish authors that he was born in Spain, as Dexter says. From there he went to Athens for the sake of philosophy, just as Seneca or Quintilian went to Rome, or as certain nobles—Jerome’s expression—came from the remotest provinces of Spain to Livy, whose eloquence flowed like a fountain of milk. Later he was brought to the faith by St. Paul and made bishop of Athens. When Dionysius was appointed in his place, he returned to his homeland to entrust his fellow citizens with the treasure of divine knowledge.

This is stated by Pineda, Jerome, Romanus, Villegas, Marieta, Trugillus in the *Life of St. Paul the Apostle*, and others. More authoritative than the rest is Ambrosius Morales, book 9 of his *History*, who, in support of his own view and ours, reports the ancient Greek commentators on St. Dionysius whom he himself had read in the Royal Library of the Escorial. Therefore, he says, there can be no doubt that Hierotheus was Spanish, since the Greek Doctors themselves confess this.

They sing his praises at length in the menologion, where they relate that, because of his outstanding uprightness of character and philosophy, he had once been enrolled among the judges of the Areopagus [Col. 0243B].

Which city in Spain he ultimately became bishop of, however, we owe solely to Dexter, who knew the ecclesiastical antiquities of Spain better than the others. It should not seem strange that the Greeks do not mention the city of Segovia, since they do not mention Paris in connection with Dionysius either. This gave rise to the question, formerly debated sharply between Greeks and Latins, concerning the two Dionysiuses. But just as they then failed to know the Gallic city, so now they fail to know the Spanish one—both omissions occurring without detriment to us.

A strong argument for Hierotheus’s return to Spain is that he had not only Dionysius as a disciple but also St. Eugenius, as we proved in its proper place. Yet he could not have met Eugenius in the East, where Eugenius was never present; he could have met him in Spain, since the city of Segovia lies within the diocese of Toledo.

The feast of St. Hierotheus is celebrated by both Greeks and Latins on 4 October.

[Col. 0243C] After I had completed such commentaries at Rome, I returned to Spain. While I happened to be staying with the Cistercian monks of the monastery of Sandoval, in the diocese of León, and was diligently examining the sacred reliquaries, I learned that the head of St. Hierotheus was preserved there. The elderly monks affirmed that this had been handed down to them by their predecessors.

The sacred head was indeed among the relics, but written testimony of the matter was lacking. Nevertheless, it occurred to me to remove the skull from the little linen cloth in which it had been kept, tightly wrapped and sewn with thread, for many years, to see whether some testimony of the matter might perhaps be found inside.

And behold, with God’s favor, in the presence of the abbot and all the monks, an extremely ancient little parchment, half a finger in length, was found with part of the skull. On it were Greek characters of this kind:

**κεφαλὴ Ἱεροθεοῦς**

That is, “the head of Hierotheus.”

An incredible joy immediately entered everyone’s minds. Over so great a gift, at the abbot’s direction, a solemn procession was held as an act of thanksgiving [Col. 0243D], and a Mass for the same divine Teacher and bishop was sung on the very day of the discovery, which was 5 April in the year of the Lord 1625, the feast dedicated to St. Isidore.

This makes more probable what Dexter writes concerning Hierotheus’s return from Athens to Spain and the church he established at Segovia. It is therefore plausible that, during the devastation by the Saracens, his sacred remains were carried by Christians to the mountains of León, at whose foot the monastery of Sandoval is situated [Col. 0244A].

## 4. Marcellus, etc.

Everything agrees with what we read in the Roman Martyrology on 7 October:

“At Rome, the holy martyrs Marcellus and Apulius, who at first adhered to Simon Magus; but when they saw the wonders that the Lord worked through the apostle Peter, they abandoned Simon, devoted themselves to apostolic teaching, and after the Passion of the Apostles received the crown of martyrdom under the consul Aurelian. They were buried not far from the city.”

Ado, Bede, Usuard, and Peter Equilinus, book 9, chapter 30, relate the same account in nearly the same words. Dexter mentions Marcellus alone.

Some say that these men are discussed in the Acts of the holy martyrs Nereus and Achilleus. They are mistaken, however, because the Marcellus discussed there did not suffer near Rome. Rather, he was St. Eugenius, archbishop of Toledo, who was previously called M. Marcellus and was afterward called Eugenius by the Christians because of his nobility; the name means “noble.”

He too was indeed a disciple of Simon and Peter, but he was distinct from that Marcellus, although related to him.

## 5. St. Theodore, etc.

The matter concerns the martyrdom of Theodore and his companions in the Roman Martyrology on 26 March, in these words:

“At Pentapolis in Libya, a province of Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Theodore, bishop; Irenaeus, deacon; and Serapion and Ammonius, readers.”

Usuard, Bede, and Equilinus, book 2, final chapter, agree.

Baronius notes that the province of Pentapolis mentioned here was also called Cyrenaica by Pliny. It is frequently mentioned in the letters of Synesius, bishop, and in the writings of Dionysius of Alexandria preserved by Eusebius.

St. Theodore was a disciple of the blessed apostle James and had succeeded St. Anathasius, bishop of Caesaraugusta, in the see of St. Mary of the Column. Zealous to spread the faith, he traveled throughout Spain and finally reached the shores of Africa, accompanied by his deacon Irenaeus and the two readers Serapion and Ammonius.

There, that is, in the province of Cyrene or Pentapolis, they were captured by pagans. Because they refused to sacrifice to false gods, they were subjected to various tortures and then beheaded [Col. 0244C].

At that time St. Crescens was bishop of Carthage, having been left there by St. Peter the Apostle, as Metaphrastes relates; and we demonstrated this more fully earlier, under the year of the Lord 50. These are his words concerning Peter:

“He came to Sirmium, a city of Spain, where he appointed Epaenetus bishop. From there he went to Carthage, a city of Africa, in which he ordained Crescens bishop.”

Crescens therefore arranged for the sacred remains of Theodore to be buried. From there he himself carried them to Gallaecia, so that what St. Theodore had stipulated in his testament, as Dexter asserts—namely, that he was to be granted burial beside St. James, his teacher—might be fulfilled.

After this, Crescens proceeded to Gaul and established the church of Vienne, as the Roman Martyrology says on 29 December.

A distinguished ancient monument to this history of St. Theodore and his companions survives in M. Maximus, who sang the whole matter in Sapphic and Adonic verses under the title: “A Sapphic poem of M. Maximus to the first holy bishops of Caesaraugusta.” It is as follows, as we promised earlier under the year of the Lord 50:

> Here at the sacred altars we burn  
> Incense, nard, and customary fragrances  
> To the throng of bishops whom this city  
> Holds as its patrons.
>
> Those whom it has as fathers, the first  
> Bishops of the faith; under these teachers  
> The city of Caesar flourishes greatly,  
> And dedicates temples to them.
>
> I praise you first, holy Athanasius,  
> And you, Theodore, in outstanding song;  
> No less worthy than our own, O chosen bishop,  
> Are you of odes.
>
> The Iberus itself saw the third and the first  
> Suffer bravely; but the second  
> Sowing sacred things throughout Libya,  
> Bright Cyrene received.
>
> Here lie the sacred ashes, buried,  
> Whom grieving Crescens commands to be buried;  
> From here Crescens lifts them, for a weightier reason,  
> As brother and guest.
>
> And the companion Irenaeus, suppliant with them,  
> Who is said to be the chief of the Levites;  
> And the two readers—but all four are killed  
> By the sword.
>
> On the twenty-fourth day of March, in blessed light,  
> The people, suppliant to you and to your sacred companions,  
> Celebrate each year the feasts  
> On which they are remembered to have suffered.

M. Maximus differs from the Martyrologies on this one point: he says that the feast of St. Theodore and his companions was celebrated at Caesaraugusta on 24 March—“the twenty-fourth day of March”—whereas the Martyrologies assign it to the 26th.

I would believe that they died on the 24th, the day on which, Maximus says, “they are remembered to have suffered,” unless perhaps an error entered the Martyrologies through the negligence of copyists. Alternatively, the day of burial may have been celebrated, as happened with other martyrs; or the feast may customarily have been transferred from that day when some interruption occurred.

I should also point out that Didacus Murillo, in his history of the Pillar, honestly confessed that he was completely unaware of what the sacred poet meant when he spoke of the relics or ashes of the martyrs:

> “Whom grieving Crescens commands to be buried.”

For he did not know who that Crescens was. Yet he was none other than the first person worthy of that name: the disciple of Paul and Peter, and at that time bishop of Carthage in Africa.

In the following verse, the reading was:

> “From here Crescens helps” [Col. 0245C]

when it must certainly be read:

> “From here Crescens lifts.”
