The meaning is that Crescens lifted the martyr’s relics from there and carried them to Spain, according to what Theodore himself had ordered. This is the “weightier reason” that compelled St. Crescens to carry him from there and place him beside the apostle James.

We possess irrefutable testimony to this in a letter of Pope St. Leo IV concerning the translation of St. James. Speaking of SS. Athanasius and Theodore, he says:

“Those two disciples and attendants, out of reverence for their teacher, ordered that after their death they should be buried by Christians beside their teacher: one at his right hand and the other at his left.”

Pope Callixtus II says the same, as Vincent of Beauvais reports in the *Historical Mirror*. Later writers—Morales, Marieta, Alderete, and the others—agree with them.

In the ancient Breviary of Córdoba I read:

“The other disciples, Athanasius and Theodore, as is recorded in the letter of Blessed Leo, were buried beside the body of the Apostle, one at his right and the other at his left.”

This very tradition has been received in the Church of Compostela [Col. 0245D].

## A.D. 71 — A.U.C. 822

At Jerusalem, the temple, greatest and most venerable in the whole world for its antiquity, religion, and throngs, was burned on the sixth day before the Ides of September [perhaps August].

## A.D. 71 — A.U.C. 822

St. Onesimus, a disciple of St. Paul from the city of Patara in Achaia, preaches throughout Spain with the holy virgins Polyxena and Sara, disciples of the apostle Andrew.

[Col. 0239] A.D. 71 — A.U.C. 822

St. Hierotheus, Spanish by nation, whom Paul converted and whose fame was made illustrious by the glory of his disciple Dionysius, went to Spain. First bishop of Athens, afterward bishop of Segovia among the Arevaci, he is considered remarkable for holiness.

[Col. 0243] A.D. 71 — A.U.C. 822

Marcellus, a relative of M. Marcellus—who was the disciple of Peter and was surnamed Eugenius—once a disciple of Simon Magus together with that same Marcellus, suffers not far from Rome.

A.D. 71 — A.U.C. 822

Theodore II, bishop of Caesaraugusta, preaching in the African Pentapolis, becomes a martyr with Irenaeus, his archdeacon, and the readers Serapion and Ammonius. Not long afterward his body, brought to Spain—as Theodore himself had ordered—lies near the tomb of St. James.

[Col. 0245] [Note: [Col. 0245D]

## A.D. 76

### 1. Paul Sergius, etc.

We have shown above, under the year 66, that Paul traversed Spain twice: first together with the apostle Saint Paul himself in the year 66, and later, having been admonished by him in a vision, in this year 76. Dexter dealt with his earlier arrival in that year 66; he now deals with the later one, and we have shed light on both in our commentary on Dexter.

The first arrival is mentioned by the first bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône in his *Topography of the Martyrs*, under the word “Corsica,” where he says:

> Corsica is an island of the Tyrrhenian Sea, near Sardinia. Here the apostle Paul preached from the city during the ten years of his freedom under Nero; from there he proceeded to Spain with Saint Paul of Narbonne.

Regarding this later preaching, during which he visited the principal cities of Spain and illumined them by his preaching, we have the celebrated testimony of Peter of Equilio, who speaks of him in Book I, chapter 60, as follows:

> After his own passion, therefore, Blessed Paul the Apostle commanded him in a vision to go to the regions of Spain and Gaul to preach.

And shortly afterward:

> He came to Narbonne, and from there, travelling throughout Spain, he preached, and returned to Narbonne.

The circuit described by Dexter should be arranged as follows: he went from Narbonne to Barcelona, and from there to Zaragoza; then to Segontia—now Sigüenza. Passing through New Castile, he visited Córdoba, and finally Hispalis, where he boarded a ship; then he returned to Narbonne across the Mediterranean. Thus, by preaching, he traversed the whole of Spain from one end to the other.

### 2. M. Pelagius, etc.

Everyone who has written about Spanish and Gallic affairs knows that Saint Saturninus, bishop of Toulouse, was a disciple of the apostle Saint Peter. Indeed, the Church of Pamplona, which recognizes him as its apostle, sings precisely this on his feast day. See the *Treasury of Preachers* under 26 November and 25 September. There Saturninus is said not merely to have come from Toulouse to Pamplona, but to have penetrated as far as the city of Toledo and to have sown there the seeds of preaching.

The *Chronicles of Prince Charles* agree, as do Primus, bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, in his *Topography of the Martyrs of Christ*; Morales, Book IX, chapter 14; Marieta, Part I, Book I, chapter 15; and, before them, Julian the archpresbyter at the beginning of his *Chronicle*. He reports that Saturninus not only preached at Toledo but also served for a time as bishop of the Toledans. See also Vaseus in his *Chronicle* and Luis Nonnius in his *Spain*, chapter 80.

Saint Braulio likewise speaks of this Saturninus in his additions to Maximus, when writing first about Saint Firminus of Pamplona and afterward bishop of Amiens:

> He was consecrated, he says, by Honoratus, bishop of Toledo, and baptized in the saving waters by Saint Saturninus, bishop of Toulouse, disciple of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, who had been sent to preach at Toulouse.

What removes all doubt in this matter is that the same assertion is made in such clear words in his authentic *Acts*. That prelate of blessed memory, Roderic Ximénez, of the Church of Toledo and historiographer of Spain, held a copy of them worthy of veneration in his library; it is now kept with his body in the royal monastery of Saint Mary of Horta, in the diocese of Sigüenza, belonging to our Cistercian order, to which the archbishop bequeathed his entire library.

In a parchment manuscript of the *Lives of the Saints* there are therefore the authentic *Acts of Saint Saturninus*, beginning: “In that course of time, therefore, etc.” There it is asserted that Saturninus was a disciple of the apostle Saint Peter in these words:

> Honestus is a good disciple of Saturninus; Saturninus is better, as Peter’s foster-son; but Christ is best of all, as Peter’s teacher—that is, master. Yet he who chose Peter in the apostolic faith also made Saturninus blessed in pastoral government, and adorned Honestus with priestly integrity.

Concerning the places illumined by his preaching, the text continues:

> O great grace of Saturninus, who traversed not only Gaul and Galicia, Septimania and Spain, but also Nesturia and Germany.

And afterward:

> When the most blessed Saturninus was preaching at Pamplona, suddenly an exceedingly large crowd of citizens gathered. They continued coming for three days, and, after seeing many signs and powerful wonders, forty thousand gentiles, strengthened by them, promptly followed the true God after receiving the bath of rebirth.

From this the error that entered the Roman Martyrology is plainly established: under 29 November it asserts that Saint Saturninus suffered martyrdom in the time of Decius. I believe this was taken from Equilio, Book I, chapter 5, where he makes the assertion rashly. For since he says there that the bishop of Toulouse was ordained by the disciples of the apostles, it would have been impossible for him to live into the time of Decius unless one wished to make him bishop for at least 150 years—especially since Saint Clement or Saint Dionysius had ordained him. Decius began to reign in A.D. 252 or 253.

Certainly, nothing about Decius is asserted in the ancient Martyrologies, as may be seen in Usuard, who has the same wording as the Roman Martyrology but not a word about Decius. Ambrosius Morales says that the common calculation has approved the view that Saturninus was sent to preach in Gaul under Claudius—namely, Nero.

If, however, that Decius was the one who put Saturninus to death, he cannot have been the emperor but must have been some prefect or proconsul. The same judgment should be made concerning the Decius under whom Saint Laurence is said to have suffered, approximately twenty years after the death of the emperor Decius.

Here I gladly follow the opinion of our Ambrosius Morales. In Book IX of his *History*, chapter 46, he notes that there existed a certain noble Roman family distinguished by the name of the Decii. Thus no one need wonder that, after the emperor Decius had died, Laurence was tortured by a Decius, and that, long before him, Saturninus was hurled to his death at Toulouse from the summit of the Capitol by a Decius.

To remove every ambiguity in this matter, Methodius—or Metrodorus—the most ancient writer on the affairs of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, explicitly states that Saint Saturninus was given as a companion to Dionysius by Saint Pope Clement, and that Dionysius, already established in Gaul, sent him to Toulouse. The author’s words are these:

> The companions of Saint Dionysius were Saint Saturninus and Marcellus.

And shortly afterward:

> Moreover, when Saint Saturninus had been sent to the regions of Aquitaine, etc.

No one is unaware that Toulouse is a city of Aquitaine.

Equilio himself says the same in Book IX, chapter 41:

> Dionysius, he says, was sent into France by Blessed Clement, successor of Peter; the priest Rusticus and the deacon Eleutherius were assigned to him as companions, and also the holy bishops Saturninus and Marcellus. He sent Marcellus to Spain—this was Saint Eugenius—and Saturninus to Aquitaine.

This must be understood as follows: Saturninus was sent into Gaul by the apostle Saint Peter, especially to the regions of Aquitaine. Nevertheless, in A.D. 76 he visited Toledo, as Dexter asserts here. From there he returned to Rome. After several years—namely, around A.D. 93—his fellow disciple Saint Clement began to sit in the chair of Saint Peter. When Clement sent Dionysius to Gaul, he joined Saturninus to him as an outstanding man, especially experienced in that province. Saturninus had already been intending of his own accord to return to his see at Toulouse; when Dionysius and his companions had taken possession of Gaul, Dionysius sent him back there.

What he accomplished there, and how he returned to Toledo again, we shall relate when treating Dexter under the years 110 and 112.

The chief fruit, however, that he brought back from his preaching at Toledo was two most holy citizens, M. Pelagius and Aulus Altimus Paternus—two, I say, illustrious lights of the Catholic Church.

Pelagius afterward became bishop of Toledo and the first bishop of all Spain. Paternus, a native of Bilbilis and therefore dear to Martial, who commended him more than once in his epigrams, became first bishop of Elusa and afterward of the Constantian community in Gaul; he won the crown by shedding his blood for Christ on 25 September.

Julian confirms this opinion in his *Chronicle* under the year 132. Speaking of Saint Honoratus, bishop of Toledo, he says:

> After several years he set out for Gaul to preach. He visited Paternus, whom Saint Saturninus had converted at Toledo and made bishop of the Elusans, etc.

He also speaks of Saint Pelagius, whom he calls M. Pelagius Agrippa. We shall deal with Paternus together with Dexter under the years 94, 112, and 130; with Pelagius, under the years 138 and 160.

In this same year of the Lord 76, Saint Quartus died in peace, as Dexter said under the year 50. We shall speak of him again under the year 105.

### A.D. 76. A.R. 827

Paul Sergius preaches at Hispalis, Córdoba, Barcelona, Zaragoza, Segontia, and many other cities of Spain; and he traverses the entire province of Spain.

### A.D. 76. A.R. 827

M. Pelagius and Aulus Altimus Paternus, citizens of Toledo, are illumined by the preaching and miracles of Saint Saturninus, disciple of Saint Peter—miracles which he performed magnificently at Toledo.

## A.D. 86

### 1. “At that time, etc.”

It is significant that he did not say, “Cletus succeeds Linus,” but “he had succeeded during that same period,” because he had succeeded him in the year 82, when Linus suffered martyrdom. Nor should anyone think that this is inconsistent with Dexter’s manner of speaking. He does not assign to every Roman Pontiff the year in which he began his pontificate; rather, he often proceeds by recapitulation, enumerating many events together.

That he regarded Anacletus and Cletus as one and the same person should not seem novel. Indeed, I do not see how a different person could be devised, since nearly all ancient Greek and Latin authors—whether they preceded Dexter himself or were his contemporaries—unhesitatingly regarded them as one, although some called him Cletus and others Anacletus.

Among these authors was the great Ignatius, “the hearer of the disciple whom Jesus loved”—I use the words of my Bernard—in his letter to Mary of Cassobola and in his letter to the Trallians. He recognizes no one other than Anacletus as Clement’s predecessor and a disciple of the apostle Peter.

Then there are Saint Irenaeus, Book III of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 12; Epiphanius, *On Heresies*, 27; Nicephorus Callistus, Book III, chapter 2; and Nicephorus the bishop in his *Chronicle*. In general, all the Greeks follow the same view.

Among the Latins are Augustine, Letter 165; Optatus of Milevis, Book II *Against Parmenian*; and, more importantly, Jerome, both in his *Chronicle* and in his *On Illustrious Men*, under Clement, where he says:

> Clement was the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter, for Linus was second and Anacletus third.

This is read exactly thus both in the Latin and in the Greek text of Sophronius. It is therefore astonishing that Baronius is said to have held the opposite opinion.

Only Tertullian, in Book III of his poems against Marcion, sang of two persons, Cletus and Anacletus; and the book attributed to Damasus on the supreme pontiffs does the same, although Onuphrius, Molanus, and Baronius deny that it is his.

I therefore strongly suspect that Cletus was later called Anacletus as a mark of honor, because of the exceptional grace of God that shone in him—just as Oppius was called Agathopius, as we said above.

I wish that greater diligence might be exercised in the Church to investigate this matter thoroughly. It is exceedingly difficult to believe that, furnished with so few authorities, she neglected to follow so many and such eminent teachers.

### 2. “Vespasian, etc.”

He had died in A.D. 81, after ruling the empire for ten years. He was succeeded by two sons: first Titus for two years; then, after Titus was removed by poison, Domitian in A.D. 83. Domitian stirred up the second persecution against the Church, as Eusebius testifies in Book III, chapter 13. Dexter soon afterward reports some of its fruits; he had dealt with the first persecution, under Nero, under the year 60.

### 3. “At Capara, etc.”

Ptolemy places Capara among the Vettones—or Vergones—of Lusitania. In that region there was once fierce conflict between Gnaeus Pompey and Aulus Trebonius, and even today many stone monuments of that war remain, namely those of soldiers killed there. They may be seen in Ambrosius Morales, Book VIII, chapter 18.

Capara still retains its name. It lies on the border of Extremadura, not far from the city of Civitas, commonly called Ciudad Rodrigo. It has been more fortunate in the martyrdom of Saints Carilippus and his companions than in the number or wealth of its inhabitants.

The feast of Saint Carilippus and his companions is celebrated on 28 April in the Martyrologies of Bede, Ado, Usuard, and the Roman Martyrology. In the latter, however, *Caralippum* is corruptly printed in place of *Carilippum*, whereas in the others, and in Equilio, Book XII, final chapter, section 131, as in Dexter, the name is written *Carilippus*.

The names of his companions are Aphrodisius, Agapius—Agapatus in Usuard and Agapitus in Equilio—and Eusebius. This is how they are named by the aforementioned authors, but no one records their acts.

### 4. “Domitian, etc.”

He took this from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, where we read:

> In the year 88, Domitian built the temple without any admixture of wood.

He is speaking of the Pantheon, now the Church of Saint Mary of the Rotunda.

Bede agrees in his Martyrology under 1 November and in his *Book on the Six Ages*, under Trajan. Baronius nevertheless disagrees in his notes under 1 November, maintaining that it was built by M. Agrippa, not by Domitian, because the following inscription still remains on the front of the temple:

> M. AGRIPPA. L. F. CONS. TERTIUM. FECIT.  
> Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, made this.

This was in the year 25 before the birth of Christ. Baronius also appeals to Dio, who says:

> The Pantheon, which Agrippa completed, etc.

The accounts can nevertheless easily be reconciled if we say that Agrippa used a wooden roof structure in the Pantheon—that is, in the portico, where his inscription appears. The difference in the work itself proves that Agrippa built only the portico, whereas Domitian completed the temple proper in new work, without a wooden roof structure, as it is seen today.

### 5. “He was also the first, etc.”

Eusebius likewise has this:

> In the year 89 of the Lord, Domitian was the first to order himself to be called “Lord and God.”

Suetonius testifies to this in his *Life of Domitian*, chapter 13, saying:

> With equal arrogance, when dictating a circular letter in the name of his procurators, he began it as follows: “Our Lord and God commands that this be done.”

After this, it became customary that no one should address him otherwise, even in writing or speech.

Martial calls him precisely this in Book VIII, in the final epigram:

> Since a crowd gives you, Augustus, a multitude of complaining little books,  
> We too, because we give our little poems to our lord,  
> Know that you can be a god alike in affairs and in the Muses,  
> And that these garlands too are pleasing to you.

Thus he grants him the status of a god. “By your poets, Augustus,” etc.

Statius likewise calls Domitian “lord and god” in Book IV of the *Silvae*. Indeed, Philostratus states in his *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, Book VII, that the evil of flattery had reached such a point that, on the advice of the famous Jew Josephus, Domitian dared to be called “son of the Virgin.”

### 6. “Saint Julianus, etc.”

What he says—“he was transferred to Vicus”—should not be understood as a translation of the sacred body, since Julianus lived for several more years and died a martyr in A.D. 92 or 93, as is clear from Dexter. Rather, it refers to exile, by which he was condemned by Domitian and transferred from the nurturing City to Spain, just as John the Theologian was also transferred to Patmos at Domitian’s command.

Julianus had been a disciple of the apostle Peter and a colleague of Eugenius. He was born at Toledo and preached the Gospel to his fellow citizens before Eugenius. He was called bishop of Toledo and of all Carpetania, as Dexter states under the years 91 and 94.

Julian the archpresbyter agrees at the beginning of his *Chronicle*. There, after reporting the diptych—or list—of the Toledan bishops customarily recited during the Mass instituted by Saint Isidore, he adds:

> This was the first diptych, in which the martyrs are not included: namely, James—the apostle who founded the Church of Toledo—Elpidius, Julianus, Saturninus, and M. Marcellus Eugenius, because it is established that they were martyrs.

The priest prayed there for the souls of the bishops who had fallen asleep, as is clear from the Missal of Saint Isidore. For this reason the names of the martyr bishops did not appear in it together with the others.

That Julianus was dear to Martial is sufficiently clear, for Martial addressed four epigrams to him under the name Lucius Julius. Dexter admits that this was his name below, under the year 94, although there is some disagreement between Martial and Dexter: Martial calls him L. Julius, whereas Dexter calls him L. Julianus, and even L. Magnus Julianus. Perhaps this difference also arose from his baptism.

Do you ask for the epigrams? In Book I, epigram 15, Martial advises him to live today and not tomorrow, perhaps moved by the fact that Saint Julius or Julianus professed that he would accomplish something better on the following day, whereas on the present day he regarded himself as a sinner. Martial turns this into a poem in his customary fashion:

> O Julianus, worthy to be remembered after all my friends,  
> If long loyalty and hoary obligations have any force,  
> Your thirtieth consulship is now almost upon you for the second time—  
> For he was nearly sixty years old, being a disciple of Saint Peter—  
> And your life scarcely counts more than a few days.  
> You will not have postponed wisely what you see may be denied,  
> And you should regard only what has been as truly yours.

Shortly afterward he adds:

> Believe me, it is not the speech of a wise man to say, “I shall live.”  
> Tomorrow’s life is too late; live today.

Julianus disliked his friend’s always singing playful and humorous verses, and therefore often urged Martial to apply his mind to serious subjects. On this theme he wrote Epigram 107 of the same Book II:

> You often say to me, dearest Lucius Julianus:  
> “Write something great; you are a lazy man.  
> Give us leisure, but such leisure as Maecenas once gave  
> To Flaccus and to his own Virgil.”

And after a few lines:

> Young men do not wish to place their yokes upon barren fields;  
> Rich soil tires them, but the labor itself is pleasing.

He wrote these verses while Julianus was living at Rome. He addressed two others to him while he was already residing in Spain. One of these, Book IV, Epigram 55, was sent to Toledo and mentions many Spanish names:

> Lucius, glory of your times,  
> You do not allow ancient Gaurus and our Tagus  
> To yield to eloquent Arpis;  
> Born among Argive cities,  
> Let Thebes sing in verse, or Mycenae,  
> Or famed Rhodes, or the wrestling grounds  
> Of lustful Leda’s Lacedaemon.  
> We who are born among the Celts and from the Iberians—  
> Let us not be ashamed, in a gracious poem,  
> To repeat the harder names of our native land.

He continues by listing certain proper names and characteristics of Bilbilis and of the neighboring towns of Celtiberia, which anyone may see there.

Finally, in Book IX, Epigram 98, he relates to the same man, as though he were absent, his good fortune and happiness, over which a certain rival was gnawing with envy:

> Someone, dearest Julianus, is bursting with envy  
> Because Rome reads me; someone is bursting with envy, etc.

That is, because we are always pointed out by every crowd; because both Caesars—brothers Titus and Domitian—granted me the right of fathers; because I have a pleasant estate beneath the City and a small house in the City; because I am agreeable to my friends; because I am a frequent guest; because I am loved and approved.

He concludes:

> May everyone who bursts with envy burst indeed.

Martial had such confidence in this friendship that, although they had differed in their manner of life for several years, he sometimes disclosed his own ideas to Julianus.

The rest concerning Saint Julianus may be found in the places mentioned.

### 7. “C. Valerius Lentulus, etc.”

We dealt in our commentaries under the year 60 with Laureolus, a Christian performed by Lentulus in a comic presentation, especially on the basis of Juvenal, who says:

> Even swift Lentulus acted Laureolus well,  
> Who, in my judgment, was truly deserving of the cross.

And Martial, whose Epigram 9 we also presented:

> As Prometheus, bound upon the Scythian cliff, etc.

There Martial relates the true passion of a certain Christian martyr under the guise of the fictional story of Laureolus the bandit, who was being acted.

Many writers report that Domitian, in his excessive cruelty, was accustomed to represent tragic accidents from real life upon the bodies of wretched people in the theater. Tacitus too, in his *Life of Agricola*, adds:

> Nero withdrew his eyes and ordered crimes to be committed, but did not watch them. Under Domitian, the chief part of misery was to see and to be seen; our sighs were recorded, and to mark the pallor of so many men, that savage face and the redness with which he defended himself against shame were sufficient.

### 8. “Flavius Clemens, etc.”

The martyrdom of this man was attested not only by Catholic writers but also by pagan authors, Suetonius and Dio.

Suetonius says in his *Life of Domitian*, chapter 15:

> Finally, he suddenly killed Flavius Clemens, his cousin, a man of the most contemptible inactivity—this is how he calls a man who, in order to devote himself to Christ, did not wish to give himself over to public affairs—and whose very young sons he had openly designated as his successors, ordering one to be called Vespasian and the other Domitian instead of their former names. He suddenly killed him on the slightest suspicion—almost during his very consulship. By this deed above all he hastened his own end.

Dio writes as follows:

> Domitian put many others to death, but especially Flavius Clemens the consul, although he was his nephew and had married Flavia Domitilla, a relative of Domitian himself. But for what reason? The charge of atheism—ἀθεότης, that is, contempt for the gods—was brought against both. For this reason many who had turned to the customs of the Jews—that is, of the Christians—from paganism were condemned: some were killed, others were stripped of their possessions. Domitilla alone was exiled to Pandateria.

Cardinal Baronius rightly laments that so distinguished a martyr of Christ was omitted from the catalogue or Martyrology of the saints. But another Flavius—Dexter—has now recorded both his martyrdom and the day, namely 21 November, so that the Church may at some time restore him.

Martial addressed Epigram 93 of Book X to him, beginning:

> If first, Clemens, you should see the Euganean shores of Helicaon  
> And the painted fields upon their vine-covered hills, etc.

He then adds, concerning his consulship:

> Poems, now stitched upon the purple-bordered toga, etc.

There was another Flavius Clemens of the same name, a disciple of Saint Peter, the paternal uncle of Saint Clement the pope, and the first bishop of Metz in Gaul. He died in peace as a confessor on the 17th of the same month; Molanus mentions him on that day, and Peter writes his life in Book X, chapter 113, of his *Catalogue*.

I fear, however, that because of the similarity of the names, he may attribute to this confessor what belongs to the martyr Flavius Clemens. For he says that he was consul at Rome and the paternal uncle of Saint Clement the pope.

### 9. “Thraseas, etc.”

In the printed edition, *Helvidias* was corruptly read in place of *Servilia*. There were Barea Soranus and Thrasea Paetus, men of the highest distinction and consular rank; Servilia was the daughter of Barea, who was then proconsul of Syria. Even the pagans lament that all these people were wickedly put to death.

Juvenal writes:

> The Stoic killed Barea,  
> The informer killed his friend  
> And the old man’s disciple.

Martial writes of Thrasea in Book IV, Epigram 54, addressed to Colinus:

> Thrasea, more steadfast than Thrasea himself.

Of both men Cornelius Tacitus writes in Book XVI:

> After slaughtering so many distinguished men, Nero finally desired to destroy virtue itself, by killing Barea Soranus and Thrasea Paetus, against both of whom he had long been hostile.

What charge was brought against them? Tacitus himself tells us. Barea was accused because of the proconsulship of Asia that he had administered—not, he says, on account of any crime he had committed, but because of his justice and diligence.

Regarding Servilia, his daughter, Tacitus writes:

> Beyond this, he connected the daughter of the father with the recent danger, because she had given money generously to magicians—that is, to the poor of Christ.

Servilia was therefore summoned to the Senate. The aged parent and his daughter stood separately before the tribunal of the consuls. She was more than twenty years old, recently widowed and desolate after her husband, Annaeus Pollio, had been driven into exile. She looked toward her father, whose dangers she seemed to have increased.

Then, when the accuser asked whether she had sold her bridal ornaments and the necklace removed from her neck in order to obtain money for the practice of magical arts, she first lay prostrate on the ground, weeping and remaining silent for a long time. Then, after embracing the altars and the altar itself, she said:

> I have invoked no impious gods, no sacred rites, and nothing more calamitous in my prayers than that you, Caesar, and you, Fathers, might preserve this excellent father safe and unharmed.

Tacitus goes on to relate the lamentable death of both. Whether he wishes it or not, whatever he says about magicians and whatever he says about embracing the altar, he sufficiently indicates that they were Christians and were killed for contempt of the gods, since they had distributed their wealth to Christ’s poor.

Why, indeed, was an altar placed before them unless they were contemptuous of the gods? Thus what Dexter asserts here is true: many people held that they were Christians, a view also accepted by Baronius under the year 68, section 28.

Let the reader note this: Dexter does not mention Thrasea and Barea here because they were killed by Domitian together with Flavius Clemens. It is certain that they were put to death by Nero twenty years earlier, a fact that even Tacitus does not conceal. Rather, Dexter mentions them because the pagan authors who write about Clemens also discuss them, and because their deaths and the causes of their deaths were similar.

The same should be understood as having been said about Helvidius Priscus, Thrasea’s son-in-law, concerning whom Tacitus gives similar information in the aforementioned Book XVI of the *Annals*.

### 10. “He flourished, etc.”

This was borrowed from Martial, Book IV, Epigram 55, where, among other memorable matters that he relates about his native province of Celtiberia, he mentions the Suelli as javelin throwers.

After first writing:

> We who are born among the Celts and from the Iberians—  
> Let us not be ashamed, in a gracious poem,  
> To repeat the harder names of our native land,

he adds, among other things:

> And the sure-handed Suelli with the light javelin.

The printed manuscripts are corrupt at this point. Instead of *Suellos* they have *Silaos*. Matthew Rader nevertheless admits in the marginal notes of his Martial that the old manuscripts read *Suevos*, which comes closer to the truth.

The Suelli javelin throwers were so called from a town of the same name in Celtiberia. Dexter teaches here that they were transferred from there to Brigantium, a distinguished city of Galicia, now Coruña. He says the same under the year 430, when the fury of the Vandals was raging in Africa.

In the map of ancient Spain that Villanovanus drew in his edition of Ptolemy, a small town named Suelo is marked. He is mistaken, however, in assigning its location: he places it not in Celtiberia but on the shore of the Strait of Cádiz, where Estepona now stands.

We should rather follow the testimony of Martial and Dexter.

### 11. “Among the people of Messana, etc.”

Nothing is more venerable among the citizens of that most illustrious city, and nothing is equally accepted by Christian tradition, than the belief that their predecessors received a letter from the most blessed Mother of God while she was still living among human beings. In memory of so great a benefit, the metropolitan church is called *la Madona de Littrio*—that is, “of the Letter,” or “of the epistle”—which is said to be reverently preserved there.

Peter Canisius speaks of it in Book V, *On the Mother of God*, chapter 1:

> Among the Sicilians there is the distinguished republic of Messana, which proclaims that it received a letter sent by that Virgin Mother and, as I hear, reverently preserves it in its archives.

Among others, Father Francisco Arias, distinguished for piety and learning, also accepts it in his *Spiritual Progress*, in the treatise *On the Imitation of the Virgin*. Dexter speaks of it again under the year 430, when it was found once more in the archives.

I found it in Spanish in the library of our distinguished monastery of Despina, and I have decided to reproduce it here word for word.

> Mary, daughter of Joachim, of the tribe of Judah, of the house of David, most humble mother of Jesus Christ crucified: to all the people of the city of Messana, greeting and the blessing of the eternal Father.
>
> We know that you of this city have sent messengers and ambassadors with great faith, confessing with profound understanding that my Son is both man and God, the Only-begotten of the eternal Father; and likewise that, after his glorious resurrection, he ascended into heaven. In all things you recognize the true path of truth through the teaching and preaching of our apostle Paul.
>
> Therefore we give our blessing to you and to this city of ours, and we promise always to keep you under our perpetual protection and defense.

Rendered into Latin, it reads:

> Mary, daughter of Joachim, of the tribe of Judah and house of David, most humble mother of Jesus Christ crucified, to all citizens of Messana, greeting and the blessing of the eternal Father.
>
> We know that you sent messengers and envoys with great faith, confessing with full recognition that my Son is both man and God, the Only-begotten of the eternal Father; and likewise that after his glorious resurrection he ascended into heaven, recognizing in all things the sure path of truth through the teaching and preaching of our apostle Paul.
>
> Therefore we impart our blessing to you and to this city of ours, and promise always to keep you under our protection and defense.

Florence likewise boasts that it was honored by a similar favor from the Mother of God, as Jerome Savonarola testifies. He preached on this matter to the Florentines on 25 October 1495, and the sermon is preserved among his works. The text of the letter is as follows:

> Florence, beloved by God, by the Lord Jesus Christ, my Son, and by me: keep the faith, persist in prayers, strengthen yourself through patience. For by these things you will attain everlasting salvation with God.

The authors cited above concerning Messana also give credence to this letter. We shall discuss the Virgin’s letter to Ignatius when treating Dexter under the year 116 of the Lord.

### 12. “At Castra-Caecilia, etc.”

Here Dexter mentions not only Saint Jonas, a disciple of Saint Dionysius, but also under the years 112 and 130. From this it is clear that Jonas traversed Spain twice: first in the year 86 or 87, preaching the word of God, especially at Castra-Caecilia in Lusitania and in the towns surrounding it.

The Roman Martyrology, under 22 September, calls it the “Castran district.” Equilio relates that, after becoming priest of that place, Jonas was sustained by green herbs and cold water, in Book VIII, chapter 106.

This was his first arrival in Spain, before Saint Dionysius—whose disciple he had been at Athens—crossed into Gaul as the legate of Saint Clement in A.D. 93. Some therefore think that our Jonas returned to Gaul at that time as Dionysius’s companion.

There, after devoting himself for some time to preaching, he again traversed Spain in the year 112 and visited Saint M. Marcellus Eugenius, his teacher Dionysius’s fellow disciple, as Dexter says. Finally, he returned to Gaul in the year 130.

At that time the governor Julianus sent three lictors to Paris, where Jonas was then devoted to preaching, to seize and kill him. These are Equilio’s words. They found him near Paris, undaunted by any fear, unmoved by threats, and in no way abandoning his teaching. They beat him and beheaded him on the tenth day before the Kalends of October.

Taking up his severed head in his hands—thus imitating his teacher Dionysius in this as well—he proceeded approximately one mile to the place where the holy martyr had chosen his burial site. There he collapsed and died, and was buried there, amid a wonderful fragrance, at the place called Mount of Saint Jonas, or Jona.

Galesinus thought that he suffered under Domitian, under the governor Fesceninus. He is mistaken, however, since Jonas died under Hadrian in the year 130, under the governor Julianus.

Thus, when the Roman Martyrology says:

> At the Castran district, Saint Jonas, priest and martyr, who, having gone into Gaul with Saint Dionysius at the command of the prefect Julianus, was beaten with clubs and completed his martyrdom by the sword,

it does not identify the town where the martyrdom took place. Equilio was mistaken on this point. It would rather be necessary to say “near Paris,” as Galesinus says in his Martyrology.

The place intended is the town that, especially because of that teacher, gloried in Dexter’s age: Castra-Caecilia, or Castra-Caeciliana. It is now called, in corrupted form, Cáceres. It lies between the Guadiana and the Tagus in Extremadura, formerly part of Lusitania, and was a very distinguished place both for the families of its citizens and for the antiquity of its foundation.

For, as Morales states in Book VIII of his *History*, chapter 18, the consul Caecilius Metellus, after defeating Hirtuleius there, bestowed his own name and that of his camps upon the town. Hence it was called Castra-Caecilia, or, as others prefer, Castra-Caeciliana.

Only Arnoldus Mylius, in his *Geographical Synonymy*, reads Castra-Viceliana. A manuscript of Ptolemy also corruptly has Liciniana, in Lusitania near Emerita.

The same Metellus founded the colony of Metellinum, now Medellín, in the same region, likewise named after his cognomen, as we shall say elsewhere.

To prevent anyone from being deceived, I should point out that Castra-Lelia is also found in Lusitania, but it is a town entirely different from Castra-Caecilia. For, even according to Dexter himself below, under the year 308, Castra-Lelia was situated beside the port and city of Cales at the mouth of the Douro, on the shore of the Ocean, now Porto, from which the kingdom of Portugal takes its name. Castra-Caecilia, on the other hand, was in the inland parts of Lusitania. We shall discuss it in its proper place.

Correct Molanus on the basis of what has been said, for he reads: “On 5 August, at Castro-Corboilo, Saint Jonas the martyr.” He himself knows neither the martyr, nor the town, nor the day of the martyrdom. Nevertheless, his reading “Castro-Corboilo” comes closest to Castra-Caecilia.

### 13. At Caraca, etc.

The feast day of the holy martyrs Aemilianus and Geronius was celebrated in the Cordoban Breviary on 20 September. Galesinus likewise mentions them in his Martyrology on that same day, saying: “In Spain, the holy martyrs Aemilianus and Geronius.” From Dexter we learn two new facts: the time of their martyrdom, namely, during the persecution of Domitian, around the year of the Lord 87, and the city in which they were put to death, Caraca. This is the city we now call Guadalajara, according to Marinaeus Siculus, Morales, Nonnius, Mariana, and others. The manuscript of Antoninus corruptly reads *Ariaca*. In his Life of Sertorius, Plutarch relates that, after Sertorius had been defeated by Metellus, he pitched his camp not far from the Caracitani, beside the river Tagonius, and fought with them a memorable battle. Morales and Nonnius are mistaken in chapter 73 of their *History of Spain* when they think that the river Tagonius is called the Henares by Plutarch because Caraca lies on its banks. It is in fact the Tajuna, into which the Henares flows, as we shall show in the year 308. The Caracitani, moreover, were those who lived between the Henares and the Tajuna.

Since we are treating here of the holy martyr Geronius of Caraca, I have thought it appropriate to revive the noble memory of Geruntius, martyr and first bishop of Italica, whose memory had disappeared from the writings of the Spanish authors; he too was killed in these very times for the name of Christ. Concerning him the Roman Martyrology has the following entry for 25 August:

“At Italica in Spain, Saint Geruntius, bishop, who, preaching the Gospel in that province in the time of the Apostles, after many labors rested in prison.”

I suspect that Geruntius was ordained bishop of Italica by Saint Pius, bishop of Seville and disciple of Saint James; and perhaps he was a disciple of that Apostle himself, or certainly of Paul. Formerly the whole Church of Spain sang his deeds in a sacred hymn, which still exists today in the so-called Mozarabic Breviary. It is as follows.

#### Hymn on Saint Geruntius, bishop of Italica and martyr

Let us sing with worthy praises  
and celebrate with our voices  
the sacred bishop of Christ,  
Geruntius the confessor.

He is said to have shone forth as a prophet  
in apostolic times  
and to have preached  
the supreme Father of the mighty Son.

And while he journeyed, renowned,  
through the western region,  
at last the wrath of the Gentiles  
dragged him to his passion.

But soon, by order of the governor,  
he was burdened with iron chains;  
amid the dreadful shadows of the prison,  
he was delivered into the executioner’s power.

They say that, bound with fetters  
amid the pallid darkness,  
he gave his soul to heaven,  
torn from his sacred body.

Thus, already blessed among  
the company of the Apostles,  
he rejoices in heavenly glory  
and in the radiant grace of Christ.

For, crowned with a double distinction,  
he shines and glitters with a double reward:  
with the title of priesthood  
and with the reward of confession.

Let glory resound to the Father  
and to Christ the only-begotten,  
with the Spirit, the Paraclete,  
unto ages of ages. Amen.

The chapter has the following text:

“Glorious and merciful Lord, who granted that your most blessed confessor Geruntius, bishop, should confess you exceedingly with his lips, and wished you to be praised in the assembly of the just through his confession, so that, having confessed you on earth, you might make him rejoice when glorifying him in the council of the saints: we ask for the gift of your grace, that through his prayers you may grant us to be cleansed from the contagion of sin, rescued from everlasting fires, and brought to attain the blessedness of your glory.”

The aforesaid Breviary also contains an entire proper office, five prayers, two blessings, and other materials that show that Saint Geruntius had, in ancient times, a most illustrious memory in Spain.

---

**A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** During this period Saint Anacletus, or Cletus, had succeeded Linus; Linus, however, had succeeded Peter in the Roman see.

**A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** Titus succeeded Vespasian, and Domitian, the most cruel emperor, succeeded Titus. He launched the second persecution against the Church.

**A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** At Capara in Lusitania, Carilippus and his companions suffered martyrdom.

**[Col. 0249] A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** The emperor Domitian built a certain temple without a roof.

**A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** He was also the first of the emperors to have himself called a god.

**A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** Saint Julian, a disciple of Saint Peter and dear to Martial, was transferred to Vico.

**[Col. 0251] A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** C. Valerius Lentulus, a former consul, in order to please Domitian, played the Christian Laureolus.

**A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** Flavius Clemens, a former consul and a friend of Martial, was killed for the faith on 21 November.

**A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** Thraseas, Helvidius, Servilia, and Bareas were handed over by certain Christians. *(The name Helvidius was missing.)*

**A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** At that time a cohort of Celtiberians flourished in Spain; it is now at Brigantium. It has Suelli javelin-throwers, from the town now called Suello in Celtiberia, a name taken—though in corrupted form—from the Suelli themselves, who were javelin-throwers.

**[Col. 0253] A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** Among the people of Messana the memory of the Blessed Virgin Mary is celebrated; she sent them a gracious letter.

**A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** At Castra-Caecilia in Lusitania, Saint Jonas, a disciple of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, preaches, and afterward returns to Gaul.

**[Col. 0255] A.D. 86. A.R. 837.** At Caraca in Carpetania, the holy martyrs Aemilianus and Geronius steadfastly suffered martyrdom for the faith of Christ.

### [Note: [Col. 0256B]]

**A.D. 88—From Mary Magdalene, etc.** Thirty years earlier, namely in the year 48 of the Lord, Dexter had recorded Magdalene’s arrival in Gaul. At that time, when the most blessed Mother of God had been taken up into heaven, Magdalene herself, together with her brothers and friends, committed herself to the sea and, saved in a contemptible wooden vessel, reached Massilia. Now, after spending thirty years in a cave devoted to penitence and contemplation, so much so that she was several times carried aloft by angels, she finally flew to her heavenly Bridegroom, celebrated by miracles both while living and after death. Read Equilinus, book VI, chapter 124, who reports further details about her thirty years of penitence and her miracles.

---

**A.D. 88. A.R. 839.** Mary Magdalene, illustrious for miracles, wonderfully devoted to divine praises and contemplation, migrated to Gaul.

### [Note: [Col. 0256C]]

**A.D. 90—Mancius, etc.** Dexter repeats this more fully at the end of his *Chronicle*, under the year 430, saying:

“In that same year the relics of Saint Memmius Mancius, bishop of Ebora in Lusitania and the first apostle of that city, were discovered. After first converting the people of Châlons in Gaul, he crossed over into Spain and preached at Ebora, where he also suffered martyrdom. He was a Roman citizen and a disciple of Christ, and from the year 36 of Christ until the year 106 he devoted himself to preaching in Gaul and Spain. At last, under Trajan, he suffered martyrdom—as I have said—for the name of Christ.”

The memory of Saint Mancius is exceedingly celebrated among all the writers on Spanish affairs. Vasaeus discusses him under the year 100; Resendius, in his *Antiquities of Ebora*; Villegas, Sanctorus, Trugillus, and Marieta on 15 May; and Mariana in his *History of Spain*. His history is given in the Breviaries of Ebora, Burgos, and Palencia in these words:

#### Passion of Saint Mancius the martyr

He suffered martyrdom at the hands of Jews or pagans in the territory of Elbora. Born in the Roman regions and sent to Spain, he preached the word of God as best he could. Traveling from region to region, he came to Elbora in the province of Lusitania, where he found a Christian people oppressed by unbelievers.

Therefore the blessed Mancius, as a soldier of Christ, armed with the breastplate of faith and trusting in his cross, girded himself against the unbelievers and said:

“I cannot listen to false gods. I must not be a false witness. For love of my God, whom the Jews crucified, I do not refuse punishments; indeed, I seek the death through which eternal life may be granted to me.”

While he was saying these things against them, Saint Mancius was dragged away to punishment. Every garment having been stripped from his body, he was torn apart with his limbs stretched out [Al. *spread apart*], bound with ropes, and beaten with countless blows, as though the limbs clothed by the confession of faith could be stripped of their garments.

Although he was always cheerful in appearance amid his bonds and tortures, he was brought before the prefect Validus and before the Jews who accused him. Validus said to him:

“Listen, Mancius; cease this preaching and worship our gods.”

Mancius replied:

“I do not fear your tortures and punishments.”

Then the prefect Validus ordered him to be beaten with clubs and mangled by many tortures. But the martyr of Christ prayed, saying:

“I give you thanks, Lord, who have enabled me to conquer the tortures of the executioners. Command me to come to you.”

And a voice was heard from heaven:

“Come, our beloved, to me.”

When he said, “Father, into your hands, etc.,” that holy soul departed from the body on 20 May.

Some, however, report that this blessed Mancius was a disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ and served the Lord at the supper when he washed the disciples’ feet.

Thus far the Breviary of Palencia. During the devastation of Spain by the Saracens in the year 714, the body of the holy martyr was transferred to that diocese. In his honor the town called Villanueva de San Mancius was built, and he rests in the monastery of Saint Benedict. In the year 1591, by order of Philip II, the Catholic king, a portion of his relics was transferred back to the see of Ebora, through the efforts of Theotonius de Braganza, archbishop of Ebora and a kinsman of the king.

In truth, what happened in the case of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite among the Greeks and Gauls, I find to have happened likewise in the case of Saint Mancius among the Gauls and Spaniards. Since the Greeks knew nothing about their Dionysius after he had departed from Athens, they believed him to have been a confessor; but the Gauls, who knew of his martyrdom, celebrated him as a martyr. Precisely the same happened with Saint Mancius. Since he did not complete his martyrdom in Gaul, the Gauls celebrate his feast as that of a confessor and bishop; but the Spaniards, who knew his martyrdom well, since it took place at Ebora, celebrate an office for him as a martyr. Yet they too proceed incompletely, because they do not preserve the memory of his episcopate, which was nevertheless sufficiently known to the Gauls.

The duplication of his name also gave rise to error. Since he was called Memmius Mancius in the Roman manner, they celebrate Memmius—or Memnius—there, while these celebrate Mancius; and the confusion even entered the Roman Martyrology, where two feasts are held for one and the same saint. One is on 15 May, in the Spanish manner:

“At Ebora in Lusitania, Saint Mancius the martyr.”

The other is on 5 August, in the following words, in the Gallic manner. These words sufficiently indicate that he was a Roman citizen and a disciple of Christ, whom we call Mancius:

“At Châlons in Gaul, Saint Memmius, a Roman citizen, who, consecrated bishop of that city by Saint Peter, brought the people entrusted to him to the truth of the Gospel.”

Bede adds that, among countless other miracles, he raised a dead man to life. Gregory of Tours discusses him in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 66, and Vincent of Beauvais in the *Speculum*, book IX, chapters 45 and 46. But the Gallic writers, as is their custom, wrote only about what he did in Gaul. The same is true of Equilinus, who followed them in book VII, chapter 25, where he says:

“Memmius, bishop of Châlons, a noble Roman, consecrated bishop by the apostle Saint Peter, was sent to Gaul with Saint Dionysius and other bishops for the sake of preaching.”

But in this the author contradicts himself, because, having been sent by the apostle Peter, Memmius could in no way have traveled with Dionysius, since Dionysius was not sent to Gaul until the pontificate of Clement.

He continues:

“But when they were eighteen miles from the city, Maximian, his subdeacon, died. Memmius returned to Peter and announced the death of his companion. Having received from the Apostle a piece of the fringe of his garment, he returned, touched the still-unburied corpse, and immediately the dead man rose again.”

When he speaks of “the city,” if Dexter is to be believed—or rather, since he is to be believed—understand Jerusalem, not Rome. In the year of the Lord 36, when Dexter says that Mancius began his preaching ministry, the Apostle had not yet come to Rome. Since Saint James was sent by Peter to Spain in that same year, as is clear from what was said above, it is plausible that Mancius was sent with James.

Given this, I would believe that the miracle of raising his companion was wrongly attributed to Saint Mancius. According to Equilinus himself, book VI, chapter 109, it happened to Saint Fronto, bishop of Périgueux, who was sent by Blessed Peter from Rome to the Gallic city of Périgueux with the presbyter George. When George died on the journey, Fronto returned to Peter, received the Apostle’s staff, and, placing it upon the dead man, raised him.

Certainly, if Mancius was traveling with James, he did not need to return to Peter. But, be that as it may, “the Lord also displayed many other signs through them,” he says.

When Mancius arrived at the city of Châlons and found the people difficult to convert, he began to devote himself to contemplation in a cave one mile from the city, in a deserted place, and there became renowned for many miracles. For he raised a noble boy who had fallen into the little river called the Nauta, which flows beside the city, and had drowned. I believe that Bede was speaking of this dead boy. By this marvelous sign he converted many to Christ. Thus the people led him honorably into the city.

At the very entrance of the city he also cleansed three lepers and gave sight to as many blind people. He likewise cast a demon out of a possessed man. Finally, the account says that he governed his see for eighty years; I read seventy. This agrees with Dexter, who teaches that his episcopate and preaching ministry began in the year of the Lord 35 and continued until 106, when he suffered martyrdom. Between those years there are seventy years, which he is said to have occupied the see.

Yet he did not sit only at Châlons, as they suppose, throughout this entire period; he also did so at Ebora in Spain. Nor is his body at Châlons, as Gregory of Tours thought, except perhaps some of his relics. See how remarkably Dexter’s account harmonizes with this. As for the claim that Mancius was instructed under the Lord’s own teaching, some extend it even to the number seventy-two, so that Mancius might have been one of those disciples. This, however, is not sufficiently clear. It is enough that he knew the teaching of Christ; I have no concern for the rest.

In this same year of the Lord 90, the following statement about Fabius Quintilianus is found in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, as supplemented by Saint Jerome:

“Quintilianus, from Calagurris in Spain, who was the first at Rome to receive a public school and a salary from the treasury, became famous.”

It is a remarkable thing that a Spaniard should have been the very first to teach the Italians rhetoric in the Latin language and, for that reason, to receive a salary from the treasury. Ausonius says of him in the *Parentalia*, number 2:

“Although Calagurris may claim Fabius as her foster-son,  
Quintilianus holds the contested palm.”

---

**A.D. 90. A.R. 841.** Saint Mancius [Al. Saint Manlius], a Roman citizen and disciple of Christ, the first bishop of the people of Ebora in Lusitania, who had previously preached in Gaul, flourished; after many labors he departed as a martyr in the year 106.

---

### [Note: [Col. 0258D]]

**A.D. 91—1. At Uxama, etc.** We read in Ptolemy that there were two Uxamas in Spain: one among the Autrigones, surnamed Barca; the other among the Arevaci, surnamed Argella. The latter is today called Osma. It is not sufficiently clear where the other, which is discussed here, was specifically located. Nevertheless, from the site indicated by Ptolemy, it is Orduna. For the Autrigones bordered the Cantabri, while the northernmost city of the Autrigones was Flaviobriga, now Bilbao. Not very far inland from it lay Uxama-Barca, at the place where Orduna is separated from Bilbao.

The martyrs who are said here to have suffered at Uxama-Barca are mentioned by Peter Equilinus in book XI, final chapter, number 251, in these words:

“Trophimus, Oceanus, and Eustorgius the bishop suffered martyrdom on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October.”

He corruptly reads *Oceanus* in place of *Ovantii* [reading uncertain], and *Eustorgius* for *Astorgius*, but the transition between these forms is easy. Equilinus admits that the saints whom he lists in that chapter were taken from the Martyrology of Jerome, Ado, or Usuard, and transcribed by him word for word.

**2. Glabrio.** What follows in this commentary should not be restricted precisely to the year 91; it could have occurred between 91 and 93, since in Dexter the following year is 94. In fact, the martyrdom of the consul Glabrio occurred in the year of the Lord 93, as Dio Cassius, although a pagan, reports in these words:

“Acilius Glabrio, the consul, together with others, was accused of *atheotēs* (ἀθεότητος), that is, contempt for the gods, because he had adopted the customs of the Jews”—for that is what they called the Christians. “While he was still serving as consul, he was summoned to Alba for the Juvenalia. Since he persisted in his position, he was sent into the theater to fight an enormous lion and be torn apart by it. But the lion not only did not injure him; he himself killed it splendidly. Therefore afterward, for the same reason—that he did not worship the Roman gods—he was ordered to be killed.”

Baronius assigns this to the year of the Lord 94; but, as we have seen from the martyrdom of the Apostles, it precedes Dexter by one year.

**3. Nereus, etc.** The author’s primary purpose here is not to record the martyrdom of these holy persons, although he mentions it incidentally, but rather the consolation which they received while exiled on the island of Pontia, while M. Marcellus was staying in the city, through the frequent letters they exchanged.

Some letters of the holy Nereus and Achilleus to Marcellus are extant in Surius, volume III, under 12 May. In them they ask his judgment concerning the question raised there by Furius and Priscus, disciples of Simon Magus, who had been exiled there because of their practice of magic, concerning the holiness of their master. For they were trying to seduce those living on the island into worshiping Simon as the Son of God and believing that the apostle Peter had been unjustly hostile to him.

I have thought it appropriate to insert the letters here.

“Nereus and Achilleus, servants of Christ Jesus, eternal salvation to their brother and fellow disciple Marcellus.

“Exiled to the prison of the island of Pontia on account of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, we rejoice indeed; but our joy is disturbed by Furius and Priscus, disciples of Simon, who have been transported here into exile because of their magical arts. They say that Simon was free from guilt and that the apostle Peter cursed him without cause.

“When we told the inhabitants of the island not to place their trust in them, we recalled your distinguished and trustworthy character, which is able through written testimony to make them certain what sort of life Simon Magus led. Since you were his disciple, you know and have thoroughly investigated all his affairs. We ask that you not hesitate to write them all out, so that innocent people may be freed from these men’s frauds and deceptions.

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.”

To this letter M. Marcellus replied as follows:

“Marcellus, servant of Jesus Christ, to the holy confessors Nereus and Achilleus.

“After reading your letter, I have been filled with joy, because I understood that you remain steadfast in the faith and are fighting manfully for the truth. Since you write that Simon’s innocence has been alleged against you, I shall partially unfold his life, so that the rest may be inferred from the little I relate.

“When I had placed myself under his instruction, I later recognized that the man was wicked, a murderer of infants, a sorcerer, and a housebreaker. I left him and joined myself to my holy Lord, the apostle Peter. When Simon Magus denounced him and inflamed the Roman people with hatred against him, suddenly, at the very place where Simon was accusing Peter, a widow passed by amid a great crowd, carrying her only son in deepest grief.

“When Saint Peter saw this, he said to the people who believed Simon: ‘Take the dead man down from the bier, and recognize as true the faith of whoever raises him.’

“When the people had done this, Simon said: ‘If I restore this man to life, will you kill Peter?’

“The whole crowd replied: ‘We will burn him alive.’

“Then Simon, through the agency of demons, caused the corpse to move a little. When they saw this, the people raised their voices in praise of Simon and threatened Peter with destruction.

“But Peter, having scarcely obtained silence, said: ‘If he is alive, let him speak, walk, eat food, and return to his home. If he does not do these things, do not doubt that Simon is a deceiver.’

“Then the people cried out with one voice: ‘If Simon does not do this, let him himself suffer the punishment with which he wanted Peter to be afflicted.’

“Simon, pretending anger, tried to flee; but the people detained him amid much reproach.

“Then the apostle Peter, raising his hands to heaven, said: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, who told us, “In my name cast out demons, heal the sick, raise the dead,” raise this boy, so that all this crowd may recognize that you are God, and that there is no other besides you, who live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever.’

“Immediately the boy rose and threw himself at the feet of the apostle Peter, saying: ‘I saw the Lord Jesus Christ commanding the angels that, because of your prayers, they should restore me, an orphan, to my widowed mother.’

“Then the people cried out: ‘There is one God, whom Peter preaches.’

“But Simon, by his tricks, fashioned the appearance of a dog’s head for himself and began to flee. When the people wanted to burn him in the flames, having seized him, Peter said: ‘Our Teacher taught us to return good for evil,’ and he caused Simon to be released.

“When Simon came to me, thinking that I did not know what had happened, he tied a huge dog at the entrance to my house, saying: ‘Let us see whether Peter will come in to you as usual.’

“An hour later Peter came. After making the sign of the cross, he released the dog and ordered it to show Simon that he should cease deceiving the people through the agency of demons, the people for whom Christ had shed his blood.

“When I saw these things, I hastened to Peter and received him reverently into my house. The dog pursued Simon; and when it had knocked him down, Peter commanded it in the name of Christ not to bite his body. It did not touch his body, but tore his clothes so thoroughly that no part of his body remained covered.

“The people, especially the boys, pursued him together with the dog and expelled him beyond the city walls like a wolf. Unable to endure this disgrace, he hid himself for an entire year.

“Afterward he was commended to Nero, who admitted him into his friendship—an evil man more wicked than Simon himself.

“The Lord appeared in a vision to the apostle Peter and said: ‘Simon and Nero, full of the evil spirit, are plotting against you. But do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will join the apostle Paul to you; he will enter the city tomorrow, and after seven months you will fight Simon together. When he has been defeated and thrust into Tartarus, you will come together to me as victors.’

“The next day Paul came to Rome. But since you yourselves were present and witnessed how they contended with Simon, it seems superfluous for me to relate it to you, especially since Saint Linus wrote the entire account in Greek to the Churches of the East.”

Thus M. Marcellus writes to the holy exiles about Simon Magus and the apostle Peter.

What follows concerns Petronilla, the daughter of the apostle Peter, my lord. Since you diligently ask what the end of her life was, I shall note it briefly. These details seem to belong to a new letter, since in the letter transcribed above the martyrs asked nothing about Petronilla. We also assigned it to the year of the Lord 34, except that there we reported only what concerned Petronilla, although the letter itself also relates the martyrdom of Saint Felicula, her companion, and of Saint Nicomedes the presbyter.

Other letters of the holy martyrs Eutyches, Victorinus, and Maro to the same Marcellus are also extant, concerning the martyrdom of the aforementioned Nereus and Achilleus, who were put to death at Terracina under Memmius Rufus, the consular governor.

After reading these letters, Marcellus sent his own brother to the island—the author of their history says—and he stayed there with these confessors of Christ for one year. He then returned to Marcellus and reported to him that Eutyches and his companions had received their crowns from the tyrant, as had Sulpitius and Servilianus, and finally the holy virgins Flavia Domitilla with her companions Euphrosina and Theodora. They were confined in a chamber at Terracina and consumed by fire under the emperor Trajan, at least in the year of the Lord 100, although Saint Flavia had been exiled under Domitian, as is asserted in the same place, around the year 90 or 91.

Nevertheless, it must be kept in view that at this time not one but two Flavia Domitillas were honored with a noble martyrdom. One was the wife of the consul Flavius Clemens, of whom Dio says that she was related by blood to Domitian and was exiled by him to the island of Pandataria because she did not worship the ancestral gods. Dexter mentions her martyrdom under Trajan in the year of Christ 100.

The other was the most holy virgin, the niece of the same consul Flavius Clemens through his sister Plautilla, who likewise suffered under Trajan. Concerning her Eusebius, drawing on Brutius, says under the year 99:

“Brutius writes that many Christians suffered martyrdom under Domitian, among them Flavia Domitilla, the niece through his sister of the consul Flavius Clemens, who was exiled to the island of Pontia because she professed herself a Christian. She suffered death for Christ on 7 May; but Nereus and Achilleus, her eunuchs, were beheaded in the preceding year, on 12 May.”

See Baronius both in his Notes and in his *Annals* under the year 68.

That they were fellow disciples of Eugenius and disciples of the apostle Saint Peter is sufficiently clear, not only from the letters just cited but also from the Epistle to the Romans, where Paul, wishing to go to Rome, orders that Nereus be greeted among others. Since Paul himself had not yet seen Rome, it follows that Nereus was a disciple of Peter and not of Paul.

**4. All Spain, etc.** We have said more than enough above about Saint James and about the pilgrimage to his sacred body that was customary in those times, especially since Saint Cletus, who flourished in this period, defended pilgrimages to the saints by issuing an edict.

**5. Saint John the Theologian, etc.** Dionysius had foretold to John his release from exile on the island of Patmos in a special letter which he sent to him. At its conclusion he said:

“I shall be all the more worthy of belief if I speak what I have learned from God—things that have been made known to you beforehand. For you are to be released from your confinement on Patmos and return to the land of Asia. There you will perform works imitating the good God—I understand this of the Gospel—and hand them down to posterity.”

John’s release from Patmos, and the joy it brought to all Christians, needs no proof. Equilinus, book II, chapter 7, speaking of this, says:

“Saint John, who had been carried into exile amid dishonor, was led back to Ephesus with honor, while the entire people came out to meet him and cried: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

But why does Dexter place John’s return from exile in this year? He was in fact sent into exile at this time, rather than returning from it.

Baronius consistently asserts that John was taken to Patmos in the year 92 under Domitian, after emerging stronger from the boiling cauldron of oil at Rome; but that he was brought back in the year 98, when, according to Dio, Nerva ordered all who had been accused of impiety toward the gods to be acquitted and the exiles to be returned to their homeland. Jerome also attests this in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under John. Metaphrastes adds that he was brought back by Trajan, which must have occurred at least in the year 100.

Dexter therefore ought in this year to have discussed John’s exile rather than his return. Yet the matter assumed as certain is not agreed upon among the learned. Arethas of Caesarea, in his commentary on the Apocalypse, thinks that John was exiled under Nero, not Domitian. It is quite plausible that Nero, who insisted that the Church of Christ must be utterly destroyed, persecuted not only Peter and Paul but also John, the surviving Apostle. For who would have allowed John alone to act freely?

Again, Epiphanius, in heresy 51, even says that John returned from Patmos under Claudius—by Claudius I understand Nero.

No one should be surprised that Dexter asserts that John returned from Patmos to Asia around the year of the Lord 93. The opposite does not at all follow from the testimony of Dio that was cited, since it merely says that the exiles were returned to their homeland. Was John therefore brought back by Nerva? What evidence is there? One would first have to establish that he was in exile at that time, which is asserted but not proved.

I add that, even if he may have been in exile, not everyone was brought back by force of that edict. The virgin Flavia Domitilla, for example, remained on the island of Pontia from the time of Domitian until the time of Trajan, under whom she suffered martyrdom, as the Acts of Domitilla herself attest concerning her and her companions.

But this is sufficient, in one way or another, for defending Dexter’s assertion.

**6. Philip, etc.** This man was a great lover of God—as the name *Philotheus*, bestowed upon him for his merits, indicates—and a citizen of Milan. While he was still a pagan, Nero appointed him governor of the province of the Arevaci. In that office he was found by Saint Paul and converted to the faith. Dexter discussed his conversion under the year 64.

After the death of the Apostles, which he witnessed, Philip returned to Milan. There he was present at the martyrdom of his friends and fellow citizens Gervasius and Protasius, conducted their funeral, and wrote their history. It was discovered by Saint Ambrose together with the relics of the saints. It is extant among Ambrose’s works and in Surius, volume III, under 19 June. It begins:

“I, Philip, servant of Christ, took the bodies of the saints from within my house with my son and buried them. Their mother was called Valeria and their father Vitalis, etc.”

It ends:

“When this had been done, I, Philip, servant of Christ, secretly took the holy bodies with my son and, with God alone as witness, buried them in my house in this marble ark, believing that through their prayers I would obtain the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.”

That they were killed under Nero is attested by Metaphrastes in their Life. Thus you can see that everything is consistent, and you should not believe that Philotheus was a different Philip from the disciple of Paul.

Baronius, in his Notes on 19 June, suspects that Gervasius and his brother were not killed under Nero, as Metaphrastes maintains, but under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. If this were accepted, the chronological discrepancy would also prove that there were two different Philips.

He is moved by the fact that the judge Astasius, who killed them, is said by that Milanese Philip to have set out at that time for the war raised by the Marcomanni. The Marcomannic War, however, was fought under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus in the year 171, as we learn from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius. More than a hundred years separate that year from Nero’s death.

Moreover, the priests of the idols are said to have told Astasius: “If you wish to return happily and victorious to our emperors, compel Gervasius and Protasius to sacrifice.” This plurality of emperors does not readily suit Nero, who ruled alone, but it suits Lucius Verus and Marcus Aurelius very well.

Certainly, if we did not have the clear testimony of Metaphrastes, and if we had to proceed by conjectures, we could not be brought with difficulty to Baronius’s opinion. But we possess a statement stronger than conjectures, and what he brings forward in opposition does not prove his case.

A war against the Marcomanni could have been waged in Nero’s time, especially when the more distinguished nations—Gaul and Spain—were rebelling against Nero. Who could accuse this of falsehood? The fact that the principal war against them took place in the year 171 does not rule out their having begun to rebel many years earlier. Indeed, we commonly see that this is how such matters occur, especially since Astasius alone, merely a companion, is said to have set out to suppress them.

If the manuscript is uncorrupted—a possibility I would not readily admit—Astasius could have called Nero’s entire household “the emperors”; or the Senate and the emperor; or Nero and Galba, who was already ruling in Spain; or Nero alone, by a figurative expression such as we use for the sake of enlarging a speech when we say “the Ciceros, Antonys, Julii, Scaevolas,” and so forth.

[Col. 0263C] After Peter and Paul had been translated to heaven, Philip attached himself to Clement, by whom he was sent to Spain as legate of the apostolic see at the beginning of Clement’s pontificate, namely in the year 93. A celebrated testimony to this exists in Methodius, a Greek and very ancient author, in the *Life of Saint Dionysius*, where we read as follows:

> At that time Saint Clement had appointed a certain Philip bishop over the Spaniards; and he had given him the same authority which the divine Clement himself had received from Peter, saying: “Go forth into the western regions and preach the Gospel of the kingdom of heaven. The power of binding and loosing shall also be yours, so that through you the Gospel of Christ may likewise be spread far and wide, and you may deserve to hear from the Lord, as a faithful servant: ‘Well done, good servant,’ etc.”

Ambrosius Morales and Juan de Mariana also mention this same Philip Philotheus, except that Morales did not rightly suspect that he coincided with Hierotheus. Saint Braulio likewise wrote several things, worthy of remembrance, in his additions to M. Maximus, which I have judged particularly appropriate to this place. He says:

> A celebrated memory of Saint Philip is preserved both in Gaul and in Spain. Saint Clement sent him before Eugenius into Spain and Gaul. He came to Rouen with Leo, bishop of Rouen and afterward of the Vascones, and with Gervasius. (Saint Gervasius, too, visited Spain before his martyrdom.) He preached in Gaul, Cantabria, among the Vascones, and throughout Spain. He was called Philotheus by surname. Under Nero he governed the province of the Arevaci as a pagan in Spain. This Saint Philip, who was then a deacon and companion of Leo, returned to Rome while Peter was still alive, in the year 67, and was present at the martyrdom of Peter and Paul. Having followed Saint Clement as his teacher, he was made bishop by him and afterward sent as legate to Spain.

Philip therefore visited Spain three times: first as a pagan, while holding the office of governor of the Arevaci; second as the deacon of Leo, bishop of Rouen and of the Vascones; and finally as Clement’s legate. Moreover, Julian, at the beginning of his *Chronicle*, states that Philip sat as bishop at Toledo for some time, when he preached there. I believe this occurred after the martyrdom of Saint Julian, and that Philip succeeded Saint Eugenius shortly afterward. We shall speak of him again this year, no. 9.

**7. Saint Julian, etc.** His memory still exists in the Roman Martyrology on 7 January, in these words: “On the same day, Saint Julian the martyr.” From this derive Molanus in his additions to Usuard, Galesinus, and the other more recent writers. Until now it was unknown who this Julian was, and Baronius too was unaware of him; but many things are now made clear by Dexter’s *Chronicle* which, without it, would have remained unknown.

**8. Aulus Cornelius Palma, etc.** That in those days many Spaniards were held in high esteem among the Romans is demonstrated by both Senecas, Lucan, Silius, Martial, and Quintilian—and above all by Trajan, who at that time had been raised to the summit of imperial power. Among the others Aulus Cornelius Palma, a nobleman of Toledo, shone especially brightly. Much later, namely in the year 101, he entered upon the consulship at Rome with Gaius Sotius Senecio, as may be seen in the *Fasti* of Cassiodorus and in Onuphrius. The Cornelius Palma who was made most illustrious by the successful completion of the Arabian war belonged to this family.

The arrival of Saint M. Eugenius, sent by Saint Pope Clement, occurred during the duumvirate of Aulus Cornelius Palma; Clement had entered upon the pontificate in this very year, 93. As for Dexter’s statement here that the primacy of Spain was designated in the Church of Toledo, this does not mean that it happened in this year, as he himself testifies under the year 105. Rather, since he is introducing Saint Eugenius into Spain for the first time and is about to say much about him, he briefly announces at the outset what he will later discuss at length. We shall deal with him, together with Dexter, under the years 100, 105, 110, 112, and 130, when he received the palm of martyrdom.

**9. M. Mancinus, etc.** Dexter had said that Philip Philotheus preached not only at Toledo, Zaragoza, Seville, and Valencia, but also at Barcelona. Now the Barcelonan author specifically reveals to his fellow citizens under whose duumvirate Philip had preached at Barcelona and that he had spent several months there.

Two epigrams of Martial addressed to Mancinus survive: one in Book I, beginning:

> *Bis tibi Triceni fuimus, Mancine, vocati, etc.*  
> “Twice thirty times, Mancinus, we were summoned to you, etc.”

The other is in Book IV and begins (no. 61):

> *Donasse amicum tibi ducenta, Mancine;*  
> “That your friend gave you two hundred, Mancinus…”

They contain nothing but jokes and wit, signs of no ordinary friendship.]

**A.D. 91. A.R. 842.** At Uxamebarcha among the Autrigones of Spain, the holy martyrs Trophimus, Ovantius, and Astorgius, bishops, were steadfastly put to death for the faith of Christ in the same persecution.

[Col. 0259] **A.D. 91. A.R. 842.** Glabrio, the Roman consul, is killed for confessing Christ.

**A.D. 91. A.R. 842.** Nereus, Achilleus, and Flavia Domitilla, having been exiled, were refreshed by the frequent letters of Saint M. Marcellus, later bishop of Toledo; at last they flew to the crown of martyrdom, slain for the faith.

[Col. 0261] **A.D. 91. A.R. 842.** Throughout Spain the memory of Saint James, the apostle and son of Zebedee, their first shepherd and eminent teacher, is celebrated.

**A.D. 91. A.R. 842.** John the Theologian is recalled from exile amid the rejoicing of the Churches of the whole world; all congratulate him on his return by sending letters.

**A.D. 91.
