A.R. 842.** Philip, surnamed Philotheus, who had previously buried at Milan the bodies of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, his fellow citizens of Milan; and who, having been converted in the Laminitan Field by Saint Paul, followed him and attached himself to Clement, by whom he was sent as legate to Spain, preached at Toledo, Barcelona, Zaragoza, Seville, Valencia, and many other cities.

[Col. 0263] **A.D. 91. A.R. 842.** Saint Julian, a citizen of Toledo, suffers martyrdom at Toledo on 7 January. He was a bishop.

**A.D. 91. A.R. 842.** Marcus Marcellus came to Toledo with Aulus Cornelius Palma, a man of clarissimus rank, a citizen of Toledo, and a Christian duumvir; there he established the principal see of all Spain, as it were in its center. He better organized the metropolitan sees begun by Saint James and greatly advanced the Church of all Spain.

**A.D. 91. A.R. 842.** Under M. Mancinus, duumvir of Barcelona, the same Philip visited Barcelona and remained there for several months.

[Note: [Col. 0264D]

**A.D. 94.—1. Saint Clement.** This letter is the fourth among those written by Saint Clement. It begins: “Clement, bishop of the city of Rome, to his dearest brothers Julius and Julian, etc. Brothers, all teachers who have been appointed for the salvation of souls, and bishops who have been consecrated for winning souls, must…” In it he rebukes them because they permitted the baptized children of pagans to live with their parents, although the Lord had said in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 10: “I have come to separate a man from his father,” etc.

Since Saint Julian was taken away by martyrdom in the year of the Lord 93, I think it must necessarily be asserted either that Clement gave the letter to one whom he did not know had been sent to heaven, or that this Julian was a different person from that one—whether at that time the same person was called the Carpetanian bishop who was called the Toletan, or whether they were different men, is unclear.

That Julius who is now called Abulensis could not have been bishop of Abula while Saint Secundus, the disciple of James, was still alive. Rather, he was a chorepiscopus and administrator of the diocese while Secundus traveled through other cities preaching. Nevertheless, Dexter could call him a bishop because he became the successor of Saint Secundus. Unless, finally, someone wishes him not to have been a bishop but a noble citizen of Abula, when he received Saint Clement’s letter—for the text also permits this, since it says only “and to Julius of Abula.”

I suspect that this was the distinguished martyr who was slaughtered for Christ at Gelduba in Turdetania of Baetica. He is mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on 20 December in these words: “At Gelduba, Saint Julius the martyr.” In Usuard, however, we corruptly read: “In the Thracian city of Gelduba, etc.” instead of “in the Turdetanian city of Gelduba.” No city of that name is found in Thrace; consequently the word “Thrace” has been removed from the Roman Martyrology. In Turdetania of Spain there is a Gelduba, which the manuscripts of Ptolemy read as Galduba, others as Calduba; it is now generally called Gelbes, and is the seat of the count of Gelbes near Seville.

At this place, in the printed edition of Dexter, the following was added: “At Amphitria, now Fita, Saint Gregory, bishop of Complutum, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January.” But this is plainly the error of a copyist, since it did not happen at this time but later, in the year 366, as we shall say in that place together with Dexter. Saint Gregory flourished in the year 360. Indeed, where it reads that he died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, it should be corrected to read the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January. We shall discuss this at the appropriate place.

**2. The Bilbilitani, etc.** An intolerable error had entered this verse in the printed manuscript, for it read: “The Bilbilitani believed in Christ with paternal affection.” It ought rather to say “with filial affection.” But neither this suits the context nor does it have the flavor of Dexter’s phrase. He himself states below, under the year 122, that the famous Paternus, a disciple of Saint Saturninus, was indeed a native of Toledo but nevertheless a citizen of Bilbilis. Thus, before he crossed into Gaul, where he became bishop and apostle of the Elusates and the Constantian people, he brought his own homeland to the knowledge of Christ.

At that time Martial was living at Bilbilis, whence he sent Book XII to Rome, as is clear from the preface addressed to Priscus and from epigram 3 of the same book. There he often met Paternus, an old friend. Nevertheless, because he differed from him in religion, Martial characterized him in epigram 43 as avaricious—perhaps because Paternus did not immediately squander his inheritance, and because the alms he gave secretly remained hidden from Martial. The epigram begins at no. 53 of Book XII:

> *Nummi cum tibi sint, opesque tantae,*  
> *Quantas civis habet, Paterne, rarus,*  
> *Largiris nihil, etc.*

> “Though you have money and such great wealth,  
> such as a rare citizen possesses, Paternus,  
> you give nothing, etc.”

We changed the phrase *affectu paterno* (“with paternal affection”) to *effante Paterno*, for *effans* was very common in ancient stone inscriptions, as Resendius asserts in his letter to Ambrosius Morales, which is included in *Hispania Illustrata*.

The ancient Bilbilis was situated not at the confluence of the Salón, where Calatayud now stands, but on the summit of a mountain, half a league away, according to Barrerius and Nonnius in their *Spain*, chapter 75—although Calatayud grew from the ruins of Bilbilis. The ancient city has now been replaced by the small town of Baubula, which retains the remnants of the name and the territory.

Bilbilis is frequently mentioned in Martial, Book I, epigram 49, *On the Places of Spain*, addressed to Licinianus, a fellow citizen returning there:

> *Vir Celtiberis non tacende gentibus,*  
> *Nostraeque laus Hispaniae:*  
> *Videbis altam Liciane Bilbilim,*  
> *Aquis, et armis nobilem, etc.*

> “Man not to be silent among the Celtiberian peoples,  
> and glory of our Spain:  
> you will see, Licinianus, lofty Bilbilis,  
> famous for its waters and its arms, etc.”

And in epigram 61, addressed to the same man, he says:

> *Duosque Senecas, unicumque Lucanum*  
> *Facunda loquitur Corduba.*  
> *Gaudent jocosae Canio suo Gades,*  
> *Emerita Deciano meo.*  
> *Te, Liciane, gloriabitur nostra,*  
> *Nec me tacebit Bilbilis.*

> “Eloquent Córdoba speaks of its two Senecas  
> and its single Lucan.  
> Playful Cádiz rejoices in its Canus,  
> and Emerita in my Decianus.  
> Our Bilbilis will boast of you, Licinianus,  
> nor will it be silent about me.”

After spending thirty-four years at Rome and longing to return to his homeland, he wrote epigram 103 of Book X, addressed to the fields of Bilbilis:

> *Municipes Augusta mihi quos Bilbilis agri*  
> *Monte creat, rapidis quos Salo cingit aquis.*

> “My fellow citizens, whom the fields of Augusta Bilbilis have produced for me on a mountain which the swift waters of the Salón encircle.”

And epigram 104, where he addresses the book as follows:

> *Hispanae pete Tarraconis arces:*  
> *Illinc te rota tollet, et citatus*  
> *Altam Bilbilim, et tuum Salonem*  
> *Quinto forsitan essedo videbis.*

> “Seek the citadels of Spanish Tarragona. From there the wheel will carry you, and, traveling swiftly, perhaps on the fifth carriage, you will see lofty Bilbilis and your Salón.”

See also epigram 55 of Book IV, addressed to Lucius. We gave it above.

**3. Gaius Prochorus, etc.** The printed manuscript was extremely corrupt at this point, for it read: “Gaius Prochorus wrote the Gospel and the deeds of John, one of the seven deacons,” as though John the Evangelist were one of the seven deacons chosen by the Apostles for the ministry to widows, rather than Prochorus himself.

That Prochorus wrote the Gospel at John’s dictation, and how this was expressed by Metaphrastes in the *Life of Saint John*, is as follows:

> “John commands a certain one of the seven to follow him; he was called Prochorus, so that John himself might record what came from God and had been dictated to him, while Prochorus recorded what came from John. Then John climbed to the summit of the mountain and, like Samuel, stood upright; like Moses, he was depicted with his hands raised, and, his mind withdrawn from the senses, he directed his whole thought toward what he desired. What followed from this? Terrifying thunder and dread, flashes of lightning striking continuously with violent crash and sudden brilliance, etc. Meanwhile Prochorus, lying prostrate and seemingly lifeless, could scarcely endure being amid such spectacles. John himself stood terrified, although love had cast fear far away. At last the thunder was transformed into a voice and rang out clearly: ‘In the beginning was the Word,’ etc. Prochorus, who by divine appointment was close by, saw the light, although trembling slightly; he heard no one. Gradually restraining his fear, with trembling hand he wrote down what had been taken from that voice, until the holy Gospel was completed.”

Equilinus supports Metaphrastes in Book II, chapter 7. Athanasius, too, in the *Synopsis*, attributes the writing of this Gospel to Caius, although his statement is less credible when he says that Caius was the beloved one of the Apostles. That man was not Gaius Prochorus but Gaius Oppius, as we have explained at length elsewhere.

Moreover, that Prochorus himself also wrote the deeds of John the Evangelist is attested by the *Acts* themselves, which are preserved in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*. Although they have been corrupted in places by heretics, many serious and authoritative writers nevertheless accept them.

[Col. 0267A] **4. L. Magnus Julianus, etc.** This is the complete name of Saint Julian, about whom enough has been said. Here mention is now made of his miracles and reputation after his victory.

**5. Octogessa, etc.** According to Morales, Book VIII of his *History of Spain*, chapter 28, Octogessa was a town of no little importance situated at the confluence of the Ebro, five leagues from Lérida, in or near the district of the Ilergetes, where it now stands. At this place Saint Agathoclia completed her most illustrious martyrdom under Domitian. Her distinguished memory still remains, and her feast is celebrated by the Latins in the Roman Martyrology on 17 September in these words:

> “On the same day, Saint Agathoclia, the maidservant of an unbelieving woman. After being tormented by her for a long time with blows and other sufferings so that she would deny Christ, she was finally brought before the judge. When she persisted in confessing the faith despite being more cruelly mangled, her tongue was cut out and she was thrown into the fire.”

The Greeks tell the story more fully in the *Menologion* on the same day. I shall give what I found translated by Cardinal Sirlet:

> “On the same day, the birthday of Saint Agathoclia the martyr, a servant”—for so it calls her. “Saint Agathoclia, a servant of a certain Christian named Nicholas and his wife Paulina, was a Christian and feared God. Every day she was tortured by her unbelieving mistress, a worshiper of idols, who for eight years struck Agathoclia on the head with rough stones and forced her to walk barefoot in winter and cold to gather wood. For eight full years she tried to persuade her to worship idols. When Agathoclia utterly refused, she was mangled, her tongue was cut out, and she was thrown into prison, where she was afflicted with hunger. Finally, when fire was put around her neck, she exchanged the present life for the eternal.”

**6. Saint Theodosius, etc.** Saint Theodosius was the successor in the see of Barcelona of Saint Etherius, the disciple of Saint James. Concerning him Dexter says below, under the year 100, no. 8, that the Christians of Barcelona advanced no less through the glory of miracles, the power of teaching, and the example of Saint Theodosius, their bishop, than did the Toletans through the teaching and miracles of Saint Eugenius.

Therefore, when Dexter says here “the sixth day before the Kalends of February,” this should not be referred to his death, as though it occurred in this year. It should instead be read appositively, with the sense: “Saint Theodosius II, bishop of Barcelona—[he flourishes], though he is celebrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.”]

**A.D. 94. A.R. 845.** Saint Clement writes to Julian, bishop of Carpetania, and to Julius of Abula.

[Col. 0265] **A.D. 94. A.R. 845.** The Bilbilitani believed in Christ with Paternus speaking (*effante Paterno*).

**A.D. 94. A.R. 845.** Gaius Prochorus, one of the seven deacons, wrote the Gospel and the deeds of John.

[Col. 0267] **A.D. 94. A.R. 845.** L. Magnus Julianus, a citizen of Toledo and martyr, is held in high esteem.

**A.D. 94. A.R. 845.** At Octogessa in Spain, Saint Agathoclia suffered martyrdom with manly courage.

**A.D. 94. A.R. 845.** Saint Theodosius II, bishop of Barcelona, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.

[Note: [Col. 0267C]

**A.D. 95.—1. In Carpetania, etc.** The memory of Saint Alexander the martyr at Pydna was once venerated by the Greeks, as is clear from the *Menologion*. He is celebrated on 14 March, and Molanus also includes him on that date.

Dexter asserts that Pydna was a town in Carpetania, called in his own time by the somewhat corrupted name Pyotium. Unless one believes that “Pyotium” was the invention of some later person who added it in the margin as an explanation, after which it was mixed into the text by some ignorant copyist—which I would not rashly deny, especially since the novelty of the word suggests it—this may be accepted. But let the reader judge. It is now called Pyoz; or, if Dexter’s text is trusted, it is not improbable that the name had already begun to be corrupted at that time, so that Pydna was called Pyotium. There was also a city of Pydna in Macedonia, which Ptolemy places in Pieria.

**2. At Aquae Quintianae, etc.** Ptolemy places Aquae Quintianae among the Seburri, peoples of the Galician Lucenses, at the site of, or near, modern Oviedo. Moletius and Millius maintain that it is now called Aquas Caldas.

Many towns in Spain were formerly named from *Aquae*. There were Aquae Sextianae, which Pliny mentions and which is believed to be the Lucense city now called Lugo. There were also Aquae Calidae, now Orense; and Aquae Cellenae, or Gallinae, as the *Itinerary of Antoninus* calls it—a town not far from Orense toward Tui, now Los Baños de Melgazo or Pregigueiro, in the territory of the monastery of Saint Mary of Melón, of our Cistercian order.

There were likewise Aquae Durae near Osset, which M. Maximus discusses under the year 506, and which Morales, in his *Antiquities*, under the entry “Italica,” asserts was once called Constantia Julia, near Italica. There were also Aquae Calidae in Ptolemy, among the Autetani of Catalonia, formerly called Vicus Aquarius, according to Villanovano, and now Vich, an episcopal city. The place near Toledo now called Talavera, a noble town in the diocese of Toledo, was also called Aquae.

The holy martyrs Dativus, Julian, Vincentius, and their companions, who are mentioned here, still have a special commemoration in the Roman Martyrology on 27 January, in these words: “Also, the holy Dativus, Julian, Vincentius, and twenty-seven other martyrs.” Bede also celebrates them on that day, except that instead of Dativus he corruptly has Doti, whom Galesinus imitated in his Martyrology.

**3. Saint Ovidius, etc.** If we consider the period in which Saint Ovidius flourished and Dexter’s purpose, I would believe him to be the man who voluntarily accompanied Caesonius Maximus when Nero drove him into exile. Martial wrote two epigrams about this in Book VII, which we transcribed when discussing Caesonias under the year 66. He also sang twice of Ovidius’s April birthday in Book IX.

The first is epigram 52:

> *Si credis mihi, Quinte (quod mireris)*  
> *Natales Ovidi tuos Apriles,*  
> *Ut nostras amo Martias kalendas.*  
> *Felix utraque lux, diesque nobis*  
> *Signandi melioribus lapillis!*  
> *Hic vitam tribuit, sed hic amicum,*  
> *Plus dant, Quinte, mihi tuae kalendae.*

> “If you believe me, Quintus—though you may wonder—  
> I love your April birthday  
> as I love my own March Kalends.  
> Happy are both lights, and days  
> to be marked with better pebbles!  
> One gave me life, but the other gave me a friend;  
> your Kalends, Quintus, give me more.”

There is also another epigram, number 53, which begins: “On your birthday, Quintus, etc.” Epigram 85 of Book I and epigram 99 of Book IX are also addressed to him.

When he had become bishop of Braga, he brought the holy women Marina, Quiteria, and their sisters to the faith and martyrdom. An elegant hymn concerning this exists in the work of Sandoval, bishop of Tui and Pamplona, in his *Book of the Bishops of Tui*, where among other things I read:

> *Gaude, sacerdos Ovidi,*  
> *Tu Braccarensis pontifex,*  
> *Qui meruisti filias*  
> *Tot ad polos transmittere.*

> “Rejoice, O priest Ovidius,  
> you bishop of Braga,  
> who were deemed worthy to send  
> so many daughters to the heavens.”

We shall give it under the year 136.

Saint Ovidius is discussed again below, under the year of the Lord 110.

**4. In Arsa Mariana, etc.** An error entered the manuscript Martyrology: “Asia” was written instead of “Arsa.” Once this had occurred, since the word *Mariana* did not agree with “Asia,” it was easily changed into *Minori*, and almost all the printed editions read it this way—the Roman Martyrology, that of Ado, and that of Usuard—under 8 July:

> “In Asia Minor, Saints Aquila and Priscilla, his wife, concerning whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles.”

Galesinus, however, a learned and careful man, did not read “in Asia” but “in Africa Minor,” for no other reason, evidently, than that he had discovered that they did not die in Asia. Yet he had no certain reason for transferring them to Africa. It was in fact customary for the Roman Martyrology to designate the cities in which saints rested rather than vast regions, leaving behind a confused knowledge of geography.

But what wonder that he did not know the city, when those who were ignorant of the martyrdom of these saints also did not know it? Those whom they did not know to have been martyrs in Spain they made confessors in Asia Minor.

The Greeks, indeed, celebrate them as martyrs in the *Horologion* on 13 February, in these words, which Galesinus himself translated into Latin:

> “The holy martyrs Aquila and Priscilla. These spouses, instructed in the word of truth by the blessed apostle Paul and then baptized, joined themselves to him as companions wherever he went, and together with him endured many hardships and labors for the faith. After his martyrdom, since they never ceased preaching Christ, they were seized by the worshipers of idols, first tortured bitterly and cruelly, and finally, having been beheaded, they received the palms of martyrdom.”

There was formerly, in the Marian Mountains of Baetica—today the Sierra Morena—a town of no little importance called Arsa. Scipio captured it while pursuing Viriathus, as Appian of Alexandria and Morales, Book VII, chapter 53, affirm. From these mountains the name *Asia Mariana* was derived.

When Aquila and Priscilla arrived there spreading the word of God, they were killed for the truth they preached. Dexter had taught earlier, under the year 70, that Saint Aquila—undoubtedly together with his wife Priscilla—was sent to Spain by the apostle Paul and settled at Heraclea near the Strait of Hercules. From there it was easy for him to illuminate the Marian Mountains with the light of the Gospel.

Ambrosius Morales learnedly believes that Arsa is the place now called Azuaga, not far from Fuente Obejuna, which lies near Córdoba. There considerable remains of a very ancient city are found. Pliny mentions Arsa when discussing Baeturia in Book III.

**5. The town of Accatucci, etc.** I would believe that one should read *Araducta in Bracara* instead of *Accatucci in Baetica*. For Ptolemy places Araducta among the Bracarii of Lusitania, between the Douro and the Minho, where the noble city of Porto now stands, which gave its name to Portugal.

Unless it was Attuvi, a town in Baetica mentioned by Pliny in Book III, called by the Romans Claritas Julia, and now Villa de Espejo near Córdoba. For this reason I think that Saint Julian, the companion of Saints Dativus, Vincentius, and their companions, originated here; we said above, under no. 2, that they suffered at Aquae Quintianae.

Others may perhaps think that one should read *Aruci in Baeturia*, now Villa de Aroche near Cazalla in Baetica, according to Ambrosius Morales, under “Baeturia,” folio 101. There, among other monuments of Roman antiquity, an inscription on a stone of this sort still survives:

> **M. ATTERIO. PAVLINO. M. F. QVI TVMVLTVARIO.**  
> **BAETICAE. BELLO. ASSVRGENTE.**  
> **MVLTA. PRO. REP. ARVCITANA.**  
> **BELLO. RETINENDA. FORTISSIME. GESSERAT.**  
> **ARVCITANI. VETERES. ET. IVVENES.**  
> **OPT. CIVI.**

> “To Marcus Atterius Paulinus, son of Marcus, who, when the war in Baetica broke out, had most courageously performed many services for the Arucitan state, which had to be preserved in the war; the old and young Arucitani [dedicated this] to their excellent citizen.”

But here let each person retain his own judgment.]

**A.D. 95. A.R. 846.** In Carpetania, Saint Alexander the martyr, of Pydna or Pyotium.

**A.D. 95. A.R. 846.** At Aquae Quintianae in Galicia of Spain, the holy martyrs of Christ Julian, Dativus, Vincentius, and twenty-seven other companions.

**A.D. 95. A.R. 846.** Saint Ovidius, a Roman citizen and bishop of Braga, succeeds Saint Basil; the latter, however—

**A.D. 95. A.R. 846.** Saint Peter, on the Kalends of November.

**A.D. 95. A.R. 846.** At Arsa Mariana in Spain, Aquila and Priscilla suffer martyrdom.

[Col. 0269] **A.D. 95. A.R. 846.** The town of Accatucci [alternatively, Attuvi] in Baetica celebrates the birthday of Saint Julian the martyr, whom we said suffered at Aquae Quintianae.

[Note: [Col. 0269D]

**A.D. 100.—1. During this period, etc.** The author has completed the first century from the birth of Christ and now proceeds to narrate what followed. First of all, what he had previously written briefly, as it were at the threshold of the second century, concerning Saint Marcus Marcellus, he now reviews chapter by chapter, explaining his ancestry, nobility, and discipline. We know all these things from the testimony of the saints Nereus and Achilleus.

It is related in their *Life*—in Surius, volume 3—that when, on the island of Pontia, the populace was being led by Furius and Priscus, men wholly devoted to magic, to assent to the teaching of Simon Magus and reject the apostle Peter, Nereus and Achilleus opposed them. They said to the people living on the island:

> “Do you know Marcellus, the son of Marcus the prefect?”

They answered:

> “Who could possibly be unaware of him?”

Nereus and Achilleus then said:

> “Will you accept his testimony concerning Simon and Peter?”

They replied:

> “He is utterly mad if he refuses to trust so great a man.”

Nereus and Achilleus said:

> “Then do this for your salvation: until we write to him and he answers us, withdraw yourselves from their teaching.”

And this was done. We gave the letters themselves earlier, when discussing these martyrs under the year 91. From them it is clear that M. Marcellus was the son of the prefect of the city and therefore belonged to the household of Nero, and that he was one of those whose greetings Paul sent from Rome to the Philippians while detained in Nero’s chains, saying: “All the saints greet you, especially those who are of Caesar’s household.” At first he had wholly devoted himself to the teaching of Simon Magus, and afterward to that of Saint Peter.

That he accompanied Peter on his journeys we demonstrated when we discussed Peter’s arrival in Spain. When Dexter now says that Marcellus “flourishes at Rome,” this should not be understood as though he were still at Rome in this very year 100 of the Lord. Rather, he flourished during this period—that is, shortly before or afterward. We had already said under the year 93 that he left Rome with Dionysius. Nor did he remain at Toledo continuously until this year 100, since, as Dexter now says, he had completed long journeys in Italy, Gaul, and Spain.

When Dexter adds, “who was given as a companion by Saint Clement to Dionysius when he was going to Gaul,” he excludes the modern opinion of those who say that Saint Eugenius, or Marcellus, was Saint Dionysius’s disciple, whereas he was in fact his fellow disciple and was designated by Saint Clement as his companion in preaching.

I understand this exactly from Methodius in the *Life of Saint Dionysius*, who adds among other things:

> “The companions of Saint Dionysius were Saturninus, Marcellus, and Lucianus. They were joined to him for this purpose: so that, on the testimony of two or three witnesses, the Christian faith might be delivered to unfamiliar regions.”

Petrus de Natalibus, Book IX, chapter 41, expresses the same view:

> “After some time Dionysius was sent by the blessed Clement into Gaul; the holy bishops Saturninus and Marcellus, and Lucianus the presbyter, were also assigned as his companions.”

Nor is this surprising, since both were disciples of the same Apostles and each had learned the elements of theology under the discipline of Hierotheus, as I shall now say.

Marcellus could be called Dionysius’s disciple in this one respect: he was ordained bishop by Dionysius in the city of Arles, sent by him from there into Spain, and finally instructed by him in many books which he gave him, about which we shall speak at length shortly.

Therefore Dexter’s words, “made bishop of Arles,” do not mean that he was appointed bishop of Arles, but that he was ordained at Arles, for the following words immediately add: “and sent to Spain.”

Speaking of this, Methodius says:

> “When they had thus gathered together and were traveling, they came to the harbor of the city of Arles. Then Saint Dionysius sent Marcellus into Spain, so that there he might commend the word of Christ’s life to the Churches.”

Equilinus says:

> “When they all came to Arles, they began to preach the word of God. Then Dionysius, relying on the authority of the supreme Pontiff, sent Marcellus into Spain.”

But how shall we demonstrate that this Marcellus was Eugenius and not some other disciple of Dionysius?

Juan de Mariana, Book IV of his *History of Spain*, chapter 4, says that this is neither new nor unheard-of, but has long been believed by many. Nevertheless, he reports that others preferred Philip Philotheus to be Eugenius, rather than M. Marcellus; he himself left the question unresolved. His words are:

> “Some believe that a certain Philip, sent by Clement as bishop to Spain, or at least Marcellus, whom Dionysius added to Philip as a companion from Gaul, as Michael Syngellus testifies, was Eugenius himself; and that the one name came from innate nobility, while the other was received from his parents.”

Mariana says that what moved them was the fact that no mention of Eugenius is found in the writings of the ancients. Yet this proves no more against Marcellus than against Philip.

I do not deny that this argument alone is inconclusive. Nevertheless, from what Mariana himself concedes, and from facts certain among all writers, it is sufficiently deduced that our Eugenius was not Philip but Marcellus.

Everyone admits—and Mariana himself agrees with them—that Philip was sent to Spain not by Dionysius but by Clement. They also admit that Marcellus was the man whom Dionysius sent to Spain; this is reported by Methodius himself, the most ancient writer of the acts of Saint Dionysius, whose words we have already given.

As for Eugenius, nothing is more certain than that he was sent from Gaul to Spain by Dionysius. In the ancient Toletan Breviary, published according to the rite of the Roman Church, there is a hymn beginning:

> *Nova resultent gaudia.*

“Let new joys resound.”

Later in the same hymn we read:

> *Doctus alumnus Graeciae*  
> *Misit hunc Dionysius,*  
> *Ut esset solis radius,*  
> *In tenebris Hispaniae.*

> “Dionysius sent this learned foster-son of Greece,  
> so that he might be a ray of the sun  
> in the darkness of Spain.”

In the hymn of the Breviary according to the rule of Saint Isidore, we likewise read another hymn in honor of Saint Eugenius, beginning: *S. Eugenii digna memoria* (“Worthy is the memory of Saint Eugenius”). In it Saint Dionysius is called his father, since Eugenius was plainly his son in the episcopal order, or his spiritual creation:

> *Doctor Hispaniae revisit Galliam,*  
> *Docti praesentiam Doctoris Galliae*  
> *(Dionysii)*  
> *Fideli captans pectore.*  
> *Patrem desiderat, votum prosequitur, etc.*

> “The teacher of Spain revisits Gaul,  
> seeking with faithful heart  
> the presence of the learned teacher of Gaul  
> [Dionysius].  
> He longs for his father and pursues his desire, etc.”

Moreover, the proper martyrology of the monastery of Broni, where the body of the holy martyr long rested, and whose concluding notice Molanus inserted into his *Usuard*, says:

> “On the same day, Saint Eugenius, archbishop and martyr of the Toletan see, who was ordained by the blessed Dionysius and sent to preach the Holy Trinity to the nations.”

Finally, all who committed the life of Saint Eugenius to writing or discussed him—Equilinus, Book X of the *Catalogue*, chapter 62; Vincent of Beauvais, Book X of the *Historical Mirror*, chapter 35; Marinaeus Siculus, Book V of his *History of Spain*; Morales, Book IX, chapter 26; Garibay, Book XII, chapter 9; Marieta, Part I, Book I, chapter 17 onward; Cianca, Book III *On Saint Secundus*, chapter 10; Illescas, Book VI of the *Pontifical History*, chapter 15; Sanctoro Villegas and Truxillo under 15 November; Blasius Ortiz, chapter 11 of his description of the Toletan church; Antonius de Ribera in his book *On the Translation of Saint Eugenius*; Padilla; and Alcocer—all testify with one voice that the principal and unique teacher of Spain whom Dionysius sent into Spain was Eugenius.

Therefore, since it is entirely certain that Marcellus was sent by Saint Dionysius, we must affirm that Marcellus and Eugenius were precisely one and the same person. This is especially so because Philip acquired an entirely different name for himself, namely Philotheus. The name Eugenius, however, which is a most proper indication of nobility, fits M. Marcellus particularly well, since he was the son of the prefect of the city and a most noble Roman.

If someone asks when Saint Marcellus Eugenius left Rome with Dionysius and received from him the authority to preach in Spain, and why he is now called by Dexter the legate of Pope Saint Clement, the question is easily resolved if one observes the difference in time. He was first sent by Dionysius; afterward he received from Clement the office and full authority of a legate—namely, as soon as Clement had been informed of his departure for Spain.]

## [Col. 0272B] 2. Romulus, etc.

The Roman Martyrology briefly and clearly recounts his martyrdom on 5 September:

> On the same day, Saint Romulus, prefect of Trajan’s court, who, detesting the emperor’s cruelty toward Christians, was scourged with rods and beheaded.

The Greeks relate this more briefly in the Menologion, although they first mention that eleven thousand Christians were deported by that same Trajan to distant regions because of their faith in Christ. This plainly refers to what Dexter writes about Romulus: that he was first deported to Spain by Trajan and later, while persevering in his resolve, was brutally beheaded in Celtiberia.

There is no doubt that Metaphrastes was misled when he says that Romulus was brought into Trajan’s presence, interrogated, and condemned, if he means that he suffered at Rome. His account can nevertheless be reconciled with the facts if we understand him to be recounting what took place in Trajan’s presence without specifying either the place or the time of the sentence’s execution. Romulus was indeed questioned by the emperor about the faith, and he truly received from him a capital sentence; but between these events and his beheading came his exile to Spain.

Metaphrastes is also mistaken when he says that Trajan sent that multitude of Christians into exile at Melitene, a city of Armenia. For since the Greeks treat Romulus and Eudoxius, Zeno, Marcharius, and the others together, on the same day and in the same section of their Martyrology, and since these men—namely Eudoxius and his companions—suffered at Melitene in Armenia under Diocletian, Metaphrastes has confused them with Romulus and the eleven thousand deported by Trajan. Yet everything is clearly distinguished in the Menologion, just as in the Roman Martyrology.

The companions of Saint Romulus, therefore, were not deported to Melitene in Armenia; rather, it was Eudoxius and his companions who were. Romulus, on the other hand, was sent to Spain—a destination that I do not object to seeing represented in the Menologion by the expression “distant regions.”

Romulus was therefore the first fruit that Spain received from Trajan’s persecution: a Spaniard and an inhabitant of Italica, elevated by an emperor who was likewise Spanish and from Italica, first because of his love for his homeland, to the prefecture of the imperial court, and afterward deprived by that same emperor of both his office and, at the same time, his belt of office and his head. Alas! Such is usually the faithfulness of the wicked.

No one is unaware that Trajan was a Spaniard, born at Italica, a city of Baetica in the province of Turdetania. The sole dissenters are Aurelius Victor and his follower Onuphrius, who, although they assert that Trajan derived his origin from that place, nevertheless say that he was born at Tudertum in Italy.

But, as you see, they read “Italy” for “Italica” and “Tudertum” for “Turdetania,” fabricating a city from a province and a province from a city. Appian of Alexandria, Eutropius, and Eusebius, however, together with the earlier authorities cited and employed in support of the truth by Morales and Baronius, openly contradict them.

Eusebius says in his Chronicle, under the year 100:

> Trajan, having been made emperor at Agrippina in Gaul, was born at Italica in Spain.

Cyriacus of Ancona reports that a column was found at Marguessa in Spain when ruins were cleared away for construction, bearing this inscription. Morales also cites it, book IX, chapter 28; Onuphrius, book II of *The Fasti*, p. 218; and Lipsius in his commentary on Pliny, 124:

> IMP. CAES. NERVAE, TRAIANO.  
> AVG. GERMANICO. DACICO.  
> PARTHICO. PONT. MAX.  
> TRIB. POT. V. COS. VI. PP. DE.  
> ROMANO. IMP. DE. PATERNA.  
> ET. AVITA. HISPANIAE. PATRIA.  
> ET. DE. OMNI. HOMINVM.  
> GENERE. MERITISS. POPVLARES.  
> PROVINCIAE. AREVATVM.  
> OPT. PRINCIPI.

That Trajan deserved very well of Spain is confirmed by Martial, an eyewitness, who, after returning to his homeland, wrote the following about him in book XII, epigram 9:

> The palm rules our Iberians, most gentle Caesar,  
> and foreign peace enjoys a peaceful yoke.  
> Therefore, rejoicing, we give thanks for so great a gift:  
> you have sent your own character into our lands.

## 3. Saint M. Marcellus, etc.

Dexter is about to recount the deeds of Saint Eugenius piece by piece. In number 1 of this year 100 he had already stated that Eugenius had established himself at Toledo; now, in number 3, he discusses his preaching. He will treat of his miracles in number 7 and of the fruit of his preaching in number 8, while always adding something new. Here he says that Eugenius had already been marked by the priestly order when he came to Spain with Paul. He also newly introduces information about his arrival: previously, he had spoken only of Eugenius’s coming with Peter; hence he now mentions three arrivals—his first with Peter in the year 50, his second with Paul in the year 64, and his third when he was sent by Dionysius in the year 100.

## 4. Rufus, etc.

The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on 21 November:

> On the same day, the birthday of Blessed Rufus, about whom Saint Paul the Apostle writes to the Romans.

Usuard has:

> The birthday of Blessed Rufus, etc.

Ado and Bede also speak of him. Equilius, book X, chapter 92.

He was the son of Simon of Cyrene and the brother of Alexander, whom Mark mentions in chapter 15 of his Gospel. He first became bishop of Thebes, according to Dorotheus in the *Synopsis*, as well as Ado and Equilinus. Nevertheless, the Church of Dertosa—now Tortosa—professes that he came from there to Spain for the sake of preaching and eventually settled at Dertosa. That church celebrates his feast on 12 November and declares in the lessons of its Breviary that it received this tradition from its ancestors.

Morales, book IX, chapter 11; Marieta, *On the Saints of Spain*, first part, book V, chapter 75, and fourth part, book XXII, under the heading “Tortosa”; Vincentius Dominicus, *On the Saints of Catalonia*; and others who have treated his history relate the same.

Dexter will discuss his brother Alexander, who suffered martyrdom at Carthage with Zosimus and Candidus, below, under the year 112.

Braulio, or Heleca, says the following in his additions to the Chronicle of Maximus:

> The memory of the saints Rufus and Alexander, sons of Simon of Cyrene—who is called Niger by some—is celebrated. Simon came to Spain with his sons in the company of Saint Paul, and preached there; previously he had gone there in the company of the blessed James and had preached there at that time. Saint Peter is said to have consecrated him bishop, together with others. He died at Jerusalem and is honored on the first of December.

In the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 13, we read about Simon:

> Now there were in the Church at Antioch prophets and teachers, among whom were Barnabas and Simon who was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, etc.

Hilary, Ambrose, Bede, and Leo, whom Maldonado cites, maintain that Simon—and consequently his sons—was a Gentile. Maldonado himself believes him to have been a Jew, but without foundation. The fact that Mark calls him the brother of Alexander and Rufus, as though they were well-known men, does not prove that he was a Jew; for when Mark wrote his Gospel, many converts from the Gentiles were already very well known.

## 5. Syrmium, etc.

In the Roman Martyrology, under 26 March, we read:

> At Syrmium, the holy martyrs Montanus the priest and Maxima, who were plunged into a river because of their faith in Christ.

Jerome, in his Martyrology, followed by Equilinus in book III, chapter 233, writes that they were drowned not in a river but in the sea. Usuard likewise affirms this:

> Montanus the priest and Maxima the virgin, says Jerome, suffered at the town of Syrmium. While they confessed the Lord Christ aloud, they were seized by the unbelievers, bound with iron chains, and both were thrown into the sea, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April.

Usuard writes:

> At Syrmium, the holy martyrs Montanus the priest and Maxima, who were thrown into the sea.

Rabanus and Notherus add in their Martyrologies that Saint Maxima was the wife of Blessed Montanus the priest, and that their bodies were later found nine miles from the city. From this one may see the error that entered the Roman Martyrology, where “river” appears instead of “sea.”

But why discuss this? In order to determine in what part of the world this Syrmium was situated. There is a city of that name in Transpadane Lombardy, now called Sirmio Castello; another in Lower Pannonia, or Hungary, situated on the river Sava; and finally another in Spain, which Floriano de Ocampo identifies with present-day Motril, Villanovano with Vélez-Málaga, and some with Fregiliana in the kingdom of Granada. It was there that Saint Peter appointed Epaenetus bishop.

Metaphrastes says:

> Peter came to the city of Syrmium in Spain, where, after he had appointed Epaenetus bishop, etc.

Whether this Syrmium is identified with Motril, Vélez-Málaga, or Fregiliana, it lies on the Mediterranean coast of Baetica, toward Africa. Metaphrastes therefore gives an orderly account when he says that the Apostle proceeded from Spanish Syrmium and arrived at Carthage in Africa:

> He came to the city of Syrmium in Spain; after appointing Epaenetus bishop there, he proceeded to the city of Carthage in Africa.

Thus the account agrees perfectly with the truth.

Since Jerome, Usuard, and Equilinus establish that the holy martyrs Montanus and Maxima were thrown into the sea, and since of all the cities bearing the name Syrmium only the Spanish one lies by the sea—for the Syrmium of Pannonia and that of Lombardy lie far inland—it necessarily follows that these martyrs of Christ were crowned at Syrmium in Spain, as Dexter asserts here.

Galesinus is therefore mistaken. Believing that there was only one Syrmium, in Pannonia, he changed “sea” into “river”—a readily accomplished alteration—and named the river that flows past Pannonian Syrmium, the Sava. More difficult still, he writes that they were killed by Diocletian. He offers no authority for either claim and therefore should be followed in neither. Indeed, he confuses this Montanus, the companion of Saint Maxima the virgin, with another Montanus, the companion of Saint Irenaeus the bishop, Demetrius the deacon, and Pollio the lector, who suffered under Diocletian by different kinds of death. For, as Equilinus writes in book IV, chapter 94, Irenaeus and Montanus were thrown into a river, Demetrius was beheaded, and Pollio was burned by flames. Nevertheless, as regards Irenaeus, the Roman Martyrology on 25 March says that he was not suffocated but completed his martyrdom by being beheaded.

## 6. At Castrum Altum, etc.

From the principal geographers—Charles Clusius, Arnoldus Mylius, Abraham Ortelius—and from the maps of William Ganson, we learn that the Tugian pass, otherwise called the Silver Mountain, was the mountain commonly known as Sierra de Alcaraz. A town called Castro still remains there.

Castrum Altum was famous for the killing of Hamilcar, about whom Livy writes in book XIV, and after him Mariana in book II, chapter 7, and Florianus in book IV, chapter 16. Saint Secundus is said to have advanced his seeds of preaching as far as this place. He later offered his throat for Christ at Abula, the last of Saint James’s disciples to do so. Through his intercession God worked many miracles, not only in that city but also in the neighboring towns and cities. On this subject see the *Treasury of Preachers*, volume II, 1 May.

In the year of Our Lord 1519, the body of Saint Secundus again came to light in the church that he himself had built and dedicated to the Savior, and which had already received the name of Saint Lucy. It was discovered beneath the ground, by God’s great favor and to the joy of the citizens of Abula and of all Spain. It bore a gold ring set with a shining sapphire, on which these letters were engraved:

> SANCTUS SECUNDUS.

A chalice was found with the sacred body, bearing the inscription:

> Andrea Petruci orto da Siena fece questo cal.

That is, “Andrea Petruci, born at Siena, made this chalice.” Since the inscription is in the modern Italian language, it suggests that the chalice had been repaired and decorated not long before.

Finally, in 1594, the body was transferred with the most solemn ceremony and display to the cathedral church by the most illustrious and reverend Lord Don Jerónimo Manrique, bishop of Abula. God honored the translation with frequent miracles, which Antonio de Cianca records in a history specially published on the subject.

## 7. M. Marcellus, etc.

It is reasonable to believe that so noble a Roman, and one of such distinguished talent, devoted himself diligently in his youth to oratory and poetry, especially since Nero himself, the ruler of the Roman Empire, boasted that he excelled everyone in both arts.

Indeed, that same Marcellus Eugenius composed a most elegant poem on the martyrdom of Saint Dionysius, as Hilduin testifies in the *Life of Saint Dionysius*, with Morales agreeing with him; the work was still preserved in Hilduin’s possession. Dexter discusses it in his Chronicle under the year 130.

There are also some indications of his prose writings in those letters to Saints Nereus and Achilleus, which were discussed above. Nor is it surprising that he was dear to Persius, Juvenal, Seneca, Catullus—also called Galbus—and Statius, since they were the more distinguished poets of his age and lived in the same city with him.

Not only the Church of Toledo but also many other churches in Spain annually read on his feast day that he performed many miracles during his preaching at Toledo. Among them, the Church of Palencia used to recite the following in its own Breviary:

> He converted the Gentile population of the province of Toledo to the Christian faith by the example of his life, the uprightness of his conduct, Catholic preaching, and the confirmation provided by miracles.

Truxillus likewise writes:

> He remained for a long time at Toledo, persevering in his preaching and shining forth with many miracles. In this way he converted countless people to the faith of Christ.

## 8. The people of Toledo

See the preceding annotation, and what we said under the year 94 concerning Saint Theodosius, bishop of Barcelona.

## 9. The greatness of the people of Toledo, etc.

The archives of Toledo provide the veins of this most pure spring. Six hundred years later, Julian, archpriest of Saint Justa, examined them and admits that he found there many things worthy of knowledge, including those letters of the Pharisees to the Hebrew inhabitants of Toledo and other materials of the same kind.

When the author says, “I governed that city for two years,” I understand him to mean that he was a duumvir at Toledo. The duumvirate lasted two years because each year one of the two duumvirs was elected, and thus each of them governed the city for two years.

Toledo ought indeed to regard it as a great distinction to have recognized as its governor so eminent a man, who, through the election of the emperor Theodosius, went on to enjoy the prefecture of the East itself.

## 10. He is famous, etc.

Possidonius mentions the quaestorship of M. Marcellus. He writes—according to Ravisius in the *Cornucopia*—that Marcellus collected a tribute of six hundred talents from Celtiberia in Spain.

Budaeus infers:

> From this one may conjecture that the Celtiberian people were extremely numerous and rich in money.

Catullus called a certain Celtiberian “the son of cavernous Celtiberia,” because it abounded in gold and silver mines, as though it were filled with countless caverns like those of rabbits.

## 11. Dionysius, etc.

This too has hitherto been unheard of. For who does not know that Dionysius dedicated his books to Timothy, bishop of Ephesus and disciple of Paul? Indeed, they appear to bear an inscription of this kind:

> To Timothy, bishop of Ephesus.

Let us begin the discussion from this point.

I do not deny that such an inscription is found in some printed copies of Dionysius’s works. But it was not placed there by the author; rather, it was added by an incompetent copyist on his own initiative. The genuine inscription of the book *On the Divine Names* is:

> Dionysius the priest to Timothy his fellow priest.

Saint Thomas gives this inscription in his commentaries; Sixtus of Siena gives it in book II of his *Holy Library*, letter D; and most recently Lansellius has printed it in his *Areopagitica*. It can also easily be inferred from the inscriptions of the other books—*On the Celestial Hierarchy*, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, and *On Mystical Theology*—which he wrote to the same Timothy. All of them begin:

> Dionysius the priest to Timothy his fellow priest.

There can therefore be no doubt that the book *On the Divine Names* also bore such an inscription. This will become even clearer from what follows.

We also admit that many men, and very distinguished ones, believed that this Timothy to whom Dionysius dedicated his books was the same man to whom Paul dedicated two epistles and whom he appointed bishop of Ephesus. Among them was that most illustrious Saint Maximus, who added Greek annotations to the works of Dionysius, later published by Lansellius.

It should not, however, be surprising that they fell into this easy error. When they heard the name Timothy and failed to distinguish the periods, the more famous Timothy, the disciple of Paul, naturally first came to mind. Yet there is no doubt that these same men would have believed nothing less readily had they noticed—as was not difficult—that the Apostle’s disciple had already been taken away by martyrdom when Dionysius dictated these books. Many other considerations prove the same thing so clearly that no room for doubt remains. Cardinal Baronius ultimately acknowledged this under the year 109, volume II of the *Annals*.

What are these considerations?

Saint Timothy, bishop of Ephesus, was put to death under the emperor Domitian, at the time when Saint John the Apostle was exiled to the island of Patmos, or at least before John himself was released from exile and returned to Ephesus. His disciple Polycrates, and after him Metaphrastes in Surius, volume I, 24 January, testify to this. Metaphrastes says that when John was exiled to Patmos, he left Timothy at Ephesus; yet the enemy did not permit Timothy himself to live long in his episcopal see. When John was released from exile, he found that Timothy had departed to God.

Since it is otherwise established that John saw his Apocalypse at Patmos but wrote his Gospel after returning to Ephesus—as testified by Irenaeus in book V near the end, Epiphanius in heresy 51, Dorotheus in the *Synopsis*, Abdias in book VIII of the *Apostolic History*, Athanasius in the *Synopsis*, Jerome in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under John, Eusebius in his *Chronicle* and in book III of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 18, and Nicephorus in book II, chapter 24, and book III, chapter 9—it follows that Timothy was removed from this life before John wrote his Gospel and published his Apocalypse at Ephesus.

John had seen the Apocalypse at Patmos toward the end of Domitian’s reign, according to Irenaeus, or, which amounts to the same thing, in the fourteenth year of Domitian, according to Eusebius. Dionysius, however, frequently inserts testimonies from both John’s Gospel and Apocalypse into his books. Who, then, does not see that Dionysius wrote after John, and even more certainly after the death of Timothy, bishop of Ephesus?

He cites John’s Gospel in *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 4 at the end, and in chapters 2 and 15; and in *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 2, part 2, the passage:

> But to all who received him, he gave power, etc.

And in part 1:

> He will keep my word, and we shall come to him, etc.

He cites it elsewhere as well.

He cites the Apocalypse nine times in *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapters 2 and 15; and in *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 1 and chapter 3, part 3, where he says:

> Whether that wholly secret and mystical vision of the beloved disciple, etc.

In *On the Divine Names*, chapter 5, he cites Revelation 1:

> Who is, and who was, and who is to come.

Moreover, in chapter 4 of *On the Divine Names* he cites Saint Ignatius from the *Epistle to the Romans*, saying—for the divine Ignatius writes:

> My love has been crucified.

Ignatius plainly wrote this while traveling toward Rome in chains and hastening toward martyrdom. In that epistle to the Romans he says:

> From Syria to Rome I fight with wild beasts, chained night and day on land and sea with twelve leopards—that is, the soldiers who guard me—etc.

That this happened under Trajan is attested by the Martyrology on 1 February. Jerome, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Ignatius, following Eusebius in his *Chronicle*, states that Ignatius suffered in the eleventh year of Trajan, that is, in the year 110 or 111 of Christ.

We must consequently admit that Dionysius wrote the book *On the Divine Names* after the martyrdom of Saint Ignatius, at the time when Dionysius was preaching in Gaul. At least fifteen or sixteen years earlier, Timothy had been stoned to death.

Cardinal Baronius had until now supported us, moved especially by this testimony concerning Ignatius. But now, departing from his former position, he suggests that the reference to Ignatius was inserted into Dionysius’s book by someone after Ignatius’s death.

I do not know how such a solution could have pleased so great a man. If we may, without the testimony of any ancient manuscript, remove the reference to Ignatius from Dionysius’s book by our own authority, I do not know on what grounds we could deny that the same could be done elsewhere. Once this principle is admitted, nothing in the writings of the saints would remain certain.

We must therefore stand by the agreement of all the Latin and Greek manuscripts that contain the passage. Baronius would not even achieve his purpose by removing this one reference. It would be necessary to erase from more than thirty passages in the works of Dionysius the testimonies drawn from the Gospel and Apocalypse of John, since these too were written after Timothy’s death. But since these passages are the very sinews of the whole discourse, the books themselves would also be destroyed. God forbid.

Three further arguments of the same kind are supplied by the books themselves.

First, when addressing the Timothy to whom he dedicates his books six hundred times, Dionysius cites statements from both of Saint Paul’s Epistles to Timothy. In *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 2, and in *On the Divine Names*, chapter 5, he cites 1 Timothy 1:

> To the King of the ages, invisible, etc.

In *On the Divine Names*, chapter 7, and *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 2, part 2, he cites 1 Timothy 2:

> Who desires all human beings to be saved, etc.

In *On the Divine Names*, chapter 8, he cites 2 Timothy:

> God remains faithful; he cannot deny himself.

He cites other passages both in *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 2, part 1, and in the letter to Demophilus, as well as frequently elsewhere.

If he were addressing the Ephesian Timothy, would he never, even when citing the Apostle’s Epistles written to Timothy himself, say, “Paul rightly wrote this or that to you”? Would he never even make the slightest allusion to something written to him in those letters? This seems to me incredible.

Second, Dionysius always calls him “son” in *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 1:

> Most holy son Timothy,

and at the end of the same book:

> These many things, son, etc.

In *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 2:

> But you, O son, etc.

And in *On the Divine Names*, chapter 2, part 1.

No sane person will persuade himself that Dionysius ever called that great Timothy “son”—the disciple older than Dionysius himself and bishop of Ephesus—whom Paul so honored that he inscribed six letters jointly in his own name and Timothy’s, saying, “Paul and Timothy,” namely two to the Corinthians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, and one to Philemon.

Would Dionysius call inferior the man whom Paul made his equal in the ministry of preaching?

Saint Maximus long ago saw the difficulty and said in his scholia on *On the Divine Names*:

> We must ask how the great Dionysius calls Timothy “son.” Either, as I think, he says this because he was more advanced than Timothy in years and superior in philosophy; or because, in imitation of the Lord, he would say, “Children, do you have anything to eat?”; or because those who practice the simplicity that is according to God were called children.

But who does not see that all these explanations are forced and strained? Even if Dionysius were using that form of speech improperly and by some rhetorical figure, he would use it only once at most. Here, however, he always calls him “son,” especially since, although Timothy was converted in his youth, he would have been extremely old when Dionysius wrote, if he had not already died.

Third, consider again how far that Saint Timothy was removed from Dionysius, so that Dionysius would not call him “son” even once.

No one should doubt that Timothy always held greater authority among the disciples than Titus, since Paul honored him more. Yet when Dionysius writes to Titus—for he also addressed an epistle to him, which Trithemius entitles *The Book of Symbolic Theology*—does he call him “son”? On the contrary, he calls him “high priest.” The inscription of the letter or book is:

> To Titus the high priest.

And in the letter itself he calls Titus “most honorable,” not “son.” It begins:

> Saint Timothy, most honorable Titus, etc.

Would Dionysius, who addresses a disciple of lesser standing with such reverence, call the disciple of greater rank and merit “son”?

There is another point worthy of the closest attention. Timothy—whoever he may be to whom these books were written—was taught by Dionysius. Dionysius wrote so many books to him for this very purpose.

Moreover, both Timothy and Dionysius spent some time under the instruction of the divine Hierotheus, as is clear from *On the Divine Names*:

> For when our illustrious teacher Hierotheus, etc., by whom we were instructed after Saint Paul, etc.

And again, in *On the Divine Names*, chapter 7:

> That man, marvelously understanding the matter by living experience, the divine sun of us both and of our teacher, said: “What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1).

No sane person will believe that the Timothy who was the equal of the Apostles, nourished at Paul’s breast and continually instructed by him in the milk of doctrine throughout the Apostle’s life, was, after Paul’s death, devoted to Dionysius’s teaching and became his disciple, or that, while the Apostle was still alive, he diligently listened to Hierotheus teaching first at Athens and afterward in Spain.

We are therefore compelled to seek another Timothy to whom all these details apply, and to admit that he was the man to whom Dionysius dedicated his works.

Cardinal Baronius suspected that this man was Timothy, the son of Saint Pudens the senator and brother of the holy virgins Pudentiana and Praxedes. He is also mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on 25 June. It is established that he was a contemporary of Dionysius, a hearer of the Apostles, and a priest, just as Dionysius continually calls him:

> Dionysius the priest to Timothy his fellow priest.

This would indeed be no slight conjecture if we were dealing only with conjectures. But we possess the weighty testimony of Dexter, from whom we may not depart without manifest reason. Dexter testifies that this Timothy was M. Marcellus Eugenius, whom Dionysius himself called Timothy because of the excellence of his intellect. I add: also because of the nobility of his lineage, since *Eugenius* means “noble.”

The assignment of such Greek names should not seem either new or unusual. Indeed, although Latin was the Romans’ common language at that time, Greek was the classical language among the learned and occupied nearly the place that Latin now occupies among us. Hence Greek cognomens were assigned to certain persons in accordance with their merits.

Thus Dionysius called Eugenius “Timothy,” which means “honor of God,” because Eugenius honored the infancy of the Church by his intellectual gifts and noble birth.

Nor, if we do not wish to accept Dexter’s testimony gratuitously, is anything lacking in Eugenius that is required of the true Timothy. He was Dionysius’s fellow disciple under Paul’s instruction and came with him to Spain, as we have already said. He was also able to meet and hear Hierotheus under his instruction, both at Athens and later in Spain, at Segovia. Eugenius was descended on his mother’s side from the most illustrious Athenian nobility, as Dexter will show a little farther below.

Moreover, Eugenius was a very well-known disciple of Dionysius, as everyone admits in the account of his life. This also agrees with the Breviary of Saint Isidore, in the hymn for his martyrdom, which says:

> The Doctor of Spain, Eugenius, revisited Gaul,  
> seeking with faithful heart  
> the presence of the learned Doctor of Gaul.  
> He longs for his father, Dionysius,  
> and pursues his desire, etc.

If we ask who was called Dionysius’s “son”—for he calls the one to whom he dedicates his books “son”—we shall find Eugenius, of whom it is said:

> He longs for his father, etc.

No one else fits. Eugenius was not only a son by instruction but much more by creation, or ordination—for we have already seen that Eugenius was ordained by Dionysius.

Moreover, Dionysius addresses Timothy as a bishop. This alone, leaving aside everything else, completely excludes Timothy, the brother of Saints Pudentiana and Praxedes, who was only a priest.

But from where do we derive Timothy’s episcopate? Clearly, from the very inscription of the books:

> Dionysius the priest to Timothy his fellow priest.

The word “priest” must be understood of Timothy in the same sense in which Dionysius himself calls himself a priest. For “fellow priest” means one who is a priest together with another and belongs to the same order.

It is certain that Dionysius understood the episcopal order and dignity by the word “priest,” since at that time he was preaching in Gaul as a bishop. Timothy, therefore, his fellow priest, was also a bishop, just as Eugenius was.

Paul uses “priest” in this sense when he says to Titus:

> Appoint priests in every city, of this sort: if anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, etc.

There he necessarily means bishops, as Theophylact noted in that passage. For when he explains why such priests are to be chosen, he adds:

> For a bishop must be blameless, etc.

He speaks in the same way in 1 Timothy 4:

> Do not neglect the grace that was given you with the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate.

Theophylact says that this means “of the bishops.”

Finally, from *On the Divine Names*, chapter 3, we learn that the Timothy whom Dionysius calls “son” was at that time absent from Gaul, where Dionysius was, but was not very far away, since communication between them was frequent.

Dionysius speaks to Timothy about the book of Hierotheus, which Timothy had received from Dionysius and returned to him, so that Timothy might explain more fully what Hierotheus, “that divine man,” had set forth in condensed style while reverently expounding the mysteries. Dionysius writes:

> Moreover, you yourself have often urged us toward the same thing, and you sent the book itself to us as something exceedingly excellent, as stated above.

If Timothy often urged him, they did not live far apart; and if Timothy sent him the book, they were not present with one another.

Everything is readily explained if Dionysius was in Gaul while Timothy was in Spain.

This also makes it easy to identify the reason why the books of Dionysius were unknown to Eusebius and Jerome. They were still being kept in Spain, where they had been sent; Dexter, being a Spaniard, read them, while Jerome and Eusebius remained unaware of them.

Yet if they had been sent to Rome and beyond, there is no doubt that Jerome would have encountered them and discussed them in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Some respond that in that book Jerome discussed only authors whose works were present in Eusebius’s library. This is asserted without foundation and against Jerome’s purpose and Dexter’s contention, as is clear from Jerome’s prologue.

Finally, I will not pass over these words of Dionysius in his epistle to Titus:

> Saint Timothy, most honorable Titus, I do not know whether I have written anything concerning theological signs of which he himself departed ignorant.

These words not only fail to support the opponents but confirm our position. Dionysius would not say this of someone who was not his disciple. Rather, he indicates that Timothy was his friend and that he had read Dionysius’s books in his own hands.

I read the following about Eugenius below in Dexter, under the year 220:

> Titus, surnamed Justus—the same man who received Paul at Corinth, for Acts 18 says, “He entered the house of a certain man named Titus Justus, a worshiper of God”—having become bishop, first followed Saint Paul and soon preached the Gospel in Carpetania, where the memory of him and the greatness of his miracles are celebrated.

This will be discussed in its proper place. For now, however, the following too must be read in Dexter:

> There exists a certain letter said to have been addressed to M. Marcellus, prelate of Toledo, whom it calls “son” and “Timothy,” that is, “honored by God”; for the other Timothy, to whom this letter was written, had already departed from the living.

There is no doubt that such a letter was by Saint Dionysius, for who else would have called M. Marcellus “son”? But this letter perished together with many other works of the same holy Doctor: namely, with the book *On Divine Hymns*, mentioned in *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 7; with the book *On Symbolic Theology*, cited in *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 15, in *On the Divine Names*, chapters 1 and 13, in *On Mystical Theology*, chapter 3, and in the Epistle to Titus; with the book *On Intelligible and Sensible Things*, cited in *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapters 1 and 2; with the book *On the Legal, or Priestly, Hierarchy*, cited in *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3; with the book *Theological Hypotyposes*, mentioned in *On the Divine Names*, chapters 1 and 2, and in *On Mystical Theology*, chapter 3; with the book *On the Soul*, cited in *On the Divine Names*, chapter 4; and with the book *On Divine and Just Judgment*, also cited in chapter 4 of that work.

What wonder if that letter suffered shipwreck together with so many and such valuable works?

Nevertheless, there survives another book by the same Dionysius, concerning the passion of Blessed Eutropius, his companion. Pope Calixtus II translated it into Latin after finding it written in Greek at Constantinople.

It survives in Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum Historiale*, book X, chapter 18, under the heading “Concerning the text of the passion of Saint Eutropius.”

I shall reproduce Vincent’s words together with the beginning of the text, since it clearly asserts that Dionysius was born at Athens and yet was bishop of Paris:

> This blessed Dionysius, he says, the companion of Blessed Eutropius and bishop of Paris, wrote his passion in Greek letters and sent it by the hand of Blessed Clement the pope to his relatives—that is, his kinsmen—in Greece who already believed in Christ. Pope Calixtus II later found this passion at Constantinople, in the school of the Greeks, in a certain codex containing the passions of many holy martyrs, and translated it from Greek into Latin. It begins as follows:

Dionysius, bishop and Greek by descent, sends greetings in Christ to the Most Reverend Father Clement.

We inform you that Eutropius, whom you sent with me to these regions to preach the name of Christ, received the crown of martyrdom at the hands of the Gentiles at the city of Xantona, for the faith of the Lord. Therefore I humbly beseech Your Paternity not to delay sending this account of his passion, as soon as you are able, to my kinsmen, acquaintances, and faithful friends in the regions of Greece, especially at Athens, so that those who received with me from Blessed Paul the washing of new birth, when they hear that a glorious martyr suffered a cruel death for the faith of Christ, may rejoice that they have endured tribulations and hardships for Christ’s name.

At the end it is necessary to observe that Dexter did not deal with the books of Dionysius in the year 100 because they were supposedly written in that year—for it is established that they were written after the martyrdom of Saint Ignatius, which took place after the year 100—but because, having once begun speaking of Dionysius, Marcellus, and Eugenius, he decided to insert this account concerning them, especially since he did not say that it happened in this year, but “during this period,” namely, at the beginning of the second century of the years of Christ the Lord.

### 12. Flavia Domitilla, etc.

We dealt with her under the year 91, when we discussed her niece Domitilla. Here Dexter adds another surname of this Domitilla, the wife of the consul Flavius Clemens, namely Sabina, by which she could be distinguished from the other Domitilla.

### 13. Miraculously, etc.

When we dealt with the miracles of Saint Eugenius, enough and more than enough was said about the spread of the faith throughout Spain. This may also easily be inferred if we consider those great champions and teachers of the faith who in those times devoted themselves to preaching in Spain: namely Titus, Onesimus, Saturninus, Philip, Philotheus, Firminus, Paulus Sergius, Probus Paternus, Rufus, Alexander, Secundus, Theodosius, and Ovidius, concerning whom we have already spoken in their proper places.

Pliny the Younger, in Book X of his *Letters*, Letter 97, addressed to Trajan himself, discusses the persecution of Christians living throughout the whole world, which was the third in sequence and began under Trajan at the beginning of his reign. He says that some Christians who had fallen away from the faith had been led to commit the crime three years earlier—namely, at the beginning of Trajan’s reign, as Baronius explains—others several years earlier, under Domitian, and still others two years earlier, while Nero’s persecution was still continuing. Therefore Eusebius is mistaken when he maintains that the third persecution began in the tenth year of Trajan. Dexter discusses this same Pliny the Younger, who is also believed to have suffered for Christ, under the year 220.

### 14. Among the Olcades, etc.

Livy, Book XXI, states that Hannibal the Carthaginian, intending to attack the Saguntines, first led his army into the territory of the Olcades. Concerning the territory and situation of the Olcades he says:

> Beyond the Iberus, that people belonged more to the sphere of Carthaginian influence than to its actual dominion. He captured and plundered Carteia, a wealthy city and the chief city of that people. The lesser cities, struck with fear by this event, accepted his authority after a tribute had been imposed.

He then adds:

> At the beginning of spring the war was carried against the Vaccaei. Hermandica and Arbocala, cities of the Cartheians, were captured by force. When the fugitives from Hermandica had joined themselves to the exiles of the Olcades, they stirred up the Carpetani. Attacking Hannibal as he returned from the Vaccaei, not far from the river Tagus, they threw his heavily burdened column into confusion with the spoils.

The Carpetani, together with their Olcadian and Vaccaeian auxiliaries, numbered one hundred thousand—most of the latter came from Helmandica, which we now call Salamanca, according to Turnebus, *Adversaria*, Book III, chapter 18, and Godelefus in his notes on Livy. They would have been an unconquered army if the battle had been fought on level ground.

It may therefore be inferred that the Olcades, like the Vaccaei, were neighbors of the Carpetani, since, after being put to flight by Hannibal, they fled to the Carpetani—clearly to their neighbors. Nebrissensis believed that the Olcades occupied that part of Carpetania where Ocana now stands; Mariana in his *History of Spain* and Ludovicus Nonius in his *Hispania*, chapter 47, followed him. But what is superior to all the rest is the present testimony of Dexter, by which the Olcades are called part of Carpetania. Plutarch and Polybius, Book III, agree with Livy. The only dissenting authority is Stephanus of Byzantium, who thought that the chief city of the Olcades, Carteia, was the city situated not far from New Carthage, although the two places are in fact very different from one another.

Among the Olcades, therefore, according to Dexter, the holy martyrs Antonina, a virgin, and Alexander, a soldier, suffered for Christ, although others believe that they were killed at Constantinople, where their feast day was celebrated annually as though they had been fellow citizens. It should not, however, seem strange that people born there were killed in Spain; this often happened during times of persecution, when Christians migrated from one place to another. We have said enough about this above.

Their acts are found in Surius, volume 3, and are related in abbreviated form in the Roman Martyrology, where it is said under 3 May:

> At Constantinople, the holy martyrs Alexander, a soldier, and Antonina, a virgin. Under the governor Festus she was condemned to a brothel; Alexander, who had remained there on her behalf, led her out secretly after changing his clothing. He was afterward ordered to suffer torture with her. Both were thrown into the fire for Christ after their hands had been cut off, and, having completed a noble contest, they were crowned.

When you hear “at Constantinople,” however, please understand not the place of their martyrdom but the place of their commemoration. For we gather from the Greek Menologion, under 8 June, that their bodies were eventually brought there for the most part.

A considerable error has crept into the Roman Martyrology when it says that they suffered in the persecution of Maximian. The Acts say only: “When persecution was taking place in those days”; they do not at all specify which persecution it was or by which ruler it was stirred up. Molanus likewise says nothing more in his additions to Usuard, under the same day. All, however, write that they suffered under the governor Festus. Yet Festus is remembered not in Thrace, where Constantinople is situated, but in Spain; nor does he belong to the time of Maximian, but to that of Domitian. In the Olcades, at the bridge of Alcántara, he erected this inscription for the emperors Vespasian, Titus, and Domitian, which can still be seen engraved in the marble:

> IMP. CAESAR. VESPASIANO AVGVSTO. PONT. MAX.  
> TRIB. POT. X. IMPER. XX. PP. COSS. IX.  
> IMPERATORI. TITO VESP. CAESAR. AVG. F. COSS. VI.  
> [lacuna]  
> *(The memory of Domitian was erased by decree of the senate, as Suetonius testifies.)*  
> CALPETANO RANTIO QVIRINALI.  
> VALERIO FESTO LEG. AVG. PR. PR. etc.

Valerius Festus was therefore legate of the emperors Titus and Domitian and propraetor of Spain at the time when Dexter reports that Alexander and Antonina suffered. We are consequently compelled to admit that they died in Domitian’s persecution, around the year of the Lord 99 or 98; for the stone was erected at that time, as Morales noted in Book IX, chapter 25.

This agrees with Dexter’s statement that in the year 100 the holy martyrs were transferred, not killed. They were transferred, I say, from the pit into which they had been buried after fire had been added, as the Acts relate. They continue:

> Immediately Festus became speechless, and, overcome by a demon, expired on the seventh day. The holy martyrs of Christ, Alexander and Antonina, completed their martyrdom on 3 May, at the ninth hour, on Saturday.

It is worthwhile, however, to hear the Menologion under 8 June:

> The contest of the holy martyrs Alexander and Antonina. These holy martyrs were from the village of Cardemo. Blessed Antonina lived a chaste and holy life. When she was arrested by the governor Festus and could not be swayed by any arguments to deny Christ and serve the demons, she was shut up in a brothel. After she had been detained there for three days in fasting, a light shone in the prison during the night; thunder sounded, the prison doors were shattered, and a voice descended from heaven exhorting her to rise and take food. When she had eaten and was strengthened, she stood before the governor. Since she again could not be persuaded to offer sacrifices to idols, she was thrown down and beaten with blows and was once more taken to the brothel.
>
> Alexander, awakened by divine revelation, entered the place. Since he was young—for he was eighteen years old—it could easily have appeared that he had approached it for an immoral act. He secretly led the holy virgin out of the house, covering her head with his cloak, while he himself remained there in her place. Shortly afterward, when the matter became known through the soldiers who had come to violate the saint, Alexander was brought before the governor and beaten. The extremities of both their hands and feet were cut off. Finally, they were thrown into a pit of fire, their whole bodies smeared with liquid pitch, and, with Christ’s help, they attained a blessed end.
>
> Their feast is celebrated at Constantinople, where their holy and precious relics are kept; from them the cures of many diseases flow forth.

### 15. L. Sabinus Probus, etc.

Here Dexter begins to discuss certain outstanding disciples of Paul whom he had in Spain and elsewhere, and their departure to God. First he speaks of Probus, whom he had brought to the faith with his wife Xantippe at Laminum; then of his mother-in-law Claudia Xantippe; then of his wife, Quinta Marcella Xantippe, daughter of that Claudia and sister of Saint Eugenius, bishop of Toledo; and also of Polyxena, her companion, and certain others.

Probus presided as bishop at Ravenna and, renowned for miracles, departed to heaven. His annual commemoration is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 10 November in these words:

> At Ravenna, Saint Probus, bishop, renowned for miracles.

Equilinus gives a distinguished eulogy of him in Book X, chapter 45, and Molanus includes it in his Usuard:

> Probus, bishop of the Ravennates, became renowned in that same city. He was gentle and pious, most devout in faith, distinguished in appearance, radiant in works, wise in speech, and full of the grace of the Holy Spirit. He cured all the sick who came to him, whatever illness afflicted them, and drove unclean spirits from the possessed. After, as the time of his life’s setting approached, he saw angelic hosts, his holy soul immediately departed from his body on 10 November. His sons buried him in the church dedicated to his name, where he lives through miracles and virtues.

Consult Rubeus, Book I of his *History of Ravenna*, although he is greatly mistaken in assigning the date of Probus’s episcopate.

### 16. Claudia Paphensis Candida, etc.

She was called Paphensis because she came from the city of Paphos in Cyprus. It is said that there she was converted to the faith by Paul, together with her husband Lucius, the proconsul Paulus Sergius, and many others, after witnessing the blindness that the apostle inflicted upon Elymas the Magus. Metaphrastes testifies in his commentary on the journeys of Peter and Paul that many people at that time, together with the proconsul, gave their names to the faith.
