Candida went to Rome with her husband Lucius, and she and Rogatus and Cassian were crowned with martyrdom. Their annual commemoration is assigned in the Roman Martyrology to 1 December, although Bede discusses Candida alone.

### 17. L. Macedonica, etc.

The Greek name Λυδία (*Lydia*) was mistakenly changed into the Latin Lucia, with the Greek upsilon υ changed into the Latin *u*, as often happens. Some, more corruptly, call her Luceia, changing δ into ει.

She was Lydia the seller of purple from the city of Thyatira, whose heart the Lord opened to attend to what Paul was saying when he preached at Philippi. This is clear from the fact that she is Macedonian and a disciple of Paul. Her conversion is related in Acts 16, together with the vision granted to Paul on her account, beginning with these words:

> A vision appeared to Paul during the night: a certain Macedonian man was standing and pleading with him, saying, “Cross over into Macedonia and help us,” etc.

Anyone may find the passage there under the name of Lydia the seller of purple.

She is mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on 3 August. Nevertheless, I would believe that she is the same as the Lucia who is said to have suffered at Rome with twenty-two others on 29 June. Baronius believes her to be the woman whose life Equilinus wrote in Book VI, chapter 4. If that were so, we would consequently be compelled to say that, since Dexter makes clear that she suffered under the governor Rucius, and since another Riccius Varus, a persecutor of martyrs, is found in the time of Diocletian, Equilinus derived his error from this and believed that Luceia suffered under Diocletian.

It would nevertheless be enough to consider that the name Ricciovarus is entirely different from Rucius and that the former did not torture martyrs at Rome at all, but in Gaul, as is clear from the martyrdom of Saints Crispinus and Crispinianus and many others.

For the rest, I believe that someone quite different wrote the life in that passage, because the Luceia about whom it speaks was a virgin at the time of her martyrdom and exceptionally beautiful. A certain barbarian king named Aceius was passionately in love with her, and she was afterward killed at Rome with him alone. None of this can apply to Lydia and her companions.

### 18. Xantippe, etc.

When Dexter recorded Paul’s preaching in Spain under the year 64, he discussed the conversion of Xantippe; under the year 71 he discussed the arrival of Polyxena, her sister, with Onesimus from Achaia. Now he discusses their deaths. We shall say more about them below, under number 10.

### 19. M. Luppus, etc.

It is difficult to believe that these four names—Marcus, Luppus, Philip, and Lucius—belong to one and the same man, namely Lucius, Candida’s husband. I would rather believe that they designate three distinguished martyrs, disciples of Paul: M. Luppus, concerning whom the Greeks speak in the Menologion on 23 August, as does the Roman Martyrology on the same day; Philip Philotheus, who, returning from Spain to Italy, from which he originated, ultimately became bishop in Picenum and offered his throat for Christ on 22 October, the day on which his feast is celebrated there and his memory is preserved in the Roman Martyrology; and finally Lucius, the husband of Claudia Candida Paphensis, whose name is read together with that of his wife in the Roman Martyrology on 1 December.

### 20. Quinta Marcella, etc.

This is particularly relevant. When Dexter was speaking of Xantippe and intended to write much in praise of Saint Eugenius, he now discloses what he had previously concealed: Eugenius and Xantippe were siblings, being the children of Marcus Marcellus and Claudia Xantippe. The former was prefect at Rome, while the latter was born of the most noble lineage of the Athenians.

Each child bore part of the father’s name. The man was called Marcus Marcellus, while the woman was called Quinta Marcella; she also received from her mother the surname Xantippe. Martial noted her mother’s height in Book VIII, Epigram 59, with his customary wit:

> You could equal the summit of the Palatine colossus  
> if you, Claudia, were a foot and a half shorter.

Paul also mentions her when writing to Timothy in the final chapter of the Second Epistle:

> Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers greet you.

Saint Xantippe, her daughter, died in Spain and was buried by her brother.

### 21. Saint Vincent, etc.

Galesinus records the memory of this most noble martyr and bishop in his martyrology under 6 June, in these words:

> At Mevia, Saint Vincent, bishop, who, having overcome tortures and having tamed the wild beasts to which he was exposed, departed to heaven to receive the reward of victory in piety.

In his notes, however, while attempting to clarify the place of martyrdom, he is entirely mistaken. He says “at Mevia,” perhaps “at Media,” which is a city of Thrace.

It is even more surprising that this happened to an Italian, who ought to have known Mevania in Italy—even if he was ignorant of Mevania in Spain—as a town of Umbria, commonly called Bevagna, as Leander Albertus and Arnoldus Milius testify in their geographical synonymy.

Another Italian, Bishop Equilinus, will correct the Italian’s error. In Book V of his *Catalogue*, chapter 93, he writes the life and death of Saint Vincent of the city of Mevia, or Mevania, in complete agreement with Dexter, as you can now see:

> Vincent, bishop of the city of Mevia, was arrested by a certain Capitolinus, governor of Tuscany, who had gathered Christian bishops bound in chains at Perugia for punishment. Together with his brother Benignus the deacon, he was brought to the temple of Mars to sacrifice to the gods. When he prayed, all the idols were overturned, and demons came out howling. They killed many pagans, striking six hundred of them to death with blows; and, compelled by the power of Christ, they released all the Christians who were bound in chains.
>
> Through this miracle many of the Gentiles received the faith, among them a certain Mavertius, previously an exceedingly cruel count, who had gathered bishops from the neighboring regions and was converted.
>
> Thus far, Equilinus says, these events occurred at Perugia in Italy, and Dexter also firmly asserts this when he says, “He goes to Italy.”
>
> Equilinus continues: When the Christians were transferring themselves with the bishop to another place and were singing psalms, Capitolinus sent men. After Vincent had been taken away, he had the others killed by the sword. A certain devout man named Extasius rescued the body of Benignus the deacon from among the others and buried it not far from Portulium on 1 May.
>
> Several days later Capitolinus had Vincent brought out, tortured for a long time, beaten with stones, stretched on the rack, and burned with flames, and then committed him to prison. There, when the doors were opened by divine power, heavenly light shone upon him.
>
> When the governor heard this, he ordered him to be drowned in the sea. After he had been thrown into the water, an angel brought him back to the shore. Those who had drowned him, seeing this, were converted, and carried him on their shoulders all the way to their own city of Mevia.
>
> Dexter maintains that these events occurred at Carthage in Spain, and rightly so. For Portulium, today called Portela, where his brother Benignus was buried, lies not in Italy but near Carthage. Moreover, if the story were transferred to Perugia—or to Mevania in Italy, which lies near Perugia—he could not have been thrown into the sea, since both cities lie inland, far from the sea on every side; Carthage, however, lies on the coast.

Therefore, what Equilinus says about the Christians transferring themselves with the bishop to another place must certainly be understood of their journey into the province of Carthage. Capitolinus also hastened there, completing the persecution he had begun—either because he had the opportunity to persecute Christians dispersed throughout the whole world, as one may reasonably believe from the emperor’s zeal, or because he was inflamed by anger and flushed with shame, knowing that the rulers of Spain would provide him assistance.

Equilinus continues:

> Meanwhile, after Capitolinus died, Vincent was detained by his successor Porphyrius and exposed to wild beasts; but they did him no harm. He was ordered to be killed in a very deep pit of water. Instead, the earth opened and swallowed the water, and swallowed eighteen men who were fleeing from it.
>
> Vincent returned to his cell and, on the following Sunday, after celebrating Mass before the people, gave up his spirit, on 6 June. A matron named Luceria purchased his body from the Gentiles, who had seized it to burn it, and buried it on her estate called the Field of Salvation, between Portulium and Levaniam, forty-four miles from the city, where it lies today, renowned for miracles.

Now observe the agreement with Dexter, so that it cannot be doubted that he suffered and was buried near Carthage. Dexter says:

> He is brought back to Mevia, and was torn apart by C. Porphyrius, the successor of Capitolinus. Now the body of the holy martyr and bishop lies in the town of Deltanum, commonly called Cotana, not far from Elisraea, between Postella and Leviniam, now Lebrella, forty-four miles from Carthage.

Those towns still exist near Carthage: Lebrella, or Lebrilla, lies to the north; Portella, now Portilla, to the south. In place of the Field of Salvation, which Dexter calls Cotona or Totana, there is La Venta Cotana, situated between the two towns.

We discussed Assotum, near Carthage, to which Saint Vincent’s episcopal see is said to have been transferred, under the year 54, on the occasion of Saint Euphrasius, who preached there.

### 22. Mevania, etc.

This island appears to be the one now called Islagruesa, near Carthage. Mevania in Italy, as we have already said, lies near Spoleto in Umbria and is commonly called Bevagna.

There is also an island in the British Sea, inhabited by Spaniards, situated between England and Ireland, which is now called Man but was formerly called Mevania, according to Humphrey Llwyd, printed with Milius and Ortelius. In the latter, however, it is corruptly read *Menavia* instead of *Mevania*.

Near this island lies the island called Mona, which was the seat of the ancient Druids and is now called Anglesey, according to the same authorities. Dexter discusses it, saying:

> Near an island not far distant from Britain, or England, which is the same thing.

### 23. Antima Maximilla, etc.

Her memory is famous from the martyrdom of Saint Andrew, written by the bishops and clergy of Achaia. She herself buried the Apostle’s body, embalmed with the finest spices.

In Equilinus, Book I, chapter 8, where we read:

> He also converted to Christ the wife of Aegeas the proconsul, and Maximilla the senatorial lady, and many of the people,

it should be read without the conjunction:

> He also converted to Christ the wife of Aegeas the proconsul, Maximilla the senatorial lady, etc.,

so that two disciples of Andrew are not fabricated from one.

Her martyrdom is celebrated among the Greeks under the name Antima on 4 May, and also among the Latins, as can be seen in the Roman, Usuard’s, Bede’s, and Ado’s martyrologies, except that some read Antonia instead of Antima, while others read Antonina.

Another error has entered Equilinus, Book II, chapter 123, where he calls her a virgin, although neither the Greeks, nor the Roman Martyrology, nor Bede, nor Usuard, nor the others call her a virgin.

Hear the account of her martyrdom in the Roman Martyrology:

> At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Antonia—I read Antima—the martyr, who, after being tortured excessively and afflicted with various torments, was hung by one arm for three days, detained in prison for two years—others read, “thrust into prison for two years”—and finally burned in the confession of the Lord by the governor Priscillianus.

She is discussed under the name Antonia Maximilla, a most distinguished woman, in the life of Pliny the Younger prefixed to his works. The words are excerpted from Pliny’s own Book X, Letter 5, where he says to Trajan:

> Likewise, I ask that you grant the rights of Roman citizenship to the freedmen of Antonia Maximilla, a most distinguished woman.

And in the following letter:

> I give thanks, Lord, that you have without delay granted the rights of Roman citizenship to the freedmen of a woman necessary to me.

It is very well known that *necessarius* often signifies a relative or kinsman. Thus Maximilla may truly be called by Dexter a blood relative of Pliny.

### 24. Stacteus, etc.

Procorus relates in the Acts of the Apostle John the miraculous return to life of Stacteus, performed by the Apostle at Ephesus. From this Equilinus derives the following passage in Book II, chapter 7:

> The Apostle began to preach much against riches. It happened that a certain young man named Stacteus, who had married thirty days earlier, was carried out dead for burial. Moved by compassion and by the prayers and tears of his widowed mother and of his parents—namely, Stacteus’s parents and those of his wife—the Apostle prayed and raised him from the dead, etc.

All the martyrologies testify that Stacteus’s father was called Getulius. We read, however, the name Zoticus in the records of the Church of Saint Angelo in the Fish Market at Rome, where the body of that man rests with his wife Symphorosa, Stacteus, and their other children, transferred there from Tibur. The inscription reads:

> Here rest the bodies of the holy martyrs Symphorosa, her husband Zoticus, and their sons, etc.

Baronius includes it in his notes under 18 July, which is dedicated to their martyrdom in all the martyrologies.

Africanus wrote their deeds, printed by Mombritius in volume II; Equilinus relates them very briefly in Book VI, chapter 3, where he says that, of the seven brothers, Stacteus died after being pierced through on the ground by many spears; Crescent after being pierced through the throat; Julian in the chest; Nemesius in the heart; Primitivus through the navel; Justin after being torn limb from limb; and Eugenius after being split from the chest down to the lower parts. Their mother Symphorosa was first beaten with slaps, then hung by her hair, and finally thrown into a river.

Zoticus had already died at Rome on the Salarian Way, together with Cerealis and others: he was burned by flames, and, still half alive, beaten on the head with clubs, on 10 June, as can be seen in the martyrologies.

They all received the martyr’s crown under the emperor Hadrian, who assumed the reins of empire in the year of the Lord 119.

---

[Col. 0271] **A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** During this period, as some writers report, Saint Marcellus, a Roman citizen, surnamed Eugenius, most dear to Nero, a disciple of Saint Peter, from Caesar’s household and family, formerly a disciple of Simon Magus and the son of the prefect Marcus Marcellus, flourished at Rome as Saint Peter’s constant companion on his journeys. He was given by Saint Clement, Roman pontiff, as a companion to Saint Dionysius the Areopagite when he was going to Gaul. After long journeys in Italy, Gaul, and Spain, he became Saint Clement’s legate, was made bishop of Arles by Blessed Dionysius, and sent to Spain, where he finally settled at Toledo.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Saint Romulus, prefect of the emperor Trajan, a native of Italica and a Spaniard, was banished by Trajan himself to Spain and suffered martyrdom in Celtiberia.

[Col. 0273] **A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Saint Marcus Marcellus Eugenius, who followed Paul the Presbyter when he came to Spain, now preaches again at Toledo as bishop.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Rufus, returning from Thebes to Spain, presides as bishop at Tortosa.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** At Sirmium in Spain, the holy martyrs Montanus the presbyter and Maxima, most renowned martyrs of Christ.

[Col. 0275] **A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** At Castrum Altum near Tugia, Saint Secundus the bishop, a disciple of Saint James and the last martyr among his companions, preaches.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Marcus Marcellus, an outstanding poet and orator, to whom Persius dedicated his fourth satire, renowned for his friendships with Juvenal, Persius, Seneca, Gallus, and Statius, flourishes through frequent miracles.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** The people of Toledo made great progress through the teaching of Saint Marcus Marcellus, just as the Christians at Barcelona advanced through the glory of miracles and through the virtue of the teaching and example of Bishop Theodosius.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** A very close relationship was formed between the people of Toledo and those of Barcelona. I, Dexter, governed that city for two years, and I confess that I found many things worthy of knowledge in its archives, expressed in his own words.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** At Toledo the memory is celebrated of Marcus Marcellus, prefect of Rome, who in the time of Claudius was quinquennial quaestor in Hither Spain and repaired the walls of Carthage Spartaria.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Dionysius the Areopagite dedicated the books *On the Divine Names* to Eugenius Marcellus, called Timothy because of his exceptional intelligence.

[Col. 0281] **A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Flavia Domitilla Sabina, wife of the consul Flavius Clemens, was killed for the faith.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** The faith of Christ spread miraculously throughout all Spain. The number of the faithful increased, and the sword of persecution was not weakened.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** At the territory of the Olcades in Carpetania of Tarraconensis Spain, but not far from Valencia, Alexander the soldier and Antonina the virgin were transferred—as some maintain—and suffered martyrdom there on 11 April. They had come here from Constantinople and are honored at Constantinople as citizens, although they suffered their illustrious martyrdom elsewhere. Their acts are found in various places, as established by public testimony.

[Col. 0283] **A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** L. Sabinus Probus, converted by Paul in the territory of Laminum in Spain, died as bishop at Ravenna.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Claudia Paphensis Candida became a martyr at Rome.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Lucia the Macedonian suffered under the governor Rucius together with many others.

[Col. 0285] **A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Xantippe and Polyxena praised God in Spain with unwavering faith.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** M. Lupus, Philip, and Lucius, Candida’s husband, obtained the palm of martyrdom.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Quintus Marcella Xantippe was the daughter of Marcus Marcellus, prefect of Rome, and the sister of Marcus Marcellus Eugenius, bishop of Toledo. Saint Paul converted her to the faith at Laminum when he saw golden letters on her forehead, as she was returning from Italy to Spain. When she died, her holy brother Marcellus committed her to burial. Her mother Claudia Xantippe, a Roman citizen and descended from the splendidest Athenian lineage, was of bodily stature taller than ordinary; Martial jokes about her.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Saint Vincent, bishop of Mevia or Mevania near Urci, a city of Spain on the boundary of Baetica and Tarraconensis, went to Italy. Brought back to Spain by the judge Capitolinus, tortured at Carthage Spartaria, and returned to Mevia, he was torn apart by C. Porphyrius, Capitolinus’s successor.

His episcopal see at Mevania [variant: Mevia] was later transferred to Azotus, which subsequently began to be called Erotus under a somewhat corrupted name. The body of the holy martyr and bishop now lies in the town of Deltanum, commonly called Totana, not far from Elisraea, between Postella and Leviniam—now called Lebrella—forty-four miles from Carthage.

[Col. 0287] **A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** There is an island called Mevania near Carthage Spartaria. From it, some people who departed founded in Italy a city called Mevania, near an island not far from Britain.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Antima Maximilla, wife of Aegeas, proconsul of Patrae in Achaia, converted by Blessed Andrew, hid herself in a cave after her husband’s death. She was from Novum Comum and a blood relative of Pliny the Younger. She later married C. Fonteius Capito and, after being taken to Nicomedia, suffered for the faith of Christ on 4 May.

**A.D. 100. A.R. 851.** Stacteus, the son of Zoticus or of a pagan—who was staying at Ephesus on business—died and was restored to life by John. Zoticus and Symphorosa, with their children, were converted to the faith. After returning to Italy, they suffered martyrdom.

[Col. 0289]

## A.D. 101. A.R. 852. Domitian, etc.

Dexter, in his customary manner, recapitulates the emperors who succeeded one another in the Roman Empire from Domitian through Trajan. In the year of the Lord 86 he had said that Titus succeeded Vespasian and Domitian succeeded Titus; now he takes up the thread of the narrative again from Domitian himself and brings it to an end with Trajan.

Domitian reigned for fifteen years and was killed in the year of the Lord 98. Nerva Cocceius succeeded him. Nerva held power for a short time—one year, four months, and nine days—and died at the beginning of his tenth year, on the Kalends of February.

Martial celebrated his accession in Spain in Book XII, Epigram 6, whose beginning is:

> Nerva, gentlest of the rulers in the Ausonian palace,  
> etc.

He had also extolled Nerva’s eloquence and excellence in poetry appropriately in Books VIII and IX.

For the rest, Nerva, intending to benefit the Roman Empire—Dio says—without considering those related to him by blood, adopted as his son and named Caesar Marcus Ulpius Trajan, a Spaniard who was then serving with the army in Germany, believing him to be an upright man worthy to guide the reins of empire.

What wonder if Martial, himself also a Spaniard, desired the empire for a Spaniard? In Book X, Epigram 34, he says:

> May the gods grant you, prince Trajan, whatever you deserve,  
> and may what they wish to bestow be ratified forever, etc.

He so highly praises Trajan’s fairness and justice that in Book XI, Epigram 6, he claims that if the ancient Roman senators returned from the Elysian grove, they would approve Trajan’s election in accordance with their wishes. In him Camillus would have found a defender of liberty, Fabricius an incorruptible judge, and Brutus a vigorous commander; even Sulla, though most bloodthirsty, would yield to him, and Crassus would give away his wealth:

> If Cato himself, recalled from the underworld shadows of Dis,  
> were restored, he would become a Caesarean.

Finally, persisting in his own error, Trajan performed an act of grateful recognition in this year, 101, by enrolling Nerva among the gods.

**A.D. 101. A.R. 852.** Domitian succeeded Titus, Nerva Cocceius succeeded Domitian, and Trajan succeeded Nerva. By decree of the senate, with his son Trajan taking charge of the matter, Nerva was enrolled among the gods.

[Col. 0289]

## A.D. 104. A.R. 855. Trajan concerning the Dacians, etc.

He transcribed the words together with their meaning from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius.

**A.D. 104. A.R. 855.** In this year Trajan celebrated a triumph over the Dacians and Scythians.

[Col. 0289]

## A.D. 105. 1. In the following year, etc.

This too was taken from Eusebius, who nevertheless relates many other deeds of Trajan, saying:

> Trajan, after defeating King Decebalus, made Dacia a province; he received the Iberians, Sarmatians, Osroenians, Arabs, Bosporans, and Colchians into allegiance; he occupied Seleucia, Ctesiphon, and Babylon; and he maintained a fleet in the Red Sea and arranged for the cities of India to be devastated by it.

Thus one may see how much Rome owed to Trajan and how far he extended his empire.

Martial sings of this achievement in Book XII, Epigram 8, when he says:

> Rome, goddess of lands and nations,  
> equal to none and second to none,  
> now rejoicing that it would count  
> so many ages under Trajan,  
> and seeing in so great a leader  
> a brave, youthful, and warlike soldier,  
> said: “With such a ruler as my champion,  
> I can show the Parthian nobles,  
> the leaders of the Seres,  
> the Thracians, Sarmatians, Getae, and Britons  
> a Caesar. Come!”

Some call the Dacian king Decebalus, as do Xiphilinus and Eusebius; others call him Diurpaneus, as Orosius does in Book VII, chapter 10.

## 2. Saint John, etc.

Among the canonical books there is one under this title: “The elder, to the chosen Lady and her children.” Although formerly it was disputed whether these letters belonged to John the Apostle or to another John called “the Elder,” and although Jerome, in his *On Illustrious Men*, said of the Apostle John, “The letters are asserted to be by John the presbyter, whose second tomb is still shown today at Ephesus,” he also says concerning Papias:

“It appears from the catalogue of names itself [a certain testimony of Papias] that there was another John, who is numbered among the Apostles, and another John the Elder.”

We have mentioned this because of the opinion cited above, which we reported as having been handed down by many: namely, that the two later letters of John belonged not to the Apostle but to the presbyter.

Dexter, however, following the better opinion, wrote long ago concerning the author of John’s second letter [Col. 0290B] what the Council of Trent later decreed in its fourth session, in the decree concerning the canonical Scriptures. The Apostle calls this woman “the Chosen One” because of the excellence of her faith and because, as Dexter maintains, she flourished at that time in extraordinary generosity and charity, like a mother of the Ephesian Church. Her proper name was Drusia, or Drusiana, as we learn from Prochorus’s *Life of John*. He also relates that, when the Apostle entered the city on his return from exile, Drusiana, his disciple, who had been consumed with longing for his arrival, was carried out dead. Her parents, as well as the poor, orphans, and widows whom she had assisted in their need, were weeping and lamenting bitterly.

The Apostle therefore ordered the bier to be set down and the body to be released from its bindings. Calling her by her own name, he commanded her to rise and, returning home, prepare him something to eat. She immediately rose, as though called not from death but from sleep, and carried out his command. Many were converted through this miracle. Bishop Equilinus transcribed these details from the writings of Saint Prochorus in Book II of his *Catalogue*, chapter 7. [Col. 0290C]

## 3. Undumeni, etc.

Bishop Equilinus, Book II, final chapter, number 313, agrees with Dexter, except that where Dexter has *Undumeni* he reads *Unduni*. He says: “Victor, bishop and confessor, rested at Unduni on the fifth day before the Ides of November,” that is, on the ninth day of that month.

There was indeed another Victor, bishop of Le Mans, whom the Roman Martyrology commemorates on 1 September; but he is very different from our Victor. As you see, our Victor flourished in the year of the Lord 105 and rested at Unduni, or Undumeni, near Valencia in Spain. The other was a contemporary of Saint Martin of Tours, in the time of Theodosius, as is clear from Bede’s Martyrology and other sources.

It is uncertain whether he was Bishop Victor of Valencia or bishop of another city, although Dexter asserts that some people maintain this. For my part, I would suppose that Unda, near Valencia, was the town situated by the sea and the river, commonly called Grao, or somewhere near it.

## 4. Saint Quartus, etc.

Whatever may pertain to this matter has been stated by us under the year of the Lord 50, when, together with Dexter, we discussed Saint Peter’s arrival in Spain. Consult what was said there.

[Col. 0291A]

## 5. Nathanael, etc.

Blessed is the man who deserved to have John as the chronicler of his virtues—John who praises him in the first and final chapters of his Gospel—and to have Jesus himself as his praiser, for Jesus said of him to the Apostles: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.”

If this could be said of him before Christ’s special instruction, what could be said after his discipline had been completed?

The ancient authors have held various opinions about Nathanael. Some thought that he was the holy Ursinus who was sent by the Apostles as bishop to the city of Bourges. Vincent of Beauvais in his *Historical Mirror* and Equilinus in Book I, chapter 9, report this as the opinion of certain others.

Others thought that he was Simon the Cananaean; the Greeks affirm this in their *Menologion* on the sixth day before the Ides of May. Rupert, however, identified him with Saint Bartholomew, and Cornelius Jansenius followed him in his *Harmony of the Gospels*. Yet neither identification is sufficiently probable, since Nathanael is shown to have been distinct from the others on the basis of many considerations, and especially from the place of his burial.

Ursinus, a confessor, was buried at Bourges. The Apostle Simeon preached in Egypt and suffered martyrdom in Persia. Bartholomew preached and suffered in India. All this is established by the Roman Martyrology and those of Bede, Ado, and Usuard.

Nathanael, however, was buried in the city of Treuga, or Treuga in Spain. There is no doubt that he labored zealously in preaching throughout the provinces of Spain.

Hear how Equilinus, borrowing the statement from Vincent, published this account:

“Nathanael, a disciple from the town of Cana in Galilee, was one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ, etc. The body of this Nathanael rests near the city of Treuga, etc. After completing the ministry of preaching, he happily rested in God on the day before the Kalends of December.”

Treuga is believed to be the place which Ptolemy’s text corruptly calls *Turiga*. Ptolemy places it beside the Seventh Twin Legion—that is, present-day León—if the geographical coordinates are correctly evaluated, as Michael Villanovanus did in the tables of ancient Spain which he added to Ptolemy.

Dexter adds that others contend that Nathanael lies in Galicia, near Trigundum—an obscure territory or small town in his own day—near Brigantium. They are guided by nothing more substantial than a certain similarity between the names Treuga and Trigundum. Dexter therefore adheres to the former opinion.

Baronius, in Volume I of his *Annals*, and Maldonado, in his commentary on the first chapter of John, learnedly reject Rupert’s opinion. Rupert relied only on conjectures: namely, that among the Evangelists John, who mentions Nathanael, says nothing about Bartholomew, while Matthew, Mark, and Luke, who introduce Bartholomew, say nothing about Nathanael. He also argued that both are presented as companions of Philip.

Augustine and Gregory, however, oppose this view; Baronius cites them, as does the common judgment of the Church. The Greeks seem to have only this in their favor: that Simon is called “the Cananaean,” as Nathanael likewise is said to have been. But who does not see that two disciples of Christ could often have come from the same town? Enough on this subject.

## 6. After some years, etc.

Dexter had already mentioned this under the year 91, saying:

“Aulus Cornelius Palma, a citizen of Toledo and a Christian duumvir, and M. Marcellus came to Toledo and there established the principal see of all Spain, since it was situated at its center.”

Now, in its proper place, he discusses the elevation of the same Church of Toledo to primacy. He explains what counsel Saint Eugenius used in establishing it and how early he first undertook the matter, so that for this reason he convened a council of bishops and distinguished men of the faith.

He names six persons in all: two bishops, two martyrs, and two princes. We have already discussed Epitectus, bishop of Zaragoza, several times above, and likewise Philip Philotheus, bishop and legate of Saint Clement.

Saint Vitalis was the first archpresbyter of the Church of Toledo. We shall speak shortly, under the year 110, of his martyrdom with Felicula and Zeno.

Saint Avitus went to the Fortunate Islands—the Canaries—to preach the Gospel and was crowned with martyrdom for Christ. Primus, the first bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, said the same in his *Topography of the Holy Martyrs of Christ*, in these words:

“The island of Canaria in the Atlantic Ocean: here the faith of Christ was extended; here was the martyr Avitus.”

Perhaps this was the Avitus whom Martial often addresses: in Book I, epigram 16; at the beginning of Book IX; and in Book X, epigram 96.

We have said something about the earlier duumvir, Aulus Cornelius Palma. P. Turacus, or Turanus, is, in my opinion, the man to whom Martial wrote Epigram 78 of Book V, whose beginning is:

“Si tristi domicenio laboras  
Turani, potes esurire mecum, etc.”

“If you are troubled by a gloomy dinner,  
Turanus, you can go hungry with me, etc.”

See how much respect and affection Martial shows him. After several lines he adds:

“Parva est caenula, quis potest negare?  
Sed finges nihil, audiesve fictum,  
Et vultu placidus tuo recumbes, etc.”

“The dinner is modest—who can deny it?  
But you will invent nothing, nor hear anything invented,  
And you will recline with a serene expression, etc.”

Thus Saint Eugenius, having summoned such men to himself, established Toledo as the primatial see—not indeed as the particular bishop of that Church, but as the legate of Pope Saint Clement, together with his other legate Philotheus, and with the presence and assent of Saint Epitectus, bishop of Zaragoza. Because of the merits of his city, Epitectus could claim for himself the primacy of Spain, especially since Saint James the Apostle had endowed his Church with a special prerogative, as one that had deserved well of the Most Holy Mother of God.

Let us now examine what rules the Apostles formerly gave concerning the assignment of primacies, so that from them we may judge the council of Saint Eugenius.

Saint Peter had formerly taught that the primates of Churches should be established in that city from which all the cities of the same province had been accustomed to receive their laws.

Pope Saint Anacletus, discussing this matter in his second letter to the bishops of Italy—cited by Gratian, Distinction 99, chapter “Provinces”—says:

“Provinces were divided long before Christ’s coming, for the most part; and afterward the same division was renewed by the Apostles and by the blessed Clement, our predecessor.”

He continues:

“Where formerly the primates of the world and the first judicial authority had existed, to them those who lived throughout the other cities used to flee when necessity required it—those who could not, or were not permitted to, take refuge in the court of the emperor or of kings—because of their oppressions or injustices; and whenever necessary they appealed to them, just as their law prescribed.

“In those same cities or places they ordered our patriarchs or primates—the two offices have one form, although their names differ—to be established by divine and ecclesiastical laws. To them bishops were to flee when necessary and appeal to them; they alone were to enjoy the title of primate.

“The remaining metropolitan cities, which had lesser judges, although they were greater than the counts, were to have their own metropolitans, who were to obey the primates named above justly, just as had been arranged in secular law. They were to be known not as primates but as metropolitans or archbishops.”

He then adds, in his third letter, that bishops were to be established in other cities where counts had formerly been accustomed to reside, and presbyters in small cities, towns, and villages.

Lucius taught the same thing in his second letter to Stephen I, chapter 5; it is cited in Distinction 80, chapter “Cities,” as follows:

“Cities and places over which primates are to preside were established not by modern rulers but many ages before Christ’s coming. Even the pagans appealed to their primates in the more important affairs. After Christ’s coming, however, the Apostles and their successors placed patriarchs or primates in those cities.”

From this there arose a question concerning the city to be chosen for the primate. All Spain had not previously obeyed one and the same city; rather, according to the different divisions it had undergone at different times, the pagans appealed to different primates.

At one period, when Spain was divided into Citerior and Ulterior Spain, with reference to the Ebro, the Romans appointed two proconsuls, propraetors, legates, quaestors, or governors: one for Citerior Spain and the other for Ulterior Spain.

Licinius Larcius under Vespasian, L. Albinus under Domitian, Celer under the same emperor, and Q. Rufinus Galerius under Hadrian governed only Citerior Spain, while other men were appointed to administer Ulterior Spain.

According to the division by which Spain was divided into three provinces—Tarraconensis, Baetica, and Lusitania—three governors were likewise sent to them. Claudius Umbonius Silo was sent to Baetica; likewise Aulus Caecina under Nero, Caecilius Classicus under Domitian, and Baebius Massa under Trajan. Shortly afterward Herennius Senecio, himself a native of Baetica, governed it.

Validius governed Lusitania, and Valerius Julianus Tarraconensis, to omit the others.

Not all the provinces of Spain, therefore, obeyed one and the same city within Spain, where, according to the law of Blessed Peter, the primacy of Spain could be placed.

This was especially so because Spain did not possess one single city that was the noblest of all. In every part of Spain there were cities that contended with the others in distinction and nobility. As Pomponius Mela, a writer of this period and country, says in Book III, chapter 6:

“Among the inland cities, the most famous in Tarraconensis were Palantia and Numantia, and now— that is, in his own age—Caesaraugusta; in Lusitania, Emerita; in Baetica, Astigi, Hispalis, and Corduba.”

Either several primates therefore had to be established, corresponding to the number of provinces, or, if there was to be one, it did not seem possible to preserve Saint Peter’s general rule.

The fathers of that council, or synod, assembled to choose the primate of the Church of Spain, could nevertheless have adopted another line of reasoning, based on what Saint Clement wrote to the Apostle James in his first letter:

“In those cities where formerly among the Gentiles their chief flamines and their chief teachers of the law existed,” he says, “Blessed Peter commanded that primates of bishops or patriarchs be established.

“But in those cities where the archflamines of the aforementioned people formerly existed—although they held lesser authority than the primates mentioned—he commanded that archbishops be established.”

It was therefore necessary to consider the chief center of the destruction of pagan religion and there establish the primate of the Catholic Church of Spain. Since, under pagan worship, the other cities had not been dependent upon any single city, but among those living according to the prescription of Mosaic law, the other cities depended upon Toledo, because there was located the most celebrated synagogue in the entire West—of which we said much above under the years of the Lord 34 and 37—it could have happened that Saint Eugenius, moved by this consideration, established the principal see at Toledo, so that from the place from which the old law had gone forth, the word of God and the grace of the Gospel might also go forth, in accordance with Saint Clement’s statement:

“Where the chief teachers of the law existed, Blessed Peter commanded that primates of bishops or patriarchs be established.” [Col. 0294A]

Finally, the principal consideration was that Toledo lies at the navel of Spain, situated at its center, as Dexter says in one place. Everyone was therefore obliged to look toward the primate as toward a center, so that all might await judgment from him without great expense or inconvenience.

Whatever may be said of the motives, the fact itself cannot be doubted, since the see of Toledo, on account of its greatness and primacy, has repeatedly gained victory over the Churches of Tarragona and Braga, not only in the writings of authors but also in contentious judicial proceedings.

It is especially important that Dexter of Barcelona, a writer who treated this matter with such care, nowhere mentions a primacy of Tarragona. Yet no one could doubt that, if the Apostles or their disciples had formerly decreed otherwise concerning the primacy, they would never have taken away from Tarragona what they gave to Toledo.

Moreover, when Constantine the Great again divided the metropolitan sees in Spain, he acknowledged Toledo as the principal one by naming it first among the others and subjecting nineteen bishops immediately to its jurisdiction. Anyone may see this in Lucas of Tuy and in Archbishop Loaysa, who explains at length and clearly many matters concerning the primacy of Toledo in his notes on Gundemar’s decree.

We may therefore answer the others with the words of Pope Anicetus in his letter to the bishops of Gaul:

“Let no archbishops be called primates except those who hold the principal cities whose bishops the Apostles and the successors of the Apostles regularly established as primates and patriarchs.”

Those who treated the primate with such precision doubtless also dealt with the other metropolitan sees. Since Saint James, the first of all in Spain, had established not a few bishoprics—including Toledo, Braga, and Tarragona, where he appointed the bishops Elpidius, Peter, and Agathodorus—when the affairs of the faith had been propagated much more abundantly, Eugenius and Philotheus arranged the Churches in a more convenient order. Dexter taught this concerning Eugenius under the year of the Lord 91 or 93.

A.D. 105. A.U.C. 856. In the following year, after defeating Decebalus, he makes Dacia a province.

A.D. 105. A.U.C. 856. Saint John wrote his second letter to Drusia, the chosen woman, who at that time flourished like a mother of that Church through extraordinary generosity and charity.

A.D. 105. A.U.C. 856. At Undumeni—which is now called Unda, a town near Valencia—Saint Victor, believed to have been bishop of Valencia.

A.D. 105. A.U.C. 856. Saint Quartus, a disciple of the Apostles, traversed Spain twice: once after James and again after being left behind by Paul. At Berela—which is now called Baetyrus, by others Baetica or Gonciolum in Spain—he is now famous for many miracles.

[Col. 0291]

A.D. 105. A.U.C. 856. Nathanael, one of the Lord’s seventy disciples, rests in the city of Treuga, near the Seventh Twin Legion. Others say that he lies near the town of Trigundum, close to Brigantium in Galicia, now an obscure territory.

A.D. 105. A.U.C. 856. Several years after his arrival in Spain, Saint Eugenius, together with M. Marcellus, discusses the primacy of Spain with holy and distinguished men: Epitectus of Zaragoza; Philotheus, his companion on his journey and also a legate of Saint Clement; Vitalis and Avitus, the latter of whom later went to the Fortunate Islands and became a martyr; Aulus Cornelius Palma and P. Turanus, Catholic men and duumvirs of Toledo; and many bishops assembled from Carpetania and elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0294C]]

## A.D. 110—1. Not long afterward, etc.

In the printed copy, *at* stood in place of *haud*, but this is exceedingly corrupt.

It may perhaps seem novel that Dexter brings Dionysius into Spain. Yet anyone who remembers that he was appointed legate by Saint Clement not merely for Gaul—although he labored more extensively there and died there—but for the entire West, will lay aside his astonishment. It was therefore incumbent upon him also to visit, at least at some time, the principal province among all the provinces of the West, especially at the period when Saint Eugenius, his dearest son and in a certain sense his disciple, was establishing the metropolitan Churches and the primacy and was seriously treating their affairs.

We have, moreover, very weighty testimony for this truth from Saint Methodius, who says in his *Life*:

“Saint Dionysius, inflamed by the warmth of the Holy Spirit and filled with apostolic authority, faithfully distributed throughout all the regions of Hesperia whatever divine oracles he had received from the Holy Spirit together with Saint Clement to be disseminated among the nations.”

Who does not know that the Greeks called Spain Hesperia, and that Latin writers also used this name more than once? Martial, for example, speaking of Corduba in Book IX, Epigram 61, whose beginning is “In Tartessian lands,” says:

“And the living gold leaf clothes the Hesperian sheep.”

I add the sacred hymn of the Gothic Breviary of Toledo, which asserts the arrival of the same Saint Dionysius the Areopagite in Spain. It begins: “Worthy memory of Saint Eugenius.” Later it says:

“The fosterling of Greece visits Spain;

The teacher of Spain revisits Gaul,

Seeking with faithful heart

The presence of the learned teacher of Gaul.”

The meaning is this: Dionysius the Areopagite, fosterling of Greece, visits Spain; Eugenius, teacher of Spain, in turn revisits Gaul in order to meet Dionysius, teacher of Gaul. We shall discuss this later.

The hymn therefore calls Dionysius a fosterling of Greece. The same title appears in another hymn of a Toledo Breviary according to the Roman rite, where it says that Dionysius sent Eugenius into Spain:

“The learned fosterling of Greece,

Dionysius sent him,

So that he might be a ray of the sun

In the western darkness.”

In the printed copy published at Zaragoza, this clause is added:

“Thirty Catholic writers wrote against the blasphemies of the philosopher Porphyry.”

But this ought to be placed not under the year 110, but under 310, as it appears in my copy. I shall discuss it in its proper place.

## 2. Saint Peter, etc.

You will find many things said by us about him above, under the years of the Lord 37 and 66; consult those passages.

We also said some things about Basileus there. Concerning Ovidius, see the year 95; we shall speak of him again under the year 138, when Dexter begins his account of Saint Marina and her sisters.

## 3. Saint Firminus, etc.

All those who have written his deeds, especially Equilinus, Book VIII, chapter 119; Morales, Book IX, chapter 15; Trugillus; Sanctorus; and Villegas under 25 September; Mariana, Book IV of his *History of Spain*, chapter 3; Marieta, *On the Saints of Spain*, Part I, Book I, chapter 16; and others, report that he was a citizen of Pamplona.

The Church of Pamplona itself professes the same in the ecclesiastical offices of this saint. It reads that he was born to the senator Firmus, was converted to the faith by Blessed Saturninus, a disciple of Saint Peter, while still a young man, was instructed in the sacred Scriptures by the presbyter Saint Honestus, and was ordained bishop by Saint Honoratus. At last he was slaughtered for Christ at Amiens.

The *Acts of Saint Saturninus* agree with this in every respect. We said above, under the year 76, that these Acts survive at Horta in the manuscript of Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo. Among other things, they say that Fortunatus and Faustinus, noble men of Pamplona, were converted to the faith together with Firmus, senator of that city and father of Saint Firminus, through the work of Saint Saturninus, the disciple of Blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles.

The account continues:

“Firmus, therefore, when he had become wholly subject to Christ’s dominion and was held in the highest esteem in the district of Pamplona, handed over his firstborn son to the aforementioned presbyter Honestus, the client of Saturninus. He was taught by him every literary discipline and every commerce of faith. Much later he was ordained bishop by Honoratus, the bishop of Toledo and successor of Saturninus.

“After thirty years had passed, Firminus went to the city of Agen and there, together with a certain presbyter Astasius, won a great people for Christ. Later he converted to the Lord a very large people of his fosterlings—that is, the people of Pamplona, whom he had spiritually nurtured.

“Crossing the river Vigenna, he afterward went to the city of Angers and there made a great multitude of pagans serve God. Finally, going toward the Germanic region, he entered the city of Beauvais; remaining there, he was chosen bishop by the believers and recalled many from the worship of idols.

“Then he went to the town of Amiens and joined thirty thousand souls to God. Finally, he was beheaded in the prison-house.”

Thus far the *Acts*.

The authors differ greatly when they identify the judge and executioner of Saint Firminus. Usuard says that he suffered under Ricciovarus; consequently the Roman Martyrology added that it occurred during the persecution of Diocletian. It says:

“At Amiens in Gaul, the blessed Firminus, bishop, who during the persecution of Diocletian, under the governor Ricciovarus, after various tortures obtained martyrdom by beheading.”

Everyone who knows that he was a disciple of Saint Saturninus knows how far this is from the truth.

Equilinus maintains that at first, at Beauvais, he was repeatedly beaten almost to death for confessing Christ by the governor Valesius; that he was then held in a foul prison by Sergius, Valesius’s successor; and that, after being released through the fury of the people, he was beheaded at Amiens by the governors Longinus and Sebastian, who, fearing the people, did not execute him publicly but in prison.

Trugillus, in his *Treasure of Sermons*, recognizes only Longinus and Sebastian as the governors under whom he suffered martyrdom. Dexter, however, now says that he suffered under the governor Julian.

What, then, should be thought amid such darkness?

Dexter should certainly be followed. There is no question concerning Valerius and Sergius, through whose agency he began to suffer but did not complete his martyrdom. As for Longinus and Sebastian, we think that they were not the principal governors of the province but executioners, and that the governor was Julian.

Dexter’s opinion is supported by the fact that we find many other martyrs of that period in Gaul suffering martyrdom under Julian. Thus the Roman Martyrology itself says this of Saint Jonah, a disciple of Saint Dionysius, on 22 September; and Equilinus writes the same of Saint Lucian and his companions, associates of Dionysius, in Book II, chapter 55.

This consideration strongly supports our position, since Lucian suffered martyrdom at Beauvais, where Saint Firminus began to suffer and was repeatedly scourged almost to death.

It was also the custom of this Julian to send lictors here and there to drag away the martyrs, as Equilinus writes in the cited Book II, chapter 55, and Book VIII, chapter 106. From this anyone may easily believe that Longinus and Sebastian were his lictors.

As for Ricciovarus, perhaps the governor was called Riccius Julianus. We discussed the governor Riccius of this period when treating of Lydia of Macedonia. Later, however, the mistaken belief arose that Riccius and Ricciovarus were one and the same person.

In any event, Saint Firminus was a citizen and bishop of Pamplona, and he preached as far as Toledo, as Dexter declares here.

The first bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône agrees with him in his *Topography*, under the word “Pompelona,” saying:

“Pompelon, a city of Spain, the metropolis of Navarre. Firminus was born here. Ordained presbyter by Saint Honoratus, bishop of Toledo, he preached at Amiens in Gaul, and there departed this life as bishop and martyr.”

From this we must necessarily conclude that Dexter is not saying under the year 110 that Firminus suffered martyrdom at that time, but that he was still flourishing in virtue and preaching while young. Otherwise Saint Honoratus would not have been bishop of Toledo until after the martyrdom of Saint Eugenius.

[Col. 0297A]

## 4. At Hispalis he flourishes, etc.

In former times there were two men named Florentius at Hispalis, conspicuous for outstanding holiness, but carried away at different times and by different kinds of death.

The older was the son of Rusticus Bolanus, a Spanish man of consular rank. According to Cassiodorus and Onuphrius, Rusticus held the Roman consulship with Calpurnius Piso in the year of the Lord 113, and again in the year 118 with Trajan.

His son Florentius, whose full name was M. Bolanus Florentius, was converted to the faith by the Apostles at Castro Tile, or Sila or Asila, in the Turdetanian region of Baetica near Hispalis. Ptolemy and Villanova place Asila there in their map of ancient Spain. At last Florentius offered his throat for Christ on 27 October, as the Roman Martyrology, Bede, Usuard, Ado, and Galesinus attest, as does Equilinus in Book XI, final chapter, number 304. Dexter places his death in the year of the Lord 116.

The other Saint Florentius, a confessor, rested in peace in the year 485. His ancient epitaph reads:

“The holy Florentius of God rested in peace on 23 February. He lived fifty-three years and was buried on 15 March in the year of the Lord 485.”

Trugillus and Villegas give this account on that day, which is also recorded in the Roman Martyrology on 23 February:

“At Hispalis in Spain, the blessed Florentius, confessor.”

Trugillus adds that local tradition held him to have been a Spaniard born of a distinguished and noble family.

Since this account was received from the tradition of the Church of Hispalis, and since that Church does not celebrate in February the feast of a confessor but celebrates in October the feast of a martyr, the reference should not be understood of Saint Florentius the confessor. It should be understood of Saint M. Bolanus Florentius, the martyr of Christ, whose noble lineage is known.

M. Maximus gives a distinguished commendation of both men in his *Chronicle* under the year 612, saying:

“The memory of both Florentii of Hispalis flourishes throughout Spain: the first, who was called Rusticus because of his father’s name, to whom Pliny the Younger wrote, the martyr who suffered under Trajan; the second, the confessor, under Zeno, bishop of Hispalis.”

Maximus treats Zeno himself under the year 483 and asserts that Pope Felix appointed him legate *a latere* in Spain.

We shall speak again of Saint Florentius the martyr below, with Dexter, under the aforementioned year 116.

## 5. Flavius Rutilius, etc.

This year concerns his flight to Spain; in the year 116, his martyrdom.

Tertullian mentions him in Book *On Flight in Persecution*, chapter 5:

“Rutilius,” he says, “a most holy martyr, after having fled persecution so many times from place to place, and having even, as he thought, purchased safety with money, after all the security he had arranged for himself, was unexpectedly seized and brought before the governor. Torn by torments—I suppose as punishment for his flight—and then handed over to the flames, he attributed to God’s mercy the passion he had sought to avoid.”

The Roman Martyrology adopted almost these words on 2 August, except for Tertullian’s error in the phrase “torn apart, I suppose as punishment for his flight.” In this he acted as a Montanist and falsely attempted to assert that the faithful were not permitted to flee during persecution, even though Christ the Lord expressly said: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another.”

[Col. 0297D]

## 6. Saint Vitalis, etc.

The most illustrious Lord Sancho of Ávila—first bishop of Jaén, then of Sigüenza, and finally of Plasencia—has forestalled us in this labor and taken its crown. Distinguished no less by learning and writings than by the nobility of his blood, while he was bishop at Jaén he published a special book on the life and martyrdom of Saint Vitalis, the first archpresbyter of Toledo under Saint Eugenius I, bishop of Toledo. I ask you, candid reader, also to read it in full.

There he confirms his account with the testimony of Dexter as it stands here.

The Roman Martyrology, Usuard, Ado, Bede, Galesinus, and Wandalbert commemorate Saint Vitalis the presbyter, together with his companions Zeno and Felicula, on 14 February. Equilinus also treats them in Book XI, final chapter, number 64.

After remaining for some time at Toledo, Vitalis departed from Chersonesus—that is, the peninsula, or Peñíscola, of Valencia—and journeyed with his companions to Rome, where they received the palms of martyrdom.

## 7. Marcellus, etc.

There exists a Book IV of Papinius Statius’s *Silvae* dedicated to Marcellus.

Petrus Crinitus thought that this was Marcellus Victorinus, to whom Fabius Quintilian sent his books on the *Institutes of Oratory*. But if the periods in which the two men flourished are weighed carefully, we must acknowledge that Marcellus Victorinus, to whom Quintilian gave his books around the year of the Lord 90, was the father of this Marcellus, to whom Statius dedicated a *Silva* in the year 110. Statius sings much of this man’s youth, flourishing in letters and physical strength.

The poem begins:

“Run swiftly through the Euboean fields, my letter,  
And enter the roads along which noble Appia extends…”

He orders the letter to go to Rome, for:

“There you will see Marcellus, outstanding in form and character,  
And recognize him by his lofty head.”

He praises his eloquence:

“Certainly now the Latin laws no longer mingle their disputes,  
The sluggish year enjoys peace, and the returning harvests  
Have dismissed the forum. No longer does a crowd of defendants  
Fill your vestibule, nor do complaining clients ask you to go out.  
Your eloquence, already most renowned, rises high in fame  
And surpasses the years of young men.”

He praises his intellect:

“Happy in his concerns, for whom neither Heliconian garlands  
Nor the unwarlike laurels from the summit of Parnassus are dear,  
But whose intellect flourishes, girded for great undertakings.”

And shortly afterward:

“But if Atropos grants you the course of a long life,  
Perhaps you will go forth to rein in the Ausonian cohorts,  
Or the peoples of the Rhine and the shores of dark Thule.”

Hear what he says about his strength:

“For your strength lies not only in powerful eloquence;  
Your limbs are suited to war,  
And your muscles can bear the weight of a heavy cuirass.”

But what of his ancestry?

“Rise, then, and as a boy catch up with your youthful father,  
Blessed in your mother’s lineage and in your father’s virtue.  
Now fortunate glory, gentle in her Tyrian lap,  
Nurtures you and rejoices in promising you all the curule offices, etc.”

From this you may see how dear he was to Hadrian, then Caesar-designate and not long afterward emperor: a Hispano-Roman man to a Hispano-Roman prince, learned and noble, if there was any such man in Rome.

[Col. 0298D]

## 8. Saint Arcadius, etc.

Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, celebrated his outstanding contest in a noble encomium. Lipomanus includes his sermon in Volume II, and Surius in Volume I.

The Roman Martyrology, Bede, and Usuard commemorate him on 12 January in these words:

“On the same day, Saint Arcadius, illustrious by birth and miracles.”

Petrus Equilinus briefly recounts all his deeds in Book II, chapter 67, saying:

“Arcadius the martyr, as Bishop Zeno of Verona writes, was crowned with a glorious passion. His martyrdom was so remarkable that in one body there were as many punishments as there are visible limbs.

“When, because of the fury of the persecution—without doubt Trajan’s—he had fled from the city and was hiding, he was captured by pagans and brought before the judge. While he confessed Christ, the pagans devised a new form of punishment: his hands and legs were cut off at the joints, and he was left alive. Thus, covered in his own blood, after enduring prolonged torment, he gave up his spirit on the day before the Ides of January.”

We owe Dexter our knowledge of the place consecrated by the blood of this great martyr.

Ursaona, also called Ursao by some and Ursuna by others, was a noble Turdetanian city in Baetica, today Osuna; Ptolemy calls it Urbona. Morales, in Book VIII, chapter 43, asserts that the Romans called it Gemina Urbanorum. He also discusses it in Book IX, chapter 32, and Book VII, chapter 48; Ludovicus Nonnius treats it in chapter 15 of his *Spain*, as do others.

Saint Leo and his companions were also crowned with martyrdom there in the year 115, as we shall say below when treating the matter with Dexter.

A.D. 110. A.U.C. 861. Not long afterward Saint Dionysius the Areopagite visited Spain, having been appointed legate of the whole West by Blessed Clement.

[Col. 0295]

A.D. 110. A.U.C. 861. Saint Peter, bishop of Braga and martyr, at the town of Rato in the territory of Braga, not far from Bracara Augusta—he had undergone a glorious martyrdom for the faith of Christ in the year of the Lord 45—is held in still greater renown because of his numerous and celebrated miracles. Basileus succeeded him, and afterward Ovidius, a Roman citizen.

A.D. 110. A.U.C. 861. Saint Firminus, citizen and bishop of Pamplona, disciple of Saint Saturninus, who likewise had been a hearer of Saint Peter, suffers at Amiens under the governor Julian. Before this, however, he preached throughout Spain as far as Toledo and spread through the province far and wide.

[Col. 0297]

A.D. 110. A.U.C. 861. At Hispalis the holy M. Bolanus Florentius, a citizen of Hispalis, flourishes.

A.D. 110. A.U.C. 861. Flavius Rutilius, fleeing, came to Corduba in Spain, but at last suffered martyrdom in Africa.

A.D. 110. A.R. 861. Saint Vitalis, the first archpriest of the Toletans [among those whom we know to have come], who had come to Toledo with Zeno and Felicula and, returning from the Chersonese to Rome, undertook a wondrous contest—the account of which is written to the Churches of the whole West.

A.D. 110. A.R. 861. Marcellus, son of the brother of Saint Marcellus, a pious man, is dear—as was also his uncle—to the emperor Hadrian; to him Papinius Statius once dedicated *Silvae*, as to a most learned man.

A.D. 110. A.R. 861. Saint Arcadius suffered at Ursaona in Baetica on 12 January.

[Col. 0299] [Note: [Col. 0299B]]

### A.D. 112

1. **Saint Marcellus, etc.** This is fourth in order among the Hispanic councils of which even a slight memory survives. The first was that famous council of Iliberis, concerning which Dexter says under the year 57:

“Some of the disciples of Saint James, while they were assembling for the council of Iliberis, were crowned after being burned in the flames under Alotus, Nero’s judge.”

The second was the Chersonesian, or Peninsular, council, concerning which the same author says under the year 60:

“When the holy bishops, disciples of Saint James, had assembled in the Chersonesian city near Valencia in Spain for the purpose of a council, Basileus of Carthage, Eugenius of Valencia, and others were put to death under the same judge.”

The third was held by Saint Eugenius at Toledo, for dividing the metropolitan Churches and designating the primacy. The fourth was also held at Toledo, where, after the bishops of Carpetania and others had been assembled, matters of faith and Christian morals were discussed under the presidency of Eugenius, in this year 112. I have no doubt that other councils were celebrated by the holy apostles and their disciples while they remained in Spain for the sake of preaching, but no memory of them survives.

2. **Jonas, etc.** Consult what we said about him under the year 86. We shall speak of him again with Dexter under the year 130.

3. **At Asta, etc.** Ptolemy mentions the city of Asta in Baetica, not far from Nebrissa among the Turdetanian peoples. It was certainly esteemed by the Romans, who adorned it with the privileges of a Roman colony and, as Pliny records, called it *Asta Regia*. Titus Livy also reports, in book XXXIX, that after C. C. Catinius had routed the Lusitanians in the territory of Asta, he captured Asta, but, having imprudently climbed the walls, was struck and died a few days later.

Moletius, Milius, and Nonius—Nonius in chapter 13 of his *Hispania*, and the others in Ortelius’s *Synonymy of Places*—suspected that Asta is now Xerez de la Frontera. It is certain, however, that it lay near the estuary of the Baetis River, the port of Menestheus in Strabo, identified by some with Puerto de Sanlúcar de Barrameda.

Ambrosius de Morales, in his *Antiquities of Spain*, under the entry “Asta,” discovered the true site of Asta. It is now called by the inhabitants *la mesa de Asta*, “the table of Asta.” It lies between the noble city of Xerez de la Frontera and the port of Santa María. Its position agrees with the distance from Gades to Asta given by Antoninus in his itinerary from Gades to Corduba.

This city was splendidly ennobled by the martyrdom of three most valiant martyrs of Christ, Honorius, Eutychius, and Stephen, as the archdeacon of Ronda, Don Laurentius de Padilla, in his *Saints of Spain*, and Vasaeus in his *Chronicle of Spain* attest. From them Morales, book X, chapter 28; Marieta, part I, book II, chapter 36; and Trugillus, under 21 November, derived their account. Trugillus says:

“In the most noble city of Asta in Baetica, in the time of the Romans, as the archdeacon of Ronda and Vasaeus report, these three glorious martyrs suffered in former times; their feast is celebrated on 21 November.”

The Roman Martyrology also commemorates them on that day:

“In Spain, Saints Honorius, Eutychius, and Stephen, martyrs.”

Consult also the following note.

4. **Saint Eutychius, etc.** In Acts of the Apostles, chapter XX, the raising of the young man Eutychus at Troas by Paul is especially famous. Luke says:

“A certain young man named Eutychus was sitting on the window, and, as Paul continued speaking for a long time, being overcome by deep sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. Paul went down and fell upon him, and embracing him said, while those standing by were present: ‘Do not be troubled, for his life is in him.’ Then they brought the boy alive, and were not a little comforted.”

After Paul’s death he attached himself to Saint John the Apostle, placing himself under his instruction. The Greeks affirm this in the Menologion; from them the Roman Martyrology, Molanus in his additions to Usuard, and Galesinus record it under 24 August.

The Greeks also relate that, for the sake of preaching, he traveled through many provinces and regions, and that in them he overthrew temples of idols by prayer poured forth to God. For this he endured prisons, blows, and fires, yet was divinely rescued from every danger; and, renowned for the glory of his holy and wondrous deeds, he fell asleep in the Lord. Accordingly, the Roman Martyrology says:

“On the same day, Saint Eutychius, disciple of blessed John the Evangelist, who, having endured prisons, blows, and fires in many regions for preaching the Gospel, at last rested in peace.”

I wonder why Baronius, in his correction of the Martyrology, erased the title “martyr,” since the Greeks, from whom he borrowed this testimony, call him not merely a martyr but a *hieromartyr*—a priestly martyr. Molanus likewise took this from them when he wrote:

“On 24 August, Saint Eutychius, hieromartyr and disciple of Saint John the Theologian.”

Dexter writes no less:

“Having suffered at Tela among the Vaccaeans in Spain, he gloriously departed to the Lord when his martyrdom was complete.”

Therefore, when he is said to have been rescued from every danger, this should not be understood to mean that he afterward spent a long time in peace.

[Col. 0300D] It may reasonably be doubted, however, whether this is the same Saint Eutychius whose feast Ado, Bede, Usuard, Galesinus, and the Roman Martyrology affirm is celebrated in Spain on 11 December. The doubt is especially prompted by the fact that some write that he was a confessor. Thus Peter of Equilinum, book XI, chapter 130, no. 5, says:

“Eutychius the confessor, whose deeds are recorded—as Ado says—whose feast is celebrated in Spain on the third day before the Ides of December.”

The Roman Martyrology calls him a martyr; Bede, Usuard, and Galesinus attach neither designation, but merely say:

“In Spain, Saint Eutychius, whose deeds are recorded.”

Trugillus likewise asserts that neither designation can be established from the Martyrologies.

We therefore see that all these details correspond exactly to Eutychius, disciple of the apostles John and Paul, for authors differ in their accounts both of his end and of his crown of martyrdom. He is the one whose deeds are recorded especially among the Greeks in the Menologion, as Baronius noted under 24 August; and he is celebrated in Spain precisely because he suffered at Tela near Palentia.

If he is not the same man, it is unknown who this third Eutychius might be, and it would be strange for Dexter to have omitted him. Baronius seems to confuse him with Eutychius, companion of Honorius and Stephen, for he says that he suffered near Gades. Asta, however, was the city of Honorius and his companions near Gades. Others indiscriminately wish there to have been three Eutychii. If they produce anything new, I shall not oppose them.

For the present, however, I do not think that the Eutychius commemorated on 11 December is different from the disciple of John who is honored among the Greeks on 24 August and who suffered at Tela. It is not unusual for the same saint to be celebrated by Latins and Greeks on different days.

Whatever the case may be, that ancient Tela was not an insignificant or unknown city in Spain. It had its own bishop for many years, until its see was transferred to Palentia in the year 480, according to Maximus. Ptolemy also knew it among the Vaccaeans near Palentia, entirely different from Tyle, which was near Hispalis. Nevertheless, in Ptolemy’s manuscript, “Gela” is corruptly read in place of “Tela”; in ancient characters, G and T readily pass into one another. The same author speaks again of the preserved memory of this saint under the year of the Lord 299.

5. **Paternus, etc.** Read what we said about him under the year 91; we shall speak of him again under the year 130.

[Col. 0301C]

6. **The Pantheon, etc.** This agrees with Eusebius in his *Chronicle* under this very year 112. “The Pantheon,” he says, “at Rome was burned by lightning.” See Baronius in the *Annals*, volume II, and Orosius.

7. **The Three Gallaecias, etc.** This too was borrowed from the same *Chronicle*, where it is asserted in almost the same words. Orosius has the same account in book VII, chapter 12.

8. **Pliny, etc.** Eusebius says:

“Pliny the Younger of Novocomum is regarded as a distinguished orator and historian; many works of his talent survive.”

9. **Saint Saturninus, etc.** Consult what we wrote under the year 76, when we discussed his first arrival in Spain.

10. **At Carthage, etc.** We discussed Saint Rufus with Dexter under the year 100, when he occupied the episcopal see of Dertosa. Saint Polycarp mentions him together with Zosimus in his letter to the Philippians. He writes:

“I urge all of you to adhere to the word of righteousness and patience, which you saw with your own eyes not only in those most blessed men, namely Ignatius, Zosimus, and Rufus, but also in others who are among you”—

therefore Zosimus and Rufus were not Philippians, but had preached to the Philippians—

“and in Paul and the other apostles.”

Since, as you see, Zosimus was Rufus’s companion in preaching the word, it is not surprising that he received the crown of martyrdom together with Rufus’s brother Alexander, especially since it is established that Rufus rested at Dertosa. At that time Alexander, together with Zosimus, filling Spain with the word, reached New Carthage, which the ancients called Spartaria because of the abundance of spartum.

What Dexter says—“Alexander suffers with Candidus and Zosimus and their companions”—Ado explains in his Martyrology under 11 March. From Ado, Equilinus, book III, chapter 191, gives the following account:

“On the fifth day before the Ides of March, Heraclius [in some copies, Hiradus], Zosimus, Alexander, Candidus, Piperion, and twenty other companions suffered as martyrs at Carthage for confessing the name of Christ and received from the Lord the triumph of victory.”

A substantial error therefore entered the Roman Martyrology, corrected and enlarged by Cardinal Baronius but still corrupt in this part. In place of Saint Alexander, it reads the city Alexandria; and, breaking apart the undivided fellowship of the martyrs, it divides them so that some are said to have suffered at Carthage and others at Alexandria. For it says:

“At Carthage, the feast of Saints Heraclius and Zosimus; at Alexandria, the passion of Saints Candidus, Piperion, and twenty others.”

Yet not only Ado, but also Bede, Equilinus, Usuard, with Molanus’s additions, Galesinus, and others expressly contradict this and equally affirm that all were companions and suffered together at Carthage.

Indeed, if Candidus, Piperion, and the twenty companions had suffered at Alexandria, their memory would undoubtedly survive among the Greeks. They are entirely without such a memory, and this is no slight argument that all died among the Latins, namely at Carthage.

Certainly, the manuscript that Baronius cites in his support should not be valued so highly that it alone is believed to be correct while all the other authors, however venerable their antiquity, are judged corrupt. Galesinus, however, should not be followed when he says that they suffered under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, for this is found nowhere else; he added it on his own authority.

We are now freed from another, still older error into which those fall who read in Bede, Ado, and Usuard—and consequently in the Roman Martyrology, which borrowed from them—the following entry under 18 December:

“At Philippi in Macedonia, Saints Rufus and Zosimus, martyrs, who belonged to that number of disciples through whom the primitive Church was founded among Jews and Greeks. Blessed Polycarp writes of their glorious contest in his letter to the Philippians.”

They believe that Rufus and Zosimus were crowned with martyrdom at Philippi on that day—unless perhaps the words “at Philippi” indicate the place of the feast, not the place of their martyrdom.

This notice was certainly taken solely from Polycarp. Yet Polycarp does not at all assert that they died at Philippi; rather, he says that they suffered much while preaching, or, which is the same thing, that they taught the Philippians with much labor and patience. For he compares them with Saint Ignatius, who did not suffer at Philippi but at Rome, and with Paul and the other apostles. He says that the Philippians saw these men preaching with all patience:

“I urge all of you to adhere to the word of righteousness and patience, which you saw with steadfast faith not only in those most blessed men, Ignatius, Zosimus, and Rufus, but also in others who are among you, and in Paul and the other apostles.”

I believe that the authors of the Martyrologies also slipped slightly at this point. For wherever they could find saints, they inserted them into their books so that the memory of such great fathers would not perish. Innumerable examples of this exist in the Martyrologies: many are recorded there solely on the basis of knowledge derived from Paul’s letters, under 25 June, 4 October, and elsewhere. When they read that Zosimus and Rufus were highly praised by Polycarp and that they had sown the word of righteousness and patience at Philippi in Macedonia, while finding no other information about them, they immediately recorded them as having suffered at Philippi.

Now, however, since we know that they suffered in other places, there is no reason to believe that these were different men. See what we presented above under the year 100 concerning Saint Simeon the Cyrenian and his sons, when discussing Rufus; there we used the testimony of Saint Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta.

A.D. 112. A.R. 863. Saint Marcellus Eugenius holds at Toledo a council composed of the bishops of Carpetania and others, concerning matters of faith and morals.

A.D. 112. A.R. 863. Jonas, disciple of Dionysius the Areopagite, visits Saint Marcellus Eugenius, his teacher Dionysius’s fellow disciple.

A.D. 112. A.R. 863. At Asta in Baetica, Spain, the holy martyrs of Christ Honorius, Eutychius, and Stephen, truly apostolic men.

A.D. 112. A.R. 863. Saint Eutychius, disciple of Saint Paul, was thrown from a window while Paul was preaching and restored to life. He later followed Saint John the Evangelist. Having suffered at Tela among the Vaccaeans in Spain, he gloriously departed to the Lord when his martyrdom was complete.

[Col. 0301] A.D. 112. A.R. 863. Paternus, a Toletan by birth and a citizen of Bilbilis, yet at Rome a familiar and dear friend of Martial, flourishes.

A.D. 112. A.R. 863. The Roman Pantheon was struck from heaven.

A.D. 112. A.R. 863. Three cities of Gallaecia were destroyed by a great earthquake.

A.D. 112. A.R. 863. Pliny the Younger of Novocomum is regarded as a distinguished orator.

A.D. 112. A.R. 863. Saint Saturninus, bishop of Toulouse, visits Toledo for the second time.

A.D. 112. A.R. 863. At Carthage Spartaria, Saint Alexander, brother of Rufus, the first bishop of Dertosa in Tarraconian Spain, son of Simon the Cyrenian, who carried Christ’s cross after him, suffers martyrdom with Candidus, Zosimus, and their companions. In religion Simon follows his sons and is not deprived of the due reward for having carried the cross after Christ; for, after many good works, he rests peacefully at Jerusalem.

[Col. 0303] [Note: [Col. 0303A]]

### A.D. 115

1. **At Hispalis, etc.** I believe that the similarity of the names of these holy martyrs and of the city was the reason for the forgetfulness by which they have until now been buried. Since they are called Justus and Rufinus and are said to have suffered at Hispalis, where the most celebrated holy virgins and martyrs Justa and Rufina are honored, it is not surprising that everything became confused through the confusion of that age.

In truth, it is clear that they share only their names and differ in every other respect: in time, sex, and companions. These men have Macarius as their companion in the crown and—as you will now see—Theophilus; those women had no companion. These were men, those women. These suffered under Trajan in the year 115, as you see; those suffered under Diocletian Caesar and the governor Diogenianus around the year 287, as Trugillus noted, or rather in the year 306, when the persecution of Diocletian raged more fiercely in Spain.

Finally, these are celebrated on 28 February, while those are celebrated on 17 and 19 July. The Church of Hispalis celebrates their feast on 17 July, whereas the Roman Martyrology, Usuard, Bede, and Equilinus place it on 19 July.

We shall discuss the most holy virgins when we reach the time of Diocletian; for now, let us discuss the men.

Equilinus mentions them in book XI, chapter 130, number 80:

“Macarius and Rufinus, Justus and Theophilus, are crowned with martyrdom on the day before the Kalends of March.”

Yet in book VI, chapter 117, he had dealt at length with Saints Justa and Rufina.

Usuard, with Molanus’s additions, says:

“On the same day, Saints Macarius and Rufinus, Justus and Theophilus.”

Yet on 19 July he discusses Justa and Rufina.

The old Roman Martyrology says:
