“On the day before the Kalends of March, the feast of the holy martyrs Macarius, Rufinus, Justus, and Theophilus.”

Baronius adds “at Rome,” but this is his own addition and has no authority, for none of the others names the city. If a city were to be supplied, it ought to be Hispalis in Spain, not Rome.

Galesinus mentions only Justus and Rufinus under 27 July and admits that they suffered in Spain:

“In Spain, Saints Justus and Rufinus, martyrs, who, having been seized in the same persecution for the faith of Christ, after various interrogations under torture by which they nobly testified to their religion, completed the course of their martyrdom amid great admiration.”

In his notes he adds that he derived this from the book and tables of the monk Nicolas.

He nevertheless goes beyond the evidence when he considers them to have suffered under Maximian, and even more when, under 28 February, he joins Justus and Macarius to Cerealis, Pupulus, and others, whom Bede asserts suffered at Alexandria without Justus and Macarius. Concerning Justa and Rufina he wrote correctly under 17 and 19 July.

2. **At Ursaona, etc.** Equilinus mentions only the martyr Leo in book XI, chapter 130, no. 82, borrowing from Saint Jerome’s Martyrology, in these words:

“Leo the martyr suffered on the same day,” that is, on the Kalends of March themselves.

The Roman Martyrology names some of his companions on that day:

“Likewise, the feast of the holy martyrs Leo, Donatus, Abundantius, Nicephorus, and nine others.”

Baronius asserts in his notes that these names were restored from the old Martyrology of the monastery of Saint Cyriacus. We discussed Ursaona under the year 110.

3. **Trajan, Armenia, etc.** Eusebius and Jerome say this word for word in the *Chronicle*.

A.D. 115. A.R. 866. At Hispalis in Baetica, Spain, Macarius, Justus, and Rufinus, martyrs, suffer in the same persecution.

A.D. 115. A.R. 866. At Ursaona in Baetica, Saint Leo the martyr and his companions.

A.D. 115. A.R. 866. Trajan makes Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia into provinces.

[Note: [Col. 0304A]]

### A.D. 116

1. **The earthquake, etc.** The authors mentioned above also record this under the same year, drawing on Xiphilinus and Orosius.

2. **The Jews, etc.** They too give the account, though somewhat more fully:

“The Jews who were in Libya fought against their foreign fellow-inhabitants; likewise in Egypt and Alexandria, and also at Cyrene and in the Thebaid, they engaged in great revolt. At Alexandria, however, the Gentile party prevailed”—

Dio also speaks of these events—

“and in the year 118: when the Jews of Mesopotamia rebelled, the emperor Trajan ordered Lysias Quietus to exterminate them from the province. Quietus drew up his forces against them and killed countless thousands of them; for this reason he was appointed governor of Judaea by the emperor. In the year 119 the Jews destroyed the city of Salamis in Cyprus after killing the Gentiles within it.”

These events occurred under Trajan; the events that took place under Hadrian against the Jews are assigned to the year 121. Consult Orosius, book VII, chapter 12.

3. **Saint Marcus Bolanus, etc.** Under the year 110 he had discussed him, when he flourished in the reputation of noble sanctity; now he discusses his martyrdom and his father. See what we noted under that year.

That there was formerly in Baetica a most noble lineage of the Rustici may be inferred, not without reason, from the marble epitaph of Clodius Rusticus, which, according to Morales, book IX of his *History*, chapter 38 or 39, still existed in his day near the town of Castro del Río, near Corduba.

Martial also sang of the funeral of Antistius Rusticus in book IX of his *Epigrams*. Its beginning, under number 30, is:

“Antistius Rusticus died on the savage shores of Cappadocia,

Rusticus—O land guilty of a mournful crime, etc.”

To him, living at Rome, Martial had given another epigram in book VIII, *Epigrams* 22:

“You seem to me cruel, etc.”

4. **The letters, etc.** It is plainly deduced from the letter now extant that Saint Ignatius wrote not one but several letters to the most blessed Virgin, Mother of God. In it Ignatius says:

“I have also written other letters to you, and have asked about the same matters.”

Saint Bernard also recognizes and celebrates several such letters in sermon 7 on Psalm 90, *Qui habitat*, where he says:

“That great Ignatius, a hearer of the disciple whom Jesus loved, our martyr, whose precious relics enrich our poverty, greets Mary, the bearer of Christ, in several letters that he wrote to her. What an outstanding title of dignity and commendation of immense honor!”

Here is the letter itself, written by one newly converted to the faith who desired fuller instruction concerning its mysteries.

**TO CHRIST-BEARING MARY, HER IGNATIUS.**

You ought to strengthen and console me, a neophyte and your disciple through John. I have learned innumerable things about your Jesus by report and have been astonished by what I have heard. From you, however, who were always intimately [variant: intimately familiar] joined to him and aware of his secrets, I earnestly desire to become more certain of what I have heard. I have also written other letters to you and asked about the same matters. Farewell; and may the neophytes who are with me be strengthened by you, through you, and in you.

Dexter also teaches that the Mother of God wrote back to Ignatius under the year 430. Speaking of the letters, then especially famous, he says:

“The letters of the Blessed Virgin to Saint Ignatius, and his letters to the most holy Virgin, are now passed from hand to hand among the faithful.”

Therefore Dexter offers testimony not merely concerning the report of ancient times, which he recorded in this year 116, but also concerning what he himself had seen with his own eyes—for in that year 430 he was writing a complete history. It follows that several letters of the Mother of God existed at that time, though we regret that they have perished except for this one.

**TO IGNATIUS, HER BELOVED DISCIPLE, THE HUMBLE HANDMAID OF CHRIST JESUS.**

The things about Jesus that you heard and learned from John are true. Believe them, cling to them, hold firmly to your Christian profession, and conform your conduct and life to that profession. I shall come with John to see you and those who are with you. Stand firm and act manfully in the faith; do not let the severity of persecution disturb you. Let your spirit prevail and rejoice in God your Savior. Amen.

I know that the authenticity of letters of this sort is regarded with suspicion by many, especially because Jerome, when discussing Ignatius in his book *On Illustrious Men*, does not mention these among his other letters. But a negative argument cannot prevail when positive testimonies from distinguished authors are present. Would the works of Dionysius therefore be spurious because Jerome did not mention them? Far from it.

If Jerome was silent, his contemporary Dexter spoke; Bernard also spoke, and he is not known ever to have placed faith in apocryphal writings. The most serious scholars accept these letters: the Carthusian, Marianus Victorius, Symphorianus Clamperius, Peter Canisius, Aeneas Sylvius, Sixtus of Siena, Franciscus Arias, and countless others whom it would take too long to enumerate.

It is clear from the letters themselves that Saint John converted Ignatius to the faith before Ignatius accompanied the Mother of God to Ephesus. We discussed this with Dexter under the year 41, when Ignatius, alone without her at the beginning of his evangelical preaching, like a son of thunder, sent swift rays of evangelical light into Asia. Consult what we said about these matters again under the year 86, where we discussed the letters of the same Blessed Virgin sent to the people of Messana and Florence.

5. **Rutilius, etc.** In the printed edition, “Rusticus” stood in place of “Rutilius,” but this is plainly an error; for the martyr mentioned by Tertullian was named Rutilius.

Again, the statement that he was sent to Spain and became a martyr should not be understood as though he completed his martyrdom in Spain. He suffered in Africa after eventually departing from Spain, as Dexter himself noted under the year 110. The meaning is: Rutilius, who was sent to Spain and at one time remained at Corduba, eventually became a martyr—namely, in Africa.

The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on 2 August. Marcus Maximus, in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 612, when that author flourished, left a twofold record of his memory, then famous in Spain:

1. “The memory of Rutilius, who suffered under Trajan in Africa, having fled to Spain and afterward remained at Corduba, is famous here.”

2. “In Africa the memory of the martyr Rutilius is celebrated, whom Septimius Tertullian mentions prominently in his book *On Flight*.”

We gave his words under the year 110; consult them there.]

A.D. 116. A.R. 867. An earthquake almost destroyed the entire city of Antioch.

A.D. 116. A.R. 867. The Jews who were in Libya fight against their fellow-countrymen.

A.D. 116. A.R. 867. Saint Marcus Bolanus Florentius, son of Rusticus Bolanus, a Spanish consular, disciple of the holy apostles, was converted at Tyle—now Sylae—near Hispalis and suffered on 27 October.

A.D. 116. A.R. 867. The letters of Saint Ignatius to the Blessed Virgin are held in high renown.

[Col. 0305] A.D. 116. A.R. 867. Rutilius, sent to Spain, becomes a martyr. Tertullian mentions him with a notably distinguished commendation.

[Note: [Col. 0306A]]

### A.D. 120

1. **Diocles, etc.** Ptolemy mentions Laconimurgum near Capara, or Caparra, a city of no little importance, in his map of Lusitania. Caparra still preserves its name today, and an inn of that name stands on the road from Salamanca to Mérida, not far from the Tagus River.

C. Apuleius Diocles proudly claimed Laconimurgum as his birthplace. He was famous for his noble skill in driving horses, whether they were harnessed to his chariot, driven without a chariot, driven in pairs, in fours, or in a thousand other arrangements.

At Rome there survives a marble record of his remarkable performances, in which he surpassed everyone—a noble monument of such great antiquity in the Campus Martius, in the house of the Checchini family. Philander reproduced it in his notes on Vitruvius, Aldus in his *Orthography*, and the author of the book *Roman Antiquities*. Morales also wrote something about it in book IX, chapter 6.

Let us reproduce the inscriptions themselves, which we ourselves read in that house last year, 1623.

**C. Apuleius Diocles, charioteer of the Red faction, a Spaniard by nation, a Lusitanian, aged 42 years, 7 months, 23 days.**

He first drove for the White faction, under the consulship of Auiolus and Corellius Pansa, [lacuna]; he drove for the same White faction under the consulship of Acilius Glabrio and C. Bellicius Torquatus, [lacuna]; he drove for the Green faction under the consulship of Torquatus Asprenatis II and Annius Libo, and first won [lacuna]; in the Red faction, under the consulship of Laenates Pontianus and Annius Rufinus, he drove a four-horse chariot for 24 years, starting from the gate [lacuna].

Of 257 starts [lacuna], 62 from the procession, 110 single [races], he won [infinity sign] 64. Thereafter he won greater prizes: 92, 30, 32, and with these three six-horse teams, 40, 28 [lacuna]. Thereafter one six-horse team, 63. Of the pairs he won 347. Three-horse teams for 15,000 sesterces, 4 [lacuna]. Of the three-horse teams he won 51. For 15,000 sesterces he won [lacuna]. He came to the honor [infinity sign] [lacuna]. Second places, 861; third places, 576; fourth places for [infinity sign] sesterces. He came out unsuccessfully [infinity sign] 351. Against the Blue faction he won 60; against the White faction he won 90. Thereafter, for 32 [lacuna], 8 [lacuna], 358, 63, 120 sesterces.

Moreover, he won three pairs of horses: one against the White faction and two against the Green. He entered and won 885; he succeeded and won 67 [lacuna]. In various types of competition he won 42. He seized and won [lacuna] 2. Against the Green faction, 216; against the Blue, 205; against the White, 81. I made nine teams of three-year-old horses and one of two-year-olds.

**His distinctions.**

[Lacuna] to him, in the year when he first became victorious with four-horse teams; twice he seized [victory], twice it is contained in the acts that Auilius Teren[tianus] of his faction was the first of all to win [infinity sign] 11, of which in one year, by winning the most, he won [lacuna]. He first achieved one hundred victories; the victor of 103 [races], he won 88 individual [races].

Still increasing the glory of his title, he surpassed Thallus of his faction, who was the first in the Red faction [lacuna]. Diocles was the most outstanding of all charioteers: in a year beginning under another [charioteer?], victorious in 133 [races], he won 117 individual [races]. By this title he surpassed the charioteers of all factions who had ever taken part in the circus [lacuna].

It was rightly marked with universal admiration that, in a year beginning under another [charioteer?], with Cottynus and Pompeianus as his two lead horses, he won 99, 60, 1, 54, 10, 1, 30, 2 [lacuna]. As victor of the Green faction, [infinity sign] 25.

The first of all since the founding of the city to win for 50,000 sesterces, he won 7. Diocles surpassed him; with three lead horses, Abigeus, Lucidus, and Paratus, when the other had won 50,000 sesterces, Diocles won 9 [lacuna].

Omnem, Venustus, and Epaphroditus, three thousand-race charioteers of the Blue faction, having won 11 for 50,000 sesterces, Diocles, with Pompeianus and Lucidus as his two lead horses, won [lacuna].

As victor of the Green faction, [infinity sign] 25; and Flavius Scorpus, victor 2, 48; and Pompeius Musclosus, victor 3, 599. Three victorious charioteers, with 632 for 50,000 sesterces, won 28 [lacuna].

The most outstanding victor, [infinity sign] 462, won 29 for 50,000 sesterces. Diocles shines with a most noble title: when Fortunatus of the Green faction, in [competition] with Victor Tuscus, the victor of 386, had won 9 for 50,000 sesterces, Diocles [lacuna].

[R.] 100, 2, won 10, 60, 1 [lacuna]. Through new achievements and titles never before recorded, Diocles stands out: on one day, with six-horse teams sent out for 40,000 sesterces, he twice emerged victorious over both [opponents], and furthermore [lacuna].

With his own seven horses joined together in a team—a contest never previously seen with this number of horses—he stood out as victor for 50,000 sesterces with Abigeus, and in other contests without a whip for 30,000 [lacuna]. Since he seemed to have distinguished himself by these innovations, he was adorned with a double glory.

Among the thousand-race charioteers, Pontius Epaphroditus of the Blue faction appears to hold first place. In the times of Antoninus Augustus Pius, he alone was victorious [infinity sign] 467 times and won 911 individual [races]. But Diocles, surpassing him, was victorious [infinity sign] 362 times and among individual [races] won [infinity sign] 64.

In those same times [lacuna] and won 467. Diocles seized victory and won 551. Diocles the charioteer, in the year when he won 127, with Abigeus, Lucidus, and Pompeianus as three lead horses, was victor 103 among [the most] outstanding charioteers [lacuna].

Among the outstanding charioteers with African lead horses, Pontius Epaphroditus of the Blue faction won the most. With the *bubulus* team he won 133. Pompeius Musclosus of the Green faction [lacuna] 115. Diocles, having surpassed them with Pompeianus as lead horse, was victorious 152 times and won 144 individual [races].

Adding to his titles, with Cottynus, Galata, Abigeus, Lucidus, and Pompeianus as five lead horses, he was victorious 445 times and won 397 individual [races]. The rest is missing through the injury of time.

You see, reader, Diocles carrying off innumerable victories from all the charioteers who had until then existed in the world in one or another of the four factions. These factions, as appears, took their names from their colors: White, Blue, Green, and Red.

A marble base for a statue of Diocles also survives. His two sons erected it in the temple of Fortuna, with the following inscription:

**To C. Apuleius Diocles, first charioteer of the Red faction, a Spaniard by nation:**

**To Fortuna Primigenia, by decree of the decurions, C. Apuleius Nymphidianus and Nymphidia, a woman, his children.**

It stands at Praeneste in the bishop’s house. Morales, book IX of his *History of Spain*, chapter 6; Philander; Aldus Manutius; and, most recently, Janus Gruterus in his book *Ancient Inscriptions of the Roman World*, under the heading “Inscriptions Dedicated to the Gods,” reproduce it.

Fuscus the Spaniard of the Blue faction also flourished in the same art of chariot driving. He died at Tarraco in Spain, where, outside the city, on the road leading to the shrine of the Virgin of Miracles, the following inscription still remains on a marble base:

**To the divine spirits.**

**For Fuscus of the Blue faction we dedicated this altar,**

**his devoted and loving comrades:**

**so that all might know the monument and pledge of love.**

**You earned an unblemished reputation and the praise of the course;**

**you contended with many and feared no poor man;**

**though subjected to envy, you were always silent and brave.**

**You lived beautifully; as a mortal, you died by fate.**

**Whoever you are, traveler, seeking such a man, stop;**

**read through it, if you remember, if you know what sort of man he was.**

**Let everyone fear Fortune. Yet you will say one thing:**

**Fuscus has the titles of death; death has the tomb;**

**the stone covers his bones. All is well; may Fortune favor you.**

**We pour tears for the innocent man, now wine, and pray**

**that you may lie peacefully: no one is like you.**

**ΤΟΥΣ. ϹΟΥΣ. ΑΓΩΝΑΣ. ΑΙΩΝ. ΛΑΛΗϹΕΙ.**

That is: “The age will speak of your contests.”

Because of the similarity of his profession and homeland, it is pleasing finally to insert here the epitaph of Eutyches the charioteer. It is carved in marble at Tarraco, in the gardens of Don Antonio Agustín, archbishop and a man renowned throughout the world for his exceptional learning. It is as follows:

**To the divine spirits.**

**To Eutyches the charioteer, aged 22.**

**Flavius Rufinus and Sempronius Diophanes**

**[dedicated this monument] to their well-deserving servant and brother.**

**Here rest in this rough charioteer’s tomb the bones**

**of one not ignorant of guiding reins with his hand.**

**I, who dared to mount four-horse chariots,**

**was nevertheless not removed from two-horse teams.**

**Cruel fates envied my years,**

**fates against which you cannot lay hands.**

**Nor was the glory of the Circus granted me in death,**

**so that the pious crowd might not shed tears for me.**

**Burning illnesses consumed my inward parts,**

**which medical hands could not overcome.**

**Scatter flowers over my grave, I beg you, traveler;**

**perhaps you yourself favored me while I lived.**

But let us pass on to other matters.]

A.D. 120. A.R. 871. Diocles, a Lusitanian charioteer from the town of Laconimurgum near Capara, flourishes through the performance of marvelous feats of chariot driving.

[Col. 0307] [Note: [Col. 0308B]]

A. C. 121.—1. Hadrian. Eusebius says for this year: “Hadrian captured the Jews who were rebelling against the Romans for the second time.” For the year 120, however, he had said: “Hadrian, jealous of Trajan’s glory, recalled the armies from Assyria, Mesopotamia, and Armenia, provinces which Trajan had made.” Trajan had in fact died in the year of Our Lord 119, after ruling for 19 years, 2 months, and 15 days; before his death he had adopted as Caesar Hadrian, the son of his cousin. Eusebius says the following under the year 120: “Hadrian was born at Italica in Spain and was the son of Trajan’s cousin”; so that one may see the error of those who claim that he was born at Hadria in Picenum, and of those who say that he was born at Rome, although there is no one who does not affirm that he derived his lineage from Italica in Spain. Consult the most learned Ambrosius Morales, book IX, chapter 31. In support of his position he cites Orosius, Eutropius, Aulus Gellius, and others, and reports that, after Aelius Hadrian had once received the empire, he returned to Spain on one occasion and was almost killed by a slave at Tarraco.

2. The same Hadrian, etc. Eusebius says: “Hadrian remitted the arrears of the city’s taxes by publicly burning the records; he also made very many people free from those very taxes.”

A. C. 121. A. R. 872. The emperor Hadrian dispersed the Jewish captives. He also relaxed the public taxes and granted freedom.

[Note: [Col. 0308C]

A. C. 122.—1. Plutarch, etc. Eusebius under this year: “Plutarch of Chaeronea, Sextus, Agathobulus, and Oenomaus are regarded as distinguished philosophers.”

2. War, etc. Eusebius: “War was waged against the Sauromatians.” See Orosius, book VII, chapter 13, and Marcoduranus, his commentator, in the notes on that chapter.]

A. C. 122. A. R. 873. Plutarch of Chaeronea, Agathobulus, Sextus, and Oenomaus are judged illustrious for the renown of their learning.

A. C. 122. A. R. 873. A savage and cruel war was waged against the Sauromatians.

[Note: [Col. 0308C]

A. C. 124.—Into Libya, etc. Eusebius has it in the plural: “Hadrian led colonists into Libya”—a province of Africa—which had been devastated by the Jews.]

A. C. 124. A. R. 875. A colony was sent into Libya, which had been devastated by the Jews.

[Note: [Col. 0308D]

A. C. 125.—Hadrian, etc. What does Eusebius say? “When the Athenians requested laws, Hadrian compiled their legal system from the books of Draco, Solon, and the others.”]

A. C. 125. A. R. 876. When the Athenians requested laws, Hadrian gave them a legal code.

[Note: [Col. 0308D]

A. C. 128.—To Hadrian, Quadratus, etc. This too was taken from Eusebius, both in the Chronicle and in book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapters 3 and 8. Jerome likewise says in his book *On Illustrious Men*: “Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, was appointed successor to Publius, bishop of Athens. When Hadrian had spent the winter at Athens, he presented him with a book composed in defense of our religion, very useful and full of reason and faith,” etc.

Regarding Aristides he says: “Aristides, an Athenian philosopher of the greatest eloquence and, while retaining his former character, a disciple of Christ, presented to the emperor Hadrian at the same time as Quadratus a volume containing an account of our doctrine”—that is, an *Apology for the Christians*—which survives to this day among lovers of learning as evidence of his intellectual ability.

These two Athenian men presented their books to Hadrian while he was staying at Athens, because at that time he was extremely devoted to his idols, and anyone who wished to rise against the Christians believed that he would thereby be rendering service to the emperor. On these matters also consult Orosius, book VII, chapter 13. Saint Quadratus is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology, by Bede, Usuard, and others on 26 May; Aristides, however, is commemorated on 31 August, where the same things are related in their praise.]

A. C. 128. A. R. 879. Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, and Aristides, both Athenians, presented books in defense of the Christian religion to Hadrian.

[Col. 0309B] [Note: [Col. 0309B]

A. C. 130.—1. Serenus Grannius, etc. Eusebius says the following in his Chronicle: “Serenus Grannius, a legate and exceptionally noble man, sent a letter back to the emperor, saying that it was utterly unjust that the blood of innocent people should be surrendered to the cries of the mob, and that they should be made guilty of nothing except their name and sect. Moved by this, Hadrian wrote to Minicius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, that Christians were not to be condemned without charges being brought against them; a copy of this letter survives to our own day.”

The same author offers it to readers in book IV, chapter 9, of his *History*. It begins: “I have received a letter written by Serenus Grannius, a most distinguished man, in whose place you yourself have been appointed.” A little later it says: “By Hercules, if anyone should attempt such a thing in order to calumniate them, rebuke such a person severely for his wickedness and cruelty, and take diligent care that he pay the penalty he deserves.”

Eusebius differs from Dexter in this respect: Eusebius refers the matter in his Chronicle to the year 128, when he is discussing the books of Quadratus and Aristides presented to Hadrian in defense of the religion; Dexter, however, assigns Hadrian’s rescript to Minicius to the year 130—and much more correctly, since some time must plainly have elapsed between Serenus’s letter and Hadrian’s rescript, which was given to Serenus’s successor, not to Serenus himself.

Galesinus, when discussing Quadratus, assigns all these events to the year 134, but none of the ancient authorities supports him. Read Orosius, book VII, chapter 13, on this matter.

2. In this year Calocerus, etc. We discussed him under the years 37 and 44; consult what was said there. His feast day in the Roman Martyrology is 11 February. Rubeus discusses him in book I of his *History of Ravenna*, as does Surius in volume VII, together with the Ravenna tables cited by Baronius.

Let us, however, reproduce Rubeus’s words under the year 127: “Calocerus, a Greek, was appointed archbishop of Ravenna in place of Martianus, with a dove descending from heaven and resting upon him. Having obtained peace in all things under Hadrian, and with God granting efficacy and strength to his words through his constant exhortation, he persuaded nearly all the Ravennates, after they had abandoned their false gods, to adhere to the holy religion, so that very few were left who did not receive the worship and knowledge of the true God.”

A little later he says: “During the pontificate of Telesphorus, Calocerus, having passed his hundredth year in vigorous old age, exchanged death for life on the third Ides of February (11 February). He was buried not far from Abderitus, the second bishop of Ravenna. The latter, he asserts, was so called because he was born at Abdera. There was, in fact, a city of that name in Baetica in Spain, which Villanovanus believes to have been Almería, and another in Thrace; but it is not known of which city he was a citizen.”

3. Saint and most holy martyr Marcellus, etc. You have been given sufficient information about him under the years 91, 100, 105, 110, and 112. The most holy martyrdom of the pontiff is celebrated in a sacred hymn of the Gothic Breviary of Toledo, which I have decided to insert here for his honor.

**The worthy memory of Saint Eugenius—**

[Col. 0310B]

let the Church of Rucurit—or “the companions”—clap its hands;

Gaul rejoices, enriched by the sacred pledge

of so great a martyrdom.

The fosterling of Greece visits Spain,

namely Dionysius, that is, Eugenius;

the teacher of Spain revisits Gaul,

and, seeking with faithful heart

the presence of the learned teacher of Gaul,

he longs for his father and pursues his desire.

He had already nearly arrived when the enemy grew angry;

the holy man is seized, whom the sword pierces,

tearing his head from his body.

His body is lowered into the nearby lake;

the pledge is entrusted to the excellent guardian.

Freshly cast in, it remains for the longest time—

the body beneath the water.

Hercoldus suffers; to him the vision of God

speaks from this place through Dionysius:

the saint is recovered at the price of healing,

to be placed in worthy honor.

To the Father be glory, to the Son be honor,

power, might, praise, and jubilation;

may an equal share arise

for the companion Spirit,

so that they may stand firm in equal strength. Amen.

Regarding those verses in which Hilduinus most elegantly celebrated the martyrdom of Saint Dionysius, he asserts in the Life of Saint Dionysius—which is preserved in Surius—that he possessed them. We explained earlier why Marcellus is now called a disciple and now a fellow disciple.

Saint Marcellus the Martyr died at the age of ninety, in the year of Christ 130, if—as is reasonable—he was nearly thirty years old at the time of the apostles’ death, having spent his vigorous years under their instruction.

Many writers discuss the complete history of Saint Eugenius: how, while making his way toward Gaul, he obtained the crown of martyrdom; how he was thrown into the Marcassian Lake; how, after two hundred years in that watery hiding place, he was brought forth freshly, through a revelation made by Saint Dionysius to the nobleman Hercolaus, together with the miraculous gift of health granted to him as a glorious sign; how he was honored with due respect; the countless miracles customarily performed at his tomb; and the various translations of so great a martyr’s relics.

One should consult Vincentius, *Speculum*, book X, chapter 35; Equilinus, book X, chapter 62; Marinaeus Siculus, book V; Trugillus; Sanctorus; Villegas; and Ribadeneira on 15 November, together with the Roman Martyrology and those of Bede, Usuard, Ado, Maurolycus, and Galesinus. One should also consult Garibay, book XII, chapter 9; Mariana, book IV, chapter 4; Marieta, part I, book I, chapter 17; Morales, book IX, chapter 26; Maldonatus in the Breviary of Burgos; Illescas, book VI, chapter 15; Ortizius, *Description of the Church of Toledo*, chapter 11; Antonius de Rivera, *On His Translation*; and Cianca, book III of the *Blessed Secundus*, chapter 10.

His illustrious deeds were once reviewed at the Council of Liège, and the Church ordered that they be read, as is clear from the Acts of Saint Gerard, abbot of Bromium, chapter 14, in Surius, volume V.

The sacred relics of Eugenius were first translated to the monastery of Bromium, then to Saint-Denis in Paris; afterward one arm was brought to Toledo in the time of Archbishop Roderic, whose celebrated history of Spanish affairs is extant; finally, under King Philip II the Catholic, the entire body was translated to its proper see at Toledo, buried with the greatest honor, and carried on royal shoulders into the chapel beneath the high altar.

I should note in passing that many of the authors mentioned above have failed in various ways concerning the chronology of Saint Eugenius’s years. It would take too long for me to list each error individually, and anyone can readily correct them from what we have said.

4. Jonas, etc. See what we said about him under the years 86 and 112. I believe that he suffered martyrdom this year or around this time in the district of Castrum, otherwise called Castra Caecilia, in Lusitania.

5. Aulus Altimus, etc. We reported his conversion under the year 76, his preaching at Bilbilis under the year 94, and his reputation for holiness under the year 112. Julian the archpresbyter of Saint Justa has left testimony in his Chronicle under the year 132 that he was bishop of Elusa; we shall quote his words for that year. He subsequently founded the Church of Constance, where he ended his life in martyrdom for the name of Christ. The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on 23 September: “In the territory of Constance, Saint Paternus, bishop and martyr.” Democares mentions him in *On the Sacrifice of the Mass* and asserts that he was the first bishop of Constance.

6. Aquis near Toledo, etc. Ptolemy, in his map of Carpetania, places Libora near Toledo. Pliny calls it Ebura; others call it Elbora. Titus Livy discusses it in book XL, saying: “Quintus Flaccus, at the beginning of spring, led his army into Carpetania and pitched his camp beside the town of Ebura, placing a small garrison in the city.”

From this arose the dispute between Bartholomaeus Quebedus and Resendius concerning Ebura. Quebedus maintained that there were two Eburas: one in Lusitania, which still retains its name and renown, and another in Carpetania, commonly called Talavera. Resendius, however, contentiously asserted that there was only one, namely the Lusitanian city. But Livy plainly contradicts him, as you see.

Mariana and Mantuanus revived the old controversy. What Mariana had vigorously demonstrated in book IV, chapter 13, namely that Talavera was once called Ebura of Carpetania, supported by Livy’s testimony, Mantuanus contentiously refuted. Mariana is supported by Nebrissensis, Marius Aretius in Ludovicus Nonnius’s book, chapter 63 of his *Spain*, Tarapha, Millius, Villanovanus, and Ambrosius Morales in *Antiquities of Spain*, under “Ebura,” folio 101.

Ebura, which we have called Talavera, was also known by another name, Aquis, as M. Maximus testifies under the year of Our Lord 580: “Ebora, which is also Aquis in Carpetania.”

Moreover, Saint Pigmenius—or Pimenius, as others read it—is reverently mentioned in the Twelfth Council of Toledo. There it was discussed that the episcopal title and dignity recently established in the Church of Saint Pimenius at the urging of King Wamba should be abolished. The text says:

“For he said that he had been compelled by royal force to establish a new arrangement of episcopal honor in the monastery of the little village of Aquis, in which the venerable body of the most holy confessor Pimenius rests with due honor,” etc.

The fact that the Fathers call Pimenius a holy confessor does not invalidate Dexter’s assertion that he suffered much for Christ, since Dexter does not say that he ended his life in the very act of martyrdom, but only that he suffered many things. This rather suggests that he was not a martyr.

There was, indeed, another Pimenius, bishop of Dumium, who subscribed to the Sixth Council of Toledo in the Spanish era 676, or in the year of Our Lord 638. His name appears forty-second among the subscriptions of the bishops, in these words: “I, Pimenius, bishop of the Church of Dumium, have subscribed.”

Eight years earlier, namely in the year of Christ 630, Spanish era 668, Pimenius, bishop of Assidonia, consecrated the church of Saint James, now an oratory at Medina Sidonia, where the following inscription is preserved in marble:

**THIS BASILICA WAS DEDICATED**

**ON THE XVII KALENDS OF JANUARY, IN THE SECOND YEAR OF THE PONTIFICATE OF PIMENIUS,**

**ERA DCLXVIII.**

Ambrosius Morales, book XII, chapter 50—and following him Mariana, book VI, chapters 5 and 14, Yepes, *Benedictine Century* 1 under the year 563, *Century* 2 under the year 675, and *Century* 3 under the year 682—believed that the Pimenius mentioned by the Fathers of the Twelfth Council of Toledo was none other than the one found as bishop of Dumium, or perhaps also as bishop of Assidonia.

But beyond doubt they are far from the truth. Saint Pimenius was not a bishop; the Fathers of the Twelfth Council of Toledo call him only a confessor; and he is much older than the other Pimenius, since he was a familiar associate of Saint Eugenius Marcellus, whereas the latter flourished five hundred years afterward.

Loaysa is also mistaken, when in the margin of the Twelfth Council of Toledo he says: “Pimenius was abbot and bishop of the monastery of Dumium.” If they believe that the monastery and bishopric of Dumium were located in the town of Aquis, they fall into an obvious error, since the monastic see of Dumium existed in Gallaecia, whereas Aquis was near Toledo.

They also plainly contradict the council, which admits that there was only one bishop of Aquis, named Cuniuldus, whom King Wamba ordered to be ordained out of devotion to the most holy confessor of Christ. Yet Cuniuldus was deposed in that same council and reduced to the rank of a monk under an abbot. Here are the council’s words:

“This Cuniuldus, who appears to have been appointed bishop, shall no longer rely upon privilege, but shall in every respect be subjected to the rule of the abbot, as he has been until now.”

The monastery of Dumium, however, enjoyed episcopal dignity for many years.

Nor should one immediately conclude, merely from hearing that Saint Pimenius lies in the monastery of the little village of Aquis, that he was a monk or abbot of that monastery. Rather, the monastery may have been founded long afterward in honor of his tomb. Likewise, the fact that Aquis is now called a little village does not imply that it was also a little village under the Romans, rather than a distinguished city; it only shows that, by the time of the Twelfth Council, it was small—namely, because it had been destroyed by Gothic violence.]

A. C. 130. A. R. 881. Serenus Grannius, a legate, learned and exceptionally noble, sent a letter to Hadrian, showing that it was unworthy to expose Christians to wild beasts at the cries of the people without proof of a crime. Moved by this, Hadrian issued a rescript that no Christian should be prosecuted as guilty without a crime being established, on the basis of an accusation directed merely against his religion.

A. C. 130. A. R. 881. In this year Saint Calocerus, a disciple of Saint James and bishop of Ravenna, more than a hundred years old and renowned for the glory of his miracles, departed to heaven.

A. C. 130. A. R. 881. Saint and most holy martyr Marcellus Eugenius, bishop of Toledo and legate of Saint Clement, went to Gaul to discuss important matters with Dionysius. He preached at Toulouse and is believed to have become bishop of that city after the death of Saint Saturninus, its bishop and martyr. From there, knowing of the martyrdom of Saint Dionysius, his fellow disciple, he celebrated it in a most elegant poem; and near Paris he was beheaded by the soldiers of Trajan Hadrian, to whom he himself had been dear, in defense of the faith.

[Col. 0311] A. C. 130. A. R. 881. Jonas, a disciple of Dionysius the Areopagite, preached in Gaul.

A. C. 130. A. R. 881. Aulus Altimus Paternus, a citizen of Toledo, converted to the faith by Saint Saturninus, bishop of Toulouse, became bishop of Elusa. Dear to Eugenius and Dionysius, he suffered martyrdom in Gaul. He was also bishop of Constance; but, wandering through Gaul, he preached the word of God in the manner of the apostles.

A. C. 130. A. R. 881. At Aquis near Toledo, Saint Pimenius, exceedingly close to Eugenius, a man of outstanding virtue, suffered many things for Christ.

[Col. 0313] [Note: [Col. 0313A]

A. C. 132.—Saint Honoratus, etc. In the diptychs of the bishops of the holy Church of Toledo, contained in the Gothic Missal, Saint Honoratus is named first, because martyrs are not listed there, but only confessors; among these Saint Honoratus was the first, as successor to the great martyr Eugenius.

Speaking of him in this very year of Our Lord 132, Julian says: “Saint Honoratus, a Spaniard of Conchana, succeeded Saint Eugenius Marcellus. After some years he went to Gaul to preach and visited Paternus, whom Saint Saturninus had converted at Toledo and made bishop of Elusa. Leaving Hermolaus as his successor, of whom we shall speak immediately, he departed approximately four years after the departure of Saint Marcellus.”

Saint Braulio, or Heleca, says the following in his additions to Maximus: “Saint Honoratus is celebrated in Spain, a Cantabrian by birth and bishop of Toledo. While preaching through various provinces and returning to his homeland of Conchana for the sake of preaching, he died a glorious confessor on 31 December in the year of Our Lord 140.”

Primus, bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, agrees in his *Topography of the Martyrs of Christ*, under “Conchana,” where he writes: “Conchana, a city of the Cantabri in Spain. Here Honoratus, bishop of Toledo, was born. He consecrated Firminus, bishop and martyr of Amiens, and here he departed as a confessor.”

Equilinus must therefore be corrected, book VIII, chapter 119. When discussing Saint Honoratus, bishop of Toledo, to whom Saint Firminus went, he reads “bishop of Toulouse.” Not only do the other authorities we have cited oppose him, but so does the catalogue of the bishops of Toulouse, since no bishop named Honoratus is found at Toulouse during that period. Trugillus was involved in the same error; avoid it in this matter as well.

As for Conchana, Dexter appears to assert that it was the city of Concha, now called Cuenca, situated among the Celtiberians, to which the bishopric of Valeria was transferred. He nevertheless leaves it uncertain whether it may rather have been Conchana, which Ptolemy names first among the Cantabrian cities. If we consider the location assigned by Ptolemy, it seems to have been succeeded by Cumana, a town of Biscay, formerly called Cantabria. But let each person follow his own judgment.]

A. C. 132. A. R. 882. Saint Honoratus was born at Concana—according to some, a city of the Celtiberians; according to others, of the Cantabri. After the departure of Saint and most holy martyr Marcellus, bishop of Toledo, he preached at Toledo and is counted second after Marcellus.

[Note: [Col. 0313C]

A. C. 134.—1. Salvius, etc. Eusebius also records this in his Chronicle under this very year. What is meant by the statement that Salvius Julianus established a perpetual edict is explained by Baronius from Justinian’s work *On the Clarification of the Ancient Law*. He says that the laws of the praetors in the provinces were annual and perished together with their authors. Salvius Julianus, however, a jurist, established by written enactment that all cities should follow the laws and customs of Rome, and not the reverse. Thus, through Hadrian’s authority, the edict became perpetual.

2. Hadrian, etc. Eusebius gives a somewhat fuller account: “After Hadrian had constructed many magnificent buildings at Athens, he held a contest and built a library of marvelous workmanship.” He was indeed extremely learned and, because of his love of philosophy, remained at Athens for a long time, as you see.

3. Ten thousand, etc. The Roman Martyrology preserves a distinguished commemoration of the ten thousand saints crucified, on 22 June: “On Mount Ararat, the passion of the ten thousand holy martyrs who were crucified.” Saint Achacius was their leader, and Anastasius the librarian translated their acts from Greek manuscripts into Latin. I had the opportunity to read them in a very ancient parchment manuscript of the library of my monastery at Nucala. Peter Equilinus, book V, chapter 137, and Lipelous in volume II of the *Lives of the Saints*, give a summary of them.

Some have doubted the reliability of those acts because certain details in them are difficult to believe, especially that they were instructed in the mysteries of the faith by an angel who appeared visibly to the entire army more than once, and who on one occasion lived among them for thirty continuous days; and that they prayed to the Lord that all who invoked them in any necessity might obtain from the Lord the fulfillment of their petition, and that those who fasted in silence on the vigil of their passion might merit one year’s remission of sins. Immediately afterward a voice fell from heaven, calling them to the heavenly kingdoms.

What connection do these things have with the humility in which the holy martyrs excelled? For this reason Molanus says in his notes on the Additions of Usuard: “Certain learned men are displeased by some things in these acts.” Rodulphus de Rivo went even further, believing nothing of what is reported there and considering Achacius and his ten thousand companions to be a fable, as though they had endured all the torments that Christ suffered. Baronius nevertheless attacked him on the basis of his merits in his Notes; consult him, please, so that you may not be surprised when you hear that so many men were crucified together.

I cannot and do not wish to deny that some things in those acts deserve correction, especially the matters we have mentioned, since such acts were certainly corrupted by someone. But thanks be to God, by whose will I found preserved in the ancient breviaries of certain Churches of Spain the pure and genuine history of these martyrs, which had long been anxiously sought.

Dexter had already held up the torch, saying that Achacius and his companions had been brought to the faith and strengthened in martyrdom by Hermolaus, archbishop of Toledo, their companion in suffering and crown, and one far more glorious than they. For this angel had evangelized them, many in Spain and some in Armenia; therefore their memory ought to have been preserved in Spain.

Let us therefore hear the Spanish writers. M. Maximus, at the end of his Chronicle, says: “The memory in Spain of the ten thousand soldiers who suffered at Ararat is most famous, with Hermolaus, archbishop of Toledo, as their teacher and companion; he instructed them in the faith and encouraged them.”

But what have soldiers who were ravaging Armenia to do with the archbishop of Toledo? Or what had Hermolaus to do with them? He adds: “These holy soldiers were for the most part Spaniards; their commander was Heliades, and their principal soldiers, together with the commander, were Agathius—or Achatius—and the Primicerius.”

Hear Julian in his Chronicle under the year 134: “Saint Hermolaus followed to Rome the Christian soldiers, a good many of whom he had either converted to the faith by his preaching or baptized in Spain, leaving M. Pelagius Agrippa as successor to his diocese of Toledo; from there he went on to Armenia, and on Mount Ararat underwent with them an altogether most glorious martyrdom.”

He adds that in the year 396 his sacred relics were finally brought to Toledo and buried with due honor by Audentius, then bishop of Toledo. “Audentius,” he says, “bishop of Toledo, caused the relics of Saint Hermolaus, sixth bishop of Toledo and martyr, to be buried with honor. He converted ten thousand soldiers and followed them into exile in Armenia.”

You will not be surprised, reader, to hear that so many thousands left Spain if you have read, even cursorily, what the pagans write about the courage of Spanish soldiers.

As for the genuine history of these martyrs, which I said exists in the ancient breviaries of Spain, I shall produce it from a very old Palatine Breviary, a copy of which the royal historiographer M. Aegidius Guldisalvi Davila made available to me.

Thus, on 22 June, for the feast of Saint Achatius and his companions, it contains the following history for the matins readings:

“The passion and memory of the ten thousand martyrs is celebrated on the tenth day before the Kalends of July. They were all killed on one day under the emperor Hadrian and six other kings who came to his aid.

“When they were being compelled to sacrifice to idols, they said to him: ‘To deaf and mute idols, O Emperor, we do not offer incense; rather, we offer to our Lord Jesus Christ a living and spotless sacrifice, namely ourselves. He descended from heaven and deigned to be born of a Virgin and to be afflicted with many evils. Finally, he also wished to be crucified for us, though you, Caesar, do not know him.’

“Then the enraged emperor ordered them to be tortured for a long time and afflicted with many sufferings; finally, he ordered them to be crucified. All the torments that Christ Jesus our Lord suffered were inflicted upon them, and they endured them for the Lord with courageous spirit and the firmest faith.

“Among them Hermolaus the archbishop suffered, he who had baptized them.” Thus it is clear that they were brought to the faith not by an angel but by Hermolaus the archbishop.

“The armies of the kings who had come to the aid of the emperor Hadrian numbered thirty thousand soldiers, and it was from them that these holy martyrs suffered.

“The place where they were crucified is therefore a very great mountain called Ararat, situated approximately fifteen stadia from the city of Alexandria”—Alexandria in Armenia, not in Egypt.

“At the sixth hour of that day a great earthquake occurred; rocks were split, the sun was also darkened, and darkness came over the land. All the signs that appeared during the Lord’s passion were also seen there.”

Consider, I ask, the zeal of the ancient saints in spreading the faith of Christ: Hermolaus left the see of Toledo in order to instruct an army of martyrs, and followed it even to the shedding of blood and the pouring out of life. This is not surprising, since he saw the illustrious bishops of that same see, Eugenius and Honoratus, depart for Gaul for the sake of preaching, entrusting the see to others.

4. Metellinum, etc. We have said elsewhere that Metellinum, commonly called Medellín, took its name from the consul Caecilius Metellus, as Ambrosius Morales testifies in book VIII, chapter 18, and book IX, chapter 32, and that it was formerly called the Colony of Metellinum.

The passion of Saint Eusebius Palatinus and nine companions is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 5 March, where it says: “On the same day, the passion of the holy martyrs Eusebius Palatinus and nine others.” It is added in almost the same words by Bede, Usuard, and Equilinus, book XI of the *Catalogue of the Saints*, chapter 130, no. 84.

No one identifies the place of their martyrdom except Dexter. Galesinus is therefore mistaken when, without authority, he says that they suffered at Antioch. His other wording, however, is elegant: “Saint Eusebius Palatinus and his nine companions, whose struggle and battle for the faith in that very persecution of Trajan”—that is, the persecution promulgated by Trajan and continued by Hadrian—“was as illustrious as the Lord’s adornment of his victors with the dignity of an extraordinary heavenly reward.”

I think Saint Eusebius is called Palatinus because he was at some time a Spaniard and a courtier of the Spanish emperor.]

A. C. 134. A. R. 885. Salvius Julianus issued the perpetual edict.

A. C. 134. A. R. 885. The emperor Hadrian left a library at Athens.

A. C. 134. A. R. 885. The ten thousand martyrs at Ararat, with Hermolaus, archbishop of Toledo, as their teacher and companion.

[Col. 0315] A. C. 134. A. R. 885. At Metellinum in Lusitania, the holy martyrs Eusebius Palatinus and nine others suffered steadfastly for the faith of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0315D]

A. C. 135.—1. The Jews, etc. Eusebius says the same thing in his Chronicle under this year: “The Jews took up arms and devastated Palestine while Tynius Rufus held the province; Hadrian sent him an army to crush the rebels.” Dio recounts this more fully; see Baronius, volume II of the *Annals*, and Orosius, book VII, chapter 13.

2. Favorinus, etc. You have these very words in the Chronicle of Eusebius.]

A. C. 135. A. R. 886. The Jews took up arms and devastated Palestine while Tynius Rufus was governor of the province; Hadrian sent him an army to crush the rebels.

A. C. 135. A. R. 886. Favorinus and Palaemon were regarded as distinguished rhetoricians.

[Note: [Col. 0316A]

A. C. 136.—Basilides, etc. The Author also takes this from Eusebius: “In that same year, Cochebas, or Bar-Cochebas, leader of the Jewish faction, killed the Christians with every kind of torture because they refused to provide assistance against the Roman army.” The following year, 137, he adds: “The Jewish war in Palestine came to an end, the affairs of the Jews having been completely suppressed; from that time permission to enter Jerusalem was also withdrawn.”]

A. C. 136. A. R. 887. Basilides, the heresiarch from whom the Gnostics derived their name, was prominent at Alexandria.

[Note: [Col. 0316A]

A. C. 138.—1. Marcus, etc. Eusebius also has this very statement in his Chronicle. But why had no one converted from paganism previously been elected bishop of Jerusalem? Severus, in book II of his *History*, answers that the observance of the legal rites continued there until this time; once those rites had been removed, Marcus was elected first of all.

2. At Barcelona, etc. These precious martyrs of Christ, although their city and religion are passed over in silence, are commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 27 March in these words: “On the same day, the holy Philetus, a senator, Lydia—or Leda—his wife, and their sons Macedonius and Theoprepis, together with Amphilochius the commander and Cronidas the *commentariensis*, who were slain for confessing Christ.”

I believe that Cronidas was not a *commentariensis* responsible for guarding the prison, but an official of the army. See Baronius in his Notes.

Baronius nevertheless handled the matter less successfully in inserting their commemoration into the Martyrology again on the following day. For 28 March he writes: “Likewise, the holy Philetus and his companions, who suffered martyrdom under the emperor Hadrian.”

In his Notes he says: “The Greeks discuss these same persons in the Menologion, where the names of the others are also given explicitly: Lydia, his wife; Macedonius and Theoprepis, his sons; Amphilochius the commander; and Cronidas the *commentariensis*.”

Yet, as I infer from Dexter, the Greeks and Latins discuss these martyrs on 27 March, while on 28 March they mention the fifty-five companions of that same Philetus who suffered on the day following his death.]

3. [The following section appears to have fallen out of the text.] At Osca in Baetica, etc. The Greeks celebrate the feast of the holy martyrs Theodore and Philippa on 20 September, except that, instead of Ὦσχε—that is, Osca or Oscha—modern manuscripts corruptly read Πέργη, Perge. Once this error had been admitted, since Perge lies in the province of Pamphylia, it was easy to add, for the sake of clarity, “Perge in Pamphylia.”

The Menologion gives the following account of their martyrdom: “On the same day, the commemoration of the holy martyr Theodore, who, under the emperor Antoninus and the governor Theodotus, was fastened to a piece of wood and suspended. He lived for three days and afterward departed to the Lord. Certain devout men took care of his sacred relics with ointments and cloths and placed them in a distinguished location. On the same day, the holy martyr Philippa, mother of Saint Theodore, was brought to completion by the sword.”

The Roman Martyrology borrowed their commemoration from the Greeks. Thus, instead of Osca in Baetica, now called Huescar, it has “Perge in Pamphylia.” It says: “The holy martyrs Theodore and Philippa, his mother, together with their companion martyrs, under the emperor Antoninus.”

The words “and their companions” also crept in. For neither in the Greek accounts from which Baronius took these martyrs, nor in Dexter, from whom the Greeks, in my opinion, took them, are more than Theodore and Philippa said to have suffered.

I also understand the statement that they were slaughtered under Antoninus to mean that Antoninus was not yet emperor, but had been designated Caesar by Hadrian, who died in the following year.

4. Saint Pelagius, etc. His venerable memory is preserved in the first diptychs of the Church of Toledo, which begin as follows: “For the spirits of Honoratus, Pelagius, Quintinus, Vincentius, Paulatus, who rest,” etc. He is named there after Saint Honoratus, although he succeeded Saint Hermolaus, who is not included in the aforementioned diptychs because he was a martyr, as Julianus Petri affirms in his Chronicle. His words under the year 134 are those we transcribed above: “Saint Hermolaus, having baptized Christian soldiers in Spain, left M. Pelagius as successor to his diocese,” etc.

This is the Pelagius whom Saint Saturninus brought to the faith at Toledo. See what we said about him above under the year 76.

What Dexter asserts here—that Saint Pelagius was appointed bishop by Saint Honoratus—does not contradict Julian’s statement: “Saint Hermolaus, leaving Pelagius as successor to his diocese.” It could have happened that, before Hermolaus left Spain, Pelagius was consecrated by Saint Honoratus, who had been bishop of that same see and was still alive.]

### 5. Of Amphilochium, etc.

St. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter 2, says: “The Gallaeci are so called from their whiteness, for they are fairer than the other peoples of Spain. Nor is this surprising, since Gallaecia is farther north than the other provinces of Spain; and everyone knows that the farther any people inclines toward the north, the farther it is from the sun and the fairer its skin becomes. Gallaecia, however, is called from *gala, galaktos*, which in Greek means ‘milk’; for these people,” Isidore adds, “that is, the Gallaeci, claim a Greek origin. They are consequently skilled by natural intelligence. For after the end of the Trojan War, Teucer, hated by his father Telamon because of the death of his brother Ajax, and not being received into the kingdom, withdrew to Cyprus, where he founded a city named Salamis after his ancient homeland; from there he proceeded to Gallaecia, settled there, and gave the people their name from the place—its northern position and its color—etc.”

There is no doubt that Isidore borrowed this from Strabo, book III of the *Geography*. According to Strabo, the city of Auriensis, commonly called Orense, was named Amphilochium after Amphilochus, the companion of Teucer, who there ended his days; and, says the ancient historian Justin, book XLIV, the people of that part of Gallaecia are called Amphilogi. He had also prefaced the statement: “The Gallaeci claim a Greek origin.” Let no one regard this as either surprising or novel, since we also know that other Spanish cities were founded by Greeks, such as Saguntum and Emporiae, to pass over the rest.

Concerning Saguntum, Isidore says in book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1: “The Greeks, coming from the island of Zacynthus, founded Saguntum in Spain.” Concerning Emporiae, there still exists an ancient inscription on marble, cited by Morales in his *Antiquities of Spain*, and by Villadamor and Pujades in book III, chapter 85, of his *History of Catalonia*, as follows:

> The Greek people of Emporiae founded this temple of Ephesian Diana in that age when, having neither abandoned the Greek language nor adopted the native Iberian idiom, they yielded to Roman customs, language, laws, and rule, under the consuls Marcus Cethegus and Lucius Apronius.

As for Amphilochium, it is preferable to consult Ludovicus Nonnius in his *Hispania*, chapter 53, where he cites Beutherus and Alvarus Gomez. Indeed, St. Athanasius, a disciple of the apostle St. James, states in the life of St. Peter of Braga, his fellow disciple—an excerpt from which we quoted above under the year 37—that this same St. Peter founded and established the Church of Amphilochium in Gallaecia.

Having thus briefly discussed the place of martyrdom of St. Marina, or Margaret, virgin and martyr—whatever may properly be asserted concerning the true location of Amphilochium, whether it stood where Orense now exists, or somewhat farther from the river Miño, toward the mountains, at the place called Holy Waters, where the body of the most holy virgin and the memorials of her passion are preserved today, a matter about which I am not greatly troubled—we must now examine one important question: whether St. Marina, who suffered at Amphilochium, a town of Gallaecia, was different from St. Margaret, who contended with the satanic dragon in prison, or whether she was one and the same person.

I see that the Spanish authors Villegas, Sanctorum, and Trugillo incline to the view that there were altogether two women, one Greek and the other Spanish. They are moved by no consideration other than that they read that Margaret is celebrated by the Greeks, is commonly said in the Martyrologies to have suffered at Antioch, and that in Gallaecia a Spanish Marina underwent martyrdom. But if they had weighed the matter carefully, as they ought to have done, they would have reached the opposite conclusion. I am confident that all who henceforth consider what we are about to say with an even balance will admit that the two were in every respect one and the same.

Dexter plainly asserts this in the present passage. For when he says that she was called Marina or Margaret and suffered at Amphilochium in Gallaecia for the faith and chastity, he clearly teaches that they differed only in name, and that Margaret was no other than Marina; that she died not at Antioch but at Amphilochium, not in Greece but in Gallaecia:

> At Amphilochium in Gallaecia, St. Marina or Margaret, virgin and martyr, suffered for the Christian faith and chastity.

Later, assigning the discovery of her body to the year 300, he says:

> In Gallaecia, a province of Spain, the body of St. Marina or Margaret, virgin and martyr, who suffered there, was found.

But learn from M. Maximus what caused this difference of names, as well as the new testimony of a very ancient author in support of the same truth. In his *Chronicle*, under the year 556, Maximus says:

> In Spain the memory of St. Marina, a Spanish virgin and martyr of Gallaecia, is especially vigorous. Some called her Margaret, others Gemma Marina. She suffered at the city of Amphilochium in Gallaecia under the judge Olybrius and the emperor Hadrian.

Add to this Julian of Toledo, who in the year 130 of his *Chronicle* sometimes calls her Gemma and sometimes Marina; we shall shortly quote his words.

Here, then, are the sources of the entire confusion: the Greek name of the city and the name of the virgin herself. Since Amphilochia, or Amphilochium—for they are the same name—is Greek, the virgin herself was consequently believed to be Greek. This was unjustified, however, for we have shown from Strabo, Justin, and others that there were many Greek cities in Spain founded by the Greeks, and that Amphilochia was among them.

And since the holy virgin was properly named Gemma Marina, some called her Margaret, which means “sea-pearl” (*marina gemma*; in Spanish, *perla*); others formerly called her Gemma Marina, some merely Gemma, and many, for the sake of brevity, called her Marina.

All the images that exist in Gallaecia and throughout Spain in honor of the Spanish Marina—some of which I have seen, very ancient indeed—show a demon or dragon placed at her feet and the sign of the cross in the virgin’s hand. No one doubts that this is the characteristic representation of St. Margaret.

Molanus also bears witness that the Spaniards are persuaded that Margaret is their Marina, since she came from Antioch in Gallaecia, although he too incorrectly writes Antioch for Amphilochia. And to see that both accounts are true, turn your eyes to the Greeks and investigate whether they themselves possess any certain and established knowledge concerning this same virgin.

Some, whom Usuard followed, called the city in which she suffered Alexandria; others called it Antioch, which, stated without qualification, denotes the patriarchal city of Syria, and Bede agreed with them. Finally, others believed it to be Antioch of Pisidia. Their very variety and inconsistency in the names evidently betrays their ignorance. Since they did not recognize any one of the aforesaid cities as the scene of so great a virgin’s contest, they sought another. The Greeks, however, had an easy opportunity for error in the name of the city itself, since *Amphilochia* (Ἀμφιλοχία) differs little from *Antiochia* (Ἀντιοχία).

It is also remarkable—and no one has hitherto explained it—why the Greeks have always called this virgin Marina, as may be seen in the *Menologion*, the *Horologion*, Symeon Metaphrastes, and others. Lipomanus, Molanus, and Baronius acknowledge this. Yet among Latin authors there is agreement that she is the woman whom the Latins themselves call Margaret.

If she is a Greek virgin, and the Greeks nowhere call her Margaret, how, I ask, do the Latins know that their Margaret is none other than the Greeks’ Marina? Indeed, Marina is a Latin name derived from *mare*, “sea,” whereas Margaret is Greek and signifies the same as “sea-pearl.” But let us pass to other matters.

Whatever is said about Margaret in her history agrees in every respect with the Gallaecian Marina: namely, that she was the daughter of a certain pagan magnate; that for the sake of her upbringing she was entrusted to a rustic nurse, who instructed her in the Christian faith; that she died in order to preserve her chastity and faith; and that she was judged and condemned to death by Olybrius.

Metaphrastes relates all these things about his Marina, and we find them in ancient manuscript codices that I read in various libraries, as well as in others cited by Baronius, which he himself had seen and which were written by a certain Theotimus or Timotheus, an eyewitness, concerning the life of St. Marina or Margaret.

We read nothing less concerning St. Marina of Gallaecia. She was the daughter of a pagan prince; because she had been born in a single birth with eight other sisters, she was ordered to be drowned in a river, but through the compassion of the midwife she was brought to a village and entrusted to a rustic nurse, from whom she received the faith of Christ. She suffered for the Christian faith and chastity, as L. Dexter testifies, and under the judge Olybrius she was crowned with martyrdom, as M. Maximus taught.

I find, moreover, that Olybrius stirred up persecution against Christians in the West and crowned St. Regina, a virgin, with martyrdom in the city of Alisia, not far from Massilia; and that he treated her in a manner similar to that in which he later acted when he reached Gallaecia and encountered Marina. Equilinus says in her life, book VIII, chapter 47:

> While the prefect Olybrius was travelling from Alisia to the city of Massilia, he saw a girl and, attracted by her beauty, had her brought before him, etc.

Concerning Marina or Margaret he says in book VI, chapter 120:

> When she had reached the age of fifteen and was tending her nurse’s sheep with other virgins, the prefect Olybrius, passing that way, burned with love for her and sent boys to bring her to him, etc.

I possess a distinguished testimony to the same matter and an excellent monument of genuine antiquity: the Breviary of Palencia. In it the history of St. Margaret is precisely the same as that which is read concerning St. Marina of Gallaecia. I have decided to insert it here because it has the character of a genuine narrative, with those points expunged that are written less truthfully or fittingly in Equilinus.

The aforesaid Breviary, therefore, having celebrated the feast of St. Margaret on the third day before the Ides of July—that is, July 13—and afterward celebrating the feast of St. Marina on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August—that is, July 18—contains the following lessons for Matins:

> When madness possessed the minds of unhappy men and sacrilegious fury burned so that they might worship and adore deaf and mute idols, I, Theotimus, believing in Christ Jesus and instructed in literary learning, resolved to write the deeds of St. Marina the virgin, and how she fought against the ancient enemy.
>
> Blessed Marina, therefore, born of pagan parents, was entrusted to a certain matron to be raised in a city fifteen *stadia* distant from the city of Amphilochium. [The true name of the city ennobled by St. Marina’s blood should be noted.] Carefully instructed by this woman in the faith of Christ and having received the grace of baptism, she heard of the contests of the martyrs and vehemently desired to become a participant in them.
>
> When Olybrius, governor of Amphilochium, was travelling toward that city, he encountered Marina on the road. When he ordered her to be seized, she began to invoke the Lord, saying: “Have mercy on your servant, Lord Jesus Christ, and do not destroy my soul with the impious.”
>
> The governor then summoned her and said: “Of what condition are you? Free or a slave?” Marina replied: “I am free, and a servant of Christ.”
>
> Then he ordered her to be thrown into prison and commanded that she be brought before him the following day. When he could not separate her from the love of Christ, he ordered her to be hung up and torn with extremely sharp rods until her blood flowed.
>
> But blessed Marina, strengthened by the power of God, neither sighed nor groaned, nor even displayed a sorrowful expression. While she was still preaching the Lord, the governor, thinking that he was being mocked, ordered her flesh to be furrowed with iron combs down to the bones, so severely that the people, and the tyrant himself, were moved to compassion.
>
> Olybrius then said to her: “Take thought, girl, for your youth, and yield to me, lest you lose the flower of your beauty.”
>
> Marina replied: “Wicked counselor! This torture is the salvation of the soul. Shameless dog, insatiable lion, you have power over the flesh, but Christ preserves the soul that he redeemed.”
>
> At this the tyrant said: “Now I shall spare nothing; now I shall show no mercy. She mocks those who advise her, blasphemes the gods, and despises torments.”
>
> She was therefore shut up in a very dark prison, but immediately it was illumined by immense light. The devil, appearing in the form of a dragon as though about to devour her, suddenly vanished when she opposed to him the sign of the cross.
>
> On the following day the virgin was brought before the judge. Refusing to sacrifice in the presence of the assembled people, she was burned; and blazing torches being placed at her sides, her freshly lacerated flesh was burned through to the innermost parts. Everyone marveled that so frail a girl could endure such torments. But when the insane judge saw that she could not be overcome by so many tortures, he finally ordered her to be beheaded on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.

At the other feast of the same virgin, under the name Margaret, the following is added:

> On the following day she was brought before the judge Olybrius, and burning lamps were placed against her sides. Then, bound hand and foot, she was plunged into water; but after she prayed, she was delivered, and the people cried out: “Great is the God of the Christians!” As a result, five thousand of them received the crown of martyrdom, while Margaret was beheaded.

Memorials of this event are still visible at the place of her burial: a small oven over which she was burned and a spring in which she was immersed. Thus, as Equilinus says, the intensity of the suffering was increased by the exchange of punishments. The healing power of the water, however, which fever sufferers received through contact with the virgin, continues to the present day; and, borrowing its name from this circumstance, it is called “Holy Waters.”

When Metaphrastes says that Marina’s father was called Aedesius and was a priest of idols, I think this resulted from a scribal error: someone read *Aedesius* for *Catelius* and “priest of idols” for “worshiper of idols” in some corrupt manuscript. From Aedesius, some made Theodosius. Thus the names of places and persons, through continual alteration, degenerate into corruption, until at last no one knows how to distinguish the true reading, the form of the word having been entirely changed.

Most writers do not call him a priest or worshiper of idols, but rather a patriarch of the pagans. This comes closest to the truth, for in Greek *patriarch* denotes in Latin a leading man, or rather a provincial prince, such as St. Marina’s father is known to have been, as we shall soon say.

There is no less disagreement concerning the day of her martyrdom. Usuard, Ado, and Bede assign it to June 18; some whom Equilinus cites, to July 13; the Greeks celebrate it on July 17; the Spaniards on July 18; and the Roman Martyrology on July 20.

In the same Martyrology, corrected by Baronius, under June 18, where Usuard, Bede, and Ado deal with Marina, these words appear:

> At Alexandria, the passion of St. Marina the virgin.

Here the first and chief error is the assertion that she suffered at Alexandria, whereas it is clear that the reading should be *at Amphilochium*. Nor is Baronius’s explanation in his Notes satisfactory, when he says that the Marina mentioned here was not a martyr but the nun who, in *The Lives of the Fathers*, part I, chapter 44, is said to have persevered until death among men under male dress and under the name Marinus. That woman did not die on June 18 but on July 16, as Equilinus says in book VI, chapter 108. Moreover, the Martyrology’s own text contradicts this explanation through the word “passion,” which, whether he wishes it or not, signifies martyrdom.

I would believe that in different provinces different feast days were customarily celebrated in honor of St. Marina for the sake of greater convenience, although the true day of her death was the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August—that is, July 20—as her history and the Roman Martyrology state. I shall say more about her when I have dealt with her other sisters.

### 6. Wilgefortis, etc.

Molanus writes the following under July 20:

> In Portugal, the feast of St. Wilgefortis, virgin and martyr, who, dying on the cross for love of chastity and the Christian faith, happily passed to the Lord.

Accordingly, the Roman Martyrology reads on the same day:

> In Lusitania, St. Wilgefortis, virgin and martyr, who, contending for the Christian faith and chastity, merited a glorious triumph on the cross.

In the additions to the ancient, or first, edition of Usuard’s Martyrology, printed at Louvain by Welleus in 1568, Molanus adds:

> Likewise, Wilgefortis, virgin and martyr, daughter of the king of Portugal, whom some call in Latin Liberata and in German Ontkommer.

Here he acknowledges that Liberata and Wilgefortis are the same person, since Wilgefortis is called Liberata in Latin according to the custom of her native country.

From this one may first see that this most blessed virgin was once famous even among foreign peoples, since the Germans invoked her under a different name, Ontkommer; others called her Wilgefortis; and others finally Liberata.

But because Dexter, in the present passage concerning her name and under the year 155 while treating her sister Marciana, also mentions the other eight sisters, saying:

> At Toledo, St. Marciana, daughter of Catelius, prince of Lusitania, suffers, together with eight other virgins, her sisters,

I shall include here the history of all of them together, as I read it in the ancient and venerable Breviaries of Spain, where it was customarily read in the divine offices on the feast of St. Liberata. I saw the Segovia and Palencia Breviaries, which contain the following:

There was a noble king among the neighboring peoples of the West, named Catellius. The capital of his kingdom was Balchagia, also called Belcagia or Balchadia, later known as the city of Estuciana. He had taken as his noble wife a woman named Calsia.

By divine permission it happened that the aforesaid queen, fruitful in numerous offspring, gave birth to nine daughters on a single day. When this became known, the queen, overcome by great shame, conceived the inhuman plan of killing them all, so that the matter would not come to the knowledge of her husband and the people.

Having devised this wicked plan, she summoned the midwife, named Sila, who was close to her and knew her secrets, and ordered her secretly and carefully to carry the entire group of infants to the river and there, with no one aware, plunge them all into the depths of the whirlpool.

O the invention of a woman—or rather of the devil! O a female more savage than any wild beast, who intended to destroy with a horrible death, at the very entrance of life, the daughters whom she had scarcely brought into the world!

But merciful God, who is accustomed to draw good from the evil deeds of human beings, determined otherwise concerning these infants. The aforesaid midwife, moved by compassion for the little girls and by love of God, found an opportunity to go to a village inhabited by Christians in the suburb of the city. There she sought suitable nurses and entrusted each girl to a different one for upbringing.

The nurses received them, caused them to be regenerated by the washing of the sacred font, and gave them names. Their names were as follows: Genibera, Victoria, Eumelia, Gemma—which is Margaret—Marciana, Germana, Basilia, Quiteria, and Liberata.

As time passed and they grew up, through living and conversing with Christians they learned their lineage and origin. Later, when a fierce persecution against Christians arose from the Romans and agents were sent through all the cities to compel the faithful to offer profane sacrifices, these blessed sisters were found in that village and cruelly dragged before the presence of their royal father.

After many questions, Genibera replied:

> “If you ask about our lineage, we are your daughters; if about our condition, we are servants of Christ.”

The king, learning with great astonishment from his wife’s confession that these were his daughters, tried by gentle words to persuade them to abandon the worship of Christ. He gave them a period of delay in order that they might agree with him. But, warned by an angel, they all fled, encouraging one another, praying and weeping together, and then separating from each other.

They were all captured by the persecutors in different places and completed their martyrdom.

Thus far the aforesaid Breviaries. The same account is also found in a very ancient manuscript Sanctorale preserved in the library of the Holy Church of Toledo and called “the Emerald” because of its external color.

Lest anyone regard as incredible the assertion that all nine girls were born in one and the same birth, let him know that it has happened more than once for numerous offspring to be brought into the world simultaneously. Dacianus the Assyrian, in his *Oration against the Greeks*, states that two women gave birth to thirty children at once:

> “What have I to do,” he says, “with the little woman Peridymene, who gave birth to thirty infants in a single delivery, which many consider a miracle? It ought rather to be regarded as the fruit of great excess; and that woman should appear abominable, being like the Roman sow, which is likewise said to have received a certain sacred veneration because of a similar event.”

What surpasses all admiration in this matter is what Gaufridus, a monk of Villers, relates in a letter to St. Ida: namely, that Margaret, countess of Holland and daughter of Count Florentius, gave birth in the year of the Lord 1276 to 364 children at one time. An inscription cut into stone, visible in the Cistercian monastery of Losdun, gives credibility to this birth, however prodigious:

> The illustrious lady Margaret, daughter of Lord Florentius, Count of Holland, whose mother was Mechtildis, daughter of Henry, Duke of Brabant, and who also had a brother, William, King of Germany, gave birth in the year of salvation 1276, in the forty-second year of her age, on Good Friday itself, at the ninth hour before noon, to 364 living infants of mixed sex. After they had received the sacrament of baptism in a certain basin from the venerable bishop Lord Guy, the suffragan, in the presence of several nobles and magnates, and after the males had been given the name John and the females the name Elizabeth, the souls of all of them, together with their mother’s soul, returned to God to live eternally, while their bodies rest beneath this stone.

Gaufridus’s letter is preserved in Bernard of Brito’s *Cistercian Chronicle*, book VI, at the final chapter.
