Many also know that not many years ago Maria Marcella, of the French family in Lusitania, born in the town of Anelle in the diocese of Braga, gave birth to seven male children at once—not merely alive, but all of whom reached the priesthood and parish dignity. They were commemorated by an inscription on marble in their mother’s tomb in the Chapel of St. Dominic in the town of Chaves. There are many witnesses to this event.

But to return to Calsia’s delivery: apart from the Breviaries mentioned above, our distinguished chronologer Julian expressly affirms the same in the year 130:

> These divine sisters, Genivera, Victoria, Eumelia, Germana, Gemma—that is, Marina—Marciana, Quiteria, Basilissa, and Wilgefortis or Liberata, were born in a single birth in the city of Gallaecia called Balcagia, now Baiona, near the city called Tui.

Many important authors also accept this same history, especially Marieta in book IV, part I, chapter 12, of his *Saints of Spain*, and Sandoval, bishop of Tui, in his book on the Church of Tui, in the section on St. Ovidius, who instructed them in the faith more fully than their nurses.

Formerly the feast of all nine together was celebrated in Spain on January 18, although each has a day assigned to her own martyrdom: Genivera on November 1; Victoria on November 17; Liberata, together with her sister Margaret, on July 20; Germana on January 19; Marciana on July 12; Basilia on November 1; and Eumelia on December 1.

Morales discusses them in book X, chapter 27, of his *History of Spain*, as does Villegas in volume I of the *Flos Sanctorum*.

But now let us investigate what happened to each of them.

#### I. St. Genivera

St. Genivera, who is customarily named first among the sisters, was separated from the others at Balcagia, or Baiona, at the angel’s command. She settled at Tui, where she was seized by the persecutors. When she could not be drawn away from the faith of Christ either by threats or by flattery, she was crowned with martyrdom.

Julian reports this under the year 130, saying:

> St. Genivera suffers at Tui on November 1.

Her name is sufficiently famous there, for through devotion to her many women are customarily called Genivera, commonly Ginebra.

#### St. Victoria

Victoria, having taken the young Acisclus as her companion, reached Córdoba. After various conversations with Dione, proconsul of Baetica, the two were cruelly scourged and thrown into a most dreadful prison. There they were nourished and refreshed for many days by four angels.

They were then thrown into the river Baetis with extremely heavy stones fastened around their necks. They were not drowned; rather, they were strengthened and delivered by Jesus the Lord himself. Next they were bound upon wheels over a slow fire, but after they prayed the fire was extinguished, having first burned many of the executioners.

Finally Victoria’s breasts and tongue were cut off, and her breast was flayed; the breasts gave milk instead of blood. At last she was pierced with arrows and passed in a renowned martyrdom to her bridegroom. Acisclus, however, was beheaded on November 17.

Prudentius celebrates their triumph in hymn 4; so does Isidore in the hymn of the Gothic Breviary, as well as Trugillus, Villegas, and Marieta.

Some incorrectly list them among the children of St. Marcellus the Centurion. Baronius also carefully noted this in his Notes for that day. Marcellus suffered under the emperor Diocletian around the year 300. It is likewise established that St. Victoria was not the daughter of Marcellus but of Catellius, and that she flourished around the year 130. Julian states precisely this in his *Chronicle* under the year 130, where, discussing the place of martyrdom of the nine sisters, he says of Victoria:

> Victoria is said to have suffered at Córdoba with Acisclus—or Zoilus—the young man.

If he wishes to identify Zoilus with Acisclus, however, he cannot be followed, since the two were very different from each other. We shall discuss Zoilus under the year 300.

Nor is there any reason why Victoria and Acisclus should be called siblings, since they were not the children of St. Marcellus. None of the ancient writers calls them brother and sister, as may be seen in Bede, Ado, Usuard, Equilinus, and the Palencia Breviary. There is therefore no doubt that the word “siblings” entered the Roman Martyrology by mistake and should be removed from its text.

Ado relates that a wondrous and perpetual miracle was customarily seen every year on their feast day at Córdoba, where they are venerated as patrons:

> They are honored there, buried together; and there also, in memory of their precious death, roses that arise by divine power on the same day of their martyrdom are gathered every year, although they suffered in winter, on November 17, and no roses are gathered on any other day during that season.

See Equilinus, book X, chapter 70, and Usuard under November 17.

#### St. Eumelia

St. Eumelia is also called Euphemia, as appears from Dexter in the present passage, where he says:

> In the same Gallaecia, St. Euphemia, virgin and martyr.

The name of the city of Abobriga, where she received the crown of martyrdom, seems to be missing. We should read Dexter as follows:

> At Abobriga, in the same Gallaecia, St. Euphemia, etc.

For it is certain that she was killed there. Julian reports this in his *Chronicle*, saying:

> Eumelia is honored in the city of Abobriga in Gallaecia on December 1.

M. Maximus, under the year 531 of the Lord, states that Abobriga, or Obobriga—as he himself writes it—is the city now called Auriensis, commonly Orense. He says:

> Martin, later bishop of Dumium, instructs Riccarius in the faith in the city of Auriensis, formerly called Obobriga Regia.

According to Maximus, therefore, one would have to admit that the same city was called Amphilochium by the Greeks, Aquae Calidae by the Latins, Obobriga by the Spaniards, and Warmsee by the Suevi—that is, “warm lake”—while from the surrounding district, as we show elsewhere, it was called Auriensis, now Orense. Consequently Euphemia too would have lived in the same city as Gemma Marina and would have suffered martyrdom there for Christ.

It seems more probable to me that Abobriga was another city, whose ruins still remain in the diocese of Orense, at a place called by the inhabitants “the Streets of St. Euphemia.” They hold by a firm tradition that she suffered martyrdom there. Some have called that city Chalcedon, but incorrectly.

Those who confuse the Chalcedonian saint with the Spanish Euphemia must therefore be corrected. They have dared to transfer Chalcedon, the famous city of Bithynia in Asia, to Spain. Ferdinand Petri Guzman was entangled in this error in his *Scholastic Valerius*, when he said that Chalcedon once stood near Tui, at the confluence of the Miño, in Gallaecia.

Sandoval adds in his book on the Church of Tui, folio 5:

> Its site still seems to be a league from the banks of the Limia, or Lethe, in a branch of those very rugged mountains called the Xerez, on the border of Galicia, in the parish of St. Salvador de Marin and in the bishopric of Orense. Beside the valley and the hot river, the local people call this site the Streets of St. Euphemia, because there, in places that are very high and precipitous, the tyrants inflicted many torments on the saint.

It is ten leagues from the city of Orense. But one matter is that our Euphemia very probably received the palm of martyrdom there; another is that Chalcedon stood there.

Certainly these authors were moved by no consideration other than that they had read that St. Euphemia died at Chalcedon, without distinguishing between provinces and periods separated by equal distances. One place was in Gallaecia, the other in Bithynia; one in Spain, the other in Asia; the Spanish woman suffered in the year 138 or 139, under Hadrian, whereas the Greek woman suffered under Diocletian, around the year 300.

The confusion even entered certain Breviaries of Spain. In the Compostellan and Bracarensian Breviaries, Chalcedon is placed in Gallaecia, and only one Euphemia is counted. The Church of Orense, however, assigns a separate feast to each and celebrates the one whose body it preserves on July 26, the day after the octave of St. Marina, her sister; it celebrates the Chalcedonian saint on September 16, the day on which she is honored throughout the universal Church.

After many years had passed, in the year 1153, at the place where St. Euphemia had suffered and been buried, an innocent girl who was tending sheep saw among the rocks a hand adorned with a beautiful ring. When she grasped it, she suddenly lost the power of speech.

When she returned to her father and indicated by signs as best she could what had happened, they went to the hand of the virgin, and both the ring and the girl’s speech were restored. A voice from heaven was then heard:

> Here lies the body of St. Euphemia. Take care, therefore, to remove it from this place at once and bury it honorably in the Church of St. Marina, which is nearby.

Obeying the angelic voice, he carried out the command he had received. What had been denied to others, however, Peter Seguin, bishop of Orense, obtained through earnest prayers and fasts. He honorably transferred the body of St. Euphemia to his cathedral church and placed it in a gilded sarcophagus beneath an iron grille, in a chapel situated to the right of the high altar. I often read the inscription there:

> St. Euphemia, virgin and martyr.

The feast of her translation is celebrated on August 7. Peter Seguin himself and his successor Alfonso commended its history to posterity in writing, and it is recounted in the lessons of the proper Breviary, together with many other miracles.

See Trugillus in his *Thesaurus Concionatorum*, under September 16. He says that the virgin’s ring is still held in high honor and is customarily applied to the sick as a miracle.

Equilinus mentions the same Euphemia in book XI, chapter 130, number 119:

> Euphemia, virgin and martyr, received the crown on the Ides of April.

At the beginning of that chapter he acknowledges that he borrowed this from Jerome’s Martyrology.

But how great a discrepancy in feast days shall we find concerning Euphemia! Julian asserts that in his time she was honored on December 1; Equilinus says that she died on April 13; the Church of Orense celebrates her feast on July 26 and her translation on August 7.

These dates may be reconciled as follows. The true day of her martyrdom had hitherto been unknown. It is now established from Jerome and Equilinus; but those who did not know it transferred her feast to the following octave of St. Marina, her virgin sister—that is, to July 26. Formerly, for greater convenience, it was observed on December 1. But let us now turn to other matters.

#### St. Germana

When the sisters separated from one another at the angel’s command, Germana crossed the sea and migrated to Africa. There, defending the faith of Christ, she gave her life together with eight other companions.

Their memory is preserved in the Roman Martyrology on January 19, where we read:

> In Africa, the holy martyrs Paul, Gerontius, Januarius, Saturninus, Successus, Julius, Cattus, Pia, and Germana.

Cardinal Baronius restored their names to the Roman Martyrology, from which they had fallen out, using ancient manuscript codices of St. Cyriacus at the Baths. Nevertheless, only the name of Saturninus, together with nine companions, had been placed under March 22, and the names have not yet been removed from the Roman Curia’s corrected edition.

That this Germana was one of the other eight Gallaecian sisters is expressly acknowledged by Julian in his *Chronicle*, where he says:

> St. Germana, sister of these women, suffers at Carthage in Africa.

Thus the Martyrologies read under January 19:

> In Africa, the holy martyrs Paul, Gerontius, etc., Pia, and Germana.

#### St. Gemma Marina, or Margaret

Enough, and more than enough, has been said about her above. Bonad, Hieronymus Vida, and Baptista Mantuanus celebrated her acts in excellent poems.

#### St. Marciana

The Roman Martyrology under July 12 reads:

> At Toledo, St. Marciana, virgin and martyr, who, having been thrown to beasts for the faith of Christ and torn apart by a bull, was crowned with martyrdom.

Julian, however, discussing the nine sisters in his *Chronicle*, says:

> Marciana suffered at Toledo in the year 155, somewhat after her sisters, on July 12.

That is the year in which Dexter mentions her, and we shall work with him to clarify everything that concerns her.

## Saint Quiteria

She is the best known among the other sisters, since many Spaniards have described her deeds, especially Marieta, book IV, part I, chapters 17, 18, and 19; Villegas, Trugillus, and others. Her sacred relics are reverently preserved in the town of Marguelizza, in the diocese of Toledo, and in her honor many women in Spain are named Quiteria.

Julianus, in the passage cited, says of her:

> At this time Saint Quiteria, Genivera, Marina, Marciana, Wilgefortis or Liberata, and four other virgins and martyrs, daughters of L. Catellius, a Bracaran consular official and ruler of Lusitania—[a verb is missing, such as “suffered”]—together with other companions and Bishop Valentinus, who suffered a celebrated martyrdom in Spain with Quiteria in Vescetania, the province neighboring Toledo to the south, at the town of Adura, now called Marguelizza, on 22 May; Saint Quiteria is held in high esteem there.

For *Vescetania* one should read *Vetonia*, which is the province nearest Carpetania. Molanus must therefore be corrected in his additions to Usuard, where he reads Gascony instead of Vetonia, although he is to be followed in the rest. He says:

> On the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in Gascony, Saint Quiteria, virgin, who endured an outstanding martyrdom together with many others.

We do not know why the Roman Martyrology makes no mention of her companions, for it says only:

> In Spain, Saint Quiteria, virgin and martyr.

To make the truth clear, let us introduce a brief history of this same virgin, preserved in the ancient records of the holy Church of Toledo, in a very old manuscript Breviary which I was permitted to see in the library. The same account is also found in the Breviary of Palencia:

> Blessed Quiteria, although her parents were alien to the Christian religion, was nevertheless, according to the common estimation of the present age, born of the noblest stock. Her father was called Catillius and her mother Calsia. They flourished in power, exalted by royal authority, and their city was called Belcagia.
>
> Their daughter, therefore, blessed Quiteria, while according to her custom—after the sisters had separated from one another—she was one day wholly intent upon heaven in devout prayers, behold, an angel of the Lord suddenly arrived and addressed the blessed virgin, saying: “Blessed virgin, blessed are you, for, adorned in heaven with an incorruptible diadem, you will deserve to be called the bride of the eternal King. Now, therefore, follow me to Mount Oria.”
>
> At these words the blessed virgin, accompanied by the angel, climbed that mountain, and there did not cease each day to entreat the Lord with prayers. Again the angel addressed her: “Arise, virgin.” Having received his blessing, she descended from the mountain and returned to the city, where her father questioned her about marriage. But she prayed to the Lord, to whose marriage she had devoted herself.
>
> Immediately the angel came and encouraged her, saying: “Do not be afraid, but leave the land of your birth and cross over to the valley of Aufragia, where the Lord has appointed for you the crown of martyrdom, and on Mount Columbianus a resting place for your bones, in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle.”
>
> Blessed Quiteria arose, with thirty companions of the virginal sex and eight distinguished men, and reached the aforesaid place, where King Leutinus—or Lencianus—an apostate, ruled. After he had spoken with her at length and could not turn her away from her good purpose, he ordered her to be thrown into prison with her companions. There she converted the king himself to Christ and healed a multitude of people from various illnesses.
>
> While these things were happening, her father sent Dumanus—or Germanus—to whom he wished to betroth her, and ordered him and his soldiers to kill her with the sword if he found her first. When Dumanus found her, he killed her, together with many others, on the aforesaid mountain. After her head had been cut off, blessed Quiteria immediately took it in her hands and carried it seventy-two stadia, as far as the aforementioned tomb, where she lies in the city of Adura. It is now called Marguelizza, reduced to a small town in the kingdom of Toledo.

The author of the *Thesaurus Concionatorum* adds that the martyrdom of blessed Quiteria occurred around the year of the Lord 100, at the very beginnings when Christianity began in France, in the time of blessed Dionysius. He does not, however, specify the particular year, as Dexter does.

Saint Quiteria is invoked for the healing of the bites of rabid dogs. Thus, among the other prayers that were long customarily said for such sufferers according to the order of Saint Bernard, especially in the monastery of Saint Mary of Mount Salvation in the diocese of Cuenca, the following collect holds a principal place and is thought to have a most beneficial effect:

> Grant, almighty God, that, just as you adorned blessed Quiteria with virginity and martyrdom, and as she bound the devil by your power and converted the king with a great multitude of people, so by her constant prayers you may free us from diabolical madness and from all its continual diseases. Through our Lord, etc.

Since the Life we have described lacks the story of the binding of the devil, we are compelled to say that it was omitted because of the brevity deliberately observed in the Breviaries. We think, however, that this occurred while Quiteria was living in solitude on Mount Oria.

The eighth in the order of the sisters was Saint Basilia, or Basilla, as others write. Departing from her sisters at an angel’s command, she reached the city of Syrmium, where she purchased eternal life with the price of her blood in exchange for temporal life.

Syrmium was a city of Baetica, where Saint Peter the Apostle had appointed blessed Epaenetus bishop. We have said much elsewhere about him and about the city itself, in the years 50 and 100.

Of the same Basilla, Equilinus, book XI, chapter 130, number 232, says:

> Saint Basilla fell asleep in the Lord at Syrmium itself, namely on 29 August.

The Roman Martyrology also deals with her on that same day, except that *Syrmium* is corruptly printed as *Smyrna*. It says:

> At Smyrna, the birthday of Saint Basilla.

It is surprising that neither source mentions either her virginity or her martyrdom. Julianus, however, recognizes her as a virgin and martyr, like her other sisters, when he says:

> At this time Saint Quiteria, Genivera, etc., Basilia, virgins and martyrs, daughters of L. Catellius, etc.

The ancient Breviaries of Spain also acknowledge this, for we read in them:

> All of them, seized by persecutors in various places, completed their martyrdom.

Julianus speaks specifically of the martyrdom of Saint Basilia somewhat further on, although in his copy *Syria* is corruptly written instead of *Syrmium*. He says:

> In Syria—I read, in Syrmium—the martyrdom of Saint Basilia, sister of Saint Quiteria of Spain, is celebrated.

When Jerome de la Higuera read *Syria* in his copy, he composed an elegant hymn to these holy virgins. It was printed by Sandoval, bishop of Tuy, in his history of the Church of Tuy. In it he praises at length the fact that all parts of the world were ennobled by the blood of these virgins and sisters: Basilia having fallen in Syria of Asia, Germana at Carthage in Africa, and the others in Europe. He says:

> You, Syria, O Basilia,
>
> And Africa, honor Germana;
>
> And Genivera, the city of Tuy,
>
> Nearest to the Ocean.
>
> And Eumelia, Abobriga,
>
> The head of Gallaecia, honors,
>
> Celebrating with annual worship,
>
> Resounding with fitting song.
>
> Through Africa, through Asia,
>
> And through the regions of Europe,
>
> Scattered by heavenly command,
>
> You consecrated the world with blood.
>
> O thrice-blessed Spain,
>
> Content with three regions;
>
> It sees its three regions
>
> Reddened by your purple.

I confess that, in those ancient and golden ages of faith, it would not seem at all difficult for me to believe that a delicate virgin born in Spain suffered martyrdom in Syria, since many examples of this kind are available in what has been said above. Nor would it be strange or unprecedented for someone to make a pilgrimage to Palestine out of devotion.

Nevertheless, I consider the reading *Syrmium* more credible. Since we know a Syrmium in Spain, we have no need to seek Saint Basilia in foreign and extremely distant regions.

Some are pleased to think that our Basilia was that Basilissa who, as the wife of Saint Julian, martyred at Antioch, persevered in virginity. Her feast is celebrated on 9 January, and her body, together with that of her husband, was transferred in earlier years to the monastery of Saint Julian of Samos. Chronology, however, does not permit this, since Saint Julian suffered under Diocletian, whereas Saint Basilia suffered no fewer than 160 years earlier, namely in the days of which we are speaking.

I say nothing for the moment of the difference in the manner of death and in the names themselves: one obtained the palm of martyrdom, while the other rested in peace; one was called Basilia, the other Basilissa.

I cannot remain silent about the aforementioned hymn, because of its elegance. I shall give it with the preceding verses cut away:

> O noble offspring
>
> Of Catillius, descendant of the Lusitanians,
>
> Nobler in faith
>
> Than you were in blood.
>
> Genivera and Eumelia,
>
> Germana and Basilia,
>
> Happy four-horse chariot of virgins,
>
> And perhaps spur of martyrs.
>
> *(Here insert the preceding verses.)*
>
> If you wished to add
>
> Five remaining sisters to these,
>
> You would make a blessed company
>
> Even of nine Muses.
>
> Would not these nine excellent Muses
>
> Better than the profane ones
>
> Kindle the consecrated breasts of poets
>
> With divine heat?
>
> Not so does Olympus shine
>
> With blazing torches,
>
> When fertile night raises up
>
> Limbs weakened by sleep.
>
> O unbroken martyrs,
>
> And most chaste virgins:
>
> You set before your virgins
>
> A sign leading to martyrdom.
>
> Rejoice, priest of Ovid,
>
> You bishop of Bracara,
>
> Who deserved to send
>
> So many daughters to the heavens.
>
> Come, holy virgins,
>
> And do not despise
>
> The vows, voices, and prayers
>
> Of those who pour them out from the heart.
>
> Favor the true tears
>
> Which we pour out before Christ,
>
> So that he, gentle through your prayers,
>
> May grant forgiveness.

Saint Wilgefortis, or Liberata, is usually listed last among the sisters; Dexter deals with her especially. Trugillus says that, after the sisters’ departure, Liberata—who seemed to excel among the others in faith and religion—converted many pagans by her example and holy words. While she was living a solitary life in a certain desert, many Christians and pagans alike flocked to her.

Two matters concerning her may be doubted: one concerns the kind of martyrdom, the other the city in which it occurred. Molanus, whom Baronius transferred into the Roman Martyrology, maintains that she triumphed after being placed upon a cross. The Breviaries of Sigüenza and Palencia state that she was beheaded. The latter says:

> After all her sisters had been sent to the heavenly kingdoms, blessed Liberata was finally tortured with many torments. Since she could not be torn away from the faith, she departed to the Lord by the cutting off of her head. And thus, liberated from being submerged in the river—when she was born—liberated from the error of unbelief through baptism, liberated from corruption of the flesh—for she suffered in order to preserve her chastity—and liberated from the prison of the body through the triumph of martyrdom, she reached Christ free.

It is nevertheless plausible that she underwent both forms of punishment, as well as many others. It can easily be believed that she was first placed upon a cross and then, when she had preached Christ God upon it for a long time, her head was cut off so that she would not bring the whole people to him.

That crucifixion does not immediately inflict death is sufficiently demonstrated by what Mark says in chapter 15:

> Pilate wondered whether he had already died,

namely after six hours from the crucifixion; and by the case of Andrew, who lived upon the cross for three days.

That it was customary finally to kill those once placed upon a cross with a sword may be inferred from what we read in John, chapter 19:

> Then the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man, and of the other who had been crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs; nevertheless he was not left without a wound, for one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance.

If we examine the records of the ancients, we find that the cross, the *patibulum*, and the fork—which were regarded as forms of the same punishment—were not the final penalty of the condemned, according to Callistratus, in the title *On Capital Punishments*, section “Famosas,” in the Digest *On Punishments*, and Isidore, book V of the *Etymologies*.

Baronius gathers this in his notes on 7 April from the following passage of Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 49:

> The Senate judged him and ordered that he be sought for punishment according to ancestral custom. He asked what sort of punishment that was; and when he learned that the neck of a naked man was inserted into a fork—behold, the accused was first placed upon a cross; what happened next?—and that his body was beaten to death with rods, and finally thrown headlong from a rock, etc.

Similarly, even today in England those convicted of treason against the royal majesty are placed upon a cross; then, after the rope has been cut, they are cut down with swords while half alive.

I have said this for those who, satisfied with merely reading the text of Baronius’s Martyrology, might believe that Saint Liberata was fastened to a true cross. I myself certainly do not affirm this. For it is clear from the most ancient records of the Spanish Churches that she was not placed upon a cross, but, after enduring many torments with unconquered courage, finally ended her life by the cutting off of her head.

What is said about the cross must be understood altogether as referring to the *equuleus*—the rack. There is no doubt that this is contained under the words “tortured with many torments, since she could not be torn away from the faith,” and so forth.

That the ancients sometimes customarily called the *equuleus* a cross is declared by Cardinal Baronius himself in his notes on 22 January. He says:

> You also have the *equuleus* represented in a certain manner as a cross. These are the words of Theophilus, a companion of Saint Dorothea, while hanging on the rack: “Behold, now I am a Christian, because I am suspended on a cross.”

The author of the Life of Saint Dorothea adds that Theophilus spoke correctly, for, he says, the *equuleus* bears a certain likeness to a cross.

Baronius therefore maintains that the *equuleus* was an upright, strong, screw-operated post with a transverse beam that could be tightened and loosened, to which the limbs were tied and stretched at the torturer’s discretion. This agrees with the words of Saint Romanus in Prudentius’s tenth hymn of the *Peristephanon*:

> You think me wretched because I hang with arms bent backward,
>
> Stretched out; because my feet are torn apart;
>
> Because the joints resound with cracking sinews.

They therefore called every upright post from which a condemned person hung a cross. Hence Seneca, book *To Marcia on Consolation*, says:

> I see crosses there—not of one single kind, but fashioned differently by different people. Some hang a man with his head turned toward the ground; others drive a post through his private parts; others spread his arms upon a crossbeam, etc.

That Wilgefortis was suspended upon the *equuleus* and torn apart upon it was the reason she is said to have been placed upon a cross. Usually, however, martyrs were taken down from it and beheaded with a sword. Thus, concerning the aforementioned Theophilus, who declared that he was hanging on a cross, the Roman Martyrology itself admits:

> Tortured most cruelly on the rack, he was finally struck down with the sword.

It asserts the same concerning Saint Dorothea, on the same day, namely 6 February.

I have a most fitting example of the entire matter in Saint Eulalia of Barcelona. The Roman Martyrology, on 12 February, says that she received the glorious crown of martyrdom upon a cross. Yet the records of the Church of Barcelona, and the ancient Breviaries of Palencia and Astorga, report that she was suspended upon the rack by Decianus and finally—according to the *Thesaurus Concionatorum* and Equilinus, book I, chapter 54—beheaded outside the city walls.

No author except Baronius says that she was fastened to a true cross. Isidore, in the Mozarabic Breviary, sings as follows on her feast:

> Seeking the patron of the cross, she is suspended on a cross.

This must nevertheless be understood altogether as referring to the *equuleus*, as we shall demonstrate more fully in its proper place, in Commentary 3 on the year 300.

There is disagreement among authorities about the city that Saint Wilgefortis, or Liberata, consecrated with her blood. Julianus seems to assert that she died near the Lusitanian town of Castraleuca, for he says:

> Victoria is said to have suffered at Córdoba, and Wilgefortis or Liberata in Lusitania, at Castraleuca.

Ptolemy mentions it in his map of Lusitania among the Celtic peoples.

The learned Gaspar Losada, in a manuscript defense of the Lectionary of Sigüenza, vigorously argues that Castraleuca was a notable town in the bishopric of La Guardia, or Egitaniensis, now called Castelblanco. For *Castraleuca* is a Latin-Greek expression formed from *castrum*, which in Latin means “castle,” and λευκότον (*leukoton*), which in Greek means “white.” Hence Leucothea is the White Goddess.

The reasoning is extremely subtle, if it were not contradicted by Dexter, who expressly states in this passage that she suffered at Amphilochium, which is a city of Orense. Dexter must certainly be preferred to Julianus.

I add that Castraleuca, which Ptolemy mentions, is by no means Castelblanco. That town was situated among the Celtic peoples, between Lisbon and the Sacred Promontory, for Ptolemy places it there. Castelblanco, however, lies much farther north, near Egitani­um, between the Douro and the Tagus.

Dexter’s words nevertheless object to us in the year 308:

> In Lusitania, in the city of Callensis, which lies near Castralaelia—or, corruptly, is said to have been called so—Saint Wilgefortis flourishes, having suffered death for the faith and chastity.

He argues that one should read *Castraleuca*, not *Castralaelia*, as Julianus reads it.

But from these words we do not at all establish—even if we read *Castraleuca*—that she suffered martyrdom there. We establish only that she flourished in the year 308, which could have happened after her body had been transferred there.

Indeed, we cannot even establish that she still flourished at Castraleuca, but rather in the city of Callensis, which is near Castraleuca.

The city of Callensis in Lusitania can be no other than Porto, an episcopal see. Hence everyone knows that the name *Portucalle* was formed from the two names. Mariana expressly states this in book I of his *History*, chapter 4:

> At the mouth of the Douro, where it flows into the Ocean, there was once the city of Cale, now called Caia. From it and Porto the name Portucale was formed, and from Portucale Lusitania is now called Portugal.

Let us also cite the classical Lusitanian author whom Losada himself greatly esteems, Resendius. In his treatise on the municipality of Évora, he says:

> The most noble city of Callensis is today called Portugallensis.

I likewise cite Carolus Clusius and Arnoldus Mylius, who assert the same in their *Geographical Synonymy of Places* apud Ortelius.

It must therefore be admitted that Saint Liberata died at Amphilochium after her sister Margaret, and that she was afterward transferred to the city of Callensis, or Portugallensis, where she became renowned for miracles in the year of the Lord 308.

I retain, however, the reading *Castralaelia* in Dexter, since Castraleuca is not near the city of Callensis. Moreover, it is certain, on the authority of Titus Livy, book XXVIII, that Laelius—famous throughout all antiquity—established his camps in various parts of Spain when he was waging war against the Carthaginians and Phoenicians.

Thus, just as certain towns were called *Castra Viceliana* from Vicelius and *Castra Metellinensia* from Metellus, so another was called *Castralaelia* from Laelius, near the city of Callensis. I therefore think that the error is rather in Julianus’s copy, and that *Castralaelia* should be read instead of *Castraleuca*.

In any case, the body of Saint Liberata was transferred from there to Sigüenza. The following is read on this matter in an ancient Breviary of that Church:

> After the martyrdom of Saint Liberata, in the course of time, she was buried in this gracious Church by Simon, then bishop of Sigüenza. During his episcopate, by apostolic authority, it was transferred from the regular to the secular clergy in the year of the Lord 120.
>
> Later, the illustrious Frederick of Portugal, then bishop of Sigüenza and afterward archbishop of Zaragoza under the name of this blessed virgin, built a royal chapel. There the holy body was honorably transferred on 15 July 1537, enclosed within a silver chest and a polished stone sarcophagus, with miracles being displayed. Her shift was so saturated with fresh blood that it seemed as though the blood had been shed the previous day.
>
> Also present were the venerable relics of Saints John and Thomas the Apostles, Stephen, Ignatius, Blaise, Gamaliel, and Sixtus, together with those of many martyrs, confessors, and virgins. People gathered from every direction to attend the translation and to obtain the plenary indulgence granted by Hadrian VI, Clement VII, and Paul III, then Roman pontiff, while the most Christian and invincible Roman emperor Charles V reigned in Spain.

What is said about the indulgence granted by three pontiffs in honor of the translation I understand as follows: it was first obtained from Hadrian in 1522; after his death it was obtained again from Clement around 1524, but the matter was delayed until the time of Paul, during whose pontificate the translation is said to have taken place, and was finally confirmed by him around 1534.

The most blessed virgin rests in a sarcophagus of varied and wonderfully polished jasper, the finest of its kind in Spain. Her feast is celebrated by the Church of Sigüenza with the office of a double feast of the first class and an octave, as that of its patroness.

See what Albarus Lupus wrote about her in his Lusitanian Martyrology, etc. Alphonsus Chacon, in book II of the *Martyrs of Caradigna*, although he is mistaken about the date of her martyrdom, since he supposes that she suffered under Diocletian, whereas it is certain that she died under Hadrian, nevertheless acknowledges that she was the sister of Saint Quiteria.

It would finally be unworthy of silence to omit what Julianus relates about Saint Sila, the nurse:

> When I accompanied Lord Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, through Lusitania and Gallaecia, I came to Jomarium, where the headquarters of the military order of Christ is located. There, near the church, was Saint Sila, virgin and martyr, whose body is preserved there. She is believed to be the virgin who bore and raised the nine virgin sisters—Quiteria, Liberata, and the other Lusitanian women. The anniversary of her martyrdom is celebrated on the Kalends of November. She is believed to have suffered not long after the virgins suffered.

Julianus himself also testifies that, down to his own age, the solemn cult of all the sisters together continued. He says:

> In my time Saint Quiteria and her eight sisters were venerated throughout Spain with great devotion. They were the daughters of L. Catellius Severus—or, according to another reading, of “a man”—consular official and governor of Gallaecia and Lusitania, a citizen of Bracara and ruler of that land. Their feast day was 18 January.

### 7. In the same Gallaecia, Saint Euphemia, etc.

We have said enough about her in the third position among her sisters.

### A.D. 138; A.R. 889

Mark is appointed the first bishop of the Gentiles at Jerusalem.

### A.D. 138; A.R. 889

At Barcelona in Spain, Saint Philetus the Senator, his wife Laeda, their children, and fifty-five other martyrs.

### [Col. 0317] A.D. 138; A.R. 889

Saint Pelagius is appointed by Saint Honoratus bishop of Toledo. He presides over the see of Toledo for twenty-six years and several additional months. He was a truly pious and praiseworthy man.

### A.D. 138; A.R. 889

At Amphilochium in Gallaecia of Spain, Saint Marina, or Margaret, virgin and martyr, suffered for the Christian faith and chastity.

### [Col. 0321] A.D. 138; A.R. 889

Wilgefortis, or Liberata, daughter of Catellius, ruler of the Lusitanians, suffered at Amphilochium.

### [Col. 0323] A.D. 138; A.R. 889

At Abobriga in the same Gallaecia, Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr.

### [Col. 0331] Note

#### A.D. 139—1. “In this year,” etc.

The authors disagree about the year of Hadrian’s death. Eusebius, whom Baronius follows, asserts that he died in the year of the Lord 140, after reigning twenty years and eleven months. Ambrosius Morales, however, agrees with Onuphrius and Dexter.

Regarding the day, Spartianus says:

> He died at Baiae on 10 July and was temporarily buried at Puteoli in Cicero’s villa.

From there he was transferred to Rome, according to Julius Capitolinus and Dio, who all state that Antoninus Pius succeeded him. Antoninus was born at Rome and received this name from his piety, having previously been called Titus Aurelius Fulvius Boionius.

#### 2. “Aulus Victor,” etc.

He succeeded Saint Theodosius, bishop of that see, about whom the Author had spoken in the year of the Lord 100. Whether he succeeded him immediately is not clear.

#### 3. “At Ulia in Baetica,” etc.

Ambrosius Morales, book VIII of his *History*, chapter 35, teaches that Ulia is now called Monte-Major and lies five leagues from Córdoba. In book IX, chapter 41, he asserts that a stone column still stands in the church of Monte-Major, erected by the people of Ulia to the emperor Antoninus Caracalla, as is clear from its inscription. He discusses the same matter in his *Antiquities*, folio 88.

Ptolemy mentions this city among the Turdetanian towns of Baetica, although in his manuscript we now corruptly read *Julia* instead of *Ulia*. Villanovanus, its commentator, is mistaken when he writes *Velia* and asserts that it is commonly now called *Belia*, for there is no city or town of that name in Spain.

At Ulia, therefore, or Monte-Major, near Córdoba, Saint Quadratus the bishop flourished. His feast is celebrated on 21 August in the Roman Martyrology and in Molanus’s additions to Usuard. Equilinus also treats of him in book VII, chapter 90, although he confuses this Quadratus with Quadratus, a disciple of the Apostles and bishop of Athens, who presented an apology for the faith to the emperor Hadrian. Dexter treated the latter above in the year 128, as did Jerome in his book *On Illustrious Men*.

They are nevertheless entirely different persons, as Equilinus himself is forced to admit, for he writes of them as different men: of the disciple of the Apostles in book V, chapter 47, and of our bishop in book VII, chapter 90.

What he adds—that Quadratus wrote about the Parthian war fought under the emperor Severus, and committed to writing the life and deeds of Avisius Cassius—cannot possibly apply to the Athenian bishop and disciple of the Apostles. The Parthian war under Severus took place in the year 200 of Christ, by which time that Quadratus, who is known to have been an old man in Hadrian’s time as a disciple of the Apostles, was no longer alive.

Therefore, the book on the Parthian war must necessarily have had another author.

The Roman Martyrology commemorates both Quadrati: the Athenian on 26 May and the Ulian on 21 August, although—as often happens in other cases—it omits the name of the city. Since no one mentions any other bishop and saint Quadratus, however, it is sufficiently indicated that the one discussed there is the Ulian.

#### 4. “The holy martyrs of Christ Facundus,” etc.

The town and river Caea still exist not far from the famous monastery of Saint Facundus in the region of León, formerly within the territory of the Gallaecian Lucenses. The place was made far more renowned by the blood of the holy brothers Facundus and Primitivus.

Their glorious martyrdom is related by the ancient Breviaries of Spain, from which the more recent authors Villegas, Maldonatus, Sanctorus, Trugillus, and others took their accounts. Molanus and Galesinus celebrate their annual memory on 27 November with this eulogy, the day on which they received the crowns of immortality:

> In Gallaecia, beside the river Caea, the birthday of the holy martyrs Facundus and Primitivus, to whom, after they had endured and overcome many torments, two crowns were brought by angels.

When the governor Atticus heard this, he said:

> Let their heads be cut off, lest there be a grove for the crowns.

The torments which they are said to have endured beforehand are reported in this manner in the ancient Breviaries: first, the cutting off of their fingers; the crushing of their shins in heavy fetters; the stench and horror of prison; a burning furnace, in which they remained unharmed for three days; food mixed with poison; iron claws; flames applied to their sides over fresh wounds; burning lime poured into their mouths; the cruel gouging out of their eyes; binding and hanging from a stake for three days; and finally, after their former health had miraculously been restored, a cruel flaying.

While the holy martyrs were undergoing such torments, the ancient records say, one of the bystanders cried out in a loud voice:

> I see two angels descending from heaven with two crowns, which they hold in their hands.

Then Atticus ordered their heads to be cut off, so that there would be no place for the crowns. When their heads were cut off, milk flowed out together with the blood.

The time at which this occurred is reported in very different ways. Some maintain that they died under the consuls Atticus and Praetextatus, namely in the year of the Lord 242. I believe this arose for no other reason than that they read that the judge who killed them was called Atticus. Others place it under the emperor Heliogabalus in 222. Lucas of Tuy and Trugillus come closer to the truth by placing it in 168, under the emperor Marcus Aurelius. Dexter places it in 139, at the beginning of the reign of Antoninus.

At the very least, all agree that they suffered long before the reign of Diocletian. It is therefore beyond doubt that Vasseus in his *Chronicle* and Marinaeus Siculus in book V are mistaken when they believe that these men were sons of Saint Marcellus, the centurion of the Legion, who did not hesitate to give his life for Christ in the persecution of Diocletian, around the year of the Lord 306.

Consequently, Baronius was also wrong to insert this claim into the Roman Martyrology, since neither Usuard, nor Molanus, nor Galesinus had it, and since the older Breviaries of Spain contradict it, together with Morales, book IX, chapter 40, and book X, chapter 19, and Antonius Yepes, Benedictine century 3, year 752, chapter 2. The claim is that Saints Facundus and Primitivus were sons of Saint Marcellus and died under Diocletian. He says:

> In Gallaecia, beside the river Caea, the holy Facundus and Primitivus, sons of Saint Marcellus the martyr, suffered under the emperor Diocletian and the governor Atticus.

Both statements must be removed from the text of the Martyrology.

### A.D. 139; A.R. 890

On 6 July of this year, Trajan Hadrian dies, and Antoninus Pius, adopted by him, succeeds him in the empire.

### A.D. 139; A.R. 890

Aulus Victor, bishop of Barcelona, presides for thirty-eight years.

### A.D. 139; A.R. 890

At Ulia in Baetica, Saint Quadratus the bishop flourishes.

### A.D. 139; A.R. 890

The holy martyrs of Christ Facundus and Primitivus, from the city of Caea in Gallaecia, were killed for Christ beside the river Caea.

### [Col. 0333] Note

#### A.D. 140—“Antoninus,” etc.

Eusebius has exactly the same entry in his *Chronicle*, and apparently Isidore took it from him in his own work, whether that Isidore was of Seville or of Córdoba; this will have to be examined in its proper place, namely in the year 384.

In this same year Saint Honoratus, formerly bishop of Toledo, went up to heaven. Saint Braulio commemorates him in his additions to the *Martyrology of Maximus*, saying:

> Saint Honoratus is celebrated in Spain, a Cantabrian by nation and bishop of Toledo. While preaching through various provinces and returning to his homeland of Cuenca for the sake of preaching, he died a glorious confessor on 31 December in the year of the Lord 140.

We have said more about him in the years 132 and 138.

### A.D. 140; A.R. 891

In this year the emperor Antoninus Pius is called “father of his country.”

### [Col. 0333C] Note

#### A.D. 141—“This,” etc.

Jerome wrote the same thing about Galen in his *Chronicle of Eusebius* under this year, and Isidore did so in his own. Let the physicians, whose chief he is, discuss his deeds.

### A.D. 141; A.R. 892

At this time Galen of Pergamum, the physician, flourished at Rome.

### [Col. 0333C] Note

#### A.D. 143—“Justin,” etc.

The ecclesiastical calendars themselves mention this matter on 13 April, as may be seen in the Roman Martyrology, on which day the martyrdom of Saint Justin the philosopher is commemorated. Consult Paulus Orosius, book VII, chapter 14.

As for the year in which he presented his book on behalf of the religion to the emperor, Baronius, in volume II of the *Annals*, thinks that he offered it to Antoninus Pius in the year of the Lord 149, although he had written the same work earlier, in 143.

The Roman Martyrology, however, states that he gave it to Antoninus’s successors, namely Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, which must have occurred after the year 163.

Eusebius and Dexter support the view that it was given to Antoninus Pius in the year of the Lord 143.

Jerome, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, says that Saint Justin wrote and offered not one book only, but two different books to different Caesars. He says:

> He labored greatly on behalf of the religion of Christ, so much so that he gave Antoninus Pius, his sons, and the Senate a book written against the Gentiles, and was not ashamed of the disgrace of the cross; and another book to the successors of that same Antoninus, Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

After he had vigorously defended the faith at Rome through books and disputations, wearing the dress of philosophers, and had rebuked the Cynic Crescentus, who blasphemed much against the Christians, as a glutton, fearful of death, and a follower of luxury and lust, he was finally accused, through Crescentus’s hostility and intrigues, of being a Christian, and shed his blood for Christ.

### A.D. 143; A.R. 894

Justin the philosopher presented a book on behalf of the religion to Antoninus.

### [Col. 0334B] Note

#### A.D. 145—1. “Valentinus,” etc.

All this has been taken from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius. The ancient Fathers contended against Valentinus: Tertullian wrote a special book against him, as well as book *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 30; Irenaeus, book II, chapter 4; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 31; and later Theodoret, book I of the *Compendium of Heretical Fables*.

The impious dreamer imagined thirty aeons, fifteen male and an equal number female, and Christ arising from their mixture and being sent into the Virgin’s womb, from whom, he falsely claimed, Christ received no more than water receives from a channel.

## 2. Concordia, etc.

Ptolemy recognized the city of Concordia in Lusitania; its situation corresponds to the town of Tomas, where, as we have said, Saint Silas, the nurse of Quiteria and her sisters, rests. Nearby flows the Beselga River, from which, it seems, the name Besulci was derived by Dexter [Col. 0334C]. The ancient Martyrologies—the Roman and Usuard’s—and, among the more recent, that of Galesinus, commemorate the holy martyrs Donatus and his companions on 17 February; Galesinus mentions them on two days, namely the aforementioned day and 23 March. Equilinus likewise mentions them in Book XI of his *Catalogue*, chapter 130, no. 69. The companions of Saint Donatus were Secundianus and Romulus, together with eighty-six others. The Roman Martyrology has this concerning them:

> At Concordia, the holy martyrs Donatus, Secundianus, and Romulus, together with eighty-six others who shared the same crown.

The others use almost the same words. Galesinus, however, is mistaken in his notes on 17 February when he suspects that they died under Julian the Apostate, in the year of the Lord 364, since, as you see, they suffered under Antoninus.

A.D. 145. A.R. 896. Valentinus the heretic became known; he continued until the time of Anicetus.

A.D. 145. A.R. 896. At Concordia in Lusitania, now called Besulci, the holy martyrs of Christ Donatus and his companions suffered greatly [var.: also].

[Note: [Col. 0334C]

A.D. 149.—Arianus, etc. You will read these very words in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* under this year.

] A.D. 149. A.R. 900. Arianus, a philosopher of Nicomedia, and Maximus of Tyre became known.

[Note: [Col. 0334C]

A.D. 150.—Apollonius, etc. This was borrowed from the same source, except that Eusebius gives the name of Caesar Verus, whose tutors Apollonius and Basilides are said to have been. Baronius, however, under the year [Col. 0334D] 189, believes that this Apollonius Chalcidius was first a pagan, afterward a Christian, and finally a martyr of Christ.

] A.D. 150. A.R. 901. Apollonius the Stoic, a Chalcidian by nationality, and Basilides of Syropolis, distinguished philosophers, are known; they were tutors of Caesar.

[Col. 0335] [Note: [Col. 0335A]

A.D. 155.—At Toledo she suffers, etc. All this account of Saint Marciana had been transferred, through the carelessness of a copyist or writer, to the year 255 in the printed Zaragoza manuscript. It is clear, however, that it must be restored to this place, since it concerns the year of the virgin’s passion, which was A.D. 155, as Julian expressly acknowledges in his *Chronicle*, having borrowed the information from no other source than Dexter. “Marciana,” he says, “suffered at Toledo in the year 155, somewhat after her sisters, on 12 July.”

Indeed, what happened to our Marciana of Toledo also happened to Martiana of Africa, just as what happened to Eulalia of Mérida happened to Eulalia of Barcelona: the similarity of their names and of certain features of their sufferings brought about confusion in the history; and once this confusion had arisen, someone was not lacking who denied that there were two, making one out of the two. The same thing happened in those cases in every respect. Both were called Eulalia; both endured wounds, the rack, iron claws, and burning torches; then it was added that from each woman’s mouth her soul flew into the heavens in the form of a very white dove. Hence Equilinus, writing of the woman of Mérida in Book I, chapter 54—whose feast is celebrated on 10 December—asserts that she died at Barcelona, making one person out of two.

The same thing happened to the Marcianas. Besides the similarity of their names, they were killed by similar martyrdoms, for each was thrown to wild beasts and torn apart by a bull. Therefore Baronius, in his notes on 12 July, believed that there had been only one. The very text of the Roman Martyrology, however, resists this conclusion, for it acknowledges that one died at Caesarea in Mauretania, Africa, and the other at Toledo. Concerning the African woman it says:

> On 9 January, or the fifth day before the Ides of January, in Caesarea of Mauretania, Saint Marciana the virgin, who, having been handed over to the beasts, completed her martyrdom.

Concerning the woman of Toledo, however:

> On 12 July, or the fourth day before the Ides of July, at Toledo, Saint Marciana, virgin and martyr, who, having been thrown to the beasts for the faith of Christ and torn apart by a bull, was crowned by martyrdom.

The same conclusion is resisted, as you see, by Dexter and Julian, who report that she suffered at Toledo and was the sister of eight other virgins and martyrs. Julian also adds:

> Another Marciana is mentioned in the Martyrologies, and although she died after being torn apart by a bull, nevertheless this woman [the one of Toledo] is much older.

It is remarkable with what praises the ancient people of Toledo celebrated Blessed Marciana. A proper and solemn office for her exists in the Gothic Breviary, where a sacred hymn relates how, moved by the divine Spirit, she shattered an idol erected over a spring; how, after she had been captured and scourged and handed over to procurers three times, she was suddenly freed three times when a wall miraculously appeared between the virgin and the procurer; and how, afterward given to the beasts to be devoured, she was kissed by a lion, wounded by a bull at the breasts, and finally killed by a leopard with a slight bite, after which she flew to her Bridegroom. Hear, please, the hymn that sings these things more sweetly:

> Let the voice of the Church  
> Celebrate the triumph of the sacred martyr;  
> Let one song resound for all,  
> In praise of the virgin Marciana.
>
> She attains the reward  
> Of her passion as she advances;  
> Willingly she dares, prepared,  
> To enter the arena of glory.
>
> For when she saw the image  
> Of the demon standing before her,  
> She struck it down. Beneath it  
> A broad stream perpetually flowed  
> At her feet.
>
> Soon, beaten with scourges, she is dragged  
> To the lofty halls of the prefect;  
> And in unlawful games [var.: before the aediles]  
> The virgin’s body is thrown down.
>
> When the robber of chastity  
> Pursues her among the shadows,  
> A wall, offered from heaven,  
> Shuts him out from the temple.
>
> Then bound to a stake,  
> She is confined amid profane speech;  
> But blasphemy bears its punishment—  
> Ruin and flames.
>
> Sent out to the beasts,  
> A lion rushes swiftly toward her;  
> He comes to adore  
> The virgin, not to eat her.
>
> Then a bull leaps forward,  
> Terrible in form and bellowing;  
> With a blow he furrows  
> Her tender breasts, wounding them.
>
> Afterward a swift beast,  
> With a spotted covering,  
> At last tears the girl’s limbs  
> With its deadly tooth.
>
> After these triumphs, her soul,  
> Escaping the bonds of the body,  
> Joyfully seeks the free  
> Heights of the highest heaven.
>
> To God the Father, etc.

What is said in the sixth verse—“But blasphemy bears its punishment, ruin and flames”—is intended to signify that the blasphemer who clamored for her to be handed over to the beasts paid the penalty for his blasphemy. He was called Budarius and was Jewish by nationality. For when the spirit of the devout virgin departed from her body, at that very moment the house of the blasphemer Budarius, together with everyone who was there, was consumed by a divine fire.

The house was frequently rebuilt by Budarius’s Jewish relatives, but it fell into ruin; and many who afterward gathered stones for its construction were seen carrying them to their burial. To this day there remains concerning that house an enduring sentence of the blessed martyr, and it continues destined to remain forever.

I have taken this word for word from the *Life of Saint Marciana*, preserved in a very old parchment manuscript in the library of the monastery of Saint Bernard outside the walls of Toledo; in every respect it agrees with the story of the hymn. Equilinus gives the same account more briefly in Book II, chapter 58, but under the name of Saint Marciana of Caesarea.

What Saint Marciana did—seeking an opportunity for martyrdom by breaking the idol—was afterward prohibited by canon 60 of the Council of Elvira, which says:

> If anyone breaks idols and is killed at that place, since this is not written in the Gospel and is never found to have been done under the apostles, it has been decreed that he is not to be received among the number of martyrs.

Baronius learnedly explains how far this was permitted after Constantine’s laws concerning the destruction of idols had been issued, under 9 April, on the occasion of Saint Eusychius, who was killed by Julian the Apostate because he had overturned a shrine of Fortune.

Our Marciana, however, appears to be exempt from the canon’s ruling because she suffered before the council, during the consulship of Aelius and Lateranus, as Dexter teaches. A mistake must have entered the printed manuscript of Dexter, so that it reads *Licentius* instead of *Lateranus*. Yet it is clear from Onuphrius and others that in the year of the Lord 155 the consulship was held by L. Aelius Aurelius Caesar, son of the emperor Pius, and Sextilius Lateranus. From this it is evident that the martyrdom of Marciana of Toledo should in no way be assigned to the year 255, as that manuscript had it, but to the year 155, as is proved by the consuls.]

A.D. 155. A.R. 906. At Toledo Saint Marciana suffers; she was the daughter of Catellius Regulus of Lusitania and the sister of eight other virgins, during the consulship of Aelius [var.: Licentius] and Lateranus.

[Note: [Col. 0336D]

A.D. 156.—1. Under Anicetus, etc. If we followed the Baronian chronology of the Roman pontiffs, we would be compelled entirely to depart from Dexter’s opinion. For since Baronius asserts that Anicetus began to sit in the year of the Lord 137, when his predecessor Saint Pius was removed by martyrdom, it could not follow from his view that Polycarp came to Rome in the year 156, while Anicetus was already seated there.

Saint Irenaeus, Saint Jerome, and Eusebius, however, oppose Baronius. Irenaeus of Lyons, in Book III, chapter 3, says:

> For it was he—namely Polycarp—who, having come to Rome under Anicetus, converted many of those heretics whom we have mentioned to the Church of God, proclaiming this one and only truth which he had received from the apostles and which the Church transmits.

Jerome likewise says the following in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Polycarp:

> Because of certain questions concerning the day of Easter, under the emperor Antoninus Pius, while Anicetus governed the Church in Rome, he came to Rome, where he restored to the faith very many believers who had been deceived by the persuasion of Marcion and Valentinus. Later, while Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus were reigning, he was handed over to the fire at Smyrna.

Certainly, if Polycarp came under Anicetus while Antoninus Pius was then reigning, Anicetus had begun to sit before the year of the Lord 163, although Baronius himself says that Antoninus died then. Therefore Anicetus’s pontificate cannot in any way be postponed to the year 167, as Baronius contends. [Col. 0337B]

Eusebius agrees entirely with Dexter, for he says in the *Chronicle*:

> In the year 156, Anicetus, the tenth bishop, holds the episcopate of the Roman Church; under him Polycarp, coming to Rome, corrected many from heretical error.

Add to this Ambrosius Morales, a most exact chronographer, who asserts that Saint Anicetus began to sit from the year of the Lord 153. Dominicus Tempesta of Rome agreed with him in his *Lives of the Supreme Pontiffs*, published at Rome in 1596, with illustrations.

2. At Blanda in Spain, etc. “In Spain” was added to distinguish this city from another city of the same name in Lucania, or Basilicata, a province of the Kingdom of Naples, which Ptolemy mentions in his maps of Italy. In Spain, likewise, Ptolemy recognizes Blanda among the Laletani of Tarraconensis; it is now called Blanes, according to Florianus de Ocampo, Villanova, and Arnoldus Millius.

Here, therefore, under the emperor Antoninus, the holy martyrs of Christ Bonosus and Maximianus were crowned by martyrdom. Their memory, with blessing, remains in the Martyrologies on 21 August, where Ado also asserts that their acts of martyrdom exist. Usuard likewise says:

> On the same day, the holy martyrs Bonosus and Maximianus, whose acts are preserved.

Equilinus, in Book XI, chapter 138, no. 218, says:

> Bonosus and Maximianus suffered as martyrs on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September; Ado says that their deeds are preserved.

Galesinus reports that Bede also remembered them, and says:

> On this same day, the holy martyrs Bonosus and Maximianus, whose deeds for the faith are read as having been bravely accomplished.

The Roman Martyrology says nothing about their acts because, as Baronius observes in his notes, they seem already to have disappeared—alas!—to the loss of the saints’ glory. They have been found nowhere, but, as we trust, God will someday bring those acts to light. See other persons of the same name under the year 308.]

A.D. 156. A.R. 907. Under Pope Anicetus, Saint Polycarp came to Rome; remarkable in doctrine and in the example of his life, he freed many from errors.

[Col. 0337] A.D. 156. A.R. 907. At Blanda in Spain the holy martyrs Bonosus and Maximianus suffer.

[Note: [Col. 0337C]

A.D. 160.—1. At Carthage, etc. Cardinal Baronius revived the memory of the holy martyrs Modestus and Julian, who suffered at Carthage and whose names had disappeared from the Roman Martyrology through the carelessness of copyists. Having found them in ancient manuscript codices at Rome, he recorded them in these words:

> On 12 February, or the day before the Ides of February, at Carthage, the holy martyrs Modestus and Julian.

2. At Interamnium Flavium, etc. In the printed Dexter the name of the city where Saint Domnina and her sisters received the crown of martyrdom was missing. That they should be read as having died at Interamnium Flavium is proved by Saint Proculus, who, as everyone acknowledges, suffered in the same town as she did, and, according to Dexter, below under the year 175 completed his martyrdom there. He says:

> At Interamnium Flavium in Spain, Saint Proculus the martyr.

They all suffered on the same day, namely 14 April. Galesinus has the following on that day:

> At Interamnium, Saint Proculus the martyr, and likewise Saint Domnina the virgin and her companions, who, because of their illustrious confessions of the faith, were granted the crowns of martyrdom and enjoy eternal glory.

He cites ancient manuscript codices, as well as Bede and Usuard. Equilinus, in Book XI, chapter 130, no. 121, says:

> Proculus the martyr and Domnina the virgin with her virgin companions suffered at Interamnium on that very day.

Usuard and the Roman Martyrology read as follows:

> At Interamnium, Blessed Proculus the martyr, and likewise Saint Domnina the virgin with her virgin companions, crowned.

Ado agrees on the same day.

Baronius believed that they suffered at Interamnium in Italy, as though there were no other city of that name in the world. Ptolemy, however, clearly describes two Interamnia in Spain: one in the Asturian region near Lucus Asturum, or Oviedo; the other not far from Asturica itself. The latter bore not only the name Interamnium but also the surname Flavium, because it had been established in honor of Flavius Vespasian.

For, as Morales testifies in Book IX, chapter 25 of his *History*, many cities in Spain were given the name Flavia from him, such as Flaviobriga, Iria Flavia, Flavium Brigantium, and, among the others, Interamnis Flavia. It was called Interamnis, or Interamnium [by others, Interamnum], because it lay between two rivers.

Morales thought that this Interamnium Flavium was the town of Fuente en Calada, in the diocese of Astorga, one and a half leagues from the monastery of Nucal. In this, however, he departed completely from the truth, since Fuente en Calada is not situated between rivers, whereas nearby lies the ancient and noble town of Benavente, which is not merely located between rivers but between the broad and abundant rivers Esla and Órbigo. These rivers surround or, rather, touch Benavente on either side.

Therefore there can be no doubt that Benavente was formerly called Interamnium Flavium, and that the most holy champions of Christ, Proculus, Domnina, and her sisters, reddened it with their blood.

To remove every further doubt, we have the *Itinerary of the Emperor Antoninus*, from which this is plainly inferred by the distances it gives. On the route from Asturica to Tarraco, the passage through Interamnium is noted; the route necessarily passes through Benavente, not through Fuentecalada. There it is stated that Interamnium Flavium lies thirty miles from Asturica. Antoninus states the same on the route from Bracara to Asturica, whose beginning is Salabiana, and on another whose beginning is Lamia. He repeats the same on the route from Asturica to Burdigala. I have brought all these passages together so that no one may suppose that a mistake has entered the number thirty miles.

Our conclusion is thereby clearly established. From Asturica to Fuentecalada there are not thirty miles, that is, ten leagues, but eighteen miles, or six leagues. From Asturica to Benavente, however, there are certainly thirty miles, or ten leagues.

3. Pelagius, etc. It is clear from the chronology of the bishops of Toledo, which Archbishop Loaysa published together with the Gothic councils, that Patruinus, or Paternus—he was also called Patruinus, Patrinus, or Pater­nus—succeeded Pelagius, bishop of Toledo.

It is remarkable how far Loaysa departed from the truth when he said that Patruinus was present at the First Council of Toledo and there overthrew the resurgent heresy of Priscillian. That council was held in the year of the Lord 205, as we shall show in its proper place. At that time, even according to Loaysa himself, Saint Asturius was bishop of Toledo, and his name is found among the nineteen bishops who were present there.

Patruinus, or Paternus, who is listed first, was bishop of Braga. We shall demonstrate this below in the place cited and in the commentaries under the years 386. Loaysa himself could easily have noticed this, since he reports that between Patruinus and Asturius, who was bishop in the year 405, seven others intervened: Turibius, Quintius, Vincentius, Paulatus, Natalis, Olympius, and Audentius. There can be no doubt that these men held the episcopal office for many years.

There is therefore no way that Patruinus could have attended that council, which took place around the year 400. Indeed, he flourished many years earlier and held the see for twenty-nine years, namely from the year 160 until 179. We shall discuss him below under the years 185 and 208.]

A.D. 160. At Carthage in Spain, Modestus and Julian flourish.

A.D. 160. At Interamnium Flavium, the virgin Domnina with her distinguished sisters, martyrs of Christ.

A.D. 160. Patruinus succeeds Pelagius, bishop of Toledo; a faithful man, he presides over that see for twenty-nine years.

[Col. 0339] [Note: [Col. 0339A]

A.D. 162.—This year, etc. Cardinal Baronius postpones the death of Antoninus Pius to the following year, 163. Eusebius, however, supports Dexter in the *Chronicle*, saying:

> In the year of the Lord 162, at his villa called Lorium, twelve miles from the city, M. Antoninus died in the seventy-second year of his life. M. Antoninus, also called Verus, ruled the Romans for fourteen years, and Lucius Aurelius Commodus for nineteen years and one month. Pius had ruled for twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty-six days.

The two Caesars shared the names Aelius, Aurelius, Verus, and Antoninus, but differed in their praenomina, Marcus and Lucius. The latter was also called Ceionius and Commodus.

Julius Capitolinus in his *Life of Pius*, Dio in his *Life of Hadrian*, Justin in his *Apology to Antoninus*, Spartianus in his *Life of Hadrian*, Theophilus of Antioch, and Galen in his book *Against Those Who Wrote Concerning Types* discuss this difference and agreement of names; Baronius follows and cites them.

It is worth observing, however, that Marcus Aurelius descended on his father’s side from the Spaniards. His great-great-grandfather, namely, was Annius Verus the Spaniard. Julius Capitolinus records this, and Morales, following him, notes it in Book IX, chapter 28. Many monuments were also erected to him in Spain. At Málaga there still stands a marble column bearing the inscription:

> M. Aurelius Antoninus Pius Augustus, etc.

At Barcelona there is another:

> To Faustina Augusta, wife of the emperor; to Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, by decree of the decurions.

Finally, Orosius, in Book VII, chapter 14, agrees concerning the death of Antoninus Pius and the choice of his successors.

] A.D. 162. A.R. 913. In this year, on the Nones of March, Antoninus Pius died. Two succeeded him: one, Marcus Antoninus Verus; the other, Lucius Aurelius Ceionius.

[Note: [Col. 0339C]

A.D. 165.—For Caesar Lucius, etc. Eusebius says exactly this in the *Chronicle* under this year, and almost in the same words, for he says:

> While Caesar Lucius was sacrificing at Athens, a fire was seen to be carried across the sky from east to west.

] A.D. 165. A.R. 916. While Caesar Lucius was sacrificing at Athens, a fire was seen to be carried across the sky from east to west, and not without a miraculous vision.

[Note: [Col. 0339C]

A.D. 166.—Vologeses, etc. Eusebius also records this under the year 166. Orosius says in Book VII, chapter 17, that he devastated Armenia, Cappadocia, and Syria. The Parthian war was waged against Vologeses, in which he was defeated. Dio says much about this in his account of Antoninus.

Misius Severianus, first commander of the Roman troops, lost his army and his life after being pierced by a weapon; but Caesar Lucius, betrothed to the daughter of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, obtained the victory. On this matter see Xiphilinus and Julius Capitolinus in their account of Antoninus.

] A.D. 166. A.R. 917. Vologeses, king of the Parthians, devastated the neighboring provinces.

[Note: [Col. 0339C]

A.D. 167.—1. Seleucia, etc. On the promontory of Syrian Antioch there stands Seleucia, formerly founded by Seleucus Nicator, as Josephus testifies in Book XVIII, chapter 16 of the *Antiquities*. Saint Paul traveled through it, as Luke relates in Acts 13; today it is called Soldino.

When Vologeses, king of the Parthians, captured this city and devastated the surrounding provinces, it was an object of fear to all Syria. It was later recaptured in war by the Roman army under the command of Caesar Lucius, together with three hundred thousand people. Eusebius also relates this with Dexter under this year. Orosius reports that forty thousand were captured.

2. At Pisa, etc. Eusebius himself records the same account of the philosopher Peregrinus, but under the following year.]

A.D. 167. A.R. 918. The city of Seleucia in Syria was captured together with three hundred thousand people.

A.D. 167. A.R. 918. At Pisa, the philosopher Peregrinus threw himself alive upon a pyre that he had built from pieces of wood.

[Note: [Col. 0340A]

A.D. 168.—At Masia in Spain, etc. The Martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, and the Roman Martyrology speak of Saint Pasycrates on 25 May, relating that he was crowned by martyrdom together with Saint Valention and two others.

A corruption entered their codices when some read *Moesia* and others *Mysia* instead of *Masia*. This is sufficiently demonstrated by the fact that throughout Mysia, or Moesia, there is no city or town called Dorostorus. Ptolemy, indeed, recognizes Dorticum in Book III, chapter 7, of Mysia—but not Dorostorum—situated beside the Danube.

Hence, because the name of the place was unknown, it came about that different authors gave it different names. Theodoret, in Book III, chapter 6, calls it Dorostolum and places it in Thrace, that is, outside Mysia. Cedrenus, in his *Summary of History*, calls it Distro; Cardinal Baronius noted this under 25 May, letter b. It is no wonder that a place could not be found which did not exist.

In Spain, however, there was not Moesia or Mysia but the city of Masia. Pliny reports that bricks were made at the city of Masia in Further Spain which, once dried, did not sink in water. According to Stephanus, Masia also belonged to the Tartessians, or Baeticans. The name referred not only to the city but also to the surrounding region, which was called Masia; Vitruvius likewise sometimes acknowledges this, although he writes *Maxia* with an x. In a more corrupt form Ptolemy calls it Maxilia, near Hispalis.

Villanova places it in the Turdetani of Baetica, near Mount Termarium, on his map of ancient Spain. Today the quicksilver mines known commonly as Almadén are located there.

I have no doubt, therefore, that Saint Pasycrates and his companions were inhabitants of Masia Tartessica in Spain and that they flourished there at the place called Dorotum. Among Greek authors the transition from Μάσια (*Masia*) to Μοέσια (*Moesia*) was easy; once this error had been admitted, Μύσια (*Mysia*) could more easily be written, since that Pontic province is spelled in both ways. From this one may see how much light Dexter contributes to ecclesiastical history.

Peter Equilinus also discussed Saint Pasycrates and his companions in Book XI, chapter 130, no. 151, but deliberately refrained from naming the city because of the uncertainty of the reading.

The holy martyrs of Christ Julius and Hesychius should be thought to have belonged to the same city, province, and place. The Latin Martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Ado, and the Roman Martyrology celebrate them as having suffered at “Dorostorum,” as they say, in Moesia. Julius is commemorated on 27 May in these words:

> At Dorostorum in Mysia, the passion of Blessed Julius, who, in the time of the emperor Alexander, when he was a veteran and had completed his military service, was arrested by officials and brought before the governor Maximus. In his presence, while he cursed the idols and most steadfastly professed the name of Christ, he was punished with a capital sentence.

When he was being led to his passion, Equilinus adds in Book V, chapter 56, a certain Christian soldier named Hesychius, his very close friend, commended himself to him in prayer and kissed him. The soldiers then seized Hesychius also, and he suffered twenty days later, as will be said below, on 15 June, namely in Book V, chapter 119, where he again says of Hesychius:

> Having been tormented in prison for many days, he was finally crowned with martyrdom when the sword struck him in his confession of Christ.

A significant argument in this matter is that the Greek Menologies make no mention at all of the holy martyrs Julius and Hesychius. Yet if they had been martyrs of Mysia, a Greek province, they would certainly not have omitted their memory. Since they are celebrated only by the Latins, they are beyond doubt Latin martyrs.

Once this is granted, no other Masia can be assigned in Europe whose inhabitants were made illustrious by their passions, apart from our Baetican Masia, which we have discussed.

I hold the same view concerning Saint Dasius, bishop and martyr, whose memory is observed in the Roman Martyrology on 20 November. Because he refused to consent to the indecencies of the festival of Saturn, he was beaten under the judge Bassus.

For the Martyrology says that he suffered at Dorostorum in Mysia, just as it says of the martyrs mentioned above. We have shown, however, that there was never any city called Dorostorum in Mysia.

As for Dasius, the Greeks seem not to know who he was when they celebrate his memory. In the Menology they say that he was a soldier flourishing in youth and beauty, whereas the records of the Roman Martyrology make clear that he was a bishop—unless one would rather suppose that a mistake entered the Roman Martyrology rather than the Greek one.

The Roman Martyrology also says that Saint Aemilianus the martyr, who received the palm of martyrdom under the governor Capitolinus in the time of Julian the Apostate because he had broken idols, was burned on 18 July, since he suffered at Dorostorum in Mysia. The Greek Menology, however, gives a different reading: at Durostulum in Mysia. His memory was exceedingly celebrated among the Greeks, for the emperor Basil restored his church at some time, as Cedrenus records in his *Summary of History*, under Basil.]

A.D. 168. A.R. 919. At Masia in Spain, at the place called Dorotum, Saint Pasycrates, a remarkable man in his manner of life [var.: conversion] and in all his works.

[Col. 0341] [Note: [Col. 0341B]

A.D. 169.—1. Marcus, etc. Irenaeus discusses Marcus, the disciple of Valentinus, at great length in Book I, chapters 8 and 9, *Against Heresies*. He says:

> Marcus was exceedingly skilled in magical deception, by which he led astray many men and not a few women.

A little farther on:

> He devotes himself especially to women, and particularly to those who are honorable, dressed in purple, and very wealthy. Often attempting to bring them over, he says to them with flattering words: “I wish to make you share in my grace. The place of your greatness is among us; we must come together as one. Receive first from me and through me the grace. Prepare yourself as a bride awaiting her bridegroom, so that you may be what I am and I may be what you are. Establish in your bridal chamber the seed of light. Behold, my grace rises within you. Open your mouth and prophesy.”
>
> When the woman replies, “I have never prophesied; I do not know how to prophesy,” he performs certain invocations again, to her astonishment, and says to the woman whom he is seducing: “Open your mouth and speak whatever you wish, and you will prophesy.”
>
> The woman, deceived and elated by what has been said, warming her soul with the suspicion that she is beginning to prophesy, dares to speak deliriously and whatever happens to come into her mind—everything vainly and boldly. From then on she thinks herself a prophetess and gives thanks to Marcus for having shared his grace with her. She longs to reward him, not only by giving from her substance—which is how he gathered great wealth—but also through physical union, and she desires to be united with him in every respect.

You have seen the deception of this diabolical man, drawn in vivid colors by the holy Irenaeus, his contemporary. But was he content to seduce women in the eastern regions? Not at all.
