Irenaeus himself testifies that he also came to the West. Concerning what happened to Marcus and his followers in Gaul near the Rhône, he adds:

> Saying and doing such things, they also led many women astray in the regions near the Rhône, which are our own regions. Some of these, having consciences seared, even make public confession.

He reports in the following manner how others resisted them:

> Some of the most faithful women, who possess the fear of God and are not seducible—women whom he had attempted to seduce in the same way as the others, commanding them to prophesy—blew upon him and anathematized him and separated themselves from this madman, who pretended to breathe forth the divine. They knew for certain that prophecy is not bestowed upon human beings by Marcus the magician, but upon those to whom God from above grants his grace.

This is precisely what Dexter relates here as having happened to him at Toledo and Valencia in Lusitania:

> When he entered Carpetania, having been driven from Toledo and wishing to corrupt Valencia of Lusitania, he was badly treated in that province. He corrupted some little women, but was mocked by others.

Jerome agrees with Irenaeus in his commentary on Isaiah 64, saying that the Gnostics, through Marcus the Egyptian, first deceived noble women of Gaul near the Rhône and afterward noble women of Spain.

When Dexter says that the Spaniards, warned by Peter in his Second Epistle and repeatedly by Paul, resisted Marcus, this should not be understood to mean that they alone were warned by the apostles. Rather, the Spaniards, when reading the apostles’ Epistles, found in the prophetic writings and teachings a lifelike and detestable portrait of Marcus.

Indeed, Peter, the chief of the apostles, wrote almost his entire Second Epistle against future heretics, and most clearly against this Marcus. In chapter 2 he says:

> There will be false teachers among you, who will introduce destructive sects, and many will follow their debaucheries; through them the way of truth will be blasphemed. In their greed they will trade in you with fabricated words. Their judgment has not been idle for a long time, and their destruction does not sleep.

And below:

> These people, like irrational animals, naturally born for capture and destruction, blaspheming in matters they do not understand, will perish in their corruption, receiving the reward of wrongdoing. They regard the pleasures of the day as delights; their eyes are full of adultery and of unceasing sin; they entice unstable souls.

He develops many other points of the same kind throughout chapters 2 and 3.

Paul likewise gave the same warning both elsewhere and in the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 4:

> The Spirit clearly says that in the latter times some will depart from the faith, attending to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons—there is Marcus’s magic—speaking lies in hypocrisy, etc.

In the Second Epistle, chapter 3, he says:

> But know this, that in the last days perilous times will come. People will be lovers of themselves, greedy, boastful, proud, lovers of pleasures rather than of God. Avoid them.

Why? Consider Marcus:

> For among them are those who creep into households and capture little women burdened with sins and led by various desires.

Nothing could have been said more clearly. Nor did the Apostle fail to warn the Hebrews of Spain in the Epistle that he wrote to them concerning Marcus’s future arrival. For in the final chapter he says:

> Do not be led away by various and foreign teachings, for it is best to establish the heart by grace, not by foods.

What wonder, then, if the Catholic Spaniards, men and women, instructed by so many and such great warnings, mocked Marcus the worst of heretics and drove him dishonorably from their provinces?

2. Caesar Lucius, etc. Eusebius agrees in the *Chronicle*, almost in the same words. Read Orosius, Book VII, chapter 15.]

A.D. 169. A.R. 920. Marcus the heretic came to Spain. The Spaniards, however, having been warned by Peter in his Second Epistle and repeatedly by Paul, resisted him. When he entered Carpetania, he was driven from Toledo; and when he wished to corrupt Valencia of Lusitania, he was badly treated in that province. He corrupted some little women, but was mocked by others.

A.D. 169. A.R. 920. Caesar Lucius triumphs over the Parthians with his brother Commodus.

[Col. 0343] [Note: [Col. 0343A]

A.D. 170.—1. In the persecution, etc. Eusebius says the following in the *Chronicle*:

> In the year of the Lord 170, when persecution arose in Asia, Polycarp and Pionius suffered martyrdom; their written passions are also said to be extant.

This persecution was initiated by Marcus Aurelius. It was the fourth in order, if, with Dexter, we say that the first was under Nero, the second under Domitian, and the third under Trajan; Dexter says under the year 86, concerning Domitian, that he launched the second persecution against the Church. Orosius agrees in the chapter cited, 15, as does Jerome, whom we shall now cite.

The feast of Saint Polycarp is observed in the Roman Martyrology on 26 January, where his acts are summarized in the words of Jerome’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> Polycarp, a disciple of the apostle John and ordained by him bishop of Smyrna, was the chief man of all Asia. For he had as teachers and had seen some of the apostles and those who had seen the Lord. Because of certain questions concerning the day of Easter, under the emperor Antoninus Pius, while Anicetus governed the Church in Rome—around the year of the Lord 168—he came to Rome, where he restored to the faith very many believers who had been deceived by the persuasion of Marcion and Valentinus.
>
> When he happened by chance to meet Marcion, and Marcion said, “Do you recognize us?” Polycarp replied, “I recognize the firstborn of the devil.”
>
> Later, while Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus were reigning, during the fourth persecution after Nero, while the proconsul was seated at Smyrna and the entire people were shouting against him in the amphitheater, he was handed over to the fire.

Irenaeus discusses him in *Against Heresies*, Book II, chapter 3; Eusebius in Book IV, chapter 14, and Book V, chapter 24; Gregory of Tours in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 86; and others.

The martyrdom of Saint Pionius is recorded in the same Martyrology on 1 February in these words:

“At Smyrna, Saint Pionius, presbyter and martyr, who, after writing Apologies for the Christian faith and after the misery of imprisonment, during which he strengthened many of the brethren by his exhortations to endure martyrdom, was tormented by many tortures, fastened with nails, and placed upon a blazing pyre; thus he obtained a blessed end for Christ. Fifteen others also suffered with him.”

I regard the words “after writing Apologies for the Christian faith” as suspect. In Usuard, who has the entire sentence, they are absent; and if Pionius had written Apologies, Jerome would not have failed to honor and record his writings when listing ecclesiastical writers, nor would Eusebius have failed to mention his writings in Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 14, or elsewhere.

More difficult is what Dexter says at this point: that Pionius died in the same persecution in which Polycarp perished. For in his Acts, preserved by Surius in volume I under 1 February, he is said to have suffered in the persecution of Decius, when Decius was consul for the third time and Gratus for the second—that is, in the year of the Lord 254—not under Lucius Verus and Marcus Aurelius Commodus. This is more strongly supported by Cardinal Baronius, both in volume II of his *Annals* under that year and in his notes to the Roman Martyrology under 1 February.

In any event, whatever the truth about the Acts may be, Dexter followed Eusebius, who wrote almost the same words in his *Chronicle* and, toward the end of Book IV, chapter 14 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, says, on the testimony of a letter from the Church of Smyrna, that Pionius was crowned with martyrdom at precisely the same time as Polycarp.

Although Baronius interprets this as referring to the same month or day, it is clear from what Eusebius writes in his *Chronicle* that it refers not to the month or day but to the period of the same persecution, since he says: “When persecution arose in Asia” (in the year 170), “Polycarp and Pionius suffered martyrdom at Smyrna.” Peter de Natalibus agrees with Eusebius in Book III, chapter 68 of his *Catalogue of the Saints*, where, citing Eusebius’s Book IV of the *History*, he teaches that Pionius was killed in the time of the emperor Antoninus.

**2. Very many in Gaul, etc.** Since the fourth persecution, which arose under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, was universal throughout the whole world, it is certain that it also reached Gaul and Spain; but it is not clear who then died for the faith of Christ. At that time Valerius Julianus, governor of the province of Tarraconensis, and Gallus Maximianus, proconsul, held office in Spain, together with Fabius Rusticus and Aemilius Pontianus, whom Ambrosius Morales discusses in Book IX, chapter 38, of his *History*. Julius Atticus Accilianus was also proconsul under the same emperors, as the same author relates in chapter 40. Thus, under these officials, many martyrs in Spain flew to heaven.

Aurelius Prudentius provides distinguished testimony to this fact. In his sacred hymn on the martyrs of Caesaraugusta, he affirms that many in Spain were crowned with martyrdom not merely in one or two persecutions, but in all of them, although he himself speaks of Caesaraugusta, saying:

> As often as a savage storm,
> in ancient tempests, shook the afflicted world,
> a harsher frenzy unleashed its wrath
> upon this shrine.
>
> Nor did any rage depart without our glory,
> or devoid of illustrious blood;
> the number of martyrs always increased
> beneath every hailstorm.

See, therefore, that in every persecution not only were many in Spain adorned with martyrdom, but their number always increased beneath every hailstorm.

**A.D. 170. A.U.C. 921.** When persecution arose in Asia, Polycarp and Pionius suffered.

**A.D. 170. A.U.C. 921.** Very many were killed in Gaul and Spain for the name of Christ.

[Note: **A.D. 171.—1. The plague, etc.** Eusebius has the following in his *Chronicle* for this very year: “A plague seized many provinces; Rome was partly afflicted.” Tertullian speaks of this pestilence in *Apology*, chapter 40, as follows: “They think Christians responsible for every public disaster and every popular misfortune. If the Tiber rises against the walls, if the Nile does not rise into the fields, if the sky stands still, if the earth moves; if there is famine, if there is plague: ‘To the lion at once with the Christians!’”

Julius Capitolinus writes of the same plague in his life of Marcus Aurelius. He also states that the Moors gained strength at that time and devastated the Spains, though a war was waged against them through the generals. Galen likewise discusses it in *On Simple Medicines*, chapter 9; *On Prognosis from the Pulse*, Book III, chapter 3; *On Common Sickness*, Book III, chapter 1; and Book VI, chapter 9. See also Lampridius and Orosius, Book VII, chapter 15. We shall say at that place that this plague spread through almost the entire world and lasted until the year 175.

**2. The Romans against the Sarmatians, etc.** Eusebius’s *Chronicle* agrees for this year. Roman historians of Roman affairs discuss this war against the Sarmatians, or Sauromatians, the Dacians, the Quadi, and the Marcomanni; Cardinal Baronius does so with them in volume II of his *Annals* under the year 171.

While the emperor Lucius Verus was advancing to subdue them, he was struck by apoplexy and died, as we shall say shortly. The Sarmatians lived to the north, in the region where the Poles, Ruthenians, and Tartars now dwell. The Dacians were neighbors of the Danube and the Hercynian Forest; most writers say that they formerly inhabited part of Hungary and later withdrew to the maritime regions of Norway. The Marcomanni, peoples of inner Germany and inhabitants of the Hercynian Forest, are today called Moravians. Finally, the Quadi were formerly a people of Bohemia, as were the Marcomanni. Jerome once wrote of them: “The Sarmatians, Quadi, Vandals, and countless other peoples delight in the flesh of horses and foxes.” See Orosius at the cited place.

**3. Saint Soter, etc.** After Saint Anicetus had been crowned with the glory of martyrdom, while the persecution of Marcus Aurelius and Commodus was raging intensely, Saint Soter was appointed to govern the Roman Church, the twelfth after Saint Peter. I say “twelfth” according to the opinion of Dexter, Eusebius, and other ancient writers, who consider Cletus and Anacletus to have been one and the same man.

In what year Soter was elected remains uncertain. Cardinal Baronius inclines to the view that he was not appointed until the year 175. Others think that he was appointed in 163 but killed in 171; this is the view followed by Onuphrius, Morales, and Tempesta. Some refer his appointment to the year 169. Eusebius, however, thinks that he was elected in this year, 171; for in his *Chronicle* under 171 he says: “Soter assumed the episcopate of the Roman Church for fourteen years.”

Amid such a diversity of opinions, Dexter used such skill that he merely said that Soter governed the Church in the year 171, a point on which several agree; but he did not determine whether Soter entered upon the episcopate in that very year or had assumed it earlier, on which there is much greater disagreement.]

**A.D. 171. A.U.C. 922.** A plague invades many provinces and Rome as well.

**A.D. 171. A.U.C. 922.** The Romans fight against the Sarmatians, Dacians, Quadi, and Marcomanni.

**A.D. 171. A.U.C. 922.** Saint Soter governs the Roman Church, which is sufficiently afflicted.

[Note: **A.D. 172.—Lucius the emperor, etc.** Eusebius says the following in his *Chronicle* for this very year: “Lucius the emperor, in the ninth year of his reign—or, as some think, the eleventh—was struck by apoplexy and died between Concordia and Altinum, while seated with his brother in a carriage.” He had undertaken an expedition against the rebellious Marcomanni and Sauromatians; but he died while on the march, as we said above.

Concordia is a town of Venetia not far from Altinum and from the river Liquentia. Pliny discusses it in Book III, chapter 18. There was another city of this name in Baetica in Spain, from which the people were called Concordienses, as the same Pliny relates in Book IV, chapter 22. We shall discuss it elsewhere, under the year 418.]

**A.D. 172. A.U.C. 923.** The emperor Lucius is struck by apoplexy near Concordia.

[Note: **A.D. 173.—Asianus of Sardica, etc.** Eusebius’s *Chronicle* agrees, almost in the same words: “Asianus, bishop of Sardica, presented an Apology for the Christians to the illustrious emperor Antoninus.” His name was Melito; he was Asian by nationality and bishop of Sardica.

The statement that he gave Antoninus an Apology for the Christian religion must be understood not of Antoninus Pius but of Marcus Aurelius Verus, who was also called Antoninus. Jerome says the following about Melito in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 34: “Melito the Asian, bishop of Sardica, presented a book on behalf of Christian doctrine to the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus, who had been a pupil of the orator Fronto. He also wrote other works, among which are those that we shall list: *On Passover*, Book XI; *On the Life of the Prophets*, Book I; and so forth.”

Tertullian, in the seven books he wrote against the Church on behalf of Montanus, says that Melito’s elegant and declamatory talent was considered by many of our people to be that of one of the prophets. A book *On the Passing of the Virgin* is also attributed to him; nevertheless, Pope Gelasius counts it among the apocryphal works, in Distinction XV, chapter “Holy Roman [Church].” Whether it was actually his, however, is uncertain.]

**A.D. 173. A.U.C. 924.** Asianus of Sardica presents an Apology to Antoninus.

**A.D. 173. A.U.C. 924.** Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis, is held in high esteem.

**A.D. 173. A.U.C. 924.** Also Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, and Pynetus of Crete.

[Note: **A.D. 174.—1. Apollinaris, etc.** Eusebius likewise records this in his *Chronicle* under this very year and calls him an Asian. Jerome writes the following about him in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 36: “Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, flourished under the emperor Marcus Antoninus for the second time, to whom he also presented a distinguished volume on behalf of the Christian faith. Five other books of his against the Gentiles remain, two *On Truth*, and one against the Cataphrygians, who had then first arisen with the mad prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla, when Montanus was beginning.”

His feast is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 8 January. Eusebius discusses him again in Book V of his *History*, chapters 6, 15, and 18; Jerome also mentions him in Letter 84, to Magnus.

**2. Dionysius, etc.** Eusebius says in his *Chronicle* for this year: “Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, is held in high esteem.” He discusses his deeds and writings in Book IV of his *History*, chapter 22.

Jerome also praises him both in the aforementioned Letter 84 and in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where the following is read in chapter 37: “Dionysius, bishop of the Church of Corinth, possessed such eloquence and diligence that by his letters he instructed not only the people of his own city and province but also the bishops of other cities and provinces. Among these letters is one to the Lacedaemonians, another to the Athenians, a third to the Nicomedians, a fourth to the Cretans, a fifth to the Church of Amastris and to the other Churches of Pontus, a sixth to the Gnos­sians and to Pynitus, bishop of that same city, a seventh to the Romans, which he wrote to their bishop Soter, and an eighth to the holy woman Chrysophora.”

He flourished under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus. His feast is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology and in Usuard on 8 April. The Roman Martyrology adds: “He so honored the Roman pontiffs that he was accustomed to have their letters read publicly in church on Sundays.”

**3. Pynetus, etc.** Eusebius writes in his *Chronicle*: “Pynetus—or Pynitus—of Crete, a most eloquent man, is held in high esteem.”

Jerome says in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 38: “Pynitus, bishop of Gnos­sus, a city of Crete, wrote a very elegant letter to Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, in which he teaches that the people should not always be nourished with milk, lest, like infants, they should be overtaken by the final day; rather, they must also consume solid food, so that they may advance into spiritual maturity. He too flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.”

Eusebius discusses him again in Book IV of his *History*, chapters 20 and 22, and Nicephorus in Book IV, chapter 8. His feast is assigned in the Martyrologies of Bede, Ado, and Usuard to 10 October, on which day the Roman Martyrology praises him in this way: “On the island of Crete, the blessed Pynitus, one of the most distinguished among bishops. He was bishop of the city of Gnos­sus and flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus; in his writings he left behind, as in a kind of mirror, a living image of himself.”]

[Note: **A.D. 175.—1. So great throughout the whole world, etc.** Eusebius has the same words in his *Chronicle* under this very year. We discussed the same pestilence above, under the year 171, when it began to spread.

**2. At Interamnum Flavium, etc.** Above, in the annotations for the year 160, we showed that Interamnum Flavium was an ancient and noble city, which we now call Benavente, a place very well known for the county of the most noble and distinguished family of the Pimentels. There Saint Domnina the virgin and her sisters suffered an outstanding martyrdom. Now, however, the subject is Saint Proculus the martyr, who was crowned in the same city.

There is considerable confusion among writers concerning Saint Proculus of Interamnum. Three Proculi are found to have been crowned with martyrdom in the same city, and Cardinal Baronius dealt with this problem unsuccessfully. Although the three are entirely different, he believed there were only two, as is clear from his notes to the Roman Martyrology under 14 February, 14 April, and 1 December, on which their memories are celebrated annually.

The first of these Proculi—that is, the one who received the eternal crown on 14 February—was an Athenian citizen. While he was at Rome with his fellow citizens Ephebus and Apollonius, he was brought to the faith by Saint Valentine, bishop of Interamnum in Italy, and shortly afterward deserved to be crowned with martyrdom at Interamnum.

The Roman Martyrology says of him on that day: “At Interamnum, Saint Valentine, bishop and martyr. In the same place, the holy martyrs Proculus, Ephebus, and Apollonius, who, while keeping vigil beside the body of Saint Valentine, were arrested by order of the governor Leontius and struck down with the sword.”

Peter, in Book III, chapter 122 of his *Catalogue*, Mombritius in volume II, and Surius in volume I report his Acts together with the Life of Valentine; before them, Rhabanus did so in his Martyrology under the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March.

Another Proculus also suffered in the same city on 1 December. The Roman Martyrology says of him: “At Interamnum, Saint Proculus, bishop and martyr, who, after many outstanding works, was ordered by Totila, king of the Goths, to be beheaded.”

Peter, in Book I, chapter 15 of his *Catalogue*, preserves his Acts and asserts that he came from the regions of Syria to Rome in the time of the emperor Justin; that he was ordained a priest by Saint Valentine, bishop of Interamnum; that he succeeded him in the episcopate after Valentine had been raised to martyrdom; and that he was finally beheaded by order of Totila.

I nevertheless think that this man was not bishop of Interamnum but of Narnia, and that the Valentine whom he succeeded in the episcopate was likewise a bishop of Narnia, not of Interamnum. An error must have entered the text, so that “of Interamnum” was written instead of “of Narnia,” through confusion with another Valentine and Proculus of that city.

I am led to this conclusion by the fact that Usuard does not read “at Interamnum” but “in the city of Narnia.” Moreover, in the ancient manuscripts of the Roman Martyrology, especially in the oldest one preserved at Rome in the Church of Saint Cyriacus, we read: “At Narnia, the feast of Saint Proculus, bishop and martyr.”

Whatever the name of the city may be, it is certain that this Proculus was different from the first. The former was a secular citizen, whereas this one was a bishop; the former suffered under Roman emperors who were persecuting the Church, whereas this one suffered under Totila, many years later. Nor is it surprising that there were two bishops and martyrs named Valentine, since in other cases as well the Acts, martyrdoms, and chronological distance clearly show them to have been very different men.

A feast is celebrated on 14 April for another Saint Proculus who suffered martyrdom at Interamnum, together with Saint Domnina and her companions. Baronius, confusing him with the other Proculus just discussed, believed him to have been a bishop; and the error entered even the Roman Martyrology. Yet before Baronius’s correction, the title “bishop” was absent from the text. The other Martyrologies strongly support this reading.

Usuard has only: “At Interamnum, the blessed martyr Proculus. Likewise, the virgin Saint Domnina and her virgin companions, crowned.” Bede and Ado have the same words, and Peter Galesinus agrees, writing: “At Interamnum, Saint Proculus the martyr; likewise Domnina the virgin and her companions,” and so forth.

Peter of Equilinum, in Book XI, chapter 130, number 121 of his *Catalogue*, likewise writes: “The martyr Proculus and the virgin Domnina, with her virgin companions, suffered at Interamnum on that same day.”

From this it is clear that this Proculus was in no way a bishop but only a martyr, as Dexter calls him here; and he was made illustrious by the blood he shed, as Domnina and her sisters had previously been. Thus the other two Proculi triumphed in Italy, whereas this one triumphed in Spain. See what we said about him and Domnina under the year 160.

**3. By the prayers of the Christians, etc.** Eusebius discusses this more fully in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 176. “The emperor Antoninus,” he says, “while many wars were arising against him, was often personally present and often sent the most distinguished commanders. On one occasion, when an army fighting with him in the region of the Quadi was stubbornly oppressed by thirst, rain was sent from heaven; while, by contrast, lightning pursued the Germans and Sarmatians and killed very many of them.”

There survives a letter of Marcus Aurelius, a most weighty emperor, in which he testifies that the thirst of the German army was relieved by rain obtained, perhaps, through the prayers of Christian soldiers. Baronius reproduces this letter from a manuscript in the Vatican Library under the year 176, as does Onuphrius in Book II of his *Feasts*.

Many pagan writers of Roman history mention this miraculous rain and victory, but, driven by hatred of the Christian faith, they assign the glory to others. Julius Capitolinus attributes it to Marcus Aurelius himself; Dio to a certain magician named Arnuphis; some to an unknown magician named Julian. Xiphilinus rightly rebukes Dio for falsehood, both because Marcus Aurelius never consulted magicians or took pleasure in their practices and because no one has ever mentioned any such Arnuphis.

As for the victory over the Quadi and Marcomanni and the rain obtained through the aid of the Christians, Claudian discusses it in Book I of his *Sixth Consulate of Honorius*; Tertullian in *Apology*, chapter 5, and *To Scapula*, chapter 4; and Eusebius again in Book V, chapter 5, citing Apollinaris of Hierapolis, whom Dexter discussed shortly above.

A notable testimony to so great a miracle still exists on the Column of Marcus Aurelius, now called the Column of Saint Paul in Rome, where the entire history of the event can be seen carved in marble. Baronius had a copy of it made and inserted it into his *Annals*.

Everyone writes that the legion through whose aid the victory was obtained was given the name “Thunderbolt” (*Fulminatrix*). The inscription on the tomb which Julius Ioschus, a soldier of that same legion, erected for his freedman Julius Secundus sufficiently testifies that the soldiers in it were Spaniards. We read it in Morales, Book IX, chapter 38, in these words:

“For Julius Secundus, who lived thirty-nine years, ten days of May. Julius Ioschus, of the Twelfth Thunderbolt Legion, erected this monument for his deserving freedman.”

See Orosius, Book VII, chapter 15.]

**A.D. 175. A.U.C. 926.** So great was the destruction throughout the world from the spreading pestilence that almost the entire Roman army was destroyed.

**A.D. 175. A.U.C. 926.** At Interamnum Flavium in Spain, Saint Proculus the martyr.

**A.D. 175. A.U.C. 926.** Through the prayers of the Christians, when Antoninus was fighting against the Quadi and fearing the destruction of his troops, rain and victory were granted.

[Note: **A.D. 180.—1. Antoninus, etc.** Eusebius agrees; these are his words for this very year: “Antoninus makes his son Commodus his associate in the government.” Lampridius discusses this in his Life of Commodus, as do others. Understand this Antoninus to be none other than Marcus Aurelius. See Orosius, Book VII, chapter 15.

**2. Utriculi, etc.** Strabo, in Book III of his *Geography*, places Baetis fourth among the principal cities of the province of Baetica, after Corduba, Gades, and Hispalis. Whether the river Baetis and the entire province of Baetica received their names from it, or whether this city took its name from the river, I do not dare to determine.

The Latins called it Utriculum, because it was situated, as it were, in the middle of the womb of all Baetica. Today, with its name slightly altered, it is called Utrera and lies near Hispalis.

It was here that the distinguished Lucius was born, outstanding in oratorical ability in his own time; later he flourished greatly at Rome. Lucas of Tuy mentions him with great praise in the prologue to his *Chronicle*, when he makes a brief catalogue of distinguished men born in Spain.

**3. At this time, etc.** Saint Peter of Alexandria, bishop and martyr, taught with force and elegance that Christians could buy off the harassment they suffered from pagans with money. Some prove that this is established from Acts, chapter XVII. There we read that, when a riot arose at Thessalonica against the disciples, the Jews cried out: “These men who are stirring up the city have come here also, and Jason has received them; they all act against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.” They stirred up the crowd and the city authorities when they heard this. “But after receiving satisfaction from Jason and the others, they released them.”

I say, after receiving pecuniary satisfaction from Jason and the others, so that they might desist for a little while from their harassment, until they could secretly send Paul and Silas away. Hence the Evangelist adds: “But the brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea.”

Tertullian writes about this sort of buying off, or commercial exchange, of harassment, which was customary in his time, in *On Flight in Persecution*, chapter 12; and in chapter 13 he says: “Finally, it is little if one or another is thus rescued for a price; they have imposed tribute upon entire Churches wholesale.”

If we are to believe that this happened in any particular place, there is no doubt that it was in Spain, where there was a greater abundance of gold and silver and an immense Roman desire for it. It was easy for Tertullian, living in Africa, to know of the Spanish Church’s monetary ransom, since it is otherwise clear from the letters of Cyprian and Augustine that the Churches of Spain and Africa maintained constant intercourse and communion with one another.]

**A.D. 180. A.U.C. 932.** Antoninus makes his son Commodus his associate in the empire.

**A.D. 180. A.U.C. 932.** Lucius was born at Utriculum, a city in Baetica formerly called Baetis, near Hispalis. He flourishes at Rome, distinguished for the excellence of his talent.

**A.D. 180. A.U.C. 932.** At this time all the Churches of Spain, like those throughout the rest of the world, purchased peace from the pagans.

[Note: **A.D. 182.—1. Antoninus, etc.** Eusebius writes in his *Chronicle*: “Antoninus—that is, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus—after returning victorious from the Sarmatians and Marcomanni, was so lavish in the presentation of public spectacles that he exhibited one hundred lions at once,” namely, for the Roman people to see at the games.

**2. All the Churches, etc.** This is precisely what Tertullian says in the passage cited above, chapter 13 of *On Flight*, when he writes: “It is little if one or another is thus rescued for a price; they have imposed tribute upon entire Churches wholesale.”

“Wholesale” means not individually, but with all the Churches of the world gathered into one body and mass; they purchased peace from the pagans with money. Lampridius, citing the old historian Marius Maximus, writes of the emperor Commodus that he sold various forms of punishment and burials.

**3. Smyrna, etc.** These statements too are borrowed from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, where he says under this very year: “The city of Smyrna in Asia fell in an earthquake; for its restoration, exemption from tribute for ten years was granted.

**4. Antoninus, etc.** Eusebius also agrees in his *Chronicle*: “Antoninus,” he says, “died of illness in Pannonia. Commodus reigned thirteen years and fifteen days in Rome.” Read Orosius at the cited place.]

**A.D. 182. A.U.C. 933.** The emperor Antoninus exhibited more than one hundred lions.

**A.D. 182. A.U.C. 933.** All the Churches of the world purchased peace from the pagans with money.

**A.D. 182. A.U.C. 933.** Smyrna, a city of Asia, collapsed after being shaken by an earthquake; for its restoration, a ten-year remission of tribute was granted.

**A.D. 182. A.U.C. 933.** The emperor Antoninus died of illness in Pannonia.

**A.D. 182. A.U.C. 933.** His son Commodus succeeded him in the Roman empire.

[Note: **A.D. 185.—1. The temple of Serapis, etc.** Eusebius writes: “The temple of Serapis at Alexandria was burned.” The Egyptians worshiped Serapis under the image of an ox; he was also customarily called Apis and Osiris, and by the Greeks, Pluto. Plutarch discusses him in his separate book *On Isis and Osiris*, as do others.

Other fires occurred in the City during his reign. Orosius writes about them in Book VII, chapter 16: “The punishment of the City followed the king’s crimes, for the Capitol was struck by lightning, and the resulting fire consumed in a raging whirlwind that library, assembled with the care and diligence of our ancestors, together with the neighboring buildings. Then another fire subsequently broke out at Rome, leveling the temple of Vesta, the Palatine, and a very large part of the City.” So much for him.

**2. Irenaeus the bishop, etc.** Eusebius has the same words for this very year of the Lord 185. Jerome agrees in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 45, where he discusses him at length and confirms, on the testimony of the martyr Polycarp, that he was a disciple of Saint Pothinus, bishop and martyr of Lyons, whom he succeeded in governing that Church.

“He flourished especially,” Jerome says, “under the emperor Commodus, who had succeeded Marcus Antoninus Verus in the empire; and in the excellent commentary which he wrote *On the Monarchy* to Florinus, toward the end he indicates that he had lived near the apostolic age.”

Eusebius discusses the council which Saint Irenaeus held at Lyons under Pope Victor concerning the question of the date of Easter in Book V of his *History*, chapter 22. That it was convened around the year 190 is established by the period of Victor’s pontificate, which, according to Onuphrius, Morales, and the more ancient authorities, began in the year of the Lord 186, although Baronius postpones the beginning of his pontificate to the year 194.

**3. At Flaviobriga, etc.** Ptolemy places Flaviobriga among the Autrigones, peoples of Tarraconese Spain, on the shore of the Cantabrian Ocean. If we trust Villanovano, it is the place we now call Fuenterrabía. John Mariana thinks it was Bermeo, or was situated not far from Bilbao. So he writes in Book IV, chapter 4 of his *History of Spain*.

Flaviumbrigantium was a very different city; it is now called Betanzos in Galicia. Thus Saint Victor suffered martyrdom at Flaviobriga with his companions under the emperor Commodus. Their feast is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 17 October, where his companions are called Alexander and Marianus. Molanus also mentions them in his Additions to Usuard, as do Galesinus and other more recent authors of Martyrologies.

Peter of Equilinum, in Book XI, chapter 130, number 293 of his *Catalogue of the Saints*, makes Victor a bishop, for he says: “Bishop Victor, and the martyrs Alexander and Marianus, suffered on that same day,” namely, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, or 17 October.

**4. Very many colleges, etc.** It was certainly a most ancient custom of the Church to gather Christian boys together and educate them for the clergy, so that in their youth they might absorb the rudiments of the Catholic faith, sacred letters, and upright morals, and be instructed in matters belonging to ecclesiastical rites.

Hence we often see that bishops were crowned with martyrdom together with boys—namely, with boys whom they were teaching sacred letters and ecclesiastical rites. Of Saint Blaise, the famous bishop and martyr of Sebaste, we read in his Acts and Martyrologies that he was beheaded together with two boys.

Victor of Utica writes of Saint Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, in Book III of his *History of the Vandal Persecution*—and the same is found in the Roman Martyrology under 13 July—that many lectors and little children suffered with him. “They were twelve in number,” Victor says. “Yielding neither to flatteries nor threats, and acting bravely and manfully lest they be torn away from the Catholic Church, they obtained the crown of martyrdom. Carthage now honors them with extraordinary affection and has received a choir of boys as if they were the twelve apostles.”

Spain likewise witnessed this at Pamplona in the case of Saint Valens, a most holy bishop, who was killed with three boys on 21 May. We shall discuss them in their proper place, together with Dexter, under the year of the Lord 300.

Among the colleges whose memory survives, which were once established in Spain for educating the young, the most famous is the one that Saint Isidore founded at Hispalis, in which Saint Ildefonsus was a fellow student. John Mariana discusses it in Book VI, chapter 10 of his *History of Spain*. “Ildefonsus,” he says, “was sent to Hispalis out of a desire to acquire cultivated learning and was admitted to the college which, as has been said, Isidore had built for the education of youth. He entrusted himself to that most learned man to be polished and refined, and he did not leave his side until, trained in every liberal discipline, he had completed the whole circle of the arts.”

The Life of Isidore agrees; it is accustomed to be read annually in the divine offices in the Churches of Spain, with the approval of the Apostolic See. There we read: “He built monasteries and established colleges, in which, devoting himself to sacred studies and divine readings, he instructed many disciples who flocked to him, among whom was the blessed Ildefonsus,” and so forth.

It is clear that the earlier bishops of the principal Churches of Spain were moved by a similar zeal. Dexter’s statement here gives sufficiently credible evidence that, through their diligence, colleges for educating youth for the clergy were once established. Such institutions were especially necessary at that time, when persecution was raging and it was not permissible for every Christian to educate his children for the clergy wherever he wished. In the principal cities, therefore, it seemed necessary to gather the boys into colleges and educate them there.

Dexter discusses these institutions again under the year of the Lord 370, saying: “The colleges for young men being educated for the clergy, which had been interrupted through the negligence of the times, were restored through the diligence of Saint Audentius, bishop of Toledo, and the other bishops.”

**5. Patrunio, etc.** He is called Patruinus by some and, more corruptly, Paternus by others. We discussed his election as bishop of Toledo together with Dexter under the year 160; but from that account a considerable doubt seems to arise. For there he is said to have presided for twenty-nine years, namely, from the year 160, in which he was elected.

“Patruinus, a faithful man,” he says, “succeeds Pelagius, bishop of Toledo; he presides over that see for twenty-nine years.” Now, however, under the year of the Lord 185, it is asserted that Turibius, bishop of Toledo, was substituted for Patruinus—namely, after only twenty-five years, the interval between 160 and 185.

The difficulty is increased by the fact that below, under the year of the Lord 208, the author says: “Quinctius, bishop of Toledo, succeeds Patruinus; he presides over that see for twelve years.” Two points here seem less consistent with the truth: first, that Quinctius, or Quinctinus, succeeded Patruinus, although above he said that Turibius was his successor; and second, that Patruinus remained in the see of Toledo until the year 208. For in that case he would not have held it for twenty-nine years, as he had previously said, but for forty-eight, namely, from 160 to 208.

To resolve these doubts, one might suppose that there were two Patruini in the see of Toledo—or, if one prefers, one named Patruinus and another named Paternus—one preceding and the other following Turibius, and having Quinctius as his successor. When it is said that the former held the see for twenty-nine years, an error could easily have entered the writing, so that someone read 29 instead of 25. The similarity of the numerals 5 and 9 could easily have deceived either reader or copyist.

That explanation may seem probable to others, but another seems more probable to me, one that resolves everything without multiplying the number of Patruini without compelling necessity. I therefore think that Patruinus, after holding the see of Toledo for twenty-five years, left it under the impulse of zeal for preaching or pilgrimage, leaving Turibius as his successor. This should not seem novel, but rather customary among his predecessors, as Dexter showed above concerning Saints Eugenius, Honoratus, and Hermolaus.

Then, after spending twenty years in preaching and pilgrimage, he returned to Toledo. When Turibius resigned or died, around the year of the Lord 204, Patruinus again sat as bishop for four years. These years, added to the twenty-five during which he had first presided, complete the total of twenty-nine specified by Dexter.

Thus it follows that he began to preside in the year 160; that Turibius succeeded him in 185; that in 208 he had Quinctius as his successor; and that throughout this whole period he held the episcopal see of Toledo for only twenty-nine years.

Our view is also supported by the fact that if the Patruinus succeeded by Quinctius were different from the one succeeded by Turibius, Dexter would have called him “the second of that name,” just as he did below in the case of Olympius, the second bishop of the same see of Toledo, under the year 424. Yet he entirely omitted such a designation, indicating that there was one and the same Patruinus.

Turibius, bishop of Toledo, is mentioned in the chronology of the bishops of Toledo which Loaysa, himself likewise archbishop of Toledo, edited in the volume of the Councils of Spain. In that chronology, he is placed as the successor of Patruinus and the predecessor of Quinctius. But in the chronology of the years, where he is said to have flourished after the year of the Lord 396, the author is completely mistaken, as we have shown elsewhere, namely, under the year 160. What sort of man he was, and how great, Dexter alone has taught.]

But what he asserts—that St. Irenaeus sent him his five books Against Heresies—will doubtless seem novel to many; nor is this surprising, since, so far as we know, Dexter alone wrote it. Yet although it cannot be clearly demonstrated from Irenaeus’s own testimony, it is by no means contrary to his writings. These circulate without the name of the person to whom they were dedicated; indeed, the assertion of our author can be inferred from them with considerable probability.

For he wrote these books at Lugdunum in Gaul, on the bank of the Rhône, as he acknowledges in the preface to the first, saying: “But you will not demand from us, who live among the Gauls and are for the most part drawn away into a barbarous language, the art of eloquence, etc.” He sends them, however, to an educated and distinguished man living in another region that had been infected by the filth of the Gnostics, just as the province of Lugdunum had been. Concerning the latter, Irenaeus says in Book I, chapter 9: “By saying and doing such things, they also seduced many women in those regions which are ours, in the Rhone districts, etc.”

Jerome indicates what province was similarly corrupted by them, in his commentary on Isaiah 64, where he asserts that the Gnostics first deceived the noble women of Gaul around the Rhône, and afterward those of Spain, “mixing pleasure with fables and arrogating to the name of science what belonged to their ignorance.” In his letter to Theodora he praises the piety of her husband, Lacinius, because, while the heresies of Basilides, the chief of the Gnostics, were ravaging Spain, he had not accepted Armigil, Barbelon, Abraxas, Balsamum, and the ridiculous Leusibara, together with the other things that were more monstrosities than names, which they shamelessly boasted had been drawn from Hebrew sources in order to excite the minds of the ignorant and of silly women. And in his commentary on Amos 3 he calls Balsamum and Barbelon “Iberian absurdities.”

Spain, therefore, was infected to some extent by the heresies of Basilides, Valentinus, and Marcus, and consequently needed the remedy of Irenaeus, who had learned their absurdities most thoroughly in the East and had fought them with all his strength in his own diocese. To whom could Irenaeus more suitably entrust his weapons among the Spanish prelates than Turibius, primate of the Spains? Especially since the heretic Marcus had attempted to infect his city of Toledo, as Dexter states above under the year of Our Lord 169.

The frequent transmission of Irenaeus’s letters and books to the man to whom he dedicated his work may likewise serve as evidence that he did not dedicate it to some Eastern bishop, but to someone living not far from his own province. For whenever he completed one of the five books into which he had arranged his entire work on heresies, he immediately sent it to him. Thus, in the preface to Book III he says:

“We have sent you books, of which the first contains the opinions of all those [the Gnostics], and displays their customs and the character of their way of life. In the second, what they wrongly teach has been destroyed and overthrown. In this third book, we shall bring forward demonstrations from the sacred Scriptures, so that nothing may be lacking to you of the matters you had requested; indeed, beyond what you expected, you may receive from us opportunities for refuting and overthrowing those who teach wrongly in any manner.”

In the preface to Book IV he says:

“Sending you this fourth book, dearest friend, of the work concerning the detection and overthrow of false knowledge—which we promised—we have confirmed by the sayings of the Lord what we previously stated, so that you too, as you requested, may receive from us on every side opportunities for refuting all heretics, and may not allow them, once thoroughly blunted, to proceed any further into the depths of error or to be suffocated in the sea of ignorance; but, turning them toward the harbor of truth, you may cause them to receive their salvation.”

Finally, in the preface to Book V:

“Having most carefully dealt with all the heretics in the four books which we previously published for you, and having exposed their teachings in this fifth book, we shall endeavor, from the remaining teachings of Our Lord and from the apostolic Epistles, to provide demonstrations, as you requested of us, since we obey your command, etc.”

Among these passages it is pleasing, in passing, to observe how highly our Turibius was regarded by Irenaeus, since he professes himself obedient to Turibius’s command. Irenaeus also commends his learning and wisdom, as he writes to him in the preface to Book I:

“You will receive with affection what has been written to you with affection, and you yourself will increase it within you, so as to be more capable than we are. Just as we formerly labored, when you sought to learn their opinions, not only to make them clear to you but also to provide you with means by which we might demonstrate them to be false, so you too will effectively minister to the others according to the grace given you by the Lord, so that people may no longer be drawn away by their persuasion.”

But these observations seem sufficient for our present purpose.

**A.C. 185. A.R. 936.** The celebrated temple of Serapis in Alexandria was burned.

**A.C. 185. A.R. 936.** Irenaeus, distinguished bishop of Lugdunum, was held in high regard.

**A.C. 185. A.R. 936.** At Flaviobriga in Spain, St. Victor the martyr and his companions suffered various tortures and were put to death.

**A.C. 185. A.R. 936.** Throughout Spain, numerous schools for young men intended for the clergy were established through the diligence of the bishops, especially at Caesaraugusta, Tarraco, Hispalis, Carthage, Toledo, Bracara Augusta, and Illiberri, the principal cities.

**[Col. 0351] A.C. 185. A.R. 936.** Turibius, a learned and educated man, was appointed bishop of Toledo in succession to Patruinus. He suffered many hardships from the pagans on behalf of the faith. He is said to have been born at Rome and to have come to Spain; to him St. Irenaeus, bishop of Lugdunum, sent, in response to his letters, the book Against Heresies, as to a very close friend.

**[Col. 0353] [Note: [Col. 0353C]**

**A.C. 186.—The Baths, etc.** Eusebius says in his *Chronicle* for this very year: “The Commodian Baths were constructed at Rome.”

**] A.C. 186. A.R. 937.** Baths were constructed at Rome by order of the emperor Commodus.

**[Note: [Col. 0353C]**

**A.C. 190.—Apollonius, etc.** Eusebius in Book V, chapter 20, and Jerome in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 52, recount the outstanding deed of this most holy man. Jerome’s words were transferred to the *Roman Martyrology* under April 18, where the feast of his martyrdom is recorded:

“At Rome, the blessed Apollonius, a senator, who under the emperor Commodus and the prefect Perennis was betrayed by a slave because he was a Christian. Ordered to give an account of his faith, he composed a remarkable volume, which he read in the senate; nevertheless, by decree of the senate, he was beheaded for Christ.”

Bede, Usuard, and Ado also discuss him on the same day, as does Equilinus in Book IV, chapter 62. Eusebius likewise assigns the martyrdom of St. Apollonius the senator to the year 190 in his *Chronicle*, although Cardinal Baronius places it in the preceding year.

**] A.C. 190. A.R. 941.** Apollonius, an outstanding worshiper of Christ and a senator, presented a book in defense of the faith to the Roman senate and was beheaded.

**[Note: [Col. 0354A]**

**A.C. 193.—Commodus, etc.** Eusebius says for this year: “Commodus kills many nobles and provides remarkable spectacles for the Roman people.” Consult Orosius, Book VII, chapter 16.

**] A.C. 193. A.R. 944.** Commodus provided the Roman people with remarkable spectacles.

**[Note: [Col. 0354A]**

**A.C. 195. 1.—The wicked emperor Commodus, etc.** Lampridius writes in his *Life* that Commodus burst forth into such great crimes that, amid the public outcry of the people, he was called “more cruel than Nero and more impure than Domitian.” But at last he paid the deserved penalty for his crimes, being strangled in the house of Vestilianus. For Eusebius writes in his *Chronicle* for this very year: “Commodus is strangled in the house of Vestilianus.” This clause was absent from the Caesaraugusta edition of Dexter, but a printer’s error was noted on the page of corrections for the same impression.

**2. He succeeded, etc.** The Roman historians discuss Aelius Pertinax, and Baronius draws on them under the year 195; according to his calculation, Pertinax reigned only eighty-two days. Eusebius, however, says in his *Chronicle* that he reigned six months.

**3. Pertinax, etc.** Eusebius records the following in his *Chronicle*: “When the senate urged Pertinax to name his wife Augusta and his son Caesar, he refused, declaring that it was enough that he himself reigned against his will.” Truly, this was a statement worthy not of a pagan but of a Christian ruler.

**4. Pertinax is killed, etc.** Dexter writes this also in the very words of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. Consult Orosius, Book VII, chapter 16; Xiphilinus; Eutropius; and Capitolinus.

**5. Severus, etc.** Aelius Pertinax was succeeded by Didius Salvius Julianus, who held the reins of the empire for nearly seven months, according to Orosius, Book VII, chapter 16. During these days Pescennius Niger in Syria and Albinus in Britain had simultaneously seized—or rather torn apart—the Roman empire. At last Albinus yielded to Severus, who, in memory of Aelius, also wished to be called Pertinax, according to Spartianus; the triumphal arch at Rome, at the foot of the Capitoline Hill, likewise gives him this name. He began to reign in the year 196, as Eusebius states in his *Chronicle*.

**] A.C. 195. A.R. 946.** The wicked emperor Commodus was killed in the house of Vestilianus.

**A.C. 195. A.R. 946.** Aelius Pertinax succeeded to the Roman empire and reigned six months.

**A.C. 195. A.R. 946.** When the senate urged Pertinax to name his wife Augusta and his son Caesar, he rejected the proposal, saying that it was enough that he had himself accepted and governed the Roman empire unwillingly.

**A.C. 195. A.R. 946.** Pertinax was killed in the Palace through the crime of Julianus the jurist, whom Severus later killed at the Milvian Bridge.

**A.C. 195. A.R. 946.** Severus, also called Pertinax, succeeded the emperor Julianus.

**[Note: [Col. 0354C]**

**A.C. 197.—Clement of Alexandria, etc.** In the Caesaraugusta edition of Dexter, the name *Espannensius* was printed most corruptly in place of *Pantaenus*. Yet *Pantaenus* must certainly be read; he was Clement of Alexandria’s teacher in the interpretation of the sacred writings. Eusebius writes of both in his *Chronicle* under the year 197:

“Clement, presbyter of the Alexandrian Church, and Pantaenus, a Stoic philosopher, are held to be most eloquent in disputing our doctrine.”

Clement is placed before Pantaenus—the pupil before the teacher—perhaps because his writings are more prominent. Pantaenus, however, has been entered in the catalogue of the saints, on July 7, in the *Roman Martyrology*, in these words:

“At Alexandria, the feast of St. Pantaenus, an apostolic man adorned with every kind of learning. He possessed such zeal and love for the word of God that, inflamed with faith and devotion, he went even to preach the Gospel of Christ to the nations hidden in the most remote recesses of the East. At last he returned to Alexandria and rested in peace under Antoninus Caracalla, the son of Severus.”

Jerome writes in Book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 46:

“Pantaenus, a philosopher of the Stoic school, possessed, according to an ancient custom at Alexandria—where, from the time of Mark the Evangelist, there had always been ecclesiastical teachers—such prudence and learning both in the divine Scriptures and in secular literature that, when requested by envoys of that nation, he was sent to India by Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria. There he found that Bartholomew, one of the twelve apostles, had preached the coming of the Lord Jesus according to the Gospel of Matthew; this Gospel, written in Hebrew characters, he brought back with him to Alexandria. Many of his commentaries on sacred Scripture still exist, but he benefited the Church more by his living voice. He taught under the emperor Severus and Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla.”

Concerning Clement, Jerome says in chapter 48 of the same book:

“Clement, presbyter of the Alexandrian Church and a pupil of Pantaenus, whom we mentioned above, took charge of the ecclesiastical school at Alexandria after Pantaenus’s death.”

After listing the titles of the books he wrote, Jerome adds: “It is certain that Origen was his pupil.” Clement flourished during the reigns of Severus and his son Antoninus.

Eusebius also says much about Pantaenus in Book IV of his *History*, chapter 10; Jerome in his letter to Magnus; Nicephorus in Book IV, chapter 32, and Book V, chapter 10; and Bede, Ado, and Usuard on July 7. Equilinus discusses him in Book VI, chapter 65.

**] A.C. 197. A.R. 948.** Clement, presbyter of Alexandria, and Pantaenus, the Stoic philosopher, were regarded as outstandingly courageous in disputation on behalf of our faith.

**[Col. 0355] [Note: [Col. 0355C]**

**A.C. 198.—Polycrates, etc.** Dexter was corruptly printed with *Polycarpus*. Eusebius says in his *Chronicle* for this year:

“Polycrates and Bachylus, bishops of the province of Asia, are held in high repute.”

St. Jerome writes in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 54:

“Bachylus, bishop of Corinth, was also held in high esteem under the same emperor Severus. On the subject of Easter, on behalf of all the bishops who were in Achaia, he composed a book full of learning.”

Of Polycrates Jerome writes in the following chapter:

“Polycrates, bishop of the Ephesians, together with the other bishops of Asia who, according to a certain ancient custom, celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, wrote a synodal letter against Victor, bishop of Rome. In it he declares that he follows the authority of the apostle John and of the ancients.”

After quoting a fragment of the same letter, Jerome adds: “He flourished in the time of the emperor Severus.”

Peter Equilinus discusses Polycrates in Book XI of the *Catalogue*, chapter 16, and Bachylus in chapter 81.

**] A.C. 198. A.R. 949.** Polycrates and Bachylus, bishops of the province of Asia, are regarded as distinguished men.

**[Col. 0355C] [Note: [Col. 0355C]**

**A.C. 199.—Under Victor, etc.** Eusebius treats this matter at somewhat greater length in his *Chronicle*:

“When a question arose among the bishops as to whether Easter should be observed according to the law of Moses, Victor, bishop of the city of Rome; Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem; Polycrates; Irenaeus; Bachylus; and very many pastors of the Churches published in writing what seemed probable to them.”

In this very year Victor convened a council at Rome for this purpose, and many other councils were held elsewhere: one in Gaul, presided over by St. Irenaeus; another at Caesarea, presided over by Bishop Theophilus, whom Bede mentions in his book *On the Spring Equinox*; another in Pontus, presided over by Bishop Palmas; another at Corinth, presided over by Bachylus; and finally another in the province of the Osrhoeni, concerning which Eusebius writes in Book V of his *History*, chapter 22.

The opinion of all these councils was that Holy Easter should be celebrated every year on the Lord’s Day. Against them, Polycrates convened a council in Asia, where it was decreed that Easter should be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon, as Moses had prescribed in the Law. The followers of this doctrine were called Quartodecimans.

Since the matter is well known, it is enough to have said so little about it. Victor’s feast day is observed in the Roman, Usuardian, and other martyrologies on the fifth day before the Kalends of August—that is, July 28—when he earned the crown of martyrdom under Severus. St. Jerome discusses him in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 44; Eusebius in Book V, chapter 22; Augustine in Letter 165; and Optatus of Milevis in Book II *Against Parmenian*.

**] A.C. 199. A.R. 950.** Under Pope Victor, a serious controversy arose concerning Easter.

**[Note: [Col. 0356A]**

**A.C. 200. 1.—The Jewish war, etc.** Cardinal Baronius, who is invariably one year ahead of Eusebius’s chronology, assigns the Jewish war to the preceding year, namely 199. Dexter, however, agrees with Eusebius; Eusebius’s words are: “In the year of Our Lord 200, the Jewish and Samaritan war arose or was renewed.”

Dio and Spartianus discuss this war, and Tertullian mentions it in his *Apologeticus*, chapter 21. The Jews had rebelled because they were burdened by the oppressive exaction of taxes, and for this reason they killed Pescennius Niger, who had tyrannized over the Roman empire in Syria. Clodius Albinus, following Pescennius, invaded Judaea and Syria, but, being pursued by Severus unto death, fled elsewhere.

**2. Severus, etc.** Baronius thinks that the emperor Severus won a victory over the Parthians in the year of Our Lord 205. Eusebius, whom Dexter consistently follows, says this under the year 200:

“Severus defeated the Parthians and the Adiabenes, and so devastated the inner Arabs that he made their region a Roman province. For this reason he was surnamed Parthicus, Arabicus, and Adiabenicus.”

Ancient inscriptions of Severus Pertinax still exist at Rome, in which he is called Parthicus, Arabicus, and Adiabenicus. At Malaga in Spain a temple was also built to Mars, whose inscription is given by Ambrosius Morales:

“To the emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus, Pius, Pertinax, Augustus, Parthicus, Arabicus, Adiabenus, peacemaker of the world and founder of the Roman empire, in his honor the commonwealth of Malaga [dedicated] this temple to Mars, by decree.”

Parthia borders the province of Media. Its inhabitants were formerly very skilled with the bow, by which they inflicted great harm even while fleeing from the enemy. They were extremely persistent enemies of the Roman name, and they surrounded and annihilated Crassus with his entire army by an ambush.

Adiabenē was formerly called Mesopotamia and Asia, a region very famous in sacred literature, which Pliny describes in Book V. According to Strabo, *Geography*, Book XVI, the Adiabenes were a people between the Euphrates and the Tigris, and their region bordered the eastern side of Assyria.

By the Arabia that Dexter calls “inner,” I understand the region otherwise called the Desert, which borders Mesopotamia. Osorius discusses this victory in Book VII, chapter 17.

**] A.C. 200. A.R. 951.** The Jewish and Samaritan war was renewed. The emperor Severus defeated the Parthians and the Adiabenes and nearly annihilated the Arabs.

**[Note: [Col. 0356D]**

**A.C. 202.—Under Severus, etc.** Eusebius writes in his *Chronicle* for this very year:

“While Severus was emperor, the Severan Baths were constructed at Antioch and Rome, and the Septizonium was built.”

I read *septizonium*, meaning a building with seven tiers of columns, instead of *septizodium*, which was read previously.

**] A.C. 202. A.R. 953.** Under the emperor Severus, the Septizonium and baths were built at Rome.

**[Col. 0357] [Note: [Col. 0357A]**

**A.C. 204.—Persecution, etc.** Eusebius records the same event under this year in his *Chronicle*, saying:

“During a persecution raised against the Christians, Leonides, the father of Origen, was taken away by a glorious death of martyrdom.”

In Book VI of his *History*, chapters 2 and 3, he reports that Origen, a young man of seventeen, sent his father Leonides a letter in prison with these words:

“Stand firm, Father; endure martyrdom courageously, and undertake nothing else on our account.”

For Leonides feared that, out of consideration for his wife and seven children, whom he was leaving poor and orphaned, he might purchase his life through apostasy.

The annual memory of Leonides is celebrated in the *Roman Martyrology* on April 22, where Bede, Ado, Usuard, and others also mention him. Eusebius discusses his martyrdom again in Book VI, chapter 11; Nicephorus in Book V, chapter 2; Jerome in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers* under Origen; Suidas; and others.

This was the fifth persecution under Severus among those which the Church suffered from the pagans, as Orosius acknowledges in Book VII, chapter 17.

**] A.C. 204. A.R. 955.** A persecution was raised against the Church, in which Leonides, the father of Origen, was crowned with glorious martyrdom.

**[Note: [Col. 0357A]**

**A.C. 206.—Alexander, etc.** This Alexander was first bishop of Caesarea in Palestine and afterward of Jerusalem, succeeding St. Narcissus. His feast is celebrated by the Greeks in the *Menologion* on May 15, but by the Latins on March 18, as can be seen in Bede, Ado, and Usuard. The *Roman Martyrology* records the following about him:

“At Caesarea in Palestine, the feast of the blessed Alexander, bishop. He came from Cappadocia, from his own city—that is, Caesarea of Cappadocia—where he was bishop, and, moved by a desire to see the holy places, came to Jerusalem. Since Narcissus, bishop of that city, was already advanced in age and governing the Church, Alexander received its leadership by divine revelation. Later, during the persecution of Decius, when he was distinguished by the venerable gray hair of his great age, he was led to Caesarea in Palestine and shut up in prison; there, for confessing Christ, he completed his martyrdom.”

Eusebius narrates his deeds in Book VI of his *History*, chapters 8 and 32; Nicephorus in Book V, chapters 9 and 10; and Jerome in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 72, where he discusses Alexander’s letters to the Antinoites, to the Antiochenes, to Origen, and on behalf of Origen, etc.

**] A.C. 206. A.R. 957.** Alexander is celebrated for his confession of the faith.

**[Note: [Col. 0357B]**

**A.C. 208. 1.—Clodius Albinus, etc.** Eusebius agrees under this year in his *Chronicle*, saying:

“After C. Albinus, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul, was killed at Lugdunum, Severus transferred the war to the Britons. There, in order to make the recovered provinces safer from barbarian invasion, he built a wall extending 132 miles from sea to sea.”

Consult Orosius, Book VII, chapter 17.

**2. At Carthage in Spain, etc.** All the martyrologies summarize the noble martyrdom of the most holy virgin Gudenis in nearly the same words:

“At Carthage, St. Gudenis, virgin, who, by order of the proconsul Rufinus, suffered on account of her confession of Christ. At four different times she was stretched upon the rack and tortured by the horrible tearing of hooks; after being afflicted for a long time in the squalor of prison, she was finally struck down by the sword.”

This is the wording of the *Roman Martyrology*, to which Bede, Ado, Usuard, and Equilinus agree verbatim, except that where the Roman Martyrology reads “afflicted for a long time in the squalor of prison,” others—including Equilinus in Book VI, chapter 112—read “afflicted for a still longer time”; others, such as Usuard and Galesinus, read “afflicted for the longest time.”

From this one can see not only that the blessed virgin of Christ was afflicted with the utmost savagery and dreadful tortures, but also that she was tormented and killed over a long period. This is sufficiently indicated by the statement that she was tortured not once but four times, and at different periods, by stretching on the rack and by the horrible tearing of hooks.

As for which Carthage was the place of her death, African or Spanish, a matter neglected by the others, Dexter explained it by saying: “At Carthage in Spain,” so that no one afterward would think her to have been African. Dexter also agrees about the name of the proconsul by whom she was killed, namely Rufinus. For it is established that during these days Quintus Rufinus Galerius governed Nearer Spain, whose city is New Carthage, as Ambrosius Morales proves—although he was concerned with another matter—in Book IX of his *History of Spain*, chapter 35.

The consulship of Geta and Plautianus, under whom she is said to have suffered, fell in the year of Christ 205, as Cardinal Baronius correctly proves from Cassiodorus in Volume II of his *Annals* and in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology*. Therefore, in the year 205, St. Gudenis, virgin of Carthage, suffered martyrdom. Dexter places her somewhat later because he is at the same time recording the memory of all the martyrs who suffered for Christ in this persecution under Severus and Commodus.

Finally, what the printed Dexter says—that she suffered on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of Quintilis—must be corrected. All the martyrologies say that she was killed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, which is called Sextilis, not Quintilis, because it was the sixth month from March, the beginning of the ancient year.

**3. Blitabrum, etc.** Ambrosius Morales reports in Book VII of his *History*, chapter 13, that Flaminius, proconsul of Nearer Spain, subdued by right of war the city of Blitabrum, or Litabrum, and had Corribilo, its lord, taken into chains.

Litabrum was situated near the Carpetanian mountains, as Dexter asserts. It is mentioned in the Second Council of Toledo, in the second letter of Montanus, archbishop of Toledo, where it is named together with Segovia and Cauca, now Coca. For this reason Loaysa teaches in his notes that Blitabrum was near Segovia.

Here, therefore, St. Auditus gave his neck for the Lord Christ. In Dexter’s age his feast was solemnly celebrated on November 1.

**[Col. 0358C] 4. St. Andeolus, etc.** The authors do not agree about the city distinguished by the martyrdom of St. Andeolus. Some read *Nivaria*, or the territory called Nivariense after it; others read *Vivaria* or *Vivarium*, and the territory of Vivariense. The latter reading is found in some manuscripts of the martyrologies, as can be seen in the edition of Ado by Surius and in that of Usuard by Molanus. Many others retain the former, including Peter, bishop of Equilinus, in Book IV, chapter 111, and Maurolicus.

Since Vivarium is a town in Narbonese Gaul, commonly called Viviers in Vivarais, many have therefore believed that Andeolus died in Gaul. For the sake of explanation, they added the words “in Gaul” to the text of the martyrologies. Thus in the Roman Martyrology we read under May 1:

“In Gaul, in the territory of Vivariensis, the blessed Andeolus, subdeacon, etc.”

This opinion was encouraged by the fact that everyone vaguely agrees that St. Andeolus preached in Gaul, having been sent from the East by St. Polycarp for that purpose.

Those, however, who retain the reading *Nivaria* must agree with Dexter, since no city in all Gaul was ever distinguished by that name. According to Antonius Nebrissensis and Charles Estienne in their historical dictionaries, Nivaria was a city of Spain between Salamanca and Complutum, named, I believe, from its perpetual snow, just as one of the Fortunate Islands, now La Gomera, was formerly also called Nivaria from its perpetual snow; Pliny discusses it in Book VI, chapter 32.

Nivaria, therefore, which lay between Salamanca and Complutum, is undoubtedly the city which, according to Dexter, bordered the territory of the Carpetani, since it is clear that the boundaries of the Carpetanian province extended that far. The fact that Andeolus preached in Gaul does not prevent him from afterward traveling through Spain in his preaching and receiving there, in the city of Nivaria, among the peoples of the Vettones and Carpetani, the crown of martyrdom.

We should therefore follow Dexter, as the most ancient of all the authors, and retain the reading *Nivaria*.

But how much did St. Andeolus suffer for the name of Christ? Ado, from whom the other martyrologies took the account, writes:

“St. Andeolus, subdeacon, whom St. Polycarp sent from the East with the blessed Benignus and Andochius, priests, and Thyrsus, subdeacon, to preach the word of God in Gaul. When the emperor Severus learned through his preaching—while Andeolus was at Novaria of Carpetania—he ordered him to be scourged most cruelly with thorny clubs and thrown into prison. On the following day, when he was brought out and Severus saw that he could not be overcome, he ordered a sword to be made from very hard wood, after the likeness of a sword, and commanded that Andeolus’s head be split in the shape of a cross. When this had been done, his brain being dashed upon the ground, he was taken away by a glorious death.”

The Roman Martyrology, that of Usuard, and Bede relate the matter in nearly the same words, as do Galesinus and Maurolicus.

**5. Lucius, etc.** Anyone may rightly wonder whether this is the same Lucius whom, twenty-eight years earlier—that is, in the year of Christ 180—Dexter had said was born at Utriculus near Hispalis and had flourished at Rome with a reputation for outstanding talent, since both the name and the period agree.

**6. Quinctius, etc.** Above, under the year 185, we explained how one should understand the statement that Quinctius succeeded Patruinus in the see of Toledo, since Turibius intervened between them. Consult what was said there.

It is worth noting, however, that a certain ignorant scholar introduced into the text itself the variant readings of proper names that had been written in the margins of ancient manuscripts. Hence, in the printed Dexter, the names are often given in two readings, in a highly corrupt form. This is especially the case here, where the text reads:

“Quinctus, or Quinctianus, bishop of Toledo, succeeds Patruinus, or Paternus,”

although one reading should have been placed in the text and the other in the margin. While others demonstrate that one or the other of these readings is correct, it seems more probable to me that they were called Quinctius and Patruinus.

**7. In Spain, etc.** Many at the Second Council of Nicaea proved that the use of sacred images originated with the apostles; the same is taught by St. John Damascene in his orations on images.

It is certain that the use and veneration of sacred images were introduced by the apostles in Spain no less than in the other provinces of the whole world, since everywhere they preached the same forms of worship and customs, alike in every respect.

These points agree with what Dexter had stated under the year 50: that St. Peter brought sacred images from Antioch to Spain; they also agree with what we noted there.

As for the added statement concerning the image of St. Christopher—“Among these, in our time, the last was the image of the giant St. Christopher after his passion”—the manuscript is corrupt, and I do not know what it means by saying that it was “the last after his passion.”

One thing is certain: these words cannot be referred to the period now under discussion, since St. Christopher was killed fifty years later, under the emperor Decius. Rather, Dexter mentioned them by a kind of anticipation. Since he says “in our time,” it is sufficiently clear that the words must be adapted to the time of the author himself, as though he had said that in his own time the image of St. Christopher the martyr was the most celebrated in Spain.

This is amply confirmed by the use of the sacred image, which is found to have been observed in all the churches of Spain from time immemorial. For there is no ancient church that lacks an image of him.

It is also clear from St. Eulogius, Book II, chapter 11 of the *Memorial of the Saints*, that in the time of the Goths there existed at Córdoba a notable monastery of St. Christopher the martyr, and that afterward some of its monks were crowned with martyrdom under the tyranny of the Arabs.

In the Toledan Breviary of St. Isidore there is an extremely ancient hymn in which the deeds of St. Christopher are sung. Its beginning is:

> O blessed author of the world and creator of all things;

and there it is asserted that his sacred relics are fittingly venerated at Toledo.

As for his gigantic stature, which some have interpreted allegorically, the hymn says:

> Graceful in stature, yet more graceful in mind,  
> Shining in appearance, vibrant in heart, and radiant in hair,  
> Christopher sounds forth Christ with his mouth and Christ in his heart.

The ancient breviaries of Spain agree with this. In the Palentian Breviary one reads: “Tall in stature, possessing a terrifying appearance”; in the Asturician Breviary: “Tall in body, terrifying in countenance.” Equilinus, drawing on ancient manuscript codices, writes in Book VI of his *Catalogue*, chapter 135: “Terrifying in countenance and of extraordinarily tall stature.”

Nor do the relics venerated today with great honor in the Asturician Church permit us to doubt this matter, for part of the jaw has molar teeth half the size of a walnut.

Finally, Cardinal Baronius admits in his notes under July 25 that the cult of the martyr Christopher was once widespread and deeply religious in Spain.

### 8. Secundus of Asti, etc.

There were formerly two cities bearing the name Asta: one in Liguria, a province of Italy, and the other in Baetica in Spain; both are very well known among ancient writers. Pomponius deals with the Spanish city in book III; Ptolemy mentions it in his map of Baetica, from which the estuary of Asta was named, between the Sacred Promontory and the Pillars of Hercules. Only the name of the city remains—*la mesa de Asta*—and it preserves there the memory of ancient events (see what we said concerning the saints Eutychius and Honorius, when treating the year of Our Lord 112).

The Ligurian Asta still preserves the name Asti, between Genoa and Milan. But as to which of these two cities Secundus, the martyr of Asti, died for Christ, the authorities do not seem to agree. For in the Roman Martyrology on 24 March, and in the additions to Usuard published by Molanus, it is merely said: “In the city of Asti, Saint Secundus the martyr” [Col. 0360D]. The Italians maintain that he was Italian and died at Asta in Liguria; Dexter, however—if the text has not been corrupted—places him in Baetica, at the confluence of the river Lethes, which is still called the Guadalete, a name meaning “the river Lethes.”

Yet if the things related in his Life are true, as it appears in Peter Equilinus, book IV, chapter 12, and in Mombritius, volume II of the *Lives of the Saints*, in the Life of Saint Martianus [Col. 0361A], and in what is read in the martyrdom of Saints Faustinus and Jovita, Equilinus, book III, chapter 127, and of Saint Calocerus, the same book, chapter 208, I strongly suspect that an error entered Dexter’s manuscript, and that *Baetica* should be read for *Italia*. For all the saints whom we have just mentioned as his companions were also friends of Saint Secundus of Asti, and under the same judge, Sapritius, during the persecution of the emperor Hadrian, they received the palms of martyrdom. Yet all of them suffered in cities of Liguria and of other Italian provinces: Martianus at Dertona, Faustinus and Jovita at Brescia, Calocerus at Albenga—which is a Ligurian city not far from Monaco—and Secundus at Asta.

What Dexter records concerning the river Tanagrus or Tanarus, at whose confluence Saint Secundus suffered, agrees with this. For that river flows past the Italian Asta, not the Spanish one, and is today called the Taner:

> When he was riding outside the city of Asti, a dove flew down and settled upon Secundus’s head; and when Secundus had come to the river Tanarus, he saw an angel walking upon the water and strengthening him in the faith.

That these things happened in Italy is made clear by what follows:

> After this Secundus went to Milan, where the angel brought Faustinus and Jovita out of prison.

And below:

> But when Secundus was returning, it was already night, and he had come to the bank of the Po, the angel took hold of his horse’s bridle, carried him across the water, led him as far as Dertona, and brought him into the prison to Martianus.

And further on it is added:

> He also brought Secundus out of the closed prison and led him as far as the city of Asti, etc.

There he was ultimately crowned by Sapritius.

Furthermore, after many years the venerable body of Saint Secundus was found at the Italian Asta, and authentic accounts of its discovery and translation were sent to Cardinal Baronius, as he himself reports in his notes for 29 March.
