Finally, M. Maximus writes the following at the end of his *Chronicle*, under the year of Our Lord 612:

> The memory of Saint Secundus of Asti is celebrated in Italy, in the city of Asta in Spain, a Roman colony and, in apostolic times, an episcopal see.

This not only asserts that Secundus of Asti suffered in Italy, but also that he was celebrated at the Spanish Asta because it was a colony of Roman soldiers, established by them in memory of the Italian Asta, whose citizens they were. Dexter again discusses the memory of this same martyr preserved at Asta in Baetica under the year 300.

But regarding his statement that the Tanarus or Tanagrus was also accustomed to be called the Lethes, it is certain that there really is a river Lethes in Africa, near the extremity of the Syrtis, flowing past the city of Berenice. Since, however, it is swallowed up by a fissure in the earth and, after running underground for several miles, bursts forth near Berenice in a great volume of water, the inhabitants were persuaded that it emerged from the underworld.

There are nevertheless other rivers of this name, which Strabo lists in books X and XIV: one near Magnesia in Asia, and another in Crete, flowing not far from Gortyna. In Lusitania there is also the Limia, which Strabo and others call the Lethes. Pomponius Mela, discussing it in book III, chapter 1, says:

> The mouth of the Tagus, the Naebis, the Minius, and the Limia, whose surname is “the river of forgetfulness.”

In Baetica, however, another river still retains the name Guadalete, which is interpreted as “the son of Lethes” [Col. 0361D]—for *guada* means “river” in the language of the Arabs—and it waters ancient Asta.

It must also be maintained that the Tanarus of Italy was formerly called the Lethes. When the people of Asta were building a new colony in Spain, they gave the river the name Tanagrus, or Tanarus, and also Lethes, just as they gave the city the name Asta, in memory of their native Italian city and river. It is well established that the Spaniards often did the same thing in the New World.

### 9. Tertullian flourishes, etc.

The same account may be found in the *Chronicle* of Eusebius and in Jerome’s version, under the year of Our Lord 210. Jerome, however, says in book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 63:

> Tertullian the presbyter is now placed first, after Victor and Apollonius, among the Latins; he was of the province of Africa, of the city of Carthage, and his father was a centurion in the proconsular service, etc.

But since the reader will find much scattered information about this man, who is known to everyone, it is enough to have said little about him.

---

**A.D. 208. A.R. 959.** After Clodius Albinus, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul, was killed near Lyons, Severus makes war upon the Britons.

**A.D. 208. A.R. 959.** At Carthage in Spain, Geta and Plautianus being consuls.

**A.D. 208. A.R. 959.** The virgin Gudenes suffers martyrdom on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of Sextilis [alternatively, Quintilis].

**A.D. 208. A.R. 959.** At Blitabri, near Segovia, by the Carpetanian mountains in the province of Tarraconensis, Saint Auditus the martyr, 1 November.

**A.D. 208. A.R. 959.** Saint Andeolus, having traversed Gaul and all Carpetania in Spain, preaches at the city of Nivaria, adjoining the borders of the Carpetanians, and suffers martyrdom under Severus.

**[Col. 0359] A.D. 208. A.R. 959.** Lucius, bishop of Barcelona, presides for four years.

**A.D. 208. A.R. 959.** Quintus, bishop of Toledo, succeeds Patrinus and presides in the see for twelve years.

**A.D. 208. A.R. 959.** In Spain, from apostolic times, the use and veneration of sacred images is widespread; among them, in our country, the latest was the image of the giant Saint Christopher, derived from his Passion.

**A.D. 208. A.R. 959.** Secundus of Asti flourishes in Spain but suffers martyrdom in Baetica, near the river Tanagrus, otherwise called the Lethes.

**[Col. 0361] A.D. 208. A.R. 959.** Tertullian the African, son of a man who was a proconsular centurion, flourishes.

[Note: **[Col. 0362A]**

**A.D. 211.—Origen, etc.** Eusebius has the following under the year 212: “Origen is educated in Alexandria in all branches of study.” Jerome and others discuss him in book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 64.

]

**A.D. 211. A.R. 962.** Origen is celebrated at Alexandria in every field of learning.

[Note: **[Col. 0362A]**

**A.D. 212.—Fulta, etc.** He succeeded Lucius in the episcopate in this very year. For above Dexter had said, under the year of Christ 208, that Lucius had sat at Barcelona for four years, which were completed in this year 212. Dexter frequently mentions the bishops of Barcelona; this is not surprising, since, writing in his native Barcelona, he would have had at hand the catalogue of the bishops of that see.

]

**A.D. 212. A.R. 963.** Fulta, bishop of Barcelona, for twelve years.

[Note: **[Col. 0362B]**

**A.D. 213.—Severus, etc.** The *Chronicle* of Eusebius has the same words under this very year, and Cardinal Baronius agrees. He ruled for seventeen years, eight months, and three days. Consult Orosius, a friend of our author, book 7, chapter 17.

]

**A.D. 213. A.R. 964.** The emperor Severus dies at York in Britain.

[Note: **[Col. 0362B]**

**A.D. 214.—Asclepiades, etc.** Eusebius, in the *Chronicle* and in books VI, chapters 10 and 15, asserts that he was a new bishop of the see of Antioch. Jerome, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 48, says of Clement of Alexandria:

> There exists, he says, a letter of Alexander, bishop of the Jerusalemites, who later governed the Church with Narcissus, congratulating the Antiochians on the ordination of Asclepiades the confessor.

He was substituted for Serapion, bishop of Antioch, whose memory is celebrated on 29 October. The feast of Asclepiades, however, is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology and in those of Bede, Ado, and Usuard on 18 October, the day on which he suffered martyrdom. There is disagreement concerning the date of his martyrdom: Usuard and Ado hold that he suffered under Decius, whereas the Roman Martyrology places it under Macrinus. Cardinal Baronius follows the latter view, since it can sufficiently be inferred from the cited writings of Eusebius and from Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 19, and book V, chapters 10 and 26.

]

**A.D. 214. A.R. 965.** Asclepiades, bishop of Antioch, flourishes remarkably.

[Note: **[Col. 0362C]**

**A.D. 217.—Antoninus, etc.** According to Spartianus, Caracalla received this surname from the type of garment he wore. Dio relates that the garment had been torn apart and sewn together from many pieces. Consult what Bede says about Caracalla’s clothing in book I of *The History of the English*, chapter 7, when he writes about Saint Alban. Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*, discusses the baths of Antoninus under this year.

]

**A.D. 217. A.R. 968.** Antoninus builds at Rome the baths named after himself.

[Note: **[Col. 0362C]**

**A.D. 218.—Antoninus, etc.** Eusebius likewise says under the present year:

> Antoninus was so unrestrained in lust that he took his stepmother Julia as his wife.

Spartianus, relating his crimes, says:

> Yet he was the most savage of all and—to sum him up in one word—a parricide and incestuous; an enemy of his father, his brother, and his mother.

Orosius agrees, book VII, chapter 18.

]

**A.D. 218. A.R. 969.** Antoninus was so extraordinary in his lust that he resolved to take his stepmother Julia as his wife.

[Note: **[Col. 0362D]**

**A.D. 219.—1. Antoninus is killed, etc.** Carrhae was a city of Mesopotamia beyond Edessa. It was made famous by the blood shed there when Crassus and the Roman army were defeated; Pliny mentions it in book V, chapter 24, and Lucan when he says:

> Carrhae stained Assyria with Latin blood.

It was made still more famous by the death of Antoninus Caracalla. For, as Rufus the consul reports, he perished within the Euphrates near the city of Edessa, when he had dismounted from his horse to relieve his bladder. He was killed by the centurion Martianus at the instigation of Macrinus, who nevertheless later enrolled him among the gods, built him a temple, and assigned him Salii and companions, as Spartianus records.

The authorities disagree about the age at which he was killed. Dio writes that he had reached only twenty-nine, while Spartianus gives forty-three. Eusebius, however, notes in his *Chronicle* that he was in the forty-fourth year of his age, saying:

> Antoninus is killed between Edessa and Carrhae in the forty-fourth year of his age.

Dexter follows this account under the present year.

**2. Macrinus, etc.** Opilius Macrinus, a native of Caesarea in Mauretania, was serving as prefect of the praetorian guard when, after Caracalla was killed, he was proclaimed emperor by the Roman army together with his son Diadumenianus. They too were killed after a year, namely in the year of Our Lord 220. This is demonstrated most clearly by Dio, Julius Capitolinus, and Eusebius in his *Chronicle*, and Orosius agrees in the chapter cited above, chapter 18.

]

**A.D. 219. A.R. 970.** Antoninus is killed near Carrhae in the forty-fourth year of his age.

**[Col. 0363] A.D. 219. A.R. 970.** Macrinus is made emperor. He reigns for one year.

[Note: **[Col. 0363B]**

**A.D. 220.—1. At the Circensian games, etc.** Eusebius, or Jerome in the *Chronicle*, has these exact words under this very year. The Vulcanalia were festivals dedicated to Vulcan and customarily held in the month of August, as may be gathered from Columella, book XI of *On Agriculture*, chapter 3. The Circensian games were a type of chariot competition, first instituted in honor of the counsels of the gods; on this matter see Gellius, book III, chapter 10.

**2. There exists a certain letter, etc.** When, under the year of Our Lord 100, the subject of Marcus Marcellus Eugenius arose, we also discussed this letter in Commentary 2. We lamented that it is still missing, together with the other works of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, to the considerable detriment of scholars. For this letter was undoubtedly his; otherwise he would not have called Saint Eugenius his son. He very frequently calls him by the same name in the books which he sent to him under the name of Timothy, as we proved in that place. He mentions the letter under this year, not because it was written at that time, but because it was held in high repute.

**3. Titus, surnamed, etc.** There is famous testimony in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter XVIII, concerning the surname Justus borne by Titus. When Paul came to Corinth, it says:

> He entered the house of a certain man named Titus Justus, whose house was next to the synagogue.

As for the other things related here about Titus, Peter Equilinus, bishop, in whose work I always find an immense treasure, as though in a storehouse of all antiquity, relates the following in book VII of the *Catalogue*, chapter 118, while writing the life of Saint Titus, disciple of the apostle Paul. Among other things he says that Paul ordained Titus bishop of Crete and, leaving him in Crete, departed.

After two years Titus came to Paul at Rome and remained with him until his execution by Nero; he buried his body together with Luke the Evangelist. We likewise learn from the Apostle about his episcopate in Crete, at the beginning of the Epistle which he addressed to Titus:

> For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might correct what remains to be done and appoint presbyters in each city, as I also instructed you.

It is not sufficiently clear when he left Titus in Crete. It nevertheless appears more probable that this happened when Paul was being brought as a prisoner from Caesarea to Rome, because he had appealed to Caesar. At that time Luke, his companion, testifies that they sailed past Crete, where Paul wished to winter, after spending a considerable time there. He says:

> Since the wind prevented us, we sailed under the lee of Crete near Salmone, and, sailing with difficulty along its coast, we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Thalassa. After much time had passed, navigation was no longer safe, and since the harbor was not suitable for wintering, most of them decided to sail from there, if somehow they could reach Phoenix and winter there, a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest.

It was then, therefore, that he left Titus as bishop of Crete, and afterward wrote to him, calling him to himself, in chapter III.

I understand the two years of which Equilinus says, “After two years Titus came to Paul at Rome,” as the years which Paul spent in chains at Rome. Of these it is said at the end of the Acts:

> He remained for a full two years in his own rented lodging.

Now what Equilinus adds—“He was also with him [Paul] until his execution by Nero”—is directed toward proving that Titus went with Paul to Spain. For if Titus was never separated from the Apostle after those two years, it is necessary that wherever Paul went, Titus went also. We have already established above, on the testimony of many Fathers, especially Chrysostom, that after completing those two years Paul visited Spain. Chrysostom’s golden words are:

> After he had spent two years in chains at Rome, he was finally released; then he departed for Spain, etc.

Theodoret likewise says:

> For two years he first lived by himself at Rome, staying in his own rented lodging; but after he had departed from there for Spain and had also delivered the divine Gospel to them, he returned.

Dexter adds that Titus returned again to Spain and preached in Carpetania with Eugenius. This can be inferred without difficulty from what we proved under the year of Our Lord 100, Commentary 2: namely, that Saint Dionysius the Areopagite dedicated his books to Saint Eugenius of Toledo. Once what we established there is accepted, what we are maintaining about Titus follows in the same way.

For that this Titus was familiar with the man to whom the books of Dionysius were dedicated, and was frequently admitted to conversation with him, is demonstrated by the letter of that same Dionysius to Titus. It says:

> Holy Timothy [that is, Eugenius], most honorable Titus, I do not know whether I have written anything concerning theological signs of which he himself departed ignorant, etc.

This implies that Titus had read the books which Dionysius had dedicated to Eugenius Timothy, and that each had communicated their teaching to the other through personal exchanges and frequent discussions. Titus thereby took occasion to ask Dionysius certain questions, which Dionysius treats in that letter. Since Dionysius was at that time in Gaul and Eugenius in Carpetania in Spain, it follows that Titus also preached for a time in Carpetania.

But how do we know that Pliny Secundus the Younger was converted to the faith in Crete through the work of Saint Titus? From his acts, written by Zenas the jurist and disciple of the Apostle, and quoted by Equilinus in the place cited. After Zenas had said that Titus had returned to Crete and led many to the faith of Christ, and had ordained presbyters and deacons, he adds:

> One day, as he was passing before the palace which Secundus the proconsul—he was Pliny Secundus the Younger—was building at the emperor’s command in the name of Jupiter, he cursed it; and immediately the entire structure was destroyed.

Is this not what Dexter had said in these words?

> This Titus converted Pliny the Younger to the faith in the island of Crete, where, at Trajan’s command, he had erected a temple to Jupiter.

The acts continue:

> Then Secundus came to Titus with tears, asking him to preserve him unharmed from the destruction of the work. Titus commanded him to begin the work in the name of the one God of the Christians, so that he might be able to complete it; and this was done. When the work had been completed, Secundus was baptized with his son.

He was the nephew on his mother’s side of Gaius Pliny Secundus, whose distinguished commentaries *On the Nature of Things* are extant. The work of Pliny Secundus the Younger, however, which survives is his *Letters*, and the *Panegyric* addressed to Caesar Trajan, in which he gives thanks for the consulship obtained through Trajan’s auspices. He also conferred certain benefits upon the Spaniards: he helped Quintilian’s impoverished daughter with a dowry, and, when the poet Martial withdrew from the city to Spain, he furnished him with travelling expenses, as he himself testifies in his letters. He discusses the martyrs who suffered under Trajan in book I, letter 97.

Some, moreover, think that Pliny himself eventually suffered martyrdom at his native Comum. They infer this from the fact that on 6 August, or Sextilis, he is found with five others in the Roman Martyrology among the martyrs, one of whom is named Secundus. We read there:

> At Comum, the passion of the holy martyrs Carpophorus, Exanthus, Cassius, Severinus, Secundus, and Licinius, who were beheaded in their confession of Christ.

Galesinus mentions these martyrs from the ancient records of the Churches of Milan, Bergamo, and Aquileia.

The citizens of Comum were certainly unaware of this history when, in the year of Our Lord 1498, they had the following inscription carved in marble before the church of the Blessed Virgin, in honor of their fellow citizen Pliny the Younger, without the title of martyr. Volaterranus reports it in book 18:

> To Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus,
>
> who, through his consulship, augurate, military service,
>
> pleading of cases, composition of poems and histories,
>
> and most brilliant praise of Caesar Trajan Augustus,
>
> and through the immense generosity he showed toward his native land,
>
> conferred upon it an immortal ornament;
>
> the council of Comum set up this monument
>
> for its beloved fellow citizen, after receiving honor.
>
> 1498,
>
> on the Kalends of May.
>
> I had completed my service, but then I was distinguished by ancient honor;
>
> I lived, I died: now too I have life.

On the right side of this inscription there is another memorial to Gaius Pliny Secundus the Elder, which you, reader, may read in the same Volaterranus.

]

**A.D. 220. A.R. 971.** During the Circensian games of the Vulcanalia, an amphitheater at Rome is burned.

**A.D. 220. A.R. 971.** There exists a certain letter, circulated to Marcus Marcellus, bishop of Toledo, whom it calls “son” and “Timothy,” that is, “honored by God.” For the other Timothy had already died by the time this letter was written.

**A.D. 220. A.R. 971.** Titus, surnamed Justus, having first followed Saint Paul and then Eugenius, is made bishop and preaches in Carpetania, where his memory and the greatness of his miracles are celebrated. This Titus converted Pliny the Younger, returning from Bithynia and Pontus, on the island of Crete, where at Trajan’s command he had erected a temple to Jupiter. Some also believe that he suffered martyrdom at Comum on the seventh day of Sextilis.

[Note: **[Col. 0365D]**

**A.D. 222.—1. Vincentius, etc.** A major error had entered the printed Caesaraugustan manuscript. An unintelligible division had truncated the words in this manner:

> Vincentius, bishop of Toledo, succeeds Quinctus, or Quinctinus.
>
> Likewise bishop of Toledo; he presides for twenty-three years and died at Mevia.

It was understood as though there were another bishop of Toledo besides Quinctus, whereas there is only one sentence, exactly as we have set it out in the text. Vincentius’s name is found among the archbishops of Toledo in the catalogue given by Loaysa, and he is said to have sat after Quinctus. Yet there is a similar error concerning the year in which he took up the see, as there is concerning Quinctus and his predecessors; we have discussed this sufficiently in the appropriate places.

**2. At Hippo, etc.** The distinguished Carpetanian city of Hippo is mentioned by Livy, book XXXIX, in these words:

> In the same year in Spain, the praetors Gaius Calpurnius and Lucius Quinctius, having brought their forces out of winter quarters in early spring and joined them in Baeturia, advanced into Carpetania, where the enemy’s camp was located. Not far from the cities of Hippo and Toledo, a battle arose between the foragers.

Its memory is also preserved in Ptolemy’s *Geography*, where, however, it is corruptly written *Hispinon*, and still more corruptly *Ispinum*, near Libora and Toledo. From its location it is sufficiently clear that it is the place which, with a slight change of name, we now call Hiepes, not far from Toledo [Col. 0366B] and Libora, or Talavera.

Glabrius should be consulted on this matter in his scholia on Livy’s testimony, where he says:

> No one, so far as I know, mentions Hippo among the Carpetanians.

In his notes on book XXV he says:

> There are many names of cities in this author, especially Spanish ones, which, because of the corruption of manuscripts through the injury of time, you will not readily find elsewhere. I wished to state this generally in a single word, so that the reader would not torment himself excessively, as happened to foolish me. Yet one must pardon an outsider, and one wholly ignorant of Spanish affairs.

Morales discusses Hippo in his *Spanish Antiquities*, under the word “Baeturia,” folio 101, although he admits that he does not know the true site of ancient Hippo. There was also a famous city of this name in Africa, over which Saint Augustine presided.

As for the homeland of the holy martyrs Quiricus and Julitta, there is no single, uniform opinion. Many hold that they came from Iconium, a city of Isauria, as we read in the Greek menologion on the Ides of July; some manuscript codices likewise say this, and Peter Equilinus follows them in book VI, chapter 101.

Spanish writers, however, insist that they were Spaniards, as does Damianus a Goes, a learned and distinguished author, in his *Spain*, which appears in *Hispania Illustrata*. Vasaeus follows him in his *Chronicle*, as does Marinaeus Siculus in book V.

Primus Cabilonensis likewise follows this view in his *Spiritual Map of the World*, letter I, saying:

> Iconium, a city of Spain. From there came Quiricus, a boy of three years, who with his mother Julitta suffered martyrdom under the emperor Alexander in the year of Our Lord 230, on 15 July.

The ancient manuscripts must therefore be corrected, and for what they read, “from Iconium of Isauria,” we should read, “from Hippo, a city of Spain,” as Dexter reads here.

Marinaeus understands the statement that the holy martyrs fled to Tarsus in Cilicia to avoid persecution as meaning that they migrated from Spain to Asia. He says:

> Finally, when Julitta was brought before the governor and he asked from what province or city she came, and what her proper name was, she replied: “From the province of Spain, indeed; and from the leading citizens of the city of the Hipponians, I migrated to Cilicia, fleeing your persecutions. I stayed at Tarsus; and since I am truly a Christian, my name is Julitta.”

Dexter, however, proves that this was taken from apocryphal sources, for he writes that they received the palms of martyrdom at Hippo in Carpetania, not at Tarsus in Cilicia.

Once Hippo in Spain had been turned into Iconium in Isauria, it was easy to add Tarsus in Cilicia and to invent their flight, along with the other falsehoods assembled there. Certainly, if Julitta had needed to flee with her trembling son from Hippo, I would sooner read *Tartessus* in the manuscript than *Tarsus*, since Tartessus was a city of the same Spain. It would have been extremely difficult for a noble and delicate woman, with a most tender infant, to undertake so long a journey as that from Spain to Cilicia.

The disagreement among their opponents also supports our position. Some substitute Antioch for Tarsus in Cilicia and write that they were killed there; Usuard and many Latins follow this account. This is no slight indication that both groups drew uncertain conclusions.

Moreover, the bodies of these blessed martyrs have been preserved in Spain. The boy Quiricus rests with great honor in the church bearing his name in the city of Burgos, which is adorned with an abbatial mitre. He also has churches in many Spanish cities, bearing names altered only slightly, such as Saint Quirce, including the church of the Cistercian nuns at Valladolid.

As for what certain acts relate—that the bodies of Saints Quiricus and Julitta were brought from the East to Gaul by Saint Amator, bishop of Auxerre—this belongs to the same class as the other material mixed in there. For it is certain that Pope Gelasius, at the Roman council whose decree is preserved in Distinction 15, chapter *Sancta Romana*, rejected the history or acts of Saints Quiricus and Julitta as apocryphal.

I myself came upon these acts while examining a very ancient manuscript of the library of Nucala. They begin:

> At that time, under the governor Alexander, etc.

They contain dreadful and incredible tortures of the saints, visible struggles of the boy with a demon, and conversations and replies beyond what his age could comprehend. They say that he strengthened his wavering mother in the faith; that the executioners fashioned seven burning obelisks for the boy, two in his eyes, two in his ears, two in his mouth, and the remaining one in his heart; and, the text says, “they became like ice,” along with other things beyond all credibility and moral edification.

Canus passed a severe judgment on these accounts in his book *On Places*.

The true history, however, is the one which the Roman Martyrology, following Simeon Metaphrastes and a certain Bishop Theodore, embraces in these words under 16 June:

> Of the holy martyrs Quiricus and Julitta, his mother, under the emperor Diocletian. Quiricus, a little boy of three years, while lamenting with an inconsolable grief his mother, who was being cruelly scourged with sinews before the governor Alexander, was dashed against the steps of the tribunal and died. Julitta, after savage blows and severe tortures, completed the course of her martyrdom by beheading.

This account nevertheless requires correction in saying that they suffered under Diocletian, since we know that they were killed under the emperor Alexander; and in calling Alexander the governor rather than the emperor. Both points contradict Dexter, as well as the most authentic history, which Equilinus transcribes from ancient manuscripts in book VI, chapter 101. He asserts that they died under the emperor Alexander, around the year of Our Lord 230. Yet when the author says that they were brought before Alexander, the name “Alexander” must be understood as referring to the emperor’s legate.

We shall discuss the discovery of their bodies below, under the year 300.

]

**A.D. 222. A.R. 973.** Vincentius, bishop of Toledo, succeeds Quinctus, likewise bishop of Toledo; he presides for twenty-three years. He dies at Mevia.

**A.D. 222. A.R. 973.** At Hippo in Carpetania, the holy martyrs of Christ, Quiricus and Julitta, win the crown under the emperor Alexander.

[Col. 0367] [Note: **[Col. 0367D]**

**A.D. 224.—Antoninus, etc.** This was the Antoninus called Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Heliogabalus, son of Antoninus Caracalla, as Eusebius writes in his *Chronicle*. Cardinal Baronius follows him and holds that Antoninus ruled for three years, nine months, and four days. Lampridius and Herodian, book V, describe his most impure behavior at length. Consult Orosius, book VII, chapter 18.

]

**A.D. 224. A.R. 975.** Antoninus is killed at Rome in a military disturbance.

[Note: **[Col. 0368A]**

**A.D. 228.—Ulpianus, etc.** Alexander succeeded Heliogabalus. He sought out and employed the most learned counselors, namely Fabius Sabinus, called the Cato of his age; Domitius; Ulpianus, the most skilled jurist; Julius Paulus, the illustrious Venetian; and other disciples of Papinian.

Ulpianus, extremely hostile to Christians, enacted a law preserved in book 3 of the *Digest*, *On the Office of the Governor*; book VII, *On the Office of the Proconsul*; and book IV, *On the Division of Inheritances*. By it he wished severe punishment to be inflicted upon sacrilegious persons who despised the gods and their temples, and he prohibited prophetic books, which he also called magical books.

Eusebius and Isidore discuss him under this very year in their *Chronicles*. He presided over the execution of Saint Quiriacus, bishop of Ostia, and his companions, whose memory is celebrated on 23 August.

]

**A.D. 228. A.R. 979.** Ulpianus the jurist, distinguished as assessor to the emperor Alexander, flourishes greatly at this time.

[Note: **[Col. 0368A]**

**A.D. 229.—At Rome, etc.** Eusebius says under this year:

> The Alexandrian Baths at Rome were completed.

Among other things Lampridius says of Alexander:

> He was also extremely skilled in haruspicy, a great bird-diviner, *ornēoskopos* (ὀρνεοσκόπος), so that he surpassed the augurs of the Vascones, the Spaniards, and the Pannonians.

]

**A.D. 229. A.R. 980.** At Rome the baths called the Alexandrian Baths are completed.

[Note: **[Col. 0368B]**

**A.D. 230.—1. Gemianus, etc.** He was also called Geminus. Jerome says of him in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 75:

> Geminus, he says, a presbyter of the Church of Antioch, composed a few monuments of his learning. He flourished under the emperor Alexander and under Zebennus, bishop of his city.

Of Hippolytus he says in chapter 71:

> Hippolytus, bishop of a certain church—I have not been able to learn the name of the city—also for this reason is omitted by Dexter. He wrote a reckoning of Easter and a canon of the times, extending to the first year of the emperor Alexander; and he discovered the sixteen-year cycle, which the Greeks call an *ekkekaidekaetērida* (ἑκκαιδεκαετηρίδα), etc.

These words contain a catalogue of his books.

Of Beryllus he writes in chapter 70:

> Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, after governing the Church gloriously for some time, finally fell into the heresy that denies Christ before the Incarnation. Corrected by Origen, he wrote various short works, especially letters, in which he thanked Origen, etc.

He flourished under Alexander, the son of Mamaea, and under Maximinus and Gordian, who succeeded him in the empire.

Eusebius discusses these three writers under this year in his *Chronicle*, in almost the same words as Dexter.

]

## 2. In Lusitania

There were formerly three cities in Spain called Salaria. One of them lay among the Oretani, above Oreto Germanorum; another among the Bastetani, near the borders of the kingdom of Valencia. Ptolemy mentions both in his map of Tarraconensian Spain. There was also another in Lusitania, called Salatia in Ptolemy’s manuscript, said to have stood on the shore of the Ocean below Cape Barbarum, not far from the mouth of the Callepodius River, where Setúbal is now situated.

According to Dexter, Gracilianus and Felicissima there suffered a glorious martyrdom. Their memory is celebrated by Usuard on 12 August in these words:

> In the city of Phalaris, the passion of the holy Gracilianus and the virgin Felicissima, whose faces were first battered with stones for Christ, and thereafter they were struck with the sword and received the desired palm of martyrdom.

Equilinus mentions them in Book XI, chapter 130, no. 213, saying:

> Gracilianus and the virgin Felicissima suffered in the city of Phalaris on the day before the Ides of August, that is, on the twelfth day of that month.

However, an error entered the manuscripts of both authors: instead of “the city of Salaria,” they read “the city of Phalaris.” This caused some to read Falari in Picenum, which Pliny mentions in Book III, chapter 13. But when this interpretation found less favor with others, they substituted Faleriae for Falari or Phalari. Petrus Galesinus appears to have been the first to do this in his Martyrology. Yet in his notes he cites only Usuard, who does not write this way; nevertheless, Galesinus admits that the manuscripts lack the city’s name.

Cardinal Baronius followed him and newly wrote in the Roman Martyrology: “At Faleriae in Tuscia, the passion of the holy Gracilianus,” and so forth. He was moved by no other consideration than the records of the Church of Castellana in Tuscia, where the relics of the holy martyrs are preserved. Those records read Faleriae, not Falari or Salariae.

But since there is no evidence establishing that those records preserve a certain and infallible reading, we cannot reject Dexter’s very ancient testimony. Indeed, the very fact that the bodies of the holy martyrs are not preserved at Faleriae, but in the city of Castellana in the same province, sufficiently proves that they did not die at Faleriae, but in another region situated a considerable distance away. For the bodies of saints are not easily transferred from place to place, except so that they may be kept in a safer location during a general devastation of the province or during persecution. This happened, for example, with the saints of Spain during the devastation caused by the Saracens. We therefore believe that the holy Gracilianus and Felicissima were transferred from the Lusitanian city of Salaria to Castellana in Tuscia.

But after Spain’s Salaria had been destroyed and consigned to oblivion, the manuscripts were altered, and the martyrs were believed to have been killed at Faleriae, a well-known city, although they had been born under the sky of Salaria, situated very far away. Certainly, if they had been martyrs of Faleriae, Faleriae would at some time have reclaimed its deposit from the city of Castellana. Yet it is not known to have done so in any way; indeed, it has always been unaware that they were its own. We should therefore rejoice with Dexter, who has brought us light amid such great darkness.

**A.D. 230. A.R. 981.** Gemianus, a presbyter of Antioch; Hippolytus; and Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, are considered distinguished writers.

**A.D. 230. A.R. 981.** In the Lusitanian city of Salaria, called an imperial city, the martyrs Gracilianus and Felicissima are celebrated with outstanding praise.

[Col. 0369B — Note]

**A.D. 234.—Alexander, etc.** These statements differ little from the words of Eusebius, who writes in his Chronicle for this year:

> Alexander was exceptionally devoted to his mother Mammaea, and for that reason beloved by everyone. He established colleges in which girls called Mammeae and boys called Mammeani would be raised in memory of his mother, as Lampridius writes in the year 984 of the City. He also built the Mammean bridge over the River Anio, which is still called Ponte Mammolo, three miles from the City; Cicero speaks of it in his book On Famous Orators.

That Mammaea was a Christian is attested by Orosius in Book VII, chapter 18, who says:

> His mother Mammaea, a Christian woman, arranged to hear the presbyter Origen.

This also seems to be suggested by Jerome, who will be cited below.

**A.D. 234. A.R. 985.** The emperor Alexander was exceptionally devoted to his mother Mammaea.

[Col. 0369C — Note]

**A.D. 235.—Origen, etc.** Eusebius mentions Origen’s same journey in his Chronicle for this year, as does Jerome in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 64:

> When Origen was already in middle age and, because of the churches of Achaea, which were troubled by numerous heresies, was traveling through Palestine toward Athens under the authority of an ecclesiastical letter, he was ordained presbyter by Theoclistus and Alexander, bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem.

A little later Jerome writes:

> How great his reputation was appears from the fact that Firmilianus, bishop of Caesarea, invited him together with all Cappadocia and kept him there for a long time. It is also shown by the fact that, when he was invited by Mammaea, the religious mother of the emperor Alexander, he went to Antioch and was treated with the highest honor.

**A.D. 235. A.R. 986.** Origen departed from Alexandria for Caesarea in Palestine.

[Col. 0370A — Note]

**A.D. 237.—Alexander.** Eusebius’s Chronicle records nearly the same words, and Baronius follows him in asserting that Alexander was killed in this year, after he had ruled for thirteen years and nine days, and that he died at Moguntiacum, a distinguished city of Germany. Cornelius Tacitus, Ammianus, the Alexandrian, Ptolemy, Orosius, and others call it Moguntiacum.

**A.D. 237. A.R. 988.** The emperor Alexander was killed at Moguntiacum in a military mutiny.

[Col. 0370A — Note]

**A.D. 238.—Maximinus, etc.** What is here called a common soldier is explained by Eusebius, translated into Latin by Saint Jerome, as meaning “from the military ranks,” for he says:

> Maximinus was the first to be chosen emperor by the army from the military ranks, without the authority of the Senate.

This is sufficiently established by Lampridius and others.

**A.D. 238. A.R. 989.** Maximinus, a common soldier, is elected without senatorial authority.

[Col. 0370A — Note]

**A.D. 239.—Maximinus against the Church, etc.** Eusebius writes in his Chronicle for this very year:

> Maximinus undertakes a persecution against the priests of the churches.

This was the sixth in order among the persecutions suffered by the Catholic Church, as Dexter himself acknowledges below under the year of the Lord 260. Consult Orosius, Book VII, chapter 19.

**A.D. 239. A.R. 990.** Maximinus launches a persecution against the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0370B — Note]

**A.D. 240.—Maximinus is killed by Pupienus, etc.** Eusebius likewise writes this in the present year. Dexter evidently borrowed from him much of what concerns the history of the emperors. Pupienus traced an ancient origin from Gades in Spain, as Morales noted from older sources under the year of Christ 239.

**A.D. 240. A.R. 991.** Maximinus is killed by Pupienus at Aquileia in Italy.

[Col. 0370B — Note]

**A.D. 241.—Gordian, etc.** These statements agree with what Julius Capitolinus, Paulus Orosius in Book VII, chapter 19, and Eutropius, likewise in Book VII, write. Eusebius also says in his Chronicle:

> When Gordian entered Rome, Pupienus and Galbinus [elsewhere Balbinus], who had seized the empire, were killed in the palace.

**A.D. 241. A.R. 992.** Gordian is elected emperor, and Pupienus and Galbinus are killed at Rome.

[Col. 0370B — Note]

**A.D. 243.—Gordian, etc.** Eusebius also attests this in the same year. Gordian defeated Sapor, king of the Persians, drove him from Syria, recovered Antioch, and subdued Carrhae and Nisibis. Orosius, Capitolinus, and Eutropius, cited above, write about this.

**A.D. 243. A.R. 994.** Gordian, still far too young, overcomes the Parthian battle lines.

[Col. 0370C — Note]

**A.D. 244.—Philip, etc.** Some writers, whom Cardinal Baronius follows, teach that Gordian ruled for six years, namely from the year of the Lord 239, when he seized power in Africa, until 246, when he was killed by Philip. Dexter, however, deals with Gordian only from his election, that is, from the time when, after Pupienus and Galbinus had been removed, he began to reign alone; the election fell in the year of the Lord 241.

His death occurred not in 246 but in 244; besides Dexter, this is taught by Eusebius in his Chronicle. Philip was prefect of the praetorian guard when he killed Gordian as Gordian was returning home from the slaughter of the Parthians. Philip was converted to the Christian faith, together with his son Philip, by Saint Pontius the martyr, who later went to Gaul for the sake of preaching and suffered martyrdom at Nicea. In the year of the Lord 247, Philip admitted his son, likewise called Philip, into a share of the kingdom, as Eusebius recorded in his Chronicle.

**A.D. 244. A.R. 995.** Philip, prefect of the praetorian guard, kills Gordian near Rome.

[Col. 0371A — Note]

**A.D. 245.—Pomponius Paulatus, etc.** We know from the catalogue of the bishops of Toledo, published by Loaysa in the volume of the Councils of Spain, that Paulatus succeeded Vincentius in the first see of Toledo, although the years during which each held office are not assigned there. We should therefore owe this information to Dexter, as well as the name Pomponius.

It is consequently established that Vincentius, bishop of Toledo, died in the year 245, since he began his pontificate in 222 and held it for twenty-three years. As for Dexter’s earlier note that he died at Mevia, we believe this happened because, out of reverence for Saint Vincent, bishop of Mivia and a distinguished early martyr of that name in Spain, he often used to visit Mevia, so that he might be supported by the merits of the saint whose name it bore. We discussed Saint Vincent of Mivia under the year 100.

Maximus adds the following about Pomponius Paulatus in his Chronicle under the year 612:

> The memory of Pomponius Paulatus, bishop of Toledo, is famous throughout Spain. Saint Cyprian of Carthage wrote to him, and he enjoyed a very close friendship and kinship with Narcissus, bishop of Braga [of whom more later].

He adds the following about Paulatus’s family:

> He was exceedingly noble, the brother of Pomponius Bassus, a former consul and twice consul; and the paternal uncle of another Pomponius Bassus, also a former consul.

Cassiodorus records that Pomponius Bassus entered the consulship with Aurelius Fuscus in the year 1010 of the City, A.D. 259. Paulatus is discussed again below under the years 285, 286, and 430.

An error had entered Dexter’s manuscript at this point, whereby Pomponius was called Paulatus or Palmatius. Palmatius, however, was a quite different bishop, who held the see of Toledo after Sintitio in the year 472; Maximus discusses him in his Chronicle.

**A.D. 245. A.R. 996.** Pomponius Paulatus, bishop of Toledo, succeeds Vincentius of Toledo as well; an eloquent and devout man, he held office for thirty-six years.

[Col. 0371B — Note]

**A.D. 246.—At Osca, etc.** The city of Osca still flourishes in the kingdom of Aragon, in the region where the Ilergetes once bordered the Vescetani, or Autetani. This caused some, like Dexter, to place Osca among the Vescetani or Autetani, while others, like Ptolemy, placed it among the Ilergetes.

Dexter’s testimony deserves greater confidence, since he was born not far away. Today the city is called Huesca; it is adorned with a very distinguished academy and an episcopal see. It is still more distinguished, however, by the blood of its citizens, the saints Orentius and Patientia, and by the sacred relics of the blessed married couple. Above all human glory, it is distinguished as the birthplace of that great and most renowned martyr throughout the world, Laurence, archdeacon of the Roman Church.

Laurence was born at Osca in Vescetania to the holy martyrs Orentius and Patientia. He had a brother, marked by his father’s name, who governed as bishop the city of Auch in Gaul and, renowned for his holiness, received the title of confessor. He is celebrated on earth with festive joy on the Kalends of May, the day on which his name is read in Usuard’s Martyrology and in the Roman Martyrology. The Roman Martyrology reads:

> At Auch, Saint Orentius, bishop.

Usuard gives a fuller account:

> Near the city of Auch, Saint Orentius, bishop, who, adorned with virtues, is said to have rested in a holy death.

Ado also discusses him in his Martyrology, but mistakenly thinks that he was bishop of Toulouse.

As for the parents of Laurence and Orentius, some, unaware of their martyrdom, celebrated their feast under the title of confessors. Dexter’s testimony establishes that they suffered martyrdom in the year of the Lord 246, during the persecution of Maximinus and Gallienus. The Roman Martyrology likewise declares this, recording under the Kalends of May:

> At Osca in Spain, the holy martyrs Orentius and Patientia.

Cardinal Baronius says:

> In the Florilegium of the Saints of Spain, drawn from the ancient records of the Church of Osca, these are said to have been the parents of Saint Laurence the martyr.

The author of the Treasury of Preachers writes about Saint Laurence under 10 August:

> He was Spanish by birth, from the city of Osca in the kingdom of Aragon. His parents, namely Orentius and Patientia, were saints, and the aforementioned Church also celebrates an office for them.

Morales, Marieta, and others discuss the same matter.

As for Laurence himself, in the Life of Saint Laurence formerly read in churches, which Surius printed from very ancient manuscript books—I read two of these manuscripts, written on parchment, in the Vatican Library, shelf 27, numbers, as I believe, 1192 and 1194—we read:

> Caesar said to him: “Tell us your lineage.” Blessed Laurence replied: “As far as lineage is concerned, I am a Spaniard; but I was raised and educated at Rome, and from my cradle I have been a Christian, instructed in every holy and divine law.”

Ado has precisely the same words in his Martyrology under 10 August. Equilinus writes in Book VII, chapter 43:

> He was Spanish by birth and was a disciple of Blessed Sixtus II.

Hieronymus Vida says in his hymn to Saint Laurence, which begins “Tantane te juvenum”:

> I would celebrate your praises in no feigned song,  
> Since, born of no ignoble stock in Iberian soil,  
> As a child you left your sweet homeland  
> And your dear parents, captivated by love of flourishing Italy, and so forth.

As he was going to martyrdom, Vida writes:

> He went rejoicing, eager, as once a young man goes to the bridal chamber  
> Of his promised wife, toward the new joys of his first night.  
> Yet whenever he halted upon the bank  
> Of the pleasant Tiber, gazing at the breezes  
> And the depths of heaven, turned toward the setting sun,  
> He said: “I shall no longer look upon you,  
> Spain, rich in fruitful kingdoms,  
> Nor upon you, rivers of my homeland, and beloved parents,  
> Who perhaps are entertaining the vain hope of my return.”

When he was about to lie upon the gridiron, Vida has him say:

> Again he spoke, gazing at heaven and the setting sun:  
> “Riding through the heights of heaven, sun, and beneficent splendor of day,  
> Since you hasten to bathe yourself in the Iberian flood,  
> Those whom Spain now separates upon distant shores,” and so forth.

Finally, in the hymn beginning “Huc ades,” he addresses Laurence and asks him to come:

> Whether the Tagus and the borders of your homeland  
> Now hold you back, sweet land, and so forth.

Saint Vincent Ferrer explains on what occasion Laurence came to Rome in a sermon on the same martyr:

> I say first that Blessed Laurence, like a good tree planted in the garden of the holy Church, bore the fruit of personal abstinence, because he always abstained from vices, sins, and the vanities of the world in three places: first in the city of Osca, second in Caesaraugusta, and third in Rome. As for the first, it should be known that he was born at Osca, of a noble family, and although he was raised in the houses of the great. Secondly, he abstained at Caesaraugusta, because when he had reached the age of discretion, he left his father’s house and went to Caesaraugusta to study. Thirdly, he went to Rome. And behold, Saint Sixtus, the pope, while going to celebrate the Council of Toledo, passed through Caesaraugusta. Having heard of Blessed Laurence’s reputation, he summoned him; and, learning of his holiness, took him with him, and so forth.

Vincent is wonderfully corroborated by the French writer Petrus Rossetus, easily the foremost of the poets of his time. He wrote Laurence’s Life in a highly elegant heroic poem called the Laurentiad. Among other passages he wrote:

> To him who asked such questions, having set aside fear of death,  
> The steadfast hero Laurence quickly replied:  
>  
> Spain gave me my first beginnings,  
> While Sixtus, chief priest, proclaimed  
> The covenant of our sacred faith in farthest Hesperia—  
> He whom you recently crushed beneath the cruel sword, though innocent.  
>  
> There I learned to know Christ and the saving rites;  
> Once, too, the water of the sacred stream washed my head.  
> He brought me here as a boy from the furthest shores  
> Of Hesperia. We spent our years together  
> During the reign of Philip. The chief priest Sixtus,  
> The great and holy man, was offering incense at the altars, and so forth.

The same Rossetus, in his Panegyric of the Salazars, dedicated to Tristán Salazar, archbishop of Sens, attests that the illustrious lineage of the Salazars once flourished at Numantia in Spain and resisted the Romans gloriously. From there it grew into a great family, and among the sons of that stock it had Blessed Laurence above all:

> Moreover, you should seek him from the Salazarian stock, and so forth.  
>  
> Later the great family grew; from it Laurence arose,  
> Who bore the burning coals upon the grate.

He does not reveal where he obtained this information. It is nevertheless established that the Salazars always held Saint Laurence as their principal patron above all others, and that some of the ancients boasted of being related to him.

Nor should we omit what Marinaeus Siculus reports in Book V:

> They say that he was the son of a certain leader of Spain, whom a demon had carried from his cradle as an infant into a forest. But Blessed Sixtus, while preaching in that same province, found him miraculously beneath a laurel tree, called him Laurence, and ordered that he be raised and taught with diligent care. When he had grown up, he brought him with him to Rome, where he later became a pontiff and appointed Laurence archdeacon.

Consult Vaseus in his Chronicles, to pass over the other writers of Spanish history.

What more is there to say? I have no doubt that Prudentius also recalled the native city of the holy archdeacon in his sacred hymn when, addressing the martyr near its end, he said:

> As though you were always present,  
> You embrace your urban disciples  
> With a nursing breast  
> And nourish them with a father’s love.

He then adds:

> Among these, O glory of Christ,  
> Hear also the rustic poet, and so forth.

Yet at that time the poet was not among the Romans but among the Spaniards, for shortly before he had said:

> The Iberian Basque separates us,  
> Removed by two Alpine ranges.

Enough has been said about a matter known to everyone.

**A.D. 246. A.R. 997.** At Osca in Vescetania, the holy martyrs Orentius and Patientia, parents of Saint Laurence, the martyr and archdeacon who suffered at Rome; and Saint Orentius, confessor and bishop of Auch.

[Col. 0373C — Note]

**A.D. 248.—Saint Melchiades, etc.** It may seem novel to some that Dexter presents that great pastor of the Roman and universal Church, Melchiades, whom everyone until now has described as African, as having been born in Spain. But it is one thing to have been African by origin and another to have arisen in Spain. Dexter himself acknowledges both below, under the year of the Lord 299, where he says:

> Melchiades, African by descent, born in the Spanish city of Mantua of the Carpetani, flourishes at Rome in the glory of holiness and learning.

We do not deny, therefore, that Melchiades derived his origin from Africa; at the same time, we assert that he was born in Spain, namely at Mantua, formerly a city of the noble province of Carpetania, as can be seen in Ptolemy’s map of Tarraconensian Spain. It is now the capital of all Spain and of the Spanish monarchy, called Madrid or Matritum by the Saracens after its name was changed. The body of modern writers agrees on this, although Julianus Petri resists the view in his Chronicle.

Speaking of the recent death of Saint Isidore the Farmer, newly enrolled among the saints, Julianus writes:

> In the year of the Lord 973. In this year Saint Isidore the Farmer died at Magerit—which he calls Matritum—although some falsely call it Mantua of the Carpetani. He was a devout man, fervent in charity, and renowned throughout Spain for many celebrated miracles, both while alive and after his death, on 28 November.

Nevertheless, as far as Melchiades’ homeland is concerned, Julianus entirely follows Dexter under the year 245:

> Miltiades, who later became pope, was born in Spain, though of African parents, near the city of Mantua of the Carpetani.

We also have in favor of this truth the Reverend Father Alfonso Chacón in the life of that pontiff, and the highly learned man and our friend Aegidius Gundisalvi Davila, the royal chronologer, in the special history of Madrid that he recently published.

But lest any suspicion arise from the homeland of the authors mentioned, or anyone think that they wrote this out of love for Spain, since all of them are Spaniards, I shall also cite a French author of unquestionably great authority and free from every suspicion: Primus, bishop of Chalon, who writes the following in his Spiritual Map of the World when discussing Mantua of Carpetania:

> Mantua, an inland city of Tarraconensian Spain. Here Pope Melchiades was born; he was martyred at Rome under Maxentius.

I shall add a Sicilian author, lest Italy appear to have been silent about this truth. He is Franciscus Maurolicus, in the topography of the martyrs appended to his Martyrology, where he reports and embraces the words of Primus of Chalon.

There are many proofs that navigation and communication between Spain and Africa were once very frequent. Saint Marcellus, a centurion taken from the Spanish city of León to Africa, suffered martyrdom at Caesarea in Mauretania. From that same Caesarea, the holy martyrs Felix and Cucuphas came to Spain and were killed for Christ at Gerunda. Saint Paschasius, born at Salamanca with his companions, offered his neck in Africa under the Arian king Genseric.

I omit Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in Africa, although he was born at Toledo in Spain; we shall discuss him in his proper place with Maximus, the continuator of Dexter. I omit the case of Felix and Basilides of Spain, which was dealt with by Saint Cyprian of Carthage, and the great disciples of Augustine—Paulus Orosius, Eucharius the presbyter, Hector Ferrandus, and others—since we shall discuss them below.

It is nevertheless certain, and generally accepted, that many people once migrated from Africa to Spain, whether for commercial purposes or for some other business capable of causing the mutual movement of citizens between neighboring provinces. Among these people, and no less distinguished than the rest, were the parents of Saint Melchiades, who went to Mantua of the Carpetani and there received the gift of so great a son’s birth.

**A.D. 248. A.R. 999.** Saint Melchiades, who later became Roman pontiff, is born in Spain.

[Col. 0374D — Note]

**A.D. 249.—While the Philips were reigning, etc.** By a special providence of God it came about that Rome celebrated the thousandth year of its foundation under Christian emperors. On this matter, read Cardinal Baronius, volume II, and Eusebius in his Chronicle, who narrates the event in nearly the same words as Dexter. Also read the Acts of Saint Pontius the martyr in Surius, volume VII, under 14 May.

**A.D. 249. A.R. 1000.** While the Philips were reigning, Rome reached the thousandth year of its foundation. On this occasion innumerable beasts were killed in the circus, and theatrical games were presented for three days and nights, while the people remained awake, with great magnificence and rejoicing among the Roman citizens.

[Col. 0374D — Note]

**A.D. 252.—1. Philip, etc.** Eusebius places the death of the Philips in the following year. Equilinus, however, considers both Philips worthy to be counted among the martyrs in Book XI, chapter 92, because they were killed by Decius, whom they themselves had appointed Caesar, out of hatred for the Christian faith.

When Decius returned victoriously from Gaul to Rome, Philip the Elder met him as far as Verona as a mark of respect. Decius declared that it was unworthy for Roman gods to be despised and scorned by emperors. After winning certain men over to revolt, and with their agreement, he cruelly slaughtered the emperor while he was resting in his bed. He then departed from Verona, kept the other Philip at Rome by equal wickedness and deceit, and killed him while he was confessing Christ.

See what the author says at greater length about this matter when he discusses the treasures that they gave to the Roman Church, which later brought Saint Laurence his palm of martyrdom.

The following memorial of the Philips exists in the Royal Church of Toledo:

> To the emperor Caesar Marcus Julius Philip, Pious, Fortunate, Augustus, holder of tribunician power, father of the country and consul. The most devoted people of Toledo dedicated this to his divine power and majesty.

The following exists at Lisbon:

> To the emperor Caesar Julius Philip, Pious, Fortunate, Augustus, Chief Pontiff, holder of tribunician power for the second time, father of the country, consul for the third time. At Felicitas Julia Olisipo.

Ambrosius Morales carefully noted that the latter Lisbon memorial was erected after Philip had become a Christian, since it omits the words “to his divine power and majesty,” which usually appear in the former Toledan inscription and in nearly all inscriptions to pagan emperors.

**2. Decius, etc.** On Decius’s succession to the empire of the Philips, read Cardinal Baronius and all those who have treated Roman affairs, as well as Eusebius, who supplies Dexter’s words in the year of the Lord 254. His name was Quintus Herennius Etruscus Messius Decius, as Morales notes from an inscription at Valencia in Spain.

**3. Out of hatred, etc.** The same thing can also be seen in Eusebius’s Chronicle under the year 254. This was the fiercest persecution, commonly held to have been the seventh among those which the Church suffered from the pagans; Dexter likewise asserts this somewhat below under the year 260. Read Equilinus, Book II, chapter 92.

**4. Antonius, etc.** This too was borrowed from Eusebius’s Chronicle. That he was born in this year, 253, is inferred from the fact that he is known to have died in the twenty-first year of Constantius’s reign, namely in the year of Christ 358, as Jerome teaches in his Chronicle, when Antonius was 105 years old. Jerome himself says this in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, in the notice on Antonius, as does the great Athanasius in his Life of him.

**5. At this time, etc.** Eusebius likewise has this in his Chronicle.

**A.D. 252. A.R. 1003.** Philip the Elder was killed at Verona, and the Younger at Rome.

**A.D. 252. A.R. 1003.** Decius, born at Budalia in Lower Pannonia, reigns.

**A.D. 252. A.R. 1003.** Out of hatred for the Christian Philips, Decius launches a persecution.

**A.D. 252. A.R. 1003.** Antonius, later patriarch of the monks in Egypt, is born.

**A.D. 252. A.R. 1003.** At this time the amphitheater at Rome was consumed by flames.

[Col. 0375C — Note]

**A.D. 255.—1. At Rome, in the Church, etc.** Saint Fabian had held the papacy for fourteen years, eleven months, and eleven days, and received the crown of martyrdom in the year 254. The see remained vacant for one year; consequently Saint Cornelius, who succeeded Fabian, was ordained in the year 255. Cardinal Baronius holds that his election fell in the year 254. But we have already shown above that this author almost invariably differs from Eusebius’s and Dexter’s chronology by one year. Consult Dexter’s catalogue of Fabian’s predecessors below, under the year of the Lord 260, no. 3.

**2. Felix, etc.** The extensive and frequent communication between the churches of Spain and Africa in the time of Saint Cyprian, in the case of Basilides, bishop of Asturica, and Martial, bishop of Mérida, is abundantly demonstrated.

During the persecution of Decius, the two aforementioned bishops, terrified by fear of the imminent death, sacrificed to the idols of the pagans—alas!—attended pagan associations and banquets, fell into the crime of blasphemy, and finally buried dead Christians, which was entirely forbidden, in common graves together with dead pagans.

For this reason they were deposed by their clergy and congregations, and the Catholics Felix and Sabinus, vigorous champions of the faith, were advanced to their sees. To obtain approval of these elections and depositions, the newly elected Sabinus and Felix were sent to the African Church with letters from another Felix, a presbyter, and from the congregations of León and Astorga, as well as from Aelius the deacon and the congregation of Mérida.

When they arrived at Carthage, the great city of Africa, Saint Cyprian, then bishop and metropolitan of that see, summoned thirty-five other bishops. When all had gathered together and were celebrating a provincial council for this reason, the letter of the presbyter Felix and the letters of the three churches of Spain were opened and publicly read before everyone. After the matter had been carefully considered, it was judged that Basilides and Martial had been rightly deposed, while Felix and Sabinus had been canonically elected. In the name of all the council’s bishops, a common responsive letter was then sent to the presbyter Felix and to the three aforementioned congregations of Spain.

Such letters are preserved in Cyprian, Book I, Letter 4—Letter 68 in Pamelius’s edition—and the entire history is contained there.

We can therefore easily escape the error in which innumerable people became entangled: they thought that, in the case of Basilides and Martial, a certain bishop Felix of Caesaraugusta had sent special letters to the bishops of Africa.

They are moved by the fact that in Cyprian’s printed copies they read these words:

> And another Felix of Caesaraugusta, a worshiper of the faith and defender of the truth, indicates in his letter that Basilides and Martial have been defiled by the infamous document of idolatry.

Among others, Martin Carrillo, abbot of Montearagón, held this view in his Catalogue of the Bishops of Caesaraugusta, printed at Cagliari in 1611, where he states:

> In the year of the Lord 255, Saint Felix, bishop of Caesaraugusta. Saint Cyprian calls him a worshiper of the faith and a defender of the truth.

Murillo followed him in his History of Caesaraugusta, as did other writers on the affairs of Aragon.

What surprises me more is that equally learned and careful men, Ambrosius Morales and Caesar Baronius, held the same opinion. Morales did so in Book IX, chapter 45, under the year 255; Baronius in volume II of his Annals, under the year 258. Baronius writes:

> To these he also added his own private letters, written in the same case, from Saint Felix, bishop of Caesaraugusta, of whom Saint Cyprian himself says so excellently: “Felix of Caesaraugusta,” and so forth.

But, leaving aside for the moment the reading “Felix of Caesaraugusta,” which will be discussed shortly, Felix is entirely gratuitously and without foundation called a bishop of Caesaraugusta. He is nowhere found as a bishop, since all the authors mentioned above find no record of him anywhere except in this letter of Cyprian. If the letter is read attentively, it provides no basis for saying that he was a bishop. It merely says:

> Felix of Caesaraugusta, a worshiper of the faith and a defender of the truth, indicates in his letter, and so forth.

There is absolutely no mention of an episcopate. On the contrary, in the same letter he is expressly called a presbyter—something I am astonished that so many learned men failed to notice.

But where will you find this? Certainly at the beginning and in the heading of the letter, for it says:

> Caecilius Cyprianus, Primus, Polycarpus, and the others, thirty-six in all, to Felix the presbyter and to the congregations residing at León and Astorga.

It also says:

> To Aelius the deacon and to the congregation of Mérida, the brethren residing there, greeting in the Lord.

And:

> When we had gathered together, dearest brothers, we read your letter, which you sent to us through our fellow bishops Felix and Sabinus, for the integrity of your faith and for the love of God, and so forth.

Here one sees, first of all, that the Carthaginian council of thirty-six bishops writes back to Felix—not to a bishop, but to a presbyter—and then to the congregations of León and Astorga, and finally to Aelius the deacon of Mérida and to that Church’s congregation.

Nor will anyone deny that these letters were addressed to Felix the presbyter and to the congregations of León and Astorga because Saint Cyprian and the fathers of that council had received letters from them. All who had written to the council about the case of Basilides and Martial were named at the beginning of the letter, for it says:

> We have read your letters, which you sent to us.

Therefore, when the letter later says:

> Consequently, just as you wrote, dearest brothers [namely, the congregations of Astorga, León, and Mérida], and as our colleagues Felix and Sabinus affirm [namely, orally, since they were the bishops who carried those letters, about whom the council fathers had said at the beginning: “We have read your letters, which you sent to us through our fellow bishops Felix and Sabinus, for the integrity of your faith”], and as another Felix of Caesaraugusta, a worshiper of the faith and defender of the truth, indicates in his letter, and so forth—

when, I say, it says this, it undoubtedly speaks of the Felix who had written a letter to the synod. For this reason the reply is now addressed to him when it says:

> To Felix the presbyter and to the congregations, and so forth.

He was therefore a presbyter, not a bishop.

I would not have him confused with that other bishop Felix, who, together with the bishop Sabinus, carried the letter of the presbyter Felix and of the congregations of León and Astorga, and so forth; Cyprian clearly distinguishes them.

[Col. 0377C] As for the name of the Church of which he was presbyter, the manuscripts of Cyprian read *Caesaraugusta* in a most corrupt form, whereas it should read *Vallata Urbicua*, as Dexter has it. It was a small city, and was therefore called *Urbicua*, or because it lay at the confluence of the river Urbicus. Nevertheless, it was fortified and surrounded by substantial walls; for it was the city which Fulvius Flaccus, praetor of Nearer Spain, once undertook to subdue and besieged—as Morales reports from Livy, book XL, in book VII, chapter 18—although Morales himself does not know where it was located. Certainly its proximity to Asturica is sufficiently demonstrated by the name of the river Urbicus, now called the Órbigo, which either received its name from Urbica Vallata or gave that city its name, as I believe; Charles Estienne mentions it in his *Dictionary* under the letter V. It is now Vaneza, or perhaps Puente de Órbigo. For the Emperor Antoninus also places Vallata in his *Itinerary* sixteen Roman miles, or five leagues, from Asturica toward the east, as may be seen in the route from Asturica to Tarraco [Col. 0377D] and in the route from Asturica to Bordeaux. Yet the site is the one now occupied by Vaneza.

This also agrees with the matter under discussion, which concerned Basilides, bishop of Asturica. The presbyter of the Asturican territory ought indeed to have accused him, since a man from Caesaraugusta, so far distant, could scarcely have known his offenses thoroughly or opposed him with sufficient courage, especially during the time of that great persecution which Decius was stirring up against the Church. Cyprian himself, at the beginning of the letter, just as he associates the deacon Aelius with the people of Emerita, since Aelius was writing against his own bishop Martial, likewise associates the presbyter Felix with the peoples residing at León and Asturica, because he was writing against Basilides, bishop of Asturica. He says: “To Felix the presbyter, and to the peoples residing at León and Asturica,” thereby indicating that this Felix was a presbyter of the Asturican territory. See, I beg you, reader, from how great a darkness Dexter delivers us.

### 3. “At this time in the city of Belsinia,” etc.

Pliny, book XIX, chapter VIII, states that Carpetania was formerly famous both for the abundance and the quality of its cumin, and that from this there arose the village of Cuminarium. At that place there now exists a town exceptionally fertile in the same cumin, Santa Cruz de la Zarza, near Voles. The learned Aurelius de Frías, a man highly distinguished for investigating the antiquities of Spain, recognized this, as Morales reports in book IX, chapter 34. The location agrees with the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, where, on the route from Emerita to Caesaraugusta through Lusitania, eighteen Roman miles before Titulcia—which is now Bayona de Aranjuez—the village of Cuminarium is placed. Santa Cruz now stands there.

But the Cuminaria of which Dexter speaks cannot be Santa Cruz de la Zarza, since that place was situated near Belsinia, or Belsinum, now called Borja, as Villanova testifies in his notes on Ptolemy’s geographical tables. In Dexter’s printed text the name is corruptly written *Vestinia*. There certainly were Vestini in Italy, neighboring the Sabines and Picentes, whose highly praised cheeses Martial mentions in book XIII:

> If you wish to eat a frugal breakfast without meat,  
> this lump comes to you from a Vestinian flock.

Pliny discusses the same people in book III, chapter 5. In Spain, however, we read *Belsini*, not *Vestini*. Not far from Belsinia was Bellica, which is falsely read as *Tullica* in Villanova’s tables. I think this is the place now called Belilla, famous because a cymbal is often miraculously struck there as an omen of great events. For both Belsinia and Bellica are placed by Ptolemy not far from Turiasona. Pliny declares Bellica to be a municipium under the jurisdiction of Caesaraugusta.

Dexter differs from Ptolemy in placing both cities in Carpetania, whereas Ptolemy places them in Celtiberia. In this matter Dexter should be followed, since he was a Spanish author writing about Spanish affairs. Ptolemy was easily misled because Carpetania lies close to Celtiberia, and the boundaries of the two regions cannot readily be determined.

These remarks concern the cities assigned at this point. When I investigated who that woman was whom Dexter calls a priestess of Venus, the powerful and extremely wealthy woman Lucilla came to mind. She forced Majorinus into the Carthaginian Church against Caecilianus. Augustine discusses her in book I, chapter 3, *Against Parmenianus*, and in book III, chapters 27–29, *Against Cresconius*; Optatus of Milevis also discusses her in book I, *Against Parmenianus*. It supports this identification that she lived in the province of Numidia. Yet the text calls her *Numia Varia*, and I do not know whether *Numia* is corrupt for *Numida*, meaning a woman named Varia, or for *Numidia*, the place where she lived. I cannot altogether conjecture how she could have been at one time in Spain and at another in Numidia, nor why we should trouble ourselves greatly with determining this more precisely.

### 4. “Likewise at this same time,” etc.

This most blessed virgin was highly celebrated among the ancients, and Aldhelm, bishop of the West Saxons, sang her life in elegant verse in book II of *The Praise of Virginity*. Surius transferred this account to volume VI, under 23 December, the feast of the same virgin. Ado writes sufficiently about her, and we read the same account in Equilinus, book I, chapter 83.

She was born at Rome and betrothed to Eugenius the Pagan. Warned beforehand by an angelic vision, she was led by her sister, Saint Anatholia, to preserve her virginity. When she refused to marry, Eugenius feared that his property would be confiscated if he publicly accused her of being a Christian. He therefore arranged with the Emperor Decius that she should be sent into exile outside the city, to her own estates. The same happened to Anatholia, who had been betrothed to Titus Aurelius, a noble Roman.

At that time Victoria converted the city of Turbula to Christ after killing a monstrous dragon. Spreading the hundredfold fruit of virginity, she gathered a choir of seventy-three virgins, over whom she presided, distinguished by much learning and the grace of miracles. At length, through the machinations of Eugenius her betrothed, she received the crown of martyrdom, being struck through the heart with a sword, as Usuard and the Roman Martyrology record on 23 December.

[Col. 0379B] All authorities agree on these matters. But there is considerable disagreement concerning the place and province where Saint Victoria suffered martyrdom. Equilinus, whom many more recent writers have followed, says that it occurred in the city of Tibulana, sixteen miles from Rome. This is supported by the statement that she suffered among the Marsi, who, however, were in Italy, not Spain.

Dexter, on the other hand, disagrees with them and maintains that it occurred at Turbula, among the Bastetani of Tarraconian Spain. This seems most probable to me because Aldhelm reads *Tribula* for the city when he writes:

> Meanwhile, leaving Rome, the virgin Victoria  
> is led in exile to the city of Tribulana.

That name certainly comes closer to *Turbula* than to *Tibulum*. Moreover, the ancient and proper name of the Italian city was *Tibur*, not *Tibuli*, although the latter is now commonly used in a form preserved by long usage, as may be seen in all reputable authors. Certainly, according to Ptolemy, Turbula was situated among the Bastetani of Tarraconian Spain, where Teruel is now found.

Villanovan is undoubtedly mistaken when he maintains that Teruel was Thyarjulia and not Turbula. For his own tables of ancient Spain show that Thyarjulia was situated not far from Tarraco and almost beside the sea, whereas Teruel is more than forty leagues from Tarraco and twenty-four from the sea. This is precisely the position in which Turbula stood.

Nor is it an objection that Saint Victoria, a Roman woman, is said to have been taken to her fiancé’s estates, so that one might suppose those estates to have been near Rome. The Romans, after subjugating Spain, possessed estates there as well.

A similar difficulty arises for those seeking the name of the city where Saint Anatholia, Victoria’s sister, suffered. In Ado’s manuscripts, and likewise in the printed edition, she is said to have suffered in the city of Thyre. The words are:

> On 7 July, in the city of Thyre, the passion of the holy Anatholia and Audax under the Emperor Decius: Anatholia, the virgin of Christ, afflicted with various kinds of wounds and finally pierced through with a sword [Col. 0379D] in prayer. Audax too was handed over to custody, and without delay was crowned by sentence of death.

Since she was believed to have been killed in Italy, some read *Thyre* instead of *Thyro*, others *Thurium*. The Roman Martyrology added “at Lake Bolsena,” thereby asserting that she suffered in Tuscany. Finally, Cardinal Baronius, at the report and urging of Curtius Francus, canon of Saint Peter’s, erased the words “in the city of Thyre at Lake Bolsena” [Col. 0380A] and wrote in their place “in the city of Thora at Lake Velinus,” as though it were permissible for anyone to move Saint Anatholia wherever he wished.

I would rather believe, as may be gathered from her history, that she died not far from Saint Victoria, in the city of Tyar, in the city of Tyar of the Hercaones in Tarraconian Spain. The river Thuria, which flows past Valencia, seems to have received its name from that place. Hence the Acts of Saint Anatholia read *Thurium*.

When Saint Victoria, according to Dexter, and Saint Anatholia, according to Equilinus, are said to have suffered among the Marsi, this should not be understood of the people specifically called Marsi, who lived near the Samnites—now Abruzzo—in the kingdom of Naples, where neither Thyre, Thora, nor Thurium is found. Rather, all those who cured people afflicted by the bite of serpents with their saliva were customarily called Marsi. Charles Estienne noted this, among others, in his *Dictionary*. Or at least the name referred to those who waged war against serpents. It is clear that Victoria and Anatholia converted such people to Christ after killing certain great serpents [Col. 0380B]. This meaning is sufficiently evident from Aldhelm, whose words are:

> And the Marsian too, who by his song brings forth the grim dipsas  
> (that is, a serpent),  
> burned, while the beast gnawed the holy limbs  
> with terrible teeth and open jaws;  
> suddenly he was healed, breaking the bonds of the chelydros.

And again:

> He who had earlier coiled the inert Marsian in his spiral  
> therefore hastened to believe in Christ,  
> recognizing his own salvation through such power.

When the Roman Martyrology, in speaking of Saint Victoria, begins, “At Rome, Saint Victoria,” it certainly does not say “at Rome” because she suffered there, since everyone agrees that she suffered elsewhere than at Rome, but because her feast is celebrated there, she being a Roman citizen.

### 5. “In Lusitania,” etc.

The Acts of Saints Felix and his companions are preserved in Surius, volume II, under 23 April [Col. 0380C]. On that day Usuard and the Roman Martyrology briefly summarize their acts in these words:

> In the city of Valencia, the feast of the holy Felix the presbyter, Fortunatus, and Achilleus the deacons, who, after converting the greater part of the said city to the faith of Christ, were thrust into prison by the commander Cornelius. Then, after being beaten for a very long time and having their legs broken, they were fastened around the circumference of wheels; they also endured smoke while suspended from the rack, and finally were put to death by the sword.

Bede, Ado, and the others agree with this account.

There is considerable controversy, however, over which city of Valencia was honored by the blood of these saints. Many teach that it was a city of Gaul, and this is how it is written in the Roman Martyrology. There is no reason for surprise, since the same is found in Usuard and Ado. Dexter, however, maintains that it was in Spain. This opinion pleased many others, especially Bishop Equilinus, book IV, chapter 83, where he says:

> Felix the presbyter, Fortunatus and Achilleus the deacons and martyrs, sent by Saint Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, to preach in the city of Valencia, which is a city of Spain, etc.

The same is read in the Chronicle of King Alfonso. Serious authorities agree: John Vasseus in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 200; Beuterus, who asserts that at Setavi in the kingdom of Valencia there is a church of these holy martyrs, whom the citizens venerate as their apostles; and Laurentius Padilla.

It may plausibly be inferred from what we said above that Saint Irenaeus wrote his books against the Gnostic heresies to the bishop of Toledo, so that the Spaniards would have something with which to refute the Gnostics who had entered their territory.

For the same purpose, therefore, Irenaeus sent his disciples to preach in Spain. Their sacred bodies are also preserved not in Gaul but in Spain, in the monastery of Saint George of Azueolo, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the kingdom of Navarre, as Yepes testifies in the sixth century of his Benedictine Chronicle, under the year 1052, chapter 10.

But since many cities bore the same name of Valencia, not everyone held the same opinion concerning the city enlightened by Saint Felix and his companions.
