Beuterus and some others maintain that it was the city which gives its special name to the kingdom of Valencia. Dexter, however, says that it was among the Vettones, not in Tarraconian Spain but in Lusitania, and that it is now called Valencia de Alcántara. There is another near Tuy in Galicia, one near Bilbao, and another formerly called Coyanca, now Valencia de Don Juan. These are not under discussion here, but rather the city situated among the Vettones.

### 6. “A pestilential disease,” etc.

Orosius, book VII, chapter 71; Gregory of Nyssa in his discourse on Gregory Thaumaturgus; Eusebius, book VII, chapter 17 and in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 255; and Saint Pontius in the *Life of Saint Cyprian* discuss the pestilence that was spreading throughout the world at this time. Among pagan authors, Eutropius discusses it in his account of Gallus and Volusianus. Saint Cyprian wrote a book on mortality because of it, and Dionysius of Alexandria wrote letters on the same subject, which Eusebius cites in the chapter mentioned. The disease began to spread in Ethiopia, then extended throughout the whole world, and lasted ten years.]

**A.D. 255. A.U.C. 1006.** At Rome, in the Roman Church, Cornelius succeeds Fabianus.

**A.D. 255. A.U.C. 1006.** Felix, presbyter of Vallata Urbicua among the Vaccaei, writes to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, concerning Basilides, bishop of Asturica, and accuses him of the gravest crimes.

[Col. 0377] **A.D. 255. A.U.C. 1006.** At this time, in the city of Belsinia in Carpetania, near Bellica, which is now called Cuminaria, Numia Varia, priestess of Venus, a woman of exceptional wealth and influence, flourishes.

**A.D. 255. A.U.C. 1006.** Likewise at this same time—although others prefer to place it under the Emperor Pius Aurelius—in Spain, at Turbula among the Bastetani, Saint Victoria, among the people called Marsi, fleeing from Rome to the Spains, where her fiancé’s estates were located, arrives. After some time, on 23 December, she gloriously completes the crown of virginity with the glory of martyrdom, suffering for the faith of Christ.

**A.D. 255. A.U.C. 1006.** In the Lusitanian city of Valencia among the Vettones, the holy martyrs of Christ Felix, Fortunatus, and Achilleus suffer martyrdom on 23 April, having been sent by Saint Irenaeus to preach against the heretics, the Gnostics.

[Col. 0381] **A.D. 255. A.U.C. 1006.** A pestilential disease miserably infects many provinces of the world, especially Alexandria and Egypt, as is recorded in the substantial work on mortality written by Dionysius and Cyprian.

[Note: [Col. 0381B]

### A.D. 256—1. “Lucius,” etc.

Some hold that the pontificate of Saint Lucius, who succeeded Saint Cornelius, began in the year 253 and ended on 4 March 255, the day on which it is commemorated in the Martyrologies. Others, whom Baronius follows, hold that it began on 14 September 255, when Cornelius was taken away by martyrdom, and continued until 4 March 257. It is clear that these agree with Dexter, who teaches that Lucius governed the Church in the year 256 [Col. 0381C]; but he does not state that Lucius began or ended his pontificate at that time.

### 2. “Gallus and Volusianus,” etc.

Eusebius develops this matter at somewhat greater length in his *Chronicle*. “Gallus and Volusianus,” he says, “having departed from the city against Aemilianus, who was stirring up revolution in Moesia, were killed at the Forum Flaminium, or, as others think, at Interamna.” Eutropius discusses the same men in the passage cited above.

At the time when they reigned, Hostilianus had seized Spain. His memory survives engraved on marble at Valencia, where he is called “C. Valens Hostilianus Messius Quincius.”]

**A.D. 256. A.U.C. 1007.** Pope Lucius holds and governs the Roman Church.

**A.D. 256. A.U.C. 1007.** Gallus and Volusianus, having set out against Aemilianus, are killed.

[Note: [Col. 0381C]

### A.D. 257—“Valerianus,” etc.

Eusebius likewise records this in his *Chronicle*, almost in the same words.]

**A.D. 257. A.U.C. 1008.** Valerian is proclaimed emperor by the army in Raetia.

[Note: [Col. 0381C]

### A.D. 259—“Cyprian,” etc.

There is no single consensus concerning the true year of Saint Cyprian’s death. Pamelius, whom Baronius follows, believes that he received the crown of martyrdom in the year of the Lord 261, because certain Acts of his martyrdom say that he was killed under the consulship of Fuscus and Bassus, whose consulship fell in that year. He also argues that Cyprian survived Saint Sixtus II, since the letter to Successus narrates Sixtus’s martyrdom (in Pamelius’s edition, no. 82), although they maintain that Successus continued alive in the pontificate until the year 261.

Others, however, and more ancient authorities assign Saint Cyprian’s martyrdom to the year 259, including Eusebius in his *Chronicle*, who agrees with Dexter even in wording. We should believe that Saint Jerome held the same view, since for the most part his *Chronicle* concerning Latin affairs is based on that of Eusebius.

This is supported by Onuphrius, Morales, Tempesta, and others, who with substantial agreement teach that Saint Sixtus was taken up by martyrdom in this very year, 259, on 6 August. Yet all acknowledge that Saint Cyprian survived Sixtus by only forty days, which elapsed between the day of Sixtus’s martyrdom and 14 September, the day of Cyprian’s martyrdom.

The consulship of Fuscus and Bassus cannot be an obstacle, for those Acts were not known before Pamelius’s edition, and their authority is not established. At the very least, it is not so great that it could prejudice the opinion of so many distinguished men. If in other respects they agree with the passion written by the deacon Saint Pontius [Col. 0382B], their testimony should be accepted; nevertheless, some ignorant person could have added the consulship. But enough on this. Dexter discusses the fame of Saint Cyprian, which filled the Spains, below under the year 285.]

**A.D. 259. A.U.C. 1010.** Cyprian, first a rhetorician at Carthage, then a presbyter, and finally bishop of Carthage, is consecrated through martyrdom.

[Note: [Col. 0382B]

### A.D. 260—1. “A persecution having been stirred up,” etc.

Eusebius gives almost the same words in his *Chronicle* under this very year: “Valerian,” he says, “having stirred up a persecution against the Christians, is immediately captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, and there grows old in miserable slavery.” Trebellius Pollio, Aurelius Victor, Eutropius, and Dionysius of Alexandria, cited by Eusebius in book VII, chapter 9, discuss this remarkable judgment of God.

Indeed, Constantine the Great says in his *Oration to the Holy Assembly*: “Because you, Valerian, by displaying the same cruelty toward the servants of God, set before the eyes of all the just and holy judgment of God; when you had been captured and were being led away in chains, dressed in purple and the rest of the royal apparel, at length, by order of Sapor, king of the Persians, you were flayed and preserved in salt, setting up before the eyes of all an everlasting trophy of your misfortune.” He was captured through the treachery of the commander Macrianus while leading the Roman army against the Persians.

### 2. “At Viana in Galicia,” etc.

There is a city of that name in Portugal, situated on the Ocean and famous for the commerce of foreign nations. To its north, however, the ruins of an older Viana are visible above a mountain; it is of this place that Dexter writes here.

Festus Rufus Avienus also seems once to have mentioned it. Sandoval, bishop of Tuy, asserts that Avienus’s works are preserved in manuscript in the library of Sculiaria, when he discusses the holy martyrs Saturninus, Theophilus, and Revocata in book 45 of his work on the bishops of Tuy.

The Roman Martyrology, Galesinus, and the additions to Usuard by Molanus, under 6 February, discuss the same martyrs, but without naming the city. The Roman Martyrology says: “On the same day, the holy martyrs Saturninus, Theophilus, and Revocata.” Baronius notes that the ancient manuscripts agree with this. Peter Equilinus, book XI, chapter 130, no. 52, says: “Saturninus, Theophilus, and Revocata suffered martyrdom on the same day.”

Galesinus is mistaken when he prefixes the name Rome, saying [Col. 0383A]: “Likewise at Rome, the holy martyrs Saturninus,” etc. This author, however, is accustomed to assign to Rome those saints whom he finds in the Roman Martyrology, as may be seen in many other cases where the Roman Martyrology does not mention their cities.

Dexter calls Valerian’s persecution the same as that which began under Decius, and therefore the seventh in order. Others, who take a different view, call it the eighth. Certainly Jerome, in his book *On Illustrious Men* under Methodius and in the *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, as well as Optatus in book III, assert that the persecution under Decius and Valerian was one and the same. On this matter see Baronius in his notes on the Roman Martyrology under 10 August, letter b.

The words that follow in the text concerning the sixth persecution under Maximinus—namely, that it arose in the year 239—were exceedingly corrupt in Dexter’s printed text. It read there: “In the year 230 from the Nativity of the Lord, 2 September,” whereas it must certainly read: “In the year 239 from the Nativity of the Lord,” since Dexter himself admits this above.]

**A.D. 260. A.U.C. 1011.** Having stirred up a persecution against the Christians, Valerian is captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, and serves a miserable slavery.

**A.D. 260. A.U.C. 1011.** At Viana in Galicia, near the city of Tuy, the holy martyrs Theophilus, Saturninus, and the virgin Revocata suffer under Julius Minervius, during the persecution of the Emperor Valerian, which is the seventh and the same as that under Decius. The sixth was under the Emperor Maximinus, in the year 239 from the Nativity of the Lord.

**A.D. 260. A.U.C. 1011.** In the see of Peter, Callistus succeeds Zephyrinus; Urban succeeds Callistus; Calpurnius Pontianus succeeds Urban; Anterus succeeds Pontianus; Fabianus succeeds Anterus; Cornelius succeeds Fabianus; Lucius succeeds Cornelius; Stephen succeeds Lucius; Sixtus succeeds Stephen; and Saint Dionysius succeeds Sixtus.

**A.D. 260. A.U.C. 1011.** At Rome, Laurence, a Spaniard from Huesca, suffers under Sixtus.

**A.D. 260. A.U.C. 1011.** At Toledo, a council is convened under the legate of Pope Sixtus.

[Note: [Col. 0383C]

### A.D. 263—“Saint Celerina,” etc.

We must understand, or perhaps the manuscript is missing, something such as “she flourished in the glory of miracles,” for since the text says that she lived in the time of Nero, it is clear that her death cannot possibly be assigned to this period, namely the year of the Lord 263, but rather her memory and the glory of her miracles.

Saint Celerina is prominently remembered in the *Life of Saint Torpes*, which is found in Mombritius, volume II. Rabanus, in his *Martyrology* under 29 March, gives an extensive account of her conversion and deeds.

Equilinus, book V, chapter 8, after narrating the martyrdom of Saint Torpes at Pisa, a city of Tuscany, adds:

> His body was placed in a rotten little boat with a dog and a rooster and exposed to the sea, either to be devoured by beasts or to sink into the water. But under the guidance of an angel the boat reached Spain. A Christian senator named Celerina, who possessed half the kingdom, was divinely warned in a dream, and the saint’s body was found in the harbor called Sinos. It was honorably buried beside the shore on 17 May, and afterward a church was built over it in her name. His feast is celebrated there on the day of his burial.

Regarding Celerina’s holiness, Galesinus says in his *Martyrology* under 17 May:

> In Spain, Saint Celerina, queen of that province—that is, I understand, a ruler or senator—who, inflamed with zeal for the Christian religion, both lived a devout life and, with royal resources, built a temple with marvelous workmanship and dedicated it to God in the name of the blessed martyr Torpes, leaving it as an everlasting monument of her devotion.

He had previously written:

> At Pisa in Tuscany, Saint Torpes, whose feast is 29 April; but on this day the translation to Spain is celebrated, which occurred miraculously in that very year in which he suffered martyrdom.

In his notes he asserts that Torpes suffered in the year of the Lord 64. Dexter adds that Celerina, besides her piety, eventually suffered martyrdom. It is sufficiently probable that this noble woman, who so publicly professed the Christian faith, was dragged to execution when Nero’s persecution intensified, since no Christian was spared, and still less the nobles, who could advance the faith.

As for the name Celerina, Pliny, book III, and Ptolemy in his table of Tarraconian Spain state that there were once certain peoples in Galicia, above the Gronniques and Bracara, called the Celerini. Ptolemy says that they lived along the river Avo, now called the Avia. Celerina therefore seems to have been named after Lucius Pompeius Celerinus, whose great-granddaughter she was; I believe he received that name from the Celerini whom he had conquered.

That the stock of the Pompeii existed in Spain is demonstrated by Pliny’s account of Sextus Pompeius: while, as governor of Nearer Spain, he was supervising the winnowing of grain in his granaries, he was seized by an attack of gout and plunged himself into the wheat up to his knees. When he was lifted out, his feet had miraculously dried, and afterward he used that remedy.

The first of the Pompeii to cross into Spain was Quintus Pompeius, sent against the Numantines. They defeated him, and he made a disgraceful and dishonorable peace, as Florus reports in book II. His grandson was Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, who went to Spain against Sertorius, joined forces with Metellus, and destroyed Sertorius and his entire faction. His son, also named Gnaeus Pompeius, was defeated in a land battle near Munda, a city of Spain.

Saint Celerina was therefore a fortunate descendant of the Pompeii, and she received the relics of Saint Torpes at Sinos. The town itself still exists in Lusitania, retaining its ancient name, on the shore of the Ocean, and is sufficiently famous for its harbor and fishing.]

**A.D. 263. A.U.C. 1014.** Saint Celerina in Lusitania, great-granddaughter of Lucius Pompeius Celerinus, after receiving at the Port of Sines the sacred relics of Saint Torpes, the martyr under Nero, was an outstanding martyr of Christ . . . . .

[Col. 0385] [Note: [Col. 0385A]

### A.D. 268—1. “Calydonius,” etc.

His letter to Saint Cyprian is preserved among Cyprian’s letters as no. 19, elsewhere book V, letter 15. His zeal for the Catholic faith shines clearly in it. He writes as follows concerning those whom he had reconciled after their lapse:

> Calydonius sends greetings to Cyprian and the fellow presbyters residing at Carthage. The circumstances of the times make it necessary that we should not grant peace rashly. But I ought to write to you, since those who, after sacrificing, were tested again and became exiles seem to me to have washed away their former offense by abandoning their estates and houses, doing penance, and following Christ.
>
> Felix, therefore, who was serving as a presbyter under Decimus, my nearest neighbor—indeed, I came to know this Felix more fully—and his wife Victoria, and Lucius, faithful men, have become exiles and abandoned their estates, which the treasury now possesses. Further, whether acting on her own or through them, a woman named Bona, who was dragged by her husband to sacrifice, although she knew that the offense had not been committed by her—for while others held her hands, they themselves sacrificed—began to protest in these words: “I did not do it; you did it.” Thus she too became an exile.
>
> Since all were seeking peace, saying, “We have recovered the faith which we had lost; having done penance, we have publicly confessed Christ,” although it seems to me that they ought to receive peace, nevertheless I have deferred them to your judgment, lest I appear to presume rashly. Therefore, if anything is approved by common counsel, write to me. Greet our people; you are ours. I wish you every happiness and good health.

Cyprian replied to Calydonius’s questions. Although that reply itself does not survive, Cyprian mentions it in letter 20, saying:

> What my colleague Calydonius wrote to me in defense of the faith, and what I wrote in reply, I have sent to you both for reading.

Moreover, when the schismatic Novatus rose up against the Church, Calydonius was sent to the mountains against him, as is clear from Cyprian’s letter 38. Letter 39 contains the sentence that he issued against certain lapsed Christians [Col. 0385C], sent to Herculanus and his companions:

> We have excluded from communion Felicissimus and Augendus, likewise Repostus among the exiles, and Irene of the Rutili, and Paula the seamstress, as you ought to know from my annotation. We have likewise excluded Sophronius, himself among the exiles, and Soliassus the wool-worker, etc.

Finally, Calydonius was held in such high esteem that when a new schism of the Novatians arose at Rome against Saint Cornelius in the Roman Church, he was sent with Bishop Fortunatus to suppress it, as is clear from Cyprian’s letters 42 and 45.

No one should infer from Calydonius’s great familiarity with Cyprian that Dexter must be wrong in placing him as a bishop in Africa rather than at Bracara in Spain. His episcopate cannot be doubted, since Cyprian calls him “my colleague” in letter 20. We have already shown above, in the case of Basilides, that the Spanish bishops had much friendship and familiarity with Cyprian and the Africans; we shall demonstrate the same again in its proper place, in the case of Orosius and others.

Even if it be granted that Calydonius was a bishop in Africa while Cyprian was alive, he could have been transferred from there to the see of Bracara after the letters written by Cyprian—especially if, being filled with zeal for the faith, he came to Spain for the purpose of preaching. We often see this happen in other cases, and also in the case of his successor, Saint Narcissus. Although bishop of Bracara, Narcissus nevertheless preached in Raetia; then he returned to Spain and suffered martyrdom at Gerunda. We shall discuss him again below under the year 277, when he was crowned with his own blood.

I would only point out here that from the present year, 268, when Narcissus is said to have succeeded Calydonius, until 277, when Narcissus was killed in the persecution of Aurelian, only ten years intervened. No one should therefore think that a chronological discrepancy could have prevented the Bracaran episcopate attributed to Narcissus by Dexter.

Furthermore, that Caledonius was bishop of Bracara and wrote the life of Saint Peter of Ratistum—the first bishop of that see and a disciple of Saint James—is entirely clear from the letter of Hugh, bishop of Porto, to Mauritius of Bracara, which we included among Dexter’s encomia, where a fragment of his life is preserved.

### 2. “Gallienus,” etc.

His endurance in the face of the disasters he suffered was so great that he even habitually joked about them, such was the depth of his moral corruption. When he learned that Egypt had defected from the Roman Empire, he said: “What? Can we not do without Egyptian linen?” When Gaul had been lost, he laughed and said: “And is the Republic not safe without the cloaks of high officials?” When Asia had been devastated by the incursions of the Alamanni and Scythians, he said: “What? Can we not do without Aphonites?”

Orosius discusses these disasters at length. In book VII, chapter 22, among many other things, he says:

> Suddenly, everywhere, by God’s permission, the nations that had been placed and left around the Empire were released, and with the reins loosened they rushed into every Roman frontier. The Germans, having penetrated the Alps, Raetia, and all Italy, reached as far as Ravenna.

This is the incursion of the Germans into Italy, which Dexter discusses here.

> The Alamanni, ranging throughout Gaul, also crossed into Italy.

Dexter likewise asserts this in no. 3: “The Germans having devastated,” etc.

The Alamanni were a western portion of the Germans living along the Rhine, and thus could readily cross into Gaul and Italy. The Germans proper were the more easterly nation, and, being near Asia, had easy access through Asia itself and as far as Italy [Col. 0386C] and Ravenna.

For these same disasters, see Eusebius in his *Chronicle* under the year 264. He nevertheless adds under the year 266: “With the Germans occupying Spain, Tarraco was captured.” On this subject Orosius says in the passage cited:

> The farther Germans, having laid waste to it, possess Spain;

and shortly afterward:

> There still remain throughout the provinces, amid the ruins of great cities, small and poor dwellings, preserving signs of misery and traces of their former names. Among these we too point out our Tarraco in Spain, as a consolation amid recent misery.

Dexter discusses these matters again under the year 424.]

### 3. The Germans, etc.

Consult the preceding note.

### 4. At Tarracona, etc.

The martyrdom of Saints Fructuosus, Augurius, and Eulogius was exceedingly celebrated, not only in Spain but also in Africa and almost everywhere in the world, as Saint Augustine demonstrates in Sermon 101 *On Various Subjects*, delivered on their feast. Their acts, received from the shorthand writers and authenticated by public testimony, exist in [Col. 0386D] very ancient manuscript codices; from these they are printed by Surius in volume I, by Baronius in volume II of the *Annals* under the year 262, and by Mombritius in volume I. Prudentius likewise formerly celebrated them in a special hymn in the *Peristephanon*, whose beginning is:

> Happy Tarraco, Fructuosus, for your [victories], etc.

[Col. 0387A] Bede, Ado, Usuard, and the Roman Martyrology briefly treated them in their own Martyrologies. The Roman Martyrology contains these words, under 21 January:

> At Tarracona in Spain, the holy martyrs Fructuosus, bishop, and Augurius and Eulogius, deacons. In the time of Gallienus they were first thrown into prison and then cast into the flames. When their bonds had been burned away, they stretched out their hands in the form of a cross and, praying, completed their martyrdom. On the anniversary of their birth, Saint Augustine preached a sermon to the people.

All the authors and Martyrologies just cited agree that they completed their martyrdom under the emperor Gallienus. Prudentius agrees, saying:

> If you have understanding, condemn the old woman’s doctrine:  
> It was commanded by the voice of Caesar Gallienus;  
> What the prince worships, let us all worship.

Primus of Châlons likewise says under the word *Tarracon* in his *Spiritual Map of the World*:

> Tarracon, a city of Hispania Tarraconensis; here Fructuosus, bishop, and Augurius and Eulogius, deacons, were martyrs under Aemilianus the governor, while Gallienus was emperor.

I read their martyrs’ acts in the old Breviary of Salamanca [Col. 0387B]; they agree in every respect with what Surius published. Formerly their feast was also celebrated in the Breviary of Saint Isidore, with a proper office and Prudentius’s hymn.

The constancy of Saint Fructuosus, the bishop, was truly admirable. When the lictors seized him without shoes, he answered without the slightest change in demeanor, “Let us go—or, if you wish, put on my shoe.” Later, when he was to enter the pyre barefoot and the Augustal lictor wished to remove his shoes, he said, “I will remove them myself: strong, joyful, and confident in the Lord’s promise.” Many of the bystanders saw his soul and those of his companions enter the opened heaven amid rejoicing.

There was also another Fructuosus in Spain, a native of Segovia and now its patron, who flourished around the year of the Lord 690; his feast is celebrated at Segovia on 25 October. Saint Fructuosus of Braga, bishop, who attended the Tenth Council of Toledo, is also celebrated at Braga on 16 April, the day on which he is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology.

Finally, I would observe that the claim that Saints Eulogius and Fructuosus were his fellow citizens is owed solely to Dexter [Col. 0387C]; no other author whom I have seen mentions their native city.

### 2. In the imperial succession, etc.

What he had done with the Roman pontiffs under the year 260, he now does with the Roman emperors: that is, he compiles a series of thirteen emperors. Although he mentions all of them individually in their proper places, he now recounts their continuous succession in summary, proceeding from the more recent to their predecessors.

Some are missing through the carelessness of copyists, as is reasonable to believe. Thus, between Valerian and Decius, Gallus, Volusianus, and Aemilianus are absent; and after Balbinus, Maximus and Pupienus should have been written. Between Alexander and Macrinus, Diadumenianus and Heliogabalus are absent.

He calls Aurelius Antoninus Geta, the brother of Caracalla, who was named Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Geta. The Antoninus whom he places as Severus’s predecessor was otherwise called Pescennius Niger. This should not be attributed to the author’s negligence, since he clearly mentions all of them in their proper places. [Col. 0387D]

### 3. At Uxama Barca, etc.

We discussed Uxama Barca, which was a city of the Autrigones, above under the year 91, and demonstrated that it was different from the place now called Osma; we judged it to have been Orduna. [Col. 0388A]

The distinguished memory of Saint Fortunatus and his twenty-eight companions is recorded in the Roman Martyrology under 26 February in these words:

> Likewise, Saints Fortunatus, Felix, and twenty-seven others, martyrs.

Thus the name of one of the twenty-eight companions is given as Felix. Baronius asserts in his Notes that, because these names had disappeared from the Martyrology through the negligence of copyists, they were eventually restored from ancient manuscript codices.

There were also other martyrs bearing the same names who were killed in different Spanish cities; we shall discuss them in their proper places together with Dexter.

### 4. At Ambratia, etc.

The bishop of Tuy, Sandoval, learnedly notes in his work *On the Affairs of Tuy* that Ambratia was the city we now call Plasencia. He does so while discussing Saint Epitatius, or Epictetus, who was first appointed bishop of Tuy by Saint Peter of Braga, whose disciple he was, and afterward became apostle and bishop of Ambratia.

There is now a small tower within Plasencia that retains the name Ambratia, commonly called the Torre de Ambroz. Perhaps the ancient city was built there and later transferred to Plasencia. Sandoval’s words should be noted:

> Ambracia lies in the boundaries of ancient Lusitania, as appears from the stones and memorials found at its ancient site, and from the mountains and banks of the surrounding region. Among the inhabitants it is widely accepted that it was a settlement of Greeks, like Tuy. To these people, as to members of his own nation and blood—for Dexter notes that he was a citizen of Ambratia—Saint Epitatius, bishop of Tuy, went to preach and convert the people of Ambracia, or Plasencia. To this day, at Plasencia they recognize Saint Epitatius as their apostle and first preacher of the faith, for which he was martyred in that city.

Thus far Sandoval. His statement that Ambratia was founded by Greeks appears consistent with what we read in Ptolemy, Strabo, and Pliny: in Epirus, a province of Greece, there once existed a city named Ambratia—now Arta—and the sea gulf was called the Ambracian Gulf after it. It is certain that Greeks crossed into Spain and founded there not a few cities, giving them the names of their own cities so that they might in some fashion preserve the memory of their homeland. [Col. 0388C]

As for Saint Epitatius, there is a notable record of him in the manuscript Missal and Martyrology of Plasencia, dated 1357. Under 23 May the Calendar contains these words:

> Saint Epitatius, first bishop of Tuy and of Ambratia.

The Martyrology has:

> In Spain, Saints Epitatius and Basileus, bishops: the former our bishop and bishop of Tuy, disciples of Peter, bishop of Braga.

The Roman Martyrology agrees, celebrating both fellow disciples on the same day:

> In Spain, Saints Epitatius, bishop, and Basileus, martyrs.

At this point Baronius says:

> The old and more recent manuscripts also speak of these men, as does the *Flower of the Saints of Spain*, namely the works of Alfonso de Villegas, Basilio Santoro, and Marieta.

Molanus has the same words in his *Additions to Usuard*:

> In Spain, Epitatius, bishop, and Basileus.

In the margin he adds that Epitatius is elsewhere read as Epictetus. But the Roman Martyrology and Molanus are deficient in calling only Epitatius a bishop. Equilinus does better in book XI of the *Catalogus*, chapter 130, number 148, where he calls both bishops:

> Epitatius and Basileus, bishops in Spain, are celebrated on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

Yet in this very respect he, like Molanus, is deficient, because they pass over the martyrdom of both in silence. Nevertheless, the Roman Martyrology, together with Dexter, expressly records it from ancient manuscripts. [Col. 0389A]

Above, we gave a distinguished account of these same men found in a fragment of the works of Saint Athanasius concerning Saints Basileus and Epitatius. There, while discussing Saint Peter of Braga, a disciple of the apostle Saint James, he says:

> This apostolic man came to Braga. He wrote letters filled with the apostolic spirit to the churches in which he appointed bishops, such as the bishop of Iria, the bishop of Amphilochia, the bishop of Eminium, and the bishop of Portus, where he installed Saint Basileus, his fellow disciple. After Basileus was taken away through martyrdom, he succeeded him in the see of Braga, and appointed Epitatius to Tuy.

These holy and wholly apostolic men—Peter, Basileus, and Epitatius—did not, like the apostles, always remain in one city. Wherever the Holy Spirit carried them, they went. Thus Epitatius preached not only in the district of Tuy but also in Ambratia, a city of Lusitania. They adorned their preaching with signs and a variety of languages. Nor did they go out to preach alone, but accompanied by many disciples, as Christ, Peter, James, and the other apostles had done. [Col. 0389B]

Saint Caledonius also testifies in Peter’s Life that this same Peter sowed the seeds of God’s word at Ambratia. We transcribed a fragment of that work among Dexter’s testimonies from a letter of Hugh.

We have said enough in its proper place, under the year of the Lord 37, about Saint Basileus II, bishop of Braga and disciple of the apostle Saint James.

Dexter again discusses Saint Epitatius under the year 277, where he says of the time of his martyrdom:

> He is believed to have suffered the most severe torments at the beginning of Nero’s reign.

We likewise have Julian’s testimony in his Chronicle under the year 252:

> At Tuy and elsewhere the memory flourishes of Saint Epitatius, the first bishop and martyr of Tuy.

And under the year 584:

> From the ruins of Ambratia, where Saint Epitatius, the first bishop of Tuy, suffered, Neufila, bishop of Tuy, transferred his relics to Tuy. Bishop Anastasius consecrated a church to him.

Finally, I would observe that the text printed at Zaragoza was corrupted when it read, “At Ambratia in Lusitania, Saint Epictetus [Col. 0389C], a citizen and bishop of that same city and a martyr of Christ,” whereas the other codices have, as we gave it above, “his memory flourishes,” which is also how Sandoval read it.

At the very least, it is certain that Saint Epitatius did not suffer martyrdom in this year, since we know that he flourished under the rule of Nero.

### 5. He began the see of Ilerda, etc.

In the records of the Roman Martyrology we have the memory of Saint Licerius, bishop of Ilerda in Spain, under 27 August, in these words:

> At Ilerda in Hispania Tarraconensis, Saint Licerius, bishop.

Baronius writes:

> He is commemorated in the church of Ilerda; mention of him is also found in its records and in the *Flower of the Saints of Spain* by Alfonso de Villegas.

Dexter asserts that he was the first bishop of that see. This is what is signified by the words, “He began the see of Ilerda,” etc. More clearly, below, under the year of the Lord 311, he says:

> Saint Licerius, bishop of Carensis [or Carinensis] in Spain, is celebrated at Ilerda, to which he is said to have been transferred together with his see.

He was therefore initially bishop of Carensis and transferred his see from there to Ilerda, now Lérida.

Antoninus mentions the town of Care on the route between Liminium and Caesaraugusta. Pliny, book III, chapter 3, asserts that the Carenses were a Spanish people neighboring the Complutenses. But they were situated far from Ilerda and were otherwise called Caracitanes; today they are the people of Guadalajara. Appian says that Careon was a city of Spain.

Pliny also discusses the Carrinensian territory of Spain in book II, chapter 104, saying that two springs rise there, one rejecting everything and the other absorbing everything. What Paulatus wrote to Saint Licerius in the letters mentioned here by Dexter, we cannot determine, since we have not been able to see them. I believe they were written concerning the transfer of his bishopric, since the matter was understood to concern Paulatus as primate.

We shall discuss again, somewhat farther below under the year 283, Paulatus, the bishop of Toledo who flourished at this time, together with the author.

### 6. Saint Marinus, etc.

While I was carefully investigating who this Saint Marinus might have been, the first to come to mind was that famous martyr and soldier Marinus, killed at Caesarea on 3 March. His beheaded body was being received by the senator Asterius upon his shoulders and upon the garment that had been spread beneath him; for the honor he paid the martyr, Asterius himself immediately received martyrdom.

Yet all the Martyrologies declare that this man died not in Mauritania but in Palestine, as does Eusebius, bishop of that city, in book VII, chapter 14 [Col. 0390B], from whom Nicephorus drew material in book VI, chapters 13 and 14. They agree, however, concerning the time of his martyrdom: he was killed in the persecution of Valerian and had been a soldier of Palestine. From this it may at least plausibly be inferred that he was a Spaniard, for we have shown that the Roman garrison in Palestine consisted of Spanish soldiers.

I therefore suspect that the word “Mauritania” was added in Dexter’s codex or substituted by someone for “Palestine.” One might also suspect that our Marinus was the man who was killed in Africa together with Januarius and other companions and is celebrated on 10 July by Bede, Ado, and the Roman Martyrology. But the time at which these men were killed for Christ is not reported.

### 7. At Carthage, etc.

The Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Bede discuss the most holy martyrs Heraclius and Zosimus, who were killed at Carthage for confessing Christ, under 11 March. Galesinus adds that they suffered under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, enemies of the faith [Col. 0390C], as Dexter records here.

Equilinus discusses them in book III, chapter 191. Yet in this matter all have held differing opinions: whether they had other companions in their crown—Alexander, Candidus, Piperion, and twenty others—or not.

Ado counts these three as companions of Heraclius and Zosimus. Galesinus counts Candidus, Piperion, and twenty others, omitting Alexander; Molanus follows him in the *Additions to Usuard*. The Roman Martyrology, however, reads “Alexandria,” the city, rather than “Alexander” the martyr, and divides the passage into two periods in this way:

> At Carthage, the holy martyrs Heraclius and Zosimus.  
> At Alexandria, the passion of the holy Candidus and Piperion and twenty others.

Baronius teaches that this is found in ancient manuscript codices, and we consider it entirely correct, being confirmed by Dexter’s testimony, who writes that only Heraclius and Zosimus were killed at Carthage—not the African city, but the Spanish city called Spartaria.]

### A.D. 268. A.R. 1019

Calydonius [or Caledonius, or Caldonius] of Braga, to whom Saint Cyprian writes, is succeeded by Narcissus.

### A.D. 268. A.R. 1019

Gallienus proved a most corrupt emperor. While he was emperor, the Germans reached as far as Ravenna.

### A.D. 268. A.R. 1019

The Germans, after ravaging Gaul, came into Italy again.

### A.D. 268. A.R. 1019

At Tarracona in Spain, the holy martyrs of Christ Eulogius, a citizen of that city, Fructuosus, a citizen and bishop, and Augurius suffered martyrdom together for Christ’s name.

[Col. 0387] ### A.D. 268. A.R. 1019

In the imperial succession, Gallienus was preceded by Valerian, Valerian by Decius, Decius by Philip, father and son, the first Christian Caesars; they were followed by Gordian, Gordian by Balbinus, Balbinus by Maximinus, Maximinus by Alexander, Alexander by Macrinus, Macrinus by Caracalla, Caracalla by Aurelius, Aurelius by Severus, and Severus in the empire by Antoninus.

### A.D. 268. A.R. 1019

At Uxama Barca, among the Autrigones, a people of Spain, Saint Fortunatus, distinguished martyr of Christ, and twenty-eight companions with him.

### A.D. 268. A.R. 1019

At Ambratia in Lusitania, the memory flourishes of Saint Epitectus [or Epictetus], a citizen, bishop, and martyr of Christ of that same city.

[Col. 0389] ### A.D. 268. A.R. 1019

Saint Licerius, a most holy man, began the see of Ilerda. Paulatus, bishop of Toledo, sent him a letter.

### A.D. 268. A.R. 1019

Saint Marinus [possibly Marcellus], a Spaniard by nationality, suffers at Caesarea in Mauritania.

### A.D. 268. A.R. 1019

At Carthage in Spain, under the emperors Gallienus and Valerian, Heraclius and Zosimus became distinguished martyrs for Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0390D]]

### A.D. 270.—1. At Flaviobriga, etc.

Ptolemy mentions Flaviobriga among the Autrigones of Hispania Tarraconensis, on the borders of the Cantabri. Villanova now believes it to have been Fuenterabia; Tarapha believes it to have been Bilbao. But Bilbao was called Flavionavia by Carlo Stefano and others.

I agree with Juan de Mariana, book IV of *The History of Spain*, chapter 4, who asserts that the ruins sufficiently prove that it existed near Bermeo. Morales, book IX, chapter 25, believes that it received this name at its foundation from the emperor Flavius Vespasianus [Col. 0391A]. Dexter says here that it was called, for the sake of brevity, Flavia or Flaviades.

As for Saint Julian, the young man who suffered there, we have an epitome of his acts in Equilinus, book V, chapter 142. I have thought it worthwhile to insert it here because, as I believe, it is found nowhere else:

> Julian, a youthful martyr eighteen years old, suffered in the city of Flaviades during the time of Caesar Decius, under the governor Martianus. The governor detained him and urged him to sacrifice. When he refused, he ordered him to be beaten with clubs; then he had him lifted onto the rack and severely scourged, after which he ordered him taken down and thrown into prison.
>
> The young man’s mother, Asclepiodora, was summoned. The governor urged her to induce her son by her exhortations to offer sacrifice to the gods. She requested a delay of three days, during which the mother strengthened her son in confessing Christ.
>
> When the three days had elapsed, Julian was brought out of custody by order of the governor. Since he despised sacrificing to the gods, the governor ordered a sack to be brought with serpents and sand, and commanded the martyr of Christ [Col. 0391B] to be sewn inside it and thrown into the sea—for Flaviobriga lies on the Cantabrian coast—so that he might perish both by suffocation in the water and by the bites of the wild creatures.
>
> His body, tossed by the waves to an island called Proconessus—one of the Sporades in the Propontis, not far from Constantinople, concerning which see Pliny, book V, final chapter—was found by Christians living there and buried on a mountain of that land. There it rested for a long time without any veneration.
>
> Many years later, during summer, when a storm at sea was swelling, the sea destroyed the part of the mountain where the coffin had been placed. The stone coffin was cast into the sea and, by divine guidance, floated above the waves. The waves carried it to the harbor of the city of Ariminum, situated on the Adriatic Sea, and cast it ashore.
>
> The citizens, astonished—for they had come to the harbor and had seen the coffin floating upon the water with light shining above it—placed the tomb with its sacred body on a cart. They wished to take it to the principal church, but they could not move it from the spot in any way, nor could they open the coffin.
>
> At last, after several days of prayers and fasts, John, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter outside the city, easily moved the tomb with its body after it had been placed on a vehicle and brought it to his church. When the tomb was gently opened, he found the body of Saint Julian the martyr entirely incorrupt, together with his clothing. The epitaph of his passion was also found there, and he read it aloud before everyone.
>
> In the same coffin were seven heads of unknown martyrs. The body, together with the coffin, was deposited in that place and rests there to the present. He suffered on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, that is, on 23 June.

The statement that he suffered under Decius must be interpreted in the same way as what we read concerning the martyrdom of Laurence: namely, that he died in the persecution of Decius, which many have regarded as identical with the persecution of Valerian.

### 2. At Carthage, etc.

The feast of Saint Hippolytus, who suffered together with Saints Felix and Symphronius, is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 3 February. Their memory also exists in the very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Cyriacus at the Baths, as Baronius notes.

Nevertheless, they were wrongly believed to have suffered in Africa, since Dexter makes clear that they underwent martyrdom in Carthage Spartaria in Spain. We therefore believe that some people thought them Africans because they read that they were killed at Carthage. Only Dexter records that Saint Hippolytus was bishop of Carthage.

### 3. Gallienus, etc.

Eusebius likewise records this in the Chronicle under this year.

### 4. Under Gallienus, etc.

This too agrees with Eusebius and the others.

### 5. Claudius defeats the Goths, etc.

Eusebius records this under the year of the Lord 272, and Dexter does not disagree, since he relates it between 270 and 273.

### 6. Claudius, etc.

Trebellius, among others, discusses the death of Claudius, which occurred at Firmum in this year, as does Eusebius in the Chronicle under the year 272.]

### A.D. 270. A.R. 1021

At Flaviobriga in Spain, under the governor Martianus, Saint Julian, a young man, was a martyr. This city is called Flavias by others.

[Col. 0391] ### A.D. 270. A.R. 1021

At Carthage in Spain, Saint Hippolytus, bishop of that city, together with other martyrs, suffered.

### A.D. 270. A.R. 1021

Gallienus, an indolent emperor, was killed at Milan.

### A.D. 270. A.R. 1021

Claudius was appointed to the Roman Empire in place of Gallienus.

### A.D. 270. A.R. 1021

Claudius defeated the Goths, who were ravaging Illyricum and Macedonia. For this reason a golden shield was placed in the Curia and a statue in the Capitol.

### A.D. 270. A.R. 1021

Claudius died not long afterward at Firmum from illness.

[Note: [Col. 0392A]]

### A.D. 273.—1. Quintillus, etc.

Eusebius says this under the present year:

> Quintillus, the brother of Claudius, was named Augustus by the Senate and was killed at Aquileia on the seventeenth day of his reign.

Trebellius discusses the same man in his account of Claudius.

### 2. Aurelianus, etc.

This was taken from Vopiscus. Eusebius has the following in his Chronicle:

> Aurelianus, when Tetricus betrayed his own army at Châlons, recovered Gaul.

His name was Domitius Valerius Aurelianus. His generosity was especially conspicuous in that he distributed tunics to the people individually, as well as grain, oil, and wine, according to Sextus Aurelius.

Concerning Tetricus, the commander of the army in Gaul and Spain, the emperor Claudius wrote in a letter addressed to the Senate and the Roman People:

> Tetricus holds Gaul and Spain, the strength of the Republic.

Equilinus relates that Aurelianus stayed for some time in Spain, while discussing Saint Sabianus the martyr in book III, chapter 42.

At Barcelona there is a distinguished memorial of Aurelianus, mentioned by Morales under the year 276, in which he is called Lucius Domitius Aurelianus.]

### A.D. 273. A.R. 1024

Quintillus, the brother of Claudius, was named emperor by the Senate.

### A.D. 273. A.R. 1024

When Tetricus betrayed his army, Aurelianus recovered Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 0392B]]

### A.D. 276.—1. Eusebius of Laodicea, etc.

The other Eusebius, namely Eusebius of Caesarea, also discusses him, both under this year in the Chronicle [Col. 0392C] and in book VII, chapter 10, of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

### 2. Aurelianus at Rome, etc.

Trebellius Pollio relates that, after the death of her husband Odaenathus, Zenobia, queen of the Palmyrenes, ruled the Roman empire in Syria. Palmyra is a region of Syria, so called from the city of that name situated within Roman territory, according to Ptolemy, book V, chapter 15, and Pliny, book V, chapter 25.

She was one of the thirty tyrants who usurped the world during the time of Gallienus. Eventually she was captured by Aurelianus and led in his triumph; through the clemency of the emperor she was granted an estate at Tibur, where she lived honorably.

Trebellius adds that she possessed such chastity that she had intercourse with her husband only for the sake of producing children. Otherwise, she was accustomed to be worshiped by her subjects with almost Persian royal ceremony. She proceeded to public assemblies wearing a helmet, with a purple border and hanging jewels; she had a clear voice and strict morals; she was highly skilled in Greek and Egyptian, knew Latin as well, and had epitomized the histories of the East and of Alexandria. [Col. 0393A]

Eusebius adds that even today a family at Rome is called the Zenobian family after her. When the Senate reproached Aurelianus for triumphing over a woman, he is said to have spoken at length in her praise.

Because Baronius says that she was Judaean and endowed with singular chastity and many other virtues, he suspects that she was a Christian, since Gentiles commonly called Christians “Judaeans.”

Claudius wrote in a letter addressed to the Senate:

> Zenobia possesses all the archers—something shameful to say.

The same authors write about Tetricus, who was led in the same triumph by Aurelius.]

### A.D. 276. A.R. 1027

Eusebius, distinguished bishop of Laodicea, is held in high regard.

### A.D. 276. A.R. 1027

Tetricus and Zenobia preceded Aurelianus in his triumph at Rome. Later Tetricus became governor of Lucania, while Zenobia afterward enjoyed the highest honor at Rome among the pagans.

[Col. 0393] [Note: [Col. 0393A]]

### A.D. 277.—1. Aurelianus, etc.

Eusebius agrees in both accounts in his Chronicle—or rather Saint Jerome, who inserted Roman affairs into Eusebius’s Chronicle—drawing from Vopiscus, who says the following about the city walls:

> Aurelianus enlarged the city walls so that their circuit enclosed nearly fifty thousand paces.

The same author also discusses the temple of the Sun erected by Aurelianus.

### 2. Saint Narcissus, etc.

A great error had entered the codex printed at Zaragoza through the negligence of librarians and copyists, so that it was read as saying that he suffered in the year of the Lord 86 [Col. 0393B]. Yet it is certain that he suffered at Gerunda, not in the persecution of Domitian but in that of Aurelianus.

Dexter had long before noted, under the year 268, that he was bishop of Braga and successor to Caledonius. Marcus Maximus, at the end of his Chronicle, says that he was a citizen of Scallabis in Lusitania and was summoned from there to the see of Braga. He was subsequently divinely warned to leave the people of Braga, travel to Vindelicia, and bring the Rhaetians to the faith.

Finally, when he was returning to Spain, he was detained at Gerunda by Lucius Caesonnius Macer Lucillus Rufinianus, a man of consular rank and governor of Hispania Citerior. After receiving three wounds—in the throat, mouth, and leg—he was finally brought to completion together with his archdeacon Felix, under the consulship of Augustus Aurelianus II and Gaius Julius Capitolinus, which was the year of Christ 276.

Here are this author’s words:

> At this time the memory of Saint Narcissus, bishop of Braga in Spain and apostle of the Rhaetians, was celebrated in the city of Gerunda, where he suffered under Aurelianus. He was a citizen of Scallabis in Lusitania. Divinely warned, he left the people of Braga and went to Vindelicia.
>
> He suffered at Gerunda under Lucius Caesonnius Macer Lucillus Rufinianus, a man of consular rank and governor of Hispania Citerior, under the consulship of Lucius Domitius Aurelianus Augustus II and Gaius Julius Capitolinus. Narcissus, after receiving three wounds—in the throat, mouth, and leg—was finally brought to completion together with Felix the archdeacon.

Narcissus succeeded Caledonius, to whom Saint Cyprian wrote and whose letters he transmitted to all the metropolitans of Spain. The same Marcus Maximus later makes clear that Pomponius Paulatus, bishop of Toledo, was bound to him by ties of friendship and kinship.

Some maintain that Saint Narcissus was born at Gerunda and was a citizen of that city. They are supported by the old lessons of the Augsburg Breviary and by the ancient records of Gerunda. But this does not rule out his having lived for some time at Scallabis and having been elected bishop of Braga; after traveling through Rhaetia, he could finally have returned to his homeland, Gerunda. There, while exercising the office of bishop for three full years, he was slaughtered while celebrating the sacred rites together with his deacon Felix.

I readily agree with this, provided they do not maintain that he suffered under Diocletian, but under Domitius Aurelianus, as the Roman Martyrology states. The ancient manuscript codex of Baronius, which he himself mentions in volume II under the year 303, reads *Domitianus* instead of *Domitius*, through a slight error. Baronius corrected it rather unsuccessfully, thinking that *Diocletianus* should be read, having been advised to do so by Velser. The ancient epitaph of Saint Narcissus’s tomb nevertheless agrees with them, asserting that he suffered in the year of the Lord 297. But Dexter and Maximus are much older, and we follow them.

It is certain from the acts of Saint Afra of Augsburg, a noble martyr, that this Narcissus converted her from prostitution and brought her to the faith and to a better way of life. Molanus testifies to this in his appendix to the Martyrology of Usuard.

The acts of Saint Afra are found in Surius, volume IV, under 5 August, and in Vicelius’s *Hagiologium*. Vincent of Beauvais, book VII of his special *History*, chapter 28; Saint Antoninus, part I, title VIII, chapter 1, section 18; Father Antonius Beuterus; and Vasaeus in their Spanish Chronicles agree with this, as do the more recent authors Villegas and Ribadeneyra in the *Flower of the Saints of Spain*.

From these sources it is proved that those who identify Narcissus, the preacher of Afra and apostle of the Rhaetians, not with this Narcissus of Gerunda but with the bishop of Jerusalem, are mistaken; that bishop had died many years earlier.

Both Baronius and Galesinus agree. Galesinus writes in his Martyrology:

> Saint Narcissus, bishop and martyr. He won a new household for God in Rhaetia. Nine months later he went from there to Gerunda in Spain and during three years converted many from the errors of impiety to the faith of Christ. In that ministry he received the crown of martyrdom together with Felix the deacon.

This is also asserted in the Augsburg Breviary printed at Rome in the year of the Lord 1570 by Otto Truchsess, cardinal and bishop of Augsburg, where his feast is celebrated as that of its patron and apostle on 29 October. The Roman Martyrology commemorates Narcissus and his deacon Felix on 18 March.

Rhaetia is a distinguished province of Germany—now the Grisons—bordering the Alps and the sources of the Danube. Vindelicia adjoins it to the east; its chief city is Augusta, now called Augsburg, where Saint Afra was converted to the faith by Narcissus.

As for Saint Felix, the companion and deacon of Saint Narcissus in the crown of martyrdom and in office, Cardinal Baronius believed in his Notes under 18 March that he was the same Felix who, the brother of Saint Cucuphas, the martyr of Barcelona, suffered at Gerunda on 1 August, the day on which he is celebrated in the Martyrologies of Ado, Bede, Usuard, the Roman Martyrology, Galesinus, and others.

Nevertheless, from the accounts given there we are compelled to admit that two Felixes suffered martyrdom for Christ at Gerunda. One suffered under Aurelianus in the year of the Lord 276 or 277, the other under Diocletian in the year 300. The former was killed by Lucillus Rufinianus, the latter by the governor Dacianus, as the Roman Martyrology states. Moreover, one received the crown of martyrdom on 18 March and the other on 1 August.

One matter might nevertheless raise suspicion concerning the two Felixes: in the acts of Saint Felix we read that he not only suffered at Gerunda but was of Scyllitan origin. Yet we know from Marcus Maximus that Saint Narcissus’s companion, the deacon Felix, was from Scallabis. It could therefore easily be believed that his deacon Felix was likewise from Scallabis and that *Scyllitanus* was incorrectly read for *Scallabitanus*.

That he went from there to Caesarea for the sake of study presents no difficulty, since travel from Lusitania to Africa was frequent at that time, as we have shown more than once above. Perhaps, however, this should be understood not of Caesarea in Mauritania but of Caesarea Augusta, from which a journey to Gerunda would have been easy.

But there can be no doubt that two sufficiently distinct Felixes were killed at Gerunda. One, born at Caesarea in Mauritania, was killed in the year of the Lord 300; we shall discuss him below under that year, Commentary 3, number 6, on the testimony of Saint Eulogius and the Breviary of Saint Isidore. The other was the deacon of Saint Narcissus, the bishop, whom we have discussed here.

Zurita and others who have treated Spanish affairs relate the miracle of the flies that emerged from Saint Narcissus’s tomb and afflicted the armies of the kings of Sicily and France in defense of Gerunda, which they had besieged.

[Col. 0395A] ### 3. Aurelianus raises a persecution, etc.

Eusebius relates this in his Chronicle under the year 278. He asserts that, when Aurelianus had stirred up a persecution against the Church, lightning fell beside him and his companions, and that not long afterward he was killed between Constantinople and Heraclea.

This was Aurelianus’s eighth persecution, according to the teaching of Dexter given under the year of the Lord 260. See Vopiscus on the death of Aurelianus.

### 4. He was succeeded by, etc.

Eusebius and the other authors likewise say this, drawing from Vopiscus.

### 5. The Parthians, etc.

The same authors agree. His name was Marcus Aurelius Valerius Probus. He began his rule in the year of the Lord 279, for the brothers Tacitus and Florianus held the reins of the empire for only eight months and were killed in that same year.

### 6. His memory flourishes, etc.

He is speaking of Saint Epitatius, or Epictetus, about whom we have said enough under the year 268.]

### A.D. 277. A.R. 1028

Aurelianus built a temple to the Sun at Rome and restored the city walls, which had collapsed through the passage of time, making them stronger.

### A.D. 277. A.R. 1028

Saint Narcissus, bishop of Braga and martyr, who preached in Rhaetia, suffered at Gerunda.

[Col. 0395] ### A.D. 277. A.R. 1028

Aurelianus began a persecution against the Christians; not long afterward he was killed between Constantinople and Heraclea.

### A.D. 277. A.R. 1028

Tacitus succeeded him in the empire, and after Tacitus, Florianus.

### A.D. 277. A.R. 1028

After them Probus began his imperial rule, which he held for six years.

### A.D. 277. A.R. 1028

At Tuy the memory flourishes of its first bishop, a saint and disciple of Saint Peter of Braga. He is believed to have suffered the most severe torments at the beginning of Nero’s reign.

[Note: [Col. 0395A]]

### A.D. 280.—1. Anatolius, etc.

Saint Jerome inserted his name with great praise in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* [Col. 0395B], saying:

> Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, flourished under the emperors Probus and Carus. He was a man of remarkable learning in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, and so forth.

He was also distinguished for holiness, since his feast is celebrated on 3 July in the Martyrologies of Usuard, Ado, and the Roman Martyrology. Eusebius discusses him in the Chronicle under this very year and in book VII, chapter 26; so do Nicephorus, book VI, chapter 36, and others.

### 2. The insane heresy, etc.

Eusebius has the same words under the year 281. Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, in Catechesis 6, states that Manes, from whom the Manichaeans received their name, began to spread his impiety under the emperor Probus. Saint Leo the pope likewise asserts this in Sermon 2 for Pentecost, as does Cassiodorus in his Chronicle and Epiphanius in Heresy 66.

Bede disagrees, asserting in his book *On the Six Ages* that it began under Tacitus, while Zonaras, in part III of his *Annals*, says that it began under Carus. We follow the more ancient authorities.

3. Probus allowed the Gauls and Pannonians to possess vineyards, etc. Eusebius in the *Chronicle* under the year [Col. 0395C] 282 says: “Probus,” he says, “granted vineyards to the Gauls and Pannonians,” and adds: “He also gave the fertile and golden mountain, planted by military labor, to the provincials for cultivation.”

A.D. 280. A.R. 1031. Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea and a philosopher, is highly praised.

A.D. 280. A.R. 1031. The insane heresy of the Manichaeans arose as a general evil.

A.D. 280. A.R. 1031. Probus permitted the Gauls and Pannonians to have vineyards.

[Note: [Col. 0395C]

A.D. 285.—1. Probus of Sirmium, etc. In the same year Eusebius has this in his *Chronicle*: “Probus was killed during a military mutiny at Sirmium, in a tower called Ferrata. He ruled the empire for six years”; Baronius reckons only five. Bonosus, born in Spain and descended from England, and a certain Saturninus rebelled against Probus. Concerning them see Ambrosio Morales, book IX, chapter 49, who asserts that a memorial of Probus still exists at Granada in the royal palace called the Alhambra.

2. Carus, etc. Eusebius—or Jerome—in the *Chronicle* likewise records this.

[Col. 0396A] 3. The Olcades, etc. We have said enough about Saint Antoninus and Alexander above, under the year 100, where we discussed the Olcades.

4. Carmonia, etc. Therefore there were formerly two cities in Spain called Carmonia: one near Hispalis, which Ptolemy mentions among the Turdetani; the other, of which Dexter now speaks, in Carpetania. Its memory is certainly preserved in Appian of Alexandria’s *Roman History*, when he is dealing with Galba. For when Galba, serving as praetor of Spain, had been driven into flight by the Lusitanians and was leaving Lusitania with some cavalry, Appian asserts that he first reached Carmonia, or Carmena. But for those leaving ancient Lusitania, the cities of Carpetania are the first to be encountered, not those of Turdetania, especially in the area adjoining Hispalis where Carmonia lies.

To this day, between Toledo and Torrijos, there remains a town called Carmena, bearing nearly the same name. Saint Justina is said to have suffered there on the last day of November, the date on which she is placed by the Roman Martyrology, Molanus, Galesinus, and Equilinus, book II, chapter [Col. 0396B] 130, no. 1. Nevertheless, they all suppress the kind of martyrdom and the name of the place itself, asserting only that she was a virgin and martyr crowned on that day. Baronius asserts that her name is also found in the oldest manuscript codices of the Roman Martyrology.

5. Varinus, etc. The acts of the saints Chrysanthus and Daria, the virgin and his wife, whose feast is celebrated in the Latin Martyrologies on 25 October and in the Greek ones on 19 March, are found in Surius, volume V, and Lipomanus, volume VII, having been added to the Greek accounts by Metaphrastes; among the Latins, however, they are found in manuscript codices of many libraries. Everywhere we read that they were written by Varinus and Armentarius, under these words, which Molanus cites from the Latin Passion:

“We, Varinus and Armenus, brothers, made priests by Saint Stephen in the apostolic see, have written all these things just as they happened, and have sent them to all the Churches throughout the East and West.”

From this it may be inferred that they also sent those acts to the Spanish Church, which was highly distinguished in the West. Among the Spanish bishops, the bishop of Toledo held the foremost place; consequently the acts of the martyrs had to be sent to him as well. At that time Pomponius Paulatus governed the see of Toledo, as you see, so that nothing is lacking from the truth asserted by Dexter. The martyrs, indeed, suffered under the emperor Numerian, as everyone testifies. Numerian, according to Baronius, entered upon and relinquished the empire in the year 284; the writers were ordained priests by Pope Saint Stephen, who suffered martyrdom in the year 260; and in the year 285 they wrote the martyrs’ acts.

We discussed Paulatus above, under the year of the Lord 245, and shall discuss him again below, under the year 286. Moreover, Varinus and Armentarius seem to have been the very men who had been the fiancés of the holy virgins and martyrs Rufina and Secunda. The time, homeland, and names agree, as anyone can easily discover from their acts in Surius, volume IV, under 10 July, and in Equilinus, book VI, chapter 78.

6. Cyprian, etc. The fame of Saint Cyprian spread widely after his martyrdom, especially in Spain, as Prudentius clearly noted in hymn 13, saying:

> He rules not only the peoples of Libya, and the regions extending eastward  
> To the setting of the sun; he cherishes the Gauls and instructs the Britons;  
> He presides over Hesperia and sows Christ among the farthest Iberians.  
> At last, he is a teacher on earth, and likewise a martyr in heaven;  
> Here he instructs men; there, as their patron, he gives holy gifts.

7. Turigii, etc. John Molanus, in his additions to Usuard, mentions the holy martyrs Felix and Regula, who suffered at Turigium, or Turego, in these words: “At Turego, the natal day of the holy Felix and Regula.” Turegum—today Torrijos—is situated in Celtiberia, twelve Roman miles, or four Spanish leagues, from Bilbilis, or Calatayud, a sufficiently well-known town.

Even today the holy martyrs of Christ, Regula and Felix, are held in the highest honor there, and their relics are piously preserved and venerated, with a considerable gathering of neighboring peoples. A spring or pool also remains, where the inhabitants, following a tradition received from their ancestors, say that the martyrs were thrown in order to be tortured. I learned this from a very trustworthy citizen while traveling that way toward Rome in the year 1621.

In the Martyrology of Saint Notker, under 3 September, this noble account of them is found:

> The nativity of the holy martyrs Felix and Regula, his sister. These martyrs, belonging to the company of Mauritius and his companions, journeying through the vast wilderness called Darona toward the regions of . . . , arrived at . . . ; and, stopping at a certain place beside the river . . . , they devoted themselves with complete religious zeal to vigils and prayers. While these most holy brothers and sisters were engaged in such practices, messengers sent by the most impious Maximilian arrived, either to compel the saints of God to sacrifice to idols or not to delay in punishing them with various tortures.  
>   
> Therefore the blessed martyrs, courageously resisting the sacrilegious demands, were bound to iron wheels glowing with fire and were further tormented by indescribable tortures. Blessed Regula was laid upon boiling pitch, and the executioner was also ordered to give her boiling lead to drink. Since they could not be torn away from Christ by any severity of punishment, it was ordered that their heads be cut off. Once this had been done, the decapitated martyrs carried their severed heads in their own hands and transported them fifty cubits from the place where they had been beheaded.

8. Theodosius, etc. This, I believe, is that Theodosius whom Dexter had mentioned above, under the year 100, saying: “The people of Barcelona advanced in the glory of miracles, in the power of the teaching and example of Saint Theodosius, bishop, just as the people of Toledo did through the teaching of Saint Eugenius, whose contemporary and friend he was.” Under the year 94 he also asserts that Saint Theodosius was the second bishop of Barcelona, as successor to Saint Etherius, the disciple of the apostle Saint James, and that his feast is celebrated on 27 January.

9. Saint Praecellius, etc. We discussed under the year [Col. 0397D] 222 the city of Hippo in Carpetania, of which Saint Praecellius was a citizen; it is now called Hiepes.

10. Saint Severus at Barcelona, etc. For a long time and with much uncertainty, scholars investigating the matter debated whether there had been only one Severus, bishop and martyr of Barcelona, or two. We now know that there were two entirely distinct men: one suffered at the beginning of Diocletian’s persecution, the other during the time of the emperor Constantine; the former at the hands of pagans, the latter at the hands of Arian Goths.

Dexter refers here to the first; he refers to the second below, under the year 352, saying: “At Barcelona Saint Severus suffers for the sake of religion at the hands of the Arian heretics, while he was governing that see rightly and piously.”

Heleca followed Dexter in his additions to Maximus: “At this time,” he says, “two Severuses, bishops and martyrs of Barcelona, are said to shine with the glory of miracles and signs; the elder flourished under Diocletian, the other under Constantine.”

Vasaeus discusses the elder in his *Chronicle* under the year 306; Laurentius Padilla in the *Thesaurus Concionatorum* and Villegas under 6 November. The feast of the younger is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology in these words:

> At Barcelona, Saint Severus, bishop and martyr, who, because of the Catholic faith, received the crown of martyrdom after a nail had been driven into his head.

That the younger is the one who died with a nail driven into his head is sufficiently established from Molanus’s additions to Usuard. In the first edition he says:

> This man was one of the seventy bishops who established the Gothic laws in Spain. He was crowned with martyrdom by the Gothic barbarians who inhabited Catalonia, after a nail had been driven into his head, in the year of Christ 683.

He is mistaken, however, in assigning the year of his martyrdom, as we have seen from Dexter and Maximus. In the later edition of Usuard he said only:

> At Barcelona, the natal day of Saint Severus, bishop and martyr, who was pierced in the head with a nail by the Goths.

Galesinus has the same account under 6 November.

It happened, nevertheless, that because of the similarity of their names, one and the same man was thought to have suffered both in Diocletian’s persecution and to have been crowned after being pierced through the head with a nail. Thus the error entered even into the lessons of the Breviary of Barcelona.

The first Severus had four clerics and one farmer, named Emiterius, as companions in the crown of martyrdom. He suffered martyrdom at a place near Barcelona called Castro Octaviano, [Col. 0398C] and their bodies rest together in the church of Saint Cucuphas. The head of the second, pierced with a nail, is preserved in the major church.

Trugillus writes about them in the *Thesaurus Concionatorum*, as do Marieta, part I, book I, chapter 23; Morales, book X, chapter 4; and, most recently, Yepes in the *Benedictine Chronicle*, century 3, under the year of Christ 778, chapter 1. The house of Saint Severus, as I believe, the younger one, is still shown at Barcelona.

11. Dejobriga, etc. Or, if you prefer, Deobriga, as others have it. Ptolemy testifies that two cities of this name formerly existed in Spain: one among the Vettones of ancient Lusitania, not far from the Tagus River and Alcántara; the other among the Autrigones, the peoples of Navarre, where Tafalla now stands, or nearby, if Ptolemy’s placement is reliable.

In which of these two places Saints Lupus and Saturninus received the crown of martyrdom, I would not dare to assert, since Dexter did not specify it. Their feast, nevertheless, is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 14 October. Although they are not expressly called martyrs there, they are nevertheless placed among the martyrs. [Col. 0398D]

Equilinus expressly states this in book XI, chapter 130, no. 288, in these words:

> The martyrs Saturninus and Lupus suffered on the day before the Ides of October.

Bede deals only with Lupus; but Baronius correctly noted that in the oldest manuscript codices both are treated together. Molanus followed this in his additions to Usuard.]

A.D. 285. A.R. 1036. Probus is seized and killed in a military mutiny at Sirmium.

A.D. 285. A.R. 1036. Carus is placed in charge of the Roman empire by order of the Senate.

A.D. 285. A.R. 1036. Alexander and the virgin Antonina are celebrated as having suffered among the Olcades of Spain.

A.D. 285. A.R. 1036. At Carmonia [called Carmena], in Carpetania, the virgin and martyr Justina becomes a martyr; she suffers on the last day of November.

A.D. 285. A.R. 1036. Varinus and Armentarius, Romans, wrote to Paulatus, bishop of Toledo, concerning the martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria.

[Col. 0397] A.D. 285. A.R. 1036. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, flourished greatly among the Spaniards at that time because of his reputation for learning and holiness.

A.D. 285. A.R. 1036. At Turigium [or Tigurinum], in Celtiberia of Spain, the holy martyrs of Christ Felix and Regula, whose sacred relics are venerated by the devout attendance of neighboring peoples.

A.D. 285. A.R. 1036. Theodosius, bishop of Barcelona, is held in renown.

A.D. 285. A.R. 1036. Saint Praecellius, a Roman martyr and a Spanish citizen of Hippo, is held in marvelous renown for the glory of his martyrdom on 25 May.

A.D. 285. A.R. 1036. At Barcelona, Saint Severus, bishop and martyr of that city.

A.D. 285. A.R. 1036. At Dejobriga in Spain, the holy martyrs Lupus and Saturninus.

[Col. 0399] [Note: [Col. 0399A]

A.D. 286.—1. Diocletian, etc. The fury and madness of the persecution aroused by Diocletian extended chiefly through the year 300 and continued until the year 306. He was not, however, emperor before he began persecuting Christians. It is especially clear concerning Spain that certain people were crowned with the laurel of martyrdom at the beginning of Diocletian’s reign. Thus the acts of the holy virgins of Seville, Justa and Rufina, assert that they were killed at the beginning of Diocletian’s reign, in the year of the Lord 287; this is reported in the *Thesaurus Concionatorum* under 19 July. But we shall discuss them later. According to Baronius, Diocletian began to rule in the year 284.

2. Pomp. Paulatus, etc. We have said a great deal about Pomponius Paulatus, bishop of Toledo, above. One point, however, is not easily explained: Dexter asserts that Paulatus began his pontificate in the year of the Lord 245 and held it for [Col. 0399B] thirty-six years, but now says that Melanthius succeeded him in 286, that is, after forty years.

One may reply, however, that the see of Toledo remained vacant for four years during the intensity of the persecution; nor does the author appear to contradict himself, for he does not assert that Paulatus died in this year 286, but only that Melanthius succeeded Paulatus. Or perhaps the numbers have been corrupted, so that someone wrote XXXVI instead of XL.

We shall speak below of Melanthius, his successor, who attended the Council of Elvira, provided that we first observe how greatly Loaysa’s catalogue departs from the truth in this matter. He places Melanthius in the year 313 and Paulatus in the year 396, as though Paulatus had been Melanthius’s seventh successor, although it is perfectly clear from what has been said that he was his predecessor. Indeed, nearly the whole chronology of that catalogue is filled with errors.

### Note on Saint Tyrsus the Martyr

The memory of that great martyr Tyrsus, patron of the people of Toledo, claims this place for itself. For, while still a catechumen and bound by the oath of military service, he is said to have departed from Toledo under the pontificate of Paulatus and gone to Greece, where he made the distinguished city of Apollonia still more illustrious by shedding his blood for the faith of Christ.

Since these matters are little known to many, I thought it appropriate to pause and demonstrate something concerning them. Greek writers, ignorant of Tyrsus’s Spanish origin, proclaim him only as a Greek martyr; consequently, some assign him a Greek ancestry, as may be seen in the author of his life preserved by Metaphrastes.

The ignorance of the Greeks, however, cannot harm the people of Toledo, since the testimony of ancient authors supports them. Julian, archpriest of Saint Justa, who was present when Toledo was recovered from Moorish rule by Alfonso VI, king of Castile and León, twice mentions this matter in his *Chronicle*. Under the year of the Lord 252 he says:

> Saint Tyrsus, a citizen of Toledo and a catechumen, departs from Toledo; in the city of Apollonia in Greece he gives an illustrious testimony to the faith.

Under the year 773 he says:

> Cyxilla founded the church of Saint Tyrsus at Toledo, a citizen of Toledo who suffered at Apollonia in Greece. The holy man departed from Toledo under Paulatus, the Toledan governor, as a catechumen; and Cyxilla himself, the bishop, composed a poem for him.

Paulatus had begun his episcopate, according to Dexter, in the year of the Lord 245 and held it until 286, when he died. That very hymn is preserved in the Gothic Breviary of Saint Isidore, where the acts of the holy martyr are sung with great purity, together with a proper ecclesiastical office in his honor, customarily sung on his feast day.

In that hymn, too, Cyxilla the author calls Tyrsus, in the name of the people of Toledo, their *patronus vernulus*, meaning their natural patron and fellow citizen. Among other lines it says:

> We ask you, martyr, our own countryman, with tears:  
> Through you may the almighty Creator quickly  
> Remove this harsh yoke under which we suffer, etc.

And somewhat farther on:

> This temple, Lord, Cyxilla founded;  
> May he receive here a worthy place in heaven.

There also exists a letter from Silo, king of Oviedo in Spain, addressed to the same Cyxilla, bishop of Toledo. Silo ruled in Asturias during the time of the Saracen tyranny, around the year of the Lord 777. In the letter he asks Cyxilla for a hymn recently composed in honor of Saint Tyrsus of Toledo and congratulates him on the temple then erected at Toledo.

I wish to insert the letter here because it not only confirms what we intend to establish, but also many other matters that we have related with Dexter in their proper places: concerning the holy martyrs Philibert and Fabricianus, abbots who suffered at Titulcia, and concerning Saints Vincent and Laetus, likewise martyrs of Toledo, who were killed at Libyso. We have promised to include it more than once. It is worthy of its barbarous age.

> To the most holy and God-beloved Cyxillanus, archbishop of the Church of Toledo, Silo, king of Oviedo and Pravia, sends greetings.
>
> By the hands of Elipandus, archdeacon, and Peter, deacon—your men—I received the letters of Your Paternity and of the faithful who, together with you in the city, eat the bread of sorrow. I grieve that you are living here in such misery, and I feel great compassion for you because you suffer so many evils among these death-dealing Saracens. Not content with imposing such lawless taxes upon you, they seek you daily for death.
>
> You are in great danger for your lives because you have begun to build there a church of Saint Tyrsus the martyr near the larger church of Melchitas. Alguazil Zuleima Yusuf Abenabdil, who governs Toledo, wanted to kill you; but when you appealed to the judge Muhammad Abenramin, he ordered you released and granted permission to build in return for the money [Col. 0400C] you gave him.
>
> These Moors do nothing except under the pretext of profit. Nevertheless, I am writing to him to thank him for the favor he showed you, and I ask him to protect you. I also ask him to grant permission for Argericus, formerly abbot of Agali, to return to you. He often told me that he had no reason to believe that Muhammad Abenramin wished to kill him when he was governor of Toledo. For when Saint Nicholas the martyr of Ledesma, who was born among you, the son of Alcamani and brother of Galafri, became a Christian, that man was not in the town; and it was merely because of suspicion concerning this affair that Abenramin, the uncle of the aforesaid Nicholas, wished to kill him.
>
> If I cannot help him by intervening with that man, I shall at least honor and support the saint. His sister Sarra, a good woman, died at Pravia, and I had her buried with the honor that a holy woman deserved.
>
> The blessing you sent to Queen Adosinda has been received by her in good will, together with the relics, which we shall place in the church at Oviedo when it is completed. I intend to be buried with the queen in the church of Saint John at Pravia.
>
> The queen is now sending some small gifts for your new church of Saint Tyrsus the martyr, which I have already heard that you have completed: a silver chalice and paten, together with a ewer and its spout, and on the lid the crown of our kingdom, with your name and mine written in abbreviation in this form, C. S. It will be used to give the blood of the Lord to the people.
>
> I have heard that you composed a hymn for the dedication of Saint Tyrsus the martyr and citizen of Toledo, as your envoys reported to me.
