You have also composed another hymn about Saint Vincent and Laetus of Toledo, who suffered, as they told me, under Caecilius Apollinaris, governor of the Spains, in the city of Libyso. Let Your Paternity send these hymns to me, so that our clergy may have something to sing.
>
> We are sending you a hymn about the holy martyrs Philibert and his companion, who suffered in the city of Titulcia—whom I have heard were Toledans—under Marcus Aurelius Valentinian, in the year 283, when Melanthius was archbishop of Toledo.
>
> We have also sent you Arcarius and Magnus, abbots and men worthy of honor, to console you and to speak face to face concerning our affairs and yours. Treat them with humanity and charity. Pray for me and for the queen. May God preserve you. Amen.
>
> At Pravia, 24 February, in the era 815.

That year was A.D. 777, when Spain was oppressed beneath the exceedingly harsh yoke of the Saracens.

Many centuries later, in our own time, when a royal hospice was being built near the summit of the church of the Blessed Virgin at Toledo, the walls and ruins of the long-destroyed church of Saint Tyrsus appeared beneath the earth. Among the rubble, not without God’s providence, a vessel-cover was found—the one that the wife of King Silo had sent to Cyxilla—with the royal crown and the initial letters [Col. 0401B] [Col. 0401C] of both men in the following form.

From this evidence it was discovered that the temple of Saint Tyrsus, citizen and patron of Toledo, had stood there. At that time the protection of Saint Tyrsus returned to people’s memory. In order that the Catholic king Philip II might share in this renewed joy—for the discovery occurred in the year of Christ 1595—Don Alfonso de Cárcamo, royal governor of the city, sent him the recently discovered vessel-cover, together with King Silo’s letter and the conclusion of the hymn of Saint Tyrsus composed by Cyxilla.

Nevertheless, some began to express doubts about the authenticity of the letter and the martyr’s homeland, so varied are human opinions. They said that it was impossible for King Silo to have written to Bishop Cyxilla, because Cyxilla had died in the year 750, in the ninth year of his episcopate, according to John Vasaeus in his *Chronicle of Spain*, whereas Silo did not begin to reign until the year 774, when he succeeded King Aurelius.

They also observed from the letter itself that it was not addressed to Cyxilla but to Cyxillanus; yet the bishop of Toledo was not called Cyxillanus but Cyxilla.

Regarding Tyrsus, they added that the hymn did not prove that he had been a Toledan. When it says, “We ask you, martyr, *vernule*, with tears,” they said that *vernule* should not be joined to “martyr,” as though *vernule* were a vocative; rather, it should be joined to *poscimus*, so that the sense would be:

“We, *vernulae*, who were born in these very houses and subjected to servitude under the Saracens, ask you with tears, O martyr,” etc.

Hence, they said, the following line is added: “Through you may the almighty Creator quickly remove this harsh yoke under which we suffer.”

For *vernula* is a diminutive of *verna*, meaning a slave born in his master’s household, as may be seen in Martial, book XIV, where he says of the *crepitacillum*:

> If some weeping-girl, a household slave, hangs around your neck,  
> Let her shake these chattering rattles with her tender hand.

Plautus in *Miles Gloriosus* and *Amphitryon*, Tibullus in book II, elegy 1, Horace in book I of the *Satires*, Festus and the cited Caelius, and, to omit the rest, Paulus in the *Digest*, title *De legatis* 3, law 97, section “if others,” all testify that *verna* means a slave.

These arguments were also sent to King Philip, who entrusted the matter for examination to learned men, especially Alfonso de Villegas, author of the *Flos Sanctorum*, and the celebrated writer Stephen Garibay. Their judgment was unanimous: the objections did not prevent Saint Tyrsus from having been a Toledan or the letter of Silo from being genuine.

I read the letters that both men wrote to the king in the vernacular language on this matter, which the aforementioned Don Alfonso de Cárcamo had printed. Among other things, Villegas said:

> “I was asked to give my opinion on this matter, and after carefully considering what both sides alleged, I said and maintain that I believe with the greatest certainty that Saint Tyrsus the martyr was a native of Toledo, both on account of the hymn of Saint Isidore and of Silo’s letter to Cyxilla, as well as for other reasons that I gave and presented,” etc.

Vasaeus was plainly mistaken when he asserted that Cyxillanus began his pontificate in the year of the Lord 741 and died in 750. For from the catalogue and chronology of the bishops of Toledo compiled by Loaysa, it is certain that Cyxillanus succeeded Urban in the year of the Lord 775 and died in 784. Elipandus was then elected in his place, and he is frequently mentioned in the Council of Frankfurt.

Silo received the royal diadem in the era 812, that is, in the year of Christ 774, as Sebastian, bishop of Salamanca, left on record in his *Chronicle*:

> In the era 812, after the end of Aurelius, Silo succeeded to the kingdom.

This unimpeachable witness lived at nearly that time, namely under Alfonso, Silo’s successor. Silo died in the era 829, or in the year of Christ 791. I have as evidence for this a privilege of Alfonso the Chaste, his successor, granted to the monastery of Saint Vincent of Monteforte in the kingdom of Galicia, where it says:

> In the era 829, Alfonso was consecrated king on 14 September.

From this one may see that Silo’s reign coincided with Cyxilla’s pontificate. Silo began to be king in the year of the Lord [Col. 0402C] 774, while Cyxilla became bishop in the year of the Lord 775. The letter was dated in the era 815, or the year of the Lord 777—that is, in Silo’s fourth year and Cyxilla’s third.

The objection concerning the inflection of the name Cyxilla arose from ignorance of the ancient inflection of Gothic names ending in *-a*. Although some people customarily decline such names according to the first declension, they were formerly declined according to the third: for example, *Wamba, Wambanis; Egila, Egilanis; Cyxilla, Cyxillanis*, as is plainly evident in the Gothic councils and in the writers of those times.

Moreover, the line of the hymn, “We ask you, martyr, *vernule*, with tears,” is being interpreted perversely when it is dragged away from the customary meaning in which the word is used consistently throughout the hymns of that same Gothic Breviary and assigned other senses.

It means the same as *vernaculus*, a word denoting something native or natural. Thus we speak of a native language and a native flavor, as Cicero does in the *Brutus*, and of a domestic or native crime, in Cicero’s *Against Verres*, book 6, and of a native pruning, that is, one customary in our region, in Pliny, book XVII. Pliny also, in book XIV, chapter 2, calls Italy’s foremost nobility *vernacular*.

In this sense the same Breviary uses the word *vernulus, -a, -um* as an adjective, both in the hymn of Saint Leocadia, the Toledan virgin sprung from the highest nobility, where it says:

> You are our illustrious fellow citizen,  
> You are our native patroness;  
> From the boundary of this city,  
> Drive far away all weariness.

And also in the hymn of the apostle Saint James, the special and almost natural patron of Spain:

> O truly worthy and most holy apostle,  
> Illustrious shining head of Spain,  
> Our protector and native patron, etc.

In precisely this sense, without doubt, that vocative *vernule* must be understood in the hymn of Saint Tyrsus.

But let us present the hymn in full for the benefit of the devout, of whom there is a great number in Spain. The very common female name Teresa was also derived from him, as Villegas correctly noted in the aforementioned letter to the Catholic king.

### Hymn in Praise of Saint Tyrsus the Martyr, Composed by Cyxilla, Bishop of Toledo

> Rejoice exceedingly, assembly of the faithful;  
> Today is the solemn feast  
> Of the illustrious martyr. Sing boldly  
> In praise of the Lord and his power.
>
> He considers the joys of the heavenly homeland;  
> Tyrsus, the holy man, cast away all worldly things,  
> Though at first he scarcely believed in God;  
> Suddenly he was inspired by the holy breath.
>
> Seeing the savage judge, he rebukes him:  
> “Why,” he says, “do you torture the Lord’s saints  
> With exceedingly cruel punishments?  
> Unhappy man, you are destined to be burned  
> In the fire of Erebus.”
>
> Immediately the raging enemy Combritius  
> Was oppressing the times  
> Of those who worship the Lord on earth;  
> Many shining thousands of saints  
> Had been slain as martyrs.
>
> The holy Leucius strives for the Lord,  
> Eager to surrender his chosen soul;  
> Innocent, he endured various kinds  
> Of punishment, receiving heavenly rewards.
>
> The athlete Tyrsus, nimble on his feet, walking on,  
> Found the impious king.  
> He seized and held him, admonishing and teaching him  
> To cease worshiping false idols.
>
> Then, pretending a cheerful expression, he spoke:  
> “Tyrsus, I wish you, following my counsel,  
> To give your assent and sacrifice to the gods,  
> That you may receive great stores of gifts.”
>
> The saint replied: “It is clear, impious man,  
> That the utterly wicked one dwells wholly within you,  
> Now a depraved and envious serpent.  
> May you perish with such a dreadful ruler.”
>
> He orders the *gustrum* [a vessel?] to be brought swiftly;  
> Full of water, it submerges the martyr’s head,  
> And commands that the remaining body  
> Be struck more fiercely with knotted clubs.
>
> But the servant of the Lord, with a most holy voice,  
> Rebukes the wretched judge from the vessel:  
> “Recognize the Lord, slippery and envious man,  
> When you behold his great and glorious works.”
>
> A high and lofty mound is built,  
> With swords fixed in order all around;  
> The saint is placed upon its blessed summit  
> And falls upon the swords to receive  
> His faithful limbs.
>
> Great are you, Lord, above all gods,  
> Most wondrous to those who believe in you.  
> For the wicked you become a snare;  
> The saint in heaven glorifies  
> The omnipotence of Christ.
>
> Defeated, the insatiable and terrible beast  
> Does not cease, but devises new tortures,  
> Thirsting to conquer the martyr;  
> But the holy Lord struck terror into evil.
>
> “Do not be afraid, Tyrsus,” says the angel;  
> “I have been sent to you  
> By the Lord God, to remove all your punishments,  
> And you will be able to conquer  
> The worst of enemies.”
>
> Hear, Lord: the impious man plans  
> To impose burdens, every kind of bond,  
> Boiling oil, lead, and claw-like instruments,  
> To overcome and kill the holy martyr.
>
> Seeing that he accomplished nothing by his own strength,  
> He orders the saint to be thrown headlong  
> Into the sea, so that human eyes might not see him,  
> Thirty stadia out from the shore.
>
> How wondrous are your works, Lord!  
> Angels bring the martyr back in their hands  
> And resound with sweet song;  
> The judge was not worthy to see an angel.
>
> We ought fully to recount the deeds,  
> The benefits he bestowed in response to the saint’s merits:  
> Three guilty judges, hidden in the earth,  
> Whom the earth repeatedly cast out dead.
>
> The people beseech the martyr, saying:  
> “We pray, Lord; command at once  
> That the earth receive the bodies of the judges,  
> So that they may provide utterly rotten food  
> For the worms.”
>
> Weeping mercifully, he receives the oracle,  
> Pointing out the place where the bodies  
> Should be buried. “Grant pardon,” we humbly ask,  
> O martyr; we believe in God.
>
> Let the hearts of all who desire  
> To seek the joys of the heavenly homeland rejoice;  
> Let them make little of every harmful thing,  
> Which flies away from the face of the wind  
> Like straw.
>
> We ask you, martyr, our native patron, with tears;  
> Through you may the almighty Creator quickly  
> Remove this harsh yoke under which we suffer,  
> And make the ages joyful forever.
>
> Now, supreme Lord, look upon the wounded;  
> Erase the bond of guilt from your people;  
> Mercifully regard our groaning,  
> Giving us help at the fitting time.
>
> Grant rest to all the dead, O best of Lords;  
> Give us prosperous times.  
> Grant sustenance to the poor and aid to widows;  
> May all receive what they piously request.
>
> This temple, Lord, Cyxilla founded;  
> May he receive here a worthy place in heaven,  
> And sing songs with the highest citizens,  
> Rejoicing throughout all the ages.
>
> May our glory rejoice in you forever,  
> Who alone are Lord, threefold and one;  
> Holding the ages under eternal rule,  
> Ruling all things and commanding everything.
>
> Grant this, Unbegotten One, through the Only-begotten,  
> Who reigns forever with the Holy Spirit;  
> You contain Olympus by eternal judgment,  
> Sustaining the dry earth by everlasting rule.
>
> Amen.

The following passages, recited by the Gothic Church in the proper office of his feast day, will shed much light on this history. I have thought it worthwhile to cite them:

**Capitulum.** Author of light, fount of light, and brightness of immeasurable splendour, Christ, only-begotten offspring of the unbegotten Father: for your athlete Tyrsus, thirsting for the cleansing bath of the everlasting fountain, you sent from heaven a messenger bearing light, that he might inwardly illumine him whom you had kindled within, so that he might become a lamp for the feet and a constant illuminator of the mind. Blaze, we beseech you, in our minds with the blessed fervour of your fire, which you promised with your own mouth to send from on high, so that, burning inwardly, it may illumine us to burn out vices, and outwardly to attain eternal rewards. Our most merciful Father, who are in heaven, etc.; but deliver us.

**Blessing.** May Christ, the Son of God, through whom the most blessed martyr Tyrsus first enjoyed suffering before baptism, enrich us with the gift of eternity, so that he may reward us with the everlasting prize of blessing. Amen.

And may he who, carried by angels, brought him back to the shore after he had been thrown into the sea, associate you with himself, rejoicing in the dwellings of heaven. Amen.

May you always invoke as God and Father the one whom that same martyr Tyrsus also invoked beneath the waters with an unfettered voice. Amen.

**Prayer.** “As we come to you, Lord, etc., we ask that, just as you did not permit your martyr to be cut apart by saws, so, through his intercession, you may not allow us to be separated for any reason from the womb of Mother Church,” etc.

The acts of Saint Tyrsus and his companions Leucius and Callinicus, who completed their martyrdom at Apollonia, are found intact in Metaphrastes. Lipomanus took them from him in volume V, and Surius in volume VI, under 14 December, on which day the Greeks celebrate them. The Latins, however, celebrate them on 28 January, as do Bede, Ado, Usuard, the Roman Martyrology, and Equilinus, book III, chapter 39.

Moreover, so that the reader may not be deceived, he should know that there are many other martyrs named Tyrsus, entirely different from ours. One of them suffered at Augustodunum in Gaul, together with his companions Andochius and Felix, on 24 September; another suffered with Saturninus at Alexandria, on 31 January; and another with Projectus on the 24th of the same month. Baronius nevertheless erred concerning the last when he believed that the hymn of the Gothic Breviary of Saint Isidore dealt with Tyrsus and Projectus, although it is manifestly about Tyrsus, Leucius, and Callinicus. But enough concerning these matters.

[Col. 0405A] 3. Carus, etc. Eusebius says the very same thing in the *Chronicle* under this year:

> Carus of Narbonne, after devastating the entire region of the Parthians and capturing Coche and Ctesiphon, the most famous cities of the enemy, died after being struck by lightning while he was pitching his camp beside the Tigris.

A memorial of the emperor Carus exists at Tarragona, in the church of Saint Michael, erected by Marcus Aurelius Valentinian, governor of Hither Spain. Concerning it, see Ambrosio Morales, as well as his account of another memorial existing on the island of Ibiza.

4. Carinus, etc. Eusebius has the exact words in the *Chronicle* under the year 287. Carinus and Numerian were sons of the emperor Carus. A memorial of Carinus carved in marble exists at Tarragona, and another at Muro Viejo, or Saguntum. Morales discusses them in book IX, chapter 49.

This very year, 287, the most holy martyrs and virgins of Christ Justa and Rufina were crowned with martyrdom, on 19 July. Their acts are found in the sacred hymn of the Breviary of St. Isidore, where their proper office is also read (we shall give their hymn below, under the year 300 [Col. 0405B]); also in the Lessons of the Sevillian Breviary; and in Morales, book X, chapter 16; Marieta, book IV, chapter 11; Villegas; and the *Sanctorale* under 19 July. Earlier accounts are found in Bellovacensis, book XIII of the *Speculum historiale*, chapter 34; Equilinus, book VI, chapter 117; and Trugillus in the *Thesaurus Concionatorum*. They suffered under the judge Diogenianus, and their feast is solemnly celebrated in all the Martyrologies on the aforesaid day.

There were formerly two other martyrs bearing the same names, killed in the same city—namely Justus and Rufinus, together with their companion Macarius, in the year of the Lord 115. Concerning them, see Dexter in the place indicated there. For the rest, it should not be surprising that a single Dexter did not remember absolutely all the martyrs of Spain; we are human beings, after all, and allowance must be made for the earliest writers if something is missing from their accounts which was later discovered by more recent authors building upon their labors.]

## A.D. 286; A.R. 1037

Diocletian the emperor began to rage against the Church.

## A.D. 286; A.R. 1037

Melantius, a holy man and later an outstanding confessor of Christ, succeeded Pomponius Paulatus [or *Paeviatus*], bishop of Toledo.

## A.D. 286; A.R. 1037 [Col. 0405]

Carus the emperor, after occupying several Parthian cities, Coche and Ctesiphon, set up camp on the river Tigris and, while successfully pursuing his enterprise, was struck by lightning and died.

## A.D. 286; A.R. 1037

Carinus the emperor, defeated in battle, was killed at Margum.

[Note: [Col. 0405B]

## A.D. 290—1. In Campania, etc.

In the acts of St. Sebastian (in Surius, volume I, under 20 January) there is an ancient and distinguished account of the martyr St. Vitalis, whom Sebastian himself, together with the saints Mark and Marcellian and several other friends of theirs, converted to the faith of Christ; it is also written that Sebastian himself raised them all from the sacred font, and that St. Polycarp baptized them. The names of the friends of Mark and Marcellian were Aristion, Crescentianus, Eutychianus, Urbanus, Vitalis, and Justus.

Molanus notes in his commentary on Usuard’s Martyrology under 2 July that, in the acts of St. Sebastian edited by Livinus, page F. 8, St. Vitalis, Aristion, and their companions are expressly said to have been sent into Campania into exile and to have there received the crown of martyrdom. Ado has the same account in his Martyrology under 2 July, and Equilinus reproduces it in book VI, chapter 42, in these words:

“Aristo, Crescentianus, Eutychianus, Urbanus, Vitalis, Justus, Felicissimus, Felix, Marcia, and Symphorosa, martyrs: all in Campania were crowned with glorious martyrdom for the truth of the faith and the confession of the Christian name, on the sixth day before the Nones of July, as Ado says from the Martyrology of Jerome.”

Usuard, Bede, and the more recent authors have almost the same words. The Roman Martyrology assigns the time of their passion, namely when the persecution of Diocletian was raging. Moreover, Martia was the mother of the holy brothers Mark and Marcellian; the others were their friends and relatives.

As for St. Vitalis, it is reasonable to believe that, being a nobleman, he served in the army and therefore traveled from Spain to Italy. We possess a noble memorial of the most holy martyr, an epigram by Valderedus, bishop of Zaragoza. In the time of Pope Sergius I, under King Egica, he attended the Third Council of Zaragoza in the year of the Lord 691 and the Fourteenth Council of Toledo; and he had sent Freydebad, abbot, to the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, celebrated under King Ervig, so that he might assent to the acts of the council.

The aforesaid epigram exists under this title:

**Valderedus, bishop of Zaragoza, on St. Vitalis the martyr, father of the holy martyrs of Complutum, Justus and Pastor**

Hail, Vitalis, most valiant martyr of Christ,  
Who are also called the father of martyrs.

Your homeland was Complutum, but your rustic dwelling Thermeda;  
They say that you fathered Justus and Pastor.

The same madness, seizing you all, carried you to the stars:  
The place was not the same, but the time was nearly the same.

For after a few years the father suffered near Fundia,  
Before his sons; yet the palm was one for all three.

Rejoice in your lot, Vitalis, and in the lot  
Of your happy children; you will rightly be blessed.

Now Arcobriga embraces you, the victor, with both arms—  
This land, close to Capua in soil.

Three times your limbs were torn away from the place; three times,  
Moved from heaven, they sought their ancient resting place.

There the earth holds the bones of the Spanish martyr;  
The Spaniard envies Italy this glory.

Pray for us, Vitalis, radiant martyr;  
Remember your homeland, as you remember Spain.

This monument of venerable antiquity agrees wonderfully with Dexter’s testimony. It asserts that St. Vitalis was born at Thermeda near Complutum, that he was the father of the holy martyrs of Complutum, and that he himself was killed for Christ near Fundana, a city in Campania of Italy—now Terralabor and a province of the Kingdom of Naples. It also adds the place of his martyrdom and burial, as well as that great miracle involving the sacred relics: his body, torn limb from limb and thrown along different roads, had all its members moved again by heavenly power and returned to its former place; and this same miracle was repeated a third time. This is how I understand the words, “Three times your limbs were torn away from the place,” and so forth.

Ptolemy mentions Thermeda among the Carpetani; Valderedus calls it the rustic village of Complutum. I believe it to be the same place that Appian of Alexandria calls Termantia, where Pompey withdrew after defeating the Numantines. More learned historians assert that Numantia was not far away, at the place where Pons Garay now stands, near the city of Soria; Morales agrees with them in his *Antiquitates Hispaniae*, under the word “Numantia,” folio 104, although he himself did not know the location of Thermantia.

### 2. In Octaviola, etc.

Formerly, not far from Bermeo, there was Octaviola, which Ptolemy mentions in Cantabria. As its name indicates, it was so called after Octavian Augustus, who had been there to conquer the Cantabrians. What Dexter adds—that Octaviola was situated in Vezozabia—is intended to identify the ancient name of that province, namely Vezozabia, which we now call Vizcaya, in a somewhat corrupted form, and which the Romans called Cantabria.

Thus, in that town, the holy martyrs of Christ Maximus and Dadas suffered martyrdom. The Greeks celebrate their memory in the Menologion on 13 April, and assert that St. Quintilian also died with them for the Lord, in these words:

“On the same day, the holy martyrs Maximus, Quintilian, and Dadas, struck down by the sword under the emperors Maximian and Diocletian.”

They are also commemorated in the same Martyrology on 18 July; but in the Roman Martyrology, under 13 April, they are said to have suffered during the persecution of Diocletian. Metaphrastes published their acts, followed by Lipomanus and Surius in volume II. Their beginning is: “At the time when Maximus and Maximian were reigning,” and so forth.

The substance of the acts is condensed by Galesinus in his Martyrology as follows:

“On 13 April, the holy martyrs Maximus, Quintilian, and Dadas. When Maximian and Diocletian were persecuting the Church of God, these men were arrested. During the judicial interrogations they freely confessed that they were Christians and were confined in prison. There, by Satan’s deceit, they saw in a dream that they were speaking against themselves; but when they awoke and, at the angel’s warning, had confirmed themselves more firmly in the same confession, the next morning the impious were unable to turn them from their purpose. Rather, they professed the religion of Christ with more confident spirit and greater freedom. First they were beaten with rods, then thrown again into prison, and finally, after enduring other torments, they were struck with the sword and won the palm of martyrdom.”

The acts add that the holy martyrs Maximus, Quintilian, and Dadas were brothers; Maximus held the office of lector; and they were killed in the town of Ozobia. “When,” they say, “the martyrs had reached the place called Ozobia and had marked their bodies with the sign of Christ, they were struck down with axes by the executioner.”

Nevertheless, according to Dexter, one should read *Ozobia*, or, in full, *Vezozabia*, as is clear from what has been said. Molanus also discusses them in his additions to Usuard. In the diocese of Piacenza there is a town called Vezocana; some may wish to claim that these holy martyrs came from there. But if it is established that Octaviola formerly existed nearby, I shall not object—although I have not yet been able to ascertain that it existed there.

### 3. At Tela, etc.

See what we noted earlier, under the year of the Lord 112, concerning Tela, a city of the Vaccaei.

The Greeks discuss the martyrs Eleutherius, Theodosius, and Zoilus, from whom Galesinus borrowed the following:

“On the same day”—that is, 13 April—“the blessed martyrs Eleutherius the Persian, Theodosius, and Zoilus, who, fighting for Christ, obtained the reward for the contest which they had bravely undertaken and completed.”

The fact that Eleutherius is called a Persian does not prevent him from having suffered at Tela in Spain. In the vast extent of the Roman Empire, soldiers were very often sent here and there for purposes of garrison duty. And just as we read of many Spaniards killed in other, very distant regions of the world, so it will not be surprising if we hear that one Persian was beheaded in Spain.

### 4. At Rome, etc.

The memory of the most blessed martyrs Zeno and his 10,203 companions, killed at Rome under Diocletian for Christ, is celebrated in all the Latin Martyrologies—the Roman, those of Ado, Bede, Usuard, Maurolycus, and Galesinus—and in Equilinus, book VI, chapter 75. His words, taken from Ado, are:

“Zeno and 10,203 other martyrs of Christ suffered martyrdom at Rome, at the perpetually flowing Gutta. They were slaughtered by various punishments and, glorifying the Lord Christ in their bodies, deserved to receive the crowns of heavenly triumph from the hand of the Lord.”

All the aforesaid Martyrologies agree both in the number and in the place of martyrdom. The perpetually flowing Gutta is the place otherwise called *ad Aquas Salvias*, where the apostle Paul was beheaded, and where the monastery of Saints Vincent and Anastasius stands—a place customarily called the Three Fountains.

Here one may see how an error entered a manuscript of Usuard preserved by Molanus. Through the judgment and in a different hand from another copyist, the words of Usuard—“at Rome, at the perpetually flowing Gutta”—were explained by adding, “which is otherwise called the Church of St. Mary of the Fountain beyond the Tiber.” This is certainly incorrect, since that church is far removed from the other; and even today, at the aforesaid Gutta, the tomb of the holy martyrs Zeno and his companions remains famous.

Baronius notes in the acts of Pope St. Marcellus, under the year 298, that by order of Diocletian and Maximian all the legions stationed everywhere were inspected. Those found among them to be Christian soldiers were stripped of their military status, completely disarmed, and brought to Rome in chains, as though they were registered slaves, to be assigned to the construction of the baths. After the baths had been completed, all those who had remained steadfast in confessing Christ and had not been broken by any labor were condemned to death together, lest, relieved by the completion of their labor—and since their number was enormous—they should undertake something against the empire. Their number was found to be 10,203.

“All of them,” he says, “together with Zeno the tribune, who seemed to excel among them in rank, were led outside the City through the Trigemina Gate, and in the hollow of the valley, at the place called the perpetually flowing Gutta at Aquae Salviae, all were killed together on 7 July.”

He adds:

“Thus it came about, by God’s providence, that the immense mass of the Baths of Diocletian was built through the sweat of those Christian soldiers, confessors, and finally martyrs. Since it remains intact—while the other baths have nearly collapsed and are insignificant—it is now the Church of St. Mary of the Angels.”

As for the number, in the extant copy of Dexter we read only that Zeno had 1,202 companions, whereas all the aforesaid Martyrologies and authors give 10,203. Some have thought that the word “ten” is missing from Dexter’s copy, so that one should read not merely “one thousand” but “ten thousand.” As for their being called 202 or 203, that makes little difference, since the variation depends on whether Zeno himself is counted with the others or reported separately from their number.

It seems more probable to me that St. Zeno had 10,202 companions, but that not all of them were Spanish soldiers; rather, 1,202 were Spanish, while the remaining 9,000 came from other regions, if what we have reported from Baronius is true.

Dexter also assigns the province of St. Zeno and his companions as Celtiberia, which extended from the Carpetani as far as Zaragoza.

### 5. At Senagis, etc.

Senagis is named fifth among the Fathers of the Council of Illiberis, of which we shall speak later. In some manuscripts, however, he is corruptly called bishop of Epagrensis, and in others, even more corruptly, of Bignerrensis, although it is clear from Dexter that at that time he was bishop of Braga. We shall return to this matter below, under the year 300.

### 6. At Clunia, etc.

Clunia was formerly a most distinguished city of Spain, having been ennobled by the privileges of a colony and a judicial assize. Ptolemy provides evidence that it was a colony. As for its status as an assize-center or tribunal for legal cases, Vasaeus states in his *Chronicle* that at Clunia, not many years ago, among the ruins of the city, a seal was found bearing the inscription **CONVENTUS CLUNIENSIS**, which is preserved by the Count of Clunia.

Suetonius, in his life of Galba, mentions a priest of Jupiter of Clunia, whose prophecies were held in high esteem. He says that Galba was confirmed in his resolve to assume the empire by favorable auspices, especially because the priest of Jupiter at Clunia had drawn those verses from the innermost sanctuary while fortified by a profound sleep.

Many traces of ancient Clunia still remain, six Spanish miles from Uxama—called *leucae*—with a Roman amphitheater, in the territory of the hermitage of St. Mary of the Castle. Near that place there is a town that retains almost the name of Clunia, commonly called Coruña.

Those who confuse it with the royal city of Galicia are plainly mistaken; there the assize-court is now located. Moletius is also mistaken when he says that it is now called Ciudad Real, since both places are far from the Arevaci, among whom Ptolemy places Clunia. Morales, book VIII of his *Historia Hispaniae*, chapter 23, agrees with our view, as do Vasaeus, Florianus de Ocampo, Mariana, and Nebrissensis.

When Dexter asserts that Clunia was formerly the boundary of Celtiberia, his purpose is to show that the boundaries of the Celtiberians and the Arevaci had been changed in his time, so that the city which had formerly been the boundary of the Celtiberians was now within the territory of the Arevaci—that is, Clunia.

The memory of the holy martyr Saturninus and his companions, who were killed there for Christ, is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology under 16 October, with the name of one of his companions also recorded, in these words:

“Also, the holy Saturninus, Nereus, and 365 other martyrs.”

The ancient manuscripts cited by Baronius agree, as does Molanus in his additions to Usuard, and Equilinus, book XI, chapter 30, number 291. The latter asserts that Saturninus was a priest, for he says:

“Saturninus the priest and Nereus suffered with 365 others on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of November.”

It therefore seems that ten martyrs are missing from Dexter’s copy, since all the aforesaid authors read 365, whereas there only 355 are given.]

## A.D. 290; A.R. 1041

In Campania of Italy, St. Vitalis the Spaniard, from the town of Thermeda in Carpetania, father of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor, who suffered near Complutum; converted to the faith through the exhortations of St. Sebastian, he suffers martyrdom with others.

## A.D. 290; A.R. 1041

At Octaviola in Vezozabia, the holy martyrs Maximus and Dadas.

## A.D. 290; A.R. 1041 [Col. 0407]

At Tela, a city of Spain, the holy martyrs Eleutherius the Persian, Theodosius, and Zoilus.

## A.D. 290; A.R. 1041

At Rome, the holy martyr Zeno and 1,202 Spanish martyrs from Celtiberia, who suffered gloriously.

## A.D. 290; A.R. 1041

Senagis, bishop of Braga, flourished and took part in the Council of Illiberis.

## A.D. 290; A.R. 1041

At Clunia, formerly the boundary of Celtiberia, 355 martyrs, with St. Saturninus as their companion.

[Col. 0409] [Note: [Col. 0409B]

## A.D. 296—1. At Complutum, etc.

All the Martyrologies celebrate the feast of the most blessed infants of Christ and noble martyrs Justus and Pastor on 6 August—those of Bede, Usuard, and Ado, as well as the Roman Martyrology—in these words:

“At Complutum in Spain, the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor, brothers. While they were still being instructed in letters, they threw down their school tablets and ran of their own accord to martyrdom. Soon, ordered by the governor Dacianus to be seized and beaten with clubs, they strengthened each other most steadfastly with mutual exhortations; then they were led outside the city and slaughtered by the executioner.”

Equilinus has almost the same account in book VII, chapter 32, but adds:

“The pagans themselves saw their souls carried up to heaven by angels singing to Christ from that very place. Their bodies, however, were buried by Christians at the place where they had suffered, and they shone with many signs.”

St. Eulogius treated them with the highest praise in book I of his *Memoriale Sanctorum*, as did Morales there, together with the other historians of Spanish affairs. Before them all, Prudentius wrote of them in *Peristephanon*, hymn 4, saying:

The blood of Justus, to whom Pastor clings,  
A double burden and a twofold gift,  
Complutum will gladly bear,  
Holding the limbs of both within its embrace.

Surius published their acts from Marinus Siculus in volume I. I possess older acts, once recited in the churches, which I extracted from the ancient Breviary of the Church of Palencia, where they were celebrated under their own office. I shall not hesitate to place them here for the benefit of the people of Complutum:

“In those days, while the most cruel Dacianus was passing through the city of Complutum, and almost the whole city had learned of his dreadful reputation, two most holy infants, Justus and Pastor, having abandoned the school tablets on which their tender years were being instructed in letters, no longer began to go to the studies of this world or to teachers. Rather, like proven disciples of Christ, they ran with joyful devotion to the spectacle of their own martyrdom.

“When they anxiously observed and attentively grasped in their hearts what the fury of the mad Dacianus was preparing, Dacianus was informed that these two little boys were Christians, that they had been born of Christian parents, and that they had come to the spectacle so that, if his clemency should call for Christians, they might offer themselves voluntarily for punishment.

“When the most cruel Dacianus had carefully considered this, he was immediately moved by the anger of indignation. He ordered them to be seized without a hearing and commanded that they be beaten, fearing that, if they were brought into his presence for interrogation, they might prepare the souls of the bystanders to confess Christ, or that, if he could not prevail against them, he might see his own wickedness overcome by children.

“When they had been seized, before they suffered punishment, the holy martyrs, inspired by an angel of God, joyfully encouraged one another in these words.

“Justus said: ‘Do not fear, brother Pastor, this temporal death. Do not try to avoid the blows of those who beat your tender body. Do not fear the sword hanging over you. For if, with God’s approval, it should happen that we depart from here, then, hastening to his glory, we shall receive in the future age a more worthy strength from him—a strength that will not diminish our littleness but will lead us to the more perfect age of martyrs and angels.’

“To him the most holy Pastor said: ‘It is fitting, brother Justus, that you exhort me in this way, so that, together with your brother Pastor, you may receive the justice which you bear in your name. It is an easy thing for us to have our little bodies slaughtered and our blood poured out for the confession of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that in the heavenly sanctuary of Christ we may be permitted to adore his divine body and precious blood.’

“But when the violent executioners who had been sent heard them speaking such things with one accord, they reported to Dacianus what orders he should give concerning those whom they had heard consoling one another so boldly in the name of God.

“When he heard this, Dacianus, astonished, said: ‘They are not worthy to be brought before our sight—those who have refused to preserve the tender strength of their infancy and have not preferred to adore the venerable worship of our gods.’

“Immediately he ordered them to be slaughtered with the sword far from the city.

“They suffered around the year of the Lord 298.” [Col. 0410C]

Thus far the Breviary of Palencia.

Moreover, the extremely hard stone on which he ordered the heads of the blessed martyrs to be struck, out of reverence for their tender strength, became soft; receiving their heads into itself, it reproduced their images, and for a long time poured forth oil abundantly. I have often venerated the clearest traces of both miracles at Complutum, in the chapel of the saints.

We shall discuss the discovery of the relics of the saints Justus and Pastor, and the church and episcopal see erected over them by St. Serrano, below, with Dexter under the year 423, where we shall provide the hymn composed by him in praise of these same holy martyrs.

### 2. At Carthage, etc.

The sixth consulship of Diocletian, as Baronius also testifies, fell in the year of Christ 296, as Dexter asserts. Cassiodorus, Bishop Idatius of Lamego, Onuphrius, and others write that Constantius Caesar was his colleague. Therefore, I think, an error entered Dexter’s copy, which reads “Crispinus.”

As for the holy virgin and martyr Charitina, who suffered much for the Lord at Carthage in that year, we possess acts written in ancient times and rendered into Greek by Metaphrastes, but now translated anew into Latin through the diligence of Aloysius Lipomanus, in volume VI, and printed by Surius in his volume V. Their beginning is: “At one time impiety held dominion,” and so forth.

Galesinus summarized their principal points in his Martyrology under 5 October in these words:

“St. Charitina, virgin and martyr, who, under the emperor Diocletian, accused before the prefect on account of the Christian faith, freely professed that she worshiped Christ as God. First her head was shaved and she was sprinkled with glowing coals; then, with a great stone fastened to her neck, she was thrown into the sea. From there she emerged by divine assistance and showed herself to the prefect. After she had struck all who were present with astonishment at the marvel, her teeth were torn out and the fingers of her hands and feet were cut off, and so she attained the palm of martyrdom.”

The Roman Martyrology has nearly the same account and says that she suffered under the consul Domitius. I think, however, that one should read “under Decimius.” For it is established that at that time Decimius Germanianus was proconsul of Baetica, and to this day the following inscription is read at Córdoba on a stone which Morales reports in book IX, chapter 26.

Galesinus should be blamed for saying, “in Greece, St. Charitina,” as though the fact that she is celebrated by the Greeks established that she died in Greece. The Roman Martyrology more prudently refrained from naming her homeland, since it did not know it. The Greek Menologion likewise refrained from doing so; under 5 October it has these words:

“The feast of the holy martyr Charitina, who lived under the emperor Diocletian and the governor Domitius—I read ‘Decimius’—and was the slave of a certain Claudius. When the governor heard about her, he wrote to her master that he should send her to him for investigation, as a Christian. The master was therefore saddened and, clothed in sackcloth, mourned for her as one who would soon die.

“But the slave herself consoled him, saying: ‘Master, do not grieve. For I shall be reckoned an acceptable victim to God, for my sins and yours, and shall go to the joys.’

“When he said, ‘Remember me before the heavenly King,’ she was sent to the governor. Having been brought before him and confessed Christ, she was shaved, laid upon burning coals, and afterward, tied to a heavy stone, thrown into the sea. Having come out of it, she appeared to the governor, who tortured her with many other torments. After the nails of her hands and feet had been cut off, she commended her spirit to God.”

This is what is found there.

### 3. In the See of Christ, etc.

He reviews those Roman Pontiffs who sat in the See of Peter from St. Sixtus II, the teacher of Blessed Laurence, down to the present time. They are Sixtus, Dionysius, Felix, Eutychianus, Caius, and Marcellinus.

St. Dionysius died on 26 December of the year of the Lord 271—if we believe Baronius—having occupied the see for 11 years, 3 months, and 14 days. St. Felix was killed for the Lord on 20 May of the year 273, having occupied the see for 2 years, 5 months, and 1 day. St. Eutychianus suffered on 8 December of the year of the Lord 283. St. Caius was crowned with martyrdom on 22 April of the year 296, after occupying the see for 12 years, 4 months, and 4 days. Marcellinus succeeded him and was killed on 26 April; we shall speak of him again below.

### 4. At Heraclea, etc.

We showed under the year 70 that Heraclea was a city of Spain situated opposite the island of Cádiz. Concerning the holy martyrs Felix and Januarius, who were killed there, Usuard has the following under 7 January:

“At the city of Heraclea, Felix and Januarius.”

Equilinus, however, in book XI, chapter 130, number 18, says:

“Felix and Januarius suffered in the city of Heraclea on 7 January.”

The Roman Martyrology on that same day has:

“At the city of Heraclea, the holy martyrs Felix and Januarius.”

Baronius testifies in his notes that the ancient manuscripts agree with this. The Greeks also discuss them in the Menologion, adding Fortunatus and Septimius as companions under 16 April. From this account Galesinus has the following:

“The holy martyrs Felix the bishop, Januarius the priest, Fortunatus, and Septimius. When the edicts of Diocletian and Maximian Caesar concerning the burning of the books of the Christian faith throughout the world had been published, they steadfastly and resolutely refused either to surrender the books or to sacrifice to idols. For this reason they were tortured in various ways and most willingly offered their necks for the glory of Christ.”]

## A.D. 296; A.R. 1847

## A.D. 296; A.R. 1847

At Carthage in Spain, St. Charitina, virgin and martyr, under the consulship of Diocletian for the sixth time and Crispinus, most noble Caesars.

In the Roman See of Christ and Peter, Dionysius succeeds Sixtus, Felix succeeds Dionysius, Eutychianus succeeds Felix, Caius succeeds Eutychianus, and the pontiff Marcellinus succeeds Caius.

## A.D. 296; A.R. 1047

At Heraclea in Spain, near the Strait of Hercules, the most holy martyrs of Christ Felix and Januarius.

[Note: [Col. 0411D]

## A.D. 298

In the consulship of Faustus and Gallus, St. Marcellus, a centurion of the Trajanic Legion, suffered martyrdom for Christ at Tingis in Mauretania, where he had been brought from the city of León, of which he was a citizen. His acts are extant in Surius and Baronius; their beginning is: “In the city of Tingis, while Fortunatus was serving as governor,” and so forth. He was crowned on 30 October, on which day he is celebrated by the Roman Martyrology, Bede, Usuard, Ado, and the others.

By his wife St. Nonia he had the most holy martyrs of Christ Claudius, Lupercus, and Victoricus, who were killed near León; Emeterius and Celedonius, who were killed at Calahorra; Servandus and Germanus, who were killed at Mérida; and Faustus, Januarius, and Martial, who were killed at Córdoba for the Lord Christ. Their memory is famous in all the Martyrologies and in the histories of Spanish affairs. Consult Ambrosius Morales, book X of his *Historia*, chapters 20 through 24; Marieta, part I, book II, beginning with chapter 41; Villegas; Trugillus; the *Sanctorale*; and the others.

As for the reason why Dexter did not mention them, I cannot guess. I more readily believe that their names were omitted through the carelessness of those who copied them. For it is not credible that Dexter was unaware of so many of the more distinguished martyrs of Spain.

Their feasts were formerly celebrated with proper offices or hymns in the Gothic Breviary of St. Isidore. There, in honor of Saints Emeterius and Celedonius, a hymn composed by Aurelius Prudentius was sung on 3 March. It begins, “The names of two martyrs are written in heaven,” and appears at the beginning of the *Peristephanon*. It should not, however, be left unmentioned that after the middle of the hymn it asserts that their ring and handkerchief were taken up into heaven before the eyes of all:

That hidden glory is not concealed,  
Nor does it grow old with time—  
For the gifts they sent upward  
Flew through the air,  
Showing by their ascent  
The way open to heaven.

As a figure of their faith,  
The ring is borne upon a cloud;  
Here the handkerchief, they say,  
Gives the pledge of their mouth.  
Snatched away by their final breath,  
They enter the innermost light.

Through the axis of the melting heavens  
The gleam of gold is hidden,  
And the woven whiteness escapes  
The long-following gaze.  
They are carried upward to the stars  
And are seen no more.

The assembled crowd saw this;  
The executioner himself saw it.  
He held back his hand, hesitated,  
And grew pale with astonishment;  
Yet he completed the blow,  
So that the glory might not perish.

Do you now believe, once-brutish  
Paganism of the Vascones,  
Which cruel error  
Sacrificed this sacred blood?  
Do you believe that the spirits  
Of the victims were taken to God?

After recounting the miracles that frequently occurred at the tomb of the holy martyrs, he adds:

This blessing the Savior himself  
Granted for our enjoyment,  
When he consecrated the limbs  
Of the martyrs to our town.  
They now preserve the settlers  
Whom the Ebro waters.

The same gifts of the martyrs, openly lifted into heaven, are discussed in the blessing of the aforesaid office in these words:

**Blessing.** May almighty God, to whom the most blessed martyrs Emeterius and Celedonius, as a sign of confession and faith, sent their handkerchief and ring to be carried up to heaven, preserve you through both gifts of grace. Amen.

May, through them, you who are strong in the virtue of faith and confession be counted citizens of the eternal heavenly homeland, whose twin feast you celebrate today with rejoicing. Amen.

As the fostered people rejoice in their double reception of the bodies, so may the whole Church rejoice that it is guarded and defended by their patronage. Amen.

As for Saints Faustus, Januarius, and Martial, a hymn is likewise found in the same Breviary, in which their acts are recounted. I am pleased to insert it here also for the benefit of scholars:

The noble company rejoices,  
Filled with God’s grace;  
The splendid solemnity  
Of three holy martyrs is at hand.

The blessed Trinity  
Built an everlasting temple for itself;  
From it a new  
And sweetest song is drawn.

These three men, in harmony,  
Come to their passion,  
To conquer the wicked enemy  
In the name of the Trinity.

Faustus, the kindly first,  
Speaks: “The passion of this time  
Is not worthy, brothers,  
Of the glory that is to come.”

Blessed Januarius says:  
“An open door is before us;  
For us … joy;  
May we enjoy the excellent heaven.”

Behold Martial urges onward  
The ascent of all the blessed  
To the glory of God;  
He rejoices happily in their fellowship.

Then Martial began:

“For the sake of eternal glory  
We must despise idols  
And the cruelty  
Of the judge.”

At once the governor began to rage.  
He ordered the saints’ teeth, noses, ears,  
Lips, and even eyebrows  
To be cut off.

The blessed martyrs say:

“Unjust and wicked judge,  
Why do you afflict God’s servants?  
Why do you worship  
False gods?”

Then the tyrant was inflamed  
With fury and said:  
“Cast these men into the fire,  
Who dare despise our commands.”

The blessed martyrs enter  
The furnace joyfully. They sing  
A hymn to God, and a new song  
With devout harmonies.

They cast off the burden of the flesh  
And send their spirits to the stars.  
They see Christ, whom they love,  
With the saints of God and the angels. Glory, etc.

Nor does it seem that the prayer referring to the names of these martyrs should be omitted. It is as follows:

“May Faustus favor the wretched and oppressed with his prayers. May Januarius, the outstanding leader, open for us the gate of heavenly life. May Martial obtain whatever the fostered people, with devoted hearts, desire to have done for themselves on account of their sins.”

But enough of these matters.]

[Col. 0413] [Note: [Col. 0413D]

## A.D. 299—1. At Tela, etc.

We have said enough in the preceding material, under the year of the Lord 112, concerning the city of Tela, situated near Palencia, where we discussed St. Eutychius the martyr. Now Dexter asserts that his memory was celebrated.

[Col. 0414A] **2. Avitus, etc.**

He continues the undertaking once begun, namely, the continuation of the succession of the bishops of Barcelona. This is not surprising, since he himself was born at Barcelona.

**3. Melchiades, etc.**

This was the fifty-first year of the life of St. Melchiades, since he had been born in the year of the Lord 246. We said enough about him under that year, and one might wish to find that material here as well.

This Melchiades is not the same as the one concerning whom Jerome, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, states that he wrote a substantial volume against Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla, as well as other books against the pagans and Jews. That Melchiades flourished under Marcus Aurelius Commodus, whereas our Melchiades flourished under Diocletian. Equilinus is therefore mistaken in book I, chapter 52, where he confuses them.

The learning and teaching of our Melchiades are also abundantly attested by a letter written to Marinus, Leontius, and Benedictus, bishops of Spain. It still exists in volume I of the Councils, where he discusses the qualities of bishops and the sacrament of Confirmation.]

## A.D. 299; A.R. 1050

At Tela in Spain, near Palencia, a very powerful city of the Vaccaei, the distinguished memory of the most holy martyr Eutychius.

## A.D. 299; A.R. 1050

Avitus, bishop of Barcelona, a man of outstanding learning.

## A.D. 299; A.R. 1050

Melchiades, an African by birth, born in the Spanish city of Mantua of the Carpetani, flourishes at Rome in the glory of holiness and learning.

[Note: [Col. 0414A]

A.D. 300.—1. Agauni, etc. We enter the year of Christ 300, which abounded more than the others in crowns of holy martyrs; for that reason it is described more fully by Dexter. It begins with the holy sisters Faith and Sabina, who were born in Spain and finally suffered at Agen in Aquitania of Gaul, under the governor Dacian. The feast day of Faith (or Fides) is indeed celebrated on 6 October in the Roman Martyrology and those of Bede, Usuard, and Ado, in nearly the same words, namely:

> In the Gallic city of Agen, the birthday of Saint Faith, virgin and martyr, by whose example the blessed Caprasius was encouraged to undergo the contest of martyrdom.

Her Acts exist in Mombritius, volume I, and in Surius, volume VII, who reduced them to a brief summary. Equilinus, book IX, chapter 26, says:

> Faith, a virgin and martyr, suffered at the city of Agen under the governor Dacian. Since she was noble, she consecrated her virginity to God from infancy. Though young in years, she was advanced in spirit. She was seized by the governor Dacian in the city of Agen and ordered to sacrifice to the gods. While she confessed Christ, she was stretched out upon an iron grate with her limbs spread apart, and with coals placed beneath her and fat thrown upon the flames. While she was being roasted in this way, she converted many by the example of her courage and encouraged them to martyrdom. Among them, the blessed Caprasius, strengthened by a divine sign, was fortified for the contest. Blessed Faith, after many struggles worthy of God, was beheaded in confession of Christ’s name and honorably buried in a tomb in the city of Agen on the day before the Nones of October.

So far Equilinus. Eventually her sacred body was brought to Spain and honorably buried in the monastery of Saint Cucuphas in the principality of Catalonia, as Yepes reports from ancient records in his Benedictine Chronicle under the year 778.

Let this suffice concerning Faith. As for Saint Sabina, not only Dexter but also the archpriest of Murcia in his Valerius, book III, title 3, chapter 5—whom Morales cites in book X of his History, chapter 29—and Vasaeus in his Chronicle under the year 306, testify that she was the companion of Saint Faith and that both had originated at Mérida in Spain. While fleeing persecution, they finally triumphed at Agen in Gaul after Dacian, that most savage enemy of the Christian name, had been defeated. Dexter’s manuscript has *Civitatensi* in place of *Emeritensi* (“at Mérida”); but which reading contains the truth, or in which one the error entered, I cannot determine. Finally, observe that Dexter read *Agauni* instead of *Agenni*. We shall shortly discuss Saint Vincent of Agen.

2. Urenae, etc. Saint Vincent the martyr, archdeacon of Saint Valerius, bishop of Zaragoza, made the memory of that bishop illustrious; in Vincent’s Acts we have much information about Valerius. His feast is celebrated on 28 January in the Roman Martyrology, but in the Toledan Breviary on the following day. Dexter says that he was taken up into heaven on the 10th of the same month; and, unless there is an error in the manuscript, we must believe that the feast of his translation is celebrated on the 28th or 29th.

As regards the manner of his death, almost everyone has hitherto called him a confessor. Dexter, however, writes that he suffered—namely, because he suffered in exile, full of hardships; and it is not unprecedented for this kind of death to be called martyrdom. D. Ferdinand de Mendoza noted this admirably in his work on the Council of Iliberis, chapter 4. The Roman Martyrology, agreeing with the Greek Menologion, calls seven Armenian brothers—Orentius, Herois, and the others—martyrs, although they died peacefully in the Lord in exile on 24 June, after suffering many hardships.

There is also disagreement among the authors concerning the place of his suffering, or death. Morales, book X, chapter 7, together with others, maintains that he completed his final day at Annet, on the bank of the river called the Cinca, in the district of Ribagorza, and was buried there in the castle of Estrada. Marieta agrees with him in book V of his *Saints of Spain*, chapter 23. Dexter, however, writes that Valerius died at Urena.

Urena is a town of some importance in Old Castile, distinguished by the title of a county. But there seems to have been another place of that name in Ribagorza, to which Saint Valerius was banished and where he died; from there he was taken to the castle of Estrada and buried. We shall show below that Saint Valerius was present at the synod of Iliberis. It follows that what is said here about his passion has been reported in advance, since he went to heaven around the year of Christ 206.

Here I gladly insert Heleca’s addition to the Chronicle of Maximus, written in praise of Saint Valerius:

> Zaragoza should be considered fortunate: under Bishop Valerius it possessed two Vincentiuses, both distinguished by the honor of the archdiaconate—one from Osca in Spain, the other from Agen in Gaul. The elder, Vincent of Agen, was sent into Gaul by Saint Valerius for the sake of preaching. He was succeeded by the younger Vincent, who provided a splendid example of virtue and innocence. Both suffered in the persecution of Diocletian: the latter in 287, the former in 304. Both were afterward buried in the Spanish city of Valencia. The former was brought to the Sacred Promontory; the latter was brought to Gaul, to the Castrense monastery, around the year 850, while the Spaniard was brought there in 757, when Valencia was being besieged by Abderrahman. Prudentius celebrates both: the one from Agen briefly, when he says:
>
> “From there your palm, Vincent, was born;
>
> from here also the clergy produced a triumph.”
>
> But he treats the one from Osca at greater length, beginning: “Was not Vincent, who had to die abroad …,” continuing for many verses of the poem.

These most holy deacons had many sacred churches in Spain and Gaul. At Toledo, one was built by Gundemar in honor of Saint Vincent the Spanish deacon and by Julian, archbishop of Toledo. Another was built in honor of Saint Vincent of Agen, in an elevated part of the royal city, of whom Julian was exceedingly devoted. He composed this poem for him:

> To Vincent, who endured, steadfast martyr at Agen,
>
> sacred deacon, by whose blood you fly to the stars:
>
> the deadly sword took your head from you,
>
> but by that sword you received a sacred, undying crown.
>
Gaul bore you, and Augusta Caesarea taught you as a minister;

> under the piety of Valerius, you flourished.
>
> Sacred Gaul received you again as you taught the holy words;
>
> Maximianus, poor in mind, killed you with the sword.
>
> After your ashes, the loving bishop Murila carried you also;
>
> Valentinus himself kept watch over you at his own dwelling.
>
> At last, as the years rolled on, Andualdus joyfully
>
> called you back to your ancestral home and himself was ordered to return.
>
> Pray for us, Vincent, glorious martyr,
>
> to whom Julian himself asks your aid:
>
> he who built a temple for you with a devoted heart
>
> and gave it an outward work in which you might be venerated.

Thus far Heleca. From this, as you see, the old question debated between the Gauls and the Lusitanians concerning the burial place of Saint Vincent the deacon and martyr is resolved. Aymo writes that he was transferred to Valencia, to the Castrense monastery; yet that Vincent was not the one from Osca but the one from Agen.

Moreover, the feast of Saint Vincent of Agen the martyr is celebrated on 9 July, as is clear from the Martyrologies of Rome, Bede, Usuard, and Ado. Saint Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 105, writes that an account of his passion existed among the inhabitants of Agen; he discusses him again in book VII of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 35. Equilinus does so in book XI, chapter 130, no. 167; the Council of Chalon, chapter 1; and Venantius in an epigram concerning the same saint. We shall discuss Saint Vincent of Osca below.

3. Mademarius, etc. He succeeded Avitus of Barcelona, as is clear from what was said in the preceding year.

4. At Seville, etc. The memory of the holy martyrs Carpophorus and Abundius is celebrated on 10 December in all the Martyrologies—the Roman, those of Bede, Usuard, and Ado—and their Acts are summarized there. Equilinus gives a somewhat fuller account in these words, book I, chapter 54:

> Carpophorus, a priest, and Abundius, a deacon, suffered at the Spanish city of Seville during the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, under the governor Marcian. Seized by him, they were first beaten with clubs; then they were confined in prison for several days, deprived of all food and drink. From there they were miraculously led out by an angel. While proclaiming Christ to the people, they were seized again, and their faces were battered with stones. After this they were raised upon the rack and tortured for a long time, and then again tormented in prison for many days. Finally, in confession of the faith, they were struck with the sword on the fourth day before the Ides of December.

Mombritius has their Acts in volume I. Yet both he and Bracchesius, who published them at Camerino in 1586, fall into the error of believing that these holy martyrs suffered not at Seville but at Spoleto in Italy. Bede demonstrates their mistake by teaching that they were killed at Seville. Usuard and Ado read “at the city of Hispolia” instead of “at the city of Seville.” The ancients derived *Hispolitanam* from *Hispalis*, as Gregory the Great does in the prologue to the *Moralia*. The city of Spoleto, however, lacks the first two letters.

Baronius adds in his notes on 10 December:

> But, surpassing all these sources, the catalogue of the bishops of Seville lists Carpophorus as a bishop and martyr.

That is, he was not merely a priest but also a bishop. Villegas in his *Flower of the Saints*, Trugillus in his *Treasury of Sermons*, Vasaeus in his Chronicle, and the Évora Breviary cited by Vasaeus agree.

Every doubt is finally removed by the statement in the Acts of these same martyrs that the same judge, Marcian, inflicted many blows at that time upon Saint Brictius, bishop of Martula. It is certain that Martula—now called Mértola—is in Spain, thirty leagues from Seville, as we shall show under the year 308. Yet no city of that name is found in Italy. I have read the learned treatise of Thaddeus Donnola on the place of the martyrdom of Saint Felix of Spello; there, however, he argues that our martyrs too were from Spello. In truth, he adduces nothing compelling on this point. Indeed, he himself concedes that Saint Brictius’ city is not found in Italy, whether it is called Martula or Martana.

5. Iliberis, etc. This resolves the old question concerning the year in which the Council of Iliberis was convened and held. The matter was disputed not only between Catholics and heretics but also among Catholics themselves.

Arnaldus Pontanus successfully refuted the Magdeburg Centuriators in his *Chronography* under the year of Christ 794, because they foolishly subtracted four hundred years of antiquity from the council by asserting that it had been held around the year 700. Alanus Copus defeated the English in dialogue 4 of *On the English*, because they claimed that the Fathers of that council had died no more than four hundred years earlier. The absurdity of both positions is so clear to anyone reading the council’s own canons and the subscriptions of the Fathers that no refutation is needed.

Did Hosius, who took part in the council, therefore not flourish under Constantine? Or did Valerius of Zaragoza, who suffered chains and exile at the hands of Dacian, the minister of Diocletian; Melanthius of Toledo, who committed Saint Leocadia, martyred under Dacian, to burial; and Sabinus of Seville, who buried the body of Saint Rufina after she had been killed by the same governor—all of whom signed the Council of Iliberis—prolong their lives until the year 700 or 1100? Where was the persecution of Christians by idolaters, so frequently mentioned in the council’s canons?

I return to the Catholics, who differ little among themselves. Onuphrius Panvinus asserts in his *Fasti* that the Council of Iliberis was convened in the year of the Lord 313. Ambrosius de Morales, book X of his *History of Spain*, chapter 31, maintains that it was held in the year of Christ 324. Antonius Augustinus, in a letter to Hieronymus Blanca, places it in the following year, that is, 325. Petrus Gregorius of Toulouse, book XXII of his *Syntagma*, chapter 13, no. 12, rejects it to the year of the Lord 336; and Joannes Vasaeus, in his *Chronicle of Spain*, to 338. Some refrain from assigning a definite year and are content to say that it was convened around the time of Nicaea. Baronius differs from all of them, maintaining that it was held in the year 305 after Christ’s birth.

What, then, seems certain to us amid such disagreement? Surely, we must agree in every respect with Dexter, who flourished nearest to those times; he writes that it occurred in the year of the Lord 300. It follows that it is older than all councils whose canons survive—not only Nicaea but also those of Neocaesarea, Ancyra, and even Arles.

D. Ferdinand de Mendoza proved this with singular and admirable learning in his excellent work written under the title *For Confirming the Council of Iliberis*, addressed to Pope Clement VIII, especially in book I, chapter 1.

That such a council was held while persecution against Christians was active, and consequently under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, before Constantine’s reign, is so evident from its Acts that it requires no proof. Many canons deal with this matter. Thus canon 60 provides that no one is to be honored as a martyr if he broke idols and was killed for doing so:

> If anyone breaks idols and is killed there, since it is not written in the Gospel, nor is it ever found to have been done by the apostles, it has been decided that he is not to be received among the number of martyrs.

Canon 25 concerns the letters of communion issued by confessors. These were given by Christ’s martyrs while they were in prison, after publicly confessing their faith and usually overcoming some tortures. Hence they were called confessional letters, as having been given by confessors. At that time the name applied only to those who, through public confession, had prepared a path for themselves to martyrdom.

Canon 58 establishes an examination of such letters, since many forged letters from confessors for the sake of profit. It orders that everywhere, and especially in the place where the chief episcopal see had been established, those who issued letters of communion should be questioned, and their testimony should confirm that everything was in order. This is plainly evidence that persecution was then active.

Canon 59 likewise prohibits this:

> No Christian, like a pagan, is to go up to the Capitolian idol for the purpose of sacrificing or looking on.

Canon 1 concerns those who after baptism sacrificed to idols; canon 2, pagan priests after baptism; canon 15, the marriage of those who come from paganism; and canon 16, faithful girls, forbidding them to marry unbelievers. I pass over the other canons dealing with the same subject.

It is therefore clear that the council was held before Constantine’s reign, under Diocletian and Maximian, when persecution was active and idolatry ruled throughout the world. In the Councils of Ancyra and Neocaesarea, which preceded Nicaea, no mention is made of persecution. Cardinal Baronius regards this as an irrefutable argument that they were not held before the year of the Lord 314, when, after the tyrant Maximian had been killed in the East, frequent gatherings of bishops soon began to be held.

He further observes that Ancyra dealt with the restoration of the lapsed through penance, whereas Neocaesarea did not. Ancyra was held immediately after persecution had been quieted, when many had lapsed; Neocaesarea, however, was held after the lapsed had been restored, when peace had already been granted to the churches.

We also have an important testimony on the same matter from Pope Innocent I in his letter to Exsuperius. Without naming the Council of Iliberis, he plainly states that it was held when persecutions in the Church were frequent. These are the words of that great pontiff:

> This question too has been raised: what ought to be observed concerning those who, after baptism, have been devoted throughout their lives to the pleasures of unrestrained desire and seek reconciliation at the end of life? Concerning them, the earlier practice was stricter; the later, with mercy intervening, is more lenient. For the earlier custom prevailed that penance was granted but communion was denied. Since at that time persecutions in the Church were frequent, lest the easy granting of communion make people confident of reconciliation and fail to recall them from falling, communion was rightly denied, while penance was granted so that everything might not be refused. But after the Lord restored peace to his Church and fear had been removed, it was decided that communion should be given to those departing this life.

So Innocent writes. What, I ask, was that earlier or ancient custom and practice by which communion was denied even at death to incontinent Christians, unless it was the rule established by canon 7 of the Council of Iliberis?

> If, after a lapse into adultery and after the appointed periods, anyone among the faithful should again commit fornication after having performed penance, it has been decided that he should not receive communion even at the end.

Certainly this does not appear to have been established by any other council. Yet once peace had been granted to the Church, it was abolished.

As for the Council of Arles, it is proved by this argument that Iliberis was still older: Arles borrowed seven canons from it—namely, canon 4 concerning charioteers; canon 5 concerning theatrical performers; canon 6 concerning those who wish to believe during illness; canon 7 concerning those who hold pagan magistracies; canon 9 concerning the letters of confessors; canon 11 concerning marriage with unbelievers; and canon 23 concerning apostates.

That Arles received these from Iliberis follows from the fact that Arles was held by Constantine’s order in the year 315, when persecution had already subsided and died out. Moreover, Hosius took part in Iliberis before the Council of Arles was held. From the time of Pope Melchiades, at least from the year of Christ 312, Hosius had attached himself to Constantine’s side. Constantine kept him occupied for many years outside Spain in difficult ecclesiastical affairs, so that he could not return to Spain before Constantine’s death.

It is plainly unreasonable to suppose that the celebration of Iliberis was postponed until after his death. I shall say nothing for the moment of the fact that Iliberis makes no mention of the blasphemy of Arius—a matter it certainly could not have passed over in silence had that heresy already arisen.

D. Ferdinand de Mendoza proves, in the place cited, that Hosius was occupied by Constantine for many years in the following manner.

In the year of the Lord 312, when Constantine II and Licinius II were consuls, Constantine wrote to Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, instructing him to receive 3,000 *folles* of money and distribute them to the poor at Hosius’ discretion:

> When, therefore, you have arranged to receive the aforementioned sum of money, order that these funds be distributed among all those whose names have been written on the list sent to you by Hosius.

Thus Hosius was then advising the emperor concerning provisions for the poor.

Again, in the year of the Lord 313, Donatus of Casis-Nigris was condemned in the Roman council under Pope Melchiades. He then brought his case before the emperor through Anulinus, proconsul of Africa, as Optatus of Milevis records in book I *Against Parmenianus*. For this reason Constantine convened the Council of Arles, attended by two hundred Fathers from Spain, Gaul, Italy, and Africa, in the year of the Lord 315.

Papirius Massonus, in his *Life of Melchiades*, preserves a letter of Constantine to Aelasius—I would rather read “Anulinus”—in which he orders that the African bishops, after crossing the Strait of Gibraltar, should travel through Baetica and Tarraconensis to Arles.

There Donatus was condemned again and again appealed to Caesar. Nevertheless, in the year of Christ 316, when Sabinus and Rufinus were consuls, Constantine, at the prompting and dictation of Hosius, issued a sentence against him and confirmed the decision rendered by the council. Hosius was therefore at that time attached to the emperor’s side.

Then, in the following year, 317, when Gallicanus and Bassus were consuls, a dispute arose between Arius and Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, and the matter was brought before the emperor. At that time, according to Eusebius, book II of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 63, Licinius, Constantine’s rival for the empire, had been destroyed, and supreme authority over the whole empire had fallen to Constantine. He was preparing to depart for the East.

In that same year, while at Sardica, he issued a constitution and sent it to Octavianus, count of Spain, dictated by Hosius of Corduba. It ordered that anyone who abducted a maiden of illustrious rank, invaded any territory, or was discovered in any fault or crime should immediately be subjected to the public laws within the province where he had committed the offense. The purpose was to prevent nobles, who could be punished only by emperors because of their immunity, from becoming insolent under the pretext of that privilege.

As is clear from the constitution itself, in book I *On Accusations* of the Theodosian Code, it was directed particularly to the people of Corduba, whom Hosius was striving to reform.

To calm the disturbances caused by Arius, the emperor sent this same Hosius to Alexandria. There Hosius convened a synod for that purpose and also settled the question of the manner of celebrating Easter, which in those days was being vigorously disputed in both Churches.

In the year of the Lord 321, Constantine issued a constitution concerning manumissions in the Church, when Crispus II and Constantine II were consuls. It is preserved in book IV, title 7, of the Theodosian Code, and was issued at Hosius’ prompting.

During those same years he issued many other constitutions for establishing and restoring churches and concerning their immunity and that of the clergy. He did nothing without Hosius’ counsel. Hosius did not separate from his side for the benefit of all the churches, continually bringing to the ears of the emperor and his mother what was advantageous to Christianity.

In the year of the Lord 324—or, as others prefer, 325—by Constantine’s command and with the will and approval of Sylvester and the universal Church, Hosius presided over the Council of Nicaea. There, after Arius had been condemned, he issued the Creed that is sung in the awesome sacrifice of the Mass.

Occupied with so many and such great affairs, Hosius could not possibly return to Spain during almost the whole period of the life of Constantine the Great. From this our purpose follows plainly: the Council of Iliberis, in which Hosius took part, necessarily had to be convened before the times just mentioned.

A further, not insignificant conjecture supports this. If the synod of Iliberis had been held under Constantine’s rule, there can be no doubt that Hosius would have presided over it, since his authority with Constantine was so great that the emperor appointed him—or caused him to be appointed—president of all the synods, as is clearly testified by the Alexandrian, Nicaean, and Sardican councils held under his direction.

Yet the Council of Iliberis was presided over not by Hosius but by Felix, bishop of Acci, although Hosius signed second among its nineteen Fathers.

But what are we to make of Saint Isidore’s assertion in book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 15, that the canons of councils began in Constantine’s time? Perhaps the canons of Iliberis were not written at the council itself in the form and wording in which they now exist, but afterward. Dexter seems to imply this below. After discussing the celebration of the council in item 5, he adds in item 12, after several other matters, that Saint Felix, archdeacon of Toledo, collected and arranged the canons of the Council of Iliberis together with Saint Hosius, bishop of Corduba. This may suggest that, after collecting fuller written acts of the council, they later distilled from them the brief canons that now survive; and this could have happened after Nicaea.

To answer the objection, however, it is enough to say with Baronius and D. Ferdinand that Isidore was speaking only of the canons of general councils. Iliberis was merely a provincial council. For my part, I do not think the antiquity of Iliberis is harmed by Isidore’s statement that the canons of councils began in Constantine’s time, since the council was held while Constantine was alive. Or, if the reference is to the period of the empire, it may rightly be said, in this general sense, that something done around that period was done in his time.

Morales notes that the oldest manuscript codices have the era 362 written in them, which falls in the year of the Lord 324. This can be seen in the Vigilian manuscript and in the Smaragdine, both preserved in the royal library of Saint Lawrence at the Escorial. Yet such codices do not exceed Gothic antiquity. Thus the era was prefixed to the Acts of the council by ignorant Gothic scribes. The canons themselves, as we have seen, nevertheless contradict it.

Let us now say something about the Fathers who assembled there.

The Acts say that “the holy and religious bishops sat together in the Church of Iliberis”; that is:

1. Felix of Acci. He was certainly a great man, who deserved to exercise the office of president among such Fathers. Yet by the rank of his see—which is now called Guadix—he was among the lesser bishops. Melamius, the primate of all Spain, was present, as were three other metropolitans, not to mention Hosius, who presided over more important synods.

2. Hosius of Corduba, about whom much has now been said. Julian, his own priest, attended with him.
