3. Sabinus of Seville, a metropolitan. His memory is celebrated in the Acts of the holy women Sabina and Rufina, whose bodies, marked with the purple distinction of martyrdom, he helped to bury. Loaysa writes in his notes on this council that there were formerly two bishops of this name: the first succeeded Marcellus, while the second succeeded Martianus.

4. Camerinus of Tucci. Tucci was a distinguished city of Baetica in Spain, once a Roman colony and an episcopal see. It was also called Augustagemella and is now Martos, not far from Jaén, as Ambrosius Morales proves in book IX, chapter 32. This see belonged to the metropolitan church of Seville, as did Corduba.

5. Senagris of Braga. Dexter discussed him under the year 290. It is therefore clear that the manuscripts of this council need correction, since some make Senagris the bishop of Évora, while others make him bishop of Biguerris.

In itself it is sufficiently clear that both readings are corrupt. There was never any bishopric of Évora in Spain or nearby whose memory survives. Biguerris, moreover, was in Gaul, far from Iliberis. Everyone agrees that this council was provincial, assembled solely from Spanish bishops. Nor is it probable that, when persecution was raging—the period in which it was held—foreign bishops could safely come to the council, when not even all the Spaniards were permitted to do so.

6. Secundinus of Castulo. We have explained what and where Castulo was in the Commentary on the year 66. The city once possessed a fairly important episcopal see under the metropolitan church of Toledo. Secundinus’ successor as bishop was Anianus, who in the year of the Lord 347 took part in and signed the Council of Sardica together with Hosius.

7. Pardus [or Pantardus] of Mentesa. Some have thought that Mentesa was the city of Jaén itself. Morales, however, more correctly maintains that it stood near Cazorla, in the forest of Saint Thomas; the ruins themselves give considerable evidence of this. See Morales, book VI of his *History of Spain*, chapter 5. It was formerly under the metropolitan church of Toledo.

8. Flavius of Iliberis. Some manuscripts have *Eliberritanus*, but the disagreement is minor. The city that the Spaniards and Latins once called Iliberis was afterward called Eliberis by the Goths, as Mendoza, cited above, noted. Its see was a suffragan of Seville, and the council was held there.

9. Cantonius of Vergium. In some places he is called *Corsicanus*, but incorrectly. Corsica is not the name of an episcopal city but of an island, and it is neither in Spain nor near it. The bishop of Vergium was subject to Toledo. The Gulf of Vergium, named after that city, is perfectly well known: it lies between the promontories of Caridemo and Scombraria, commonly called Cabo de Gata and Cabo de Palos. Consult what we said about it under the year 54.

10. Liberius of Mérida. This bishop was extremely famous in his own age, for he took part not only in the synod of Iliberis but also in that of Arles and signed its acts. At Arles several of his priests were present with him, as was Florentius, his deacon, who succeeded him and was one of the Fathers of the Council of Sardica, as his subscriptions prove. See Morales, book X, chapters 32 and 36.

11. Saint Valerius of Zaragoza. This is that man renowned for holiness whom the glory of his archdeacon Vincent made especially illustrious. The Church throughout the world sings of and admires Vincent’s most glorious martyrdom.

Since several bishops of that see with the same name lived in that age, some believe that the Saint Valerius who took part in Iliberis was not the first of that name—the companion of Saint Vincent—but the second. This opinion arose from the false assumption on which those authors incorrectly rely: that the council was held in the year 324 after Christ, or around that time, when Saint Valerius had undoubtedly already exchanged his troubled and anguished life for death. But how far this is from the truth has been amply shown above.

Indeed, since the council was held while the persecution of Diocletian was active, as its canons show, no one other than the teacher of Vincent should be said to have attended it. For this reason many believe that Saint Vincent was also present there, and not without reason. Archdeacons nowhere abandoned their bishops but stood beside them in councils, as is clear from the Council of Arles and others. The argument applies even more strongly to Vincent, since, because Saint Valerius was hindered by an impediment of speech, Vincent served as the bishop’s voice.

We have a celebrated testimony to this from Maximus, who sings of the same martyr in the following hymn:

> From here you emerge radiant—  
> from the seat of Blessed Mary of the Column—  
> to be admired in the armor of faith;
>
> from there you give instruction to the soil of Valencia.
>
> In the great assembly at Iliberis
>
> you give signs of your steadfast heart and faith.
>
> You grieve, O Valerius, most courageous father,
>
> for such a heart; would you not enter battle with this companion?

D. Ferdinand de Mendoza, in the place cited, also subscribes to this opinion.

12. Decentius of León. This see is well known to everyone.

13. Melanthius of Toledo. I believe that he signed not because the thirteenth place fell to him according to his dignity—for the council seems rather to have been convened at his command as primate, according to Dexter—but because, as I suppose, the Fathers who were on the side of the fortunate president had signed up to that point; now Melanthius, as the head of the other side, signs first. Unless one prefers to suppose that everyone signed in a disorderly fashion, without regard to rank.

We said much about Melanthius under the year 287, and we shall speak of him again below under the year 310. Saint Felix of Toledo, his archdeacon, attended with him. Shortly afterward Felix received the crown of martyrdom at Seville. Together with Hosius, he arranged the canons of the Council of Iliberis; we shall discuss him later under item 12.

14. Januarius of Caliabria, or Saliabria, an episcopal city subject to the metropolitan church of Mérida. Morales thinks that it was situated where Montánchez now stands, in book X, chapter 32. The council manuscripts should therefore be corrected where they read *Salaria* or, in others, *Sabaria*, now Alcázar de la Sal; this is incorrect, since that place was not an episcopal see.

15. Vincent of Ossonoba. There was once a very well-known city of this name, adorned with cathedral dignity and subject to Mérida, not far from the Sacred Promontory. If Barrerius is right, it stood where Estômbar now is; or, according to Morales, Resende, and Mariana, where Selves, an episcopal city, now stands.

16. Quintianus of Elvora. This was the name given by the Goths to Ebura, a distinguished city of Lusitania whose see was subject to Mérida.

17. Successus of Eliocroca. It was an episcopal city under the metropolitan church of Toledo. We discussed it above under the year 54, where we suspected that it was Valladolid. Liberatus, his priest, attended with Bishop Successus.

18. Eutychianus of Basti. The city is now called Baza and no longer has a bishop, although it once did; it belonged to the metropolitan church of Toledo.

19. Patricius of Málaga. It likewise now has a bishop and is commonly called Málaga; it was under the metropolitan church of Seville.

This concludes our discussion of the bishops and their cities who attended the synod of Iliberis. Let us now speak of the priests residing there. The Acts of the council state:

“Twenty-six priests also being present”—supply, “who are as follows,” or something similar:

1. Restitutus, priest of Elepel. This is how it was written by a Gothic scribe, although it should be read “of Ilipula.” That town was under the bishop of Iliberis and stood where Granada now is. Hence Mount Saint, in the lead tablets discovered there, is called Ilipulitanus. Saint Restitutus was crowned with martyrdom, as we shall say below with Dexter, together with his companions Castor and Crispulus, who also attended the council.

2. Natalis of Orsuna, namely a priest; the word “priest” is understood in the other entries as well. Natalis was later raised to the see of Toledo after Melanthius, about whom much will be said in its proper places. Orsuna itself is now Osuna.

3. Maurus of Iliturgi, today Andújar el Viejo. Consult the year 54.

4. Lamponius of Carula. I read “of Calduba,” a town among the Turdetani of Baetica.

5. Barbatus of Adingi. *Aurigi* is preferable; according to Morales, in *Antiquities of Spain*, folio 74, this is Jaén.

6. Felicissimus of Atubi, today Villa de Espejo, near Corduba, formerly Claritas Julia. See Morales, book VIII, chapter 48.

7. Leo of Acinippo. In Ptolemy, this is a town in Celtic Baetica.

8. Liberatus of Eliocroca. On this place, consult what was said in the notes on Successus, bishop 17.

9. Januarius of Lauro. Today this is Lora, near Écija.

10. Januarius of Barbesola. I think it should be read “of Barbesola,” which more or less retains its name in the Strait of Gibraltar.

11. Victorius of Gabrum, otherwise of Egabrum, formerly an episcopal city now called Cabra.

12. Titus of Vinc. I suppose this is now called Vilches, in the Marian forest.

13. Eucharius of the Municipality, that is, of the Municipality of Alba, now called Arjona.

14. Victor of Ulia. According to Morales, book VIII, chapter 35, this is now Montemayor, near Corduba.

15. Silvanus of Sagalbina. I read “of Salambina,” now Salobreña, not far from Málaga.

16. Januarius of Urci. It stood on the Mediterranean coast, at the place where Tarraconensis was separated from Baetica.

17. Leo of Gemella, namely Augusta, formerly called Tucci and now Martos.

18. Turrinus of Castelbona. More correctly, it should be read “of Castulone,” whose bishop was also present.

19. Luxurius of Drona. Otherwise Urbona, in Baetica, according to Ptolemy.

20. Emeritus of Barca. It seems to be Uxama Barca, now called Osma.

21. Eumantius of Solia. It was a town near Granada among the Turduli, otherwise called Selia.

22. Eumentianus of Ossigi. I would more willingly read “Astigi,” which is Écija, since no one knows of Ossigi.

[Col. 0423C] 23. Evexes of Carthage, in place of his bishop, who was absent.

24. Julian of Corduba. He seems to have been a companion of the great Hosius. The names of two others are missing; nevertheless, if we believe Dexter, one of them was Juvencus, the very well-known Christian poet. For below, under the year of the Lord 337, he says:

> At Salamanca among the Vettones, Saint Juvencus the presbyter, who, according to some, took part in the Council of Iliberis.

See, candid reader, how great the reverence with which the gathering at Iliberis ought to be regarded, at which so many martyrs of Christ and so many outstanding confessors and teachers of the Catholic faith assembled. With what face, then, do some dare to speak of it with insufficient reverence? We shall deal with these people more suitably under the year 311, where Dexter writes that a council was assembled at Toledo for its defense.

A very different council from this was the Council of Iliberis held while Nero was persecuting the Church, at which many of the disciples of [Col. 0424A] the apostle Saint James obtained the crown of martyrdom. Concerning it, consult what was said above under the year of the Lord 57.

6. Of Histonium, etc. Dexter taught above, under the year 222, that Cyricus and Julitta bravely endured martyrdom at Hippo in Carpetania. There we too defended his opinion at greater length, saying that Hippo was the town now called Hieppes.

After eighty years, however, the bodies of the holy martyrs were found at Histonium, where they had been brought and hidden by the faithful out of fear of persecution. Histonium is the place now called Histo, near San Felices—commonly Saelices—and Villascusa, in the district of Cuenca. Saint Cyricus now rests at Burgos in Spain, in a church dedicated to his name, which has been raised to the dignity of an abbey in his honor; its abbot holds his seat of dignity in the metropolitan church.

7. In Gallaecia, etc. Consult what we noted about Saint Marina under the year 138, where we showed at greater length that she is the same person as Margaret, who until now was believed to be Greek.

[Col. 0424B] 8. Saint Justus, etc. According to Dexter, there were two bishops of Vic in Catalonia bearing the name Justus. The first flourished in the year 300 and continued until 320; the second in the year 380. Concerning him, see below under the year 382, to which the blessed Ambrose wrote.

There was also another pontiff of the same name at Urgell, not far from the city of Vic—now Vich—who took part in the Second Council of Toledo, in the 565th year of Caesar. This is the year 327 after the birth of Christ; his feast is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 28 May.

9. Near Lingonae, etc. Eusebius uses almost the same words in his Chronicle under this year, 300. Consult Eutropius, Book IX, Sextus Aurelius, and Orosius, Book VII, chapter 25, on these matters.

10. Galerius Maxim, etc. You will find this also in fuller form in Eusebius at the cited place and year. Orosius likewise reports it in the cited chapter 25.

11. Veturius, etc. Eusebius records this under the year 301. Baronius mentions it under the year 297, and the Roman Martyrology, on 20 February, states that Veturius, Diocletian’s master of soldiers, caused such a slaughter of blessed martyrs at Tyre in Phoenicia that only God’s knowledge can count their number.

It should not, however, be inferred from this that Diocletian’s persecution began in this year, 301, in such a way that no worshiper of Christ had previously been crowned with martyrdom either by it or by its agents. Rather, the persecution received greater force that year and stirred the emperor against the Christians more than usual. Nevertheless, it is also certain that later, in the year 306, the persecution was aggravated beyond measure; for this reason Eusebius writes that the event occurred in that year, calling it the fiercest of all.

Dexter, however, now embraces the principal period of the persecution from the year 300 to 307 and at the same time enumerates all the martyrs who suffered in it, without assigning them to particular years.

12. Felix, etc. This is the holy martyr Felix mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on 2 May, where he is said to have been crowned with martyrdom at Seville. For that reason he is commonly called Felix of Seville. Nevertheless, Marieta writes in *On the Saints of Spain*, Book II, chapter 99, that he was a deacon of Toledo.

A clear notice of him is preserved in M. Maximus, in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 612, where he says:

> The memory of Saint Felix, the deacon of Toledo, flourishes at Seville. When he was sent by Saint Melanthius, whose archdeacon he was, from Toledo to Saint Sabinus, bishop of Seville, he suffered at Seville on 2 May.

The Toledan Breviary of Saint Isidore has a proper office for him, whose chapter begins:

> Your martyr Felix, Lord, approved by his name and consecrated by his gift: while by his name you call him and by your gift you consecrate him, etc.

We spoke of the same man above, number 5. Great credit must be given to Dexter for having consecrated to immortality the memory of so great a man, who, as the very first, arranged the conciliar canons in their proper form, a form preserved by all councils through so many succeeding years. Under what right he calls Hosius of Corduba a saint, however, must be considered below, under the year 360.

[Col. 0425B] 13. L. Valerius, etc. Berossus the Chaldaean, a native of Babylonia, wrote his history 300 years before the birth of Christ the Lord, according to Josephus, Book I of *The Antiquities of the Jews* and *Against Apion the Grammarian*. In those passages Josephus states that Berossus extracted the whole of Chaldaean history, copied all antiquity as though he were an official recorder of public trust, and, among other things, mentioned the great Flood and named Noah and his sons.

Metasthenes, in his book *On Judgments*, and Diodorus Siculus, Book III, also discuss him. Pliny adds, in Book VII, chapter 37, that Berossus the Athenian taught Chaldaean disciplines, especially astrology, in the Greek language, and that for this reason the Athenians set up for him, in the public gymnasium, a gilded statue with a tongue.

Whether the work published by Annius of Viterbo, together with appended commentaries, was genuinely produced by Berossus or, as many believe, forged, I do not undertake to determine. I read only in Dexter that L. Valerius Hispanus once arranged fragments of Berossus into five parts. [Col. 0425C] Yet I do not find his name in the new Berossus, although the number of books agrees.

As I understand it, Dexter calls them “fragments” not because they were portions of the books of Berossus’s own history, but because they were materials found in Metasthenes, Josephus, and other authors, which L. Valerius collected in a single volume.

14. Mellaria, etc. There were formerly two cities in Baetica bearing this name. One belonged to the Corduban jurisdiction; Pliny mentions it, and now, according to Morales in *Antiquities*, folios 97 and 98, it is called Fuente Obejuna. The other stood beside the Strait of Cádiz and is now Bejar de la Miel. It was the birthplace of Pomponius Mela, as he himself testifies near the end of Book II, chapter 6, in these words:

> And where we come from, surrounded by the strait, is Mellaria.

Let anyone who wishes believe Carlo Stefano, who claims that Mellaria received its name from the golden apples that Hercules brought there from Libya. You will never find it called *Malaria*, as would have been necessary, but always *Mellaria*, evidently from honey, whose excellence and abundance were found there; and even now the name retains that sound.

Furthermore, the name and martyrdom of Saint Firmus of Mellaria are honored by Greeks and Latins on 1 June, as may be seen in the *Menologion* and the Roman Martyrology. The Greek text reads as follows:

> On the same day, Saint Firmus the martyr, who, under the emperor Maximian, was seized for the faith of Christ and led before the governor named Magnus [read: Marcus]. Since he could not be persuaded to sacrifice to idols, he was stripped naked and beaten with sinews; suspended, he was torn apart, and, after the structure of his entire body had been broken, he was finally beheaded and obtained the crown of his contest.

The Roman Martyrology reads:

> Likewise Saint Firmus the martyr, who during the persecution of Maximian, after being afflicted with the most savage blows and struck with stones, was finally beheaded.

Dexter has almost the same account word for word, except that, instead of “struck with stones,” he has, in agreement with the Greek, “burned with torches.” This is a very different kind of martyrdom and was very often inflicted on those suspended on the *equuleus*.

We discussed M. Aurelius Verus, under whom Saint Firmus was killed, under the year 286.

15. Of Iria Flavia, etc. The most holy virgin and martyr Susanna rests in the holy Compostellan Church among the other relics of the saints, with which her shrine is richly filled.

The body of this same Saint Susanna was transferred from Iria Flavia to Compostela—as is believed—by the blessed Diego Ramírez, the first archbishop of Compostela, when he arranged for the bodies of the holy martyrs Cucuphas and Silvester and various other relics to be transferred from different places to his own see, around the year 1102 of human salvation, as the records of the Compostellan history relate.

Unless perhaps, during the time of Pope Urban II and King Alfonso, surnamed the Chaste, when the episcopal see of Iria Flavia was transferred to Compostela, the relics of Saint Susanna were also transferred with the see, namely in the year of the Lord 1096.

Some people confused the Saint Susanna of Iria whom we are discussing with Saint Susanna, likewise a virgin and martyr of Braga, the sister of Saint Victor the martyr and catechumen. Deceived by the identical name and nationality of the two women, they added that the Susanna who rests at Compostela had been transferred from the territory of Braga together with the body of Saint Victor.

This was the opinion of Father Lobo at the end of his Portuguese translation of the Roman Martyrology, on 12 April, when he discussed the Portuguese saints. Yet from the very things he noted there, the opposite is sufficiently proved. For he states that in October 1590 the tomb of Saint Susanna of Braga was opened in a church of the territory of Braga dedicated to her name, in the presence of Don Augustine de Castro, archbishop of Braga, and that the sacred bones of that same virgin were found in it.

Therefore, they must by no means be thought to have been transferred from there, especially since Dexter’s testimony proves the distinctness of the two Susannas. He discusses the Susanna of Braga below, in this same year, toward its end.

16. At Caea, etc. The Greeks preserve a celebrated memory of Saint Antonina the martyr in the *Menologion* on 1 March. From there the Roman Martyrology received its account, in almost the same words, as follows:

> On the same day, Saint Antonina the martyr, who, during the persecution of Diocletian, after mocking the gods of the pagans, was subjected to various tortures, enclosed in a certain vessel, and sunk in the marsh of the city of Caea.

The Greek text, as found in Cardinal Sirletus, reads:

> On the same day, Saint Antonina. She was from the city of Caea and, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, endured severe and various tortures for confessing Christ and mocking the empty idols. Finally, enclosed in a certain vessel, she was thrown into the marsh of Caea and commended her spirit to the Lord.

Baronius, in his notes, thought that Saint Antonina had been killed on the well-known island of Caea in the Aegean Sea, moved by the fact that he saw the Greeks honoring her memory. Dexter, however, firmly asserts that she was crowned in Spain. Above, when we discussed the holy martyrs Facundus and Primitivus of Caea under the year 139, we showed at greater length that Caea was a city and river of that name among the Vaccaei.

17. During this period, etc. See what we noted in the preceding commentary, number 11. He surely prefaced this statement so that, under this one heading, he might include all those who suffered martyrdom in Spain during Diocletian’s persecution, especially up to the year 306, when the persecution raged more violently, as Eusebius also records in his Chronicle.

18. The Council of Suessa, etc. The event of the Council of Suessa was very well known and celebrated among all writers. At it Saint Marcellinus voluntarily conceded and, without being judged at all by the Fathers, pronounced a severe judgment against himself.

Consult Cardinal Baronius and Equilinus, Book IV, chapter 89. Baronius states that eighty-eight Fathers assembled at Suessa, a city of Campania—now Sessa in the Kingdom of Naples. No one should therefore find it implausible that certain bishops from Spain, Gaul, and Germany—as Dexter asserts—were present there, for such a number of bishops could not at that time have assembled from Italy alone.

Nor should anyone think that the severity of the persecution prevented them from traveling from Spain to Suessa, since access was easily granted to them in ordinary clothing; and the cause was exceedingly urgent. I would believe that Hosius was present there, as the leading Father of the councils of his time. But more about him later.

19. At Juliobriga, etc. The Greek *Menologion* commemorates Saint Lucia the martyr and her companions with the highest praise. From it the Roman Martyrology has the following entry on 6 July, or the day before the Nones of that month:

> On the same day, Saint Lucia the martyr, who, a native of Campania, was seized and cruelly tortured by Rixiovarus and converted him to Christ. With them were Antoninus, Severinus, Diodorus, Dion, and seventeen others, who shared in the suffering of their companion and in the crown.

The Greeks continue with their names in greater detail, in these words:

> This Saint Lucia is not the same as the woman who came from Sicily, but was born in the region of Campania and was detained by Rixiovarus. When she was compelled to sacrifice to idols, and steadfastly refused, she shed her blood for the name of Christ. When Rixiovarus himself had been converted through her agency to faith in Christ, Antoninus, Severinus, Diodorus, Dion, Apollonius, Apamus, Papyranus, Cotyus, Oronus, Dapimus, Satyrus, Victor, and nine others became sharers in the crown.

As for the city where the most holy woman suffered, Pliny, in Book III, chapter 3, and Book IV, chapter 10, states that Juliobriga was forty miles from the sources of the river Iberus. For this reason Ambrose Morales suspects that it stood between Santander and Bermeo, on the ocean coast; hence some also mention the port of Juliobriga.

This seems quite difficult to me, since Ptolemy states that it was an inland city of the Cantabri. I therefore agree more readily with Villanueva, Ortelius, and others, who unanimously assert that Juliobriga is now called Logroño. [Col. 0427D] Its distance from the sources of the Iberus, as reported by Pliny, and its inland position agree sufficiently with this.

Nor does the fact that a port of Juliobriga is found present an obstacle. It is mentioned below when Saint Aza and his fellow martyrs are discussed, and this could have happened because the city, although inland, possessed a territory extending as far as the coast. Flaviobriga certainly stood on that same maritime coast, but Juliobriga was inland.

20. In this most savage persecution, etc. Bede discusses the holy martyrs Felix, Luciolus, and their companions in his *Martyrology* on 3 March. The ancient manuscripts and the Roman Martyrology agree, in these words:

> On the same day, the passion of the holy Felix, Luciolus, Fortunatus, Marcia, and their companions; likewise of the holy soldiers Cleonicus, Eutropius, and Basiliscus, who, during the persecution of Maximian, under the governor Asclepiades, gloriously triumphed through the punishment of the cross.

The Greeks discuss the same martyrs in the *Menologion* and add that, before the punishment of the cross, they endured many other tortures at the hands of Asclepiades. The Greek account reads:

> These men served as soldiers under the emperor Maximian. When they were denounced as Christians, they endured many tortures under the governor Asclepiades and, after the cross itself, became martyrs and departed to heaven.

Galesinus, following Bede, writes that all these were companions: Felix, Luciolus, Fortunatus, Marcia, Herod, Antigonius, Januarius, Tertulla, Gavianus, Quiriulus, another Felix, Florianus, and Donatus.

We discussed Ebura, a city of Carpetania now called Talavera, ennobled by the trophies of so many martyrs, under the year 130, number 6.

21. Of Iria Flavia, etc. Some have made one person out of the two Cucuphases, believing that he suffered at Barcelona. Yet that they are entirely distinct is proved not only by Dexter, who asserts that one suffered at Iria Flavia, a well-known town of Gallaecia, while no one doubts that the other died at Barcelona, but is also made clear by the fact that one rests at Compostela in the Church of the Apostle Saint James, whereas the other rests at Saint-Denis in Paris, where he was brought from Barcelona.

On this subject see Morales, Book X, chapter 2; Marieta, Part I, Book II, chapters 7 and 8; the *Flos sanctorum*; the *Treasury of Preachers*; and the other Spanish authors, together with all the Martyrologies on 25 July and Saint Eulogius, Book I of the *Memorial of the Saints*.

As for Cucuphas of Iria, Father Lobo thought in the Portuguese Martyrology, on 12 April, that he had been transferred from Braga to Compostela together with Saint Susanna and Saint Silvester the martyrs.

Although it is true that all were transferred at the same time by Don Diego, archbishop of Compostela, in 1102, they were not all brought from Braga. Only Saint Silvester was brought from there, as will be explained later; Susanna and Cucuphas had been resting at Iria Flavia.

Unless someone wishes to say that these two were first brought from Iria to Braga, their metropolitan see, and then from there to Compostela together with the body of Saint Silvester—a view that does not seem implausible.

The acts of Saint Cucuphas of Barcelona are preserved in Surius, volume IV, on 25 July, and in Equilinus, Book VI, chapter 136. They are sung more felicitously, however, in Sapphic verse, in a sacred hymn read in the Toledan Breviary, which we insert here for the benefit of learned readers.

> O Barcelona, flourishing with joy because of Cucuphas,  
> Honor the tomb of the holy body;  
> And, revering the place of the sacred sepulcher,  
> Scatter privet blossoms.
>
> This illustrious gift the Scyllitan  
> City sent you, and it gave the blessed one  
> To the peoples of Gerunda,  
> That he might be honored by lot.
>
> These men, their tombs’ honor set apart,  
> Go to guard their native seats:  
> Here the court of Barcelona is celebrated,  
> There that of Gerunda.
>
> Hence the blood of this gracious Cucuphas  
> Has become fixed in our region;  
> And there, placing his limbs here among us,  
> He grants us life.
>
> Here, full of faith and returning Christ’s love,  
> He suffers the tyrant hostile to the light;  
> And soon, tortured by twelve times  
> Two soldiers, he is ground down for blessedness.
>
> Struck by the excessive blows of the raging man,  
> He pours out his entrails as though they were doomed;  
> But, restored, he receives them again  
> Into his body, sound for the moment.
>
> Sent into the flames, by prayers he destroys  
> The threatening force of the fire brought near;  
> The flame cannot burn too fiercely  
> In the blessed body.
>
> Ordered to be burned by the torches  
> Of a glowing grating, the fuel of the heat grows;  
> Yet the flame does no harm to him [lacuna]  
> Of the punishments.
>
> Thereafter he first endures  
> Sharp iron thorns striking him with blows;  
> And thus, his head cut off, into the heavens  
> His spirit breathes forth.
>
> Now favor, O Martyr, the prayers of your clients;  
> Instruct the citizen, protect the people;  
> And soothe the devout hearts of priests  
> With love of peace.
>
> With guilt removed, may the soul grow strong;  
> May we all be filled with heavenly Bread;  
> And may the Spirit adorn the limbs  
> Corrupted by fallen guilt.

22. At Augustobriga, etc. Ambrose Morales notes, in Book VIII of his *History*, final chapter, that Dion mentions certain colonies in Spain named after Augustus, including one called Augustobriga. For, as we have said elsewhere, *briga* in the ancient language of Spain means “city,” so that *Augustobriga* means “the city of Augustus.”

According to the same Morales, one of these cities stood near Numantia, where Aldea el Muro now lies; the ruins themselves testify to the size of the ancient city. Another stood near Burgos, and a third not far from Guadalupe, where Villardelpedroso now stands. Carlo Clusius also accepted this view.

Ptolemy mentions the first two: the first among the Pelendones near Numantia, the second among the Vettones. Florianus de Ocampo thought the latter was the city of Burgos, but Nonius rejects his opinion with clear arguments in chapter 55 of his *Spain*. Molecius is also mistaken in thinking that Medina Coeli was called Augustobriga. See Morales as well, Book IX, chapter 28.

As for the holy martyrs who suffered at Augustobriga—I cannot determine which of the three cities is meant—namely Absolonius, [Col. 0429D] Heraclius, and Largus, they have a celebrated feast on 2 March in Bede, the Roman Martyrology, Molanus, Galesinus, and others.

Accordingly, a serious error entered the Roman Martyrology when it stated that they were killed at Caesarea in Cappadocia and added Bishop Lucius, while excluding Heraclius, who was said to have died with others at the Roman Port. Its words are:

> At the Roman Port, the holy martyrs Paul, Heraclius, Secundilla, and Januaria. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the holy martyrs Bishop Lucius, Absalon, and Lorgius.

Bede proves that the reading in all these matters had been badly corrupted; it was from him that they were introduced into the Roman Martyrology. For Bede joined Heraclius with Absalon and Largus, as Dexter does, but separated the others in such a way that Paul alone is said to have been killed at the Roman Port, and Lucius at Caesarea in Cappadocia, while no place of martyrdom is assigned to Absalon, Heraclius, and Largus.

Molanus agrees with Bede in his additions to Usuard, where he writes:

> Likewise, of Lucius the bishop at Caesarea in Cappadocia; and of the holy martyrs Absalon, Lorgius, and Heraclius. At the Roman Port, of Paul, Secundola, and Januaria.

Galesinus also agrees with both:

> On the same day, the holy martyrs Absalon, Heraclius, and Largus.

In the notes he adds:

> Thus Bede and the manuscripts; others have Heraclius and Largus, or Lorgius.

Certainly the ancient text of the Roman Martyrology agreed with this, but it was altered by Baronius on the authority—I do not know of which manuscript. Nevertheless, it should be read in the notes on 28 July, under letter F, where he learnedly discusses that form of exceedingly atrocious punishment first devised by Mezentius. In it, the bodies of living persons were tied and fastened face to face against corpses, so that each corresponding part of the limbs was fitted to another and the two bodies decayed together. Virgil mentions this in Book VIII of the *Aeneid*, and Valerius Maximus in Book IX, chapter 2, concerning cruelty, example 10.

23. At Munobriga, etc. There were formerly various cities in Spain bearing this name, or nearly the same name. Ptolemy assigns three Mirobrigas: one in ancient Lusitania near Ebura; a second among the Turditani of Baetica, not far from Seville, perhaps Almadén; and a third among the Oretani of Tarraconensis, near Oretum and Libysosa, in the territory of Calatrava.

Morales mentions Medobriga in Lusitania in Book IX, chapter 28, and states in Book VIII, chapter 33, that it stood on the borders of Lusitania. The same author, in his *Antiquities*, under “Beturia,” folio 98, says that one Mirobriga stood where the town of Capilla now lies, near Fuente Ovejuna in Baetica. In Book IX of his *History*, chapter 1, on the basis of a marble inscription preserved in the city of Ciudad Real, he conjectures that another Mirobriga existed there.

Whatever may finally be true of these places, it is certain that Munobriga, or Munobrica, was entirely different from them, since it still exists in Celtiberia, twelve miles from Bilbilis—that is, four leagues from Calatayud—and, with its name little changed, is now called Munébrega.

The Greeks still preserve the memory of Saint Demetrius, who suffered there, in the *Menologion* on 15 November. On the same day Galesinus gives the following account:

> Saint Demetrius the martyr. Accused of the Christian faith, he was brought before Publius the prefect. There, not only did he profess the Christian religion with great freedom of speech, but he also vehemently attacked the superstition of the false gods. By the prefect’s order he was beheaded and obtained the martyr’s palm, which he had so greatly desired.

Understand this Publius to be Dacianus, who was called Publius Dacianus, as Morales observed from other acts of the martyrs; at that time he was inflicting martyrdom on the saints in Spain.

24. At Carthage, etc. The memory of the holy martyrs Philemon and Domninus is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 21 March and in the Greek *Menologion*, from which it was transferred into the Roman Martyrology. Neither, however, specifies the place of their passion, which we nevertheless learn from Dexter.

This sufficiently proves that they were not killed in Greece, since the Greeks did not know the place of their execution. We have used this argument elsewhere.

[Col. 0431A] 25. At the same time, etc. The *Menologion* of the Greeks contains, on 19 November, a notable commemoration of Saint Aza and his fellow martyrs, together with their acts reduced to a brief summary.

One point in it nevertheless deserves correction: it calls their region Isaurian, or Isauria, whereas it ought rather to be called Auria, or Auriensis. For, according to Dexter, they were crowned with martyrdom at Tude or at the Hot Springs, which lie in the district of Auria in Gallaecia.

The city of Tui lies in the Auriensis region, which still preserves its meaning among the inhabitants and is called *Vega d’Oro*. The city of the Hot Springs is Auriensis, commonly Orense, as Luis Nonius among others noted in chapter 53 of his *Spain*. That city, called the Hot Springs because of the very warm springs enjoyed at Burgos, is called Auriensis from the situation of the region or district.

The Greeks could easily have been deceived, since there is little difference in sound between our Iria and their Isauria, when they read that the martyrs had suffered in the Auriensis region. Since they knew only the Isaurian region—situated at the foot of Mount Taurus near Cilicia—they attributed the error, as is reasonable to believe, to the manuscript.

But let us give the words of the *Menologion*:

> On 19 November, the commemoration of Saint Aza. He was from the region of the Isaurians [I read: Aurians] and served as a soldier under the emperor Diocletian. After abandoning military service, he lived in the wilderness, performing many cures and miracles. He was denounced by certain hunters and handed over to the tribune Aquilinus with 150 soldiers who had come to capture him; but, when they saw his miracles and were returning, they had been converted to Christ. For through his prayers he had brought forth water and refreshed the thirsty.
>
> The tribune subjected the holy martyr Aza, to terrify many, to numerous blows; he suspended him on a wheel and tore him with iron claws, then threw him into a furnace. When the flame itself had been extinguished and the blessed martyr remained unharmed, the tribune’s wife and daughter were converted to the faith of Christ. The tribune then ordered the heads of the 150 soldiers to be cut off and had his wife and daughter beheaded with them. Afterward the holy martyr was completed by the sword.

The Roman Martyrology also discusses them. Since it received their memory from the Greeks, it is for this reason that it says they suffered in Isauria. In the older manuscripts of the Roman Martyrology, however, and in all printed editions before the Gregorian correction, they are absent. This proves that they were formerly not recognized but were borrowed from the *Menologion* at the time of that correction, as happened with many others.

Galesinus likewise extracted the following from it:

> The holy martyrs Aza and his companions. Aza, who hid in the wilderness and was renowned for the holiness of his life and the glory of his miracles, was seized by Diocletian’s soldiers and brought before the tribunal of the prefect Aquilinus. By the prefect’s order he was hung from above by his hair and flayed with iron claws. Then he was thrown into a blazing furnace; when, by divine aid, he emerged unharmed and by this miracle converted the prefect’s wife and daughter to the faith, he was condemned to death together with them and with the soldiers—150 in number—whom he had likewise led to the Christian religion by another miracle.

The printed text of Dexter must also be corrected at Zaragoza, because it corruptly calls Saint Aza “Ara” and thinks that Aza was a woman, when it says: “Saint Ara the martyr suffered.”

[Col. 0432A] 26. At Tarragona, etc. The Greeks celebrate a feast for these saints in the *Menologion* on 23 March. From it the Roman Martyrology has the following entry on the same day:

> Likewise, the crowns of the holy martyrs Domitius, Pelagia, Aquila, Eparchius, and Theodosia.

From this it is clear that Eparchius is missing from Dexter’s text.

27. At Carthage, etc. Bede mentions Saint Concessa the martyr, who was killed at Carthage, on 8 April; the Roman Martyrology and other more recent writers have followed him.

28. In the city of Solia, etc. It is uncertain whether it should be read “Selia,” since in Ptolemy’s text the city Selia is placed among the Turduli of Baetica, not Solia. It stood on the bank of the river Baetis, near Ilipa Magna, or Martos.

This Marcellus seems to have been that bishop of Seville who is said to have flourished at this time in the catalogue of the bishops of that see. Loaysa also discusses him in the notes on the Council of Iliberis. He was the first of that name, and Sabinus succeeded him.

29. Seori, etc. The name of this town is written in various ways. The ancient legend of Saint Centolla has *Saria*, and Morales accepts this reading in Book X, chapter 17. Ptolemy, however, calls it *Savia*, while Dexter’s manuscript has *Seorim*; it is now called Siero.

Whatever the form of the word, it is clear that the place lay among the Pelendones, a Cantabrian people. As for the holy martyrs, their acts are found in the Burgos Breviary, Maldonado, Trugillo, Morales, Villegas, and others.

What surpasses the others, however, is the account of Ferdinand Petri Guzamius in his *Scholastic Valerius of Histories*, Book III, title 3, chapter 5. He states that Saint Centolla was born at Toledo to a father named Regulus, then went from there to Saria in Cantabria, and suffered under the governor Eglisius at the very confluence of the Iberus. Morales reports this in Book X, chapter 17, and Venerus on folio 116; Marieta follows them in Part I, Book IV, chapter 10.

The man whom Valerius calls Regulus is called by Dexter L. Ragonius Quintianus. Their sacred relics were transferred after many centuries, in the time of Alfonso X [or: the Wise], to the Church of Burgos, which celebrates their feast on 13 August; the Roman Martyrology also discusses them on that day.

Centolla was a virgin, whereas Helena, her companion, was a widow, as Trugillo noted among others.

At this point Dexter’s printed text was extremely corrupt. Instead of the sign “(”, half of a parenthesis, it read the letter C as though it signified someone’s name; from this it again mangled the sentence and divided one passage into two that yielded no sense.

The whole passage should nevertheless be read within parentheses as follows:

> At Catana the most courageous holy virgin Agatha suffered under this man’s father, L. Quintianus.

Thus the lower passage, which concerns Saint Helena, coheres with the preceding material concerning Saint Centolla.

I find the name Quintianus in use in Spain at precisely this period, for Bishop Quintianus of Évora took part in the Council of Iliberis.

The consulship of L. Ragonius Quintianus—the man meant here—fell in the year 987 from the founding of the City, that is, in the year 236 of the Lord. He had Severus as his colleague, according to Cassiodorus and others. In the year of the Lord 252, during the third consulship of Decius, Saint Agatha the virgin was killed at Catana, and at Ravenna, under the same Decius, Saints Fusca and Maura were killed, as is clear from the Roman Martyrology on 5 and 13 February.

If this Quintianus was the father of Saint Centolla, he must have fathered her at Toledo several years after his consulship, lest we make the virgin excessively old at the time of her martyrdom. Yet it would not be remarkable if she were killed at the age of sixty, for it is known that Saint Apollonia was killed at a fairly advanced age.

Nevertheless, I would believe that father and son bore the same names and that the consulship should be assigned to the father.

30. At Voluca, etc. Ptolemy mentions this city among the Arevaci near Numantia; in my opinion, it is Berlanga.

The body of the most blessed virgin and martyr Victoria rests with due honor in the metropolitan church of Burgos. Until now, popular error had believed her to be one of Saint Ursula’s sisters and the daughter of a certain Sicilian prince and Saint Gerasina, but these two claims contradict each other. All Saint Ursula’s companions were from Greater Britain, or England, which is separated from Sicily by a great distance of land and sea.

Therefore, those said to be the parents of Saint Victoria were actually her fellow martyrs, whom Dexter discusses here. Their feast is celebrated at Burgos on 10 November.

There were also other women of this name in Spain; see the annotations under the years 130 and 406.

31. At Asta in Spain, etc. Consult what we wrote under the year 208.

### 32. At Oretum, etc.

Ptolemy calls it *Oreton Germanorum*, from which the people called Oretani took their name; Strabo corruptly has *Oria*. Many, including Tarapha, Villanueva, and Carolus Clusius, believed that ancient Oretum is now called Calatrava. But Morales, in his discussion of *Oreton* in the *Antiquities*, learnedly proves that it was located not there but near Calatrava, where a little church now seems to have been built in honor of the Blessed Mother of God, between Granátula and Calatrava on the bank of the Xabalón River. The ruins themselves and the name of the hermitage alike bear witness to this; for it is called Santa María de Oreto, otherwise del Azuqueça.

Some have found it more difficult to accept what is asserted about Saint Spyridon—namely, that he was bishop of Toledo and fought nobly at Oretum for Christ. For Spyridon was bishop in Cyprus, as Rufinus, book I, chapter 5; Sozomen, book I, chapter 11; Socrates [Col. 0433C], book I, chapter 8; and his acts, published by his disciple Triphyllius and printed by Surius, make clear.

Nevertheless, if anyone wished to assert that there were two Spyridons, one Cypriot and the other Toledan, he could not be manifestly convicted of falsehood. I myself judge it more probable that the Spyridon mentioned by Dexter and Rufinus was one and the same man: born on the island of Cyprus, he went to Spain and, on account of the excellence of his life, became bishop of Toledo; finally, after many years, he returned to his homeland and was elected bishop of Trimithus. From there he went to Nicaea for the general council and also attended the Council of Sardica. Thus everything is consistent.

This is supported by the fact that the Roman Martyrology says of Saint Spyridon on 14 December that he was one of those confessors whom Maximian condemned to the mines after having one eye gouged out and the left knee severed. Who does not know that the principal mines possessed by the Roman Empire were in Spain? We have demonstrated this at length elsewhere from the Book of Maccabees and other sources. [Col. 0434A] Saint Spyridon, therefore, was condemned by Maximian to the Oretanian gold or silver mines, after he had governed the Church of Toledo for some time; and at Oretum, condemned to the mines, he fought nobly for Christ’s name. But he was released through the intervention of the emperor Constantine and Hosius of Córdoba, and returned to Cyprus. For the rest, consult his acts.

### 33. At Ilipa, etc.

In ancient times there were many cities in Spain bearing this name. Pliny mentions three: in book XXVIII, chapter 2, the Ilipae of Italica in the conventus of Hispalis, near the municipality of Axati; and in book I, chapter 3, Ilipa Laus among the Bastetani, and Ilipa Minor in the conventus of Astigi. Ptolemy mentions two: one in Turdetania near Nebrissa, the other, surnamed the Great, among the Turduli.

I agree with Ambrosio de Morales, who in his discussion of *Ilipa* in the *Antiquities*, folios 87–90, learnedly proves from Strabo and others that Ilipa Magna stood in the Marianus forest—the Sierra Morena—where Peñaflor is now situated. The other Ilipa, mentioned at times by Livy, is Zalamea [Col. 0434B] in the Serenian forest.

As for the holy martyrs Restitutus and his companions, Bede and the Roman Martyrology speak of them on 10 June in these words: “In Spain, the holy martyrs Crispulus and Restitutus.” Ado mentions them on the following day. Dexter alone mentions Castor and his Cantabrian companions.

Restitutus, a presbyter of Ilipa—corruptly written *Elepelitanus*—is found as the first of those presbyters who attended the Council of Elvira, in Loaysa, Zurita, and Genebrard. Concerning the condemnation of Christians to the stone quarries, consult Cardinal Baronius in his notes for 16 February, under “condemned to the mines.” Certainly the ruggedness of Cantabria is responsible for the fact that there have always been quarries there, and that its people excelled by natural ability in cutting and polishing stone.

### 34. At Patavonium, etc.

Ptolemy places Patavonium among the Astures, beneath the city of Asturica. Morales, book X, chapter 33, believes it to be what we now call Vaneza. The tribune of the Flavian cohort resided there. [Col. 0434C]

Peter, in the *Catalogue*, book XI, chapter 130, no. 77, mentions the holy martyrs Felix, Fortunatus, and their companions, and asserts that they were killed for the Lord on the fourth day before the Kalends of March.

### 35. At the city of Heraclea, etc.

We discussed the city of Heraclea, formerly situated at Calpe on the strait, above, under the year of Christ 70.

### 36. At Argenteola, etc.

Ptolemy mentions this city among the Astures, and Molecius, in Ortelius’s *Synonymy of Places*, asserts that it is now called Medules. But, in my opinion, he read *Medules* corruptly instead of *Aviles*.

The memory of the holy martyrs Saturninus, Theophilus, and Revocata is preserved in the Roman Martyrology on 6 February in these words: “On the same day, the holy martyrs Saturninus, Theophilus, and Revocata.” The ancient manuscripts agree, as does Equilinus, book XI, chapter 130, no. 52.

We read the same names under the year 260 in Dexter; nevertheless, the difference of times and places shows that they were different persons. These martyrs were killed in the year 300 at Argenteola among the Astures, whereas those others were killed in the year 260 at Vienne in Gallaecia.

[Col. 0435A]

### 37. In the Eastern region, etc.

Modern writers, enveloped in a great darkness of confusion, have formed various opinions about the city and region where the holy virgin Sother suffered for Christ. They read in Bede that she perished “in the East”; in other writers, that she was Roman by birth, that her body was preserved at Rome, and that it had been transferred by Sergius the Younger to the church of Equitius. Moreover, they understood Saint Ambrose to indicate that she suffered nowhere but Rome when he speaks of her in books III and IV *On Virgins*. Hence Baronius said that she suffered at Rome on the Appian Way, in his notes for 10 February. He cites the reading of a manuscript Martyrology from the monastery of Saint Cyriacus and of the Cassinese Martyrology, which reads: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, the passion of Saint Soteris the virgin.”

Others believed that she suffered in some eastern province, such as Equilinus, book III, chapter 3, who writes: “Sothera the virgin suffered in the regions of the East.” Yet all were deceived by error. In the first place, the text of the Roman Martyrology was changed without sufficient authority or consideration; formerly it consistently read “in the East.” Nor is it sufficient that two manuscripts of some antiquity have a different reading, since all the authors of the Martyrologies stand against it—namely Bede, Usuard, and Ado, to whom Galesinus, Maurolicus, and others agree. All these unanimously have: “In the East, Saint Soteris the virgin,” etc.

Now Dexter has shed light on the doubtful matter, so that what was formerly read as “a Roman virgin suffered in the East” may be understood not of eastern Asia but of the eastern town of Palamós in Spain. The holy virgin had evidently reached that place while fleeing persecution, and there she was seized and carried off to punishment. Perhaps her parents possessed estates in Spain, and she herself was traveling there.

In time, however, her body was brought to Rome—as happened with other martyrs—and was first buried on the Appian Way. This gave rise to the belief among some that she had suffered on the Appian Way. It was later transferred to the church of Equitius.

Ambrose says of her in his *Exhortation to Virgins*:

> “But did Soteris not care for her appearance—as we bring forward the intimate example of a pious parent? Although she was extremely beautiful in face, and a noble virgin descended from an illustrious family, she set aside her ancestors’ consulships and prefectures for the sake of sacred faith. When ordered to sacrifice, she did not consent. They were indeed able to furrow her face with stripes, but they could not in the least furrow the face of her virtue.”

The same Ambrose says to his sister:

> “In the time of persecution she was raised even through servile insults to the height of persecution. She gave to the executioner that very face which, amid the tortures of the whole body, had usually been free from injury, and which was accustomed to behold rather than suffer torments. She was so strong and patient that, when she offered her tender cheeks to punishment, the executioner grew weary from striking before the martyr yielded to the injury. She did not bend her face, turn her countenance, or shed tears. Finally, when she had overcome every other kind of punishment, she found the sword she had sought.”

Again he says:

> “The savage persecutor ordered her to be struck on the cheeks, so that the tender virgin might yield either to pain or to shame. But when she heard this command, she uncovered her face, unveiled and exposed to the sun, and to martyrdom; willingly she met the outrage, offering her face so that the sacrifice of martyrdom might take place where the testimony of modesty is accustomed to reside.”

Whom, then, did Ambrose offer to virgins as an example to follow? Why should Saint Monica of that age not have presented her as an example of chastity? Finally, Dexter’s statement that she was crowned with martyrdom in the year of the Lord 304 is confirmed by the acts of Saint Pancratius, where we read that this occurred under the ninth consulship of Diocletian and the eighth of Maximian. Their consulships did indeed fall in the aforesaid year of Christ, as Baronius noted in the place cited.

### 38. The Goths, etc.

Concerning this kind of Gothic devastation, read Saint Isidore’s history of the Goths, and John and Olaus Magnus, historians of Gothic affairs.

As for Dexter’s mention here of the Constantinopolitans, it should not be understood as though Constantine had already given his own name to Byzantium in those very days, since he had not yet risen to imperial power. But since, in Dexter’s time, Byzantium was called Constantinople, he could call the Byzantines Constantinopolitans, since they were one and the same people, whatever name was used for them.

But how can it stand with what he asserts elsewhere—that the Goths, taught by the Byzantines, were accustomed to strike bronze cymbals with wooden instruments—if Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, invented the use of bells or cymbals, as the name derived from his city seems to indicate?

Yet Paulinus instituted something quite different from what the Goths are said to have done: namely, towers, which he devised for placing bells in an elevated position. Otherwise, Hieronymus Magius and Angelus Roca infer from sacred and profane authors that the use of little bells was extremely ancient; they have published books on little bells or bells, which the reader may consult.

### 39. In this year, etc.

He is speaking of the year of the Lord 304, but the statement requires correction. It was said that Diocletian had entered upon the consulship seven times and Maximian nine times, whereas it is certain that the reading must be reversed: Diocletian nine times and Maximian seven times. This is gathered from all the fasti. [Col. 0436C]

### 40. In this year, etc.

At this time innumerable people were slaughtered in Spain by Dacian and by Diocletian’s other governors; their names are in the book of life.

At Ágreda, a very well-known town of Spain, there is a field held in great veneration, with a temple formerly erected over it, in memory and honor of many holy martyrs who were killed there by Dacian in defense of the Christian faith. It is consequently called the Field of the Martyrs. Morales mentions it in book X, chapter 6.

### 41. In the preceding year, etc.

Eusebius reports this in his *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 305, where he discusses this triumph. Consult, among others, what Orosius writes in book VII, chapter 25, about Narseus and his conflicts with Maximian.

### 42. Not long afterward, etc.

Eusebius in his *Chronicle* and in book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapters 26 and 29, testifies that this occurred in the year of the Lord 307. Constantine the Great also mentions it in the address he delivered to the Fathers assembled at the Council of Nicaea, as do the acts of Saint Menas and his companions, where it is said that they laid aside the purple, overcome by grief because they had been unable to prevail against Christ’s faithful.

Eusebius states that Diocletian abdicated the empire and the purple at Nicomedia, while Maximian did so at Milan. Nevertheless, the persecution against Christians, once proclaimed throughout the world, continued.

### 43. They suffer, etc.

All the Martyrologies speak of Saint Felix, who suffered at Gerunda, on 1 August. Usuard, in a brief eulogy, writes:

> “In Spain, in the city of Gerunda, the feast of Saint Felix, whom the judge Dacian ordered, after various kinds of torture had been inflicted, to be torn with hooks and then lacerated to the bone; and he ordered the wounds to be renewed by blows for so long, until Felix returned his unconquered spirit to Christ.”

Prudentius also mentions him in the fourth hymn of the *Peristephanon*, as does Saint Eulogius in the *Memoriale Sanctorum*, and Gregory of Tours in *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 92. An ancient hymn recounting his acts is also found in the Breviary of Saint Isidore, namely:

#### Hymn on Saint Felix, martyr of Gerunda

God, fountain of everlasting life, light and source of light,  
look upon the people singing the festival of the great martyr;  
receive the prayers of those who plead, accept the songs of praise.

Behold, we celebrate the honors of your blessed Felix;  
loosen the bonds of the tongue, granting resonant songs,  
so that we may duly proclaim your mighty deeds.

For this man, while studying the letters  
of worldly learning in the city of Caesarea in Mauretania,  
abandoned the famous language of the arts to follow you.

Hearing that the faithful were being punished, he immediately reached Gerunda.  
At the governor’s command he was seized and thrust into prison;  
loaded with iron chains, he conversed with angels.

He was brought before the altar to offer sacrifice to bloody idols.  
He rejected the infamous deed and confessed Christ aloud.  
The crowd roared, stripping his bones with two-pronged hooks.

Indeed, bound to mules, his limbs were torn apart;  
thrown into the sea, he was submerged beneath the swelling waves.

An angel mingled with him and opened his blessed mouth in songs.

He endured every torture with a courageous breast;  
after punishments, chains, hooks, and blows,  
leaving the prison of the flesh, he departed to the heavenly realms.

O most fortunate Gerunda, O blessed city,  
you fear no evil, supported by so great a martyr;  
whoever gathers here obtains what he requests.

Here demons, crushed by God’s power, are mangled,  
beaten, bound, and fiercely burned;  
smoke and ash possess no strength.

Here the desired salvation flows down for the weary, though it is heavenly;  
sight is opened to the blind, speech comes to the mute,  
the deaf here recover their ears, and the lame leap up.

Therefore we all pray to you, one supreme Trinity,  
that through the martyr’s intercession you remove our sins,  
repel every harmful thing, and grant prosperity.

May the clergy shine with life, and may the priest flourish;  
may the faithful people feel that they have obtained what they seek.  
May every age and sex, through this patron, receive glory, etc.

Of Saint Maximus, his companion, Dexter alone, so far as I know, writes. Moreover, it is sufficiently established from the letter sent by Berengarius, bishop of Gerunda, together with the clergy and people of Gerunda, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August in the year of the Lord 1087, to the congregation of Saint Afra in the city of Augsburg—preserved by Velserus in the life of that saint—that two Felixes were crowned with martyrdom at Gerunda and were very clearly distinct, not one person, as many have believed merely because of the identity of their names. The letter says especially:

> “We send a gift, namely some bones mixed with earth and blood, together with the clothing of our most holy teacher Felix, martyr of Christ—that is, the one whom we regard as an apostle and prophet, not the one who is called the deacon of the most blessed Narcissus; for he was transferred by the most pious king of the Franks, Charles, and rests honorably in the city of Paris.”

The sacred body of Saint Felix whom Dexter is now discussing is preserved in the cathedral of Gerunda, while his head is in the collegiate church dedicated to his name. In some churches of Spain he was formerly celebrated with a proper office, which I read in the Breviary of Palencia. Consult what we said under the year 277.

### 44. At Rhoda, etc.

It still largely retains its name and is called Rueda; there is a famous Cistercian monastery there, at the confluence of the Ebro.

There is another city or town of this name in Spain, now called Rosas, above Barcelona on the very shore of the Mediterranean. Ptolemy mentions it among the Indigetes under the name Rhoda, and Strabo under the name Rhodopes. Morales also discusses it in the *Antiquities*, folio 85, as does Florianus de Ocampo in book II, chapter 4, and book III, chapter 27, of his *History of Spain*.

But Dexter is speaking of Celtiberian Rhoda, where he says that the holy martyrs Dionysius and Ammonius gave their necks for Christ. Their feast falls on 14 February, as may be seen in Bede, Ado, and Usuard, in these words: “Likewise, Saints Dionysius and Ammonius, who were beheaded.”

In the correction of the Roman Martyrology, the adverb *item* was wrongly changed to *ibidem*. Yet the Martyrologies of the authors mentioned prove, without any authority for the change, that the original reading should be retained: nowhere are they said to have suffered *ibidem*, that is, at Alexandria, where the preceding martyrs had been killed, but *item*, that is, “likewise,” on that same day.

### 45. At Iturissa, etc.

Ptolemy mentions this city among the Vascones of Tarraconensian Spain. Villanueva, in his marginal notes, Carolus Stephanus, and others say that it is Sangüesa in Navarre. Pomponius Mela discusses it in book III of *On the Situation of the World*, and Pliny mentions the people of Iturissa.

The Greeks, in the *Menologion*, mention on 19 April the holy martyrs Socrates and Dionysius, pierced with spears, and on the following day Saint Victor with his remaining companions.

The Roman Martyrology has the following on 19 April:

> “On the same day, the holy martyrs Socrates and Dionysius, who confessed [Christ] by spears.”

And on 20 April:

> “On the same day, the holy martyrs Victor, Zoticus, Zeno, Acindinus, Caesarius, Severianus, Chrysophorus, and Theonas, who, subjected to various trials under Diocletian, completed their martyrdom.”

They therefore did not suffer martyrdom on one and the same day, but on different days, as you see. Dexter’s manuscript has *Christophoro* instead of *Chrysophoro*, with one letter varied.

### 46. In the Metellinian wilderness, etc.

Today it is Medellín. Consult what we noted about that city under the year 134.

The Greeks celebrate the name and memory of the sanctity of the admirable Saint Theodore on 20 April. On that day the Roman Martyrology says:

> “On the same day, Saint Theodore the confessor, surnamed Trichinas from the rough garment of haircloth with which he was clothed. He shone with many virtues, especially against demons; from his body an ointment flowed forth and bestowed health upon the sick.”

This was taken from the Greeks, who in the *Menologion* have:

> “Because of the hardships and severity of life to which he subjected himself, he was afflicted by cold and frost for Christ’s sake and covered his body with a thick, rough garment. Hence he was surnamed Trichinas. For this reason he received power against demons. Having lived in this way and departed to the Lord whom he desired, he grants health to all the faithful through the ointment that flows from his holy tomb.”

But why do the Greeks not disclose the name of the place where he rests? For no other reason than that they did not know it, although Dexter records it. We have discussed him more fully in our *Apology for the Author*.

### 47. At Carthage, etc.

The Roman Martyrology records the holy Felix and his twenty companions on 23 March, drawing on Bede and Uvandelbertus. Until now, however, they have been believed to have suffered martyrdom in Africa because they were found killed at Carthage. Whether they are the same persons whose feast is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 3 February, in these words—“There likewise, the holy martyrs Felix, Symphronius, Hippolytus, and their companions”—is not clear to me.

### 48. At Toledo, etc.

The Roman Martyrology speaks on 2 May of Saint Felix the deacon who suffered at Hispalis; that feast was also customarily celebrated at Hispalis and Toledo. See Marieta, book II, chapter 99.

Much is found about him in the Breviary of Saint Isidore. A proper office for this martyr is recited there, together with a hymn from the Common of Martyrs; but nothing is said that bears on the history of his contest. Everything alludes rather to the name Felix, as in a certain chapter: “Your martyr Felix, Lord, approved both by name and by gift, while you call him by his name and consecrate him by his gift,” etc.

The memory of the holy virgins Justa and Rufina may be introduced here. They received the crown of martyrdom in the same city and brought glory to all Spain. But since their acts are extremely famous and have been described by many, we shall give only the hymn customarily sung on their feast in the Breviary of Saint Isidore.

#### Hymn

Here are the crimson blossoms of the virgins,  
green with the gentle heavenly dew;  
their vessels of heaven, marked with the stars,  
have been tested in the fiery flame of heaven.

First anointed with showers of oil,  
they kindle the torches of their hearts toward heaven,  
overcoming the treachery of night and the enemy’s assault  
in the glorious light of faith.

Behold, Justa and likewise Rufina,  
shining in merits and illustrious conduct:  
virgins by their distinct names,  
but martyrs by the single name of their devotion.

Illustrious by the laws of the Lord,  
in the earthen vessels of their bodies they uniquely bear his treasure.  
They sell the little vessels for a price,  
and with the gain provide sustenance for the poor.

But by these supports the cunning craftsman  
breaks the earthen vessels [lacuna]  
lest the human vessel climb into heaven  
and dust become heavenly glory.

Hence steadfast faith receives martyrdom,  
flaring up in the broken vessel,  
granting rewards to the female sex,  
by which they may rise to the lofty stars.

For this reason, Christ, life, salvation, and way, truth,  
we ask you with utmost prayers:  
through their intercession consecrate us to yourself,  
you whose favor was won by the voice of their faith.

Make the lamp of the mind, O virgins,  
free from the flow of the body,  
so that, carrying hearts warmed by steadfast vows,  
we may possess the heavenly kingdoms.

May our glory continually rejoice in you,  
who alone are Lord, triune and one,  
holding the ages under everlasting dominion  
and ruling all things, commanding everything.

Amen.

The feast of the holy virgins and martyrs of Hispalis is celebrated in the Roman and other Martyrologies on 9 July. On that day Villegas, Sanctorus, Trugillus, Marieta, Maldonatus, and the ancient Breviaries of various churches write about them. We discussed them under the year 287, when some say that they suffered martyrdom.

### 49. At Caesaraugusta, etc.

The great slaughter of the holy martyrs killed at Caesaraugusta under the most impious Dacian has customarily been celebrated by the faithful on 3 November under the name “the innumerable.” On that day Usuard and the Roman Martyrology have the following in identical words:

> “At Caesaraugusta, the innumerable holy martyrs who, under the governor Dacian, wonderfully fell for Christ.”

For when Dacian—as Vincent of Beauvais and Equilinus, book X, chapter 17, relate—saw that the more he tried to destroy the Christians, the more their faith multiplied and their fellowship increased, he pretended to restore peace to the churches and sent a deceptive edict permitting hidden Christians to practice their religion according to their laws.

When they came out into public and praised Christ, and their multitude gathered in the aforesaid city, he assembled a pagan army and ordered the city gates closed so that none of them could escape. Thus the armed pagans came out from their hiding places and slaughtered with swords all the Christians found there. They gathered the bodies into enormous heaps, burned them, and scattered the ashes to the wind.

Nevertheless, by the wondrous providence of God, the ashes remained whiter than snow. They were therefore gathered into balls and deserved to be called the White Mass.

Prudentius says the following about them in hymn 6 of the *Peristephanon*, speaking of Caesaraugusta:

> Alone you prepared to meet the Lord  
> more numerous throngs of martyrs;  
> alone, rich in abundant devotion,  
> you enjoy the light.
>
> Scarcely can populous Carthage,  
> the parent of the world,  
> scarcely Rome herself, enthroned,  
> deserve to surpass you in this honor.
>
> Sacred blood, sacrificed at every gate,  
> shut out the hateful race  
> of demons and drove away the black darkness  
> from the purified city.

And shortly afterward:

> No frenzy among us ever departed without praise,  
> nor was any number lacking in the bright blood  
> of martyrs; beneath every hailstorm  
> their number always increased.

Saint Isidore says of Caesaraugusta in book XV of the *Etymologies*: “It is illustrious, flourishing through the burials of holy martyrs.”

I read in a large, very ancient manuscript at Toledo, in our convent of Saint Bernard outside the walls, a history of the innumerable martyrs of Caesaraugusta. Its title is: “The Passion of the Innumerable Holy Martyrs, Whose Bodies Are before the Church Called Holy of Holies, under the Governor Dacian,” etc. Its opening is: “The deeds of the ancient purified men,” etc.

It is contained on three large parchment leaves under no. 75. One thing must certainly be noted: the pious devotion of the ancients called their church Holy of Holies, out of reverence for so many relics. I read their lessons in the Breviary of Palencia, where they are said to have suffered under the year of the Lord 291. Morales, book X, chapter 6; Trugillus, Marieta, Vasaeus, Villegas, and the other writers also discuss them.

### 50. Likewise, Saint Encratis there, etc.

The Roman Martyrology says of her on 16 April:

> “There likewise”—that is, at Caesaraugusta—“Saint Encratis, virgin and martyr, who, after her body had been lacerated, one breast cut off, and her liver torn out, was nevertheless still alive and shut up in prison until her wounded body putrefied.”

Prudentius sang of her contest in the *Peristephanon*, saying:

> Here also, Encratis, lie the bones  
> of your virtues, by which, as a violent virgin,  
> you disgraced the spirit of the savage world.

And other passages worthy of reading, some of which we shall soon append.

Her martyrdom is narrated together with the history of the innumerable martyrs in the aforesaid manuscript of Saint Bernard at Toledo. The Breviary of Salamanca records that she was the daughter of a certain petty king of Portugal and that she was being led by her maternal uncle Lupercius and seventeen other prominent men to be given in marriage to the Marquis of the Rhône.

But the holy virgin, seeking an opportunity for martyrdom, set out and reached Caesaraugusta. There she attacked Dacian and challenged him to a contest. The aforementioned Breviary adds that Dacian immediately ordered her to be beaten in his presence with the fiercest whips; then, after she had been beaten and bound, she was dragged by a horse’s tail through the entire city because she had blasphemed the most sacred emperors. Thereafter further tortures were inflicted upon her sacred and tender body, as the Martyrology relates. Among them, a nail was driven into her head; its hole can still be seen today in the sacred skull.

After many centuries, in the year of the Lord 1389, on 13 March, the body of the most holy virgin was found in a marble tomb with this inscription:

> “The sacred body of Blessed Engratia, virgin and martyr.”

It was accompanied by the testimony of Bishop Prudentius, who had committed her to burial.

Morales, book X, chapter 5; Marieta, book IV, chapters 3 and 4; Yepes, second century, year of the Lord 657, chapter 1; Villegas, Trugillus, and the others also discuss her.

Moreover, Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta, sang of her as follows:

> For Encratis, beloved in heaven because of her snow-white character  
> and snow-white modesty, and even more beloved because of her martyrdom,  
> pleases the Father of heaven and earth, as Christ’s bride,  
> and remains the faithful patroness of Caesaraugusta.
>
> She ennobles the city by her poured-out blood and mutilated body,  
> left alone by the combs in her tomb.  
> While living in the body, she sees temples dedicated to herself:  
> a laurel worthy of the vigor of her soul, an honor worthy of her.
>
> Look upon me and my flock, most holy Virgin,  
> for whom we offer our hearts to you in place of temples.  
> As our patroness, keep every evil from your walls,  
> bless us with salvation, and shut the gates against our enemies.

What Maximus says—“While living in the body, she sees temples dedicated to herself”—refers to the following words of Prudentius:

> None of the martyrs, while life remained,  
> was granted to dwell upon our earth;  
> you alone, surviving your own death,  
> live in the world.
>
> You live and recount the sequence of your punishment,  
> retaining the remains of your slaughtered flesh;  
> you tell how dreadful wounds  
> bear bitter furrows.
>
> The barbarous torturer tore your entire side;  
> blood was poured out, limbs were lacerated;  
> your breast, with its nipple cut away,  
> was exposed, with the heart beneath.
>
> We saw part of your liver torn out,  
> lying far away beneath the pressure of the hooks;  
> death, which drives something of your life away,  
> has touched you also, though you live.
>
> Although the jealous sword of the persecutor  
> denied you the final death,  
> punishment nevertheless crowns you, martyr,  
> as though you had been completely slain.

From these lines he concludes:

> Christ himself gave Caesaraugusta  
> this new title for our enjoyment:  
> that a house dedicated to a martyr  
> who lives forever should stand there.

It is as though he had said: Christ granted Caesaraugusta a special privilege above other cities, so that it might enjoy a new kind of church—for *title* signifies a church. While other cities erect titles for martyrs who have died, Caesaraugusta built a house and title for a martyr who lives forever—that is, for a martyr who is both martyr and living person, a wondrous and unprecedented thing—namely, for Saint Encratis.

Prudentius also sang in the same hymn of the celebrated martyrdom of the seventeen saints who suffered with her. Its opening is: “Twice nine of our people beneath one,” etc. Their solemn memory is preserved in the Martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Ado, the Roman Martyrology, and the more recent Martyrologies; Vasaeus and all the authors cited concerning Encratis also discuss them.

As for their names, the Roman Martyrology gives fourteen and says that the remaining four were called Saturnini. Here are its words:

> “At Caesaraugusta in Spain, the feast of the eighteen holy martyrs: Optatus, Lupercus, Successus, Martialis, Urbanus, Julia, Quintilianus, Publius, Fronto, Felix, Caecilianus, Eventius, Primitivus, Apodemius, and four others who are reported to have been called Saturnini. All these, under Dacian, governor of the Spains, were subjected to punishments and killed together; Prudentius adorned their illustrious martyrdom in verse.”

He borrowed their names and their order from Prudentius, who writes:

> Therefore, rich in six times three sacred candidates,  
> together with Optatus and Lupercus,  
> go on composing for yourself in psalms  
> the senate enrolled here.
>
> Tell of Successus, sing of Martialis;  
> let death be sung together with Urbanus;  
> let the song resound for Julia,  
> and likewise for Quintilianus.
>
> Let the choir proclaim Publius  
> and unfold what kind of trophy was Fronto’s;  
> what good Felix endured, and what fierce  
> Caecilianus suffered.
>
> How great a quantity of blood, Eventius,  
> stained your battles; how much, Primitivus,  
> while praise remembers your living triumphs,  
> was the glory of Apodemius.
>
> Four men remain thereafter  
> whose name must be extolled, though the meter refuses it;  
> ancient tradition records  
> that they were called Saturnini.

But all the other authors not only vary the order and sequence of the names; they also give the names of all eighteen and affirm that none of them was called Saturninus. Hear the words of Usuard, with whom Ado and Equilinus agree:

> “At Caesaraugusta, the eighteen holy martyrs Quintilianus, Cassianus, Matutinus, Publius, Urbanus, Martialis, Faustus, Successus, Felix, Januarius, Primitivus, Eventius, Caecilianus, Optatus, Fronto, Lupercus, Apodemius, and Julius. All these under Dacian,” etc.

Marieta agrees in part I, book II, chapter 103. More importantly, the very ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint Bernard at Toledo mentioned above has exactly the same reading.

Thus four of their names are missing from the Roman Martyrology: Cassianus, Faustus, Januarius, and Matutinus. As Prudentius says, the ancients called these four Saturnini—that is, by an ancestral surname or for some other reason.

But what does Prudentius mean when he says:

> Four men remain thereafter  
> whose name must be extolled, though the meter refuses it;  
> ancient tradition records  
> that they were called Saturnini?

Ambrosius Morales, book X, chapter 5, believes that Prudentius refrained from their proper names because they would not fit the rules of Sapphic meter, and that this is what he wished to signify by “though the meter refuses it.”
