This opinion does not satisfy me. As Father Lupus correctly noted in his annotations to the Lusitanian Martyrology, there can be no doubt that Cassianus and Faustus could easily fit the Sapphic measure, while Januarius and Matutinus could fit in the vocative case.

What Prudentius asserts, therefore, is something quite different: namely, that the name by which ancient tradition calls those four saints—*Saturnini*—could in no way find a place in this kind of meter, because it consists of four long syllables, whereas the first syllable, *Sa*, would necessarily have to be short in the phrase “whom they call Saturnini.” For the first foot is a trochee, consisting of a long and a short syllable.

Prudentius therefore asks pardon. The common name of such great ancient martyrs should not be suppressed merely because of the strict rules of meter. Thus he adds:

> Love of golden names makes little  
> of the laws of verse and the care of speech;  
> concern for the saints is never idle,  
> nor ever uncultivated.
>
> The method of art is complete: to recite to Christ  
> the forms of names that have been recorded,  
> which the book of heaven holds, to be unfolded  
> at the proper time.

There is also a dispute about one of them: whether the person was male or female. Some manuscripts of Prudentius and the Roman Martyrology in Baronius call the person Julia; the ancient Toledan manuscript, Usuard, and the others call the person Julius. Equilinus follows the latter. Both are plausible; neither is certain.

The bodies of the eighteen saints were buried near the body of Saint Engratia and were found together with it. On one of the tombs there was this inscription:

> “The body of Saint Lupercus, his uncle, martyr”—

that is, the uncle of Saint Engratia.

### 51. Likewise, Saint Lambertus there, etc.

What is related here about Saint Lambertus is well known to all writers on Spanish affairs. Morales, book X, chapter 6; Villegas; Trugillus; Vasaeus; and the others report it in essentially the same way.

Saint Lambertus was a farmer and the slave of a certain pagan. Accused by his master before the judge on account of his faith, he was rewarded with beheading while he was leading oxen and plowing in the field. Then, taking his head in his own hands and guided by the oxen and angels, he proceeded to the tombs of the other martyrs. When he arrived there, he said: “The saints shall exult in glory”; and the other martyrs answered: “They shall rejoice in their resting places.” After saying this, he joined their company.

I saw this story carved in images on the marble of the tomb of Saint Lambertus near Saint Engratia’s sepulcher.

For him, consult the Roman Martyrology on 16 April.

Saints Caius and Crementius also suffered with the aforementioned martyrs. Concerning them Prudentius says in his hymn of the Eighteen Martyrs:

> With Caius added—for he must not be passed over—  
> and you, Crementius, to whom it befell  
> to bear bloodless glory from the second—
In the contest of praise. The Roman Martyrology explains this on the aforementioned day as follows: “In the same city, Saints Caius and Crementius, who, having confessed a second time and persevering in the faith of Christ, tasted the cup of martyrdom.” Their being said to have confessed a second time, or to have been honored in a second contest of praise, is intended to signify that they failed in the first struggle but, moved to repentance, presented themselves for a second contest and gained the crown. Hence Prudentius adds:

> Both confessed the Lord and stood  
> Firmly against the robbers’ fury;  
> Both gently tasted the sleep  
> Of martyrdom.

Moreover, since they are said to have borne the bloodless honor of martyrdom and to have tasted its sleep gently, I think this must refer to their being strangled with ropes, or hurled headlong into a river, without the shedding of blood.

## APPENDIX ON SAINT VINCENT, MARTYR

Beyond doubt, in the copies of Dexter available to us, the notice of Saint Vincent the Levite and martyr is missing. Throughout the universal Church he is celebrated as second in renown only to Laurence. For the most famous of all martyrs could not have been concealed from Dexter, who is shown to have possessed a knowledge of the Spanish martyrs more distinctive than that of any other writer whose works survive. The omission should rather be attributed to the copyist’s fault. Yet the same copyist is also proved to have omitted Eulalia of Barcelona, whom a writer from Barcelona—Dexter, writing at Barcelona—would certainly not have passed over.

Moreover, Saint Braulio made certain additions to Dexter which absolutely presuppose that the memory of Saints Vincent and Eulalia of Barcelona had not been omitted. For the year of the Lord 304, in which both were killed, he writes:

> Around this time the Catholics of Valencia erect a noble tomb for Saint Vincent on the shore of the Saguntine sea, and most reverently place the body of the unconquered martyr in a deep location beneath the lowest altar of the sanctuary. This church is frequented by constant visitation. They also visit and venerate with a certain singular devotion the places where he was imprisoned and where he suffered martyrdom.

For the year 312 he writes:

> At Barcelona, says Braulio, the citizens build a church by the sea for Saint Eulalia, virgin, martyr, citizen, and their patroness.

Certainly, if Dexter had made no mention whatever of Vincent and Eulalia, Braulio would not merely have added the erection of churches, but much more likely the contests of those martyrs themselves.

Concerning the tomb erected over the body of Saint Vincent, Equilinus says in his second book, chapter 3, from his acts:

> The loosened corpse was carried by the waves onto the shore. It was discovered by a certain widowed matron, who was directed to it by the saint himself, and she buried it in a small basilica together with certain faithful believers. When the persecution had ceased, the body was brought to the city of Valencia and buried more honorably beside its walls.

We have the testimony of Prudentius himself that Saint Vincent was not tortured to death at Valencia, but near the ruined walls of Saguntum, in an obscure place. I wish to note this for those who have held the opposite opinion. For in the hymn on the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, written while he himself was at Zaragoza, he says:

> He is ours, although far from here, in an unknown city,  
> He suffered and gave glory to his tomb,  
> A victor near the shore of lofty  
> Saguntum, perhaps.

This agrees with the addition quoted above from Saint Braulio.

As for the place made illustrious by the birthplace of Saint Vincent, there is some dispute among the authors. Some, including Morales in book X, chapter 8 or 9, believe that he was born at Zaragoza; others say at Huesca. Prudentius appears to favor them when, in the same hymn, he asserts that Saint Vincent ought to be numbered among the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza because he drew his blood from that place:

> Surely they will be added to the ancient number:  
> The living girl after the trial of punishment;  
> And the death of Vincent, whose blood from here  
> Is the source and honor.

I judge their opinion to be entirely true, since it is defended by the more authoritative and more numerous witnesses, among them Heleca, bishop of Zaragoza, whose words we quoted earlier when discussing Saint Valerius the bishop.

Certainly the people of Huesca preserve this tradition as something received from their ancestors, and they point out the house of Eutychius and Enola, the parents of Saint Vincent. Many breviaries of different Spanish churches agree with them. Among these, the one of Salamanca says:

> Since we intend to hand down to the knowledge of the faithful the triumph of Saint Vincent, it is fitting briefly to make known the nobility of his family. For he was born of Eutychius, who was the well-known son of Agrestus the consul; his mother, Enola, is known to have been born in the city of Huesca, and so forth.

To this may be added that Saint Vincent came from the same homeland and was a kinsman of Saint Laurence, who nevertheless was from Huesca, as we proved in its proper place.

M. Maximus expressed this clearly in an epigram on Vincent, which I have thought worth appending here:

> Recalling for Vincent the splendid crown from his contest,  
> The sweet Levite, outstanding head of the Levites:  
> The sacred house that has gained the name of the firm Column—  
> That is, of the Pillar—  
> For you, destined to conquer, it was dust and shadow.  
>  
> O most celebrated one among the seven ministers  
> In the See.

Prudentius said this:

> Here Vincent cries aloud,  
> A Levite of the sacred tribe,  
> Minister of God’s altar,  
> One of the seven milk-white columns.

Nebrissensis explained this as meaning that the bishop of Zaragoza had seven deacons, after the apostolic model, just as the Acts of the Apostles records that an equal number had once been established for the see of Jerusalem in chapter 6. Among these seven deacons, Vincent of Zaragoza was the first.

I believe the same was true of the other bishops, for they all had an archdeacon, that is, one superior to the other deacons. Thus Prudentius says of Saint Laurence in the hymn:

> He is first among the seven men  
> Who stand nearest the altar:  
> A Levite exalted in rank  
> And superior to the others.

Thus Maximus says:

> O most celebrated one among the seven ministers  
> In the See,

which corresponds to what he had said earlier:

> Sweet head of the Levites:

> Martyr, be present to our prayers and supplications.  
> Hence you emerge, resplendent, to be seen in the weapons of faith;  
> From there you give instruction to the soil of Valencia.  
> And among the people of Iliberris  
> You give the greatest signs of your unbroken courage and faith.  
> We discussed this above.  
>  
> You are witness, O most valiant father Valerius, of such courage:  
> Do you not enter battle with this companion?  
> Sacred archdeacon, whose concern is the sanctuary,  
> You teach the sacred ranks that stand beside you.  
>  
> That powerful Laurence was your kinsman, powerful  
> To extinguish the fires from tortured limbs.  
> He gave you splendid lessons in shining forth,  
> And he himself gives them to others; you are equal in this art.  
>  
> He wins a crown at Rome; you yourself win an equal one in your homeland.  
> The homeland is the same for both, the laurel and the strength the same.  
> Look upon us, present in your starry vesture, O minister,  
> And help your citizens, yourself also a citizen.

The fact that Prudentius says that Vincent drew his blood from Zaragoza does not exclude his having been born at Huesca, provided that one of his own people was from Zaragoza.

Many things concerning the same Saint Vincent are found in the Breviary of Saint Isidore. Among them is a hymn beginning:

> The wondrous passion is present  
> Of the holy martyr Levite,  
> For whom, aflame with glorious virtue,  
> The crown is given to Vincent the conqueror, and so forth.

And in the chapter reading:

> The solemn and most renowned feast of your witness, Lord, is present; it is displayed before the eyes of mortals in its annual recurrence. In it Vincent, your martyr, wondrously conquering and tested both on land—that is, on earth—and at sea, is conquered neither by earthly punishments nor fettered by marine whirlpools, and so forth.

Further on he is called “the Preacher of light.”

It would be lengthy to pursue individually all that the holy martyrs have written about so great a martyr. Consult Baronius in his notes for 22 January, and Molanus in the same place; especially the martyrology of Rabanus, who describes all the contests of Blessed Vincent in a brief epitome.

## 52. At Toledo, Saint Leocadia, etc.

The authors of all the martyrologies mention her: Bede, Usuard, Ado, the Roman Martyrology, and the others; as do Vasaeus, Laurentius de Padilla, Mariana, Marieta, Villegas, Trugillus, Maldonado, and the Sicilian Marinaeus.

In the Palencian Breviary her acts are recounted in these words:

> The most impious emperors Diocletian and Maximian appointed the exceedingly cruel Dacian as governor, assigning him to overthrow it rather than to govern it. After the slaughter of many saints, he entered the city of Toledo. There he found Leocadia, a virgin dedicated to God, born of a most noble family, who, with vigilant devotion, ceased neither by day nor by night from prayer.
>
> When Dacian ordered her to be brought before him, he addressed her as follows: “Why does such a light and empty delusion deceive you, so that, born of so distinguished a family, you have abandoned the rites of our gods and offer yourself in service to some Christ whom I know not?”
>
> Blessed Leocadia replied: “Your persuasion will not recall me from my purpose concerning Christ, for I have devoted myself to serving him. Neither the mockery of your words nor the allurements of my birth, by which you try to persuade me, will draw me away from the service of my Lord Jesus Christ, who, redeeming us with his precious blood, has granted us great freedom.”
>
> Enraged, Dacian ordered her to be thrown into prison, bound with the tightest chains, until he could devise punishments and tortures with which to afflict her. Then he departed for the city of Elbora and sent many saints to the Lord by the shedding of their blood.
>
> When news of this had reached Saint Leocadia in Toledo, she knelt in prayer. Having completed her prayer in the very place where she was confined, she commended her spirit to the Lord and sent it to heaven.

In the sixth response, the special notice of the martyrdom of Saint Eulalia attributes to her what the common lessons had said: that the report of the deaths of many martyrs had reached Leocadia’s ears.

The Breviary of Salamanca and many others of the churches of Spain agree. Moreover, what Dexter adds concerning the hard stone into which Saint Leocadia gently impressed the sign of the cross with her thumb is shown to be entirely true by her hymn, which I read in the Palencian Breviary. It runs as follows:

> With a pure heart  
> She entreated God;  
> On the prison wall  
> She pressed her thumb.
>
> The thumb entered thus  
> Into the hard stone,  
> So that she marked a cross  
> As in soft butter.
>
> Thus, O Christ, mark  
> Our hardened hearts,  
> So that with a mind worthy of you  
> We may follow you in purity.

In the Toledan Breviary of Archbishop Siliceus I read the following, with scarcely altered wording:

> The thumb entered thus  
> Into the very hard rock,  
> So that she marked a cross  
> As in soft wax.

To this day, in the cavern of Saint Leocadia’s prison, near the altar of the virgin on the Gospel side, there remains in the wall the stone marked by her thumb with a cross. It is guarded beneath an iron grating. When I was at Toledo in the year of the Lord 1621, I venerated it.

The altar itself is constructed of alabaster marble and divided into three scenes, each representing an episode of Saint Leocadia’s martyrdom. In the first, on the Gospel side, she is presented to Dacian; in the second, in the middle of the altar, she is cruelly scourged by his attendants; in the third, toward the Epistle side, she is shut in prison, lying on the bare ground and giving up her spirit.

From this one may see how mistaken are all those who believe that Saint Leocadia was worn down solely by imprisonment and endured no other torture. Indeed, the hymn customarily sung in her honor in the Gothic Breviary affirms that she was “seized,” that is, beaten with blows. I gladly insert it here:

> The solemn feast  
> Of most holy Leocadia has arisen,  
> She who, scorning the vanity of earth,  
> Passed to the kingdom of heaven.
>
> Come, all of you, as suppliants;  
> Reveal the guilt of your hearts.  
> Fulfill your vows with rejoicing  
> And render thanks to God.
>
> For this noble virgin,  
> Born of illustrious stock,  
> Having boldly confessed Christ,  
> Willingly endured punishments.
>
> Seized at the governor’s command,  
> She is bound with iron hooks,  
> So that, under the weight of her chains,  
> The girl’s faith might yield.
>
> There, seeking to please Christ  
> Through abstinence,  
> She offers in return praises and thanks  
> And presents the sacrifices of prayer.
>
> But as soon as she learned  
> Of Saint Eulalia’s sacred death,  
> In the bonds of prison  
> She poured forth her spirit to heaven.
>
> Now, holy virgin, we ask,  
> And we beg with tears,  
> That you wash away our disgrace  
> And carry our vows before Christ.
>
> You, our illustrious fellow citizen,  
> You are the patroness of Vernula:  
> From the boundaries of this city  
> Drive far away affliction.
>
> Let no enemy prevail here,  
> Nor sickness or want.  
> Let every harmful thing depart,  
> And let prosperity be bestowed.
>
> Thus may life abound in blessings,  
> Yet may our hearts not be stained by luxury.  
> From every crime  
> May indulgence be granted.
>
> To God be everlasting glory  
> And an abundance of thanksgiving,  
> Who willed all ages  
> And reigns before the ages. Amen.

The account in the Salamanca Breviary adds that the enraged Dacian ordered many soldiers to afflict her with numerous tortures: “Then, hastening to Elbora,” and so forth. This at least suggests that she was beaten with scourges.

The fact that she did not end her life by the sword is shown by her being perpetually called a confessor in the ecclesiastical office of the Gothic Breviary. Thus the same prayer says:

> Your virgin, Christ, Leocadia, has become glorious. Compared with the rising dawn, beautiful and chosen like the sun, she is proved like the moon; while shining with a brighter light and gleaming like the full moon in confession, and persisting like the blazing sun, knowing no diminution of herself, in the work of holiness. Grant us, therefore, that through her we may merit from you the indulgence we ask, since now, for our sins, we either pour out tears or offer groans. Amen.

This passage is claimed by Saint Braulio’s addition to Dexter. In the year of the Lord 312, the faithful of Toledo erected a sacred church to Saint Leocadia, martyr and citizen, at the place where she lies buried. It is the second sacred building in that city and is especially frequented. Several councils of Toledo were held there.

## APPENDIX ON THE SAINTS NAMED EULALIA

In passing, when Dexter mentions Saint Eulalia of Mérida, he seems in his original work to have spoken more fully, at the proper place, both of her and of her companion and fellow virgin, Saint Julia. We regret that this is missing from our manuscript, as is the notice of Saint Eulalia of Barcelona.

One remarkable feature is evident in both: not only did they share the same name, the same age, and the same persecution, but they were also honored in death by exceedingly similar kinds of martyrdom and by comparable miracles. It is therefore not surprising that some foreign authors confused them. Equilinus is shown to have done so in book I, chapter 54, when he supposes that the Eulalia celebrated on 10 December, instructed by the priest Donatus, was the Eulalia of Barcelona. This is false and contradicts his own account, for only six chapters earlier in the same book Equilinus mentioned Eulalia of Mérida while discussing Saint Leocadia. Later, forgetting what he had written, he confused the two.

Prudentius sang the acts of Eulalia of Mérida with great clarity in the *Peristephanon*. This hymn was customarily recited in the Breviary of Saint Isidore on the feast of the virgin herself. Reduced to an epitome, Ado expressed the account as follows in his Martyrology:

> At Mérida, a city of Spain, the natal day of Saint Eulalia, virgin, who, when she was thirteen years old, endured many tortures by order of the governor Dacian—read Calpurnian, whom the acts call Dacian’s subordinate, as I believe—and finally, suspended on the rack and torn with hooks, with burning torches placed on either side of her, gave up her spirit after inhaling the fire. In the sight of Christians she went up to heaven in the form of a snow-white dove.
>
> By order of the governor her blessed body hung upon the wood for three days. But although human honors were denied her, heavenly gifts were granted. Snow fell upon the girl’s body, so that what the fire placed on both sides had consumed with its burning heat might, covered with snowy whiteness, be made white by divine grace. Thus, reverently taken down by Christians and placed with due devotion beneath a sacred altar, she is made illustrious by the glory of miracles.

This is taken from the aforementioned Aurelius Prudentius. Hear now, I ask, what Prudentius himself writes of the same martyr in the hymn beginning:

> Noble by birth, Eulalia,  
> Nobler still in mind and character,  
> The holy virgin adorns Mérida,  
> From whose breast she was born,  
> And cherishes it with love.

Concerning her martyrdom, a little farther on:

> Without delay the twin executioners  
> Tear her slender breast,  
> And the claw strikes the virgin’s side  
> On either side and cuts to the bones,  
> While Eulalia counts the wounds.

Again, when she had been placed on the rack and burned with lamps set at her sides, and nevertheless had been surrounded by a pyre, he adds:

> The crackling flame flies into her face;  
> Fed through her hair, it seizes her head,  
> Surpasses its crown.  
> The virgin, desiring a swift death,  
> Approaches the pyre  
> And drinks it with her mouth.
>
> From there a dove suddenly flashes forth,  
> Whiter than snow in appearance,  
> Leaving the martyr’s mouth and following the stars.  
> This was Eulalia’s spirit,  
> Milky-white, swift, and innocent.
>
> Behold, icy winter brings down snow  
> And covers the entire marketplace;  
> It covers Eulalia’s limbs as well,  
> Lying beneath the frozen sky,  
> In place of a little cloak or linen cloth.

I deliberately omit the rest, since the hymn itself surpasses all others.

Quiricus, bishop of the see of Toledo and successor of Saint Ildefonsus, recounts nearly as much concerning Eulalia of Barcelona in a hymn which he composed in her honor and inserted into the Toledan Breviary. He took part in the eleventh Council of Toledo, held in the era 713, that is, in the year of the Lord 675. The hymn runs as follows:

> Here shines the honor of the martyr Eulalia’s tomb,  
> Which she marked with the sacred stigma of her passion.  
> It calls everyone to come; all gather to approach.
>
> The offspring of this stock, or the assembled throng,  
> Barcelona, ever increased by noble lineage,  
> A flourishing crown of citizens, an illustrious faithful people:
>
> Look upon your virgin, how she is a herald of glory;  
> Tested in faith, she so terrifies the raging judge,  
> Preaching the honor of the cross and the sign of salvation.
>
> For she is *catomata*, placed upon the rack;  
> She is beaten, torn with hooks, and burned by flames,  
> Knowing no end to her praise amid these things.
>
> Embracing the patron of the cross, she is hung upon the cross;  
> There snow from the heavens protects her body for its honor.  
> Thus, filled with holy warmth, she endured her passion.
>
> From her mouth, when her limbs had been released,  
> A dove springs forth to travel through the air,  
> Proclaiming that the virgin has conquered in the heavenly dwellings.
>
> Yet the dove, eager to precede God’s girl,  
> Is lifted in joy once the law of death has been fulfilled;  
> Thus, with laughter, it moistens her face and consoles the hearts of those who weep.
>
> Fortunate Barcelona, you are raised illustrious throughout the world,  
> You who retain in your bosom so salutary and pious a pledge,  
> Namely, the fellowship of so great a body.
>
> O blessed bride of Christ, most merciful virgin,  
> Receive now the vows and sighs of each person;  
> Beg Christ in prayer to hear those who groan.
>
> Remove what is burdensome, what accuses us to our destruction in death;  
> Let pestilential disease depart, let the enemy’s sword be overthrown.  
> Let life be tranquil for all, let the times be peaceful.
>
> May we not serve unjust factions in mind;  
> May rebellious flesh not reject the gentle yoke of Christ;  
> But may all shine with the holiness of Christ’s ardor.
>
> Meet your fellow citizens as a fellow citizen and extend salvation;  
> Be thus our patroness in the communication of grace,  
> As you are near the heavens in the favor of glory.
>
> Amid these things Quiricus himself, mingling his own prayer, laments:
>
> Quiricus himself, who consecrated the place of your tomb  
> According to monastic ordinances,  
> For the honor of the eternal Godhead,
>
> So that you may remember me in heaven  
> After the bonds of the flesh;  
> And that you may powerfully complete  
> What I have accomplished here only imperfectly,  
> I consecrate these vows and this song to you.
>
> Glory forever to the Father, Son, and Paraclete,  
> Praise, power, strength, and abundance of thanksgiving  
> To him whom all things confess as God  
> For ages upon ages. Amen.

See, I ask you, reader, how similar jewels the Sun of justice produced in our sea, so that they seem to differ only in city, parents, and the day of their passion.

Nor should anyone suppose that they differ even in this respect: that the one from Barcelona is said to have been killed on a cross, while the one from Mérida was killed on a rack. For we likewise read of Eulalia of Mérida in a certain prayer of the Gothic Breviary, which says:

> Lord Jesus Christ, who, while the body of your most blessed virgin Eulalia hung upon the cross, clothed it with a final sprinkling, so that both whiteness might clothe the virgin and refreshment the martyr.

The acts of the same most blessed virgin, recited on her feast in the Salamanca Breviary, likewise assert this, for they say:

> After these things Blessed Eulalia, tortured by various kinds of torment, hung upon a cross and gloried above all these things, and so forth.

I am nevertheless convinced that when both are said to have been hung upon a cross, this should not be understood strictly as an actual cross, but as a rack which bore the shape of a cross. For what Quiricus and the Roman Martyrology assert—that the woman of Barcelona gave up her spirit while suspended on a cross—is stated in explicit terms by her acts, which I read both at the beginning of the very ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint Bernard of Toledo, “In those days, Saint Eulalia of Barcelona, citizen and inhabitant, etc.,” and in the Palencian Breviary: she gave up her soul after being raised upon a rack.

The cross of Eulalia of Mérida is also clearly identified as having been of this kind in a certain hymn of the Gothic Breviary, which I shall give later. It says:

> Then upon a cut-down stake,  
> With her arms drawn upward,  
> The girl’s side is beaten,  
> And naked she is burned by flames.

This was undoubtedly the form of a rack.

As for what the Salamanca Breviary says of Eulalia of Mérida—that from the cross she penetrated the heavens in the form of a dove—the acts preserved in the aforementioned Palencian Breviary assert that this was said of the rack.

Consult what we noted to this effect when discussing Saint Wilgeforte in the year 138. But since we have never yet seen the genuine and sincere acts themselves published, I have decided, for the benefit of scholars, to bring them forward as they are preserved in the Palencian, Salamancan, and Astorgan Breviaries.

## LIFE OF SAINT EULALIA OF MÉRIDA

The passion of the holy and most blessed virgin Eulalia, which took place in the city of Mérida under the governor Calpurnian, on the fourth day before the Ides of December.

> In those days the most blessed virgin Eulalia, a devout girl, had Liberius, a leading citizen of the city of Mérida, as her father. When she was about thirteen years old, fearing God, chaste in mind and body, and modest in religion, she was taught from the beginnings of her childhood by a certain priest, Donatus, to confess Christ.
>
> When she had entered the years of adolescence, she preserved with a stronger spirit the faith which she had conceived in holy devotion. Thus, while Blessed Eulalia, a citizen and inhabitant of the province of Lusitania, was staying beyond Mérida, nearly thirty-eight miles away, within the boundaries of the province of Baetica, in a village called Proncianus, together with the confessor Felix and other God-fearing companions, and was continuing in the praises of God, Calpurnian entered the city of Mérida, persecuting Christians.
>
> When Blessed Eulalia was informed that messengers had arrived in a public vehicle to take her to Mérida, and that the care of her parent kept her concealed at home, the courageous virgin nevertheless rose during the night and, immediately moving swiftly in the vehicle, proceeded joyfully, hastening with all her heart toward martyrdom.
>
> Her fellow virgin Julia also accompanied her. As they traveled, Blessed Eulalia said to her: “Let it be known to you, lady sister, that I am going last, but I shall suffer first.”
>
> When they had approached the city of the people of Mérida, a certain Jew met Blessed Eulalia and said to her: “Go, offer incense, so that you may live.”
>
> The holy virgin replied: “May the Lord increase your years, for I desire to die for Christ.”
>
> Then, led to her passion, she addressed Calpurnian, the governor of the city of Mérida, as follows:
>
> “Why do you enter the city, enemy of God Most High? Why do you persecute Christians and strive to destroy God’s virgin?” The Lord teaches me in his truth, and you will not take my chastity from me, for you will not seduce my youth.”
>
> The governor Calpurnian said: “O little child, before you grow, you seek to destroy the flower of your age.”
>
> Blessed Eulalia replied: “I am about thirteen years old. Do you think that my childhood can be disturbed by your terror? This transient life is enough for me; and because I take no delight in the allurements of earthly life, I await the other blessed life, in which I shall become happier through the gift of God.”
>
> The governor Calpurnian said: “Do not let this wretched vanity deceive you. Come and sacrifice to the gods according to the imperial command, so that you may escape tortures, be honored, and obtain a rich husband.”
>
> Blessed Eulalia replied: “I have an immortal rich bridegroom, Christ, who will destroy you and your people, and your father the devil, who is called Satan.”
>
> Then the governor ordered her to be sent to prison. Beforehand, however, he ordered her to be brought before him and, wishing to persuade her with flattering and deceptive words, said: “Consider your childhood; look at yourself; have pity on yourself. Go, offer incense, so that you may live.”
>
> But Blessed Eulalia, full of faith, firm in virtue, and not fearing to persevere in her work until death, replied: “I am a Christian; I will not do it.”
>
> Then Calpurnian, inflamed by turbulent fury, thinking that the modest virgin should be corrected on the back of her body in the manner of children, ordered through the official in charge that she be *catomized*—that is, beaten on the buttocks while held upon another’s shoulders.
>
> Blessed Eulalia said to him: “You have power over my body, but no one can have power over my soul except God alone.”
>
> While her delicate and holy body was being *catomized*, she endured the blows inflicted upon her with an even spirit. Trusting in the great glory of God, she steadfastly and courageously cursed Caesar the king and his gods.
>
> But the angels of the Lord protected Blessed Eulalia. When the governor heard this and delayed pronouncing sentence upon the girl, the virgin Eulalia, persevering in steadfastness, boldly full of faith, and with a free voice so that everyone could hear, said:
>
> “Calpurnian, pronounce sentence. For to your kings and their gods I repeat what I have often said: I have cursed them, and I curse them.”
>
> When he heard these words of the blessed virgin, Calpurnian was greatly angered and inflamed with excessive fury. He ordered a tribunal to be prepared for himself in the forum on the following day.
>
> Then, in accordance with his sentence, he ordered the blessed virgin to be tortured. First he ordered her to be beaten with wet rods, her breasts to be drenched with burning oil, and her to be plunged alive into lime, with water poured over her and a pot of molten lead placed above her.
>
> Finally, when Calpurnian saw that he was defeated and confounded, he ordered Blessed Eulalia to be led outside the city, suspended upon a rack, torn with hooks, burning lamps to be applied around her sides, and her to be burned alive by flames.
>
> After Blessed Eulalia had been tormented by various kinds of torture, while hanging upon the cross she gloried above all these things. Recalling what she had prepared herself for from childhood, she said before all who heard:
>
> “It is necessary to believe in the one true God, the heavenly Father, and to adore Jesus Christ, his almighty Son, together with the Holy Spirit, who is blessed forever.”
>
> Thus, blessed and glorious, hastening toward the Lord at her end, she hurried so that she might go more quickly. Therefore, when flames of fire had been applied from both sides, she opened her mouth, drew in their force, and increased the blaze. After this, the spirit of the holy martyr passed from her mouth to the Lord in the form of a dove, in the sight of everyone.

The miracle of the snow, which we have already mentioned, is absent, as is the martyrdom of Saint Julia, her companion.

However, what the account says about her being ordered to be *catomized* means nothing other than that she was lifted onto another’s shoulders and, in the manner of children, beaten on the buttocks. For *κατωμαδόν* (*katōmadon*) means “to place something upon the shoulders,” as Baronius correctly noted in his notes on the Martyrology for 15 June, letter b, from Suidas, Hippocrates, and Josephus. This is clearly suggested by the words of the acts which we have just quoted: “Thinking that the modest virgin should be corrected on the back of her body in the manner of children”; and immediately afterward comes: “He ordered her to be catomized.” The same thing is meant by what is said of Eulalia of Barcelona in the hymn quoted above: “For she is placed upon the rack, *catomata*.”

Likewise, Saint Vitus the boy is said by Ado and Bede to have been beaten with *catomi* in the manner of children, as were Saint Barida and others.

But I shall give you another hymn of Eulalia of Mérida, the virgin, which was customarily sung in the Breviary of Saint Isidore.

## Praises of Blessed Eulalia

> Let us sing with a pure heart  
> The praises of blessed Eulalia,  
> Whom Christ consecrated among the martyrs  
> With chaste blood.
>
> Shut behind harsh doors  
> And among strong bolts,  
> Knowing neither sleep nor food,  
> She sang wakefully to Christ.
>
> The prison guard marvels at the light of the dread Godhead in her chains:  
> In the narrowness of prison,  
> The joys of her blessed mind.
>
> The judge, disturbed by fury,  
> Rises with bloodstained jaws  
> And rebukes the delay of night,  
> About to offer a holy victim.
>
> With joyful first blows  
> The girl of Christ is beaten,  
> Yet she utterly refuses  
> To consecrate an impious offering to the altars.
>
> Then upon a cut-down stake,  
> With her arms drawn upward,  
> The girl’s side is beaten,  
> And naked she is burned by flames.
>
> The victorious spirit departs,  
> Leaving the body pale.  
> May God, by the law of death,  
> Lead what has been lost to life.
>
> Glory, etc.

## 53. There are some who say, etc.

Certain persons, whom Ambrosius Morales reports in book IX, chapter 48, believed that Saints Parmena, Helimena, and Chrysolitus, priests, and Lucius and Mutius, deacons, were crowned with martyrdom at Córdoba in Spain. The acts themselves plainly prove them to have been deceived. Those acts, together with the acts of Saints Abdon and Senen of Persia and especially of Saint Laurence the martyr, are found in Surius, volume IV, on 10 August, where they are said to have suffered in Persia under the emperor Decius, before Saint Laurence.

The Persians have their own Córdoba, or Corduena, which Equilinus, in book IV, chapter 79, corruptly calls Cordula. Dexter nevertheless asserts that some people say relics were brought from there to our Córdoba in these days. If this is true, I would believe that it happened because certain Spanish people from Córdoba—perhaps soldiers—arranged to bring the bodies of the holy martyrs from Persia to their homeland. Or the reverse may have happened: the Persians themselves may have migrated to Spain with the relics and proceeded toward Córdoba, which had long before been founded by them.

Indeed, Pliny, in book III, chapter 1, reports from M. Varro that Persians once reached Spain with their colonies.

In this place in the printed Dexter there was a notice of Saint Firmus, beginning “From the city of Mellaria in Spain, etc.” We have excluded it from this place because it had been written shortly above, in the year 300, in the same words, and was repeated here by another ignorant compiler.

## 54. The holy martyrs of Christ, etc.

We have noted more than once that Elbora, or Ebora, of Carpetania is the city now called Talavera. On this matter there was a considerable dispute between Quevedo and Resendius, recorded in *Hispania Illustrata*. Mantuanus raised this very dispute against Mariana, but unjustly, driven more by a desire to contradict than by love of truth.

Certainly, that there was an Ebura in Carpetania is so clearly established by the testimony of Livy that anyone who does not see it appears blind in broad daylight. For in book XL, speaking of the war of Quintus Fulvius Flaccus with the Celtiberians, he says:

> At the beginning of spring he led the army into Carpetania and pitched camp near the town of Ebura, placing a small garrison in the city. A few days later the Celtiberians, etc.

Moreover, the acts of Saints Vincent and his sisters establish that they were born at Elbora and captured there by Dacian. From there they fled as far as Abula, where they were also killed.

That this Elbora was not in Lusitania but between Toledo and Abula—where Talavera is situated—is sufficiently demonstrated by the route itself which Dacian and the martyrs traveled. The acts say that Dacian bound Leocadia in chains at Toledo, then departed for Elbora, and finally reached Abula. The same is asserted concerning Saint Vincent and his sisters.

If someone should say that Dacian traveled from Toledo in Lusitania to Elbora and from there to Abula, he would be claiming that a very distorted route was taken. Ancient tradition stands against this, for the road by which the holy martyrs entered Abula still exists and is held in great veneration. It runs toward Talavera and Toledo through the pass where Carpetania was separated from the peoples of Bastetania. But if they had come from Elbora in Lusitania, they could not possibly have traveled by that road.

Furthermore, at Talavera there exists, and is held in great veneration, a stone which Saint Vincent trod upon. It became soft through contact with his holy feet and both expressed and retains their image, as is read in the life of the same saints.

Resendius contends that another similar stone at Ebura in Lusitania is held in equal honor. To me, however, this seems to have been said—or even done—for the sake of disputation. I would believe that he himself would yield to the dispute if he had been granted the opportunity to examine Dexter’s present testimony, by which the whole question is settled.

As for the saints themselves, they are renowned throughout the world, since their victory is celebrated by all. Usuard says on 27 October:

> In Spain, in the city of Ávila, the passion of the holy saints Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta, who were first stretched upon the rack so severely that all the joints of their limbs were dislocated. Then their heads were placed upon stones and crushed with powerful blows until their brains were scattered; thus they completed their martyrdom, under the governor Dacian.

I believe that *powerful blows* should be read instead of *powerful rods*; for the Acts state that the heads of the martyrs were crushed not with rods but with clubs. Ado, Bede, and the Roman Martyrology retain Usuard’s wording. All the historians of Spanish affairs discuss them—Vasaeus, Marinaeus, Morales, Mariana, Marieta, Villegas, Trugillus, and others—as does Equilinus, book IX, chapter 114. Saint Braulio adds the following under the year of the Lord 314, attributing it to Dexter:

> At Ávila a church is also erected to the sacred martyrs Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta, at the place where they suffered.

But let us give their genuine Acts, as they appear in the Palencia Breviaries and in the very ancient manuscript codex of the library of Saint Bernard of Toledo, under number 72.

> In those days, when the impious tyrant Dacian had inflicted great massacres of the saints throughout many cities, he came to Évora and immediately ordered all his officials to ensure that any Christians they found were brought before him. At once they seized a young man named Vincent, whose merit was commensurate with his name, and brought him before Dacian.
>
> When Dacian saw him, wishing to deceive him by flattery, he said: “Of what sect are you?”
>
> Vincent, whose spirit already clung to heaven, replied: “I worship Christ, from whose name I am called a Christian.”
>
> Dacian said: “I pardon your youth, since you have not yet reached the solid strength of maturity in wisdom. Nevertheless, you will be well advised if you listen to me as to your father and sacrifice to the gods.”
>
> Vincent said: “They lack sound understanding who, abandoning the living God, worship stones and wood.”
>
> At these and similar replies, Dacian, filled with fury, said: “Either let him sacrifice to the god Jupiter, or let him be subjected to various punishments and condemned to the most disgraceful death.”
>
> As he was being led away to sacrifice to Jupiter, suddenly the stone beneath his foot was miraculously softened so completely that those standing nearby thought it had become dust; and just as the impression of any metal is made in wax, so that stone displayed and retained the imprint of his foot. This marvel remains commemorated to the present day.
>
> Terrified by so great a miracle, the soldiers said: “The worshipers of our gods have never performed anything like this.” Therefore they asked Dacian that Vincent be kept under guard at home. When this was granted, many people, through his preaching, surrendered their souls to the Lord over the course of three days.
>
> Then his two sisters, Sabina and Christeta, entered the cell where he was bound and uttered these words amid groaning:
>
> “To whom are you leaving us, destined to perish? Who, do you think, will be our lord? Or who will protect our virginity? Brother, calm your ear for a little while and listen to our lamentable proposal; at the same time let us flee. If, while fleeing from our persecutors, we are overtaken, let us surrender our souls to God together. But if we escape, then just as we have led a long life with you in modesty, so holiness will be heaped up for us by God.”
>
> Vincent, overcome by his sisters’ lamentations, fled with them, and together they took refuge in Ávila. The persecutors caught up with them there; having found them in that city, they cruelly afflicted them with blows. They were stretched upon the rack upward and downward and finally, with clubs and stones, their brains were crushed and they completed their martyrdom. They were buried there, about the year 306.
>
> Later, however, during the reign of King Ferdinand the Great in Spain, their bodies were translated—as the testimony of many asserts: namely, the body of Saint Vincent to León, that of Saint Sabina to Palencia, and that of Saint Christeta to Saint Peter of Arlanza, in the Spanish Era 1097. We should not believe that their bodies were translated entire, but rather a substantial portion of them, since their sacred remains are still held in great veneration at Ávila.

This translation is confirmed by an inscription carved in marble that remains intact on the wall of the cloister of the Church of Saint Isidore at León. It bears the barbarous diction of that period, as I myself read it in the year of the Lord 1621:

> This hall which you see was once built of mud, dedicated to Saint John the Baptist; recently the most excellent Ferdinand and Queen Sancha built it of stone. At that time they brought here from the city of Seville the body of Saint Isidore the bishop, at the dedication of this church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, in the Spanish Era 1101. Then, in the Spanish Era 1103, on the sixth day before the Ides of May, they brought here from the city of Ávila the body of Saint Vincent, brother of Saints Sabina and Christeta.

The body of Saint Vincent—“a substantial portion,” as I have said—rests in a silver reliquary above the high altar of the same church, with this inscription:

> This little shrine shines with the honor of two saints:
>
> In the Spanish Era 1097.

Formerly, together with Saint Vincent, a substantial part of the jawbone of Saint John the Baptist was kept there. Therefore the shrine was said to shine in honor of two saints; but later it was removed from there for the devotion of the people and is kept in the sacristy. Morales supports all this in book X, chapter 12.

For the benefit of the learned, I would also like to append the hymn concerning these martyrs found in the Mozarabic Breviary of Saint Isidore.

### Hymn for the feast of the holy martyrs Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta

*[Col. 0454D]*

Here the Lord of powers graciously summons you, devout people,  
to bring fervent vows with banquets to the courts of his witnesses,  
and may he place you in heaven’s inmost regions.

United with the martyrs, unite your joys;  
let a devout voice offer gifts to Vincent;  
let the heavenly writing sing Sabina,  
and Christeta, the good lady.

These spurned the wretched gains of the world,  
the crafty sufferings of men amid hardships.  
Their crimson necks yield laurels to you in all things,  
O Christ the King.

O God, simple and Trinity, one Godhead,  
we ask that, through their prayers, you hear  
what we ourselves request with fervent hearts;  
O immeasurable one, graciously grant it.

Let there be glory to you, triune Deity,  
who, being one, hold and judge all things;  
through unending ages  
you generously make good things prosper beyond measure. Amen.

### 55. At Alba near Acci, etc.

Alba was indeed a municipium called Alba Urgabonensis. The place is now Arjona, which received its name from Urgabo, between the cities of Acci and Giennium—that is, between Guadix and Jaén. Thus Morales says in *Antiquities*, under the word “Mentesa,” folio 74, asserting that an inscription still exists at Alba, or Arjona, carved in stone in honor of the emperor Hadrian:

> To the Emperor Caesar, son of the deified Trajan Parthicus, grandson of the deified Nerva, Trajan Hadrian Augustus, chief pontiff, invested with tribunician power fourteen times, father of his country: the municipium of Alba Urgabonensis has dedicated this.

The Roman Martyrology celebrates the feast of the holy martyrs Apollo, Isacius, and Crotatus on 21 April, in these words:

> Likewise, the holy martyrs Apollo, Isacius, and Crotatus, who suffered under Diocletian.

The Greeks also remember them in the Menologion, whose words are:

> On the same day, the contest of the holy martyrs Apollo, Isacius, and Crotatus, who were brought to completion by hunger and the sword under the emperor Diocletian, in whose army they served.

Only to Dexter is owed the information concerning their city.

### 56. At Bracara, etc.

In the Lusitanian Martyrology printed at Coimbra in the year of the Lord 1591, the memory of Saint Silvester the martyr, crowned in the territory of Bracara under Diocletian, appears on 12 April. His body was translated to the Church of Compostela in the year 1102 by Diego, the first archbishop of that see, as the Compostelan Annals report.

### 57. At Córdoba, etc.

Usuard and the Roman Martyrology remember that Saint Secundinus suffered at Córdoba on 21 May. Vasaeus asserts that he was killed in the persecution of Diocletian. Roa gives his Acts from an ancient Cordoban Breviary in his *Cordoban Saints*. They begin:

> At the time when Diocletian was persecuting the Church and Spain with the greatest fury, etc.

Their substance is that Secundinus was arrested by the judge and entered into various conversations and disputations with him, by which he refuted the falsehood of the gods and displayed the majesty of the true God. The judge then attempted in a thousand ways to draw Christ’s soldier away from the faith, either by enticing him with promises or by threatening him with terrors; and at last, when he saw that he was casting his words uselessly to the winds, he tried the gravest punishments upon him and inflicted death itself with atrocious cruelty.

The Church of Córdoba celebrates the feast of its martyr every year on the same day, 21 May; the Church of Cuenca and others also celebrated it before the reform of the Roman Breviary. There is also mention in the Acts of Saints Justa and Rufina of Diogenianus, under whose rule Secundinus is said to have suffered; he was governor of Baetica under Diocletian. Saint Eulogius remembers Saint Secundinus with the highest praise in book II of his *Memorial of the Saints*. Morales discusses him in book X, chapter 25; Mariana in book II, chapter 28; as do Villegas and the others, and Equilinus, book III, chapter 130, number 145.

Under the aforementioned judge Diogenianus, as the chronology demonstrates, twenty martyrs of Christ were crowned at Córdoba in glorious martyrdom. The principal among them is recognized as the young Saint Zoilus. The authors of all the Martyrologies remember them—Bede, Usuard, Ado, and the others, together with the Roman Martyrology, which has these words on 27 June:

> At Córdoba, the holy martyrs Zoilus and nineteen others.

On that day Galesinus says:

> At Córdoba in Spain, Saint Zoilus the martyr and his nineteen companions, who, under the emperor Diocletian, were crowned with distinction after glorious struggles undertaken for piety.

Equilinus has similar material in book VI, chapter 16. The outstanding deeds and torments that Saint Zoilus endured for Christ are recited in the Cordoban, Palencian, Salamancan, and other Breviaries. Marieta includes them in *Spanish Saints*, part I, book II; they also appear in the *Flower of the Saints* of Alfonso de Villegas, in Basilius Sanctorus, in the *Thesaurus Concionatorum*, and most recently in Roa’s book on the Saints of Córdoba—to pass over Morales, Vasaeus, Lucius Marinaeus, and others.

Moreover, the Toledan Breviary of Saint Isidore recites at his feast the following hymn, composed from various excerpts of Prudentius: it was made as a hymn in praise of the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, as can be seen from the numbers marked in the margin.

### Hymn for the feast of Saint Zoilus the martyr

*[Col. 0456B]*

**From verse 4:**

The martyr’s deeds and Zoilus’ crown  
will hasten to meet Christ;  
the precious city too, bearing  
the victor’s gifts.

**From verse 24:**

The citizens honor these as though  
their own earth enclosed the very limbs  
and, embracing them in their ancestral tomb,  
preserved the bones of the blessed martyr.

**From verse 26:**

Our own man, and first in our own arena,  
anointed with the oil of virtue  
and faith, learned to subdue  
the dreadful enemy by his strength.

**From verse 29:**

While life remained, no martyr  
was granted to dwell in our lands;  
you alone, surviving your own death,  
live throughout the world.

**From verse 15:**

Alone, you prepared  
for the Lord more numerous deeds of virtue;  
alone, rich in piety,  
you enjoy abundant light.

**From verse 19:**

You may believe that the homeland is owed  
to the sacred crowns of the martyr,  
from which the choir rises  
and extends toward heaven, clothed in snowy nobility.

**From verse 20:**

From there, Zoilus, your palm arose;  
from here the clergy produced such triumph:  
here the mitred house of priests  
celebrates its vow.

### 58. Gloria, etc.

I corrected this in several places by collating it with copies of Prudentius. Among the other torments that Saint Zoilus endured bravely, one was especially remarkable: after an opening had been cut in the lower part of his back, the cruel torturer pulled out his kidneys and flanks; nevertheless, he remained alive for some time and continued praising God. Therefore, what Prudentius had sung concerning Saint Engratia—“While life remained, no martyr,” and so forth—is rightly sung of Zoilus as well in the aforementioned hymn.

There is someone who wishes to confuse him with Acisclus, the companion of Saint Victoria of Córdoba, as Julian did in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 130. Yet they had undergone martyrdom for Christ much earlier, namely in that same year.

As for why Dexter did not mention so great a martyr and his companions in his *Chronicle*—unless one should attribute it to a defect in the manuscript or a copyist’s error, which I would readily believe—the following explanation occurs to me. Saint Zoilus lay hidden for many years in an obscure tomb, cast out by the pagans, until, in the time of Sisebut, king of the Goths, he was revealed by divine revelation to Venerable Agapitus, bishop of that city, discovered by him, and placed in a fitting position of honor. These are the words of Ado and Equilinus. Marinaeus recounts the matter more fully in book V of *Memorable Events of Spain*, which Surius transcribed in volume 7. Galesinus agrees at the cited place.

Concerning the Church of Saint Zoilus, erected by Agapitus, Saint Eulogius writes in book II, chapter 6, of his *Memorial of the Saints*; Albarus reports in his Life that Eulogius served there in the clerical office. It is therefore not surprising if Dexter had no knowledge of that martyr, although one difficulty remains: Prudentius, a contemporary of Dexter and of Saint Zoilus, mentions him in the hymn mentioned above. Nevertheless, it could still have happened that the martyr remained unknown to Dexter if he had not read that hymn. This is not improbable, since, although he discusses other books of Prudentius in this *Chronicle*, he does not mention the hymns.

Finally, in the year 1070, Fernando Gómez, count of Carrión, translated the body of Saint Zoilus to his own city, where he built in his name the well-known Benedictine monastery. I should not omit to say that the Reverend Father Fray Ildephonsus Truxillus, now general procurator in the city, my dearest companion and friend, has sung the deeds of the holy martyr in two thousand octonary verses of Spanish poetry, in an elegant style; these poems are to be published someday.

### 59. At Nertobriga, etc.

Ptolemy testifies that there were formerly two cities of this name in Spain. One was among the Turdetani of Baetica; Morales proves from a stone found there, bearing the inscription **NERTOB**, that it is now called Fregenal, in *Antiquities*, under the word “Beturia,” folio 100. The other was in Celtiberia and is mentioned by Appian. Dexter is speaking of this second city, which seems to have been situated where Almunta now stands, as the author of the *Geographical Dictionary* asserts—namely, at the confluence of the Salon, not far from Bilbilis, toward Zaragoza.

The memory of the holy martyrs Theopompus and Synesius is found in the Roman Martyrology on 21 May. Their Acts are given by Equilinus, book V of the *Catalogue*, chapter 33. However, when he makes Theopompus bishop of Nicomedia, Cardinal Baronius clearly proves in his notes that Equilinus was mistaken, since in the time of Diocletian, under whom Theopompus suffered, the bishops of Nicomedia were first Cyril and then Anthimus. Nor is this surprising, since instead of Nicomedia one should read, as we have it in Dexter, Nertobriga.

Again, what happened in the Acts of other martyrs certainly happened here as well: the emperor by whose order the persecution was launched is introduced as though he himself were the judge, questioning the martyrs under torture, although it was not he but his subordinate who carried out the execution. Their corrected Acts read as follows:

> Theopompus, bishop of Nertobriga, suffered together with a certain Synesius under the emperor Diocletian. When Theopompus the bishop was led to a shrine and refused to worship the images, he was sent into a fiery furnace, in which he remained unharmed for a day and a night. At night he came out from there, preceded by heavenly light, and reached the judge’s palace. With all the doors divinely opened, he approached the judge’s bedchamber, declared that he was alive, and returned to the furnace. In the morning he was found singing psalms in its midst and entirely unburned.
>
> When the judge attributed this to his magic and wished to test it, he had a dog thrown into the furnace; the dog was immediately consumed by fire. After this Theopompus was held in prison for twenty-two days without any food, but, strengthened by the Lord, he was brought out with a cheerful countenance.
>
> Then, by order of the judge, his right eye was gouged out. When he returned to prison, however, the Lord restored it to him. When the judge again attributed this to magical arts, he summoned to himself a certain Egyptian, a great magician named Theonas, and led him to the bishop so that he might kill him by his tricks; but first he wished to see his power.
>
> The magician had a most savage bull brought before him. After speaking certain words into its ear, he suddenly tore it into two parts, and when the pieces were weighed on a scale, they balanced equally. Then the magician offered Theopompus magical cakes of flour and a cup filled with poison and demons. When Theopompus tasted all these things without injury, the magician was converted. He was handed over to prison with Theopompus, who baptized him, and the name Synesius was given to him.
>
> The saint was then brought out, stretched supine on the ground, and bound to stakes. A great stone, scarcely carried by eight men, was placed upon his belly; but the stone rose of its own accord and leapt more than fifteen cubits away. Next he was hung from a height by his feet, head downward, with a huge stone fastened to his neck. When the rope by which he was held was cut, so that he might be dragged suddenly to the ground and torn apart, he stood on his feet without any injury. Finally, he was beheaded.
>
> Synesius, however, was placed in a pit dug in the ground and covered with earth. Horses were driven over it so that they might press the earth down with their hooves, and thus he departed to Christ. Their bodies were buried in the same tomb at Nertobriga, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

Some have asserted, in the time of Dexter, that Synesius too was a bishop. If this were so, it would necessarily follow that they did not die at the same time, but that Synesius survived for some period and was eventually killed at Nertobriga as well.

### 60. At Alexandria, etc.

Whatever Dexter writes here concerning Saint Catherine is found in her Acts edited by Metaphrastes and in the Roman Breviary—whether concerning the forty philosophers whom she overcame, or rather fifty, as some report; or concerning the Augusta Faustina and the commander Porphyry, whom she converted and who were crowned with martyrdom before her.

Equilinus has the same material in book X, chapter 105, adding what Baronius noted: namely, that one should not read that she was killed under Maxentius, but under the tyrant Maximinus. Blessed Catherine was always held in great esteem in Spain, and for that reason Dexter mentions her among the Spanish martyrs, of whom he was speaking particularly in this passage. Hence, a little later, under the year 309, he speaks of her again, saying:

> Ega brought the memory of Saint Catherine from the East into Spain.

### 61. In the territory of Bracara, etc.

Vasaeus discusses Saint Susanna the virgin in his *Chronicle* under the year 306. She suffered at Bracara and was the sister of Saint Victor the martyr, who was baptized in his own blood. She is also mentioned in the Lusitanian Martyrology, toward the end, among the saints of Lusitania, on 12 April. The Compostelan Annals assert that Don Diego, archbishop of Compostela, translated the body of Saint Susanna, virgin and martyr of Bracara, from the place where she had previously been buried to his own see in the year of the Lord 1102.

More than three hundred years later, namely in 1590, Don Augustine de Castro, archbishop of Bracara, ordered her tomb to be opened again. A considerable number of the virgin’s bones were found in it, proving that her entire body had not been translated to Compostela.

### 62. At Pamplona, etc.

In Dexter’s codex printed at Zaragoza, “Saint Valerius” was read; but Bede, Ado, the Roman Martyrology, and ancient manuscripts prove that “Saint Valent” should be read. All of these preserve the memory of his feast on 21 May. On that day the Roman Martyrology says:

> On the same day, Saint Valent, bishop, who was killed together with three boys.

Molanus adds from a certain Martyrology:

> At Augia, which leads him through joys with glad vows.

This seems to assert that his feast was celebrated in the monastery of Augia, renowned throughout the world, near Constance. I believe this was because the bodies of Saint Valent the bishop and the boys were translated from Pamplona to Augia by the emperor Charlemagne.

### 63. At Clunia, etc.

We proved above, under the year 290, when discussing Saint Saturninus and his companion martyrs, that ancient Clunia was the modern Coruña del Conde, not Coruña, the capital of the kingdom of Galicia.

Concerning Saint Meletius and his companions, their wives and children, the Roman Martyrology says on 24 May:

> On the same day, the holy martyrs Meletius, commander of an army, and his two hundred and fifty-two companions, who completed their martyrdom by various kinds of death. Likewise, the holy martyrs Susanna, Marciana, and Palladia, wives of the aforementioned soldiers, who were broken to death together with their little children.

In his notes Baronius attests that they are also discussed on that day in the Menologion, where their Acts are related at greater length. There, under 24 May, the following is found:

> On the same day, Saint Meletius, commander of the army, John and Stephen, officers, and their multitude, who endured the contest with them—two hundred and fifty martyrs, together with women and children.
>
> When Saint Meletius freely and steadfastly professed the faith of Christ and overthrew by his prayers the detestable idols worshiped in the temples of the pagans, soldiers were sent by the governor Maximus to detain Meletius and those who were with him. When they were led away and in no way consented to sacrifice, they were beaten with wooden staffs, their sides were torn, and they were crushed with iron hammers; finally, they were nailed to a piece of wood.
>
> When their foreheads were again beaten with iron hammers, Saint Meletius was suspended and fastened to a pine tree and departed to God. His companions Stephen and John were beheaded and likewise died for the faith of Christ. The soldiers who were with Saint Meletius were struck down with the sword.
>
> Susanna, Marciana, and Palladia, the wives of the holy martyrs, were, together with their infants, broken to death by executioners at the governor’s command. The executioners are said to have breathed out their souls immediately after committing the crime.
>
> Moreover, when Cyrianus and Christianus, still very young, were questioned by the governor whether they thought Jupiter or Christ was greater, and they answered that Christ was greater, they were beheaded.
>
> On the same day, the contest of Saint Serapion the Egyptian martyr and of those who suffered with him at the same time. He was beheaded together with the magician Callinicus for the faith of Christ. Festus, Faustus, Marcellus, Theodorus, Melecion, Sergius, Marcellinus, and with them Felix, Photinus, Theodoriscus, Mercurius, and Didymus—some companions, some tribunes, and some commanders—were all thrown into a furnace and completed their martyrdom.

Thus far the Menologion.

### 64. At Segisama, etc.

Ptolemy asserts that Segisama Julia was a city of the Vaccaei, and his scholiast Villanovanus says that it is now called Simancas. Ptolemy also places Segisamunculum among the Autrigones, peoples of the Cantabri, where Santa Gadea now stands. This seems to be the Segisama in whose territory Augustus Caesar established his camp in order to subjugate Cantabria, as Morales reports from the ancient sources in book VIII, chapter 53.

Whichever of these cities it may have been that Saint Papius made illustrious by his blood, although Dexter does not specify it here, it will become clear from what he notes below concerning Saint Britius that it was the Segisama, or Segisamon, of the Vaccaei.

The memory of Saint Papius is preserved among the Greeks in the Menologion on 28 June. From it the Roman Martyrology took the following:

> On the same day, Saint Papius the martyr, who, during the persecution of Diocletian, was beaten with whips and thrown into a cauldron full of boiling oil and fat. After suffering other terrible punishments, he was finally crowned when his neck was offered.

These words entirely agree with what Dexter writes about him. Galesinus says on the same day:

> Saint Papius the martyr, who, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, after enduring many punishments for Christ with unconquered spirit—punishments terrible even to describe—was finally crowned when his neck was offered.

The Greeks, however, say:

> This man, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, followed and preached the faith of Christ the Lord, which he had received from his ancestors. For confessing it, he was beaten with whips and thrown into a cauldron filled with boiling oil and fat. He remained there for seven days, clothed in fire as in a garment. This caused astonishment in everyone and converted many to the faith of Christ.

Agaunum in Gaul: the holy virgins and martyrs Faith and Sabina, Spanish by home and lineage, from the city of Civitas, suffered under Dacian, the most cruel governor of Gaul and Spain.

*[Col. 0415]*

At Ureña, Bishop Valerius of Zaragoza suffers on 10 January, leaving to posterity an example of steadfastness.

Mademarius, bishop of Barcelona, outstanding.

At Seville in Spain, the martyrs Carpophorus and Abundius, born and raised there, were cruelly killed for Christ.

*[Col. 0417]*

At Iliberri in Baetica, a council of many bishops is convened. Felix, bishop of Acci, presides. It is held by order and mandate of Melantius, bishop of Toledo and primate of the bishops of Spain.

*[Col. 0423]*

At Histonium in Spain, the bodies of the most holy martyrs Cyricus and Julitta were discovered, having once been brought there from elsewhere.

In the province of Gallaecia in Spain, the body of Saint Marina, or Margaret, virgin and martyr, who suffered there, was discovered.

Saint Justus, bishop of Vich, renowned for holiness, about the year 320.

Near Langres, Caesar Constantius killed sixty thousand Germans in a single battle and destroyed them.

Galerius Maximianus, defeated by Narseus in battle, ran before the chariot of the emperor Diocletian wearing the imperial purple.

The centurion Veturius harshly persecutes Christian soldiers.

Felix, archdeacon of Toledo, who collected and arranged the canons of the Council of Iliberri together with Saint Hosius of Córdoba, flourishes remarkably.

*[Col. 0425]*

L. Valerius Hispanus arranged the fragments of Berossus into five parts.

At Mellaria, a city of Baetica in Spain, Saint Firmus the martyr, who, after being afflicted with the harshest wounds and burned with lamps, finally completed his martyrdom by having his head cut off under the governor of Spain, M. Aurelius Verus, a man of consular rank. In the course of time his body was also brought to Rome, and he is especially honored on the first day of July.

At Iria Flavia in Gallaecia, Saint Susanna, virgin and martyr.

At the city of Caea in Spain, among the Vaccaei, Saint Antonina the martyr.

*[Col. 0427]*

During this period the persecution of Diocletian rages with greater violence.

The Council of Sinuessa is held in the case of Pope Marcellinus, who had burned incense at Rome, with many bishops present; some prelates from Gaul, Germany, and Spain are also present.

At Juliobriga in Spain, Saint Lucia the martyr, who came to Spain from the region of Campania. She was seized by Ritiovarus, whom she converted to the faith; after he abandoned her, she was seized by another judge and suffered with other companions on the day before the Nones of July.

In this most severe persecution, at Ebura among the Carpetani, the holy martyrs of Christ Felix, Luciolus, Fortunatus, and Eusebius were crucified by Asclepiades, the governor of Spain.

At Iria Flavia in Spain, Saint Cucuphas, martyr of Christ.

*[Col. 0429]*

At Augustobriga in Spain, at the same time, the holy martyrs Absalonius, Heraclius, and Largus were killed for Christ—these were killed, while those others were yoked.

At Munobriga among the Celtiberians, Saint Demetrius the martyr.

At Carthage Spartaria, the martyrs Philemon and Domninus.

*[Col. 0431]*

At the same time, at Tude, or Aquae Calidae, a distinguished town of Gallaecia through which the river Miño flows, Saint Aza the martyr suffered, together with his glorious fellow soldiers.

At Tarragona in Spain, the crowns of the holy martyrs Domitius, Pelagia, Aquila, and Theodosia.

At Carthage in Spain, the distinguished martyr Saint Concessa.

In the city of Solia in Baetica, Saint Marcellus—Hispanic, as is believed—a bishop, an exceptionally devout and learned man.

At Seori in Cantabria, Saint Centolla, a citizen of Toledo, daughter of the consul Lucius Ragonus Quintianus—at Catania, under her father L. Quintianus, the most courageous holy virgin Agatha suffered—suffered together with the widow Helena during the persecution of Diocletian.

*[Col. 0433]*

At Voluca near Numantia, Saint Victoria with her companions.

At Asta in Baetica, Saint Secundus the martyr is honored.

At Oretum in Tarraconian Spain, Saint Spiridion, formerly bishop of Toledo, who fought gloriously for the name of Christ.

At Ilipula in Spain, Saint Restitutus—so it is believed—a presbyter, teacher of Castor and his Cantabrian companions of the quarries. This Castor, the martyr Crispulus, and the Restitutus of whom we spoke earlier were present at the Council of Iliberri in Baetica.

At Patavonium among the Astures, the most glorious martyrs of Christ Saturninus, Felix, Fortunatus, and other companion martyrs.

In the city of Heraclea on the Spanish promontory of Calpe, Saint Lucia the martyr.

At Argenteola among the Astures, the holy martyrs of Christ Saturninus, Theophilus, and Revocata suffered for Christ.

*[Col. 0435]*

In the eastern part of Spain, in the city of Palemo, Saint Sotera, virgin and martyr, who, following the custom of slaves, received slaps upon the face and completed an illustrious martyrdom in the Lord. Saint Monica, the worthy mother of Augustine, held her up as an example of chastity. She came to Spain as a pilgrim in the year of the Lord 304.

The Goths ravage the Empire. They had adopted many customs from the people of Constantinople, including the practice of striking bronze cymbals with wooden instruments on Friday of Holy Week.

In this year the emperor Diocletian Valerius Jovius entered the consulship for the ninth time, and Maximianus Valerius Herculeus for the seventh.

In this same year many suffered martyrdom throughout Spain.

In the preceding year Diocletian and Maximian, the Augusti, celebrated a triumph at Rome with splendid pomp and pageantry. Before their chariot came the wife, sisters, and children of Narseus, together with all the booty by which the emperors had stripped the Parthians.

Not long afterward, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, those same Augusti abdicated the imperial purple.

*[Col. 0437]*

Nevertheless, the savage persecution of Diocletian continues.

At Gerunda in Spain, the holy martyrs Felix and Maximus suffer.

At Rhoda in Celtiberian Spain, the holy martyrs Dionysius and Ammonius.

At Iturissa among the Vascones, the holy martyrs Socrates, Dionysius, Victor, Zoticus, Arcadius, Caesar­ius, and Severinus, who, tortured in various ways under Diocletian, completed their martyrdom. Christophorus, Antonius, and Theonas were added to them and were tortured in various ways.

In the wilderness of Metellinum in Lusitania, Theodorus the Admirable.

*[Col. 0439]*

At Carthage in Spain, Felix the bishop and martyr, with his companions.

At Toledo and Seville, Saint Felix, a deacon of Toledo, suffered at Seville under Dacian, the most cruel governor of all Spain.

At Zaragoza, an innumerable multitude of martyrs of every age, condition, and both sexes suffered.

*[Col. 0441]*

There also Saint Encratis, virgin and martyr from the city of Bracara Augusta. Eighteen martyrs also suffered there.

*[Col. 0443]*

There also Saint Lambertus, who, carrying his severed head in his hands and guided by an angel, was joined to the number of the holy martyrs.

*[Col. 0445]*

At Toledo, Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr, who, already scourged, had been thrust into a dreadful prison. When she heard of the martyrdom of Saint Eulalia of Mérida, she marked the stone of the prison in prayer with the sign of the cross using her virgin thumb. The imprint of her fingers and the cross remain there to this day. She surrendered her undefiled spirit to God in prayer.

*[Col. 0451]*

Some say that relics of the holy Parmena and his companions, who suffered in Persia, were recently brought from Persia to Córdoba, a city of Baetica in Spain, called Patricia.

The holy martyrs of Christ Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta, his sisters, who were born in the town of Évora in Carpetania and suffered at Ávila, triumphed over the enemy through a most glorious form of martyrdom.

*[Col. 0455]*

At Alba near Acci in Baetica, the holy martyrs of Christ Apollo, Isacius, and their glorious companion Crotatus.

At Bracara in Lusitania, Saint Silvester suffered for Christ.

At Córdoba in Baetica, Saint Secundinus the martyr and citizen of Córdoba, who, under the judge Diogenianus, through the struggle of contests, overcoming the judge’s cruelty and enduring many torments bravely, carried away the palm of martyrdom.

*[Col. 0457]*

At Nertobriga in Celtiberia, the holy martyrs Synesius and Theopompus. Some even believe that these were bishops of two cities of Spain, although they do not specify which cities they were.

A.D. 300. A.R. 1051. In Alexandria, Saint Catherine, virgin and martyr, suffered under the Emperor Maximinus, after overcoming forty philosophers; the Empress Augusta having preceded her, Porphyrius the commander too suffered with the army.

A.D. 300. A.R. 1051. In the territory of Braga, Saint Susanna, virgin and martyr, suffered for the faith; she was the sister of Saint Victor the martyr and catechumen.

[Col. 0459] A.D. 300. A.R. 1051. At Pompilona, Saint Valens, bishop of Pompilona in Spain and martyr; three boys, companions of his crown, suffered with him.

A.D. 300. A.R. 1051. At Clunia in Spain, the most valiant martyrs of Christ, Meletius, commander of the army, and two others, glorified God through various kinds of torture; and their holy wives, Susanna, Marciana, and Palladia, having had their necks broken together with their children, obtained the crown.

A.D. 300. A.R. 1051. At Segisamona in Spain, Saint Papius the martyr, who, after being beaten with scourges and thrown into a cauldron filled with boiling oil and melting fat, and enduring other torments more severe than these, was beheaded.

[Note: [Col. 0460C]

A.D. 308.—1. At the city of Martula, etc. You will find much about Saint Britius in the Acts of the holy martyrs of Seville, Carpophorus and Abundius, in Mombritius, volume I. Usuard, Ado, the Roman Martyrology, Galesinus, and more recent writers also discuss him on 9 July. I shall give the words of Usuard, from whom the others borrowed:

“At the city of Martula, Saint Britius, bishop and confessor, who, after enduring many things for his confession of the Lord and being strengthened by a holy angel and by the blessed apostle Peter, winning great multitudes of believing peoples [Col. 0461A] for almighty God, rested in peace.”

The Roman Martyrology states the name of the judge, saying: “Under the judge Marcianus he endured many things in confession of the Lord,” and so forth. Equilinus gives a fuller account of his acts in book VI, chapter 74:

“Britius,” he says, “was renowned as bishop in the city of Martula. While preaching Christ the Lord, he was seized by the judge Marcianus, who ordered the governor that his mouth be long beaten with a stone; then that he be hoisted onto the rack and cruelly tortured. Since he persisted in confessing God, he was thrown into prison. When night came, the whole city was shaken by a tremendous earthquake, and Marcianus was crushed beneath a falling wall. Britius, however, visited by an angel and by the blessed apostle Peter, was led out of prison. Thereafter, preaching the Gospel of Christ throughout the surrounding region for a long time and winning great multitudes of peoples for almighty God, he rested in peace on the seventh day before the Ides of July. Those standing by saw his soul swiftly ascending into heaven in the form of a snow-white dove.”

In almost everything Equilinus agrees with Dexter; nor is it surprising that such accounts should be found in the aforementioned Acts, [Col. 0461B] which we believe were precisely those sent from Spain to Eusebius of Caesarea by the agency of the Emperor Constantine the Great, together with the others from which he compiled his vast work on the deeds of the martyrs. This work, written in Greek, is said to be found in the royal library of Saint Laurence at the Escorial. Eusebius was also the first author of a Martyrology, as Bede expressly testifies in his book of Retractations on the Acts of the Apostles, volume VI, and in book II on Mark, chapter 26; as do Hilduin in the preface to the Life of Saint Dionysius and Saint Notker in his Martyrology on the seventh day before the Kalends of May. Molanus proves the matter extensively and learnedly in his book On Martyrologies, chapter 2, under the title “On the Martyrologies of Eusebius and Jerome”; and Pamelius, cited by him, admitted it. This is regardless of the letter to Chromatius and Heliodorus circulated under Jerome’s name before the Martyrology of Usuard, which Cassiodorus nevertheless accepts in On Divine Institutions, chapter 32. We shall defend these matters expressly below, under the year of the Lord 384.
