Now, concerning the city of Martula, [Col. 0461C] it is sufficiently clear from the Acts of the saints Carpophorus and Abundius, who suffered under the same judge Marcianus near Seville, that it was first of all in Spain, not far from Seville. It is certainly the place now called Mertula, situated within the borders of Lusitania at the confluence of the river Anas, not far from Beja, beside the town of Alcoutim. Formerly it was called Myrtilis, or Julia Myrtilis, by Pliny in book VIII, chapter 22, and by Ptolemy in his map of Lusitania. Villanova is mistaken in claiming that Julia Myrtilis is now Baena, which nevertheless is not in Lusitania, as everyone places Myrtilis, but in Baetica, between Córdoba and Alcalá la Real. It is certain and well known that many places in Spain received the surname Julia from Julius [Col. 0462A] Caesar; Morales observed this in book IX, chapter 32. Such places include Julia Claritas, Julia Virtus, Julia Contributa, Julia Concordia, and so forth in Baetica.

Finally, I would note that what others attribute to the apostle Saint Peter—namely, the liberation of Britius from his bonds—Dexter, on the report of others, attributes to Peter, bishop of Braga: first, because Britius was a bishop of Évora in Lusitania; and second, because that Peter too was called “the apostle” by the Lusitanians, just as the fathers of the council of Braga under Bishop Pancratian called him. Consult the acts of this council, which we shall give under the year 423.

2. At Serpa, etc. The memory of Saints Hilarion and Proclus, who were killed in the time of the Emperor Trajan, is preserved in the Roman Martyrology on 12 July. On that day the Greeks read the following in their Menologion:

“Of the holy martyrs Proclus and Hilary. First, Saint Proclus, arrested under the Emperor Trajan, is brought before the court. He freely professes his faith before the prefect Maximus, and by his order is immediately burned with torches on his shoulders and belly. Then, with a stone fastened to his feet, he is hung aloft upon a wooden beam; afterward he is pierced with a dense volley of arrows, and [Col. 0462B], wounded by them, departs to the Lord. Next, Hilary, the blessed Proclus’s cousin, after confessing himself a Christian, is suspended and beaten; and, dragged for three miles, he is beheaded and buried with Saint Proclus.”

Consult Peter Galesinus on this same day. Concerning Saint Hilarion he says: “After various torments in confessing the faith, he is finally crowned by offering his neck.” Dexter also has this account.

As for the question of what city of Baetica Serpa was, or where it was [Col. 0462C] situated, I have not been able to investigate it. There were indeed the Caepori, a people of Nearer Spain, according to Pliny, book IV, chapter 20; but whether they were named from Serpa is unclear. Perhaps it is now called Sequia, near Alcalá la Real.

3. In Lusitania, etc. Consult what we left recorded under the year 138. Meanwhile, in place of “Near Castralaelia,” which stood in the printed edition, read “Situated near Castralaelia.”

4. At Urgabona, etc. It is now called Arjona, formerly a distinguished municipium, as we showed above from the testimony of our Morales, commentary 4 on the year 300, number 3, under the words “At Alba near Acci.” The martyrs discussed here are certainly different from those treated above under the year 156, even though both pairs bear the same names: the former are called Bonosus and Maximianus, and these are likewise called Bonosus and Maximianus. The difference of cities and times certainly proves them to be different, since the former are read to have suffered at Blanda in the year 156, while these suffered at Urgabona in 308.

5. At Carthage, etc. Their feast day is designated from ancient manuscript codices in the Roman Martyrology on 10 August, in these words:

“At Carthage, the holy virgins [Col. 0463A] and martyrs Bassa, Paula, and Agathonica.”

The edition of Dexter printed at Zaragoza has Beata instead of Bassa, but this is corrupt. The Greeks also discuss them in their Menologion on 23 June, where they relate that, when they had perhaps gone to Rome and happened to be present at the noble martyrdom of Saint Agrippina, a virgin who suffered under Diocletian, they secretly received her body and transferred it to Sicily, where it subsequently became renowned through many miracles. From there, however, when they crossed over to Spain, they too obtained the palms of martyrdom at Carthage.

6. At Titulcia, etc. Ambrosius Morales, in Antiquities of Spain, under the heading “Carpetania,” folio 77, asserts that ancient Titulcia was situated where the town of Bayona now stands, near the Royal Green Town of Aranjuez. A little earlier, Aurelio de Frías had held the same opinion; he was a man who had long and successfully occupied himself with investigating the antiquities of Spain. Both men saw that the position given by Ptolemy agreed with this location and that substantial traces remained in the ruins. Ptolemy mentions it among the Carpetani, not far from Mantua.

But what they themselves put forward with some hesitation, [Col. 0463B] we, now enlightened by the authority of Dexter, affirm without hesitation. Since Titulcia was situated where the Tagonius joins the Fenario—commonly called the Henares and the Tajuna—so that they converge into one and the same channel, it is necessary that ancient Titulcia once occupied the site of modern Bayona, which is situated above Aranjuez.

Moreover, the memory of the holy martyrs and abbots Philibert and Fabricianus remains fixed in the Roman Martyrology on 22 August, under these words:

“In Spain, the holy martyrs Fabricianus and Philibert.”

Their feast was celebrated in Spain with no ordinary solemnity, as is clear from the Breviary of Saint Isidore, where on the aforesaid day the following rubric is found:

“Of the holy abbots and martyrs Fabricianus and Philibert: everything is to be said as for several martyrs, with nine lessons.”

The Spanish king Silo also mentions them in a letter to Cixilla, bishop of Toledo, under the Spanish Era 815. He says:

“We send you a hymn concerning the holy martyrs Philibert and his companion, [Col. 0463C] who suffered in the city of Titulcia (whom we have heard were Toledans) under Marcus Aurelius Valentinianus, in the year of the Lord 283, when Melanthius was archbishop of Toledo.”

We gave Silo’s entire letter when discussing Tyrsus under the year 286, where we said a few things about Marcus Aurelius Valentinianus, a man of consular rank and propraetor of Nearer Spain, who, having been sent by the Emperor Carus, continued for some time under Diocletian.

When you hear them called monks or abbots, please do not imagine that they observed the institution of Basil, Augustine, or Benedict, who had not yet been born. Rather, it was that kind of monasticism which took its beginning from Saint Mark, and about which Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, while in Gaul, wrote in his book On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy. Hence we learn that this type of monasticism was introduced into Spain before Saint Antony began gathering and instructing monks, as is readily established from the nativity and year of martyrdom of the holy monks Fabricianus and Philibert, which we also noted above.

[Col. 0463D] 7. At Carthage, etc. The Roman Martyrology treats of Saint Candida and her companions on 20 September, [Col. 0464A] in these words:

“At Carthage, Saint Candida, virgin and martyr, who, under the Emperor Maximian, was torn apart by blows over her entire body and crowned with martyrdom. Likewise, the holy martyrs Susanna, daughter of Arthemius, a priest of idols, and Martha.”

The Greeks also discuss the two latter women in their Menologion on this day. A feast of Saint Candida was formerly celebrated in the Church of Córdoba, as is evident from its Breviary; Baronius and Galesinus took their accounts from its tables.

But let us give their acts, as the Greeks relate them:

“On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Susanna, martyr of Christ, daughter of Arthemius, a priest of idols, and of Martha, who was descended from the Jews. After her parents died, Martha was baptized by the presbyter Sylvanus and instructed in the faith of Christ. She afterward distributed her possessions to the poor and, having abandoned the world, entered a monastery and became a nun. Although dressed in male clothing instead of female attire, she arranged to be called John. Later, after being accused by another woman of having used force against her in a masculine manner, she was discovered to be a virgin in male clothing; and, when her sex was discovered, she refuted the woman who had accused her.

“Having gone to the city of Solia, she was reported [Col. 0464B] to the governor Alexander because she persuaded many pagans not to worship idols. He seized her and tortured her severely. Nevertheless, many were converted to the faith of Christ through her miracles. Finally, after being thrown into prison, she gave her spirit to God.”

Thus far the account.

The presbyter Sylvanus, by whom Saint Martha was instructed in the faith of Christ, was one of those presbyters who attended the Council of Elvira, as is clear from the subscriptions. The city of Solia was situated not far from Carthage; we have discussed it above. In the Greek text it is called Heliopolis—meaning “city of the sun.” In the same way, on 11 November the Greeks speak of Saint Vincent, deacon of Zaragoza and martyr, and say that he suffered at Augustopolis in Spain, as though they were saying “the city of Augustus,” that is, Zaragoza.

8. The relics, etc. The eighth of January is dedicated to Saint Lucian of Beauvais in all the Martyrologies, those of Rome, Bede, Usuard, and Ado. Vincent [Col. 0464C] of Beauvais discusses him in the Historical Mirror, book X, chapter 25; Antoninus, title VI, chapter 26, section 3; and Equilinus, book II, chapter 55. Yet all of them seem to have failed in calling him a presbyter, since he was made bishop of Beauvais by the blessed Dionysius, as Methodius explicitly stated in the Acts of that same Dionysius, about which we have said much in its proper place.

The village mentioned here was formerly called Vicus Aquarius; now it is commonly called Vich in Catalonia.

[Col. 0464D] 9. Of James, etc. The present testimony of Dexter has generated such immense scandal for some people that they have not only declared it false and fictitious but have also attached the same accusation to the entire book, as though it had been fabricated chiefly to commend the mystery of the Immaculate Conception by the testimony of Dexter, a most weighty author.

But, to say this first, Dexter is unjustly deprived of the honor of an entire book and of so much labor because one or another sentence has been found in it to which objection may be made—as though it could not have been corrupted in any part of itself for almost twelve hundred [Col. 0465A] years. They should therefore say, and more readily persuade others, that the codex was corrupted at this point and that such a clause was added by some defender of the Immaculate Conception, rather than that the whole book was fabricated and invented chiefly for that purpose.

Although there are many highly authoritative statements of the holy Fathers in favor of the Immaculate Conception of the Mother of God, about which we have treated elsewhere in a special book printed this year, 1624, at Lyon by Jacob Cardon and Peter Cavellat under the title The Holy Fathers Vindicated in the Cause of the Immaculate Conception, I am nevertheless certain beyond doubt that the present testimony neither harms nor benefits the advocates of either side. It was received by Dexter in a quite different sense from that in which they understand it; it contains a truth so certain that no Catholic can deny it; and it is far from necessary to regard it as foreign to Dexter’s opinion or to believe that it bears the odor of an insufficiently genuine antiquity.

What, then, does it mean? Simply that Saint James instituted in Spain a feast of the Immaculate Incarnation of the Word of God. Who would deny that James did this? He must be exceedingly ignorant [Col. 0465B] who does not know that the holy apostles taught and celebrated throughout the Christian world the Lord’s Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, and likewise his Incarnation. Therefore James too, while preaching the Gospel in Spain, must be believed to have done the same.

This feast of the pure and immaculate Conception of Mary, the Mother of God, is what Dexter calls it, using the word “conception” not in the passive but in the active sense: that is, for the conception by which the Virgin Mother of God, without stain or blemish, conceived the Son of God in her most chaste womb—not for the conception by which she herself was conceived by the blessed Anna.

Nor should anyone think that we are twisting the aforesaid words into a foreign meaning merely because nowadays the word “conception,” when attributed to the blessed Virgin, is understood passively. Many proofs show that formerly it was accustomed to be understood actively. To omit its use in that sense by the Lord when he spoke of the punishment of original sin [Col. 0465C] in Genesis III, in the words “I will multiply your conceptions”—or, as another translation has it, “your pregnancies”—let it suffice to observe that the ancients, when designating the feast of the Conception, did not use the expression “the conception of the Mother of God,” but rather “the conception of Saint Anna.”

Thus the Greeks say in their Menologion on 9 December: “The pure conception of the blessed Anna, the grandmother of God and of our Lord.” This is what we call “the conception of the holy Mother of God.” The Syrians use precisely the same expression in their calendar on 9 December: “The conception of righteous Anna in our Lady, the Mother of God.”

I also read the holy Fathers frequently calling the Virgin’s conception the conception by which she conceived God himself. Thus Bernard, in Sermon 4 on the Vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, says:

“Observe, and you will find conception without seed: what is more glorious than a holy and sincere conception, in which there is nothing shameful, nothing filthy, nothing corrupt?”

And Cyprian—or one of his contemporaries—in his sermon On the Cardinal Works of Christ, On the Nativity, says:

“O righteous Virgin, full of every righteousness, how singular your conception!”

[Col. 0465D] It was singular, of course, because it was accomplished without the seed of a man. He therefore adds: “When the Holy Spirit overshadowed her, the burning of original sin was extinguished”—that is, the lustful itch—and therefore it was not fitting that an innocent woman should be afflicted, and so forth.

Bernard, again, in Homily 4 on “He Was Sent,” calls the Baptist’s conception the conception of Elizabeth. Nor is this surprising, since “conception” is more properly the name of an action than of a passivity.

This is certainly the sense conveyed by those words of the tenth liturgy from the Greeks, published by Claudius Spence:

“We who have obtained joy in your conception, O wholly immaculate one, greet you, crying out with the angel: Hail,” and so forth.

Some, however, wrongly wish to understand these words of passive conception, against the very context, which plainly concerns the angelic Annunciation.

Nor do I think that any other sense is yielded by the words of a certain prayer found in the Breviary of Saint Isidore:

“Lord Jesus Christ, who so honored the Virgin Mother that, through the grace of her conception, we find her before you to be an incomparable intercessor,” and so forth.

We certainly find her to be an intercessor when she conceived the Word of God, not when she was conceived.

Furthermore, the same conclusion follows if it is true that, according to Paul Orosius, a contemporary of Dexter, Mauritius de Villaprobata in his Crown, Mariana in Sermon 16, and Bernardinus de Busti in Sermon 8 On the Conception, part 3, report that Jerome wrote in a certain letter to Saint Eustochium, his disciple:

“Before God I know, and in truth I have found, that no woman suffers danger in childbirth over whom the grace of Mary is devoutly invoked and the day of her conception is celebrated”—that is, because she conceived without shame so that she might give birth without pain.

This was the grace of Mary appropriate to women in danger during childbirth: to seek aid from her who, in the conception of her Son, received the grace of being pregnant without burden and giving birth without pain, as Bernard says somewhere.

[Col. 0466B] Finally, from this point we shall vindicate the Apostolic Canon from the difficult sense in which it is commonly understood. I mean the canon found in the books of Saint Ctesiphon, a disciple of the apostle James, discovered at the Holy Mount of Hipula near Granada together with traces of venerable antiquity. Saint Ctesiphon says that the holy apostles, under an anathema, defined in a certain council that the Virgin Mother of God was preserved, at the very moment of her conception, from every contagion of original sin and made free from every stain of sin.

The author’s words in the book On the Foundation of the Church, as they are commonly circulated, translated from the Arabic in which they were written into Latin, are these:

“That Virgin, that Mary, that holy woman was preserved from original sin at the first moment of her conception and free from every fault. And whoever does not think thus will not attain eternal salvation.”

I do not believe that the words were translated literally. They could be translated even more felicitously and easily, for the words “preserved from original sin at the first moment of her conception” [Col. 0466C] belong to the very recent style of the theologians of our age; it would rather be rendered: “she was freed from the evil of the first origin at the moment of her conception,” or something similar.

But whatever may be said of the translation, the sense is easy and necessary: namely, that all Catholics must embrace and profess, under threat of eternal life or death, that the Virgin Mary, at the very first moment of her conception—when, remaining a virgin, she conceived the Word of God—was preserved from original sin; that is, from the punishments inflicted upon the first woman and upon all others in her because of original guilt, in the words:

“I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions; in sorrow you shall bear children, and you shall be under your husband’s power, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III).

No one who has handled the writings of Scripture and the Fathers even with his fingertips will deny that in them “sin” is very commonly taken to mean punishment.

The fact that this is the legitimate and necessary sense of the canon is shown by the appended anathema. For [Col. 0466D] who would say that people who think contrary to what the apostles taught can be saved? Or that the apostles could have erred in issuing canons? Yet many have so far been saved without faith in the mystery of passive conception.

Moreover, why would the apostles issue a canon concerning a matter that was neither necessary nor disputed among the heretics of their time? If it were necessary for salvation, Paul, when he wrote so extensively to the Romans about original sin, would certainly also have mentioned it.

The apostles, therefore, were far from the sense that some attribute to this canon. When they defined something altogether necessary for salvation—such as the mystery of the immaculate conception by which the Word of God, through the power of the Holy Spirit, became man—and when all the words appear to fit that meaning, there is no reason to twist them into foreign [Col. 0467A] senses that cannot stand with the truth. By doing so we inflict a manifest injury upon the sacred books and force them to be rejected among the apocryphal and worthless, whereas we ought to direct all our efforts toward finding in them only a doctrine worthy of the apostles.

I understand the council at which this canon was issued to have been none other than the council which the apostles held when they were about to depart from one another, at which they composed the Creed. I understand the canon to be none other than the words of the Creed: “And was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.” Saint Ctesiphon extracted the sense of this statement, perhaps using the words in which the apostles defined it before formally constructing the Creed. For before they composed the form of faith with complete precision, it is likely that the apostles discussed its mysteries more fully and spoke many words besides those contained in the Creed.

I believe that Ctesiphon meant nothing different when he said elsewhere that “the first sin did not touch Mary”—by “sin,” I mean the punishment of Eve’s first sin [Col. 0467B] inflicted upon her daughters: namely, because she neither conceived with sorrows nor gave birth with pain.

To explain this fully, it is necessary to add here the preceding words, from which the mind of Saint Ctesiphon may more easily be understood. In book I, entitled The Foundation of the Church, after treating systematically of all the dogmas of the Christian faith, and after discussing most exactly the creation and fall of the angels, the formation of the first parents of the human race, and their sin, which was propagated to all human beings, he finally proceeded to explain human redemption. In section 24 he says:

“Jesus was sent into Mary from the house of David, without a man; and she was a virgin after childbirth, as she was during it and before it.”

To explain this, he immediately adds in section 25:

“Adam was created without parents, and Eve from a father without a mother, in grace. Section 26: For the perfection of the creature”—another version has “of creation”—“Jesus was created in the mother without a father; therefore the first guilt did not apprehend [Col. 0467C] Mary.”

More skilled Arabists agree on this translation, except that, in place of the particle “therefore,” for which the original Arabic text has *Hinda delique*, someone translates “then”; and in place of the verb “apprehended,” some translate “comprehended,” while others translate “touched.” However it may be taken, everything comes to the same point.

For what Saint Ctesiphon had undertaken to prove in section 24 was not the preservation of the Mother of God from original sin in her formation, but her perpetual virginity, as the words themselves make clear:

“Jesus was sent into Mary without a man; and she was a virgin after childbirth, as she was during it and before it.”

How this should be understood he suggests by examples from the procreation of the first parents. Adam was made without father or mother; Eve came from a father—that is, from the man’s rib—without the cooperation of a mother. What wonder, then, if the new Adam, Jesus, was made from a mother alone, without the agency of a father?

Indeed, for the perfection of the creature or creation, as another reading has it, it was fitting that some new human being should be formed from a mother without the aid of a father. Thus all conceivable modes of generation would exist in the world: with father and mother, as we are all born; without father and mother, as Adam alone was formed; from the father only, as Eve was; and finally from the mother without [Col. 0467D] the father, which the Lord Jesus alone chose for himself.

Theologians commonly use this argument from the Fathers. From it, in turn, the article of Catholic faith concerning Mary’s perpetual virginity follows most correctly and immediately, which was the author’s intention: namely, that she conceived and gave birth as a virgin.

But that she was preserved from the first guilt was neither relevant to the point nor immediately inferred; it followed only very remotely. More importantly, it was not a matter of faith, whereas his purpose was to treat only of the articles of faith.

[Col. 0468A] “But,” you say, “does he not speak most clearly of the first guilt, which without doubt was original sin?” I admit that he does, but nevertheless he speaks of it in the sense in which its absence is necessarily connected with perpetual virginity: namely, so that by the name “first guilt,” or “the first and original sin,” is understood the sentence once inflicted by God upon Eve and all her daughters:

“I will multiply your conceptions and your sorrows; in sorrow you shall bear children, and you shall be under your husband’s power” (Gen. III).

This sentence neither comprehended nor touched Mary in whole or in part, precisely because she conceived the Lord without a man. The translator expressed this clearly when he wrote: “And then the first guilt did not apprehend Mary.” For, at the incarnation of the divine Word, it was not the time for formal original guilt to be contracted, but for the punishment and sentence due to it.

If, however, we translate not “then” but “therefore,” “wherefore,” or something similar—for *Hinda delique* is an inferential particle—the same sense cannot fail to be conveyed. It indicates that the fact that original sin did not apprehend Mary necessarily follows from what has just been said: “Jesus was begotten in the mother without a father.” This is the article [Col. 0468B] concerning the Virgin Mother, from which it follows by necessary consequence that, in the generation of her Son, she suffered no sorrows, in childbirth no pains, and that she was not subjected to a man. This is to say: “Therefore the first sin did not touch Mary.”

To this may be added that precisely the same statement is found very frequently in the other books of that holy mountain, so that anyone may easily understand that Saint Ctesiphon meant nothing else here. In one of those books it is asserted that the curse of Eve—“you shall be under your husband’s power”—did not comprehend Mary; in another, that the afflictions of pregnant women were far from her, concerning which the curse had said, “I will multiply your conceptions and your sorrows.” For, to use Bernard’s words, she bore without burden and gave birth to the Son without pain.

Finally, another passage asserts that the angel would in no way have said to her, “Hail, full of grace,” and so forth, if the first [Col. 0468C] sin had comprehended her. Here, as you see, the subject is Mary at the time of the angelic Annunciation, when she was not capable of original guilt but only of its punishment.

Here, then, is the genuine interpretation of the sacred books, according to which no doctrine of the Virgin’s preservation from original sin at her own conception, and nothing contrary to apostolic teaching, is imposed upon them.

To return, therefore, to Dexter: let it henceforth be certain to everyone that he meant nothing else here than that the Spaniards received the feast of the angelic Annunciation from their apostle James.

This also agrees with what we read in Augustine, Rufinus, and others: when the apostles composed the Creed in sections, Peter first said, “I believe in God the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth”; Andrew said, “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord”; and our James, in third place, added the clause, “And was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.” This evidently indicates that this mystery had always been sweeter to him than the others. For this reason he arranged for the first temple to be erected at Zaragoza in its honor, as M. Maximus splendidly sang in the hymn he composed on the erection of that temple, where he says:

[Col. 0468D] > She showed herself gracious to him  
> *(the Mother of God to James)*  
>   
> And at her feast-day  
>   
> Of the golden Conception,  
>   
> Temple dedications endure [reading uncertain].  
>   
> From this day of the Conception  
>   
> James teaches the Spaniards;  
>   
> And he proclaims it, as do the other apostles,  
>   
> Free from every stain  
>   
> *(that is, a conception accomplished without seed).*

That Maximus is speaking of conception understood actively is sufficiently proved by his assertion that James proclaimed that conception free from sins which the other apostles proclaimed free from every stain. Everyone can see that this is the active conception of the Virgin. [Col. 0469A]

This is shown even more clearly by what he adds:

> From this the custom has its beginning,  
>   
> Of continually celebrating this day  
>   
> Among the Iberian peoples,  
>   
> Which endures even to this day.

Whose feast of conception lasted from the beginnings of the Catholic Church to the author’s time, and afterward, if not the active conception?

Certainly the epithets used by Dexter—“pure” and “immaculate”—properly belong to it, since the Church has sufficiently adopted them, both in that hymn:

> Remember, Author of salvation,  
>   
> That once, in being born  
>   
> From an undefiled Virgin,  
>   
> You took the form of our body, [Col. 0469B]

and in the responsory:

> Holy and immaculate virginity,  
>   
> With what praises shall we extol you? …

Finally, we are led to the same conclusion by the particular and heartfelt devotion which the Spaniards formerly had toward the mystery of virginal conception. Not content with honoring it through the common ecclesiastical feast on 25 April, the Tenth Council of Toledo established a second celebration of it on 18 December, since the earlier feast fell during Lent.

The devotion to this mystery was therefore so deeply rooted in the hearts of the Spaniards that it both demonstrates that they received it from that great teacher of theirs and especially commends it in the erection of the Pillar at Zaragoza. But enough has been said, since these remarks seem sufficient for understanding Dexter.

11. At Ulyssipona, etc. Also called Ulyssipona, after its founder Ulysses, and commonly Lisbon, it is adorned no less—indeed, much more—with the blood of its holy citizens Verissimus, Maxima, and Julia than with the daily treasures brought there from the Orient [Col. 0469C] Indies. They died under the ministers of Diocletian on the Kalends of October, on which day they are commemorated in all the Martyrologies. Since these most celebrated martyrs and siblings are known to everyone, there is no reason to prolong our discussion of them. Let Morales, book X, chapter 14, Villegas, Trugillus, and the others be consulted.

I myself read their acts in a very ancient parchment manuscript in the Library of Saint Bernard of Toledo, number 64, beginning: “In those times, when throughout all the provinces,” and so forth.

12. In the same place, etc. You should understand that, together with Dexter, these same people are again discussed under the year 353, but here they are mentioned incidentally and by way of anticipation, since the subject was the holy martyrs of Ulyssipona, whose fellow citizens these too were. Therefore the words “they are celebrated” should not be referred to the time under discussion in the Chronicle, but to the time of the writer.

13. At Secura, etc. The pass of Secura—commonly called the Sierra de Segura—is famous on the borders of Tarraconensis and Baetica [Col. 0469D] in Spain. From it two rivers spring forth: the Baetis toward the west and the Tader toward the east.

Concerning [Col. 0470A] the latter, Hieronymus Paulus writes in his book On the Rivers of Spain:

“The river Tader flows toward New Carthage. It rises in the mountains touched by the Baetis; passing Murcia and Aureola, now called Orihuela, it empties into the Ebusitan or Iberian Sea. The common people call it the Segura.”

Morales gives nearly the same account in his Antiquities, under the headings “Mentesa,” folio 72, and “Ilorci,” folio 81. Pliny discusses the same river in book III, chapters 1 and 3; and, if we may trust Villanueva, Ptolemy calls it the Terebis.

Near its sources there is still a place called Castel Segura, a rural settlement preserving the memory of ancient Secura.

Moreover, Saint Briena is discussed at length in the Life of Saint Febronia, written by Thomais, a disciple of both women, preserved by Metaphrastes, and published by Surius in volume III under 15 June, the day on which Saint Febronia’s feast is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology, where she is said to have suffered under Diocletian.

The material that Dexter writes here about Saint Briena is absent from that work, perhaps because the events that occurred in Spain, where Saint Briena suffered, could not have reached the notice of Thomais, who was situated in Syria. Nevertheless, that she was always famous [Col. 0470B] in Spain is at least proved by the fact that many women, borrowing their name from her with only slight alteration, are called Briandas.

### 14. At Munda, etc.

That exceedingly famous city of Munda was made renowned throughout the world by the war which Julius Caesar undertook against the younger Gnaeus Pompey. In that battle such slaughter was inflicted on both sides that Caesar, after his victory, besieging the enemy who had fled into the city, constructed a rampart from the piled-up corpses. Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 18, on the testimony of Dio, book XLIII, further asserts the no less portentous fact that from that time a palm-shoot arose there: whenever stones bearing a palm were broken, they were found.

According to the same authority, Munda was a Roman colony; Morales observed this in the ancient coins, book VIII of his *History*, chapter 44. Silius once wrote of it:

> “And Munda, destined once more to produce Emathian struggles.”

It still preserves almost its ancient name, being now called Monda, at the foot of the pass of Tolox near Cartima, five Spanish miles distant from Murcia. It lay either on the borders of the Bastetani and Celtiberians, as Ptolemy holds, or among the Celtiberians themselves, as Dexter prefers—unless one would rather count the Bastetani among the Celtiberians. See Nonius, in his *Spain*, chapter 28.

Moreover, the memory of Saint Felicianus, who suffered there, is preserved in the Roman Martyrology on 20 October and in Molanus’s additions to Usuard. In these, however, a correction is needed: they read *Minda* instead of *Munda*, as follows:

> “At Minda, the birthday of Saint Felicianus, bishop and martyr.”

The reading should be “At Munda, etc.” Baronius also suspected this in his notes, although, because he lacked Dexter’s manuscript, he did not entirely attain the true reading. We now possess it from Dexter, together with the time of the martyrdom and the name of the city over which he presided, namely Málaga.

In the old Breviary of Córdoba, Saint Felicianus the martyr is celebrated on 21 July; Galesinus also commemorates him on that day, saying:

> “At Córdoba in Spain, Saint Felicianus the martyr.”

Father Roa likewise writes of him in his *Cordoban Saints*. I believe that he is different from our bishop, as can sufficiently be inferred from the city and the ecclesiastical rank.

### 15. At Baeta, etc.

It was so called from the river Baetis, which flows nearby—or, if one prefers the reverse explanation, because the river received its name from the city. From the position of the province, however, since it lies almost at the navel or in the middle of the womb of Baetica, it received the name *Utriculi*. It is now called Utrera and lies between Seville and Marchena.

The Greeks celebrate in their *Menologion*, on 9 September, the feast of Saint Strato, who suffered there, and of Rufinus and others. On that day the Roman Martyrology has:

> “On the same day, the passion of Saint Strato, who, bound to two trees and torn apart, completed his martyrdom for Christ. Likewise, of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Rufinianus, brothers.”

I read *Rufinianus* with the Greeks. Galesinus, following the same Greek sources, says on 8 September:

> “Of the holy brothers and martyrs Rufinus and Rufinianus, who were struck with the sword for their confession of the faith. Likewise, of Saint Artemidorus the martyr, who, cast into the flames, gave a splendid testimony to his admirable piety and faith. Likewise, of Saint Severus the martyr, who endured every torment for Christ and at last, by the strength of his steadfast courage, offered his neck.”

Thus far Galesinus. Yet he is mistaken when he says that Saint Strato suffered at Nicomedia with others on 17 September. He inserted this on his own authority, without a source, for the Greeks say nothing of the kind. Their words are:

> “The birthday of Blessed Strato, who, bound to two cedars and cut into two parts, was joined to the heavenly ones for his confession of Christ. On the same day, the contest of Saints Rufus and Rufinianus, who, being brothers by birth, were struck with the sword for their confession of the Christian faith. Saint Severus also suffered in the same way. On the same day Saint Artemidorus was consumed by fire.”

This is what they say for 9 September. As for the other holy martyrs Rufus and Rufinianus, from the city of Apollonia, the Greeks speak of them on 17 June and 6 July. It is therefore demonstrated that they are entirely different from our martyrs.

### 16. At Ispali, etc.

This is a very different city from that celebrated Seville of the province of Baetica. Orthelius confesses that he did not know its location on the map of ancient Spain, but Dexter identifies it. Certainly Pliny mentions the peoples of Ispalum in Tarraconensian Spain, in book III; they must have been situated far from the Seville of Baetica.

The Roman Martyrology speaks of the holy martyrs who suffered there on 10 September in these words:

> “Likewise, the holy martyrs Apellius, Lucas, and Clement.”

The Greeks, in their *Menologion*, and Galesinus following them, speak on 9 September of Theodore and Oceanus, who, placed in the fire for the faith of Christ, “attained eternal glory by an outstanding testimony of true and divine piety,” as Galesinus puts it. Consult the following note.

### 17. At Tucci, etc.

All writers agree that the city of Tucci stood where Peña de Martos now stands, near Jaén. Above all, consult Morales, book IX, chapter 32; Orthelius; Clusius; Stephanus; and others. Ptolemy also mentions it among the Turduli of Baetica.

It was formerly a Roman colony and, under the law of the Gospel, an episcopal see subject to the metropolitan of Seville. Its bishop Camerinus took part in the Council of Iliberis.

As for the holy martyrs crowned there, the Greeks speak of them in their *Menologion* on 4 September, and the Roman Martyrology has:

> “Likewise, the holy martyrs Theodore, Oceanus, Ammianus, and Julianus, who, their feet having been cut apart, were cast into the fire and completed their martyrdom under the emperor Maximian.”

Galesinus gives a fuller account of their sufferings, in these words:

> “The holy martyrs Theodore, Oceanus, Ammianus, and Julianus. Under the emperor Maximian, they were first flayed with combs for the Lord Christ; then, after being cast into boiling baths, they escaped from them unharmed by divine aid. Seized again afterward and led into a vast wilderness, each of their limbs was cut off and their legs were broken; then, placed in the fire, they went up to heaven while continually praying to God.”

It follows from this that the name of Saint Ammianus is missing from Dexter’s manuscript, since all authorities name him among the martyrs just mentioned.

Whether Theodore and Oceanus, who suffered at Tucci, are the same as Theodore and Oceanus of Seville, whom we discussed recently, may rightly be questioned. Yet, however much their names agree, the difference between the cities in which they were killed, together with Dexter’s testimony, makes it sufficiently clear that they are different men. For the moment I omit the fact that the former were crowned with martyrdom on 9 September, while the latter were crowned on the 4th of the same month. The Greeks agree with this also, as can be seen in the *Menologion*.

### 18. At Tarragona, etc.

The holy martyr Maginus—whom some incorrectly call Magnus and others Maximus—is commemorated with distinction in the Roman Martyrology on 25 August, in these words:

> “At Tarragona, Saint Maginus the martyr,”

where, of course, his feast is celebrated with solemn rites.

Master Ludovicus Icarte, in his account of Tarragona, as reported by Beuterus and asserted by Morales, book IX, chapter 43, says that Maginus lived as a solitary in a cave in the Bufagrana wilderness, six Spanish miles from the city. He was seized by the governor and brought to Tarragona, where he was thrown into prison. Yet he was divinely rescued from there and restored to his former cave. Captured again, tortured in various ways, and finally beheaded, he departed victoriously into heaven.

They are mistaken, however, when they read *Maximinus* instead of the emperor Maximian and consequently assign his death to the year of the Lord 240, whereas Dexter makes clear that he was killed under Maximian around the year 308.

The faithful still venerate Saint Maginus’s cave and visit it with pious devotion, since God glorifies it with daily miracles through the merits of the holy martyr. Marieta also writes of him, book II, part I, chapter 43; as do Mariana, book IV, chapter 9; Trugillus, in the *Treasury*; and many others.

### 19. In the city of Capara, etc.

The place still retains the name of the city and is called Caparra, with the doubled *r*. We discussed it above under the year 86.

The Roman Martyrology contains an honorable mention of Saint Mark the martyr and his companions on 3 July, in these words:

> “On the same day, the holy martyrs Mark and Mucianus, who were struck down with the sword for Christ. When a very young boy warned them in a loud voice not to sacrifice to idols, he was ordered to be beaten with rods; and when he confessed Christ still more fervently, he was killed together with a certain Paul, who was encouraging the martyrs.”

The Greeks give a fuller account of the same acts in their *Menologion*.

### 20. In Spain, etc.

For Juliobriga and the port of Juliobriga, consult what we said under the year 300, commentary 2, number 3, when discussing Saint Lucia, a citizen of that city.

The Greeks give an extensive account in their *Menologion* of Saint Ananias and many other holy martyrs who were his companions. From them Galesinus inserted the following into his Martyrology under 27 January:

> “On the same day, Saint Ananias the martyr, who, under Caesar Diocletian and before the prefect Maximus, voluntarily professed the Christian faith and vehemently attacked the worship of idols. Accordingly, he was seized and first beaten with rods; then he was pierced with red-hot awls. Afterward, his wounds were rubbed with salt and vinegar, and he was confined in prison so that he might be killed there by hunger. But it came to pass by divine providence that for seven days he was nourished with heavenly food. When Peter, the prison guard, observed this, he abandoned his impiety and embraced the Christian religion. For this reason, by order of the prefect, he was bound to a wheel together with Ananias and both were placed upon a gridiron. A fire was lit beneath them; but when it was suddenly and miraculously extinguished, the torturers, perceiving the wonder of what had occurred, openly confessed Christ as God. Thus the seven men, together with Ananias and Peter, were thrown into the sea and attained the palm of martyrdom.”

Thus far the acts as given by Galesinus.

### 21. At Pamia, etc.

Modern writers committed a very serious error when they believed that Saint Antoninus, a citizen of Palencia, was Gallic by birth and descent. They had read in the acts of his martyrdom that he was born and killed at Pamia, or Apamia; since they did not know of a city of that name in Spain but did know one in Gaul, they assigned that city to the martyr.

It is surprising that they did not assign him to Apamia in Syria, since the name is the same in both cases and the Syrian city is the more famous. But Dexter now dispels the darkness by demonstrating that Pamia was in the territory of the Vaccaei, on the river Arlanza, where the city of Palencia now stands; and that Antoninus was born and killed at Pamia, and nowhere else than where the city now lies.

Certainly, how long his body has lain at Palencia exceeds human memory, since no one anywhere knows that it was brought from elsewhere. His church celebrates its discovery but knows nothing of a translation. He was placed beneath the earth in his tomb during the disaster inflicted on Spain by the Moors, on account of the violence of the times; after they had been subdued, this heavenly treasure was found again.

The acts of the martyr also omit the name of Gaul. They are too well known to be repeated here. They are found in Saint Antoninus of Florence, *Historical Part*, I, title 8, chapter 1; in Equilinus, book VIII, chapter 24; in Mombritius, volume I; and in the Breviary of Palencia. The word “Gaul,” however, should be removed from the latter and from the Roman Martyrology, since the old manuscripts of the latter, as well as the Martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Ado, and the modern Martyrology of Galesinus, lack it.

Baronius was misled by the modern registers of Palencia, which he himself cites. Galesinus gives the following brief epitome:

> “At Apamia, Saint Antoninus the martyr, whose head was cut off for Christ Jesus and whose body was torn limb from limb in the final persecution of the emperor Diocletian.”

### 22. At Emerita, etc.

She is a very well-known virgin, celebrated in the writings of the Spaniards: Vasaeus, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 306; Morales, book X, chapter 10; Marieta, book IV, chapter 64; Trugillus, Villegas, and Sanctorius, under 23 November. On that day the Roman Martyrology says:

> “At Emerita in Spain, Saint Lucretia, virgin and martyr, who completed her martyrdom under the governor Dacian during the persecution of Diocletian.”

Usuard also speaks of her on the same day, as does Equilinus, book II, chapter 130, number 330.

### 23. Ega brought, etc.

Consult what we noted above concerning Saint Catherine under the year 300, commentary 3.

### 24. At Pax Augusta, etc.

We settled the old and stubborn controversy concerning the location of this city in the notes under the year 64, and proved that it was not Beja in Portugal but Badajoz in Extremadura, in the kingdom of Castile. It would be tedious to repeat everything.

The sacred names of Saints Vincentius, Orentius, and Victor are recorded in the Roman Martyrology on 22 January, where they are said to have been crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian. Bede, Usuard, and Ado likewise have this account.

The acts, written by Aetherius, bishop of Embrun, were published from manuscript sources by Surius, volume I. Equilinus abridged them as follows, book II, chapter 112:

> “Vincentius and Orentius suffered martyrdom in Spain during the reigns of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, under Rufinus, governor of the Spains. This Rufinus had crowned Saint Cucuphas at Barcelona while serving as Dacian’s legate. Inflamed by the ardor of faith, they voluntarily presented themselves before the judge and courageously confessed Christ; by order of the governor they were condemned to death. A certain Victor, a Levite who had received them as guests, buried their bodies. For this reason he too was seized by the judge; his arms were cut off at the elbows, and he was ordered to be beheaded in the same place where they had suffered. When Victor’s father, who was himself a Christian, saw this, he took flight. But, urged by his wife Aquilina, he returned and was beheaded together with his son.
>
> “Pontius the bishop, warned by divine revelation, placed all their bodies on a wagon and was carrying them back to their former regions in Italy. When they reached the vicinity of the city of Embrun, the oxen stopped and were unable to go any farther. There the bodies of the martyrs were buried, the will of God having thereby been made known.”

Everything agrees with Dexter’s statements. What the Martyrologies say—“At Embrun in Gaul, the holy martyrs, etc.”—must be understood not of the place of martyrdom but of the place of burial and celebration.

The brothers of Saint Victor, whom Dexter calls companions of Saints Vincentius and Orentius, are also omitted from the Martyrologies. See concerning them Morales, book X, chapter 14, and Marieta, part I, book II, chapter 39.

### 25. At the See of Peter, etc.

Having ended the succession of the Roman pontiffs with Marcellinus in the year of the Lord 296, he now continues it as far as Saint Sylvester, who succeeded Saint Melchiades, Spanish by homeland—of Marava in Carpetania—but African by descent.

We have treated Melchiades sufficiently under the years 248 and 299, and shall do so again under the year 311.

Saint Marcellinus was taken away by martyrdom in the year 304, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, after having held the see for almost eight years. Saint Marcellus was killed for the Lord in the year 309, after the fifth year of his pontificate. Saint Eusebius continued his pontificate into the year 311, until 26 September of that year. Saint Melchiades continued until the year 313, on 10 December, and sat for three years, seven months, and eight days.

This entire chronology agrees with Baronius’s *Annals*.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At the city of Martula [or Mertile] in Lusitania, as is established from the Martyrology of Eusebius of Caesarea, which he composed at the command of the emperor Constantine, Saint Bricius, believed to have been bishop of Évora, was seized by Marcianus, governor of Lusitania, and endured many sufferings for his confession of the faith.

He also preached at Castulo, near the river Tagus, which flows past that city. Then, returning to Segisamo, a city of the Vaccaei, where he had preached earlier, he preached there again. After traversing almost the whole of Spain, he returned to Martula and was seized by the aforementioned judge.

He was then tortured on the rack, afterward cast into prison, and then, when a violent earthquake arose throughout the city and a wall collapsed, Marcianus was crushed beneath it. Saint Bricius was then led out of the public prison by Peter—some believe him to have been bishop of Braga—and encouraged by an angel.

Preaching far and wide throughout Baetica, Lusitania, and Tarraconensian Spain, he returned to his own city and, full of days and holy works, departed victoriously to heaven on the seventh day before the Ides of July. Those standing by testified that his soul flew away like a most radiant dove, enriched by the most beautiful merits.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Serpa in Baetica flourished the holy martyrs Proculus and Hilarion, whom the Greeks also celebrate because of the glory of their holiness. They suffered under the emperor Trajan and the governor Marcus Aurelius.

Proculus was first burned on the shoulders and belly with torches; afterward, wounded by repeated blows from weapons, he died. Hilarion, after various torments, finally completed his martyrdom by decapitation.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

In the Lusitanian city of Calles, situated near Castralaelia, Saint Wilgefortis flourished; she suffered death for the faith and for chastity.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Urgabona in Baetica, under the governor Dacian, the martyrs Bonosus and Maximinus.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Carthage Spartaria, under Dacian, governor of Spain and Gaul, the holy virgins, brides, and martyrs of Christ—Bassa, Paula, and Agathonica—who, victorious, obtained a double crown.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Titulcia in Carpetania, near the city of Thermeda, the holy martyrs and monks of Christ, Philibertus and Fabritianus, who dedicated to God Almighty and to the Blessed Virgin the monastery of Tagonium, at the confluence of the Fenarius and Tagonius rivers.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Carthage in Spain, Saint Candida, virgin and martyr, who, miserably torn by blows, finally suffered martyrdom together with Susanna, the daughter of a priest of the idols, and Martha.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

The relics of Saint Lucianus, bishop of Beauvais, are transferred to Vicus.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

Through the preaching of James, the feast of the immaculate and undefiled Conception of Mary, the Mother of God, is celebrated in Spain.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Ulyssippo in Lusitania, the holy martyrs of Christ Verissimus, Maxima, and Julia, sisters of the same martyr and fellow-participants in his martyrdom.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

In the same place, Anastasius the presbyter, Placidus, and Genesius are also celebrated.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Secura, on the border of Baetica, which is also called the Tader, Saint Briena, companion of Saint Febronia. She came to the Spains and suffered in the province of Tarragona, where she is held in greater honor.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At the city of Munda in Celtiberia, Saint Felicianus, bishop of Málaga and an outstanding martyr of Christ.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Baeta, a city in Hispania Baetica, also called Baetis Utriculum, Saint Strato, martyr of Christ, who was bound between two trees. When they were torn apart, he was dismembered for the name of Christ and flew away to heaven. In the same place were the holy martyrs, citizens and brothers, Rufinus, Rufinianus, Artemidorus, and Severus.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Ispali, near Gaul, in the Pyrenean mountains of Spain, the holy martyrs Theodore, Oceanus, Apellius, Lucas, and Clement.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Tucci in Hispania Baetica, now also called Torisia, the holy martyrs Theodore, Oceanus, and Julianus, who, their legs having been broken, were cast into the fire and gloriously crowned.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Tarragona in Spain, Saint Maginus, who, after enduring many torments for Christ, flew with joyful spirit to the glorious palm of martyrdom.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

In the city of Capara, a city of Lusitania, Saint Mark and his companions.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

In Spain, at the port of Juliobriga, Saint Ananias the martyr and his companions, who prevailed after enduring many torments.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Pamia in Tarraconensian Spain, in the town of the Vaccaei on the river Arlanza, the passion of Saint Antoninus the martyr.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Emerita Augusta in Lusitania, Saint Lucretia, virgin and martyr.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

Ega brought from the East the memory of Saint Catherine into Spain.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At Pax Augusta, situated on the river Ana, the triumph of the holy martyrs Vincentius, Orentius, and others; Pontius Paulinus having been divinely warned, their bodies, through the ministry of angels, came to rest at the city of Embrun.

## A.D. 308. A.R. 1059

At the See of Peter, Marcellinus succeeded Caius; Marcellus succeeded Marcellinus; Eusebius succeeded Marcellus; Melchiades succeeded Eusebius. Melchiades was Spanish by homeland and birth, but African by descent. Saint Sylvester succeeded Melchiades; under him, during the reign of the emperor Constantine, happiness and golden peace returned to the Churches.

## [Note: [Col. 0475A]]

### A.D. 310—1. Constantius, etc.

When Vopiscus and Eutropius speak of the abdication of the empire by Diocletian and Maximian, they say:

> “Thus the empire was divided, so that Constantius Chlorus governed Gaul, Spain, Italy, and Africa, while Galerius governed Illyricum, Greece, and the East.”

That Chlorus deserved extremely well of Spain is demonstrated by the mitigation of the persecution. Under his rule no one is recorded as having been crowned with martyrdom. Indeed, as Eusebius writes in book I of the *Life of Constantine*, he expelled from his palace those who denied that they were Christians although they were, while those who confessed that they were Christians he honored, considering them faithful to himself because they were faithful to God.

At Córdoba there remains an inscription carved in stone, which Morales, book X, chapter 18, and others report:

> “To the most valiant and most indulgent prince, our lord Constantius, perpetual victor, always Augustus. Decimius Germinianus, most illustrious man, governor of the province of Baetica, most devoted to his name and majesty.”

As for the duration of Constantius’s reign, some assign him only two or three years. Eusebius, however, agrees with Dexter, who assigns him sixteen years. In his *Chronicle*, Eusebius has the following words under this very year of Christ 310:

> “Constantius died at York in Britain in the sixteenth year of his reign. After him his son Constantine, etc.”

### 2. About thirty, etc.

This clause, which belonged to the year 310, had been placed in the year 110 through the error of copyists; compelled by the sequence of the dates, we have moved it.

Porphyry lived in the time of the emperor Aurelian, being a disciple of Plotinus and a fellow student of Origen. Eusebius and Apollinaris of Laodicea, however, lived in the time of Constantius and Constantine.

Jerome mentions some of those who wrote against Porphyry in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Concerning Eusebius, he says in his catalogue of works:

> “Against Porphyry, who was writing at the same time in Sicily, as some believe, thirty books; of these only twenty have reached me.”

Concerning Apollinaris he says:

> “There exist his works against Porphyry, which, among his other writings, are held in especially high esteem.”

Of Methodius he writes:

> “Methodius, bishop first of Olympus in Lycia and afterward of Tyre, composed books against Porphyry in polished and well-ordered language, etc.”

But alas! how many of the scholarly labors of our forefathers have perished!

### 3. Natalis, etc.

Natalis is mentioned in the catalogue of the bishops of Toledo published by Loaysa. That catalogue is defective, however, in making him the successor of Paulatus, since he actually assumed the episcopate after Melanthius.

His name also appears after Melanthius in the diptychs of the Missal of Saint Isidore. The printing of Cardinal Ximénez must nevertheless be corrected, since it names Melanthius twice; at the second occurrence Natalis should be written, as follows:

> “For the spirits of Pausantius, Honoratus, Pelagius, Quintinus, Vincentius, Paulatus, Melanthius, Natalis, Georgius, Olympius, etc.”

He took part in the Council of Iliberis and subscribed as the second among the presbyters in these words:

> “Natalis of Orsuna,”

which indicates that at that time he was the presbyter of that city.

Constantius Chlorus Augustus, who had deserved exceedingly well of Spain, died in Britain after the sixteenth year of his reign.

## A.D. 310. A.R. 1061

Approximately thirty Catholic writers wrote against the blasphemies of the philosopher Porphyry. Among them were several Spaniards.

Natalis, bishop of Toledo, succeeded the most holy confessor Melanthius, who, in keeping with the circumstances of that age, suffered greatly in defense of the Catholic Church against heretics and pagans.
