## [Note: [Col. 0475D]]

### A.D. 311—1. The council, etc.

No one whom I have seen, apart from Dexter, mentions this council. Yet it is sufficiently established from a letter of Saint Melchiades the pope—preserved in volume I of the Councils—that a certain synod was held by the bishops of Spain at this time. In that letter he replies to Marinus, Leontius, Benedictus, and the other bishops of Spain concerning what they had asked about the qualifications of bishops and the sacrament of Extreme Unction.

This was under the consuls Datus Rubrius and Volusianus, whose consulship falls in the year of Christ 314. Consult also Morales under this same year, book X.

Nevertheless, this has nothing in common with the council mentioned here, since the bishops referred very different matters to Pope Melchiades from those which Dexter says were treated in such a council at Toledo.

What those matters were can be inferred from the acts of Iliberis itself, for in its defense the council was evidently convened. It seemed extremely harsh that any Christian should be denied Holy Communion not merely for a long period but for all the days of his life, and be deprived of the heavenly viaticum at the point of death. This was especially so because the council ordered this most severe penalty not only for perpetrators of idolatry, magic, and similar grave crimes, but also for those who, after baptism, fell once or twice into the contagion of adultery.

This is clear from canon 7, where we read:

> “If, after falling into adultery and after the appointed period, someone who has done penance should again commit fornication, it has been decided that he shall not receive Communion even at the end.”

This penalty was imposed twenty times for various crimes in the same canons of the council. What wonder, then, if many thought it harsh and, when the people became disorderly, it was necessary to convene another council concerning these matters?

Perhaps other articles also seemed to require explanation or modification, such as the provision established by canon 34:

> “It has been decided that candles should not be lit in the cemetery during the day.”

And what is added in the following canon, 35:

> “It has been decided to prohibit women from keeping vigil in the cemetery.”

And again what canon 36 adds:

> “It has been decided that there ought to be no paintings in a church.”

This did not, of course, prohibit the use of profane images but, as it seems, of sacred ones, as the following words indicate:

> “So that what is worshiped and adored may not be painted on the walls.”

These regulations appeared to prohibit actions that were, in fact, noble expressions of Christianity.

I therefore think that the following event arose from this situation. Augustine relates in book I *Against the Letter of Parmenianus* that Hosius, whose zeal had burned brilliantly in that council, was hated by certain people and falsely accused before the Spanish bishops of many crimes. Their accusations grew so powerful that he eventually received from them a sentence of condemnation. Once the envy and malice of his adversaries had been exposed, however, he was acquitted by the bishops of Gaul—undoubtedly those gathered at the Council of Arles, as Mendoza learnedly argues—with the Spanish Fathers likewise consenting to the same acquittal.

The fact that the condemnation of Hosius mentioned above took place in this Council of Toledo is demonstrated by both the timing and the cause. Augustine relates the matter in the cited book, chapter 4, on the occasion that the Donatists—whom Hosius had formerly harassed as their chief opponent, since he was a defender of Caecilianus—were boasting of Hosius’s condemnation. Augustine’s words are:

> “As for what they say about Hosius of Córdoba, they must be required to prove not only that he was such a man as they claim—for this could be proved by hired false witnesses—but also that it was manifest to those with whom they assert that he communicated that he was such a man. Unless they prove this, they say in vain that they knew what he was like, because he could not harm those who did not know. By separating themselves from those innocent men, they cannot be innocent on account of the sacrilegious wickedness of that separation.
>
> “This is the more credible if Hosius, having been condemned by the Spaniards, was acquitted by the Gauls. It could have happened that the Spaniards, deceived by false accusers and ensnared by the cunning fraud of their plots, pronounced sentence against an innocent man, and afterward, peacefully and in Christian humility, yielded to the judgment of their colleagues, to whom his innocence had been demonstrated.”

And shortly afterward:

> “They never revealed so openly why they refused to be corrected even after separation as when they denounce the Spaniards because, after their sentences had been pronounced, they yielded to inquiry and to a later judgment. For just as the latter action proceeded from Christian gentleness, so the former proceeded from diabolical contentiousness.”

As for the cause of the great hatred conceived by his adversaries against Hosius, I infer that it was his zeal, which burned against sinners and the wicked. For in the same Augustine, chapter 8 of the aforementioned book, I read that his enemies branded him with the charge of cruelty, as though, guided by suspicions, he customarily condemned people unheard.

Parmenianus complained, Augustine says:

> “That when they had been defeated before ecclesiastical judges, and so that they could not prove before him”—namely Constantine—“what they were saying, they were led to the field, that is, to punishment. They accused him of having ordered this savagely, at the suggestion of Hosius the Spaniard—condemning the unheard on the basis of their own suspicions, as always.”

Augustine nevertheless excuses him in this way:

> “As though another person might not have believed, more humanely and more plausibly, that this was done at the suggestion of Hosius as bishop, so that the emperor might bend the sentence toward a milder punishment, however monstrous the crime, namely the sacrilegious schism.”

From this, then, we may conjecture that Hosius was accused of cruelty before the Spanish bishops, on the occasion provided by the severity of the penalties imposed through the canons issued by Hosius. Although a sentence may have been passed against Hosius personally concerning several crimes falsely charged against him, the authority of the Council of Iliberis nevertheless remained restored and unimpaired.

This is established not only by Dexter’s present testimony but also by the fact that the council’s authority was perpetually used and honored in the Church by later Fathers and councils.

First, the Council of Arles borrowed seven canons from it: canon 4, concerning charioteers; canon 5, concerning theatrical performers; canon 6, concerning those who wish to believe during illness; canon 7, concerning those who hold the offices of pagan magistrates; canon 9, concerning letters from confessors; canon 11, concerning marriages with unbelievers; and canon 23, concerning apostates.

The Council of Nicaea borrowed five: canon 3, concerning women living in the household of clergy; canon 5, concerning the reconciliation of those excommunicated by their own bishop; canon 10, concerning heretics not being ordained and the deposition of those who have been ordained; canon 13, concerning sinful catechumens; and canon 18, concerning clergy who accept interest.

The Council of Sardica likewise took from it canon 14, which is canon 21 in the Council of Iliberis. There Hosius silently alludes to it, saying:

> “I remember that at the preceding council our brothers decreed that if any layman failed to attend the assembly for three successive Sundays, he should be deprived of Communion.”

In the eleventh Council of Toledo, held under King Wamba in the Caesarean era 713, chapter 13 cites canon 29 of Iliberis.

The Council of Soissons, held in the year of the Lord 853, reports canon 75 of Iliberis in the acts of session 6, at the end of its final canon.

The Council of Worms, under King Louis in the year of the Lord 868, admits canon 5 of Iliberis in canon 39.

The Council of Mainz, under Bishop Rabanus, receives canons 5 and 63 of Iliberis in canon 22. Another Council of Mainz, under Bishop Arnulf in the year 888, cites and admits canon 13 of the same council in canon 26; and the Council of Cologne, under Charles the Fat, praises and renews that same canon in canon 6 of its own.

The Second Council of Arles, in Brucardus, book XVII, chapter 53, and in Ivo, part IX of the *Decretum*, chapter 103, as well as the Roman *Penitential* in Antonius Augustinus, title I, chapter 27, cite canon 63 from Iliberis.

Furthermore, Rabanus in his *Penitential*; Theodore the Greek, Isidore, and Saint Martin of Braga in their collections of councils; Gratian, Ivo, and Brucardus in their *Decrees*—all borrowed much from the same Council of Iliberis.

More important than all the rest, Pope Hadrian I, in chapters 60 and 61 of his collection of *Decrees*, cites canons 52 and 75 of Iliberis.

From this one may see how great was the perpetual reverence in which the council was held in the Church, and how little consideration certain people have shown—whom, out of regard for modesty, I do not name—when they diminished the honor of such great Fathers.

But if that harsh penalty which the council imposed seems excessive—depriving offenders of Viaticum at the point of death—it was nevertheless necessary in view of the troubles of the time. In this respect Pope Innocent himself defends the council in his letter to Exuperius of Toulouse, whose words we quoted above. The other objections raised against it are irrelevant. For candles are not absolutely forbidden when lit in cemeteries; rather, what is forbidden is their superstitious use—namely, the belief of the ignorant populace that by means of them the holy martyrs could be summoned back to give answers. The reason for the prohibition is then added: “For the spirits of the saints must not be disturbed”—just as Samuel, recalled from the dead, said to Saul: “Why have you disturbed me?” (1 Sam. 28).

It should also be noted that the council did not prohibit candles from being lit at the tombs of martyrs during the nighttime, but only during the day; for the canon says: “It has been decided that candles should not be lit in the cemetery during the day.” Here another superstition is exposed: simple believers thought that candles were lit to illuminate the souls of the dead, who were hiding in darkness, rather than to signify the faith of the living. Candles were permitted to be lit at night because at that time the living themselves, who kept vigil at the tombs of the saints, needed the light of a candle.

In later times, however, after the peoples had been cleansed of pagan superstitions, the prohibition ceased.

The objection raised concerning canon 35 is more easily answered. Women were indeed forbidden to keep vigil in cemeteries, but the council added the reason for the prohibition: they often committed crimes secretly under the pretext of prayer. It did not therefore prohibit vigils as such, as though they were intrinsically unlawful—far from it—but because some women were misusing them.

The same judgment must be made concerning canon 36. It does not absolutely prohibit the use of images, but forbids their being painted on the walls of churches. This was either because, during the persecution then raging, churches would often remain in the power of the pagans, and the images would be exposed to their mockery; or because, when the coatings of the walls were easily torn away, the images of the saints would be disfigured; or finally because, at that time, images of the saints were held in such great reverence among the faithful that it did not seem fitting for them to be painted on just any material. All these considerations are sufficiently indicated as the reason for the council’s prohibition in the words: “Lest what is worshiped and adored be painted on the walls.”

But let this suffice for our present purpose. If anyone desires a fuller exposition of these canons, let him consult D. Fernando de Mendoza in the cited book; Alanus Copus, *Dialogue* 5, chapter 16; and, among more recent theologians, Vazquez, Suarez, and Lorca in their commentaries on question 25, part III of St. Thomas, articles 3 and 6.

### 2. Saint Licerius, etc.

Saint Licerius flourished in the year of the Lord 268, when we discussed him together with Dexter, who nevertheless deals here with the renown and glory of his name. Antoninus mentions the city of Carensis, of which Saint Licerius is said to have been bishop, in his *Itinerary* between Laminium and Caesaraugusta. Pliny also wrote about the Carenses living near Complutum, in book III of his *Natural History*, chapter 3; but he confuses them with the Caracitani, or Caracenses, so called from Caraca, which is now called Guadalajara.

### 3. From the year 306, etc.

He calls Helena not a concubine or an innkeeper, as some have wrongly done, but a woman of noble rank, as the facts required. Baronius agrees with this in the same year, 306. There he observes that envy caused the daughter of a most noble Briton, with whom Constantius Chlorus had been received as a guest, to be called an innkeeper’s daughter; and that she was called a concubine because she was separated from him when he took Theodora, the daughter of Maximian, as his wife. Yet Helena was the emperor’s true wife and bore Constantine the Great from a legitimate marriage.

As for the beginning of this imperial rule, everyone agrees that it began in the year of the Lord 306, from which Baronius believes that Constantius Chlorus, his father, was taken from the living in that year. Yet this cannot be reconciled with the testimony of Eusebius, a writer of that period, who asserts that Constantius died in the year of Christ 310, as Dexter stated.

But how can it be reconciled with what the same Eusebius writes—that Constantine ruled for thirty years and ten months and died in the year 337? Certainly, if we rely only on Dexter’s assertion that Constantine began to rule in Hispania while his father was still alive, from the year 306 onward, nearly thirty-one years elapsed between 306 and 337. From this, no doubt, arose his close relationship with Hosius of Corduba—especially since his mother Helena remained with her son in Hispania. That relationship was so longstanding that in the year of the Lord 312 she sent him a letter in his support, of which I shall now speak.

---

### A.D. 311. A.U.C. 1062. The Council of Toledo is convened in defense of the Council of Iliberris.

[Col. 0477] **A.D. 311. A.U.C. 1062.** Saint Licerius, bishop of Carensis, is celebrated at Ilerda in Hispania; he is said to have been transferred there together with his see.

[Col. 0479] **A.D. 311. A.U.C. 1062.** From the year 306, Constantine, the son of Constantius Chlorus, surnamed the Great, succeeded his father in the government of the empire and of Hispania; his mother was Helena, a woman of noble rank from Britain.

[Col. 0479] **[Note: [Col. 0479B]]**

**A.D. 312.—This year, etc.** Eusebius recounts the event at greater length in book IX of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 8, in book I of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 32, and in his panegyric after the victory. In the *Chronicle*, however, he records it briefly under this very year: “Maxentius,” he says, “was defeated and killed by Constantine near the Milvian Bridge, in the sixth year of his reign.” If the year of Christ 312 was the sixth year of his reign, it is necessary that he began to reign in 306, as we have already proved.

Prudentius also sang of this victory of the Cross in the first book of his work *Against Symmachus*, in the section on the Power of the Cross, in these words:

> By this sign, unconquered avenger, having crossed the Alps,  
> Constantine freed miserable servitude;  
> When pestilential Maxentius roared in his palace,  
> You were mourning the hundred condemned to a long imprisonment—  
> As you yourself know, Fathers—and the bridegroom grieving  
> Over the interrupted pledges of his promised bride,  
> Seized by a cruel guardsman and, plunged into darkness,  
> Suffering amid harsh chains.

And shortly afterward:

> Milvian Bridge bears witness to the arrival in the city  
> Of the Christ-worshiping commander,  
> Hurling the tyrant into the Tiber’s waters,  
> And to the majesty that gave the king his victorious arms;  
> To the sign which the avenging right hand carried before him;  
> To the standard that shone with such a device:  
> Christ, woven in purple and glittering gold,  
> Marked the labarum; Christ inscribed  
> The emblems of the shields; a cross was fixed  
> And burned upon the highest crests.

And below:

> … Then that senate  
> Reverenced the title of the avenging army  
> And the august name of Christ,  
> Which shone brightly upon the weapons.

After Maxentius had been defeated through the power of the Cross shown to Constantine in heaven, Eusebius testifies in book I of his *Life of Constantine*, chapter 36, that the emperor devoted himself entirely to the erection of churches and the establishment of peace throughout the universal Church. His words are these: “Moreover, he supplied the churches with abundant resources, raised temples to great heights, enlarged those that had been built, adorned the sanctuaries of the Church with monuments enriched in many ways, relieved the poverty of the needy by various distributions of money,” and so forth.

At Hosius’s urging, he gave the Lateran Palace to Pope Melchiades. That he issued a rescript concerning the restoration or erection of the churches of Hispania before all others is inferred from the fact that Hosius was his adviser in all these matters. Hosius undoubtedly attended to the affairs of the churches of Corduba and of the other churches in his province, especially since he had long been in communication with Helena, the emperor’s mother. Even the enemies of the Church acknowledged this: Evagrius and Zosimus. The latter’s words are these:

> A certain man of Spanish origin, whose name was Aegyptius—for they called Hosius “the Egyptian,” as a term of disparagement, as though he were a magician—was brought to Rome and became familiar with the palace women, who were undoubtedly Helena and her attendants. Admitted to an interview with Constantine, he affirmed that the doctrine of the Christians possessed the power to abolish every sin.

Evagrius uses almost the same words, except that instead of “a certain man of Spanish origin, whose name was Aegyptius,” he has: “A certain Egyptian from Hiberia”—that is, Hispania—“had come to Rome,” and so forth.

There is also extant a letter of Constantine to Caecilianus, bishop of Carthage, in which the emperor says: “Therefore, since you have taken care to receive the stated sum of money, order it to be distributed among all those whose names were previously written on the schedule sent to you by Hosius.” Clearly, throughout the world money for the construction and necessities of the churches was distributed according to Hosius’s decision.

Finally, what is said here about the Gospel having first been preached to all the churches of Hispania does not mean that it intends to establish the primacy of the Church in Hispania—far from it—but refers to the priority in time of the Gospel’s preaching there; this matter has been sufficiently discussed above.

Juvencus, who was writing there during these days, bears witness also to the peace granted by Constantine to the churches of Hispania. At the end of his work he says:

> This peace of Christ has been granted to me; this peace of the world,  
> Which Constantine, the generous ruler of the open earth,  
> Fosters—he is present, worthy of gratitude for his merit;  
> He alone among kings dreads that the burden  
> Of the sacred name should be imposed upon him.

In this year, 312, according to Braulio’s additions, a church at Barcelona was built in honor of Saint Eulalia, and one at Toledo in honor of Saint Leocadia. In the same author, under the year 314, we read:

> At Caesaraugusta, the most august church of Blessed Mary, built by Blessed James, son of Zebedee, was restored with expanded spaces, and is venerated with no less devotion and attendance.

A church was also erected at Abula for the holy martyrs Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta, at the place where they suffered; as well as other churches besides these. All were built throughout the various regions at the expense of the most holy queen Helena Augusta.

---

### A.D. 312. A.U.C. 1063.

In this year, after the tyrant Maxentius had been defeated and drowned in the Tiber at the Milvian Bridge, Constantine the Great, warned by the miraculous sign of the Cross, triumphed most gloriously; and the greatest tranquility shone upon the churches. For the temples destroyed by the edicts of the emperors were restored throughout the whole world, and especially in Hispania, under the care above all of his mother Helena and Hosius, bishop of Corduba in Hispania. Thus the province which had first seen the rays of the clearest evangelical light might also be the first to rejoice in the blessings of peace and its fruits.

[Col. 0481] **[Note: [Col. 0481A]]**

**A.D. 316.—The synod, etc.** Both synods are very celebrated and well known. Regarding the time at which they were held, Baronius, having sensed the truth, first asserts that the Council of Ancyra was celebrated before the Council of Neocaesarea, because at Ancyra there is discussion of restoring the lapsed through penance, which points to a time close to the persecution; whereas at Neocaesarea nothing of this kind is asserted, since by then the restoration of the lapsed had already been dealt with.

As for the year, we have Dexter’s testimony, which Baronius did not possess. For that reason he conjectured that the Council of Ancyra was celebrated in 314, although it was held two years later.

] **A.D. 316. A.U.C. 1067.** The Synod of Ancyra, with 24 canons, and also the Synod of Neocaesarea, with 12 canons, are celebrated at the same time.

[Col. 0481] **[Note: [Col. 0481A]]**

**A.D. 317.—1. Alexander, etc.** This is that great Alexander who, as the predecessor of Saint Athanasius, labored so strenuously for the Church of God against Arius, the presbyter of his own church. Some place him nineteenth in the catalogue of the Alexandrian bishops, as may be seen in Equilinus, book XI, chapter 6; Dexter places him twentieth. All agree that he occupied the see for seven years. Achillas succeeded him.

[Col. 0481B] **2. L. Caecilius, etc.** Jerome discusses Caecilius Lactantius Firmianus, whose books of the *Institutions* are extant, in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. He says that Lactantius was a disciple of Arnobius, who taught rhetoric most successfully in Africa under Diocletian; that Lactantius was brought from there to Nicomedia, where he also taught rhetoric; and that, because of the scarcity of students in that Greek city, he turned to writing. In extreme old age he became the tutor in Gaul of Crispus, the son of Caesar Constantine.

Eusebius says of him: “He was the most eloquent man of his time; yet in this life he was so poor that he often lacked even necessities, let alone luxuries.” This is what Eusebius says in the *Chronicle*.

Some have believed him to be an African, but without sufficient foundation. The fact that he attached himself to Arnobius as a disciple in Africa does not prove that he was born there; for under Augustine we know that the Spaniard Orosius pursued his studies in Africa. I therefore accept Dexter’s statement that Lactantius was born in Hispania, since none of the ancients contradicts it; I am compelled to agree with him in every respect.

The fact that Lactantius died at Nicaea around this time leads me to believe that he was summoned to the Council of Nicaea by Constantine’s command and there finally—or shortly beforehand, or during the council’s celebration—closed his life.

] **A.D. 317. A.U.C. 1068.** Alexander, twentieth bishop of Alexandria, presides for seven years.

**A.D. 317. A.U.C. 1068.** L. Caecilius Lactantius Firmianus, a Spaniard and tutor of Crispus Caesar, the son of Constantine, poor and despised, dies at Nicaea.

[Col. 0481] **[Note: [Col. 0481C]]**

**A.D. 324.—At Nicaea, etc.** There is no general agreement concerning the date of the Council of Nicaea. Cassiodorus insists that it was celebrated in 328; Eusebius places it in 324. More recently Morales disagreed with them, and Baronius follows his opinion by assigning it to the year 325.

Dexter follows Eusebius, but which of the two has the stronger position? I would think that there is not much difference among them. If there is any disagreement, it is perhaps a disagreement among the others themselves, but none between them and Dexter. For either we are speaking of the council’s conclusion—in which case Cassiodorus indicates the year 328, believing that the Fathers spent a full three years on it, as Nicephorus also writes in book VIII, chapter 26; on this view, it must have begun toward the end of 324—or, if those who place its completion in 325 are correct, they must consequently assert that it began in 324. I consider this entirely true, since it is confirmed by the year assigned by Hosius to the council itself, namely the Caesarean era 363, which is the year of the Lord 325. Dexter and Eusebius are speaking of the beginning of the council.

But not everyone understands Dexter’s statement—“In the place of Sylvester, Hosius, bishop of Corduba, an outstanding confessor, presides”—in the same sense. The more common view is that Hosius was the legate of Saint Sylvester, Roman pontiff, and presided over the Council of Nicaea in that capacity. Nevertheless, learned and respected writers contend that Hosius was in no way the legate of the Roman See at the Nicene Synod, but subscribed in the name of his own province. These writers are Didacus Valdesius, counselor of the royal convent of Valladolid, in book 2 of *On the Dignity of the Kings and Kingdoms of Hispania*, chapter 2, and D. Joannes de Salazar, archdeacon of Úbeda, in his book *On the Coming of Saint James*.

The subscriptions of the Fathers themselves clearly demonstrate this. They all append the name of their province, and from each province only one man subscribes, even if several had attended. This is easily confirmed in the case of the Spanish bishops. Eusebius writes that not only Hosius but many others came, in the words quoted below—and Dexter mentions some of them—yet Hosius alone subscribes for all Hispania.

The matter is also confirmed by the testimony of ancient writers. All unanimously attest that the legates of Saint Sylvester were the presbyters Victor and Vincentius, whereas no one says this of Hosius. Theodore, in book I, chapter 7, after stating that Sylvester was unable to attend because of his advanced age, adds:

> But he sent two presbyters, granting them authority to assent to the acts of that council.

He says nothing about Hosius. Socrates, book I, chapter 3; Sozomen, book I, chapter 16; and Cassiodorus, book II of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 1, write the same.

Eusebius does not disagree; rather, in book III, chapter 7, he writes in the same sense when discussing the Fathers who came to Nicaea:

> Among them was one man from Hispania, distinguished both by name and by the renown of his reputation, who attended that assembly with many others. Although the bishop of that city which holds imperial power—that is, Rome—was prevented from attending by advancing age, his presbyters, who were present, supplied his place.

What could be clearer? Certainly, if Hosius had been Sylvester’s legate, Eusebius would have said that he supplied the place of the Roman bishop. Yet he did not do so; indeed, by affirming this of others, he appears plainly to deny it of Hosius.

But why delay, when the Fathers themselves, writing to Sylvester after the council had been completed, show that Hosius and the others were altogether distinct from the legates? Here are the words of the letter:

> To the most blessed pope of the city of Rome, Sylvester, to be revered with all honor: Hosius, bishop of the province of Hispania, of the city of Corduba; Macarius of the Church of Constantinople; and Victor and Vincentius, presbyters ordained in the city of Rome by your direction; and so forth.

The names of the other Fathers follow. Hosius is therefore not said to have been ordained by Sylvester’s direction; only the two presbyters, Victor and Vincentius, are so described.

The same conclusion follows from the subscriptions themselves. The presbyters subscribe as follows:

> Victor and Vincentius, presbyters of the city of Rome, have written this on behalf of the venerable man, our holy father Sylvester, bishop and pope, believing as it has been written above.

Hosius, however, subscribes in this manner:

> Hosius, bishop of the city of Corduba in the province of Hispania, said: I believe as it has been written above.

The other Fathers subscribe in the same manner—for example, Alexander of Alexandria the Great, of the province of Egypt; Nicasius of Divio, of the province of Gaul; and so forth.

But one matter troubled everyone: how could Hosius have presided over the Catholic Synod of Nicaea if he was not the Roman pontiff’s legate? The acts of the council themselves show that he presided. He proposed and defined everything that had to be treated, with the agreement of the other Fathers, and he himself composed the Nicene Creed.

This objection, however, should not be regarded as so weighty that it compels us to assert something contrary to the facts. We freely concede that if Sylvester had been present, he ought to have presided over the council; and if he had appointed a president, his decision and appointment would have had to be followed. But he sent presbyters to give assent to the acts of the council in his name, not to preside over the bishops. Thus the authority of presiding remained with the body of the council, especially since in the early times of the Church concern for truth was greater than concern for precedence.

The Fathers themselves, for the most just reasons—and with the approval also of Constantine, who was present—decided that Hosius should discharge the office of president, on account of the excellence of his learning and the merits of his confession of faith. Or perhaps they did so because consideration was given to the Christian status of the provinces, as the authors mentioned above argue on substantial grounds. We have already sufficiently established that Hispania was the first of all the pagan provinces to be brought to the faith of Christ.

I consider it more probable that both considerations were taken into account: Constantine and the Fathers. Thus, when the author writes, “In the place of Sylvester, Hosius presided,” he means that Hosius occupied in the council the seat which Sylvester would have occupied had he been present.

**2. Natalis, etc.** From this testimony of Dexter I infer the following. If we consider the original use of the term *natales* for the saints, the impious festival days came to be called *natales* because their lists—called calendars—were first written by Natalis, bishop of Toledo. Later, however, the name appeared suitable for signifying the death of the saints: they were not born on earth from flesh, as Chrysologus said in sermon 129, but from earth to heaven, from labor to rest, from temptations to tranquility, from torments to delights—not fleeting delights, but strong, stable, and eternal ones.

Or perhaps the term arose for the reason given by Saint Eucherius of Lyon—wrongly thought to have been Eusebius of Emesa—in homily 50 on Genesis:

> We call the days of the blessed martyrs their birthdays, because when the life of martyrdom and faith in glory consigns them to death, it gives them birth into eternity; and through brief suffering it brings forth everlasting joys.

Certainly, if the days had been called *natales* because of death, which is changed into true life, only those festivals of the saints that concerned the death of martyrs and other blessed persons would bear that name. But the matter is otherwise. The sixth day of May, for example, is called by the ancients the birthday of Saint John the Evangelist, yet it is not celebrated in memory of his death but of the miracle that occurred at the Latin Gate. Thus Usuardus writes:

> The birthday of Saint John the Apostle, when by order of Domitian he was brought from Ephesus to Rome and, before the assembled senate, was thrown into a vessel of boiling oil at the Latin Gate, but was not harmed.

The feast of Saint Peter’s Chair is also called a birthday by Augustine in his sermon on that feast. Saint Leo calls the dedication of a church its birthday in his sermon on the same subject, as Molanus noted under 1 August.

You may therefore suppose that these days began to be called *natales* because the calendars of the Church’s festivals began to be written and arranged by Bishop Natalis. The matter is no different from the case of Peter, bishop of Equilinum, whom some customarily call Peter of Natalibus because he composed a vast work on the birthdays of the saints, although his proper name was Peter of Venice, as he himself left on record in his prologue.

Add to this that the deaths of the holy martyrs were not called *natales* before the time of Natalis, but only afterward. What some quote from Origen, in homily 3 on Job, is irrelevant, for there he merely says: “We therefore do not celebrate the day of birth but of death, because those who appear to die do not die.” Still less does the testimony of D. Cyprian bear on the matter, whether one considers his letters 34 or 37, whatever Pamelius may attempt.

**3. Under Natalis, etc.** This Council of Toledo is discussed by the *General History of Hispania*, circulated under the name of King Alfonso X the Wise, and by the history of the city of Toledo. Morales drew from these sources and from a very ancient manuscript codex of the Church of Toledo.

At that council, with the Roman pontiff’s assent—an assent which it is reasonable to attribute to ecclesiastical matters carried out by that emperor—ancient boundaries of metropolitan and diocesan churches were discussed, and all Hispania was divided into five metropolitan sees:

1. Toledo  
2. Tarragona  
3. Braga  
4. Mérida  
5. Seville  

They are listed in the order of dignity in which they have been named.

Tarragona had ten:

### A.D. 324. A.U.C. 1075.

At Nicaea in Bithynia, the holy and universal synod of 318 bishops is convened against the heretic Arius. In the place of Sylvester, Hosius, bishop of Corduba, an outstanding confessor, presides. The Spanish bishops of Seville and Barcelona also attended, as did Natalis of Toledo and many others from the provinces of Baetica and Tarraconensis.

[Col. 0483] **A.D. 324. A.U.C. 1075.** Natalis sent to Constantine the birthdays of the martyrs and the calendars.

**A.D. 324. A.U.C. 1075.** Under Natalis, bishop and pontiff of Toledo, and presiding by Constantine’s order, the Council of Toledo is convened. The ancient episcopal sees that had lost their boundaries recovered them.

[Col. 0483] **[Note: [Col. 0484C]]**

**A.D. 330.—Arnobius, etc.** Jerome asserts in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers* that Arnobius taught rhetoric most successfully at Sicca in Africa and wrote against the pagans; his books are commonly extant. But since Jerome says that he flourished under Diocletian, it is necessary either that this year concerns only his reputation after death, or that he reached an advanced old age. Jerome again discusses him in the *Chronicle* under this very year.

] **A.D. 330. A.U.C. 1081.** Arnobius, a rhetorician teaching in Africa, is held in high repute.

[Col. 0483] **[Note: [Col. 0484C]]**

**A.D. 335.—When he had died, etc.** In this year Saint Sylvester exchanged earth for heaven on the last day of December, having occupied the see, according to Baronius’s calculation, for 21 years, 10 months, and 1 day. Saint Mark was elected in his place in the year 336; after Saint Mark’s death, Saint Julius also ascended the apostolic see, as Onuphrius, Morales, and others hold, although others believe that Saint Mark occupied the Roman see for several years. The author’s opinion is the more common.

] **A.D. 335. A.U.C. 1086.** After Sylvester’s death, Saint Mark succeeded to the See of Peter, and the following year Saint Julius succeeded Saint Mark.

[Col. 0483] **[Note: [Col. 0484D]]**

**A.D. 337.—1. This year, etc.** Baronius proves this at length under this very year from Jerome, Socrates, Rufinus, Sozomen, and others. I urge you to consult him concerning the great deeds Constantine performed for the Church of God.

Because of his outstanding virtues, he was numbered among the saints by the Greeks and is celebrated with festive joy on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, or on the twelfth day before the Kalends, as Molanus has it:

> On the twenty-first day of May, the feast of the great kings, equal to the Apostles, Constantine and Helena.

He is also included by Equilinus in his *Catalogue of the Saints*, book V, chapter 26, under the title “On Saint Constantine the Emperor.”

Near Mérida in Hispania there is an ancient stone bearing the following inscription, which Morales gives in book X, chapter 36:

> The Emperor Caesar Flavius Constantine Augustus,  
> Cultivator of peace and justice,  
> Founder of public tranquility,  
> Author of religion and faith,  
> Having remitted the tributes throughout the neighboring provinces,  
> Restored the road.

He left his empire to his three sons. Constantine received Hispania, Gaul, and Germania; Constantius received the entire East; Constans received Italy, Africa, and Illyricum.

**[Col. 0485B] 2. At Salamanca, etc.** The fame of so great a man will endure forever with his distinguished works. In former times he was praised for his merits by D. Jerome, both in the *Chronicle* under the year 332 and in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. His words are these:

> Juvencus, a Spaniard of very noble birth and a presbyter, composed four books transferring the four Gospels almost word for word into hexameter verse, along with certain other works in the same meter relating to the order of the sacraments.

The prologue of his work on the Gospels begins: “Nothing immortal is held within the structure of the world.” At the conclusion he suggests that he wrote while the emperor Constantine was still alive.

Equilinus also discusses him in book XI, chapter 121. We shall speak again of his reputation under the year of the Lord 407.

] **A.D. 337. A.U.C. 1088.** This year was mournful and disastrous for the Christian state. On the second day before the Kalends of June, the emperor Constantine—Pious, Fortunate, and Augustus, and the true defender of religion—died at Constantinople, leaving his three sons as his successors.

**A.D. 337. A.U.C. 1088.** At Salamanca among the Vectones, Saint Juvencus the presbyter died. According to some, he attended the Council of Iliberris.

[Col. 0485] **[Note: [Col. 0485B]]**

**A.D. 341.—Ablavius, etc.** This was borrowed from the *Chronicle* of Blessed Jerome. Eunapius calls Ablavius the plaything and ball of fortune, always devising something new: born in the lowest station, he rose above the power of an emperor, but was killed by Constantius. Ammianus also discusses him in book XXII, as does Zosimus in book II and the aforementioned Eunapius in his *Lives of the Philosophers*.

] **A.D. 341. A.U.C. 1092.** Ablavius, prefect of the praetorium, and many others, were killed.

[Col. 0485] **[Note: [Col. 0485C]]**

**A.D. 344.—Many, etc.** You will also read this in Jerome’s *Chronicle*.

] **A.D. 344. A.U.C. 1093.** Many cities of the East collapsed in a terrible earthquake.

[Col. 0485] **[Note: [Col. 0485C]]**

**A.D. 347.—Titianus, etc.** Jerome has the same account in his *Chronicle*. He was different from Tatian the Christian rhetorician, who wrote books against the Gentiles, from whom he had been converted to the faith. Eusebius discusses him in book IV of his *History*, chapter 16, and Jerome himself in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 39. The latter flourished under Marcus Aurelius, the former under the sons of Constantine. This man was called Titianus; the other, Tatianus.

] **A.D. 347. A.U.C. 1098.** Titianus, an eloquent man holding the prefecture of the praetorium, went to Gaul.

[Col. 0485] **[Note: [Col. 0485C]]**

**A.D. 350.—A great, etc.** We read about this same eclipse, which occurred in this year, in the *Chronicle* of Saint Jerome.

] **A.D. 350. A.U.C. 1101.** There was a great eclipse of the sun in this year.

[Col. 0485] **[Note: [Col. 0485C]]**

**A.D. 352.—1. Natalis, etc.** Good God, how feeble until now has been the memory among the people of Toledo of their holy and truly great bishop Olympius! Yet they ought to glory in him no less than the people of Lyon in Irenaeus, the Carthaginians in Cyprian, the Milanese in Ambrose, and, to put it in a single word, the cities and nations of the Church in all her teachers.

For if you seek learning, he was most erudite; if dignity, a bishop; if character, a saint; and if antiquity, exceedingly ancient. Only the unstable and perpetual vicissitudes of Spanish affairs could have obscured so great a star. But thanks be to God, Dexter has emerged from the hiding places in which he had lain concealed for so many centuries. He has brought Olympius once more into the light and before the eyes of all, restoring to Hispania its teacher and to Toledo its bishop.

But—and this is what I find more astonishing—the light of Olympius was never entirely absent from Spanish monuments. If only some degree of diligence had been applied, everything that Dexter now brings forth concerning Saint Olympius could have been made public.

I shall establish each point that he records. Among the letters of Gregory Nazianzen, five are found addressed to Olympius: namely, letter 40, which begins, “Again the occasion,” etc.; and letter 41, “You are our ruler, even after your rule,” where he says:

> The great Olympius is no longer with us, nor does he hold the governance of our affairs; once again we have become a second-rate Cappadocia, whereas you had made us first.

There is also letter 76, which begins, “This is almost more grievous to me than the illness itself”; letter 77, at the beginning, “And old age itself, now gray,” etc.; and finally letter 78, “Again I write when I ought to be present,” etc.

These letters indicate that before becoming a bishop Olympius had been governor and ruler of Cappadocia. But whether this same Olympius was the bishop cannot be established from the letters alone, unless supporting evidence is sought elsewhere.

That Olympius was a bishop in Thrace, of the city of Aenus, and was exiled from there together with Theodulus, likewise bishop of Trajanopolis in Thrace—indeed, that they were even sought for execution because they favored Athanasius and the orthodox faith and persecuted Ursacius, Valens, and the Arians—is narrated by the Council of Jerusalem in Sozomen’s *Tripartite History*, book IV, chapter 38, in the letter in support of Athanasius. Speaking there of Athanasius’s adversaries, it says:

> The reports made against Athanasius gained such force that the emperor Constantius ordered him to be killed wherever he might be found, together with Theodulus and Olympius, bishops of the churches of Thrace.

Athanasius likewise writes in his letter to those leading the solitary life:

> They expelled Diodorus, a bishop, from his see. They likewise attacked Olympius of Aenus and Theodulus of Trajanopolis—both bishops of Thrace, good and orthodox men, hostile to heresy—with accusations: first, when the emperor Constantius sent an edict in response to the accusations of the Eusebians; and again when the Eusebians revived the memory of that matter.

He calls the Arians “Eusebians” because Eusebius had been their standard-bearer. The edict ordered not only that these men be expelled from their cities and churches, but also that they be punished by capital sentence wherever they were found.

Athanasius repeats the same account in his *Apology for His Flight*. This explains why Olympius became joined to Hosius by a special friendship, especially at the Council of Sardica. There, at Olympius’s urging, Hosius modified the law he had enacted in chapter 14 concerning the permanent residence of prelates in their own churches. Under that law they could be absent for no more than three weeks at most; Hosius adjusted it so that it would not apply to those who had been forcibly expelled from their sees.

Thus chapter 21 says:

> Hosius the bishop said: At the suggestion of our brother and fellow bishop Olympius, this also seemed good: if anyone has suffered violence and, fleeing danger, has come to another city, he should not be forbidden to remain there for as long as he is either able to return or receives a remedy for the injury he has suffered.

Olympius also subscribed to the Council of Gangra, held under Saint Sylvester in the year of the Lord 324.

After the assembly at Sardica had been dissolved, Olympius accompanied Hosius to Spain. We shall shortly prove that this was the time when Athanasius was brought there by him; and Hosius himself, writing to Constantius, had promised, saying among other things:

> “I promised them [the Arians] that, if Athanasius were found guilty, I would expel him by every means; but if he were found innocent, and he exposed you as calumniators, and you nevertheless rejected him, I would persuade him to come with me to Spain.”

Likewise, I do not doubt that Hosius acted in this matter with Olympius concurring in the judgment concerning Athanasius. However his arrival in Spain occurred, it is certain that there he was once again elected bishop and published books against the heretics. We learn this from St. Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book I, chapters 3 and 7, where he says:

> “Olympius, a Spanish bishop, a man of great glory in the Church and in Christ, said in a certain ecclesiastical sermon: ‘If faith had ever remained incorrupt upon earth and had kept firmly fixed the traces which it abandoned after they had been marked out, it would never have spread a fault through the offspring by the deadly transgression of the first-formed man, so that sin might be born with man.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “Saint Olympius says: ‘A fault was spread from the first-formed man through the offspring, so that sin might be born with man,’ etc.”

O judgment truly to be valued above all gold and riches! O words whose magnificence can never be sufficiently praised! Olympius, a Spanish bishop, a man of great glory in the Church and in Christ.

That this Olympius, whose testimony Augustine reports, was the same man who had been bishop of Thrace cannot be doubted. Augustine says of the man whom he calls a Spanish bishop that he was a man “of great glory in the Church and in Christ”; by these words he indicates that he was that Olympius who in those days was a great and glorious man in the Church, since he had subscribed the general councils of his time and had shone there with the glory of outstanding learning. For Christ he endured exile and many great hardships, and he was sought even unto death no less than Athanasius.

But what a man of great glory! Shall I state in one word how highly Augustine regarded him? In *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book II, chapter 10, Augustine numbers him among the foremost and greatest Fathers and Doctors of the Catholic Church, saying:

> “For this Catholic truth, holy and blessed priests, outstanding in their treatment of the divine Scriptures—Irenaeus, Cyprian, Rethicius, Olympius, Hilary, Ambrose, Gregory, Innocent, Basil; and to these I add, whether you wish it or not, the presbyter Jerome.”

Again, in the following book, book III, chapter 17, he names the same men in the same order and calls them “holy bishops of God and memorable teachers.”

Consult Baronius, volume V, under the year 405, number 58, and Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 23. Gennadius says that Olympius was Spanish by nationality:

> “Olympius, Spanish by nationality, a bishop, wrote a book on faith against those who attribute blame to nature and not to free choice, showing that evil was implanted in nature not by creation but by disobedience.”

I would believe that he traveled from Spain to Constantinople under the pretext of official business during the time of Constantine, and that there he was made bishop in Thrace—for Constantinople is in Thrace—but that, having been expelled from there because of his adherence to the faith, he returned once more to his native Spain together with Hosius.

That he became bishop of Toledo after Natalis is shown both by the lists of the bishops of Toledo, preserved by Loaysa or in the library of the holy Church of Toledo, in which Olympius appears as Natalis’s successor, and also by the diptychs of the Mozarabic Breviary of St. Isidore, where Olympius’s name is recited daily among the other names in the canon of the Mass.

His sanctity likewise cannot be doubted, since Augustine says, “Saint Olympius said,” and inserts him in his proper place among the other holy Fathers of the Church. It is also noteworthy that his name is included in the Roman Martyrology on June 12 in these words:

> “In Thrace, Saint Olympius, bishop, who, expelled from his see by the Arians, died a confessor.”

Let all the people of Toledo, and all Spaniards, therefore see how highly they ought henceforth to esteem their teacher. But we shall speak of him again below, under the year 356.

## A.D. 352. A.R. 1103

Olympius, a devout and most learned man, succeeds Natalis as bishop of Toledo. Gregory Nazianzenus wrote to him on several occasions. He had previously been bishop in Thrace; having been sent into exile, he came to Spain and was elected by the Toledans in Natalis’s place. By publishing books, he fought wonderfully against the heretics of his time.

## A.D. 352. A.R. 1103

Saint Orosius, uncle of Orosius of Tarragona, is flourishing at Rome.

## A.D. 352. A.R. 1103

At Barcelona, Saint Severus suffers for the faith at the hands of the heretical Arians while he was governing that see in holiness and piety.

## A.D. 352. A.R. 1103

The saints Vincent and Laetus, born of Turibius, a citizen of Toledo, and Severa, of Aquae or Ebora near Toledo in Carpetania, twins, are renowned for their miraculous works.

[Note: **1. Saint Orosius, etc.** He is written of in the acts of Saint Eusebius, priest and martyr, in Mombritius, vol. I: Saint Orosius buried Eusebius’s body together with Saint Gregory, their fellow priest. We also read this in the Roman Martyrology on August 14. On that passage Cardinal Baronius says of the church of Saint Eusebius: “The venerable bodies of Saints Eusebius, Orosius, and Paulinus are kept there, together with many relics of other martyrs.” See also Equilinus, *Catalogue*, book VII, chapter 62. Saint Orosius was the paternal uncle of Paul Orosius, to whom Dexter dedicated the present work. Saint Orosius died in 366, as we shall say in its place, after he had begotten by a lawful wife, before becoming a priest, another Paul Orosius, who died at Carthage. But of these matters below.

**2. At Barcelona, etc.** This Severus differs from the man who, as bishop of the same city, suffered martyrdom in the year of the Lord 285, as Dexter noted there. Heleca, bishop of Zaragoza, treats of both in his additions to M. Maximus, in these words: “At this time”—namely 360, when he himself flourished—“two martyr-bishops named Severus of Barcelona are said to be renowned with the glory of miracles and signs: the elder flourished under Diocletian, the other under Constantius.” Vasaeus treats of the former in his *Chronicle* under 306; Morales, book X, chapter 4; Marieta, book I, part I, chapter 23; and Trugillus and Villegas, who maintain that four priests were crowned with martyrdom together with him. Molanus treats of the latter under November 6, saying: “At Barcelona, the feast of Saint Severus, bishop and martyr, who was pierced through the head with a nail by the Goths.” In the *Additions*, according to Baronius’s notes: “He was one of the seventy bishops who made the Gothic laws in Spain. He was crowned with martyrdom in the year of Christ 683, his head pierced with a nail by the barbarian Goths inhabiting Catalonia.” Baronius rightly doubts their reliability, however, and it is unknown whence Molanus derived this, especially since the name of Severus of Barcelona is nowhere found in the councils of Spain, which were frequently held in those ancient times. Dexter also conflicts with this account, writing that he was killed in this year, 352, not more than three hundred years later. Moreover, he suffered not at the hands of Goths, who had not yet come into Spain, but at the hands of Arians. Accordingly, those words were removed in the final 1583 edition of Molanus, printed at Antwerp by Philip Nutius.

**3. Saints Vincent, etc.** We have said enough concerning the city of Aquae or Ebora under Saint Pigmenius, at the year 130, and Saints Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta, at 300. The feast day of the holy martyrs Vincent and Laetus is celebrated annually at Toledo on September 1 according to the rite or Breviary of Saint Isidore; their names occur in the Roman Martyrology on that day under the words: “In Spain, the holy martyrs Vincent and Laetus.” Baronius may be consulted there. Further information concerning them is to be had from the letter of Silo, king of Oviedo, to Cixila, bishop of Toledo, which we supplied above when discussing Saint Thyrsus. There Silo states that Cixila had composed a hymn in honor of these martyrs: “I have heard,” says Silo, “that you composed another hymn concerning Saints Vincent and Laetus of Toledo, who suffered, as your envoys reported to me”—such barbarity did the Latin idiom of the time exhibit—“under Caecilius Apollinaris, governor of the Spains, in the city of Lybisoca. Let your Paternity send it to me, that our clerics may have something to sing.” Marieta treats of them in book II, chapter 102, and Basilius Sanctorus, under September. Lybisoca was the place now called Lezuca, near Alcaraz. Consult what we noted concerning that city under the year 64.]

## A.D. 353. A.R. 1104

After Julius’s death, Saint Liberius succeeds to the see of Peter.

## A.D. 353. A.R. 1104

Gratianus, bishop of Carthage in Spain, born at Baga, near Carthage—formerly called Thiar—consecrates at Lybissosa a church of the holy martyrs Vincent and Laetus, who suffered martyrdom there.

## A.D. 353. A.R. 1104

At Mantua in Carpetania, Anastasius the presbyter, Placidus, Genesius, and their companions are held in honor; they later suffered together there an illustrious martyrdom for the faith of Christ under Julian.

[Note: **A.D. 353.—1. Julius, etc.** Some place Liberius’s election in the year of the Lord 351, Baronius in 352, but Dexter in 353; Onuphrius and Morales agree with Dexter. As for Liberius’s sanctity, Equilinus must be rejected, both in book VII, chapter 62, and in book XI, chapter 2, where he brands him with the mark of heresy. His innocence and sanctity, however, are attested by the great Athanasius in his letter to those leading the solitary life. Equilinus is not even consistent with himself, since later, in book XI, chapter 130, number 258, he numbers Liberius among the saints whom he says he excerpted from the select martyrologies of Jerome, Bede, Usuard, and Ado. Molanus also discusses him in his additions to Usuard, under September 23, in these words: “At Rome, Saint Liberius, pope and confessor.” Thus one need no longer wonder at the title “saint” with which Dexter honors him.

**2. Gratianus, etc.** By Baga I understand the city now called Baza, situated approximately in the territory of Carthage.

**3. At Mantua, etc.** The author had mentioned these same martyrs above, under the year 300, in connection with Verissimus and his sisters of Lisbon, since these too had likewise been born and brought up at Lisbon. He now discusses them—not because they were killed this year, for they were later put to death under Julian in the year 362, but because those three singular champions of Christ, Anastasius the presbyter, Placidus, and Genesius, had gone to Mantua in Carpetania and flourished there as examples of miraculous works and virtues; others were added to their crown. The acts of such great martyrs have perished, to the great loss of our royal city, though their memory has not wholly disappeared. For in the Roman Martyrology, on October 11, we read:

> “Likewise, the passion of the holy Anastasius the presbyter, Placidus, Genesius, and their companions.”

Baronius admits that he found the same account in ancient manuscripts.]

[Note: **A.D. 356.—1. Hosius, etc.** St. Athanasius recounts the event and the letters themselves word for word in his letter to those leading the solitary life. Since they are most worthy of reading, I have decided to reproduce them verbatim. After reporting the hardships inflicted upon Pope Liberius by Constantius and the other Arians, he continues:

> “After committing such and so many crimes, they still thought they had done nothing at all so long as that great man Hosius had not experienced their malice. They therefore sought to extend their fury against such a great and eminent man. They showed no reverence for him because he was the father of bishops; they were not moved by shame because he was a confessor; they paid no regard to the fact that he had spent sixty years and more since his confession”—as may be inferred from this, he had been seized by pagans in or around the year of the Lord 294 and afflicted with blows and tortures for confessing Christ—“but, despising everything alike, they fixed their eyes solely upon their heresy: men who truly neither feared God nor respected human beings.

> “They therefore approached Constantius and addressed him in these words: ‘We have done everything. We have driven the Roman pontiff into exile, and before him we made very many bishops exiles; we have filled every place with terror. Yet all your efforts are counted as nothing, and we have accomplished nothing, so long as Hosius remains. For as long as he remains in his own place, everyone seems to remain in his own Church. By his words and by the authority of his faith he can turn everyone against us. He is the head of the councils; if he writes anything, he is heard everywhere. He formulated the creed at the Council of Nicaea and everywhere exposed the Arians as heretics. If he remains in his present position, the exile of the others is useless, for our heresy is forced to yield. Begin, therefore, to persecute him also, and do not think that his age should spare him; our heresy has no regard for the gray hairs of the elderly.’

> “When Constantius heard these words, he thought he must not delay. Knowing the man and the great authority possessed by that old man, he wrote and issued an order that Hosius should come to him, just as he had initially attempted to win over Liberius. When Hosius arrived, the emperor entreated him and received him with his customary words, by which he usually deceived others, urging him to subscribe against us and to enter into communion with the Arians. The old man could scarcely bear even hearing of such a thing, and was distressed merely to hear the sound of their words. He brought the emperor, terrified by the great force of their arguments, back from his position, and so returned to his own country and Church.”

“Understand ‘Corduba,’” the commentator adds; “for Hosius had been summoned from there, and, after convincing Constantius, returned there once more.” But for how long, do you suppose, was he permitted to enjoy the quiet he desired?

> “When the Arians again lamented and provoked the emperor, and the eunuchs, lending support to their arguments, inflamed him still further, he again wrote to Hosius with threats. Hosius was subjected to insults, but did not on that account abandon his position; he firmly held to his purpose, for he had built his dwelling upon the solid rock of faith. He spoke with complete freedom against the heresy, treating the rains and winds of threatening letters as nothing.

> “Constantius therefore wrote to him repeatedly, sometimes flattering him and calling him ‘father,’ sometimes threatening him, counting up those who had been exiled, and addressing him in these words: ‘Will you alone still remain an enemy of the heresy? Obey and write against Athanasius; for whoever writes against him plainly embraces the Arian doctrines with us.’ Hosius was not at all frightened by this. Amid the insults he suffered, he wrote the following letter, which we have read ourselves and have appended at the end. How free it is!”

### Hosius to the Emperor Constantius, Greetings

I fulfilled the duty of confession when persecution was first stirred up by your grandfather Maximian. If you too are stirring up persecution, I am even now prepared to endure anything rather than shed innocent blood and betray the truth. I can never approve of your writing such things or issuing threats of this sort.

Cease writing in this manner. Do not think with Arius; do not listen to the Orientals; do not trust Ursacius and Valens. What they say, they say not because of Athanasius but because of their own heresy. Believe me: I could be your grandfather in age.

I myself was present at the Council of Sardica when you and your blessed brother Constans summoned us all there. I myself voluntarily challenged the enemies of Athanasius when they came to the church where I was staying, asking them to produce whatever they had against him. I promised them security and assured them that they should expect nothing other than a just judgment in every matter. I did this not once but twice. If they did not wish the matter to be examined by the whole council, I offered to serve as their judge. I promised them that if Athanasius were found guilty, we would expel him by every means; but if he were found innocent, and exposed you as calumniators, and you nevertheless rejected him, I would persuade him to come with me to Spain.

Athanasius accepted these conditions and objected to nothing. They, however, withdrew, dissenting from everything alike. Athanasius was afterward summoned by your letters and came to your camp. He ordered all his enemies who were present at Antioch to be summoned individually, so that either they might refute him or be refuted, and either prove in his presence that he had done the things of which they accused him or cease calumniating him in his absence. They could not even endure your issuing this command to them, and they utterly rejected such conditions.

Why, then, do you now listen to his detractors? Why do you tolerate the accusations of Valens and Ursacius, who have acknowledged in repentance and in writing that they made false accusations? They confessed their fraud voluntarily, not under compulsion, as they claim; no soldiers were present there, and your brother knew nothing of it. Nothing of the sort that is now being done was taking place under him. They came voluntarily to Rome and, in the presence of the bishop and the presbyters who were there, set down their confession in writing, after they had previously sent Athanasius peaceful and friendly letters.

If they wish to allege that they were subjected to force, and regard that as an evil, then you too should abandon your use of force. Do not write letters or send agents; release those who have been banished into exile, lest, while you inquire into the use of force, they should exercise even greater force against them in your name.

What action of this sort was taken by Constans? Which bishop was exiled there? When did he take part in ecclesiastical judgments? Which Palatine official used force to compel a written statement against anyone? Let Valens and his associates produce something comparable and have something to bring as an accusation.

Cease, I beg you, and remember that you are mortal. Fear the day of judgment; preserve yourself pure for that day. Do not involve yourself in ecclesiastical matters, and do not command us in this sphere. Rather, learn these things from us. God has entrusted imperial power to you; he has entrusted the affairs of the Church to us. Just as one who maliciously attacks your authority contradicts the divine ordinance, so you must beware lest, by drawing the affairs of the Church to yourself, you become liable to grave guilt.

“It is written: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.’” It is therefore not lawful for us to hold imperial power on earth, nor do you, emperor, possess the authority over incense and sacred things. I write these things out of concern for your salvation. As for the matters about which you write in your letters, accept this as my position:

I neither sit with the Arians nor support them; rather, I condemn their heresy by an anathema. Nor do I subscribe to the accusations against Athanasius, whom we, the Roman Church, and the whole council have pronounced innocent. For when you had learned and examined the matter, you yourself summoned Athanasius and granted him permission to return with honor to his homeland and Church.

What, then, is the reason for this great change, when his enemies are the same men they were before? What they now whisper, they did not dare utter in his presence; they had been murmuring these things before you summoned Athanasius. At that time, when I confronted them, as I said above, and ordered them to produce evidence of their charges, they could bring nothing forward. If they had been able to produce anything, they would not have fled so shamefully.

Who, then, has induced you to forget, after so long a time, your own letters and words? Restrain yourself, I beg you. Do not lend your ears to evil men, and do not make yourself guilty by exchanging favors with them. For whatever indulgence you grant them, you alone will be compelled to answer for in judgment.

They seek through you to injure their enemy and want you to be the instrument of their malice, so that through you they may sow their detestable heresy in the Church. It is not the part of a prudent man to cast himself into certain danger for the sake of gratifying another’s desire.

Cease, I beg you, and listen to me, Constantius. It is fitting both that I should write this and that you should not despise it.”

Thus far the letter of Hosius.

O truly golden letter, filled with the spirit of God’s freedom! For he was truly wise: “Where the Spirit of God is, there is freedom.” Accordingly, Athanasius rightly added this conclusion:

> “That Abrahamic old man, truly Hosius—that is, holy—both thought and wrote these things.”

And truly he was an Abrahamic old man, since, according to the testimony of Athanasius himself, indeed even of his enemies, he was the father of bishops and the head of councils. From this it follows that he was the father of the faith, for he himself formulated the creed at the Council of Nicaea, and all Catholics have inherited his faith. Nothing could be more glorious than this title.

Athanasius then proceeds to recount the new accusations by which Hosius was again attacked by the Africans, saying:

> “He did not lay aside his plots, nor cease seeking opportunities for accusation; rather, he threatened ever more gravely to overcome him by force and bring him over to his side, or to expel him if he refused obedience. But just as the commanders and satraps of Babylon, diligently seeking an accusation against Daniel, could find none except in the law of his God, so now the satraps of impiety could not even invent anything against the old man. He was known to everyone and was regarded as truly Hosius according to his name—that is, holy—and his life was irreproachable, unless they borrowed a charge from his hatred of heresy.

> “They accused him, therefore, not as those men accused Daniel before Darius, who heard such accusations unwillingly, but as Jezebel accused Naboth and as the Jews acted before Herod. He not only refuses to subscribe against Athanasius, but also condemns us on Athanasius’s account. He pursues the heresy with such hatred that he writes to others that it is better to endure death than to become traitors to the truth. He says that Athanasius, his beloved brother, is suffering persecution because of the heresy, and that Liberius, bishop of Rome, and many others are being tested by plots.

> “When Constantius Caesar, the champion of impiety, heard this, and learned that others throughout Spain held the same opinion as Hosius, he summoned them and tried to induce them to subscribe; but when he was unable to compel them, he summoned Hosius and kept him in exile for a full year at Sirmium. That impious man showed no fear either of God or of the affection which his father, Constantine the Great, had held for Hosius. That inhuman man paid no regard to the old age of one already nearly a hundred years old. The new Ahab, the second Baltassar of our age, neglected everything out of love for the heresy.

> “He therefore used such force against the old man and held him by such devices that, afflicted and worn down by misfortunes, Hosius at last, and only with difficulty, entered into communion with Ursacius and Valens, yet without subscribing against Athanasius. But even then Constantius did not regard the matter as insignificant. At the point of death, as though in his testament, Hosius protested against their violence, condemned the Arian heresy, and forbade anyone to approve or receive it.

> “But we shall speak of these things again below, when we discuss Hosius’s death under the year 360.”

Who, observing these things, would not appropriately cry out to the Lord:

> “Astonishment and horror have overtaken the earth; heaven has been stunned by this, and the earth has shuddered more and more.”

The fathers of peoples and teachers of the faith are removed, and the impious are thrust into the Church. Who, seeing Pope Liberius driven from Rome into exile, great Hosius suffering so many evils, and so many bishops from Spain and other regions carried into exile, would not clearly perceive that all the accusations against Athanasius and the others were false, and that everything was teeming with fraud? For what, I ask, was Liberius’s crime? Or what could be censured in the old man Hosius?

Thus far Athanasius concerning Hosius.

**2. Olympius, etc.** Coelestinus, consul of the province of Baetica, is mentioned in the Theodosian Code, from which Morales drew his account in *History of Spain*, under the year of the Lord 356, book X. He was crowned with martyrdom at Rome in the year 362 under Julian the Apostate, on May 2, when his feast, together with that of his companions, is commended in the Roman Martyrology.

As for St. Gregory, bishop of Toledo, who is discussed here and is said to have died at Amphitria—commonly called Hita—in Carpetania on December 20, Equilinus places him in his catalogue, book XI, chapter 130, number 17. He appears in the diptychs of the holy bishops of Toledo preserved in the liturgy of St. Isidore’s Missal, immediately before St. Olympius.

Indeed, St. Gregory is considered one of those about whom St. Athanasius wrote to the solitary ascetics:

> “For who, seeing the father of bishops, the great Hosius, suffering so many evils, and bishops from Spain and other regions being carried into exile, would not perceive that all the accusations against Athanasius were false?”

And again:

> “When Constantius Caesar, the champion of impiety, heard this, and learned that others throughout Spain held the same opinion as Hosius,” etc.

Here something highly worthy of note is that many have been deceived into believing that this Gregory was St. Gregory of Baetica, the bishop of Iliberris and companion of St. Lucifer, of whom Jerome said in his *Chronicle*, under the year 374:

> “Lucifer, bishop of Caralis, dies; together with Gregory, bishop of Spain, he never joined in the perversity of Rimini.”

Yet the Gregory meant here was Gregory of Toledo. This is necessarily demonstrated by the fact that the Baetican Gregory had not yet risen to the episcopate in the very year of St. Lucifer’s death, as we shall show below; nor, so far as we know, did he ever suffer exile or accompany Lucifer.

Gregory of Toledo, however, was led into exile and suffered many hardships. Together with St. Lucifer, at the false council of Rimini, he strongly opposed Ursacius and Valens. This is sufficiently indicated by Jerome’s words cited above. Jerome does not call him Gregory of Baetica or Gregory of Iliberris, but “a bishop of Spain,” a designation that properly belongs only to the primate of Toledo.

We shall discuss him again below, under the year of the Lord 366. I would nevertheless note that Sihignia, mentioned here, is now called Illescas, as may be inferred by comparing the ancient location of Sihignia with that of Illescas.

**3. Celebris, etc.** Julian mentions the council held at Corduba in favor of Athanasius in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 350. It was undoubtedly one of those which St. Athanasius says were convened on his behalf in his letter to Epictetus, when he writes:

> “At councils held in various places throughout Gaul, Spain, and at Rome, all who were present in those assemblies, moved by one spirit and with a common decision, struck with an anathema those men who flee the light and still hide themselves, holding the opinions of Arius—I mean Auxentius of Milan, Ursacius, and Valens.”

What council, I ask, was that council held in Spain at which Ursacius, Valens, and the other Arians were struck with an anathema? I read of no other than the council of Corduba. That it was held at Corduba is indicated by the see and presence of Hosius. Since he was the patron of councils, there can be no doubt that he would convene one in his own city to establish the Catholic faith, especially in a time of urgent necessity.

For it was necessary publicly to excuse—or even to accuse before the assembled senate of the Fathers—the conduct of the man who had entered into communion with Valens and Ursacius amid public scandal, though under fear of death, after he had once been permitted to return home. It was necessary to make his faith clear: he had never opposed the faith he had formulated at Nicaea, nor had he ever opposed Athanasius.

The emperor Constantius had indeed convened a false council at Rimini in favor of the Arians in the year of the Lord 359—not 259, as the text of Severus’s *History*, book II, appears to read—where some bishops were subtly compelled to subscribe against Athanasius. Hosius entered into communion with Ursacius and Valens, but only on the condition that he would not subscribe against Athanasius. Athanasius himself left this on record in his letter to those leading the solitary life, where, speaking of the threats made by the emperor Constantius against Hosius, he says:

> “He used such force against the old man and held him so tightly that, afflicted and worn down by misfortunes, he finally, and only with difficulty, entered into communion with Ursacius and Valens, but without subscribing against Athanasius.”

Yet even then he did not regard the matter as insignificant, etc.

Speaking of these events, Sozomen, book IV, chapter 5, says:

> “The old man, as the report goes, was severely beaten there with blows,” etc.

Socrates, book II, chapter 24, says:

> “As soon as that old man refused to assent to their faith, blows were inflicted upon him and his limbs were twisted by instruments.”

Theodoret has the same account in book II, chapter 15.

Behold the fall of great Hosius and of certain other Fathers at Rimini. Since we are certain of his recantation on Athanasius’s testimony, and since they themselves recanted this in no council other than the council of Corduba, we are compelled to acknowledge the council of Corduba and to accept what Damasus said about it:

> “From the very beginning, the matter was corrected by those same men who at Rimini were being compelled to revoke or retract, until they confessed that the matter had been stolen from them by deception.”

At the time of the deception at Rimini, Hosius was already a hundred years old, as Athanasius said to the solitary ascetics:

> “That inhuman man paid no regard to the old age of a man already a hundred years old.”

Of those whom Dexter reports as having attended the council of Corduba, several subscribed the acts of Sardica: Costus, first bishop of Barcelona and afterward of Zaragoza; Florentius, metropolitan of Mérida; Praetextatus of Barcelona; Idatius of Ebora; and, in place of Anianus of Cástulo, who had attended Sardica, his successor Marcellus.

Domitianus of Astorga had also attended Sardica, but Dexter is silent about him here. Perhaps, being detained in exile, he was unable to go to Corduba.

**4. At Sentica, etc.** That Sentica was the ancient and noble city of Zamora is sufficiently demonstrated by Ptolemy, who places Sentica among the Vaccaei above the Durius, almost at the beginning of Lusitania. Zamora is unquestionably located there. Mariana, book VI, chapter 10, and Álvar Gómez, book III of *The Deeds of Ximénez, Archbishop of Toledo*, teach the same, along with others.

Villanovanus is mistaken in wishing to identify it with Sarabis, for Ptolemy places Sarabis near Pincia, where Tordesillas is located, whereas Sentica lies somewhat farther downstream.

The tomb of Saint Baudelius—which the Vulgate calls Saint Baal—seen at Zamora in the church of Saint Torquatus agrees with this identification. Its inscription, written in ancient characters, says that he suffered martyrdom for Christ there, at Monte Concilii near the city walls, together with his companions.

This Baudelius is therefore quite different from the other Baudelius who was killed at Nîmes in Gaul, whose feast is celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of June.]

## A.D. 356. A.R. 1107

Hosius writes a frank letter to Constantius Augustus.

## A.D. 356. A.R. 1107

Gregory, a holy man who attended the council of Rimini and strongly opposed Ursacius and Valens, succeeds Olympius in that see. Olympius, a most celebrated and holy man, suffered many incredible hardships for the sake of the faith—for he had been exiled three times in defense of the Catholic faith, abroad and also in Spain, including at Toledo. He published books dedicated to Coelestinus, consul of Baetica, who later became a martyr.

Gregory is exiled to Minorca for the sake of the faith. A letter of congratulation is sent to him while he is residing at the town of Sihignia in Carpetania, twenty-four Roman miles from Toledo on the road to Complutum; Bishop Hilary of Poitiers also frequently sends him letters.

## A.D. 356. A.R. 1107

The memory of Saint Olympius is held in great honor among the Toledans. In the year 345 he attended the council of Corduba in the case of Athanasius, to which many bishops assembled from Spain, Gaul, Italy, and Germany. Besides Olympius, these included Costus of Zaragoza, Marcellus of Cástulo, Florentius of Mérida, Praetextatus of Barcelona, and others—one hundred in all—who also acquitted Athanasius.

## A.D. 356. A.R. 1107
