At Sentica in Spain, Baudelius, Julia, and other martyrs are venerated; they had suffered in Spain during other persecutions.

[Note: **A.D. 360.—1. Gregory, etc.** We have said enough about St. Gregory of Toledo under the preceding year. That St. Hilary of Poitiers flourished in these days is clear from his own works on the councils, especially the council of Rimini, and from Jerome’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and elsewhere. Hilary was exiled for the faith at the same time as Gregory, but after the death of Constantius Augustus both eventually returned to their sees. We shall discuss Audentius, Gregory’s successor, below.]

[Col. 0495C] 2. Hosius, etc. The most learned Cardinal Baronius has indeed vindicated Hosius from the injury commonly done him, when he is suddenly said to have died with his mouth twisted because of the unjust judgment delivered against Saint Gregory of Iliberri, for which he supposedly immediately experienced divine vengeance. This imposture is usually attributed to Saint Isidore of Seville, since it is found in some manuscripts of the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; but the older copies preserved in the royal library of Saint Lawrence show how false this is, for they contain no such story. It was doubtless borrowed from the ravings of Marcellinus the Arian, as Baronius proves thoroughly. The very learned Don Ferdinand de Mendoza, in his defense of the church of Iliberri, attributes it to Theodiscus, deposed from the see of Seville by Gregory, whereas others attribute it to Marcellinus.

Certainly the unanimous judgment of the holy Fathers agrees in treating Hosius himself as a saint, for after his death they call him truly holy, and truly Hosius—that is, Hosius in both reality and name—for *Hosius* means “holy” in Greek, as can be seen in Athanasius, Hilary, and others. [Col. 0495D] Indeed, Primus of Chalon-sur-Saône lists him among the saints in his *Spiritual Topography*, under the entry “Corduba.” There he says:

“Corduba, a city of Baetica: here are the martyrs Solomon, Perfectus, Secundianus, Peter, Aventius, Jeremiah, Fandilas, Zoilus, Paul, and Leovigildus; and Christopher. Here Hosius, bishop, companion of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, of Hilary of Poitiers, of Eusebius of Vercelli, and of Meletius, bishop of Antioch, departs as a confessor.”

And, what is most important, the Church of Syria celebrates the feast of Saint Hosius on November 5, and has his name written in its calendar in these words: “The solemn feast of Hosius.” The archbishop of Damascus, serving in the city as envoy for the patriarch of that nation, also testifies that many churches in the East are dedicated to this saint’s name and that he is held there in especial veneration.

But let us hear Athanasius himself, who, in his letter to the Solitaries, reports that Hosius died in a far more illustrious manner than Marcellinus relates. He did not, he says, fall from a judicial throne with his mouth twisted, but confessed the faith of the Council of Nicaea with a clear voice and tranquil mind. “When he was about to die,” Athanasius says of Hosius, “as though in his testament, he protested against the violence inflicted upon him at Rimini by the ministers of Constantius, condemned the Arian heresy, anathematized it, and forbade anyone to approve or accept it.” These facts are reported almost exactly by Dexter, so that one may see truth agreeing with truth.

Let us add something that most clearly refutes the aforesaid fiction: in this very year, in which Hosius died—namely, the year of Christ 360—Saint Gregory was not yet bishop of Iliberri. Indeed, he did not become so until the year of Christ 390, after another thirty years, as we shall show in its place together with Dexter; yet in that fiction he is already asserted to be bishop. Moreover, it is established that Gregory survived beyond the year of the Lord 407, which proves that he was of a much later age than Hosius, although the contrary is asserted in that tale.

3. At Carthage, etc. There exists a book *On the Wrath of God*, which Jerome calls “very beautiful” in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Lactantius. Its beginning is: “I have often observed, Donatus, that very many people think that God is not angry,” etc.

Usuard deals with Donatus himself, who suffered martyrdom, on March 1: “On the same day, Saint Donatus the martyr, who suffered at Carthage under the judge Ursatius and the tribune Marcellinus.” Ado writes somewhat more fully that he was devoted to military service and was therefore beheaded by the military tribune. From Ado derive Equilinus, book III, chapter 163, and Galesinus, on the same day. They nevertheless deserve correction because they have added on their own authority that he was killed in Africa, as though there had been no Carthage other than the African one.

The judge’s name is read differently. In Dexter’s manuscript it is Veranius; in Usuard, Ursatius; in Equilinus, Nisatius. Which reading is the more accurate is difficult to determine.

4. At Tarragona, etc. The feast day of the holy martyrs Crispilus—also called Crispinus—and his companions appears in the Roman Martyrology and in the martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, and Ado on December 5. Their names are Crispilus, Julius, Potamia, Felix, Gratus, and seven others with them.

As for the name of the city ennobled by their blood, the manuscripts display the greatest corruption. Molanus has *Thagora* in Usuard; Equilinus, book XI, final chapter, no. 3, has *Togara*; Baronius, in the Martyrology, has *Thagura*. Once that reading is admitted, the narrative is transferred to Africa, where Thagura is a city of Numidia mentioned by Antoninus in his *Itinerary*; the Martyrology accordingly adds, “at Thagura in Africa,” although it is already clear from Dexter that the reading should be “at Tarragona.”

The copyist’s confusion was easy: *Tarrago*—or *Tarraco*—was transformed into *Tagora* by transposing the syllables *go* and *ra*. Errors of this kind are found everywhere in ancient manuscripts.

5. Maxima, etc. Equilinus discusses her, together with the deeds of Saint Ansanus the martyr, in book I, chapter 14. He says that Saint Maxima, a virgin, was born in the territory of Tanagrum; that when she came to Rome she lifted Saint Ansanus, then twelve years old, from the sacred font, while the priest Protasius supplied the baptismal water; but that afterward, when she was arrested by the persecutors, she was first handed over to prison for many days and then beaten with clubs until she breathed her last on the Kalends of December. She is commemorated on that day in the Roman Martyrology and elsewhere. Ansanus was later killed for Christ as an old man. We discussed the river Tanagrus of Spain above, under the year 208, no. 8.

6. At Caraca, etc. That city is now called Guadalajara, as we noted under the year 86. The feast of Saint Perseveranda, a virgin, is celebrated on June 26 in Usuard and the Roman Martyrology. Equilinus mentions her in book XI, chapter 130, no. 160.

7. At Verovisca, etc. Today it is generally called Virbiesca, retaining nearly the ancient name. It is a very well-known town in the diocese of Burgos. Ptolemy mentions it among the Autrigones, as one of the towns of that region.

In book XI of the *Speculum*, chapters 86 and 87, the Belvacensis preserves the acts of Saint Mary the Virgin, who suffered martyrdom there; Equilinus does so in book X, chapter 4. The substance of the story is as follows:

Blessed Mary was the slave of Tertullus, an idolater and a leading man among his people. While he was celebrating his son’s birthday and offering gifts to idols, Mary, devoted according to Christian custom to fasting, was accused before Tertullus by a fellow servant because, being attached to Christian rites, she refused to eat food sacrificed to idols. For this reason her master cruelly scourged her and confined her in a prison at home.

When the city governor learned of this, he ordered Mary to be brought before his tribunal. There she was publicly torn with iron claws so savagely that the people, drenched in tears, cried out to the governor. He then abandoned her, and she was filled with a heavenly vision of angels; at the divine command she fled outside the city.

When the attendants pursued her, she took refuge inside a fissure in a certain rock. The fissure immediately closed by divine intervention and sheltered the martyr within its substance, while a portion of her clothing remained outside as evidence of so great a miracle.

The governor summoned the people to break apart the rock, attributing the event to magic. But as soon as his ministers attempted to lay their impious hands upon it, a great flash arose from the east, accompanied by thunder and a crash, so that they thought everything was collapsing. The earth immediately shook, and behold, two horsemen came from the heavenly throne, shining with great radiance. Their bridles, saddles, and all their trappings glittered with heavenly fire like lamps.

Many of those standing around fell dead. Others—more numerous—who had fled to the temple of the idols were likewise burned when the temple itself was struck by lightning. Altogether 2,700 people died. The survivors, numbering about 3,000, loudly proclaimed the greatness of Mary’s God and were led to the true faith.

The Christians then easily extracted the Virgin’s body from the marble—for she had died there—and buried it honorably.

This is approximately the account of the Belvacensis, who nevertheless gives the name of the city, saying:

“The acts report that the governor, moved partly by anger and partly by astonishment, ordered Philocomus, the chief magistrate of the city of Verovisca, to hurry to the place mentioned and to bring with him an innumerable multitude to remove the stone,” etc.

Thus the printed manuscripts read. They have *Verovensium* corruptly instead of *Veroviscensium*; even more corruptly, the margin gives *Netromensium*; and most corruptly of all, Equilinus reads “at Nicomedia.”

As for the day of her passion, some assign it to November 1, as do Usuard, the Roman Martyrology, and Equilinus; others—namely Galesinus and the very ancient Cremona Martyrology, which he used—place it on March 17.

They differ greatly among themselves, however. The former do not call her a slave, but merely Mary, and say that she completed her martyrdom after being stretched on the rack and torn by claws, whereas Mary the Slave died after taking refuge within the rock. I am convinced that these were two different women named Mary, and that our Mary belongs to March 17. Indeed, when some say that she suffered under Hadrian, this must be understood of the other Mary, the martyr; for Dexter places our Mary under Julian.

8. At Capara, etc. We have discussed Capara elsewhere; it is now called Caparra, on the road by which one travels from Salamanca to Mérida.

As for the holy martyrs mentioned here, Dexter contains two other pairs with the same names. One pair consists of Felix and Fortunatus, disciples of Saint Irenaeus, who suffered at Valencia around the year 255; the other consists likewise of Felix and Fortunatus of Patavonium, under the year 300. A third pair is now added at Capara.

Unless someone wishes to claim that those said to be venerated at Capara were these very disciples of Irenaeus—a claim that would nevertheless be made without sufficient reason, although it could not be proved false.

9. At Toledo, etc. This is that Vincent whom Marcellinus mentions with great praise in his little work. Baronius, under the year 371, reports his words as follows:

“Mention is also made in the same book of Marcellinus of Vincent, a Spanish priest, who, because he refused to communicate with such Arians, had suffered the gravest injuries at the hands of the bishops Lucius and Hyginus. For when they burst into the church with clubs, where the people involved had gathered, they killed several of them there; some of these, although distinguished by the honor of the decurionate, were nevertheless thrust into prison, and one of them was killed. When the same Vincent was holding assemblies with his people in the countryside, they attacked them and caused such confusion that, after the altar had been removed, they placed it beneath their feet as an object of contempt, like an idol.”

Hyginus was indeed bishop of Córdoba. He was touched by the Arian heresy and afterward by that of Priscillian; for this reason he persecuted Vincent, the Catholic priest, with such savagery. In the end he paid the penalty for such great crimes, as we shall say below with Dexter under the year 384. Meanwhile Vincent was living in exile at Toledo, distinguished for his piety and intelligence.

Another Vincent was the priest and companion of Saint Jerome in these times; Jerome discusses him at length in Letter 61.

In this same year, 360, Saint Jerome’s *Chronicle* also mentions Peter of Zaragoza, who taught rhetoric with distinction. His words are: “Peter of Zaragoza, a distinguished teacher of rhetoric, is teaching.”

A.D. 360. A.R. 1111. Bishop Gregory of Toledo shared his affairs with Blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; and while Hilary was in exile, Audentius, archdeacon and citizen of Toledo, administered the affairs of the Church in Gregory’s absence with remarkable ability.

A.D. 360. A.R. 1111. Hosius, well over a hundred years old, departed in holiness and piety; in his testament he professed the faith of the Council of Nicaea and declared that it had never been his intention to depart from it by even the breadth of a fingernail, whether through threats or promises.

A.D. 360. A.R. 1111. At Carthage Spartaria, during the most impious persecution of Julian, Donatus, a Spanish martyr to whom Lactantius addressed his book *On the Wrath of God*, suffered under the judge Veranus.

A.D. 360. A.R. 1111. At Tarragona in Hispania Citerior, Crispilus the martyr and others.

[Col. 0497] A.D. 360. A.R. 1111. Maxima, a virgin of Caurium, from the town of Tanagrum, suffers at Rome.

A.D. 360. A.R. 1111. At Caraca in Carpetania, Perseveranda, a virgin devoted to God.

A.D. 360. A.R. 1111. At Verovisca in Spain, Saint Mary the Slave, a virgin.

A.D. 360. A.R. 1111. At Capara in Vettonia, the holy martyrs Felix and Fortunatus are venerated.

A.D. 360. A.R. 1111. At Toledo, Vincent of Córdoba flourishes, distinguished for piety and intelligence.

[Col. 0497] [Note: [Col. 0498D]]

A.D. 364.—1. Jovianus, etc. Julian had seized the empire in the year of the Lord 362; but in the year 364 he was killed in the war against the Persians, at the age of thirty-one, in the first year of his reign, nine months less nine days. Saint John of Damascus, in his first Oration *On Images*, reports that he was killed by the hand of Saint Mercury the martyr and that he breathed out his soul with these words: “You have conquered, Nazarene.” The source is Theodoret, book III of his *History*, chapter 35, and from him Nicephorus, book X, chapter 35.

Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople, gives a lengthy account of Julian’s cruel savagery toward Christians in his *Oration on the Quadragesimal Fast*, in volume V of Lipomanus. Jovian, a most pious and Christian prince, succeeded him, but reigned only seven months and twenty days. As Ammianus reports in book 25, he died either from the fumes of burning coals or from the fresh plaster of his bedchamber.

2. The Illyrian Synod, etc. In the printed manuscript of Dexter, *Illiciana* was read, but incorrectly. This synod was held in Illyricum in the year 365, according to Cardinal Baronius. Theodoret discusses it in book IV, chapter 8; Sozomen in book VI, chapter 12; and Hilary in the fragments of the Council of Rimini. It was presided over by the priest Elpidius, legate of the pope.

A.D. 364. A.R. 1115. Jovian, a Catholic, is appointed emperor in succession to Julian the Apostate.

[Col. 0499] A.D. 364. A.R. 1115. The Ilician Synod is convened at approximately the same time.

[Col. 0499] [Note: [Col. 0499A]]

A.D. 366.—1. Gregory, etc. Consult what we noted under the year 360 concerning Gregory and Audentius.

The feast day of Saint Gregory the bishop, who died at Amphitria, is recorded by Equilinus in book XI, chapter 130, no. 17, in these words: “Gregory the bishop became renowned on this same day”—namely, December 20—“at Amphitria.” He had indeed been exiled to Minorca; from there he went to Amphitria, where he ended his life.

Audentius is commemorated in the diptychs of the Mass of the Missal of Saint Isidore; he is placed after Saint Gregory of Toledo, likewise a bishop.

2. Saint Paul, etc. Dexter dealt with Saint Orosius under the year 352. He was the uncle of Paul Orosius the famous writer and disciple of Saint Augustine; he was also the brother of the elder Paul Orosius, whose son and biographer the younger Orosius was. His death is recorded this year in these words: “The elder Saint Paul Orosius remained at Rome.”

3. Liberius, etc. The birthplace of Saint Damasus has long been disputed contentiously. The Portuguese wish him to have been Portuguese; the people of Mantua insist that he was a citizen of their own city; nor are there lacking people from Tarragona who claim him as a Tarragonese.

But thanks be to God, Dexter has settled the question by assigning him to the people of Mantua—and rightly. There are still those who have read at Madrid, in the parish church of Saint Saviour, an inscription carved in marble in ancient lettering, asserting that the most holy pontiff was baptized in that church, since he was born in its parish. Perhaps he was descended from Portuguese parents; from this the other opinion may have arisen, just as we saw happen with Saint Melchiades above, under the years 248 and 299.

Consult the learned history of Madrid by Aegidius Gundisalvus Davila, the royal historiographer, where he defends that city as the birthplace of Saint Damasus.

Nor can the following addition in the printed manuscript of Dexter harm our case: “Some make him a Portuguese from Igeditania, others a Tarragonese.” It does not, I say, harm us, because it is clear that these words were added later and eventually transferred from the margin into the text. Dexter could not have written them, since, being a contemporary of Damasus and a member of the same province—that is, Spain—and having likewise been educated at Rome, he could not have been ignorant of the true city of Damasus’s birth and then left the matter unresolved.

Indeed, even if that reading is admitted, we still have it from Dexter’s own meaning that Damasus was from Mantua in Carpetania. Dexter states this affirmatively and in the first place, as his own view. When reporting the other opinions, he says, “Some make him Portuguese, others Tarragonese”; but when he speaks of Mantua he does not say “some” or “certain people say or make him so.” Instead he says absolutely: “Damasus succeeds Liberius, from Mantua of the Carpetanians.”

Since the praises of so great a Father have been sung by countless people, we would rather remain silent than speak of them. Consult Baronius, volume IV. I cannot, however, keep silent about one thing: the Catholic Church owes this one man the Latin edition of the sacred Scriptures and the custom of singing divine praises in the choirs.

He began his pontificate in the year of the Lord 367 and sat for approximately seventeen years and three months.

A.D. 366. A.R. 1117. Audentius, the first successor to Gregory in the see of Toledo, was born at Toledo and came from Sihignia, a town of Hispania in Carpetania, twenty-four miles from Toledo. He was a man of outstanding holiness, flourishing in the praise of a keen intelligence and judgment against all heretics. Saint Gregory of Toledo was translated from Amphitria to Toledo and was received among the saints of Spain on December 20.

A.D. 366. A.R. 1117. Saint Paul Orosius the elder remained at Rome; his son by his wife, Paul Orosius the younger, died at Carthage and was brought to Rome.

A.D. 366. A.R. 1117. Damasus, from Mantua of the Carpetanians, succeeds Liberius.

[Col. 0499] [Note: [Col. 0500B]]

A.D. 368.—1. Frequent synods, etc. In writing to the bishops of Spain, Saint Lucius the pope had ordered them to celebrate synods frequently, as had been the custom of the universal Church from apostolic times. The letter itself is extant in volume I of the old edition of the Councils. We now have Dexter’s testimony that this command was obeyed in these times.

In the printed manuscript, *Trucum* was read corruptly; *Tritium* has been restored in its place. Tritium, surnamed Melatum, was a not insignificant town among the Berones; it is now called Tafalla in the kingdom of Navarre. Ptolemy places another town nearby, where Tudela now stands or not far from it.

2. Audentius, etc. Gennadius discusses him in his book *On Illustrious Men*: “Audentius,” he says, “a Spanish bishop, wrote against the Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians, and especially, with particular attention, against the Photinians, who are now called Bonosians, a book entitled *On the Faith against All Heretics*. In it he showed that the Son of God was co-eternal with the Father from antiquity and that he did not then receive the beginning of his divinity from God the Father when, having become man through God the Creator, he was conceived and born from Mary, the Virgin Mother.”

Baronius also discusses him under the year 389.

3. Corcheia, etc. At precisely these times Matronianus flourished in Spain. Jerome writes of him in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Matronianus, of the province of Spain, was highly learned and, in metrical composition, comparable to the ancients.” Works of his talent, composed in various meters, survive.

Whether Dexter is speaking of this same man here, whether he had two names, or whether we have *Marcius* as a corruption of *Matronianus*, I would not dare decide. One thing, however, is certainly lamentable: Matronianus defected to Priscillian, as we shall say immediately.

4. Against Julian, etc. Among the others, Gregory of Nazianzus and Cyril of Alexandria distinguished themselves in refuting Julian.

A.D. 368. A.R. 1119. Frequent synods are said to have been assembled throughout Spain; they were convened especially at Toledo and near Tritium in Varia.

A.D. 368. A.R. 1119. Audentius, bishop of Toledo, to whom Saint Basil writes, publishes books and fights against the Arians and Photinians.

A.D. 368. A.R. 1119. At Corcheia in Spain, Marcius, a lyric poet, flourishes.

A.D. 368. A.R. 1119. More than sixty most wise, eloquent, and thoroughly Catholic Doctors write against Julian the Apostate.

[Col. 0501] [Note: [Col. 0501A]]

A.D. 369.—1. The Roman Synod, etc. It was presided over by Saint Damasus the pope, who indeed convened three synods at Rome: the first at the beginning of his pontificate against Ursatius and Valens; the second this year against Auxentius; and the third against the Apollinarians around the seventh year of his pontificate.

2. Saint Ambrose, etc. Here is the knot that must be untied, which often caused Cardinal Baronius anxiety and compelled him to depart from the common opinion. Until then, it had been believed that Saint Ambrose’s ordination occurred in the year 369, and all who wrote before Baronius, following the chronology of Ambrose’s deeds, held this view.

Baronius, however, moves it five years later, namely to the year of the Lord 374, relying also on the authority of Saint Jerome’s *Chronicle*. Under the eleventh year of the emperor Valentinian, when Gratian was consul for the third time and Equitius was consul, Jerome writes:

“After the belated death of Auxentius, with Ambrose appointed at Milan, all Italy is converted to the true faith.”

Some have interpreted these words as though Jerome meant that all Italy could not have been converted to the true faith before the belated death of Auxentius, even though Ambrose had been appointed bishop.

Baronius rightly attacks this interpretation, since the testimonies of Paulinus, Rufinus, Sozomen, and Theodoret clearly establish that Ambrose was not promoted to the episcopate until after the death of Auxentius, the Arian bishop. Accordingly, in the lessons of the Roman Breviary we read:

“At the command of Probus he came with authority to Milan, where, after Auxentius the Arian bishop had died, the people were divided over the choice of his successor.”

Nor is the view he himself maintains supported by any greater probability—namely, that Jerome’s words show that three events occurred together in that year: the death of Auxentius, the ordination of Ambrose, and the conversion of all Italy to the true faith. But where is the evidence for this?

“Certainly,” he says in his notes on December 7, “these events are mentioned only in the year in which they occurred. Otherwise Jerome must have been mistaken and, through some negligence, placed events of his own times, which by design should have been arranged year by year, in a period far removed from their actual time.”

Yet I am astonished that so learned a man should so readily accuse Jerome of negligence if Jerome had not intended what Baronius supposes.

Who does not see that it is difficult to believe that all Italy, which had so long suffered under the Arian heresy, was converted to the true faith in one and the same year? Surely such a universal restoration required much effort, labor, and time.

That is in fact what happened. Ambrose was ordained in 369, and after five or six years of exertion and preaching, namely in the year of Christ 374 assigned by Jerome, he reaped the fruit of Italy’s conversion. His words themselves sufficiently indicate this. Jerome’s principal concern in that passage is to discuss the conversion of Italy; before that conversion he places the death of Auxentius and the ordination of Ambrose because the conversion originated from them. He suggests that those two events preceded the conversion; he nowhere asserts that they occurred in the same year.

Baronius is nevertheless very emphatic in proving that there were two men named Auxentius at Milan. We frankly admit this, although it makes no difference to us whether one or several men bore that name, provided we establish at least that Saint Ambrose was not ordained in the same year as Italy’s restoration; Dexter deals with the year of the ordination, while Jerome deals with the restoration, presupposing the prior ordination after the death of the elder Auxentius.

A.D. 369. A.R. 1120. A Roman Synod is assembled against the Arian heretics.

A.D. 369. A.R. 1120. Ambrose, formerly a judge, becomes bishop of Milan.

[Col. 0501] [Note: [Col. 0502A]]

A.D. 370.—1. Colleges, etc. Consult what we noted under the year of the Lord 185 concerning colleges for training young men for the clergy in Spain.

2. Gregory of Nazianzus, etc. The fame of the most celebrated of all the Doctors requires neither our exposition nor any account of his struggle against the heretics. See Baronius, volume IV.

3. Asturius, etc. This is that Saint Asturius Serrano who later became archbishop of Toledo and whom Saint Ildefonsus mentions with praise in his book *On Illustrious Men*. His body is preserved in the Holy Church of Oviedo, which venerates his memory under the name of Saint Serrano on March 8. We shall discuss him more fully below, over many years—namely, 380, 396, 406, 423, and 424.

4. Aquilius, etc. Jerome writes of him in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Aquilius Severus in Spain, of the family of that Severus to whom Lactantius addressed two books of letters, composed a volume resembling an itinerary, containing the course of his entire life, in prose as well as verse. He called it *katastrophē* (καταστροφή, ‘conclusion’) or *peira* (πεῖρα, ‘experience’), and died under the emperor Valentinian.”

5. Under Pacianus, etc. We shall discuss Orosius under the year of the Lord 400. Of Pacianus, Dexter’s father, Jerome writes in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

“Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona in the heights of the Pyrenees, distinguished for chastity and eloquence, and equally in life and speech, wrote various short works, including *Kerdos* (Κέρδος, ‘Gain’) and one against the Novatians. He died under the emperor Theodosius, already in extreme old age.”

His works, dedicated to Symphorianus, survive in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*. His name is written in both the new and old Roman Martyrologies and in Usuard, on March 9. Equilinus also discusses him in book XI of his *Catalogue*, chapter 123.

A.D. 370. A.R. 1121. Colleges for educating young men for the clerical state, interrupted through the negligence of the times, are restored through the diligence of Saint Audentius, bishop of Toledo, and other bishops.

A.D. 370. A.R. 1121. Gregory of Nazianzus fights fiercely against the heretics.

A.D. 370. A.R. 1121. Asturius, known in Carpetania at Villasicca, flourishes as a young man in the Church of Toledo, distinguished for piety and intelligence.

A.D. 370. A.R. 1121. Aquilius Severus, a native of Toledo and descended from another Aquilius Severus, to whom Lactantius wrote two books of letters, is held in great esteem at this time.

A.D. 370. A.R. 1121. Under Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona, Paul Orosius the Younger is born, a citizen of Tarragona and disciple of Saint Augustine.

[Col. 0501] [Note: [Col. 0502C]]

A.D. 375.—Valentinian, etc. Saint Jerome brought his *Chronicles* to an end, writing in this very year:

“Valentinian died at Brigetio from a sudden rupture of blood, which in Greek is called apoplexy. After him Gratian, having taken his brother Valentinian into the empire, reigns with his uncle Valens.”

A.D. 375. A.R. 1126. Valentinian, a Catholic emperor and pious man, died; his son Gratian succeeded him in the empire.

[Col. 0503] [Note: [Col. 0503A]]

A.D. 380.—1. Adelphus, etc. At this very time there was a certain Adelphius, from whom the Adelphian heretics took their name, as Theodoret writes in book IV, chapter 10.

Compelled by Flavian, bishop of Antioch, this man confessed that he believed that the washing of baptism did not itself confer grace upon those who received it worthily, but that grace came through the prayers of the priest who administered it. He also said that the Holy Spirit visibly descended in baptism and rendered the baptized person free from every stimulus of lust, and consequently free from the obligation of fasting. Indeed, he maintained that the Holy Trinity itself was seen by the recipients without a veil.

O madness! Whether this was the same man of whom Dexter speaks here may be questioned, since their times coincide; but their locations differ greatly, since the former lived in Greece and the latter in Spain.

We discussed the Carenses, a people near Ilerda, under the year of the Lord 311. I shall not omit that in the acts of Charlemagne an Adelphus is found as prince of the Cauci. Sent by Charlemagne with a strong force into Britain, he returned victorious.

[Col. 0503B] 2. Vesania, etc. We said under the year 169 that that Marcus the Gnostic infected a number of women in Spain; consult what was said there.

Severus Sulpicius treats Priscillian’s madness and deeds in book II of his *Sacred History*, and Morales discusses them at length from him in book X, chapters 34 and 35; their accounts agree in every respect with Dexter’s writings.

Saint Jerome also discusses him in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. The bishops of the provinces of Carthage, Tarragona, Lusitania, and Baetica set out his errors at length in the rule of faith contained in the First Council of Toledo. It comprises eighteen articles, including these: that not everything in the world was created by God; that God is not three Persons; that the Word did not assume flesh; and many other ravings of the Gnostics, which it would take too long to enumerate individually.

Augustine discusses Priscillian and his followers in his book *On Heresies*, chapter 70, and in the second book of his *Retractations*, chapter 11. We shall explain in their proper places how, through the authority of many councils, the corruption of the Priscillianists was suppressed, and what became of the founder and his followers.

3. Flourishes, etc. Authors disagree about the city whose birth gave distinction to Prudentius Clemens. Some insist that he was born at Calagurris, among them Antonius Nebrissensis and Juan de Mariana in book IV, chapter 17; others place his birth at Zaragoza, as Aldus preferred in his *Life of Prudentius*.

Most recently, Mantuanus departs from both opinions in his notes on that passage of Mariana and attempts at length to prove that Prudentius was born at Salia, among the Saleni, who lived along the Cantabrian Ocean.

No one, however, fails to believe that he can derive his opinion with certainty from Prudentius’s own writings. Nebrissensis and Mariana use passages in which the poet calls the city of Calagurris his own, particularly from the hymn on the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, where, speaking of Saints Emeterius and Chelidonius, he says:

> Our Calagurris will bear both,  
> whom we venerate.

In another hymn concerning the same martyrs:

[Col. 0503D]

> This good the Savior himself granted us to enjoy,  
> when he consecrated the martyrs’ bodies to our town.

Here he calls Calagurris “our town.”

Aldus and his followers are supported by two other passages. One comes from the aforementioned hymn on the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, at its beginning:

[Col. 0504A]

> Twice nine, our people, beneath one  
> tomb, guard the ashes of the martyrs;  
> Zaragoza we call the city—  
> so great is the matter entrusted to it.

The other comes from the hymn on Saint Vincent, archdeacon of Zaragoza:

> He is ours—though far from here, in an unknown city,  
> having suffered, he gave glory  
> to the tomb, a victor, near the shore  
> of lofty Saguntum.

And:

> Ours also is the boy in the arena—  
> that is, the Zaragoza arena—  
> anointed with the art of virtue  
> and the oil of faith. He learned to subdue  
> the dreadful enemy by his strength.

Mantuanus, however, counters that Prudentius also calls Tarragona his own, although no one has ever imagined that he was born there. For in the hymn on Saint Fructuosus and his companions, who suffered at Tarragona, he says:

[Col. 0504B]

> O triple honor, O threefold summit,  
> by which the head of our city is raised,  
> surpassing all the cities of Iberia.

“Therefore,” he says, “one cannot derive from this any certain knowledge of his city. He calls many cities his own, plainly for no other reason than that they were subject to the jurisdiction of Tarragona in Spain. For all three belong to that province: Calagurris, Zaragoza, and Tarragona.”

He proves that Prudentius was born at Salia in Asturias from the prologue to the *Cathemerinon*, where he writes:

> While this flying life was passing,  
> gray hair suddenly crept upon me in old age,  
> accusing me of having forgotten ancient Salia, the consul,  
> under whom my first day dawned.

The sense, he supposes, is that gray hair suddenly crept upon him in his old age, accusing him of having forgotten the ancient consul—that is, that ancient year under which his first day at Salia had dawned.

It was indeed customary for the years themselves to be called by the names of the consuls, since they were always distinguished by the new consuls. Martial sufficiently proves this in book I:

> Your thirtieth consulship is now almost twice upon you;

that is, “you are nearly sixty years old.” Cicero also says in the *Brutus*, “He would have him born under the most recent consuls,” meaning “in the preceding year.”

But when someone undertakes new paths while abandoning the well-trodden and familiar ones, it is not surprising that he alone goes astray in the wilderness. This happened precisely to Mantuanus. In investigating Prudentius’s birthplace, he refused to follow either Calagurris or Zaragoza, the paths his predecessors had worn smooth, and leaped into a certain Salia that no one had ever previously discovered.

We were looking for the city ennobled by Prudentius’s birth, and behold, he identifies a river. For Salia is a river, as Pomponius himself attests in book III, chapter 1, in these words:

“From the river which they call the Salia, the shores gradually begin to recede,” etc.

That there was never a city of this name there is shown by the fact that neither Pomponius himself, nor Pliny, nor Ptolemy, nor Strabo—in short, no geographer ever—mentions such a city in that region of Spain. They do mention the river.

Nor does the statement that the Saleni lived there prove that a city of this name existed there, as he believes. Indeed, if that were true, it would be the chief city of the region, since the people would have received their name from it; and no one listing the cities of the Saleni would omit Salia.

Once this has been established—a point that cannot be called into doubt—Prudentius’s words cannot properly be applied to the river. For when, speaking of his gray hair, he says:

> Accusing me of having forgotten ancient Salia, the consul,  
> under whom my first day dawned,

no one will say that Prudentius meant that he was born in a river.

What, then, is the true sense of the poem? Clearly, it is the sense followed by Dexter and Morales, and almost reached by Nebrissensis—except that, misled by corrupt manuscripts, they called the consul Mesalia rather than Salia.

Prudentius, therefore, was born under the consulship of Salia and Philippus. According to the *Fasti* of Onuphrius and Idatius, their consulship fell in the year of the Lord 348. Thus, in the year 380, in which he is said to have flourished, he was thirty-two years old.

I say that he flourished in rhetorical ability, concerning which he himself says in the same prologue to the *Cathemerinon*:

> My earliest age wept  
> beneath the resounding rods; soon the toga taught me,
Infected with vices, speaking falsely not without guilt.

[Col. 0505B] And again:

Then quarrels armed their troubled minds,  
and a wickedly stubborn desire  
to conquer lay beneath harsh misfortunes.

He was born at Caesaraugusta, as Dexter relates, of a father from Caesaraugusta and a mother from Calagurris; hence he called each city his own on several occasions. He also called Tarraco his own, because at some point he had been its governor, having been appointed by the emperor, as we shall say below. What Mantuanus objects against this is too easily answered to require a lengthy refutation. He says: “The colleague of Philip in the consulship was called Salea, not Salia.” And I reply: “Those peoples of Asturias were called Saleni, from Salea, not from Salia; therefore the river too must be called Salea.” But if he does not wish us to dispute over a single letter in “Salia” as his text has it, let him likewise not dispute over “Salia” in our text—or else in both places. Again he says: “If Salia had been consul, he would by no means have been distinguished by the name ‘the elder,’ since there had never been another consul of that name.” I reply: “What if he called him ‘the elder’ with reference to the consul’s age? What if, among the suffect consuls whose names have not survived, there had been another of that name before him?” But enough of this.

4. Asturius, etc. We have spoken of him above and shall discuss him again below.

5. Gulphilas, etc. Baronius treats him more fully under the year 370, where, drawing on Sozomen, book VI, chapter 37, he asserts that, while Gulphilas was serving as envoy to the emperor, King Athanaric, in consideration of him, allowed the Christians scattered among the Goths to settle in Thrace; and that although at first he had agreed with the Arians, he later repented and, having accepted the Catholic faith, attended the council at Constantinople with Acacius and Eudoxius. He also instructed the Goths to embrace piety and the true worship of God; and, he says, “was the first to discover letters among them,” translating the sacred writings into their native language. His likeness, with the alphabet of the letters he devised above it, is preserved in the Vatican Library, over Bookcase 27. Some call him Gulphilas, others Vulphilas, but the difference is slight.]

A.D. 380. A.R. 1131. Adelphus, appointed teacher of rhetoric to the people of Carens in Spain, distinguished for his learning, talent, and eloquence.

A.D. 380. A.R. 1131. The madness of the Gnostics, spreading in Spain from the disciples of Marcus, attacked Priscillian, a nobleman born in Gallaecia, and Spain at the same time. He became a torch for his own people, for the citizens of his homeland, and for those nearby—a man of keen intelligence.

A.D. 380. A.R. 1131. Flavius Prudentius flourishes, born at Caesaraugusta of a father from Caesaraugusta and a mother from Calagurris, during the consulship of Salia.

[Col. 0505] A.D. 380. A.R. 1131. Asturius, surnamed Serranus, becomes lector under Audientius of Toledo.

A.D. 380. A.R. 1131. Gulphilas the Goth, inventor of Gothic letters and bishop, is highly praised for his learning and talent.

[Col. 0505] [Note: [Col. 0505D]

A.D. 382.—1. Lampadius, etc. He succeeded Symmachus in the urban prefecture. “After Symmachus,” says Ammianus, book XXVII, “the urban prefecture was given to Lampadius. He transferred to the poor and needy in the Vatican the expenditures customarily displayed in the lavish presentation of public entertainments; for this reason he stirred up the populace against himself, so that it came close to setting fire with torches to his house, which stood opposite the Baths of Constantine.” Hence, I believe, arose the tradition that he crossed over into Spain, where, on account of his piety and learning, he deserved to be promoted to the see of Oretania. He is found attending the council of Toledo, called the First, in the year 400, as we shall say in its proper place.

2. Dracontius, etc. Consult Saint Isidore’s book On Illustrious Men concerning Dracontius; there he enumerates his books and praises his talent. I believe that Saint Athanasius addressed to this same Dracontius the letter entitled “To Dracontius,” for we now learn from Dexter that Dracontius, brought from the East—where he was known to Athanasius—and living in exile in Spain, remained there after Athanasius’s death, which occurred in A.D. 372. Some think that Adelphus attended the council of Caesaraugusta, discussed below, and they say that “Adelphus” should be read in place of “Ampelius,” which our codices have.

3. Justus, etc. In the printed edition of Dexter, “to another Justus” is added, but I do not know whom this refers to. There was indeed another Justus in Spain, bishop of Urgell, whose feast day is recorded in the Roman Martyrology on 28 May; but he was much more recent than Dexter, so Dexter could not have had him in mind. Two letters of Saint Ambrose written to Justus are extant: one in book I of the letters, letter 1; the other in book VIII, letter 2, which is number 63 in the sequence. In them, at Justus’s request, Ambrose explains several questions concerning the sacred Scriptures. In the first he explains the meaning of the didrachm, half of which a Hebrew was commanded to offer for the redemption of his soul. It begins: “Ambrose to Justus: You rightly urge me, brother, to turn the conversations of letters and the speech of absent friends toward an interpretation of the heavenly oracle,” etc. In the second he proves that the ancients—whom many deny to have written according to art—wrote according to grace, which surpasses every art; nevertheless, those who wrote about art discovered art in their writings. Consult these letters, since they are filled with learned seriousness.

4. Crematus, etc. In this passage the printed Caesaraugustan codex has most corruptly confused the death of Constans with that of Valens, reading: “Crematus, with Valens at Helenema, a city of Gaul,” etc. It is established from Jerome’s Chronicle under A.D. 353 that the emperor Constans was killed not far from Spain, in a fortress called Helena, a town of Narbonese Gaul. But everyone who mentions Valens—Sozomen, Socrates, Rufinus, Theodoret, Ammianus, Nicephorus, and the rest—reports that Valens was burned not at Helena in Gaul, but at the imperial estate of Melantiadas in Greece, near Constantinople. For, having departed from Constantinople for the imperial estate of Melantiadas with his army, he halted there. When battle was joined with Fritigern, king of the Goths, from whom he had refused a request for peace, Valens was put to flight and carried into a peasant’s hut; the hut and Valens burned together. Ammianus adds, in book XXXI, that voices had shortly before been heard at Antioch crying: “Let Valens burn alive.”

This occurred, according to Baronius’s reckoning, in A.D. 378. Since Dexter states that Theodosius was taken by Gratian into partnership in the empire in A.D. 382, it follows that he was not appointed immediately after Valens’s death, but in the fourth year afterward. Therefore one should not read “at Helena,” nor “at Helenema,” as that codex has it, but “at Melantiadas”; and not “of Gaul,” but “of Greece.” Morales and Baronius have gathered much concerning the election of Theodosius and his Italian birthplace. Marcellinus begins his Chronicle as follows:

“During the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius, Theodosius, a Spaniard from Italica, the divine Trajan’s city, was made emperor by Augustus Gratian at Sirmium, thirty-nine days after the death of Valens, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, to govern only the Eastern Empire. He was a deeply religious man and a propagator of the Catholic Church, to be preferred to all the princes of the East,” etc.

Only Idatius of Lamecum, an ancient bishop in Gallaecia, makes him originate from that same Gallaecia. For in his Chronicle he says: “Theodosius, a Spaniard by nation, from the province of Gallaecia, from the city of Cauca,” which today is called Coca, between Braga and Valencia.

5. Priscillianus, etc. Consult Severus, book II of the Sacred History, and what we brought forward above under the year 380.

6. Gratianus, etc. Baronius has collected much about him in volume IV from Sozomen, Theodoret, and others; consult those works.

7. Saint Augustalis, etc. We shall discuss him again under the year 388, when he was enrolled among the saints with the approval of the bishops of Gaul. Here, however, his death is under consideration, which occurred at Arles on 7 September. Bede and the Roman Martyrology commemorate him on that very day. Bede has the following: “At Arles in Gaul, Saint Augustalis, bishop and confessor.” Cardinal Baronius nevertheless found this difficult, because Saint Augustalis is found to have subscribed to the First Council of Orange, presided over by Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles. Hence he concludes that Saint Augustalis could not at the same time have been bishop of Arles. This is especially so because in the lists of the bishops of Arles transcribed by Demochares no one of that name is found. Bede, however, did not assert that he was bishop of Arles, but that his feast was celebrated at Arles, where his body, of course, rests; and these are very different claims. He was in fact bishop of Iliberris in Spain, and while he was staying in Gaul to attend the Council of Ariminum, he died. Therefore the word “Arles” must by all means be restored in the Roman Martyrology, so that it agrees with Bede’s testimony, from which it was taken.

8. Martinus, etc. His life, written by Severus, made him famous throughout the whole world even while he was still alive. It was the sixth year of his episcopate; for when he was eighty-one years old—which coincided with his revered death in A.D. 402—he had been a bishop for twenty-six years. Consult Baronius’s notes under 11 November.

9. At the same time, etc. I believe this was the holy Marcellus who is called bishop of Apamea in the Greek Menologion on 14 August. He was killed by a faction of pagans in the eleventh year of the emperor Theodosius because, supported by divine protection, he had demolished the temple of Jupiter at Apamea. The statement that he suffered in Syria appears to have arisen from the error of a copyist who, hearing “Apamea,” added “Syria” by way of explanation, as though there were no other cities of that name in the world. Above we saw that the city of the Vaccaeans called Palentia was formerly known as Apamea, or Pamea; its bishopric is none other than that of Tela. For, according to M. Maximus in his Chronicle under A.D. 480, the see of Tela was transferred to the city of Palentia. Thus, when Saint Marcellus is called bishop of Tela or of Apamea, the two descriptions amount to the same thing.

The date of his martyrdom also fits, for he is said to have suffered in the eleventh year of Theodosius. By Theodosius’s command, all the pagan temples that still remained throughout the world—and especially in Spain, his homeland—were demolished. The Roman Martyrology followed the Greek codices; therefore the word “Syria” must likewise be removed from it.

10. Theodosius, etc. Equilinus, book XI, chapter 93, under the heading “On Saint Theodosius the Great, Emperor,” has the following among other things: “He is listed by the Greeks in their catalogue of saints and venerated under the name of a most holy confessor. He destroyed all the ancient shrines and temples of idols and ordered them destroyed throughout the Roman world; and he wonderfully increased the worship of Christ and the faith.” You will read the same in Theodoret, Sozomen, Nicephorus, and the others.

In this matter alone Spain may boast among the other nations of the world: that it gave so great a man both to the Empire and to the Church. Latinus Pacatus pursued the praises of both at length in his panegyric, where, among many other things, he says:

“Spain is first your mother, a land happier than all other lands, to which the supreme Maker of the universe granted more generously than to other peoples the task of cultivation and, indeed, of enrichment. Subject neither to the scorching heat of the south nor to the cold of the north, she is warmed by the temperate climate of both axes. On one side she is crowned by the Pyrenean mountains, on another by the tides of the Ocean, and on another by the shores of the Tyrrhenian Sea; enclosed by the skillful design of nature as though she were another world.

“Add so many distinguished cities; add all her cultivated and uncultivated lands, either rich in fruits or filled with flocks; add the wealth of her gold-bearing rivers; add her mines shining with gems. I know that the poets’ fables were invented to delight the ears, since they attributed to certain peoples marvels which, although true, are unique; I shall not now investigate their truth. Let Gargara, as it is written, be fertile in its yield of grain; let Mevania be remembered for its cattle; let Campania be judged by Mount Gaurus; let Lydia be celebrated for the river Pactolus—provided that whatever is praised anywhere rises to Spain alone.

“She has produced the toughest soldiers, the most experienced commanders, the most eloquent orators, and the most illustrious poets. She is the mother of judges; she is the mother of princes. She sent that Trajan to the Empire, and afterward Hadrian. The Empire owes you to her. Let the Cretan land yield to these lands, boasting of the cradle of little Jupiter; let Delos, trodden by its twin divinities, yield; and let Thebes, made noble by its fosterling Hercules, yield. We do not know whether to trust what we have heard; Spain has given us a god whom we see.”

Read the rest in Pacatus himself.]

A.D. 382. A.R. 1133. Lampadius, formerly prefect of the city, comes to Spain; a good and learned man, he becomes bishop of Oretania.

A.D. 382. A.R. 1133. The bishops Dracontius and Adelphus are exiled in Spain.

A.D. 382. A.R. 1133. Saint Ambrose writes to Justus [lacuna], bishop of Vic.

A.D. 382. A.R. 1133. When the heretical emperor Valens was burned at the city of Melantiadas in Greece, Gratian makes Theodosius, the son of the admirable Theodosius, co-ruler of the Empire—a pious man, born at Italica in Baetica.

[Col. 0507] A.D. 382. A.R. 1133. Priscillian, a heretic—headlong, capable of enduring difficulties, versatile in talent, crafty, and eloquent—is raging greatly.

A.D. 382. A.R. 1133. Gratian, a highly religious emperor, favors the Christian religion and is approved by the churches spread throughout the city.

A.D. 382. A.R. 1133. Saint Augustalis, bishop of Iliberris, dies in Gaul, where he had long remained on behalf of the Catholics.

A.D. 382. A.R. 1133. Martin, bishop of Tours, exceptionally renowned for apostolic virtues, is celebrated for the glory of his miracles.

A.D. 382. A.R. 1133. At the same time Marcellus, bishop of Tela, flourishes in Spain. Tela is a city of the Vaccaeans near Palentia.

A.D. 382. A.R. 1133. The emperor Theodosius restores the fallen state in the eastern regions and zealously favors the Christian religion.

[Col. 0509] [Note: [Col. 0509A]

A.D. 384.—1. Gratianus, etc. Some place the death of Gratian in the preceding year, as does Baronius, whose reckoning, however, generally precedes Dexter’s calculation by one year. Gratian was killed by the tyrant Maximus, who, although professing the Catholic faith, seized power in Spain, England, and Britain. Gildas the Wise, in his work On the Ruin of Britain, says that Maximus stretched one wing toward Spain and the other toward Italy and established the imperial throne at Trier. Socrates, book V, chapter 11, says that he was British by descent; Sozimus, however, makes him Spanish. Baronius proves that he was a relative of Constantine the Great, named Flavius Clemens Maximus, and that he was hailed as emperor by the soldiers in Britain. Consult Idatius and Marcellinus in their Chronicles.

2. Eucharius, etc. Saint Augustine discusses him in his Sermon on the Miracles of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. Through the merits of that martyr, Eucharius was miraculously freed from a serious illness and once restored to life. “Eucharius,” he says, “a presbyter from Spain living at Calama, was suffering from an old disease of stone. Through the memorial of the martyr Stephen, which Bishop Possidius had brought there, he was restored to health. The same Eucharius later died when another illness grew severe and lay in such a condition that his thumbs were already being tied. But through the help of the aforementioned martyr, when [something] had been brought back from his memorial and the tunic of the presbyter himself was laid upon his body as he lay there, he was raised up.”

These events did not occur in this year, but after Paul Orosius first brought the relics of the most holy protomartyr into the West. Dexter merely says that Eucharius flourished in Africa in this year.

3. The Council of Milan, etc. This council is mentioned by the bishops Heliodorus and Chromatius in a letter to Saint Jerome concerning the compilation of a martyrology; there they also speak of Saint Gregory, bishop of Corduba:

“When the most religious Augustus Theodosius had entered the city of Milan and had invited all the bishops of Italy to himself,” etc.

Further on they write:

“The most Christian prince began to prefer Saint Gregory, bishop of the Church of Corduba, because every day—whether, while not fasting, he celebrated the morning Masses, or, while fasting, the evening Masses—he recalled very many names of those martyrs whose feast days were being observed,” etc.

From this arose the occasion for composing a martyrology in the Church. At that time Jerome briefly collected in a small work what Eusebius had written at greater length in one book about the deeds of the martyrs, and called it a Martyrology. Both the letter to Jerome and Jerome’s reply have customarily been placed before all the martyrological codices in the world. We have thought it necessary to insert them here; we shall discuss their authenticity afterward.

LETTER OF CHROMATIUS AND HELIODORUS, BISHOPS, TO THE BLESSED JEROME, CONCERNING THE COMPILATION OF A MARTYROLOGY.

[Col. 0509D] To the holy lord Father Jerome, Chromatius and Heliodorus, bishops, greetings in the Lord.

When the most religious Augustus Theodosius had entered the city of Milan and invited all the bishops of Italy to himself, while investigating the case of certain bishops who had polluted their souls with the dregs of Arianism, it happened that our humble selves were also present at that council. When the matters that had to be said had been said and the matters that had to be defined had been defined, the most Christian prince began to prefer Saint Gregory, bishop of the Church of Corduba, because every day—whether, while not fasting, he celebrated the morning Masses, or, while fasting, the evening Masses—he recalled very many names of those martyrs whose feast days were being observed.

And so we all resolved to write to your charity, asking you to search the most famous liturgical records in the archive of Saint Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, and send us the feasts of the martyrs, so that through your holy diligence we might offer this service to the martyrs more fully and perfectly, to the honor of God.

Thus far they. Jerome’s letter, bearing the following heading, reads as follows:

THE RESPONSE OF BLESSED JEROME TO THEM ON THE SAME MATTER.

To Chromatius and Heliodorus, holy bishops: Jerome, presbyter.

It is established that our Lord Jesus Christ receives every day the triumphs of his martyrs, whose passions we find to have been written by Saint Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea. For when the emperor Constantine had entered Caesarea and told the aforementioned bishop to ask for some benefits advantageous to the Church of Caesarea, Eusebius is reported to have replied that the Church was enriched by its own resources and was compelled by no necessity to seek benefits. Nevertheless, he said that he had an unshakable desire: that whatever had been done in the Roman state concerning the saints of God, as judges succeeded judges throughout the Roman world, should be diligently investigated by examining the public records; and that the martyrs who had won the palm of victory—under which judge, in which province or city, on what day, and with what perseverance in their passion—should be taken from the archives themselves and sent to Eusebius by imperial command.

Thus it came about that, being a suitable chronicler, he both composed an ecclesiastical history and, as a diligent historian, set forth the trophies of nearly all the martyrs of all the Roman provinces, so that, offering sacrifice to God every day, people might remember their names. They would honor those who on the very day when the sacrifice was offered had proved victorious over the devil and, endowed with the triumph of their martyrdom and rejoicing in it, had come to their king, Christ.

For this reason we have written down the feasts of each month and of each day, so that, when you deign to command it, you may believe that it will provide an enduring memorial of our humble work, since throughout so many years the holy names of the saints will have been celebrated festively on every day.

And since on each day the names of more than eight hundred or nine hundred martyrs from different provinces and different cities have been recorded—so that there is no day that cannot be found entered among the number of five hundred, except the day of the Kalends of January—I considered that among innumerable crowds the reader’s mind might become weary within a single month. To prevent this, I have briefly and concisely mentioned, in their proper places and above all others, those who belong to the most solemn celebration, so that, once weariness has been cut away, a single little book might suffice in place of them all.

In the first part of the little book we have written down the feasts of all the blessed apostles, so that varying days might not divide those whom the one dignity of the apostolate made exalted together in heavenly glory.

Thus far Jerome.

[Col. 0510D] Nothing is so secure, so well protected, or so supported by venerable antiquity that more recent writers have not called it into doubt. Molanus began to question the authenticity of these letters, and Baronius ultimately rejected them altogether as fabrications in his work On the Roman Martyrology. To support this conclusion, he gathers many varied arguments from every direction.

First, in chapter 6, he attempts to overturn what many had hitherto believed: that Eusebius of Caesarea’s book on the martyrs was nothing other than a concise collection of all the holy martyrs, composed in the brevity characteristic of martyrologies, and therefore called a Martyrology. “How falsely this is said,” he argues, “is proved nowhere more clearly than by Eusebius’s own testimony: in book IV, chapter 14, concerning Saint Pionius; in book V, chapters 2 and 4, concerning the letter of the Church of Lyons; and in chapter 20, where, speaking of Saint Apollonius the senator, he asserts that he wrote the acts of all these men in full in his book On the Martyrs. The aforementioned letter and the apologetic speech of Saint Apollonius before the senate, which Jerome calls an ‘insigne volume,’ are found there. Could one book, one volume, have contained the acts of so many martyrs, when it could scarcely have sufficed merely to list their names? Indeed, if Eusebius had had to write out at such length, as he did elsewhere, the deeds of the holy martyrs of the entire Catholic Church, not one book, nor a hundred, nor even a thousand would have sufficed; indeed, the world itself could not have contained the books that would have had to be written on the subject.”

[Col. 0511B] This, however, is not a weighty objection. From Eusebius himself it is clear—and from no other testimonies than those Baronius cites—that he wrote not a thousand, not a hundred, nor many books on the deeds of the martyrs, but only one. Since he never praises it for its size, there is no reason to believe that it was enormous. Indeed, what he elsewhere called a book, he sometimes calls a little book.

Thus, when speaking of Saint Pionius in book IV, chapter 14, he says:

“Finally, those who wish to know what sort of death he suffered, and how remarkable it was, in addition to all the other deeds he performed with such great admiration, we refer to the little book published by us containing in one collection the martyrdoms of the ancient saints; it fully embraces all his acts.”

But how could the deeds of so many martyrs be contained in a single little book? Certainly because, for the most part, it briefly included the history of Christ’s martyrs and contained nothing more than the names of their city and governor, and the kind of martyrdom they suffered—since nothing else could be learned about them—although in other cases it set forth their deeds and sayings more fully.

The Martyrology of Ado may serve as an example. It fills only a few pages, yet the acts, interrogations, answers, and miracles of many martyrs are written in it, and even letters, as can be seen in the entries for Saint Anastasia and Chrysogonus.

Nor am I troubled by the fact that Saint Apollonius is said by Jerome to have written an “insigne volume,” and that this is also contained in Eusebius’s book On the Martyrs. That volume is not called “insigne” because of its great size, but because of the dignity and completeness of the work. Jerome uses the expression in precisely the same way in his book On Illustrious Men, where he says that blessed Pontius, Saint Cyprian’s deacon, wrote an “insigne volume” on Cyprian’s martyrdom, although it is plainly very brief.

Baronius presses the matter further in the following chapter, chapter 7, claiming that these two letters are stuffed with many falsehoods, which expose their imposture:

1. Contrary to ancient custom, Chromatius and Heliodorus, the bishops, call Jerome the presbyter “Father”; and this should be considered all the more objectionable because they say that they are writing as the Fathers of the Council of Milan.

2. They mention the aforementioned council, supposedly convened by the emperor Theodosius, although the silence of writers from that period sufficiently proves it to be a mere fiction. No one mentions it.

3. In speaking of Gregory of Corduba, they mention evening Masses, although Augustine, in letter 118, chapter 5, testifies that such Masses were celebrated in the Church only on Thursday of Holy Week; and they say that the feasts of martyrs were celebrated on fast days, although the very different custom of the Church in that period is evident from canon 51 of the Council of Laodicea, in the collection of Saint Martin of Dumium, chapter 48, and 33, question 1, “It is not permitted in Lent.”

4. They call Eusebius “Saint,” although Jerome calls him the standard-bearer, champion, and leader of the Arians in books I and II of his Apology against Rufinus and elsewhere.

5. The letter differs from Jerome’s style.

6. Finally, the second letter asserts that no Catholic martyr had ever suffered on the Kalends of January, which is plainly false from the Roman Martyrology and others.

That is Baronius’s argument.

It is nevertheless very surprising that so learned a man, led by slight conjectures, attempted to overthrow these letters, which were certainly recognized and held in veneration for more than eight hundred years by illustrious writers of exceptional authority—namely Cassiodorus, Bede, and Strabo. In the Church of God, their judgments have nowhere been praised for frivolity, but everywhere for seriousness.

Hear the words of each. Cassiodorus, in chapter 32 of On the Institutes of Divine Learning, says:

“Read constantly the lives of the Fathers, the confessions of the faithful, and the passions of the martyrs, the patterns of the future blessedness; among other works, you will undoubtedly find them in the letter of Saint Jerome addressed to Chromatius and Heliodorus. They flourished throughout the whole world, so that holy imitation, urging you forward, may lead you to the heavenly kingdom.”

Consider, I ask, how universally accepted it was in Cassiodorus’s time that this letter, together with the Martyrology, was Jerome’s work, since Cassiodorus directs his readers to it as a source from which to draw the spirit of devotion.

Bede, in his Retractation on the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 1, says:

“The book of the Martyrology also bears witness, being entitled with the name and preface of blessed Jerome, although Jerome himself is said not to have been the author of that book but its translator, while Eusebius was its author.”

By the preface I understand the letter we are now discussing.

Walafrid Strabo writes in book 28 of On Ecclesiastical Matters:

“Jerome, following Eusebius of Caesarea, composed a Martyrology for the cycle of the year. He was asked by the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus to compose this work because Theodosius, the religious emperor, praised Gregory, bishop of Corduba, at a council of bishops for recalling every day the names of many of those martyrs whose feast days were being celebrated while he celebrated Masses.”

These words are taken verbatim from the letter of Chromatius and Heliodorus. Should the authority of so many and such great Doctors be set aside, so that anyone may follow his own inclination in a serious matter that ought to have been confirmed or rejected not by conjectures but by the testimony of the ancients?

What has been devised against the truth cannot be true, as will become clear when we examine individually the objections he has brought against us.

1. It is a minor point that a presbyter should be called “Father” by bishops, if the presbyter is Jerome, who at that time was regarded as a father of the faith and a Doctor of the Church. Perhaps the reason was the dignity of the cardinal presbyter, although Baronius denies this and Chaconius defends it in a special work. In Rome I see an irrefragable testimony to it whenever I look around the apse of the principal altar of the Church of Saint Mary Major. There, in a very ancient mosaic from the time of Sixtus III, who was a little younger than Jerome, the same holy Doctor is shown wearing episcopal insignia, ascending a chair and covered with a mitre—the emblem of cardinal presbyters—and delivering a sermon to the holy women Paula and Eustochium. The inscription reads: “Saint Jerome delivers a sermon to Paula and Eustochium.”

2. Baronius cites no ancient writer who denies the Council of Milan. We have cited three most serious Doctors; and even if they were absent, the argument, being negative, would prove nothing against a letter that affirms the council. Add to this the fact that the author Dexter, who lived at that time, also mentions the council, as well as the history of the letters. We shall discuss the date of this council shortly.

3. Baronius himself admits that evening Masses were a custom in the Church that varied according to region. This may be seen in Cyprian’s letter 63, with the notes of Pamelius, and in the acts of the Council of Agde, canon 13, distinction 15. Baronius says that he does not resist the point on that account, and therefore neither do we.

What he adds concerning the celebration of the feasts of martyrs on fast days is not correctly stated. The letter of Heliodorus does not say that the feasts of martyrs were celebrated on those days, but that, while celebrating Masses even on those days, Gregory recalled the names of many martyrs. I understand this as referring to commemorations, or collects, as they were customarily called, or to the names of the saints invoked in the canon. Perhaps Saint Gregory invoked the martyrs of that day in that very place.

4. Perhaps the title of sanctity given to Eusebius was added by someone else in the letter. Who could deny that this was possible in codices of such great antiquity? We see such additions throughout the writings of the holy Doctors and even in the sacred Scriptures themselves. Jerome himself could also have added it, for in that age, as Baronius too admits, the title of sanctity was more commonly used and was therefore customarily applied to every bishop.

5. Nor does the style differ greatly from Jerome’s, although it is not implausible that Jerome first wrote the letters in an eloquent style, but that they were translated into Greek by Sophronius and then rendered back into Latin without their former elegance and wit.

6. The letter is falsely charged with asserting that no martyr suffered on the Kalends of January. It says only that there is no day that cannot be found entered among the number of five hundred, except the day of the Kalends of January. What does it matter that thirty-four martyrs are recorded on the Kalends of January in the Roman Martyrology and elsewhere? The claim is merely that five hundred were not killed on that day, although, according to Jerome’s testimony, that number is found for the other days of the year in Eusebius’s book On the Martyrs.

Consider, I ask, how little weight there is in all the objections Baronius brings against the authenticity of those letters. In his anger against them, he accused them five times of imposture, three times of fabrication, twice of falsehood, and once of error; he called them at one time frivolous, at another false, at another mendacious. Yet his own conjectures, which are entirely without authorial support, he declared to be as clear as the light of day. Still, I prefer to deal with him more moderately and always to write with restraint.

The date of the celebration of the Council of Milan is somewhat more difficult to determine. Many believe that Theodosius entered Italy only twice: once in the ninth year of his reign, which Marcellinus records in his Chronicle, to fight Maximus; and again in the sixteenth year, to fight the equally tyrannical Eugenius. Baronius, in chapter 7 of his On the Roman Martyrology, insists that the council could have occurred at neither time, because Jerome and Ambrose, who described the deeds of Theodosius, do not mention it. But this argument, being negative, cannot be conclusive.

It could therefore have occurred in either of those periods. Since Dexter places the council in A.D. 384, which, according to his reckoning, was the third year of Theodosius’s reign, we are compelled to admit that Theodosius came to Italy three times: to overthrow the remnants of idolatry and Arianism and to carry the body of the emperor Valentinian to Constantinople. It is established that Valentinian was transported by Theodosius to Greece in the year when Antoninus and Siagrius were consuls and was buried there honorably.

4. Priamus, etc. In the printed codex of Dexter, “Pyramus” was corruptly read in place of “Priamus.” He ruled over the Franks in eastern Francia, the third after Pharamond. Pharamond was succeeded by his brother Marcomer, and Marcomer by his son, named Priamus. Priamus is said to have held power around A.D. 423 and to have been succeeded by Genebald, as you may see in Trithemius’s book On the Origin of the Franks and in others. Prosper of Aquitaine also mentions this Priamus in his Chronicle, under the fourth year of Gratian Augustus, in Canisius, volume I of Ancient Readings.

### 5. At Emerita, etc.

Severus Sulpicius reports in Book II of his *Sacred History* that, when the contagion of Priscillian’s perfidy had gradually spread through most parts of Spain, some of the bishops also became corrupted. Among them, Instantius and Salvianus had undertaken to defend that sect not merely by agreement but also under a kind of conspiracy. When Bishop Hyginus of Córdoba, who was living nearby, learned of this, he reported the matter to Idatius, surnamed Clarus, a priest of Emerita who was advanced in age. Idatius then summoned the bishops of the neighboring provinces and convened a council at Emerita to condemn the heresy of Priscillian; this is the council of which Dexter is now speaking.

Reason itself strongly supports this conclusion. Idatius was the metropolitan of Lusitania and, endowed with that authority and adorned with great learning, he could easily expel that heresy from his own boundaries as quickly as possible—especially since Priscillian had arisen in Gallaecia and his heresy was spreading there with greater fervor; Idatius himself, being bishop of Braga, was its metropolitan, and the condemnation of the heresy therefore particularly concerned him. For this reason he added new measures to what he had done at the Council of Emerita: he wrote a notable volume against all Priscillian’s errors. Saint Isidore says the following about it in his *Book of Illustrious Men*:

> Idatius, a bishop of the Spains, distinguished both by his name and by his eloquence, wrote a certain book in the form of an *Apology*. In it he exposes the detestable doctrines of Priscillian, his magical practices, and the disgraces of his lusts; showing that a certain Marcus of Memphis, highly skilled in magic, was the teacher of the Nians and of Priscillian.

This great man, who had deserved so well of the Catholic faith in opposition to Priscillian and his followers, nevertheless had to endure Severus as a detractor. Among other things, Severus wrote of him in the passage cited:

> Certainly I declare that Idatius had no regard for anything and no reverence for anything sacred; for he was bold, talkative, shameless, and presumptuous.

But to whom, reader, should one rather give assent—to Sulpicius or to Isidore? Isidore calls Idatius distinguished both by name and by eloquence; and yet this “great man” was bold and talkative? Did he have regard for nothing and reverence for nothing sacred? This alone I know: Priscillian was persecuted by him throughout the whole world and, through his agency, was finally driven back from the whole world, as I shall now relate.

### 6. A second synod, etc.

Idatius was not content with the condemnation at the Council of Emerita alone; he also caused another council to be convened in Lusitania. Concerning these councils, the other Idatius, bishop of Lamego, says in his *Chronicle*, under the seventh year of Theodosius the Great:

> Priscillian, turning toward the heresy of the Gnostics, was judged by several councils of bishops; he went to Italy and to Rome, etc.

Here he admits that not merely one but several councils were convened against Priscillian. Canon 1 of the First Council of Toledo mentions a certain synod held earlier by the Lusitanian bishops. This can be none other than the one of which Dexter is now speaking.

### 7. At Caesaraugusta, etc.

It was chiefly at this council that the heresy of Priscillian was condemned. Many bishops attended it, not only from Spain but also from Gaul, and Phegadius, bishop of Agen, presided. Severus mentions this synod in Book II of his *Sacred History*, from which Ambrosius Morales, in Book X, chapter 44, Vasaeus, Mariana, and others drew their accounts.

A certain Council of Caesaraugusta appears in the volume of the Councils of Spain. It was held—as its heading states—in the Spanish Era 418, that is, in the year of the Lord 380. It contains eight canons, and twelve bishops subscribe to it; the first is Phegadius, or, which is the same thing, Fetadius. García de Loaysa, in his notes, thought that this was entirely different from the Council of Caesaraugusta at which the errors of the Priscillianists were condemned. He says:

> There was another Council of Caesaraugusta after this one, at which the heresy of Priscillian was first condemned. The bishops of Aquitaine also attended it, as did Itacius and Idatius, who subscribed to this council and acted vigorously in eradicating Priscillian’s impiety. Severus Sulpicius, Book II.

So far he.

However, if the names of the bishops whom Dexter reports as having attended that Council—the council from which the aforesaid heresy received its condemnation—are compared with those whose subscriptions are preserved in the acts of this council of eight canons, we shall doubtless find that it was one and the same Council of Caesaraugusta. In both accounts Phegadius is said to have presided; yet he had previously presided over the Council of Valence in Gaul in the year 374, as Baronius maintains in his *Annals*, under title 4. In other manuscripts he is called Phoebadius, and in others Saebadius. Jerome discusses him in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, stating that he wrote a book against the Arians and certain other treatises, and that he was still living in extreme old age.

In both accounts the bishop of Bordeaux, Delphinus, is placed second, although in the acts of the council he is simply called Delphinus, whereas Dexter calls him the bishop of Bordeaux. In those days Saint Delphinus presided at Bordeaux, as Severus asserts in Book II, and Baronius in his notes for 24 December, the day on which the Roman Martyrology reads:

> At Bordeaux, Saint Delphinus, bishop, who shone in holiness in the time of Theodosius.

Many letters of Saint Paulinus of Nola to him are extant.

Again, if we preserve the order of the subscriptions, the bishops of Toulouse and Elne, whom Dexter gives without their names, appear to be those whom the acts of the council call Eutychianus and Apellius. Idatius is named in both accounts, and Dexter explains that he was the metropolitan of Braga. The same is evident in the case of Audentius, metropolitan of Toledo, whom Loaysa nevertheless corruptly calls Augentius. This is not surprising, since he did not know that Audentius was a bishop of Toledo.
