Moreover, Cartherius subscribes in both accounts, as do Valerius and Lupus; Dexter, however, specifies their bishoprics. Cartherius was bishop of Uxama, Valerius bishop of Caesaraugusta, and Lupus bishop of Teles. The manuscripts of the councils should incidentally be corrected, since they read *Lucius* instead of *Lupus*.

As for Valerius, Loaysa thinks that he was the same man who attended the Council of Iliberri. He is entirely mistaken. It is not credible that the man who, already made a bishop in the year of the Lord 300, attended the Council of Iliberri could have lived to such an age and remained in the episcopate for another eighty-four years. The Council of Caesaraugusta falls in this year, 384, or, as the acts have it, in 380.

The same refutation applies to what Loaysa says about Bishop Eutychianus: namely, that he was the bishop of Basti because a bishop of Basti by that name is found subscribed at the Council of Iliberri. Similarity of name, especially when the dates are widely discordant, cannot establish the identity of a person.

Finally, a bishop of Ossonoba is mentioned in both accounts. Severus calls him Itacius, whereas Dexter’s manuscript reads Etherius. Which of the two should be corrected is difficult to determine.

Besides these bishops, Dexter writes that Saint Martin of Tours and Emilas of Barcelona also attended the Council of Caesaraugusta. The acts of that council add Splendonius and Symphosius. There is no contradiction here, since all of them could have been present.

Emilas was later degraded at the First Council of Toledo, and a sentence of suspension was pronounced against Symphosius, because afterward they fell into the errors of Priscillian. We shall discuss this below, under the year of the Lord 386.

It is quite credible that Martin was present at Caesaraugusta. He was no less zealous for the faith than Saint Delphinus of Bordeaux, or than the bishop of Toulouse, who had come from Gaul to the council for the condemnation of the Priscillianist heresy.

At that council Instantius and Salvianus, bishops of Gallaecia, were condemned, together with Hyginus—or Adiginsius—of Córdoba, who had already fallen into the heresy that he had initially abhorred. So Severus says in the passage cited.

It is therefore clear that not two Councils of Caesaraugusta, but one, was convened against Priscillian—whether it was held in 380, as the acts state, or in 384, as Dexter writes and as is more probable, as is evident from what has just been said.

After I had written this, I found that Severinus Binius held the same opinion. He proves it also from the very canons that survive, as anyone can easily read in Volume I of his *Councils*. I was certainly pleased that so learned a man had also arrived at this truth.

As for whose negligence or malice caused the manifest condemnation of the Priscillianists to be separated from the acts of the council, so that only twelve canons concerning reform remain, in which nothing explicit about such an error is found, I cannot easily say. If there is room for suspicion, I should think that the material was perhaps rejected by the copyists because it was to be set out at length shortly afterward in the First Council of Toledo, where it now appears—unless someone prefers to suppose that it was removed from the acts through the deceit of the Priscillians themselves, though Toledo later took it up again.

There still seems, however, to be a decree against Priscillian, although not explicitly, in canon 7:

> Let no one assume for himself the name of teacher.

Priscillian had done precisely this without the authority of the Church, assuming for himself the name and office of teacher even though he was a layman.

The celebrated memory of this council also survives in the sentence issued by the First Council of Toledo against Symphosius, Dictinius, and the other bishops of Gallaecia, in these words:

> Although, after long deliberation, it was indeed after the Council of Caesaraugusta, at which a sentence had been pronounced against certain individuals—namely, Salvianus, Instantius, and Hyginus—and although Symphosius alone was present on one day, etc.

Later, Bishop Vegetinus is absolved because, having become a bishop before the Council of Caesaraugusta, he had condemned the books of Priscillian together with their author.

But enough on this subject.

### 8. Isidore, etc.

The surname *Senior* is necessarily required because, during Dexter’s lifetime, another Isidore flourished who was younger than him; for that reason he was given the surname *Junior*. Otherwise, how could one be called “the Elder” if there were no younger person from whom he was distinguished?

Those who believe that the name *Junior* was given to Isidore of Seville to distinguish him from the Elder of Córdoba are therefore completely mistaken. Not one but two men of that name flourished at Córdoba in published writings, and between them the distinction of Elder and Younger was necessary, since both were from Córdoba. Between the truly Sevillian Isidore and the two men of Córdoba, the distinction of their dioceses was sufficient.

Certainly Dexter could not have called the Elder “of Córdoba” with reference to the Sevillian, who flourished many centuries after him and died in the year of the Lord 636.

I find four writers of this name in Spain: namely, two from Córdoba. The Elder of these, as Dexter asserts, wrote a chronicle extending from the first consulship of Theodosius to his own time; he was not, however, a bishop.

The Younger was a bishop of Córdoba after Hyginus and Gregory, as we shall soon say. He wrote the books of the *Allegories*, which are extant among the works of the Sevillian; also a commentary on the year 380, addressed to Orosius; a commentary on the four books of Kings; and an exceptionally elegant commentary on the Gospel of Luke. Dexter mentions all these works under the years 388, 423, and 430, where he again discusses him.

The third, and the Great, Isidore was the bishop of Seville. His writings, collected into a single body at the command of Philip II, the Catholic monarch of Spain, we read and admire.

Finally, the fourth was a bishop of Badajoz and likewise the author of a certain chronicle of Spain. Vasaeus read a copy of it; it was written in a very barbarous style and in Gothic, as the circumstances of his age required. Thus three Isidores are found to have written chronicles.

The Elder of Córdoba continued Eusebius and Jerome, just as Prosper of Aquitaine, Victor of Tunis, Idatius of Lamego, and Marcellinus Comes did, from the beginning of Theodosius’ reign down to the time of each writer.

The Younger of Córdoba refrained from writing a chronicle. The Sevillian, however, wrote—as Saint Braulio reports in his *Life*—not from the time of Theodosius but from the beginning of the world down to his own time, in a single book compiled with excessive brevity. It is extant among the works of that holy teacher and appears to be an abridgment of Eusebius and others.

Isidore of Badajoz still lies hidden in the recesses of the Spanish libraries. It is extant in the library of the major College of Oviedo at Salamanca, and elsewhere. Vasaeus and Morales testify in the prologue to their *History of Spain* that they saw his chronicle.

As for the chronicle of the Elder of Córdoba, I think that it was brought to light again by Lucas of Tuy, although in his work it is joined to the chronicle of Eusebius. This seems probable to me because Lucas professes to be copying the chronicle of Saint Isidore, yet produces a chronicle very different from that of Saint Isidore of Seville, as will be clear to anyone who compares the two. It must therefore belong to another Isidore, and to no one other than the Elder of Córdoba.

I would nevertheless point out that Lucas appended the final words of the Sevillian’s chronicle to his own, believing that both had been produced by the same author.

### 9. Hyginus, etc.

Under this bishop the Elder Isidore continued the chronicles of Eusebius. This is precisely the man who first of all detected Priscillian’s errors and reported them to Idatius of Braga. Yet shortly afterward—as is so often the condition of human affairs—he himself fell into the same heresy, and relapsed into it once and again.

At last, after he had been accused before Maximus, who was ruling in Gaul and Spain, through the agency of that same Idatius, he was brought to Trier, where the emperor was residing, and condemned to exile.

Saint Ambrose lamented his old age when writing to Valentinian, in these words:

> I willingly undertook the journey, although many believed that I would not escape the ambushes, being moved by this one grief alone: that I discovered that the aged Bishop Hyginus was being led into exile, a man for whom only his final breath now remained. When I had urged his companions not to allow the old man to be driven out without clothing or bedding, I myself was driven out as well.

Perhaps Ambrose grieved that an old man would be exiled to an island full of serpents, as Lero was at that time. Later Saint Honoratus of Arles freed it from them by his virtue, as Baronius reports elsewhere under the year 445, number 2. Baronius also notes under the year 387 that this Hyginus was the bitterest enemy of the Luciferians, against whom Marcellinus and Faustinus accordingly bark in their customary manner.

Dexter discusses his successor in the bishopric of Córdoba under the year 388.

The island here called Lero is not the island of that name lying in the Aegean Sea off the coast of Caria, about which Strabo writes in Book XXIV and Pliny also writes. It is the island otherwise called Lerinum in the Gallic Sea, commonly known as Saint Honorat, famous for the monastery of Lérins. Maximus could not have sent the exile to Greece, since his rule did not extend beyond Italy, Gaul, and Spain; and in Greece Valentinian and Theodosius were ruling.

### 10. The Ambratians, etc.

Earlier, under the year 268, we showed that the city now called Placentia was formerly called Ambratia in Spain. Dexter now notes that Placentia of Cantabria, near the town of Bermeo, still preserves its name at the mouth of the Cantabrian Ocean. It was founded by the ancient Ambratians, or Placentians, who gave it the name of their own city.

### 11. Ambrose, etc.

The books themselves are extant and bear witness to these matters: namely, the five books *On the Faith* addressed to the Emperor Gratian, in which Ambrose instructed him concerning the errors of the Arians, and another book bearing the special title *On the Divinity and Consubstantiality of the Son against the Arians*.

### A.D. 384. A.R. 1135

The Emperor Gratian, a catechumen, is killed on 25 August. Flavius Maximus, a Catholic man, is proclaimed Emperor of Gaul, Britain, and Spain by the soldiers, tyrannically.

### A.D. 384. A.R. 1135

Eucharius, a Toletan presbyter, flourishes in exile in Spain.

### A.D. 384. A.R. 1135

Theodosius Augustus attended the Council of Milan, where he made excellent use of the services of Saint Gregory, bishop of Córdoba.

### A.D. 384. A.R. 1135

Priamus ruled in Gaul around this same time.

### A.D. 384. A.R. 1135

At Emerita Augusta in Spain, Idatius, bishop and metropolitan pontiff of Lusitania, convened a council against Priscillian.

### A.D. 384. A.R. 1135

A second synod was held in Lusitania.

### A.D. 384. A.R. 1135

A second council was convened at Caesaraugusta. Phaegadius, bishop, presided [lacuna] and there attended the bishop of Bordeaux, the bishop of Toulouse, and the bishop of Elne, who, having come from Lusitania, died at Ganaca, a town of Veracium, westward, twenty-eight thousand paces from Toledo.

Idatius, metropolitan of Braga, also attended; as did Audentius, metropolitan of Toledo; Etherius, bishop of Ossonoba; Cartherius of Uxama; Lupus, bishop of Teles; Valerius, bishop of Caesaraugusta; and others, including Emilas of Barcelona and also Saint Martin of Tours from Gaul.

Isidore the Elder of Córdoba continued his chronicle from the first consulship of Theodosius.

### A.D. 384. A.R. 1135

Hyginus, bishop of Córdoba, having been touched by the heresy of the Priscillianists, which he had formerly detested, was brought in chains from Spain to Trier by order of Maximus. Later, after being convicted of the crime, he was sent into exile on the island of Lero in Gaul.

### A.D. 384. A.R. 1135

The Ambratians from Lusitania built Placentia in Cantabria.

### A.D. 384. A.R. 1135

Ambrose became renowned through the books he published against the Arians.

[Note: [Col. 0518B]]

## A.D. 385

### 1. Audentius, etc.

He wrote a book not only against the Priscillianists but against all heretics. Gennadius mentions it with praise in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, chapter 14, saying:

> Audentius, a Spanish bishop, wrote against the Manichaeans, the Sabellians, and the Arians, and especially, with particular purpose, against the Photinians, who are now called Bonosians, a book entitled *On the Faith against All Heretics*. In it he shows that the antiquity of the Son of God was coeternal with the Father, and that He did not then receive the beginning of His divinity from God the Father when, as man, He was conceived and born of Mary, the Virgin Mother, with God as the maker.

I think that “Priscillianist” should be substituted for “Photinian,” since Audentius argued chiefly against Priscillian. This is especially so because Priscillian combined into one body the errors of the Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians, as is clearly evident from the rule of faith against the Priscillianists read by the bishops of Spain at the First Council of Toledo.

In that rule eighteen errors are condemned. The first is that there is not one first principle of created things; the second, that God is only one person; the third, that the Word assumed flesh alone; the fourth, that Christ is unbegotten; and so forth.

The first of these propositions was asserted by the Manichaeans, the second by the Sabellians, and the third and fourth likewise by the Arians. Other errors peculiar to Priscillian are added: that astrology must be believed, that marriage is not permitted, and that meat must not be eaten but execrated.

Finally, at the end of the aforesaid rule, the following is appended:

> If anyone follows or professes the sect of Priscillian in these errors, let him be anathema.

It is therefore clear that Audentius, the archbishop of Toledo, when he wrote against the Priscillianists, necessarily attacked almost all heretics at the same time.

### 2. Exuperantius, etc.

He is found among those who subscribed to the First Council of Toledo. Loaysa, I do not know from what defect in a manuscript, conjectured that he was the bishop of Lugo in Gallaecia, although he was in fact bishop of Uxama.

The older editions make clear that it was not Exuperantius but Leona who was bishop of Lugo. They read as follows:

> Leona of Gallaecia, from the ecclesiastical district of the city of Lugo and the municipality of Celenis;

while the bishopric of Exuperantius is not specified.

The bishops of Ravenna celebrate their own bishop—our Exuperantius had been transferred there—on 30 May, and his name appears in the Roman Martyrology on that day. Baronius notes from the records of the Church of Ravenna that he flourished in the time of the Emperor Honorius, the son of Theodosius, who began to reign in the year of the Lord 395. Thus it can be seen that the dates do not conflict.

A bishop of this name subscribed at that very time, together with Saint Ambrose, to the Council of Aquileia, under the name Exuperius of Dertona. If, as others prefer, the reading is *Dertosensis*, he should be regarded as no other than our Exuperius. He had been transferred from the see of Oxama to the see of Dertona—now called Tortosa—and, together with the other bishops of Spain, met Saint Ambrose concerning the errors of Priscillian.

After accompanying him from there, they celebrated the Synod of Aquileia. It was then easy to make Exuperantius bishop of Ravenna, since Ravenna lies near Aquileia.

While he was still devoted to secular military service, Jerome sent him a letter (*Epistle* 35, Volume II), in which, among other things, he wrote the following about his holiness:

> Who would not love the man who, under a military cloak and in military dress, performs the works of the prophets, and overcomes the outward man, who promises one thing, by the inward man, who was formed in the image of the Creator, etc.?

Here is a living likeness of Martin as a soldier and, likewise, later invested with the episcopal mitre.

Dexter mentions him several times later, namely under the years 388 and 407.

### 3. Helpidius, etc.

Severus discusses in Book II of his *Sacred History* the rhetorician Helpidius, a man of great eloquence, who in Spain went over to the sect of the Gnostics through the preaching of Marcus the Egyptian:

> Marcus, he says, having come from Egypt and born at Memphis, first introduced that superstition into Spain. His hearers were a certain Agape, a woman of no low standing, and the rhetorician Helpidius.

Jerome adds in his work *Against the Pelagians, addressed to Ctesiphon*, that a woman named Agape seduced Helpidius, and that Galla, joined to him—not by race but by name—left the heresy an heir in the form of a sister who ran here and there.

This Helpidius cannot possibly have been the father of the man whom Dexter discusses here, since more than two hundred years intervened between them. The earlier Helpidius was alive in the year of Christ 169, when he was deceived by Marcus and Agape; the later Helpidius is said to have flourished in the year 385.

Perhaps the latter derived his origin from the former; and whereas the former, led astray by error, had disgraced his homeland, the latter adorned it by undertaking writings and disputations against the Priscillianists, offspring of the Gnostics. For this, I think, the words of Dexter refer: “he flourishes exceedingly.” Such words could certainly not be said of a heretical man.

### 4. At Lucus Augustus, etc.

This city is now called Lugo, from *Lucus*. It is the metropolis of the Lucenses of Gallaecia and is distinguished by its bishopric; still more so because it was deemed worthy to have Saint Forcatus as its bishop.

Equilinus, in Book XI of his *Catalogue*, chapter 130, number 193, states that his feast is celebrated on the day before the Ides of July, that is, on 14 July. In his work the name is written not with *F* but with *Ph*: *Phorcatus*.

### A.D. 385. A.R. 1136

Audentius, bishop of Toledo, flourished remarkably through the books he published against Priscillian and through the public disputations he held against the Priscillianists.

### A.D. 385. A.R. 1136

Exuperantius, formerly a military man, was transferred as bishop of Uxama to Ravenna, a city of Italy; Saint Jerome wrote to him.

### A.D. 385. A.R. 1136

Helpidius, son of Helpidius, a Spaniard, flourished exceedingly.

### A.D. 385. A.R. 1136

At Lucus Augustus in Spain, Saint Forcatus, bishop.

[Col. 0519] [Note: [Col. 0520A]]

## A.D. 386

### At Toledo, etc.

They inflicted an enormous injury upon all posterity who collected the acts of several Toletan councils into a single body and gave it the name of the First Council of Toledo. The result was that the acts of each council became confused, and what had plainly been formed from many councils was believed to be only one.

Since I am about to make a claim contrary to everyone’s expectation, I must explain the matter, lest anyone think that I am speaking out of my head. Yet what doubt can there be about something so evident?

In the acts circulated under the name of the First Council of Toledo, including those revised by Loaysa, there is a rule of faith against all heresies and especially against the Priscillianists. It was composed by the bishops of Carthage, Tarragona, Lusitania, and Baetica, and it is said that they sent it, together with a command of Pope Leo, to Balconius, bishop of Braga.

Saint Leo, however, did not ascend the Roman pontificate until the year of the Lord 440. The title of the council, therefore, conflicts violently with the rule of faith. The council is said to have been held in the Spanish Era 438—that is, in the year of Christ 400, during the consulship of Stilicho—whereas the rule was sent more than forty years later, together with a command of Pope Leo, to the bishop of Braga. Consequently, these two items cannot possibly refer to one and the same council but must belong to different councils.

Moreover, the acts under discussion mention another, older Council of Toledo. When the canons of the present council had been promulgated, the fathers ordered that the professions of Symphosius, Dictinius, and the other bishops who had withdrawn from Priscillian’s sect should be extracted from the full acts of the Council of Toledo. The very words of the acts are:

> The professions of the lords Symphosius and Dictinius, bishops of holy memory, and of the lord Comasius, then a presbyter and now of holy memory, were excerpted from the full acts—professions which, together with the others, they made in the Council of Toledo concerning the condemnation of Priscillian or his sect.

Certainly, if such professions had been made in this present Council of Toledo, the fathers would not have said that they had made them “in the Council of Toledo,” but “in this council.” Furthermore, Symphosius and Dictinius are called bishops of holy memory, which could not be said of those who were presently alive. More importantly, Comasius is said to have been a presbyter when he abjured the heresy: “of the lord Comasius, then a presbyter,” etc. By this one expression it is clearly asserted that he did not make his profession in the present Council of Toledo but at another time—when he was a presbyter, not now, when he was a bishop.

Again, in the sentence against the fallen bishops, which was ordered to be read, it is prescribed that all who had been reconciled should subscribe to the council:

> Having received the form from the council, if they subscribe, they too shall remain in the contemplation of heavenly peace.

Yet none of them is found among the names of the nineteen fathers of this council: neither Symphosius, Dictinius, Comasius, Vegetinus, nor Anterus. It is certain, however, that they subscribed to the acts and canons of the Council of Toledo from which they received reconciliation; otherwise they would appear to disagree with that council and not to obey it.

Listen to further extraordinary matters. In the aforesaid sentence, which was inflicted at an earlier Council of Toledo and read at a later one against the bishops who followed Priscillian’s sect—namely Symphosius, Dictinius, and the others—Paternus, bishop of Braga, is excluded from communion with the other bishops because he had been ordained by Symphosius at a time when Symphosius was tainted with the contagion of Priscillian. Paternus is ordered to await absolution from the Roman Pontiff.

Yet this very Paternus is found to have presided at the Council of Toledo commonly called the First, and, as its president, subscribed first. At his command all the council’s matters were proposed and discussed, as is clear from the acts themselves.

Would anyone therefore have assumed in the same council both the person of supreme judge and the person of the accused? Certainly not.

Nor is what Loaysa noted plausible: that Paternus, the president of the Council of Toledo, was a bishop of Toledo rather than of Braga. This cannot stand, because Asturius, who at that time was the bishop of Toledo, subscribed to the same council.

Loaysa denies this, but denies what is true. For, as he himself admits together with Saint Ildephonsus in the *Book of Illustrious Men*, Asturius succeeded Audentius in the episcopate. But Audentius had already died by the time of this Council of Toledo. He had subscribed to the Council of Caesaraugusta held in the year of the Lord 384, as we said in that passage; whereas he does not subscribe to this Council of Toledo, held not many years later. Asturius does.

And why should I delay, when in the aforesaid sentence issued against Symphosius and his associates Paternus is expressly named not as a Toletan but as a bishop of Braga?

If someone asks how it could have happened that Paternus of Braga, after once appearing as an accused man at Toledo, later became president of the Council of Toledo, I answer that this must be attributed to the merits of the man. He had never fallen into heresy; indeed, the sentence itself praises him for defending the truth of the Catholic faith and exposing the error of other heretics.

For this reason he was permitted to exercise his episcopal functions in his Church of Braga and was merely forbidden for a time to communicate with the other bishops. The sole reason was that he had allowed himself to be ordained by Symphosius, at a time when nearly all the bishops of his province had turned toward the doctrines of Priscillian.

Hear the words of the sentence:

> Although we gladly embrace Paternus, bishop of Braga, because of his defense of the truth of the Catholic faith and his public exposure of the error of heresy, we have permitted him to retain the Church in which he had been bishop. We shall also receive him into our communion when the Apostolic See has sent its reply.

Thus, after he had easily obtained favor and absolution in this matter, Paternus, once he had received communion, became greatly esteemed by all on account of his merits and rose to the presidency of the Council of Toledo.

What contradiction is there in this?

Dexter therefore speaks worthily of him below, under the year 407:

> Saint Paternus, bishop of Braga, who presided over the Council of Toledo of nineteen bishops, died after being afflicted by many labors and illnesses. A man exceptionally learned and devout.

What more is needed? Does it seem insignificant that the acts themselves of the Council of Toledo commonly believed to be the First mention an earlier council? The same acts provide knowledge of another still earlier council, with respect to which the council believed to be the First is, at a minimum, the third.

But how is this shown? By the sentence issued against Symphosius, Dictinius, and their associates. Is it not sufficiently clear from what has been said that the sentence was issued at an earlier council, different from the one at which it was ordered to be read?

At that earlier council, therefore, the sentence asserts that the aforesaid bishops had avoided the presence and judgment of a council previously announced in the city of Toledo. Another council had consequently been held, the sight of which they had scorned.

The fathers say in the sentence they issued:

> We are known to have shown great patience, although they had avoided the council previously announced in the city of Toledo, to which we summoned them and at which we would have heard why they had not fulfilled the conditions that they themselves had established in the presence and hearing of Saint Ambrose.

As you see, that council was held while Saint Ambrose was still alive. The council in which the sentence was finally pronounced, however, was held shortly after his death, since those who had been punished were ordered to await the reply of Saint Simplicianus, bishop of Milan and successor to Ambrose:

> Awaiting, by the same precedent, what the present Pope and Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, may write in reply.

Observe, I beg you, how different were the times at which those two earlier councils were held.

In addition to all this, the same acts contain a letter of Pope Saint Innocent I addressed to the fathers assembled in a Council of Toledo. But Saint Innocent did not ascend the Apostolic See until the year of the Lord 402, whereas the sentence—which, as its heading shows, is recorded as having been issued on 11 September in the Spanish Era 438, that is, in the year of the Lord 400—necessarily follows that he wrote to fathers assembled at a very different council from the one at which the aforesaid sentence was issued.

Nor will you henceforth, benevolent reader, be surprised when you find a great many canons attributed to the Council of Toledo in Gratian, Ivo, and Burchard, although they are found in none of the printed Toletan councils. Examples of this kind are found in Gratian’s *Decree*: Book 10, Question 1, *Relata*; Book 12, Question 2, *Sancimus*; Book 16, Question 1, *Plures baptismales*; and Book 27, Question 2, *Statutum est*.

They are also found in Gregory’s *Decretals*, Book I, Title 2, chapter 3, *Officium*; Title 24, chapter 1; Title 26, chapter 1; Title 27, chapter 2; and many others in Ivo, Burchard, and Martin of Braga. They are found at the end of the First Council of Toledo in the volumes of the councils and in Loaysa.

It is certainly not surprising that many canons of this kind should be found if, in addition to those that have been published, many other Councils of Toledo were formerly held.

But how many councils, and which ones, are contained under the name of the First Council, you ask?

Without doubt, five. So many can be extracted from the acts themselves and, as you may see truth agreeing with truth, the same number are recorded as having been held by Dexter and his continuator M. Maximus.

The first of these is said by Dexter to have been convened in the present year, namely 386, against all the rebellious bishops of Priscillian’s sect, who were being pressed very vigorously.

The second was held near the year 390. Concerning it he says:

> A second synod is held at Toledo, after Damasus, the Roman pontiff, had already died in the year 384, and Saint Siricius had succeeded him.

This same synod, however, is said to have begun several years earlier.

The third was held in the year 400. He says of it:

> Under this pontiff, Siricius, a certain synod is convened at Toledo.

The fourth is described as follows:

> In the year of the Lord 405, during the second consulship of Stilicho and that of Flavius Anthemius, a council is convened at Toledo; and Saint Innocent writes to the fathers gathered at this council.

Finally, Maximus writes the following concerning the fifth under the year of Christ 448:

> With Turibius, bishop of Astorga and legate of Pope Saint Leo, presiding, many bishops and abbots assemble at Toledo in Spain against the errors of Priscillian, which had again begun to sprout, although previously they had been entirely suppressed and driven out of all Spain.

You have seen five councils of Toledo distinguished by these authors. Now you will easily discover that just as many are derived from the Acts called the First. The fifth is mentioned quite explicitly in the Rule of Faith that was sent by the Fathers of the council to Balconius of Braga together with Pope Leo’s command. The fourth is answered by the letter itself of Saint Innocent, which begins, “Innocent to all the bishops assembled in the synod at Toledo,” etc.; and it could in no way have been addressed to the council in which judgment was pronounced against Symphosius and his associates. That council was celebrated in the year of the Lord 400, as I shall now explain. Innocent, however, did not ascend the chair of Peter until 402, as everyone knows and as we shall prove below. That mention is made in the Acts of the other three has already been proved by us.

The professions of faith of Symphosius, Dictinius, and Comasius, together with their associates, and the judgment pronounced against them, therefore belong to the third council; for it is said to have been issued at its head on the third day before the Ides of September, in the Spanish Era 438. Idatius of Lamecum makes the same assertion in his *Chronicle*, dating it to the fifth year of the reigns of Arcadius and Honorius, Era 438, which is the year of the Lord 400. The second is indicated by the statement in the judgment: “And although previously they had avoided the council summoned in the city of Toledo.” The first, finally, is indicated by the earlier profession that Dictinius had made in the council of Toledo, which he himself plainly recalls in the later words: “This I reproach myself for having said: that God and man have one nature”; and shortly afterward: “In my earlier self-reproach, and at the beginning of my conversion, whatever I wrote,” etc.

Now hear the cause and sequence of these councils. When, in the first council of Toledo, all the rebellious bishops of the Priscillianist sect were being pressed very forcefully by the Fathers, they were compelled to condemn all their errors in themselves. Nevertheless Symphosius, Dictinius, and the other rebels again fell away and withdrew to Italy. But Saint Ambrose of Milan, to whom they communicated their arguments, compelled them to return to a sound mind.

Meanwhile, when they were summoned to a new council of Toledo, they refused to attend, around the year 390. Indeed, Bishop Symphosius, acting contrary to Saint Ambrose’s written decision—which had forbidden Dictinius, while still a presbyter, to be ordained bishop until the absolution of Saint Siricius, Roman Pontiff, had been obtained—nevertheless ordained Dictinius bishop of Astorga in fact. At last, however, both men, having repented, received a judgment concerning their errors in the following council of Toledo, in the year of Christ 400.

In the year 405, moreover, when a new schism had arisen among the bishops of Spain, it became necessary to apply a remedy in a new council; for many had not accepted the previous judgment. Saint Innocent therefore wrote to them:

> “Often, and with more than sufficient cause, concern for the dissension and schism of the Churches has kept me anxious. Rumor declares that this evil is advancing daily through the Spanish provinces with ever-widening separation. The necessary moment has arisen when so great a correction can no longer be delayed, and an appropriate remedy must be provided,” etc.

Saint Paternus of Braga presided over this council—for he could not have presided over the other one, since in the preceding year, 400, he had been recently ordained by Symphosius and had in some sense acted as a defendant. Those nineteen bishops whose subscriptions survive also took part in it; they likewise issued twenty canons, circulated publicly in the Acts. Baronius distinguished these two synods in the appendix to volume five of the *Annals*.

After more than forty years, the Priscillianists again began to flourish, while Leo the Great governed the chair of Peter. In the year 448, Saint Turibius, bishop of Astorga and successor of Dictinius, convened a new council at Toledo. In it the most foul heresy of Priscillian was finally buried. At this council copies of the professions of Symphosius and his associates, together with the judgment pronounced against them, were ordered to be read from the complete official records. Here also the Rule of Faith was issued, divided into seventeen canons, and sent to Balconius; armed with it, the metropolitan himself could confound and punish the Priscillianists, who had their principal seat there in Gallaecia.

These five councils, then, have been confused under the title of the First Council. This was perhaps not wholly unreasonable, since all were celebrated for the same purpose, namely, the abolition of the heresy of Priscillian. Nevertheless, it is clear from what has been said in these commentaries that many other councils were convened at Toledo from the beginning of the nascent Church; in comparison with them, the oldest of the five mentioned above is not yet the seventh. For, to review briefly the writings of Dexter, Saint Eugenius convened the first of all the councils, for the establishment of the primacy of Toledo, around the year of the Lord 105, and another around 112, concerning matters of faith and morals.

Then, under Saint Gregory, bishop of Toledo, Saint Sixtus’s papal legate convened a council at Toledo in the year of the Lord 260; Saint Vincent Ferrer wrote that it had been celebrated by Sixtus himself. In addition, under Natalis, bishop of Toledo, two councils were celebrated: one in 311, in defense of the Council of Elvira; the other, by order of Constantine, in 324 or thereabouts, where the ancient sees that had lost their boundaries recovered them.

In the year 366 and those following, under Pope Damasus and Audentius, bishop of Toledo, frequent synods are said to have been gathered at Toledo at various times. These were followed by the five councils against the Priscillianists. After the fifth, convened by Saint Turibius under Pope Leo, another council was held in 458, as M. Maximus reports, for the reception of the faith of the Council of Chalcedon. Castinus was then presiding over the Church of Toledo. After all this, the council commonly called the Second Council of Toledo was convened in the year of the Lord 531, under Amalaric, king of the Goths, by Montanus, bishop of Toledo, as may be seen in the same Maximus.

It was necessary to say this once for a fuller understanding of the Councils of Toledo; the rest we shall note in their proper places.]

## A.D. 386; Spanish Era 1137

A council is held at Toledo against all the rebellious bishops of the Priscillianist sect, who are being pressed with great force.

[Col. 0523] [Note: [Col. 0524A]]

## A.D. 388 — 1

The just punishment inflicted upon Priscillian by the tyrant-emperor Maximus at Trier, and the death of Maximus himself, are treated at length by Severus in the place cited. Idatius of Lamecum, a bishop in Spain and an author of the same period, arranged this history year by year in his *Chronicle*, recently published by Jacob Sirmond in the year of the Lord 1619.

Idatius’s words are therefore as follows:

> “Era 423”—that is, the year of Christ 385—“Priscillian, turning toward the heresy of the Gnostics, was ordained bishop of Ávila by bishops whom he had gathered to himself in the same depravity. Condemned by several councils of bishops, he went to Italy and to Rome. When he was not even received into the presence of the holy bishops Damasus and Ambrose, he returned with those who had accompanied him to Gaul. There likewise he was judged a heretic by Saint Martin, the bishop, and by other bishops, at the Council of Bordeaux, which, according to Severus, was convened by order of Maximus. He appealed to the emperor, because Maximus at that time possessed imperial power in Gaul.”

Again:

> “Era 425”—the year of the Lord 387—“Priscillian, expelled from the episcopate because of the aforesaid heresy, and with him the layman Latronianus and several of his followers, were put to death at Trier under the tyrant Maximus. From that time the heresy of the Priscillianists invaded Gallaecia.”

Finally, concerning the death of the tyrant himself, he adds:

> “Era 426”—the year of Christ 388—“the tyrant Maximus is killed by Theodosius at the third milestone from Aquileia, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. At the same time, or in that same year, in Gaul Maximus’s son, named Victor, was killed by Count Arbogast.”

Again, in his *Consular Fasti*, under the same year, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the second time and Cynegius, Idatius says:

> “In that same year the public enemy, the tyrant Maximus, is killed by Theodosius Augustus at the third milestone from Aquileia, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. His son Victor was also killed in Gaul a few days later by a count of Theodosius.”

See the agreement between Idatius and Dexter in assigning the year of Maximus’s death, although they disagree about the day.

If we believe Zosimus, Maximus was Spanish by birth, as was the emperor Theodosius himself, and even the consul Cynegius, prefect of the East. Concerning Cynegius’s death, achievements, and burial, Idatius records the following in his *Fasti*:

> “Cynegius, prefect of the East, died at Constantinople during his consulship. He restored all the provinces, which had been corrupted by long decay, to their former condition; he penetrated as far as Egypt and overturned the images of the nations. Therefore, with the great mourning of the entire population, his body was escorted to the Apostles”—thus he calls the church of the Apostles at Constantinople—“on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April. After a year his wife Achantia transported him on foot to Spain.”

He had said nearly the same thing about Cynegius in the *Chronicle* under the year 388. Marcellinus likewise discusses the destruction of Maximus and his son Victor under the same consuls, and adds:

> “When Count Andragathius learned of Maximus’s death, he threw himself headlong from a ship into the waves and was drowned.”

## 2

Saint Augustalis, etc. Above, under the year 382, Dexter had noted Saint Augustalis’s death in Gaul. Now he identifies the city and records that the Catholic bishops were ordered to offer him veneration. His memory appears in the Roman Martyrology and in Bede on 7 September.

Baronius, uncertain of his see, changed Bede’s wording, “At Arles, Saint Augustalis, bishop and confessor,” to “In Gaul, Saint Augustalis,” because no bishop of that name appears in the lists of the bishops of Arles edited by Demochares. This was unreasonable, however, since Bede does not assert that he had been bishop of Arles, but only that his feast was celebrated there, because he had evidently ended his life and been buried there.

Baronius also adds that Augustalis is found among the signatories of the First Council of Orange under Pope Leo; at that time Saint Hilary presided over the church of Arles. This has no bearing on the matter, because this Augustalis is far different from our Augustalis of Elvira. It is certain that the Elviran died in 382, whereas Saint Leo did not begin his Roman pontificate until 440.

## 3

Several bishops, etc. This is made clear by the Acts of the Council of Toledo called the First. In the judgment delivered against Symphosius and Dictinius we read:

> “From the letter of Ambrose, of holy memory, which he had sent to us after the Council of Saragossa, we are known to have shown great patience, so that, if they condemned the things they had wrongly done and fulfilled the conditions contained in the letter, they might return to peace; unless they had first avoided the council summoned in the city of Toledo, to which we would summon them and hear why they had not fulfilled the conditions that they themselves had imposed upon themselves in the presence and hearing of Saint Ambrose.”

These words indicate that Symphosius, Dictinius, and their associates, against whom that judgment was delivered, had met Saint Ambrose; that, in response to his admonitions, they had not merely been restored to a sound mind, but had also, in his presence and hearing, imposed upon themselves the penance that they owed and promised to fulfill certain conditions. Yet at the time of that Council of Toledo, whose presence they avoided, they had still not fulfilled them.

The judgment adds below:

> “Moreover, Symphosius should prove that the pressure of the multitude of the people forced him to ordain Dictinius bishop, although Saint Ambrose had decreed that Dictinius should remain in the place of a presbyter and not receive an advancement of honor.”

Hence it is clear how truthfully Dexter asserts that Dictinius, while not yet a bishop, met Saint Ambrose.

The truth of Dictinius’s own confession is splendidly attested by the confession preserved in the Acts of that council; still more splendidly by his holy life and his death, made illustrious by miracles. For this reason he is celebrated by the Church of Astorga among the saints, with a double office of the second class, on 3 June. His ancient Breviary contains the following collect:

> Almighty and everlasting God, who grant us to celebrate today’s feast in honor of Blessed Dictinius, your confessor and bishop: grant, we beseech you, that through his glorious merits and continual intercessions, with you as our guide, we may deserve to attain the joys of eternal life. Through our Lord.

In the litany he is named among the bishops who are confessors, as a patron; he also has an ancient church dedicated to his name, which is now the house of the Friars Preachers.

When you hear that Dictinius and Symphosius met Saint Ambrose, do not understand this as though they had slighted the apostolic see—far be such a thought—but rather as meaning that they came to him so that he might explain the true doctrines to them, since the reputation of his teaching had spread throughout all Spain. The matter was no different from the later occasion when Orosius went to Augustine in Africa on behalf of the bishops of Spain, or from the much earlier occasion when two other bishops, one of Asturias and one of Mérida, met Saint Cyprian concerning the case of Martial and Basilides.

## 4

Augustalis, etc. At the time when the case of Priscillian was being handled, while Bishop Idatius, his principal adversary, was active, Gregory was praetorian prefect in Gaul, as Severus states explicitly in Book II of his *Sacred History*. Speaking of Idatius as he hurried to Gaul, Severus says:

> “There he approached Gregory the Prefect. When Gregory learned what had happened, he ordered the authors of the disturbances to be seized and brought before him, and reported everything to the emperor, so that he might close the way by which the heretics sought to obtain influence.”

That Gregory was then abruptly transferred from this office to the episcopate in Spain is written by Pope Saint Innocent in his letter to the bishops assembled at the Council of Toledo. He reproaches them there because some men were being promoted from secular prefectures—where they had undoubtedly often incurred irregularity—to the episcopate. Among these, he says, had been Gregory and Rufinus:

> “For concerning the ordinations which, through the fault of a wicked custom, we know the Spanish bishops to celebrate: how many do we find to have been summoned to the priesthood from among those who, after receiving the grace of baptism, had been engaged in forensic practice and had taken up the obstinacy of pursuing office, among whom Rufinus and Gregory are said to have been? How many from the military, men who obeyed authorities and necessarily carried out severe commands? How many from the ranks of the municipal councillors?” etc.

Saint Exuperantius was raised from military service to the episcopate of Uxama; Gregory the Younger of Córdoba was raised from the prefecture of Cappadocia, as I shall say below in section 6.

Gregory, however, after being raised to the see of Elvira, shone with no ordinary holiness and learning, as we shall say with Dexter below under the years 407 and 423, when he died.

Consider, reader, I beg you, how cleverly the little tale has been fabricated about the pitiable death of Hosius, supposedly caused by the curse of Saint Gregory, bishop of Elvira. Gregory, however, was still a young man practicing at the bar and did not ascend the episcopal chair until more than thirty years later, in 390. We dealt with this matter under the year 360, and Baronius, learnedly, proves in the *Annals*, at the place cited there, that it was an invention of Marcellinus Comes.

## 5

Severus, etc. M. Maximus mentions the same man in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 432, saying: “Severus, bishop of Lamecum, flourishes through his writings.” He attended the First Council of Toledo. Indeed, his name is found among the nineteen subscribed Fathers, in thirteenth place in the edition of Archbishop Loaysa, but in seventh place in the old edition of the *Councils*. In the printed codex of Dexter he is called bishop of Malaca; but Maximus’s testimony establishes that he was bishop of Lamecum, or Lamacensis, as Maximus himself calls him. Perhaps Saint Paulinus wrote to him the letters which, according to Gennadius, were addressed to Severus.

## 6

Hyginus, etc. When Hyginus, who was in exile at Lerida, died—as we discussed at length under the year 384—Gregory succeeded him in the see of Córdoba. Gregory had previously been praetorian prefect of Cappadocia, as Dexter himself asserts below under the year 424. He also mentions him with praise at the end of the *Chronicle*. He is called the Younger in relation to Gregory, Hyginus’s predecessor, whose praises the great Theodosius recounted at the Council of Milan; this was noted there under the year of the Lord 384. Hyginus succeeded this Gregory; Gregory the Younger succeeded Hyginus; and Isidore, himself also called the Younger, succeeded Gregory. Recall also what was noted there concerning him, because of the memory of Isidore the Elder.

## 7

Prudentius, etc. He himself declares this in explicit words in the preface to the *Cathemerinon*, saying:

> Twice in the exercise of the laws,  
> I governed the reins of noble cities;  
> I restored civil justice to the good and struck terror into the accused.  
>   
> At last, raised in rank of service,  
> The emperor’s piety exalted me,  
> Ordering me, once admitted, to stand nearer, in the next rank.

Perhaps, instead of “Twice in the exercise of the laws,” one ought to read “Thrice in the exercise of the laws”; otherwise, how can it be true that he governed by legal authority the three cities of Toledo, Córdoba, and Saragossa, unless one says that he governed one for a full three-year term and the others for half that time? The statement that follows, that he went to Rome in his fortieth year, must refer to his age; for he had been born in the consulship of Philippus and Salia, in the year of the Lord 348. Thus he entered upon his fortieth year in A.D. 388, with which Dexter is now chiefly concerned. Therefore the reading in the printed Saragossa copy, “In the year 400 he went to Rome,” was introduced by scribal error; the error is evident because below Prudentius is said to have been writing at Rome in the year 396.

## 8

Synod, etc. We have counted this as the second among the councils convened at Toledo against the Priscillianists. It is said to have been begun over several years because the bishops infected by the contagion of Priscillian were repeatedly summoned to it; when they refused, the synod was deferred, and at last it was celebrated without them, as was proved above from the wording of the judgment delivered against them.

Saint Damasus had departed this life in the year of the Lord 384. Siricius succeeded him the following year and governed the Church until 398; his successor Anastasius did so until 402, when Saint Innocent was elected. Innocent wrote concerning reform to the Fathers celebrating the synod of Toledo in the year 405. Baronius agrees with us and the others in volumes IV and V of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*.

## 9

Claudian, etc. Not everyone has held the same opinion about Claudian’s homeland. Petrarch makes him a Spaniard; Landinus, a Florentine; Girardus makes him an Egyptian from Alexandria, following what Suidas taught. Indeed, Claudian himself sometimes wrote in this way, in his letter to the proconsul Gennadius:

> “The common glory of Italy, known to the peoples of Greece and to our Nile.”

Everyone knows, however, that the Nile waters the Egyptian city of Alexandria. I consider this to be true, and Dexter does not contradict it. He does not write that Claudian was born in Spain, but that he originated from Spain, evidently deriving his family from there; nor do I think Petrarch intended anything else.

Landinus alone proceeds without an authority, and perhaps he is caught in an ambiguity. He had a Florentine who was especially closely connected with him in friendship, a man of distinction whose books on agriculture are read among the Greeks, and to whom Claudian himself dedicated Books III of *The Rape of Proserpina*. There also survives an elegy under both their names, beginning:

> “When Orpheus was spending his leisure with songs in the quiet hours.”

There is no doubt that the ambiguity arose from this, so that Landinus came to believe that one and the same Claudian was both a Spaniard and a Florentine, with “Florentine” functioning almost as the former’s proper surname.

As for Dexter’s opinion, a significant indication of its truth is provided by the fact that Claudian everywhere customarily expands upon Spain’s praises, while he is silent about the encomia of the other provinces of the world. I shall give several examples.

In the book entitled *The Praise of Serena, Wife of Stilicho*, he says:

> What worthy thing, Spain, can human speech  
> Recall of your lands? The sun is first raised  
> From the sea by India; you, when daylight is spent,  
> Wash the weary horses of the sun, and in your waters  
> The stars find rest.  
>   
> Rich in horses, generous in crops, precious in metals,  
> Fertile in pious princes: the ages owe  
> Trajan to you; from these springs flowed  
> The line of Aelia  
>   
> [Note: “Aelia” refers to the line of Hadrian.]  
>   
> Hence the elder father, hence the diadems  
> Of the young brothers.  
>   
> For other peoples whom Rome received by treaty  
> Or subdued by arms are dragged away  
> For the varied uses of the empire:  
> The crops of Pharia and the harvest of Carthage  
> Are devoted to the nourishment of the camps;  
> Gaul supplies the strength of soldiers;  
> The cavalry squadrons of Illyria sweat;  
> Iberia alone has brought a new revenue  
> To Latian affairs—the Augusti. Crops, treasuries,  
> And soldiers gather from everywhere,  
> And are recruited from the whole world;  
> She produces those who rule all these things.  
> Nor was she content to be judged by the fame  
> Of her men, unless she surpassed them equally  
> In mothers, shining with competing glory  
> In either sex, and gave Flaccilla, Maria,  
> And beautiful Serena.  
>   
> [Note: Here he turns to Serena.]  
>   
> They say that at your birth the Tagus, swelling  
> Through rich fields, overflowed with wealth;  
> Gallaecia smiled with flowers, and the beautiful Durius  
> With rose-colored banks. The Cantabrian everywhere  
> Changed his sheepfold for purple fleece;  
> The Ocean spewed gems upon the neighboring shore;  
> The southern wind, pale from the excavated mountains,  
> Did not wander idly; veins of gold, offered  
> At sacred births, vomit their wealth for all;  
> And beneath the caves of the Pyrenees  
> Nymphs gathered the fiery Ceraunian stones  
> Amid thunderbolts.

Latinus Pacatus said nearly the same things about Theodosius.

Again, in the marriage poem for Honorius Augustus and Maria, the Spanish daughter of Stilicho:

> Let the Iberians hear from afar,  
> From whom the seed of the imperial palace came,  
> Where the house, heavy with laurels,  
> Pregnant with empire, scarcely counts its triumphs.  
>   
> The husband has his father from this side  
> —that is, Honorius has Theodosius—  
> And the girl her mother from that side  
> —Maria has Serena, Stilicho’s wife—  
> And from either branch, drawn together,  
> The imperial line returns through a fiery origin.  
>   
> Let the groves of the Baetis be adorned,  
> Let the Tagus swell with gold;  
> And let the Ocean, begetter of the race,  
> Revel beneath its glassy waves.

In the panegyric on Honorius’s fourth consulship he addresses him as follows:

> Having received all others willingly,  
> The palace brought you forth alone;  
> Fortunate, you grew up in your father’s purple,  
> And limbs never profaned by ordinary dress  
> Fell into sacred folds. Spain brought forth  
> Your father from her golden waters;  
> The Bosphorus rejoices in you as its fosterling;  
>   
> [Note: He was born at Constantinople in the East, on the Thracian Bosphorus, to a Spanish father.]  
>   
> Your origin rises from the western frontier,  
> But the Dawn is your nurse. For so great a pledge  
> The two sides contend: each hemisphere claims you  
> As its citizen.

Again, in Book II of *The Praise of Stilicho*, he leads the provinces of the world to Rome, demanding that they seek Stilicho’s consulship. Among the others he introduces Spain first, in these words:

> They gather at the temple of the goddess  
> —I understand this as the Temple of Peace—  
> Which shines white on the Palatine hill.  
> Then Spain, first, her hair bound with the pale leaves  
> Of Minerva and woven through with the glittering  
> Golden garment of the Tagus, speaks these words:  
>   
> “Whatever I have ever asked, Stilicho,  
> He has always granted me, and he has begrudged  
> His honors only to himself. He was able  
> To disregard the authority of his imperial father-in-law;  
> Now he denies it even to his son-in-law.  
> If he will not receive it from the world he rules  
> As its commander, let him at least receive it  
> As a kinsman from the palace.  
>   
> Does he think it a small thing that, embracing  
> The Iberian offspring, he supports my grandsons  
> With unshaken right”—  
>   
> [Note: He means Honorius and Arcadius.]  
>   
> “—so that purple may commend the Baetis of their fathers?  
> That he may fertilize the kingdom with Maria’s  
> Beautiful offspring? That he is expected  
> To be the grandfather of the Lord?”  
>   
> [Note: Stilicho was indeed expected to become grandfather of the future Caesar when he married his daughter Maria to Honorius Augustus.]

Likewise, in the book on the consulship of Manlius Theodorus, he wrote:

> “The sluggish Saône, the swift Rhône, and the wealthy Iberus.”

And below:

> May every steed that resounds with proud neighing  
> Around the Baetis illuminate it; the steed that drinks  
> The splendid waters of the Tagus and sprinkles  
> Its mane with dripping gold.

Let these examples be understood not merely in favor of Dexter, who makes Claudian originate from Spain and whose affection for Spanish affairs is always and abundantly displayed, revealing a blood connection, but much more in favor of the emperors Honorius and Arcadius, whose names had fallen out of the copy of Dexter through the fault of the copyists. He could not have forgotten such great princes, since, in accordance with the practice of his *Chronicle*, he reconstructed the sequence of the other events. We shall say a little more about them and about Stilicho below, under the years 400 and 405.

## 10

“Wonderfully,” etc. Consult what was said about the same matter under the year 385. I believe the Council of Tarragona mentioned here to be the council convened by Himerius, metropolitan of Tarragona, for the reception of the canons of Pope Siricius. These appear in the letter sent to Himerius in the consulship of Arcadius and Bauto, that is, in the year of Christ 385. There are fifteen canons in all. At the end of the letter Himerius is ordered to communicate them to the bishops of the provinces of Carthage, Baetica, Lusitania, and Gallaecia, and not merely to those of Tarragona. It therefore appears that the bishops of the whole Spanish nation assembled with him.

## 11

Vigilantius, etc. Cardinal Baronius thought in the *Annals* that this heretic had been born at Calagurris in Spain, and that Saint Jerome supported him while writing against Vigilantius. Gennadius, however, contradicts him in Book 35 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, or *On Illustrious Men*, writing as follows:

> “Vigilantius the presbyter, a Gaul by nation, held a church in the Spanish parish of Barcelona. He too wrote certain things, indeed out of zeal for religion, but seduced by human praise and presuming beyond his powers: a man polished in language but untrained in the meaning of Scripture. With perverse ingenuity he expounded the second vision of Daniel, and said other frivolous things, which must necessarily be set forth in the catalogue of heretics.”

Everything Dexter writes agrees with this: namely, that Vigilantius was born in Gaul and became a presbyter of a church in the diocese of Barcelona. For a long time he lived at Calagurris—not the place flourishing on the banks of the Iberus that is commonly called Calahorra, but the place formerly situated at the foot of the Pyrenees in the district of Barcelona. Ausonius mentions it in his letters to Paulinus.

After writing in Letter 24 that Paulinus was living at Barcelona, he says:

> Why do I complain, and attack the crimes of the eastern monster?  
> The western bank of the Tagus afflicts me; Punic Barcelona afflicts me;  
> The snowy ridges of the two-sea Pyrenees afflict me.

He evidently meant that his Paulinus was being detained there. In Letter 25 he adds:

> Will Bilbilis, or Calagurris clinging to its crags,  
> Then possess my glory, the glory of my homeland,  
> The crown and summit of the senate?

It is as though he had said that Calagurris clinging to the Pyrenean crags possessed his Paulinus, whom he had nevertheless said was living at Barcelona among the snowy ridges of the Pyrenees. He plainly indicates that this Calagurris was near Barcelona.

Morales treats both Barcelonas at length in his *Antiquities of Spain*, as does Nonius in chapter 81. One was called Nasica, the other Fibularia, which still exists today. Vigilantius, therefore, was born in Gaul. Crossing the Pyrenees from there, he settled at Calagurris in the district of Barcelona and became presbyter of its church.

Nor does Jerome disagree with this; indeed, he presents the matter in such clear words that Marianus Victorius, summarizing the argument of his book against Vigilantius, wrote:

> “Vigilantius, a Gaul by nation, presbyter of the Church of Barcelona, which is in Spain,” etc.

What could be clearer than the very beginning of the book?

> “Many monsters have been generated throughout the world. We read of Centaurs and Sirens, etc., in the books of the poets. Spain has produced the three-formed Geryon; Gaul alone had no monsters, but always abounded in the bravest and most eloquent men. Suddenly Vigilantius arose—or, more truly, Dormitantius—who with an unclean spirit fights against the Spirit of Christ.”

From where, I ask, did Vigilantius suddenly arise for Jerome? From nowhere other than Gaul, which before him had been ignorant of monsters. This cannot be applied to Spain, since it must necessarily refer to the province just named, and that province is not Spain but Gaul. It also matters that Jerome wonders at the origin of this monster. It would not have been astonishing if he had been born in Spain, which had produced its own three-formed Geryon; but Gaul alone had not possessed monsters. Hence Jerome’s greater astonishment arose from his origin there.

Why rely on conjectures when Jerome later gives us the name of the city in which Vigilantius was born, namely Convenae? According to Ptolemy, Pliny, and the other authorities, this city was situated in Aquitaine and was commonly called Comminges or Commenge. Hear Jerome:

> “He answers to his ancestry, so that, born from the seed of brigands and Convenae”—whom Gnaeus Pompey, after conquering Spain and hastening to return for his triumph, brought down from the Pyrenean heights and gathered into one town, from which the city acquired the name Convenae—“he may continue to practice brigandage against the Church of God.”

No one, therefore, should doubt that Vigilantius was born in Gaul. Everyone nevertheless admits that he went from there to Calagurris and served as presbyter until, after corrupting several churches of Spain, he was expelled by the Spaniards into Gaul. He was living there at the time when the pious man Sisinius was sent to Jerome by the holy presbyters Riparius and Desiderius of Barcelona, as Jerome himself expressly states:

> “This Calagurritan tavernkeeper”—so Jerome says—“and, perversely on account of the name of the village, this mute Quintilian, mixes water with wine; and from his former trade”—he apparently had first been a tavernkeeper at Calagurris—“he attempts to join the poisons of his treachery to the Catholic faith.”

And below:

> “Shame upon the sacrilege! He is said to have bishops as accomplices in his crime, if indeed they should be called bishops who do not ordain deacons unless they have first taken wives.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The authors of this little statement of mine are the holy presbyters Riparius and Desiderius. They write that their parishes are stained by the neighborhood of this man, and they sent books through their brother Sisinius, which he vomited up while snoring amid his drunken feasts. They report that some have been found who, favoring his vices, assent to his blasphemies. But how many and how great are they? He attacked virginity, hated chastity, and at the banquets of worldly people protested against the fasts of the saints while philosophizing among the drinking vessels. Indeed, he dared to open his foul mouth upward and utter the vilest stench against the relics of the holy martyrs, and to call us, who venerate them, ash-worshippers and idolaters because we honor the bones of dead men.”

The following words indicate that he eventually withdrew to Gaul:

> “Gaul endures an enemy native to herself, and sees a man with a disturbed head, one who ought to be bound in the chains of Hippocrates, sitting in the Church.”

And below:

> “You who live at the foot of the Pyrenees and are a neighbor of Iberia,” etc.

And again:

> “He attacks the churches of Gaul.”

See how true everything Dexter writes about him is. Incidentally, note Jerome’s words, “Gaul endures an enemy native to herself,” by which he plainly asserts that Vigilantius was a Gaul. For what else does it mean to be a native enemy than to be a domestic one?

Finally, I would point out that at the Council of Toledo held in the year of the Lord 400, Emila, or Emilius, was deposed with the other Priscillianist bishops. He was evidently the bishop of Barcelona whom Dexter had said took part in the Council of Saragossa. It is therefore clear that what Dexter now asserts is true: Vigilantius had corrupted the Church of Barcelona.

Later Sidonius Apollinaris and Palmatius, bishop of Toledo, wrote against Vigilantius, according to M. Maximus in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 476.]

## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

On the sixth day before the Kalends of September, Sextus Flavius Maximus was killed together with his son Victor. In this one respect at least he deserves the highest praise: he exposed the frauds of the heresiarch Priscillian, expelled him from Spain, and, when Priscillian resisted obeying first the Council of Saragossa and then the Council of Bordeaux, forced him to go to Trier. At last he inflicted worthy punishment upon the impure and wicked man; although the proper legal procedure was not observed, he nevertheless ordered that the convicted man be punished by the sword.

[Col. 0525] ## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

Saint Augustalis, bishop of Elvira, died at Arles and was enrolled among the saints; his memory is celebrated on 7 September.

## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

Several bishops of the Priscillianist faction fled to Ambrose, bishop of Milan, who was most closely united with the Catholic bishops of Spain by the bond of faith and friendship. They were deeply repentant of their former life and errors and strove, by confession, to return to the bosom of the Church. Among them were Dictinius, then a presbyter and later bishop of Astorga; Symphosius, bishop of Gallaecia; and several others.

## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

Gregory, formerly praetorian prefect of Gaul and already advanced in years, succeeded Augustalis in the Baetican see of Elvira. He was a supremely devout man and exceptionally learned in the liberal arts.

## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

Severus, bishop of Malaca [variant: Lamecum], wrote a book to his sister on virginity.

[Col. 0527] ## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

Gregory the Younger succeeded Hyginus at Córdoba. He wrote to Orosius concerning the year 380.

## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

Prudentius, after governing Toledo, Córdoba, and Saragossa in Spain with distinction, became a commander and was regarded as a most celebrated orator and a marvelous poet. In the year 400 he went to Rome.

## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

A second council is held at Toledo, after Damasus, Roman pontiff, had already died in the year 384 and Saint Siricius had succeeded him. This same synod, however, had been initiated several years earlier.

## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

The poet Claudian, originally from Spain, flourishes at Rome.

[Col. 0529] ## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

Exuperantius, a Spanish bishop, flourishes wonderfully. He was an illustrious bishop of Italy and took part in the Council of Tarragona.

## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

Vigilantius the heretic, a native of Calagurris, from Gaul.

[Col. 0531] ## A.D. 388; Spanish Era 1139

He corrupts the Church of Barcelona, where he had been a presbyter, and other churches of Spain. Saint Jerome wrote against him.

[Note: [Col. 0531C]

## A.D. 396—1. “By the holy man,” etc.

What some have called into question—whether Paulinus of Nola was that author whose poems circulate under the name of Pontius Paulinus—is now settled by Dexter’s testimony. For it is asserted that the same man lived at Barcelona, was honored with the priesthood (as we read concerning the poet in his own works), and afterward, endowed with great poverty of spirit, distributed all his possessions to the poor and to captives. Gregory the Great writes this about the bishop of Nola in Book III, chapter 1, of the *Dialogues*.

Cardinal Baronius, under the year of the Lord 395, notes that Saint Paulinus, while still living in Spain, wrote Book II of the *Natalitia*. Uranius the presbyter indeed writes that Saint Paulinus was born at Bordeaux and had a wife named Therasia. Since the name Therasia was in use nowhere except in the Spanish regions, this sufficiently shows that she was Spanish.

Moreover, Ausonius of Bordeaux sent many letters from Bordeaux to his nephew Pontius Paulinus, who was living at Barcelona in Spain—namely, letters 19 through 25. The nineteenth begins, “Tartesian Calpe had already confined the horses of the Sun,” and the twenty-fifth bears the title, “Ausonius to Pontius Paulinus, his son.” There he complains that Paulinus had abandoned Bordeaux, his fatherland, and with it the religion of his homeland, having been converted to the faith of Christ. In Letter 24 he says:

> Why do I complain, and pursue the crimes of the monster of the East?
>
> The bank of the western Tagus wounds me; Punic Barcelona wounds me;
>
> the snowy heights of the Pyrenees between two seas wound me.
>
> But if a tolerable boundary lay between us across the intervening valleys, etc.,
>
> then I would embrace you as one suited to my own arms.
>
> Now, beyond the Alps and the marble Pyrenees,
>
> stand the houses of Caesaraugusta, and Tarraco near the Tyrrhenian [Sea],
>
> and Barcelona added above the oyster-bearing sea.

He intimates that Paulinus had not always remained in one place in Spain, for he adds:

> And you, wandering through Spain’s whole and lengthy expanse,
>
> forgetful of your ancestors, trusting foreign friends, etc.

In Letter 25, which begins:

> This fourth letter has revealed to you my familiar complaints,

he complains:

> Speaking much and remaining wholly silent, neither of us is pleasing.
>
> Nor can I conceal the yoke which free devotion never bears,
>
> nor does it love to set truth below pleasing words.
>
> Have you changed your character, dearest Paulinus?
>
> Is it the Vasconian forest, the snowy lodgings
>
> of the Pyrenees, and forgetfulness of our own sky that have done this?
>
> What punishment might I not rightly invoke upon you, Iberian land?
>
> May the Carthaginians ravage you; may faithless Hannibal burn you;
>
> may exiled Sertorius again seek you as the seat of war.
>
> Then who will possess my glory, the glory of my fatherland,
>
> and the summit of the senate—that is, of Bordeaux?
>
> Will it be Bilbilis, or Calagurris clinging to its crags?
>
> Or Ilerda, which from its exposed, rugged ruins
>
> looks down upon the arid torrent of the Sicoris? etc.

Paulinus also sent Ausonius several replies from Spain, defending himself concerning his adoption of the Christian religion. The first begins:

> Why do you command the Muses, renounced and entrusted to my care, father,
>
> to return? Take hold of sacred studies;
>
> let profane things be set aside.

The second bears the title *Defense on Account of the Religion Adopted*. There he responds to the objections concerning the barbarous names of Spain, and among other things says:

> Why do you cast before me the vast forests
>
> of Vasconia and the snowy lodgings of the Pyrenees?
>
> As though fixed upon the very threshold, am I to conduct my life
>
> in the Spanish region, with no place for me anywhere,
>
> in countryside or city, across the whole world’s highest expanse,
>
> where wealthy Spain stretches on, watching suns submerged in the sea?

A little earlier he says:

> Believe me, therefore, my father:
>
> we are neither forgetful of the sky nor living without understanding,
>
> nor do we move about among human places, etc.

He began the third letter as follows:

> Spare, I beg you, tearing apart your own,
>
> and do not wish to mingle bitter things with those of a father, etc.

These statements agree with what Saint Paulinus of Nola writes to Alypius, bishop of Tagaste. This letter is numbered 35 among Augustine’s letters. Paulinus says that he was baptized at Bordeaux by Saint Delphinus and raised to the order of the priesthood at Barcelona in Spain by Bishop Lampadius—or Lampius—while the people shouted and caused an uproar for that purpose. The letter is addressed:

> To the most deservedly honored and most blessed father, Alypius: Paulinus and Therasia, sinners.

For with his most holy wife Therasia he traveled as a stranger, as though with a sister, in the highest continence. As long as he lived, he gave and received letters under the names of both, as is clear from Letters 31, 32, 33, 34, and 35 among Augustine’s letters.

In the aforementioned Letter 35 he writes:

> Although I was baptized by Delphinus at Bordeaux and consecrated by Lampadius at Barcelona in Spain through the force of a suddenly inflamed crowd, nevertheless I have always been nourished in the faith by Ambrose’s love, and now I am being cherished in the order of the priesthood.

In Letter 6, to Severus, he likewise says:

> Hasten, he says, to come to us . . . . . We are now staying in the city of Barcelona, as I had written before. After those letters in which you replied, on the Lord’s day on which he deigned to be born in the flesh, I was suddenly seized—as he himself bears witness—by the force of the multitude, though I believe by his own arrangement, and was initiated into the priesthood. I confess that I was unwilling, not because I despised the place, etc.

Behold how true Dexter’s account is.

Yet a learned man in the city once objected to me that what Dexter asserts could not possibly agree with the truth—namely, that in the year of the Lord 396 Saint Paulinus was ordained priest by Lampadius, bishop of Barcelona, since Paulinus himself writes to Alypius in the aforementioned letter that he had been ordained before Augustine’s baptism. Augustine’s baptism occurred in the year of the Lord 389, when Timasius and Protus were consuls, as Cardinal Baronius clearly proves from Augustine’s writings. Indeed, Paulinus had already come to Italy and had become renowned at Milan. Thus spoke the man, whose name, out of respect, I conceal in silence.

But if he had carefully considered the words of the letter, he would easily have recognized that none of what he alleged is found there. Paulinus merely says that Alypius had heard something of his reputation when Alypius himself was being initiated at Milan together with Augustine. He also asserts that, when he wrote the letter, he had already been admitted to the rank of presbyter. But he gives not even the slightest indication that Alypius had heard this at Milan while he was being catechized. Rather, the letter implies that, not only after Augustine and Alypius had been baptized, but also after Alypius had become bishop, Paulinus had been more abundantly instructed in the faith by Ambrose at Milan and had afterward been ordained at Barcelona.

Here are Paulinus’s very words:

> You indicated to me that you had already learned at Milan about the title of our humility, when you were being initiated there. I confess that I desire to learn this more carefully, so that I may know you in every respect; and I shall rejoice all the more if, when you received our father Ambrose, you were either initiated into the faith or consecrated to the priesthood, so that we may both appear to have the same author.
>
> For although I was baptized by Delphinus at Bordeaux and consecrated by Lampadius at Barcelona in Spain through the force of a suddenly inflamed crowd, nevertheless I have always been nourished in the faith by Ambrose’s love, and now I am being cherished in the order of the priesthood. Finally, he wished to claim me for his own clergy, so that, although I live in different places, I might be considered his presbyter.

Paulinus narrates all this to Alypius as something new and previously unknown to him, things that had occurred after Alypius’s initiation. But enough has been said about this trivial matter.

For the remaining matters concerning the holiness of the blessed Paulinus and Therasia, one should consult Uranius, in his *Book on the Passing of Saint Paulinus*, and Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 1. Gregory relates Paulinus’s voluntary captivity in place of the son of a widow of Nola, and his liberation together with all the citizens of his city. One should also consult Augustine’s letters, especially Letter 34, whose title contains the following commendation of the persons mentioned above:

> To our most beloved and sincere lords, truly most blessed and endowed with the most abundant grace of God, our brothers Paulinus and Therasia: Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

The account of Gregory of Tours in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 107, is also most worthy of remembrance:

> He therefore departed with his wife, as though intending to travel to another region, possessing nothing except his own status. After a long time, when he was sought by the inhabitants of his region and could nowhere be found, a merchant from that city—Bordeaux—came to this city, Nola, where the blessed man was serving through a heavenly gift. When he saw him, he immediately threw himself upon the ground and, embracing the holy man’s feet, said: “This is the blessed Paulinus, known throughout the whole world. Although his fellow citizens sought him earnestly, he could nowhere be found.” When the merchant recounted all his deeds, those who heard him were astonished. Without delay, Paulinus, who was serving as a priest at Nola, was himself appointed in place of the bishop.

See also Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 48, and the other authors cited by Baronius in his notes on June 22.

Nor should we omit what Ausonius wrote in the *Parentalia*: namely, that other Paulinuses, relatives of the man mentioned above, also came down from Bordeaux into Spain and flourished there. For first, a certain Paulinus governed Tarraco. Of him he says in number 24:

> For Tarraco of Iberia offered you a tribunal,
>
> seeking to be your client.

This man’s son married Megentia, Ausonius’s sister, and by her had two children in Spain: one, Paulinus, who died in his youth; and Driadia, who also died in Spain, as he himself says in number 23:

> She died far away in the Spanish region,
>
