> between her mother’s hands and her father’s kisses.

The most fortunate offspring of this family was therefore Saint Paulinus. In his youth he left Bordeaux and fled to his relatives in Spain, where he took Therasia as his wife.

Ausonius himself also says that, at the same time, Dinamius of Bordeaux, a man distinguished in the rhetorical arts, did something similar. In the aforementioned number 24 of the *Parentalia*, he writes of him:

> Whom wounded reputation drove away on a charge of adultery,
>
> whom little Ilerda sheltered in its hiding places;
>
> whom a Spanish wife enriched while he lay concealed,
>
> for there, under an altered name, you were a rhetorician.
>
> A rhetorician disguised under the surname Flavinius, etc.

It is also worthy of remembrance that, while Saint Paulinus was at Complutum in Spain with his wife, the blessed Therasia, their son Celsus, still a boy and renowned for holiness, died. His dear parents buried him near the tomb of the holy boys Justus and Pastor. A panegyric composed by Saint Paulinus on the death of his son still exists. It begins, “Formerly a child of illustrious fathers,” and among other things says:

> We believe, Celsus, that he plays with you,
>
> a participant in the eternal green fields of joy and life.
>
> We entrusted him in the city of Complutum,
>
> joined by covenant with the martyrs in a nearby tomb,
>
> so that from the nearby blood of the saints he may draw that
>
> by which he may cleanse our souls in that fire.
>
> For perhaps this little drop of our own blood
>
> will one day also be light to our hearts.

Concerning Lampadius, bishop of Barcelona, who ordained Saint Paulinus priest, I should note that he was present at the council called the First Council of Toledo, and likewise at the First Council of Milevis in Africa. His name is found subscribed in both places: in the acts of the First Council of Toledo, and in Augustine’s Letter 92, where the African council is discussed.

In the letter of Paulinus and Therasia to Alypius, the reading *Lampius* is found incorrectly in place of *Lampadius*. But if you ask how, since Emilas governed the see of Barcelona between Pacianus and Lampadius, Dexter can now assert that Lampadius succeeded Pacianus, I will answer that Emilas was deprived of the priesthood on account of the heresy of Priscillian and Vigilantius, as can be seen in the acts of the First Council of Toledo. For this reason his name was rejected from their catalogue of bishops.

### 2. Asturius, etc.

We discussed him above, under the year 370. We shall discuss his holiness again below, under the years 406, 423, and 424.

### 3. Prudentius, etc.

This should be understood of the book *Psychomachia*, that is, *The Conflict of the Soul*. For he wrote the book *Cathemerinon*, that is, a work on divine matters, in the fifty-seventh year of his life, as he himself states in the prologue. Since he was born when Salia and Philippus were consuls—in other words, in the year of Christ 348—it follows that he wrote *Cathemerinon* in the year 404, for fifty-seven years separate that year from this one. He says:

> Ten periods of five years have now passed,
>
> and, if I am not mistaken, the revolving hinge
>
> rolls on a seventh year besides,
>
> while we enjoy the circling sun.
>
> The limit approaches, and God now brings near
>
> the day that borders upon old age.
>
> What useful thing have we accomplished
>
> in so great a span of time?

After recounting the events of his life, he adds:

> Yet, at the very final end,
>
> let the sinful soul cast off its folly;
>
> if it cannot celebrate God by its merits,
>
> let it at least celebrate him with its voice.
>
> Let the day continue in hymns,
>
> and let no night be free from singing to the Lord.
>
> Let it fight against heresies
>
> and examine the Catholic faith.
>
> Let it trample the sacred things of the nations;
>
> let Rome bring defilement upon your idols;
>
> let it devote its song to the martyrs
>
> and praise the apostles.

He wrote about all these matters, but not in the same year. For he composed *Peristephanon*, *Apotheosis*, *Hamartigenia*, and the two books against Symmachus afterward, while living in Spain, as we shall say in their proper place.

A.D. 396. A.R. 1147. Paulinus became a presbyter under the holy bishop Lampadius [or Lampius] of Barcelona, who succeeded my holy father Pacianus. Not long afterward, endowed with great poverty of spirit, he sold everything.

[Col. 0533] A.D. 396. A.R. 1147. Asturius, surnamed Serranus, who had succeeded the most holy man Audentius in the see of Toledo, is venerated as a holy man.

[Col. 0535] A.D. 396. A.R. 1147. Prudentius, the lyric poet of Caesaraugusta, writes at Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0535B]

### A.D. 398. “To Siricius,” etc.

Cardinal Baronius asserts this together with the more ancient authorities.]

A.D. 398. A.R. 1149. Anastasius succeeded Siricius in the Roman See of Saint Peter.

[Note: [Col. 0535B]

### A.D. 400—1. “Under this pontiff,” etc.

That is, under Anastasius, whom Dexter had just said immediately succeeded Siricius in the See of Peter. In this council a decision was issued concerning Symphosius and Dictinius, together with the other bishops converted from the sect of Priscillian. We discussed this matter at length above, under the year of the Lord 386, where we established that this was the third of the councils assembled at Toledo against the Priscillianists.

In this same year, 400, which was the fifth year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, Bishop Idatius makes honorable mention of such a Council of Toledo in his *Chronicle*, in these words:

> In the province of Carthaginensis, in the city of Toledo, a synod of bishops was assembled. In it—as is contained in the acts—Symphosius and Dictinius, together with other Galician bishops, followers of Priscillian, condemned his most blasphemous heresy, along with its author, by subscribing their profession.
>
> Certain regulations were also established concerning the discipline of the Church. Ortigius the bishop participated in the same council. He had been ordained at Caelenis, but, having been driven out on account of the Catholic faith through the factional activity of the Priscillianists, he lived in exile.
>
> The sentence of the council itself, as can be gathered from the acts, says concerning Ortigius: “We declare that our brother Ortigius is to be restored to the churches from which he had been expelled.”

Ortigius is found subscribed to the following Council of Toledo, in the year of the Lord 405. We have already said much about it and shall speak of it again in its proper place.

### 2. “Paul Orosius,” etc.

Orosius himself discusses his mission from Spain to Augustine in the consultation addressed to Augustine concerning the affairs of his mission. This consultation is prefixed to the book *On the Errors of the Priscillianists and Origenists*, which is found in Volume VI of Augustine’s works. Augustine himself also discusses it in Letter 102, to Evodius.

Three matters in Dexter’s account require explanation here: the time at which the mission occurred; by whom Orosius was sent to Africa; and for what reason.

As to the date, Caesar Baronius assigns it to the year of the Lord 414, but the illustrious cardinal does not reveal where he obtained this information. Perhaps he inferred it from the fact that, after carrying out his mission, Orosius was sent by Augustine to Jerusalem to Saint Jerome, and that he was present there when the relics of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr were revealed to the presbyter Lucian. He afterward brought a substantial portion of them to the West, the first to do so. This is known not only from Augustine’s Sermon 32 *On Various Matters*, but also from the testimony of Marcellinus Comes in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 416.

If the discovery occurred in the preceding year, as Marcellinus writes, and as is clear both from Lucian’s own letter and from the *Fasti* of Idatius of Lamacum, it would seem to follow that Orosius’s mission to Augustine took place one year before the discovery of the relics—namely, in 414.

But by which bishops was he sent? Baronius says that he was sent by Eutropius and Paulus, since these men are named in the memorandum, or consultation, concerning Orosius’s mission. Dexter maintains that he was sent by Heros, Prudentius, and Lazarus.

There appears to be no less disagreement concerning the purpose of the mission. Baronius asserts that Orosius went to Augustine to consult him concerning the errors of the Priscillianists and Origenists. Dexter, however, says that Orosius went to the African bishops assembled for a general council, carrying letters from Heros and his associates, and that he brought with him the canons of the Council of Caesaraugusta held some time earlier, in order to have them approved by the African Fathers.

Nevertheless, if the matter itself is subjected to rigorous examination, we shall find nothing in Dexter’s writing that departs from the truth.

In this year Orosius was twenty-five or twenty-six years old, since he had been born—as we saw above—in the year of the Lord 375. The statement in the Caesaraugusta manuscript that he was born in 382 or 384 was a copyist’s error, which I corrected from another manuscript. He had also been ordained a presbyter in the prime of his youth.

Saint Augustine certainly recognized Orosius as a young presbyter, for in Letter 102 he says:

> On the occasion of a certain most devoted young presbyter, Orosius, who came to us from the farthest part of Spain, inflamed solely by zeal for the holy Scriptures, etc.

Nor is it surprising that Orosius is said to have gone to Africa in the twenty-fifth year of his life, in the very flower of youth—namely, in the year of Christ 400. He was not sent as a council father, but rather acted as an intermediary. Perhaps, using his youth as an excuse, he resisted for some time. But the bishops of Spain, delighted by the capacity of his intellect, wished him to become a disciple of the great Augustine, and they compelled the young man. At length, attracted by the desire to hear so great a teacher, he went to him.

This can certainly be learned from the words that Orosius himself writes in the aforementioned consultation:

> “I have been sent to you,” he says to Augustine, “by God; concerning you I hope through him. When I consider how it came about that I should come here, I understand why I came. Without my will, without necessity, without consent, I left my homeland, driven by a certain hidden force, until I was brought to the shore of this land. At last I came to my senses and understood that I had been commanded to come to you.”

Once Orosius had been placed under Augustine’s instruction, there is no reason to suppose that he was weaned from the rich nourishment of that teaching in that same year or the next and sent off to the East. On the contrary, it is consistent with reason to judge that he spent several years with Augustine, devoting himself to literary studies, and that, having advanced in them, he finally went to Jerome at the time when the relics of the holy Protomartyr were discovered.

It also follows that Orosius did not return to Spain until many years later. Yet if he had gone to Africa chiefly to obtain a written answer to the questions he had brought, and not to pursue his studies, he ought to have returned immediately after receiving Augustine’s reply.

Another indication is that, as soon as he arrived there, he did not obtain Augustine’s response to the questions of the Priscillianists and Origenists. Some time passed before he did so, evidently because Augustine had first to be freed from other obligations of dictation. Orosius himself says this at the beginning of the aforementioned consultation:

> To the most blessed Father Augustine, bishop, from Orosius. I had already made a suggestion to Your Holiness, but I was planning to present the memorandum concerning the matter suggested when I perceived that you had been completely freed from the other demands of dictation, etc.

Finally, the very subject of the errors of Priscillian—which was also the reason Orosius was sent by the Spanish bishops—sufficiently proves that Orosius was sent to Africa before the year of the Lord 405. Augustine’s judgment and that of the African Fathers were sought so that, after seeing them, the Priscillianists might come to their senses. Yet in that very year they were convicted and confessed, and were admitted to peace at a council of nineteen bishops held at Toledo. We shall discuss it in its proper place. Their errors then fell silent until the year of Christ 418, when they began to sprout again; through the efforts of Saint Turibius of Astorga, they finally disappeared at the Council of Toledo in the year of the Lord 448.

It is therefore clear that Orosius migrated to Africa long before the year 414, as some believe—indeed, before 405. It is especially consistent with reason to accept Dexter’s opinion, according to which he was sent in the year 400, after the Priscillianists had been condemned at the Council of Caesaraugusta. Orosius is said to have carried away its eight canons.

Nor can the claim stand that he was sent by the bishops Eutropius and Paulus. Orosius himself—the only witness through whom we know of those men—does not say that they directed him to Augustine. Rather, he says that, after he himself had spent some time with Augustine, they sent their letters to Augustine about the same matter, though by a completely different route. When Orosius learned this, he himself hastened to bring the business to completion.

Here are Orosius’s own words:

> I had already made a suggestion to Your Holiness, but I was planning to present the memorandum concerning the matter suggested when I perceived that you had been completely freed from the other demands of dictation. But since my lords, your sons, the bishops Eutropius and Paulus, moved by the same concern for the salvation of all as your young servant, have already submitted a memorandum concerning certain heresies, etc.

You see, reader, that Paulus and Eutropius did not send Orosius to Augustine. They dealt with Augustine concerning the same matter through another intermediary, which is something quite different.

There therefore remains room for Dexter’s assertion that Orosius was sent by the bishops Heros—or Herotes, as others call him—Lazarus, and Prudentius. This is so true that the Council of Carthage itself expressed it in precise words in its letter to Pope Innocent, whose words we shall soon quote.

Heros and Lazarus are prominently mentioned by Zosimus, the Roman pontiff, in letters that Baronius transcribed in Volume V of the *Annals* from a manuscript of the Vatican Library. Prosper of Aquitaine also records the matter in his *Chronicle*. From these sources it is clear that Heros and Lazarus pursued the heretic Coelestius with great zeal, and that for this reason they were deceitfully misrepresented by Coelestius before Zosimus. At Coelestius’s persuasion, the pontiff believed serious charges against both men.

Thus, in his first letter to Aurelius and the bishops of Africa, Zosimus wrote:

> With regard to the letter of Heros and Lazarus, submitted in their earlier report—for they had written to the Africans against Pelagius and Coelestius—it is certainly most evident that this matter was hastened with the fervor of faith and the utmost readiness.

Further on he says:

> When he was questioned about them, he stated that he had known Lazarus only in passing, but that Heros, after offering satisfaction for having thought differently concerning an unknown and absent man, had departed with gratitude . . . . . It became clear that these men, despite the established orders and in opposition from the people and clergy, had claimed priestly offices within Gaul as unknown foreigners. They themselves renounced these offices by their own judgment, and we, although we followed also their subsequent repentance, removed them from priestly rank and office.

In the later letter he says:

> Lazarus has an old habit of accusing innocence through many councils. He was found to be a diabolical accuser of our fellow bishop Britius of the city of Tours. At a synod at Turin he received the sentence of a calumniator from Proculus of Marseilles. Through that same Proculus he was made a priest for many years by a tyrannical judgment and defender of the city of Aix. When affliction opposed him and penetrated his vulnerable condition, he broke into the priestly throne, almost sprinkling it with the blood of an innocent man. There the shadow of priesthood remained over him until the image of imperial power remained with the tyrant. After the destruction of his patron, he voluntarily stripped himself of that office and condemned himself by his own withdrawal.
>
> Everything concerning Heros was similar: the same tyrant, the patron of slaughter, the crowd of opposing presbyters, chains and imprisonment, and the subjection of the entire city; and a similar punishment through renunciation of the priesthood.

But that all these matters were brought before the Roman pontiff in a highly distorted form is sufficiently proved by the fact that the letters themselves were written in defense of the heretics Pelagius and Coelestius. Whatever they maliciously suggested against the Catholic bishops is contained in those letters.

If a Catholic writer is to be trusted, Prosper writes the following about Heros in his *Chronicle*:

> Heros, a holy man and disciple of the blessed Martin, was presiding as bishop over the town of Arles when he was driven out by the people of that city, though innocent and guilty of no accusation. In his place Patroclus was ordained, a friend and associate of Constantius, the master of the soldiers, whose favor was being sought through him. This matter became the cause of great discord among the bishops of that region.

There is no doubt that the same thing happened to Lazarus, since Coelestius told Zosimus the same story about both men.

After resigning their sees, they departed from Aquitaine into the neighboring province of Catalonia. There Heros was elected to the see of Dertosa and Lazarus to that of Vich, as Dexter writes. The letter of the Council of Carthage to Pope Innocent also establishes that they were bishops in Spain, as I shall now explain.

In any event, I believe they had not yet come to Spain in this year 400. When Dexter calls them bishops of Dertosa and Vich, he is referring to the time at which he himself wrote his *Chronicle*, not to the year of Orosius’s mission. Thus the words “Heros, I say, of Dertosa,” etc., convey this material sense: “Heros, I say, who is now bishop of Dertosa,” etc.

I have nothing further to say concerning Prudentius, except that he was bishop of Ilerda, as Dexter writes.

Thus those who later pursued Pelagius and Coelestius with the greatest severity had earlier also attacked the Priscillianists and Origenists fiercely.

The letters written against Pelagius and Coelestius by Heros and Lazarus, and delivered by Orosius to the African bishops, are mentioned in the letter of the Council of Carthage to Pope Innocent, which is numbered 90 among Augustine’s letters. It says:

> When, according to custom, we had solemnly come to the Church of Carthage, and a synod had been assembled from among us concerning various matters, our fellow presbyter Orosius gave us a letter from our holy brothers and fellow priests Heros and Lazarus. We have determined that its text should be appended here, etc.

But the letters themselves have perished.

As for the Origenists, Orosius reports in his consultation that two Tarraconensian men named Avitus, driven from their homeland, brought certain errors back into it: one, a follower of Victorinus, had gone to Rome; the other, a follower of Origen, to Jerusalem. The latter carried with him Origen’s books *Periarchon* (*On First Principles*) and preached the errors with which they abound. Among other things, he taught that the Word of the Father had successively assumed the natures of all the orders of angelic rulers into his hypostasis, and finally the human nature.

A certain holy Basil, a Greek—as Orosius himself calls him—had come to Spain with these men, teaching the same doctrines repeatedly, although it is unknown who he was.

That all of them, however, were refuted by the writings of Saint Augustine and abandoned their undertakings is sufficiently clear from the fact that Dexter later mentions them with honor and praise under the year of the Lord 429. It is also shown by the fact that no memory of such errors occurs in any Spanish council of this period.

Another Avitus, also a Spanish presbyter, was different from these men. He was present at Jerusalem when the relics of Saint Stephen were revealed, translated Lucian’s letter from Greek into Latin, and gave it to Orosius to carry to the West together with the relics.

The difference is indicated first by the difference of homeland. The two former men were from Tarraco, according to the testimony of Orosius and Dexter; this Avitus was Lusitanian, as Idatius expressly writes in the *Fasti* under the consulship of Honorius X and Theodosius the Younger VI:

> From these proceedings there remain, he says, letters of the aforementioned presbyter Lucian and of Saint Avitus, presbyter of Braga, who were then living at Jerusalem.

Thus Avitus dedicated his translation to Balconius, bishop of Braga, who is mentioned in the acts of the First Council of Toledo and likewise of the First Council of Braga.

The difference is also shown by the time and place. When the relics were discovered, this Avitus was present, whereas the others who had brought the *Periarchon* from there to Spain had returned several years earlier.]

A.D. 400. A.R. 1151. During this pontificate a certain synod was assembled at Toledo.

A.D. 400. A.R. 1151. Paul Orosius, having received letters from the bishops Heros, Prudentius, and Lazarus—Heros, I say, of Dertosa; Prudentius of Ilerda; and Lazarus of Vich—hurried to the African bishops assembled for a certain general council, bringing with him the canons collected from the Council of Toledo held some time earlier.

[Col. 0539] [Note: [Col. 0539B]

### A.D. 401. “Innocent,” etc.

Not everyone agrees on the year of Innocent’s election. Idatius assigns it to the eighth year of Arcadius and Honorius, which was the year of Christ 403. Marcellinus and the others assign it to the consulship of Arcadius V and Honorius V, whom Baronius follows. That is the year of the Lord 402. Dexter alone, among those I have seen, reports that he was elected in the year of the Lord 401, from the founding of the City 1152.

The opinion of Marcellinus has prevailed among authors. But since Dexter wrote during those very days and is older than all the others, he seems worthy of being heard above them all.

Jerome mourns the death of Pope Anastasius in Letter 16 to Principia. From this the Roman Martyrology took the following words for April 27:

> He was not permitted to remain long in Rome, lest the head of the world be mutilated under such a bishop.

For not long after his death Rome was captured by the Goths: in the year 410, namely, under Varane and Tertullus as sole consul, according to Marcellinus; or in the following year, according to Idatius in his *Chronicle*.

] A.D. 401. A.R. 1152. Innocent I, of this name, succeeded Anastasius.

[Note: [Col. 0539C]

### A.D. 405. “Stilicho,” etc.

The memory of this council must be sought in the letter of Saint Innocent I, Roman Pontiff. From it we learn that, after some time had passed in his pontificate during which he had delayed writing, he wrote to all the bishops assembled in the Council of Toledo. Since he was elected in the year 401 or 402, it follows that the letter was sent in 405 or approximately then. He says:

> Innocent sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops assembled in the Council of Toledo, his most beloved brothers. Often, and excessively, while anxiety kept me troubled concerning the schism of division among the churches—a calamity which rumor reports to be advancing more broadly through Spain each day by degrees of separation—the necessary time has arisen when so great a correction can no longer be delayed, etc.

All writers affirm that this occurred in the year 405, the second consulship of Stilicho, which he held with Flavius Anthemius. Perhaps for this reason the acts of this council were confused with those of the preceding Council of Toledo, since both were held while Stilicho was consul.

I make no distinction concerning the number of the consulship, since it is certain that Stilicho’s first consulship fell in the year of the Lord 400 and his second in 405, as Idatius, Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, and the others testify.

Moreover, the surviving subscriptions of nineteen bishops prove that this council necessarily belonged to this year, since Paternus—namely, the bishop of Braga—subscribes first of all, because he served as its president. Yet in the preceding council of the year 400 he had temporarily received a sentence of light condemnation.

We discussed this matter, and the other matters relating to this council, above under the year of the Lord 386.

Saint Asturius, bishop of Toledo and bishop of the principal see, attended together with the others. So did Marcellus of Coria, according to Dexter’s opinion under the year 424, although in the manuscript of Saint Michael’s he is called bishop of Seville, as in Loaysa; Severus of Lamacum, or Malaca, whom we already discussed under the year 388; Olympius, the second of that name among the bishops of Toledo, who later succeeded Saint Asturius in 424, but at this time was bishop of another see; Saint Hilary of Arles, as I believe, who flourished in Aquitaine in these days; Ortigius, bishop of Caelenis in Galicia, who had been absolved in the preceding Council of Toledo and restored to his see; Lampadius of Barcelona, who had honored Saint Paulinus with the priesthood; Saint Exuperantius, bishop of Ravenna, about whom much has been said above; and Leonas, bishop of Lugo, as the ancient subscriptions report.

I was unable to discover the sees of the others: Aphrodisius, Licinianus, Leporius, Jucundus, Lampadius, Serenus, Florus, Statius, and Aurelianus.

] A.D. 405. A.R. 1156. In the second consulship of Stilicho and the consulship of Flavius Anthemius, a council was convened at Toledo, and Saint Innocent wrote to the Fathers gathered in this council.

[Note: [Col. 0540B]

A.D. 406.—1. Leporius, etc. It is not universally agreed who this Leporius was, for some maintain that two men of this name existed at this time: one from the household of Saint Augustine, whom Augustine himself mentions in Sermon 50, *On Various Subjects*; [Col. 0540C] the other, infected with the corruption of Pelagius and opposed to the grace of God, disseminated a perverse doctrine in Gaul but, admonished by Augustine, recanted in a *palinode*. Gennadius discusses him in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 59, and Cassian in *On the Incarnation*, books I and VII. They add that he is wrongly called bishop of Utica in Spain, since Utica is in Africa, not Spain, and that Leporius was not a Spaniard but a Gaul or Briton, as Pitsaeus argues in *On English Writers*.

I excuse Cardinal Baronius, who lacked Dexter, but I am astonished at those who, having seen Dexter, still resist him. For since he explicitly asserts that the man who changed his opinion and was restored to sound judgment was a monk from Augustine’s household and had Augustine himself as his teacher, there is no basis on which one can distinguish one from the other; moreover, none of the ancients mentions two men of this name practicing monasticism under Augustine’s direction. Someone might perhaps object that the distinction can be inferred from their ages: when one changed his opinion in mature age, the other had not yet passed beyond the years of youth. For Augustine, his hair already sprinkled with gray, reports that he received Leporius into the monastery; and this seems to have occurred after the other’s lapse, preaching of error, and eventual recantation, following many years of monastic life.

Yet this is mistaken, for none of these things is established by the authors’ writings. But let us grant that Augustine wrote that Sermon 50 when his hair was sprinkled with gray, since he says in it: “I whom, by God’s favor, you see as your bishop came as a young man to this city, etc.,” [Col. 0540D] and, “These gray hairs are not fitting,” etc. Even so, he does not present Leporius’s conversion and the beginning of his monastic life as recent or as having occurred in those very days, but as something that had taken place many years earlier. Here are his own words:

“There was a certain Leporius, distinguished by secular nobility and exceedingly wealthy, comparable in many respects to Pinianus. Wishing to abandon all his possessions and, poor among Christ’s poor, to serve God with Augustine’s brothers, Augustine did not receive him until he had distributed all his goods and had seen him reduced to complete poverty. He had also suggested to him that he should establish from his wealth a monastery, as well as a hospice and a basilica of the Martyrs.”

Does not the expression “There was a certain Leporius” use the past tense and indicate an event that had occurred many years earlier? Leporius, therefore, could have done many things by the time Augustine’s hair was gray. Indeed, the manner of speaking indicates someone absent, as Leporius was when he had spent some time in Gaul.

“But,” someone says, “in that sermon Augustine praises him, and he would not praise a heretic.”

I agree—but for how long had he been immersed in error? And once he had been restored to sound judgment [Col. 0541A] and was presenting himself as an example of repentance, why, I ask, should he not have been praised? Especially since Augustine is speaking there only of his conversion from secular life to the monastic life, which had undoubtedly been exemplary; his lapse had nothing to do with the purpose of that sermon.

The statement added about his bishopric at Utica arises from ignorance of the topography of ancient Spain. For the testimony of Appian of Alexandria establishes that there was a city of Utica in Spain, from which Viriathus once drove out the Roman garrisons after he himself had withdrawn, defeated by Quintus Pompeius. The order of the narrative also proves that Utica was a city of Baetica, for he places it between Ebora in Lusitania and the peoples of Tarraconensian Spain, precisely where the more northerly region of Baetica lies, as we see in the maps of Ptolemy. See also Ambrosius Morales, *On the Antiquities of Spain*, book VII, chapter 49, concerning this Utica, and what we noted under the year of Christ 66.

I care nothing about Leporius’s homeland, although I believe him to have been an African, on Augustine’s testimony, provided that he was a bishop in Spain. [Col. 0541B]

What Dexter asserts—that Leporius, a bishop, changed his lost or erroneous opinion—seems somewhat more difficult. For Gennadius and Cassian say that he fell before the priesthood. “Leporius,” says Gennadius, “while still a monk and afterward a priest, presuming upon the purity of his life, which he believed he had obtained solely by his own judgment and effort, rather than through God’s assistance, began to follow the Pelagian doctrine. But, admonished by the Gallic teachers and corrected by God in Africa through Augustine, he wrote a little book about his correction,” and so forth.

Cassian, however, says:

“Leporius, then a monk and now a priest, who, proceeding from the teaching—or rather the depravity—of Pelagius” (in respect of the error, not of monastic discipline, as someone told me, since this would make Leporius a monk not of Augustine but of Pelagius), “was among the first, or among the chief, defenders of that heresy in Gaul. Admonished by us and corrected by God” (through Augustine), “he condemned his badly conceived conviction so magnificently that his correction is scarcely less admirable than the unshaken faith of many others. Thus, having come to his senses, where he then was and now is, he confessed his error both with sorrow and without shame; he also sent letters of confession and lamentation to all the cities of Gaul,” and so forth.

These letters are extant in Baronius, volume V, under the year of the Lord 420; they begin: “What should I say first about myself, O my revered lords?” etc.

Since, therefore, he fell and was corrected before becoming a priest, how can Dexter call him a bishop? Certainly the words “Bishop of Utica” are written appositionally, so that the meaning is: Leporius, who at the time of this writing is now bishop of Utica, formerly a monk from the household of Saint Augustine, etc. Nor is this different from what Cassian said of him—“then a monk, now a priest”—or from Gennadius—“still a monk, afterward a priest.” For the man who, after his lapse, deserved to be ordained a priest was afterward also judged worthy to rise to the episcopate. [Col. 0541C]

Hence it undoubtedly follows that he is a different person from the bishop Leporius who subscribed to the council called the First Council of Toledo in the year of the Lord 405, since the man under discussion had not yet been ordained at that time. Unless someone wishes to say that Dexter assigned the whole of this account to this year because he did not know the true date of Leporius’s correction; yet it is clear from the subscriptions mentioned above that it occurred before the council.

I should also note that Cassian’s words, “He was among the first defenders of that heresy,” were spoken especially with reference to the period in which he preached Pelagius’s error before others. For when Leporius himself fell and was corrected, Pelagius had not yet been condemned in any council. He was first condemned in the year of the Lord 416, when Orosius took part in the councils of Milevis and Carthage under Bishop Silvanus. Leporius was therefore more readily corrected through Augustine, his teacher, and, as appears, had not been obstinate.

Some people still cannot accept that Leporius is called a monk from the household of Saint Augustine, because they refuse to admit that Augustine instituted monasticism and will allow only regular canons. No one should doubt that this is said for the sake of controversy, not truth. For nothing is equally clear from the writings of the most holy Doctor as that he himself was a monk and an institutor of monks.

This is shown by the objection made to him by Petilianus, the insolent leader of the Donatists, who knew Augustine well in Africa. Augustine himself reports it in book III of *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, chapter 40, saying:

“Next, with his accursed mouth he proceeded to denounce monasteries and monks, accusing me also of having instituted this form of life. He does not know at all what this way of life is, or rather, although it is known throughout the whole world, he pretended that he did not know it.”

Petilianus therefore objected to Augustine that he was the institutor of monks. Yet when the holy Doctor answers him, he does not deny that he was a monk and the father of monks; he denies only that he should be called the new inventor or institutor of monasticism, [Col. 0541D] since this way of life was already known throughout the whole world—something Petilianus either did not know or pretended not to know.

Augustine himself expressly acknowledges this, both in other places and especially in his exposition of Psalm 132, “Behold, how good,” etc., where he says:

“What then do those people say who insult us on account of the name of monks?”

Although Augustine was not the first inventor of monasticism in the world, he was nevertheless the first to introduce it into Africa, as can be established from various writings of Augustine. Among others, Cardinal Baronius has demonstrated this learnedly in volume IV of his *Annals*, under the year of the Lord 391, saying:

“Saint Augustine was the first to introduce the institutions of the monastic life into Africa; he himself began to observe them and handed them on to others for observance. Hence it happened that the Donatists thought that this kind of life had been devised by him.”

Indeed, we learn from Augustine himself, *Retractations*, book II, chapter 21, that monasteries began to exist at Carthage in his own time, as though previously there had been no monastery there; this was when he wrote his work *On the Work of Monks*.

Moreover, from the letters sent by Saint Paulinus to Alypius—extant among Augustine’s letters as number 35—it is clear that the monastic life in Africa, which Augustine had first brought there from Italy when he returned to his native land, had already been spread far and wide by fruitful propagation within only six years, the period between Augustine’s arrival in Africa and the date of the aforementioned letter. Among other things, Paulinus addresses Alypius as follows:

“We earnestly and dutifully ask that you greet, if they are willing, the blessed companions and imitators of your holiness in the Lord—our brothers—serving the Lord in Catholic devotion, both in the churches and in the monasteries at Carthage, Tagaste, Hippo Regius, and throughout all your parishes and all the places in Africa known to you,” etc.

The same is evident from Possidius, *Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 11. “Thus,” says Baronius, “you can clearly see that from one monastery of Augustine the entire Catholic Church of Africa was filled, within a short time, with monasteries deriving from that one.” [Col. 0542A]

What caused Augustine to begin establishing regular canons, however, he himself explains clearly in Sermon 1, *On the Common Life of Clerics*: namely, that when he became a bishop, so that he could attend to his episcopal office and receive visiting guests with courtesy—as was then expected of bishops—he could no longer live in the monastery in the wilderness with the monks as before. Therefore, gathering together the clerics who had previously lived within the city walls for the service of the altar, he established a monastery of clerics.

These clerics differed from monks only in that they were assigned to the altar and lived within the city, whereas monks lived in the countryside and had not been ordained to sacred orders. Nevertheless, when necessary, clerics were made from among the monks, and those whom Augustine had tested in the monastery of monks he afterward brought into the city, from where they were often promoted to the episcopate.

These points are certain to me from the writings of the holy Doctor, especially from the following words:

“I came to the episcopate. I saw that a bishop necessarily had to show continual kindness to all who came or passed through; if I did not do this, I would be called an inhuman bishop. But if this custom were permitted in the monastery”—that is, the monastery of monks—“it would be improper”—that is, it would not suit monastic quiet. “Therefore I wished to have in this episcopal house a monastery of clerics with me.”

Here he makes clear the true reason for founding regular clerics. But since many people have written many things about this matter, and the controversy has been vigorously disputed on both sides, I have decided to add nothing further, since what has already been said is sufficient for my purpose, lest anyone despise the monastic life of Leporius under Augustine’s discipline, as Dexter asserts.

2. Ilorci, etc. Today it is called Lorca, as Morales demonstrated at length in *Spanish Antiquities*, under the word “Ilorci,” folio 81; and that the river Tader, or Staber, flows past it is shown by Pliny, book III, chapters 1 and 3.

As for Saint Victoria, who is discussed here, I believe her to be the one whose remains rest at Burgos in Spain and who is honored throughout the entire archbishopric with a double office on 10 November, as can be seen in the calendar of the diocese of Burgos.

For the belief of Mariana and others that she was a companion of Saint Ursula and her eleven thousand companions, and the daughter of the king of Sicily by Saint Gerasina, killed together with them, is not probable. How could the daughter of a Sicilian king and her mother, the queen, have been joined with Ursula the Briton and crowned at Cologne on the Rhine in Germany?

It is true that Saint Ursula was struck down by the Huns at that same time or shortly before. Victoria, however, was not killed by the Huns but by the Vandals, who, not long after those days, afflicted Baetica in Spain and its neighboring regions, where Ilorci lies, slaughtering many Christians.

It is also established from Dexter that she was not a virgin but a widow, and that before receiving the crown of martyrdom she had flourished in exceptional holiness.

A.D. 406. A.R. 1157. Bishop Leporius of Utica in Baetica, formerly a monk from the household of Saint Augustine, changes his former erroneous opinion after being admonished by Saint Augustine, his teacher.

[Col. 0543] A.D. 406. A.R. 1157. At Ilorci in Tarraconensian Spain, Saint Victoria, a widow distinguished for exceptional holiness, is struck down by the Vandals, as is believed.

[Note: [Col. 0544A]]

A.D. 407.—1. Asturius, etc. At the time when Flavius Maximus ruled in Spain and Gaul, Saint Audentius governed the see of Toledo. Saint Asturius, surnamed Serranus, was his contemporary and friend, as is clear from what has been said and from the chronology explained by Dexter.

That Saint Gregory of Hiberrita was dear to Placidia Augusta, the daughter of Theodosius the Great, is proclaimed by the book *On Faith* written to her. Cardinal Baronius considers this Placidia Augusta to have been the sister of the emperor Theodosius, although Marcellinus and Hydatius, writers of that period, assert that she was not his sister but his daughter, as L. Dexter maintains.

In his account of the sack of the City by Alaric, king of the Goths, Hydatius writes under the year of the Lord 410, A.R. 448:

“Placidia, daughter of Theodosius and sister of the emperor Honorius, was captured by the Goths in the City.”

Under A.R. 453 he records her marriage to Ataulf, Alaric’s successor:

“Ataulf took Placidia as his wife at Narbonne; in this people thought Daniel’s prophecy had been fulfilled, which says: ‘The daughter of the king of the south shall be joined to the king of the north,’ although no offspring from her survived.”

We shall discuss this matter at the end of these commentaries. Again, after Ataulf was killed at Barcelona in the year of the Lord 416, Hydatius adds:

“Constantius took Placidia as his wife.”

Later he discusses the emperor Valentinian, the son of Constantius and Placidia, born to them in the year of the Lord 419; Constantius’s elevation to the imperial rank by Honorius in 420; his death the following year, in which his third consulship fell; and the death of Placidia Augusta in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of her son Valentinian, and in the year of Christ 451.

Marcellinus agrees with all this. He says that Alaric left the City after abducting Placidia, the sister of the emperor Honorius, whom he later gave in marriage to his kinsman Ataulf. Later, after Ataulf’s death, he says that Wallia, king of the Goths, having made peace with Honorius, gave his widowed sister Placidia to him. He also adds the other matters concerning Constantius and Valentinian, her husband and son, which we read in Hydatius.

In the year of the Lord 424, under the consuls Victor and Castinus, Placidia, the mother of Valentinian, was named Augusta. We shall show in its proper place, under the year of the Lord 423, that this is the same Placidia to whom Gregory’s book is dedicated. Orosius, book VII, Zosimus, book VI, and Paul the Deacon, book XIII, also discuss this Placidia.

2. Caesarobriga, etc. Ptolemy mentions Oliva in Vectonia, not far from Salamanca. It was formerly called Caesarobriga, and now, bearing the title of a county, it is subject to the wife and son of Don Rodrigo Calderón.

Enough has been said above about Juvencus, under the year of his death and of Christ our Lord 337. Dexter now discusses his reputation for learning and holiness.

3. Saint Paternus, etc. He was discussed at length above when the subject of the councils of Toledo arose, under the years of the Lord 386 and 405. Pancratianus succeeded him, as we shall soon say.

[Col. 0545A] 4. Exuperantius, etc. Much was said above about his deeds under the years 385 and 388; consult those passages. Rufinus, whom Dexter mentions, is the man referred to in the letter of Pope Saint Innocent to the Council of Toledo, where it is said:

“How many of those who, after receiving the grace of Baptism, engaged in forensic practice and adopted the stubbornness of pursuing their own interests have we found summoned to the priesthood? Among their number Rufinus and Gregory are reported.”

That he was a bishop in Spain is also established by the same letter.

A.D. 407. A.R. 1158. Asturius, bishop of Toledo, surnamed Serranos, was greatly loved by the emperor Flavius Maximus and was a friend of Saint Audentius. Gregory, also a Baetician, already advanced to extreme old age but still vigorous and possessing unimpaired powers of mind and body, was especially dear to Galla Placidia Augusta, first the wife of Ataulf, king of the Visigoths, and afterward of Constantius the emperor. She, the daughter of Theodosius the elder by his first wife, is magnificently praised.

A.D. 407. A.R. 1158. Juvencus spent several years at Caesarobriga, now called Oliva near Ambratia in Vectonia, and is said to have been born there. From there he went to Salamanca, where the distinguished memory of this learned and holy man flourishes greatly.

A.D. 407. A.R. 1158. Saint Paternus, bishop of Braga, who presided over the Council of Toledo of nineteen bishops, died troubled by many labors and illnesses. He was an exceptionally learned and devout man.

[Col. 0545] A.D. 407. A.R. 1158. Exuperantius, who came from the city of Ravenna to Spain on business and took part in the Council of Toledo, flourishes with distinction; and Rufinus, bishop of Tarragona, formerly an advocate.

[Note: [Col. 0545A]]

A.D. 417.—Paul Orosius, etc. The distinguished work of this great man is extant and is in everyone’s hands, together with the learned notes of Francis Fabricius of Marcodurum. He had returned from Palestine to Africa in the year of the Lord 416. At Diospolis he had seen Pelagius and Coelestius acquitted by bishops assembled in synod, as though they were free from every error which they had concealed by their lies. Having been encouraged by the zeal of the bishops Heros and Lazarus, whose recent letters he had received, he caused two African councils to be held, the Second Council of Milevis and the Council of Carthage, at which the aforementioned heretics were condemned, as Augustine records in Letter 90 and Baronius demonstrates learnedly.

Since at that time the Roman Empire was being weakened by the invasions of many barbarian nations—Alans, Goths, Sueves, and Vandals—and many Romans, lamenting the Roman name, asserted that the decline of the Roman state had been brought about by the Christian religion, Orosius, at Augustine’s urging, wrote seven books of universal history. In them, to use the words of Gennadius, “by recounting nearly all the calamities and miseries of the ages of the world and the disturbances of wars, he shows that it is more consistent with Christian observance that the Roman state should still endure despite its deserts and that, through the peace of the worship of God, the Empire should be kept at peace.”

He began writing in the second year after his return, namely in the year of Christ 417, as Dexter asserts, and completed the work three years later, in the year of Christ 419. For at the end of the seventh book he says:

“With Christ’s assistance, I have completed, according to your command, most blessed Father Augustine, from the beginning of the world to the present day—that is, through 5,618 years.”

Since he plainly follows the computation of the Septuagint translators, according to which Christ was born in the year 5,199 from the creation of the world, as the Roman Martyrology testifies, it follows that the year 5,618 from the creation of the world, in which Orosius’s *Hormesta* was completed, corresponds to the year 419 from the birth of Christ, as will be clear to anyone who makes the calculation.

Dexter therefore very correctly uses the word “begins” for the year of Christ 417, even though Marcellinus uses the word “wrote” without qualification when he says:

“Under the consuls Theodosius VII and Palladius, Orosius, a priest of Spanish origin, composed seven books of histories.”

Let us also add what Andreas Scotus thought about the title of the book, *Hormesta*, in a letter addressed to Peter Cholinus:

“Why was this history of Orosius formerly entitled *Ormesta*? In my judgment, through corruption and the fault of the barbarous age. The title should rather be *Orchestra of the World*, as the most learned Pighius first saw in his *Hercules Prodicius*. Was it because it represents, as it were, a theater of historical events? Or because it begins with a description of the world? Lipsius explains what an orchestra is in his *Amphitheatre*, chapter 14, and Julius Pollux in his *Onomasticon*, book IV, chapter 19.”

Certainly Trithemius, in *On Illustrious Men*, under Orosius, reads *Hormesta of the World*, just as Dexter does here.

At this point I should note that one of those who lamented the Christian name and attributed the fall of the Roman Empire to the change of religion was Symmachus, prefect of the City. He presented a report to the emperors Valentinian I, Theodosius I, and Arcadius in defense of the ancient worship of the gods and against the Christians. Prudentius nevertheless attacked him with all his strength in two published books of poems and answered his objections learnedly and subtly in book II, where, among other things, he introduces Rome, by personification, speaking thus to her citizens:

> “I live piously because of you, though formerly, I confess,  
> I lived by the impious worship of Jupiter. For what bloody thing  
> Did he not hand down, or what gentle and peaceful thing  
> Did he demand for himself?  
> While he feared that the worship of Christ would grow bold,  
> He raged and stained the wretched age with blood.  
>   
> Yet some do not hesitate to reproach you  
> With these ill-omened wars, after we rejected  
> The altars of the temples. They assert that the Libyan Hannibal  
> Was driven back from the threshold of the Colline Gate by Jupiter’s command and Mars’s,  
> And that the victorious Senones were driven from the citadel of the Capitol,  
> While the gods fought upon the lofty rock.  
>   
> Let those who thrust upon me once more  
> My former disaster and ancient sufferings  
> Look upon me in your age. Now no barbarian enemy  
> Strikes my gates with a spear,” etc.

The verses that follow celebrate Stilicho’s victory, obtained under Christ’s leadership, over Radagaisus and two hundred thousand Scythians or Getae, who in the year of Christ 406, under the sixth consulship of Arcadius and the consulship of Probus, had flooded all Italy, as Marcellinus records in his *Chronicle*.

I have introduced this material to show that Prudentius dealt with the same subject ten years before Orosius. He wrote after Radagaisus had been overthrown and before Alaric destroyed the City and before the Alans, Vandals, and Sueves invaded the Roman provinces of Gaul and Spain, as those words indicate: “No barbarian enemy strikes my gates with a spear.”

According to Marcellinus, Radagaisus was defeated in the year of the Lord 406, and the City was destroyed in 410, under the sole consulship of Varane. The barbarians entered Spain, according to the eyewitness testimony of Hydatius, in the year 447 of Caesar, that is, in the year of Christ 409.

Indeed, as Marcellinus says, in the year of Christ 408, under the consuls Bassus and Philippus, Stilicho—whose two daughters, Maria and Thermantia, were each married to Honorius, although both died virgins—despised Honorius and, desiring his kingdom, incited the peoples of the Alans, Sueves, and Vandals against the emperor by means of gifts and money, because he wanted to appoint his own son Eucherius, a pagan who was plotting against the Christians, as Caesar. Yet Stilicho was killed together with Eucherius when his treachery was discovered.

If, I say, these events truly occurred in the year mentioned, Prudentius must have written against Symmachus in the preceding year, namely 407, for that year lies between the slaughter of Radagaisus and Stilicho’s treason.

At the very least, Eucherius’s paganism seems suspicious to me. It is difficult to believe that Stilicho, by Serena, the sister of Theodosius the Great, had a pagan son, especially since Prudentius, in book II *Against the Pagan Symmachus*, extols Stilicho with great praise for his profession of the Catholic faith:

> “The leader of the army and of the Empire,  
> The Christ-bearing young man, was ours”—he is speaking of Honorius—“and his companion  
> And father was Stilicho. One God, Christ, belonged to both.  
> Worshiping his altars and with the cross  
> Inscribed upon their foreheads, the trumpets sounded;  
> The first spear of the dragon advanced before them,  
> Bearing aloft the emblem of Christ,” etc.

A.D. 417. A.R. 1168. Paul Orosius, son of Flavius Lucius Orosius, a relative of my father Pacianus and a citizen of Tarragona, begins with great distinction his *Hormesta*, that is, *Chronicle of the World*, which he undertook to write at the urging and letters of Saint Augustine, bishop.

[Col. 0547] [Note: [Col. 0547A]]

A.D. 418.—1. Paul, etc. So far I have been unable to find anything about this Paul of Massilia.

2. . . . etc. In some manuscripts words of this sort were inserted here:

“Emperor Avitus crossed into Spain and, having laid aside the dignity of the Empire, hurried by forced marches to Gaul.”

But these words have been transferred from elsewhere. Dexter could not have known Avitus as having been elevated to the Empire, since, according to Hydatius and Prosper Tiro in the *Chronicle*, he was raised to that position in the year of the Lord 455.

3. Heresy, etc. Perhaps those who had been removed from the priesthood and episcopate by the sword of the Council of Toledo were responsible for this: namely, Herena, Donatus, Acurius, and Emilius, or Emila. For they proclaimed that Priscillian had been unjustly killed and venerated him as a martyr, as is written in their own statement.

Severus, speaking of them, said: “The bodies of the slain were brought back to Spain, and their funerals were celebrated with great ceremonies.” Their madness, however, was finally quieted later, when Saint Turibius dealt with it in the year of the Lord 448, as is recorded in the council called the First Council of Braga.

[Col. 0547B] 4. Paul, etc. Jerome’s Letter 21 was written to him. Since Jerome himself says in it that he saw this Paul at Concordia in Italy, while elsewhere Dexter calls him a Lusitanian, and since there is another Concordia in Lusitania not far from Lisbon, the point we noted elsewhere arises again: when the Italians ruled Spain, they frequently gave cities newly founded by them there the names of their own cities.

It is therefore not surprising if the peoples of Concordia in Spain had relations with the people of Concordia in Italy and if passage from one to the other was easy. I believe this is what happened in Paul’s case: born at Concordia in Lusitania, he went to Concordia in Italy, where he was encountered by Saint Jerome, as is clear from Jerome’s book *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Tertullian.

Whoever does not approve this explanation may say that the coincidence happened by chance; I would not care. Or it may be said that he was indeed a Lusitanian but was called Concordian from the city whose parish he governed.

Jerome addressed Letter 21 of the first volume to him. Among other things he says:

“Behold, as the circle of a hundred years of age revolves, while you continually observe the Lord’s commandments and meditate upon the blessedness of the life to come through present examples, your eyes remain vigorous with pure light, your feet plant firm steps, your hearing is penetrating, your teeth are white, your voice sonorous, your body solid and full of vitality. Your gray hair is at odds with your strength; your powers disagree with your age. Neither does more advanced old age dissolve the tenacity of your memory, nor does cold blood blunt the sharpness of your warm intelligence; nor does a brow furrowed with wrinkles roughen your face; finally, your trembling hand does not guide the wandering stylus along the curved paths of the wax tablet,” etc., which you may read.

5. Constantius, etc. At the time when the Alans, Sueves, and Vandals invaded Spain, some of the Romans themselves rebelled in Gaul, especially Constantine with his son Constans. After seizing imperial power, Constantine made Constans Caesar, although Constans had formerly been a monk.

They were killed three years after the usurpation by Constantius, the general of Honorius, later Caesar, husband of Placidia and father of the younger Valentinian: Constantine at Arles and Constans at Vienne. Hydatius and Marcellinus record this under the consuls Honorius IX and Theodosius IV, in the year of Christ 411.

Again, according to Hydatius, in 416 Constantius drove Ataulf, king of the Goths, out so that he abandoned Narbonne and headed for Spain. After Ataulf was removed from the world, Wallia, his successor, made peace with the same Constantius.

In the following year, 417, Wallia, acting in the interests of the Roman name, inflicted an immense slaughter of barbarians within Spain. But in 418, when the conflict they had been waging had been interrupted, the Goths were recalled to Gaul by Constantius.

This is what Hydatius records. From it you can see that Constantius was in the regions of Spain in the year of the Lord 418, as Dexter writes, and consequently that he was plundering there.

A.D. 418. A.R. 1169. Paul, bishop of Massilia, is held in high renown.

A.D. 418. A.R. 1169. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

A.D. 418. A.R. 1169. The heresy of the Priscillianists grows vigorously again in Spain.

A.D. 418. A.R. 1169. Jerome writes to Paul of Concordia, a Lusitanian.

A.D. 418. A.R. 1169. Constantius plunders in the regions of Spain.

[Note: [Col. 0548A]]

A.D. 419.—1. Province, etc. Although no document survives concerning the separation of those churches into two provinces and metropolitan sees, a considerable memory of it remains in ancient records, by which it is sufficiently established that the division took place at approximately this time.

For in the year of the Lord 385, under the consuls Arcadius and Bauto, Siricius, Roman Pontiff, wrote a decretal letter to Himerius of Tarragona and to all the metropolitans of Spain. He names them individually, placing Carthaginensis first, then Baetica of Seville, and afterward Lusitania and Gallaecia—that is, Emerita and Braga—without mentioning Toledo or Carpetania. This was evidently because Carthaginensis included Toledo under its jurisdiction.

Moreover, in the council called the First Council of Toledo, it is said that a rule of faith was drawn up against all the heresies of Priscillian by the bishops of Carthaginensis, Tarragona, Lusitania, Baetica, and Gallaecia; and the same is afterward reported in the council called the First Council of Braga under Lucretius, bishop of Braga. There again Toledo is included under Carthaginensis.

This is not surprising, since, as is clear from the reorganization of the provincial sees carried out at Toledo under the emperor Constantine the Great, Carthaginensis was placed subject to Toledo. We discussed this in its proper place under the year 324.

It follows that this arrangement continued at least until the year 400 or 405, when the aforementioned rule was composed. Consequently, those are mistaken who think that the separation took place before the time of Saint Anterus, pope, who had died much earlier, in the year of the Lord 238.

Again, in the Chronicle of Maximus, under the year of the Lord 448, the provinces are found distinguished. It says there:

“The Alans, invading Carpetania and the province of Carthaginensis in Spain, occupy them after laying waste to many cities.”

In the council called the Third Council of Toledo, at which, under the leadership of Saint Leander of Seville, the Goths abandoned the Arian heresy, there subscribed Dominicus, metropolitan of Carthage Spartaria, and Epiphanius Helladius, metropolitan of Toledo. This occurred in the year of the Lord 390.

As for Saint Elpidius, the first bishop of Toledo, ordained by the holy apostle James, we have discussed him sufficiently elsewhere.

2. Saint Maxentia, etc. She is honorably mentioned in the martyrology of Galesinus on 30 April, in these words:

“In the territory of the people of Trent, Saint Maxentia, widow. She was the mother of Saint Vigilius, bishop, and shone forth with such exceptional piety and religious devotion that God wished to confirm the renown of her holiness through many miracles.”

In the notes he adds:

“Altemanius, bishop of Trent, wrote her life.”

The feast day of her son, Saint Vigilius, bishop and martyr, is celebrated on 26 June. At that time, while he was endeavoring to eradicate the remnants of idolatry completely, he was struck by savage and barbarous men with a shower of stones and fulfilled martyrdom in the name of Christ, as the Roman Martyrology, Usuard, and Ado record.

### 3. Canali, etc.

That there were very numerous communities of monks in Spain at this period is sufficiently clear from the records of councils and the letters of the supreme pontiffs. For in the Council of Saragossa of the year 384—or, as others prefer, 380—the sixth and eighth canons deal with monks, and in the First Council of Toledo the sixth canon concerns nuns. Siricius, likewise, the Roman pontiff, in his letter to Himerius of Tarragona and to all the bishops of Spain—a letter divided into articles or responses—lays down several regulations concerning monks in the seventh and fourteenth responses.

I shall omit the holy monks and abbots Fabricianus and Philibertus, who built a monastery at Titultia, where the rivers Fenarius and Tagonius meet, and who, there taken up to heaven through martyrdom, flew forth in the year of the Lord 308, as we noted above together with Dexter.

We must now consider who these monks were who, to distinguish them from the others, were called “Black,” and who were introduced into Spain from the year of the Lord 393. It is certain that they were in no way followers of the discipline of Saint Benedict, since he was born several years later. Moreover, among the ancient monks no mention is found of the color of their habit. Indeed, Benedict himself, who wrote their Rule and imitated the customs of the ancient Fathers, says this when discussing clothing in chapter 55:

> Let monks not complain about the color or coarseness of such things, but use whatever can be found in the province where they live, or whatever can be bought more cheaply.

They therefore did not all go about dressed in one and the same color, even within a single monastery, but in different colors, according to what they could buy most cheaply. I understand this, however, to refer to the natural colors of wool—such as brown, ash-colored, black, nearly black, or reddish-brown—for artificial colors were by no means permitted to them.

Indeed, that white was not used among them was expressly asserted by Peter the Venerable in Book I, Letter 28, where he reproves the Cistercians for using white, contrary to the custom of all monks. He says:

> You make yourselves saints, exceptional men, truly monks throughout the whole world, while all the others are false and corrupt according to the meaning of the name; you alone distinguish yourselves from all others. Hence you display a habit of unusual color and, to distinguish yourselves from the monks of almost the entire world, show yourselves white among the black.

And further:

> You reject the color more suited to humility and abasement, and assume the color by which joy and solemnity are represented even in Scripture—namely, white. Since you are placed in the valley of tears, commanded to devote yourselves always to mourning and never to joy, garments signifying mourning and penitence ought to suit you. Yet, on the contrary, you display happiness amid misery, joy amid sorrow, delight amid mourning, and gladness in the whiteness of your clothing.

Whatever may be said about the contentious spirit that induced the Venerable Peter to write this—something I am not concerned with here—we nevertheless learn from his testimony that the color white was far removed from the ancient monks. For Metaphrastes, in the Life of Saints Galation and Episteme, also tells of a certain old monk named Honofrius who covered his monastic habit with a white garment so that he would not be recognized.

Likewise, in the Life of Saint Martin, we read that Anatolius, one of his disciples, deceived by an angel of Satan, said one day to the other monks:

> Behold, this night an angel brought me a white garment from heaven. Clothed in it, I shall move about among you, and this will be a sign to you that I am endowed with God’s power, since I have been given God’s garment.

If white clothing had been customary among monks, such a garment could not have served as a distinguishing sign.

Regarding the color black, the following is especially persuasive: the aforementioned Peter of Cluny asserts that, as far as he knew, Saint Martin was the first of all monks to use it. It follows, he says, that his monks also adopted it:

> Certainly, this blackness of clothing was devised by the Fathers in ancient times for the sake of humility. For of that great and admirable, truly monastic Martin, it is not written that he went forth in a white and short cloak, but in a black and flowing mantle.

Severus reports the same in Dialogue 2:

> But when the beasts of burden saw Martin close beside them, covered in a rough garment and a black, flowing mantle, they retreated in fear a little to the other side.

The same author, in Martin’s Life, reports that Martin built very many monasteries, not only at Milan and Tours but also in other provinces, where great communities of monks lived according to his example. Concerning a certain woman whom he had converted to the faith, he says:

> She grew so strong through his virtues and example that there is now no place there which is not either extremely well supplied with churches or filled with monasteries.

The seeds of these institutions were therefore also planted in Spain, as is said here; and this is not surprising, since Spain lies not far from that region of Gaul inhabited by Saint Martin.

### A.D. 419. A.R. 1170

The province of Carthaginensis, which until then had been one province and had been subject to Toledo, was divided by Saint Elpidius, through the ambition of certain bishops, into Carthaginensis and Carpetania. Some think that this division had already taken place before the time of the Roman pontiff Anterus, and that the province was called Toletana.

### A.D. 419. A.R. 1170

Saint Maxentia of Spain, of Caurium, flourishes at Tridentum.

### A.D. 419. A.R. 1170

At Canali in Lusitania, Black monks, from the year 393 onward.

### Note

#### A.D. 423.—1. “He died,” etc.

We have said much about him under the years of the Lord 388 and 406; and his feast day is sufficiently celebrated in the martyrology of Usuard, which Galesinus follows in his own, on 24 April. A book *On the Faith* is extant in the volumes of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, and Jerome also mentions it in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

As for Augusta, to whom the book was dedicated, Paul the Deacon expressly teaches in Book XIII of *The Deeds of the Lombards*—in agreement with Dexter—that she was called not merely Placidia but Galla Placidia, although someone has denied this. Peter likewise, in Book XI, chapter 93 of his *Catalogue*, relates it as a certain and well-known fact that the surname Galla was added to Placidia from her mother Galla, the wife of Theodosius.

The title of the book, as found by Achille Statius in a very ancient manuscript, reads:

> Gregory of Baetica, bishop of the see of Iliberris, to Galla Placidia Augusta, a book on the Trinity and the Faith against the Arians.

Within the work she is treated as faithful and Catholic; this is less suitable to the earlier Galla, but most appropriate to the later one.

A clear indication of Gregory’s extreme old age is that Jerome wrote his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* in the fourteenth year of Theodosius—that is, in the year of Christ 393—and then said that Gregory, being in the final stage of old age, was still alive. Since he is now said to have died thirty years later, he must have died at almost a hundred years of age.

#### 2. “Vincentius,” etc.

This Valerius was the third bishop of Saragossa of that name. The first had subscribed at Iliberris, the second at Saragossa. This one, however, is called Valerianus by others: so he is called by Dexter himself below, under the year of the Lord 430, and by Aurelius Prudentius, who dedicated his *Hippolytus* to him under the title *The Passion of the Martyr Hippolytus, to Valerianus the Bishop*. It begins with these words:

> We saw countless ashes of saints in the city of Romulus,  
> O Valerianus, sacred to Christ, etc.

When Prudentius had returned from Rome to Saragossa and had reverently visited Saint Hippolytus among the other relics of the saints, he conceived a special devotion toward him and wrote his martyrdom to his own bishop Valerianus, asking that it might be added:

> May this day also run for you  
> among the solemn days of Cyprian, or Chelidonius,  
> and of Eulalia.

That this Valerianus was Prudentius’s pastor and bishop is established by what he adds at the end of the work, among other prayers:

> Thus, when I remain at last upon the grassy field,  
> may you, as a diligent shepherd, bring back your sick sheep.

That Prudentius had this bishop in Spain after returning from Rome is also demonstrated by the fact that he wrote the book *Peristephanon* in Spain after his return. Thus, in the hymn on Saint Laurence, he says:

> The Iberian Basque country separates us,  
> kept apart by two Alpine ranges;  
> beyond the Cotian peaks,  
> beyond the snowy Pyrenees.  
>   
> Scarcely is the fame known, hidden away,  
> of how full of saints Rome is;  
> how richly the Urban soil  
> blooms with sacred tombs.

He had said the same in the poem on Hippolytus, for among other things he adds:

> But since we lack these blessings  
> and cannot behold before our eyes  
> the traces of blood,  
> we gaze at heaven from afar.

#### 3. “Theodosius,” etc.

Orosius narrates the death of Theodosius in Book VII, chapter 33; from him Cardinal Baronius derives his account, as do Paul the Deacon and others.

Valens had received a prediction concerning his successor: that his name would begin with the letters *Theo*. In order to thwart this prediction, he ordered many people to be killed whose names perhaps were Theophilus or Theodorus. Thus, driven by this madness, he arranged for the death of the exceptionally capable general Theodosius, born in Spain, who had stabilized the tottering affairs of the Empire in Africa after defeating the usurpers. He also arranged for the death of that man’s son, likewise named Theodosius.

The son whom God had destined for imperial rule fled. At that time still a catechumen, the elder man arranged to be baptized before he was killed. Having received the water of the sacred font and, at the same time, shed his blood, he was impiously and tyrannically slaughtered and departed to the Lord. Hence, as Dexter writes, he was later counted by some among the martyrs.

#### 4. “A great dispute,” etc.

By decree of the so-called First Council of Toledo, certain bishops from among the Priscillianists were deprived of their dignity, while others retained their dignity but were temporarily denied communion with the other bishops—namely, until communion should be granted to them by the pope or by Saint Simplicianus, as is stated there in the sentence issued against the Priscillianists. From this, without doubt, the dispute mentioned here arose.

#### 5. “He writes,” etc.

The book of *Allegories* mentioned here is extant among the works of Saint Isidore of Seville. From the catalogue of Isidore’s works compiled by his disciples Ildefonsus and Braulio, however, it is clear that this was the work of another Isidore, not Isidore of Seville.

Why this man is called the Younger of Córdoba has been explained by us above, under the year of the Lord 384, where we discussed the Elder of Córdoba, who wrote a chronicle.

#### 6. “From the year,” etc.

He gives a fuller account of the barbarian invasion of the Scythians, by which Italy, Gaul, Africa, Asia, and nearly the entire Roman Empire were shaken in those days, especially Spain. Idatius of Lamego, a writer and eyewitness of that period in Spain, relates it.

He first indicated in the consular fasti from what origin so great an evil had arisen, saying:

> In the consulship of Valens V and Valentinian, the Goths were defeated and expelled by the Hunnic people, and were received into Romania, out of mercy and by order of the Emperor Valens.

This was the year 376 after Christ’s birth. In the following year, during the consulship of Gratian IV and Merobaudes:

> The nation of the Goths, which had been received out of mercy, rebelled against the Romans. Counts with soldiers were sent to defeat them, and they fought with the Goths.

In the year 378, during the consulship of Valens VI and Valentinian II:

> Throughout the entire year the Goths lived in and ravaged the dioceses of Thrace, Scythia, and Moesia; then they advanced as far as the gates of Constantinople.

In the year 379, the first year of the Emperor Theodosius:

> The Romans fought many battles with the Goths. Then victories were announced over the Goths, Alans, and Huns on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December.

After peace had nevertheless been made with the Huns, Athanaric, king of the Goths, entered Constantinople in the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius—that is, in the year of Christ 381. After his death, the entire Gothic nation, together with its king, surrendered itself to Romania on the fifth day before the Nones of October in the following year.

As a result, the Roman emperors made use of Gothic auxiliary forces whenever necessity required. Thus they employed them against the usurper Radagaisus, who had flooded all Italy with two hundred thousand of his followers; but he was defeated by the Huns and Goths under the consulship of Arcadius VI and Probus, in the year of the Lord 406, as Marcellinus relates in his *Chronicle*.

From the same source we also learn that, in the consulship of Bassus and Philippus, in the year of Christ 408, Stilicho, despising the Emperor Honorius and coveting his kingdom, stirred up the peoples of the Alans, Suevi, and Vandals against Honorius’s rule by attracting them with gifts and money. He wished to appoint his son Eucherius Caesar. Stilicho paid the penalty for his treachery by his own death, while the barbarians, becoming more insolent, invaded the provinces of the Empire.

In the following year, when Constans, the son of the usurper Constantine, was acting against Didymus and Verinianus, as Prosper asserts in his *Chronicle*, the Alans, Vandals, and Suevi entered Spain—namely, in the 447th year of the Caesarian era, or the year of Christ 409, as Idatius and the others record. This occurred in the consulship of Honorius VIII and Theodosius, son of Arcadius, III, in the year 410.

The barbarians divided Spain among themselves, so that Gallaecia fell to the Vandals and Suevi, Lusitania and the province of Carthaginensis to the Alans, while Baetica fell solely to the Vandals. What preceded this partition we shall explain below with Dexter, under the year of the Lord 424.

The Goths did not enter Spain until the year of the Lord 416, under their king Ataulf, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place.

I also find that Salvianus of Marseille noted that the devastation of the barbarians had occurred throughout the Roman Empire because the sins of mankind demanded it. After discussing the invasion of Gaul as a just judgment of God, he adds in Book VII of *On Providence*:

> Why did the same, or perhaps greater, vices not destroy Spain—Spain which, even if heavenly wrath had handed it over to any other barbarians, nevertheless endured punishments worthy of its crimes, as enemies of purity? But this was added to reveal their condemnation for their shamelessness: that they should be handed over especially to the Vandals, that is, to chaste barbarians.  
>   
> In this captivity of the Spaniards God wished to show in two ways how much he hated the lust of the flesh and how much he loved chastity: he both placed the Vandals above them because of their exceptional chastity and subjected the Spaniards because of their exceptional shamelessness.  
>   
> What then? Were there not throughout the whole world barbarians stronger than those to whom Spain could have been handed over? There were many—indeed, unless I am mistaken, all of them. But for that reason he opposed the weakest enemies to them, so that he might show that it is not strength but the cause that prevails, and that we were not then overwhelmed by the power of the most cowardly of enemies, but conquered solely by the impurity of our own vices.

So far Salvianus.

When the aforementioned barbarians began to plunder Spain, Pancratianus, bishop of Braga, summoned a synod of the bishops subject to him, so that by a conciliar decree it might make provision concerning the articles of the faith that were being attacked by the barbarians, and concerning the safe preservation of the relics of the saints, lest they should be mocked and treated with derision by them.

The original document of this council is preserved in a worm-eaten and very ancient manuscript of the library of the monastery of Eburobriga belonging to our order. It was extracted from that manuscript and published in Volume II of the *Monarchy of Lusitania*, compiled by Father Bernardo Brito, a monk of our order and royal historiographer. Since it is highly relevant to our subject, and few people have access to it, I have decided to insert it here verbatim.

## Council of Braga under Pancratianus, Bishop of the First See

### Chapter I

When the bishops had assembled—Elipandus of Coimbra, Pamerius of Egitania, Arisbertus of Portugal, Deusdedit of Lugo, Galesius of Mérida, Pontamius of Eminium, Tiburtius of Lamego, Agathius of Iria, and Petrus of Numantia—in the church of Saint Mary of Braga, the Lord Pancratianus, bishop of the first see, said:

> It is known to you, my brothers and companions, how the barbarian peoples are devastating all Spain, overthrowing temples, killing the servants of God by the sword, and profaning the memorials of the saints, their bones, tombs, and cemeteries.
