They are breaking the power of the Empire, now shaking everything like straw before the face of the wind. Except for Celtiberia and Carpetania, everything else as far as the Pyrenees now lies under their power.  
>   
> Since this evil is already upon our heads, I wished to summon you, so that each man might make provision for his own people and all of us together for the common calamity of the Church. Let us provide, my companions, a remedy for souls, lest the multitude of labors and afflictions compel them to enter the assembly of the impious, stand in the way of sinners, sit in the seat of pestilence, and apostatize from the true faith.  
>   
> For this purpose let us place before the eyes of our subjects examples of our steadfastness, suffering for Christ some portion of the many torments that he endured for us. Since some of the Alans, Suevi, and Vandals are idolaters, while others profess the heresy of Arius, it has seemed good to me, with your approval, to issue a declaration against such errors for the greater firmness of the faith. What is your judgment?

All replied:

> A just, pious, holy, and necessary undertaking.

### Chapter II

Pancratianus:

> I believe in the one Word begotten by the Father himself before the ages, God from true God, of the same substance as the Father, without whom nothing was made and through whom all things were created.

All the bishops:

> We likewise believe.

Pancratianus:

> I believe in the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Word, one with them in the Godhead, who spoke through the mouths of the prophets, sat above the apostles, and filled Mary, the Mother of Christ.

All the bishops:

> We likewise believe.

Pancratianus:

> I believe that in this Trinity there is neither greater nor lesser, neither earlier nor later; but that among the three distinct persons there is one equality, one Godhead, one divinity.

All the bishops:

> We likewise believe.

Pancratianus:

> I condemn, excommunicate, reject, and anathematize all who think, hold, or preach anything contrary to this.

All the bishops:

> We likewise condemn them.

Pancratianus:

> I believe that the gods of the nations are demons: they have mouths but do not speak; eyes but do not see; ears but do not hear; nor is there breath in their mouths.

All:

> We likewise believe.

Pancratianus:

> I believe that our God, three in persons and one in essence, made all things from nothing; that he created our father Adam from the earth and Eve from his side; that he destroyed the world by the waters; that he gave the Law to Moses; and that in the last days he visited us through his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh.

All:

> We likewise believe.

Pancratianus:

> I condemn, reject, curse, and anathematize all who hold, think, or preach anything contrary to this.

All the bishops:

> We likewise condemn them.

### Chapter III

Pancratianus:

> Now, if it pleases all of you, let us determine what ought to be done concerning the relics of the saints, especially those of our father and the apostle of this region, Peter of Ratiaria, whom James, the kinsman of the Lord, sent here to save souls.

Elipandus of Coimbra rose and said:

> We cannot all do this in one way. But, if it pleases you, let each man act according to the opportunity of the time. The barbarians are among us; they are pressing Lisbon, they possess Mérida and likewise Astorga, and before long they will be upon us. Let each man depart to his own place, strengthen the faithful, and honorably conceal the bodies of the saints. Then let him send you a report from the places and caves where they are afterward deposited, lest, as time passes, they fall into oblivion.

All:

> This counsel seems to us just, good, and appropriate to the necessities of the time.

Pancratianus:

> It seems the same to me as it does to you. Go in peace.

All:

> Let our brother Pontamius alone remain, because of the destruction of his church at Eminium, which the barbarians are harassing.

### Chapter IV

Pontamius said:

> Let me go also, so that I may strengthen my sheep and suffer with them, for the name of Christ, labors and anxieties. For I did not accept the office of bishop in prosperity, but in hardship.

Pancratianus:

> An excellent statement and a just decision. I approve your departure. May God preserve you.

All:

> May God preserve you in the good decision that we likewise approve.

All together:

> Let us depart in the peace of Jesus Christ.

### Signatures

Pancratianus, bishop of Braga, in the name of God; Gelasius, bishop of Mérida, in the name of God; Elipandus, bishop of Coimbra, in the name of God; Pomerius, bishop of Egitania; Arisbertus, bishop of Portugal; Deusdedit, bishop of Lugo, in the name of God; Pontamius, bishop of Eminium; Tiburius, bishop of Lamego; Agathius, bishop of Iria; Petrus, bishop of Numantia, in the name of God.

Thus far the Council of Braga.

Saint Augustine discusses the flight of the bishops of Spain amid this disaster, and their afflictions through hardships and anguish, in Letter 180 to Honoratus, who had consulted him whether it was permissible for a bishop to flee at such a time, as some Spaniards had done. He replies:

> Thus, indeed, the holy bishops fled from Spain, after their peoples had partly escaped through flight, partly been killed, partly been consumed by siege, and partly been scattered into captivity. But many more remained there because those who remained under the weight of those dangers remained with them. If some abandoned their peoples, that is precisely what we say ought not to be done. Such men were not instructed by divine authority, but were overcome either by human error or by fear.

Augustine certainly seems to have had in mind what was decreed in this Council of Braga. The bishop Pontamius of Eminium must be counted among those of whom he said: “Many more remained there with those who remained,” and so forth.

But how do we know that this council was held at this time? From the fact that its records assert that at that time the barbarian nations of the Alans, Suevi, and Vandals held all the rest of the country as far as the Pyrenees under their power, except for Carpetania and Celtiberia; that they were pressing Lisbon, possessing Mérida and Astorga, and holding the district of Eminium in Gallaecia; and that they had not yet reached Braga, although their arrival was imminent.

All these events must be assigned to the very year in which they entered Spain. For in the following year, as both Dexter and Idatius testify, Lusitania and Gallaecia were devastated by the Suevi and Alans, and Braga and the sees of its neighboring bishops were situated there.

Moreover, since the records make no mention of the Goths, but only of the Alans, Vandals, and Suevi, we must infer that the council was held before the Goths entered Spain—namely, seven years after the others had entered.

It is also relevant that not long afterward, in the year of the Lord 415, the presbyter Avitus dedicated to Balchonius, bishop of Braga, his translation from Greek into Latin of Lucian’s letter concerning the discovery of the body of the protomartyr Stephen. Balchonius was still alive at the time of the Council of Toledo celebrated by Saint Turibius, legate of Saint Leo the pope, in the year of the Lord 448, when the barbarians possessed the whole of Spain without opposition.

We are therefore compelled to say that Pancratianus preceded Balchonius, died before the year 415, and held the aforesaid council somewhat earlier. Father Caracciolus, a Neapolitan cleric regular, likewise transcribed it in his controversy concerning the arrival of Saint James in Spain.

#### 7. “Marabaudes,” etc.

Some heroic poems by him are extant in Volume XV of the latest edition of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, under the title *Merobaudes the Spanish Schoolman, on Christ*. Their opening is:

> The true offspring of God, older than all the ages,

They appear to have been written against the error of the Arians.

#### 8. “Asturius,” etc.

Saint Ildefonsus relates the matter concerning the discovery and translation of the holy martyrs in his book *On Illustrious Men*, under Asturius, in these words:

> Blessed in his priesthood and worthy of a miracle, he deserved to discover in an earthly tomb the bodies of those with whom he would be joined in heaven. While exercising the priesthood of his see, he is said to have been warned by a divine revelation to search for the martyrs of God buried in the district of Complutum, situated nearly sixty miles from his city. Hastening there, he found those whom both the earth’s mound and the oblivion of time had covered, and brought them forth into the light and glory of earthly knowledge. When they had been discovered, he refused to return to his see; bound to the saints alike by service and constant attendance, he brought his final day to a close.

This is what we read in Ildefonsus concerning the revelation made to Asturius about the saints. We should not, however, suppose that he discovered them as though it were unknown in what city or church they lay buried. For shortly before this we saw that Saint Paulinus had buried his son Celsus at Complutum near the holy martyrs. Rather, the precise location of their tomb, since it lay beneath the earth, had faded from human memory.

The office composed by Saint Asturius in their honor is also extant in the Mozarabic Breviary of Saint Isidore, together with a hymn which I have decided to append here for the benefit of the learned and the devotion of all.

## Hymn on the Holy Martyrs of Complutum

O everlasting Word of God, brought forth from the Father’s mouth,  
you who, applying an instrument to the weakness of infants,  
give them breath to breathe forth the sound of their voices:

Be graciously present to us; loosen the fibers of our throats,  
equip our mouths with speech, fill our hearts with tears,  
that we may sing the feasts of the holy ones in worthy hymns.

Behold Justus; behold Pastor—both joined by blood,  
whom the loving bond of brotherhood had united,  
and whom the unity of sacred suffering made equal.

Yet while they were being kept in school and instructed in letters,  
hearing that the tyrant was entering the city as a persecutor,  
they immediately left the school and brought forward their writing tablets.

Then they hastened to the presence of the governor,  
and, following the cross of Christ, armed their weak bodies,  
so that they might bravely accomplish the triumphs of martyrdom.

Suddenly they announced this to Dacianus, saying:

Behold, little ones are coming, professing Christ,  
and freely ready  
to undergo the suffering of death and slaughter.

But the governor, thrown into turmoil, stirred up his fury  
and shouted to his savage ministers that they should seize them,  
ordering that their tender bodies be torn with clubs.

Then, behold, they addressed the sacred words to one another:

> It is time for us to receive the punishments of this body,  
> by which we may possess future joy with the angels.

Dacianus soon heard the martyrs’ steadfastness  
and, aroused to fury, dictated this sentence:

> Let both brothers be killed and perish by a dreadful death.

At once the enraged attendants dragged them  
to an open field, which they say was called Laudabile.  
There they were struck with the sword and crowned with blood.

O truly blessed place, where the holy blood  
of these little ones is hidden for the salvation of the peoples,  
and where many signs of healing flow to the sick.

Here, indeed, divine power conquers the wrath of demons,  
heals the ulcer, restores the limbs, and eases the pain;  
it receives the vows of all and raises up those who fall.

Now, city, rejoice, trusting in the passion of your saints,  
Complutum, made blessed by the blood with which you were washed;  
and soon render the vows due in twin songs.

Here we ask you, God, to hear us as we pray:  
drive away diseases, loosen bonds, and forgive sins,  
and grant that, unharmed, we may seek the homeland to come.

For love of your name, grant that we, your little servants,  
may love nothing temporal, love one another,  
follow you, sing of you, and enjoy you forever.

Praise to you throughout all time, undivided Trinity;  
praise, honor, supreme power, singular glory,  
which may proclaim you God through the ages of ages. Amen.

As for the bodies of these most holy martyrs, during the time of the Saracen devastation—that is, in the year of the Lord 714—they were transferred to Huesca by Saint Urbicius of Bordeaux. Having removed them from Complutum out of fear of the Moors, he first carried them to Bordeaux and then to Huesca, the celebrated city of Aragon. There they shine forth through many miracles and, even to the present time, have been remarkably preserved incorrupt, 1,328 years after their illustrious martyrdom.

Many citizens and clergy of Huesca witnessed this a few years ago. Among them was Don Vincentius Claveria, at that time a prebendary of the church of the holy martyrs and now auditor of the most illustrious Lord Cardinal of Trejo. He reverently handled the bodies with his own hands and repeatedly confessed to me under oath that they were full of flesh.

With them were found the breeches of the other of the two, together with stockings and a linen cloth, soaked with blood that appeared almost fresh—a miraculous sight. Moreover, part of the relics, through the efforts of Philip II, the Catholic King, was transferred to Complutum in the year 1568 and solemnly restored to its ancient see. Consult Morales, *History of Spain*, Book X, chapter 9.

As for Ildefonsus’s assertion concerning Saint Asturius—that he was ninth among the bishops of Toledo—it certainly refers to what he had read in Dexter: that Asturius was ninth in number among the bishop-writers. Otherwise he would have made a wholly false statement, since the catalogue of the bishops of that see, printed by Loaysa, although mutilated and defective, makes it clear that Asturius was at least the twelfth after Saint Eugenius the Martyr. Indeed, in Dexter he appears as the eighteenth, or twice ninth.

By the nine writers of Toledo I understand the following: Eugenius, Turibius, Paulatus, Melantius, Natalis, Olympius I, Gregorius, Audentius, and Asturius himself. We have listed their labors and works in their proper places together with Dexter.

### A.D. 423. A.R. 1174

Gregory of Baetica died, having previously dedicated his book *On the Faith*, or *On the Trinity*, to Galla Placidia Augusta, a most distinguished woman.

### A.D. 423. A.R. 1174

Valerius was appointed bishop of Saragossa in place of Vincentius.

### A.D. 423. A.R. 1174

Theodosius, father of the elder Theodosius, who died in Africa through the treachery of heretics, is counted by some among the martyrs.

### A.D. 423. A.R. 1174

A great dispute arose among our bishops because the Catholics would not restore to ecclesiastical dignity those who had fallen into the Priscillianist heresy—although they did restore them to penitence—or admit them to communion with their dignity.

### A.D. 423. A.R. 1174

At this time Isidore the Younger, bishop of Córdoba, wrote a book of *Allegories* to Paul Orosius of Tarragona and had written a work on Luke.

### A.D. 423. A.R. 1174

From the year 410 the Suevi began to possess Gallaecia, after Lusitania had been devastated.

### A.D. 423. A.R. 1174

Marabaudes, a lyric poet, blind, flourishes at Barcelona.

### A.D. 423. A.R. 1174

Asturius of Toledo, after the bodies of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor had first been transferred within the walls of the city of Complutum, honored them with a basilica, although their memory had been completely erased by the earth that covered them. Leaving the see of Toledo, he remained at Complutum and wrote their life and deeds, as well as a hymn and office for the holy martyrs. Among bishop-writers he is ninth in number.

A.D. 424.—1. The Goths, etc. Here they are listed in the reverse order from that in which they entered Spain. Orosius and Hydatius list them as follows: “The Alans, Vandals, and Suebi enter together, and afterward the Goths”—something not without a hidden significance, as we shall show at the end of these Commentaries. Dexter, however, reverses the order, evidently because, in the reverse order, the stronger peoples received greater power within Spain. For the Goths endured longest in their kingdom; the Suebi somewhat less, but much longer than the Vandals and Alans. Of the latter, the Alans were the first of all to be conquered and disappear, while the Vandals soon afterward migrated to Africa, abandoning Spain. We shall discuss this matter more fully at the end of the work.

Concerning the calamity that Dexter mentions here, we have Hydatius’s notable testimony, which I am pleased to reproduce verbatim. He writes in his Chronicle under Caesar’s era 447, that is, in the fifteenth year of Arcadius and Honorius:

“The barbarians who had entered Spain ravage it with hostile slaughter. Pestilence performs its part no less fiercely. Again, in the sixteenth year of those emperors:

“While the barbarians rage throughout Spain and the evil of pestilence rages no less, a tyrannical tax-collector plunders wealth and stored goods in the cities, and the soldier exhausts them. Terrible famine spreads, to such an extent that human flesh was eaten by human beings under the force of hunger; mothers, too, were nourished by the bodies of their children, whom they had killed or cooked themselves. Beasts, accustomed to the corpses of those slain by the sword, famine, and pestilence, kill the stronger among human beings wherever they find them; and, feeding upon their flesh, they run wild everywhere in the destruction of the human race. And thus, with four scourges—the sword, famine, pestilence, and beasts—raging everywhere throughout the whole world, the announcements previously proclaimed by the Lord through his prophets are fulfilled.”

He means Jeremiah and Zechariah. The former, in chapter 15, foretold the following in God’s name:

“Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; those destined for captivity, to captivity. And I shall appoint over them four kinds of punishment, says the Lord: the sword for slaughter, dogs for tearing apart, the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth for devouring and scattering.”

Where the words “those destined for death, to death,” announce the sudden destruction of many by various forms of death—by sword, famine, and the tearing apart of beasts—they necessarily signify pestilence, which together with the other three completes the four kinds of scourge.

Zechariah, however, says in chapter 11:

“I will not pasture you. What is dying, let it die; what is being cut off, let it be cut off; and let those who remain devour each the flesh of his neighbor.”

These kinds of scourge are certainly the same as those which Hydatius reports as having occurred in Spain. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that the prophets mentioned above literally directed these words against the Israelite people at God’s command, as will readily be clear to those who examine their context. For Jeremiah immediately adds:

“And I shall give them over to the heat of all the kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, for everything that he did in Jerusalem.”

Zechariah, on the other hand, plainly speaks of the scourges by which Jerusalem was overthrown because of Christ’s killing. Hence, in the figure of the Lord’s sale—as Matthew explains in chapter 27—he says:

“And they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver.”

Nevertheless, the divine Spirit may secondarily have had such calamities in Spain in view; this is undoubtedly what Hydatius maintains.

He then adds, under the seventeenth year of Arcadius:

“After the provinces of Spain had been overthrown by the ravages of the aforementioned scourges, the barbarians, converted to the making of peace through the Lord’s mercy, divided the regions of the provinces among themselves by lot for habitation. The Vandals occupied Gallaecia, and the Suebi the region situated at the western extremity of the Ocean Sea; the Alans received the provinces of Lusitania and Carthaginensis; and the Vandals surnamed Silingi received Baetica by lot. The Spaniards who remained in the cities and fortresses after the scourges submitted themselves to the slavery of the barbarians ruling throughout the provinces.”

Orosius discusses the destruction of Tarraco in book 7, chapter 22, and, as it was his homeland, laments it.

[Col. 0557B]

2. Theodosius, etc. You should understand the statement that Theodosius the Younger ruled from the year of the Lord 402 in this sense: in that year—when Arcadius was consul for the fifth time and Honorius likewise for the fifth time, according to Marcellinus—he was created Caesar. For in his Chronicle, under that year, he says: “Theodosius the Younger was created Caesar in the place where his father and paternal uncle had been.”

The statement that he flourished from the year 424 should be understood as referring to the fact that, after the death of his father and paternal uncle, Arcadius and Honorius, he alone then obtained the imperial monarchy. This is plainly confirmed by Hydatius under that year, which in his chronology is the final year of Honorius, the first year of the 301st Olympiad, Caesar’s era 462, and the year of Christ 423. He writes:

“Roman year 41. Theodosius, son of Arcadius, who had been reigning for several years in the eastern regions, after the death of his father and, following the death of his paternal uncle Honorius, held the monarchy of the empire, being twenty-six years old.”

3. Peter, etc. Augustine dedicated to him his book On the Soul and Its Origin; Paul Orosius had labored against a certain Origenist named Avitus while traveling from the West to the East. Augustine speaks of the same man again in book 2 of his Retractions, chapter 56:

“Vincentius Victor,” he says, “in Caesarean Mauritania found, among a certain Spanish presbyter named Peter, a little work of mine in which I had written about the origin of the soul,” and so forth.

4. Cauriae, etc. Gregory of Tours wrote an illustrious account of her martyrdom in his History of the Franks, book 2, chapter 2. Although he suppresses her name, he relates it as follows:

“A devout Spanish virgin, exceedingly wealthy in possessions and, according to the dignity of the world, distinguished by senatorial nobility—and, nobler than all these things, eminent in the Catholic faith and serving Almighty God blamelessly—was brought to this trial. When she had been presented before King Trasamund the Arian, he first began to entice her with persuasive words to be rebaptized. When she repelled his poisonous dart with the weapons of faith, the king ordered her possessions to be taken away—she who already possessed the kingdom of paradise in her mind—and then, after subjecting her to torments, ordered her to be tortured without hope of preserving her present life.

“After many interrogations and after the treasures of earthly possessions had been taken away, when she still could not be broken so that she would renounce the blessed Trinity, she was forcibly led to be rebaptized. When she was being compelled by force to be plunged into that filthy bath, she cried out: ‘I believe that the Father, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, is of one substance and essence.’ By a fitting excretion she polluted all the waters—that is, she had a bowel movement. From there she was led to the formal judicial examination and, after the rack, flames, and claws, was consecrated to the Lord Christ by the severing of her head.”

Thus far Gregory, who likewise affirms that other Catholics in Spain were persecuted by the same Vandal king, tortured by various kinds of torment, and finally punished with death and crowned with martyrdom.

He must nevertheless be corrected in asserting that Saint Vincentia the virgin suffered under Trasamund. Trasamund assumed the kingdom many years later, not while the Vandals were in Spain but after they had migrated to Africa, as is clear from the Life of Fulgentius of Ruspe and other authors. Moreover, that many Spaniards received the crown of martyrdom from the barbarians at that time is clearly demonstrated by the acts of the Council of Braga transcribed above. You should also consult chapter 1.

[Col. 0559B]

5. Near Tude, etc. He calls the town Viana, situated between the Douro and Minho, a region that once belonged to Gallaecia but is now part of Portugal.

The feast day of Saints Maximilian and Valentinian is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 29 October, and the ancient manuscripts agree. Molanus also mentions them in his Additions to Usuard. In the Roman Martyrology Maximilian is now called a martyr, while Valentinian is called a confessor. This must be understood in the sense in which the title “confessor” was given only to those who had begun martyrdom and had confessed the faith of Christ before a judge. In this sense the two most blessed bishops of Viana were admirably examined by the Vandals concerning the faith.

Molanus was nevertheless deceived in joining the city of Viana—which belonged with the preceding reading concerning the aforementioned saints—to the following passage, where Blessed Theodore the abbot is discussed, as though Saint Theodore had died at Vienna or Viana, rather than the aforementioned holy bishops having attained distinction through the glory of their confession. Yet no memory of that abbot is found at Vienna in Gaul, either in the work of Gregory of Tours, who wrote about the glory of the confessors of Gaul, or in the Historical Mirror of the Beauvais author.

Nor is this surprising, since this is Saint Theodore who succeeded his holy teacher Pachomius in the governance of the monastery, and whose many illustrious deeds Cassian relates in his Conferences, as does Gennadius in his book On Illustrious Men. Equilinus drew something from these accounts in book 1, chapter 173, of his Catalogue.

Thus the Martyrology seems to need to be read as follows on 29 October:

“On the same day, the holy bishops Maximilian, martyr, and Valentinian, confessor, at Viana. Likewise, the burial of Blessed Theodore the abbot.”

The context was made more obscure by those who placed between these two notices the birthdays of other saints—namely, Narcissus of Jerusalem and John, bishop of Autun—though the ancient codices lack them.

[Col. 0559C]

6. Rufus, etc. Severus recorded the event in the Life of Saint Martin, in these words:

“It was nevertheless observed that at almost the same time there was in Spain a young man who, having acquired authority for himself through many signs, was carried so far that he claimed to be Elijah. When many rashly believed this, he added that he was Christ. In this matter he so dazzled them that a certain bishop named Rufus worshiped him as God; for this reason we afterward saw Rufus removed from the episcopate.”

This Rufus was from Charia, a province of Asia Minor in which Tripolis, Antioch, and Leocadia are situated, as may be seen in Ptolemy, Geography, book 5, chapter 2, map 1.

7. Saint Asturius, etc. Saint Ildefonsus supports this account concerning the burial of Saint Asturius Serrani. He says:

“When these men had been found”—he is speaking of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor at Complutum—“he refused to return to his see and, bound to the saints by both service and constant devotion, brought his final day to its close. Nevertheless, no one occupied his see while he lived, though he was absent from Toledo. Hence, as antiquity relates, he is recognized as the ninth priest in Toledo and the first in Complutum.”

From that time until Spain’s devastation by the Saracens, the bishops of Complutum are found subscribing to the councils of Spain.

As for his assertion that Asturius was the ninth of the bishops of Toledo, we explained this above. I do not know where Ildefonsus obtained the information unless from the Chronicles of Dexter. I believe that he had those Chronicles in mind when he said, “as antiquity relates,” and so forth. For no one older than Dexter who wrote these things could be found, since Dexter wrote his Chronicle in these times.

After many years, the body of Saint Asturius was transferred to Oviedo during Spain’s captivity under the harsh yoke of the Saracens. There it rests honorably buried in the holy chapel commonly called the Cámara Santa, in a wooden chest. When this was opened on 25 July 1572, it gave forth the fragrance of heavenly spices, as Ambrosius Morales reports in book 13, chapter 38, of his History. It bears the title of Saint Serrano, namely, the man who was called Asturius Serrano.

The Church of Oviedo celebrates his feast on 8 March under the name of Saint Serrano, bishop and confessor, as I found in the calendar of the Spanish saints printed at Madrid in 1614.

[Col. 0560C]

We learn from Dexter that Martin succeeded Asturius in the principal see of Toledo; after Martin had briefly assumed office, Olympius II of that name succeeded him, then Foetadius succeeded Olympius, and Isicius succeeded Foetadius.

From this the catalogue of the bishops of Toledo published by the learned Loaysa among the Spanish councils must be partly corrected and partly expanded. For he confuses Martin with Majorianus and omits Olympius II, whose name nevertheless appears among the Fathers of the council called the First Council of Toledo. The first Olympius had already departed to heaven in the fourth place before Asturius, while the second had not yet ascended the aforementioned see, which Asturius held.

He also omits Foetadius. We shall discuss him and the others in their proper places.

8. The heretics, etc. The Priscillianists were flourishing again in these times, though Saint Turibius later eradicated and destroyed them.

9. Under Olympius, etc. Consider, I ask you, the antiquity of the library of the Holy Church of Toledo, which in this respect too can be compared with any other in the world. It contains many manuscript books of the saints that have not yet seen the light, as well as an incredible treasure of Arabic books. Would that that holy Church would undertake to provide them in Latin, for its own benefit and that of the entire Christian world.

[Col. 0561A]

10. The memory of Gregory, etc. We said much about him in treating the Council of Milan under the year of the Lord 384; you should consult that discussion.

11. Innocentius, etc. The entire account of the conversion of Innocentius and Theodosius, or Theodore, together with the whole synagogue of the city of Magona on the island of Minorca—a conversion brought about by the power of Saint Stephen’s relics, which Orosius had carried there, and preceded by many miracles—is narrated at length by Severus, bishop of Minorca, in an encyclical letter that he sent to the whole Christian world. Cardinal Baronius published it, transcribed from an old manuscript in the Vatican Library, in volume 5 of his Annals under the year of the Lord 418.

It would be lengthy to insert it here, yet I cannot omit everything. He says:

“Almost in these very days a certain presbyter, outstanding in holiness, came from Jerusalem”—he is speaking of Orosius—“and stayed for some time at Magona. After he was unable to cross over to Spain as he wished, he decided to return to Africa. Then, when he had decided to carry to Spain the relics of Blessed Stephen, which had recently been revealed, he placed them in the church of the aforementioned town, undoubtedly inspired by the martyr himself.

“The Christians, inflamed by devotion to the protomartyr, began to discuss the conversion of the Jews. From this arose a considerable conflict. By a great miracle of God, although the Jewish women hurled innumerable weapons and stones at the Christians, they injured none of them. Yet when one Christian threw a single stone, a Jew was gravely wounded in the head.

“The conversion of their synagogue was repeatedly shown in dreams to some Jews, especially to Theodore, the high priest and the richest of them all. The first to be converted were Innocentius and Meletius.”

Who these men were may be learned from the letter mentioned above:

“Two leading Jews, Meletius, the brother of Theodore, and Innocentius, who had recently fled the devastation of Spain and come to this island with their families—as they themselves now confirm, even with the solemn interposition of the sacraments—went together to a certain cave, or rather cliff, accompanied by two Jews of humble origin who had chosen these men as leaders of their common flight.

“The beginning of their conversion came about because, by God’s merciful arrangement, this word—‘Christ, in your name’—clung tenaciously to Meletius, so that he could not drive it from his memory. When the matter was disclosed to Innocentius and he tried to consign it to oblivion with the foulest words, but accomplished nothing, they entered a very narrow path. Darkness of thought obscured the light of their eyes, and they lost the path they had been following unknowingly, remaining in deserted and impassable places.

“When they were torn by thorns or blocked by brambles, and after they had covered their bodies with long wounds, they first reached such anxiety and then such despair and fear that they were compelled to admit that they were suffering these things by the just judgment of God because of their unbelief.

“Therefore, invoking the name of Christ—which earlier, when it thrust itself upon them of its own accord, they had rejected—they seized the path that led them, against their will and intention, back to the town, their legs already lacerated.

“After they had been converted to the faith, Theodore too was converted after three days, and with him the whole synagogue.”

Meanwhile many miracles occurred, reproducing the ancient exodus of the Hebrews from Egyptian slavery. For a globe of fire was seen over the church in place of the pillar of cloud. Very fine hail also fell, like manna, possessing the taste of honey. Moreover, rain preceded them as they went to baptism, so that when the Christians discovered what was happening they said: “Look, it is already raining; know that the Jews are about to approach the faith of Christ.” At the conversion of Artemisia, the wife of Meletius, the taste of honey was likewise produced, like the waters of Marah that had been turned into sweetness (Exodus 15).

Of the synagogue of the entire city, only two Spanish sisters resisted the Holy Spirit’s call: one was the wife of Innocentius, the other a widowed relative who had children. Concerning their remarkable conversion, Severus writes:

“For nearly four days the wife of Innocentius received the word of salvation that we were pressing upon her with stopped ears. When she could be moved neither by any threats, prayers, nor tears of Innocentius her husband, the whole company of the brethren gathered, at Innocentius’s request, in the house where she lived, deeply grieved that one woman should resist the fullness of so great a joy.

“Since for a long time we accomplished nothing by pouring empty words into deaf ears, we fled to the familiar refuge of prayer. Thus, almost until the third hour, the army of our leader Jesus fought against the enemy Amalek through the exertions of hymns and prayers. Then, when we were almost despairing and were preparing to withdraw, we summoned everyone to prayer again with renewed strength, and for a long time we lay prostrate and wept.

“When, at the conclusion of the prayer, she cried out ‘Amen,’ she added that she believed and wished to become a Christian.”

But what happened to her widowed sister?

“When the venerable matron with her children saw that Innocentius, her sister’s husband, had been converted, she immediately boarded a ship, with our permission—and indeed at our urging—because she could not be moved toward the faith of Christ either by words or miracles.

“On the eighth day, when we had decided to return”—Severus, that is, to the city of his see—“that widow, Innocentius’s relative, was brought back from the sea. She suddenly threw herself at my knees and tearfully begged for the help of our faith.

“To her I said: ‘Why, woman, did you wish with such fickleness of spirit to abandon your brothers?’

“She replied: ‘The prophet Jonah too wished to flee from the presence of the Lord, yet he fulfilled God’s will, though unwillingly. Therefore receive not only me but these orphans as well, and nourish them for Christ.’

“With these words, uttered wondrously, she pressed her two little sons upon me amid tears. Who did not weep for joy? Whom did the greatness of that happiness not force to shed tears? I received the sheep whom we had thought alone among the whole flock to have gone astray, and with her twin offspring I brought her back to Christ’s sheepfold.”

As for the date of this conversion, at the end of Severus’s letter it is said to have occurred after the eleventh consulship of Honorius and the second consulship of Constantius, the victor. These consulships fell in the year of the Lord 417. Therefore, if the event occurred immediately afterward, it must be assigned to the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, that is, the year of Christ 418, as Baronius believes. This is especially so because Severus himself says that it occurred when Paul Orosius was returning from Jerusalem to Spain and Africa with the relics of Saint Stephen the protomartyr; and it has been shown that this occurred in the year just mentioned.

Dexter, however, perhaps unaware of Severus’s letter, or because the event occurred several years after the consulship mentioned above, assigns it to the year of the Lord 424.

[Col. 0563A]

12. The feast, etc. At the end of the history of the Finding of the Holy Cross it is asserted—as, among others, Equilinus relates in book 4, chapter 117, of his Catalogue—that Saint Helena, the mother of the Emperor Constantine, established an annual feast throughout the world in its memory. No one should doubt that this was proclaimed and announced to all by Pope Sylvester, and that in those days it was customarily celebrated with special veneration. Dexter affirms this.

13. Prudentius, etc. His final work was the Handbook of the New and Old Testament. In its preface he quite plainly asserts that he had finally been received into the sacred house of the Virgin of the Pillar in order to write the Handbook. For after stating that not all the vessels of a rich man’s house are golden, but that some are also earthen, though necessary for use, he adds:

“Christ fits me, in my father’s court,  
Like a worn little vessel, to  
Perishable uses,  
And allows me to remain in a corner.

“Behold, we undertake an earthen service  
Within the palace of salvation.”

What does “to enter within the palace of salvation” mean except to write within the house of God? He declares that he remains in its corner, and Dexter likewise notes this.

I suspect that Prudentius should be read as follows: “Christ fits me, in my mother’s court, to perishable uses,” instead of “in my father’s court,” and so forth, since he lived in a corner of the temple of Christ’s Mother, as Dexter writes.

As for his age, since we proved above, under the year 380, that his birth fell in the consulship of Salia and Philippus—or, which is the same thing, in the year of the Lord 348—it follows that he died at the age of seventy-seven, since he is said to have died this year, 425. His books are full of his struggles with idolaters, Jews, and heretics of every kind.

14. The second synod, etc. The word “second” indicates here that the memory of some synod is missing—namely, the African Synod of Telepte, which he mentions a little later when discussing Majorianus, bishop of Toledo, who attended it. Because of the proximity of the names, he consequently wrote, “the second synod of Telensis,” and so forth. I find no mention of that council anywhere except in Dexter.

15. Foetadius, etc. His memory was absent from the catalogues of the bishops of Toledo, but it will have to be restored from Dexter.

16. Honorius, etc. The letter that Minervius had sent to Jerome and that the monk Sisinius had brought, together with the letters of Exuperius and Alexander, is answered by Letter 152 itself, and Jerome dedicates his Malachias to them. Prosper of Aquitaine also discusses the same men in his Chronicle under the twenty-eighth year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, namely the year of Christ 422, saying:

“Honoratus, Minervius, Castor, and Jovianus, fathers of individual monasteries, flourish in Gaul.”

[Col. 0564A]

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. The Goths, Suebi, Vandals, and Alans, northern peoples who had invaded Spain somewhat earlier, ravage it with pitiful slaughter and fires. They completely destroy many cities, among them Tarraco, setting them ablaze, and kill many thousands of people with the sword; while very many others perish everywhere as pestilence and famine rage.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. Theodosius the Younger, who has ruled since the year 402, flourishes.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. Peter the Younger, a Toledan presbyter, is said to flourish in Africa.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. At Cauria in Spain, a Catholic Lusitanian virgin named Vincentia is subjected by the Arian heretics to almost immeasurable tortures because, having once been baptized as a Catholic, she refused to be baptized again by the heretics. This year, on the Ides of March, she is gravely tortured and departs to heaven as a virgin and martyr.

[Col. 0559]

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. Near Tude in Gallaecia, in the town of Viana, the holy bishops Maximianus and Valentinian, confessors, shine forth.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. Rufus, from Charia, is ordained bishop in Spain. After being marvelously deceived for several years while following a certain pseudo-Christ, he is removed from the episcopal rank by the judgment of a numerous council.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. When Saint Asturius, surnamed Serrano, dies in a good old age, a burial is provided for him in the church of Saints Justus and Pastor, built at Complutum. Martin succeeds him in the see of Toledo; Olympius II succeeds Martin.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. The Priscillianist heretics are disgracefully expelled from Ambratia, the city of the Vettones, by Splendonius, bishop of that city; similarly, they are expelled with no less disgrace by Marcello, bishop of Cauria.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. Under Olympius II of Toledo, the space of the principal church of Toledo is enlarged, and the church is endowed with an illustrious library.

[Col. 0561]

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. The memory of Gregory of Córdoba is celebrated everywhere. He was prefect of the praetorium of Cappadocia and the brother of Count Olympius.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. Innocentius the Spaniard, from Ebora in the city of the Carpetani, flees with many companions to the island of Minorca because of the Goths’ movement and their burning of the Spanish cities, and is converted to the faith. The Jew Theodosius followed him not long afterward.

[Col. 0563]

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. The feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross, instituted by Sylvester, is widely celebrated.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. Prudentius, returning from Rome to Caesaraugusta, full of years and illustrious works, dies peacefully at the see of Saint Mary of Caesaraugusta after many struggles with all the heretics of his time.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. A second synod is held at Telensis in Spain, at which Domitianus, bishop of that city, confirms the synodal acts. This see of Telensis was regarded as one of the foremost in Spain.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. Foetadius succeeds the holy man Olympius in the see of Toledo.

A.D. 424. A.R. 1175. Honorius, Minervius, and Jovianus, men of the highest distinction and holiness, assume responsibility for individual monasteries.

[Note: [Col. 0564A]]

A.D. 426.—Saint Jerome, etc. Prosper of Aquitaine assigns the death of the holy doctor to the consulship of Theodosius IX and Constantius III, namely the year of the Lord 420. Dexter places it six years later, that is, in 426. Which of them wrote more accurately I would find difficult to judge, especially because nothing among the writers of that period was nearly so unknown and uncertain as the death of Jerome.

Indeed, Hydatius writes in his Chronicle under the eleventh year of Theodosius the Younger, that is, the year of Christ 433:

“The account has not disclosed at what time the holy John”—the bishop of Jerusalem—“Jerome, and the others whom we mentioned above died.”

Earlier he had said that Juvenal presided at Jerusalem, as he had learned from the report of Germanus, a presbyter from the Arabian region who had come from there to Gallaecia, and from other Greeks. They nevertheless reported nothing about the death of Saint Jerome. Hydatius himself had stated in the year of the Lord 407, that is, the thirteenth year of Arcadius and Honorius, that he had seen Jerome at Jerusalem while still a boy and very young, visiting the holy places.

Moreover, Marcellinus, having no certain knowledge of the death of that holy doctor, treated it not under the year in which it might be believed to have occurred, but under the year in which he had completed his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, namely the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius the Great, when Arcadius was consul again with Rufinus. He writes:

“Up to this fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius, Blessed Jerome, beginning with the apostle Peter after the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ and ending with himself, wrote accounts of 135 illustrious ecclesiastical men. He lived at Bethlehem, where he also founded a monastery for himself, and he brought his life to an end at a very advanced age.”

Yet he recorded Augustine’s death, which he knew with certainty, under the year of the Lord 430, when Florentius and Dionysius were consuls.

As for Jerome’s age, the authorities vary. Bede, Ado, and Usuard in his Martyrology, followed by Sigebert in his Chronicle, assert that he died at the age of ninety-eight or ninety-nine, whereas Prosper says ninety-one. Cardinal Baronius maintains that he did not reach eighty but attained only seventy-eight or seventy-nine.

Nevertheless, all agree that he ended his life at a very advanced age, as Marcellinus says—or, which is the same thing in Dexter, that he departed to heaven already decrepit. For, according to Ptolemy, in the final chapter of the Tetrabiblos, decrepit age begins at sixty-eight.

A.D. 426. A.R. 1177. Saint Jerome of Dalmatia, a most holy and learned man, while residing at Bethlehem, departs to heaven already decrepit.

[Note: [Col. 0564C]]

A.D. 428.—1. Foetadius, etc. The memory of Bishop Isicius appears in the Catalogue of the Bishops of Toledo. From this we learn that Sedulius of Oretum was a bishop in Spain. This does not, however, rule out his having been born in Ireland, as many believe, since Isicius himself, the bishop of Toledo, was a Palestinian monk. Whether two Seduliuses once flourished in poetry, or only one, is not for this place to determine.

[Col. 0565A]

2. Celebrated, etc. This was that great Olympius whom Augustine calls an illustrious teacher of the Church and a saint when he cites his book. Consult what we wrote about Olympius I of that name under the year of the Lord 356, for he is the man under discussion here.

A.D. 428. A.R. 1179. Isicius, a Palestinian monk, succeeds the bishop of Toledo, Foetadius. He detains his friend Sedulius, bishop of Oretum, at Toledo for the sake of preaching. Distinguished by God’s gift in poetry and oratory, Sedulius composes many books.

[Col. 0565]

A.D. 428. A.R. 1179. The memory of the pious bishop Olympius is celebrated in Carpetania; his book on the faith is carefully read there and elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0565A]]

A.D. 429.—1. Isicius, etc. This too is found in the Catalogue of the Bishops of Toledo, where Majorianus is nevertheless confused with Martin. They are entirely different men, since Martin preceded Olympius II, Foetadius, and Isicius in that same see, whereas Majorianus succeeded Isicius. The Caesaraugustan manuscript of Dexter is involved in the same error and deserves a similar correction.

2. Vincentius, etc. This author is well known to everyone, since his book Against Heresies is in everyone’s hands and is read with great praise; his name has also been entered into the tables of the ecclesiastical calendar or Martyrology on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, that is, 24 May.

Gennadius discusses him in chapter 64 of his Catalogue of Illustrious Men. He writes that Vincentius died while Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian were reigning, namely around the year 434, the period under discussion by Baronius, or shortly afterward. In the year 429, however, he embraced the life and discipline of a monk in the monastery on the island of Lérins, under its abbot Saint Honoratus, later bishop of Arles. Consult also Equilinus, book 5, chapter 72, concerning Vincentius.

“And many presbyters,” etc. Enough was said about these men under the year 417, when the discussion concerned Paul Orosius, who carried an embassy to Augustine against them. Since Dexter now says that they were flourishing, we believe that they had been brought back to sound understanding by the writings of that same Augustine.

3. To Paul of Tarragona, etc. Some are troubled when they hear the name of the Augustinian order in those days, since neither the different institutions of monks were then called orders nor was the designation “Augustinian” known to have been in use. Hence they consider this passage spurious, invented by some ignorant person for the benefit of the hermits of Saint Augustine.

It cannot certainly be denied that these are unusual expressions for that age, when the institutions of monks differed little or not at all from one another. The words “of the Augustinian order” could easily have been added in the margin of Dexter’s manuscript by someone and then, as frequently happens, inserted into the text by another copyist.

Nevertheless, I would not believe that this was done in our own times, but many years ago by Eutrando, the continuator of this Chronicle, who flourished in the year of the Lord 960, or by some other ancient and learned man. For Dexter’s Chronicle did not come down to us through the hands of some Augustinian, but through the learned Jesuit Thomas de Turrealba, who copied the manuscript after it had been removed from the Benedictine library at Fulda and sent it to Spain. We discussed this matter at length in the preface to the work.

It is nevertheless worth observing that the name of the order was not as new as many believe. I find it used by Saint Zacharias, the Roman pontiff, in a privilege granted to the monastery of Cassino in March of the year of the Lord 742, which I myself inspected with my own eyes in the present year, 1623, in its archive, where the autograph itself is preserved.

There Zacharias reports that an angel from heaven said to Saint Benedict, who was deeply saddened by the future destruction of his monastery under the Lombards:

“Do not grieve, most excellent and most chosen Benedict, over what you have learned will happen to this place. For what has once been decreed by God is immutable and irrevocable. Only the souls of those dwelling in this place have been granted to you by your merit. But the consolation of Almighty God will come, and it will restore this place to a state broader and better than that in which it now stands; and the teaching of this order will once again shine from this place throughout the whole world.”

Thus far Zacharias—or rather, the angel speaking to Benedict. It follows that, according to Zacharias, in Benedict’s time the order was called the Order of Saint Benedict.

As for the text, the word *Tarraconensi* should not be joined to the following word *episcopo*, but rather separated from it and joined to the preceding *Paulo*. Thus the meaning is not that he was bishop of Tarragona—for he was only bishop of Caldaqua—but that Paul, a native of Tarragona, was bishop of Caldaqua, and that Boniface succeeded him in the episcopate. Augustine wrote to this Paul in Letter 216, from which it is clear that Paul had been his disciple, for Augustine says: “For I owe you most of all, because in Christ Jesus through the Gospel I begot you.” Nevertheless, he sharply rebukes him because he had burdened the Church of Caldaqua, or Cataqua, beyond necessity with debts:

“For since you do not cease to involve yourself more and more, so that even after your renunciation you have inserted yourself into the affairs which you renounced”—thus, evidently, he had professed regular vows under Augustine’s direction—“and are said to live in that profession, although the frugality of your Church cannot suffice for you, why do you seek my communion?” and so forth.

In Letter 124, addressed to the count Olympius, he warmly commends Boniface, who had already been appointed to the same see in Paul’s place, asking that the debts incurred by his predecessor be forgiven him; he repeats this request in Letter 129.

**4.** [lacuna] In the Caesaraugustan manuscript the following words were added at this point: “Petronius Maximus Augustus, deposed at Complutum, dies.” They were nevertheless inserted here incorrectly by some plagiarist, since it is certain that after Dextrus’s death, in the year of the Lord 455, when Valentinian III and Anthemius were consuls—as Prosper of Tyre reports in his *Chronicle*—and after Valentinian had been killed, Petronius Maximus was raised to the imperial dignity. He was killed, however, after seventy-two days and dragged through the City.

**5. Goths under the leadership of Castinus, etc.** Idatius writes the following about Castinus in his *Chronicle*, in the twenty-eighth year of Arcadius and Honorius, but in the year of Christ 422:

“Castinus, master of the soldiers, brings war against the Vandals in Baetica with a large force and Gothic auxiliaries. When he had pressed them so hard by the force of his siege that they were already preparing to surrender, he imprudently engaged them in open battle. Deceived by the treachery of the auxiliaries, he was defeated and fled to Tarragona. On his return he devastated the Carpetanian region.”

Castinus had been consul in the year of the Lord 424, with Victor as his colleague.

**6. Capreolus, etc.** Saint Capreolus, who is said at this time to have written to the Toledan deacon of that name, was bishop of Carthage in Africa. Quodvultdeus succeeded him in the episcopate. Through the deacon Bassula he wrote to the Fathers assembled at the Council of Ephesus, as Liberatus reports in chapter 5 of his *Breviary*, and Peltanus in the *Acts of that Synod*, volume II, chapter 19.

**7. The Goths, etc.** That is, under Castinus, master of the soldiers, when they devastated the whole of Carpetania.

**8. At Toledo, etc.** Gennadius, chapter 62, records the following about this Philip, a disciple of Saint Jerome:

“Philip, a Spanish presbyter”—[another reading: “excellent,” but tastelessly]—“a hearer of Jerome, composed a commentary on Job and published books in simple style. I have read his familiar letters, very witty, exhorting people to endure the greatest poverty and sufferings. He died during the reigns of Marcian and Avitus,” that is, around the year 455.

**9. Idatius Clarus, etc.** Saint Isidore discusses him in his book *On Illustrious Men*, and we have followed him in the preceding material for the years 382 and thereafter.

**10. Meco, etc.** It still retains its ancient name, although reduced to a small town, and is called Meco, almost four miles from Complutum.

**11. Twenty, etc.** This is undoubtedly the war about which Idatius speaks in the words that we quoted above in number 5. Prosper of Tyre also says of the same event in his *Chronicle*, under the eighth year of Theodosius, which was the year of our Lord 430:

“Nearly twenty thousand soldiers fighting against the Vandals in Spain were killed.”

**A.D. 429. Era 1180.** Isicius has Majorian as his successor; Majorian indeed took part in the African Council of Telepte.

**A.D. 429. Era 1180.** Vincentius, formerly a Palatine official, becomes a monk of Lérins; and many presbyters named Avitus flourish as citizens of Tarragona.

**A.D. 429. Era 1180.** Boniface, also bishop of Caldaqua and of the Augustinian order, succeeds Paul of Tarragona.

**A.D. 429. Era 1180.** [lacuna]

**A.D. 429. Era 1180.** The Goths, under Castinus, devastate the Carpetanian region.

**A.D. 429. Era 1180.** Saint Capreolus writes to Capreolus, a Toledan deacon.

**A.D. 429. Era 1180.** The Goths invade Complutum not long afterward.

**A.D. 429. Era 1180.** Philip, a disciple of Jerome, is renowned at Toledo.

**A.D. 429. Era 1180.** Idatius Clarus is held in high esteem in Spain.

**A.D. 429. Era 1180.** The Goths devastate Meco, a city near Complutum on the borders of Carpetania, with immense fury and cruelty.

**A.D. 429. Era 1180.** Nearly twenty thousand soldiers fighting against the Vandals slaughter one another atrociously in various battles.

[Note: **A.D. 430–431. The saints, etc.** Saint Prosper narrates their most illustrious contest in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 437 in these words:

“At about this time four Spanish men—Arcadius, Probus, Paschasius, and Eutychius—had long been held in esteem by Genseric for their wisdom and faithful service. The king ordered them to pass over into the Arian sect, so that he might make them more closely attached to himself. But they steadfastly rejected the crime; and when the barbarian was aroused to the most violent anger, they were first proscribed, then driven into exile, afterward tortured with the most atrocious punishments, and finally killed by different forms of death. Thus they miserably met their end in glorious martyrdom.

“The boy Paulillus, however, the brother of Paschasius and Eutychius, was highly favored by the king because of the elegance of his appearance and his intelligence. Since no threats could drive him from his profession and love of the Catholic faith, he was beaten for a long time with clubs and condemned to infamous slavery. He was not killed, as it appears, lest even that age should glory in the defeat of the impious king’s savagery. These men were the firstfruits of the Vandal persecution.”

Moreover, while Saint Arcadius and his companions were detained in chains, Honoratus, bishop of the city of Constantina, according to Gennadius in his book *On Illustrious Men*, wrote them letters exhorting them to martyrdom; these letters are extant in the *Library of the Fathers*. They begin:

“Go on, faithful soul; go on, confessor of the Trinity,” and so forth, since he detested the doctrine of the Arians. He also writes among other things:

“Behold, Christ rejoices and looks upon you; the angels rejoice and assist you. With you is the whole company of the martyrs who preceded you; the martyrs await you, defend you, and extend the crown. I beg you, hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown. The Catholic Church awaits you as her martyr, so that she may honor you as her Stephen,” and so forth.

Some manuscripts have *Antoninus* instead of *Honoratus, and they report that he was the author of this letter. At that very time there was indeed an Antoninus, bishop of Mérida, as Idatius, his associate and friend, writes in his *Chronicle* under the twenty-first year of Theodosius the Younger. Yet there can be no doubt that he had seen the holy martyrs, since in earlier years, when the Vandal king Genseric entered Mérida against Hermigarius the Suevian, the king was accompanied by these men, who were devoted to his faithful service.

Idatius records the following about that expedition of Genseric:

“In the fifth year of Theodosius the Younger, the 302nd Olympiad, and the year of Christ 428, King Genseric crossed from the coast of the province of Baetica to Mauritania and Africa with all the Vandals and their families, leaving Spain in the month of May. Before he crossed, he was informed that Hermigarius the Suevian was plundering the neighboring provinces along his route. He turned back with some of his men and caught the plunderer in Lusitania. Not far from Mérida—which Hermigarius had treated with contempt, to the injury of the holy martyr Eulalia—many of those who were with him having been killed by Genseric, he seized what he thought was a swifter means of escape, fled into the river Ana, and perished there, hurled down by the arm of God. When he had thus been destroyed, Genseric immediately resumed the voyage he had begun.”

Arcadius and his companions traveled with him. When Antoninus learned that they had become confessors, he sent them the letters mentioned above. They are commemorated in the Roman and Usuardian martyrologies on November 13.

**2. To Valerian, etc.** Saint Cyril of Alexandria dedicated his *Expositions* to Bishop Valerian, described there as the bishop of Iconium. He was one of the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus against Nestorius, as the subscriptions show. Whether this same man afterward went to Spain and occupied the see of Zaragoza—as we have often seen happen in the case of others, especially Olympius and Isicius—or whether the person mentioned here was another man of the same name is not sufficiently clear. Certainly, we have already established through the testimony of Prudentius that Valerian then held the Church of Zaragoza.

**3. This too, etc.** The mountain mentioned here is called Saint Mammes. On its summit it has a small hermitage, which I visited several times because the place and mountain belong to the monastery of Santa María del Monte de los Ramos in the diocese of Ourense, where I lived for some time. A feast is held there every year on August 7 in honor of Saint Mammes the martyr. Nevertheless, it is commonly believed among the inhabitants of that region that their own Mammes lived on that mountain, so that it might easily be thought that he was a different person from the Caesarean martyr of Cappadocia, whom the Roman Church celebrates on August 17 and the Greeks on September 2.

**4. A dreadful persecution grows, etc.** Idatius reports in his *Chronicle*, under the fourth year of Theodosius the Younger, that Genseric, king of the Vandals, abandoned the Catholic faith that he had first professed and passed over to the doctrine of the Arians. From this his persecution of the Catholics took its origin. Victor of Utica treats the matter at length, as does the Roman Martyrology on various days concerning its fruits.

**5. The cohorts, etc.** Nearly the same words are found under the year of Christ 86. I do not know whether they were inserted here again through the fault of copyists, or whether this was done to mention that cohort as still flourishing at this time against the Vandals and Suevi.

**6. The letters, etc.** Consult what we said about them above under the year of the Lord 116.

**7. At the same time, etc.** Dextrus mentions the Blessed Virgin’s letter to the people of Messana twice: once when it first began to circulate, newly written, under the year of the Lord 86; and again when it was found anew in the archive, as happens here.

**8. At the same time they were brought, etc.** John Marieta writes about its translation in book IV of *The Saints of Spain*, chapter 67. He asserts that its sacred relics are held in great veneration near the city of Vitoria in Cantabria, and that its church lies between Salvatierra—which Dextrus calls *Salvia terra*—and Santa Cruz de Campezo, in the Alava forest, commonly called the Sierra de Alava.

**9. And in that same year, etc.** We said much, and matters highly worthy of knowledge, about Saint Memmius above under the year of the Lord 90; consult that discussion. In the printed Caesaraugustan manuscript, after those words, the text under the year 106 lacked the following: “He preached in Gaul and Spain.” We supplied these words from other manuscripts.

**10. Throughout Spain, etc.** We dealt with Pomponius Paulatus under the year of the Lord 245, and with Caledonius under the year 268.

**11. They flourished, etc.** See what we said about this Isidore under the year of the Lord 423 and earlier under the year 384. There is some difficulty concerning his surname. The printed manuscript of Dextrus calls him first *the Younger* and afterward *the Elder*. I am convinced that this was caused by a copyist’s error. For although the name could easily have been altered by more recent authors—namely, by those who recognized Isidore of Seville, in relation to whom this earlier Isidore of Córdoba ought certainly to have been called *the Elder*—Dextrus, who did not know Isidore of Seville, could not have had him in mind. Therefore, it is certain that Dextrus called this man of Córdoba simply *the Younger*. A different judgment must be made about M. Maximus, his continuator. Since M. Maximus recognized Isidore of Seville, he quite properly called this much earlier Isidore of Córdoba *the Elder*, under the year of Christ 432.

**12. When I was writing this, etc.** Much that could be said here has been noted in the *Apology for this Work*, where we answered those arguments by which some people attempt to draw conclusions against the work’s authenticity. Consult that discussion. The author had brought his *Chronicle* to an end in the year of Christ 430, when he dedicated it to Jerome, as is clear from the letter addressed to Orosius at the beginning of the work. It could not, however, have reached Jerome’s hands, since he had passed to God in 426. Nevertheless, even in the year 433, the eleventh year of Arcadius, nothing certain was being said in Spain about Jerome’s death, as Idatius writes in his *Chronicle*. No one, therefore, should wonder that a *Chronicle* sent to him in 430—four years after his blessed departure—could not have reached his hands.

After Dextrus learned of this some years later, he reviewed his work again, completed it, and enriched it—not in its chronology of years, but in the opinions that he interwove throughout the entire work, as is evident from his recollection of Jerome’s death, which he mentioned under the year of the Lord 426. Thus enriched and enlarged, he dedicated it once more to his friend and kinsman Paulus Orosius, putting the final hand to the work in the year of the Lord 440. This is what he means when he says, “When I was writing this,” and the other chronological indications recorded there correspond to that year: the foundation of Rome, the era of Caesar, and the reign in Spain of Theodoredus, king of the Goths.

For the foundation of the City, as was stated at the beginning, preceded the birth of Christ by 751 years, while the era preceded it by 38 years. Therefore, the year of the Lord 440 must necessarily be the year 1191 from the foundation of Rome and the year 478 of the era of Caesar.

Furthermore, according to Idatius, in the twenty-fourth year of the empire of Arcadius and Honorius, after Walia, king of the Goths, died, Theodoredus succeeded him in the kingdom—Idatius himself calls him *Theodoredus*. That year was the year 418 from the birth of the Lord; from then until 440 there are twenty-two years of Theodoredus’s reign, as recorded by Dextrus.

Sigeric, the successor of Ataulphus, had preceded Walia. Orosius in book VII and M. Maximus under the year of the Lord 435 also recorded this. But because Sigeric spent only a very few days in the kingdom, and perhaps was killed before he had even been crowned, his name is not ordinarily included in the catalog of the kings of the Goths in Spain. Thus Prosper and Idatius, in their *Chronicles*, state simply that Walia succeeded Ataulphus, making no mention of Sigeric.

Idatius says:

“Ataulphus, driven out by the patrician Constantius so that he might leave Narbonne and seek Spain, was murdered by a certain Goth at Barcelona during a private conversation. Walia succeeded him in the kingdom and, having soon made peace with the patrician Constantius, opposed the Alans and the Siling Vandals who were settled in Lusitania and Baetica.”

Constantius was therefore responsible for the Goths’ invasion of Spain. Shortly before, they had made Narbonne the capital of their kingdom with the assent of the Romans. Galla Placidia, the sister of Arcadius and Honorius, who had been captured by Alaric during the sack of Rome, had married Ataulphus, his successor.

Regarding her, Idatius says under the twentieth year of Arcadius:

“Ataulphus took Placidia as his wife at Narbonne.”

In this, people think that Daniel’s prophecy was fulfilled: “The daughter of the king of the South shall be joined to the king of the North, yet no offspring of hers shall remain.” Her husband Ataulphus was indeed murdered shortly after entering Barcelona, together with six sons, by a certain Goth who perhaps begrudged him his Roman stock, during a private conversation. Dextrus asserted this in their epitaph, which remains carved on a marble tomb at Barcelona. Vasaeus in his *Chronicle of Spain*, Morales in book XI, chapter 14, Ludovicus Nonius in his *Spain*, chapter 88, Hieronymus Pujades of Barcelona in his *General History of Catalonia*, and others reproduce it word for word. It reads:

“Here you lie, King Ataulphus, with your six offspring.”

And also:

“Your envious people killed both you and your children.”

From this one may see the prophecy precisely fulfilled in him: he was indeed joined in marriage to the daughter of the king of the South—that is, of the Romans, who, in relation to the northern Goths, lie toward the South—but no offspring of hers remained, since all the sons were killed together with their father. Placidia, however, was restored to her brother Honorius and, by her new husband Constantius Caesar, bore Valentinian the Younger to the imperial power.

Saint Isidore and Lucas of Tuy subscribed to this account in their *Chronicles*, as did Rodrigo of Toledo in book II of his *History of Spain*, chapter 6.

To understand clearly that the Prophet literally spoke about Placidia and Ataulphus, it is worthwhile to examine what he himself relates beforehand. In chapter 10, Daniel first states that the angel who guarded his people, and whom the prince of the kingdom of Persia had resisted for twenty-one days, said to him:

“I have come to teach you what shall happen to your people in the latter days.”

This extends, evidently, from the third year of Cyrus, king of Persia, to the day of the final judgment and resurrection. The final part of the prophecy must necessarily be understood of that time:

“At that time your people shall be saved, every one who is found written in the book. And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life and others to everlasting disgrace.”

At the beginning, however—namely, in chapter 11—he deals with the destruction and weakening of three monarchies, the Persian, Greek, and Roman. The Persian monarchy was destined to come to an end after the fourth king from the time of the vision.

“And now,” he says in chapter 11, “I will announce the truth to you. Behold, three more kings shall arise in Persia, and the fourth shall become exceedingly rich beyond them all. When he has grown strong through his wealth, he shall stir everyone up against the king of Greece.”

This was the downfall of the Persian kingdom and the beginning of the Greek kingdom: Darius, king of the Persians, was defeated by Alexander the Great. Of him Daniel adds:

“But a mighty king shall arise”—namely, of the Greeks—“and shall rule with great power and do whatever he pleases.”

His kingdom, however, was divided at his death among four lesser rulers: Ptolemy, Seleucus, Philip, and Antigonus, as the First Book of Maccabees relates. This was signified to Daniel by the angel in these words:

“When he has arisen”—that is, when Alexander has ascended to the greater fullness of majesty and established the position of his ascent—“his kingdom shall be broken and divided toward the four winds of heaven, but not among his descendants and not according to the power with which he ruled; for his kingdom shall be torn apart even among foreigners.”

Once the Greek kingdom had been torn apart and diminished, the Romans obtained the supremacy. Their king the Prophet appears to call the king of the South, because, in relation to Greece and Macedonia, Italy, the seat of the Roman ruler, lies toward the South.

“And the king of the South shall grow strong,” he says, “and one of his princes shall prevail over him and shall rule with great dominion, for his dominion shall be great.”

But behold the decline of the Roman monarchy. The Romans, harassed by northern peoples—namely, by the Goths—were compelled to enter into peace and friendship with them. This is signified by the words:

“And after the end of the years they shall be joined in alliance.”

Marcellinus discusses this alliance in his *Chronicle* under the third year of Theodosius the Great:

“Athanaric, king of the Goths, with whom the emperor Theodosius had made a treaty, came to Constantinople in the month of January.”

But when war again flared up between them, after Rome had been captured by Alaric, king of the Goths, and among the spoils there was the daughter of that same Theodosius, finally, for the sake of peace, Placidia herself was joined in marriage to Ataulphus, the successor of Alaric. The angel indicates this when he adds:

“And the daughter of the king of the South shall come to the king of the North to make an alliance; but she shall not retain the strength of her arm, nor shall her offspring endure.”

That this was said literally of Placidia and Ataulphus can be denied only by those who refuse to understand the king of the South as the king of the Romans. Let them decide for themselves. It is certain that the Roman monarchy was weakened by none other than the Goths, and the Greek monarchy by none other than the Romans. With equal certainty, therefore, we may understand the king of the North to signify the king of the Goths, since the Goths were born in northern regions and conspired against the Romans.

Daniel is therefore speaking literally of that daughter of the Roman king who, for the sake of peace and alliance, was joined in marriage to the king of the Goths. She was none other than Galla Placidia.

Nor is it an objection that she was captured by the Goths during the sack of the City, whereas Daniel says that she came to make an alliance. Although she was first captured, she was nevertheless joined in marriage willingly and not against her will. For, as Zosimus writes in book VI:

“Placidia, the sister of the emperor”—Honorius—“remained with Alaric, fulfilling in a certain sense the role of a hostage, yet enjoying every honor and royal treatment.”

No force was therefore used against her. She herself willingly offered herself in marriage to Ataulphus for the sake of peace. For, as Orosius says in book VII, chapter 40:

“For this reason Ataulphus strove to abstain from war and to pursue peace, being especially guided and moderated by the persuasion and counsel of Placidia, his wife, a woman of exceptionally keen intelligence, of sufficiently proven religion, and suited to every work of good order.”

The other signs recorded by Daniel are likewise fulfilled in her. “Her offspring shall not endure”: all the sons born to Ataulphus were indeed killed with him, as we have already said.

The following statement also came to pass in Placidia’s case:

“And she shall be surrendered, and those who brought her, her young men.”

For, according to Marcellinus in his *Chronicle* under the consulship of Constantius and Constans, Walia, the successor of Ataulphus, after making peace with the emperor Honorius, restored Placidia, his sister, to him as a widow. There can be no doubt that her young men, who attended her, were restored as well.

The angel then continues his account of the many military conflicts that were to take place between the two kings—the king of the South and the king of the North—which we read as having been fulfilled in the histories of the Romans and Goths. Idatius discusses them specifically, though very briefly, in his *Chronicle*. It would be lengthy and tedious to list them all one by one.

Nevertheless, I should note that Saint Jerome, whom the other interpreters of Daniel followed, thought that the kings of the South and North in this passage were not the Roman and Gothic kings, but the Syrian and Egyptian kings, the divided successors of Alexander of Macedon. A long war was waged between them. The king of Syria was called the king of the North, and the Egyptian king the king of the South, because, in relation to Palestine—the region under discussion—their kingdoms lie toward those directions.

It also happened that the daughter of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, named Berenice, was given in marriage to Antiochus, king of Syria, in order to establish and strengthen peace between them. She had a son by her husband and lost him; and she was surrendered, together with her attendants, to Laodice, her husband’s concubine, who arranged for both of them to be killed by poison and the sword.

On this matter I have nothing else to say except that anyone is free to pass judgment. Both interpretations are probable. Perhaps the sacred text admits both meanings, and both may have been signified by the same words. It is not implausible that Daniel was told for this reason:

“But you, Daniel, close up the words and seal the book until the appointed time. Many shall pass through it, and knowledge shall be multiplied.”

It is as though he had said that their interpretation would be not one but manifold—not merely conjectural in any fashion, but true and grounded in knowledge. For he does not say, “Interpretation shall be multiplied,” but, “Knowledge shall be multiplied.”]

**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** The holy martyrs, natives of Salamanca, cross from Spain to Africa; among them are Arcadius and his companions.

**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** Cyril writes to Valerian [variant: Valerius], bishop of Zaragoza.

**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** At this time the body of Saint Mammes, the Caesarean martyr, was brought to Galicia and is preserved on a high mountain. Others, however, think that it is the body of Saint Mammes the Hermit, who rested there no more than a few years ago.

**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** A dreadful persecution of the Vandals against the Catholics grows in Africa.

**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** Of the cohorts in Spain, the most distinguished at this time is reckoned to be that of the Celtiberians. It is stationed at Brigantium and has Suelli javelin-men from the town of Gelo, corruptly called *Suelli* by the soldiers themselves; they excel in the art of throwing javelins.

**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** The letters of the Blessed Virgin to Saint Ignatius, and Saint Ignatius’ letter to the Most Holy Virgin, are now being handled by the hands of the faithful.

**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** At the same time, a letter written in Hebrew by the Blessed Virgin to those same citizens of Messana was found in the Messanian archive, and it is held in the highest esteem.

**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** At the same time, the sacred relics of the virgin Theodosia, who suffered martyrdom at Caesarea in Palestine under Maximian, were brought to Spain and conveyed with the greatest honor to the obscure town of Hacid in Cantabria, called Salvia terra.
