**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** In that same year the relics of Saint Memmius Mancius, bishop of Évora in Lusitania and the first apostle of that city, were found. After first converting the people of Châlons in Gaul, he crossed into Spain and preached at Évora, where he also suffered martyrdom. He was a Roman citizen and a disciple of Christ. From the year 36 of Christ until the year 106 he preached in Gaul and Spain, and under Trajan he suffered martyrdom, as I have said, for the name of Christ.

**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** The memory of Pomponius Paulatus, Caledonius of Braga, and Lucian, bishop of Zaragoza, was celebrated throughout Spain. Besides being distinguished writers, they took part with other Africans in a council at Carthage and subscribed its acts.

**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** The works of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Córdoba, on Luke and the Kings were flourishing. He died in the year of the Lord 430. He shone with outstanding learning and a reputation for remarkable holiness. He was succeeded in the episcopal see of Córdoba by Gregory, a most holy and learned man, around the year 400. He was bishop for thirty years.

**A.D. 430. Era 1181.** When I was writing this, King Theodoredus was reigning in Spain. His twenty-second year was in progress; the year from the foundation of Rome was 1191, from Christ 440, and in the era 478. I was then eighty-two years old, already entering decrepitude. This king succeeded Walia, Walia succeeded Sigeric, and Sigeric succeeded Ataulphus, who was killed at Barcelona, our native city, on August 21 in the year 416. In his memory I composed this poem:

> Born from the mighty warlike race of the Goths,  
> Here you lie, King Ataulphus, with your six sons.  
> You were the first to dare descend to the Spanish shores,  
> And many thousands of men accompanied you.  
> Your envious people then killed both you and your sons;  
> Afterwards great Barcelona embraced you, mourning.

# APPENDIX

## ON DANIEL’S PROPHECY OF THE FOUR ANIMALS (S)*

### § I. Introduction

While I was examining the aforementioned prophecy of Daniel as expounded by Idatius, I came upon another prophecy, far more excellent, contained in chapter 7 of that holy prophet: the prophecy of the four mystical animals, or kingdoms, shown to him together. Its fulfillment appears in every respect to refer to these very times, with which we are now dealing in connection with Dextrus, and to the entry of the barbarians into Spain and the Gothic kings who ruled there.

Let the reader not be astonished, I ask, or become distrustful when he hears that something in Spain was foreseen by the prophets for fulfillment. Spain is no less worthy of prophetic predictions than Egypt, Ethiopia, and other barbarian nations, concerning which many things are found foretold by the prophets. And certainly, if—as is certain—the prophecies are to be understood chiefly as directed toward the progress and advancement of the Church, why, I ask, would the prophets have passed over in silence what we see so gloriously in Spain: the increase of the faith and its dominion, founded upon the deepest roots?

Was it then such an insignificant matter that the Christian faith should have been exceptionally and uniquely revered there from the beginning of the nascent Church, and cultivated, defended, and propagated with a purity surpassed by nothing, so that nothing about it should be recorded in the sacred Scriptures?

But let us grant that nothing concerning it is found among the other prophets—a matter which we have nevertheless discussed more than once in these commentaries. Surely such a great matter ought to have been treated by Daniel, to whom, among the other chroniclers of the Church, a special prerogative was given. For while the others dealt with matters pertaining either solely to the Jewish people or to the mysteries of the faith in respect of their substance—as may be seen in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the rest—Daniel, like a new and universal chronicler among the prophets, wrote uniquely and with the greatest precision about the monarchies and kingdoms that would rule throughout the world, about the number of their kings, and about their chronology.

Thus, in chapter 2, under the image of the statue seen by Nebuchadnezzar—a statue with a golden head, a silver chest and arms, a bronze belly and thighs, iron legs, and feet partly of iron and partly of clay—he ingeniously discussed the four principal monarchies of the world, namely those of the Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, and Romans. He also treated specifically, in chapter 5, the swift end of the Assyrian or Chaldean monarchy, explaining the three words that the monarch Belshazzar saw written on the wall during a public banquet.

In chapter 6 he gave the chronology of the twelve months after which Nebuchadnezzar was to undergo his transformation. In chapter 8, under the figures of the ram and the he-goat fighting one another, he discussed the power of the Persian kingdom and the beginnings of the Greek kingdom under Alexander the Great, extending to Antiochus; he also treated the innumerable evils inflicted by Antiochus upon the people of God in the time of the Maccabees, and Antiochus’ miserable death.

Again, in chapter 9, he foretold that the kingdom of the Jews would endure for sixty-nine weeks—that is, nearly five hundred years. I leave aside what we have just explained with Idatius concerning the disputes between the kings of the South and North and the events affecting the people of God until the end of the ages, which are related by the prophet himself in chapters 10, 11, and 12.

Since it was therefore proper to the prophet Daniel to deal with great kingdoms and monarchies that would rule in the world until its end, how could he have kept silent about the one kingdom of the kings of Spain that has spread most widely throughout the world, subjected another world to the faith, and appears more than the others to concern the growth, defense, and glory of the Church?

I have said this so that no one may recoil at once from the novelty of the interpretation, but may read patiently. For everything that Daniel foretold in that chapter 7 under discussion will be seen to have been fulfilled in Spain—although no one has hitherto found it verified anywhere. The earlier interpretations, even by the admission of their own authors, are full of obvious contradictions; whereas the interpretation that we embrace distributes and explains everything easily and coherently.

To proceed in an orderly fashion, however, it is necessary first to set out the actual context of the prophetic prediction and what others have thought it signifies. After we have shown that none of those interpretations fits the words of the prophecy, we shall finally, God willing, propose and defend our own interpretation. In it, I hope, there will be nothing that does not accord with the prophetic words, nothing forced, and nothing accommodated by violence.

### § II. Daniel’s Prophecy, Chapter 7

In the first year of Belshazzar, king of Babylon, Daniel saw a dream. The vision of his head came to him upon his bed, and, writing down the dream, he summarized it in brief language and gave the following condensed account:

“I was watching in my night vision, and behold, the four winds of heaven were fighting upon the great sea, and four great beasts were coming up from the sea, different from one another.

“The first was like a lioness and had the wings of an eagle. I watched until its wings were plucked out; it was lifted from the earth, stood upon its feet like a man, and a human heart was given to it.

“And behold, another beast, like a bear, stood on one side; three rows were in its mouth and in its teeth, and they were saying to it: ‘Rise, devour much flesh.’

“After this I watched, and behold, another beast like a leopard, and it had wings like a bird—four of them upon it—and the beast had four heads, and authority was given to it.

“After this I watched in the night vision, and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and extraordinary, and exceedingly strong. It had great iron teeth; it was eating and crushing, and trampling the remainder under its feet. It was different from all the other beasts that I had seen before it, and it had ten horns.

“I was considering the horns, and behold, another little horn arose from among them, and three of the first horns were plucked up before it. And behold, eyes like human eyes were in this horn, and a mouth speaking great things.”

I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat down. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head was like clean wool. His throne was flames of fire; its wheels were burning fire. A stream of fire, swift-flowing, issued from before him. A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him. The court sat, and the books were opened.

I watched because of the sound of the great words that the horn was speaking. I saw that the beast was slain, its body perished, and it was given over to be burned with fire. As for the other beasts, their dominion was taken away, but an extension of life was allotted to them for a time and a season.

Then I watched in the night vision, and behold, one like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven. He came as far as the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And to him was given dominion, honor, and a kingdom; all peoples, tribes, and languages would serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.

My spirit shuddered. I, Daniel, was terrified by these things, and the visions of my head troubled me. I approached one of those who stood by and sought the truth from him concerning all these things. He told me the interpretation of the words and instructed me:

“These four great beasts are four kingdoms that shall arise from the earth. But the saints of the Most High God shall receive the kingdom, and they shall possess the kingdom forever and ever.”

After this I wished to learn carefully about the fourth beast, which was very different from all the others and exceedingly terrifying. Its teeth and claws were of iron; it devoured and crushed, and trampled the remainder with its feet. I also wished to learn about the ten horns that it had on its head, and about the other horn that had arisen, before which three horns had fallen; and about that horn which had eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and which was larger than the others.

I watched, and behold, that horn made war against the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days came and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High. Then the time arrived, and the saints obtained the kingdom.

And he said:

“The fourth beast shall be a fourth kingdom on earth, which shall be greater than all the kingdoms. It shall devour the whole earth, trample it down, and crush it. As for the ten horns of that kingdom, they shall be ten kings; and another shall arise after them. He shall be more powerful than the earlier ones, shall humble three kings, speak words against the Most High, and crush the saints of the Most High. He shall think that he can change times and laws, and they shall be delivered into his hand for a time, times, and half a time. But the court shall sit, so that his dominion may be taken away, crushed, and destroyed utterly.

“Then the kingdom, dominion, and greatness of the kingdom beneath the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High. His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all kings shall serve and obey him.”

Thus far the end of the account. I, Daniel, was greatly troubled by my thoughts, and my face changed within me; but I kept the matter in my heart.

## § III. What in the Vulgate and common interpretation of this prophecy appears to contradict its own words

This prophecy contains chiefly three subjects: the history of the four animals, or kingdoms; the solemn judgment held by God; and, finally, the handing over of an everlasting and unending kingdom to his people, the saints.

Until now there has been remarkable agreement among all interpreters of Daniel in explaining these matters. The older Fathers paved the way for the others—those whom Saint Jerome, together with Eusebius of Caesarea, mentions in the prologue to Daniel: Theodoret, Bede, and Rupert. Albert the Great, Hugh of Saint-Cher, Nicholas of Lyra, and all the more recent interpreters followed in their footsteps: Hector Pintus, Pereira, Cornelius a Lapide, and others.

They therefore agree in asserting that those four animals symbolically foreshadowed the four best-known monarchies: the Assyrian, Persian, Greek, and Roman monarchies. Once these had finally been removed from the midst, the universal judgment of the human race would be held, and the eternal kingdom would be handed over to the saints and elect.

Accordingly, they maintain that the final horn of the fourth beast must be Antichrist, since the following words suit him:

“He shall speak words against the Most High and crush the saints of the Most High.”

They also apply to him the words:

“I saw that the beast was slain, its body perished, and it was given over to be burned with fire”—

especially when the Son of Man came with the clouds of heaven, when the thrones were set in place and the Ancient of Days sat down, and when the court sat and the books were opened.

Only the Rabbis have so far dissented from this view. They maintain that the saints to whom the kingdom was given after the beast was slain were the Maccabees, and that the last king who persecuted them was signified by the horn—namely, Antiochus.

But Antiochus was not the eleventh king of his realm, as would have been necessary if he were foreshadowed by that horn. Nor can anything else be suitably accommodated to this explanation. But let us leave the vain Jews; they will remain all the more thoroughly defeated by the refutation of the other opinion.

That other interpretation, however, contains so many elements that fail to cohere that anyone can easily form a judgment about it. Certainly the older Fathers have a legitimate excuse for embracing it, since in their time the prophecy had not yet been fulfilled. The more recent interpreters, on the other hand, are not without excuse for following so many and such distinguished leaders, although they encountered immense difficulties—appropriating to themselves Plutarch’s saying: “If we have erred, we had great leaders.”

Certainly Jerome does not so much follow that common interpretation concerning the four monarchies as report and refute it. Overcome by the difficulties, he prefaced the beginning of his commentary on this chapter with these words:

“In the earlier chapters, the order of history is followed: what happened under Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, and Darius—or Cyrus—in the matter of miraculous signs. But in these chapters—that is, from chapter 7 through chapter 12—dreams are narrated that appeared to particular persons at particular times. The prophet alone is aware of them, and among barbarian nations they possess no great significance or revelatory force; they are described merely so that the memory of what was seen may endure among later generations.”

But what is not verified in the monarchies just mentioned? I shall touch briefly on many points.

First, all four kingdoms signified by the beasts are predicted by the angel as being about to arise:

“These four great beasts are four kingdoms that shall arise from the earth.”

But this could not have been said of those monarchies at the time of the prophecy, since the Babylonian, or Chaldean, monarchy had not merely already arisen but was almost dead, given that this vision is said to have been shown in the first year of Belshazzar, king of Babylon, in which that predicted monarchy came to an end—as Daniel himself testifies in chapter 5.

Moreover, these animals arose together from the sea, agitated by the blasts of the winds. “I watched,” he says, “in my vision, and behold, the four winds of heaven were fighting upon the great sea, and four great beasts were ascending from the sea, different from one another.”

Those monarchies, however, did not arise together, but successively over the course of many years. Each later one arose through the destruction of the earlier: the Persians subdued the Assyrians, or Chaldeans; after 230 years of Persian rule, a Greek army under Alexander destroyed the Persians; at Alexander’s death his monarchy was divided into three kingdoms—the Syrian, Macedonian, and Egyptian. Having become more powerful than these, the Romans established and preserved a monarchy for five hundred years, from the Second Punic War until the destruction of the city by Alaric in the year 1164 from the founding of Rome.

Again, when each beast is applied to a particular monarchy, new ambiguities arise.

Of the second beast it is said that there were three rows of teeth in its mouth. But this would apply more readily to the third monarchy, that of the Greeks, than to the second. For the Greek monarchy was divided, as I have said, into three kingdoms warring against one another; this did not happen to the second monarchy.

They reply that the detail is fulfilled in the three Persian princes who presided over 120 satraps. Through them, they say, the entire empire was governed, as Daniel himself testifies in chapter 6.

But I ask: what flesh were they ordered to devour? We read nothing of their cruelty. Indeed, Daniel himself was one of the three, since chapter 6 says:

“Darius was pleased and appointed 120 satraps over the kingdom, to be throughout his entire kingdom, and over them three princes, one of whom was Daniel.”

Let them consider what sort of cruelty they attribute to him, so that the words “Arise, eat much flesh” may in some fashion truly be applied to him.

Furthermore, what does it mean that the third beast is said to have had four heads and the same number of wings? It is certainly clear that there were neither only four nor only eight kings in the Greek monarchy; and Alexander’s empire was divided into only three kingdoms.

As for the fourth beast, which is described as more terrifying than the others, they maintain that it signifies the Roman Empire. But nothing could be more difficult, since that beast is said to have only eleven kings until the judgment. How many decades of Roman emperors were there? For the angel explained to Daniel that the horns represented an equal number of kings of that fourth kingdom.

Moreover, let them decide whether they wish to make Antichrist a Roman emperor and the last king of his monarchy, since it is asserted of the eleventh horn of the fourth beast that it will be the final king of the kingdom signified by it:

“The ten horns of that kingdom shall be ten kings; and another shall arise after them. He shall be more powerful than the earlier ones, shall humble three kings, and shall speak words against the Most High,” and so forth.

The opinion expressed by Annius of Viterbo in his questions on the Apocalypse is no more substantial: he claimed that the final horn signified Muhammad, the false prophet. None of the things said about that horn is fulfilled in Muhammad. He was not the last ruler of that fourth monarchy, as is said of the horn, but the beginning of a new one. He did not follow ten other kings, did not humble three of them, and we do not read that any judgment was carried out at his death or that his body was burned with fire.

Furthermore, who does not see that the judgment foreseen by Daniel in this passage is wrongly interpreted as the final judgment of the entire human race? Christ the Lord is not appointed judge in it, although faith teaches that he will be judge at the end. Rather, it is the eternal Father—the first Person of the most holy Trinity.

Nor is the human race brought before that judgment to receive rewards or punishments individually according to its deeds. Instead, it is the Redeemer of the human race himself who is presented, since he is said to have been offered to his Father.

Here are the prophet’s words:

“I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat down; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head was like clean wool.”

This is plainly a vivid and most fitting representation of the eternal Father. The prophet then adds the number of those standing before him:

“A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him.”

Everyone can see that this refers to the angelic spirits who minister to God.

But who is said to have been presented at so great a judgment?

“I watched,” he says, “and behold, one like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven and came as far as the Ancient of Days.”

Was he a judge about to sit, before whom human beings were to be brought? Certainly not. He himself was presented to the Judge, and they presented him before him.

A favorable sentence was then pronounced on his behalf:

“And he gave him”—the Father and Judge—“dominion, honor, and a kingdom; all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.”

Then, after the beast was slain, the kingdom was given to the people of the saints of the Most High.

It is also very important to note that at the end of the vision it is expressly asserted that, after the judgment shown to Daniel, many kings would rule beneath heaven and would serve and obey the monarchy of the people of the saints.

Therefore, the final kingdom, or monarchy, of the people of the saints under discussion here cannot in any way signify the heavenly joys of the blessed. For after the kingdom of heaven has been bodily received by them, no people or king could remain beneath heaven, whereas the prophet declares that many peoples and kings will remain under it, in these words:

“The court shall sit, so that dominion may be taken away, crushed, and destroyed utterly. But the kingdom, dominion, and greatness of the kingdom beneath the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, and all kings shall serve and obey him.”

He does not say that this kingdom is to be above heaven or contained in heaven, but beneath the whole heaven, with all kings obeying it.

The statement that the beast’s dominion “shall perish utterly” also makes clear that the end of the world still lies ahead after that judgment, and that the world has not yet ended.

Furthermore, once the judgment had been completed and the fourth beast slain, it is said of the other three that life was granted to them for a fixed period, though without power or dominion:

“As for the other beasts, their dominion was taken away, but an extension of life was allotted to them for a time and a season.”

No one would dare assert that, after the universal judgment, some nations would be left beneath heaven for a time in this present life.

Thus, whether we examine individually the beasts, the judgment, or the kingdom given afterward to the people of the saints, the common interpretation appears to suffer innumerable and insurmountable difficulties. In the interpretation that we shall now set forth, all these difficulties cease: everything coheres with the vision, everything corresponds, and in every part there is found a remarkable agreement with the reality signified.

Moreover, the origin and destruction of those four monarchies had already been shown in chapter 2 under the symbol of the statue seen by Nebuchadnezzar, made from four different metals. It is therefore unlikely that Daniel would again record the same matter in writing, especially since the angel did not explain this as a vision of the same thing, but of something new and different. Let us therefore seek what else is signified here.

## § IV. A new and exact interpretation of the same prophecy concerning the Alans, Vandals, Sueves, and Goths invading Spain; and concerning the Catholic monarchy

Come, then, let us now explain Daniel’s prophetic vision concerning the barbarians invading Spain. Jerome himself noted that barbarian nations are signified by these beasts, saying:

“The savagery and cruelty of kingdoms are represented by the name of beasts.”

Accordingly, in the year of the Lord 409, in the Caesarean Era 447, in the fifteenth year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, during the eighth consulship of Honorius and the third of Theodosius, son of Arcadius, on the third day before the Ides of October, which was also a Tuesday, the Alans, Vandals, and Sueves—three barbarian nations—entered Spain.

In the year of the Lord 416, which was the Caesarean Era 454 and the twenty-second year of the reign of the emperors just mentioned, the Goths, under their king Ataulphus, entered the same country.

All authors agree on these facts. The most exact writer on the subject was also an eyewitness, Hydatius, bishop of Lamego, whose guidance and stimulus led us to undertake this work.

The four beasts ascending from the sea are therefore these four barbarian nations, raised up at that time for the destruction of Spain, when almost the entire world was shaken, as though from its four corners, under the figure of the same number of winds, and tyrants everywhere, breathing war, conspired against the Roman Empire.

Indeed, the fact that they are said to have been stirred up by four winds is fulfilled literally in this respect: two generals who rebelled against two emperors brought the four beasts mentioned above against the Roman Empire from the most distant lands.

For the count Stilicho, despising the emperor Honorius and coveting his realm, stirred up the peoples of the Alans, Sueves, and Vandals against Honorius’s kingdom, enticing them with gifts and money. Rufinus, meanwhile, while plotting against the emperor Arcadius, made Alaric, king of the Goths, hostile to the state.

These are the words of Marcellinus Comes in his Chronicle, under the years of the Lord 395 and 408.

The statement that they later ascended from the sea is explained by the angel as meaning that the sea itself signifies the world, since what are first said to have ascended from the sea are later said to have arisen from the earth.

Nevertheless, it can also easily be understood that these nations entered Spain from the sea by way of the four winds of heaven, since Spain is almost entirely surrounded by seas. We know that the Alans occupied the western region, namely Lusitania; the Vandals the southern region, that is, Baetica; the Sueves the northern region, namely Galicia and Asturias; and the Goths entered from the east, at Barcelona.

To this may be added the fact that nowhere else in the world are four barbarian nations found to have entered together except Spain. Although the Alans, Vandals, Sueves, and Goths also entered Italy, Gaul, and Germany, they did not enter those lands alone, as they did Spain. The Huns and Heruli entered together with them, and later the Lombards; all of these, however, kept away from Spain.

Thus only in Spain did four nations enter—neither more nor fewer. Most importantly, all the circumstances of the prophecy are fulfilled in Spain alone.

First, the order of the beasts corresponds to the order of the nations entering Spain. Hydatius and Orosius name them in this order. Hydatius says:

“The Alans, Vandals, and Sueves entered Spain,”

and, seven years later:

“Ataulphus with the Goths entered Barcelona.”

Orosius, in book 7, at the end, says:

“Although the kings of the Alans, Vandals, and Sueves had made an agreement with us on the same terms,” and so forth.

The first beast therefore signifies the Alans, the second the Vandals, the third the Sueves, and the fourth the Goths—and with complete precision, since the distinctive signs of each one are described.

### The first beast: the Alans

The first beast is said to have had three characteristics.

1. It was like a lioness, since it considered itself queen of the others; for among animals the lion possesses dominion.

2. It had the wings of an eagle, that is, a proud king; for the eagle is an emblem of a king. Just as kings are signified by the horns and heads of beasts, so they are signified by wings. In general, by an equal principle of interpretation, whatever they are said to have above them represents kings.

3. Its feathers were quickly stripped away, and royal dignity was taken from it:

“I watched until its wings were plucked out, and it was lifted from the earth; it stood upon two feet like a man.”

This means that it came to support others, having embraced servitude. The creature that had been the most arrogant of all, boasting greatly of itself and assuming the savagery of a wild beast, became gentle and tractable.

This is what is meant by the words:

“And the heart of a man was given to it.”

The Alans are represented by this symbol in every respect.

They had power over the Vandals and Sueves and despised the Goths. When the Vandals and Sueves together occupied Galicia alone, the Alans received the more important provinces of Spain, namely Carthaginensis and Lusitania.

“The Vandals occupy Galicia,” says Hydatius, under the year of the Lord 411, “and the Sueves [occupy] the western region situated at the edge of the Ocean; the Alans, the provinces of Lusitania and Carthaginensis.”

We have, then, a sufficiently exact representation of the Alans in the lioness possessing eagle’s wings. But how do we derive their swift abolition from the passage? How many years, I ask, did their pride fly? They did not complete ten, if Hydatius is to be believed. In the year of the Lord 418, the twenty-fourth year of Arcadius and Honorius, he writes:

“The Alans, who held power over the Vandals and Sueves, were so thoroughly defeated by the Goths that, after their king Atace—called Ajax by others—had been killed, the few survivors, with the name of their kingdom abolished”—behold how their wings were overturned—“submitted themselves under the protection of Gunderic, king of the Vandals, who had settled in Galicia.”

Thus it is verified in that nation that it stood upon its feet like a man and was given a human heart.

They were destroyed by Wallia, king of the Goths, who in that same year, to use Hydatius’s words, “for the sake of the Roman name inflicted the greatest slaughter upon the barbarians within Spain.”

Some believe that the Catalans are so called as though they were “Goth-Alans,” because the Alans, subjected to the Goths, occupied that part of Spain and both peoples gave their name to the province.

Some may also find it pleasing, and not without mystery, that the Alans are signified by the lioness mentioned above, so that the name of the beast would indicate the name of the nation signified. Someone may perhaps wish to make the same observation about the first letter of the second beast and the corresponding nation, namely that the Vandals are signified by the bear. But let us pursue stronger arguments.

### The second beast: the Vandals

Three features are also said of the second beast, and they fit the Vandals exactly.

1. It was like a bear. In this image, according to Daniel’s interpreters, a frugal diet accompanied by hardness and ferocity is indicated.

2. There were three rows in its mouth and teeth. This signifies that the kingdom was to be divided into three parts and would exercise ferocity everywhere.

3. Finally, it alone among the other beasts was told:

“Arise, eat much flesh.”

These three characteristics rightly apply to the Vandals. Salvian of Marseilles, in book 7 of *On Providence*, praises especially their frugality of life—signified by the symbol of the bear—and the chastity that follows from it.

They are said to have had three rows of teeth in their mouth because, while each of the other nations never separated from itself, the Vandals occupied three different provinces.

First, some of the Vandals settled near the Sueves in Galicia; others, called the Silingi, turned toward Baetica; finally, the stronger among them seized and devastated Africa.

We are taught to believe this from Orosius, Isidore, and Hydatius. The words of the latter, followed by the other two, are these:

“In the seventeenth year of Arcadius and Honorius: the Vandals occupy Galicia; the Sueves and Alans, the provinces of Lusitania and Carthaginensis; and the Vandals called Silingi receive Baetica, from whom Vandalusia later began to be named.

“Then, in the fifth year of Theodosius, King Gaiseric crossed from the coast of the province of Baetica to Mauretania and Africa, together with all the Vandals and their families, leaving Spain in the month of May.”

Everywhere, however, they exercised their teeth—that is, their ferocity—against the servants of Christ, plundering all their possessions and cruelly slaughtering the wretched.

Earlier we spoke of Saint Vincent of Caurium in Baetica, crowned with martyrdom by the Vandals, and of the holy martyrs Arcadius and his companions, killed by the same people. Concerning those whom they slaughtered at Braga, the metropolitan city of Galicia, Hydatius himself writes under the years of the Lord 420 and 427.

And as though they had eaten too little Christian flesh, they are again ordered to arise and eat much flesh. This signifies that the Vandals rose from the settlements they had previously held in Spain and crossed over into Africa, where they launched that famous persecution, now called Vandalic, to introduce Arianism. It consecrated many tens of thousands of martyrs to God and was recorded by Victor of Vita.

For this reason the Vandalic beast was certainly told, “Eat much flesh,” something that is said of none of the other beasts.

It alone also seems to fit the statement that it “stood in one part,” namely because, while the others remained in Spain, the Vandals alone were separated from them and moved to another region—that is, to Africa.

### The third beast: the Sueves

In the third beast there are just as many noteworthy features as in the others.

1. It was like a leopard. Since the leopard belongs to the lion’s kind, it signifies royal majesty.

2. It had wings like a bird, four above it, and the beast also had four heads. Since whatever the kingdom typified by the beast is said to have above it represents its king, the four wings and four heads above the third beast signify eight kings who, in the course of time, would govern that kingdom.

3. It is specifically written of this beast that “dominion was given to it,” although this was not said of the first two. This clearly indicates that the nation signified by this beast would establish and possess a particular kingdom, extending over a long period through the lives of many kings.

Nothing could represent the Sueves more precisely. They possessed a distinct kingdom in Spain, which neither the Alans nor the Vandals established. They eventually reached such great power that M. Maximus writes of their king Rechila in his Chronicle under the year of the Lord 448:

“Rechila, king of the Sueves, becomes almost monarch of the whole of Spain.”

Their kingdom lasted from the year 411, when they withdrew into Galicia, until the third year of the emperor Maurice and the year of Christ 588, according to John of Biclaro in his Chronicle; or, as M. Maximus says, until the year of the Lord 586, when they were subdued by Leovigild, king of the Goths, after 177 or 179 years of Galician rule. During that period they maintained their royal court at Braga.

For this reason some now call the inhabitants of that province Sevos, as though they were Sueves.

Throughout the aforementioned period of 177 years, they are said to have had only eight kings, in the following order:

I. Hermenricus, the first to establish the throne of the Suevic kingdom in Spain. According to Hydatius, he lived until the year of the Lord 440 and left his son Rechila as successor to the kingdom.

II. Rechila died in the year of the Lord 447, the twenty-fourth year of Theodosius the Younger.

III. He was succeeded by his son Ricciarius, who was killed in the second year of the reign of Emperor Marcian, in December, by Theodoric, king of the Goths.

IV. After Ricciarius died without a successor, Maldra was chosen by the Sueves. He was killed in the fourth year of his reign.

V. He was succeeded by Remismundus.

VI. Remismundus was succeeded by Arianimirus, or Theodomirus, distinguished by a double name because at first he favored the Arians, but afterward confessed the divinity of Christ. Hence he was first called Arianimirus and later Theodomirus.

VII. Miro assumed the government of the Sueves.

VIII. Evoricus, under whom the entire line of Suevic kings, together with the crown, came to an end.

Thus the account is drawn from Hydatius, M. Maximus, Biclaro, and Isidore. Although some writers, including Maximus, vary in arranging the kings—for he places Ricciarius not third after Rechila but fifth, between Remismundus and Arianimirus—no one increases or diminishes the number eight.

The four tyrants who attempted on several occasions to seize the kingdom must be excluded from this number: Frantanes rebelled against King Maldra; Fumarius against Remismundus; Andeca against Miro; and finally Malluricus against Andeca. All authors unanimously call them tyrants, not kings.

Thus the third beast, the Suevic leopard, had four wings above it and four heads, and dominion was given to it. Dominion is not said to have been given either to the Vandals or the Alans, since their wings were quickly plucked away and they “stood in one part”: the Alans were destroyed in Lusitania before they obtained a succession of kings, while the Vandals withdrew to Africa.

But why are the first four Suevic kings called wings and the last four heads, rather than all being called heads or all wings?

As I understand it, the reason is that the first four plundered different and distant provinces of Spain with incredible speed, while the later kings, having attained peace, governed their peoples quietly.

Hermenricus repeatedly ravaged those parts of Galicia that were not under his rule. Rechila first reached Mérida and afterward attacked the provinces of Baetica and Carthaginensis. Ricciarius devastated the Basque country and then Zaragoza and Lérida. Maldra plundered Lisbon and the whole of Lusitania, as Hydatius records in his account of his deeds.

But Remismundus, Arianimirus, Miro, and Evoricus are recorded as having cared only for their own kingdom.

Therefore the first four kings are most precisely represented by the four wings, and the later four by the four heads. They are not all called wings or all called heads.

### The fourth beast: the Goths

Finally, we shall speak of the fourth beast, in which Daniel foresaw four noteworthy features.

1. It was more astonishing and terrifying than the others and exceedingly strong, since it had large iron teeth and likewise iron claws. With its mouth and feet alike it crushed, trampled, and tore apart everything placed before it.

2. It was unlike the others and, so far as we know, had no definite form.

3. It had ten horns, after which another small horn arose among them.

Much is said about this horn: it grew so large that it became greater than the other horns; three horns fell at its appearance; it had eyes like human eyes; and it also had a mouth speaking great—or immense—things.

4. Finally, because of the sound of the great words spoken by that horn, the beast was slain, its body perished, and it was given over to be burned with fire.

We are led to understand it through the angelic interpretation given to Daniel:

“The fourth beast shall be a fourth kingdom on earth, which shall be greater than all the kingdoms. It shall devour the whole earth, trample it down, and crush it. The ten horns of that kingdom shall be ten kings; and another shall arise after them. He shall be more powerful than the earlier ones, shall humble three kings, speak words against the Most High, and crush the saints of the Most High.”

Regarding the pride and duration of his rule, the angel adds:

“He shall think that he can change times and laws, and they shall be delivered into his hand”—

namely, the saints, of whom he had earlier said that the horn “made war against the saints and prevailed over them.”

For how long? Until the end. Then at last the kingdom, dominion, and greatness beneath the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High. All kings shall serve and obey that people, and its kingdom shall be everlasting.

It is truly remarkable how well all these details fit the Gothic people and their kings reigning in Spain.

They are the fourth beast and the fourth kingdom, since they entered Spain after the other three nations. They were stronger and more ferocious than the others and inflicted greater slaughter in Spain. They were unlike the rest and did not present the definite form of any animal—that is, neither of a lioness, nor a bear, nor a leopard, nor any other beast that could clearly be described.

They did not enter Spain as enemies and plunderers, as the other barbarian nations did, but under the title of defenders of the Roman Empire, although they deceived everyone and attempted to drive the Romans from Spain no less than the other peoples.

Concerning the barbarians acting under the Roman name, Hydatius writes under the twenty-third year of Arcadius and Honorius, the second year after the Goths’ entry:

“Wallia, king of the Goths, inflicted the greatest slaughter upon the barbarians within Spain for the sake of the Roman name.”

In the following year he writes:

“The Silingian Vandals in Baetica were all destroyed by King Wallia. The Alans also were so thoroughly defeated by the Goths that, after their king had been killed, they submitted themselves to the protection of the Vandals.”

Who would not have called the Goths the most faithful auxiliaries of the Romans? Yet nothing could have been further from their intentions. When the opportunity arose, they betrayed to the Vandals, through fraud and deception, the Roman army that they had openly promised to assist—at the very moment when victory was already being spoken of.

Hydatius is also a witness to this. Under the twenty-eighth year of Arcadius he says:

“Castinus, master of the Roman soldiery, brought war against the Vandals in Baetica with a large force and with Gothic auxiliaries. When he had pressed them so severely by the force of the siege that they were already preparing to surrender, he rashly engaged them in open battle and, deceived by the treachery of the auxiliaries, fled defeated to Tarragona.”

Since, therefore, no one recognized the fourth beast as the Goths, it is not surprising that its appearance is not described but is said to be unlike the others.

As for the number of kings of this nation, symbolized by the ten horns, it had ten—neither more nor fewer—from Ataulf, who was the first of the Goths to enter Spain, down to Liuba, whom Leovigild succeeded as the eleventh. Whatever is said concerning the eleventh horn is verified to the letter in him, as I shall soon show. The first was, as we have said, Ataulf, who was killed at Barcelona in A.D. 416. II. Wallia, who reigned for two years and died in 418. III. Theodored, who was killed and died in A.D. 455. IV. His son Thorism, or Thorismund, who was killed the following year. V. His brother Theodoric succeeded him; he was slaughtered in 464 by his brother Euric. VI. Euric himself, who died at Arles in Gothic Gaul in A.D. 482, and was succeeded by Alaric. VII. Alaric reigned for twenty-three years, until A.D. 506. VIII. His son Amalaric succeeded him, the grandson through his daughter of Theodoric, king of Italy; he was still an infant and did not exceed the age of a boy. At that time Theodoric governed Spain on behalf of his grandson. IX. Athanagild, who held the reins of government until the second year of Justin the Younger, namely A.D. 567, when, as Viclarensis says, Athanagild, king of the Goths, ended his life in Spain, and Liuba was elevated to the throne in his place. Liuba was therefore the tenth among the Gothic kings of Spain. For all these matters I have three eyewitness authorities: Idatius, Maximus, and John of Biclaro.

[Col. 0586C] There are, however, some who place Sigeric after Ataulf and before Wallia. Yet he did not ascend the royal throne, and for that reason he is not admitted by Prosper and Idatius into the catalogue of the Gothic kings. We have said enough about him above. During Amalaric’s minority, Gesalec likewise seized his kingdom, but Theodoric, who was administering the government, resisted his tyranny. Gesalec, however, died as an exile and wanderer in Gaul in A.D. 510. Isidore, whom more recent writers follow, adds three others before Athanagild—namely Theudis, Theudisclus, and Agila. Yet they were tyrants rather than true kings, and for that reason Marcus Maximus, who followed Gothic affairs more precisely in chronological order, excluded them from the catalogue of kings, judging them unworthy of so great an honor. Lucas of Tuy did the same; indeed, according to his testimony, Isidore too did so, although Lucas copied Isidore’s Chronicle word for word from purer originals, as appears, than those now extant. For certainly the Chronicle of the Goths that survives among Isidore’s works under his name is riddled with innumerable errors in its dates, names, order and succession of kings, and other matters—errors that anyone can readily detect by comparing it with the councils, Idatius, Viclarensis, and the other authorities. Thus there were only ten Gothic kings down to Liuba.

Nevertheless, while Liuba was reigning, Leovigild—the eleventh horn—received a part of the kingdom. Of him it could truly be said: “Behold, another little horn arose from among them.” For he established a small kingdom for himself in the midst of his brother’s kingdom. Viclarensis, the chronicler of his deeds, recorded it thus:

> In the third year of Justin the Younger, Leovigild, the brother of King Liuba, was appointed, while his brother was still alive, to the kingdom of Nearer Spain.

Moreover, after his rise three kings fell: Liuba of the Goths, and Miro and Evoric of the Suevi. He added their kingdoms to his own, as the same Viclarensis writes. Thus the following was fulfilled in him: “Another horn had arisen, before which three horns had fallen, and it was greater than the others.” It was much greater, since he was the first of all to bring under his power the whole of Spain, which had previously been subject to many kings and various princes. To accomplish this, he had to subjugate by war Vasconia, Bastetania, the region of Malaga, the territory of Córdoba, and that of Sidonia, along with other provinces and cities; destroy the kingdom of the Suevi, who held power in Galicia; and finally add Narbonese Gaul to his dominions. Hence he is most appropriately said to have devoured the whole earth, trampled it underfoot, and crushed it.

He also spoke great and enormous things against the Most High, pouring forth blasphemies against the divinity of Christ, as the champion of the Arians. For this reason he waged war against the saints and prevailed over them. Nothing could be truer or more consistent with the text. For the unanimous testimony of the authorities is that Leovigild declared the fiercest war against the Catholics, whose cause his son Hermenegild had undertaken to defend, and that he continually prevailed against them.

Hear the words of Marcus Maximus, who committed to writing what he himself had seen:

> In A.D. 580 Hermenegild undertakes the defense of the Catholics. Again, when public war was declared between his father Leovigild and Prince Hermenegild—for his father had warned him, in the cause of the Catholic peoples, not to revolt from him—Leovigild besieges his son at Seville. Through the treachery of the Romans he is handed over to his father, and after being held in harsh imprisonment at Seville, bound and shackled, he is subjected to severe oppression. At last he is released after hostages have been given.

In 581:

> Leovigild again besieges his son Hermenegild at the town of Osset in Lusitania; after capturing him, he takes him to Toledo and commits him to prison.

Furthermore, in 583:

> Leovigild again besieges his son Hermenegild at Seville.

And in 584:

> Leovigild gathers an army against his son Hermenegild. He calls Miro, king of the Suevi, and many enemies to his aid against his son.

In 585:

> Hermenegild escapes from Seville, is captured at Córdoba, and is held first at Seville, then at Toledo, and finally at Valencia, where he remains in captivity for several months.

What more is needed? The savage beast prevailed to such an extent that he caused his son to be beheaded. Before this, he had launched a general persecution against the Catholics and had fiercely persecuted and exiled their principal bishops. At his command Saint Leander of Seville and Saint Licinianus, bishop of Cartagena, were banished to Constantinople; Saint Mausona of Mérida to Complutum; Saint Euphemius of Toledo to Barcelona; Saint Bonitus of Complutum to Zaragoza; Saint Fulgentius of Astigi, and others elsewhere, endured exile in defense of Catholic truth, through the agency of the wicked king Leovigild. Marcus Maximus of Zaragoza, then a bishop and himself an eyewitness, records this under the year A.D. 583. Thus he waged war against the saints and prevailed over them.

But what does the statement that “the eyes like the eyes of a man were in this horn” mean? It means that, in combating the saints, he was not moved merely by his own blind imagination, but also by the instigation of many bishops, who were called the eyes of the Church. Indeed, he even held councils concerning the same matter. Hear the words of Marcus Maximus under the year A.D. 581:

> Leovigild again besieges his son Hermenegild, takes him captive to Toledo, and commits him to prison.

But behold the eyes of this horn:

> He convenes a synod of Arian bishops and of those belonging to his faction, presided over by Paschasius, bishop of the Church of Saint Eulalia of Toledo. Vincent, bishop of Zaragoza, attends; Sumnia and Nepotianus, intruded bishops of the Church of Mérida; Ugnus of Barcelona; Murita of Valencia; Argimundus of Porto; Gardingus, bishop of Tui; and others of the same sect.

Elated by the support of so many Fathers, it is no wonder that Leovigild thought he could change the times and laws of his kingdom and his sect. Viclarensis provides an example of this. Since the inviolable law of the Arians required that no Catholic be permitted to pass over to them unless he were rebaptized in their Zenosian washing (*lavacro ... Zenoso*), Leovigild, after convening a council of his bishops, abrogated the law and enacted a new one in these words:

> Those who come from the Roman religion to our Catholic faith—they thus miserably called their own religion—should not be baptized, but should be received merely through the laying on of hands and the reception of communion, and glory should be given to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.

As a result—miserable to relate—many of our people, as Viclarensis says, were impelled more by desire to turn aside into the Arian doctrine through this deception.

But what is meant by the statement that he warred against the saints and prevailed over them, and that they were delivered into his hand “for a time, times, and half a time”? Clearly, these words indicate how many years he was to reign. Since the word “time” does not designate a determinate and clearly defined number of years, it will be necessary to seek some definite period in which the singular “time,” together with the plural “times,” and half of the double period called “half a time,” may comprise the years of his reign.

We find this in Leovigild, who, according to Viclarensis, spent seventeen and a half years in his most impious rule. For if by the singular “time” we understand a period of five years, by “times” ten years, and by “half a time” half of five years—that is, two and a half years—then “a time, times, and half a time” will amount to seventeen and a half years, neither more nor fewer.

When these years had passed, because of the great words that the horn had spoken against the Most High, the beast was killed and its body perished. Most justly, after that period, Leovigild paid the penalty for such enormous crimes, deprived both of his kingdom and of his life. In the death of that king the beast was killed, by the judgment of the supreme Judge, and its body likewise perished. For it was not he alone who perished: his entire sect, pierced by the sword of the word of God, was destroyed and fell, and the body of that beast was delivered to be burned with fire.

This too was fulfilled literally when Recared, the Catholic king, after removing his father from the world, publicly burned at the gates of Toledo all the books of the Arian perfidy that had supplied strength to the beast. Marcus Maximus witnessed this and testified to it in his Chronicle under A.D. 589, where, speaking of the beginnings of Recared’s reign, he says:

> The books of the Arian perfidy are burned at the gates of Toledo.

Then the thrones were set up, and the Ancient of Days, judging from heaven in favor of and in justice for the Son of the Most High, caused judgment also to be solemnly celebrated on earth at Toledo. There, while seventy-two bishops of all Spain and Gothic Gaul were seated, the perfidy of Arius was condemned.

The fact itself—which was destined to produce such great glory for God—demonstrates that innumerable hosts of angels, inspiring what was right, were also present at that holy assembly. So too does the day on which the council was celebrated, 8 May, the day on which the feast of Saint Michael and the angels is observed in the Church, as is evident from the acts of that same synod. Thus Daniel’s words, “thousands of thousands ministered to him,” and so forth, may be understood literally not only of the holy bishops but also of the angels themselves.

Then the books were opened. The writings of the great Fathers, especially those who had celebrated the Council of Nicaea, were examined, and the books of the holy Prophets and the Gospels were read. The case of Christ the Lord was argued, and a divine sentence was pronounced in their favor, so that the following was fulfilled to the letter:

> One like a Son of Man came and reached the Ancient of Days; they brought him before him, and he gave him power, honor, and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him.

Concerning these words Jerome says:

> If the whole of this were understood by the Arian heresy in a pious sense, it would by no means bring an accusation of inequality against the Son of God.

He plainly acknowledges that by this judgment the Arian heresy was condemned.

When these things had been accomplished, the great kingdom of that fourth beast was taken away from it by judgment and delivered to the people of the saints of the Most High. This occurred when Arianism had been abolished throughout Spain and the Spanish kingdom, now Catholic, had been handed over to the truly Catholic king Recared, in whom the Catholic monarchy was founded.

He also enacted most sacred laws for it, which still survive in the twelve books of the laws of the Visigoths. With the agreement of the entire council, he acquired the title “Glorious King,” a title which his successors used uniquely for many generations in all public documents, as can be seen in the headings and subscriptions of the laws contained in those twelve books and in the acts of all the councils of Spain. In these, the kings of Spain are perpetually styled by the Fathers “Glorious,” and many also “Most Glorious.” When they addressed the kings, they used the designation “Glory” in place of the titles “Majesty,” “Highness,” or “Serenity,” which we now employ.

The same usage can also be found among all the writers of that period, namely Isidore, Ildefonsus, Marcus Maximus, and the others. We shall discuss this matter more fully in our commentaries on that same Maximus, under A.D. 590. There we shall also demonstrate the antiquity of the title “Catholic King,” which likewise derives its origin from that time and succeeded to the title “Glorious.”

Both titles, however, are highly appropriate to the matter of which we are speaking: the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kings were called Glorious and Catholic by the great design of God. From the very titles, as from a sign, we might infer who that truly Catholic and glorious people was of whom Daniel spoke so much.

As for the perpetuity of that kingdom, which the same prophet foretold, it is plainly established that from Recared onward down to Philip IV, who now reigns happily, there has never been a Catholic king absent from Spain for the entire period of 1,030 years. Nor has the Spanish people itself, by God’s gift, ever departed from the Catholic faith.

Although, because its sins demanded it, the people was for a time punished by the scourge of the Saracens, the Glorious and Catholic king Pelagius nevertheless maintained sovereignty over it in the mountains. Indeed, in all the cities of Spain, public churches were granted by the Saracens to the Spanish Catholics under the burden of an enormous tribute. In those churches the people, however much crushed beneath the harshest yoke, never hesitated publicly to profess the Catholic faith. During that period countless Spaniards at Córdoba and elsewhere attained the crown of martyrdom. One of those martyrs, Saint Eulogius—elected to the primatial see of Toledo—described their glorious triumphs in a most polished style.

Moreover, by God’s mercy the Spaniards not only shook the impious yoke from their necks but also gradually began to extend the Catholic monarchy. They subjugated and acquired many great and powerful dominions in Europe, Africa, and Asia, which it would take too long to enumerate individually. Finally, contrary to the expectation of all the ages, they added to these the New World, discovered and subjugated by them, made it Catholic, and made it part of the kingdom of the saints. In their fellowship, which extends so widely throughout the world, no one who is not Catholic is permitted to dwell—a circumstance that makes it all the more properly describable as the people of the saints.

Since these things are so, we believe, on no futile foundation, that this Catholic monarchy was foreshown to the prophet Daniel in chapter 7. Four barbarian devastations by beasts preceded it; it took its beginning with the destruction of the Arian perfidy and the glorification of the Son of God; and in it everything Daniel notes, even the smallest details, is verified to the letter, as we have seen.

We hope that the remaining promises of the same prophetic prediction—those made by God concerning the still greater expansion and perpetuity of the people of the saints—will likewise be fulfilled in it. May God Almighty deign to accomplish this for his greater glory.

[Col. 0591A] This work was almost already laboring beneath the press when I came upon a prophetic prediction—shall I call it similar, or the same?—which had been written by Jeremiah but explained by the venerable Abbot Joachim in his commentaries on Jeremiah, chapter 49.

There the prophet threatens Elam, declaring that God will bring four winds of heaven from the four quarters of the world, so that he may scatter Elam among all the winds and disperse it into every region of the earth. Nevertheless, he also foretells a time when God will set his throne in Elam and place it over the whole earth.

These are the prophet’s words:

> The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah the prophet against Elam: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will break the bow of Elam and the sum of their strength; and I will bring upon Elam four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and I will scatter them in all these winds, and there shall be no nation to which the fugitives of Elam shall not come. I will make Elam terrified before its enemies and in the sight of those who seek its life, and I will bring evil upon them, the anger of my wrath, says the Lord; and I will send the sword after them until I consume them. I will set my throne in Elam and destroy from there kings and princes, says the Lord. But in the last days I will bring back the captives of Elam, says the Lord.

So much for the prophet. Joachim, a man of great authority in the interpretation of prophets, insists that this must be understood of the Spaniards. He says:

> “Against Elam,” and so forth: After an intervening visitation, he will impel the descendants of the Spaniards and Western nations, whom the sword of persecution had worn down, toward the faith of Catholic inspiration.

We have shown that this took place under the Catholic king Recared. Compare, I ask you, reader, Jeremiah’s prophecy with Daniel’s prophecy. When you discover that they differ in nothing from one another, you will recognize that Abbot Joachim stands on our side.

Let these things be said subject to the correction of Holy Mother Church and to the judgment of anyone who judges better. To that judgment I most willingly submit this entire commentary.

[Col. 0591]

# APOLOGETICUS FOR L. DEXTER AGAINST A RECENT OPPONENT

## DEDICATORY EPISTLE

To the Most Reverend Father and Lord, Brother Valerian de Spinosa, Master of Sacred Theology, General Reformer of the Regular Observance of Saint Bernard of the Cistercian Order throughout Spain, and Abbot of the royal monastery of Saint Mary of Palazuelos, etc., his most honored lord, Brother Francis de Bivar sends greetings and prays for eternal blessings.

Our cause is at stake, Most Reverend Prelate, whenever anyone in any way diminishes the honor of the Cistercian religious order, whose reformer you are, or when anyone attempts to take away the treasures of our fatherland or obscure our glory. We certainly share the same fatherland and religious order: the latter gives life, the former confers honor; the one cares for the body, the other for the soul. Therefore we must fight for both together.

The antiquity of the order, and the well-established succession that followed from Benedict, our first father, has always been so evident among all people that it is astonishing that anyone, however scrupulous, could have called it into question. Nevertheless, someone attempted to do so, and Dexter too found an adversary. Which of the two is more intolerable, I would not easily judge. Neither could be passed over without satisfaction, and the task of dealing with both fell to me.

But since I am to choose a patron to sustain this singular contest, and since I have always recognized you as my patron in both matters alike—one who shines equally with the splendors of learning and virtue—I could not, nor did I wish to, choose anyone else.

Therefore sustain with me these contests, which I dedicate to your name, and encourage me as I fight manfully. The victory will belong to you, after God, with whom I trust you will reign eternally.

Farewell, Most Reverend Father.

Rome, 18 September 1624.

# THE APOLOGETIC RESPONSE TO PENNOTTUS’S OBJECTIONS AGAINST DEXTER’S CHRONICLE BEGINS

[Col. 0591]

## § I. The Purpose of the Apology Is Set Forth

[Col. 0591C]

I had almost withdrawn my hand from defending Dexter when I was challenged once more to battle and compelled to insert my hand on his behalf—not, indeed, against an open enemy, for that would have been less unpleasant, but against one whose friendship I embrace most willingly.

I have injured no one and deceived no one; but, touched inwardly by the pain of my heart, I am drawn beyond my customary limits. There is one thing from which I shall never withdraw, if God grants it, and another into which I very much wish not to fall: the former is moderation, the latter insult. The one greatly assists persuasion; the other causes serious harm and offends the minds of readers.

However much I see that both we and our work have been attacked, I shall never be brought to return evil for evil and abuse for abuse, since I profess the humble condition of a religious man. Rather, in the words of the Apostle (Romans 12), I shall strive, insofar as it is granted me from above, to overcome evil with good.

Near the beginning of the present year, A.D. 1624, there appeared from the press of the Reverend Apostolic Chamber a General History of the Entire Sacred Order of Clerics Regular Canons in Three Parts, by the Reverend Father Gabriel Pennottus of Novara, a regular canon of the Lateran Congregation. In it, an exceptionally learned man, cultivated equally in theology and eloquence, a professor and moderator of the Vespers chair at Salamanca and preacher to His Catholic Majesty, Brother John Márquez, is attacked concerning a question that had for many years been vigorously disputed between the canons and the hermits on both sides: the right of succession to the inheritance of the great Aurelius Augustine.

Since Márquez had more than once used the authority of L. Dexter and his continuator M. Maximus to support his positions, our Pennottus seized the opportunity to inveigh against those most eminent men, Dexter and Maximus. By weakening their authority, if possible, he thought that they would no longer cause him any difficulty.

At that time he had perhaps obtained a copy of Dexter from Doctor John de Salasmalo, theologian and prior of the celebrated Church of Saint Mary of the Pillar at Zaragoza. By a single night’s work he read through the entire Chronicle, comparing parts with parts and statements with statements, and, putting pen to paper, gathered and appended many observations here and there. In this way, the authority of the Chronicle seemed to him to be shown not merely to waver—which would have been little—but to be branded as fabrication or fable.

Since he knew that Dexter had a defender in Rome, he came more than once, with his customary kindness, to my usual residence at Saint Mautus [reading uncertain] to communicate to me the notes he had prepared. Out of the reverence owed to so great a man, I examined his notes once and again. He frankly admitted that they were the work of a single night and had been written rapidly.

After several days, in familiar conversation, I took care to answer all of them orally and in order. I added that, if he wished, I would also respond to them in writing. Yet he did not cease to hesitate over two points: one concerned a certain Leporius, who had been led from Pelagianism to the Catholic faith by the work of his teacher Augustine, whom he believed to have been two different men; the other concerned several distinguished men whom we read in M. Maximus as having belonged either to the order of the hermits of Saint Augustine or to the order of Saint Benedict.

He maintained that the hermits of Saint Augustine had not been taught by Augustine himself, and that those names designating membership in this or that saint’s order were much more recent than M. Maximus. I too indicated that these expressions seemed suspicious to me, although we disagreed about whether Leporius was one person or two.

He declared that this was sufficient for his purpose and that he would do nothing further concerning Dexter. With the strength of our friendship entirely diminished, he departed, and on several occasions he revealed this in familiar conversations with Doctor Salasmalo.

But can a mother forget the child of her womb? The son he had conceived that night could not be consigned to oblivion. He therefore allowed it to see the light and had the entire little work, exactly as it lay, printed in Book I, chapters 52 and 53, of his Tripartite History, as though nothing had been done about it. We give thanks that he added nothing. Thus there will still be something for us to work over anew in order to answer his objections.

For the rest, I do not sufficiently understand how the case that this man undertook in that book against the Venerable Father Master Brother John Márquez concerning the origin and institution of the hermits assisted his purpose, or how the origin of the Cistercian order, or the causes of its institution, helped him—even in particular—so that, turning aside from his stated purpose, he attacked the Cistercians with all his strength, insisting that their institution did not descend from Saint Benedict, openly criticizing their blessed fathers and the splendor of their monasteries, and at times doing so with insufficient reverence.

Yet I have no doubt that he would not have done this if he had spoken carefully and had known that Cistercian monks can demonstrate their Benedictine descent much more clearly than regular canons can demonstrate their Augustinian descent; that Cistercian monasteries not only borrowed their splendor from nowhere else but also bestowed it upon many other orders; or that the venerable Abbot Joachim of Fiore, wonderfully distinguished by God through miracles and virtues in life and death, regarded as blessed throughout Calabria, and repeatedly defended in his honor by the Apostolic See.

If Pennottus knew these facts, he would certainly not detract from Joachim so fiercely. He devoted two chapters of his work to this matter: chapter 51 of the first book and chapter 2 of the second. Without doubt he would refrain from those insults which could be poured out only upon a thoroughly depraved man.

For what else does it mean to wish to summon Joachim back from the underworld, giving him the name Goliath in mockery so as to measure his strength—this is how Pennottus honors him in that chapter 51—than to profess that the founder of the most blessed Florensian congregation, flourishing in the Church and a branch of the Cistercian order of Saint Bernard, lies buried in hell?

But how can Master Márquez, in the prologue to his book, wonder that Pennottus turned aside from attacking the Reverend Father Antonio Daza concerning some question of the Augustinian profession of Saint Francis to criticize the origin of the Reverend Fathers, the regular canons, if Pennottus himself remains caught in the same offense and turns aside from fighting the hermits of Saint Augustine to provoke the Cistercians?

His words are almost the same as those we used shortly before, namely:

> Besides, I still do not sufficiently understand how the origin of the canonical order, or the causes of its institution, or even anything specifically related to it, can have assisted the case that this man undertook in that book against the venerable Father Antonio Daza concerning the origin and institution of the Friars Minor, or of the hermits. For although he wrote at the very beginning of his book that his sole purpose in it was to defend his order against the injuries inflicted upon it by Antonio Daza, nevertheless, after drawing up his battle line against him, he deliberately turned aside and transferred the whole burden of the conflict to the canonical order, and so forth.

Certainly, in criticizing another, he is caught in the same fault himself. For this reason it will be enough for me to do only this: following the prophetic saying, “I will set him before his own face” (Psalm 49), I shall show that in all the matters for which he censures others, he himself is manifestly at fault, so that he may learn not to think too highly of himself, but to fear lest, after preaching to others, he himself should become blameworthy.

He must therefore be taught that he judged the Chronicle of Dexter and Maximus less correctly than he should have, and that he unjustly hurled his darts against the Cistercian monks, who had injured neither him nor their own order. I would wish that he be taught this by more learned men; but while the others whose duty it is to deal with this matter are becoming fully informed, it cannot be otherwise than that I, the least of all, should admonish him concerning certain points.

I trust in his goodness that, once he knows the truth, he will frankly acknowledge that I was moved by just causes—namely, zeal for truth, for my nation, and for my religious order—not against him, whom I deeply respect and praise, but against the reputation of my author and my order, which in his writings he injured more through the heat of his style than through any deliberate intention.

## § II. How Many and How Great Objections Pennottus Devised to Blunt the Authority of This Chronicle

To begin, then, from the egg, as the saying goes, before examining the matters contained in the Chronicle itself, Pennottus raises three objections that he judges greatly weaken its credibility. They concern three points on which Spanish writers disagree among themselves when they discuss it: its preservation, its discovery, and finally the discrepancy among the various manuscripts.

As for its preservation, some deny that it was preserved and affirm that it perished through the injuries of time. Baronius asserts this in volume 4 of the Ecclesiastical Annals under A.D. 392.

Others maintain that it was preserved in the library of the monastery of Fulda, to which it was brought from Spain, together with other manuscripts, on the orders of the emperor Charlemagne during the time of the Saracen invasion. This is what Euthrandus says in his letter to Regismundus, bishop of Iliberis.

As for its discoverer, some assert that it was the aforementioned Euthrandus, who flourished around A.D. 390. Others believe it was the most illustrious Lord Brother Augustine of Jesus, archbishop of Braga. While traveling through Germany to visit the monasteries of his order—for he was then prior general of the hermits of Saint Augustine—he supposedly came upon Dexter’s manuscript among the books at Fulda. From it he had two copies made, one of which he gave as a gift to Philip II, the Catholic king, while reserving the other for his own use.

This is the account of John Calderón. Gaspar Álvarez de Losada, however, directly opposes him, denying that Lord Augustine of Jesus ever found Dexter in Germany.

Others then attribute the discovery to the Reverend Father Thomas Torralba, a priest of the Society of Jesus from Ocaña. They say that, having found it at Fulda, he sent it in A.D. 1594 to Father Jerome de la Higuera, a theologian of the same Society and a man who had rendered valuable service to ecclesiastical antiquity. Nevertheless, others assert that it was found not at Fulda but at Worms.

Finally, Gaspar Escolano states that for many years Dexter’s Chronicle had existed at Toledo, in the monastery of Sisla, to which Lord Pedro Pecha, formerly bishop of Jaén, had given it as a gift.

From this Pennottus considers the imposture of the Chronicle sufficiently exposed, and even more so from the discrepancy among the manuscripts circulated under Dexter’s name. In the copy used by Márquez there are certain passages absent from Calderón’s printed work, especially under A.D. 424. The author’s name itself is written in various ways: the printed manuscript calls him Fl. L. Dexter, whereas the manuscript followed by Márquez calls him M. L. Dexter.

Many believe that the work is complete, while Escolano considers it merely an abridgment. Pennottus is led to this conclusion because Dexter’s Chronicle, according to Jerome, was a history of every kind, and therefore must have been extremely extensive. Consequently it must have been much fuller than what now circulates under his name; otherwise the work would scarcely correspond to its title.

It is also reported that Lord John Pérez, bishop of Segorbe, possessed another Chronicle of Dexter, very different from those mentioned above. Concerning this, the learned Father Murillo says in the prologue to his book on the foundation of the Sacred Chapel of the Pillar:

> It seems not so much an abridgment as a corruption of Dexter’s Chronicle; for in it certain things are found contrary to truth and to the seriousness of history, and unworthy of so great an author.

But, as Pennottus says, this is the chief point of all: if one asks which of the copies just mentioned is the one to which we should grant credibility as the legitimate text, what answer can be given?

Brother Diego Murillo had in his hands an abridgment of this Chronicle that differed in many respects from the one printed at Zaragoza and departed from the truth. For this reason it is rejected by John Calderón, who arranged for it to be printed, in his preface to the reader.

Yet the manuscript that Calderón himself printed is nevertheless proved to be the most corrupt of all. It was printed with many instances of carelessness, as will be apparent to anyone who reads it. Nor are there lacking those who say that the Chronicle of M. Maximus was recently corrupted by the Magdeburg Centuriators.

From this Pennottus extracts four conclusions:

1. At the very least, there is as yet no certainty concerning an ancient copy of this Chronicle, much less concerning a legitimate autograph.

2. The Fulda manuscript was corrupted by the Magdeburg heretics.

3. The copy used by Márquez was not Dexter’s complete history, but only a corrupted abridgment.

4. The Chronicle printed at Zaragoza is full of very numerous errors; consequently no certain argument can be drawn from either of them as though from Dexter’s authority.

Such is Pennottus’s judgment concerning the Chronicle of Dexter and Maximus, recently published, derived—as I may put it—from external arguments alone. For when he examines the internal details one by one, he maintains that many things are found to conflict both with one another and with the truth.

Would you like to know what things? I shall briefly touch upon his statements.

In the letter prefixed as a dedication to Jerome, there are three difficulties.

First, Dexter claims to have continued his Chronicle to A.D. 430, although Jerome had mentioned it forty years earlier in his book On Illustrious Men. The work was plainly composed in A.D. 390, as is evident from its conclusion, and Baronius proves this in the Ecclesiastical Annals.

Second, Dexter says that his work could not have reached Jerome’s hands, since Jerome was already dead. But who would believe that from A.D. 390, when—according to Jerome—the book had been written, until A.D. 426, when, even according to Dexter himself, Jerome ceased to live, Jerome never received, during that interval of thirty-six years, a work dedicated to him by so powerful a man?

Third, in the same letter the author admits that when he dedicated the work to Orosius, the year was A.D. 430, while at the end of his history Dexter writes that, when he completed it, the year was A.D. 440.

Much more, he thinks, are proved false in the course of the history, and from among them he has selected the following examples, relating to various years of the chronology.

Under the year of Christ 27 it is falsely stated: “Saint Petronilla, ten years old, flourishes as the daughter of the Apostle Saint Peter by marriage.” For this is rejected by Saint Augustine, *Against Adimantus*, chapter 17, and by Baronius under the year of the Lord 69, number 33—and rightly so; for how could a girl then ten years old have been flourishing?

Moreover, under the year of the Lord 37, he says that James son of Zebedee was the author of the canonical epistle, which everyone considers false, and contrary to the tradition of the Roman Church, which commands that it be read on the feast of Saint James the Less.
