In the same place, by the twelve tribes that were in the Dispersion, to whom James addresses the epistle, he wishes Jews then living in Spain to be understood. This fiction, he says, when restricted to them alone, is plainly contrary to Sacred Scripture, the Fourth Book of Kings. How prematurely this was said, you will see below. Meanwhile, reader, patiently endure the notes with which this religious man wounds us. “Contrary to the tradition,” he says, “of the Church, and plainly contrary to Sacred Scripture.” They would be more tolerable if they stood alone; but now he adds other notes of unbelief. For, contrary to the Gospel history in John, chapter 2, it is asserted under the same year that the Jews who were in Jerusalem, by letters sent to them, sought the agreement of the Spanish Jews concerning the death of Christ. For after the raising of Lazarus and the convocation of the council at which Christ’s destruction was decreed, they no longer sought the agreement of others, but issued an order for his arrest, as those words show: “But the chief priests and Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, so that they might seize him.” And he calls the contrary opinion a most empty fiction.

Again, under the year 38, it is falsely stated that in that year Saul reached Jerusalem after his conversion; for Paul himself writes the opposite in Galatians, chapter 1: “Immediately [after the conversion] I did not go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away to Arabia and returned again to Damascus; then after three years I went up to Jerusalem”—which did not occur until the year of the Lord 41.

Under the year of the Lord 86, he extends the pontificate of Linus to that date. “This,” he says, “is so false that there is no need to prove its falsity.”

[Col. 0598A] Likewise, under the year 156, he says that Saint Polycarp went to Rome that year, under Anicetus; yet Anicetus was not appointed pope before the year 167.

“But even if,” says Pennottus, “we grant him many other errors concerning the calculation of the years, under the year 384 Iginius of Córdoba is said to have been exiled to Léron, an island of Gaul. Yet before the arrival of Saint Hilary, around the year of grace 440, it was rendered uninhabitable by serpents, as Baronius notes under the year 445, number 5, volume V.”

Under the year of the Lord 396, the author says that Paulinus of Nola was ordained priest at Barcelona; yet Paulinus himself writes to Alypius, in Letter 35 among the Augustinian letters, that this occurred before Augustine’s baptism. Augustine’s baptism, however, took place in the year of the Lord [Col. 0598B] 387 or 388, as Pennottus himself proved in Book I, chapter 4, numbers 3 and 6, adding that the imposture of this Chronicle can thereby be plainly exposed: “For how could so distinguished a historian, concerning the events of his own times and those that had occurred in his own home—that is, at Barcelona—and concerning a person so prominent as Paulinus, have erred so carelessly, so negligently, and so disgracefully?”

Under the year 400, Orosius is sent as envoy of the Spanish bishops to the fathers of an African council, already an ordained priest, as is clear from Augustine’s Letter 90. Yet in this Chronicle he is said to have been born in the year of the Lord 384, from which it is proved that he had not exceeded his sixteenth year. What consistency among these facts, I ask?

[Col. 0598C] Under the year 406, it is asserted that Leporius, Bishop of Utica in Baetica, was brought back from Pelagianism into the bosom of the Church by Augustine, his teacher. Apart from this being an evident falsehood in history—for this Leporius was Bishop of Utica in Africa, not in Baetica—it is also an intolerable insult inflicted upon Saint Augustine and his community, from which, by God’s grace, neither heresiarchs nor heretics emerged, at least while he was alive—as this Leporius did.

Finally, since at the end of the Chronicle Dexter is said to have been seventy-two years old in the year of the Lord 440, although he had already completed it in the year 390, as is made clear from Jerome’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, it follows that he wrote his book when he was only twenty years old, and that at that age he was prefect of the praetorium—which seems altogether incredible.

Thus far Pennottus has attacked the codex of Dexter. Next he proceeds to gather many other objections against its continuator, M. Maximus, whose work he contends is still more corrupt in many ways. First, under the year 432, he calls Isidore, the author of the book *Allegories*, “the Elder,” disagreeing with Dexter, who called him “the Younger” under the year 430; and whereas the former says that Isidore dedicated the book of *Allegories* to Paul Orosius of Tarragona, this author maintains that it was addressed to Paul Orosius, Bishop of León.

Again, under the year 439, he places the death of Dexter, although Dexter had earlier said of himself that he had set the final hand to his work in the year 440.

[Col. 0599A] Likewise, under the year 471, he writes that Paul Orosius died at more than one hundred years of age, although he had completed only eighty-eight, since, according to Dexter, he was born in the year 384.

Under the year of the Lord 474, he calls the holy African martyrs Liberatus and his companions, who suffered under Himmeric, king of the Vandals, Augustinian monks. This term is much more recent than M. Maximus and was perhaps added by later writers, or by the Magdeburg historians.

Under the year 486, Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe is said to have been of Toledan origin, although he was African and was born at Telepte, not Toledo, to Carthaginian parents of the senatorial order, not Toledans, as is clear from his acts.

In the year of the Lord 514, Saint Vincent, martyr of León, is said to have professed the order of Saint Benedict shortly before suffering martyrdom. Yet Saint Benedict did not gather monks until the year 525, and his monks did not cross into Spain until 646. Moreover, that expression—“of the order after Saint Benedict”—was not then in use.

The same is true of what is said under the year 531 about Saint Turibius having received the habit at Rome from Saint Benedict. For Saint Benedict never lived in Rome after becoming a monk, nor did his monks inhabit Rome before 567.

Under the year 534, the author says that Gennadius of Marseille died, although he had died forty years earlier, since he offered his books to Pope Gelasius for correction and was a contemporary of Saints Prosper, Hilary, and Cassian.

In the year 562, it is wrongly asserted that King Athanagild, having summoned monks from Italy, built the Agallian monastery at Toledo, although he was a heretical Arian or a pagan, as Baronius noted from Tuditanus, volume VII, under the year 567, number 17. In the same place, that king is said to have built the monastery of Sisla, which presents the same difficulty; and it is said to have been built by Saint Augustine, although Julian calls it Saint Mary’s, and in other codices it is said to have been erected in the year 424.

Under the year 568, it is altogether false, says Pennottus, that the Church of Saint Mary of the Column at Zaragoza was inhabited by monks of Saint Benedict. Rather, the institution of canons living under a rule, planted by the most holy Apostles, has continued to this day, under God’s protection. Nor should the following statement be omitted: “And nearby there was a monastery of Benedictine monks.” The expression “of Benedictines” is new, and the verb “there was” suggests that the monastery had already been destroyed at that time. Yet this is incredible, since the monasteries of Saint Benedict were scarcely beginning to spring up then.

In the year 575, Saint Donatus is said to have been the first to bring from Africa into Spain the richer and milder rule of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, and to have built the Servitan monastery. “A foolish fiction indeed,” says the censor. “For Augustine’s rule is milder than all others and requires restriction, not mitigation,” [Col. 0600A] as the canon *What the Fear of God Requires concerning the State of Monks* states. Saint Ildefonsus and the other writers on Spanish affairs, when they speak of Saint Donatus, do not mention the rule of Augustine. Moreover, the author himself admits below, under the year of the Lord 590, that the Servitan monastery belonged to the order of Saint Benedict.

Under the year 590, M. Maximus is said to have been made archdeacon of Zaragoza after having been abbot of the Benedictines, which is contrary to the practice of that time.

Finally, under the year 606, Muhammad is said to have ravaged Spain. “This,” says Pennottus, “is a conspicuous falsehood, for Muhammad never saw Spain, as is more widely known than anything requiring proof; nor did his followers invade it until the year of the Lord 713, as Baronius proves from Tuditanus, volume VI, and elsewhere.” These, then, are his statements concerning M. Maximus.

[Col. 0600B] After M. Maximus, Dexter also had Euthrandus, or Liudprand of Pavia, as a continuator. John Celderon arranged for the printing of his dedicatory letter to Regimundus, Bishop of Ribera. Pennottus, nevertheless, hurled several darts against it. For the deacon did not write his *Antipodosis* while still a deacon of Pavia, but while already Bishop of Cremona; nor around the year of Christ 860, but in 962, as is clear from the preface to Book III and as Baronius proves under the year 963; nor while he was an exile at Fulda, but while returning from his embassy to Constantinople. If he was the subdeacon of Saint Bonitus, Archbishop of Toledo, he must have lived in the year of the Lord 860, when Bonitus flourished, according to Murillo. And why was Euthrandus’s continuation not printed together with Dexter and Maximus, but rejected as spurious? If it is spurious, then Dexter’s Chronicle itself, and Maximus’s continuation—which derive their credibility from Euthrandus’s letter—will likewise be spurious.

§ III. Pennottus’s *Tripartite History* is entangled in the same knots with which he attempts to bind Dexter’s *Omnimoda History*.

When I pause at this point, it occurs to me that, if I wished, I could justly hurl against Pennottus himself the words that he rather vehemently directs in Book II of his *Tripartite History*, chapter 18, number 3, against the learned and religious man, R. P. Constantine Cajetan:

“This Constantinian apparatus, however, and such a great clamor of words, swollen and puffed up with so many ornaments of mockery, is not so solid that it could not be shattered altogether by a single blow and dissolved into the air; nor is it of such weight that we ought to apply hand to pen in order to refute it. For even if everything were as he boasts concerning Dexter, Maximus, and Euthrandus—which we nevertheless deny in every respect—all would collapse with that one blow if we were to say that, amid such a clamor of words swollen and puffed up with so many ornaments of mockery, nothing else is proved than that the book is not canonical, and that its author has not been raised to the rank of an Evangelist, so that he could not at times depart from the truth. The differences among the codices and copies, however, plainly prove the antiquity of the work. For if it were a more recent fiction, it could never have undergone such various transcriptions. Nor ought we to apply hand to pen to refute it, since everything he has objected, each in its proper place, has been set forth by us in these commentaries.”

Nevertheless, I prefer to embrace the modesty that befits religious men, although at times we have judged it necessary to place his excesses before his eyes, so that he may see how indulgently we treat him. Thus we may avoid incurring what he charged against Constantine for following John the Baptist Brachesius, a man whom Baronius praised highly for piety and learning: “The blind gives guidance to the blind, and both fall into the pit.” For what benefit to the cause is there in his jesting somewhat irreverently about ours—that Pennottus’s imagination concerning this or that matter is cold—and in other remarks of that kind, which he hurls as darts against Constantine? Or how can these things be referred to the glory of God, as he does in chapter 19, number 8, when, at the end of Constantine’s *Apology*, after the aforesaid and other insults, he adds:

“I have written these things to vindicate them for the glory of God and the canonical profession of Saint Herculanus”—for this was the issue disputed among them—“not in order to return an injury”?

Unless perhaps one excuses him by agreeing with what he begs in chapter 18, number 7: “Bear with me, I beseech you, in my slowness.” We therefore judge that such things should be avoided; for “if anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor has the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 11 and 16). But to the matter.

Before, however, we descend to resolve the individual knots objected to us, I wish to satisfy Pennottus with one common decision concerning them all: namely, that he himself is caught in the same snare as we are, and that his work is entangled in all the headings of argument that he has hurled against us. When we have seen his industry set it free from these, we shall more easily dissolve the objections directed against us by following his example. This is what we promised above (§ I, no. 4): to set him against his own face, so that, when he sees himself held by the same bonds, he may cease attacking us.

Thus, to speak briefly, the five headings to which all the objections may be reduced are these:

1. The title of the work and the author’s intention.

2. Contradictions of statements and inconsistencies, which indicate either carelessness or diversity of authors.

3. Assertions of things difficult to believe.

4. New words, unused in the ancient periods of the authors.

5. Manifest falsehoods unworthy of a learned author.

The Reverend Father contends that all these weaken the authority of these Chronicles. For they do not seem to correspond to the title *Omnimoda History*, since they mention only a few matters; and they abound throughout in inconsistencies, falsehoods, and incredible assertions, both in their dates and in their statements; and they repeatedly use new expressions such as “the order of the Hermits of Saint Augustine,” “the order of Saint Benedict,” and similar terms.

But why does he not see that anyone could hurl just as many darts against his own work? His work, first of all, does not correspond to its title. Is not the title prefixed to it *A Tripartite General History of the Entire Sacred Order of Clerical Canons*? From reading the title, one would believe that the work concerns not only regular canons but also secular canons; for both the former and the latter are clerical canons, and at least one of the three divisions of the history would seem to concern them. Yet nothing about them is found in the entire work. Therefore, no one would judge rashly if he concluded that the work before us is not Pennottus’s complete work, but that a substantial part of it has perished.

For if he did not intend to write anything about secular canons, the title ought to have been changed to say, “A Tripartite History of Regular Canons,” instead of “of Clerical Canons,” which also includes the secular.

But the essential point is that the title itself promises a canonical history, whereas the book does not provide one. History is recognized by the writer’s method, not by the matters narrated. Natural history and natural philosophy, for example, may deal with the same subjects—Pliny’s *Natural History* and Aristotle’s *Natural Philosophy*—but the latter proceeds by discussion in scholastic style, while the former proceeds by simple exposition.

Similarly, one may compose either a history or, so to speak, a question-book concerning regular canons; which of the two it is must be recognized from its style and method. Now the style of this book that R. Pennottus produces is wholly scholastic. He proposes questions and various opinions concerning them, prefacing them with noteworthy observations in order to untangle them; he then draws conclusions and proves them individually. From the conclusions he sometimes derives corollaries, and finally takes care to answer the arguments in an orderly fashion.

What do these things have in common with historical style? Certainly, if someone read the title of the book without the book, and later perhaps came upon the book without its title, he could never be persuaded that the book was what that title promised, or that the author had assigned that title to it. It would rather deserve to be called *The Metaphysical Genesis of the Regular Canons*—“Genesis,” I say, because it explains their spiritual descent; “metaphysical,” because it proceeds through the highest causes, claiming that this order began with God himself and with the first causes of the whole Christian religion, namely, the Apostles of Christ our Lord. At times it even goes beyond the bounds of Christianity and contends that the order originated with the Nazarenes and Levites of the Old Law, and that Saint Paul favors such antiquity when he writes to the Hebrews (see Book II of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 2). And it does all this in the manner of controversies, as metaphysicians are accustomed to do.

Although even within scholastic style the author goes too far, since approved scholastics strongly abhor the marks of censure, whereas he acts as a universal censor of the living and the dead, even in the most trivial matters. He frequently calls the statements of others, when they do not conform to his own, “errors,” “shameful lapses,” “stupid fictions,” and “resounding falsehoods,” contrary to Sacred Scripture and very often contrary to Gospel history. He also now casts down the same authors to the depths and now lifts them to the heavens, according as they seem to support or hinder him.

Thus he contends that Cardinal Baronius, deliberately, fell ten times into error in his history of Augustine (Book I, chapter 42), and endeavors to show by many arguments that Baronius’s authority provides far too weak a foundation for proving Augustine’s monastic profession. Later, however, in Book II, chapters 10 and 34, he makes so much of Baronius that he wishes matters of equal importance—namely, the regular canonicate of Saint Martin of Tours and of Saint Patrick, the apostle of the Irish, whom their chroniclers nevertheless always called monks—to stand firm on Baronius’s authority alone.

Similarly, when defending the cause of the hermits, he considers Brother Jerome the Roman, to mention no others, to be of no value; nevertheless, in Book II, chapter 10, he places almost the entire weight of his most serious assertion concerning the canonicate of Saint Hilary of Poitiers upon the shoulders of that same Roman.

He strongly praises Francis of Pisa when he argues that it cannot properly be inferred from the name “abbot” that the Agallian monastery was subject to Benedictine rules. Yet he insists that the same Francis must be rejected by everyone because he said that it could not be established from that name that the monastery belonged to the canons of Saint Augustine. He writes all this together in the same book, chapter 31, numbers 9 and 10.

Indeed, such inequality of style is as far removed from approved scholastics as the book’s title is from the book.

Whether he himself had a censor even before he wrote the book, he perhaps did not notice, although on its very first pages he supplies all readers with the judgment of the great Father of the Church, Sixtus IV. In a document issued by his own authority in the year of the Lord 1484 at Saint Peter’s—beginning, “He who commanded the Apostles”—he gives the following judgment concerning books of this subject:

“Indeed, not without singular displeasure of our mind, it has repeatedly come to our ears for some time that among our beloved sons, the regular canons of the Order of Saint Augustine of the Lateran Congregation, and the Friars of the Order of Hermits of the same Blessed Augustine, a certain unnecessary and less praiseworthy controversy has begun to arise concerning the habit of that most distinguished doctor of the Church, Augustine, and concerning the institution of these orders, each side thinking and preaching differently. Nor have they hesitated to compose books on such trifles, and to read them and give them to others to read, not without scandal and disturbance of the minds of the readers and of other Christian faithful. Through such absurdities they hasten to lose those whom they ought to win for God.

“We, considering that whether the illustrious light of the Church, Augustine, wore any other habit besides that of episcopal dignity, or subjected himself to another profession, is irrelevant to the matter—whether one affirms or denies it—except insofar as a superfluous controversy seeks to gain advantage from it, and wishing to remove from the midst and utterly root out such an enormous offense and dangerous controversies, by our own authority, etc.”

He then imposes the penalty of automatic excommunication upon those who defend either side in published writings or in any other manner; they may be absolved from it only by the Roman Pontiff, except in the hour of death.

I am not unaware that the very weighty judgment of the Salamancan theologians was that this decree had either never been observed or had long since been revoked by contrary custom, and that the illustrious cardinals of the Sacred Congregation of the Index of Forbidden Books did not dissent from them. Nevertheless, everyone can see that they dealt only with the sentence of excommunication, which transgressors would no longer incur, because they judged that it was not in vigorous observance, insofar as there remained an opportunity to write on either side.

But concerning the Pope’s theological judgment, so to speak, upon books of this kind—that is, his judgment that they contained a less necessary controversy; that their authors had not hesitated to compose books about such trifles, not without scandal and disturbance of the minds of readers; and consequently that the controversy was superfluous and that such an enormous offense and dangerous disputes ought to be removed—concerning this censure and judgment of the Supreme Pontiff, they could say nothing. For this pertains not to law but to fact. Yet the fact is plainly established, since the authentic example of the aforesaid letter remains in the archive of the monastery of Saint Mary of Peace, as Pennottus himself, who produces it, admits.

[Col. 0604B] The universal censor, therefore, could not escape the censure of so great a Pontiff. The Lateran canons ought especially to revere him, since by his gift they received the Church of Saint Mary of Peace, which they now inhabit, after they had been expelled from the Lateran Basilica by the power of the Roman people. Concerning this matter Pennottus himself produces the papal diploma of Sixtus in Book III, chapter 33, number 3.

But one should attribute to the natural sharpness of the man any excess that may be found in the frequent censures of such a work. For his pious intention is sufficiently evident to us, since at the very beginning he promised all readers in his prologue that, to the best of his ability, he would refrain from heaping injuries and insults upon his adversaries and would make his case by reason alone. Yet, having forgotten this promise, he was unable to restrain his biting style. We would criticize the work much more severely if the skill of the Roman master of the Sacred Palace had not tempered it in many places before it was committed to print. But let us proceed to the remaining headings.

§ IV. Some of Pennottus’s inconsistencies are exposed.

As for the inconsistencies, or contradictions of statements, by which he attempts to show that our Chronicle is spurious, I ask fair-minded readers to judge how much trouble this very argument causes Pennottus, in whose work, after the study of a rather short time, I have found contradictions of this kind.

In Book II, chapter 73, number 2, he asserts that the Order of the Most Holy Trinity for the Redemption of Captives was confirmed by Innocent III in the year 1209. In the following chapter—chapter 74—he says that it was confirmed by the same pope in the year 1198. In the former place he reports that the order’s founders were sent by Innocent to the canons of Saint Victor in Paris to learn their regular institutions, as is clear from the apostolic letters of that same Innocent, printed in Book I of his *Register*. Yet those letters by no means assert that the order was endowed with the rule of Saint Augustine.

In the later chapter, however, chapter 74, he places this order fourth among those instituted under the rule of Saint Augustine. Nevertheless, it is clear from other letters of the same Pontiff in the same *Register* that the order was endowed with a special rule dictated by that Pontiff himself. But it is absolutely certain that it never observed Augustine’s rule.

Moreover, in the aforesaid chapter 74 he places the Order of the Hermits of Fabali as differing in origin from the Order of the Hermits of Brittini and from that of Blessed John the Good; nevertheless, in Book I, chapter 25, number 4, and chapter 47 at the beginning, he contends that it was one and the same congregation with those of Brittini and John the Good.

Again, in Book II, chapter 30, number 1, he writes that the most august Church of Saint Mary of the Pillar throughout the world was built by angelic hands; but in chapter 11 of the same book, number 3, he contends that it was built by Saint James, son of Zebedee. The latter is most certainly true, as all the documents preserved in that church teach; we have reported them at length under the year of Christ 38.

Thus, to omit innumerable Doctors, Calixtus III reports in a letter given at Rome on the ninth day before the Kalends of October 1456, in these words:

“The faithful of Christ worship and venerate with great devotion and reverence an image of the same Blessed Mary and of her Son in a certain chapel of that church, which was built at the command of the said Blessed Mary by the said Blessed James and was called the Angelic Chamber of the Mother of God of the Pillar, etc.”

An ancient history reverently preserved there also bears witness to this when it says that Blessed Mary spoke to the Apostle James:

“Behold, James, my son, the designated place assigned to my name, in which, through your industry, my church is to be built in my memory.”

From these words the Offertory of the Mass of the proper office of that feast was formerly composed. I shall not hesitate to insert it here, since it makes the matter clear:

“Almighty and eternal God, who deigned that your most sacred Mother, while she was still living, should come among the choirs of angels upon a marble column sent down by you from on high, so that the Basilica of the Pillar might be built in her honor by the protomartyr, the Apostle James, and his most holy disciples: grant, we beseech you, that through her merits and intercession what we ask with faithful mind may be obtained. You who live, etc.”

Here you see that the column—or *Pillar*—was sent down from on high and carried by the hands of angels, whereas the Basilica of the Pillar, or the Column, was built by Saint James and his disciples.

I pass over many of Pennottus’s inconsistencies: for example, that he now elevates and now depresses the same authors, as we have already said; that he sometimes takes the word “monks” in the broadest sense and usually in the strictest, so that regular canons may share in the monks’ advantages but not in their punishments and defects; and that he inflicts upon others the censures that he does not tolerate being brought against himself.

In Book II, chapter 19, number 8, he impatiently complains that R. P. Constantine Cajetan calls regular canons “Good Fathers”; yet in Book I, chapter 47, number 2, he most patiently calls Master John Marquez “Good Marquez.”

He likewise abhors Constantine’s claim that the canonicate of Herculanus is drawn from foul sources; yet he does not hesitate to write that Augustine’s monastic profession was drawn by the hermits from foul sources.

Similarly, in Book I, chapter 51, number 1, he mocks Marquez for saying that the testimony of Blessed Joachim the Abbot could stand against twenty adversaries. Nevertheless, in Book II, chapter 18, number 10, he contends that two regular canons in the cause of the canons themselves have greater authority than ten authorities of Arnoldus and Brachesius, or even of Trithemius, cited by Father Constantine in the cause of Saint Herculanus. This amounts to saying that they are worth more than thirty; for who does not see that ten Arnolduses, ten Brachesiuses, and ten Trithemiuses make thirty?

But the chief point is this: the very Chronicle of Dexter and Maximus, which he expressly rejects in the passages cited above, he later admits more than once, asserting that it was undoubtedly corrupted by some person attached either to the hermits or to the Benedictines, as may be seen in Book I, chapter 56, number 4, and chapter 57, number 8, and elsewhere.

From all this I am persuaded that such a work is not Pennottus’s alone, but was officiously corrupted by someone. For surely there will be someone who, by comparing statements with statements and parts with parts, will laugh or grow angry, just as he himself said, quite falsely, about comparing Dexter’s codices with one another in Book I, chapter 52, number 5.

Now, concerning matters difficult to believe, I wish to submit one among many to the touchstone: namely, the proposition that R. P. Pennottus intends to persuade us of throughout his entire book—that the order of regular canons was instituted by the holy Apostles and that it has continued in those who survive today. It is not enough, he says, that it derive its origin from Saint Augustine.

But this is as true as if someone were to say that the Benedictine monks belong to the same order as Saints Antony, Pachomius, Hilarion, and the others who formerly inhabited the Thebaid and Palestine; or that all the congregations of monks throughout the world, including the mendicants, belong to one and the same order. If this were granted, there could be no doubt that they too were instituted by the holy Apostles. For religious profession is nothing other than directing one’s life according to the prescription of evangelical perfection.

Yet everyone can see that when one discusses the primitive origin of a particular order, the name “order” is not being taken generically, in which sense it includes all religious communities of monks, but specifically, insofar as one is distinguished from another. Nor would anyone patiently listen to Franciscans or [Col. 0606D] Dominicans boasting of such antiquity that they traced their origin back to Christ our Lord. Who would say such a thing?

Now it is as plain as day that the regular clergy is divided into many different families or congregations, just as monasticism is. Why, then, when the canons of Frisonaria or the Lateran are under discussion, is the entire religious clergy taken as one body? Is every individual congregation so lacking in holy and illustrious men that it cannot emerge honorably into the light by itself? Far from it: they are all most illustrious and need no assistance from others.

It therefore remains that we speak of each one individually when we intend to investigate the antiquity of its origin. Accordingly, we gladly admit that clerics were instructed in religious disciplines by the holy Apostles of God, and that they were reformed many times by councils and Fathers. But we must confess no less concerning monks, who are also frequently mentioned in councils and were reformed at various times and in various provinces.

Nor can any plausible reason for distinction between the two be assigned. For if someone says that all clerics are directed toward the same end by the very nature of the clergy, and agree in every respect toward that end—that is, in their designation for the service of the altar, the administration of the sacraments, and the preaching of the word of God—but differ only accidentally, so to speak, in the various constitutions of their congregations, which nevertheless is insufficient to diversify the orders of clerics, let him know that the same argument presses equally in the case of monks.

Monks indeed agree uniformly in their essential matters and differ only through various constitutions, which are little different from one another. Nor do the constitutions of one monastic order differ more from those of another than the constitutions of the various congregations of regular canons differ among themselves. Indeed, the mendicant orders come very close to the institution of the canons, since they were instituted to assist bishops in preaching the word of God and administering to the faithful the sacraments of confession and the Eucharist.

But if someone insists that Saint Augustine did not intend to introduce a new order of canons into the Church, but to reform an ancient one—so that there would be one and the same order instructed by his precepts and instituted earlier by the Fathers of the primitive Church—he will, I say, make little progress.

For if Blessed Benedict never undertook to establish a new order of monks or a new kind of life, but only to instruct the ancient coenobitic life—as is clear from the first chapter of his rule, where, after setting forth four kinds of monks, namely, anchorites, coenobites, sarabaites, and gyrovagues, he passes over the others and says: “With the Lord’s help, let us proceed to establish the strongest kind, the coenobites.”

[Col. 0607D] Let us add another point closely related to this, and no less difficult to believe: namely, that St. Augustine wrote a rule for his canons. Yet this is proved false by that negative argument which Pennottus elsewhere regards as conclusive. For in Book I, chapter 45, he says:

“In historical matters, an argument from negatives proves, and sometimes demonstrates, a point, as when all historians are silent.” And below: “The conclusion is drawn not only from the silence of the sacred canons, but from that of all councils, pontiffs, and histories; from such unanimous silence the conclusion follows not merely probably, but demonstratively.”

Thus, since St. Augustine himself composed his book of *Retractations*, in which he mentioned all the books he had composed up to that time; and since his disciple Possidius published a very full catalogue of those same works; yet neither of them made any mention of a rule for clerics or monks—indeed, no writer or council cited such a rule under Augustine’s name until the year 1100—[Col. 0608A] it remains that we must acknowledge that St. Augustine never composed such a rule at all, but that it was later, around the year of the Lord 1100, extracted from Letter 109, which he dictated to certain nuns on the occasion of a dispute they were having with their prioress (*praeposita*), as is clear from the letter’s context. Otherwise Possidius—and Augustine himself—would have to be accused of negligence and forgetfulness for failing to mention so distinguished a work, something Pennottus himself abhors in Book I, chapter 42, no. 8.

But there is no reason to linger over a matter so obvious, which not only Cardinal Bellarmine observed and judged in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, but which the regular canons themselves also recognized. [Col. 0608B] Among them Simon Werlinus, provost of St. Mary’s at Diest, expressly defended this position in his *Correction of the Monastic Rule of St. Augustine* (printed at Munich in 1618 by Nicolaus Henricus), and Bernard Vindirigus agrees with him in his *Corrected Critic*, printed at Vellamere in 1621 by Georgius Medellanus.

Nor are there lacking in Pennottus’s *Tripartite History* new expressions and words that make the work sufficiently suspect of having been corrupted by someone else. For who are the “Benedictinensian” monks? Or who is the writer Tuditanus? Monks are indeed called *Benedictini* after St. Benedict; but *Benedictinenses* would necessarily have to be derived from a certain St. Benedictinus, not from St. Benedict. Yet throughout almost the entire work he avoids calling them *Benedictini*. Moreover, everyone hitherto has said Luke of Tuy and the city of Tuy; here, contrary to universal usage, the form *Tuditanus* is used. I say nothing of *the progress of his order* for *the advancement of his order*, or *the benevolent reader* for *the kindly reader*: these are certainly novel expressions. But these are minor matters.

[Col. 0608C] Let us now descend to assertions that diverge from the truth. For it will be proved step by step that the *Tripartite History* is not the work of the very learned R. P. Pennottus—for it is not to be supposed that such a man wrote false assertions—and that the *Chronicle of Dexter*, which lies before us, is a fabricated product.

First of all, it is contrary to the truth that the holy patriarch Benedict made no provision for clerics in his Rule. Pennottus expressly wrote this in Book II, chapter 18, no. 4, and at the end of no. 7 says:

“St. Benedict prescribed his rule of life not for clerics but for laymen; in it there is not even a word about clerical monks.”

[Col. 0608D] And yet the most blessed teacher devotes two entire chapters of his Rule—chapters 60 and 62—to regulating the priests of the monastery. The title of the first is, “On Priests Who Desire to Live in the Monastery.” There he orders them to submit themselves entirely to the yoke of the Rule, to take a place after the abbot, and to have clerics who are not yet priests placed in a middle rank. The title of the second is, “On the Priests of the Monastery,” where he makes many provisions concerning those who are raised to orders after becoming monks. Certainly, if Pennottus had merely read the titles of the chapters of the Rule, he would have been spared this error.

[Col. 0609A] But this resembles what he writes about Paul Orosius in Book I, chapter 38, no. 4: namely, that Orosius used the word “monks” so broadly in Book VII, chapter 17, of his *Ormesta* that it included all Christians who, abandoning the many activities of worldly affairs, devoted themselves to a single work of faith. In this way, Pennottus says, regular clerics too are included under the name “monks.”

But if he had read the words immediately following those of Orosius—setting aside the fact that he incorrectly cites Orosius’s chapter 17, when it is actually chapter 33—he would plainly have found that Orosius meant only anchorites by that name. For, speaking of the emperor Valens, Orosius says:

“With the unrestrained boldness of his freedom, he enacted a law that monks—that is, Christians who, abandoning the many activities of worldly affairs, devote themselves to a single work of faith—should be compelled into military service. Those vast solitudes of Egypt and its widespread sands, which because of thirst, barrenness, and the extremely dangerous abundance of snakes human habitation did not know, had been filled by a great multitude of monks living together. Tribunes and soldiers were sent there; under another name, that of persecution, they dragged away the holy and true soldiers of God, and there they slaughtered many troops of the saints.”

[Col. 0609B] Let him therefore consider whether he wishes to draw anchorites also into the institution of the canons, however proper it is for canons to live in the churches of cities. But these are minor matters.

§ V. The rights of the Cistercian order, injured by Pennottus, are defended

[Col. 0609C] More intolerable, and farther removed from every appearance of probability, is what he asserts in Book I, chapter 50, no. 5: that the Cistercian monks—and he says the same of the Vallombrosans, Camaldolese, and Sylvestrines—derive no more immediately from the institution of Blessed Father Benedict than the Hieronymite Hermits derive from St. Jerome. He maintains that the Augustinian Hermits are so called because, through apostolic generosity, they were endowed with the rule and title of Blessed Augustine.

He ought to have remembered that he promised at the end of his prologue:

“I shall endeavor, to the best of my ability, to defend our rights without injury to others; for it is in no way my purpose or intention to touch upon the rights of other orders, or to dispute in this work about their antiquity, origin, or dignity, unless compelled to do so by the opposing side.”

He promised well, but fulfilled his promise badly. Who, I ask, compelled him to detract from the antiquity, origin, and dignity of so many holy orders? Yet the opposing side had said nothing about such matters, so that he could not claim to have been compelled by it.

[Col. 0609D] Indeed, if matters were as he writes, it would nevertheless be somewhat tolerable. It would matter little to us whether he kept his promises. If anyone had ever placed the matter in dispute, I would not object. Or if, when he was writing this, he had not had at hand the means of learning the truth about the origin of the Cistercian order, I would forgive his ignorance. But now he not only fails to keep his own statements; he denies, without any foundation, merely through his own will and haste in writing, a matter that had never been disputed and was as well known to the blind as to barbers.

This is especially blameworthy because, at the very time, he had received from me a book on the origin of the Cistercian order, written not by some modern author but by the order’s own founders. There the most holy founders explicitly demonstrate that the Cistercian order was not some new invention in the Church, but a reform of the monastic order of St. Benedict.

[Col. 0610A] Let R. P. Pennottus consider, then, whether the reformed Lateran regular canons brought into reform by the Frigidionians—or Frissonarians—are of a different order from the ancient Laterans; or whether the Frissonarians themselves, whose reform began in the year 1400, as he reports in Book III, chapter 6, do not belong to the ancient order of regular canons.

Nothing is more opposed to this throughout his entire work. Nor is that surprising, since the reform of an ancient order—especially a reform undertaken by religious men who had formerly professed that same order but were living under a looser observance, and directed toward restoring the order to its primitive vigor—is so far from the construction of a new order that, undoubtedly, the reformers are closer to the ancient order precisely in proportion as the reform itself approaches the true institution of its founders.

[Col. 0610B] Or let him say which, among the very diverse congregations of the Friars Minor, are more truly Franciscans: the Conventuals or the Observants? The Reformed, or Discalced, or the Capuchins? Yet the more recently reformed are continually newer with respect to the modern reform, while they more securely attain the primitive inheritance of their fathers.

I shall now produce the testimonies of the founders of the Cistercian order, which I had previously lent to Pennottus himself, so that he may at least read that the order truly descends from the institution of St. Benedict.

[Col. 0610C] The title of the book is: *The Origin of the Sacred Cistercian Order, by St. Robert, St. Alberic, and St. Stephen, Its First Founders, Carefully Written Five Hundred Years Ago.*

The prologue reads:

“We, the first founders of this Church of Cîteaux, make known to our successors in the present writing how canonically, with what authority, by which persons, and at what times the monastery and their manner of life began, so that, once the sincere truth of this matter has been disclosed, they may love more steadfastly both the place and the observance of the holy Rule which, by God’s grace, we have in some measure begun there,” and so forth.

The book begins as follows:

[Col. 0610D] “In the year 1098 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Robert of Molesme, of blessed memory, the first abbot of the church founded at Molesme in the diocese of Langres, and the brothers of that same monastery, came to the venerable Hugh, then legate of the Apostolic See and archbishop of the Church of Lyon. They promised that they would order their life under the protection of St. Benedict’s Rule; and for this reason they earnestly begged him to extend to them, so that they might carry it out more freely, the support of his assistance and the strength of apostolic authority. The legate gladly favoring their request laid the foundation of their undertaking with the following letter.”

Hugh, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the Apostolic See, to Robert, abbot of Molesme, and to the brothers who desire to serve God with him according to the Rule of St. Benedict:

“Let it be known to all who rejoice in the advancement of Holy Mother Church that you and certain sons of yours, brothers of the monastery of Molesme, appeared at Lyon in our presence and professed that you wished henceforth to adhere more strictly and perfectly to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, which up to that time you had observed lukewarmly and negligently in that monastery. Since it is clear that this cannot be accomplished in the aforementioned place because of numerous impediments, we have judged it beneficial for the welfare of both parties—that is, of those departing and of those remaining there—that you withdraw to another place which divine generosity shall designate for you, and there serve the Lord more healthfully and peacefully.

[Col. 0611A] “Therefore, to you who were then present—Robert the abbot, and the brothers Alberic, Odo, John, Stephen, Letaldus, and Peter—as well as to all whom you shall decide to associate with yourselves in accordance with the Rule and by common counsel, we then gave our advice that you preserve this holy purpose; we command you to persevere in it; and by apostolic authority, through the impression of our seal, we confirm it perpetually.”

[Col. 0611B] The authors go on to relate how, departing from there, they withdrew to the wilderness of Cîteaux and built the Cistercian monastery there. From that monastery the reform itself was afterward spread throughout the world, chiefly through the efforts of Blessed Bernard.

It was therefore not newly arrived men recently drawn from the world who restored the Cistercian order, but Benedictine monks of the monastery of Molesme, moved by the fact that they had hitherto observed too lukewarmly the Rule which they had professed.

For these men, as chapter 4 says, while situated at Molesme, often spoke among themselves—impelled by the grace of God—about the transgression of the Rule of Blessed Benedict, the father of monks, and grieved when they saw that they and the other monks had promised under solemn profession to observe this Rule but had scarcely kept it. For this reason, by the authority of the legate of the Apostolic See, as we have already mentioned, they came to this solitude so that they might fulfill their profession through the observance of the holy Rule, and so forth.

[Col. 0611C] The authors then append the apostolic letters of Urban II and likewise of Paschal II, Roman Pontiffs, together with letters of two cardinals and the bishop of Chalon, as well as two further letters of the aforementioned legate Hugh, by which the reform itself was confirmed.

All historians relate our origin in precisely the same way, as may be seen in Caesarius, *Dialogue on Miracles*, Book I, chapter 1; Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, Book XXV, chapters 94 and 95; and Antoninus, who reproduces the account word for word from him; in Sigebert, or his continuator Robert, under the year 1098; and in all who have mentioned the origin of that order. More recently the same account appears in Aubertus Miraeus, Barnabas de Montalvo, and Bernard of Brito in their Cistercian chronicles, and most exactly in the *Evangelical Laurel* of the very reverend and most celebrated R. P. Fr. Angelus Manrique, public professor of theology at Salamanca—to omit innumerable others.

[Col. 0611D] The words of Caesarius deserve notice:

“Keep this firmly in mind: the author of our undertaking is the Holy Spirit; its institutor is St. Benedict; its intercessor is the venerable abbot Robert.”

From this arose a dispute between the reformed Cistercians and the Cluniacs, such as frequently arises between reformed and unreformed members of the same order concerning observance or transgression of the Rule. It may be seen in Peter the Venerable, Book III of his letters, letter 28, to St. Bernard, and Book V, letter 16, to the same man. There he responds to twelve articles of the Rule of St. Benedict in which the Cistercians accused the Cluniacs of falling short, and he objects to us concerning the change in the color of the habit. Nevertheless, our members maintained that this change was permitted by the prescription of the Rule in chapter 55.

[Col. 0612A] Bernard himself also discusses this question in his *Apology to William, Abbot*, where he openly calls the order of St. Benedict his own order.

From all this, then, let R. P. Pennottus consider how greatly he detracts from the rights of the Cistercian order when he writes that it does not descend from St. Benedict, its founding father.

Nor should he object that authors commonly do not call it the Cistercian congregation but simply the Cistercian order. This does not make it distinct from the order of St. Benedict as essentially different—if I may use his scholastic terminology—but only as accidentally different. We have treated this matter more fully elsewhere, in a special treatise on the proper meaning of the word “order.”

[Col. 0612B] The same judgment must be formed concerning the other reforms of the order of St. Benedict. St. Romuald, from whom the Camaldolese derive; St. John Gualbert, from whom the Vallombrosans derive; and St. Silvester, from whom the Sylvestrines derive, were black-robed monks and sought to reform their order.

[Col. 0612C] What, moreover, are we to make of Pennottus’s assertion in Book II, chapter 73, no. 1?

“But the monastic order received not only its origin but also its principal illuminators from that same order of canons.”

After listing certain saints who formerly passed from the canons to the Benedictines, he adds:

“The matter is still much more evident in the case of the Cistercians, since one Malachy, a regular canon in Ireland, founded so many Cistercian monasteries, and entire monasteries of canons passed over to the Cistercians, as is evident in the abbey of Alna, belonging to the regular canons of Liège, which St. Bernard changed into a Cistercian monastery. The prior of the monastery of York also went over to the Cistercians with nearly all the brothers of that monastery, for whom St. Bernard himself wrote to the abbot of York the letter numbered 95 in the collection. Blessed Humbert seems to have been among their number; the same Blessed Bernard recounted his praises in a sermon delivered on him.”

So much for Pennottus. But whatever the truth of these matters may be, let readers consider which of the two groups was truly illuminated: the canons who passed over to the Cistercians under the pretext of attaining reform and sanctity, or the Cistercians who received the canons into their bosom and raised them to the highest summit of sanctity?

[Col. 0612D] There can be no doubt that they became holier and were made illustrious. For the canons did not pass to the Cistercians in order to illuminate or perfect them, but in order to become more perfect and more illustrious themselves.

Bernard himself judged similarly in a comparable case. He says in Letter 142:

“This, I say—this most certainly—made you who were illustrious more illustrious, you who were holy more holy; and wherever this discourse was spread, it filled everything with the fragrance of sweetness . . . With what joyful embrace the multitude of Cistercians received you,” and so forth.

If someone should say that our order too was made illustrious by the arrival of such men, we do not deny it—but no differently from the way in which an order is made illustrious by distinguished men coming from the world. Who does not see, then, that the world itself could equally boast that it had made all the orders illustrious?

[Col. 0613A] Moreover, we deny that St. Malachy was a regular canon, since it is more truthful that he was always a monk, and that by the time he founded monasteries in Ireland for the Cistercians, he had already joined them. For we know with certainty from the final chapter of the *Life of St. Bernard*, written by his secretary, who attended his funeral, that St. Bernard was buried in St. Malachy’s habit, and conversely St. Malachy in Bernard’s clothing.

For this reason the Cistercians continually include him in the catalogue of their saints and celebrate him every year with solemn office as one of their own. Yet Pennottus once considered this same argument effective for proving that St. Herculanus was a regular canon, namely because he is honored with solemn office by the regular canons.

[Col. 0613B] Again, the monastery of Alna—for that is its name, not Alva—had professed the Rule of St. Augustine for only four years, as Miraeus reports in his *Cistercian Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1148. Since its institution was therefore still young, it was easy for it to pass to something more excellent.

But where, I ask, did Pennottus find that this monastery of York, from which the prior and certain other brothers hastened to the Cistercians, belonged to the canonical order? If he thinks it was the cathedral church itself, then, setting aside the fact that he rather freely assumes in Book II, chapter 37, no. 6, that it belonged to canons and not to monks of St. Benedict, he makes an even freer assertion when he says that the prior and his brothers left it.

For nothing of the sort can be drawn from Bernard’s letter—which is Letter 94, not 95, as Pennottus claims—and the title suggests the opposite. It reads:

“To the abbot of a certain monastery of York, from which the prior had departed with several brothers.”

When it says “a certain monastery of York,” it sufficiently indicates that this was not the cathedral church itself, but another church in the same diocese.

[Col. 0613C] The case of Blessed Humbert is easier. Neither from St. Bernard’s sermon preached at his death, nor from his *Life*, which is found in Book III of the *Cistercian Origin*, chapters 4 and 5, nor from anywhere else can it be established that he was a monk of York or one of those who were reformed with the prior.

Indeed, the opposite follows quite clearly from the fact that, according to Bernard himself, Humbert lived with him almost from the very beginning of the monastery of Clairvaux. But the conversion of the prior and the York brothers occurred much later, as is clear from the letter written by Bernard—if we consider its place among his other letters—when he was working to suppress the schism of Anacletus, at a time when he was already famous throughout the world.

[Col. 0613D] We do not, however, wish to deny that the mellifluous doctor admitted many regular canons into his order and rejected others. This may be seen in the case of the man who illustrated Bernard’s patience by striking him on the cheek when Bernard refused to admit him to the order; the incident is fully related in Book III of the *Life of Bernard*, chapter 6. But let us proceed to other matters.

I pass over the Council of Rheims celebrated by Blessed Eugene III, which Pennottus, in Book I, chapter 19, no. 1, attributes to Eugene II, thereby making the reform of the regular canons carried out there much more ancient. Yet the acts of the Council of Rheims themselves contradict this, as do all who have written the acts of Eugene or Bernard; Bernard was present and defended the unity of the Trinity against Gilbert Porretanus. He himself discusses this matter in Sermon 80 on the *Song of Songs*.

[Col. 0614A] I come now to Blessed Joachim, whom our friend attacks undeservedly and immoderately.

§ VI. Blessed Abbot Joachim is defended against the calumnies of Pennottus and others

There are two matters in the teachings of the venerable abbot Joachim which Pennottus believes to be damaging. The first is that, in his introduction to the exposition of the Apocalypse, Joachim prophesied concerning the order of hermits. The second is that he maintained that the regular canons instituted by St. Rufus around the year of the Lord 1100 were then first endowed by him with the Rule of St. Augustine.

[Col. 0614B] This is how he reports Joachim’s views, and he attacks them so violently that he greatly exceeds the bounds of courtesy and religious propriety. For even if matters were as he reports them, and the holy abbot had written what Pennottus attributes to him, they were not matters of such importance that the office of the Holy Inquisition should thunder against him on their account, or that, without hearing him, a sentence of condemnation should be issued against him on the basis of the misunderstood testimony of certain persons—a condemnation, I say, of eternal death and of the person by the general Council of Lateran.

“It remains,” he says in Book I, chapter 41, “that we examine only the testimony of Abbot Joachim and see whether perhaps Goliath has been recalled from the underworld, possessing such strength that he alone can rightly stand against twenty.”

And shortly afterward, in no. 2:

“Whether we may rightly count Joachim among the prophets, I shall report what learned men have written about him.”

[Col. 0614C] Here he constructs his case by calling St. Antoninus, Cardinals Bellarmine and Baronius, and Alfonso de Castro as witnesses. After hearing them as best he can, he mockingly adds:

“From these and the other things said above, you may see how highly this new prophet should be esteemed, whom Marquez presents as such a vigorous soldier that he alone can stand against twenty armed men.”

In Book II, chapter 2, as though Joachim had previously been unknown to him, he cites him as follows:

“Thus the first opinion concerning the origin of the canonical order is that of a certain abbot named Joachim, in his exposition of the Apocalypse. He asserts that the order of regular canons began around the year of the Lord 1100 in the regions of Gaul, under a certain bishop named Rufus, who first handed the Rule of St. Augustine to those canons; and from him the congregation of regular canons derived its origin, which for that reason was called the congregation of St. Rufus.”

[Col. 0614D]

And after a little more:

“This opinion of Joachim, especially as explained and expanded in this manner, contains not one but many manifest and palpable errors.”

In the course of the chapter he enumerates ten of them. In passing, he treats the most reverend Lord Bishop Antonio Massa Galesinus, a very learned man of his age, with the same honor because he followed Joachim in this matter. He says:

“I omit Antonio Massa Galesinus, who, following Abbot Joachim, poured forth many absurdities, by which he most clearly displayed the venality of his mind, the shallowness of his intellect, and his ignorance,” and so forth.

Is this how one may treat men of such gravity? But the hand that is against everyone will have to withstand everyone’s hand.

[Col. 0615A] As far as Joachim is concerned, it is obvious that Pennottus did not read the writings he cites, nor did he recognize who Joachim was or what standing he held in the Church. Everything is cited incorrectly. The prophecy concerning the order of hermits is not found in the introduction to the Apocalypse, but in the exposition of chapter 14, at the words:

“And another angel came out of the temple, having also a sharp sickle,” and so forth.

As for the canons instituted by St. Rufus, Joachim does not discuss them in his exposition of the Apocalypse, but in chapter 20 of the introduction. One can see that the good soldier has, as the saying goes, changed horses.

Certainly, in a matter of such importance, on which the honor of a holy man depended, no one will absolve Pennottus from the fault of notable carelessness in failing to read Joachim, when it would have been very easy for him to consult the works either in the Vatican Library, or in that of St. Peter at the Golden Mountain, splendidly supplied by R. P. Luke Wadding, or in the Anician Library of the Gregorian College, or in that of the most illustrious Lord Giovanni Battista Coccini, dean of the Sacred Rota. His works could be found there and in other libraries of Rome.

[Col. 0615B] What if Joachim had been less opposed to Pennottus’s efforts? What if he had favored them? It would not have been enough to raise his teaching to the heavens; no one would have defended so vigorously the spirit of the abbot, distinguished by the gift of prophecy, as Pennottus himself. For he strongly honors even authors of inferior rank who happen to favor him, out of gratitude.

I hope, nevertheless, that Joachim will henceforth be held in great esteem by him, since he more than anyone else defends the cause of the clerics. For there is nothing he emphasizes equally throughout all his works more than that the order of clerics preceded the order of monks. He expressly asserts and proves this in Book II of the *Concordance of the Two Testaments*, treated in chapter 5, and in chapter 19 of the introduction to the Apocalypse.

[Col. 0615C] In the following chapter, chapter 20, he compares twelve orders or congregations of religious men to the twelve patriarchs, the sons of Jacob. First he lists six congregations of clerics, represented by the six sons of Leah, Jacob’s first wife in relation to Rachel; then he sets forth as a type the same number of monks and religious soldiers, represented by the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, the handmaids, and of Rachel.

I gladly quote his words, so that Pennottus may see that he has hitherto misunderstood the holy abbot when he discusses the canons of St. Rufus. To make clear what is being said, he assigns the sons of Jacob to the individual orders.

[Col. 0615D] “The first order of religious men was instituted by the apostles in the primitive Church, and it is represented by Reuben.

“The second was instituted at Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians; and it is represented by Simeon.

“The third was instituted at Alexandria. Concerning it, as Ecclesiastical History reports, Philo the Jew related many things worthy of praise, commending its sobriety and manner of life; and it is represented by Levi.

“The fourth order was instituted in Africa by Blessed Augustine; and it is represented by Judah.

“The fifth order was that of the regular canons instituted in the western regions. Since it follows, in part, the Rule which it observes, it too is called the order of St. Augustine; and it is represented by Issachar.

“The sixth order appears to be that of the Premonstratensian canons; and it is represented by Zebulun.”

This concerns the sons of Leah.

[Col. 0616A] After speaking of these six orders of clerics, he adds an account of an equal number of orders of monks:

“Bilhah, Rachel’s handmaid, bore a son in the form of the order of monks, which was instituted in the Greek Church by the holy Fathers. This order, therefore, is represented by Dan, the son of Bilhah the handmaid.

“Bilhah then bore a second son named Naphtali, who seems to represent the order of monks in the West—namely, those instructed under the discipline of the holy Father Benedict—and she ceased bearing.

“Leah too, emulating her sister in this matter, gave her handmaid Zilpah to her husband. She bore Gad and Asher, representing two orders of lay brothers who flourished in those times in the regions of the East: the Hospitallers, now called the Order of St. John, and the Knights Templar.

[Col. 0616B] “Finally, he says that two monastic orders, represented by Joseph and Benjamin, the sons of Rachel and the last of all the brothers, had not yet begun in his own time. Nor is this surprising, since they were to be the most illustrious orders of the Preachers and the Friars Minor, concerning whom Joachim clearly prophesied in his commentaries on Jeremiah.”

Let Pennottus now consider, I ask, whom Joachim favors more: clerics or monks.

As for what he writes about the regular canons of the fifth order, it is clear that this must be understood of a certain congregation—namely, the one in Gaul that was canonically endowed with the Rule of St. Augustine, and that had begun to be called “regular canons” by the doubled name of canon and rule.

Joachim does not promise what year this occurred. And when he asserts that it was instituted by St. Rufus, he writes this not from his own authority but from the report of others. Perhaps that order was commonly said to have been instituted by St. Rufus because it was instituted in his monastery, and from there spread from St. Rufus to many other places.

[Col. 0616C] Nevertheless, the precedence of the clerics should not be understood so rigidly according to the blessed man’s mind as though a great span of time separated the institution of the clerics from that of the monks. For in the preceding chapter—chapter 19 of the introduction—he maintains that both arose in the primitive Church, saying:

“When the first state had been entered and the second begun—which began with Christ the Lord—the orders of clerics and monks immediately began: undoubtedly in the primitive Church, where they maintained both the ecclesiastical life by preaching and the monastic order through common life.”

So great was the communion of these two orders in this second state that there were clerics living communally like monks, and monks to whom clerical duties were entrusted.

[Col. 0616D] Furthermore, concerning chapter 14 of the Apocalypse he writes:

“An order will arise which appears to be new, but is not, clothed in black garments and girded above with a belt; it will be the order of hermits,” and so forth.

Whether Pennottus wishes it or not, this is clearly a prophecy concerning the Hermits of St. Augustine, since Joachim depicted them in vivid colors before they had yet been given that habit and girdle—as R. P. Luke Wadding proves at length—and before they had been united into a single order.

[Col. 0617A] For Pennottus’s response in Book I, chapter 51—that Joachim could have been speaking of the Williamite or Jambonite hermits, after whom he prophesied around the year of the Lord 1200—is far from the truth and shows that he has little memory. For shortly before, in chapter 46, no. 5, he had said of the Williamites:

“It is clear that the habit of the hermits of St. William was entirely different, both from the hermits of that order who remained in that habit—which was not a black cowl but a white tunic with a white mantle—and hence they were called White Mantles.”

Concerning the Jambonites, or hermits of Friar John Buono, he asserts in the following chapter, chapter 47, no. 1, that before the union made by Innocent IV they did not have a black habit, but one very similar to the habit of the Friars Minor. He also reports a letter of Cardinal William, their protector, in which he says of them after they had been united:

“And because their habit, which seemed conformed to the habit of the Friars Minor, was in some way causing scandal among certain people, by the command and authority of the two cardinals who were then exercising the office of legate in the regions of Lombardy, they chose the black habit which you still wear.”

He adds: “When they were already called the Hermite Brothers of John Buono,” and so forth.

[Col. 0617B] That they later also adopted the girdle is clear from the apostolic letters of Gregory IX, which Pennottus himself reports in the same chapter 47, no. 7.

Joachim therefore depicted the habit and belt of the hermits before they existed in reality. Nor is this surprising, since he also plainly foretold the orders of the Friars Minor and the Preachers, and caused their patriarchs to be depicted in vivid colors at St. Mark’s in Venice wearing the habit which they later adopted. He foretold many other things as well, so that it is more evident that he possessed an extraordinary prophetic spirit than that this needs to be demonstrated at length.

[Col. 0617C] So that these matters may become known to everyone, and so that Joachim’s innocence may be established against the testimony presented by Pennottus’s adversaries, I shall not hesitate to bring forward some of those who stand on his side, briefly and concisely, as the occasion permits.

First of all I present St. Cyril, the glory of the Carmelite order, who, from Carmel, wrote to Joachim, then living in Calabria, asking him to explain a prophecy divinely revealed to Cyril, in these words:

“Since God has bestowed upon you, as upon a second John the Evangelist, the wondrous grace of knowing future things, I humbly ask, reverend Father, that you deign to explain this prophecy more briefly, so that we may be able to penetrate more clearly the abyss of this divine gift. Break open the nut; reveal what is dense, so that the brightness of the most brilliant Sun may shine forth for all.”

[Col. 0617D] A letter of this kind exists together with Joachim’s works in the Vatican Library and in another library of the monastery of St. Faith of the Cistercian order near Zaragoza. Jacobus de Voragine also reports it in the *Life of St. Cyril*.

The *Chronicle of the Masters General of the Order of St. Dominic* contains the following:

“The venerable abbot Joachim, founder of the Florense order, prophetically showing his brothers the habit which the said Master Reginald had received from the Blessed Virgin, caused it to be painted in a certain monastery of his order in Calabria and also to be represented in the Church of St. Mark at Venice in a mosaic image, saying: ‘Soon there will arise in the Church of God a new order of teachers,’” and so forth.

[Col. 0618A] Henry of Vrimaria, in his treatise on the origin of the order of the Hermits of St. Augustine, adduces Joachim’s prophecy, which we discussed a little earlier.

Robert of Licio, bishop of Aquino, in Sermon 45 on the Saints, which concerns Blessed Francis, says:

“Moreover, Abbot Joachim, a man of extraordinary holiness and distinguished by a prophetic spirit, said in one of his little books: ‘There will be two men, one from here and the other from there, who represent two orders: one an Italian from Tuscany, the other a Spaniard from Spain,’” and so forth.

Of Francis he adds:

“He caused him to be painted in the Church of St. Mark at Venice with the stigmata above the door of the sacristy, just as those who look upon it today can see.”

Ptolemy of Lucca, in his *Chronicle*:

“During the time of Lucius III, Abbot Joachim flourished in Calabria, celebrated for his learning and prophecy.”

[Col. 0618B] Trithemius, Book II, *On Illustrious Men of St. Benedict*, chapter 117.

Matthaeus Palmerius, in his continuation of the *Chronicle*: “Joachim the abbot, a man full of the prophetic spirit and learned in the science of sacred letters, flourished in Calabria under Urban II.”

Pandolphus Collenutius, Book IV of the *History of Naples*, when discussing the emperor Henry VI, who was amazed that his wife Constance, then about fifty years old, was pregnant, writes that when Henry learned that she was pregnant, he sought to have the matter confirmed by Abbot Joachim. Joachim was flourishing at that time and was distinguished by his reputation for the prophetic spirit. The abbot assured Henry that Constance had conceived by Henry himself, and that she would give birth to a boy; he also foretold all the events of the child’s life and how Henry himself, shortly afterward, would die in the field of Malearum near Messina, etc.

Joannes Nicolaus Doglion, Part III of the *Compendium of Universal History*: “Abbot Joachim,” he says, “foretold to both kings—that is, Philip of France and Richard of England—that their expedition would be fruitless, because the time had not yet arrived for recovering the holy city; the outcome of events proved the truth of this.”

Paulus Aemilius, in the history of the monastery of Carbone, while discussing the emperor Henry VI, says: “After Joachim the abbot had foretold future events,” etc.

Petrus Rodulphus, in his *Seraphic History*, when discussing the image of Saint Francis, writes as follows: “Before the appearance of this saint, Abbot Joachim of Fiore, a man of outstanding holiness and conspicuous for the prophetic spirit, [had him depicted] in the church of Saint Mark at Venice,” etc. The image is still seen today in the vault of the church. A certain ingenious poet expressed the same in these verses:

> And before he had arisen in the world, in the church  
> Which under Mark’s name is second to none throughout the world,  
> He stands depicted among the Venetians, represented for many long years.

He adds: “Abbot Joachim was a man of outstanding and almost divine intellect. He glossed the Apocalypse, in which he foretold many things concerning the Orders of Mendicants, whose truth the outcome of events made clear.”

Arnoldus Wion, Part II of the *Tree of Life*, Book V, chapter 89, branch 9, collects many testimonies in praise of the prophetic spirit in which Joachim flourished. For the same purpose he cites Leander of Bologna in his *Life* of Joachim. He also asserts that the naval victory over the Turks at the Echinades Islands, won under the leadership of the most serene Don John of Austria in the year of salvation 1571, had been foreseen and announced by Joachim nearly four hundred years earlier, as the authors of the *Triumph of the Catholic Church* understood very clearly from his books on the Apocalypse.

Gabriel Barrius, in his *Life* of Joachim, which begins, “Joannes Joachim was an abbot,” etc., after listing his books, adds: “In them it is clear that he possessed the prophetic spirit; for he prophesied many things, of which many have been fulfilled and the rest remain to be fulfilled. For he foretold that Greece would be given over to the nations because of its treachery toward the Roman Church, and that the founders of the Orders of Preachers and Friars Minor would soon arise; indeed, he foretold them at the very doors of the Church.” He continues at length in this vein. But the prophecy concerning the subjugation of Greece by the Saracens appears in the *Commentaries on Jeremiah*, on chapters 1 and 48, in unmistakable words.

Sylvester Meucius, in the preface to his *Commentaries on the Apocalypse*, extols Joachim with many praises on account of the prophetic spirit with which he abounded.

Paschalinus Regiselinus, in his dedicatory letter to the prophecies of blessed Joachim, says: “Everyone knows that whatever the Abbot wrapped up in his sayings received the exact fulfillment of its events.”

I pass over many others, such as Angelus Manrique, the most learned theologian of our age, an outstanding preacher of the word of God and public professor of theology at Salamanca, in his *Evangelical Laurel*; Barnabas de Montalbo in the *Cistercian Chronicle*; and Jacobus Graecus Syllaneus in the *Chronicle of the Order of Fiore*; together with others who fought splendidly on Joachim’s behalf. Nor are illustrious poets lacking who affirm the same opinion. For Dante, in the third part of the *Paradiso*, says:

> Here is Rabanus, and at my side shines  
> The Calabrian Abbot Joachim,  
> Endowed with the prophetic spirit.

Philippus Phasianus echoes him in unequal verses published in Joachim’s praise, which Graecus reports.

The author of the epitaph affixed to his tomb also says, among other things:

> For he knew then the sayings of the Fathers who had been  
> Sheltered beneath the cloud, and he knew what was to be done.  
> As a truthful prophet he foretold many things;  
> Many were fulfilled, as the day made manifest by its light.

As a crowning testimony I shall add Seraphinus of Fermo, a canon regular of the Lateran, whom R. P. Pennottus extols with extraordinary praises in Book III, chapter 29, no. 5. He calls him “a venerable and most holy canon, and a most fervent herald of the word of God, who enlightened his age by his holy preaching, whose words,” he says, “were like a blazing fire and like a hammer crushing rocks.” By his counsel and persuasion above all, two congregations of regular clerics were founded: one of Saint Paul the Beheaded at Milan, the other of the priests of the Good Jesus at Ravenna. After laboring through many efforts for the glory of God and the salvation of souls, and publishing various booklets full of the fire of divine love and exceedingly useful for spiritual edification, he died at Bologna, etc.

Since these statements are true as they came from his mouth, it will be surprising if Pennottus did not prefer the judgment of so great a man. But what then? In his *Commentaries on Revelation*, chapter 9—the work he himself mentions in Book III, chapter 55, no. 6—he says the following about Joachim: “I would not wish this exposition of this chapter to be attributed to my own ingenuity, and therefore to be considered less credible. Let whatever Joachim, Ubertinus, and others write concerning these matters be read, and everything becomes clear; for whatever they prophesied, we see to have been fulfilled.”

Here, candid reader, are more than twenty witnesses whom we set against the four or five produced by Pennottus on the opposing side. Between them there is not only the most obvious difference in number, but also in their knowledge of what they testify. Our witnesses are, so to speak, eyewitnesses: they write what they themselves read in Joachim’s books and saw fulfilled in reality. The witnesses on the opposing side cannot be eyewitnesses, since they attribute to Joachim something he never wrote.

For Vincent of Beauvais, whom Saint Antoninus transcribes—and therefore reports by hearsay—blames Joachim for having foretold that the end of the world would occur within two generations, that is, within sixty years. Yet he never stated this affirmatively anywhere, but only expressed it as a doubt, as may be seen at the end of the *Concordia*, where he discusses the matter expressly.

Nor should it seem surprising that the holy abbot wrote somewhat hesitantly about Christ’s imminent judgment, since other holy Fathers improperly assigned a short term to it. Bernard reports this of Saint Norbert, founder of the Premonstratensian canons, in Letter 56; Bernard had received it from Norbert’s own mouth.

Nevertheless, Vincent and Antoninus stand on our side when they lend credence to certain of Joachim’s predictions—namely, the prediction that the time had not yet arrived for the kings of England and France to recover the Holy Land, and others of the same kind.

Cardinal Bellarmine, who is cited in second place, makes no assertion, but leaves the judgment to others, as his words show in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Joachim.

As for what Cardinal Baronius writes in volume XII of the *Annals*, under the year 1164—that Joachim, as an opponent of Peter Lombard, was condemned at the Lateran Council—who does not see that this is improperly stated?
