It was not the person of the abbot that was condemned, but the book on the unity and essence of the Trinity which he had published.

Here are the words of the council, chapter 2:

> We therefore condemn and reject the book, or treatise, which Abbot Joachim published against Master Peter Lombard, concerning the unity or essence of the Trinity, because it asserted in that work that the unity of the Holy Trinity is not real and individual, but merely analogous, just as several men are called one people.

Pennottus, however, suppressed the council’s exculpation of Joachim’s person, which it immediately adds:

> Nevertheless, we do not wish any derogation to be made on this account from the monastery of Fiore, of which Joachim himself was the founder, where both the regular institution and the salutary observance remain; especially since Joachim himself ordered all his writings to be submitted to us for the judgment of the Apostolic See, to be approved or corrected. He dictated a letter, which he signed with his own hand, in which he firmly confessed that he held the faith held by the Roman Church, etc.

This letter itself was printed together with the commentaries on the Apocalypse. It begins, “To all to whom this letter may come,” and ends:

> I, Abbot Joachim, wrote this document and confirmed it with my own hand, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1200; and I confess that I hold the faith as it is contained herein. I, Brother Joachim, Abbot of Fiore.

Appended to the same letter is a letter of Pope Clement II, in which, among other things, he says:

> Since, then, at the command and exhortation of our predecessor, Pope Lucius of blessed memory, you are said to have begun an exposition of the Apocalypse and the work of the *Concordia*, and afterward to have composed it by the authority of the Lord Pope Urban, his successor, we admonish and exhort your Charity in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters that, bringing your labors in this matter to the eagerly desired and proper conclusion, with the grace of the Lord assisting you, you should complete that work for the benefit of your neighbors and diligently endeavor to correct it. And when the opportunity arises, come to us as soon as possible, presenting yourself for examination and judgment by the Apostolic See. For if you should wish to keep it hidden, consider carefully how you may appease the offense of the supreme Head of the Household by making satisfaction for the talent entrusted to you.
>
> Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, in the first year of our pontificate.

From this you may see that Joachim did not rashly assume the office of doctor or writer in the Church, but did so at the urging and command of three supreme pontiffs—Lucius, Urban, and Clement. If he nevertheless fell into error in some respect, you should believe that this occurred through the profound providence of God, namely so that he might be reminded of his own frailty and, having flown so high above nature, might not at some point become presumptuous, but might remain fearful.

Nevertheless, there were people who, led by a spirit of malice, defamed Joachim and his Florentine monastic followers by accusing them of heresy. One such person was a certain bishop of Lucca, whom Honorius III nevertheless severely restrained in a letter sent to him from Saint Peter’s on the fourth day before the Nones of December, in the first year of his pontificate. Jacobus Graecus reports the letter in section 20 of the *Chronology of the Order of Fiore*, and Paschalinus Regiselinus in the preface to Joachim’s prophecies.

The same Honorius added another letter in the fifth year of his pontificate. It is preserved in volume 3 of his *Register*, under number 268 in the Vatican archives. I received it from R. P. Fr. Luca Wadding, and it runs as follows:

> Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to his venerable brothers, the archbishop of Cosenza and the bishop of Bisignano.
>
> It has been brought before us on behalf of our beloved sons, the abbots and convent of the Order of Fiore, both of its head and of its members, that the one who envies the salvation of men and their peace, taking occasion from the fact that the book which Abbot Joachim of blessed memory published against Master Peter Lombard of blessed memory was condemned in a general council, has stirred up against them certain prelates, both clerics and laymen, superiors and subjects. In order to turn them away from the leisure of contemplation, these men stretch ropes into a snare for their feet and place a stumbling-block beside their path, reproaching them by asserting that the same abbot, who was the father and founder of their order, is regarded by the Church of God as a heretic.
>
> For this reason they not only turn simple people, who partake of milk, away from association with that order, but also cause those strong in faith, who have learned to use solid food and habitually have their senses trained to discern good and evil, to begin wavering regarding the institutions of that order.
>
> Although the aforementioned book or treatise was condemned in the council mentioned, nevertheless, since Joachim himself ordered all his writings to be submitted to the Roman Pontiff for the judgment of the Apostolic See, to be approved or corrected, dictating a letter which he signed with his own hand and in which he firmly confessed that he held the faith held by the Roman Church, which by the Lord’s disposition is the mother and teacher of all the faithful, we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters that throughout Calabria you cause it to be publicly announced that we regard him as a Catholic man and a follower of the holy orthodox faith, and that the regular observance which he instituted is salutary. Those who thereafter presume to disparage or insult the said order shall be punished with an appropriate penalty, once the truth has been ascertained and, after prior admonition, the obstacle of appeal having been removed.
>
> Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

However, so far as I infer from reading Joachim’s works, he was accused before Innocent and the council through the cunning of certain monks of his own order, whom imprudent zeal was burning; and the words of the book *On the Unity of the Trinity* were twisted into a meaning foreign to the author’s mind, so that he might be charged with error in the full assembly of the Fathers. Or perhaps something was maliciously added to his books.

Jacobus Graecus certainly suspected this before us, saying in section 22:

> Whether anything was added to that work before it was presented to the council must be left to God’s judgment to examine.

For Joachim himself seems to have foretold this very thing in chapter 11 of Jeremiah, on the words, “To the men of Anathoth, who seek your life.”

Whether these things are true, let my readers judge from what I shall set forth below.

Joachim professed the Cistercian order at the monastery of Corazzo, in the diocese of Martirano, which had proceeded from the filiation of Fossanova, around the year 1150. Nevertheless, while building the monastery of Fiore, he introduced a new reform into the Cistercian order, which was called Florentine from its head. As a result, he incurred the hatred of certain Cistercians, who mocked his prophecies and searched his writings with great care, eagerly seeking an opportunity to accuse him.

I would believe that he or most of them acted out of good motives in their zeal against him, and that the dispute between them proceeded no differently from the ancient dispute between Chrysostom and Epiphanius.

Whatever the case, in Joachim’s book *On the Substance or Unity of the Trinity* they found grounds by which they could subject him to the Church’s severe judgment. He apparently explained the unity of the Trinity in the same manner in which Christ, through John, asserted that those whom he loves become one with God; or in the manner in which the three tribes of Judah, Benjamin, and Levi are said together to be one people. He also added that the simple divine substance cannot be conceived apart from the persons—as Peter Lombard seemed to have done in Book I of the *Sentences*, distinction 3—unless one were to think with Sabellius and Arius.

They therefore brought this matter before the council, and the aforementioned book received a sentence of condemnation in the year of the Lord 1215, in the sense which its words appeared to imply.

Joachim, however, was less able to defend himself, since in the preceding year, 1214 from the Lord’s Incarnation, he had ended his earthly life on the last day of March, as Jacobus Graecus makes clear in his *Chronology*, section 36.

Nevertheless, eighteen years before his condemnation he had foretold it in explicit words, namely in the year 1197, when he composed his commentaries on Jeremiah, as he himself testifies when he says on chapter 24: “For the year 1197 is now underway,” etc.

The prophecy appears at chapter 11 and is so clear that it names the book and the subject of the book later to be condemned, as well as the accusers and the Roman pontiff who would condemn it.

On the words, “Come, let us put wood in his bread, and let us cut him off from the land of the living, so that his name may be remembered no more,” he says:

> They will place a stumbling-block in order to extinguish sound doctrine and overthrow the name of the teacher to whom the meaning of Daniel will be revealed.

That teacher is Joachim himself, who unraveled the most hidden prophecies of Daniel, in chapter 12 of the Apocalypse and elsewhere.

> For it will happen that the supreme pontiff will make the truth known, so that one may be condemned—that is, so that a teacher may die for the people—in order that the whole nation may not perish in error.

Thus Zedekiah rises up against Jeremiah, condemns the book—what could be clearer?—and severs the Trinity from unity—the title of the book is expressed here. He cuts the teacher’s sentence with the scribe’s knife, alluding to chapter 36 of Jeremiah:

> When Jehudi had read three or four pages, he cut the scroll with the scribe’s knife.

And shortly afterward he says:

> He designates the supreme pontiff who will come after Celestine, whoever he may be.

Everyone knows that Innocent III, who condemned the book, succeeded Celestine. Since the star disappeared—that is, since, after Joachim’s death, the brilliance of his understanding disappeared—spiritual intelligence will be extinguished through deceit and delivered over through envy, and he will think of destroying it.

As for the fact that the bishops of the churches and the Pharisees—that is, the abbots, priors, and religious of the Cistercian order—assembled a council, perhaps a general one, all of this must be referred to that teacher of truth whom the sixth angel describes, or rather under whom the book of truth is shown open in the hand of another angel.

These matters become much clearer from what he immediately adds. Explaining the words, “Therefore thus says the Lord to the men of Anathoth who seek your life and say, ‘You shall not prophesy in the name of the Lord, and you shall die by our hands.’ Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: ‘Behold, I will visit punishment upon them; their young men shall die by the sword, their sons and daughters shall die of famine, and no remnant shall remain of them. For I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their visitation,’” he says:

> It follows: “To the men of Anathoth who seek your life.” From certain Cistercians this iniquity will proceed: that the teacher may not prophesy in the name of the Lord and may die at their hands—that is, through their actions and councils—in other words, may be condemned. For it was through their action that the book was condemned in the general council.

But what follows from this? So that truth may correspond to truth, he foretells the lamentable decline of the Cistercian order—which, if only we had not seen it with our own eyes:

> “Their young men shall die by the sword,” etc.

The young men are the priors; the sons are the monks; the daughters are the monasteries, which had been distributed through filiations, or their obediences. The first will fall by the sword of the civil power—that is, into the hands of commendatory superiors. The second will fail through famine of Catholic doctrine. The remnants—that is, the powers of the order—will remain in a state of diminished regular observance.

> “For I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth,” that is, upon the higher prelates of the Cistercians, “the year of their visitation,” that is, the year of the tribulation imposed upon them.

Nevertheless, later, in chapter 35 of Jeremiah, he foretells the continuation of the same order in some of its sons. For after stating that Jonadab son of Rechab commanded his sons not to drink wine or build houses, but to dwell in tents, he directs his speech to Saint Bernard, who prohibited his monks both from preaching and from wandering about, and commanded them simply to remain subject in the monasteries . . . .

As for the statement that some of the seed of Jonadab would not be lacking, who would always stand in the presence of the Lord, it seems that the Cistercian religious order will continue until the end of the world.

By this prophecy, the first congregation of the observance of Saint Bernard was foretold before all others. In the kingdoms of Spain it began to be instituted from the year of the Lord 14 . . . ; with God’s favor, through the merits of Saint Bernard, it sustains the former splendor of the order. Then came the observance of the Italian congregation, and finally the reform of the monks of Fuliens. Through all these, it has come about that never until now has anyone from the seed of Jonadab—or of the honey-flowing Bernard—failed to stand in the presence of the Lord.

To return, then, to the earlier matter: the meaning of the prophecy is clear. Namely, the sons of Anathoth—that is, the Cistercians—would take offense at his teaching. To quiet this offense, the pontiff would be declared bound to pronounce that one person should be condemned in the book *On the Unity of the Trinity*, over whose interpretation the offense had arisen. That pontiff would be none other than the one who succeeded Celestine.

That pontiff was Innocent III. He convened the general Lateran Council, at which, besides seventy archbishops and four hundred bishops, eight hundred abbots were present, most of them from the Cistercian order. There, at the prompting of certain of these men, he condemned Joachim’s book *On the Unity of the Trinity*.

It should nevertheless be noted that when Joachim says, “He condemns the book, severs the Trinity from unity, and with the scribe’s knife [cuts] the teacher’s sentence,” the word “severs” is significant, because elsewhere in the same book he declares his own position. For he says certain things that seem sufficiently to draw him toward the Catholic understanding—if, indeed, this is the same book called the *Ten-Stringed Psalter*, otherwise entitled *On the Unity of the Trinity*.

But if it was a different book, it nevertheless appears to have been seriously corrupted because it abandoned the Catholic position which Joachim had deliberately defended in the *Psalter*. There, in Book I, distinction 1, he says:

> We all confess this with one voice and one confession: There is one God without confusion of persons; three in persons without division of substance.

And again:

> This substance which is God is one, supremely one, exceedingly simple—more simple than can be expressed—and one nature. Nor do we deny the Trinity in confessing one substance; rather, we shudder at the divisions of parts which the carnal intellect imagines for itself . . . .

> Therefore the three are one and the one is three: not divided in nature, like earth, water, and fire; not separated in persons, like three men of the same nature.

And below:

> Hence he is simply said to be one who is truly the triune God.

And shortly afterward:

> Let us confess one God, supremely one; let us confess him triune and truly triune.

He says many things of this kind, which certainly contain Catholic doctrine. They cannot stand together with the claim that he believed the unity of the substance of the three persons was no greater than that of many human beings among themselves, or of human beings with God.

Indeed, when he used such comparisons to explain the unity of the Trinity, he first stated that the examples were dissimilar:

> How, he says, to speak not of a similar thing but of a dissimilar one: the three tribes of Judah, Benjamin, and Levi are called one people. For when I say “one people,” I do not assign some fourth thing; I say that unity exists in those three and that they are not cut off or divided from the house of David, as the remaining ten tribes were.

He therefore abhorred only those who asserted that, besides the three persons, there was some fourth thing—namely, the divine substance—really distinct from them. Perhaps he had heard some theologians of his time making this assertion. For he says:

> Moreover, I do not know who, which is worse than these things, has dared to assign three things apart from the substance as a new invention.

Against them he cries out:

> O human temerity, how always blind! O presumption always hostile to piety! If you have conceived the simple divine substance in such a way that you imagine it apart from the persons—that is, if you have believed it distinct—you have cloaked Sabellius beneath Arius. If you separate three persons from the substance, you excuse Arius beneath the covering of Sabellius.

Joachim’s rivals judged these words to have been directed against Peter Lombard, since Lombard had said in Book I, distinction 5, that the divine substance is neither begotten, nor proceeding, nor begetting.

Joachim nevertheless did not mention him by name. If perhaps he was attacking him, he understood his words in the sense that Lombard wished to say that the divine substance is not the thing that is begotten, begetting, or proceeding; and that would be erroneous to assert. Yet the Master’s words must be understood in their formal sense.

Let others judge these matters. For me, it is enough that Joachim’s intention was sound and that he himself foretold both his own affliction and his condemnation concerning this very matter.

Let these things, then, have been said in Cardinal Baronius’s interest, in response to the witnesses produced by Pennottus for Joachim’s condemnation.

But Alphonsus de Castro, though otherwise a learned man, plainly cannot be an eyewitness. He charges the holy abbot with an error—namely, that the apostles did not preach the Gospel according to the spiritual understanding, but only according to the letter—yet he asserts that he did not find Joachim making this claim in those works, but that Guido the Carmelite noted it about him. “Therefore,” he says, “let us trust Guido in this matter.”

I cannot sufficiently wonder at the judgment of so great a man. Was the matter so trivial? Was the reputation of a Catholic so insignificant that, in a matter not established by written evidence, one ought to trust a single person whose source of knowledge was unknown rather than protect the honor of an innocent man?

In any event, I have no doubt that Guido misunderstood the three states of the world which the holy abbot frequently emphasizes in his writings. The first extends from Adam to Christ, the second from Christ to the time of our holy father Benedict, and the third from him to the end of the world. In the first, human beings lived according to the flesh; in the second, partly according to the flesh and partly according to the spirit; in the third, according to the spirit alone.

He deals especially with these matters in chapter 5 of the *Introduction to the Apocalypse*, and expressly in Book II, treatise 1, of the *Concordia*, beginning at chapter 5 and continuing thereafter.

From this it might appear that, until Saint Benedict, human beings had not lived purely according to the spirit, as though he had been the first preacher of the spiritual understanding of the Gospel, and not the apostles.

But if the aforementioned authors had carefully read Joachim’s writings, they would not have fallen into such obvious ignorance. His intention is altogether different, as he explains both elsewhere and especially in Book IV, chapter 3, of the *Concordia*.

In the first state, only signs preceded, because everything happened to them in the form of things to come. In the second, signs and things signified followed one another: the things written in the New Testament were signified by the realities of the earlier period, and in turn signified other things that would come later in the spiritual sense. In the third, once the signs had been removed, only the things signified followed; none of the things that then happen or will happen can be taken as a figure of some future thing.

This is suggested when it is said that in the first state everything is flesh—that is, a figure or spirit of future things—and that in the third there is nothing that is a figure, but everything is figured, as though it were the spirit of past things. In the second state, however, both are found together because of the excellence of the New Testament, to which it belongs that one may find in it both the spirit of past things and the figure of future things.

If you are surprised that he takes the beginning of the third state from Saint Benedict rather than from other saints of the New Testament, I can readily answer you from the teaching of the *Concordia*, Book II, treatise 1, chapters 14–18. Those three states were not divided arbitrarily, but according to the same number of generations, just as in Matthew, chapter 1, the human state from Abraham to Christ comprises three groups of fourteen generations—that is, forty-two generations. Joachim explains in detail there how this is to be applied.

The spiritual life of the third state can also be said to have been verified in this respect: from Saint Benedict onward, the swarms of monks, among whom the spiritual life has its place, began to multiply far more than before.

Since these things are so, there is no reason for Joachim to be continually accused of error, nor for the reverence due to a holy man to be withheld from him. God, who rewards the humble, made his holiness of life known through almost innumerable miracles. The venerable archbishop Lucas of Cosenza, a disciple of Joachim, described them in a substantial volume; Jacobus Graecus, prior of Fiore, drew upon him in a book published on this matter, which is preserved in the archive of that monastery, while a copy of it is held in the Anician Library of the Gregorian College in Rome.

Let our Pennottus see what sort of man he was whom he hopes will rise from the dead—and how appropriately the name “Goliath” is applied to holy men.

### § VII. Pennottus’s objections against the Chronicles of Dextrus and Maximus are answered

Since R. P. Pennottus sees that his own work is caught in the same bonds with which he seeks to bind our *Chronicle*, it remains for him henceforth to deal more gently with us. He should learn from his own misfortune that arguments can easily be hurled against any book, although whether this is done justly or unjustly must be left to the judgment of readers.

We shall now apply our responses to his objections, so that everyone may see that none of them can weaken the authority of the *Chronicle*.

First, whatever has so far been said by various people about the preservation and discovery of the *Chronicle* arises from the same principle. They differed from one another according to popular opinion, which is ordinarily different in different places, and not according to any true knowledge that they themselves possessed.

I say this with reference to Father Joannes Calderon, who presented as popular opinion what he wrote about the *Chronicle* discovered by the archbishop of Braga, rather than as a report received from Father Jerome de la Higuera or Father Thomas de Torralba, to whom the discovery is owed.

Nor is this contradicted by the claim that it was first discovered by Euthrandus, or that one of his copies was at some point in Sisla. We proved both statements to be true in the first part of our preface, to the satisfaction of our readers.

The discrepancy among the manuscripts arose because Father Higuera, when many people requested the *Chronicle* and he was unable to provide everyone with the complete work—which had not yet been printed—copied different conclusions or abbreviations according to the diversity of the requests.

Thus, to the bishop of Tui, since he was a Benedictine, he sent only those portions that seemed to concern the Order of Saint Benedict or the saints of the bishopric of Tui, as Prudentius de Sandoval himself asserts in his book on the Church of Tui.

To the most illustrious archbishop of Braga, who was an Augustinian by profession, he sent matters concerning his archbishopric and order, as Losada affirms.

He satisfied many others in the same way, according to the differences among the provinces. From these abbreviations various copies were made, undoubtedly always teeming with new errors. One of them was certainly the copy belonging to the bishop of Segorbe.

Master Joannes Marquez did not use the complete *Chronicle*, but a certain abbreviation. Murillo obtained a complete copy from Father Higuera himself, but it was printed very corruptly at Zaragoza. It was therefore necessary to correct it by comparison with other copies, as I did, collating it with the copy preserved at Toledo in the library of the count of Mora, corrected and collated by Father Higuera himself, and with another copy preserved in the royal library of Saint Lawrence at the Escorial.

I have demonstrated at length in the preliminary defense of the *Chronicle* that full confidence should be placed in this corrected copy, which I now publish.

I am not readily persuaded by the claim that the text was corrupted by the Magdeburgians, since no passage that smacks of heresy or could in any way assist their errors is found in the entire codex. Unless one wishes to attribute to those heretics certain transcriptions or even repetitions of sentences which, as we have shown in their proper places, occur in the work, this is what Father Higuera supposed, moved by his knowledge that the Magdeburgians had corrupted books and libraries. But he did not know that this had certainly happened to Dextrus as well.

Certainly, if the *Chronicle* had been corrupted by heretics, it would not have escaped their heresies.

The objections that Pennottus raises against Dextrus’s dedicatory letter have already been answered twice: in § 2 of the preliminary *Apology*, and in the commentary on the year 430, at the final words of the *Chronicle*.

Moreover, we have proved at the appropriate place, by the testimony of many witnesses, that Saint Petronilla was truly the daughter of the blessed prince of the apostles by marriage, where we answered Baronius’s objections.

Nor does Saint Augustine, in Book I *Against Adimantus*, contradict us, as Pennottus believes. Although in chapter 17 he seems to assert that the story of Peter’s daughter healed of paralysis, and that of the gardener’s daughter who died at Peter’s prayer, was taken from apocryphal sources, he does not assert that it is apocryphal for the apostle Peter to have had a daughter. Rather, he says that she was healed through Peter’s prayers.

At the same time, the term “apocryphal” seems to include everything that is not narrated at all in sacred Scripture. For that is called apocryphal which is not authentic.

Here are Augustine’s words:

> The Manichaeans, in their great blindness, condemn these things—namely, miracles performed by divine power—although in the apocrypha they read as something great both what I mentioned concerning the Apostle Thomas and the healing, through the prayers of her father Peter, of Peter’s daughter who was paralyzed, and the death, at the prayer of that same Peter, of the gardener’s daughter. They answer that these things were useful to them, so that the one might be released from paralysis and the other might die; nevertheless, they do not deny that it happened at the Apostle’s prayer.

These are Augustine’s words. But, as you see, they do not bear on the matter. He does not deny that such persons existed, but that those miracles are authentic.

Pennottus also went seriously astray when he wrote that it was contrary to the tradition of the Church to assert that the canonical Epistle of James was written not by James the Less but by James the Greater, on the grounds that it is read in the first nocturn of the Roman Breviary on the feast of the former. Certainly in this matter that outstanding theologian is plainly shown to be ignorant of what is required for something to be regarded as deriving from ecclesiastical tradition, since it is established that the histories of the saints [Col. 0629A] read in the Breviary do not possess unavoidable certainty; besides, that epistle could be read on that day by an accommodation based on the name James. It was enough for the correctors of the Breviary that St. Jerome attributed it to James the Less in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. And Pennottus himself refuses to accept the readings concerning St. Herculanus approved by the Sacred Congregation of the Most Illustrious Cardinals of Sacred Rites, because they say that he was a Benedictine by profession.

Moreover, it is so far from being the tradition of the Church that the epistle itself belonged to James the Less that in our commentaries we demonstrated, from the tradition of the entire Spanish and Syrian Churches and from the matter itself, that it was the work of James the Greater and the first writing of the entire New Testament. Reread what we said there under the year 37, nos. 6 and 7, and you will see with what probability Dextri’s opinion is endowed.

Pennottus went further astray when he said that what Dexter asserts—that the twelve tribes to which James sent the epistle were within Spain—is an invention and plainly contrary to Sacred Scripture in the Fourth Book of Kings. If this were so, no one would deny that it was heretical. But whether he himself read or understood that book will easily be clear to everyone from what we wrote at length in the aforementioned place, no. 5; and, lest we seem to be doing the same thing again here, we do not repeat it. Nevertheless, we willingly pardon our friend’s sharp criticism, including the criticism by which he says that it contradicts the Gospel history of John 11 that the Jews of Jerusalem, by letters sent, consulted the Jews of Spain about Christ’s death. We dealt with this matter at length under the year of the Lord 35, commentary 2, no. 1, and under the year 37, commentary 3, [Col. 0629C] no. 1. From these discussions it will become plain who understood the Gospel more correctly, and it will also be clear that the objection is rather feebly founded on the words of John 11.

Good heavens, how falsely he slanders Dexter! Under the year 38 we proved that Saul was converted into Paul in the year of Christ 36, on 25 January—that is, in the second year after the Lord’s Ascension—as the Roman Church declares in its martyrology; and Baronius agrees with it in his notes for that day. Since Paul himself states that he came to Jerusalem after three years, it is necessary that his arrival fell in the year of the Lord 38, as Dexter asserts. For the whole of the year 36 must be counted, since Paul’s conversion occurred at its beginning, namely on 25 January.

Dexter therefore does not mean that Paul came to Jerusalem after his conversion—that is, immediately after he was converted—as Pennottus supposes on his own authority; rather, he means that in the year of the Lord 38 Paul came after his conversion, that is, already converted: plainly, not before his conversion, but in the year of the Lord 38, which was the third year after it. But where did Pennottus get the idea that Paul was not converted before the year 38 of the Lord, and did not ascend to Jerusalem before the year 41? Dexter asserts neither of these things, nor does anyone offer even a remotely probable conjecture in their favor.

It is not true that Dexter asserts that Linus’s pontificate extended to the year of the Lord 86. For the words, “In the year of Christ 86, at about the same time St. Anacletus, or Cletus, had succeeded Linus,” do not mean that he succeeded him in that very year. Since the text says *had succeeded*, it plainly indicates that he had succeeded him before the year 86 itself; [Col. 0630A] it does not specify the year. Nevertheless, it is certain that here too, as elsewhere, Dexter followed the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, who extends the episcopate of Linus to the year 72. And if more recent writers disagree with these authorities, that matters little, since Dexter could not have heard them but only the earlier writers, whom everyone ought to follow in a matter so obscure and ancient.

Pennottus ought at the very least to have deleted this from his notes, since I had previously warned him of the error. What Dexter asserts here—namely, that Polycarp came to Rome under Anicetus—is so true that later writers among the ancient Doctors affirmed it, and it will not be safe to resist them: Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, chapter 3; Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Polycarp; and Eusebius in the *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord [Col. 0630B] 156. Up to this point, other modern writers have agreed with them. We gave their words in the commentary under this same year.

Indeed, Higinius was sent away to Lerone precisely because the island was full of snakes, so that he would die more certainly; and perhaps for this reason Ambrose, writing to Valentinian, grieved over the exile of the old man. See what we said on this matter under the year 384.

As for the objection he makes concerning St. Paulinus, how far it is from the point we explained expressly above under the year 396 itself. Although, out of respect for Pennottus’s name, we suppressed both his name and the place, since at that time he had not yet published his *Tripartite History*, the reader will find there the knot untied and the objection resting on a false foundation.

The objection would indeed be valid if the printed codex used by Pennottus had not been corrupted. Nevertheless, he ought to have corrected it from other, more accurate copies. In that statement—“Under Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona, Paul Orosius is born,” and so forth—the year is not 384 of the Lord but 370, as can be seen in its proper place. Once this is granted, the objection collapses. For in the year 400, when he is said to have been sent by the Spanish bishops to the Africans, he was thirty years old and indeed a young man, although a presbyter; for that is what Augustine calls him, to whom he was chiefly sent. We discussed the embassy itself at length under the year 400.

What is said about there having been two Leporii we proved to be poorly established in the commentary under the year 406, where we replied to Pennottus while suppressing his name. He is moved chiefly by the fear that some disciple of Augustine might be found to have inclined toward heresy. But this is a very slight consideration, and it does not diminish the glory of so great a pastor: one diseased sheep does not do so, any more than one Judas diminishes Christ’s teaching, especially since this Leporius is later said to have been brought back to a sound mind through Augustine’s efforts. Moreover, in the aforementioned place we showed, on the testimony of Appian of Alexandria and Ambrosius Morales, that there was a Utica in Spain bearing precisely the same name as the African city.

Finally, the last objection he makes against the *Chronicle* of Dexter concerning the year in which it was completed was answered twice above: in section 2 of the preliminary Apology and in the commentary on the final words of the *Chronicle*. There, I think, the reader will find everything he could desire.

The objection Pennottus devised concerning M. Maximus has the following answer. What if the text itself is corrupt, and has “the younger” where it should have “the elder”? Certainly, in a very ancient author this would not be surprising. But I believe that no error entered there. The person who was “the younger” in Dexter’s time was Isidore, in relation to an earlier man; later, in the time of M. Maximus, who flourished more than two hundred years afterward, he was called “the elder,” with reference to St. Isidore of Seville, who was then held in high regard by everyone. Thus the man whom Dexter necessarily called “the younger,” because he knew no other younger person, Maximus called “the elder,” since he recognized a more recent one.

As for Dexter’s statement that the book of *Allegories* was dedicated to Paul Orosius of Tarragona, while Maximus asserts that it was dedicated to Orosius, bishop of León, these statements are not contradictory. Maximus explains what Dexter had expressed less clearly, lest anyone believe that the book had been dedicated to Paul Orosius, Augustine’s disciple, rather than to another man of the same name and homeland who had nevertheless been raised to the see of León. For it is clear from Dexter’s testimony under the year 366 and from M. Maximus’s under the year 602 that others bearing that name existed.

All the manuscript codices state that Dexter died in the year of the Lord 444, not 439; and the printed Caesaraugustan copy, corrected by the hand of the person who reviewed it, is commonly circulated.

Maximus is certainly right to say that Paul Orosius died more than a hundred years old in the year of Christ 471, since he was born in 370, as the more accurate codices have it. We have said enough about this in our response to the eleventh objection against Dexter.

I also regard that word as suspect, but I do not believe that it was added by the Augustinian hermits. Rather, I attribute it to Euthrandus or to some other ancient scholiast or annotator. We said enough about this in the commentary under the year 429, no. 3. Nor is the word itself wholly alien to the ancient manner of speaking of writers, since Pope Zacharias of Rome, who lived not long after M. Maximus, called the Order of St. Benedict by that name in a privilege granted by him to the venerable monastery of Monte Cassino. We gave his words in that place.

Here Pennottus is easily astonished, although other authors also acknowledge precisely what Maximus writes concerning St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, as may be seen in Equilinus, book II, chapter 32, in Juan Marieta’s *On the Saints of Spain*, and elsewhere.

I have just spoken of that expression, “the Order of St. Benedict,” in no. [Col. 0631D] 4. Pennottus, however, hostile to the Benedictines because a fierce dispute has arisen between the two sides over the antiquity of their orders, unjustly and gratuitously diminishes the antiquity of the Order of St. Benedict and violently postpones the foundations of monasteries in Spain until the year of the Lord 646. Since he does not prove this, he is shown to be speaking on his own authority; and at least in this matter, of which he is formally a party and therefore strongly suspect, he should not be heard.

But what if St. Vincent of León, while traveling to Italy around the year of the Lord 544, received the habit from the hand of St. Benedict, who, according to Pennottus himself, had begun to gather monks in the year 525, and then returned to his homeland, where in the year 546 he suffered martyrdom under Richillan, the heretical Suevian king?

[Col. 0632A] The same defect affects what he objects in seventh place concerning the monastic habit received by St. Turibius at Rome. For he himself must prove what he puts forward; since he does not do so, his labor is fruitless.

What if Maximus was at times mistaken in this matter? The time of death of very distinguished men has often been uncertain, as in the case of Augustine, Jerome, and others; and sometimes “good Homer nods.” Only the sacred authors have been granted by heaven never to err.

He is exceedingly scrupulous in refusing to swallow a gnat, while he does not refuse to swallow a camel in his own affairs. Athanagild was indeed infected with the dregs of Arianism, but he respected the holiness of monks. For such is the power of holiness that it compels love and reverence even from pagans and opponents of the orthodox faith. [Col. 0632B] But Athanagild was not so attached to his error that, even if uncertain about religion, he did not adhere greatly to the Catholic faith. Indeed, he was said inwardly to agree with the Catholics. Nor is it surprising that he built or restored monasteries of monks, as he is said to have restored the monastery of Sysla.

As for the name of that monastery, I am not greatly concerned. It may have been built in honor of several saints at once, as we see elsewhere; or it may have acquired one name when it was built and another when it was rebuilt.

Here is the camel that Pennottus does not refuse to swallow. He asserts that the church of St. Mary of the Pillar had been occupied by regular canons continuously from apostolic times to the present, although it is established that it passed to the regular clergy in the year of the Lord 1141 through the favor of Pope Innocent II. The apostolic letters issued that year on this matter, which was the twelfth year of his pontificate, are preserved in the archive of that venerable church, together with others of Eugene III from 1146, the second year of his pontificate, and others of Alexander III from 1173, the twelfth year of his pontificate. The canons of that church cite and produce these letters in their case concerning precedence, which they conduct with the other cathedrals of Aragon; Augustine Morlanes reports them in his pleading for the church of the Pillar, part 2, no. 383.

As for Maximus’s statement in the *Chronicle* that he himself spent many days under the rule of St. Benedict in the church of St. Mary of the Column, and that his monastery had been established nearby, its sole purpose is to indicate that, when the Benedictines first arrived in Zaragoza, they occupied a building adjoining or near the aforementioned church. From there they daily approached to perform the sacred rite before the image of the Blessed Mother of God, until a monastery was built for them at Massas Sanctas. This could have been done in a short time. Nevertheless, it could subsequently be truthfully said that before this there had been a monastery of monks of St. Benedict near the church of the Pillar.

For what else is a monastery than a house inhabited by monks? We see this every day also among reformed monks, who first turn an ordinary enough house into a monastery by adding only enclosure and a little bell at the entrance; from it they generally move soon afterward to a new building, leaving the name of the old monastery with the former house.

From this, rather, Cardinal Bellarmine’s opinion gains strength—an opinion agreeable to the regular canons themselves, namely to Simon Uverlin, provost of St. Mary at Diessen, whom Bernard Winding follows. The most holy Doctor instructed his monks or canons not through a written rule but by word of mouth and example, as was customary among the other Fathers of ancient times.

Let them produce for us in Augustine himself, or in Possidius, in the catalogues of his works prepared with the greatest care, even a slight mention of a written rule. This argument plainly proves that Augustine wrote no rule for his disciples—at least according to Pennottus’s opinion, as we noted above in section 4, no. 5, of this apologetic response. This is why St. Ildefonsus and the others who discuss Donatus—with the exception of M. Maximus—do not mention an Augustinian rule introduced by them into Spain.

Maximus, however, by the name “rule of St. Augustine” does not understand any written document, but rather a manner and norm of life handed down orally by Augustine to his followers. This must certainly be thought to have been very rigorous, given the fervor of that age, and therefore it could later have been mitigated by St. Donatus so that it might be adapted to a colder region such as Spain in comparison with Africa.

The rule now in our hands appears to have been extracted from Letter 109, in which, with the gender changed, it is reproduced word for word. It is an instruction for the life of nuns, which Augustine undertook to place before them on the occasion of the controversy they were having with their superior. Hence it says nothing there about presbyters, clerics, or preachers. And if one presbyter is mentioned, that very fact proves that the rule was written for women, for it commands that greater obedience be given to the presbyter who cares for all than to the superior. This has no place among men, since the superior must be obeyed above all; but it is appropriate among women, over whom a single presbyter is placed and must be obeyed above the regular superior.

Or let them show who that presbyter ever was who was placed over canons or hermits above their regular superior. If they invent someone, let them show where they derive him from; for without an author they should not be heard.

This is why the rule composed from the letter is so mild, since it was given to fragile women; and perhaps it did not contain a complete institution of all regular activities, being less suited to an epistolary treatment. What is added concerning the Servitan monastery is easily resolved if we say that at that time there were two places of that name in Spain, one following the prescription of St. Augustine and the other operating under the rule of St. Benedict. This is not surprising, since in that age all monks were commonly called *Servants of God*.

Unless you prefer to say that the monastery founded by St. Donatus in the year of the Lord 575 submitted, after a few years, to the rule of St. Benedict, under which a Servitan abbot is found in the year of Christ 590. This is quite plausible, since in former times no monk sought a diversity of orders, but rather an easier way to find perfection.

How he disguises his knowledge of antiquity, so that it seems strange to him that monks were accustomed to be taken from monasteries into the clergy, even by force. I know that Pennottus is not ignorant of this; in his *Tripartite History* he often emphasizes the same point, even bringing forward sacred canons. Therefore no one can be surprised that M. Maximus was taken from the monastery to the archdeaconate of Zaragoza and from there to the episcopal throne itself.

What if classical writers had repeatedly written the same thing? Certainly St. Isidore has it in the *Chronicle*, which Lucas of Tuy revised at the command of Queen Berengaria; and Tuy himself—or “Tuditanus,” as Pennottus calls him—to whom he also pays considerable tribute for his merits, agrees with him. Most importantly, St. Ildefonsus agrees in his continuation of Isidore’s *Chronicle*.

Thus, in the year of the Lord 606, Muhammad the false prophet invaded Spain under the pretext of trade and preaching. But he was expelled from there with shame through the efforts of Isidore of Seville. God willing, we shall speak about this in the commentary on M. Maximus, which we are preparing and will publish shortly. For now, let this suffice in defense of Maximus himself.

Nothing is brought against Euthrandus that puts us under pressure, since we do not assert that he composed his *Antipodosis* while he was still a deacon or in exile; none of this follows from the letter of its continuation.

When Pennottus says that Euthrandus extended the *Antipodosis* to the era 963, he confuses the era with the year, as Ambrosius Morales learnedly noted that many people of his time did in his *Antiquities of Spain*.

Furthermore, Bonisus, bishop of Toledo, under whom Euthrandus was subdeacon, was not the first of that name, elected in the year of the Lord 863, but the third, elected at Toledo in the year 946. Julian explicitly noted this in the *Chronicle* under that year, saying:

> “The third Bonisus had been elected. Under him was Euthrandus, or Luitprandus of Pavia, a historian of no small reputation and likewise an outstanding poet.”

Calderon could not have printed his *Chronicle*, since it had not reached his hands, but only the bare letter. Nor had Father Jerome de la Higuera Morillo communicated Euthrandus to him, from whom Father Calderon received Dexter and Maximus—not because he judged them spurious, but because it was wearisome to write out in his own hand as many copies as different friends or learned men demanded from him each day.

He communicated various fragments to many people according to each person’s need—for example, to Sandoval, bishop of Tuy, Gaspar Machado, and others. To Father Gabriel Vasquez, however, he gave Euthrandus’s letter because it would greatly serve the cause of Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, in the question concerning the Sonship of Christ in the third part of St. Thomas, volume I. Hence, I believe, certain people took it up in support of Dexter’s *Chronicle*.

It remains for me to bring this treatise to an end with the words of my Bernard, with which he concluded his apologetic letter written to the abbot of Prémontré; it is letter 252 among his letters:

> “Since these things are so, you have no reason to complain about us, since, as it appears, we have greater justice for complaining about you. It remains for you to love those who love you, especially being concerned to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. But I, Father, whatever you may do, have resolved always to love you, even though I am not loved” (Ephesians 4).

> “Let him seek occasions who wishes to withdraw from a friend. My concern has been and will be neither to give any of my friends a just cause for separation from me nor to search out in another what would make this friendship feigned and that one neglected. And because, according to the prophet (Isaiah 41), ‘What is joined is good,’ you may loosen—or rather break—your bond with me, but I cannot break it with you. I shall cling to you even if you do not wish it; I shall cling to you even if I myself do not wish it, since, if I have been foolish, you forced me to it—you who, although warned, have tried to break even my wall.”

**PAULUS OROSIUS, HISPANIC PRESBYTER**

[Col. 0635]

# DEDICATORY LETTER OF SIGEBERT HAVERCAMP

To the most excellent man NICOLAS GRIIS, councillor of state to the most serene king of Denmark, Norway, etc., and likewise in the supreme court of justice, and extraordinary envoy of His Majesty to the States of the United Provinces, from SIGEBERT HAVERCAMP.

When once the Roman Empire, as exhausted bodies commonly do, was wasting away through old age and, like the great masses of a foundation damaged by decay and storms, was contemplating its own ruin, the people who had once conquered the world did not turn their eyes as they ought to have done. Rather, they believed that the Eternal City, which they had fashioned for themselves in their hopes and inscriptions, was perishing through the anger of the gods after its former sacred rites had been changed, though it had outlived its ancient glory.

They alleged that the contagions of the new religion were not only infecting all the provinces everywhere but also filling both the old and the new Rome. They said that, together with the temples of the gods, divine benevolence had been shut up; that the warnings of the deities had ceased together with sacrifices and divination; and that dangers could neither be avoided nor met because the omens by which their ancestors had been accustomed to receive warnings about such matters were being neglected.

This crude speech, heard among the pagans, burst into still more savage abuse after Rome—the city that had once ruled the world and was still mistress of Italy and the Western Empire—had been captured and plundered by the Goths. The common people, touched by their ancient superstition, blamed this disaster of the Empire and these calamities of the world on the Christian name. All the pagans openly cried out that every evil had rushed upon the lands of the Roman Empire in a single mass from the moment when, after the old sacred rites had been abolished and the divine power of the gods despised, only the name of Christ was publicly worshiped.

Against this mad opinion, worthy of a blind religion, Orosius—a Spaniard by nationality and a presbyter by status—took up his pen at the urging of Augustine, the outstanding bishop of Hippo. His purpose was not to overcome the foolishness of worshiping so many deities, to expose the vanity of adoring the dead and empty names, or to denounce the shamefulness of those religions—for many had done these things before him. Rather, he wished to show that the condition of the world was by no means worse while the public worship of the true God and the accepted Christian religion prevailed than it had always and everywhere been from the beginning.

For immediately after the creation of this universe, all evils entered the world together with the sin of the first man: wars, robberies, murders, calamities of every kind, and whatever proud conquerors, the harshness of heaven, the earth’s refusal to produce crops, deadly pestilences, fires, collapses, and floods have forced miserable mortals to endure. Indeed, even Rome herself, whose days were counted by triumphs, scarcely ever breathed free from the evils that he recounts extensively and in great number.

The entire kind of writing Orosius undertook thus concerns a varied and multifaceted history. Beginning with the creation of the world, he travels through the three kingdoms by which the world was oppressed and measures the boundaries, destinies, and periods of the Roman Empire. He records what remarkable, pitiable, shameful, and—unless historians worthy of belief asserted it—incredible things occurred under each consul, in each province of the Empire, and even in Rome itself.

Thus no one could justly condemn the present times unless he were ignorant of the past and were utterly a stranger to reading the writers who carefully committed to writing the events that occurred in their own times.

For if, while safely removed from the dangers of war, it is not unpleasant to watch uncertain struggles and to rejoice in the misfortunes from which one is personally free, then the recollection of events accomplished by illustrious men through varied fortune, great struggles, and all their strength cannot fail to be pleasurable. Historians bring us in, as it were, to inspect these events in a picture; and each one who holds our minds more strongly either through the seasoning of his language or through the variety of his subject matter is accustomed to be praised and sought out.

Among these, no one will deny that Orosius occupies a respectable second place, since he briefly describes the disasters and miseries of the entire world from its beginning down to his own times and arranges them suitably according to their periods.

This was above all the reason that moved me, most excellent and noble sir, willingly to dedicate a new edition of so useful a writer to your name. Although, amid all kinds of writing, you devote the few hours left free from your demanding duties, I have often heard you affirm that you take pleasure in none more than in the ancient historians.

Accordingly, among the select books gathered with discriminating care from the whole range of scholarly pursuits, your library shines especially brightly through these works. It does not please merely by its ornament and attract the eyes of those who praise it, but lies open for the use of its owner and friends: for them, for various reasons; for him, so that he may gather advice and precepts useful to him in the splendid office he holds by comparing ancient affairs with modern ones. For the dead are the best counsellors. And when the mind, wearied by cares, seeks rest, it should seek it above all not in empty pleasure for the ears or eyes, but in the solid admiration of outstanding examples and intellects.

Among the dead who customarily teach the living, I ask you to grant a place to our Orosius, who for more than a century has suffered from neglected external appearance and typographical elegance—qualities in which the good fortune of ancient authors now excels—and who has not been cleansed with sufficient diligence of the errors remaining in the text.

According to the capacity of my abilities, and under the guidance of the most ancient manuscripts, I have carefully reviewed him from beginning to end. I have also taken as much care as possible to ensure that his external appearance would not cause embarrassment.

Leiden, 1 December 1737.

[Col. 0637]

# PREFACE OF SIGEBERT HAVERCAMP

SIGEBERT HAVERCAMPUS GREETS THE BENEVOLENT READER.

[Col. 0637A] When learning returned, Paulus Orosius was among the ancient authors whom the first leaders and promoters of the art of printing brought into public light. He enjoyed the good fortune that, before the end of the fifteenth century, he appeared in no fewer than three different places in respectable form, and was committed to the presses in the year 1504 itself.

Among the editions that I had long ago acquired, under a fortunate star—for chance and fortune have great influence even in such matters—while concentrating on this author, I assigned first place to the Italian edition, which is splendid whether one considers the elegance of its letters or the beauty of its paper.

Although neither the city in which the book was printed, nor the printer’s name, nor finally the year in which it appeared is recorded either at the beginning or at the end, scholars agree that it was published at Vicenza. For the purpose of ensuring that it would be read accurately, Aeneas Vulpes presided over this edition. Both his homeland and his rank are apparent from certain lines, printed in capital letters opposite the first page of Orosius himself. The inscription, which forms a little rectangular panel there, reads:

> “Know, most courteous reader, that Aeneas Vulpes of Vicenza, prior of Holy Cross, with the assistance of Laurentius of Brescia, corrected as accurately as he could the Histories of Paulus Orosius contained in this volume. If you think that anything should be added from your own ingenuity, either better or more suitable, I beg you to do so while preserving his honor intact, which is the duty of a grateful spirit.”

At the final page of the book the following is read:

[Col. 0637C] Bartholomaeus Paiellus, knight of Vicenza, on St. Orosius.

As the title itself teaches in the first margin:

> “My name is Orosius.”

Whatever error belonged to the scribes:

> “Aeneas removed from me.”

And he handed me over to be printed to no one else,

> “Hermann, but to you alone.”

Hermann, the name and glory of this art,

> “And the praise of your Cologne.”

If anyone wishes to know the disturbances, wars, and killings,

> “And disasters of the world,”

from the very origin of the world

> “down to our own times, let him read me.”

From these lines we now recognize not only the corrector of the book, Aeneas Vulpes of Vicenza, but also the editor, Hermann of Cologne.

The editions that followed in Italy all reproduce these verses at the end of the book, although silently omitting the name of Bartholomaeus Paiellus, and although they were printed in another city—namely Venice—and by other printers.

It is easy to see how the distinguished Fabricius, although following Clericus, whom he cites, was led into error when he states in volume I of his *Latin Library*, p. 736, that the oldest Basel edition was revised and printed by a certain Aeneas at the workshop of Leonhardus, without an indication of the year, although it could easily be seen to have appeared long before the end of the fifteenth century.

In all the editions that appeared after that of Hermann of Cologne, those verses and the commendation resulting from the work of Aeneas Vulpes were appended gratuitously, although most depart from his correction and reading.

That Hermann of Cologne was called by his homeland; he had another surname. He printed his books not at Cologne or elsewhere in Germany, but in Italy, at Vicenza and other places, as is clear from the *Typographical Annals* of the distinguished Michael Maittaire, volume I, p. 136:

> “At Vicenza, Hermann LEVILAPIS of Cologne, at the expense of Antonio, Gerard, John, Peter, and Bartholomew, brothers, and of certain sons of S. Zanoto of Piacenza, citizens of Verona. With Benedict Trevisan and Angelo Michele as magistrates.”

The surname Levilapis was likewise adopted by Hermann through a transformation of language; otherwise it sounded different in his native tongue. We learn this from the same book of Michael Maittaire. For the man whom he had likewise called Hermann Levilapis on p. 33, he calls Liechtenstein by his native name on p. 108, in these words:

> “Aeneas Vulpes of Vicenza, prior of Holy Cross, with the assistance of Laurentius of Brescia, corrected the Histories of Paulus Orosius, which Hermann Liechtenstein committed to the press, although the year is not indicated.”

From the same book we also learn both forms of his surname, the cities in which he published his books, the years in which he did so, and the year of his death, volume I, p. 224:

> “Hermann Levilapis of Cologne, at Vicenza—at the expense of Antonio, Gerard, John, Peter, and Bartholomew, brothers, and of certain sons of S. Zanoto of Piacenza, citizens of Verona—1475, 1476. Hermann de Levilapide, at the expense of Nicolaus Peter of Haarlem, a German of Holland, 1477. Hermann Liechtenstein, or Lichtenstein, of Cologne, 1478, 1479, 1480. At Treviso, 1477. At Venice, 1483, 1484, 1486, 1487, 1488, 1490, 1493, 1494, in which year he died. See Vincent, *Speculum*, 1494.”

Hermann therefore began to mark the year of publication of the book around 1475. From this it is clear that an edition of Orosius published by him existed before that year, which is why I have often called it in my notes the first and principal edition, although another edition of Orosius could dispute its primacy or priority in antiquity. That edition bears a date and was not omitted by the most diligent scholar in the *Typographical Annals*, although it is extremely rare to find; he records it in volume I, p. 305.

This book was printed in German Gothic type at Augsburg in 1471 by Johannes Schuszler. In this edition, which surpasses all the other old editions in quality and was copied with the utmost fidelity from an excellent manuscript, the following is prefixed to Orosius’s own prologue:

> “The Prologue of Paulus Orosius the historiographer, disciple of St. Augustine the bishop, a man of most eloquent Spanish birth, against the complaints of the Christians” [*Cristiani*; printed as “Cristiani” and “nois,” sic] “in seven books.”

At the very end of the book are these words:

> “The seven books of blessed Paulus Orosius, presbyter, against the complaints of the Christians” [printed *Xptani* and *nois*, sic] “end happily, printed by Johannes Schuszler, citizen of the most flourishing city of Augsburg. In the year from the saving birth of the Virgin Mary one thousand four hundred and seventy, around the seventh day before the Nones of June.”

Orosius then appeared for the third time at Venice through the work of Octavianus Scotus in 1483. At the end of that edition the following is found:

> “Here ends the seventh and final book of Paulus Orosius, a most distinguished man, addressed to Aurelius Augustine, bishop and outstanding Doctor. Printed at Venice through the work and expense of Octavianus Scotus of Modena, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1483, on the third day before the Kalends of August, under Giovanni Mocenigo, illustrious doge of Venice.”

This edition displays red and illuminated letters, as the first edition also commonly boasts at its front and at the beginning of its chapters.

After that it was again published at Venice through the work and expense—as is likewise read at the end—of Bernardo Veneto de Vitalibus, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1500, on 12 October, during the reign of Lord Agostino Barbarigo.

From that time onward Orosius often tired the presses. He was first printed at Paris by Johannes Barbier, who calls himself a sworn printer as well as bookseller, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1510, on 13 November. Then, again at Paris in 1524, he was published by Johannes Parvus, printed by Peter Vidovaeus, and edited by Sebastian Menginus.

The Cologne printers subsequently reprinted this author more than once, especially in 1526, an edition for which Gerard Bolsuinge, who wrote the preface to it, took considerable care. Eucharius Cervicornus printed it, as the title page says; at the expense, however, of M. Godefridus Hittorpius, a citizen of Cologne, as we are informed on the final page, in the month of June. Hittorpius likewise calls himself by that name in the Cologne edition that came from the workshop of Jaspar Gennepaeus in 1542 and was undertaken by Joannes Caesarius, whose preface is read at the beginning of that edition. At the end of the book appear these words: “At the expense and with the funds of M. Godefridus Hittorpius, citizen of Cologne, in the month of August 1542.” We shall henceforth call this edition Hittorpian, and the earlier one Bolsuingian. I have learned little about Bolsuinge; Joannes Caesarius, however, was a German from Jülich and published many works between 1520 and 1540, printed chiefly at Cologne by Eucharius Cervicornus. Among them was the complete work of C. Pliny’s *Natural History* in 1524, purged, as its title reports, of very many errors.

More than the others, Franciscus Fabricius Marcoduranus rendered a service to Orosius: a man distinguished by many services to the republic of letters. In 1561 he prepared a new edition of Orosius, furnished with notes; he issued it again in 1573 and finally a third time in 1582. Thirty-three years later Andreas Scottus, a name well known among scholars, also published Orosius. He added nothing of his own, but besides Fabricius’s notes he appended excerpts from the *Annotations* of Ludovicus Lautius, a Belgian and priest of Ghent. In this latest edition of Orosius, which had seemed to surpass all the others up to that time, I discovered very many errors—errors that reveal the careless eye of the man who supervised the undertaking. Nor did Fabricius himself, although he worked with exceptional skill in emending and elucidating Orosius, seem to have achieved complete success, since he appears to have indulged himself too much in dealing with this author, as Barthius testifies in *Adversaria*, book XXXVI, chapter 17.

Accordingly, learned men long ago rightly judged that Orosius deserved to be reviewed anew with greater care against manuscript copies—especially since, from the year 1615, when Andreas Scottus’s Mainz edition appeared, Orosius had lain untouched by any man of letters for more than one hundred and twenty years, despite the great eagerness with which ancient authors were being brought back into print. Yet so many editions had previously followed one another, and such a varied, extensive, and altogether necessary history existed.

Not content, therefore, with those earlier and ancient editions, all of which had been available to me, I judged that assistance should be sought especially from manuscript codices. When I had obtained eleven of this kind, I considered myself adequately equipped. Five of them were supplied by the library at Leiden, or Lugdunum Batavorum; three came from Florence, and one from Utrecht. I also possess one myself, and finally I obtained a collation of an ancient codex made with the utmost care by the celebrated Jacobus Gronovius. His most worthy son, Abrahamus Gronovius, made it available to me, and I discovered that this codex agrees very closely with the third of those from Leiden.

My own codex, written in columns on parchment and formerly acquired from the Hulsian Library, is of the highest quality and was of great use to me. The Utrecht codex was collated with great industry by Otto Arntzenius, now indefatigable head of the Gouda School. It is indeed one of the more recent codices and is very corrupt, but it nevertheless contains certain readings in which it agrees with the best manuscripts.

Among the five manuscripts supplied by the library of the academy at Leiden, one is preserved in the Perizonian bequest. It bears the title *On the Orchestra of the World* and was written on paper in 1463, and is therefore quite recent; nevertheless, it is very good and comparable with the oldest manuscripts. Of the remaining four Leiden codices, I usually mention first the one that once belonged to Nicolaus Heinsius and afterward to Isaac Vossius, and that has Justin attached to it.

In this book, written on parchment, certain verses had been prefixed to it. I cannot present them in their entirety, because the outer part of the parchment has been torn away. The following, however, could be read:

> This sacred codex of Orosius clearly reckons  
> the globe of the earth and the boundaries and locations of places.  
>   
> The world after it was made, and the first man formed thereafter;  
> the earth after the flood had been poured over all of it in retribution;  
> the ark, by divine gift, having preserved a few.  
>   
> From this came evil wars, deaths, conflicts, battles, quarrels,  
> disgraces, hostilities, incest, disputes, frauds;  
>   
> sects of error, parricides, thefts, robbery,  
> [lacuna]  
>   
> [Almost the entire torn column is missing.]  
>   
> [lacuna]  
>   
> He would see with his eyes, so that each might be instructed by it.  
>   
> I have transmitted this to you, not so that you may learn  
> [Col. 0641B] my doctrines, but so that you might become a truthful judge of yourself.  
>   
> For then the envious hand will cease to gnaw at it in this way.

The second Leiden codex is marked at the end as having been written by the hand of Brother Everardus of Novongium. At the beginning it bears this title: *The Seven Books of Orosius on the Disasters and Miseries of the Ancients*. At the end these words are read: “The books of Orosius the priest, on the disasters and ancient miseries of the world, written by the hand of Brother Everardus of Novongium.”

The third Orosian codex known to us also contains the books of Justin and is entitled *Orosius’s Book of Histories on the Ormesta of the World*. At the end of the seventh book a verse is subscribed, which also appears in the first codex:

> Here ends the sacred codex of the priest Orosius.

The fourth, finally, is a parchment manuscript that once belonged to Isaac Vossius and passed with his other manuscripts, by purchase, into the library at Leiden.

These, then, were the aids I obtained in my own country. I did not, however, think that I should rest content with them. Since I knew that the Laurentian Library in Florence carefully preserved the oldest of all Orosius’s surviving manuscript codices, magnificently written in Lombardic script, I did not rest until I had brought its harvest into this work.

The prefect of the Laurentian Library, Antonius Maria Biscionius, collated this exceptional codex for me with the most reverent care, through the agency of Dom. Albertus Mazzolenus, an old friend who procured this favor for me, using his own hand and eyes, in the year 1729. That most ancient codex, written in the format of a large quarto, bears, as the most diligent examiner noted, the appearance of an age of nearly a thousand years. He also sent me a drawing of its letters to be engraved on copper; it will be found on page 70.

This Lombardic codex, also mentioned by Mabillon in *De Re Diplomatica*, book V, p. 354, begins in a mutilated condition, for it is defective at the beginning of the first book, and the entire seventh book is missing. Nor did the service of this most courteous man end with the collation of this codex, which is preserved in that library in bookcase 65, no. 1: he also sent me an equally careful collation of two other codices. One of these is preserved in bookcase 65, no. 35, and is considered to belong to the thirteenth century; the other is kept there under no. 37 and is assigned to the fourteenth century.

In the latter of these, since the former is also damaged at the beginning, the title of the book is: “The first book of Paulus Orosius, priest of Spain, on the calamities of the whole world.” Finally, below the dedications and prefaces you will find the account of orthography, extracted and sent to me, which may be observed especially in that most ancient codex.

Against these manuscript codices and all the old editions I therefore reviewed Orosius with the care that the author deserved—a writer whose refinement, we must acknowledge, had lacked supporters for more than a hundred years. For the observations that learned men had scattered throughout his work had been collected with a very sparing hand, and anyone who compares the manuscripts will see how much healing Orosius has received from them and from their more careful examination than that undertaken by earlier editors.

Although this writer did not flourish in the golden or silver age of Latin, and can scarcely retain a place for himself even in the bronze age, and although at times, according to the understanding of his century, he is carried away by old wives’ tales—for example, by the story of the tracks left by the wheels of the chariots of the Egyptians who pursued the Israelites, tracks supposedly still visible—nevertheless, both because of the multifaceted history of his work, compressed with useful brevity and carefully arranged according to the succession of times and Roman consuls, and because he makes use of the great historians and annalists whose complete works we now seek in vain, and who held the first place in that field, he is generally held in high esteem by all learned people.

Concerning the word *Hormesta*, which some codices give as the title of Orosius’s book, while others wish to substitute *Orchestra*, one may consult Joannes Albertus Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina*, book IV, chapter 3, or volume III, p. 537, where he cites several learned men who have discussed the word. After weighing their arguments, however, neither form seems genuine to me.

Since in certain copies I find written *de ormesia mundi*, I believe this to be nothing other than a corruption derived from the words *de miseria mundi*—“on the misery of the world”—and I believe this to be the true title, because the author alludes to it throughout his entire work. He wrote these seven books at Augustine’s urging for no other reason than to show [Note: [Col. 0641] Book I, chapter I, p. 6: “I have undertaken to trace the beginning of human misery from the beginning of the human being who sinned,” etc.] that misery was born together with sin and did not enter the Roman Empire along with the Christian religion, but had existed from the most ancient times throughout the entire world, and had never been absent from the Roman Empire even when that empire was flourishing most vigorously.

Orosius’s little book entitled *Apology, or On Free Choice against the Pelagians*, does not properly belong to his Histories. Fabricius added it to the second edition that he prepared, and afterward it appeared in the other editions as well. We therefore did not wish it to be absent from this new edition, especially since it is a notable monument of its age and contains excerpts from Pelagius’s lost writings, from which the savage doctrines of that man may be recognized. Farewell.

[Col. 0643]

# VARIOUS DEDICATIONS AND PREFACES

## LETTER OF LUDOVICUS THIBOUST OF PARIS TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS YOUTHS, LUDOVICUS AND ANDREAS GUILLARDUS, PATRICIANS OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED CHARACTER

[Col. 0643A]

Most illustrious youths,

Those who have worked most carefully to examine the monuments of writers and to weigh them as though they had been skillfully arranged on a bookstand have rightly and wisely observed that none are more commendable or more excellent than those who have copied out, from the faithful monuments of history, the notable deeds performed by their ancestors, their admirable counsels, and the unexpected outcomes of events, with a rich abundance of examples.

For history—which Cicero, the foremost father of eloquence, calls “the witness of time, the light of truth, the life of memory, and the messenger of antiquity”—provides these things in abundance, offers them most generously, and supplies them most richly. Through them, people, eager to emulate the distinguished customs of the ancients, may become better prepared and better equipped for the blessed life; while, wishing to avoid blameworthy and shameful deeds, they may not merely fear such things but flee them, assail them, and spurn them.

No one can provide more carefully for posterity, nor publish anything from which every class, sex, and age may promise itself either greater assistance in letters or a more abundant storehouse for the formation of character, than history—that is, the teacher and guide of living well and happily. From it comes knowledge of all things, and from it people can draw lessons by which advantage may be gained both in public and private affairs.

Indeed, no literary monuments can be found in any respect that do not need the assistance of history and do not kiss its footprints. Nor should we now pass over the lawmakers, who would perform their office badly and could not properly establish a state unless they had thoroughly mastered the narration of deeds. From it they will inspect the character of individuals as though in a model and mirror of human life; then, having carefully gathered them together, they will select those who may contribute to the common advantage of all, bring them forward, and proclaim them.

Philosophy too cannot adequately explain precepts concerning morals, nor discuss the conduct of domestic affairs and the entire skill of administering and organizing the commonwealth without a manifold narration of examples. Everyone knows that teaching through examples is more useful and effective than teaching through precepts.

Nature has arranged matters so that people are summoned to the pursuit of glory by the examples of outstanding men; and, drawn onward by them, they strive either to imitate or to attain only what is excellent and honorable. It also happens that, while contemplating the vicissitudes of human affairs, they learn to regulate Fortune—now blowing forward, now backward—by alternately spreading the sails, and carefully to observe the attacks of Fortune herself as she changes.

[Col. 0644A]

Moreover, it is well established that people are deterred from the life of the wicked even by fear alone—whether of disgrace or of punishment.
