Thus we read in Plutarch that it was the custom of the Lacedaemonians, during festivals, to bring before the banquets slaves who had been made drunk, infamous gluttons, and men driven mad by wine, so that, by the example of drunken men, they might teach the young how much evil the most filthy drunkenness contained.

For this reason I would maintain that nothing more useful or more excellent than history can be found, and that there is no faculty or discipline that would not yield to it as to a teacher of right living.

Among those who transmitted this most excellent kind of writing, we must plainly acknowledge that Paulus Orosius flourished and deserved well of human affairs. Although he promises to write of the conflicts of the human race, its desires, and the various outcomes of its calamities, he nevertheless embraced with the greatest fidelity the continuous sequence of history, from the creation of the world to the memory of his own times. In accordance with the purpose of his work, he brought together pestilences, earthquakes, unheard-of devastations, unexpected disasters, and portentous marvels of events.

Nor was he without the praises of eloquence. His lucid brevity, arranged with a more substantial narration of events, overflowing with weighty reflections and distinguished by an unavoidable variety, shines and gleams, and drives the reader to scarcely believe that so much artistry of expression could be contained in this little volume.

Alexander of Aphrodisias, in his *Problems*, gives a physical explanation of why people of short stature are generally wiser than tall people: namely, because in them the soul is compressed and compacted throughout the whole body, whereas in tall people it is stretched out lengthwise and becomes dispersed. Papinius expressed this in the following verse:

> Greater virtue ruled in a small body.

For this reason Homer describes Odysseus as short and prudent, but Ajax as tall and more foolish. Into this problem I have willingly turned aside, as into a bypath, thinking that the same solution might be offered concerning the prudence of our historiographer, who in this short work describes at length the deeds of so many past centuries. He observes a brevity that is neither obscure nor meager, but which, the more restrained it is, is all the more prudent and lucid.

Indeed, I myself, prompted by many considerations, most distinguished youths, advise and exhort you to receive with cheerful countenance and serene brow this most excellent work, dedicated specifically to you. From it you will carry away much pleasure, much benefit, and no less happiness. It is a work no less fruitful than delightful.

I have written brief annotations on its pages in the margins and compiled a literary index of them, so that the subjects of the annotations might be more readily understood and the annotations themselves more easily found. This labor was by no means unpleasant to me, since I thought that in this way I would make my work worthwhile and publish something that might assist your learning in attaining the distinguished heights of both virtue and letters.

Farewell, and cherish with lasting devotion this little work as a testimony of my love and esteem for you.

## LETTER OF JOANNES CAESARIUS TO GEORGIUS A SEINA

To the illustrious and noble Lord Georgius a Seina, of the renowned and distinguished family of the counts of Wittgenstein, canon and chief secretary of the metropolitan church of Cologne, archdeacon and provost of the churches of Saint Patroclus at Soest, a not insignificant town of Westphalia, and of Saint Gereon and the Apostles at Cologne, that most famous city of the Ubii; his lord, patron, and most highly esteemed protector, Joannes Caesarius sends greetings.

[Col. 0645B]

The divine Aurelius Augustine, besides the gentleness of spirit that he displayed from his earliest youth and preserved throughout his life, and besides the sanctity of life by which, soon after his conversion to Christianity, he began to become renowned before God and humanity and afterward became conspicuously famous while he lived, was a man of truly great judgment. This was so both in profane and secular matters, but especially in divine and sacred letters. After he had given his name to Christ in the sacred font, he examined, read, and reread them with the greatest diligence. He labored energetically to elucidate and explain them, and left to posterity nearly countless books written by himself.

While, among his other studies, this man was engaged in composing that great work, the volume he entitled *The City of God*, which he arranged in twenty-two books, he argued with great acuteness in the first ten against unbelievers, commonly called pagans and enemies of the Christian name. These men attributed the impending ruin of the Roman Empire—which had by that time begun to decline—to Christian piety, faith, and religion.

In those books, therefore, this man refutes and confounds them with the gravest and most certain testimonies drawn from approved historians. Indeed, he very clearly shows and demonstrates that it would not be a new event, or even something to be regarded as a miracle, for the Roman Empire eventually to come to an end or at least to decline. For it is perfectly clear, and has been handed down in the writings of historians, annalists, and even chroniclers, that kingdoms and empires have repeatedly either been utterly overthrown or transferred elsewhere.

Examples may be drawn from the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Macedonians, or Greeks, even under that false religion which, long before the coming of Christ our Savior, had occupied and deceived nearly the whole world. What, I ask, was that religion other than the most destructive worship of false gods—or, more truly, of demons?

Moreover, so that those impious and blasphemous haters and revilers of the Christian religion might have nothing left with which to disguise their cunning, shifting malice, and slander against Christians—or rather, so that the piety of that most holy man’s undertaking might at last be made evident to the whole world—the same man encouraged Paulus Orosius the priest, a man who at that time was especially close to him and highly practiced in reading histories, to undertake the composition of histories from the creation of the world down to his own times.

In this way those slanderous men might at last, even against their will, understand and recognize that the Christian religion was not the cause of the Roman Empire’s apparent decline, but rather the grave and dreadful crimes and wickedness of human beings, with divine providence undoubtedly arranging and governing all things according to its will for the common salvation and correction of the human race.

Orosius therefore obeyed the exhortation—or rather the command—of so great a man, and, as he himself candidly testifies in the preface to his work, he did so willingly, although he realized that the task would be extremely difficult. He immediately undertook to write the histories, beginning with the origin of the world and arranging them in seven books. Having gathered annals from everywhere, as is probable, and undoubtedly aided by the not insignificant historians who had preceded him, he fashioned those seven books into a work that is certainly not inelegant and should not be ranked far below the other historians. Indeed, it may perhaps be preferred to them on this point: throughout the whole work the author joins to his narration of events a comparison and calculation of periods and years.

For it is of no small importance that someone who wishes to know what events occurred at different times should also possess a definite account and awareness of the times in which those events took place.

Because this work had already been printed several times, though meanwhile swarming with many errors despite the repeated attempts of various people to cleanse and purify it, it now appears again through the care and expense of Master Gotfridus Hittorpius, a citizen of Cologne of no inferior rank, a man, by Hercules, both industrious and honorable. It has first been reviewed with no small diligence, partly by us and partly by certain others, and purged of its remaining errors; it now comes to light in a form considerably different from that in which it has hitherto appeared, and has at the same time been printed in highly attractive type.

When I was considering and reflecting to whom among the leading men I should dedicate and address our labor and study in this work, so that it might rest upon his protection, your favor first came to mind, illustrious and noble Count—and not without good reason. I have often experienced your favor and goodwill toward me, not without some benefit and advantage to myself.

Therefore, in order at last to declare and display, however inadequately, at least some gratitude toward you and my inclination of mind toward you—for I have long desired to do so, most discerning and most worthy man—I now offer and dedicate this little gift to your favor and generosity. I do not doubt that your goodwill toward me will receive it, however small it may be, with a fair and gracious spirit, since by your prudence you are accustomed to look not at the thing given or offered but rather at the disposition with which it is given and offered.

Once I have established this as certain, there is nothing by which I should not rightly congratulate myself in your name. May Your Grace fare well. Cologne, the day before the Kalends of August.

## LETTER OF GERARDUS BOLSUINGE TO THE LORD ARCHBISHOP, LORD HERMANNUS

To the Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, Lord Quirinus, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See bishop of Cyrene, vicar general in pontificals of the most reverend and illustrious prince and our lord, Lord Hermannus, archbishop of the Holy Church of Cologne, arch-chancellor of the Holy Roman Empire in Italy, prince-elector, duke of Westphalia and Angaria, hereditary legate, and so forth:

Gerardus Bolsuinge of Recklinghausen sends greetings.

[Col. 0647B]

Since there are many men today, Reverend Father and most learned Bishop, who strive to deserve well of the republic of letters by restoring the monuments of antiquity, among the very first in their number is the most upright and excellent Godefridus Hittorpius. He never fails to publish, at his own expense, some work of ancient learning in a form either more purified or more polished.

Recently he approached me and asked me to rescue that Paulus Orosius, collated with ancient and manuscript copies, insofar as I could, from the myriad of errors by which it had hitherto been so mutilated, corrupted, and disfigured through either the sleepiness, laziness, or—if you prefer—inertia of both scribes and printers, that it rightly deterred not only the less educated but even learned men from reading it.

Nor, by Hercules, was that a mistaken judgment regarding the author himself. For that single Orosius, a man who appears to have been deeply learned in all good letters, including divine letters, is one to whom alone, and rightly, credence ought to be given in histories. As a Christian endowed with sound and uncorrupted judgment, attached privately to no faction and devoted to no nation or people, he gathered from the best histories and annals written from the beginning of the human race onward—and at the prompting and command of the divine Augustine, who assigned him this task (for it is clear that the purpose of both writers was the same: Augustine, in the twenty-two books of *The City of God*, and Orosius, in these seven books, drove away the false suspicions and calumnies of the pagans or heathen)—those things which, beyond dispute, appeared wholly free and separated from every passion and vanity.

Throughout his work he introduced, at suitable points, the finest and most salutary seasonings of the Christian heart, which will certainly benefit the devout and thoughtful reader no less than the histories themselves.

To this must also be added that, through the benefit of this excellent man, we are enabled to see more clearly a countless number of matters by no means unworthy of notice, of which scarcely any trace survives elsewhere today because their original sources have perished. Among these are many things that he faithfully copied, in the fullest good faith, from the most trustworthy monuments of Livy’s industry, long ago lost through the injustice of time—or rather through the negligence of men.

Furthermore, if someone is prevented by other occupations from reading through all the histories of all authors, here he has something like a complete compendium, containing the choicest and most necessary material from them all, so that it may serve in place of all histories.

To celebrate the *ἐγκώμιον*—“encomium”—of histories according to its deserts is beyond my powers, and this place does not permit it. I shall therefore merely silence the detractors with something like a club, using Cicero’s saying: “To be ignorant of what was done before you were born is to remain always a child.”

But no one will see or judge more exactly how much oil and labor were spent in restoring this author than one who compares this copy with every kind of earlier exemplar, both manuscript and printed.

For why should I enumerate—or rather, set before you—the more than one hundred verses that had been omitted here and there with the integrity of the sense mutilated? Nevertheless, lest anyone think me boastful, I shall point out a few of the many examples.

Let the beginning of the third chapter of Book II be compared, where these words were missing:

> “Semiramis, his wife, succeeded him, as I have said. She too reigned for forty-two years, etc.”

Likewise, to pass over other examples, in chapter 17 of Book V, approximately six lines were required, although otherwise no coherent sentence existed there:

> “On the appointed day, Metellus, innocent but condemned by judges belonging to the same faction through a criminal act, departed into exile amid the grief of the whole City; and what follows up to ‘with infamous enterprises.’”

Similarly, in the following chapter of the same book, no fewer than three lines had been omitted, namely:

> “For just as they had stood stunned with fear of the enemy, some leaning against tree trunks, others against rocks, and others supporting themselves on their weapons, etc.”

What should I say of the many thousands of words either restored or returned to their proper places?

In this matter three very ancient written copies brought us no little assistance. One of them was supplied by the library of the cathedral church of Cologne; it was scarcely written in characters or letter-forms that could now be recognized or read.

Yet who but someone who has experienced it himself could believe how difficult it was, amid such variety or disagreement among the codices—when the manuscripts disagreed most sharply both with the printed copies and with one another—to judge what ought to be erased or retained, and what ought instead to be substituted?

Moreover, who does not know how ignorantly, not to say disgracefully, this book was once divided into chapters *per ὄρον λύρας* (“by the boundary of the lyre”; the printed Greek phrase is obscure, perhaps corrupt)? It was divided in such a way that not only was no regard paid to differences of subject or history, but speeches were often split apart and separated in the middle of periods, indeed even in the middle of clauses of thought; while, conversely, passages that most needed to be divided and separated were enclosed and glued together.

And how foolishly, I ask, and ineptly, had he added arguments that were entirely irrelevant and unrelated to the subject? Finally, how improperly and without any judgment this same book had hitherto been circulated as divided into sections, I believe no one who has read it at all can fail to know.

If our small labor has assisted in any of these matters, more through diligence than effectiveness, I ask all students to judge it fairly and favorably. And whatever labor this may have been, receive it, most upright Bishop, dedicated to you, with the same expression and disposition with which the Persian king Artaxerxes is said to have once received a poor man’s trifling but simple gift—water drawn from a nearby river in his cupped hands—valuing the intention and inclination of spirit rather than the thing itself.

May Your Reverence prosper happily. Cologne, in the year 1526, on the Ides of June themselves.

## LETTER OF FRANCISCUS FABRICIUS MARCODURANUS TO LORD JOANNES ULATTENUS

To the most eminent and distinguished Lord Joannes Ulattenus, provost of Aachen, Kranenburg, and Kerpen; chancellor of the most illustrious prince Wilhelm, Duke of Jülich, Cleves, and Berg, and so forth; his patron:

Franciscus Fabricius Marcoduranus sends greetings.

Since all who have committed to writing the things they first discovered, or afterward cultivated and illuminated by letters, have deserved well of posterity, most distinguished sir, surely no one has deserved better than those who have entrusted deeds to history and handed them down to memory. The works that the most serious men—Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, and other philosophers—have written about the pursuit of virtue and the rejection of vice are rightly held in high esteem; yet, I think, no one will deny that what Herodotus, Thucydides, Theopompus, Ephorus, and the other historians committed to the records of the annals has greater force for pursuing noble actions and avoiding their opposites. The former teach what people ought to do, the latter what they have nobly done; the former have given many precepts concerning the cultivation of justice, courage, and temperance; the latter demonstrate who has lived justly, courageously, and moderately.

Nor will one who exhorts people to justice accomplish more by the Socratic method than by the examples of Aristides, Fabricius, and others. Antonius therefore rightly calls history, when he adorns it with his praises in Cicero, “the teacher of life.” Great thanks are owed to the writers of history, who by their diligence have brought it about that, through learning about past events, we may behold as in a mirror what in human life is praised or blamed, approved or condemned.

Nevertheless, no one is so ignorant of affairs or so estranged from letters that he does not know that all who have written histories should not be held in equal estimation, nor the same usefulness expected from all their writings. Some have wished, by narrating ancient events, merely to bathe the ears, as it were, in a kind of pleasure and to captivate them with the allurements of words; others have treated deeds performed wisely, justly, piously, courageously, and moderately in splendid and elevated language; others, neglecting verbal ornament, have presented useful events, certainly, but not illuminated by the lights of eloquence. Above all, those should be selected and diligently read who can cultivate not only the language but also equip the mind with an abundance of many important matters.

Yet if we do not despise those from whom nothing at all is supplied beyond verbal ornament, certainly those are very fastidious who shrink from writers who, in brief and simple speech, have comprehended events most worthy of knowledge—especially if it is clear that they have enclosed themselves within the boundaries of truth so completely that they never stepped outside them and were moved in writing by neither favor nor hostility.

I do not think it necessary at this time to establish at greater length that this is true of Paul Orosius; but I shall by no means omit what young men will strive to learn about this author of ours. A brief account of his life, written by Gennadius in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, survives; it is also found at the beginning of the *History* in manuscript copies, as we have published it.

He was a Christian, born and brought up in Spain; but, eager for learning, he left his own people and homeland. To gain a clear understanding of the matters in religion that he desired to know more thoroughly, he crossed over to Africa to Aurelius Augustine. This was around the year of Christ 400.

While he was with Augustine, he consulted him about the Priscillianists and about certain opinions of Origen. Augustine answered this consultation in the book that survives under the title *Against the Priscillianists and Origenists, to Orosius*.

Meanwhile Rome was captured by Alaric, king of the Goths, and the Romans suffered a great disaster; the enemies attributed its cause to the Christian religion. Against them, Orosius, at Augustine’s command, composed these seven books of Histories.

Gelasius I, together with seventy bishops, passed judgment concerning them, and the words of his decree are these: “We commend Orosius, a most learned man, because he arranged matters of great necessity against the calumnies of the pagans and wove them together with remarkable brevity.”

Afterward, on Augustine’s advice—as Augustine himself writes to Evodius—Orosius went to Bethlehem to Saint Jerome. Augustine commended him in these words:

“Behold, there has come to me a religious young man, a brother in the peace of the Catholic faith, a son in age, and in rank our fellow presbyter, Orosius: watchful in intellect, ready in speech, burning with zeal, desiring to be a useful vessel in the house of the Lord, for refuting the false and destructive doctrines that have slaughtered the souls of the Spaniards far more unhappily than the barbarian sword has slaughtered their bodies, and so forth.”

I shall not mention here how often, and how willingly, learned men make use of this writer’s authority and testimony, nor how much historical memory survives in Orosius that cannot be found elsewhere after the loss of so much in Livy, Tacitus, and other historians. I will say only this: it ought to have been regretted that the history of so great a man, and so productive a history, had until now circulated in such a corrupt form.

Thirty-five years ago Gerard Bolsuinge had compared it with several manuscript copies. The learned Johannes Caesarius afterward labored to correct it. Yet it is plainly necessary to conclude either that their copies were not transcribed with sufficient care, or that they themselves did not examine the work accurately enough, since I have detected so many errors left by them after I began comparing their books with three manuscripts.

Nor was I content merely to call upon old books for the correction of this so distinguished history. Since I had long before learned, from collating many Greek and Latin authors, that written books are often disfigured by numerous errors, I collected and, as it were, summoned into one place all the authors whom I could remember having written anything about the matters touched upon by Orosius. Who they were, and how many, will appear from our Annotations. In them I have attempted not only to support this edition but also to illuminate Roman history, so that young men who wished to know more fully what Orosius has briefly summarized might, instructed by this notice of ours, know where those matters were to be sought and satisfy their thirst by reading them.

I undertook this with great effort and zeal; what I have achieved, however, I willingly leave to the judgment of others. Among them, you, most distinguished patron, are in my eyes the equivalent of all. Your goodwill and your judgment will be the richest fruit of these vigils of mine.

In undertaking, planning, and completing this work, I certainly had the public benefit of the young foremost in view. Yet, while laboring together with Orosius for your sake, I also looked upon you with a grateful remembrance of your benefits toward me—and not without reason. For if, from the time when you first embraced me, I determined that everything proceeding from me was owed to you, how much fuller that disposition of mine ought now to be, after you wished, with the greatest expression of goodwill, to receive my son from the sacred font of baptism!

Since this bond of relationship is regarded as especially close by the sanction of the emperor Justinian, I consider that it imposes upon me the heaviest burden of respect. As its witness, I now send Orosius to you. I think that he rightly appears under your name, because you—who, placed at the highest level of dignity, wisely care for and preside over the tranquillity of your homeland—remember that you began, nourished, enlarged, and strengthened your knowledge of histories from your earliest years, and even now, when the gravest affairs of the commonwealth allow it, have not made a habit of avoiding the reading of historians.

Since you do this not for the sake of acquiring knowledge but of recalling it, no histories are read more conveniently than those who have written the deeds of famous men and peoples *in epitome* (ἐν ἐπιτομῇ, that is, “in abridgment”). Since Orosius has fulfilled this task with the utmost fidelity, on the testimony of very serious men, I do not think it necessary to demonstrate it here at greater length. Nor do I doubt that the man is sufficiently commended to you who, beginning his History from the origin of the world, carried it down almost to his own times through a little more than five thousand six hundred years.

I also trust that you will approve our labor. Therefore, just as Timanthes left Agamemnon’s grief to be judged, so we leave it to you to estimate our love and devotion toward you.

We pray Christ, the Best and Greatest, to preserve you long in safety for your homeland and for us. Farewell, patron whom I especially revere.

Düsseldorf, the day after the Ides of March, in the year from the birth of Christ 1561.

## PROLOGUE TO THE READER BY JOANNES RUREMONDUS, A DISCIPLE

If, friendly reader, you take pleasure in enjoying more fully  
the final events through histories beginning with the world’s origin,  
why do you cling so closely to the mutilated volumes of the ancients,  
which cannot in any respect relieve your hunger?

Behold, Orosius returns, released into the thin air,  
shining with Francis’s more brilliant light.

Although formerly he had been carried to the lips of the people,  
he himself had not yet been stripped of his filth;  
but just as an apple, usually rosy in color,  
which leaves its mother’s branches before its time,  
abandons the honor of its nourishing skin  
where the sun’s heat cooks the rind,  
while the rest remains full of its former vigor,  
so much error had weakened Orosius on one side,  
while on the other he had been only half restored from his blemishes.

Now behold him coming to you, with the foulness and decay removed,  
a child endowed with the learned honor of Fabricius.

If the ancients can have deserved some favor,  
though they often lighten the bonds of history,  
can Orosius, now cut by the avenging file, be displeasing—  
he who courageously bore his weapons for Christ?

For as soon as Roman power began to decline  
and the people declared Christ to be the source of evil,  
he wove annals from the world’s first seed,  
always showing that the earth is burdened with disasters.

And to dispel the lies of the foolish crowd,  
which could darken Christ’s radiance,  
he taught, refuting their frauds with marvelous brevity,  
that the Romulan scepters flourished through the faith of Christ’s people.

Hence we, who are covered as though by a dense cloud of sorrows  
and are always a crowd buried beneath troubles,  
flee from assigning the causes of evils to Christ,  
and learn to bear, undergo, and endure disasters.

Therefore take up Orosius, snatched from the dust of corruption,  
if any small concern for your own welfare can touch you.

His speech, no empty one, will not bring you the weariness of reading;  
the living grace of his eloquence runs onward.

The sad procession of errors will no longer delay you;  
through Fabricius’s service, Orosius comes forth bereft of them.

If anything seems immersed in blind darkness,  
which your intellectual capacity cannot penetrate,  
our most illustrious Gymnasium’s light,  
Francis, makes it clear by the brilliance of his commentary.

Just as he follows the monuments of ancient men,  
so he draws places forth from the clouded darkness of events.

If the labors of this man can please you  
and move your thoughts without end,  
then, diligent reader, take up Orosius’s little books,  
which he offers here to you with grateful zeal.

## LETTER OF ANDREAS SCHOTTUS OF ANTWERP, S.J., TO PETER CHOLINUS, PRINTER OF COLOGNE AGRIPPINA, IN UBII TERRITORY, GREETING

Those who have handed down to the memory of posterity instructions for reading history—which is exceedingly useful for human life, since it is the teacher of morals—have for the most part thought it more convenient to begin with epitomes and abridgments. They judge that one should take one’s beginning either from L. Florus in Roman history, or from the writer *On Illustrious Men*, or finally from Paul Orosius in Greek and Latin history, and proceed gradually to those vast historians, the writers of the histories of the greater nations and of the Roman Republic: Titus Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Plutarch, Appian, Dio, Polybius, and the rest.

The epitomes of L. Julius Florus—or, if Vinetus is right and the manuscripts bear that name, the work of L. Annaeus Seneca—have been illuminated by the commentaries of learned men: Johannes Camer­tus, Elias Vinetus, Johannes Stadius, Gruterus, and the selected notes of the distinguished Justus Lipsius. On the author *On the Illustrious Men of the City of Rome*, Dominicus Machanaeus, Philippus Puncherius, and, in Germany, Lycosthenes once made such observations as they could. Finally, we certainly wished to lend our hand to Cornelius Nepos by preparing him for publication.

As for Orosius, whom, excellent Cholinus, you are preparing to print for the fourth time or more in your presses, our friend Myllus has informed me by letter that he has been so illuminated by the commentary of Franciscus Fabricius, a most learned man, that he seems to have brought light not only to Paul Orosius but to the whole history of the Greeks and Romans.

Nevertheless, Ludovicus Lautius of Belgium once compared those seven books again with your manuscripts and those of Cologne. I revised the Notes at your particular request and found that a large part consisted of Fabricius’s Notes. I therefore separated them, so that the reader would not be compelled to read the same things twice with annoyance, and so that an Aesopian crow adorned with another’s feathers would not provoke laughter. I have assigned each note to its proper author and send them to you, so that, if you think fit, you may join them to the others, with some addition concerning variant readings.

As for the observations that we wrote in the margin while reading and correcting the text, when we were publishing the complete *Fasti of the Magistrates* and *Roman Annals* of Stephanus Vinandus Pighius in the Plantinian press, I earnestly beg and beseech you to judge them favorably.

In the meantime, by way of a conclusion, we shall add one point that occurred to none of those men: why this History of Orosius was once entitled *Ormesia of the World*. In my opinion, this was an error caused by the barbarous age, when not only Greek letters but also Latin letters belonged to very few people, lay neglected, and had fallen silent.

The title should rather have been *Orchestra*. The first to see and name this was the same most learned Pighius in the *Hercules Prodicius*. That book concerns the best education of a prince and describes the journey toward Rome of Charles, son of the Duke of Cleves and Jülich, in the sacred jubilee year 1575. In that year, while in the embrace of Gregory XIII at Rome, that prince of the highest promise died; he was buried in the church of Blessed Mary of the Souls, very near the tomb of Adrian VI, the Belgian Supreme Pontiff.

“But why *Orchestra*?” you will ask. Is it because it represents the theater of historical events, as it were? Or because it begins with a description of the world? What the Orchestra is, however, our Lipsius explains in his *Amphitheatre*, chapter 14, and Julius Pollux in his *Onomasticon*, book 4, chapter 19.

Farewell, my Cholinus, and enjoy this work of ours on Orosius, whatever its worth.

Antwerp, 1614.

## GALLANDIUS’S NOTICE CONCERNING PAUL OROSIUS

Paul Orosius, a presbyter, Spanish by nationality and a citizen of Tarragona, flourished almost at the end of the reign of the emperor Honorius, as Gennadius writes [Note: Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 39.].

The author himself reveals his people and homeland in these words [Note: Orosius, *History*, book 7, chapter 22]: “There still exist throughout the provinces, amid the ruins of great cities, small and poor settlements preserving the marks of their miseries and the tokens of their names. Among them we too, in Spain, display our own Tarragona as a consolation for our recent misery.”

From Spain he undertook his journey to Africa for the purpose of bringing back from Saint Augustine a remedy and salvation for his fellow countrymen infected with the wicked errors of heretics. We learn this both from the holy teacher himself and especially from Orosius.

Augustine, in his letter to Saint Jerome [Note: Augustine, letter 166, paragraph 2, works, volume 2, page 583], says:

“Behold, there has come to me a religious young man, a brother in the peace of the Catholic faith, a son in age, and in rank our fellow presbyter, Orosius: watchful in intellect, ready in speech, burning with zeal, desiring to be a useful vessel in the house of the Lord, for refuting the false and destructive doctrines that have slaughtered the souls of the Spaniards far more unhappily than the barbarian sword has slaughtered their bodies. For he hurried to us from the shore of the ocean, summoned by the report that from me he could hear whatever he wished to know about the matters he wished to know.”

Again, writing to Bishop Evodius [Note: Augustine, letter 169, paragraph 13, same volume, page 608], he mentions “the most holy and zealous young presbyter Orosius, who,” he says, “came to us from the farthest part of Spain, that is, from the shore of the ocean, inflamed solely by the ardor of the Holy Scriptures.”

This is Augustine.

Orosius himself, addressing the holy teacher in the same sense, writes as follows [Note: Orosius, *Consultation to Augustine*, section 1]:

“I have been sent to you by God; through you I hope in him, when I consider how it came about that I should come here. I recognize why I have come. Without will, without necessity, without consent, I departed from my homeland, driven by some hidden force, until I was brought to the shore of this land. Only then did I recover the understanding that I had been commanded to come to you. Do not judge me impudent, if you accept me as one who confesses . . . . We have been torn apart by wicked teachers more grievously than by the bloodiest enemies. We confess the offense; you see the wound. What alone remains, with the Lord’s help, grant us: medicine.”

From these statements it is therefore perfectly clear that they are mistaken who assert either that Orosius was sent to Africa to Saint Augustine by Eutropius and Paulus, apparently Spanish bishops [Note: Tillemont, volume 13, page 1006, note 57 on Saint Augustine], or that he was sent there by Herotes and Lazarus, bishops of Gaul.

Orosius does mention the first two bishops [Note: Orosius, *Consultation*, cited above]; but from his words they appear either to have gone to Africa before him or at least to have been there at the same time as he was, so that, like Orosius himself, they might seek and receive help from Saint Augustine for the salvation of the Spaniards. For this reason the same holy father dedicated to them his book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness* [Note: Augustine, works, volume 10, page 167].

The latter bishops of Gaul, Herotes and Lazarus, after both had been driven from their own sees and had gone to Palestine to oppose the Pelagians, found Orosius already living there—as we shall presently say—for that very reason. Since he was already planning to return to Africa, they gave him a letter for the Council of Carthage, as Augustine testifies [Note: Augustine, letter 175, paragraph 1, works, volume 2, page 617].

Thus none of the bishops mentioned was the author of Orosius’s journey to Africa. He had left his homeland “without will, without necessity, without consent,” driven by some hidden force, as we have just heard him say.

Nor does what he narrates elsewhere [Note: Orosius, *History*, book 3, chapter 20] about persecution inflicted upon him by barbarians in his own homeland seem to contradict this assertion of Orosius. At that time the Goths and Suevi had invaded Spain, and he may consequently have been compelled by necessity to seek safety by flight in order to avoid that persecution.

For he did withdraw his foot from Spain, driven by the force of barbarian persecution. Yet he could have gone elsewhere, in a sound and free state of mind, rather than to the African shores, where he might live more safely—and therefore “without necessity,” as he himself says—and so he finally fled there willingly.

Let us hear Orosius himself on this matter [Note: the same, ibid., book 5, chapter 2]:

“But as I fled at the first disturbance, whatever it was, of my mind, because I was secure concerning the place of refuge—for everywhere is my homeland, everywhere my law and religion—Africa has now received me as willingly as I approached confidently. This Africa, I say, has now received me with simple peace, in her own bosom, under the common law.”

And the rest, which are certainly worthy of being read through in the author himself.

Together with learned men [Note: Benedictine editors, notice, volume 10 of Augustine’s works, page 165, near the end; Ballerini, *Observations*, book 1, chapter 4, paragraph 4, page 863 of volume 4 of the works of Noris] we place Orosius’s first arrival in Africa either after the beginning of the year 415 or before the middle of that same year. This differs from the view of Noris [Note: Noris, *Pelagian History*, book 1, chapter 6, page 68 and following, works, volume 1] and his follower Pagi [Note: Pagi, on the year 414, paragraph 6], both of whom preferred to set the event in the preceding year, 414.

Thus, while Orosius was staying with Augustine at Hippo, after he had presented the holy teacher with the reason for his journey, he afterward offered him a *Consultation*, or *Commonitorium*, concerning the error of the Priscillianists and Origenists, earnestly asking him [Note: Orosius, *Consultation to Augustine*, section 4] to hasten to apply a remedy after examining all the diseases.

Augustine agreed to Orosius’s request and, in response to his *Consultation*, dedicated a book to him [Note: Augustine, works, volume 8, page 611]. The holy father mentions both works once and again [Note: Augustine, *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 44, works, volume 1, page 57, and letter 169, paragraph 13, volume 2, page 608].

Since one of Orosius’s questions concerned the origin of the soul, and since Saint Augustine declared himself unequal to solving this most difficult question, he judged that our Spanish presbyter should be sent to the greatest teacher, Jerome. Among other things, he gave him two letters addressed to Jerome, the first of which begins as follows [Note: Augustine, letter 166, paragraph 2, volume 2, page 584]:

“I taught the man Orosius what I could; what I could not, I pointed out where he might learn it, and I encouraged him to go to you.”

He makes the same point elsewhere also, writing to Bishop Evodius [Note: the same, letter 166, paragraph 13, page 608].

Orosius obeyed Augustine. Speaking therefore of his arrival in Palestine, he says [Note: Orosius, *Apology*, section 3]:

“I was staying in Bethlehem, entrusted by Father Augustine, so that I might learn the fear of the Lord, sitting at Jerome’s feet.”

Jerome himself, writing back to Augustine, says [Note: Jerome, letter 134, paragraph 1, works, volume 1, page 1036, Verona edition]:

“I received Orosius the presbyter, an honorable man, my brother, the son of your esteem, both because of his own merit and at your command.”

After receiving from Augustine two letters to Jerome, written in the spring of 415, Orosius therefore left Hippo at once and went to Palestine. It will become clear from what follows that he was already there at the end of July of that same year, 415.

While Orosius was staying with Jerome and had related everything that had been done at Carthage against the Pelagians, John of Jerusalem, having heard these things, decided to deal with the matter judicially. John had been deceived by Pelagius, who was likewise living there, and regarded him as orthodox. Accordingly, after summoning a public synod, he called Orosius before it.

Subsequently, after being branded by the deceitful tactics of his adversaries as an advocate of heretical depravity, Orosius published an apologetic book in which, pursuing his defense at length, he attacks Pelagius alone.

It would be lengthy to go through one by one the events said to have occurred at that assembly. It will be better to learn them from the *Apology* of our author himself, which we shall present below. For the purposes of our undertaking, however, we think it appropriate meanwhile to note one or two points.

First, it seems necessary to establish that the Jerusalem assembly belongs to the year 415, when Orosius, departing from Africa in the spring and making for Palestine, as we saw above, arrived there. We learn from Orosius himself that the date on which the assembly was held was 28 July.

For it is established [Note: Orosius, *Apology*, section 7] that he returned to Jerusalem forty-seven days after the assembly had been held, on the first day of the Encaenia. That day was 13 September, as Nicephorus reports [Note: Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 8, chapter 50, volume 1, page 653]: “It was the thirteenth day of the month of September.” Valesius [Note: Valesius, on Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book 4, chapter 46] correctly observed this, and after him Tillemont [Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, volume 13, page 668].

Noris [Note: Noris, *Pelagian History*, book 1, chapter 7, works, volume 1, page 74], the Benedictines [Note: the Benedictines, Appendix to volume 10 of Augustine, page 74, note], Vallarsi [Note: Vallarsi, on Jerome’s works, volume 2, page 375 near the end, and volume 1 in the recension of letter 133], and others, however, deceived by the translator Langus, who rendered Nicephorus’s words while engaged in another matter, assert that the day was the fourteenth of September and that the first day of the Encaenia fell on 14 September.

Pagi made the same error [Note: Pagi, on the year 415, paragraph 4], following Noris as he usually did and forgetting himself—for earlier, when copying Valesius, he had correctly stated that the Encaenia of the Jerusalem church had been celebrated on 13 September [Note: the same, on the year 335, paragraphs 3 and 6].

If, therefore, you count back Orosius’s forty-seven days from 13 September, you arrive at 28 July, on which the Jerusalem assembly was held.

The second point that we believe especially relevant to our undertaking concerns the attribution to our author, together with learned men, of the *Apology* just mentioned.

Jansenius thinks that this excellent little work was written by someone as an exercise [Note: Jansenius, *Augustinus*, volume 1, page 26, Leuven edition, 1640]. Wastelius added to what he drew from Jansenius that the author of Orosius’s little work was guilty of Novatianism and Nestorianism [Note: Wastelius, volume 2, *Vindications*, book 3, section 5, pages 568 and following].

“To use Labbé’s words [Note: Labbé, *Councils*, volume 3, page 363, Venice edition], this is not the place to inveigh more bitterly either against the bishop of Ypres or against the Carmelite Wastelius, who sought, by frivolous but outwardly disguised arguments, to cast suspicion of forgery (νοθεία) upon that outstanding apologetic work, while almost the entire army of learned men resists them.”

To refute them, however, Augustine alone is at hand. He is found to have incorporated into his book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* excerpts from the proceedings of the Jerusalem assembly arranged by Orosius in his *Apology* [Note: Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapters 14, 15, 16, 17, and 30].

To make this more evident to the reader, consult, if you wish, the most distinguished men who vigorously defended the authenticity of this *Apology*: first of all Noris [Note: Noris, *Pelagian History*, book 1, chapter 7, works, volume 1, pages 74 and following] and Garnerius [Note: Garnerius, Dissertation 6, chapter 3, on Marius Mercator, volume 1, page 354, or in the *Augustinian Appendix*, page 248]. They were later followed by Pagi [Note: Pagi, on the year 415, paragraph 3], Papebrochius [Note: Papebrochius, preliminary treatise to volume 3 of the *Acta Sanctorum* for May, page XXI], Tillemont [Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, volume 13, page 1008, note 59 on Saint Augustine], Natalis Alexander [Note: Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, fifth century, chapter 3, article 6, paragraph 2, page 44], and others.

The *Apology* is therefore rightly attributed to Orosius.

“For,” as Garnerius says [Note: Garnerius, Dissertation 6, cited *Augustinian Appendix*, page 250 near the end], “it has Augustine’s testimony; its style demonstrates the author; the manuscript codices bear the name of Orosius; and the only opponents are those whose interest it is that so great and ancient a writer, and above all so noble a disciple of Jerome and Augustine, should not furnish weapons with which he once defeated Pelagius and with which Catholics now in turn defeat them.”

This is what the learned man says. Finally, emphasizing the excellence of the work again, he adds:

“Only two of the questions raised by Pelagius are treated in this book: one concerning the power of free will, the other concerning human perfection in mortal life. Jerome was agitating these two questions in the East and had persuaded the presbyters of his party of them, so that they thereby brought great unpopularity upon Pelagius. Both questions, however, are resolved in this *Apology of Orosius* with such subtlety, according to the exactness of the Schools (ἀκρίβεια), and with such solidity, according to the rule of faith, that I do not hesitate to affirm that scarcely anything better was written in ancient times, nor does anything more useful survive from the monuments of antiquity for later ages.”

The discussion of Orosius’s *Apology* must not yet be broken off. It has been discovered that a considerable portion of the final part of this little work [Note: Orosius, *Apology*, section 33] was incorporated from Saint Augustine’s book *On Nature and Grace* [Note: Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, chapters 13 through 21 and chapters 3 through 13]. These passages are therefore rightly excised by learned scholars.

Schottus was the first to detect this addition [Note: Schottus, preface to Orosius’s *Apology*, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris, volume 15, page 800]; afterward Vossius explained it more fully [Note: Vossius, *Pelagian History*, book 1, chapter 17]. Elsewhere, treating the same matter, Vossius believes that it happened by chance [Note: the same, *On Latin History*, book 2, chapter 14, pages 218 and following] that some copyist mixed into the Orosian material several pages of Augustine, placing them in reverse order and transposing them.

“Once these passages,” he adds, “had been introduced through some carelessness and afterward joined to the Orosian material, it happened that they were read as though they were Orosian by a reader who was inattentive and not very familiar with Augustine’s writings.”

On this matter, if you have the leisure, see also Noris [Note: Noris, *Pelagian History*, book 1, chapter 7, page 76], Garnerius [Note: Garnerius, in the cited *Augustinian Appendix*, page 250 near the end], and Tillemont [Note: Tillemont, volume 13, page 1008, note 59].

Following the guidance of these learned men, we have therefore published the Augustinian excerpts separately from Orosius’s *Apology* and have informed the reader in the notes below about their inversion and transposition. We may well wonder why Havercamp neglected this task.

It is especially worth noting also that, since the text of the *Apology* appears in many places corrupted in Havercamp’s edition, we have diligently cleansed it as far as lay within our power. We followed Schottus’s example, although it was less carefully corrected, because no other was available. We could have produced an even more accurate text if the excerpts preserved either by Labbé [Note: Labbé, *Councils*, volume 3, pages 363 and following, Venice-Labbé edition] or by the Benedictines [Note: the Benedictines, Appendix to volume 10 of the works of Saint Augustine, pages 79 and following] had come to our aid at a more suitable time.

Nevertheless, in order to remedy this difficulty in some fashion, we compared our copy, already issued from the press, with the excerpts just mentioned. Whatever we discovered in them that seemed worthy of notice, we transcribed below at the end among the passages requiring correction.

But let the discussion at last return to its proper course. Thus Orosius, still staying in Palestine in December of the year 415, was hastening his journey to Africa with extraordinary eagerness, as we learn from Avitus’ letter to Palchonius [Note: Avitus’ letter, in Baronius under the year 415, § 3, and in the Appendix to vol. VII of Augustine’s works, p. 2.]; and accordingly, setting out from there in the spring of the following year, 416, he went to Augustine by prior agreement [Note: Augustine, Letter 161, no. 2, works, vol. II, p. 584.]. “On his return,” says Gennadius [Note: Gennadius, On Illustrious Men, chap. 39.], “he was the first to bring to the West the relics of blessed Stephen, the first martyr, which had shortly before been discovered.” The aforementioned Avitus had previously reported the same thing [Note: Avitus, letter, cited above.]. In addition, he brought with him Jerome’s letter to Augustine [Note: Jerome, Letter 134, works, vol. I, p. 1036.], as well as the letter of Heros and Lazarus to the African bishops concerning Pelagius and Coelestius, the authors of an utterly wicked error to be anathematized by all [Note: Augustine, Letter 175, vol. II, p. 617.].

After returning from the East to Africa, Orosius set his hand to composing the seven books of the *Histories*, at Augustine’s urging and command [Note: Orosius, preface to the *Histories* and book VII, chap. 43.], and dedicated them to that holy teacher. Marcellinus reports that this work was written by Orosius during the consulship of Theodosius VII and Palladius [Note: Marcellinus, *Chronicle*, under the year 416, among the works of Sirmond, vol. II, p. 357, Paris edition.], that is, in the year 416. For the author himself testifies [Note: Orosius, preface.] that he began his *Histories* at the time when Augustine was engaged in completing the eleventh book of *The City of God*, that is, in the year 416, as learned men have judged [Note: Benedictines, preface to vol. VII of Augustine’s works.]; and that he completed them in the following year, 417, namely after Vallia, king of the Goths [Note: Orosius, *Histories*, book VII, chap. 43.], had concluded a very favorable peace with the emperor Honorius after giving the choicest hostages. On this dating of the time, see Baronius [Note: Baronius, under the year 414, § 14.], but especially Tillemont [Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XIII, pp. 698 and 1010, note 62.].

Moreover, that Orosius wrote his *Histories* while he was staying in Africa is attested by the author himself, an entirely reliable witness. For near the beginning of book V he says [Note: Orosius, book V, chap. 2.]:

> NOW AFRICA HAS RECEIVED ME as willingly as I approached it confidently: NOW THIS AFRICA HAS RECEIVED ME in simple peace, in her own bosom, by common right.

Furthermore, when the work had already been completed and he was still staying in the same region, he seems to have addressed Augustine in person. Thus, at the beginning [Note: The same, preface.]:

> I have obeyed your commands, most blessed father Augustine,

he says; and at the end [Note: The same, book VII, chap. 43.]:

> I have completed it, with Christ’s help, according to your command, most blessed father Augustine, etc.

Nor did Tillemont think otherwise [Note: Tillemont, cited above, vol. XIII, p. 698.]. From these facts, therefore, we understand that Pagius was entirely mistaken in asserting, without documentary evidence [Note: Pagius, under the year 417, § 23.], that this work had been written by Orosius in Spain.

After completing the books of the *Histories*, presenting them to Augustine, and obtaining his approval, Orosius left Africa at the end of the year 417 and undertook a journey to Spain, carrying among other things the relics of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, which he had received from Avitus, as we saw above, in order to deliver them to Palchonius, bishop of Braga. On this journey he turned aside to the island of Minorca and stayed for a short time at Magona. But since at that time the Spaniards were being besieged by the Goths, and he could not be transported there as he wished, he decided to return once more to Africa, as we learn from the encyclical letter of Severus, bishop of Minorca [Note: Severus’ letter, in Baronius under the year 418, § 46.]. What happened to Orosius thereafter is completely unknown.

Now, to return to his *History*, we find that it was held in great esteem among the ancients. For scarcely had it been completed and published for the general reading when its author is said to have been adorned with praises. Prosper, a disciple of Saint Augustine [Note: Prosper, *Chronicle*, among his works, p. m. 428.], says:

> Orosius, a Spanish presbyter, an eloquent man and a student of history, is distinguished;

and Gennadius copied these words [Note: Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chap. 39.]. An anonymous African author, nearly contemporary with Prosper, calls Orosius “a most learned man” and “the historiographer Orosius” [Note: Anonymous author, *On the Promises and Predictions*, part II, chap. 33, no. 4, in the Appendix to Prosper’s works.]. Sidonius, in listing various ecclesiastical writers, praises Orosius’ abundance in expression and his readily flowing eloquence [Note: Sidonius, book IV, letter 3, among the works of Sirmond, vol. I, p. 932.]. Gelasius, the supreme pontiff of the Church [Note: Gelasius, *Decree*, § 3, in Fontanini, appendix to *Ancient Gardens*, p. 326.], says:

> We commend Orosius, a most learned man, who composed for us a *History* greatly needed against the accusations of the pagans and wove it together with marvelous brevity.

Cassiodorus likewise does not pass over Orosius; he calls him a compiler who brings together the times of Christians and of pagans [Note: Cassiodorus, *On Divine and Secular Learning*, chap. 17.].

We omit the judgments of more recent writers concerning this Orosian work. If desired, they may be found collected with sufficient care by an English author [Note: Thomas Pope Blount, *Censura celebrium auctorum*, p. 290.]. We also omit discussion of the title-word, whether *Hormesta* or *Ormesta*, under which the seven books of our author’s *Histories* are commonly inscribed, according to Cangius [Note: Cangius, *Latin Glossary*, entries “Hormesta” and “Ormesta.”], in manuscript codices; for Fabricius has treated the matter with the greatest diligence [Note: Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediæ et infimæ Latinitatis*, vol. V, p. 520.], though one addition should be made to what he has related, which Gerdesius reports from Withofius [Note: Gerdesius, *Groningae Miscellanea*, vol. II, fasc. 2, p. 382.].

For the rest, although this work of Orosius is not free from blemishes—ones which very learned men have recognized, including Baronius in various places, Scaliger in his *Annotations on Eusebius*, Petavius in his books *On the Doctrine of Time*, Norisius in the *Pisan Cenotaphs*, and others—“it is nevertheless,” to use the words of the recent editor [Note: Havercamp, preface to Orosius, near the end.], “generally held in high esteem among all learned men, both because of the manifold history of the work itself, gathered together in a brevity that is not unhelpful and carefully arranged according to the reckoning of times and the Roman consuls, and especially because he made use of the great historians and annalists—whole works of whom we now seek in vain—and of authors who held the first rank in that field.”

We have arranged for an edition of Orosius’ *History* to be printed—the latest edition, published at Leiden in 1738 by the most learned Havercamp—since it was carefully collated both with the older printed copies and with the authority of the manuscripts, especially the ancient Lombard manuscript of the Florentine Medicean Library [Note: Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, book V, p. 354.], which Mabillon mentions.

There is one point that we think should be noted. Orosius, calculating the course of time that he embraced in composing his *History* and extended from the creation of the world to his own age, says as follows [Note: Orosius, *Histories*, book VII, chap. 43, near the end.]:

> I have completed … from the beginning of the world up to the present day, through 5,618 years,

that is, five thousand six hundred and eighteen years, etc. Thus the more accurate older printed editions read—although some others, with one numeral transposed, incorrectly display *VM. DXC. XVIII*, while nevertheless retaining the final number XVIII. Thus also the very learned Baronius [Note: Baronius, under the year 414, § 15.], Vossius [Note: Vossius, book II of *On Latin History*, chap. 14, p. 216.], Pagius [Note: Pagius, under the year 417, § 23.] and Tillemont [Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XIII, p. 1010, note 42 on Saint Augustine.] read it correctly. But Havercamp, running his eyes over the numerical signs too hastily, wrote “through one thousand six hundred and seventeen years” instead of “eighteen.” Since this error escaped our notice when Havercamp’s copy was committed to type, we now point it out as something to be corrected in our own edition [Note: Orosius, *Histories*, book VII, chap. 43.].

The same inscription, identifying Orosius as a presbyter, is also found in the Utrecht and Perizonius manuscripts; in certain manuscripts the same title is given to him at the end, and in the first and third Leiden editions it is enclosed in this verse:

## THE SEVEN BOOKS OF THE HISTORIES OF PAUL OROSIUS, A SPANIARD AND PRESBYTER

(C)

### Preface: TO AURELIUS AUGUSTINE

**1** I have obeyed your commands, most blessed father Augustine—and would that I had done so as effectively as willingly! Although I am little moved in either direction concerning whether I have acted rightly or wrongly [Note: “Little in either direction.” My parchment manuscript prefers “little in both directions.” The third Florentine reads “equally little in either direction.” The third and fourth Leiden editions read “for a little while in either direction.” The same edition correctly deletes *recte*, and shortly afterward writes *praeceperas*. The Utrecht manuscript reads “whether rightly or wrongly.”], for you have already undertaken to judge whether I was able to do what you commanded [Note: “For you, now, in that matter.” The fourth Leiden edition reads, “But you, now, in a matter of justice.”], while I am content with the testimony of obedience alone—if indeed I have honored it by my willingness and effort.

For in the great house of a great householder, although there are many animals of different kinds, useful for the management of the household [Note: “Yet it is not the least important.” My manuscript, the third Leiden edition, and the third Florentine read “not, however,” and the latter shortly afterward has *institutum* instead of *insitum*.], the care of dogs is not the least important. For they alone have been endowed by nature with the disposition to be willingly driven toward the purpose for which they are prepared [Note: “Toward that for which they are prepared.” Some older printed editions read “toward that for which they are prepared,” among them the very first. All the manuscripts, however, read “toward that which they are prepared for,” as does the Augsburg edition. Fabricius therefore inserted the little word *ad*, which was necessarily required and seems to have fallen out because the word *id* occurred twice with another word between them.], and, by a certain innate pattern of obedience, to be held suspended solely by the expectation of disciplined fear [Note: “Of disciplined fear.” Here some manuscripts—the second and third Florentine, the second Leiden, the Utrecht manuscript, and older printed editions—give *tremoris* (“trembling”) instead of *timoris* (“fear”). The remaining Leiden manuscripts, as well as my own, have *timoris*, and Fabricius rightly preferred it, since trembling arises from fear. The third Leiden edition reads *pergendi* rather than *peragendi*. Shortly afterward, the second Leiden edition and the Utrecht manuscript add *sunt* to “as much … superior to brute animals as they approach rational beings.” The former places *mox animalibus* after *rationabilibus* and also reads *appropinquantes*.], until they are sent by a nod or sign to carry out their task.

For they have their own appetites: in proportion as they are superior to brute animals, they approach rational beings; namely, the ability to distinguish, to love, and to serve. For when they distinguish between their masters and strangers [Note: “Not those whom.” The second Florentine reads incorrectly, “not only those.” For Orosius says that love for their masters is innate in dogs, so that, impelled by it, they bark at strangers and pursue them—not because they naturally hate them, but in defense of their master.], they do not hate those whom they pursue [Note: “But they show jealousy toward those whom they love.” Our manuscripts have *his*, not *hos*. The verb ζηλοῦν (“to be jealous of,” “to show zeal for”) is also found in sacred writings with the dative. Fabricius. — All the Utrecht and Leiden manuscripts have *sed*, followed by *his* or *hiis*, as does the first edition; the second and third Florentine manuscripts, as well as the Hittorp edition, have *hos*. Fabricius’ *his* is supported by the Augsburg edition, the Perizonius codex, and my manuscript.], but they show jealousy toward those whom they love. And while loving their master and the household, they do not keep watch as though their bodies were naturally suited for it, but remain vigilant out of the anxious awareness of their love.

Hence also, in the mystical sacrament in the Gospels, we read that the little dogs eat the crumbs [Note: “The little dogs under the table.” It is also read as “from the table.” In Matthew, chapter 15, the Greek is: τὰ κυνάρια ἐσθίει ἀπὸ τῶν ψιχίων τῶν πιπτόντων ἀπὸ τῆς τραπέζης τῶν κυρίων αὐτῶν, “the little dogs eat from the crumbs falling from the table of their masters.” Fabricius. — The third Leiden edition has *catuli*, “puppies.”] under the table of their masters [Note: “Under the table of their masters.” The final word is deleted by Perizonius, the Utrecht manuscript, the second Leiden edition, and the second and third Florentine manuscripts. It is also absent from the Augsburg edition and my codex. The fourth Leiden edition prefers *mensis* (“tables”). The Greek from which the passage is taken nevertheless requires it. Shortly afterward, certain printed editions insert *mulier*, “the woman.”], and the Canaanite woman was not ashamed to say it, nor did the Lord disdain to hear it.

Blessed Tobias likewise, following an angel as his guide, did not reject having a dog as his companion [Note: “Blessed Tobias as well.” Tobit, chapter 6.]. Therefore, joined to your universal love by a special bond [Note: “Joined to your love by my special love.” The third Florentine reads “by your love.” I prefer the reading found in the oldest second Leiden manuscript, the Utrecht manuscript, and the first edition: “joined to your universal love and by a special bond.”], I willingly obeyed your will.

For since my submission ought to render an achievement to the command of your fatherly authority [Note: “Ought to have been made.” So all the manuscripts and printed editions read; one Utrecht manuscript has “you ought to have expended the work.” Hence I suspect that there is an ancient corruption here; for I do not sufficiently understand what this is meant to convey. If Orosius wishes to suggest that his submission to the fatherly command of Aurelius Augustine ought to have become this work, he has expressed himself rather awkwardly and unworthily of the judgment by which he was distinguished. I therefore suspect that Orosius wrote not *factum* (“made”) but *fructum* (“fruit”). He owed the command and labor of Augustine, his teacher and spiritual father, the fruit that would demonstrate how much he had advanced under that teacher. He now presents this fruit and offers it to him to whom he professes that he owes it.], and that everything should be yours which returns to you from you—my work [Note: “And let the whole thing be yours, etc.” I corrected this passage, corrupted by faulty punctuation. Earlier editions read: “and let the whole thing be yours, which, having come from you [the Utrecht edition adds *sit*], returns to you; I have made this work more complete by my own sole contribution, because I did it willingly.” The punctuation should plainly be placed after *opus meum*. Orosius is saying that the whole of his work may deservedly be called Aurelius Augustine’s, since it proceeded from him—that is, it was written at his urging and command—and that it therefore deservedly ought to be offered to him. The third Florentine transposes the words *tuum sit*. The first and fourth Leiden manuscripts read: “and let the whole thing be yours, which is from you and returns to you”; the third reads: “and let the whole thing which is from you be yours, and let it return to you”; the second reads: “the same work, namely, let the whole thing be yours, which is from you.” In the first three manuscripts the opening words should be referred to a gloss explaining “let the whole thing be yours.”], I have made it more complete by this one contribution of mine, that I did it willingly [Note: “More complete by this one contribution of mine.” Many manuscripts do not recognize *meo*, including the second Florentine, the Utrecht and Perizonius manuscripts, the first, second, and third Leiden manuscripts, and the first edition, as well as the Augsburg edition. It is retained by the third Florentine, my codex, and the fourth Leiden edition, which last reads “by this alone of mine.” Yet *meo* may be absent, since the sense plainly shows that Orosius is speaking of his own work, not another’s. “To you, father Augustine,” he says, “I owe the fruit; I offer to you the work undertaken under your auspices and admonitions, which for that reason may and ought properly to be called yours. The glory of obedience belongs to me, and I have made it more complete by this alone, that I did it willingly.” At the beginning of his preface he had promised this obedience to his teacher’s commands in the words, “I have obeyed your commands, most blessed father Augustine—and would that I had done so as effectively as willingly!”], you had commanded me to write against the empty perversity of those who, being strangers to the City of God, are called pagans—or gentiles—from the crossroads and villages of rural places [Note: “Strangers to the City of God.” He alludes to the eminent work of his teacher Aurelius Augustine, which he entitled *The City of God* and whose tenth book he had published when Orosius made this work public.]; those who set their minds on earthly things [Note: Thus nearly all the manuscripts display the passage. One or two, with the printed editions, read *quia terrena sapiunt* (“because they set their minds on earthly things”), as though gentiles were called such because they set their minds on earthly things. I cannot extract that meaning from the passage. Rather, he calls those who are strangers to the City of God “pagans” and “gentiles”; he says that these set their minds on earthly things, and that, since they do not seek the future, etc.], who, while they do not seek the future, either forget the past or do not know it [Note: “But the past.” The Augsburg edition does not recognize *autem*, nor do the Venetian edition or the Perizonius manuscript; Hittorp deletes the following *aut*, as does the third Leiden edition. Worse, the first and Augsburg editions do not delete *non* in the preceding words, *non quaerant*. Shortly afterward, the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts read *obliviscuntur et nesciunt*.], and regard the present age alone as exceptionally beset by evils [Note: “The present alone.” The second Florentine, the first edition, the Augsburg edition, and the Venetian edition read “the present, however”; the third Florentine reads “the present alone.” Shortly afterward comes “certain most hostile [things].”], and denounce it for this sole reason: that Christ is believed in and God is worshiped, while idols are worshiped less [Note: The first and third Leiden editions read “are not worshiped.” But the common reading is more correct, since the pagan religion had not yet been completely abolished. Shortly afterward: “in the books of the *Histories*,” in the Perizonius manuscript.].

You had therefore commanded me to explain, in a brief and orderly composition, whatever I might find throughout the elapsed ages in all the annalistic and historical records presently available: whatever was grievous in wars, corrupted by diseases, sorrowful through famine, terrifying through earthquakes, extraordinary through floods, dreadful through volcanic eruptions, savage through lightning strikes and hailstorms, or miserable through parricides and crimes.

This was especially so since your Reverence, occupied with completing the eleventh book against these very pagans [Note: “Against these very people.” From this it is learned at what time Orosius wrote this history: namely, after the capture of Rome under the emperor Honorius, in the year of Christ 410. We shall discuss this in the twenty-ninth chapter of the final book. Since Augustine had already completed the tenth book of *The City of God* and was then writing the eleventh, our Orosius undertook to write these things. Fabricius.], should not be occupied with a small work: for ten books had already appeared [Note: “Rising rays.” In the second Florentine, *velut* was written above the line. The Augsburg edition reads “like the rays of the rising sun,” as though the following words alluded to the rays of the sun, whereas the subsequent context shows that the metaphor is taken from fires by which signals were given.], which, like rising rays, as soon as they had been lifted from the watchtower of ecclesiastical splendor [Note: “Raised from the watchtower, etc.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden editions read incorrectly, “carried down from the watchtower.” The propriety of the expression is evident from Lucan, book VI, verse 278:

> Caesar had scarcely perceived the battles,  
> lifted up on the watchtower disclosed by the fire.]

shone throughout the whole world [Note: The Hittorp edition reads “throughout the whole world” in the dative.]. Nor should your holy son Julian, a Carthaginian and servant of God, be denied satisfaction in this matter [Note: “To his petition.” The common reading is “to your petition.” I consider the former preferable. Lautius. — *Suae*, instead of *tuae*, is confirmed by the second, third, and fourth Florentine and Leiden manuscripts, the Utrecht and Perizonius manuscripts, and the first and Augsburg editions. I have restored *poposcit* (“he requested”) from these and, in addition, the Perizonius manuscript, the third Florentine, my manuscript, and the Venetian editions, in place of *poposcisti* (“you requested”), which appeared in the common editions; for the subject here is Julian, not Augustine. Augustine had evidently commanded Orosius to compose this work, while Julian required Orosius to complete what he had undertaken. The Utrecht manuscript has *ea fiducia* (“with that confidence”) instead of *eadem* (“the same”).], with the same confidence with which he had requested it. I applied myself to the task, and first of all pressed myself down in embarrassment [Note: “In embarrassment.” The first and third Leiden editions read “in a state of embarrassment.” Shortly afterward they read *videantur* (“may seem”), where the third and fourth Florentine editions have *videbatur* (“seemed”).], since, whenever I reflected upon it, the disasters of the present age seemed to have boiled over beyond measure.

**5** For I discovered that past days were not only as grievous as the present, but even more cruelly wretched in proportion as they were farther removed from the remedy of true religion. Thus this investigation rightly made clear that death, greedy for blood, had reigned while religion was unknown [Note: “Which would restrain them from bloodshed.” The fourth Leiden edition reads *prohibuerit* (“which would have restrained”) and my manuscript *prohibet* (“which restrains bloodshed”).], religion which would restrain them from bloodshed. When this one began to shine, that other became stupefied [Note: “When this one began to shine, that other became stupefied.” Fabricius’ earlier editions read *illucescente*, as do the older manuscripts, the second and third Florentine, my manuscript, most of the Leiden manuscripts, and the Perizonius manuscript. The Mainz edition changed it to *conlucescente*, which I found only in the second Leiden manuscript and which seems less suitable because of the collision of similar sounds. Some manuscripts—the second and third Florentine, the third Leiden, and my manuscript—incorrectly read *constipuisse* instead of *constupuisse*. Orosius wrote *constupuisse*, as he often uses the simple verb *stupere*; Tertullian also uses *stupor*. In his *Apology*, chap. 37, p. 113, appropriately for the sense of this passage, he writes: “Without doubt you would have been terrified at your solitude, at the silence of things, and at a certain stupor, as though the world were dead.” The same author speaks of a divinity that is utterly nonexistent as *stupentem* (“stupefied”), in *Against the Valentinians*, chap. 7. The second Leiden manuscript and the Utrecht manuscript have *obstupuisse* (“had become utterly stupefied”).]—that one being brought to an end when this one already prevails [Note: The third Leiden edition reads “when this one would already prevail”; the first Leiden edition reads “when this one would prevail.” Shortly afterward, the second Leiden edition and the Augsburg edition have “now utterly nonexistent”; the fourth Leiden edition, “now that one”; the Utrecht manuscript, “now utterly that one.” Then the third Florentine and the Augsburg and first editions incorrectly read *regnavit* (“reigned”) instead of *regnabit* (“will reign”).], that one being destined to be utterly nonexistent when this one alone shall reign.

This statement excludes, of course, those final days set apart and removed at the end of the age, at the appearing of Antichrist, or even at the completion of the judgment. Concerning those times the Lord Christ foretold through the Holy Scriptures—and also by his own solemn testimony—that there would be future tribulations such as had not occurred before [Note: The Augsburg and first editions read *fuerant* (“had been”). Shortly afterward, for *semper* (“always”), the first Leiden edition has *semper fuit* (“has always been”). In the phrases “at the appearing” and “at the completion,” the second Florentine deletes the second *sub*. For the final word of this preface, *consequetur* (“will follow”), the Venetian editions have *sequetur* (“will follow”), while the Augsburg edition has *consequatur* (“may follow”).], when, according to the measure of that very one who is both now and always, the testing of the holy and the destruction of the impious will come through the intolerable and more grievous calamities of those times.

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER ONE

He shows from what point other writers have begun their histories, and from what point he himself intends to begin and how far to carry his; meanwhile he includes remarks on the earliest times and on the origin or cause of evils.

[Note: “And since almost all.” Most manuscript books, and nearly all printed editions which divide this writer’s books into chapters, make these words the beginning of the first chapter. Others, including Perizonius, the third Florentine manuscript, and the third Leiden edition, begin Book One with the following chapter, perhaps more correctly. But in the Augsburg edition of Johann Schuszler it begins with “I begin,” etc.; and after “as though shaken and awakened to a new providence” (for so it is read), there is written, “The Prologue ends.” Then follows: “The seven books of Paul Orosius, presbyter and historiographer, disciple of Saint Augustine the bishop, against the complainants against the Christian name, begin.” The title “presbyter” is likewise given to this writer at the beginning of the Prologue itself in the same edition, where the rubric reads: “Prologue to seven books of Paul Orosius, presbyter, historiographer, disciple of Saint Augustine, a man of Spanish origin and most eloquent, against the complainants against the Christian name.”]

And since almost all men, both among Greeks and among Latins, who have zealously undertaken writing and have perpetuated in words the deeds of kings and peoples for enduring remembrance [Note: “Of kings and peoples.” The Augsburg and Venetian editions read “of things and peoples.”] have made Ninus, son of Belus and king of the Assyrians, the beginning of their writing [Note: “Have perpetuated in words.” The fourth Leiden edition deletes *verbis* (“in words”). Shortly afterward the third Florentine has “and the beginning of writing.”]; although, in their blind opinion, they wish the origin of the world and the creation of humankind to be believed without beginning, they nevertheless determine that kingdoms and wars began with him. As though, indeed, the human race had lived like cattle up to that point, and only then, as if stirred and awakened to a new [Note: “Providence.” The Augsburg edition reads *prudentiam* (“prudence”). Lucretius, IV.14:] providence.

So that the heedless age of children might be deceived.] shaken and roused to providence, may have awakened [Note: “May have awakened.” Thus several manuscripts and printed editions, better than *vigilarit* or *vigilaret*, as others have it.
