The second Florentine manuscript has *vigilaverit*.] I have undertaken to trace the beginning of human misery [Note: “From the beginning of sinful humanity.” The second and third Florentine manuscripts have “from the beginning of the sin of humanity.” The first, second, third, and fourth Leiden editions have “from the beginning of the sin of the first man.” The Utrecht edition has “from the beginning of the sinning first man.” I see no reason to depart from the standard reading, which the others confirm.] from the beginning of the sinning man, intending to touch on only a few matters [7], and those briefly. [Note: “There are, however, from Adam.” Many manuscripts place here the rubric of this first chapter, including the first Florentine manuscript, Utrecht, and my manuscript: “There are, however, from the beginning of the world, from Adam,” etc.; the second Leiden manuscript.] [Note: “I have undertaken to trace.” The third Leiden edition has “I have undertaken to teach.” But the first, second, and fourth have “I have undertaken to teach,” which the Utrecht edition also approves. If anything must be changed, I would prefer *deducere* (“to trace”) with my manuscripts: Orosius repeatedly traces the miseries of the world from its first origin and brings them down to his own times. Immediately afterward, the Venetian editions have *deliberatis* (“having deliberated”) instead of *delibatis* (“having briefly touched upon”).]

[Col. 0669B] There are, however, from Adam, the first man, to Ninus, [Col. 0670A] the great king, as they call him, at whose time Abraham was born: [Note: “Three thousand one hundred and eighty-four years.” We find this number in all the books, and, because of the variation found in the earliest periods, we have wished to leave it attested. The variation arose from the diversity of the Hebrew and Greek books; see, among others, Augustine, *The City of God*, book 15, chapter 10. Eusebius, Orosius, Cassiodorus, and later writers followed the Greeks more than the Hebrews. According to Eusebius, Abraham was born in the forty-third year of the reign of King Ninus. FABRICIUS.] three thousand one hundred and eighty-four years, which all historians have either omitted or failed to know.

From Ninus, or Abraham, [Note: “When peace had been made.” The second Florentine manuscript reads “when wars had been made throughout the whole world,” etc. In its margin: others read, “when he made peace with the Parthians, the gates of Janus were closed, and wars,” etc.] [Note: “Or Abraham.” The third Florentine manuscript has “or from Abraham,” and immediately afterward “to the birth of the Lord,” instead of “of Christ.”] to Caesar Augustus—that is, to the birth of Christ, which occurred in the forty-second year of Caesar’s reign—when, peace having been made with the Parthians, the gates of Janus were closed and wars ceased throughout the world, two thousand and fifteen years are reckoned, during which [Note: “Among themselves.” The Leiden and Utrecht editions have *inter se* (“among themselves”), and the Venetian editions likewise transpose the words. All of them, however, delete the conjunction *et* before *quindecim*.] doers and writers of all things wore away leisure and business among themselves. [Note: “Authors and writers.” The editions have *auctores* (“authors”), but my reading is proved correct by Sallust: “Although the writer and the doer of deeds are by no means followed by equal glory.” LAUTIUS.—Lautius’s emendation is confirmed by the second and third Florentine manuscripts, and seems certain. In the second Florentine manuscript, *tribuerunt* (“they assigned”) is mistakenly written for *triverunt* (“they wore away”).]

Therefore the subject itself requires us to touch upon from these books only a very few matters, as briefly as possible. These books, speaking of the origin of the world, established the credibility of past events by announcing future ones and by the subsequent confirmation of those announcements. [Note: “To touch upon.” With broad agreement, the word *eorum* (“of them”) is deleted; it entered the editions through an interpolation in Hittorp. It is absent from the first and second Florentine manuscripts, all the Leiden manuscripts, Perizonius, Utrecht, and my manuscript, as well as the first edition, the Augsburg edition, and the Venetian editions. Some manuscripts and editions have *contingere* (“to encounter”) instead of *attingere* (“to touch upon”), as does Fabricius; but this is wrong. *Contingere* concerns the time at which something happens, whereas *attingere* is used of a writer such as Orosius, who excerpts the writings of earlier authors.] [Note: “Speaking.” The second and fourth Leiden editions have *linquentes* (“leaving aside”). The following I explain as follows: “Those books,” he says, “which teach us the true origin of the world, establish that faith cannot be denied them in matters which they alone attest to have happened, since those things which they predict in the same books as future later received confirmation through their fulfillment.” The second Florentine manuscript has *subsequentia* (“subsequent things”) instead of *subsequa*, and the third Leiden edition has *communis sit* (“is common”) instead of *communis est*.] [Note: “Not because [*non quo*] we seem to impose their authority.” The standard text has *quod*, but I found *quo* in the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts, as well as in Perizonius and my manuscript; both Florentine manuscripts and the first and Augsburg editions support them. Some witnesses also write *quo* in what follows, “but because it is worthwhile,” including the second and third Leiden manuscripts, my manuscript, and Utrecht. Where the earlier *quo* or *quod* is lacking, however, I consider *quod* preferable in the latter passage.] 

Not because we seem to impose their authority on anyone, but because it is worthwhile to call attention to the commonly held opinion, [8] which we share with everyone. [Note: “First, because.” In the second Florentine manuscript, the later word has *quidem* (“indeed”) written above it by another hand.]

[Col. 0670B] First, because if divine providence, which, [Note: “Which, just as it is good, is also pious and just.” The words *et pia* (“and pious”) had entered here from some unknown gloss. LAUTIUS.—The third Leiden edition acknowledges *pia* but not *bona* (“good”); both the second and third Florentine manuscripts and Perizonius omit *bona*, which Lautius wishes to delete. The Augsburg edition, the Utrecht edition, and my manuscript acknowledge neither word. Nevertheless, I strongly doubt that *pia* should be deleted—indeed, I deny it—for when Orosius declares divine providence good, he derives that goodness from piety and justice. The following discussion of man and his nature, which corresponds to this division and contrasts with the divine nature, shows that this was Orosius’s intention: just as the needy must be governed piously, so the excessively free must be corrected justly, and so forth. For this reading, the Augsburg and first editions have *et juste corripi* (“and must be corrected justly”); the first edition also has “of immoderate freedom.”] just as it is good, is also pious and just, [Col. 0671A] [Note: “The world and man are governed.” The third Leiden edition has “this world and man.” The Augsburg edition reads *agitur* (“is governed”); another has *regitur hic mundus et homo* (“this world and man are governed”), according to the practice by which the earliest editions sometimes faithfully reproduce what they found in written manuscripts. Others transpose the words as *agitur et homo et mundus* (“man and the world are governed”), as does the first undated edition, published under the care of Aeneas Vulpes of Vicenza, and the Venetian editions.] the world and man are governed: but man, who is both weak and rebellious through the changeability of his nature and the freedom of his license, [Note: “Both weak and rebellious.” From the second Florentine manuscript, the third Leiden edition, and the first and Augsburg editions, I have added the conjunction *et* (“and”): “and he is rebellious through weakness.” The third Florentine manuscript reads *gubernare* (“to govern”), as do the first edition and the Venetian editions.] just as a needy person must be governed piously, so one who abuses freedom without restraint must necessarily be corrected justly: rightly, from the beginning of humanity, he perceives that this world is exercised by alternating good and evil, [Note: “This world.” The third Florentine manuscript has *hunc modum* (“this pattern”), incorrectly; the preceding words, “the world and man are governed,” correspond to the present reading.] whoever sees the human race through himself and in himself. [Note: “Whoever sees through himself and in himself, and so forth.” That is, whoever recognizes both that he himself is a human being, endowed with that weakness which cannot be absent from the human race, and that other human beings are like himself and of the same nature as himself. The third Leiden edition has: “whoever sees through himself and through himself—the human race” [*quis per se, atque per se h. g.*].]

Then, since we are taught that sin and the punishment of sin began with the first man; and further, since even those [Note: “Those who begin from the intervening periods.” The Augsburg edition has *ipsi* (“they themselves”), and so forth; the third Leiden edition has *isti* (“those”).] who begin from the intervening periods, although they have nowhere remembered the earlier events, [Note: “Nowhere.” The third Florentine manuscript has *numquam* (“never”).] have described nothing but wars and disasters—which wars must be called nothing other than evils tending toward one another; [Note: “Tending.” Hittorp’s edition and others have *urguentia* (“pressing”); but he calls evils ‘tending toward one another,’ just as above he says that this world is exercised through alternating goods and evils.] but such evils as then [9] existed, just as they exist now, insofar as they exist, [Note: “Such.” The second and third Florentine manuscripts, the fourth Leiden manuscript, and my manuscript read “evils of this world.” But ‘such evils’ are those which tend toward one another.] [Note: “Insofar as they exist.” The final word has dropped out of some editions and manuscripts; in these, too, one reads “to disclose the beginning of that matter” instead of “for us to disclose that matter,” and so forth.] are without doubt either manifest sins or hidden punishments of sins—what prevents us from disclosing the beginning of that matter whose body they have set forth, and from showing that those earlier ages, which we shall demonstrate to have been far more numerous, endured similar miseries, even if by the thinnest account? [Note: “Those earlier ages.” The later word is absent from the fourth Leiden edition. *Monstravimus* (“we have shown”) appears instead of *monstrabimus* (“we shall show”) in the second and fourth Leiden editions, the third Florentine manuscript, and the Augsburg edition; it is a common scribal error.]

I am therefore about to speak of the period from the foundation of the world to the foundation of the City, and thereafter to the rule of Caesar and the birth of Christ, from which time the empire remained over the world under the power of the City; [Note: “The empire remained.” The Utrecht edition, Perizonius, and the third Leiden edition have *mansit imperium* (“the empire remained”).] or even down to our own days, [Note: “Down to the days.” The second Leiden manuscript has *ad dies* (“to the days”).] [Note: “Insofar as I shall have been able to devote myself to knowing it.” All the standard editions and manuscripts preserve *vocare* (“to call”), but the most learned Palmerius advised me to change that inept word to the very Latin *vacare* (“to devote oneself”); because of his outstanding judgment in restoring authors, I gladly followed him, and, if I have not restored Orosius’s own word, I have at least restored the meaning. LAUTIUS.—*Ad cognitionem* (“to knowledge”) is deleted by Perizonius.] insofar as I shall have been able to devote myself to knowing it, [Note: “I shall have been able to devote myself.” Lautius praises Palmerius’s ingenuity. But the first and Augsburg editions had already printed this reading, which is further confirmed by the second, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, Perizonius, Utrecht, my manuscript, and the Florentine manuscripts: the third clearly reads it, while in the second *vacare* is written above *vocare*.] I deem it necessary, as I am about to display from a watchtower the struggles of the human race and the world, as though burning with evils in its several parts and set alight by the torch of desire, [Note: “Struggles.” The second Florentine manuscript has *conflictationem* (“struggle”); the fourth Leiden manuscript has *conflictiones* (“conflicts”). The third Leiden manuscript has *divisas* (“divided”) for *diversas* (“several”), and, like the fourth, deletes *malis* (“with evils”) in “the world burning with evils.”] [Note: “From a watchtower.” The Augsburg edition, Perizonius manuscript, and the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts have *specula*; the third has *speculo*.] first to set forth the earth itself, inhabited by the human race, as it was divided into three parts by our ancestors, [Note: “Divided three ways.” The Utrecht edition and the third Leiden edition have *trifarie distributum* (“divided in three ways”); the second Leiden edition has *trifarie distributus* (“divided three ways”). The third Florentine manuscript, my manuscript, and the first and Augsburg editions support the reading *distributum trifariam* (“divided into three parts”). The second manuscript has *multifariam distributum* (“divided into many parts”), with *trifariam* (“into three parts”) written above it. Accordingly, all these witnesses also write *determinatum* (“determined”) below.] and then to explain it as marked out by regions and provinces, so that, [Note: “More easily.” The second Leiden edition and the Utrecht edition have *facile* (“easily”).] when local disasters of wars and diseases are displayed, [Note: “Will be displayed.” The fourth Leiden edition has *ostenduntur* (“are displayed”).] those who are devoted to study may acquire knowledge not only of events and times, [Note: “But also knowledge of places.” In the third Leiden manuscript the following rubric is found: “[Col. 0672D] The Preface ends. The first book of the Histories of Saint Orosius, *De Ormesta mundi* [‘On the Ormesta of the world’], begins.” In the Perizonian manuscript, the following rubric is likewise prefixed to the next chapter as though it were the first: “The first book of Paul Orosius, priest, of the Histories *De Hormesta [superscribed: Orchestra] mundi* [‘On the Hormesta of the world’], against the Pagans, begins.” The third Florentine manuscript likewise reads: “The book of Orosius on the Calamities of the World begins.” On the title of this book, and on whether one should read *Orchestra*, *Ormesta*, or *Hormesta*, see our Preface.] but also of places.

**10. CHAPTER II.** Our ancestors divided the world into three parts; he gives a very concise description of their position, regions, and more celebrated places.

[Col. 0672B]

[Note: [Col. 0672D] “Our predecessors.” The later word is deleted by Perizonius, whose same manuscript soon reads “and its parts,” with the intervening word “three” removed. The reader should be advised that this entire chapter of Orosius, which treats the division of the world, is found almost verbatim among certain excerpts repeatedly published in a little work entitled *The Cosmography of Aethicus*.]

Our predecessors held the whole globe of the earth, enclosed by Ocean’s rim, to be three-sided; and they called its three parts Asia, Europe, and Africa, although some thought that there were two—namely Asia and then Africa—to be reckoned as part of Europe. [Note: [Col. 0673B] “To be reckoned as part of Europe.” The old editions—the first, the Augustan, and the Venetian—give the accusative and read *in Europam accipiendam* (“to be reckoned into Europe”). The learned man and my very dear friend Henricus Cannegieter has shown at length, in his dissertation on Avienus, chapter 19, pp. 300–301, that ancient writers used the preposition *in* indiscriminately with the accusative and ablative, generally consulting the ear. In Aethicus’s *Cosmography* either another reading or an interpretation of the common text occurs, for there it reads: “They determined that Africa should be added to Europe.” Shortly afterward the first Leiden manuscript, whose leaf is damaged from the words “Ninus, the great (as they say) king,” begins again here, namely with the words “Asia in three parts.” For *putarint* (“they may have thought”), the second Leiden manuscript has *putarent* (“they thought”).]

Asia, surrounded on three sides by the Ocean, extends across the whole breadth of the eastern region. [Note: [Col. 0673C] “Across the breadth.” Perizonius and Meus have *transfusi plagam* (“the breadth poured across”).] [Note: [Col. 0673B] “Asia in three parts.” Orosius follows Pomponius Mela, who writes of Asia in Book I, chapter 2: “The Ocean touches it on three sides, differing in name as it differs in location: the Eastern Ocean on the east, the Indian on the south, and the Scythian on the north.”] Toward the west, on its right-hand side, it touches Europe, which begins beneath the northern axis; [Note: [Col. 0673C] “On its right.” Meus and the third Leiden manuscript have *ad dextram sui* (“on its right”).] while on the left it leaves Africa. [Note: [Col. 0673C] “It touches Europe.” The third Florentine manuscript has *contrahit*, as though it wished to read “it draws together,” or *contra agit Europam*, “it confronts Europe,” instead of “it meets Europe”; or, as Pomponius Mela says in Book I, chapter 2, “it comes to meet the approaching [continent].” Yet I do not think Orosius wrote this in that form. He properly says that Europe, beginning beneath the northern axis, is touched by Asia; Africa, on the other hand, is left on the left, since Europe is narrow toward the north where it joins Asia, whereas Africa extends far away on the left, as is clear to anyone looking at maps depicting the position of the lands. Aethicus’s *Cosmography* agrees with the common reading.]

Beneath Egypt and Syria it has the sea which we generally call the Mediterranean, or Great, Sea. Europe begins, as I have said, beneath the northern region, at the river Tanais, [Note: [Col. 0673C] “As I have said, beneath the northern region.” These words are absent from the Ulm manuscript and the first and Augustan editions; these editions have *septentrionalis* (“northern”) for *septentrionis* and read “Europe begins [in] the northern [region],” as though this were opposed to what follows somewhat later, “the western [ocean] of Europe in Spain.” In Aethicus, with words slightly altered, one reads: “Europe begins beneath the northern region at the river Tanais,” etc.] where the Riphaean Mountains, turned away from the Sarmatian Ocean, pour forth the river Tanais. [Note: [Col. 0673C] “But on the left.” The final word is deleted by the Ulm manuscript and by the first and Augustan editions.] As it passes beyond the altars and boundaries of Alexander the Great, situated within the territory of the Roxolani, it enlarges the Maeotian marshes. [Note: [Col. 0673D] “Where the Riphaean Mountains.” For *qua* (“where”), the Ulm manuscript and the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts have *quo* (“by which”); shortly afterward the third has *infundunt* (“pour into”) and then *secundas oras* (“secondary shores”) instead of *aras* (“altars”), and *fundunt* (“pour forth”). The second and third Florentine manuscripts, as well as the first and Augustan editions, read *fluvium fundunt* (“pour forth the river”).] [Note: [Col. 0673D] “Within the territory of the Roxolani.” In this chapter, which gives a brief description of the world, there are several barbarous names not easily found in other writers. We have therefore thought that the authority of ancient books should be given considerable weight. In the present passage, however, we have retained the printed reading *in Roxolanorum finibus* (“within the territory of the Roxolani”), although the manuscripts have *Rhobascorum*, as others have also noted. The second and third Florentine manuscripts, the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, Meus, the Ulm manuscript, the old editions, and Aethicus have *Robascorum* or *Rhobascorum*. The second Leiden manuscript has *Robastorum*, as do Perizonius and the Ulm manuscript; the Augustan edition has *rochbaos bascorum*. Shortly afterward the second Florentine manuscript has *finibus situs Meotidas* (“situated at the borders of the Maeotides”); in the margin it gives alternatively *Scithas Meotidasque*, while the third has *fimbria sices Meocidas*.] [Note: [Col. 0674B] “It enlarges the marshes.” The third Leiden manuscript has *augent paludes* (“they enlarge the marshes”), as though the Riphaean Mountains, extended so far by the course of the waters, enlarged the Maeotian marshes.]

The immense overflow of these marshes enters widely into the Euxine Pontus beside the city of Theodosia. [Note: [Col. 0674B] “Overflow.” Aethicus has *inundatio* (“inundation”), a reading confirmed here by my manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0674B] “Theodosia.” Mela lists it among the Cimmerian towns in Book II, chapter 1: “The Satarchae hold the places tending toward the marsh; in the Cimmerian Bosporus are the towns Myrmecion, Panticapaeum, Theodosia, and Hermisium; in the Euxine Sea, and so forth.”] From there, beside Constantinople, long narrow straits are sent out until this sea, which we call the Mediterranean, receives them. [Note: [Col. 0674B] “Long straits are sent out.” That is, “the sea is narrowed over a considerable distance.” The manuscripts and editions that read *emittuntur* (“are sent out”) are the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, Perizonius, and Meus; the others read *mittuntur* (“are sent”), which is also preserved in Aethicus’s excerpts. The common text has *longe* (“far”).] [Note: [Col. 0674C] “This sea which we call the Mediterranean.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has *mare quod* (“the sea which”), with *hoc* deleted; the second has *mare hoc Nostrum quod dicimus*; Perizonius has *mare hoc Magnum quod dicimus* (“this Great Sea, as we call it”); the Ulm manuscript has *mare hoc Nostrum quod Magnum dicimus*.]

The western Ocean is the boundary of Europe in Spain, especially where the Pillars of Hercules are seen beside the islands of Gades and the tide of the Ocean is admitted through the straits of the Tyrrhenian Sea. [Note: [Col. 0674C] “Is its boundary.” Certain old editions, such as those of Hittorp and Cervicorn, or Bolswing, read *termino est* (“is a boundary”), as does the second Florentine manuscript, although with the reading found in the third Florentine manuscript and all the other manuscripts and editions, as well as in Aethicus, written above it: *terminus est* (“is the boundary”). The third Leiden manuscript presents what follows thus: “and especially where, beside the islands of Gades, the flood of the Ocean is sent through the straits of the Tyrrhenian Sea.”]

The beginning of Africa is at the borders of Egypt and the city of Alexandria, where the city of Paraetonium is situated upon this Great Sea, which washes between all the regions and lands. [Note: [Col. 0674C] “Paraetonium.” The third Florentine manuscript has *Parentorium*, the second, as well as the Augustan edition, *Parethonio*, and Aethicus’s excerpts *Partheno*.] [Note: [Col. 0674C] “Upon this Great Sea.” Since this is found thus in Aethicus and nearly all the manuscripts agree in reading it, I do not know why the editions transpose the words to *mare hoc* (“this sea”). For *interluit* (“washes between”), the second Leiden manuscript has *interfluit* (“flows between”), as do the third Florentine and the Ulm manuscripts.]

From there, through the places which the inhabitants call Catabathmon, not far from the camp of Alexander the Great, and above Lake Caleartium, it proceeds beside the borders of the Avasitae, crosses the Ethiopian deserts, and reaches the southern Ocean. [Note: [Col. 0674D] “From there through the places.” The third and fourth Leiden manuscripts, together with the first and Augustan editions, prefer *inde* (“from there”). For *Catabathmon*, those editions have *Catabathynon*, the Ulm manuscript *Cathapatmon*, and the third Florentine *Chatabitinum*, in which *a Chaxitre* is read instead of *castris* (“camp”).] [Note: [Col. 0674D] “Above Lake Caleartium.” Gerard Bolswing, who corrected Hittorp’s first edition from ancient books, noted from them the readings *Alearsum* and *Chalearsum*. In the manuscripts we found *Halearzum*, *Calearsum*, and *Caleartum*. FABRICIUS. —I too found great variety in the manuscripts: the second Florentine has *Calearzum*, the third and Meus *Chalearcum*, the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts *Calearsum*, the Ulm manuscript *Helearzum*, Perizonius *Calearzarum*, the Augustan edition *Leazarum*, and Aethicus *Galearum*. Yet the first edition preserves *Caleartium*, as do all the Venetian editions.] [Note: [Col. 0674D] “The borders of the upper peoples.” The second Florentine manuscript has *superiora fine* (“the upper regions as a boundary”) in the margin, and *superiores fines* (“the borders of the upper peoples”).]

[Note: [Col. 0675B] “Of the Avasitae.” The first edition and the Venetian editions have *Anasitarum*, and this is also found in the Ulm and Perizonian manuscripts. The first and third Leiden manuscripts have *Ausitarum*.]

The western boundaries of Africa are the same as those of Europe, namely the mouths of the Gaditanian strait. Its farthest boundary is Mount Atlas and the islands called the Fortunate Islands. [Note: [Col. 0675B] “Crossing it transversely.” The third Leiden manuscript has *missa transversum*, with *in* deleted; the fourth has *emissa in transversum* (“sent across transversely”).] [Note: [Col. 0675B] “And since I have briefly given.” In Aethicus’s *Cosmography*, p. 724 of Gronovius’s edition, at the end of Mela’s work, it reads: “We have briefly described the divisions of the three parts among themselves; but, so that nothing may be lacking for complete instruction, I shall also indicate the regions, situations, and boundaries of the provinces of the parts themselves, so that the reader may recognize everything without tedium, or even the number of the peoples who dwell there. Asia has, from its central front toward the east, etc.” I have cited this to show that the section of the *Cosmography* published under the name of Aethicus was drawn from Orosius, with a few alterations. I think that this work was written later than Orosius’s time.]

And since I have briefly given the general divisions of the threefold world, I shall also indicate the regions of the several parts, as I promised. Asia has, at the middle of its eastern front, in the Eastern Ocean, the mouths of the river Ganges, and on the left the promontory Caligardamna; [Note: [Col. 0675B] “On the left.” The Perizonian manuscript has *in sinistro* (“on the left”).] [Note: [Col. 0675C] “The promontory Caligardamna.” Thus in the old manuscripts, whereas the printed editions read *Calligicum*. FABRICIUS. —The second Florentine manuscript has *Caligar damana*, the third, written together, *Caligardamana*. The same form occurs in Fabricius’s earlier editions and the Augustan edition, as well as in the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, the Ulm and Perizonian manuscripts. The second Leiden manuscript has *Caligardama*, Meus *Caligardamnen*, and the earliest edition *Caligardamanam*. Aethicus’s *Cosmography* has *Calidardam*. Vincent of Beauvais has *Taligardamana*, with the initial C transferred to the following word *Taprobane*, which he spells *Caprobana*. In Vincent’s *Speculum Historiale*, Book V, chapter 47, an excerpt from Orosius on the situation of Asia occurs, beginning “Asia at the middle” and continuing “to the many other inhabited islands.” The Venetian editions, Hittorp, and Bolswing have *Calligicum*, which they unquestionably took from manuscripts, since the Venetian editions—at least the first, for the others follow it—were printed from manuscripts. It therefore seems that *Calligicum* is corrupt for *Colligicum*, for which Pliny too has *Coliacum* in Book VI, chapter 22. As Christoph Cellarius observed in Volume II of *Ancient Geography*, or *Notice of the Ancient World*, p. 877, Greek writers call this promontory Κῶρυ ἄκρον καὶ Κολλίγικον (“the Cory headland and Colligicum”).]

Beneath it, toward the Eurus, lies the island Taprobane. [Note: [Col. 0675D] “Beneath which lies.” The Venetian editions have *cui sumanet* (“beneath which lies”), a form also found in the first edition.] [Note: [Col. 0675D] “Taprobane.” All the Leiden manuscripts have *Taprobrana* here and below. Most learned authorities agree that this is the island now commonly called Ceylon; see Christoph Cellarius’s *Notice of the Ancient World*, Volume II, pp. 876–877.] From it the Indian Ocean begins to be called by that name. On the right it has the Imai Mountains, where the Caucasus ends, and the promontory Samara. [Note: [Col. 0675D] “The Imai Mountains.” The old edition, the first edition, the Venetian editions, Hittorp, and Bolswing have *Emodos montes* (“the Emodian Mountains”); the Augustan edition has *Tinavi montis*; Vincent of Beauvais *Timani montis*. The second Florentine manuscript has *Inmavi montis*, and the third has *montis* in the sea. The Ulm manuscript has *ima in montium*, Perizonius and Meus *Imani montis*, and all the Leiden manuscripts *Immavi montis*. In all these, *montis* is written instead of *montes* according to ancient usage, or *jugum* (“range”) should be supplied, as in Aethicus’s *Cosmography*, where it reads: “on the right—or from the right—it has the mountain range of the Imai.” Pliny teaches in Book VI, chapter 17, that Imaus is joined to Emodus and the other ranges: “Imaus, Emodus, Parapamisus, and Caucasus are joined together; from them India descends into an immense plain resembling Egypt.” He also says that the promontory of Emodus is called Imanus.] [Note: [Col. 0676B] “Samara.” Some read *Samara*, including Vincent of Beauvais and Aethicus; this is confirmed by the second and third Florentine manuscripts, except that the latter has *Somora*. The first Leiden manuscript, Perizonius, Meus, and the Augustan edition retain *Samaram*; the first edition and the Ulm manuscript do likewise. Hittorp and Bolswing prefer *Samarae*; the second Leiden manuscript has *Samarata*, and the third *Samarata*. Those who read *Samara* take it as the neuter plural accusative.] To the north of it lie the mouths of the river Octorogorra, from which the ocean is called the Seric Ocean. [Note: [Col. 0676C] “To the north of which lie.” Aethicus departs from the common reading, for he has: “which lies to the north, at the mouths,” and so forth.] [Note: [Col. 0676C] “Octorogorra.” Vincent of Beauvais has *Ortorogortae*; Aethicus’s *Cosmography* has *Octacordis* or *Octocordis*; the Augustan edition *Ottoroborrae*. All the manuscripts and the remaining editions have either *Ottorogorrae* or *Octorogorrae*. Cellarius lists Octorocorrhae beside the Emodian and Seric Mountains in Volume II of *Ancient Geography*, p. 889. Some editions and manuscripts have *Syricus* through the common error, instead of *Sericus*.]

Within these boundaries lies India. On the west it has the river Indus, which is received by the Red Sea; [Note: [Col. 0676C] “On the west.” The Ulm manuscript has *ad occidentem* (“toward the west”). Vincent of Beauvais changes the river Indus into the river Melus.] to the north, Mount Caucasus; the remainder, as I have said, is bounded by the Eastern and Indian Oceans. [Note: [Col. 0676C] “Which is received by the Red Sea.” Perizonius more smoothly transposes the words to *mari Rubro* (“by the Red Sea”). Vincent has: “which runs into the Red Sea.”] [Note: [Col. 0676C] “The remainder, as I have said.” That is, the remainder of India. The first, second, and third Leiden manuscripts read: “the remainder, as I have said, is bounded by the Eastern and Indian Oceans.” Hittorp and Bolswing, inserting the words “the remaining part,” have: “the remaining part, as I have said, is bounded by the Eastern and Indian Oceans.” The common reading is supported by the second and third Florentine manuscripts, the fourth Leiden manuscript, Perizonius, the Ulm manuscript, and Meus.]

It contains forty-four peoples, apart from the island of Taprobane, which has ten cities, and apart from the many other inhabited islands. [Note: [Col. 0676D] “The many other inhabited islands.” Thus in the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts and in all the other manuscripts except the second Leiden and the Ulm manuscripts, which have “the remaining inhabited islands, very many.” Hittorp and Bolswing also prefer *quam plurimis* (“very many”), contrary to all the other old witnesses.]

From the river Indus, which is in the east, to the river Tigris, which is in the west, these are the regions: [Note: [Col. 0676D] “Which is in the east.” The first Leiden manuscript deletes *est* (“is”), and shortly afterward, together with the Augustan edition, reads “which is in the west,” not badly.] Aracosia, Parthia, Assyria, Persia, and Media, mountainous and rugged in their terrain. [Note: [Col. 0676D] “Persia.” Many manuscripts—including the second and third Florentine, the first, second, and fourth Leiden, and the Ulm manuscripts—together with Bolswing’s, the Augustan, Venetian, and first editions, read *Persida* instead of *Persia*, as I think, in accordance with the form found in my manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0677B] “Mountainous and rugged.” The third Leiden manuscript, Meus, and Perizonius have *montuoso* (“mountainous”), as does Bolswing’s edition with the Venetian editions. Both forms are used by Latin writers. Thus, alongside *montoso atque aspero* (“mountainous and rugged”), one finds *montosis asperis* (“rugged mountains”) together in Pliny, Harduin’s edition, Volume II, p. 401; elsewhere, however, *montuosis partibus* (“mountainous regions”) and *montuosa planis* (“mountainous [regions] with plains”) are preferable, in the same work, pp. 108 and 49. Pliny himself used *montosa* in Volume II, p. 3, or Book XVI, chapter 5: “already in mountainous and level places.”]

These regions have Mount Caucasus to the north, and to the south the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. [Note: [Col. 0677B] “These have to the north.” The third Leiden manuscript, Meus, and the Ulm manuscript refer this only to Media and read: “This has to the north,” etc.] In their midst are the principal rivers Hydaspes and Arbis. [Note: [Col. 0677B] “In their midst.” Meus has *in medio sui* (“in its midst”).] [Note: [Col. 0677B] “Hydaspes and Arbis.” Aethicus’s *Cosmography* has *Hydraspem et Carbin*. The Augustan edition has *Indaspen et Arbimin*. The second Florentine has *Ydaspen et Arbin*, corrected by another hand to *Arben*; the third has *Iadasper et Arbra*. The second Leiden manuscript, together with the Augustan, Venetian, and first editions, has *Hydaspen et Arabin* or *Arabim*; the third Leiden has *Ara Arbim*. Cellarius, *Ancient Geography*, Volume II, p. 849, shows that this river, which is in Gedrosia, is written in various ways by ancient authors: *Arbin, Arabin, Arabium, Artabin,* and *Artabium*.]

There are thirty-two peoples in these regions. But in general it is called Parthia, although Sacred Scripture often calls the whole [region] Media. [Note: [Col. 0677C] “Sacred Scripture.” The Augustan edition has *scripturae sacrae*, since these words are frequently exchanged in the manuscripts and old editions. Shortly afterward the same edition reads “from the river Tigris, therefore.” Somewhat later, the word *saepe* (“often”) is absent from the third Florentine manuscript; that manuscript reads *montem Taurum* (“Mount Taurus”) instead of *montem Tauri*.]

From the river Tigris to the river Euphrates lies Mesopotamia, beginning in the north between Mount Taurus and the Caucasus. [Note: [Col. 0677C] “To its south.” The third Florentine manuscript has *cui a meridie* (“to it from the south”).] To the south of it come Babylonia, then Chaldaea, and finally Arabia Eudaemon, which extends eastward in a narrow strip of land between the Persian Gulf and the Arabian Gulf. There are twenty-eight peoples in these regions. [Note: [Col. 0677C] “Twenty-eight.” We inserted *et* (“and”) from the better manuscripts. The fourth Leiden manuscript has twenty-four; in the third Leiden manuscript the latter word is deleted.] [Note: [Col. 0677C] “Arabia Eudaemon.” The first edition of all establishes the passage thus: “finally Arabia, and then that region between the Persian Gulf…” But the manuscripts and the Augustan edition support *Eudaemon*, which has been deleted.]

From the river Euphrates, which is in the east, to the Mediterranean Sea, which is in the west, and then from the north—that is, from the city of Dacusa, situated on the border of Cappadocia and Armenia, not far from the place where the Euphrates rises—to Egypt and the extremity of the Arabian Gulf, which lies to the south, Syria extends westward from the Red Sea—that is, from the Ocean—in a long and narrow belt thickly set with rocks and islands. [Note: [Col. 0677D] “From the city of Dacusa.” Thus we have established the text from the same books, instead of the common forms *Dascuta* and *Dagusa*. Pliny calls this town *Dascusa* in Book VI, chapter 24, and Book VI, chapter 19. FABRICIUS. —The name of this city is written variously not only in Orosius’s manuscripts but also in those of other writers, as may be seen in Cellarius’s *Ancient Geography*, Volume II, p. 353, and in the notes of the distinguished Petrus Wesseling on the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, p. 209. Among Orosius’s manuscripts, *Dacusa* is clearly given by the second Florentine, the Perizonian manuscript, and Meus; *Dotusa* by the third Florentine; *Decusa* by the first, second, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts and the Ulm manuscript; Aethicus’s *Cosmography* has *Adcusa*. The first edition also prefers *Dacusa*, as does the Augustan edition. All the Venetian editions, Hittorp, and Bolswing—or Cervicorn—have *Dascuta*, with *Dagusa* noted in the margin as an alternative. Fabricius’s editions have *Dacusa*, which he defends in his notes. The names of cities, especially less famous ones, are found written—and in antiquity pronounced—in more than one way, as we recently demonstrated from the example of Saxia, a Cretan city, in the *Collection of Writings on the True Pronunciation of the Greek Language*.]

[Note: [Col. 0678B] “And the extremity of the Arabian Gulf.” The Venetian editions have *et ad*, and so forth; the first edition of all has “and to the extremity of the Gulf of Arabia.” Shortly afterward the third Leiden manuscript deletes *est* and reads “which lies to the south.”] [Note: [Col. 0678B] “Crowded.” The Augustan edition has *creberrimis* (“very crowded”); somewhat later the second Florentine has *ostenditur* (“is shown”) instead of *extenditur* (“extends”).] Syria, which is thus generally named, possesses the greatest provinces: Commagene, Phoenicia, and Palestine, apart from the Saracens and Nabataeans, whose peoples number twelve. [Note: [Col. 0678B] “Syria extends.” Up to this point all the editions have been disfigured by a very serious error arising from bad punctuation, of the kind also frequently found in manuscripts. In all of them a major pause is placed after *extenditur* (“extends”), although the sense should not be separated there and is incomplete unless the word is joined with *Syria*, as I found it in my excellent parchment manuscript. The passage had previously been read: “from the Ocean it extends westward. Syria is generally so called, having the greatest provinces,” and so forth. The first edition and the others read similarly, except that the Augustan edition more correctly restores *habetque* (“and possesses”), a reading confirmed by the four Leiden manuscripts and the Ulm manuscript, which have *habetque maximas provincias*. The sole Perizonian manuscript, although paper and recent, is often better than many parchment and older manuscripts; it improves the passage by inserting *quae sic* (“which is thus”) after *Syria*. Accordingly, relying on these supports, we have established the passage as: “Syria extends, which is thus generally called, and possesses the greatest provinces,” although the second and third Florentine manuscripts and Meus have *habens* (“having”) with the same sense.]

[Note: [Col. 0678C] “Commagene.” The first edition, Hittorp, and Cervicorn read *Commagenen*, closer to the Greek spelling. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts consistently have *Commagenam*, as does the Augustan edition and Aethicus’s *Cosmography*. The first edition and the twelve Venetian editions transpose the final words.] In the head of Syria lies Cappadocia, which has Armenia to the east, Asia to the west, and to the north the Themiscyrian plains and the Cimmerian Sea. [Note: [Col. 0678D] “Themiscyrian.” The manuscripts contain, as often, monstrous variations: *chemis cyrios* in the second Florentine; *Themisciros* in the third; *Themisterios* in the Ulm and second Leiden manuscripts; *Themistrios* in Perizonius; and shortly afterward *Cimbricum* (“Cimbrian”) instead of *Cimmericum* in the first Leiden manuscript. The Themiscyrian plains—written with *y* rather than *i*, contrary to Fabricius—are well known among Greek geographers and writers for their fertility.] To the south it has Mount Taurus, beneath which lie Cilicia and Isauria, as far as the Gulf of Issus, which faces the island of Cyprus. [Note: [Col. 0678D] “As far as the Gulf of Issus.” Hittorp and Cervicorn, or Bolswing, have *usque ad Cilicinum sinum* (“as far as the Cilician Gulf”). The first, Augustan, and Fabrician editions have *usque ad Cilicum sinum*, as do the second and third Florentine manuscripts and all the Leiden manuscripts, Meus, and Perizonius; the Ulm manuscript changes nothing except deleting *ad*. The error is so old that it is also found in Aethicus’s *Cosmography*. Yet the text should be written as I have restored it, *usque ad Issicum sinum* (“as far as the Gulf of Issus”). The Venetian codices lead us to this reading; the first edition printed in that city in 1483 has *Isicus*, which later editions there corrected to *Isicum*, recognizing it as either a scribal or typographical error.]

The region of Asia—or, more properly, Asia Minor—apart from its eastern portion, which projects toward Cappadocia and Syria, is surrounded on every side by the sea: on the north by the Pontus Euxinus, on the west by the Propontis and the Hellespont, and on the south by the Mediterranean Sea, where Mount Olympus is located. [Note: [Col. 0679B] “The region of Asia.” The second and fourth Leiden manuscripts have *Asia regio* (“the region of Asia”); the first and third have *Asia vero regio* (“the region of Asia, indeed”). All the others, together with Aethicus’s *Cosmography*, support the common reading.] [Note: [Col. 0679B] “Which advances toward Cappadocia.” The second Florentine has *quae* instead of *qua*; Perizonius has *et Syriam* rather than *Syriamque*.]

Lower Egypt has Syria Palestina to the east, Libya to the west, the Mediterranean Sea to the north, and to the south the mountain called Climax, Upper Egypt, and the river Nile. [Note: [Col. 0679B] “To the south.” Perizonius has *ad meridiem* (“toward the south”). Shortly afterward the third Florentine has “there is Mount Olympus,” although the words had been absent from the text and are supplied in the margin.] [Note: [Col. 0679B] “Climax.” The third Florentine has *Dimax*. In Fabricius’s editions it is incorrectly written *Clymax*, contrary to the Greek origin of the name, derived from steps or ladders. Greek writers call this mountain Κλίμακα (*Klimaka*), famous for the narrowness of its passes, and place it not far from Phaselis, the last city of Lycia toward the borders of Pamphylia, as Polybius, Book I, chapter 72, Plutarch in his *Life of Alexander*, p. 674, and others state.]

The Nile, which seems to emerge from the shore of the Red Sea where that sea begins, at a place called the emporium of Mossylon. [Note: [Col. 0679C] “Which begins from the side of the sea.” In former times *littore* (“shore”) was read here, which is a very dry expression indeed. LAUTIUS.] [Note: [Col. 0679C] “From the shore.” Lautius could not accept this reading and therefore judged that it should be changed. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts and editions unanimously preserve it. It is certain that the sources of the Nile were formerly unknown, and that various, even absurd, opinions about the origin of this famous river were consequently transmitted. Among them this may have been one: that the sources emerged from the shore of the Red Sea where it begins, near Mossylon. It is certainly neither novel nor unknown in our own times for springs to issue in a sandy shore, or even beneath the waters at the shore, and to burst forth and boil up with great force. Moreover, since Orosius names Mossylon, its position beside the sea seems to support the old reading, so that some of the ancients may have believed that the sources of the Nile emerged not “from the side” but “from the shore” at which Mossylon was situated, where the Red Sea begins.]

It then flows for a long distance toward the west, forming in its midst an island called Meroe; finally, bending toward the north and increased by seasonal floods, it waters the flatlands of Egypt. [Note: [Col. 0680B] “Toward the north.” The second and third Florentine manuscripts have *a septentrione* (“from the north”); for *tempestivis* (“seasonal”), the first and Venetian editions have *tempestivisque* (“and seasonal”).] [Note: [Col. 0680C] “It waters the plains of Egypt.” The second Florentine manuscript has *inrigat*, and the Augustan edition *irrigat*; for *plana* (“plains”), the second Leiden manuscript has *plagam* (“region”) and the Ulm manuscript *plaga*.] [Note: [Col. 0680B] “Forming an island.” Thus the Augustan edition and certain manuscripts; others have *faciens insulam* (“forming an island”). The second Leiden manuscript has *dein* instead of *deinde* (“then”).] [Note: [Col. 0679D] “The emporium of Mossylon.” The correct form of the name of this promontory and emporium at the beginning of the Red Sea, where the ancients testify that cinnamon was customarily brought, is *Mossylon*, *Mosylon*, or rather *Moisylon*, as it is written in the third Leiden manuscript, according to the origin of the name. Aethicus’s *Cosmography* and Pliny, Book VI, chapter 29, Volume I of Harduin’s edition, pp. 342–343, give the following forms: “The Mossylic promontory and harbor, to which cinnamon is brought. To this point Sesostris led his army.” Shortly afterward: “Juba wishes the Atlantic Sea to begin at the Mossylic promontory.” Harduin notes that it is now called Cape Guardafui. Aethicus’s *Cosmography*, p. 725, has: “To the south, Mount Climax, Upper Egypt, and the river Nile, which seems to emerge from the shore of the Red Sea where that sea begins, at the place called the emporium of Mossylon.” Some manuscripts have *Moissylon* there, and the name was also corrupted in various ways in Orosius’s manuscripts: the second Florentine has *Mossilonporium*, with *Monstilonporium* written above it; the first and second Leiden manuscripts, as well as the Ulm manuscript, have *Mosselon*; the Augustan edition has *Moysilon*. Some manuscripts and editions write *Mosilon*, correctly with *y* in Perizonius, since Ptolemy calls it Μόσυλον ἄκρον καὶ ἐμπόριον (“the promontory and emporium of Mosylon”). A notable reading follows in the second Leiden and Ulm manuscripts, which append after these words *id est ortus aquae* (“that is, the source of the water”), explaining the word *Mosylon*. This strongly confirms the old and consistent manuscript reading *de littore* (“from the shore”), not *de latere* (“from the side”), against Lautius; for if the emporium received its name from the rising of waters, and if it was situated on the shore beside the sea, some could have believed that the sources of the Nile were born there from the shore.]

Some writers say that this river has its source not far from Atlas, is immediately swallowed up by the sands, then, after a short interval, bursts forth from an immense lake, and from there flows as far as the Ocean, eastward through the Ethiopian deserts, and, bending again to the left, descends toward Egypt. [Note: [Col. 0680C] “Is swallowed up by the sands.” Perizonius has *ab arenis mergi* (“is swallowed up by the sands”).] [Note: [Col. 0680C] “Immense.” Meus has *et vastissimo* (“and immense”); the second Leiden manuscript has *faustissimo* (“most favorable”).] [Note: [Col. 0680C] “Through the Ethiopian deserts.” The second Leiden and Ulm manuscripts have *Aethiopiae deserta* (“the deserts of Ethiopia”); shortly afterward the second and third Florentine manuscripts have *rursumque* (“and again”).] [Note: [Col. 0680C] “To the left.” The first, second, and third Leiden manuscripts add *partem* (“side”).] It is indeed true that there is a great river of this kind, with such a source and such a course, and that it truly produces all the marvels of the Nile. [Note: [Col. 0680C] “It produces all the marvels of the Nile.” The first edition has *tot tantaque monstra gignat* (“produces so many and such great marvels”), as do the Venetian editions. Aethicus’s *Cosmography* reads: “It is indeed clear that there is such a manifest and great river, with such a source and such a course that it is understood to be the Nile; for it produces marvels and other similar things.” Orosius here reports the opinion of those who followed the view of Juba the Younger, king of Mauretania and a distinguished historian. Juba had sought the sources of the Nile in Lower Mauretania and Mount Atlas. Pliny, Book V, chapter 9, or Volume I, p. 255, writes: “As King Juba was able to discover, it has its origin in a mountain of Lower Mauretania, not far from the Ocean, immediately stagnating in a lake called the Nilides. Fish called *alabetae*, *coracini*, and *siluri* are found there. A crocodile is also seen there today, dedicated by him at Caesarea in the temple of Isis as evidence of this.” He then gives a vivid description of that river, not unlike Orosius’s. A passage of Ammianus Marcellinus is also usefully cited by Harduin in *Emendationes*, 31, p. 295, from Book XXII, p. 229: “King Juba, relying on the text of Punic books, explains that it rises from a certain mountain situated in Mauretania and overlooking the Ocean; and he says that this was revealed by the fact that fish, plants, and beasts resembling those found in the Nile are produced throughout those marshes.”]

The barbarians near the source call it Dara; the other inhabitants call it Nuchul. [Note: [Col. 0680D] “Certainly near the source.” With the help of the Cologne manuscript I have corrected this passage. It formerly read: *quem utique proprie* (“which they properly…”), though this is clearly inappropriate, as what follows proves: “but the other inhabitants call it Nuchul.” Thus “near the source,” that is, where it arises. LAUTIUS. —On the contrary, it had been read in this way long before Lautius, who consulted only Fabricius’s editions: in the first edition, the Augustan edition, the Venetian editions, Hittorp, Cervicorn, and all the ancient books, as well as in the manuscripts, which often write *ppe* in their customary fashion, except that the first and fourth Leiden manuscripts have *propemodum* (“almost”). I scarcely know how *proprie* (“properly”) entered Fabricius’s editions. The second Florentine has *utice* instead of *utique*, as though it wished to read “of Utica”; but that city, near Carthage, is extremely far from the source of the Nile, which Juba sought near Atlas in Mauretania.] [Note: [Col. 0681B] “They call it Dara.” Those barbarians who are near or inhabit the source—as must be understood—call this river, or the beginning of its course, Dara; those who dwell farther away, that is, the other inhabitants, call it Nuchul. Aethicus likewise has *Dara* and *Nuchul*. The manuscripts vary: the second Florentine has *Nehul*; the third and Meus *Nuhul*; the fourth Leiden, the first edition, the Augustan edition, and the Venetian editions *Nuhul*; the second Leiden *Nichul*; the Ulm manuscript omits the words “but the other inhabitants,” beginning with N.] But this river, in the territory of a people called Libya Aegyptia, not far from the river which, as we have said, bursts forth from the shore of the Red Sea, is swallowed up in an immense lake. [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Nuchul.” The ending proves that this is an African name; I think that, by inflection into the usage of the Latin language, it became *Nilides*, as it is read in Pliny at the cited passage. Aethicus also has *Dara* and *Nuchul*, though the manuscripts vary. The second Florentine has *Nehul*, the third and Meus *Nuhul*, the fourth Leiden and the old, Augustan, and Venetian editions *Nuhul*, while the second Leiden has *Nichul* and the Ulm manuscript omits the phrase beginning “but the other inhabitants.”] [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Libya Aegyptia.” Two manuscripts have *Libyo Aegyptiae*. Pliny, Book V, chapter 7, has *Libyaegyptii*, and says that they live above the Gaetuli. FABRICIUS. —The land of these peoples is called Libya Aegyptia, and the peoples themselves Libyaegyptians, as though they were Libyans mixed with Egyptians. Harduin notes that they were located west of the Thebaid, where the deserts of Barca and Libya now are, in his note on this passage of Pliny, Book V, chapter 8: “In the inner circuit of Africa, toward the south, and above the Gaetuli, with deserts intervening, the Libyaegyptians are the first inhabitants, followed by the Leucaethiopians.” The second Florentine and Perizonius have *Libyoaegyptiae*. The first, second, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts and the Ulm manuscript have *Libya* or *Libia Aegyptiae*. Three Leiden manuscripts have *vocatur* (“is called”), and since this also occurs in Aethicus’s *Cosmography*, I have adopted that reading. Some of Fabricius’s editions have *Libya Aegyptiis*.]

Unless perhaps it pours forth by a hidden course into the bed of the river that descends from the east. Upper Egypt extends a long distance toward the east; to the north it has the Arabian Gulf, and to the south the Ocean. For it begins in the west from Lower Egypt and is bounded on the east by the Red Sea, where there are twenty-four peoples. [Note: [Col. 0681D] “It is swallowed up.” The Augustan edition has *assumitur* (“is received”); shortly afterward the first edition has *eructet* (“it pours forth”).] [Note: [Col. 0681D] “Toward the east.” The Augustan edition has *ab oriente* (“from the east”), and instead of *ubi* (“where”) has *ibi* (“there”).]

And since we have described the southern part of all Asia, it remains to explain the part that is left, from east to north. Mount Caucasus first rises between the Colchi, who are above the Cimmerian Sea, and the Albani, who are beside the Caspian Sea; [Note: [Col. 0681D] “The southern part.” The second Leiden and Ulm manuscripts delete the latter word, reading simply “we have described the meridian part of all Asia.”] [Note: [Col. 0681D] “As far as the extreme east.” Meus has “as far as the east.” The Augustan edition and]
ms. Flor. tert. “up to the extreme east.” Ultr. deletes only the preceding *primum* (“first”).

As far as the furthest east, there appears to be a single mountain chain, but it bears many names; and many wish this same chain to be regarded as part of Mount Taurus, because in reality Parchoatras, a mountain of Armenia situated between Taurus and Caucasus, is thought to join Taurus with Caucasus. But that this is not so is shown by the Euphrates, which, issuing from the root of Mount Parchoatras and heading southward, cuts off Taurus itself on the left-hand side. Thus the Caucasus itself, between the Colchians and Albanians, where it also has passes, is called Mount Caucasus.

From the Caspian Gates to the Armenian Gates, or to the source of the river Tigris, between Armenia and Iberia, the mountains are called the Acroceraunian Mountains. From the source of the Tigris to the city of Carrhae, [Col. 0683A] between the Massagetae and the Parthians, is Mount Ariobarzanes. From the city of Carrhae to the town of Cathippi, between the Hyrcanians and the Bactrians, is Mount Memarmali, where amomum grows. The next chain is called Mount Parthau. From the town of Cathippi to the village of Saphrim, between the Dahae and Araucae and the Parthyenae, is Mount Oscobares, where the river Ganges rises and laser grows. From the source of the river Ganges to the sources of the river Ottorogorra, which lie to the north, are the mountain-dwellers, the Paropamisadae, and Mount Taurus.

From the sources of Ottorogorra to the city of Ottorogorra, [Col. 0684A] between the Huns, Scythians, and Gandaridae, is Mount Caucasus. Finally, between the Eoae and the Pasiadras is Mount Imaus, where the river Chrysorrhoas and the promontory of Samara reach the eastern ocean. Accordingly, from Mount Imaus—that is, from the lower end of the Caucasus—and along the eastern right-hand side, where the Seric Ocean extends, [Col. 0685A] up to the Boreian promontory and the Boreian River, thence along the Scythian Sea, which lies to the north, to the Caspian Sea, which lies to the west, and to the extent—

[Col. 0682B] **Mount Taurus.** The first edition has *Tauri montes* (“the mountains of Taurus”); Aethicus has *Tauri montem* (“Mount Taurus”).

[Col. 0682B] **Parchoatras.** Strabo has *Parachoatras*, Pliny *Choatras*. Flor. sec. has *Parcho hatras*, but Flor. tert. clearly has *Parchoatras*. Lugd. Bat. pr. has *Parthoatras*, quart. *Parchoastras*, and Meus *Parchoatas*. The remaining witnesses preserve the customary spelling, as do Aethicus and the older printed editions; Hittorp has *Parchoateas*.

[Col. 0682B] **That this is not so.** This is found in Aethicus and in the manuscripts Flor. sec., Lugd. Batt. pr., tert., and quart., as well as in the Augustan edition. Others transpose the words as *ita non esse* (“that it is not so”). Hittorp and Bolsuing have *non ita se habere posse* (“that it cannot be so”).

[Col. 0682B] **Which, from the root.** *Qui radice* (“which [from] the root”) occurs with the Fabrician editions, Flor. sec. and tert., Lugd. Bat. pr., and Periz.; *qui a radice* (“which from the root”) occurs except in Aethicus, Meus, and the Augustan edition. But Lugd. Batt. sec., tert., quart., the remaining editions, and the Mainz edition prefer *qui de radice* (“which from the root”).

[Col. 0682C] **Leaves Taurus out.** Hittorp’s edition inserts *montem* (“the mountain”), followed by Bolsuing; it is absent from the others, as well as from the manuscripts. The Augustan edition, however, changes the sense through punctuation: “It leaves Taurus out. On the right, therefore, is Caucasus itself,” and so forth.

[Col. 0682C] **It has passes.** The first edition says that “Mount Caucasus is said to have passes”; Ultr. consistently has *portas* (“gates”) in place of *portas habere*.

[Col. 0682C] **Tigris.** Some manuscripts and editions have *Tigris* here and throughout.

[Col. 0682C] **Carrhae.** Lugd. Batt. pr., sec., and tert., together with some printed editions, write *Charras*. Latin and Greek writers prefer expressing the name without aspiration, and this usage is confirmed by coins, such as those published by Haymius. Since we also possess others of the same kind in our museum, we have had several of them depicted. [Col. 0683C] Some of these coins display the head of Apollo on the obverse, others that of Jupiter. The first two, which Haymius depicted in the *Thesaurus Britannicus*, vol. II, p. 117, have the head of Apollo; but my four, by no means those of Apollo, display the bearded head of Jupiter. Although they are not very dissimilar, I ordered them to be brought together and engraved, so that it might be clear that the head on them is Jupiter’s, not Apollo’s. Why on the reverse a half wolf appears, surrounded by the rays of a star, is obscure—unless perhaps this side pertains to the worship of Apollo and Diana; hence on nearly all the coins of this city struck under the Roman emperors, a crescent moon is seen together with the sun’s star.

[Col. 0683C] **Ariobarzanes.** The first edition has *Ariobarzones*. The manuscript Lugd. Bat. pr. has *Ariorbarzanes*. Lugd. Batt. pr. tert. adds *dicitur* (“is called”) after the name of the mountain.

[Col. 0683C] **Memarmali.** Lugd. Bat. pr. has *Memarmoli*, sec. *Memoli*, and quart. and Perizon. *Marmali*.

[Col. 0683D] **Is called Parthau.** Lugd. Bat. pr. has *Parchau*. Aethicus has *Partao*. Hittorp and Bolsuing prefer *appellatur* (“is called”) to *dicitur*.

[Col. 0683D] **The Dahae and Araucae.** Bolsuing wrote this as *Dahas ac Araucas*, whereas the readings had previously been *Dahassacaraucas* and *Dachastauriocas*. Our older witnesses have either *Daassacauracas* or *Daassacaraucas*. Flor. sec. has *Dasseraucas*, with *Dastauraucas* in the margin; Flor. tert. (with which Meus agrees) has *Daas et Sacaraucas*. Lugd. Bat. has *Dacaustaraucas*, sec. *Duas Satauracas*, tert. *Dachastaraucas*, quart. *Dachaustraucas*, Perizon. *Dahassa Carautas*, and Ultr. *Duas Sacaurautas*. Among the printed editions are *Dahassaraucos* in the first, *Dachas Tarucas* in the Augustan, and *Dahassaraucas* in the Venetian editions. Hittorp has *Dagas ac Araucas*. In Aethicus’s *Cosmographia* it is *Dapsassa Cauracas*.

[Col. 0683D] **The Parthyenae.** Flor. pr. has *Parhieas*. A superscript *f* is added, as though it should read *Parthinas*. Lugd. Bat. pr. has *Parchyenas*. Meus has *Parthrenas*. The Augustan edition has *Parthynas*. Aethicus has *Parthenasis mons Oschobaris* (“Mount Oschobaris of the Parthenases”).

[Col. 0684A] **Oscobares.** Flor. sec. has *Achobares*, tert. *Osobalers*, and Meus *Oscobates*. The Augustan edition has *Oschobates*.

[Col. 0684B] **Ottorogorra.** Flor. sec. has *a fontibus Octorogorrae* (“from the sources of Octorogorra”) and shortly afterward *ad civitatem Ottorogorrem* (“to the city of Ottorogorres”); Flor. tert. has *a fontibus Ottorogorrae* and shortly afterward *ad civitatem Otorogorum*. Lugd. Batt. pr. and quart. write *Octorogorrae* and *Octorogorram*, as do the first editions and the Venetian editions. The remaining witnesses, as well as Aethicus’s *Cosmographia*, have *Ottorogorrae* and *Ottorogorram*. Cellarius, vol. II, pp. 888–889, calls it *Ottorocorrha Serica*, a town near the Ottorocorrha Mountains.

[Col. 0684B] **The mountain-dwellers, the Paropamisadae.** The usual reading is *Montana Paropamissadae* (“the mountains of the Paropamissadae”); we have followed the old books. Stephanus writes:

> Παροπάμισσος πόλεως ὄρος Ἰνδικῆς, ἀφ᾽ οὗπερ Παροπαμισσάδαι οἱ παροικοῦντες. Ἀπολλόδωρος δὲ ἐν δευτέρῳ περὶ γῆς, ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν φησι τὸ ὄρος κεκλῆσθαι, οἱ δὲ τοῦτο κατοικοῦντες Παροπαμισσάδαι.

“Paropamissus is a mountain of an Indian city, from which the inhabitants dwelling around it are called Paropamissadae. Apollodorus, however, in the second book of his work *On the Earth*, says that the mountain was named from them, and that those who inhabit it are called Paropamissadae.”

In Arrian this name is written sometimes with a single sigma, sometimes with the double sigma *σσ*; but in Diodorus and in Eustathius, the commentator on Dionysius, it has a single sigma.

FABRICIUS. — Flor. sec. has *Paropadissadae*, with a superscript *n*, as though it should read *Paropanisadae*; tert. has *Paropanissadae*; Lugd. Batt. pr., sec., and quart. have *Paropanisadae*; the remaining manuscripts have *Paropamisadae*. Lugd. Batt. pr. and tert. additionally insert the conjunction *et* (“and”). Shortly afterward Meus reads *Taurus est* (“there is Taurus”).

[Col. 0684C] **The Huns and Scythians.** Flor. pr. has *inter unos* (“between the Unos”), with an *h* written above it, but it is corrected there to *in Hunas* (“among the Huns”). Flor. sec. has *inter Funos Sitas*. Lugd. Batt. pr. and quart. have *Chunos et Scithas*, sec. *Hunos*, tert. *Chimos*, and Periz. and Ultr. *Hunos Scitas*. Meus has *Funoscitas*. The customary reading is correct, and it also occurs in Aethicus. Procopius likewise mentions the Huns as inhabitants of this mountain, *Gothic War* IV.3, p. 160, where he is discussing the parts of the Caucasus toward the east and south:

> Οἱ δὲ πρὸς ἀνίσχοντα ἤλιον καὶ ἄνεμον νότον, ἐς τὰς διεξόδους ἐξικνοῦνται αὐτὰς, αἳ τὰ τῆδε ᾠκημένα Οὑννικὰ ἔθνη ἐς τὴν γῆν τῶν Περσῶν καὶ Ῥωμαίων ἄγουσιν.

“But those passages that face the rising sun and the south wind reach the exits themselves, which lead the Hunnic peoples dwelling there into the land of the Persians and Romans.”

He then mentions the Huns who are called Sabiri, and other Hunnic peoples in the same region.

[Col. 0684D] **Gandaridae.** Lugd. Batt. quart. and Perizon. have *Gangaridae*. The name is written both ways.

[Col. 0684D] **The Eoae and the Pasiadras.** The first edition has *Eosas et Pasiadras*. Lugd. Bat. quart., Perizon., and Meus double the *s* in *Pasiadras*, as does Flor. tert.; Flor. sec. likewise has *Passiadras*, but *tro* is written above it, as though it were intended to be *Passitroas*. Lugd. Bat. sec. has *Paidras*.

[Col. 0684D] **Imaus.** This name is variously corrupted in the manuscripts here and below. Flor. sec. has *Inmavus*, tert. *Immanus*, Lugd. Bat. pr. *Emaavus*, with a note “read *Thimavus*”; tert. and quart. *Emavus*, sec. *Ymavus*; Ultr. and Periz. *Imanus*; the first edition *Imavus*; and the Augustan edition *Timavus*.

[Col. 0684D] **Samara.** The Augustan edition has *Samora*, followed shortly by the first editions and the Venetian editions. *Syricus* for *Sericus* in the Ultr. manuscript is an ordinary scribal error.

[Col. 0684D] **And along the eastern right-hand side.** Flor. sec. has *et dextra orientis partem* (“and the eastern right-hand side”), but it is corrected to *et usque ad dextram* (“and as far as the right-hand side”), and so forth.

[Col. 0685B] **Thence along.** Lugd. Batt. pr., tert., and quart. have *exinde tenus* (“thence along”), while the first editions, Hittorp, the Venetian editions, and Bolsuing have *inde tenus*. The *et* is deleted by the Augustan edition and does not appear in the Florentine manuscripts.

[Col. 0685B] **Extent.** Lugd. Batt. sec., quart., and Ultr. have *extensum*. [Col. 0685C] Flor. tert. has *extremum*. The customary reading is better. Ovid calls Mount Tmolus *extentus utroque clivo* (“stretched along both slopes”) in *Metamorphoses* XI, line 150:

Late the steep Tmolus stiffens in its lofty ascent,  
and, extending along either slope, is bounded on this side by Sardis, on that by little Hypaepa.

[Note: “To the south.” All the manuscripts consistently prefer this to “from the south,” which appears in most printed editions except the Augustan edition.]

the outstretched ridge of the Caucasus, which is to the south; the peoples of the Hyrcanians and Scythians number forty-two;

[Note: “Forty-two.” Three manuscripts assign a larger number, with the Augustan edition and the first and third Leiden manuscripts; the fourth gives four. Shortly afterward, the Augustan edition and Meus have “dispersion” instead of “expanse,” and Meus has “far” instead of “widely.”]

 they wander widely because of the unproductive expanse of their lands. The Caspian Sea rises under the northern region from the Ocean; both of its shores around the Ocean, and its deserted and uncultivated places, are considered part of it.

[Note: “Both around the Ocean.” The first Leiden manuscript reads “both parts around the Ocean”; the fourth has “on this side” instead of “around.” Meus deletes the conjunction *and*.]

From there it extends southward through long narrow passages, until, having broadened over great distances, it is terminated by the roots of the Caucasus Mountains.

[Note: “Is terminated.” The first Leiden manuscript has “is terminated.” In this connection, the third Florentine manuscript may be thought to write “it broadens” above instead of “having broadened.”]

[Note: “At the east.” The Augustan edition has “from the east.”]

Thus, from the Caspian Sea, which lies to the east, along the shore of the northern Ocean as far as the river Tanais and the Maeotian marshes, which lie to the west, along the shore of the Cimmerian Sea—which lies from the southwest as far as the summit and gates of the Caucasus, which lie to the south—there are thirty-four peoples.

[Note: “Along the shore.” The second and third Florentine manuscripts read “along the shores,” as does Perizonius; the others retain the received reading with Aethicus.]

[Note: “To the south.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “from the south.”]

[Note: “Thirty-four.” The third Florentine manuscript has “four and thirty.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, now less generous, assign only thirty-two.]

[Note: “Maeotian marshes.” The first edition has “Maeotian marshes” with the adjective in another form.]

But, generally speaking, the region adjoining further Albania, beneath the Caspian Sea and mountain, is called the land of the Amazons.

[Note: “Is called.” This is the reading of the second Florentine manuscript, as well as the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, Meus, and Perizonius. The second Leiden manuscript has “is named.” The editions generally have “is designated,” except the Augustan edition, which has “is called.” The manuscripts of Aethicus likewise show variation in the wording.]

The boundaries of Asia have now been set out as briefly as possible. I shall now traverse Europe with my pen, insofar as human knowledge permits.

[Note: “They have been set out.” The second and third Florentine manuscripts and the fourth Leiden manuscript read “they have been explained.” The first editions and the Venetian editions read “but they have been set out”; the same editions below have “now, however,” and so forth. Some editions, such as those of Hittorp and Bolswing, have “although very briefly.”]

[Note: “Insofar as human knowledge permits.” Formerly the text was printed “as far as knowledge is granted,” and the manuscripts had a form meaning “and is climbed.” Hence this reading was extracted as the genuine one and, unless I am mistaken, agrees especially well with the neighboring expression. LAUT.—But then the text would have to read “is ascended.” Nevertheless, I do not depart from the received reading, which is confirmed by all the Florentine manuscripts and all those I have examined, nor would I rashly adopt another reading with Andreas Scotus. Aethicus’ *Cosmography* also confirms the received text, interpreting it in the same way: “insofar as it is granted to human condition.”]

From the Riphaean Mountains, the river Tanais, and the Maeotian marshes, which lie to the east, along the shore of the northern Ocean as far as Belgic Gaul and the river Rhine, which lies to the west, and then as far as the Danube, also called the Ister, which flows from the south toward the east and is received by the sea, the boundaries are as follows: to the east lies Alania; in the middle is Dacia, where Gothia too is situated; then comes Germany, most of which is occupied by the Suebi. The peoples of all these regions number fifty-four.

[Note: “To the south.” The Augustan edition has “toward the south.” The conjunction *and* is omitted by the older editions through the Fabrician editions, contrary to all the manuscripts I have examined or collated, and contrary also to Aethicus’ *Cosmography*. The Ister, or Danube, therefore begins in the south, where it rises; then, directing its course toward the east, it continues until it flows into the sea and empties itself.]

[Note: “Where Gothia too is situated.” The same edition reads “there Gothia too is situated,” and then “and Germany is situated.”]

[Note: “The Suebi occupy.” Thus in the manuscripts and older editions. Hittorp and the Bolswing edition read “the Suebi possess.”]

[Note: “There are peoples.” Thus in the manuscripts. The editions transpose the words and read “there are fifty-four peoples.”]

Now I shall describe whatever the Danube separates from the barbarian sea as far as the Mediterranean Sea.

[Note: “From the barbarian sea.” The second Leiden and Ultrajectine manuscripts add “Ocean”; the fourth adds “sea.” The second and third Florentine manuscripts wrongly have “Mysia” for “Moesia,” here and below.]

Moesia has on the east the mouths of the river Danube; on the southeast, Thrace; on the south, Macedonia; on the southwest, Dalmatia; on the west, Istria; on the northwest, Pannonia; and on the north, the Danube.

Thrace has on the east the gulf of the Propontis and the city of Constantinople, formerly called Byzantium; on the north, part of Dalmatia and the gulf of the Pontus Euxinus; on the west and southwest, Macedonia; and on the south, the Aegean Sea.

Macedonia has on the east the Aegean Sea; on the north, Thrace; on the southeast, Euboea and the Macedonian Gulf; on the south, Achaea; and on the southwest, the Acroceraunian Mountains in the narrow part of the Adriatic Gulf. These mountains lie opposite Apulia and Brundisium; on the west, Macedonia has Dalmatia; on the northwest, Dardania; and on the north, Moesia.

[Note: “The Acroceraunian Mountains.” They are also called the Acroceraunia. Horace, in the first book of the *Odes*, writes: “Who saw the swollen sea and the infamous Acroceraunian cliffs.” Diodorus, book forty-one, writes in Greek: “He crossed toward the peaks called the Ceraunian Mountains.” FABR.—The second Florentine manuscript reads “the Acroceanian Mountains.” All the Leiden manuscripts, as well as Perizonius and Fabricius, read “the Acroceraunian Mountains.” Meus has “of the Acroceraunian sea” instead of “of the gulf.”]

[Note: “Which mountains are.” Hittorp and the Bolswing editions, contrary to all the other editions and all the manuscripts, insert *siti* (“situated”). The second Leiden manuscript and the Ultrajectine manuscript additionally omit *sunt* (“are”).]

[Note: “And Brundisium.” This is the reading preferred by the manuscripts and the older printed editions; the others have “and Brundisium.”]

[Note: “On the west.” The fourth Leiden manuscript prefixes *and*.]

Achaea is almost entirely surrounded by sea. For on the east it has the Myrtoan Sea; on the southeast, the Cretan Sea; on the south, the Ionian Sea; on the southwest and west, the islands Cephallenia and Cassiope; on the north, the Gulf of Corinth; and on the northeast, a narrow ridge of land by which it is joined to Macedonia—or rather to Attica. This place is called the Isthmus, and Corinth is situated there, having the city of Athens not far away in Attica to the north.

[Note: “The Cretan Sea.” The first edition has “the Arctic Sea.”]

[Note: “By which it is joined to Macedonia.” The second Leiden manuscript and Perizonius read “by which”; the fourth has “by whom,” and so forth.]

[Note: “Where Corinth is situated.” The latter word is absent from the Augustan edition.]

[Note: “Having Athens in Attica to the north.” The third and fourth Leiden manuscripts read “having Athens in Attica,” and the first edition agrees with them, also reading “to the north.” The first Leiden manuscript has “facing Attica to the north.” In Aethicus’ *Cosmography* we read: “Here, in Attica to the north, not far away, is the city of Athens.” Correct this to: “From here, in Attica, ...”]

Dalmatia has on the east Macedonia; on the northeast, Dardania; on the north, Moesia; on the west, Istria, the Liburnian Gulf, and the Liburnian Islands; and on the south, the Adriatic Gulf.

Pannonia, Noricum, and Raetia have on the east Moesia; on the south, Istria; on the southwest, the Pennine Alps; on the west, Belgic Gaul; on the northwest, the source of the Danube and the boundary that separates Germany from Gaul between the Danube and Gaul; and on the north, the Danube and Germany.

[Note: “Separates.” The first and Venetian editions have “distinguishes.” The Augustan edition deletes the following conjunction *and*.]

[Note: “The Pennine Alps.” This is clearly written in the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts and in the Perizonian manuscript, and the Augustan edition has “Pennine.” Meus, together with the second Leiden manuscript and the second Florentine manuscript, writes “Apennine” or “Apenninian”; the third Florentine manuscript, the first edition, and the first Leiden manuscript likewise have “Apennine.” Livy demonstrates that these Alps are called Pennine from the god Penninus, not Poenine, as some claim—especially Greek writers—because of the passage of the Carthaginians and Hannibal. In book 21, chapter 38, he writes: “Nor is it likely that the routes to Gaul were then open—at any rate those leading to Pennine—since they were blocked by half-German peoples; and, by Hercules, if anyone has been moved by these mountains, the Veragri, inhabitants of that ridge, know that their name was not bestowed from any passage of the Carthaginians, but from the one whom the mountaineers call Penninus, consecrated upon the highest summit.”]

Italy extends from the northwest toward the southeast. It has the Tyrrhenian Sea on the southwest and the Adriatic Gulf on the north. The part of it that is common and contiguous with the mainland is blocked by the barrier of the Alps. These Alps, rising from the Gallic Sea above the Ligurian Gulf, first shut off the territory of the Narbonenses, then Gaul and Raetia, until they end in the Liburnian Gulf.

[Note: “By which it is contiguous with the mainland.” The first and second Leiden manuscripts, as well as the Augustan edition, read “which,” rather than “by which.”]

[Note: “Which rise from the Gallic Sea above the Ligurian Gulf.” The second Leiden manuscript has “which”; the Augustan edition has “which rise from the Gallic Sea through the Ligurian Gulf”; the Ultrajectine manuscript likewise has “through the Ligurian Gulf.”]

[Note: “Until they end in the Liburnian Gulf.” The second Leiden manuscript has “until they are fixed”; the fourth has “until they end in the Liburnian Gulf.”]

Belgic Gaul has on the east the boundary of the river Rhine and Germany; on the southeast, the Pennine Alps; on the south, the province of Narbonensis; on the west, the province of Lugdunensis; on the northwest, the British Ocean; and on the north, the island of Britain.

[Note: “On the southeast.” The first, second, and third Leiden manuscripts and the Augustan edition add “has.” Here again Perizonius and the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts write “the Pennine Alps,” as does the first manuscript, though in the first manuscript a second hand has written “from the” before it, indicating “the Apennine Alps.”]

Lugdunensis Gaul, stretched lengthwise and bent into a narrow form, almost encircles the province of Aquitania. It has Belgic Gaul on the east; on the south, that part of the province of Narbonensis where the city of Arelas is situated; and, along the Gallic Sea, the river Rhône is received.
