[Note: “Britain.” The Ultrajectine manuscript and the first, Venetian, and Augustan editions have “British.” A little later they add “Gaul,” and again have “Belgic”; the Ultrajectine manuscript has “Aquitanian” instead of “the province of Aquitania.” The first, Augustan, and Venetian editions have “Arelatum” instead of “Arelas.”]

[Note: “And by the sea.” The fourth Leiden manuscript inserts “where”; the second writes “is received” instead of “is taken up.”]

The province of Narbonensis, a part of Gaul, has on the east the Cottian Alps; on the west, Hispania; on the northwest, Aquitania; on the north, Lugdunensis Gaul; on the northeast, Belgic Gaul; and on the south, the Gallic Sea, which lies between Sardinia and the Balearic Islands. At its front, where the river Rhône flows out into the sea, it has the Stoechades Islands.

[Note: “The Cottian Alps.” This is the correct name. The first and third Leiden manuscripts have “Gottian,” the second “Chotian,” the fourth “Cothician,” Perizonius “Cotian,” and Meus, incorrectly, “Cutian,” as with many place-names.]

[Note: “On the west.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “on the western side,” and immediately afterward the second, third, and fourth have “Aquitania.”]

[Note: “Lugdunensis.” Some editions place “Gaul” before it, but the word is absent from the manuscripts.]

[Note: “The Balearic Islands.” The second and fourth Leiden manuscripts delete the first word, “islands.”]

The province of Aquitania is driven into a circuit by the oblique course of the river Loire, which is for the most part its boundary. It has on the northwest the Ocean, which is called the Aquitanian Gulf; on the west, the Spanish provinces; on the north and east, Lugdunensis; and on the southeast and south, the province of Narbonensis.

[Note: “Aquitania.” The Ultrajectine manuscript has “Aquitania,” and deletes “its” from the following phrase.]

[Note: “The Ocean on the northwest.” The Augustan edition has “the Ocean”; the first and Venetian editions read “on the northwest it has the Ocean.” The Ultrajectine manuscript has “the Spanish peoples.”]

Hispania as a whole is triangular in the arrangement of its land and, being surrounded by the Ocean and the Tyrrhenian Sea, is made almost an island.

[Note: “As a whole.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts, the first editions, the Augustan edition, and the Venetian editions have “as a whole” in a form referring to the situation rather than to Hispania. Aethicus’ *Cosmography* supports the received reading. The verb “is” is omitted by both Florentine manuscripts, the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts, Perizonius, and Meus, as is the conjunction after “Tyrrhenian” in the first and third Leiden manuscripts.]

Its first angle, facing east, is enclosed on the right by the province of Aquitania and on the left by the Balearic Sea, and is inserted into the territory of the Narbonenses.

[Note: “The nearer angle.” The fourth Leiden manuscript reads “the nearer one.” The same manuscript later reads “on the right it has the province of Aquitania,” a reading also found in the third. The Florentine manuscripts and Venetian editions delete the final word after “its angle.”]

The second angle extends toward the northwest. There lies the city of Brigantia in Callecia, where it raises a very lofty lighthouse, one of the few works worthy of remembrance, as a lookout toward Britain.

[Note: “Where Brigantia in Callecia is situated.” Thus we have written from an old book, instead of the reading in the printed editions, “of Gallaecia.” Diodorus, book thirty-seven, says in Greek: “Brigantium, a city of Callaecia.” FABR.—The second Florentine manuscript has “Galleciae,” with an i written above it to indicate “Galliciae,” as appears in the second Florentine manuscript, the Leiden manuscripts, the Ultrajectine manuscript, and Aethicus’ *Cosmography*. The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts have “of Gaul”; Perizonius has “Galleciae”; Meus, “Galiciae.” But “Callaecia” is correct. Besides Diodorus, Dio Cassius, when speaking of Caesar, calls it a city of Callaecia, book thirty-seven, page 54: “Having sailed past Brigantium, a city of Callaecia.” This shows that it was a coastal town, a fact admirably confirmed by this passage of Orosius; for the lighthouse of a memorable work could not elsewhere have served sailors. Some manuscripts arrange the following words thus: “it is situated, and raises a very lofty lighthouse, among the few works worthy of remembrance, as a spectacle toward Britain.” The first Leiden manuscript reads: “it is situated, and raises a very lofty lighthouse, and among the few works worthy of remembrance raises it as a spectacle toward Britain.” The third Leiden manuscript has “it is situated, which also has”; the second and third Florentine manuscripts have “a mirror” instead of “a spectacle.” The Ultrajectine manuscript reads “is raised as a spectacle toward Britain.” The first and Venetian editions have “extends as a lookout toward Britain.” Aethicus’ *Cosmography* reads: “Where the city Brigantia of Gallicia is situated, and a very lofty lighthouse is raised—some have ‘toward’—and among the few works worthy of remembrance it is raised as a lookout toward Britain.”]

Its third angle is where the islands of Gades, stretching toward the southwest, look across the intervening gulf of the Ocean toward Mount Atlas.

[Note: “Where.” The second, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, the second Florentine manuscript, and the Ultrajectine manuscript have “where,” as does the first edition and all the old editions before the Fabrician editions. Meus preserves “qua.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “toward the southwest.”]

Hither Hispania Citerior begins: the Pyrenean passes extend along its northern side as far as the Cantabrians and Asturians; from there, through the Vaccaei and Oretani, whom it has on the west, Carthage, situated on the shore of Our Sea, forms its boundary.

[Note: “Beginning.” The word is absent from Perizonius; the others preserve it, as does Aethicus: “on the east it begins from the Pyrenean passes.” Meus has “the Pyrenean pass” in the singular.]

[Note: “As far as.” The latter word is deleted by the second Leiden manuscript.]

[Note: “Oretani.” The first edition has “Oreatani,” and Meus subsequently has “whom it has placed on the west, on the shore of Our Sea, Carthage determines.” The first edition reads “which it has situated on the west, on the shore of Our Sea, determines Carthage.”]

Hispania Ulterior has on the east the Vaccaei, Celtiberians, and Oretani; on the north, the Ocean; on the west, the Ocean; and on the south, the Strait of the Gaditanian Ocean, through which Our Sea, called the Tyrrhenian Sea, flows in.

[Note: “From which.” The Augustan edition has “from there, Our Sea,” and the Venetian editions likewise.]

Since the Ocean contains islands called Britain and Hibernia, which lie on the far side of Gaul, facing Hispania, they will be briefly described.

[Note: “On the far side of Gaul.” “Far side,” not “opposite,” is correctly found in the manuscripts. FABRIC.—“Far side” is also read in Aethicus’ *Cosmography* and in the second Florentine manuscript; most of the others, together with the old editions, read “opposite.”]

Britain, an island of the Ocean, extends lengthwise toward the north. On the south it has Gaul, whose nearest shore, for those crossing over, is opened up by the city called the port of Rhutupiae. Not far from the Morini, it looks toward the Menapii and Batavi, situated to the southwest.

[Note: “From the Morini.” The first and Venetian editions have “from the Moryni.” The third and fourth Leiden manuscripts and Perizonius have “from the Morini”; the second, fourth, and Perizonius subsequently have “Menapii,” while the Ultrajectine manuscript has “Batavi” for “Batrasii” in the first edition.]

[Note: “The city opens.” The same words describe these places in Aethicus’ *Cosmography*. But the fourth Leiden and Ultrajectine manuscripts read “the city appears,” contrary to the others and to the author’s intention. Orosius uses the geographical expression “the British city opens the nearest shore of Gaul to those crossing,” meaning that the sea passage there was so narrow that the shores of Gaul could be seen from it. For that reason there was formerly frequent passage from there into Gaul and from Gaul into Britain, before the port of Dubris—now Dover—took over that function. It lay opposite Boulogne, from which, or from Gessoriacum, ships sailed directly from Gaul. Ammianus Marcellinus, book 20, chapter 1, writes: “Having observed a favorable wind, he is carried to Rutupiae, situated opposite, and seeks London.” The same author, book 27, chapter 8: “When he had come to the shore of Boulogne, from there, after crossing the narrower strait, he was carried to Rutupiae, a tranquil station opposite.”]

[Note: “The port of Rhutupiae.” The spelling and designation of the name vary not only in manuscripts and printed editions but also among ancient authors. The first and third Leiden manuscripts have “the port of Rutupiae.” Meus has “the port of Rhutupiae.” Antoninus’ *Itinerary* has “Ritupae”; other writers generally use “Rutupiae” or “Ritupiae.” The distinguished Petrus Wesselingius observes in his notes to Antoninus’ *Itinerary*, p. 473, that the plural is used because two fortresses were placed there at the harbor; the one toward the north was called Regulbium, whose name survives today in Reculver. As evidence he cites, besides the *Notitia Dignitatum* of the Western Empire, John Battely’s *On the Antiquities of Rutupiae*, published at Oxford.]

It has a length of eight hundred thousand paces and a width of two hundred thousand. Behind it, where it is open to the boundless Ocean, it has the Orcades Islands, of which twenty are deserted and thirteen inhabited.

[Note: “In length.” Since “in width” follows immediately afterward, it is surprising that some editions, contrary to Aethicus and all the manuscripts, should have allowed “in the long direction” to enter the text. Below, in the description of Cyprus, its extent is likewise described as “in length and in width.” The fourth Leiden manuscript adds “three” at the beginning of “eight hundred thousand paces.”]

[Note: “The Orcades.” This is the reading of the better manuscripts; some editions have “Orcades,” a variation also found in Aethicus’ *Cosmography*.]

[Note: “Thirteen are inhabited.” Aethicus and the Augustan edition have “fourteen are inhabited”; the first and Venetian editions, Hittorp, and Bolswing have “thirteen are inhabited,” contrary to all the manuscripts and also to Aethicus’ *Cosmography*. The first edition and the Florentine manuscripts have “Tile” instead of “Thule”; the Augustan edition has “Thile.” The second Leiden manuscript then reads “which, through the boundless Ocean,” and so forth.]

Then there is the island of Thule, separated from the others by an immense distance and situated toward the northwest in the middle of the Ocean; it is scarcely known to a few.

[Note: “Situated in the middle of the Ocean.” The Ultrajectine manuscript has “situated in the middle of the Ocean”; the first editions, Hittorp, Bolswing, and the second and third Florentine manuscripts have “situated in the Ocean”; Perizonius and Meus likewise have this form.]

The island of Hibernia, situated between Britain and Hispania, extends over a greater distance from the southwest toward the north. Its forward regions, facing the Cantabrian Ocean, look across a broad interval toward the city of Brigantia in Callecia, which lies opposite them from the southwest toward the northwest, especially from the promontory where the mouth of the river Scena is situated and where the Velabri and Luceni dwell.

[Note: “A longer distance.” The Ultrajectine manuscript has “situated, over a longer distance,” and so forth. The first and Venetian editions have “situated, which extends over a greater distance from the southwest.” Perizonius reads “is gathered together.”]

[Note: “The mouth of the river Scena.” The name of the river is absent from the Ultrajectine manuscript; in Aethicus’ *Cosmography* it is called the Sacana. The second and third Florentine manuscripts, Meus, and the first edition write “Sena”; the others read “Scena,” which agrees with its modern name. Cellarius, book 2, chapter 4, p. 441, testifies that it was called the Scennon.]

[Note: “And the Luceni.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts have “Lugenique”; the Augustan edition has “Velabri Luceni,” deleting the conjunction in the Ultrajectine manuscript. Perizonius has “over a broad interval” instead of “over a spacious interval.”]

This island is nearer to Britain and narrower in the extent of its land, but, because of the temperateness of its climate and soil, it is more productive; it is inhabited by the peoples of the Scots.

[Note: “But because of the temperateness of its climate and soil.” The common text has “of its climate and sun,” a childish tautology. LAUT.—Andreas Scotus added in the margin of the Mainz edition “and soil,” more correctly and appropriately. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts, the printed editions, and Aethicus’ *Cosmography* itself prefer “because of the temperateness of its climate and sun,” except my parchment manuscripts, which clearly read “because of the temperateness of its climate and soil.” I would prefer “because of the temperateness of its soil and climate,” since *temperies* properly concerns the air or climate; and Orosius praises Hibernia for enjoying a temperate climate and fertile soil. A little later, “of the Scots” is preceded by “among,” also in the fourth Leiden manuscript.]

Near to it is the island of Mevania, itself by no means small in extent and fertile in soil; it too is inhabited by the peoples of the Scots.

[Note: “The island of Mevania.” The Augustan edition has “the nearby island of Mevania.” For Mevania, the first and third Leiden manuscripts have “Evann,” the second and Ultrajectine manuscripts “Eumania,” and the fourth “Eumonia.”]

[Note: “Fertile in soil.” The Ultrajectine manuscript and the Augustan edition have “fertile alone,” but the Fabrician editions note in the margin the word “soil.” I have preferred “in soil,” also on the authority of Aethicus’ *Cosmography*: just as above he praised Hibernia for its climate and soil, so now he commends Mevania for its soil and extent. The first edition reads “by no means small in extent, fertile in soil.” The Venetian editions often follow it.]

These are the boundaries of all Europe.

Africa, as I have said, our ancestors described as constituting a third part of the world, following the principles of division rather than measurements of distances. The Great Sea, rising from the Ocean in the west and inclining more toward the south, forms the boundary of Africa, which is compressed between it and the Ocean into a narrower space.

[Note: “Together with a third part of the world.” The second Leiden manuscript deletes “of the world”; the Ultrajectine manuscript deletes “together with,” reading “a third part.” The first Leiden manuscript has “together with nearly a third part of the world,” and so forth. The second Florentine manuscript, the third, the second, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, and the printed editions read “should be described,” rather than “should be accepted.”]

[Note: “This sea.” The Perizonian manuscript, together with Hittorp’s edition, transposes the words and reads “Since this great sea.”]

[Note: “Inclining more.” The first word is absent from the Perizonian manuscript.]

[Note: “Forms.” The second and third Florentine manuscripts, the first, second, and third Leiden manuscripts, Meus, the Ultrajectine manuscript, and the first, Augustan, and Venetian editions have “formed.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “formed” with an abbreviated spelling, and Perizonius has a corrupt form.]

Consequently, although some, recognizing that it is equal in length but much narrower, judged it shameless to call it a third part, they preferred to designate Africa as a portion of Europe’s second division.

[Note: “Shameless.” Meus, the third Florentine manuscript, and the Augustan edition have “modest.” The second and third Leiden manuscripts, Meus, and Perizonius delete “are”; the first edition, together with the Venetian editions, transposes “to call a part.”]

[Note: “To Europe.” This reading is supported by the strong agreement of the second and third Florentine manuscripts, the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts, the Ultrajectine manuscript, and Meus. The Augustan edition also preserves it. Perizonius and the third Leiden manuscript retain the received reading. We noted above that ancient writers used the preposition *in* indiscriminately with the fourth and sixth cases.]

[Note: “A portion of the second.” Thus I read it. The printed editions have “a portion of a portion of the second,” following Hittorp’s edition. The manuscripts vary greatly: the second and third Florentine manuscripts have “that is, a portion of the second,” a reading supported by the fourth Leiden manuscript, Perizonius, and Meus. The first and third Leiden manuscripts have “that is, the second portion”; the second and the Ultrajectine manuscript have “that is, that second portion.” The first edition and the Venetian editions have “and a second portion”; the Augustan edition has “a second portion.” In his description of Africa especially, Aethicus alters Orosius’ words and paraphrases the passage thus: “But they judged it to be reckoned in Europe, that is, so that they would not call it similar to two parts, but subject to one of the two.”]

Moreover, since far more land in Africa remains uncultivated and unknown because of the sun’s heat than in Europe because of the cold, for almost all animals and plants approach the greatest cold more patiently and tolerably than the greatest heat, that is the reason why Africa appears smaller in every respect, both in its land and in its peoples: for by its own nature it has less space, and because of the harshness of its climate it has more desert.

[Note: “Because both by its own nature.” The first and Venetian editions have “and because by its own nature”; the third Leiden manuscript has “because from its own nature.” Both Florentine manuscripts and the Venetian editions have “has less space.”]

[Note: “Much more.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “much more greatly.”]

[Note: “Since everything.” The middle word is missing in Fabricius’ edition; hence “approach” is altered there to “they approach.”]

Its description by provinces and peoples is as follows.

Libya Cyrenaica and Pentapolis, after Egypt, is the first region of Africa.

It begins at the city of Paraetonium and the Catabathmon Mountains; from there it extends along the sea as far as the Altars of the Philaeni. Behind it, as far as the southern Ocean, are the peoples of the Libyans, Ethiopians, and Garamantes.

[Note: “After Egypt.” The second Leiden manuscript and the Ultrajectine manuscript read “which is after Egypt.”]

[Note: “Paraetonium.” Aethicus has the erroneous form “Parthenium.”]

[Note: “The Libyans, Ethiopians.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts simply have “of the Ethiopians.” Meus and the third Florentine manuscript have “Libyans, Ethiopians.” The first edition, together with Aethicus’ *Cosmography*, has “Libyans, Ethiopians”; the Augustan edition has “Libyans of the Ethiopians”; the second Florentine manuscript has “Libyo-Ethiopians”; the Ultrajectine manuscript has “of Libya, Ethiopians.” I judge the correct text to be: “the peoples of Libya, of the Ethiopians, and of the Garamantes.” For all these peoples are divided into several nations. The Libyo-Ethiopians, or inhabitants of Egyptian Libya, whom he mentioned above, are different from these; and from that passage it appears that the name “Libyo-Ethiopians” was first restored here in Hittorp’s edition, then in the editions of Bolswing, Fabricius, and Andreas Scotus of Mainz.]

This region has Egypt on the east; the Libyan Sea on the north; on the west, the Greater Syrtes and the Troglodytes, opposite whom lies the island of Calypso; and on the south, the Aethiopian Ocean.

[Note: “It has.” The latter word is absent from the second Florentine manuscript. Some manuscripts have “from here,” in place of “it has.”]

[Note: “Calypso.” The third Florentine manuscript has “Calypsa,” and the Augustan edition “Calyps.” Latin writers call this island *Calypso*, as Pliny does in book 3, at the end of chapter 10: “The promontory Lacynium; before its shore, an island called Dioscuron, ten thousand paces from the mainland; another, Calypso, which Homer is thought to have called Ogygia.” Orosius follows the Greek inflection, and Aethicus follows him. Scylax’s *Periplus*, p. 5 in Hudson’s edition, reads in Greek: “The sanctuary of Hera at Lacinium and the island Calypso, on which Odysseus lived with Calypso.” Homer calls this island Ogygia, where Calypso, daughter of Atlas, lived, *Odyssey* 2.244. The Perizonian manuscript has “the island Calyopso.”]

The province of Tripolitana, also called Subventana or the region of the Arzuges, where the great city of Leptis is situated—although the Arzuges are generally so called along the entire length of Africa—has on the east the Altars of the Philaeni, between the Greater Syrtes and the Troglodytes; on the north, the Sicilian Sea, or rather the Adriatic, and the Lesser Syrtes; on the west, Byzacium as far as Lake Salinarum; and on the south, the barbarian Getuli, the Nothabres, and the Garamantes, extending as far as the Aethiopian Ocean.

[Note: “The region of the Arzuges.” We have found the form “Azotum,” which some have written above the text, in none of the ancient manuscripts. FABRIC.—The second Florentine manuscript has “Arzutum,” the first Leiden manuscript “Arguzum,” and the third “Arrugum”; later manuscripts likewise have “Arguzes” and “Arruges.”]

[Note: “Byzacium.” The common text mistakenly reads “Byzantium.” See Pliny, book 5, chapter 4, concerning Byzacium. In the ancient *Register of Dignities and Administrations* it is written both “Byzacium” and “Bisacium.” FABR.—The first, second, and third Leiden manuscripts have “Bizantium” here and below; the third has “Bizagium.” The remaining witnesses preserve the correct reading. The Augustan edition has “Bizachium.”]

[Note: “As far as the lake.” The first Leiden manuscript deletes “as far as.”]

[Note: “The Nothabres.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts have “Nabazares”; the second and Meus “Natabres”; the fourth and Perizonius “Nathabres.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts then have “Garamantes.”]

Byzacium, Zeugis, and Numidia. We find that Zeugis was formerly not the name of a single administrative district but the general name of the whole province.

[Note: “Zeugis.” The second Florentine manuscript has “Zeuges” here and below, as does the Augustan edition.]

[Note: “Had been the name.” Some manuscripts transpose the words and read “had been its name.”]

Byzacium is where the city of Hadrumetum is situated; Zeugis, where great Carthage is situated; Numidia, where the cities of Hippo Regius and Rusiccada are situated.

[Note: “The city of Hadrumetum.” The first Leiden manuscript has “Hadrumeta, the city”; the latter word is absent from Meus.]

[Note: “Rusiccada.” Pliny, book 5, chapter 3, and Mela, book 1, chapter 7, have “Rusicade.” The first, second, and third Leiden manuscripts, as well as the Ultrajectine manuscript, have “Rusicada”; the fourth has “Rusicida”; the first edition has “Nisiccada.”]

These regions have on the east the Lesser Syrtes and Lake Salinarum; on the north, Our Sea, facing the islands of Sicily and Sardinia; on the west, Mauritania Sitifensis; and on the south, the Uzara Mountains. Beyond them are the peoples of the Ethiopians, extending as far as the Aethiopian Ocean.

[Note: “On the west.” The first Leiden manuscript has “on the western side.”]

[Note: “The Uzara Mountains.” Meus has “the Uazara Mountains.” The Cervicorn edition has “the springs of Uzara,” a reading also found in the first and Venetian editions. The second Florentine manuscript has “Mount Suzara”; the third has “the Vazara Mountains.” Soon afterward, the Ultrajectine manuscript deletes the first word in *qui in ad oceanum* (“which [extend] to the Ocean”).]

[Col. 0694A] [Note: [Col. 0693D] Mauretania Sitifensis and Caesariensis. The first, third, and fourth Leiden editions, together with the first printed edition, read “the Mauretaniae Sitifenses and Caesarienses.” In the first edition, however, a division is placed after *Caesarienses*, as though this belonged to what preceded it. Soon afterward, the third Leiden edition and Perizonius have *habent* (“have”) instead of *habet* (“has”).]

Mauretania Sitifensis and Caesariensis have Numidia to the east, the Mediterranean Sea to the north, the river Malva to the west [Note: [Col. 0694B] *Malvam*. This river divides the two Mauretanias. The river is called *Malva* in the first, second, fourth, and Ultrajectine Leiden manuscripts. In the first edition, however, *Muluca* is written above it.], and Mount Astrixis to the south [Note: [Col. 0694B] *Astrixim*. The second Florentine manuscript has *Astrinxim*; the third, *Astrixim*. The first Leiden manuscript has *Astrinxi*, but adds “read *Astricii*.”], which divides the inhabited land from the lying sands [Note: [Col. 0694B] *As far as the Ocean*. Meursius deletes the middle word.] extending as far as the Ocean. [Note: [Col. 0694B] *In which the Gangines wander*. The first edition and the Venetian editions read *et oberrant* (“and wander”).] In these regions the Ethiopian Gangines also wander.

Tingitana Mauretania is the final region of Africa. [Note: [Col. 0694B] *This has*. The first Leiden edition has “And this has,” and so forth.] It has the river Malva to the east, the Mediterranean Sea to the north as far as the Strait of Gades, [Note: [Col. 0694B] *Which*. The Augustan edition has *quo* (“by which”).] which [Note: [Col. 0694C] *Between Abenne and Calpe*. It is written variously as *Havennem*, *Habennen*, and *Abennen*. He means the two Pillars of Hercules: one, European, is called Calpe by the barbarians and Ἀλύβα (*Alyba*) by the Greeks; the other, Libyan, is called Abenne by the former and Κυννηγετικὴ (*Kynēgetikē*) by the latter, according to Eustathius in his commentary on Dionysius. FABRICIUS.—The second Florentine manuscript and all the Leiden manuscripts, as well as Meursius, read “between Avenne and Calpis”; the Ultrajectine, “between Avene and Calpen”; the third Florentine, “between Habenne and Calpis”; the Augustan edition, “between Avenne and Calpes.” The Ultrajectine soon deletes *coarctatur* (“is constricted”).] is constricted between Abenne and Calpe, two promontories opposed to one another. To the west it has Mount Atlas and the Atlantic Ocean; to the southwest, Mount Hesperius; to the south, the peoples [Note: [Col. 0694C] *Aulolum*. The third Florentine manuscript, Meursius, and the third Leiden edition have *Aulososum*.] called Aulolum, whom they now call [32] [Note: [Col. 0694C] *Galaulas*. Thus the first edition, together with the Venetians and Fabricius. The Hittorpian and Cervicornian editions have *Gaulales*, which is also found in the first and third Leiden manuscripts; the fourth has *Gaulades*; the second Florentine, the third, and Meursius have *Galaulas*; the third Florentine has *Galaulolas*.] Galaulas, extending as far as the Hesperian Ocean. This is [Note: [Col. 0694C] *The boundary of the whole*. Thus in the Florentine manuscripts and in Meursius. The first edition and the Venetians, together with Hittorp, have “the boundary of the whole”; Bolsuing, with Fabricius and certain manuscripts, “the universal boundary of Africa.”] the boundary of all Africa.

Now I shall measure the locations, names, and dimensions of the islands [Col. 0694B] in the Mediterranean Sea. [Note: [Col. 0694D] *Locations, names, and dimensions*. Meursius has “locations and names and dimensions.” Soon afterward, the Augustan edition has *spatia demetiar* (“I shall measure the dimensions”); others have *dimetiar*, and both readings have been admitted into the text.]

The island of Cyprus is enclosed on the east by the Syrian Sea, [Note: [Col. 0694D] *Which they call the Issic Gulf*. The second Florentine manuscript has “which they call the Missic Gulf”; the third, “which they call the Misic Gulf.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, Meursius, the first edition, and the Venetian editions have “which they call the Missic Gulf.” The Augustan edition has “the Mesic Gulf”; the Ultrajectine, “the Missic Gulf.” The legitimate reading is preserved by the second Leiden manuscript and Perizonius. The error arose from an abbreviation in writing and the transposition of the letter *m*, producing *qm Issicum* (“which [is] Issic”).] on the west by the Pamphylian Sea, on the north by the Cilician Aulon, [Note: [Col. 0694D] *Cilician Aulon*. The first edition has “Aulon of Cilicia.” The Venetians, followed by the Paris edition, have “the Cilician Vulona.” Soon afterward, the Florentine manuscripts have *Phoenicis* instead of *Phoenices*.] and on the south by the sea of Syria and Phoenicia. Its length [Note: [Col. 0694D] *In length … in breadth*. Certain editions, such as the first, the Venetians, the Augustan, and the Bolsuingian, here and below have *in longum* (“lengthwise”) and *in latum* (“breadthwise”).] is 175 miles, and its breadth 125 miles.

The island of Crete is bounded on the east by the Carpathian Sea, on the west and north by the Cretan Sea, [Note: [Col. 0695B] *On the south by the Libyan Sea*. The word *mari* (“sea”) has fallen out of the Fabrician and Mainz editions, although it is found in all the other manuscripts and printed editions.] and on the south by the Libyan Sea, which they also call the Adriatic. [Note: [Col. 0695B] *It has in length 172 miles and in breadth 50*. The Augustan edition has: “This has in length 172 miles, in breadth 50.” But the first edition has: “It has in length 177 miles and in breadth 50.”] It has in length 172 miles and in breadth 50. [Note: [Col. 0695C] *In those [manuscripts] and in breadth*. The second and third Florentine manuscripts, the second, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, Meursius, Perizonius, and certain editions delete the conjunction *et* (“and”). For “172,” the first Leiden manuscript counts four hundred and seventy-two.] 

The Cyclades Islands, of which Rhodes is the first on the east, Tenedos lies to the north, Carpathos to the south, and Cythera to the west, are bounded on the east by the shores of Asia, on the west [Note: [Col. 0695C] *By the Icarius Sea*. The Augustan edition has “by the Ionian Sea.”] by the Icarius Sea, on the north by the Aegean Sea, and on the south by the Carpathian Sea. There are, in all, fifty-three Cyclades. [Note: [Col. 0695C] *Fifty-three*. As commonly happens among authors, the number of these islands differs in the printed editions and manuscripts. The second Florentine manuscript writes and enumerates fifty-three; all the Leiden manuscripts, as well as the Ultrajectine and the Augustan edition, have fifty-four; the received reading is retained by Perizonius and Meursius together with the other editions.] [33] These extend from north to south [Note: [Col. 0695D] *Fifty miles*. Here and below, the fourth Leiden manuscript prefers *mille* (“one thousand”) to *millia* (“thousands”). There is great variation in the number of miles. The second Florentine manuscript, together with the first and Augustan editions, has 500 miles; all the Leiden manuscripts and the Ultrajectine support it. The third Florentine has 50 miles, a number retained by Meursius, Perizonius, and most editions. Soon afterward, the Ultrajectine has “from east to west.”] for fifty miles, and from east to west for two hundred miles.

The island of Sicily has three promontories: one called Pelorum, [Note: [Col. 0695D] *Pelorum*. The first edition, as well as the Paris edition, has *Pelorus*; below they likewise have *Pachynus* and *Lilybaeus*.] which faces north, and near which lies the city of Messana; the second, called Pachynum, beneath which lies the city of Syracuse, [Note: [Col. 0695D] *Faces the southeast*. The Ultrajectine and the fourth Leiden edition place this phrase first.] faces the southeast; the third, called Lilybaeum, where a city of the same name is also situated, [Note: [Col. 0695D] *Is directed*. The first edition has *dirigiturque* (“and is directed”).] is directed toward the west.

This island has [Note: [Col. 0695D] *From Pelorum to Pachynum, 159 miles*. One manuscript has 149, others 159. If we follow Strabo’s stadia, the smaller number seems more likely to be correct. FABRICIUS.] from Pelorum to Pachynum 159 miles, [Note: [Col. 0696B] *One hundred and fifty-nine*. The second Florentine has 169; the first Leiden, together with the first edition and Aethicus, 149.] and from Pachynum to Lilybaeum [Note: [Col. 0696B] *One hundred and seventy-seven*. The first edition, together with the Venetian and Paris editions and the third Leiden manuscript, adds *millia* (“miles”) at the end; that manuscript, however, writes 187 miles. Aethicus likewise has 174 miles.] 177 miles.

To the east this island is enclosed by the Adriatic Sea, to the south by the African Sea, which lies opposite the Subventani and the Lesser Syrtes; to the west and north it has the Tyrrhenian Sea; from the north [Note: [Col. 0696C] *As far as the southeast*. The second Florentine, the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, Perizonius, the Ultrajectine, and the first, Augustan, and Venetian editions insert *ad* (“toward”). The other manuscripts and editions delete it.] as far as the southeast, the Adriatic Strait, which divides the Tauromenitans of Sicily from the Bruttians of Italy.

The islands of Sardinia and Corsica are separated by a narrow strait, that is, [Note: [Col. 0696C] *Twenty miles*. The first edition and the Venetian editions have “twenty miles.”] twenty miles. Sardinia has on the south, opposite Numidia, the Caralitani; opposite the island of Corsica—that is, toward the north—it has the Ulbienses. Its [Note: [Col. 0696C] *In length*. The Hittorpian edition has *in longum* (“lengthwise”).] length is 230 [34] miles, [Note: [Col. 0696C] *Two hundred and thirty*. The Augustan edition has 320, and the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts acknowledge the same number.] and its breadth [Note: [Col. 0696C] *Two hundred and eighty*. Thus the Augustan edition and several manuscripts. Others, including the Perizonian manuscript and the second Florentine, have 180. In Aethicus’s *Cosmography*, the hundreds have dropped out, and only 80 is written.] 280 miles.

It has to the east [Note: [Col. 0696C] *And to the north*. The second and third Florentine manuscripts, Meursius, and the first edition have “and to the north.”] and north [Note: [Col. 0696C] *The Tyrrhenian Sea*. Thus the Ultrajectine and the first, second, and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the first, Augustan, and Venetian editions. The others have “the Tyrrhenic Sea,” which I do not prefer, since Aethicus also writes “Tyrrhenian,” and Orosius soon afterward writes “Sardinian,” not “Sardic,” although the latter is found there—only in my parchment manuscripts.] the Tyrrhenian Sea, which faces [Note: [Col. 0696D] *The harbor of the city of Rome*. The first edition has “and the harbor of the city”; the Paris edition, “and the harbor of the Roman city”; Aethicus’s *Cosmography*, “the harbor of the eternal city of Rome.” The manuscripts preserve the received reading.] the harbor [Col. 0696B] of the city of Rome; to the west, the Sardinian Sea; to the southwest, the distant Balearic Islands; to the south, the Numidian Gulf; and to the north, as I have said, Corsica.

The island of Corsica is angular, with many promontories. It has [Note: [Col. 0696D] *From the east*. The second and fourth Leiden manuscripts add “and from the north.”] to the east the Tyrrhenian Sea [Note: [Col. 0696D] *And the harbor of the City*. The second and fourth Leiden manuscripts have “which faces the harbor of the City.” Then, after *Urbis* (“City”), they add *Romae* (“of Rome”), together with the first and third editions and the Ultrajectine. But this seems to have entered from what precedes, as though from a gloss; for in the Augustan edition it reads, “that is, of Rome.”], and the harbor of the City; to the south, Sardinia; to the west, [Note: [Col. 0696D] *The distant Balearic Islands*. I added the last two words to Orosius from the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts, because they also occur in Aethicus’s *Cosmography*.] the distant Balearic Islands; and to the northwest and north, the Ligurian Gulf. [Col. 0697A] Its length is [Note: [Col. 0697B] *In length, miles*. Certain editions have *in longum* (“lengthwise”), and soon afterward the first Leiden manuscript has *mille passus* (“one thousand paces”) instead of “twenty-six.”] 160 miles and its breadth 26 miles.

There are two Balearic Islands, Major and Minor, each of which contains two towns. Major has Tarraco, a city of Hispania; Minor has [Note: [Col. 0697B] *Barcino*. The manuscripts read *Barcelonam*, *Barchilonam*, *Barcinolam*, and *Barcilon*. In some, above this, are found *Tarraconam*, *Tragonam*, and so forth.] Barcino [Note: [Col. 0697B] *Toward the north*. The word *in* (“toward”) is absent from the first Leiden manuscript. Soon afterward, the Augustan edition has *habent* (“they have”) instead of *habet* (“it has”).] opposite it toward the north. Beneath Major lies the island of Ebusus.

Then, to the east, [the islands have] Sardinia; to the north, the Gallic Sea; to the south and southwest, the Mauretanian Sea; [Note: [Col. 0697B] *To the west it faces the Iberian Sea*. This sentence is absent from the Augustan edition. That edition, together with four Leiden manuscripts, reads *spectant pelagus* (“they face the sea”), as though the subject were the Balearic Islands and not Corsica. After *Mauritanicum*, the second Florentine deletes *pelagus* (“sea”).] to the west, they face the Iberian Sea.

These are the islands situated from the Hellespont all the way to the Ocean throughout the Great Sea, and they are regarded as especially renowned both for their cultivation and for their historical memory.

[35] I have briefly surveyed, as best I could, the provinces and islands [Note: [Col. 0697C] *Of the whole world*. The first Leiden manuscript transposes the words.] of the whole world. Now I shall set forth the local miseries [Note: [Col. 0697C] *Of individual peoples*. All the Leiden manuscripts have “of peoples and islands,” and the second, together with the Ultrajectine, additionally reads “of individual peoples and islands.” But Meursius, with Perizonius, upholds the received reading apart from the Florentine manuscripts, and I judge it to be the true and genuine one.] of individual peoples, as they have existed without interruption from the beginning, and how [Note: [Col. 0697C] *And in what ways*. The third and fourth Leiden manuscripts delete *et* (“and”).] and in what ways they arose [Col. 0697B] and at what times [Note: [Col. 0697C] *At what times they arose*. The fourth Leiden manuscript deletes *que* after *quibus*. In the first Leiden manuscript, *temporibus* (“times”) is written above the line. It could appropriately be added, for Orosius will now relate not only what evils occurred and how, with respect to their magnitude, and to whom, with respect to peoples or nations, but also at what times they occurred. In this final respect especially Orosius’s diligence is evident; for this reason he is commonly kept at hand by all learned men, and his authority is regularly employed. I therefore think the passage should be read as follows: “Now I shall set forth the local miseries of peoples, and of individuals, as they have existed without interruption from the beginning: how, by whom, and at what times they arose,” and so forth.] they arose, insofar as I shall be able, I will relate.

## CHAPTER III. On the Flood in the time of Noah

[Note: [Col. 0697D] When, after the making and adornment of this world, the human being whom God had made upright and unstained had subjected himself to death, and consequently the human race, corrupted by lusts, had become utterly sullied by sins. The Venetian manuscript returned the words “had subjected himself to death” to Orosius. Likewise, it returned the word “utterly”; Marcoduranus omitted it. I have changed *obsorbuisset* and *obsurbuisset* to *obsorduisset*. This is perhaps correct. *Obsorbuisset* or *obsurduisset* might also be correct. LAUT.—Apart from the Venetian and Paris editions, Hittorp, and Cervicornus, the first edition also displays “had subjected himself to death”; but neither the Augustan edition nor any of the manuscripts we consulted recognizes this addition. The first edition also has *funditus absorberetur* (“would be utterly engulfed”), for which the Venetian and Paris editions have *funditus obsorberetur*. But in all the Florentine and other manuscripts that I examined, the reading is *peccatis obsorduisset*, a verb corresponding to *immaculatum* (“unstained”), which occurs above. The Mainz edition, edited by Andreas Schottus, reads: “the human being whom He had made upright and unstained according to His own image,” inserting three words contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts and editions.]

When, after the making and adornment of this world, [Col. 0698A] the human being whom God had made upright and unstained [Note: [Col. 0698B] *And consequently the human race, corrupted by lusts, had become sullied by sins*. The common editions add before these words, “had subjected himself to death.” Since we found this in none of the ancient books, we deleted it as an interpolation, without prejudging the matter. FABRICIUS.] and consequently the human race, corrupted by lusts, had become utterly sullied by sins, an unjust license was immediately followed by a just punishment. [36]

The sentence of the Creator and Judge God, assigned to the sinful human being and to the earth because of the human being, and destined to endure forever while human beings inhabit the earth, is endured by all, whether unwillingly we approve it by denial or confessing it submit to it. [Note: [Col. 0698C] *Even unwillingly*. The first edition has *videlicet* (“namely”).] Its weakness brands itself as a witness upon stubborn minds, unless faithful Scripture has instructed them otherwise. [Note: [Col. 0698C] *And afterward, when the flood had been poured out in Noah’s time*. The last two words are absent from the ancient books and may appropriately be omitted. FABRICIUS.—The Ultrajectine and Meursius manuscripts delete them. Among the Leiden manuscripts, the second and third have *suffuso sub Noe in omni terra* (“when [the sea] had been poured out under Noah over the whole earth”); the fourth has *refuso sub Noe ipso in omni terra* (“when [the sea] itself had been poured out under Noah over the whole earth”); the others, together with the ancient editions, have *refuso sub Noe in omni terra* (“when [the sea] had been poured out under Noah over the whole earth”). Soon afterward, Meursius and the second Florentine manuscript have *missoque diluvio* (“and when the flood had been sent”) instead of *immissoque* (“and when the flood had been sent in”).]

Then, when the sea had been poured over the whole earth and the flood had been sent in, so that, with the entire world covered, there was one expanse of sky and sea, the whole human race was destroyed, with a few preserved in the ark, by the merit of their faith, to re-establish its origin, as the most truthful writers teach with complete clarity. [Note: [Col. 0698D] *The most truthful writers*. Perizonius deletes the first word, but the Hittorpian and Bolsuingian editions read “the most truthful writers and teachers.”] 

Yet even those who, ignorant of past times and of the very author of time, nevertheless learned this from the evidence and conjecture of stones, [Note: [Col. 0698D] *From the evidence and conjecture of stones*. In Genesis 8 we read that Noah’s ark came to rest upon the mountains of Ararat—that is, of Armenia—where, according to Jerome, its traces remain to this day. Jerome discusses Ararat likewise in the eleventh book of his commentary on Isaiah. Josephus, *Antiquities*, book I, writes that the Armenians gave the place where Noah came out of the ark the name ἀποβατήριον (“place of disembarkation”). FABRICIUS.—“From judgment and inference”: thus I read it on the authority of the Cologne manuscript, not *conjectura* (“conjecture”). LAUT.—I change nothing, although the Augustan edition also has *judicio* (“judgment”). Soon afterward, the Ultrajectine has “and shells and oysters.”] which we often see rough with shells and oysters, and even hollowed out by waters in remote mountains, bore witness to it. And although we could still bring forward matters of this kind that are both worthy of narration and certain on the basis of trustworthy evidence [Note: [Col. 0699B] *By us*. The Perizonian manuscript deletes these words.], nevertheless let these statements suffice as the two principal facts: concerning the transgression of the first human being and the condemnation of his offspring and life, and then [Note: [Col. 0699B] *The destruction*. The second Florentine has “concerning the destruction.”] the destruction of the whole human race. Let it suffice, provided only that, if anything which pagan historians recorded in some orderly fashion [Note: [Col. 0699B] *Occurred*. The older editions have *contigerint* (“may have occurred”); the Augustan edition has *contigerint aliquo ordine* (“may have occurred in some orderly fashion”).] from our history is found, it may be set forth more fully, together with the rest, in the very order in which [Note: [Col. 0699B] *They occurred*. The second Florentine has *incurrerunt* (“they occurred”); the third, *incurrerat* (“it had occurred”).] they occurred.

## 37 CHAPTER IV. On Ninus and Semiramis and their kingdoms

One thousand three hundred years before the founding of the City, [Note: [Col. 0699B] *Ninus, king of the Assyrians*. Ninus was not the first but the third king of the Assyrians, as is known from Berossus. But because Ninus was “the first of those handed down into history and memory,” as Diodorus writes at the beginning of Book II, historians—including Ctesias, Diodorus, Eusebius, Justin, Orosius, Cassiodorus, and others—began their accounts with Ninus. FABRICIUS.] Ninus, king of the Assyrians, was the first, as they themselves claim, to carry arms abroad, driven by a desire to extend his rule. He conducted a bloody war for fifty years throughout Asia. [Note: [Col. 0699B] *For fifty years*. The Venetian edition has “for fifty years.”] Rising from the south [Note: [Col. 0699B] *And from the Red Sea*. The first Leiden edition has “from the Red Sea”; the fourth has “and from the Red Sea.” The Venetian editions likewise.] and from the Red Sea, [Col. 0700A] he devastated and conquered the Pontus Euxinus beneath the farthest north, and stirred up the Scythian barbarian people, still at that time [Note: [Col. 0699C] *Unwarlike and innocent*. The common reading is “both unwarlike and innocent,” but the Venetian editions, together with the first and Augustan editions, and three Leiden manuscripts and Perizonius, delete *et* (“and”).] unwarlike and innocent, [Note: [Col. 0699C] *He roused its dormant ferocity*. We corrected this passage on the authority of the manuscripts, although the common reading could be tolerated. FABRICIUS.—Not only can the old reading *excitare* (“to rouse”) be tolerated, but it ought to be preferred to the new *excitavit* (“he roused”), with the manuscripts supporting it. Three of them, together with the Florentine manuscripts, Perizonius, and Meursius, read *excitare*, not *excitavit*. Ninus, it says, taught the Scythian barbarian people, still at that time unwarlike and innocent, “to rouse its dormant ferocity and to recognize its own strength,” and so forth. The first and third Leiden manuscripts have *Scythiamque barbariam*; the fourth, *Scythiamque barbaricam*; the second and the Ultrajectine, *Scythicamque barbariem*. In the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, Meursius, and Perizonius, the reading is *torpentem*, not *torpentemque*, as in the printed editions, or *torpentem* as in Perizonius.] teaching it to rouse its dormant ferocity [Note: [Col. 0699C] *Ferocity*. The Hittorpian and Bolsuingian editions have *saevitiae* (“of ferocity”).], to recognize its own strength, [Note: [Col. 0699C] *And to live no longer on the milk of animals but on human blood, and so forth*. Thus all the manuscripts and the first and Augustan editions. But Hittorp and Bolsuing, together with the Paris and Venetian editions, have “and no longer to drink the milk of animals but human blood.” Concerning the Scythians, Justin, Book II, chapter 2: “They feed on milk and honey.” A verse hurled at Tiberius in Rome is not unlike Orosius’s wording; Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 59:

> He loathes wine, because now this man thirsts for blood;  
> He drinks it eagerly, as once he drank unmixed wine.] and ultimately [Note: [Col. 0699D] *He taught them to conquer while being conquered*. Thus all the Leiden manuscripts. The others have “he taught them to conquer while he conquers,” so that *vincit* (“he conquers”) refers to Ninus himself. But the conquered themselves, while they are conquered, learn the arts of conquering, by which they had previously fallen while still inexperienced, and through which, hardened, they later prevailed over their enemies. For Ninus was the first to bring war against neighboring peoples and subdued, as far as the borders of Libya, nations still inexperienced in resistance. Justin, Book I, chapter 1.] he taught them to conquer while being conquered.

[38] Finally, he overcame and killed Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, whom they also report to have been the inventor of magical arts, after defeating him in battle. Then, while attacking a city that was revolting against him, [Note: [Col. 0700B] *Struck by an arrow*. The common editions and some manuscripts have *sagittae ictu* (“by the stroke of an arrow”). I preferred the reading of the Florentine manuscripts, Perizonius, and Meursius, which had previously appeared in the Augustan edition. Aelian gives a different account of Ninus’s death, *Various History*, Book VII, chapter 1, which seems to belong among fables. Justin, in the cited passage, simply says that after Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, had been killed, Ninus himself died, leaving behind his minor son Ninya.] he died, struck by an arrow. [Note: [Col. 0700C] *After his death, his wife Semiramis succeeded him*. Diodorus discusses Semiramis at length in Book II. FABRICIUS.] After his death, his wife Semiramis succeeded him, a man in courage, presenting herself in dress as a son. [Note: [Col. 0700C] *Presenting a son in appearance*. Correctly so, since she pretended to be a son rather than Ninus’s wife, and a boy rather than a woman. See Justin, Book I, chapter 2. *Woman* is wrong. All the Leiden manuscripts, together with the Ultrajectine, have “a son in spirit and appearance”; the second Florentine, “a son in spirit and appearance”; the Venetian editions, the Augustan, and the first edition, “carrying a man in spirit and appearance”; the Bolsuingian edition, “carrying a son in spirit and appearance.”] She exercised peoples already rendered eager by long familiarity with blood through forty-two years of massacring nations.

Not content, as a woman, with the boundaries that she had received from her husband, then the sole warrior, [Note: [Col. 0700C] *For fifty years*. Some manuscripts and editions have *in quinquaginta annis* (“over fifty years”). Others more correctly delete *in* (“in”). Meursius has “over forty-four years.”] and that had been acquired over fifty years, [Col. 0700B] she added Ethiopia to her rule, [Note: [Col. 0700D] *Overwhelmed in war and drenched in blood*. Two Florentine manuscripts and all the Leiden manuscripts, together with Meursius, Perizonius, and the Ultrajectine, have “pressed down in war,” and so forth. The first and Augustan editions likewise display this reading. The printed first and Venetian editions have *illitam* (“smeared”) instead of *interlitam* (“drenched”). Some manuscripts soon afterward have “to her rule.”] after crushing it in war and drenching it in blood. [Note: [Col. 0700D] *She also made war against the Indians*. Besides Diodorus, see Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 2. Strabo, Book XV, reports from Megasthenes that Semiramis died before she departed from India. FABRICIUS.] She also made war against the Indians, [Note: [Col. 0700D] *By which*. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the older printed editions, have *quo* (“by which”).] [the country] into which, apart from her and Alexander the Great, no one entered.

This was crueler and more grievous at that time than it is now: to pursue and slaughter peoples living in peace, because then among them there were neither wars abroad nor such extensive exercises of desire at home. Thus she, burning with lust and thirsting for blood, amid unceasing [Note: [Col. 0701B] *And adulteries*. Three manuscripts—namely, Meursius and the two Florentine manuscripts—increase the phrase by adding *et* (“and”); the Augustan edition adds still more, reading “amid unceasing banquets and adulteries and murders.” Perhaps that is more correct.] adulteries and murders, [Note: [Col. 0701B] *When she had delighted in all those whom, summoned in royal fashion and treated as prostitutes, she had enjoyed in intercourse, etc.* By following the faulty edition and punctuation of Hittorp and Bolsuing, Fabricius and Schottus greatly obscure the meaning of this passage. In their editions it reads: “when, having delighted in intercourse with all those summoned to the palace and treated as prostitutes, she killed them.” Orosius’s meaning is that Semiramis received royally all those whom she desired lustfully; but after she had rolled about with them in shameful love affairs, becoming weary of them and desiring others and new lovers, she killed them all. The Augustan edition has: “when she had delighted in those treated as prostitutes in intercourse, and had killed them.”] when she had delighted in all those whom, summoned to the palace in royal fashion and treated as prostitutes, she had enjoyed in intercourse, killed them, and finally, [Note: [Col. 0701B] *With a son shamefully conceived*. Orosius’s words seem to indicate that this son of Semiramis, whom writers call Ninya, was not begotten by Ninus but conceived through promiscuous intercourse. For that reason he was exposed by his mother, but later recognized and received into the bed of his mother the queen—first secretly and lustfully, then openly and under the name of marriage.] with a son shamefully conceived, impiously exposed, [Note: [Col. 0701C] *Recognized incestuously*. My parchment manuscripts and the Augustan edition have *incestu* (“through incest”); this reading is also found in Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum Historiale*, which contains many excerpts from Orosius and others, Book II, chapter 103. The Augustan edition, together with my manuscripts, displays the earlier words in the plural, without any sense: “finally, with sons shamefully conceived, exposed, recognized through incest.” Instead of *obtexit* (“covered”), the Ultrajectine has *detexit* (“uncovered”).] covered her private disgrace with a public crime.

For she ordered that, with no respect for nature conveyed between parents and children, [Note: [Col. 0701C] *Concerning the pursuit of marriages*. The word *de* (“concerning”) is also inserted by Vincent of Beauvais.] the pursuit of marriages [Note: [Col. 0701C] *Should become free for anyone who wished it*. This is clearly the true reading of the passage, as is shown by chapter 16 of this book: “With the whole earth subjected and open to them, it was free to seize whatever each person wished.” Vincent of Beauvais reads, “so that it became free for anyone who wished it.” The first Leiden manuscript has “for anyone whom it might please, it would become free”; the second, “so that it might be free for anyone whom it pleased”; the third, “for anyone whom it pleased, it would become a freedman.” The Ultrajectine has “concerning marriages”—deleting *appetendis* (“to be pursued”)—“so that whatever pleased anyone might become permitted.”] should become free for anyone who wished it.

## 40 CHAPTER V. How the region of Pentapolis was struck and burned by heaven on account of the unspeakable crimes of lust

[Col. 0702A]

One thousand one hundred and sixty years before the founding of the City, a region bordering Arabia, [Note: [Col. 0701D] *One thousand one hundred and sixty*. The Augustan edition has 3,160.] which at that time [Note: [Col. 0701D] *Pentapolis*. It does not seem to me that this district bore this name before its destruction; rather, afterward writers called it so from the number of its five cities, four of which were destroyed by fire while one survived. The same designation occurs in the book entitled *Wisdom*, chapter 10, verse 6, where the just Lot is described as escaping the καταβάσιον πῦρ Πενταπόλεως, “the descending fire of Pentapolis.”] was called Pentapolis, was utterly burned by heavenly fire. [Note: [Col. 0701D] *Among others*. In other copies the faulty reading *inter alia* (“among other things”) is found. The passage is in Tacitus, Book XXI. On this region, see also Egesippus, Book IV, chapter 18. FABRICIUS.—Some printed editions, contrary to the manuscripts, have *inter alia*, but besides Tacitus, *Histories*, Book V, chapter 7, Solinus, Strabo, and others also remember this disaster.] Among others, Cornelius Tacitus reports this, saying:

“Not far from there are fields which, as they say, were once fertile, [Note: [Col. 0702B] *Fields*. All the Leiden manuscripts, the Ultrajectine, and certain editions have *campos* (“fields”).] and inhabited by great cities, [Note: [Col. 0702B] *And by great cities*. The Ultrajectine manuscript has “by great cities.” The Florentine has “by great men,” though *viribus* (“strength”) had previously stood there. The second Florentine, together with Meursius and Perizonius, has “by great strength.” Tacitus preserves the received reading, and both sacred Scripture and Orosius below sufficiently attest that they had been great cities. Soon afterward, the Perizonian manuscript and the Augustan and Venetian editions have *habitas* (“inhabited”) instead of *habitatas* (“inhabited”).] were burned by thunderbolts,” [Note: [Col. 0702B] *Burned by the stroke of lightning*. Pichena showed that this should be read thus, not *fulminum ictu* (“by the stroke of lightning”) as an alteration of Tacitus. The older editions and all the manuscripts of Orosius support it except the Ultrajectine and the first, second, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, which have *ictu*. The discharge of lightning indicates God’s anger. In Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 46, Juno, sharpening her indignation by the example of Pallas, who had burned the fleet of the Argives with lightning, says: ]

Jupiter himself hurled swift fire from the clouds. Tertullian calls it “fiery rain” in the *Apology*, chapter 4, p. 343: “When the neighboring regions, Sodom and Gomorrah, were scorched by fiery rain.”] They had burned by the stroke of lightning; but traces remain, and that the earth itself, [Note: “Solid in appearance.” It is commonly read *solida*, “solid.” In Tacitus the wording is *terramque specie torridam*, “and the earth, hot in appearance.” FABR. — Among the manuscripts that prefer *specie solida*, “solid in appearance,” are the first and second Leiden manuscripts, agreeing with my copy. The second and third Florentine manuscripts, as well as the first editions, those of Hittorp, Bolsuing, and Venice, likewise read *specie solida*; the Augsburg edition and the remaining manuscripts have *specie solidam*, a reading apparently supported by Tacitus’s *torridam*. It is uncertain, however, whether *solidam* or *torridam* should be read in Tacitus. Since Orosius copied Tacitus, he seems to have reproduced his very words. I would not doubt this were it not that Justin’s wording is altered when he discusses Joseph below, in chapter 7. What appears externally and what actually exists are set against each other. If, then, the earth appears hot externally, there is no reason to wonder if the crops touched by it turn to ash. Tacitus continues: “For everything produced spontaneously, or sown by hand, whether it grew only to the height of grass or flower, or matured to its usual appearance, withers away black and empty as though into ash.” Add Tertullian, *Apology*, loc. cit.: “The earth still smells of the fire, and if any tree fruits attempt to grow there, they exist only for the eyes; once touched, they turn to ash.” Just as the fruits are solid only in appearance, so the earth itself is solid only in appearance; within, it is barren, burned out, and parched. In place of *frugiferam*, “fruit-bearing,” one of the Leiden manuscripts has *fructiferam*.] solid in appearance, had lost its productive power.

And although at this point he said nothing about cities burned because of human sins, as though unaware of the matter, a little later, as if he had forgotten his own plan, [Note: “He adds and says.” The first edition has *subjecit et ait*, “he added and said,” followed by the Venetian and Hittorp editions; the second and third Florentine manuscripts likewise have *ait*, “he says.”] he adds and says: [Note: “I, just as I would grant that famous…” *Inclytas* also occurs in the old manuscripts, but Tacitus has *Judaicas*, “Jewish.” FABR. — This was changed in the better editions of Tacitus.]

“I, just as I would grant that once-famous cities [Col. 0703A] burned with heavenly fire, so I think that the earth was infected and corrupted by the lake’s exhalation.”

By saying this, although unwillingly, he openly revealed—with respect to the burned cities, which unquestionably perished because of the guilt of sinners—[Note: “Were consumed.” The first, Venetian, and Hittorp editions, as well as the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, have *conflagraverant*, “had been consumed.”] and by confessing that he both knew and acknowledged the fact, [Note: “And that he knew and acknowledged it.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts read *scisse confessus*, “having confessed that he knew,” with the remaining words deleted. The second Leiden manuscript has *scisse se confessus*.] that he did not lack confidence in his knowledge, but rather the will to express what he knew—a point which [Note: “By me now.” This is the reading of the Augsburg edition and the first and third Leiden manuscripts. Others commonly have *nunc a me*, “now by me.” Immediately afterward, *profertur*, “is brought forward,” occurs with the Venetian and first editions.] I shall now set forth more fully. [Note: “On the border of Arabia and Palestine.” Moses discusses the destruction of these cities in Genesis 19. FABR. My parchment copy has *in confinibus*, “in the borders.”]

On the border of Arabia and Palestine, where the mountains, receding on either side, enclose the plains below, [Note: “The mountains released on either side.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts read: “where, the mountains being released on either side, the plains lying below are received”; the Augsburg edition reads likewise, except that it has *demissis*, “lowered.” A mountain is *demissus* when it gradually broadens from its summit toward the plain; Orosius seems to call *dimissi montes* those that are divided and separated through the middle of the plain.] there were five cities: Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboim, and Zoar. But Zoar was small among them; [Note: “Those were broad and large.” Some printed editions have “large and broad”; the first and third Leiden manuscripts have “broad and large”; the Augsburg edition has “but those were broad and large.”] the others were broad and large—for they possessed both the fertility of the soil and the river Jordan, which spread across the level land and, dividing it most advantageously, supplied an increase of abundance.

For this entire region, using its blessings badly, [Col. 0703B] abundance became the cause of evils. [Note: “For from abundance…” My manuscript has “and from luxury.” But the four Leiden manuscripts arrange the passage as follows: “For from the abundance of foul luxury lusts grew strong.”]

For from abundance came luxury, and from luxury foul lusts grew strong, so that males rushed upon males, committing indecency without regard even to place, status, [Col. 0704A] or age. [Note: “They rushed.” Some manuscripts and printed editions have *proruerunt*, “they rushed”; others have *proruerint*, “they may have rushed.”]

Therefore God, angered, rained fire and sulfur upon this land, and, having burned the entire region together with its peoples and cities, condemned it to eternal destruction as a perpetual witness to his judgment, [Note: “He condemned it to eternal destruction.” Some transpose the words as “he condemned it with eternal destruction.” The first edition, together with the first manuscript, has *damnatione*, “condemnation,” instead of *perditione*, “destruction.” Immediately afterward the third Florentine manuscript has *quondam forma*, “the former appearance.”] so that even now the region’s shape is indeed visible, but it is found to be [Note: “A region of ash.” After these words, the 1471 Augsburg edition of Johann Schuszler inserts the following passage: “There green fruits and formed clusters of grapes, so as to arouse desire in those who eat them: if you pluck them, they split apart into ash and raise smoke, as though they were burning.” But since these words occur verbatim in Hegesippus—or rather, in Saint Ambrose—and were taken from there, they do not seem to have originated with Orosius. The passage in Hegesippus occurs in book 4, chapter 18, *On the Destruction of Jerusalem*: “There green fruits and formed clusters of grapes, so as to arouse in those who look at them a desire to eat them. If you pluck them, they split apart and dissolve into ash, and raise smoke as though they were still burning.” In the following phrase, the Perizonius manuscript has *vallem*, “valley,” instead of *convallem*, “hollow valley.”]

a region of ash, and the entire hollow valley which the Jordan had watered is now covered by a sea. [Note: “Covers.” The Augsburg edition and the first and third Leiden manuscripts have *tegit*, “covers.”]

And so great was the fury of divine indignation over matters—as they are thought to be—so small [Note: “And so great was the divine indignation over matters—as they are thought to be—so small.” Some books have “the judgment of divine indignation was aroused”; others have “fury was aroused,” a reading retained by Marcoduranus. I think both readings entered the text from a scribe’s gloss. I therefore removed them, in elegant Latin and with the support also of the Cologne manuscript. LAUT. — The very first edition has: “And so, over matters—as they are thought to be—small, the judgment of divine indignation was aroused.” The second, or Augsburg, edition reproduces Lautius’s reading from the Cologne manuscript; Hittorp and Bolsuing, together with the Venetians, follow the first edition. Among the manuscripts, the Utrecht manuscript and the second and third Leiden manuscripts have *furor*, “fury.” But the second and third Florentine manuscripts, and the first Leiden manuscript together with Perizonius’s and my own, support Lautius’s correction. Since copyists did not understand the expression, they corrupted it; thus the fourth Leiden manuscript reads: “So great was the divine indignation over matters—as they were thought to be—small.” The following words are not recognized by the first edition, which is followed by the Venetian editions.]

that, because those people, misusing blessings, [Note: “The fruits of mercies.” All the editions contain here a very disgraceful error, reading *fructus miseriarum*, “fruits of miseries.” We learn the true reading from the fourth Leiden manuscript and my own. All the others retain the received error; these words are very often exchanged in manuscripts. In this passage my manuscript has *Al. miseriarum*, “alternatively, miseries,” written in the margin. The good things bestowed upon us from heaven, which the wicked misuse, are not fruits of miseries but fruits of God’s mercies—for it is God who is under discussion here. The Utrecht manuscript has the word *et*, “and,” immediately before *nutrimenta*, “nourishments.”]

had made the fruits of mercies into nourishments for lusts, the very earth that had contained these cities, first burned by fires and afterward overwhelmed by waters, might perish from the sight of all humanity forever. [Note: “Might perish from common sight.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts have *communi pereat adspectu*, “may perish from common sight”; the second and fourth have *communi periret adspectu*, “might perish from common sight.” Incorrectly. Suetonius, *Life of Vespasian*, chapter 11: “Therefore the emperor too regularly visited the place of his origin, while the villa remained as it had once been, so that nothing might be lost to the accustomed sight of his eyes.”]

## Chapter VI. A comparison of the Sodomite and Roman disasters

[Col. 0704B]

Therefore now, if it pleases them, let those who spit upon Christ, whom we have shown to be the judge of the ages, distinguish—as far as lies in them—the causes of Sodom and Rome, and compare their punishments. I need not review these matters at length, especially because they are known to everyone. Yet how gladly I would accept their judgments if they would faithfully confess what they think: [Note: “Although what…” This is found in the very first edition, and I do not doubt that it can preserve its proper place better than *quid*, “what,” which all the others commonly substitute for *quod*, “that,” except the Augsburg edition, which has *quidquid*, “whatever,” with a tolerable sense. My manuscript and the third Florentine likewise have *quod*. The first and fourth Leiden manuscripts have: “And although what they say about Christian times…”] although I do not think it should be taken too seriously that a few of them murmur about Christian times, and do so in corners, [Note: “They murmur.” The first Leiden manuscript has *murmurant*, “they murmur.”] when the thought and speech of the entire Roman people, in one harmonious voice and with equal judgment, [Note: “Is known.” Perizonius has *est cognitus*, “has become known.”] are known.

Indeed, that sentiment most unmistakably testified that their habitual practice of pleasures had faltered in its attachment to them for a little while, with only a slight and passing disturbance, [Note: “For a short while, his accustomed practice.” My parchment copy has *pari consuetudine*, “with the same practice.”] when he cried out freely: [Note: “So that he might cry out freely.” The third Florentine has *ubi libere conclamaret*, “when he cried out freely”; the fourth Leiden manuscript has *ut libere clamaret*, “so that he might cry out.”]

“If it received back the Circus, nothing would have happened to it.” [Note: “That nothing had been done to him.” The Augsburg edition and the Utrecht manuscript transpose the words: “that nothing had happened to him.”] That is, the swords of the Goths had done nothing at Rome, if the Romans were allowed to watch the Circus games. [Note: “If it be granted.” The first edition has *si concederetur*, “if it were granted,” rather than *si concedatur*, “if it be granted.”]

Unless perhaps—[Note: “As is the custom among most people.” The Augsburg edition gives, ironically: “as courage is found among most people,” a reading that should not be dismissed because of what follows. The second and third Florentine manuscripts have “as is customary among most people.”] as is especially the custom at the present time—those who regard even a small anxiety arising after a long period of rest as intolerable labor [Note: “That has arisen.” The Utrecht manuscript has *obortamque*, “that has arisen”; the second and third Florentine manuscripts have *parum obortam*, “a little anxiety that has arisen.”] place these most gentle admonitions [Note: “These.” One Leiden manuscript has *tantas*, “so great”; the third Florentine has “these so very gentle admonitions.”]—by which we are all at some time touched—[Note: “By which we are touched.” The first edition and the Paris edition have *restringimur*, “we are constrained”; the Augsburg edition has *adstringimur*, “we are bound”; the first Leiden manuscript has *constringimur*, “we are compelled”; the third has *constringuntur*, “they are compelled.”] before the punishments of others, having heard and read about them; [Note: “Of others.” The first edition has *alienis*, “of those belonging to others”; the Augsburg edition has *praeponant*, “let them place before.”] I warn them at least by this very outcome of the Sodomites and Gomorrhans, so that [Note: “From this very matter.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has *ex hoc ipso*, “from this very matter”; the Utrecht manuscript has *vel de hoc ipso*, “or from this very matter.”] they may learn and understand how God punished sinners, how he can punish them, and how he will punish them.

## Chapter VII. The battle between the Telchines and the Carpathians and King Phoroneus; also the flood of Achaia

[Col. 0705D]

One thousand and seventy years before the founding of the City [Note: “The Telchines and Carpathians.” We have written *Telchines*, not *Telchises*, because Orosius immediately says that Rhodes was occupied by them; those who occupied Rhodes are called Telchines by the Greeks. Besides Strabo, Diodorus, book 5, mentions them: *τὴν δὲ νῆσον τὴν ὀνομαζομένην Ῥόδον κατῴκησαν οἱ προσαγορευόμενοι Τελχῖνες*, that is, “The island called Rhodes was first inhabited by those called Telchines.” In Eusebius’s *Chronicle* the event is described thus: “The Teltaphites and Carsatians undertake war against Phoroneus and the Parrhasians.” One manuscript reads *Carsatii*. FABR. — The old editions give these names as follows. The first, Augsburg, and Paris editions have *Thelcises et Carsathii*. Hittorp, together with the Venetian editions, has *Telchises et Carpathii*, as does Bolsuing. The second Florentine has *Thelcises et Cariani*; the third, *Thelcises et Chariatii*. The Utrecht and first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, as well as my own and Perizonius’s, all have *Telchises*, but instead of *Carpathii* they read: the first and third, *Carthasi*; the second and Utrecht manuscript, *Carsathii*; the fourth, *Cartharassi*; my manuscript, *Chariavi*; and Perizonius, *Charrathii*. Fabricius correctly changed the first name to *Telchines*, a form also preserved in the second Leiden manuscript and written above *Telchises* in the first. Apart from the authors cited by Fabricius, this reading is clearly supported by Pausanias and Apollodorus. Apollodorus, *Library*, book 2, chapter 1, writes that Phoroneus was the son of Inachus and king of the entire land afterward called the Peloponnese. He says that Phoroneus left a son, Apis, from whom that region was called Apia: Phoroneus, he says, *ὑπὸ Θελξίονος καὶ Τελχῖνος ἐπιβουλευθεὶς, ἄπαις ἀπέθανε*, “attacked by the plots of Thelxion and Telchin, died childless.” But according to the ancient Sicyonian traditions, reported by Pausanias, book 2, chapter 5, p. 123, Aegialeus first ruled that part of the Peloponnese which was called Aegialus after him, and there founded the city of Aegialea. He left a son, Europs, who had Telchin as a son; Telchin’s son was Apis, who fathered Thelxion. The descendants of Telchin were called Telchinii, and inhabited not only Rhodes but also Cyprus, as we shall soon say.]

the Telchines and [Col. 0707A] [Note: “The Carpathians.” If these people fought alongside the Telchines against Phoroneus, king of the Argives, they too must have inhabited the Peloponnese. But there were no Carpathians there, nor does anyone mention Carpathians in that land. The name is therefore corrupt in Orosius, as the multitude of variant readings also shows. I restore *Carnasii*, or *Carpasii*. My source for this emendation is Pausanias, who assigns to Messenia, in the Peloponnese, a region called *Καρνάσιον*, Carnasium, also known as Oechalia, book 4, chapter 11, p. 283; there he acknowledges the Messenian town of Carnasium, book 8, chapter 35, p. 670. In the same place he mentions the celebrated Carnasian grove, *Καρνάσιον ἄλσος*, through which the river Charadros flows, book 4, chapter 33, p. 362. I think that the Carnasians were also called Carpathians, since they seem to have left the Peloponnese together with the Telchines and gone to the island of Cyprus, where they founded the famous city of Carpasia. Strabo mentions it in book 14, p. 682—or p. 1001 of the latest edition—where the nearby island of Carpasia is also described. Two coins of Carpasia in Cyprus are extant, attesting the worship of the Cyprian Venus. On them appear the goddess’s head, a friendly star, and a winged boy about to shoot an arrow from a bow, with the inscription *ΚΑΡΠΑΣΙΩΝ*, “of the Carpasian people.”]

the Carpathians fought a stubborn battle [Note: “Against Phoroneus.” He was the second king of the Argives, according to Eusebius, and Plato mentions him in the *Timaeus*. Pausanias, book 2, writes that he compelled the Argives, previously scattered and living separately, to submit to the authority of a single city. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, says that *Αἰζειὸν καὶ Φορωνέα*, “Aegialeus and Phoroneus,” were the first to rule in the Peloponnese. FABRICIUS. — Apollodorus, *Library*, book 2, chapter 1, relates that Inachus was born from Oceanus and Tethys and gave his name to the river Inachus of the Argives; by Melissa, daughter of Oceanus, he had Phoroneus and Aegialeus. Phoroneus is said to have ruled the whole Peloponnese, after expelling his adversaries, the Telchines and Carnasians, or Carpathians. Pausanias, book 2, chapter 20, p. 155, records that the tomb of Phoroneus still existed and that sacrifices were performed for him among the Corinthians even in his own day.]

against Phoroneus, king of the Argives, and the [Note: “Parapasian people.” Some have written that *Paphasii* should also be read. I found *parapasios* in one manuscript and *Parphasios* in others. FABRIC. — Since no Parapasii are found in the Peloponnese, this name too seems corrupt. It appears in various forms. Of the Florentine manuscripts, the second has *Parapasios*, the third *Parphasyos*; of the Leiden manuscripts, the first and third have *Parachasios*, the second *Parasios*, and the fourth *Parapasios*; Perizonius has *Parthasios*, my manuscript *Parphasios*, and the Utrecht manuscript *Pharrasios*. All the printed editions have *Paraphasios*, except the Augsburg edition, which has *Pharphasios*; Hittorp and Bolsuing have *Paphasios* in the margin. I judge that *Parrhasios* should be restored, as the true reading is indicated by the second Leiden manuscript. The Parrhasians are known in the Peloponnese and are mentioned in Arcadia by Pausanias, book 8, chapter 27, p. 654. Among the Olympic victors was a not insignificant Arcadian Parrhasian named Demarchus, mentioned by the same Pausanias, book 6, chapter 8, p. 471.]
