Parapasian people, [Note: “With uncertain hope, and so forth.” The first edition, together with the Venetian editions, gives the entire passage as follows: “One thousand and seventy years before the founding of the City, while the Telchines, and so forth,” taking the words to mean that they “held hope without the fruit of victory.”] with uncertain hope and without the fruit of victory.

The same Telchines and Carpathians, defeated in battle shortly afterward, [Note: “Fugitives from their homeland and ignorant of circumstances, believing that they…” The common text reads *credentes quia se*, “believing because they,” without any coherent sense and most ineptly for the history. LAUT. — Although Lautius’s emendation may appeal to some, it does not please me. A very slight alteration leaves no harshness in the meaning. In Orosius’s manuscripts the words *quia* and *quod* are exchanged with one another a thousand times; therefore *quod* should unquestionably be restored here in place of *quia*. The reading found in the other manuscripts, *quoque*, is contradicted by what precedes, *ignarique rerum*, “ignorant of circumstances.” Since they were fugitives from their homeland, they sought a safe place of exile; ignorant of circumstances, they believed that by occupying Rhodes—which was both an island and farther from the Peloponnese—they could completely withdraw from contact with all human beings. I therefore retain *credentes*, “believing,” and restore *quod*, “that,” in place of *quia*.]

fugitives from their homeland and ignorant of circumstances, believing that they could completely withdraw from contact with the entire human habitation, took possession of the island of Rhodes, which [Note: “Ophiussa.” Stephanus writes: *Ῥόδος νήσος ἐπιφανεστάτη ἐκαλεῖτο Ὀφιοῦσα καὶ Ἀνθραΐα*, “The most famous island of Rhodes was called Ophiussa and Anthraia.” In Strabo and in the translator of Dionysius the African, *Ὀφίουσα* is read. FABR. — This name is also mentioned in Hyginus, *Poetic Astronomy*, book 2, chapter 14, concerning Phorbas. Whenever a fleet approaching from afar was seen, the Rhodians used to sacrifice to him. For when their citizens, after their island had been occupied by a multitude of snakes, called it Ophiussa, and among the multitude of wild beasts there was a dragon of immense size, and so forth.]

was formerly called Ophiussa, as a seemingly secure possession. [Note: “A secure possession.” This is the reading of the Utrecht, Florentine, first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, and my own; the fourth additionally has *sibi in medio auget*, “increases for itself in the midst.” But it is shown that the Carpasian and Telchinian peoples—or Telchinii—not only found a secure possession on Rhodes but also on Cyprus. This is demonstrated by the Cypriot city of Carpasia, discussed above, and by the testimony of Pausanias, book 9, chapter 19, p. 746. When he mentions Teumessus in Boeotia, he says that a temple of Minerva Telchinia, without an image, existed there, and adds: *Ἐς δὲ τήν ἐπίκλησιν αὐτῆς ἔστιν εἰκάζειν, ὡς, τῶν ἐν Κύπρῳ ποτὲ οἰκησάντων Τελχίνων ἀφικομένη μοῖρα ἐς Βοιωτοὺς, ἱερὸν ἱδρύσατο Ἀθηνᾶς Τελχινίας*, “It may be conjectured from her epithet that a group of the Telchines who once lived in Cyprus came to Boeotia and founded a temple of Athena Telchinia.”]

One thousand and forty years before the founding of the City, a savage flood in Achaia caused enormous devastation throughout nearly the entire province. [Note: “Because it was that of Ogyges.” Augustine, *City of God*, book 18, chapter 3, says that writers disagree about when Ogyges himself lived, in whose time the flood occurred. Orosius followed the same account as Eusebius. FABR. — *Ogygii* is written incorrectly; according to the Greek ending followed by Orosius’s manuscripts, the Latin form should be *Ogygi*, as in the Venetian editions and the first edition. Tatian, chapter 60, assigns Ogyges to the time of Phoroneus: *Κατὰ Φορωνέα τὸν κατ᾽ Ἴναχον, μνημονεύεται, παρ᾽ Ἀθηναίοις Ὤγυγος, ἐφ᾽ οὗ κατακλυσμὸς ὁ πρῶτος*, “In the time of Phoroneus, successor of Inachus, Ogyges is remembered among the Athenians, under whom the first flood occurred.”]

Because it occurred during the time of Ogyges, who was then [Note: “Founder and king of Eleusis.” My manuscript transposes the words as “king and founder.” Instead of *nomen*, “name,” the Utrecht manuscript has *id non*, apparently intending *id nomen*, “that name.” The Thebans seem, with stronger justification, to have claimed Ogyges for themselves, since Thebes itself was called Ogygian because of his fame, and the oldest gate at Thebes was called Ogygian. See Pausanias, book 9, chapters 5 and 8, pp. 719 and 728. Nevertheless, the Eleusinians, tracing their origins to him, say that the town Eleusis, or Eleusina, was founded by the hero Eleusis, son of Ogyges, according to Pausanias in the same work; he criticizes their freedom to invent such stories in book 1, chapter 38, p. 93.]

founder and king of Eleusis, it gave its name to the place and the period.

## Chapter VIII. The barrenness and famine of Egypt, which Joseph relieved by his resourcefulness; and the vanity of the Egyptian priests

[Note: “One thousand and eight years before the founding of the City.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts have “in the year before the founding of the City,” as does the Augsburg edition, which writes *MIX* instead of *MVIII*. The first edition and the Venetian editions, agreeing with the first Leiden manuscript, change this number to *MXLVIII*. The second and third Florentine manuscripts have *MXL* years from the founding of the City. For *primum*, “first,” below, the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts have *primo*, “at first”; afterward the first edition and the Venetian editions add *legimus*, “we read,” and then write, “as the historian Pompeius relates.” The word *refert*, “relates,” also occurs in the Hittorp and Bolsuing editions.]

One thousand and eight years before the founding of the City, there first occurred in Egypt an unusual and distasteful abundance, and afterward a continuous and intolerable famine, which Joseph, a just and wise man, relieved through divine providence. [Note: “May have come to his aid.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts have *subveniret*, “might come to his aid.” Orosius himself below has *congregasset*, “had gathered.” In Perizonius’s Justin, *dein*, “then,” is absent. The second Florentine has *docent*, “they teach,” instead of *docet*, “he teaches.”] The historian Pompeius and his epitomator Justin testify to this. Among other things, Justin says:

“Joseph was the youngest in age among his brothers. Fearing his exceptional intelligence, his brothers sold him to foreign merchants after seizing him. Taken by them to Egypt, he acquired there, through his skillful intelligence, [Note: “There.” This word is absent from three Leiden manuscripts.] a knowledge of magical arts, and within a short time [Note: “In a short time.” All the Leiden manuscripts have *in brevi*.] became exceedingly dear to the king. For he was both extraordinarily perceptive in interpreting prodigies and the first to establish the interpretation of dreams. Nothing concerning divine or human law seemed unknown to him, so much so that, foreseeing many years in advance the future barrenness of the fields, [Note: “He had gathered the crops.” These words are not found in Pompeius or Justin but were inserted into Orosius’s text, as we observed above in the excerpt from Tacitus, p. 40. *Congregasset* is used as above, in the second note, in certain manuscripts in place of *subveniret*.]

he had gathered the crops. His achievements were so remarkable that his answers seemed to come not from a human being but from God.” [Note: “To be given.” The two Florentine manuscripts, the Utrecht manuscript, the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts, Perizonius’s manuscript, and my own omit *dari*, “to be given.”]

Joseph’s son [Note: “Was Moses.” This gloss occurs in the second Leiden manuscript and the Utrecht manuscript: “Moses was not his son according to the flesh but according to nature, because Moses was the son of Amram.”] was Moses, whom, besides the inheritance of his father’s knowledge, the beauty of his appearance also commended. But when the Egyptians suffered from scabies and vitiligo, [Note: “Scabies and vitiligo.” The same is read below in chapter 10, whereas the commonly printed books of Justin have *scabiem et pruriginem*, “scabies and itching.” I possess a manuscript copy of Justin in which *scabiem et uliginem*, “scabies and moisture,” is read—incorrectly, certainly, but in such a way that traces of the true reading remain. FABR.] they were warned by an oracle and expelled him, together with the sick, beyond the borders of Egypt, lest the disease spread to more people. [Note: “Him.” This is absent from the fourth Leiden manuscript.] This is Justin.

But since this same Moses—whom they themselves attest to have been wise and learned—[Note: “They attest.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts and Perizonius have *testantur*, “they attest.”] recorded these events more fully and accurately, as having been accomplished by himself and his people, their ignorance must first be remedied; [Note: “Must be supplied: thereafter.” *Est* is deleted by Perizonius and by me; the first and third Leiden manuscripts read *hinc*, “hence.”] then the deceitful malice of the Egyptian priests must be refuted. They either tried by cunning—which is the more evident explanation—to conceal from memory the manifest anger and mercy of the true God [Note: “Of the true God.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts omit *veri*, “true.”] by a confused, piecemeal account, lest, to the disgrace of their idols, they should rightly show that he was to be worshiped, since they had taught that these evils were foretold by his counsel and averted by his aid; [Note: “Him to be worshiped.” The second Leiden manuscript and the Utrecht manuscript have *Joseph* instead of *eum*, “him,” as though they intended “Joseph’s God.” But the reading should perhaps be *Deum colendum*, “God to be worshiped,” since the opposition between idols and God occurs more than once in Tertullian’s *Apology*.] or perhaps, if we interpret them more indulgently, [Col. 0711A] they forgot.

For that Joseph of ours, who was a servant of the true God, [Note: “And, as a creature of his Lord.” The third Leiden manuscript has *et pro curatura domini sui*, “and for the care of his lord”; the first has *et procurator*, “and as steward,” and so forth. Yet what follows shows that the common reading should not be changed. Although the Egyptians were idolaters, they were nevertheless creatures of God; therefore Joseph was piously and attentively concerned for them as creatures of his Lord. The same manuscripts afterward read *cujus provisione*, “by whose providence”; the fourth Leiden manuscript likewise has *cujus*, “whose.”] piously and attentively concerned for the creature of his Lord, by whose providence they themselves abounded in grain as though they were priests, [Note: “But because.” The first Leiden manuscript has *sed qui*, “but those who.”] but because they were false priests, they did not grieve together with the others who were hungry.

Indeed, whoever wishes forgets; [Note: “Whoever wishes forgets.” A sentence of Cicero from the speech *For Murena*. FABR.] whoever suffers remembers. Ausonius, in *The Caesars*, epigram 12, on Domitian:

“Until now you had produced twin just men, Flavian race;

why did a third man take away those whom two had given?

Scarcely is it worth having possessed them, since the gifts of the good …”

What has caused harm, though brief, pains forever; he who suffers pain remembers. [Note: [Col. 0711C] “Summary.” The first, third, and augmented Leiden editions read *argumentum* (“summary”).] Although the records and official annals are silent about the chronology of this period, the land of Egypt itself bears witness on its own behalf: after it had then been brought under royal authority and restored to its cultivators, it paid from all its produce, continuously down to the present, a tax of one-fifth. [Note: [Col. 0711C] “Down to the present.” The second Florentine manuscript and the fourth Leiden edition read *usque nunc* (“until now”); in the Augustan edition *suo* is absent after *fructu*. Instead of *exsolvit* (“paid”), the first edition and the Venetian editions, together with the Paris edition, read *persolvit* (“paid in full”).]

[Note: [Col. 0711D] “This famine, then, was great.” This chronological indication is taken from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, and is also found in Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.4. The narrative itself is found in Genesis 44 and in Book II of Josephus’s *Antiquities*. FABR.—It is absent from my copy.] This, then, was a great famine under the Egyptian king [Note: [Col. 0711D] “Diapolitan.” The first editions, Venetian and Parisian, read *Diapolito*; the Augustan edition and the manuscripts, *Diopolita*; both Florentine manuscripts and my copy, *Diopolita*; the Ultrajectine and second Leiden editions, *Diospolita*; the fourth, *Dioopolita*; the first and third, *Diupolita*. Perizonius has *Heliopolita*, which is also written above the line in the first Leiden edition.] Diapolitan, whose name was [Note: [Col. 0711D] “Amasis.” My copy has *Amosis*; the Ultrajectine, *Amosum*.] Amasis, at the time when Baleus ruled the Assyrians and Apis the Argives.

There were seven years of famine, preceded by seven other years of abundance; Joseph, our Joseph, gathered and stored up through his own prudence the harvest that would have been lost all the more carelessly because it had been produced in such abundance, and preserved the whole of Egypt. [Note: [Col. 0711D] “Produced.” The first and third Leiden editions read *notam* (“known”) instead of *natam*.]

[Note: [Col. 0711D] “He acquired.” The second Leiden edition adds *et* (“and”).] He acquired all the Egyptians’ money for Pharaoh and, in the most just administration, rendered glory to God: “to whom tax, tax; to whom honor, honor.” [Note: [Col. 0711D] “To whom tax, tax.” This passage occurs in Paul, Romans 13. FABR.] He collected everyone’s livestock, lands, and assessments. [Note: [Col. 0712B] “And everyone’s livestock.” The first Leiden edition reads *omniumque pecora et terras* (“and everyone’s livestock and lands”); Perizonius has *omnium terras censusque ac pecora collegit* (“he collected everyone’s lands, assessments, and livestock”).] But those who had sold themselves together with their lands in return for an assessment of the due payment, he released on the fixed agreement of a fifth part. [Note: [Col. 0712B] “Who had sold themselves with their lands.” Some printed editions and manuscripts read *qui semetipsos* (“who had sold themselves”), a less pleasing expression. The same witnesses have *statutae* instead of *statuta*. Instead of *laxavit* (“released”), the first and third Leiden editions have *locavit* (“placed”). Instead of *vendiderant* (“had sold”), others read *vendiderunt* (“sold”).]

Who, then, would believe that this Joseph, whom God appointed author of the Egyptians’ preservation, could so quickly have fallen from their memory that shortly afterward they enslaved his sons and his entire family, afflicted them with forced labor, and destroyed them by slaughter? [Note: [Col. 0712C] “Of the preservation.” The Augustan edition and the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts read *conservandae* (“to be preserved”) instead of *conservatae*.] [Note: [Col. 0712C] “Had fallen from memory.” So the Florentine manuscripts, the Leiden manuscripts, and all the others, except the second Leiden and Ultrajectine manuscripts, which, together with the printed editions, read *excidisse memoria* (“had fallen from memory”); the Augustan edition also has *memoriae*.] [Note: [Col. 0712C] “Into servitude.” The fourth Leiden edition reads *servituti*.] [Note: [Col. 0712C] “Afflicted.” Andreas Scottus noted this reading in the margin of the Mainz edition; it is confirmed by three Leiden manuscripts, the first, third, and fourth, except that the first has *affixerint*. The common text reads *affecerint*.]

For this reason it is not surprising if even now some are found who, while they have turned away the sword hanging over their own necks by displaying the Christian name, either conceal or defame the very name of Christ, by which alone they are saved. [Note: [Col. 0712C] “Some are found.” Perizonius’s manuscript reads *si nunc quoque reperiuntur*; the first, second, and fourth Leiden editions read *si nunc quoque aliqui reperiantur*.] [Note: [Col. 0712C] “By which alone they are saved.” The fourth Leiden edition has *quo solo salvi sunt* (“by which alone they are saved”); the third Florentine, *quo salvi sunt*; the second, *quo salvati sunt*.] Or they assert that they are burdened by the times of those through whose merits they are liberated. [Note: [Col. 0712D] “Defame.” The fourth Leiden edition reads *diffamant*.]

## CHAPTER IX  
### Of the flood under the kings Amphictyon and Deucalion, the Ethiopian plague, and Father Liber devastating India

In the year 810 before the founding of the City, Amphictyon reigned at Athens, third after Cecrops. [Note: [Col. 0712D] “Amphictyon.” Here and in Book II of Justin, *Amphitryon* is commonly written erroneously, although *Amphictyon* is to be read not only from the ancient books but also from Pausanias, Book I, where he writes that after Cecrops died Cranaus gained possession of the kingdom of Athens, and that Amphictyon expelled him by force. Concerning this flood, Augustine writes in *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 10: “At these times, as Varro wrote, while Cranaus, the successor of Cecrops, was reigning at Athens—or, according to our Eusebius and Jerome, while Cecrops still remained in power—there was a flood called Deucalion’s, because he was reigning in those regions where it occurred most severely.” FABR.]

During his reign a deluge of waters swept away most of the peoples of Thessaly, with only a few escaping through mountain refuges, especially on Mount Parnassus, around which Deucalion then held royal power. Deucalion received those who fled to him in boats and sheltered and nourished them between the two ridges of Parnassus; for this reason, they say, the human race was restored. [Note: [Col. 0712D] “The twin ridges of Parnassus.” This middle phrase is absent from the Augustan edition.] [Note: [Col. 0712D] “The human race.” The second and third Florentine manuscripts, my copy, and the Augustan edition prefer *genus hominum* (“the race of human beings”).]

At that time also, Plato bears witness that very many plagues and dreadful diseases raged in Ethiopia, almost to the point of desolation. [Note: [Col. 0713B] “He bears witness.” The first edition and the Venetian editions prefer *testatus est* (“he bore witness”).] And lest the wrath of God and the fury of war be thought to belong to separate periods, [Note: [Col. 0713B] “Divided periods.” Perizonius and my copy read *divisa tempora esse credantur* (“be thought to be divided periods”).] [Note: [Col. 0713B] “The wrath of God.” In the third Florentine manuscript *Dei* (“of God”) is absent; in the second it is supplied by another hand. It should nevertheless not be absent, for the evils recounted thus far were inflicted by God’s just judgment and wrath; what follows is an example of the fury of war and of human greed.] at that same time Father Liber subdued India with blood, filled it with slaughter, polluted it with lust—the nation, in any case, which had never been subject to any human being and was content only with its native peace. [Note: [Col. 0713B] “Father Liber subduing India.” Clitarchus likewise wrote in his histories of Alexander that Liber subdued the Indians, as the Scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius’ *Argonautica*, Book II, reports. But who this Father Liber—or Διωνυσός (*Dionysos*)—was, Arrian asks with good reason at the beginning of Book V. FABR.] [Note: [Col. 0713B] “Subject to any human being.” That is, people who had neither previously served others nor ruled over others. Something similar is said above, in Chapter IV, of the Indians living in peace: “For at that time among them there were neither fires of war abroad nor such great exercises of desire at home.” Instead of *vernacula tantum*, the fourth Leiden edition has *vernacula tamen* (“nevertheless native”).]

## CHAPTER X  
### Of God’s people afflicted in Egypt, the ten plagues of the Egyptians, the crossing of the Arabian Gulf, and the remnants of that event; and of a certain destructive heat of the sun

In the year 805 before the founding of the City, Pompey and Cornelius testify that unspeakable evils and intolerable plagues fell upon the Egyptians. [Note: [Col. 0713C] “In the year before.” Both Florentine manuscripts read *Anno autem ante* (“in the year, however, before”).] Since both of them propose to relate these events concerning the Jews, they moved me somewhat by their divergence. [Note: [Col. 0713C] “Unspeakable evils for the Egyptians.” The second Leiden edition reads *nefanda* (“abominable”); the fourth, *Aegypto* (“for Egypt”).] [Note: [Col. 0713C] “Moved me somewhat.” The later Florentine manuscript reads *Aliquantum ut me proposui diversitatem* (“somewhat, as I set out, by the divergence”). Shortly afterward, the first edition has *sua* instead of *sui*.]

For Pompey—or Justin—says as follows: [Note: [Col. 0713C] “Or Justin.” The first, Venetian, and Paris editions add *ejus abbreviator* (“his abridger”). This passage appears in Justin, Book XXXVI, chapter 2.]

“When the Egyptians were suffering from scabies and vitiligo, they were warned by an oracle and expelled Moses, together with the sick, beyond the boundaries of Egypt, lest the plague spread to more people. Thus made leader of the exiles, he stole away the sacred objects of the Egyptians. When the Egyptians attempted to recover them by force, they were driven by storms to return home.”

But Cornelius says the following about the same matter: [Note: [Col. 0713C] “But Cornelius.” This is found at the beginning of Book II of Cornelius Tacitus. The passage has been transcribed as we present it here in the manuscripts of Tacitus and Orosius. FABR. It may be found in Tacitus, *Histories* V, chapter 3.]

“Most authorities agree that, when a disease arising throughout Egypt disfigured the bodies, King Bocchoris [Note: [Col. 0713D] “King Bocchorim.” The Augustan edition reads *regem ob hoc Chorim*.], having consulted the oracle of Ammon and seeking a remedy, was ordered to cleanse his kingdom and carry that class of people, as hateful to the gods, away into other lands. [Note: [Col. 0713D] “Arising throughout Egypt.” One or two manuscripts and printed editions read: *Cum orta per Aegyptum tabes corpora foedaret* (“When a disease arising throughout Egypt disfigured the bodies”).] After the common people had been searched out and gathered and had been left in desolate places, while the rest were numb with tears, [Note: [Col. 0714B] “Numb.” The fourth Leiden edition reads *stupentibus* (“astounded”).] Moses, one of the exiles, warned them not to expect help from gods or human beings, [Note: [Col. 0714B] “In desolate places.” Three Leiden manuscripts read *vastatis locis* (“places having been laid waste”); the first editions and the Venetian editions, *vastis in locis* (“in desolate places”). Tertullian, in his *Apology*, chapter 15, page 157, similarly citing Tacitus, writes *vastis Arabiae in locis* (“in the desolate places of Arabia”). Yet *Arabiae* should not be added either here or in Tacitus; it is Tertullian’s elaboration, just as the words that follow in him, *et aquarum egentissimis* (“and most lacking in water”), are also his. Desolate places simply means deserted places.] having been abandoned by both sides, but to trust themselves as though to a heavenly leader, [Note: [Col. 0714B] “So that they should expect no.” Three Leiden manuscripts have *nequaquam* (“in no way”), which the Ultrajectine also appears to intend with *ne q q*. After *duorum* in the Venetian editions, *templorum* (“temples”) is added, and this is also found in the Paris edition.] [Note: [Col. 0714B] “Abandoned by both.” Although these words are not found in our ancient manuscripts, we have retained them because they occur in Tacitus. FABR.—They are likewise absent from all the manuscripts I consulted and from the first, Augustan, and Paris editions. The Venetian edition first supplied them, followed by all the others. Colerus reports in his notes on Tacitus that they were also absent from his manuscript; Orosius himself may have removed them, as we have already found two examples, one in Justin, page 48, and the other in this passage of Tacitus, page 40, where the wording of the authors has been altered somewhat.] [Note: [Col. 0714C] “As a leader.” The word *ut* is absent from the first, Paris, and Venetian editions and from all the manuscripts, in which the reading is *sibimet duci coelesti crederent* (“they should trust themselves to a heavenly leader”). The Augustan edition has *sibimet, duce coelesti* (“themselves, with a heavenly leader”), as though it intended the leader to be understood as God.]

“Trusting in him, by whose aid they, trusting, had first driven away their present miseries.” [Note: [Col. 0715C] “They had driven away.” This is to be read with the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts, not *propulissent* (“had driven back”), as in the common editions.] [Note: [Col. 0714C] “By whose aid first.” How greatly this passage has troubled the ingenuity of scholars can be seen in their notes on Tacitus. In that author the reading is: *sed sibimet, ut duci coelesti crederent, primo cujus auxilio credentes, praesentes miserias pepulissent* (“but that they should trust themselves as to a heavenly leader, by whose aid first, trusting, they had driven away their present miseries”). Following that example, some seem to have supplied *credentes* (“trusting”) to Orosius. It first appears in the editions of Hittorp and Bolsuing, and thereafter in the others, although all the manuscripts and the older editions—the Venetian, Parisian, Augustan, and first editions—oppose it. I can scarcely be persuaded that Tacitus wrote it thus; rather, I think the reading arose from a double textual form, as I have found more than once in Orosius’s manuscript and printed copies: when different readings occurred in the codices, both were sometimes admitted into the text, with the word *Al.*—that is, *Alius* (“another [manuscript] reads”)—added, or with nothing added. I therefore think that one of Tacitus’s exemplars had *recentes miserias* (“recent miseries”), another *praesentes* (“present miseries”); when these were joined by the copyists, *recentes* first migrated into *credentes* (“trusting”). I would therefore prefer to read *recentes miserias*, words in which Moses is exhorting the Jews to hope well for the future, strengthened by the fact that they had just endured recent miseries in Egypt, during the crossing of the Red Sea, and in the persecution by their enemies. If we wish to retain the common reading *praesentes miserias* (“present miseries”), there is no need to stir up so much confusion, since the sense, as you may find in the notes on Tacitus, is simple and sufficiently clear. Moses wishes the Jews, settled in desolate places and an inhospitable wilderness, fearful of thirst, hunger, and every sorrow in the future, to lay aside all fear, to trust themselves to a heavenly leader—one who governs them and leads them on this road not by human plans but by divine direction—and why? Because they had already experienced his aid, as is clear from what follows: in Egypt. It was plainly foolish for those who had just been rescued from present and wholly certain evils, under Moses as their leader, to fear future and uncertain ones. The beginning of this clause remains, however, which learned men can scarcely approve: *primo cujus auxilio* (“by whose aid first”). The sentence is certainly weak. In Orosius’s first edition it is punctuated as follows: *sed sibimet duci coelesti crederent primo, cujus auxilio* (“but that they should trust themselves to a heavenly leader first, by whose aid,” etc.). Some attempted to read *privo* in Tacitus. I would rather have the whole passage corrected thus: *Sed sibimet, duci coelesti, crederent porro, cujus auxilio recentes (vel praesentes) miserias pepulissent* (“But that they should henceforth trust themselves to a heavenly leader, by whose aid they had driven away their recent—or present—miseries”). For *credentes* must certainly be deleted. The Augustan edition reads *repulissent* (“had repelled”), and shortly afterward *propulsi sunt* (“were driven away”), where *sunt* appears instead of *sint*; my parchment manuscripts and the Ultrajectine also have this reading.]

Thus Cornelius says that, compelled by the Egyptians themselves, the Jews were driven into the desert, and afterward he incautiously adds that they had driven away their miseries in Egypt through the aid of Moses as their leader. [Note: [Col. 0715C] “Into the desert.” The second Florentine reads *in deserto propulsi sint*; the third, *in deserta propulsi sint*.] [Note: [Col. 0715C] “That.” Four Leiden manuscripts, both Florentine manuscripts, the Ultrajectine, and Perizonius have *quia* (“because”) here. I noted this in support of my emendation above, page 46.]

Therefore it is shown that certain things vigorously accomplished through Moses were concealed. Justin likewise asserts that Moses, expelled together with the people, stole the sacred objects of the Egyptians. [Note: [Col. 0715D] “Why.” The Ultrajectine manuscript reads *Qua in re* (“in which matter”).] [Note: [Col. 0715D] “The sacred objects of the Egyptians.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts read *atque sacra Aegyptiorum* (“and the sacred objects of the Egyptians”).] When the Egyptians attempted to recover them by force, they were compelled by storms to return home, repelled. [Note: [Col. 0715D] “And, having been repelled, to return home.” The same Leiden manuscripts read *ac pulsos domum redisse* (“and, having been driven back, to return home”). My copy has *ac repulsos domi redisse* (“and, having been repelled, to return home”).]

Here too he revealed something more, though not everything, than the other concealed. Therefore, since both bore witness to that great leader Moses, [Note: [Col. 0715D] “By him.” This is absent from the third Leiden manuscript. Thereafter the first and second Leiden manuscripts, together with the first, Venetian, and Paris editions, read *Sicut quae per eum et gesta* (“just as things were both accomplished through him”). The Augustan edition deletes *quae*; the third Leiden has *qui* instead of *quae*.] what was both done and said by him and through him will be brought forth. [Note: [Col. 0716B] “And said.” Moses explained these things in Exodus. FABR.—The first and third Leiden editions read *et facta sunt* (“and were done”).] [Note: [Col. 0716B] “Will be brought forth.” The Augustan edition has *proferuntur* (“are brought forth”), while the other old editions have *proferantur* (“may be brought forth”), a reading not without acceptable sense. Shortly afterward Perizonius and my copy delete *Aegyptii* (“the Egyptians”).]

When the Egyptians afflicted God’s people—that is, Joseph’s race—with servitude and tormented them with labor, although they had been saved by his aid, and when they further compelled them by cruel command to kill their own offspring, God ordered his people, through Moses as his messenger, to be released as free people in order to serve him. The rebellious Egyptians were driven by the most dreadful punishments. [Note: [Col. 0716B] “Most dreadful.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts have *dirissimis*, a more significant reading than the *durissimis* (“very harsh”) found in the other common editions. The Egyptian plagues were not merely harsh but altogether dreadful.] [Note: [Col. 0716B] “He drives.” The second and fourth Leiden editions, together with the Ultrajectine, read *egit* (“he drove”) instead of *agit*.]

Loaded down and crushed by ten plagues, they at last compelled those whom they had refused to release even to hasten away. [Note: [Col. 0716B] “After the waters.” The first Leiden edition reads *Post aquas enim* (“For after the waters”); the older editions, except the Augustan, read *conversas* (“changed”) for *versas*.] After the waters had been turned into blood, bringing to those burning with thirst remedies of punishment more grievous than the punishments themselves. [Note: [Col. 0716C] “Burning.” My copy reads *ardentibusque* (“and burning”), as does the third Florentine manuscript; in the second Florentine manuscript *poenarum* (“of punishments”) is then absent.] After the horrible filth of frogs, crawling through every clean and unclean place; after fiery gnats, nowhere avoidable while they darted through the entire air; [Note: [Col. 0716C] “Fiery gnats.” The Augustan edition, both Florentine manuscripts, the three Leiden manuscripts, and Perizonius have *ignitas sciniphes* (“fiery gnats,” feminine plural).] [Note: [Col. 0716C] “And nowhere avoidable while the whole air vibrated.” The first edition has *Et nusquam se toto aere vibrantes pene inevitabiles* (“and nowhere, darting through the whole air, almost unavoidable”). The four Leiden manuscripts have *vibrantes*; both Florentine manuscripts, *vitabiles*, as does the Augustan edition; the Venetian and Paris editions have *et numquam toto aere vibrantes pene inevitabiles* (“and never, darting through the whole air, almost unavoidable”).]

After dog-flies, running even through the interiors of their limbs with horrible movements and inflicting bitterly torturous as well as shameful sufferings; [Note: [Col. 0716C] “Dog-flies.” The first edition has *muscas pene caninas* (“almost dog-like flies”); the Augustan edition, *muscas etiam caninas* (“even dog-flies”).] [Note: [Col. 0716C] “With horrible movements.” The second Leiden edition and the Ultrajectine have *horrendis motibus* (“with terrifying movements”), which I would not prefer. The Augustan edition adds *cursitantibus* (“running about”).]

[Note: [Col. 0716D] “After all the cattle.” The first edition, together with the Venetian and Paris editions, reads *post grandem omnium pecorum* (“after the great [destruction] of all cattle”).] After the sudden destruction of all the cattle and beasts of burden and the general slaughter; after swelling blisters and flowing ulcers and—as they themselves preferred to say—scabies and vitiligo breaking out over their whole bodies; after hail mixed with fire, striking down men, herds, and trees everywhere; [Note: [Col. 0716D] “Effervescing.” The third Florentine and the second Leiden edition have *efferventes* (“boiling up”).] [Note: [Col. 0716D] “Mixed with fire.” Perizonius has *igne permixtam* (“mixed with fire”); the second Leiden edition and the Ultrajectine, *igne commixtam* (“mingled with fire”).] [Note: [Col. 0716D] “Striking down.” The Augustan edition and the first and third Leiden manuscripts have *prosternentem* (“striking down”).]

After clouds of locusts, exhausting everything and pursuing even the roots of the seeds; [Note: [Col. 0716D] “After [the clouds] of locusts.” The first edition, with the Venetian and Paris editions, reads *post grandem omnium pecorum* (“after the great [destruction] of all cattle”).] after darkness dreadful in its apparitions, palpable in its density and deadly in its duration. [Note: [Col. 0716D] “Density.” The Ultrajectine has *per perenni crassitudine* (“through perpetual density”).] finally, after the uniform death of the firstborn throughout Egypt and a corresponding storm of bereavement throughout all households, those who had not yielded to God’s command yielded to his punishment. [Note: [Col. 0716D] “Who had not yielded to God’s command.” The Augustan edition reads *qui jubente Deo non cesserunt* (“who did not yield when God commanded”); the Ultrajectine, *qui jubente Deo non cesserant* (“who had not yielded when God commanded”).]

But soon, in the worst repentance, they dared to pursue those who had been released and to pay the ultimate penalty for their abominable obstinacy. [Note: [Col. 0716D] “The worst repentance.” The first edition has *pessimae—i.e. pessime—poenitentes* (“repenting most wickedly”); the Venetian and Paris editions, *pessime poenitentes*; the second Florentine manuscript, *et mox pessima* (“and soon, in the worst manner,” etc.).]

For their king drove the entire Egyptian army, equipped with chariots and horsemen, against the fugitives. We can infer its size especially from this one fact: they feared and fled six hundred thousand men. But God, protector of the oppressed and avenger of the rebellious, suddenly divided the Red Sea; and, spreading apart the banks on either side, he suspended the stiffened waves upright like the sides of mountains. [Note: [Col. 0717B] “Of the oppressed.” The Augustan edition and the manuscripts of Perizonius and my copy read *oppressorum* (“of the oppressed”); three Leiden manuscripts have *defensorum* (“of the defenders”).] [Note: [Col. 0717B] “Stiffened.” The third Florentine has *rigentum*; in the second, *regientium* is written above the line with *ru*, evidently intending *rugientium* (“roaring”). The common reading is preferable: the waves were stiffened on either side and raised like marble mountains.]

Thus, summoned by the hope of a pathway through the sea, the pious entered the road of hopeless salvation without injury, while the impious entered the pit of unexpected death. [Note: [Col. 0717B] “Thus, summoned by the hope of a boundary without injury.” I altered the reading on the authority of the Paris manuscript, which had *inoffensis pelagi viis provocatis* (“summoned by unharmed paths of the sea”). This reading could also be drawn from other witnesses, though less easily, which had *inoffensi spe limitis provocati* (“summoned unharmed by the hope of a boundary”). LAUT.—“Thus the pious, summoned unharmed by the hope of a boundary,” etc. The sense is that the pious, seeing God’s wondrous work and his assisting right hand, did not fear entering the depths of the sea, as though traveling along a fixed boundary; whereas the impious, blinded by anger and hope of vengeance, followed the same path, as though it were equally safe for both. The reading *inoffensi spe limitis* is therefore correct; all the manuscripts except the Florentines support it, and the Augustan edition preserved it. The first edition, as well as the Venetian and Paris editions, wrongly has *inoffensis pelagi viis*, and the latter add *provocatis*. In what follows, the first word of *pii viam* (“the pious [entered] the road”) is absent in both Florentine manuscripts; the second reads *per viam desperatae mortis intrarent* (“they entered by the road of hopeless death”). The rest is absent.]

And so, while the Hebrews walked safely over dry ground, the masses of waters standing behind them were drawn back, and the entire population of Egypt, together with its king, was overwhelmed and killed. [Note: [Col. 0717C] “Standing.” The first and third Leiden editions have *instantium* (“pressing upon them”). If that reading is preferred, it means that no refuge was available to the Egyptians because of the speed of the waves; if the common reading is retained, it refers to the masses of water that stood on either side like mountains, were released, and then joined behind the Egyptians, leaving them no escape.]

The whole province, already tormented by the plagues, was emptied by this final slaughter. [Note: [Col. 0717D] “Previously tormented.” The second Florentine reads *ante cruciata*; the first and third Leiden editions, *ante sauciata* (“previously wounded”). My copy, together with both Florentine manuscripts, not improperly reads *hac postrema interfectione* (“by this final slaughter”); the second and fourth Leiden editions have *ac postremo interfectione*. Several early editions do not recognize the conjunction in *totaque*. Instead of *vacuata est* (“was emptied”), some editions have *evacuata est*.]

Even now there remain unmistakable monuments of these events. For the tracks of chariot wheels and the ruts of the wheels can be seen not only on the shore but also in the depths, as far as sight can penetrate. [Note: [Col. 0717D] “Tracks of wheels and ruts.” My parchment, with the support of the third Florentine manuscript, reads *rotarumque signa, orbitae* (“and the marks of the wheels, the ruts”). This does not seem to have been done arbitrarily: wherever ruts are seen, a judgment is made about chariots, because ruts are the marks of chariots.] [Note: [Col. 0717D] “In the depths.” The first and third Leiden editions read *in profundo nunc* (“now in the depths”). These things, and what follows, must be pardoned to the age and to the credulity of the Fathers.]

And if at times, whether by chance or through curiosity, they are disturbed, they are immediately restored by divine agency to their former appearance by winds and waves. [Note: [Col. 0717D] “As far as sight penetrates.” The editions and manuscripts read *admittitur* (“is admitted”), barbarously. But perhaps Orosius wrote *admittit* (“admits”), which is Latin. LAUT.—After *curiositate*, some editions add *quaedam* (“certain things”).]

Thus whoever is not taught the fear of God by the zeal of proclaiming the revealed religion may be terrified by the example of his completed vengeance and wrath. [Note: [Col. 0718B] “So that whoever is not taught.” The third Florentine has *ubi quisque* (“wherever each person”); the second, *ut quisque non docetur timorem Dei propalatae religionis studio, ira* (“so that each person who is not taught the fear of God by zeal for the revealed religion, wrath,” and likewise in the third). Three Leiden manuscripts read *ut quisquis non doceatur timore Dei vel propalatae religionis studio, ira ejus* (“so that whoever is not taught by the fear of God or by zeal for the revealed religion, his wrath”), though the fourth has *docetur* and *irae*, and the second and fourth have *propalatae*. The first edition reads *Ut si quis timorem Dei non doceatur vel propalatae religionis studio, irae ejus* (“so that if anyone is not taught the fear of God or by zeal for the revealed religion, his wrath”), followed by the Venetian and Paris editions. The Augustan edition reads: *Ut quisque, si non doceatur timore Domini, prolatae religionis studio, ira Dei transactae ultionis terreatur* (“so that each person, if not taught by the fear of the Lord, may be terrified by the wrath of God’s completed vengeance through zeal for the proclaimed religion”). Yet I see no reason to depart from the common reading, which Perizonius and my copy confirm word for word, except that my copy has *ira* instead of *irae*. Orosius’s meaning is that all these things can still be recognized today, so that anyone who, through zeal for proclaiming the religion—that is, through acknowledgment of the Christian religion as the one true and saving religion—does not allow himself to be taught, may experience God’s wrath against unbelievers and obstinate people and thus, as he puts it, be frightened by the example of the wrath of that completed vengeance.]

Even in those times such continuous and intense heat blazed up that the sun, carried across its oblique course, is said to have affected the whole world not with heat but to have scorched it with fire. Neither the Ethiopian endured heat greater than usual, nor the Scythian heat unaccustomed to him. [Note: [Col. 0718C] “The heat.” The Augustan edition has *furorem* (“fury”). In what follows, my manuscript does not recognize the first word beyond the usual form.] From this, some people, refusing to grant God ineffable power, gathered their empty little arguments [Note: [Col. 0718D] “Their empty little arguments.” I emended this from the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, supported by the first, Augustan, Venetian, and Paris editions. The common text reads and is printed: *dum non concedunt Deo ineffabilem potentiam suam, inanes ratiunculas*, etc.; indeed, I would willingly delete *ineffabilem* as well, since it is absent from my manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0718C] “While they do not grant God.” The Ultrajectine reads *dum non reddunt Deo* (“while they do not render to God”); the Augustan edition, *dum non cedunt Deo* (“while they do not yield to God”).] and wove the ridiculous myth of Phaëthon. [Note: [Col. 0718D] “The ridiculous myth of Phaëthon.” Plato’s account in the *Timaeus* agrees with this narrative. FABR.—The first and third Leiden manuscripts add *Philosophi* (“the philosophers”) after *Phaetontis*.]

## CHAPTER XI  
### Of the murder committed by the Danaids, the cruelty of Busiris, Tereus, Procne, and Philomela, and Perseus ravaging Asia

Likewise, in the year 775 before the founding of the City, fifty murders of brothers’ sons were committed in a single night between the sons of the brothers Danaus and Aegyptus. [Note: [Col. 0718D] “Between Danaus and Aegyptus.” The crime of the Danaids is well known; Virgil also mentions it in Book X of the *Aeneid*:

> And the infamous crime, in a single nuptial night,  
> the young men’s hands shamefully slaughtered, and the bloodstained bridal chambers.

FABR.—Some editions and manuscripts have *Aegisti* (“of Aegisthus”).]

Then Danaus himself, the architect of such great crimes, expelled from the kingdom that he had acquired through so many atrocities, withdrew to Argos. [Note: [Col. 0718D] “From the kingdom, etc.” The crime of Danaus’s daughters is said to have occurred after Danaus had left his homeland. For Danaus and Aegyptus were sons of Belus, king of Egypt, by Anchinoe, daughter of the Nile, according to Apollodorus, *Bibliotheca* II.1.4. Warned by an oracle, Danaus boarded a ship with his fifty daughters and fled first to Rhodes and then to the Peloponnese. When he reached Argos, he became its ruler and gave the people his own name. At that time the fifty sons of his brother came to him and asked him, after laying aside his hatred, to give them his fifty daughters as wives. All the daughters, except Hypermnestra, following the counsel of their father Danaus, killed their husbands on the first night. The names of all of them are preserved in Apollodorus. Hypermnestra spared her fiancé Lynceus because he alone of the others had not yet violated his bride’s virginity. His father, enraged, threw his daughter into chains, but later gave her to Lynceus as wife; after Danaus, Lynceus ruled at Argos. Pausanias, Book III, chapter 12, page 235, explains how Danaus married off the remaining daughters, whom their suitors rejected because of the crime they had committed. Orosius could have called them *liberos* (“children”), but used *filios* (“sons”) on account of the superior sex.]

There, having disgracefully persuaded the Argives to undertake the crime, [Note: [Col. 0719B] “Having persuaded the Argives to undertake the crime.” Pausanias, Book II, chapters 19, pages 152–153, reports that the Argives were persuaded in this way to hand the kingdom over to Danaus. When Danaus arrived at Argos, he contended for the kingdom with Gelanor, son of Sthenelus. Since both men addressed the people with many arguments, most of them highly plausible and consistent with justice, and since what Gelanor advanced did not appear at all less equitable, the case was postponed to the following day. On the next day, at dawn, a wolf attacked a herd of cattle grazing near the city wall, and it attacked the bull itself, the leader of the herd. The Argives thought that the relation between Gelanor and the bull, and between Danaus and the wolf, was especially appropriate: just as the wolf is an animal least familiar to human beings, so until that time Danaus had scarcely had any association with the Argives. Therefore, when the wolf killed the bull, the Argives, judging from the event, awarded command to Danaus. Pausanias adds that Danaus judged the wolf to have been sent by Apollo, and for that reason dedicated a temple to Lycian Apollo. Hence, on ancient coins of Argos, Apollo Lycius and the forepart of a wolf in attack are commonly depicted.]

Sthenelas, who had welcomed him as a fugitive and needy man … [Note: [Col. 0719C] “Sthenelas, who had welcomed him as a fugitive.” *Sthenelus* is commonly and corruptly read here, just as the name is corrupted in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. Pausanias, however, in the *Corinthian* account, writes that Danaus, coming from Egypt, expelled from the kingdom not Sthenelas but his son Gelanor. FABR.—The Perizonian manuscript and the old editions have *Sthelenum*; the four Leiden manuscripts and the Ultrajectine, *Sthenelaum*; my copy and the Florentine manuscripts, *Sthenelam*. Pausanias calls him Gelanor, while Apollodorus calls him Elanor or Helanor and says that he handed over the kingdom to Danaus: “and Helanor, who had previously been king, handed over the kingdom to him” (*καὶ τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτῷ παραδίδωσι Ἑλάνωρ ὁ πότε βασιλεύων*). This is plainly contrary to Pausanias, Book II, chapter 16, page 145: “Danaus, sailing from Egypt against Gelanor, son of Sthenelus, deprived the descendants of Agenor of the kingdom” (*Δαναὸς δ᾽ ἀπ᾽ Αἰγύπτου πλεύσας ἐπὶ Γελάνωρα τὸν Σθενέλα, τοὺς ἀπογόνους τοὺς Ἀγήνορος βασιλείας ἔπαυσεν*). “Danaus, sailing from Egypt, deprived Gelanor, son of Sthenelus, descendant of Agenor, of the kingdom.” Agenor was originally from Argos; this Sthenelus had been his grandfather.]

[Note: [Col. 0719D] “Had received him as a fugitive and needy man.” All manuscripts except the Cologne codices read *susceperant* (“had received”), inelegantly. LAUT.—Together with Lautius, the two Florentine manuscripts, the second Leiden edition, my copy, and Perizonius, I preferred *exceperat* (“had welcomed”) to the common *susceperat*. It is an imitation, as often occurs in Orosius, of Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.373:

> Cast out upon the shore, needy…]

I received him and, mad for the kingdom, installed him in a share of it. Soon he himself ruled. [Perizonius; the second Leiden edition reads, “and he ruled.”]

Having received a refugee and needy man, he drove him from the kingdom and himself ruled. [Note: [Col. 0720A] “Of Busiris in Egypt.” Besides Isocrates, Diodorus treats Busiris’s ξενοκτονία (“slaying of guests”) in the latter part of Book I. Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, ch. 12: “At that time, he says, Busiris, king—or rather tyrant—sacrificed his own guests to his gods.” FABRICIUS.]

In Egypt at that time there was the cruel hospitality and still more cruel religion of Busiris, the bloodiest tyrant: he offered to the gods, accomplices in his crimes, the innocent blood of his guests. [Note: “Of innocent guests.” Both Florentine manuscripts, together with the Utrecht and Perizonius manuscripts and the first Paris and Venetian editions, read this way. Others have “of innocent guests” in the genitive plural. Soon afterward the Augsburg edition reads “he offered.”]

—something unquestionably abominable to human beings: they must decide whether it would also have seemed abominable to the gods. [Note: “Something abominable, etc.” In the printed books this passage is read differently, but we have scrupled to depart even by a fingernail from the old reading. The crime of Tereus is well known from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, Book VI. FABRICIUS.—The passage is extraordinarily corrupt, and the editors and interpreters do not seem to have attained its true reading and sense. The first edition reads: “which can undoubtedly seem abominable to human beings, much more so even to the gods.” The Venetian, Parisian, Hittorpian, and Bolsuing editions follow it. The Augsburg edition has: “which can seem abominable to human beings; or would it not also seem abominable to the gods?” Fabricius: “which seems undoubtedly abominable to human beings, since it would also seem abominable to the gods.” In Schott’s Mainz edition the passage is rashly altered to: “which would undoubtedly seem abominable to human beings,” with the rest removed. In two Florentine manuscripts it reads: “which seems undoubtedly abominable to human beings; or would it also seem abominable to the gods?” Four Leiden manuscripts and the Utrecht manuscript have: “which can undoubtedly seem abominable to human beings, or does it seem more abominable to the gods?” as though *non* (“not”) ought to be inserted: “or does it not seem so,” etc. My manuscript has: “which they will have judged undoubtedly abominable to human beings; or does it seem abominable even to the gods?” The Utrecht manuscript reads exactly the same, except that it is uncertain whether a comma written above *videtur* indicates *videretur* (“would seem”). From these two readings and the traces in the Florentine manuscripts, I emend the passage as follows: “which they will have judged undoubtedly abominable to human beings; or would it also seem abominable to the gods?” Or, if a bolder emendation is permitted: “would it seem desirable,” or even “would it seem excusable.” The sense of either reading is clear. Tertullian and others favored *viderint* (“they will have judged”), as in Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 9, p. 90: “in those same trees, the shades of their temples, sheltering crimes,” and similar expressions to those which Orosius has just used: “blood for the gods, accomplices in their crimes.” Orosian usage has *videretur* for *visum fuerit* (“would have seemed”). See below, Notes, p. 64, note 6.]

At that time the parricide was added to the incest of Tereus, Procne, and Philomela, and a banquet more abominable than either crime was added through unspeakable food: because her sister’s chastity had been violated and her tongue cut out, the mother killed her little son, and the father ate him. [Note: “At that time also, Tereus.” This reading is confirmed by the second and third Florentine manuscripts (except that the third has *incestus*), by all the Leiden manuscripts, and by the Utrecht, Perizonius, and my manuscript. From these, my manuscript and the Florentines supply *Prognes* rather than *Prognae*. Most of them place *est* after *adjunctum* and delete *post additum*. Before Fabricius, the first edition, together with the Parisian and Venetian editions, read: “At that time also the parricide of Tereus, Procne, and Philomela was added to their incest, and a crime more abominable than either was added to the unspeakable food.” Hittorp and Bolsuing have the same, except that *post adjunctum* is deleted. The Augsburg edition reads: “At that time also the parricide of Tereus, Procne, and Philomela’s incest, and a crime more abominable than either, was added to the unspeakable food.”]

[Note: “At the same time Perseus.” Perseus, son of Jupiter and Danaë, went to Cepheus, son of Belus, married his daughter Andromeda, and had by her a son Perses. From him the Persians, formerly called Cephenes and Artaei, received their name. Herodotus, Book VII. FABRICIUS.]

At the same time Perseus was transported from Greece into Asia; there he subdued barbarian peoples in a severe and prolonged war, and finally, as victor, gave his name to the people he had conquered. For the Persians were called Persians after Perseus. [Note: “Were called.” Thus in most Leiden manuscripts; the fourth deletes *sunt*, as does the Augsburg edition. The first Leiden edition has simply “for from Perseus, etc.” Some editions read *vocitati* instead of *vocati*.] [Note: “Was transported.” I have added the final word on the authority of six or seven manuscripts—my own, Perizonius’s, the Utrecht manuscript, and four Leiden manuscripts. The Utrecht manuscript reads *ubi* (“where”) instead of *ibi* (“there”).]

## CHAPTER XII  
### A Mass of Many Crimes Passed over in Silence

But now I am compelled to confess that, for the convenience of bringing my account to an end, I am passing over many things amid so great a surrounding multitude of the age’s evils, and shortening everything. For I could never pass through so dense a forest unless I sometimes flew over it in frequent leaps. Since the Assyrian kingdom lasted for 1,160 years, down to Sardanapalus, and was governed by nearly fifty kings, and since it scarcely ever ceased, up to that time, either to wage or to endure wars, [Note: “Ceased.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts read *quieverint*.] what end would be found if we attempted to recount these things one by one [Note: “By enumerating.” Thus, in one Leiden manuscript, better than *numerando*, as elsewhere.]—not to mention [Note: “Not to mention.” Both Florentine manuscripts and certain printed editions read *ne dicam*; in the first Florentine manuscript *ut ne dicam* is written above the line.] describing them? Especially since the affairs of the Greeks must also be passed over, while those of the Romans must above all be reviewed. [Note: “The Greek matters that must be passed over.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts add *bella* (“wars”).] [Note: “Must be reviewed.” My manuscript and the third Florentine manuscript read *recolenda* (“must be recalled”).]

Nor is there any need now for me to enumerate the shameful deeds of Tantalus and Pelops, more shameful tales. [Note: “More shameful tales.” I deleted the conjunction *et* (“and”) preceding this phrase, with the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts.] Their king Tantalus of the Phrygians, after shamefully abducting Ganymede, son of Tros, king of the Dardanians, detained him with an even more disgraceful abuse of the conflict he had begun, as the poet Phanocles confirms, recording that a great war was stirred up on this account. [Note: “Tantalus, king.” It would be tedious to write anything about Tantalus, Cadmus, and the others mentioned in this chapter, since they are commonly known. FABRICIUS.] Whether he wishes us to understand that this same Tantalus, as a favorite of the gods, prepared the abducted boy for Jupiter’s lust by familiar pandering, since he did not hesitate to offer his own son Pelops also at Jupiter’s banquets. [Note: “Phanocles.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts have *Phanodes*, incorrectly. Phanocles was an elegiac poet who lived after Demosthenes. He is mentioned by Clement of Alexandria in the *Protrepticus*, p. 24, and in Book VI of the *Stromata*, p. 627; by Grotius in his *Excerpta* from Stobaeus, p. 262; and by Scaliger on Eusebius, p. 41. He seems to have mentioned Tantalus and Ganymede in a poem entitled *Erotes* (“Loves”) or *Kaloi* (“Beautiful Boys”), which Clement mentions in the *Protrepticus*.]

It is tedious also to recount the great struggles of Pelops himself against Dardanus and the Trojans, although they were great: because they are usually celebrated in stories, they are heard with less attention. [Note: “Are heard.” Some manuscripts and printed editions read *adjunguntur* (“are joined”).] [Note: “Usually are.” Perizonius reads *solent* (“usually are”) rather than *solita sunt* (“have usually been”).] I also pass over [Note: “I pass over.” Perizonius reads *praeterea* (“besides”), as though the sentence were connected with what precedes.] what is related by Palaephatus about Perseus, Cadmus, the Thebans, and the Spartans through the inextricable recurring cycles [Note: “Cycles.” Three Leiden manuscripts read *recessus* (“retreats”).] of alternating evils. [Note: “Cadmus.” The same manuscripts prefix the conjunction *et* (“and”).] I am silent about the crimes of the Lemnian women; I omit the tearful flight of Pandion, king of the Athenians; I conceal the hatreds, sexual outrages, and parricides of Atreus and Thyestes, hated even by heaven. [Note: “And parricides.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts direct that the conjunction be deleted.] [Note: “Tearful.” Perizonius reads *miserabilem* (“piteous”).] I omit Oedipus, the killer of his father, husband of his mother, brother of his sons, and stepfather to himself. [Note: Some printed editions also include *Oedipum* here.]

I prefer to remain silent about Eteocles and Polynices, who labored through mutual clashes so that neither of them might fail to be a parricide. [The page reference in the supplied text is 62.] I do not wish to recall Medea, wounded by savage love, rejoicing in the slaughter of her little children, and whatever else may be inferred to have been perpetrated in those times—how human beings could have endured such things, when even the stars are said to have fled from them. [Note: “Could have endured.” The third Florentine manuscript and the Augsburg edition read *sustinuerunt* (“endured”).] [Note: “Wounded by savage love.” This refers to Ennius’s passage from *Medea*:

> For never, my mistress, wandering from my house and setting foot …

> Medea, sick at heart, wounded by savage love.

The passage survives in Book II of *Rhetoric for Herennius* and is modeled on these lines of Euripides:

> For never, my mistress—  
> Medea, having sailed from the towers of the land of Iolcus,  
> Her heart struck with love for Jason …

Cicero also mentions it in the *Caelian Speech*. FABRICIUS.—The third Florentine manuscript and my own have *sauciatae* (“of her who was wounded”).]

## CHAPTER XIII  
### The Conflict between the Cretans and Athenians, and between the Lapiths and Thessalians

In the year 560 before the founding of the City, there was an exceptionally savage conflict between the Cretans and Athenians. When the peoples on both sides had been disastrously routed, the Cretans inflicted a bloodier victory: they condemned the sons of the Athenian nobility to be devoured by the Minotaur—whether it is more appropriate to call him a savage human being or a human beast, I do not know—and fattened the misshapen monster by digging out the lights of Greece. [Note: “In the year before, etc.” One of the Leiden manuscripts specifies 640 years before the founding of the City; two others specify 660.] [Note: “The most savage conflict between the Cretans.” Minos, king of the Cretans, began this war against the Athenians because of the death of Androgeus. On this matter and on the Minotaur, see Diodorus, Book IV; Plutarch, *Theseus*; and Pausanias, Book I. FABRICIUS.] [Note: “To a savage human being or a human beast.” Since all the old editions—the first, the Augsburg, Venetian, and Parisian—printed the passage in this form, Hittorp supplied the model for restoring *inhumanae bestiae* (“inhuman beast”), which Fabricius and Scottus retained, although it is wholly inelegant. They removed the contrast Orosius was making, as though he did not know whether to call the Minotaur a human being, though savage, or a beast, though human: for he could not be a human being, since he had a bull’s body, nor could he seem able to be called a beast, since he had a human face. In agreement with the oldest editions, the first and third Leiden manuscripts, the fourth, Perizonius, and my own, I have therefore restored the old reading.]

At the same time the Lapiths and Thessalians fought in conflicts of extraordinary fame. But Palaephatus, in the first book of his *Incredible Tales*, reports that the Thessalians themselves were believed and called by the Lapiths “centaurs,” because, charging about in battle, the mounted warriors appeared to be a single body composed of horses and men. [Note: “At the same time the Lapiths.” Besides Palaephatus, whom Orosius cites, Diodorus, Book IV, should be read concerning the Lapiths and Centaurs. FABRICIUS.] [Note: “In the first book.” Perizonius deletes *in* (“in”).] [Note: “Reports.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts have *prodidit* (“reported”).] [Note: “Centaurs.” Four Leiden manuscripts and the Utrecht manuscript have *hippocentaurs*.] [Note: “And men.” Perizonius reads *hominumque* (“and of men”), while my manuscript has “and men and horsemen, they seemed.”]

## CHAPTER XIV  
### Vesores, King of Egypt, Attacks the Scythians in War and Is Defeated; the Scythians Subjugate Asia

In the year 480 before the founding of the City, Vesores, king of Egypt, seeking either to unite in war or to join under his rule the southern and northern regions, almost wholly divided from one another by sky and sea, was the first to declare war on the Scythians. He first sent ambassadors to announce to the enemy the terms of submission. [Note: “Vesores, king of Egypt.” The old books variously have *Vesozes* and *Vesoges*. The printed books of Justin have *Vexores*, while my manuscript has *Vizores*, so that perhaps *Vezores* is correct. Some think that this is the king whom Herodotus, Book II, calls Σέσωστρις (*Sesostris*) and says conquered the Scythians. See Justin, Book II. FABRICIUS.—In my manuscript this Egyptian king is called *Vaesdres*; in the others I consulted he is regularly called *Vesores*, *Vezozes*, or *Vesoges*. A related name is the one Manetho gives for Sesostris, *Seosis*. See Diodorus Siculus, Book I, chapter 53.]

To this the Scythians replied to the ambassadors that the extremely wealthy king had foolishly undertaken a war against the poor—a war more to be feared by himself because of the uncertain outcomes of war: no rewards, but obvious losses. For they themselves ought not to wait until he came to them; rather, they would go voluntarily to meet the booty. [Note: “To this.” The Augsburg edition has *atque* (“and”) instead. Some editions soon afterward read *respondent* (“they reply”).] [Note: “More for himself.” The Augsburg edition and three Leiden manuscripts have “more for himself.” Soon afterward my manuscript reverses the word order. The Utrecht manuscript has *inde* (“from there”), but the error is obvious.] [Note: “Until they were approached.” The Utrecht and second Leiden editions have “until one came to them”; Perizonius has “until they come to him.”]

There was no delay, for words followed deeds. First they terrified Vesores himself and forced him to flee back to his kingdom. Then they attacked his abandoned army, seized all the equipment of war, and would have ravaged Egypt in its entirety, had they not been checked by the marshes and driven back. [Note: “By the marshes.” Perizonius and my manuscript have “unless they were held back by the marshes”; one Leiden manuscript has “unless by the marshes.” For *populassent* (“they would have ravaged”), most of the major manuscripts prefer *populavissent*.] [Note: “They were driven back.” This is found in all the manuscripts, and Orosius seems to have used it instead of the more classical *repulsi fuissent* (“they would have been driven back”), which all editions except the Augsburg, Fabrician, and Mainz editions substituted. Yet we have the same Orosian Latin above, in chapter 8, with *subveniret* for *subvenerit*, *congregasset* for *congregaverit*, and on p. 60 *videretur* for *visum fuerit*.]

Then, returning immediately, they made Asia, subdued through countless massacres, tributary to themselves. After remaining there for fifteen years without peace, they were finally recalled by the insistence of their wives, who announced that, unless they returned, they would seek children from neighboring peoples. [Note: “Announcing.” Some manuscripts have *denuntiantibus* or *renuntiantibus*, with “to them” understood.]

## CHAPTER XV  
### The Origin, Customs, and Deeds of the Amazons

Meanwhile, among the Scythians, two royal youths, Plynos and Scolopythus, driven from home by a faction of the nobles, led a great body of young men with them and settled on the coast of Pontic Cappadocia, near the river Thermodon, in the Themiscyrian plains that they had brought under their control. There they long plundered everything nearby, until they were slaughtered by a conspiracy of their neighbors. [Note: “Two royal youths.” Three Leiden manuscripts and the Utrecht manuscript read “two young kings.” We find the same variation in their names as Fabricius presents. The first is called *Plemus* in three Leiden manuscripts and *Plynus* in Perizonius. The second is also found as *Scolopeus* and *Scolopeius* in some manuscripts.] [Note: “Plynos and Scolopythus.” The latter name is written variously here and in Justin, from whom this account is taken: *Scolpythus*, *Scolopitus*, *Scolopesius*, and *Scolopetius* are all found. FABRICIUS.] [Note: “On the coast of Pontic Cappadocia.” Justin’s books have “on the coast of Cappadocia.” On Themiscyra, besides others, see Diodorus, Book II, and Stephanus: “Themiscyra, a city opposite the Thermodon; and those who inhabit the region are Themiscyrians.” FABRICIUS.—The Augsburg edition has “of Pontus and Cappadocia.” Three Leiden manuscripts have “on the coast of Pontic Cappadocia”; I have restored this reading, supported also by Bongarsius’s notes on Justin, Book II, chapter 4, where he says that his manuscripts likewise read it.]

Their wives, moved by exile and widowhood, took up arms and, so that all might acquire equal courage from their similar condition, killed the men who had survived. [Note: “The men who had survived.” *Superfuerant*, not *supererant*, is found in the old manuscripts. Ephorus, in the scholia on Apollonius’s *Argonautica*, wrote that the Amazons, having been insulted by their husbands when the men had gone to war outside their borders, killed those who had remained at home and did not receive the others when they returned. FABRICIUS.]

Then, inflamed against the enemy by the blood of their own people, they obtained vengeance for their murdered husbands through the destruction of their neighbors. [Note: “And inflamed against the enemy, etc.” In the printed editions these words are punctuated without any good sense: “and, inflamed against the enemy, they obtain through their own blood vengeance for their murdered husbands by the destruction of their neighbors.” I considered that *sanguine suo* (“by their own blood”) ought to be removed, especially since it is absent from Justin, from whom this account is taken; or that it ought to be placed after *conjugum*, giving: “the vengeance for their murdered husbands through their own blood.” But since the received reading is supported by all the manuscripts, I consider the passage sound if the punctuation is changed and *sanguine suorum* (“by the blood of their own people”) is restored from the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts and the Utrecht manuscript instead of *sanguine suo*. Orosius says that these women were inflamed against the enemy by the blood of their own people, as women who had already learned, through the death of their husbands, to shed blood, to slaughter men, and to do and endure things befitting the stronger sex.]

Then [Note: “Then they seek peace by arms.” The fourth Leiden manuscript reads, “Then they seek peace by arms.” For *enecant* (“they kill”), the old editions have *necant*.] having sought peace by arms, they entered into sexual relations with outsiders. They immediately killed the male children born from them, but carefully raised the females. They burned the right breasts of the infants so that the discharge of arrows would not be impeded; hence they were called Amazons. [Note: “With the right breasts of the infants burned.” Thus Diodorus, Book II, writes that the Amazons burned the right breast of the females, “so that, when it was raised during battles, it would not impede the movement of their bodies; and from this cause the nation of the Amazons came to receive this name.” That is: “They burned the right breast of the maidens so that its swelling would not impede bodily agility in battle; and for this reason the race of the Amazons acquired this name.” FABRICIUS.] [Note: “So that the discharge of arrows would not be impeded.” The first edition and three Leiden manuscripts have *jactu* (“by the throwing”); one manuscript and the Utrecht manuscript have *ictus* (“by the blow”). But *sagittarum jactus* (“the shooting of arrows”) seems more correct, since Justin, Book II, chapter 4, and Orosius, Book VII, chapter 36, preserve the same expression: “beyond the measure of a human throw.” Soon afterward the first edition reads “and hence the Amazons were called.”]

They had two queens, Marpesia and Lampeto, who, dividing their army into two parts, took turns overseeing the war and guarding the home. [Note: “Marpesia and Lampeto.” These names of the queens are written without any variation in our manuscript books of Orosius and Justin, not as in the printed editions, which have *Marthesia* and *Lampedo*. FABRICIUS.] [Note: “Took turns.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “guarded” instead.]

After they had conquered most of Europe, and captured a number of cities in Asia, they themselves founded Ephesus and other cities. They recalled home the principal part of their army, laden with extremely rich booty; the remainder, left behind with Queen Marpesia to defend their rule in Asia, was slaughtered in an encounter with the enemy. [Note: “They had conquered most of Europe.” This is the Latin reading in the Cologne manuscript. Some here read *maxima ex parte* (“for the most part”). LAUTIUS.—Both Florentine manuscripts, together with Perizonius, have *maxima parte* (“most of it”); the Augsburg edition has “most of Europe,” which I preferred.] [Note: “They themselves founded Ephesus and other cities.” According to Strabo, Book 11, Ephesus, Smyrna, Myrrhina, and Paphos were founded and named by the Amazons. Eustathius also mentions this in his commentary on Dionysius. FABRICIUS.—All the Leiden manuscripts and my own read “they themselves, however, founded Ephesus.”] [Note: “The remainder, left behind.” Three Leiden manuscripts have: “the remainder, left behind to defend the rule of Asia, was slaughtered with Queen Marpesia in the encounter with the enemy.” Justin supports the received reading. Perizonius has *regnum* (“kingdom”) instead of *imperium* (“rule”).]

Her place was taken by her daughter Sinope, who crowned her exceptional reputation for courage with perpetual virginity. [Note: “Her place was taken by Orithya.” Justin writes that Orithya, Marpesia’s daughter, succeeded her in the kingdom. Yet the old books have: “Her place was taken by Sinope, her daughter.” FABRICIUS.—The third Leiden manuscript has “whose place.”] [Note: “Sinope, her daughter.” All the manuscript books of Orosius, without a single exception, read not *Orithyia* but *Sinope*; the Augsburg edition, alone among the printed editions, confirms this. Nor does it trouble me that Justin reads *Orithya* and that editors have restored that name in Orosius from Justin, for I think that Justin too once read *Sinope*, as Vossius testifies that it is written above the line in his manuscript. Moreover, I judge that this name ought to be restored for two reasons: first, Sinope herself was an Amazon of great renown, after whom Sinope, the city of Pontus, derived its name and origin, as is clear from the testimonia cited by Vossius; and second, Justin and Orosius both say that, at the time when Hercules undertook his expedition against the Amazons, two sisters, namely Antiope and Orithya, ruled them. But here they do not say that two sisters or daughters succeeded Marpesia their mother in the kingdom; rather, they name one daughter of Marpesia, whom we seem to have found called Sinope.]

The peoples, stirred by this fame, had been seized by such admiration and fear that even Hercules, when ordered by his master to bring back the queen’s weapons, as though destined for unavoidable danger, gathered the whole picked and noble youth of Greece and prepared nine long ships. [Note: “Stirred.” Both Florentine manuscripts and three Leiden manuscripts have *excitatas* (“stirred”).] [Note: “So that Hercules too, when ordered, etc.” Hercules’ master was Eurystheus, who prescribed for him the twelve labors to be performed. Explaining this labor, Diodorus, Book IV, says: “When Hercules had received the command to bring back the belt of Hippolyta, the Amazon, he undertook an expedition against the Amazons.” Thus Orosius understands by “weapons” Hippolyta’s Ἱππολύτης ζωστῆρα παναίολον, “variegated girdle,” as Apollonius calls it in Book II of the *Argonautica*. See also the learned commentary of Isaac Tzetzes on Lycophron’s *Cassandra*. FABRICIUS.] [Note: “To bring the queen’s weapons.” The Amazons’ weapons are the shield and double-headed axe. Plutarch, *Greek Questions*, pp. 301–302, mentions the double-headed axe that Hercules took from the Amazon queen, the one which Omphale received from him as a gift, which later passed to the kings of Lydia, and finally became an ornament of Jupiter Labradensis in Caria. There the Amazon queen is called Hippolyta and is said to have been killed by Hercules, according to the varying form of the story. By “weapons,” Orosius may have understood the belt, for Hercules had been ordered by Eurystheus to bring it, and the armed woman could not have been stripped of her belt unless she had either been killed or defeated. This labor of Hercules is represented on two ancient coins of the emperor Macrinus, of the first and second modules, minted at Heraclea in Pontus. On them Hercules, protected by the lion’s skin and armed with his club, pursues the mounted Amazon on foot. On one, the armed queen threatens him with a double-headed axe if he does not stop pursuing her, while Hercules demands her surrender; on the other, Hercules, seizing her stripped of her weapons, holds her already captured, his club threatening.]

Yet, not content with assessing his strength, he preferred to attack unexpectedly and surround them by surprise. [Note: Some editions have “and not so greatly” or “and not only.” The first edition has “nor so much.”]

At that time two sisters ruled: Antiope and Orithya. Hercules came by sea and overwhelmed them unprepared, unarmed, and made sluggish by their neglect of peace. Among the many who were killed and captured, two sisters were retained: Antiope—Menalippe by Hercules—and Hippolyte by Theseus. [Note: “Two sisters of Antiope.” Diodorus writes that Hercules gave Antiope, one of the captives, to Theseus, and freed Menalippe after receiving the belt. Apollonius Rhodius sings that Hippolyta gave Hercules the belt so that he would free Menalippe, who had been captured by ambush. Tzetzes prefers Antiope—the woman by whom Theseus fathered Hippolytus—to Hippolyta, as Lycophron wrote: “But it is not surprising that history should be mistaken in matters so ancient,” says Plutarch in his *Theseus*, discussing this very matter. Read him. FABRICIUS.] [Note: “Were retained.” Some manuscripts delete the final word.]

But Theseus took Hippolyte as his wife; Hercules returned Menalippe to her sister and received the queen’s weapons as the price of her ransom. [Note: “After Orithya, Penthesilea.” Penthesilea, queen of the Amazons, came to the aid of the Trojans after the death of Hector. After killing a great number of Greeks, she herself was finally killed by Achilles while fighting bravely. See Diodorus, Book II, and Dictys of Crete, Book IV. FABRICIUS.—This coin, a contorniate from the Farnese Museum, preserves the memory of this Amazon and of her death at Achilles’ hands.]

After Orithya, Penthesilea gained the kingdom; from her we have received the most distinguished examples of courage among men during the Trojan War.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### Epilogue of the History of the Amazons, in Which He Attacks the Present Blindness of the Romans

[Page reference: 68; column reference: 0728A.]

Alas, how shameful is human error. Women who had fled their homeland entered Europe and Asia—that is, the largest and strongest regions of the world—roamed through them, destroyed them, and, for nearly a hundred years, held many cities by overthrowing some and founding others.
