[Note: “The largest and strongest regions of the world.” The Augsburg edition has “the largest regions of the world and the strongest.” Soon afterward one edition has “and a hundred cities.”] [Note: “And founding others.” The first edition and the third Leiden edition have “and building others”; the Parisian and Venetian editions have “in building”; the fourth Leiden manuscript has “and constructing others.”]

Yet this was not attributed to the misery of human beings and the pressure of the times. [Note: “The misery of human beings.” The Augsburg edition has the singular “misery of humanity.”] But now those Getae, who are also the Goths of the present day, whom Alexander declared ought to be avoided, whom Pyrrhus dreaded and Caesar likewise evaded, after abandoning and emptying their own settlements, have entered with all their strength into so many Roman provinces. [Note: “But now.” The final word is absent from Perizonius.] [Note: “Those Getae, who are also now Goths.” Jerome, in his commentary on Genesis, likewise testifies that the Goths were called Getae by learned men of antiquity. Dio, Book LI, and Xiphilinus, drawing on Dio in his account of Domitian, state that the Getae had settlements beyond Haemus, near the Danube. Dio also entitled a book on the history of the Goths *Getica*, as is known from the *Suda*. Claudian likewise frequently understands the Goths by the name Getae. But the Greek ecclesiastical historians call them Γότθοι (*Gothi*). FABRICIUS.—Thus Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Genesis, testifies that the Goths were called Getae by learned men of antiquity. Claudian likewise frequently understands the Goths by the name Getae; and Diodorus, Book V, states that the Getae had settlements beyond Haemus, near the Danube. But the Greek ecclesiastical historians call them Γόθοι (*Gothi*). LAUTIUS.] [Note: “Whom Alexander declared ought to be avoided.” Strabo, Book VII, writes that Alexander, during the expedition he undertook against the Thracians living beyond Haemus, penetrated to the Getae and brought their city under his power. FABRICIUS.—Orosius, Book VII, chapter 34: “Those greatest Scythian peoples, feared by all earlier powers and also avoided by Alexander, that great man, as Pompey, Cornelius, and others have testified.”] [Note: “To be avoided.” All the Leiden manuscripts and the Utrecht manuscript have *vitandos* (“to be avoided”).] [Note: “Pyrrhus.” The Leiden manuscripts have *Cyrus*, incorrectly. Alexander must be preceded by Pyrrhus, and Orosius is speaking of great kings who feared to engage the Goths, although they penetrated into their territories. Cyrus did not reach that far: when he made war on Scythia, he was disgracefully defeated and died.]

And, having displayed themselves for a long time as a terror, they now hope by entreaties to obtain a partnership in the Roman alliance, which they could have claimed by arms. They ask for the site of a small habitation, not by their own choice but at our judgment. [Note: “Leaving their own settlements.” The first, Parisian, and Venetian editions do not recognize the final word.] [Note: “And with all their strength, so many Roman provinces.” I adopted Lautius’s emendation, which Scottus received in the Mainz edition, from the third Florentine manuscript and the Utrecht manuscript. Nothing is more certain, although the reading of the principal editions—the first and Augsburg editions—can be defended: “and, safe with all their strength, they entered the Roman provinces,” meaning that they invaded the Roman provinces without resistance and thus plainly had the greater strength, should the Romans wish to test them in war. The Venetian and Parisian editions follow this reading, as do the first and fourth Leiden manuscripts. My manuscript has *totos* (“entire”). The reading found in the others, *toti Romanas*, is worthless.] [Note: “Not by their own choice.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “not by their choice”; above “their habitation,” the second Florentine manuscript has “of their habitation.” Orosius below, Book VII, chapter 38: “Therefore Alaric and the whole Gothic people, humbly and simply begging for peace and for whatever settlements might be granted.” Lucan, on pirates who feared the preparations of Pompey the Great, Book II, line 579:

> And he asked for a narrow home in a confined place of earth.]

Since the whole earth was subject to them and open before them, it was free for them to take as much as they wished and establish settlements wherever they desired. They offer themselves for the defense of the Roman kingdom—those whom unconquered kingdoms alone have feared. [Note: “Open.” This is correct. The Venetian, Parisian, Hittorpian, and Bolsuing editions print *parente* (“obeying”), against the first and Augsburg editions, which have *patente* (“being open”). The earth did not obey the Goths; rather, it lay open, subject to their eyes, so that they could burst in wherever they wished and establish settlements. Two Leiden manuscripts have *petenda* (“to be sought”).] [Note: “As much as it pleased them.” The Utrecht manuscript has “wherever it pleased”; the first edition has *quod* (“whatever”). For *fuit* (“it was”), the second Florentine manuscript has *fuisse* (“to have been”), as though the meaning were “had been free.”]

And yet blind paganism, because it does not see that these things were accomplished by Roman valor, does not believe what has been obtained through Roman faith and does not rest content, although it understands that, through the benefit of the Christian religion—which joins a kindred faith among all peoples—those men have been subjected to it without a battle, whose women destroyed the greater part of the world through immeasurable slaughter. [Note: “Who joins a kindred faith among all peoples.” Fabricius printed this form, following the older editions, all of which support it, except that the Augsburg edition reads *cognata fide* (“by a kindred faith”). All the manuscripts I examined or for which I possess a collation, however, prefer *cognitam* (“known”); this reading appears in the margin of Hittorp and the editions that followed it. The fourth Leiden manuscript additionally has *fide jungitur* (“is joined by faith”). The received reading is correct. Orosius means: “The Christian religion joins a kindred faith among all peoples,” that is, it causes all peoples, through the same faith, no longer to be strangers and enemies to one another but brothers and kin, all belonging to one body of the Church and members of one body, whose head is Christ.]

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On the Abduction of Helen and the Destruction of Troy, with an Admonition to the Reader

[Col. 0730A]

But before the founding of the City [Note: [Col. 0730B] In the year 430. We have written this on the authority of the manuscript books, whereas the common reading is “in the year 430 and more.” We shall discuss this number further in the following book, chapter 4. FABR. — The editions of Hittorp and Bolsuing print “in the year 430 and more.” But the first edition, Augustine’s, the Venetian and Parisian editions, as well as the manuscripts of Leiden, have “in the year 330,” with the remaining words deleted. All the other manuscripts approve Fabricius’s emendation. Soon afterward, “by the abduction of Helen”: three manuscripts of Leiden, and the first Decennial edition, together with the Parisian and Venetian editions.] in the year 430, the abduction of Helen, the conspiracy of the Greeks, and [Note: [Col. 0730B] The gathering of a thousand ships. The rounded number of the Greek fleet, as in Virgil, Aeneid 2, and Ovid, Metamorphoses 13: “a thousand keels.” In Euripides’ Orestes the Chorus addresses Menelaus as follows: “O you who launched the thousand-oared army upon the land of Asia, rejoice!”; where the Scholia note: “He used a complete number, for the Greeks’ ships were 1,155.” He therefore meant that there were 1,155 ships. See further material collected from various sources by Martin Delrio in his notes on Seneca the Tragedian. FABR.] the gathering of a thousand ships, followed by a ten-year siege and finally the celebrated destruction of Troy, are recorded. In that war [Note: [Col. 0730C] Ten years. With these words begins that famous Florentine codex, the first of whose testimony we have made use, venerable among all manuscript codices for its antiquity. It seemed worthwhile to insert here its beginning, with its letters painted with the greatest care in accordance with the archetype, and to display it for inspection. Soon afterward, in place of *quas*, four Leiden manuscripts, together with the Utrecht manuscript and Augustine’s first edition, have *quantas nationes*; and Augustine’s edition in particular adds *Al.* in several copies.] which was waged with the utmost savagery for ten years, how many nations and how many peoples the same storm engulfed and afflicted, the poet Homer, especially renowned, has made abundantly clear in brilliant verse [Note: [Col. 0729D] He made clear. All the manuscripts, as well as the old editions, have this reading; nor do I know why Fabricius and Scott printed *palam facit* (“makes clear”). What follows is absent from two Leiden manuscripts.] — nor is it our task now to recount the matter in order, [Note: [Col. 0729D] Because it is also long for the work. Correctly so; Augustine’s edition, which reads *opere*, should not be followed. In the first Leiden manuscript it was likewise altered by a second hand. The third Leiden manuscript has the word deleted.] since it seems both too lengthy for the work and known to everyone. Nevertheless, those who have learned the duration of that siege, the horror of the overthrow, [Note: [Col. 0730D] Slaughter. The Utrecht manuscript has *caedemque* (“and slaughter”).] the slaughter and the captivity should consider whether they are rightly offended by this present condition, whatever its character may be; [Note: [Col. 0730D] “Whom, as enemies,” etc. The meaning of this passage was more obscure, especially if a minor division were placed before these words and, as had previously been done, the punctuation were arranged as follows: “they are offended by the present condition, whom as enemies…” For then the preceding words—“let them consider whether they are rightly offended”—seemed to have to be joined with “whom as enemies,” leaving great ambiguity as to whether *hostes* (“enemies”) should be understood as nominative or accusative. Hence, I suppose, in the first and third Leiden manuscripts the letter *q*, with a superscript *o*, indicated another reading, namely *quo*. But the meaning is now clear in itself. Orosius says, in a manner very familiar to Tertullian and other Christian writers, as we said above on p. 59, that they should consider whether they are rightly offended by the condition of our present age, about which a few people complain in corners; and that those very men who complain about the present times are not treated as enemies by the Goths—whose power and multitude were described at the end of the preceding chapter—but rather that the Goths show themselves ready to fight against other barbarians on their behalf, as allies and friends, and to defend the Roman Empire. In this matter the pagans ought to have recognized not the misery of the times, nor Christians as disturbers of the peace of the Eternal City, but the mercy of God, who, for the sake of the Christian name, spares both others and the Christians themselves. What he writes here and above about the Goths and their zeal on behalf of Rome concerns the times and events more fully described by Orosius at the end of his work, or in the final chapter of Book 7.] whom, although they can pursue as enemies throughout all lands with armies equipped for war, the hidden mercy [Col. 0731A] of God, [Note: [Col. 0731B] When throughout all lands. The first word is absent from the first Leiden manuscript. In place of *instructis*, the Utrecht manuscript has *exstructis*; Augustine’s edition has *instruens*. In place of *possint*, the first and third Leiden manuscripts and the second Florentine have *possunt*. The first edition and the Parisian edition have *possent*. The Venetians delete *bello*. The words “throughout all lands” refer to the many Roman provinces which, as he wrote above, the Goths invaded with all their forces.] they pursue across every sea for the sake of peace, with hostages put forward [Note: [Col. 0731C] Having offered hostages. Perizonius reads *praeteritis obsidibus*, which produces the opposite meaning, as though Orosius had wished to say that those proud enemies had judged the Romans so favorably that they did not even wish to receive hostages from them. Nevertheless, I prefer the common reading, which indicates that the Goths demonstrated their loyalty to the Romans by giving or offering hostages from their own people.] — and lest they be thought to do these things merely from a love of quiet, [Note: [Col. 0731C] Themselves and their own dangers. The common reading has *ad pericula sua* (“toward their own dangers”). LAUT. — The editor does not say whether the Cologne manuscript used by him expresses it in this way. But I can affirm that it stands thus in the best and oldest manuscript, namely the first Florentine, as also in the two remaining manuscripts, in the fourth Leiden manuscript, in Perizonius’s copy, in my parchment manuscripts, and in Augustine’s first and the Parisian editions.] they offer themselves and their own dangers for the peace of the Romans against other peoples.

## 72. CHAPTER XVIII. The arrival of Aeneas in Italy and various disasters of the same period

After a few years had intervened, [Note: [Col. 0731C] Aeneas, an exile from Troy. What Orosius writes about Aeneas as something implanted in his own memory through the discipline of literary schooling is something boys even today learn from Virgil in school. FABR. — In the most ancient Florentine codex, the words *In Italiam adventus Aeneae* (“The arrival of Aeneas in Italy”) are written in the margin. The hand is from the same period; I thought this worth noting, so that it may be apparent how ancient was the custom of adding headings in the margins of books. In place of *praeterea*, Augustine’s edition has *interea*.] the arrival in Italy of Aeneas, an exile from Troy, [Col. 0732A] [Note: [Col. 0731D] The arrival in Italy of Aeneas, an exile from Troy. This is the reading of three Florentine codices and of my own. The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, together with Augustine’s edition, prefer *a Troja profugi*; the others have *ex Troja*, less elegantly. I do not know how, contrary to all the editions that preceded it, Scott could print in the Mainz edition: “The arrival in Italy of Aeneas, an exile from Troy, which stirred up arms,” with an inept punctuation.] what conflicts it stirred up, what wars it kindled for three years, how many peoples it involved, and how many it afflicted with hatred and destruction, [Note: [Col. 0731D] He stirred up. The first Florentine has *exciverit*; in the margin, *exercuerit*; the second has *exercuerit* in the text, but a second hand adds the letter *c*. The third has *exciverit*, with *excitaverit* written above it.] all this is branded even upon our memory by the discipline of literary schooling. [Note: [Col. 0732A] Of literary schooling. In place of *ludi litterarii*, *ludi litteralis* is found. Then, in place of *insitum*, all the old books correctly recognize *inustum*. LAUT.] [Note: [Col. 0732A] “It is *inustum*.” This is the true and genuine reading—which Lautius also saw, although I do not approve his reading *ludi litteralis disciplinae*, contrary to the manuscripts. It is confirmed by the first and second Florentine manuscripts, Perizonius’s copy, and my own, together with Augustine’s edition; the remaining editions have *insitum est*. The first and third Leiden manuscripts have *injunctum est*. The third Florentine has *inditum est*.]

In the interval of these same times, [Note: [Col. 0732B] “Intervening in the middle.” Fabricius, followed by Scott, was wrong to change this to *interjacente*, although three Leiden manuscripts have *media interjacenti*, and my copy has *medio interjacenti*. The three Florentine manuscripts, together with the old editions, preserve the correct reading; but Augustine’s edition, together with the Utrecht manuscript and Perizonius, reads *media interjacent*.] there occurred the exiles and shipwrecks of the Greeks, and the disasters of the Peloponnesians, when Codrus died, [Note: [Col. 0732B] When Codrus died. This is a well-known story from Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, Justin, Book 2, and Velleius, Book 1; Valerius Maximus, Book 5, chapter 7, differs from them in some details. Lycurgus treated the matter most elegantly in his speech *Against Leocrates*. Pausanias, Book 1, writes that Codrus was killed not far from the Ilissus by the Peloponnesians. FABR.] and the Thracians, ignorant of their fate, [Note: [Col. 0732B] The Thracians, ignorant of their fate. The Cologne manuscript has *fractorum*. Materni’s copy has *factorum*; both are wrong in light of the history. The word *ignoti*, in place of *ignari*, although many people have disturbed it in its proper place, has nevertheless been restored by us in Latin. Plautus, *Pseudolus*: “I know; you proclaim things known.” LAUT. — That the ancients exchanged the meanings of these words, using *ignoti* for *ignari*, is shown by many passages of Ovid. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 1, verse 134: “The keels have leapt upon unknown waves.” Heinsius records that the Medicean manuscript, the best one, has *ignaris* in place of this; Tacitus confirms *ignoto* as its equivalent. He also cites Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.706: “The Laurentine shore holds Mimas unaware.” Likewise Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 7.404: “Now Theseus was approaching, a son unknown to his father.” And at verse 672: “He sees the son of Aeolus, made from an unknown tree, carrying a spear in his hand.” Here the manuscripts have *ignara*, as Heinsius illustrates at length; see him. Similarly, Orosius uses *ignotus* for *ignarus*, and not without precedent. Before him, Quintilian, *Declamations* 6, p. 128: “Yet let no one be mistaken: she is not my son’s stepmother, but his mother.” See the notes there for more. I found *ignoti* for *ignari* in the six manuscripts I myself collated and in Augustine’s edition. The Utrecht codex also has this reading, but the Florentine manuscripts seem not to differ from the printed texts. In those three manuscripts, as in the Cologne manuscript, *fractorum*—which in the second was changed to *factorum*—is found, as also in the four Leiden manuscripts, my copy, Perizonius’s, the Utrecht manuscript, and Augustine’s edition. But why does Orosius call the Thracians “ignorant of their fate”? I wish the interpreters had explained this. Was some oracle given to them which, because they misunderstood it, led them to renew the war fruitlessly, as happened to others? I do not remember having read this. Hence I suspect that the passage was corrupted long ago and could be restored as follows: “when Codrus died, the Thracians, knowing their fate.” Historical probability supports this emendation. At the end of the chapter the first and second Leiden manuscripts add *addunt*.] rising to new wars, and a general upheaval throughout Asia and Greece.

## 73. CHAPTER XIX. Sardanapalus, king of the Assyrians; Phraortes, Diocles, and Astyages, kings of the Medes; Cyrus, king of the Persians

[Col. 0733A]

In the year 64 before the founding of the City, the last king among the Assyrians was Sardanapalus, [Note: [Col. 0733A] Sardanapalus. On Sardanapalus, see Justin, Book 1; Diodorus, Book 2, at length; and Velleius Paterculus, Book 1. FABR. — Just as in the manuscripts of Justin, so also in the manuscripts of Orosius the name is often written *Sardanapallus*. But in place of “in the year 64 before the founding of the City,” the second Leiden manuscript gives 65.] a man more corrupt than a woman; who, among crowds of prostitutes, [Note: [Col. 0733B] In women’s clothing. All the manuscripts consistently write this, including the three Florentine manuscripts, the four Leiden manuscripts, my copy, and Perizonius’s, together with Augustine’s edition. Those who have *femineo* seem to have followed Justin, who has *muliebri habitu* in Book 1, chapter 3, from whom Orosius drew his material.] dressed as a woman, worked purple wool with a distaff, [Note: [Col. 0733B] By his prefect Arbatus. The common text has *Arbastus* and *Arbactus* here, just as *Arbastus* and *Arbactus* are read in the following book, chapter 2; but what we have written is found in the manuscripts in both places. FABR. — All the manuscripts we consulted consistently preserve Fabricius’s reading. In place of *tunc*, which follows, the third Leiden manuscript has *e te*, as though it wished to say “at that time.”] was regarded with contempt and abhorrence by his own prefect Arbatus, who then ruled the Medes, [Note: [Col. 0733B] Was regarded. The subsequent Leiden manuscript and the Utrecht manuscript have *visus est*. Augustine’s edition has “regarded as hateful and accursed.”] and soon, when the peoples of the Medes had been summoned to war, [Note: [Col. 0733B] Summoned. The subsequent Florentine has *adscitis*; the first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Utrecht manuscript, have *excitatis*. The first Florentine transposes the following words to *ad bellum Medorum populis*. In place of *provocatus*, the subsequent Florentine has *provocatur*.] challenged to battle and defeated, [Note: [Col. 0734A] He threw himself upon the burning pyre. “In this alone,” says Justin, “did he imitate a man.” A remarkable monument of this Sardanapalus once stood in Anchiale, a city of Cilicia not far from Tarsus; Arrian left a description of it in *The Expedition of Alexander the Great*, Book 2, chapter 5, p. 66. That king was said to have founded Anchiale; hence its inhabitants celebrated him there as their founder and honored him with this remarkable monument: “The monument of Sardanapalus stood near the walls of Anchiale, and Sardanapalus himself stood upon it, striking his hands together as people do when applauding.” He then adds an inscription worthy of such a king, commanding us to eat, drink, and indulge, while the other things of this life are not worth so much as the snap of the fingers or the clapping of the hands. That monument, along with many others of the same kind, perished long ago; nevertheless, the people of Tarsus wished its memory to remain eternally in bronze, since that city too was said to have been founded by Sardanapalus. They struck coins commemorating the event and the monument, though with some discrepancy; six especially distinguished examples of this type seemed worth inserting here.] he threw himself into the burning pyre. 75 [Note: [Col. 0735B] “Thereafter.” The first edition and the third Florentine have *Exhinc*; Augustine’s edition has *Exinde*, as does the second Florentine, though this was written by a second hand; previously it had *Exin*.]

Thereafter the kingdom of the Assyrians passed to the Medes. Then, with many battles breaking out on every side [Note: [Col. 0735B] Breaking out. All the manuscripts have this unusual verb, except Perizonius’s copy and the fourth Leiden manuscript, which have *scatentibus*, as in the first editions, the Parisian and Venetian editions, and Hittorp.]—battles which it does not seem appropriate to relate in sequence—it returned by various fortunes, by the same route, to the Scythians and Chaldaeans, and again to the Medes [Note: [Col. 0735C] It returned. Fabricius has *redit*, contrary to the manuscripts and the other editions; for above also the reading is *concessit* (“passed”).]. In this compressed account one must consider how great were the collapses and disasters of nations, how many wars swept onward, when so many kingdoms of such a kind changed hands so often. [Note: [Col. 0735C] “After this, Phraortes ruled the Medes.” Here Orosius follows someone unknown and disagrees with Herodotus and Eusebius, who make Phraortes the son of Deioces and say that he succeeded him in the Median kingdom. Megasthenes and Diodorus give different names for these kings. FABR.]

After this Phraortes ruled the Medes [Note: [Col. 0735C] Ruled. The second and third Florentine manuscripts and three Leiden manuscripts have *imperavit*. The first Florentine transposes what follows: “in the wars of the Assyrians and Persians.”], and he consumed twenty-two years of his reign in almost uninterrupted wars with the Persians and Assyrians. [Note: [Col. 0735C] “After him, Diocles.” The name *Diocles* is also found in the manuscripts. In Eusebius’ *Chronicle* it is *Deiocles*; Herodotus calls him Δηιόκης (*Dēiokēs*). FABR.]

After him Diocles became king, a man most experienced in arms [Note: [Col. 0735C] Most experienced. Some manuscripts and printed editions have *expertissimus*, contrary to the older and more numerous manuscripts. That this king was not only warlike but also just and good in peace is attested by excerpts from Diodorus together with the Polybian material, edited by Henri Valois, p. 230: “Deioces, king of the Medes, when many crimes were being committed, cultivated justice and the other virtues.”] and always occupied with wars; when he died, he handed his empire, which had been widely enlarged, [Note: [Col. 0735D] Widely. The second Leiden manuscript and the Utrecht manuscript omit the word, and my copy omits *moriens* (“when he died”). Augustine’s edition has, absurdly, “of the Lacedaemonians.”] over to Astyages. [Note: [Col. 0735D] Astyages, without male offspring. This story is told by Herodotus, Book 1, and likewise by Justin, Book 1. FABR.]

Astyages, lacking male offspring, had Cyrus, born among the Persians, as his grandson. But Cyrus, as soon as he grew to manhood, gathered a Persian force and challenged his grandfather to battle. [Note: [Col. 0735D] “Then Astyages.” Augustine’s edition has *Post Astyages* (“After Astyages”).] Astyages, however, having forgotten the crime he had once committed against Harpagus, when he killed his only young son and set him before his father to eat, and lest happy ignorance deprive that most wretched bereavement of anything, reproached him with the infamous meal after displaying to the father the head and hands. [Note: [Col. 0735D] “Forgetful.” Augustine’s edition adds the gloss “namely, Astyages.”]

Forgetful, therefore, of this deed, he entrusts the entire conduct of the war to Harpagus, [Note: [Col. 0736B] He entrusts. The first editions, Venetian and Parisian, have *commisit* (“entrusted”), as does Perizonius’s copy. The four Leiden manuscripts, together with the Utrecht manuscript and the first edition, read *tradidit* (“handed over”) below. The third Leiden manuscript has *auctum* in place of *acceptum*.] who immediately hands over the army he has received to Cyrus by treachery [Note: [Col. 0736B] He hands over by treachery. The reading *tradit* is also found, as in Justin. In the printed books of Justin, however, *deditionem* is corruptly printed, whereas the old copies correctly have *proditionem*. FABR.]. When Astyages learned of this, he seized his forces and himself marched against the Persians, [Note: [Col. 0736C] More fiercely. The third Florentine deletes the conjunction.] and renewed the battle more fiercely, imposing the threat of death upon his men if anyone should attempt to withdraw from the fight [Note: [Col. 0736C] To withdraw from the battle. The Utrecht manuscript has *secedere*. The first and Parisian editions have *de praelio cedere*. The first and third Leiden manuscripts have *praelio moliretur cedere*, with *e* deleted. Perhaps the reading should be *praelio excedere*.], for he would be received by the sword [Note: [Col. 0736C] He would be received. My copy has *exciperentur*, as does the third Florentine, in which *molirentur* was written shortly before.].

Because the Medes fought under this compulsion with determined effort, the Persian line was again put to flight [Note: [Col. 0736C] Again defeated. The fourth Leiden manuscript omits the second word; in place of *pulsa*, the Utrecht manuscript has *pulsata*.], and as it gradually gave way, their mothers and wives came forward to meet them and begged them [Note: [Col. 0736C] Into the battle. The old editions, together with the first and third Leiden manuscripts, have *ut in praelium* (“that they return into battle”), but all the others disagree, as does Justin. Augustine’s edition has “they beg their husbands, etc., to…” The fourth Leiden manuscript together with the Utrecht manuscript reads “they beg them to return into battle.”] to return into battle. When they hesitated, they lifted their clothing and exposed the shameful parts of their bodies, asking [Note: [Col. 0736C] Into the wombs. The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts have *numquid*, as does Augustine’s edition, in place of *an*; the second Leiden manuscript has *an*. The common reading is found in the others and in Justin.] whether they wished to retreat into the wombs of their mothers or wives. Ashamed by this deed, they returned to the battle; and having made an assault, they forced those whom they had been fleeing to flee. There Astyages was captured. Cyrus took nothing from him except his kingdom, and placed him over the great nation of the Hyrcanians. He himself did not wish to return to the Medes [Note: [Col. 0736D] He himself did not wish to return. This is found in the best and most numerous manuscripts, as well as in Justin; others have “he did not wish to return himself.” Then the Utrecht manuscript has “Here is the end,” etc.; somewhat later, the first editions, Venetian and Parisian, have *defecerant*.]. This was the end of the Median empire. But the cities that had been tributary to the Medes revolted from Cyrus [Col. 0736B]; and this became for Cyrus the cause and origin of many wars.

## CHAPTER XX. The tyranny of Phalaris and the crimes of Aremulus, king of the Latins

At that time Phalaris of Sicily was ravaging the people of Agrigentum after seizing the tyranny [Note: [Col. 0736D] He was ravaging. All the manuscripts, together with Augustine’s edition, have this reading; Fabricius printed it, and Scott followed him. The others have *depopulabatur*, in place of which Vincent of Beauvais has *depopulatur*.]. Cruel in character and even more cruel in his inventions, inflicting every abomination upon the innocent, he eventually found someone whom he, an unjust man, could justly punish. [Note: [Col. 0736D] For Perillus. This Perillus, a worker in bronze, is called Πέριλλος τῇ τέχνῃ χαλκίουργος (“Perillus, a bronze-worker by profession”) by Plutarch in the *Parallel Lives*; Lucian calls him Πορίλαος in *Phalaris* 1. See also Pliny, Book 34, chapter 8. FABR.]

For a certain Perillus, a craftsman in bronze, seeking the tyrant’s friendship, thought up a gift suited to his cruelty and made a bronze bull, [Note: [Col. 0737B] “For which he skillfully fitted a door.” The editions have *adfabre*, but because the old word is preserved by the Cologne manuscript, we too have preferred it. LAUT. — *Fabre* is also found in the three Florentine manuscripts, in three Leiden manuscripts, in the Utrecht manuscript, in my copy, and in Perizonius’s, as well as in the older Hittorpian editions. In the first of these, it was changed to *adfabre*, which the later editions followed. But the true reading is *fabricae*, preserved by the first Leiden manuscript and by Vincent of Beauvais, who copied the entire earlier part of this chapter and inserted it into the great work he called the *Historical Mirror*, Book 3, chapter 107. Then, in place of “a door in its side,” the Utrecht manuscript has “in its side a door”; Augustine’s edition has “a door in its side.”] for which he skillfully constructed a door in its side, so that it might serve as a receptacle [Note: [Col. 0737C] For thrusting in. Vincent of Beauvais has “for thrusting in.”] for thrusting in the condemned; so that, when the person enclosed inside was roasted by fires placed beneath it, the hollow bronze would magnify the sound of the voice forced from him, [Note: [Col. 0737C] In the same place. The second and fourth Leiden manuscripts have *ibi ex*; Perizonius has *ibi*.] and, by a suitable reverberation, would send forth a dreadful imitation of the sound, so that the bellowing of an animal, rather than the groaning of a human being, would seem to emerge from the monstrous spectacle. But Phalaris, embracing the device and cursing its maker, supplied material both for vengeance and for cruelty: for he punished the craftsman himself by means of his own invention. [Note: [Col. 0737C] “By his own invention.” Augustine’s edition has *sua adinventione*.]

Somewhat earlier, there had also been among the Latins a king named Aremulus, [Note: [Col. 0737C] Aremulus. He was the twelfth king of the Latins, called Romulus Silvius in Livy; Dio calls him Ἀλλάδην (*Alladēs*) and writes more about his impiety. FABR. — *Remulus* is found in the first and third Leiden manuscripts and in Perizonius’s; also in the second and first Florentine manuscripts, both here and below, although *Aremulus* is written in the margin. The fourth Leiden manuscript has *Romulus*, as do the older editions.] who, increasing in crimes and impieties for eighteen years, was at last seized by lightning through divine judgment and, at an untimely age, paid his timely penalties [Note: [Col. 0737D] Paid. Scott printed *exsolvit*, supported by the oldest first edition, Augustine’s, and the Venetian and Parisian editions. But *dissolvit* is found in Fabricius and the other editions, as well as in every manuscript I consulted, and I did not wish to alter it. The tyrant “paid” the penalties owed, as though they were a debt incurred. Cicero similarly says *poenam dissolvere* in *Tusculan Disputations* 1.42: “I am very grateful to the man who imposed upon me a penalty which I could pay without borrowing or taking out a new loan.” He is there speaking of a Lacedaemonian condemned to death, who was led away with a cheerful expression.] . Let the Latins and Sicilians now choose, if they wish, whether they would have preferred to live in the days of Aremulus and Phalaris, when the lives of innocent people were extorted through punishments, or in these Christian times, when Roman emperors, [Note: [Col. 0737D] Themselves. The first and third Leiden manuscripts have *ipsi* (“they themselves”).] formed above all by the religion itself, after tyrannies had been crushed for the good of the state, do not exact even the injuries inflicted upon them by tyrants.

## 79. CHAPTER XXI. The war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians; the incursion of the Amazons and Cimmerians into Asia; the long siege and capture of Messene; the war of the Athenians against the Lacedaemonians; and that of the Peloponnesians and Boeotians against the Athenians

[Note: [Col. 0737D] “In the year,” etc. In place of 30, the first edition, and the Venetian and Parisian editions have 13.]

In the year 30 before the founding of the City, the greatest war between the Peloponnesians and Athenians was undertaken with all their strength and spirit. In it, through mutual slaughter, [Note: [Col. 0737D] They were compelled to this. The first two words are absent from the second Leiden manuscript.] they were forced to withdraw from one another as though defeated, [Note: [Col. 0738B] And abandon the war. My copy has “and dismiss the war.” The first, Parisian, and Venetian editions have “and depart from the war.” It is characteristic of Justin, from whom Orosius took much of his material, to use *deserere bellum* for “to abandon the war”: see Book 2, chapter 8, “the Megarians, mindful of the war inflicted upon and abandoned by the Athenians”; Book 5, chapter 2, “the war must be endured lest it be abandoned through want”; and Book 9, chapter 2, “lest want compel him to abandon the war.”] and abandon the war. At that time a sudden incursion of the Amazon nation and the Cimmerians into Asia also produced a widespread devastation and slaughter for a long time. [Note: [Col. 0738B] “A very extensive devastation for a long time.” The first edition, together with the Venetian and Parisian editions, has *diu lateque*; the third Leiden manuscript has the same. The first Florentine has *late diu*. The first and third Leiden manuscripts and Perizonius’s have *stragemque dedit*.]

In the twentieth year before the founding of the City, the Lacedaemonians, because their own maidens had been spurned [Note: [Col. 0738C] Because their maidens had been dishonored. In Justin, Book 3, from whom this account was taken, the reading is “because the maidens had been violated.” Pausanias, Book 4, writes that during the war the Messenian youths seized the maidens who were dancing the choruses of Diana; the young men, heated with wine, wished to violate them, but their leader Aristomenes returned them unharmed to their people. FABR. — All the printed and manuscript copies of Orosius have *spretas* (“despised”), although it is entirely clear from Justin that the maidens had been violated; see what learned men have noted there. Orosius seems to have used a corrupt copy of Justin in which *spretas* had occurred, or perhaps a compendium in which *stpratas* or *spratas*, with the customary abbreviation stroke above it, gave rise to the common *spretas* in the older Orosian manuscripts.] in the solemn sacrifice of the Messenians, [Note: [Col. 0738C] At the solemn Messenian sacrifice. Strabo, Book 8, p. 362—or p. 556 in the latest edition—tells us where this event took place: “The temple of Artemis at Limnae, called Limnaeum, in which the Messenians are thought to have violated the maidens who had come to the sacrifice, lies on the border of Laconia and Messenia, where both peoples used to celebrate a common festival and sacrifice. After the insult, when the Messenians did not submit to judgment, they say that the war broke out.”] declared war, 80 [Note: [Col. 0738D] For twenty years. Pausanias, Book 4, chapter 12, p. 309, also testifies that the war lasted this many years: “For the twentieth year of the war was approaching.” Then, on p. 312, he says that finally, after all their leaders and the best men had been lost, the Messenians abandoned Mount Ithome and, defeated, brought the war to an end: “After they had waged war for twenty years in all, as Tyrtaeus also recorded in verse.” The verses are these:

“Both sides fought here for nineteen years,
Always without respite, with steadfast hearts,
Warriors, the fathers of our fathers.
But in the twentieth year, leaving their rich fields,
They fled from the great mountains of Ithome.”

The verses are found joined in this way in Strabo, Book 6, p. 279, or 428; the latter part is found in Pausanias at the cited passage, and the former in the same author, Book 4, chapter 15, p. 315. On p. 312 Pausanias notes the time when the war ended: “This war came to an end in the first year of the fourteenth Olympiad.” The war with the Messenians was concluded in the twentieth year, in the war they fought against the Lacedaemonians for the first time, as these three different wars are enumerated by Diodorus Siculus, Book 15, p. 378, and by Strabo, Book 8, p. 362, or 556, on the authority of the poet and military leader of the Messenians in the second war, Tyrtaeus. [Col. 0739C] Tyrtaeus sings that the first war was fought in the time of the grandfathers. In the second war, Tyrtaeus himself was present as leader of the Lacedaemonians; the Eleans, Argives, and Pisatae had joined the Messenians as allies. At that time their king Aristodemus led the Messenians to war, Aristocrates, king of Orchomenus, led the Arcadians, and Pantaleon, son of Omphalion, led the Pisatae. What Strabo then calls the third and fourth wars concerns the revolt of the Messenians, which Pausanias, Book 4, chapter 15, p. 315, says occurred with the help of the Arcadians and Argives. This was forty years after the destruction of Ithome, in the fourth year of the twenty-third Olympiad, when Icarus of Hyperesia won the stadion race. Strabo, Book 6, p. 279, or 427, on the authority of the very ancient historian Ephorus, traces the origin of the twenty-year war not to the violation of the maidens but to the killing of Teleclus, king of the Lacedaemonians: the Messenians had killed him when he had gone there to sacrifice, while the Lacedaemonians unsuccessfully sought vengeance for his death. The insult inflicted upon the Spartan maidens occurred in the third war, which Aristomenes, the renowned leader of the Messenians, waged against the Lacedaemonians, as is clear from Pausanias, Book 4, chapter 16, p. 320. But these matters, and more besides, are commonly confused in Justin and other writers.] and after fighting for twenty years with unremitting fury, they involved the whole strength of Greece in their own ruin. [Note: [Col. 0739D] “Who, when they had bound themselves by great…” In Strabo at the cited passage, Ephorus, the distinguished historian whose work has now perished, gives a lengthy account of the origin of Tarentum, founded by the Partheniae, and says that the cause of that war and of the Lacedaemonians’ persistent anger was the unavenged death of King Teleclus.]

For, after binding themselves with great imprecations and oaths never to return home until Messene had been captured, and after being worn out by ten years of a lengthy siege without gaining any advantage from victory, [Note: [Col. 0739D] Having gained. The first Leiden manuscript adds *sunt*.] they were moved by the complaints of their wives over their prolonged widowhood and the danger of barrenness, [Note: [Col. 0739D] Protesting. Perizonius adds after this: “that, if they did not return, they would seek intercourse with their neighbors”; these words seem to have been inserted here from a similar passage occurring above at the end of chapter 15.] and were recalled. After a council had been held, they feared that, if the hope of offspring were lost, their persistence would bring ruin upon themselves more than upon the Messenians. They therefore selected from the army those who had come to reinforce the army after the oath had been sworn [Note: [Col. 0740A] The chosen men. The Utrecht manuscript and two Leiden manuscripts, together with Perizonius, have *electos*.], and sent them back to Sparta [Note: [Col. 0740A] To Sparta. The Utrecht manuscript and the second Leiden manuscript have *ad Spartam*.]. To these they permitted sexual intercourse with all the women indiscriminately [Note: [Col. 0740A] With all the women. Ephorus, in Strabo at the cited passage, restricts this to the maidens alone, as is also shown by the name given to the offspring born from it: “They ordered all the men to have intercourse with all the maidens, thinking that there would thereby be more children; and when these were born, the boys were called Partheniae.” That is, they ordered them to have intercourse with all the maidens, believing that offspring would thereby be more abundant; and those born in this way were called Partheniae, that is, “sons of maidens,” their fathers being uncertain. These were the men who, under the leadership of Phalanthus, left their homeland and founded Tarentum in Magna Graecia.] by a license sufficiently shameful, yet not advantageous. [Note: [Col. 0740B] A sufficiently shameful and nevertheless useless license. The authority of the first Florentine alone would suggest that this is the way it must be written. In addition, the third and fourth Florentine manuscripts, my copy, and Perizonius’s, as well as the first and Parisian editions, have this reading; I pay no attention to the others, which, together with certain manuscripts, give “and nevertheless not useless.” The license was in fact useless to the Lacedaemonians, indeed almost fatal. For when the Partheniae saw themselves despised and neglected in the attainment of offices, they formed a conspiracy, resolved to slaughter their fellow citizens and seize their homeland. Antiochus, in Strabo, Book 6, p. 278, or 426, gives a lengthy account of this. They had decided that, when the Hyacinthian games were being celebrated at the Amyclaeum, Phalanthus, their leader, would place a cap upon his head; at that signal they would attack the citizens, whom their long hair made recognizable above the others. But when the matter came to the attention of the Spartan magistrates through the information of certain people, once the contest had already begun, the herald came forward and announced that Phalanthus was not to place the cap upon his head. Thus, when the conspiracy of the Partheniae had been exposed and their plan dissolved, they were forced to leave the country and consequently did nothing for the Lacedaemonian state.]

The Lacedaemonians, however, persisting in their purpose, captured the Messenians by treachery, [Note: [Col. 0740C]

“They oppress the defeated with slavery.” How harsh their slavery was is explained by Tyrtaeus in his elegies and, following him, by Pausanias, Book 4, p. 313:

“Like asses worn down beneath great burdens,
Carrying for cruel masters upon their backs,
Under the compulsion of grievous necessity,
Half of all the produce that the fields bear.”

That they were also required to mourn is made clear in the following:

“Lamenting their masters, alike their wives and they,
Whenever some deadly fate seized one of them in death.”

Tyrtaeus’ verses make clear these insulting punishments inflicted upon the Messenians:

“Like asses, crushed beneath an unequal burden,
Whom cruel masters compel to carry on their backs
Half the produce that their own land bears.”

That they were also compelled to attend funerals in mournful dress may be inferred from these words:]

And they themselves, together with their wives, were compelled to mourn their masters whenever cruel death carried one of them away from life. For among the conditions of peace the Lacedaemonians had imposed upon the Messenians was that they should bind themselves by oath never to revolt from the Lacedaemonians, should bring half of their annual produce to Sparta, and should follow the funerals of Lacedaemonians, dressed in black, together with their wives.] They oppress the vanquished with slavery. But after long enduring their bloody domination amid whippings and chains, the Messenians shake off the yoke, take up arms, and renew the war. [Note: [Col. 0741B] They renew the war. Since Tyrtaeus refers the first war to the third generation before his own, it is clear that a longer interval must be placed between the two than Pausanias allowed. Compare the note above, no. 7. The interval was therefore ninety years, if the duration of each generation (γενεά) is reduced to thirty years. See Graevius on Justin, book III, chapter 5. Tyrtaeus teaches that three generations intervened, in the following verse quoted above under no. 7:

“. . . the fathers of our fathers.”

For the fathers’ fathers are three γενεαί distant from their grandchildren. The First Messenian War, which lasted twenty years, ended at the beginning of the twenty-fourth Olympiad, and is consequently acknowledged to have begun in the ninth Olympiad. Suidas, however, says that Tyrtaeus flourished in the thirty-fifth Olympiad; in its third year Messana revolted from the alliance of the Lacedaemonians, as Valesius observed from Eusebius in his notes on Diodorus’s Excerpts, p. 38.] The Lacedaemonians enlist Tyrtaeus, an Athenian poet, as their commander in the war. [Note: [Col. 0741C] Tyrtaeus, an Athenian poet. Philochorus, Callisthenes, and several others related that Tyrtaeus came from Athens and Aphidna, at the command of the oracle and at the request of the Lacedaemonians, as Strabo notes. But Strabo likewise observes that poems of his survive which show that he came into the Peloponnese from Erineus. Erineus was a Dorian city beneath Mounts Pindus and Oeta, whence Tyrtaeus called it “windy” (ἠνεμόεντα). His verses preserved by Strabo, book VIII, pp. 362 or 557, are these:

“Zeus, son of Cronus, husband of beautifully crowned Hera,
himself gave this city to the Heraclids;
with them, leaving windy Erineus,
we came to the broad island of Pelops.”

He attributes the city to the Heraclids, for Jupiter is the husband of Juno; with them, leaving windy Erineus, we came to the broad land of the Peloponnese.] After being defeated in three engagements, they replenish their lost army by calling slaves to freedom. But when even then they thought that they must abandon the struggle because of fear of danger, [Note: [Col. 0741D] The struggle should be abandoned. Instead of *certamine*, as found in the first and Paris editions—and indeed in the first, second, and third Florentine manuscripts, as well as in mine—some copies have *certamini*, which would mean “to abandon the battle” or “to desert the struggle,” though the expression is less usual. A little earlier, two manuscripts read *impleverunt* (“filled”) instead of *suppleverunt* (“replenished”), and the first Florentine manuscript has *in libertate* (“in freedom”) instead of *in libertatem* (“to freedom”).] they were once more roused by a poem composed by the poet and commander Tyrtaeus and recited before the assembly. [Note: [Col. 0742B] Tyrtaeus’s poem. This poem was composed in alternating, rather long lines. Lycurgus says that a law required it to be recited to the Spartan soldiers, assembled under the king’s command and bearing arms: “Against Leocrates,” where that poem is found. FABR.] They rush again into the struggle; [Note: [Col. 0742B] Into the struggle. The Augustan edition has *in certamina* (“into struggles”), and soon afterward *tanta autem vi* (“with such force”), as do all the manuscripts of the Ulm, Leiden, and Florentine collections, as well as mine. For *praelium* (“battle”), the first Leiden edition and the Perizonian manuscript have *bellum* (“war”); these two words are often confused in Orosius’s manuscripts. Thus below, for *in Athenienses praelio*, the first edition likewise has *bello*, and shortly afterward it has *pugnam* (“fight”) instead of *certamen*. Periz.] such was the force of their courage in the encounter that scarcely ever had a bloodier battle broken out. At last, however, victory belonged to the Lacedaemonians.

For the third time the Messenians renewed the struggle. Nor did the Lacedaemonians delay. [Note: [Col. 0742C] Many forces in support. The Augustan edition reads, “for they led many forces in support,” and shortly afterward, instead of *intentos* (“intent upon”), three Leiden manuscripts have *infestos* (“hostile”).] Both sides brought many forces to their aid. The Athenians, meanwhile, prepared to attack the Lacedaemonians from the opposite direction, while they were occupied elsewhere. Nor did the Lacedaemonians remain inactive: since they themselves were engaged against the Messenians, they sent Peloponnesians to meet the Athenians in battle.

The Athenians, after sending a small fleet to Egypt, were inferior in strength and were easily defeated in a naval engagement. Then, having recalled the fleet and increased their military strength, they summoned the enemy to battle as victors. The Lacedaemonians too, [Note: [Col. 0742C] Omitting. Perizon has *dimissis* (“having dismissed”).] abandoning the Messenians, turned their arms against the Athenians. [Note: [Col. 0742C] Long, varied, and serious battles. The first and second Florentine manuscripts, the Ulm manuscript, and Perizonus together with the Augustan edition transpose the words in this way. The usual text has “long, serious, and varied battles.” Mine, together with Perizonus, reads “for a long time, equally serious battles.” Four Leiden manuscripts add *fuerunt* (“there were”) at the end of the sentence.] For a long time the battles were varied and severe, and the outcome of the victory remained uncertain; at last, with the result still undecided, both sides withdrew. [Note: [Col. 0742C] At last. Some editions have *ac postremum*; my manuscript has *ac postremo* (“and finally”).]

[Note: [Col. 0742C] It must nevertheless be understood. My manuscript deletes the final word. I would readily remove the entire clause up to “the Spartans are called,” unless the authority of all the manuscripts stood against it. The first edition and the Paris edition read: “It must nevertheless be understood that Sparta itself is the Lacedaemonian state,” with *maxime* (“especially”) deleted—in place of which the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts have *maximam* (“greatest”)—as well as *est*. The Ulm manuscript also omits it. Then in the first Florentine manuscript, the first three Leiden manuscripts, and mine, *dicunt* (“they call”) is missing. I therefore reconstruct the passage, removing what is needlessly superfluous, as follows: “It must nevertheless be understood that Sparta itself is the Lacedaemonian state” (or, as the first Florentine manuscript has it, *Lacedaemonem*), “and that from this the Lacedaemonians are called Spartans.”]

It must nevertheless be understood that Sparta itself is the state which they also call Lacedaemon, and that from it the Lacedaemonians are called Spartans. Therefore, when the Lacedaemonians were recalled from there to the war against the Messenians, so that they would not leave the Athenians an interval of leisure, they made an agreement with the Thebans that they would restore to them the rule of Boeotia, which they had lost during the Persian War, if the Thebans would undertake the war against the Athenians. The fury of the Spartans was so great that, although entangled in two wars, they did not refuse to undertake a third, provided that they acquired enemies for their own enemies.

[Col. 0742B] The Athenians, shaken by so great a storm of wars, chose two commanders: Pericles, a man of renowned courage, and Sophocles, the writer of tragedies. [Note: [Col. 0742D] They chose. Perizonus has *eligunt* (“they choose”); the Augustan edition has *elegerunt* (“they chose”).] Dividing the army, they both ravaged the territories of the Spartans far and wide [Note: [Col. 0742D] And they ravaged the Spartan territories far and wide. Instead of *fines*, Perizonus has *civitates* (“cities”); the Augustan edition then has *depopulati* (“having ravaged”).] and added many cities of Asia to the dominion of the Athenians.

From that point onward, for fifty years, war was waged on land and sea, victory always uncertain, until the Spartans, [Note: [Col. 0743A] Their resources diminished. My parchment has *opibus imminuti* (“diminished in resources”), agreeing with the masculine plural subject.] with their resources diminished and their good faith ruined, became a reproach even to their allies. But people make little of the fact that these things weighed upon Greece through so many generations. Now, however, people cannot endure having their pleasures interrupted even occasionally or their desires hindered for a little while.

Although there is this difference between the people of that time and those of the present: the former patiently endured these intolerable things, because they had been born and [Note: [Col. 0743A] Brought up. The first Florentine and the third Leiden manuscripts read *nutriti* (“nourished”), as Scott published it; Fabricius and the others have *enutriti* (“brought up”).] brought up amid them and knew nothing better, whereas the latter, accustomed throughout their lives to a perpetual serenity of tranquility and luxury, are shaken by every even slight cloud of anxiety that gathers.

And would that they prayed to the very One who drives away even this slight unrest—the One whose gift has granted them a peace of uninterrupted duration unknown in other times!

And since I remember promising, when I was defining the order of my discourse by certain divisions, that I would speak from the creation of the world to the founding of the City, let this volume, in which I have unfolded events from the creation of the world, now come to an end, so that the following book may begin from the founding of the City. [Note: [Col. 0743B] Which. This is absent from my manuscript and from three Florentine manuscripts. It is nevertheless absolutely required, unless we delete the final word of this book, so that the sentence reads: “the following book will contain the more immediate evils of those times, among people more practiced in wickedness and more educated.” At the end of this book, the oldest Florentine manuscript has, in the same ancient hand, *contuli* (“I have collated”). In the Augustan edition, after *continebit*, the following gloss has intruded into the text: “From the creation of the world to the founding of the City, 4,487 years are reckoned. From the founding of the City to the birth of Christ, 715 are reckoned. Therefore from the origin of the world to the coming of our Lord there are 5,099 years.” It then continues: “Here ends the first book successfully.” But in the first Florentine manuscript we read: “Here ends book I of Paulus Orosius Against the Pagans; book II begins.” Much the same is found in the others, except that some write: “The Histories Against the Pagans.”] It will contain the more immediate evils of those times, among people more practiced in wickedness and more educated.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0743]

### CHAPTER ONE. On the changes of kingdoms brought about by God’s providence

[Col. 0743C]

I believe that there is now no human being who can remain unaware that God made man upright in this world; hence, even when man sins, the world is charged with guilt, and, to restrain our lack of self-control, this earth in which we live is chastised by the decline of its other animals and by the barrenness of its fruits.

Therefore, if we are God’s creation, by the merit and dispensation of God, [Note: [Col. 0743C] God’s creature. Above, book I, chapter 8, p. 49: “and, more correctly, *creatura* rather than *creatura domini sui*.” Soon afterward, three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have *merito et dispensatione* (“by right and by God’s ordering”).] who loves more than the one who made us? And who governs in a more orderly way than the one who both made and loves us? [Note: [Col. 0743D] Who both made and loves. The fourth Leiden manuscript has *dilexit* (“loved”); mine reads, “than the one who made and loves.”] Who, then, could arrange and govern what has been made more wisely and powerfully than the one who foresaw what was to be made and completed what he had foreseen? [Note: [Col. 0743D] He foresaw what was to be made. The first and Perizonian Leiden manuscripts have *praevidit* (“foresaw”); certain editions have *providet* (“provides”), the Ulm manuscript *perficit* (“completes”).]

Consequently, all power is from God, as is every ordinance; those who have not [Note: [Col. 0743D] Have read. Three Leiden manuscripts and the old editions, together with the Gronovian Collection, read *legunt* (“read”) here and again shortly afterward; Perizonus accepts *agnoscunt* (“recognize”) instead of *cognoscunt* (“know”); the first Florentine manuscript has *recognoscunt* (“recognize”), which I prefer as familiar to Christian writers. See the index to Tertullian’s *Apologeticus*, book 20, p. 191: “While we suffer, they read; while we recognize, they approve.”] read perceive this, and those who have read recognize it. But if powers are from God, how much more kingdoms, from which the remaining powers proceed! And if there are diverse kingdoms, how much more reasonably is there some greatest kingdom to which the power of all the other kingdoms is subjected? [Note: [Col. 0744D] Such as Babylonian at the beginning. The Gronovian Collection and three Leiden manuscripts have, “such as that Babylonian kingdom at the beginning.” In the margin of the first Florentine manuscript this heading is written: “The order of the kingdoms: Babylonian, Macedonian, African, Roman”; and in the second: “First, the Babylonian kingdom; second, the Macedonian; third, the African.” Orosius does not mention the dominion of the Medes and Persians, because they arose, as it were, from the Babylonian kingdom, whereas the Greeks, Romans, and Africans were entirely different peoples, distinct from one another in origin, language, and customs. The Ulm manuscript deletes *atque* (“and”) at the end. Some editions add material afterward.]

Such as the Babylonian kingdom was at the beginning, then the Macedonian, afterward the African, and finally the Roman, which endures to the present. By the same ineffable ordering, the dominion of four kingdoms was established at the four quarters of the world, rising in distinguished ranks: the Babylonian kingdom in the east, the Carthaginian in the south, the Macedonian in the north, [Note: [Col. 0745C] In the west. Three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have *ab occasu* (“from the west”).] and the Roman in the west. Between the first and the last—that is, between the Babylonian and Roman kingdoms—there came, as it were between an aged father and a little son, the African and Macedonian kingdoms, brief and intermediate, admitted by the power of time, not by hereditary right. [Note: [Col. 0745C] Admitted. The Augustan edition, together with one Leiden manuscript and the Mainz edition, has *admissi* (“admitted,” masculine plural), referring to *principatus* (“dominions”), but that antecedent is too remote.] I shall explain as clearly as possible whether this is so.

### CHAPTER TWO. A kind of epilogue to the foregoing; a comparison of the various kingdoms and periods; and the succession of kingdoms

[Col. 0745B]

The first king among the Assyrians who was able to rise above the rest was Ninus. After Ninus was killed, his wife Semiramis, queen of all Asia, restored the city of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0745C] Restored. The Ulm and second Leiden editions have *restauravit* (“restored”).] and established it as the capital of the Assyrian kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0745C] The Assyrian kingdom. The second Leiden edition has “but the Assyrian kingdom.” Shortly afterward the Augustan edition has “its power, long unshaken.” In the margin of the first Florentine manuscript is written: “Arbatus the prefect killed Sardanapalus and transferred the empire to the Medes,” in accordance with the usual practice of the manuscripts in expressing the name.]

The Assyrian kingdom stood for a long time with power unshaken. But when Arbatus, whom others call Arbaces, the prefect of the Medes and himself a Mede by nation, had killed his king Sardanapalus near Babylon, he transferred the name and supreme authority of the kingdom to the Medes. [Note: [Col. 0745D] Arbatus, whom others call Arbaces. As we have already said, this is how the ancient books read. Diodorus calls him Ἀρβαίκη, as does Eusebius in the *Chronicle*. Accordingly, the printed books of Velleius Paterculus must be corrected, where it is written, “Pharnaces the Mede deprived Sardanapalus of life and empire”; it should read, “Arbaces the Mede.” FABR. Arbatus is also found in all the Florentine manuscripts, as well as in many others and in the Augustan edition.]

Thus the kingdom of Ninus and Babylon was transferred to the Medes in the same year in which, among the Latins, Procas—father of Amulius and Numitor, and grandfather of Rhea Silvia, who was the mother of Romulus—began to reign. To demonstrate fully that all these events were arranged by ineffable mysteries and the deepest judgments of God, and did not occur through human strength or uncertain chance, all ancient histories begin with Ninus, and all Roman histories originate with Procas. [Note: [Col. 0745D] But not. The Augustan, first Paris, and Venetian editions have *non aut* (“not either”), and so forth.]

From the first year of Ninus’s reign until Semiramis began to restore Babylon, sixty-four years intervened. [Note: [Col. 0746C] Sixty-four years. The first Leiden edition reckons seventy-three years.] From the first year of Procas, when he began to reign, until the founding of the City by Romulus, an equal sixty-four years intervened. Thus, under the reign of Procas, the seed of future Rome was sown, although the sprout had not yet appeared. [Note: [Col. 0746C] The sprout had not appeared. The Augustan edition and the first and third Florentine manuscripts have *germen apparet* (“the sprout appears”); the second Florentine manuscript has *apparet* written above the line. My manuscript has “the seed had not appeared.”]

In that same year of Procas’s reign, the kingdom of Babylon failed, although Babylon itself still remained. [Note: [Col. 0746C] As Arbaces descended. Two old manuscripts, as well as the context, show that this should be read instead of *discedente* (“departing”). LAUT. This reading is supported by the first and fourth Leiden manuscripts and the Augustan edition.] When Arbatus passed over to the Medes, [Note: [Col. 0746C] The Chaldaeans retained part of the kingdom. Belochus, prefect of Babylonia, helped Arbaces against Sardanapalus. After Sardanapalus was defeated, Arbaces gained possession of the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, while Belochus retained Babylon with Assyria. FABR.] the Chaldaeans retained part of the kingdom for themselves, claiming Babylon against the Medes. Thus power over Babylonia belonged to the Medes, but ownership belonged to the Chaldaeans. The Chaldaeans, however, because of the ancient dignity of the royal city, preferred to call it not theirs but themselves Babylon’s; [Note: [Col. 0746D] To call. This is the reading of all the Florentine manuscripts, the Ulm manuscript, mine, and the Leiden manuscripts. Perizonus and some printed editions have *vocari* (“to be called”).] [Note: [Col. 0746D] Hence. The Augustan edition has *inde* (“therefore”).] hence it happened that Nabuchodonosor and the other kings after him down to Cyrus, although they are recorded as powerful through the strength of the Chaldaeans and renowned under the name of Babylonia, [Note: [Col. 0746D] In the number and rank. *Ordine* (“rank”) might have been tolerated earlier, unless the better reading in Maternus’s book were *cardine* (“order,” literally “hinge”). The Florentine manuscripts and the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts, as well as Perizonus, prefer *cardine*.] were nevertheless not counted among the illustrious kings. [Note: [Col. 0746D] Be counted. Some printed editions have *habentur* (“are counted”), contrary to the better manuscripts and nearly all the others.]

Babylon, therefore, was dishonored under the prefect Arbatus in the same year in which Rome, under King Procas—to speak precisely—was sown. [Note: [Col. 0746D] Was sown. Three Leiden manuscripts have *fundata est* (“was founded”), as does the Gronovian Collection, which deletes *illa* (“that”).]

At last Babylon was overthrown by King Cyrus at the time when Rome was first freed from the domination of the Tarquin kings. [Note: [Col. 0747C] By King Cyrus. The Ulm and second Leiden editions delete *rege* (“king”).] For, in one and the same correspondence of times, Babylon fell and Rome rose: Babylon then first endured the rule of foreigners, while Rome then first rejected even the arrogance of her own people. [Note: [Col. 0747C] The arrogance. The Augustan edition has *fastigium* (“loftiness”); my manuscript and Perizonus have *fastigium*; the first and second Leiden manuscripts have *flagitium* (“disgrace”).] Babylon, then as if dying, relinquished her inheritance; Rome, growing to maturity, then recognized herself as heir. Then the power of the East fell, and the empire of the West arose. And, lest I delay longer with words, I commit myself to the teeth of madmen, to be delivered by the protection of truth.

### CHAPTER THREE. The origin, foundation, and state of the Babylonian and Roman kingdoms were nearly alike, but their ends were different

[Col. 0747B]

Ninus reigned for fifty-two years. He was succeeded, as I have said, by his wife Semiramis; and when she too had reigned for forty-two years, [Note: [Col. 0747C] For forty-two years. The Augustan edition increases the number by fifty. The third Leiden manuscript and the Gronovian Collection have sixty-two years. Perizonus soon deletes *imperii* (“of her reign”).] in the middle of her reign she founded Babylon, the capital of the kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0747D] Babylon. This is the reading of three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection, which I adopt because *Babylon* follows. The three Florentine manuscripts have *Babylonam*; the printed editions have *Babyloniam*.] [Note: [Col. 0747D] The capital of the kingdom. Perizonus has “the capital of her kingdom”; the Augustan edition, “the kingdom’s capital.” The Gronovian Collection has *caput regni erexit* (“raised up the capital of the kingdom”) instead of *condidit* (“founded”), as if it meant “raised it into a capital.” I have not changed the common reading, since what follows supports it.]

Thus, after one thousand one hundred and nearly sixty-four years from its foundation, [Note: [Col. 0747D] Since it was founded. The third Florentine manuscript deletes this phrase; the first and third Leiden manuscripts have *postquam* (“after”), and so forth.] Babylon was stripped of its wealth and kingdom by the Medes and by Arbatus, [Note: [Col. 0748C] And by Arbatus. This is the reading of the best Florentine manuscript and of the first and fourth Leiden manuscripts; the others have “and Arbatus.”] their king but its prefect, and was deprived of its own king. [Note: [Col. 0748C] Their king. My manuscript has “their own king,” but deletes *suo* (“own”) shortly afterward. The words from “its own prefect” to “companion” are absent from the third Florentine manuscript.] Yet Babylon itself afterward remained unharmed for some time.

Rome likewise, after the same number of years—that is, one thousand one hundred and nearly sixty-four—was stormed by the Goths and their king Alaric, though he was Rome’s commander, and was stripped of her wealth; but not of her kingdom. She still remains and reigns unharmed. [Note: [Col. 0748C] And nearly. This is absent from the second Florentine manuscript and the Venetian editions.] Although the entire order of correspondence between the two cities was preserved according to such secret decrees that there too Arbatus, its prefect, seized the kingdom, while here [Note: [Col. 0748C] The prefect of this city. All the manuscripts and printed editions transpose the words: “this city’s prefect.”] its prefect Attalus attempted to reign. [Note: [Col. 0748C] Attalus. The Gronovian Collection has *Athalus*.] Yet in this city alone the profane attempt against the Christian emperor was, deservedly, rendered ineffectual. [Note: [Col. 0748C] Of the Christian emperor. The name “Honorius,” commonly added, is, I think, a gloss inserted by someone who wished to identify which emperor was meant; he is discussed in book VII, chapter 40. FABR. Fabricius rightly deleted the name Honorius, although three Leiden manuscripts together with the Gronovian Collection attest it. The Longobard Florentine manuscript, together with two others, mine, Perizonus, the Ulm manuscript, and the second Leiden edition, also deletes it.] [Note: [Col. 0748D] Assault. The Gronovian Collection and the third Leiden manuscript have *tentatio* (“attempt”).]

I have thought these matters especially worth recalling so that, now that part of the ineffable mystery of God’s judgments has been disclosed, those who foolishly grumble about Christian times may understand that one God arranged the ages: at the beginning for the Babylonians, and at the end for the Romans. It is due to his mercy that we live; but that we live miserably is due to our lack of self-control.

Behold: Babylon and Rome had a similar origin, similar power, similar greatness, similar periods, similar advantages, and similar evils; [Note: [Col. 0748D] Yet. This reading is exhibited with remarkable agreement by the three Florentine manuscripts, four Leiden manuscripts, Perizonus, mine, and finally the Ulm manuscript together with the Gronovian Collation. Of the printed editions, only the Augustan has it. All the others, rather awkwardly, write *tametsi* (“although”).] yet their endings were not alike, nor was their decline alike. Babylon lost her kingdom; Rome retains hers. Babylon was deprived of her king by his murder; Rome is secure with her emperor alive.

And why is this? Because there the disgrace of the king’s lusts was punished, whereas here the most continent justice of the Christian religion was preserved in the king. [Note: [Col. 0748D] Most continent. Perizonus deletes this; the Ulm manuscript reads “continence and justice in the king.”] There, without reverence for religion, a desire for pleasure was fulfilled by the license of madness. [Note: [Col. 0748D] A desire for pleasure. Apart from the Augustan edition, the three Florentine manuscripts have *voluntatis* (“of the will”). I prefer the common reading, since it refers back to the disgrace of lusts.] Here there were Christians who spared, Christians whom they spared, and Christians for whose memory, and in whose memory, mercy was shown.

Therefore let them cease to tear religion apart and to provoke the patience of God. [Note: [Col. 0748D] Patience. This word seems more suitable than *potentiam* (“power”), which is found in the Gronovian Collection and the first Leiden edition.] Through that patience they possess what they possess, and may they also retain this unpunished, if only they eventually desist. [Note: [Col. 0749B] “And may they also retain this,” and so forth. Although this passage is arranged in this way in all the manuscripts I consulted, and its sense is not troublesome, I greatly prefer the reading found only in the very first edition, the Paris and Venetian editions, and the notable old edition produced at Augsburg from manuscripts. There it reads: “Through which they possess what they possess; and may they also retain this unpunished, if only they eventually desist.” The final words in the Ulm manuscript, which agrees with all the others in the preceding material, are: “but let them desist at some time.” The sense is: let the Roman pagans cease tearing apart the Christian religion and provoking God’s patience, through which patience they possess what they possess—namely, an end and decline unlike that of the Babylonian empire, just as the evils of both were compared above. Indeed, he adds, may they not even be punished for their attack upon the Christian religion and their blasphemies, which will happen if they return to a better mind and desist from their ignorance and madness. The same sense remains if we accept the final reading of the Ulm manuscript, with somewhat greater emphasis: “And may they also retain this unpunished! But let them eventually desist.” That is, he says, they will retain it through God’s mercy; nevertheless, it is time to desist from their former hostility, lest by provoking the divine power too greatly they make God unappeasable.]

Let them recall with me the times of their ancestors: times most disturbed by wars, accursed for their crimes, foul with dissensions, and filled continuously with miseries. They may rightly shudder at them, because they were, and they must necessarily pray that they may not be. Let them pray, indeed, to that one God who, by hidden justice, then permitted these things to happen, and who now, by manifest mercy, ensures that they do not happen. These matters will now be set forth more fully by me, after I have reviewed the histories in order from the City’s very origin.

### CHAPTER FOUR. On the founding of Rome and the period during which it obeyed the rule of kings

[Col. 0749D]

[Note: [Col. 0749D] In the year 414 after the destruction of Troy. We restore this number, not because we judge it entirely correct, but because we find it in all the old books and do not doubt that Orosius wrote it. For when Eutropius had written that Rome was founded on the Kalends of May, in the third year of the sixth Olympiad, 419 years after the destruction of Troy, Paul the Deacon subsequently added: “Or, as Orosius prefers, 414.” I know that this is commonly read and published differently by Schonhovius, but I follow the authority of my old book, in which Eutropius’s history is set out so that the additions of Paul are separated by the insertion of his name. Thus I restore Orosius’s reading, although the accounts found in Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Solinus, chapter 2, are not without reason judged more reliable. FABR. In the Augustan edition the year is given as 414; in the others, 335. The first and fourth Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have 454, and the Florentine manuscripts agree: the first displays the numbers as “400, with fourteen written above”; the second, “four hundred fourteen”; the third, “four hundred, fourteen.” Some editions insert *igitur* (“therefore”) after *anno*, contrary to the manuscripts.]

In the year 414 after the destruction of Troy, and in the sixth Olympiad—which is customarily celebrated in its fifth year, after four years have been completed, at Elis, a city of Greece, with contests and games—Rome was founded in Italy by Romulus and Remus, twin founders. Romulus immediately stained its kingship with parricide. [Note: [Col. 0750B] Stained. My manuscript has *invadit* (“seized”).] With a matching succession of cruelty, he endowed the Sabine women, seized without lawful custom and joined in disgraceful marriages, with the blood of their husbands and parents. [Note: [Col. 0750C] Seized without lawful custom. Virgil supports this reading, although the manuscripts here have *sine mora* (“without delay”). LAUT. But the Longobard, or Florentine, manuscript and the first Leiden manuscript, together with Perizonus, the Gronovian Collation, and the Venetian editions, preserve the true reading. Perizonus also transposes the words: “the Sabine women seized without lawful custom.”]

[Note: [Col. 0750C] He endowed them with blood. This too is an imitation of Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VII, verse 318,
“By Trojan and Rutulian blood you will be endowed, maiden,” as the Poet has it. *Mulieres* (“women”), together with the Augustan edition, is inserted by the first and third Leiden editions and by the Groningen Collation. Besides Orosius, Justin also sketched this episode in book I, chapter 7: “And the wife, endowed with her husband’s blood, surrendered both her husband’s kingdom and herself to the adulterer,” concerning the wife of Candaules, king of the Lydians.]

he endowed with blood. Thus Romulus, after first killing his grandfather Numitor and then his brother Remus, seized power and founded the City. He dedicated his grandfather’s kingdom, his brother’s walls, and his father-in-law’s temple with blood; he gathered a band of criminals by promising them immunity.

[Note: [Col. 0750C] *Interfecto primum avo Numitore.* “After first killing his grandfather Numitor.” I do not remember having read this elsewhere. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0750C] *Sceleratorum manum.* “A band of criminals.” The well-known story of the asylum opened by Romulus. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0750C] *Promissa impunitate.* “By promising immunity.” The first edition has *promiscua impunitate*, “indiscriminate immunity,” as does the Paris edition in what follows.]

His first field for war was the City’s Forum, signifying that foreign and civil wars alike would never cease. He seized the women of the Sabines, whom he had enticed by treaty and games, with as much dishonor as he defended them with impiety.
