[Note: [Col. 0750D] *Sabinorum, quos, etc.* The Perizonian codex has *Sabinorum imperium, quos*, “the dominion of the Sabines, whom.” For *quos*, the fourth Leiden edition, together with the Augustan edition, has *quas*, “whom” feminine; either reading can be defended.]

[Note: [Col. 0750D] *Ducem eorum Titum Tatium.* “Their leader Titus Tatius.” I shall not recount matters familiar even to children; I shall only point out that Tatius was killed at Lavinium, not by Romulus, but by those who had quarreled with his relatives, as Dionysius, Livy, and Plutarch relate. FABR.]

He killed their aged leader Titus Tatius, who had long resisted him with arms while pursuing honorable motives of piety, but whom he killed as soon as he had admitted him to a partnership in the kingship.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] *Cum Veientibus praelium adhuc parvo nomine, sed jam magnis viribus agitatum est.* “A war with the Veientes, still insignificant in name but already great in strength.” Since all the books read *parvo nomine*, “in a small name,” here, I have altered nothing; nevertheless, I could easily be persuaded that, following John William Suntzius, we should read *momine* for *momento*, “in a small impulse,” or perhaps *molimine*, “in a small effort.” This most ingenious young man, deeply devoted to our studies and to letters, happened to be reading this passage with me and, struck by the antithesis “small in name, but already great in strength,” conjectured that *momine* ought to be restored in Orosius. Certainly, the later war which the Romans waged with the Veientes was of greater *momen*—that is, of greater force—in the year 366. LAUT. — I judge this emendation inept, unless *momen* were a word familiar to Orosius, meaning “momentum” and “impulse.” Lucretius, book III, lines 189–190:

> *Momine uti parvo possint impulsa moveri.*  
> “So that, moved by a small impulse, they may be set in motion.”
>
> *Namque movetur aqua, et tantillo momine flutat.*  
> “For water is moved and ripples with so slight an impulse.”]

A war with the Veientes, still insignificant in name but already great in strength, was undertaken. The town of Caenina was captured and destroyed.

[Note: [Col. 0751B] *Captum ac dirutum.* “Captured and destroyed.” Three Leiden codices, together with the Groningen Collation, insert *est*, “was.”]

Once they had taken up arms, they never rested—for poverty and shameful hunger would threaten them at home if they ever submitted to peace.

[Note: [Col. 0751B] *Numquam quies.* “They never rested.” Orosius deliberately adopted brevity here. I therefore deleted *fuit*, “there was,” which all editions generously supplied, relying both on the authority of the Longobardic codex, the first among the Florentine manuscripts, and on the other two, my own and the Perizonian.]

[Note: [Col. 0751C] *Domi timerentur.* “Would be feared at home.” This reading is supported by the first and second Florentine manuscripts, the two Leiden codices, the Utrecht, Perizonian, and my own manuscripts, and by the Augustan edition. The common reading is *domi timeretur*, “would be feared at home.” For *fames*, “hunger,” the first Florentine manuscript writes *famis*, also found in the second but corrected there to *fames*.]

I shall compress their unceasing conflicts, always severe in proportion to their strength, as briefly as possible.

[Note: [Col. 0751C] *Strinxerim.* “I shall compress.” The Augustan edition has *perstrinxerim*, “I shall summarize fully.” The first edition, together with the Parisian, Venetian, Hittorpian, and Bolsuing editions, has *strinxero*, “I shall have compressed.” All the manuscripts confirm the common reading.]

Tullus Hostilius, founder of military discipline, trusting in a well-trained youth,

[Note: [Col. 0751C] *Exercitae.* “Well-trained.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with my own and certain editions, read *exercitatae*. The second Florentine has *exercitae*; the Augustan has *exercitatae*, and another edition *exercitae*.]

brought war upon the Albans; and after a long period in which each side faced uncertain hope and certain defeat,

[Note: [Col. 0751C] *Certa clade.* “Certain defeat.” This reading is confirmed by the best Florentine manuscript, together with other superior manuscripts and the Augustan edition. We should not follow some printed editions and manuscripts that prefer *certaque clade*, “and certain defeat,” including the fourth Leiden edition, which has *incertaque clade*, “and uncertain defeat.” The usual punctuation is wrong: the phrase should not be divided as “and for a long time, on either side with uncertain hope,” and so forth.]

he finally brought their worst outcomes and doubtful fortunes to an end through the brief encounter of the threefold champions.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] *Tergeminorum.* “Of the threefold champions.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collation, add *populorum*, “of the peoples.”]

[Note: [Col. 0751D] *Finisse.* “To have ended.” This is found consistently in all the manuscripts instead of *finiisse*.]

When peace was again broken,

[Note: [Col. 0751D] *Dirupta.* “Broken.” The first Florentine manuscript has *disrupta*, “disrupted.”]

he had Mettus Fufetius, in the war with Fidenae,

[Note: [Col. 0751D] *Mettum Fufetium.* We have written these names as we found them written in the ancient books. Read what John Pierius in book VIII of the *Aeneid* and Sigonius in book I of his *Emendationes*, chapter 52, have written about them with great learning. FABR. — The second Leiden manuscript, the Perizonian, my own, and two Florentine manuscripts write *Metium* for *Mettum*, but the Longobardic codex preserves *Mettum*.]

held in suspense because of his planned treachery, and, while chariots dragged him in opposite directions, paid through the punishment of his divided body for the crime of his divided mind.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] *Meditata proditione suspectum.* “Suspected of planned treachery.” The old book’s reading, *suspectum*, seemed more suited to the sense of the passage, which magnifies the crimes of kings, than *suspensum*, “hanged,” found in other books. Livy and Dionysius discuss this punishment in book III. FABR. — Orosius does not magnify the crimes of kings but traces the miseries of the times. I would therefore not exchange the better reading, supported by all the better manuscripts, for the inferior reading of one or another codex. The Florentine and all the Leiden manuscripts, as well as my own and the Groningen Collation, prefer *suspensum*. It signifies mental uncertainty, such as Livy describes in Fufetius. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, line 145:

> *Dicam equidem, nec te suspensum, nate, tenebo.*  
> “I shall tell you, my son, and I shall not keep you in suspense.”]

The Latins, under the leadership of Ancus Marcius, often engaged in battle and were sometimes defeated. Tarquinius Priscus caused all the neighboring peoples—and the twelve powerful peoples of Etruria at that time—to fall in countless conflicts.

[Note: [Col. 0752B] *Potentes tunc duodecim Tusciae populos.* “The twelve powerful peoples of Etruria at that time.” Florus, book I, chapter 1, says of Tarquinius: “He subdued the twelve peoples of Etruria by frequent wars.” FABR. — The better manuscripts transpose the words: *Tusciae duodecim populos*, “the twelve peoples of Etruria.” For *concidisse*, “to have fallen,” the Perizonian has *cecidisse*, “to have been defeated.”]

While Servius Tullius was pressing them, the Veientes were defeated but not subdued.

[Note: [Col. 0752B] *Fuisse, nec domitos.* “To have been defeated, but not subdued.” These words do not appear in three Leiden manuscripts, nor in the Groningen Collation.]

The kingdom of Tarquinius Superbus, acquired through the crime of murdering his father-in-law, maintained through cruelty toward the citizens, and lost through the outrage committed against Lucretia,

[Note: [Col. 0752C] *Occisi soceri.* “Of the murdered father-in-law.” The first editions and the Venetian editions, together with the Parisian, have *occiso socero*, “with the father-in-law murdered.”]

was lost amid domestic vices and external virtues shining forth—that is, the strong towns he captured in Latium: Ardea,

[Note: [Col. 0752C] *Inter.* “Amid.” With broad agreement, three Florentine manuscripts, an equal number of Leiden manuscripts, the Perizonian and my own, together with the Augustan edition, write *et inter* instead of *et intus*, “and within.” The Groningen Collation additionally deletes *et*, which ought to be absent; it is also absent from the fourth Leiden manuscript. The common reading, *et intus domestica vitia*, “and within, domestic vices,” can be tolerated, but I would not prefer it. The subject is not kings in general but specifically the kingdom of Tarquinius Superbus, which, he says, was acquired through crime, retained through cruelty, and lost through lust—amid domestic vices and external virtues, that is, outstandingly conducted wars, and so forth.]

Ocricolum,

[Note: [Col. 0752C] *Ocricolum.* Stephanus writes: “Ocricola, a city of the Tyrrhenians”; Dionysius, in the eighteenth book of his *Roman Antiquities*, gives the ethnic name *Ocricolanus*, as he himself says. FABR.]

Suessa Pometia,

[Note: [Col. 0752C] *Suessam Pometiam.* We have written this on the authority of the ancient books. The common reading is *Sinuessam Pometiamque*, “Sinuessa and Pometia.” Eutropius says: “He subdued the city of Gabii and Suessa Pometia.” Florus, book I, chapter 7: “Thus the strong towns in Latium were captured: Ardea, Ocricolum, Gabii, Suessa Pometia.” Dionysius, book IV: “He led his forces against those called the Pomptines, who inhabited the city of Suessa.” Strabo, book V, calls it *Suessa* “of the Pontines,” although that passage is greatly corrupted in the common text. This Suessa was called Suessa Pometia to distinguish it from the town in Campania called Suessa Aurunca. It is therefore erroneous that Messalla reads: “He stormed the towns of Suessa and Pometia.” FABR. — In antiquity it was called *Pomesia*, as is shown by a remarkable silver coin in our museum. In the most ancient letters, written backward, it bears on both sides the inscription which we published in our short dissertation *On the Various Forms of Greek Letters*, found in the *Collection of Writings on the Pronunciation of the Greek Language*, pp. 211–212.]

and whatever he accomplished against Gabii, whether through his own fraud, through the punishment inflicted by his son, or through Roman strength.

But how great evils the Romans endured for 243 years under that uninterrupted domination of kings is shown not only by the expulsion of one king but also by the renunciation of the royal name and authority.

[Note: [Col. 0753B] *Per CCCXL et III annos.* “For 343 years.” The first and third Leiden editions read “for 242 years”; the fourth, together with the first and Paris editions and the Augustan edition, generously gives “244 years.” The Groningen Collation finally has “262 years.”]

[Note: [Col. 0753B] *Ejuratio regii nominis.* “Renunciation of the royal name.” Some read *abjuratio*, “abjuration,” but the Perizonian codex, together with the second Florentine, prefers *ejuratio*. The others, generally following the first Florentine, write *et juratio*, “and swearing,” and thus seem to incline toward that reading.]

For if the arrogance of only one king had been at fault, he alone ought to have been expelled, while royal dignity was preserved for better men. Therefore, after the kings had been driven from the City,

[Note: [Col. 0753B] *Propulsis.* “Having been driven away.” My manuscript has *pulsis*, “having been driven away,” which is more classical Latin.]

the Romans, thinking that they ought to take care of their own liberty rather than dominate anyone else’s,

[Note: [Col. 0753C] *Quam cuiquam.* “Rather than anyone else’s.” The Venetian editions put *potius* before these words, not understanding this idiom. Consult Barnabas Brissonius, *De Verborum Significatione*, under the word *quam*, against all the manuscripts.]

created consuls. In their hands, as though the mature age of the growing republic were being exercised in more vigorous enterprises,

[Note: [Col. 0753C] *Adulta.* “Mature.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collation, write *adulte*, that is, *adultae*, “mature.” The Augustan edition has *crescens et causis*, “growing and in its causes,” instead of *crescentis et ausis*, “of the growing [republic] and its enterprises”; the second Florentine has *ausibus*, “enterprises.”]

**96. CHAPTER V. The deeds of Brutus, the first consul. The war with the Tarquinians and Sabines. The secession of the plebs. A great famine and pestilence at Rome. The war with the Veientes and Etruscans, in which the Fabian family perished.**

[Col. 0753B]

[Note: [Col. 0753C] *Anno post Urbem conditam CCXLIV.* “In the 244th year after the founding of the City.” The same number is found in Eutropius, Messalla, and Sextus Rufus. But Dionysius, book V, writes that the Romans obeyed royal rule for 244 years. Livy likewise says at the end of book I that kings reigned at Rome for 243 years from the founding of the City until its liberation. Sigonius explained the reason for the discrepancy. FABR. — In the third Leiden edition the number is 243. Through a typographical error it entered the last of the Fabrician editions as 264; in the others and in the Mainz edition, and even in the notes to that edition, the true number is preserved, as it is given in the Longobardic codex and the other two Florentine manuscripts: 244.]

In the 244th year after the founding of the City, Brutus, the first consul among the Romans, sought not merely to equal the first founder and king of Rome in parricide but even to surpass him. For he dragged into the assembly his two adolescent sons and an equal number of young brothers of his wife, the Vitellii,

[Note: [Col. 0753D] *Suos.* “His own.” This is absent from the first and Paris editions and from the Venetian editions, as well as from the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts.]

who had been accused of wishing to restore the kings to the City,

[Note: [Col. 0753D] *In Urbem.* “Into the City.” Three Leiden manuscripts have *in Urbe*, “in the City,” as do the first and Paris editions.]

and had them brought before the assembly,

[Note: [Col. 0753D] *Insimulatos.* “Having been accused.” The same three Leiden manuscripts have *insimulato*, a scribal error that also occurred in the codex collated by Gronovius.]

where he flogged them with rods and struck them with the axe.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] *Protraxit.* “He dragged forth.” The Groningen Collation has *pertraxit*. I have not changed the reading. Virgil, *Aeneid* II, line 122:

> *Tunc Ithacus vatem magno Calchanta tumultu*  
> *Protrahit in medium.*
>
> “Then Ithacus, amid great tumult, drags the prophet Calchas into the midst.”]

He himself then fell in the war against the Veientes and Tarquinians, dying together with Aruns, the son of Superbus, who had engaged him.

[Note: [Col. 0754B] *Veientum.* The Groningen Collation has *Veientium*.]

[Note: [Col. 0754B] *Arunte.* The Longobardic codex has *Arrunte*.]

Porsena, king of the Etruscans, a most formidable supporter of the royal name,

[Note: [Col. 0754B] *Porsena, rex Etruscorum.* Latin poets sometimes lengthened and sometimes shortened the middle syllable of *Porsena*. Hence the name is found written variously. In Greek, both *Πορσίνας* and *Πορσίνος* are read. FABR.]

bringing Tarquinius upon them by force,

[Note: [Col. 0754B] *Tarquinium manu ingerens.* “Bringing Tarquinius upon them by force.” This is what the ancient books have, not *Tarquiniensium manum*, “the hand of the Tarquinians,” as in the common editions. FABR. — The Longobardic codex and the two other Florentine manuscripts, one Leiden manuscript, the Perizonian, and my own support the true reading restored by Fabricius, which is preserved among the printed editions only by the Augsburg edition. The first, third, and fourth Leiden editions, together with the Groningen Collation, read *Tarquiniensium manum*; the Utrecht manuscript has nothing beyond *Tarquinium*, and *manu ingerens* seems to have dropped out there. Porsena is said to have brought Tarquinius upon them *manu*, that is, with the greatest force. The alternative reading signifies a multitude of Tarquinians.]

terrified and blockaded the trembling City for three consecutive years.

[Note: [Col. 0754C] *Obsedit.* “Blockaded.” After this, the first Leiden manuscript contains the following remarkable gloss: “He carried glowing iron in his hand against the enemy and hurled it at them from the wall.”]

And unless the enemy had been moved by Mucius’s steadfast endurance in burning his hand,

[Note: [Col. 0754C] *Mucius constanti urendae manus.* “Mucius’s steadfastness in burning his hand.” This was Gaius Mucius, later surnamed Scaevola because of the injury to his right hand, as Livy and others relate. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0754C] *Urendae.* “Of burning.” The first and third Leiden editions have *horrendae*, “of terrifying.” The word *constanti* is absent from the Utrecht manuscript.]

or the maiden Cloelia by her admirable courage in crossing the river,

[Note: [Col. 0754C] *Admirabili.* “Admirable.” The second Florentine has *admirabilis*, “admirable,” as though the adjective should refer to Cloelia. The first edition, the Parisian, and the Venetian editions have *permovissent*, “had moved,” rather than *permovisset*; Perizonius deletes the word entirely.]

the Romans would certainly have been compelled either to endure captivity after being defeated while the enemy pressed upon them, or to submit to slavery after the king had been restored.

After this the Sabines, having gathered forces from everywhere,

[Note: [Col. 0754D] *Corrasis.* “Having gathered.” My manuscript has *contractis*, “having assembled,” a reading I would prefer, although the other appears to come from Orosius’s hand. For *undique*, “from everywhere,” the first and fourth Leiden editions have *ubique*, “everywhere,” as does the Groningen Collation, which also reads *in servitutem recepto rege subjecti*, “subject after the king had been restored to slavery.”]

marched against Rome with a great warlike display. Terrified by this danger, the Romans appointed a dictator,

[Note: [Col. 0754D] *Dictatorem creant.* “They appoint a dictator.” Eutropius says, “In the ninth year after the kings had been expelled,” and Livy and Cassiodorus write that the first dictator was appointed under the consuls Postumus Cominius and Titus Lartius. Read Sigonius’s most learned commentary on the *Fasti*. FABR.]

whose authority and power surpassed that of a consul,

[Note: [Col. 0754D] *Consulem praeiret.* That is, “surpassed consular authority,” although those who wrote *consules* in the first and fourth Leiden editions failed to notice the point.]

and this arrangement brought great advantage in that war.

[Note: [Col. 0755B] *In illo tunc bello.* “In that war at that time.” In the Fabrician and Mainz editions one looks in vain for *illud in*, “that,” although all earlier printed editions and all the manuscripts contain it.]

[Note: [Col. 0755B] *Emolumenti tulit.* “Brought advantage.” The Perizonian has *emolumenti contulit*, “conferred advantage”; the first and fourth Leiden editions and the Groningen Collation have *emolumenti tulit eis*, “brought advantage to them.”]

Then followed the secession of the plebs from the patricians.

[Note: [Col. 0755B] *Cum M. Valerio dictatore.* “With the dictator Marcus Valerius.” This Valerius’s praenomen was not Marcus but Manius, as is known from fragments of the triumphal records. Dionysius, in book VI, also calls him *Μάνιον Οὐαλέριον ἀδελφὸν Ποπιλίου τοῦ πρώτου ὑπατεύσαντος*—“Manius Valerius, the brother of Popilius, who was the first to hold the consulship.” Read Cicero’s *Brutus*. FABR.]

While the dictator Marcus Valerius was conducting the levy, the people, goaded by various injuries, occupied the Sacred Mount under arms. What could be more dreadful than this catastrophe, when the body, cut off from the head, threatened the destruction of the very part through which it breathed?

[Note: [Col. 0755C] *Pernicie.* “Catastrophe.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collation, have *pernicitate*, “swiftness.”]

[Note: [Col. 0755C] *Perditionem.* “Destruction.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has *per proditionem*, “through treachery,” as though the meaning were “its treachery.”]

[Note: [Col. 0755C] *Spirabat.* “Breathed.” The Longobardic codex and the Utrecht manuscript have *inspirabat*, “inspired.”]

[Note: [Col. 0755C] *Minitaretur.* “Threatened.” I restored this reading from *meditaretur* and *imitaretur*; the imitation is Sallustian. LAUT. — Of the manuscripts, only the Utrecht supports this reading. Nevertheless, the emendation is entirely sound and should be accepted even with the support of a single codex. For it is appropriate and correct to say that the head, in which wisdom resides, “deliberates,” while the body, which possesses the strength of the hands, “threatens.”]

And the Roman name would have been destroyed by internal disaster had a speedy reconciliation not intervened before the secession itself became known.

[Note: [Col. 0755C] *Actumque.* “And would have been destroyed.” The first Leiden edition has *Actum*, “destroyed,” and shortly afterward *ni*, “unless,” instead of *nisi*.]

[Note: [Col. 0755C] *Subrepsisset.* “Had intervened secretly.” This is the common and correct reading. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collation and the Augustan edition, have *subripuisset*, “had stolen away”; my manuscript has *surrexisset*, “had arisen.”]

The hidden disaster, advancing and threatening itself, follows with wretched success outside those open calamities of war. For, under the consulship of Titus Geganius and Publius Minucius, two of the greatest abominations among all evils—famine and pestilence—seized the exhausted City.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] *T. Geganio et P. Minucio.* “Titus Geganius and Publius Minucius.” The name of the first consul was corrupt in Orosius’s books. They were consuls in the year 261 after the founding of the City. Read Dionysius at the beginning of book VII and Livy in book II. FABR. — In three Florentine manuscripts the first consul’s name is written *Gesonius*, but in the second it is superscribed *Gessonio*, the reading found in ancient editions and in three Leiden manuscripts and my own. Perizonius gives *P. Mucio* for *P. Minucio*. The Augustan edition has *Munisio*, the first *Numisio*, and the Paris edition *Numitio*.]

The battles ceased for a little while, but the deaths did not cease.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] *A mortibus.* “From deaths.” My manuscript has *a motibus*, “from movements.” But the common reading should not be changed: the cessation was not from deaths, since famine and pestilence sent many souls—both the weak and even the strong—to the underworld.]

The Veientes and Etruscans, formidable enemies, rose up for war after joining the forces of their neighbors. They were met by the consuls Marcus Fabius and Gnaeus Manlius.

[Note: [Col. 0756B] *Manlio.* Three Leiden manuscripts have *Mallio*, a corruption that often affects this name in the manuscripts of Suetonius and other writers.]

After the oath by which the Romans had devoted themselves—swearing that they would not return to camp until after victory—the battle was so fierce, and the appearance of the defeated and the victorious so nearly alike,

[Note: [Col. 0756B] *Et victis.* The old editions have *Ut victis victoribusque par forma esset*, “so that the appearance of the defeated and the victorious was alike.” *Esset* is absent from the Augustan edition.]

that, after a great part of the army had been lost and the consul Manlius and the consular Fabius had been killed,

[Note: [Col. 0756B] *Consulari.* The Augustan edition has *proconsulari*, “proconsular.”]

the consul Marcus Fabius refused to accept the triumph offered him by the Senate, because mourning rather than triumph was owed for such losses to the republic.

[Note: [Col. 0756C] *Suscipere recusarit.* “Refused to accept.” I restored this from three Florentine manuscripts, the Utrecht manuscript, and my own, in place of *recusaret*. Perizonius deletes *suscipere*; the Groningen Collation has *recipere*, “to receive.”]

That most glorious Fabian family, remarkable in number and strength, having drawn the Veientine conflict by lot,

[Note: [Col. 0756C] *Illa numero et viribus.* “That one in number and strength.” My manuscript prefers *et numero et viribus*, “both in number and strength.” But the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collation, punctuate the passage thus: “That most glorious Fabian cohort in number and strength, having drawn the Veientine conflict.”]

demonstrated what desolation its downfall brought upon the republic; the river that destroyed them and the gate that sent them forth bear witness in names infamous to this day.

[Note: [Col. 0756C] *Veientanum.* “Veientine.” The Augustan edition has *Veientium*, “of the Veientes.”]

[Note: [Col. 0756C] *Usque ad nunc.* “To this day.” This is found in all the Florentine manuscripts and the others; the old editions have *usque nunc*, “until now.”]

[Note: [Col. 0756C] *Fluvius qui perdidit, et porta.* “The river that destroyed them, and the gate.” The river was the Cremera, and the gate was the Carmental Gate. Livy, Dionysius, and Ovid, book II of the *Fasti*. FABR. — In my manuscript, the Perizonian, and the fourth Leiden manuscript, the river’s name is written *Chiemera* for *Cremera*: “the river,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0756C] *Quae misit.* “That sent them forth.” This is preferred by the three Florentine manuscripts, the first Leiden manuscript, the Groningen Collation, the Augustan edition, and my own codex. The common editions have *quae emisit*, “which sent them out.”]

For when the 306 Fabii, truly the brightest lights of the Roman state,

[Note: [Col. 0756D] *Sex et trecenti Fabii.* “Three hundred and six Fabii.” The Augustan edition absurdly has “six thousand and three hundred Fabii.”]

had sought that a special war be decreed for them against the Veientes,

[Note: [Col. 0756D] *Veientes.* The first and third Leiden editions and the Groningen Collation have *Veientanos*, “the Veientines.”]

they strengthened the hope of their rash expedition by their initial successes. Then, led into an ambush and surrounded by the enemy, they were all slaughtered there, with only one spared to announce the disaster,

[Note: [Col. 0756D] *Ad enuntiandam cladem.* “To announce the disaster.” The Groningen Collation, the Utrecht manuscript, the first and second Leiden manuscripts, and the Perizonian have *ad nuntiandam*, “to announce”; the second Florentine has *ad denuntiandam*, “to report”; the Augustan edition has *ad enuntiandum*, “for announcing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0756D] *Reservato.* “Having been spared.” The fourth Leiden edition has *servato*, “having been preserved.”]

so that their homeland might hear more miserably that they had been lost than they had lost it.

Nor were such things happening only at Rome; every province was seething amid its own fires. And what the chief poet described in a single city, I would say of the whole world:

> “Cruel grief everywhere,
>
> Everywhere terror, and the most abundant image of death.”

**100. CHAPTER VI. Cyrus, king of the Persians, ravages the entire East, captures Babylon, a most strongly fortified city, and defeats Croesus.**

[Col. 0757A]

[Note: [Col. 0757B] *Igitur eodem tempore.* “Therefore, at the same time.” Three Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen Collation have *Igitur eo tempore*, “Therefore, at that time.”]

Therefore, at the same time, Cyrus, king of the Persians, whom I mentioned above in order to explain the history, and who was then traversing Asia, Scythia, and the entire East with his arms, while Tarquinius Superbus was oppressing the City either as king, enemy, or slave-master, Cyrus—as I said—having subdued all against whom he had gone, turned against the Assyrians and Babylonians,

[Note: [Col. 0757B] *Babyloniam.* The three Florentine manuscripts have *Babylonam*, “Babylon,” and so almost always.]

a people and a city then richer than all others. But his advance was checked by the river Gyndes,

[Note: [Col. 0757B] *Gyndes fluvius.* Since the river of India, the Ganges, is better known in histories, many manuscripts and printed editions have wrongly written that name here; all the Florentine manuscripts and my own preserve it unaltered. In the first Florentine manuscript the river is called *Gynes* in the margin: “Gynes, the river of Babylon.” But the correct form is *Gyndes*. Tibullus, book IV, elegy 1, line 141.]

… Swift [was] Cyrus’ madness: the Gyndes. Herodotus, narrating this history in Book I, chapter 189, p. 76, writes that the river Gyndes, rising in the Matienian mountains, flows through Dardania and empties into the Tigris.] The river Gyndes, second in size only to the Euphrates, obstructed him.

[Note: [Col. 0757B] For when one of the royal horses. We have had this passage printed as we find it described in all the ancient books. Orosius took the account from Herodotus, who writes as follows about the Gyndes and Cyrus: “Thereupon one of the sacred white horses, entering the river in his arrogance, tried to cross; but the river, whirling it about, carried it away beneath the water.” Here is one of the sacred horses, distinguished by its whiteness, which, driven by arrogance, entered the river and tried to cross it; but the river, twisting it about in its eddies, carried it away and submerged it. FABRICIUS.—Although all the manuscripts displayed the passage in this form, Orosius nevertheless could not, and did not, have written it so, for it would contradict Herodotus openly. That Orosius did not write it thus is confirmed by the texts of two manuscripts, those of Perizonius and Meursius, in which *horses* clearly appears; moreover, that he could not have written it thus is shown by what follows: “outstanding in whiteness and form.” For the praise of whiteness plainly belongs to the horse, whom Herodotus likewise commended for his whiteness, since the sacred horses must have been of that color. We have restored the whole passage from the manuscript reading. Where the printed editions give *Nam cum unum* (“For when one”), ten manuscripts—and better ones—together with the Augustan edition and Vincent of Beauvais, omit the middle word *cum*. Meursius alone supplies *merserat* (“had submerged”), but it is clear that the passage cannot be read otherwise if one reads with all the manuscripts *nam unum*, omitting the spurious *cum*. Of the remaining manuscripts and printed editions, some give *mersisset* (“had submerged”), others *merserunt* (“they submerged”). The older editions, except the Augustan one—the first edition, the Venetian editions, and the Parisian edition—mention not only the horse but also the rider. In them the passage reads: “For when one of the royal horses, outstanding in whiteness and form, together with its rider, persuaded by confidence that it could cross, etc.”; and a little later: “after it had swallowed horse and rider.” But this reading is contradicted by all the manuscripts I have examined.]

For when one of the royal horses, outstanding in whiteness and form,

[Note: [Col. 0757D] “Outstanding.” The first Parisian and Venetian editions have *praecipuum* (“distinguished”).]

persuaded by confidence that it could cross,

[Note: [Col. 0758B] “Persuaded.” The first edition has *persuaso*, so that it is to be joined with *cum equite* (“with its rider”), which occurs in that edition.]

was seized and hurled down and submerged by the whirlpools that rose in the rapacious channel when their course was obstructed by the ford.

[Note: [Col. 0758B] “Whirlpools obstructed by the ford.” The first Parisian and Venetian editions have *offensi vada vorticis*. Some manuscripts, through a familiar error, have *vertices*.]

[Note: [Col. 0758B] “For he threatened that he would make it”—Herodotus writes: “And he threatened it, saying that he would make it so weak that thereafter even women would easily cross it without wetting their knees.” FABRICIUS.]

The king, angrily, resolved to punish the river, declaring that the river which had now swallowed so splendid a horse would be left crossable even by women barely wetting their knees.

[Note: [Col. 0758B] “To be left passable.” The first Parisian and Venetian editions read *a se permeabilem*, etc.; Hittorp and Bolsuing follow them. But this is absent from the Augustan edition and the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0758B] “Which now”—the first edition, the Parisian, and the Venetian editions read *qui tam* (“which so”), while Hittorp more generously included both forms; Fabricius and Scott followed him in printing “which now so splendid,” contrary to all the manuscripts and Vincent of Beauvais.]

[Note: [Col. 0758B] “In carrying it out.” The Augustan edition has *in peragendo*, as do the first Parisian edition and Scott’s Mainz edition, but contrary to the manuscripts and Vincent of Beauvais.]

Nor was he slower in carrying out his purpose: with all his forces, for an entire year, he divided the Gyndes River by means of great excavations and channels—

[Note: [Col. 0758C] “Into four hundred and sixty channels.” It should rather be written “into 360,” for Herodotus says: “Dividing it into 360 canals.” FABRICIUS.—This appears to be an old error, perhaps made by the author himself; or the copyists of Orosius may have erred in the number. Vincent of Beauvais, who excerpted this passage in Book IV, chapter 11, has the same number.]

—into four hundred and sixty channels. Having thus trained his diggers, he also diverted the Euphrates, by far the mightier river, which flowed through the middle of Babylon.

[Note: [Col. 0758C] “And thus, with fordable passages, made it dry.” Xenophon also writes this in Book VII of the *Education of Cyrus*. FABRICIUS.]

And thus, making it dry where the fords were passable, he also made a route through the broad stretches of its channel—

[Note: [Col. 0758C] “He killed it in the parts of the channel.” Thus reads one manuscript, that of Cologne, which I willingly follow because of the elegance of the expression. That *to kill* may mean *to dry up* a river is attested by Plautus, the most Latin of authors: “If I once begin, I shall draw all the life out of that well”; yet the sense is not lost if the other reading is retained. LAUT.—On the contrary, if one accepts the reading of the Cologne manuscript, one destroys Orosius’ meaning. He says that by this device of Cyrus the Euphrates was made completely dry in places where there had previously been fords that could be crossed on foot; but in places where it had formerly spread broadly and had deep waters, it was made passable to the army. Thus he “killed” it, if one may speak in this way, where dry fords had been created. Herodotus gives a fuller account of how this was accomplished and how Cyrus’ soldiers crossed by the river’s new fords and captured the city.]

—he made a passage. And he captured the city, which it was almost incredible among mortals either that human labor could have built or that human strength could destroy.

[Note: [Col. 0758D] “By labor.” The second Florentine manuscript has *labore* (“by labor”).]

For many have handed down that Babylon was founded by the giant Nimrod,

[Note: [Col. 0758D] “Nimrod.” The first and second Florentine manuscripts have *Nebrot*; the Groningen manuscript has *Nebroth*. Meursius subsequently deletes *giant*.]

and restored by Ninus or Semiramis.

[Note: [Col. 0758D] “Semiramis.” Three Florentine manuscripts have *Samiramis*. For *reparatam* (“restored”), the first Florentine manuscript has *paratam* (“prepared”).]

This city, visible from every side across the level plain, situated in a region of exceptionally fertile nature, arranged in the appearance of a camp with equal walls laid out in a square, possessed walls whose strength and size were scarcely credible even to describe—

[Note: [Col. 0759B] “Credible.” The first, Parisian, and Venetian editions have *credibili* (“credible”).]

—that is, fifty cubits in width and four times as much in height.

[Note: [Col. 0759B] “Fifty cubits in width.” Quintus Curtius, Book V: “A wall constructed of baked brick, cemented with bitumen, occupies a width of thirty-two feet; it is said that four-horse chariots could pass one another upon it without danger. The wall rises to a height of one hundred cubits; the towers are ten feet higher than the wall. The circuit of the entire work extends for 368 stades.” Strabo, Book XVI, writes that the walls were thirty-two feet thick and fifty cubits high. But Orosius follows Herodotus. Pliny, Book VI, chapter 26, writes that the walls of Babylon were two hundred feet high and fifty feet wide. FABRICIUS.—In place of the sixth case, which appears in all the manuscripts, the older editions, except the Augustan, print “width and height.” Three manuscripts from Leiden place *et* before *altitudine*; only the first and second Florentine manuscripts write it four times; it is absent from the first Leiden manuscript.]

Its circuit was enclosed by four hundred and eighty stades. The wall, constructed of baked brick and joined with poured bitumen—

[Note: [Col. 0759C] “With bitumen poured between.” Correctly *interfuso*, since the bitumen had to be liquefied: “using hot bitumen,” says Herodotus in Book I, chapter 179, p. 72. In the East bitumen served in place of lime; Pliny, Book XXXV, chapter 15, also teaches that the walls of Babylon were cemented with it. Since bitumen was produced in the lake of Idumea called Asphaltitis, it derived its name from that place and provided the inhabitants with a considerable source of income. Hence, when Antigonus, king of Asia, wished to claim possession of it for himself, Diodorus Siculus, Book XIX, p. 734, says that he was driven back from it by the inhabitants with great force.]

—was surrounded externally by a broad moat, flowing around it like a river. On the front of the walls stood one hundred bronze gates. The width itself, at the completion of the battlements, with dwellings for the defenders arranged equally on either side, contained, in the space between them, swift-moving chariots.

[Note: [Col. 0759C] “With its middle space containing swift chariots.” Thus I wrote from an old book of Cornelius Gualterus. Herodotus has: “Above the wall, along the edges, they built single-room dwellings, turned toward one another, and left between the dwellings enough space for a four-horse chariot to be driven around.” Valla: “Above the wall, around its edges, they built single-room apartments, facing one another, and left between them so much intervening space that a four-horse chariot could be turned around.” H. Stephanus published an abridged history of Cyrus, king of the Persians, taken from the Persian history of Ctesias; this agrees more closely with Xenophon’s account than with Herodotus’. FABRICIUS.—The reading which Fabricius restored from the book of Cornelius Gualterus is entirely correct. It is confirmed by that notable Lombard manuscript and by the third Florentine manuscript. All the others depart farther from it: the second Florentine has “with its middle space bound together.” This reading seems to indicate the form found in the Perizonian manuscript, “joined together.” The earlier printed editions have *actas*, except that the Augustan edition gives *vicenas*, “twenty each,” in the middle space; this reading also occurs in four Leiden manuscripts and in the Groningen manuscript, but with *sui* deleted. My manuscript seems to indicate the same reading when it writes *sui vicis*. Orosius appears to have chosen *citas quadrigas* (“swift chariots”) because this suits the breadth of the place perfectly: chariots rushing past at speed would encounter no danger of collision. For the other reading cannot be admitted, as is shown by the Herodotus cited by Fabricius, whose words in Book I, chapter 179, p. 72, state that only enough space was left between the small houses built along both edges of the walls for a four-horse chariot to be turned around. Diodorus Siculus likewise says plainly in Book II, p. 96: “The width possessed somewhat more space than would be sufficient for two horse-drawn chariots.”]

Inside were fourfold rows of houses—

[Note: [Col. 0760B] “Of habitation.” Thus all the manuscripts; some older editions prefer *habitationes* (“dwellings”).]

—remarkable for the threatening height of their dwellings.

[Note: [Col. 0760B] The Leiden manuscripts, second and fourth, add *erant* (“were”).]

[Col. 0759B] [Note: [Col. 0760B] “And yet.” The Augustan edition has *at tamen* (“but nevertheless”).]

And yet that great Babylon,

[Note: [Col. 0760C] “That first one.” The four Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen manuscript and certain older editions, do not recognize the repeated *illa* (“that”) here. All the Florentine manuscripts and the others retain it.]

that first city founded after the restoration of the human race,

[Note: [Col. 0760C] “After the restoration.” The Augustan edition has *post separationem* (“after the separation”).]

was now overcome by almost the slightest delay, captured, and overthrown.

[Note: [Col. 0760C] “Overcome by delay.” The Utrecht manuscript and three Leiden manuscripts absurdly read *muro victa* (“overcome by a wall”); the fourth Leiden manuscript has *muro videtur* (“it seems by a wall”). Some early editions have *ac subversa est* (“and was overthrown”). Meursius has *et* (“and”).]

At that time Croesus, king of the Lydians and famous for his wealth, had come to aid the Babylonians; when defeated, he fled anxiously back to his kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0760C] “Anxiously.” Some older editions have *sollicitusque* (“and anxious”).]

But Cyrus, after he invaded Babylon as an enemy, overthrew it as a victor, and organized it as a king,

[Note: [Col. 0760C] “Babylon.” The three Florentine manuscripts, as frequently elsewhere, write *Babylonem*. The four Leiden manuscripts, Perizonius, Utrecht, and Vincent of Beauvais, together with the Groningen manuscript, also have *Babylonem*. Orosius seems, following Justin’s example, to have used both *Babylonia* and *Babylone* indiscriminately.]

transferred the war to Lydia, where he easily defeated the army, already terrified by its previous defeat.

[Note: [Col. 0760C] “Terrified.” Vincent of Beauvais, in the *Speculum Historiale*, Book IV, chapter 17, writes *contritum* (“crushed”). For *ubi* (“where”), the Groningen manuscript has *ibi* (“there”), and Vincent has *fudit* (“routed”) instead of *superavit* (“defeated”).]

He also captured Croesus and, after capturing him, spared both his life and his property.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] “Both life and property.” The first, Parisian, and Venetian editions delete the first *et* (“both”), and Meursius has *captumque* without it. Vincent of Beauvais has *matrimonio* (“marriage”) shortly afterward.]

There is no need here to enlarge upon the unstable conditions of mutable affairs: Babylon, once captured, confirms that whatever has been made by labor and human hands slips and is consumed by age.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] “For whatever.” This is taken from Cicero, *Oration for Marcellus*, chapter 4: “For nothing has been made by work or by hand which old age does not eventually destroy and consume.”]

For just as Babylon’s empire was the first and most powerful, so it was the first to yield—

[Note: [Col. 0760D] “And first.” The same editions have *primum* (“first”), deleting *et* (“and”) here as well.]

—so that, as though by some right of succession, the inheritance owed to posterity might be handed down to the next age, with those generations themselves destined to preserve the same form of transmission.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] “So that, as it were.” This must be written exactly so, not as in all the printed editions except the Augustan, which have *et veluti* (“and as it were”). Our reading is also confirmed by the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts and by Meursius, together with the Groningen manuscript.]

Thus, at the first approaches of Cyrus, great Babylon and mighty Lydia fell: the most extensive arms of the East, together with its head, collapsed through the expedition of a single battle.

[Note: [Col. 0761B] “Most extensive.” The Augustan edition has *maxima* (“greatest”).]

And our people, with heedless anxiety, complain if those enormous masses of the once most powerful Roman state now tremble, shaken more by the weakness of their own old age than by foreign forces.

[Note: [Col. 0761B] “Roman.” The word is absent from Meursius and from the second and third Florentine manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0761C] “Shaken.” The Groningen manuscript has *concessisse* (“to have yielded”).]

## CHAPTER VII. Cyrus waged war against the Scythians and was defeated and killed by Queen Tomyris.

[Note: [Col. 0761C] “Therefore the same Cyrus.” The middle word is absent from the first edition, the Venetian, and the Parisian editions.]

Therefore the same Cyrus, following the success of the preceding period, waged war against the Scythians. Queen Tomyris, who then ruled that people—

[Note: [Col. 0761C] “Queen Tomyris.” In Greek, Herodotus has Τόμυρις (*Tómyris*), while Lucian in *Charon* has Τώμυρις (*Tṓmyris*). The story is also related by Justin, Book I, and Valerius Maximus, Book IX, chapter 10. FABRICIUS.—The manuscripts have *Thamyris* and *Tamyris*. Most write it in either form, as does Vincent of Beauvais in excerpts from Peter Comestor, who flourished in the eleventh century. Add the notes of Vossius on Justin, Book I, chapter 8.]

—although she could have prevented his crossing the river Araxes, allowed him to cross.

[Note: [Col. 0761C] “Although she could have prevented the crossing.” This is how it appears in Justin’s manuscript. “Although she could have prevented them from crossing the river Araxes, she permitted them to cross,” whereas the common text reads differently. FABRICIUS.]

First because of her confidence in herself, and then because of the advantage offered by the river, which enclosed the enemy.

Thus Cyrus entered Scythia and camped some distance from the river he had crossed,

[Note: [Col. 0761C] “Some distance away.” The first and second Leiden manuscripts and the fourth together with the Utrecht manuscript have *haud procul* (“not far away”), sometimes with the same meaning, as is known from Virgil, *Eclogue* 6, verse 16:

“Only so far away the garlands, fallen from his head, lay.”

There Servius explains *procul* as “near” and “close by.” Justin, Book I, chapter 8: “And so Cyrus, having transported his forces, after advancing for some distance into Scythia, pitched camp.” Yet that cannot be what is meant here, since Cyrus pitched camp a day’s march from the Araxes. Herodotus, Book I, chapter 211, p. 85, says: “Cyrus, advancing a day’s journey from the Araxes.” The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Groningen manuscript, deletes *procul*. The Augustan edition has “he pitched camp.”]

and, having arranged the same camp with cunning,

[Note: [Col. 0761D] “The same.” The Groningen manuscript and three Leiden manuscripts have *eadem castra* (“the same camp”).]

abandoned it with wine and banquets, as though he had fled in fear.

When the queen learned this, she sent a third of her forces and her adolescent son to pursue Cyrus.

[Note: [Col. 0762B] “First.” It is absent from the first Florentine manuscript. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Augustan and Groningen editions, prefer *primo*.]

[Note: [Col. 0761D] “Her adolescent son.” Herodotus names this son Σπαργαπίσης (*Spargapísēs*). FABRICIUS.—The same Herodotus relates that he was overcome by wine and captured by Cyrus; when he recovered consciousness, he asked to be released from his bonds, and once this had been granted, immediately killed himself. Justin, whom Orosius follows, tells the story less elaborately in Book I, chapter 8: “Cyrus returned during the night, overwhelmed the wounded, and killed all the Scythians together with the queen’s son.” Soon afterward, the second Leiden manuscript has *misit* (“sent”) instead of *mittit* (“sends”). In what follows, the Augustan edition likewise has *adolescentulo* (“the adolescent”).]

The barbarians, as if invited to a banquet, are first overcome by drunkenness; then, when Cyrus returned, they were all slaughtered together with the young man.

Tomyris, having lost her army and her son, prepares to assuage the grief of either mother or queen with the blood of the enemy rather than with her own tears.

[Note: [Col. 0762C] “Rather.” Following the Lombard manuscript, the other two Florentine manuscripts give this in place of the common *promptius* (“more readily”). The same reading is confirmed by the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts, together with the Utrecht, Meursius, and Perizonian manuscripts. Meursius places *diluere* (“to assuage”) after *lacrymis* (“tears”); the Augustan edition deletes *suis* (“her own”).]

She feigns distrust through despair at the disaster inflicted, and, gradually giving ground,

[Note: [Col. 0762C] “Giving ground.” The second Leiden and Utrecht manuscripts have *decedendo* (“retreating”); the latter also deletes *-que*.]

lures the arrogant enemy into an ambush.

There, having prepared an ambush among the mountains, she destroyed two hundred thousand Persians together with the king himself. Above all, the event was made remarkable by the fact that not even a messenger survived such a great disaster.

[Note: [Col. 0762C] “Of so great a disaster.” Perizonius has *tantae cladi* (“for so great a disaster”).]

[Note: [Col. 0762C] “Not even a messenger.” The first and Parisian editions have *nec nuntius quidem* (“nor even a messenger”).]

The queen ordered Cyrus’ head to be cut off and thrown into a skin filled with human blood,

[Note: [Col. 0762C] “Into a skin.” The first Florentine manuscript has *in utre* (“in a skin”).]

rebuking him not like a woman:

[Note: [Col. 0762C] “Rebuking.” Meursius has *increpans* (“rebuking”) instead of *increpitans*. He intended to imitate Virgil, *Aeneid* I.742:

“Then, rebuking Bitias, he gave it to him. Eagerly he drained the foaming cup.”]

“Sate yourself,” she said, “with the blood for which you thirsted, and in which, for thirty years, you remained insatiable.”

## CHAPTER VIII. Darius, king of the Persians, attacks the Scythians and is put to flight; he conquers Asia, Macedonia, and the Ionians. He attacks the Athenians at the cost of his own life and that of many others.

In the year 245 from the founding of the City, Darius, after Cyrus had been killed among the Scythians, perhaps gained the kingdom after a considerable interval.

[Note: [Col. 0762C] “From the founding of the City.” The first and fourth Leiden manuscripts have “after the founding of the City.”]

For Cambyses, son of Cyrus, had reigned between them.

[Note: [Col. 0762D] “Cambyses reigned between them.” Cambyses reigned seven years and five months, according to Herodotus, Book III. In excerpts from Ctesias, eighteen years are assigned to Cambyses’ reign. Lucian also discusses him in *Charon*. FABRICIUS.]

After conquering Egypt, he detested the whole religion of Egypt and demolished its ceremonies and temples.

[Note: [Col. 0762D] “Detested.” The Augustan edition adds *est* (“was”). Shortly afterward, Perizonius has *religiones* (“religions”) instead of *caeremonias* (“ceremonies”).]

[Note: [Col. 0762D] “He polluted its ceremonies and the temples of the gods.” From the notes of the old Cologne book I conjectured that this should be read as above; the common text had *deposuit* (“laid down”). But since *de* was written in the form of a contraction, it aroused suspicion; and *posuit* (“placed”) can easily become *polluit* (“polluted”) through the change of *s* into *l*. LAUT.—I think nothing should be changed, for *deposuit* in Orosius means “destroyed” or “demolished.” Justin, Book I, chapter 9, says of Cambyses: “Offended by the superstitions of the Egyptians, he ordered the temples of Apis and the other gods to be demolished.” See also Brisson, *On the Significations of Words*, under *deponere*.]

After him, two Magi also dared to creep into the kingdom under the name of the king whom they had killed; but they were soon discovered and overthrown.

[Note: [Col. 0763B] “The Magi.” Three Leiden manuscripts have “two Magi.” The Groningen manuscript and the older editions likewise have this number; but neither the Augustan edition nor the Florentine manuscripts or the others recognize it. The names of the Magi were Cometes and Oropastes according to Justin, and Patizeithes and Smerdis according to Herodotus; they held the kingdom for seven months. See Rutgers, *Various Readings*, Book I, chapter 8, p. 22. Oropastes appears to have been called Smerdis because, after Cometes—also called Patizeithes, his brother—had been ordered to kill Smerdis, the Magus assumed Smerdis’ name and acted in his place.]

[Note: [Col. 0763B] “To creep in.” In the manuscripts and in certain printed editions it is incorrectly written *obripere*. To creep into something or toward some office means to deceive the unsuspecting and obtain something under the false appearance of some virtue or right. Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 3: “Nor can Scaurus be thought to have crept upon a crude and unsuspecting state through some rudimentary quality of life.” Cicero, *Speech Against Piso*, chapter 1: “You crept into office through the error of men and the recommendation of smoky ancestral images,” which resemble you in nothing except their color; and *Speech for Gnaeus Plancius*, chapter 7: “Gnaeus Plancius did not creep into office but reached it by a direct course.”]

Therefore Darius, one of those who had restrained the audacity of the Magi by the sword, was made king by the unanimous consent of all. After he had recovered by war the Assyrians and Babylon, which had defected from Persian rule, he made war on Attyros, king of the Scythians—

[Note: [Col. 0763C] “Attyros, king.” In the old books it is read variously as *Anthiros* and *Antyros*. In the printed editions of Justin—for the king’s name is not found in our manuscript—he is called *Lanthinus*. Herodotus, who gives a full account of this war in Book IV, names the Scythian king Ἰνδάθυρσος (*Indáthur­sos*); others call him Σκυθάρκης (*Scythárkēs*). FABRICIUS.]

—principally for this reason: he had failed to obtain the marriage with Attyros’ daughter that he had requested. A truly great necessity, that seven hundred thousand men should be exposed to mortal danger for the pleasure of one man!

With an incredible force of seven hundred thousand armed men, he entered Scythia. Since the enemy did not permit a set battle and sudden attacks continually tore at the rear of his forces, he feared that his return might be denied him if the bridge over the Ister River were broken. Having lost eighty thousand warriors, he fled in panic, although he did not count this number among his losses—

[Note: [Col. 0763D] “Counted.” Perizonius has *tulerit* (“bore” or “suffered”). Shortly afterward, the third Leiden manuscript, as well as the Groningen manuscript, repeats *numerum* (“number”).]

—and what almost no one would have dared even to hope to possess, he did not notice that he had lost.

Then he attacked and conquered Asia and Macedonia.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] “Attacked.” Three Leiden manuscripts have *ingressus* (“entered”). At that time Amyntas, father of Alexander Philhellene, ruled Macedonia. Thinking it prudent to yield to a greater power, he submitted to the Persians when they demanded earth and water, and retained his kingdom and peace through the marriage of his daughter to Babari, the foremost man among the Persians. See Herodotus, Books V, chapters 17, 18, 19, and 94, and Justin, Book VII, chapter 3.]

He also defeated the Ionians in a naval engagement.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] “The Ionians in a naval engagement.” For this naval battle, in which the Ionians were defeated by the Persians, read Herodotus, Book VI. FABRICIUS.]

Then he attacked the Athenians because the Ionians had aided them against him and directed his arms against them.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] “Because the Ionians had aided them against him.” Justin says the same in Book II. Plato, in the *Menexenus*, writes: “Darius, accusing us and the Eretrians, on the pretext that we had plotted against Sardis,” etc. Plutarch, in *Aristides*, says that Darius gave as the reason for this war against the Athenians “that they had burned Sardis.” FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0764B] “Had aided them.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has *auxilio venissent* (“had come to their aid”), and the first has *in auxilio venissent* (“had come as aid”). But *juvissent* (“had aided”) is written above the line.]

When the Athenians learned that Darius was approaching—

[Note: [Col. 0764B] “Learned.” The Utrecht manuscript has *comperunt* (“learned”), and the Augustan edition has *compererant* (“had learned”).]

—although they had requested assistance from the Lacedaemonians, nevertheless, knowing that the Lacedaemonians were being detained by the leisure imposed by a four-day religious observance—

[Note: [Col. 0764B] “Because they were being detained by the leisure of a four-day religious observance.” A shameful error had intruded here, with the word *Persas* (“the Persians”) added. For it was not the Persians but the Lacedaemonians who were bound by a four-day religious observance, as Justin writes, and Herodotus states more clearly in these words: “It was the ninth day of the month; they said that they would not set out, since the lunar cycle was not yet complete.” That is, “It was the ninth day of the month, but they denied that they would lead out the army on that day because the moon had not yet completed its circuit.” Lucian, in *On Astrology*, says of Lycurgus: “He established for them a law that they should never advance to war before the moon became full.” Plato, *Laws* III, thinks that the reason they arrived late at Lacedaemon was the war they were waging with the Messenians. FABRICIUS.]

—they seized the opportunity to hope, and, having arrayed only ten thousand citizens and one thousand auxiliary Plataeans, burst forth upon the plains of Marathon against six hundred thousand enemies.

[Note: [Col. 0764C] “Ten thousand citizens.” In the common editions, except the Augustan, *armatorum civium* (“armed citizens”) is read. The word *armatorum* is rightly deleted by that edition and by all the Florentine manuscripts, two Leiden manuscripts, and the Perizonian and Meursian manuscripts. The second Leiden manuscript has *auxiliatoribus* (“helpers”) instead of *auxiliaribus* (“auxiliaries”).]

Miltiades commanded in that war. Relying more on speed than valor, he clung to the enemy at close quarters with a sufficiently swift advance before he could be driven back by a well-aimed discharge of arrows.

[Note: [Col. 0764D] “By a discharge.” The Groningen manuscript and the first and fourth Leiden manuscripts have *ictu* (“blow” or “stroke”).]

So great was the difference in the manner of fighting in that battle that on one side men seemed prepared to kill, while on the other cattle seemed prepared to die.

[Note: [Col. 0764D] “Two hundred thousand Persians on the plain of Marathon.” This is that famous victory won at Marathon under the auspices of Miltiades, about which much is found everywhere. FABRICIUS.—As the battle at Marathon itself was famous, so the Marathonian people wished its memory and the eternal proclamation of the victory to survive on their coinage. This single coin, itself distinguished and memorable, came into my collection of antiquities. On one side it displays a large letter M occupying the middle of the coin’s surface, with a grain ear inserted through the center by means of transverse lines, to indicate the fertility of the land. Beneath it is inscribed ΜΑΡΑΤ. I think this was misread by Wolfgang Lazius, who published the coin in the *Commentaries on Greek Affairs*, included in the *Thesaurus of Gronovius*, volume VI, p. 3419, printing ΜΑΡΑΘ., that is, ΜΑΡΑΘΟΝΙΩΝ, “of the Marathonians.” On the obverse of the coin there is a vulture holding a snake in its talons and a laurel branch in its beak; the former signifies the abundance and hunting of these birds, while the latter refers to the famous victory over the Persians.]

Two hundred thousand Persians fell on the fields of Marathon at that time.

[Col. 0765A] [Note: [Col. 0765C] “He felt it.” This alludes to what had just preceded: “Although he did not count this number of the lost among the losses, he did not feel what he had lost.”]

Darius felt this loss:

[Note: [Col. 0765C] “For, defeated.” The Augustan edition has *jam victus* (“already defeated”). But three Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen manuscript have *nam motus* (“for, moved”). Should one write *submotus fugatusque* (“driven away and put to flight”)?]

for, defeated and put to flight, he seized his ships and fled back to Persia. When he was renewing the war and preparing to avenge himself on the victors, he collapsed amid the preparations, in the seventy-fourth Olympiad—that is, in the year 275 from the founding of the City—at which time in Rome the maiden Popillia was buried alive for the crime of sexual misconduct.

[Note: [Col. 0765C] “The maiden Popillia.” There is great variation in the name of this Vestal. Orosius calls her *Popillia* here; Dionysius, Book VIII, calls her Ὠπιμία (*Opimia*); Livy, Book II, calls her *Oppia*. She was condemned for incest under the consulship of Marcus Fabius and Lucius Valerius; according to Dionysius, that year was 271 from the founding of the City. FABRICIUS.—The second Leiden manuscript reads 285; the third, 276; the fourth, 272; the Utrecht manuscript, 234.]

## CHAPTER IX. Xerxes, king of the Persians, receives a great defeat from a few Spartans under the command of Leonidas and is conquered by stratagem.

Xerxes, succeeding his father Darius in the kingdom, spent five years preparing the war against Greece that his father had undertaken—

[Note: [Col. 0765C] “Which Demaratus the Lacedaemonian.” Herodotus, Book VII near the end, records this in addition to Justin.]

[Note: [Col. 0765C] “His father Darius.” The fourth Leiden manuscript inserts *defuncto* (“after his death”), followed by *mox in regno succedens* (“then succeeding him in the kingdom”), as do the first, Parisian, and Venetian editions.]

—a war which Demaratus the Lacedaemonian, then living in exile at Xerxes’ court, revealed to his countrymen first on tablets covered with writing and then on wax tablets.

Therefore Xerxes, with seven hundred thousand armed men from his kingdom and three hundred thousand auxiliaries—

[Note: [Col. 0765D] “Xerxes, seven hundred thousand.” Herodotus writes that Xerxes’ infantry numbered ἑβδομήκοντα καὶ ἑκατὸν μυριάδων, that is, seventeen hundred thousand. Diodorus, Book II, says: “More than eight hundred thousand of the infantry forces were counted.” FABRICIUS.—Three Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen manuscript have *Xerxem* (“Xerxes”).]

[Note: [Col. 0765D] “From auxiliaries.” Vincent of Beauvais and the Augustan edition have *de auxiliatoribus* (“of auxiliary troops”). Two Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen manuscript, increase the number by writing *CCCC* or *CCCМ*.]

—and also twelve hundred warships with beaks—

[Note: [Col. 0765D] “Twelve hundred beaked ships.” Lysias and Isocrates write that Xerxes arrived in Greece with a fleet of 1,700 ships. We have discussed this matter more fully from Herodotus and Aeschylus in our scholia on Lysias’ *Funeral Oration*. FABRICIUS.]

—and three thousand cargo ships, as is reported to have been his force; so that it is rightly said that rivers scarcely sufficed for drinking, lands scarcely for entering, and seas scarcely for sailing, for that unexpected army and immense fleet.

[Note: [Col. 0766C] “Rivers scarcely sufficient for drinking.” The famous passage is in Juvenal, *Satire* 10:

“We believe the deep rivers failed,
and the rivers were drunk dry while the Mede dined.”

FABRICIUS.—“Leonidas” should be written, not *Leonidas* or *Leonides*. Shortly afterward, the first, Parisian, and Venetian editions have *obsistit* (“resists”) instead of *obstitit* (“resisted”); the Augustan edition has “despising the obstacle of their fewness,” and the second Florentine manuscript has “with contempt for their interposed small number.”]

Against this army so incredible for its time—whose number is now harder to establish than it then was to defeat—Leonidas, king of the Spartans, stood with four thousand men in the narrow pass of Thermopylae.

[Note: [Col. 0766D] “Leonidas, king of the Spartans, with four thousand.” Three hundred of these were Spartans. FABRICIUS.]

But Xerxes, despising the smallness of the force opposed to him, ordered the battle to be entered and hand-to-hand combat joined. Then, as one wave succeeded another, a larger and more sluggish crowd followed, since they were now neither free to rush forward—

[Note: [Col. 0766D] “Nor equipped for fighting.” Lucan, *Pharsalia* VII, verse 494, on Pompey’s battle line:

“Scarcely having room to move right hands and weapons,”]

It stood fast and, packed tight, feared its own swords.] Neither equipped to fight nor ready to flee, [Note: [Col. 0766D] “Only by the dead would it be supported.” The first edition ineptly has *subjacer*; the Paris and Venetian editions have *subjicerent*, for which the Lugdunensis Batavus manuscript has *subjiceretur*. [Col. 0767B] The sense is that the enemy ranks stood so densely packed that the compacted bodies of the slain had no room to fall to the ground, but remained upright, leaning against one another, without any vital movement to sustain them.] it was supported only by the dead, [Col. 0767A] and for three continuous days it was not a battle of two sides, but the slaughter of one people.

[Note: [Col. 0767B] “On the fourth day.” Most printed copies have “on the fourth”; but *quarta* is found in Justinus, in the editions and some manuscripts of Vincentius Bellovacensis, and in certain manuscripts of Orosius. In place of *hostem*, Vincentius writes *hostes*.]

On the fourth day, when Leonidas saw the enemy surrounding him on every side, he urged [Note: [Col. 0767C] “Auxiliary allies.” The Augustan edition, Gronovius’s collection, and the Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts—the first, third, and fourth—have *auxiliatores socios*; the second has *auxiliarios socios*. [Col. 0767D] ] . Nowhere, he said, would victors perish more honorably than in the enemy’s camp [Note: [Col. 0767D] “Would perish.” Three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, together with Meursius and Perizonius, have *esse perituros*, which is weak and does not seem to have come from Justinus, whom Orosius follows.] .

The Spartans, searching for their king but not finding him, cut down and overthrew everything, ranging through the entire camp; and amid the dense heaps of bodies they scarcely pursued the few surviving men. [Note: [Col. 0767D] “Victors without doubt.” The common printed books add *non essent* (“they would not be”), which I find in no manuscript. The battle, begun at the start of the night, continued into the greater part of the day. [Col. 0768A] At last, exhausted by victory, when each man, his limbs failing, seemed to himself to have been sated with vengeance for his own death, there, amid the obstacles formed by corpses, [Note: [Col. 0767D] “And the field, thick with …” The first edition, the Paris and Venetian editions, have: “and the thick, half-congealed field of blood, twitching, he slipped and died.” The first, third, and fourth Lugdunensis Batavus editions have *campum quoque crasso*, and so forth. [Col. 0768B] ] and across the field, twitching with thick, half-congealed blood, [Note: [Col. 0768B] “He slipped and died.” The second and fourth Lugdunensis Batavus editions have *lapsusque et mortuus est*. But all printed editions except the first, Venetian, and Paris editions present *lassus, lapsus et mortuus est* (“weary, he slipped and died”). This is wholly inept: *lassus* was first formed from the variant reading of the verb *lapsus*, and then, once both verbs had been placed in the manuscripts in accordance with common practice, was added as well.] he slipped and died.

## CHAPTER X. Xerxes is confronted in war by Themistocles, commander of the Athenians. Then, after Themistocles had alienated the Ionians from him, he puts him to flight.

Xerxes, twice defeated on land, [Note: [Col. 0768C] “Prepares a naval battle.” On the naval battle described in this chapter, consult Herodotus, Book Eight; Aeschylus, *The Persians* (Πέρσαις); Diodorus, Book Eleven; Plutarch, *Life of Themistocles*; and others. FABR.] prepares a naval battle.

But Themistocles, commander of the Athenians, having learned that the Ionians—whom, by aiding them in the earlier war, he had caused the Persian attack to turn against himself—were bringing out the fleet that had been equipped to support Xerxes, decided to entice them to his side and withdraw them from the enemy. [Col. 0768B] Since he was denied the opportunity to speak with them, he ordered messages [Note: [Col. 0768C] “To be displayed.” The old books have *symbolos*, not *symbola*, as do the printed books of Justinus. Plautus, *Bacchides*: “In his presence he immediately showed the man the token that you yourself had given him.” Herodotus, speaking of Themistocles, has: ἐντάμνων ἐν τοῖσι λίθοισι γράμματα (“cutting letters into the stones”), and so forth. Plutarch writes: Ἐνεχάραττε κατὰ τῶν λίθων ἐπιφανῆ γράμματα τοὺς μὲν εὑρίσκων ἀπὸ τύχης τοὺς δὲ αὐτὸς ἱστὰς περὶ τὰ ναύλοχα δὲ τὰς ὑδρείας, that is: “He carved conspicuous letters on the stones, finding some by chance and placing others himself near the anchorages and watering places.” FABR.] to be displayed at the places [Note: [Col. 0768C] “At which.” Some editions have *ad quae* (“to which”).] where the Ionians seemed likely to approach with their ships, [Note: [Col. 0768C] ] and fastened to rocks, [Note: [Col. 0768D] “And fastened to rocks.” The first and fourth Lugdunensis Batavus editions have *proponi symbolos funiculis, saxisque* (“tokens were to be displayed by cords and fastened to rocks”), and so forth.] addressing with a fitting reproach those who had once been allies and companions in danger, [Note: [Col. 0768D] “But now acting unjustly.” Herodotus similarly has: ἄνδρες Ἴωνες, οὐ ποιέετε δίκαια—“Ionians, you are acting unjustly.” In our manuscripts, however, the reading is *injuste desides* (“unjustly idle”). FABR. —The same reading is found, apart from the Augustan edition, in three Florentine manuscripts, one of the Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts—namely the second (the fourth writes *insistentes*)—and in Perizonius, Meursius, and the Ultricht manuscript. Yet the reproach found in Justinus makes it clear that one should write not *injuste desides*, but *injuste agentes*; this reading is preserved by the first and third Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, Gronovius’s collection, and most printed editions.] but now acting unjustly, and persuading them through a solemn exhortation to respect the rights of their ancient treaties; above all, he warned them that, once battle had been joined, they should, in the guise of retreating, hold back their oars [Note: [Col. 0768D] “And themselves.” Meursius does not recognize the conjunction *-que*. Shortly afterward, the Augustan edition reads *Xerxes igitur rex* (“King Xerxes, therefore”); several manuscripts omit *rex*, and some have *exspectator* (“awaiting”) instead of *spectator*, as they do somewhat later *exspectaretur* for *spectaretur*—a common scribal error.] and withdraw themselves from the war.

Accordingly, the king, keeping part of the ships for himself, [Col. 0769A] remains on the shore as a spectator of the battle. On the other side, [Note: [Col. 0769B] “Artemidora, queen of Halicarnassus.” I have retained the name *Artemidora*, which is found in all the books. Yet both Herodotus and Justinus, as well as Pausanias in his *Laconica*, call this queen Artemisia. Plutarch likewise mentions Ἀρτεμισία in the *Life of Themistocles*. FABR.] Artemidora, queen of Halicarnassus, who had come to Xerxes’ aid [Note: [Col. 0769B] “Had come to Xerxes.” The Augustan edition and the second Florentine manuscript have *Xerxis venerat*.] , enters the battle among the foremost commanders with the greatest ferocity, so that, by a reversal of roles, a woman’s caution could be seen in a man, and a man’s boldness in a woman.

When the battle was evenly balanced, the Ionians, following Themistocles’ instructions, gradually began to withdraw from the engagement [Note: [Col. 0769C] “Began.” The Augustan edition has *ceperant* (“had begun”).] . Their defection persuaded the Persians, already looking for an opportunity to flee, to flee openly.

In this panic many ships were sunk and captured; more, however, fearing the king’s savagery [Note: [Col. 0769C] “As though his monstrous cruelty.” The third Lugdunensis Batavus, together with Gronovius’s collection, has *cum* (“with”). Perhaps not without reason, as Orosius may once have written: “more fearing the king’s savagery than the enemy’s monstrous cruelty,” with *magis* understood.] as though it were the enemy’s monstrous cruelty, [Note: [Col. 0769C] “They scatter homeward.” This appears to have been written by Orosius from Justinus, and all the old editions present it thus. Fabricius and Scottus restored *domos* from several manuscripts that have it. The first Lugdunensis Batavus nevertheless has *domum dilabebantur* (“were scattering homeward”).] scatter homeward.

Mardonius approaches the king, distressed by so many disasters, and advises [Note: [Col. 0769C] “The king into his kingdom.” Meursius has *eum in regnum* (“him into his kingdom”).] that the king should return to his kingdom before unfavorable reports stirred up fresh disturbances at home. He himself, if the remaining forces were entrusted to him, would both exact vengeance from the enemy and avert the domestic disgrace; or, if the adverse fortunes of war [Note: [Col. 0769B] “Had persisted.” Perizonius has *perseverarent* (“should persist”).] persisted, he would indeed yield to the enemy, but nevertheless without bringing disgrace upon the king.

When the plan was approved, the army was handed over to Mardonius. Xerxes departed with a few men for Abydos, where he had built a bridge as though he were victor over the sea. But when he found the bridge destroyed by winter storms, he crossed in panic by a fishing boat. [Col. 0770A]

There was indeed something for the human race to look upon and lament [Note: [Col. 0769C] “Ought to have.” This should be written thus, as in the best manuscripts, the three Florentine manuscripts, Perizonius, and Meursius. The printed editions have *debuerat* (“ought to have”), and the manuscripts vary greatly immediately afterward.] : to observe, amid this extraordinary reversal of circumstances, one who had once hidden the very sea beneath a joined bridge [Note: [Col. 0769C] “The sea itself before him.” The first and third Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, have *prius ipsum pelagus* (“the very sea beforehand”).] now content with the narrow side of a little boat, beneath which [Note: [Col. 0769D] “Had earlier carried the sea itself.” The first Lugdunensis Batavus manuscript, the third, and Gronovius’s collection have *prius ipsum pelagus*.] the sea itself had formerly lain hidden, [Note: [Col. 0769D] “Had carried the yoke of his captivity, bound to the bridge.” We printed this from the book of Corbinianus Gualtherus; others too suspected it to be the true reading. Andreas Papius has *vinctum ponte, portasset*. FABR. —“And the yoke of his captivity, bound to the bridge,” and so forth, is an emendation of Andreas Papius, who worked so successfully in translating and correcting Dionysius’ *Orbis*. Some printed and manuscript copies have *vincto ponto* (“when the sea was bound”), others *victo Ponto* (“when the Pontus was conquered”), and others *juncto* (“when it was joined”). Cassae glandes. LAUT. —I found these readings in the manuscripts: Perizonius has *victo ponto*; the first, second, and fourth Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, the Ultricht manuscript, and Gronovius’s collection have *vecto ponte*; the first and second Florentine manuscripts, as well as Meursius, have *vincto ponte*. [Note: [Col. 0770B] “Of the cheapest.” Three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, Meursius, and Perizonius, together with Gronovius’s collection, have *et vilissimo*.
