The infantry forces entrusted to the commanders likewise wasted away through toil, hunger, [Note: [Col. 0770C] “And fear, so that they wasted away.” The first edition, together with the Venetian and Paris editions, has *ac metu tabuerunt* (“and through fear they wasted away”).] and fear; and, as the disease grew more virulent, such a plague and such a ghastly spectacle of the dying arose that the roads were filled with corpses. Even savage birds and shameless beasts, drawn by the allure of food, [Note: [Col. 0770C] “Followed the dying army.” Lucan, Book Seven, line 831:

“Now for a long time the birds, having followed the civil camp,

assemble.”

Justinus, Book Two, chapter 13: “So great was the ghastliness of the dying that the roads were filled with corpses, and birds and beasts, enticed by the lure of food, followed the army.” Aelian notes this nature of vultures in *On Animals*, Book Two, chapter 46: Καὶ μέντοι καὶ ταῖς στρατιαῖς ἕπονται γῦπες, καὶ μάλα μαντικῶς ὅτι γε εἰς πόλεμον χωροῦσιν εἰδότες, καὶ ὅτι μάχη πάσα ἐργάζεται νεκροὺς καὶ τοῦτο ἐγνωκότες—“Vultures follow armies on campaign, with extraordinary foreknowledge, knowing both that they are marching to war and that every battle produces corpses, and being aware of this.”] followed the dying [Col. 0770B] army.

## 115. CHAPTER XI. Mardonius, Xerxes’ prefect, while carrying on the remainder of the war, flees after losing his forces. Xerxes, despised by his own men as an unfortunate man, is killed.

But Mardonius, to whom Xerxes had entrusted the remainder of the war, was first inflated by brief success and soon afterward cast down into the utmost ruin. [Note: [Col. 0770D] “Olynthus.” Concerning Olynthus, Stephanus of Byzantium writes: Ὄλυνθος, πόλις Θράκης, πρὸς τῇ Σιθωνίᾳ τῆς Μακεδονίας—“Olynthus, a city of Thrace, near Sithonia in Macedonia.” It was situated in the Chalcidian region near Mount Athos; hence Thucydides, Book Four, page 283, calls it “Chalcidian Olynthus,” and Herodotus, Book Eight, chapter 127, writes that the Chalcidians possessed it even after the disaster they suffered in the Persian war. The Olynthians had revolted, or were deliberating revolt, when they were overcome by the Persians, as Herodotus relates in the preceding chapter; in Book Seven, chapter 122, he suggests that they had dealt with the Persians when he says that the Persians took ships and fellow soldiers from Torone, Galepsus, Sermyla, Mecyberna, and Olynthus, a region which, he adds, in his time was called Sithonia. Olynthus had previously been destroyed by Philip of Macedon, son of Amyntas, after the serious war waged by that free and powerful city against that most powerful king. I do not find when or by whom it was restored. The Persians did not destroy it, but, after killing its inhabitants, introduced new settlers. [Col. 0771B] Hence even today there survive coins of that most distinguished city. Of the two following coins, one silver coin is preserved in the Friderician Treasury, conspicuous for its representation of the worship of Diana and Jupiter and notable for the inscription ΟΛΟΝΤΙΩΝ (“of the Olynthians”). Goltzius supplies the other, a bronze coin, distinguished by the common bond and concord of the Toroneans and Olynthians, neighboring cities.] In fact, he captured Olynthus, [Col. 0771A] a town of Greece, [Note: [Col. 0771B] “He captured it.” Orosius follows Justinus. Herodotus, however, Book Eight, writes that Olynthus was captured not by Mardonius but by another commander, Artabazus. FABR.] .

Having attempted, by various inducements, [Note: [Col. 0771B] “By varied enticement.” The Lugdunensis Batavus manuscript has *vana* (“empty”) instead of *varia*. But Mardonius tried the Athenians’ steadfastness in vain by many methods.] to lead the Athenians to hope for peace, when he saw that their freedom could not be overcome, he burned part of the city [Note: [Col. 0771C] “After part of the city had been burned.” He means the part that the Athenians had already begun to rebuild, according to Justinus. FABR.] and transferred all his preparations for war [Note: [Col. 0771C] “He led them away.” Perizonius’s manuscript has *ducit*. Some old editions have *in omnem Boeotiam* (“into all Boeotia”) instead of *in Boeotiam omnem*.] into Boeotia.

A hundred thousand Greeks followed him there, and, battle being joined without delay, [Note: [Col. 0771C] “Mardonius, his forces having been destroyed, and so forth.” I fear that Justinus, deceived in his epitome, assigned to Mardonius matters that ought to be attributed to Artabazus, and thereby led Orosius into the same error. For Herodotus, Diodorus, Plutarch, and all the others write that Artabazus fled and Mardonius fell in the battle at Plataea. Pausanias, Book One, says that Mardonius was killed by a Spartan soldier. Ctesias, however, disagrees with them: he says that Mardonius fled after being wounded and later, sent by Xerxes to plunder Apollo’s temple, was overwhelmed and killed by a violent hailstorm. Justinus and Orosius follow him. FABR.] they forced Mardonius, his forces destroyed, [Note: [Col. 0771D] “As though from a shipwreck.” The three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, have *veluti de naufragio* (“as though from a shipwreck”).] to flee naked and with only a few men, as though from a shipwreck. For after the division of this booty [Note: [Col. 0771D] “Of this booty.” I restored this reading from the Longobard manuscript, supported by seven other manuscripts. The common editions have *istius praedae* (“of that booty”).] , Persian gold was the first corruption [Note: [Col. 0771D] “Of Greek virtue.” This reading is defended by the first edition, the editions that followed it, the Augustan edition, three Florentine manuscripts, three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, the Ultricht manuscript, Gronovius’s collection, and Vincentius Bellovacensis. The manuscripts of the second Lugdunensis Batavus, Perizonius, and Meursius, together with the Hittorp and Bolsuinge editions, prefer *Graecae virtutis* (“of Greek virtue”).] of Greek virtue.

Thus the undertaking [Note: [Col. 0772B] “The undertaking.” The Augustan edition and the third Florentine manuscript have the erroneous *inceptos*, just as the first edition and those following it have *prima*, from which [Col. 0772C] *in Boeotiam Mardonii copiae delatae sunt* (“Mardonius’ forces were brought into Boeotia”) arose. And then, “under the walls of Mycale.”] presses the wretched toward utter ruin. For, by chance, [Col. 0772A] on the same day that Mardonius’ forces were destroyed in Boeotia, part of the Persian army was fighting in Asia [Col. 0772C] beneath Mount Mycale [Note: [Col. 0772C] “Beneath Mount Mycale.” Herodotus has Ἐν Μυκάλῃ τῆς Ἰωνίης—“at Mycale in Ionia”—in his final book, where the history is described at greater length, as also in Diodorus, Book Eleven. Consult Thucydides, Book One, as well. FABR.] in a naval battle.

There a new report suddenly filled the ears [Note: [Col. 0772C] “The ears.” The first, third, and fourth Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, add the gloss *audientes* (“hearing”); the first Lugdunensis Batavus has *opes* (“resources”) instead of *copias* (“forces”).] of both fleets and peoples: Mardonius’ forces had been destroyed and the Greeks had been victorious.

A marvelous ordering of divine judgment: in Boeotia, at sunrise, battle had been joined; [Note: [Col. 0772C] “In Asia, at midday.” Herodotus writes: Τὸ μὲν ἐν Πλαταιῆσι πρωῒ ἔτι τῆς ἡμέρης ἐγίνετο, τὸ δέ ἠν Μυκάλῃ, περὶ δείλην—“The action at Plataea took place early in the day, but that at Mycale toward evening.” Orosius follows Justinus. FABR.] in Asia, at midday, it was announced on that same day, with such vast distances of sea and land lying between them!

[Note: [Col. 0772C] “To which report this especially contributed.” This is the reading of the first edition, the Paris and Venetian editions, and the Hittorp and Bolsuinge editions. The Augustan edition has: “That report especially contributed to the matter.” Fabricius and Scottus adopted this, and several manuscripts seem to confirm it. Meursius deletes *ei*; the first and third Florentine manuscripts have *qui rumore vel maxime rei astipulatus est*; the second has *rus more*, and so forth, as does the first. If we adopt the common reading, the sense is: “that report especially supported that matter,” namely, the ordering of divine judgment. But I preferred to restore the old reading, because the sentence seems to flow more suitably, especially if, instead of *clade* (“defeat”), as all copies have it, we write *clades* (“the disaster”), which the sense plainly requires; and I am surprised that this did not occur to anyone. Unless we admit this emendation, there is no noun or word in what precedes to which the following words—“and rendered them unprepared for battle,” and so forth—can refer. For what produced this result was the hearing of the allies’ disaster; Orosius might better have written *suorum* (“their own”), since it was the Persians who had perished in Greece, just as here the Persians were defeated in the naval battle.] This report especially contributed to the fact that the Persians, when they heard of the disaster of their allies, were first seized by grief and then by despair, and were rendered neither fit for battle nor capable of flight.

And so, when they had been thrown into panic and routed, the enemy, made more resolute by the success of his good fortune, attacked them.

Xerxes, after the war he had unsuccessfully waged in Greece had made him contemptible to his own people, was surrounded in the palace and killed by his prefect Artabanus [Note: [Col. 0773B] “By Artabanus.” Artabanus killed Xerxes in the year before the seventy-ninth Olympiad, according to Diodorus. FABR.] .

O times [Note: [Col. 0773C] “Worthy of longing and remembrance.” The Augustan edition has *desiderata et memoria dignissima* (“most longed for and most worthy of remembrance”).] most worthy of longing and remembrance! O days of untroubled serenity, which are set before us to look back upon as though from darkness [Note: [Col. 0773C] “As though from darkness.” The first, third, and fourth Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts and Gronovius’s collection read: “O days of untroubled virtue, which are set before us to look back upon as though they were serenities emerging from darkness.”] , in which, within the briefest interval, nineteen hundred thousand men were snatched from the vitals of a single kingdom by three wars under its three successive kings—leaving aside the most wretched Greece of that time, which surpassed in death this entire number, at which we now grow numb [Note: [Col. 0773C] “At which we now grow numb.” The Augustan edition has *de quo nunc erubescimus* (“at which we now blush”), a reading that should not be dismissed. “I am ashamed,” he says, “to admit, while complaining about our own times, the miseries of that period and the immeasurable multitude of those who perished.” If *hebescimus* is retained, it must be understood as “we are stunned.”] .

Leonidas, that most renowned of the Lacedaemonians, in this war against Xerxes—which was to be the last for him and for his enemies—after saying to his six hundred men those famous words of encouragement [Note: [Col. 0773C] “With his six hundred.” The latter word is absent from the Venetian, Paris, and first editions.] : [Note: [Col. 0773C] “Dine as though you were to sup among the dead.” This saying is reported by Plutarch and by Marcus Tullius Cicero in Book One of the *Tusculan Disputations*. FABR. —Four Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts and Gronovius’s collection add *inquit* (“he said”) after *prandete*. Shortly afterward, several manuscripts and printed editions have *auxiliatoribus* instead of *auxiliaribus*.] “Eat breakfast as though you were going to dine among the dead,” nevertheless mercifully advised the auxiliaries whom he ordered to withdraw from the battle to reserve themselves for better times.

Behold: when he promised [Note: [Col. 0773C] “When he promised.” Perizonius’s manuscript has *iste* (“that man”); the Ultricht manuscript has *promiserit* (“when he should have promised”).] future better times [Note: [Col. 0773D] “Future better things, and so forth.” Instead of *isti asserunt* (“these men assert”), the first, Paris, and Venetian editions have *istique asserunt* (“and these assert”). Several Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, punctuate the passage as follows: “Behold, when he promised future better times, these men assert better times in the past and greater ones.”] , they assert better times in the past; what else can be inferred, with both men condemning the present in their own ways, except either that good things are always available but unappreciated, [Note: [Col. 0773D] “Or never better in every respect.” Against all the manuscripts—ten of which I have consulted—as well as Gronovius’s collection and the Augustan edition, the printed editions have inserted *futura* here, reading “or never in any respect will there be better future things.”] or that there are never better things at all?

## CHAPTER XII. Rome harassed by a severe pestilence while the wars are suspended. On the war of the exiles and fugitives, and likewise of the Aequi and Volsci.

[Col. 0774A]

But at Rome, to return to the point from which I digressed—for I am not compelled by an interval of miseries to pass over to other matters, but, just as evils once boiling up everywhere were linked together by their very events, so too let them be related together [Note: [Col. 0773D] “Just as once their gathering heat.” The Longobard manuscript has *sicuti*. Meursius deletes *se*. The first and fourth Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts and Gronovius’s collection place the first syllable in *effervescentia*. The Augustan edition has *ipsa* (“the things themselves”) instead of *ipsis* (“their own”).] —for our purpose is to compare the periods of the world with one another, not to mock the sufferings of any one part of it [Note: [Col. 0773D] “Let them be referred together.” I thought *referentur* should be written, but when I consulted my manuscript I found *referantur* written there. The common editions, as do some manuscripts, have *referuntur*.] : at Rome, then, in the 290th year after the founding of the City [Note: [Col. 0774B] “In the 290th year.” This number is correctly written thus in the manuscripts, whereas it is usually printed incorrectly as 260. In the ancient Roman Fasti as well, the year in which P. Servilius Priscus and L. Aebutius Elva were consuls is numbered 290 after the founding of the City. On this very severe pestilence, see Livy, Book Three, and Dionysius, Book Nine, who writes that it began on the Kalends of September and lasted throughout that year. FABR. —The erroneous number is found in all editions before those of Fabricius; they differ only in that the Augustan edition adds one year. In the three Florentine manuscripts the correct number is expressed as follows: *CCmo nongmo* in the Longobard manuscript, or first; *ducentesimo nonagesimo* in the other two. All manuscripts preserve this number. The scribal error was corrected long ago by Pighius in *Annals*, volume one, page 123.] , with the war suspended for a short time, a severe pestilence, which had either interrupted or compelled whatever rare truces were made there, blazed violently throughout the whole state, so that, appropriately, the heavens seemed to burn with the preceding portent [Note: [Col. 0774C] “With the preceding portent.” The Augustan edition adds *vel signo* (“or sign”). When this had deteriorated into *regno* (“kingdom”) in other manuscripts, the first and fourth Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, expressed both readings: *praecedente regno, praecedente prodigio*.] , when the head of nations was aflame with so great a fire of disease.

For in that year pestilence consumed both Aebutius and Servilius, the two consuls [Col. 0774B] [Note: [Col. 0774C] “Consumed.” Perizonius’s manuscript has *absumpsit* (“wasted away”).] , destroyed most of the military forces, and wiped out many nobles, especially the common people, through loathsome corruption—although a plague that had already arisen in the preceding fourth year had also ravaged the same people [Note: [Col. 0774D] “Although already in the preceding fourth year.” One Lugdunensis Batavus manuscript, together with the Ultricht manuscript, has *quamvis jam etiam* (“although already even”).] .

In the following year, exiled citizens and fugitive slaves, led by Herdonius, a Sabine man, invaded the city. [Note: [Col. 0774D] “And they set fire to the Capitol.” No one reports that the Capitol burned at this time; therefore, contrary even to the authority of the books, I think one should read *inscenderunt* (“they climbed up”), not *incenderunt* (“they set fire to”). FABR. —In the margin of the Longobard manuscript: “Herdonius, a Sabine man, set fire to the Capitol with the slaves and killed the consul Valerius. They were driven out of the Capitol, which they had occupied, by Valerius, who fell fighting there. Add, among others, Augustine, *The City of God*, Book Three, chapter 17.] They even set fire to the Capitol. There the younger men resisted with the greatest courage under the consul and commander Valerius; but the battle was so fierce and perilous that the consul Valerius himself was killed there, and by his own death further stained the unworthy victory over slaves.

The following year, in which the consul was besieged with his defeated army, then came. For the Aequi and Volscians defeated the consul Minucius when he joined battle, and surrounded him in flight [Note: [Col. 0775B] “At Algidus.” The Venetian editions, together with the first and Paris editions, have *in Algidum* (“at Algidus,” with accusative).] at Algidus with hunger and the sword. The outcome would have been disastrous [Note: [Col. 0775B] “A close blockade.” The common editions have *arctatam* (“tightened”), but the first, Paris, and Venetian editions correctly have *arctam* (“close”); the first and third Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, likewise intended this, writing *ortam* (“arisen”).] had Quintius Cincinnatus, that outstanding dictator, not broken the close blockade by crushing the enemy.

Found [Note: [Col. 0775C] “In the countryside.” Latin usage requires this, but all the manuscripts have *in rure* (“in the countryside”), perhaps because the phrase was written as *repertus rure*.] in the countryside, summoned from the plow [Note: [Col. 0775C] “To the fasces.” Some old editions have *ad imperii fasces* (“to the fasces of authority”).] to the fasces, he accepted the office, organized an army, and soon became victorious. [Note: [Col. 0775C] “The yoke of oxen, and so forth.” The Deacon inserted this passage into his history of Eutropius. FABR.] He placed the yoke of oxen [Note: [Col. 0775C] “Upon the Aequi.” This is absent from the third Lugdunensis Batavus manuscript and Gronovius’s collection. Yet, with an intolerable error, all editions without exception read *equis* (“upon horses”).] upon the Aequi, and, holding victory as though it were a plow handle, first drove the conquered enemy before him [Note: [Col. 0775C] “Drove them before him first.” Some early editions have *per se egit primus* (“first drove them by himself”); the Augustan edition has *prae se missos primus egit* (“first drove those sent before him”).] .

## CHAPTER XIII. Famine and pestilence at Rome. Authority transferred from the consuls to the decemvirs, disastrously for the republic. Frequent earthquakes in Italy. The war with Fidenae.

[Col. 0775B]

In the year that was nearest to the three-hundredth after the founding of the City, while envoys sent to the Athenians to bring back the laws of Solon were being awaited [Note: [Col. 0775C] “To be brought back.” The first Florentine manuscript has *transferendas* (“to be transferred”). In place of *compescuit* (“restrained”), the first Lugdunensis Batavus has *consumpsit* (“consumed”).] , famine and pestilence checked Roman arms.

In that three-hundredth year itself—that is, [Note: [Col. 0775D] “In the ninety-fifth Olympiad.” I have retained the numerical variation found in other sources. I found XCV in two manuscripts and XXC in a third. Since Orosius generally follows Eusebius here, who assigns the creation of the decemvirs to the eighty-second Olympiad, consider whether that should also be written here. Dionysius places the creation of the decemvirs in the second year of the eighty-second Olympiad. Diodorus, Book Twelve, gives the eighty-fourth Olympiad. FABR.] in the ninety-fifth Olympiad, the authority of the consuls was transferred to the decemvirs for the purpose of establishing the Attic laws, and brought great ruin upon the republic.

For the first of the decemvirs, while the others yielded, continued the supreme authority for himself alone, and immediately afterward a conspiracy of the others followed, so that, despising the customary order by which the insignia of authority belonged to one man but power was shared, they all pursued everything according to their private desires.

Accordingly, among the many things they arrogantly assumed, they suddenly appeared one by one with twelve fasces each and the other insignia of authority [Note: [Col. 0775D] “Insignia of authority.” The Augustan edition and all the manuscripts without exception have *imperatoriis insignibus* (“imperial insignia”), a reading also found in Vincentius Bellovacensis.] . And, with the religious authority of the consuls cast aside [Note: [Col. 0775D] “With the consuls’ religious authority cast aside.” The first and third Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, write *obligata* (“bound”). The Augustan edition has *obligataque*; Meursius has *abnegata* (“denied”). Vincentius Bellovacensis, in his *Speculum*, has *oblitterata* (“obliterated”).] , a troop of tyrants burst forth through this new beginning of wicked government. After two tables of laws had been added to the first ten, they did very many things with the most insolent arrogance on the day when it was customary to lay down their magistracies, still wearing the same insignia [Note: [Col. 0775D] “Many things.” This error arose from an abbreviation in the fourth Lugdunensis Batavus manuscript and in Vincentius Bellovacensis, where *prima* (“first”) is written, so that it is joined with the following day.] .

The very great lust of Appius Claudius [Note: [Col. 0776C] “The lust of Appius Claudius.” The matter is well known from Dionysius, Book Eleven; Diodorus, Book Twelve; Livy, Book Three; and Eutropius, Book One. FABR.] also increased the resentment [Note: [Col. 0776B] “Greatly.” Three Florentine manuscripts, two Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, Perizonius, Gronovius’s collection, and Vincentius Bellovacensis write *maximam* (“the greatest”). The Augustan edition also has *maximam*, as though Orosius called it “the greatest resentment,” since they made perpetual the office that had been annual and administered it according to their own will. I think it should be restored to *maxime* (“greatly”). The common editions join *maxima* with *libidine*.] , for, in order to violate the virgin Virginia, he first brought forward a pretext for claiming that she was a slave.

Therefore her father Virginius, driven by grief at the loss of freedom and shame at the dishonor, [Note: [Col. 0776C] “Father Virginius, driven.” The reading *adductus* (“led”) is also found. Cicero, Book Two of *On Ends*: “L. Virginius, in the sixtieth year after liberty was recovered, killed his daughter Virginia with his own hand rather than that she should be surrendered to the lust of Appius Claudius, who was then in supreme power.” FABR.] drew his daughter, being dragged into slavery, before the eyes of the people—a pious parricide [sentence breaks off]. [Note: [Col. 0776C] “A pious parricide.” A similar expression occurs in Ovid, *Ibis*, line 311:

“Or let the adulteress, with you slain, be called pious, just as  
she by whose avenger Leucon fell was called pious.”

For the interpretation of that passage, an ancient commentator added: “Leucon, one of the kings of Pontus, killed his brother Spartacus, provoked by his wife. When Leucon wished to commit adultery with her, he was killed by him; hence Arion:

‘Leucon killed his brother for his wife, and she  
killed him: thus the cause of death was shared by both.’

This play on the words brings to mind an ancient inscription in which a woman said to have been excessively (*nimia*, for *nimium*) pious is recorded as having become impious. To shed some light upon it, I append here, from the elegant little work by Jacob Spon entitled *Research into the Antiquities and Curiosities of the City of Lyon*, page 86, the same inscription. It reads:

D. M.

[To the divine Manes.]

ETERNAL MEMORY

OF SUTIA ANTHIDIS,

WHO LIVED TWENTY-FIVE

YEARS, NINE MONTHS,

AND FIVE DAYS; WHO, WHILE

SHE WAS EXCESSIVELY DUTIFUL,

WAS MADE UN-DUTIFUL; AND TO ATTIUS PROBATIOLUS, CERIALIUS CALISTIUS,

[Col. 0777B] HER HUSBAND AND HIS FATHER,

ALSO FOR HIMSELF,

WHILE STILL LIVING,

SAW TO THE ERECTION OF [THIS MONUMENT]

[Col. 0777C] AND DEDICATED IT UNDER THE ADZE.

For this woman—and likewise for his son Attius Probatiolus—Cerialius Calistius, her husband and the latter’s father, erected that monument, in which he mourns that his wife, through excessive devotion, became undutiful. Does he hint that she had passed over to the Christian sect, while embracing their approved morals and committing this one offense, that she had attached herself to those who were accustomed to be called impious? Or, since an epitaph was written for the son at the same time, was the son’s death caused by excessive devotion, which made her undutiful against her will?

[Col. 0777A] A dutiful parricide struck down; whereupon the people, moved by the atrocious extremity of their necessity and warned by the danger threatening their liberty, seized the Aventine Mount under arms. Nor did they cease defending their liberty with weapons [Note: [Col. 0777C] “Cease.” Three Lyons editions and the Gronovian collection have *destituit* (“abandoned”) instead of *destitit* (“ceased”).] until the conspiracy of the conspirators had also deprived them of their very offices.

In the third and fifth Olympiads after the hundredth [Note: [Col. 0777C] “Olympiad.” The second and third Florentine editions, the Utrecht edition, the Gronovian collection, and Perizonius have *Olympiadem*.], for almost an entire year earthquakes were so frequent and so severe throughout Italy that Rome was wearied by continual reports of the innumerable shocks and collapses of farms and towns [Note: [Col. 0777C] “Rome was wearied by reports.” *Nuntiis* is correctly found in the manuscripts; the common text mistakenly reads *intus* (“within”). Livy writes that in these times, during the consulship of Marcus Cornelius and Lucius Papirius, houses collapsed in the countryside because of frequent earth tremors; but those consuls belong, in other chronological systems, to the second year of the eighty-fourth Olympiad, and in Diodorus to the third year of the eighty-seventh. FABR.]. Then the drought was so prolonged [Note: [Col. 0777D] “So prolonged.” Three Lyons editions remove the first *ita* (“so”), as does the Gronovian collection.] and so burning [Note: [Col. 0777D] “So prolonged and burning a drought.” Livy writes that the year 327 was greatly afflicted by drought, during the consulship of Aulus Cornelius Cossus and Titus Quinctius Pennus. FABR.] that it denied the hope of the present and following year for producing the earth’s crops [Note: [Col. 0777D] “Denied.” Three Lyons editions, Perizonius, the Utrecht edition, the Gronovian collection, and the Augustan edition have *abnegarit* (“denied”), rather than *abnegaret* (“was denying”).].

At the same time [Note: [Col. 0777D] “At the same time.” My manuscript, with Perizonius, has *isdem* (“at the same [times”]); the first and fourth Lyons editions have *his denique* (“at these, indeed”). The third Lyons edition later has *auxiliatorum* (“of helpers”) for *auxiliorum* (“of auxiliaries”).], when the Fidenates, enemies of Rome, threatened the Roman citadels with a terrifying force supported by the largest auxiliaries [Note: [Col. 0777D] “When the Fidenates were enemies.” It is also read as “Fidenas, the enemy.” Eutropius, book I, under the year 315 from the founding of the City, says: “The Fidenates rebelled against the Romans. The Veientes aided them, as did Tolumnius, king of the Veientes. The Volsci joined them as well.” See Livy, book IV, for more. FABR.], Aemilius, dictator for the third time [Note: [Col. 0778C] “Aemilius, dictator for the third time.” Mamercus Aemilius Mamercinus fought most fiercely against the Fidenates for the first time in the year 316 and returned to the City in triumph. As dictator for the third time, in 327, when the Fidenates again rebelled, he captured and destroyed Fidenae. Livy, book IV. FABR.], barely dispelled and remedied the great mass of evil when Fidenae itself had scarcely been captured [Note: [Col. 0778C] “So great.” Two Lyons editions have *tantaque* (“and so great”).]: such was the struggle of evils and passions within the city that even domestic disasters, overwhelmed by wars from abroad, were obliterated [Note: [Col. 0778C] “Domestic disasters.” The common editions have *domesticae*; our reading, taken from ancient books, is confirmed by the antithesis (*antithesis*). FABR.], or, after the losses of war, when truces had brought relief, various plagues, growing hot in sky and earth, destroyed everything with unceasing violence.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the rule of Sicily and the events that took place there

[Col. 0778C]

[Note: [Col. 0778C] “Sicily from the beginning.” The matters explained by Orosius in this chapter are recounted more fully by Justin, following Trogus, in book IV. Thucydides writes at the beginning of book VI that the Cyclopes were among the most ancient inhabitants of part of Sicily. FABR.]

Sicily, from the beginning the homeland of the Cyclopes and after them always the nurse of tyrants, was also often held captive by slaves, of whom the first fed upon human flesh, those in the middle upon tortures, and the last upon deaths; except insofar as it was held by foreigners either as booty or as a prize. To put the matter as briefly as possible, it knows no respite from miseries except now; indeed, to make the differences between the periods more evident: just as previously, among all lands, it alone always endured either internal or external disturbances, so now, among all lands, it alone never suffers them [Note: [Col. 0778D] “Never.” Some old editions and certain manuscripts add *patitur* (“suffers”), but this is contrary to the better manuscripts.].

For even—to say nothing of the duration either of that calamity by which it was oppressed or, conversely, of this peace which it enjoys—Etna itself, which then seethed with frequent eruptions amid the destruction of cities and fields, now merely smokes harmlessly, as a sign confirming the events of the past.

Therefore, for the moment passing over the tyrants, whose avenger soon became his successor [Note: [Col. 0778D] “Who became his successor as avenger.” That is, the man who overthrew the tyrant himself seized the tyranny. Thus the tyrant was killed, but the homeland was not liberated. Justin speaks similarly when discussing the tyrants of Heraclea, book XVI, chapter 5. On the tyrants of Sicily, see also book IV, chapter 2: “Cocalus seized the kingdom of the island; after him the individual cities passed under the rule of tyrants, although no land was more fertile.”], meanwhile—that is, in the year 335 from the founding of the City—when the Rhegines were suffering from dissension near Sicily, and the state, divided by disagreement into two factions [Note: [Col. 0778D] “Dissension.” Perizonius has “division”; the third Lyons edition and the Gronovian collection have “secession”; the third Florentine edition has “secessions.”], one faction summoned veterans from Himera, a city of Sicily, to its aid.

Those men, after first driving from the city the very people against whom they had been summoned, and then soon slaughtering even those for whose assistance they had come, occupied the city together with the wives and children of the allies, daring an act comparable with no tyrant [Note: [Col. 0779B] “Comparable with no tyrant.” Orosius took this from Justin, where some have improperly tried to alter the reading. The reading is confirmed by all the editions and by all the manuscripts of Orosius except the third Lyons edition, which has “of tyrants.”].

Indeed, it would have been preferable for the Rhegines to endure anything whatever [Note: [Col. 0779B] “To endure anything whatever.” The reading is found in the Cologne manuscript. Others have “anything.” Varro uses the elegant and ancient form *quotquot annis* and *quotquot kalendis* for *quotannis* and *quot kalendis*. The first and third Lyons editions, together with the Gronovian collection, read: “whatever right there might be that could be tolerated if war were added.” For whether they had served the victors by the right of captivity, or had been forced into exile after losing their homeland, they would nevertheless not have been slaughtered between their altars and ancestral hearths, leaving their homeland with wives and children as booty for the most cruel tyrants. Justin, book IV, chapter 3. The three Florentine editions, two Lyons editions together with my manuscript and Perizonius, print *quidquid vis* (“anything whatever”), which Lautius preferred on the authority of the Cologne manuscript.], than voluntarily to invite those to whom, themselves exiles, they would leave their homeland, wives, children, and household gods as booty [Note: [Col. 0779C] “So that they would voluntarily invite them.” Perizonius has *quod ultro* (“which voluntarily”).].

The Catanaeans too, when they were suffering the Syracusans as a grievous and hostile presence, requested aid from the Athenians. But the Athenians sent a fleet to Sicily, equipped more for their own purposes than for those of their allies, since they were trying both to extend their own dominion and fearing that the recently equipped Syracusan fleet might advance to the Lacedaemonians. And since the Athenians who had been sent had begun successfully, after defeating the enemy [Note: [Col. 0779C] “After defeating the enemy.” Three Lyons manuscripts—the first, third, and fourth—together with the Gronovian collection remarkably transpose the words: “They brought larger forces and a stronger army back to Sicily under the commanders Laches and Cariades, after defeating the enemy, and had begun successfully.” I have thought it necessary to note this, so that it may be clear that this reading was propagated in four manuscripts from a single source.], they brought larger forces and a stronger army back to Sicily under the commanders Laches and Charoeades [Note: [Col. 0779C] “Laches and Charoeades as commanders.” These commanders were sent to Sicily at the end of the summer of the fifth year of the Peloponnesian War, according to Thucydides, book III. In Dio, book XII, *Chabrias* is mistakenly given instead of Charoeades. FABR. The first Florentine edition has *Thariades*; the first, third, and fourth Lyons editions and Perizonius, together with the Utrecht edition, have *Cariades*; the second Lyons edition has *Chariodes*; my manuscript has *Chunades*.].

But the Catanaeans, moved by weariness of war, made a treaty with the Syracusans and rejected the Athenian assistance. Afterwards [Note: [Col. 0779D] “Afterwards.” The first and third Lyons editions have *post haec autem* (“after these things, however”).], however, when the Syracusans violated the conditions of peace in their desire for domination, they again sent envoys to Athens. These men, filthy with unkempt hair and beard, dressed in mourning garments [Note: [Col. 0779D] “Dressed in mourning garments.” The word *pannis* (“rags” or “cloths”), which is commonly added, is not found in the old book. FABR. Another manuscript reads “dressed in mourning rags”; the addition is not inappropriate. Terence has *pannis annisque obsitus*, “covered with rags and years.” Apart from the Venetian editions, all editions preceding those of Fabricius, except the Augustan, include *pannis*. I think it was inserted by those who thought something was missing, as *vestibus* (“clothing”) is similarly found in the second Florentine edition; but the Lombard manuscript, with all the others, does not recognize it. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XI.134:

“Rise, come, shed tears, and put on mourning; do not send me,
Unwept, beneath the hollow Tartarus.”

Seneca, *Hercules Furens* 626:

“Whence, father, comes this squalor,
And your wife dressed in mourning?”], begged for pity and aid both in speech and appearance.

Accordingly, a great fleet was equipped under the commanders Nicias and Lamachus [Note: [Col. 0780C] “Under the commanders Nicias and Lamachus.” The third commander was Alcibiades, but not long after reaching Sicily he was recalled home and went into exile. Thucydides, book VI; Diodorus, book XIII; Plutarch, *Alcibiades* and *Nicias*. A fuller account must be sought there. FABR.]. Sicily was attacked again with such great forces that even those who had requested their assistance feared their own allies [Note: [Col. 0780C] “So that they feared their own support.” Justin, book IV, chapter 4: “Sicily was attacked with such great forces that they were themselves a terror to those to whose aid they were being sent.”].

The Athenians immediately fought two infantry battles with favorable results; they crushed the enemy in the city and surrounded them, enclosed by the fleet stationed before them, both on land and sea [Note: [Col. 0780C] “Having crushed them.” The common editions, except the Augustan, have *confertosque* (“crowded together”), but the Lombard manuscript and all the manuscripts unanimously have *confectosque* or *confectos* (“crushed”). This expression is familiar to Orosius and must certainly be restored here. The Athenians had crushed the Syracusans in various battles and, had the Lacedaemonians not arrived, would have driven them into complete desperation, since they no longer dared leave the city. FABR.].

But the Syracusans, their affairs broken and exhausted, requested aid from the Lacedaemonians. From them Gylippus was soon sent—alone, indeed, but bearing within himself the equivalent of every defense. When he arrived and learned that the condition of the war was already declining, he gathered auxiliary forces partly in Greece and partly in Sicily and occupied places advantageous for war. Then, defeated in two battles but not intimidated, in the third engagement he killed Lamachus, put the enemy to flight, and freed his allies from the siege.

Thus [Note: [Col. 0780D] “Hence the Athenians.” The Augustan edition has *hic Athenienses* (“here the Athenians”).] the Athenians, defeated in a land battle, tried the possibilities of the sea and prepared to engage in a naval contest. When Gylippus learned this, he summoned a fleet equipped by the Lacedaemonians. The Athenians likewise sent Demosthenes and Eurymedon to replace their lost commander, with a reinforcement of troops [Note: [Col. 0780D] “Demosthenes and Eurymedon.” Greek: “Demosthenes, son of Alcisthēnes, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles.” Thucydides, book VII. FABR.].

The Peloponnesians too, with the agreement and decree of many cities, sent enormous reinforcements to the Syracusans [Note: [Col. 0780D] “Also.” The third Lyons edition has “also then.”]. Thus, under the appearance of an allied war, they carried out domestic disturbances, and, as though the contest had been transferred from Greece to Sicily by common agreement, the struggle was waged with the utmost strength on both sides [Note: [Col. 0780D] Some manuscripts and the Augustan edition read: “Thus, in order that under the appearance of an allied war they might carry out domestic disturbances, and as though the contest had been transferred from Greece to Sicily by common agreement, so …”].

The Athenians were therefore defeated in the first engagement [Note: [Col. 0780D] “Their camp also.” The fourth Lyons edition has *castraque* (“and their camp”).], and lost their camp together with all their money, public or private, and with the entire equipment of their long expedition. Their resources broken and reduced to straits, Demosthenes advised them that, while their affairs were not yet completely ruined [Note: [Col. 0781B] “While not yet wholly.” I have restored this reading, following the Lombard manuscript and the third Florentine edition, and confirmed by my manuscript, which additionally prefixes *ut* (“that”). The Utrecht edition has *dum jam nondum*; the second Florentine, *cum nondum omnino*; the common editions, *dum nodum omnino*.], however afflicted they might appear, they should return home and withdraw from Sicily [Note: [Col. 0781B] “However.” Older editions, except the Augustan, have *quantumlibet* (“however much”), as do several manuscripts; but the former expression is often used with the meaning of the latter.].

Nicias, however, made more desperate from the beginning by shame at the badly conducted enterprise, insisted on remaining [Note: [Col. 0781B] “To remain.” This is the reading of all the manuscripts, as well as the Augustan edition; the remaining common editions have *manere* (“to stay”).]. They renewed the naval engagement, and soon, through ignorance, the Syracusans were drawn into a confined part of the sea and surrounded by the enemy’s ambushes. The commander Eurymedon was the first to be killed [Note: [Col. 0781B] “The commander Eurymedon was first killed.” We have written this from the Augustinian manuscript. The others do not differ from the printed editions; in my manuscript of Justin, however, the name Eurylochus is also found instead of Eurymedon. It is known from Thucydides, book VII, Diodorus XIII, and Plutarch’s *Nicias* that Eurymedon, who commanded the right wing, was cut off from his own men and killed when he tried to surround the enemy. FABR.].

Eleven ships were burned [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Eleven ships were burned.” This is consistently found in all the books of Orosius; but in Justin, from whom this account is taken, we read: “Thirty ships, which he had commanded, were burned.” Thucydides and Diodorus mention that the enemy carried out the burning, but say nothing about the number of ships destroyed by the flames. FABR.].

Demosthenes and Nicias dismissed the fleet, as though they would escape more safely by a land expedition. Gylippus first attacked their remaining ships, numbering one hundred and thirty [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Their remaining ships, one hundred and thirty.” The same number is found in Justin. Thucydides writes that about sixty ships remained to the Athenians; Dio says that fifty remained. FABR.]. Then he began pursuing the fugitives themselves and captured and killed very many [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Very many.” The second Lyons edition has *plurimos* (“many”).].

Demosthenes avoided the disgrace of slavery by voluntary death [Note: [Col. 0781D] “Avoids.” The second and third Florentine editions have *declinavit* (“avoided”).]. [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Demosthenes [avoided] disgrace.” Apart from Justin, others say nothing about this. Plutarch writes only this in his *Nicias*: “Demosthenes himself drew his sword and struck himself, but did not die, for the enemy suddenly surrounded and captured him.” Plutarch also writes there that Timaeus gave an account of the deaths of Demosthenes and Nicias differing from Thucydides and Philistus. FABR.] Nicias, however, adds the disgrace of captivity to an unworthy and shameful life [Note: [Col. 0781D] “Nicias, however.” Two Lyons editions have *Nicias autem*.] [Note: [Col. 0781D] “Adds.” The Utrecht edition has *cumulat* (“piles up”). Pausanias, book I, p. 74, contains a detail concerning Nicias and Demosthenes, and their memory among posterity, not found elsewhere: after recounting the columns erected in honor of Athenians who had died fighting abroad, he adds: “The generals are inscribed, except Nicias, and the Plataean soldiers together with the citizens. Nicias was omitted for the following reason; and I write nothing different from Philistus, who said that Demosthenes made terms for the others, except himself, and, when he was captured, attempted to kill himself; but that Nicias’ surrender was voluntary. For these reasons Nicias was not inscribed on the column, having been judged a voluntary captive and not a man fit for war.”].

128

## CHAPTER XV. The Athenians are attacked in the war against the Lacedaemonians, with Alcibiades encouraging them and avenging his own exile

[Col. 0782A]

[Note: [Col. 0782C] “The Athenians, therefore.” Besides Justin, the events narrated by Orosius in this chapter are found in Thucydides, book VIII; Diodorus, book XIII; and Plutarch, *Alcibiades*. FABR.]

The Athenians, after struggling for two years in Sicily—not without inflicting losses upon the Lacedaemonians—were surrounded by other domestic evils. Alcibiades, previously appointed commander against Syracuse, was soon detained for trial on account of a certain accusation; then, going voluntarily into exile, he betook himself to Lacedaemon [Note: [Col. 0782C] “Lacedaemon.” Orosius wrote *Lacedaemona*, not *Lacedaemonem* as the common editions have; this is clear from Justin, whom he followed, and from the manuscripts, which have *Lacedaemona*, *Lacedaemoniam*, or finally, as required, *Lacedaemona*.]. He urged the Spartans to press the Athenians, now in confusion, with a renewed war, and not to grant them even a breathing-space before they were crushed. All Greece supported this undertaking as though, for the extinguishing of a common conflagration, resources were being gathered for the public good.

Darius too, king of the Persians [Note: [Col. 0782D] “Darius, king of the Persians.” He was the sixth king of Persia and succeeded Artaxerxes, the son of Xerxes. FABR.], remembering his father’s and grandfather’s hatred of this city, through Tissaphernes, governor of Lydia [Note: [Col. 0782D] “Tissaphernes, governor of Lydia.” Greek: “Tissaphernes was general under King Darius, son of Artaxerxes.” Tissaphernes was governor of the coastal region under Darius, son of Artaxerxes. Thucydides. FABR.], made a treaty with the Lacedaemonians and promised them the expenses of the war and military forces.

It is astonishing to say that the Athenians then possessed such great resources that, although against them—that is, against a single city—the forces of Greece, Asia, and the entire East had been brought to bear [Note: [Col. 0782D] “Against a single city.” I have altered the faulty punctuation found in all the printed editions. It had read: “that is, against a single city of Greece, an attack had been made with the forces of Asia and the whole East.” The present punctuation is more coherent. Orosius amplifies what Justin wrote in book V, chapter 2: “When the forces of the entire East were brought together to crush a single city.” He joins Asia and Greece, evidently because he had just said, “All Greece supported this undertaking.”], they seemed to have been exhausted more by fighting often and never yielding than to have been defeated [Note: [Col. 0783B] “To have been.” This is absent from the first Lyons edition and the Gronovian collection; my manuscript prefers *esse* (“to be”). The fourth Lyons edition soon adds *sed* (“but”), which should be deleted.].

For at the outset Alcibiades compelled all the allies to defect from the Athenians to the Lacedaemonians. But, attacked by the latter as well through envy and ambushes [Note: [Col. 0783B] “Attacked.” Some editions have *impetitus* (“assailed”); the second Lyons edition and the Utrecht edition have *petitus* (“sought”). Soon, *effugit* (“escaped”) is found instead of *aufugit* (“fled”) in the fourth Lyons edition.], he fled and withdrew to Tissaphernes in Media [Note: [Col. 0783C] “He withdrew to Tissaphernes in Media.” Thucydides: “In fear, he withdrew secretly to Tissaphernes.” Plutarch: “Giving himself to Tissaphernes, the king’s satrap, for security, he immediately became his chief and most influential associate.” FABR.].

Having immediately become more intimate with him through his adaptable character and persuasive eloquence [Note: [Col. 0783C] “And because of his persuasive eloquence.” Perizonius’ manuscript deletes *apti* (“apt”). The first Florentine, or Lombard, manuscript has *et aptii*; the second has *et apud eloquii*, but after *apud* was deleted, *ob* (“because of”) was written above it. I suspect that the reading should be *et ob eloquii gratiam* or *et ab eloquii gratia* (“and because of the power of his eloquence”).], he persuaded him not to aid the Lacedaemonians with such lavish resources [Note: [Col. 0783C] “Aid.” Some old editions have *adjuvaret* (“he should aid”), or *jubet* (“he orders”). The first, second, and third Lyons manuscripts, together with the Utrecht and Gronovian collections, have *adiret, jubet*; from the double writing, *juvet* (“he should aid”) arose. The ancient Augustan edition has *juvet*, as do three Florentine manuscripts and Justin, who reads: “nor should the Lacedaemonians be aided too zealously with resources.” The latter reading should be retained.], but rather to become the arbiter and spectator of this conflict, reserving the intact forces of Lydia for use against the victor [Note: [Col. 0783D] “To be reserved.” The Utrecht edition has *servandas* (“to be preserved”).].

Accordingly, Tissaphernes ordered part of the fleet, with a considerable force, to be brought to Lacedaemon, so that the Lacedaemonians might neither, relying on an abundance of support, fight under another’s danger, nor, being wholly abandoned, give up the contest they had undertaken [Note: [Col. 0783D] “Support.” Orosius favors this word in the sense in which the better Latin authors rejected it. He uses it for “auxiliaries,” as above in chapter XIV: “So that even those who had requested their support feared it.”].

130

## CHAPTER XVI. The Athenians’ severe battles against the Lacedaemonians, and the dreadful disasters and slaughter suffered on both sides

[Col. 0783B]

Among the Athenians, while domestic discord had long been raging, when danger threatened, supreme authority was transferred, by the will of the people, to the senate [Note: [Col. 0783D] “Supreme authority is transferred to the senate.” Thucydides, Diodorus, and Plutarch, in the passages cited, give a detailed account of how supreme authority was transferred to a senate of four hundred men, and likewise of Alcibiades’ return. FABR.], since leisure nourishes discord [Note: [Col. 0783D] “Leisure.” Three Lyons editions have *odio* (“hatred”), incorrectly.]. But when necessity bore down upon them, after private interests and hatreds had been set aside, they took counsel for the common good [Note: [Col. 0783D] “But when necessity.” Three Lyons editions together with the Gronovian collection omit *at* (“but”) and read: “After private interests had been set aside …”].

Yet this very arrangement, because of the pride ingrained in the people and their tyrannical passions [Note: [Col. 0784B] “Ingrained.” The first Lyons edition writes *ingenitam* (“inborn”) above the text, which has *insitam* (“implanted”).], would have been ruinous. At last Alcibiades, an exile, was recalled by the army and appointed commander of the fleet [Note: [Col. 0784B] “Appointed commander of the fleet.” Three Lyons editions together with the Gronovian collection have “appointed commander for the fleet.”].

When this became known, the leading men first tried to betray the city to the Spartans [Note: [Col. 0784B] “First.” This word is absent from my manuscript.]; then, when they had considered the plan in vain [Note: [Col. 0784B] “Had considered.” The Augustan edition has *agitassent* (“had pursued”).], they voluntarily went into exile.

Accordingly, Alcibiades, with his homeland liberated, directed the fleet against the enemy. After battle had been joined, the Athenians won the victory [Note: [Col. 0784C] “After battle had been joined.” Two victories are described: one naval and one on land, which the Athenians won over the Spartans at Cyzicus, killing their commander Mindarus. Xenophon, book I of *The Affairs of Greece*; Diodorus, book XIII; Plutarch, *Alcibiades*. FABR.].

But the greater part of the Spartan army was killed, nearly all the commanders were slain [Note: [Col. 0784C] “Nearly all.” The Utrecht edition does not recognize the first word.], and eighty ships were captured, besides those that perished by burning or sinking in the engagement [Note: [Col. 0784C] “Perished.” The third Lyons edition and the Gronovian collection have *perierant* (“had perished”). Soon, Perizonius has *in terram* (“onto land”) instead of *in terra* (“on land”), as the Augustan edition later has *in Sicilia* (“in Sicily”) instead of *in Siciliam* (“to Sicily”).]. The war was again transferred to land, and went no better for the Spartans. Broken by these events, the Lacedaemonians sought peace [Note: [Col. 0784C] “The Lacedaemonians sought peace.” Endius was the chief of the embassy sent to Athens concerning peace; at Athens, Cleophon was chiefly responsible for obstructing it. See Diodorus. FABR.], but could not obtain it.

Moreover, the Syracusan forces were recalled to Sicily when the Carthaginian war was reported to be pressing [Note: [Col. 0784C] “The Syracusan forces.” After the Athenians’ defeat in Sicily, the Aegestans, allies of the Athenians, being hard pressed by the Selinuntines and Syracusans, requested aid from the Carthaginians. They sent them a garrison under Hannibal, son of Gisco; therefore the Syracusans recalled home their own men whom they had sent to aid the Lacedaemonians against the Athenians. Xenophon and Diodorus. FABR.].

For this reason Alcibiades, with his victorious fleet, ranged throughout Asia, seizing and laying everything waste with wars, fires, and slaughter [Note: [Col. 0784D] “And with slaughter.” This is found in the manuscripts; the common editions have merely “slaughter.” Some manuscripts soon add *urbesque* (“and cities”), and most manuscripts thereafter have *recepitque* (“and recovered”).]. He captured and recovered very many cities that had defected from the alliance some time before.

Thus Alcibiades, having become a man of great renown, entered Athens amid the admiration and joy of everyone. Soon afterwards he increased his forces and advanced the army and fleet rapidly [Note: [Col. 0784D] “He advances the army and fleet *numero*.” Here *numero* is an adverb meaning “rapidly”; or, at any rate, a word specifying the number of the fleet may be missing.]. Then he again made for Asia.

The Lacedaemonians appointed Lysander commander of the fleet and of the war. Cyrus too, son of Darius [Note: [Col. 0784D] “Cyrus, son of Darius.” The common text has the disgraceful error “Cyrus, brother of Darius.” FABR.], placed in charge of Ionia and Lydia in the place of Tissaphernes, strengthened them with great resources and auxiliaries.

Lysander therefore, by a sudden attack, overwhelmed Alcibiades’ army, intent on plunder and consequently scattered and wandering everywhere. Without any battle he defeated it and slaughtered the fugitives [Note: [Col. 0784D] “Lysander and Alcibiades.” This defeat occurred in Alcibiades’ absence, through the rashness of Antiochus, whom he had placed in command of the fleet. Xenophon, book I; Diodorus XIII; Plutarch, *Alcibiades* and *Lysander*; Pausanias, book III. FABR.].

The Athenians suffered a great disaster and a wound much more grievous than the one they had inflicted shortly before [Note: [Col. 0785C] “Much more grievous.” This must certainly be written so on the evidence of the manuscripts, which agree almost unanimously. The common editions have *magno atrocius* (“more grievous than a great one”), except the Augustan, which agrees with the manuscripts.]. When this became known, the Athenians supposed that Alcibiades had arranged to avenge his ancient grief over his exile by this crime of treachery [Note: [Col. 0785C] “Ancient.” The first Lyons edition has *antiqui* (“of the ancient [grief]”).]; and therefore appointed Conon in his place [Note: [Col. 0785C] “In his place.” Some editions have *ideo in locum ejus* (“therefore in his place”); two Lyons manuscripts together with the Gronovian collection have *in loco ejus* (“in his position”).]. They entrusted to him the remaining force and supreme command of the war. Wishing at least to replenish the troops exhausted in number, he enrolled old men and boys and enlisted an army [Note: [Col. 0785C] “Enlisted.” This is the manuscript reading; the common text has *conscribit* (“enlists”).].

But such a force brought no delay to the war, since victory is usually achieved by strength, not by numbers. Accordingly, the unwarlike force was immediately either captured or killed, and so great a slaughter of the slain was made in that battle [Note: [Col. 0785C] “In that battle.” Three Lyons editions together with the Gronovian collection and the Augustan edition have “in the battle.”] that it seemed not only the kingdom but even the name of the Athenians had been destroyed.

But when their affairs were desperate, they decided to give the city to foreigners [Note: [Col. 0785D] “They decided to give the city to foreigners.” That is, to grant citizenship to foreigners. Diodorus: “They made the resident aliens citizens, and those of the other foreigners who wished to join the struggle.” FABR.], so that those who shortly before had ruled throughout Asia might now preserve at least their walls and liberty from this rabble [Note: [Col. 0785D] “Rabble.” Three Lyons editions together with the Gronovian collection have “heap” instead.]. Although even by their own judgment they were not sufficient to protect these things, despite the walls placed before them, they nevertheless prepared again to engage in a naval battle.

Fury devoid of counsel mistakes grief for courage; and as much as anger contemplates, so much audacity promises. Accordingly, with some captured and others killed, nothing at all remained even of the survivors.

Only the commander Conon, surviving both the war and his people, fearing the cruelty of his fellow citizens, withdrew to Evagoras, king of Cyprus [Note: [Col. 0785D] “He withdrew to Evagoras, king of Cyprus.” Others had noticed the error in this passage, which could easily be corrected from Justin. Xenophon, book II: “Conon sailed away with eight ships to Evagoras in Cyprus.” Isocrates, in the *Evagoras*: “Who does not know Conon, that when his city had suffered misfortune he went to Evagoras?” FABR. The text had read absurdly: “He withdrew to Cyrus, the king.” Evagoras—or Evacinas—was instead a Lacedaemonian commander, and so forth.].

But the Lacedaemonian commander, after taking away all their cities, left the Athenians nothing except an empty city—and not even that for long, for later he surrounded the city itself with a siege.

Hunger, desolation, and disease oppressed those under siege [Note: [Col. 0785D] “Oppressed.” Several manuscripts have *agebat* (“drove” or “tormented”).]. And when, after every horror of misery [Note: [Col. 0786C] “Every.” The first Lyons edition has *omnium* (“of all”).]—which it is dreadful even to recount [Note: [Col. 0786C] “It is dreadful.” The old editions, except the Augustan, have *horrori* or *horror est*; thereafter they read “nothing of former hope.”]—nothing appeared to offer hope except death, they sought peace.

133

## CHAPTER XVII. Peace is granted to the Athenians under definite laws and conditions, and thirty rulers are appointed; when they exercised tyranny, they were expelled through the efforts of Thrasybulus
A great debate therefore arose among the Spartans and their allies, since very many declared that the most troublesome city should be razed to the ground, and that its most hostile people should be abolished together with its very name. [Note: [Col. 0786C] “Since very many”: some old editions have “and since very many.”] The Spartans refused, [Note: [Col. 0786C] “They”: absent from the Gronovian Collection and the third Leiden edition.] [Note: [Col. 0786C] “Spartans refused”: Justin has this wording; Xenophon, Book II, has: “But the Lacedaemonians said that they would not enslave a Greek city which had rendered the greatest services to Greece when the greatest dangers had befallen it” (for this is how it must be read from the old manuscripts, not “which had come into being,” as it is printed). FABRICIUS.] saying that they would not permit one of the two eyes of Greece to be torn out. Moreover, they promised peace if the fortifications extending from the harbor of Piraeus into the city [Note: [Col. 0786C] “If the harbor of Piraeus”: Justin has, “If they should demolish the arms of the walls extending toward Piraeus,” where he calls the arms of the walls what the Greeks call μακρὰ σκέλη, μακρὰ τείχη, “the Long Legs,” “the Long Walls.” FABRICIUS.] were demolished [Note: [Col. 0786D] “Fortifications”: two Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have *munimenta*, “fortifications.” The Lombard manuscript intended the same, writing *monumenta*, with *u* written above the *i*. The Augustan edition has *ducentiaque*, “and extending”; several manuscripts have *verterentur*, “were turned,” in place of *everterentur*, “were demolished.” A third Florentine manuscript has *eruerentur*, “were pulled down.”] and that they should voluntarily surrender the remaining ships [Note: [Col. 0786D] “And that they should voluntarily surrender the remaining ships”: the third Leiden manuscript has “and that the remaining ships should be surrendered voluntarily.”]; and thereafter if they accepted thirty rulers chosen for themselves. [Note: [Col. 0786D] “Chosen”: Fabricius restored this from the manuscripts. It had previously been absent from the printed editions, except in the Augustan edition, which has *electos*, “elected.” A little later my manuscript has *constituunt*, “they appoint,” instead of *constituerunt*, “they appointed.”]

When they had accepted and submitted to this condition, the Lacedaemonians appointed Lysander to establish in the city the laws by which it was to obey. This was a notable year both for the capture of Athens and for the death of Darius, [Note: [Col. 0786D] “Darius, king of the Persians”: Darius died not much later, after peace had been made with the Athenians, having reigned nineteen years, according to Diodorus, Book XIII. Dionysius, however, as he himself writes, was not so much an exile as a man who came into the greatest danger of losing his tyranny. FABRICIUS. — The third Leiden manuscript and the Augustan edition delete the first of two occurrences of *et*, “and.”] king of the Persians, and the exile of Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily. Thus thirty rulers were appointed for the Athenians, and thirty tyrants arose. They first surrounded themselves with three thousand bodyguards, and soon also placed seven hundred soldiers from the victorious army around their sides. They began the future general slaughter by murdering Alcibiades. [Note: [Col. 0787B] “After Alcibiades had been murdered”: Trogus, whose account Orosius follows, seems to have written that Alcibiades was killed by the Thirty, because they—and especially Critias—persuaded Lysander, as we read in Plutarch, to arrange for Alcibiades to be killed by Pharnabazus. Plutarch and Diodorus, Book XIV, nevertheless report various causes of his death.]

As Alcibiades was fleeing, they shut him up in a room along the way, and he was burned alive. [Note: [Col. 0787B] “He was burned alive”: Plutarch writes that Alcibiades was discovered in a certain village of Phrygia by those to whom Pharnabazus had entrusted the killing. Since they did not dare enter his presence, they surrounded the house and set it on fire. Alcibiades wrapped his left hand in his cloak, drew his sword, and burst unharmed through the flames; after driving back his killers, he was overwhelmed from a distance by their weapons. But Ephorus, Book VII, as quoted by Diodorus, reports that, when the house was set alight, Alcibiades did attempt to break out, but died, impeded by the flames and missiles. FABRICIUS.] Once he had been killed, as though the avenger had been removed and they were secure, they drained the miserable remnants of the wretched city through massacres and plunder. They also butchered Theramenes, one of their own number, when they perceived that he disapproved of these actions, as an example and a warning to the rest. [Note: [Col. 0787C] “Theramenes also”: The celebrated death of Theramenes is described elegantly not only by Xenophon but also praised magnificently by Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. FABRICIUS.]

Accordingly, everyone fled in every direction from the city; but, by order of the Lacedaemonians, since hospitality was denied throughout Greece to the exiles, they all betook themselves to Argos and Thebes. [Note: [Col. 0787C] “By prohibition”: the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have *interdicto*, “by a prohibition,” rather than *interdictu*.] There they were so warmly supported by the duties of hospitality [Note: [Col. 0787C] “Were warmed”: the Venetian editions have the incorrect *foti sunt*, “were warmed,” on the authority of the manuscripts.] that they not only eased the pain of having lost their country, [Note: [Col. 0787C] “But also meditated the hope of recovering it”: the Cologne manuscript has this wording, whereas the editions improperly took over the word *recuperandi*, “of recovering.” In the Florentine Law and Digest manuscripts, *reciperare* is frequent, an old form used for *reparare*, “to restore,” just as *reciprocare* was used for *reprocare*; and Gellius has *reciperatores*. LAUT.] but also contemplated the hope of recovering it.

Among the exiles was Thrasybulus, an energetic man, distinguished among his people by the nobility of his family, who was the author of the resolve to venture something on behalf of his country. [Note: [Col. 0787C] “Thrasybulus, an energetic man”: Θρασύβουλος ὁ Τιριεὺς ὀνομαζόμενος, ὢν Ἀθηναῖος, “Thrasybulus, called the Tirian, being an Athenian,” Diodorus. FABRICIUS.]

Accordingly, the exiles, gathered from the Attic territory, seized the fortress of Phyle [Col. 0788A] [Note: [Col. 0787D] “The fortress of Phyle”: it is commonly and incorrectly printed *Phylenen*, as also in Isocrates, *On the Peace*, τῶν φυλακὴν καταλαβόντων, “of those who occupied the fortress.” In Dio, Book XLIV, οἱ τὴν φυλακὴν καταλαβόντες, “those who occupied the fortress,” occurs in place of Φυλὴν, “Phyle.” Xenophon has φυλὴν χωρίον καταλαμβάνει ἰσχυρὸν, “he occupies Phyle, a strong place.” Diodorus has κατελάβετο χωρίον τῆς Ἀττικῆς ὀνομαζόμενον Φυλὴν, ἦν δὲ τὸ φρούριον ὀχυρόν τε σφόδρα καὶ τῶν Ἀθηνῶν ἀπέχον σταδίους ἑκατόν, that is: “He occupied a fortress of Attica called Phyle; it was very strongly fortified and about one hundred stadia—approximately thirteen Roman miles—from Athens.” FABRICIUS. — From this arose the proverbial expression in Aristophanes’ *Plutus*, line 1147:

Μὴ μνησικακήσῃς, εἰ σὺ Φυλὴν κατέλαβες.

“Please do not remember the wrongs, although you have now occupied Phyle.”

Consult the Scholiast there. Leopardus long ago corrected Orosius’ passage in Gruter’s *Face Critica*, volume III, p. 400.]

[Col. 0788A] 135 and, assisted by the resources of many cities, gathered strength. [Note: [Col. 0788B] “Among whom Lysias also”: Several speeches of this excellent orator survive. Some years ago, with the aid of a manuscript, we published his most charming speech, the *Funeral Oration*, complete, and also produced a Latin version of it together with the *Defense against the Murder of Eratosthenes*. FABRICIUS.] Among those who helped them was Lysias, the Syracusan orator, who, as though coming to the aid of a city that was the common homeland of eloquence, sent five hundred soldiers with their pay. [Note: [Col. 0788B] “Five hundred soldiers”: Plutarch, in his *Life of Lysias*, states that he aided Thrasybulus with two thousand drachmas, two hundred shields, and three hundred soldiers hired at his own expense. FABRICIUS. — The Augustan edition has *mittit*, “sends,” in place of *misit*, “sent.”]

The battle was savage; but while these men fought for their own liberty and the others for foreign domination, the battle itself rendered judgment concerning their spirits and causes. [Note: [Col. 0788B] “For their own liberty”: This seems correctly opposed to what follows, “for foreign domination.” Yet the Lombard manuscript reads “for the liberty of their country,” and the Utrecht manuscript seems to intend the same; it has *pro patria propria libertate*. The earliest editions, Parisian and Venetian, and even that excellent edition issued at Augsburg, have *pro patria pro libertate*, “for their country, for liberty.” I believe the double reading in those editions reflects the manuscript wording, and that one should read either *pro patria et libertate*, “for country and liberty,” or *pro patria libertate*, “for the liberty of their country,” as the best manuscripts have it; Justin, Book V, chapter 9, also seems to confirm this: “Since on one side they fought with all their strength for their country, and on the other more securely for foreign domination.”] [Note: [Col. 0788C] “The battle itself also rendered judgment”: this passage must be restored exactly thus from the same editions and, additionally, my manuscript and the third Leiden manuscript. The common editions have *indicium*, “judgment.” Lucan imitates it in Book I, lines 126–28:

“Quis justius induit arma
Scire nefas: magno se judice quisque tuetur:
Victrix causa deis placuit, sed victa Catoni.”

“It is sinful to know who took up arms more justly: each side relies on a great judge in its own cause; the victorious cause pleased the gods, but the defeated one pleased Cato.” The earliest, Venetian, and Parisian editions have *refugerunt et ab armis*, “they fled back and from arms.”]

For the tyrants were defeated and fled back into the city, and they removed from the city guard all those Athenians whom they had previously selected for themselves as bodyguards, now suspecting them of treason. They even attempted to win Thrasybulus himself over by corruption. [Note: [Col. 0788D] “Thrasybulus himself”: Diodorus, Book XIV, had described this attempt. After the occupation of Piraeus, he writes that a great number of exiles flocked to Thrasybulus; then, in the books of Henricus Stephanus, follows *φανερὸς μὲν περὶ τινων αἰχμαλώτων διαλεγόμενος*, “openly negotiating concerning certain prisoners,” and so forth, where the words *ἦλθον δὲ καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν τριάκοντα τινες*, “and some also came from the Thirty,” or similar words, are absent. FABRICIUS.] When this hope had failed, they summoned reinforcements from Lacedaemon and again rushed into war. There two of the most savage of all the tyrants were killed. [Note: [Col. 0788D] “Two of the most savage”: namely Critias and Hippomachus, according to Xenophon and Justin. Diodorus mentions only Critias. FABRICIUS.]

Thrasybulus pursued the others, defeated and put to flight. When he realized that they were Athenians above all, [Note: [Col. 0788D] “He realized”: my manuscript, together with two Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection, has *intellexit*, “he realized,” rather than *intelligit*, “he realizes.”] he checked them with a shout, held them back with a speech, and bound them with entreaties. He placed before their eyes that the war had been undertaken against the Thirty Lords, not against wretched fellow citizens whom they wished either to flee from or to flee for refuge among. [Note: [Col. 0789B] “Whom they wished”: the third Leiden manuscript, the Gronovian Collection, and the Augustan edition have *velint*, “whom they may wish,” rather than *vellent*, “whom they wished.” The same manuscripts remove *eorum*, “of whom,” from the preceding text. A little later they also remove *esse*, “to be,” and write, with the second Leiden manuscript, *meminerint Athenienses*, “let them remember that they are Athenians.”]

Rather, all who remembered that they were Athenians ought to follow him as avengers of Athenian liberty. This exhortation [Note: [Col. 0789B] “Exhortation”: the old editions have *exhortatio*, “exhortation.” The third Leiden manuscript and the Gronovian Collection have *oratio*, “speech.”] had such power over them that they soon returned to the city and compelled the tyrants to withdraw from the citadel and migrate to Eleusis. [Note: [Col. 0789C] “To migrate to Eleusis”: some editions have *Eleusin* and *emigrare*, “to emigrate,” as well as *compellerent*, “they might compel.”]

After the Athenians had received their fellow citizens, who until then had been exiles, into the community of the city, the tyrants stirred themselves to war out of rivalry, since the liberty of others seemed to them a form of their own enslavement. [Note: [Col. 0789C] “After they received”: some editions have *exceperunt*, “received,” instead of *receperunt*.] Then, when battle had been announced, they met first as though for a conference, but were surrounded by treachery and slaughtered like victims of peace. [Note: [Col. 0789C] “Then, when battle had been announced”: the third Leiden manuscript and the Gronovian Collection have *inclita*, “renowned,” from which it is clear that this was drawn from the same source. The sense of Orosius’ words seems to be that the tyrants had announced to the Athenians the war, and the day and place of the battle. Justin, Book V, chapter 10: “They bring war upon the Athenians.”]

Thus, after they had been recalled into one body, and after the inexhaustible [Col. 0789B] tears of great joy, they renewed these first foundations [Note: [Col. 0789C] “Foundations”: the fourth Leiden manuscript and the Utrecht manuscript have *fundamenta*, “foundations,” as does the Augustan edition.] of recovered liberty, after proclaiming an oath that former disagreements and resentments should be consigned to perpetual oblivion and everlasting silence. Regarding this kind of agreement as though it were a new ordering of life and a new happiness in their condition, [Note: [Col. 0789C] “A new”: the Perizonian and Utrecht manuscripts have *novae*, “of a new,” rather than *novam*, “a new.”] they called it an amnesty, [Note: [Col. 0789C] “Amnesty”: ἀμνηστίαν, “amnesty.” Valerius Maximus, Book IV, chapter 1, concerning Thrasybulus: “He introduced a plebiscite that no mention should be made of past events.” This oblivion, “which the Athenians call ἀμνηστία, amnesty,” and so forth. Hence Plutarch, in *Civil Precepts*, calls that decree of the Athenians τὸ τῆς ἀμνηστίας ψήφισμα, “the decree of amnesty.” Marcus Tullius used this Greek word when, after the murder of Gaius Julius Caesar, he proposed that every memory of the civil discord should be erased by everlasting oblivion, *Philippic* I. Hence Velleius Paterculus, Book II: “That celebrated example of the Athenians’ decree, cited by Cicero, was approved by a decree of the Senate concerning the oblivion of past events.” Vopiscus, in *Aurelian*: “An amnesty of public offenses was also decreed under him, following the example of the Athenians,” a matter of which Tully also speaks in the *Philippics*. I discuss this at greater length because I see that some assert—as Muretus does in *Various Readings* II, chapter 15—that the word used by Cicero was not ἀμνηστίαν, “amnesty,” but μὴ μνησικακεῖν, “not to remember wrongs.” FABRICIUS. — Compare the passage of Aristophanes from *Plutus* above, p. 134, and Orosius, Book VII, chapter 6.] that is, the abolition of evils. This was the wisest measure of the Athenians, especially after such great lessons in misery, [Note: [Col. 0790B] “The wisest measure of the Athenians”: the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts, the Gronovian Collection, and some old editions have: “This was the wisest measure, and so forth.” A little later the Perizonian manuscript has *post tot*, “after so many,” instead of *post tanta*, “after such great.” After *provisio*, “measure,” the Utrecht manuscript and the Augustan edition add *esset*, “it was.”] if only human affairs might endure, with human agreement preserved, as they are ordered. [Note: [Col. 0790C] “As they are ordered”: apart from the Augustan edition, six or seven manuscripts write: “so that, as they are ordered, they might have strength.” These include the Utrecht, second, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, the Gronovian Collection, the Perizonian manuscript, and mine.]

But this same settlement [Note: [Col. 0790C] “Almost in the very words of the agreement”: rightly, the third and fourth Leiden editions and the Gronovian Collection, which print *inter pia beneplaciti verba*, “among the pious words of the agreement,” should not be followed.] was corrupted almost in the very words of the agreement, so that, scarcely two years having intervened, that Socrates, the most illustrious of philosophers, compelled by his sufferings, took his own life among them by poison. [Note: [Col. 0790C] “That Socrates”: Socrates, accused of impiety by Anytus and Meletus and condemned, drank poison in the first year of the ninety-fifth Olympiad. Laertius, Book II, and Diodorus, Book XIV. FABRICIUS.] Then, after scarcely forty years had passed—to say nothing of other matters—the same Athenians, having completely lost their liberty, served under Philip, king of the Macedonians. [Note: [Col. 0790C] “Served”: the Perizonian manuscript, the third Leiden manuscript, and the Augustan edition have *servierunt*, “served,” rather than *servierint*, “may have served.”]

Nevertheless, the Athenians, wisest of all and sufficiently instructed even by their own sufferings that the smallest things grow through concord and the greatest fall through discord, [Note: [Col. 0790C] “The smallest things grow through concord”: a Sallustian maxim from the *Jugurthine War*. FABRICIUS.] and that all things—whether good or even evil—that are done abroad are rooted in and arise from internal causes, [Note: [Col. 0790C] “And all things”: the Augustan edition omits the conjunction and shortly afterwards has *intrinsecus*, “from within,” in place of *internis*, “internal.”] wiped away their hatreds at home and restrained their wars abroad. They left to their descendants an example of their own ruin and a plan for their restoration: if, that is, because of the extreme fickleness of the human mind, what is resolved in times of distress were maintained in prosperity. [Note: [Col. 0790C] “Of their ruin”: this is the better reading, and that of nearly all the manuscripts. Some, with certain editions, have “of their ruin” in the feminine form *sua*. A little later the Augustan edition has “and concerning restoration.”]

## 138. CHAPTER XVIII

**The civil war between Artaxerxes and Cyrus, the sons of Darius, which ended in fratricide. The earthquake in Sicily, and the transformation of the island of Atalante.**

In approximately the same days, a civil war—indeed, more than civil—scarcely brought to an end except by fratricide, was being waged among the Persians.
