[Note: [Col. 0790D] “Indeed, more than civil”: Orosius intended to imitate the words with which Lucan opens his poem: “Wars more than civil across the Emathian plains.” Some old editions lack *immo*, “indeed.”] [Note: [Col. 0790D] “Civil war”: Xenophon, a participant and companion in this war, described the conflict between the two brothers Cyrus and Artaxerxes in seven books entitled Κύρου Ἀνάβασις, “The Expedition of Cyrus.” The learned Romulus Amasaeus translated them well into Latin. Diodorus, Book XIV, and Plutarch, in *Artaxerxes*, also discuss it. FABRICIUS.] For after King Darius had died, when Artaxerxes and Cyrus, his sons, disputed the kingdom, they eventually fought with great preparations, [Note: [Col. 0790D] “With great provincial forces”: the second occurrence of *magnis*, “great,” is absent from the Lombard manuscript.] amid great devastation of provinces and peoples. [Col. 0791A] The contest was waged on both sides. [Note: [Col. 0791B] “The contest was waged on both sides”: this is the reading of the Lombard and second Florentine manuscripts, three Leiden manuscripts, the Gronovian Collection, and the Utrecht manuscript. The common manuscript tradition, the first Leiden manuscript, and the third Florentine have *est utrimque certatum*, “the contest was waged on both sides.” If *est* is retained, it is better placed at the end of the sentence, as in my manuscript and the Augustan edition.]

In this conflict, when the two brothers, rushing against each other, had been brought face to face by the chance of battle, Artaxerxes was wounded first by his brother but escaped death through the speed of his horse. [Note: [Col. 0791C] “He escaped, rescued from death”: the Augustan edition has “he was rescued from death.”] Cyrus, however, soon overwhelmed by the royal cohort, brought the fighting to an end. Artaxerxes therefore, having gained both the spoils of his brother’s expedition and possession of the army, secured his power over the kingdom by fratricide. [Note: [Col. 0791C] “Secured”: the Lombard manuscript has *finivit*, “ended,” as though some preceding expression such as “he confirmed” or something similar had been present.]

Thus all Asia and Europe were being mingled in funerals and crimes, partly each within itself and partly with one another. [Note: [Col. 0791C] “Thus all”: the third and fourth Leiden editions and the Gronovian Collection have “And thus,” and several editions have “with one another” in place of “among themselves.”] Behold, in a very small space and with very few words, how many events concerning so many provinces, peoples, and cities I have not so much unfolded as entangled into a single mass of misery. [Col. 0791C] For who could relate in speech the disaster of that time, or equal its sorrows with tears? [Note: [Col. 0791C] “Who could relate the disaster”: a parody of Virgil from Book II of the *Aeneid*. FABRICIUS.]

Yet because these events, after the long passage of centuries, have faded away, they have become exercises for our intellects and amusements for our stories. [Note: [Col. 0791C] “Yet, etc.”: the Augustan edition has “But these very things which…”] [Note: [Col. 0791C] “Exercises for intellects”:  namely, material for elegant declamation. Juvenal, Satire 10, line 167: “So that you may please boys and become a declamation.”] Nevertheless, if anyone applies his mind more attentively, and mingles himself with those very causes and wars with the whole force of his mind, and then, as though stationed on a spectator’s tower, measures each period in its own qualities, I should readily say that he would judge that those events could have been so disastrously thrown into confusion only with God angry and turned away, [Note: [Col. 0791D] “With God turned away”: I think *aversante Deo*, “with God turning away,” should be restored, as in the third Leiden manuscript and the Gronovian Collection; my manuscript perhaps intended this when it wrote *adversato*, “with God opposed,” or Orosius may have written, as the Augustan edition has, *averso Deo*, “with God turned away.” Martial, concerning an unfortunate poet writing on defiled pages, Book VIII, epigram 56:

“Scribit in aversa Picens epigrammata charta:
Et dolet, averso quod facit illa deo.”

“Picens writes epigrams on the reverse of the page, and is sorry that he does this with the god turned away”—that is, with Apollo and the Muses angry. Ovid, *Amores* III.12.17:

“Aversis utinam tetigissem carmina Musis;
Phoebus et inceptum destituisset opus.”

“Would that I had touched my poems with the Muses turned away, and Phoebus had abandoned the work he had begun.”] and that these events could have been composed in this way only with God propitious and merciful. [Note: [Col. 0792B] “Could”: the Perizonian manuscript has *potuisse*, “could have,” rather than *posse*, “can.”]

After these events, in the same period, Sicily was shaken by a very violent earthquake and devastated, with enormous loss to its fields and farmsteads, while the fires of Mount Etna burst forth above it, together with hot ashes. [Note: [Col. 0792B] “After these events”: this earthquake occurred in the third year of the eighty-eighth Olympiad, the fifth year of the Peloponnesian War. Diodorus, Book XII, says: “It happened that earthquakes of such magnitude occurred in many parts of Greece that they destroyed certain coastal cities when the sea had overflowed them, and in Locris, where a peninsula had been formed, they broke the isthmus and made the island called Atalante.” That is: “At that time the earth moved in many parts of Greece so violently that the sea, pouring over them, overwhelmed certain coastal cities; and in Locris, where Atalante had been a town projecting into the sea and attached to the mainland, the force of the sea tore away the side of the land and turned it into an island.” FABRICIUS.] At that time, too, the city of Atalante, attached to Locris and joined to the mainland, was torn away by a sudden surge of the sea and left as an island in desolation. [Note: [Col. 0792C] “Torn away by a sudden surge of the sea”: the Perizonian and my manuscripts have *abscisa*, “cut away.” But the common reading *abscissa* should be retained, as is clear from the distinction made by learned men between *abscisus* and *abscissus*. Compare Duker’s notes on Florus, Book II, chapter 11, p. 227, and Oudendorp’s notes on Frontinus, p. 49.] The plague also attacked the pitiable remnant of the Athenians and ravaged it for a long time.

## 140. CHAPTER XIX

**The Romans’ dishonorable siege of Veii. The city captured and devastated by the Gauls. A comparison of that destruction with the present Gothic invasion.**

In the year 355 from the foundation of the City, the siege of Veii wore down the besiegers more than the besieged for ten continuous years. [Note: [Col. 0792C] “In the year from the foundation of the City, 355”: Cuspinianus believes this number contains an error. I, however, who think that Orosius was referring not to the time when the siege of Veii began but to the capture of the city, have refused to alter it against the testimony of the books. According to Sigonius, whose diligence in completing the *Fasti* we admire, the year of the capture of Veii was 357 from the foundation of Rome. On the siege and capture of Veii, see Livy, Book V. FABRICIUS.] For the Romans, often shattered by sudden sallies of the enemy, and, in addition, compelled to draw lots for winter campaigns, to spend the winter under hides, and finally to endure hunger and cold in the sight of the enemy, at last captured the city by tunnels and secret infiltration, without any worthy testimony to Roman courage. [Note: [Col. 0792D] “Draw lots”: my manuscript, together with the Perizonian manuscript and the Augustan edition, has *sortiri*, “to draw lots,” referring it to *coacti sunt*, “they were compelled.” The third Leiden edition and the Gronovian Collection have *postremoque*, “and finally.”] [Note: [Col. 0792D] “For ten continuous years”:  the third Leiden manuscript, the Gronovian Collection, and the Augustan edition have *continuatis*, “uninterrupted,” rather than *continuis*.] This victory, more useful than glorious, was followed first by the exile of the dictator Camillus, who had achieved it against the Veientes, [Note: [Col. 0792D] “A worthy testimony to Roman courage”: the Augustan edition has *dignae virtutis testimonio*, “a testimony to worthy courage.”] [Note: [Col. 0792D] “The exile of Camillus”:  Marcus Furius Camillus, prosecuted by Lucius Appuleius, tribune of the plebs, because the Veientine spoils had been unfairly distributed, went into exile in the fifth year after he had captured Veii. Livy and Plutarch, *Camillus*. FABRICIUS.] and thereafter by the invasion of the Gauls and the burning of the City.

If anyone can, let him compare some event of the present time with that disaster, although the injury of the present does not weigh equally against the story of the past evil. The Senonian Gauls, therefore, under the leadership of Brennus, with a very large and exceedingly strong army, while they were besieging the city of the Clusini, [Note: [Col. 0793B] “The city of the Clusini, which is now Tuscany”: here we have restored Orosius’ reading. It is more commonly known that this town was called Clusium and its inhabitants Clusini, so that no warning is needed. FABRICIUS. — My parchment manuscripts have *Clusium*, as do the Venetian editions, including the first, and the Parisian edition. Vincent of Beauvais, Book IV, chapter 81, has *Dusim*, “which is now called Tuscany.”] which is now called Tuscany, [Note: [Col. 0793C] “Which is now called Tuscany”: these words are absent from my manuscript. Older editions have *Dusia*; the Lombard manuscript has *Thuscia*; the second Florentine and other manuscripts have *Tuscia*.] saw the Roman ambassadors—who had then come to arrange peace between the two sides—fighting against them in battle. Moved by this indignation, they abandoned the siege of the town of Clusium and marched with all their strength toward Rome.

Fabius, the consul with an army, met them as they rushed forward, but did not stop them. [Note: [Col. 0793C] “Fabius, consul, with an army”: no Fabius was consul at this time; but in the year Rome was captured, three Fabii were military tribunes with consular power, according to Livy, Book V, Diodorus XIV, and Plutarch’s *Camillus*. The word *consul* was marked in the margin by an ignoramus and perhaps intruded into the text. It certainly stands out of place and disrupts the order of the words. Hence my manuscript reads “the consul with an army.”] Rather, that hostile assault, like a dry field of grain, cut down, flattened, and passed over him. [Note: [Col. 0793C] “Cut down, flattened, and passed over”: the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, have *succendit*, “set fire to,” and so forth. The Augustan edition has “set fire to, flattened, and passed over.” Since Orosius has mentioned a dry field of grain, this might seem a suitable reading. I nevertheless prefer the common reading, which Vincent of Beauvais also preserves, because of the words that follow, “flattened and passed over.”]

The river Allia bears witness to this defeat of Fabius, just as the Cremera bears witness to the defeat of the Fabii. [Note: [Col. 0793C] “It bears witness to this defeat of Fabius”: both disasters occurred on the same day, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of Sextilis; the day was subsequently called the Allia after the latter event. Livy, Book VI; Plutarch, *Camillus*; Tacitus, Book XVIII; Servius on the Seventh Book of the *Aeneid*. FABRICIUS.] For no one could easily recount a similar ruin of the Roman army, even if Rome had not additionally been set on fire.

The Gauls entered the undefended City, slaughtered the senators, who sat rigid in their homes as though they were statues, [Note: [Col. 0793D] “In their homes”: the manuscripts and some editions incorrectly have *aedibus*, “buildings,” rather than *sedibus*, “seats” or “residences.”] and, when the senators had been burned by the fire of their houses, buried them beneath the collapse of their own roofs. They shut up under siege in the citadel of Capitoline Hill all the remaining young men, who are said at that time to have numbered scarcely a thousand. [Note: [Col. 0793D] “Lying hidden”: my manuscript, the Perizonian manuscript, and the second Leiden manuscript have *latentem*, “lying hidden,” rather than *latitantem*, “lurking.”] There they wore down, subdued, and sold the wretched remnant through hunger, disease, despair, and terror. For they agreed upon a thousand pounds of gold as the price of their withdrawal—not because Rome had been of little renown among the Gauls, but because they had already so thoroughly worn it down that it could then be worth no more.

When the Gauls departed, there remained within the former circuit of the City an unsightly heap of shapeless ruins, and everywhere, amid the obstructed paths of those wandering about, an image of a voice answering among people who remained within their own enclosures unknown to others, so that the fearful ears of others were held suspended. [Note: [Col. 0793D] “And everywhere, among the obstructed…”: we have not found in the ancient manuscripts the reading which Gerard Bolsuinge wrote in the margin here, but we have faithfully transcribed what is read in them without variation. FABRICIUS. — In the margins of the Hittorp and Bolsuinge editions the following is added: “And while they wandered through the obstructed ruins, and those remaining within their own enclosures were unknown to the others, the voices of those lamenting held the frightened ears of the others suspended.”] Horror shook their minds; the silences themselves terrified them. [Col. 0794B] [Note: [Col. 0794B] “Horror…”: taken from Virgil’s account of the destruction of Troy, *Aeneid* II.755:

“Horror ubique animos simul ipsa silentia terrent.”

“Everywhere horror frightens their minds, and the very silences terrify them.” The first edition and the Venetian editions have *Horrore*, “with horror,” and *silentioque ipso terrebat*, “and the very silence terrified.”]

For the very scarcity of sound in the spacious places is itself a source of fear. [Note: [Col. 0794C] “The very scarcity of sound in spacious places”: this is how I found it written in the Augustan edition, and I believe the reading to be entirely correct. The scarcity of sound produces horror, but the horror is increased when, in broad and spacious places such as Rome, buildings lie flattened and the land stretches desolate, so that a vast silence prevails. The older printed editions, down to the Fabrician editions, have only “the very scarcity of sound.” Fabricius preferred, without adding any note, “the very scarcity in spacious places.” Although this reading is confirmed by three Florentine manuscripts, the first Leiden manuscript, and my and the Perizonian manuscripts, it is nevertheless in no way superior to the reading found in the ancient editions, three Leiden manuscripts, and the Gronovian Collection: “the very scarcity of sound.” For what does Orosius understand by “scarcity” in spacious places? If he means people, they are not mentioned in what precedes; therefore he means sound. I therefore embrace the reading of the Augustan manuscript, especially since it is further confirmed by the Utrecht manuscript.]

Hence they considered, approved, and attempted the idea of changing their residence, inhabiting another town, and being counted under another name. [Note: [Col. 0794C] “Hence they considered changing their residence”: he means the proposal to migrate to Veii, concerning which Livy speaks at the end of Book V.]

Behold the times by comparison with which the present is weighed, and at the memory of which one sighs; behold the events that inspire repentance for having chosen—or rather neglected—religion. [Note: [Col. 0794C] “For having chosen”: the sense is: “behold what those times were like, times which deserve that you should regret that the Christian religion, once publicly received under pious emperors, was in fact neglected for so long and received so late, and which should rather shame you for this.” The first edition has *rejecta*, “rejected”; the Augustan edition, *relicta*, “abandoned.”]

In truth, these two captivities are equal and may be compared with one another: that one, raging for six months, and this one, passing by in three days. [Note: [Col. 0794D] “In truth they are equal, etc.”: I think the text should read: “In truth they are equal, but let them be compared with one another,” and so forth. With a very small alteration, the meaning—which now stumbles—becomes clear and appropriate to the matter and the speech. He admits that, just as Rome was once captured by the Gauls, so it has now been captured by the Goths; but if the disasters are compared, the difference will be enormous, and so forth.] The Gauls, having extinguished the people and destroyed the City, pursuing even the name of Rome itself amid the final ashes, and the Goths, abandoning their determination to plunder, driving ignorant crowds toward places of refuge and safety—that is, holy places. [Note: [Col. 0795B] “The name itself”: old editions have *ipsius*, “of Rome itself,” contrary to the majority and better manuscripts.] There, scarcely any senator was found who had escaped even while absent; here, scarcely anyone is sought who may have perished while perhaps hiding. [Col. 0795B] I may rightly compare the number of those saved there with the number of those lost here. [Note: [Col. 0795B] “I may compare”: the Augustan edition has *comparavi*, “I compared.” The first edition has *potest comparari*, “it can be compared.” The third Leiden and Utrecht manuscripts have *comparari inter se possunt*, “they can be compared with one another.”]

Certainly, [Note: [Col. 0796A] “Certainly”: the second Florentine manuscript has *sane*, “indeed.”] what is reproached must be acknowledged: in this present disaster God has acted more severely, while human beings have acted less so, since, by carrying out Himself what they had not completed, He demonstrated why He had sent them. For it was beyond human power to set bronze beams on fire and overthrow the mass of great structures. By a stroke of lightning the Forum, together with its empty images—which, in their pitiable superstition, pretend to be either gods or men—was cast down. [Note: [Col. 0796A] “And these”: the third Leiden manuscript and the Gronovian Collection have *forumque*, “and the Forum,” perhaps because Orosius is playing on the word *forum*, here used for the marketplace.] And whatever of all these abominations the flame sent by the enemy had not reached, fire sent from heaven overthrew.

And since the material for speaking is abundant, and cannot in any way be brought to completion in this book, let this be the end of the present volume, so that in the following books we may pursue the rest. [Note: [Col. 0796B] “In the following”: the Utrecht manuscript has *sequentibus*, “in the following,” rather than *subsequentibus*.] [Note: [Col. 0796B] “Let us pursue”: the second and third Florentine manuscripts have *persequamur*, “let us pursue,” rather than *prosequamur*. The first has *subsequamur*, corrected by another hand to *persequamur*.]

# BOOK THREE

## PREFACE

[Col. 0795]

[Col. 0795B] 144

[Note: [Col. 0795C] *Et superiore*, etc. The manuscripts of Utrecht and Leiden 2 read *Superiore*, with the conjunction deleted. My manuscript and Perizonius, together with the first edition, read *ut superiore*. The third and fourth Leiden manuscripts read *Ex superiore*. The Paris editions and the Venetian editions read *Et in superiori*. But after I had testified to this, in the Groningen Collection it is repeated from chapter 18. A Virgilian imitation: “Who could explain the disaster of that time, who could recount the deaths, or match the griefs with tears?” I found the same in one of the Leiden manuscripts. For *conflictationibus*, the same manuscripts as the three Leiden copies have *conflictionibus*.]

I have already testified in the preceding book, and now I must necessarily repeat, in accordance with your instruction, that the past conflicts of the age cannot all be explained, nor explained in every respect as they occurred, since great and innumerable events have been written about at great length and by many authors; and although the writers did not have the same purposes, they nevertheless had the same events before them. For they unfold the wars, whereas we unfold the miseries of the wars.

[Note: [Col. 0795C] *Nec omnia nec per omnia*. This is the constant reading of the manuscripts, preserved from the ancient editions before the Fabrician editions only by Augustine’s edition; the others have: “and that I can explain neither all the things that happened nor them as they happened.”]

[Col. 0795C] Moreover, from this very abundance of which I complain, difficulty arises for me, and a more intricate anxiety confines me. For if I omit anything in the interest of brevity, it will be thought either that I now lacked it or that it was not present at that earlier time. But if, while striving to indicate everything without expressing everything, I compress it into concise brevity, I shall make it obscure; and so, for most people, the statements will be such that they will not even seem to have been stated.

[Note: [Col. 0795D] *Erunt dicta*. The manuscripts here too, certainly the best ones, retain the reading I have adopted: namely, the Longobard manuscript together with the two other Florentine manuscripts, those of Meus and Perizonius. All editions have *dubia* (“doubtful”), but most editors note *dicta* in the margin from the manuscripts.]

This is especially so because, in contrast, we are concerned to commend the force of events, not their outward appearance. Brevity, however, and obscurity—or rather, since brevity is always obscure—even though it offers an image of understanding, nevertheless removes the power of comprehension.

[Note: [Col. 0795D] *Aufert tamen*. The third Leiden manuscript and the Groningen Collection read *haud refert tamen* (“yet it does not matter”). The same manuscript has *noscendi* instead of *cognoscendi* above.]

[Col. 0796C] But I, knowing that both must be avoided, shall act so that, however either of the two may be moderated, neither much will appear to have been omitted nor much to have been compressed.

[Note: [Col. 0795D] *Cum utrumque vitandum sciam*, etc. This sentence is found in various forms in both the newer and older editions. [Col. 0796C] The first edition, Augustine’s edition, and the Paris edition expressed it thus: “since I know that both must be avoided, I shall do both, so that, in whatever way one or the other is moderated, neither much will seem to have been omitted nor much compressed” (Augustine’s edition has *multum*). The Venetian editions read: “but I, since I know that both must be avoided, shall do both,” etc. I also found this reading in Hittorp and Bolsuing. Yet those editions insert *ibi* (“there”), whether before *nec multa* or after it. Fabricius and Scottus did the same, though instead of *utrimque* they print *utrobique*. Although I have found *utrumque* twice in the manuscripts, I think it must certainly be removed in one of the two places. For since in some copies the reading was *cum vitandum sciam utrumque, faciam*, etc., while in others it was *cum utrumque vitandum sciam, faciam*, etc., the scribes seem, according to their usual practice, to have retained *utrumque*. I have ordered it, as a tiresome intrusion, to be expelled, together with *si* before *nec multa*, where it was wrongly inserted.]

[Note: [Col. 0796D] *Alterutra*. The Utrecht manuscript has *utraque*. Three Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection have *aliter utraque*.]

[Note: [Col. 0796D] *Nec multa*. My manuscript has *ut nec multum* (“so that not much…”). One of the Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen Collection have *non haec multum* (“not this much”).]

[Note: [Col. 0796D] *Constricta videantur*. My manuscript reads *extensa videantur* (“may seem extended”). This is not inappropriate, since omissions imply brevity, to which extension is opposed. The common reading may be explained thus: “not much will have been omitted, nor will the discourse nevertheless be excessively compressed and contracted.”]

## 146. CHAPTER I. On the peace made throughout Greece at the command of King Artaxerxes, and on the various wars waged by the Lacedaemonians with the king and the Thebans before that peace, including the account of Conon.

[Col. 0797A]

[Note: [Col. 0797B] *In the year 364 from the founding of the City*. This number is also found in Pliny, book 34, chapter 1. Livy, book 5, in Camillus’ speech, indicates that Rome was captured in the year 365 from the founding of the City. FABRICIUS. Some editions and manuscripts soon afterward have *ignorata* (“unknown”) instead of *ignotam* (“unfamiliar”). They also repeat *sibi* before it because of the unusual peace.]

In the year 364 from the founding of the City—a year which Rome experienced as extremely grievous because of the unfamiliar experience of captivity, but which Greece regarded as magnificent because of its unprecedented peace—

[Note: [Col. 0797C] *Because of the unprecedented peace*. In that year in which Rome was captured, held, burned, and sold, the Lacedaemonians ratified the peace made through Antalcidas with the Persian king—that is, they approved the peace made through Antalcidas with the king of the Persians, as Polybius says in book 1. But this peace will be discussed below. FABRICIUS.]

at that time, while the Gauls held Rome after capturing and burning it and sold it, Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, ordered all Greece through ambassadors to withdraw from arms and rest in peace, declaring that anyone who opposed the peace would be attacked by war.

The Greeks could certainly have despised him giving such an order as consistently as they had often defeated him bravely, unless they had drunk so eagerly and willingly the opportunity offered them from every side, which they had desired so avidly. For they showed how reluctantly they had undertaken what they had hitherto done, since they laid it down so readily, even on dishonorable terms.

For what could be so dishonorable to free and brave men as to lay down their arms and submit to peace at the command of one who was far away, had often been defeated, was still an enemy, and was moreover issuing threats?

[Note: [Col. 0797C] *Often defeated, still an enemy*. Fabricius and Scottus printed *saepe etiam victi adhuc hostis*, following Hittorp and Bolsuing. The editions—the Venetian, the first, and the Paris edition—have *saepe etiam victi hostis*. But among the manuscripts I consulted, none admits *etiam* there; all, in agreement with Augustine’s edition, read *saepe etiam victi, adhuc hostis*, etc. I have thus punctuated the words because Orosius enumerates four reasons why the Greeks could have rejected the author of the peace: that the Persian king was far from Greece, that he had often been defeated, that he was still their hereditary enemy in spirit, and finally that he was speaking not without threats.]

unless the very sound of the announced peace had caused the intention for war to melt away in the hearts of all, weary of war, and, after the long vigils of their labors, unexpected rest had relaxed them, yawning and stupefied, before their will had agreed to the terms of peace itself.

[Note: [Col. 0797D] *If not in the very*. The Longobard manuscript has *si non in ipso* (“if not in the very”).]

[Note: [Col. 0797D] *Voluntas pacta componeret*. The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Groningen Collection and certain old editions, has *peracta* (“completed”), which I believe arose from those copyists who sought a contraction of the writing in the middle of the word *pacta*. Orosius’ meaning here is that the Greeks, seized by an excessive desire for peace, as though their minds were stunned, embraced it at the first mention of it, even before their will—giving assent through deliberation—had recognized and approved the conditions of peace. Something similar was written above in book 2, chapter 5: “unless reconciliation, hastened before the withdrawal itself could recognize itself, had stolen in.”]

But how such great exhaustion oppressed the hearts and bodies of all the peoples throughout Greece, and persuaded their savage spirits so readily to rest in an unfamiliar leisure, I shall show as briefly as possible.

[Note: [Col. 0798B] *The Lacedaemonians, as men*. Orosius transcribed this from Justin, book 6. Xenophon, book 3, and Diodorus, book 14, give a fuller account of the same events. FABRICIUS.]

The Lacedaemonians, being men, and the Greeks being men, desired greater things in proportion to what they possessed. After they had gained possession of the Athenians,

[Note: [Col. 0798B] *After they had gained possession of the Athenians*. Those who did not understand this manner of expression unnecessarily inserted *auxilio* (“with the aid of”) before *Atheniensium*, as found in the first edition, the Paris edition, and the Venetian editions.]

they reached out in hope of ruling all Asia.

[Note: [Col. 0798C] *All Asia*. Since some manuscripts had *Graeciam* (“Greece”), which is also found in two Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen Collection, many editors printed *Asiam* (“Asia”) as a connected reading. Bolsuing, Hittorp, and the Venetian editions have *Graeciam et Asiam* (“Greece and Asia”), although the first edition and Augustine’s edition do not recognize this addition, and the better manuscripts, together with the Longobard manuscript, reject it. What follows also shows that Orosius is speaking here of Asia alone.]

Thus, making war upon the whole East,

[Note: [Col. 0798C] *They reached out*. The reading in the Perizonian manuscript, *hauserant* (“they had drunk in”), is more flattering than the one printed here, *hauserunt* (“they drank in”).]

they appointed Dercyllidas as commander for this campaign.

[Note: [Col. 0798C] *The commander Dercyllidas*. This commander is commonly and incorrectly called *Hircilides* here; in Greek his name is Δερκυλλίδας (*Dercyllidas*). FABRICIUS.]

When he saw that he had to fight against two very powerful prefects of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, Pharnabazus and Tissaphernes, he adopted a plan for the moment in order to evade the burden of a double confrontation: he attacked one after declaring war, and held the other in suspense by making peace.

[Note: [Col. 0798C] *He attacks one after declaring war*. Dercyllidas, having made an agreement with Tissaphernes on certain conditions, led his army into the territory of Pharnabazus. Xenophon and Justin. FABRICIUS.]

Pharnabazus denounced Tissaphernes before Artaxerxes, then their common king, as a traitor, especially since he had made an agreement with the enemy concerning the terms of an alliance during wartime. He urged the king to appoint in his place Conon, an Athenian who at that time happened to be living in exile in Cyprus, as commander in the naval war.

[Note: [Col. 0798D] *In his place*. The third Leiden manuscript together with the Groningen Collection has *in loco* (“in the place”).]

[Note: [Col. 0798D] *Conon, an Athenian*. You will read the same account in Diodorus, book 14. FABRICIUS. The third Leiden manuscript together with Perizonius and the Groningen Collection has *appetiit* (“he sought”) instead of *appetitur* (“he is appointed”).]

[Note: [Col. 0798D] *Having received five hundred talents of silver*. Diodorus likewise has λαβὼν ἀργυρίου τάλαντα πεντακόσια, “having received five hundred talents of silver.” FABRICIUS.]

After receiving five hundred talents of silver, Conon was summoned by Pharnabazus

[Note: [Col. 0798D] *He is summoned*. My manuscript has *vocatur* (“he is called”).]

and placed in command of the fleet. When the Lacedaemonians learned this, they too requested naval assistance from the king of Egypt, Hercynion, through ambassadors,

[Note: [Col. 0798D] *From Hercynion, king of Egypt*. Justin has *from Hercymon, king of Egypt*. Diodorus calls this king, who gave the Lacedaemonians “equipment for one hundred triremes and fifty myriads of measures of grain,” Νεφρέας, or, as it appears in other books, Νεφερέας (*Nefreus* or *Nephereus*). FABRICIUS.]

and received one hundred equipped triremes and six hundred thousand modii of grain. They also gathered substantial reinforcements from their allies everywhere.

By unanimous agreement they appointed Agesilaus commander of this campaign,

[Note: [Col. 0799B] *A man lame in one foot*. The well-known dispute over the Spartan kingship was between Leotychides, son of Agis, and Agesilaus, his brother. Leotychides wished to exclude Agesilaus from the kingship on the basis of an oracle, because Agesilaus was lame in one foot. But Agesilaus defeated him, arguing that the oracle applied to Leotychides, who was neither legitimate nor fathered by Agis. Xenophon, book 3 and in the *Agesilaus*; Plutarch, in the same work and in the *Life of Lysander*; Pausanias, book 3. FABRICIUS.]

a man lame in one foot, but in the most difficult circumstances they preferred that their king should limp rather than that the kingdom should.

Rarely have commanders so evenly matched in every form of skill come together for a single war. Exhausted by the bitterest battles against one another and stained with much blood, they withdrew from each other as though each had been unconquered.

[Note: [Col. 0799B] *Then Conon*. Justin, book 6, gives a detailed account of why Conon went to the king. FABRICIUS.]

Then Conon, having again received pay from the Great King in person,

[Note: [Col. 0799B] *By himself*. The Greeks say αὐτός and δι’ ἑαυτοῦ (“himself” and “by himself”); compare Aelian, *Various History*, book 1, chapter 21, concerning Ismenias, the Theban ambassador. [Col. 0799C]]

returned to the fleet, invaded the enemy’s territories, and stormed their towers, strongholds, and other defenses.

[Note: [Col. 0799C] *He captures*. Augustine’s edition has *impugnat* (“he attacks”). Soon afterward all the manuscripts and the better editions have *incubuit* (“he fell upon”), while others have *incumbit* (“he falls upon”).]

Like a storm breaking loose, wherever he fell he laid everything low.

[Note: [Col. 0799C] *But the Lacedaemonians, surrounded by domestic evils*. This refers to the time when, around the 96th Olympiad, almost all the allies abandoned the Lacedaemonians, who were ruling unjustly, as Cicero says in book 2 of *On Duties*. The Boeotians, Athenians, Corinthians, Argives, and others then formed a conspiracy and made war against the Lacedaemonians. For this reason Agesilaus was finally recalled from Asia. Xenophon, books 3 and 4; Diodorus, book 14; Plutarch, in the *Life of Agesilaus*; Pausanias, book 3. FABRICIUS.]

The Lacedaemonians, surrounded by domestic troubles, ceased to covet external possessions and abandoned their hope of dominion, as the danger of slavery threatened. They recalled Agesilaus, whom they had sent into Asia with the army, to assist his country.

[Note: [Col. 0799C] *Meanwhile Pisander, commander at Sparta*. It is certainly surprising that, contrary to the testimony of the ancient books, this commander has until now been called Lysander both by Justin and by Orosius, although it is certain from all the authors just mentioned that Agesilaus appointed Pisander, his wife’s brother, to command the fleet, and that Pisander, left in Asia, was defeated in a naval battle at Cnidus by Pharnabazus and Conon and perished. The fact that in the commonly circulated text of Diodorus the naval commander is called not Πείσανδρος (*Pisander*) but Περίαρχος (*Periarchus*) is without doubt an error. FABRICIUS.]

Meanwhile Pisander, the commander left at Sparta by King Agesilaus,

[Note: [Col. 0799D] *He had prepared the largest and most strongly fortified fleet at that time*. This is the consistent reading of the better manuscripts: the three Florentine manuscripts, those of Perizonius and Meus, the third Leiden manuscript, Utrecht, and the Groningen Collection, as well as Augustine’s edition and Scottus’ latest edition. The common text reads: “they had then prepared the largest and fortified fleet.”]

had prepared the largest and most strongly fortified fleet at that time. Moved by rivalry in valor with Agesilaus, so that while Agesilaus was conducting a land campaign he too might range along the coast in naval operations,

[Note: [Col. 0799D] *By rivalry*. Two Leiden manuscripts have *admiratione* (“by admiration”).]

Conon, however, directed the undertaking with twofold concern,

[Note: [Col. 0800A] *The undertaking he had undertaken*, etc. Up to this point the text had been printed: “But Conon, having undertaken the task, devoted twofold care,” etc. The first edition and those following it read similarly, but insert *omni* (“every”) after *negotio*. The reading restored from the manuscripts is much better, altered by us only through the change of a single letter. For in the three Florentine manuscripts, and in those of Meus and Perizonius—which surpass the other five considerably in quality—the reading is: “But Conon directed his attention to the undertaking he had accepted with twofold care.” In place of *impendebat* we have restored *intendebat*, which was undoubtedly the original reading. Livy uses *intendere bellum* (“to direct one’s attention to war”) in book 21, chapter 6: “Some, assigning Spain and Africa as provinces to the consuls, thought that the matter should be conducted by land and sea; others directed the whole war against Spain and Hannibal.” See also what we wrote concerning the correction of a similar passage of Orosius at the end of book 4.]

owing concern to his allies and loyalty to his country: to the latter he showed natural affection, to the former he supplied diligence. In this he was more devoted to his fellow citizens, because for their peace and freedom he was risking foreign blood, and he fought against exceedingly arrogant enemies at the king's risk and for his homeland's reward.

Thus the Persians under Conon and the Spartans under Pisander entered into a naval battle:

[Note: [Col. 0800B] *The soldiers, the rowers, and the commanders themselves*. From this passage of Orosius it is clear how the text of Justin was read in his time; it may be corrected from this passage in book 3, chapter 1, where the common text reads: “The same concern for the soldiers and all the kings existed.” The same naval battle between Conon and Pisander is described there. Nor can the common reading *regum* (“of the kings”) be defended in any way. For just as Orosius mentions soldiers, rowers, and commanders, so Justin had already described the commanders, by that name and also by their competition to win, in the preceding passage: “Moreover, Pisander, in addition to his association with Agesilaus, was also his rival in valor; and he strove not to fall short of his achievements and the splendor of his glory, nor to overturn through a brief moment of fault the dominion acquired through so many wars and generations.” He then continues: “The same concern for the soldiers,” etc.]

soldiers, rowers, and the commanders themselves were alike swept along by one ardor toward mutual slaughter.

[Note: [Col. 0800C] *The magnitude and savagery of this war reveal the condition of the Lacedaemonians, thereafter always declining*. We owe this much more elegant reading than the common one to the same Florentine manuscripts, with which my manuscript and Perizonius agree. All editions read: “The magnitude and savagery of this war having caused the condition of the Lacedaemonians thereafter always to collapse.”]

The magnitude and savagery of this war reveal the condition of the Lacedaemonians, which from that point onward continually declined.

[Note: [Col. 0800D] *For from that point flowed*. A Virgilian parody from book 2 of the *Aeneid*. FABRICIUS.]

For from that point the hopes of the Spartans seemed to flow away and to slip backward,

[Note: [Col. 0800D] *Seemed*. The common editions add *est* (“is”), which the better manuscripts and the principal editions do not recognize.]

until, struggling painfully to rise and falling back miserably,

[Note: [Col. 0800D] *Rising with difficulty and falling back wretchedly*. He describes the condition of Lacedaemon, as though it were dying, not inelegantly and again in imitation of Virgil. The poet had written of Dido in *Aeneid* 4, lines 688ff.:

> She, trying to raise her heavy eyes, again  
> Fails. The wound fixed beneath her breast hisses.  
> Three times she rises and, leaning on her elbow, lifts herself;  
> Three times she rolls back upon the bed, etc.]

it was exhausted and deprived both of power and of name. But this same battle was for the Athenians the beginning of recovering their power, just as it was for the Lacedaemonians the beginning of losing theirs.

[Note: [Col. 0801B] *The Thebans were therefore the first*. The leaders of this war, called the Boeotian War, were the Opuntian Locrians and the Phocians. The latter summoned aid from the Lacedaemonians, the former from the Thebans. The Thebans drew the Athenians over to their side. After battle was joined at Haliartus, the Lacedaemonians were defeated and Lysander fell: Xenophon, near the end of book 3; Diodorus, book 14; Pausanias, books 3 and 9; Plutarch, in the *Life of Lysander*. FABRICIUS. The Longobard manuscript has *retro ferri* (“to be carried backward”) instead of *retro referri*. Augustine’s edition has *auxiliis* (“with aids”) instead of *auxilio*. Three Leiden manuscripts together with Perizonius transpose *sublapsa retro referri*.]

The Thebans, therefore, supported by the aid of the Athenians, were the first to attack the wounded and terrified Lacedaemonians after their previous defeat, encouraged by great confidence because of the valor and skill of their commander Epaminondas. They thought that, with him, they could easily obtain rule over all Greece.

[Note: [Col. 0801C] *Because of the valor and skill of Epaminondas*. Orosius seems, misled by the words of Justin, to have thought that Epaminondas took part in this battle, which is not true. FABRICIUS.]

A land battle was therefore fought, with the Thebans winning without difficulty. Lysander too was defeated and killed in this engagement.

[Note: [Col. 0801C] *Pausanias too, the other commander*. Pausanias, who had been sent with Lysander against the Thebans, was accused because he had arrived in Boeotia too late and because he had preferred to remove the bodies of the fallen under a truce rather than after battle. Summoned to answer the charge before the court, he did not appear but fled into exile at Tegea. Xenophon and Pausanias, book 3. FABRICIUS. This was Pausanias, son of Pleistianax and grandson of that Pausanias who, after defeating Mardonius and the Persians at Plataea, stained immortal glory with depraved lust and criminal treachery. The innocence of this Pausanias—who was summoned to face capital charges for the second time by Lysander’s faction—was demonstrated by Xenophon, *Greek History*, book 3, p. 507; Plutarch, *Life of Lysander*, p. 450; Pausanias, book 3, p. 216; and Justin, book 6, chapter 4. He had first been summoned before the court because he had favored the Athenian exiles and had escaped danger only with the greatest difficulty, by an equal division of the votes. When accused a second time, he did not wish to entrust his safety to citizens angered by Lysander’s death, but fled to Tegea, to the temple of Minerva, which was a safe asylum for the unfortunate; there he died of illness. See what we have said about him in the *List of the Kings of the Lacedaemonian House of the Eurypontids*, which follows the *Life of Antigonus the Guardian*, after whom, when Cleomenes had been defeated, Lacedaemon was captured, in the *History of the Kings of Macedonia*.]

Pausanias too, the Lacedaemonian commander, accused of treason, was driven into exile.

The Thebans, having won the victory, gathered the entire army and marched toward Sparta, thinking that they would enter without difficulty a city left without defenders, since they believed that nearly all its forces, together with its king, had already been destroyed and that it had been abandoned by all its allies.

The Lacedaemonians, driven by the danger threatening their city, held whatever levy they could from untrained soldiers and advanced to meet the enemy. But once defeated, they had neither the valor nor the courage to resist the victors.

When, therefore, the slaughter was taking place on only one side,

[Note: [Col. 0801D] *King Agesilaus suddenly*. The accounts of Agesilaus’ arrival in Boeotia do not entirely agree in Justin and Orosius with those in Xenophon, Diodorus, and Plutarch. The battle was fought at Coronea; for Plutarch’s *Life of Agesilaus* incorrectly has περὶ τὴν Χαιρώνειαν (“around Chaeronea”) instead of Κορώνειαν (“Coronea”). FABRICIUS.]

King Agesilaus, summoned from Asia, suddenly and unexpectedly arrived in the midst of the war. He attacked the Thebans, already made more joyful and less vigilant by the success of their two victories, and defeated them without difficulty, especially since his own forces were still almost intact. Agesilaus himself, however, was seriously wounded.

[Note: [Col. 0802B] *He is wounded*. Augustine’s edition has *vulneratus est* (“was wounded”), a reading also recognized by the three Florentine manuscripts. [Col. 0802C]]

When the Athenians learned that the Lacedaemonians had been strengthened by their unexpected victory, they were frightened by fear of their former servitude, from which they had only just begun to breathe again. They gathered an army and joined it to the Boeotian forces as assistance,

[Note: [Col. 0802C] *From which they had then scarcely begun to breathe again*. Perizonius has “from which they had scarcely begun to breathe again.” The second Leiden manuscript and Utrecht have “from which they had then begun to breathe again.” Soon afterward Augustine’s edition has *in auxilio* (“as assistance”).]

placing it under the command of Iphicrates,

[Note: [Col. 0802C] *Under the command of Iphicrates*. Concerning Iphicrates, see Xenophon, book 4 and following; Diodorus, books 14 and 15.]

who, although still very young and scarcely twenty years old, fortified the weakness of his age with maturity of mind.

Conon too, an Athenian by birth but commander of the Persian army,

[Note: [Col. 0802C] *A man indeed*. The second occurrence of the word is deleted by the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection.]

when he heard of Agesilaus’ return, went back to devastate the fields of the Lacedaemonians.

Thus the Spartans, hemmed in and terrified by the din of enemies resounding all around them, wasted away in almost total despair.

[Note: [Col. 0802C] *But Conon, after he had been sated with the devastation*. Concerning Conon’s service to the Athenians and the honor bestowed upon him by his countrymen, Demosthenes’ speech *Against Leptines, on Immunity* gives an elegant account, in addition to the other authors whom we have often mentioned. Isocrates’ *Evagoras* should also be read. FABRICIUS.]

But Conon, after he had been sated with the extensive devastation of the enemy’s land, proceeded to Athens. He himself was sad amid the citizens’ greatest joy, since he saw that the city, once most richly adorned with people and culture,

[Note: [Col. 0802C] *Now*. Certain old editions have *tunc* (“then”).]

was now exhausted by the miserable squalor of ruins and desolation.

Accordingly, he performed a great work of piety and compassion in restoring it. For he replenished the city, emptied by the Lacedaemonians, with the spoils of the Lacedaemonians.

[Note: [Col. 0802C] *With spoils*. Certain editions, as well as the Utrecht manuscript, have *praesidiis* (“with defenses”), as if indicating the Persian resources from which Conon restored the city, formerly the defenses of the Lacedaemonians. But I do not alter the common reading, which is confirmed by Justin, who writes in book 6, chapter 52: “And so the things that had been burned were restored at the expense of the spoils,” and shortly afterward: “from the spoils of the Lacedaemonians.”]

What the Persians had burned with fire, the Persians rebuilt.

[Note: [Col. 0802D] *Meanwhile Artaxerxes, king of the Persians*. When Pharnabazus and Conon, with the royal fleet, were ravaging the coast of Laconia and attacking it with hostile actions, while Athens was being surrounded by a wall, the Lacedaemonians decided to make peace with the king of the Persians. For this reason they sent Antalcidas to Tiribazus, the king’s prefect, so that peace might be secured through his agency. For this reason the Greeks call this peace τὴν ἐπ’ Ἀνταλκίδου γενομένην εἰρήνην, “the peace made through Antalcidas,” as we demonstrated shortly before from Polybius. Read Xenophon, book 5; Diodorus, book 14; Plutarch, in the *Lives of Agesilaus* and *Artaxerxes*. Strabo mentions it at the end of book 6, and Pausanias at the beginning of book 9. FABRICIUS.]

Meanwhile Artaxerxes,

[Col. 0803A] king of the Persians, as was stated at the beginning,

[Note: [Col. 0803B] *As at the beginning*. The Utrecht and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have *sicut in principio* (“as at the beginning”). My manuscript has *sicut a principio* (“as from the beginning”).]

Here *praeruptus* is an adjective, corresponding to the Greek κρημνώδης, used substantivally, with *vastum* placed beside it as an adjective. [Note: [Col. 0810D] “In those days Alexander the Great also.” Below, in chapter 16, Orosius writes that Alexander succeeded his father Philip in the year 426 from the Founding of the City. Therefore, if Alexander assumed the kingdom of Macedonia at the age of twenty, as Plutarch and Arrian write, he was certainly born around the same time as these portents occurred. FABR.] In those days also [Note: [Col. 0810D] “Alexander the Great.” In the Longobard manuscript, Perizonius, and the Gronovian Collections, the reading is “Alexander the Great, truly,” etc.; Vincent of Beauvais has “Alexander the Great, that devourer,” etc. In the same author one reads: “He struck the earth in spring with stones for twenty-five days, in which days, etc.” The words “for twenty-five days,” derived from “from which days he was born,” should be deleted.] Alexander the Great was born—that truly great devourer of misery and most savage storm of the entire East.

[Note: [Col. 0811B] “Then also Ochus, who is also Artaxerxes.” Artaxerxes, ὁ ἐπικληθεὶς Ὦχος, “who was called Ochus,” is the twelfth Persian king in Eusebius. Under his sixth year these words are recorded: “Ochus, having captured the Jews at Apodasmos, transferred the inhabitants and settled them beside the Caspian Sea in Hyrcania.” FABR.] Then also Ochus, who is also Artaxerxes, after bringing to an end the great and prolonged war in Egypt, led a very large number of Jews into exile and ordered them to dwell in Hyrcania beside the Caspian Sea. It is believed that they remain there to the present day, increasing greatly in the prosperity of their race, and that from there they will one day break forth again [Note: [Col. 0811B] “Will break forth.” The fourth Leiden manuscript reads “having been rescued again in Judaea.” The Longobard manuscript and the third Leiden manuscript together with the Gronovian Collections read *exin*, “from there,” instead of *exinde*, “from that place.”].

During the crisis of that same war, [Note: [Col. 0811C] “Passing through, and also [destroying] Sidon.” Tripolis had revolted from the Persian king and received a garrison of three thousand Rhodians from the Egyptian king Nectanebo. When Ochus advanced from Babylon into Egypt with very large forces, he first attacked the Phoenicians, recovered Sidon for himself through the treachery of the ruler Mentor, and destroyed it. Diodorus XVI and Gemistus Pletho II discuss this at greater length. FABR. —The Venetian editions together with the Gronovian Collections prefer “Sidon.”] passing through, he also destroyed Sidon, the most prosperous city of the province of Phoenicia, and subjected Egypt to the Persian empire, [Note: [Col. 0811C] “Although previously defeated.” The printed copies read “having defeated it.” But who knows the history and does not see which reading is preferable? LAUT. —The first and third Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collections, together with Lautius, recognize “although previously defeated.” The Persians had been defeated by Nectanebo, king of Egypt, but Diodorus XV, p. 359, and XVI, p. 445, show that this was accomplished through the agency of Greek commanders.] although it had previously defeated him, but had then been subdued and crushed by the sword.

## CHAPTER VIII. He Briefly Summarizes the Disasters of the Wars Subsequently Waged by the Romans and Treats of the Closing of the Gates of Janus

[Col. 0811B]

From this point onward the Romans immediately undertook wars against the Samnites, a people powerful in wealth and arms, on behalf of the Campani and Sidicini. [Note: [Col. 0811C] “The Samnite War.” The Samnite War will be discussed below in this book; the Tarentine and Punic Wars afterward. FABR.] The Samnite War, conducted with uncertain outcome, was followed by Pyrrhus, the greatest—or nearly the greatest—enemy of the Roman name. The war with Pyrrhus was soon followed by the Punic War. And although [Note: [Col. 0811D] “Never after the death of Numa.” Numa established Janus at the lowest point of the Argiletum as an indicator of peace and war: open, to signify that the state was at war; closed, to signify that it was at peace with all peoples. Under Numa, Janus remained continuously closed for forty-three years. Livy I; Plutarch, *Numa*. FABR.] it is shown by the ever-open gates of Janus [Note: [Col. 0811D] “The gates of Janus always open.” All the manuscripts and editions before Fabricius have this reading. I do not know what induced him to print once “the gates of Janus open.” They were closed once, namely under Numa; thereafter—as Orosius wishes to say here—they remained open continuously until Augustus.] that after Numa’s death there was never any cessation from the disasters of war, nevertheless from that time the heat of evils, as though at midday, blazed imprinted across the entire sky.

Moreover, once the Punic War had begun, let whoever considers the Christian times infamous inquire, discover, and reveal whether wars, slaughter, ruin, and [Note: [Col. 0811D] “All things.” Thus the manuscripts; some old editions read “and every kind,” which also occurs somewhat later, “had ceased.”] every kind of unspeakable death ever ceased, except under Caesar Augustus. [Note: [Col. 0812B] “Except under Caesar Augustus’ rule.” After the battle of Actium, when peace had been secured by land and sea. See Book VI, chapter 22. FABR.]

Apart from him, however, during the one year between the Punic Wars, like a bird’s fleeting passage, the Romans, because the gates of Janus were closed, amid the fevers and diseases of the state, [Note: [Col. 0812C] “For this purpose.” We restore this reading from the Longobard manuscript, supported by my manuscript, Perizonius, and the Augustan edition; the common editions still read it ineptly. Orosius says, “For this purpose they were enticed by the very brief sign of peace,” and so, “growing feverish again for the worse,” etc.] were enticed by this very brief sign of peace, as by a very small draught of cold water, so that, growing feverish again for the worse, they might be afflicted much more gravely and violently [Note: [Col. 0812C] “Might be afflicted.” My copy and Perizonius read “might struggle.”].

But if it is established beyond all doubt that under Caesar Augustus peace first shone forth, after [Note: [Col. 0812C] “The Parthian peace.” Correctly so; contrary to the common reading *partam*, Suetonius has *Parthicam*. LAUT. —“Parthian” is likewise written by the three Florentine manuscripts, the four Leiden manuscripts, the Gronovian Collections, the Utrecht manuscript, my copy, Perizonius, and therefore all the manuscripts, together with the first editions. I am therefore surprised that Fabricius, Hittorp, and Bolsuing preferred *partam*. What follows is drawn from Lucan, Book I, line 60:

[Col. 0812D]

“Then, with arms laid down, let the human race care for itself,

and let every nation love one another in turn: peace, sent throughout the world,”

“May [he] restrain the iron gates of warlike Janus.”] The Parthian peace had brought the whole world of all lands into order: arms had been laid down, discord abolished, and a universal peace and new tranquility established. [Col. 0812B] It had obeyed Roman laws; it had preferred Roman laws to its own arms; having spurned their own leaders, they had chosen Roman judges. Finally, among all nations, [Note: Among all provinces. The common editions read “and among all,” but the better manuscripts do not recognize that conjunction. Instead of “among countless,” the Groningen Collection has “throughout the whole world.”] all provinces, countless cities, innumerable peoples, and the entire earth, there had been one [Note: Will. The Longobard manuscript reads “pleasure.” Somewhat later, the Augustan edition has “not even one” for “not one.”] will: freely and honorably to serve peace and to work for the common good. Previously not even one city, or one people of citizens—or, what is more remarkable, one household of brothers—had been able to maintain this continually. But if, while these things occurred under the rule of Caesar, it is nevertheless clearly evident, by the most lucid [Col. 0813A] proof, that our Lord Jesus Christ, born into this world, shone forth during Caesar’s own empire, then even those whom envy drove toward blasphemy [Note: “Envy compelled.” This is the reading of the better and older manuscripts—three Florentine copies, the Meo and Perizonian manuscripts, and the Augustan edition. The common editions read “envy compels,” and shortly afterward “the most tranquil” instead of “and the most tranquil”; three Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection read the latter.] are compelled, unwilling though they are, to acknowledge and confess that the peace of the whole world and its most tranquil serenity arose not from Caesar’s greatness but from the power of the Son of God, who appeared in Caesar’s days; and that the world itself obeyed not the emperor of one city but the Creator of the entire universe, through a universal recognition. For just as the rising sun floods the day with light, so he, mercifully arriving, clothed the world in an extended peace.

When this matter has been reached more fully, with the Lord himself bringing it to completion, [Note: “Will be brought forth.” Thus read three Florentine manuscripts, the Meo, Ultramontane, and Perizonian manuscripts, together with the Augustan edition, instead of “we bring forth,” as in the common editions. Three Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection read “will profess.”] it will be brought forth.

## CHAPTER IX. The Romans wage war against the Latins. Manlius Torquatus kills his son. Minucia, a Vestal Virgin, is condemned for incest.

[Col. 0813B] [Note: Thus, in the year 409 from the founding of the City. This was the year in which L. Manlius and P. Decius were consuls; in the ancient Fasti it is numbered 414. Since that number is far removed from the present one, I fear that an error lies here.] Accordingly, in the year 409 from the founding of the City, the Romans brought war against the rebelling Latins, with Manlius Torquatus and [Note: Decius Mus. The common text has, through an obvious error, “Muraena” instead of “Mus,” which appears in all the manuscripts here and below in chapter 21, as also in Florus, book I, chapter 14.] Decius Mus as consuls. In this war one consul was killed, while the other became a parricide. For Manlius Torquatus killed his son, a young man who had been victorious and had slain [Note: Metius of Tusculum, a noble horseman. Thus the manuscripts read, not “soldier,” as in the common editions.] Metius of Tusculum, a noble horseman and at that moment an especially defiant and insolent enemy.

[Note: The other consul. This refers to the other consul, P. Decius the father, who devoted himself in the Latin War, as Cicero and all the others relate.] The other consul, when he saw that the wing he commanded was being cut down and crushed in a renewed engagement, voluntarily threw himself into the densest ranks of the enemy and fell. Although victorious, Manlius did not deserve the customary reception by the Roman noble youths [Note: “The noble youths nevertheless went out to meet him.” Livy says that, after the war, T. Manlius returned to Rome, and that only the elders are known to have gone out to meet him; the young men both then and throughout the rest of his life avoided and cursed him. Valerius Maximus says the same, book IX, chapter 3.] that is ordinarily accorded to a triumphing man, because he was a parricide.

[Note: In the year following this one. Minucia was condemned for incest not in the immediately following year after the consulship of Manlius and Decius, but three years afterward, according to Livy, book VIII. On the punishment of Vestal Virgins, see Dionysius, book II; Plutarch, Life of Numa; and Festus, under “Sceleratus Field.”] In the year following this one, Minucia, a Vestal Virgin, was condemned for the incest she had committed and was buried alive in the field that is now called the Accursed Field.

## CHAPTER X. Very many Roman matrons were accused and condemned for poisoning.

But after a short interval, I shudder to report what occurred: [Note: In the consulship of Claudius Marcellus. M. Claudius Marcellus and C. Valerius Flaccus were consuls in the year 422, in which year an investigation into poisonings was first held at Rome. Livy, book VIII.] in the consulship of Claudius Marcellus and Valerius Flaccus, the Roman matrons burst forth with unbelievable madness and passion for crime. It was certainly a foul and pestilential year, [Note: “And unwept.” Unless this is correctly restored in Orosius in place of “and afflicted” or “and filled,” I have seen nothing anywhere. —LAUTIUS. This is an elegant emendation by Lautius, who substitutes “unwept” for “afflicted” or “filled.” He gives no authority, however, proving that *infletus* can be used for *indefletus*. Yet analogy does not stand in the way, since *fletus* occurs for *defletus* in Virgil, Aeneid VI, 481:

> Here are the Dardanids, much mourned by those above and fallen in war.

Servius notes that “much mourned” means “noble,” whose death is followed by great lamentation. Certainly the multitude of the dead and the magnitude of the slaughter are commonly demonstrated when, because of frequent and unceasing funerals, mourning is not omitted and the unmourned—or *infleti*, as Orosius seems to have written—are placed upon the funeral pyre by their relatives. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII, 610:

> They fight over the pyres and burn in others’ fires.  
> There are none to weep; unwept wander  
> The spirits of daughters and mothers, of young men and old.

Although no manuscript reads “unwept,” the Meo, Perizonian, and Ultramontane manuscripts nevertheless read “filled,” which comes close to that reading, since in manuscripts the letters *p* and *f* differ very little.] and slaughter was already everywhere being inflicted in masses, while everyone still held the simple belief that the corruption of the air was responsible. Then, when a certain slave-woman came forward as informant and accuser, many matrons were first compelled to drink the poisons they themselves had prepared; and then, as soon as they had swallowed them, [Note: “And drank.” Thus read three Florentine manuscripts together with the Perizonian and Meo manuscripts: “those who drank these.” The common editions read “so that they drank.”] they perished.

So great, moreover, was the number of matrons implicated in these crimes [Note: “Conscious of these crimes.” This is somewhat more Latin in the Cologne manuscript than in the others, which read “conscious in these crimes.” I would nevertheless prefer “conscious of this crime.” —LAUTIUS. At the end of the following chapter, however, the Ultramontane manuscript likewise reads “great among the small.”] that 370 of them are reported to have been condemned together. [Note: “So that 370 were condemned.” The manuscripts of Orosius agree on the number, but Livy writes that about 170 were condemned. Valerius, book II, chapter 1, says: “Some were condemned by capital judgment, completing the number 170.” —FABER. Three hundred and eighty is read in the first, third, and Groningen Leiden manuscripts, as well as in the Venetian, Parisian, and earliest printed editions. Pighius suspects an error in the numbers, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 333.]

## CHAPTER XI. Alexander, king of the Epirotes, is defeated and killed by the Samnites.

[Col. 0815A]

In the year 422 from the founding of the City, [Note: Alexander, king of the Epirotes. What Orosius writes in this chapter about Alexander, king of Epirus, Livy relates at length in book VIII, during the consulship of L. Papirius and C. Poetelius. See also what the Deacon added to Eutropius, and Strabo, book V, and below, chapter 18.] Alexander, king of the Epirotes and uncle of that Alexander the Great, having transported troops into Italy, was preparing war against the Romans and, while trying to strengthen his army near the cities neighboring Rome and either to obtain allies for himself or to deprive his enemies of them, was engaged in warfare. He was defeated and killed in a great battle in Lucania by the Samnites, who were supporting the Lucanian people.

But since, in reviewing Roman disasters, I have advanced somewhat far, or since I have been reminded by the mention of this Alexander, I shall, going back a few years, gather together, as far as I can, great matters from small ones. [Note: “Great matters from small ones.” Orosius may have written “great matters in small ones,” as is suggested by the comparison with the words in the preceding chapter, “implicated in these crimes.” The Ultramontane manuscript alone reads “in small ones,” but the excellent Augustan edition also seems to favor that reading.]

## CHAPTER XII. The achievements of Philip, king of Macedonia, and the peoples and cities he subdued.

[Note: In the year 400 from the founding of the City. Philip, son of Amyntas, assumed the kingdom of the Macedonians, according to Diodorus, book XVI, in the 105th Olympiad, when Cn. Genucius and L. Aemilius were consuls at Rome. The ancient Fasti, however, place these events in the year 390 from the founding of the City, and I would prefer to follow them as more reliable guides.] In the year 400 from the founding of the City, Philip, son of Amyntas and father of Alexander, having obtained the kingdom of the Macedonians, [Note: “The kingdom of the Macedonians.” The third and fourth Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection read “the kingdom of Macedonia.”] held it for twenty-five years, during which he built up all these heaps of bitterness and every mass of evils.

[Note: He was first given by his brother Alexander. In recounting these events Orosius follows Justin. Plutarch also writes in his *Life of Pelopidas* that Philip was given by his brother Alexander as a hostage to the Thebans. Diodorus, book XVI, however, says that Amyntas himself, after being defeated by the Illyrians, gave Philip, his youngest son, as a hostage to the victors, who deposited him with the Thebans. Gemistus Pletho, reporting both Plutarch’s and Diodorus’s accounts, says that Philip was first at Thebes as a hostage while his father was alive, and afterward was given a second time by his brother when the latter entered into an alliance with Pelopidas; Diodorus, book XV, is his authority for this. It must be asked, however, how Justin and Orosius can say that Philip was a hostage at Thebes for three years if, having been given by his brother, he did not escape custody until Perdiccas was defeated and killed by the Illyrians, as Diodorus and Pletho relate. For Alexander, according to the same authorities, was killed after reigning one year by Ptolemy Alorites, the illegitimate son of Amyntas. The latter then held the kingdom of Macedonia for three years; Perdiccas, Alexander’s full brother, killed him, and after spending five years on the throne was defeated and killed by the Illyrians. —FABER. I have discussed this controversy expressly in the larger work mentioned above; see there what I have brought together on the life of Alexander, the brother of Philip, and of Philip himself concerning this matter.] He had first been given by his brother Alexander as a hostage to the Thebans and was educated for three years under Epaminondas, a most vigorous commander and an eminent philosopher.

After Alexander himself had been killed through the crime of his mother Eurydice, [Note: “Killed through the crime of Eurydice his mother.” Thus the manuscripts and the Fabrician editions read. The remaining editions have “killed by the crime of his mother Eurydice,” although she had already committed the crime, and so on. Since the Augustan edition agrees with the manuscripts, Orosius here follows Justin, who stigmatizes Eurydice by this charge. The justice of that charge may be examined in our Universal History, or Royal Treasury, where, in the Life of King Philip, we demonstrated Eurydice’s innocence from the testimony of writers who lived at the same time.] although she, after committing adultery, had first killed one son and deprived her daughter of a husband by arranging a marriage with her son-in-law through the death of her husband, Philip was compelled by the people to assume the kingdom, which he had been governing on behalf of the young son of his murdered brother.

Since he was harassed abroad by the assault of enemies rising from every side and at home by the fear of repeatedly discovered plots, [Note: The first war with the Athenians. This war was conducted under Mantias, when the Athenians were attempting to give the kingdom of Macedonia to Argaeus. Diodorus. —FABER.] he first waged war against the Athenians. Having defeated them, [Note: He transferred the war to the Illyrians. Philip defeated the Illyrians in the second year of his reign and forced them to withdraw from the towns of Macedonia, according to Diodorus and Pletho. Philip joined the Thessalians to himself in the fourth year of his reign, according to the same authorities. —FABER.] he transferred his arms against the Illyrians and, after slaughtering many thousands of the enemy, captured the most famous city of Larissa.

From there he invaded Thessaly, not so much from love of victory as from ambition to possess the Thessalian cavalry, whose strength he wanted to incorporate into his army. Thus, after taking the Thessalians by surprise and reducing them to his power, he made his army invincible by joining together the strongest squadrons and forces of horse and foot.

Accordingly, after defeating the Athenians and subjecting the Thessalians, [Note: Olympias, sister of Arubas, king of the Molossians. We have written this from the excellent book of Cornelius Gualtherus, where the common reading is “Eurucha,” probably derived from “Arucha,” which appears in some manuscripts. The name of this king is written with great variation. The printed books of Justin variously have “Arymbas”; my manuscript has “Arybbas.” In Demosthenes, *Olynthiac* I, and in Diodorus, book XVI, it is Ἄρυμβας; in Plutarch, *Pyrrhus*, Ἄρυβας; in Pausanias, book I, Ἄρυββας. It must be asked on what authorities Orosius calls Olympias the sister of Arubas and Justin calls Arybbas the paternal cousin of Olympias, since Pausanias and Plutarch make it clear that Arubas was Olympias’s paternal uncle: Arubas and Neoptolemus, Olympias’s father, were sons of Alcetas. Ulpian, the interpreter of Demosthenes, calls Arymbas the θεῖος (*theios*, “paternal uncle”) of Olympias, Philip’s wife—not, as Wolff thought, her maternal uncle. Demosthenes, *Olynthiac* I, mentions Philip’s expedition against Arymbas. —FABER. The first and fourth Leiden manuscripts read “Aurubas,” with “read Aribas” written above in the first; the third reads “Cherubas”; the Perizonian manuscript “Aurubas”; three Florentine manuscripts and the others “Arubas.”] he married Olympias, sister of Arubas, king of the Molossians. Arubas, thinking that through his alliance with the Macedonians, secured by the king’s marriage connection, he would enlarge his power, was deceived by this expectation, lost his kingdom, and grew old in exile.

Then, while Philip was attacking the city of Methone, [Note: Methone. Three Florentine manuscripts write “Mothone”; the interpreters of Justin, book VII, chapter 6, also discuss that reading and the Latin form of the name. Vincent of Beauvais likewise writes “Mothone,” *Speculum Historiale* V, 18.] he lost an eye by the stroke of an arrow. [Note: He lost his eye by the shot of an arrow. This soldier is called Aster by Plutarch and Ulpian; he deprived Philip of his eye. Besides Diodorus, Strabo, book VIII, mentions this injury. Critobulus removed the arrow from Philip’s eye and healed the loss of sight without disfiguring his face, according to Pliny, book VII, chapter 37. —FABER. Aster, the one who shot the arrow, had inscribed it boastfully:

> Ἀστὴρ Φιλίππῳ θανάσιμον ἐπιπέμπει βέλος.  
> Aster sends Philip a deadly missile.

The enraged king ordered an arrow to be shot within the walls as well, inscribed with these words:

> Ἀστέρα Φίλιππος, ἢν λάβῃ, κρεμήσεται.  
> Philip will hang Aster when he captures him.

Nor did he permit the city to be surrendered on any other condition than that Aster be handed over; once handed over, he fastened him to a cross. Suidas, vol. II, p. 242, under “Caranus.” Add Strabo, book VII, p. 330, and book VIII, p. 274; Diodorus Siculus, book XVI, p. 434; Plutarch, *Parallel Lives*, p. 307; and Ptolemy Hephaestion in Photius, codex 190, p. 478.] He soon stormed and captured the city itself.

Afterward he subdued nearly all Greece, [Note: “Nearly all Greece.” Thus read the Florentine manuscripts and others, while the Perizonian and Meo manuscripts have “almost all Greece.” Some editions read “all Greece almost.”] having forestalled it by his counsels and overcome it by force. For the cities of Greece, while each desired to rule, all lost the power of ruling; and while they rushed without restraint toward mutual destruction, they finally learned, when enslaved and crushed, that what each had lost had perished for all. [Note: “Toward mutual ruin.” The Perizonian manuscript reads “toward mutual destruction.” — “All to perish.” The Meo manuscript has “all equally,” but I prefer the common reading.] [Note: “Only when crushed.” The Augustan edition reads “only when finally crushed.”]

While Philip watched their mad rivalries, as though from a vantage point, [Note: “Mad rivalries.” This is the true word, not “rivalrous wanderings,” which had occupied this passage like Cerberus; even if the Cologne manuscript did not say so, the following words readily prove it: “disputes, the tinder of wars.” —LAUTIUS. The reading “rivalrous wanderings,” of which Lautius complains, I have not found in the manuscripts; they read “intercourse,” which comes closer to his emendation, which I consider correct. The old editions also have “intercourse,” except that the Venetian editions have “rivalrous wanderings.” Hittorp’s first printed edition has “incursions,” which the later editions then followed.] [Note: “Observed.” I have restored this reading in agreement with all the manuscripts, as also below “nourishes,” instead of “was observing” and “was nourishing.” The manuscripts are joined by the Augustan edition.] and, by continually offering aid to the weaker side, cunningly fostered their disputes—the tinder of wars—he subjected both the defeated and the victors equally to himself.

But to obtain dominion over all Greece, he was given an opportunity by the immoderate domination of the Thebans. They had defeated the Lacedaemonians and Phocians and exhausted them with slaughter and plunder; then, having additionally burdened them at the common council of Greece with so great a fine that they could in no way pay it, [Note: At the common council of Greece. Diodorus has Ἐν Ἀμφικτύονι, “in the Amphictyonic council.” This war was called the Sacred and Phocian War. On it, see Diodorus and Pausanias, book X, who writes that the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi was occupied by the Phocians under the archon Agathocles, in the fourth year of the 105th Olympiad. —FABER.] they compelled them to take up arms.

Accordingly, the Phocians, under the command of Philomelus [Note: Under Philomelus. In Greek it is Φιλόμηλος ὁ Θεοτίμου; the name commonly given here, “Philomenes,” is corrupt. —FABER. In place of “for which,” the first and second Florentine manuscripts read “in whose place.”] and supported by the aid of the Lacedaemonians and Athenians, [Note: Of the Lacedaemonians and Athenians. The reason the Lacedaemonians favored the Phocians in the Sacred War and sent aid under King Archidamus, son of Agesilaus, was that a similar decree had been issued against them in the common council of the Greeks. In former times the Lacedaemonians had occupied the Cadmean citadel of Thebes through treachery. The Thebans, finding an opportunity to avenge the injury, condemned them through the Amphictyons to a fine of 500 talents; the fine was later doubled because they had failed to pay it at the appointed time. The Lacedaemonians, angered by this and unwilling to pay the fine, made the cause of the Phocians their own. The Athenians, out of hatred for Philip and fear of his desire to dominate everyone, were especially urged on by Demosthenes and brought aid to the Phocians. We have discussed this war, one of the memorable wars of Greece, more fully in our History and in the Life of Philip.] joined battle, routed the enemy, and captured the Theban camp. In the next battle, amid the immense slaughter of both peoples, Philomelus was killed. In his place the Phocians appointed Onomarchus as commander. [Note: Onomarchus as commander. Thus everyone calls him; his name is corrupt in the common text. —FABER.]

The Thebans and Thessalians, moreover, abandoning the selection of their own citizens, voluntarily chose Philip, king of Macedonia, as their commander—the very man whom they had previously struggled to repel as an enemy. [Note: When battle had been joined. This battle was fought against the Phocians in the third year of the Sacred War. More than 6,000 of the Phocian people were killed with their commander Onomarchus, and about 3,000 were captured, according to Diodorus, book XVI. —FABER. Onomarchus was not immediately defeated by Philip. Only after he had twice forced Philip himself to flee was Onomarchus defeated in a third battle. Many of the Phocians then threw themselves into the sea and reached the passing Athenian fleet unharmed. The commander Onomarchus attempted to do the same but perished; Philip crucified his corpse. Onomarchus was succeeded by the third of his brothers, Phayllus. When Phayllus died of illness, command passed to Phalaecus, the very young son of Onomarchus.
