Then the affairs of the Phocians were completely ruined by Philip’s deceit and courage; Phalaecus, having obtained permission to depart freely with his mercenaries, abandoned his people, was carried to Crete, and died there.] When battle had been joined and the Phocians had been slaughtered almost to annihilation, victory fell to Philip.

[Note: But the Athenians, having heard the outcome of the war. Philip, after defeating Onomarchus, was hastening to Thermopylae so that he might wage war against the Phocians in their own territory. But the Athenians, sailing around by ship, prevented him from passing, according to Diodorus and Libanius in the introduction to Demosthenes’ speech *On the Peace*. —FABER.] But the Athenians, having heard the outcome of the war, occupied the narrow pass of Thermopylae so that Philip would not enter Greece, just as they had earlier occupied it when the Persians were approaching.

When Philip therefore saw that, because Thermopylae had been fortified, he was shut out from entering Greece and that war had been prepared against him, he turned against his allies. He invaded as enemies the cities whose commander he had recently been and which had stood open to him in gratitude and welcome; he cruelly plundered them. Completely erasing every consciousness of alliance, he sold the wives and children of all under the auctioneer’s crown, and he also overturned and stripped all the temples. Yet for twenty-five years he was never defeated, as though by angry gods. [Note: “As though defeated by angry gods.” Below, chapter 14: “Nor could he be prevented by the angry gods, whom he had always despised and whose altars, temples, and images he had overturned, from obtaining the most chosen death, as it seemed to him.” After these words, the entire passage found above in book II, chapter 3, is inserted in the Augustan edition, beginning “Therefore, for this reason above all, I have thought these matters worthy of commemoration” and ending “and there were Christians who spared, and Christians whom they spared.”]

After this he crossed into Cappadocia, where he waged war with equal treachery; he captured neighboring kings by deceit and killed them, and subjected all Cappadocia to the power of Macedonia. [Note: Cappadocia. This is false, and Philip never penetrated as far as Asian Cappadocia. Therefore here and in Justin, book VIII, chapter 3, as the interpreters observed there, “Chalcis” or “Chalcidice” should be restored. At this time Philip undertook an expedition into Thracian Chalcidice and harassed in war the Greek cities situated around the Strymonic and Singitic Gulfs. Compare Diodorus Siculus, book XVI, p. 450. Shortly afterward some editions read “in allied cities” instead of “among allied cities.”]

From there, after the slaughter, fires, and plundering carried out in allied cities, he turned his acts of parricide against his brothers. Fearing those born from his stepmother as coheirs of the kingdom, [Note: Born from his stepmother. Amyntas, Philip’s father, had three sons by Gygaea: Archelaus, Argaeus, and Menelaus. Philip had killed one of them; the other two fled to Olynthus, a city that had initially supported Philip and had received from him as gifts the cities of Potidaea and Anthemus. But when the Olynthians saw that Philip was luring them into a trap, they conspired against him with the Athenians, and they would not easily have been defeated if they had not been betrayed by their commanders, Lasthenes and Euthycrates, who had been bribed by Philip. See what we have collected under the thirteenth year of Philip.] he began to kill them. Having killed one of them, [Note: Two fled to Olynthus. Justin, book VIII, makes this the cause of the Olynthian War; neither Diodorus nor Libanius mentions it. The war was waged, according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, who cites Philochorus, in the year before the 108th Olympiad, under the archon Callimachus. In the following year, according to Diodorus, Olynthus was captured. —FABER.] two fled to Olynthus. [Note: “To Olynthus.” Contrary to the old editions, all the manuscripts retain the preposition *in*; Fabricius printed “Olynthus” without it.] Philip soon attacked it as an enemy, filled the ancient and flourishing city with slaughter and blood, emptied it of its wealth and inhabitants, and also dragged out his brothers and put them to punishment and death.

[Col. 0820A] [Note: Then, when. Thus the better manuscripts and the Longobard manuscript read; others have “then, after the destruction,” and so on.] Then, elated by the destruction of his allies and the murder of his brothers, he thought that everything he had conceived was permitted to him. He invaded the gold-bearing regions of Thessaly and the silver mines of Thrace. And, so that he might leave no law or religious obligation inviolate, after seizing the sea and scattering his fleet, [Note: He also began to practice piracy. Besides Justin, book IV, chapter 3, Demosthenes teaches us this in the First Philippic, p. 18, the Second Philippic, p. 29, and the speech *On the Crown*, p. 329: after landing on Lemnos, Philip carried off some Athenian citizens from there and attempted to occupy the island of Imbros; he even carried away the sacred Athenian trireme near Marathon.] he also began to practice piracy.

Moreover, when two brothers, kings of Thrace, disputing over the boundaries of their kingdom, had by mutual agreement chosen him as judge, Philip, following his customary character, entered the judicial proceeding as though it were a war, with an army drawn up, and deprived the unsuspecting young men of life and kingdom. [Note: The two brothers, kings of Thrace. See whether Cersobleptes and Amadocus are meant; Demosthenes discusses them in *Against Aristocrates*. It is certain from Demosthenes, Aeschines, and Pletho that Cersobleptes was attacked by Philip when the Athenians made peace with him. The peace made with Philip by the Athenians, under the archon Themistocles, lasted seven years, as Dionysius writes to Ammaeus. —FABER. If these men are meant, Philip did not kill them but compelled them to follow his side—certainly Cersobleptes, who ruled Thrace near the Chersonese and possessed Cardia, the largest city in the Chersonese. This Cersobleptes, son of Cotys and king of Thrace, was surprised by Philip’s unexpected arrival, forced to make a treaty with him, and compelled to give his son as a hostage. Later, defecting from Philip and again subdued in war, he was required to pay tribute to him.]

The Athenians, who had earlier repelled Philip’s entry by fortifying Thermopylae, now voluntarily sought his peace and reminded the most treacherous enemy that they had neglected to guard the entrance. The other cities of Greece as well, so that they might devote themselves more intently to civil wars, voluntarily subjected themselves to foreign rule under the pretext of peace and alliance. This happened especially when the Thessalians and Boeotians asked Philip to present himself as the publicly declared commander against the Phocians and to wage the war he had undertaken, while the Athenians and Lacedaemonians joined them and struggled, through payment and entreaty, either to delay or to remove the war. [Note: “To wage the war.” The Augustan edition reads “to wage the war of Greece,” perhaps not incorrectly. Since the Sacred War was against the Phocians, who had stripped the offerings from the Delphic Apollo, it could be called the war of Greece. The Boeotians made Philip commander and leader of that war only when, exhausted by adverse circumstances, they could no longer resist the Phocians, who, in support of King Phalaecus—who had handled affairs badly—had appointed three commanders to direct the war.]

Philip secretly made different promises to the two sides. [Col. 0821A] He swore to the Phocians that he would grant them peace and pardon. [Note: That he would grant peace and pardon to the Phocians. Aeschines, returning from Philip, reported to the Athenians that Philip had confirmed this promise to them; Demosthenes discusses the matter in *On the Embassy* and *On the Crown*. —FABER.] To the Thessalians he promised that he would soon come to their aid with an army, but he forbade both sides to prepare for war.

Accordingly, Philip, having drawn up his forces, confidently entered the pass of Thermopylae, and fortified it by stationing garrisons. [Note: “Fortified.” The Meo manuscript together with the first and third Florentine manuscripts reads “fortifies”; the second Florentine manuscript “fortified.” Shortly afterward, instead of “the first,” the Augustan edition and certain manuscripts read “at first.” The three Florentine manuscripts have “but all Greece” instead of “but also all Greece.”]

Then, for the first time, not only the Phocians but all Greece felt that it had been captured. For Philip first delivered the Phocians, having broken faith and trampled upon his oath, to unspeakable mutilation. From there he ravaged the cities and territories of all the others, and by his bloody presence ensured that he would be feared even when absent.

When he returned to his kingdom, like shepherds [Note: Who drive their flocks. Thus the Cologne manuscript reads; I do not change it to “sheep.” For just as we now say *genua* (“knees”), so the ancients said *pecua* (“flocks”). Thus, just as we now say *genua*, they then said *pecua*. —LAUTIUS. Philip, king and father of Perseus, later did the same when he was planning war against the Romans. Compare his Life and History.] who drive their flocks now through summer pastures, now through winter ones, he transferred peoples and cities wherever he thought particular places ought to be filled or abandoned, according to his own will.

Everywhere a pitiable spectacle and the most atrocious kind of misery lay before the eyes: destruction endured without invasion, captivity without war, exile without crime, domination without a conqueror. Fear, poured over the miserable amid the goads of injustice, oppressed them; [Note: “And the thing itself.” The Meo manuscript has “and the thing itself also.” Instead of “for those who feared,” some manuscripts and editions read “to be feared”; the Augustan edition reads “it was to be feared.”] pain grew through the very concealment of it: the deeper it was driven down, the more it grew, because they were not permitted to express it, fearing that even their tears might be counted as defiance.

He set some peoples, torn from their homes, opposite the territories of enemies; he stationed others at the farthest boundaries of his kingdom; he distributed certain peoples, out of jealousy of their strength, as reinforcements for exhausted cities, lest they should be able to do what they were believed capable of doing. Thus that once most glorious body of flourishing Greece collapsed into many torn fragments, its liberty first extinguished.

## CHAPTER XIII. Philip besieges Byzantium unsuccessfully. He attacks Scythia in war and conquers it. The Triballi seize the spoils from him.

[Col. 0822A]

But when he had carried this out in several Greek cities and nevertheless kept them all crushed by fear, inferring the wealth of all from the spoils of a few, he judged Byzantium, a necessary maritime city, useful for completing an equal devastation everywhere. [Note: [Col. 0821D] Deeming Byzantium a necessary maritime city. The treaties of friendship and alliance between Philip and the Byzantines remained in force until the archonship of Nicomachus; but in the following year, which was the first of the 110th Olympiad, Philip first attempted to capture Perinthus and, having been repulsed from there, besieged Byzantium. At that time he sent a letter to the Athenians, accusing them of violating the treaty and declaring war against them. Dionysius, drawing on Philochorus, clearly relates all these events. Philip’s letter survives among Demosthenes’ Philippic orations. FABR.] He considered it a distinguished city, excellently suited to serve as a refuge for him by land and sea, [Note: [Col. 0822C] For himself by land and sea. The Augustan edition has “for his forces by land and sea.” The Groningen Collection has only “by land and sea.”] and immediately surrounded it with a siege when it resisted him. [Note: [Col. 0822C] This Byzantium. Cassiodorus writes that Byzantium was founded during the reign of Tullus Hostilius. Eustathius, in his commentary on Dionysius, reports how Byzantium received its name. FABR.] This Byzantium, once founded by Pausanias, king of the Spartans, but later enlarged by Constantine, a Christian ruler, and called Constantinople, [Note: [Col. 0822C] Called Constantinople. See below, Book VII, chapter 28. FABR.] is now the seat of the most glorious empire and the capital of the entire East.

But after a long and fruitless siege, in order to recover by plundering the money he had exhausted through the siege, [Col. 0822B] Philip took up piracy. Accordingly, he sold one hundred and seventy ships packed with merchandise, [Note: [Col. 0822C] One hundred and seventy ships. The third Leiden edition, together with the Groningen Collection and the Augustan edition, counts one hundred and eighty; but Justinus is to be preferred to the common reading.] and supplied some relief to his panting poverty. From there he divided his army, partly to carry on plunder and partly to maintain the siege. He himself set out with his bravest troops and captured many cities of the Chersonese; after defeating their peoples, he carried off their wealth.

He also crossed into Scythia with his son Alexander, intending to plunder. [Note: [Col. 0822C] He crossed over. The third Leiden edition has “he crosses”; the Augustan edition, “he crossed.”] At that time Atheas was king of the Scythians. [Note: [Col. 0822D] At that time Atheas was king of the Scythians. I have retained the king’s name as it appears in the printed editions, although in the manuscripts it is read Atheas and Natheas; in the printed books of Justinus it is Mattheas, and in our manuscript Metheas. FABR. — In almost all the manuscripts of Orosius, and likewise now in Justinus, Atheas is read; this was in fact the man’s name. The Venetian editions have, “At that time Etheas ruled the Scythians.”] Since he was being hard pressed by a war with the Istrians, he requested assistance from Philip through the Apollonians. [Note: [Col. 0822D] Assistance from Philip. All the manuscripts, with one or two exceptions, prefer this reading to “assistance.” In place of “he requested,” Perizonius reads “he requests.”] But when the king of the Istrians had soon died, and he had been freed both from fear of the war and from the need for assistance, he dissolved the treaty of alliance made with Philip.

Philip, abandoning the siege of Byzantium, attacked the Scythian war with all his forces; [Col. 0822C] and when battle was joined, although the Scythians were superior both in numbers and in valor, they were defeated by Philip’s trickery. In that battle twenty thousand boys and women of the Scythian nation were captured, and a great quantity of livestock was carried away. No gold or silver was found; [Note: [Col. 0822D] Gold and silver. My text, together with Justinus, has “no gold or silver.” [Col. 0823C] Shortly afterward, my text, together with certain editions, has “were sent.”] this circumstance first gave credibility to the poverty of Scythia.

Twenty thousand noble mares, sufficient for breeding, were sent to Macedonia. But as Philip was returning, the Triballi met him in battle, and Philip was wounded in the thigh so severely that his horse was killed through his body. [Note: [Col. 0823C] When everyone. Certain editions have “and when everyone”; the Venetian editions, “and when everyone had”; the Augustan edition soon afterward has “having turned,” in place of “turned.”] When everyone thought him dead, they turned to flight and lost their plunder. Then, after a brief interval while he recovered from his wound, he rested in peace.

As soon as he recovered, however, he made war upon the Athenians. Since they were placed in such a critical situation, they admitted the Thebans, once their enemies, but then their allies, [Note: [Col. 0823C] The Thebans, once enemies. “The Lacedaemonians” had evidently been read here in place of “the Thebans.” For when Philip occupied Elatea, the Athenians, prevented by the timing of events from sending envoys to the other allies, won the Thebans over to their side through the eloquence of Demosthenes. See Demosthenes, Against Ctesiphon; Diodorus, Book XVI; Plutarch, Life of Demosthenes. [Col. 0823D] FABR.] and wearied the cities of all Greece with embassies, urging them to attack the common enemy with united strength. Accordingly, several cities joined themselves to the Athenians, while fear of war drew others to Philip. [Col. 0823B]

When battle was joined, [Note: [Col. 0823D] When battle was joined. This battle was fought at Chaeronea, according to Diodorus, Plutarch, and Strabo, Book IX.] although the Athenians were far superior in the number of their soldiers, they were nevertheless defeated by the endurance of the Macedonians, hardened through continual wars. The outcome itself showed that this battle was much more terrible than all the preceding wars. For that day brought to an end throughout Greece the glory of acquired dominion and the condition of its most ancient freedom.

## CHAPTER XIV. Philip’s cruelty toward the Thebans and his death

Afterward Philip inflicted a most bloody victory upon the Thebans and Lacedaemonians. [Note: [Col. 0823D] Against the Thebans and Lacedaemonians. This is also how it stands in the manuscripts, although no other accounts mention cruelty toward the Lacedaemonians, and Justinus, whom Orosius follows, mentions only the Thebans. FABR.] Indeed, he struck some of the leading men of the cities with the axe, drove others into exile, and deprived them all of their property. He restored to their homeland those who had long ago been expelled by their fellow citizens; from among them he appointed three hundred exiles as judges and governors, so that, by healing their ancient grief through a new authority, they might not allow the peoples whom he had oppressed so miserably to breathe again in hope of liberty.

Moreover, having selected a large number of soldiers [Note: [Col. 0823D] As a reserve. The Lombard manuscript has “as a reserve.”] throughout Greece to support the royal plan, he organized two hundred thousand infantry and fifteen thousand cavalry, apart from the Macedonian army [Note: [Col. 0823D] Of the Macedonians. Four Leiden editions, together with the Groningen Collection and the Augustan edition, have “Macedonian.”] and an immeasurable barbarian host, [Note: [Col. 0823D] Barbarian multitude. The same manuscripts and the Augustan edition have *barbaria* (“barbarian multitude”). This also appears in the first and second Florentine manuscripts, although in the second it has been restored as *barbarie*. [Col. 0824C]] intending to send them into Asia for the Persian expedition. [Note: [Col. 0824C] Three commanders, namely Parmenion, etc. Diodorus and Pletho say that two commanders were sent ahead, namely Attalus and Parmenion; they give a fairly full account of Philip’s death. FABR.]

And while the forces mentioned above were gathering from Greece, Alexander—who was the brother of Olympias, his wife—and later [Note: [Col. 0824C] Struck down by the Sabines in Lucania. Livius writes that he was killed by a Lucanian exile. Gemisthus writes: “Having crossed into Italy to assist the Tarentines, he fought bravely in a certain battle and died.” [Col. 0824D] FABR. — The Augustan edition has “by the Samnites,” as does the Ultr. manuscript, which writes “by the Samnites.”] was struck down by the Sabines in Lucania, [Note: [Col. 0824C] Struck down by the Sabines in Lucania. Livius writes that he was killed by a Lucanian exile. Gemisthus writes: “Having crossed into Italy to assist the Tarentines, he fought bravely in a certain battle and died.” [Col. 0824D] FABR. — The Augustan edition has “by the Samnites,” as does the Ultr. manuscript, which writes “by the Samnites.”] Philip had appointed him king of Epirus in return for the sexual violation committed against him, and had decided to celebrate his marriage by giving him his daughter Cleopatra.

When, on the day before his death, he was asked what end was most desirable for a man, he is said to have replied that the best was one that could come suddenly and swiftly, by an unexpected weapon, to a brave man who, after the glory of his virtues, was reigning in peace, without bodily struggle or disgrace of spirit. That is precisely what befell him shortly afterward. [Note: [Col. 0824D] Befell him. The Lombard, third Florentine, second Leiden, my manuscript, and Perizonius prefer “befell”; the others have “happened.”]

Nor could the angry gods—whom he had always despised and whose altars, temples, and images he had overthrown—prevent him from attaining the most select death, as it seemed to him. [Note: [Col. 0824D] The most select. Since, apart from the Augustan edition, three Leiden manuscripts, my manuscript, the Groningen Collection, and the Lombard manuscript all have this reading, I believe it derives from Orosius; the printed editions have “the most chosen.”]

For on the day of the wedding, while he was proceeding to the magnificently prepared games between the two Alexanders, his son and his son-in-law, he was surrounded and killed in a narrow passage, without guards, by Pausanias, a noble Macedonian youth. [Note: [Col. 0824D] In a narrow passage. My manuscript has “in a narrow place”; three Leiden manuscripts have “between narrow passages.” Shortly afterward the first Leiden manuscript has “he is killed.”]

Let them now proclaim these things loudly and celebrate them with many voices, as though the praises and fortunate deeds of brave men—by which the bitterest disasters of others are turned into pleasing tales—were worthy of praise, provided that they themselves never lament with a sadder narration the wrongs by which they are at times afflicted. If, however, they wish merely to move others who listen to their complaints as deeply as they themselves felt them while enduring them, let them first compare past events, not with the present, [Note: [Col. 0825C] But let deeds be compared with deeds. In the Groningen Collection this is given more fully: “but let deeds be compared with deeds.” That is, one should not compare past times with present times for those who now suffer injustice; rather, the evil deeds of the past should be compared with present wrongs, and present blessings with past blessings. He forbids comparison of the past with the present because, although the past may have inflicted greater misery, it is considered less grievous since it no longer exists; present events, even if they cause only slight anxiety, are felt more heavily. It is readily apparent, however, that this is a gloss added by someone wishing to clarify the meaning of Orosius’ words.] but let deeds be compared with deeds; and let them judge both, on the basis of hearsay, as though they were impartial arbiters of others’ affairs. For twenty-five years the fraud, ferocity, and domination of a single king kept in motion the burning of cities, the destruction of wars, the subjugation of provinces, the slaughter of men, the plundering of wealth, the seizure of livestock, the sale of the dead, and the enslavement of the living. [Note: [Col. 0825C] As though they were certain. The Augustan edition, together with the Ultr. manuscript, deletes “certain.” Nor does it appear in the three Florentine manuscripts or the second Leiden manuscript.]

## CHAPTER XV. The Samnites capture the Roman forces. The Romans break the treaty they had made and capture Satricum.

These events, impressed upon our memory as an example of misery through Philip, would be sufficient even if Alexander had not succeeded him in the kingdom. I shall briefly suspend the account of Alexander’s wars—indeed, of the world’s disasters that followed in ordered succession under his wars—in order, at the appropriate point in the chronology, to insert the Roman events. [Note: [Col. 0825C] In the year 426 from the founding of the City. According to the consuls listed in the Capitoline records, this year was 432 after the founding of the City. FABR.]

In the year 426 from the founding of the City, the famous Caudine Forks made the Romans notorious for a remarkable disgrace. For although in the preceding war twenty thousand Samnites had fallen when Fabius, master of the cavalry, joined battle, [Note: [Col. 0825D] Twenty thousand Samnites, when Fabius was master of the cavalry. The same number of enemy dead appears in Livy, Book VIII, where these events are narrated at considerable length. Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus, whom Orosius means here, was master of the cavalry under the dictator Lucius Papirius Cursor, four years before the Caudine disgrace. In addition to Livy, see Eutropius, Book II, and Valerius Maximus, Book II, chapter 2. FABR.] the Samnites settled at the Caudine Forks with more watchful care and more carefully prepared equipment.

There, when they had enclosed the consuls Veturius and Postumius and all the Roman forces within the narrowness of the terrain and among their weapons, [Note: [Col. 0825D] The consuls Veturius and Postumius. Titus Veturius and Spurius Postumius were consuls for the second time when the Romans fought disastrously at Caudium and the legions were sent under the yoke. Cicero, *De Officiis* III; Livy VI; Florus I, chapter 16; Augustine, *City of God* III, chapter 17. FABR.] Pontius, their commander, abused the security produced by victory to such an extent that he thought it necessary to consult his father Herennius about whether he should kill the trapped men or spare them. He chose to preserve them alive for disgrace. It was well known that the Romans had often before been defeated and killed, but had never been captured [Note: [Col. 0826C] But never captured. The fourth Leiden edition has “never captured”; the second has “yet never captured.” The following word, “could,” is absent from my manuscript and Perizonius.] or compelled to surrender.

Thus the Samnites, having won the victory, ordered the entire Roman army, shamefully captured and stripped even of its arms and clothing—except that each man was allowed a single cheap covering for the concealment of his body’s private parts—to be sent under the yoke and subjected to servitude, while they arranged for it to proceed in a long ceremonial procession. Having taken six hundred Roman cavalrymen as hostages, they sent the consuls back, burdened with disgrace but deprived of everything else.

Why should I labor in words to magnify the stain of this most shameful treaty, when I would rather have remained silent? The Romans today would either not exist at all or would serve under Samnite domination if, when subjected to the Samnites, they had kept faith with the treaty that they wish their own subjects to observe.

In the following year the Romans broke the agreement ratified with the Samnites and forced them into war, [Note: [Col. 0826C] Which was undertaken under the consul Papirius. Orosius and Eutropius follow those authorities who report that the Romans achieved success against the Samnites under the consul Lucius Papirius, not under the master of the cavalry; Livy says that this is disputed. FABR.] which was undertaken under the consul Papirius and brought great slaughter upon both peoples.

While on one side anger over the recent disgrace and on the other the glory of the recent victory spurred the combatants on, [Note: [Col. 0826C] Spurred them on. Some manuscripts and editions read “stimulated,” including the second Leiden manuscript. Below, Book VI, chapter 18, concerning Caesar: “The people, spurred by grief, dragged his body into the Forum and burned it with fragments of the tribunal platforms and benches.” Ovid also uses the verb *instimulare*, *Fasti* VI.507:

“Saturnia, having disguised herself as a goddess,  
spurs on the Latin Bacchae through deceitful sounds.”

For “recent disgrace,” three Leiden manuscripts have “the preceding disgrace.”] at last the Romans conquered by dying stubbornly. They did not cease either to be slaughtered or to slaughter until, after the Samnites had been defeated and their commander captured, they had imposed the yoke upon him. [Note: [Col. 0826D] And their commander captured. This is the reading of the Lombard manuscript, or the first Florentine, and it is likewise corrected in the second Florentine; the printed editions have “with the commander captured.” After “they restored,” Perizonius’ manuscript adds “of servitude,” while my manuscript subsequently reads “the same” instead of “the same thing.”]

Then the same Papirius, after expelling the Samnite garrison from Satricum, stormed and captured it. [Page 180] At that time Papirius was regarded among the Romans as so warlike and energetic that, when Alexander the Great was said to be planning to descend from the East and conquer Africa by force, [Note: [Col. 0826D] And from there. The Augustan edition has “and then.” The words “and energetic,” which appear in the other editions, are absent from the Augustan and Venetian editions, as also from Vincent of Beauvais, Book VI, chapter 7.] and then cross over into Italy, the Romans considered that, among all the excellent commanders then in their republic, Papirius would be the foremost man capable of withstanding Alexander’s assault.

## CHAPTER XVI. Alexander, succeeding Philip, subdues the Thebans, Illyrians, Thracians, and other cities, and defeats Darius.

Accordingly, in the year 426 from the founding of the City, Alexander succeeded his father Philip in the kingdom. He gave the first proof of his spirit and courage by rapidly suppressing the disturbances of the Greeks, whose instigator in urging them to revolt from Macedonian rule had been the orator Demosthenes, corrupted by Persian gold. [Note: [Col. 0827B] The orator Demosthenes, corrupted by Persian gold. Aeschines brings this charge against Demosthenes in his speech *Against Ctesiphon* in these words: “But now the royal gold has overflowed and supported his expenditure; yet even this will not be enough, for no wealth has ever been so great as to overcome a wicked character.” These lines should be read in this form from the manuscript of Aeschines and from Diodorus’ book published by Henri Estienne. Their meaning is: “Now an abundant supply of Persian gold supports his expenses; yet even this will not be enough, for no wealth has ever been so great that it could overcome depraved morals.” FABR.]

Accordingly, when the Athenians begged him to refrain from war, he spared them and additionally released them from fear of a fine. [Note: [Col. 0827B] He released them from fear of a fine. The printed editions have “from great fear”; the manuscripts, “from fear of a fine.” I have restored the historical reading. LAUT. — The Lombard manuscript clearly has “from fear of a fine.”]

But he destroyed the Thebans, together with their city demolished, [Note: [Col. 0827B] The Thebans together with their city destroyed. For the destruction of Thebes, see Diodorus, Plutarch, Arrian, Book I, and Pausanias in the *Boeotica*. FABR. — [Col. 0827C] Together with it demolished. This is how the manuscripts read; but since some old editions recognize only “with the city demolished,” perhaps the reading should be “when their city had been demolished, he destroyed them.”] and sold the survivors under the crown. [Note: [Col. 0827C] The remaining cities. Many editions insert “however,” against the agreement of the manuscripts. Many of the same editions also delete the word that appears after “the Illyrians.”] He made the remaining cities of Achaea and Thessaly tributary. He also subdued the Illyrians and Thracians, turning his war against them soon afterward. [Note: [Col. 0827C] The Illyrians and Thracians as well. Alexander subjected these peoples to his rule before he destroyed Thebes. Diodorus and Arrian. FABR.]

Then, as he was about to depart for the Persian war, he killed all his relatives and close associates. [Note: [Col. 0827C] All his relatives, etc. Among the most prominent were Amyntas, son of King Perdiccas, who had been Philip of Macedon’s elder brother. Philip had spared him and had given him his daughter by the Illyrian Audata, Cynna or Cynnan, a woman of heroic spirit. After her husband’s death, despite Alexander’s advice, she refused to marry again and was killed by Perdiccas after the king’s death. Next came the brothers of Lyncestes, sons of Aeropus, who had once contested the kingdom with Philip. Their names were Heromenes, Arrabaeus, and Alexander. Alexander was spared while he was in Europe because he had been the first to hail the king; afterward, however, he was killed in Asia. Olympias had already put Caranus, Philip’s son by Cleopatra, to death in a cruel manner. See these matters and the rest of Alexander the Great’s history in the Life of Alexander that I have written.]

His army consisted of thirty-two thousand infantry, four thousand two hundred cavalry, and one hundred and eighty ships. [Note: [Col. 0827D] They were in his army. Arrian writes that Alexander had in his army infantry “not much more than thirty thousand” (*οὐ πολλῷ πλείους τρισμυρίων*) and cavalry “more than five thousand” (*ὑπὲρ τοὺς πεντακισχιλίους*). Plutarch, in his Life of Alexander, says that the writers disagree about the number of troops: those who give the smallest number count thirty thousand infantry and five thousand cavalry; those who give the largest count thirty-four thousand infantry and four thousand cavalry. Diodorus writes that there were thirty thousand infantry and four thousand five hundred cavalry. FABR. — The Lombard manuscript reads thirty thousand. Some old editions read: “There were in his army thirty-two thousand infantry, four thousand five hundred cavalry, and one hundred and eighty ships.” In place of “more admirable,” three Florentine manuscripts have “more marvelous.”]

With this very small force he conquered the whole world. Whether it is more astonishing that he conquered it or that he dared to attack it is uncertain. [Note: [Col. 0828B] That he conquered it. The Augustan edition reads: “whether it is more astonishing that he conquered it, or that he dared to attack it,” deleting both occurrences of “that”; the first is also absent from the Ultr. manuscript.]

At his first encounter with King Darius, six hundred thousand Persians stood in battle formation; they turned their backs, overcome no less by Alexander’s strategy than by the valor of the Macedonians. [Note: [Col. 0828B] At his first encounter with King Darius. This first battle was fought at the Granicus River. On the numbers, see Arrian: “The Persian cavalry numbered about twenty thousand, while the foreign mercenary infantry fell only slightly short of twenty thousand.” Diodorus writes: “The entire cavalry numbered more than ten thousand, while the Persian infantry numbered no fewer than one million.” FABR.]

There was therefore a great slaughter of the Persians. [Note: [Col. 0828B] There was a great slaughter of the Persians. It is reported, on Plutarch’s authority, that twenty thousand Persian infantry and two thousand cavalry fell. FABR.] In Alexander’s army, however, one hundred and twenty cavalrymen and only nine infantrymen were lost. [Note: [Col. 0828C] In Alexander’s army. In the figures Orosius follows Justinus. Arrian writes that in Alexander’s army at the first encounter about twenty-five cavalrymen were killed, and afterward more than sixty; about thirty infantrymen also fell. But Aristobulus, according to Plutarch, wrote that thirty-four of Alexander’s troops were killed, nine of them infantrymen. In the following book, chapter 1, Orosius says: “Although nearly four hundred thousand of the enemy were killed, only nine infantrymen were missing from Alexander’s army.” FABR. — Almost all the manuscripts of Orosius delete “in Alexander’s army,” writing simply “Alexander’s army,” etc.]

Next he attacked and captured Gordium, a city of Phrygia, now called Sardis, which had been besieged, and handed it over to plunder. [Note: [Col. 0828C] Gordium of Phrygia. This is also found without variation in the manuscripts. My copy of Justinus likewise has “after this he proceeds to the city of Gordium,” where the printed editions have “Gordium.” Curtius, Book III, names the town Gordium, as do the Greeks, Γόρδιον (*Gordion*). On the Gordian knot, see Plutarch, *Alexander*; Arrian, Book II; Curtius III; Justinus XI; and Erasmus, *Adagia*. FABR. — [Col. 0828D] Attacked and captured. The Lombard manuscript more correctly has “attacked and captured” than the reading found in all the others, “conquered and captured.”]

When he was informed that Darius was approaching with large forces, he feared the narrowness of the terrain in which he was situated, crossed Mount Taurus with astonishing speed, covered five hundred stades in a single day’s march, and reached Tarsus. There, when he descended, sweating, into the exceedingly cold river Cydnus, [Note: [Col. 0828D] When, sweating, he entered the Cydnus. On the Cydnus, see Curtius, Book III. Some write that Alexander contracted the illness from which he was restored by the skill of Philip of Acarnania not in the river Cydnus but from exhaustion; see Plutarch and Arrian. Diodorus makes no mention at all of the river Cydnus. FABR. — [Col. 0828D] Exceedingly cold. The first Paris and Venetian editions have “very cold.” This is incorrect, for Justinus XI.8 also reads: “He threw himself into the exceedingly cold water.”]

he stiffened and, because of the contraction of his muscles, came close to death.

Meanwhile Darius advanced into battle with three hundred thousand infantry and one hundred thousand cavalry. [Note: [Col. 0829B] Darius with 300,000. Arrian writes: “The entire army with Darius was said to consist of about six hundred thousand men capable of fighting.” FABR.] This multitude of enemies troubled Alexander greatly, especially in view of his own small numbers, although he had long since learned, after overcoming six hundred thousand enemies with that same small force, not only not to fear battle but even to hope for victory.

Accordingly, when both armies had taken their positions within a spear’s cast of each other, and the commanders, running among the peoples who were awaiting the signal, sharpened their courage with various exhortations, battle was joined on both sides with immense spirit. In it both kings, Alexander and Darius, were wounded. [Note: [Col. 0829B] Both Alexander and Darius were wounded. For Alexander’s wound, which grazed his right thigh, see Diodorus, Plutarch, Arrian, and Curtius. Apart from Justinus, no one mentions Darius as having been wounded in this battle. FABR.] The contest remained uncertain until Darius fled. [Note: [Col. 0829C] Until he fled. This is the reading of three Florentine manuscripts together with Perizonius’ manuscript. The common reading is “until he fled completely.”]

After this came the slaughter of the Persians. Eighty thousand infantry and ten thousand cavalry were killed, while forty thousand were captured. [Note: [Col. 0829C] Eighty thousand infantry and ten thousand cavalry. The number of Persian cavalry killed is the same in Diodorus, Curtius, Justinus, and Orosius; Justinus gives sixty-one thousand infantry, Curtius one hundred thousand, and Diodorus more than one hundred and twenty thousand. Plutarch says that Alexander struck down “more than one hundred and ten thousand of the enemy” (*ὑπὲρ ἔνδεκα μυριάτας τῶν πολεμίων*). FABR.]

Of the Macedonians, one hundred and thirty infantrymen and one hundred and fifty cavalrymen fell. [Note: [Col. 0829C] Of the Macedonians, one hundred and thirty infantrymen. This is Justinus’ figure, and Diodorus agrees, writing: “Of the Macedonians, about three hundred infantrymen died, and about one hundred and fifty cavalrymen.” Curtius, however, writes: “On Alexander’s side there were four hundred and four wounded; altogether thirty-two infantrymen were missing, and one hundred and fifty cavalrymen were killed.” FABR.]

A great quantity of gold and other wealth was found in the Persian camp. [Note: [Col. 0829D] Was found. The better manuscripts and nearly all the others delete this phrase.] Among the captives in the camp were Darius’ mother, his wife—who was also his sister—and his two daughters.

Since Darius could not obtain their ransom even after offering half his kingdom, he gathered all the forces of Persia and the assistance of its allies for a third time and renewed the war.

While Darius was carrying out these preparations, Alexander sent Parmenion with troops to attack the Persian fleet, while he himself set out for Syria. There, when many kings of the East wearing fillets came voluntarily to meet him, [Note: [Col. 0829D] With kings wearing fillets, etc. The editions have “with islanders,” perhaps because I once read the following in the work of the most noble and accomplished young man Peter von Broich of Agrippina: “With what islanders, then, did they come to meet him?” Or did Orosius suppose that fillets were the insignia of kings? You may laugh freely. LAUT. — Yet in Justinus, from whom this passage is taken, Book XI, chapter 10, we read: “Then he set out for Syria, where many kings of the East wearing fillets came to meet him.” Here too the manuscripts of Orosius read “fillets,” as do Fabricius’ editions. I am therefore surprised that in Scott’s Mainz edition “fillets” is placed in the margin and “islanders” in the text.] he admitted some to his alliance and destroyed others. [Note: [Col. 0829D] He admitted others. This is correctly found in three Florentine manuscripts and the other better manuscripts. Other copies, together with certain editions, incorrectly have “he bound,” “he chose,” or “he sent away.” FABR. — [Col. 0830B] He admitted others. The manuscripts have “he admitted,” not “he bound.”]

He crushed and captured Tyre, the most ancient and flourishing city, which resisted him in reliance upon its Carthaginian kinsmen. [Note: [Col. 0830B] The very ancient city of Tyre. Tyre was captured by Alexander in the seventh month after its siege began, in the seventh year of the 112th Olympiad, as Diodorus XVII, Arrian II, and Curtius IV relate at length. FABR.]

From there he swept through Cilicia, Rhodes, and Egypt in persistent fury. Then he proceeded to the temple of Jupiter Ammon [Note: [Col. 0830C] From there to the temple of Jupiter Ammon. Diodorus, Plutarch, Arrian, Curtius, and Justinus say so much about this temple and Alexander’s journey to Ammon that it would be tedious to offer any further note. FABR.] in order, by a lie devised for the moment, to remove from himself the disgrace of an uncertain father and the infamy of an adulterous mother. [Note: [Col. 0830C] Devised for the moment. The first and third Leiden editions have “devised for the temple.”] [Note: [Col. 0830C] Disgrace. The Augustan edition has “ignorance.”] [Note: [Col. 0830C] Of an incestuous father. This is how the manuscripts read. But to remove the reading formerly printed, “uncertain,” who would not say that this better suits the adulterous mother? LAUT. — The better and more numerous manuscripts have “uncertain,” not “incestuous.” Nor do I see how it better suits the adulterous mother. Could she not have been adulterous without incest? The father necessarily was uncertain if Alexander had been conceived through adultery.]

For, having summoned the priest of the shrine to him, he secretly instructed him about the answer he wished to receive as though he were consulting the god, as their historians report. Thus Alexander was certain—and revealed to us—that, with the gods themselves silent and deaf, either it lay within the priest’s power to fabricate whatever he wished, or within the will of the consulter to hear whatever he preferred.

Returning from Ammon to the third Persian war, he founded Alexandria in Egypt. [Note: [Col. 0830C] He founded Alexandria in Egypt. Livy, Book VIII, Solinus, and Cassiodorus state that Alexandria in Egypt was founded in the year 427 from the founding of the City, under the consuls Gaius Poetelius and Lucius Papirius. The other matter is discussed below, chapter 18. [Col. 0830D] FABR.]

## CHAPTER XVII. Darius’ final battle with Alexander and his death
[Note: [Col. 0830D] “But Darius, after abandoning hope of peace, [had] 304,000 infantry.” My Justin is therefore more correct: “Then, after abandoning hope of peace, Darius renews the war with 400,000 infantry,” etc., rather than the commonly read “with 40,000 infantry.” There is, however, some variation among those who enumerate Darius’s army. Plutarch, in his *Alexander*, writes that Darius advanced to meet Alexander with “ἑκατὸν μυριάσιν στρατοῦ,” that is, with ten hundred-thousands of troops, among whom, as Diodorus counts them, there were 800,000 infantry and 200,000 cavalry. Arrian, in Book III, writes that Darius had nearly 40,000 cavalry and 400,000 infantry. In Curtius’s books it is read as follows: “The total army numbered 45,000 cavalry; the infantry line amounted to 200,000,” but I fear that the 200,000 here is corrupt for “a hundred ten-thousands.” FABR.]

But Darius, after abandoning hope of peace, opposed to Alexander, returning from Egypt, 404,000 infantry and 100,000 cavalry [Col. 0831A] at Tarsus in battle. [Note: [Col. 0831B] “He opposes him in battle at Tarsus.” I do not think there is any student of history whom this passage would not trouble, especially since all authors state that this final battle between Alexander and Darius was fought not in Cilicia, where Tarsus is, but in Assyria, and yet Orosius has left the text written thus; [Col. 0831C] all the books bear witness to it. What, then, shall we say? I fear indeed that Justin, whom Orosius follows as his source, misled him: when Justin had written that Darius, in flight, crossed the bridge of the Cydnus River—which flows past Tarsus—Orosius may have thought that the battle was fought at Tarsus. But this battle was fought in Assyria, beyond the Lycus, in the plains of Aturia, at a village called Gaugamela, according to Strabo in Book XVI. Although Dionysius of Halicarnassus, addressing Ammaeus, calls this battle “τὴν ἐν Ἀρβήλοις μάχην,” “the battle at Arbela,” and Curtius calls it “the battle at Arbela,” while Diodorus concludes his account thus, “ἡ μὲν οὖν περὶ Ἄρβηλα γενομένη παράταξις τοιοῦτον ἔσχε τὸ πέρας,” “Thus the battle formation that took place around Arbela had such an ending,” nevertheless Plutarch, in his *Alexander*, writes: “Τὴν δὲ μεγάλην μάχην πρὸς Δαρεῖον οὐκ ἐν Ἀρβήλοις, ὥσπερ οἱ πολλοὶ γράφουσιν, ἀλλὰ ἐν Γαυγαμήλοις γενέσθαι συνέπεσεν,” that is, “It happened that the great battle with Darius was fought not at Arbela, as most writers record, but at Gaugamela.” Arrian agrees with Strabo and Plutarch in Book III, where he reports that Darius placed his camp at Gaugamela, by the Bumadus River, about sixty stades from the town of Arbela. Read him also in Book VI. FABR.—Orosius’s error is manifest; he seems to have read Justin carelessly.]

Nor was there any delay in the battle: all rushed blindly, in mad fury, upon the sword. The Macedonians were spirited, having so often defeated their enemies; the Persians, preferring death unless they should win. Rarely in any battle was so much bloodshed. But when Darius saw his men being defeated, although prepared to die in battle, he was compelled, at the urging of his own men, to flee. In this battle the strength and kingdoms of Asia [Note: [Col. 0831D] “Fell.” Perizonius reads, not badly, “collapsed.” Soon afterward the edition of Augustine has “came under control.”] collapsed, and the entire East passed under the power of the Macedonian empire. Thus all the Persians’ confidence was so worn down in this war that afterward no one dared to rebel, and the Persians patiently accepted the yoke of slavery after an empire lasting so many years. [Note: [Col. 0831D] “Accepted.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection, read “would accept.” The Augustan edition has “accepted.”]

Alexander [Note: [Col. 0831D] “Alexander for thirty-four consecutive days.” The same number appears in Justin, in my manuscript and in Robert Estienne’s printed book, while other copies commonly read forty, and others eighty-three. FABR.—In the first and fourth Leiden manuscripts, “thirty-seven consecutive days.” Vincent of Beauvais likewise reads thirty-seven days in *Historical Mirror*, Book V, chapter 37. There, he reports: “Persepolis, the capital city of the Persian kingdom, illustrious for many years and filled with the wealth of the whole world,” etc.] spent thirty-four consecutive days inspecting the spoils of the camp; he attacked Persepolis, [Note: [Col. 0831D] “Persepolis, the capital of the Persian kingdom.” Concerning the capture and plundering of Persepolis and its immense wealth, Diodorus in the latter part of Book XVII and Curtius in Book V should be read. Strabo mentions it in Book XV. FABR.] the capital of the Persian kingdom, [Note: [Col. 0832B] “A most famous city.” Three Florentine manuscripts, the Ultramontane manuscript, the Groningen collection, my manuscript, and Perizonius delete “city,” as does the printed Augustan edition.] a most famous city, crowded with the wealth of the entire world. [Note: [Col. 0832C] “But when he had discovered that Darius was being held captive by his relatives.” Bessus and Nabarzanes bound Darius in golden fetters, as Curtius and Justin write, and left him on the road pierced by many wounds. Diodorus, Plutarch, Arrian, Curtius, and Justin discuss this extensively. FABR.] But when he learned that Darius was being held by his relatives, bound in golden fetters, he decided to pursue him. Accordingly, after ordering [Note: [Col. 0832C] “To follow.” Fabricius rightly printed this, following the manuscripts and the better editions. Justin, Book XI, chapter 15: “And so, when he had ordered the army to follow, he set out with six thousand cavalry,” etc. In some copies “he pursued” and “he followed,” as well as “with a thousand soldiers he set out,” are incorrect.] the army to follow, he himself set out with six thousand cavalry and found him abandoned alone on the road, pierced by many wounds and breathing out the last of his life through those wounds. [Note: [Col. 0832C] “He ordered him to be carried out and buried in the tombs of his ancestors.” The ordinary copies have “to be carried back into the tombs,” a barbarous expression. The Cologne manuscript has “to be carried out into the tombs,” from which I restored the text’s reading; though certainly Apollo need not be consulted to determine whether it is correct. The first editions, the Augustan, Parisian, and Venetian editions have “he ordered him to be carried back and buried in the tombs of his ancestors.” This is the reading in the manuscripts; but if one wishes the author to speak more Latinly, the passage should be reshaped as: “to be placed in the tomb—or tombs—of his ancestors, and to be buried there.” Compare Tacitus, *Annals* III.4 and IV.44; Suetonius, *Augustus* 101 and *Tiberius* 15.]

He ordered this man, dead, to be carried back with empty compassion into the tombs of his ancestors and buried there. He held in cruel captivity not only his mother or wife, but even his little daughters. [Note: [Col. 0832D] “He held.” This is the reading of all the manuscripts. Some printed editions have “he detained.”]

Amid so great a multitude of disasters—an account difficult to believe—within three battles and as many years, 1,500,000 infantry and cavalry were consumed. These came, indeed, from that kingdom and those peoples from whom, not many more years earlier, 1,900,000 are reported to have been routed. Yet beyond these catastrophes, during the same three years, many cities of Asia were crushed, all Syria was devastated, Tyre destroyed, Cilicia drained of its resources, Cappadocia subdued, and Egypt [Note: [Col. 0832D] “Was subjected.” The first Florentine manuscript, that is, the Lombard manuscript, my manuscript, and the third Leiden manuscript, together with the Groningen collection, read “was added.” Perhaps “was afflicted” should be understood.] subjected. The island of Rhodes, too, trembling, voluntarily submitted to slavery; many provinces beneath Mount Taurus were subjected; and Mount Taurus itself, after long resisting the yoke, was subdued, conquered, and forced to accept it.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The wars of Agis, king of the Spartans; of Alexander of Epirus; and of Zopyrion, the governor; the peoples subdued by Alexander after Darius’s death; and his cruelty toward his own men.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] “And lest perhaps now.” Three Florentine manuscripts, likewise three Leiden manuscripts, my manuscript, Perizonius, the Groningen collection, and the Augustan edition read “then,” which cannot be defended in its place, since “then also” occurs immediately afterward in the same copies. Fabricius therefore restored “now.” But the older editions—the first, Parisian, Venetian, Bolsingian, and Hittorpian—seem more correct in omitting it; all of them print: “And lest anyone perhaps should suppose,” etc.]

And lest anyone now suppose that only the East was subdued by Alexander’s power, or that only Italy was exhausted by Roman unrest, at that time also war was being waged in Greece by Agis, king of the Spartans; in Lucania by Alexander, king of Epirus; and in Scythia by Zopyrion, the governor. [Note: [Col. 0833B] “Of whom Agis the Lacedaemonian.” Curtius described this war of the Greeks against Antipater, governor of Macedonia, in fuller detail in Book VI, but only the outcome of the battle has come down to us. Besides Justin, Diodorus also writes about it in Book XVII. Pausanias mentions it in Book III. FABR.] Agis the Lacedaemonian, with all Greece roused and rebelling alongside him, engaged Antipater’s very powerful forces and, amid great slaughter on both sides, fell himself. [Note: [Col. 0833B] “Fell.” The Augustan edition has “died.”]

Alexander, meanwhile, in Italy, aspiring to rule the West and emulating Alexander the Great, after waging numerous and serious wars there, was defeated by the Bruttians and Lucanians, [Note: [Col. 0833C] “And his body.” The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Groningen collection, has “his body for burial”; the first and second have “and his body for burial.”] and his body was sold for burial. Zopyrion, governor of Pontus, gathered an army of 30,000 and dared to make war upon the Scythians; he was slaughtered to the last man and utterly destroyed along with all his forces. Thus Alexander the Great, [Col. 0833B] after Darius’s death, [Note: [Col. 0833C] “Subdued the Hyrcanians and Mardians.” Concerning the Hyrcanians and Mardians, neighboring peoples, and the subjugation of Hyrcania, see Diodorus XVI, Arrian III, and Curtius VII. FABR.] subdued the Hyrcanians and Mardians. While he was still intent upon war there, [Note: [Col. 0833C] “Thalestris or Minothaea.” Diodorus calls this queen of the Amazons Thalestris, “Θάληστρις”; Curtius calls her Thalestris. They report that she came to Alexander, evidently following Cleitarchus, Polycritus, Onesicritus, Antigenes, and Ister. But Aristobulus, Ptolemy, and the other writers named by Plutarch said that this was fiction. FABR.] Thalestris or Minothaea, [Note: [Col. 0833C] “Queen.” This is absent from all the manuscripts, nor do the older editions before Hittorp, Bolsing, and the Fabrician editions contain it. Soon afterward, three Leiden manuscripts have “roused” for “excited.”] a queen, an impudent Amazon, came to him with three hundred women, having been stirred by the desire to conceive offspring from him.

After this he attacked the Parthians, [Note: [Col. 0833D] “Attacked.” Some Leiden manuscripts have “attacked them,” followed by “although they resisted for a long time,” etc.] whom he almost annihilated before he defeated them, though they resisted for a long time. [Note: [Col. 0833D] “From there, the Drangae.” This is rightly written here; in the commonly printed books it is incorrectly “Dracae.” Arrian calls them “Δράγγας” and Diodorus calls their region “τὴν Δραγγινὴν.” FABR.] From there he subdued the Drangae, [Note: [Col. 0833D] “Evergetae.” They received this name, meaning “benefactors,” from Cyrus, king of the Persians, since previously they were called Ariaspae, as in Arrian and Curtius, or Arimaspi, as Diodorus has it. FABR.] the Evergetae, [Col. 0834A] [Note: [Col. 0833D] “Parimas, Parapamenos, Adaspios.” I find these forms in the manuscripts of Orosius and Justin, but I have nothing further to say about them. Besides Justin, Book XII, Curtius in Book VII and Arrian in Book IV discuss the founding of Alexandria on the River Tanais. FABR.] Parimas, Parapamenos, Adaspios, and the other peoples who lived at the foot of the Caucasus, establishing there the city of Alexandria on the River Tanais.

But his cruelty toward his own men was no less than his fury against the enemy. [Note: [Col. 0834B] “Amyntas bears witness to this.” All who have written about Alexander’s deeds discuss these matters. Concerning Parmenion and his son Philotas, who were killed, see Diodorus in the latter part of Book XVII, Plutarch in his *Alexander*, Arrian in Book III, and Curtius in Books VI and VII. Concerning Alexandria in Egypt, see above at the end of Chapter 16. FABR.] This is shown by the murder of Amyntas, his cousin; the killing of his stepmother and brothers; the slaughter of Parmenion and Philotas; and the destruction of Attalus, Eurylochus, Pausanias, and many Macedonian leaders. [Note: [Col. 0834B] “Clitus, too, advanced in years.” His name in Greek is “Κλεῖτος”; therefore the common form “Clytum” is incorrect. On Clitus, see Curtius VIII, Arrian IV, and Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* IV. “When King Alexander had killed Clitus, his intimate friend, he scarcely kept his hands from himself.” FABR.]

Clitus, too, advanced in years and a longtime friend, was wickedly killed. When, at a banquet, relying on the intimacy of their friendship, he defended the memory of his father Philip against the king, who was preferring his own achievements to those of his father, in vain, [Note: [Col. 0834C] “By the offended king, in vain.” The sense requires this transposition: “he defended the memory of his father in vain, with the king offended,” etc., unless “in vain” means “unjustly” or “undeservedly.”] he was pierced through with a hunting spear by the angered king. [Note: [Col. 0834C] “Pierced through with a hunting spear.” Curtius writes that Alexander pierced Clitus’s side with a spear. Arrian reports that some said Clitus was killed with a “λόγχη” [spear], others with a “σαρίσσα” [sarissa]; Plutarch calls it an “αἰχμή” [spear]. FABR.] As he died, he bloodied the common banquet. [Note: [Col. 0834C] “Bloodied in death.” My manuscript has “bloodied by death.”]

But Alexander, insatiable of human blood, [Note: [Col. 0834C] “Insatiable.” I find this in all the manuscripts, except that the first Leiden manuscript has “unsatisfied.” All the printed editions likewise have “insatiable,” except the Augustan edition, which has “inexhaustibly insatiable,” as Fabricius and Scott printed it. Cicero, *Speech for Publius Sestius*, chapter 51: “Booklets were often pawned even for wine; the insatiable belly remained, while supplies failed.”] whether of enemies [Col. 0834B] or even of allies, nevertheless always [Note: [Col. 0834C] “Thirsted for fresh blood.” An epigram on Tiberius in Suetonius, chapter 59:

“He scorns wine because now this man thirsts for blood.”] thirsted for fresh blood. Therefore, pressing forward into wars with relentless attack, [Note: [Col. 0834D] “The Chorasmii and Dahae.” The manuscripts of Orosius and Justin have “Dahae,” not “Dacae”; Curtius likewise names them this way in Books VII and VIII. The Greeks call them “Δάαι.” Those whom Justin and Orosius call “Chorasmiani” are called “Χωρασμενοί” by Arrian in Book IV and Strabo in Book XI; Spitamenes fled to them. Pliny, Book VI, chapter 16, calls them the Chorasmii. FABR.] he accepted into submission the Chorasmii and Dahae, an unconquered people. [Note: [Col. 0834D] “The philosopher Callisthenes.” On the death of Callisthenes of Olynthus, see at length Arrian IV, Plutarch’s *Alexander*, and Curtius VIII. Marcus Tullius, *For Rabirius Postumus*: “We are told that Callisthenes, an educated man and companion of Alexander the Great, was killed by Alexander.” FABR.] He killed the philosopher Callisthenes, who had been his fellow student under Aristotle, along with many other leaders, because Callisthenes, rejecting the customary form of greeting, would not worship him as a god.

## CHAPTER XIX. Alexander subdues India; defeats King Porus; subjects cities and peoples.

[Col. 0835A]

After this [Note: [Col. 0835B] “He set out for India.” Perizonius has “he set out for India.”] he set out for India, so that he might bring his empire to the Ocean and the farthest East. [Note: [Col. 0835B] “He approached the city of Nysa.” Strabo, Arrian, Dionysius, and Eustathius call this Indian city “Νύσσα” [Nysa]; Arrian discusses it at length at the beginning of Book III. FABR.] He approached the city of Nysa, [Note: [Col. 0835B] “The Daedalian mountains.” Cicero, Book VIII: “From there they reached the region called Daedala.” FABR.] the Daedalian mountains, [Note: [Col. 0835B] “And the kingdom of Cleophis.” Cleophis, the mother of Assacanus, ruled that region after her son’s death, at the time when Alexander came into India. Justin XII; Curtius VIII. The chief town of that region was called by Arrian “Μάοσαγα,” by Diodorus “Μάσσακα,” by Strabo “Μαγόσα,” and by Curtius Mazaga; Alexander besieged it and captured it by surrender. FABR.] and conquered the kingdom of Queen Cleophis. When she had surrendered, [Note: [Col. 0835B] “Redeemed the kingdom by intercourse.” Besides Justin XII.7 and Curtius VIII.10, Diodorus Siculus also mentions this woman in Book XVII, p. 554. She is said to have borne a son by Alexander, whose descendants ruled this part of India for a long time; but she herself afterward acquired the disgraceful title of royal concubine.] she redeemed her kingdom by sexual intercourse.

After Alexander had traversed and subdued India, when he reached a rock of extraordinary ruggedness and height, [Note: [Col. 0835C] “To a rock of extraordinary ruggedness.” According to Diodorus and Arrian, this rock was called “πέτρα ἄορνος,” “the Aornian rock.” Hence Curtius’s books must be corrected, where they read: “The armed inhabitants occupied a rock named Dorinim,” since one should read “Aornon” or “Aornim,” as in some copies of Diodorus. FABR.] into which many peoples had fled, [Note: [Col. 0835C] “Into which many peoples.” Four Leiden manuscripts together with the third Florentine, the Ultramontane, and the Groningen collection have “in which,” etc. Soon afterward my manuscript has “by assault,” and then “through rivalry.”] he learned that Hercules had been prevented by an earthquake from capturing the same rock. Moved by rivalry, so that he might surpass the deeds of Hercules, he seized the rock with the greatest labor and danger and accepted all the peoples of the place into submission. [Note: [Col. 0835C] “With Porus, the most valiant.” Diodorus in Book XVII, Arrian in Book V, and Curtius at the end of Book VIII write that the war with Porus was fought with losses among the Macedonians. Plutarch recounts the affair with Porus from Alexander’s letters. FABR.] He fought a most bloody war with Porus, the bravest king of the Indians. [Col. 0836A] In it Alexander engaged Porus himself in single combat and, when his horse had been killed and he had been thrown down, escaped the immediate danger of death through the intervention of his guards. [Note: [Col. 0835C] “And, when his horse had been killed, he was thrown down.” Some report that Bucephalus, Alexander’s horse, was killed in this battle. Plutarch and Arrian. FABR.] Porus, pierced by many wounds, was captured. Restored to his kingdom as a mark of his valor, [Note: [Col. 0835C] “There he founded two cities.” “Τὴν μὲν Νίκαιαν, τῆς νίκης τῆς κατ᾽ Ἰνδῶν ἐπώνυμον ὠνόμασε, τὴν δὲ Βουκεφάλαν, ἐς τοῦ ἵππου τοῦ Βουκεφάλου τὴν μνήμην ὃς ἀπέθανεν αὐτοῦ.” “He named one Nicaea, after the victory won over the Indians, and the other Bucephala, in memory of his horse Bucephalus, which had died there.” Diodorus writes the same, as do Strabo in Book XV; but whereas Diodorus and Arrian call the second city “Βουκεφάλα,” Plutarch calls it “Βουκεφαλία.” In our manuscripts it is “Nicaea and Bucephalen.” FABR.] he founded two cities there, Nicaea and Bucephala, which he ordered to be so called after the name of his horse.

[Note: [Col. 0835C] “From there, the Adrestae.” This is the form in the ancient manuscripts, not the commonly printed “Arestae.” Diodorus calls them “Ἀνδρεστάς,” and Arrian “Ἀδραιστάς.” FABR.] From there the Adrestae, [Note: [Col. 0835C] “The Cathaeans.” The printed editions have “Statheni”; the ancient copies have “Cathaeni,” and therefore, following Arrian, I printed “Cathaeans.” In Diodorus’s books one reads corruptly “εἰς τὴν τῶν Καθαρῶν χώραν” for “Καθαίων,” with αρ written for αι; this is made clear by Strabo, Book XV. FABR.—Four Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen collection have “Catheni.”] the Cathaeans, [Note: [Col. 0836B] “The Praesidae and Gandaridae.” In the manuscripts of Orosius the reading is not “Passidae” but “Praesidae”; in the ancient copies of Justin, “Praesidiae.” Plutarch, in his *Alexander*, writes “Γανδαρίτας καὶ Πραισίους,” although immediately afterward one reads “οἱ Πραισιαίων βασιλεῖς.” Diodorus has: “Beyond this dwell the peoples of the Tabraesii and Gandaridae, and their king is Xandrames.” Curtius writes: “Beyond the river lived the Gandaridae and Pharasii, whose king was Aggrammes.” Comparing these passages, it seems that Diodorus should read “Πραισίων,” Curtius “Praesii,” and “Xandrames.” FABR.—The better and more numerous manuscripts, as also in Curtius, have “Gangaridae.”] the Praesidae and Gangaridae, were conquered by the Macedonians after their armies had been slaughtered.

When they had reached [Note: [Col. 0836B] “To Chofides.” It is also read as “Cophides,” and in Justin’s books as “Euphites” or “Cuphites.” I am uncertain about this name. Perhaps the person intended is the one called Sophites by Curtius and “Σωπείθης” by Diodorus and Strabo. For when Alexander had advanced to the Hyphasis River in his kingdom, he was recalled by the soldiers’ pleas; but the others say nothing about a battle. FABR.—The three Florentine manuscripts read “Chofides.” The second Leiden manuscript has “Confides.” The others generally have “Cophides.” Yet all the manuscripts have “when they had reached,” not “and when they had reached.” Of these readings, one of “cavalry” and “enemies” seems superfluous. Perizonius and the Augustan edition seem more correctly to delete “cavalry.” I think Curtius is discussing all these peoples, although he names only two, when he writes that their king Agrammes blocked the roads with 20,000 cavalry and 200,000 infantry. The number of cavalry perhaps dropped out of Orosius, as also from Justin XII.8, from whom Orosius drew his material.] Chofides, they joined battle there against 200,000 enemy cavalry. Though by then worn down by age, troubled in spirit, and exhausted in strength, they won with difficulty; in memory of the event they built a camp more magnificent than usual.

From there Alexander [Note: [Col. 0836C] “To the Acesines River.” Dionysius the African writes of this, verse 1138:

“Then the navigable Hydaspes receives the Acesines,
which is drawn obliquely from the cliffs.”] proceeded to the Acesines River. By it he was carried down to the Ocean. [Note: [Col. 0836C] “There, the Gessones and Siboi.” The printed books of Justin have “Gessones Asybosque”; our ancient copy has “Jacensanos Sibosque.” Of the former Diodorus writes: “When they came to the region where the Hydaspes joins the Acesines, after disembarking the soldiers he led his forces against those called the Siboi.” Curtius, Book IX: “They had reached the region where the Hydaspes joins the Acesines; from there it flows down into the territory of the Siboi.” In the common text, however, “Sobii” is read here and “Ἴβους” there, both corruptly. FABR.—My copy has “Gesonas”; the three Florentine manuscripts have “Gesones.”] There he crushed the Gessones and Siboi, whom Hercules had founded.

[Note: [Col. 0836C] “From there to the Malli and Oxydracae.” We have corrected this, following the traces of the corrupted ancient reading in the books of Orosius and Justin. You will recognize that it must be read this way from the history given by Curtius in Book IX, Arrian in Book VI, and Diodorus in Book XVII. For what is read in Diodorus, “Συρακούσας,” is corrupt, as Henri Estienne observed; but I am surprised that so learned a man did not see that “Ὀξυδράκας” should be restored. FABR.] From there [Col. 0837A] he sailed toward the Malli and Oxydracae, [Col. 0837B] peoples who met him with 80,000 infantry and 60,000 cavalry. [Note: [Col. 0837B] “Eighty thousand infantry.” Diodorus also writes that they had “πεζοὺς πλείους τῶν ὀκτακισμυρίων,” more than 80,000 infantry. Hence Curtius’s books must be corrected, where they have: “Nine thousand assembled infantry were under arms.” In the number of cavalry, Orosius and Justin do not agree with Diodorus and Curtius. FABR.]

After the battle had begun, a long, uncertain, and bloody struggle at last gave the Macedonians an almost sorrowful victory. [Note: [Col. 0837C] “A sad victory, almost.” Following the old editions, Fabricius printed “almost the whole sad victory,” against the manuscripts, none of which acknowledges “whole,” nor does that word appear in the Augustan edition.] For when the enemy forces had been routed, Alexander led his army toward the city. [Note: [Col. 0837C] “And when he had climbed the wall.” The printed editions have “ascended”; the written books have “extended,” from which others may judge whether I have rightly restored Orosius’s ancient word. LAUT.—The reading should be restored from the manuscripts: “And when he himself had first climbed the wall.” The written copies transpose the words in this way; some have “extended,” “ascended,” or “had fallen out,” but the Lombard manuscript clearly has “had climbed.” On the proper use of the verb *escendere*, see Cortius’s notes on Sallust, p. 355. Above, Orosius used the verb *inscendere*, Book II, chapter 12: “They invaded and climbed the Capitol.” Thus it should be read there, not—as it is commonly printed—“set fire to and burned the Capitol.” For he followed Augustine, who, in *The City of God* III.17, has in the better manuscripts, in the same history of the assault on the Capitol: “Where they were, when Valerius the consul was killed while defending the Capitol that had been climbed by exiles and slaves.”]

And when he had first climbed the wall, thinking the city empty, he alone leapt inside. When hostile men surrounded him on every side, it is incredible to say that neither the multitude of enemies, nor the great force of their missiles, nor so great a clamor of attackers terrified him: alone, he cut down and routed many thousands. But when he perceived that he was being overwhelmed by the crowd surrounding him, [Note: [Col. 0837D] “With the barrier of the wall behind him.” The second Florentine manuscript has “by the obstacle of the wall.” Soon afterward, instead of “having defended,” the third Florentine and my manuscript have “safe.”] he protected his rear with the wall as a barrier and more easily held off his opponents until, in response to the danger threatening him and the cries of the enemy, the entire army burst in through the broken walls. In that battle, [Note: [Col. 0837D] “Pierced by an arrow beneath the breast.” Diodorus: “τοξευθεὶς ὑπὸ τὸν μαστόν,” “shot beneath the breast.” Plutarch: “περὶ τὸν μαστόν,” “around the breast.” Arrian: “ὑπὲρ τὸν μαστόν,” “above the breast.” Curtius: “An Indian discharged an arrow two cubits long, so that it pierced the chest and lodged slightly above the right side.” FABR.] pierced beneath the breast by an arrow, [Note: [Col. 0837D] “With his knee fixed.” Or should it be “with his knee bent”?] with his knee fixed, he fought until he killed the man by whom [Note: [Col. 0837D] “He had been wounded.” Perizonius has “had been wounded.”] he had been wounded.

Then, after boarding ships and traveling along the shores of the Ocean, he reached a certain city, [Col. 0838A] [Note: [Col. 0837D] “Over which King Ambira presided.” Ambira is also found in our ancient copies; in Justin XII one reads: “When he had come to the city of King Ambiger.” Strabo says that this occurred in the territory of the Orites; Diodorus names the city Harmatelia, in the territory of the Brahmans; Curtius places it in the kingdom of Sambi. FABR.—In the first Leiden manuscript the king’s name is written Abira; in the fourth, Ahira.] over which King Ambira presided. During the assault on the city he lost a large part of his army to the arrows of the enemy, which had been smeared with poison. [Note: [Col. 0838B] “He lost.” Perizonius’s manuscript has “destroyed.”] Afterwards, when a herb shown to him in a dream had been given as a drink to the wounded and assistance had been brought to the rest, he stormed and captured the city.

## CHAPTER XX. All the provinces, terrified, sent ambassadors to Alexander seeking peace. Alexander died by poison. An address to the readers.

After, as it were, having completed his circuit, [Note: [Col. 0838B] “After the goal had been rounded.” This is the correct reading, preserved by the Lombard manuscript together with the manuscripts and better editions. Some manuscripts have: “After, as though he had traversed India as far as the Ocean and entered the Indus River.”] he entered the Indus River from the Ocean and quickly returned to Babylon, where [Note: [Col. 0838C] “Where they awaited him.” The Augustan edition has “there they awaited him.”] the ambassadors of the provinces of the entire world, terrified, awaited him: namely, those of the Carthaginians and of all the cities of Africa, and also of the Spaniards, Gauls, [Col. 0838B] Sicily, and Sardinia; [Note: [Col. 0838C] “Of a very large part of Italy besides.” From Italy came ambassadors from the Bruttians, Lucanians, and Etruscans. Some have also written that Romans came; but Arrian does not consider this true. FABR.—Arrian, Book VII, chapter 15, p. 224, discusses the report of this Roman embassy in such a way that he dares neither affirm nor entirely reject it. But Cleitarchus clearly asserts it in Pliny, *Natural History* III, p. 152 of Hardouin’s edition. Indeed, if the Carthaginians sent Hamilcar Rhodian there to investigate Alexander’s schemes, why should the Romans not also have sent one of their own for the same purpose, or even in the name of an embassy—especially since Orosius reports that Alexander’s military success so moved them that they looked around for a commander to use against him and placed their chief confidence in the consul Papirius, as he explains above in Chapter 15?] and, besides, those of most of Italy. [Col. 0839A]

Such fear of the commander established in the far East had seized the peoples of the far West [Note: [Col. 0838D] “Of the farthest West.” The Augustan edition has “in the farthest West.” Below, Book VI, chapter 21: “Meanwhile, the ambassadors of the Indians and Scythians, having crossed the whole world, at last found Caesar at Tarraco, a city of Hither Spain, beyond which they could no longer search; and they transferred to Caesar the glory of Alexander the Great. Just as the embassy of Spaniards and Gauls approached him in the middle East at Babylon, seeking peace, so the eastern Indian and northern Scythian approached this man in Spain, at the farthest point of the West, as a suppliant, with a customary gift.”] that you might see a foreign embassy coming from the place to which you would scarcely believe that news had reached. But Alexander, at Babylon, while still thirsting for blood and having poorly disciplined his greed, [Note: [Col. 0839B] “When he had drunk poison, he died.” Justin and Orosius follow those who wrote that Alexander was killed by poison. Plutarch and Arrian reject this account; read them. FABR.—The story that Alexander was given poison is fiction, which certain writers embellished in various ways. Plutarch, in his *Alexander*, p. 707, clearly demonstrates this, and no suspicion of poison arose before Olympias invented this accusation against the household of Antipater and Cassander, whom she hated with feminine resentment. See the *History of the Life of Alexander* that we have composed, in more than one place.] died when he had drunk poison through the plotting of his attendants.

O hard mind of human beings, and heart always inhuman! I myself, who review these matters in order to assert the alternating misery of all ages, when recounting so great an evil—an evil by which the whole world trembled, whether from death itself or from fear of death—did I shed tears with my eyes? Did I grieve in my heart? Did I, turning these things over, make the sufferings of my ancestors my own on account of the common condition of life? Yet whenever I speak about myself—how I first saw unknown barbarians, how I avoided hostile men, how I won the favor of rulers, [Note: [Col. 0839C] “I won them over.” The Lombard manuscript and the fourth Leiden manuscript have “I won them over.” I do not change the text, since *eblandiri* means to elicit and obtain something by flattering. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, final book, letter 19: “Now, my dear Capito, work hard—or rather, flatter and accomplish it—that Plato’s,” etc.] how I guarded against the faithless, how I escaped those lying in wait, and finally how, when pursuers at sea were attacking me with rocks [Note: [Col. 0839C] “And spears.” All manuscripts and editions have “spears,” except the Augustan edition, which has “watchtowers,” as though the passage concerned ambushes from a lookout; I do not think so. The same edition has “those pressing upon” for “those seeking.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “those adding”; but the first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection, have “those attending.” In what follows he alludes to the Homeric story of Aeneas, who was rescued from the hands of his enemies by the gods, surrounded by a cloud.] and spears, [Col. 0839B] and were almost already seizing me with their hands, I escaped, enveloped in a sudden fog—I would like all who hear me to be moved to tears, and silently I would grieve over those who do not grieve, reflecting upon the hardness of those who do not believe what they themselves have not endured. [Note: [Col. 0839D] “The Spaniard and the Maurine.” Our ancient copies have “the Spaniard and the seafarer.” FABR.—I am surprised that Fabricius neither found the true reading in the manuscripts nor devised it himself. For what are “the Spanish Maurine” or “Marinus”?
