It must certainly be read as it appears in the Augustan edition and in the first and third Leiden manuscripts, in my manuscript, in Perizonius, in the Groningen collection, and finally in the three Florentine manuscripts: “the Spaniard and the Morinian,” although the Lombard manuscript, or first Florentine, writes “Morenus.” The Morini are appropriately joined with the Spaniards, being even farther removed from Asia; they are called “the farthest of peoples” by Virgil in *Aeneid* VIII.727:]

The Morini, the furthest people of mankind, and the two-horned Rhine.

[Note: [Col. 0840B] These formerly belonged to the Celts; ancient writers also affirm that Celts were seen among the ambassadors at that time, as may be gathered from the passage of Arrian indicated by us. Orosius himself therefore joins the embassy of the Spaniards and Gauls—that is, the Celts—in Book VI, chapter 21, as is clear from the words cited above in note 5.]

The Spaniard and the Morinian came to Babylon to supplicate Alexander, and sought out that bloodstained master through Assyria and India so that he might not receive an enemy, traversing the limits of the earth and unhappily known to both oceans; yet the memory of so violent a necessity has either failed through forgetfulness or become insignificant through the passage of time. And we suppose that what will cling to perpetual remembrance is that, while most of the world was secure, a fugitive brigand violated one corner of it—as though, to say nothing of the Indian and Assyrian in reversed circumstances, even the Spaniard himself, who suffers the enemy, had asked for the peace of the Goths and Suevi.

[Note: [Col. 0840C] “But if those [times]”: the three Florentine manuscripts, agreeing with Meus, read “But if any [such times].”]

[Note: [Col. 0840C] “Was conquered”: my manuscript, together with Perizonius and three Leiden manuscripts, deletes this phrase here because it occurs again immediately afterward.]

[Note: [Col. 0840C] “And even now very many”: four Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection read “very many indeed.” But the common reading is preferable, because “if those times of Alexander,” etc., has preceded. The Augustan edition gives both readings: “very many indeed” or “even now very many.”]

But if those times of Alexander are judged worthy of praise rather on account of the valor by which the whole world was conquered than detestable on account of the ruin by which the whole world was overturned, then even now many will be found who think them worthy of praise because they conquered many peoples and regard the miseries of others as their own happiness.

But let someone say: “These are enemies of Romania.”

[Note: [Col. 0840C] “Anyone”: all the manuscripts read *quisquam*; the common printed editions have the same reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0840C–D] “These are enemies of Romania”: Fabricius wrote here “They are enemies of the Romans,” alarmed, I suppose, by the apparent absurdity of the word *Romania*. But since the Cologne manuscript has this reading, I did not hesitate to recognize it as Orosian, especially because in Book VII he also speaks thus: “And, to speak in common terms, Gothia would be what Romania had been.” LAUTERBACH.—Lauterbach is entirely right; three Florentine manuscripts confirm the reading, among them the best and oldest, written in Lombardic characters.]

It will be answered: This is also how Alexander then appeared to the entire East; and the Romans likewise appeared in this way to others when they attacked peoples who were living in peace and were unknown to them. But those men sought to acquire kingdoms, whereas these seek to overthrow them. The ruin inflicted by an enemy and the judgments of the victor are distinct: for the former first afflicted those whom they later organized under their own laws; and the latter now disturb in a hostile manner those things which—may God not permit it—if they should possess them after subduing them, they would endeavor to arrange according to their own custom, telling posterity that they were great kings, although now they are adjudged by us to be the most savage enemies.

[Note: *Hostiliter turbant, quae* (“they disturb in a hostile manner those things which”) is how this passage of Orosius must altogether be read and punctuated. Some manuscripts and printed editions inserted *regna* (“kingdoms”), reading “they disturb the kingdoms.” But neither the old editions nor the three Florentine manuscripts, nor Meus, Perizon, or the fourth Leiden manuscript together with the Groningen Collection, recognize that word. Furthermore, instead of *in quo non* (“in which not”), which most manuscripts read for the parenthetical words *quod non permiserit Deus* (“which may God not permit”), the first and third Florentine manuscripts (the second has erased it), Meus, Perizon, Utrecht, the Groningen Collection, and the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts read *quae*; in the first Leiden manuscript one page is missing. Thus all the manuscripts, as well as the Augustan edition, are corrupt.]

[Note: [Col. 0841C] “Whatever name such deeds may be assigned”: I have restored this from the three Florentine and three Leiden manuscripts and all the rest, as well as the old editions, in place of the common reading “but whatever deeds.” Immediately afterward, one or two of the same witnesses read “such” in place of “such deeds.”]

[Note: [Col. 0841C] “In the present age”: Perizonius and the old editions read “at this time.” But Orosius very frequently inserts *in hoc* into his discourse.]

[Note: [Col. 0841C] “And thus both”: this is the reading of all manuscripts. The old editions read, “and thus both work to our advantage.” The Augustan edition reads, “and thus both work to our advantage,” and absurdly reads at the end of the chapter “of the Romans rather than of the Persians.”]

Whatever name such deeds may be assigned—that is, whether they are called miseries or virtues—when compared with earlier events, both are lesser in the present age; and thus both work to our advantage in comparison with Alexander and the Persians: if what exists now must be called valor, the enemies’ valor is lesser; if misery, the Romans’ misery is lesser.

## Chapter XXI. The conspiracy and defeat of the Etruscans, Umbrians, Samnites, and Gauls against the Romans.

[Note: In the year 450 from the founding of the City. This year, in which Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus for the fifth time and Publius Decius Mus for the fourth time were consuls, is dated in the Capitoline Fasti from the founding of the City as 458. Livy gives it as 457; he describes this war in Book X. FABRICIUS.]

In the year 450 from the founding of the City, when Fabius Maximus was consul for the fifth time and Decius Mus for the fourth, four of Italy’s bravest and most flourishing peoples joined together in one army and alliance. For the Etruscans, Umbrians, Samnites, and Gauls, conspiring in a single host, attempted to destroy the Romans. The Romans’ spirits were shaken by this war, and their confidence was undermined; nor did they dare to place complete reliance on their own strength.

[Note: [Col. 0841C–D] The Groningen Collection reads “and [they were] shaken”; the second Leiden manuscript and Perizonius, together with the old editions, read “and confidence was undermined.” Both are Latin idioms.]

[Note: [Col. 0841D] Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection and Perizonius, read, “nor did they dare to place complete reliance on their strength.”]

Thinking it safer to engage the enemy in several wars than in major ones, they divided them by strategy.

[Note: [Col. 0841D] The first edition and those following it read: “thinking it safer to divide the enemy by strategy, they involved themselves in several wars rather than serious ones.” The Lombardic manuscript has *totius* in place of *tutius*, a reading preferred in the Venetian editions.]

Thus, after sending some of their own men ahead to ravage the enemy territory in Umbria and Etruria, they compelled the army of the Umbrians and Etruscans to return to defend their own lands, and hastened to enter upon war with the Samnites and Gauls.

[Note: Livy mentions only that the Etruscans were compelled by the report of the devastation to return to defend their territory; it may be inferred from him that the Umbrians did not take part in the battle. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: This war was fought in the territory of Sentinum, *ἐν τῇ τῶν Σεντινατῶν χώρᾳ*—“in the land of the people of Sentinum,” as Polybius says in Book II. FABRICIUS.]

In this war, when the Romans were being hard pressed by the Gauls’ attack, the consul Decius was killed.

[Note: [Col. 0841D–0842C] This was the second of the Decii, whom Cicero says in the *Cato* spurred their horses toward voluntary death. The son, imitating his father, devoted himself in his fourth consulship, in Book II of *On Ends*. Cicero, however, writes in *Tusculan Disputations* I that Decius the son, fighting the Etruscans, exposed himself to the weapons of the enemy; in this he differs from others, who write that this Decius fought the Gauls. FABRICIUS.]

Fabius, however, after a great slaughter of Decius’s forces, finally won. In that battle, forty thousand Samnites or Gauls are reported to have been killed, while seven thousand Romans were destroyed—only from the division of Decius, who was killed.

[Note: The Leiden third and fourth manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, read “fifty thousand.”]

It is reported that, apart from the Etruscans and Umbrians, whom the Romans cleverly drew away from the war, the Samnites and Gauls had one hundred forty thousand three hundred thirty infantry and forty-four thousand cavalry; Livy gives these figures. He also says that one thousand charioteers stood armed against the Roman line.

[Note: [Col. 0842C] “One hundred forty thousand four hundred thirty infantry, and forty-six thousand cavalry”: thus these figures are read in the excellent manuscript of Cornelius Gualter; Livy likewise reports this number from the annals of other writers. FABRICIUS.—The same number is found in the three Florentine manuscripts, Meus, Perizonius, and the first Leiden manuscript, except that Meus, Perizonius, the second Leiden manuscript, and the Groningen Collection give forty-seven thousand cavalry.]

But, as has often been said, just as the Romans’ domestic peace was always interrupted by foreign wars, so their foreign successes were burdened by internal diseases.

[Note: [Col. 0842C–D] “Foreign successes”: *Τὰς ἔξωθεν εὐτυχίας καὶ εὐημερίας*, “external good fortune and prosperity.” The common reading, contrary to the authority of the ancient books, is “events.” Livy also mentions the pestilence by which this year was grievous. FABRICIUS.]

Thus their great spirits were oppressed from every direction in every possible way.

[Note: [Col. 0842D] The old editions read *omnimode*; both forms are Latin and occur more than once in Lucretius.]

Pestilence weighed down this bloody and mournful victory of theirs, and the funeral processions of those who met them polluted the triumphal ceremonies.

[Note: [Col. 0842D] There was no sense in the preceding words because the passage was incorrectly punctuated by placing a full stop before “this.” We remedied it by the smallest alteration, restoring a lighter punctuation mark.]

There was no one to whom joy over a triumph could be recommended, since the entire city either sighed for the sick or mourned the dead.

## Chapter XXII. The Romans, defeated by the Samnites, defeat them in turn; an unbearable pestilence afflicts the Romans. Again they overcome the Samnites, and the Samnites fall. The consul Curius successfully wages war against the Sabines. The Romans suffer a shameful defeat at the hands of the Gauls and their allies.

[Note: The following year. This year had Lucius Postumius Megellus and Marcus Atilius Regulus as consuls; “its chronology is rather uncertain,” says Livy in Book X. Consult him. FABRICIUS.]

The following year, when the Samnites had renewed the war, the Romans were defeated and fled into their camp. Afterwards, the Samnites, assuming a new appearance and spirit—that is, with their weapons and clothing silver-plated and with their minds prepared to die if they did not win—offered themselves for battle.

[Note: [Col. 0843B] The third and fourth Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen Collection add “twenty-four thousand” after this.]

[Note: The armor and the spirit prepared for combat are briefly indicated here; Livy gives a full account at the end of Book X. FABRICIUS.]

Against them the consul Papirius was sent with an army.

[Note: [Col. 0843B] This is Lucius Papirius Cursor, colleague in the consulship of Spurius Carvilius in the year 460 after Rome’s foundation; Valerius Maximus also mentions him, apart from Livy, in Book VII, chapter 2, concerning the keeper of the sacred chickens. FABRICIUS.]

Although the pullarii augurs, making a vain prediction, tried to prevent him from engaging, he mocked them and completed the war as successfully as he had undertaken it resolutely. In this battle twelve thousand of the enemy are reported to have been killed and three thousand captured.

[Note: The third Leiden manuscript reports twenty thousand enemy dead and four thousand captured. The Groningen Collection and Vincent of Beauvais, Book VI, chapter 6, agree concerning the number of captives.]

But this victory too—truly worthy of praise, since the false auspices had been unable to hinder it—was suddenly spoiled by the outbreak of disease.

[Note: [Col. 0843B–C] Perizonius, the third Leiden manuscript, the Groningen Collection, and the Augustan edition read *aruspices* (“diviners”) for *auspices*. The same edition reads *arripuit* (“undertook”) for *corripuit* (“seized”) below.] For such a great and unbearable pestilence then seized the city that, in order to calm it by whatever means possible, they thought the Sibylline Books should be consulted and brought from Epidaurus that dreadful serpent,

[Note: Livy wrote about this matter at the end of Book X and continued it in Book XI, as is known from the epitome, where a serpent or snake is mentioned. Consult Pausanias, Book II, and Ovid, Book XV of the *Metamorphoses*. FABRICIUS.]

together with the very stone of Aesculapius.

[Note: We find a record of this story on an ancient Roman as, struck by the quaestor Eppius. It displays the customary type of the asses: the double head of Janus and a ship. But between the two temples of the double Janus appears a mark of remarkable antiquity, namely an altar decorated with ribbons, on which lies a stone shaped like a cone or half an egg, around which a serpent coils. That serpent represents the Epidaurian snake itself and the god; the stone represents the very stone of which Orosius speaks; and the altar represents the worship of Aesculapius, whom the Romans solemnly received when they brought the god over. Eppius seems to have used this type because perhaps one of his ancestors had been in charge of this undertaking. The figure on his coin is as follows.]

They brought it over together with the stone of Aesculapius—as though pestilence had either not previously been brought under control or had not arisen afterward.

[Note: [Col. 0843D] The Augustan edition reads “led it [there]” rather than “brought it over.”]

Moreover, in the following year but one, the consul Fabius Gurges fought unsuccessfully against the Samnites.

[Note: The following year but one: the year after Lucius Papirius, when Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges and Decimus Junius Brutus Scaeva were consuls. Robortellus is certainly mistaken, for he everywhere takes *alterum* to mean “second.” FABRICIUS.]

For, having lost his army, he was defeated and fled back to Rome.

[Note: Eutropius, Book II, reports that three thousand men were killed. FABRICIUS.]

Therefore, when the senate was deliberating about removing him from office, his father, Fabius Maximus, pleaded against his son’s disgrace and voluntarily offered to go as his son’s lieutenant, if the son were granted the opportunity to remove the disgrace and wage war again. After this was granted, and battle had been joined, he suddenly saw his son the consul fighting, hemmed in by the Samnite commander Pontius and surrounded by the enemy’s hostile weapons. The pious old man, mounted on horseback, thrust himself into the midst of the battle line.

[Note: Meus reads “into the midst of the enemy’s battle line,” which is wrong. The edition of Mainz reads *ignem* (“fire”) instead of *agmen* (“battle line”), which is worse.]

Moved by this deed, the Romans threw their entire line into the fight there, until they captured the commander himself, Pontius, after destroying and overpowering the enemy army. In that battle twenty thousand Samnites were killed, while four thousand, together with their king, were captured; and at last the Samnite war—which had continued for forty-nine years amid much Roman slaughter—was ended by the capture of its commander.

[Note: In some copies the number is incorrectly given as fifty-nine. For if the year in which Quintus Fabius was consul for the fifth time and Publius Decius for the fourth is correctly called by Livy the forty-sixth year of the Samnite war, this must be the forty-ninth. FABRICIUS. The number fifty-nine is found in some manuscripts and in Vincent of Beauvais, Book VI, chapter 8, where, somewhat earlier, the words “with their king Pontius” are read.]

[Note: [Col. 0844D] In the following year, in 463 from the foundation of the City, Manius Curius Dentatus was consul with Publius Cornelius Rufinus. Eutropius writes that both defeated the Samnites; Cicero in the *Cato* shows that Curius triumphed over the Samnites, and this is also written in the book *On Illustrious Men*. Orosius mentions only what was done among the Sabines, as does Florus in Book I, chapter 15. FABRICIUS.]

In the following year war was waged against the Sabines under the consul Curius. There the consul himself showed how many thousands of men had been killed and how many captured: when he wished to report in the senate the extent of the Sabine territory acquired and the multitude of the people captured, he was unable to state the number.

[Note: In the second Florentine manuscript, “to explain the number.”]

[Note: [Col. 0844D] According to the Capitoline Fasti, which we follow as the most trustworthy guides, this is the year 470, when Publius Cornelius Dolabella and Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus were consuls. Pighius also corrects the numerical error in *Annals*, vol. I, p. 414. FABRICIUS.]

In the year 463 from the founding of the City, when Dolabella and Domitius were consuls, the Lucanians, Bruttians, and Samnites, having also formed an alliance with the Etruscans and Senonian Gauls, were plotting to renew the war against the Romans.

[Note: According to Polybius in Book II, these ambassadors were sent by Marcus Curius to Gaul *ὑπὲρ τῶν αἰχμαλώτων*—“for the ransom of the captives”; but the Gauls, *παρασπονδήσαντες ἐπανείλοντο*—“having violated the law of nations, killed them.” The loss of Livy has therefore inflicted great damage on history, for at the beginning of Book XII he had explained the matter at length. FABRICIUS.]

The Romans sent ambassadors to entreat the Gauls. When the Gauls had killed them, the praetor Caecilius was sent with an army to avenge the ambassadors’ death and suppress the enemy’s uprising; but he was overwhelmed and killed by the Etruscans and Gauls.

[Note: Augustine mentions this praetor Caecilius in *The City of God*, Book III, chapter 17, and in the epitome of Livy he is named the praetor Lucius Caecilius. From this one recognizes the error of Sipontinus, who translated Polybius’s *Λευκίου τοῦ στρατηγοῦ τελευτήσαντος* as “with Lucius the consul lost.” As for the remnants of the Gauls, Publius Dolabella destroyed them in Etruria at Lake Vadimo, as Florus says in Book I, chapter 13, *περὶ τὴν Οὐάδμονα προσαγορευομένην λίμνην*—“at the lake called Vadimo.” Polybius. FABRICIUS.]

Seven military tribunes were also killed in that battle, and many nobles were slaughtered; thirteen thousand Roman soldiers were laid low in that war.

[Note: I have deleted what was senselessly inserted after *millia* (“thousands”) in all the printed editions and manuscripts, doing so on the authority of the Longobardic manuscript. Instead of thirteen thousand, the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, count eighteen thousand; and instead of “in that war,” some manuscripts read “in the war.”]

Thus, whenever the Gauls have risen up, Rome has been worn down with all her resources, so that under the present invasion of the Goths she ought all the more to remember the Gauls.

## Chapter XXIII. After Alexander, king of Macedonia, was killed by poison, his commanders divided the whole world among themselves and consumed one another in mutual wars.

[Col. 0845B]

But now I am recalled to review, during those same periods in which the Romans suffered these disasters, what wars the Macedonian commanders waged among themselves—those who, after Alexander’s death, received different provinces by lot and consumed one another in mutual wars. I seem to behold their most tumultuous period as though, from a mountain watchtower, I were looking by night upon some immense camp, seeing nothing across the great expanse of the plain except innumerable fires: so, throughout the entire kingdom of Macedonia—that is, throughout all Asia, most of Europe, and the greater part of Libya—did dreadful masses of wars suddenly blaze forth. Although they devastated especially the places in which they broke out, they threw all the remaining regions into confusion through the terror of rumor, as though through a darkness of smoke.

But I shall by no means unfold the wars and destructions of so many kings and kingdoms unless I first disclose the kingdoms themselves together with their kings. Alexander, therefore, for twelve years held the trembling world beneath him by the sword.

[Note: [Col. 0845D] “Alexander for twelve years.” Cicero says (*Philippics* V): “Alexander the Macedonian, having begun to accomplish the greatest deeds from early youth, died in his thirty-third year.” For he lived thirty-two years and eight months, and reigned twelve years and eight months. Arrian, at the end of Book VII. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0845C] “During these same periods.” The older editions read, “during the same periods.”]

His commanders, however, tore it apart for fourteen years and, like greedy whelps, ripped to pieces a rich prey laid low by a great lion; then, provoked against one another to quarrel by rivalry over the spoil, they ruined one another.

[Note: [Col. 0845D] “Greedy.” Perizonius reads *greedily*, and *tore apart* instead of *dilaniaverunt*.]

Accordingly, Egypt first fell by lot to Ptolemy, together with part of Africa and Arabia.

[Note: [Col. 0845D] “First to Ptolemy.” This is Πτολεμαῖος ὁ Λαγοῦ, “Ptolemy son of Lagos,” the first king of Egypt. From him onward, those who ruled Egypt down to Auletes—whom Aulus Gabinius restored after the Alexandrians had expelled him—and his son—whom Gaius Julius Caesar killed—bore the name Ptolemy.]

[Note: [Col. 0846B] “Egypt.” This must certainly be restored from the agreement of the manuscripts; Fabricius and the common editions incorrectly have *of Egypt*.]

Laomedon of Mytilene received Syria, adjoining that province; Philotas received Cilicia, and Philo the Illyrian received Illyria.

[Note: [Col. 0846B] “Laomedon of Mytilene.” Λαομέδων ὁ Μιτυληναῖος, “Laomedon of Mytilene,” to whom Syria together with Phoenicia was given, as Curtius writes in his last book.]

[Note: [Col. 0846C] “Philotas received Cilicia, and Philo the Illyrian [received Illyria].” This is also how it is read in our manuscript of Justin’s Book XIII; in the printed editions, *Philotas with his son, and the Illyrians* is corruptly read.]

Atropatus was placed over Greater Media, and the father-in-law of Perdiccas over Lesser Media.

[Note: [Col. 0846C] “Atropatus of Greater Media.” Ἀτροπάτης ὁ τῆς Μηδίας σατράπης, “Atropatus, satrap of Media,” occurs in Arrian, Book VII. From this it is evident that not only Justin and Orosius must be emended, but also Diodorus, where Book XVIII has Ἀτράτῃ δὲ Μηδίαν, with the two letters οπ omitted in the middle.]

[Note: [Col. 0846C] “The father-in-law of Perdiccas over Lesser [Media].” This is also found in the manuscripts; but Justin has, “Alcetas, the brother of Perdiccas, is placed over Lesser Media.” Ἀλκέτας ὁ ἀδελφὸς Περδίκκου, “Alcetas, the brother of Perdiccas,” is named by Diodorus in Book XVIII.]

The Susian people were assigned to Scynus, and Greater Phrygia to Antigonus, son of Philip. Nearchus received Lycia and Pamphylia, Cassander Caria, and Menander Lydia. Leonnatus received Lesser Phrygia.

[Note: [Col. 0846C] “The Susian people to Scynus.” Apart from Justin and Orosius, no one else, so far as I know, mentions Scynus. Antipater later gave τὴν Συσιανήν, “Susiana,” to Antigonus; to Perdiccas he had first assigned Pamphylia, Lycia, and τὴν μεγάλην καλουμένην Φρυγίαν, “the great Phrygia so called,” according to Diodorus. Orosius, however, following Justin, writes that Pamphylia and Lycia were given to Nearchus, whom he commonly calls Learchus. Nearchus is discussed by Diodorus, Plutarch, and Arrian.]

[Note: [Col. 0846D] “Menander [received] Lydia.” Menander is also found in the manuscripts of Justin and Orosius, but one may fear that the well-known Menander has migrated into this place in place of the unknown Meleager. For Diodorus writes that Lydia was assigned to Meleager.]

[Note: [Col. 0846D] “Lesser Phrygia.” Diodorus has Τὴν ἐφ’ Ἑλλησπόντῳ Φρυγίαν, “Phrygia on the Hellespont.”]

Thrace and the regions bordering the Pontic Sea went to Lysimachus; Cappadocia together with Paphlagonia was given to Eumenes. The supreme command of the army passed to Seleucus, son of Antiochus; Cassander, son of Antipater, was placed over the king’s bodyguards and attendants.

[Note: [Col. 0846D] “Thrace and the regions of the Pontic [Sea].” Diodorus says, “To Lysimachus were given Thrace and the neighboring peoples along the Pontic Sea.”]

[Note: [Col. 0847B] “Seleucus, son of Antiochus.” This is Seleucus, “who had become king of the part of Asia beyond the Euphrates,” as Appian says in his *Syrian Wars*: he ruled in Greater Asia and Syria.]

[Note: [Col. 0847B] “Is placed over.” Perizonius reads, “is placed before.”]

In farther Bactria and the regions of India, the former prefects who had begun their service under Alexander remained in office.

[Note: [Col. 0847B] “Under Alexander.” The third Leiden edition and Gronovius’s collection read, “by Alexander.”]

Taxiles held the Seres, situated between the two rivers, the Hydaspes and the Indus.

[Note: [Col. 0847B] “The Seres.” Our manuscript of Justin also has *Seres*, whereas the printed editions read, “But matters…”]

Pithon, son of Agenor, was sent to the colonies founded in India.

[Note: [Col. 0847B] “Pithon, son of Agenor.” Πεíθων or Πíθων ὁ Ἀγήνορος, “Pithon son of Agenor,” occurs in Diodorus and Arrian. From this it can be known how the name should be written.]

Oxyartes received the Parapamisadian territories on the borders of the Caucasus.

[Note: [Col. 0847C] “The borders of the Caucasus.” Nearly all the manuscripts, in strong agreement, have *at the border*, namely the first and third Florentine manuscripts together with four Leiden manuscripts, Meursius, Perizonius, and Gronovius’s collection. Orosius meant to indicate that these peoples were situated at the extreme ridges of the Caucasus. In Justin, Book XIII, chapter 4, Graevius reads *and the end* instead of *and the borders of the Caucasus*. In the same author, *Oxyartes* should be restored from Orosius in place of *Extarches*, or *Oxyarches*, as it stands in the Lombard manuscript and certain others.]

[Note: [Col. 0847C] “Oxyartes.” This name is correctly written *Oxyartes* in Gualther’s book; from it the common form *Axiarches* was produced. Diodorus writes: τὴν καὶ παρὰ τὸν Καύκασον κειμένην, ὀνομαζομένην δὲ Παροπισαδῶν, προσώρισεν Ὀξυάρτῃ τῷ Βακτριανῷ βασιλεῖ, τοῦ τὴν θυγατέρα Ῥωξάνην γεγαμηκῶς ἦν Ἀλέξανδρος—“He assigned the territory lying by the Caucasus, called that of the Paropamisadae, to Oxyartes, king of the Bactrians, whose daughter Roxane Alexander had married.” Thus Trogus said *the Parapamisadian territories*, that is, τὴν τῶν Παροπαμισαδῶν χώραν, “the territory of the Paropamisadae.”]

Arachosia and Gedrosia were assigned to Sibyrtius.

[Note: [Col. 0847D] “To Sibyrtius.” Diodorus has Σιβυρτίῳ ἔδωκεν Ἀραχωσίαν καὶ Κεδρωσίαν, “He gave Arachosia and Gedrosia to Sibyrtius.” Arrian, speaking of the same Sibyrtius, says: τούτῳ Ἀραχωτῶν τε καὶ Γεδρωσίων ἄρχειν ἐδόθη, “To him was given rule over the Aracho­tians and Gedrosians.” Plutarch also names Γεδρωσίαν, whereas Diodorus has Κεδρωσίαν. Our manuscripts read *Cedrosique*. In our ancient manuscript Justin’s mutilated passage is preserved intact as follows: “The Arachosians and Cedrosians are handed over to Sibyrtius; the Drangians and Araeans to Stasanor.” Arrian calls him Στασάνωρ ὁ Ἀρείων καὶ Δράγγων σατράπης, “Stasanor, satrap of the Areians and Drangians.” Diodorus likewise says, “To Stasanor of Soli he assigned Areia and Drangiana.”]

Stasanor received the Drangians and Areians. Amyntas drew Bactria, Scythaeus the Sogdians; Nicanor received Parthia, Philippus Hyrcania, Phrataphernes Armenia, Tlepolemus Persia, Peucestes Babylon, Archon the Pelasgians, and Archelaus Mesopotamia.

[Note: [Col. 0847D] “Amyntas.” In Diodorus this is Philippus, where we read: Φιλίππῳ προσώρισε Βακτριανὴν καὶ Σαρδιανήν, Φραταφέρνῃ Παρθυαΐαν, καὶ Ὑρκανίαν, Πευκέστῃ Περσίδα, Τληπολέμῳ Καρμανίαν, Ἄρχωνι Βαβυλονίαν, Ἀρχεσιλάῳ Μεσοποταμίαν—“To Philippus he assigned Bactria and Sardiana; to Phrataphernes, Parthia and Hyrcania; to Peucestes, Persia; to Tlepolemus, Carmania; to Archon, Babylonia; and to Archelaus, Mesopotamia.” Here one sees that Scythaeus and Nicanor are not mentioned. Our emendation is further supported by that authority, which I neglected in the name *Archelaus*, as it appears in the ancient copies.]

The cause and origin of the wars was a letter of King Alexander, in which he ordered all exiles to be restored to their country and liberty.

[Note: [Col. 0848B] “The letter of Alexander.” This letter was read aloud at the Olympic festival, as Justin says in Book XIII—Ολυμπιάσιν, as the Greeks say—and it is preserved in Diodorus, Book XVIII.]

The powerful men of the Greek cities, fearing that the exiles, once restored to freedom, might plan vengeance, revolted from the kingdom of Macedonia.

The Athenians were the first to wage war against Antipater, to whom Greece had fallen by lot. They assembled an army of thirty thousand and two hundred ships.

[Note: [Col. 0848B] “The Athenians were the first.” This war, which the Greeks waged against Antipater, was called the Lamian War and is described at length by Diodorus in Book XVIII.]

Through the orator Demosthenes they also brought Sicyon, Argos, Corinth, and the other cities into alliance with themselves, and surrounded Antipater with a siege.

[Note: [Col. 0848C] “Through Demosthenes.” On account of this service Demosthenes, who had been condemned because of the money received from Harpalus and had gone into exile, was recalled. See Plutarch, *Demosthenes*; Justin, Book XIII; and Pausanias, Book I. Three Florentine manuscripts together with Meursius and Perizonius later read *had come* instead of *had fallen by lot*.]

There their commander Leosthenes was killed, pierced by a missile thrown from the walls.

[Note: [Col. 0848C] “Pierced by a missile thrown from the walls.” Diodorus says: Πληγεὶς εἰς τὴν κεφαλὴν λίθῳ παραχρῆμα ἔπεσε, “Struck on the head by a stone, he immediately fell.” Consult him also concerning the death of Leonnatus.]

The Athenians encountered Leonnatus, who was bringing aid to Antipater, shattered his forces, and killed him.

Perdiccas, however, made war on Ariarathes, king of Cappadocia, and defeated him.

[Note: [Col. 0848C] “Ariarathes of the Cappadocians.” Diodorus calls him Ἀριαράθην τῆς Καππαδοκίας δυνάστην, “Ariarathes, ruler of Cappadocia.” Plutarch mentions him in the *Life of Eumenes*.]

In that victory he gained nothing except wounds and dangers, for all the inhabitants, before the assault on their city, had set fire to their houses and burned themselves and all they possessed.

[Note: [Col. 0848C] “For all, before the assault.” Here one sees the usefulness of epitomes. Trogus had first described what Perdiccas did in Cappadocia with King Ariarathes, then in Pisidia with the Larandaeans and Isaurians; Justin so mutilated the material that scarcely one body remained from the two. The Isaurians therefore inflicted this cruelty upon themselves and their own people, as Diodorus writes in Book XVIII, where he also explains the war between Antigonus and Perdiccas.]

After this, a very serious war arose between Antigonus and Perdiccas, with many provinces and islands torn apart because aid was either refused or given. For a long time they deliberated whether the war should be transferred to Macedonia or fought in Asia. At last Perdiccas himself marched against Egypt with a huge army. Thus Macedonia, while its commanders advanced in two directions, took up arms against its own vitals.

Ptolemy, equipped with the resources of Egypt and the forces of Cyrene, prepared to meet Perdiccas in war. Meanwhile Neoptolemus and Eumenes fought one another in a most bloody battle.

[Note: [Col. 0848D] “Neoptolemus and Eumenes.” Neoptolemus, left by Perdiccas to assist Eumenes, shared his plans with the adversaries and prepared an ambush for Eumenes. When this was revealed, he was compelled to fight him in battle, came into the utmost danger, and lost nearly all his forces. See Diodorus, Plutarch in the *Life of Eumenes*, and Justin, Book XIII.]

Neoptolemus, defeated, fled to Antipater and urged him to attack Eumenes unexpectedly. Eumenes, believing that this would happen, caught the plotters in their own ambush.

[Note: [Col. 0849B] “Unexpectedly.” The third Florentine manuscript and the Meursian manuscript read, “unexpectedly.”]

In that war Polyperchon was killed; Neoptolemus and Eumenes were pierced by mutual wounds, but Neoptolemus died and Eumenes escaped victorious.

[Note: [Col. 0849B] “Polyperchon was killed.” Apart from Justin, no one says anything about Polyperchon’s being killed in this battle. Diodorus and Plutarch record that the commander Craterus fell in this battle on Perdiccas’s side. Consult them concerning Eumenes’s engagement with Neoptolemus and their mutual wounds. Fabricius adds: Justin is mistaken concerning Polyperchon’s death; he lived long after these events, as we have shown in the *History*, or *Life*, of Antigonus and in the *Life* of Cassander. He seems to have died of old age at approximately the same time that Cassander died of dropsy. The events recounted throughout this chapter are explained more fully at the end of Volume I and throughout Volume II of the *Universal History*.]

Perdiccas, having engaged Ptolemy in a bitter war, lost his forces and was himself also killed.

Eumenes, Pithon, the Illyrian, and Alcetas, brother of Perdiccas, were declared enemies by the Macedonians, and war against them was assigned to Antigonus.

[Note: [Col. 0849C] “Was assigned to Antigonus.” The printed editions incorrectly have *by Antigonus*. Diodorus says: Ἀντιγόνῳ προστεταγμένον ἦν καταπολεμῆσαι Εὐμένην τε καὶ Ἀλκέταν, “Antigonus had been charged with making war upon Eumenes and Alcetas.”]

Eumenes and Antigonus therefore joined battle with the greatest forces on both sides. Eumenes was defeated and fled to a very strongly fortified castle, from which he requested aid through envoys from Antipater, then the most powerful man.

[Note: [Col. 0849D] “To a certain fortress.” Plutarch, in the *Life of Eumenes*, has καταφυγὼν εἰς Νῶρα χωρίον ἐν μεθορίῳ Λυκαονίας καὶ Καππαδοκίας, “having fled to Nora, a fortress on the border of Lycaonia and Cappadocia.” Diodorus also discusses this fortress.]

Terrified by this message, Antigonus withdrew from the siege. Yet Eumenes still had neither firm hope nor certain safety. Therefore, as a final expedient, he asked the Argyraspids—so called because of their silver-plated shields, that is, soldiers who had served under Alexander—for aid.

[Note: [Col. 0849D] “The Argyraspids.” Diodorus and Plutarch discuss these men and their treachery.]

They listened arrogantly to their commander while he arranged the battle; defeated by Antigonus, deprived of their camp, they lost their wives and children and everything they had acquired under Alexander. Later they shamefully asked the victor, through envoys, to restore what they had lost. Antigonus promised that he would, if they brought Eumenes to him in chains.

[Note: [Col. 0849D] “He promised that he would restore it.” The Lombard manuscript, the first and third Leiden manuscripts together with Gronovius’s collection, and finally the manuscripts of Perizonius and Meursius require the deletion of *he*.]

Thus enticed by the hope of recovery, they committed the most disgraceful treachery: they brought their own commander, whose standards they had followed shortly before, captive and chained—though they themselves were captives—and soon afterward were scattered through Antigonus’s army in the deepest disgrace.

Meanwhile Eurydice, wife of Arrhidaeus, king of the Macedonians, carried out many wicked acts in her husband’s name through Cassander.

[Note: [Col. 0849D] “King Arrhidaeus.” Arrhidaeus was the son of Philip, the father of Alexander the Great. After Philip’s death, he was made king by the Macedonians and took the name Philip. According to Diodorus at the beginning of Book XVIII, he reigned six years and four months.]

She had advanced him—whom she had shamefully taken as her lover—to the highest eminence through every grade of office; through the woman’s lust he afflicted many Greek cities.

[Note: [Col. 0850B] “She carried out wicked acts.” Meursius, Perizonius, the four Leiden manuscripts together with Gronovius’s collection, and the Augustan edition read, “carries out wicked acts” or “acts wickedly.”]

Then Olympias, mother of King Alexander, encouraged by Polyperchon, came from Epirus into Macedonia under the escort of King Aeacidas of the Molossians.

[Note: [Col. 0850C] “King Aeacidas.” He was the father of Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, who is mentioned shortly afterward and in the following book.]

When she was barred from entering by Eurydice, and the Macedonians were supporting Eurydice, Olympias ordered King Arrhidaeus and Eurydice to be killed. She herself, however, soon paid the deserved penalty for her cruelty. For after carrying out many murders of leading men with feminine audacity, she heard of Cassander’s arrival and, distrusting the Macedonians, withdrew with her daughter-in-law Roxane and her grandson Hercules into the city of Pydna.

[Note: [Col. 0850C] “With Roxane, her daughter-in-law.” Roxane, daughter of Oxyartes the Bactrian, was one of Alexander’s wives. Consult Arrian, Book VII.]

[Note: [Col. 0850B] “Hercules.” In the printed editions the name *Pictuam* is corruptly read, whereas the manuscript correctly has *Pydnam*. Diodorus says of Olympias: Αὐτὴ δὲ παρῆλθεν εἰς Πύδναν, ἔχουσα τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Ἀλεξάνδρου, καὶ τὴν μητέρα αὐτοῦ Ῥωξάνην, “She herself went to Pydna, taking with her Alexander’s son and his mother Roxane.” Thus Olympias did not take Alexander the Great’s son Hercules, born to Barsine, with her to Pydna, but Alexander, Roxane’s son. See Diodorus, Book XIX. Shortly afterward, the third Leiden manuscript together with Gronovius’s collection and the Augustan edition read *they strongly fortify* instead of *they eagerly fortify*.]

There she was immediately captured and killed by Cassander.

[Note: [Col. 0850C] “Where she was immediately.” This is how all the manuscripts and the Augustan edition read; the printed editions have, “and there immediately.”]

[Note: [Col. 0850C] “And was killed.” The conjunction *and*, recognized by all the manuscripts, is wrongly omitted in the printed editions.]

The son of Alexander the Great was sent with his mother to be held under guard in the citadel of Amphipolis.

After Perdiccas, Alcetas, Polyperchon, and the other commanders—whose enumeration would be tedious—had been killed by various means, the wars among Alexander’s successors seemed to have ended.

[Note: [Col. 0850D] “By various means.” I have restored the passage in this way from the Cologne manuscript, which had *by various parties*, correctly, I think, because some were killed secretly and others openly. The common editions print *of the opposing faction*. “The alliance having again been made”: all the editions have *made*, concerning which they may see to it themselves. “Of the opposing faction” here means the same as “by both sides.”]

Then Antigonus, burning with the desire to rule, pretended that he would liberate Hercules, the king’s son, from the siege at Amphipolis.

[Note: [Col. 0850D] “To liberate Hercules by war.” Justin, Book XV, says: “He publicized that he wished to free the son of his king Alexander from the siege at Amphipolis.” Thus the son intended here is not Barsine’s but Roxane’s; Diodorus in Book XIX and Pausanias in Books I and IX write that he was named Alexander.]

When this became known, Ptolemy and Cassander, having formed an alliance with Lysimachus and Seleucus, eagerly prepared war by land and sea. Antigonus was defeated in that war together with his son Demetrius.

[Note: [Col. 0850D] “He was defeated together with his son Demetrius.” Demetrius alone, while Antigonus had gone toward the Hellespont, engaged Ptolemy near the town of Gaza and was defeated. See Diodorus, Book XIX; Pausanias, Book I; and Plutarch, *Life of Demetrius*.]

Cassander, having shared in Ptolemy’s victory, encountered the Autariatae while returning to Apollonia.

[Note: [Col. 0851B] “He encountered the Autariatae.” In the Meursian manuscript and in Perizonius, the ultra-Leiden manuscript, the Leiden manuscript, three Florentine manuscripts, and Gronovius’s collection, the reading is *Avienitae*, or *Aviniatae*, *Abienatae*, *Avicinatae*. The Augustan edition has *Aveniatae*. From these readings it is clear that *Autariatae* should be restored in place of *Abderitae*, as in the common editions. No one can doubt this, since they are similarly mentioned by Justin, Book XV, chapter 2: “While this was happening, Cassander, returning from Apollonia, encountered the Autariatae, who, because of the multitude of frogs and mice, were seeking new settlements after abandoning their native soil.” The Autariatae were a warlike nation and later also served under Lysimachus against Demetrius. But the Abderitae, drawn from corrupt ancient editions of Justin, from which the editors ordered them to depart, also occupied the place of the Autariatae in Orosius. Thus Orosius was not misled by corrupt copies of Justin, as the distinguished Graevius judged in his edition of Justin; rather, both authors were badly treated by overzealous correctors.]

They were emigrating from their ancestral land and ancient dwellings because of the intolerable multitude of frogs and mice, and, under a truce meanwhile offered, were seeking new settlements.

But Cassander, recognizing both the valor and the numbers of the people, feared that, driven by necessity, they might shake Macedonia with war and invade it. He therefore received them into alliance and settled them in the remotest borders of Macedonia.

When Hercules, son of Alexander, was already fourteen years old, Cassander feared—

[Note: [Col. 0851C] “Hercules, son of Alexander.” Polyperchon was preparing to restore him to the kingdom, but, induced by Cassander’s great promises, he killed him. See Diodorus, Book XX, who adds that Hercules was then about seventeen years old.]

[Note: [Col. 0851D] “Fearing that the Macedonians might…” Because Cassander sought the kingdom of Macedonia, he could not be secure while Alexander’s son lived. Thus he removed both Hercules and Alexander: the former was Alexander’s son by Barsine, the latter his son by Roxane. Cassander made an agreement with Polyperchon, who intended to lead Hercules back to his father’s kingdom; by words and gifts he corrupted Polyperchon, to whom he also ceded the whole Peloponnese, so that he would kill the young man, who would grow to the ruin of them both and would eventually be unable to repay Polyperchon with an equivalent favor. Thus Hercules was strangled at a banquet in Polyperchon’s house, by Polyperchon’s own order. All the Macedonians would have defected to Hercules and Polyperchon had this crime not been committed. In none of the manuscripts I consulted did I find *Macedonians*; all instead read *all*, as does the Augustan edition. Orosius, together with the others, is mistaken in confusing Hercules, Barsine’s son, with Alexander, Roxane’s son.]

—he secretly arranged for him and his mother to be killed.

Ptolemy again engaged Demetrius in a naval battle.

[Note: [Col. 0852C] “Ptolemy again with Demetrius.” This naval battle, in which Ptolemy was defeated and fled to Egypt, was fought near Cyprus and is carefully described by Diodorus in Book XX and Plutarch in the *Life of Demetrius*. Pausanias, Book I, mentions the royal title; Diodorus and Plutarch also do so.]

When he had lost almost his entire fleet and army, he was defeated and fled to Egypt. Elated by this victory, Antigonus ordered that he be called king together with his son Demetrius.

[Note: [Col. 0852C] “That he be called king.” The Augustan edition reads, “that he and his son Demetrius be called king,” and so forth.]

All the others followed this example and assumed the royal name and dignity for themselves.

Ptolemy and Cassander, together with the other commanders of the opposing faction, saw that Antigonus was deceiving them one by one. They therefore encouraged one another by letter, agreed upon a time and place for assembling, and prepared war against Antigonus with their united forces.

Cassander, entangled in wars with neighboring peoples, sent Lysimachus, the most distinguished commander of all, with a large force to aid his allies on his behalf. Seleucus also descended from Greater Asia and joined the conflict as a new enemy of Antigonus.

This Seleucus had fought many wars in the East among the allies of the Macedonian kingdom. At the outset he conquered and captured Babylon by war. He subdued the Bactrians as they rose in new rebellions. He then crossed into India, which after Alexander’s death had killed Alexander’s prefects as though it had thrown off a yoke removed from its neck, under the leadership of a certain Androcottus, who claimed its freedom.

[Note: [Col. 0852C] “Androcottus.” He is also read as *Androcottus* and, in Justin, *Sandrocottus*. The authority of Strabo, Book XV, confirms our reading. Plutarch describes the battle in which Antigonus fell in the *Life of Demetrius*. Pausanias mentions it in Book I. In Arrian, Book VII, we read that the battle was fought ἐν Ἰψῷ, “at Ipsus.” Fabricius adds: On the authority of the Lombard manuscript and the better copies I restored *Androcottus*.]

Later, acting cruelly toward the citizens whom he had defended from foreign domination, he himself oppressed them under servitude.

Against this Androcottus, Seleucus fought many serious wars. At last, after securing the conditions of his kingdom and making a peace treaty, he withdrew.

The forces of Ptolemy and his allies were then united, and battle was joined. The more powerful the preparations, the heavier the disaster. For in that battle almost all the strength of the Macedonian kingdom fell. Antigonus himself was killed in the fighting; but the end of this war became the beginning of another. Since the victors could not agree about the spoil, they were again divided into two factions.

Seleucus joined Demetrius, while Ptolemy joined Lysimachus.

[Note: [Col. 0852C] “Seleucus [joined] Demetrius.” At that time Seleucus married Stratonice, daughter of Demetrius and Phila. See Plutarch, *Life of Demetrius*.]

After Cassander’s death, his son Philip succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 0852D] “After Cassander’s death.” Cassander wasted away from dropsy while still alive, worms bursting out everywhere; his eldest son Philip, having already entered upon the kingship, perished from the disease of his wasting body. See Pausanias, Book IX. Shortly afterward some manuscripts and editions read, “New wars arise in Macedonia.”]

Thus, as though from the beginning, new wars arose in Macedonia. Antipater stabbed to death with his own hand his mother, Thessalonice, wife of Cassander, although she was pitiably begging for her life.

[Note: [Col. 0852D] “Antipater [killed] Thessalonice.” Cassander left three sons at his death: Philip, Antipater, and Alexander. Philip died at the beginning of his reign. Antipater killed his mother Thessalonice, daughter of Philip, son of Amyntas, and Nicasipolis, because she favored Alexander more. Alexander, after seeking the aid of Pyrrhus and Demetrius, was killed by Demetrius. See Plutarch, *Lives of Pyrrhus and Demetrius*; Pausanias, Book IX; and Justin, Book XVI.]

His brother Alexander, while preparing war against his brother to avenge their mother, was intercepted and killed by Demetrius, whose aid he had requested.

Lysimachus, being hard pressed in a most hostile war by the Thracian king Dromichetes, was unable to fight against Demetrius.

[Note: [Col. 0853C] “Doricetes.” Gualther’s book has *Dori*, a reading also found by others in their manuscripts. I think *Dromichetes* is correct; Pausanias names him thus in Book I. Plutarch also mentions Δρομικαῖτος, “Dromichetes,” in the *Life of Demetrius*, and writes that Lysimachus was captured by him and treated humanely and royally. Strabo discusses him in Book VII. Fabricius adds: I too found *Dori the king* in all the manuscripts, and suspect that *Doricetes* arose from it. The true name is Dromichetes, as Fabricius asserted.]

Demetrius, elated by the enlargement of Greece and of all Macedonia, planned to cross into Asia.

Ptolemy, Seleucus, and Lysimachus, having learned from their earlier contest how great the strength of concord was, again formed an alliance and, joining their armies, transferred the war to Europe against Demetrius.

[Note: [Col. 0853C] “Having formed an alliance.” All the manuscripts consistently read this, as does the Augustan edition. Therefore the spurious *having made an alliance*, which Lautius also noticed above at number 47, must be removed.]

Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, joined them as a companion and ally in the war, hoping that Demetrius could be driven from Macedonia—and his hope was not in vain.

[Note: [Col. 0853C] “He joined them as a companion.” What Orosius writes here about Pyrrhus is pursued at greater length by Plutarch in his *Life of Pyrrhus*.]

For when Demetrius’s army was corrupted and he himself had been put to flight, Pyrrhus seized the kingdom of Macedonia.

[Note: [Col. 0853C] “Nor was his hope in vain.” Some copies and editions read, “nor was his hope frustrated.”]

Then Lysimachus killed his son-in-law Antipater, who was plotting against him,

[Note: [Col. 0853C] “His son-in-law Antipater.” He means Antipater, son of Cassander, whom I mentioned shortly before.]

and, hating his own son Agathocles beyond all human measure, killed him as well.

[Note: [Col. 0853D] “And his son Agathocles.” Agathocles was killed by the deceit and plotting of Arsinoe, wife of Lysimachus and sister of Lysandra, who was with Agathocles, as Pausanias writes in Book I. Strabo, Book XIII, says that Lysimachus was compelled by wicked intimates to kill his son Agathocles.]

During those same days, the city of Lysimachia, destroyed by a most terrifying earthquake and crushing its people, became a cruel tomb.

[Note: [Col. 0854C] “The city of Lysimachia.” Lysimachus founded it after destroying the city of the Cardians, on the isthmus of the Thracian Chersonese. See Pausanias, Book I. Strabo, Book X, discusses its destruction. Concerning the deaths of Lysimachus and Seleucus, consult Pausanias, Book I. Polybius, Book II, writes that they died around the 124th Olympiad.]

[Note: [Col. 0854C] “By a most terrifying earthquake.” The Augustan edition has “by most terrifying earthquakes.”]

All Lysimachus’s allies deserted him as he continually stained himself with murders of his own kin. They defected to Seleucus and urged him, already inclined through rivalry for the kingdom, to make war on Lysimachus.

[Note: [Col. 0854C] “But Lysimachus.” Three Leiden manuscripts together with Gronovius’s collection read, “But when Lysimachus had been abandoned by his allies.”]

It was a spectacle of the most shameful kind: two kings, Lysimachus seventy-four years old and Seleucus seventy-seven, contending in battle to seize one another’s kingdoms, standing in the line and bearing arms.

This was the last war of Alexander’s fellow soldiers, but it was preserved as an example of human misery. Although, after thirty-four of Alexander’s commanders had perished, they alone possessed the world, and although they did not look toward the narrow limits of their old age and life, they thought that the boundaries of the whole world were narrow for their empire.

[Note: [Col. 0854C] “That the boundaries were narrow, and so forth.” I have restored this from the best manuscripts and the older editions; the common editions have “and narrower.” Juvenal imitates the thought concerning Alexander in Satire 10, verse 170:

> “And as upon the cliffs of Gyara and little Seriphos  
> he seethes, enclosed within the narrow boundary of the world.”]

In that war Lysimachus, after fifteen children had already been lost—some killed and some dead before the battle—was killed last.

[Note: [Col. 0854C] “Last.” Three Leiden manuscripts and Gronovius’s collection read, “last of all.”]

Thus Lysimachus became the conclusion of the Macedonian conflict.

[Note: [Col. 0854D] “The conclusion of the battle.” A tasteless jest has been sought from the Greek meaning of the name Lysimachus.]

But Seleucus did not enjoy so great a victory with impunity. He too, after seventy-seven years, found no rest in a natural death; instead, his life was miserably torn from him and ended in something like a premature death. For, when Ptolemy—whose sister Lysimachus had married—

[Note: [Col. 0854C] “Whose sister Lysimachus [had married].” Lysandra was Ptolemy’s sister and Lysimachus’s wife. See Pausanias.]

—pressed upon him, Seleucus was surrounded by a plot and killed.

These are the dealings among parents and children, brothers and relatives, in matters of kinship and alliance. Such was the value they placed upon divine and human religion.

Let those who now know how to live with enemies and refrain from hostilities through the intervention of Christian faith alone and merely through the solemn oath of an oath-taking sacrament blush at the memory of the past. For it is proved beyond doubt that they do not act as those men once did,

> “who ratified treaties with a slaughtered sow,”

but because now, between Barbarians and Romans, while calling their Creator and Lord to witness, they keep, when the Gospels are employed as an oath, as great a faith as nature could not then preserve even between parents and children.

Now let this be the end of the Macedonian war and also the end of the book, especially since from this point onward the wars of Pyrrhus begin, and the Punic wars soon follow.

# BOOK FOUR

## PREFACE

[Col. 0853]

[Col. 0853D]

Virgil reports that Aeneas said this when, after his own dangers and the shipwrecks of his companions, he was reluctantly consoling the survivors:

[Note: [Col. 0853D] “That Aeneas said.” The passage is found in Virgil, *Aeneid* Book I, verse 207.]

[Col. 0854D] “After his dangers…”

[Note: [Col. 0854D] “After his own dangers.” Three manuscripts from the Leiden collection together with Gronovius’s collection delete *his own*. Shortly afterward, in place of *the remaining companions*, the first of these manuscripts reads *his companions*, and then *he might console* instead of *he consoled*.]

[Source ends here.]

Perhaps one day it will also be a pleasure to remember these things. [Col. 0855A] Once aptly fashioned, this sentence always conveys its threefold force through the most diverse effects [Note: [Col. 0855B] *Through the most diverse effects.* Thus restored from all the manuscripts and editions before Fabricius; nor do I see why he preferred to print, on his own authority, “through the most diverse emotions.” [Col. 0855C] For diverse emotions are grief and joy and the like; but diverse effects are those which we experience through hearing or seeing, hoping or sensing—things that have a very different effect on a person, although they differ greatly in magnitude. Thus a present evil, however slight, produces in us the effect of making us bear it more heavily because it is present than other, more serious evils, because they have passed or seem far away. For “aptly fashioned,” my manuscript reads “aptly spoken.”], since past events are regarded as all the more agreeable in words the more grievous they are reported to have been in deeds; and future events, while they become desirable through weariness with present things, are always believed to be better. But no fair comparison with miseries can in any respect be applied to present circumstances, because these things that actually exist afflict us with far greater distress, however slight they may be, than those things which, whether past or future, are said to be great but meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0855C] *Are then entirely nonexistent.* I have improved the obscure passage by supplying the distinction. In my manuscript and the Venetian editions, *then* is absent; nevertheless two Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, restore it.] are then entirely nonexistent. For example, if someone, kept awake by the nighttime irritation of fleas and anxious because of it, should recall other nights that he once endured for a long time amid the fiercest fevers, without doubt he will bear the restlessness of the former more impatiently than the memory of the latter. [Col. 0855B] Yet although this may seem so to everyone’s senses according to the circumstances of time, is there nevertheless anyone who, even in the midst of that anxiety, would declare that fleas are more grievous than fevers? Or who would take it more bitterly that he is awake while healthy than that, while dying, he had been unable to sleep?

Since this is so, I concede to these delicate and querulous people, to some extent, that they may think grievous, when they experience them, those things of which we are now sometimes [Note: [Col. 0855C] *We are admonished.* Thus the manuscripts and the better editions of Bolland and Hittorp; *we are moved* in other witnesses.] warned, because this is expedient. [Note: [Col. 0855C] *Yet I do not connive.* This must unquestionably be restored, and I found it written so in the first Leiden manuscript and in the earliest Paris and Venetian editions, as well as in those of Bolland and Hittorp. The Augustan, Fabrician, and latest edition of Scott instead restored *I restrain*. That word is indeed found in all the manuscripts except the first Leiden one; but I would venture to affirm that it did not come from the author and plainly contradicts his meaning. Indeed, since I see that in the oldest of all the manuscripts of Orosius—the Florentine or Lombard manuscript—*conhibeo* is written, I have no doubt that *cohibeo* arose in the others from *conniveo*, as it ought to have done.] Yet I do not connive at their asserting this by comparing it with more serious things.

Suppose someone, leaving his very soft bed and exceedingly comfortable bedroom in the morning, were to see the backs of the pools [Note: [Col. 0855D] *The backs of the pools.* In the printed editions the reading is one hardly capable of being more absurd in Orosius, namely *the backs of the ceilings*, although all the manuscripts, together with that excellent edition of Augustine, give *the backs of the pools*. For what are “the backs of ceilings,” and how could someone, leaping from his bed and leaving his bedroom, see ceilings in the streets or squares? The backs of pools, stiffened by the nighttime frost, are the summits of stagnant water or rainwater, such as is usually found in hollows or lower places in the ground. Virgil, *Georgics* I.24:

> Especially if, in the uncertain months, the overflowing river  
> Breaks out and holds everything far and wide beneath its covering mud:  
> From this the hollow pools sweat with warm moisture.

In speaking of the backs of pools, he imitates Virgil, though not very aptly. Virgil called the sea’s surface a *back*, but in poetic phrasing he was not speaking of the upper surface of the sea, but of short, accumulated and compacted sandbanks in an unfavorable place among the waves; if ships become stuck on them, they can scarcely be drawn away unless the waves rise. Virgil’s passages are *Aeneid* I.114:

> An immense back upon the surface of the sea,

and *Aeneid* X.303:

> For struck upon the shallows, while it hangs upon an unfavorable back.

] stiff with frost and the grasses white with hoar, and, prompted by the unexpected sight, were to say, “It is cold today,” I would certainly not consider him blameworthy, since he would have spoken either according to common usage or from his own perception.

But if, trembling, he were to hurry back into his bedroom and, wrapping himself in his bedding [Note: [Col. 0856C] *Wrapping himself in it.* The first Leiden manuscript and the fourth, together with Gronovius’s collection, read “placing himself upon it.”], or hiding himself still more deeply, were to cry out that the cold was altogether as great as it had ever been on the Apennines when Hannibal lost his elephants, horses, and the greater part of his army, shut in and overwhelmed by the snows [Note: [Col. 0856D] *When Hannibal had his elephants.* Hannibal’s passage into Italy and the losses he suffered will be discussed below, chapter 14.], I would not merely refuse to tolerate him, sickening in his childish extravagance as he said these things; I would drag him from the very bedding that bore witness to his leisure, out before the people and the public. Once he had been brought outside, I would show him children playing in and upon that frost, [Note: [Col. 0856D] *Rejoicing and sweating.* Three Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, give only “rejoicing”; all the manuscripts spell it *jocundantes*. But in mine it reads “striking,” as though the author meant snowballs compacted from the snow and their throwing or striking.] rejoicing and sweating, so that it might be demonstrated that his wordy triviality, corrupted by luxurious upbringing, might be taught that the harshness lay not in the weather but in his own sluggishness [Note: [Col. 0856D] *Sluggishness.* Thus most manuscripts, together with the Lombard manuscript, have *segnitiam* instead of *segnitiem*.]; and, in judging things by comparison, that it might be proved not that greater men had endured small things, but that he himself was not equal even to enduring small things [Note: [Col. 0855D] *It would be proved that he was inadequate even to endure small things.* The earliest edition, and the Paris and Venetian editions that followed it, read “they would prove sufficiently.” Since the second Florentine manuscript writes above, instead of “it might be demonstrated: and when things are compared,” “to demonstrate, and when things are compared,” those manuscripts seem to suggest that one should read “as though he demonstrated, and then proved sufficiently”; but I have not altered the common reading.].

I shall establish this even more clearly by recalling the disasters of the past, beginning, as the order requires, with the war against Pyrrhus, whose cause and origin were as follows.

## CHAPTER I. On the war of the Tarentines, whom Pyrrhus of Epirus assisted against the Romans

[Col. 0857A]

[Note: [Col. 0857B] *In the year 464 from the founding of the City.* All the manuscripts have 464, not 454, as is commonly read. But Orosius here too, following his usual practice, counts fewer years than other writers. Gellius, book XVII, last chapter, says: “About 470 years after the founding of the City, war was undertaken against King Pyrrhus.” Some place the Tarentine war and the war with King Pyrrhus in year 472, as in the *Annals* of Stephen Pighius; others refer it to 473 after the founding of the City. — Fabricius. In three Florentine manuscripts it reads “in the 464th year.” But mine, together with the third Leiden manuscript, Gronovius’s collection, and the Augustan edition, add ten and read 474.]

In the year 464 from the founding of the City, the Tarentines, having caught sight of the Roman fleet as it happened to be passing by, attacked it as an enemy while viewing it from the theater [Note: [Col. 0857C] *From the theater as a spectacle.* This theater overlooked the Tarentine harbor toward the sea. While games were being celebrated there, the Tarentines saw the Roman fleet rowing toward the shore, took the Romans for enemies, rushed out, and attacked without distinction. Florus, book I, chapter 18. — The old editions, with which my manuscript agrees, prefer “from the spectacle.”], scarcely five ships escaping by flight. The rest of the fleet, dragged back into the harbor, was destroyed; the naval commanders were slaughtered, all who were fit for war were killed, and the remainder were sold for a price.

The Romans immediately sent ambassadors to Tarentum to complain of the injuries inflicted upon them; [Note: [Col. 0857C] *Beaten by the same men.* Livy also writes, book XII, that the Roman envoys were beaten by the Tarentines. Valerius, book XII, chapter 2, says that, besides suffering the gravest injuries, one of them was even splashed with urine. — Fabricius.] but after being beaten by the same men, they returned bearing injuries made still worse. For these reasons a great war broke out.

The Romans, reckoning how many and how great enemies were clamoring all around them, were driven by the utmost necessity to compel even the proletarians to take up arms—that is, to enroll in military service those who had always remained in the City for the sake of producing offspring; for concern about offspring is useless unless provision is made for present circumstances. [Note: [Col. 0857C] *There is concern.* All the manuscripts read “there is concern,” rather than “concern exists.”]

Accordingly, the Roman army, under the consul Aemilius, rushed into the entire territory of the Tarentines [Note: [Col. 0857C] *With the consul Aemilius.* If Aemilius had brought an action for damages before the praetor against those who published this author before us, no one would deny it—especially since he could prosecute those men as defendants not only on the testimony of the annalistic record but also on that of all the ancient books, and could prove that he had conducted this affair against the Tarentines, not Laevinus, to whom they attributed it, as though Laevinus alone had conducted the affair with the Tarentines and their allies. Yet in the epitome of Livy, book XII, we read that before Laevinus several commanders fought successfully against them in a number of battles. Among these was L. Aemilius Barbula, consul with Q. Marcius Philippus in the year 472 from the founding of the City; having conducted the matter successfully, he triumphed in the year after his consulship. Concerning this, the Capitoline Triumphs read:

> L. AEMILIUS Q. F. Q. N. BARBULA. IN THE YEAR 473. AS PROCONSUL. OVER THE TARENTINES, SAMNITES, AND SALENTINES. ON THE SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF QUINTILIS.

— Fabricius.] and ravaged everything with fire and sword, stormed very many towns, and cruelly avenged the insult insolently inflicted upon him.

Then Pyrrhus greatly strengthened the Tarentines, who were supported by very many garrisons of neighboring peoples [Note: [Col. 0857D] *Supported by very many of their neighbors, etc.* Three Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, read “supported by a very great force of neighboring peoples.” Instead of *fultos*, the first Florentine manuscript has *fultus*.], and, because of the magnitude of his forces and plans, transferred the whole burden and title of the war to himself. For, wishing to avenge Tarentum, a city founded by Lacedaemonians and related to Greece [Note: [Col. 0858B] *For Tarentum, as being founded by Lacedaemonians.* Strabo discusses the origin and resources of the Tarentines in book VI. — Fabricius.], he was the first to bring into Italy the entire strength of Epirus, Thessaly, and Macedonia, including twenty elephants, previously unseen by the Romans [Note: [Col. 0858B] *Elephants as well.* Read Pliny, book VIII, chapter 6, and Solinus, chapter 38. — The number twenty-five is found in Augustine’s edition.], making himself terrifying by land, sea, men, horses, weapons, and finally beasts, as well as by his strength and stratagems.

Only he was caught by the ambiguous response of that most vain Delphic spirit, that most mendacious impostor whom they themselves proclaim a great prophet [Note: [Col. 0858B] *Caught by the response.* He means the response which Ennius expressed in this verse:

> I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, can conquer the Romans.

Cicero, *On Divination* II; Arnobius, final book: “Ennius invented Apollo’s responses, when Apollo had already ceased to compose verses.” — Fabricius.], and met the end of one who had not consulted the oracle [Note: [Col. 0858C] *He met the end of one who had not consulted it.* This is found in all the ancient witnesses, with this meaning: Pyrrhus, deceived by Apollo’s oracle, perished by the fate by which he would have perished even had he not consulted the oracle. — In all the old editions except the Augustan, which is the best, the text previously read foolishly, “the kind of end he thought he had consulted.”].

Thus, near Heraclea, a city of Campania [Note: [Col. 0858C] *At Heraclea.* Florus, book I, chapter 18, and Plutarch, *Life of Pyrrhus*, give the same location for this battle: “He encamped in the plain between the city of Pandosia and Heraclea” (*κατεστρατοπέδευσεν ἐν τῷ μεταξὺ πεδίῳ Πανδοσίας πόλεως καὶ Ἡρακλείας*). — Fabricius.], and the river Siris [Note: [Col. 0858C] *And the river Siris.* The name is commonly and incorrectly printed here and in Florus as *Lyris*. It is in fact the river Σίρις, as in Plutarch, Strabo book VI, and Stephanus’s *On Cities*. Pliny, book III, chapter 11: “Heraclea lies between the Siris and the Aciris.” — Fabricius.], the first battle between King Pyrrhus and the consul Laevinus [Note: [Col. 0858D] *The consul Laevinus.* P. Valerius Laevinus was consul with Ti. Coruncanius in the year 473. In the manuscripts of Plutarch, the first syllable of Laevinus’s name is corrupted: Ἀλβῖνος is read instead of Λαιβῖνος. The same corruption appears in the latest Basel edition, which reads *he rode forward to the river* (*προΐππευσε τῷ ποταμῷ*) instead of *he rode forward against the river* (*προσΐππευσε*). I will also mention in passing that the commander of the Ferentan squadron, called Ὄπλακος in Plutarch’s manuscripts, is called Obsidium in my manuscript of Florus; his name is absent from the printed books. — Fabricius. All the manuscripts, instead of “he was exhausted,” read “it was exhausted.” A little later, in the first Leiden manuscript, the words *the hand of the beast* are preceded by this gloss: “with which it supplies itself with food, and which fights on its behalf like a human hand.”] was fought. The day was consumed by the fiercest struggle, with both sides intent on dying and knowing nothing of flight.

When the elephants were brought in among the opposing ranks—terrible in appearance, oppressive in smell, and terrifying in bulk—the Romans, unaccustomed to this new kind of warfare, were surrounded and frightened; their horses especially panicked, and they scattered. But after Minucius, the first spearman of the Fourth Legion [Note: [Col. 0859C] *But after Minucius.* Florus says of this: “C. Minucius, a spearman of the Fourth Legion, demonstrated that the beasts could die by cutting off the trunk of one of them.” — Fabricius.], cut off with his sword the beast’s outstretched trunk as it reached toward him, and forced the animal, thrown into confusion by the pain of its wound, to turn away from the battle and rage against its own side, the elephants’ uncontrolled movements began to throw everything into confusion and disorder. The battle was brought to an end, with the help of night.

That the Romans had been defeated was revealed by their disgraceful flight. Their losses are reported as fourteen thousand eight hundred and eighty infantry [Note: [Col. 0859C] *Fourteen thousand infantry.* This number is found in all the manuscripts. Dionysius says that slightly fewer than fifteen thousand Romans fell; Jerome gives only seven thousand. — Fabricius.], while one thousand three hundred and ten were captured [Note: [Col. 0859C] *Captured, 1,310.* This number is complete in one manuscript; in the others the common number is written, though there had previously been another. Eutropius says that Pyrrhus captured 1,800 Romans. — In Augustine’s edition the number captured is given as 14,980.], two hundred and forty-two cavalry were killed, eight hundred and two captured, and twenty-two standards lost [Note: [Col. 0859C] *The cavalry killed were 242.* In Gualther’s book the number is 246. The variation arose because II and V often merge, as the reverse also happens. — The number Fabricius reports from his manuscript is also found in all the manuscripts I consulted.].

But the number of Pyrrhus’s allies who were killed has not been handed down to memory [Note: [Col. 0859C] *For how great the opposing number was.* Dionysius and Jerome reported the number of Pyrrhus’s dead, which Orosius says had not been preserved: Dionysius wrote that thirteen thousand were killed, Jerome that not quite four thousand, following Plutarch. — All the manuscripts have *commendare* somewhat later, instead of *commemorare*.], chiefly because it is the custom of ancient writers not to record the number of slain on the victorious side, lest the losses of the victor stain the glory of victory. This is excepted when so few fall that the small number of the dead increases admiration and dread of their valor, as happened in the first encounter of the Persian war at Alexander the Great’s battle [Note: [Col. 0859D] *In the first Persian war.* We discussed this in the preceding book, chapter 16.], where, although nearly four hundred thousand of the enemy were killed, only nine infantrymen from Alexander’s army are reported to have been missing.

But Pyrrhus testified to gods and men to the severity of the disaster he had suffered in this war by affixing an inscription in the temple of Tarentine Jupiter, on which he wrote:

> Those who had previously been unconquered men, O excellent father Olympus,  
> I conquered in battle, and I was conquered by those same men.  
>
> [Note: [Col. 0859D] *Men who had previously been unconquered.* The verses, as I have restored them in the text, are unquestionably Ennian and had previously been wrongly conflated with what follows. *Fuvere* for *fuere* is ancient, like many forms which our learned Palmerius has elegantly extracted in his *Spicilegia*. — Laut.]

When his allies reproached him [Note: [Col. 0859D] *Was reproached.* All the manuscripts read “was reproached” in the imperfect subjunctive.], asking why he called himself defeated when he had won, he is said to have replied: “If I win another victory in the same manner, I shall return to Epirus without a single soldier.”

Meanwhile the Roman army, after fleeing secretly from the camp once defeated, perceived that the pitiable disaster of the war had been increased and compounded by still more grievous prodigies. For some foragers who had gone forward were suddenly seized, as though by a hostile storm arising amid a terrible crash of the sky, and burned by dreadful thunderbolts. Indeed, the same whirlwind struck down thirty-four of them [Note: [Col. 0860C] *Indeed, thirty-three of them.* I conjectured that this should be read; otherwise it was impossible to make Orosius intelligible. The printed and manuscript copies read: “the same whirlwind struck down some of them, leaving them half-dead.” — Laut.] [Note: [Col. 0860C] *Thirty-four.* Ten of these are absent from three Leiden manuscripts together with Gronovius’s collection. The remaining manuscripts write XXX and IV.], leaving twenty-two half-dead, while very many pack animals were killed and captured [Note: [Col. 0860C] *Very many.* My manuscript, together with four Leiden manuscripts and Gronovius’s collection, reads “a great many.” Instead of “captured,” perhaps “destroyed” or “carried away” should be read.], so that what occurred may rightly be described not as a sign of future devastation [Note: [Col. 0860C] *Not a sign of future devastation.* Perizonius reads, “so that it may seem to have occurred not as a sign,” etc. My manuscript, together with four Leiden manuscripts and Perizonius’s collection, reads, “to have occurred not as a sign,” etc.] but as devastation itself.

The second battle between Pyrrhus and the Roman consuls [Note: [Col. 0860C] *The second battle between Pyrrhus and the Romans.* This battle was fought with Pyrrhus while P. Sulpicius and P. Decius Mus were consuls, in the year 474. Eutropius says: “P. Sulpicius and Decius, the consuls, were sent against the commander Pyrrhus. When battle was joined, Pyrrhus was wounded, his elephants were killed, twenty thousand of the enemy were slain, and only five thousand Romans.” — Fabricius.] took place in the territory of Apulia [Note: [Col. 0860D] *In the territory of Apulia.* Plutarch writes in his *Pyrrhus* that the battle was fought περὶ Ἄσκλον, “near Asculum”; Florus says: “Then in Apulia, near Asculum, the fighting went better.” — Fabricius.], where the disaster of war fell upon both sides, but especially upon Pyrrhus, while victory went to the Romans.

For when the outcome of the battle hung in doubt, with everyone for a long time rushing fiercely toward mutual slaughter, Pyrrhus, wounded by a thrust through the arm, was the first to withdraw from the battle. Fabricius, too, who was then a legate, was wounded. It was discovered that the elephants could be wounded in the first battle and driven to flight; later, fires placed beneath their hindquarters and softer parts drove them mad, and, carrying burning structures around in frantic terror, they became the destruction of their own side.

Five thousand Romans were killed in that battle; twenty thousand of Pyrrhus’s army were thrown down [Note: [Col. 0860D] *Twenty thousand.* The second Florentine manuscript additionally recognizes “three,” but that word is written above the line. The first edition and those that followed it give four thousand instead of five thousand.]. Fifty-three of the king’s standards were taken, and eleven Roman standards were lost.
