Pyrrhus, broken by the war, was summoned to Sicily to assume command after the death of Agathocles, king of Syracuse [Note: [Col. 0860D] *After Agathocles had died.* Who this Agathocles was and by what means he rose to the kingship may be learned fully from book XIX of Diodorus Siculus; more is said about him in chapter 6. — Fabricius.], and went to Syracuse.

## CHAPTER II. The Romans are seized by a dreadful plague; a third war is waged with Pyrrhus, who is routed and perishes

[Col. 0861A]

But the misery of the Romans does not cease for any interval [Note: [Col. 0861B] *But the Romans’.* The old editions read, “But even the Romans’.”]. A respite from warfare is consumed by the evils of disease [Note: [Col. 0861B] *By the evils of diseases.* The third Florentine manuscript reads, “by the mass of diseases.”]; and when fighting ceases abroad, anger from heaven is enacted within.

For when Fabius Gurges and C. Genucius Clepsina were again consuls, a severe plague invaded the City and its territory. Seizing everyone, but especially women and cattle, it emptied the future of offspring by killing fetuses in the womb; and through premature births, miscarriages were forcibly brought forth and cast away at the danger of the mothers. Thus it was believed that the succession would fail and that the race of living creatures would disappear, because the proper order of vital birth had been taken away [Note: [Col. 0861C] *Would disappear.* My manuscript reads “would fail.”].

Meanwhile Pyrrhus, having returned from Sicily [Note: [Col. 0861C] *Pyrrhus, having returned from Sicily.* When M. Curius Dentatus and L. Cornelius Lentulus were consuls, Pyrrhus was recalled to Italy by the Tarentines and Samnites. Curius, sent against him as consul, defeated his army and expelled him from Italy. Plutarch, *Pyrrhus*; Livy, book XIV; Justin, book XXIII; Eutropius, book II. — Fabricius.], was met by the consul Curius. This was the third war against the Epirotes, fought in Lucania on the Arusian plains [Note: [Col. 0861C] *In Lucania on the Arusian plains.* Florus also writes that the final battle with Pyrrhus was fought on the Arusian plains of Lucania. Frontinus, book IV, likewise, in explaining Pyrrhus’s battle formation, says that he was defeated on the Arusian plains near Beneventum. — Fabricius.].

Accordingly, at the first clash, when Pyrrhus’s soldiers were thrown into confusion by the Roman assault [Note: [Col. 0861C] *By the assault.* In Fabricius’s editions and most of the common editions, *assault* is incorrectly read in the accusative. The older editions and the more ancient manuscripts read *by the assault*, for Pyrrhus’s soldiers were thrown into confusion by an assault made by the Romans, not because of an assault that was still to come. I have restored what follows from the manuscripts and old editions. The common editions read “while they looked around for a means of flight.”], and, looking about for flight, were attempting to withdraw from the battle, Pyrrhus ordered the elephants to be brought forward from reserve.

The Romans, now accustomed to fighting beasts, had prepared small darts wrapped in tow and smeared with pitch, with barbs attached to make them cling; they hurled these flaming weapons at the backs and towers of the beasts. They easily turned the raging, burning animals back upon those whose support they had been [Note: [Col. 0861D] *Whose support they had been.* Augustine’s edition reads, “for whose support they had been.”].

They say that the king had eighty thousand infantry in that battle and six thousand cavalry. Of these, thirty-three thousand are reported killed [Note: [Col. 0861D] *Thirty-three thousand are reported killed.* Eutropius: “On that day twenty-three thousand of the enemy were killed.” — Fabricius. In Augustine’s edition the number is specified as thirty thousand, with three hundred captured. The number captured is the same in Gronovius’s collection.], while one thousand three hundred were captured.

At last, in the fifth year after he had come, Pyrrhus fled defeated from Italy [Note: [Col. 0861D] *Only in the fifth year, Pyrrhus.* Plutarch: “Thus Pyrrhus was driven from his hopes concerning Italy and Sicily, after spending six years in the wars there” (*Οὕτω μὲν ἐξέπεσε τῶν Ἰταλικῶν καὶ Σικελικῶν ἐλπίδων ὁ Πύῤῥος, ἐξαετῆ χρόνον ἀναλώσας περὶ τοὺς ἐκεῖ πολέμους*). — Fabricius.]; after many very serious wars, he was misled by his desire for the Spartan kingdom and perished in Greece, at Argos, the most flourishing city of Achaea, struck by a stone [Note: [Col. 0861D] *Struck by a stone, he fell dead.* The author of *On Illustrious Men* writes that Pyrrhus was felled by a roof tile; Plutarch also names a κεραμίς, which an Argive woman threw from a roof onto his head. — Fabricius. Some old editions read “perished” instead of “fell dead.” We discussed Pyrrhus’s death at greater length at the end of his Life.].

At that time also, among the Romans, Sextilia, a Vestal virgin, convicted and condemned for incest, was buried alive at the Colline Gate [Note: [Col. 0862B] *Then also Sextilia.* Sextilia’s condemnation for incest after an alliance with Ptolemy, king of Egypt, is known from Livy’s epitome, book XIV. This affair occurred, according to Eutropius, when C. Fabricius Luscinus and C. Claudius Canina were consuls, in the year 480 from the founding of the City according to the Capitoline Fasti, which we follow. — Fabricius. The third Leiden manuscript reads *Vestilia*.].

## CHAPTER III. The Romans defeat the Tarentines and their Carthaginian auxiliaries, and punish the Eighth Legion

[Col. 0862B]

[Note: [Col. 0862C] *In the year 475 from the founding of the City.* According to others, this year is 481 from the founding of the City, when L. Papirius Cursor and Sp. Carvilius Maximus were again consuls and war was declared against the Samnites, Bruttians, and Lucanians together with the Tarentine people, as Livy says in book XXIV. They completed the Tarentine and Samnite wars and triumphed over the Tarentines, Samnites, Lucanians, and Bruttians, as is known from the Capitoline Tablets. — Fabricius.]

In the year 475 from the founding of the City, when they learned of Pyrrhus’s death, the Tarentines once again stirred up new arms against the Romans and requested and received the aid of the Carthaginians through ambassadors [Note: [Col. 0862C] *The aid of the Carthaginians.* Here Carlo Sigonio, a man of exceptionally keen intelligence and great learning, correctly emended Livy’s epitome, book XIV: “The Carthaginian fleet came to the aid of the Tarentines; by this act the treaty was violated by them,” whereas earlier *Mamertines* had been incorrectly read instead of *Tarentines*.].

Battle was joined, and the Romans won. There the Carthaginians, although they had not yet been declared enemies, realized that they could nevertheless be defeated by the Romans.

In the following year [Note: [Col. 0862D] *In the following year.* This was the year 482 from the founding of the City, with L. Genucius Clepsina and C. Quinctius as consuls. — Fabricius.], Roman severity cut down a large part of its own entrails. For, when Pyrrhus had long since been approaching [Note: [Col. 0862D] *When Pyrrhus had already been approaching.* That is, nine years earlier. At that time the Campanian Legion had been sent with its commander D. Jubellius as a garrison to Rhegium; after killing the people of Rhegium, it occupied the city. Livy, book XII, and Polybius, book I, give a fuller account. Valerius, book II, also discusses the matter. — Fabricius.], the Eighth Legion, losing confidence in Roman prospects, dared a new crime and killed all the Rheginians whom it had been assigned to protect [Note: [Col. 0862D] *Having dared a new crime, all the Rheginians.* The common text incorrectly reads *increased* instead of *having dared*. Polybius writes of the soldiers of this legion: “Having driven out some of the citizens and slaughtered others, they took possession of the city” (*Καὶ τοὺς μὲν ἐκβαλόντες, τοὺς δὲ ἀποσφάξαντες τῶν πολιτῶν κατέσχον τὴν πόλιν*). — Fabricius.].

It claimed all the booty and the town itself for its own. Genucius the consul was ordered to punish such criminal deserters for this deed. After besieging the city of Rhegium and capturing them all [Note: [Col. 0863C] *And, having captured them all, he himself.* Polybius writes: “After gaining the victory, they destroyed most of them during the capture of the city, since they resisted fiercely, foreseeing the danger that awaited them; but they took alive more than three hundred. These men were sent to Rome, where the praetors led them into the forum, flogged them all with rods according to their custom, and beheaded every one of them.” — Fabricius.], he inflicted deserved punishments upon the remaining deserters and robbers. But he sent the Roman soldiers of the entire legion to Rome. By order of the people, they were beaten with rods in the middle of the forum [Note: [Col. 0863C] *Were beaten, and so forth, by order of the Roman people.* Without exception all the manuscripts, supported by Augustine’s edition, place *were* here; the printed editions place it after *beheaded*.] and struck with axes.

Rome then seemed to itself to have conquered when it killed its own entire legion [Note: [Col. 0863D] *The legion.* In Fabricius’s editions, the correct reading is placed in the margin, while the text gives *delegation*. Scott’s edition follows the latter, rather poorly, although it is contrary to the manuscripts and old editions and even to Orosius himself, who states above in this chapter that this was the Eighth Legion.], which would unquestionably have been defeated had it lost its men in battle against the enemy.

## CHAPTER IV. On certain dreadful prodigies and on the Picentine war

[Col. 0863B]

[Note: [Col. 0863D] *In the year 477 from the founding of the City.* This year is the one immediately preceding the consulship of Sempronius Sophus and is distinct from the year 484 from the founding of the City. — Fabricius. In the first Florentine manuscript it is written as 470, as in mine and Perizonius’s; the fourth Leiden manuscript has 480.]

In the year 477 from the founding of the City, obscene and dreadful prodigies were either seen at Rome or reported there. The temple of Salus was shattered by a lightning strike, and part of the wall at the same place was, as they say, struck from heaven.

Three wolves entered the city before dawn and carried in a half-eaten corpse. They left it scattered limb by limb in the forum when they themselves were frightened away by the noise of the people [Note: [Col. 0863D] *They left it.* My manuscript reads “they departed.”].

At Formiae, the walls were scorched and shattered on every side by many lightning strikes. In the territory of Cales, a flame suddenly burst forth from a split in the earth [Note: [Col. 0863D] *Burst forth.* The first Florentine manuscript reads “suddenly burst forth everywhere.”], and, boiling up terribly for three days and three nights, burned five *iugera* of farmland to ash, utterly exhausting its fertile substance, so that it is reported to have consumed not only crops but also trees with their deepest roots [Note: [Col. 0863D] *So that.* The first word is absent from my manuscript.].

In the following year [Note: [Col. 0863D] *In the year following this.* P. Sempronius Sophus was consul with App. Claudius Crassus in the year 485, and both triumphed over the Picentes. — Fabricius.], the consul Sempronius led an army against the Picentes.

When both battle lines had taken position within a spear’s cast of one another [Note: [Col. 0864C] *And when the lines had already been drawn up.* Augustine’s edition reads, “and when the lines had now been drawn up.”], the earth suddenly trembled with such a dreadful crash that both armies, stunned by the wonder, were paralyzed with fear [Note: [Col. 0864C] *The earth trembled with a dreadful crash.* Florus, book I, chapter 19, also recalls this earthquake and the Picentine war. Frontinus, book I, writes how Sempronius restored the soldiers’ courage after they had been terrified by the earthquake. — Fabricius.].

For a long time the peoples on both sides, stunned, hesitated [Note: [Col. 0864C] *They hesitated.* Three Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, read “were in turmoil”; a little later they read *human* rather than *of men*, and, together with certain old editions, “about to receive” and “the earth,” instead of “about to receive the earth.” The common editions were incorrectly punctuated: “They remained motionless. With consciousness of the undertaking already prejudged, at last…”]. With their consciences already prejudging the undertaking, at last they rushed forward and joined battle.

That war was so mournful that it may rightly be said that the earth trembled then with a dreadful groan because it was about to receive so much human blood. The very few Romans who survived that battle won.

## CHAPTER V. Prodigies are seen again. The freedmen of the Volsinians conspire against their masters, whom the Romans assisted. Rome is again seized by plague.

[Col. 0864B] In the year 480 from the founding of the City, amid many portents [Note: [Col. 0864C] “Among many portents.” The Deacon mentioned these portents in his additions to Eutropius. FABR.], blood was seen to flow from the earth and milk from the sky. For in very many places gore gushed forth from springs, and, as though milk had been let down drop by drop from the clouds in the appearance of rain, showers of an ominous kind, as they themselves thought, drenched the earth.

At that time the Carthaginians, having given aid against the Romans to the Tarentines, were challenged by the Senate through ambassadors; and, having already presumed to commit perjury, they compounded the most disgraceful stain of a broken treaty. [Note: [Col. 0864C] “At that time also the Vulsinians.” Florus, book I, chapter 21, writes about this matter: “The last of the Italians to remain loyal were the Vulsinians, the wealthiest of the Etruscans. They implored aid against their former slaves, who had turned the freedom granted them by their masters against those masters and, having transferred the commonwealth to themselves, ruled it. But these too paid the penalty under Fabius Gurges.” In the Capitoline Triumphs we read that the consuls M. Valerius and Flaccus celebrated a triumph over the Vulsinians in the year 489, at the beginning of the First Punic War. FABR.]

At that time also the Vulsinians, the most prosperous of the Etruscans, [Note: [Col. 0864D] “They nearly perished through luxury.” Florus, first edition: “They nearly perished through luxury,” a reading supported by the third Leiden manuscript and the Gronovian manuscript. Meus has “they perished through luxury.” The second and fourth Leiden manuscripts, as well as the Utrecht manuscript and another cited in the Notes to Aurelius Victor, p. 169, have “they perished through the punishment of luxury.” The outcome, however, stands against this reading, since they were restored by the Romans. Accordingly Aurelius Victor, in On Illustrious Men, chapter 36, simply wrote: “Volsinii, a noble town of Etruria, nearly perished through luxury.”], nearly perished through luxury.

For when they had extended license until it became customary [Note: [Col. 0864D] “Extended.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “spread.”], habitually made their slaves free, admitted them to their banquets [Note: [Col. 0864D] “Admitted.” This is how the verb is written in the manuscripts. The common editions incorrectly read “they alleged.”], and honored them with marriages, the freedmen, having been admitted to a share in power, planned to usurp its fullness by crime [Col. 0865A] [Note: [Col. 0865C] “Planned.” Thus the manuscripts and better editions; some have “undertook.”]. Having been released from the yoke of servitude, they burned with ambition for domination; and those whom, as subjects, they had patiently loved as masters, they now, as free men, cursed because they remembered that they had been masters. [Note: [Col. 0865C] “Because they remembered that they had been masters.” This is the elegant reading of the first and third Florentine manuscripts; the common reading is “those whom they had loved as masters.” For they could not endure before their eyes that reproach of their former slavery, and they hated their benefactors because they had been their masters.] [Note: [Col. 0865C] “And so the freedmen, conspiring.” On the insolence of the Vulsinian slaves, read Valerius, book IX, chapter 1. FABR.]

And so the freedmen, conspiring in a criminal undertaking—for their multitude was so great that they could seize power without opposition—captured the city and claimed it solely for their own class. They criminally seized their masters’ estates and wives, drove their masters far away as exiles, and the wretched men, banished and destitute, came to Rome. There, after their misery had been displayed and their complaint lamented, through Roman severity they were both avenged and restored.

In the year 481 from the founding of the City [Note: [Col. 0865C] “A great pestilence.” Augustine mentions this pestilence in The City of God, book III, chapter 17. FABR.], a great pestilence broke out at Rome. I shall be content merely to indicate its horror, since I cannot fill it out in words. If the length of time during which it lasted is considered, it extended beyond two years in its devastation; if the depopulation it caused is considered, a census was taken that asked not how many people had perished but how many had survived; and if the violence with which it afflicted them is considered, the Sibylline Books bear witness: they declared that it had been imposed by heavenly anger.

[Col. 0865B] But lest anyone be offended by an attempted alteration of the wording [Note: [Col. 0865C] “But lest anyone be offended by an attempted alteration.” This reading occurs in Walther’s book; we have eagerly accepted it after rejecting the readings commonly printed. FABR.—The printed editions had: “But lest anyone be offended, as though a quibble had been attempted”; in the Augustan edition: “But by no means during the tempest,” and so forth. In the manuscripts, instead of “a quibble had been attempted,” one finds “an attempted violation,” “during the tempest,” or “an attempted quibble,” as in three Florentine manuscripts. Meus has “an attempted quibble may offend.” Of all these readings I prefer Fabricius’ reading.], because, when the Sibyl speaks of angry gods, we may seem to have spoken of heavenly anger, let him hear and understand that although such things are usually brought about through aerial powers, nevertheless they are not brought about at all without the will of almighty God.

At the same time [Note: [Col. 0865D] “Capparonia.” The manuscripts have “Capparronia.” FABR.—The first Leiden edition has “the captured Roman Vestal virgin.”] Capparonia, a Vestal virgin, perished by hanging after being accused of incest; her seducer and the slaves who were privy to the crime were punished.

Behold how many and how great events we can enumerate as having happened consecutively in individual years [Col. 0865C], among which certainly there was rarely, or scarcely ever, a year in which nothing sorrowful [Note: [Col. 0865D] “Was done.” None of the manuscripts recognizes the clause “was done,” which the printed editions add, nor does the Augustan edition. The meaning is that nothing sorrowful was publicly done, without a war.], was done.

And this was so even though those same writers, whose assigned task was rather to praise, took care to avoid enumerating the miseries, lest they offend the very people about whom and for whom these things were written, and lest they appear to terrify their listeners by examples of the past rather than instruct them.

But we, placed at the end of the ages, cannot know the evils of the Romans except through those who praised the Romans. From this it may be understood how great those evils were that were suppressed out of a desire to avoid horror, since so many are found [Note: [Col. 0865D] “Are found.” The first Florus edition, together with the Augustan edition and the third Leiden manuscript, has “are discovered.”] that were able to seep out only faintly amid the praises.

## CHAPTER VI. On the origin of the Carthaginians and the varied fortune they enjoyed before the First Punic War

[Col. 0866B] And since from this point the Punic Wars now follow, the subject itself requires that we say something about Carthage, which [Note: [Col. 0865D] “Seventy-two years before the city of Rome.” Thus Justin, book XVIII, concerning Carthage: “This city was founded seventy-two years before Rome.” In the Epitome of Livy, book XXXI, we read that Carthage was captured seven hundred years after it had been founded. Therefore, since Scipio captured Carthage in the year 607 from the founding of the City, it is found to have been founded ninety-three years before Rome. But in the Chronicle of Eusebius, Carthage is found to have been founded about forty years before the capture of Troy. Appian begins his Libyan, or Carthaginian, history as follows: Καρχηδόνα τὴν ἐν Λιβύῃ Φοίνικες ᾤκισαν ἔτεσι πεντήκοντα πρὸ ἁλώσεως Ἰλίου, “The Phoenicians founded Carthage, which is in Libya, fifty years before the capture of Ilium.” FABR.]

we find was founded by Elisa seventy-two years before the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0866C] “Seventy-two.” The first and third Florentine manuscripts, and likewise originally the second Florus manuscript, have “seventy-two” in the nominative form.], [Note: [Col. 0866C] “By Elisa.” She was surnamed Dido. Appian says: Οἰκισταὶ δ᾽ αὐτῆς ἐγένοντο Ξῶρός τε, καὶ Καρχηδών· ὡς δὲ Ῥωμαῖοι καὶ αὐτοὶ Καρχηδόνιοι νομίζουσι, Διδὼ γυνὴ Τυρία, “Its founders were Xorus and Carchedon; but, as the Romans and the Carthaginians themselves believe, Dido, a Tyrian woman.” Virgil discusses the matter at greater length in book I of the Aeneid. FABR.], and let us recount at least a few things about its disasters and domestic misfortunes, as Pompeius Trogus and Justin set them forth. [Note: [Col. 0866D] “As Pompeius Trogus.” What Orosius writes about the Carthaginians in this chapter is found in Justin, drawing on Trogus, book XVIII and following. FABR.]

The Carthaginians [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Native.” The first Leiden manuscript and certain editions have “as it were native.” The Augustan edition subsequently has “of discord.”] always possessed a native and internal evil among themselves: discord. Harassed disastrously by it, they never experienced any period prosperous abroad or peaceful at home.

But when, among their other evils, they were also suffering from pestilence, they used homicides as remedies. For they sacrificed human beings as victims, and brought to the altars children not yet of puberty, whose age would even arouse the pity of enemies. [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Children not yet of puberty.” The Carthaginians were accustomed to sacrifice their finest sons to Saturn, according to Diodorus, book XX. FABR.—The Leiden manuscripts together with the Gronovian manuscript have “in an unripe age,” a circumstance that also, etc.]

I do not find what, above all, should be examined about this kind of worship—or rather sacrilege [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Concerning this kind of worship.” The Augustan edition has “concerning this kind of sacrifice.” My manuscript has “concerning whose kind of worship,” and so forth.] . For if some demons dared to prescribe such rites [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Such rites, etc.” The Augustan edition reads “in such a rite.” Hence I suspect that what follows is corrupt in all the manuscripts, and that the passage should read as follows: “For if some demons dared to propitiate [read ‘prescribe,’ rather than ‘command’] by such a rite, so that the killing of human beings might satisfy them with the deaths of human beings,” etc. For this reason the following passage says that those whom the pestilence had not seized should kill others. Those who sacrificed human beings killed them; but they themselves were killed to win the demons’ favor.], it must be understood that they were enlisted as agents and assistants of the pestilence, so that they might kill those whom it had not seized. For it is customary to offer healthy and unblemished victims [Note: [Col. 0867C] “Thus they.” In Fabricius’ and Scott’s editions, the word “however” has been inserted: “thus, however, they.” Earlier editions have “so that they,” which is also found in the second Leiden manuscript and the Gronovian manuscript. But the middle word is deleted by the three Florentine manuscripts, Meus, Perizonius, and Utrecht, and we do not need it.], and thus they were not calming diseases but preventing them.

And so the Carthaginians, with the gods hostile on account of such rites [Note: [Col. 0867C] “With the gods hostile.” Some manuscripts have “with the gods averted,” or “with the gods opposed.”], as Pompeius Trogus and Justin admit, but, as is clear among us, with God angered because of their presumption and impiety, after they had long fought unsuccessfully in Sicily, transferred the war to Sardinia and were defeated even more disastrously. Consequently they ordered their commander Mazeus and the few soldiers who had survived to go into exile. [Note: [Col. 0867C] “Their commander Mazeus.” In the common editions of Justin this commander is called Machaeus; our manuscript agrees with the manuscripts of Orosius. FABR.—In the first Florus manuscript the name of this commander is written Himelcho, as also in the second and in the second and fifth Leiden manuscripts and in Perizonius; in my manuscript he is called Himilco.]

When the exiles, seeking pardon through ambassadors, were rejected [Note: [Col. 0867C] “Were rejected.” The Augustan edition has “and were rejected.”], they surrounded their homeland with war and siege.

Thereupon Mazeus, the leader of the exiles, crucified Carthalo, his son and a priest of Hercules, because he came toward him dressed in purple, as though mocking him [Note: [Col. 0867C] “Came toward him.” Thus all the manuscripts, instead of “had come toward him,” which appears in the common editions.], [Note: [Col. 0867D] “Before the eyes.” Meus, together with three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian manuscript, has “in the eyes.”] before the eyes of his country, just as he was, [Note: [Col. 0867D] “Just as he was.” Ὡς εἶχεν, ὡς ἔτυχε, “as he was, as he happened to be.” The common editions therefore wrongly write, against the evidence of the ancient books, “just as he was worthy.” FABR.] and hung him with his purple robe and fillets. [Note: [Col. 0867D] “With his purple robe and fillets.” Three Leiden manuscripts together with the Gronovian manuscript have “in purple and fillets.” Either reading can be defended from Justin. In book XVIII, chapter 7, where he gives the command, “What else are you doing in that purple and those crowns?” a little later he says, “and so, with his apparel, he ordered him to be fastened to a very high cross in the sight of the city.”]

After a few days [Note: [Col. 0867D] “After a few days.” The older editions have “but after a few days.” The manuscripts do not contain “but.” The Augustan edition, two Leiden manuscripts, and the Gronovian manuscript have “and after a few days.” But Justin has “then, after a few days,” etc.], he captured the city itself. After killing many senators and ruling in blood, he was killed.

These events took place in the time of Cyrus, king of the Persians.

After this, when Imilco, king of the Carthaginians [Note: [Col. 0868B] “Imilco, king of Carthage.” In the printed books of Justin he is Amilco; in the manuscripts, Imilco; in Greek, Ἰμίλκων. He was king of the Carthaginians in the ninety-seventh Olympiad and conducted the war in Sicily unsuccessfully against Dionysius the Elder. After capturing Achradina, one part of Syracuse, he plundered the temples of Ceres and Proserpina, and thereafter his army suffered from a very severe pestilence, as Diodorus records in book XIV. FABR.], was waging war in Sicily, he suddenly lost his army to a dreadful pestilence.

And no delay followed: with the sick falling in crowds, each person was quickly seized and soon died, and no one was even buried [Note: [Col. 0868C] “Nor did the sick delay.” Thus the most excellent Franciscus Modius advised me that it should be read, from “this sickness is.” LAUT.—The common editions and manuscripts rightly have “by diseases,” which must be construed with “each person was quickly seized.”]. When news of this disaster filled Carthage, stunned by sudden grief, the city was thrown into confusion, as though it had been captured. [Note: [Col. 0868C] “As though it had been captured.” The last word is not recognized by three Leiden manuscripts together with the Gronovian manuscript.]

Everything resounded with wailing; doors were shut everywhere; all private and public business was abandoned; everyone hurried to the harbor [Note: [Col. 0868C] “They hurried.” The Augustan edition and three Leiden manuscripts together with the Gronovian manuscript have “they returned.” But the first edition has “they hurry,” and the Venetian editions followed it.], and, as the survivors came ashore from the ships, they questioned them [Note: [Col. 0868C] “They question.” Thus, together with Justin, book XIX, chapter 2, the manuscripts of Perizonius and Meus require that it be restored. The common editions have “they questioned.”] about their own people.

When the wretched inhabitants understood from those men—who remained silent or groaned [Note: [Col. 0868C] “While they were silent.” The common editions have “while they spoke,” but all the manuscripts and the Augustan edition have “while they were silent,” which is much more expressive.]—what had happened to their people, then along the entire shore the voices of mourners and the wails and sorrowful lamentations of the unhappy mothers were heard.

Meanwhile the commander himself came forth from his ship [Note: [Col. 0868D] “Comes forth.” Some printed editions have “coming out, he proceeds.”], stripped of his belt and dressed in a filthy, servile tunic. At the sight of him [Col. 0868B] [Note: [Col. 0868D] “The ranks of mourners gather.” The manuscripts of Meus and Perizonius have “the mourning ranks,” which may be acceptable, since “the voices of mourners” has just preceded it. But Justin too reads, in book XIX, chapter 3: “At the sight of him the ranks of mourners gathered.”] the ranks of mourners gathered around him.

He too raised his hands toward heaven, accusing and lamenting now his own misfortune, now that of the state. At last, crying out through the city, he entered his house and dismissed with a final farewell all those who had followed him weeping. Then, having barred the doors and even excluded his sons, he ended both his grief and his life with a sword.

These events took place in the time of Darius.

After this, a certain Hanno, a Carthaginian whose private wealth surpassed the resources of the state, conceived a desire to seize power. He judged the following plan useful: under the pretense of arranging his only daughter’s wedding, he would kill over drinks all the senators whose dignity he thought would obstruct his plans [Note: [Col. 0869C] “Would obstruct.” The manuscripts of Longobardus and other older manuscripts, as well as Vincent of Beauvais, who excerpted this passage in book IV, chapter 93, support this reading; some manuscripts and editions have “would have obstructed.” Quintilian, book II, chapter 12, says: “I see some who would obstruct me right at the threshold.” Shortly afterward Meus has “undertakings” instead of “begun undertakings.”].

When the matter was exposed by the servants, it was avoided without retaliation, lest the discovery should cause more trouble in the case of so powerful a man than the plan itself had caused. [Note: [Col. 0869C] “So powerful.” This word is absent from Vincent and from the manuscripts of Meus, Perizonius, three Leiden manuscripts, the Gronovian manuscript, and several older editions. In most of these same witnesses, “established” occurs shortly afterward instead of “appointed.”]

Frustrated in this plan, Hanno prepared to undertake the crime by another contrivance. He stirred up the slaves, intending suddenly to overwhelm the unwary city. But when he realized that he had been betrayed and forestalled before the day appointed for the killings, he seized, with an armed force of twenty thousand slaves [Note: [Col. 0869C] “With twenty thousand.” The Augustan edition has twenty-four thousand. Several later manuscripts have “he seized a fortified place with armed slaves,” and so does Vincent of Beauvais.], a certain fortress.

While there he incited the Africans and the king of the Moors, he was captured. First he was beaten with rods; then his eyes were gouged out and his hands and legs broken, as though punishment were being exacted from each of his limbs; finally he was killed in the sight of the people. His body, mangled by the blows [Note: [Col. 0869C] “Mangling.” Some of the first editions have “mangled and fastened to a cross,” as does Vincent of Beauvais.], was fastened to a cross, and all his sons and relatives were handed over to punishment, so that no one of that family might ever plan either to imitate him or to avenge him.

These events took place in the time of Philip.

After this, when the Carthaginians learned that Tyre, the originator of their lineage, had been captured and destroyed by Alexander the Great, fearing that he might cross over to Africa, they sent a certain Hamilcar, surnamed Rhodanus, a man outstanding in eloquence and skill, to investigate Alexander’s actions.

Received by Parmenion as though he were a deserter, and afterward admitted into the king’s military service, he reported everything to his fellow citizens on written tablets [Col. 0870A] and then with the wax scraped over them [Note: [Col. 0869D] “And afterward covered with wax.” A similar stratagem is attributed above, in book II, chapter 9, to Demaratus the Lacedaemonian.].

When he returned to Carthage after Alexander’s death, they killed him, not merely out of ingratitude but also from cruel envy, as though he had sold the city to the king [Note: [Col. 0869D] “As though he had sold the city to the king.” I have made this reading from the corrupt readings “had avenged” and “had vindicated.” A similar usage occurs in Justin, where this verb means “to sell”; and I do not doubt that the reader will approve it. LAUT.—The printed editions wrongly have “had vindicated”; either “had revealed” or “had sold” should be written. From the notes of Bongarsius and Berneccerus on Justin, book XXI, chapter 6, it is clear that both expressions can properly be used to mean “to offer for sale.” In four Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian manuscript I found “had revealed.” The Augustan edition represented both readings, printing “had revealed or had vindicated,” the latter word having displaced “had sold” in the remaining manuscripts.].

Then, when they were waging continual and never entirely successful wars against the Sicilians and had surrounded Syracuse, at that time the most flourishing city in Sicily, with a siege, they were brought to the extremity of despair after Agathocles, king of Sicily, had outmaneuvered them by an extraordinary stratagem [Note: [Col. 0870C] “They were brought.” Thus I prefer it, with all the manuscripts and older editions, to “they were driven,” which appears in more recent editions.].

For when Agathocles was being besieged by the Carthaginians near Syracuse, and saw that he was neither a match for them in war, given the equipment of his forces, nor able to endure the siege because of insufficient pay [Note: [Col. 0870C] “Sufficiency of pay.” The Augustan edition has “sufficiency of pay” in the accusative.], he formed a plan prudently and concealed it even more effectively, and crossed over into Africa with his army [Note: [Col. 0870C] “He crossed over.” The Longobard manuscript together with that of Meus has “he crossed over” in the perfect tense.]. There he disclosed to his men what he was planning [Col. 0870B] and then instructed them what needed to be done.

Immediately, with one accord, they first burned the ships in which they had come [Note: [Col. 0870C] “They burned.” Most manuscripts have “they set fire to.” Justin, book XXII, chapter 6: “He ordered all the ships to be burned with the army’s consent.”], so that there would be no hope of retreat.

Then, as he laid waste to everything toward which he had directed his march, burning farms and fortresses, he encountered a certain Hanno with thirty thousand Carthaginians [Note: [Col. 0870D] “A certain Hanno with thirty thousand.” Justin says the matter occurred thus in book XXII. Diodorus, however, writes that not only Hanno but also Bomilcar was sent against Agathocles with an army consisting of no fewer than forty thousand infantry, one thousand cavalry, and two thousand chariots. Agathocles opposed to them first his son Archagathus with two thousand infantry and five hundred cavalry; then three thousand Syracusans; then three thousand Greeks and equal numbers of Samnites, Etruscans, and Gauls. Diodorus says that in the battle two hundred Greeks and no more than one thousand Carthaginians fell, although some have written six thousand. FABR.] opposing him [Note: [Col. 0870D] “He encountered.” The Longobard manuscript has “he had an encounter with.”]. He killed Hanno with two thousand of his own men [Note: [Col. 0870D] “With two thousand.” In Justin, from whom this account is taken, three thousand are said to have perished. He writes in book XXII, chapter 6: “When battle had been joined, two thousand Sicilians and three thousand Carthaginians fell with their commander.” But it is wholly incredible that, as Orosius would have it, only two men from Agathocles’ army fell. Hence I suspect that in Justin “two” should mean “two thousand,” just as the following “three” means “three thousand.” The Carthaginians’ defeat was much more severe, since they lost not only many more men but also their commander Hanno.].

Agathocles himself lost only two men in that war.

By this battle the courage of the Africans was extraordinarily broken and that of his own men immeasurably increased. He captured cities and fortresses, carried off enormous spoils, and slaughtered many thousands of the enemy. Then he established his camp five miles from Carthage, so that from the walls of the city itself they could watch the loss of their richest possessions, the devastation of the fields, and the burning of the farms.

To the present disasters was added a more grievous report: the army of the Africans, together with its commander, was said to have been destroyed in Sicily. In fact Antander, Agathocles’ brother [Note: [Col. 0871B] “Antander, Agathocles’ brother.” The common editions corruptly read “Andro.” Read Diodorus, who explains all these matters at length. FABR.], had overwhelmed it while it was off its guard and almost inactive.

When this news was spread throughout Africa, not only the tributary cities but also allied kings defected from the Carthaginians. Among them Ophellas, king of Cyrene [Note: [Col. 0871B] “Ophellas, king of Cyrene.” Diodorus, book XX: Ὁ δ᾽ Ὀφέλλας ἦν μὲν τῶν φίλων τῶν συνεστρατευμένων Ἀλεξάνδρῳ, κυριεύων δὲ τῶν περὶ Κυρήνην πόλεων, καὶ δυνάμεος ἁδρᾶς, περιεβάλετο ταῖς ἐλπίσι μείζονα δυναστείαν, that is: “Ophellas was one of Alexander’s friends who had served with him; but, since he held the cities around Cyrene and a large force under his authority, he conceived hopes of a greater sovereignty.” FABR.—This Ophellas had married Eurydice, an Athenian girl of noble descent from the ancient line of Miltiades. After Ophellas’ death, Demetrius Poliorcetes received her among his wives, to the great joy of the Athenians. The account we wrote about this may be consulted in our Catholic History, published in the vernacular, vol. I, p. 345.], also made an agreement with Agathocles to share the war, while eagerly aspiring to rule Africa.

But after they had joined their armies and camps into one, Ophellas was surrounded and killed through Agathocles’ flatteries and ambushes [Note: [Col. 0871C] “He was killed.” Meus has “he is killed”; in the same manuscript, shortly afterward, “he overcame” is written instead of “he overcomes.”].

The Carthaginians, gathering forces from every direction, burst into war. Agathocles, who had Ophellas’ forces with him, engaged them and defeated them in a fierce battle, with great slaughter on both sides.

The crisis of this battle brought such despair upon the Carthaginians that, had a mutiny not arisen in Agathocles’ army, Bomilcar, commander of the Carthaginians [Note: [Col. 0871C] “Bomilcar, commander of the Carthaginians.” The common editions incorrectly call him Hamilcar. He is in fact Βομίλκας; when he seized royal power at Carthage, he was killed, as Diodorus writes. FABR.], would have gone over to him with his army.

For this offense he was fastened to a gallows in the middle of the marketplace by order of the Carthaginians and provided his countrymen with a cruel spectacle.

After Agathocles’ death, when the Carthaginians ravaged Sicily with a prepared fleet, they were repeatedly defeated by land and sea by King Pyrrhus, summoned from Epirus to Italy; finally they turned their attention to the Roman wars. [Note: [Col. 0871D] “Alas!” The Longobard manuscript and that of Meus have “for grief.”]

Alas! Do those who complain about recent events read such things about the ancients [Note: [Col. 0871D] “About recent events.” Perizonius has “about the events just mentioned.”]? Indeed they read them, and they interpret them not with fairness but with rivalry.

For they are pierced by that immense and ineffable goad, which they themselves do not discern [Note: [Col. 0871D] “Which they themselves do not discern.” I emended this from my manuscript, the first Leiden manuscript, and the Gronovian manuscript, with the support also of three Florentine manuscripts. The common editions have “which they themselves distinguish,” but that fits less well.], not because of difficult times but because of Christian times.

And this is the discharge of an envious ulcer: whatever is done under an accursed name appears more grievous [Note: [Col. 0871D] “Whatever is done under an accursed…” The Augustan edition has “whatever is accursed.” The sense of the common reading is: “Whatever is done under an accursed [name], that is, under the name or in the time that we curse, appears more atrocious.” This is clear from what follows, where he says that nothing can be rightly done by anyone in the eyes of enemies who curse him and therefore indiscriminately curse everything he does.], just as among us it is often the case, in the eyes of enemies, that those whom they curse appear to do nothing that is not wicked, nothing that is not shameful, [Note: [Col. 0871D] “Nothing that is merely incidental, nothing that is not a wound for themselves.” This is the reading of all the ancient books. *Subsicivum* or *subsecivum* is what the Greeks call πάρεργον, something alien to the principal matter and, so to speak, superfluous. The metaphor is taken from the portions of land left over in land assignments, called *subseciva*, about which Frontinus writes. FABR.—The printed editions have “nothing that is incidental, nothing that is full of wounds,” in place of “nothing that is a wound for themselves”; this fits both the sense and the rhetorical form of the period less well. But I do not know what “incidental” or *subsicivum* means here. Nor do I think Orosius means what Franciscus Fabricius says, namely what the Greeks call πάρεργον and what truly signifies “superfluous,” although it is read consistently in all the books. LAUT.—What Fabricius asserts to be the reading of all ancient books can apply only to those he himself examined. The manuscripts I consulted differ. For *subsicivum*, the first Leiden manuscript, older than the others, has *saevum*. The second and fourth Leiden manuscripts and the Utrecht manuscript have *suscenum* or *suscevum*; the older editions substituted *obscaenum*, except the Augustan edition, which reads *subscivum*. Orosius perhaps wrote *subscaevum*, meaning “somewhat ill-fated” or “of evil omen.” In this sense *scaevum* is used by Arnobius, Against the Pagans, book V, p. 159: “Lest some ill-omened person interrupt the nuptial joys.” For “a wound for themselves,” the first Leiden manuscript and the Gronovian manuscript have *vulnerosum*, a word worthy of Orosius’ age, though it is also found in the earliest editions and is joined in the Augustan edition with the other reading, “a wound for themselves,” both being received into the text. The Longobard manuscript reads: “nothing that is wicked, nothing that is *subsichivum* [sic], nothing that is a wound for themselves.” The others do not differ from the more recent common editions.], doing nothing, in word or deed, that is not incidental or to their own hurt—and yet doing this almost simply [Note: [Col. 0872D] “And yet almost simply.” Some read “and yet simply,” as do two Leiden manuscripts and several older editions. Others read “and now almost simply,” including the three Florentine manuscripts, Meus, Perizonius, the Gronovian manuscript, and “and yet similarly.” The common reading seems to mean: “And yet what is seized upon so harshly by enemies and turned to evil is generally done simply and almost without malicious intent.”].

For envy so distorts the mind that, by nature, it does not see what is straight. Such are these people—but much more wretched, because they are enemies of God and therefore enemies of truth. Of them we speak these things with tears [Note: [Col. 0872D] “We say these things with tears.” He is referring to the words of the Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Philippians, chapter III, verse 18.], and, if they permit it, we admonish them compassionately so that we may heal them.

They see these things with a diseased eye, and therefore whatever they see appears double to them. Blinded and confused by the darkness of wickedness, they fall into such a condition that, seeing less, they see more, although they cannot see what is as it is [Col. 0873A] [Note: [Col. 0873C] “They can.” The manuscript of Perizonius and the Augustan edition have “they are able.”].

They consider the scourges of a father more severe than the fires of an enemy; they call God, who caresses, admonishes, and redeems, harsher than the devil, who persecutes, dominates, and slaughters.

Yet if they understood that he was a father, they would rejoice in correction; and if the fruit of instruction were foreseen, discipline would be bearable. Moreover, because of the hope now given to the nations, though previously it had not been given, they would consider sufferings lighter, even if they endured heavier ones.

Yet they can also learn contempt for miseries [Note: [Col. 0873C] “Contempt.” The Longobard manuscript, Meus, Perizonius, two Leiden manuscripts, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Gronovian manuscript prefer *contemptus* in the plural; among the editions, the Augustan edition has the common reading *contemptum*. After “learn” the fourth Leiden manuscript adds “to praise.”] from their own people, among whom the greatest evils were valued as the greatest goods, provided only that they might attain glory renowned and illustrious in fame [Note: [Col. 0873C] “Glory of fame.” Perizonius has “glory celebrated by fame,” and so forth, which is better expressed. At the end of the chapter the older editions have “they were able” instead of “they might have been able.”].

From this it may be gathered how much we, to whom blessed eternity is promised, must endure for life, when they were able to endure so much for fame.

## CHAPTER VII. The achievements of the Romans against the Syracusans and Carthaginians, and the outcomes of various wars. The conspiracy of slaves and naval allies.

[Note: [Col. 0873C] In the 483rd year from the founding of the City. This year, in which the First Punic War began, is assigned various numbers by historians; in the Capitoline Fasti it is 489. FABR.]

In the 483rd year from the founding of the City, when Appius Claudius and Quintus Fabius were consuls, the Romans sent assistance to the Mamertines—whose city, Messana, was a famous city of Sicily—against Hiero, king of Syracuse, and against the Carthaginian forces allied with Hiero; they also sent the consul Appius Claudius with an army. He so swiftly defeated the Syracusans and Carthaginians that the king himself, terrified by the magnitude of the disaster, declared that he had been defeated before he had even engaged in battle.

[Note: [Col. 0873C] Appius Claudius. All manuscripts and the Augustan edition have “Appius Claudius,” that is, “with Appius Claudius.”]

[Note: [Col. 0873C] Quintus Fabius. Orosius alone, so far as I know, compares Fabius as consul with Appius Claudius. In his place, all other records have Flaccus, who is described in the Capitoline Fasti as follows: “M. FULVIUS Q. F. M. N. FLACCUS.” On the deeds of Appius Claudius against the Carthaginians and King Hiero, see Polybius, Book I; Livy, Book XVI; and Florus, Book II, chapter 2. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Was a city. The Perizonius manuscript has “was a city.”]

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Assistance. All manuscripts have “assistance”; the Augustan edition has “for assistance,” while the printed editions have “as assistance.”]

[Note: [Col. 0873D] And Appius Claudius. Since the printed editions do not recognize the conjunction “and,” which appears in all the manuscripts, they substituted “for assistance” above for “assistance.”]

Thereafter, with his strength broken and his confidence lost, he humbly begged for peace and received it; but by order of the consuls he was fined two hundred talents of silver.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Who thereafter, with his strength broken. The common reading is “with unbroken strength,” which the text itself disproves. LAUT.—It is a ridiculous error found in all the printed editions. For what does “with unbroken strength” or “from unbroken strength” mean? Lautius is therefore right.]

[Note: [Col. 0873D] The consuls besieged Agrigentum. He means the consuls of the third year of this war, Lucius Postumius Megellus and Quintus Mamilius Vitulus. They conducted operations at Agrigentum and captured the town. See Polybius, Book I. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Agrigentum. The old editions read: “The consuls therefore, going to Agrigentum, a city of Sicily, there the garrisons, etc.” [Col. 0874C], contrary to all the manuscripts and the Augustan edition.]

The consuls surrounded Agrigentum, a city of Sicily, together with the Carthaginian garrisons there, by siegeworks and a rampart. When the elderly Hannibal, the Carthaginian commander, enclosed within that siege had been reduced to the greatest extremity, Hanno, the new commander of the Carthaginians, arrived unexpectedly with fifteen hundred cavalry, thirty thousand infantry, and thirty elephants, and for a short time delayed the capture of the city. But soon afterward the city was taken. The Carthaginians were defeated and routed in a great battle; eleven elephants were captured, and all the Agrigentines were sold under the auctioneer’s crown.

[Note: [Col. 0874C] The Agrigentines. The first Leiden manuscript has: “All the Agrigentines were sold under the crown.”]

The elder Hannibal escaped by breaking out with a few men.

[Note: [Col. 0874C] Gnaeus Cornelius Asina, Gaius Duilius. These were consuls in the fifth year of this war, and in the 493rd year from the founding of the City. What Orosius writes about the speed with which the fleet was prepared is found in Florus, Book II. FABR.]

When Gnaeus Cornelius Asina and Gaius Duilius were consuls, and the elder Hannibal was ravaging the Italian coast with a fleet of seventy ships, the Romans likewise ordered a fleet to be built and equipped; the consul Duilius quickly carried this out.

[Note: [Col. 0874C] Ordered. Some old editions have “order.”]

For within sixty days after the trees had been felled, a fleet of one hundred and thirty ships was launched and lay at anchor.

[Note: [Col. 0874C] Within the sixtieth day. All the manuscripts that I consulted, as well as Vincent of Beauvais, Book VI, chapter 34, have “within sixty days.” The first edition has “within seventy days”; the Paris and Venetian editions have “within seventy day.” Later the Augustan edition has “within sixty days after the trees had been cut,” instead of “after the trees had been.”]

[Note: [Col. 0874C] A fleet of one hundred and thirty ships. Florus gives the number as one hundred and sixty. FABR.]

Cornelius Asina, the other consul, set out with sixteen ships for the island of Lipara.

[Note: [Col. 0874C] With sixteen. The Augustan edition has “with seventeen.”]

[Note: [Col. 0874C] Set out for. The manuscripts of the Longobard family and the second Florentine manuscript, together with Perizonius, require this form instead of “sought.”]

There, having been summoned by Hannibal, as though to a peace conference, he was captured by Punic treachery and killed in chains.

[Note: [Col. 0874C] Where he was captured by Hannibal. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection and the Augustan edition, have “There he was captured by Hannibal,” which is not objectionable, since what follows is “when Duilius.” Vincent of Beauvais also confirms this reading.]

When Duilius, the other consul, heard of this, he set out with thirty ships against Hannibal. A naval battle was joined. Hannibal, after losing the ship on which he had been carried, escaped in a boat; thirty-one of his ships were captured, thirteen were sunk, three thousand men were killed, and seven thousand are reported to have been captured.

[Note: [Col. 0874D] When Duilius. This is Gaius Duilius, son of Marcus, who was the first to defeat the Carthaginians in a naval battle. See Cicero, Cato; Valerius, Book III, chapter 3; and Pliny, Book XXXIV, chapter 5. FABR.—After the excerpt from Orosius about Duilius, Vincent of Beauvais adds the following in his *Speculum Historiale*, at the same place: “This man, whom Orosius calls Duilius, Helinandus”—a writer and compiler who lived shortly before Vincent’s time—“says was the same man whom Jerome, in Book I against Jovinianus, calls Duellus. Concerning Duillius or Duellius—as he is often called in the manuscripts—or Duellus, as Jerome calls him, the following is found there: ‘Duellus, who first celebrated a triumph at Rome for a naval victory, married a maiden named Ilia, of such modesty that even in that age, when immorality was a monstrosity rather than a vice, she was an example. Now when he was already old and his body trembled, during a certain quarrel he heard it reproached that his breath smelled foul. Sadly he went home. When he complained to his wife, asking why she had never warned him so that he might remedy the defect, she replied: “I would have done so, unless I had thought that all men’s breath smelled that way.”’”]

[Note: [Col. 0875C] Thirty-one ships. The same number appears in Eutropius, except that he writes that fourteen ships were sunk. Polybius reports that the Carthaginians lost fifty ships in this battle. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0875C] Seven thousand were reported captured. Three Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen Collection count three thousand prisoners. Vincent of Beauvais agrees with them.]

Afterward, when Gaius Aquillius Florus and Lucius Cornelius Scipio were consuls, the Carthaginians appointed Hanno, who had been substituted for Hannibal, to command the naval battle for the defense of Sardinia and Corsica. Defeated by the consul Scipio and having lost his army, Hanno threw himself into the thick of the enemy and was killed there.

[Note: [Col. 0875C] Lucius Cornelius Scipio. The printed editions insert the conjunction “and” between the names of the consuls, but none of the manuscripts recognizes it.]

[Note: [Col. 0875C] In the place of. The second Florentine manuscript has “in the place.”]

[Note: [Col. 0875C] There he was killed. Hanno, commander of the Carthaginians, died fighting with the greatest courage near the town of Olbia. See Valerius, Book V, chapter 1. FABR.—In my manuscript: “He was killed.” Hanno fell before the walls of Olbia, a town of Sardinia. Because of his courage, Valerius Maximus, Book V, chapter 1, example 2, reports that Scipio Asina, the Roman commander—whose brother had been captured and killed by the elder Hannibal—honorably carried his body from his own tent and gave it a magnificent funeral. Silius Italicus also mentions him in Book VI, line 670:

“He sees also the final honors of the dead citizen:

Scipio was celebrating the funeral of the Carthaginian commander,

Victorious in the Sardinian land.”]

In that same year, three thousand slaves and four thousand naval allies conspired to destroy the city of Rome; and unless the betrayal, once discovered, had forestalled the plot, the city, left without a defense, would have perished by the hand of slaves.

[Note: [Col. 0875D] The betrayal, once discovered. My manuscript has “the betrayal, once revealed.” Apart from Orosius, Zonaras also mentions this danger, *Annals*, Book II.]

235

## CHAPTER VIII

The Romans, marching against the city of Camerina, fall into an ambush. The elder Hannibal is stoned to death by his own men. Regulus ravages Lipara and Melita. Clupea surrenders to the Romans. Regulus wins a victory over the Carthaginians after killing a serpent of enormous size.

[Note: [Col. 0875D] In the following year. This year is 495 from the founding of the City in the Capitoline Fasti, when Aulus Atilius Calatinus and Gaius Sulpicius Paterculus were consuls. FABR.]

In the following year, the consul Calatinus, marching against Camerina, a city of Sicily, rashly led his army into a narrow pass that the Carthaginian forces had long before fortified.

[Note: [Col. 0875D] Calpurnius Flamma. Livy, Book XXII, Florus, Book II, and the author of *On Illustrious Men* call this tribune by that name; Pliny, Book XXII, chapter 6, calls him Marcus Calpurnius Flamma; Cato calls him Quintus Caedicius; Quadrigarius calls him Laberius. See Gellius, Book III, chapter 7, and Frontinus, Book I. FABR.]

Since he had absolutely no opportunity either to resist or to escape, he was saved by the courage and efforts of Calpurnius Flamma. Calpurnius selected a band of three hundred men, seized a hill occupied by the enemy, and drew all the Carthaginians against himself by fighting, until the Roman army passed through the enclosed defile while the enemy was not pressing it.

[Note: [Col. 0876B] With a band of three hundred men. All the manuscripts prefer this reading to “three hundred.”]

All three hundred were killed in that battle; Calpurnius alone escaped, although pierced by many wounds and covered with corpses.

[Note: [Col. 0876B] In that battle. The common editions have “in that engagement,” but Orosius, following the example of Sallust, very often uses *bellum* for “battle,” and all the manuscripts require “battle” here.]

The elder Hannibal, again placed in command of the fleet by the Carthaginians, unfortunately engaged the Romans in a naval battle and was defeated. When a mutiny arose, he was stoned to death by his own army.

[Note: [Col. 0876C] Again placed in command of the fleet by the Carthaginians. This is the reading of all the manuscripts and old editions. Fabricius changed it to “placed in command of the Carthaginian fleet again.”]

[Note: [Col. 0876C] He died covered with stones. In the Livian Epitome, Book XVII, Hannibal’s death is recorded as follows: “Hannibal, commander of the Carthaginians, after the fleet which he had commanded was defeated, was lifted onto a cross by his soldiers.” Polybius writes of him: “Not many years afterward, having been surrounded by the Romans in Sardinia, in a certain harbor, and having lost many of his ships, he was immediately seized by the Carthaginians who had survived and crucified.” That is: “Not long afterward, having been surrounded by the Romans in a certain harbor in Sardinia, after losing a great number of ships, he was immediately seized and crucified by the Carthaginians who had escaped. FABR.—Understand the passage thus: after he had been covered with stones during the mutiny, his corpse was afterward lifted onto a cross in the same tumult.”]

The consul Atilius ravaged and destroyed Lipara and Melita, famous islands of Sicily.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] Consul Atilius. Gaius Atilius Regulus is meant. In the eighth year of this war he was consul with Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio and celebrated a naval triumph over the Carthaginians, as recorded in the Capitoline tablets. FABR.]

The consuls were ordered to transfer the war to Africa. They set out for Sicily with three hundred and thirty ships, where Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians, and Hanno, commander of the fleet, met them. In the ensuing naval battle the Carthaginians were put to flight and lost sixty-four ships.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] The consuls into Africa. These consuls were Marcus Atilius Regulus and Lucius Manlius Vulso, according to Polybius, Eutropius, and Florus; consult those authors. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0876D] With three hundred and thirty ships. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have “with four hundred and thirty ships.”]

The victorious consuls were transported to Africa and were the first of all to receive the city of Clupea into surrender.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] First of all. The Augustan edition has “first of all” in the neuter form.]

From there, as they advanced against Carthage, they ravaged three hundred fortresses or more and carried their hostile standards around Carthage.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] Or more. My manuscript has “and more.”]

The consul Manlius, departing from Africa with his victorious fleet, brought back to Rome twenty-seven thousand captives together with immense spoils.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] From Africa. Three Florentine manuscripts, together with Perizonius, the third Leiden manuscript, and the Groningen Collection, read “Africa,” omitting *ab*.]

Regulus, having drawn the Carthaginian war by lot, marched with his army and pitched camp not far from the river Bagrada. There, while a serpent of extraordinary size was devouring many soldiers who had descended to the river out of necessity to obtain water, Regulus set out with his army to destroy the beast.

[Note: [Col. 0877C] A serpent of extraordinary size. Valerius, at the end of Book I, writes that Livy related this story of the serpent with equal care and eloquence at the beginning of Book XVIII. Gellius, Book VI, chapter 3, also recounts it from Tubero. FABR.]

But the javelins, striking its back, accomplished nothing, and every blow of the weapons was ineffectual: they slipped across the dreadful lattice of its scales as though across an oblique tortoise-shell formation of shields, and were repelled by the body itself in a marvelous manner, so that they did not wound it. When Regulus saw that a great number of men were being crushed by its bite, trampled by its attack, and even deprived of life by its poisonous breath, he ordered ballistae to be brought forward. Through these, a stone of the size used against walls was hurled into its spine and loosened the structure of its entire body.

[Note: [Col. 0877C] To bring up the ballistae. Some manuscripts and editions have “to bring up the ballistae.”]

[Note: [Col. 0877C] A stone used against walls. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have “a millstone-sized rock.” I found the same reading in Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum Historiale*, Book VI, chapter 35.]

The nature of a serpent is indeed such that, although it appears to lack feet, it is nevertheless equipped with ribs and scales arranged in an even pattern from the top of its throat to the bottom of its belly, so that it rests on its scales as though on claws and on its ribs as though on legs.

For it does not move like a worm, which has no rigid spine and unfolds its motion by successively extending the contracted parts of its little body in a straight line and contracting the extended parts. Rather, by alternating efforts, it moves its sinuous sides in a winding motion, so that along the outer curve of its spine it stretches the stiff row of ribs, while by means of the ribs, which by nature are straight at their upper ends, it fixes the claw-like points of its scales.

[Note: [Col. 0877C] And in a straight line. The printed editions of Fabricius incorrectly merged the phrase into “indirectly.” A little earlier they also incorrectly print “is equipped” instead of “is arranged,” which is found in the manuscripts.]

By doing this alternately and rapidly, it travels not only across level ground but also climbs convex surfaces, equipped with as many tracks as it has ribs.

The consequence of this arrangement is that, if it is struck anywhere on the body between the belly and the head, once weakened it cannot continue its course.

[Note: [Col. 0877C] It cannot continue its course. The Augustan edition reads, not unreasonably, “it cannot move away,” namely, because it is forced to remain in the place where it received the wound.]

For wherever that blow falls, it breaks the spine by which the rib-legs and the movement of the body are driven.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] Wherever that blow falls. Instead of “that blow,” the common editions, except the Augustan, have “those blows.” But the Longobard manuscript, together with three Leiden manuscripts, the Groningen Collection, and Perizonius, requires “that blow.” My manuscript has “there the blow,” which can also sufficiently defend the passage.]

Therefore this serpent, which for so long had resisted so many javelins without being wounded, yielded helplessly to the blow of a single stone and was soon surrounded by weapons and easily overcome.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] This serpent. The first and second Florentine manuscripts and several others read “this serpent” with the feminine form, followed by “which,” as well as “surrounded” and “overcome.”]

Its hide was carried to Rome—said to have measured one hundred and twenty feet—and for a long time it was an object of wonder to everyone.

Regulus waged a most savage war against three commanders: two Hasdrubals and Hamilcar, summoned from Sicily. In that war seventeen thousand Carthaginians were killed, five thousand were captured, eighteen elephants were led away, and eighty-two towns surrendered to the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] Regulus against three commanders. Eutropius gives three unnamed commanders. Polybius names Hasdrubal, Bostar, and Hamilcar. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0877D] Seventeen thousand were killed. Eutropius says that nineteen thousand of the enemy fell. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0878C] Eighty-two towns. Eutropius says that he received seventy-four communities into alliance. FABR.]

238

## CHAPTER IX

The Carthaginians, after being denied peace, gather assistance from everywhere; under the Lacedaemonian commander Xanthippus they defeat the Romans and capture Regulus; Aemilius and Fulvius avenge that outrage.

[Col. 0878B]

The Carthaginians, broken by wars and exhausted by disasters, asked Regulus for peace. But when they heard the intolerable and harsh terms of peace, they judged it safer to die armed than to live in misery, and decided to purchase not only the assistance of the Spaniards and Gauls, of whom they already had very many, but also that of the Greeks.

[Note: [Col. 0878C] Harsh terms. Polybius, Book I, and Eutropius, Book II, say the same. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0878C] Having sworn themselves. Because the manuscripts had this reading, Fabricius placed it in the margin, preferring to retain the common text as the safer course. The written reading can be defended if one understands it in the Greek manner. LAUT.—In the manuscripts that I consulted I found “considering it safer.”]

Accordingly, they summoned Xanthippus, king of the Lacedaemonians, with auxiliary forces and placed him in command of the war.

[Note: [Col. 0878C] Xanthippus, king of the Lacedaemonians. No one, so far as I know, says that this man was king of the Lacedaemonians; all say that he was a commander sent to the Carthaginians. Cicero calls him “Xanthippus the Lacedaemonian” in Book III *On Duties*. Polybius says: “A certain Xanthippus, a Lacedaemonian man, who had received the Spartan training and possessed moderate experience in military affairs.”]

After inspecting the Carthaginian forces and leading them out into the field, Xanthippus greatly improved their deployment and engaged the Romans in battle. There was a great slaughter of Roman forces. Thirty thousand Romans were struck down in that engagement.

[Note: [Col. 0878D] Of Roman forces. My manuscript and the first Leiden manuscript, together with Scott’s edition, have “of Roman forces.” Three Florentine manuscripts have “of Roman soldiers.” “Of Roman forces” sounds better, indicating Roman strength rather than Roman men.]

[Note: [Col. 0878D] For thirty thousand. Appian, in his *Libyca*, says: “Of the thirty thousand men whom Atilius commanded, only a few barely escaped to the city of Aspis; all the rest were partly killed and partly captured.” Polybius and Eutropius report that two thousand escaped. FABR.]

That famous commander Regulus was captured with five hundred men and, thrown into chains, furnished the Carthaginians with a glorious triumph only in the tenth year of the Punic War.

[Note: [Col. 0878D] That famous commander. Some manuscripts have “a famous man,” others “both,” and others “a famous commander.” The Florentine or Longobard manuscript has “a famous commander,” as do most manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0879C] Only in the tenth year. The tenth year of this war followed the consulship of Regulus and Manlius, when Fulvius and Aemilius were consuls; Sigonius correctly thinks that Regulus was captured in that year. Appian, speaking of the captives, says: “And with them the general Atilius, who had been consul, was a prisoner.” Cicero, however, writes in Book III *On Duties*: “Marcus Atilius Regulus, when he had been captured by ambush in Africa during his second consulship,” and so forth. FABR.]

Xanthippus, conscious of so bold a deed and fearing a reversal of unstable fortunes, immediately departed from Africa for Greece.

[Note: [Col. 0879C] Xanthippus, of so bold a deed. For the reasons why Xanthippus suddenly left Africa, see Polybius and Appian. FABR.—Orosius follows Polybius, whom one should consult in Book I, chapter 36. The Romans commonly followed another account, one that was disgraceful to the Carthaginians; Appian recounts it at length at the beginning of his *Punic War*, and Silius Italicus pursues it in these words in Book VI, line 680:

“And the treacherous band, casting him from the stern,

though he called upon the gods in vain, sank into the sea

the Amyclaean commander; and for you, Regulus,

Xanthippus was paying upon the waves the savage penalty

of a death he had deserved.”]

Then the consuls Aemilius Paulus and Fulvius Nobiliore, having heard of Regulus’s capture and the defeat of the Roman army, were ordered to cross into Africa with a fleet of three hundred ships. They set out for Clupea.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] With a fleet of three hundred ships. The number is the same in Eutropius; Polybius gives three hundred and fifty. FABR.]

The Carthaginians immediately came there with an equal fleet, and the naval battle could not be postponed. One hundred and four Carthaginian ships were sunk, thirty were captured with their fighting men, and in addition thirty-five thousand soldiers from their ranks were killed. Of the Romans, nine ships were sunk and eleven hundred soldiers perished.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] In addition, thirty-five thousand. In the printed books of Eutropius the number is fifteen thousand enemy soldiers killed or captured. But since our manuscript has “five thousand,” I think that the figure indicating thirty thousand has been lost.]

[Note: [Col. 0879D] From their own ranks. This is absent from the old editions before the Bolsingian and Hittorp editions. In those editions, “discovered” appears shortly afterward incorrectly instead of “sunk”; the Augustan edition, together with the manuscripts, has “sunk.”]

The consuls pitched camp near Clupea. The two Hannos, commanders of the Carthaginians, again assembled there with a large army; when battle was joined, they lost nine thousand soldiers.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] But even then. All the manuscripts have “but as then,” and so forth; a smaller pause should, however, be placed after “were overwhelmed.”]

Yet Roman prosperity was never lasting, and whatever successes they achieved were immediately overwhelmed by great masses of disaster. When the Roman fleet was returning to Italy laden with booty, it was destroyed in a dreadful shipwreck.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] For out of three hundred ships. Eutropius gives a different account: “There was such a storm that, out of 463 ships, only 80 could scarcely be saved.” Polybius likewise says: “For of the three hundred and sixty-four ships, only eighty happened to remain.” FABR.]

For out of three hundred ships, two hundred and twenty perished, and only eighty were scarcely saved after their cargoes had been thrown overboard.

[Note: [Col. 0880C] Two hundred and twenty, etc. The first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have “two hundred and thirty perished; seventy were scarcely saved,” and so forth.]

Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians, was sent with an army into Numidia and Mauretania. After treating all the people with hostility and bloodshed because they were said to have willingly welcomed Regulus, he fined the survivors one thousand talents of silver and twenty thousand cattle. He crucified the leading men of all the peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0880C] Willingly. This is absent from two Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen Collection.]

In the third year, as savage fury always quickly forgets its dangers, the consuls Servilius Caepio and Sempronius Blaesus crossed into Africa with two hundred and sixty ships. They ravaged the entire coastline lying around the Syrtes and, advancing farther inland, captured and destroyed many cities and carried immense booty down to the fleet.

[Note: [Col. 0880C] In the third year. Here Orosius counts the last two years together, for only one year intervened between these consuls and the earlier consuls Paulus and Nobiliore. See Polybius and Eutropius on the deeds of these consuls. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0880C] With two hundred. Restore this reading from the Augustan manuscript; the others have “with two hundred.”]

[Note: [Col. 0880C] They carried down. Two Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection and the Augustan edition, have “they brought down.”]

From there, as they were returning to Italy, they were wrecked near the promontory of Palinurus, which projects into the sea from the Lucanian mountains, and disastrously lost one hundred and fifty cargo ships and the distinguished booty they had acquired by cruelty.

[Note: [Col. 0880C] When they were returning to Italy. The Augustan edition has “when they were returning to Italy.”]

Among the Romans, the enormity of their miseries at last overcame their shameful greed. For the Fathers, who had become utterly weary of naval affairs, decreed that no fleet of more than sixty ships should be maintained for the defense of Italy. Yet, driven by their unrestrained greed, they immediately violated this decree.

[Note: [Col. 0880C] Had become utterly weary. All the printed editions except the Augustan have changed this to “was,” as though that were better Latin; but all the manuscripts consistently write “had become,” which seems to have originated with Orosius himself, who belonged to the same age.]

[Note: [Col. 0880D] Moreover, the consul Cotta. Gaius Aurelius Cotta was consul with Publius Servilius Geminus in the 501st year of the City; the Capitoline tablets record that he triumphed over the Carthaginians and Sicilians. FABR.]

Moreover, the consul Cotta crossed into Sicily and fought the Carthaginians and Sicilians in many battles on land and sea. Throughout Sicily he left behind heaps of unburied dead, partly enemies and partly even allies.

[Note: [Col. 0880D] Unburied slaughter. The common editions have “inhuman slaughter,” which is certainly inhumane. LAUT.—Lautius’s reading is supported not only by those manuscripts from which it was restored in later editions, such as those of Bolsing and Hittorp, but also by the first and third Florentine manuscripts, my own manuscript, and the manuscript once owned by Perizonius. The second Florentine manuscript has “countless slaughter.” Cotta appears to have held proconsular authority in Sicily that year. The word “even” is absent from two Leiden manuscripts.]

When Lucius Caecilius Metellus and Gaius Furius Pacilus were consuls, Hasdrubal, the new commander of the Carthaginians, arrived from Africa at Lilybaeum with one hundred and thirty elephants and more than thirty thousand cavalry and infantry. He immediately engaged the consul Metellus in battle near Panormus.

[Note: [Col. 0880D] Furius Pacilus. Pacilus, not Placidus, is the cognomen of Furius in the Capitoline Fasti, whose authority is of the greatest weight for us. On Metellus’s deeds, see Polybius and Eutropius. FABR.]

But Metellus, fearing the great force of the beasts, first drove them, with great skill, either into flight or to their deaths, and thus easily defeated the enemy’s very large force. Twenty thousand Carthaginians were killed in that battle; twenty-six elephants were also killed, while one hundred and four were captured and led through Italy, providing the Italian peoples with a most remarkable spectacle.

[Note: [Col. 0881B] One hundred and four were captured and led through Italy. Eutropius says that Metellus led 130 elephants through Italy. Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 6, writes that Metellus transported 142 into Italy. But in the Epitome, Book XIX, we read that 120 were led in Metellus’s triumph. FABR.]

Hasdrubal fled with a few men to Lilybaeum and, in his absence, was condemned to death by the Carthaginians.

241

## CHAPTER X

How the Carthaginians, after peace had been denied them, cruelly killed Regulus; and how the Romans, after fighting unsuccessfully in Sicily once and again, finally prevailed.

[Col. 0881B]

After this, the Carthaginians, exhausted by so many disasters, decided that peace must be sought from the Romans. For this purpose they thought that Atilius Regulus, formerly the Roman commander whom they had held captive for five years, should be sent among the other ambassadors in a position of special prominence.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] Roman. The Augustan edition has “of the Romans.”] They had him return from Italy after peace had not been obtained; with his eyelids cut off, they bound him to a framework and killed him by keeping him awake.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] Atilius for this purpose. After the Carthaginians were defeated by Metellus, Regulus was sent under oath to Rome and the Senate. He refused to have the prisoners returned and went back to Carthage for punishment. Cicero discusses the matter in Book III *On Duties* and mentions it in many other places. See Livy, Book XVIII; Eutropius, Book II; Valerius, Book I, chapter 1; Gellius, Book VI, chapter 4; Horace, Book III, Ode 5; and Silius, Book VI. FABR.]
