[Note: [Col. 0881C] With his eyelids cut off. These are Cicero’s words concerning Regulus’s punishment in his speech *Against Piso*. When Marcus Tullius says that Regulus was killed on a machine, Appian expresses it as follows: “The Carthaginians shut him into a cage fitted with spikes on every side and destroyed him.” FABR.]

Then Atilius Regulus and Manlius Vulso, both again consuls, set out for Lilybaeum with a fleet of two hundred ships and four legions.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] The other Atilius Regulus. Gaius Atilius Regulus and Lucius Manlius Vulso were again consuls in the year 503. The names of these consuls are complete in my manuscript of Justin, Book XLI, except that, in the old form of writing, “Bulsone” appears instead of “Vulsone”; hence “Pisone” arose in the printed editions. Polybius recounts at length what these consuls did against the Carthaginians. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0881D] They set out. This final word appears only in my manuscript and is absent from the others.]

The Romans attempted to besiege the town, situated on a promontory; but when Hannibal, the son of Hamilcar, arrived, they were defeated, lost most of their army, and escaped only with difficulty.

[Note: [Col. 0881D] After them, the consul Claudius. This is Publius Claudius, son of Appius. When the sacred chickens would not eat after being released from their cage, he ordered them thrown into the water so that they might drink, since they did not wish to eat. Cicero, Book II *On the Nature of the Gods*. FABR.]

After them, the consul Claudius set out against the enemy for the harbor of Drepanum with a fleet of one hundred and twenty ships. There he was soon intercepted by the Carthaginian fleet and defeated.

[Note: [Col. 0881D] With a fleet of one hundred and twenty ships. Polybius adds three ships and recounts the entire affair at length. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0881D] He set out against the enemy. My manuscript adds “was.” Shortly afterward, in place of “there,” Perizonius’s manuscript reads “there immediately,” while all the others have “where immediately.” Most of them then delete “was” after “defeated.” I therefore think the passage should be reconstructed as follows: “He set out against the enemy, where he was soon intercepted by the Carthaginian fleet and defeated, although he himself,” and so forth. In three Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen Collection, “was received” appears instead of “was intercepted.”]

He himself fled with thirty ships to the camp at Lilybaeum. All the rest—that is, ninety—were either captured or sunk. Eight thousand soldiers were killed, and twenty thousand are reported to have been captured.

[Note: [Col. 0882C] He fled. My manuscript has “he escaped,” and shortly afterward “were sunk” instead of “were destroyed.” The Augustan edition has “were destroyed.” My manuscript has “are carried away” instead of “are reported.”]

Gaius Junius, Claudius’s colleague, also lost his entire fleet in a shipwreck.

[Note: [Col. 0882C] In the following year as well. This account, inserted by the deacon who incorporated material into Eutropius’s history, is commonly read as part of Eutropius. FABR.]

In the following year as well, the Punic fleet crossed into Italy and ravaged many parts of it far and wide.

[Note: [Col. 0882C] Following. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have “next.”]

Meanwhile Lutatius, having crossed into Sicily with a fleet of three hundred ships, while stirring up battle near the city of Drepanum in the front ranks, was pierced through the thigh and rescued only with the greatest difficulty when he was already being overwhelmed.

[Note: [Col. 0882C] Lutatius with a fleet of three hundred ships. Gaius Lutatius Catulus was consul with Aulus Postumius Albinus in the year 506 from the founding of the City. We have written “Catulus crossed over with a fleet of three hundred ships” on the authority of old books, whereas the common reading has “a fleet of two hundred ships.” Eutropius likewise states that Catulus went to Sicily with three hundred ships. I cannot be persuaded that the Roman people possessed no other public ships besides those two hundred quinqueremes which Polybius says were built by private citizens. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0882C] He engaged among the leading men. We restored this reading on the authority of the Longobard manuscript, also supported by the second and third Florentine manuscripts. The common editions ineptly read “he engaged among the leading men of Sicily.” The variant “of Sicily” seems to have arisen in some manuscripts from *ciet* or *cieret*, after which both readings were combined. Hence *cieret* is absent from the Augustan edition and the Groningen Collection, while the first and fourth Leiden manuscripts have *gerit* instead. My manuscript also has the better reading “he engages among the leading men,” but a line is drawn above *ciet*, apparently indicating that *cieret* should be written there. The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Groningen Collection, reads “among the first men.”]

The Carthaginians, under Hanno, then advanced toward Sicily with four hundred ships and large forces. Lutatius was no less energetic; indeed, with remarkable speed he anticipated the Carthaginians’ plans.

After the fleets of both sides had anchored close to one another near the island of Aegates and had remained there throughout the night with their anchors almost interwoven, Lutatius gave the signal for battle at daybreak.

[Note: [Col. 0882D] Near the island of Aegates. Polybius says: “He sailed toward Aegusa, the island lying before Lilybaeum.” Silius, Book I:

“... he longs to wipe away the shame of his ancestors from Aegates.”

Eutropius says that the battle was fought on the sixth day before the Ides of March. FABR.]

As the battle grew more violent, Hanno was defeated, turned his ship away, and was the first of the commanders to flee. A considerable part of his army went with him to Africa; others took refuge at Lilybaeum.

[Note: [Col. 0883C] Set out. The Longobard manuscript has “set out.”]

Sixty-three Punic ships were captured and one hundred and twenty-five were sunk. Thirty-two thousand men were captured, and fourteen thousand were killed.

[Note: [Col. 0883C] Sixty-three Punic ships were captured. In its numbers, Orosius’s text generally agrees with Eutropius; it differs greatly from Polybius. FABR.]

The Romans, however, lost twelve ships by sinking.

Lutatius then came to the city of Eryx, which the Carthaginians held; there, after battle was joined, he killed two thousand Carthaginians.

## CHAPTER XI

How the Carthaginians obtained peace on stated terms and at a price; how Rome suffered a disastrous flood of the Tiber and the devastation of a certain fire; and concerning the war against the Falisci.

Then the Carthaginians, in urgent haste, sent first to the consul Lutatius and then to Rome, begging for peace; and they immediately obtained it on the terms previously proposed. [Note: “Previously proposed.” The Florentine manuscript of the second class, together with the Augustan edition, reads *ante positis*, “set forth earlier.” Perhaps this is better.] The terms were that they should withdraw from Sicily and Sardinia; [Note: “That they should withdraw from Sicily and Sardinia.” Polybius: “The Carthaginians are to withdraw from all Sicily and from the islands that lie between Italy and Sicily.” Thus: “Let the Carthaginians withdraw from all Sicily and the islands that lie between Italy and Sicily.” Livy, Book XXI: “After suffering naval defeat at the Aegates, the Carthaginians surrendered Sicily and Sardinia.” FABR.] and, in compensation for the expenses of the war, [Note: “And in compensation for the expenses of the war.” Polybius: “The Carthaginians shall pay to the Romans, over twenty years, two thousand two hundred Euboean talents of silver.” Thus: “The Carthaginians shall pay the Romans, for twenty years, two thousand two hundred Euboean talents.” He adds immediately that the ten commissioners altered the period of payment and added one thousand talents.] and, in compensation for the expenses of the war, should pay three thousand [Note: “Talents.” The Florentine manuscripts read *tres, talentum*—“three, one talent.” Some early editions soon afterward read *portionibus* instead of *pensionibus*, “installments” instead of “payments.”] Euboean talents of refined silver in equal installments over twenty years.

This peace was concluded [Note: “After the twenty-third year.” Polybius and Livy, who reckon the time from the outbreak of this war, write that it occurred in the twenty-fourth year; but Orosius counts from the consulship of Appius Claudius and Quintus Fulvius, under whom the First Punic War began.] after the twenty-third year from the beginning of the First Punic War. Who, I ask, could set forth in words the war waged for twenty-three years between two states? How many kings of the Carthaginians, how many Roman consuls, how many columns of armies, what numbers of ships it gathered, shattered, and overwhelmed? And only then, when those matters have been fully weighed, let judgment be passed upon the present circumstances.

[Note: “In the year 507 from the founding of the City.” This year, in which Quintus Lutatius and Aulus Manlius were consuls, is recorded in the Capitoline Fasti as the year 512. Here one sees that Orosius, as above, likewise counts five years fewer here. FABR.]

In the year 507 from the founding of the City, a sudden overthrow of Rome herself forestalled the Romans’ triumph. For I should not speak rashly when I say that no sooner had even a modest joy come to Rome than a most grievous mourning suddenly overwhelmed it. When Quintus Lutatius and Aulus Manlius were consuls, diverse disasters of fire and water nearly consumed the City. [Note: “Under the consulship of Quintus Lutatius and Aulus Manlius.” We have removed the surname Catulus, which is given to Lutatius in Orosius’s books, since he belonged not to the family of the Catuli but to that of the Cercōnes, and is so recorded in the Capitoline Fasti: “Q. LUTATIUS C. F. C. N. CERCO.” FABR. — In Fabricius’s editions and in Scottus’s edition the surname Catulus is omitted; it appears in the others, as well as in all the manuscripts—certainly contrary to the truth, unless we say that Orosius himself was mistaken.]

For the Tiber, swollen by unaccustomed rains and overflowing beyond expectation either in duration or in volume, destroyed all the buildings of Rome [Note: “Built on level ground.” The third Leiden manuscript reads “threw down those situated on level ground,” and Vincent of Beauvais also reads this in Book VI, chapter 38. The Augustan edition has “threw down those situated on flat ground.”] situated on the plain. The different conditions of the places converged in a single destruction: for the slower overflow dissolved whatever it held by soaking it, while whatever the torrent’s course encountered it struck down by force. A devastation of fire, more grievous than the terrible disaster of the waters, followed. That fire—its origin uncertain—spread through many parts of the City, and besides producing a pitiable slaughter of people and houses, consumed in a single conflagration such a quantity of wealth as many foreign victories could scarcely have supplied. [Note: “Could scarcely have supplied.” All the manuscripts have *non possent*, “could not have supplied,” rather than *vix possent*. Vincent of Beauvais likewise has the former reading.]

Then, as it ravaged everything around the Forum, [Note: “It seized the temple of Vesta.” Livy records that the temple of Vesta burned at night; Valerius, Book I, chapter 4, gives the same account. During this fire Metellus, the chief pontiff, while rescuing the Palladium from the temple of Vesta, lost his eyesight. Pliny, Book VII, chapter 43, and Plutarch in the *Parallel Lives* are authorities for this. FABR.] it seized the temple of Vesta. And although even the gods did not come to their own aid, the temporary fire overcame that fire which was thought eternal. Consequently Metellus, while rescuing the gods from the flames, escaped only after his arm had been half burned. [Note: “With his arm half burned.” Some manuscripts and printed editions read “carried away with his arm half burned.” Vincent calls Metellus the chief pontiff.]

Under the consulship of Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus and Publius Valerius Falto, the Romans waged war against the Faliscans, and in that battle fifteen thousand Faliscans were killed. [Note: “Under the consulship of Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus and Publius Valerius Falto.” These consuls held office in year 515 according to the Capitoline Fasti. Orosius’s assignment of the Faliscan War to this year therefore differs from Eutropius, who says that it occurred three years earlier, under the consulship of Cercō and Torquatus; the Capitoline tablets record that those men celebrated a triumph over the Faliscans. FABR.]

## CHAPTER XII. The Cisalpine Gauls, new and hostile enemies of the Romans, defeated; rebellious Sardinia subdued; the Carthaginians obtaining peace only with difficulty; the gates of Janus closed for one year

In that same year the Cisalpine Gauls arose as new enemies, and the war against them had varying outcomes. In the first engagement [Note: “Of the consul Valerius.” Six manuscripts read *Valerio consule*, “under the consul Valerius.”] three thousand five hundred Romans fell under the consul Valerius; in the second, fourteen thousand Gauls were killed [Note: “Fourteen.” The Augustan edition has “thirteen.” Above, *viginti* is absent from the second Leiden manuscript.], and two thousand were captured. But because of the earlier defeat, the consul was denied a triumph.

Under the consulship of Titus Manlius Torquatus and Gaius Atilius Bulbus, [Note: “The island of Sardinia revolted.” Polybius, at the end of Book I, and Eutropius, Book III, discuss this matter. FABR.] the island of Sardinia revolted, at the instigation of the Carthaginians; hence the Sardinians were soon subdued and crushed. Since the Carthaginians had violated the peace which they themselves [Note: “Had requested.” The Augustan edition reads *poposcerant*, “had requested.”] had requested, it was resolved to make war upon them.

The Carthaginians, on the other hand, begged for peace in supplication. When two embassies had been sent and achieved nothing, and afterward ten leading men had likewise pleaded twice without obtaining it, at last they gained it through the speech of Hanno, the least distinguished of the ambassadors. [Note: “They obtained it through his speech.” We do not know what speech this Hanno, the least distinguished of the ambassadors, delivered, because of the injury of time and the scarcity of writings. Let a similar service to his country therefore be added here: at the end of the Second Punic War, Hasdrubal the Kid became memorable both then and now through the pointed reply he gave to the Roman senate in the Curia. When a certain senator, hostile to the Carthaginians and to peace, shouted, “By what gods will you make the treaty, since you deceived the gods by whom the former treaty was made?” Hasdrubal is said to have replied, “By those same gods, who are equally hostile to those who violate treaties.” Livy, Book XXX, chapter 42.]

In that year the gate of Janus Geminus was closed, because there was nowhere a war in that year—something that had occurred only under King Numa Pompilius. [Note: “In this year the gate of Janus.” We mentioned this matter in chapter 8 of Book III. Plutarch, in *Numa*, says: “When Marcus Atilius and Titus Manlius were consuls, the temple of Janus was closed for not very long, and then immediately opened again when war broke out.” Thus: “Under the consulship of Marcus Atilius and Titus Manlius, the temple of Janus was closed for a short time, but was immediately opened again when war arose.” FABR.]

From this point we must finally be silent, and it is best to pass over in silence those periods with which our own times cannot possibly be compared, lest by this clamour we provoke the detractors of their own days to attack us. Behold: the gates of Janus were closed; there was no war abroad for the Romans; Rome, containing all her offspring resting in her bosom, did not sigh. And when was this? After the First Punic War. After how much time? [Note: “After 440 years.” The reading “450” is also found, but the other number is more accurate, since approximately that many years are reckoned from the beginning of Hostilius’s reign to Manlius and Atilius. FABR. — The Longobard manuscript has “after 350 years”; the first and third Florentine manuscripts, three Leiden manuscripts, the Gronovian Collection, and the manuscripts of Meus and Perizonius, as well as the Utrecht manuscript and the Augustan edition, have “450”; the old editions give “460.”] After four hundred and forty years. For how long? One year. And what followed in the next year? To say nothing of the rest, the Gallic War—and Hannibal with the Second Punic War.

Alas for me that I have learned of these things and exposed them! [Note: “And exposed them.” The Augustan edition reads “enumerated”; the third Leiden edition reads “questioned.”] How ashamed I am even of having done so! Was this peace of one year—or rather, this shadow of peace—a soothing of miseries or an incentive to evils? Did that tiny drop of oil, falling into the midst of a great flame, extinguish the fuel of so great a fire, or feed it? Did a small amount of cold water swallowed during the fiercest fevers cure the sick man, or rather inflame him?

For nearly seven hundred years—that is, from Hostilius Tullus to Caesar Augustus—the Roman entrails did not sweat blood for only one summer. And amid the many ages of great centuries, the wretched City, truly a wretched mother, scarcely rested for one brief period from fear of mourning, not to say from mourning itself. If anyone had possessed so little rest in his life, would he even be said to have lived? Or if anyone were tormented by pains and tortures throughout an entire year, but spent only one day in the middle of that year in tranquility and without struggles, would he receive from it any relief from his sufferings, or would he not count the entire year among his miseries? [Note: “Would be tormented.” All the manuscripts have *agatur*, apparently because the small stroke normally written above the letters was omitted.]

“But they,” he says, “placed this year as a glorious sign of tireless courage; and would that it had passed as an oblivion of continuous disaster!” [Note: “Had passed as an oblivion of continuous disaster.” The Augustan edition has “had passed continuously”; the Gronovian Collection has “had passed continuously.”]

For just as leprosy is recognized in the human body only when a different color appears here and there among healthy areas of skin, whereas if it spreads everywhere so that it makes everything a single color, however false that color may be, the distinction disappears; [Note: “Makes everything a false color.” This should be read rather than “makes everything adulterous,” as in more recent editions. The subject is leprosy, which spreads so that it makes everything one color—namely white, though this color is false because it is not a pure and healthy brightness. The reading *faciat* is supplied by the old editions and the manuscripts; *adulterini* comes from the Augustan edition. Venetian editions read *adulterari faciat*, “causes to become discolored.”] so, if unremitting toil had flowed on with equal endurance, without any desire for respite, the exertion would have been called the force of will and the choice of habit.

But when, during this tiny interval of leisure, [Note: “This little interval.” The Longobard manuscript has *pausillum*; the third Florentine manuscript, together with the Meus manuscript and the Augustan edition, has *pauxillum*; the second Florentine and the third Leiden manuscript, together with the Gronovian Collection, have *pusillum*.] the joys of the greater [Note: “The joys of the greater.” The Perizonian manuscript has “the joys of the greater with such danger.”] or the efforts of the lesser [Note: “Are set aside.” The Augustan edition reads “are inclined”; the third Leiden edition reads “are redeemed.” The Gronovian Collection and the third Leiden edition read “are distinguished,” as does the former instead of “is distinguished.”] are so greatly turned aside, it is certainly discernible both how much pleasure this brief period possessed and how much bitterness that long one contained: that is, how welcome that rest would have been if it had lasted, and how intolerable this unending misery must have been if it could have been avoided by any means. [Note: “By any means.” The best manuscripts—three Florentine manuscripts, those of Meus and Perizonius—do not contain *arte*, “means.” The first editions and the Venetian editions also omit it. The phrase is used in the sense in which Virgil uses *aliqua* in *Eclogue* III.15:

> And if you had not harmed in some way, you would have died.

That is, “to some extent” or “by some means,” as Servius explains.]

## CHAPTER XIII. The death of Hamilcar; the Roman war against the Illyrians and its cause; the war against the Cisalpine Gauls, and likewise against the Insubrian Gauls; various prodigies; a new defeat of the Gauls and the war against the Istrians

[Note: “In the year 517 from the founding of the City.” Hamilcar, Hannibal’s father, was killed in Spain, according to Cassiodorus, under the consulship of Marcus Aemilius Barbula and Marcus Junius Pera; that year is 522 from the founding of the City in the Capitoline Fasti. Polybius discusses Hamilcar’s death more fully at the beginning of Book II. FABR.]

In the year 517 from the founding of the City, Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians, was killed by the Spaniards in war, while secretly preparing another war against the Romans.

[Note: “The following year the Roman ambassadors.” Polybius, Book II, names the ambassadors Gaius and Lucius Coruncanius. They were sent to Teuta, queen of the Illyrians, because of injuries inflicted upon Italian merchants, and one of them was killed at the queen’s command, as Polybius also records. In the epitome of Book XX one reads: “War was declared against the Illyrians because one of the ambassadors sent to them was killed.” Appian likewise mentions the killing of the Coruncanii by the Illyrians in his *Illyrian History*. Florus, Book II, chapter 5, writes that the Roman ambassadors were killed during the reign of Teuta. Pliny, Book XXXIV, chapter 6, names the ambassadors Publius Junius and Titus Coruncanius; after Teuta, queen of the Illyrians, had killed them, statues were set up for them on the Rostra. FABR.]

In the following year Roman ambassadors were killed by the Illyrians. Afterward a most savage war was waged against the Illyrians themselves. In it many towns and peoples were destroyed, and the survivors surrendered under the consulship of Fulvius and Postumius.

In the third year thereafter, pontiffs, wickedly exercising power through sacrilegious sacrifices, brought mourning upon the wretched City. For the decemvirs, having returned to the custom of ancient superstition, [Note: “Having undertaken the custom of ancient superstition.” Meus has *pristinae*, “former,” instead of *priscae*, “ancient.” But where the common editions read *aggressi*, “having undertaken,” all the manuscripts, together with the same edition, have *egressi*, “having departed.” This reading seems to lead us to the true text: “For the decemvirs, having returned to the custom of ancient superstition.” Quintilian, in the preface to Book I, section 8, gives a similar example: “Then some, scorning the labor of speaking well, returned to forming minds and establishing laws of life.” A similar sacrifice occurs in Livy somewhat later, in Hannibal’s time, Book XXII, chapter 57.] buried alive in the cattle market a Gallic man and a Gallic woman together with a Greek woman. [Note: “A Gallic man and a Gallic woman.” Plutarch says in the *Roman Questions*: “They buried alive in the place called the Cattle Market two men and two women, the men Greeks and the women Gauls.” Plutarch also says in *Marcellus* that they did this on the basis of the Sibylline Books, at the beginning of the Cisalpine Gallic War. FABR.]

But this magical binding immediately turned against them. For those dreadful deaths of foreigners which they had inflicted, they atoned for by the most shameful slaughter of their own people. Accordingly, under the consulship of Lucius Aemilius Papus and Gaius Atilius Regulus, [Note: “Lucius Aemilius Papus.” The surname Catulus is commonly and incorrectly added here to Aemilius, as Paulus is in Pliny, Book III, chapter 20. In the Capitoline Fasti these consuls are named in year 528: “C. AEMILIUS, Q. F. CN. N. PAPUS. C. ATILIUS, M. F. M. N. REGULUS.” Polybius, Book II, Plutarch in *Marcellus*, Livy, Book XX, Florus, Book II, chapter 4, and Eutropius, Book II, describe this Gallic War. FABR.]

the Senate was struck with great terror by the revolt of Cisalpine Gaul, especially when it was reported that an enormous army was also approaching from farther Gaul. [Note: “Especially of the Gaesati.” I have taken this name from the excellent manuscript of Cornelius Gualtherus. Polybius writes: “Therefore the greatest peoples, the Insubres and Boii, having formed an alliance with one another, immediately sent envoys to the Gauls who inhabit the regions around the Alps and the Rhône and who are called Gaesati because they serve as mercenaries; for this word properly signifies that.” In Plutarch’s *Marcellus* the name is corrupted: “and they summoned Gauls who serve as mercenaries, who are called Gerati.” I attribute this corruption to those who thought that the name was derived from *geras*, “reward.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII:

> [lacuna]
>
> Each brandishes two Alpine spears in his hand.

FABR.]

The Gaesati were especially prominent; the name refers not to a nation but to Gallic mercenaries. Therefore the consuls, alarmed, gathered the strength of all Italy for the defense of the empire. Once this had been done, eight hundred thousand armed men are reported to have been present in the armies of the two consuls, as the historian Fabius, who took part in that same war, wrote. [Note: “As the historian Fabius.” This was Quintus Fabius Pictor, who lived at this time and took part not only in this war but also, as Livy says, shortly afterward in the Second Punic War. Eutropius says of him: “It is handed down by the historian Fabius, who took part in that war, that 800,000 men were prepared for it.” Pliny, Book III, chapter 20, writes that at this time Italy armed 80,000 cavalry and 700,000 infantry. FABR.]

Of these, the Romans and Campanians numbered 348,200 infantry and 26,600 cavalry; the rest were allied troops. [Note: “Of these, Romans and Campanians.” Polybius writes: “The number of Romans and Campanians enrolled was approximately 250,000 infantry, and in addition there were 23,000 cavalry.” FABR.]

When battle was joined near Arretium, the consul Atilius was killed. Eight hundred thousand Romans fled, although not even a loss as great as should have frightened them had been inflicted upon their own side. For historians report that only three thousand of them were killed at that time. [Note: “Historians report.” Fabricius and Scottus read “the historian,” contrary to all the manuscripts and editions. The preceding word *eorum*, “of them,” is absent from some manuscripts and editions. The third Leiden manuscript omits *est*, which occurs at the end of the sentence.] This makes their disgrace and shame all the greater: with so few lost, so vast an army fled, thereby revealing that in their other victories they had prevailed not through strength of spirit but through the outcome of battles.

For who, I ask, would believe that this number even existed in the Roman army, let alone that it fled? After this, a second battle was fought with the Gauls, in which fully forty thousand Gauls were slaughtered.

In the following year, when Manlius Torquatus and Fulvius Flaccus were consuls, [Note: “The first across the Po.” This is mentioned in the Livian epitome, Book XX. FABR.] they were the first to lead Roman legions across the Po. There they fought the Insubrian Gauls, of whom twenty-three thousand were killed and five thousand captured. [Note: “Five thousand were captured.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection and the Augustan edition, report six thousand captives and thirty-three thousand killed. The Augustan edition agrees concerning the number captured.]

Then, in the year immediately following this one, dreadful prodigies terrified the wretched City. Wretched indeed was the City, terrified on one side by the roar of enemies and on the other by the wickedness of demons. For in Picenum a river flowed with blood; in Etruria the sky was seen to burn; at Ariminum, during the night, a bright light shone; and three moons appeared to rise in different regions of the sky. [Note: “For in Picenum.” The Deacon inserted an account of these prodigies into Eutropius, but in the wrong place. Plutarch mentions the same events in *Marcellus*: “When Flaminius and Furius, the consuls, had led great forces against the Insubres, the river that flows through the land of Picenum was seen to run with blood, and it was reported that three moons had appeared around the city of Ariminum.” Thus: “When Flaminius and Furius were consuls and had led great forces against the Insubres, a river flowing through Picenum was seen to run with blood, and it was reported that three moons had appeared around Ariminum.” FABR. — Plutarch’s passage shows that the common reading should be preferred to the alternative found in the earliest editions: “blood flowed from the river.” For *effulsisse*, “to have shone forth,” the manuscripts commonly have *offulsisse* or *obfulsisse*.]

At that time, too, Caria and the island of Rhodes were so violently shaken by a great earthquake that, as roofs collapsed everywhere, [Note: “That enormous colossus also fell.” Strabo discusses this colossus in Book XIV, and Pliny in Book XXXIV, chapter 7. FABR.] that famous enormous colossus also fell.

In the same year, the consul Flaminius, disregarding the auspices by which he had been forbidden to fight, engaged the Gauls and defeated them. [Note: “In that war.” The Perizonian manuscript reads “in this war.”] In that battle nine thousand Gauls were killed and seventeen thousand captured.

After this, the consul Claudius destroyed thirty thousand Gaesati. [Note: “Afterward, the consul Claudius.” This was Marcus Claudius Marcellus, who was consul five times afterward. Plutarch, Polybius, Eutropius, and others discuss his victory over the Insubres. FABR.] There, advancing into the front line himself, he killed their king Virdomarus. [Note: “King Virdomarus.” The common form Viridomarus is incorrect. Propertius, Book IV, has:

> Virdomarus, who claimed his descent from the Rhine itself.

In Plutarch’s *Marcellus* the reading is “the king of the Gaesati, Britomarus,” instead of Virdomarus. In the Capitoline record of triumphs the enemy leader is called Virdumarus. FABR.]

He also captured Mediolanum, a most flourishing city, among the many Insubrian towns that he had forced to surrender.

Then the Istrians, new enemies, arose. The consuls Cornelius and Minucius subdued them, though at the cost of much Roman blood. [Note: “The Istrians.” Eutropius says that war was waged against the Istrians under the consulship of Minucius Rufus and Publius Cornelius, because they had plundered Roman ships carrying grain; after much Roman blood had been shed, they were subdued. FABR. — “Much, indeed.” The first edition reads *multo equidem*, “much, certainly.”]

Here that ancient Roman appetite for disgraceful glory, even through parricide, emerges briefly again. For Fabius, a former censor, killed Fabius Buteo, his own son, after accusing him of theft—a deed which the father certainly judged worthy of punishment even by parricide, although the laws prescribed for any person no more than a financial penalty [Note: “A financial penalty.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “a fine to be paid in money.”] or, at most, exile [Note: “Or at the utmost, exile.” The Longobard manuscript, together with the second Florentine, two Leiden manuscripts, and the Perizonian manuscript, reads “or exile at the utmost.”] for such a crime. [Note: “For any human being.” Three Leiden manuscripts have “for any man.”]

## CHAPTER XIV. The Second Punic War: Hannibal inflicted enormous slaughter upon the Romans, opening a road through the Gauls

[Note: “In the year 534 from the founding of the City.” In this year Marcus Livius and Lucius Aemilius were consuls; Polybius, Book III, records that Saguntum was captured by Hannibal. Consult what Sigonius diligently annotated on Livy’s Book XXI. FABR.]

In the year 534 from the founding of the City, Hannibal, commander of the Carthaginians, first attacked Saguntum, the most flourishing city of Spain and a friend of the Roman people, [Note: “Attacked in war.” All the manuscripts, as well as the best Augustan edition, read *bello impetitam*, “attacked in war.” Most of the common editions have *bello petitam*, “sought in war.”] then surrounded it with a siege and tormented it with hunger. It endured everything, bravely and in consideration of the loyalty which it had pledged to the Romans, [Note: “Had pledged.” I prefer this reading, found in three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection, to *devoverant*, “had pledged,” as others have it.] worthy and unworthy alike; and only in the eighth month did he finally destroy it.

He most unjustly refused even to allow the Roman ambassadors sent to him to appear before him. [Note: “He kept them from his presence.” The manuscripts have *abstinuit*, not *abstituit*. Livy, Book VIII: “Although fortune kept him away from the Roman war.” FABR.]

From that point, out of hatred for the Roman name—a hatred which, when he was nine years old, he had sworn most faithfully, though otherwise most faithlessly, before the altars, to his father Hamilcar—under the consulship of Publius Cornelius Scipio and Tiberius Sempronius Longus, he crossed the Pyrenees Mountains. [Note: “The Pyrenees Mountains.” Apart from Vincent of Beauvais, who excerpted this chapter in the *Historical Mirror*, Book VI, chapter 42, all the manuscripts and old editions prefer the plural; the more recent editions have the singular.]

With the sword he opened a road through the fiercest peoples of Gaul, and only on the ninth day reached the Alps from the Pyrenees. There, while he defeated in battle the mountain Gauls who resisted his ascent and cut through impassable cliffs with fire and iron, he remained for four days; only on the fifth day, after the greatest exertion, did he reach the level ground. [Note: “To the plains.” Some Italian manuscripts and editions add “of Italy,” as does Vincent of Beauvais.]

They reckon that his army then consisted of one hundred thousand infantry and twenty thousand cavalry. [Note: “One hundred thousand.” All the manuscripts, except the fourth Leiden manuscript, which has “one hundred thousand,” read “one hundred thousand cavalry and twenty thousand infantry.”] [Note: “Twenty thousand cavalry.” The common reading, “thirty thousand,” is erroneous. Amid the great variation, those who write that there were one hundred thousand infantry and twenty thousand cavalry are the most numerous; Livy is their authority. Consult him concerning these matters. FABR.]

The consul Scipio was the first to confront Hannibal. When battle was joined near the Ticinus, Scipio himself, severely wounded, escaped death only because of his son Scipio, still wearing the purple-bordered boy’s garment, who afterward received the surname Africanus. Nearly the entire Roman army was killed there.

Battle was then fought, under the same consul, at the river Trebia, and the Romans were again defeated with equal disaster. The consul Sempronius, learning of his colleague’s misfortune, returned from Sicily with his army; engaging the enemy similarly at the same river, he lost his army and escaped almost alone. [Note: “In that war, however.” Hannibal was wounded while attacking Emporium near Placentia, according to Livy, Book XXI, and Appian in his account of Hannibal’s deeds. FABR.]

In that war Hannibal too was wounded. Later, when he crossed into Etruria at the beginning of spring, he was caught by a storm on the summit of the Apennines. [Note: “On the summit of the Apennines.” Livy discusses this at the end of Book XXI. FABR.] For two continuous days he remained immobilized with his army, enclosed and laden with snow, [Note: “Enclosed by snow.” Elsewhere the reading is *navibus*, “by ships.” If this is not a scribal error, I wonder where it came from.] and froze stiff. There a great number of men, many pack animals, and nearly all the elephants perished from the severity of the cold. [Note: “Nearly all the elephants.” Most printed editions insert *autem*, “however,” contrary to the manuscripts and Vincent of Beauvais.]

Meanwhile the other Scipio, the consul’s brother, fought many battles in Spain; he also defeated and captured Mago, a commander of the Carthaginians. [Note: “Mago, commander of the Carthaginians.” The manuscripts also have Mago, although Polybius and Livy make it certain that it was not Mago but Hanno whom Gnaeus Cornelius, the brother of Publius Scipio, captured. FABR. — For this reason the distinguished Oudendorp urges that Hanno or Hannon be restored here as well; see his note on Frontinus, p. 174.]

## CHAPTER XV. Many strange prodigies appeared everywhere at that time; Hannibal, by a stratagem, nearly annihilated the army of the consul Flaminius

[Note: “At that time, dreadful prodigies.” These prodigies are found in Livy at the beginning of Book XXII and in Plutarch’s *Fabius*. FABR.]

At that time the Romans were also terrified by dreadful prodigies. The disk of the sun appeared to diminish; at Arpi shields were seen in the sky; the sun itself seemed to have fought with the moon; at Capena [Note: “During the day.” The Augustan edition, the Leiden manuscript, and the Gronovian Collection read “in the daytime.” Shortly afterward, the Gronovian Collection has “in the chest.”] two moons appeared during the day; in Sardinia two shields sweated blood; among the Faliscans the sky seemed to split open as though by a great chasm; and at Antium bloody ears of grain fell into the reapers’ basket.

Therefore Hannibal, knowing that the consul Flaminius was alone in the camp, advanced at the beginning of spring and seized the nearer road, although it was marshy, so that he might overwhelm him unprepared more quickly. At that time the Sarnus, swollen and spreading widely, had left behind fields hanging loose and dissolved. Concerning these it was said:

[lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0892D] “And the Sarnus, which waters the seas.” This is a Virgilian half-line from Book VII of the *Aeneid*. FABR.] And the Sarnus, which waters the seas. When Hannibal advanced into these regions with his army, the mists rising especially from the marsh [Note: [Col. 0892D] “Were exhaled.” My manuscript, with Perizonius and certain editions, reads *exhalabant* (“were exhaled”).] deprived him of visibility, and he lost a large part of his allies and pack animals. He himself, riding upon the one elephant that alone had survived, barely escaped the difficulty of the journey; but he lost the eye that had long been diseased because of the violent cold, sleeplessness, and exertion. [Note: [Col. 0892D] “With which he had long been ill.” The Cologne manuscript has *egerat* (“had done”), from which Fabricius derived *aegrotaverat* (“had been ill”). LAUT.—All the manuscripts consistently read, “with which he had long been ill,” as does Vincent of Beauvais, who nevertheless adds *yet*, reading, “yet he lost the eye,” etc. The printed editions therefore needlessly read *had been sick*.]

When he had come close to the camp of the consul Flaminius, he provoked Flaminius to battle by ravaging the surrounding districts. [Note: [Col. 0893C] “This battle took place at Lake Trasimene.” In Plutarch’s *Fabius* there is an error, *περὶ τὴν καλουμένην Θρασυνίαν λίμνην* (“at the lake called Thrasymene”). Polybius calls it *τὴν Τεαμένην λίμνην* (“the Teamenian Lake”). See Silius, Book V, and Valerius, Book I. FABR.] This battle was fought at Lake Trasimene, where the Roman army, most disastrously surrounded by Hannibal’s stratagem, was utterly slaughtered. The consul himself too was killed; twenty-five thousand Romans are reported to have fallen in that battle, and six thousand to have been captured. [Note: [Col. 0893C] “Twenty-five thousand Romans.” In the battle at Trasimene, Eutropius writes that twenty-five thousand Romans were killed and the rest fled; Polybius and Livy report fifteen thousand killed and six thousand falling into Maharbal’s power; Appian states that twenty thousand fell with Flaminius and ten thousand were captured by Maharbal. The authors also disagree about Hannibal’s losses. FABR.—The fourth manuscript of Leiden reads “twenty thousand.” The first edition reports twenty-three thousand killed. For *in eo praelio* (“in that battle”), Vincent of Beauvais reads *in ipso praelio* (“in the very battle”).] Of Hannibal’s army, however, two thousand fell. This was a famous contest at Lake Trasimene, with so great a Roman disaster, especially since the fury of the combatants became so intense [Note: [Col. 0893C] “That they did not perceive the most severe earthquake.” Livy, Book XXII, and Plutarch in his *Fabius* discuss this. FABR.] that the combatants did not perceive the most severe earthquake—which, occurring at that very moment with such violence, is reported to have destroyed cities, shifted mountains, split rocks, and forced rivers backward. [Col. 0893B]

The ruin inflicted at Trasimene was followed by the battle of Cannae, although the interval was occupied by the dictatorship of Fabius Maximus, who delayed Hannibal’s advance by his policy of postponement. [Note: [Col. 0893D] “Of Fabius Maximus.” Concerning him Ennius wrote:

> One man, by delaying, restored our fortunes.

Cicero, *On Duties*, and in the *Cato*. FABR.]

## CHAPTER XVI. On the lamentable disaster of the Romans at Cannae; on the plan of abandoning Italy, how the Romans recovered their breath and rebuilt their army; and also on various battles.

[Note: [Col. 0893D] “In the year 540 from the founding of the City.” Eutropius counts it this way, and Orosius follows him in describing the disaster at Cannae. For others this is the year 537, as for Pighius in the *Roman Annals*. FABR.] In the year 540 from the founding of the City, when L. Aemilius Paulus and C. Terentius Varro were consuls and had been sent against Hannibal, almost all the forces on which Roman hope rested were disastrously lost at Cannae, a town of Apulia, through the impatience of the consul Varro. For in that battle [Note: [Col. 0893D] “Forty-four thousand.” Livy says that forty thousand infantry and two thousand seven hundred cavalry were killed. Appian and Plutarch write that fifty thousand were killed in this battle. FABR.] forty-four thousand Romans were killed, although a large part of Hannibal’s army was also slain. Yet in no Punic war were the Romans brought so near utter destruction. The consul Aemilius Paulus perished; [Note: [Col. 0893D] “In it.” Three Leiden-Batavian manuscripts add *bello* (“war”), as does the Groningen Collection.] twenty men of consular or praetorian rank were killed; thirty senators were either captured or slain; three hundred noblemen, forty thousand infantrymen, and three thousand five hundred cavalrymen also perished. The consul Varro fled to Venusia with fifty cavalrymen.

There is no doubt that that would have been the final day of the Roman state if Hannibal, immediately after his victory, had hastened to invade the City. As a token of his victory, Hannibal sent three measures of gold rings to Carthage. [Note: [Col. 0894C] “Three measures of rings.” Pliny, Book XXXIII, chapter 50, reports that Hannibal sent three measures of rings to Carthage. See Livy, Book XXIII. In Lucian Hannibal boasts that he killed so many Romans in one day “that he measured out their rings by the medimni.” FABR.] [Note: [Col. 0894C] “From the hands.” Codex Meus has “from the hands.”] He had stripped them from the hands of the slain Roman knights and senators.

So extreme, however, was the final despair of the republic among the Romans who remained [Note: [Col. 0894C] “That the senators considered abandoning Italy.” According to Livy, Book XXII, this plan to abandon Italy was not devised at Rome by the senators, but by the survivors of the disaster at Cannae who had fled to Canusium. FABR.] that they thought a plan had to be made for abandoning Italy and seeking new homes. This plan would have been approved at the urging of Caecilius Metellus, had not the military tribune Cornelius Scipio, [Note: [Col. 0894C] “The same man who was later Africanus.” This is the reading of the manuscripts and old editions; the word *who* is absent from more recent editions.] the same man who was later called Africanus, drawn his sword, deterred them, and instead compelled them to swear an oath in his words in defense of their country.

The Romans, daring to breathe again as though returning from the underworld, elected Decimus Junius dictator. [Note: [Col. 0894C] “The dictator Decimus Junius.” Livy and Plutarch in the *Fabius Maximus* call this dictator Junius, and learned men think him to be the man who appears in the Capitoline Fasti as consul in the year 523 under the name *M. Junius, D. F. D. N. Pera*. FABR.] After holding a levy beginning with those seventeen years old, he hastily gathered four legions from every source, an army immature and poorly organized. At that time they also compelled slaves of tested strength and willingness—whether volunteers or, if necessary, purchased at public expense under the title of freedom [Note: [Col. 0894C] “Whether volunteers or purchased at public expense.” Orosius indicates that the authors did not transmit the same account concerning the armed slaves. Livy says that the dictator armed eight thousand slaves purchased publicly. Appian, in his account of Hannibal, states that the senate freed eight thousand slaves, their masters voluntarily donating them. FABR.—Soon afterward, Vincent of Beauvais: “to the military oath.”]—to take the military oath.

They removed the weapons that were lacking from the temples, and private wealth replenished the impoverished treasury. Thus the equestrian order and thus the alarmed plebs, forgetting their private interests, acted with a common purpose. [Note: [Col. 0894D] “Acted with a common purpose.” Although this is the reading of the manuscripts and older editions, the Fabrician editions have *acted in the common interest*, which Scott did not correct even in his latest edition.]

The dictator Junius too, recalling an ancient deed from Rome’s misery, [Note: [Col. 0894D] “Recalling an ancient deed from Rome’s misery.” All the manuscripts have this, except that the Lombard manuscript has simply *recalling*. The printed editions, such as those of Hittorp and Bolsuing, read *recalling the condition*. But the older editions also favor *recalling an ancient deed*. A little later some editions have *permitted*, wrongly, for *promised*.] by an edict opened, as it were, an asylum and, promising immunity, enrolled in the army any men who were burdened by crimes and debts, for the reinforcement of the army. Their number was six thousand men. [Note: [Col. 0895C] “Was six thousand men.” The third Leiden manuscript and the Groningen Collection omit *men*. The Augustan edition counts seven thousand men. A little later, in *of the Roman state*, my manuscript adds *of the whole Roman state*.]

But Campania—or rather all Italy—deserted to Hannibal, having entirely abandoned hope of restoring the Roman state. After this, the praetor Lucius Postumius, sent to fight the Gauls [Note: [Col. 0895C] “Sent to fight the Gauls.” This was the Latin wording in the manuscripts, but the printed editions had added *to fight*, I do not know why. LAUT.—On the contrary, both *sent* and *to fight* appear in the manuscripts. The ten manuscripts I consulted unanimously give *sent to fight*, that is, “sent for the purpose of fighting.” I do not see why the editors changed this Greek construction to *ordered*, which is found everywhere except in the first and Augustan editions.] was killed together with his army.

Then, when Sempronius Gracchus and Q. Fabius Maximus were consuls, Claudius Marcellus, designated proconsul after serving as praetor, [Note: [Col. 0895C] “Routed Hannibal’s army in battle.” This battle was fought by Marcellus at Nola. Livy, Book XXIII, and Plutarch in his *Marcellus*. FABR.] routed Hannibal’s army in battle, and was the first, after such great disasters to the republic, to give hope that Hannibal could be defeated.

In Spain, the Scipios defeated Hasdrubal, commander of the Carthaginians, who was preparing an army for Italy, in a very serious war. [Note: [Col. 0895C] “They overwhelmed him in a very serious war.” Perizonius inserts *after being defeated* after *war*. Three Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection delete the first syllable of *overwhelmed*.] For they reduced his army by the death or capture of thirty-five thousand soldiers. [Note: [Col. 0895D] “By killing or capturing them.” The Codex Meus, or Augustan edition, has this reading: “they encountered killing or capture.”] They enticed the Celtiberian soldiers—the first foreign force that the Romans began to have in their camps—by payment, and brought them over from the enemy’s alliance into their own camp. [Note: [Col. 0895D] “The first.” Three Leiden manuscripts have *the largest*, as does the Utrecht manuscript, wrongly. The older editions have *when first*, except for the distinguished Augustan edition.]

Sempronius Gracchus, proconsul, was led into an ambush and killed by a certain Lucanian who had been his guest. [Note: [Col. 0895D] “By his Lucanian guest.” Appian and Livy, Book XXV, call this man Flavius Lucanus; there you will also find the story of Centenius and Fulvius. FABR.—It is enough to have given this warning once: Latin authors, and Orosius throughout, used *proconsule* in the ablative for the nominative; all the manuscripts preserve this, and I think it should be printed accordingly. LAUT.—It is enough to have said this once; our manuscripts also confirm it.]

Centenius Penula, a centurion, voluntarily requested that a war against Hannibal be assigned to him. Hannibal killed him together with the eight thousand soldiers whom he had led into battle. [Note: [Col. 0896C] “Whom he had led into battle.” This is the reading of the better manuscripts and printed editions. Others have “whom he had led into the line” or “whom he had led in the battle line.”] After him, Cn. Fulvius, the praetor, was defeated by Hannibal, lost his army, and barely escaped.

It is shameful to recall this. What shall I say: that the Romans were more wicked, or more wretched? Rather, more truly, either a wicked misery or a miserable wickedness. [Note: [Col. 0896C] “Who would believe it?” The Augustan edition reads, “For who would believe it?”]

Who would believe that at the time when the treasury of the Roman people was begging private citizens for a meager contribution, a soldier in the camp was no one but a boy, a slave, a criminal, or a debtor—and even then the number was still inadequate; [Note: [Col. 0896C] “The number was adequate.” I scrupled to depart from the manuscript codices, all of which read thus, rather than, as the printed editions do, “the number was adequate.”] when almost the entire senate in the senate-house seemed newly recruited; finally, when all things had been so diminished and broken [Note: [Col. 0896C] “Was despaired of.” Codex Meus has *desperabant* (“they despaired”), but three Leiden-Batavian manuscripts with the Groningen Collation, the Perizonius codex, and the Augustan edition prefer *desperabatur* (“there was despair”).] that a plan to abandon Italy was being considered— [Note: [Col. 0896C] “At that time.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, repeat *who would believe it* here.] who would believe that at that time, when even one domestic war, as we have said, could not possibly be endured, [Note: [Col. 0896C] “Could not possibly be endured.” This is the reading of the manuscripts and better printed editions. Others have, “could scarcely be endured in any way.”] [Note: [Col. 0896D] “Three additional, etc.” Some older editions read: “Who would believe that three additional overseas wars were undertaken?” The Augustan edition reads: “Three additional overseas wars were undertaken.”] three additional overseas wars were undertaken? One in Macedonia [Note: [Col. 0896D] “Against Philip.” Livy, Books XXIII and XXIV, and Eutropius, Book III, treat the war against Philip, king of Macedonia. For the campaign in Sardinia against the Carthaginians and Sardinians under T. Manlius, see Livy, Book XXIII, and Silius, Book XII. FABR.] against Philip, the most powerful king of Macedonia; another in Spain against Hasdrubal, Hannibal’s brother; and a third in Sardinia against the Sardinians and another Hasdrubal, commander of the Carthaginians. In addition to these there was the fourth war, Hannibal’s, by which they were being crushed in Italy. And yet their courageous despair against either side advanced toward better things: for in all these wars they fought in despair, and by fighting they conquered.

From this it is clearly shown that the times then were not more peaceful for leisure, but that men were stronger in the face of misery.

## CHAPTER XVII. Claudius Marcellus captures Syracuse. Hannibal terrifies the Romans at the Anio, but is not given the opportunity to overwhelm them.

[Note: [Col. 0896D] “In the year from the founding of the City.” 543. M. Marcellus, consul for the third time, was sent to Sicily in the year 539 from the founding of the City; he besieged Syracuse and captured it in the third year afterward. Polybius, Book VIII; Livy, Book XXIV; Plutarch in his *Marcellus*; Cicero, *Against Verres*. FABR.] In the year 543 from the founding of the City, Claudius Marcellus barely captured Syracuse, the wealthiest city of Sicily, in a second assault. Although he had long been besieging it, he had been unable to take it because he was repulsed by the machines of Archimedes, a Syracusan citizen endowed with marvelous ingenuity. [Col. 0897A]

Ten years after Hannibal had come into Italy, [Note: [Col. 0897B] “Ten years later.” Eutropius too counts this as the tenth year of the war, whereas others count it as the eighth. FABR.] when Cn. Fulvius and P. Sulpicius were consuls, [Note: [Col. 0897B] “Cn. Fulvius, P. Sulpicius.” The Fabrician and Scott editions wrongly omit the praenomen Publius, although it is absent from some manuscripts. Since the better books do not recognize the conjunction *and*, we have omitted it, as Fabricius also deleted it.] Hannibal moved his army out of Campania. With immense devastation of everything, he proceeded along the Latin road through the territory of Sidicinum and Suessanum [Note: [Col. 0897C] “Through Sidicinian and Suessanian territory.” *Suessanum*, not *Sinuessanum*, is found in the manuscripts of Orosius and Eutropius. Livy, Book XXVI, leads Hannibal by way of Suessula, the territory of the Alifani, and the Casinate territory; Sigonius reads *Suessulanum*. Silius, Book XII, after passing through this territory, sings as follows:

Then they traverse the Sidicine fields with swift battalions,  
and Treicia of Cales, dwellings named for you, Orithyia;  
thence the Alifan field, not unploughed by Bacchus,  
and Casinum’s countryside, inhabited by nymphs,  
are laid waste, and so forth. FABR.] he settled beside the river Anio, three miles from the City. [Note: [Col. 0897C] “Three miles from the City.” So Livy: “Meanwhile Hannibal moved his camp to the river Anio, three miles from the City.” Florus, Book II, chapter 6, says that Hannibal pitched camp at the third milestone. Pliny, Book XV, chapter 18, says that the Punic camp was fortified at the third milestone. Eutropius, however, says that Hannibal advanced as far as the fourth mile-marker from the City, and Appian agrees; in his book on Hannibal’s affairs he writes that Hannibal pitched his camp at the Anio, thirty-two stades from the City. But Polybius, Book IX, says: “He secretly crossed the river Anio and approached so closely that he established his camp no more than forty stades from Rome.” Hannibal, without the Romans’ knowledge, crossed the Anio and came so near that he established his camp no more than forty stades, or five Roman miles, from the City. FABR.—Vincent of Beauvais has “three miles.”]

He settled there amid incredible fear throughout the entire State. The senate and people were agitated by different anxieties, while even the matrons, driven mad by terror, ran along the fortifications and eagerly carried stones onto the walls, desiring to be the first to fight before the walls. [Note: [Col. 0897D] “Onto the walls.” The Lombard Collection, with three Leiden-Batavian manuscripts from the Groningen Collation, reads “on the walls.”] Hannibal himself, advancing threateningly with his light cavalry, came as far as the Colline Gate. [Note: [Col. 0897D] “As far as the Colline Gate.” Cicero, *First Philippic*: “Hannibal, I believe, was at the gates.” Livy discusses all these matters at length. FABR.] Then he drew all his forces up for battle.

The consuls and the proconsul Fulvius also did not decline battle. [Note: [Col. 0897D] “The consuls and Fulvius the proconsul.” This passage is correctly read in all the manuscripts, and I cannot sufficiently marvel at the negligence of those who, careless of history, corrupted so much against the ancient books. The consuls were Cn. Fulvius Centumalus and P. Sulpicius Galba. Q. Fulvius Flaccus, however, who had been consul the previous year and was already besieging Capua with Appius, had been summoned from there and had his camp between the Esquiline and Colline Gates. Livy and all the others. Livy’s words, Book XXVI, chapter 11, are: “Nor did Flaccus and the consuls decline the contest.” FABR.—The older editions, except the Augustan, contain a shameful error when they read: “But the consuls Fulvius and Publius also did not decline battle.”]

But when the battle lines, drawn up on both sides, had taken position, [Note: [Col. 0898C] “When the battle lines had been drawn up on both sides.” My codex with the third Florentine prefers “when the battle line had been drawn up on either side.” But the second Florentine is more idiomatic Latin: “when the battle lines, prepared on both sides, had taken position.”] with Rome before their eyes and the victor’s reward awaiting them, [Note: [Col. 0898C] “The victor’s reward.” Vincent of Beauvais, and some editions and manuscripts, have *of victory*.] such a great storm suddenly poured from the clouds, mixed with hail, that the confused ranks, barely holding on to their weapons, withdrew into their own camps.

Then, when calm weather had returned and the forces had come back into the field and battle line, a second storm, more violent than the first, again poured down. It restrained the courage of mortals with greater fear and forced the terrified armies to flee back into their tents. At this point Hannibal, turning his thoughts to religion, is said to have declared that the will to take Rome was being denied him at one moment, and the opportunity at another.

Let the detractors of the true God answer me here: was it Roman courage that prevented Hannibal from seizing and overthrowing Rome, or divine mercy? Or perhaps those who have been preserved are ashamed to confess what Hannibal both feared as a victor and demonstrated by his withdrawal? [Note: [Col. 0898C] “Hannibal.” My manuscript, like the Utrecht manuscript, reads *Annibalem* (“Hannibal,” accusative), but I would not have mentioned this if the Lombard manuscript and the other two very ancient Florentine manuscripts did not also read it so. Hence I suspect that the manuscripts once read *abstulit* (“removed”) in place of the following *obstitit* (“prevented”), for which some editions have *restitit* (“resisted”). God’s mercy, that is, removed and drove Hannibal away from the walls of Rome by a sudden storm, when human hands could not have kept him from taking it.]

But if it is clear that this divine protection came through rain from heaven, [Note: [Col. 0898D] “Through rain.” Rain often afforded the Romans great benefit in doubtful circumstances. Orosius here treats the same argument and in the same manner as Tertullian in chapter V of the *Apology*.] and if the rain itself is supplied at suitable and necessary times only through Christ, who is the true God, I think that this can be known with sufficient certainty even from facts of this kind, and cannot be denied. [Note: [Col. 0898D] “From facts of this kind.” Since the words seem not to cohere sufficiently well, the first, Paris, and Venetian editions insert *hominibus* (“by men”), contrary to all manuscripts. Perhaps the author wrote *ab hujusmodi servatis* (“by persons saved in such a way”), for which, written in the usual abbreviated manner, *satis* seems afterward to have replaced it. Our emendation certainly corresponds to what he said above: “perhaps those who have been preserved are ashamed to confess.”] This is especially so now, when, as a demonstration of his power, during distressing drought it regularly happens that rain is requested, now by pagans, now by Christians. Nor has it ever happened, even in the testimony of those very people, that the desired rains came except on a day when Christ was permitted to be invoked and Christians to pray. [Note: [Col. 0898D] “On which Christ is invoked.” The second Leiden manuscript, together with Perizonius, reads “on which Christ is invoked” in the form “on which to invoke Christ,” and “Christians are permitted to pray.” For *is permitted*, my manuscript has *they permit*.]

Without doubt, then, it is established that Rome was preserved by this same true God, who is Christ Jesus, acting according to the purpose of his ineffable judgment: at that time, for belief in the faith that was to come; and now punished in its unbelieving part. [Note: [Col. 0898D] “Because of its unbelieving part.” The Augustan edition reads, “because of its slowness.”]

But in Spain both Scipios were killed by Hasdrubal, Hannibal’s brother. [Note: [Col. 0898D] “By his brother Hasdrubal.” This should be read, not *of Hasdrubal*. Hasdrubal Barca, Hannibal’s brother, destroyed P. Scipio and his army; on the twenty-ninth day afterward, after joining forces with Mago and the other Hasdrubal, son of Gisgo, he overwhelmed Cn. Scipio. Livy, Book XXV; Appian, *On Spanish Affairs*; Silius, Book XIII; Valerius, Book III, chapter 7; Eutropius, Book III. Cicero, *For Balbus*: “When the two thunderbolts of our empire, Cn. and P. Scipio, had suddenly perished in Spain.” FABR.]

In Campania, Capua was captured by the proconsul Q. Fulvius. [Col. 0899A] The leading men of the Campanians [Note: [Col. 0899B] “The leading men of the Campanians.” Livy, Book XXVI, where the history of Capua is explained, says that there were about twenty-seven senators. M. Cato states that Capua had stood for approximately 260 years before it was captured by the Romans. At this time, however, after its capture, it was reduced to the status of a prefecture, according to Velleius, Book II. Read Cicero, *Against Rullus*. FABR.—Several printed editions insert *moreover*, contrary to the manuscripts.] committed suicide by poison. Fulvius put the entire senate of Capua to death with punishments, even though the Roman senate forbade it. [Note: [Col. 0899C] “By punishments.” The Augustan edition and Vincent of Beauvais agree with the manuscripts, all of which have *by punishments*. The printed editions wrongly have the singular, *by punishment*.]

After the Scipios had been killed in Spain, while everyone hesitated in fear, Scipio, still very young, voluntarily presented himself. [Note: [Col. 0899C] “Scipio, still very young.” Scipio was about twenty-four years old. Livy, Book XXVI; Appian, *On Spanish Affairs*; Valerius, Book III, chapter 9. This is P. Cornelius Scipio, who was later called Africanus. FABR.] And when the treasury was in shameful poverty, at the urging of Claudius Marcellus and Valerius Laevinus, who were then consuls, all the senators openly brought their coined gold and silver to the quaestors for public use. They left themselves and their sons nothing except one ring and one amulet each, and afterward [Note: [Col. 0899C] “And afterward for their daughters, etc.” The excellent Augustan edition again agrees with the manuscripts. For the other old editions read, “and afterward they left one ounce each to their daughters and wives.”] no more than one ounce of gold each for their daughters and wives, and no more than one pound of silver each.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the various disasters suffered on both sides by the Romans and Carthaginians, as victory inclined now this way, now that.

[Col. 0899B]

[Note: [Col. 0899C] Scipio was twenty-four years old. We have already discussed Scipio’s age. Yet in the Epitome of Polybius, book X, we read: “For, being in his twenty-seventh year, he first undertook actions which most people had altogether despaired of,” and thereafter the author explains at length how New Carthage was captured by him; Livy follows him in this near the end of book XXVI. The same account is found in Appian, *On the Spanish Affairs*, and in Silius, book XV. FABR. — Indeed, the manuscripts Lugd. Bat. III and IV, together with the Gronovian Collection, assign Scipio precisely the same age. The others retain the common reading. In the Augustan edition and in those same Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, “Scipio Africanus” is read. But that name did not yet belong to him at that time. Shortly afterward, Lugd. Bat. IV, together with the Gronovian Collection and certain editions, has “in Hispania”; in contrast, all the Florentine manuscripts and the others have “Hispaniam.”]

Scipio, twenty-four years old, having drawn by lot a proconsular command in Spain and directing his mind especially toward avenging his father and uncle, crossed the Pyrenees and at the first assault captured New Carthage, [Col. 0900A] where the Carthaginians had their largest military stores, strong garrisons, and great supplies of gold and silver. [Note: [Col. 0899D] “The largest military stores.” The Collection agrees with three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Augustan editions in reading “great military stores.”] There also he sent to Rome, among the other prisoners, Mago, Hannibal’s brother, whom he had captured. [Note: [Col. 0899D] “Of the Carthaginians.” Perizonius’s manuscript reads “of the Africans.”]

[Note: [Col. 0900B] “Laevinus, the consul, returning from Macedonia.” What Orosius writes here concerning the operations of the consul M. Valerius Laevinus in Sicily he took from Eutropius. Livy writes that Agrigentum was not stormed but captured through treachery. He likewise says that Hanno was not captured by Laevinus but escaped through a rear gate and fled across to Africa. FABR.]

Laevinus, the consul, returning from Macedonia, stormed Agrigentum, a city of Sicily; there he captured Hanno, commander of the Africans, [Note: [Col. 0900B] “Forty communities.” Lugd. Bat. III, together with the Gronovian Collection, counts forty-six, a number also found in certain manuscripts of Eutropius. But immediately afterward those same witnesses say that twenty-seven were stormed.] accepted forty communities into surrender, and stormed twenty-six. In Italy Hannibal killed the proconsul Cn. Fulvius, together with eleven military tribunes and seventeen thousand soldiers. [Note: [Col. 0900B] “Cn. Fulvius, the proconsul.” Fulvius was killed by Hannibal at Herdonea, as Livy relates at the beginning of book XXVII and Appian in *On Hannibal’s Affairs*. Plutarch too, in his *Marcellus*, reports that eleven military tribunes fell with Fulvius, whereas Livy gives twelve. Sigonius is right in this matter: here we have written seventeen thousand soldiers killed, not six thousand, as is commonly read, first because this is found in all the written books, and second because it is unlikely that Orosius, who made it his purpose to magnify disasters, would here have reduced a number reported by others. Livy elsewhere gives thirteen thousand killed, and elsewhere says that no more than seven thousand were killed. Appian and Eutropius report eight thousand; Plutarch says, “the greater part of the army.” FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0900C] “The consul Marcellus.” Livy, book XXVII, and Plutarch in his *Marcellus* relate this. FABR.]

The consul Marcellus fought Hannibal continuously for three days. On the first day they withdrew after an evenly matched battle; on the next the consul was defeated; on the third he was victorious, killed eight thousand of the enemy, and forced Hannibal himself, together with the survivors, to flee into camp. [Note: [Col. 0900C] “The consul Fabius Maximus.” Q. Fabius Maximus, consul for the fifth time, recovered Tarentum through treachery, as Livy writes in book XXVII, and Plutarch in his *Fabius* and Appian in *On Hannibal’s Affairs*; consult those authors also concerning the death of Marcellus. FABR.]

The consul Fabius Maximus again stormed and captured Tarentum, which had defected from the Romans. [Col. 0900B] There he destroyed Hannibal’s immense forces, together with their commander Carthalo, sold thirty thousand prisoners, and deposited the proceeds in the treasury.

[Note: [Col. 0900C] “In the following year, etc.” This passage is reported by Orosius with excessive carelessness and inattentiveness, if indeed it originated with him. For a few lines later it says that Hannibal killed both consuls, Marcellus and Crispinus, after surrounding them in an ambush. It was therefore superfluous to say the same thing about Marcellus here. Moreover, it is false that Marcellus was killed by Hannibal together with his army. Both consuls had gone out to reconnoiter; Numidian cavalry attacked them from ambush, killed Marcellus, and severely wounded Crispinus. The latter saved himself and his army by flight at that time, but died somewhat later from his wounds. To free Orosius from blame in a matter so obvious and so fully described by Livy and others, the author’s words may be amended with little alteration and an appropriate sense: “In the following year, in Italy, the consul Claudius Marcellus was set against Hannibal with an army. Scipio in Spain, etc.” Lugd. Bat. I then deletes *est*.]

In the following year, in Italy, the consul Claudius Marcellus was killed by Hannibal together with his army. [Note: [Col. 0900D] “Scipio in Spain.” A fragment of Polybius concerning this survives from book VIII, from which Livy drew his account. Consult Appian as well in his Spanish history. FABR.]

Scipio in Spain defeated the Carthaginian commander Hasdrubal [Col. 0901A] and stripped him of his camp. In addition, he brought eighty communities under his control, either by surrender or by war. Having sold the Africans at auction, he released the Spaniards free of charge. Hannibal killed both consuls, Marcellus and Crispinus, after surrounding them in an ambush.

[Note: [Col. 0901B] “Claudius Nero and M. Livius.” These men were consuls in the year 546 from the founding of the City. They crushed Hannibal’s brother Hasdrubal, who had come with a large army; Polybius, book XI, Livy XXVII, Appian *On Hannibal’s Affairs*, Silius book XV, Suetonius in his *Tiberius*, Florus, Eutropius, and others relate this. FABR.]

When the consuls Claudius Nero and M. Livius Salinator were in office, Hasdrubal, Hannibal’s brother, was coming from Spain through Gaul into Italy. The Carthaginians had ordered him to join his brother with his forces, and he was bringing with him substantial auxiliary troops from Spain and Gaul. [Note: [Col. 0901C] “He was bringing.” My manuscript reads “he was leading.”] Since, by his swift advance, word had reached the consuls that he had already descended from the Alps, [Note: [Col. 0901C] “To the consuls.” My manuscript, together with the Gronovian Collection, reads “he had been betrayed to the consuls,” as though he had descended shortly before; “had descended” should therefore be read.] he was intercepted by the Roman army without Hannibal’s knowledge and killed together with his entire army. For a long time the outcome of the battle remained uncertain, especially because the elephants were harassing the Roman line; these [Col. 0901B] were killed by the Roman soldiers, [Note: [Col. 0901C] “Were killed.” These words are absent not only from my manuscript, as also from the Utrecht and Perizonius manuscripts, but likewise from the Lombard manuscript and two other Florentine manuscripts. Since these five manuscripts are far superior to the others, they may arouse some suspicion, especially because a little later the account says not that the elephants were killed by the skirmishers but that they were driven back and killed by the Carthaginians and Hasdrubal himself. Nevertheless, the sense requires something of this kind. Perhaps Orosius wrote “were cut down,” which can also mean “wounded,” and thus may here suggest that the beasts, after being wounded and harassed, were driven back. Although Livy too implies that several elephants were killed by the Romans during the battle itself, book XXVII, chapter 51: “More elephants were killed by their own drivers than by the enemy.”] whom they call *velites* because of their darting about. [Note: [Col. 0901D] “Whom they call velites because of their darting about.” Festus says: “Velites are called lightly equipped soldiers, as if *volites*, that is, ‘flying men.’” FABR.]

This kind of military service had recently been devised: young men chosen for their agility would sit behind the cavalrymen with their own weapons; then, when they approached the enemy, they would leap down from the horses and, now fighting on foot themselves, immediately harass the enemy from another direction while the cavalrymen who had carried them engaged in battle. Thus, when the elephants had been driven back by these *velites* and could no longer be controlled by their own men, they were killed by driving a smith’s chisel between their ears. [Col. 0902A] The commander Hasdrubal himself had first devised this method of killing a beast when necessary. [Note: [Col. 0901D] “The same commander Hasdrubal.” The Gronovian Collection does not have “same.” But the Augustan edition reads *isdem* instead of *iisdem*, and Lugd. Bat. III reads *penes* instead of “the Carthaginian commander Hasdrubal.”]

This battle was fought by the Carthaginians at the Metaurus River, where Hasdrubal was defeated, like the battle at Lake Trasimene; [Note: [Col. 0901D] “The Metaurus.” Three Florentine manuscripts, as well as my manuscript and Perizonius’s, have *Metaurum*, perhaps because *penes* was written in an earlier copy in place of *Poenis*, from which the third Florentine manuscript and the Augustan edition have *penes Metaurum*, and from these the Gronovian Collection has “this battle was fought near the Metaurus River.”] and at Sena, a city of Picenum, as at that village of Cannae. [Note: [Col. 0901D] “And Sena of Picenum.” The corrupted form *Caesena* is commonly read. Livy, Appian, Eutropius, the author of *On Illustrious Men*, and Silius write that the battle was fought at Sena. Hence Cicero, in the *Brutus*, calls it the Battle of Sena, in which Salinator vowed games to Juventas. FABR.]

For fifty-eight thousand of Hasdrubal’s army were killed there, and five thousand four hundred were captured. [Note: [Col. 0902B] “For fifty-eight thousand.” This number is found in our manuscripts, and the Deacon inserted the same number into his Eutropius from Orosius. But Livy’s books give fifty-six thousand enemy dead, five thousand four hundred captured. Polybius publishes a much smaller number: he writes that approximately ten thousand Carthaginians and Gauls, and nearly two thousand Romans, were killed. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0902C] “Four thousand.” Three Florentine manuscripts, as well as my manuscript, Perizonius’s, the Gronovian Collection, Lugd. Bat. III, and all the old editions add *autem* (“however”) after these words.]

Four thousand Roman citizens were found among them and brought back, which was a consolation to the victorious consuls. For eight thousand also fell from their army. Hannibal’s brother Hasdrubal’s head was thrown before the camp. When he saw it and at the same time learned of the Carthaginians’ defeat, [Note: [Col. 0902C] “In the thirteenth year after he had come into Italy.” The same wording is found in the additions of the Deacon to Eutropius. FABR.] in the thirteenth year after he had come into Italy, he withdrew to the Bruttians.

After this, for one entire year, a respite from the tumult of war seemed to intervene between Hannibal and the Romans, because the disturbance of illness afflicted the camps, and a very severe pestilence [Note: [Col. 0902C] “Afflicted both armies.” This is better read from the Cologne manuscript as *angebatur* than as *agebatur*. LAUT. — My manuscript, Perizonius’s, Lugd. Bat. III, and two Florentine manuscripts, together with the old editions, have *utrique exercitus angebantur* (“both armies were afflicted”); the first Florentine manuscript, or Lombard manuscript, has *utriusque exercitus angebantur* (“the army of each side was afflicted”). Whichever reading one chooses, it is clear that the verb *angi* (“to be afflicted”) must be retained, and with better justification than *agi* (“to be conducted”), which is preferred by the manuscripts and editions that favor *agebatur*. For the distinction between these expressions, see the distinguished Arentzenius’s note on Aurelius Victor, p. 347.] afflicted both armies.

[Note: [Col. 0902D] “Meanwhile Scipio.” Livy, book XXVIII, and Appian in his Spanish history relate these events. A fragment of Polybius from book XI also survives; comparing it with Livy’s account would be highly useful to students. FABR.]

Meanwhile Scipio, having reduced all Spain into a province from the Pyrenees to the Ocean, came to Rome. [Note: [Col. 0902D] “Consul with Licinius.” P. Cornelius Scipio and P. Licinius Crassus Dives were consuls in the year 543 from the founding of the City. In that year Scipio obtained the province of Sicily, and in the following year crossed into Africa; Livy, book XXIX. Appian in his Libyan history and Eutropius, book III, also relate this. By comparing their accounts, you will learn—as Livy too admits—that the authors do not agree on every point. FABR.]

Having been elected consul with Licinius Crassus, he crossed into Africa, killed Hanno, son of Hamilcar and commander of the Carthaginians, and destroyed his army partly by slaughter and partly by capture; for [Note: [Col. 0902D] “Eleven thousand.” Lugd. Bat. III, together with the Gronovian Collection and the Augustan edition, has forty thousand.
