The same number is found in excerpts from Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, book VI, chapter 51.] he killed eleven thousand Carthaginians in that battle.

The consul Sempronius engaged Hannibal and was defeated, [Note: [Col. 0903C] “Fled back to Rome.” Livy, at the end of book IX, writes that P. Sempronius, defeated by Hannibal in the territory of Croton, returned to camp and thereafter, after summoning Licinius Crassus, fought successfully. FABR.] and fled back to Rome. Scipio in Africa attacked the winter quarters of the Carthaginians and those of the Numidians, both of which were not far from Utica, and at midnight [Note: [Col. 0903C] “He caused them to be set on fire.” Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with Vincent of Beauvais and the Gronovian Collection, read “he set them on fire.”] caused them to be set on fire. The Carthaginians, alarmed and thinking that the fire had arisen by accident, ran unarmed to extinguish it; and so they were easily overwhelmed by armed men. [Note: [Col. 0903C] “They were overwhelmed.” The Augustan edition has “they were defeated or overwhelmed.” The Venetian editions likewise have both readings joined together, as can often be seen in old editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0903C] “Forty thousand in both camps.” Livy gives this number. Appian says: “Of the enemy, nearly thirty thousand were killed, and two thousand four hundred were taken prisoner.” FABR.]

In both camps forty thousand men were consumed by fire and sword, [Note: [Col. 0903C] “Five thousand were captured.” Lugd. Bat. IV, closer to Appian’s number, says that two thousand were captured. [Col. 0903D]] five thousand were captured, and the commanders themselves, dreadfully burned, [Note: [Col. 0903D] “Escaped with difficulty.” The first Florentine manuscript has “escaped with difficulty”; the third has “fled away with difficulty”; another has “retreated with difficulty.”] escaped with difficulty. The commander Hasdrubal fled to Carthage.

[Note: [Col. 0903D] “And so Syphax and Hasdrubal.” Livy and Appian give a full account of all these events; consult them. FABR.]

Accordingly, Syphax and Hasdrubal soon rebuilt a very large army and again engaged Scipio; defeated, they fled. Laelius and Massanissa captured Syphax as he fled; the rest of the multitude took refuge at Cirta, [Note: [Col. 0903D] “Took refuge.” The Augustan edition has “fled for refuge.” My manuscript has simply “fled.” Shortly afterward Perizonius reads “accepted into surrender” instead of “received.”] which Massanissa, after besieging it, received into surrender. He brought Syphax, bound in chains, [Note: [Col. 0903D] “To Scipio, etc.” Vincent of Beauvais prefers: “He brought Syphax, bound in chains, to Scipio.”] to Scipio; Scipio entrusted him to Laelius to be taken to Rome with enormous spoils and a great number of prisoners. [Note: [Col. 0903D] “To Rome.” This is absent from eight manuscripts—namely, three Florentine manuscripts, three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, my manuscript, and Perizonius’s—as well as from Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, book VI, chapter 51.]

## CHAPTER XIX  
### That Hannibal, recalled to Africa, was defeated and put to flight by Scipio, and that the Romans granted peace to the Carthaginians

When Hannibal was ordered to return to Africa to aid the exhausted Carthaginians, [Note: [Col. 0903D] “He left Italy weeping.” Eutropius has the same; Livy says that he scarcely restrained his tears. FABR.] he left Italy weeping, after killing all the soldiers of Italian origin who were unwilling to follow him. [Note: [Col. 0904C] “All of Italian origin.” Appian discusses this at the end of his book *On Hannibal’s Affairs*. FABR.]

As he approached the African shore, he ordered one of the sailors to climb the ship’s mast and look out from there to determine what region they held. [Note: [Col. 0904C] “He replied that he had seen a ruined tomb.” Livy writes: “When he said that a ruined tomb faced the prow, Hannibal, regarding it as an evil omen, ordered the helmsman to sail past it and brought the fleet to Leptis.” FABR. — Vincent of Beauvais has “to look out.”]

The sailor replied that he had seen a ruined tomb. Hannibal, regarding the words as an evil omen, changed course, landed his forces at the town of Leptis, [Note: [Col. 0904C] “Who immediately.” This reading is found in all the manuscripts and also in Vincent of Beauvais, so that the reference is to Hannibal, not to Leptis, as the editions have devised. The Augustan edition agrees with the manuscripts, always scrupulously preserving the wording of its own copy.] and, after immediately restoring his forces, [Note: [Col. 0904C] “Came to Carthage.” He did not approach the city itself, but Zama, which is five days’ journey from Carthage, as Livy relates in book XXX and Polybius in book XV. They give a fuller account of the commanders’ conference. FABR.] came to Carthage. Then [Note: [Col. 0904C] “Sought a conference with Scipio.” This is the reading of the manuscripts. Most editions, however, have “he sought Scipio’s conference.” The Augustan edition alone has “he came to a conference with Scipio.” Where it says, “When there the two men had long…,” four manuscripts have *petit* (“seeks”) instead of *petiit* (“sought”).] he sought a conference with Scipio.

[Note: [Col. 0904D] “When there the two men had long.” This is the reading of the manuscripts. The old editions have, “There, when they had long…”] There, after the two most illustrious commanders had for a long time gazed at one another in stunned mutual admiration, [Note: [Col. 0904D] “Had gazed.” Lugd. Bat. I has “had looked at one another.”] the negotiations for peace having failed, battle was joined. It was arranged with the great skill of the commanders, fought with the great masses of their forces, and brought to completion by the great strength of the soldiers; and it gave victory to the Romans. Eighty elephants were either captured or killed. [Note: [Col. 0904D] “Twenty thousand five hundred Carthaginians were killed.” Appian says: “Twenty-five thousand of the enemy were killed.” Polybius and Livy write that more than twenty thousand Carthaginians were killed. Consult these same authors concerning Hannibal’s flight and concerning the peace and its conditions. FABR.]

After Hannibal had tried every expedient both before and during the battle, he escaped amid the confusion with a few men—indeed, scarcely four horsemen—and fled to Hadrumetum. Later he came to Carthage, thirty-six years after he had left it [Note: [Col. 0904D] “As a little boy.” Perizonius’s manuscript has “as a small child.”] as a little boy with his father. [Note: [Col. 0904D] “And having consulted the senate.” My manuscript has “and while consulting the senate,” which is also found in the Augustan edition.]

He persuaded the senate, when it was deliberating, that no hope remained except in seeking peace. In the consulship of Cn. Cornelius Lentulus and P. Aelius Paetus, peace was granted to the Carthaginians through Scipio, with the consent of the senate and the Roman people. Nevertheless, more than five hundred ships were taken out to sea and burned in sight of the city.

Scipio, already at that time bearing the surname Africanus, entered the City in triumph. Terentius, who later became a comic poet, [Note: [Col. 0904D] “Terentius, who later became a comic poet.” What Orosius writes here about the comic poet Terentius, Livy, in books XXX and XXXVIII, records concerning Q. Terentius Culleo, a Roman senator whom Scipio received among the prisoners. Fenestella too refuted those who had written that Terentius was captured in Africa and brought to Rome. FABR. — Although this reading is found in all the manuscripts, and also in Vincent of Beauvais, book VI, chapter 52, Pighius, under the year 552 from the founding of the City, volume II of the *Annals*, p. 241, calls it an impudent gloss introduced through the ignorance of copyists. I wish that were so! But I fear that Orosius read Livy too carelessly and hastily. For the words “who later became a comic poet,” as well as the phrase above concerning Scipio “who later became Africanus,” have the stamp of Orosius’s style. He appears to have believed that Publius Terentius, later a comic writer, had been one of the noble—or, as some editions read, most noble—Carthaginian captives, and that before the triumph he had been released from servitude and granted freedom, and for that reason had followed the triumphal chariot of Scipio, his benefactor. For if we remove only the words “who later became a comic poet” as a gloss, there still remain the badly connected words “from the noble Carthaginian captives.” Q. Terentius Culleo, to whom Livy and others say that this good fortune occurred, cannot be said to have been one of the noble Carthaginian captives, because he was one of the Roman captives held by the Carthaginians; Roman captives in Greece are described in the same way in the following chapter. Moreover, the text should then read “of the freedom that had been granted” or, as in the following chapter, “of the freedom that had been wiped away,” not “of the freedom bestowed,” since one Roman could not bestow freedom on another Roman, which belonged to him by the same right as to himself, as a Roman. A master, however, customarily bestows freedom on a slave; thus that Publius Terentius, who later became a comic poet, was manumitted.]

Terentius, who later became a comic poet, followed behind the triumphal chariot wearing the cap of liberty, as one of the noble [Col. 0905A] Carthaginian captives—this cap being the mark of the freedom granted to him.

## CHAPTER XX  
### On the Macedonian war, in which the Romans fought variously and in different ways, chiefly against the Macedonians and Antiochus, king of Syria, with victory shifting now to one side and now to the other
[Note: [Col. 0905D] In the year 546 from the founding of the City. In the Capitoline Fasti this year is 552 from the founding of the City. The First Macedonian War, which the Romans undertook in this year, is also called the Philippic War, after the king against whom it was waged. Livy treats it in Book 31 and following books, Florus in Book II, chapter 7, and Eutropius in Book IV. FABR.]

In the year 546 from the founding of the City, the Second Punic War came to an end; it had lasted seventeen years. The Macedonian War immediately succeeded it.

[Note: [Col. 0905D] That Quinctius Flamininus. T. Quinctius Flamininus, son of Titus, grandson of Lucius, consul, is found in the Capitoline Fasti in the year 555. He drew Macedonia by lot and fought successfully against Philip at the passes of Epirus; in the following year, after defeating him, he granted him peace. See Polybius, Book 17; Livy, Books 32 and 33; and Plutarch, Life of Flamininus. The cognomen Flamininus is correctly written in Cornelius Gualther’s book, although in other books and commonly elsewhere it is written incorrectly. Concerning Nabis, see, besides Livy and Plutarch, Pausanias, Book IV, and Justin, Books 30 and 31. FABR.]

Quinctius Flamininus, who had drawn this province by lot as consul, after many extremely severe battles in which the Macedonians were defeated, granted peace to Philip. Then he fought against the Lacedaemonians; after defeating Nabis, their commander, he led before his chariot the most distinguished hostages, Demetrius, Philip’s son, and Armenes.

[Note: [Col. 0906C] Armenes. He died in Italy among the Romans. Demetrius was later restored to his father Philip.]

The Roman captives who had been sold throughout Greece under Hannibal were all recovered. With their heads shaved, as a sign that their enslavement had been removed, they followed the triumphal chariot.

[Note: [Col. 0906C] At the same time, the Insubrians. This action against the Gauls was carried out by the praetor L. Furius Purpureo when P. Sulpicius Galba and C. Aurelius Cotta were consuls, in the year 553 from the founding of the City. Livy, Book 30. FABR.]

At the same time, the Insubrians, Boii, and Cenomani, having joined their forces under the leadership of Hamilcar the Carthaginian, who had remained in Italy, laid waste to Cremona and Placentia, but were defeated by the praetor L. Furius in a very difficult war.

Later, as proconsul, Flamininus subdued in war King Philip, together with the Thracians, Macedonians, Illyrians, and many other peoples who had come to his aid.

[Note: [Col. 0906C] To his aid. Three Leiden manuscripts, with Gronovius’s manuscript, read: “who had come to his assistance.”]

[Note: [Col. 0906C] The Macedonians were defeated. He means the battle in which Philip, king of the Macedonians, was defeated by T. Quinctius at Cynoscephalae. Livy described it at the beginning of Book 33; but since the account there was lost, not without considerable damage to the historical record, it has been preserved, by an exceptional favor, in fragments of Polybius, Book 17. There, what Orosius reports from Polybius is written as follows: “Of the Macedonians, all told about eight thousand died, while no fewer than five thousand were captured alive.” Plutarch gives the same number of slain. FABR.]

The Macedonians were defeated and lost their camp. Polybius writes that eight thousand of the enemy were killed that day and five thousand captured.

[Note: [Col. 0906D] Killed that day. Thus read the better manuscripts—six in number, namely three Florentine manuscripts, those of Perizonius and myself, and one of the Leiden manuscripts—supported by Gronovius’s manuscript. Others read “at the same time.”]

[Note: [Col. 0906D] Five thousand captured. In three more recent manuscripts the number of slain is set at nine thousand and that of captives at six thousand, but contrary to Polybius. Shortly afterward, the manuscript of Perizonius reads *victorum* (“of the victors”) for *victoris* (“of the victor”).]

Valerius says that forty thousand were slaughtered. Claudius, however, records that thirty-two thousand were killed. But this variation among the writers is certainly falsehood. The cause of the falsehood is clearly flattery: they strive to heap praise upon the victor and exalt the valor of their country, whether for the benefit of their contemporaries or of posterity. Otherwise, if the number had not been investigated, no number of any kind would have been stated.

If it is glorious for a commander and his country to have destroyed very many enemies, how much more joyful for the country and gratifying for the commander must it appear to have lost either none or very few of its own men! Thus it is perfectly clear that, with the same shamelessness with which the number of slain enemies is increased, the losses of the allies are also diminished or even wholly concealed.

[Note: [Col. 0906D] Therefore Sempronius. C. Sempronius Tuditanus, praetor in Hither Spain, was defeated in battle and died not long afterward from a serious wound. Livy, Book 33. Appian calls him Sempronius Tudertinus in his Spanish History. FABR.]

Accordingly, Sempronius Tuditanus was overwhelmed in battle in Hither Spain and killed together with the entire Roman army.

[Note: [Col. 0906D] The consul Marcellus. M. Claudius Marcellus and L. Furius Purpureo were consuls in the year 557 from the founding of the City, and during that magistracy conducted operations in Etruria. Livy, Book 33. FABR.]

The consul Marcellus was overwhelmed by the Boii in Etruria and lost a large part of his army; afterward the other consul, Furius, came to his aid. Thus they ravaged the entire nation of the Boii with fire and sword and almost annihilated it.

When L. Valerius Flaccus and M. Porcius Cato were consuls,

[Note: [Col. 0907B] Antiochus, king of Syria. Livy discusses him and Hannibal’s journey to him; see also Appian, On the Affairs of Hannibal and his Syrian History, and Justin, Book 31. FABR.]

Antiochus, king of Syria, crossed from Asia into Europe while preparing war against the Roman people.

[Note: [Col. 0907C] Were being circulated. The Augustan edition reads *ferebantur* (“were being reported”), as does Scott’s edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0907C] To Rome. Thus the better manuscripts; others read *Romae* (“at Rome”).]

[Note: [Col. 0907C] Tribune of the plebs. The Longobard manuscript, like that of Perizonius, reads “for the tribune of the plebs.”]

[Note: [Col. 0907D] Publius Digitius. In Gualther’s book Digitius has no praenomen. At the beginning of Book 35 Livy calls him Sextus Digitius and records the other events that Orosius briefly recounts here. FABR.]

and captured their king.

[Note: [Col. 0908B] Very much. The fourth Leiden manuscript and the Augustan edition read “many.” The latter edition soon afterward also reads “of both peoples.”]

[Note: [Col. 0908C] By whose defenses. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s manuscript, read “from whose defenses.”]

reaching Ephesus.

[Note: [Col. 0908C] He is said to have had sixty thousand armed men. According to Livy, this number was given by Valerius Antias. Appian, however, writes that approximately ten thousand of Antiochus’s army were killed or captured. FABR.]

He is said to have had sixty thousand armed men, of whom forty thousand were killed and more than five thousand captured.

The other consul, Scipio, engaged the nation of the Boii,

[Note: [Col. 0908C] In which battle twenty thousand of the enemy. Valerius Antias writes that twenty-eight thousand of the enemy were killed, three thousand four hundred captured, and that 124 military standards, 1,200 horses, and 247 wagons were taken. Livy. FABR.]

and in that battle killed twenty thousand of the enemy.

[Note: [Col. 0908C] In that battle. Perizonius reads “in that war,” as often elsewhere.]

In the following year Scipio

[Note: [Col. 0908C] The following year. Africanus’s brother L. Scipio completed the Antiochene War and was consequently called Asiaticus. Livy, Book 37. FABR.]

In Further Spain,

[Note: [Col. 0908D] Lucius Aemilius as proconsul. Lucius Aemilius Paulus, while Scipio and Glabrio were consuls, received Further Spain by lot and governed it with consular authority as proconsul. [Note: [Col. 0908D] So completely. This does not appear in the same Augustan edition.]

it is clear that not even a messenger survived, so that the Massilians had to report the annihilation itself at Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0909C] Fulvius, consul from Greece. In the year 564 from the founding of the City, M. Fulvius Nobilior was consul with Cn. Manlius Vulso. Livy, Book 38, says that the war in Gallograecia was conducted by Manlius, not Fulvius. See also Florus, Book II, chapter 11, and Appian, Syrian History. On Gallograecia, see Livy and Justin, Book 25. FABR.]

Fulvius, consul, crossed from Greece into Gallograecia, which is now Galatia, and reached Mount Olympus, to which all the Gallograecians had fled with their wives and children. There he fought a most bitter battle. From their higher positions the enemy severely battered the Romans with arrows,

[Note: [Col. 0909C] With huge stones. Thus read the manuscripts, with the conjunction *que* deleted, although some printed editions retain it.]

huge stones, and other weapons; but at last the Romans broke through to close combat with the enemy. Forty thousand Gallograecians are said to have been killed in that battle.

[Note: [Col. 0909C] Crushed. The fourth Leiden manuscript and the Augustan edition read “worn down,” a reading also found in Vincent of Beauvais, Book VI, chapter 58, who continues, “at last, breaking through,” and so forth, and reports that they killed forty thousand Gallograecians.]

The consul Marcius set out against the Ligurians and was defeated, losing four thousand soldiers. Had he not, despite his defeat, quickly retreated to the camp, he would have suffered the same massacre that Baebius had earlier suffered at the hands of those same enemies.

When M. Claudius Marcellus and Q. Fabius Labeo were consuls, King Philip,

[Note: [Col. 0909C] Who had killed the envoys of the Roman people. Philip did not kill Roman envoys; rather, he cruelly slaughtered the Maronites, whom the Senate had ordered him to restore to liberty. Livy, Book 39. On Demetrius’s murder, see the same author, Book 40, and Plutarch, Life of Aemilius Paulus. FABR.]

who had killed the envoys of the Roman people, obtained pardon because of the most respectful pleas of his son Demetrius,

[Note: [Col. 0909D] His son. In two Leiden manuscripts only *filii* (“of his son”) is found.]

whom he had sent as an envoy. Yet immediately afterward, treating that same son as a friend of the Romans and a traitor to himself, he killed him with poison, assisted in the parricide by the son’s own brother, who was unsuspecting of the wickedness against them both.

In the same year Scipio Africanus, long living in exile from the City that had shown him no gratitude,

[Note: [Col. 0909D] Living in exile for a long time. The Augustan edition orders that the earlier word be *exsulare* (“to live in exile”).]

died of illness at the town of Liternum.

[Note: [Col. 0909D] At Liternum. For the death of Africanus, see Livy, Book 39. There he also records the deaths of Hannibal and Philopoemen, as do Plutarch in his Lives of Flamininus and Philopoemen and Justin, Book 32. FABR.]

In those same days Hannibal, when the Romans demanded that he be surrendered by Prusias, king of Bithynia, killed himself with poison.

[Note: [Col. 0909D] Philopoemen, commander of the Achaeans, was captured and killed by the Messenians. In Sicily at that time. I am surprised that Marcoduranus did not notice the corruption here, when he printed this passage in such confused divisions: “captured and killed by the Messenians in Sicily.” LAUT.—It is likewise incorrect to write *Philopoemenes* and *Messanis*, since he is called the commander Philopoemen, and those who captured him are called the Messenians, in Justin, Book 32, chapter 1.]

Philopoemen, commander of the Achaeans, was captured and killed by the Messenians. At that time in Sicily an island of Vulcan,

[Note: [Col. 0910C] The island of Vulcan, and so forth. The Augustan edition reads “the Vulcanian island, which had not previously existed, suddenly emerging from the sea to everyone’s amazement,” and so forth. Instead of *in mari* (“in the sea”), which appears in the Vulgate edition, two Leiden manuscripts, my manuscript, and that of Perizonius read *mari* (“from the sea”), as do three Florentine manuscripts and the Venetian editions. I have therefore rejected *in*, which is superfluous.]

which had not existed before, suddenly emerged from the sea amid everyone’s wonder and remains there to this day.

[Note: [Col. 0910C] Q. Fulvius Flaccus. When Baebius and Aemilius were consuls, he received Hither Spain as praetor and in the following year defeated the Celtiberians. Livy, Book 40. Appian, in his Spanish History, attributes the action to Fulvius as consul, if Beraldus translated correctly, for I have not yet seen the Greek book published by Henri Estienne. FABR.]

The praetor Q. Fulvius Flaccus routed twenty-three thousand men in a great battle in Hither Spain

[Note: [Col. 0910C] Twenty-three thousand. The Augustan edition has thirty-three thousand.]

and captured four thousand.

[Note: [Col. 0910C] Ti. Sempronius Gracchus. Gracchus succeeded Fulvius in Spain, according to Appian. See the Epitome of Book 41. FABR.]

Ti. Sempronius Gracchus in Further Spain compelled 105 towns, emptied and battered by war, to surrender.

[Note: [Col. 0910C] One hundred and five towns. Several old editions read 150. Two Leiden manuscripts read 152.]

That same summer L. Postumius also killed forty thousand of the enemy in battle in Hither Spain. Gracchus, again as praetor in the same region, stormed and captured two hundred towns.

[Note: [Col. 0910D] He stormed and captured. My manuscript reads “attacked and captured.”]

When Lepidus and Mucius were consuls,

[Note: [Col. 0910D] When Lepidus and Mucius were consuls. M. Aemilius Lepidus and P. Mucius Scaevola were consuls in the year 578 from the founding of the City. FABR.]

the extremely warlike tribe of the Bastarnae, enticed by Perseus, son of Philip, with the hope of plunder and by the opportunity to cross the Ister River,

[Note: [Col. 0910D] The tribe of the Bastarnae. Before the time of Perseus, his father Philip had already incited this tribe and neighboring peoples to war against the Romans. See what we have written about them in the Major Work, in the Life of Philip, son of Demetrius.]

was destroyed without any battle or enemy.

[Note: [Col. 0910D] Without any battle. The first Longobard manuscript reads “without any battle.”]

For at that time the Danube, also called the Ister, happened to be covered with thick ice, making an easy crossing on foot possible. Accordingly, when an immeasurable multitude of men and horses crossed in one vast column without due caution, the ice, cracking under the enormous weight and the jolting of those walking upon it, split apart; the icy crust, finally overcome and shattered, abandoned the entire column that it had long supported to the depths of the waters. Then, when the same ice formed again over the fragments that hindered it, it submerged them. A few from the entire population escaped along both banks, scarcely alive and with their entrails mangled.

When P. Licinius Crassus and C. Cassius Longinus were consuls,

[Note: [Col. 0910D] The Macedonian War. Livy sets out the Second Macedonian War in Books 41–45. See also Plutarch, Life of Aemilius Paulus; Florus, Book II, chapter 12; and Eutropius, Book IV. On the auxiliaries of both sides, see Livy, Book 42. FABR.]

the Macedonian War was waged, rightly reckoned among the greatest wars. At first all Italy, then Ptolemy, king of Egypt, Ariarathes of Cappadocia, Eumenes of Asia, and Masinissa of Numidia were allies of the Romans. The Thracians under their king Cotys, and all the Illyrians under their king Gentius, followed Perseus and the Macedonians.

Thus Perseus met the consul Crassus as he arrived.

[Note: [Col. 0911B] And when battle had been joined, they were miserably defeated. Livy discusses this battle in Book 42. Plutarch writes in his *Apophthegmata*: “Publius Licinius, consul and commander, defeated in cavalry battle by Perseus, king of the Macedonians, lost 2,800 men, some of whom fell and others were captured.” FABR.]

When battle was joined, the Romans were miserably defeated and fled. In the following engagement, the losses of both sides were nearly equal, and they withdrew into winter quarters.

Then Perseus, after the Roman army had been crushed in many battles, crossed into Illyricum and captured by fighting the town of Sulcanum, which was defended by Roman garrisons.

[Note: [Col. 0911C] The town of Sulcanum. *Sulcanum* appears in Gualther’s book; Livy, Book 43, writes that Perseus captured Uscana and that the Roman garrison there fell into his power. FABR.—*Sulcamum* is read in three Florentine manuscripts; my manuscript and two Leiden manuscripts read *Sulcanium*.]

[Note: [Col. 0911C] He captured it by fighting. From the uncertain conjecture *pugnare coepit* (“he began to fight”), which appeared in the Cologne and Venetian editions, Fabricius had printed *pugnando cepit* (“he captured it by fighting”). LAUT.—Fabricius restored the text in this form from the manuscripts, which read *pugnando*.]

There he killed some of the large number of Roman garrison troops, sold others as slaves, and led others with him into Macedonia.

Afterward L. Aemilius Paulus, consul, fought against him and defeated him.

[Note: [Col. 0911C] For he killed twenty thousand infantry. Livy, Book 44, says that about twenty thousand men were killed. Plutarch writes: “It is reported that more than twenty-five thousand were killed.” FABR.]

For he killed twenty thousand infantry in that war. The king escaped with his cavalry,

but was immediately captured and driven in triumph before the chariot with his sons. Afterwards,

[Note: [Col. 0911C] In custody at Alba. Perseus was first placed in custody at Alba; later, released from prison at the decision of Aemilius Paulus, he died after having endured a miserable life for ten years, according to Diodorus Siculus, Book 31. Velleius writes that Perseus died at Alba four years later while in free custody. FABR.—Concerning Gentius, king of the Illyrians; Perseus himself; his sons; and the fate of his entire household, see the Life of Perseus at the end of our History of the Kings of Macedonia.]

he died in custody at Alba. His younger son learned the craft of metalworking at Rome in order to endure his poverty, and there he wasted away.

Many other wars, with very different outcomes, were waged everywhere against numerous peoples; I have omitted them for the sake of brevity.

## CHAPTER XXI  
**Scipio Africanus devastated Spain; Scipio Nasica opposed the construction of a theater; Galba dealt not very honorably with the Lusitanians**

[Col. 0912A]

[Note: [Col. 0911D] In the year 600 from the founding of the City. In other sources this year is 602. The Deacon inserted this passage of Orosius into the history of Eutropius. FABR.]

In the year 600 from the founding of the City, when L. Licinius Lucullus and A. Postumius Albinus were consuls, a great fear of the Celtiberians seized all the Romans. Among all of them there was no one who dared to go to Spain, either as a soldier or as an envoy.

[Note: [Col. 0911D] P. Scipio. On the military service of Scipio Aemilianus, see the Livian Epitome, Book 48. FABR.]

P. Scipio, who was later called Africanus, voluntarily offered himself for military service in Spain, although Macedonia had already been assigned to him by lot.

Accordingly, he set out for Spain and inflicted great slaughter upon the peoples there, often performing the duty of a soldier more than that of a commander.

[Note: [Col. 0911D] Even of a soldier. Some old editions read “even so much the duty of a soldier,” and so forth; but the omission is more elegant.]

For he also killed, in single combat, a barbarian who had challenged him.

[Note: [Col. 0911D] For he killed a barbarian who had challenged him. Appian records that this happened during the siege of the town of Intercatia in his Spanish History, as does the author of *On Illustrious Men*. In the Livian Epitome, the reading is commonly corrupted to “of the captured city”; in the old manuscripts it reads “of the intercepted city,” instead of “of Intercatia.” FABR.]

The praetor Servius Galba, however, was defeated by the Lusitanians in a great battle. After losing his entire army, he himself barely escaped with a few men.

[Note: [Col. 0912B] But Servius Galba. This is Servius Sulpicius Galba, whom Appian and Suetonius discuss in the Life of Galba. “Sergius Galba,” instead of “Servius,” had previously been read incorrectly. FABR.]

At the same time the censors decided that a stone theater should be built in the City.

[Note: [Col. 0912C] At the same time the censors. See the Epitome of Book 48. FABR.]

Scipio Nasica vigorously opposed its construction, saying that it would be most hostile to a warlike people because it would nurture idleness

[Note: [Col. 0912C] And a contrivance of wantonness. Fabricius printed this form, following certain old editions; but all the Florentine manuscripts, as well as the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts, and also my manuscript and Perizonius’s, read “and a contrivance for wantonness.” In that sense Nasica said that the theater was a most hostile contrivance for nurturing both idleness and wantonness. The first editions and the Augustan edition, together with the Venetian editions, also support this reading. The first Leiden manuscript offers another reading: “for proclaiming idleness and a contrivance of wantonness,” which is not without its own appeal. Tertullian likewise regarded the theater as a contrivance of wantonness in *On the Spectacles*, chapter 10: “The censors often destroyed theaters that were springing up again, taking thought for morals, since they foresaw the great danger to them from wantonness.” Valerius Maximus also noted that sitting in the theater brought idleness to a warlike people, II.4.2: “Indeed, a senatorial decree was enacted that no one should set up benches in the City or within a mile of it, or sit and watch the games, so that the manliness of standing—an attribute proper to the Roman people—might be joined to the relaxation of the spirit.” Velleius Paterculus, Book I, chapter 15; Appian, Civil Wars, Book I, p. 367; Livy, Epitome 48; and Augustine, Orosius’s teacher, in *The City of God*, Book I, chapter 6, also discuss Scipio Nasica’s action: “When the Senate was attempting to build the auditorium of the theater, Nasica, the chief pontiff, restrained it and persuaded it not to allow Greek luxury to creep into the manly morals of the country; and he arranged that the Senate should subsequently prohibit the benches that the state had long since begun to use at the spectacle of the games, after they had been assembled for the occasion.”]

and a contrivance of wantonness. He influenced the Senate so greatly that it not only ordered everything acquired for the theater to be sold but also prohibited the placing of benches at the games.

Therefore let our people understand—for whom anything encountered outside the entertainment of lust is an offense—that because they themselves feel and admit that they are weaker than their enemies, theaters are to be blamed for this, not the times. They should not blaspheme the true God, who has forbidden such things down to the present day, but should abominate their gods or demons, who demanded them, since in a sufficiently profound demonstration of their malignity they required such a sacrifice that they might be nourished not so much by the blood poured out from cattle as by the virtue of human beings laid low.

For certainly at that time there was no lack of enemies, famine, diseases, or prodigies; indeed, there were very many of them. But there were no theaters, where—as incredible as it is to say—at the altar of wantonness the victims of virtue are slaughtered.

[Note: [Col. 0913C] Victims of virtues. The Augustan editions read “the virtues of human beings are slaughtered as victims.”]

At one time the Carthaginians thought it appropriate to sacrifice human beings, but that wrongly conceived belief was soon abandoned. By contrast, the Romans were driven to devote themselves to destruction.

[Note: [Col. 0913C] They devoted themselves to destruction. The Augustan edition adds “on account of the theater.”]

[Note: [Col. 0913C] It happened, it happens, it is loved, and so forth. This is a difficult passage, which I scarcely understand adequately; the same seems to have happened to the commentators, since they passed over it without explanation. All the old editions except the Augustan have: “They admit that it happened in this way, and they shout that it should happen.” The third Florentine manuscript reads the same. The Utrecht manuscript is not far from it, reading: “He admits that it happened and it is shouted that it should happen.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts and the fourth—although the second reads, “It happened, he admits, and it is shouted that it should happen”—together with Gronovius’s manuscript, offer this reading: “It happened, it is sung in this way, and it is shouted that it should happen.” But the Longobard manuscript, or first Florentine manuscript, and the second Florentine manuscript plainly read: “It happened, it happens, it is loved, and it is shouted that it should happen,” except that the second has *amatus* (“loved”) instead of *amatur*. From this it is evident that Fabricius derived his reading from the manuscripts. My manuscript, Perizonius’s, and the Augustan edition—the best of all, as often happens—agree with the Florentine manuscripts and present the same reading here. The sense of the words appears to be this: sitting in the theater and remaining seated there, as it was formerly done, is also done now. The wretched people love this stain upon virtue and demand with continual shouts that it happen again—that is, that they be permitted to watch the games more often. He is attacking the madness of his own time concerning theatrical games, similar to the vanity of the circus, about which he wrote in Book I, chapter 6: “He most unmistakably testified that custom had wavered only briefly and through some small and slight movement toward pleasures, when he freely shouted that, if the circus were restored to him, nothing had been done to him—that is, that the swords of the Goths had accomplished nothing at Rome if the Romans were permitted to watch the circus games.”]

“It happened, it happens, it is loved, and it is shouted that it should happen”: those who might perhaps be offended by the slaughter of a sheep belonging to their flock rejoice at the destruction of the virtue of their own hearts. Rather, let them blush before Nasica, whom they think should be reproached by Christians; and let them complain not to us about the enemies they have always had, but to him about the theater whose existence he had forbidden.

[Note: [Col. 0914C] Therefore, in Spain, Servius Galba. Appian attributes this event to Lucullus; but Cicero in *Brutus*, Suetonius in the Life of Galba, and Valerius Maximus, Book IX, chapter 6, agree with Orosius. FABR.]

Accordingly, in Spain the praetor Servius Galba received the Lusitanians living this side of the Tagus River into surrender and then criminally killed them. Pretending that he would take care of their interests, he surrounded them with soldiers and struck down all of them, unarmed and unsuspecting. This act later became, because of Roman treachery, the cause of the greatest disturbance throughout Spain.

## CHAPTER XXII  
**The Third Punic War. The consuls who set out to destroy Carthage were put to flight. Meanwhile, concerning its situation**

[Col. 0914A]

In the 602nd year from the founding of the City, in the consulship of L. Censorinus and M. Manilius, the Third Punic War broke out. [Note: [Col. 0914C] The Third Punic War. This war is set out in the Livian Epitome, Books XLIX, L, and LI. It is narrated by Appian in the Libyca, by Plutarch in his Life of Cato, by Eutropius in Book IV, and by Florus in Book II, chapter 15. FABR.]

Accordingly, when the Senate had determined that Carthage must be destroyed, the consuls set out for Africa, and Scipio, then military tribune, established their position near Utica at the camp of the Elder Africanus. [Note: [Col. 0914C] The camp of the Elder Africanus. He means the Cornelian Camp, discussed by Caesar in Book II of the *Commentaries on the Civil War* and by Lucan in Book IV. FABR.]

There, after summoning the Carthaginians and ordering them to hand over their arms and ships, and without delay, such a quantity of weapons was suddenly surrendered that all Africa could easily have been armed from them. But after the Carthaginians had handed over their weapons and had been ordered to withdraw ten miles from the city, away from the sea, [Note: [Col. 0914C] Ten thousand paces. Appian gives eighty stades, which corresponds to this number. FABR.] they turned their grief into desperation, determined either to defend their state or to be buried with and through it. They appointed two commanders for themselves, both named Hasdrubal. [Note: [Col. 0914C] First to make weapons. Thus all the manuscripts; the old editions have *armaque* (“and weapons”). A little earlier, Gronovius’s collection has “and through it.”]

Beginning first to manufacture weapons, they made up for their lack of bronze and iron with supplies of gold and silver ore. The consuls decided to attack Carthage, whose site is said to have been as follows: [Note: [Col. 0914C] Its site. My manuscript has “of whose site it then was,” and so forth.]

Its circuit enclosed by a wall was twenty thousand paces, and almost the whole city was surrounded by the sea, except at the entrance, which opened for three thousand paces. [Note: [Col. 0914C] Twenty thousand. In our old copies it is twenty-two thousand. [Col. 0914D] Appian accurately describes the site of Carthage in his *Libyca*, which should be read above all concerning the events of the Third Punic War. FABR. — Whatever number of paces Fabricius found in his manuscripts is likewise found in ours. Six excellent manuscripts—namely, three Florentine copies, the copies of Meus, Perizonius, and the second Leiden manuscript—write “twenty-two thousand paces”; the fourth Leiden manuscript has “twenty-two thousand.” But the first among these, together with the third and Gronovius’s collection, has “thirty thousand” or “thirty thousand paces,” as does the Augustan edition. This ought to be noted, because Appian, otherwise careful, does not expressly state how many thousand paces the walls of Carthage enclosed. Besides Appian, Polybius, Book I, chapter 73, and Strabo, Book XVIII, p. 572, also describe the site of the city of Carthage.]

That place had a wall thirty feet thick, built of squared stone, and forty cubits high. The citadel, called Byrsa, occupied somewhat more than two thousand paces. On one side the common wall of the city and Byrsa overlooked the sea, which they called a lagoon, because, through the projection of an extended tongue of land, it was made calm. [Note: [Col. 0915B] They called it a lagoon. All the manuscripts and the Augustan edition have “they call it.” Immediately afterward, the same edition and four Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, have *strangulatur* (“is constricted”) instead of *stagnabatur* (“was made a lagoon”). But the Perizonius manuscript reads *tranquillatur* (“is made calm”), not ineptly so, and perhaps the Ulm manuscript intended the same, though it corruptly reads *stranquillatur*. Since I see this reading, *tranquillatur*, confirmed by the Longobard manuscript and two other very ancient Florentine manuscripts, I have adopted it and rejected the common reading. Pliny, Book II, chapter 103, p. 124: “In winter the sea is warmer, in autumn saltier; every sea is calmed by oil.”]

Accordingly, although the consuls had demolished a considerable section of the wall by battering it with siege engines, they were nevertheless defeated and driven back by the Carthaginians. Scipio protected the fleeing Romans after driving the enemy back within the walls. Censorinus returned to Rome. [Note: [Col. 0915B] Censorinus returned to the City. Appian says, Κηνσωρίνος ἐς Ῥώμην ᾤχετο ἀρχαιρεσιάσων, “Censorinus departed for Rome to hold the elections.” FABR.]

Manilius, abandoning Carthage, turned his arms against Hasdrubal. After Massanissa’s death, Scipio divided the kingdom of Numidia among Massanissa’s three sons. When he had returned to the area around Carthage, Manilius captured and plundered the city of Tezaga. Twelve thousand Africans were killed there and six thousand were captured.

Hasdrubal, the commander of the Carthaginians, the grandson of Massanissa, was killed by his own men in the senate-house with fragments of benches, because of suspicion of treason. [Note: [Col. 0915C] Hasdrubal. He said above that the Carthaginians had appointed two commanders for themselves, both named Hasdrubal. One of them was away from the city with a large force of soldiers, hostile to his country because of his condemnation; Appian narrates the cause at greater length in Book [On the Punic War], p. 41, where there is a ridiculous error by the translator and editors. This Hasdrubal had waged war unsuccessfully against Massanissa, losing his entire army to the sword, plague, and famine. After a disgraceful agreement had been made, the survivors were dismissed; Gulussa, Massanissa’s son, attacked them with Numidian cavalry in a sufficiently treacherous manner and slaughtered them while they were unarmed, so that very few returned to Carthage. After narrating this, Appian continues: Καὶ σὺν αὐτοῖς Ἀσδρούβας τε ὁ στρατηγὸς, καὶ ἕτεροι τῶν ἐπιφανῶν. This, through astonishing carelessness, has been translated: “The commander Hasdrubal himself was among those who were missed, together with other nobles.” The opposite is true, and it should be translated: “Among them were the commander Hasdrubal himself”—for the preceding words, with which this is connected, are ὀλίγοι πάμπαν ἐς Καρχηδόνα περιεσώθησαν, “Very few at all reached Carthage safely”—“and the rest of the nobility.” For it immediately follows how the Carthaginians, in order to clear themselves before the Romans concerning the war waged against Massanissa, declared Hasdrubal and the other nobles liable to capital punishment.]

[Note: [Col. 0915D] Massanissa’s grandson. Appian has Θυγατριδοῦς Μασσανάσου, “Massanissa’s daughter’s son.” FABR.]

The praetor Juventius, having engaged Pseudo-Philip in Macedonia, was killed, together with the entire Roman army, in a very severe defeat. [Note: [Col. 0915D] The praetor Juventius. The Livian Epitome has M. Juventius, whom Eutropius calls P. Juventius; both of them, as does Florus in Book II, chapter 14, assign to him this Third Macedonian War. FABR.] [Note: [Col. 0915D] In a very severe defeat. The Augustan edition and two Leiden manuscripts have “in a great defeat.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII. The pitiable overthrow and destruction of Carthage

In the 606th year from the founding of the City—that is, in the fiftieth year after the Second Punic War—in the consulship of Cn. Cornelius Lentulus and L. Mummius, P. Scipio, consul of the preceding year, undertook, as his final destiny, to destroy Carthage. [Note: [Col. 0915D] He enters the Cothon. Appian describes how Scipio seized the harbor called the Cothon in his *Libyca*. FABR. — Although Appian calls the Cothon a harbor on p. 79, where he says that Scipio attacked both Byrsa, the citadel, and the harbor called Cothon—ἐπεχείρει καὶ τῶν λιμένων τῷ καλουμένῳ Κώθωνι, that is, “and the harbor which they call Cothon”—properly speaking it was a small island lying beneath Byrsa, on which the Carthaginians’ shipyards were located. Strabo, Book XVII, p. 832: Ὑπόκεινται τῇ ἀκροπόλει οἵτε λιμένες καὶ ὁ Κώθων, νησίον περιφερὲς εὐρίπῳ περιεχόμενον, ἔχοντι νεωσοίκους ἑκαθέρωθεν κύκλῳ: “Beneath the citadel lie the harbors and the Cothon, a small round island enclosed by a channel, with shipyards arranged in a circle on either side.”]

He entered the Cothon. [Note: [Col. 0916C] While there, and so forth. The Augustan edition has “there,” and so forth.] While fighting continued there for six uninterrupted days and nights, the final desperation of the Carthaginians drove them to surrender, asking that those whom the disasters of war had left alive might at least be permitted to serve. The first group to descend was a sufficiently pitiable procession of women; afterward came the men, in a still more wretched condition. [Note: [Col. 0916C] For there were twenty-five thousand women. Appian says, Καὶ ἐξῄεσαν αὐτίκα μυριάδες πέντε ἀνδρῶν ἅμα καὶ γυναικῶν, that is, “Immediately fifty thousand men and women came out.” FABR.]

It is handed down that there were twenty-five thousand women and thirty thousand men. King Hasdrubal surrendered himself voluntarily. [Note: [Col. 0916C] Surrendered. The first Leiden manuscript and Perizonius have “surrendered himself.”] The deserters who had occupied the temple of Aesculapius threw themselves down voluntarily and were consumed by fire.

Hasdrubal’s wife threw herself and her two sons into the midst of the flames, with a man’s grief and a woman’s fury, [Note: [Col. 0916C] Hasdrubal’s wife. Read Appian and Florus concerning her death and her reproaches against her husband, the traitor. Valerius, Book III, chapter 2, writes that she cast herself, together with her three sons, into the fire of her burning homeland. FABR. — Hence Strabo writes of this noble and courageous woman, in the same passage, that on the summit of Byrsa there was a temple of Aesculapius, ὅπερ κατὰ τὴν ἅλωσιν ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ Ἀσδρούβα συνιάρησεν [perhaps συνεπύρησεν] αὐτῇ, that is, “which Hasdrubal’s wife, when the city was captured, burned together with it.”] thereby sharing the same end in death as the last queen of Carthage that the first had once shared. The city itself burned for seventeen uninterrupted days and offered a pitiable spectacle of the changing condition of human affairs to its victorious conquerors. [Note: [Col. 0916C] Concerning the changing condition of human affairs, and so forth. So much so that it moved the victorious Scipio to tears—as also happened to Titus in the case of Jerusalem and that famous Temple—and elicited from him the following prophetic utterance:

Ἔσσεται ἧμαρ ὅταν ποτ᾽ ὀλώλῃ Ἴλιος ἵρη,

Καὶ Πρίαμος, καὶ λαὸς ἐϋμελίω Πριάμοιο.

“There will be a day when sacred Ilium shall perish, and Priam and the people of spear-bearing Priam.” The accompanying Latin rendering is: “And now the day will come when great Ilium falls, and Priam, and the people of war-mighty Priam collapse.”

This is attested by Appian, p. 82, who adds the following: Πολυβίου δ᾽ αὐτὸν ἐρομένου σὺν παῤῥησίᾳ (καὶ γὰρ ἦν αὐτοῦ καὶ διδάσκαλος) ὅ, τι βούλοιτο ὁ λόγος, φασὶν, οὐ φυλαξάμην [perhaps φυλαξάμενον], ὀνομάσαι τὴν πατρίδα σαφῶς, ὑπέρ ἧς ἄρα, ἐς τ᾽ ἀνθρώπεια ἀφορῶν, ἐδεδίει· καὶ τάδε μὲν Πολύβιος αὐτὸς ἀκούσας συγγράφει.

“When Polybius asked him frankly what the saying meant—for he was also his teacher—they say that he did not refrain [perhaps read *φυλαξάμενον*, ‘having refrained’] from clearly naming the homeland for which, looking to human affairs, he was afraid; Polybius himself records this after hearing it.” Certainly, when his teacher Polybius asked him familiarly what those words meant, he frankly admitted that the thought of his homeland had come to him, for which, considering the vicissitudes of human affairs, he feared. Polybius himself records this in his *Histories*. For “his victors,” Perizonius has only “victors.”]

Carthage was destroyed, every piece of wall-stone having been crushed into dust, in the seven-hundredth year after it had been founded. The entire multitude of captives, except for a few leading men, was sold. [Note: [Col. 0917B] Thus, in the fourth year after the war had begun. Those who did not think this expression, confirmed by all the better manuscripts, customary changed *quam* to *postquam* (“after”), as happened in some old editions. But the Augustan edition, following its manuscript, changed nothing. For *venumdata* (“sold”), many manuscripts and editions prefer *vendita* (“sold”), and likewise *coeptum* (“begun”) instead of *incoeptum*.]

Thus, in the fourth year after the war had begun, the Third Punic War was brought to an end. But although I have sought with the greatest diligence, being nevertheless a man of slower understanding, nowhere has the cause of the Third Punic War become clear to me—what cause could have so inflamed Carthage that it was decided she ought justly to be overthrown. This troubles me especially: if, as in the earlier wars, an evident cause and grievance had provoked the rising power, there would have been no need for deliberation.

But while some Romans decided that Carthage had to be destroyed for the sake of Rome’s perpetual security, others judged that Carthage should be left unharmed in its established condition, for the sake of the continual concern for Roman virtue which it would always devote to itself through suspicion of a rival city—lest Roman vigor, continually exercised by wars, should be dissolved through security and leisure into languid idleness. [Note: [Col. 0917B] Since others, for the sake of Rome’s perpetual security. The originator and chief advocate of this opinion was M. Cato; Nasica held the opposite view. See Livy, Book XLIX, and Plutarch, *Life of Cato the Elder*. FABR. — I think there is some corruption hidden in these words. For *quae* is replaced by *quam* in the Longobard manuscript and other better witnesses, as well as in all the old editions; many of the same have *impenderent* instead of *impenderet*. I therefore correct the passage thus: “which they should always intensify for themselves through suspicion of a rival city,” namely virtue; the opposite, *intendetur socordia* (“sluggishness will be increased”), occurs in Tacitus, *Annals* II.39. Here *intendere* means “to increase” or “to promote.” Similarly Orosius above, Book III, p. 149: “He was pursuing the undertaking with redoubled care.”] I find that the cause arose not from any injury inflicted by the aggressive Carthaginians, but from the inconstancy of the Romans, who had grown sluggish.

If this is so, why do they charge the Christian age with its dullness and rust—outwardly sluggish, inwardly consumed—when, nearly six hundred years earlier, they lost that great whetstone of their brilliance and sharpness, Carthage, just as their own wise and cautious men had foretold? Accordingly, I shall bring the volume to an end, lest by striking too forcefully, after temporarily dispersing the rust, I should find, where I cannot draw out the necessary sharpness, a useless harshness. Yet I would by no means fear the harshness that met me, if I found hope of inward sharpness.

# BOOK FIVE

## CHAPTER I. That the Romans’ prosperity, gained through the disasters of others, brought them more harm than benefit; and likewise that their own times were better than earlier times

I know that some may be disturbed by what follows, because Roman victories are multiplying through the slaughter of many nations and cities. [Note: [Col. 0917C] Are increasing. The Augustan edition has “increased.”] If they consider this carefully, they will find that more harm has occurred than benefit. For so many slave wars, allied wars, civil wars, and wars of the fugitives must not be regarded as trivial—wars that produced no profit at all, but great misery. [Note: [Col. 0917D] But I overlook this. Nearly all the manuscripts have *cohibeo* (“I restrain”). In the first Florentine manuscript this page is torn; in the second it reads *conhibeo*, with a dot beneath the *n*, as though the letter were superfluous. Our correction is confirmed in the Preface to Book IV above, p. 212: “Yet I do not overlook this, even though they should assert it by comparing greater things.”]

But I overlook this, so that, as they wish, it may appear to have been so, and therefore I imagine they will say: [Note: [Col. 0918C] “What is there in these times?” All the manuscripts generally have “and what is there in these times”; Perizonius has “in those times.”]

“What could be happier than these times, in which triumphs follow one another without interruption, victories are celebrated, spoils are wealthy, processions splendid, great kings are led before the chariot, and conquered nations are driven along in a long procession?” [Note: [Col. 0918D] Kings before the chariot. The old editions have “kings before the chariots.” Hittorp and Bolswinus, as often elsewhere, have “kings.”]

The brief answer will be that they themselves are accustomed to complain about their times, and that we have undertaken to speak on behalf of those same times—times that are acknowledged to belong not merely to one city, but to the whole world.

Look how happily Rome conquers: whatever lies outside Rome is conquered just as unhappily. How highly, then, should we value this drop of hard-won prosperity, to which the happiness of one city is attributed amid such a mass of misery, through which the overthrow of the whole world is being carried out? Or, if those times are thought happy because the resources of one state were increased, why should they not rather be judged most unhappy, in which the most powerful kingdoms of many nations—nations both wretchedly devastated and well ordered—fell? [Note: [Col. 0918D] “Most unhappy.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, add “times.”] [Note: [Col. 0918D] “And well ordered nations.” Perizonius has “and almost countless nations,” not implausibly.]

Or did Carthage perhaps see things differently when, after a hundred and twenty years during which she alternately trembled at the disasters of war and the terms of peace, she changed peace into war and war into peace—now through rebellious determination, now through entreaties? [Note: [Col. 0918D] “Now through rebellious determination,” and so forth. I do not know how Fabricius could have approved the reading that, following the editions of Hittorp and Bolswinus, he adopted: “now through rebellious determination, now through the supplications of war she changed peace, now through peace she changed wars.” These words are badly both punctuated and written. I punctuate and emend the rest from the manuscripts and old editions as follows: “now through rebellious determination” (that is, with hostile intent and with a plan suited to the occasion, by which they might later wage war more effectively after restoring their strength), “now through supplications” (for these were prayers genuinely and sincerely offered, as the defeated, worn down by the hardships of war and longing for the benefits of peace), “she changed war into peace, and peace into wars.” Almost all manuscripts have *bellis* (“wars”), which does correspond to the *bella* (“wars”) that follows, but produces a harsh sound. The second Florentine manuscript reads *bello* (“war”), which I prefer to the others. *Supplicia*, ἱκεσίαι, used for “supplications,” occurs in the best authors, such as Varro, Tacitus, and Sallust. Sallust, *Catiline* 60: “The aid of the gods is not secured by vows or womanly supplications.”]

Finally, when wretched citizens were everywhere throwing themselves into the fire in utter desperation, the whole city became one funeral pyre. Even now, for Carthage—small in site and deprived of walls—it is part of its misery to hear what it once was.

Let Spain express her own judgment, when for two hundred years she watered her fields everywhere with her own blood, unable either to repel or endure an unwelcome enemy who harassed her openly at her very doors; when, broken by the slaughter of wars, emptied by sieges and famine, with wives and children killed, her people, from their wretched gathering together for relief from misery, slaughtered one another. [Note: [Col. 0919D] “With their own.” The Augustan edition has “each in different places.” Perhaps one should read “in their own cities, scattered,” or “with their own cities overthrown,” and so forth.] [Note: [Col. 0919D] “And mutual slaughter.” Just as he has recently recalled the ruin of Carthage, so now he refers to the destruction of Numantia. I have removed the punctuation that was wrongly placed after “broken,” and put it before that word.]

What did Italy herself finally think of her times? Let her say. Why did she contradict, resist, and oppose her own Romans for four hundred years, if their happiness was not her unhappiness, and if it did not obstruct the Romans from becoming masters of the world through the common good? [Note: [Col. 0919D] “Hers.” This is absent from the second Leiden manuscript.]

I do not ask what the innumerable peoples of diverse nations, once free for a long time but then defeated in war, removed from their homelands, sold for a price, and scattered in slavery, would at that time have preferred for themselves, what they thought of the Romans, or how they judged their times. [Note: [Col. 0919D] “In slavery.” The third Leiden manuscript and Gronovius’s collection have “in servitude.” In my manuscript, “then” is absent.]

I omit the case of kings of great wealth, great strength, and great renown, long supreme in power, but eventually captured, bound in servile chains, sent beneath the yoke, driven before the chariot, and slaughtered in prison. [Note: [Col. 0919D] “Beneath the yoke.” The second Florentine manuscript has “under the yoke.”] [Note: [Col. 0920C] “Slaughtered in prison.” Some old manuscripts read “thrust into prison.” FABR. — Gronovius’s collection likewise has “thrust into prison.” But the common reading is entirely sound.]

To seek the opinion of such men would be as foolish as failing to grieve over their misery.

Let us consult ourselves—yes, ourselves, I say—and the choice of life to which we have consented. Our ancestors waged wars, wearied by wars, and, seeking peace, offered tribute. [Note: [Col. 0920C] “Waged.” The first Florentine manuscript has “had waged.”] Tribute is the price of peace. We pay tribute so that we may not suffer wars; and by this means we occupy and remain in the harbor to which they at last fled in order to escape the storms of their troubles.

Let us therefore look at our own times: are they happy? [Note: [Col. 0920C] “Our times.” The common editions rightly read thus, although some manuscripts—including Perizonius and three Florentine copies—write “let us,” etc.; over the third of these the common reading is written.] Certainly we consider them happier than those earlier times, because what they finally chose, we possess continually. The unrest of wars, by which they were worn down, is unknown to us. In the leisure that they tasted only slightly after the reign of Caesar and the birth of Christ, we are born and grow old. What was for them the required payment of servitude is for us the free contribution of defense. So great is the difference between past and present times that what Rome extorted by the sword from our people for the use of her luxury, she now contributes together with us for the use of the commonwealth. [Note: [Col. 0920D] “From our people.” The preposition is absent from the Longobard manuscript, where it reads simply “our people.”]

Or if someone says that the Roman enemies were more tolerable to our parents than the Goths are to us, let him hear and understand how differently his situation appears to him from the way it is treated in relation to himself.

Formerly, when wars raged throughout the world, each province lived under its own kings, its own laws, and its own customs; nor was there any fellowship of affections where diversity of powers prevailed. Finally, what could bring unrestrained and barbarous peoples into a common society, when religion itself separated them, since they had been formed by diverse rites of worship? [Note: [Col. 0920D] “What, then?” Since, apart from the Augustan edition, three Florentine manuscripts, as well as the copies of Meus, Perizonius, Ulm, and the third Leiden manuscript, present the text in this form, I think Orosius also wrote *quid* (“what”), not *quis* (“who”), as appears in the common editions. Instead of *diversitas* (“diversity”), the first Florentine manuscript has *adversitas* (“hostility”).]

If anyone, overcome then by the bitterness of his troubles, abandoned his homeland with the enemy, what unknown place did he, himself unknown, approach? What people, generally regarded as an enemy, did he appeal to as an enemy? To whom did he entrust himself at their first encounter, invited neither by fellowship of name, nor brought in by sharing of law, nor made secure by unity of religion? [Note: [Col. 0920D] “Brought in.” The Ulm manuscript has “devoted,” as do some old editions.]

Did Busiris in Egypt, that most impious sacrificer of unlucky foreigners who happened to fall into his hands, provide too little example? [Note: [Col. 0920D] Busiris in Egypt. Read in Book I, chapter 11, concerning the cruel hospitality of Busiris. FABR.] Did the shores of Tauric Diana, most cruel toward strangers, provide too little? [Note: [Col. 0921C] “The shores of Tauric Diana.” The reading in the common editions, “the sacrificial rite of Tauric Diana,” is entirely inelegant, or rather “cruel rites.” Against all the manuscripts—which consistently present the reading we have followed, and which is also preserved in the Augustan edition—we have retained it. It also agrees with reason and history. Orosius is not indicating danger or uncertainty, as though it were a question whether sacrifices were performed there; rather, he calls them shores most cruel to guests because, as he says in the following chapter:

“. . . we are barred from the hospitality of the shore,

and they stir up wars and forbid us to set foot upon the first land;

nor do they grant even to shipwrecked men the safety

which the gods have allowed.”

But he says that it is still more cruel that in that place, under the pretext of sacred rites, wretched men were twice sacrificed and slaughtered.]

Did Thrace, with its Polymnestor, remain criminal even toward close relatives who were guests? [Note: [Col. 0921D] Thrace with Polymnestor. Euripides writes in the *Hecuba* concerning Polymnestor, king of the Thracians, who killed Polydorus, entrusted to his protection. FABR.]

And, lest I seem to linger over antiquities, Rome itself bears witness in the case of Pompey, who was killed; Egypt bears witness in the case of Ptolemy, who killed him. [Note: [Col. 0921D] “Concerning Ptolemy, the killer.” Correctly so; nor should we follow the three Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, which read “concerning the king who was killed.” In the Venetian editions *rege* (“king”) is absent, as it is in the Paris and first editions.]

## CHAPTER II. That for Orosius, as a Christian, every place is a homeland, and access is secure everywhere

For me, fleeing from the first disturbance of whatever kind, because I am secure in the place of refuge to which I flee, every place is a homeland, and everywhere my law and religion are with me. Now Africa has welcomed me as willingly as I approached it confidently. Now, I say, this Africa has received me with an uncomplicated peace, in its own embrace, under the common law, concerning which it was once said—and truly said:

“. . . we are barred from the hospitality of the shore,

they stir up wars and forbid us to set foot upon the first land.”

Now, of its own accord, it opens wide its benevolent bosom to receive companions in its religion and peace, and of its own accord invites the weary to come where it may cherish them.

The breadth of the East, the abundance of the North, the southern expanse, and the most generous and secure homes of the great islands belong to me by right and by name. For I approach Christians and Romans as a Roman and a Christian. I do not fear the gods of my host; I do not fear his religion as my death; I do not find such a place as I must dread, where the owner is permitted to do whatever he wishes while the stranger is not permitted to do what is proper. [Note: [Col. 0922C] “Where there is the law of hospitality.” I prefer this reading, found in three Leiden manuscripts and Gronovius’s collection, to *hospitis* (“of the host”), which others prefer. The three examples that he reviewed in the preceding chapter are answered here by his own times. The example of Busiris corresponds to “I do not fear the gods of my host”; the rites of Tauric Diana to “I do not fear his religion as my death”; and the crime and treachery of Polymnestor toward his guest, the son of Priam, to “I do not have such a place.”] Where is there a law of hospitality that is not mine?

There is one God, who, at the times when he wished to make himself known, established this unity of rule, and is loved and feared by all. The same laws, subject to the one God, rule everywhere. Wherever I approach as a stranger, I do not fear sudden violence as one abandoned.

Among Romans, as I have said, I am a Roman; among Christians, a Christian; among human beings, a human being. By the laws I appeal to the commonwealth; by religion, to conscience; by fellowship, to nature.

For a time I use every land as though it were my homeland, because that homeland which is true—and which I love—is not on earth at all. I have lost nothing where I loved nothing; and I possess everything when the one whom I love is with me, especially since he is the same among all people, making me not merely known to all but also their neighbor. He does not abandon the needy, because the earth and its fullness belong to him, and from them he commanded that all things be shared by all.

These are the blessings of our times, which our ancestors did not possess in full either in the tranquility of the present, or in hope of the future, or in a common refuge. Consequently, they waged unending wars, because the sharing of places of refuge was not free to them: by remaining in their own settlements, they were either unhappily killed or disgracefully enslaved. This will become clearer and more evident to them when the deeds of earlier times have been set out in order.

## CHAPTER III. The Achaean War and the destruction of Corinth

In the 606th year from the founding of the City—that is, in the same year in which Carthage was destroyed—in the consulship of Cn. Cornelius Lentulus and L. Mummius, the destruction of Corinth followed upon the overthrow of Carthage, and the wretched conflagration of two most powerful cities shone forth in different parts of the world within a short interval of time.

For when the praetor Metellus had defeated the allied Achaeans and Boeotians in two wars—that is, first at Thermopylae and then in Phocis—[Note: [Col. 0922D] “He had defeated them in Phocis.” The first Florentine, or Longobard, manuscript has “had defeated them in Phocis.” Thus, taken together, the second Florentine and four Leiden manuscripts, as well as the copies of Meus, Perizonius, and Ulm, and Gronovius’s collection, have “had defeated them in Phocis” or “Phocis.” I think one should write “had defeated them in Phocis.” Phocis is a region of Greece not far from the Peloponnese, whereas Phocaea is a city of Ionia in Asia. Moreover, Orosius’s sentence is disjointed if we retain what follows, “of whom.” The remedy is to write “of these.”]

the historian Claudius reports that twenty thousand were killed in the first war and seven thousand in the second. Valerius Antias confirms that the fighting took place in Achaea and that twenty thousand Achaeans fell with their commander Diaeus. [Note: [Col. 0923C] With their commander Diaeus. The commander’s name, commonly corrupted to Dienus, is correctly written in the old manuscripts; Pausanias also calls him Diaeus, Δίαιος. FABR.]

Polybius the Achaean, although he was then in Africa with Scipio, nevertheless asserts that fighting occurred once in Achaea under the command of Critolaus, since he could not have been unaware of the disaster at home. He teaches that Diaeus, bringing soldiers from Arcadia, was defeated together with his army by the same praetor Metellus.

But we have already said something about the conflicting accounts of historians. Let this exposed and ill-known mark of their falsehoods suffice, since those who disagree even about matters they themselves witnessed clearly show that little credence should be given to their other accounts. [Note: [Col. 0923C] “An ill-known mark of falsehoods.” The three Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, wrongly reject the second *nota* (“mark”). “That mark of falsehoods,” because it was badly known—that is, sufficiently unfamiliar and encrusted with lies—is exposed by Orosius. Some old editions have *quare* (“wherefore”) instead of *quia* (“because”).]

Accordingly, after the defenses of all Achaea had been destroyed, and while the praetor Metellus was planning the overthrow of the abandoned cities, the consul Mummius arrived unexpectedly in the camp with a few men. He immediately dismissed Metellus and captured Corinth without delay, a city then by far the richest in the entire world. For throughout many preceding centuries it had been, as it were, the workshop of every artisan and every craft, and the common marketplace of Asia and Europe. [Note: [Col. 0923D] “To the captives.” Who are these captives—Corinthians? But they were sold under the auctioneer’s spear. Or others? I scarcely think so, since the Romans did not usually keep captives except the more distinguished ones, who were to be led in a triumph; they sold the rest into slavery. Perhaps one should write *cuivis* (“to anyone”). For booty was ordinarily guarded by persons specifically chosen and assigned to that duty, a practice to which Virgil alludes, *Aeneid* II, 762:

“Chosen guards, Phoenix and grim Ulysses,

were guarding the spoil.”

But Mummius seems to have permitted his soldiers to plunder and pillage everyone and everything without distinction; this certainly contributes to the misery of the captured city and the destruction of the precious objects there.]

Permission to plunder was cruelly granted even to the captives, so that everything was filled with slaughter and fires, and from the circuit of the walls the conflagration poured forth, as though from a furnace, narrowed into a single peak. Thus, after most of the population had been consumed by sword and flames, the rest was sold under the crown.

After the city had been burned, the walls were demolished to their foundations. The wall-stone was reduced to dust, and immense booty was seized. Indeed, because of the multitude and variety of the statues and images, when gold, silver, bronze, and all the metals together had melted and flowed into one mass amid that conflagration of the city, a new kind of metal was produced. From it—or, as tradition relates, in imitation of it—came Corinthian bronze and Corinthian vessels. [Note: [Col. 0924C] Corinthian bronze. Concerning Corinthian bronze, read Pliny, Book XXXIV. But if you wish to know what the ancients transmitted concerning the origin of Corinthian bronze, read Muretus, *Various Readings*, Book III, chapter 5. FABR.]

## CHAPTER IV. The war in Spain with Viriathus; the bloody conflict with the Lusitanians and the Salassian Gauls; the great plague at Rome; and other Roman wars with the Numantines and with Mithridates
Under the same consuls, [Note: [Col. 0924C] Viriathus in Spain. Viriathus, whose name appears on an ancient stone excavated in Lusitania containing the will of Gallus Favonius. In excerpts from Diodorus, book 32, his name is Οὐιρίατος, in which the τ seems superfluous. Diodorus writes much about him, especially the following concerning his fairness in distributing booty: “He was also fair in the distributions of spoils, and according to merit he singled out those who had performed brave deeds for rewards.” Hence Cicero says in *On Duties* II that Viriathus the Lusitanian possessed great wealth because of his equal distribution of booty. For the account of events involving Viriathus, see Appian, *Iberica*; Livy, books LII and LIV; Florus, book II, chapter 17; Velleius II; and Eutropius IV. FABR.]

Viriathus in Spain, a Lusitanian by birth [Col. 0924B], a shepherd and bandit, first by harassing the roads, then by ravaging the provinces, and finally by defeating, routing [Note: [Col. 0924C] “Subjugating.” The older editions have *subjiciendo*, “subjecting.”], and subduing the armies of Roman praetors and consuls, became a source of the greatest terror to all the Romans. For as he crossed widely and roamed through the territories, C. Vetilius the praetor confronted him at the rivers Iberus and Tagus, the greatest and most widely separated [Note: [Col. 0924C] “The greatest and most diverse.” In the second Florentine manuscript, *maxima et* is absent. In the third, *maxima et diversissima* is written. [Col. 0924D] The older editions have *maxima et diversorum*, “the greatest of diverse [regions].”] rivers of those regions [Note: [Col. 0924D] “C. Vetilius the praetor.” C. Vetilius also appears in Appian’s *Iberica*, translated by Beraldus; M. Vetilius appears in the *Epitome of Livy*, book LII; Sex. Vetilius in the additions of Paulus Diaconus to Eutropius; and Diodorus has στρατηγὸν Οὐϊτέλλιον, “the general Vitellius.” FABR.]. Vetilius immediately lost almost his entire army, slaughtered to the point of annihilation, and he himself scarcely escaped by flight with a few men [Note: [Col. 0924D] “Having escaped by flight, he got away.” Livy, by contrast, says that Vetilius was captured; Diodorus and Appian say that he was captured and killed. FABR.].

Then the same Viriathus routed the praetor C. Plautius, who had been broken by many battles. Later Claudius Unimanus [Note: [Col. 0924D] “Claudius Unimanus.” Florus also mentions Claudius, as does the author of *On Illustrious Men*, who writes that after Claudius, C. Nigidius was defeated by Viriathus. FABR.], sent against Viriathus with a great military force [Note: [Col. 0924D] “With a great military establishment.” The first edition has *cum magno apparatu belli instructi*, “with a great preparation and military equipment.”], as though to erase the disgrace of the earlier defeat, himself increased the disgrace by a more shameful one. For when he engaged Viriathus, he lost all the forces that he had brought with him [Note: [Col. 0925B] “Had led down.” Perizonius has *duxerat*; three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection and the Augustan edition, have *adduxerat*; the Utrecht manuscript has *deduxit*.], as well as the greatest strength of the Roman army. Viriathus fixed Roman striped ceremonial robes (*trabeae*), fasces, and other insignia upon his mountains as trophies [Note: [Col. 0925B] “As trophies.” The first Leiden manuscript has *velut tropaea*, “as though trophies.”].

At the same time, three hundred Lusitanians engaged one thousand Romans in a certain defile. In that battle, Claudius reports, seventy Lusitanians and three hundred and twenty Romans were killed [Note: [Col. 0925B] “Seventy Lusitanians.” The Augustan edition has twenty Lusitanians.]. When the victorious Lusitanians, scattered and secure, were departing, one of them, separated far from the others, was himself caught on foot by horsemen surrounding him [Note: [Col. 0925C] “When, with horsemen surrounding him, etc.” Three Leiden manuscripts have “when he himself had been caught by the horsemen surrounding him.” But my manuscript and Perizonius, together with the Augustan and Venetian editions, have “when, with horsemen surrounding him, he himself was caught on foot,” which I prefer to the commonly printed reading. Fabricius printed “when he himself, on foot, had been caught by horsemen surrounding him,” etc. The editions preceding his, as well as all the manuscripts, reject *pedestris*, “on foot,” in place of *pedes*, “on foot.”]. Having pierced the horse of one of them with his spear, he cut off the horseman’s head with a single stroke of his sword. Thus he struck them all with fear that, while everyone watched, he himself could depart contemptuously and at leisure.

[293] When Appius Claudius and Q. Caecilius Metellus were consuls [Note: [Col. 0925C] “When Appius Claudius and Q. Caecilius Metellus were consuls.” Appius Claudius Pulcher and Q. Metellus Macedonicus were consuls in the year 620 from the founding of the City. In our old manuscripts it is stated that Appius lost five thousand soldiers in the war against the Salassi, so that the number lost would equal the number killed. Hence a triumph was rightly denied to Appius. Valerius, book II, chapter 3. FABR.], Appius Claudius engaged the Salassi, a Gallic people, and, defeated, lost five thousand soldiers [Note: [Col. 0925C] “Five thousand.” Fabricius found this number in his manuscripts and, content to place it in the margin, retained ten thousand, as it stood in the common text, except in the Augustan edition. In that edition, as also in eleven manuscripts, the number is five thousand. Since I have found the true number, I have ordered the false one to be expelled.]. After renewing the battle, he killed five thousand of the enemy. But since a law had established that anyone who killed five thousand enemies had the right to triumph [Note: [Col. 0925D] “Whoever had killed five thousand.” This was the prescribed number required for seeking a triumph.
