See Casaubon on Suetonius, *Julius*, chapter 76. FABR.], he too would have sought a triumph; because of his earlier losses, however, he could not obtain one. Therefore, with disgraceful shamelessness and ambition, he triumphed at his own private expense [Note: [Col. 0925D] “He triumphed at private expense.” Otherwise, expenses were supplied from the treasury for those celebrating a triumph, as Livy indicates in book XXXIII. This is something for young students of Roman history to observe. FABR.].

When L. Caecilius Metellus and Q. Fabius Maximus Servilianus were consuls, among other portents an androgyne was seen at Rome [Note: [Col. 0925D] “An androgyne was seen at Rome.” This androgyne was born at Luna, not at Rome. Julius Obsequens writes that in the same consulship there was such a great pestilence at Luna that, with corpses lying everywhere in public, there were not enough people to bury them. FABR.—In the third and fourth Leiden editions, *visus*, “was seen,” is absent.]. By order of the haruspices it was submerged in the sea; but that impious expiation accomplished nothing. For a pestilence suddenly arose so great that those responsible for conducting funerals were at first insufficient and then no longer existed [Note: [Col. 0925D] “And so also.” Three Florentine manuscripts together with the second Leiden manuscript have *jamque etiam*, “and now also”; Perizonius has *tunc etiam*, “then also.” The older editions have “and so great houses, etc.” [Col. 0926B] But the Augustan edition, preferable to the others, reads “so that even great houses, etc., remained.”]. Thus even great houses remained empty of the living and full of the dead. Vast inheritances lay within, with no heirs at all. Finally, people were denied not only the possibility of living in the City, but even of approaching it, so foully did the stench of corpses, which were wasting beneath roofs and on their beds throughout the City, exhale [Note: [Col. 0926B] “Were exhaled.” The Perizonian manuscript, together with the Augustan edition, has *exhalabant*, “they exhaled.”].

That cruel expiation, preparing a road to death by the death of human beings [Col. 0926B] [Note: [Col. 0926B] “Preparing.” The first and second Florentine manuscripts, as well as three Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection, have *struens*, “preparing.”], finally became known to the Romans, who amid their misery were growing ashamed of how miserable and empty it was. Previously, it had been regarded as a means of forestalling the impending disaster, and thus the pestilence followed [Note: [Col. 0926C] “Followed.” Three Florentine manuscripts, the Augustan edition, and the same reading elsewhere have *consecuta est*. Orosius often uses this for *subsecuta est*, “followed,” which certain older editions and the second Leiden manuscript have. My manuscript has *secuta est*, “followed,” while the first Leiden manuscript has *exorta est*, “arose”; above it is written *consecuta est*.]. Yet the pestilence was fulfilled without any satisfaction through sacrifices, simply through a chastisement completed according to the measure of the hidden judgment—but so it was. If those craftsmen of deception, the haruspices [Note: [Col. 0926C] “Those craftsmen of deception, the haruspices.” Columella I.12: “The haruspices, through empty superstition, drive uncultivated minds to expense.” Hence Hannibal’s memorable remark to King Prusias, whose entrails did not seem to predict a favorable battle that day: “Do you prefer to believe a piece of veal rather than an experienced commander?” Cicero, *On Divination* II, chapter 24. Orosius calls the haruspices “hunters of outcomes and builders of deceit” later in this chapter.], had, as they commonly do, celebrated some rite at the very moment when the diseases were beginning to subside, they would undoubtedly have claimed for themselves, for their gods, and for their rites the glory of restored health [Note: [Col. 0926C] “By their aids and rites.” All manuscripts and printed editions have *sibi diis et ritibus*, “for themselves, the gods, and the rites.” But let them not accuse me of rashness before they see how they can defend their reading. LAUT.—Although Lautius asserts this concerning the printed editions and manuscripts, he shows how few of each kind he has examined. For *subsidiis*, which he prefers, was printed before him by the Bolsuing edition, and before Bolsuing by the Paris and Venetian editions. Only the Hittorp edition has *insidiis*, “by ambushes.” Since the common reading is confirmed by the manuscripts, including the best, and also produces good sense, I do not think it should be abandoned. Of the eleven manuscripts I consulted, all have either *sub diis et ritibus suis*, “under their gods and rites,” as do the first and third Leiden manuscripts with the Groningen Collection, or *sibi, dis [or sibi et diis] et ritibus suis*, “for themselves, the gods, and their rites,” as do the three Florentine manuscripts and all the others. But can Orosius’s meaning really not be defended? Would those haruspices not have attributed remissions of disease and the glory of healing both to themselves, to their own gods, and to those rites? For *reductae*, “restored,” three Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection prefer *productae*, “brought forth.”]. Thus the wretched and wickedly religious city was mocked by lies from which it could not be freed [Note: [Col. 0927C] “And toward sacrileges, etc.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have “Thus the wretched and sacrilegious, badly religious city.” The Augustan manuscript also reads this way and additionally has “and the badly religious city.”].

Therefore Fabius the consul, fighting against the Lusitanians and Viriathus [Note: [Col. 0927C] “Fabius the consul.” For Appian’s account of Fabius Servilianus’s actions against Viriathus, see Appian. FABR.], liberated the town of Baccia [Note: [Col. 0927C] “Baccia.” All the manuscripts have *Buccia*, except that my manuscript has *Buccina*.], which Viriathus was besieging, by driving off the enemy, and received it, together with many other forts, into surrender. He committed an act that would be execrable even among the most remote barbarians of Scythia, let alone according to Roman faithfulness and restraint. For he cut off the hands of five hundred of their chiefs, whom he had received, after inviting them under the terms of an alliance, by right of surrender [Note: [Col. 0927C] “For five hundred of their chiefs.” Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 2, and Frontinus, book IV, discuss Fabius’s severity. FABR.].

Pompey, consul of the following year, entered the territory of the Numantines and, after suffering a very great defeat, withdrew, not only with almost his entire army routed, but also with many of the nobles who were serving under him killed [Note: [Col. 0927C] “Who were serving with him.” This is the reading of all manuscripts and better editions. Those who did not understand the expression changed it to “those of his military service.”]. But Viriathus, after wearing down Roman generals and armies for fourteen years, was killed through the treachery of his own men. In this one matter alone the Romans acted bravely against him: they judged his assassins unworthy of a reward. But I could not only now, but often elsewhere, insert those inscrutable wars of the East [Note: [Col. 0927D] “Inscrutable.” My manuscript has *exsecrabilia*, “execrable.”], which almost never begin or end except through crimes; but the wars of the Romans, with whom our discussion is concerned, are so numerous that foreign ones may rightly be disdained.

For at that time Mithridates, king of the Parthians, sixth in succession from Arsaces, after defeating the governor Demetrius, invaded Babylon and all its territory as a victor. Moreover, he subdued all the peoples living between the river Hydaspes and the Indus. He extended his bloody rule as far as India as well; he defeated and captured Demetrius himself when Demetrius met him in a second battle. After Demetrius had been captured, a certain Diodotus [Note: [Col. 0927D] “A certain Diodotus.” All the older editions have *Diodotus*, whereas the printed editions read *Theodotus*. Sigonius also testifies that in old books of the *Epitome* of book LII he read “by a certain Diodotus.” Appian likewise names the same man Διόδοτος, “Diodotus.” FABR.—Here Orosius is seriously mistaken and does not follow his own authority, Justin. Justin writes of this Diodotus, or Tryphon—for he assumed that name together with the royal power—as follows in book XXXVI, chapter 1: “Meanwhile, in Syria, Tryphon, who had endeavored to have himself appointed by the people as guardian of Antiochus, the stepson of Demetrius, after killing his ward, seized the kingdom of Syria.” Tryphon killed his ward Antiochus VI, son of Alexander Theopator. According to Appian, in his book on the Syrian War, p. 132, this Antiochus seems also to have borne the name Alexander, where Tryphon is said to have killed “the child Alexander, son of Alexander the Bastard and the daughter of Ptolemy”—παιδίον Ἀλέξανδρον ἐξ Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ νόθου καὶ τῆς Πτολεμαίου θυγατρός. Nor could he have been Demetrius’s stepson, as Justin writes, because the guardian killed the ten-year-old Antiochus through physicians who pretended that the boy was suffering from a stone. See the *Epitome of Livy*, book LV.] usurped his kingdom and royal name together with Alexander, his son. Later, so that he would not have as a partner in possession the son whom he had made a partner in the danger of seizing the kingdom, he killed Alexander himself.

When M. Aemilius Lepidus and C. Hostilius Mancinus were consuls [Note: [Col. 0928C] “M. Aemilius Lepidus and C. Hostilius.” These men were consuls in the year 616 from the founding of the City. Obsequens explains the portents that occurred then. FABR.], various portents appeared, and, insofar as lay within their power, they were dealt with according to custom. But favorable circumstances do not always support the haruspices, those hunters of outcomes and builders of deception. For the consul Mancinus, after receiving the army from Popillius near Numantia [Note: [Col. 0928C] “After receiving it from Popillius.” *Popillio* is correct in the old manuscripts; hence some changed it to *Pompilio*, others to *Pompeio*. Appian also records that M. Popillius Laenas, consul of the preceding year, was succeeded by Mancinus at Numantia. FABR.], conducted all his battles so unsuccessfully and was driven to such utter desperation that he was forced to make a most shameful treaty with the Numantines [Note: [Col. 0928D] “A most shameful treaty.” Everyone should read Cicero, book III of *On Duties*, concerning the treaty Mancinus made with the Numantines. FABR.—The Augustan edition continues: “and always to be reproached by the Roman name.” This does not occur in the other editions or manuscripts.], although Pompey shortly before had already made an equally disgraceful treaty with those same Numantines. The Senate ordered that the treaty be dissolved and Mancinus be handed over to the Numantines [Note: [Col. 0928D] “Be dissolved.” Several manuscripts together with the older editions have *dissolvit*, “dissolved it.”]. His body stripped naked and his hands bound behind his back [Note: [Col. 0928D] “With his hands.” The first and third Florentine manuscripts, together with the Utrecht, my manuscript, Perizonius, and the second Leiden manuscript, have *manibusque*, “and with his hands.” The Augustan edition and three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have *manibus quoque*, “also with his hands.”], he was placed before the gates of Numantia. Remaining there until nightfall, abandoned by his own people but not received by the enemy, he presented a pitiable spectacle to both sides.

## CHAPTER V. How unjustly the Romans handed Mancinus over to the Numantines; concerning Brutus’s slaughter of the Gallaeci and Lepidus’s defeat by the Vaccaei

At this point grief demands an outcry [Note: [Col. 0928D] “Demands.” Perizonius has “will compel.”]. Why, Romans, do you falsely claim for yourselves those great names—justice, faithfulness, courage, and mercy [Note: [Col. 0928D] “Justice and faithfulness.” Some older editions have “justice and faithfulness.”]? Learn these things more truly from the Numantines. Was courage required? They conquered by fighting. Was faithfulness demanded? Trusting others as they trusted themselves, they released those whom they could have killed, in accordance with the treaty. Was justice to be commended? The Senate itself silently commended it when those same Numantines, through their envoys, requested either only an inviolate peace or the return of all those whom they had released alive after receiving them as pledges of peace. Did mercy seem to require examination? They gave sufficient proof, either by releasing the enemy army to live or by refusing to accept Mancinus for punishment [Note: [Col. 0929C] “Sufficient evidence.” The Augustan edition, together with three Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen Collection, adds *indicium*, “evidence.”].

Was Mancinus not to be handed over, the man who, by displaying the shield of the treaty, prevented the impending slaughter of a defeated army; who preserved the endangered strength of his country for better times [Note: [Col. 0929C] “Those in danger.” The Augustan edition has *periclitantis*, “of the one in danger.”]? Or, if the treaty that had been made was displeasing, why was the soldier who had been redeemed by this pledge either received when he returned or not returned when he was demanded? Or, if some provision for preserving the soldiers was approved, why was Mancinus, who made that agreement, handed over alone [Note: [Col. 0929C] “Was handed over?” After these words, the Augustan edition contains a lacuna of thirteen lines, which has unfortunately entered there from elsewhere in Orosius. It begins “Although among…” and ends “…nature was able to preserve.”]?

Recently Varro, so that battle might be joined too hastily, pushed forward his resisting colleague Paulus; he drove a frightened army headlong; and at those infamous Cannae, notorious for Roman defeats, he did not arrange his unfortunate forces for battle [Note: [Col. 0929D] “But exposed them to death.” This is imitated from Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.126:

> “And, covered, he refuses  
> To betray anyone by his voice or expose him to death.”], but exposed them to death. There more than forty thousand Roman soldiers were lost solely through his own impatience, by which Hannibal had long anticipated victory for himself. After also losing his colleague Paulus—for what kind of man was he?—Varro finally dared to return almost alone to the City with the utmost shamelessness, and he received the reward of his shamelessness. For public thanks were given to him in the Senate because he had not despaired of the republic, although he himself had made it desperate [Note: [Col. 0929D] “For thanks were given to him.” Livy writes in book XXII that the Senate thanked Varro when he returned to the City. Valerius, book III, chapter 4. FABR.].

Mancinus, on the other hand, who had struggled not to lose an army surrounded by the fortunes of war, was condemned by that same Senate to surrender. I know that the Romans also disliked that conduct in Varro, but it was excused on account of the circumstances; and in Mancinus it was approved, but the action was judged according to the circumstances [Note: [Col. 0930C] “And therefore.” Perhaps one should read “equally therefore.”]. Thus from the beginning you brought it about [Col. 0930A] that neither a citizen would act suitably for an ungrateful country nor an enemy trust faithfully those who were faithless [Note: [Col. 0930C] “So that neither a citizen.” Because of Mancinus’s example, a citizen will fear providing a similar service to his country; because of the Numantines’ example, an enemy will fear trusting any conditions of peace.].

Meanwhile Brutus in Further Spain [Note: [Col. 0930C] “Brutus in Further Spain.” D. Junius Brutus was consul in the year 615 from the City’s foundation. He was assigned Further Spain and, after defeating the Gallaeci, earned the surname derived from that victory. See Appian, *Iberica*; Strabo, book III; Livy, books LV and LVI; Florus, book II, chapter 17; and Velleius II. FABR.] defeated sixty thousand Gallaeci, who had come to aid the Lusitanians [Note: [Col. 0930D] “As aid.” All the Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection and the Augustan edition, have *in auxilium*, “as aid.”], in a very harsh and difficult war, although he had surrounded them while they were off guard. Fifty thousand of them are reported to have been killed in that battle, six thousand captured, and only a few to have escaped by flight.

In Hither Spain, Lepidus, as proconsul, persistently attempted to subdue the Vaccaei, an innocent and suppliant people, even though the Senate prohibited him from doing so [Note: [Col. 0930D] “Even though the Senate prohibited it.” Cinna and Caecilius, envoys sent to Lepidus in Spain, brought a senatorial decree warning that Lepidus should not attack the Vaccaei in war. Appian. FABR.]. But soon he paid the penalty for his wicked persistence by suffering a very grave defeat. Six thousand Romans were killed in this unjust war, with perfect justice; the rest escaped after being stripped of their camp and even losing their weapons. This defeat under Lepidus was no less disgraceful than that under Mancinus [Note: [Col. 0930D] “This under Lepidus.” The common texts read “under Metellus.” The *Epitome* of book LVI reads: “With a different outcome, M. Aemilius Lepidus, as proconsul, conducted operations against the Vaccaei and suffered a defeat like that at Numantia.” FABR.].

Let the Spaniards, battered and exhausted by so many wars—or at least the Romans themselves, subdued by such continuous defeats and conquered so many times—now ascribe these times to themselves as a period of good fortune [Note: [Col. 0930D] “Thus now.” Certain older editions have “why now.”], so that I will not even reproach them by counting how many of their praetors, legates, consuls, legions, and armies have been destroyed. I shall consider only how great was the madness produced by fear. The Roman soldier was so stupefied that he could no longer restrain his foot or steel his courage even for a trial of battle; but as soon as he saw a Spaniard, his distinctive enemy, he fled and almost believed himself conquered before he could be seen.

From this it is clear that those wretched times were judged in the same way by both sides: the Spaniards, although they could win, nevertheless unwillingly abandoned their sweet leisure and endured foreign wars, while the Romans, the more shamelessly they intruded upon another people’s peace, were defeated all the more disgracefully.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning a monstrous child born at Rome, the eruption of Aetna, and the servile war in Sicily

When Sex. Fulvius Flaccus and Q. Calpurnius Piso were consuls [Note: [Col. 0930D] “Sex. Fulvius Flaccus and Q. Calpurnius.” These men were consuls in the year 618 from the City’s foundation. Obsequens, however, writes that the child was born not during the consulship of these men but during that of their predecessors, P. Furius and Sex. Atilius Serranus. To the present consuls he assigns the eruption of Aetna and other portents. FABR.], a four-handed child was born at Rome from a female slave [Note: [Col. 0931C] “Was born.” The better manuscripts—namely, three Florentine manuscripts, my manuscript, and Perizonius—delete the later occurrence of the verb.], with four eyes, the same number of ears, and a double male nature. In Sicily, Mount Aetna belched forth and poured out vast fires. Like torrents rushing headlong down slopes, the flames burned whatever was nearest; farther things they scorched with hot ashes, which flew widely about with heavy vapor. This is a native kind of portent in Sicily, which customarily does not foretell evil but inflicts it.

In the territory of Bononia, crops sprang forth on trees [Note: [Col. 0931C] “Sprang forth.” This is the reading of the six or seven best manuscripts. The common text has “were born.”]. Then in Sicily a servile war arose [Note: [Col. 0931C] “A war in Sicily.” This servile war was stirred up by Eunus the Syrian from Apamea, a slave belonging to Antigenes of Enna. Diodorus Siculus describes the cause, disaster, and entire course of this war in book XXXIV; Henricus Stephanus published a Latin version of it. Florus discusses the same war in book III, chapter 19, and Livy in book LVI. Appian mentions it in book I. FABR.], so serious and savage in the number of slaves, the organization of its forces, and the magnitude of its strength [Note: [Col. 0931C] “The magnitude of its strength.” Against all the manuscripts, the editors had inserted the conjunction *et*, “and”; I have removed it.], that it terrified not only Roman praetors, whom it utterly routed, but even the consuls [Note: [Col. 0931C] “I will not say the praetors.” Florus writes that the camps of four praetors—Manilius, Lentulus, Piso, and Hypsaeus—were captured by the slaves [Col. 0931D]. Diodorus names one, L. Hypsaeus, who went from Rome to Sicily with eight thousand Sicilian soldiers and was defeated by the slaves in battle. The consuls will be discussed below. FABR.].

For seventy thousand slaves are reported to have conspired at that time to take up arms, excluding the city of Messana, which kept its slaves, treated generously, in peace. Sicily was all the more wretched in this respect because, being an island and never possessing a condition of sufficiently secure law [Note: [Col. 0931D] “Of suitable legal standing.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, add *fuit*, “was.” Some manuscripts and printed editions also add *est*, “is,” after *insula*.], it was now subject to tyrants and now to slaves: the former exacting servitude through wicked domination, the latter perversely exchanging liberty for domination. This was especially so because, with the sea closed around it on every side, Sicily could not easily expel its internal evil.

For it nourished a viper’s conception toward its own destruction [Note: [Col. 0931D] “Toward its destruction.” This must be completely reconstructed from the first and second Florentine manuscripts and Perizonius. My manuscript has “in its destruction”; the common text has “of its destruction.”], enlarged by its own lust and destined to survive through its own death. The outbreak of this servile tumult, however, was all the rarer among other such events and therefore all the more savage [Note: [Col. 0931D] “Is more savage.” The word *est*, “is,” is absent from my manuscript. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have “is more cruel.” My manuscript also has “is moved” instead of “is stirred.” But the passage beginning “because it is stirred by intention…” is written in the Perizonian manuscript as follows: “By what intention … that servile [movement] may destroy.”]: a free multitude is stirred by the desire to increase its country, a servile multitude by the desire to destroy it.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Numantia and its destruction by Scipio Africanus

[Col. 0932A]

[Note: [Col. 0931D] In the year 620 from the founding of the City. Some write that in this year Scipio was not made consul and sent to besiege Numantia, but that Numantia was conquered by him. FABR.]

In the year 620 from the founding of the City, when a greater disgrace concerning the treaty concluded at Numantia than that once suffered at the Caudine Forks weighed upon the shame of the Roman face, Scipio Africanus, elected consul with the consent of all the tribes, was sent with an army to besiege Numantia. [Note: [Col. 0932C] “With the consent of all the tribes.” I do not know on what grounds certain other correctors wrote, “By the consent of all, he is made consul from tribune,” since the manuscripts read otherwise. FABR. The cause appears to have been that in certain manuscripts they found the corrupt reading “of all the tribunes.” Thus it is written in the first and third Leiden copies and also in the Groningen Collection; it is absent in the Augustan edition. Shortly afterward, for “to capture” certain old editions, the second Florentine, and the first Leiden copy have “to capture”; and three Leiden copies, together with the Groningen Collection, have “of slaves also” in place of “of their own men.”]

Numantia, situated in Nearer Spain not far from the Vaccaei and Cantabri, at the head of Gallaecia, was the last stronghold of the Celtiberians. [Note: [Col. 0932C] For fourteen years Numantia alone held out against an army of forty thousand with four thousand Celtiberians. Florus, book II, chapter 18: “Numantia, with four thousand Celtiberians, sustained an army of forty thousand for fourteen years.” Appian, in his *Spanish History*, writes that before the war the Numantines numbered no more than eight thousand. Consult him concerning Scipio’s operations at Numantia. FABR.] For fourteen years, with only four thousand of its own people, it not only endured forty thousand Romans but even defeated them and subjected them to shameful treaties.

Accordingly, when Scipio Africanus entered Spain, he did not immediately throw himself against the enemy, as though he might catch them off guard; for he knew that this kind of people would never become so relaxed in body and spirit that they would not surpass the equipment of others by the very quality of their physical condition. [Note: [Col. 0932D] “This kind.” The Longobard manuscript and three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Augustan copy, read “this kind.”] Instead, for some time he trained his own soldiers in the camp as though in schools. After he had spent the whole of summer and the entire winter without even attempting battle, he nevertheless made scarcely any progress by this diligence. For when an opportunity for battle arose, the Roman army, overwhelmed by the attack of the Numantines, turned its back. [Note: [Col. 0932D] “Turned its back.” My copy has *terga vertit*, “turned its back.” This is better expressed.]

But, after the consul reproached them and threatened them, throwing himself before them and restraining them with his hand, they at last became indignant and returned against the enemy; and they compelled those from whom they had been fleeing to flee. It is difficult then to credit the report: the Numantines both put the Romans to flight, and the Romans saw them fleeing. [Note: [Col. 0932D] “The Numantines also put to flight.” Editions preceding those of Fabricius, as well as the Augustan, Venetian, and Paris editions, read: “It is difficult to credit the report: the Numantines also put to flight,” and so forth. Other editions, including Bolsuing’s, read: “It is difficult then to credit the report, and the Numantines fled,” and so forth. In the Fabrician editions, Hittorp printed *fugêre* for *fugiere*; since this could scarcely be tolerated, Scott replaced it with *fugere*. But the true reading is *et fugavere*, “and they put to flight,” which is explicitly given by the Longobard copy and mine, and is also indicated by those copies in which *effugavere* is written, such as the Utrecht and second Florentine copies, together with the Groningen Collection. Above, where my copy reads *vidêre*, “they saw,” it has *vicêre*, “they conquered.”]

Therefore, although Scipio rejoiced and gloried because the event had occurred beyond expectation, he nevertheless declared that no further war ought to be undertaken against them. [Note: [Col. 0933C] “War against them.” The common editions read *bellum*, “war,” incorrectly and contrary to the better manuscripts—the first Florentine, mine, and Perizonius’s—which are joined by three Leiden copies, the Groningen Collection, and the Utrecht copy.]

Thus Scipio judged that he should press his unexpected successes. He enclosed the city itself with a siege and surrounded it with a trench. [Note: [Col. 0933C] “He surrounded it also with a trench.” All manuscripts and old editions approve this reading. But the editions following Bolsuing read, “and he surrounded it with a trench.”] The trench was ten feet wide and twenty feet deep. He then fortified the rampart itself, constructed with pointed stakes, with numerous towers, so that if the enemy attempted any breakthrough while making a sortie, he would no longer fight as a besieger with the besieged, but, the positions being reversed, as the besieged with the besieger.

Numantia, situated on a hill not far from the river Durius, enclosed three thousand paces within the circuit of its walls. [Note: [Col. 0933C] “Three thousand paces in circumference.” Appian likewise writes that Numantia had a circumference of twenty-four stadia. FABR.] Some, however, assert that it occupied only a small area and had no wall. [Note: [Col. 0933C] “Hence it is credible that they enclosed this extent of ground.” The first and third Leiden copies do not contain the verb *est*, “is.” All manuscripts and printed editions, however, read *quia*, “because,” for *quod*, “that.” I have restored *quod*. In all the manuscripts of Orosius I have observed that copyists very frequently and everywhere wrote *quia* for *quod*. Although the editions have correctly amended this elsewhere, they neglected to do so here, where it was especially necessary. The last part is written in the Longobard copy and the latest Leiden manuscripts.]

Hence it is credible that, while they were hard pressed by the war, they had enclosed this extent of ground for the care and protection of livestock, or even for the convenience of cultivating the land, while themselves occupying a small citadel fortified by nature. Otherwise, not to fortify so great an expanse of city for so small a number of people seemed more like betraying it than protecting it.

The Numantines, therefore, after being shut in for a long time and slaughtered by hunger, offered their surrender, provided that tolerable terms were imposed. They often even begged for the opportunity of a fair fight, so that they might be allowed to die like men.

At last they all suddenly burst out through two gates, having first taken a large quantity of drink—not wine, for that region does not produce it, but a juice of grain prepared by an art, which they call *celia*, from its being heated. [Note: [Col. 0933C–D] “They call it *celia*.” Florus also mentions this drink. FABR.—See Pontanus, *Danish History*, p. 766.]

For the power of the moistened grain’s germ is awakened by fire; then it is dried and afterward reduced to meal, and it is mixed with a soft juice, by which fermentation adds a sharp flavor and the warmth of intoxication. [Note: [Col. 0933D] “For that power is awakened by fire,” and so forth. This is the reading of the second Florentine manuscript and is the only one that should be approved; it is also found in three Leiden copies together with the Groningen Collection. The very first edition supports it. All the others read, “for that fiery power is awakened.” The first Florentine and the first Leiden copy omit *ignem*, “fire,” and read, “for that power is awakened,” and so forth. My copy offers a new reading differing from the others: “for that power awakens the fire of the germ of heated grain,” as though “fire” indicated the boldness that the drink aroused in those who consumed it. But since the text continues, “and afterward it is dried,” I prefer the other wording. The word *germinis*, “of the germ,” may be absent; nevertheless, Orosius seems to have said *germen madefactae frugis* for the swollen grains of wheat moistened with poured water, as they usually are when they begin to germinate.]

Thus, warmed by this drink after their long hunger, they offered themselves for battle. The fierce struggle lasted a long time and brought the Romans to the brink of danger; and once again the Romans would have proved, by fleeing, that they could fight against the Numantines, had they not been fighting under Scipio. [Note: [Col. 0933D–0934C] “That they could fight.” Three Leiden copies, together with the Groningen Collection and the Augustan edition, read *pugnare*, “fight.”]

The Numantines, after their bravest men had been killed, yielded in battle; yet, keeping their ranks in order, they did not return to the city like fugitives, and they refused to receive the bodies of the slain when these were brought for burial. [Note: [Col. 0934C] “Yet keeping their ranks in order.” After this, the Fabrician, Scottian, and Hittorpian editions read *non separantes se*, “not separating themselves.” This is an obvious gloss, unknown to all the old editions and manuscripts, and deserves to be removed.]

Finally, with every hope transformed into despair and all resolved upon death, they set fire to the enclosed city from within; and all together were consumed by sword, poison, and fire.

The Romans gained nothing at all from the defeated except their own security. For after Numantia had been destroyed, they considered that they had not so much defeated the Numantines as escaped from them. [Note: [Col. 0934C] “They considered that they had more.” Three Leiden copies, together with the Groningen Collection and the Augustan edition, read *vicisse magis*, “had more truly conquered,” with *se*, “themselves,” removed. The Longobard copy reads *vicisse re magis*, “had more truly conquered in fact.”]

[Note: [Col. 0934C–D] “Than that they had escaped.” That is, “they thought.” The reading *qua*, “by which,” found in some editions contrary to the manuscripts, does not fit here. The Romans judged the matter so in their minds, but in words they were always grandiloquent, even in disasters. Similar examples occur in Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, chapter 28, p. 391: “What crown did Cannae deserve? From where, to flee was the highest achievement of valor.” Concerning Hannibal, Horace, book IV, ode 4, lines 49 ff.:

> And at last the treacherous Hannibal said:  
> “Deer, the prey of ravening wolves,  
> We pursue of our own accord—  
> For to deceive and escape them is triumph.”

Sallust, *Jugurthine War*, chapter 104, concerning Jugurtha, Bocchus, and others: “And the fierce leaders themselves, who had not fled, acted as victors.” The distinguished Wasse gives more and other examples.]

Not one Numantine was held by the victor’s chain; therefore Rome did not witness a triumph on their account. Among the poor there was no gold or silver that could have survived the fire; fire consumed their weapons and clothing. [Note: [Col. 0934D] “Not one Numantine was held by the victor’s chain.” Florus writes the same; but Appian reports that Scipio, reserving fifty for his triumph, sold the rest under the crown. In this manner Scipio Africanus Aemilianus, within a year and three months of his arrival, after surrounding Numantia with siege works and destroying it, levelled it with the ground, as Velleius writes in book II. FABR.]

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Sedition of the Gracchi and the Inheritance of Attalus, King of Pergamum

Accordingly, at the time when these events were taking place at Numantia, seditions of the Gracchi were being stirred up at Rome. [Note: [Col. 0934D] “The seditions of the Gracchi.” Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus was killed, because of the seditions he had provoked, while tribune of the plebs, when Publius Mucius and Lucius Calpurnius were consuls—the year in which Scipio destroyed Numantia. See Plutarch, *Life of the Gracchi*, Appian, book I of the *Civil Wars*, Livy, Velleius, Florus, and others. FABR.]

But when Scipio, after destroying Numantia, was arranging the other peoples of Spain under peace, he consulted a certain Tiresus, a Celtic prince, asking by what means the Numantine state had either previously endured unconquered or afterward been destroyed. [Note: [Col. 0935B] “A certain Tiresus.” In Cornelius Gualther’s book he is called *Thyreus*, while the name appears variously elsewhere. I found *Thyresus* in the Longobard copy and *Thiresus* in the Augustan edition.]

Tiresus replied: “Concord was unconquered; discord brought destruction.” [Note: [Col. 0935B] “Concord was unconquered; discord brought destruction.” This reading is neither satisfactory nor internally consistent. If *concordia* is nominative, the following *invicta* does not agree with *exitio fuit*. If it is ablative, the text should read *concordiā invictā, discordiā victā fuit*. The manuscripts offer no help except Perizonius’s copy, which supplies: “Concord was a defense; discord was destruction.” This is certainly far superior to the common reading. In Orosius, “unconquered concord” means concord that no sedition or ambition broke. Nevertheless, I would prefer the shorter and more rounded wording: “Concord was a defense; discord was destruction.” I scarcely doubt that *invicta*, “unconquered,” flowed here from the preceding words, “had previously endured unconquered.”]

The Romans accepted this as though it had been said to and about themselves, since news was already reaching them that the entire City was divided by seditions. [Note: [Col. 0935C] “Said to and about themselves.” The Longobard copy reads “said by themselves about themselves.”] [Note: [Col. 0935C] “By seditions.” All the manuscripts, together with the excellent Augustan edition, require this reading in place of “by sedition,” found in the other editions. Shortly afterward, the second Leiden copy, together with the Utrecht copy, reads “destroyed” for “chosen.”]

After Carthage and Numantia had been destroyed, a useful comparison concerning foresight perished among the Romans, and an infamous rivalry arising from ambition came into being. [Note: [Col. 0935C–D] “Perishes among the Romans.” This elegant reading is drawn from the Longobard copy. For what purpose would the words read thus far serve? “Among the Romans there arises a useful comparison concerning foresight, and an infamous rivalry concerning ambition arises.” Although everyone had been able to digest this harsh and inept wording, Perizonius’s copy nevertheless rejects the second *oritur*, “arises,” and reads: “Among the Romans there arises a useful comparison concerning foresight, and an infamous rivalry concerning ambition.” But our correction from the Longobard copy is the truest. For the Romans, having lost that whetstone of their virtue which the more prudent members of the Senate feared, as Orosius says above in book III, at the end of the final chapter, not only became relaxed through leisure but were also disturbed, harassed, and oppressed by seditions, discords, and civil wars. In the phrase “a useful comparison concerning foresight,” it would be surprising if Orosius had not had Justin in mind, who writes in a similar situation concerning the Athenians after the death of Epaminondas, book VI, chapter 9: “When they had lost the man whom they had been accustomed to emulate, they became slack and torpid; instead of spending their revenues, as formerly, on fleets and armies, they squandered them on festivals and the apparatus of games.”]

Gracchus, tribune of the plebs, was angry with the nobility because he had been marked out as one of the authors of the Numantine treaty. [Note: [Col. 0935D] “With the nobility.” Certain manuscripts once read “with the Senate,” as is clear from mine and Perizonius’s copy, in which both readings occur.] [Note: [Col. 0935D–0936B] “As one of the authors of the Numantine treaty.” Read about the cause of the Gracchan sedition in Plutarch, Appian, Livy, and Velleius. Hence Cicero, *On the Response of the Haruspices*: “For resentment over the Numantine treaty, in whose conclusion he had taken part as quaestor to the consul Gaius Mancinus, and the severity of the Senate in rejecting that treaty, caused Tiberius Gracchus grief and fear; and this matter compelled that brave and distinguished man to abandon the authority of the fathers.” FABR.]

He resolved to distribute among the people the land that had until then been held by private individuals. [Note: [Col. 0936B] “To distribute the land among the people.” Gracchus proposed an agrarian law: “No one should possess more than five hundred plethra”—that is, no one should hold more than five hundred *iugera* of public land. Whatever was held beyond that amount was to be distributed among the plebs. See Plutarch and Appian.]

When the tribune Octavius opposed him, he deprived him of his authority and appointed Minucius as his successor. [Note: [Col. 0936B] “Tribune Octavius.” Appian, Plutarch, and Livy, book LVIII, name him Marcus Octavius. The printed books of Florus have Gnaeus Octavius; my manuscript has Gaius. FABR.] [Note: [Col. 0936B] “His successor Minucius.” Plutarch has Μούκιον (*Moukion*), “Mucius,” instead of Μινούκιον (*Minoukion*), “Minucius.” In Appian the name is Κοΐντος Μούμμιος (*Koïntos Moummios*), “Quintus Mummius.” FABR.]

For these reasons anger seized the Senate and arrogance seized the people. [Note: [Col. 0936B–C] “Seized.” Three Leiden copies, together with the Groningen Collection, have *invasit*, “seized,” with the word marked as doubtful.]

At that time Attalus, son of Eumenes, dying, had ordered by his will that the Roman people should succeed him as heir to the empire of Asia. [Note: [Col. 0936C] “Attalus, son of Eumenes.” Concerning Attalus and his inheritance, see Plutarch, *Life of the Gracchi*; Strabo, book XIII; Livy, book LVIII; Velleius; Sextus Rufus; and others.] [Note: [Col. 0936C] “As heir.” This word is absent from the first Leiden copy.]

Seeking the people’s favor by means of money, Gracchus introduced a law that the money which had belonged to Attalus should be distributed among the people. [Note: [Col. 0936C] “That the money.” All the Leiden copies, together with the Groningen Collection and the Utrecht copy, read “that the money itself.”]

When Nasica opposed him, Pompey also promised that he would prosecute Gracchus as soon as he had left office. [Note: [Col. 0936C] “Promised.” The first and third Leiden copies, together with the Groningen Collection, read *spondet*, “he promises.”] [Note: [Col. 0936C] “Had left office.” This is correctly written in Gualther’s book, whereas other copies corruptly read “had entered office.” The better reading is confirmed by the three Florentine copies, Perizonius’s copy, and mine, except that mine reads “from office.”]

## CHAPTER IX. On the Death of Gracchus and the Servile War in Sicily, among the Athenians, and at Delos

As Gracchus strove to remain tribune of the plebs in the following year, and as he was inflaming popular disturbances on the day of the elections, the nobility, instigated by Nasica, became inflamed and drove the plebs away with fragments of the benches. [Note: [Col. 0936C] “At the instigation of Nasica.” Livy says this. Cicero says in the *Brutus* that Gracchus was killed under the leadership of Nasica. See Velleius Paterculus concerning Nasica.]

Gracchus, fleeing down the steps that are above the Calpurnian arch, after throwing off his cloak, was struck by a fragment of a bench and fell. [Note: [Col. 0936C–D] “By the steps that are above the Calpurnian arch.” This is how all the old books read, instead of the common version, “by which one goes above the Calpurnian arch.” Appian: ἀνῃρέθη παρὰ τὰς θύρας παρὰ τοὺς τῶν βασιλέων ἀνδριάντας, “He was killed near the doors, beside the statues of the kings.” Tiberius was killed not far from the entrance to the Capitol, where the statues of the kings stood. FABR.] [Note: [Col. 0936D] “After throwing off his cloak and fleeing.” Plutarch: αὐτοῦ δὲ τοῦ Τιβερίου φεύγοντος ἀντελάβετό τις τῶν ἱματίων· ὁ δὲ τὸν τήβεννον ἀφεὶς καὶ φεύγων ἐν τοῖς χιτῶσιν ἐσφάλη, that is: “While Tiberius was fleeing, someone seized him by his clothing. He, having abandoned his toga and fleeing in his tunic, fell.” FABR.—Perizonius reads “after removing his garment.”]

After rising again, he was killed by another blow from a club that struck his brain. [Note: [Col. 0937B] “A club struck his brain.” Perizonius reads “with the club having struck his brain.” This is not bad.]

Two hundred others were also killed in that sedition, and their bodies were thrown into the Tiber. The unburied corpse of Gracchus himself likewise wasted away. [Note: [Col. 0937B] “Two hundred besides.” Plutarch: τῶν δὲ ἄλλων ἀπέθανον ὑπὲρ τριακοσίους, “Of the others, more than three hundred were killed.” FABR.]

Moreover, the contagion of a servile war, having arisen in Sicily, infected many provinces far and wide. [Note: [Col. 0937B–C] “The servile contagion infected many.” Diodorus, in the translation of Henry Stephens: “When the report of the slaves’ victory had spread, the slaves already in Rome had been inflamed to revolt by a conspiracy among themselves; in Attica, more than a thousand had likewise risen, and similarly at Delos and in many other places.” This is relevant to the statement of Obsequens: “Many thousands of slaves in Italy who had conspired were with difficulty arrested and consumed by punishment.” FABR.]

For at Minturnae four hundred and fifty slaves were crucified, and at Sinuessa nearly four thousand slaves were suppressed by Quintus Metellus and Gnaeus Servilius Caepio. [Note: [Col. 0937C] “Four hundred and fifty slaves at Minturnae.” The fourth Leiden copy gives a number one hundred less. In three Leiden copies and the Groningen Collection, *servis*, “slaves,” is absent; shortly afterward, the first and second copies number seven thousand instead of four thousand.]

The same servile uprising was also put down in the Athenian mines by the praetor Heraclitus. At Delos too, slaves swelling with a new revolt were suppressed when the townspeople forestalled them. [Note: [Col. 0937C] “At Delos.” All the manuscripts prefer this form to *Delum*, “Delos.”] Apart from that first spark of the Sicilian evil from which, like sparks flashing out, these different conflagrations were kindled. [Note: [Col. 0937C–D] “From which these, like sparks, kindled.” I have corrected this partly by conjecture and partly with the help of the manuscripts. All the manuscripts read *seminarunt*, “they sowed,” a reading also found in the single Augustan edition. All the others, contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts, read *seminavit*, “he sowed.” The error arose because, since the manuscripts frequently write *e* for *ae*, the editors failed to notice that *istae*, “these,” rather than *iste*, “this,” should be written in all the editions that printed “from which this, like a spark,” and so forth. Thus they made two errors without any acceptable sense. Although *istae* appears in Scott’s edition, the sense that could be drawn from it while retaining *seminavit* is unclear.]

In Sicily, after the consul Fulvius, the consul Piso captured the town of Mamertium, where he killed eight thousand fugitives. Those whom he was able to capture he fastened to the gallows. [Note: [Col. 0937D] “After the consul Fulvius.” The servile war arose in Sicily, and when the praetors had been unable to suppress it, it was entrusted to the consul Gaius Fulvius. Livy, book LVI. Fulvius was consul with Africanus the Younger in the year 619. FABR.] [Note: [Col. 0937D] “The consul Piso.” Lucius Calpurnius Piso was consul in the year after Fulvius and successfully conducted the war against the fugitives in Sicily, as Valerius shows in book II, chapter 2, and book IV, chapter 3, in addition to Orosius. FABR.]

When the consul Rupilius succeeded him, he too recovered Tauromenium and Enna by force of arms, the strongest refuges of the fugitives, [Note: [Col. 0937D–0938B] “When Rupilius the consul succeeded him.” Rutilius is commonly called consul by everyone, including Diodorus. But in the Capitoline Fasti for the year 621, Publius Rupilius is consul with Publius Popillius Laenas: “Publius Rupilius, son of Publius, grandson of Publius.” Cicero likewise says in *Against Verres*: “Under the consuls Publius Popillius and Publius Rupilius, that place was held by runaway slaves, barbarians, and enemies.” He is speaking of Enna, which the common editions clumsily changed here to Aetna. Diodorus gives a detailed account of Tauromenium and Enna, which Rupilius captured, and of the completion of the servile war. He writes that Eunus, the author of this war, miserably perished in prison at Morgantina, his body dissolving into a mass of lice. Plutarch, in *Life of Sulla*: λέγεται τὸν ἄρξαντα τοῦ δουλικοῦ πολέμου περὶ Σικελίαν δραπέτην, Εὔνουν ὄνομα, μετὰ τὴν ἅλωσιν εἰς Ῥώμην ἀγόμενον ὑπὸ φθειριάσεως ἀποθανεῖν, that is: “It is reported that Eunus, the runaway named as the instigator of the servile war in Sicily, died of a disease of lice when he was being taken to Rome after his capture.” FABR.—Rutilius is named throughout the Orosian manuscripts, but corruptly.]

where, it is reported, more than twenty thousand slaves were then slaughtered. [Note: [Col. 0938C] “Where more than.” Three Leiden copies, together with the Utrecht and Groningen copies and the Augustan edition, delete *ubi*, “where.” The Perizonian manuscript does the same.]

Truly, this was a wretched and insoluble cause for war. The masters would necessarily have perished unless they met the insolence of the slaves with the sword. Yet even in the battles of these most grievous losses and in the still more grievous gains of victory, as many were destroyed by the defeated as were lost by the victors.

## 308 CHAPTER X. On the War of Aristonicus; on the Crimes of Ptolemy, King of the Alexandrians; on Antiochus, Defeated by Phraates; and on the Fires of Aetna and Lipara

[Note: [Col. 0938C] “In the year, etc.” The third Leiden copy and the Groningen Collection place this event one year earlier.]

In the year 622 from the founding of the City, Publius Licinius Crassus, consul and chief pontiff, was sent with a fully equipped army against Aristonicus, the brother of Attalus, who had taken possession of Asia, which had been left to the Romans by will. [Note: [Col. 0938C] “Aristonicus, the brother of Attalus.” Aristonicus was the son of Eumenes, not born in a legitimate marriage but begotten by an Ephesian courtesan, the daughter of a certain cithara-player, according to Justin, book XXXVI. See also Livy, book LIX; Florus, book II, final chapter; Velleius; and Eutropius. Cicero’s *Second Philippic* should also be consulted.]

Moreover, supported by the great kings—that is, Nicomedes of Bithynia, Mithridates of Pontus and Armenia, Ariarathes of Cappadocia, and Pylaemenes of Paphlagonia—with their enormous forces, he nevertheless was defeated in battle. [Note: [Col. 0938C–0940B] “By the great kings, etc.” Eutropius, book IV, p. 188: “Licinius Crassus was sent against him, having unlimited auxiliaries from kings. For Nicomedes, king of Bithynia, helped the Romans; so did Mithridates of Pontus, with whom there was later a very serious war; Ariarathes of Cappadocia; and Pylaemenes of Paphlagonia. Crassus was nevertheless defeated and killed in battle.” Learned men have already noted Eutropius’s error in confusing Mithridates the father with the son. The father was surnamed Evergetes, as is clear from his coin; the son was surnamed Eupator. The name Pylaemenes—which seems to have been common to many kings of Paphlagonia—is rendered incorrectly in some manuscripts and old editions as Philomenes, Philimenes, or in other forms. Fabricius also neglected the diphthong in the name, which is preserved on the very rare coins of the ancient king Pylaemenes. I have appended an image of the bronze coin that I myself possess, remarkable for its beauty, workmanship, and brilliance, as well as another silver coin, also from our collection, of Ariarathes, king of Cappadocia, and of Nicomedes, the second king of Bithynia of that name. Finally, I appended a silver coin of Mithridates, taken from the distinguished posthumous work of Vaillant, *The Empire of the Achaemenids*. Vaillant believes that the era of the kings of Pontus is marked on it on p. 61, and that this establishes which King Mithridates the coin should be attributed to. I, however, do not think that coin should be attributed to the ancient Mithridates, nor that the head visible on the coin is the head of a king, but rather that it is the head of a Roman emperor, specifically Claudius. Accordingly, the coin should be attributed to that Mithridates who lived in the time of Claudius, concerning whom Dio Cassius writes explicitly in book LX, p. 670: Ἄλλῳ τέ τινι Μιθριδάτῃ, τὸ γένος ἀπ’ ἐκείνου τοῦ πάνυ ἔχοντι, τὸν Βόσπορον ἐχαρίσατο, “He granted the Bosporus to another Mithridates, who traced his lineage to that great Mithridates.” We shall illustrate this conjecture more fully in a larger work containing the coins of all the Greek kings, which, having long ago been engraved in copper at our expense, will, with God’s favor, soon be issued from the press.]

After the battle had been joined, he was defeated; and when the army had been routed after a very great slaughter, he himself, already surrounded by the enemy and nearly captured, struck a Thracian in the eye with the staff he had used for his horse. The barbarian, blazing with anger and pain, pierced Crassus’s side with his sword. Thus, by devising a manner of death for himself, he escaped both disgrace and slavery. [Note: [Col. 0939D] “The staff with which he had handled the horse.” Valerius also records this in book III, chapter 2. FABR.—For *impegit*, “struck,” Perizonius’s copy reads *injecit*, “thrust.”]

The consul Perperna, who had succeeded Crassus, heard of Crassus’s death and the defeat of the Roman army and hurried rapidly into Asia. He attacked Aristonicus, who was taking his ease after his recent victory, with an unexpected war, and, stripping him of all his forces, put him to flight. When he had surrounded the city of Stratonicea, to which Aristonicus had fled, with a siege, he compelled him, exhausted by hunger, to surrender. The consul Perperna, seized by illness at Pergamum, died. [Note: [Col. 0939D] “Aristonicus, etc.” This is the reading of the manuscripts and the Augustan copy. The old editions read: “But Aristonicus, led to Rome—or to the city of Rome—was strangled in prison.” For *strangulatus est*, “was strangled,” the third Leiden copy, together with the Groningen Collection, prefers *strangulatus*, “strangled”; Perizonius has *strangulatur*, “is strangled.”]

Aristonicus was strangled in prison at Rome by order of the Senate.

In the same year, Ptolemy, king of the Alexandrians, gave a more wretched end to his life than his life itself had been. [Note: [Col. 0939D–0940D] “Ptolemy, king of Alexandria.” He means Ptolemy VII, king of the Alexandrians, who was called Euergetes II and Physcon and lived most disgracefully, as Strabo writes in book XVII. What Orosius writes here about Ptolemy and Antiochus he took from Livy, book LIX, as the epitome of that book demonstrates. FABR.] He had first violated his own sister and then taken her in marriage; finally, he cast her off in a manner even more disgraceful than the way in which he had married her. He took his own stepdaughter—that is, the daughter of his sister and wife—as his wife. He killed his own son, whom he had fathered by his sister, as well as his brother’s son. Therefore, execrable for such incest and parricides, he was driven from the kingdom by the Alexandrians. [Note: [Col. 0940D] “For such incests.” The Augustan edition reads *incestubus*, “incestuous acts.”]

At the same time, Antiochus, not content with Babylonia, Ecbatana, and the whole empire of Media, engaged in battle against Phraates, king of the Parthians, and was defeated. Although he appeared to have one hundred thousand armed men in his army, he dragged along more than two hundred thousand camp-followers and sutlers, mixed with prostitutes and actors. Thus, easily overwhelmed by the strength of the Parthians, he perished together with his entire army. [Note: [Col. 0940D] “One hundred thousand armed men.” The king’s great softness and indolence are being indicated: he led to war twice as many useless followers as armed men. There is no reason to alter the number found in the old books. FABR.]

When Gaius Sempronius Tuditanus and Manius Aquillius were consuls, Publius Scipio Africanus, having publicly declared the day before that he was in danger of his life because he had learned that this was being threatened against him as he labored for his country by wicked and ungrateful men, was found lifeless in his bedchamber the next morning. I have not rashly included this among the greatest Roman disasters, especially since Africanus’s strength and moderation had such influence in that city that, while he lived, it was easily believed that neither a social nor a civil war could arise. [Note: [Col. 0941C] “Having declared.” The Augustan edition reads *contestantem*, “declaring.”] [Note: [Col. 0941C] “The next morning.” The best manuscripts—the three Florentine copies, mine, and Perizonius’s—read “the next morning lifeless,” and so forth. In the second Florentine copy, *die*, “day,” is written above the line.]

Some say that he was killed by the treachery of his wife Sempronia, the sister of the Gracchi, so that a wicked family, born—as I believe—for the ruin of its country would not, amid the impious seditions of its men, prove even more monstrous through the crimes of its women. [Note: [Col. 0941C–D] “Some say that he was killed by his wife.” Suspicion of his wife Sempronia appears in the Livian epitome, and of Sempronia and her mother-in-law Cornelia in Appian, book I. Hence Cicero said in the *Dream of Scipio*: “If you escape the impious hands of your relatives.” Gaius Carbo, tribune of the plebs, was also thought to have used violence against Africanus, as he writes in the twenty-first letter to Paetus. FABR.] [Note: [Col. 0941D] “And for the ruin.” This is the reading of the second Florentine copy, while the first and third Florentine copies read “for ruin.” All the remaining manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection and the Augustan edition, read “unto ruin.” For *patriae suae*, “of its country,” three Leiden copies and the Groningen Collection read *patriae*, “of the country.”]

When Marcus Aemilius and Lucius Orestes were consuls, Aetna, shaken by a vast tremor, overflowed with fiery globes. On another day the island of Lipara and the sea surrounding it boiled so violently that it dissolved even scorched rocks, tore away the ship’s planking after melting its wax fastenings, boiled dead fish and those floating on the surface, and suffocated human beings as well—unless they were able to flee farther away—by the repeated inhalation of hot air, which burned their internal organs.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Great and Destructive Force of Locusts in Africa, Whose Death and Putrefaction Produced a Horrible and Unheard-of Pestilence
M. Plautius Hypsaeus and M. Fulvius Flaccus being consuls, scarcely had Africa, still resting from the devastation of the wars, found peace when a dreadful and unprecedented calamity followed. For when enormous swarms of locusts had gathered throughout Africa,

> [Note: [Col. 0941D] “Enormous locusts.” What Orosius writes in this chapter about the monstrous force of the locusts in Africa and the pestilence arising from them was related by Livy in Book LX, whose Epitome reads as follows: “It is reported that a pestilence arose in Africa from an immense multitude of locusts and then from the heaps of their corpses.” Obsequens also mentions the same event. FABR.]

and had not merely already stripped away every hope of crops,

> [Col. 0941C] 312

all the grasses, including part of their roots, and the leaves of the trees together with the tender branches, but had even gnawed through the bitter bark and dry wood,

> [Note: [Col. 0941D] “Had gnawed through.” The Leiden third edition has *praerosissent* (“had gnawed beforehand”); but the other Leiden editions, together with Gronovius’s Collection and the manuscripts of Meus and Perizonius, have *perroderent* (“were gnawing through”), which is perhaps better.]

they were suddenly seized by the wind,

> [Note: [Col. 0942C] “Seized by the wind.” I prefer this reading, with the Perizonius manuscript, the third Leiden edition, and Gronovius’s Collection, to *arreptae* (“snatched up”), which appears in all the other manuscripts and editions, except the Augustan edition, which likewise reads *abreptae*.]

and, driven together into balls and carried for a long time through the air, were plunged into the African sea.

When the waves, driven by the wind, had pushed their immense heaps far along the extensive shores, the foul and exceedingly pestilential odor—beyond all expectation—which the decaying and putrefying mass exhaled produced such a pestilence among all living creatures alike that the rotting corpses scattered everywhere, as birds, cattle, and wild animals were destroyed by the corruption of the air, increased the contagion of the disease.

But how great was the plague among human beings I myself shudder throughout my body as I relate. For it is reported that in Numidia, where King Micipsa then ruled,

> [Note: [Col. 0942C] “King Micipsa.” He is discussed below, chapter 15. FABR.]

eight hundred thousand people perished,

> [Note: [Col. 0942C] “Eight hundred.” Some editions have “eighty,” but that number is inconsistent with the size of Numidia and the great number of its inhabitants.]

while along the coast, especially adjacent to the Carthaginian and Utican shores, more than two hundred thousand died. At Utica itself thirty thousand soldiers, who had been assigned to defend all Africa, were killed and swept away.

This disaster

> [Note: [Col. 0942C] “So sudden and so violent.” The first *tam* (“so”) was omitted in the editions of Fabricius and Scott, contrary to all the manuscripts and editions. [Col. 0942D] Shortly afterward, Perizonius and Meus read *exstitit* (“arose”) instead of *institit* (“pressed upon us”).]

was so sudden and so violent that it is said that at Utica, in a single day and through a single gate, more than fifteen hundred of those younger men were carried out dead.

> [Note: [Col. 0942D] “Fifteen hundred.” The Augustan edition has “twelve hundred.”]

Nevertheless, with the peace and favor of almighty God—of whose mercy, and in whose confidence, I speak—let me say this:

> [Note: [Col. 0942D] “Of whose.” In the first Florentine edition, *de* (“of”) is absent.]

although in our own times locusts sometimes arise in different regions and often cause damage, though tolerable,

> [Note: [Col. 0942D] “Arise.” Perizonius has the singular *exoriatur*; shortly afterward, instead of “in different regions,” he reads “at different times.”]

never in Christian times has such an inextricable force of evil occurred that the plague of locusts, which while alive could in no way have been endured, should cause greater harm when dead; and that which, while alive, would have destroyed everything, once destroyed itself, should have brought about the more general destruction of all things, so that it would have been desirable

> [Note: [Col. 0942D] “Lest it should have perished.” I restored this reading from the Longobard manuscript; the common reading is “lest it perish.”]

that it had not perished.

## CHAPTER XII. On Carthage restored, and on the sedition and death of Gaius Gracchus

> [Note: [Col. 0942D] In the 627th year from the founding of the City. Other authorities give the year as 630. The names of the consuls have been terribly corrupted in the common texts; in the best books they are correct, except that they wrongly give Metellus the first name Lucius instead of Quintus. FABR.]

In the 627th year from the founding of the City, Quintus Caecilius Metellus and Titus Quinctius Flamininus being consuls, Carthage in Africa was ordered to be restored. At last, in the twenty-second year after its destruction, it was restored and refilled by the settlement of families of Roman citizens who were to inhabit it, an ominous portent having first occurred.

> [Note: [Col. 0942D] “Carthage in Africa was ordered to be restored.” Eutropius writes that Carthage was repaired by order of the senate. Appian indicates that this was decreed by the senate. Plutarch, in his *Life of the Gracchi*, states that the tribune Rubrius brought before the people a proposal for founding a colony at Carthage. FABR.]

For when surveyors had been sent to mark out the Carthaginian territory and found that stakes, fixed as boundary markers, had been torn out at night by wolves with their teeth and gnawed,

> [Note: [Col. 0943B] “At night.” The common editions add *et* (“and”), but the manuscripts do not recognize the conjunction.]

there was for some time uncertainty whether it was advantageous to Roman peace for Carthage to be rebuilt.

> [Note: [Col. 0943B] “In the same year Gaius Gracchus.” Gaius Sempronius Gracchus continued as tribune of the plebs for two years, as we noted in the argument of the speech *On the Consular Provinces*, and during that period enacted many laws, concerning which see Appian, Plutarch, Livy, Asconius, and Velleius. FABR.]

In the same year Gaius Gracchus, brother of that Gracchus who had already been killed in a sedition, was created tribune of the plebs amid tumult and became a great calamity for the state. For after he had often stirred the Roman people into the bitterest seditions by means of lavish distributions and excessive promises,

> [Note: [Col. 0943C] “Had stirred up.” Perizonius has “had summoned”; some editions have “had incited.”]

especially on account of the agrarian law,

> [Note: [Col. 0943C] “On account of the agrarian law.” Latin writers sometimes omit the word *causa* or *gratia* with the genitive, as is clear from examples of the ancients and from the authority of learned men cited by Joannes Arntzenius in his notes on Victor, p. 55. For this reason that learned man wishes the word to be absent here in accordance with the manuscripts. I would not object if more or better manuscripts supported him. But since he relies on the worst of all, the Utrecht manuscript, which contains very frequent omissions of words and a forest of errors, I think the word may be retained with all the other manuscripts.]

for which his brother Tiberius Gracchus had also been killed, he eventually withdrew from the tribunate, Minucius succeeding him.

> [Note: [Col. 0943C] “With Minucius as his successor.” It appears that his colleagues substituted Minucius in Gracchus’s place, although Gracchus had been elected tribune of the plebs for the third time by a very large majority. Plutarch mentions this Minucius; Florus does so in Book III, chapter 15. The author of *On Illustrious Men* calls him Minucius Rufus. FABR.]

When Minucius, tribune of the plebs, had overturned most of the measures of his predecessor Gracchus and repealed his laws, Gaius Gracchus, accompanied by a vast crowd and by Fulvius Flaccus, ascended the Capitol, where an assembly was being held. After a great tumult had arisen there,

> [Note: [Col. 0943D] “A certain herald.” Atilius, the herald of the consul Opimius, appears in the book *On Illustrious Men*. Plutarch calls him “Quintus Antyllius, the servant of Opimius” (Ὀπιμίου ὑπηρέτης Κοῖντος Ἀντίλλιος); in Appian he is called both Atilius and Antilius. FABR.]

a certain herald was killed by the Gracchan party, as though this were the signal for war. Flaccus, surrounded by his two armed sons and accompanied also by Gracchus, who was wearing the toga and concealing a short sword under his left arm, although he had unsuccessfully sent ahead a herald to summon the slaves to freedom, occupied the Janiculum as though it were a citadel.

> [Note: [Col. 0943D] “The Janiculum as though it were a citadel.” This is how the passage is read in all the old books. Everyone writes that the Aventine was occupied, and the following reference to the public slope, by which one ascended the Aventine, shows that the Aventine must be understood. FABR.]

> [Note: [Col. 0943D] “Against D. Brutus.” Contrary to all the manuscripts and despite the Augustan edition, all the other editions have restored *contra quem D. Brutus* (“against whom D. Brutus”), as though *contra* here could not mean “on the other side.”]

Against them the former consul D. Brutus rushed from the Publician Slope with great force.

> [Note: [Col. 0943D] “D. Brutus.” He was discussed above, in chapter 5. FABR.]

> [Note: [Col. 0943D] “From the Publician Slope.” This reading is preserved in the better Florentine manuscripts and in Perizonius, and is preferable to *publico* (“public”), found in some other and later editions. It received its name from the Publicii. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book IV, p. 38: “The Publician Slope was named after the plebeian aediles Publicius, who built it at public expense.” They were brothers; Festus says: “The Publician Slope is so called because the two brothers L. and M. Publicius Malleolus, curule aediles, built it from money received after condemning cattle dealers, so that vehicles could reach the Aventine from the Velia.” Ovid likewise called it Publician in the *Fasti*, 5.293:

> “They dwell on part of the slope, which then was a steep cliff;
>
> Now it is a useful road, and they call it Publician.”]

There Flaccus fought for a long time with the utmost determination. Gracchus, after withdrawing into the temple of Minerva, wished to fall upon his sword, but was restrained by the intervention of Laetorius.

> [Note: [Col. 0944C] “By the intervention of Laetorius.” We restored *Laetorii* from Gualther’s excellent manuscript; in the others *Lictoris* (“of the lictor”) is written incorrectly. The error arose because the common texts write *Lectorium* instead of *Laetorio*. But in that excellent manuscript the name is *Laetorius* not only here but also below, in chapter 21, where we shall show that this is how the name ought to be written. In the passage of Plutarch just cited, Λικιννίου is undoubtedly corruptly printed instead of Λαιτωρίου. For the men called Pomponius and Licinnius there are called Pomponius and Laetorius by the author of *On Illustrious Men* and by Valerius Maximus, Book IV, chapter 7. On the loyalty of Pomponius, a Roman knight, toward Gracchus, see Velleius Paterculus. FABR.]

Thus, while the battle remained uncertain for a long time,

> [Note: [Col. 0944C] “At last the archers.” Plutarch has Τοξόται Κρῆτες, “Cretan archers.”]

at last the archers sent by Opimius scattered the massed crowd.

> [Note: [Col. 0944C] “Sent by Opimius.” The Augustan edition has “sent by the consul Opimius.”]

The two Flacci, father and son, having leapt from the temple of Luna into a private house and barred the doors, were stabbed after the lattice wall had been broken through.

> [Note: [Col. 0944D] “Into a private house.” Appian has εἰς ἐργαστήριον ἀνδρὸς γνωρίμου, “into the workshop of a well-known man.” FABR.]

Gracchus,

> [Note: [Col. 0944D] “Gracchus, for a long time on his own behalf.” Appian says: Γράκχος διὰ τῆς ξυλίνης γεφύρας ἐς τὸ πέραν τοῦ ποταμοῦ καταφυγὼν εἰς ἄλσος τι μεθ’ ἑνὸς θεράποντος, ὑπέσχε τῷ δράποντι [probably a corruption for θεράποντι] τὴν σφαγὴν καταλαμβανόμενος, that is: “Gracchus, fleeing across the wooden bridge to the other side of the Tiber into a certain grove with one slave, when he was already being captured there, offered his neck to the slave.” The author of *On Illustrious Men* calls it the grove of Furina, perhaps of the Furies; for Plutarch has ἱερὸν ἄλσος τῶν Ἐριννύων, “the sacred grove of the Erinyes.” Velleius and the author of *On Illustrious Men* call the slave Euporus; Plutarch calls him Philocrates. See Valerius, Book VI, chapter 8. FABR.]

> [Note: [Col. 0944D] “For a long time.” This is absent from some manuscripts and editions.]

while his friends fought and died for him for a long time, reached the sublician bridge only with difficulty; and there, lest he be captured alive, he offered his neck to his slave.

> [Note: [Col. 0945B] “He offered.” The Utrecht manuscript has “he handed over,” which is inappropriate. On the expression “to offer one’s neck” in voluntary death, see Joannes Arntzenius on Aurelius Victor, p. 257.]

Gracchus’s severed head was brought to the consul, while his body was carried to the town of Misenum, to his mother Cornelia.

> [Note: [Col. 0945B] “Severed.” The first Leiden edition has “cut off.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0945B] “Was carried away.” The Augustan edition has “was brought”; the first Leiden manuscript has “was conveyed.”]

This Cornelia, daughter of the elder Africanus, had withdrawn to Misenum after the death of her first son.

> [Note: [Col. 0945B] “Had withdrawn to Misenum after the death of her first son.” This reading appeared correctly in the first edition and afterward in the Paris and Venetian editions, but all the others have “Misenum, as I have decided, had withdrawn after the death of her first son.” But where did Orosius say this? Certainly not in this chapter, nor above in chapter 9, where he discussed the killing of Tiberius Gracchus. Therefore the phrase, although it occurs in the manuscripts and the Augustan edition, cannot be tolerated.]

Gracchus’s property was confiscated.

> [Note: [Col. 0945C] “The young Flaccus.” Appian calls him Quintus Flaccus and says that he was sent by his father as an envoy; Cicero says in *Against Catiline* that he was killed in prison while still under age. Velleius says: “A young man of distinguished appearance, not yet eighteen years old, free from his father’s crimes, the son of Fulvius Flaccus, whom his father had sent as an envoy concerning the terms, was killed by Opimius.” FABR.]

The young Flaccus was killed in the *robur*.

> [Note: [Col. 0945C] “In the *robur*.” In prison, *robur* denotes the place into which a class of criminals was thrown, according to Festus. Livy, Book XXXVIII: “So that a most distinguished man may be confined in prison among nocturnal thieves and robbers, and expire in the *robur* and darkness.” FABR.]

Two hundred and fifty of the Gracchan faction are reported to have been killed on the Aventine.

> [Note: [Col. 0945C] “Two hundred and fifty.” This is more plausible than the three thousand whom Plutarch says were killed. [Col. 0945D] FABR. For *caesi* (“were killed”), Perizonius and Meus report *caesi fuisse* (“to have been killed”).]

The consul Opimius was brave in war, but equally cruel in the investigation.

> [Note: [Col. 0946B] “In the investigation.” The Augustan edition, together with three Leiden manuscripts and Gronovius’s Collection, has “in the inquiry,” which is the more appropriate reading.]

For he killed more than three thousand people by judicial punishments; among them many innocent men were killed without even having had their case stated.

> [Note: [Col. 0946B] “More than three thousand.” The same manuscripts, agreeing with the three Florentine manuscripts, have “more than three thousand,” which could be restored. The same Leiden manuscripts later read *nec* (“nor”) instead of *ne*, without any stated reason.]

## CHAPTER XIII. That the Balearic Islands were subdued by Metellus, the Allobroges defeated by Domitius, and Etna erupted again

At the same time,

> [Note: [Col. 0946B] “Metellus and the Balearic Islands.” On the Balearic war, see Livy, Book LX, and Florus, Book III, chapter 8. FABR.]

Metellus traversed the Balearic Islands in war and subdued them; he also suppressed the piratical attacks that were then arising from those same people by slaughtering many of the inhabitants.

> [Note: [Col. 0946B] “By war.” This is absent from the Augustan edition.]

> [Note: [Col. 0946C] “Which was then arising from those same people.” The first Leiden edition has “which was arising from those same people”; Meus has “which was then arising from those same people.”]

Cnaeus Domitius, as proconsul,

> [Note: [Col. 0946C] “Domitius as proconsul.” Cnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus was consul with Gaius Fannius in the year 631. On the war he waged against the Allobroges, see Livy, Book LXI; Eutropius, Book IV; and Suetonius, *Life of Nero*. FABR.]

defeated the Gallic Allobroges near the town of Vindalium in a very severe battle, especially when the enemy’s horses and the enemy themselves, terrified by the novel appearance of the elephants, fled in confusion. Twenty thousand Allobroges are reported to have been killed there, and three thousand were captured.

> [Note: [Col. 0946C] “There.” This is absent from the second Leiden edition.]

At the same time Mount Etna erupted with greater violence than usual and, pouring forth streams of fire and spreading them widely around, overwhelmed the city of Catana and its territory, so that the roofs of the buildings, scorched and weighed down by hot ashes, collapsed. To alleviate this disaster, the senate remitted ten years of taxes to the people of Catana.

> [Col. 0945B] 319

## CHAPTER XIV. The consul Fabius routed Bituitus, king of the Arverni, though equipped with great forces, with a small army; Quintus Marcius routed other Gauls

> [Note: [Col. 0946C] In the 638th year from the founding of the City. Others give this year as the 633rd from the founding of the City. On the Allobrogian war, see Appian, *Celtica*; Strabo, Book IV; Livy, Book LXI; and Florus, Book III, chapter 2. FABR.]

In the 628th year from the founding of the City, the consul Fabius

> [Col. 0946B]

confronted Bituitus, king of the Arverni, a Gallic people,

> [Note: [Col. 0946C] “Bituitus.” Ancient bronze coins survive that are attributed to this king and bear the inscriptions ΒΙΤΟΥΚΟϹ and ΒΙΤΟΥΙΟϹ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ, “of Bituitus the king.” Beger reproduced and explained them in volume III of the *Brandenburg Thesaurus*, p. 6; I have appended them with their proper scale preserved. On Bituitus himself, a man of extraordinary height, almost miraculous, see Florus, Book III, chapter 2. FABR.]

as he was preparing for war with the greatest resources,

> [Note: [Col. 0945D] “Of Gaul.” The Augustan edition has “Gallic.”]

and met him with so small an army that Bituitus boasted that the few Romans would scarcely suffice as food for the dogs he had with him in his marching column.

> [Note: [Col. 0945D] “For the dogs, which, etc.” This passage shows that it was customary among the Gauls, when setting out for war, to take dogs with them. Strabo, an author scarcely surpassed, did not fail to note this in Book IV, p. 199, or in the newest edition p. 305, where he discusses Britain and praises, among other things, the British mastiffs: Καὶ κύνες εὐφυεῖς πρὸς τὰς κυνηγεσίας. Κελτοὶ δὲ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς πολέμους χρῶνται καὶ τούτοις, καὶ τοῖς ἐπιχωρίοις. “There are also dogs naturally well suited to hunting. The Gauls—or Celts—use these in war as well, as well as those bred among themselves.”]

When he realized that one bridge over the Rhône was insufficient for transferring his forces, he constructed another from boats joined together and connected by chains,

> [Col. 0947A]

laying and fastening planks across it.

> [Note: [Col. 0947C] “Laid across.” Meus has “placed over it.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0947C] “Constructed.” Meus has “built”; Perizonius and two Florentine manuscripts have “built.” But the Longobard manuscript has “constructed.”]

The battle was joined and fought fiercely for a long time. The Gauls were defeated and turned to flight. As each man looked to his own safety, their columns became recklessly crowded together, and in their hurried crossing they broke the fastenings of the bridge and soon sank along with the boats.
