> [Note: [Col. 0947C] “And in their hurried crossing.” The conjunction *et* is absent in the Augustan edition; instead of *transitu* (“crossing”), the first Leiden edition reads *censu*.]

> [Note: [Col. 0947C] “The battle being joined.” The battle was fought at the river Isara on the sixth day before the Ides of August, according to Pliny, Book VII, chapter 50.]

Bituitus’s army is said to have contained 180,000 armed men, of whom 150,000 were either killed or drowned.

> [Note: [Col. 0947C] “One hundred and fifty thousand.” This number appears in all our manuscripts. Livy says that 120,000 men from Bituitus’s army were killed. Appian likewise gives 120,000 (δώδεκα μυριάδας). FABR.]

The consul Quintus Marcius attacked in war a people of Gauls settled at the foot of the Alps.

> [Note: [Col. 0947D] “The consul Quintus Marcius.” Quintus Marcius Rex was consul with Marcus Porcius Cato in the year 635. On Marcius’s action, see Livy, Book LXII. FABR.]

> [Note: [Col. 0947D] “At the foot.” Meus has “at the feet.”]

When they saw themselves surrounded by the Roman forces and realized that they would be unequal to the war, they killed their wives and children and threw themselves into the flames. Those who, because the Romans had forestalled them, had not been allowed to complete their intended deaths and had been captured consumed themselves, some by the sword, some by hanging, and some by refusing food. Not a single child survived who, out of love of life, would endure the condition of slavery.

> [Note: [Col. 0947D] “Who, etc., of slavery.” Perizonius has “who by the condition of slavery preserved his life from death.”]

## CHAPTER XV. On the Jugurthine War, in which the Romans fought variously against Jugurtha, king of the Numidians

> [Note: [Col. 0947D] In the 639th year from the founding of the City. Others give this year as 642. The Jugurthine War is known from Sallust. Livy’s Epitome, Book LXIV, should be read together with what follows. In Orosius one will find certain matters not expressed in the same way by Sallust. FABR.—In the third Leiden edition, as also in Gronovius’s Collection, the number 632 is read; but in the second and fourth Leiden editions, Perizonius, and Meus, 635 is read.]

In the 639th year from the founding of the City, Publius Scipio Nasica and Lucius Calpurnius Bestia being consuls, the Roman people and senate jointly declared war against Jugurtha, king of the Numidians.

But I shall touch briefly on Jugurtha only in outline and for the purpose of mentioning him, since there is sufficient knowledge among everyone—thanks to the splendid abundance of writers—both of his varied and intolerable character and of the deeds he performed with equal deceit and energy.

> [Note: [Col. 0947D] “Sufficient.” The Augustan edition has “satisfying.” For *praestrinxerim* (“I shall touch upon”), the first Florentine edition has *strinxerim* (“I shall touch upon”). Shortly afterward, the first Florentine edition removes the conjunction *et* from *ita et* (“so also”).]

Jugurtha, therefore, the adopted son of Micipsa, king of the Numidians, and appointed heir together with his natural sons,

> [Note: [Col. 0947D] “And appointed heir.” Meus reads *haeresque institutus* (“and appointed heir”) and omits *ejus* (“his”) before “sons.”]

first killed his co-heirs—namely, Hiempsal—and then expelled Adherbal from Africa after defeating him in war.

> [Note: [Col. 0947D] “Adherbal.” The three Leiden editions, together with Gronovius’s Collection, read *Haderbalem*.] Next he corrupted the consul Calpurnius, who had been sent against him, with money and brought him to the most shameful terms of peace.

Moreover, when he himself had come to Rome,

> [Note: [Col. 0948C] “Had come.” The same manuscripts read *pervenisset* (“had arrived”).]

after corrupting or attempting to corrupt everyone with money, he mingled seditions and dissensions throughout the city. As he was leaving,

> [Note: [Col. 0948C] “Which.” The Augustan edition reads *qua cum egrederetur* (“as he was leaving it”).]

he marked it with a sufficiently infamous saying:

> “O venal city, and destined to perish quickly if it should find a buyer!”

In the following year he crushed in war, at Calama, Aulus Postumius, the brother of the consul Postumius, whom the latter had placed in command of an army of forty thousand armed men, while he was greedily coveting the royal treasures stored in that city.

> [Col. 0948C] 322

> [Note: [Col. 0948C] “Forty thousand.” I restored this from the manuscripts; the common editions have “forty thousand” in the ablative, which cannot be tolerated because of the similar construction that follows.]

Having defeated him, he exacted a most disgraceful treaty

> [Note: [Col. 0948C] “From him when defeated.” I think it should be written *eique victo*, or *cui quoque victo*; the conjunction has been deleted. The Venetian editions, together with the first edition, prefer *cui victo*. Instead of *oppressit* (“crushed”), the Augustan edition and the third Leiden edition, together with Gronovius’s Collection, have *compressit*.]

and joined almost the whole of Africa, which was defecting from the Romans, to his own kingdom.

> [Note: [Col. 0948C] “Exacted.” Perizonius reads *extorsit* (“extorted”).]

> [Note: [Col. 0948C] “Joined it to his kingdom.” The Augustan edition has “added it beneath his kingdom.”]

Afterward, however, restrained by the integrity and discipline of the consul Metellus, and defeated in two battles, he saw, while he himself was present, his Numidia being ravaged and unable to be defended. Forced by Metellus to surrender, he gave three hundred hostages, promised that he would supply grain and other provisions, and returned more than three thousand deserters.

> [Note: [Col. 0948C] “More than three thousand deserters.” This is the reading of the Longobard manuscript. Other copies have “three thousand more” or “more than three thousand deserters.”]

Then, because he was uncertain of the peace and did not restrain the raids of wicked men,

> [Note: [Col. 0948D] “Did not restrain.” The three Leiden editions, together with Gronovius’s Collection and the three Florentine manuscripts, prescribe this spelling. The common reading is *prohiberet*.]

> [Note: [Col. 0948D] “Uncertain in peace.” The Augustan edition has “received into peace” or “received peace.” But peace was not granted to Jugurtha; Marius immediately succeeded Metellus. Yet Jugurtha, pursued by Metellus according to his usual methods, although he had thus far done what was commanded after handing over the deserters, nevertheless had good reason to distrust the Romans.]

he was broken by the consul Gaius Marius, who possessed almost as much cunning as Jugurtha himself, and by the strength of the Romans—especially after Marius by deception surrounded and captured Capsa, founded, as they say, by Phoenician Hercules and then filled to overflowing with royal treasures.

> [Note: [Col. 0948D] “Then.” This is absent from the three Leiden editions and Gronovius’s Collection.]

> [Note: [Col. 0948D] “Capsa, founded by Phoenician Hercules.” Sallustius calls him Libyan Hercules. Strabo, in the final book, calls Capsa “the treasury of Jugurtha” (Κάψαν τὸ γαζοφυλάκιον τοῦ Ἰουγούρθα). FABR.]

Then, despairing of his own affairs and forces,

> [Note: [Col. 0948D] “Of his own affairs.” The common editions add *et* (“and”), “and of his own affairs,” contrary to the manuscripts.]

Jugurtha formed an alliance with Bocchus, king of the Moors. Greatly strengthened by Bocchus’s cavalry, he wore down Marius’s army with the most frequent incursions.

At last, near Cirta, an ancient city and the royal seat of Massanissa, he met the Romans, who were preparing to storm it, equipped with sixty thousand cavalry.

> [Note: [Col. 0949B] “An ancient city.” Meus has “a very ancient city.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0949B] “Sixty thousand.” The third Leiden edition and Gronovius’s Collection have “forty thousand”; the Augustan edition has “equipped with sixty thousand cavalry.”]

Never had any battle been more tumultuous or more terrifying for a Roman soldier. The dust raised by the movement and roar of the horsemen rushing about and charging covered the sky from beneath, took away the daylight, and spread night over the scene. So great a storm of missiles descended that no part of the body was safe from blows. Their sight was hindered from looking ahead by the darkness, and they lacked the opportunity to take precautions because of the crowding.

> [Note: [Col. 0949C] “By the crowding of the multitude.” This is the reading of the three Florentine manuscripts, with Meus in support. The common reading, *compressionem multitudinis* (“the crowding of the multitude”), is wholly inept. Roman soldiers were prevented from avoiding the enemy missiles for two reasons: first, because, when the missiles were thrown from afar, they could not see them through the darkness; then, when they had come close, they could not evade them by moving their bodies. Virgil, *Aeneid* V.438, on Entellus: “With his body alone, and with watchful eyes, he escapes the weapons.” They could not free themselves because of the crowding of the multitude, since they feared their own swords and had no room to step aside or backward, as Lucan says of Pompey’s army, *Pharsalia* VII.492: “Pompey’s battle-line, packed in dense masses, had joined its weapons in a row with shields interlocked; it had scarcely room to move hands and weapons, and, pressed tight, feared its own swords.” Sallust, *Jugurthine War* 102: “Without standards, without ranks, cavalry and infantry were mingled.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0949C] “A more tumultuous battle.” In this battle Marius defeated Jugurtha and Bocchus at Cirta, according to Florus, Book III, chapter 1. FABR.]

The Moorish and Numidian horsemen did not try to find a well-positioned enemy by a well-aimed cast of a weapon; rather, they threw their javelins at random, certain that the wounds would not be random.

> [Note: [Col. 0949D] “At an opportune moment.” Perizonius has “opportunely.” A few manuscripts have *tela* (“weapons”) below instead of *pila* (“javelins”).]

Thus the Roman cavalry and infantry were forced to mass together in one place.

> [Note: [Col. 0949D] “The cavalry into one place.” These words were omitted through an unfortunate lapse in some manuscripts and are neglected in all editions except the first, the Augustan, and the Paris edition. For where else could the cavalry have been at that time except in the same place as the infantry? Indeed, the crowding was all the more severe because infantry and cavalry were packed together. Sallustius, *Jugurthine War*, chapter 102: “Without standards, without ranks, cavalry and infantry mingled.”]

Night intervened and gave them a respite from so great a danger.

The next day presented the same appearance of war and danger.

> [Note: [Col. 0950B] “Appearance.” Some manuscripts add *erat* (“was”), but the better ones do not.]

The soldier could not break out against the enemy, although his sword was drawn,

> [Note: [Col. 0950C] “Was not able.” The first edition has “was not able to strike,” followed also by the Paris and Venetian editions. > [Note: [Col. 0950C] “Could not flee.” All the manuscripts I consulted prefer “could flee.” Either reading can be tolerated.]

> [Col. 0950C] 324

> [Note: [Col. 0950C] “Now the third day.” Some old editions unnecessarily add *illuxerat* (“had dawned”), contrary to the manuscripts and the Augustan edition. A little later, with equal licence, they add *et cum universo* (“and with the entire”) for *universo* (“with the entire”). The third day had now arrived, and no help appeared from any direction; everywhere the dreadful spectacle of death confronted them. At last the consul Marius, with bold despair, opened a path through hope: with the entire army at once he burst out from the rampart and gave himself simultaneously to the plain and to battle.

When the enemy again surrounded them and not only tore apart the rear of the column but also struck the center from a distance after casting their weapons, and when the Romans, thrown into confusion, were further exhausted almost to the limit of despair by the heat of the sun, their inability to endure thirst, and death surrounding them,

> [Note: [Col. 0950C] “Exhausted.” All the manuscripts have the singular “exhausted”; the Augustan and first editions, and the Paris and Venetian editions, have the singular “wearied.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0950C] “Was an unexpected salvation.” Some manuscripts and editions have *salutis* (“of salvation”) in the genitive, but less correctly.] A sudden rain supplied the thirsty and overheated Romans with cooling relief and drink.

Moreover, it made the Moorish and Numidian spear-shafts—which they customarily hurl by hand without thongs—slippery and therefore useless. Their shields, which they carried as convenient and protective coverings made from stretched and hardened elephant hide, also have this property: they absorb water they receive like a sponge and consequently become unwieldy from their sudden weight. Since the shields could not be carried about, they could no longer provide protection.

Thus, when the Moors and Numidians were unexpectedly thrown into confusion and deprived of their equipment, Bocchus and Jugurtha fled.

After this, the ninety thousand armed men whom those same kings had set against the Romans in the final battle are also reported to have been slaughtered to the last man, the Romans being victorious.

> [Note: [Col. 0950D] “Ninety thousand armed men.” I have accepted the number found in Gualther’s manuscript. > [Note: [Col. 0950D] “Through the envoy Sulla.” All the others call Sulla Marius’s quaestor. FABR.]

and soon afterward was strangled in prison.

> [Note: [Col. 0951B] “And soon afterward in prison.” We restored the conjunction *et* from all the manuscripts, supported by the Augustan edition. Some editions remove the latter word *suis* (“his”) from “with his sons.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0951B] “An obscene portent.” This portent occurred three years before the Jugurthine War, under the consuls Manius Acilius Balbus and Gaius Porcius Cato, in the year 639, as Obsequens writes. FABR.]

A short time after this,

### 327. CHAPTER XVI

[Note: [Col. 0952C] In the year 642 from the founding of the City. In other authorities this is the year 648 A.U.C. At that time Rome experienced not merely the greatest grief but also fear that the Cimbri might immediately cross the Alps and destroy Italy.

At the same time, [Note: [Col. 0953C] Q. Fabius Maximus’ son. Fabius Maximus killed his adolescent son, who had been banished to the country, with the aid of two slaves, instruments of the parricide, [Col. 0954A] and immediately freed those slaves as the reward for their crime. > By what means he might attempt an entrance, and by what path  
> Drive the Trojans shut in from the rampart and scatter them onto the plain.

For *effunderet* (“might pour forth”), most manuscripts read *refunderet* (“might pour back”).] into the open plain, decided to march into Italy in three columns.

After the enemy had departed, Marius moved his camp and occupied a hill that overlooked the plain and the river where the enemy had spread out. FABR.] and everyone was reproaching him with complaints, he replied that water was indeed in sight, but that it had to be won by the sword.

On the fourth day the battle lines on both sides were again brought out onto the plain, and they fought almost until noon with nearly equal danger. But afterward, as the sun grew hot, the loose bodies of the Gauls melted away like snow; and until nightfall the slaughter continued rather than the battle.

[Note: [Col. 0954C] Two hundred thousand armed men. Eutropius gives the same number of dead and captured. In the *Epitome of Livy*, LXVIII, ninety thousand are said to have been captured. Two hundred thousand armed men were killed in that war, eighty thousand were captured, [Note: [Col. 0954D] Scarcely three thousand. [Note: [Col. 0954D] Their women. See Valerius Maximus, Book VI, chapter 1.] Their women, with greater courage [Note: [Col. 0954D] Than if they had conquered. [Note: [Col. 0954D] Sacred virgins. That is, Vestals. Florus’ words are in Book III, chapter 3: “For, when an embassy had been sent to Marius, they did not obtain freedom and priesthood,” etc. But the learned man did not consider the following passage of Valerius Maximus, Book VI, chapter 3: “The wives of the Teutones begged the victorious Marius that they might be sent as gifts to the Vestal virgins, affirming that they, like those women, would remain untouched by intercourse with men.” I think that the women of the Cimbri asked for the latter, not priesthood itself, making an absurd request of that kind, but that they might be servants of the Vestals and of the sacred rites—something tolerable both to the defeated and to the victors. When they did not obtain what they had requested, all of them killed themselves with the sword or by hanging, after dashing their little children against rocks.

[Note: [Col. 0955C] This concerns the Tigurini and Ambrones. FABR.]

This is what happened to the Tigurini and Ambrones. But the Teutones and Cimbri, with their forces intact, crossed the snowy Alps and had overrun the plains of Italy. [Note: [Col. 0955C] Had overrun. This is how the majority of manuscripts read, as does the Augustan edition. Others have “overran.”] There, while their harsh constitution was for a long time softened by gentler breezes, drinking, food, and baths, Marius, consul for the fifth time, and Catulus were sent against them. FABR.] they followed Hannibal’s strategy: they arranged the battle in a fog but fought in sunlight.

[Note: [Col. 0956C] One woman was also found. One woman was also found who had tied two sons to her feet, with nooses passed through their necks; and when she had hanged herself to die, she dragged them down with her to be killed.

Amid these many and pitiable forms of death, two petty kings also are reported to have rushed upon one another with drawn swords. [Col. 0956B] The kings Lugius and Boiorix fell in battle. [Note: [Col. 0956C] Lugius. I found this name written thus in the manuscripts of Perizonius, in mine, and in the fourth Leiden manuscript; it is also printed thus in the Augustan edition, and seems more suitable for a barbarian than the Roman name Lucius, which the common editions have.]

Claodicus and [Note: [Col. 0956C] Cesorix. The first Leiden manuscript has Cessotrix; the third, Cesserix.] Cesorix were captured. [Note: [Col. 0956C] Claodicus. This is the spelling in three Florentine manuscripts and in the Utrecht manuscript; mine reads Claoclicus; Perizonius, Cludicus; the common editions, Claudicus; the first Leiden manuscript, Claudius.]

Thus, in these two battles, three hundred and forty thousand Gauls were killed and [Note: [Col. 0956D] One hundred and forty thousand. The Augustan edition reads one hundred and sixty thousand. [Note: [Col. 0956D] Throughout the whole city. In the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, as well as in the Groningen manuscript, *tota* (“whole”) is absent.]

[Note: [Col. 0956D] Poblicius Malleolus. Concerning this Poblicius, see Cornificius’ *Rhetorica ad Herennium*, Book I. The old copies of Livy also have “Poblicius Malleolus,” as Sigonius testifies. FABR.]

Concerning this punishment of parricides, see Modestinus, chapter 9, *Digest* “On the Pompeian Law concerning Parricide.” Cicero mentions it in his speech for Roscius of Ameria. FABR.] and thrown into the sea. Thus the Romans fulfilled both the crime and the punishment, [Note: [Col. 0957C] Hence Solon also. ### 332. CHAPTER XVII  
### On the great sedition at Rome, which arose through L. Appuleius Saturninus, C. Marius, and the others

[Note: [Col. 0957C] In the year 645. According to other annals, the sixth consulship of Marius falls in the year 653. FABR.]

In the year 645 from the founding of the City, after the Cimbrian and Teutonic war and the fifth consulship of Marius, in which the security of Roman power is judged to have been legally preserved, that security was so shaken in the sixth consulship of the same C. Marius that it nearly collapsed through internal disaster.

To unfold and traverse the labyrinths of dissension and the impenetrable causes of seditions seems both troublesome and lengthy to me. It is enough, surely, to touch briefly upon the fact that L. Appuleius Saturninus was the first author of the disturbance that was raised. He was an extremely bitter enemy of Q. Metellus Numidicus, a man of the highest distinction, [Note: [Col. 0957C] Who, when censor. Q. Metellus, censor during Marius’ fifth consulship, marked Saturninus with a censorial note; he was then subjected to insults by an agitated crowd. Cicero, *For Sextius*; Valerius, Book IX, chapter 7; Appian, Book I. FABR.] who, after having been dragged from his house when he had been elected censor and had taken refuge in the Capitol, was besieged there by an armed multitude and driven out through the indignation of the Roman knights, after a great slaughter had taken place before the Capitol. [Note: [Col. 0957D] After a great slaughter. The second and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen manuscript, read “slaughters were carried out,” with *est* understood.]

Saturninus and Glaucia, through the treachery of the consul C. Marius, then killed A. Nonius, their rival. [Note: [Col. 0957D] A. Nonius. I have written this form, since some manuscripts read Annonium and others Anunium. Appian calls him Νώνιον (*Nōnion*), and in Plutarch’s *Marius* the phrase ὁ Ὀνίου φόνος (*the murder of Onias*) is corruptly printed in place of ὁ Νυνίου. Florus, Book III, chapter 16, also corruptly has *Annio*, with one letter omitted; it should be read as *A. Nonio*. FABR.—Perizonius also has Annium; the others have Anunium or Annonium.]

In the following year, Marius being consul for the sixth time, Glaucia praetor, and Saturninus [Col. 0957C] tribune of the plebs, [Note: [Col. 0957D] Tribune of the plebs. This is how the Cologne manuscript reads, and Livy does so more than once, instead of *plebis*. LAUT.—The Orosian manuscripts regularly display this form.] conspired to drive Metellus Numidicus into exile by whatever means they could.

[Note: [Col. 0957D] After a prosecution had been initiated. Saturninus prosecuted Metellus because he had refused to swear allegiance to his agrarian law. Cicero, *For Sextius*; Livy, Book LXIX; Appian, Plutarch, and others. FABR.]

After charges had been brought against him, Metellus, though innocent, was condemned criminally by judges supplied by the same faction and departed into exile amid the grief of the entire City.

[Note: [Col. 0958C] The same Saturninus. The first Leiden manuscript reads *inde Saturninus* (“then Saturninus”).]

The same Saturninus, fearing that Memmius, an energetic and upright man, would become consul, killed him as he was fleeing during a sudden riot, [Note: [Col. 0958C] P. Mettius. In writing this name I have followed the excellent book of Cor. Gualther. FABR.—Perizonius and mine have P. Mettius; the Leiden manuscripts, Publius Vectoius.] after he had been smashed to pieces with a misshapen club by P. Mettius, his henchman.

As the Senate and Roman people raged at such great evils inflicted on the state, the consul Marius, adapting his character to the moment, mingled with the party of the respectable citizens and calmed the aroused plebs with a gentle speech.

Saturninus, with infamous ventures, [Note: [Col. 0958C] With infamous ventures. Thus the manuscripts read, not *ausibus*, as in the common editions.] held an assembly in his own house, where some called him king and others commander.

Marius, having arranged the plebs in companies, [Col. 0958B] [Note: [Col. 0958C] The other consul. L. Valerius Flaccus. For when C. Marius and L. Valerius were consuls, the Senate entrusted the defense of the state to them; Cicero, *Catiline* I, *Philippics* VIII. For a fuller history, see the speech *For Rabirius on a Charge of Treason*. FABR.] stationed the other consul with troops on a hill, while he himself fortified the gates.

A battle was fought in the Forum. Saturninus, driven from the Forum by Marius’ men, took refuge in the Capitol.

[Note: [Col. 0958C] Marius cut the pipes. Cicero: “Marius ordered the pipes by which water was supplied to the temples and precincts of Jupiter Optimus Maximus to be cut.” Plutarch: τοὺς ὀχετοὺς ἀπέκοψεν (*he cut off the conduits*). FABR.]

Marius cut the pipes through which water was conveyed there. A sufficiently terrible battle was then fought at the entrance to the Capitol, and many were killed around Saufeius and Saturninus. [Note: [Col. 0958D] Around Saufeius. C. Saufeius. Cicero and Appian have Γάϊον Σάφηιον (*Gaius Saphaios*). FABR.—I have deleted the conjunction, which is absent from the manuscripts.]

Saturninus, openly shouting and declaring that Marius was the author of all his undertakings, was himself forced by Marius, together with Saufeius and Labienus, to take refuge in the senate-house. [Note: [Col. 0958D] Into the senate-house. The Hostilian Curia, according to Velleius Paterculus. FABR.] The Roman knights broke down the doors and killed them.

C. Glaucia was dragged [Note: [Col. 0958D] From the house. All the Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen manuscript, read “from the house.”] from the house of Claudius and butchered.

[Note: [Col. 0958D] C. Furius, tribune of the plebs. Πόπλιος Φούριος δήμαρχος οὐ δ᾽ ἐλευθέρου πατρός, ἀλλ᾽ ἐξελευθέρου (*Publius Furius, tribune of the people, born not even of a free father but of a freedman*). P. Furius, tribune of the plebs, was born not to a freeborn father but to a freedman, according to Appian. Cicero, in his speech for Rabirius, calls him a man marked by every sign of disgrace. FABR.]

Furius, tribune of the plebs, decreed that the property of everyone should be confiscated.

Cn. Dolabella, Saturninus’ brother, was killed while fleeing through the vegetable market, [Col. 0958C] together with L. [Note: [Col. 0958D] L. Geganius. The Geganian family is well known in Roman history; from it came M. Geganius, three times consul during the Roman war with the Volscians. These Geganii also had the praenomen Lucius, as did L. Geganius [Col. 0959C] Macerinus, military tribune with consular power in 388 A.U.C. It is therefore pointless that three Florentine manuscripts write L. Giganius.]

Geganius.

Thus, when the authors of so great a sedition had been killed, the people enjoyed peace. [Col. 0959A] Then Cato and Pompeius proposed a bill concerning the return of Metellus Numidicus, to the joy of the entire City. [Note: [Col. 0959C] So that it might not be carried through. The majority of manuscripts read “so that it might not be completed.” Three Florentine manuscripts come closer to the true reading: “so that it might not be completed.”] The factions of the consul Marius and Furius, tribune of the plebs, intervened to prevent its passage.

Rutilius as well, a man of the utmost integrity, [Note: [Col. 0959C] Rutilius, a man of the utmost integrity. P. Rutilius Rufus, who was consul in 648, was a man with no equal in the state either in integrity or holiness. He was summoned to trial through a conspiracy of the tax farmers, against whom he had permitted no wrongdoing in his province of Asia. Imitating Socrates, he refused to beg anyone for mercy; nor did he wish his case to be pleaded more elaborately or freely than the straightforward account of the truth permitted. See Cicero, Book I of *On the Orator* and the *Brutus*; Valerius, Book VI, chapter 4; Asconius; Velleius; and others. FABR.] displayed such steadfastness of faith and innocence that, after his accusers had brought charges against him, he neither grew his hair or beard until the hearing, nor sought supporters through dirty clothing or a humble appearance, nor softened his enemies, nor influenced the judges. Even the speech granted him by the praetor was no more submissive than his spirit.

Although he was attacked by manifest falsehood and was thought by all good men rightly deserving of acquittal, he was condemned through the perjury of the judges. [Note: [Col. 0959C] When he moved to Smyrna. Hence Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, Book I:

> And marvel at the stern strength of great-hearted Rutilius,  
> Who did not make use of the condition of return that had been granted;  
> Smyrna held the man, etc.

Cicero, in his speech for Balbus, states that Rutilius, while living in exile at Smyrna, was made a citizen of that city. FABR.]

He moved to Smyrna and grew old devoted to literary studies.

### 335. CHAPTER XVIII  
### On the Social War, in which the Italian peoples, revolting from the Romans, rebelled; and also on various prodigies
[Note: [Col. 0959D] In the year 659 from the founding of the City. In the Capitoline Fasti this year is 662 from the founding of the City, when M. Livius Drusus, tribune of the plebs, stirred up a revolt; concerning this Livius, Book 71, Appian, Book 1, Florus, Book 3, chapter 17, Velleius, Book 2. Read Cicero’s Preface to the third book *On the Orator*. FABR.]

In the year 659 from the founding of the City, during the consulship of Sextus Julius Caesar and Lucius Marcius Philippus, the Social War, arising from internal causes, stirred up all Italy. [Note: [Col. 0959D] “Stirred up all Italy.” Some manuscripts and editions, less correctly, have “stirred up all of Italy.”] Since Livius Drusus, tribune of the plebs, incited all the Latins, enticed by the hope of freedom, to take up arms, when he was unable to fulfill his promises. [Note: [Col. 0959D] “When he was unable to fulfill what had been agreed.” Three Florentine manuscripts have *cum placito*, and so also my manuscript and the Venetian editions. The second Leiden edition, the Utrecht edition, and the Augustan edition read *placitum explere*; but three other Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, read *placitum expugnare*. I think one should read *cum pollicita explere non posset*, “when he was unable to fulfill what he had promised.” The Epitome of Livy, Book 71, concerning this same Livius Drusus: “When thereafter the citizenship promised to the allies could not be granted.”]

[Note: [Col. 0960C] “To this was added.” Thus the manuscripts; the old editions have *quo*, Perizonius *eoque*.]

To this was added the fact that dreadful prodigies terrified the sorrowful City. [Note: [Col. 0960C] “Dreadful prodigies.” Julius Obsequens relates these prodigies. Cicero too, in Book 1 of *On Divination*, reports several prodigies that Sisenna had described at the beginning of the Marsic War. FABR.] For at sunrise, a ball of fire flashed forth from the northern region with an immense crashing of the sky. At Arretium, while loaves were being broken at banquets, blood flowed from the middle of the loaves as if from wounds in bodies. Moreover, for seven consecutive days hailstones, mixed also with fragments of pottery, beat upon the earth over a very wide area. In Samnium, from an enormous fissure in the earth, a flame burst forth and seemed to extend up to the heavens. Furthermore, several Romans saw on their journey a sphere of golden color roll down from the sky toward the earth, grow larger, and then be carried back from the earth into the heights toward the rising sun, finally covering the sun itself with its size.

[Note: [Col. 0960C] “Drusus, distressed by such great evils.” Drusus was struck at home with a knife, which remained embedded in his side, and died within a few hours, according to Velleius. Seneca, in *On the Shortness of Life*, says that he collapsed after receiving a wound in the groin, with some people doubting whether his death had been voluntary or timely. See also Pliny, Book 28, chapter 9, and the author of *On Illustrious Men*. FABR.]

Drusus, distressed by such great evils, was killed in his own house, though the author of the deed was uncertain.

336 Accordingly, the Picentes, Vestini, Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini, Samnites, and [OCR: Lncani; probably Lucani], while still secretly planning revolt, killed at Asculum C. Servilius, the praetor sent to them as envoy, [Note: [Col. 0960C] “C. Servilius.” The books commonly and incorrectly have C. Servius; the same error occurs in Velleius. Livy, Book 67, has Q. Servilius the proconsul; Appian calls him Σερουΐλιον ἀνθύπατον, “Servilius the proconsul.” FABR.] and immediately, after closing the city, slaughtered all the Roman citizens in a massacre that had been ordered. [Note: [Col. 0960D] “Without an order for slaughter.” That is, “without it having been commanded”—a frequent meaning of this verb among authors. I mention this so that no one, following Freinshemius on Florus, Book 3, chapter 18, may try to change it to *indigna*, “unworthy.”]

Immediately the most infamous prodigies preceded this most atrocious disaster. [Note: [Col. 0960D] “Most infamous.” My manuscript has *infandissima*, “most unspeakable.”] For animals of every kind, accustomed to endure the touch of human hands gently and to live among human beings, abandoned their stalls and pastures and fled to the forests and mountains with pitiable bleating, neighing, and lowing. Even dogs, whose nature it is to be unable to exist outside human society, wandered about with tearful howls like wolves. [Note: [Col. 0960D] “Whose nature it is.” The better manuscript copies require this reading. The common editions have *quorum natura est*, “whose nature is.”]

Accordingly, the praetor Gnaeus Pompeius waged war against the Picentes by order of the senate, and was defeated. The Samnites had appointed Papius Mutilus as their commander, while the Marsi had preferred Agamemnon, the arch-pirate. [Note: [Col. 0960D] “Papius Mutilus.” Velleius has *Papius Mutilius*, but Appian names him Γάϊον Πάπιον Μότιλον (*Gaius Papius Mutilus*); Diodorus, in the excerpts of Book 37, has Γάϊον Ἀπώνιον Μότυλον (*Gaius Aponius Motylus*). FABR.]

Julius Caesar, defeated in battle by the Samnites, fled with his army slaughtered. [Note: [Col. 0960D] “Julius Caesar.” L. Julius Caesar was consul; Appian has Sextus Caesar instead. See Livy, Book 73. FABR.] The consul Rutilius chose his kinsman Marius as his legate. Marius repeatedly urged him that delay would be advantageous in the war and that the inexperienced soldiers ought to train in camp for a little while. Rutilius, thinking that Marius was doing this deceptively, despised his advice and recklessly led himself and the entire column of his army into an ambush of the Marsi. There the consul himself was killed, many nobles were slain, and eight thousand Romans were massacred.

The river Tolenus carried the weapons and bodies of the slain into the sight of Marius, the legate, and raised them up as evidence of the disaster. [Note: [Col. 0961C] “The river Tolenus.” Appian writes that Rutilius and Marius had their camps on the river Liris, not far apart, and that Marius inferred Rutilius’s defeat from the corpses being carried along by that river. FABR.]

Marius immediately gathered his forces and unexpectedly overwhelmed the victors. [Note: [Col. 0961C] “He unexpectedly overwhelmed them.” *Insperatos* is poor Latin in the historical context. All the Leiden manuscripts have *insperatus*, that is, “sudden, unforeseen, unexpected.” Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* 3.13: “The Cyrenaics do not think that every evil produces distress, but only an unforeseen and unexpected evil.”] He too killed eight thousand of the Marsi.

Caepio, led into an ambush by the Vestini and Marsi, was massacred with his army. Lucius Julius Caesar, after having been defeated and fleeing at Aesernia, gathered forces from every direction and, fighting against the Samnites and Lucani, killed many thousands of the enemy. When the army had proclaimed him commander and he had sent messengers to Rome concerning the victory, the senate laid aside the *sagum*—that is, the garment of mourning—which it had assumed when the Social War began, encouraged by this hope, and recovered the ancient dignity of the toga.

[Note: [Col. 0961C] “Marius then killed six thousand.” Plutarch mentions this battle, in which Marius killed six thousand of the enemy, in his *Life of Marius*. FABR.]

Marius then killed six thousand Marsi and stripped seven thousand of their arms. Sulla, sent with twenty-four cohorts to Aesernia, where Roman citizens and soldiers were being hard pressed by a very close siege, saved the city and its allies in a great battle and after much slaughter of the enemy.

Gnaeus Pompeius routed the Picentes in a severe battle. By this victory the senate recovered the broad-striped senatorial tunic and the other insignia of rank, since it had assumed only the togas after Caesar’s victory, when it first began to breathe again. [Note: [Col. 0961C] “The senate’s broad-striped tunic.” Thus the old books read. Livy, Book 74, says that, because of this victory, the bordered togas and other insignia of magistrates were assumed at Rome. FABR.] [Note: [Col. 0961C] “When it first began to breathe again.” All manuscripts and editions read *primum respirante*, except that some old editions read *de victoria*, and so forth. Perizonius’s manuscript has *victoria Caesaris prima*. I think one should write *respirans*. For previously, after Caesar’s victory, the senate had begun to breathe again from evils and distress; now, after that of Gnaeus Pompeius, it began to promise itself a favorable outcome. In the margin of Scott’s edition one reads *respirante civitate*, “the state breathing again,” but this is contrary to the manuscripts, which preserve the complete word.]

Porcius Cato, the praetor, and Plotius, the legate, defeated the Etruscans and Umbrians respectively, at the cost of much blood and with the greatest difficulty. [Note: [Col. 0961D] “Cato the praetor [defeated] the Etruscans.” These words too are commonly read confusedly, whereas they are distinct in the ancient copies. See Livy. FABR.]

During the consulship of Gnaeus Pompeius and Lucius Porcius Cato, Pompeius besieged the city of Asculum for a long time. [Note: [Col. 0961D] “And yet.” The Augustan edition has *quam non*, “which he would not have,” instead.] Yet he would not have captured it if he had not defeated the people who were rushing out into the field by a very severe assault. In that battle eighteen thousand Marsi were killed together with their commander Franco, and three thousand were captured.

But four thousand Italian men who had escaped from that slaughter climbed, perhaps, to the mountain ridge in a single column forced together. [Note: [Col. 0961D] “Perhaps they had climbed.” Three Florentine manuscripts have *forte consederant*, “perhaps they had settled,” except that *forte* is absent from the first Florentine manuscript. That reading is sufficiently good if *jugo* is restored in place of *jugum*, as I find it in the Augustan edition, although *conscenderant* is retained there. In the first Leiden edition *forte* is also absent.] There they were overwhelmed and stiffened in a pitiable death beneath the snow. [Note: [Col. 0962C] “They stiffened in a pitiable death.” Above, concerning Hannibal and his army, Book 4, chapter 14: “Caught by a storm on the summit of the Apennines, he remained motionless with his army for two continuous days, enclosed and burdened by snow, and grew rigid.”]

For, just as they had stood stunned by fear of the enemy, some appeared leaning against tree trunks or rocks, others resting upon their own weapons; all had their eyes open and their teeth bared, and seemed, as it were, to be alive. To those looking from a distance, there was no indication of death except their prolonged immobility, which the vitality of human life cannot endure for any length of time. [Note: [Col. 0962C] “For thus, and so forth.” Just like those who, fighting with Phineus against Perseus and transformed into stones by the petrifying face of Medusa, seemed to live on, in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 5.211.]

On the same day the Picentes engaged in battle and were defeated. Their leader Judacilius, having summoned his chiefs, after a magnificent feast and abundant drinking, urged them all to follow his example and, having drunk poison, perished. All praised his deed, but no one followed him. [Note: [Col. 0962C] “Their leader Judacilius.” Γαῖος Ἰουδακίλιος (*Gaius Judacilius*). Appian says that he took poison at Asculum. FABR.—In the Lombard manuscript the reading is *Vidacilius*, and this name is also noted in the margins of some editions.] [Note: [Col. 0962C] “Having summoned his chiefs.” The later word is deleted in the fourth Leiden manuscript, and the sentence can do without it. For *absumptus*, the first edition reads *consumptus est*, “was consumed.”]

In the year 661 from the founding of the City, when the Roman army had gone to besiege Pompeii, [Note: [Col. 0962C] “To besiege Pompeii.” This is the correct reading, retained from the ancient editions only by the Augustan edition and also preserved as a marginal annotation in the inferior manuscripts of Hitter and Bolswing. Fabricius and Scott restored it, whereas previously the text read: “when Pompeius and the Roman army had gone to besiege the Samnites.” Some manuscripts retain this reading, while others alter it. Mine has: “when Pompeius and the Roman army had gone to besiege the Samnites.” The second Leiden edition and the Utrecht edition read: “when the Roman army had gone—or departed—to besiege Asculum.” The first, third, and fourth Leiden editions, together with Gronovius’s collection, read: “when Pompeius and the Roman army had gone to besiege Asculum.”

The historical circumstances are as follows. According to Orosius, in the year 661 from the founding of the City, but according to Pighius in 665, during the consulship of Lucius Cornelius Sulla and Quintus Pompeius Rufus, the Social War was fought in Campania between Sulla, the Roman consul, and Lucius Cluentius, an Italian, together with Mutilus, the Samnite commander. The circumstances of the battle must be taken from Appian, who writes in *Civil Wars* 1, p. 380: Λεύκιος δὲ Κλοέντιος Σύλλᾳ περὶ Πομπαῖα ὄρη στρατοπεδεύοντι μάλα καταφρονητικῶς ἀπὸ σταδίων τριῶν παρεστρατοπεδεύε — “Lucius Cluentius, daring to despise Sulla, who was encamped near the Pompeian mountains, pitched his own camp three stades away.”

He then relates how they fought twice: Sulla was defeated in the first battle, but in the second he defeated the enemy and pursued them as far as the city of Nola, inflicting a great slaughter, so that thirty thousand of them perished in battle and flight, and another twenty thousand, including Cluentius himself, fell before the gates of Nola.

That the town of Pompeii was at that time attacked by the Romans is clear from the words of Velleius Paterculus, Book 2, chapter 16. In commending the memory of his ancestor Minatius Magius, he writes that, although an Asculan, he was so loyal to the Romans that, with the legion he himself had enrolled among the Hirpini, he captured Herculaneum together with T. Didius, besieged Pompeii with L. Sulla, and occupied Cosa. From Pliny we learn that Stabiae, in the Campanian territory, was destroyed by Sulla in the same disaster of war, *Natural History* 3.5, p. 157: “In the Campanian territory, the town of Stabiae existed until the consulship of Gnaeus Pompeius and Lucius Cato, on the day before the Kalends of May, when Lucius Sulla, as legate in the Social War, destroyed it; it has now become a country estate.” It follows that the calamity of Stabiae occurred in the year before the siege of Pompeii.]

and Postumius Albinus, a former consul and at that time L. Sulla’s legate, having aroused the hatred of all the soldiers against himself through intolerable arrogance, was killed by stoning. [Note: [Col. 0963C] “Postumius Albinus.” Valerius, Book 9, chapter 8, relates the killing of this Postumius Albinus. FABR.—His full name was A. Postumius Albinus. Because of the scarcity of writers, we do not know what his arrogance was; Valerius recognizes none in him, but writes that he was buried under stones by the army in the camp because of false and empty suspicions.]

The consul Sulla declared that Roman blood could be expiated only by the blood of the enemy. Moved by consciousness of this deed, the army attacked the battle in such a way that each man saw that he must perish unless he conquered. [Note: [Col. 0963D] “Because of this deed.” Perizonius has “because of that deed.”] [Note: [Col. 0963D] “Thus he attacked the battle.” The old editions have *ita pugnam adorsus est*. The fourth Leiden manuscript has *ita in pugnam exortus est*, which seems to point toward the reading preferred by the Augustan edition and by the first and second Leiden manuscripts: *ita pugnam exorsus est*.] [Note: [Col. 0963D] “Unless he conquered.” Perizonius’s manuscript has *nisi vinceret*, “unless he conquered.”]

Eighteen thousand Samnites were killed in that battle. He also pursued and killed Juventius, an Italian commander, together with a large part of his people. [Note: [Col. 0963D] “Eighteen thousand.” This is how it is printed in the Augustan edition and written in three Florentine manuscripts. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, count one thousand more. The old editions have eighteen thousand.]

The consul Porcius Cato, commanding Marius’s forces, after having performed several notable deeds, boasted that Gaius Marius had accomplished nothing greater. Therefore, when he was waging war against the Marsi at Lake Fucinus, he was struck down in the confusion of battle by Gaius Marius’s son, as though by an unknown assailant. [Note: [Col. 0963D] “By Gaius Marius’s son.” We owe this detail to Orosius, who used writers of this war whom we now lack. Eutropius, Book 5, chapter 3, p. 205: “The consul P. Rutilius was killed in it; Caepio, a noble young man, and Porcius Cato, the other consul, [were killed].” Appian likewise simply records his death in the passage cited, p. 380: Τοῦ δὲ αὐτοῦ χειμῶνος Κορνήλιος μὲν Κάτων, ὁ σύναρχος τοῦ Πομπηΐου, Μάρσοις πολεμῶν ἀνῃρέθη — “In the same winter Cornelius Cato, Pompeius’s fellow consul, was killed while waging war against the Marsi.” Cato’s death therefore preceded the victory of Sulla, who succeeded him in the consulship and command.]

The legate Gaius Gabinius was killed while storming the enemy camp. [Note: [Col. 0964C] “Gaius Gabinius.” Livy, Book 76, calls him A. Gabinius; the praenomen Gaius is absent from one manuscript. FABR.] The Marrucini and Vestini were devastated while Sulpicius, Pompeius’s legate, pursued them.

Pompaedius and Obsidius, Italian commanders, were overwhelmed and killed by the same Sulpicius in a dreadful battle beside the river THeanus. [Note: [Col. 0964C] “Pompaedius.” Thus it appears in Gualther’s book. Appian calls him Κοΐντον Πομπάδιον (*Quintus Pompaedius*), while in the books of Livy and Velleius he is called *Silo Popedius*. In Plutarch’s *Apophthegmata* he is erroneously called Πομπίου Σίλωνος, and in the *Life of Marius*, Ποπίου Σίλωνος. In Diodorus the correct form is Κοΐντος Πομπαίδιος Σίλων (*Quintus Pompaedius Silo*). FABR.—The Augustan edition too reads *Q. Pompaedius*, not *Q. Popedius*.]

[Note: [Col. 0964C] “Obsidius.” It is worth noting that the name written above this man in the parchment and most ancient manuscript—the first among the Leiden manuscripts—is L. Opidius. Orosius alone mentions Obsidius or Opidius. Pliny, Book 36, chapter 26, reports that in Samnium a little stone of the deepest black color is produced, called *obsidian*, and that glass of the same color is therefore called *obsidian glass*. Freinshemius lists the commanders of the Social War who stood against the Romans in his notes on Florus, Book 3, chapter 8.]

Pompeius entered Asculum and beat its prefects, centurions, and all its leading men with rods and struck them with the axe; he sold the slaves and all the booty under the auctioneer’s spear, and ordered the others—free, indeed, but naked and destitute—to depart. Although he hoped that the senate would use some portion of this booty to support the public pay, Pompeius contributed nothing from it to the impoverished treasury.

For at the same time, when the treasury had been completely exhausted and there was not enough money for the grain allowance, the public lands around the Capitol, which had been handed over for possession to the pontiffs, augurs, decemvirs, and flamines, were sold under the pressure of necessity, and a sufficient sum of money was received to serve as a temporary remedy for the shortage.

And indeed, at that time, wealth scraped together from every side out of all the overthrown cities and devastated lands was being heaped into the bosom of the state itself, while Rome herself, driven by shameful want, was auctioning off her principal parts. [Note: [Col. 0964D] “Into its bosom.” I prefer *in sinum*, as in the first and Augustan editions and in my and Perizonius’s manuscripts, to *in sinus*, which others and the common editions have.] [Note: [Col. 0964D] “Driven by shameful want.” The Augustan edition has *turpi vel indigente inopia*, “by shameful or pressing want.”] [Note: [Col. 0964D] “Her principal parts.” The third Leiden manuscript, together with Gronovius’s collection, has *quae praecipua sui parte auctionabatur*, “which was being auctioned in its chief parts.”]

Therefore, let anyone consider what the times were like then, when Rome, like an insatiable belly consuming everything and always hungry, more wretched herself than all the cities she was making wretched, leaving nothing and possessing nothing, was driven by the spur of domestic hunger into the continuation of the unrest of war. [Note: [Col. 0964B] “Consuming everything.” Perizonius’s manuscript has *omnia consumens*, “consuming everything,” because of what follows, I think: “as I do with all the cities.”]

At the same time, King Sothimus entered Greece with large Thracian auxiliaries and ravaged all the territory of Macedonia. Finally, defeated by the praetor Gaius Sentius, he was forced to return to his kingdom.

341 **CHAPTER XIX. On the Marian and Mithridatic Civil War, in which Sulla and Marius brought the greatest disturbances and disasters upon the state.**

[Col. 0965A]

[Note: [Col. 0965B] In the year 662 from the founding of the City. Eutropius, Book 5, counts it this way. For others it is the year 665, when L. Cornelius Sulla and Q. Pompeius Rufus were consuls. FABR.]

In the year 662 from the founding of the City, while the Social War had not yet ended, the first civil war was stirred up at Rome. In the same year the Mithridatic War was also begun—less infamous, certainly, but no less serious. [Note: [Col. 0965C] “The Mithridatic War.” The second word is absent from the Augustan edition. Shortly afterward, *primum*, “first,” is missing from the first and Venetian editions.]

Indeed, the duration of the Mithridatic War has been reported variously: whether it first began at this point, or whether it then chiefly burst into flame, especially since some report that it was waged for thirty years and others for forty. [Note: [Col. 0965C] “Some thirty, others forty.” If one counts from Sulla and Pompeius to the consuls Piso and Messalla, under whom Pompeius celebrated his triumph after the Mithridatic War was completed, one finds twenty-seven years. But Florus, Book 3, chapter 5, writes that Mithridates resisted for forty years; Appian, in his *Mithridatic War*, says that this war lasted forty-two years.] Yet although these events, carried out in the same period, flared up in a confused heap of evils, I shall nevertheless present them individually, each in its proper place, though briefly.

When Sulla was consul, and Marius was setting out for Asia with an army against Mithridates, but remained in Campania because of the remnants of the Social War, Marius sought a seventh consulship and the undertaking of the Mithridatic War. When Sulla learned of this, he, a truly impatient young man, inflamed by unrestrained anger, first took up position before the City with four legions. There he killed Gratidius, Marius’s legate, as the first victim of the civil war. [Note: [Col. 0965C] “And conversely.” Some old editions, contrary to the manuscripts, have omitted this conjunction.] [Note: [Col. 0965C] “But remaining in Campania.” Nola was obstinately holding on to its arms and was being besieged by the Roman army. Velleius. FABR.] [Note: [Col. 0965C] “Gratidius, Marius’s legate.” The soldiers slaughtered Gratidius, whom Marius had sent as his legate to Sulla to receive the legions. Valerius, Book 9, chapter 7. Plutarch, in his *Life of Marius*, writes that Marius himself sent two military tribunes to take over Sulla’s army, and that the soldiers killed them. FABR.]

Soon afterward he burst into the City with his army and asked for torches with which to set the City ablaze. While everyone hid in fear, he entered the Forum by the Sacred Way at a swift pace.

When Marius had unsuccessfully attempted to move the nobility, inflame the plebs, and finally arm the equestrian order against Sulla, he at last tried in vain to resist after enticing slaves to take up arms with the hope of freedom and booty, and withdrew to the Capitol. [Note: [Col. 0965D] “Had attempted.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, have *tentasset*. Above, for *denique*, some old editions have *deinde*.] [Note: [Col. 0965D] “Having dared to resist in vain.” The Augustan edition has *neque quidquam repugnare ausus*, “having dared to resist nothing.”]

But when Sulla’s cohorts rushed in after him, he escaped amid the great slaughter of his followers. There Sulpicius, Marius’s colleague, was struck down after being betrayed by his own slave. [Note: [Col. 0965D] “His colleague, Sulpicius.” P. Sulpicius, tribune of the plebs, had proposed a law that the Mithridatic War should be assigned to Marius and had been the author of the revolt. Livy, Book 77; Velleius 2; Valerius, Book 6, chapter 5; Appian, Book 1; Plutarch, *Lives of Marius and Sulla*; Cicero, *Brutus*; and others. FABR.]

The consuls decreed that the slave himself should be freed because he had revealed an enemy, but that, because he had betrayed his master, he should be thrown from the Tarpeian Rock.

While Marius was fleeing and had been surrounded by the persistence of his pursuers, he hid himself in the marshes of Minturnae. There, unfortunately smeared with mud and dragged out in disgrace, he was taken to Minturnae as a shameful spectacle and thrust into prison. [Note: [Col. 0965D] “In the marshes of the Minturnians.” In addition to those I have named, read Cicero’s speeches *For Sextius* and *Against Piso*. FABR.] He terrified the executioner sent against him by his mere expression.

Then, having slipped his bonds, he fled to Africa. Having summoned his son from Utica, where he was being held under guard, [Note: [Col. 0966B] “Having summoned him.” The Augustan edition has *solutoque*, “having released him.” I nevertheless prefer the common reading, for the word *observabatur*, “was being watched,” seems to indicate that he was in free custody. Moreover, Sextilius, the praetor of Africa at that time, is said to have been neither Marius’s friend nor his enemy. Thus he did nothing harsh against the elder Marius, but when he came ashore he sent a lictor to meet him and order him to leave the province. See Plutarch, *Life of Marius*, p. 429. Therefore he could not have released the son from custody. It seems rather that Marius’s son himself secretly escaped from custody. For how could the captive father, in a sudden and unprepared situation, have sent messengers across the sea to his son from Minturnae? Plutarch, *Life of Marius*, p. 428, writes that the younger Marius, together with Cethegus, reached the Numidian king Hiempsal in flight. Appian, p. 388, calls this Numidian prince Mandrestal; learn from Plutarch how great a danger he later created for the Marii and the Marian party, and about their remarkable flight.]

Marius immediately returned to Rome and joined forces with the consul Cinna in a partnership of crimes. [Note: [Col. 0966C] “Where he was in custody.” This is correctly written in the first and third Florentine manuscripts and also in my manuscript. The Augustan edition has *ubi is in custodia*, and the common editions *ubi is custodia*. Perizonius soon afterward has *servabatur*, “was being guarded.”] [Note: [Col. 0966C] “With the consul Cinna.” L. Cornelius Cinna was consul with Gnaeus Octavius after Sulla’s consulship; together they began the Octavian War, which Cicero mentions in Book 2 of *On the Nature of the Gods*. See Plutarch, *Life of Sulla*; Appian, Book 1; Livy, Books 79 and 88; Velleius; Florus; Eutropius; and others. FABR.]

Accordingly, in order to overthrow the entire state, they divided their army into four parts. [Note: [Col. 0966D] “Their army.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, have *exercitum sic in quatuor partes*, “their army thus into four parts”; shortly afterward, the Augustan edition has *quidem* in place of *siquidem*.] Three legions were assigned to Marius; Gnaeus Carbo was placed over one portion of the forces, and Sertorius took another. [Note: [Col. 0966D] “One part Sertorius.” Concerning Quintus Sertorius, see Plutarch’s *Life of Sertorius*. FABR.] This was that Sertorius who, already from this point, was an instigator and participant in the civil war and who, even after this war had ended, later stirred up another in Spain, prolonging it for many years with the greatest disasters to the Romans. [Note: [Col. 0966D] “Already from this point, an instigator of the civil war, etc.” I have restored this most excellent reading from the first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection; most old editions agree with them. The common reading, *jam hic*, is worthless. Lucan speaks similarly of Antony, Book 5, line 478: “Antony was a leader bold in every kind of warfare, even then plotting Leucas in the civil war.”] The remaining portion of the army followed Cinna.

Gnaeus Pompeius, whom the senate had summoned with an army to aid the state and who had long held himself back in expectation of revolutionary opportunities, was despised by Marius or Cinna and went over to Octavius, the other consul. Soon afterward he engaged Sertorius. The unfortunate battle was broken off by the arrival of night. Six hundred soldiers from both sides were slaughtered. [Note: [Col. 0967C] “Six hundred.” Colonus alone, drawing the complete figure from the history, wrote *sexcenteni* instead of *sexcenti*. LAUT.—Soon afterward Perizonius’s manuscript has *mixtim*, “mixed together”; the first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with Gronovius’s collection, have *permixta*.]

On the following day, when the bodies were being sorted out indiscriminately for burial, a Pompeian soldier. [Note: [Col. 0967C] “Of his own brother.” Lucan, Book 7, line 550:] [Note: [Col. 0967C] “Of his own brother.” Lucan, Book 7, line 550:]

That place had brothers; that place had parents. ] He recognized the body of his brother, whom he himself had killed. [Note: [Col. 0967C] “Both.” Some manuscripts and editions read utrimque, “on both sides”; the first Leiden edition: in concursu enim utrimque facto, “for when a clash had occurred on both sides.”]

For in the clash, the helmet deprived both men of recognition of the face, and frenzy deprived them of consideration: although there is little excuse in ignorance, since he appears not to have known his brother, whom he is undoubtedly known to have recognized as a fellow citizen. [Note: [Col. 0967C] “Having cursed.” The Augustan edition reads exsecrans, “cursing.”]

Thus the victor, more wretched than the vanquished, when he recognized both his brother’s body and his own act of fratricide, cursed the civil wars and immediately pierced his own breast with his sword; at the same time pouring forth tears and blood, he threw himself upon his brother’s corpse.

[Note: [Col. 0967C] “For the confounding” (ad confusionem). The Augustan edition adds the reading ad confessionem, “for confession.” But the older Orosian reading is sound. He says that private piety did not avail publicly, nor did it confound the Romans so that they might avoid similar examples and desist from criminal warfare.]

And what did this accomplish toward exposing the cruelty of the undertaking, when, at the very beginning of the civil wars, the infamous report spread everywhere that brothers, indeed ignorant of one another but citizens conscious of their identity, had engaged one another; that one had attacked his brother, victorious through crime, and had stripped the slain brother of his spoils; and that soon afterward, guilty of such monstrous brutality, he had, by the same sword and the same hand, through his own death, avenged the fratricide he had committed?

[Note: “Anyone.” The Perizonian manuscript made Orosius richer by one word, inserting aliquem, “anyone.” No one will deny that word’s necessity, since what follows is Numquid apud quemquam, “Did anyone at all…?” Four Leiden manuscripts and the Utrecht manuscript read Numquid intentarum animositates partium. The same reading appears in the first and second Florentine manuscripts, although it is corrected in the second.]

Did such a grievous example move anyone amid the passions of factions so great? Did the danger of crime, through the terror of error, repel anyone?

[Note: “Did these things…?” I think it should be written Num quis, haec, quae communis est, etc. “Did anyone,” he says, “tremble at these things,” that is, “before these things”—a reading confirmed by what follows: “and, overcome by conscience, withdraw from an undertaking of this sort”? For I do not see how the words can otherwise fit together adequately. Alternatively, with the correction of the Perizonian manuscript— which reads conscientia victa, “with conscience overcome,” instead of conscientia victus, “overcome by conscience”—the passage seems to require the following punctuation: “Did anyone tremble at this—an act which even with beasts is a common piety and reverence for nature—that, because what one man committed by killing and dying could be done to oneself, and did anyone, overcome by conscience, withdraw from an undertaking of this kind?”]

Did anyone tremble at this piety and reverence for nature, shared even with beasts, because what one man had committed by killing and dying could be done to oneself, and withdraw from such an undertaking, overcome by conscience? On the contrary, for nearly the following forty years the civil wars continued to such an extent that the magnitude of the praise might be thought to be proportionate to the magnitude of the crime.

[Note: “To be weighed against.” At my own risk I have adopted appendenda here in place of appetenda in the text; unless I give the true word, I should be prosecuted by the praetor for an action for damages. —Laut. We recovered this reading after Lautius from manuscripts, nearly all of which read it thus or have it written above the line as the reading intended. The common reading is appetenda, “to be desired,” which is in no way equal to the elegance of the other. Appendenda signifies an equal weighing of praise and crime. Orosius does not say that such praise is simply to be desired because of the magnitude of the crime, but that it is to be assessed by comparison, using the image of scales and of things placed upon them. The first Florentine manuscript additionally reads ad magnitudinem sceleris, “in proportion to the magnitude of the crime.”]

[Note: [Col. 0968C] “In such a warfare.” Some manuscripts and editions read in tali malitia, “in such wickedness,” and shortly afterward, fugissent, “would have fled.”]

For everyone, after such a lesson, would have shunned the dangers of fratricide in such a warfare, unless they had themselves desired fratricides. Accordingly, Marius entered the colony of Ostia by force and practiced there every kind of lust, avarice, and cruelty.

[Note: “The colony of Ostia.” Appian, Book I; Plutarch, Life of Sulla; Livy, Book LXXIX, report this.]

Pompey was struck by lightning and perished; his army, seized by pestilence, was almost entirely destroyed. For eleven thousand men from Pompey’s camp died, while six thousand from the side of the consul Octavius were lost.

[Note: “Were lost.” Perizonius reads deleta sunt, “were destroyed.” But three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read siderata sunt, as though they meant “were struck by an evil star.” The Augustan edition also prints siderata; others have debilitata sunt, “were weakened.”]

Marius stormed the cities of Antium and Aricia like an enemy and killed everyone in them except the traitors, allowing their property to be plundered by his own men.

[Note: “Antium and Aricia.” Appian has Ἄντιον καὶ Ἀρικίαν καὶ Λανούβιον, “Antium, Aricia, and Lanuvium.”]

Afterward, when the consul Cinna entered the City with his legions and Marius with the fugitives, they killed the most distinguished men of the Senate and very many men of consular rank.

[Note: “The most distinguished men.” Among them were three orators: Q. Catulus, M. Antonius, and C. Julius Caesar, concerning whom Cicero writes in the Brutus. At that time the consuls Octavius and Merula were also killed, as were Crassus the father and son and many others; concerning them see Appian, Book I; Livy, Book LXXX; Lucan, Book II; Velleius, and others.]

But how small a portion of the misery displayed is it to define in a single word the slaughter of the good, whose extent, duration, cruelty, and variety were so great? Nevertheless, it is more equitable that I should have withheld some usefulness from the account than that I should have inflicted so much horror upon the knowledge of it, whether these matters are presented to the learned or to the ignorant. For we are speaking of our fatherland, our fellow citizens, and our ancestors—people who, harassed by these evils, committed such abominable acts that even later generations shudder when they hear of them. Surely they do not wish these things to be exaggerated beyond measure, either because they know them through a sufficient degree of knowledge, or, if they do not know them, through the contemplation of compassionate reverence.

[Note: “Compassionate reverence.” The reading of the Augustan edition, in secundos, reverentiae contemplatione, “through the contemplation of reverence toward the unfortunate,” perhaps ought not to be dismissed.]

Accordingly, when Marius brought the heads of the murdered citizens to banquets, displayed them in the Capitolia,

[Note: “To the Capitolia.” Since this is the consistent reading of all the manuscripts, also approved by the Augustan edition, I do not know why all the other editions retain oblata Capitolio, “displayed at the Capitol,” as though Orosius could not, in imitation of the poets, especially Virgil, use Capitolia in the plural.]

and placed them on the Rostra,

[Note: “Placed on the Rostra.” I find this in all the manuscripts. Nevertheless, the editions restored collocata rostris, “placed on the Rostra,” instead of in rostris, “on the Rostra,” although they ought at least to have restored the preposition. But Orosius seems to have continued the ablative in all three expressions: collata therefore means “given” or “offered,” “presented.”]

and had reached his seventh consulship together with Cinna as consul for the third time, he was finally carried off by a belated death at the beginning of his consular power.

[Note: “When Cinna was consul for the third time.” In the year 667 from the founding of the City, when C. Marius was consul for the seventh time and Cinna for the second time, Marius died at the beginning of his consulship, on the Ides of January, according to Livy, Book LXXX, and Plutarch, Life of Marius. L. Valerius Flaccus was substituted in his place; he is discussed in the following book.]

Cinna made up for the slaughter of the good by the massacre of the wicked. For when the insatiable band of fugitives introduced by Marius had become intent upon plunder and supplied no share of the booty to the consuls, its leaders, they were summoned into the Forum as though to receive their pay, surrounded by soldiers, and killed while unarmed.

[Note: “Introduced by Marius.” Appian writes that the slaves who had fled to Cinna after being promised freedom, and who placed no limit on plunder and slaughter, were massacred by the Gauls at Cinna’s command. Plutarch relates that Sertorius killed about four thousand slaves whom Marius had used as allies in war and as bodyguards during his tyranny.]

Eight thousand fugitives were killed that day in the Forum of the City; and Cinna himself, consul for the fourth time,

[Note: “Cinna, consul for the fourth time.” During his fourth consulship Cinna was stoned to death at Ancona by his own army. See Livy, Book LXXXIII; Appian, Book I; Plutarch, Life of Pompey; and others.]

was killed by his own army.

## CHAPTER XX

How Sulla was recalled by the senators to aid his ruined fatherland, and whom he himself subdued together with his men

Meanwhile the remaining senators, who had escaped by flight the power of Cinna, the cruelty of Marius, the madness of Fimbria, and the audacity of Sertorius, having crossed over into Greece, compelled Sulla by their entreaties to bring help to his endangered—indeed, already almost ruined—fatherland. Accordingly, as soon as Sulla reached the Campanian coast, he defeated the consul Norbanus in battle. The Romans then killed seven thousand Romans, six thousand of the same group were captured by them, and one hundred and twenty-four fell on Sulla’s side.

[Note: “Seven thousand Romans then.” Eutropius gives the same number, reporting that seven thousand from Norbanus’s army were killed; Plutarch also does so. Appian, however, writes that six thousand of Norbanus’s soldiers fell and seventy of Sulla’s.]

Fabius Adrianus,

[Note: “Fabius Adrianus.” Cicero mentions this Adrianus in Against Verres, Book III. Asconius writes as follows: “In the time of Cinna, when C. Fabius Adrianus—according to some, a legate; according to others, a propraetor or praetor—held the province of Africa, he was burned alive at Utica in his praetorium because he was said to have conspired in the murder of the leading citizens after corrupting the city’s slaves.” Livy, Book LXXXVI, and Valerius, Book IX, chapter 10, also speak of him. —Fabr. We discussed this C. Fabius Adrianus, son of Gaius, at considerable length in our notes to Morell’s Thesaurus, vol. I, p. 171. There we showed that a denarius struck from public silver, or by public authority, bearing on one side a turreted female head and on the other Victory in a chariot with an ostrich, belongs to this Fabius Adrianus and was struck by him when he was propraetor in Africa, not to C. Fabius Pictor. Until then antiquarians had believed that this denarius was struck in the year when the Roman people began to use coined silver; we placed it nearly two hundred years later. Most recently, while examining ancient authors to illuminate the Life of Mithridates Eupator in the Royal Thesaurus, I found, as I believe, a brother of this Fabius, or certainly another Fabius from the same family, surnamed Adrianus. For among the commanders of L. Lucullus, who conducted the Mithridatic War after Sulla and Murena, Plutarch mentions an Adrianus who inflicted a great defeat upon the cavalry of Mithridates, sent against the Roman foragers, and destroyed it completely. When Mithridates tried to conceal the defeat of the royal cavalry, Ἀδριανὸς δὲ λαμπρὸς παρημείβετο τὸ στρατόπεδον, πολλὰς κατάγων ἁμάξας, σίτου καὶ λαφυρῶν γεμούσας: “Adrianus indeed passed the camp in splendid fashion, bringing along a great number of wagons loaded with provisions and booty.” Plutarch, Life of Lucullus, p. 502. Appian, in On the Mithridatic War, p. 365, calls this commander Fabius rather than Adrianus. He relates that, as Mithridates hurried from Armenia to recover his kingdom, ἐπέθετο Φαβίῳ τῷ δεῦρο ἐκ Λουκοὑλλου στρατηγεῖν ὑπολελειμμένῳ, καὶ τρεψάμενος αὐτὸν, ἔκτεινεν πεντακοσίους: “He attacked Fabius, who had been left here by Lucullus as commander, routed him, and killed five hundred in the battle.” He then relates how the same Fabius, after freeing the slaves who were following the camp, fought with Mithridates again and suffered an even heavier defeat. Fabius escaped with difficulty from Cabira, where he was besieged by Mithridates and freed by the arrival of Triarius, as Dio Cassius reports, calling him M. Fabius, Book XXXV, p. 4. Thus, according to Dio Cassius, one of these Fabii had the praenomen Marcus, while the coins attest that the other had the praenomen Gaius. We have added a representation of his denarius, together with another on which the head of L. Cornelius Sulla, as well as that of his colleague Pompeius Rufus, is accurately depicted.]

who held authority as propraetor, aspiring to establish a kingdom in Africa through the agency of slaves, was burned alive with his entire household by their masters at Utica, after piles of brushwood had been heaped around him.

[Note: “The praetor Damasippus.” Only Appian calls this praetor Brutus; Livy, Book LXXXVI, Velleius, Book II, and Valerius, Book IX, chapter 2, call him L. Damasippus. Cicero likewise writes in Letter 21 of Book IX, to Paetus: “For apart from this C. Carbo”—the common text corruptly reads Cn. Carbo—“whom Damasippus killed, no citizen of the Carbo family existed in the Republic.” —Fabr.]

The praetor Damasippus, at the instigation of the consul Marius,

[Note: “At the instigation of Marius.” See the preceding chapter, concerning Sertorius: “from this point the instigator and participant in the civil war.”]

summoned Q. Scaevola, C. Carbo, L. Domitius, and P. Antistius into the senate house as though for consultation, and killed them with the utmost cruelty. The bodies of those who had been killed were dragged by executioners with hooks and thrown into the Tiber.

At the same time Sulla’s commanders fought many battles against the Marian faction, with disastrous success.

[Note: “Many battles.” The Longobard manuscript requires that this be restored in place of plura, “several.”]

For Q. Metellus defeated the forces of Carrinas, seized his camp, and Cn. Pompeius inflicted a severe slaughter upon the cavalry of Carbo.

[Note: “Q. Metellus’s forces against Carrinas.” Q. Metellus Pius defeated Carrinas, his legate, at the Aesis, which Appian calls the Αἰσινὸν ποταμὸν, “the river Aesis.” In Plutarch’s Life of Pompey it is called the Ἄρσις ποταμὸς, “river Arsis,” corruptly, as I think; Plutarch writes that Carbo’s cavalry was put to flight there. —Fabr.]

The greatest battle between Sulla and the younger Marius at that time took place at Sacriportus,

[Note: “At Sacriportus.” Livy, Book LXXXVII; Velleius, Book II; and Florus, Book III, chapter 21, discuss Sulla’s victory at Sacriportus. The younger Marius, after Sulla had occupied Setia, established his camp nearby; when, while retreating, he reached Sacriportus, he drew up his line of battle, as Appian writes. Appian calls Sacriportus ἱερὸν λιμένα, “sacred harbor.” Plutarch, in his Life of Sulla, says that this battle was fought at Signia. Strabo, Book V, places Signia and Setia, neighboring towns, between the Latin and Appian Ways. —Fabr.]

in which twenty-five thousand of Marius’s army were killed, as Claudius writes.

[Note: “Twenty-five thousand were killed.” Sulla wrote that twenty thousand of the opposing side killed themselves in this battle, according to Plutarch; Eutropius gives the same number.]

Pompeius also stripped Carbo of his camp and, pursuing him as he fled, now slaughtering, now forcing him to surrender, deprived him of a very large part of his army.

Metellus overwhelmed the column of Norbanus; nine thousand of the Marian faction were killed there.

[Note: “Metellus’s attack on Norbanus’s column.” Velleius writes that this battle was fought near Faenza.]

Lucullus, when he was being besieged by Quinctius, broke out and, in a sudden battle, destroyed the besieger’s army.

[Note: “Lucullus, when [besieged] by Quinctius.” The common text incorrectly reads Quinto. Velleius and Plutarch, in the Life of Sulla, discuss M. Lucullus’s victory at Fidenae. —Fabr.]

More than ten thousand are reported to have been killed there at that time.

[Note: “More than ten thousand.” Plutarch has Ὀκτακισχιλίους ἐπὶ μυρίοις, “eight thousand in addition to ten thousand.”]

Then Sulla joined battle with Lamponius, the leader of the Samnites, and the remaining forces of Carrinas, before the very walls of the City and the Colline Gate

[Note: “At the ninth hour of the day.” Plutarch has σχεδὸν εἰς ὥραν δεκάτην ἤδη τῆς ἡμέρας καταστρεφούσης, “almost at the tenth hour, when the day was already declining.” —Fabr.]

at the ninth hour of the day and finally won after a very severe battle. Eighty thousand men are said to have been routed there; twelve thousand surrendered; and the remaining multitude, having been put to flight, was consumed by the insatiable anger of the victorious citizens.

## CHAPTER XXI

On the Sullan proscriptions and other cruel crimes

As soon as Sulla entered the City as victor,

[Note: “As soon as he entered the City.” This is the reading of the Longobard manuscript, as well as the second Florentine and second Leiden manuscripts, and finally the Perizonian manuscript; it is also printed in the Augustan edition.]

he killed, contrary to divine and human law and contrary to the faith he had pledged, three thousand unarmed and unsuspecting men who had surrendered through their envoys.

[Note: “Three thousand men.” One manuscript has four thousand, perhaps through an obvious and common error for seven thousand. The Augustan edition of Augustine, City of God, Book III, chapter 28, gives seven thousand; Livy, Book LXXXVIII, gives eight thousand; Plutarch, Life of Sulla, gives ἑξακισχιλίους, “six thousand”; Valerius, Book IX, chapter 2, gives four legions. My Florentine manuscript reads: “He ordered four thousand unarmed citizens who had surrendered to be killed in the public villa.” The common text corruptly reads in via publica, “on the public road,” an error that Sigonius also removed from Livy’s Epitome. —Fabr. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, count four thousand.]

At that time very many others were killed—not merely innocent men, but even men of Sulla’s own faction—more than nine thousand, it is said. Thus free slaughter raged throughout the City, with assassins wandering everywhere and attacking whoever was prompted by anger or tempted by booty.

[Note: “Whether anger urged them on or booty enticed them.” The Augustan edition reads vel ira praecipitabat vel praeda sollicitabat, “whether anger drove them headlong or booty enticed them.” Perhaps it should be read that way.]

Accordingly, when everyone was now openly murmuring about what each individual feared,

[Note: “Openly murmuring.” Certain old editions corruptly read aperta fronte timentibus, “fearing with an open face.” Some old editions omit the following word palam, “openly,” but it is found in all the manuscripts I have consulted.]

Q. Catulus openly said to Sulla:

[Note: “Q. Catulus openly.” Palam, “openly,” is also added in the additions of Diaconus to Eutropius. Otherwise, in place of Q. Catulus, Plutarch has C. Metellus. —Fabr.]

“With whom, then, are we ultimately going to live, if in war we kill armed men and in peace unarmed men?”

Then Sulla, on the advice of L. Fursidius,
