[Note: “L. Fursidius.” Florus mentions him; Plutarch calls him Ἀφίδιον. —Fabr. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection and the Augustan edition, call him Forsidius.]

at the prompting of L. Fursidius, a centurion of the first rank, was the first to introduce that infamous tablet of proscription.

[Note: “The first proscription consisted of eighty men.” Contrary to the authority of the ancient books, the common editions read “eighty thousand men.” Plutarch, Life of Sulla, has ὁ δ` οὖν Σύλλας εὐθὺς ὀγδοήκοντα προέγραψεν, “Sulla immediately proscribed eighty.” Thus it should be read, not προσέγραψεν, as it is printed.]

The first proscription consisted of eighty men, among whom were four former consuls: Carbo, Marius, Norbanus, and Scipio; among them also was Sertorius, at that time especially to be feared.

[Note: “And among them.” This is the reading of all the manuscripts, not interque eos, “and among them.”]

Another list, containing five hundred names, was posted. When Lollius, being confident and conscious of no wrongdoing, was reading it and suddenly encountered his own name, he was killed while, trembling, he withdrew from the Forum with his head covered. But even in the lists themselves there seemed to be neither security nor an end to the evils. For some whom they had proscribed they slaughtered; others, after they had slaughtered them, they proscribed. Nor was there a simple path to death or a single condition, so that at least in the killing of citizens the law of enemies might be observed—the law by which enemies demand nothing from the defeated beyond their lives.

[Note: “M. Marius.” Valerius, Book IX, chapter 2, calls M. Marius a praetor: “Marius, the brother of the commander himself.” Florus also does so. Lucan, Book II, describes his cruel death. —Fabr.]

Sulla ordered M. Marius to be dragged from a shepherd’s hut, bound,

[Note: “And having been led.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read vinctumque, “having been bound.”]

and taken across the Tiber to the tomb of the Lutatii, where, after his eyes had been gouged out and his limbs cut into pieces or even broken, he was put to death. After him, P. Laetorius and the senator Venuleius were killed.

[Note: “P. Laetorius.” I think this is the man whom Sulla, as consul together with the elder Marius, proscribed, and whom Appian calls Λαιτώριον, “Laetorius.” It should be written Laetorius, not Lectorius, as is known from Greek books and ancient Latin works, and also from the Capitoline Fasti, where, in the year 496 from the founding of the City, we find M. Laetorius M. F. M. N. Plancianus, master of the cavalry under the dictator Q. Ogulnius Gallus. Valerius Maximus calls this man not P. Laetorius but M. Plaetorius; in some books of Orosius the praenomen of Laetorius is joined to the name itself. —Fabr. The Perizonian manuscript has P. Lectorius; mine has P. Vectorius; the first Leiden manuscript has L. Lictorius.]

[Note: “Venuleius.” Three Leiden manuscripts read Belnuleius. During Cicero’s time there was a certain Venuleius among the quaestors, perhaps this man’s son. The office of triumvir was the first step toward public honors, namely, the office of those in charge of striking coin, and was scarcely worth mentioning; therefore I do not believe Orosius inserted it here. The passage requires correction and should plainly be written as it appears in my most reliable manuscripts: “And the senator Venuleius were killed.” Appian also calls that Laetorius a senator in Book I of the Civil War, p. 386; but Appian and Orosius do not seem to be speaking of the same man. For Laetorius, proscribed together with the elder Marius and Sulla, bore the praenomen Marcus. The name Plaetorius therefore seems more suitable here; and in place of what the common editions have hitherto printed—“After him P. Laetorius the senator and Venuleius the triumvir were killed”—the passage should be restored in full as: “Plaetorius the senator and Venuleius were killed,” with both praenomina omitted. For Valerius Maximus, Book IX, chapter 2, immediately joins the slaughter of Plaetorius to Sulla’s cruelty toward Marcus Marius: “But he also slaughtered M. Plaetorius on the spot, because he had fallen there fainting at the punishment of M. Marius—a new punisher of mercy, in whose eyes to look upon crime with disapproval was itself a crime.” I also seem to have discovered in my manuscript the error through which the word triumvir intruded here. I found the words Marci Marii written as axirci Marii, so that axir ends one line and ci begins the next. Since the same thing appears to have been written in other manuscripts, the correctors thought they had easily removed the error by putting ιιιvir in place of axir and M in place of ci, and then moving occisi, “were killed,” to after ιιιvir.]

The head of M. Marius was sent to Praeneste;

[Note: “Sent to Praeneste.” The editions insert est, “was,” contrary to all the manuscripts.]

when C. Marius saw it, overcome by utter despair while he was being besieged by Lucretius, he met Telesinus in mutual death so as not to fall into the hands of his enemies.

[Note: “With Telesinus.” The same account appears in Livy’s Epitome. Others, however, have written differently about the death of Marius, as in Velleius. —Fabr.]

And while he drove his hand more violently into his advancing opponent’s hand,

[Note: “Against the advancing man.” The first Leiden manuscript reads in incurrentem, “against the attacking man.”]

the hand of the man striking him was weakened around his own wound.

[Note: “He drives.” I have restored adigit from better manuscripts, two Florentine manuscripts, mine, and the Perizonian. The common text has adegit, except in the Augustan edition.]

Thus, after that man had been killed, Marius, lightly wounded himself, offered his neck to his slave.

[Note: “Neck.” I found cervices, “necks,” in all the manuscripts except mine and the Perizonian manuscript.]

Sulla slaughtered the praetor Carrinas. From there he went to Praeneste and ordered all the leaders of the Marian forces—that is, the legates, quaestors, prefects, and tribunes—to be killed.

Pompeius dragged Carbo, who was attempting to flee from the island of Cossura to Egypt, back to Sicily, and killed him there, along with many of his companions.

[Note: “From the island of Cossura.” Two manuscripts have Cossura, not Cossyra. One corruptly reads Corsica, just as in the Epitome, Book LXXXIX, it reads Corcyra. Appian writes: Κάρβωνα δ` ἐκ Λιβύης ἐς Σικιλίαν μετὰ πολλῶν ἐπιφανῶν, καὶ ἀπ` αὐτῶν ἐς Κοσσύραν νῆσον ὑποφεύγοντα, πέμψας τινάς ὁ Πομπήϊος συνελάμβανε: “Pompey sent men and captured Carbo, who was fleeing from Africa to Sicily with many distinguished companions and from there to the island of Cossura.” On the Capitoline monuments are recorded naval triumphs of Ser. Fulvius Nobilior and M. Aemilius Paulus over the Cossurans and Poeni in the year 499 from the founding of the City. —Fabr.]

Sulla was created dictator, so that the lust for domination and cruelty might both be armed and concealed by the reverence owed to an honorable and preeminent title.

Pompey crossed over into Africa and, making a sortie near Utica, killed eighteen thousand men.

[Note: “Eighteen thousand.” The first Leiden manuscript reads nineteen thousand.]

In that war Domitius, the Marian commander, was killed while resisting among the leading men.

[Note: “Among the leading men.” My manuscript and the third Florentine manuscript read inter primos, “among the foremost.” In the same manuscript idem, “the same,” appears below in place of idemque, “and the same.”]

The same Pompey pursued Hiertam, king of Numidia,

[Note: “Hiertam, king of Numidia.” All the manuscript books have Hiertam; my ancient Eutropius likewise calls him Hierdam, while the printed editions have Hierbam, Plutarch Ἱάρφαν, and the Epitome Hieram. —Fabr.]

and had him, while fleeing, stripped of all his forces by Bogud, son of Bocchus, king of the Moors. He returned immediately to Bulla,

[Note: “Bulla.” Pliny, Book V, chapter 3, and the Itinerary of Antoninus mention this city of Numidia, calling it Bulla Regia.]

and, after the town had been handed over to Pompey, Pompey killed him.

## CHAPTER XXII

The author presents a kind of epilogue to what has been said. On the new disturbance raised by Lepidus

[Col. 0975A]

[Note: [Col. 0975C] After P. Servilius had therefore been elected. P. Servilius Vatia and Appius Claudius Pulcher were consuls in the year 673, and after they had been elected consuls Sulla voluntarily resigned the dictatorship. Appian, Book I; Plutarch, *Sulla*. FABR.]

After P. Servilius and Appius Claudius had been elected consuls, Sulla was at last seen as a private citizen. [Note: [Col. 0975C] Sulla was at last seen. Some copies read “was seen”; the Venetian editions read “Lucius Sulla was at last a private citizen.”]

With this conclusion, two most disastrous wars came to an end: the Social, or Italian, War and Sulla’s Civil War. These, prolonged for ten years, consumed more than 150,000 Romans; and in this civil war Rome lost so many of her finest men and native soldiers as the census had found in her at an earlier period, when she was already looking around to confront Alexander the Great, though in separate generations. [Note: [Col. 0975C] In separate generations. The first and third editions of Leiden, with the Gronovian Collection, read “of an undivided generation”; the Augustan edition, “in undivided generations.”]

Moreover, twenty-four men of consular rank, six of praetorian rank, sixty who had held the aedileship, and nearly two hundred senators were lost, apart from the countless peoples of all Italy who were destroyed indiscriminately and without consideration—peoples whom no one, if he is able, can deny that Rome conquered at the same cost to herself at which Italy lost them. [Note: [Col. 0975C] Twenty-four. The fourth Leiden edition counts one more.] [Note: [Col. 0975B] Whom. That is, the peoples of Italy; some old editions read corruptly *qua*, or *quomodo*, or *quod*, as does the Perizonian manuscript, in order to deny the construction.] [Note: [Col. 0975D] Conquered. The first Florentine edition reads “conquered.”]

Shame! Do these times perhaps also require an ambiguous comparison? [Note: [Col. 0975D] Shame! Others read “Alas!”] Indeed, they require it above all, they say. For what is more fitting than to compare civil wars with civil wars? Or will someone perhaps say that in these times there have not been civil wars? To this we shall reply that they ought more properly to be called social wars, but that it is advantageous for us if they are called civil wars. For when everything is declared equal in causes, names, and purposes, Christian religion’s reverence claims so much more for itself in these matters, the less the enraged power of the victor has presumed. [Note: [Col. 0975D] “And for us.” Perizonius wrongly reads “but not.”] [Note: [Col. 0975D] In names. Thus all the manuscripts and the Augustan edition; the common editions read “in names also.”] [Note: [Col. 0975D] The enraged power of the victor. Three Leiden editions, with the Gronovian Collection, read “the power of the enraged victor.”]

For when wicked tyrants, generally rushing rashly upon the state and having usurped royal authority, have overwhelmed the body of the Roman Empire, and as a result have either introduced wars that were unjust in themselves or stirred up wars that were just against themselves, raised and equipped by the peoples of Britain and Gaul; [Note: [Col. 0975D] Raised and equipped by the peoples of Britain and Gaul. He means Carausius, Allectus, Constantine, and other tyrants of that period, whom he says were “raised,” that is, supported, by the Britons and Gauls. Yet I have found the word *erecti* in no manuscript; all have *creati*, as does the Augustan edition. Therefore I judge that *erecti* cannot be retained against the agreement of the manuscripts. My manuscript reads “both raised and equipped.” Did Orosius write: “raised and equipped by the peoples of Britain and Gaul”?]

—when these wars are as near to foreign wars as they are distant from civil wars, by what right should they be called anything other than social wars, since the Romans themselves never called even the wars of Sertorius, Perperna, Crixus, or Spartacus civil wars? [Note: [Col. 0976C] Or Crixus. We shall speak of Crixus, the leader of the gladiators, below, in the final chapter. The printed editions commonly read incorrectly “or Crassus.” FABR.]

In such a defect or rebellion of allies, there would now at least be less ill will if perhaps there were a serious battle or a bloody victory. Yet since in these times everything brings more necessity and less shame—that is, the cause, the battle, and the victory—whether for extinguishing the insolence of tyrants, restraining the rebellion of allies, or branding an example of vengeance, who could doubt how much more mildly and mercifully the so-called civil wars are now being stirred up—indeed, rather suppressed than waged? [Note: [Col. 0976C] In these times. Three Florentine manuscripts read “in these times,” deleting *in*; this is not bad.]

Who, in these times, has heard of a single civil war lasting ten years? Who remembers that in one war 150,000 men were slaughtered—enemies by enemies, not to mention citizens by citizens? Who has learned that in peacetime such a multitude of the best and most distinguished men, too numerous to recount, was butchered? Finally, who has feared or read or experienced those infamous lists of those destined to be killed? [Note: [Col. 0976D] “Read, experienced.” The Augustan edition reads: “feared, written, experienced, and not known.” The opposing pairs are those who wrote and those who feared, each in their respective turns, and likewise those who experienced and those who did not know, since both those listed and those not listed among them perished. I prefer the common reading.]

And is it not rather known to all that, having been brought together under one peace and made secure by the same salvation, the defeated and the victorious alike rejoiced in a common happiness, and that even among so many provinces, cities, and peoples of the entire Roman Empire scarcely a few ever existed whom a just vengeance condemned, even against the will of the victor? [Note: [Col. 0976D] And also. Some manuscripts read “also”; perhaps “and even” is better.]

And, so that I do not burden words with words, I would not rashly say that even in war so great a band of common soldiers has just now been destroyed as the number of nobles then slaughtered in peacetime. [Note: [Col. 0976D] “As were slaughtered in peacetime among the nobles.” The same three manuscripts, with the Gronovian Collection, read here “as were slaughtered even in peacetime among the nobles”; above, however, they read “not merely destroyed.”]

Therefore, after Sulla’s death, Lepidus, champion of the Marian party, rising against Catulus, the Sullan leader, revived the ashes of the civil wars. [Note: [Col. 0976D] After Sulla’s death, Lepidus. Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Quintus Lutatius Catulus were consuls in the year 675 from the founding of the City. Sallust, Book I of the *Histories*, says: “I have set down the deeds of the Roman people in war and at home during the consulship of M. Lepidus and Q. Catulus.” On the disagreement between these consuls, see Cicero, *Catiline* III; Livy, Book XC; Appian I; Plutarch, *Sulla* and *Pompey*; Eutropius and others. FABR.]

Twice then battle was joined. Very many Romans were killed—already pitiful because of their mere scarcity, yet still raging with that same madness. The city of Alba was attacked under siege and tormented by the extremity of famine, but was preserved when its wretched survivors surrendered. There Scipio, Lepidus’ son, was captured and killed. [Note: [Col. 0977C] Brutus in Cisalpine Gaul. This was Marcus Junius Brutus, father of the Brutus who killed Caesar; see Plutarch, *Pompey* and *Brutus*. FABR.]

Brutus, fleeing into Cisalpine Gaul, was pursued by Pompey and killed near Rhegium. Thus this civil war, no less through Catulus’ clemency than through weariness of Sulla’s cruelty, vanished with the same speed with which it had flared up, like fire in straw.

**355 CHAPTER XXIII. On four new wars undertaken by the Romans: the Spanish, Pamphylian, Macedonian, and Dalmatian wars**

[Col. 0977B]

[Note: [Col. 0977C] In the year 673 from the founding of the City. He means the year in which Lepidus and Catulus were consuls; we have called it 675 from the founding of Rome. Eutropius, at the beginning of Book IV, confirms that these four wars arose during their consulship. FABR.]

In the year 673 from the founding of the City, while the din of wars resounded everywhere—one of them in Spain, another in Pamphylia, a third in Macedonia, and a fourth in Dalmatia—the Roman state, still bloodless and exhausted from its internal destruction as though from fevers, was compelled to repel by arms the bravest peoples of the West and the North. [Note: [Col. 0977C] Still bloodless. Perizonius’ manuscript reads “bloodless everywhere.” The same manuscript counts the year as 677 instead of 673.]

For Sertorius, a man powerful through deceit and audacity, who had belonged to the Marian party and was fleeing from Sulla, slipped away from Africa into the Spains and stirred the most warlike peoples to arms. [Note: [Col. 0977C] Most warlike. Some old editions add “and most savage”; they then read “into arms from arms,” contrary to the better manuscripts.]

Against him, to state the matter briefly, two commanders were sent, Metellus and Domitius. [Note: [Col. 0977C] Were sent. The Augustan edition reads “were sent.”] Domitius was overwhelmed, together with his army, by Hirtuleius, Sertorius’ commander. [Note: [Col. 0977C] Domitius by Hirtuleius. In our manuscripts of Orosius, Eutropius, and Florus the name is *Hirculeius*. Livy, Book XC, calls him the quaestor Hirculeius. Plutarch refers to the same man in *Sertorius* with these words: “Having defeated Domitius Caelusius [perhaps Calvinius], who was proconsul of the other Spain, through his quaestor.” Plutarch also mentions Thoranius, Metellus’ lieutenant, whom Sertorius killed together with his army. My Florus manuscript likewise reads: “While on this side Domitius and Thorius, and on that side the brothers of Hirtuleius, were making preliminary attacks.” The printed editions read “while on this side Domitius and cohorts.” FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 0977D] Overwhelmed together with his army. Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus had obtained Citerior Spain as proconsul; Metellus, inferior to Sertorius in strength, had summoned him from there. Sallust, fragment of Book II: “Metellus summoned Domitius, the proconsul in Citerior Spain, with all the forces he had prepared.” Plutarch and Eutropius likewise report that he was overwhelmed and killed together with his army by Lucius Hirtuleius. Plutarch, *Sertorius*, p. 574: “Having defeated Domitius and Lucius, who was proconsul of the other Spain, through his quaestor, etc., he killed him.” They translate: “Domitius and Lucius Manlius, etc.” But I think *Lucium* should be written, and translated as follows: “He also killed Lucius Domitius, proconsul of the other Spain, after defeating him through his quaestor.” For Domitius was proconsul of Citerior Spain, whereas Manlius—or rather Manilius—was proconsul of Gaul. Moreover, Domitius fell in battle; Manilius escaped by a shameful flight after losing his army. Eutropius, Book VI, chapter 1: “Domitius was killed by Hirtuleius, Sertorius’ commander. The defeat was suffered near the river Anas.” Florus, Book III, chapter 22: “The first engagements were conducted through lieutenants, while on this side Domitius and Thorius, and on that side the brothers Hirtuleius, were making preliminary attacks; soon the former were overwhelmed at Segovia and the latter at the river Anas.” If you compare this with the passages cited from Plutarch, where he also speaks of Thorius’ death, you will see that our emendation is confirmed and that there is no place there for L. Manilius. Somewhat later, the fourth Leiden edition reads *sociarentur* instead of *consociarentur*.”]

Manilius, proconsul of Gaul, crossed into Spain with three legions and 1,500 cavalry and joined battle with Hirtuleius under unfavorable conditions. Stripped by him of his camp and forces, he fled almost alone into the town of Herda. [Note: [Col. 0978C] Manilius, the proconsul. One manuscript reads *Manilius*, the others *Manlius*. In Plutarch the passage reads: “so that Lucius Lollius came to him as an auxiliary from the region around Narbo in Gaul,” where Sigonius reads “so that Lucius Manilius came to him.” FABR. The manuscripts I consulted, almost all of them—including the Lombard manuscript—correctly write *Hirtuleius*, both here and below; and again *Hirtuleius* where Orosius later speaks of the death of the Hirtuleian brothers. Hirtuleius, the man in question here, was one of Sertorius’ commanders together with his brother and is counted among his quaestors. In all the manuscripts, *Manlius* is written instead of *Manilius*, but incorrectly.]

Metellus, worn out by many battles, wandered through byways and wearied the enemy by delay, until he joined Pompey’s camp. Pompey, having gathered his army near Pallantia, attempted unsuccessfully to defend the city of Lauron, which Sertorius was then besieging, and, defeated, fled. [Note: [Col. 0978D] Near Pallantia. Other copies read *Polentia*, incorrectly. Strabo, Book III, discusses Pallantia; Pliny, Book III, chapter 3, the people of Pallantia; Plutarch and Appian, the destruction of Lauron. FABR. The fourth Leiden edition and my manuscript read *Palentium*.]

After defeating and routing Pompey, Sertorius captured Lauron and ravaged it with the utmost brutality. [Note: [Col. 0978D] The remaining force of the Lauronenses. Plutarch gives a different account in *Sertorius*, saying that Sertorius spared the Lauronenses and dismissed them. FABR.] The remaining force of the Lauronenses, which had survived the slaughter, he led into Lusitania in pitiable captivity.

He boasted that Pompey—that is, that Roman commander—had been defeated by him; Pompey whom Rome, endowed with great confidence in him, had sent to this war not as proconsul but as though he were several consuls. [Note: [Col. 0978D] Not as proconsul. Read Plutarch, *Pompey*. FABR. Somewhat later, instead of “1,000 cavalry,” the common editions read “and 1,000 cavalry,” contrary to the manuscripts.]

Galba writes that Pompey then had 30,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry; he records that Sertorius had 60,000 infantry and 8,000 cavalry. Afterwards Hirtuleius engaged Metellus near Italica, a city of Baetica, and lost 20,000 soldiers; defeated, he fled with a few men into Lusitania. [Note: [Col. 0979C] Hirtuleius with Metellus. On Metellus’ victory over Hirtuleius, see Livy, Book XCI, and Frontinus, *Stratagems*, Book II. FABR. Sallust, fragment of Book II: “They confronted the commander and provoked battle, so that missiles came to Metellus’ cloak and to Hirtuleius’ arm.”]

Pompey captured Segida, a distinguished city of Celtiberia. [Note: [Col. 0979C] Segida. All the manuscripts read *Belgida*, as do the old editions up to Fabricius, who gives no reason for his emendation. I find neither Belgida nor Segida in Celtiberia; Ptolemy and others recognize Balsion or Belsinua there, which comes closest to Belgida, as does Cesata or Cesada, whose spelling does not differ greatly from *Segida*.]

Sertorius then engaged Pompey and killed 10,000 of his soldiers. On the other wing, while Pompey was victorious, Sertorius himself lost nearly as many. [Note: [Col. 0979C] With Pompey victorious. Thus three Florentine manuscripts, my manuscript, and Perizonius, as well as the first and Augustan editions with the Venetian editions. Four Leiden manuscripts, together with some editions, read “while Pompey was exerting force.” Utrecht and the Gronovian Collection read “while Pompey, exerting force, was victorious.”]

Many other battles were fought between them. Memmius, Pompey’s quaestor and also the husband of his sister, was killed. [Note: [Col. 0979C] Memmius, the quaestor. Plutarch, *Sertorius*, says that Memmius was killed in the territory of Seguntia. On Memmius, Pompey’s quaestor, see Cicero, *For Balbus*. FABR.]

The brothers Hirtuleius were killed. [Note: [Col. 0979D] The Hirtuleian brothers were killed. Their standing among Sertorius’ commanders is clear from Frontinus, *Stratagems*, Book II, chapter 7: “When Quintus Sertorius was fighting in battle, he stabbed with a dagger the barbarian who had announced to him that Hirtuleius had perished, lest the news spread to others and thereby weaken the courage of his men.”]

Perperna, who had joined himself to Sertorius, was crushed. [Note: [Col. 0979D] Perperna. That the name ought to be written *Perperna*, not *Perpenna*, is shown by the Capitoline Fasti, in which, in the year 661, Marcus Perperna is paired with Claudius Pulcher as consul; Dio, Book XLI, likewise calls him *Perpernas* in Greek, Περπέρνας. There is therefore no doubt that in Plutarch and Appian scribes substituted Περπένναν for *Perperna*, especially since in the edition of Appian’s *Iberica* published by Henri Estienne this Perperna is called Περπέρνας. FABR.]

Finally, Sertorius himself, in the tenth year after the war began, was killed by the treachery of his own men, like Viriathus, and brought the war to an end, giving the Romans a victory without glory. [Note: [Col. 0980C] Sertorius only in the tenth year. Eutropius’ books say that Sertorius was killed by his own men in the eighteenth year, but Cuspinianus correctly emends this to “only in the eighth year.” Appian likewise writes of Sertorius’ achievements: “What remained of Sulla’s deeds was that of Sertorius, which lasted eight years.” Sertorius was killed in the eighth year of his command, but the war was concluded in the tenth, according to Livy, Book XCVI. FABR.]

Nevertheless, part of his army later followed Perperna; defeated by Pompey, Perperna was killed together with his entire army. All the cities, however, having surrendered voluntarily and without delay, were received except for two: Uxama and Calagurris. Pompey demolished Uxama; Afranius destroyed Calagurris, which had been worn down by a relentless siege and driven by pitiable want to the most infamous food, through a final slaughter and conflagration.

The assassins of Sertorius did not even think that a reward ought to be requested from the Romans, since they remembered that one had previously been denied to the assassins of Viriathus. And although at that time they had not completed Rome’s security for any reward, nevertheless Spain, always brave in loyalty and strength, which had given the state the best and most invincible kings, has never, from the beginning until the present day, sent forth any tyrant raised from within herself or allowed one invading her from outside to depart alive and powerful. [Note: [Col. 0980C] “Best and most invincible.” The conjunction is deleted by all except the Augustan edition, the Lombard manuscript, the third Florentine manuscript, and the third Leiden manuscript. Perhaps one of the two words, “best” and “most invincible,” is a variant reading.]

Meanwhile Claudius drew the Macedonian war by lot and attacked the various peoples surrounding the Rhodope Mountains, who at that time were savagely ravaging Macedonia—for among the other horrors, dreadful to relate and hear, that they inflicted on captives, when a drinking vessel was needed they seized human skulls, still bloody and covered with hair, with the brains left within their inner hollows and incompletely scooped out, and greedily and without horror used them like genuine drinking cups. The most bloodthirsty and savage among them were the Scordisci. Thus Claudius, as I have said, attempted to drive them from the borders of Macedonia by war and exposed himself to great masses of troubles. [Note: [Col. 0980C] “Whence, being troubled in mind and surrounded by cares.” This reading occurs in all our manuscripts; in its place other printed editions corruptly read: “Since he was carrying these matters in his mind, surrounded by cares,” etc. FABR. The manuscripts all confirm Fabricius’ emendation, as does the Augustan edition.]

As a result, being distressed in mind, surrounded by cares, and additionally seized by illness, he died.

His successor Scribonius, avoiding the force of the peoples attacked in the preceding war, turned his arms toward Dardania and conquered it. [Note: [Col. 0980D] His successor Scribonius. Gaius Scribonius Curio, who was consul with Gnaeus Octavius in the year 677, succeeded Appius Claudius in Macedonia; see Eutropius, Book VI, and Livy, Books XCII and XCV. Cicero mentions Curio’s triumph from Macedonia in *Against Piso*. FABR.]

Publius Servilius, a former consul, attacked Cilicia and Pamphylia with the utmost cruelty and, while striving to bring them under control, nearly destroyed them. He captured Lycia and its cities after besieging and overwhelming them. Moreover, having traversed Mount Olympus, he overthrew Phaselis and demolished Corycus. [Note: [Col. 0980D] He overthrew Phaselis. The name of Phaselis has commonly been corrupted. Dionysius, verse 854:

“Other Pamphylian cities follow in succession:
Corycus, Pargete, and windy Phaselis.”

Sallust, Book I of the *Histories*, describing Servilius’ achievements, says “to Olympus and Phaselis,” and likewise “to Corycus,” according to Priscian, Book XV. Cicero, *Against Verres* V: “That Phaselis which Publius Servilius captured had not previously been a city but had belonged to Cilicians and pirates,” etc. FABR.]

He also explored the slopes of Mount Taurus that descend toward Cilicia and brought the Isaurians, broken in war, under his authority. [Note: [Col. 0981C] Brought under his authority. Fabricius printed this reading, whereas all earlier editions had “brought into surrender,” the usual expression when an enemy submits, and it is found in four Leiden manuscripts, in Perizonius, and in my manuscript, though my manuscript reads “received into surrender.” The Lombard manuscript, however, supports Fabricius’ reading. Pomponius likewise says *to come under authority* in *On the Origin and Succession of Magistracies*, chapter 18, p. 275, ed. Ruperti, section on the Origin of Law: “Then Sardinia was captured, soon Sicily, likewise Spain, then the province of Narbonensis; as many praetors as there were provinces were elected, which had come under authority.” Thus “he brought under authority” amounts to the same as “he made a province of the Roman people.”]

He was the first of the Romans to lead an army across the Taurus and made it the boundary of his march. When the three years over which the war had lasted had elapsed, he assumed the name Isauricus.

Cosconius, having drawn Illyricum as proconsul, crushed and subdued Dalmatia and after two years finally stormed and captured Salona, a most flourishing city. [Note: [Col. 0981C] Cosconius, the proconsul. On Cosconius’ achievements, see Eutropius, Book VI, where the manuscripts give him the praenomen Gnaeus, incorrectly in my view: he was Gaius Cosconius, whose letter made it clear that a legion had been solicited by Bulbus in Illyricum, as Cicero testifies in *For Cluentius*. FABR.]

**CHAPTER XXIV. On the war of the fugitives, or gladiators, and its disasters**

[Note: [Col. 0981D] In the year 679 from the founding of the City. For Eutropius this is the year 678; for others, 630, in which Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus and Gaius Cassius were consuls. FABR.]

In the year 679 from the founding of the City, when Lucullus and Cassius were consuls, seventy-four gladiators escaped from the training school of Gnaeus Lentulus at Capua. [Note: [Col. 0981D] Seventy-four gladiators. Livy and Eutropius give the same number; Appian, seventy gladiators, μονομάχους ἑβδομήκοντα; Plutarch, in *Crassus*, “eighty-two short of a hundred.” FABR. The fourth Leiden edition counts forty-four; but the third, together with the Gronovian Collection and the manuscripts of Me, Perizonius, and the three Florentine manuscripts, counts or writes “sixty-four.”]

They immediately occupied Mount Vesuvius under the leadership of Crixus and Oenomaus, Gauls, and Spartacus, a Thracian. [Note: [Col. 0981D] Crixus and Oenomaus. Not only Appian but also the old books prove that these are the commanders’ names. FABR.] Bursting out from there, they stormed the camp of the praetor Clodius, who had surrounded them with a siege. [Note: [Col. 0981D] Of the praetor Clodius. Livy, Book XCV, has Claudius Pulcher as the legate; Florus, Book III, chapter 20, Clodius Glaber; Plutarch, Κλώδιον στρατηγὸν, “the general Clodius.” FABR.] After putting Clodius to flight, they turned everything into plunder. [Note: [Col. 0982B] Turned. Most manuscript copies, together with the Augustan edition, read “turned away.”]

From there, having been led around through Consentia and Metapontum, they quickly gathered enormous forces. For Crixus is reported to have had a multitude of 10,000, while Spartacus had three times that number. [Note: [Col. 0982B] Is reported. Thus almost all the manuscripts require it to be written, not “is said.”] Oenomaus, however, had already been killed in the earlier war. [Note: [Col. 0982C] In the earlier war. Two manuscripts and the two Leiden manuscripts, with the Gronovian Collection, read “in the earlier war,” deleting *in*.]

And so, while they mingled everything with slaughter, fires, robbery, and rape, at the funeral rites of a captive matron who had killed herself from grief at the violation of her honor, they presented a gladiatorial spectacle from 400 captives—namely, men who had been intended to be spectators but were to become performers, since the leaders were rather trainers of gladiators than soldiers. [Note: [Col. 0982C] At the funeral rites of a captive woman. Appian writes: “Spartacus sacrificed 300 Roman captives to Crixus and marched toward Rome with 120,000 Roman infantry.” Thus Spartacus sent 300 Roman captives as funeral offerings to Crixus and advanced on the City with 120,000 infantry. Florus derives this account: “He celebrated the funerals of the dead commanders with the rites of generals and ordered captives to fight with weapons around the pyre.” FABR. I would soon prefer *munus gladiatorium*—“a gladiatorial spectacle”—to “of gladiators.”]

Then the consuls Gellius and Lentulus were sent against them with an army. [Note: [Col. 0982C] Were sent. Some manuscripts read “were sent.”] Gellius defeated Crixus, who was fighting most fiercely, in battle; Lentulus, overcome by Spartacus, fled. Afterwards, when both consuls had uselessly united their forces, they suffered a severe defeat and fled. Next, Spartacus defeated in battle and killed the proconsul Gaius Cassius. [Note: [Col. 0982C] The same. The first Florentine manuscript reads “in the same place.”]

Thus, with the state terrified by almost as great a fear as that with which it had trembled when Hannibal roared near the gates, the Senate sent Crassus with the consular legions and a new reinforcement of soldiers. [Note: [Col. 0982C] Of the consuls. This is absent from the Augustan edition, but three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection incorrectly write “the consul,” meaning the forces of both consuls, as Florus puts it in Book III, chapter 20. That Crassus, who was then praetor, had the armies of both consuls at that time is attested by Plutarch in *Crassus*, p. 548. After saying that both consuls, Gellius and Lentulus, had been sent against the fugitives, he adds that the Senate, hostile to the consuls, ordered them to exercise no authority and entrusted the war to Crassus.]

As soon as he engaged the fugitives in battle, he killed 6,000 of them and captured 900. Then, before he attacked Spartacus himself, who was encamped at the headwaters of the river Silarus, he defeated his Gallic auxiliaries and the Germans. [Note: [Col. 0982D] At the headwaters of the Silarus. On the Silarus, also called Silaris, see Strabo, Book V, near the end, and Pliny, Book III, chapters 103 and 5. On the number killed, see Livy, Book XCVII. FABR.] Of these, together with their commanders, he killed 30,000 men. [Note: [Col. 0982D] His auxiliaries. The latter word is absent from Perizonius; afterward my manuscript reads “and defeated the Germans in battle.”]

Finally, he engaged Spartacus himself in an arranged battle and routed the greatest forces of fugitives with him. For 60,000 of them are reported to have been killed and 6,000 captured; 3,000 Roman citizens were recovered. [Note: [Col. 0982D] Sixty thousand of them. Perizonius counts 40,000.] The rest, who had escaped from this war and were wandering about, were worn down through persistent pursuit by several commanders. [Note: [Col. 0983C] Were worn down. The Augustan edition reads “were crushed.”]

But I repeat again and again: do these times require any comparison here? Who, I ask, would not shudder to hear not merely of such wars but even of the names of such wars—foreign, servile, social, civil, and those of fugitives? [Note: [Col. 0983C] “Such.” The second Florentine manuscript reads “of such great wars.” Later, instead of “of the fugitives,” Perizonius and my manuscript correctly read “of the fugitives also.”]

And even so they do not follow one another like the waves of a disturbed sea, however great the masses, but, aroused everywhere by different causes, names, forms, and evils, they pile up and rush together. [Note: [Col. 0983C] Which nevertheless. Almost all the manuscripts write *nec* instead of *ne*; all the Leiden manuscripts, with the Gronovian Collection, and likewise my manuscript and Perizonius, delete *quidem*.] [Note: [Col. 0983C] However great. The first Leiden edition reads “however great”; the wording of the others is uncertain.] [Note: [Col. 0983C] And piled up. I confidently inserted this reading, praised by Palmerius, in place of the common *coacervata*, and I do not yet doubt that others will approve it. LAUT.]

To take up what immediately precedes, and to pass over that infamous servile war, the Jugurthine War had not yet ceased to thunder from the southwest when the Cimbrian War was already flashing like lightning from the northwest. [Note: [Col. 0983C] Had not yet ceased to thunder. The second Leiden edition, three Florentine manuscripts, and the Augustan edition read “had not yet completely ceased to thunder”; the Gronovian Collection seems to intend the same, with three other Leiden manuscripts, in which the reading is variously transmitted as “had not yet known the thunder,” “had not yet stirred after being destroyed,” or “had not yet stirred what had been destroyed.” My manuscript reads “had not yet thundered completely.” Later some editions add “and already the Cimbrian war,” and somewhat afterward “and already the Social War.” Old editions.]

The monstrous and vast torrents of blood shed by those Cimbrian clouds were still being discussed, when already the Social War— [Note: [Col. 0983D] “The clouds of war, etc.” Virgil, *Aeneid* X, 809:

“Aeneas, while the whole cloud of war thunders.”

Sustains.] The mists of war [362] that were continually about to gather into a great cloud of evils were being exhaled by wretched Italy. Even after the endless and repeated storm of the Italian war, it was by no means possible to travel safely through Italy: thus everyone, apart from those most perilous abysses of hostile cities, staggered amid a peace that had been dissolved and made slippery. Rome was already bringing forth for itself the destruction of Marius and Cinna, while from the opposite direction the East and the North—namely, the Mithridatic [Note: [Col. 0983D] The Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, three Florentine manuscripts, and the Gronovian Collection add *bellum*, “war.”]—were threatening another disaster; and that Mithridatic war, begun earlier, is now extended farther and farther.

From the Marian torch the funeral pyre of Sulla’s disaster was kindled; from that most grievous pyre, burning brands of the Sullan and civil war were scattered through many regions of the earth, and many conflagrations spread from a single firebrand. For Lepidus and Scipio in Italy, Brutus in Gaul, Domitius, Cinna’s son-in-law, in Africa, Carbo in Cossura and Sicily, Perperna in Liguria, and afterward with Sertorius in Spain—and Sertorius, the most savage of them all, in that same Spain—raising these civil wars, or whatever other name they should be called, made many things out of one, great things out of a small beginning [Note: [Col. 0983D] The old editions read, “made great things out of the smallest beginning.” All the manuscripts have “out of a great thing, great things”; Perizonius alone has “made greater things out of a great thing,” which I consider superior to the others. For that first civil or social war was not insignificant, and the later wars arose from it.].

Apart from those three enormous wars which were then called foreign—namely, the Pamphylian, Macedonian, and Dalmatian wars—and also apart from that great Mithridatic war, by far the longest [Note: [Col. 0983D] They reject this superlative and write *diuturno*, “long-lasting.” The three Florentine manuscripts, three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, my manuscript, Perizonius, and the Gronovian Collection support the superlative.], most hostile, and most dreadful of all, then, while the Spanish war with Sertorius had not yet ended—indeed, while Sertorius himself was still alive—this war of fugitives, or, to speak more accurately, gladiatorial [Col. 0984B] war, broke out: no longer something to be watched by a few [Note: [Col. 0983D] That is, for amusement in the amphitheater, where idle spectators watched imprisoned gladiators fight one another.], but something to be feared everywhere.

Because it is called a war of fugitives, let no one regard it as insignificant on account of its name. In it the two consuls were often defeated individually, and sometimes together with armies joined in vain; very many nobles were slaughtered. The fugitives themselves numbered more than one hundred thousand, and they were slain. From this we admonish Italy herself to console herself for the harassment inflicted by present foreign enemies by remembering past troubles [Note: [Col. 0984C] “And let her go forth into herself, and not think that she is being torn apart incomparably.” Here I have subdued the monsters of Hercules. All the manuscripts read, “from themselves and within themselves tearing apart incomparably”—a confused reading. Yet, if I may claim the credit, I have supplied *exeatque in se ipsa* in place of *de ex se atque in se ipsa*, and I owe *nec putet se* to the Venetian manuscript. The Venetian editions, however, read, “and let her go forth into herself, and not think that she is being torn apart with incomparable cruelty”; this is also the reading of all the old editions except the Augustan edition, which has, “from themselves and within themselves, and herself incomparably more cruelly torn apart by her own people.” The Longobard manuscript has essentially the same reading, except that it expands it: “from themselves and within themselves, and let her herself know that she has been incomparably more cruelly torn apart by her own people.” The four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, the Gronovian Collection, and Perizonius agree substantially with this. My manuscript reads, “from themselves and within themselves; and let her know that she herself has been incomparably more cruelly torn apart by her own people.” This alone seems to me the true correction of the passage. I do not grant Lautius the applause he claims for himself, for the present foreign troubles of which Orosius speaks must have something opposed to them, and this is lacking in Lautius’ correction but found in ours—namely, those past wars or disasters, “from themselves and within themselves.” The corrupt readings of the second and third Florentine manuscripts also contribute something to this correction. The second, with the agreement of the Ultramontane manuscript, reads, “and let her go forth into herself, and let her herself know that she has been incomparably more cruelly torn apart by her own people” (the Florentine manuscript originally had *dilacerantum*, corrected to *dilaceratam*); the third reads, “and let her go forth into herself, and let her herself know that she has been incomparably more cruelly torn apart”—with *afflictam*, “afflicted,” written above it. Fabricius and Scottus published, “of past troubles, from themselves and within themselves incomparably more cruelly tearing her apart.”] from themselves and within themselves; and let her herself know that she has been incomparably more cruelly torn apart by her own people.

For this reason [Note: [Col. 0984D] The better manuscripts direct that it be read this way; others, and the common editions, have “to this fifth volume now.”], I shall now bring this fifth volume to an end, so that the civil wars mingled everywhere with foreign wars—both those already mentioned and those that follow, since they have been joined together in the sequence of time [Note: [Col. 0985A] My manuscript has *miserie temporum*, “of the misery of the times.”] and in the evils that followed them [Note: [Col. 0985A] The second Florentine manuscript has “and in the evils that followed”; another manuscript has “as evils followed.” In the Longobard manuscript, after this passage appears: “Here ends Book V of Paulus Orosius. Book VI begins.” A note concerning that distinguished manuscript follows in the same handwriting: “This manuscript was completed in the workshop of Viliaric, a copyist. Pray for me, the scribe, so that you may have the Lord as your protector.”]—may at least be separated by the limit of the books.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0985]

## CHAPTER ONE. The One God, according to the judgment both of the Gentiles and of Christians

[Col. 0985A]

[Col. 0985B] All human beings, whatever their sect, way of life, or homeland [Note: [Col. 0985C] Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, the Gronovian Collection, my manuscript, and the first Florentine manuscript, deleting the first *vel*, prefer “whatever his sect, way of life, or homeland.” The old editions transpose the words “whether sect or way of life.”], are always so raised toward the prospect of wisdom by the natural good [Note: [Col. 0985C] The Gronovian Collection reads *exiguntur*, “are required.” Immediately afterward, the first Florentine manuscript omits *ut*.] that, although they may not in practice place the rational mind before bodily pleasure, they nevertheless know by judgment that it ought to be preferred. This mind, enlightened under the guidance of reason [Note: [Col. 0985C] My manuscript incorrectly has *lustrata*, “purified,” and immediately afterward the third Lugd. Bat. manuscript has *gemino*, “twofold,” instead of the genuine reading.], rises amid the virtues, toward which it is inclined by an inborn favor, although it leans toward vices, and looks out upon the knowledge of God as though from a citadel [Note: [Col. 0985C] “For anyone can temporarily despise God, but no one can be wholly ignorant of him.” Hence Tertullian called the soul “naturally Christian” in *Apologeticus* 17, p. 176, after writing: “Do you wish us to prove this from the testimony of the soul itself? Although it is confined by the prison of the body, although it is hemmed in by depraved teachings, although it is enervated by lusts and desires, although it is enslaved to false gods, yet when it recovers its senses…”].

For anyone can temporarily despise God, but no one can be wholly ignorant of him [Note: [Col. 0985C] The first and fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscripts have “in so great a degree” instead of “wholly.”]. Hence certain people, while believing that God was present in many things, fashioned many gods out of indiscriminate fear [Note: [Col. 0985D] Some old editions read, “while believing in many gods, they fashioned many gods out of indiscriminate fear.” But the meaning of Orosius’ words is this: while some suppose that divinity is present in many things, and that the gods themselves, distinguished as though into a household, each perform separate functions, they fail to discern the indivisible deity and so fashion many gods for themselves to worship.].

But from this position there has now been a particularly great departure, both because the authority of truth has been at work and because reason itself has examined the matter. For their philosophers also [Note: [Col. 0985D] See what we noted concerning Plato and Thales in Tertullian’s *Apologeticus* 46, p. 387.], to say nothing of our saints [Note: [Col. 0985D] The first Lugd. Bat. manuscript has *sacris*, “sacred things.” My manuscript and Perizonius have *scis*, from which the variation in reading arose.], while they seek and investigate everything with concentrated intellectual effort [Note: [Col. 0986C] The second Lugd. Bat. manuscript and the Ultramontane manuscript have *intente*, “attentively.” Immediately afterward, the Ultramontane manuscript omits *omnia*.], discovered one God, the author of all things [Note: [Col. 0986C] The fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript has “we discovered.”], to whom all things are referred [Note: [Col. 0986C] My manuscript has *referrentur*, “would be referred,” which I preferred.]. Hence even now the pagans [Note: [Col. 0986C] The first Lugd. Bat. manuscript has *quod*, “which,” instead of *quos*, “whom.”], whom manifest truth convicts more of obstinacy than of ignorance, when they are challenged by us, admit that they do not follow several gods but venerate many ministers under one great God [Note: [Col. 0986C] The first Florentine manuscript omits *magno*, “great.”].

There remains, therefore, a confused disagreement concerning the understanding of the true God, through the many conjectures by which he is understood, since nearly everyone has one opinion about there being one God [Note: [Col. 0986C] The fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript has “a confused distinction,” which is wrong. Everyone, he says, agrees that there is one God, but within this agreement there are confusedly many opinions held by many people.]. Human inquiry has reached this point, although with labor [Note: [Col. 0986C] “Although with labor, it was able to go this far.” Fabricius added *deliberare*, “to deliberate,” incorrectly. The verb is elegantly used absolutely. Virgil, *Aeneid* II: “Thus far, sister Acca, I was able.” Lautius. Fabricius acted rashly in inserting that word against all the manuscripts and all the old editions. Most old editions have *patuit*, “was open,” but the Augustan edition, along with the manuscripts, has *potuit*, “was able.” The manuscripts and better editions prefer *etsi*, “although,” or *et sic*, “and thus,” found in three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection.], but when reasoning failed [Note: [Col. 0986D] The first edition and those following it have *deficit*, “fails.”], faith came to the rescue [Note: [Col. 0986D] Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts have *supervenit*, “came afterward.”]. For unless we believe, we shall not understand [Note: [Col. 0986D] The first and third Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Augustan edition, have “we do not understand.”]. Hear it from him himself, and believe God himself, if you wish to know what is true concerning God.

Thus the same one and true God, in whom, as we have said, every sect, although arising from diverse opinions, comes together, changing kingdoms, arranging times, and also punishing sins, chose the weak things of the world [Note: [Col. 0986D] From Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians 1:27.] to confound the strong [Col. 0987A]; and he founded the Roman empire by taking as its shepherd a man of the poorest condition [Note: [Col. 0987B] Romulus, brought up by Faustulus, master of the royal flock. Livy I.4.]. This empire, after it had long been advanced by kings and consuls [Note: [Col. 0987B] Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have *profectum*, “advanced forth.”], when it had gained possession of Asia, Africa, and Europe [Note: [Col. 0987B] All the Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection insert *imperio*, “by its empire.” The Ultramontane manuscript has *imperiis*, “by empires,” through the hand of an inexperienced scribe who did not know that *potiri* is joined with the genitive, as in Sallust, *Catiline* 47, *urbis potiri*, “to gain possession of the city.” The first Florentine manuscript reverses Africa and Europe.], he brought together under one emperor [Note: [Col. 0987C] The first Lugd. Bat. manuscript has *eumdem*, “the same,” without *-que*. Some printed editions omit *clementissimum*, “most merciful.”], the same emperor both most courageous and most merciful, all things being arranged according to his order [Note: [Col. 0987C] Four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Ultramontane manuscript and the Gronovian Collection, have *concessit*, “granted.” He is speaking of Augustus.].

Under this emperor, whom almost all nations rightly honored with love mingled with fear, the true God—who had been worshiped by the ignorant with anxious superstition—opened that great fountain of his knowledge [Note: [Col. 0987C] The second word is absent from the first and fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and from the Gronovian Collection. Some old editions likewise have simply “his fountain.”], and, intending to teach human beings more openly through a human being, sent his Son, who performed works surpassing human power, and who rebuked the demons [Note: [Col. 0987C] My manuscript has *coarguerint*, “they would have rebuked,” instead of *coarguentem*, “rebuking.”], whom some might have thought gods, so that those very persons who had not believed him as a human being might believe him, because of his works, to be God’s [Note: [Col. 0987C] All the Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Ultramontane manuscript and the Gronovian Collection, have *tamquam Deo*, “as God,” rather than *tamquam Dei*, “as God’s.” But the latter agrees with the remaining manuscripts and with the passage from which this is taken, John 10:37–38.].

Then, so that the glory of the new name and the swift report of the announced salvation might travel unhindered and rapidly in profound silence [Note: [Col. 0987D] The first Florentine manuscript deletes *in* and reads “in profound silence.”] and the broadest peace [Note: [Col. 0987D] Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have “the broadest peace.” A third Lugd. Bat. manuscript deletes *celeriter*, “rapidly.”], or even so that, while his disciples traveled through different nations and freely offered the gifts of salvation to all, there might be a safe freedom to travel about and teach—since they were Roman citizens among Roman citizens [Note: [Col. 0987D] Some manuscripts and editions read “to depart and desert,” but incorrectly. He means not the freedom to come and go, which would accomplish nothing for the Christian religion, but the freedom to go around, teach, debate, refute, and so forth.]—this was why I thought it worth recalling.

I have mentioned this because this sixth book extends as far as Caesar Augustus, of whom these things are said [Col. 0988A]. But if some consider this most lucid reasoning invalid and assign these achievements instead to their own gods, whom they first chose by prudence and afterward invited by exceptional worship [Note: [Col. 0987D] The Augustan edition has “they chose, and then invited by exceptional worship.” In the fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript, the reading is “they invited.”], so that by their agency this great and most beautiful empire might be founded [Note: [Col. 0988B] This word is absent from the first and third Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and from the Gronovian Collection.], they boast in this way [Note: [Col. 0988C] Some manuscripts and editions have *quod*, “because,” instead of *quia*, “because,” as often happens throughout the printed and manuscript books of this author. Tertullian develops this argument more fully than others in *Apologeticus* 25, pp. 243ff.: “Since mention is specifically made of the Roman name, I shall not omit the challenge provoked by that presumption of those who say that the Romans were raised to such greatness because of their exceptionally diligent religious observance that they occupied the world,” and so forth.] because they themselves, by their excellent religious rites, deserved the special favor of the gods [Note: [Col. 0988C] This is the reading of all the manuscripts, except that Perizonius has *emeruerant*, “had deserved.” Some common editions have *meruerint*, “may have deserved.”], and, when these gods were removed or neglected [Note: [Col. 0988C] Perizonius has *discesserunt*, “they departed.”], everyone departed,

> All have withdrawn from the shrines and, with the altars abandoned,
>
> the gods by whom this empire had stood.  
> [Note: [Col. 0988C] These are Virgil’s words, *Aeneid* II: “All have withdrawn from the shrines and, with the altars abandoned, the gods by whom this empire had stood.”]

Therefore, although reverence for your holiness [Note: [Col. 0988C] He is referring to Augustine’s books *On the City of God*. The Augustan edition deletes *verissime*, “most truthfully,” reading “although you have argued many things most courageously.” The whole passage is absent from the first Florentine manuscript.] has argued many things most courageously and most truthfully, the occasion nevertheless requires me to add a few remarks.

If the Romans earned the gods’ favor by worshiping them and lost it by failing to worship them [Note: [Col. 0988D] The fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript has “and earned it”; the first and third, together with Perizonius and the Gronovian Collection, have “may have earned it,” followed shortly afterward by “may have lost it.”], then, as Romulus himself, the father of Rome, was saved amid all the disasters that assailed him from his very birth [Note: [Col. 0988D] The first word is absent from the third and fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and from Perizonius.], who earned this by worshiping them? Was it his grandfather Amulius, who exposed him to death [Note: [Col. 0988D] The old editions, except the Augustan, have “who exposed him”; the Augustan has “who exposed him to death.” The manuscripts support the former.]? Was it his father, whose identity was uncertain [Note: [Col. 0988D] Perizonius has “who was uncertain?”]? Was it his mother Rhea, guilty of sexual misconduct? Was it the Alban ancestors, who themselves from the beginning persecuted the shoots of the Roman name [Note: [Col. 0988D] These two words are absent from the Augustan edition.]? Was it all Italy, which for four hundred years, as long as it was able, longed for his destruction?

“No,” they reply, “but the gods themselves, because they knew that they were to be worshiped, protected their future worshipers.” Then they are prescient. If they are prescient, why did they bring this empire, throughout so many ages, to the summit of supreme power at precisely the time when he wished to be born among human beings and to be acknowledged as a human being [Note: [Col. 0989C] All the manuscripts and the first of the old editions, the Paris and Venetian editions, have “at the time when he wished to be born.” Bolsuingus and the editions that followed him preferred “at the time when he wished to be born as a human being,” but although I have also found this in the Augustan edition, I cannot approve it.]—after whose name both the gods themselves were despised as nothing and those whom they had advanced, together with the whole world, [Note: [Col. 0989C] I can scarcely tolerate this reading. What does it mean to “run with the whole world”? The second Florentine manuscript has the more tolerable *concurrerunt*, “converged.” But that does not satisfy me either. I therefore correct it to *corruerunt*, “fell.” Orosius’ meaning seems to be: those fictitious gods whom the Romans had chosen for themselves, and the Romans who believed that through those gods they had been raised to such power, were conquered by the power of God born among human beings and acknowledged as a human being. When his kingdom came, those fictitious gods themselves were despised and treated as nothing, and the Roman empire fell; together with the whole world, it came under the dominion of him who establishes empires and emperors, and to whom his Father had long before promised the inheritance of the whole earth and rule over all kingdoms. This seems to me Orosius’ meaning as a Christian writer.] ran? [Note: [Col. 0989D] The verb has rightly been retained; I would not change it to *inrepsit*, “crept in,” although that reading occurs in my manuscript.]

“But he crept in humbly and entered secretly,” they reply. But from something secret and humble, whence came such widespread fame, such unquestioned faith, such manifest power? By certain signs and miracles he seized and held minds anxious with superstition [Note: [Col. 0989D] All the old editions, except Hittorp’s and the Venetian editions, which incorrectly have *solitas*, and the manuscripts, read *sollicitas*. The second and first Lugd. Bat. manuscripts have *sollicitatas*, “having been troubled,” with this reading written above it in the first. I retain the common reading. Orosius rightly calls human minds “anxious with superstition,” referring to that foolish anxiety which arises from superstition.]. But if a human being could do this, the gods ought to have been able to do it even more [Note: [Col. 0990C] Four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have *potuisse*, “to have been able.”].

Or was it because he proclaimed that this power had been handed over to him by his Father that people finally arrived at an understanding of that known and unknown God, whom, as I have said, no one can grasp except through him? Nor can anyone grasp him unless he has examined and despised himself thoroughly [Note: [Col. 0990C] The Augustan edition simply has “who, with complete reflection.”], and, turning toward God’s wisdom, has transferred the entire reasoning process of seeking [Note: [Col. 0990C] This word is absent from the first Florentine manuscript. Shortly afterward, three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection read *transtulit*, “has transferred,” instead of *transtulerit*. Scottus’ edition also incorrectly has *rationem*, “reason,” rather than *ratiocinationem*, “process of reasoning.”] to the faith of believing.

Nevertheless, I shall examine the matter briefly. These gods, whom people represent as so powerful that they both advanced the Roman state when favorable and seem to have ruined it when hostile [Note: [Col. 0989C] The manuscripts have *aversi*, “when turned away”; some old editions have *adversi*, “when hostile.” Four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Ultramontane manuscript have *videbantur*, “seemed,” instead of *videantur*. My manuscript and Perizonius have “at that certain time,” as do the second and third Florentine manuscripts.], were being worshiped with the utmost devotion and intensity [Note: [Col. 0989C] Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have *diutissime*, “for a very long time.” The Ultramontane and second Lugd. Bat. manuscripts have *quamvis devotissime*, “although with the greatest devotion.”] at precisely the time when it is publicly established that Christ wished to be born and began to be proclaimed among the nations [Note: [Col. 0989C] One or two Lugd. Bat. manuscripts absurdly add “among Christians,” or “Christ.”]. Thus, although they were concerned for themselves and their worshipers, were they unable either to restrain or to repel the superstition because of which they saw that they themselves ought to be despised and their worshipers abandoned [Note: [Col. 0990D] This word is absent from the third and fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and from the Gronovian Collection.]?

Yet if they were to be forgiven because they were unwilling, they should not have been abandoned; if they were willing, their foreknowledge should have been preserved, and they ought not to have been helped beforehand [Note: [Col. 0990D] The first Paris and Venetian editions have *desperandi*, “there was no hope,” rather than *deserendi*, “of abandoning.” I have added the question mark in the preceding passage, as it removes the obscurity of the sense.].

“This is what happened,” they reply. “For we stirred up nations, inflamed kings, established laws, appointed judges, prepared punishments with executions and crosses, searched the whole world, [Note: [Col. 0990D] Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, the Ultramontane manuscript, and the Gronovian Collection, together with some editions, add *tandem*, “at last.”] to see whether the Christian name and worship could somehow be erased from the whole world.”

This was done until fruitful cruelty advanced so far amid tortures and through tortures that it occupied the imperial summit itself, through which alone it could have been prevented [Note: [Col. 0990D] Perizonius has *impediri*, “be hindered.” The third and fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with my manuscript, Perizonius, and the Gronovian Collection, have “could have been prevented.”].

“And what followed afterward?” they ask. “The Christian emperors ordered the rites to cease and the temples to be closed, and therefore:

> All have withdrawn from the shrines, with the altars abandoned,
>
> the gods by whom this empire had stood.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0990D] The Augustan edition has “with the altars abandoned and the gods,” rather than “with the altars and the gods abandoned.”]

O how great, and how unobstructed, is the light of truth, if weak and wretched eyes did not close themselves voluntarily against it when it offered itself [Note: [Col. 0990D] My parchment manuscript, with *si* deleted, reads “the Christian faith…”]!

If the Christian faith, through many past ages [Note: [Col. 0990D] The first Lugd. Bat. manuscript has “through many centuries.”], when nations, kings, laws, massacres, crosses, and deaths were raging everywhere against it [Note: [Col. 0990D] The first Lugd. Bat. manuscript omits *caedibus*, “massacres”; some old editions have *cruciatibus*, “torments,” instead of *crucibus*, “crosses.”], could in no way be restrained, but rather—as I have said—grew amid these things and through these things; while the worship of idols, already in some sense dying away of itself and ashamed of itself, ceased at a single most merciful command without any punitive terror—who can doubt that through this demonstration of understanding the creature at last learned of its Creator [Col. 0991A], whom it had sought until then through various forms of reasoning, however intensely its mind was engaged, but whose knowledge had been obscured by other things, and that it therefore immediately cleaved to his love, whom it had loved even while ignorant of him [Note: [Col. 0991C] Some old editions and manuscripts incorrectly have *quem*, “whom,” or *quam*, “which,” or *quoniam*, “because”; the fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript likewise has *statutum*, “established,” instead of *statim*, “immediately.]?

Nor, therefore, is it surprising if in a great household there are found some slaves [Note: [Col. 0991C] Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, the Gronovian Collection, and the Ultramontane manuscript have *inveniantur*, “may be found.”] who, accustomed through the habit and licentiousness of seducers, abuse their master’s patience to despise him [Note: [Col. 0991C] Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have “whence deservedly.”], and therefore God rightly rebukes the ungrateful, the unbelieving, and even the rebellious [Note: [Col. 0991C] My manuscript lacks the first *vel*, “or”; *utique*, “certainly,” which follows shortly afterward, is absent from the second Lugd. Bat. manuscript.] with various chastisements. This must always be acknowledged, but especially then [Note: [Col. 0991C] In Perizonius these words are transposed: “when throughout the whole world there was not yet any church.”], when as yet there was no church throughout the whole world that, through the intervention of the prayers of the faithful, might entreat God’s mercy and temper the world’s deserved punishments and God’s just judgment. Hence these things too, whatever they may be [Note: [Col. 0991C] Some old editions have *sint*, “may be,” instead of *sunt*, “are.”], which appear evil to human beings [Col. 0991B], were without doubt all the more severe, as will be proved by the very order in which they began.

The Mithridatic war—or, to speak more accurately, the disasters of the Mithridatic war, which involved many provinces at once [Note: [Col. 0991C] This is the reading of all the manuscripts, which I have restored. The common editions have “which carried many provinces along with it,” except the Augustan edition, which agrees with the manuscripts.]—was prolonged and extended over forty years [Note: [Col. 0991C] My parchment manuscript reads “prolonged and further prolonged.”]. For in the six hundred and sixty-second year from the founding of the City, as I have said [Note: [Col. 0991C] This was stated in the preceding book, chapter 19, where in the notes we discussed the duration of the Mithridatic war. Fabricius.], in which the first civil war had also begun [Note: [Col. 0991D] The second Lugd. Bat. manuscript has “the first,” but the three Florentine manuscripts delete it, and the third also omits “war.”], the war, growing fiercer [Note: [Col. 0991D] Some old editions connect this word with what precedes, reading *inardescere*, “to grow fiercer.” But the three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have “was growing fiercer”; in several other manuscripts and editions *vero* is also added to the following phrase.], was, in the consulship of Cicero and Antony, to use the words of the excellent poet [Note: [Col. 0991D] He alludes to Lucan, whose words occur in Book I, line 337. It is noteworthy that in the time of Orosius and Augustine Lucan was held in high esteem, and later in excessively high esteem.]:

> It was scarcely finished by barbarian poison.

But in these periods, thirty years of warfare are found [Note: [Col. 0992C] Some editions incorrectly remove the middle word. How many years that most serious Mithridatic war lasted, I have traced as far as possible through the annals in the *Universal History*, whose third volume begins with the kings of Pontus and contains more about this Mithridates.]. It is not easy to determine in what manner forty years are said by most writers [Note: [Col. 0992C] Perizonius and my manuscript have “are said.” Four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Ultramontane manuscript and the Gronovian Collection, have “are distinguished.”].

## CHAPTER TWO. Here he continues the Mithridatic war, which Sulla brought to an end

[Col. 0992A]

Therefore Mithridates, king of Pontus and Armenia [Note: [Col. 0992C] “King of Pontus and Armenia.” This is to be understood of Lesser Armenia. For Greater Armenia was ruled by Tigranes, whom this most cunning and powerful king Mithridates, his son-in-law, involved in the Roman war through the marriage of his daughter Cleopatra.], after he had attempted to deprive Nicomedes, king of Bithynia and a friend of the Roman people, of his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0992C] “After Nicomedes.” The same account is found in Eutropius, book V. See Appian’s *Mithridatic War* and Justin, book XXXVIII. FABR.], and, having been warned by the senate that, if he attempted it, war would be brought against him by the Roman people, became enraged and immediately invaded Cappadocia [Note: [Col. 0992C] “Invaded.” The fourth Leiden edition reads *invasit* (“invaded”) for *pervasit* (“overran”).]. Having expelled King Ariobarzanes from it, he devastated the whole province with fire and sword. Next he attacked Bithynia with equal destruction. He afflicted Paphlagonia with a similar outcome, driving out its kings Pylaemenes and Nicomedes.

Afterward, when he had come to Ephesus, he issued a cruel edict [Note: [Col. 0992C] “He issued a cruel edict.” Besides Appian, this edict is mentioned by Livy, book LXXVIII, Florus, book III, chapter 5, and Eutropius, book V. Hence Cicero, in *On the Manilian Law*, says: “Mithridates marked out the Roman citizens throughout all Asia, in so many cities, to be killed and slaughtered on one entire day, by one announcement and one written signal.” FABR.], ordering that throughout Asia all Roman citizens who were found should be killed on a single day [Note: [Col. 0992D] “Whoever.” The first Florence edition reads: “so that whoever should be found …”]. And it was done. It is impossible for words either to explain or to comprehend in any way what multitude of Roman citizens was then slaughtered, what grief there was in the many provinces, what groaning among those about to kill and those about to be killed alike, when each person was compelled either to betray innocent hosts and friends or to risk himself in punishment for his guests.

Archelaus also [Note: [Col. 0992D] “Also.” Absent from the Augustan edition.], the commander of Mithridates, having been sent ahead into Achaea with one hundred and twenty thousand infantry and cavalry [Note: [Col. 0992D] “With one hundred and twenty thousand.” In *Meus* the word “twenty” is absent.], gained possession of Athens and all Greece, partly by force and partly by surrender.

Sulla, to whom the Mithridatic War had fallen after his consulship [Note: [Col. 0992D] “Sulla, to whom after his consulship …” Sulla departed for the Mithridatic War after his consulship, when Cinna, already consul, was preparing an accusation against him through the tribune of the plebs Virginius. Plutarch, *Sulla*. FABR.], besieged Archelaus at the Piraeus, the port of the Athenians, which was fortified by a sevenfold wall [Note: [Col. 0992D] “Fortified by a sevenfold wall.” Thus Florus: “Then, after the Piraean port had been destroyed, fortified with six and even more walls.” Archelaus had fortified it with several walls against Sulla’s attack, as Appian writes. FABR.] [Note: [Col. 0992D] “Fortified.” Perizonius reads *munitum* (“fortified”) rather than *commun[i]tum*.]. He captured the city of Athens itself by force, and afterward [Note: [Col. 0993B] “Afterward he engaged Archelaus in a pitched battle.” This battle was fought in Boeotia at Chaeronea. Appian, Plutarch, and Eutropius write that, out of Archelaus’s 120,000 men, scarcely 10,000 escaped to Chalcis. Therefore, in the epitome of Livy, book eighty-two, where it reads “one hundred thousand of the enemy having been killed,” I think it should be written “one hundred and ten thousand.” FABR.] fought Archelaus in a pitched battle [Note: [Col. 0993B] “In a pitched battle.” Most editions read “and afterward,” being excessively permissive against the evidence of all the manuscripts. For “in a pitched battle,” the fourth Leiden edition reads “after a battle had been joined.”]. One hundred and ten thousand from Archelaus’s army are reported to have been killed, and scarcely ten thousand to have survived [Note: [Col. 0993B] “One hundred and ten thousand.” The first Leiden edition reads “ninety thousand.”].

When Mithridates learned of the defeat, he sent Archelaus the finest seventy thousand soldiers from Asia as reinforcements [Note: [Col. 0993C] “The finest seventy thousand.” Eutropius has the same number; but Appian and Plutarch have *ὀκτὼ μυριάδες*, that is, eighty thousand, whom Mithridates sent with Dorylaus to Archelaus. FABR.]. [Note: [Col. 0993C] “Seventy thousand.” Perizonius reads “eighty thousand.”] In the second battle fifteen thousand of these were killed [Note: [Col. 0993C] “Fifteen thousand in the second battle.” Although all the books of Orosius read “fifty thousand,” I nevertheless did not hesitate to restore “fifteen thousand” from my manuscript of Eutropius (for the printed editions have “twenty thousand”), especially since Appian writes: *τῶν πολεμίων ἀπώλοντο ἀμφὶ μυρίους καὶ πεντακισχιλίους*, “about fifteen thousand of the enemy perished,” and the numbers that follow cannot stand if one reads “fifty thousand.” This second battle was fought at Orchomenus. Appian, Plutarch, Florus. FABR.], and there Diogenes, the son of Archelaus, was slaughtered [Note: [Col. 0993C] “Diogenes, son of Archelaus.” *Ὁ παῖς Ἀρχελάου Διογένης* (“Diogenes, the son of Archelaus”), according to Appian. Plutarch has *Διογένης ὁ τῆς Ἀρχελάου γυναικὸς υἱός* (“Diogenes, the son of Archelaus’s wife”). FABR.].

In the third war all the forces Archelaus possessed were destroyed. For twenty thousand of his soldiers, driven into a marsh [Note: [Col. 0993D] “Driven.” Four Leiden copies, together with the Utrecht and Groningen collections, read “forced in.”], while they implored Sulla’s protection [Note: [Col. 0993D] “Implored.” Perizonius reads “reproached.”], were killed by the victor’s insatiable anger; an equal number were driven into a river and killed, and the rest of the wretched men were slaughtered everywhere [Note: [Col. 0993D] “Here and there.” *Meus* reads “scatteredly.”].

Moreover, Mithridates was intent on killing the leading men of the most distinguished cities in Asia and confiscating their property. And when he had already killed one thousand six hundred [Note: [Col. 0993D] “One thousand six hundred.” Appian also has *ἀμφὶ τοὺς χιλίους καὶ ἑξακοσίους ἄνδρας* (“about one thousand six hundred men”); consult him on this matter. FABR.] in this way [Note: [Col. 0993D] “Had killed them thus.” The preceding word is absent from *Meus* and from three Leiden or Groningen copies.], the Ephesians, fearing their example, shut the gates after excluding his garrison [Note: [Col. 0993D] “After excluding his garrison.” Some old editions read: “after excluding the garrison, they barred the gates against him.”]. The Smyrnaeans, Sardians, Colophonians, and Trallians did the same.

Mithridates, thrown into confusion, made peace with Sulla through his commander Archelaus.

Meanwhile Fimbria, an accomplice in the crimes of the Marians and the boldest of men, killed the consul Flaccus at Nicomedia, to whom he had gone as lieutenant [Note: [Col. 0994B] “To whom he had gone.” *Meus* and Perizonius read “to whom he was.”]. He then seized the army and drove Mithridates’ son from Asia to Miletopolis [Note: [Col. 0994B] “To Miletopolis.” See Strabo, book II. FABR.], attacked the king’s position, and expelled Mithridates himself from Pergamum. Pursuing him, he besieged him at Pitane; and he would certainly have captured him, if Lucullus had placed the care of the state above the civil quarrels and had wished to hem him in by sea, by placing his fleet in the way [Note: [Col. 0994B] “And hem him in by sea.” This passage had been corrupted by superfluous words and has been restored by us from the manuscripts. Plutarch, explaining the same matter in *Lucullus*, says among other things: *Εἰ Φιμβρίᾳ τότε πεισθεὶς ὁ Λούκουλλος, οὐ μακρὰν ὢν, περιήγαγεν ἐκεῖσε τὰς ναῦς καὶ συνέφραξε τὸν λιμένα τῷ στόλῳ πέρας ἂν εἶχεν ὁ πόλεμος*, that is: “If Lucullus, who was not far away, had then followed Fimbria’s advice, brought the ships around there, and blocked the harbor with his fleet, the war would have been finished.” FABR. — Previously most editions incorrectly read: “and when he wished to hem him in by sea, he was repulsed by the Ilians after placing his fleet in the way. Then Fimbria …”].
