Therefore Fimbria, angry with the Ilians, by whom he appeared to have been repulsed because of their support for Sulla’s party [Note: [Col. 0994C] “Angry with the Ilians.” Appian and Strabo, book XIII, discuss the destruction of Ilium. FABR.], utterly destroyed the city of Ilium, that ancient parent of Rome, by slaughter and fire. But Sulla immediately restored it.

The same Fimbria, at Thyatira [Note: [Col. 0994D] “At Thyatira.” *Πρὸς Θυατείροις* (“near Thyatira”), Plutarch, *Sulla*. FABR.], when he was besieged by Sulla’s army, driven to despair [Note: [Col. 0994D] “Driven.” The first Leiden edition reads “forced.”], killed himself with his own hand in the temple of Aesculapius.

373 [Note: [Col. 0994D] “Fannius and Magius.” This is read in all the handwritten books, and I judge it to be the correct reading. Although Appian’s printed book has *Λουκίους Μαγνιόν τε καὶ Φάνιον*, I nevertheless read *Μαγιόν τε καὶ Φάνιον*, especially since Asconius, in the third *Verrine*, calls these same men L. Magius and L. Fannius, although in Cicero’s book it is corruptly written “L. Magius and L. Rabius.” FABR. — The first and fourth Leiden editions have *Magnus*; all the others, as also the Augustan edition, correctly have *Magius*. Soon afterward the name Fimbria is absent from some manuscripts.].

Fannius and Magius, deserters from Fimbria’s army, joined Mithridates [Note: [Col. 0994D] “Joined themselves.” The fourth Leiden edition reads simply “joined.”]. At their urging, Mithridates made a treaty with Sertorius through envoys sent to Spain.

Sertorius sent Marcus Marius to him [Note: [Col. 0995B] “Sertorius sent to him.” Some old editions read: “Sertorius, however, sent …”] to strengthen the alliance [Note: [Col. 0995B] “Marcus Marius.” Appian calls him *Μάρκιον Οὐάρον* or, as the translator Candidus reads it, *Οὐάριον*. But Plutarch, in *Lucullus*, names him Marius, as Orosius does. FABR.]. The king kept him with him and soon made him commander in place of Archelaus, who had gone over to Sulla with his wife and children.

Marius and Eumachus, commanders sent by Mithridates against Lucullus, soon gathered a large army and encountered P. Rutilius at Chalcedon [Note: [Col. 0995C] “With P. Rutilius.” I think Rutilius was the lieutenant of M. Cotta; for Mithridates defeated Cotta on land at Chalcedon and stripped him of his magnificent fleet at sea, as Mithridates himself writes in his letter to Arsaces, preserved from book IV of Sallust’s *Histories*. On this matter, as also on the siege of Cyzicus, see Appian and Plutarch. FABR.]. They killed him together with a very large part of his army [Note: [Col. 0995C] “With part of his army.” The first Leiden edition omits the middle word, which can easily be missed; the Augustan edition substitutes “of his” for it.].

Lucullus surrounded Mithridates, who was besieging the Cyzicenes, with a trench and compelled him to suffer what he himself was doing. He sent a message to the Cyzicenes, telling them to keep their courage, by means of a soldier skilled in swimming. Suspended from two wineskins [Note: [Col. 0995C] “Suspended.” Fabricius correctly restored this from the manuscripts; most editions had: “who, hanging from two wineskins, himself holding a middle balance and paddling with his feet …”], while himself holding a middle pole and paddling with his feet, the soldier crossed seven miles. Mithridates, suffering from scarcity, ordered part of his troops, armed and arrayed, to return home. Lucullus intercepted them and destroyed them all.

For it is reported that he then killed more than fifteen thousand men [Note: [Col. 0995C] “For more than fifteen thousand.” Lucullus pursued to the Rhyndacus River those who were being sent by Mithridates into Bithynia and killed a great number of them; he captured six thousand horses and fifteen thousand men. Thus Plutarch and Appian. FABR. — In the first edition: “more than fifteen,” with *quam* (“than”) deleted.].

At that time Fannius, who had joined Mithridates, and Metrophanes, the royal governor, were defeated by Mamerchus and fled into Moesia with two thousand cavalry. From there they departed into Maeonia [Note: [Col. 0995D] “Departed.” The first Leiden edition reads “descended.”] and came into the hills and the plains of Inarimus [Note: [Col. 0995D] “The plains of Inarimus.” The common reading is “the plains and the deserts.” I have found the conjunction *et* (“and”) in none of the old manuscripts. But some have *camposque inheremos*, others *camposque inharemos*. Hence I was led to believe that Orosius wrote *camposque Inarimos*. Homer’s famous passage in the Catalogue reads:

*Εἰναρίμοις, ὅθι φασὶ Τυφωέος ἔμμεναι εὐνάς.*

“Where they say the chambers of Typhoeus are in Arimi.”

Although all the Greek writers read *εἰν Ἀρίμοις* as two words and place Arima either in Cilicia, Syria, or Lydia, Pliny nevertheless writes in book III, chapter 6, that the island Aenaria was called Inarime by Homer. Virgil, Ovid, Horace, Lucan, and the other Latin poets likewise used *Inarime*. I therefore thought that Livy, or whoever else was the source from whom Orosius derived his history, had written *campos Inarimos*, especially since the Skepsian, as reported by Strabo in book XIII [Col. 0996B], judged the opinion more probable that places the Arimi in the burned region of Mysia, and Xanthus reports that a certain Arimus once ruled in those regions. FABR. — Of the manuscripts I consulted, three Florence copies and the second Leiden copy have *in colles camposque inaremos*; *Meus* has *inheremo*; Utrecht has *Arenios*; the first and third Leiden editions have *maritimos*; the fourth, together with Perizonius, *marinos*; and the Groningen collection, *mansimos*. But I judge Fabricius’s emendation to be sound. The Homeric verse occurs in book II of the *Iliad*, in the Catalogue of Ships, verse 290. At that passage Eustathius, in the excellent and highly praiseworthy edition of Alexander Politi, volume II, p. 747, writes: *Γαῖα δ᾽ ὑπεστενάχιζεν, ὅπερ κατωτέρω παθητικῶς λέγει, στεναχίζετο. Ἐστενάχιζε δὲ καὶ πυρὸς νομὴν ἔπασχεν, οὐχ ἁπλῶς, ἀλλὰ Διὶ ὡς τερπικεραύνῳ χωομένῳ, ὅτε τ᾽ ἀμφὶ Τυφωέϊ γαῖαν ἱμάσσει εἰν Ἀρίμοις, ὅθι φασὶ Τυφωέος ἔμμεναι εὐνάς.*

“That is: ‘The earth groaned beneath them,’ which he later expresses in the passive form *στεναχίζετο*, ‘was made to groan.’ It groaned and suffered the ravaging of fire, not simply or in some ordinary way, but as if beneath an angry Zeus the Thunderer, when he lashes the earth around Typhoeus in Arimis, where they say Typhoeus’s chambers are.”].

They fell among the plains of Inarimus, where not only burned mountains and rocks darkened as if by a kind of soot are visible, but also plains made barren by scorched soil, extending for fifty miles, with no sign of fire or furnace, and decayed ashes lying suspended over the depths. In three places, moreover, smoking chasms are displayed, which the Greeks call *physai*. After wandering about in them for a long time, they were finally delivered from unexpected dangers and secretly came into the king’s camp.

Deiotarus, king of Gallograecia [Note: [Col. 0996C] “Deiotarus, king of Gallograecia.” The same appears in Livy’s Epistle to book XCIV. Eumachus, Mithridates’ governor, had invaded Phrygia; see Appian. FABR.], killed the king’s commanders in battle [Note: [Col. 0996D] “In battle.” The first and third Leiden editions, together with the Groningen collection, read “in the war.”].

Meanwhile Mithridates, besieged at Cyzicus by the very delay with which he was conducting the siege, reduced his army to great scarcity and pestilence. For he is said to have lost more than three hundred thousand men to hunger and disease during that same siege [Note: [Col. 0996D] “More than three hundred thousand.” Plutarch, in *Lucullus*, says: *Λέγονται δὲ ἐκ τοῦ παντὸς ἀκολούθων τε καὶ μαχίμων ὄχλου μυριάδες οὐ πολὺ δὴ τοῦ τριάκοντα λείπουσαι διαφθαρῆναι* (“It is said that, from the entire multitude of followers and fighting men, nearly thirty tens of thousands perished”). FABR. — The first Florence edition reads “more than three hundred,” with *quam* deleted.]. He himself secretly fled from the camp with a few men after seizing a ship [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Secretly fled.” The second Leiden edition and the Groningen collection read: “after seizing a small ship, he fled.”].

Lucullus, watching without bloodshed by his own soldiers the disaster of another, gained a new kind of victory. Soon afterward he attacked Marius and defeated and routed him. In that battle more than eleven thousand Marian soldiers are reported to have been killed [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Eleven.” Perizonius’s manuscript counts twelve thousand.].

Later Lucullus engaged the same Marius in a naval battle [Note: [Col. 0996D] “In a naval battle.” Some editions read “in war.”] and either sank or captured thirty-two royal ships and several transports [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Thirty-two.” Some old editions read thirty-five.]. Many of those whom Sulla had proscribed were killed there [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Many of these.” Perizonius’s manuscript does not acknowledge the phrase, which may be absent.].

The next day Marius was dragged out of the cave where he was hiding and paid the penalty deserved by a hostile spirit.

With the same assault Lucullus devastated Apamea and captured, stormed, and plundered Prusa beneath Mount Olympus, a very strongly fortified city [Note: [Col. 0997B] “Prusa beneath Mount Olympus.” All printed books have *prius Athan* in place of *Prusam*, but since the latter word is absent from the manuscripts and one reads *Priusam*, I have written *Prusam*. Pliny, book V, at the end: “Inland from Cius in Bithynia is Prusa, founded beneath Olympus by Hannibal.” Appian: *Βάρβας δὲ Προυσιάδα εἷλε τὴν πρὸς τῷ ὄρει* (“Barbas captured Prusias near the mountain”). On Prusias, formerly called Cius, see Strabo, book XII. FABR.].

Mithridates, sailing with a fleet toward Byzantium, was caught by a storm and lost eighty beaked ships [Note: [Col. 0997C] “Eighty beaked ships.” Appian has about sixty ships.]. As he himself was being carried down with the already battered ship [Note: [Col. 0997C] “With the ship already battered.” Three Leiden copies, together with the Groningen collection and the first Florence edition, have “with a battered ship,” or “with the ship already battered.” The same occurs in the second Florence copy, but *quassata* is written above it. Both forms are Latin, and many examples of each are found in Ovid. But *quassata* seems to have been taken from Orosius through his frequent imitation of Virgil. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 53:

“And the battered ships, while the sky was unmanageable.”], he leapt aboard the pirate Seleucus’s *myoparo*, with the pirate himself helping [Note: [Col. 0997C] “Helping.” The first Florence edition reads *juvente* (“helping”) instead of *jubente* (“ordering”), which appears in the Augustan edition.]. From there he reached Sinope, and afterward Amisus, with great difficulty [Note: [Col. 0997C] “And afterward Amisus.” This is correctly given by the manuscripts; see Appian and Plutarch.].

376 CHAPTER III. On Catiline’s incest, and the wars of the Luculli against the Bessi, Mithridates, Tigranes, and the others.

In the same year at Rome Catiline was accused of incest [Note: [Col. 0997D] “Catiline accused of incest.” Asconius mentions this trial in his speech of Cicero against his competitors, where he writes that this Fabia was a Vestal Virgin and the sister of Terentia, Cicero’s wife. Accordingly, in Plutarch’s *Cato*, one should read: *ἐν οἷς καὶ Φαβία, Τερεντίας ἀδελφή, τῆς Κικέρωνος γυναικὸς ἐκινδύνευσεν* (“among whom Fabia, sister of Terentia, Cicero’s wife, was also put in danger”). FABR.], because he was alleged to have committed it with Fabia, a Vestal Virgin [Note: [Col. 0997D] “Was alleged.” *Meus* reads “was said.” Some editions add *stuprum* (“sexual violation”) after “Vestal.”]. Supported by Catulus’s influence, Catiline escaped.

Lucullus had besieged Sinope in preparation for storming it. Seleucus, the chief pirate, and Cleochares the eunuch [Note: [Col. 0997D] “Cleochares.” Two Leiden copies, the Groningen collection, and the first edition read *Leochares*.], who were in charge of the garrison [Note: [Col. 0997D] “For the purpose.” The first Leiden edition reads “for the sake of it.”], left it plundered and burned [Note: [Col. 0997D] “Plundered.” Some manuscripts and printed copies read “stripped.” But the Augustan edition reads: “They left it, without the equipment of war, plundered and burned.”].

Lucullus, moved by the internal disaster of the wretched enemy, extinguished the fire by a swift arrival [Note: [Col. 0997D] “Arrival.” Three Leiden copies, together with the Groningen collection, read “advance.”]. Thus the unhappy city, in the reversal of enemies and allies, was destroyed from the place from which it ought to have been defended, and saved from the place from which it ought to have been destroyed.

But M. Lucullus, who had succeeded Curio in Macedonia [Note: [Col. 0998B] “M. Lucullus.” For the deeds accomplished by M. Lucullus against the Bessi and Thracians, see Eutropius and Sextus Rufus. FABR.], attacked the entire nation of the Bessi in war and received its surrender.

At the same time Metellus, praetor of Sicily, having found Sicily afflicted by that most disgraceful praetorship of C. Verres, especially while Pyrganion, the chief pirate [Note: [Col. 0998C] “Pyrganion.” We find two forms of the name of this chief pirate in our manuscripts: some call him *Pergamaenon* in their books. FABR. — In all the manuscripts I find *Pyrganion* or *Purganion*. Some editions have *Pergamenon* or *Perganion*.], was mangling it with wicked plunderings and massacres [Note: [Col. 0998C] “Mangling.” Four Leiden copies read “lacerating.”], after he had driven off the Roman fleet and taken possession of the harbor of Syracuse, compelled him soon to withdraw from Sicily after crushing him in a naval and land battle [Note: [Col. 0998C] “Which.” Perizonius reads “him.” The Augustan edition deletes the word, but the first and Venetian editions soon afterward read “him.”].

Furthermore, Lucullus, having crossed the Euphrates and Tigris, engaged Mithridates and Tigranes at the city of Tigranocerta [Note: [Col. 0998C] “At Tigranocerta.” The first Leiden edition reads *Tigranocerem*.], and with a very small force of his own killed a great number of the enemy. For thirty thousand men are reported to have been killed in that war [Note: [Col. 0998C] “For thirty thousand.” Twenty thousand is also read. But Plutarch reports that one hundred thousand infantry were killed and that, of the fifty-five thousand cavalry, only a few escaped. FABR.].

Tigranes, accompanied by scarcely one hundred and fifty cavalry [Note: [Col. 0998C] “Scarcely.” Absent from the first Florence edition.], fled, throwing away his diadem and tiara so that he would not be recognized. Then envoys from almost the entire East came as suppliants to Lucullus.

As winter was approaching, Lucullus returned through Armenia into Mesopotamia and stormed and captured the city of Nisibis, then famous in those regions [Note: [Col. 0998C] “He, as winter approached.” Nisibis, which the Greeks call Antioch of Mygdonia, was captured when L. Metellus and Q. Marcius were consuls, according to Dio, book XXXV. See also Appian and Plutarch. On Antioch, Didacus Covarruvias treats the matter in book IV of his *Various Resolutions*. FABR.]. [Note: [Col. 0998D] “In those regions at that time.” Thus all the manuscripts consistently read. The editions therefore insert the words “in those regions,” reading “then in those regions,” without justification.].

CHAPTER IV. On the Pirate and Cretan Wars, and on Pompey’s actions against Mithridates.

[Note: [Col. 0998D] “The pirates in those same days.” On the Pirate War, also called the Maritime War, see Dio, book XXXVI, and Plutarch, *Pompey*, for a detailed account. On the same subject, see Cicero, *On the Manilian Law*; Livy, book XCIX; Florus, book III, chapter 6; Velleius; and Eutropius. FABR.]

In those same days the pirates, scattered throughout all the seas [Note: [Col. 0998D] “In those days.” Perizonius reads “at that time.”], no longer merely intercepting the passage of ships but also laying waste to islands and provinces, openly joining themselves together through impunity in crime and greed for plunder [Note: [Col. 0998D] “Joining themselves together.” I preferred to print this with Perizonius’s manuscript and the oldest editions rather than *associantibus*, which some prefer.], grew to an immense power.

Cn. Pompey, after the extensive devastation which they had long inflicted on land and sea, nevertheless suppressed them with remarkable speed [Note: [Col. 0999C] “Whom Cn. Pompey …” In addition to other accounts of this war and of the pirates’ new settlement, Lucan, book II, 576:

“Who, when I bore standards shining over the whole sea,

before Cynthia had twice completed and set her sphere,

fearing every strait, the pirate abandoned the sea

and demanded a narrow dwelling in a confined land.”

For Pompey granted the pirates permission to live at Soli, a city of Cilicia, as Dio Cassius, book XXXVI, p. 18, and Strabo, p. 462, testify. Therefore this new colony called its city Pompeiopolis. I published in the first volume of the *Morellian Treasury*, p. 339, a notable coin struck in that city bearing the head of its founder Pompey. Later I also acquired another unpublished bronze, no less remarkable for rarity and preservation, indeed additionally distinguished by the newly restored city after it had changed its name. From our collection, together with the Morellian coin—both are bronze—I append it, drawn exactly from the original.].

At the same time Metellus overran the island of Crete for two years and, after subduing it in a long war, brought it under his power, exchanging the laws of Minos for Roman laws [Note: [Col. 0999C] “Crete at the same time.” On the Cretan War, see Xiphilinus in *Pompey*; Livy, book XCVIII and following; Florus, book III, chapter 7; and Velleius, book II. FABR.].

Afterward Pompey, Lucullus’s successor [Note: [Col. 0999D] “Pompey, Lucullus’s successor.” The Mithridatic War was entrusted to Pompey by the Manilian Law, which Cicero advocated. Appian, Plutarch, and Diodorus. FABR.], enclosed the king’s camp under siege in Lesser Armenia near Mount Dastracum. The king, having made a sortie by night with all his forces, decided also to drive back the pursuer in battle [Note: [Col. 0999D] “The pursuer.” Three Leiden copies, together with the Groningen collection and some editions, read “the pursuers.”]. Pompey set out to pursue the fugitives. Thus the battle was joined at night [Note: [Col. 0999D] “The battle was joined at night.” Besides Appian, Plutarch, and Dio, see Florus, book III, chapter 5, and Eutropius, book VI, who writes that Pompey killed forty thousand and lost thirty from his own army, along with two centurions. FABR.].

The moon had then risen and was behind the Romans [Note: [Col. 0999D] “Was.” The Augustan edition reads “was situated.”]. The royal troops, taking the length of the shadows for the proximity of the enemy [Note: [Col. 0999D] “The length of the shadows.” I restored this on the authority of the Lombard manuscript; the common reading is “by the length of the shadows.” But the royal troops did not infer the Romans’ proximity from the length of the shadows—for in that case they would not have wasted their missiles so ineffectually. Rather, deceived by the length of the shadows and believing that length itself indicated that the hostile army was present, they attacked the shadows as though they were bodies: *Ἐς γὰρ τὸ κενὸν οἱ βάρβαροι, ὡς καὶ ἐγγὺς αὐτῶν ὄντων, μάτην ἔπαιον* (“For the barbarians struck into empty space in vain, as though the enemies were close at hand”). Dio Cassius, book XXXVI, p. 24.], discharged all their weapons to no effect [Note: [Col. 1000B] “Discharged.” *Meus* reads “sent.”]. The Romans then attacked them as though they were unarmed and won without difficulty.

For forty thousand from the royal army were killed or captured [Note: [Col. 1000B] “The Romans wounded.” Perizonius reads “but the Romans were wounded.”], while one thousand Romans were wounded and scarcely forty were killed [Note: [Col. 1000B] “Forty killed.” The first and third Leiden editions, together with the Groningen collection, reduce the number further to twenty.].

The king escaped by flight amid the confusion of battle, aided also by the benefit of the faint light of night. Abandoned by all his friends, philosophers, writers of histories or poems, and physicians, he went alone through trackless places, leading his horse by the hand and trembling at every nocturnal sound [Note: [Col. 1000B] “Trembling.” Perizonius reads “fearing.”]. He turned aside into a certain fort [Note: [Col. 1000B] “Turned aside.” Orosius appears to have written *devertit* in the old sense of *divertit* (“turned aside”), imitating Plautus, Tacitus, Quintilian, and others. The Lombard manuscript clearly has *devertit*, as does the Groningen collection. The first Leiden edition’s *devenit* appears to be a gloss.], and from there proceeded into Armenia.

As Pompey pursued the king, he founded the city of Nicopolis between the two rivers that rise from one mountain through separate caves, namely the Euphrates and the Araxes, for exhausted and sick old soldiers who wished it [Note: [Col. 1000C] “For exhausted and sick old men.” Other copies have “for old camp-followers and sick men.” I corrected this from Walter’s book to “for exhausted old men.” Dio, book XXXVI, says: *Πόλιν ἐν τῷ χωρίῳ ἐν ᾧ ἐνενικήκει συνῴκισε τοῖς τραυματίαις, καὶ τοῖς ἀφηλικεστέροις τῶν στρατιωτῶν*, that is: “He founded a city in the place where he had won the victory, for soldiers worn out by wounds and age.” Seneca likewise said “exhausted old men.” FABR. — The third Leiden edition has *lexis*, which I also found in the Groningen collection. Should one therefore read *laesis* (“wounded”), that is, *τοῖς τραυματίαις* (“the wounded”), as Dio has? In that way three kinds of useless soldiers are enumerated: the old, the wounded, and the sick. In the second Leiden edition the text reads, as commonly, *lixis*, but in the margin “or *lassis*.” The passage of Seneca to which Fabricius referred is found in *Agamemnon*, verse 364:

“To you the very old and weary men,

their wish fulfilled, render thanks,” etc.].

He granted Tigranes forgiveness when he asked for it. He defeated three times in battle the army of Orodes, king of the Albanians, and its commanders [Note: [Col. 1000D] “Orodes, king of the Albanians.” Walter’s book has *Hierodes*, others *Horodes*. I retained *Orodes*, which appeared in the printed editions; Florus also names him Orodes, called *Ὀροίζης* by Appian and *Ὀροίσης* by Dio. FABR. — Latin writers commonly write *Orodes*, as is clear from Virgil, *Aeneid* X, 732:

“And the same man did not deign to strike down Orodes as he fled,”

and verse 737:

“An opponent not to be despised lies slain, the tall Orodes.”].

Afterward he willingly accepted Orodes’ letters and gifts for restoring peace with the Albanians [Note: [Col. 1001B] “For restoring peace with the Albanians.” I adopted the reading of Perizonius’s manuscript, which I prefer to the others. The common reading is: “and he willingly accepted Orodes’ letters and gifts for restoring peace with the Albanians.” The word *pace* (“peace”) is omitted by three Leiden copies together with the Groningen collection. It is also absent from many old editions. But my manuscript supplies another reading: “Afterward he willingly accepted Orodes’ letters and gifts for restoring peace with the Albanians.” This reading is also written above the text in the second Florence copy.].

He defeated Artoces, king of Iberia, in war [Note: [Col. 1001C] “Artoces, king of Iberia.” Dio also names him *Ἀρτώκης* in book XXXVII. In Appian’s books he is corruptly called *Ὤτοκος*; those same books have *κύρτον* corruptly for *κρύνον*, and Candidus’s translator reads it no differently. FABR.], and received all Iberia into surrender [Note: [Col. 1001C] “All of it.” The second Leiden edition reads “all of it also.”].

Then, having organized and settled Armenia, Colchis, Cappadocia, and Syria [Note: [Col. 1001C] “Having organized.” *Meus* reads “having adorned.”], he advanced from Pontus into Parthia and arrived on the fiftieth day at the city of Ecbatana, the capital of the Parthian kingdom [Note: [Col. 1001C] “At Ecbatana.” The first Leiden edition and the Groningen collection read *Ecbatanam*.].

CHAPTER V. How Mithridates killed his sons and friends, and was himself in turn killed by his son.

In Bosporus, while Mithridates was celebrating the Cerealian rites, an earthquake so severe [Note: [Col. 1001C] “Suddenly.” Absent from my manuscript.] suddenly arose [Note: [Col. 1001C] “An earthquake so severe.” Dio, Book XXXVII, says of this earthquake: “And the earthquake, the greatest earthquake ever to occur among them, destroyed many of their cities”; that is: “An earthquake greater among them at that time than ever before destroyed many cities.” FABR.] that a great disaster to cities and fields is reported to have followed from it [Note: [Col. 1001C] “From it.” Perizonius has “thereafter.”]. At the same time, Castor, Mithridates’ prefect [Note: [Col. 1001D] “Castor, Mithridates’ prefect.” Appian calls him Κάστωρ Φαναγορεύς (“Castor of Phanagoria”) and names the city Φαναγόρεια, which in the old books here is called Phanagorium. See Strabo, Book VI. FABR.], who was in charge of Phanagorium, after killing the royal friends [Note: [Col. 1001D] “Royal.” The first and fourth Lugd. Bat. editions read “of the king.”], seized the citadel and sent four of Mithridates’ sons [Note: [Col. 1001D] “Four sons.” According to Appian, these were Artaphernes, Darius, Xerxes, and Oxathres. FABR.—The manuscripts of my text and Perizonius read Xipodorus; this seems to support Fabricius’ conjecture below concerning Xiphares.] over to the Roman garrisons [Note: [Col. 1001D] “Sent over to the Romans.” My manuscript reads “sent to the Romans.”]. Mithridates, inflamed with anger, burst into crimes [Note: [Col. 1001D] “Into crimes.” The first and fourth Lugd. Bat. editions read “into crime.”]. 381 For at that time he killed a number of his friends and his son Exipodras [Note: [Col. 1001D] “Exipodras.” So far as I know, nothing is recorded about him elsewhere, unless he is the Xiphares about whom Appian writes. FABR.], although earlier he had already murdered another son named Machares [Note: [Col. 1001D] “Machares.” This name, variously corrupted in printed books, is correctly read in the manuscripts. The Greeks likewise call him Μαχάρης. FABR.—His father had made this Machares king of Bosporus; but when Mithridates’ affairs, while he himself was hiding in Armenia and was not admitted to the sight of his son-in-law Tigranes, seemed to have been reduced completely to the last extremity, his son Machares sought the Romans’ friendship in order to retain his kingdom. Therefore, when his father returned to the kingdom, he attempted in vain to clear himself and was driven to death. See the fuller account of all this in the Life of Mithridates, volume III of the Universal History. [Col. 1002C]], by parricide. Pharnaces, another of his sons, terrified by the example of his brothers [Col. 1002A], won over to himself the army that had been sent to pursue him [Note: [Col. 1002C] “*Se* (‘himself’).” The manuscripts prefer this reading here to *sese* (‘himself’), which is found in the printed editions.], and soon led it against his father.

Mithridates, after imploring his son in vain for a long time from the top of a very high wall [Note: [Col. 1002C] “In vain.” This word is absent from some of the older editions.], when he saw that Pharnaces was inexorable, is said, as he was about to die, to have cried out: “Since Pharnaces,” he said, “orders me to die [Note: [Col. 1002C] “Orders me to die.” The same editions improperly attach these words to what follows.], I pray you, ancestral gods, if you exist, that sometime he too may hear this same voice from his children” [Note: [Col. 1002C] “Sometime.” The printed editions read *quandoque* (‘sometime’); but *quandocumque* (‘whenever’) is the correct reading and is used absolutely, elegantly, for ‘at any time.’ LAUT.—The first and second Florentine manuscripts, the third Lugd. Bat. manuscript, and the Groningen manuscript read *quandocumque* (‘whenever’).].

He immediately went down to his wives, concubines, and daughters, and gave poison to them all. When he himself had swallowed it last, yet could not be killed by the poison because of the remedies with which he had often fortified his vital organs against harmful substances, and when he wandered about in vain to see whether at last the infused poison might by some means circulate through his veins, driven by the movement of his body, he invited a certain Gallic soldier [Note: [Col. 1002C] “A certain Gallic soldier.” The epitome of Book CII has: “By a Gallic soldier named Bithocus.” The author *On Illustrious Men* calls him a Gaul named Sithocus. But since Appian names him Βιτοῖτος (“Bitoetus”), consider whether in both places the name should be written Bitoetus. FABR.—Bituitus is a Gallic name, as is clear from Bituitus, king of the Arverni, who was led to Rome in triumph.], who was running about after the wall had already been broken down, and offered him his throat.

[Col. 1002B] [Note: [Col. 1002C] “This end of Mithridates’ life.” The Augustan edition reads: “Mithridates had this end of life.” Many silver coins of this Mithridates, the greatest and bravest of kings, are extant; but I once saw one, more remarkable than the rest, made of gold and formerly in the Marckian museum, whose most accurate drawing I append.] Mithridates had this end of life 382 [Note: [Col. 1002D] “And left us.” The Groningen manuscript reads “and a noble [argument].”], and left us a most powerful proof of his judgment: a man, as they say, extremely superstitious, seventy-two years old [Note: [Col. 1002D] “Seventy-two.” Some older editions read “seventy-five.” Three Florentine manuscripts read “seventy-two.” In place of *ferunt* (“they say”), those editions prefer *fertur* (“he is said”). A little later Perizonius has *senserat* (“he had perceived”) instead of *persenserat* (“he had fully perceived”).], and always accompanied by philosophers and men highly skilled in every art.

“If you exist,” he said, “ancestral gods.” Thus, by worshiping and seeking them for so long, he had come to realize that those who were thought to exist were not reliable gods. A king of extensive experience and weighed down by age, he did not understand the true God, to knowledge of whom one comes only by hearing through faith. Yet by the light of reason itself he had clearly seen that these gods were false, assigning one thing to custom and another to his own mind: “If you are gods,” he said—that is, “I, recognizing that there is a power stronger than man and superior to man, moved by the necessity of prayer, commend my diligence and excuse my ignorance.”

“I invoke the One who is, while I address the one who is not” [Note: [Col. 1003B] “I invoke the One who is.” The Cologne manuscript gives a fuller text than the others, which omit the first two words. LAUT.—For *invoco*, Perizonius reads *in eo* (“in him”). The Augustan edition presents the passage as: “I now invoke him who is, while I address him who is not God.” But the reading of both manuscripts seems to me to have the character of a gloss; the common reading is more rounded.].

Therefore it must be considered with grief and fear what punishment or judgment will await those who, contrary to the prohibition of the truth already revealed and proclaimed, follow and worship those gods [Note: [Col. 1003B] “The gods.” This is absent from my manuscript and from Perizonius, and it can be absent if, above, *eos* (“them”) is replaced by *deos* (“gods”).] concerning whom even those could already have had doubts [Note: [Col. 1003B] “Even.” This is absent from my manuscript. The first and fourth Lugd. Bat. editions read: “concerning whom even those at that time could have doubted.”], who as yet could know nothing except those same gods.

Nevertheless, I shall briefly explain what those times seemed like to the whole East, when for forty years wretched nations were worn down by the alternating devastations of such great leaders [Note: [Col. 1003C] “Such great.” Perizonius reads “two.”]: when every city, lying between such hostile forces and unavoidably exposed to their clashes [Note: [Col. 1003C] “Between.” Correctly so: the land lying between two enemies suffers disaster and loss from both. Some editions absurdly read “through famine.”], was inevitably endangered, so that it would kindle one fire from the place where it had dampened the other, and would soon suffer as punishment what it had temporarily possessed as a remedy; when the trembling embassies of the various provinces were passed alternately between the Roman commanders [Note: [Col. 1003C] “The Roman commanders succeeding one another.” Sulla, Lucullus, Cotta, Murena, and Pompey.], and between both sides—Mithridates, who was more savage by experience [Note: [Col. 1003C] “Mithridates by experience.” Several manuscripts, including the Lugd. Bat. manuscript, read “the experience of Mithridates.” He calls Mithridates “more savage by experience” because they had experienced his cruelty, while they hoped that whichever Roman followed might prove more tolerable than the one who had preceded him.], and the Romans—were transferred according to whichever the fortune of war raised up, with alternating and uncertain acts of appeasement [Note: [Col. 1003C] “And uncertain.” I have supplied the conjunction from the manuscripts.] increasing the dangers that they were remedying [Note: [Col. 1003C] “Were remedying.” The Augustan edition reads “were being remedied.”].

[Note: [Col. 1003C] “Now.” The Augustan edition, the four Lugd. Bat. editions, my manuscript, Perizonius, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Groningen manuscript read: “For what Pompey did continuously, etc.” If that reading is preferred, the end of the period should read: “I shall now set forth briefly.”]

Now what Pompey—and indeed Pompey, the most moderate of the Romans [Note: [Col. 1003C] “And indeed Pompey.” These words are absent from some of the earliest editions, as also from my manuscript and Perizonius.]—did throughout very large parts of the East, after the Mithridatic War had been concluded, I shall set forth briefly [Note: [Col. 1003D] “I shall set forth.” The first and third Lugd. Bat. editions read “I shall recount.”].

## Chapter VI. Pompey’s deeds in Syria, Phoenicia, and Judaea, and the conspiracy of Catiline

[Note: [Col. 1003D] “In the year from the founding of the City 689.” Others give the year as 690 from the founding of the City. Eutropius, Book VII, agrees with Orosius. FABR.]

In the year 689 from the founding of the City, when Marcus Tullius Cicero and Gaius Antonius were consuls, Pompey, having received news of the death of Mithridates [Note: [Col. 1003D] “Of Mithridates who had been killed.” Mithridates, his strength broken and having been defeated by Pompey in Asia, had resolved, following the example of Agathocles of Syracuse and the Roman Scipio, to transfer the war to hostile territory, disturb Italy, and, aided by Gallic forces, attack the Romans there. His son Pharnaces feared this bold plan of his aged father, lest he completely cut off from himself every hope of pardon from the Romans; by revolt and parricide, therefore, he earned from Pompey part of his father’s kingdom. Pompey boasts before Lucan that he had forced Mithridates to his death:

> I, through the passages of Scythian Pontus,  
> Forced the unconquered king, delaying Roman destiny,  
> To go to death—more fortunate than Sulla. [Col. 1004B]], attacked Coele Syria and Phoenicia in war. First he subdued the Ituraeans [Note: [Col. 1004B] “First the Ituraeans.” Strabo, Book XVI, discusses the Ituraeans and their fortresses destroyed by Pompey. In Cicero’s *Philippics* they are called Ithyreans, not very accurately. FABR.] and the Arabs [Note: [Col. 1004B] “And subdued the Arabs.” Pompey says in Lucan, Book II:

> The conquered Arab came to know me; the Heniochi, fierce in war,  
> And the Colchians, famed for the fleece they had seized, know me.  
> Cappadocia fears my standards, and Judaea, surrendered to the worship  
> Of an uncertain God, and gentle Sophene.  
> I subdued the Armenians, the savage Cilicians, and the Taurus.

], and captured their city, which they call Petra [Note: [Col. 1004C] “Which they call Petra.” Aretas, king of the Arabs, whom Pompey defeated and captured, is called by Plutarch in the *Life of Pompey* βασιλεὺς τῶν περὶ τὴν Πέτραν Ἀράβων, “king of the Arabs around Petra.” Aretas had his royal residence at Petra; see Josephus, Book XIV of the *Antiquities*, chapter 2. See Dio, Book XXXVII. FABR.—We possess a very rare bronze coin inscribed ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΑΡΕΤΟΥ (“of King Aretas”), showing the face of Aretas, king of the Arabs, or Aretes—for the name is written both ways. Another coin with a similar inscription and the additional title “Philhellene” was published by Andreas Morellius in his excellent *Specimen*. The reader, I think, will gladly look at a drawing of both. [Col. 1004D]].

Then he sent Gabinius with an army against the Jews, over whom Aristobulus, after expelling his brother Hyrcanus, was the first priest to rule as king, and against Jerusalem, their city [Col. 1005A] [Note: [Col. 1005B] “Sends.” The first Lugd. Bat. edition reads “sent.”]. He himself immediately followed and was received into the city by the senators, but was repulsed by the common people from the wall of the Temple [Note: [Col. 1005B] “Its assault.” The first and second Florentine manuscripts, together with the second Lugd. Bat. manuscript, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Groningen manuscript, read “its capture.” The same reading appears in the Augustan and Venetian editions. But my manuscript reads “he turned his attention to the assault.”]. He attacked it. The place itself made it strong, as did also a massive wall [Note: [Col. 1005B] “A massive wall.” Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Groningen manuscript, read “massive walls.” They soon read, with the Augustan edition, “for days and nights.”], and a very deep ditch; and, by making one legion succeed another without respite, day and night, he scarcely captured it in the third month [Note: [Col. 1005C] “Only in the third month.” Josephus likewise writes this in Book XIV, chapter 8; consult him. FABR.].

Thirteen thousand Jews are said to have been killed there [Note: [Col. 1005C] “Thirteen thousand.” The second Florentine manuscript reads “fourteen thousand.”]; the rest of the multitude surrendered. Pompey ordered the city walls to be demolished and leveled with the ground; and after he had executed several Jewish leaders with the axe [Note: [Col. 1005C] “Leaders.” This word is absent from some of the older editions.], he restored Hyrcanus to the priesthood and led Aristobulus captive to Rome.

Pompey himself declared in an address that he had waged this war of the East against twenty-two kings [Note: [Col. 1005C] “Kings.” The Augustan edition reads “petty kings.”] [Note: [Col. 1005C] “Pompey himself.” The first Florentine manuscript omits the first word.].

Meanwhile, during those same days, Catiline’s conspiracy against his country was conceived and exposed in the City, while in Etruria it was extinguished by civil war [Col. 1005B]. The accomplices in the conspiracy were killed at Rome. But since this history, made known by Cicero and described by Sallust [Note: [Col. 1005C] “With Cicero acting and Sallust describing it.” Above, Book I, chapter 1, p. 7: “Among them they spent all their leisure and business as actors and writers.”], is sufficiently familiar to everyone, it is enough for us now merely to have touched on it briefly.

A disturbance also arose among the Paeligni, begun by Marcellus, father and son, and, through Lucius Vettius [Note: [Col. 1005C] “Lucius Vettius.” This is Lucius Vettius the judge, about whom Cicero writes in *Against Vatinius* and in Letter 24 of Book II *To Atticus*. Dio, Book XXXVIII, names him Λούκιον Οὐέττιον. In Appian the name is incorrectly written with a single tau; Plutarch’s books on Lucullus likewise have Βρέττιόν τινα incorrectly instead of Βέττιον. FABR.—The name is written variously in the manuscripts: Vestilius, Vectitius, Butius, Hibilus; but the first Florentine manuscript correctly gives L. Vettius.], was exposed [Note: [Col. 1005C] “Was exposed.” The learned P. Wesseling, in *Probabilia*, p. 382, reads *proditis* (“after they had been exposed”), so that the word may be joined with “the Marcelli.”], and, once Catiline’s conspiracy had been disclosed, was suppressed as though its root had been cut away. Each affair was avenged: the one among the Paeligni by Bibulus, the other among the Bruttii by Cicero.

## Chapter VII. Which provinces Caesar received by lot, and how he subdued the Helvetii and the Belgae

[Col. 1006A]

[Note: [Col. 1005D] “In the year from the founding of the City 693.” All the printed books of Eutropius, including the one edited by Sconhovius, assign this year as 698 from the founding of the City; but our manuscript correctly has 693. In the Capitoline Fasti this year is 694. FABR.]

In the year 693 from the founding of the City, when Gaius Caesar and Lucius Bibulus were consuls, by the Vatinian law [Note: [Col. 1005D] “By the Vatinian law.” Publius Vatinius, tribune of the people, proposed this law to the people while Caesar and Bibulus were consuls. See Suetonius, *Julius*. FABR.] three provinces, together with seven legions [Note: [Col. 1005D] “With seven legions.” Eutropius reads: “Gaul and Illyricum were assigned to him with ten legions.” Plutarch, in his *Life of Caesar*, writes that Caesar received Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul, together with Illyricum, for five years, with four legions. For, according to Dio, Book XXXVIII, the people gave Caesar Citerior Gaul and Illyricum for five years with three legions; the Senate added Ulterior Gaul with one legion. FABR.], were assigned to Caesar for five years: Transalpine Gaul, Cisalpine Gaul, and Illyricum. The Senate later added Comata Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 1006B] “This history Suetonius.” We ourselves gladly read and interpret the appropriate portions of this history, which Caesar himself set out with the greatest diligence and eloquence, not without benefit. FABR.] Suetonius Tranquillus has explained this history at fullest length; from him we have culled suitable portions.

A certain Orgetorix had inflamed the spirit of the Helvetii, the bravest of all the Gallic peoples, especially for the reason that they were almost continually engaged in warfare with the Germans, from whom they are separated only by the Rhine [Note: [Col. 1006C] “For this was especially the reason.” Two Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and my manuscript read “for the greatest reason.” The same manuscripts soon read “from which,” rather than “from whom,” referring only to the Rhine.], hoping to invade all Gaul. He was a leader of the nation [Note: [Col. 1006C] “Orgetorix.” The memory of this man, a leading figure among his people, seems to survive on a silver coin now in Bouteroue’s possession.]. When the other nobles had seized him and forced him to face death, they nevertheless could not restrain the common people, once aroused, from setting out for plunder. After forming a conspiracy and appointing a day, they burned their villages and houses, so that no longing to return would remain [Note: [Col. 1006D] “From the hope.” The Augustan edition reads “from the hope of returning.”], and departed.

When Caesar encountered them near the Rhône River, he defeated them twice in a great and difficult war [Note: [Col. 1006D] “He defeated them twice.” First he defeated the Tigurine canton while crossing the Arar River; then, pursuing the others, he overcame them after varying fortunes. So Caesar and Dio, Book XXXVIII. One manuscript reads “he scarcely defeated them twice.” FABR.—“Twice” and “scarcely” are two different readings; this manuscript had written both in accordance with the practice of scribes. The second Lugd. Bat. manuscript likewise reads “scarcely,” as does the Augustan edition.], and compelled the defeated to surrender [Note: [Col. 1006D] “Compelled.” The second Lugd. Bat. manuscript reads “reduced.”].

When they first set out, their entire population consisted of the Helvetii [Col. 1007A], the Tulingi [Note: [Col. 1007A] “The Tulingi, etc.” The variant forms in the manuscript codices are: Tulingiorum, Latobrogiorum or Logiboiorum, Latubogiorum, Latobogiorum, or Lateboiorum; Raviricorum or Racuracorum. The Rauraci seem to be mentioned on an ancient little silver coin, whose obverse displays the adorned head of Venus with the letters R—RA, though one or two letters, V or AV, show only traces of their original form because of wear. Hence Bouteroue, p. 47, thinks that the coin may refer either to the Rauraci or to Raraurium, that is, the town called Rom near Poitiers in the *Itinerary* of Antoninus. [Col. 1007B] On the reverse an unrestrained horse is shown in free motion; beneath it are the letters IVLIO. This is interpreted either as referring to a prince or commander of that name, or to Juliobona or Luliobona in Normandy. Orosius next mentions Ariovistus, and Caesar discusses many of his deeds in his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*. His personal name seems to have been Arivus or Arivos, lengthened by the Romans into Ariovistus, as often happens with proper names. This conjecture is supported by a remarkable Gallic coin that I saw in Amsterdam in the possession of Gerard Schaak, a man extraordinarily devoted to every kind of elegance. I found a similar coin reproduced by Claudius Bouteroue in his exceedingly rare and excellent book written in French, *Curious Investigations into the Coins of France*, p. 59. On the obverse appears the head of Virtue—or, if one prefers, of armed Venus, in the manner customary among the Gauls and imitated from the Romans—with the commander’s or king’s name ARIVOS. On the reverse is a fierce horse, a symbol of liberty; around it is written SANTONOS, indicating that the Santones, or Santoni, had struck the coin, as in Lucan I, 422:

> He moves the standards, and the Santon rejoices when the enemy has been driven away.

[Col. 1007D] That the name Arivos refers to a commander or king, not to some people or city, is shown by another silver coin published there by Bouteroue, on which the name of another commander, Quintus Docius or Docimus, appears with the same helmeted female head. We append this coin together with a third coin struck by the same people. [Col. 1008A] Two silver coins of the Sequani also came into my possession. Caesar defeated among them this great king of Gaul and Germany, Ariovistus. Both coins display Mercury, or his head, recognizable by the wing that is customarily attached to his petasus, the revered god of the Gauls and Germans. A boar, the emblem of the people, is prominent. The first celebrates the leader Ninnus; the second, also struck by the Sequani and likewise published by Bouteroue, pp. 56–57, testifies to this. [Col. 1008C]] [Note: [Col. 1008C] “The Latobrogii.” Caesar calls these people the Lacobrigii. FABR.], the Latobrogii, the Rauraci, and the Boii—men and women alike—amounting to 157,000 persons [Note: [Col. 1008C] “157,000.” Caesar says: “The total number of all of them was approximately 368,000.” Plutarch writes: τριάκοντα μὲν αἱ πᾶσαι μυριάδες ὄντες, εἴκοσι δὲ αἱ μαχόμεναι, μιᾶς δέουσαι, that is: “The total number was 300,000; those capable of bearing arms numbered 190,000.” FABR.].

Of these, 47,000 fell in battle [Note: [Col. 1008C] “Of these, 47,000.” Strabo, Book IV, says of the Helvetian war: ἐν ᾧ πολέμῳ περὶ τετταράκοντα μυριάδες σωμάτων διεφθάρησαν, that is: “Approximately 400,000 persons perished.” I suspect that there is an error in this number. FABR.—Shortly afterward, the words “in battle” are absent from my manuscript and from the fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript, which then read “and the rest into their lands.”] The rest were sent back to their own lands.

[Note: [Col. 1008C] “Afterward Caesar [defeated] Ariovistus, etc.” In all the editions this passage is badly corrupted. They read: “Afterward Caesar against Ariovistus, etc.” The word “against” has been inserted wrongly and cannot fit with “he defeated,” which closes the sentence. Therefore some scribes inserted “having engaged him,” a reading found in four manuscripts: Lugd. Bat., Utrecht, Groningen, and the Augustan edition. But “against” must be deleted, as it is in the manuscripts of Perizonius and the fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript. In what follows, the words “recently” are absent from the third Lugd. Bat. manuscript, the Groningen manuscript, and some older editions.]

Afterward Caesar defeated Ariovistus, the king, who was raising and bringing with him an unbelievable host of Germans, with which he boasted that he had recently subjugated all the peoples of Gaul, among the Sequani [Col. 1008A], while Caesar’s army for a long time declined battle, terrified by the Germans’ numbers and courage [Note: [Col. 1008D] “Although for a long time.” The printed editions insert *autem* (‘however’), contrary to the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts.]. Ariovistus escaped into Germany, crossing the Rhine in a small boat [Note: [Col. 1008D] “Escaped.” The first Lugd. Bat. edition and some older editions read “fled.” The fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript, my manuscript, and Perizonius do not recognize the following “but.”]; his two wives and as many daughters were captured.

In Ariovistus’ army were the Arudes [Note: [Col. 1009B] “Arudes.” The first and third Lugd. Bat. manuscripts read Arodes, as does the Groningen manuscript.], the Marcomani [Note: [Col. 1009B] “Marcomani.” The first Lugd. Bat. manuscript reads Marcomanni; the second and third, together with the Groningen manuscript, Marcomones; likewise the first and second Florentine manuscripts read Marcomones; the third Florentine manuscript and the Utrecht manuscript read Marcomenes; finally, my manuscript, the fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript, and the Augustan edition read Marcomannes.], the Triboci [Note: [Col. 1009B] “Triboci.” So the first and second Florentine manuscripts. The third Florentine manuscript, the third Lugd. Bat. manuscript, and the Utrecht manuscript read Tribocii; the second Lugd. Bat. manuscript reads Triboicii.], the Vangiones, the Nemetes, the Edures [Note: [Col. 1009B] “Edures.” Also written Eudures. In Caesar these are the Sedusii, concerning whom various opinions are held. FABR.—I found Eduses in all the manuscripts I consulted, except that my manuscript reads both Eduses and Cluses.], and the Suevi.

The battle was especially severe against the German phalanx, which they had formed into a single column, interlocking their shields above their heads, and thus protected on every side so as to break into the Roman line. But after certain Roman soldiers, distinguished for agility and courage, leaped onto the tortoise formation [Note: [Col. 1009C] “Leaped above the covering.” Florus, Book III, chapter 10, discusses this event. FABR.] [Note: [Col. 1009C] “The covering.” The first Lugd. Bat. manuscript, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Groningen manuscript read “the formation”; the third Lugd. Bat. manuscript reads “the enclosure.”] [Note: [Col. 1009C] “Leaped.” All the Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Utrecht and Groningen manuscripts, read “loosed,” incorrectly.] and tore away the shields one by one, as though they were scales [Note: [Col. 1009C] “Torn away.” The first and third Lugd. Bat. manuscripts read “pulled away.”], they stabbed from above the bare shoulders of the trapped and uncovered men [Note: [Col. 1009C] “Of those found.” My manuscript, together with the fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript, reads “of those crushed.” But I prefer the common reading.]. Terrified by this new danger of death, the enemy broke apart their dreadful formation.

Then, turning to flight, they were slaughtered relentlessly for fifty Roman miles, and it was impossible to determine the number of Germans, either how many had taken part in the battle or how many had been killed [Col. 1009B] [Note: [Col. 1009C] “Of those killed.” The Augustan edition reads “of the one killed.”].

After this, the nation of the Belgae, which is the third part of Gaul, rose up against Caesar [Note: [Col. 1009C] “After this, the nation of the Belgae.” What follows here to the end of the chapter is discussed at length by Caesar in Book II and by Diodorus at the beginning of Book XXXIX. FABR.]. Their forces, distributed among their peoples, were as follows [Note: [Col. 1009C] “This was their force.” The Longobard manuscript reads “this force was.”].

The Bellovaci [Note: [Col. 1009C] “Bellovaci.” The second and third Florentine manuscripts, together with the second and third Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, the Groningen manuscript, and the Augustan edition, read Belluagui. The Longobard manuscript, the fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript, my manuscript, and the first edition read Bellovagi. The Utrecht manuscript reads Bellovagnes.]—who seemed to surpass the others in number and courage [Note: [Col. 1009D] “Seemed.” The first editions and those following them read “seem.”]—had 60,000 chosen armed men [Note: [Col. 1009D] “Sixty thousand armed men.” Caesar writes that the Bellovaci promised 50,000 armed men. He assigns 15,000 to the Atrebates. FABR.—The first Lugd. Bat. edition reads 40,000 instead of 60,000.];

the Suessiones, from twelve towns, had 50,000 [Note: [Col. 1009D] “Suessiones.” Most manuscripts, and almost all of them, read Suessones. Both forms of the name are found among the authors. Lucan likewise prefers Suessones, I, 423:

> And the Biturix, and the Suessones, light in their long weapons.];

the Nervii, whose savagery was said to be so untamed that, up to that time, they had never allowed merchants to bring them wine or other merchandise [Note: [Col. 1009D] “To them.” The Augustan edition deletes these unnecessary words.], lest the pleasure introduced by such goods should bring dullness upon their courage [Note: [Col. 1009D] “By which.” The Perizonian manuscript reads “from which.”] [Note: [Col. 1009D] “Introduced.” The first Lugd. Bat. edition reads “proclaimed.” Elsewhere also these words are transposed in Orosius. If the manuscript reading is preferred, the passage should be read, with the assistance of the Perizonian manuscript: “from which pleasure, once introduced, might bring dullness.”], likewise had 50,000;

the Atrebates and the Ambiani [Note: [Col. 1010B] “And the Ambiani.” Some manuscripts and editions insert “also” here.] had 10,000;

the Morini, 25,000;

the Menapii, 9,000 [Note: [Col. 1010B] “The Menapii, nine.” So the manuscripts; the printed editions read ten. Caesar writes that the Menapii promised 7,000. FABR.];

the Caleti, 10,000 [Note: [Col. 1010B] “Caleti.” The Augustan edition reads Calecii.];

the Velocasses [Note: [Col. 1010B] “Velocasses.” The fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript, as also my manuscript, reads Volocassi.] and the Veromandui, likewise 10,000 [Note: [Col. 1010B] “Veromandui.” The first and second Florentine manuscripts read Veromandi; likewise the second and third Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Utrecht manuscript, read Viromandi; Perizonius reads Volomandi; the fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript and my manuscript read Volomandi; finally, the third Florentine manuscript reads Velomandi.];

the Aduatici, 18,000 [Note: [Col. 1010C] “The Aduatici, eighteen.” One manuscript reads Atuati; Caesar has the Catuaci with 19,000. FABR.—Many manuscripts prefer Atuatici. The first and third Lugd. Bat. manuscripts reduce the number by one thousand; some editions, including the first and the Augustan, add one thousand.];

the Condrusi [Note: [Col. 1010C] “Condrusi.” The manuscripts read Condurses, Conduses, Condureses—the latter being the reading of the Longobard manuscript—and finally Dorses.], the Eburones [Note: [Col. 1010C] “Eburones.” Some manuscripts read Eborones and Eborrones.], the Caeresi [Note: [Col. 1010C] “Caeresi, Caemani.” All our manuscripts read Caerosi, Caemani. Caesar calls the former Caeresi and the latter Paemani. In the commonly circulated books of Orosius, Cenomanni was read incorrectly. Robert Estienne, whom I mention with honor, appended this epitome of Caesar’s deeds in Gaul to the *Commentaries of Caesar*, printed by him under Eutropius’ name with the greatest accuracy and diligence; there he restored these names from Caesar. FABR.—I found Cesori and Cecosi in the manuscripts; my manuscript and Perizonius have Cerosi; three Florentine manuscripts have Caerosi.], and the Caemani [Note: [Col. 1010D] “Caemani.” So the three Florentine manuscripts and other manuscripts. But the first Lugd. Bat. manuscript, together with Perizonius and the older editions, reads Cenomanni.], who are called Germans by one name, 40,000.

And thus, it is reported [Note: [Col. 1010D] “And thus.” Orosius did not write this way if we follow the manuscripts. The Longobard manuscript and the Augustan edition delete the words, simply reading: “are reported to have been,” etc. The first, second, and third Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, and the Utrecht manuscript together with the Groningen manuscript, read “and therefore they write that they were”; but the fourth, together with my manuscript and Perizonius, supported by two Florentine manuscripts, reads: “Thus they are reported to have been,” etc.] 272,000 of the finest armed men [Note: [Col. 1010D] “Two hundred seventy-two thousand.” The first Lugd. Bat. manuscript reads 282,000; in the third, I think, the word “two” was written in place of “eighty.”].

When these men suddenly burst from the forest, Caesar’s army was thrown into confusion and put to flight. After many of their men had been lost, the army at last stood firm at its commander’s exhortation and, attacking the victors, almost completely annihilated them.

## Chapter VIII. Galba’s expedition against the Veragri and Seduni; Caesar’s deeds against the conspirators allied with the Veneti; and the expeditions of Titurius Sabinus and Publius Crassus

[Col. 1011A]

[Note: [Col. 1011C] “Then Caesar.” What Orosius covers in this chapter Caesar treats at length in Book III of the *Commentaries*; students of both languages should connect these passages with what is found in Dio, Book XXXIX. FABR.]

Then Caesar, having accomplished great things in Gaul and having decided to depart for Italy, sent Galba with the Twelfth Legion [Note: [Col. 1011C] “Twelfth.” The Augustan edition has “tenth.”] to the Veragri [Note: [Col. 1011C] “Veragri.” Some manuscripts have “Beragradi.”] and Seduni [Note: [Col. 1011C] “and Seduni.” Some manuscripts have “Divos,” “Duros,” and “Sedimos.”]. When Galba had settled for the winter in a village of the Veragri called Octodurus [Note: [Col. 1011C] “Octodurus.” Thus, among others, the Longobard manuscript; other manuscripts have “Octodorus,” “Otodorus,” and “Ortodorus.”], and had assigned to the inhabitants the half of the town separated by a torrent [Note: [Col. 1011C] “Had assigned.” The second Leiden manuscript has “had ceded”; some old editions have “was divided” instead of “was separated,” which is found in the manuscripts.], he saw one day that they had departed during the night and occupied the neighboring hill [Note: [Col. 1011C] “Hill.” My manuscript, together with the fourth Leiden manuscript, has “hill” in the ablative.]. For, despising the smallness of scarcely half a legion, they considered the booty lying before them to be theirs without difficulty and summoned their neighbors to share in the slaughter and plunder [Note: [Col. 1011C] “They had summoned.” Some manuscripts and editions have “they summoned.”].

Thus Galba, surrounded and alarmed by such immediate dangers and uncertain of a definite course amid various counsels [Note: [Col. 1011C] “And.” The first Leiden manuscript, the second Florentine manuscript, and some old editions omit it.], was suddenly overwhelmed when the Gauls poured down from the mountain, surrounded the unfinished camp [Note: [Col. 1011C] “They surround.” Perizonius has “surrounding.”], and showered stones and missiles upon the few defenders along the rampart. When the camp was already being stormed, by the advice of the chief centurion Pacuvius [Note: [Col. 1011D] “Pacuvius the chief centurion.” This chief centurion is called P. Sextius Baculus by Caesar. FABR.—The fourth Leiden manuscript and mine read “Pattavius.”] and the tribune Volusenus [Note: [Col. 1011D] “Volusenus.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “Volussinus.”], all the Romans burst out through the gates [Note: [Col. 1011D] “All.” This is absent from the fourth Leiden manuscript and mine; perhaps “all together” was intended.], and, attacking the unsuspecting enemy by surprise, first threw them into confusion and then, when they had turned to flight, scattered them in a pitiable slaughter. For more than thirty thousand barbarians are reported to have been killed at that time.

Thus Caesar, who had thought that all the peoples of Gaul had already been pacified, was drawn back into a new and very great war. For while the young Publius Crassus was wintering with the Seventh Legion as far as the Ocean among the Andegavi [Note: [Col. 1011D] “Was wintering.” Perizonius has “had wintered.”], the Veneti and the other neighboring peoples suddenly conspired to take up arms [Note: [Col. 1011D] “Suddenly.” Absent from the Augustan edition], bound the Roman envoys, and informed the Romans that they would return them only if they received back their own hostages [Note: [Col. 1011D] “They would return them.” The Longobard manuscript does not support “would not acknowledge them.”]. They enlisted as allies for this war the Osismii [Note: [Col. 1011D] “Osismii.” Perizonius has “Oxismii”; the first and third Florentine manuscripts, together with the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts and mine, have “Osismii”; the first Leiden manuscript and the second Florentine have “Osissimi.”], Lexovii [Note: [Col. 1012C] “Lexovii.” The first Leiden manuscript has “Luxovii.”], Nannetes [Note: [Col. 1012C] “Nannetes.” Three Florentine manuscripts and the second and third Leiden manuscripts have “Namnetes”; Perizonius has “Naninetes.”], Ambivariti [Note: [Col. 1012C] “Ambivariti.” Caesar’s books have “Ambiliates” in this place. FABR.—Some manuscripts have “Ambibariti.”], Morini, Diablintres [Note: [Col. 1012C] “Diablintres.” The third Leiden manuscript and mine have “Diabintes”; the three Florentine manuscripts have “Diablintes,” as do the first and second Leiden manuscripts together with Perizonius.], and Menapii; they also summoned auxiliaries from Britain.

When Caesar learned through Crassus of the revolt of the peoples who had submitted, although he understood how difficult it would be to undertake the war, he nevertheless judged that so important a matter must not be neglected [Note: [Col. 1012C] “He judged.” The old editions have “judging it to be necessary,” followed by “lest the others, etc.” But the three Florentine manuscripts, four Leiden manuscripts, mine, Perizonius, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Gronovian collection omit *esse* or *est*. On the basis of their agreement, I judge that the passage should be arranged as follows: “Judging that it must not be neglected, lest the license to attempt such things be extended to the others as an example, he unsuccessfully attempted to pursue the enemy in a land battle.”]. He feared that the others might thereby be encouraged to venture upon similar undertakings. [Note: [Col. 1012C] “Therefore.” Perizonius’s manuscript and mine, supporting our emendation, omit this word.] Accordingly, he unsuccessfully attempted to pursue the enemy in a land battle [Note: [Col. 1012C] “Battle.” Mine has “war.”]; for the enemy was protected by channels of the sea that ran between them and the inaccessible inlets, as well as by secure boundaries of land [Note: [Col. 1012D] “Boundaries.” The three Florentine manuscripts have “bays.”]. He ordered long ships to be built on the river Loire [Note: [Col. 1012D] “Loire.” Some manuscripts have “Ligero” and “Ligerio.”]. These were brought down the river into the Ocean, and as soon as they appeared to the enemy, two hundred and twenty of their ships, already prepared and most fully equipped with every kind of weapon, advanced from the harbor and took position opposite them.

When Brutus surveyed the engagement and saw that the number of ships was far from equal—for the barbarians’ ships were woven together with solid timbers and reinforced by massive beams, so that they blunted the blows of the beaked ships, which struck them like stones driven against them—his first means of assistance was this: he had prepared very sharp hooks, not fixed stubbornly to poles but fastened to ropes. Whenever necessary, these hooks seized the ropes at a distance; by lowering the poles and pulling back the hooks along the ropes, they cut them through [Note: [Col. 1012D] “Aid.” The first Leiden manuscript has “assistance.”]. Once these had been swiftly dealt with, he ordered the rigging of the enemy [Col. 1013A] yards to be torn apart [Note: [Col. 1012D] “To be broken.” Some manuscripts have “to be torn apart”; the first Florentine manuscript has simply “to be cut.”].

Thus, when the yards came crashing down, he immediately rendered many ships motionless, as though captured. Others, terrified by this danger, tried to flee with their sails furled, wherever the wind might carry them [Note: [Col. 1013C] “With sails furled.” Thus the manuscripts; some old editions have “with sails spread.”]; but when the wind soon failed, they were left helpless and became a laughingstock to the Romans. Accordingly, after all the ships had been burned and those Gauls who had fought had been killed [Note: [Col. 1013C] “The Gauls; the rest.” Perizonius’s manuscript and mine have “the remaining Gauls surrendered themselves,” a reading also supported by the old editions.], all the rest surrendered themselves. But Caesar, chiefly because of the injury done to the envoys [Note: [Col. 1013C] “Because of the injury.” Mine and the fourth Leiden manuscript have “on account of the injury.”], and in order to stamp upon all their leaders a terrifying mark of an example for every undertaking [Note: [Col. 1013C] “Counsels” or “undertakings.” This word is absent from the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian collection.], had all the chiefs killed under torture and sold the rest into slavery [Note: [Col. 1013C] “To brand them with a mark.” The Augustan edition has “to inflict a mark and upon all the leaders the rest,” with several words omitted in the middle.].

At the same time [Note: [Col. 1013C] “On the same days.” Mine has “In those days.”], Titurius Sabinus utterly destroyed the Aulerci, Eburones, and Lexovii, who had killed their leading men because they did not wish to be regarded as the instigators of reviving the war [Note: [Col. 1013C] “Because they were instigators.” The old editions have “because they were the instigators.” Fabricius, however, printed the reading found in all the manuscripts. Since all agree on *cur*, not *quod*, I think we should read *cum auctores*, “since they were the instigators,” with only one letter changed.], bursting forth upon them and annihilating them in an incredible slaughter.

Publius Crassus, however, when he had reached Aquitania [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Aquitania.” The three Florentine manuscripts have “Aquitanica.”], was met by war. For the Sontiates [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Sontiates.” The Longobard manuscript has “Sotiates”; the other manuscripts and old editions have “Sociates,” and shortly afterward call the town itself “Sociatum.”], attacking the Romans with a large cavalry force and very powerful infantry, seriously harassed them for a long time. After they had been defeated, driven into the town of Sontiatum, and besieged, they saw that they could not be conquered; they surrendered their arms and were received into submission.

The Aquitani, alarmed by the defeat [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Alarmed by the defeat.” My manuscript, together with the fourth Leiden manuscript, has “alarmed by this defeat,”], gathered an army from every direction; they also summoned auxiliaries from Further Spain [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Further.” The second Florentine manuscript has “from Inner Spain.”], and appointed as commanders in the war chiefly those who had served with Sertorius [Note: [Col. 1013D] “With Sertorius.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “under Sertorius.”]. While all these were preparing to besiege Crassus, they were destroyed in their own camp when Crassus overwhelmed them. For of the Aquitani and Cantabri, of whom fifty thousand had then come to their aid [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Then.” Absent from the first and third Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian collection.], thirty-eight thousand are reported to have been killed [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Thirty-eight thousand.” The first Leiden manuscript counts one thousand fewer.].

Caesar attacked the Germans who had crossed the Rhine with immense forces and were preparing at the same time to subject all Gaul to themselves, and he slew them to the point of annihilation. Their number is reported to have been four hundred and forty thousand [Note: [Col. 1013D–1014C] “Four hundred and forty thousand.” Most old editions omit the forty thousand added to the four hundred thousand above. The same occurs in the second Florentine manuscript; but the third Florentine manuscript, three Leiden manuscripts, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Gronovian collection omit the hundreds and retain the forty thousand. Such a force certainly cannot be called immense, as Orosius does. Since the Longobard manuscript reads “a number up to four hundred and forty thousand,” without an intervening conjunction, I suspect that the later, smaller number was added from a variant reading, while Orosius originally wrote the earlier round number.]. [Note: [Col. 1014C] “They report.” The second Florentine manuscript has “are reported,” instead of “they report,” or else the preceding word *numerum* should be deleted if that reading is preferred.]

## CHAPTER IX. How Caesar subdued the Suebi and the Britons

[Note: [Col. 1014C] “Then Caesar, etc.” What Orosius summarizes in this chapter Caesar explained at length in Books IV and V of the *Commentaries*. Dio, Book XXXIX, and Plutarch in his *Life of Caesar* treat the same matters. FABR.]

Then Caesar crossed into Germany over a bridge [Note: [Col. 1014C] “Crossed over.” Thus the four Leiden manuscripts and three Florentine manuscripts; the Vulgate editions have “crossing over,” but the Augustan edition agrees with the manuscripts.], liberated the Sugambri [Note: [Col. 1014C] “Sugambri.” In our manuscripts, “Sigambri”; Dio calls them Συγγάμβρους. FABR.—Most of our manuscripts have “Sugambri.”] and Ubii from siege, and terrified the Suebi, the largest and fiercest nation, of whom many have recorded that there were one hundred districts and tribes, and all Germany, by his arrival. Soon, after dismantling the bridge [Note: [Col. 1014D] “After dismantling the bridge.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian collection, have “after cutting the bridge.”], he withdrew into Gaul [Note: [Col. 1014D] “He withdrew.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “he contended.”].

From there he came to the Morini, from whom the nearest and shortest passage to Britain leads [Note: [Col. 1014D] “To Britain.” Three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian collection have “toward Britain.”]. Having prepared about eighty transport and light cargo ships, he crossed over to Britain [Note: [Col. 1014D] “He crossed over.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts have “he crossed.”]. There, after first being exhausted by a fierce battle, he was then caught by adverse weather and lost most of his fleet and a considerable number of soldiers, while almost all his cavalry perished.

Returning to Gaul, he distributed the legions into winter quarters and ordered six hundred ships of both types to be built. Having crossed over to Britain in them again in early spring [Note: [Col. 1014D] “Having crossed over.” Thus all the Florentine and Leiden manuscripts read, rather than “having crossed them,” as is commonly printed.], while he himself advanced against the enemy with the army, the ships lying at anchor were seized by a storm: some collided with one another, while others were dashed against the sands and broken apart. Forty of them were lost; the rest were repaired with great difficulty.

The cavalry of Caesar was defeated by the Britons in the first engagement [Note: [Col. 1014D] “In the first engagement.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts, supported by the Gronovian collection, have “in the first encounter.”], and there the tribune Labienus was killed [Note: [Col. 1015B] “And there Labienus.” “Labienus” appears in the old and Robert’s manuscripts. Caesar, Book V, has “Q. Laberius Durus.” FABR.]. In a second battle, at great cost to his own men, he routed the defeated Britons [Note: [Col. 1015C] “He turned.” The first Leiden manuscript has “he turned them completely.”] and put them to flight.

From there he marched to the river Thames [Note: [Col. 1015C] “To the river Thames.” The manuscripts have “Tamensim,” “Tamniensim,” “Tamesiet,” and “Tanesin.” One or two manuscripts omit “river,” and several omit *est*.], which, they say, could be crossed by a ford at only one place. On the farther bank of this river, under the leadership of Cassivellaunus [Note: [Col. 1015C] “Under the leadership of Cassivellaunus.” The manuscripts have “Cassovellaunus”; likewise the Longobard manuscript. Others have “Cassibellaunus,” “Cassobellaunus,” “Cassopellaunus,” and finally “Cassivellanus.”], an immense multitude of enemies had taken position and had fortified the bank of the river, and nearly the entire ford beneath the water, with very sharp stakes.

When this was discovered and avoided by the Romans, the barbarians, unable to withstand the attack of the legions, hid themselves in the forests, from which they repeatedly and severely harassed the Romans by frequent sorties. Meanwhile the very powerful state of the Trinobantes, under the leadership of Androgorius [Note: [Col. 1015C] “Androgorius.” Gualther’s book has “Andragius.” Caesar calls him “Mandubracius.” FABR.—The first and third Florentine manuscripts and three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian collection, have “Androgius”; the second Florentine manuscript and the second Leiden manuscript have “Andragius.”], gave forty hostages and surrendered itself to Caesar [Note: [Col. 1015C] “Surrendered.” Some manuscripts have “gave themselves up.”]. Following this example, several other cities entered into alliance with the Romans. Guided by them, Caesar finally captured the town of Cassivellaunus [Note: [Col. 1015C] “Of Cassivellaunus.” The manuscripts have “Cassovellaunus,” “Cassobellaunus,” “Cassibellaunus,” and “Cassobellaunum.”], situated between two marshes, additionally fortified by the protection of forests, and abundantly supplied with everything, after a severe battle.

## CHAPTER X. That Caesar set out against a new conspiracy of the Gauls and subdued them again

Then Caesar, having returned from Britain [Note: [Col. 1015C] “From the Britons.” The Augustan edition has “from Britain.”] to Gaul and sent the legions into winter quarters, was surrounded and hard pressed on every side by sudden outbreaks of war. For Ambiorix, conspiring with the Eburones and Aduatuci [Note: [Col. 1016C] “Aduatuci.” In nearly all our manuscripts, here and above in Chapter 7, they are called “Atuatuci,” whom the common editions call “Aduatuci.” Dio likewise calls them Ἀτουατικοί. Caesar, Book V, says that after Cotta and Sabinus were killed they joined Ambiorix. FABR.—I also find “Atuacicis” in two Florentine and four Leiden manuscripts.], and encouraged by the counsel of the Treveri [Note: [Col. 1016C] “Of the Treveri.” The first and third Florentine manuscripts have “Treveri.”], surrounded by an ambush and killed the legates Cotta and Sabinus among the Eburones, together with the entire legion, utterly annihilating it [Note: [Col. 1016C] “Among the Eburones.” Four Leiden manuscripts have “among the Eburones.”] [Note: [Col. 1016C] “Utterly.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “at the same time.”].

Ambiorix, elated by this victory, hastily gathered the Aduatuci, the Nervii, and many others to arms and marched against the legate Cicero [Note: [Col. 1016C] “Against Cicero.” Quintus Tullius Cicero, the brother of Marcus and Caesar’s legate, is meant; Caesar, Book V, and Dio, Book XL. FABR.], who was likewise then in charge of a legion in winter quarters.

The size of the enemy forces could be inferred from this: when they were told by Roman prisoners that a rampart had to be constructed around the camp for the siege, and they had no agricultural tools, they chopped up the earth with swords and carried it away in their cloaks; yet in scarcely three hours they completed a ten-foot rampart and a fifteen-foot ditch [Note: [Col. 1016D] “A ten-foot rampart.” Caesar has eleven feet. From what follows—“for fifteen miles”—one can determine how Caesar’s text should be read, since some books have fifteen and others ten miles, a variation in which Glareanus is perplexed. FABR.] around a circumference of fifteen miles [Note: [Col. 1016D] “For fifteen miles.” Absent from the Augustan edition.]. Moreover, they built one hundred and twenty towers of extraordinary height.

When hostile columns had been attacking continuously for seven days and nights [Note: [Col. 1016D] “And the wind.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “when the wind.”], and a very strong wind suddenly arose, they hurled burning pots from slings, as well as missiles set alight in the fires and soon glowing with the flame they had caught [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Set alight.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “set on fire.”], into the camp [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Into.” The first and third Florentine manuscripts, together with three Leiden manuscripts, have “inside.”]. As a result, the wind, rushing over the roofs [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Over the roofs.” Robert’s book has “over the roof-ridges”; three Leiden manuscripts have “over all the roof-ridges,” as do the Utrecht and Gronovian collections.], quickly fanned the scattered fire.

Yet even so the Romans did not yield, though they were overwhelmed on every side by wounds, exertions, sleeplessness, fasting, and fires [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Not even then.” The fourth Leiden manuscript and some editions prefer “nor even then.”]. At last Caesar was informed that one legion had been destroyed and another was already nearly exhausted. When Caesar approached with two legions [Note: [Col. 1016D–1017C] “With two legions.” Plutarch writes that Caesar then had ἑπτακισχιλίους τοὺς σύμπαντας, “seven thousand in all.” FABR.], the enemy abandoned the siege [Note: [Col. 1017C] “They abandoned.” The first edition has “they abandoned completely,” followed by the Venetian editions;] and, gathering all their forces, rushed against him.
