Caesar deliberately concealed himself in a very small camp [Note: [Col. 1017C] “Deliberately.” In the margin of the second Leiden manuscript: “or secretly.”], and ordered the cavalry to be sent ahead to pretend flight, so that, by crossing the valley lying between them—which seemed dangerous to him—he might lure the enemy through contempt for him. When they approached, he further ordered the gates to be blocked.

Seeing this, the Gauls, as though they had already won, turned to construct an outer rampart [Note: [Col. 1017C–1017D] “To draw a rampart around the outside.” The distinguished Oudendorp, commenting on Frontinus, p. 397, reads “to draw away,” because Frontinus, Book III of the *Stratagems*, chapter 117, has that expression. But since all the manuscripts consistently prefer “to draw around,” I do not think Orosius is speaking of the Romans’ rampart, but of the Gauls’ rampart, with which they intended to enclose Caesar’s camp. In the siege of Cicero’s camp they had done the same thing: instructed by prisoners that a rampart had to be constructed around the camp during a siege, they dug the earth with swords and carried it away in their cloaks. Since this occurred shortly before in this very chapter, the same meaning must be understood here concerning the attack on Caesar’s camp. Thus Caesar defeated and destroyed the Gauls when they turned to draw an outer rampart around the camp, by which they would enclose Caesar and prevent his departure.] [Note: [Col. 1017D] “An outer rampart.”] Caesar suddenly poured out his prepared army through all the gates and, after the Gauls had been put to flight, slaughtered them in an immense massacre.

For they are reported to have numbered sixty thousand at that time [Note: [Col. 1017D] “For sixty thousand.” Plutarch, in his *Life of Caesar*, also gives this number for those who besieged Quintus Cicero’s camp. FABR.—The first and third Leiden manuscripts have forty thousand.]; only a few escaped through the impassable marshes.

Indutiomarus, chief of the Treveri, who possessed large forces of armed men, after learning of the agreement of all Gaul, decided that it would be easy to destroy the camp of Labienus and the legion under his command [Note: [Col. 1017D] “Which he commanded.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Utrecht and Gronovian collections, delete the pronoun *is*.], and then, joining forces with the Eburones and Nervii, to proceed against Caesar.

Labienus, by whatever means he could, pretended fear, and thus overthrew Indutiomarus in a sudden sortie [Note: [Col. 1017D] “He overthrew in a sudden sortie.” The reading *eruptione* is correct; the printed editions incorrectly have *irruptione*. FABR.] while Indutiomarus, made careless, was riding about before the rampart with his forces taunting the Romans [Note: [Col. 1017D] “Thus.” Absent from the Augustan edition.]. Through this victory of Labienus, the remaining efforts of the Gauls were checked, and Caesar enjoyed somewhat greater quiet during the rest of the winter.

But understanding that greater tasks of war still lay before him—especially because, having lost a large part of his army and with the rest severely wounded, he seemed not even fit to withstand, much less to suppress, the attack of the Gauls—he asked the proconsul Gnaeus Pompey to levy legions and send them to him as reinforcements. Accordingly, before the winter had ended, three legions came to him in camp.

Then Caesar, before the enemy forces could unite, prepared to attack them at the beginning of spring while they were alarmed and to crush them while dispersed in their own territories. First, therefore, he ravaged the territory of the Nervii; but he handed over to the army the booty, which was extremely abundant. Next he invaded the Menapii in three columns. They seemed to him to be strongly protected by their immense marshes and extremely dense forests; but after a great slaughter had been widely inflicted, he received the survivors, who came as suppliants, into submission [Note: [Col. 1018C] “Received.” Three Leiden manuscripts have “receives.”].

In the following battle Labienus killed the entire force of the Treveri [Note: [Col. 1018C] “Killed.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “kills.”], having drawn them into battle by stratagem [Note: [Col. 1018C] “By stratagem.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts have “beforehand.”] before they could join the Germans who were approaching, and immediately captured the state itself [Note: [Col. 1018C] “Captured.” The same manuscripts have “captured”; shortly afterward the fourth Leiden manuscript has “drawn out” instead of “drawn into battle.”].

Caesar, wishing to avenge the deaths of the legates Sabinus and Cotta, learned that Ambiorix and the Eburones, the instigators of the destroyed legion [Note: [Col. 1018C] “Ambiorix and the Eburones, etc.” The Vulgate editions read “against Ambiorix and the Eburones.” But “against” appears in none of the manuscripts; the Augustan edition, faithfully based on an excellent manuscript, likewise rejected it, and so I have banished it.], had fled into the Ardennes Forest [Note: [Col. 1018C] “Had fled.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “had defected”; the Augustan edition has “had escaped.”]. This forest is the largest in all Gaul and extends from the banks of the Rhine and the territory of the Treveri as far as the Nervii; in length it stretches for more than five hundred miles.

Realizing that it would be extremely dangerous for his men to divide themselves through obstructed and extensive forests [Note: [Col. 1018D] “Obstructed.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “blocked,” which is also found in the Augustan edition.] in pursuit of an enemy thoroughly familiar with the region [Note: [Col. 1018D] “An enemy very familiar with the places.” Robert’s book has “an enemy thoroughly familiar with the region.”], he invited all Gaul by messengers to seek out and plunder the hidden booty in the Ardennes Forest, each according to his own inclination [Note: [Col. 1018D] “He invites.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “he invited,” followed by “so that each one…”]. By this means, with Gauls dying on both sides, he avenged the greatest injuries done to the Romans without danger to any Roman. Thus, secure in this very safe method of victory [Note: [Col. 1018D] “Method of victory.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian collection, have “method of vengeance.”], he returned to Italy.

## CHAPTER XI. Caesar likewise suppresses with great slaughter a new conspiracy of the Gauls to take up arms against him

[Note: [Col. 1019B] “With Caesar.” This chapter briefly touches upon matters that Caesar explained at length in Book VII and Hirtius in Book VIII. FABR.]

When Caesar had returned to Italy, Gaul again conspired to take up arms, and many peoples joined together at once. Their leader was Vercingetorix, whose counsel immediately persuaded all the Gauls to burn their own towns voluntarily [Note: [Col. 1019B] “They burned.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “they burn.”]; the first to be burned by its own inhabitants was Biturigo [Note: [Col. 1019B] “By its own people.” This does not appear in the Longobard manuscript.].

From there they attacked Caesar, who had secretly hurried back to his army by forced marches through the province of Narbonensis. Caesar had then enclosed in a siege a town called Cenapum [Note: [Col. 1019B] “A town called Cenapum.” Cenapum is also found in the old manuscripts, though wholly corrupt. Robert Stephanus wrote “Genabum.” But since it is clear from Caesar and Dio that what Orosius attributes here to the siege of this town occurred at Avaricum, I have no doubt that the latter name has intruded in place of the former. FABR.—The fourth Leiden manuscript has “Cenabum”; the others do not differ from the Vulgate editions.]. After it had long been attacked, it was finally captured and destroyed on a rainy day [Note: [Col. 1019B] “On a rainy day.” The second Leiden manuscript adds “rainy”; others have “on a rainy day.” The Augustan edition has “on another day.”], when the ropes and sinews of the enemy’s siege engines had weakened [Note: [Col. 1019B] “Had weakened.” Four Leiden manuscripts, the Gronovian collection, and some editions have “had become weak.”], and the towers had been brought up against the walls.

Forty thousand people are reported to have been there; scarcely eighty of them escaped by flight [Note: [Col. 1019B] “Escaped.” The same manuscripts have simply “escaped” or “fell.”] to the nearest camp of the Gauls.

Moreover, the Arverni and the other neighboring peoples, having also won over the Aedui to their side, fought many battles against Caesar. When, exhausted by fighting, they had withdrawn into a certain fortress [Note: [Col. 1019B–1019C] “Into a certain fortress.” Caesar calls it Gergovia; Strabo, Γεργουία; Dio, Γοργοθυία. FABR.—These events are described by Caesar, *Gallic War* VII.41. Through the treachery of Litavicus and his brothers, this disturbance was stirred up against Caesar. The memory of this man seems to survive on three small silver coins struck at Cabillonum, as indicated by the letter C, visible on the obverse after the female heads, probably of Venus. On the reverse appears a standard-bearing horseman, or one armed with a bow, quiver, and arrows, with the letters LITA VICVS beneath. The first and third coins are taken from Bouteroue, p. 48; the middle one is in our museum.], the soldiers, eager for plunder, turned their attention to storming the town, although Caesar vainly pleaded the disadvantage of the location. Thus Caesar, pressed there by enemies bursting down from above, fled defeated after losing a large part of his army.

While these things were taking place at Alesia [Note: [Col. 1020B] “While these things were taking place at Alesia.” He uses Caesar’s words, although he has described nothing that occurred at Alesia. This town of the Mandubii is correctly called Alesia in the manuscripts of Orosius and Caesar. Plutarch likewise calls it Ἀλησία, and Diodorus Siculus, Book IV, writes that Hercules founded the town and named it Ἀλησία from ἀπὸ τῆς κατὰ τὴν στρατείαν ἄλης, “from the wandering during the campaign.” Guil. Xylander, who displayed remarkable ingenuity in translating Dio from a very corrupt exemplar, correctly recognized that the manuscript’s ἐς Σαλεσίαν was a corruption for ἐς Ἀλεσίαν. Strabo, Book IV, reads περὶ Ἀλλησίαν πόλιν Μανδιβούλων, “around Alesia, the city of the Mandubii.” FABR.—Some manuscripts have “Helestam,” “Helesiam,” and “Halestam,” whence the form “Chaiestam” also entered some old editions. Shortly afterward, three Florentine manuscripts and the second Leiden manuscript read *possint* instead of *possent*.], Vercingetorix [Note: [Col. 1020B] “Vercingetorix.” You may read a fuller account of the efforts and unhappy courage of this great man in Caesar’s *Gallic War*, Book VII, chapters 66 and following. Besides this great king, the principal commanders in the revolt were Vergasillaunus the Arvernian, a relative and, as he is called there, cousin of Vercingetorix, Caesar VII.76 and 83, who, after rendering distinguished service to his country, was captured alive by the Romans while fleeing, VII.88; Sedulius, commander and chief of the Lemovices, killed in battle; Commius the Atrebatian; and the Aedui Viridomarus and Eporedorix. The memory of most of these men, defenders of liberty and lovers of their country, is believed to have been perpetuated on the silver coins of the Gauls, which we have placed below. On the first appears what I take to be a female head, encircled by a jeweled diadem, which I believe to be Venus. On the reverse is a horse. An inscription, VERGA, is added beside the head; Claudius Bouteroue, in his *Recherche Curieuse des monnoyes de France*, p. 64, considers it to refer to Vercingetorix. On the second is a helmeted female head with the inscription VIRODV; this inscription seems to refer to Viridomarus, whose name is written variously in Caesar’s manuscripts. The other side of the coin is occupied by a horseman holding a spear in his right hand. A third coin also seems to belong to Viridomarus or Virodomarus, from the surviving letters. I take the diademed head to refer to Venus, although Bouteroue, p. 66, suspects that it is the head of King Vercingetorix. The name of Commius, or Commii, the Atrebatian, is clearly expressed on the fourth coin, which displays an enduring symbol of liberty: a horse running freely, without a bridle. The obverse bears a helmeted head with the remaining letters ARMANO.], whom all had unanimously chosen as king, urged them to ensure that all throughout Gaul who could bear arms should be ready for this war. For this was the one war from which would follow either perpetual liberty, eternal servitude, or the death of all [Note: [Col. 1021C] “From which either, etc.” Three Leiden manuscripts together with the Gronovian collection transpose the words as follows: “either eternal servitude, or perpetual liberty, or death, etc.”].

Thus, apart from the force which he had previously assembled—an unlimited number—about eight thousand cavalry and two hundred and fifty thousand infantry were gathered [Note: [Col. 1021C] “Two hundred and fifty thousand infantry.” Caesar gives approximately two hundred and forty thousand infantry. FABR.].

Then the Romans and Gauls occupied two hills facing one another [Note: [Col. 1021C] “Two.” The same Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian collection, two Florentine manuscripts, and the Augustan edition, have “two” in the accusative.]. From there, fighting through many sorties and with varying outcomes, the Romans at last defeated the Gauls through the outstanding valor of the German cavalry [Note: [Col. 1021C] “Especially.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has “especially.”], whom they had summoned as allies for their aid some time before [Note: [Col. 1021C] “They had summoned.” I have again preferred this reading from the Cologne manuscript to the printed *adsciverant*. FABR.—All the manuscripts have *acciverant*, not *adsciverant*, although Fabricius and Scott preferred the latter.].

On the following day Vercingetorix gathered all who had escaped by flight and said that he had honestly been the author of defending liberty and of breaking the treaty [Note: [Col. 1021C] “Of breaking the treaty.” All the manuscripts have *inrumpendi* or *irrumpendi*, “of breaking into,” the treaty.] and that now, whether they all offered themselves to the Romans for death or whether he alone surrendered himself on behalf of all [Note: [Col. 1021D] “Himself alone.” Some old editions and the first Florentine manuscript have “whether he alone.” The fourth Leiden manuscript reads in what follows, “he would be ready in spirit.”], he would be steadfast in spirit.

Thus the Gauls, [Note: [Col. 1021D] “The resolve which, through shame, etc.” That is:

“All assented, and what each feared for himself,”]

“They turned their united strength to one wretch’s destruction.” Virgil, *Aeneid* II.130. His address to the Gauls and the common people was: “He had undertaken that war not for his own necessities, but for the sake of common liberty; and, since one must yield to fortune, he offered himself to them for either purpose: whether they wished to satisfy the Romans by his death or to surrender him alive.” Caesar, *Gallic War* VII.89. Nor was his address to Caesar, when he surrendered, any more abject, according to Florus III.10, as he cast his ornaments and weapons before Caesar’s knees: “You have conquered,” he said, “a brave man, bravest of men.” [Col. 1022B] Vercingetorix was a man to set beside Regulus, Mancinus, and the Decii. I suppose that the merciful and noble victor treated him mercifully; for I do not remember having read what became of him.] They bore their will, which for some time they had concealed out of shame, as though adopting it on the king’s advice; immediately begging pardon for themselves, they surrendered him alone as the author of the great crime.

The Bellovaci were considered, in their own opinion, stronger than all the Gallic peoples. Under the leadership of Correus [Note: [Col. 1022B] “Under the leadership of Correus.” Thus it is written in three Florentine manuscripts and nearly all the others, except that Lugd. Bat. I has *Coreo*, and Lugd. Bat. IV and Meus have *Corbeo*. The same diversity of spelling occurs in Caesar, Book VIII, chapter 6, p. 454. Fabricius printed *Chorreo*, a reading I also found in the Augustan edition. But instead of *hi Correo duce* (“these men under Correus”), Lugd. Bat. II has there *etc.*; the Augustan edition recognizes neither *hi* nor *ibi*.], they renew the war and join themselves in this alliance of the war they had undertaken to the Ambiani, Aulerci, Caleti, Veliocasses, and Atrebates [Note: [Col. 1022B] “The Ambiani, etc.” After the Ambiani, some manuscripts call those who follow the Aulerci, Caleti, and Veliocasses *Alurci*, *Saleti* or *Saluti*, *Velocarses* or *Veliocarses*, or finally *Veliocasses*. For *Atrebates*, three Leiden manuscripts prefer *Atrebatas*. This little silver coin is thought to belong to the Caleti or Caletes: on its obverse it has a helmeted head, in Roman fashion; on its reverse, an unbridled horse rushing forward at a free gallop, with the letters ΚΑΛΕΙ . . . . Υ. Yet I doubt whether it can be assigned to the Caleti or Caletes, since the letters ΑΛ, which are joined on the coin, rather form Α and Μ, and thus may supply another reading—namely, the one observed on the second coin. But here are the very little silver denarii: the first from Bouteroue, p. 52; the other two from our museum. [Col. 1022C]], and seize a certain place surrounded and obstructed on every side by marshes. When battle was joined, they slaughter a large force of Remi that had been serving as auxiliaries to the Romans [Note: [Col. 1022D] “That was serving as auxiliaries to the Romans.” The Longobard manuscript has *qui auxilio Romanis erant* (“who were serving as auxiliaries to the Romans”). Lugd. Bat. IV more correctly reads *quae auxilio Romanis venerat* (“which had come to the Romans’ aid”).].

Then, after they themselves [Note: [Col. 1022D] “Themselves.” Some editions have *sibi* (“for themselves”).] had occupied a position prepared for an ambush, and the Romans, having discovered this, had come in battle array and orderly formation to the place of the ambush, battle was joined. The Romans enclosed the fleeing Gauls within the same fortifications of the terrain by which they had been hemmed in, and killed them all.

There Correus, refusing either flight or surrender, forced the Romans, who were pressing him in order to capture him alive, by killing them, to compel him to be killed [Note: [Col. 1023B] “The Romans, so that he might be captured alive.” Robert’s manuscript has: “By killing the Romans who pressed him in order that he might be captured alive, he compelled them to kill him. Read Hirtius, Book VIII of the *Commentaries*.” Fabricius. — Hirtius’s words, chapter 19, p. 473 of Oudendorp’s edition, are: “Meanwhile Correus, overcome by no misfortune, could not be induced either to withdraw from the battle and seek the woods or—when our men invited him to surrender—to do so; instead, fighting with the greatest courage and wounding many, he compelled the victors, carried away by anger, to hurl their weapons at him. Nor do I see why these words provide Fabricius with stronger support for the common reading, *ne vivus caperetur, instanter occidendo* (“by urgently killing him so that he might not be captured alive”), since Hirtius’s words plainly show that the Romans tried by every means to capture Correus alive. But he fiercely repulsed the enemy as they approached to seize him or urge him to surrender, wounding very many, and thus caused the enemy to kill the man whom, for the glory of the victors, they would rather have preserved alive for all to behold. I have therefore restored the better reading from all the manuscripts I consulted; it is further confirmed by the excellent Augustan edition.].

Since Caesar therefore supposed that all Gaul was pacified and would not dare to aspire to any uprisings [Note: [Col. 1023C] “To any.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection and the Augustan edition, have *aut aliquos* (“or any”).], he sent the legions into winter quarters [Note: [Col. 1023C] “He sent.” Lugd. Bat. III and the Groningen Collection read *misit* (“he sent”) rather than *dimisit* (“he dismissed”).]. He himself, however [Note: [Col. 1023C] “He himself, however.” Three Leiden manuscripts read *ipse tamen* (“he himself nevertheless”).], devastated the territory of Ambiorix, who had stirred up so many wars, with a dreadful slaughter of its inhabitants.

But Gaius Caninius [Note: [Col. 1023D] “Gaius Caninius.” Lugd. Bat. II has *G. Caninius*; the other three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have *Gallus Caninius*. That was a cognomen of the Caninii.], a legate [Note: [Col. 1023D] “A legate.” Some editions have *alter legatus* (“another legate”).], encountered war among the Pictones. There a great multitude of the enemy surrounded a legion hampered by the march and brought it to the utmost danger.

Fabius, moreover, the legate, after receiving Caninius’s letter, set out for the Pictones. There, having learned from prisoners about the advantageous nature of the terrain, he overwhelmed the unsuspecting enemy and, after inflicting great slaughter [Note: [Col. 1023D] “After inflicting slaughter.” The Augustan edition adds these words by anticipation.], carried off abundant booty. Then, when he had given Caninius a signal of his arrival, Caninius suddenly sprang forth from the whole camp [Note: [Col. 1023D] “Sprang forth.” Lugd. Bat. IV and two Florentine manuscripts have *exsiluit* (“sprang forth”). The first edition and the Venetian editions have *exsiliens se injecit hosti* (“springing forth, he threw himself upon the enemy”).] and threw himself upon the enemy. Thus, while Fabius pressed them from one side and Caninius from the other [Note: [Col. 1023D] “Pressing from the other side.” Lugd. Bat. IV has *multum insistente* (“pressing hard”).], countless Gallic forces were slaughtered in a very great and prolonged battle [Note: [Col. 1023D] “Forces.” The same manuscript has *gentes* (“peoples”).].

From there Fabius proceeded against the Carnutes [Note: [Col. 1023D] “Against the Carnutes.” The first Florentine manuscript has *ad Carnutes* (“to the Carnutes”).]. For he knew that Dumnacus [Note: [Col. 1023D] “Dumnacus.” In three Florentine manuscripts and Lugd. Bat. II, as also in the Augustan edition, I found *Domnacum*; the other manuscripts have *Dominacum* and *Donacum*.], the very ancient leader and instigator of the whole rebellion, having escaped from this war [Note: [Col. 1023D] “Having escaped.” Two Leiden manuscripts have *lapsum* (“having slipped away”).], would, if he joined the Armorican peoples, again stir up the greatest disturbances in Gaul. But he subdued them, still trembling from the novelty of the situation, with remarkable courage and speed [Note: [Col. 1023D] “But them.” I have restored this from all the manuscripts; the editions had corrupted it into *sed eos* (“but them [masculine]”), failing to observe that “to tremble” and “to subdue” refer to the peoples, not to the disturbances.].

407 Meanwhile Draptes [Note: [Col. 1024B] “Draptes.” The Paris editions, Bolsuing, Hittorp, Fabricius, and Scottus printed *Drapes*, but the true name appears to have been *Draptes*, if the manuscripts, especially the better ones, are to be followed. It is so written in Flor. I, or the Longobard codex, and Flor. II, as also in Lugd. Bat. I and III, together with the Groningen Collection and the first, Augustan, and Venetian editions. Flor. III, Lugd. Bat. II, and Utrecht indicate the same spelling when they write *Adraptes*, the first letter being redundant through duplication of the final letter of the preceding word. Yet *Drapes* occurs in my codex and in Perizonius, and the same variation is observed in Caesar’s codices.] and Lucterius [Note: [Col. 1024C] “Lucterius.” Flor. I and II have *Lycterius* or *Lycteriusque*; Flor. III, *Licterius*; Lugd. Bat. I and III, *Lipterius*; the Groningen Collection, *Lypterius*. The Augustan edition reads *Leptirius* or, conjunctively, *Lecterius*.], seeing that Caninius and the legions were present in their territory, collected forces from every quarter and occupied the town of Uxellodunum [Note: [Col. 1024C] “Uxellodunum.” The codices and manuscripts have *Velutudunum*, *Veludunum*, *Velutunum*, *Velucunum*, and *Velludonum*.]. This town stood [Note: [Col. 1024C] “Stood.” Thus the manuscripts; some editions have *pendens* (“hanging”).] on the very lofty summit of a mountain, and on two sides [Note: [Col. 1024C] “And on two.” Lugd. Bat. IV does not recognize the conjunction.] was encircled by a considerable river beneath steep slopes. Secure through a very abundant spring halfway down the descent [Note: [Col. 1024C] “Then halfway.” Lugd. Bat. II has *medio inde* (“thence halfway”).], and protected within by a plentiful supply of grain, it looked down upon the enemy’s fruitless attacks from afar. Caninius, with such Roman resources as he alone could provide [Note: [Col. 1024C] “Alone.” Lugd. Bat. II has *sola* (“alone,” feminine).], defeated in a great battle both leaders, who had been drawn out into the plain with a very large part of their forces.

[Note: [Col. 1024C] “For one of the leaders having been killed, etc.” Lucterius fled from the battle, which was very fierce, while Draptes was captured. Hirtius, *Gallic War* VIII.36, p. 490: “Draptes himself was captured in that battle.” He escaped Roman mockery. *Ibid.* 44: “Draptes (or, as Hirtius writes it, Drappes), whom I have related to have been captured by Caninius, whether through indignation and grief at his chains or fear of a harsher punishment, abstained from food for a few days and so died.” What befell the other leader he pursues shortly afterward, p. 501, in these words: “At the same time Lucterius, whom I wrote had fled from battle, having come into the power of Epasnactus the Arvernian—for he kept changing places and entrusting himself to the loyalty of many, because he seemed likely nowhere to remain long without danger, being conscious how hostile Caesar must be toward him—this Epasnactus the Arvernian, a most devoted friend of the Roman people, without any hesitation led him bound to Caesar.”] For one of the leaders having been killed, the other fled with very few men [Note: [Col. 1024D] “The other, etc.” The Augustan edition has *alterum cum paucissimis fugat* (“he puts the other to flight with very few men”).]; none returned to the town, [Col. 1025A] but Caesar was needed to assault it. Therefore, informed by messengers [Note: [Col. 1025B] “Informed.” Lugd. Bat. I and III, with the Groningen Collection, write *redditus*; shortly afterward they have *occurrit* for *accurrit*, just as *deludendum* for *delendum*.], Caesar hastened there. Having surveyed everything, he saw that, if he attempted to take it by force, his army would have to be destroyed for the enemy’s sport and spectacle: 408 [Note: [Col. 1025B] “There was one sole means of defense.” The first edition, with the Paris and Venetian editions, has *hoc solum esse praesidium*; Bolsuing and Hittorp have *unum solum esse praesidii*, which I found in all manuscripts and the Augustan edition. Fabricius restored *unum solum esse praesidium*. But since the manuscript codices reject this form, I think the expression elliptical, with *loco* (“in place”) to be understood.] there was one sole means of defense, if somehow the enemy could be cut off from water [Note: [Col. 1025C] “If somehow.” Here too the editions have been excessively free in doubling the middle word, since all manuscript codices, supported by the Augustan edition, read *quo modo*, not *quoquo modo*.]. But even this Caesar could not have accomplished [Note: [Col. 1025C] “Could not have.” This is the consistent manuscript reading; before Fabricius, *nemo potuisset* (“no one could have”) was read in vain, and Scottus wrongly restored that reading in his edition. “Unless Caesar had been Caesar, he could not have done it,” says Orosius. Here again the Augustan edition supports the manuscripts.], since the spring from which they drank issued from the middle of the side of the sloping mountain. Caesar ordered mantlets to be brought up close to the spring and a tower to be built. Immediately there was a great sortie from the town [Note: [Col. 1025C] “Immediately.” The Augustan edition has *undique* (“from every side”); shortly afterward, *trucidabantur* (“were slaughtered”).]. Though they fought without danger, and although the Romans resisted stubbornly and came up repeatedly, many Romans were nevertheless slaughtered. Accordingly, an embankment and a tower sixty feet high were constructed, whose summit could reach the level of the spring [Note: [Col. 1025C] “Could reach the level of the spring.” Nearly all manuscripts have *aequare ad fontis locum possit* (“may be level with the place of the spring”).], so that missiles could be cast on equal terms [Note: [Col. 1025B] “On equal terms.” Lugd. Bat. I and III, with the Groningen Collection, have *aeque* (“equally”).], or the downward-thrown masses of rocks from above need not be feared.

But when the townspeople saw their cattle, and also the weaker ages of human beings, dying of thirst, they filled casks with pitch, tallow, and shingles [Note: [Col. 1025D] “Filled with shingles.” The manuscripts have *scindulis*; following Hirtius, we have written *scandulis* with Robert. According to Isidore, *scandulae* are so called from cutting; they are small boards cut in strips from oak or other timber. Thus Vitruvius, II.1, writes that among certain peoples buildings are constructed from stout shingles. Cornelius Nepos states that Rome was roofed with shingles until the Pyrrhic War, 470 years; see Pliny XVI.10. Fabricius.], then set them alight and hurled them down the slope, themselves following them in a mass from the whole town. Seeing that his engines were burning and that a serious and dangerous battle threatened his men [Note: [Col. 1025D] “Seeing.” Some editions add *inminere* (“was threatening”) uselessly and contrary to the manuscripts.], Caesar ordered the cohorts to go swiftly and secretly around the town [Note: [Col. 1025D] “Around.” Thus the manuscripts require us to read, not *circuitum*.] and suddenly raise a huge shout from every side. Terrified by this, the townspeople, [Col. 1026A] wishing to run back to fortify the town, withdrew from attacking the tower or demolishing the embankment [Note: [Col. 1025D] “Withdrew.” Flor. I has *decesserunt* (“departed”). For *oppugnatione*, Lugd. Bat. II and Utrecht have *expugnatione* (“taking by assault”).]. Yet those who, protected beneath the cover of the embankment, were digging tunnels to cut the veins of the spring, found its hidden channels and, by dividing them in many directions, caused them to diminish and be consumed within themselves. When the spring had dried up, the townspeople, seized by utter desperation, surrendered themselves. Caesar, however, cut off the hands of all who had borne arms and left them alive, so that the punishment of the wicked might be more manifest even to posterity [Note: [Col. 1026B] “More manifest.” The Groningen Collection has *testatura*; Lugd. Bat. III, *testatum*; shortly afterward Lugd. Bat. II has *ut improborum* (“as of the wicked”).]. For the public example of punishment is highly effective in checking audacity, since the very present appearance of the miserable living man both reminds those who know of it to remember and compels the ignorant to inquire.

### CHAPTER XII  
### He places before our eyes, as though beneath them, the misery and calamity suffered by Gaul at Caesar’s hands

[Col. 1026B]

[Note: [Col. 1026B] “When the Gauls had been exhausted and subdued.” The Augustan edition reads, “When therefore the Gauls had been exhausted and subdued.”] When Gaul had been exhausted and subdued, Caesar returned safely with the legions to Italy [Note: [Col. 1026B] “Returned.” Two Leiden manuscripts have *redit* (“returns”).], fearing no further Gallic disturbances behind him, knowing for certain that he had left behind no one who either dared to stir, or, if he did stir, was to be feared.

Now I wish to set before our eyes an emaciated and exhausted Gaul [Note: [Col. 1026C] “Exhausted Gaul.” I do not know what moved the editors to prefer *defetam* (“worn out”) when they found *defectam* (“exhausted”) in the manuscripts and had therefore placed it in the margin. Fabricius and Scottus accepted the same corrupt reading, which all the manuscripts I consulted, together with the Augustan codex or edition, unanimously reject. Nor does anyone in his right mind seem able to prefer it, provided he pays careful attention. *Defeta* seems to signify the same thing as *effeta* in Sallust, *Catiline* 53: “And, as though Rome had been exhausted by childbirth, for many years scarcely anyone of great virtue arose there.” It can therefore refer only to sterility and to fertility exhausted by years and frequent offspring. It cannot have a place here in Orosius, where Gaul is not compared with a woman exhausted by childbirth, with wearied and drained entrails, but with a great body which, seized by a more powerful disease, has lost its vigor, strength, and blood. Thus *defecta Gallia*, with blood or strength understood, is said here just as in Pliny, Columella, and others one speaks of a man exhausted in spirit, by old age, by years, and so forth.], after those most burning fevers and inward heats that consumed the better parts of its vital powers [Note: [Col. 1026D] “Consuming the better parts of its vital powers.” This is the reading of the Longobard, or first Florentine, manuscript, as well as the second Florentine, Lugd. Bat. II, and Utrecht manuscripts. The third Florentine and Lugd. Bat. IV have *medullarum* (“of the marrow”), as though they intended *medullam* (“marrow”), which appears in Meus in a form whose final *m* seems almost like the letter *v*. In the other manuscripts and all the old editions, *molliora* (“the softer parts”) is found, a reading preferred by Fabricius and Scottus, with Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 66: “Meanwhile the soft flame lives in her marrow, and the silent wound lives beneath her breast.”], so that it may be seen how great its thinness [Col. 1027A] and pallor are [Note: [Col. 1027B] “May be.” Some old editions have *affecta sit* (“is afflicted”).], how sunk down and weakened it lies, how greatly it fears even the movements of its necessary functions, lest they recall the same onslaught of evils [Note: [Col. 1027B] “Onslaught.” Lugd. Bat. III and the Augustan edition have *occursum* (“encounter”); the Groningen Collection has *in occursum* (“to meet”).].

For the Roman army rushed upon it in a sudden assault, like a disease more powerful than a very strong body; and the disease burns all the more fiercely the less patiently it is endured. Miserable Gaul thirsted when, with the sword hanging over it, it was compelled to declare its submission to eternal slavery, with hostages also torn away. It thirsted, as I have said, for that sweetness of liberty, like cold water, so familiar and so delightful to all; and the more it understood that this was being taken from it, the more eagerly it desired it.

Hence came that frequent presumption against prohibitions, and that untimely liberty in defense of liberty [Note: [Col. 1027B] “And in defense of liberty.” Several editions prefix the conjunction *et* (“and”), but most manuscripts reject it.], and the license to seize what had been snatched away, insatiably, which seemed to extinguish the ill-conceived disaster, yet increased it [Note: [Col. 1027C] “Untimely liberty.” The same manuscripts have *inopportuna* (“untimely”), and I do not see why *importuna* (“troublesome”), which the printed editions prefer, would be more appropriate. — “And the license to seize what had been snatched away.” Two Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have *praeceptaque* (“and commands”), while the Longobard manuscript has *praeruptaque*, as though Orosius had called reckless, dangerous license *praerupta*, from the metaphor of precipices. The sense of the common reading is obscure. For *augebat* (“increased”), some editions wrongly have *angeb at* (“distressed”).].

Thus the Roman was more cunning in laying ambush before the battle; more hostile as an enemy in the battle; more savage as victor after the battle; and everything grew more cruel for subduing impatience. At last no one trusted even remedies. And so, if I could ask this nation of which we are speaking what judgment it formed at that time, while enduring these things, it would, I think, answer:

“Thus that fever then made me bloodless and cold” [Note: [Col. 1027C] “Made me bloodless and cold.” From these words it is clear that *defetam* (“worn out”) is wrongly printed at the beginning of the chapter, and that the reading of all the manuscripts is sound: *exsanguem defectamque Galliam* (“Gaul, bloodless and exhausted”), that is, bloodless and therefore, as it is called here, cold.], “so that even this [fever]” [Note: [Col. 1027C] “So that even this.” The Cologne and Maternus manuscripts insert the word *aestas* (“summer”) very appropriately. Laut. — I found the same word inserted after *etiam haec* (“even this”) in the Utrecht manuscript and in Lugd. Bat. II; it is also found in the Augustan edition and was accepted by Scottus in his edition. Yet I do not think it should therefore immediately be accepted. First, it would have to be established that in the year when Orosius wrote this, the summer was especially hot; moreover, the subject would then be summer rather than fever, so that the metaphor would not continue but a new one would be introduced. Indeed, I strongly dislike the word *aestas* here; *aestus* (“heat”) should rather be read, which corresponds to a burning fever. Orosius means that Gaul was so utterly afflicted by that fever—that is, by its suffering under Julius Caesar—that it was never able to recover its strength, nor rise even against the Goths, that is, restore its strength throughout the entire intervening period, from the time it was subdued by the Romans under Caesar until that disaster suffered by the Roman territories and Rome herself at the hands of the Goths. That disaster, by continuation of the metaphor, is called a fever which affected not only the Gauls but nearly everyone. He says that Gaul did not feel this, as though it had been deprived of sensation by its ancient disasters. I therefore retain the old reading as the genuine one.], which affected almost everyone [Note: [Col. 1028B] “Which affected almost everyone.” The first word is condemned by three manuscripts, Lugd. Bat. IV and Meus. Lugd. Bat. I omits *pene* (“almost”), which follows.], could heat or stir me” [Note: [Col. 1028C] “Affected.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have *constrinxit* (“constricted”).]; “and thus the Romans so bent me that I cannot rise even against the Goths.”

But Rome herself did not escape the disasters she inflicted. The powers of her generals and the strength of her legions were exercised and driven for a long time throughout the whole compass of the world [Note: [Col. 1028C] “Were exercised and driven.” Several manuscripts and many editions prefer *auctae* (“increased”), but wrongly. The violence of the verb *agere* and *agi* (“to drive” and “to be driven”) is well known, as is clear from the frequent pairing of *agere* and *rapere* (“to drive” and “to seize”). Roman power, therefore, having been increased too greatly, turned its strength against itself; and through the mutual disasters of those who, driven by ambition, were hastening toward the highest rank, it finally began to collapse from exhaustion and fell with a heavy crash.], forces which, rushing against one another, would win at the cost of the one whose danger brought about their victory. For the victorious Caesar, returning from Gaul, was followed by civil wars and other grave disasters; and before these came the killing of Crassus among the Parthians and the slaughter of his army.

### CHAPTER XIII  
### On the greed of Crassus, his operations against the Parthians, and his death

[Col. 1028B]

In the 697th year from the founding of the City [Note: [Col. 1028C] “In the 697th year from the founding of the City.” The same number is found in our manuscript of Eutropius, whereas the printed editions have the 699th year from the founding of the City. According to the calculation of the Capitoline Fasti, however, the year in which Gnaeus Pompey and Marcus Crassus were consuls for the second time was 698. Crassus, eager for a province, set out for Syria in military dress during his consulship itself, according to Plutarch and Dio. Fabricius.], Crassus, Pompey’s colleague in the consulship, having drawn by lot the province directed against the Parthians, a man of insatiable greed, heard of the wealth of the temple at Jerusalem, which Pompey had left untouched [Note: [Col. 1028D] “Heard of it at Jerusalem.” Josephus recounts this matter in *Antiquities* XIV, chapter 12; read it.], and turned aside into Palestine [Note: [Col. 1028D] “Turned aside.” Here too *devertit* (“turned aside”) seems to need restoring; the same was done above, in chapter 4, from the Longobard manuscript, and the Utrecht manuscript seems to indicate it by reading *revertit* (“turned back”).]. He approached Jerusalem, entered the temple [Note: [Col. 1028D] “Entered.” This is the manuscript reading. Some editions have *invadit* (“invaded”); the Augustan edition has *templumque pervadit* (“and entered throughout the temple”). For *adit* (“approached”), four Leiden manuscripts together with Utrecht have *adiit* (“approached”).], and plundered its treasures.

From there, advancing through Mesopotamia into Parthia, wherever he passed he imposed levies of auxiliary troops upon allied cities and exacted payments. As soon as he crossed the Euphrates, he immediately encountered Vageses [Note: [Col. 1028D] “Vageses.” I wrote this from Gualther’s book. Plutarch, in his *Life of Crassus*, and Appian, in the *Parthian History*—if that book was indeed written by Appian—have Οὐαγίσης (*Ouagisēs*). Fabricius. — Two Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection have *Bogessen* or *Bogessem*. The first Florentine has *Vagensem*, the second *Bogesen*, the third *Lugessem*. The Augustan edition has *Bagessen*.], the envoy sent to him by Orodes, king of the Parthians. Vageses rebuked him sharply [Note: [Col. 1029C] “Rebuked.” Some manuscripts have *increpatus* (“having been rebuked”), and nearly all have *cur* (“why”) in place of *quod* (“because”).] for crossing the Euphrates, driven by greed, contrary to the treaty of Lucullus and Pompey [Note: [Col. 1029C] “Of Lucullus and Pompey.” In some editions, contrary to the manuscripts, the conjunction *et* (“and”) has dropped out; Fabricius and Scottus should not have overlooked it, since its omission gives this passage a very different and unsuitable meaning. For greed belongs not to Pompey, whom he called most self-controlled above, but to Crassus. The act was committed by Crassus contrary first to the treaty of Lucullus and then also to that of Pompey, who had succeeded Lucullus in the Mithridatic War. [Col. 1029D]], and told him that before long he would be loaded, in place of Parthian gold, with Parthian iron.

When they had reached the vicinity of Carrhae, the Parthians suddenly attacked the Romans with Surena and Sillaces, commanders of the archers [Note: [Col. 1029D] “With Surena and Sillaces.” *Sulacea* is commonly and corruptly read; Plutarch has Σιλλάκης (*Sillakēs*). Fabricius.]. Many senators fell there, as did several men of consular rank [Note: [Col. 1029D] “Several.” The first and Augustan editions, together with the Paris and Venetian editions, have *aliqui* (“some”).], and men who had been praetors. Crassus’s son also, a young man of the highest distinction, was killed in battle. In addition, four cohorts were caught in the middle of the plain with Vargunteius and killed.

Surena, taking the cavalry, set out to pursue Crassus. After surrounding him and killing him when he was vainly seeking a conference with him, he nevertheless would have preferred to carry him away alive. A few, saved by the protection of night, escaped to Carrhae [Note: [Col. 1029D] “Carrhae.” The Augustan edition, as well as the Utrecht manuscript, consistently has *Charras*.].

When the Roman disaster became known, many eastern provinces would have defected from the alliance or allegiance of the Roman people [Note: [Col. 1029D] “Or allegiance.” Some manuscripts and editions have *et fide* (“and allegiance”).], had Cassius not, after gathering a few soldiers from the rout, checked Syria in its swelling pride with outstanding courage and self-restraint. He defeated Antiochus and his immense forces in battle and killed him. He also drove from Syria the Parthians sent by Orodes, who had already entered Antioch, and killed their commander Osaces [Note: [Col. 1029D] “Osaces.” All the Leiden manuscripts, together with Utrecht and the Groningen Collection, have *Osacen*. Cicero discusses Cassius’s actions against the Parthians and the killing of their commander Osaces in *Letters to Atticus* V, letter 20; Dio discusses it in Book 40. Fabricius.].

### CHAPTER XIV  
### On the mutability of the Roman Empire, as though in epilogue to the foregoing

Thus the Roman state is always [Note: [Col. 1029D] “Always.” This word is absent from Lugd. Bat. I and the Groningen Collection.] undergoing alternating change, like the form of the ocean sea, which differs every day: now it is raised for seven days by successive increases, now during the following equal number of days it is withdrawn by a natural loss and inward decline [Note: [Col. 1029D] “During the following.” Some editions have *consequentibus* (“following”), and two Leiden manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection have *in consequentibus* (“in the following”).].

To begin with the nearest examples, when the Cimbri and Tigurini were victorious and the Roman army perished by the river Rhône, Rome experienced the narrowest straits. Then, with the disaster of the Cimbri immediately reversed, she rose high through great successes [Note: [Col. 1030C] “Raised high.” Three Leiden manuscripts together with the third Florentine have *elevata* (“raised”).] and, forgetting her earlier failures [Col. 1030A] [Note: [Col. 1030C] “Successes.” Some editions have *provectibus* (“advances”). Several manuscripts delete *est* (“was”) immediately afterward.], became elated.

Then the vaunting of this most recent prosperity was chastised by the Italian War and the devastation under Sulla. Again, after this domestic and internal ruin, by which she was almost disemboweled and consumed to the marrow, she was restored, and indeed extended, in periods of time almost equal to the preceding ones, when Lucullus subdued Asia, Pompey Spain, and Caesar Gaul, and the Roman Empire was extended almost to the furthest boundaries of the earth.

Now this vastest expansion is followed by an immense collapse. For a Roman consul is killed among the Parthians and his army destroyed [Note: [Col. 1030C] “And the army.” The conjunction is absent from Lugd. Bat. II.]; that most savage civil war between Pompey and Caesar is joined; and amid these events Rome herself is suddenly seized by fire and burned.

In the 700th year from the founding of the City [Note: [Col. 1030C] “In the 700th year from the founding of the City.” This fire, which destroyed a very large part of the city and was regarded as a portent, actually occurred in the year 703, during the consulship of Lucius Paulus and Gaius Marcellus. Orosius cites Livy’s authority concerning it in Book VII, chapter 2. Fabricius.], a fire, whose origin is uncertain, seized a very large part of the City. They say that the city had never before been caught and devastated by so great a conflagration. For it is recorded that fourteen districts, together with the Jugarius district [Note: [Col. 1030D] “It is recorded.” Some manuscripts and the Augustan edition have *traditum est* (“it has been handed down”).], were consumed.

From this point the civil war begins, which had long been prepared by great disagreements and schemes.

### CHAPTER XV  
### On the civil war waged by Caesar and Pompey, the bloodiest of all
For when Caesar returned victorious from Gaul, he demanded that a second consulship be decreed for him while he was absent. The consul Marcellus opposed this [Note: [Col. 1030D] “By the consul Marcellus.” Roberti’s book adds: “by Bibulus, by Cato.” Since everyone writes much about these disputes, it would be tedious to wish to annotate anything here. Read Caesar, Appian, Plutarch, and the others. FABR.], with Pompey supporting him; then the Senate decreed that Caesar should not enter Rome unless he had disbanded his army [Col. 1030C], and, on the authority of the consul Marcellus, Pompey was sent with imperium to the legions stationed at Luceria. Caesar withdrew to Ravenna. Marcus Antonius and [Note: [Col. 1030D] “Quintus Cassius.” Everyone calls him this, except the books of Orosius, in which he is given the praenomen Publius.] Quintus Cassius, tribunes of the plebs, intervening on Caesar’s behalf, were forbidden by the consul Lentulus to enter the senate-house and the forum, and departed to Caesar, [Note: [Col. 1030D] “With Curio and Coelius.” This is Marcus Coelius Rufus, whose death is mentioned shortly afterward. I thought this should be noted because in Dio, at the beginning of Book XLI, Καικιλίου is twice read corruptly instead of Καιλίου, or rather Κοιλίου. FABR.] accompanied by Curio and Coelius.

[Col. 1031A] After Caesar had crossed the Rubicon River [Note: [Col. 1031C] “Crossed.” Florus, third edition: “having crossed.”], as soon as he came to Ariminum, he explained what ought to be done to the five cohorts that were then all he possessed, with which—as Livy says—he attacked the entire world. Lamenting his wrongs, he declared that the cause of the civil war was the restoration of the tribunes to their country. Through Antonius he then recovered from Lucretius the seven cohorts that were staying at Sulmo [Note: [Col. 1031C] “Recovered.” Some manuscripts read “recovers.” For “were staying,” some editions have “were there.”], and brought over to his side the three legions that were staying with Domitius at Corfinium.

Pompey and the entire Senate, alarmed as Caesar’s strength increased, crossed into Greece as though driven from Italy and chose Dyrrachium as the base from which to conduct the war. Caesar came to Rome and, breaking down the doors, seized the money that had been denied him from the treasury [Note: [Col. 1031C] The tribune of the plebs, Lucius Metellus, intervened in this affair. See Appian, Book II; Dio, Book XLI; Lucan, Book III. FABR.], bringing out from it four thousand one hundred and thirty-five pounds [Col. 1031B] of gold and nearly nine hundred thousand pounds of silver. [Note: [Col. 1031C] “Pounds of silver.” Budaeus investigates this sum in *De Asse*, Book II, p. 318; see him. The Lugdunensis Batavus, third edition, together with the Gronovian Collation, deletes “this weight” at this point.]

416 From there he departed for Ariminum to join the legions, then crossed the Alps and came to Massilia. Since he was not admitted there, he left Trebonius with three legions to besiege it [Note: [Col. 1031C] “Since he was not admitted.” Some manuscripts read *cur*, which all printed editions retain. But the second and fourth Lugdunensis Batavus read *cum*, which seems preferable here, unless we prefer *quod*, for which word *cur* is often written in Orosian manuscripts.], and hastened to Spain, which the Pompeian commanders Lucius Afranius, Marcus Petreius, and Marcus Varro held with their legions. There, after defeating Petreius and Afranius in many battles, he dismissed them after an agreement had been made [Note: [Col. 1031C] “After an agreement had been made.” Some editions insert “of an alliance” against the manuscripts.]. In Further Spain he received two legions from Marcus Varro.

Likewise his commanders—that is, Curio expelled Cato from Sicily; Valerius expelled Cotta from Sardinia; and Varus expelled Tubero from Africa [Note: [Col. 1031C] “That is.” Orosius often speaks in this way. Therefore the words that some editions have after this, “which is why,” are rightly rejected.]. Returning to Massilia, Caesar subdued it by siege and stripped it of everything except life and liberty.

[Note: [Col. 1031D] “But Dolabella.” Students should read this passage carefully, since Caesar’s own full account of the entire affair, not far from the beginning of Book III of the *Civil War*, has been lost. The same matter is related briefly by Appian and Dio, but described more fully by Lucan in Book IV. See Florus, Book IV, chapter 2. FABR.] But Dolabella [Note: [Col. 1031D] “Of Caesar’s party.” Some editions read “on Caesar’s side.”], one of Caesar’s supporters, was defeated in Illyricum by Octavius and Libo and deprived of his forces; he fled to Antonius [Note: [Col. 1031D] “To Antonius.” The first Florentine manuscript reads: “he fled to Antonius.”]. Basilus [Note: [Col. 1031D] Lucan, Book IV: “And they saw Basilus as commander.” We shall discuss this name in Chapter 18. FABR.] and Sallustius [Note: [Col. 1031D] “By individual legions.” This passage has been badly corrupted in Orosius. Since in most manuscripts one could read *Basillus et Sallustius singulas legiones*, the editors saw that the sense was incomplete in this form and gratuitously supplied *parantes* (“preparing”). This reading occupied all editions down to Fabricius, except the Augustan. Fabricius, without giving either reason or authority for his alteration, restored *dividentes* (“dividing”). The copyist of the third Florentine manuscript, likewise seeing that something was missing, wrote *ducentes* (“leading”) above the words *quibus praeerant*. But, since I found *per singulas* in three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, besides the Ultrajectine and the Gronovian Collation, I did not doubt that this was the true reading; because *per* was written in contracted form, the first editors made *parantes* from it. They were defeated by individual legions because they joined battle with the enemy not with their forces united, but each separately with the legion over which he commanded.], with the individual legions under their command, and Antonius likewise, as well as Hortensius, who was engaging the enemy with a fleet from the lower sea, all advanced together against Octavius and Libo, [Col. 1032C] 417 and were all defeated. [Note: [Col. 1032C] “And were defeated.” My manuscript deletes the conjunction *and*.] Antonius, after surrendering himself to Octavius with fifteen cohorts [Note: [Col. 1032C] The Augustan edition has “with twelve cohorts.”], was led by Libo, together with all his men, over to Pompey.

[Note: [Col. 1032C] “Curio and Sicily.” Caesar gives a full account of what is briefly touched upon here concerning Curio’s death, the assault on Salona, and Marcus Coelius and Titus Milo. FABR.] Curio crossed from Sicily into Africa with an army; King Juba immediately received him and slaughtered him together with all his forces. Octavius attempted to besiege Salona, but lost almost all the forces he had led there [Note: [Col. 1032D] “To besiege.” Some manuscripts read “to capture.”]. Coelius defected from Caesar [Col. 1032B] and joined the exiled Milo. When the two attempted to attack Capua with a force of slaves, they were killed.

At Corcyra, Bibulus, overcome by shame because the enemy had mocked the guard he had stationed before the sea and the town, exhausted himself by fasting and keeping watch.

[Note: [Col. 1032D] “Appius Claudius.” Valerius recounts this matter in Book I, Chapter 8. See Lucan, Book V. FABR.] Appius Claudius Censorinus, who was guarding Greece at Pompey’s command, wished to test the already discredited authority of the Pythian oracle. For, after forcing the prophetess to descend into the cave, he is said to have consulted her about the war, and she replied:

“This war, Roman, has nothing to do with you;  
you shall possess Euboean Coela.”

[Note: [Col. 1032D] “The skies of Euboea.” In the printed books of Valerius it is “the chamber of Euboea”; in the manuscript, “the sky of Euboea,” followed by “the sky of Euboea.” Lucan writes:

“Alone you shall possess a place of rest  
in the vast valley of the Euboean flank.” FABR.]

*Coela* is the name used for the Euboean Gulf. Thus Appius departed perplexed and uncertain about the oracle.

[Note: [Col. 1032D] “This adviser urges us, etc.” If we retain the common reading, it will mean “to consult our detractors,” that is, to say something for their advantage. I very much doubt whether that is the sense of this passage, especially since three Florentine manuscripts, as many Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, and also the Ultrajectine manuscript read: “this adviser urges us to consult our detractors.” If Orosius wrote according to the understanding of his age, it would mean the same as “to consult the detractors,” that is, “to question them,” as he immediately does with the words, “Why then,” etc. FABR.] This adviser urges us to consult our detractors [Col. 1033A]. They complain, of course, that the sacred rites of the Christians have been forbidden to them and their ceremonies abolished, [Note: [Col. 1033C] “And especially on this account.” Three Florentine manuscripts, four Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, the Gronovian Collation, and the old editions read: “and for this reason especially,” except that *ob* is absent from the Augustan edition. My manuscript and Perizonius, together with the Ultrajectine, confirm the common reading, which is sufficiently sound.] and especially on this account: since omens from entrails and prophecies have ceased, future disasters cannot be avoided because they cannot be known. [Note: [Col. 1033C] “Cannot be known.” The first and third Lugdunensis Batavus have “cannot be.”]

Why, then, long before Caesar’s rule and the birth of Christ, had faith in the Pythian oracle been abolished, as its own authorities testify? It had been abolished because it was despised. And why, in turn, was it despised, unless because it was false, vain, or doubtful? Hence the poet wisely warned us:

“The unadvised depart, and hate the seat of the Sibyl.”

[Note: [Col. 1033C] “The poet gave warning beforehand.” Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 452.]

And lest anyone should perhaps think lightly of the fact that what had been abolished and grown obsolete through contempt was some insignificant thing—that is, either the divinity or the seat—the god Apollo Pythius [Note: [Col. 1033C] “This Apollo was the Pythian.” The Augustan edition has “Apollo was the Pythonian.” In the same manuscript these words, taken from a gloss, preceded it: “Apollo succeeded the serpent Python as heir in divination. After Apollo, the Sibyl succeeded in divination.”] was said to have become heir to the seat, the divination, and the divine power after killing that great serpent [Col. 1033B] Python [Note: [Col. 1033C] “The serpent Python.” Callimachus writes of Python in the hymn to Apollo:

“Python, as you descended, the dread beast met you,  
the terrible serpent; you slew him,  
hurling swift arrows one after another.”

That is:

“A fearsome serpent, a wild beast, met him—Python—  
whom you, descending, quickly killed with your deadly bow,  
while continually directing the flying arrows with your skill.  
FABR.]

He chose to give responses there, where the divination itself seemed to have arisen together with its founder. Moreover, throughout other regions of the earth, this same deity spews forth all the madness of frenzied women, foaming at the mouth and rushing about in delirium. To him many kings of the earth hastened, as though to the living voice of a consulted god, and the Romans themselves very often sent him lavish gifts.

But if this Apollo Pythius was gradually despised, abandoned, and abolished as experience distinguished the truth, what living thing can be hoped for from a dead animal, or what truth from a deranged little woman? Finally, what will the hungry priest not fabricate,

[Col. 1033C] [Note: [Col. 1033D] “When the fat Tyrrhenian has inflated the ivory.” This is a verse of Virgil from Book II of the *Georgics*. FABR.]

“When the fat Tyrrhenian has inflated the ivory at the altars,”

after the entrails of a fat animal have been displayed? [Col. 1034A] For, as they themselves admit, Apollo himself misleads people by speaking either obscurely or falsely. Therefore let them calmly endure our forbidding, in the judgment of truth, what their ancestors were able to despise through experience, even if they themselves are unwilling for the moment to imitate them. [Note: [Col. 1033D] “Just as they themselves admit.” Previously this was confused and read: “Will the hungry man not fabricate? For, as they themselves …” LAUT.—The common reading is correct; nothing should be changed.]

Meanwhile, many kings of the East came with auxiliary forces to Pompey at Dyrrachium [Note: [Col. 1034C] “Came together.” The first Florentine manuscript has “came.”]. When Caesar arrived there, he surrounded Pompey with a siege without success, constructing a ditch around fifteen thousand paces of ground [Note: [Col. 1034C] “He himself enclosed fifteen thousand paces of ground.” Caesar does not state the length of the fortification, nor does Lucan at the beginning of Book VI. Appian, Book II, gives “two hundred and one thousand stades.” Florus writes that Caesar enclosed Pompey’s camp with a rampart sixteen thousand paces long. FABR.] while Pompey had the sea open to him.

Pompey destroyed a certain fort near the sea, which Marcellinus was defending [Note: [Col. 1034C] “Which Marcellinus was defending.” Lentulus Marcellinus was quaestor. Caesar. FABR.], and killed Caesar’s garrison stationed there. Caesar attacked Torquatus and one legion in order to overcome them. When Pompey learned of the danger threatening his allies, he concentrated all his forces there; [Col. 1034B] Caesar immediately abandoned the siege and turned against him. Torquatus, bursting out at once [Note: [Col. 1034C] “Bursting out.” The Augustan edition has “breaking out.”], pursued Caesar as he retreated. Thus Caesar’s soldiers, terrified by the danger on both sides, fled despite Caesar’s vain efforts to stop them. Pompey, however, victorious even by Caesar’s own testimony [Note: [Col. 1034C] “Victorious even by Caesar’s testimony.” After this battle was fought at Dyrrachium and Caesar was defeated, Pompey did not press the pursuit; Caesar denied that Pompey knew how to win. See Suetonius, *Julius*; Plutarch, *Pompey* and *Caesar*. FABR.], recalled the pursuing army.

Four thousand of Caesar’s soldiers, twenty-two centurions [Note: [Col. 1034D] Plutarch, in *Pompey*, has two thousand. Caesar, *Commentaries*, Book III, has thirty-two centurions, not twenty-two. FABR.—The same number, thirty-two, occurs in the first edition, as well as in the Paris and Venetian editions.], and several Roman knights [Note: [Col. 1034D] “And the cavalry.” The manuscripts and some editions delete the conjunction.] were killed in that battle. [Col. 1034D] Caesar then hastened through Epirus into Thessaly. Pompey followed with his enormous forces, and battle was joined.

Thus the lines were drawn up on both sides. [Note: [Col. 1034D] “Is drawn up.” So the better manuscripts and the old editions read, not “was drawn up.”] Pompey stationed eighty-eight cohorts in three lines. He had forty thousand infantry, six hundred cavalry on the left wing and five hundred on the right, besides many kings, senators, and Roman knights, together with a large number of light-armed troops [Col. 1035A] [Note: [Col. 1034D] “Of light-armed troops.” Three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts and the Gronovian Collation read “of light-armed men.”].

Caesar likewise arranged eighty cohorts in three lines. He had [Note: [Col. 1035B] “No fewer.” The first edition has “fewer than.” The same reading occurs in three Florentine manuscripts, two of which additionally delete “than.”] no fewer than thirty thousand infantry and one thousand cavalry.

It was a sight both to behold and to lament: the strength of Rome gathered on the Pharsalian fields and standing ready for mutual slaughter [Note: [Col. 1035B] “Pharsalian.” Three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts read “Thessalian.” The same is found in the Augustan edition.]. Had concord directed those forces, no peoples or kings could have withstood them.

At the first clash Pompey’s cavalry was driven back, exposing his left flank. Then, after the fighting had long remained uncertain on both sides, and while Pompey, on one side, urged his men, saying, “Spare the citizens” [Note: [Col. 1035C] “Spare the citizens.” We have written this from the ancient manuscripts; Florus has the same. FABR.], though he did not do so, while Caesar, on the other, did what he was pressing them to do, saying, “Soldier, strike the face,” Pompey’s entire army at last fled, and the camp was plundered.

In that battle fifteen thousand Pompeians [Note: [Col. 1035C] “Fifteen thousand.” The first and fourth Lugdunensis Batavus have twenty-two thousand.] and thirty-three centurions [Col. 1035B] were killed.

Such was the outcome of the battle at Old Pharsalus. [Note: [Col. 1035C] “Pompey fleeing.” Caesar, Book III; Plutarch, *Pompey*; Appian, Book II; Dio, Book XLII; and Velleius, Book II, discuss Pompey’s flight and death. FABR.] Pompey, fleeing, found a cargo ship at the mouth of the Peneius River and crossed into Asia. From there he went through Cyprus to Egypt. As soon as he reached the shore, he was killed at the command of the young Ptolemy, in order to win the favor of the victorious Caesar.

Pompey’s wife and sons fled. The rest of the Pompeian fleet was plundered, and everyone aboard it was brutally slaughtered. [Col. 1035C] 421 Pompey Bithynicus was also killed [Note: [Col. 1035C] “Pompey Bithynicus.” Quintus Pompeius, son of Aulus, who was called Bithynicus. Cicero, *Brutus*. FABR.—The Lugdunensis Batavus, three manuscripts together with the Gronovian Collation, delete the conjunction “and.”].

Lentulus, a former consul [Note: [Col. 1035C] “Lentulus.” Lucius Lentulus Crus, who had been consul the preceding year. Caesar writes that he was captured by the king and killed in custody. FABR.], was killed at Pelusium [Col. 1036A] [Note: [Col. 1035C] “A former consul.” The Augustan edition has “Lentulus, the former consul.”].

After settling affairs in Thessaly, Caesar came to Alexandria. When Pompey’s head and ring had been brought to him and he had seen them, he wept. After withdrawing into the palace, he was thwarted by the guardians, who prevented him from receiving money by craftily plundering their temples, so as both to make the royal treasuries appear empty and to stir up the people’s hostility to Caesar.

Moreover, the royal commander Achillas, having once been stained with Pompey’s blood, was also plotting Caesar’s death. For when he was ordered to disband the army he commanded—twenty thousand armed men—he not only disregarded the order [Note: [Col. 1035C] “But also drew up a battle line.” Two Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts read “but even drew up a battle line.”], but actually drew up a battle line.

During the battle itself, the royal fleet, which happened by chance to have been hauled ashore, was ordered to be burned. [Note: [Col. 1035C] [Col. 1035D] “That fire.” Praising this library, Titus Livy says that it was a remarkable work of royal elegance and care, as reported by Seneca in *On the Tranquility of Life*, where it is said that four hundred thousand books burned at Alexandria. Plutarch, in *Caesar*, and Dio, Book XLII, also mention the burning of the Alexandrian library. Hirtius gives a fuller account of the entire affair than anyone else in his *Alexandrian War*. FABR.] The fire, after also invading part of the city, consumed four hundred thousand books that had perhaps been stored in buildings nearby [Note: [Col. 1035D] “After it had consumed part.” The fourth Lugdunensis Batavus and the Gronovian Collation read “after it had consumed parts.” The same Collation, together with three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, does not recognize *ea* above.], a singular monument to the zeal and care of earlier generations, who had gathered together so many works of so many distinguished minds.

Hence, although even today there remain in temples—ones that we too have seen—bookcases [Note: [Col. 1035D] “Even today.” Some old editions incorrectly have “today,” which is also the reading of the manuscripts.] whose contents, after being plundered [Note: [Col. 1035D] “After they had been plundered.” Four Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, the Ultrajectine, and the Gronovian Collation read “after they had been abandoned.”], our people emptied [Note: [Col. 1035D] “By our people.” Absent from the fourth Lugdunensis Batavus.], and which in our times [Note: [Col. 1035D] “In our times.” Some old editions have “and in our times.”] they mention [Note: [Col. 1035D] “They mention.” So the manuscripts and better editions read; others have “they are mentioned.”], this is nevertheless true: it is more honorably believed that other books were sought, books that might rival the earlier labors of scholarship, [Col. 1036C] 422 than that there was any other library at that time containing four hundred thousand books which could be believed to have escaped [Col. 1037A] [Note: [Col. 1036C] “Than that there was any other library at that time, etc.” The word “any” is absent from three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts and the Gronovian Collation. I scarcely understand what Orosius’s words here mean. He seems to suggest either that there were writers who claimed that another library existed elsewhere in Alexandria at the same time and had not burned—which Orosius denies because of the number of books destroyed in the fire—or that, apart from that Alexandrian library of four hundred thousand books, there was no other public library. The latter is certainly false. The Pergamene library, which Antony gave to Cleopatra and which, according to Plutarch, *Antony*, p. 943, contained two hundred thousand volumes, collected by the kings of Pergamum in rivalry with the Ptolemies, was held in great honor both before and after this literary disaster. This was therefore a second Alexandrian library. The first stood in the part of the city called the Bruchium. Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*, Chapter 9, writes: “Ptolemy, surnamed Philadelphus, king of Alexandria, established an excellent library at Alexandria in that district of the city called the Bruchium; it is now seen abandoned.” The second library, which grew chiefly from the Pergamene collection, was in the Serapeum, a most celebrated temple of astonishing size and workmanship, which stood until the time of Theodosius the Elder. By that Christian emperor’s command it was demolished; at that time, too, the other Alexandrian, or Pergamene, library seems to have been plundered by Christians and transported elsewhere.]

Caesar later captured the island where the Pharos is located. Achillas came there with the Gabinian soldiers [Note: [Col. 1037C] “Came.” Some manuscripts and editions have “came afterward.”]. A great battle was fought. A large number of Caesar’s soldiers fell there, and all the killers of Pompey were also killed. Caesar, pressed by the force of the attacking enemy, climbed into a small boat; but when it soon sank under the weight of those following him, he swam two hundred paces to a ship, holding one hand above the water because he was carrying documents [Note: [Col. 1037C] “By swimming.” The Longobard, Meus, and third Florentine manuscripts have “he reached it by swimming.”]. Then, after being attacked in a naval engagement, he either sank or captured the royal fleet, with great good fortune [Note: [Col. 1037C] “With great good fortune.” All the manuscripts and old editions read “with ease.” Nevertheless, Paulus Diaconus preserves the common reading at the end of Book VI of his *Miscellaneous History*.].

423 **CHAPTER XVI. Caesar Restores the King to the Alexandrians, Subdues the Alexandrians, and Slaughters Many Citizens.**

[Col. 1037B]

At the Alexandrians’ request, he restored the king to them [Note: [Col. 1037C] “When the Alexandrians requested a king.” The Augustan edition has “when the Alexandrians requested a king, he restored him.”], advising him to strive to experience Roman friendship rather than Roman arms [Note: [Col. 1037C] “Strive.” The first Lugdunensis Batavus has “let him strive.”]. Yet as soon as he was free, he immediately made war, but was himself promptly destroyed together with his entire army [Note: [Col. 1037C] “As soon as he was free.” Some old editions read: “as soon as he was free, he immediately made war,” etc.]. Twenty thousand men are reported to have been killed in that war, twelve thousand to have surrendered together with seventy longships, and five hundred of the victors to have fallen [Note: [Col. 1037D] “Are said.” All the manuscripts prefer this word; the common editions have “are reported.”]. The young king himself, taken into a small boat as he attempted to flee, was drowned and killed when many men leapt into it [Note: [Col. 1037D] “His body.” The first Lugdunensis Batavus has “and his body.”]. His body was washed ashore and recognized by the evidence of his golden breastplate.

[With this sent ahead to Alexandria—the transmitted reference is materially uncertain—] Caesar compelled all the Alexandrians, through despair, to surrender, and gave the kingdom of Egypt to Cleopatra.

From there he passed through Syria and defeated Pharnaces in Pontus [Note: [Col. 1037D] “Pharnaces in Pontus.” Hirtius, *Alexandrian War*; Dio, Book XLII; and others discuss Pharnaces and the war fought against him. FABR.]. Afterward, when he came to Rome, he was created dictator and consul [Note: [Col. 1037D] “Dictator and consul.” Orosius, perhaps following Livy, clearly shows here that Caesar was made dictator and consul for the third time in the year 707 from the founding of the City, although not all annals support this dictatorship; Sigonius discusses the matter in his *Fasti*. Hirtius’s *African War* survives. All the other writers discuss the same matter; therefore, since the fact is clear, our own words are unnecessary. FABR.], crossed into Africa, and fought Juba and Scipio at Thapsus. There he killed a very large number of men. The camps of both were plundered, and sixty elephants were captured. Cato killed himself at Utica.

Juba [Note: [Col. 1037D] The first and third Lugdunensis Batavus, together with the Gronovian Collation, have “King Juba.”] offered his throat to the executioner [Note: [Col. 1038C] “After giving a payment.” Rubenius’s emendation in *Electa* I.10, “to Petreius,” is excellent. I have no doubt that Orosius wrote: “Juba offered his throat to the executioner Petreius.” For if Orosius had believed that Juba was killed by some unknown executioner after a payment had been made, he would have written below that Petreius stabbed himself with his own sword. But since he says that both died by the same means, he must necessarily be referring to the sword with which Juba first killed himself and then Petreius. That sword was sufficient both for the king and for himself. Florus, Book IV, Chapter 2.] after payment had been made. Petreius pierced himself with the same sword. Scipio, on the ship in which he had attempted to flee to Spain, but which, driven by the wind, had returned to Africa [Note: [Col. 1038C] “Forced by the wind.” The first and third Lugdunensis Batavus, the fourth together with the Gronovian Collation, have “driven by the wind, he had returned to Africa,” omitting *neglecto in*.], cut his own throat [Note: [Col. 1038C] “Himself.” The Augustan and Venetian editions have “himself” in the accusative; the Ultrajectine manuscript agrees with the present reading.]. Titus Torquatus was also killed on the same ship.

Caesar ordered the grandsons of Pompey the Great, his daughter Pompeia [Note: [Col. 1038C] “Pompeia.” The Augustan edition has “Pompey’s daughter.”], and, together with them, Faustus Sulla, Afranius, and the son of Petreius [Col. 1038B] to be killed.

Then, after entering Rome in four triumphs and arranging the restored state, [Note: [Col. 1038C] “Immediately into Spain.” Hirtius’s commentary on the Spanish War survives [Col. 1038D]. Plutarch and Dio, Book XLIII, also discuss it. FABR.] he immediately set out for Spain [Note: [Col. 1038D] The Augustan edition has “into Hispania,” singular.] against the Pompeii, the sons of Pompey. On the seventeenth day after he had left Rome [Note: [Col. 1038D] “On the seventeenth.” So three Florentine manuscripts read; others have “seventeenth.” For *quam*, the Augustan edition has *qua*.], he reached Saguntum, and at once fought many battles, with varying fortunes, against the two Pompeii, Labienus, and Attius Varus [Note: [Col. 1038D] “Attius Varus.” *Attius* is correctly read in the ancient books. Dio likewise calls him Πούπλιον Ἄττιον Οὐάρον. The ordinary books variously have *Actius* and *Accius*. In Plutarch’s *Cato*, he is corruptly called Οὐάρος Ἄππιος. FABR.].

The final battle was fought at the town of Munda [Note: [Col. 1038D] “The town of Munda.” Some manuscripts and editions have “the river Munda.”], where the fighting was carried on with such strength and the slaughter was so great that Caesar too, seeing his line being cut down and forced back while even his veterans did not blush to yield, contemplated forestalling by death the disgrace of defeat [Note: [Col. 1038D] “He contemplated.” Three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts, the Ultrajectine, and the Gronovian Collation have “he was contemplating.”]; when suddenly the army of the Pompeii turned and fled [Col. 1039A].

[Note: [Col. 1039B] “And indeed on that day.” Plutarch, in *Caesar*, writes of the battle of Munda:

“Caesar won this battle on the festival of Dionysus, on which day Pompey the Great is said to have first set out for the war; four years elapsed in the interval.”

That is:

“Caesar won this battle at the Liberalia, on the day when Pompey the Great is said to have first set out for this war, with four years having elapsed in the interval.” FABR.]

And indeed this war was fought on the very day [Note: [Col. 1039B] “This civil war was fought.” One or another of the old editions omits “war.”] on which Pompey the father had fled from Rome to conduct the war; and for four years this civil war thundered without interruption [Col. 1039B] 425 throughout the entire world [Note: [Col. 1039B] “Thundered throughout the entire world.” Unlearned scribes changed this to “held the entire world,” as happened in three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts and the Gronovian Collation. But the Augustan edition added to the true and common reading: “Alternatively, it held the whole city.”]. Titus Labienus and Attius Varus were killed in battle.
