Sextus Pompeius fled with one hundred horsemen [Note: [Col. 1039B] “With one hundred cavalry.” The first Lugdunensis Batavus has *centenario*; the other three, together with the Gronovian Collation, have “with a hundred cavalry.” Some old editions have “with one hundred horsemen.”]. His brother Gnaeus Pompeius, having quickly gathered a considerable band of Lusitanians, engaged Caesonius [Note: [Col. 1039C] “With Caesonius.” *Caesonius* is also found in the ancient texts, but perhaps *Cesennius* should be read instead. Dio calls this man Cesennius Lento; he is mentioned in the Twelfth Philippic. FABR.], was defeated, and was killed while fleeing [Note: [Col. 1039C] “And was defeated.” The Augustan edition has “there he was defeated.” In that edition too the reading is *Caesonius*, not *Cesennius*.].

The town of Munda, with immense slaughter of its inhabitants, was scarcely captured while Caesar was besieging it [Note: [Col. 1039C] “While besieging.” The third Lugdunensis Batavus has “while fighting”; the first has “while fighting and yielding.”].

**CHAPTER XVII. The Death of Caesar, and the Tumults and Wars Caused by It**

Caesar returned to Rome. [Note: [Col. 1039C] “Where, while.” The Augustan edition and the Ultrajectine manuscript have “there, while.” The speaker possesses, among several, a notable bronze coin of Julius Caesar, struck by the Corinthians in his honor as the restorer of their city. On this very finely made coin one can see the aged head of the hero Julius, worn by cares and emaciation. The names of the two duumvirs, Certus Aericius and Gaius Julius, are written on the reverse, which bears the image of the ancient Corinthian Bellerophon riding Pegasus. I have also added from our museum another bronze coin of Julius Caesar, likewise bearing his head and an image of Jupiter, though more badly damaged by time, with its letters worn away. [Col. 1040B] ] While he was gently restoring the state [Col. 1039B] contrary to the examples of his ancestors, with Brutus and Cassius as the instigators and a large part of the Senate also involved, he was stabbed to death in the senate-house [Note: [Col. 1040B] “In the senate-house.” Suetonius and all the other writers relate how Caesar was stabbed with twenty-three wounds on the Ides of March in the Curia of Pompey. FABR.] with twenty-three wounds [Col. 1040A] [Note: [Col. 1040B] “With twenty-three.” Three Lugdunensis Batavus manuscripts together with the Gronovian Collation have “twenty-four.”].

More than sixty accomplices are said to have been involved in the conspiracy [Note: [Col. 1040C] “More than sixty accomplices.” Suetonius: “A conspiracy was formed against him by more than sixty,” some of whom Cicero names in *Philippic* II and more of whom Appian names in Book II. FABR.]. The two Brutuses, Gaius Cassius, and the other associates withdrew to the Capitol with drawn daggers [Note: [Col. 1040C] “Withdrew.” Some manuscripts and editions have “retreated.”].

For a long time they deliberated whether the Capitol, together with the perpetrators of the murder, ought to be burned. The people, driven by grief [Note: [Col. 1040C] “Driven.” The Augustan edition has “stimulated.”], seized his body and burned it in the forum with fragments of platforms and benches.

Rome measured the extent of its empire by its own disasters, and, turned upon itself [Note: [Col. 1040C] “Turned.” The first and third Lugdunensis Batavus, together with the Gronovian Collation, have “having been turned.” Lucan I, 3:

“And the powerful people turned  
against their own entrails by their victorious right hand.”

The same author, ibid., verse 7:

“What madness, citizens, what such license of the sword,  
to offer Latian blood to hated nations!”

And ibid., verse 38:

“The dreadful fields of Pharsalus” [Col. 1040D] …

May [he] fill [it], and may the Punic shades be sated with blood.” Having turned the slaughter back, he avenged each individual nation there, in the very place where he had conquered it. In Asia, Europe, and Africa—not merely in the three parts of the world, but in all the corners of the three parts—he produced his gladiators. [Note: “His gladiators.” Captives, especially those who belonged to the same nation, were often compelled to fight one another in the arena; the same thing happened more frequently at the funerals of great men. Thus, at what was virtually the funeral of conquered nations, Romans fought one another in civil wars and in this way offered a kind of consolation to lands conquered by them.] And, after his enemies had been put to death, he imposed upon the wretched a spectacle of vengeance.

Yet it was not enough that the causes themselves, together with their authors, had also been destroyed: recurring seeds germinate in the same soil, producing with great toil a continuous harvest of ever-growing evils. [Note: “Germinate.” Some editions read “germinated”; the Augustan edition, “he sowed.”] [Note: “Great.” The first Florentine edition reads “evils.”] Caesar, the victor in the civil war, is killed by citizens, and the ranks of the conspirators are drawn into the slaughter of a single man. For it was certain that, because Caesar had been unjustly killed, he could have many avengers. [Note: “Because Caesar.” I think one should read, as it stands in the first edition, “that.” In the manuscripts of Orosius the words *quod*, *quia*, and *cur* are commonly confused. In some manuscripts *enim* is absent; in several, *possit* is written instead of *posset*.] And a great part of the nobility is bound together in one chain of crime, lest so great a source of evils should be supplied by the magnitude of war but restrained by the brevity of vengeance. [Note: “And a very large part.” The first Florentine edition does not recognize the conjunction *-que*.]

They say that Medea once sowed the teeth of a slain serpent, from which, like a crop appropriate to the seed, armed men emerged from the earth and soon struck one another down in battle. [Note: “That Medea.” The story occurs in Apollonius’s *Argonautica*, Book III, and Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, Book VII. FABRICIUS.] [Note: “The teeth once.” This is the reading of the better manuscripts; others have “certain teeth.”] [Note: “A crop appropriate to the seed.” This is the manuscript reading; some editions have “crops appropriate to the seed.”] Poets indeed invented these tales, But our Rome, after Caesar was killed, how many armed hosts did she bring forth from his ashes? [Note: “But this Rome of ours.” Two Leiden manuscripts, with the Groningen Collection, read “but our Rome.”] How many wars did she raise as a testimony to this wretched fertility—not things to be read to children, but spectacles to be watched by the crowds? [Note: “To be read to children.” That is, in school exercises. Juvenal, *Satire* X, line 167: “So that you may please boys and become a declamation.”] [Note: “To be watched by the crowds.” Some of them did so not without pleasure, as used to happen at gladiatorial spectacles, with which he compared the wretched Romans above.]

And yet the beginning of all these evils is pride. From it civil wars burst into flame; from it they sprouted again. [Note: “Burst into flame.” Some older editions read “arose.”] [Note: “Sprouted.” Two Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, read “of the people.”] [Note: “Pursue.” Some older editions read “persecute.” The same editions shortly afterward read “is enacted and punished,” omitting *and*, which preceded it.] Therefore the slaughter of those who unjustly pursue it is not unjust, if the rivalry of ambition is both enacted and punished through them and in them, until those who refused partnership learn to endure domination. When the whole power of government had been reduced to one man, all human beings entered upon a wholly different manner of life, so that everyone strove humbly to please and not arrogantly to give offense.

But such a salutary lesson in humility required a teacher. Accordingly, when affairs had been suitably arranged, the Lord Christ was born in the time of Caesar Augustus: [Note: “Who, although, etc.” From Paul’s Epistle to the Philippians, chapter II, verse 6.] although he existed in the form of God, he humbly assumed the form of a servant, so that the teaching of humility might at last become more effective, when throughout the whole world the punishment of pride had already become an example to everyone.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Caesar Octavian Augustus and the deeds accomplished by him

In the year 710 from the founding of the City, after Julius Caesar had been killed, Octavianus—who, by the will of his maternal uncle Julius Caesar, had assumed his inheritance and name, and who was afterward called Augustus when he gained control of affairs—had scarcely arrived at Rome as a very young man when he devoted his character to civil wars. [Note: “Octavianus.” The manuscripts are correct. For Gaius Octavius, adopted by the will of Julius Caesar, was called, according to Roman usage, Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus; see Dio, Book XLVII. FABRICIUS.] [Note: “The maternal uncle Caesar.” Orosius also calls Julius Caesar Octavianus’s maternal uncle below, chapter 20, and Suetonius, in *Augustus*, says: “Considering nothing more fitting than to avenge the death of his uncle,” although Caesar had in fact been his great-uncle. I do not know whether Orosius thought that Octavianus had been born from Caesar’s sister; this error was refuted by Joannes Pierius, Carolus Sigonius, and finally Wilhelm Xylander, who displayed remarkable evidence of his talent in translating and emending Dio’s history. FABRICIUS.] [Note: “Devoted.” I have made this out of *novit* and *vovit*. Thus in Book VII, where it reads “vowing by a secret pact,” restore “devoting.” Perhaps nothing should rashly be changed if one considers the various meaning of *voveo*. LAUT.—The verb *fovit* destroys the elegance of the passage; *novit*, which Fabricius adopted against all the older editions that preceded him, is worthless, as is *movit*, which I found in three Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen Collection. *Vovit* must unquestionably be restored, and all the remaining manuscripts and editions recognize it. Octavianus had vowed, or devoted, himself to civil wars, being still a young man when he began the five wars that he waged. The expression is like that in Lucan III, 310: “Receive hands devoted to foreign wars.”]

For a brief explanation of the accumulation of evils: he waged five civil wars—at Mutina, Philippi, Perusia, Sicily, and Actium. [Note: “He waged five civil wars.” A remarkable memorial of Caesar Octavian Augustus’s wars and victories is preserved on a most distinguished silver coin in my possession. On its obverse, without any inscription, is recognizable the head of Caesar Octavianus, adorned with the spoils of a lion in the manner of Hercules—as though the Roman Senate, by whose order the coin was struck and marked *S. C.*, acknowledged that this Hercules Alexicacus had subdued the monsters tearing apart the Roman Empire, especially Antony and Sextus Pompey. The reverse of the coin is equally notable and completes the subject through the splendor of its design, without any inscription. There one sees a globe representing the world, in the center of the field, encircled by four wreaths, together with an acrostolium and an ear of grain. I can offer two interpretations of this emblem. The four wreaths may represent Caesar’s four victories, which Orosius lists here, with the fifth victory indicated by the twofold symbol of the acrostolium and the ear of grain—that is, symbols of Sicily and the Sicilian victory, or the victory over Sextus Pompey, for he was powerful in fleets and in an abundance of grain. The other interpretation is this: we see four wreaths, but they are depicted so that the one placed above the globe surpasses the other three, which are equal in size. Thus the former signifies Caesar’s victories in general and the subjugation of the world; the three similar wreaths signify the triple triumph mentioned in chapter 20 and, specifically, the victories won in Europe, Asia, and Africa, the three parts of the world. The acrostolium signifies power at sea, while the ear of grain signifies abundance, the fertility of all things, and especially concern for grain. I also preserve another bronze coin, a witness to the Actian victory, struck at Philippi, a city of Macedonia at the foot of Mount Pangaeus. Caesar had made it a colony, and Augustus settled new colonists there. On one side are the standards of the praetorian cohorts, with their name inscribed; on the other is seen a representation of a naval Victory. The inscription *VICTORIA AVGUSTI* shows that the coin was struck after Octavianus Augustus had assumed the name Augustus.]

Of these, he concluded two—that is, the first and the last—against Marcus Antonius; the second against Brutus and Cassius; the third against Lucius Antonius; and the fourth against Sextus Pompeius, the son of Gnaeus Pompeius.

Antony, declared an enemy by the Senate, had shut up Decimus Brutus under siege at Mutina. [Note: “Antony an enemy.” Young people can learn this history most conveniently from Cicero’s letters and *Philippics*. Plutarch, Appian, Dio, and Paterculus should also be read. FABRICIUS.] The consuls Hirtius and Pansa, together with Caesar, were sent to liberate Brutus and defeat Antony. [Note: “Pansa, coming first.” Concerning the battle of Mutina, there is a letter from Galba to Cicero in Book X of the *Letters to Friends*. FABRICIUS.] Pansa, arriving first and falling into an ambush, was severely wounded by a javelin amid the losses of his men and died several days later from that same wound. Hirtius, bringing aid to his colleague, destroyed Antony’s considerable forces in a vast slaughter. [Note: “In a vast slaughter.” Elsewhere, but only there, “in one slaughter”; shortly afterward the first Leiden edition has *clades* instead of *strages*.] Caesar, for his part, guarded the camp.

In the second battle against Antony, great slaughter was inflicted on both sides. For it was then that the consul Hirtius was killed; Antony, defeated, fled, and Caesar gained the victory. [Note: “Antony, defeated, fled.” I have restored this from the consensus of the manuscripts, supported by the Augustan edition. The other common editions read “Antony was defeated.”] Decimus Brutus, having confessed his involvement in the conspiracy that killed Julius Caesar, poured forth prayers of repentance. [Note: “Poured forth.” Three Florentine manuscripts read “gave.”] Dolabella killed Trebonius, one of Caesar’s assassins, at Smyrna. [Note: “Dolabella Trebonius.” This is related by Dio in Book XLVII and Appian in Book III.] The Senate declared Dolabella an enemy. Both armies of the slain consuls obeyed Caesar.

Afterward Decimus Brutus was captured and killed in Gaul by the Sequani. [Note: “Afterward Decimus Brutus in Gaul.” Decimus Brutus was killed not by the Sequani but by Capenus the Sequanian, as Livy says in Book CXX, or in Capenus’s house by men sent by Antony, as Velleius writes. FABRICIUS.] Basillus, likewise one of the assassins, was killed by the hands of his own slaves. [Note: “Basillus.” At the end of Appian, Book III, it reads: “At the same time Minucius Basillus, himself also an assassin of Caesar, was killed by his servants.” Thus in the old manuscript the surname of the Minucian family is rightly written *Basillus*. Nor do I approve of Hieronymus Ferrarius’s changing *Basillus* to *Basilius* in the second Philippic, on the authority of a single book contrary to the evidence of the others. Indeed, I have no doubt that in Book III of *On Duties* and in Caesar’s Book V of the *Gallic War* one should read “Lucius Minucius Basillus.” Plutarch too has *Leukion Basillon* [Λεύκιον Βάσιλλον] in his *Sulla*, and surnames ordinarily end not in *-ius* but in *-us*. FABRICIUS.—The Leiden first edition has *Basillus*, but the first Florentine edition reads *Basilus*, as in Lucan IV, 416: “And they saw Basilus leading.” He belonged to the Minucian family and was called Lucius Minucius Basilus or Basillus, according to Fabricius and also Isaac Casaubon in his note on Suetonius, *Julius* chapter 80. Perhaps he was the same man who had previously supported Caesar against Pompey and whose defeat, together with his legion, by the Pompeians Orosius mentioned above in chapter 15.]

At the urging of Lepidus, Caesar received Antony back into favor; and as a pledge of the restored alliance, he took Antony’s daughter in marriage. Then, when they had approached the City and a rumor had arisen that a proscription was forthcoming, Gaius Thoranius, a former praetor who feared no such thing, was killed in his own house by a military attack, and many others were slaughtered. [Note: “Gaius Thoranius.” Concerning him, see Appian Book IV, Suetonius in *Augustus*, and, I think, Valerius Book IX, chapter 11. FABRICIUS.]

Therefore, so that unrestrained slaughter might not proceed more widely and more violently, the names of 132 senators were posted on a tablet, first under Lepidus’s authority and name, then under Antony’s, and third under Caesar’s. There Antony proscribed Tullius Cicero, his personal enemy, and Lucius Caesar, his maternal uncle; and, as an addition that aggravated the crime, he proscribed him while his mother was still alive. There Lepidus cast his own brother Lucius Paulus into the same group of the proscribed. [Note: “Into the same group of the proscribed.” Some older editions read “in the same number of the proscribed.”] Later, thirty Roman knights were added to the number of the proscribed. Many and varied killings continued for a long time; the houses of the proscribed were stripped of everything and demolished.

But Dolabella waged many wars against Cassius in Syria, and, after being defeated by him, killed himself. [Note: “He killed himself.” All the manuscript books have either this form or “he himself killed himself”; the Vulgate editions, omitting *ipse*, read “he killed himself.”] Brutus and Cassius, having assembled large armies, met at Athens and ravaged the whole of Greece. Cassius attacked the Rhodians by land and sea and forced them to surrender, leaving them nothing except their lives.

Caesar and Antony therefore pursued these same men into Macedonia with extensive preparations for war and drove them to death. Yet it is perfectly clear that this battle was brought to an end not by the valor of Antony’s party but by Caesar’s good fortune. For Caesar was ill at the time and had decided to remain in the camp in order to rest. But at the urging and entreaties of his physician, who said that he had been warned in a dream to lead Caesar out of the camp that day for the sake of his safety, he reluctantly went out among the troops onto the field. [Note: “Reluctantly.” This is the reading of the majority of the better manuscripts and editions. Others read “ill”; Suetonius, *Augustus* 91: “Although he had resolved not to leave his tent because of his health.”] [Note: “At the urging and entreaties of his physician.” Dio relates this dream and says, on Plutarch’s authority, that the physician was his friend. FABRICIUS.] Soon his camp was captured by the enemy; but the Caesarian soldiers in turn captured Cassius’s camp. Thus, driven to despair, Brutus and Cassius brought about their premature deaths before the war had ended: when they invited their assassins, Cassius offered his head and Brutus his side.

At Rome, however, Fulvia, Antony’s wife and Caesar’s mother-in-law, exercised domination like a woman. [Note: “To be counted.” All the manuscripts I examined read this; Fabricius and the other editors read “to be named.”] In this transformation of consular and royal magnificence, it is uncertain whether she should be counted as the final manifestation of declining power or the first of power beginning; certainly she was insolent even toward those through whom she was being enabled to become insolent. For she attacked Caesar, after he had returned to Brundisium, with insults, factions, and ambushes. [Note: “Attacked.” The same manuscripts read *petivit*, “sought.”] Repelled by him, she withdrew to join Antony in Greece.

Sextus Pompeius, after discovering that he had been included among the proscribed, turned to brigandage [Note: “Sextus Pompeius.” On Sextus Pompeius and his deeds and campaigns, see Livy, Books CXXVII and following; Appian, Book V; Dio, Books XLVIII and XLIX; Florus, Book IV, chapter 8. FABRICIUS.] and laid waste the entire coast of Italy with slaughter and plunder. Having seized Sicily and obstructed the grain supplies, he afflicted Rome with famine. Soon the triumvirs—Lepidus, Caesar, and Antony, or, rather, the tyrants—made peace with him. But when Pompeius immediately began to receive fugitives in violation of the agreement, he was treated as an enemy.

Menas, Pompeius’s freedman, defected to Caesar with a fleet of sixty ships, and by Caesar’s order was himself placed in command of that fleet. He immediately waged a naval battle with Statilius Taurus against Menecrates, Pompeius’s commander. [Note: “With Statilius Taurus.” Dio, Book XLVIII, says that Menas waged war against Menecrates not with Taurus but with Calvisius Sabinus. FABRICIUS.]

Then Caesar himself concluded a most bloody naval war against those same Pompeians; but immediately afterward he lost almost his entire victorious fleet in a shipwreck at Scyllaceum. [Note: “At Scyllaceum.” Dio has *Skyllaion* [Σκύλλαιον]; Appian, *Skyllakion* [Σκυλλάκιον]. Virgil, in Book III of the *Aeneid*, calls it “shipwreck-bearing Scylaceum”; Pierius and Erythraeus discuss the origin of this name. FABRICIUS.]

Ventidius defeated the Persians and Parthians when they invaded Syria in three great battles, and killed their king Pacorus in battle, on the very day on which Crassus had been killed by the Parthians. Antony, after scarcely capturing one fortress, made peace with Antiochus, so that he might appear to have completed so great an undertaking. He placed Ventidius in command of Syria and ordered him to make war upon Antigonus, who at that time had defeated the Jews, captured Jerusalem, and stripped the Temple. [Note: “Had stripped.” All the manuscripts and Vulgate editions read “had given,” but in the first Leiden manuscript it is written above the line that “had stripped” should be read; no emendation is more certain. Antigonus had waged war against Herod and his brothers for the kingdom, was captured by Ventidius, and was beheaded by Antony. Antony afterward gave the kingdom to Herod. It is remarkable that Fabricius should have invoked Josephus on his side and noted nothing concerning the absurd reading “and had given the kingdom to Herod,” since the subject is plainly Antigonus, who expelled Herod and his followers from the kingdom and power, not Antony, who made Herod king but did so only after defeating and capturing Antigonus.] He had deprived Herod of the kingdom; Antigonus, having immediately been defeated, was received in surrender.

Menas the freedman returned to Pompeius with six ships. Pompeius received him graciously, and Menas set Caesar’s fleet on fire, although Caesar had recently lost another fleet in a second shipwreck. Later, when Menas was surrounded by Agrippa in a naval battle, he went over to Caesar with six triremes. But Caesar, since this was Menas’s third defection, left him inactive, granting him only his life. [Note: “Left him inactive.” Virgil, *Aeneid* X, 699: “He lets Palmus roll helpless, with his knee severed.”]

Then Agrippa fought a naval battle between Mylas and Lipara against Demochares and Pompeius and won. [Note: “Against Demochares.” Other copies corruptly have *Democham*; Appian and Dio name him *Demochares* [Δημοχάρης]. Suetonius also correctly has *Demochares*. FABRICIUS.] There he either sank or captured thirty ships, with the rest torn apart. Pompeius fled to Messana.

Meanwhile Caesar had crossed over to Tauromenium, and Pompeius struck him with a sudden attack. [Note: “Had crossed over.” Some manuscripts read “had passed over.”] As a result, after many of his ships had been sunk and a great number of his soldiers had been lost, Caesar fled to Italy. Without any intervening delay, he returned to Sicily, where he encountered Lepidus arriving from Africa and claiming the highest authority for himself through terror, threats, and arrogance. [Note: “Without any intervening delay.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, read “without any intervening postponement.” The Augustan edition has “without any intervening delay in submission.”]

A few days later, Agrippa, by Caesar’s order, engaged Pompeius in a most violent naval battle from the shore, while Caesar watched with his line drawn up, and defeated him. [Note: “Most violent.” This is the reading of the manuscripts and the better editions, as well as the Augustan edition; others have “most violently.”] For he either sank or captured 163 ships. Pompeius escaped with difficulty in only seventeen ships.

Lepidus, swollen with the insolence of commanding twenty legions, had plundered Messana [Note: “Lepidus, with the great insolence of fifteen legions.” Dio, Book XLIX, Appian, Book V, and Velleius, Book I, give a full account of Lepidus’s disagreement with Octavian and how he was forced to abdicate. FABRICIUS.] after allowing it to his soldiers. When Caesar himself came to him, Lepidus twice rejected him and instead ordered that he be attacked with weapons; Caesar avoided the missiles by gathering his cloak around his left arm and using it to ward them off. Soon, mounting a horse, he returned to his own men. Then, advancing with an army drawn up against Lepidus, he compelled a great number of Lepidus’s legions to cross over to his side, with only a few men being killed.

At last Lepidus understood where his vanity was leading him. He laid aside his military cloak, assumed a dark garment, and, becoming a suppliant to Caesar, obtained his life and property. [Note: “A dark garment.” Some manuscripts erroneously read “a pure garment.” Dio says: “Thus Lepidus too was compelled, voluntarily to become his suppliant in a gray garment.” That is: “In this way Lepidus too was compelled, after putting on a gray garment, voluntarily to become Caesar’s suppliant.” Velleius likewise writes: “Lepidus, covered with a dark cloak, fell at Caesar’s knees.” FABRICIUS.] He was, however, permanently corrected by exile. [Note: “Corrected by exile.” The Venetian edition reads “punished,” and rightly so; nevertheless, the present reading is not foreign to Orosius. Martial, concerning his own book, IV, 10, 7: “Many erasures cannot, Faustinus, correct my jokes; one erasure can.” LAUT.—“Sent into exile,” which appears in the Augustan edition, is closer to the manuscript reading. I retain “corrected,” because this was the only remedy for Lepidus, a turbulent man, and he could not have been corrected in any other way.]

Taurus, Caesar’s commander, subdued and brought into allegiance almost the whole of Sicily, which had been ravaged and terrified by the sword. [Note: “Taurus, etc., almost the whole of Sicily.” Consider whether “Africa” should instead be read. For by Taurus’s valor Octavianus obtained both Africas, according to Dio. The Capitol—inscriptions indicate that he celebrated a triumph from Africa: “T. STATILIUS T. F. TAURUS, PROCONSUL, FROM AFRICA, in the year 719, on the day before the Kalends of July.” FABRICIUS.] At that time forty-four legions were under the single command of Caesar. The soldiers, fiercer because of their numbers, caused disturbances [Note: “Fiercer.” The Augustan edition reads “fierce.”] in order to receive lands. But Caesar, great in spirit, discharged twenty thousand soldiers; he restored thirty thousand slaves to their masters; and he crucified six thousand whose masters could not be found. [Note: “Restored.” Some Leiden manuscripts read “restored” in the singular, and shortly afterward count seven thousand instead of six thousand slaves.]

He entered the City in an ovation, and the Senate decreed that he should possess tribunician power in perpetuity. [Note: “He entered the City in an ovation.” Hence on the Capitoline triumphal inscriptions: “Imperator Caesar, son of the deified one, grandson of Gaius; for the second time triumvir for restoring the Republic; for the second time entering in an ovation from Sicily, in the year 718, on the Ides of November.” FABRICIUS.] In those days, across the Tiber, from a tavern, a fountain of oil burst forth from the earth and flowed all day in a very abundant stream. [Note: “From a shop selling provisions.” Two Leiden manuscripts read: “from the provision shop a fountain of oil burst from the earth.”]

## CHAPTER XIX. On the deeds accomplished by Antony and the Battle of Actium

[Column 1048A]

[Note: [Col. 1048C] “Antonius vero postquam.” On Antony’s disastrous war with the Parthians, besides Plutarch, see Velleius. FABR.]

But after Antony had crossed the Araxes, surrounded on every side by every kind of misfortune, he at last returned to Antioch with only a few men. For, although he always escaped defeated from all the many battles that he attempted with a multitude of cavalry and archers,

[Note: [Col. 1048C] “Vix tandem.” Some editions omit the first word.]

[Note: [Col. 1048C] “Sagittarum.” In all the manuscripts, as also in the Augustan edition, *sagittarum* is written, not *sagittariorum*, as in the common editions. Evidently the Parthians were accustomed to shoot arrows from horseback, and so those horsemen themselves were archers that there can be no doubt about the more correct reading.]

and, moreover, being hindered by the uncertain and unfamiliar places of the region,

[Note: [Col. 1048C] “Regionis.” In the Augustan edition this is removed as superfluous.]

he was compelled by the severest hunger to eat loathsome foods, and very many of the soldiers surrendered themselves to the enemy.

[Note: [Col. 1048C] “Victus semper effugeret.” In the Augustan edition it reads *victus effugeret*—*semper* having been deleted. Another edition has *effugerit*. The latter reading occurs in three Florentine manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 1048C] “Plurimique.” In almost all the manuscripts, as also in the Augustan edition, the conjunction is lacking.]

From there he crossed into Greece and ordered Pompey, who, after being defeated by Caesar, was rebuilding his army and renewing the war, to come to him with a few men. Pompey, while fleeing, was repeatedly defeated by the Antonian commanders Titius and Furnius in battles on land and sea,

[Note: [Col. 1048C] “A Titio et Furnio.” This is correctly given in the ancient books. The common text corruptly reads *Tito et Formo*. Appian and Dio likewise say that Sextus Pompey was killed by Marcus Titius and Furnius. Velleius mentions Titius. FABR.]

[Note: [Col. 1048D] “Bello.” The Augustan edition has *praelio*, since these words are often interchanged.]

and was captured; shortly afterward he was killed.

Caesar subdued and conquered Illyricum, Pannonia, and part of Italy in war. Antony captured Artabanes, king of Armenia, by treachery and deceit; binding him with a silver chain, he compelled him to disclose the royal treasures. After storming the town in which Artabanes had said that the treasures were stored, Antony carried away a large quantity of gold and silver.

[Note: [Col. 1048D] “Antonius Artabanem.” Read this history in Dio, book XLIX, and in the Livian Epitome, book CXXII. FABR.]

Elated by this wealth, he ordered war to be declared against Caesar, commanded that a divorce be announced to Octavia, Caesar’s sister and his own wife, and ordered Cleopatra to come to him from Alexandria.

[Note: [Col. 1048D] “Ipse Actium.” On the Actian War, in which Antony and Cleopatra were defeated by Caesar, see Plutarch’s *Antony*, Dio book L, Florus book IV chapter 11, Eutropius book VII, Velleius, and others. FABR. The Augustan edition has *ipse vero Actium*.]

He himself set out for Actium, where he had assembled his fleet. When he found that nearly a third of the rowers had been carried off by hunger,

[Note: [Col. 1048D] “Assumptam.” The Augustan edition has *ablatam*, “taken away.”]

he was unmoved: “Let the oars,” he said, “only be safe; for there will be no lack of rowers,”

[Note: [Col. 1048D] “Quoad.” The Augustan edition and the second Florentine manuscript have *quoadusque*, “as long as.” In three Leiden-Batavian manuscripts, as also in the Utrecht manuscript, *ad* is omitted.]

“as long as Greece has men.”

Caesar set out from Brundisium for Epirus with two hundred and thirty ships equipped with beaks. Agrippa, sent ahead by Caesar, captured many cargo ships laden with grain and arms that were coming from Egypt, Syria, and Asia to support Antony.

[Note: [Col. 1049B] “Antonio.” Four Leiden-Batavian manuscripts and the Groningen Collection have *Antonii*, “of Antony.”]

After traversing the Gulf of the Peloponnese, he stormed the city of Methone, fortified by a very strong Antonian garrison. From there he captured Corcyra; pursuing the fugitives in a naval battle, he routed them. After carrying out many bloody operations, he came to Caesar.

Antony, moved by the exhaustion and hunger of his soldiers, decided to hasten the war. He suddenly drew up his forces, advanced to Caesar’s camp, and was defeated. On the third day after the battle Antony transferred his camp to Actium, prepared to engage in a naval battle.

[Note: [Col. 1049B] “Decernere.” Three Leiden-Batavian manuscripts together with the Groningen Collection have *dimicare*, “to fight.”]

There were two hundred and thirty beaked ships belonging to Caesar, and thirty without beaks—triremes equal in speed to the Liburnian vessels—and eight legions stationed aboard the fleet, in addition to five praetorian cohorts. Antony’s fleet consisted of one hundred and seventy ships,

[Note: [Col. 1049C] “Centum et septuaginta navium.” The Augustan edition has “one hundred and eighty ships.” A little later that same edition reads *in horam* instead of *ad horam*.]

and, though inferior in number by as much, it surpassed the other in size. For the ships rose ten feet above the sea. This was a famous and great war at Actium. From the fifth hour until the seventh, with the outcome uncertain, extremely heavy slaughter was inflicted on both sides; the remainder of the day, together with the following night, turned toward Caesar’s victory.

Queen Cleopatra was the first to flee with sixty of her fastest ships.

[Note: [Col. 1049C] “Antonius quoque.” Just as the Phoenicians were pre-eminent in naval power through the fleets of Marcus Antony and Cleopatra, so, in honor of both of them and as a favorable omen, they struck coins bearing a type of naval victory. One such bronze coin was minted by the Tripolitans of Phoenicia. On its obverse it displays the jugate heads of the triumvir Marcus Antony and Queen Cleopatra; on the reverse Victory is seen standing on the prow of a ship, holding a wreath in her right hand. Around it is read ΤΡΙΠΟΛΙΤΑΝ ΕΤ . ΚΕ, “of the Tripolitans, year 25.” Tripolis, a city of Phoenicia, like the other cities of that region, used the Seleucid era on its bronze coins. Later, when Seleucus’s descendants were disputing the kingdom among themselves, a certain tyrant named Dionysius seized Tripolis and ruled it. Pompey the Great, entering Phoenicia, brought him under his power and struck him with the axe. Therefore the Tripolitans, in honor of Pompey, introduced a new era, counting their years from Pompey’s benefaction and from the reduction of Phoenicia by him to provincial status—an event that occurred in the year 691 from the founding of the City. From this it follows that this coin was struck in the year 716 from the founding of the City. Later, however, in order to honor Augustus, they rejected Pompey’s era and again used the former Seleucid era on their coins. This coin is preserved in the distinguished museum of the illustrious Lebret, prefect of the same province, at Aix-en-Provence. We have added another from our own museum, on which likewise appear the jugate heads of Marcus Antony and his wife. The woman, however, is shown by the names added beside the heads—M. ANTONIOC OKTABIA—not to be Cleopatra but Octavia, the sister of Caesar Octavianus. On my coins (I possess two), these names have been worn away by verdigris, but they are present on a similar coin belonging to Andrea Marmora, in his *History of Corcyra*, published in Italian, p. 156. The Corcyrans struck the coin under Philotas, as the inscription on the other side shows. Octavia’s head is extremely rare on ancient coins.]

Antony too, after removing the insignia of his flagship, followed his fleeing wife.

At daybreak Caesar completed the victory. It is reported that twelve thousand of the defeated fell; six thousand were wounded, of whom one thousand died while being treated.

[Note: [Col. 1050D] “Sex millia.” All the manuscripts consistently preserve this number, except that one Leiden-Batavian manuscript has four thousand. All the common editions have seven thousand, except the Augustan edition, which almost everywhere agrees with the better manuscripts.]

Antony and Cleopatra decided to send their children, together with part of the royal treasury, ahead to the Red Sea. They themselves, having stationed garrisons around the two horns of Egypt, Pelusium and Paraetonium,

[Note: [Col. 1050D] “Aegypti cornua.” The first word is absent from the Augustan edition.]

prepared a fleet and forces for renewing the war.

Caesar, having been hailed as commander for the sixth time, and himself as consul for the fourth time together with Marcus Licinius Crassus, came to Brundisium,

[Note: [Col. 1050D] “Sextum, etc.” Almost all the manuscripts prefer *sexto et quarto*, and write it thus almost everywhere.]

[Note: [Col. 1050D] “Ibique.” The Augustan edition has *ibi*, “there.” Three Florentine manuscripts likewise have *ibi*, with the conjunction *-que* deleted.]

and there, by distributing the legions, organized the garrisons of the world. From there he set out for Syria and soon approached Pelusium, where he was voluntarily received by the Antonian garrisons.

Meanwhile Cornelius Gallus, sent ahead by Caesar, received under his protection the four legions that Antony had established at Cyrene as a garrison. From there he took Paraetonium,

[Note: [Col. 1050D] “Primam.” The first Florentine manuscript has *primum*, “first.”]

the first city of Egypt on the Libyan side, and, after Antony’s defeat, captured it; immediately afterward he defeated Antony himself near Pharos.

[Note: [Col. 1050D] “Victo cepit Antonio.” The Augustan edition has *victam cepit, Antonium ipsum continuo*, “he captured it after it had been defeated, and immediately afterward Antony himself.”]

Antony undertook a cavalry battle against Caesar; he was miserably defeated in that engagement as well and fled.

On the Kalends of Sextilis, at first light, as Antony was going down to the harbor to equip the fleet, all the ships suddenly went over to Caesar. When he had thus been deprived of his sole remaining support, Antony retreated in panic with a few men into the palace.

Then, with Caesar approaching and the city in confusion, Antony stabbed himself with a sword. Still half alive, he was carried to Cleopatra in the monument into which she had shut herself, determined to die.

[Note: [Col. 1051B] “In quod.” The third Florentine manuscript, all the Leiden-Batavian manuscripts, and the Groningen Collection have *in quo*, “in which.”]

When Cleopatra realized that she was being preserved for Caesar’s triumph, she sought voluntary death. Believed to have been bitten by a serpent on the left arm,

[Note: [Col. 1051B] “In sinistro tacta brachio.” The Augustan edition deletes *in*. The third Leiden-Batavian manuscript and the Groningen Collection delete *tacta*.]

she was found lifeless, although Caesar vainly brought in the Psylli,

[Note: [Col. 1051B] “Revocare.” The second Leiden-Batavian manuscript has *evocare*, “to draw out.”]

who customarily recalled and sucked out serpent poisons from human wounds by drawing them out with their mouths.

Caesar took possession of Alexandria, by far the wealthiest and greatest of all cities, as victor. Rome too was so greatly enriched by its resources that, because of the abundance of money, the prices of estates and other goods for sale were set at twice what they had been up to that time.

By Caesar’s order, the elder son of Antony was killed, as were P. Canidius,

[Note: [Col. 1051B] “P. Canidius.” The manuscript books correctly give this name; the common text has *Caninius*. See Plutarch and Velleius. FABR.]

who had always been extremely hostile to Caesar, though also disloyal to Antony,

[Note: [Col. 1051B] “Infestissimus quidem semper.” After *quidem* was deleted, the Augustan edition preferred *infestus*, “hostile.”]

and Cassius of Parma.

[Note: [Col. 1051B] “Cassius Parmensis.” Velleius also mentions him. In Appian, book V, he is Κάσσιος ὁ Παρμήσιος, “Cassius the Parmian.” Perhaps his little poem *Orpheus* survives. FABR.]

Cassius was the final victim of Caesar’s violated father,

[Note: [Col. 1051B] “Violati patris.” This reading was proposed in place of *violatae partis*, and who would not prefer it who understands that Cassius had been one of Caesar Julius’s conspirators? LAUT.—It is remarkable that others before Lautius did not notice this, especially since all the manuscripts give the reading, either in full or, with a line drawn through the first letter, writing *ptris*. The Augustan edition too clearly has *violati patris*, not *violatae partis* as in the others. I also encountered the true reading of this passage in Paul the Deacon’s *Historia Miscella*, book VII, p. 50 of the latest edition in the *Thesaurus Italiae* of Ludovico Antonio Muratori, vol. I.]

and Q. Ovinius, chiefly because, although a Roman senator, he had not blushed to preside over the queen’s wool-spinning and weaving in the most indecent manner.

Thereafter Caesar came with infantry forces to Syria, then withdrew into Asia for winter quarters,

[Note: [Col. 1051C] “Ad hyberna.” Several manuscripts have *in hiberna*, “into winter quarters.”]

and afterward traveled through Greece to Brundisium.

[Note: [Col. 1051C] “Pervectus est.” The manuscripts have this form; some editions have *provectus est*, as though they intended *profectus est*, “he set out.”]

## CHAPTER XX

On Caesar’s Triumph and the Name Augustus; on the Roman Monarchy and Our Epiphany; Then an Explanation of the Fountain of Oil

[Note: [Col. 1051C] “In the year 725 from the founding of the City.” Dio, book LI, also reckons it this way. Caesar’s colleague in his fifth consulship was Sextus Appuleius, not Lucius, as all the others call him. FABR.]

In the year 725 from the founding of the City, when Caesar Augustus was consul for the fifth time and L. Apuleius was consul, Caesar, returning victorious from the East, entered the city on the eighth day before the Ides of January in a triple triumph.

[Note: [Col. 1052B] “The eighth day before the Ides of January.” If we follow Macrobius, *Saturnalia* book I, Caesar entered the City in a triple triumph in the month of Sextilis, not January. FABR.]

Then, for the first time, he himself closed the gates of Janus, after all the civil wars had been brought to rest and ended.

[Note: [Col. 1052B] “On this day Augustus was first hailed.” Caesar Octavianus and L. or Sextus Apuleius were consuls in the year 725 from the founding of the City, when vows were discharged at Rome for Caesar’s return and he celebrated a triple triumph there. He did not receive the name Augustus in that year, but two years later, during his seventh consulship, which he held with Agrippa as consul for the second time. At that time he also received tribunician power for ten years. From then on his coins were marked with the number of his tribunician power and with the distinguished inscription “Augustus.” The name Augustus, however, is not always added to them, since the emperor can be recognized sufficiently from his portrait, as is clear from a large bronze coin bearing a bronze circle, as there are many of this kind. On it appears the beautiful head of Caesar Augustus without any inscription. On the other side is a type belonging to the period after he had assumed the name Augustus; for while Lepidus was alive he never endured taking away from him the office of chief pontiff, whose emblem, the *apex*, can be seen there. Lepidus died in the year 741 from the founding of the City. From many other coins it is known that P. Licinius Stolo was among the monetary triumvirs of the Roman Senate; but on none, as on this one, is the title of prefect of the City assigned to him. Since the monetary triumvirate was the first step toward honors, I do not wish to conceal that I regard this coin as suspect. It is now preserved in the Caesarean Museum at Rome; I obtained its type when it formerly belonged to the Carthusians.]

On this day Augustus was first hailed by that name. The title, previously inviolate

[Note: [Col. 1053C] “Inviolatum.” I do not know what this word means here, or how the name can be called “inviolate” before Augustus. In the second Florentine manuscript it reads *inolitum*, with certain letters that had previously stood there erased. Should one write *insolitum*, “unusual”? Or does *violare* here mean “to invade” a divine title, as in Florus’s final words of book IV concerning the name Augustus—that, while he was already worshiping the earth, he might be consecrated by the name and title itself?]

and, down to the present, unattempted by other masters, was assumed by the ruler of the whole world and declared the summit of imperial power. From that same day supreme authority and power began to belong to one man and remained there—what the Greeks call a monarchy.

Moreover, no believer, nor even anyone who contradicts the faith, is unaware that this is the very same day, namely the eighth day before the Ides of January, on which we observe Epiphany, that is, the appearance or manifestation of the Lord’s sacrament. The nature and place of the present discussion do not require us to speak more fully now about the sacrament of this most faithful observance, so that we may seem to have reserved something for those who inquire and not thrust it upon the negligent.

It was nevertheless fitting to recall this faithfully, so that Caesar’s empire might be shown to have been prepared in every respect by the grace of the coming Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1053D] “For when he first.” This is taken from Suetonius’s *Augustus*. Julius Obsequens reports the same event. FABR.]

For when, after the murder of his uncle Gaius Caesar, he was returning from Apollonia and entering the City, at about the third hour,

[Note: [Col. 1053D] “Suddenly, in a clear and pure calm.” The printed editions have “in a pure and calm sky.” This is inconsiderate, especially since in chapter 1 of the final book Orosius also speaks in this way: “accustomed to a calm sky of delights,” and the manuscripts likewise omit *absit*. Thus Virgil says:

> Alas, too confident in the calmness of the sky.

The verse to which this refers occurs in *Aeneid* V, 870. The common text there reads:

> O too confident in sky and sea made calm!

But since all the ancient editions, in agreement with all the manuscripts, read *liquido ac puro sereno*, Fabricius altered the reading far too rashly and boldly, replacing it with *puro serenoque die*, “on a pure and calm day.” This was all the more inconsiderate because in Suetonius, *Augustus* chapter 95, from which this passage was taken, the wording stands exactly as it does in Orosius’s manuscripts. Casaubon illustrated Suetonius’s account there from Velleius, Dio, and Zonaras.]

suddenly, in a clear and pure calm, a circle resembling a heavenly rainbow surrounded the disk of the sun,

[Note: [Col. 1054C] “As though it displayed him as the one and most powerful.” Some old editions have “as though it displayed him as the one and most eminent.”]

as though it showed that he alone was the one and most powerful, and the sole most brilliant being in the world, in whose time the one would come who alone had made both the sun itself and the whole world, and would rule them.

Second, when, after receiving the legions of Pompey and Lepidus in Sicily, he had restored thirty thousand slaves to their masters and distributed forty-four legions under his sole command for the protection of the world, and, entering the City in an ovation, had decided that all the debts owed to the Roman people should be remitted, with even the written records being destroyed,

[Note: [Col. 1054C] “Had decreed that the fountain.” The book of Maternus correctly reads this. The following words had intruded from elsewhere: “in his days”; since they immediately follow later as well, I have moved them back from here to the place from which they came. LAUT.—Nevertheless, they are found in all the manuscripts, except that most have *ipsis* instead of *ipsius*, and mine has *illis*. The words “in the days of Caesar” also seem to correspond to “in his days.”]

in his days a most abundant fountain of oil flowed all day from the public inn (*taberna meritoria*), as I have described above.

[Note: [Col. 1054D] “Fluxisset.” The Leiden-Batavian manuscripts have *fluxit*, “flowed.”]

What sign could be clearer than that, in the days of Caesar’s rule over the whole world,

[Note: [Col. 1054D] “Future.” This word is absent from the Longobard manuscript.]

the future birth of Christ was declared? For “Christ,” in the language of the people among whom he was born,

[Note: [Col. 1054D] “In which.” Some manuscripts have *ex qua*, “from which”; others, *ex qua et in qua*, “from which and in which.”]

means “anointed.”

Thus, at the time when perpetual tribunician power was decreed to Caesar, a fountain of oil flowed all day at Rome. Under Caesar’s principate and the Roman Empire, throughout the entire day—that is, throughout the whole period of the Roman imperial power—Christ and, from him, Christians, that is, “the anointed” and, from him, “the anointed ones,” would flow abundantly and without interruption from the public inn (*taberna meritoria*), that is, from the hospitable and generous Church; all the slaves who nevertheless came to know their Lord would be restored by Caesar; while the others who were found without a master

[Note: [Col. 1054D] “Without a master.” This has been restored from the manuscripts. It was wrongly read as *sine dominio*, “without dominion.”]

would be handed over to death and punishment; and the debts of sins would be remitted under Caesar, in that City in which oil had flowed spontaneously—these were exceedingly clear signs in heaven and portents on earth for those who did not heed the voices of the prophets.

Third, when he entered the City in triumph as consul for the fifth time, on the very day mentioned above,

[Note: [Col. 1054D] “When he also [closed] Janus.” Janus was mentioned as closed at the beginning of the first book. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 298, said: “The gates of war shall be closed.” FABR.]

when he himself also closed Janus for the first time after two hundred years and assumed that most illustrious name Augustus,

[Note: [Col. 1054D] “The name Augustus.” Censorinus writes that Caesar was called Augustus by the Senate and the other citizens on the motion of Munatius Plancus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventh consulship of Caesar and the consulship of M. Vipsanius Agrippa. FABR.]

what can be believed or recognized as more trustworthy and more true than this: that, with peace, the name, and the day converging upon so great a manifestation, this day had been predestined by the hidden order of events to prepare for his obedience? For on the day when he was shortly afterward to be manifested to the world, that man both displayed the sign of peace and assumed the name of power.

But what occurred at his fourth return, when, after the Cantabrian War had ended and all the peoples had been pacified, Caesar returned to the City in confirmation of the faith we have expressed, will be set forth more effectively in its proper order.

## CHAPTER XXI

How Caesar Entered Spain and Conquered the Cantabrians and Asturians; Whom Drusus Subdued in Germany, and Cossus in Africa; and Concerning the Deeds of Tiberius, Quintilius Varus, and Agrippa

[Note: [Col. 1055C] “In the year 726 from the founding of the City.” Compare Casaubon on Suetonius, *Augustus* chapter 20.]

In the year 726 from the founding of the City, when Caesar Augustus was consul for the sixth time and M. Agrippa for the second time,

[Note: [Col. 1055C] “Caesar six times, and M. Agrippa twice.” Cassiodorus also attests that Agrippa was consul for the second time in this year. Guilielmus Xylander is therefore correct in noting, at the beginning of Dio’s fifty-third book, where τὸ γ appears, that τὸ β should be written. On the Cantabrian War, see Dio and Florus, book IV, final chapter. The same authors should also be consulted concerning the other wars mentioned here. FABR.]

Caesar, understanding that two hundred years of activity in Spain had achieved little if he allowed the Cantabrians and Asturians, the two strongest peoples of Spain, to live under their own laws, opened the gates of Janus and personally set out for Spain with an army.

The Cantabrians and Asturians are part of the province of Gallaecia,

[Note: [Col. 1055D] “Province.” This word is absent from two Leiden-Batavian manuscripts.]

where the extended ridge of the Pyrenees descends not far from the farther Ocean, toward the north.

[Note: [Col. 1055D] “Toward the north.” The Augustan edition has *sub septemtrionem*, “beneath the north.”]

They were prepared not only to defend their own freedom but also dared to seize that of their neighbors, ravaging the Vaccaei, Turmodigi,

[Note: [Col. 1055D] “Turmodigos.” Four Leiden-Batavian manuscripts, mine, Perizonius’s manuscript, the Utrecht manuscript, the Groningen Collection, and two Florentine manuscripts have *Turmogos*. The third Florentine manuscript has *Turmogas*.]

and Autrigones with continual raids.

Accordingly, Caesar established a camp near Segisama,

[Note: [Col. 1055D] “Segisama.” Two Leiden-Batavian manuscripts have *Segessimam*.]

enclosing almost the whole of Cantabria with three columns. After his army had long been worn out in vain and repeatedly brought into danger, he finally ordered a fleet to be brought from the Gulf of Aquitania across the Ocean and troops to be disembarked against the unsuspecting enemy.

[Note: [Col. 1055D] “To bring up a fleet.” This is the reading of three Florentine manuscripts, as the other manuscripts also seem to intend when they write *amoveri*. The common editions have *admovĕre*.]

Then at last the Cantabrians met the Romans beneath the walls of Belgica in a great battle and were defeated.

[Note: [Col. 1055D] “Belgica.” Learned men, in their notes on Florus book IV, final chapter, have advised that *Vellicae* should be written. The manuscripts commonly have *Atticae*; mine has *Acite*.]

They fled to Mount Vinnius,

[Note: [Col. 1056C] “Vinnium.” Mine has *Vinium*; the fourth Leiden-Batavian manuscript has *Virnium*; some editions have *Vennium*.]

which was naturally very secure, where they were almost entirely consumed by the hunger of the siege.

[Note: [Col. 1056C] “By the hunger of the siege.” Better: “by siege and hunger.”]

Next the town of Aracillum,

[Note: [Col. 1056C] “Aracillum.” This is the form in Florus; the manuscripts here commonly have *Racilium*, *Rachilium*, or *Recilium*.]

which resisted with great force and for a long time, was finally captured and destroyed.

Moreover, Antistius and Firmius, the lieutenants, subdued the farther parts of Gallaecia, planted with mountains and forests and bounded by the Ocean, through great and arduous wars. They also surrounded Mount Medullium,

[Note: [Col. 1056D] “Medullium.” I found *Medulium* in three Leiden-Batavian manuscripts.]

which overlooked the river Minho and on which a large multitude of people had taken refuge, with a ditch fifteen thousand paces in circumference, and besieged it.

Thus, when this people, savage and fierce by nature,

[Note: [Col. 1056D] “Savage by nature.” The Augustan edition has *atrox natura*, “savage by nature.”]

realized that it was neither capable of enduring the siege nor equal to undertaking the war,

[Note: [Col. 1056D] “The siege.” The same edition has *obsidionis*, “of the siege.”]

they rushed to voluntary death out of fear of slavery. Almost all of them killed themselves in a contest of desperation by fire, sword, or poison.

The Asturians, however, having established their camp beside the river Astura, would have overwhelmed the Romans through great planning and force had they not been betrayed and forestalled. They attempted suddenly to crush the three legates, divided with their legions among three camps, by attacking them with three equally large columns, but their plan was exposed through the treachery of their own people.

Carisius later engaged and defeated them in battle, though not without considerable Roman losses. A portion of them, having escaped the battle, fled to Lancia. When the soldiers were preparing to attack the surrounded city with fire, the commander Carisius obtained from his own men a suspension of the burning

[Note: [Col. 1056D] “Obtained.” Some manuscripts and editions have *imperavit*, “ordered,” but this is wrong.]

and compelled the barbarians to surrender. For he was earnestly striving to leave the city intact and unharmed as a witness to his victory.

Caesar granted this honor to the Cantabrian victory: he ordered the gates of war to be shut even then.

[Note: [Col. 1056D] “Of war.” Some manuscripts have *Jani*, “of Janus.”]

Thus Janus was closed for the second time by Caesar, and for the fourth time since the founding of the City.

[Note: [Col. 1056D] “After this Claudius Drusus.” The war with the Raetians was waged when Drusus and Piso were consuls, in the year 738 from the founding of the City.]

After this Claudius Drusus, Caesar’s stepson, having received Gaul and Raetia as his provinces, subdued with arms the greatest and strongest peoples of Germany. For at that time, as though they were hastening toward an appointed day of peace, all the peoples were stirred up in waves to test war or decide a treaty: either they would accept terms of peace if defeated, or enjoy peaceful freedom if they prevailed.

The Norici, Illyrians, Pannonians, Dalmatians, Moesi, Thracians, Dacians, Sarmatians, and many very great German peoples were, under different commanders, either defeated, restrained, or shut out by the barrier of the greatest rivers, the Rhine and the Danube.

Drusus first subdued the Usipetes in Germany, then the Tencteri and Chatti. He slaughtered the Marcomanni almost to extermination. Afterward, in a single war, he defeated the strongest nations—the Cherusci, Suebi, and Sicambri—which possessed strength from nature and experience of strength from custom, though the war was also harsh for their own people.

Their courage and savagery can be judged from this: whenever their women were enclosed among their wagons by a surprise attack of the Romans, and their weapons had run out, they hurled their small children, battered against the ground, into the faces of the enemy—using them as weapons, so to speak—and by each killing of a child they became twice murderers of their own children.

[Note: [Col. 1056D] “Twice.” This word is absent from the first and third Leiden-Batavian manuscripts.]

At that same time in Africa Cossus, Caesar’s commander, restricted the Musolani and Gaetuli,

[Note: [Col. 1056D] “Musolani.” Three Leiden-Batavian manuscripts read *Usulanos*; the Utrecht manuscript and the Groningen Collection have *Musulanos*; the second Florentine manuscript has *Muselanos*.]

who were spreading more widely,

and compelled them through fear to keep away from the Roman frontiers.

[Note: [Col. 1057D] “Cossus, commander.” On him and his deeds, see Dio book LV. FABR.]

Meanwhile, envoys of the Indians and Scythians, having crossed the whole world, finally found Caesar at Tarraco, a city of Hither Spain,

[Note: [Col. 1057D] “The envoys of the Indians.” Compare Casaubon’s notes on Suetonius, *Augustus* chapter 21.]

beyond which they could no longer seek him,

[Note: [Col. 1057D] “Beyond which.” Three Leiden-Batavian manuscripts and the Groningen Collection have *ultra quo*, “beyond which.”]

and transferred to Caesar the glory of Alexander the Great. Just as a delegation of Spaniards and Gauls had approached Alexander in the middle of the East at Babylon in contemplation of peace, so the Eastern Indian and Northern Scythian, humbly bearing a gift from his people, appealed to Caesar in the farthest West, in Spain.

After the Cantabrian War had lasted five years [the following printed word is corrupt or uncertain],

[Note: [Col. 1057D] “With a certain breathing-space from weariness.” The first and third Leiden-Batavian manuscripts have *cum quadam lassitudine*, “with a certain weariness.”]

and with all Spain reclining and restored to everlasting peace, together with a certain breathing-space from exhaustion, Caesar returned to Rome.

[Note: [Col. 1057D] “And many.” The Augustan edition does not recognize the conjunction.]

During those same days he himself conducted many wars, and many more through his commanders and lieutenants. Among the others, Piso was sent against the Vindelici. After subduing them, he came victorious to Caesar at Lugdunum.

[Note: [Col. 1057D] “To Caesar.” Several manuscripts from the Leiden-Batavian collection add *reversus*, “having returned.”]

Tiberius, Caesar’s stepson, annihilated the Pannonians, who were swelling with a renewed uprising, in a most bloody slaughter. He then immediately took up war against the Germans, from whom, victorious, he led away forty thousand captives.

This was truly a great and most terrifying war, conducted with fifteen legions over three years; as Suetonius attests, scarcely any greater war had occurred after the Punic War.

At nearly the same time, Quinctilius Varus, acting with remarkable arrogance and greed toward his subjects, was utterly destroyed by the rebelling Germans together with three legions. Caesar Augustus bore this disaster to the state so heavily that, often overcome by the force of his grief, he dashed his head against a wall and cried out: “Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!”

Agrippa defeated the Bosporans and, having recovered in war the Roman standards that they had once taken under Mithridates, compelled the defeated to surrender.

The Parthians, as though they alone were marked out for all eyes while the whole world had either been conquered or pacified, and as though all the strength of the Roman Empire had to be turned against them alone—for the memory of avenging Crassus’s slaughter still gnawed at them—voluntarily sent back to Caesar the standards they had taken after killing Crassus. After handing over royal hostages, they earned a firm treaty through a loyal supplication.

## CHAPTER XXII

Octavius Augustus, Having Established Peace Everywhere, Himself Closed Janus for the Third Time and Set the State in Order; and Concerning the Census Conducted by Caesar

[Col. 1058A]

[Note: [Col. 1057D] “Therefore, in the year…” In all manuscripts, as also in the Augustan edition, *itaque* (“therefore”) is found; the remaining codices condemned it to exile.]

Therefore, in the year 752 from the founding of the City, Caesar Augustus, after arranging peace among all peoples from East to West, from North to South, and throughout the entire circuit of the Ocean, himself then closed the gates of Janus for the third time.

[Note: [Col. 1057D] “The gates of Janus for the third time.” Suetonius also testifies that Augustus closed Janus three times. FABR.]

For nearly twelve years thereafter, they remained continuously shut in the deepest peace, as even the rust itself attested.

[Note: [Col. 1058D] “The rust attested.” None of the manuscripts recognizes *consignavit*, which is found in the editions except the Augustan edition.]

They were never opened again until the very end of Augustus’s old age, when they were struck by the Athenian revolt and the uprising of the Dacians. After the gates of Janus had therefore been closed, Augustus strove to nourish and enlarge by peace the state that he had won by war. He enacted very many laws, by which the human race might live according to the custom of disciplined reverence with free obedience, while he himself avoided the title “Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 1058D] “The title ‘Lord.’” This account is taken from Suetonius Tranquillus’s *Augustus*. FABR.]

For when, while he was watching the games, the following words had been spoken in a mime, “O just and good lord!” and everyone had applauded joyfully as though the words had been spoken about him,

[Note: [Col. 1058D] “In a certain mime.” Fabricius, against all the manuscripts, wrote *a quodam* (“by a certain person”), as though *mimus* did not equally signify both the play and the actor. LAUT.]

he immediately restrained the unbecoming flattery with hand and expression, and on the following day rebuked it in a most severe edict. Thereafter he did not permit even his children or grandchildren to call him “lord,” whether seriously or in jest.

[Note: [Col. 1058D] “Thereafter.” The Leiden edition was the first, together with the Augustan edition, to print *post haec* (“after this”).]

[Note: [Col. 1058D] “At that time.” Some manuscripts have *eodem tempore* (“at the same time”).]

Therefore, at that time—that is, in the year in which Caesar, by God’s ordering, established the firmest and truest peace—Christ was born. This peace served his coming; and at his birth the rejoicing angels sang, with human beings listening: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

At the same time, this man, to whom supreme authority over all things had fallen, did not allow himself to be called “lord of men”;

[Col. 1058B]

indeed, he did not dare to do so, at the very moment when the true Lord of the whole human race was born among human beings.

In that same year, this same Caesar—whom God had predestined for such great mysteries—

[Note: [Col. 1058D] “Had predestined.” Three Leiden manuscripts have *praesignaverat* (“had marked out beforehand”).]

first ordered a census to be taken throughout every province and all people to be registered,

[Note: [Col. 1058D] “A census to be taken.” This census is well known from Luke. FABR.]

at the time when God also deigned to be seen as a human being and to exist as one. Christ was therefore born at that time and immediately registered in the Roman census at his birth. This was that first and most celebrated declaration which, through the public registration of each individual, marked Caesar as ruler of all and the Romans as masters of the world; in it, he himself also—who had made all human beings—willed to be found a human being and to be registered among human beings.

[Col. 1059A]

This had never at all been granted, from the founding of the world and the beginning of the human race, in this manner—not even under the Babylonian or Macedonian kingdoms, to say nothing of any lesser kingdom.

There can be no doubt that it is open to the knowledge, faith, and observation of all that our Lord Jesus Christ, by his nod, increased and defended this city and raised it to this summit of power. When he came, he especially wished to belong to it, and so he was necessarily to be called a Roman citizen, registered by a Roman census.

Therefore, since we have reached the point at which the Lord Christ first illumined this world by his coming and gave Caesar the most tranquil kingdom, I shall also bring this sixth book to a close here. In the seventh book, if—with the Lord’s help—I shall have enough strength,

[Note: [Col. 1059A] “If I shall have enough.” The first Florentine manuscript, the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read *suffecero* (“if I shall have enough”) rather than *suffecerim* (“if I should have enough”).]

I shall set forth the beginnings of the Christian age, and how it grew increasingly amid the hands that sought to restrain it, and how, though it is still advancing, it is gnawed by the attacks of those very people to whom we are compelled to make this reply. [Note: [Col. 1060A] “What persecutions.” Two Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read: “what persecution of Christians was carried out.”]

Since I have not been silent from the beginning about human beings’ sinning and being punished for their sins, I shall now also explain what persecutions were inflicted upon Christians and what punishments followed them, apart from the fact that all people are generally inclined to sin and are therefore corrected individually.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1059]

## 450 CHAPTER ONE

That the one true God, creator of the world and of all things, willed to make known to human beings, through the One—that is, Christ—both his power and his patience.

[Col. 1059B]

[Note: [Col. 1059C] “Sufficient.” Some old editions have *sufficienter* (“sufficiently”). This entire seventh book is lacking in the Lombard manuscript.]

Sufficient evidence, I think, has been gathered by which it can be plainly demonstrated, without any hidden mystery of the kind possessed by only a few believers, that the one true God whom the Christian faith proclaims both created the world and, whenever he willed, created his creature,

[Note: [Col. 1059C] “And arranged it in many ways, when he was unknown in many ways.” The latter words in the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts and in the Gronovian Collection are expressed as follows: “when he was unknown to many.” Some old editions read similarly and add something further to the earlier wording by printing “through many periods of time.” Since the phrase *cum per unicum* (“when through the One,” namely Christ) follows shortly afterward, I retain *per multa* here as well. The apparent meaning is that God created the world and arranged it in many ways (*per multa*, that is, in manifold ways), while he was unknown to the Gentiles in many ways (*per multa*, again meaning “in manifold ways”).]

and arranged it in many ways while he was unknown in many ways, and confirmed it through the One when he was revealed through the One. At the same time, his power and patience shone forth through arguments of many kinds.

[Note: [Col. 1059C] “His patience as well.” The third and fourth Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, prefer *sapientiam* (“wisdom”). I do not agree; what follows is “that such great patience is joined to such great power,” and shortly afterward, “What need was there for such great patience?”]

Here, I understand that I have briefly offended narrow and depressed minds, because such great patience is joined to such great power.

[Note: [Col. 1059D] “Is joined.” The first Leiden manuscript has *misceatur* (“may be joined”).]

For they say: If he was powerful enough to create the world, to establish the peace of the world,

[Col. 1059C]

and to make the worship and knowledge of himself known to the world,

[Note: [Col. 1059D] “To make known to the world the worship, etc.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, have “to make known the worship and knowledge of himself” and delete the remaining words. They have *fuerit* (“was”) instead of *fuit* (“was”).]

why was there a need for such patience—or, as they themselves think, for such destructive patience—that in the end what came about through human errors, disasters, and sufferings could instead have begun at the beginning through the power of the God whom you proclaim?

[Note: [Col. 1060C] “Could have begun?” The second Florentine manuscript superscribes *forte* (“perhaps”), *debuisset* (“ought to have”) being another possibility.]

[Note: [Col. 1060C] “To these indeed.” The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Gronovian Collection, has *quibus quippe* (“to these, indeed”). The same witnesses shortly afterward have *mereretur* (“might deserve”).]

I could answer them truthfully that the human race was created and established from the beginning for this purpose: that, living under religion and in peace without labor, it might earn eternity as the reward of obedience. But it abused the Creator’s goodness,

[Note: [Col. 1060C] “Of him who grants freedom.” Three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have *indulgentiae* (“of indulgence”). A little later, certain old Ultramarine and other editions read *contumaciam* (“rebelliousness”) instead of *contumacem* (“rebellious”). Thus one might read: “turned the freedom of indulgence into rebelliousness, and license, through contempt, into forgetfulness,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 1060C] “License, and.” The Perizonian manuscript has *licentiamque* (“and license”), etc.]

turning the freedom he granted into rebelliousness and turning license, through contempt, into forgetfulness.

[Note: [Col. 1060C] “Turned aside.” I restored this reading from the Perizonian manuscript and the Augustan editions; previously *defluxisse* (“had flowed away”) was read.]

[Note: [Col. 1060C] “And just.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, have *istamque* (“and that”). I change nothing, for he is disputing against those who charged that patience of God was unjust and destructive.]

Therefore God’s patience is now just, and just in both respects: neither does contempt wholly destroy the one toward whom he may wish to show mercy,

[Note: [Col. 1060C] “And allow him to be afflicted with hardships.” Some manuscripts have “and be afflicted by hardships.” [Col. 1060D] The Augustan edition transposes the final words of the sentence: “while powerful contempt permits…”]

and powerful contempt permits him, while God wills, to be afflicted with hardships. Then, since it is just, he always applies governance even to one who is ignorant, so that at some time he may piously restore to the repentant the possibility of his former grace.

But although these things are spoken most truthfully and forcefully,

[Note: [Col. 1060D] “Are spoken.” Some manuscripts and editions have *dicantur* (“may be spoken”).]

they nevertheless require a faithful and obedient hearer. As for me,

[Col. 1061C] [Note: [Col. 1061C] “I shall see, etc.” Fabricius correctly reads this way; certain old editions foolishly have “if I shall see whether anyone of those who will believe…”]

I shall see whether anyone will believe in the future, but for now I am dealing with unbelievers. I shall present more readily those arguments which they themselves, even if they refuse to approve them, cannot disprove.

[Note: [Col. 1061C] “Which they themselves, even if they cannot approve…” I prefer this reading from the Perizonian manuscript to the common text, which has “which they themselves, even if they do not wish to approve…”]

Therefore, so far as the conscience of human minds is concerned, we both live under the reverence of religion and the acknowledgment and worship of a heavenly power, differing only in faith:

[Note: [Col. 1061C] “Both.” This is the consistent reading of the manuscripts and old editions, except for the Hittorf, Fabrician, and Scott editions, which inelegantly have *utique* (“certainly”), contrary to the sense of what follows.]

for it is our position to confess that all things consist from one God and through one God; theirs is to believe that there are as many gods as there are elements.

[Note: [Col. 1061C] “Because it is ours.” This reading, found also in the three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection, is preferable, since it refers back to *fide* (“faith”) above, rather than to *quia* (“because”), as in the editions. [Col. 1061D]]

If it was within the power of the God whom you proclaim to make the Roman empire so great and so exalted, why did his patience prevent it from becoming so earlier?

To this they will receive the same answer in the same words: If it was within the power of the gods whom you proclaim to make the Roman empire so great and so exalted, why did their patience prevent it from becoming so earlier?

Were the gods themselves not yet in existence? Or did Rome itself not yet exist? Or were they not worshiped? Or did this empire not yet seem suitable?

[Note: [Col. 1061D] “Not yet suitable.” Together with the Augustan edition, the manuscripts require us to adopt this reading instead of *nondum* (“not yet”).]

If the gods did not yet exist, the argument comes to an end.

[Note: [Col. 1061D] “The argument comes to an end.” Some manuscripts have *cesset intentio* (“let the argument come to an end”).]

For why should I now investigate their delay in a place where I do not even find nature itself?

[Note: [Col. 1061D] “For what purpose.” I think one should read “To what end,” etc. A little later the Perizonian manuscript has “nor Rome itself.”]

But if they were gods, then either their power, as they themselves judge, or their patience is at fault: patience, if it existed; power, if it was lacking. Or, if it seems more persuasive to say that gods existed then who could have advanced Rome, but that the Romans who could rightfully be advanced did not yet exist, we are asking about the power of the author of things, not the skill of a craftsman.

For the question concerns great gods, as they suppose, not the most worthless artisans, whose art ceases unless material is supplied.

[Note: [Col. 1061D] “Ready at hand.” Three Leiden manuscripts—the first, third, and fourth—together with the Gronovian Collection, have *praestantius* (“more excellent”); and shortly afterward I think *quam* (“than”) should be read for *quia apud* (“because under”).]

For if it was always ready for them to know beforehand and to will—indeed, since foreknowledge under omnipotence concerns only their own works, that is, to know beforehand whatever they were going to will, with the foreknowledge accompanied by the will—then the work ought not to have been awaited but created, especially since they say that their Jupiter was accustomed to turn heaps of ants into peoples of human beings as a game.

As for their concern with religious rites, I do not think it needs to be reviewed, since amid uninterrupted sacred observances there was no end and no respite from continuous disasters, except when Christ, the Savior of the world, shone forth. Although I think I have already sufficiently shown that the peace of the Roman empire was predestined for his coming, I shall nevertheless try to add a few further points.

## CHAPTER TWO

That Babylon and Rome, and their kingdoms, agree in most respects; concerning the four monarchies of the world, a certain burning of Rome, and the ages of Christ and Abraham.

[Note: [Col. 1061D] “At the beginning of the second.” Read Book II, chapter 1. FABR.]

At the beginning of the second book, when I was briefly treating the periods of Rome’s foundation in the course of my writing, I composed a number of comparisons between Babylon, the city of the Assyrians and then mistress of the nations, and Rome, now likewise ruling the nations:

[Note: [Col. 1061D] “Compared.” Perhaps one should read *comparata* (“compared”).]

Babylon had been the first empire, Rome the last; Babylon gradually declined, while Rome slowly grew stronger;
