[Note: [Col. 1062C] “Growing stronger.” The Perizonian manuscript has *crescens* (“growing”), which, as much more Latin, deserved to be accepted if other manuscripts also supported it.]

Babylon lost its final king at a single moment, while Rome first gained one;

[Note: [Col. 1062C] “Rome first had one.” The second Leiden manuscript, the Meuse manuscript, two Florentine manuscripts, and the Augustan edition have *cum isti* (“while Rome had one”); Perizonius more correctly reads *tum isti* (“then Rome had one”). Three other Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, have *quo isti*, etc. A little later, instead of *in mortem* (“to death”), the first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the second Florentine manuscript and the Gronovian Collection, have *in morte* (“in death”).]

Babylon was then attacked by Cyrus, captured, and collapsed as though into death, while Rome, confidently rising after the expulsion of its kings, began to use free counsels. Especially noteworthy is that, when Rome was asserting its freedom, the people of the Jews—who had been serving under kings in Babylon—also returned, their freedom restored, to holy Jerusalem,

and rebuilt the temple of the Lord, as had been foretold by the prophets.

[Note: [Col. 1062C] “And the temple.” Three Leiden manuscripts have *templum quoque* (“the temple also”).]

[Note: [Col. 1062C] “Rebuilt.” Four Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, have *reformaret* (“might rebuild”).]

Moreover, I had said that between the Babylonian kingdom, which had existed in the East, and the Roman kingdom, which arose in the West,

[Note: [Col. 1062C] “Was nourished for the inheritance of the East.” We owe this excellent reading to the first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts, the Perizonian manuscript, and the Gronovian Collection. The first editions and the Augustan edition had also shown that it should be read this way, but all the others preferred *haereditate Orientis* (“by the inheritance of the East”), thereby removing all elegance and producing the opposite meaning. For the Roman empire was not nourished by the inheritance of the East, but the Macedonian empire was—the empire that flourished in Asia before the Roman empire, at the time when the Roman empire first arose in the West. But that rising Roman empire was gradually nourished as the heir of the East, first swallowing up each neighboring possession and then satisfying itself with possession of the East.]

it was nourished as the heir of the East,

[Note: [Col. 1062D] “Was nourished.” Some manuscripts and editions have *nutriebatur* (“was nourished”).]

while the Macedonian and African kingdoms, that is, as though from the South and North, briefly held the roles of protector and guardian.

I know that no one has ever doubted that the Babylonian and Roman kingdoms are rightly called the kingdoms of East and West. The Macedonian kingdom was in the North: this is shown both by the region of the sky itself and by the altars of Alexander the Great, which still stand beneath the Rhipaean Mountains.

[Note: [Col. 1063C] “Was.” This is absent from most manuscripts. A little later, the Perizonian manuscript has *tum* (“then”) instead of *cum* (“when”). Two Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, have *doceant* (“show”) instead of *docent* (“show”).]

The historical records and the monuments of cities alike show that Carthage surpassed all Africa and extended the boundaries of its kingdom not only into Sicily, Sardinia, and the other neighboring islands, but also into Spain.

It was also said that the numbers of years of Babylon, devastated by the Medes, and Rome, attacked by the Goths, coincided very closely.

[Note: [Col. 1063C] “Coincided.” This is the reading of three Leiden manuscripts, the Perizonian manuscript, the Gronovian Collection, and the Augustan editions. The common editions have *cucurrisse* (“ran”).]

Now I add this point, so that it may become clearer that God alone is the arbiter of all ages, kingdoms, and places. The Carthaginian kingdom stood, from its foundation until its overthrow, for a little more than seven hundred years;

[Col. 1063B]

[Note: [Col. 1063C] “Likewise the Macedonian kingdom.” The kingdom of Macedonia had thirty-five kings, from the houses of the Heraclids or Temenids, Cassander, and Antigonus; it endured no longer than 566 years, as we have shown at the end of the *Macedonian History*, p. 279, vol. II of the *Universal History*.

The Macedonian kingdom likewise stood, from Caranus to Perseus, for somewhat less than seven hundred years. Yet both were brought to an end by that number seven,

[Note: [Col. 1063C] “That number.” This word is absent from the second and third Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection.]

by which all things are judged.

[Note: [Col. 1063C] “Are judged.” The Augustan edition has *dijudicantur* (“are adjudged”).]

Rome itself, although its empire was perfected and advanced toward the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, nevertheless stumbled slightly, even it, upon encountering this number. For in the seven-hundredth year of its foundation, a fire, arising from an unknown source, consumed fourteen of its districts.

[Note: [Col. 1063D] “Its districts.” The second word is absent from three Leiden manuscripts. This fire is also mentioned above, Book VI, chapter 14.] It was never devastated by a greater fire, as Livy says; so much so that several years later Caesar Augustus distributed a large sum from the public treasury for the restoration of what had then been burned.

I could also show that this same doubled number belonged to Babylon, which, after one thousand four hundred and more years, was finally captured by King Cyrus, if consideration of the present subject did not call me back.

This, however, I gladly add: in the forty-third year of that first of all kings, Ninus—although his father Belus is also obscurely reported to have been the first to reign—

[Note: [Col. 1063D] “First.” Some manuscripts and editions have *primum* (“first,” adverbially).]

[Note: [Col. 1063D] “In the forty-third.” The four Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, subtract one year.]

the holy Abraham was born,

[Note: [Col. 1063D] “To whom were spoken.” The Augustan edition has “to whom were given.”]

to whom the promises were spoken,

[Note: [Col. 1063D] “Promises.” Perizonius has *promissiones* (“promises”); shortly afterward, together with three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection, he has *repromissus* (“promised”).]

from whose offspring Christ was promised.

Then, when nearly the forty-second year had elapsed after Augustus Caesar—the first of all emperors—had begun to rule, Christ was born, the one promised to Abraham under Ninus, the first king, although Caesar, Augustus’s father, had been more a surveyor and establisher of the empire than an emperor.

[Note: [Col. 1063D] “Founder of the empire.” He speaks in such a way as to compare Caesar with Belus and Augustus with Ninus. *Metator* is a military term; it referred to one sent ahead by a commander to survey and mark out a place suitable for a camp. Lucan, *Pharsalia* 1.381:

“To pitch a camp above the Tuscan Tiber’s waters,  
I, the bold surveyor, shall come into Hesperian fields.”]

[Note: [Col. 1064C] “I mean.” Several manuscripts have *ergo* (“therefore”).]

[Note: [Col. 1064C] “After nearly completing the forty-second year.” This is also the year of Christ’s birth according to Eusebius; nevertheless, some write that Christ was born in the forty-first year of Augustus’s rule, and others in the forty-fourth. FABR.]

He was born on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, when all the beginnings of the coming year first begin to grow. Thus it came about that, since Abraham was born in the forty-third year, Christ’s birth corresponded to the end of the forty-second year, so that he himself was not born during part of a third year, but rather the third year itself began with him.

[Note: [Col. 1064D] “Corresponded.” Some manuscripts have *convenerit* (“has corresponded”).]

[Note: [Col. 1064D] “Might arise.” Three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection have *ostenderetur* (“might be shown”).]

That year was filled with such great and such unprecedented blessings that, even without my setting them forth, I think they are sufficiently known: a single peace for all throughout the whole world,

[Note: [Col. 1064D] “A peace for all.” The first and fourth Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, have “a single peace for all, and not by a cessation but by an abolition of wars,” etc.]

the twin gates of Janus closed; the roots of wars eradicated, not merely suppressed; and that first and greatest census.

[Note: [Col. 1064D] “Was.” Two Florentine manuscripts and the Perizonian manuscript are said to delete this word.]

In it, all the creation of the great nations swore allegiance to the one name of Caesar,

[Note: [Col. 1064D] “All the creation of the great nations.” The Augustan edition deletes *magnarum* (“great”). The Perizonian manuscript omits *juravit* (“swore”). The first, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection read: “all the creation of the great nations swore allegiance.”]

and through their participation in the census they were made members of one society.

## 457 CHAPTER THREE

When Christ was born for the salvation of humanity, how he was immediately persecuted; concerning the great famine at Rome and the perpetual peace.

Therefore, in the year 752 from the founding of the City,

[Note: [Col. 1064D] “In the year 752 from the founding of the City.” Cassiodorus writes that Christ was born under the consulship of Gnaeus Lentulus and Marcus Messalla, which falls in the year 750 of the City. FABR.]

Christ was born, bringing saving faith to the world, truly the rock set in the midst of all things: whoever stumbled against it would be shattered, while whoever believed would be saved; truly a blazing fire, by which whoever follows it is illumined and whoever tests it is burned.

Christ himself is the head of Christians, the savior of the good, the punisher of the wicked, and the judge of all. Establishing by word and deed the pattern for those who would follow,

[Note: [Col. 1065C] “For those who would follow.” Some editions have *secuturis* (“for those who follow”).]

he taught all the more clearly that those who would receive persecutions for the sake of eternal life ought to be patient in them.

[Note: [Col. 1065C] “In persecutions.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, have “in the persecution which they would receive,” etc.]

As soon as he had appeared to the world, brought forth by a virgin, he began to undergo his own sufferings.

[Note: [Col. 1065C] “His own sufferings.” The final word does not appear in the Perizonian manuscript. Some manuscripts and editions have “from sufferings.”]

For as soon as Herod, king of Judaea, learned that he had been born, he resolved to kill him and, while pursuing one child, slaughtered very many infants.

[Note: [Col. 1065D] “From this.” The third Leiden manuscript has *hic* (“here”), so that the reference is to Christ; the following passages likewise return to him.]

From this comes deserved punishment when the wicked make an unjust attack. From this it follows that insofar as the world is conducted peacefully, it is through the grace of believers, while insofar as it is disturbed disastrously, it is through the punishment of blasphemers. Christians faithful to him are secure in every respect: either the rest of eternal life is safe for them, or even this present life becomes gain. I shall demonstrate this more readily by relating events in order and by letting the events themselves speak.

After the Redeemer of the world, the Lord Jesus Christ, came to earth and was registered as a Roman citizen in Caesar’s census, while for twelve years, as I have said, the gates of war were held shut by the most blessed tranquility of peace, Caesar Augustus sent Gaius, his grandson, to organize the provinces of Egypt and Syria. Passing from Egypt through the territory of Palestine, he refused to worship at Jerusalem in the temple of God, which was then holy and celebrated,

[Note: [Col. 1065D] “As Suetonius says.” In *Augustus*, chapter 93. FABR.]

as Suetonius Tranquillus reports.

[Note: [Col. 1065D] “When Augustus learned this, etc.” The first edition and the Venetian editions that followed it read, “when Augustus learned this, as he had done what was wrong, he praised him for having acted wisely.”]

When Augustus learned this from him, he praised him for having acted wisely, using a faulty judgment.

Therefore, in the forty-eighth year of Caesar’s reign, such a dreadful famine overtook the Romans that Caesar ordered the families of gladiators and all foreigners, along with the greatest numbers of slaves, except physicians and teachers,

[Col. 1065C]

to be expelled from the City.

[Note: [Col. 1065D] “To be expelled from the City.” The Perizonian manuscript has *extrudi Urbe* (“to be driven out of the City”).]

Thus, since the ruler sinned against God’s holy one and the people were corrected through famine, the severity of the punishment revealed the magnitude of the offense.

[Note: [Col. 1065D] “Next, etc.” Consult Lipsius, *Antiquae Lectiones* II.8.]

Next, to speak in the words of Cornelius Tacitus,

[Note: [Col. 1065D] “To speak.” The Perizonian manuscript has “to use the words.”]

when old Augustus had opened Janus, while new peoples at the farthest boundaries of the earth were repeatedly sought, sometimes with advantage and sometimes at a cost, it remained open until the reign of Vespasian. Thus far Cornelius.

Moreover, when the city of Jerusalem had then been captured and overthrown, as the prophets had foretold, and the Jews had been extinguished, Titus—who had been appointed by God’s judgment to avenge the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—closed Janus in triumph with his father Vespasian.

[Note: [Col. 1065D] “With Vespasian.” The second Leiden manuscript has “under Vespasian.”]

Therefore, although Janus was opened toward the end of Caesar’s reign, nevertheless for a long time afterward, even though the army was under arms, no wars made their noise. Hence the Lord Jesus Christ himself also said in the Gospels, when in those times the whole world was living in complete tranquility and a single peace covered all nations,

[Note: [Col. 1065D] “Covered.” That is, “covered,” “adorned,” or “crowned.”]

and when his disciples asked him about the conclusion of the times to come,

[Note: [Col. 1066C] “About the conclusion of the times.” This is the reading of the manuscripts and better editions; others have “about the conjunction” or “condition” of the times.]

among other things he said:

[Note: [Col. 1066C] “He said.” Some manuscripts have “among other things he said.” The words occur in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 24.]

“But you will hear of wars and reports of wars. See that you are not troubled. For these things must happen, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be pestilences, famines, and earthquakes in various places. But all these things are the beginnings of sorrows. Then they will hand you over to tribulation and kill you, and you will be hated by all nations because of my name.”

[Note: [Col. 1066D] “Nations.” This word is absent from the second Florentine manuscript.]

By teaching this through divine providence, he strengthened believers by warning them beforehand and confounded unbelievers by predicting what was to come.

## CHAPTER FOUR

Concerning the life and deeds of Tiberius Caesar; how he embraced Christ; and concerning his cruelty toward very many people.

In the year 767 from the founding of the City, after the death of Caesar Augustus, Tiberius Caesar obtained the imperial power and remained in it for twenty-three years.

[Note: Tiberius Caesar. A fuller account of the life and deeds of Tiberius, here briefly sketched, is found in Dio, Tacitus, Suetonius, and Zonaras. FABR.]

He himself waged no wars personally, nor, indeed, through his generals any serious ones, except that occasional outbreaks of peoples, foreseen in advance, were quickly suppressed in certain places. In the fourth year of his reign, Germanicus, son of Drusus and father of Caligula, celebrated a triumph over the Germans, against whom he had been sent by the aged Augustus.

For most of his reign Tiberius governed the state with great and serious moderation, to such an extent that, when certain governors advised that the tribute of the provinces should be increased, he wrote to them: “It is the duty of a good shepherd to shear the flock, not to flay it.”

[Note: Not to skin it. Perizonius has “not to strip it,” which is a gloss.]

But after the Lord Christ had suffered

[Note: Lord Christ. Some early Augustan editions and others insert “Jesus.”]

and risen from the dead, and had sent his disciples to preach

[Note: “Sent away.” Some manuscripts and editions read “sent.”]

, Pilate, governor of the province of Palestine, reported to the emperor Tiberius and to the Senate concerning the passion of Christ,

[Note: And the resurrection. The third Leiden manuscript and the Groningen collection read “and concerning the resurrection.”]

and concerning the miracles that had been openly performed

[Note: “Openly.” The same third Leiden manuscript deletes this word.]

either by Christ himself or by his disciples in his name,

[Note: Either by his disciples. The Perizonius manuscript transposes the words: “or by his disciples in his name,” and so forth.]

and concerning the fact that, as the faith of very many rapidly increased, God was being believed in.

[Note: Pilate, the governor. Concerning Pontius Pilate, governor of Palestine, and his deeds, see Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XVIII. Pilate’s letter to Tiberius concerning the resurrection of Christ is found in Hegesippus. Compare what we noted concerning a similar passage of Tertullian in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 5, pp. 57–58. FABR.]

With the support of great popular approval, Tiberius brought a motion before the Senate that Christ should be regarded as God.

[Note: Should be regarded as God. The third Leiden manuscript and the Groningen collection read “among the gods.”]

The Senate, angered that the matter had not first been referred to it according to custom, so that it might itself decide beforehand whether this worship should be accepted, refused to consecrate Christ and ordered by decree that Christians be expelled from the City—especially since Sejanus, Tiberius’s prefect, was obstinately opposing the acceptance of this religion.

[Note: Sejanus. No one is unaware of the great influence Sejanus possessed with Tiberius. The municipalities, following Tiberius’s judgment, heaped every kind of honor upon Sejanus while he was alive; but after his death, when he had paid the penalties for his crime against the imperial household and for his perverse ambition, they persecuted his memory in every way. I possess two bronze coins, distinguished by a double mark, although they do not differ from one another in type. When Tiberius had adopted Sejanus as his colleague in his fifth consulship, the Bilbilitani in Spain struck coins bearing the face and inscription of the emperor Tiberius; on the other side they joined that famous pair of consuls in the inscription. The memorable legend reads: **MVNicipium AVGVSTA BIBILIS TIberio CAESARE V. Lucio AELIO SEIANO COnSulibus**—“The municipality Augusta Bilbilis, Tiberius Caesar being consul for the fifth time and Lucius Aelius Sejanus being consuls.” The other coin has the same workmanship, inscription, and type. But on it Sejanus’s name, praenomen, and cognomen can be seen erased with a graver; the bottom of the incision made by the graver is somewhat hollowed out. This shows that the erasure was made during Tiberius’s own time or immediately after Sejanus’s death, since the noble rust—which antiquarians call the patina—occupies the bottom there with the same color and the same patina as the rest of the coin’s entire surface. Thus this memorable coin teaches us that the fury directed against Sejanus’s honors and memory extended not only to throwing down statues, breaking marble, and removing publicly erected inscriptions, but also to the Roman mint in a Spanish municipality. One of these coins therefore underwent the fate of Sejanus’s erased honor; the other, whether then buried in the earth or hidden elsewhere, escaped. I carefully preserve both and have appended an exceedingly accurate drawing of each.]

Nevertheless, by an edict Tiberius threatened the accusers of Christians with death. Thus, little by little, that highly celebrated moderation of Tiberius Caesar was altered

[Note: “Altered.” The Groningen collection reads “diminished.” The word “is” is absent from the Augustan edition.]

as punishment for the Senate’s opposition. For whatever he did according to his own will became a pleasure to him; and from the gentlest of princes the fiercest beast burst into flame.

[Note: “It was a pleasure.” The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Groningen collection, reads “pleasure was made,” or “became a pleasure.”]

For he proscribed very many senators and compelled them to die. He had selected twenty patrician men for his counsel; scarcely two of them did he leave unharmed, while he killed the rest on various pretexts.

[Note: “He had selected.” So my manuscript reads, as do Perizonius, two Leiden manuscripts, and the Groningen collection; the Utrecht manuscript and older editions instead direct that one should write “he had ordered [them] to be chosen,” not “he had selected,” as found in the editions of Fabricius and Scotius.]

He killed his prefect Sejanus, who was plotting revolution. He destroyed his sons Drusus and Germanicus, of whom Drusus was his natural son and Germanicus his adopted son, with unmistakable signs of poison. He killed the sons of his own son Germanicus.

My spirit shudders to recount his deeds individually,

[Note: “My spirit shudders.” With “spirit” deleted, three Leiden manuscripts, together with Perizonius, read “I shudder”; the Augustan edition also has “I shudder,” while the second Florentine manuscript reads “I shudder.”]

and I am ashamed, for he boiled over with such a frenzy of lust and cruelty that those who had despised being saved by Christ the King were punished by Caesar the King.

In the twelfth year of this reign, however, a new and incredible disaster occurred near the city of Fidenae. While the people were watching a gladiatorial spectacle, the amphitheater’s seating collapsed, and more than twenty thousand people were killed.

[Note: “It killed more than twenty thousand people.” In recounting the severe punishment of that cruel spectacle, Tacitus, who describes this disaster vividly, reports a larger number, adding the wounded as well: “Fifty thousand people were disabled or crushed in that accident,” *Annals* IV.62–63.]

A truly fitting example of so great a correction for posterity: people had gathered, eager to watch the deaths of human beings, at the very time when God had willed to become human in order to provide for the salvation of human beings.

[Note: “Then, in the seventeenth year of the same reign.” We have retained this number, although not without reason many follow Eusebius, who assigns the passion of Christ to the eighteenth year of Tiberius. FABR.—The eighteenth year is found in the fourth Leiden manuscript.]

Then, in the seventeenth year of the same reign, when the Lord Jesus Christ had indeed voluntarily delivered himself to suffering, but had been impiously seized by the Jews and fastened to the cross, a tremendous earthquake occurred throughout the world. Rocks were split apart in the mountains,

[Note: “Were split apart.” Several manuscripts delete the second occurrence of “were split apart.”]

and many parts of the greatest cities collapsed after being shaken more violently than usual. On that same day, at the sixth hour of the day, the sun was completely darkened,

[Note: “The sun was completely darkened.” Some older editions and the third Leiden manuscript read “darkened throughout the whole world.”]

and suddenly a dreadful night was spread over the earth, and, as it is said:

[Note: “And the impious ages feared everlasting night.” This is a verse from Virgil, *Georgics* I.468:

> Who would dare call the sun false?  
> He also often warns that blind tumults are threatening,  
> and that treachery and open wars are swelling.  
> He also, mourning Rome after Caesar had been slain,  
> when he covered his shining head with dark rust,  
> says that the impious ages feared everlasting night.]

“And the impious ages feared everlasting night.”

[Note: Virgil’s passage is quoted here as an editorial example concerning the darkness.]

It is therefore clear that neither the moon came between the light of the sun nor clouds obstructed it, since the fourteenth-day moon is reported to have been very far from the sun’s sight, despite occupying the whole region of the sky,

[Note: “The moon on that same day came between the sky.” This is the best reading, instead of “the moon on that day came between the whole region of the sky,” which, I do not know from what philosophy, has been introduced. LAUT.]

[Note: “The moon occupying the whole sky.” The third Leiden manuscript reads “the moon having measured out the region of the sky.” The Augustan edition has: “on the fourteenth day, the moon occupying the whole region of the sky,” and so forth.]

and the stars are said to have shone then during the daylight hours—or rather, throughout that dreadful night, across the whole sky. This is attested not only by the faith of the holy Gospels but also by several Greek books.

From that time onward, after the passion of the Lord, whom the Jews persecuted as far as lay within their power, continuous disasters have resounded against the Jews without interruption, until they are emptied out, scattered, and brought to an end.

[Note: “Resound.” Some older editions read “resound continually”; the Augustan edition, “sound forth.”]

Tiberius accordingly relegated their swelling youth to provinces with a harsher climate, under the pretext of military service,

[Note: “Their youth.” These are the words of Suetonius, *Tiberius* 36.]

[Note: “Swelling.” I am surprised that this word is found nowhere except in the Cologne manuscript. LAUT.—I have found it in no manuscripts, nor does it occur in Suetonius, from whom this passage is taken.]

and removed from the City the remaining members of that same people, or those pursuing similar practices, under penalty of perpetual slavery unless they obeyed.

[Note: “Or pursuing similar practices.” Tacitus, *Annals* II.85: “Action was also taken concerning the expulsion of Egyptian and Jewish rites; and a decree of the Senate was made that four thousand of the freedman class, infected with that superstition and of suitable age, should be transported to the island of Sardinia to suppress brigandage there; and if they should perish from the severity of the climate, it would be a cheap loss. The rest were to leave Italy unless, by a fixed day, they abandoned their profane rites.”]

Certainly, he remitted the tribute of the cities of Asia that had been destroyed by that earthquake and also granted them their own liberty.

[Note: “The cities of Asia.” Besides the historians, ancient coins attest this liberality of Tiberius; since they are well known to the public, I pass them over. But it is false that the cities of Asia suffered this disaster in the earthquake that occurred near the time of Christ’s death, since it is established that it happened several years later. See Tacitus, *Annals* II.47, and others.]

He died amid ambiguous indications of poisoning.

## CHAPTER V. The Character, Deeds, and Cruel Crimes of Caius Caligula Caesar

[Col. 1069C]

In the year 790 from the founding of the City, Caius Caligula, the third emperor after Augustus,

[Note: Caius Caligula. Concerning Caligula, see Suetonius and Dio, as well as Eutropius, Book VII, and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II. FABR.]

began to reign and remained in power for not quite four years. He was the most depraved man of all who had preceded him, and seemed truly to have been appointed as a punishment for the Romans who blasphemed and the Jews who persecuted.

To give a brief account of the magnitude of his cruelty,

[Note: “I shall give an account.” I restored this reading from the Augustan edition, supported by all the manuscripts. The common editions have “I shall express”; but below in this chapter Orosius uses the word “give an account” again: “for the purpose of giving an account of the complaints,” in reference to Philo.]

he is said to have exclaimed:

[Note: “Would that,” and so forth. See Suetonius, life of that monster, chapters 30–31.]

“Would that the Roman people had a single neck!”

He often complained about the circumstances of his times,

[Note: “About the circumstances.” The Perizonius manuscript reads “about the circumstances” in the plural.]

because they were marked by no public calamities.

O blessed beginnings of the Christian age, how greatly have you prevailed in human affairs, since even human cruelty could desire disasters more readily than it could find them! Behold: in the midst of general tranquility, savage ferocity complains of hunger;

> Impious Fury, sitting within,  
> cruelly enthroned upon arms,  
> bound behind by a hundred alien knots,  
> roars horribly with bloodstained mouth.

Rebellious slaves and fugitive gladiators terrified Rome, overturned Italy, and devastated Sicily; they were already feared by nearly the entire human race throughout the whole world. But in the days of salvation—that is, in Christian times—not even an enemy emperor can tear apart the peace.

For this emperor, setting out with a great and incredible display, went in search of an enemy with forces that had nothing to do, traversed Germany and Gaul, and halted on the shore of the Ocean, near the view of Britain. When he had received into submission Minocynobellinus, the son of the king of the Britons, who had been driven out by his father and was wandering about with a few companions,

[Note: Minocynobellinus. Suetonius, *Caligula* 44, has “Adminius, son of Cinobellinus, king of the Britons.” FABR.—Casaubon, in his note on Suetonius, thinks that Orosius wrote: “When he had received Adminius—or rather Arminius—son of Cinobellinus, king of the Britons,” and so forth. This conjecture is highly plausible.]

he returned to Rome when the opportunity for war had failed him.

At the same time the Jews, who even then were being harassed everywhere by deserved disasters because of Christ’s passion, having raised a sedition at Alexandria, were defeated and slaughtered and driven from the city.

[Note: “And driven from the city.” Some older editions read “and driven from the City”; the third Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen collection read “and expelled from the city”; Perizonius reads “and driven out of the city.”]

To present their complaints, they sent a certain Philo, a man especially learned,

[Col. 1071A]

as an ambassador to Caesar.

[Note: “They sent.” Two Florentine manuscripts read “they had sent.”]

But Caligula, hostile to all people and especially to the Jews, rejected Philo’s embassy,

[Note: “Philo’s embassy rejected.” Concerning this embassy, see Eusebius, Book II, chapter 5, and Josephus, Book VIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 10. FABR.]

and ordered all the sacred buildings of the Jews, especially that ancient sanctuary at Jerusalem,

[Note: “At Jerusalem.” The first word is absent from the second Florentine manuscript.]

to be profaned with pagan sacrifices and filled with statues and images, and commanded that he himself be worshiped there as God.

[Note: “But Pilate.” Pilate took his own life in the second year of Caligula’s reign, according to Cassiodorus and Eusebius. FABR.]

But Pilate, the governor who had pronounced the sentence of condemnation against Christ, after encountering and provoking numerous seditions at Jerusalem, was so constricted by the anguish inflicted by Caius that, stabbing himself with his own hand, he sought a shortened escape from his miseries through the speed of death.

Caius Caligula added this crime also to his lusts: he first polluted his sisters by incest and then condemned them to exile.

[Note: “His sisters.” The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Groningen collection, reads “his sisters also.” Shortly afterward, some older editions have “whom he polluted and condemned.” The names of the sisters, which still survive on several coins of that emperor, were Drusilla, Julia, and Agrippina. I once saw in the Marckian museum a large medallion of remarkable weight and singular workmanship, on which **LIVIA** had been engraved instead of **IVLIA**. This, together with several other features, made the coin—otherwise enormous in size and thickness—suspect. After the museum was dispersed, it was carried away to Brabant. I had previously taken an impression of it; its depiction and dimensions are as follows:]

Afterward he ordered all the exiles to be killed together.

[Note: “He ordered all the exiles to be killed together.” Suetonius, *Life of Caligula*, chapter 28, adds the reason: “Having recalled a certain man from an old exile, he asked him what he had usually done there. When the man replied flatteringly, ‘I always prayed to the gods that Tiberius would perish, as happened, and that you would reign,’ Caligula imagined that his own exiles were also praying for his death and sent men around the islands to massacre them all.”]

He himself was killed by his own bodyguards.

Two documents were found in his private quarters.

[Note: “In his private quarters.” The Groningen collection reads “in private.”] On one, a dagger had been written as the identifying symbol; on the other, a sword. Both contained the names and identifying marks of distinguished men of both the senatorial and equestrian orders who had been destined for death.

A huge chest was also discovered containing cups of various poisons,

[Note: “Containing cups of poisons.” These last two words occurred in one Venetian manuscript but are lacking in all the others. LAUT.—The expression is nevertheless inept, since the poisons were pure and not yet mixed. I have found it in no manuscripts. Suetonius, *Caligula* 49, reads: “A huge chest was also found, full of various poisons”; Orosius may perhaps have written the same.]

and when these were sunk into the sea on the orders of Caesar Claudius,

[Note: “When they had been sunk.” The Perizonius manuscript reads “when they had been immersed.”]

the waters are said to have been contaminated, causing the death of many fish, whose corpses the tide cast about along the nearby shores.

[Note: “A great indication indeed.” I restored this reading with the manuscripts, the Augustan edition, and Scotius; the remaining common editions have “a great indication, however.”]

This was truly a great indication of God’s mercy: on account of the help of grace soon to be believed by part of the people, and as a tempering of his wrath against the people then stubbornly refusing to believe, so that the number of human beings who had escaped the death prepared for them might be understood from the multitude of fish that had been killed; and so that everyone might recognize

[Note: “Might recognize.” Thus the manuscripts; the common editions have “might become known.”]

what such a great quantity of poison, increased by human ingenuity, could have done in that wretched city—since, when carelessly poured out, it even polluted the sea.

## CHAPTER VI. The Life and Deeds of Claudius Tiberius Caesar, and the Extremely Severe Famine at Rome under His Reign

[Col. 1072B]

In the year 795 from the founding of the City, Tiberius Claudius, the fourth emperor after Augustus, obtained the throne and remained in it for fourteen years.

[Note: Tiberius Claudius. Concerning Claudius Caesar, see Suetonius, Dio, Eutropius, and Sextus Aurelius. He ruled for thirteen years, eight months, and twenty days. Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XX, chapter 5; Xiphilinus, epitome of Dio. FABR.]

At the beginning of his reign,

[Note: “At the beginning of his reign.” In the second year, under the consulship of Saturninus and Venustus, according to Cassiodorus. See Eusebius, *Chronicle*. The Augustan edition reads “from the beginning.” FABR.]

Peter, the apostle of our Lord Jesus Christ,

[Note: “Of our Lord.” “Our” is absent from Perizonius and the second and third Florentine manuscripts. The second Florentine manuscript also lacks “of Christ.”]

came to Rome and taught the saving faith to all believers through faithful words, confirming it by the most powerful miracles. From that time onward Christians began to exist at Rome.

[Note: “From that time.” The Leiden manuscripts read “also from then.”]

Rome recognized that this benefit had been conferred upon its faith.

[Note: “For.” The first Leiden manuscripts read “now.”]

For when, after Caligula had been killed, the Senate and consuls had resolved to abolish the imperial power, restore the republic to its ancient order, and completely overthrow the whole family of the Caesars,

[Note: “And to sweep away.” The second Florentine manuscript has “verendaque,” a corrupt reading of “everrendaque,” which I found, perhaps not without reason, in the Perizonius manuscript.]

[Note: “Much.” This word is absent from the first and third Leiden manuscripts and from the Groningen collection.]

Claudius, as soon as he had secured the imperial power, displayed an extraordinary and previously unknown clemency at Rome,

[Note: “Previously unknown at Rome.” Above the second Florentine manuscript is written, perhaps, “to this Rome.”]

lest, once begun, vengeance should rage against so great a multitude of nobles. He erased from memory those two days during which an unfortunate consultation and debate concerning the state of the republic had taken place, and permanently decreed pardon and oblivion for everything done or said during them.

[Note: “Those two days.” This passage is correctly read in the manuscripts, as is clear from Suetonius, *Claudius* 1. FABR.—The reading “that judgment” was formerly found, but the Venetian restoration is supported by what immediately follows: “and he decreed pardon and oblivion for all deeds and words committed during it.” LAUT.—All the manuscripts and the Augustan edition have “two days,” as Fabricius correctly restored it; one would rightly miss “judgment” in those who reproduce it from corrupt editions.]

Thus he voluntarily confirmed that famous Athenian amnesty

[Note: “Thus that.” Some manuscripts read “thus also that.”]

which the Senate, at Cicero’s urging, had attempted to introduce at Rome after Julius Caesar had been killed, but which had come to nothing when Antony and Octavian burst in to avenge the murdered Caesar. Although Claudius was being impelled toward the slaughter of the conspirators by a much more savage cause,

[Note: “Much.” This word is absent from the first and third Leiden manuscripts and from the Groningen collection.]

he established the amnesty by spontaneous clemency, although no one had asked for it.

[Note: “Of the conspirators.” The Perizonius manuscript reads “of the plotters.”]

[Note: “Was being impelled.” This appears to be Orosius’s word, restored from the agreement of the manuscripts. The common editions read “was being driven.”]

At the same time a great miracle of God’s present grace occurred. Furius Camillus Scribonianus, governor of Dalmatia, was plotting civil war and had enticed many very strong legions to change their oath.

Accordingly, when the day had been announced for all to assemble from every direction before the new emperor,

[Note: “On the appointed day.” Perizonius reads “on the day given.”]

neither the eagles could be adorned nor could the standards be moved or disturbed in any way.

[Note: “Nor could the eagles be adorned.” In Suetonius, *Claudius* 13, the reading is “nor could the eagle be adorned.” Since Orosius has “eagles” in the plural, Casaubon asks whether all the eagles had conspired in this portent. I may in turn ask whether all the standards conspired in the same portent—or rather in the same deception.]

The army, moved by faith in so great and so unusual a miracle and converted to repentance, immediately killed Scribonianus, who was abandoned on the fifth day, and continued to observe its former military oath.

It is well known that nothing has ever been more grievous or destructive to the city of Rome than civil wars. Therefore, on account of the arrival of the apostle Peter and the tender beginnings of the Christians, still scarcely numerous and only just emerging into the profession of the holy faith,

[Note: “For the profession.” I found this reading in the Cologne manuscript and have no doubt that Orosius wrote it, rather than “for departure.” LAUT.]

who could deny that this rising tyranny and that emerging civil war were divinely suppressed? Who could point to a similar example from earlier times of the suppression of civil wars?

In the fourth year of his reign, Claudius, wishing to display himself as a ruler useful to the state,

[Note: Some manuscripts read “wishing to show himself a useful ruler to the republic.”]

sought war everywhere and victory in every direction. Accordingly, he undertook an expedition against Britain. The island had been thrown into turmoil because deserters had not been restored;

[Note: “Had not been restored.” The Cologne and Maternus manuscripts have the most correct reading, instead of “had not been returned.” But whoever refuses to accept this word I refer to the jurists. LAUT.—I also found it in the better manuscripts.]

he crossed over into the island, which no one had dared to approach either before Julius Caesar or after him.

There, to use the words of Suetonius Tranquillus, without any battle or bloodshed, within a very few days he received the greater part of the island into submission.

[Note: “As Suetonius puts it.” Suetonius, *Claudius* 17. FABR.—Most manuscripts delete the conjunction in “and he crossed over.”]

He also added the Orkney Islands, situated in the Ocean beyond Britain, to the Roman Empire and returned to Rome in the sixth month after his departure.

Let anyone now compare, if he wishes, under one island, time with time, war with war, Caesar with Caesar.

[Note: “Under one island.” I found this reading in four manuscripts: two Florentine manuscripts, the Utrecht manuscript, my own, and Perizonius. All the common editions read “island and island,” which is wholly inept. For he is speaking of one island, Britain, where first Caesar, but not without disaster, and then Claudius, most successfully, waged war. Orosius is therefore not speaking of an island that can be compared with an island; he is comparing the deeds and victories by which he says Claudius took the palm from Caesar in Britain.]

For I make no comparison concerning the outcome,

[Note: “I make no comparison.” Thus read several manuscripts and the Augustan edition. Others have “I do not report anything.”]

since one was a most fortunate victory and the other a most bitter disaster. And so at last let Rome recognize that, through the hidden providence of God, in the advancement of its affairs it had previously possessed a share of good fortune; once it has accepted this recognition, it enjoys complete happiness, insofar as it is not corrupted by the stumbling-blocks of blasphemy.

In the same year of his reign a most severe famine occurred throughout Syria,

[Note: “The very severe famine.” Concerning this famine, see Luke in the *Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 11; Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XX, chapter 2; and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 8. FABR.]

which the prophets had also foretold.

[Note: “Had foretold.” The third Leiden manuscript reads “had announced beforehand.”]

For the needs of the Christians at Jerusalem, Helena, queen of the Adiabenes, who had converted to the faith of Christ, supplied grain brought from Egypt in the greatest abundance.

[Note: “Converted to the faith of Christ.” The falsity of this statement has been demonstrated at length from Josephus by the great Scaliger in his notes on Eusebius, p. 192, and by the distinguished Wesseling, who, in an entire chapter, showed that Queen Helena, together with her sons Izates and Monobazus, had adopted Jewish rites, *Observations*, Book I, chapter 9, p. 28.]

In the fifth year of his reign, between the islands of Thera and Therasia, an island rose from the depths, extending over a distance of thirty stadia.

[Note: “Between Thera.” Cassiodorus and Eusebius also have this reading in the *Chronicle*. Concerning Thera and Therasia, see Strabo, Book X. Some editions introduce “a monstrous beast” instead of “island.”]

In the seventh year of his reign,

[Note: “In the seventh year of his reign.” Concerning this sedition, see Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XX, chapter 4, and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 19.]

under the procurator of Judea, Cumanus, such a great sedition arose at Jerusalem during the days of Unleavened Bread that, when the people were hemmed in at the exit of the gates, thirty thousand Jews are reported to have been struck down by slaughter and suffocated by the crush.

In the ninth year of the same reign, Josephus reports that the Jews were expelled from Rome by Claudius.

[Note: “Josephus reports this.” Spanheim says that Orosius falsely claims this to be found in Josephus, *Works*, p. 558.]

But Suetonius moves me more, for he says as follows:

[Note: “But Suetonius moves me more.” Suetonius, *Claudius* 24. FABR.]

“Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome, who were continually rioting at the instigation of Christ.”

Whether Claudius ordered Jews who were rioting against Christ to be restrained and suppressed, or whether he also wished Christians to be expelled at the same time, as people belonging to a related religion,

[Note: “As people belonging to a related religion.” Compare what we wrote in the notes to Tertullian’s *Apologeticus*, p. 503.]

cannot in any way be determined.

Nevertheless, in the following year such a great famine occurred at Rome that the emperor, seized by the people in the middle of the Forum and shamefully attacked with insults and fragments of bread, barely escaped the fury of the enraged crowd by fleeing through a back door into the palace.

[Note: “Through a back door.” The Latins call this a rear entrance. Suetonius reports the same event, chapter 18, saying that Claudius “could escape to the palace only with difficulty and through a back door.”]

After a short interval he killed thirty-five senators and three hundred Roman knights on the most trivial pretexts. He himself died with unmistakable signs of poisoning.

[Note: “With unmistakable signs of poisoning.” Concerning Tiberius, at the end of the preceding chapter, Orosius cautiously wrote that he died “amid ambiguous signs of poisoning.” Concerning Claudius, who was killed by poisonous mushrooms through the agency of Agrippina and Nero, the matter was so obvious that his successor Nero was not ashamed to say that mushrooms were food for the gods. I once saw at Amsterdam, in the collection of Gerard Schaakius, a silver medallion of exceptional beauty and quality commemorating that deification of Claudius, accomplished through mushrooms. Nero ordered it struck in honor of his father, who had already been made divine; his head is visible on the reverse. I have also appended another small bronze coin from our museum. It was struck in some colony and likewise displays the heads of Claudius and Nero; in keeping with the adoption, it was struck while Claudius was alive, since letters remain beside his head indicating his consulship; it was struck [the source breaks off].]

## CHAPTER VII. The Depraved Character and Criminal Deeds of Nero Claudius Caesar
In the year 808 from the founding of the City, Nero Caesar, the fifth emperor after Augustus, gained the principate and remained in it for not quite fourteen years. He followed—or rather surpassed—his uncle Gaius Caligula in every vice and crime, exercising wantonness, lust, luxury, avarice, and cruelty through every conceivable offense.

[Note: Nero Caesar. If you wish to learn about the life and deeds of Nero, read, besides Suetonius and Dio’s Epitome, Tacitus, Books XIII, XIV, XV, and XVI. FABR.]

Driven by wantonness, he visited almost all the theaters of Italy and Greece, even adopting the disgrace of various costumes; he often imagined that he had surpassed heralds, cithara-players, tragic actors, and charioteers.

[Note: *Cerices*. The printed editions have *cerites* and *scenicos*; although the former may be genuine, the text has been properly restored. For among the Greeks, κήρυκες (*kērykes*) are theatrical performers. LAUT.—In the manuscripts I found these readings: *ceritas* in three Leiden manuscripts (the fourth has *scenicos*), in the Groningen Collection, and in the Perizonius manuscript; in the second Florence manuscript, *cerriscas*; in the third, as also in my manuscript, *cericas*, which comes closest to *cerycas*, as Beroaldus emends it in his notes to Suetonius, p. 671.]

Moreover, he was so agitated by such great lusts that he is reported not to have refrained even from his mother, sister, or any respect owed to blood relationship; and he married a man, being himself received by a man as a wife.

His luxury was so unrestrained that he fished with golden nets drawn out by purple cords, and bathed in cold and hot perfumes.

[Note: *Unrestrained*. The Augustan edition has *ineffrenatae*; it intended *infrenatae*.]

[Note: *Bathed*. Some manuscripts have *lavaretur*.]

He is also said never to have made a journey with fewer than a thousand carriages.

Finally, he turned the burning of Rome into a spectacle for his own pleasure.

[Note: The burning of the city of Rome. Tacitus discusses this fire in Book XV. FABR.]

For six days and seven nights, while the city burned, the imperial eyes feasted upon the sight. The warehouses built of squared stone, and those great ancient apartment blocks which the spreading flames could not reach, were shaken and set on fire by massive engines once prepared for foreign wars; the unhappy populace was driven toward the shelter of monuments and tombs.

[Note: *Which, as he moved about, etc.* The first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, read *qua* (“by which”) instead of *quas* (“which”); this is not unreasonable.]

He himself watched the scene from that lofty Maecenatian tower and, delighted by the beauty of the flames—as he said—sang the *Iliad* in tragic costume.

His avarice was so outrageous that, after this burning of the City—which Augustus had boasted he had made marble after finding it brick—

[Note: *Had restored*. The Perizonius manuscript has *reliquisse* (“had left”).]

he allowed no one to approach the remains of his property, but himself carried away everything that had survived the flames in any manner.

[Note: *The remains of the burned things*. Thus the Venetian manuscript; all the others read *suarum* (“of his own things”), which History declares to be preferable. LAUT.—Indeed, Suetonius insists that the true reading should not be disturbed. In chapter 38 he has the same words: “He allowed no one to approach the remains of his property.”]

[Note: *A hundred times a hundred thousand, etc.* Orosius relates this, though Casaubon says he does not know from what source it was taken, in his notes to Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 38.]

He ordered the Senate to provide him annually with a hundred million sesterces for expenses. He deprived very many senators of their property without any stated reason. In a single day, applying torture as well, he completely wiped out the entire assessed wealth of all the merchants.

He was so maddened by a frenzy of cruelty that he killed a large part of the Senate and nearly destroyed the equestrian order. Nor did he abstain even from parricide: he ruthlessly brought down his mother, brother, sister, wife, and all his other relatives and relations.

[Note: His mother, brother, etc. Agrippina, Britannicus, Octavia, and Poppaea. I have chosen to append exceptional coins of all of them. The first coin, from my own collection, is silver and exceptionally beautiful; it displays the facing heads of Agrippina and Nero. The second, also preserved by me and made of bronze, displays the face of Britannicus, as the Greek inscription confirms. The surviving portion of the letters and the double axe, commonly seen on the coins of that city, show that it was struck at Thyatira. The third is a Greek coin of the unhappy Octavia, with Nero’s head on the other side; the people of Teos struck it, and Morellius published it in his *Specimen*. Finally, I found a fourth in what was once the Marckian Museum, or that of Monsieur de Leur; it too is bronze and was struck in a Greek city, displaying the portraits of Poppaea and Nero, with their names and titles attached. [Column 1077D; Column 1078B.]]

His heap of crimes was increased by the audacity of his impiety toward God. For he was the first at Rome to inflict punishments and deaths upon Christians, and ordered them to be tortured throughout all the provinces by a similar persecution. In an attempt to eradicate the very name, he killed the most blessed apostles of Christ: Peter by the cross, Paul by the sword.

[Note: Christians subjected to punishments. Tacitus mentions this in Book XV; Suetonius, chapter 16. Read Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 52; Hegesippus, Book III; and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 25. FABR.]

Soon afterward, disasters arising on every side overwhelmed the wretched city in heaps. For in the following autumn such a pestilence settled upon the City that thirty thousand deaths were entered in the records of Libitina. Then the British disaster followed immediately, in which two leading towns were seized amid the great destruction and slaughter of citizens and allies.

Furthermore, after the loss of the great provinces of Armenia in the East, Roman legions were sent beneath the Parthian yoke, and Syria was retained only with difficulty. In Asia three cities—Laodicea, Hierapolis, and Colossae—collapsed in an earthquake.

But when Nero learned that Galba had been proclaimed emperor in Spain by the army,

[Note: Galba in Spain. I possess a coin of this emperor, larger than those usually called of the first size. On it is an elegant representation of Galba addressing the soldiers by whom he had been made emperor; I have appended a drawing of it. [Column 1078D.]]

his whole spirit and hope collapsed. While he was devising incredible evils to disturb—or rather overthrow—the state, the Senate declared him an enemy. Fleeing in the most disgraceful manner, he killed himself at the fourth milestone from the City, and with him the entire family of the Caesars was destroyed.

[Note: *He killed himself*. Some editions omit *sese*.]

[Note: *Was destroyed*. The second Florence manuscript has *consummata est* (“was completed”).]

## CHAPTER VIII. The rule, character, and crimes of Galba, Otho, and Vitellius

[Note: *In the year from the City, etc.* The third Florence manuscript and certain old editions count two fewer years.]

In the year 824 from the founding of the City, Galba seized power in Spain.

[Note: Galba in Spain. Read Tacitus, Book XV, and Suetonius. Above all, Plutarch’s carefully written life of Galba should be read. He also described Otho; Xiphilinus, Suetonius, Eutropius, and others discuss him. FABR.]

As soon as he learned of Nero’s death, he came to Rome. Since he offended everyone by his avarice, cruelty, and sluggishness, he adopted Piso, a noble and energetic young man, as his son and successor. With him he was slaughtered by Otho in the seventh month of his reign.

Rome paid for the recent injuries inflicted upon the Christian religion with the slaughter of rulers and the outbreak of civil wars. Those standards of the legions which, at the arrival of the apostle Peter in the City, had been divinely restrained from being torn down and used to stir up the civil war then being prepared by Scribonianus, after Peter had been killed in the City and Christians had been mangled by various punishments, broke loose throughout the whole world.

[Note: *In the City*. The Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, add *Roma* (“Rome”). Then, instead of *agitarentur* (“were being stirred up”), the second Florence manuscript reads *agerentur* (“were being carried on”).]

For Galba had immediately risen in Spain; when he was soon overthrown, Otho in Rome, Vitellius in Germany, and Vespasian in Syria simultaneously seized authority and arms. Even unwillingly, let them acknowledge both the power and the mercy of God: in Christian times they may observe with what speed such great fires of war were both kindled and quenched, although previously great and prolonged disasters had arisen from the slightest causes, while now the crashing uproar of immense evils resounding everywhere was quieted with the least effort.

[Note: *Resounding*. The Augustan edition has *increpantes* (“reproaching”); the Venetian manuscripts have *constrepantes* (“resounding”).]

[Note: *Quieted*. I read *soporentur* (“were lulled to sleep”).]

For by then there was at Rome, although harassed by persecution, a Church that prayed to Christ, the judge of all, even for its enemies and persecutors.

Accordingly, after Otho had seized power amid tumult and slaughter, following the killing of Galba and Piso at Rome, and soon learned that Vitellius had been created emperor in Gaul by the Germanic legions,

[Note: *He prepared a civil war*. The Perizonius manuscript has *bellum civile molitur* (“he is preparing a civil war”), followed by *cumque*, etc.]

he set about a civil war. At first he emerged victorious in three minor battles: one near the Alps, another near Placentia, and a third near the place called Castor.

[Note: *Castor’s*. Perizonius has *Castores*, as do the two Florence manuscripts. Nevertheless, Suetonius reads *Castoris*, chapter 9, and *ad Castoris* (“at Castor’s”), which is the name of the place.]

But in the fourth battle, at Bebriacum,

[Note: Bebriacum. Tacitus also has *Bebriacum*, Book VIII of the *Histories*, as do Eutropius, Book VII, Suetonius, and Sextus Aurelius. Yet I do not think the reading in Gualther’s book should be neglected, namely *Betriacum*, since Plutarch also has Βητριακόν (*Bētriakon*) in his *Life of Otho*. FABR.]

when he realized that his men were being defeated, he killed himself in the third month after beginning to rule.

[Note: *In the third month*. This explains why bronze coins of this emperor are said not to be found—that is, coins struck by the monetary triumvirs of the Roman Senate. For several gold coins and many silver ones are known, and Egyptian bronze coins also survive, such as one I once examined in the Marckian Museum and had carefully drawn. I have nevertheless seen one bronze coin of the second size, neither Greek nor Egyptian, but marked with Latin letters; it might rightly be called a cross for antiquarians, since, to tell the truth, I would not dare confidently decide whether it is counterfeit or genuine. It is preserved at Amsterdam in the richly endowed collection of Goswin Uilenbroek. I have appended drawings of both coins. Among other places, such coins are also preserved at Aix-en-Provence in the select collection of Lebret. One Greek coin of Otho is kept there, depicting his victory, with the bust of a winged goddess attached at the shoulders. A coin of Claudius is also preserved in the same collection, of the type believed to have been struck at Antioch and marked with an *S.C.* enclosed in a laurel wreath. This coin bears at the neck a mark comprising the joined letters expressing Otho’s name and the title of emperor. I have also gladly appended drawings of these.]

Vitellius, victorious, came to Rome. There, while he acted cruelly and wickedly in many ways and, with an incredible appetite for gluttony, burdened human life with disgrace, after learning about Vespasian he first attempted to lay down the imperial power.

[Note: *First attempted to lay down the imperial power*. Thus it stands in the Augustan manuscript and the other manuscripts; the common editions have *non deponere est molitus* (“he did not attempt to lay down”), as though it were not. The Florence manuscripts later read *post* (“after”), while some have *postea* (“afterward”).]

Later, encouraged by certain people, he drove Sabinus, the brother of Vespasian, who at that time suspected no evil, together with the other Flavians into the Capitol.

[Note: Sabinus, Vespasian’s brother. Xiphilinus says of Sabinus in his account of Vitellius: συγγενὴς οὗτος Οὐεσπασιανοῦ, “This man was a relative of Vespasian.” Tacitus, Eutropius, and the others agree with Orosius. FABR.]

After setting the temple on fire, and with flame and ruin mingled together, he gave them all a common and simultaneous death and burial.

[Note: *And gave them a burial mound*. The common editions have *tumultum dedit* (“he gave a tumult”). They certainly gave him that. LAUT.—It is surprising that Fabricius could have accepted this reading in certain editions, since the Bolswing edition had already supplied the better reading, which is also found in the Augustan edition, in the better manuscripts, and was accepted by Scottus. Once he discovered the error, Fabricius himself corrected it in one of his own copies.]

Afterward, when his army abandoned him for Vespasian’s cause, he became frightened as the enemy was already approaching. He had shut himself into a small room near the palace; he was dragged out of it in the most disgraceful manner and led naked through the Sacred Way, while everyone threw dung into his face. He was brought into the Forum and, in the eighth month after he had usurped the throne,

[Note: The brief reign of Vitellius explains why his bronze coins of the first size are very rare, while those inscribed in Greek are exceedingly rare. Hence Vaillant declares in *Numismata Imperatorum Graecorum*, p. 20: “Vitellius’s coins are seen only from Egypt, and are rarer than those of Otho.” I have included this all the more willingly so as not to deprive curious readers of the sight of two exceedingly rare and outstanding coins of this emperor, which I carefully preserve in the more private part of my collection. One, remarkable for its beauty and completeness, displays Vitellius’s bare head with this inscription: ΑΥΛΟΣ ΟΥΙΤΕΛΛΙΟΣ ΚΑΙΣΑΡ ΓΕΡΜΑΝΙΚΟΣ, “Aulus Vitellius Caesar Germanicus.” On the other side Victory is seen hastening forward with a wreath and laurel; the first year of his reign is indicated by the letters ΛΥΚΑΒΑΝΤΟΣ Α, “the first year.” The type celebrates victory over Otho.

The other coin, likewise inscribed in Greek, is more noteworthy because it was not struck in Egypt and thus belongs to a class whose existence escaped Vaillant, although no one saw more coins of this kind than he did. It displays the laureate head of Vitellius, with the inscription ΑΥΛΟΣ ΟΥΙΤΕΛΛΙΟΣ ΚΑΙΣΑΡ ΣΕΒ..., “Aulus Vitellius Caesar Aug[ustus].” On the other side appears Diana Lucifera, or Ceres, holding a torch in either hand. From the letters worn away by the injury of time, three letters, ΤΕΑ., remain. They may designate Telmessus, a city of Caria, Lycia, or Pisidia, unless we read ΤΕΑ. as the middle part of a proper name, or some other city lies hidden under those letters. Both coins are unquestionably genuine. [Column 1082C; Column 1083C.]

I also possess bronze coins of the first size, already published by others; among the rest, I preserve two of the second size, the first of which has not previously been published with that type. It too celebrates victory over Otho, which the emperor attributes to the agreement of the armies. The later coin boasts of restored liberty, which the voracious beast, devoted to his throat and belly rather than a human being, had miserably oppressed.]

He was tortured at the Gemonian stairs by repeated stabbings with countless tiny blows and was then dragged away by a hook,

[Note: *And thrown into the Tiber*. The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Groningen Collection, has *in Tiberim missus* (“sent into the Tiber”).]

and cast into the Tiber; he was denied even a common burial.

[Note: *Many, etc.* See Tacitus, Book IV of the *Histories*, chapters 1 and 2, where the misery of the City at that time is described more fully, as well as how the soldiers acted as conquerors through slaughter and plunder, while Domitian, the emperor’s son, acted through sexual outrages and adulteries.]

For several days, Vespasian’s soldiers raged against the Senate and the Roman people through many abominable forms of indiscriminate slaughter.

## CHAPTER IX. How Vespasian Augustus and Titus suppressed the rebellious Jews, leveled the city of Jerusalem and its temple to the ground, and their other deeds

In the year 825 from the founding of the City, after that brief but turbulent period of tyrants had been dispelled, a tranquil calm returned under Vespasian’s leadership.

For, to begin somewhat earlier,

[Note: *Somewhat earlier*. The second Florence manuscript has *paulo anterius* (“a little earlier”); certain editions have *latius* (“more broadly”).]

after the passion of Christ, the Jews, wholly deprived of God’s favor, were surrounded on every side by every kind of evil. Certain men, misled on Mount Carmel by oracles promising that leaders arising from Judaea would gain possession of power,

[Note: *On Mount Carmel*. This is correctly read in the manuscripts. Read Suetonius, *Vespasian*, chapter 4; Josephus’s books on the Jewish War provide everything abundantly. FABR.]

and drawing the prediction toward themselves, broke out into rebellion.

[Note: *And after the Roman garrisons had been destroyed*. The fourth Leiden manuscript has *cunctis exstinctisque* (“after all had been destroyed”); the Augustan edition has *cumque exstinctis Romanis* (“and when the Romans had been destroyed”).]

After destroying the Roman garrisons, they also defeated the governor of Syria who had come to bring assistance, having seized the eagle and slaughtered the troops.

[Note: *The eagle having been seized*. This is taken from Suetonius, where the same account occurs in *Vespasian*, chapter 4. Learned men have tried both to emend and to explain Suetonius’s words in various ways. I cannot pass over Christian Wormius’s explanation, which I found in Book II of his work *On the Corrupt Traces of Hebrew Antiquities in Tacitus and Martial*. His words, on page 4, are these:

“An especially noteworthy passage of Suetonius offers me the means of demonstrating this, in the fourth chapter of his *Life of Flavius Vespasian*, p. 462: ‘The Jews, drawing matters toward themselves, rebelled; after killing the commander and seizing the eagle, they routed the consular governor of Syria who had come to bring assistance.’ Some deny that the governor of Syria was killed—namely Gessius Florus—although Josephus expressly writes in his *Life*, p. 1000: Ὁ δ᾽ ἐπελθὼν καὶ συμβαλὼν μάχῃ ἐνικήθη, πολλῶν τῶν μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ πεσόντων, καὶ γίνεται τοῦ Γεσσίου πταῖσμα συμφορὰ τοῦ παντὸς ἡμῶν ἔθνους. ‘He returned, engaged in battle, and was defeated, many of those with him falling; and the defeat of Gessius became the calamity of our entire nation.’

“Many claim that Suetonius gratuitously says the Roman eagle was seized, although, if the matter is properly examined, the historian is treated with great injustice. Suetonius says that Florus came to bring assistance after the eagle had been seized—that is, he arrived long after the eagle had been taken. But how does Suetonius understand the eagle to have been seized? In battle? Certainly not. Rather, he refers to the ἀετὸν χρύσεον μέγαν, ‘the great golden eagle,’ which Herod had caused to be hung as a symbol of Roman sovereignty over the greater part of the temple. The Jewish populace threw this down amid great turmoil, as Josephus records in Book XVII of the *Jewish Antiquities* and Book I of the *Jewish War*.”]

To them Nero sent Vespasian, who took his elder son Titus with him among the commanders and transferred many strong legions with him into Syria.

After he had captured many of their towns, he confined the Jews in the city of Jerusalem, where they had gathered especially for the feast, by means of a siege.

[Note: *Into the City*. The Augustan edition has *in urbe* (“in the city”).]

When he learned of Nero’s death, and at the urging of many kings and commanders—especially Josephus, the Jewish leader, who, after being captured and thrown into chains, had stated with complete confidence, as Suetonius reports, that he would soon be released by that same man, but as emperor—Vespasian gained the imperial power.

He left his son Titus in the camp to direct the siege of Jerusalem and traveled to Rome through Alexandria.

[Note: *Was thrown into chains*. Some manuscripts have *coerceretur* (“was restrained”).]

[Note: *But as emperor*. Some manuscripts have *sed ab imperatore* (“but by the emperor”).]

[Note: *To direct*. The second Florence manuscript deletes *ad* and reads *procuratione* (“in the direction”), with *procuratore* (“director”) written above it.]

After learning of Vitellius’s death, he remained for a short time in Alexandria,

[Note: *For a short time*. The third Leiden manuscript and the Groningen Collection have *paululum* (“a little while”).]

while Titus, pressing the Jews with a great and prolonged siege, at last broke through the city walls with engines and every kind of military apparatus, though not without much bloodshed among his own men.

But to storm the inner fortification of the temple, which a multitude of priests and leaders defended after shutting themselves inside it,

[Note: *Shut inside*. The Groningen Collection has *reclusam*; the Augustan edition has *inclusam*. All the other manuscripts preserve the common reading.]

greater force and delay were required.

After it had nevertheless been brought under his power, he admired its workmanship and antiquity and deliberated for a long time whether he should burn it as an incitement to the enemy or preserve it as a memorial of victory. But since the Church of God was already flourishing abundantly throughout the whole world, it had to be removed by God’s judgment as something withered and empty, useful for no good purpose.

Accordingly, Titus, proclaimed emperor by the army, burned and demolished the temple in Jerusalem. From the day of its original construction until the day of its final destruction, it had stood for 1,102 years.

[Note: *In Jerusalem*. The Augustan and second Florence editions delete the preceding word.]

[Note: *Final*. The second Florence manuscript has *ultimam*, “the final [day],” as somewhat earlier it has *prima*, “the first [day].”]

He leveled all the walls of the city to the ground.

[Note: *All*. Absent from the second Leiden manuscript.]

[Note: *Leveled*. The fourth Leiden manuscript, the Augustan manuscript, and the second Florence manuscript have *aequavit* (“made equal”).]

Cornelius and Suetonius report that six hundred thousand Jews were killed in that war.

[Note: Six hundred thousand Jews. The same number is found in Eusebius. Besides Josephus, read Hegesippus, Book V. FABR.]

Josephus the Jew, who had commanded them in that war and had obtained pardon and favor with Vespasian on account of the previously mentioned prediction,

[Note: Josephus writes. The second Florence manuscript has *scripsit* (“wrote”).]

writes that 1,100,000 perished by the sword and famine. The remaining Jews, he says, were scattered throughout the world under various conditions, and their number is reported to have been 90,000 persons.

[Note: *Ninety*. The third Leiden manuscript and the Groningen Collection have *nongenta* (“nine hundred”).]

[Note: Vespasian and Titus. Many coins of various kinds celebrate this victory and triumph. I shall mention a beautiful unpublished coin that I preserve, of the first size, on which Victory hands a trophy to the emperor standing opposite; the inscription VICTORIAE AUGUSTI, “To the Victory of Augustus,” explains the purpose of the type.

To commemorate the concord of Titus and Domitian, I shall also mention another beautiful unpublished coin in my possession, of the same size. On it Domitian and Titus stand facing one another in togas and join their right hands, with the goddess Pietas between them. The inscription on this splendid coin is PIETAS AUGUSTI, “The Piety of Augustus.”]

Vespasian and Titus, the emperors, entered the City while celebrating a magnificent triumph over the Jews. Among the 320 triumphs that had been celebrated from the founding of the City up to that time, this was a spectacle beautiful and previously unknown to all mortals: father and son were carried in a single triumphal chariot and brought back a most glorious victory over those who had attacked father and son.

[Note: *Up to that time*. The Augustan edition and several manuscripts prefer *usque ad id tempus* (“up to that time”).]

[Note: *It was a spectacle*. The final word is absent from the Augustan edition.]

Immediately suppressing all wars and disturbances, at home and abroad, they proclaimed peace throughout the whole world and decreed that the double-gated shrine of Janus should be closed—only the sixth time, they judged, since the founding of the City.

[Note: *Only the sixth time*. Strictly speaking, it was the seventh; but Nero is not counted because he closed it without cause, as Casaubon says. See his notes to Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 22.]

[Note: *And disturbances*. Not found in the Perizonius manuscript.]

Rightly was the same honor paid to vengeance for the Lord’s Passion that had also been assigned to his Nativity.

Then, without any disturbance of war, the Roman state advanced to immense power. Achaea, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, Samos, Thrace, Cilicia,

[Note: Commagene. Compare Spanheim, *Orbis Romanus*, p. 260.]

and Commagene, now for the first time reduced to provinces, obeyed Roman governors and laws.

[Note: Achaea, etc. The same account is found in Eutropius, Book VII, and Suetonius, *Vespasian*, chapter 8. FABR.]

In the ninth year of his reign, three cities in Cyprus collapsed in an earthquake, and Rome suffered a great pestilence. Vespasian died in his own villa near the Sabines, in the ninth year of his principate, from a disorder of the bowels.

[Note: The year from the founding of the City. Xiphilinus and Suetonius write extensively about the life of Titus; Eutropius and Sextus Aurelius more briefly. FABR.]

In the year 828 from the founding of the City, Titus, excluding Otho and Vitellius from the number of the rulers, was the eighth emperor after Augustus and reigned for two years after Vespasian.

His rule was so peaceful that he is said not to have shed the blood of anyone at all in administering the state. Yet at that time a sudden fire broke out at Rome and burned a great many public buildings.

Then the summit of Mount Vesuvius also burst open and is said to have poured forth great fires,

[Note: Vesuvius. Read about the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in Xiphilinus’s account of Titus; Suetonius mentions it in *Titus*, chapter 8, and Pliny in his *Letters*. FABR.]

which destroyed the neighboring parts of the region, together with towns and inhabitants, in torrents of flame.

[Note: *The neighboring region*. The Groningen Collection has *vicinas regiones* (“the neighboring regions”).]

Titus died of illness, amid the immense mourning of all, in the same villa in which his father had died.

## CHAPTER X. The rule, achievements, and crimes of Flavius Domitian Caesar

In the year 830 from the founding of the City,

[Note: Domitian. On Domitian, read Xiphilinus, Suetonius, Eutropius, and Aurelius Victor. FABR.]

Domitian, the brother of Titus and the ninth emperor after Augustus, succeeded his brother in the kingship.

For fifteen years he gradually advanced through every degree of crime until he dared to attack the Church of Christ, firmly established throughout the world, by issuing everywhere edicts of the most savage persecution.

[Note: *To this point*. In one of the Leiden manuscripts this is deleted; in another it reads *modestus ad hoc* (“modest up to this point”). A little later, instead of *trusit* (“drove into exile”), the Augustan edition has *miserabiliter trusit* (“drove miserably into exile”).]

He fell into such arrogance that he ordered himself to be called, written of, and worshiped as lord and god.

He killed the most distinguished men of the Senate, some openly for reasons of both envy and plunder, and drove others into exile, ordering them to be murdered there.

In the excesses of his lust he did whatever can be imagined.

[Note: *Can be imagined*. The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Groningen Collection, has *excogitari* (“can be devised”).]

[Note: *Very many buildings of the city*. The two Florence manuscripts have *plurima urbis* (“very many buildings of the city”), but with the following words destroyed.]

He built a great many buildings in the city, after destroying the resources of the Roman people.

He waged war against the Germans and Dacians through his generals, with equal ruin to the state: while at Rome he himself tore apart the Senate and people, abroad an army badly maneuvered was worn down by the continuous slaughter inflicted by the enemy.

For if I were to unfold at length how great were the battles fought by Diurpaneus, king of the Dacians, against the commander Fuscus, and how great were the Roman disasters,

[Note: *Diurpaneus*. Gualther’s book has *Diurpanis*; Xiphilinus names the Dacian king Decebalus. Read him, since Tacitus, whom Orosius mentions, has not come down to us. FABR.]

I would unfold them at length, unless Cornelius Tacitus, who composed this history with the greatest care, had said that Sallustius Crispus and many other authors had decreed that the number of those killed should be withheld, and that he himself had especially chosen the same course.

Nevertheless, Domitian, carried away by the most perverse boasting, celebrated a triumph under the name of conquered enemies over destroyed legions. Inflated with the same arrogance by which he wished to be worshiped as a god, he ordered persecution to be inflicted upon Christians, being the second after Nero to do so.

[Note: The second after Nero. Compare Tertullian’s *Apology* and the notes to it, p. 60.]

At that time the most blessed apostle John was also exiled to the island of Patmos.

[Note: The most blessed John. Sophronius writes that the apostle John was sent into exile in the thirteenth year of Domitian’s reign. The same account appears in the *Chronicle* of Eusebius. FABR.]

Among the Jews, it was likewise ordered that those of David’s lineage should be sought out and killed through the severity of tortures and the bloodiest interrogation, while the holy prophets were both envied and believed, as though someone from David’s seed might still arise who could obtain the kingdom.

Nevertheless, Domitian was soon cruelly killed by his own people in the palace.

[Note: *Cruelly*. The Perizonius manuscript has *justissime* (“with complete justice”).]
