His corpse was carried out by undertakers on a common bier and buried in the most disgraceful manner.

## CHAPTER XI. The rule of Cocceius Nerva Caesar

In the year 846 from the founding of the City,

[Note: Although Eutropius. Eutropius writes this at the beginning of Book VIII. FABR.]

although Eutropius wrote that this was the fiftieth year,

[Note: Nerva. On Nerva, read Xiphilinus, Eutropius, and Aurelius. FABR.]

Nerva, a very old man, was made emperor—the tenth after Augustus—by Petronius, prefect of the praetorian guard, and Parthenius the eunuch,

[Note: The murderer of Domitian. The second Florence manuscript has *interfecto Domitiano* (“with Domitian killed”).]

the murderer of Domitian.

[Note: Trajan, etc. Coins testifying to this adoption, already published by antiquarians, survive. Therefore I prefer to present here an unpublished Greek coin, one of the rarer coins of this emperor. Around Nerva’s laureate head is written ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡ ΝΕΡΟΥΑ ΚΑΙΣΑΡ ΣΕΒΑΣτος, “Emperor Nerva Caesar Augustus.” On the other side appears a hexastyle temple, with the inscription ΚΥΖικήνων ΕΠΙ Τίτου ΠΟΜΠΩΝΙΟΥ ΑΝθυπάτου B, “Of the Cyzicenes, under Titus Pomponius, proconsul, year two.” This coin is notable both otherwise and because the title and name of the proconsul are appended. It is preserved in the museum of Hermann Horstius.]

He adopted Trajan as his successor, through whom he truly, by divine providence, provided for the distressed state.

[Note: *The distressed state*. The excellent Augustan edition adds *ad felicitatem afflictae reipublicae* (“for the happiness of the distressed state”) and reads the remainder as *divina provisione consuluit* (“he provided by divine providence”). It is correctly written that, by divine providence, provision for the distressed state was made through the emperor Trajan. Under Nerva, since he was an aged emperor, the state was indeed revived during his brief reign; but under Trajan, and during his sufficiently long reign, it flexed its strength, not merely repelling the barbarians but conquering almost the entire East. Thus Rome seemed to itself to aspire to eternity, a flattering title it employed, as is clear from this remarkable medallion preserved among the Pisan Coins.]

In his first edict he recalled all exiles. Accordingly, the apostle John, released by this general act of clemency, returned to Ephesus. After completing one year of his reign, Nerva died, overcome by illness.

[Note: In his first edict, etc. Compare what we noted concerning Tertullian’s *Apology*, p. 61.]

## CHAPTER XII. The rule and achievements of Ulpius Trajan Caesar Augustus
In the year 847 from the founding of the City, Trajan, a Spaniard by birth and the eleventh emperor after Augustus, assumed the reins of government when Nerva handed them over to him, and held them for nineteen years.[^c0122-1] At Agrippina, a city of Gaul, he received the insignia of imperial authority; soon afterward he restored Germany beyond the Rhine to its former condition.[^c0122-2] He subdued many peoples beyond the Danube. He made the regions beyond the Euphrates and Tigris into provinces. He occupied Seleucia, Ctesiphon, and Babylon.

While persecuting the Christians, deceived by error, he was the third after Nero to order that those found everywhere should be compelled to sacrifice to idols and that those who refused should be put to death. When very many were being killed, Pliny the Younger,[^c0122-3] who had been appointed among the other judges to carry out the persecution, informed him by report that these people, apart from their confession of Christ and their respectable gatherings, did nothing contrary to Roman laws, and that, because of the confidence inspired by an innocent confession, death seemed to no one grievous or terrifying. Trajan immediately moderated his edict by more lenient rescripts.[^c0122-4]

Nevertheless, the Golden House at Rome, built by Nero at the expense of all private and public resources,[^c0122-5] was soon afterward consumed by a sudden conflagration, so that it might be understood that the persecution sent also by another against the very monuments of the one from whom it had first arisen was being punished in the author himself.[^c0122-6]

Four cities of Asia were overthrown by an earthquake: Heleia,[^c0122-7] Myrina, Pitane, and Syme; and two cities of Greece, those of the Opuntians and the Oritians. Three cities of Galatia were destroyed by the same earthquake. The Pantheon at Rome was burned by lightning. An earthquake almost completely demolished the city of Antioch.[^c0122-8]

Then, in an astonishing upheaval, the Jews, as though driven mad by frenzy, broke out simultaneously in various parts of the world. Throughout Libya they waged the most savage wars against the inhabitants. The land was then so thoroughly depopulated by the slaughter of its residents that, unless the emperor Hadrian had later brought colonies there from elsewhere, the country would have remained entirely empty, its inhabitants wiped away.[^c0122-9] They disturbed all Egypt, Cyrene, and the Thebaid with bloody uprisings. In Alexandria, however, they were defeated and crushed in battle. War was also brought against the rebels in Mesopotamia by order of the emperor. Thus many thousands of them were destroyed in a vast slaughter.[^c0122-10] Indeed, they destroyed Salamis, a city of Cyprus, after killing all its inhabitants.[^c0122-11]

Trajan, as some report, died at Seleucia, a city of Isauria, from an intestinal discharge.[^c0122-12]

## CHAPTER XIII. Aelius Hadrian Caesar and his reign

In the year 867 from the founding of the City,[^c0122-13] Hadrian, son of Trajan’s cousin,[^c0122-14] the twelfth emperor after Augustus, assumed the principate and ruled for twenty-one years. Through Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, and Aristides of Athens, a man full of faith and wisdom, and through the legate Serenus Granius, he was instructed and educated by books composed concerning the Christian religion. He therefore ordered, by a letter sent to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia,[^c0122-15] that no one should be permitted to condemn Christians without an accusation of crime or proof.

He likewise was immediately called “Father of His Country” in the Senate, beyond the custom of his ancestors,[^c0122-16] and his wife was made Augusta.[^c0122-17] Hadrian regulated the state by the most just laws. He waged war against the Sarmatians and defeated them. The Jews, driven into agitation by the disturbance arising from their crimes and ravaging Palestine, once their own province, he finally subdued in a slaughter of the utmost severity.[^c0122-18] He also avenged the Christians whom they, under the leadership of Cochebas, tortured because they would not support them against the Romans. He ordered that no Jew should have permission to enter Jerusalem, while the city was permitted only to Christians; and he himself restored it to an excellent condition by constructing its walls, ordering that it be called Aelia, from his own praenomen.

## CHAPTER XIV. The reign of Antoninus Pius Caesar

In the year 888 from the founding of the City,[^c0122-19] Antoninus, surnamed Pius, created emperor as the thirteenth after Augustus, governed the state with his sons Aurelius and Lucius for twenty-three years less a fraction,[^c0122-20] so peacefully and reverently that he was deservedly called Pius and Father of His Country.

In his time Valentinus, the arch-heretic, and Cerdo, the teacher of Marcion, came to Rome.[^c0122-21] But Justin the philosopher gave Antoninus a book composed in defense of the Christian religion,[^c0122-22] and he made him favorable toward the Christians.[^c0122-23] Antoninus, seized by illness at the twelfth milestone from the City, died.

## CHAPTER XV. What Marcus Antoninus Verus did during his reign

In the year 911 from the founding of the City,[^c0122-24] Marcus Antoninus Verus, the fourteenth after Augustus, assumed the rule together with his brother Aurelius Commodus,[^c0122-25] and remained in it for nineteen years.[^c0122-26] These men were the first to protect the state on equal terms; afterward they waged war against the Parthians with admirable courage and success.

Lucius Antoninus Verus departed for that war. For Vologaeses, king of the Parthians, had devastated Armenia, Cappadocia, and Lycia in a serious invasion. But Antoninus, through the achievements of his energetic commanders, captured Seleucia, a city of Assyria situated on the Hydaspes River, together with four hundred thousand men, and celebrated a triumph for the Parthian victory with his brother. Not long afterward, while sitting with his brother in a vehicle, he was suffocated by a sudden illness, which the Greeks call *apoplexy*, and died.

After his death Marcus Antoninus alone governed the state. During the Parthian war, however, serious persecutions of Christians, the fourth after Nero, arose in Asia and Gaul at his command, and many of the saints were crowned with martyrdom.[^c0122-27]

A plague followed, spreading through many provinces.[^c0122-28] It devastated all Italy with so great a pestilence that villas, fields, and towns everywhere, left without cultivator or inhabitant, fell into ruins and forests.[^c0122-29] The Roman army and all the legions stationed widely in distant winter quarters are said to have been so depleted that the Marcomannic War, which broke out immediately afterward, was not conducted except with a new levy of soldiers, which Marcus Antoninus kept continually for three years at Carnuntum.[^c0122-30][^c0122-51]

That this war was administered by the providence of God is most clearly demonstrated by many arguments, and above all by a letter of the very serious and restrained emperor.[^c0122-31] For when peoples of barbarous savagery and innumerable in number had risen up—that is, the Marcomanni, Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, Suevi, and almost the whole of Germany—and the army, having advanced as far as the territory of the Quadi, was surrounded by the enemy and, because of the scarcity of water, was suffering a danger from thirst more immediate than that from the enemy,[^c0122-32] certain soldiers, poured out in prayer, publicly invoked the name of Christ with sudden and great steadfastness of faith.[^c0122-33][^c0122-52] So great a force of rain was poured out that it refreshed the Romans most abundantly and without harm, while it terrified the barbarians with frequent strokes of lightning, especially since many of them were killed, and drove them into flight.

The Romans pursued them, cutting them down to the point of annihilation, and won a most glorious victory, one that ought to be preferred to nearly all the triumphal titles of the ancients, with a rough and small number of soldiers but with the most powerful aid of Christ.[^c0122-34] Letters of the emperor Antoninus are also said still to exist among many people, in which he acknowledges that, through the invocation of Christ’s name by Christian soldiers, the thirst was driven away and the victory granted.

Antoninus also associated his son Commodus with the government. He remitted throughout all the provinces the taxes of past years, and ordered that all the malicious records of fiscal lawsuits, which had been heaped up in the Forum, be burned at once. By new constitutions he moderated the harsher laws. Finally, while stationed in Pannonia, he died of a sudden illness.

## CHAPTER XVI. The reigns of Lucius Antoninus Commodus, Publius Aelius Pertinax, and Didius Julianus, Caesars and Augusti

In the year 930 from the founding of the City,[^c0122-35] Lucius Antoninus Commodus, the fifteenth emperor after Augustus, succeeded his father in the government,[^c0122-36] and remained in it for thirteen years.[^c0122-37] He waged war successfully against the Germans.[^c0122-38] Otherwise, corrupted by every disgrace of luxury and obscenity, he very often fought with gladiatorial weapons in the training school and frequently exposed himself to wild beasts in the amphitheater. He also killed very many senators, especially those whom he observed to excel in nobility and industry.

The punishment of the City followed the king’s crimes. For the Capitol was struck by lightning, and the resulting fire, carried by a devouring whirlwind, burned that library, assembled through the care and diligence of the ancestors, together with the nearby buildings. Then another fire, which later broke out at Rome, leveled the temple of Vesta, the palace, and a large part of the City with the ground. Commodus, harmful to everyone, is said to have been strangled and killed in the house of Vestilianus; even while alive he was judged an enemy of the human race.

After him the Senate created the elderly Helvius Pertinax,[^c0122-39] the sixteenth emperor after Augustus. He was killed in the palace in the seventh month after he had begun to rule, through the crime of the jurist Julianus.[^c0122-40]

Julianus, after Pertinax had been murdered, seized the empire. But soon he was defeated in civil war by Severus at the Milvian Bridge[^c0122-41] and was killed, in the seventh month after he had begun to reign. Thus one year was consumed between Pertinax and Julianus.

## CHAPTER XVII. The reign of Septimius Severus Pertinax Caesar Augustus, and how he afflicted the Christians

In the year 944 from the founding of the City,[^c0122-42] Severus, an African from Tripolitania, from the town of Lepcis, wished to be called Pertinax after the name of the emperor whose death he had avenged.[^c0122-53] He was the seventeenth emperor after Augustus and, having obtained the abandoned empire, held it for eighteen years.[^c0122-43] Naturally savage and continually harassed by many wars, he governed the state with great courage indeed, but with the greatest labor.[^c0122-54]

He defeated and killed Pescennius Niger, who had aspired to tyranny in Egypt and Syria, at Cyzicus.[^c0122-55] He subdued with the sword the Jews and Samaritans who were attempting rebellion.[^c0122-44] He overcame the Parthians, the Arabs, and the Adiabenians. In the fifth persecution after Nero he tortured the Christians, and many of the saints throughout the provinces were crowned with martyrdom.

Heavenly vengeance immediately followed this profane presumption of Severus against the Christians and the Church of God.[^c0122-45] For Severus was immediately carried—or rather dragged back—to Gaul from Syria, to a third civil war: he had already waged one at Rome against Julianus and another in Syria against Pescennius; a third was being raised by Clodius Albinus,[^c0122-46] the associate of Julianus in the murder of Pertinax, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul. A great deal of Roman blood was shed on both sides in that war. Albinus, however, was defeated and killed at Lyons.

Severus, victorious in Britain, was dragged there with almost all his allies having perished.[^c0122-47] After repeatedly fighting great and serious battles, he thought that the part of the island which he had recovered should be separated from the remaining unconquered peoples by a rampart. Thus he constructed a great ditch and a very strong wall, additionally strengthened by frequent towers, extending for 132 Roman miles from sea to sea.[^c0122-48] There, near the town of Eboracum, he died of illness.

He left two sons, Bassianus and Geta.[^c0122-49][^c0122-50] Geta, declared a public enemy, died. Bassianus, having assumed the surname Antoninus, obtained the empire.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The reigns of Aurelius Antoninus Caracalla, Opilius Macrinus, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Heliogabalus, and Aurelius Alexander Severus

### Notes

[^c0122-1]: **For nineteen years.** Xiphilinus, drawing from Dio, adds six months; Cassiodorus gives four months and fifteen days.

[^c0122-2]: **He restored Germany beyond the Rhine to its former condition.** He subdued many peoples beyond the Danube. There is an enormous number of coins of every kind celebrating the victories and triumphs of Trajan. I shall append only one from the Pisan *Numismata*, commemorating his arrival in Rome and his return from the Dacian war, together with another Greek and unpublished coin.

On the obverse of the Greek coin is seen the bust of Trajan, laureate; his chest and shoulders are armed with cuirass and aegis, and engraved on the breastplate is a representation of a cavalry expedition, with this inscription around the edge of the coin:

**ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡ ΚΑΙΣΑΡ ΤΡΑΙΑΝΟΣ ΣΕΒΑΣΤΟΣ ΓΕΡΜΑΝΙΚΟΣ ΔΑΚΙΚΟΣ**

“Emperor Caesar Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus.”

On the reverse is a notable representation of victory in the East. For the East is visible, readily recognized by its cloak, scepter, and radiate crown, standing upon a swift four-horse chariot, with its right hand raised, as it is usually represented. Above the horses’ heads flies Victory with a trophy. Beneath is added the sixteenth year of the reign:

**ΛΥΚΑΒΑΝΤΟΣ ΙΞ**

“Year sixteen.”

[^c0122-3]: **Pliny the Younger.** Pliny’s letter to Trajan concerning the Christians is found in Book X.

[^c0122-4]: **He moderated the edict.** He tempered the edict. See the notes on Tertullian’s *Apologeticus*, p. 59.

[^c0122-5]: **At the expense of all private resources.** Some older editions read: “at the expense of so many private [resources],” and so forth.

[^c0122-6]: **In the author himself.** The word *auctore* is absent from the Augustan edition.

[^c0122-7]: **Heleia.** A town of Mesopotamia, not far from Carrhae. Ammianus Marcellinus calls it Hileia; Ptolemy calls it Eleia or Iliia.

[^c0122-8]: **Antioch.** The Gronovian Collection reads *Antiochiae*; but the Augustan edition, the second Florentine manuscript, and Perizonius, together with the Ultrajectine manuscript, read *in Antiochia*. This reading also seems to be favored by the second Florentine manuscript, which writes *in Anthioniciam*.

[^c0122-9]: **Unless Hadrian had later brought colonies there from elsewhere.** The land was so thoroughly depopulated that, unless Hadrian afterward led colonies collected from elsewhere into it, the country would have remained entirely empty, its inhabitants wiped away.

[^c0122-10]: **A vast slaughter.** The wording is simply “many thousands of them were destroyed by a vast slaughter.”

[^c0122-11]: **Indeed, Salamis.** The word *sane*, “indeed” or “certainly,” is absent from some manuscripts, and perhaps conceals some corruption.

[^c0122-12]: **At Seleucia.** This is the reading of Eutropius, Eusebius, and Cassiodorus. Xiphilinus, however, has: “And when he came to Selinus of Cilicia, which we also call Trajanopolis, he suddenly died.”

[^c0122-13]: **Hadrian.** Hadrian’s life, written from Dio by Xiphilinus and from Spartianus, is extant.

[^c0122-14]: **Son of Trajan’s cousin.** This has been edited from the Lyon manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection. It is surprising that the editors retained “daughter of a cousin” without even consulting Spartianus, whose words in *Hadrian*, chapter 1, are: “Hadrian’s father, Aelius Hadrianus, surnamed Afer, was the cousin of the emperor Trajan.”

[^c0122-15]: **By a letter sent to Minucius.** A copy of this letter is read in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 9.

[^c0122-16]: **Father of His Country.** This title is inscribed on nearly all his coins, and indeed on both sides of the medallion found among the Pisan coins. Although the Senate immediately conferred the name Father of His Country on the new emperor, Spartianus indicates, apparently under a show of refusal, that he accepted it: “He postponed the name Father of His Country, which had been conferred on him, immediately and again later, because Augustus had earned this title only late in life” (*Life of Hadrian*, chapter 6).

[^c0122-17]: **And his wife was made Augusta.** Justly so, for it was through her favor and through her faction, acting through Plotina, that he attained the empire. Compare Spartianus, chapters 2 and 4. A notable medallion of Sabina Augusta is found among the Caesarian coins. On it she is likened to Ceres, with her head crowned with ears of grain, and to the Mother of the Gods, carried by a lion.

[^c0122-18]: **The Jews, driven into agitation.** On this war see Xiphilinus, who writes that Hadrian, after establishing a colony at Jerusalem, called the city Aelia Capitolina.

[^c0122-19]: **Antoninus.** The life of Antoninus Pius, written by Capitolinus for Diocletian, is extant.

A very beautiful Greek medallion of this Antoninus came to my attention. On the side bearing the head is this inscription:

**ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡ ΚΑΙΣΑΡ ΤΙΤΟΣ ΑΙΛΙΟΣ ΑΔΡΙΑΝΟΣ ΑΝΤΩΝΙΝΟΣ**

“Emperor Caesar Titus Aelius Hadrianus.”

On the other side the emperor stands in a two-horse chariot and holds with his right hand his wife Faustina, veiled with the *flammeum* like a newly married bride, while holding a spear in his left. By this representation, as though of Bacchus and Ariadne, the Smyrnaeans flatter the emperor, as is clear from the inscription, which reads:

**... ΟΣΣΛΙΑΝΟΣ**

I think this should be read:

**ΑΙΛΙΟΣ ΑΙΛΙΑΝΟΣ ΣΤΡΑΤΗΓΟΣ ΑΝΕΘΗΚΕ ΣΜΥΡΝΑΙΟΣ ΝΕΩΚΟΡΟΙΣ**

“Aelius Aelianus, the strategus, dedicated it to the neocorate Smyrnaeans.”

[^c0122-20]: **With his sons, Aurelius and Lucius.** Marcus Aurelius was a son-in-law of Antoninus Pius, as was Lucius Verus. Aurelius, however, was adopted by Pius at Hadrian’s command, on the condition that he in turn adopt Lucius. See Julius Capitolinus, *Life of Marcus Antoninus*, chapter 5. We have arranged for the likenesses of both to be placed before this note, taken from a coin in the Caesarian Museum.

[^c0122-21]: **Valentinus, the arch-heretic.** See Eusebius, *History*, Book IV, chapter 16 and following. Justin’s book, among his works printed by Robert Estienne, is extant.

[^c0122-22]: **A book composed in defense of the Christian religion.** Perizonius and three Lyon manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “composed concerning the Christian religion.” The first Lyon manuscript then reads: “composed and delivered it to Antoninus.”

[^c0122-23]: **He made him favorable toward the Christians.** The common editions add “men,” but Perizonius and the Augustan edition properly omit it as unnecessary. Perhaps the reading should be: “he made him favorable toward all Christians.”

[^c0122-24]: **Marcus Antoninus.** Capitolinus also wrote this Antoninus’s life. Xiphilinus drew his account of him from Dio.

[^c0122-25]: **Together with his brother Aurelius Commodus.** Marcus Aurelius, while still a boy, initially bore the name of his grandfather Verus and that of Catilius Severus, his maternal great-grandfather. After his father’s death Hadrian called him Annius Verissimus; after receiving the *toga virilis*, he was called Annius Verus. Capitolinus, *Life of Marcus*, chapter 1.

His colleague in the empire, his relation by marriage and adopted son, had the full name Lucius Ceionius Aelius Commodus Verus Antoninus. By Hadrian’s will he was called Aelius; through his association with Antoninus he was called Verus and Antoninus. Capitolinus, *Life of Verus*, chapter 1.

[^c0122-26]: **For nineteen years.** These two were the first to govern the state jointly. Hence their faces are frequently joined, as on the large-module coins from the Royal Museum placed opposite the following page.

[^c0122-27]: **Persecutions of Christians.** The source reads that the persecutions arose “in Asia and Gaul” by his command.

[^c0122-28]: **A plague followed.** On this plague see Lampridius and Eusebius in the *Chronicle*.

[^c0122-29]: **Into ruins and forests.** Three Lyon manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection and the Ultrajectine manuscript, read “into thorns and forests,” which is not unacceptable. A little later, instead of *exortum est*, “broke out,” some manuscripts read *secutum est*, “followed.”

[^c0122-30]: **At Carnuntum.** This city in Pannonia ought to be written *Carnuntum*. The forms *Carnutum*, *Carnicium*, *Carnotum*, and *Carnuntium* are incorrectly found in manuscripts and editions. Eutropius, Book VIII, chapter 13, p. 365: “When he had persisted continuously for three years at Carnuntum.” Spartianus, *Life of Severus*, chapter 5: “He was proclaimed emperor at Carnuntum on the Ides of August.” Hence, in an ancient inscription in Gruter, p. 1032, no. 2: **NATVS CARNVNTO**, “born at Carnuntum.”

[^c0122-31]: **The emperor.** Perizonius reads “the emperors.”

[^c0122-32]: **A danger from thirst more immediate.** Four Lyon manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection and the Ultrajectine manuscript, read *tum praesentis*, “then of the present”; but *praesentius*, “more immediate,” correctly describes the danger from thirst rather than the danger impending from the enemy.

[^c0122-33]: **Certain soldiers.** These were the Melitene soldiers, concerning whom Xiphilinus speaks against Dio in his account of the Philosopher Antoninus. See also Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 5.

[^c0122-34]: **They won a most glorious victory.** The memory of this victory is preserved by a remarkable medallion, distinguished by its type, weight, and quality, formerly kept in the Marckian Museum and now in the Cronenburg Museum at The Hague. I present a carefully made drawing of it.

[^c0122-35]: **Lucius Antoninus Commodus.** Lampridius, Xiphilinus, and Herodian, Book I, wrote Commodus’s life.

[^c0122-36]: **Succeeded his father in the government.** Two Lyon manuscripts read “succeeded his father in the kingdom.”

[^c0122-37]: **For thirteen years.**

[^c0122-38]: **Against the Germans.** After his father’s death he immediately abandoned the German war. Later, however, he successfully waged many wars through his legates. Lampridius, *Life of Commodus*, chapter 13: “Nevertheless, while he lived in this way, the Moors were defeated under him through his legates, the Dacians were defeated, and Pannonia was brought into order; in Britain, Germany, and Dacia the provincials were refusing his authority. All these matters were settled through commanders.” Hence the surname *Britannicus* appears on the large-module coin that follows. It was formerly in the Marckian Museum and is now found in the Cronenburg Museum.

[^c0122-39]: **Aelius Pertinax.** Capitolinus wrote Pertinax’s life. Herodian treats him in Book II, as do Xiphilinus and Eutropius.

The editors’ ability to digest the name Aelius is surprising, since all writers, and the excellent witnesses to matters of this kind, as well as inscriptions and coins, call him Helvius, not Aelius. The first and fourth Lyon manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection read not *Aelius* but *Elvius*; in the second Lyon manuscript, the Ultrajectine manuscript, the secondary codex, and the Augustan edition, *Helvius* is clearly recognized.

I preserve a large-module bronze coin of this emperor, inscribed in Greek and exceedingly rare, purchased at a truly shameful price, which I invoke as a witness to the name. Beside the laureate head of Pertinax it reads:

**ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡ ΚΑΙΣΑΡ ΠΟΥΒΛΙΟΣ ΠΕΛΥΙΟΣ ΠΕΡΤΙΝΑΞ ΣΕΒΑΣΤΟΣ**

“Emperor Caesar Publius Helvius Pertinax Augustus.”

On the other side the emperor is seen standing in a four-horse chariot, holding a wreath in his right hand and a spear and reins in his left, with the mark of his first year of rule:

**ΛΥΚΑΒΑΝΤΟΣ Α**

[^c0122-40]: **Through the crime of Julianus.** Julianus’s great-grandfather had been a jurist. He had a wife, Manlia Scantilla, who incited her husband, from desire for power, to purchase the empire from the soldiers with the money in which he abounded. I have placed below bronze coins of both, of remarkable workmanship, of what is called the second module. I myself preserve the one of Didius Julianus; I once saw the other in the Marckian Museum. But on closer examination the obverse seemed to have been corrupted from Julia Severus into Scantilla of Julianus.

[^c0122-41]: **At the Milvian Bridge.** This is how the manuscripts give the name of the bridge, here and also below in chapter 28; nor do I find it written otherwise in the ancient books of Sallustius.

[^c0122-42]: **In the year 944.** Some Lyon manuscripts read 943, others 946.

[^c0122-43]: **For eighteen years.** Three Lyon manuscripts, two Florentine manuscripts, Perizonius’s codex, the Ultrajectine manuscript, the Gronovian Collection, and the Augustan edition count seventeen years.

[^c0122-44]: **He subdued them.** Some older editions read “he checked them.”

[^c0122-45]: **Heavenly vengeance immediately followed.** The Lyon manuscript reads *apta*, “fitting,” rather than *acta*, “deeds.” Perhaps *aperta*, “manifest,” should be read.

[^c0122-46]: **Clodius Albinus.** A large-module coin of his, once preserved at Rome but now transferred with others of its kind to the Caesarian Treasury, is celebrated as follows. It shows the face of Clodius Albinus without a laurel wreath; a military cloak adorns his chest and shoulders. The inscription reads:

**DECIMVS CLODIVS SEPTIMIVS ALBINVS CAESAR**

On the other side is a type common to many silver and other coins of Clodius: Minerva, who from her dress and inscription is understood to be the Bringer of Peace. The inscription reads:

**MINERVAE PACIFERAE COS. II**

[^c0122-47]: **Dragged there with almost all his allies having perished.** On Severus’s expedition to Britain, in addition to the authors cited above, Cassiodorus also writes.

[^c0122-48]: **A ditch and wall extending 132 miles.** Four Lyon manuscripts, together with the Ultrajectine manuscript and the Gronovian Collection, read “the largest ditch.” Scott, in his edition of Victor, p. 533, showed from comparison with other writers that the number contains an excess hundred. Whether the fault lies with the copyists or with Orosius himself seems uncertain: not only do all the manuscripts display the same number, but so does Paul the Deacon’s *Miscellaneous History*, which uses Orosius’s words in many places, as is clear in Muratori’s *Collection, or Treasury*, vol. I, p. 65.

[^c0122-49]: **He left two sons.** This is the reading of the manuscripts and the Augustan edition. The other editions less correctly read: “Leaving two sons, Bassianus…”

[^c0122-50]: **Bassianus and Geta.** Spartianus, in *Life of Severus*, chapter 20, writes from Aelius Maurus, freedman of Phlegon of Tralles, that Septimius Severus rejoiced immoderately because he was leaving two Antonini with equal authority over the state, following the example of Pius, who left Verus and Marcus Antoninus, his adopted sons, to the state. This was better, he says, because the former gave adopted sons as rulers of the Roman state, while the latter gave his own natural sons.

The later pair illuminates Orosius’s words above in chapter 14 concerning Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, who are there called the sons of Antoninus Pius, although Verus was properly his grandson, adopted by Marcus. Add Capitolinus, *Life of Verus*, chapter 11.

The harmony between the brothers Antoninus and Geta, the sons of Severus, was extremely poor, although they are often joined in inscriptions and on coins, as on this large-module Greek coin in the Caesarian Treasury. On its obverse it displays the two heads of the brothers: Antoninus laureate and Geta bareheaded, with the inscription:

**ΜΑΡΚΟΣ ΑΥΡΗΛΙΟΣ ΑΝΤΩΝΕΙΝΟΣ ΠΟΥΒΛΙΟΣ ΣΕΠΤΙΜΙΟΣ ΓΕΤΑΣ**

“Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, Publius Septimius Geta.”

On the reverse is a representation of Apollo, or his priest, and Aesculapius, with this inscription:

**ΑΡΧΙΕΡΕΩΣ ΓΑΙΟΥ ΦΛΑΒΙΟΥ ΜΑΞΙΜΟΥ ΑΛΙΚΑΡΝΑΣΣΕΩΝ**

“Under the high priest Gaius Flavius Maximus, of the Halicarnassians.”

It is preserved in the Caesarian Treasury.

[^c0122-51]: **It is said to have been conducted.** Some witnesses read *esse*, “to be,” instead of *fuisse*, “to have been”; in the Lyon manuscripts the following word *argumentis* is corrupted as *adjumentis*.

[^c0122-52]: **They made [the invocation].** The manuscripts and editions have *quidam fecerant*, “certain men had made [it].”

[^c0122-53]: **He wished to be called Pertinax.** Countless silver and bronze coins bear this surname. Two especially noteworthy coins, hitherto neither seen nor published by antiquaries, may be brought to light: one bears a Latin, the other a Greek inscription.

The first has this legend around Severus’s laureate head: **IMP. CAES. L. SEPTIMIVS SEVERVS PERTINAX AVG.** — “Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Pertinax Augustus.” On the reverse stands the god Lunus, in distinctive attire, holding a spear in his right hand, leaning on a column with his left, and holding Victory standing on a globe; he congratulates the emperor on victories won throughout the world. Behind him stands a cock, while he presses his left foot upon a bovine head. The god Lunus was worshipped elsewhere in the East, and also at Antioch in Pisidia. The coin was struck there, as is shown by the surrounding inscription **COL. CAES. ANTIOCHENSIS**, “the Caesarean colony of Antioch”; for it had been made a Roman colony by Augustus, which explains the Latin legend.

The Greek coin, remarkable both otherwise and for its size and weight, displays Severus’s laureate head, with a military cloak over the shoulders and an incuse mark of Ephesian Diana before the chin. Around it is written: **ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡ ΚΑΙΣΑΡ ΛΟΥΚΙΟΣ ΣΕΠΤΙΜΙΟΣ ΣΕΟΥΗΡΟΣ ΠΕΡΤΙΝΑΞ** — “Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Pertinax.” On the reverse the emperor’s prudence and courage are commended by the representation of Hercules and Minerva, who apparently join right hands with an altar between them. The coin was struck by the Acrasiotae in Lydia, as the legend declares: **ΑΚΡΑΣΙΩΤΩΝ ΕΠΙ ΣΤΡΑΤΗΓΟΥ ΣΤΡΑΤΟΝΕΙΚΙΑΝΟΥ Γ** — “Of the Acrasiotae, under the strategus Stratonicianus, third [year].” This splendid coin, one of the foremost in the largest module, is preserved in the Horstian Museum.

[^c0122-54]: **Continually.** Three Lyon manuscripts, the Ultrajectine manuscript, and the Gronovian Collection read *saepe*, “often.”

[^c0122-55]: **Pescennius Niger.** Those authors just named also treat Pescennius Niger. Collectors know how rarely coins of this emperor are found; most are compelled to do without them. I possess a completely intact silver coin, though its design has been published by others. More remarkable is a Greek-inscribed bronze coin of the largest module, kept at the Farnese Treasury at Parma; its design is given in the Farnese Museum, table XVIII, no. 1.

I have cited that coin all the more gladly so that those whom distance prevents from seeing it may compare a very similar one formerly in the Marckian Museum, from which I obtained drawings of many of that most courteous man’s rarer coins. It may now be inspected at The Hague in the possession of Godard Cronenburg, whose museum boasts many exceedingly rare coins. On both coins appears the bearded, laureate head of Pescennius Niger, with a military cloak upon the shoulders, and this inscription: **ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡ ΚΑΙΣΑΡ ΓΑΙΟΣ ΠΕΣΚΕΝΝΙΟΣ ΝΙΓΕΡΟΣ** (in the Cronenburg coin, **ΝΙΓΕΡΩΣ**) **ΣΕΒΑΣΤΟΣ** — “Emperor Caesar Gaius Pescennius Niger Augustus.” On the reverse Ceres stands, holding ears of grain in her lowered right hand and a burning torch in her left; a serpent is before her feet. The inscription is **ΑΝΤΙΟΧΕΩΝ ΝΕΟΚΟΡΩΝ** — “Of the Antiochene neocori.” The material of the coin, that is, the bronze itself, approaches the hardness of iron.

This coin, like most of those I have published and the many more that I still possess for publication, was drawn for me, with the highest skill and exact likeness to the originals, by Franciscus van Mieris, the most diligent craftsman in these matters and most expert painter, grandson of the celebrated Franciscus van Mieris.

In the year 962 from the founding of the City, Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus, also called Caracalla [Note: “Caracalla.” Explaining the origin of this name, Xiphilinus has Καράκαλλον. Spartianus wrote his life; Herodian discusses him in Book IV. FABR.], the eighteenth to assume the principate after Augustus [Note: “Created, he remained for years,” etc. The printed editions have “and he remained in it for years.” Trifles. LAUT. — I think the received text should not lightly be altered.], remained in it for not quite seven years [Col. 1108A]. He was harsher than his father [Note: “He lived.” Perizonius’s manuscript orders that this be deleted.], and was more uncontrolled in lust than all other men [Note: “But among all men.” This addition is found in manuscripts and in the Augustan edition [Col. 1107B]. The others read, “more uncontrolled in lust than all men,” etc.]. He even took his stepmother Julia as his wife [Note: “Julia.” Already notorious for adulteries during her marriage to Severus. In Spartianus’s Life of Severus, chapter 18: “Domitian was less cautious, for he kept Julia as his wife, a woman notorious for adulteries and even an accomplice in the conspiracy.” The people of Aegeae and Smyrna represented her likeness as that of Cleopatra on an unusually large coin, which I possess: a very beautiful, perfectly preserved, and extremely rare piece. On the obverse of the coin appears Julia’s head, with this inscription: ΙΟΥΛΙΑΝ ΔΟΜΝΑΝ ϹΕΒΑΣΤΗΝ, “Julia Domna Augusta,” that is, “they honor Julia Domna Augusta.” On the reverse appears the head of Cleopatra, once queen of Egypt, recognizable by the royal diadem and the asp placed against her neck. Around the coin one reads the names of the cities: ϹΜΥΡΝΑΙΩΝ ΑΔΡΙΑΝΩΝ ΑΙΓΕΩΝ ΕΤΟΥϹ . . ., “of the Hadrianean Smyrnaeans, of the Aegeatae, year . . .”] 505

Here, while preparing a war against the Parthians, he was surrounded by the enemy and killed between Edessa and Carrhae. After him, the nineteenth after Augustus, Opellius [Note: “Opellius Macrinus.” Concerning him, see Capitolinus, Xiphilinus, and Herodian, Books IV and V. FABR. — I possess several unpublished coins of this emperor and their types, but I present two: one from the Lebret collection and the other from my own. The former, struck at the Colonia Julia Berytus, displays, though somewhat crudely, the customary type of the colony. The latter, struck at Rome, is excellently engraved. On its obverse appears the laureate head of Macrinus, with a military cloak over his shoulders, and this inscription: IMPerator CAESar Marcus OPELius SEVerus MAcrinus AUGustus. On the reverse stands Jupiter with thunderbolt and spear; around him is written PONTIFex MA- - - - - -S II. Pater Patriae, “Father of the Fatherland.”] Opellius 506 Macrinus, who was prefect of the praetorian guard [Note: “Praetorian.” Several manuscripts read praetorii.], seized the empire together with his son Diadumenus [Note: “With his son Diadumenus.” The historians praise the beauty of Diadumenus, or Diadumenianus, in several places [Col. 1108D]. It is also evident on coins, as on this Caesarean coin struck at the Colonia Julia Augusta Felix Berytus.], but after completing a year he was immediately killed at Archelais in a military uprising [Note: “Archelais.” Two Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read Dulaidem or Dualaidem; Perizonius reads Archeidem. This is wrong, for Eusebius and George Syncellus also call it Archelais. It was a village of Bithynia, as appears from Capitolinus’s Life of Macrinus, chapter 10: “While fleeing with a few men and his son, Macrinus was killed with Diadumenianus in a certain village of Bithynia.”].

In the year 970 from the founding of the City, M. Aurelius Antoninus [Note: “M. Aurelius Antoninus.” Concerning Antoninus Heliogabalus, see Lampridius and Herodian, Book V. FABR. — The empire came into the hands of his grandmother Julia Maesa, a most cunning woman, by the arts with which Capitolinus describes this episode in his Life of Macrinus, chapter 9: “There was a certain woman, Maesa, or Varia, from the city of Emesa, sister of Julia, the wife of Severus Pertinax the African. After the death of Antoninus Bassianus she had been expelled from the imperial household through Macrinus’s arrogance; yet Macrinus granted her everything that she had accumulated over a long period. She had two daughters, Semiamira and Mamaea. The elder had a son named Heliogabalus, who also took the name of Bassianus and Antoninus. For the Phoenicians call Heliogabalus the sun. Heliogabalus was conspicuous for his beauty, stature, and priesthood, and was known to everyone who came to the temple, especially to the soldiers.” To these men Maesa, or Varia, said that Bassianus was the son of Antoninus, and this gradually became known to all the soldiers. He then relates how she drew the legions away from Macrinus and overthrew him with astonishing boldness. I have chosen to quote this passage from Capitolinus at some length so that it may be understood why, on a certain coin modeled on Faustina, the wife of Marcus, Maesa is called Mater Castrorum, “Mother of the Camps,” a title previously unheard of or unknown in connection with an Augusta. This coin rightly occupies a place among the rarer pieces in my collection, both because of that unusual inscription and because it is silver and of large module. On its obverse appears the head of Julia Maesa, with this inscription: ΙΟΥΛΙΑ ΜΑΙϹΑ ϹΕΒΑϹΤΗ ΜΗΤΗΡ ϹΤΡΑΤΙΑϹ, “Julia Maesa Augusta, Mother of the Camps.” On the reverse is the bust of Isis, raising her right hand to her breast; her head is crowned with a lotus, and the inscription Λ. Γ. indicates the third year of Heliogabalus’s reign. The coin is therefore Egyptian, of fairly pure though not completely pure silver. [Col. 1109C] We have also appended an unpublished bronze Greek coin of Heliogabalus himself, highly worthy of attention, since it was struck by the Cyrrhestians with the type of Jupiter Cataebates. Its owner, Gerard Schaakius of Amsterdam, a man devoted to every form of elegance, permitted us to have it drawn. On the obverse appears the laureate head of Heliogabalus, with this inscription: ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡΑ ΚΑΙϹΑΡΑ ΜΑΡΚΟΝ ΑΥΡΗΛΙΟΝ ΑΝΤΩΝΙΝΟΝ, “Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus,” that is, “they honor him.” On the reverse appears that Jupiter known to scholars by his epithet, in a six-columned temple; his very epithet is also inscribed, along with the people who worshiped him: ΚΥΡΡΗϹΤΩΝ ΔΙΟϹ ΚΑΤΑΙΒΑΤΟΥ, “of the Cyrrhestians, of Jupiter Cataebates.”].

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, the twentieth after Augustus, having obtained the empire, held it for four years. He was a priest of the temple of Heliogabalus and left behind no reputable memory of himself, only the infamy of sexual violations, crimes, and every form of obscenity [Col. 1110A]. When a military uprising broke out, he was killed at Rome together with his mother [Note: “He was killed together with his mother.” Julia Soaemias, or Semiamira, as Capitolinus calls her.] 507

In the year 974 from the founding of the City, Aurelius Alexander [Note: “Aurelius Alexander.” Lampridius also wrote Alexander’s life; Herodian discusses him in Book VI. FABR.], the twenty-first after Augustus, was proclaimed emperor by the will of the Senate and the army, and held the office for thirteen years, deserving the highest praise for his justice [Note: “His mother Mamaea.” She too was killed with her son in the same uprising. The son did much through her counsel, and therefore they are often joined on coins, as on this unusually large coin from Caesarea. [Col. 1109D] On it are seen the facing heads of Alexander and Mamaea, with this inscription: IMPerator SEVERUS ALEXANDER AUGustus. IVLIA MAMMAEA AUGusta MATER AUGusti, “Emperor Severus Alexander Augustus. Julia Mamaea Augusta, Mother of Augustus.” On the reverse sits Roma Victrix, with Victory crowning her; Jupiter stands to her right. She herself sits upon a starry globe, holding a scepter in her left hand and leaning her right hand upon a circle, symbol of eternity. Across the orb of this circle four little boys can be seen playing, as though to signify that the eternal City would never lack descendants. The inscription reads TEMPORUM FELICITAS, “The happiness of the ages.”].

His mother Mamaea, 508 [Col. 1111A] a Christian, took care to hear the presbyter Origen. For, as soon as he had undertaken an expedition against the Persians, he defeated Xerxes, their king [Note: “Xerxes.” He is likewise named by Cassiodorus, whose source is Herodian: Ἀρταξέρξης ὁ Περσῶν βασιλεύς, “Artaxerxes, king of the Persians.” FABR.], in a very great war. With Ulpian as his adviser, he displayed the greatest moderation in governing the state; but he was killed in a military uprising at Mainz.

509 CHAPTER XIX. The reigns of Julius Maximinus and the younger Gordian, and the persecution of the Christians.

In the year 987 from the founding of the City, Maximinus [Note: “Maximinus.” Capitolinus wrote the lives of the two Maximini, father and son; Herodian discusses him in Books VII and VIII. FABR. — He was remarkable for the massive size and strength of his limbs and joints, on account of which the people of Perge compared him with Hercules on an unusually large coin that I possess. On the obverse is seen the laureate head of Maximinus, with a military cloak over his shoulders, and this inscription: ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡ ΓΑΙΟΣ ΙΟΥΛΙΟΣ ΟΥΗΡΟΣ ΜΑΞΙΜΕΙΝΟϹ ϹΕΒΑϹΤΟϹ, “Emperor Gaius Julius Verus Maximinus Augustus.” On the reverse appears Hercules, holding a club in both hands; ΠΕΡΓΑΙΩΝ, “of the Pergans,” is inscribed. The type of the coin is placed below.] the twenty-second after Augustus, was proclaimed emperor by the army, without the consent of the Senate, after he had successfully conducted the war in Germany [Col. 1111B] [Note: “Was created.” The Augustan edition reads “was made.”]. He then launched a persecution against the Christians, the sixth after Nero, and exercised it. But immediately— that is, in the third year of his reign—he was killed by Pupienus at Aquileia, thus bringing an end both to his persecution and to his life. He had undertaken the persecution chiefly because of the Christian household of Alexander, whom he had succeeded, and of his mother Mamaea, and especially because of the presbyter Origen: he had sent orders for the persecution of priests and clerics, that is, teachers.

In the year 991 from the founding of the City, Gordian, the twenty-third after Augustus, was proclaimed emperor and remained in office for six years. For Pupienus, the slayer of Maximinus [Note: “Pupienus, the slayer.” Concerning Pupienus and Albinus, see Eutropius, Book IX. In place of Pupienus, Capitolinus and Herodian have Maximus. He included the three Gordians in a single book. FABR.], and his brother [Note: “And his brother.” Orosius wrongly calls them brothers: they were colleagues in the empire but were not related. Nor was their harmony brotherly; they could have protected themselves against plots and military unrest if one had not distrusted the other because of evil suspicions. In other respects they were a noble pair of emperors, whom I once saw together on a remarkable coin of Marckian weight and size. When his collection was dispersed, it went to Brabant; although I rightly regarded it as less than genuine, I nevertheless preserved its drawing because of its exceptional workmanship and the striking resemblance of both men to their finest coins, and I judged it worthy of being seen.] Balbinus [Note: “Balbinus.” Since so many coins of this emperor survive, and many manuscripts correctly give this name, it is strange that all editions—even those of Fabricius, except the latest edition of Andreas Schottus—read Albinus. Only the Augsburg edition gives Balbinus, and it is supported by three Leiden manuscripts, the Gronovian Collection, Perizonius’s manuscript, and both Florentine manuscripts, except that in one of the latter the first letter was erased and Albinus remained. That name seems to have taken possession of several manuscripts because of the Caesar Clodius Albinus, mentioned in chapter 17. [Col. 1112D] The titles and names of Balbinus on the coin quoted here are: IMPerator CAESar Decimus CAELius BALBINVS AVGustus, “Emperor Caesar Decimus Caelius Balbinus Augustus.” On the other side, those of Pupienus are: IMPerator CAESar Marcus CLODius PVPIENVS MAXIMVS AVGustus, “Emperor Caesar Marcus Clodius Pupienus Maximus Augustus.”], who had usurped the empire, were soon killed in the palace. 510

Gordian, still a very young boy, was about to depart for the East to wage war against the Parthians [Col. 1112B] [Note: “About to depart for the East for the Parthian war.” This departure is indicated by the decoration of the shield that Gordian carries in his right hand on an unusually large Caesarean coin [Col. 1113A]. On it appears the bust of Gordian, laureate and wearing a military cloak over his shoulders; he holds a spear in his right hand and a shield in his left. On the shield is depicted an emperor on horseback, preceded by Victory and followed by a soldier. The inscription on that side of the coin is IMPerator GORDIANVS PIVS FELIX AVGustus, “Emperor Gordianus Pius Felix Augustus.” On the reverse one reads FIDES EXERCITVS, “The loyalty of the army.” Its type is a military figure joining hands with the emperor and thus giving the oath, with military standards between them; behind the emperor stands Victory holding a palm; at their feet two rivers recline, perhaps representing the Tiber and the Tigris.], as Eutropius writes, opened the gates of Janus [Note: “Eutropius.” Book IX, chapter 11, p. 395: “Gordian, still a very young man, having taken Tranquillina as his wife at Rome, opened the double gates of Janus and set out for the East, bringing war upon the Parthians, who were already preparing to break forth. He conducted the war successfully and afflicted the Persians in great battles.”]. I do not remember anyone writing that after Vespasian and Titus anyone had closed them, although Cornelius Tacitus reports that Vespasian himself opened them again after a year [Note: “Cornelius Tacitus reports.” Not in those books that survive for us from so great a wreck, but in books that Orosius read in his own day, as is clear from the words of that same Tacitus quoted above in chapter 9.].

Accordingly, after Gordian had successfully fought great battles against the Parthians, he was killed through the treachery of his own men not far from Circesium on the Euphrates [Note: “Circesium.” A town of Mesopotamia between Nicephorium and the confluence of the Chaboras, at the angle formed by the Chaboras and the Euphrates, where a tomb was erected for the unfortunate young man. Eutropius, Book IX, chapter 11, p. 396: “A soldier built a tomb for him at the twentieth milestone from Circesium, a fortress now belonging to the Romans and overlooking the Euphrates.”].

512 CHAPTER XX. The empire of M. Julius Philippus with his son.

In the year 997 from the founding of the City [Col. 1114A], Philippus, the twenty-fourth after Augustus, was proclaimed emperor [Note: “Philippus.” Concerning Philippus the father and Philippus the son, see Eutropius and Sextus Aurelius. FABR. — I possess a Greek coin of this Philippus. On its obverse is his laureate head, with a military cloak over his shoulders, and the inscription ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡ ΚΑΙΣΑΡ ΜΑΡΚΟΣ ΙΟΥΛΙΟΣ ΦΙΛΙΠΠΟΣ, “Emperor Caesar Marcus Julius Philippus.” On the reverse the people of Ancyra struck Fortune with a grain measure on her head, with this inscription: ΑΓΚΥΡΑΝΩΝ ΕΠΙ ΜΑΡΚΟΥ ΖΟΙΛΟΥ ΑΡΧΙΕΡΕΩΣ Α. ΤΟ Β, “of the Ancyrans, under Marcus Zoilus, chief priest, for the first and second time.”], made his son Philippus his associate in the kingdom [Note: “Philippus his son,” etc. Hence he too appears on coins with the title Augustus, as on a large Greek coin that I possess, struck at Laodicea. It shows Philippus’s laureate head on the obverse, with a military cloak over his shoulders, and this inscription: ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡ ΚΑΙΣΑΡ ΜΑΡΚΟΣ ΙΟΥΛΙΟΣ ΦΙΛΙΠΠΟΣ ΑΥΓΟΥΣΤΟΣ, “Emperor Caesar Marcus Julius Philippus Augustus.” On the reverse stands a female figure wearing a grain measure on her head, holding a small image in her right hand and a cornucopia in her left. The inscription reads ΑΟΔΙΚΕΩΝ ΝΕΩΚΟΡΩΝ, “of the Laodiceans, temple-wardens.” [Col. 1115A] I also possess two extremely rare bronze coins of Maximus, the son of Maximinus, struck in Roman colonies. On the first, the bare head of Caesar Maximus bears the inscription IVLius VERUS MAXIMUS CAESAR. On the reverse his mother, the wife of Maximinus, is represented by the Roman colony seated in the guise of the goddess Pudicitia. That city was Pella in Macedonia, once the homeland of Alexander the Great, as appears from this inscription: COLonia IVLia AUGusta PELLA. The second was struck in the city once called Ilium and later named Alexandria after Alexander the Great; under Roman rule it was called Alexandria Troas. Beside the bare head of Caesar Maximus is the inscription JVLius VERus MAXIMVS. On the reverse one reads TROas, COLonia AVGusta. The customary symbol of the Troad appears there: the Roman eagle standing upon the head of an ox, which is the colony’s type. Since these coins have not yet been published by others, I have been pleased to append them.], and remained in office for seven years. He was the first of all the emperors to be a Christian, and after his third year of rule [Col. 1115A], the thousandth year from Rome’s foundation was completed [Note: “The thousandth year from the foundation.” Rome’s thousandth completed year fell in the third year of Philippus’s reign. Cassiodorus. FABR. — Several coins survive that attest this celebration and these secular games held by the Philippi. Among them is one of unusually large module, which we present here from the distinguished collection of the often-mentioned Illustrious Lebret; it is highly noteworthy. On the obverse are joined the heads of Philippus and Otacilia, while opposite them appears the head of their son Philippus. The appropriate inscription for all three reads CONCORDIA AVGVSTORVM, “Harmony of the Augusti.” On the reverse is the magnificent structure of the Circus, with chariots racing and the remaining letters AVGG. The complete inscription seems to have been SAECVLa es AVGG., that is, “of the Augusti.”].

Thus this birthday-year, the most august of all those previously celebrated, was commemorated by a Christian emperor with magnificent games. There is no doubt that Philippus gained from Christ and the Church the favor and honor of such devotion, since no author shows that he ascended the Capitol or sacrificed the customary victims. 515 Nevertheless, both men, though in different places, were killed by military revolt and through the treachery of Decius.

CHAPTER XXI. The empire of Quintus Trajanus Decius and Gallus Hostilianus with his son Volusianus.

In the year 1004 from the founding of the City [Col. 1116A], Decius, instigator and suppressor of civil war, after killing the Philippi, seized the empire as the twenty-fifth after Augustus and held it for three years. Immediately, by the very act through which he showed that he had killed the Philippi also for this reason [Note: “The Philippi.” Several manuscripts write Philippum.], he issued deadly edicts for the persecution and execution of Christians, the seventh such persecutor after Nero, and sent many of the saints from their tortures to the crowns of Christ [Col. 1117A] [Note: “Tortures.” Nearly all manuscripts read this more correctly, I think, than crucibus, “crosses,” which occurs in most vulgate editions.]. He also appointed his son Caesar, and together with him was soon killed in the midst of the barbarians. 516

In the year 1007 from the founding of the City, Gallus Hostilianus, the twenty-sixth after Augustus, obtained the kingdom and held it for scarcely two years with his son Volusianus [Note: “Scarcely two years.” The Augustan edition has “two years” (deleting vix, “scarcely”) “with his son Volusianus he held it.”] [Note: “He held it.” Perizonius reads “he maintained it.”]. The vengeance for the violated Christian name arose, and for as long as the edicts of Decius continued to lay the Churches low, the plague of incredible diseases extended [Note: “The plague of diseases.” Eusebius says that Cyprian, in his work On Mortality, is a witness to this plague. FABR.]. Almost no Roman province, city, or household was left that was not afflicted and emptied by that general pestilence [Note: “And emptied.” I have restored the manuscript reading; the reading in the vulgate editions, “and laid waste,” seems to be a gloss.]. Gallus and Volusianus became notable only for this disaster; while preparing a civil war against Aemilianus, who was attempting a revolution, they were killed. Nevertheless, Aemilianus was destroyed in the third month of the tyranny he had seized [Note: “Of the tyranny he had seized.” Absent from the Augustan edition.] [Col. 1117B].

CHAPTER XXII. How and how long Valerian and Gallienus ruled. Meanwhile, concerning the persecution of the Church and its vengeance through various wars and the conspiracy of tyrants.

In the year 1010 from the founding of the City, two emperors were appointed, twenty-seventh in succession after Augustus [Col. 1117D]. Valerian was proclaimed Augustus by the army in Raetia [Note: “Valerian in Raetia.” For Valerian and Gallienus, Trebellius Pollio, who wrote the life of each, should be read. FABR.]. Gallienus, however, was proclaimed by the Senate at Rome [Note: “But Gallienus at Rome by the Senate.” Several manuscripts and nearly all printed editions add, “and was made Caesar, and remained,” etc. I have deleted this worthless fragment on the authority of the Florentine manuscripts and the Augustan edition. Orosius has just said that two emperors were appointed together; he now states where and by whom: the father in Raetia by the army, the son at Rome by the Senate. Below he also calls him a colleague, but a Caesar was not the colleague of an emperor.]. Gallienus remained unhappily in power for fifteen years, while the human race briefly drew breath from that continual and severe pestilence, heavier than usual. The heedless soldiery calls forth its own punishment. Impiety feels its scourges when tormented, but, hardened against the one who scourges it, does not recognize him [Note: “Tormented.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “exercised.”].

To say nothing of earlier events, after the persecution of the Christians by Decius, a great pestilence afflicted the entire Roman Empire. Iniquity deceived itself, ensnared by a perverse judgment to its own destruction, in supposing that the pestilence was a common accident and that death arising from disease was the end of nature, not a punishment [Note: “And occurring,” etc. Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read: “that it was a common case of an occurrence, which thought that death, even when arising from diseases, was the end of nature, not a punishment.” Then, in the following words, in place of “the wrath of God,” etc., the second Florentine manuscript has “God’s wrath,” etc.]. Again, therefore, and in a short time, it provokes God’s anger by its criminal actions, destined to receive a blow that will force it at some point to remember [Note: “At some point.” The Augustan edition reads “for a while.”].

For Valerian, as soon as he seized the empire, the eighth after Nero, ordered Christians to be compelled through torture to idolatry, and those who refused to do so to be killed; the blood of the saints was poured out across the entire breadth of the Roman realm. Valerian, the author of the wicked edict, was immediately captured by Sapor, king of the Persians. The emperor of the Roman people grew old in the most disgraceful slavery among the Persians, receiving throughout his life the continuous condemnation of this infamous office: he himself, bent low upon the ground, raised the king, as he mounted his horse, not with his hands but with his back [Note: “This … condemnation.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “this condemnation,” etc.; then “condemnation.”] [Note: “To mount above him.” The second, third, and fourth Leiden manuscripts correctly restore this reading; the other manuscripts and printed editions have “always going to mount,” which is inept. The scribes found in their manuscripts the abbreviation sp or sup, with a line above two letters of the first word or drawn across the final letter of the second; hence some interpreted it as semper rather than super or supra.]. And Gallienus, terrified by so conspicuous a judgment of God and moved by the example of so wretched a colleague [Note: “And so wretched.” Three Leiden manuscripts read tamquam, “as though,” etc.], restored peace to the Churches with anxious repentance.

But the perpetual captivity of one impious man, abominable beyond measure, does not balance the measure of injury and vengeance against so many thousands of tortured saints; and the blood of the righteous, crying out to God, begs to be avenged in the very earth where it was shed [Note: “But he does not compensate.” The vulgate editions read “but without compensating.” I have preferred the reading of Perizonius and the third Leiden manuscript. The expression is characteristic of the Iron Age: “he compensates against so many thousands,” etc. He might have written “and the blood of the righteous against,” etc.; perhaps contra has been displaced.]. For a just punishment was demanded not only of the sole author of the edict [Note: “Punishment.” Some manuscripts read supplicii, others supplicio, both incorrectly. The punishment that the impious man was to suffer was not demanded only of Valerian, who had issued bloody edicts against the Christians, but also of his ministers, etc.]; it was also just that the executioners, informers, accusers, spectators, judges, and finally all who by silent consent assented to the most unjust cruelty should be struck by the same blow of vengeance, since God is the knower of secrets and since most of those men were scattered throughout all the provinces [Note: “Assented.” All manuscripts, together with the better old editions, prefer this to assentiebantur.].

Suddenly, by God’s permission [Note: “By God’s permission.” Four Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “by God’s command.”] [Col. 1118C], the nations that had been placed around and held back for this purpose were released on every side; with the reins loosened, they rushed into all the borders of the Romans. The Germans, having penetrated the Alps, Raetia, and all Italy, reached Ravenna. The Alamanni [Note: “Alamanni.” This should be written Alamanni, not Alemanni, as is evident from a coin of Constantine bearing ALAMANNIA GAVDIUM ROMANORUM, “Alamannia, joy of the Romans.”] ravaged the Gauls and also crossed into Italy. Greece, Macedonia, Pontus, and Asia were destroyed by the inundation of the Goths. For Dacia beyond the Danube was lost forever. The Quadi and Sarmatians devastated the Pannonias. The farther Germans, having laid it waste, took possession of Spain. The Parthians seized Mesopotamia and gnawed away at Syria [Note: “Gnawed away.” Four Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection and the Augustan edition, read contrahunt, as though they wished to make the possession of Syria by the Parthians more restricted, that is, smaller. The second Florentine manuscript reads conradunt, the third congradiunt.].

Still today, throughout the various provinces, small and impoverished settlements survive amid the ruins of great cities, preserving the signs of misery and the traces of their names [Note: “Poor settlements.” The Cologne and Maternian editions, together with six other printed books, read aedes, “buildings.” But let Stellio’s guts burst! Orosius proves that sedes, “settlements,” must be read when he says, “among which we too display our own Tarragona in Spain.” Tarragona was therefore in the jurisdiction of Hispania Tarraconensis, that is, of Hispania Citerior, and Orosius was from there. LAUT. — I too found sedes in four Leiden manuscripts, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Gronovian Collection [Col. 1119C], so Lautius’s emendation cannot be doubted; the Augustan edition had already printed it long ago from an excellent manuscript. Both Florentine manuscripts likewise read it.]. Among them we too display our own Tarragona in Spain as a consolation for recent misery [Note: “Recent misery.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection and the Utrecht manuscript, read “present misery.”]. And lest any part of the Roman body perhaps remain untouched by this laceration, tyrants conspired within [Note: “Tyrants conspire within.” Thirty tyrants arose in the Roman Empire at that time; Pollio’s book concerning them survives. FABR.]; civil wars arose, and Roman blood was poured out everywhere while Romans and barbarians alike raged [Col. 1119B]. But soon God’s anger turned into mercy, and the greater pattern of the vengeance that had begun was reckoned as a full measure rather than as punishment.

Accordingly, first Ingenuus [Note: “Ingenuus.” I have restored the name from Trebellius Pollio and from coins. The printed editions incorrectly read Genuus.], who had assumed the imperial purple, was killed at Mursa. Postumus seized the tyranny in Gaul, to the great advantage of the state. For ten years [Col. 1120A], using great courage and moderation, he both expelled the hostile rulers and restored the ruined provinces to their former appearance, but he was killed in a military mutiny. Aemilianus was crushed at Mainz while attempting a revolution. After the death of Postumus, Marius seized the empire in the same place, but was immediately killed. Then Victorinus was voluntarily chosen by the Gauls [Note: “And shortly afterward.” The Augustan edition reads “shortly afterward,”] and shortly afterward was killed. Tetricus succeeded him; at that time he was administering the office of governor of Aquitania [Note: “Of Aquitania.” Three Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection read Aquitaniae. The ancients wrote it both ways.], and endured many military mutinies [Note: “Many.” Nearly all manuscripts lack the conjunction -que.].

In the East, however, the Persians, defeated and driven back by a certain Odaenathus, who had gathered a rustic force, were repelled; Syria was defended and Mesopotamia recovered, and the rustic inhabitants of Syria, together with their Odaenathus, advanced in victory as far as Ctesiphon [Note: “But Gallienus, when he had abandoned the state.” Nevertheless, he left coins with sufficiently magnificent titles and types, on which Hercules appears as the conqueror of tyrants and monsters, as may be gathered from a large Caesarean coin that has been illustrated.]. But Gallienus, after abandoning the state and devoting himself to lust at Milan [Col. 1120B], was killed.

520 CHAPTER XXIII. The emperors Flavius Claudius, Aurelius Quintillus, and Valerius Aurelianus.

In the year 1025 from the founding of the City, Claudius [Note: “Claudius.” Trebellius wrote Claudius’s life. Vopiscus wrote Aurelian’s and also mentions Quintillus. Eutropius and Aurelius should also be read. FABR. — A Greek coin of this Claudius, struck in Egypt, as is believed, in the second year of his reign, refers to his famous victory over the Goths, which Orosius mentions. The reverse bears the type of Victory. On the obverse is the laureate head of Tacitus, with the inscription ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡ ΚΑΙΣΑΡ ΚΛΑΥΔΙΟΣ ϹΕΒΑϹΤΟΣ, “Emperor Caesar Claudius Augustus.” My other coin of the same Claudius has the same inscription; on it appears the customary eagle symbol found on such bronze coins.], the twenty-eighth after Augustus, assumed the empire by the will of the Senate and immediately attacked the Goths, who had been ravaging Illyricum and Macedonia for fifteen years [Note: “Already for fifteen years.” The first word is absent from the Augustan edition.], and destroyed them in an incredible massacre. For this the Senate decreed a golden shield in the Curia and an equally golden statue in the Capitol [Note: “An equally golden statue.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “an equestrian golden statue,” but incorrectly. Trebellius Pollio, Life of Claudius, chapter 3: “A golden shield—or, as the grammarians say, a golden shield—was placed for him by the unanimous judgment of the Senate in the Roman Curia, as it is still seen today. His likeness was represented upon the breastplate. For him, something granted to no one before, the Roman people at their own expense placed in the Capitol, before the temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest, a ten-foot golden statue.”]. But before he had completed two years in power, he was seized by illness and died at Sirmium.

After Claudius’s death, his brother Quintillus was chosen emperor by the army. He was a man of singular moderation, and the only one who should be preferred to his brother; nevertheless, he was killed on the seventeenth day of his reign [Note: “On the seventeenth day of his reign.” Perizonius and the third Leiden manuscript, together with the Gronovian Collection, delete imperii; the Augustan edition adds sui.].

In the year 1027 from the founding of the City, Aurelianus [Note: “Aurelianus.” Rome numbered him among its most warlike emperors. I possess a highly remarkable Greek coin of this prince, except that it has suffered some blemish from age and verdigris. On its obverse appears Aurelian’s bust, radiate, with his right hand raised and holding a globe in his left; a military cloak hangs from his chest and shoulders. The surviving letters of the inscription are . . . . . . . . . ΑΙΑΝΟϹ ΑΥΓ., “Aurelianus Augustus.” The other side of the coin is no less noteworthy: Aurelian, wearing a toga, joins his right hand with that of his wife, with an altar between them. Around the coin are the letters ΥΠΟ ΤΕΡΤΥΛΛ . . . . . . . . . . . ΩΝ, meaning that the coin was struck under a certain Tertullus or Tertullianus, in a Greek city whose final two letters alone can be read.], the twenty-ninth to obtain the empire, held it for five years and six months, a man outstanding in military ability [Note: “Outstanding in military industry.” Four Leiden manuscripts and the Utrecht manuscript, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “most experienced in military industry.”]. Undertaking an expedition to the Danube, he routed the Goths in great battles [Note: “Routed.” Some older editions read “struck down.”] and fixed the Roman dominion within its ancient boundaries [Col. 1121B]. Then turning toward the East, he brought Zenobia under his power—she had claimed for herself Syria, which she had recovered after the murder of her husband Odaenathus—more by the terror of battle than by battle itself [Note: “More by the terror of battle.” Four Leiden manuscripts and the Utrecht manuscript, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “more by the terror of battles.”].

In Gaul, Tetricus, quite unable to withstand the mutinies of his soldiers, wrote:

“Rescue me from these evils, unconquered one,”

and by this act became a traitor to his own army; Aurelian overcame him without difficulty [Note: “Rescue me from these.” Read Pollio’s Life of the Tyrant Tetricus. FABR. — Taken from Virgil, Aeneid VI, 365.].

Thus he triumphed in great glory as the restorer of the East and the North. He fortified the city of Rome with stronger walls [Note: “The city of Rome.” Perizonius reads “and the city of Rome.”]. Finally, when, as the ninth after Nero, he decreed that persecution should be undertaken against the Christians [Note: “Should be undertaken.” This is absent from four Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection and can be omitted.], a thunderbolt fell before him, greatly terrifying those standing around; not long afterward he was killed while on the road.

523 CHAPTER XXIV. The emperors Claudius Tacitus, Annius Florianus, Aurelius Valerius Probus, and M. Aurelius Carus.

In the year 1032 from the founding of the City, Tacitus, having attained the imperial power as the thirtieth emperor, was killed in Pontus in the sixth month. After him Florianus, meeting the same fate in his rule, was killed only in the third month at Tarsus.

In the year 1033 from the founding of the City, Probus, the thirty-first to obtain the throne, held it for six years [and four months]. [Note: “And four months” is absent from the Augustan edition.] He completely liberated Gaul, which had long been occupied by the barbarians, through many severe battles, finally destroying the enemies. [Note: Some editions have “after many [battles],” rather than “through many [battles].”]

Thereafter he waged two civil wars, and indeed with very great bloodshed. [Note: “And indeed” is preferred by the Leiden and Perizonian editions to *equidem*, “indeed”; two Florentine manuscripts confirm it.] One was in the East, in which he crushed and captured Saturninus, who had relied upon tyranny; the other in which he killed Proculus and Bonosus after they had been overcome in great battles near Agrippina. [Note: Some manuscripts more correctly have *Saturninum* than *Saturnium*, which appears in others and in the common editions.]

[Note: The lives of Tacitus, Florianus, Probus, Saturninus, Proculus, and Bonosus, written by Flavius Vopiscus, are extant; read them.]

He himself was killed at Sirmium, in an iron-clad tower, during a military disturbance. [Note: Herodian, book seven, calls Sirmium “the greatest city of the Paeonians.”]

In the year 1039 from the founding of the City, Carus of Narbo, the thirty-second, assumed the imperial power and held it for two years. [Note: The first and third Leiden editions, together with the Groningen Collection, have “for a period of two years.”] After he had made his sons Carinus and Numerian co-rulers, [Note: The Leiden editions prefer *fecisset*, “had made,” to *effecisset*, “had appointed” or “had brought about,” found in the common editions.] he entered the Parthian war. Having captured the two most distinguished cities of the Parthians, Cochem and Ctesiphon, he perished after being struck by lightning in his camp beyond the Tigris.

[Note: Regarding Carus, see Vopiscus and Sextus Aurelius. Consult the same authors concerning Carinus and Numerian.]

[Note: Some manuscripts from our collection have *Choten*, *Cothem*, and *Chocem*; the Augustan edition has *Achem*. Schönhovius’s Eutropius has *Corchen*, while my manuscript has *Soaenen*. The true name is Cochem. See Cellarius’s *Geography*.]

Numerian, who had been with his father, was killed on the return journey through the treachery of his father-in-law Aper.

[Note: Numerian was a remarkable prince, gifted in speech and verse, and commendable for his devotion to his father; he was all the more regretted because his brother Carinus was turning toward every kind of evil. All his coins are far from common. Many are found in bronze, though of the smallest size; those of larger and largest size are especially rare. Among a sufficiently large and select number of coins of the largest size—commonly called medallions—I possess a beautiful coin of this Numerian, of the greatest size, of the finest quality, and far removed from every suspicion of forgery.

Its unusual size and the thickness of the bronze are not its only recommendations; its exceptionally noble type is also noteworthy. On the obverse is a bust of Numerian, laureate, wearing the trabea and adorned with the imperial insignia. In his right hand he holds an ivory staff, at whose top is an eagle; in his left he holds a globe, upon which Victory stands, turned toward the emperor as though about to crown him. Around it is written: **IMPerator Caesar NVMERIANVS Pius Felix AVGustus COnSul**.

The reverse displays the two emperors, Carus and Numerian, standing on a platform with the prefect of the praetorian guard and addressing the soldiers with their right hands extended. Several military figures stand by, with eagles and legionary standards, ready to hear the emperors’ speech. The inscription is **ADLOCVTIO AVGG**, that is, “of the Augusti.” I do not refer the third letter G—whose part appears incomplete and sunken among the others—to Carinus; rather, as commonly happens when a coin is struck, the bronze must have shifted somewhat from its place and thereby received that form.

The coin itself is unpublished and was acquired by us from the former Marckian collection. It is exactly of this size and design.]

## CHAPTER XXV

### How C. Aurelius Valerius Diocletianus ruled, and what was done under and through him. The Roman Empire is divided for the first time.

In the year 1041 from the founding of the City, Diocletian, the thirty-third emperor chosen by the army, ruled for twenty years. [Note: I restored “ruled” from the Augustan edition; the others have “was.”]

As soon as he possessed the opportunity to exercise power, he killed Aper, the murderer of Numerian, with his own hand.

[Note: We can learn from Vopiscus, *Life of Numerian*, chapters 14 and 15, why Diocletian killed Aper with his own hand. A Druid had foretold to him that he would become emperor once he had killed Aper. Accordingly, as Vopiscus relates, whenever he had the opportunity while hunting, he always killed boars with his own hand.

Finally, when Aurelian had received the imperial power, and likewise when Probus, Tacitus, and Carus had received it, Diocletian said: “I always kill boars, but another always enjoys the dish.” It is now well known and commonly reported that, after he had killed the prefect of the praetorian guard, Aper, he is said to have declared: “At last I have killed the fated boar.”

In the preceding passage Vopiscus relates that his grandfather and Maximian were aware of this matter and saying: “Maximian knew it, as did my grandfather, from whom he himself had learned this saying from the Druid.” Read the passage beginning, “Those who knew this saying,” and so forth.]

He then overcame Carinus, whom Carus had left as Caesar in Dalmatia, living disgracefully, in a very difficult war and with the greatest effort.

Afterward, when Amandus and Aelianus in Gaul had raised a band of peasants—whom they called *Vacaudae*—and had stirred up destructive disturbances, he made Maximian, surnamed Herculeus, Caesar and sent him into Gaul. Maximian easily subdued the ignorant and disordered band of country people by military valor. [Note: *Vacaudas.* Eutropius in Schönhovius has the name *Bacaudarum*; my manuscript has *Bagaudarum*. What Orosius writes here is also found in Eutropius, book nine, and in Sextus Aurelius. The first Florentine manuscript and the first and third Leiden editions have *Bacaudas*; the third Florentine, *Bacuades*; the fourth Leiden, *Baugaudas*; the second, *Baticadas*; Perizonius, *Bangandas*; the Augustan edition, *Bagandas*. Compare Eutropius and Victor.]

[Note: “Subdued.” *Composuit*, “ordered” or “brought into order,” fits the disordered band better than *compescuit*, “restrained,” found in the common editions. I have retained *composuit*, although it also appears in two Florentine editions and in Perizonius.]

Then a certain Carausius, low-born indeed but ready in judgment and action, was stationed to watch the shores of the Ocean, which the Franks and Saxons were then ravaging. Since he was acting more to the ruin than to the advantage of the state—returning booty seized from the pirates in no part to its owners, but claiming it for himself alone—he aroused suspicion. [Note: “Returning booty seized from the pirates in no part to its owners.” The first and third Leiden editions have this wording, adding that it was “not restored in any part to its owners.”]

[Note: “He aroused suspicion.” I restored this from the Perizonian manuscript in place of the inept “arousing,” which is found in the others and in the common editions.]
