[Note: “That he would allow even the enemies themselves to attack the frontiers through an artful negligence.” Since *quia* and *quod* are frequently confused in the manuscripts of Orosius, *quod* should plainly be restored here in place of *quia*.]

For this reason, ordered by Maximian to be killed, he assumed the purple and seized Britain. [Note: Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, have *admitteret*, “would admit,” rather than *permitteret*, “would permit.”] [Note: Some manuscripts express *Britannia* here and below in the singular.]

Thus, throughout all the frontiers of the Roman Empire, the crashes of sudden disturbances resounded: Carausius rebelling in Britain, Achilleus in Egypt, while the Quinquegentiani were also harassing Africa; and Narseus, king of the Persians, was pressing the East with war. [Note: Concerning the Quinquegentiani, compare what learned men have noted on page 423 of Aurelius Victor and page 436 of Eutropius.]

Moved by this danger, Diocletian made Maximian Herculeus Augustus instead of Caesar, and chose Constantius and Maximian Galerius as Caesars.

Constantius took Theodora, the stepdaughter of Herculeus Maximian, as his wife; by her he fathered six sons, the brothers of Constantine.

Carausius, after most vigorously claiming and retaining Britain for himself for seven years, was finally killed through the treachery of his associate Allectus.

[Note: “At last, through the treachery of Allectus,” and so forth. I possess several coins of Carausius and Allectus, with various types; it was enough to produce one of each. I added to them an exceptional Carausius coin of the first size, from the Lebretian collection. All are bronze.]

Allectus afterward held the island wrested from Carausius for three years. Asclepiodotus, prefect of the praetorian guard, crushed him and recovered Britain after ten years.

Constantius Caesar, however, in Gaul, after his army had been routed by the Alamanni in the first battle, barely escaped himself; but in the second battle a sufficiently favorable victory followed.

For sixty thousand Alamanni are reported to have been killed in a few hours. [Note: Four Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, count seventy thousand Alamanni.]

Maximian Augustus, moreover, subdued the Quinquegentiani in Africa.

Diocletian, for his part, captured and killed Achilleus at Alexandria after besieging him for eight months. But, using his victory without restraint, he gave Alexandria over to plunder and stained all Egypt with proscriptions and massacres.

Furthermore, Galerius Maximian, after having already fought Narseus in two battles, encountered and was defeated by him in a third between Callinicum and Carrhae. Having lost his forces, he fled back to Diocletian. [Note: *Callinicum.* This town of Mesopotamia should be written *Callinicum*, not *Gallinicum*, *Gallienicum*, or *Gallianicum*, as it appears in the manuscripts and editions. The derivation of the name and the work of geographers make this clear. See Cellarius.]

Diocletian received him with extreme arrogance, so that he is reported to have run in his purple robe before Diocletian’s carriage for several miles.

Nevertheless, he used this insult as a whetstone for valor; by it he sharpened his mind, its rust of royal arrogance having been worn away. Accordingly, he soon gathered forces from all sides through Illyricum and Moesia and immediately returned against the enemy. [Note: The first Leiden edition has “and at once.”]

He overcame Narseus with great planning and strength. After the Persian forces had been destroyed and Narseus himself put to flight, he invaded his camp, captured his wives, sisters, and children, seized an immense quantity of Persian treasure, and led away very many Persian nobles as prisoners.

On his return to Mesopotamia he was received by Diocletian with the highest honors.

Afterward, the same commanders fought vigorously against the Carpi and the Basternae. They then defeated the Sarmatians and dispersed their extremely numerous captive multitude among the garrisons of the Roman frontiers. [Note: The third Leiden edition, together with the Groningen Collection, has *captivorum*, “of captives,” rather than *captivam*, “captive”; this better suits the sense.]

Meanwhile Diocletian in the East and Maximian Herculeus in the West ordered churches to be devastated and Christians to be afflicted and killed, in the tenth persecution after Nero. This persecution was longer and more savage than nearly all those that had preceded it.

For ten years it was carried on without interruption through the burning of churches, the proscription of the innocent, and the slaughter of martyrs.

Then came an earthquake in Syria, in which, as roofs collapsed everywhere at Tyre and Sidon, many thousands of people were crushed.

In the second year of the persecution, Diocletian compelled Maximian, against his will, to lay down the purple and the imperial power together, so that, with younger men substituted for them in the government of the state, they themselves might grow old in private leisure.

[Note: Diocletian afterward lived quietly in retirement at Salona, whereas Maximian, just as he had unwillingly laid down the imperial power, later vainly aspired again to the dignity he had once surrendered. While he was plotting impious frauds against his son-in-law Constantine, he paid the deserved penalties of the crime he had conceived, having been caught in the very act.

The coins of both Augusti are common. Many Greek examples may also be observed, but struck in Egypt. We preserve, among others of this kind, two such coins. On the first is the face of Diocletian, with the inscription **ΔΙΟΚΛΗΤΙΑΝΟϹ ϹΕΒαστος**, “Diocletian Augustus.” On the other side is a figure of Hope, holding a flower in her right hand and lifting her garment with her left. The year of the imperial reign appears as **Λυκάβαντος ΕΝΑΤΟΥ**, “in the ninth year.”

On the coin of Maximian, the fourth year of his reign is marked **Λυκάβαντος Δʹ**. The type customary on Egyptian coins—a spread eagle holding a crown in its beak, with a star at its side—is visible.

Around Maximian’s head is written **Αυτοκράτωρ Καίσαρ ΜΑρκος ΟΥΑλέριος ΜΑΞΙΜΙΑΝΟϹ ϹΕΒαστος**, “Emperor Caesar Marcus Valerius Maximianus Augustus.”]

Thus, on a single day, Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid down the authority of the empire and its ceremonial insignia. [Note: “They laid down.” This is preferred by the second Florentine manuscript and four Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection; the common editions have “they placed,” although above also the text says *deponere*, not *ponere*.]

Galerius and Constantius, the Augusti, for the first time divided the Roman Empire into two parts: Galerius Maximian received Illyricum, Asia, and the East; Constantius received Italy, Africa, Spain, and Gaul.

But Constantius, a most peaceful man, content with Gaul and Spain alone, ceded the remaining regions to Galerius.

Galerius chose two Caesars: Maximinus, whom he established in the East, and Severus, to whom he entrusted Italy; he himself was established in Illyricum.

Constantius Augustus, a man of the greatest gentleness and courtesy, died in Britain. He left his son Constantine, born of his concubine Helena, as emperor of the Gauls.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### Constantine the Great, Emperor, Caesar, Augustus. Meanwhile he elegantly refutes the objections of his opponents concerning the Church’s most recent ten-year devastation.

In the year 1061 from the founding of the City, Constantine, the thirty-fourth emperor after Augustus, received the reins of the empire from his father Constantius and held them most successfully for thirty-one years. [Note: Constantine’s life was described at length by Eusebius in five books. See also Sextus Aurelius and Eutropius. Several manuscripts, together with the Augustan edition, add “from his own father.”]

Suddenly I am confronted, and certain people mock me with exultant cries:

“Ah!” they say. “At last you have come, long awaited, into our pits. We were waiting for you to descend here; here we crush you once you have fallen; here, bewildered, we hold you. Until now we have endured you as you artfully and cunningly adapted the chance changes of the times to the vengeance of the Christians.

Sometimes, moved by the appearance of probability—for we are ignorant of divine mysteries—we turned pale with fear. But now our Maximian has emptied the entire stage of your drama, and an impregnable column has upheld the antiquity of our religion. [Note: Some older editions have “our antiquated religion,” rather than “the antiquity of our religion.”]

[Note: “An impregnable column shone.” The third Leiden manuscript and Perizonius have “he shone with an impregnable column.” But the common reading is sound, and its meaning is this: Maximian supported the antiquity of our religion, which had been attacked but remained victorious and steadfast, like a stable and firm column standing in its place. Cicero, *Oration for Rabirius Postumus*, chapter 16: “He caught him as he was falling, did not allow him to collapse; he supported and sustained him by his resources, fortune, and loyalty.”]

For ten years your churches were overthrown, as you yourself admit; Christians throughout the world were torn apart by tortures and emptied out by death. We have your explicit testimony that no earlier persecution was either so severe or so prolonged.

And yet behold: amid the most peaceful blessings of the times, even the emperors who carried out these things enjoyed extraordinary happiness. [Note: The first Leiden edition has “there were the most peaceful blessings of the times.”] [Note: The second Leiden edition has “extraordinary felicity,” rather than “extraordinary happiness.”]

There was no famine at home, no pestilence, no war abroad except a voluntary one, by which strength could be exercised without being endangered. Moreover, there was a circumstance previously unknown to the human race: several kings at once endured partnership and shared power in great harmony, and their common authority now looked after the common welfare—something that had never happened before.

Furthermore—and this too has hitherto been unknown to mortal experience—those greatest emperors, although persecutors, laid aside their honors and adopted repose. In private life, which men judge to be most blessed and the highest good of a good life, they attained this as though it were a reward, precisely when the persecution they had begun was raging throughout the world at the midpoint of its course.

Are you also claiming that this happiness befell them as a punishment in those times, and trying to frighten us by this as well?”

To them I would reply humbly that, armed with the greatest concern for piety, I am reminding them of truths, not frightening them with falsehoods.

The Church of Christ suffered ten persecutions, from Nero to Maximian. [Note: The second Leiden edition has “ten persecutors,” rather than “ten persecutions.”] [Note: Some manuscripts have “endured” rather than “suffered.”]

Nine calamities followed immediately as vengeance, as they themselves do not deny. [Note: Four Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection and the Perizonian manuscript, have “from the traces.”]

Nor do I argue over the word, whether they appear to have been deserved punishments or accidental changes, although by their own testimony and by that of the events themselves they were disasters. [Note: The manuscripts and the second Florentine have *premo*, “I press,” while the Augustan edition has *promo*, “I bring forward.” The sense is: “I do not wish to dispute whether,” and so forth.]

In the tenth persecution, the wretched and blind think that there is uncertainty, not seeing that it was all the more grievous for them because it was less understood.

For “the impious is scourged, and does not feel it.” [Note: These words are from Jeremiah 5:3.]

When this has been explained, although unwillingly because of the very truth of the events, they will confess that these are the wounds inflicted by the greatest punishment of the Maximian persecution. Even now they suffer from them, and they suffer to such an extent that they cry out and provoke us also to cry back at them, anxiously considering how their shouting may be silenced. [Note: Only the Augustan edition has “to condemn themselves,” rather than “to cry back.” The passage is obscure. The apparent meaning is that, feeling their misery and crying out from pain, the wretched compel us in turn to cry out at them, anxious about how we may restrain their shouting.]

## CHAPTER XXVII

### A comparison of the Israelite and Christian peoples, and likewise of the Egyptian and Roman peoples: how the former suffered nearly identical things on God’s behalf in afflictions, while the latter suffered them from God in punishments.

In the first book we explained that Pompeius Trogus and Cornelius Tacitus had recalled—though not fully—that our Moses, whose testimony is reliable even by their own witness, had faithfully and sufficiently stated that the Egyptians and their king, when they tried to recall the people of God, intent and ready to serve their own God, to mud and straw in order to obstruct their devotion, were afflicted with ten exceedingly bitter plagues. [Note: The first and fourth Leiden editions have “in the first book,” rather than “in the first little book.”] [Note: The third Leiden edition has “with the sharpest plagues,” rather than “with the most bitter plagues.”]

Then, subdued by the violence of their evils, they not only forced them to depart in haste but also loaded them with their own silver and gold vessels. [Note: “Their own” is absent from the Augustan edition, which soon afterward prefers “to have heaped up.”]

Afterward, having forgotten their plague and desiring the unlawful spoil, and also jealous of another’s religion, they eagerly pursued the innocent. When they had all finally been overtaken in the Red Sea, they perished there utterly.

What I now relate and proclaim—although perhaps not accepted as credible—must nevertheless be proved by the outcome, because these things were done as a figure of our own history. [Note: “As a figure of our own” is taken from 1 Corinthians 10:6.]

Both peoples belong to one God; the cause of both peoples is one. The synagogue of the Israelites was subjected to the Egyptians; the Church of the Christians has been subjected to the Romans. The Egyptians persecuted; the Romans also persecuted. There were ten acts of opposition there against Moses; here, ten edicts against Christ. There were different plagues of the Egyptians there; here, different calamities of the Romans.

To compare even the plagues with one another, insofar as the figure may be compared with its form:

There, the first punishment brought blood, either flowing commonly from the wells or running in the rivers. Here, the first plague under Nero brought it about that everywhere there was the blood of the dying, corrupted by diseases in the City or poured out in wars throughout the world.

There, the following plague revealed frogs croaking and leaping throughout the inner rooms; they nearly caused famine for the inhabitants and drove them into exile. Here, the following punishment under Domitian similarly showed that, through the wicked and unrestrained movements of his attendants and soldiers, carrying out the bloodiest commands of the emperor, nearly all Roman citizens were reduced to want and scattered into exile.

There, the third affliction consisted of gnats—that is, the smallest and most savage flies—which, often in the middle of the heat, gathered densely in desolate places, swarming in formation, and used to settle with a shrill flight, lodging among the hair of humans and the bristles of cattle with a burning bite. [Note: The Leiden manuscripts and the Perizonian manuscript have “most savage” rather than “and most savage.”]

[Note: “And they usually settle with a shrill flight.” Until now, an extremely inept reading occupied all editions except the Augustan one. All of them read “and they usually settle in no flight,” which is nevertheless an unresolved defect, since the manuscripts offered no help. All the manuscripts I examined have either *in nullo* (“in no”) as printed, or *ac et nullo*, as the third Florentine has, or *et in ullo*, as the second Florentine has. The last comes closest to the true reading, *tinnulo volatu*, “with a shrill flight,” which I eagerly restored to the text, though not without profound respect for the distinguished Augustan edition.]

Here, likewise, the third plague under Trajan stirred up the Jews. Although previously scattered everywhere and now quiet, as though they scarcely existed, they were suddenly aroused by a violent impulse and raged throughout the world against those among whom they lived, without great destruction of the many cities which frequent earthquakes overthrew at the same time. [Note: Many manuscripts have “with immense destruction” rather than “with great destruction.”]

There, in the fourth plague, there were dog-flies, savage fosterers of corruption and mothers of worms. [Note: “Savage fosterers” is more pleasing, as it occurs in three Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen Collection, than “fosterers of corruption,” which the others and the common editions provide.]

Here, likewise, the fourth plague under Marcus Antoninus was a pestilence poured over many provinces. It gave all Italy, including the entire city of Rome, and the Roman army, scattered across distant frontiers and different winter quarters, over to death and corruption and worms. [Note: The second Leiden edition and the Groningen Collection have “in different places” rather than “and different winter quarters.”] [Note: Three Leiden manuscripts, together with Perizonius and the Groningen Collection, have “dissolved by death,” rather than “dissolved into death.”]

There, the fifth punishment was completed by the sudden death of cattle and beasts of burden. Here, similarly, in the fifth retribution under the persecutor Severus, through very frequent civil wars the state’s own entrails and supports—that is, the populations of the provinces and the legions of soldiers—were shattered.

There, the sixth affliction brought swollen blisters and running ulcers. Here, likewise, the sixth punishment, which followed the persecution of Maximinus, grew swollen. Maximinus had ordered bishops and clergy in particular, leaving aside the common people—that is, the leaders of the churches—to be slaughtered. Inflamed by frequent anger and envy, it burst forth not through the slaughter of the multitude but through the wounds and deaths of rulers and powerful men. [Note: Some manuscripts and the Augustan edition have “the deaths of dying rulers,” rather than “the deaths of rulers.”]

[Note: “It burst forth.” The Cologne manuscript has *exaltata*, “raised up,” from which Fabricius fashioned his reading *exaltata*, but less skillfully. The editors should by no means have altered *exalata* or *exhalata*, which they found in the manuscripts, to *exaltata*. This was not Fabricius’s own doing; rather, he followed too confidently the earlier editions, all of which had adopted the bad reading. In my manuscript and in the Utrecht manuscript I found *exalata*, as also in the Augustan edition, which faithfully reproduces everywhere even the faulty readings of its excellent manuscript. Four Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen Collection, correctly have *exhalata*. In this passage *exhalata est* means “it boiled over” or “it burst forth.”]

There, the seventh plague is recorded as hail poured down after the air had been gathered together, bringing destruction to humans, beasts of burden, and crops. [Note: “The air having been gathered.” Those who printed “hail poured down with the air gathered” paid no attention to ordinary experience. All editions before Fabricius and the manuscripts preserve the natural reading, and reason itself teaches that clouds are gathered together and condensed when a heavier rain or hailstorm approaches.] [Note: “To beasts of burden and crops.” It was equally foolishly printed as “to beasts of burden and crops,” although some manuscripts read it that way.]

Here, similarly, the seventh plague under Gallus and Volusianus, who succeeded the persecutor Decius, soon killed, was the pestilence poured out after the air had been corrupted. It spread through all the regions of the Roman empire from East to West and not only destroyed nearly every kind of human being and animal but also—

[Note: The Perizonian manuscript has “the persecutor,” rather than “to the persecutor.”]

It corrupted the lakes and infected the pastures with poison.

[Note: “And it corrupted the lakes,” and so forth. This is the better reading of the manuscripts. Some omit the conjunction. The lines are taken from Virgil, *Georgics* 3.480:

> And gave every kind of cattle, every kind of wild beast, to death,  
> And corrupted the lakes, infected the pastures with poison.]

There, the eighth affliction of Egypt was caused by locusts raised up everywhere, occupying, wearing away, and covering everything. [Note: In some manuscripts only the middle verb occurs. Perhaps the rest arose from variant readings. “Wearing away everything” or “covering and wearing away everything” is sufficient.]

Here, the eighth likewise was brought upon the overthrow of the Roman world by peoples raised up everywhere, who destroyed all the provinces with massacres and fires.

There, the ninth disturbance consisted of prolonged, dense, and almost tangible darkness, threatening more danger than it caused. [Note: Two Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen Collection have “penetrable,” rather than “almost tangible.”]

Here, likewise, the ninth punishment occurred when, under Aurelian, who had decreed persecution, a terrible and mournful thunderbolt fell amid dreadful storms at his very feet. It showed what so great an avenger could do when such retribution was demanded, unless he were also merciful and patient.

Nevertheless, within the following six months, three emperors—Aurelian, Tacitus, and Florianus—were killed for different reasons.

There, finally, the tenth and last of all the plagues was the killing of the sons whom each man had first begotten. [Note: The Augustan edition has “of the sons who were killed,” rather than “the killing of sons.”]

Here, no less, the tenth—that is, the last—punishment of all was the destruction of all the idols, which they had formerly loved above all.

There, the king perceived, proved, and feared the power of God, and therefore allowed the people of God to depart free. [Note: The Augustan manuscript reads: “Here the tyrants enlarged the Church of God, freed from persecution, with honors.” But the author is speaking about Constantine the Great, as is clear from the word “believed,” set in opposition to the preceding “feared.” The received reading is therefore sound.]

Here, the king perceived, proved, and believed in the power of God, and therefore allowed the people of God to be free.

There, afterward, the people of God were never again brought back into slavery; here, afterward, the people of God were never again compelled to idolatry.

There, the precious vessels of the Egyptians were handed over to the Hebrews; here, the chief pagan temples passed to the Christian churches.

Indeed, as I said, I think this must be announced: just as eternal destruction rushed upon the Egyptians when, after the ten plagues, they attempted to pursue the Hebrews who had been released, through the sea brought upon them from above, so a persecution of the gentiles, which will one day come upon us, awaits us as we travel freely, until we cross the Red Sea—that is, the fire of judgment—with our Lord Jesus Christ as leader and judge.

But those into whom the form of the Egyptians is transferred, raging with the gravest permission of God during the time for which power has been allowed them, will persecute Christians with torments. [Note: “Raging.” I wrote this from the traces preserved in the Cologne manuscript. What connection does the reading *servientes*, “serving,” found here, have? The Fabrician editions somehow introduced *servientes*; the older editions and the manuscripts have *saevientes*, “raging,” as required.]

[Note: “Will persecute Christians with torments.” The Perizonian manuscript, the Augustan edition, the first edition, and the Venetian editions have this reading; the first Leiden edition has “they torture [Christians] with persecutions.” Orosius seems to be indicating the future persecutions of the Church under another, spiritual Egypt, namely those foretold in John’s Apocalypse. The passage concerning the punishment of Antichrist and of all who resemble him is also taken from there.]

Nevertheless, all these enemies of Christ, together with their king Antichrist, received into the lake of eternal fire—which is entered while it is not seen because of the great darkness obstructing it—will obtain everlasting destruction and burn in immortal punishments.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### The reigns and deeds of Constantine the Great Augustus, Maxentius, Licinius, and Maximian. Also concerning the heretic Arius and his condemned doctrine.

Therefore, when Constantine had died, as I have said, in Britain, Constantine was made emperor. [Note: [Col. 1134C] “Was made.” In most manuscripts *est* (“was”) has dropped out.] He was the first of the Christian emperors, [Note: [Col. 1134D] “Of the emperors.” Two Florentine manuscripts read *imperator*, “emperor.”] with the exception of Philip, who, as it seems to me, was appointed a Christian for only a very few years, and for this sole purpose: that Rome’s thousandth year might be dedicated to Christ rather than to idols. [Note: [Col. 1134D] “Might be dedicated.” Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, and also the Utrecht and Perizonius manuscripts, read *dedicaretur*; this reading is also written above the line in the second Florentine manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 1134D] “But from Constantine.” Most manuscripts read, “But from Constantine all [emperors] have always been Christians,” etc., with *autem* deleted.] From Constantine onward, all emperors have always been created Christians [Col. 1134B] down to the present day, [Note: [Col. 1134D] “To the present day.” Four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “to this present day.”] with the exception of Julian, whom a destructive life abandoned while he was plotting impiously, as they say. [Note: [Col. 1134D] “Plotting.” The second Florentine manuscript has *machinatum*, “having plotted.”]

This is that slow but certain punishment of the pagans. Hence the healthy become insane; hence those who have not been wounded are pierced with remorse. [Note: [Col. 1134D] “Those who have not been wounded.” The Perizonius manuscript reads, “the wounded are not pierced with remorse.” This is incorrect, as is clear from the context.] Hence those who laugh groan; hence the living waste away; hence those whom no one persecutes are secretly tortured. Hence now very few remain who have never been punished by any persecutor.

Nevertheless, I shall explain what end awaited those persecutors whose impunity they attempt not only to boast of but even to flaunt.

While Constantine was vigorously administering the state in Gaul, the praetorian soldiers at Rome proclaimed Maxentius, the son of Herculeus, who was living as a private citizen in Lucania, Augustus. Maximianus Herculeus, already a private citizen after being Augustus, but still a public persecutor, was stirred by the opportunity presented by his son, who had laid down the imperial power, and seized tyranny. Galerius Augustus sent Severus Caesar against Maxentius at Rome with an army. [Note: [Col. 1134D] “He sent him with an army.” Some older editions read, “he sends him with an army.”] While Severus was besieging the City, he was abandoned and betrayed through the crime of his own soldiers; fleeing from there, he was killed at Ravenna.

Maximianus Herculeus, the persecutor and, after being Augustus, a tyrant, attempted to strip his son—already firmly established [Col. 1135A] in the imperial power [Note: [Col. 1135C] “In the imperial power.” Some manuscripts delete *in*.]—of his royal clothing and authority. [Note: [Col. 1135C] “Attempted to strip.” Four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts read *spoliare conatus est*, “attempted to strip,” as do the Utrecht and Gronovian manuscripts and some older editions; the Augustan edition has *exspoliare conatus*.] But openly terrified by the soldiers’ insults and tumult, [Note: [Col. 1135C] “By insults and tumult.” The Perizonius manuscript reads, “having been convicted”; but *autem* is absent from two Lugd. Bat. manuscripts.] he went to Gaul in order, through his son-in-law Constantine, who was equally joined to him in his schemes, to remove the empire; but he was detected and betrayed by his daughter, then put to flight, and finally seized and killed at Massilia.

After Severus had been killed, Galerius created Licinius emperor. Although Galerius himself had added still more atrocious edicts to the persecution sent forth by Diocletian and Maximian, [Note: [Col. 1135C] “Sent forth.” The Augustan edition reads *passam*, “suffered.”] and after he had exhausted the provinces of every kind of human being for ten years, his inward organs putrefied and his vital powers dissolved. Beyond the horror of human misery, he even vomited worms; and when the physicians could no longer endure the stench, they were repeatedly killed at his command. [Note: [Col. 1135C] “And the physicians.” Thus correctly in the first editions, the Venetian editions, and the Scottish edition; nothing in the later editions supports the word *neque*, “nor,” which appears in Fabricius and others.]

Then, rebuked by a certain physician who drew courage from despair, Galerius was told that the wrath of God was his punishment and that for this reason he could not be cured by physicians. He issued widely circulated edicts recalling the Christians from exile. But, unable to endure his sufferings, he brought violence upon his own life. [Note: [Col. 1135C] “Thus then was the state.” The manuscripts transpose these words. I do not know how the reading “Thus now is the state,” which occurs in the Fabrician and Scottish editions, could have been tolerated and repeatedly reproduced.]

Thus the state was then under four new rulers: Constantine and Maxentius, the sons of Augusti, and Licinius and Maximinus, new men. [Note: [Col. 1135D] “Maximinus.” The manuscripts restore the man’s name. The common reading, *Maximiano*, is inept.] Constantine granted peace to the churches after ten years during which they had been harassed by persecutors. Then civil war broke out between Constantine and Maxentius. [Note: [Col. 1135D] “Broke out.” The Augustan edition reads *ortum est*, “arose.”] Maxentius, wearied by many battles, was finally defeated and killed at the Mulvian Bridge. [Note: [Col. 1135D] “Wearied.” Four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Utrecht and Gronovian manuscripts, read “agitated”; the Augustan edition has “put to flight.”]

Maximinus, the most hostile instigator and executor of the persecution of the Christians, died at Tarsus while preparing a civil war against Licinius. Licinius, suddenly aroused to madness, ordered all Christians to be expelled from his palace.

Soon war flared up between Licinius himself and Constantine. Constantine first defeated Licinius, the husband of his sister, in Pannonia, and then crushed him at Cibalae. Having gained possession of all Greece, he repeatedly restrained Licinius, who was rising against him by land and sea, and finally forced him to surrender. [Note: [Col. 1135D] “And restrained him.” The Augustan edition reads, “and crushed him.”]

But, following the example of his father-in-law Maximianus Herculeus, Constantine ordered Licinius, now a private citizen, to be killed, lest he should once again take up the purple, which he had laid down, to the ruin of the state; since, when all the agents of the wicked persecution had already been destroyed, fitting punishment demanded this man too as a persecutor, insofar as he had been able to exert himself. [Note: [Col. 1135D] “Although all the ministers.” This passage was corrupted in the editions as follows: “Although all the ministers of the wicked persecution had by then been destroyed, fitting punishment demanded that he too, insofar as he was able, should exercise persecution.” I first restored *cum* from the oldest editions, the Paris and Venetian editions; then, on the authority of the two Florentine manuscripts and Perizonius, as well as the Augustan and several other earliest editions, I changed *persecutionem*, “persecution,” to *persecutorem*, “persecutor.” In some manuscripts I read *exserere* instead of *exercere*; marginal notes in the editions of Hittorp and Bolswing testify to this. Nor do I reject that reading, for one says *exserere principem* and similar expressions. Licinius was therefore a persecutor insofar as he could be by himself, and would have been more savage if Constantine had allowed it. Thus divine vengeance rightly awaited him, since he alone remained.]

Constantine’s sons, Crispus and Constantine, and Licinius the Younger, the son of Licinius Augustus and Constantine’s nephew through his sister, were made Caesars.

In those days [Col. 1136B] Arius, a presbyter of the city of Alexandria, deviating from the truth of the Catholic faith, established a destructive doctrine for many. [Note: [Col. 1136C] “Arius, of the city of Alexandria.” The ecclesiastical writers have said so much about Arius and the Council of Nicaea that I think I ought to remain silent. —FABR.]

As soon as he first became known—or marked out—in Alexandria among the confused crowd of his followers and opponents, he was expelled from the Church by Alexander, then bishop of that same city. [Note: [Col. 1136C] “He became.” Two Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, delete *est* (“was”).] When he also incited the people whom he had led astray to sedition, an assembly of three hundred and eighteen bishops was held at Nicaea, a city of Bithynia. [Note: [Col. 1136C] “Whom he had led into error.” Four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with Perizonius, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Gronovian Collection, read: “and when he had stirred up the men whom he had led into this error,” and so forth.] Through them the destructive and wretched Arian doctrine was most clearly detected, publicly exposed, and rejected. [Note: [Col. 1136C] “Destructive and wretched.” Four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, Perizonius, the Utrecht and Gronovian manuscripts, and both Florentine manuscripts add *esse*, “to be.”]

But amid these events there lie hidden the reasons why the emperor Constantine turned the avenging sword and the punishment destined for the impious even against members of his own household. For he killed his son Crispus and Licinius, his sister’s son. [Note: [Col. 1136D] “Licinius, his sister’s son.” I do not know where the absurd reading found in Fabricius and the Scottish editions entered against all the manuscripts and editions: “and Licinius, his son, his sister’s son, he killed.” It is as though anyone could have thought of Licinius’s father, who had already been killed.]

Moreover, Constantine subdued many peoples in various battles. He founded a city bearing his own name. [Note: [Col. 1136D] “A city bearing his own name.” He means Constantinople, which had previously been Byzantium. —FABR.] [Note: [Col. 1136D] “Of his own name.” This reading of all the manuscripts, and also of the Augustan edition, is preferable to *nomine suo* (“in his own name”), which appears in the other common editions. Hence innumerable coins of every size are found celebrating Constantinople, founded by Constantine the Great. They occur everywhere. But I possess an extremely rare coin of Constantine the Great in pure silver and of the largest size, remarkable both for its unusual magnitude and for its most splendid inscription. [Col. 1137B] The first Christian emperor and founder of the new Rome is compared with Caesar Augustus, enlarger of the Roman empire, who had made Rome marble after it had been brick. On the obverse is the head of Constantine the Great, encircled by a jeweled crown (in place of which a laurel crown is seen on a similar coin in Bandurius); on the reverse is a huge laurel crown inscribed with the name of Caesar, placed beside Constantine’s head, not with Constantine’s own name but with that of Augustus, whom he was assimilating himself to. Thus the complete inscription of the coin, struck at Lyons and surpassing all others in its titles, is: *CAESAR AVGVSTVS* (“Caesar Augustus”). The size and image of the coin are as follows:]

He established a city of his own name, the first—or perhaps the only one—of the Roman kings to do so. This city alone, free from idols and founded within so brief a time by a Christian emperor, was advanced to such a degree that, in form and power, it could rightly be compared with Rome, which had been advanced through so many centuries and miseries. [Note: [Col. 1137C] “In form and power.” The second Florentine manuscript reads “in form as in power”; the other reads “both in form and power.”] [Note: [Col. 1137C] “Could be compared.” All the manuscripts and reason itself show that this is how the passage should be read. In the common editions, except the first and the Paris edition, the inept reading *posset*, “could,” appears.]

Then, in due and pious order, Constantine was the first to reverse the situation by an edict, since he decreed that the temples of the pagans should be closed without any human slaughter.

Soon afterward he destroyed the bravest and most numerous peoples of the Goths in the very heart of barbarian territory—that is, in the region of the Sarmatians.

He crushed a certain Calocerus, who was attempting revolution in Cyprus. [Note: [Col. 1137C] “Calocerus.” The first and third Lugd. Bat. editions, together with the Gronovian Collection, read *Calotherum*; the two Florentine editions, together with the Utrecht edition, have *Calocherum*; Perizonius has *Calochareum*.]

At his thirtieth anniversary celebrations he appointed Dalmatius Caesar. As he was preparing war against the Persians, he died in a public residence near Nicomedia, handing over the well-ordered state to his sons.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The Emperors Constantine, Constantius, and Constans; and, meanwhile, Magnentius seizing the empire, and Decentius

[Col. 1137B]

In the year 1092 from the founding of the City, Constantius, the thirty-fifth emperor, acquired the empire together with his brothers Constantine and Constans and held it for twenty-four years. [Note: [Col. 1137C] “Constantius, etc.” From the manuscripts and older editions I have restored the text in this form, which is more appropriate than the version published by Fabricius and others: “Constantine, the thirty-fifth, with Constantius and Constans, etc.” Constantius survived the others, whereas Constantine died immediately.] [Note: [Col. 1137C] “His brothers.” For the three sons of Constantine who succeeded him in the empire, see Eutropius, last book. —FABR.] [Note: [Col. 1137C] “For twenty-four years.” The Augustan edition incorrectly has “twenty-three”; he died in the twenty-fifth year of his reign and therefore ruled for twenty-four full years.]

Among Constantine’s successors there was also Dalmatius Caesar, his brother’s son, [Note: [Col. 1137D] “His brother’s son.” Four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, Perizonius, and Utrecht read “the son of his own brother.”] but he was immediately cut down by a military faction. [Note: [Col. 1137D] “By a faction.” The first and third Lugd. Bat. editions read “by sedition.”] [Note: [Col. 1138C] “He was cut down.” That is, “he was taken away prematurely.” Some scribes, not understanding the verb, wrote “he was deceived.”]

Meanwhile, the devil’s ever-malignant persecution of the true God [Note: [Col. 1138C] “The devil’s persecution.” The second Florentine manuscript reads “diabolical persecution”; the third, together with the Augustan edition, reads “the persecution of the devil.”—]—which from the beginning of the world until now has disturbed the slippery hearts of human beings by spreading clouds of errors [Note: [Col. 1138C] “Spread.” The two Florentine manuscripts and Perizonius read *effusis*, “poured out.”] over the sincere path of faith and religion—after it had ceased to persecute the Church of Christ through zeal for idolatry, when Christian emperors were turning the highest royal power toward better things, devised another scheme by which, through those same Christian emperors, it might harass the Church of Christ.

Accordingly, Arius, the author of the new error, and his other disciples gained ready and easy access to the familiarity of the emperor Constantius. Constantius was persuaded to believe that there were certain degrees within God; and he who had departed through the door from the error of idolatry was led back again into its bosom, while seeking gods within God, as through a false door. [Note: [Col. 1138C] “Back into its bosom, while.” Most books read “having returned into the bosom of the same,” but I can find no sense in the word *dum* there and have therefore altered the text. “Boldly, you will say.” Boldly indeed, but no less suitably. —LAUT. Although all the manuscripts and the Augustan edition write it in this way, the corrupt reading of the other editions—“having returned into the bosom of the same, he seeks gods within God”—was nevertheless followed by most later editions, except the Scottish one, in which the passage is correctly arranged.]

Thus power, deceived by a perverted zeal, was armed, and under the name of piety the force of persecution was set in motion. A dispute arose over the new choice of a name, so that the churches might belong rather to the Arians than to the Catholics. [Note: [Col. 1138C] “Over the new choice of a name.” Some manuscripts and editions read “over the choice of a new name,” and so forth.]

Then followed a terrible earthquake which leveled many cities of the East to the ground. [Note: [Col. 1138D] “Leveled to the ground.” Some manuscripts omit the first word.]

Constantine, while pursuing his brother Constans in war, rashly exposing himself to danger through reckless insolence, was killed by his commanders. [Note: [Col. 1139C] “While pursuing.” The second Florentine manuscript has “having pursued”; the Augustan edition and the Perizonius manuscript have “pursues.”] [Note: [Col. 1139C] “To dangers.” The Augustan edition reads “to danger.”]

Constantius fought nine battles against the Persians and Sapor, who had devastated Mesopotamia, with little success. [Note: [Col. 1139D] “Had devastated.” Two Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with Perizonius and the second Florentine manuscript, have the singular “had devastated.”] Finally, compelled by the mutiny and lack of discipline of his soldiers to attack at night, he lost, after nearly achieving victory, the victory that had almost been completed, being himself defeated in addition.

Afterward, when Constans had surrendered himself to intolerable vices and purchased the soldiers’ favor by punishing the provincials, [Note: [Col. 1139D] “Afterward, when Constans.” Constans is inserted from the same manuscripts as above, to which the other two Lugd. Bat. manuscripts and the Gronovian Collection are added. By omitting his name, as the editions do, Orosius is done a grave injustice as though ignorant of history.] he was killed by the treachery of Magnentius in a town called Helena, near Spain. [Note: [Col. 1139D] “Called Helena.” Eutropius writes that Constans died not far from Spain, in a fortress called Helena. Schonhovius incorrectly reads *castris*, “in the camp,” as is clear from Cassiodorus and Jerome’s Chronicle. —FABR.]

For Magnentius seized the empire at Augustodunum and immediately extended his power through Gaul, Africa, and Italy. In Illyricum [Col. 1140B] the soldiers created Vetranio, an elderly man, emperor for themselves. [Note: [Col. 1140D] “Vetranio.” This name is also written in this form in my copy of Eutropius. —FABR.] He was by nature simple and agreeable to everyone, but had never learned even the first elements of letters.

Thus, while the old emperor sometimes unwillingly practiced his first letters and syllables, [Note: [Col. 1140D] “While he practiced his first letters.” Perizonius and the fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript read “when he first practiced.”] Constantius—who, inflamed by vengeance for his brother, was then preparing war against Magnentius—ordered him to lay down the empire. Vetranio cast off both the purple and his letters, and, content with the leisure of a private citizen, left the palace and the school at the same time. [Note: [Col. 1140D] “And the school.” Perizonius has “and the schools.”]

Then Nepotianus, the son of Constantine’s sister, seized the empire at Rome, relying on a band of gladiators. Since he was wicked and therefore hated by everyone, he was subsequently crushed by the generals of Magnentius.

That terrible war between Constantius and Magnentius followed, fought near the city of Mursa, in which the destruction of much Roman strength caused harm even to later generations. Magnentius nevertheless was defeated and fled, and not long afterward killed himself at Lugdunum. Decentius, his brother, whom he had placed in charge of Gaul as Caesar, also ended his life by hanging at Senones.

Constantius immediately appointed Gallus, his uncle’s son, Caesar. But when Gallus again acted cruelly and tyrannically, Constantius killed him shortly after appointing him. He also took care to surround and crush without delay Sylvanus, who was aspiring to revolution throughout Gaul.

Accordingly, after Sylvanus had been killed, Constantius sent Julian, his cousin and Gallus’s brother, to Gaul, having created him Caesar. Thus Julian Caesar restored the Gauls, which had been overthrown and oppressed by the enemy, to their former condition with the greatest vigor. [Note: [Col. 1140D] “By the enemy.” Most manuscripts have this; others read “by the enemies.”]

With a small force he routed a great multitude of Alamanni. He bound the Germans to the Rhine. [Note: [Col. 1140D] “To the Rhine, etc.” Perizonius reads, “he separated the Germans from the Rhine by the river.”]

Elated by these successes, he usurped the dignity of Augustus; and soon, invading Italy and Illyricum, he deprived Constantius, who was occupied with wars against the Parthians, of part of his kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1140D] “In Parthian battles.” Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “in wars,” which is more Latin, though Orosius uses the terms interchangeably.]

When Constantius learned of Julian’s crime, he abandoned the Parthian expedition. As he was returning to the civil war, he died on the road between Cilicia and Cappadocia.

Thus the man who, by breaking the peace and unity of the Catholic faith, armed Christians against Christians and—so to speak—tore apart the members of the Church in civil war, spent, exhausted, and consumed the entire troubled period of his reign and the most burdensome span of his life in civil wars stirred up even among relatives and blood relations. [Note: [Col. 1141C] “By breaking the peace.” I prefer *discussa pace*, “with the peace broken,” which is found in the third Lugd. Bat. manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 1141C] “Arming.” Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with Perizonius and the Gronovian Collection, read “had armed.”] [Note: [Col. 1141C] “Troubled.” The Augustan edition has “of his troubled reign”; all the Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, have “the troubled period of his reign,” with *sui* omitted. This is not incorrect.]

## CHAPTER XXX. Flavius Claudius Julianus, emperor and Caesar

In the year 1116 from the founding of the City, Julian, formerly Caesar [Note: [Col. 1141C] “Formerly Caesar.” Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, both Florentine manuscripts, and the Venetian editions, read “already for some time Caesar”; shortly afterward, when he gained control of affairs, the second Florentine manuscript reads “already Caesar.”] and afterward the thirty-sixth ruler after Augustus, alone held supreme power for one year and eight months. He attacked the Christian religion by craft rather than by force, striving to induce the denial of the faith of Christ [Col. 1141B] and the acceptance of the worship of idols. [Note: [Col. 1141C] “And the worship of idols.” Julian’s madness in these matters is evident from one of his small bronze coins, on which the head of Serapis and the figure of Isis in a ship can be seen, with vows publicly offered by that impious man to those Egyptian idols. [Col. 1141D]]

Nevertheless, by an open edict he ordered that no Christian should be a professor of the liberal studies. [Note: [Col. 1141D] “That no one, etc.” Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, omit *quis*, “anyone”; Perizonius reads, “that no Christian should be a professor of the liberal studies.”]

Yet, as we have learned from our ancestors, [Note: [Col. 1142C] “From our ancestors.” The first and third Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, omit this phrase.] all of them almost everywhere embraced the conditions of the command and preferred to abandon their office rather than their faith.

Julian, however, while preparing war against the Parthians and drawing Roman forces gathered from every direction toward the destruction he had determined upon for himself, vowed Christian blood to his gods, intending openly to persecute the churches if he could attain victory. [Note: [Col. 1142C] “The churches.” Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, Perizonius, and the Gronovian Collection read “the Church.” One of these soon afterward has *posset*, “could,” instead of *potuisset*, “could have.” The second Florentine manuscript here reads, “preparing persecution for the churches.”]

For he also ordered an amphitheater to be built at Jerusalem, in which, after returning from the Parthians, he would cast the bishops, monks, and all the holy men of that place before beasts even fiercer than those made savage by art, and would watch them being torn apart.

Accordingly, after he had moved his camp from Ctesiphon and had been led into the desert by the treachery of a certain deserter, the army was wasted by thirst, the heat of the sun, and, in addition, the labor of the sands. [Note: [Col. 1142C] “Into the desert.” The Augustan edition reads “into a desert.”] The emperor, anxious amid such great dangers, wandered incautiously through the vast stretches of the desert. [Note: [Col. 1142C] “Through the vast desert.” Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with Perizonius and the Gronovian Collection, read “while he wandered through vast deserts”; the second Lugd. Bat. manuscript has “while he wandered through the vastness of the desert.”] [Note: [Col. 1142C] “Incautiously.” Perizonius has “incautious.”] He was struck by the spear of an enemy horseman whom he encountered and died. [Note: [Col. 1142C] “Thus merciful is God.” The first and third Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “and thus merciful is God.”] Thus merciful God dissolved the impious counsels by the death of the impious man.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Jovianus, emperor, Caesar, and Augustus

In the year 1117 from the founding of the City, [Note: [Col. 1142C] “Jovinianus.” On this man see Eutropius, at the end of Book X, Ammianus, Book XXV, and Sextus Aurelius. —FABR. The manuscripts more correctly write *Jovianus*, which is also the reading on coins.] Jovianus, the thirty-seventh emperor, was chosen by the army at the greatest crisis of affairs. Since he was both trapped by the unfavorable terrain and surrounded by the enemy, and could find no means of escape, he made a treaty with Sapor, king of the Persians—a treaty, as they think, not very honorable, but nevertheless sufficiently necessary. [Note: [Col. 1142D] “Not very honorable, as they think.” Against the manuscripts and the Augustan edition, all the other editions, perpetuating the error, ineptly read, “not very honorable, they think.”] In order to free the Roman army safely and unharmed not only from enemy attack but also from the danger posed by the terrain, he ceded to the Persians the town of Nisibis and part of Upper Mesopotamia.

From there, while returning to Illyricum and traveling through Galatia, he retired to sleep in a certain newly built room. He was oppressed and suffocated by the heat of the coals and the odor of the walls recently coated with plaster. [Note: [Col. 1142D] “Oppressed.” Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with Perizonius and the Gronovian Collection, read “heavily oppressed.”] He died only in the eighth month after he had begun to rule.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Flavius Valerius Valentinianus, emperor, Caesar, and Augustus, with his brother Valens; and concerning Gratian, already Caesar

[Col. 1142C] [Note: [Col. 1142D] “In the year, etc.” What Orosius writes from this point onward is also pursued by Paul the Deacon in the history which he appended to Eutropius. Whoever wishes may seek it there; since we have found nothing in it requiring annotation, we end here. —FABR.]

In the year 1118 from the founding of the City, Valentinianus, the thirty-eighth emperor, was made emperor at Nicaea with the consent of the soldiers, and remained in that position for eleven years. Although, as a Christian of uncorrupted faith, he faithfully fulfilled the military oath, and, under Julian [Note: [Col. 1143C] “And under Julian.” The conjunction *et* is omitted by the first Lugd. Bat. manuscript together with the Gronovian Collection.] Augustus [Note: [Col. 1143C] “Augustus.” It is absent from the second and third Lugd. Bat. manuscripts.] had served as tribune of the Scutarii, the sacrilegious emperor ordered him either to sacrifice to idols or to leave the army. Knowing faithfully [Note: [Col. 1143C] “Faithfully.” It is absent from the second Lugd. Bat. manuscript.] that God’s judgments were more severe [Note: [Col. 1143C] “And more severe.” The third and fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “more severe.”] and his promises better, he withdrew voluntarily.

Thus, after a brief interval, Julian was killed and Jovianus died; Christ repaid the man who had lost his tribuneship for the name of Christ by giving him the imperial power in place of his persecutor. Valentinianus later made his brother Valens a partner in the empire, and killed Procopius the usurper and many of his followers. [Note: [Col. 1143C] “And Procopius.” In all the manuscripts I consulted, *et*, “and,” is absent, as it is in the Augustan edition.]

An earthquake occurred throughout the entire world and shook the sea, which had also been thrown into confusion, so violently that the sea, overflowing into the neighboring flatlands, is reported to have destroyed many island cities, which were shaken and undermined. [Note: [Col. 1143C] “Throughout the entire world.” Some editions read “throughout the entire inhabited world.”]

Valens, baptized and persuaded by Eudoxius, a supporter of Arian doctrine, [Note: [Col. 1143C] “Arian.” The second Florentine manuscript reads “of the Arians.”] turned toward the most savage heresy. Yet he long concealed his malignant persecution [Note: [Col. 1143D] “Concealed.” The Augustan edition reads “covered over.”] and did not combine authority with his will, so long as he was restrained by the authority of his living brother. For he was observing how much power the faithful emperor might exercise in avenging the faith, [Note: [Col. 1143D] “In avenging the faith.” Three Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “in avenging the faithful emperor.”] since, as a soldier, he had once shown such constancy in preserving it. [Note: [Col. 1143D] “Might exercise.” The first edition has “might extend”; these words are often confused, both in other authors and in Orosius.]

In the third year of their rule, Gratianus, the son of Valentinianus, was made emperor. In that same year, at Atrebates, genuine wool fell from the clouds mixed with rain.

Moreover, Athanaricus, king of the Goths, persecuted the Christians in his nation with the greatest cruelty and raised many barbarians [Note: [Col. 1143D] “Barbarians.” Perizonius reads “Christians”; the third Florentine manuscript reads “barbarians.”] who had been killed for their faith to the crown of martyrdom. Nevertheless, many of them fled into Roman territory, [Note: [Col. 1143D] “Into Roman territory.” Perizonius reads “to Roman territory.”] not trembling [Note: [Col. 1143D] “Not trembling.” Four Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian and Utrecht manuscripts, read “fearlessly.”] as though to enemies, but confidently, [Note: [Col. 1143D] “As though.” Most of the same manuscripts read “wandering.”] knowing that they were going to brothers, for the confession of Christ. [Note: [Col. 1143D] “For Christ’s.” The Augustan edition reads “for the one nearby.”]

Valentinianus crushed the Saxons at the very borders of the Franks. They were a people settled along the shores of the Ocean and amid impassable marshes, terrible for their courage and agility and dangerous to the Roman frontiers, while they were planning a massive incursion. [Note: [Col. 1143D] “With a massive effort.” The first Lugd. Bat. edition reads “an incursion long ago.”] [Note: [Col. 1143D] “While planning.” All the manuscripts favor this form, so that the participle refers to the Saxons, not the singular form referring to the people, as in the common editions.]

There is likewise the new name of the Burgundians, new enemies, who, more than eighty thousand armed men strong, as they say, settled along the bank of the Rhine. [Note: [Col. 1144C] “Eighty thousand.” The Augustan edition gives a double reading, adding seventy thousand as well.] [Note: [Col. 1144C] “Of the Rhine.” The second Florentine manuscript has “of the Rhone.”]

These, after Inner Germany had once been subdued, had been distributed among military camps by Drusus and Tiberius, the adoptive sons of Caesar, [Note: [Col. 1144C] “Of Caesar.” The Paris and Venetian editions, together with the Augustan edition, add “of Augustus,” which I do not reject, although I have not found it in the manuscripts.] and had grown into a great people, [Note: [Col. 1144C] “To have grown into a great people.” As though this could not be connected with what follows without some supporting prop, all the editions except the Augustan, against all the manuscripts, inserted *aiunt*, “they say,” printing “they say that they had grown into a great people,” although the phrase depends on what precedes, “who had once been distributed by Drusus and Tiberius.” Gaul still bears witness to this.] and thus had also taken their name from their occupation, because they commonly call the numerous dwellings established along the frontier *burgi*, “forts.”

That they possess a very powerful and destructive force is also attested today by Gaul, in which they have established themselves by presumed occupation. Yet, by God’s providence, now that all have become Christians, [Note: [Col. 1144D] “Christians.” This word is absent from the Perizonius manuscript.] they live gently and innocently [Note: [Col. 1144D] “Gently, innocently.” The second Florentine manuscript reads “gentle and innocent”; the first Lugd. Bat. edition has “they live gently and innocently.”] in the Catholic faith, having received our clergy whom they obey—not as though among subjected Gauls, [Note: [Col. 1144D] “Gaul.” The Perizonius manuscript reads “the Gauls.”] but truly as Christian brothers.

In the eleventh year of his reign, when the Sarmatians had spread throughout Pannonia and were ravaging it, Valentinianus prepared war against them. At the town of Brigition, [Note: [Col. 1144D] “At Brigition.” Ammianus Marcellinus calls it Bregition; for the circumstances of Valentinianus’s death, see book XXX, chapter 5.] he was suffocated and died from a sudden effusion of blood, a condition which the Greeks call *apoplexis* (“apoplexy”). [Note: [Col. 1144D] “Which the Greeks call.” All the Lugd. Bat. manuscripts, together with the Gronovian Collection, read “which the Greeks call *apoplexis*.”]

After him Gratianus, his son, [Note: [Col. 1144D] “His son.” The first Lugd. Bat. edition has “his own son.”] held the empire of the West. While his uncle Valens was established in the eastern regions, Gratianus also [Note: [Col. 1144D] “Also.” The fourth Lugd. Bat. manuscript and the Gronovian Collection omit the word.] made Valentinianus, his very young brother, a partner in the empire.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The Emperor Valens: how he punished the Christians and what wars he waged; and concerning the reign of Gratianus

[Col. 1144C]

In the year 1128 from the founding of the City, Valens, thirty-ninth in succession, held the empire for four years after Valentinian’s death. [Note: “To whom alone, when he was acting impiously, he could have blushed.” The Leiden editions, four in number, together with the Gronovian and Utrecht collections, read: “to whom alone, when he could have blushed at acting impiously”; this reading also occurs in the second Florentine manuscript, though the final letter has been erased in *ageret*. Perizonius reads: “who alone, while acting impiously, ought to have blushed.” The passage will be sound if, deleting *et*, one writes: “to whom alone, when he was acting impiously, he could have blushed.” Or Valens could have blushed before his brother Valentinian alone, a man especially orthodox in the Christian faith, if, while Valentinian lived, he had departed from the purity of the faith. It was very easy for *ageret et* to arise from the final syllable of *ageret* being duplicated.] To him alone, though he was acting impiously, Valens might have been able to blush; yet he immediately issued, as though with unrestrained audacity, a law that monks—that is, Christians who devote themselves to the one work of faith, having abandoned the manifold activity of secular affairs—were to be compelled into military service. [Note: “Of liberty.” The first and Paris editions read *liber* (“free”). The second Florentine manuscript has *libera audacia* (“free audacity”).] [Note: “Devote themselves.” Some old editions read *redegerant* (“had devoted themselves”).]

At that time the vast deserts of Egypt and the stretches of sand—regions unknown to human habitation because of their thirst, barrenness, and the exceedingly dangerous abundance of snakes—had been filled by a great multitude of resident monks. [Note: “Tribunes were sent there.” The earlier word *huc* (“there”) is absent from the third Leiden manuscript and the Gronovian collection.] Tribunes and soldiers were sent there to drag away, under another name for persecution, the holy and true soldiers of God. [Note: “And true soldiers of God.” The Augustan edition reads “and venerable soldiers of God.”] [Note: “Under another name for persecution.” The Perizonian manuscript has “under the alien name of persecution.”]

There many companies of saints were killed. [Note: Since this is the unanimous reading of all the manuscripts, without even one exception, those first editors must be pronounced rash who, at their own peril, changed *interfecta sunt* (“were killed”) into *interfecerunt* (“they killed”); this alteration then seized all subsequent editions, with the sole exception of the Augustan edition, which, in reproducing the readings of its manuscript—including corrupt and duplicated readings—takes the place of an outstanding codex.]

What was done throughout the various provinces everywhere, by these and similar orders, against the Catholic churches and peoples of right belief, may be sufficiently indicated by the very choice to pass it over in silence. [Note: “To pass over in silence.” In the second Florentine manuscript this is written above the line, though against Orosius; perhaps *dicendi* (“of speaking”) should be read.]

Meanwhile, in the regions of Africa, Firmus [Note: “Firmus.” The Perizonian manuscript reads *Firmius*.], having stirred up the Moorish tribes and proclaimed himself king, devastated Africa and Mauretania. He captured Caesarea, the most distinguished city of Mauretania, by treachery, then filled it with slaughter and fires, and handed it over to the barbarians as plunder. Accordingly, Count Theodosius—the father of Theodosius who later became emperor—sent by Valentinian, broke the Moorish tribes in many battles. [Note: “Broke.” The second Florentine manuscript reads “broke and routed.”] He compelled Firmus himself, beaten down and crushed, to die. [Note: “Firmus himself.” The Perizonian manuscript has “Firmius himself.”]

Afterward, when with the most experienced foresight he had rendered all Africa together with Mauretania better than before by his laws, [Note: “Had restored it to better laws than before.” The phrase *legibus* (“under laws”) rests on no authority except that of the editors; it is found in none of the manuscripts, nor in the Augustan edition. Yet, following the first and Paris editions, Bolsuingius, Fabricius, and others accepted it without hesitation. The corruption is therefore concealed, although it does not appear at first sight; and it lies particularly in the word *pristinis* (“former”), which, since it is written in the manuscripts—certainly in mine—with fewer and contracted letters as *pitis*, seems to suggest something other than *pristinis*. Perhaps the reading should be *partibus* (“regions”) or *principibus* (“rulers”), namely Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian. For *meliorem* (“better”), the Gronovian collection gives *melioratam* (“improved”).] [Note: “Urging.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian collection and the Utrecht manuscript, read *stimulante* (“urging”); but *instimulare* is Orosius’ own word. Compare above, chapter 6: “he was urged on to the slaughter of the conspirators.”] when envy urged and insinuated itself, [Note: “When he had been ordered to be killed.” In the second Florentine manuscript is written above the line: “by Valens.” Valesius, in his note to Ammianus Marcellinus, book 29, chapter 5, identified the year in which this undeserved killing of Theodosius occurred from Jerome’s *Chronicle*.] and he was ordered to be killed, he preferred to be baptized at Carthage for the remission of sins. [Note: “He preferred.” The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Gronovian collection, reads *preoperavit*, perhaps for *properavit* (“hastened”).] After he had obtained the sacrament of Christ that he had sought, [Note: “Which.” The fourth Leiden manuscript has *quem* (“whom”), so that the reference would be to Christ.] after a glorious life in this world, and secure also of eternal life, he willingly offered his throat to the executioner.

Meanwhile the emperor Gratian, still very young, seeing an immeasurable multitude of enemies pouring into Roman territory, relying on the power of Christ, gave himself over to the enemy with a force of soldiers vastly inferior in number. [Note: “Vastly inferior in number.” Some old editions read “vastly inferior,” and so forth.] At once, near Argentaria, a town of Gaul, he brought to an end a most terrifying war with incredible success. For more than thirty thousand Alamanni are said to have been killed in that battle, with very little loss to the Romans. [Note: “An immeasurable multitude.” The third Leiden manuscript, Perizonius, and the Gronovian collection read “an innumerable multitude.”]

In the thirteenth year of Valens’ reign—that is, shortly after Valens had carried out the mutilation of the churches and the slaughter of the saints throughout the whole East—the root of our miseries put forth an abundant growth of branches all at once. For the nation of the Huns, long shut off by inaccessible mountains, suddenly inflamed by savage fury, blazed against the Goths. [Note: “The nation of the Huns.” Some old editions read “the race of the Huns.”] [Note: “Shut off by mountains.” The Augustan edition reads “closed in by mountains.”] It drove them, scattered and thrown into confusion, from their ancient settlements. [Note: “Scattered and thrown into confusion.” Perizonius reads “scattered and disturbed”; the second Florentine manuscript reads “and drove them about everywhere in confusion.”]

The Goths, fleeing across the Danube, were received by Valens without any agreement of alliance; they did not even hand over their weapons to the Romans, so that they might be more safely trusted by the barbarians. Then, driven by the intolerable greed of the commander Maximus, by hunger and wrongs, they rose in arms. Having defeated Valens’ army and mingled with the population throughout Thrace, they defiled everything at once with slaughter, fires, and plunder.

Valens, having departed from Antioch, and being dragged toward the final outcome of an unlucky war, was stirred by late repentance for his greatest sin and ordered the bishops and the other saints to be recalled from exile. [Note: “And the other saints.” Three Leiden manuscripts read “and the other saints’ [companions].” Soon afterward the Venetian editions read *bellis* (“wars”) instead of *exsiliis* (“exiles”).]

Thus, in the fifteenth year of his reign, he fought that lamentable war in Thrace against the Goths, who by then were thoroughly equipped through practice in arms and abundance of resources. [Note: “Lamentable.” Perizonius reads “truly lamentable.”] At the very first attack, the Roman cavalry squadrons were thrown into confusion by the Goths and abandoned the exposed protection of the infantry. Then the infantry legions, surrounded on every side by the enemy’s cavalry, first overwhelmed by clouds of arrows, and afterward, when in their madness they were scattered by fear and forced along the byways, were utterly cut down and perished beneath the swords and spears of their pursuers. [Note: “And first.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Gronovian collection, omit *ac* (“and”), which is unnecessary here.] [Note: “Overwhelmed.” Perizonius reads “were overwhelmed.”]

The emperor himself, wounded by an arrow and turned to flight, was scarcely carried away and hidden in the hut of a certain little farmstead. [Note: “Wounded.” Three Leiden manuscripts, Perizonius, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Gronovian collection read *sauciatus* (“having been wounded”).] [Note: “Scarcely.” The fourth Leiden manuscript reads *aeger* (“sick”).] He was discovered by the pursuing enemy and, after a fire had been set beneath him, was consumed. And so that this might provide posterity with a more terrible example of his punishment and of divine indignation, [Note: “Might provide posterity with an example.” Perizonius, the third Leiden manuscript, and the Gronovian collection read “might have stood as an example to posterity.” The less corrupt reading is *exsisteret posteris exemplo*.] he was deprived even of ordinary burial. [Note: “Terrible.” The second Florentine manuscript and the Augustan edition read *terribilis* (“terrible,” nominative).]

Let the pagans console themselves—but only in this respect—with the stubbornness and wretchedness of their people: that in the times of Christian rulers and under Christian kings such great disasters were heaped together, burdening the already pressed neck of the state: provinces overthrown, an army destroyed, an emperor burned. This is truly a great matter for our grief, and all the more pitiable because it is so unusual. [Note: “In this respect alone.” The Gronovian collection has *sclo*, with a line written above for *saeculo* (“age”); the second Florentine manuscript reads “in this place.”] [Note: “Rulers.” The Leiden editions read *legibus* (“laws”).]

But what consolation does this provide for the pagans, who plainly see—and recognize even in these events—that a persecutor of the churches was punished? [Note: “Plainly see.” The Gronovian collection reads *provident* (“foresee”); Perizonius, *parvipendent* (“make light of”).] [Note: “Does it provide.” The third Leiden manuscript reads “has provided.”] One God delivered one faith, spread one church throughout the whole world, looks upon this church, loves it, and defends it. [Note: “Loves.” The third Leiden manuscript and the Gronovian collection read “guides.”] Let each person shelter himself under whatever name he wishes: if he is not joined to this church, he is an outsider; if he attacks it, he is its enemy. [Note: “Each person himself.” Some manuscripts and editions read “each individual.”]

Let the pagans console themselves as much as they wish by the punishments of Jews and heretics; let them acknowledge, at least from this example of Valens’ destruction, that there is one and the same God, and that he is not a respecter of persons. [Note: “And the same.” The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Gronovian collection, reads “and one.”]

Earlier, the Goths had humbly requested through envoys that bishops be sent to them, from whom they might learn the rule of the Christian faith. The emperor Valens, in his ruinous depravity, sent teachers of the Arian doctrine. [Note: “Depravity.” Some old editions read “held fast by depravity.”] The Goths retained the first rudiment of the faith that they received. [Note: “Rudiment.” The second Florentine manuscript reads *rudimento* (“as a rudiment”).] Thus, by the just judgment of God, they burned alive the very man through whom they too, though dead, will burn through the fault of error. [Note: The first edition, the Paris edition, and the Venetian editions insert here the following words: “Valens, abandoning the rule of the Catholic faith that he had formerly possessed, entangled himself in the perverse doctrine of the Arians.” Lautius noted: “I marvel and am astonished that these words, although they appear excellently in the Venetian printed book, are absent from all the others.” But I assert—indeed, I assert plainly—that these words are not Orosius’ own; they stood in the margin as the content of the speech, as many such marginal additions occur in the manuscripts of Orosius, and the first editors transferred them into the text. I affirm further that they are found in no manuscript, nor in the Augustan edition; Fabricius therefore rightly omitted them, while Scotus was wrong to include them in his edition.]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How wisely the emperor Gratian governed the empire; Theodosius rules the East and Thrace; and concerning Arcadius and Maximus

In the year 1132 from the founding of the City, Gratian, fortieth after Augustus, held the empire for six years after Valens’ death, although he had already long been reigning together with his uncle Valens and his brother Valentinian. Seeing that the condition of the state was afflicted and almost collapsed, he selected Theodosius, likewise a Spaniard, by the same foresight with which Nerva had once selected Trajan, a Spaniard, through whom the state was restored. At Sirmium he clothed him in the purple [Note: “He clothed him in the purple.” Thus the Gronovian collection and the Utrecht manuscript read, better than the others, which write *purpuram* (“the purple garment”), as the word is commonly printed.] and placed him simultaneously over the empire of the East and of Thrace, [Note: “Using more perfect judgment in this.” The same manuscripts, and also the second and third Leiden manuscripts, have this reading. In the common editions *usus* (“using”) is absent.] displaying more perfect judgment in this: although Theodosius had been the equal of Trajan in all the virtues of human life, he surpassed him without comparison in the sacrament of faith and the worship of religion. [Note: “He had been his equal.” Perizonius’ manuscript prefers “he himself had been equal”; three Leiden manuscripts together with the Gronovian collection read “he himself had been first.” I would prefer “he had been equal to him.” That is, Theodosius was equal to Trajan, meaning similar, in all respects, but better and more fortunate because he had been instructed in knowledge of the true God.]

The former was a persecutor; this man was a propagator of the Church. Thus not even one natural son was granted to Trajan, in whom he might rejoice as his successor, [Note: “Not even one natural son.” The Augustan edition omits *quidem* (“indeed”); the Perizonian manuscript has *proprius* (“natural”). Yet it should not be rejected, since Hadrian was regarded as his son, as though by adoption, in the designation of the succession, and thereafter frequently added Trajan’s name to his own.] whereas the glorious offspring of this man now rules both East and West through successive generations down to the present. [Note: “The East and the West alike.” Perizonius reads “the East and the West”; the second Florentine manuscript, together with the third Leiden manuscript, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Gronovian collection, reads “both the East and the West.”]

[Note: “Therefore, just as, etc.” In Perizonius, the second and fourth Leiden manuscripts, and the Gronovian collection, *ut* (“just as”) is absent, though it is necessary here: the sense is, “just as Theodosius believed that the afflicted state, etc., was to be restored, so ….” If *ut* is removed, the following should read “and placing all his confidence,” as in the first and Venetian editions.] Therefore, just as Theodosius believed that the state, afflicted by God’s anger, was to be restored by his mercy, [Note: “Of his mercy.” The second and third Florentine manuscripts and three Leiden manuscripts, together with Perizonius and the Gronovian collection, prefer *Dei* (“of God”) to *illius* (“of his”); the third Leiden manuscript and the Gronovian collection likewise write *Dei* again instead of *sui* (“of himself”).] placing all his confidence in the help of Christ, he attacked without hesitation those greatest Scythian peoples, feared by all earlier generations and avoided even by that Alexander the Great, as Pompey and Cornelius testify, but now, after the Roman army had been destroyed, fully equipped with Roman horses and weapons—that is, the Alans, Huns, and Goths. [Note: “Even by that Alexander the Great.” Some manuscripts read “even by Alexander the Great”; the third Florentine manuscript has “avoided by that Alexander the Great.”] He defeated them in great and numerous battles. [Note: “Without hesitation.” This word is incorrectly absent from two Leiden manuscripts and the Utrecht manuscript.]

He entered Constantinople in triumph. [Note: “He entered in triumph.” Perizonius reads “having entered in triumph.”] And lest he wear away even that small remnant of the Roman army by continual warfare, [Note: “That very army.” It is absent from some old editions.] he made a treaty with Athanaric, king of the Goths. [Note: “Wear away.” The editions of Fabricius and Scotus most perversely read *deterreret* (“terrify”), a corruption they would certainly have avoided had they consulted the Venetian and Paris editions and those of Hittorp and Bolsuingius. Those editions correctly preserve the verb most appropriate here, although the Augustan edition and some manuscripts, such as the third Leiden and the Utrecht manuscripts, are corrupt.
