The correct reading is found in mine, in Perizonius, and in two Florentine manuscripts.]

As soon as Athanaric came to Constantinople, he died. [Note: “All the Goths.” The Augustan edition reads “but all the Goths,” and so forth.] All the Gothic peoples, seeing the virtue and kindness of Theodosius after their king’s death, surrendered themselves to the Roman empire.

[Note: “In those same days the Persians.” Some old editions read “In these days the Persians”; the Perizonian manuscript reads “In those same times the Persians.”] In those same days the Persians—who, after Julian had been killed and the other emperors repeatedly defeated, and now after Valens too had been put to flight, were belching forth, with raw insolence, their satisfaction at their most recent victory—sent envoys of their own accord to Theodosius at Constantinople and humbly requested peace. [Note: “Even now.” Two Leiden manuscripts, the Utrecht manuscript, Perizonius, and the Gronovian collection read “but now.”] [Note: “Were belching forth.” The Augustan edition reads “were vomiting forth.”] [Note: “And humbly requested peace.” This is the reading favored by the better manuscripts, the Augustan edition, and the editions of Fabricius. Others have “requesting peace humbly.” In the third Florentine manuscript the conjunction *-que* is absent.] A treaty was then concluded, by which the whole East has enjoyed the utmost tranquility down to the present. [Note: “Down to the present.” The third Leiden manuscript, together with the Gronovian collection, reads “until now.”]

Meanwhile, when Theodosius had subdued the barbarian peoples in the East and finally restored the Thracian provinces to freedom from the enemy, and had made his son Arcadius his colleague in the empire, Maximus—a vigorous and upright man [Note: “Vigorous and upright.” The Perizonian manuscript deletes *et* (“and”).], worthy of Augustus, had he not risen through tyranny against the faith of his oath—was almost unwillingly proclaimed emperor by the army in Britain and crossed into Gaul. There he terrified Gratian Augustus by a sudden attack; when Gratian was planning to cross into Italy, Maximus ensnared and killed him by treachery, and drove his brother Valentinian Augustus from Italy.

Valentinian, fleeing to the East, was received by Theodosius with fatherly affection and soon restored to the empire. [Note: “Fleeing.” Perizonius reads simply “fleeing.”]

## CHAPTER XXXV. The wars fought by the emperor Caesar Augustus Theodosius; meanwhile, the deaths of Maximus, Andragathius, and Valentinian, and the destruction by Theodosius of Arbogastes and the tyrant Eugenius

In the year 1138 from the founding of the City, Theodosius, forty-first in succession, obtained sole control of the Roman world after Gratian had been killed by Maximus, and remained in it for eleven years, although he had already reigned for six years in the East while Gratian was still alive.

Therefore, moved by just and necessary causes to civil war, when the blood of one murdered Augustus demanded vengeance [Note: “Demanded.” Without any sense, the Fabrician editions, Scotus’s final edition, and several old editions read *exigeretur* (“was demanded”), contrary to all the manuscripts.] and the restoration of the other, who was in exile, pleaded for it, he placed his hope in God and rushed against the tyrant Maximus, greater only in faith—for he was far inferior in the whole preparation of military equipment. [Note: “Was.” This is absent from two Florentine manuscripts and from the Utrecht, Perizonian, and third Leiden manuscripts. The latter soon read *belli* (“of war”) instead of *bellici* (“military”).]

At that time Maximus was seated at Aquileia, enjoying the spectacle of his victory. His commander, Count Andragathius, directed the whole war. With very large forces of soldiers, and with the strength of those great forces, he had fortified all the approaches through the Alps and across the rivers by an outstanding strategy. But, by the ineffable judgment of God, while preparing to anticipate and overwhelm the unwary enemy by a naval expedition, he voluntarily abandoned the very barriers he had blocked. [Note: “Thus Theodosius.” The Augustan edition reads “And so Theodosius, with no one knowing,” and so forth.]

Thus Theodosius crossed the empty Alps [Note: “Crossed.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with Perizonius, read *transmeavit* (“passed across”).] unobserved—let me not say unopposed—[Note: “Empty.” This is the reading favored by all the manuscripts and by the better old editions. The editions of Fabricius and others have *vacuatas* (“emptied”).] and, arriving unexpectedly at Aquileia [Note: “And to Aquileia.” The Augustan edition reads “and to Aquileia.”], shut in, without treachery [Note: “And without dispute.” I found this reading in the Augustan edition and in the Perizonian manuscript, as also in both Florentine manuscripts. The common editions omit *sine* (“without”).], captured, and killed that great enemy, the savage Maximus, who by the mere terror of his name [Note: “By the mere terror of his name.” The Leiden manuscripts, with Perizonius, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Gronovian collection, read “by great terror of his name”; Perizonius also has “by great terror and threats.” The common reading is more significant.] exacted tribute and military payments even from the most ferocious German peoples. [Note: “Captured and killed.” The common editions read “and killed.” But the reading found in the manuscripts and in the Augustan edition, with *et* removed, is smoother.]

Valentinian, having recovered Italy, gained possession of the empire. When Count Andragathius learned of Maximus’ death, he threw himself headlong from a ship into the waves and was drowned. Theodosius received a bloodless victory, God having brought it about.

Behold how, under Christian kings and in Christian times, civil wars are settled when they cannot be avoided. Victory was attained, a city was stormed, a tyrant was seized—and this is little enough. Behold, on the other side [Note: “On the other side.” This is likewise the reading of the manuscripts, rather than the common editions’ “from the other side.”], the enemy army was defeated, and the tyrant’s commander, more savage than the tyrant himself, was forced to die; such great ambushes were dissolved and rendered futile, such great preparations emptied of their force. [Note: “Were.” This is absent from the Perizonian manuscript.] Yet no one devised tricks, no one drew up a battle line, and finally no one, if one may say so, drew a sword from its sheath. A most terrifying war was brought to an end without bloodshed, through victory, and in the victory through the deaths of two men.

And lest anyone think that this happened by chance, so that the power of God—by which all things are both administered and judged—might be displayed by the testimony of its revelation [Note: “Displayed.” Two Leiden manuscripts read “and displayed.”] and force the minds of those who resist either to confusion or to faith, I shall recount something both unknown to everyone and known to everyone.

After this war, in which Maximus was killed, many things, as we all recognize, followed Theodosius and his son Honorius, both foreign wars and civil wars, down to the present. [Note: “Followed Theodosius …” This is the reading of both Florentine manuscripts, three Leiden manuscripts, Perizonius, the Utrecht manuscript, the Gronovian collection, and the old editions. The third Leiden manuscript reads “followed through Theodosius.” Fabricius and Scotus, however, print “followed Theodosius.”] Yet nearly all of them, even down to the present day, and indeed with the benefit of a simple and holy victory, have subsided with either no bloodshed or very little.

Accordingly, the younger Valentinian, restored to the throne after Maximus and his son Victor had been destroyed—the son whom Maximus had left as emperor over the Gauls [Note: “Had left.” Some manuscripts read “had appointed.” Soon afterward the Leiden manuscripts and the Gronovian collection prefer *transiit* (“crossed”) to *transivit* (“went across”).]—himself crossed into Gaul. There, while the state was living in peace and tranquility, he was, as they report, strangled at Vienne by the treachery of his commander Arbogastes, and was hanged in a noose so that it might be thought that he had inflicted death upon himself voluntarily.

After Valentinian Augustus died, Arbogastes soon dared to create the tyrant Eugenius, and chose a man on whom he might impose the title of emperor, while he himself intended to exercise the imperial power. [Note: “Eugenius.” Some manuscripts read “and then Eugenius”; the Perizonian manuscript has “and he chose,” instead of “and he selected.”] A barbarian in spirit, judgment, strength, audacity, and excessive power, he assembled from every quarter innumerable and invincible forces, supported either by Roman garrisons or by barbarian auxiliaries, relying in one place on authority and in another on kinship. It is unnecessary to expand in words a history known even to the eyes of many, and better understood by those who witnessed it.

That Theodosius always proved victorious through the power of God, not through confidence in man, is demonstrated especially by Arbogastes in both instances. On the earlier occasion, when he obeyed Theodosius, he himself, though the least of men, captured Maximus, who was equipped with such great forces. [Note: “The least.” Some old editions read *minimis* (“with the least”), but this is an allusion to the name *Maximus* (“the greatest”), which has just preceded.] Now, when he rose against that same Theodosius after gathering the strength of the Gauls and Franks, relying [Note: “Relying.” The third Leiden manuscript reads *nisus*.] also on the special worship of idols, he nevertheless fell with great ease. [Note: “Ease.” Some manuscripts have the less appropriate reading *felicitate* (“success”).]

Eugenius and Arbogastes had deployed their battle lines across the plain and occupied the narrow sides of the Alps and the impassable passes, cleverly setting ambushes in advance, [Note: “So that, even if.” Three Leiden manuscripts read simply “even if.”] so that, even if they were inferior in number and strength, they might nevertheless be victorious through the disposition of the war alone. [Note: “The narrow sides of the Alps.” The Leiden manuscripts, together with Perizonius, the Utrecht manuscript, and the Gronovian collection, read *alta* (“high”), which I do not prefer to the common reading, since the passage had been blocked where it was narrow.] But Theodosius, stationed on the highest Alps, deprived of food and sleep, knowing that he was abandoned by his own men but not knowing that he was enclosed by those of the enemy, prayed to the Lord Christ alone, the only one who could do all things: his body stretched upon the ground, his mind fixed upon heaven.

Then, after passing the sleepless night in continuous prayer, leaving behind pools of tears, almost as witnesses, which he had offered as the price of heavenly protection, he confidently seized his weapons, alone, knowing that he was not alone. He gave the signal for battle with the sign of the cross and threw himself into the war, confident that he would be victorious even if no one followed him. [Note: “He gave the signal for battle with the sign of the cross.” I have removed at this point a most foolish and lengthy gloss which disfigured all the editions except the Augustan, and I have also altered the punctuation above. The common text read: “He confidently seized his weapons alone, knowing that he was not only to be protected by the sign of the cross but also destined to gain victory; fortifying himself with the sign of the cross, he gave the sign of victory, and with the sign of the cross gave the signal for battle,” and so forth. This stood against all the manuscript books, something I am surprised Fabricius did not notice. Lautius saw no more than Fabricius did, for he writes concerning this passage: “Marcoduranus added: ‘and with the sign of the cross gave the signal for battle,’ which was found neither in the Cologne manuscript nor in the manuscripts of Maternus.”]

The first path to salvation was provided by Arbitio, a commander of the enemy forces. [Note: “Arbitio.” The Augustan edition and some other old editions, together with the Perizonian manuscripts and the third Leiden manuscript, have *Arbitio*; the second Leiden manuscript reads *Arbicio*.] When he had received the unsuspecting emperor amid the ambushes arranged around him, he turned in reverence toward the Augustus who stood before him, and not only freed him from danger but also supplied him with assistance.

When they reached the adjoining spaces where battle was to be joined [Note: “The adjoining spaces where battle was to be joined.” Perizonius and the third Leiden manuscript, with the Gronovian collection, read *miscendae* (“to be joined”); the common editions read *inmiscendae*. The second Florentine manuscript has *in continua inmiscenda*.], immediately a great and indescribable whirlwind of winds rushed into the faces of the enemy. Arrows hurled by our men were carried through the air [Note: “Through the air.” The manuscripts prefer *per aera* to *aerem*.] and, borne across the great void beyond the measure of human throwing, [Note: “By the hand of our men.” The Perizonian manuscript usefully adds the final word, absent from the common editions.] were scarcely ever allowed to fall before they struck their targets. [Note: “Throw.” Some manuscripts read “blow.”] [Note: “Carried across the great void.” The Cologne manuscript and the printed editions have “carried back in the air by hand”; from these words I inferred that reading. If it is wrong, let the judgment belong to others. All the old editions and all the manuscripts I have consulted exhibit “carried across the great void.” I therefore wonder how Fabricius and Scotus obtained “carried by hand in the air,” for that is how it appears in their editions.]

The unbroken whirlwind now battered the faces and breasts of the enemy, their shields having been struck violently. [Note: “Now with shields violently struck.” All the manuscripts consulted, as well as the Augustan edition, read *nunc illisis graviter scutis*; the common editions have *nunc illis*, which is very unsatisfactory.] [Note: “Battered.” Some manuscripts read “beat.”] Now it closed them in when their shields were pressed stubbornly against them. [Note: The meaning is that the whirlwind drove some shields of the enemy so violently against their breasts and faces that it scarcely allowed them the opportunity to breathe.] Now, when the shields had been violently torn away—whether snatched from their hands by the savage whirlwind or bent back so that they exposed their unprotected faces to wounds—it left them naked. Now, when they continually held up their shields to ward off the force of the storm, it drove the same men who carried them backward onto their backs. [Note: “Now when they had been held up.” This refers to the soldiers opposing the force of the storm by holding up their shields; by the same force of the whirlwind they were thrown backward.]

The weapons which they themselves had hurled with force were caught by the winds, bent backward by the violence of the blast, and driven back to strike the very men who had cast them, unhappily piercing them. [Note: “Bent backward by the force.” Two Florentine manuscripts read “with the force bent backward.”]

Human fear looked to its own safety. For immediately, after the small force of our men had been scattered, the enemy army prostrated itself before the victorious Theodosius. Eugenius was captured and killed. Arbogastes struck himself with his own hand. [Note: “With his own hand.” Some manuscripts read “with his own hand himself,” or “himself with his own hand.”]

Thus here too civil war was extinguished by the blood of two men, apart from those ten thousand Goths whom Arbogastes is said to have utterly destroyed after Theodosius had sent them ahead. To have lost them was gain, and to have been defeated was victory. [Note: “Was extinguished.” The earlier Leiden manuscript reads “was destroyed,” though *restinctum* (“extinguished”) is written above it. Some old editions read “was restricted.”]

I do not insult our detractors. Let them produce a single war, from the beginning of the founding of the City, undertaken from such pious necessity, brought to an end with such divine success, and quieted with such merciful kindness, in which neither the battle demanded a grievous slaughter nor the victory a bloody vengeance. Then perhaps I shall concede that this does not appear to have been granted to the faith of a Christian commander—although I am not troubled by this testimony, since one of their own, an outstanding poet but a most stubborn pagan, bore witness in the following verses [Note: “Verses of this kind.” Some manuscripts read “words of this kind.”] both to God and to man:

> O one exceedingly beloved by God,  
> The heavens serve you,  
> And the winds, conspiring, come to the trumpet-call.

[Note: “The heavens serve you.” In the Augustan edition the following appears:

> O truly beloved by God, for whom Aeolus pours  
> Armed storms from the stars; the heavens serve you,  
> And the winds, conspiring, come to the trumpet-call.

These verses are found in Claudian, *On the Third Consulship of Honorius*, verse 96, except that there *Cui fundit ab antris* (“for whom he pours from the caves”) appears at the end of the first verse instead of *Cui fudit ab astris* (“for whom he poured from the stars”). Orosius, however, seems unwilling to admit the reference to Aeolus, a pagan god, and therefore shortened the verses. Some manuscripts read *ad humillima classica venti* (“the winds to the very humblest trumpet-call”), from which the first word arose through a variant reading.]

Thus it was judged from heaven between the one side, humbly placing its hope in God alone even without human support, and the other, relying most arrogantly on its own strength and on idols.

[Note: “Theodosius, however.” It is pleasing to append a gold coin of this most victorious and truly most Christian emperor, which once existed in the Marckian museum. On its obverse appears a bust-length image of Theodosius. His right hand holds a spear; his left holds a shield marked with the device of a cavalry expedition. His chest is covered by a cuirass and his head by a jeweled helmet. Around it is written: “Our Lord Theodosius, Pious, Fortunate Augustus.” On the reverse sits New Rome. At her feet appears the prow of a ship with its steering-oar, a symbol of maritime power. In her right hand she holds a spear; in her left, a small Victory standing upon a globe. The concord of Theodosius and Arcadius is praised by the inscription: “The Concord of the Augusti.” As the inscription shows, the coin was struck at Constantinople.]

Theodosius, having restored and pacified the state, died at Milan.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The empire and achievements of the Caesars Arcadius, Theodosius the Younger, and Honorius; the treachery and schemes of Gildo, nevertheless suppressed by Mascezel

[Col. 1155A]

In the year 1149 from the founding of the City, [Note: [Col. 1155B] Arcadius … and Honorius. These two, sons of Theodosius, divided the Roman Empire and its portions between themselves, at their father’s will, after the sons of Constantine the Great. Neither of them had shoulders sufficient for the burden, and under them the Roman state was miserably afflicted by the cunning and deceit of their guardians and by barbarian invasions. It seemed appropriate to append a gold coin of each Augustus. On the coin of Arcadius, once taken from the Marckian collection at Gaza, the Virtue of the Romans is praised, though under an unwarlike prince it shone forth only faintly; on the coin of Honorius his long reign is celebrated. Concerning it, Bandurius may be consulted, from whose work the coin of Honorius was taken. [Col. 1155D]] Arcadius Augustus, whose son Theodosius now rules the East, and Honorius Augustus, his brother, upon whom the commonwealth now depends, began, in the forty-second position, to hold the empire jointly, with only their residences divided. [Note: [Col. 1155D] “And he lived.” Perizonius reads “he lived”; the three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection, read “and so he lived.”] Arcadius lived twelve years after his father’s death and, as he was dying, handed over supreme power to his very young son Theodosius. [Note: [Col. 1155D] “To his son.” Several manuscripts, together with the Augsburg edition, do not contain “his.”]

Meanwhile Count Gildo, who at the beginning of their reign governed Africa, as soon as he learned that Theodosius had died, [Note: [Col. 1155D] “Or, as some report.” Perizonius’s manuscript, the first and third Leiden manuscripts, and the Groningen collection read “as some report.”] or, as some report, having been moved by a certain envy, [Col. 1155B] [Note: [Col. 1155D] “To join Africa to the regions of the Eastern Empire,” and so forth. The Augsburg edition inserts “his” between “of the empire” and “regions.” Gildo either wished to add to Africa, whose administration he held, the eastern provinces as well, or to seize tyranny in Africa alone and claim for himself that portion of the Roman Empire, torn away from the rest of the body. [Col. 1156B]] attempted to attach Africa to the territories of the Eastern Empire; or, as another opinion maintains, thinking that there would be little hope in children, especially since previously scarcely anyone of tender age left in the empire without such support had easily survived to the maturity of manhood, [Note: [Col. 1156B] “Had survived.” Perizonius and the first Leiden manuscript, together with the Groningen collection, read “had reached.” Soon afterward these same manuscripts, together with some others from Leiden, …] and that these were almost the only ones to be found whom, because of their father’s and their own outstanding faithfulness, Christ’s protection had advanced even when divided and abandoned. [Note: [Col. 1156B] “Africa, cut off.” In three Leiden manuscripts, Perizonius, and the Groningen collection, one reads “a citadel seized” instead. Perhaps the passage should read: “He dared to seize Africa, cut off from participation in the commonwealth, and to usurp a citadel for himself.” For it is well known that Latin writers commonly use “to seize and hold a citadel” of an acquired tyranny. See what we noted on Tertullian’s *Apology*, p. 48.] He dared to usurp Africa, cut off from participation in the commonwealth, being content with the license of a barbarian rather than puffed up with the ambition of royal pretension.

His brother was Mascezil, [Note: [Col. 1156C] “Mascezil.” This name is written in various ways in the manuscripts of Orosius and also in those of the Deacon. The first Leiden manuscript has *Mascebiel* here, but *Masceibel* below; the second has *Mascelzel*; the second Florentine manuscript and the Augsburg edition, *Mascezel*; the third and fourth Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen collection, *Masceibel*; and the Perizonian manuscript, *Maseczel*.] who, horrified by his brother’s schemes for revolution, returned to Italy, leaving two adolescent sons with the African army. Gildo, regarding both his brother’s absence and the presence of his sons with suspicion, ensnared the young men by treachery and killed them. Mascezil, therefore, was sent against him as an enemy, to be pursued in war; and the recent grief of his own bereavement promised that he would be a suitable administrator of the commonwealth. Thus Mascezil, having already learned from Theodosius how much, in the most desperate circumstances, a human being’s prayer through faith in Christ could obtain from God’s mercy, [Note: [Col. 1156C] “The man’s prayer,” and so forth. The Augsburg edition supplies this reading: “prayer through faith and God’s mercy obtained,” which is not implausible.] went to the island of Capraria. [Note: [Col. 1156C] The second Florentine manuscript reads *Capria*.] From there he took with him, moved by his prayers, several holy servants of God. [Note: [Col. 1156C] Perizonius reads “some.”] With these, continuing day and night in prayers, fasts, and psalms, he earned victory without battle and vengeance without slaughter. [Col. 1156B] [Note: [Col. 1156D] “And of the night.” Perizonius, together with several Leiden manuscripts, reads “and of the night.”]

Ardalio is the name of a river that flows between the cities of Thebaste and Metridera. [Note: [Col. 1156D] In place of *Metridera*, the two Florentine manuscripts read *Admedera*; the second Leiden manuscript and Ultr., *Ammedera*; the fourth Leiden manuscript and Perizonius, *Mederam*; the first Leiden manuscript, *Oomeodora*; the third, together with the Groningen collection, *Odmeodera*; and the Augsburg edition, *Admereda*. Yet in Paul the Deacon, Book XIII, p. 90, I find that it flows between the cities of Tereste and Amedara.] There, with a small force—that is, with five thousand soldiers, as they say—he pitched camp against seventy thousand enemies. [Note: [Col. 1156D] “Having pitched camp.” Perizonius reads “he pitched camp.”] [Note: [Col. 1156D] “Against seventy thousand enemies.” The third Leiden manuscript and the Groningen collection count forty thousand.] After a delay, when he wished to leave the place and cross the narrow passages of the valley lying before him, [Note: [Col. 1156D] “And the opposing narrow passages of the valley lying before him.” The Perizonian manuscript and the Groningen collection read: “and the opposing narrow passages of the valleys lying before him,” and so forth. In the Deacon one reads: “and when he wished to cross the narrow passages of the valleys lying before him.”] during the intervening night, [Note: [Col. 1156D] The Deacon likewise reads *intercurrente nocte*, “during the intervening night”; but the Augsburg edition and the second Leiden manuscript with Ultr. prefer *incurrente nocte*, “as night came on.” The other three Leiden manuscripts, with Perizonius and the Groningen collection, read *insistente nocte*, “as night pressed on.”] he seemed in a dream to see the blessed bishop Ambrose, who had died shortly before at Milan. Ambrose indicated with his hand and, striking the ground three times with his staff, said: “Here, here, here.” Mascezil understood this by a prudent conjecture to mean that the merit of the one announcing it signified confidence in victory, the word signified the place, and the number signified the day. [Note: [Col. 1157C] “Rightly announcing.” *Merito* appears to be the ablative of merit, not an adverb; it therefore means “through the merit of Ambrose, now numbered among the blessed.” Perizonius reads *meritoque*, “and rightly.”]

He halted, [Note: [Col. 1157C] “He remained.” This is how it is read in the Deacon, and likewise in the Ultr. and Groningen manuscripts; it is not objectionable. The common editions read “he halted.”] and only on the third day, after spending the night awake in prayers and hymns, fortified by the very mysteries of the heavenly sacraments, he advanced against the enemy surrounding him. [Note: [Col. 1157C] “He advanced.” The three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection and the Perizonian manuscript, read “he advances.”] [Note: [Col. 1157C] “By the very mysteries.” Some older editions read “fortified by them.”] [Note: [Col. 1157D] “And when he was addressing them.” The Augsburg edition reads “and when he was already addressing them.”] When he was already addressing those who first came forward with pious words of peace, he struck with his sword on the arm a standard-bearer who insolently resisted and was on the point of starting the fight. [Note: [Col. 1157D] “Insolently.” The Perizonian manuscript reads “violently.”] He forced him, his hand disabled by the wound, to lower the standard forward. At this sight, the remaining cohorts thought that the earlier troops had already surrendered and vied with one another in handing themselves over to Mascezil, turning their standards toward him. [Col. 1157B]

The barbarians, a great multitude of whom Gildo had led to war, abandoned by their soldiers, fled in different directions. [Note: [Col. 1157D] “Gildo.” Concerning Gildo’s movement and crimes, there survives a letter of Quintus Aurelius Symmachus addressed to Stilicho, Book IV, Letter 4.] Gildo himself also attempted flight, seized a ship, [Note: [Col. 1157D] “When he had put out to sea.” The word *ut* is absent from the three Leiden manuscripts.] put out into the open sea, and then, brought back to Africa, died by strangulation after several days.

We would be in danger, in recounting such great miracles, of being charged with the shamelessness of deliberate falsehood, unless the consciousness of those who were present still anticipated our voice. No ambush was laid, no bribery occurred: seventy thousand enemies were defeated almost without a battle. The defeated man fled for a time, lest, if victorious and angered, he should dare more. He was transported to a different place, [Note: [Col. 1157D] “So that his brother would not know that he had been killed.” The manuscripts and the editions of Fabricius correctly read this. In other copies it was very badly written: “so that he would not be known to have been killed by his brother.” The Augsburg edition reads: “so that his brother would not know that he had been killed, that his brother had killed him,” thereby justifying the killing of the murdered man. Orosius’s meaning is that Gildo was cast into a place different from that of his brother Mascezil and killed there, so that his brother would not order the death by which his sons’ bereavement would be avenged.] so that his brother would not know that he had been killed, [Note: [Col. 1157D] “By which, when he was killed, vengeance was taken.” All the Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection, read this as “by which vengeance is taken when he is killed”; the Florentine manuscripts and older editions read “by which vengeance is taken on those killed,” namely, Mascezil’s sons.] and by whose killing his brother was avenged.

But that same Mascezil, uplifted by the insolence of prosperity, set aside the company of the saints, with whom he had previously conquered while serving God, and even dared to violate a church; he did not hesitate to drag certain people out of it. [Col. 1158A] Punishment followed the sacrilegious man. [Note: [Col. 1158C] “The sacrilegious man.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection, read “the sacrilege.”] For after those whom he had dragged from the church to punishment had survived and were mocking him, after some time he alone was also punished. [Note: [Col. 1158C] The manuscripts transpose these words, reading “and he alone himself,” rather than “alone and himself.” In the Augsburg edition and the Ultr. manuscript, *et* is deleted.] He demonstrated in his own person that divine judgment is always vigilant toward both sides: when he hoped, he was helped; and when he despised, he was killed. [Note: [Col. 1158C] “And he demonstrated.” Correctly so—not “and he appealed,” as appears in the first and third Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen collection.] [Note: [Col. 1158C] “Always.” This is absent from the three Leiden manuscripts, as well as from the Perizonian manuscript and the Groningen collection.]

**CHAPTER XXXVII. On the crime of Rufinus and Stilicho; and likewise on Rhadagaisus, king of the Goths: how he terrified Rome and was defeated**

Meanwhile, since the elder Emperor Theodosius had entrusted the care and education of the boys of the two imperial courts respectively to the foremost men—that is, Rufinus for the Eastern court and Stilicho for the Western Empire—the outcome of each showed what each had done or attempted to do. [Note: [Col. 1158D] “Foremost.” The Perizonian manuscript reads “most powerful,” incorrectly.] One sought the royal eminence for himself, the other for his son; and, when affairs were suddenly thrown into confusion, so that the necessity of the commonwealth might conceal the crime of ambition, the one brought barbarian peoples in, while the other encouraged them.

I say nothing of King Alaric, often defeated and often hemmed in with his Goths, yet always released. [Note: [Col. 1158D] “I say nothing of the unfortunate wars.” Perizonius and the first and third Leiden manuscripts direct that this be written so. The reading in the common editions arose from a variant reading, as the Augsburg edition shows, where both readings are joined to *wars*.] I say nothing of the unfortunate wars fought at Pollentia. [Note: [Col. 1158D] Pollentia was a city of Liguria; there was also another of that name in Picenum. Both letters were doubled—*Pollentia*—as the better manuscripts write it, not *Polentia*, as in the common editions.] The supreme command of the war had been entrusted to a barbarian and pagan commander, namely Saul. [Note: [Col. 1158D] Some older editions read “under the commander,” to whom the entire conduct of the war was entrusted; but this conflicts with the manuscripts and with the true meaning.] Through his wickedness, the most revered days and holy Easter were violated, and the retreating enemy was forced to fight because of religious observance. [Note: [Col. 1158D] “The most revered day and holy Easter.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection, read “the day’s—or God’s—Easter.”] When, in a brief demonstration of God’s judgment, it showed both what his favor could accomplish and what vengeance demanded, we defeated while fighting and were defeated while victorious. [Note: [Col. 1158D] “Vengeance.” Some older editions add “divine” redundantly.]

I say nothing of the frequent mutual destructions among the barbarians, when two Gothic bands, and then the Alans and Huns, devastated one another in various slaughters. [Note: [Col. 1158D] Perizonius reads “when they devastated one another.”]

Rhadagaisus, by far the most savage of all ancient and contemporary enemies, inundated all Italy with a sudden attack. [Col. 1159A] [Note: [Col. 1159C] “Inundated.” This is Orosius’s word; the Augsburg edition gives “invaded” as its gloss.] For they say that there were more than two hundred thousand Goths in his people. Besides this incredible multitude and untamed valor, he was a pagan and a Scythian; and, as is customary among such barbarian peoples, he had vowed to pour out all the blood of the Roman race as a libation to his gods. [Note: [Col. 1159C] “Of this kind.” Perizonius reads “of the same kind”; the first and third Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection, read “of that same nation.”]

When he was therefore threatening the Roman strongholds, all the pagans in the City gathered together, proclaiming that the enemy was at hand, powerful both through his abundance of forces and, above all, through the protection of the gods; but that the City had therefore been abandoned and would soon perish because it had lost its gods and sacred rites. [Note: [Col. 1159C] “Had lost them.” Perizonius reads “had lost them” in the past tense.] Great lamentations were heard everywhere, and immediately discussion began about recovering and celebrating the rites. [Note: [Col. 1159C] The first Leiden manuscript had “about sudden rites” in the text, with the true reading added in the margin.] Throughout the City blasphemies raged; the name of Christ was publicly burdened with insults, as though it were some plague of the present age. [Note: [Col. 1159C] “Is burdened with insults.” I prefer this reading, found in Perizonius, the three Leiden manuscripts, and the Groningen collection, to “is weighed down by reproaches,” which the other manuscripts and editions have.]

And so, by God’s ineffable judgment, it came about that, since grace was owed to the pious and punishment to the impious in a mixed population, it was necessary to permit enemies who would convict a city, obstinate in the majority and resistant, by harsher scourges than usual. [Note: [Col. 1159D] Perizonius reads “it was necessary.”] Yet not those who, carried away without distinction, would destroy the city by uncontrolled slaughter. [Note: [Col. 1159D] The Augsburg edition adds “enemies.”] Two peoples of the Goths, with their two most powerful kings, were then raging through the Roman provinces. [Note: [Col. 1159D] All nine manuscripts that I consulted for this passage, together with the Groningen collection and the Augsburg manuscript, read *bacchabantur*, “were raging.” If this reading is accepted, the earlier *oportebatque*, “it was necessary,” should be changed to *oportebat*, and a new sentence should begin with “two peoples of the Goths,” placing a stronger punctuation after “would destroy.”]

One of them was Christian and closer to Roman ways. [Note: [Col. 1160C] “In slaughter.” Three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection, read “unto slaughter”; nothing need be changed, since shortly afterward the other is said to have loved slaughter itself in slaughter.] [Note: [Col. 1159D] “And more Roman.” I do not know why the editions of Fabricius and Scottus have *propriorque*, “nearer,” which is no more satisfactory than *propitiorque Romano*, “more favorable to the Romans,” found in the Perizonian and Augsburg manuscripts. The phrase means “less barbarous and closer to Roman customs.”] And, as events showed, gentle in slaughter through fear of God; the other was pagan, [Note: [Col. 1160C] “Barbarian.” This word has dropped out of the first and third Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen collection.] barbarian, and truly Scythian, loving not merely glory or booty but slaughter itself, in slaughter, with insatiable cruelty. This latter, now having taken Italy into his embrace, was shaking Rome with terror from nearby. [Note: [Col. 1160C] Some manuscripts read: “He was shaking Rome, trembling with terror, from the neighboring place.”]

Therefore, if power of vengeance had been granted to this man, whom the Romans considered especially terrifying because he invited the favor of the gods by sacrificial observances, and if uncontrolled slaughter had burned without the fruit of correction, the final error would have grown worse than the first. For, if it were believed that Rome had fallen into the hands of a pagan and idolater, not only would the surviving pagans have been indisputably persuaded to restore the worship of idols, but Christians too would have been dangerously confused: the Christians would be terrified by the precedent, and the pagans strengthened by the example. [Note: [Col. 1160C] “Excessive slaughter.” Some editions incorrectly read “more excessive than slaughter.”] [Note: [Col. 1160C] “To have fallen.” Perizonius and the Groningen collection read the plural “to have fallen,” which yields no sound sense.]

Therefore God, the just disposer of the human race, willed the pagan enemy to perish [Note: [Col. 1160C] “Just.” The three Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection, read “most just.”] and permitted the Christian to prevail, so that the pagan and blaspheming Romans would both be confounded by the destruction of the former and punished by the sending of the latter against them—especially since the admirable self-restraint of the Emperor Honorius toward the king and his most holy faith deserved no small measure of divine mercy. [Note: [Col. 1160C] The first Leiden manuscript reads: “and his most holy faith deserved the aid of divine mercy.”]

Support was indeed granted against that most savage enemy Rhadagaisus by the courage of other enemies, who with their forces inclined toward assistance. Uldin and Sarus, leaders of the Huns and Goths, [Note: [Col. 1160C] The Deacon reads *Virdinus*; the Venetian editions have *Uldinus*.] [Note: [Col. 1160D] “Sarus.” Two Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection, read *Parus*.] appeared in support of the Romans. But God does not allow the matter to appear to have been accomplished by human power, or by the valor of men and especially of enemies.

He drove Rhadagaisus, terrified by divine intervention, into the Faesulan mountains. [Note: [Col. 1160D] In the first Florentine manuscript, the final letter in these two words appears to have been erased.] There, according to those who report the smallest number, [Note: [Col. 1160D] “Two hundred thousand.” The third Leiden manuscript and the Groningen collection read seven hundred thousand.] he enclosed two hundred thousand men, lacking both counsel and food, on the dry and rugged ridge of the mountain, hemmed in on every side by fear. The armies that had earlier thought Italy too narrow drove themselves, in the hope of hiding, onto a single small summit. [Note: [Col. 1160D] The Augsburg edition reads “onto one, and onto a small summit.”]

Why delay with details? There was no battle line arranged for combat; neither fury nor fear made uncertainty prefer battle; there was no slaughter, no blood was shed, nor, finally—which is usually counted a form of good fortune—were the losses of battle compensated by the outcome of victory. [Note: [Col. 1160D] “Compensated by the outcome of victory.” The first and second Leiden manuscripts, together with the Groningen collection, read “were compensated by the outcome of victory.”] [Note: [Col. 1160D] Perizonius, three Leiden manuscripts, and the Groningen collection read “nor finally, which is counted as a matter of good fortune.” The Venetian editions and the Augsburg edition, deleting *non*, read “which is usually counted as a matter of good fortune.”] While our men were eating, drinking, and playing, those immense and savage enemies were exhausted by hunger, thirst, and weakness.

This is too little, unless they also know that he was captured, chained, and placed under the yoke; that man whom the Romans feared, and that idolater whose sacrifices they pretended to fear more than his weapons, they might look upon as defeated and bound without a battle, beneath the yoke and chains. [Note: [Col. 1160D] “And chained.” This appears in none of the manuscripts I consulted, nor in the Augsburg edition. Yet it corresponds to what follows, where it is said that he was defeated without battle—or, as Perizonius reads, captured and bound—and that they looked upon him beneath the yoke and chains.]

King Rhadagaisus, therefore, alone placing his hope in flight, secretly abandoned his men and fell into ours’ hands. He was captured, held for a short time, and then killed. [Note: [Col. 1161C] Perizonius’s manuscript, together with two or three Leiden manuscripts and the Groningen collection, reads: “captured, held briefly, and then killed.”] It is said that such a great multitude of captive Goths remained that, like the cheapest livestock, whole herds of human beings were sold everywhere for a single gold coin. But God allowed nothing of that people to remain. For immediately, when all those who were being purchased died, what their wicked buyers had not shamefully spent on their price, they mercifully expended on their burial.

Ungrateful Rome, which, as it has now learned, suffers the oblique mercy of God’s judgment—not for the remission but for the repression of its presumption in idolatry—was therefore not to endure the full anger of God immediately, because of the pious remembrance of the living and the dead saints, [Note: [Col. 1161C] “Thus immediately.” The Groningen collection reads “thus immediately, just as because of the living,” and so forth.] [Note: [Col. 1161C] The Augsburg edition reads “of the ancestors” rather than “of the saints.”] if perhaps, humbled, it might repent and learn faith through experience. For a short time, then, the attack of King Alaric, an enemy but a Christian, [Note: [Col. 1161D] The first Leiden manuscript reads *aliquanto*, “somewhat,” rather than *aliquantulo*, “for a little while.”] was postponed. [Note: [Col. 1161D] The fourth Leiden manuscript reads “was delayed.” In the first Leiden manuscript the text has *defertur queat*, “may be deferred,” but this is corrected to *differri queat*, as in the third manuscript. The common reading is sound. Orosius means that Rome, although it prides itself on the title of Eternal City, will nevertheless eventually perish through God’s anger; yet God postpones his anger so that, if Rome—having not been destroyed by Rhadagaisus, to whom this was not granted because he was a pagan—should repent, it might be punished more gently by Alaric, a Christian, and thus learn faith and, through faith, submit fruitfully to divine chastisements. Compare the end of the following chapter.]

**CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the schemes of Count Stilicho and on his death and that of Eucherius**

Meanwhile Count Stilicho, born of the stock of the Vandals, an unwarlike, greedy, faithless, and deceitful people, thinking little of the fact that he ruled under an emperor, was striving by any means to support his son Eucherius in attaining the imperial power. Eucherius, as many report, had contemplated the persecution of Christians from the time when, as a private citizen, he was still a boy. [Note: [Col. 1162C] “For the imperial power.” The Augsburg edition and nearly all the manuscripts I have examined have this reading, not “in the empire,” as in the common editions.]

For this reason Stilicho secretly supported Alaric and the entire Gothic nation, which was humbly and straightforwardly asking for peace and for any settlement whatsoever; but publicly, while denying them both the opportunity for war and that of peace, he kept them in reserve to wear down and terrify the commonwealth. Moreover, he deliberately summoned other peoples intolerable in their forces and strength, by whom the provinces of Gaul and Spain are now oppressed—namely, the Alans, Suebi, and Vandals—and, together with them, the Burgundians, driven on by the same movement. [Note: [Col. 1162C] The Augsburg edition reads “and by fear of them all together,” which I do not reject.] Once the fear of the Roman name had been wiped away, he roused them to arms. [Col. 1162B]

Meanwhile he wanted them to shake the banks of the Rhine and strike Gaul, hoping, in his misery, [Note: [Col. 1162C] “Meanwhile he wished them to shake the banks,” and so forth. Earlier editions placed no punctuation before these words, and consequently obscured their meaning. The Augsburg edition reads “the very banks,” for “the banks,” and “of them all,” for “of them.”] [Note: [Col. 1162C] “That he could also force.” In Orosius’s manuscripts *quia* frequently stands for *quod*, and the two are interchanged in most codices here; we follow those which write *quod*. Perizonius has *qua*, “by which.”] that under such a crisis of necessity he could force the imperial power from his son-in-law into his son, [Note: [Col. 1162C] “Could also force the empire from his son-in-law into his son.” Stilicho’s son-in-law was Honorius, who had married Stilicho’s daughter; but while preparing a kingdom for his son Eucherius, Stilicho sought to wrest it from his son-in-law Honorius. The Perizonian manuscript offers a new reading: “by which he could also force the imperial power, held by his tender son,” and so forth. The common reading is sound.] and that barbarian peoples could be suppressed as easily as they could be stirred up.

When this scene of so many crimes was therefore exposed to the Emperor Honorius and the Roman army, the army was justly aroused and Stilicho was killed. In order to clothe one boy in the purple, he had delivered up the blood of the entire human race. [Note: [Col. 1162D] “Should put on the purple.” The Augsburg edition and the better manuscripts read this; others have “should put on the purple garment.”] [Note: [Col. 1162D] “He delivered up.” This has been restored from the Florentine manuscripts and the Augsburg edition; other copies read “he gave.”]

Eucherius too was killed. To win the favor of the pagans, he threatened to inaugurate his reign by restoring the temples and overthrowing the churches. A few retainers together with them were also punished for such great schemes. Thus, at the very small cost of punishing a few, the Church of Christ was both freed and avenged together with the religious emperor. [Col. 1162C] [Note: [Col. 1162D] “And by the punishment of a few.” Several manuscripts read “by the punishment of a few.”]

After such a great increase of blasphemies and no repentance, that final punishment, long delayed and long suspended over the City, overtook it. [Note: [Col. 1162D] The Perizonian manuscript reads “after so great an increase and such atonements of blasphemies.”]

**CHAPTER XXXIX. How Rome was invaded, plundered, and burned by the Goths, while Christians alone remained safe and free**

Alaric appeared, besieged trembling Rome, [Note: [Col. 1163C] “Disturbs, bursts in.” Perizonius, together with Ultr. and two Leiden manuscripts, reads “having disturbed, or having greatly disturbed, he bursts in.”] disturbed it, and burst in. Yet he first issued an order [Note: [Col. 1163C] “First.” This word is absent from the Augsburg edition.] that, if anyone had fled for refuge to holy places, and especially to the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, [Note: [Col. 1163C] The Perizonian manuscript likewise reads “they should take refuge.”] they should above all leave such people inviolate and secure. Then, as far as they could, while intent on booty, they should refrain from bloodshed.

It also happened—so that this invasion of the City might be shown to have been brought about more by God’s indignation than by the enemy’s strength—that blessed Innocent, [Note: [Col. 1163D] “Of the Roman Church.” The Augsburg edition reads “of the Roman City.” In the same edition *Lot* is missing, and shortly afterward it prefers “of the sinful people at that time,” and so forth.] bishop of the Roman Church, was then staying at Ravenna by God’s hidden providence, like the righteous Lot rescued from Sodom, and did not see the destruction of the sinful people.

As the barbarians were running through the City, one of the Goths, both a powerful man and a Christian, found an elderly sacred virgin of God in a certain ecclesiastical house. He honorably asked her for gold and silver. She faithfully promised that she possessed a great deal and would immediately produce it, and she did so. [Note: [Col. 1163D] “She.” Perizonius reads “to him.”] When the treasures had been displayed, and the barbarian was astonished by their size, weight, and beauty, and also by the unfamiliar character of the vessels, [Note: [Col. 1163D] Some editions read “saw” instead of “understood.”] Christ’s virgin said to the barbarian: “These are the sacred vessels used in the ministry of the apostle Peter. Take them, if you dare; as for the deed, you must see to it.” “For I cannot defend them, nor do I dare to keep them.” [Note: [Col. 1163D] “For I cannot defend them, nor do I dare to keep them.” Fabricius restored this reading from his manuscripts; previously, except in the Augsburg edition, the text read “nor do I dare to contend for them.” The Perizonian manuscript and the fourth Leiden manuscript and Ultr. read: “Since I cannot, or cannot at all, defend them, I do not dare to keep them.”]

The barbarian, moved to reverence for religion by fear of God and faith in the virgin, reported these things by a messenger to Alaric. Alaric immediately ordered all the vessels to be carried to the apostle’s basilica as they were, [Note: [Col. 1163D] “All of them.” This is absent from the Perizonian manuscript, which shortly afterward reads “the same things, with protection.”] and ordered the virgin, together with all the Christians who joined her, to be escorted there under the same protection.

That house was, as they say, far from the holy sites, with much of the City lying between them. [Note: [Col. 1164C] Some editions read “from the holy sites,” without “far.” The Augsburg edition and the better manuscripts require “far,” rather than the common reading “at a distance, as they say.”] Thus, to the great spectacle of everyone, the vessels were arranged one by one and carried openly, each raised above a person’s head; golden and silver vessels were displayed, and the pious procession was protected on every side by drawn swords. Hymns were sung publicly, with Romans and barbarians singing together to God. [Note: [Col. 1164C] The Augsburg edition reads the singular “a hymn”; some copies have “the hymn.”] Amid the destruction of the City, the trumpet of salvation sounded far and wide, inviting and striking even all those who were hiding in secret places.

Everywhere people ran to the vessels of Peter—the vessels of Christ. Many pagans also mingled with the Christians in profession, though not in faith, [Note: [Col. 1164C] “Though not in faith.” Read this way from the manuscripts and the Augsburg edition; the common editions read “if not in faith.”] and through this, nevertheless, they escaped for a time, only to be more thoroughly confounded. The more abundantly the Romans fleeing for refuge gathered, the more eagerly the barbarian protectors surrounded them.

O sacred and ineffable discrimination of divine judgment! O holy and saving river, which, rising from a small house and flowing through a blessed channel toward the holy sites, carried wandering and endangered souls, by its pious force, into the embrace of salvation! O glorious trumpet of Christian warfare, which, inviting all alike to life with the sweetest melody, left those whom it did not rouse to salvation in their disobedience [Note: [Col. 1164D] Perizonius and the fourth Leiden manuscript read “to life” rather than “to salvation.”] without excuse for death. [Note: [Col. 1164D] “Inexcusable.” The fourth Leiden manuscript reads “entangled.”]

I think this mystery, which was enacted in the carrying of the vessels, the singing of hymns, and the leading of the people, was like a great sieve. Through it, from the gathering of the Roman people, as from a great mass of grain, living kernels flowed out through all the openings of hiding places throughout the entire circuit of the City, moved either by circumstance or by truth; yet all believed in the salvation present at that moment, and were received from the storehouse of the Lord’s preparation. [Note: [Col. 1164D] “From the granary.” Two Florentine manuscripts read “and from the granary.”] The rest, like dung [Note: [Col. 1164D] The Augsburg edition and the Florentine manuscripts read “like dung” or “as dung.”] and like straw, condemned in advance by their own unbelief or disobedience, remained for destruction and burning.

Who could fully comprehend these things amid such abundant miracles, or proclaim them in praises worthy of them? [Note: [Col. 1164D] “Comprehend.” The same edition reads “will comprehend.”] On the third day after entering the City, the barbarians voluntarily departed. [Note: [Col. 1164D] Some manuscripts read “having nevertheless done so,” rather than “having indeed done so.”] They did set fire to a number of buildings, but not even to as many as the disaster had consumed in the seven-hundredth year of the City’s foundation. [Note: [Col. 1164D] One manuscript reads “as many as in the seven-hundredth year.”]

For if I recall the conflagration which their own emperor Nero staged for spectacles, there can unquestionably be no comparison between what the prince’s wantonness caused and what the victor’s anger has now inflicted. Nor should I mention the Gauls in such a comparison, [Note: [Col. 1165C] Perizonius and the three Leiden manuscripts read “Nor should I mention the Gauls.”] who for almost the continuous span of a year possessed the crushed ashes of the burned and overturned City. [Note: [Col. 1165C] The three Leiden manuscripts read: “for almost the continuous span of a year they possessed the crushed ashes, with the remaining structures destroyed.” Some older editions have “for nearly an entire year.”]

And lest anyone perhaps doubt that the enemies had been permitted this as a correction of the proud, wanton, and blasphemous City, at the same time the most famous places of the City were destroyed by lightning—places that the enemy could not set ablaze. [Note: [Col. 1165C] “Were destroyed.” The first and third Leiden manuscripts read “were torn apart,” which is not without merit. The Augsburg edition reads “of the proud and wretched city”; the Perizonian manuscript reads “of the proud, wanton, blasphemous, and wretched city.” This reading is not objectionable.]

**CHAPTER XL. On the invasion and devastation of the Alans, Suebi, and Vandals; and likewise on the tyrant Gratian and the Emperor Constantine among the Britons; and on the deeds and deaths of Didymus and Verinianus**

[Col. 1165B]

[Note: [Col. 1165C] “And so in the year.” Three copies from Lyon, to which Perizonius, the Utrecht edition, and Gronovius’s collection are added, do not recognize the second reading.]

And so, in the year 1164 from the founding of the City, the invasion of Rome by Alaric took place. Although the memory of this event is recent [Note: [Col. 1165C] “May be.” The Augustan edition has “is.”], nevertheless, if anyone were to see the population of the Roman people itself and hear its voice, he would think that nothing had happened—as they themselves also admit—unless he were perhaps shown by the ruins still remaining from the fire [Note: [Col. 1165C] “With ruins still standing.” Three Lyon editions, together with Gronovius’s collection, have “with standing ruins.”]. In that invasion Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius and sister of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius [Note: [Col. 1165C] “Sister of the emperors.” Three Lyon editions together with Gronovius read “sister of the emperor, having been carried away.”], was captured by Ataulf, a kinsman of Alaric [Note: [Col. 1165D] “Was captured.” Three Lyon editions, two Florentine manuscripts, Perizonius, and Gronovius’s collection omit the verb “was.”], and taken as his wife, as though Rome, by divine judgment, had surrendered her as a special pledge and hostage. Thus joined in marriage to the most powerful barbarian king [Note: [Col. 1165D] “Of the most powerful barbarian king.” So the Augustan edition; the others have “of the most powerful barbarian king,” which is harsh to the ear. The first Lyon edition deletes “king,” as do two Florentine manuscripts.], she proved greatly advantageous to the state.

Meanwhile, two years before the invasion of Rome, the peoples of the Alans, Suebi, and Vandals, roused by Stilicho, as I have said, together with many other peoples [Col. 1166A] accompanying them, crushed the Franks, crossed the Rhine, invaded Gaul, and advanced in a direct thrust as far as the Pyrenees. Repulsed for a time by that barrier, they poured back through the surrounding provinces.

While these peoples were raging through Gaul, in Britain Gratian, a townsman of that island, was made tyrant and killed. In his place Constantine, from the lowest ranks of the army, was chosen solely because of the hope attached to his name and without any merit of courage. 577 As soon as he seized the imperial power, he crossed into Gaul. [Note: [Col. 1165D] “There often.” The first and third Lyon editions have “where often.”] There he was frequently deceived by the barbarians through uncertain treaties and proved more a loss than a benefit to the state.

[Note: [Col. 1165D] “He sent judges into Spain.” Many editions read, “But he sent judges into Spain”; this is contrary to the manuscripts.]

He sent judges into Spain. When the provinces had accepted them in obedience [Note: [Col. 1165D] “Had accepted.” Three Lyon editions together with Gronovius’s collection have “had heard.” Not Verinianus but Viridianus is the name of one of these men according to Paul the Deacon.], two young brothers of noble birth and wealth, Didymus and Verinianus [Note: [Col. 1166C] “They did not take up.” Nearly all manuscripts have “not to take up,” which is well and correctly expressed in Latin, but it is uncertain whether Orosius wrote it. The words that follow, I think, will easily be understood by only a few in their transmitted form. The printed editions have “they did not take up, lest they should act against the tyrant,” etc. If a stronger pause is placed after “they did not take up,” the sense becomes clearer, especially if “nor” is substituted for “lest,” or if “lest” is understood to have the same meaning as “nor.” The meaning is this: these young men did not even take up arms for tyranny—that is, for their own tyranny, as Orosius makes clear below—against the tyrant, but for the emperor and their country, against the tyrant and the barbarians. The manuscripts that have “to take up” delete “lest,” but without justification, although some of them also insert, pointlessly, between “the tyrant” and “and indeed,” the words “they themselves,” and then remove “and the barbarians.”], did not take up arms even for tyranny against the tyrant; rather, they attempted to defend themselves and their country for the rightful emperor, against the tyrant and the barbarians. This was evident from the very sequence of events.

[Note: [Col. 1166D] “Secretly.” This is absent from the Augustan manuscript and from two Florentine manuscripts, which have “secretly.”]

For no one undertakes a tyranny except by first preparing it quickly in secret and then arming himself openly; its essence is that, after assuming the diadem and purple [Note: [Col. 1166D] “And the purple.” Two Lyon manuscripts have “or the purple.”], he should be seen before he is known. These men, however, for a very long time [Note: [Col. 1166D] Perizonius has “at the first time.”] gathered only their own household slaves [Note: [Col. 1166D] “From their own estates.” The first and third Lyon editions have “from their own garrisons.”] from their private estates and fed them at their own expense, without concealing their purpose, and proceeded toward the passes of the Pyrenees without disturbing anyone.

Against them [Note: [Col. 1166D] Perizonius has “against whom.”] Constantine sent his son Constans—alas! made Caesar from a monk—together with certain barbarians [Note: [Col. 1166D] “Certain.” This is absent from the Lyon manuscripts and from Gronovius’s collection], who, having once been received into alliance and recruited into the army, were called Honoriaci [Note: [Col. 1166D] In some manuscripts they are called “Honoriani,” in others “Honoriaci”; Perizonius calls them “Honoraciaci.”], into Spain.

Here the first stain of the disaster appeared [Note: [Col. 1166D] The Lyon edition, together with Perizonius and Gronovius’s collection, adds “was.”]. For after those brothers, who were attempting to guard the Pyrenean Alps with a private force, had been killed, these barbarians were first granted the opportunity to plunder in the Palatine plains [Note: [Col. 1167C] “In the Palatine plains.” Four Lyon editions together with Perizonius, Gronovius’s collection, and the Augustan edition have “in the Palestinian plains.”], as the reward of victory. Thereafter the defense of the aforesaid mountain and its passes was entrusted to them, the faithful and useful protection of the peasants having been removed.

Thus the Honoriaci, having been steeped in plunder and enticed by abundance [Note: [Col. 1167C] The Augustan edition has “allured” instead of “enticed.”], so that the crime itself might enjoy greater impunity [Note: [Col. 1167C] I have emended this passage from the Augustan edition, which reads as follows: “so that the crime itself might have greater license.” The common editions read “so that there might be greater license for their crimes.” For this, three Lyon editions together with Gronovius’s collection and the Utrecht edition have, more suitably, “for the crimes themselves”; Perizonius has “so that they themselves might have greater license for crime.”], betrayed the guard of the Pyrenees and opened its passes, and admitted into the provinces of Spain all the peoples wandering through Gaul. They themselves also joined those peoples. After carrying out for some time great and bloody raids, and after the grave devastation of property and people [Note: [Col. 1167C] Three Lyon editions have “of slaves and people.”], of which they themselves too now repent [Note: [Col. 1167C] Since this reading is found in all the manuscripts, as also in the Augustan edition, I have banished the reading which the editors substituted at their discretion, “of which they themselves repent,” etc.], they now remain there, having received by lot and distributed among them the land they possess to this day. [Note: [Col. 1167C] Paul the Deacon, at the end of Book XIII, says: “And so, after many massacres, fires, and plunderings, the barbarians at last, their settlements divided, turned to the plow and began to cherish the Romans who remained as friends.”]

## CHAPTER XLI. An Epilogue, as It Were, of What Has Been Said; Also, That All Have Justly Suffered All Things, Whether They Were Pious or Impious

[Col. 1167B]

I would now have much opportunity to speak about matters of this kind [Note: [Col. 1167D] Two Florentine manuscripts have “of matters of this sort.”], if the hidden conscience within each person did not speak, according to all human beings, in each person’s mind.

Spain has been invaded; it has suffered slaughter and devastation. Nothing new, certainly [Note: [Col. 1167D] Some manuscripts have “nothing new.”], for this is what it now [Note: [Col. 1167D] The final word is absent from three Lyon manuscripts.] endured for two years [Note: [Col. 1167D] “That.” This is not found in the same manuscripts, nor in the Augustan edition.] while the hostile sword raged [Note: [Col. 1167D] I prefer “raged,” with Perizonius and the Perizonian manuscript, to “rages,” which appears in the others]—what it once suffered for two hundred years at the hands of the Romans, and what, under the emperor Gallienus, it endured for nearly twelve years while the Germans were overthrowing everything.

Nevertheless, who, being conscious of himself, his actions, and even his thoughts, and fearing God’s judgments, would not confess that he has justly suffered everything, or at least suffered only a little? Or how could anyone who does not understand himself and does not fear God fail to have suffered these things justly—and indeed only a little?

[Note: [Col. 1167D] “Since these things are so.” The editions of Fabricius and Scott have “since all these things are so,” ineptly and contrary to the manuscripts. Perizonius has “since these things are just.”]

Since these things are so, God’s mercy nevertheless, with the same compassion with which he had formerly foretold it, brought about this result: in accordance with his Gospel, by which he continually admonished us [Note: [Col. 1168C] Three Lyon editions, together with Perizonius and Gronovius’s collection, have “commanded” instead of “admonished.”], “When they persecute you in one city, flee to another” [Note: [Col. 1168C] “When they persecute you, etc.” The first Lyon edition and Perizonius have “But if they persecute you, etc.” It occurs in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 10.], whoever wished to leave and depart could use those same barbarians as hired servants and protectors.

At that time they themselves voluntarily offered this service. And those who, after killing everyone, could have taken everything demanded only a portion of the payment for their service and for transporting the burdens [Note: [Col. 1168C] The second Florentine manuscript has “for the transportation.” They were content, of course, with the money given for transporting the goods which, as they escorted those departing, they carried to another place for their use.]. This was indeed done by very many people [Note: [Col. 1168C] This phrase is absent from the Augustan edition].

But those who did not believe God’s Gospel, being obstinate—or, if they had not even heard it, doubly obstinate [Note: [Col. 1168D] “Or if.” “Or” is absent from two Lyon manuscripts.], did not make room for wrath [Note: [Col. 1168D] The first Lyon edition has “and did not make room”; Perizonius has “and did not believe.”], and were justly seized and crushed by the wrath that came upon them.

And yet, immediately afterward, the barbarians, cursing their swords, turned to the plow and now cherish the Romans who remained as allies and friends. Thus some Romans are now found among them who would rather endure poor freedom among barbarians than tributary anxiety among Romans.

[Note: [Col. 1168D] “And yet.” The Augustan edition has “as though.”]

And yet, if the barbarians had been admitted into Roman territories for this one reason alone—that, as is commonly reported, throughout East and West the churches of Christ are filled with Huns and Suebi, Vandals and Burgundians, and diverse and innumerable peoples of believers [Note: [Col. 1168D] “Are filled.” The first Lyon edition has “might be filled.”], God’s mercy would seem worthy of praise and exaltation [Note: [Col. 1168D] Three Lyon editions, together with Gronovius’s collection, have “seems” instead of “would seem.”]. For even though this occurred at our own weakening, so many peoples would receive knowledge of the truth [Note: [Col. 1168D] The same manuscripts have “might have received”; Perizonius has “had received.”]—a knowledge which, certainly, they could not have found except on this occasion [Note: [Col. 1168D] Perizonius has “could not have found.”].

For what loss is there for a Christian longing for eternal life in being taken away from this age, at whatever time and by whatever means? But what gain is there for a pagan hardened against the faith amid Christians if he prolongs his day a little longer, when conversion is hopeless for one who is going to die? [Note: [Col. 1169C] The first, third, and fourth Lyon editions, together with Gronovius’s collection, have “whenever he is going to die”; the second has “when he is going to die.” All of them, together with Perizonius, add “for whom conversion is hopeless.” The common reading can nevertheless defend itself.]

And because God’s judgments are ineffable, so that we can neither know all of them nor explain what we do know [Note: [Col. 1169C] The first and third Lyon editions, together with Gronovius’s collection, have “fulfill” instead of “explain.”], I shall briefly express this point: those who know that God’s judgment is correction should justly endure it, however it may occur [Note: [Col. 1169C] The old editions have “correction” instead of “chastisement.”]—those who do not know should justly endure it [Note: [Col. 1169C] These words correspond to what was said above: “Nevertheless, who, being conscious of himself, his actions, etc., would not confess that he has justly suffered everything?” The Augustan edition therefore reads ineptly, “who know that it should justly be endured, and that those who do not know should unjustly endure it.”].

581 ## CHAPTER XLII. A Catalogue Is Given of Certain Tyrants Who Were Ultimately Destroyed, All Through the Efforts of Count Constantius

In the year 1165 from the founding of the City, the emperor Honorius, seeing that nothing could be done against the barbarians while so many tyrants opposed him, ordered that the tyrants themselves should first be destroyed [Note: [Col. 1169C] “Should be destroyed.” So two Florentine manuscripts, Perizonius, the Utrecht edition, and the third Lyon edition. The others, as well as the printed editions, have “orders them to destroy.”]. The chief command of this war was entrusted to Count Constantius. Only then did the state realize both what an advantage it had finally gained in a Roman commander and what destruction it had endured for so long under barbarian commanders.

Accordingly, Count Constantius set out with an army for Gaul, besieged Constantine the emperor at the city of Arles [Note: [Col. 1169C] The printed editions and some manuscripts have “Arles” in the accusative, since the name is ordinarily written in either form; but the Deacon also has “at Arles,” deleting “the city,” which some manuscripts of Orosius likewise omit.], captured him, and killed him.

Now, to speak as briefly as possible about the catalogue of tyrants: Constans, the son of Constantine, was killed at Vienne by his own count Gerontius, a wicked and disreputable man [Note: [Col. 1169C] All the Lyon manuscripts, together with Perizonius and Gronovius’s collection, have “more wicked than upright.”], who installed a certain Maximus in his place [Note: [Col. 1169C] Perizonius has “appointed.”]. Gerontius himself, however, was killed by his own soldiers.

Maximus, stripped of the purple and abandoned by the Gallic soldiers, who were transferred to Africa and later recalled to Italy, now lives in exile among the barbarians in Spain in poverty [Note: [Col. 1169C] The second Lyon edition has “lives in exile in barbarous Spain in poverty.” Paul the Deacon, at the beginning of Book XIV, says: “He [Constantius], as soon as he entered Gaul, immediately destroyed the tyrant Constantine at Arles. Constans, his son, was killed at Vienne by Gerontius, his count. Gerontius, having installed Maximus in his place, was himself slaughtered by his own soldiers. Maximus, then stripped of the purple, died in poverty while living in exile in Spain.”].

Later Jovinus, a man of the highest nobility in Gaul, fell as soon as he rose up in tyranny [Note: [Col. 1170C] The Augustan edition has “and he fell”; the first and third Lyon editions, together with Gronovius’s collection, have “and he died.” Perizonius has “rose up.”]. His brother Sebastianus chose only this: to die as a tyrant. 582 For as soon as he was created, he was killed [Note: [Col. 1170C] All the Lyon manuscripts, together with the Utrecht edition, Perizonius, Meursius, and Gronovius’s collection—and therefore all the manuscripts—delete “was,” which the printed editions insert, except the Augustan edition, thus reading “as soon as he was created, he was killed.”].

What shall I say about the most unfortunate Attalus, for whom being killed among tyrants was an honor and dying a gain? In making him emperor, unmaking him, remaking him, and unmaking him again, all more quickly than these things can almost be said, Alaric laughed at the farce and watched the spectacle of imperial power. Nor is it surprising that he was miserably played in this performance [Note: [Col. 1170C] “If he was rightly subjected to this spectacle.” Three Lyon editions, together with Gronovius’s collection, have “if he was rightly subjected to this display.”], since his shadow-consul Tertullus dared to say in the senate:

“I shall speak to you, Conscript Fathers, as consul and pontiff. I hold one of these offices [Note: [Col. 1170C] “I hope for the other.” That is, the pontificate, if the worship of idols were restored and his own shadow-emperor continued in power. Paul the Deacon badly transmitted Orosius’s passage, writing at the beginning of Book XIV: “Tertullus the consul, who boasted in the senate that he would become emperor, nevertheless perished in a similar manner.”], and I hope for the other”—hoping from one who had no hope, and certainly accursed because [Note: [Col. 1170C] Three Lyon editions, together with Gronovius’s collection and the Perizonian manuscript, read “who” instead of “because.”] he had placed his hope in a human being.

Thus Attalus, like an empty image of imperial power, was carried with the Goths as far as Spain. Departing from there by ship and attempting uncertain ventures, he was captured at sea and brought to Count Constantius. Then he was presented to the emperor Honorius, and, with one hand cut off, was left alive.

Meanwhile, Heraclianus was sent as count of Africa. While that same Attalus was bearing the shadow of imperial power, Heraclianus vigorously defended Africa against the judges sent by him and attained the consulship [Note: [Col. 1170C] The Augustan edition has “attained” instead of “secured.”]. Elated by this distinction, he took as his son-in-law his domestic officer Sabinus [Note: [Col. 1170C] The second Florentine manuscript has “Sabinus the judge, his companion.”], a man clever in intellect, diligent in industry, and deserving of being called wise if he had devoted the strength of his mind to peaceful pursuits.

While he was suffering and provoking suspicions of certain dangers together with him, the African grain supply was detained for some time outside the regular order. 583 Finally, with an immense fleet—certainly sufficiently incredible for our own times [Note: [Col. 1171C] Perizonius has “quite enough” instead of “certainly.”]—he made for Rome [Note: [Col. 1171C] The printed editions, except the Augustan, have “and sufficiently incredible”; but the manuscripts do not recognize “and,” which also damages the sense.]. For he is said then to have had 3,700 ships—a number which histories report to have existed neither under Xerxes, that celebrated king of the Persians, nor under Alexander the Great, nor under any other king.

As soon as he had disembarked on the shore while advancing with his army toward the City, he was frightened by the approach of Count Marinus and put to flight. Seizing a ship, he returned alone to Carthage, where he was immediately killed by a military force.

His son-in-law Sabinus fled to Constantinople. From there, after some time [Note: [Col. 1171C] The second Florentine manuscript and the third Lyon edition, together with Gronovius’s collection, have “after some time” in place of “after a little time”; the second Lyon edition also has “after some time.” I have supplied the phrase at the end of the sentence from the manuscripts.], he was brought back and condemned to exile.

This entire catalogue, as I have said, of either manifest tyrants or disobedient commanders, the emperor Honorius, through his excellent piety and good fortune, deserved to see killed [Note: [Col. 1171C] “Deserved to see killed.” Through extreme negligence, not only in all the printed editions but also in all the manuscripts except the first and third Lyon editions and Gronovius’s collection, the verb “to see killed” had been omitted, without which the meaning is extremely ridiculous.]; Count Constantius accomplished with great diligence and speed.

And rightly so, because in those days, at the command of Honorius and with the assistance of Constantius, peace and unity were restored throughout the whole of Africa to the Catholic Church. The body of Christ, which we are, was healed after its division had been repaired [Note: [Col. 1171D] Four Lyon editions, Gronovius’s collection, and the Venetian editions have “separation” instead of “division.”]. The execution of the holy command was entrusted to the tribune Marcellinus [Note: [Col. 1171D] The Augustan edition has “a good man, especially,” instead of “a man especially prudent.”], a man especially prudent and energetic and most eager for every good pursuit. Count Marinus killed him at Carthage—whether goaded by zeal or corrupted by gold is uncertain [Note: [Col. 1171D] He was the man who had stripped Heraclianus of his forces in Italy and was afterward sent to Africa with command.]. Marinus was immediately recalled from Africa, reduced to private status, and dismissed either for punishment or for the repentance of his conscience.

584 ## CHAPTER XLIII. How the Goths Were Expelled; What Their King Ataulf Established; Concerning the Gothic Kings Sigeric and Wallia

[Col. 1171C]
