In the year 1168 from the founding of the City, Count Constantius, stationed at Arles, a city of Gaul, with great diligence in carrying out his plans, expelled the Goths from Narbonne and forced them to withdraw into Spain. He did this by especially prohibiting and blocking every supply of ships and the use of travel and commerce by foreigners.

At that time Ataulf was king over the Gothic peoples. After the invasion of Rome and the death of Alaric, he had succeeded Alaric as king, having taken Placidia, as I have said, the emperor’s sister, captive as his wife.

As was often heard, and as was proved by his final end [Note: [Col. 1171D] “By his final end.” Three Lyon editions have “at his final end.”], he was an eager follower of peace. He preferred to serve the emperor Honorius faithfully and to devote the strength of the Goths to the defense of the Roman state.

For I myself heard a certain man from Narbonne, a distinguished soldier under Theodosius and also a religious, prudent, and grave man [Note: [Col. 1171D] The same manuscripts have “prudent” instead of “prudent and grave.”], reporting to the most blessed presbyter Jerome at Bethlehem, a town of Palestine [Note: [Col. 1171D] Three Lyon manuscripts, Gronovius’s collection, and the Augustan edition write “reporting”; this is also how it ought to be written. The common text is exceedingly inept: “with the presbyter Jerome reporting, I heard him,” as though Orosius meant that he had heard that Narbonese man from Jerome, although he indicates that he himself had been present at the conversation. Some Lyon manuscripts, as well as Gronovius’s collection, then have “I confess that I heard,” or “I confess that I heard him,” and afterward indicate that he himself had been present.], that he had been extremely close to Ataulf at Narbonne.

From him he had often learned under oath that, since Ataulf was excessive in spirit, strength, and intelligence, he was accustomed to say that he had ardently desired above all things that, once the Roman name had been obliterated, the whole Roman land might both become and be called the empire of the Goths; that there might be, as I may put it popularly, a Gothia where there had been a Romania [Note: [Col. 1172C] On this designation, which ought not to be disturbed, see Spanheim, *Orbis Romanus*, p. 166]; and that Ataulf might become what Caesar Augustus once had been.

But when long experience had proved that the Goths could in no way obey laws because of their unrestrained barbarism, and that laws could not be removed from the state, without which the state is not a state [Note: [Col. 1172D] The Augustan edition has “would not be a state” instead of “is not a state.”], he said that he had chosen at least [Note: [Col. 1172D] The common editions have “salvation” instead of “at least,” except the Venetian and Augustan editions and the first edition of all, in which “salvation” certainly gives no sound sense. All the manuscripts I examined have “at least.” The third Florentine manuscript reads “he chose at least.”] to seek glory for himself by restoring the Roman name to its full integrity and enlarging it through the strength of the Goths, so that he might be regarded by posterity as the author of Rome’s restoration, since he had been unable to be its transformer.

For this reason he abstained from war; for this reason he strove for peace, especially guided in all works of good ordering by the persuasion and counsel of his wife Placidia, a woman of exceptionally sharp intelligence and of sufficiently good religious character [Note: [Col. 1172D] By common agreement these same copies write “not sufficiently approved,” rather than “sufficiently good.”].

While he was most zealously pursuing the securing and offering of that peace, he was killed at Barcelona, a city of Spain, as is reported, by the treachery of his own people.

After him Sigeric was made king by the Goths. Although he too was inclined toward peace by God’s judgment, he was nevertheless killed by his own people.

Then Wallia succeeded to the kingship, chosen by the Goths for the purpose of breaking the peace and appointed by God for the purpose of confirming it [Note: [Col. 1173C] Most manuscripts have “ordained” instead of “chosen.”].

He, therefore, greatly terrified by God’s judgment—for in the preceding year, when a large Gothic force equipped with arms and ships was preparing to cross into Africa, it had been caught by a storm twelve miles from the strait of Cádiz and had perished in a pitiable end [Note: [Col. 1173C] The second Lyon edition, with excessive mercy, has “almost perished.”]—and mindful also of the disaster suffered under Alaric, when the Goths attempted to cross into Sicily and, in sight of their own people, were miserably seized and drowned, made an excellent peace with the emperor Honorius, giving the finest hostages.

He returned to her brother Placidia, the emperor’s sister, whom he had kept honorably and chastely. He offered his own danger for Rome’s security [Note: [Col. 1173C] The fourth Lyon edition and Perizonius have “for Roman fellowship.”], so that he might fight against the other peoples who had settled throughout Spain and win for the Romans [Note: [Col. 1173C] The first and fourth Lyon editions have “and win for the Romans.”].

Although the other kings of the Alans, Vandals, and Suebi had likewise made a pact with us [Note: [Col. 1173C] Certain editions have “despised”; three Lyon manuscripts have “joined together.”], they sent word to the emperor Honorius:

“Keep peace with everyone; accept hostages from everyone [Note: [Col. 1173C] The same manuscripts have “and accept us as hostages,” with “from everyone” deleted.]. We fight among ourselves; we perish for ourselves [Note: [Col. 1173C] So I write with four Lyon manuscripts, the second Florentine manuscript, Perizonius, other manuscripts, and the Augustan edition. The common editions incorrectly have “we fight with one another; we perish for ourselves.”]; we win for you [Note: [Col. 1173C] The fourth Lyon edition has “we shall win for you.”]. Your state will have an immortal gain [Note: [Col. 1174C] All the manuscripts contain “it will be an immortal gain,” from which it is clear that they require us to read: “it will be an immortal gain for your state.” In the Perizonian manuscript and the third Lyon edition, “it will be” is absent.], if we both perish [Note: [Col. 1174C] Above, chapter 35: “Thus too, here, civil war was quenched by the blood of two peoples, apart from those ten thousand Goths whom Arbogastes is said to have sent ahead from Theodosius and utterly destroyed. Their loss was certainly a gain, and to be defeated was to conquer.”]

Who would believe these things unless events themselves proved them? [Note: [Col. 1174C] The Augustan edition has “who would believe?”; the Perizonian manuscript has “Who would know these things unless events taught them?”]

And so we learn from frequent and reliable reports that wars among the peoples are now being waged daily in Spain and that massacres are being inflicted on both sides among the barbarians. They report especially that Wallia, king of the Goths, is intent on bringing peace to completion.

From this I shall concede, in any event [Note: [Col. 1174C] Perizonius has “both” instead of “in any event.”], that Christian times may be criticized freely [Note: In the manuscripts of the first Lyon edition, “freely” is written above “willingly.” The Augustan edition has “properly.”], if anything can be shown to have occurred with comparable good fortune from the beginning of the world until now.

We have, I think, made clear and demonstrated that innumerable wars have been silenced almost by word rather than by the finger, that very many tyrants have been destroyed, and that the fiercest peoples have been restrained, confined, subdued, and emptied of power with very little bloodshed, without a struggle, and almost without slaughter.

It remains for our detractors to repent of their efforts and blush before the truth; and to believe, fear, love, and follow the true and only God, who can do all things—God whose works, including those they consider evil, they have learned to be good.

With Christ’s help, according to your command, most blessed Father Augustine, I have explained from the beginning of the world [Note: [Col. 1174C] Three Lyon editions have “up to” instead of “until.”] until the present day—that is, over 5,617 years—the desires and punishments of sinful human beings, the conflicts of the world, and the judgments of God, as briefly and simply as I could [Note: [Col. 1174C] Three Lyon editions have “as I was able.”], distinguishing Christian times from that former confusion of unbelief, especially because of the present grace of Christ.

Thus I now enjoy, with certainty, the fruit of my obedience—the one and only fruit that I ought to desire. As for the quality of the works, you must judge it, since you commanded that they be assigned to you [Note: [Col. 1174C] The Augustan edition has “to be judged” instead of “to be assigned.”] if you publish them, and judged by you if you destroy them.

[Col. 1173]

## PAUL OROSIUS, HISPANIC PRESBYTER, APOLOGETIC BOOK AGAINST PELAGIUS, ON THE FREEDOM OF THE WILL (C)

[Col. 1173D] 588

### 1.

It is not a matter of ability or presumption on my part, most blessed priests, but of the most urgent and almost extreme necessity, as you yourselves acknowledge, that I should now appear before you.

Indeed, I was compelled to do so by injury: not merely as the defender of my own faith, but also as the exposer of another’s faithlessness. For just as I ought to devote myself to my own vindication—though I speak of conscience not my own but another’s [Note: [Col. 1175] Preferring Andrew Schott’s reading, Gallandius has “because of conscience”; “but I speak of conscience,” etc.]—so I am compelled, for the sake of faith and zeal, to point out the wolves discovered among the flock; yet I say that the zeal is not mine but Christ’s.

Nor, although I am the least of all, do I presume to do anything rashly. It is my necessity to expose the injury I have suffered; let those who inflicted it be made known to everyone.

For it is both God’s will and his ordinance that the evil which was being endured through patience should necessarily be exposed and that, through the contest of their fury, those receiving the reward their error deserved should bring about not merely the denunciation of the most wicked doctrines, but also the identification of the persons who must be corrected.

For the fathers and martyrs who have already rested, and who were united in concord—Cyprian, Hilary, and Ambrose—and those who even now must necessarily remain in the flesh, who are the pillars and foundations of the Catholic Church, Aurelius Augustine and Jerome, have already published many proven works against this unspeakable heresy, without identifying the names of the heretics.

Nevertheless, this abhorrence of the most poisonous doctrines also has living dead men and dead living men even now. Origen, Priscillian, and Jovinian, long dead among themselves, live in these men; indeed, they not only live but also speak through them.

Now Pelagius and Coelestius, if they persist in these things as living dead men, behold, hiss openly against the Church—which is pitiable—and, what is much more pitiable, within the Church. Like impious serpents, they lick mouths infected by their quivering tongues, while they besiege the holy and most strongly fortified seat into which they have subtly crept, frightening all the faithful lest we fly together to that once most secure refuge in Zion.

2. Against this serpent, and against the breath that suffocates, the most blessed men whom we mentioned above certainly prepare many and varied sweet-smelling ointments from the Scriptures; and, to refresh the fevered hearts of the peoples, they burn the most fragrant incense together with an offering of prayer. But it is not enough to contend with an almost uncertain author and, by substituting opposites for opposites, to temper the air infected by the pestilential breath, unless the serpents themselves are dragged into the open [Col. 1175D] and crushed. For when, merely to protect the head, they expose the rest of the body to mutilation and injury, thinking there is no harm so long as that part alone is freed from danger which contains within itself many poisonous tongues—even if all the limbs are cut off—it seems sufficient for us at least to temper and remedy the stench, but not to remove them from their innermost recesses, as though there could be any end to the foul exhalation unless its author were brought to an end. And amid these matters Solomon’s testimony now comes to mind: “One builds, another destroys; what profit do they have except labor?” [Ecclesiasticus 34:28; Col. 1176A].

There stands also the most savage Goliath, swollen with pride and bloated with carnal power, confident that he can accomplish everything by himself: his head, hands, and entire body clothed in an immense array, with his armor-bearer behind him. Although he himself does not fight, he nevertheless supplies every support of bronze and iron. Nor is it surprising that Scripture, foreseeing this situation appropriately, declares: “The Philistines stood upon the mountain on this side” (1 Samuel 17:3). For the opponent of heresy is expelled from the Church, while the heretic is found being nourished in the Church’s bosom; and therefore the Holy Spirit declares Israel to stand on one side, and the enemy on the other. This has often happened. For even King David, a pious father toward his impious son, is driven from Jerusalem after laying aside the royal attire, and immediately afterward the tyrant Absalom enters [Col. 1176B]. Thus Goliath stands, alas, on this side—that is, in the Church—and not only stands, but also challenges; and for many days he reproaches holy Israel with its evident fear.

3. Lest, I beg you, most blessed priests, anyone should think that under the guise of Goliath I am claiming glory in David’s name, you wished me to share in your contest, so that I might join you as an assistant, not as its author. I was hiding in Bethlehem, unknown, an outsider, and poor. Why do I, wretched man, speak in this way? Perhaps I shall again be marked for boasting, since David himself was such a man and came from there.

I was therefore hiding in Bethlehem, entrusted by my father Augustine with learning the fear of the Lord, sitting at Jerome’s feet. From there, summoned by you to Jerusalem, I came. Then, at the command of Bishop John, I sat down together with you in your assembly. Immediately you all asked my humble self that, if I knew anything about what had taken place in Africa concerning this heresy which Pelagius and Coelestius had sown, I should report it faithfully and plainly.

I briefly explained to your assembly, as best I could, that Coelestius, who had already insinuated himself toward the honor of the presbyterate, had been exposed, heard, convicted, confessed, and condemned by the Church at Carthage in the judgment of many bishops, and had fled from Africa; but that, concerning Pelagius’s book, blessed Augustine had given a most complete reply at the request and disclosure of Pelagius’s own disciples. I also had in my hands a letter of the aforesaid bishop, which he had recently composed for Sicily and in which he reported many questions raised by the heretics [Col. 1176C]. You ordered me to read it there, and I read it. At this, Bishop John requested that Pelagius be brought in before us. Out of reverence for his paternal authority, and because you thought it useful for the proceedings that Pelagius should be refuted more effectively by the bishop in person, permission was granted for him to be admitted.

4. Once Pelagius had been admitted, you all unanimously asked him: “Did you acknowledge that you had taught these doctrines to which Bishop Augustine had replied?”

He immediately answered: “And who is Augustine to me?”

When everyone shouted that a man who blasphemed against the bishop—from whose mouth the Lord had granted healing to the unity of all Africa—should be expelled not only from that assembly but from the entire Church, Bishop John immediately ordered him, plainly a layman, to sit openly among the presbyters as one accused of heresy in the midst of Catholics. Then he said: “I am Augustine,” assuming, as it were, the person of the man who was present, so that, through the authority of the one who had been injured, he might pardon more freely and calm the hearts of those who were grieving.

We then said to him: “If you assume Augustine’s person, follow Augustine’s judgment.”

Then that same bishop said to all of us: “Were the things now being read spoken against others, or do you think that Pelagius should be addressed concerning them? If, however, you have something to say against Pelagius himself, bring it forth.”

With your approval I said: “Pelagius told me that he teaches that a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes.”

Pelagius replied, in your hearing: “I cannot deny that I both said this and say it.”

I immediately continued: “The African synod condemned this in Coelestius; Bishop Augustine, as you have heard, rejected it in his writings; he now condemns it in Pelagius’s own writings in his reply; and blessed Jerome has also condemned it—Jerome whose eloquence the whole West awaits like dew upon a fleece. For many heretics have already been overthrown together with their doctrines by his opposition, and he condemned this in his letter which he recently published to Ctesiphon. Likewise, in the book which he is now writing, he refutes it by setting out the dispute in the form of a dialogue.”

[Note: [Col. 1177D] He is speaking of the Dialogue which he wrote against the Pelagians.]

“For this is the slippery task: to hold the dragon in the Antichrist, so that he cannot escape” [Col. 1177C].

5. Bishop John, however, hearing none of these things, tried to compel us to acknowledge that we were his accusers while he was the judge. Everyone answered repeatedly: “We are not this man’s accusers; rather, we are informing you what your brothers and our fathers thought and decreed concerning this heresy, which a layman is now publicly preaching, lest—especially without your knowledge—it disturb your Church, to whose bosom we have fled.”

But when he repeatedly tried, under the pretext of teaching us, to lead us toward some form of confession, he said that the Lord had said to Abraham, “Walk before me and be without blemish” (Genesis 17:1), and that Zechariah and Elizabeth had both been declared righteous before the Lord, walking in all the Lord’s commandments without reproach (Luke 1:6) [Col. 1177D]. Several of us knew that he was producing something said by Origen.

I answered him: “We are sons of the Catholic Church. Do not require us, father, to dare to be teachers over teachers or judges over judges. The fathers whom the universal Church throughout the world approves, whose communion you are glad that we embrace, have decreed that these doctrines are damnable. Since they approve this judgment, it is right for us to obey them. Why do you ask the sons what they think, when you hear what the fathers decree? [Col. 1178A]”

6. But while he debated for a long time, and while, because of the incompetence of the interpreter unknown to us—whom the distinguished and religious men, the presbyters Posserius and Avitus, and Dominus ex Duce, repeatedly refuted for interpreting badly, suppressing much, or suggesting one thing from another—our proceedings, as I said, were usually either altered or passed over in silence, Bishop John said: “If he were to say that a human being could do this without God’s help, it would be a very evil and condemnable statement. But now, since he adds that a human being can be without sin, not without God’s help, what do you say? Or do you perhaps deny God’s help?”

I replied: “With those men whom I have mentioned above, who are even now witnesses and bear testimony, anathema to the one who denies God’s help. Certainly I do not deny it, especially since I have refuted the heretics on the contrary point.”

Then, when we had understood the judge and exposed the interpreter, we cried out: “He is a Latin heretic, we are Latins, and this is a heresy more familiar to Latins; it ought to be discussed by Latin judges, and it is almost shameless for him to adjudicate it himself.” Since we were not his accusers, and since I alone was being thrust forward as a suspect, many found it necessary to say: “No one can be at once a heretic, an advocate, and a judge.”

After many other proceedings, Bishop John delivered his final judgment. At last he confirmed our request and intention: brothers and letters should be sent to blessed Innocent, the Roman pope, and everyone would follow whatever he decreed. But Pelagius, as a heretic, was to remain silent under an imposed prohibition, and our men were to refrain from insulting and humiliating the convicted John. We all agreed to this judgment. After giving thanks, making peace, and completing a prayer as a testimony to the peace, we departed [Col. 1178C].

7. But now, after forty-seven days, when on the first day of the Encaenia I had hurried, as I was accustomed to do when I was present, to attend upon Bishop John, I immediately received from him, in place of a greeting, the mark of a false accusation. For he said to me: “Why are you coming to me, you who have blasphemed?”

He wished, I believe, to be understood as saying: “Do not touch me, because I am clean and without sin” (Isaiah 65:5).

[Note: [Col. 1178D] Gallandius corrects the text to *nae credo* (“I suppose indeed”).]

But, conscious of nothing against myself, I asked: “When, or in whose hearing, or what sort of statement was made that could be attributed to blasphemy?”

The bishop replied: “I heard you say that even with God’s help a human being cannot be without sin.”

Most blessed priests, as you yourselves, the whole brotherhood, and the holy men who stand beside this testimony out of love for truth are witnesses, I immediately testified, saying: “Such a statement as the bishop now intends to attribute to me had never previously proceeded from my mouth”—although, by repeatedly rehearsing this wretched falsehood in frequent explanation, I seem not so much to have vindicated myself as to have exposed another [Col. 1179A].

I grant, then, that I said whatever that statement was. How, however, did a Greek ignorant of Latin hear it? Or, if he heard a sacrilegious statement, why did he not immediately convict the blasphemer, or, to act more mildly, why did not a pious father admonish an unwary son to restrain the license of dangerous speech? Instead, after a very long lapse of time, he himself brought the accusation, he himself gave the testimony, and he himself pronounced the judgment, assuming in his own person the offices of every crime—especially though he was instructed by the Gospel reading that our Lord Jesus was not condemned without the testimony of a ruler.

On one side my brothers stood beside me; on the other, false brothers. Then, in the same assembly, the presbyters Avitus and Vitalis sat on one side with me; on the other was some unknown interpreter; and then there were the men approved both by the world and by God, the presbyter Passerius and Dominus ex Duce. At the request of Bishop John himself, they had been summoned and brought from your assembly so that, on account of their experience and faith, they might serve as interpreters. He himself too was among you: in that circumstance it is no less astonishing that he heard than that he saw how such a great statement could pass by hostile colleagues and hearers and enter the unaware ears of an informed listener.

8. But I am driven on by the heat of truth, and I am pressing the matter beyond the proper bounds of my position. It is preferable to grant that the interpreter made a mistake in speaking than to suppose that the bishop fabricated the matter in hearing it—and that now, in order to exact the return for the favor he showed the heretics, he is seeking false witnesses to support him. No one should now be surprised that false witnesses were sought out and found in Jerusalem by priests and elders [Note: [Col. 1179D; 1180D] Gallandius likewise prefers *conquiri* (“to be sought out”) to the manuscript reading *conqueri*.]: the blood of Stephen cries this out; the standards of the Lord’s cross signify it; and the persecution now stirred up by them also demonstrates it.

Whether these things appear to have been rashly believed by the bishop, maliciously fabricated, or ignorantly misunderstood, I entrust to Christ the judge to examine. Far be it from me ever, a poor, sinful, unknown man, to dare to appeal from a bishop, and especially from the bishop of Jerusalem, to other bishops. My simplicity and vindication before the most eminent Trinity, the omnipotent God, and all his Catholic servants are enough for me [Col. 1179D].

Most blessed priests, with you writing these same things and bearing witness together with me, I call God as witness over my soul: in that assembly of yours I uttered no blasphemy with my mouth, nor did I say the sort of words which Bishop John has brought against me—namely, “that even with God’s help a human being cannot be without sin.”

I also wish to satisfy the contention of those who are unaware of the matter, lest perhaps, although you did not hear it from me, you should think that I did say it and thus labor under an ambiguous testimony. I wish also to satisfy common rumor, lest, while people do not believe that a bishop can lie, they should suppose that an innocent man sinned through some other credulity. And who does not know the authors of such accusations, whether in the case of Susanna or in the stoning of Naboth? [Col. 1180A]

[Note: [Col. 1179D] Gallandius prefers *tantos* (“so great”) here.]

9. And lest anyone perhaps be unaware that Jerusalem has never lacked either the support of silver or the lashes of soldiers for the shedding of Christian blood, now that I think myself free from this statement, free by your faith and free by my conscience, I shall try, after examining the ambiguity of the very words, to inquire how those who assert that we answered in this way appear themselves to have asked the question. Perhaps, by the form of their question, the secret of their doctrine will be exposed, so that, by striking them with reciprocal wounds, the arrows they have shot may more surely punish their sender [Col. 1180B].

For they say that our answer was: “Even with God’s help, a human being cannot be without sin.” If anyone should think that this must be understood in such a way that it affirms, under the weakness of human beings, that God cannot do it, and suspects something impossible for God’s omnipotence in any creature of heaven, earth, or the underworld, I would call such a person not merely blasphemous by my judgment, but anathema, to be detested—indeed, either to be condemned by divine fire after the example of Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10), or, like Dathan and Abiram in their destruction (Deuteronomy 11), to be swallowed alive by the opening of the earth and plunged into hell.

Both groups, in the presumption of their hearts, detracted from God’s power: the former by offering strange fire, as though God needed it; the latter by resisting Moses and distrusting that they could be brought into the promised land. God can do everything, and he can always do whatever he wills. As powerful as he is in making from nothing, so easily does he perfect what has been made. For the power to do so lies with him whenever he wills (Wisdom 12).

This is confessed by grace granted according to the Spirit; this is attested by the law written according to the letter; this is understood by the natural law throughout the universe; this is displayed by the ordered movement of the world. For what pagan would dare to say this, when the distinct elements of heaven, earth, and sea are always before his eyes? What Jew could suspect it, however little knowledge of the law delivered through Moses has reached him, when he both reads and believes that the depths lay bare when the waves of the Red Sea were split apart, and that the sea provided a safe path on dry land for those who walked upon it (Exodus 14:18); and that the Jordan, divided, flowed backward toward its source with its waters turned back (Joshua 3) [Col. 1180D]; or that Elijah, a mortal in the body, was carried up by the fire of a fiery chariot without being harmed (2 Kings 2); or that Habakkuk, laden with prepared food, was transported immediately from Judea to Babylon and brought back at once, in order to serve a meal to the righteous man fasting among hungry beasts—as the common edition relates (Daniel 14)? [Alternative reading: “to serve a meal, during the fast, to the righteous man among hungry beasts.”]

What Christian would admit this into his heart, even into an atom of thought—one who knows that Lazarus, dead for four days, his limbs already stinking and liquid flowing within his loosened skin, sprang forth to the Lord’s devoted service (John 11); who has read that the man blind from birth, now advanced in age, suddenly became vigorous through the restoration of his sight (John 9); who has witnessed that winds, waves, storms, and the elements contending with one another were simultaneously calmed when they heard the Lord’s rebuking command (Matthew 8); who believes that Peter, weighed down by the burden of the flesh and about to deny the Lord three times in succession, walked upon the swollen waves with feet suspended above them (Matthew 14)?

10. I therefore think that all human beings—whether endowed with outstanding faith and wisdom or otherwise—venerate, believe, and confess that God can do everything. For he is universally called omnipotent by the whole creation because he can do everything [Col. 1181B]. And he alone is God who says: “These things are impossible with human beings” (Luke 18:27). Elsewhere he teaches, saying: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Therefore he can do everything in a human being, since he himself can do everything.

But why does earth and ashes grow proud enough to say, “A human being can,” when God can? The Apostle cries out: “By his grace I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain, but I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

What do you see, heedless presumer, in the fact that he said “with me”? Pay attention to the fact that he first said “not I.” Therefore, between these two words—“not I” and “with me”—stands the grace of God, whose gift it truly is both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13), and yet through the human will [Col. 1181C].

Thus the human conscience confesses when it says “not I”; the grace of God grants the “with me.” The Apostle cries out: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10). For he remembered the Lord’s preaching: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John 6:44). And again elsewhere: “I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

And in another place, speaking of the Holy Spirit, he says: “It is expedient for you that I go away; for if I do not go away, that Comforter will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7).

11. Unhappy man, according to the truth of God’s judgment! The Father draws you, the Son is with you, and the Spirit comforts you; yet amid such a great surrounding presence of divine majesty you dare to say: “With the grace of God helping me, I am what I am by my own ability”?

For now, after this amendment joined to your ancient error, you assert: “A human being can be without sin with God’s help.” Yet in your book, which you entitled by the name of *Testimonies*, this same judgment is written in these words: “A human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes.” No grace of God, no help, is named there. Although you frequently speak about God’s grace, you say that I did not deny it because I did not mention it; rather, I should be understood to have asserted it because I did not deny it.

As though Susanna should be believed to have confessed adultery merely because she did not deny it when others accused her, or as though the Lord Jesus approved the testimony of false witnesses because he remained silent. If, among you, not denying is the same as asserting, and remaining silent is the same as shouting, David’s prayer is useless: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door around my lips” (Psalm 140:3). And it is useless for me to confirm, by witnesses and testimony, that I did not say what I am accused of saying, if another person could hear what my speech did not say.

But I grant that you think something never said should be accepted as though it had been said. What shall we do, then, with the fact that, when we examine the meaning, we find a difference in the wording, and that discordant connections do not cohere, since the very page itself does not admit words that contradict one another? You write: “A human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes.” And, as blessed Father Jerome explained this same statement in the letter he is writing to Ctesiphon [Col. 1182B], at the end, as though awakening from a very deep sleep, you add: “Not without God’s help?”

For in this the truth itself opposes and protests against you. Why, through disdainful swelling and nauseated shame, do you keep the help of God—unnecessary to you, as you judge everything easy—from your mouth? “With your lips you honor me, but your heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13). In an action, two agents are not needed for what is easy for one; and the grace of divinity inserts itself in vain where a human being admits that he can easily accomplish something alone, if he wishes.

You said that the commandments are easy for one who wishes; but I also assert that even what is difficult can be fulfilled. Yet however you promise that a human being can accomplish this, you accuse the Lord of envy, since, by adding his help, he supposedly tries to claim for himself what a human being could have fulfilled alone through the will.

Either take away from the human being the claim “if he wishes,” and attribute to grace the fact that he can; or, since you grant that a human being can when he wishes, remove your feigned, flattering, and incoherent participation of grace, and openly confess the blasphemy that proceeds from the abundance of your heart [Col. 1182C].

12. But it is not my task to investigate these matters at greater length, especially since the most blessed fathers Augustine and Jerome have supplied the western provinces with the fullest proof of the heresy already convicted. Let me return to the question proposed above, to which I approached not because confidence in my ability had stirred me up, but because injury had moved me [Col. 1182D].

You say that in this age a human being can be without sin with God’s help. You say, “A human being can”; I say, “God can.”

The three boys in the furnace were not harmed by the flame blazing within it (Daniel 3). Which of them could do what happened contrary to nature—the boys themselves, or the fourth in their midst, who was like the Son of God?

The leper cries out: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me” (Matthew 8:2), making his will manifest through his ability and confirming his ability through his will. For he alone is the one in whom willing and being able coincide whenever he wills.

The blind came to him to be illumined, praying, and Jesus said to them: “Do you believe that I can do this?” (Matthew 9:28). The Lord Christ judges it worthy of the highest reward of faith if anyone believes that the Son of God can do these things, while our Britannicus, as soon as he wills, is confident that he can do them himself [Col. 1183A].

To the faithful paralytic the Lord says: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven” (Matthew 9:20). And now this new teacher and minister of tables has dared to presume forgiveness of sins more from his own ability, and does not wait to hear it from the Lord?

The scribes, not understanding the truth, murmur and say: “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” (Mark 2:7). But this man judges sins to have been abolished even though he does not know that God has forgiven them.

13. Behold, inflated by the spirit of your flesh, as though it were above nothing, proud in your free will, you boast and say: “I am a sinner because I wish to be; I sin while I wish to sin; but when I wish again, I can be without sin.”

What you say—“I sin when I wish”—is true, because even what you have not done in deed, you have done in thought. Again, “when I wish, I do not sin” is indeed difficult and hard, and is not entirely within one’s power, but nevertheless it is not doubtful that it can sometimes happen. But for one who has sinned at some time to be without sin is impossible without the sole grace of baptism, where it is said in the person of the Lord: “Your sins are forgiven you.” I am persuaded to believe this because I am permitted to hear it.

Therefore I do not accept, do not presume, and do not hear the claim that I can be without sin in this corruption in which we live. For if David prays to the Lord: “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you” (Psalm 51:6); and if, according to the Apocalypse of John, the dead are to be judged from the things they sinned before God, from the things written in the books, receiving according to their works (Revelation 20:12), why should I presume to judge myself, if I know that I shall be judged even concerning that very judgment?

Or, if those sacred books are opened only at the judgment and contain equally the good and evil deeds of our life, to provide the examination of judgment on the scales, how do we know, without examination, in this life and before death, that those things have been abolished which we read will be brought forth not only after death but even after the resurrection?

I had power to sin; I do not have power to free myself from sin. It is mine to pray; it is not mine to be absolved. Once I have given myself to sin, I have become the slave of the accuser and the defendant of the judge. Because of the support furnished by my constant prayers, I may have hope in the good judge; but I cannot, without fear for my conscience, vindicate myself as innocent before the sentence is pronounced.

For the Apostle says: “Do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then each one will receive praise from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5). Otherwise, if it lies within human power to make oneself free from one’s own sin, either Christ is not a judge, or he is one in vain [Col. 1183D].

14. But you say: “I spoke of a human being without sin in this sense: when a sinner groans, then he will be saved—that is, then he will begin to belong to salvation; nevertheless, he will not immediately be without sin.”

For when the Lord entered the house of the believing Zacchaeus, he said: “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9). Surely, if one person believed, did the entire household immediately become without sin, when the beginning of salvation entered the house through its believing head? [Col. 1184A]

[Note: [Col. 1183] Schott reads *majore* (“greater”), and perhaps then *credente* (“believing”). Gallandius.]

For David also groaned after he had sinned. And although he deserved to hear that his offense had been forgiven, he nevertheless later atoned for it through exile and very great disgrace, so that it might plainly appear both that punishment was paid in the present and that forgiveness was to be granted in the future. In this way God granted great mercy to the sinner who groaned, purifying through temporary correction the sin that deserved death.

Ananias is told concerning Paul, who was making his complaint about the persecution with fear: “I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts 9:16). Thus, when Paul was released there where he had bound Christ through persecution, he soon became troubled unto death by suffering for Christ and was glorified in the resurrection [Col. 1184B].

This happens because “mercy and truth always go before the face of God” (Psalm 89:15): if, in the present time, a voluntary sacrifice is offered by one who groans, so that truth may be realized in mercy—a spirit afflicted and a heart contrite—then at the end mercy will be preferred to judgment.

15. The Lord Christ is both believed and hoped to come in the glory of God the Father, to judge the living and the dead. At his appearance, as Scripture testifies, heaven and earth will flee (Revelation 20:11). Yet there are people who, whether through ignorance—to say nothing of conscience—do not judge themselves subject to the coming judgment, and who do not tremble at the Lord’s arrival and the illumination of his radiance, when the elements burn and the world perishes (2 Peter 3:10).

I fear that they will be among those of whom the Lord gives warning: “For many will say on that day” (namely, people speaking from that carnal arrogance by which they deceived others, and who were righteous not so much before God as still in their own eyes): “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name perform mighty works?” And then I shall declare to them and say: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7:22–23) [Col. 1184C].

The prophet David is said, in the person of Christ: “Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle, or who will rest upon your holy mountain? The one who walks without blemish and practices righteousness” (Psalm 15:1–2). This truly means: the one who can be, and is, without sin.

For the Lord himself says of himself: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he found nothing belonging to me” (John 14:30). For what does the devil have? Without doubt, sin. “From the beginning the devil is a liar” (1 John 3:8; John 8:44), whereas my Lord is the one who speaks truth in his heart and has not acted deceitfully with his tongue (Psalm 15:3).

A great and powerful angel, as Scripture testifies, cries out in heaven: “Who is worthy to open the book and loose its seals?” No one was able—in heaven, on earth, or under the earth—to open the book or to look upon it (Revelation 5:2–3). John weeps and mourns greatly because no one was found worthy among all rational creatures to open the book and look upon it.

One of the elders consoles the weeping John and says: “Do not weep, John. Behold, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, to open the book and loose its seals” (Revelation 5:5).

Who, I ask, is this book, which no one was worthy to receive from the hand of the One who lives forever except the one who walks without blemish and practices righteousness (Psalm 15:2)? It is not enough that he be without blemish; it is not enough that he be a lamb, unless he was also slain, unless he crowned the purity of his life with the testimony of his passion, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God (Revelation 5:6)—namely, without doubt, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isaiah 11:2–3).

What, then, is this book? As I believe, it is the book of judgment. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22) [Col. 1185B].

16. Alas! I am forced to say what I dreaded even to think. Behold, Pelagius too, who has dared to profess himself without blemish and without sin, consequently considers himself worthy to receive the book and the judgment. It is the next step for him to say to himself: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again,” and to prepare himself to be a companion on Christ’s throne.

Wretched man! He does not instead understand that he is preparing himself as a forerunner for the coming of Antichrist, who, when he has been revealed, “exalts himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped” (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4), in keeping with this man who already sets himself alongside the only-begotten Son of God.

The Lamb of God, the Son of God, in order to receive the book from the Father’s hand, displays the marks of his passion; he does not declare the victory accomplished except in death and resurrection. Yet my *anamartētos* (ἀναμάρτητος), my “sinless” man, claims that perfection of an immaculate life is possible for him while eating, drinking, and sleeping [Col. 1185C].

Our Lord Jesus, after a forty-day fast, was tempted three times by the devil and overcame him three times; the devil withdrew from him—not forever, but “for a time” (Luke 4:13), to return more fiercely, through the Apostle’s denial, even unto the death of the cross. Yet our *apathēs* (ἀπαθὴς), our “passionless” man, confidently maintains that, once the temptations have been defeated—as he thinks—together with their author, he can no longer be tempted or disturbed.

That perfect Lamb, the one who not only has no sin but also takes away the sin of the world, and who has seven horns upon his head, was not sufficient to repel the tempter so completely that he would not return. Yet this mutilated man of ours, smooth upon the forehead, *monophthalmos* (μονόφθαλμος), “one-eyed,” does not think that he needs protection upon his head, since he presumes such ability in the flesh [Col. 1185D].

Wretched man, who, according to the Gospel (John 15:22, 24), might perhaps have no sin if he were blind! But perhaps, because the seven eyes are the seven spirits, he boasts that he abounds in all of them and that, as though the sevenfold powers of grace had been heaped together within him, his inner person flourishes in their virtues—especially since he boasts of as many titles for his doctrines.

Thus it may be that in his own judgment he considers himself filled with the spirit of wisdom, especially because he says that God’s commandments are easy; amply endowed with the spirit of understanding, because he foreknows and proclaims that all sinners together with the ungodly are condemned to eternal fire; rich in the spirit of counsel, because he advises that evil should not even be thought; powerful in the spirit of might, because he affirms that a human being can be without sin; inflated with the spirit of knowledge, because he hopes that no one can be without sin unless he has knowledge of the law; and abounding in the spirit of piety, because he teaches that an enemy is to be loved as a friend, forgetting that he himself said: “An enemy must not be trusted in any way.”

How can he be adorned with the spirit of the fear of God, when, after much drunkenness, he finally awoke and added: “A human being can be without sin, not without God’s help”? And by these steps of presumption, as I think, he does not fear ascending until he is so exalted that he says that, in the likeness of Christ, filled with perfect power, the Holy Spirit descended wholly upon him and remained with him.

Yet this was given by God the Father to Christ alone, to whom he also gave “the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9), who alone is without sin and walks without blemish, and with whom the very anointing of holiness remains.

But we run in the fragrance of his ointments, and meanwhile, as the Lord goes before us, we catch sweet breaths of life from the wafting of the life-giving breeze over us (Song of Songs 1:3) [Col. 1186B].

### 17

But you say: “Why do you assail me with such grave insult? Why do you load me with envy in such arrogant words? Would I dare compare myself, a servant, with my Lord? Would I, earth and ashes, compare myself with the Word of God? Should I, subject to death, be called the equal of the conqueror of death?”

Indeed, O condemned wickedness, by giving testimony to God you humble yourself in words; but your meaning speaks otherwise among the pagans. You say, “A human being can be without sin.” Again and repeatedly I say: the human being who can do this is Christ. Either claim the name, or lay aside your confidence. God granted this to one alone, and that only to the firstborn among many brothers (Rom. VIII, 9). This is how it is handed down in the catholic faith; this is what we hold.

Certainly, our Lord warned the unbelievers: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me. Another will come in his own name; perhaps you will receive him” (John V, 43). Either, as sinners, follow with us the one whom we believe to be without sin, the same only-begotten Son, or, if you are that other one, acknowledge it.

He is the Lord Jesus who, after conquering death and triumphing over the devil, ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to human beings (Ps. LXVII, 19). “From his fullness we have all received” (John I, 16), as the Apostle teaches: “To each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. IV, 7). And to the Romans the same teacher of the nations writes: “For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment. And to each one according as God has allotted the measure of faith” (Rom. XII, 3).

Then to the Corinthians he proclaims: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of workings, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of ministries” (1 Cor. XII, 4–6)—of graces and virtues. He adds: “But all these things one and the same Spirit brings about, distributing to each one as he wills” (ibid. 11).

Then, by comparing the members of the human body, he makes clear that the body of the Church’s unity, through its differing modes of activity, comes together in a single harmony of perfection. He proves that there is absolutely no member that does not need the help and articulation of another, with the Lord himself established as the head, in whom “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. II, 3).

Therefore he also gave us understanding, through which we might know “that the Word is in Christ Jesus” (1 John V, 20), in whom “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II, 9). The Holy Spirit descended upon him and remained in him, according to John’s testimony (John I, 32), and thereby declared him to be the Lord.

Therefore, if no one possesses anything except because he asks it from you (Matt. V, 42), and no one receives anything except according to the division and measure allotted to him, and whoever has received something needs another’s help in preserving it, by what madness, I ask, does one who is insufficient in his individuality promise himself something from the fullness?

The Evangelist testifies concerning the Lord: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I, 9). But the Lord says to his apostles: “You are the light of this world” (Matt. V, 14). There, in the Lord alone, the whole light is present, because it is true; here, in all the apostles, there is indeed light, but light derived from the one who is wholly light.

And since this is so in the apostles, in whose election the whole body of the Church was included, what can we—yes, we individually—be seen as after them except, in the words of the apostle Peter, ignorant people who believe only through faith in the evangelical and prophetic message, “like a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. I, 19)?

> [Note: [Col. 1187D] Gallandius, inserting *Qua*, adds in a footnote: “Thus Schott’s edition correctly. Havercamp has it incorrectly as *Quum*.”]

When we have been enlightened, we too are persuaded that “lamps prepared in good works” should be burning in our hands (Luke XII, 35). These lamps, exhausted by manifold temptations, are always endangered both by their own weakness and by the blow inflicted by another.

Therefore the Lord also says in the Gospel: “And if the light that is in us is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?” (Matt. VI, 23).

### 18

But I grant that this light, however small it may be, remains with unfailing strength until the end—that is, that he does not lose the gift he has received as a special grace. Otherwise the fullness of light is present throughout and no darkness remains. By “darkness,” I mean the ignorance arising from the filth of sin.

What if it is a reasonable principle that, to the extent that light is lacking, to that same extent darkness remains? Moreover, it is extremely difficult for darkness not to contain some stumbling block. A human being established in a certain measure of light and in the remnants of darkness, desiring the good but not fleeing evil, must both have assistance available and not be without sin.

If this seems obscurely stated to anyone, let him take an example from human conduct. Two individuals possess different gifts: one has the gift of being humble in silence, the other of being persuasive in teaching. The one who cherishes silence—if he is perhaps asked to give an account of his faith—do you suppose that he assumes no deception in his humility?

Or do you readily suppose that a simple person is free from buffoonery; cheerful in speech, cautious in anger, patient in negligence, gentle in laziness, learned without boastfulness, submissive without envy, and free from that general darkness of all good works, the desire for empty glory?

If this is understood piously and reverently, let each one of us apply the comparison to himself, so that he condemns himself more in preferring what is better than justifies himself by despising what is lesser. Thus, at last, he will join the members together with one another, especially if, with a single love surrounding the bones like skin and with the sinews joined together through their mutual need, a person understands that the grace he possesses is a gift, not a merit. Let him glory in the Lord more for the source from which he received it than grow angry over what he did not receive.

For when we were by nature children of wrath because of our transgression, we became [Note: [Col. 1187D] Schottus, followed by Gallandius, adds the word *children*] children of mercy through the Lord’s clemency, deserving nothing except condemnation (Eph. II, 3–4).

Let us not press a complaint upon the Lord concerning what we have not received; rather, let us repay him with thanks for what we have received, and attribute glory to him alone, our Creator and Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ. God appointed him as an expiation through his blood (Rom. III, 25), so that at his name every knee might bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. II, 10). Every flesh will see him judging in that foretold power, and every tongue will confess to him.

Therefore the Apostle also says: “For this reason we strive, whether absent or present, to please him. For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. V, 9–10). And elsewhere: “For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God” (Rom. XIV, 10).

The apostle Paul also said that he would stand before the tribunal of God and, together with the others, render an account of what he had done through the body. Yet Pelagius confidently dares to say: “Thus I complete the whole of perfection in the flesh, so that I expect nothing from the judge’s goodness.”

On that day, the righteous, hearing the praises of their works from the Judge, will nevertheless ask as though unaware: “Lord, when did we see you and do these things for you?” (Matt. XXV, 37). Yet this man, our great expert in the law, recognizes the day, hour, and moment when he will enter the final dwelling beyond which there is no other, the dwelling of complete holiness.

### 19

Or perhaps he protests and says: “It would rightly be called madness—or, not to say, pride—if these reproaches were brought against me when I said that a human being could be without sin without God’s assistance. But now that I add assistance, I assert nothing difficult. Do you perhaps deny God’s assistance?”

For a little while I grant your slander, so that, while what I wish to convict you of may appear to be exposed in me, we may both be found together: I more thoroughly purified in my defense, and you more clearly exposed in your confusion.

This has always been my faithful and certain conviction: God supplies his assistance not only to his own body, which is the Church, to which he generously grants the special gifts of his grace because of the believers’ faith, but also to all the nations throughout this world, because of his long-suffering and eternal clemency.

He does not supply it, as you assert with your disciple Coelestius—whose hidden nature of impious doctrines has already been crushed before the African council—only in natural goodness and in free choice, as though one general grace had been bestowed upon all alike. Rather, he supplies it specifically, day by day, through times, days, moments, and **ἄτομας**—indivisible instants—to all and to each individually.

For Scripture says: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matt. V, 45). But perhaps you reply: “The well-ordered nature preserves its own order, and therefore God, once the elemental courses have been established, produces from them whatever he produces.”

What, then, do you think of the part of the sentence that follows: “He gives rain upon the just and the unjust” (ibid.)? Certainly, the one who gives, gives when he wishes and where he wishes—either administering an established arrangement or pouring out his own generosity.

And lest, in accordance with the madness of your impiety, you attempt to empty even this of meaning, hear the prophet testifying to this truth: “He summons the waters of the sea and pours them out over the face of the earth; the Lord is his name” (Amos V, 8).

What shall I say about the true hope of the human race, since “everyone who plows, plows in hope” (1 Cor. IX, 10)? To hope, however, is not a matter of one’s own ability but of another’s generosity. When someone has sown and the cultivator has hidden the scattered seed in the earth’s bosom, he has nothing more to do except raise his eyes to heaven and pray—not to the earth to which he entrusted it, but to the God in whom he has believed—that he may enrich his labor with either morning or evening rain.

And, to make use even of spiritual testimony for ordinary matters, “neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. III, 7).

Measure how much I rejoice in God’s assistance by the fact that I prove it to be supplied individually even to the nations, so that it might be clear to us whom we ought to avoid until the end and whom we ought to invoke without ceasing.

### 20

The devil is questioned by the Lord: “From where have you come?” He replied: “Going around the earth and traversing what is beneath heaven, I am here” (Job I, 7).

I ask you: is this concern of the devil a good will or an evil one? You must admit that it is entirely evil. The complaint that follows also demonstrates this.

This manifestation of the devil occurred in Job’s time, that is, in the time of Moses. Certainly, at that time there was no Judea, no Jerusalem, and no Church throughout the world. As yet the whole Gentile world had no knowledge of God; nevertheless, the devil was already going around the earth and traversing everything beneath heaven. He was driven by the restless concern of his own malice to deceive and scatter the human race.

Therefore, when you see such great wickedness of the devil pressing upon ignorant human beings for their destruction, do you believe that God’s grace for their protection played no part in this? Or perhaps you think it was said in vain: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. XXIII, 1)?

But to prove more clearly that God’s assistance is present and operates through individuals, behold: while the devil testifies concerning the whole, he is questioned about one person. God says: “Have you noticed my servant Job, that there is no one like him on earth?” (Job I, 8).

The Lord knows each individual specifically, and the devil knows each one as well: the Lord by the power of nature, the devil through the labor of wickedness; the devil in order to tempt, the Lord in order to test.

Job is praised by the Creator while his adversary objects. The Lord wishes to judge the work of the human being, which he himself works within him; but even the devil confesses concerning assistance. For he says: “Have you not fenced around what is outside his house and what is inside his house?” (ibid. 10).

At the enemy’s request, God strips his servant through temptation but does not leave him naked: he takes away his possessions and gives grace. “Behold,” he says, “everything that he has I give into your hand; only do not touch him himself” (ibid. 12).

That is not enough. The envious one rages and tries to inflict death; but, on the contrary, by God’s dispensation he is restrained, and grace is not taken away. The prey requested by the plunderer is brought forth, [Note: [Col. 1189D] Perhaps the reading is *promitur* or *permittitur*, unless one prefers *premitur*. Gallandius says that *promitur* must certainly be read, following Schott’s edition; immediately afterward, before *rursus*, he adds the conjunction *et*, which Schottus also printed.] and once again a guardian is assigned to guard his prey.

For it is said to him: “Behold, I deliver him to you; only preserve his life” (Job II, 6). Let no one therefore conclude from this that the devil labors merely to seduce the soul while it is in the body, unless he also seeks to tear it away from the body. If the merciful God’s protection did not fortify the wounded and weakened human being and continually confront every assault of the devil’s plots, this would indeed be possible.

### 21

You have, I think, sufficient proof among the Gentiles of cooperating grace. Receive also a clear indication concerning that particular gift which he generously bestows upon the Church and his own body.

The apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians: “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you were enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you, so that you lack nothing in any grace” (1 Cor. I, 4–7).

And again: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand and boast” (Rom. V, 1–2).

Therefore the apostle Peter also admonishes us, saying: “Receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls. Concerning this salvation the prophets searched and examined carefully, who prophesied about the grace of God destined for us” (1 Pet. I, 9–10).

From this it has been demonstrated most clearly that God’s assistance is lacking to no human being, especially since both the deceiver presses upon us and weakness is present within us. The slander of the blind accuser who says, “Perhaps you deny God’s assistance?” has been confused and overturned.

But since we have mentioned Job, let us say what was also recorded in the preceding testimony, when the Lord said: “A blameless man, a true worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil” (Job II, 3).

You frequently assert that a human being can be without sin, proving it by saying that such a person existed—namely, that Job was called by God’s testimony a blameless and true man, and that Zechariah is also shown in the Gospel to have been without complaint.

The Lord said of Job, “A blameless man” (Luke I, 6). Did he say, “without sin”? Sin is conceived in thought, whereas a crime is manifested only in an act.

Being without complaint is also attributed to the knowledge and judgment of those who are able readily to observe gentleness in the face but do not know the battles of the heart. Therefore Paul confidently commands, saying: “The bishop must be blameless” (Tit. I, 6).

And elsewhere he gives a general testimony concerning the Corinthians and asserts: “So that you lack no grace, awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will also confirm you to the end, blameless” (1 Cor. I, 7–8).

Behold: Paul confirms by his testimony that they will be blameless to the end, yet immediately afterward, in the same letter, he rebukes them, writing: “It is altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another” (1 Cor. VI, 7).

Under one heading and concerning the same persons there is both “blameless” and “fault.” Thus he shows that someone is not immediately asserted to be without fault merely because he is called blameless.

For the Lord Jesus also said: “John came neither eating nor drinking” (Luke VII, 33). And again it is written: “His food was locusts and wild honey” (Matt. III, 4). Are we to believe, on the basis of either statement, that John did not eat or that the Lord spoke falsely?

On the contrary, the truth is present in both: John did consume some food as nourishment for the flesh, while the Lord truly said of John that he did not eat either with others or what others ate. He was showing that he and the holy Scriptures often conceal God’s knowledge while revealing human opinions.

For this reason, whenever Scripture mentions someone as both just and without complaint, it is rightly understood according to the capacity of the time and according to that final judgment of God to which the conscience of all is subjected and every tongue confesses.

### 22

Finally, understand clearly that Job’s justification, and the permission of his sufferings in the flesh, brought about—by God’s provident counsel—the confusion of the presumptuous devil. Thus, while the human being was praised for the Creator’s honor, with the Lord himself approving, the angel who brought the charge of unbelief was punished.

Again, lest he inflict a more serious wound upon his servant while healing him and, through care of the flesh, wound the soul—that is, lest blessed Job, having overcome so great a temptation and having everything doubled and restored, be lifted up into pride and fall under the judgment of the devil—he is warned by hidden things that, although he was praised outwardly for his righteousness, he nevertheless ought to know that inwardly he must remain subject to the one by whom he was protected.

For the Lord says to him: “Who is this that hides counsel from me, containing words in his heart and thinking that I am concealed from him? Gird your loins like a man. I will question you, and you answer me. Where were you when I founded the earth? Tell me, if you possess knowledge” (Job XXXVIII, 2–4, according to the Septuagint).

After a long instruction in correction—or a doctrine of reproof—Job, replying to the Lord, said: “What [Note: [Col. 1191D] Gallandius prints *ego* and adds in a footnote: “The editions have it incorrectly as *Quid ergo*. The Septuagint reads, Τί ἔτι ἐγὼ κρίνομαι ἐλέγχων Κύριον—‘Why am I still judged, reproving the Lord?’ Nevertheless, just as Orosius here, reproved by the Lord, so too Saint Augustine reads it, as Nobilius notes.”] therefore am I judged, having been admonished and reproved by the Lord, hearing such things when I am nothing?” (Job XXXIX, 33, according to the Septuagint).

Such also was Zechariah, a man without complaint, worthy of human honor and worthy of the testimony of Scripture. Perhaps some swelling of pride was already tickling him because of this; perhaps he was beginning to trust reputation more than conscience. Through the reproving angel he is accused of the mark of unbelief and chastised with temporary silence.

Therefore Paul also says: “Let the one who thinks he stands take care lest he fall” (1 Cor. X, 12). And as though pronouncing judgment upon human beings in general, he says of himself: “I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. IX, 27).

Thus, for someone to be called blameless and without complaint is not a testimony of perfection but an example of conduct.

### 23

But wherever Scripture pronounces someone immaculate, as David says, “Blessed are the immaculate in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 1), I believe sound doctrine has been handed down: truly blessed are those who are immaculate in the way—that is, who walk in the truth with perfect faith, turning neither to the right nor to the left through heretical perversity.

The way is Christ, who leads to the Father through the Holy Spirit (John XIV, 6). Therefore the person who, without spot or defilement and not corrupted by those whose speech spreads like cancer (2 Tim. II, 17), hears, believes, and understands the glory of the venerable Trinity remains blessed and immaculate in faith.

Thus it is also said to Abraham: “Walk before me and be without blemish” (Gen. XVII, 1). Abraham, who believed God and “it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. IV, 3, 22), must necessarily be reminded to be perfect and without blemish in what he believed, saw, and rejoiced in (John VIII, 36). He was established as the father of many nations in faith (Gen. XVII, 5; Rom. IV, 18), and as the bosom of the faithful, so that all of us who hope in God with faithful Abraham may be at rest.

“Blessed are the immaculate in the way,” it is written, for “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. V, 7).

But if you wish to hear what sort of immaculate person David seeks in prayer, lay aside your vain confidence in your own ability. Prostrate in prayer, join yourself to the prophet in prayer, weeping and saying together with him: “Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those belonging to another. If they do not rule over me, then I shall be immaculate” (Ps. XVIII, 13–14).

Unhappy man that I am! When shall I avoid offenses that I do not yet understand?

Peter loves Christ and never turns away from love. By the Lord’s testimony to his love, he is now established as the rock and foundation of the Church (Matt. XVI, 18), and now is corrected with the name of Satan (ibid. 23).

While he is always acting with one and the same disposition, he is told first: “Flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid. 17); then again he is told: “You do not understand the things of God, but the things of human beings” (ibid. 23).

The Apostle was chosen because of his love and confounded because of his love, possessing sin because of the excess of his affection. When the Lord announced his passion, the impatience of love made him say: “Be favorable to yourself, Lord; this shall not happen to you” (Matt. XVI, 22).

### 24

O misery of the miserable! If Peter sinned in loving Christ in some respect, who understands his offenses? (Ps. XVIII, 13).

The prophet cries out, and cries out in the Holy Spirit. He is the one of whom the Lord had said: “My hand will assist him, and my arm will strengthen him, and the enemy will gain nothing against him” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 22–23). Pay attention to what he cries: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults” (Ps. XVIII, 23).

That chosen David, “according to the heart” (1 Sam. XIII, 14); the one whom God promised he would make to carry out all his will (ibid.; Acts XIII, 22); the one whom he anointed king; the one to whom he gave the sanctification of the prophetic spirit—astonished at the intrusion of sins, cries out to the Lord and implores him to be cleansed from his hidden faults.

And elsewhere the Lord says to him: “You shall not build a house for my name, because you are a warrior and have shed blood” (1 Chron. XXVIII, 3)—as though he could not have so cleansed him by removing every stain that he might prepare him as worthy for a worthy work.

David was not cleansed even unto death; instead, when his son was preferred for the construction of the Temple, he condemned himself. And [Note: [Col. 1193D] Schott identifies Goliath and his armor-bearer as Pelagius and Coelestius.] Goliath, with his armor-bearer, slanders me: why does the Lord not do in this man what he has never done in the world?

The Ecclesiastes says: “There is nothing new under the sun, nor can anyone say, ‘Behold, this is new’; it has already existed in the ages that were before us” (Eccl. I, 10). Yet the instructor in new doctrines affirms that what has never happened can occur.

Do not ask whether something has existed if you do not doubt that it can exist.

God wished a temple to be built for his name, and wished that it should be constructed only by one who was innocent and completely without blemish. For this purpose two kings are chosen with all their strength, each to provide assistance; protection is promised to both.

To David, God says: “My truth and my mercy are with him” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 25). Concerning Solomon he testifies: “I have chosen him for myself as a son, and I will be a father to him” (1 Chron. XXVIII, 6).

Of these two, one prepares the Lord’s Temple and the other builds it: the old man prepares it, the young man completes it. For it is fitting that a holy person should build the Lord’s holy Temple.

As I have said, the old man prepares it, but as though after he had ceased to sin; the young man completes it, yet almost as though he had not begun to sin. The former sinned before; the latter afterward. The former, because of his many sins, did not deserve to build; the latter, by sinning greatly, abandoned what he had built.

And amid all this, holy providence wonderfully arranged matters for itself, so that between two ages it might find, according to the capacity of the time, what could not exist perpetually in a human being. Each at some time did not sin, yet neither could be without sin:

“So that God may be true, but every human being a liar” (Rom. III, 4; Ps. CXV, 11), as it is written: “The sons of human beings are vain; the sons of human beings are liars in the balance” (Ps. LXI, 10).

### 25

Although they possessed God’s grace and assistance, neither David nor Solomon was able to be without sin or to preserve that state. Yet the son of Jovinian hopes that almighty God will change the entire order of things for him and his disciples. If this should perhaps not happen, will he accuse God of inability?

“Human beings can be without sin,” he says, “yet with God’s assistance.”

What am I to do? For the moment I will tolerate the new cloth fastened to the old garment, until the worse tear exposes the falsehood of this wretched correction.

For I grant that, contrary to the leader of truth, who said, “A human being can, if he wishes,” he may appear to have said, “A human being can with God’s assistance.”

Now at last my argument must be recalled, as it were, to the beginning of the proposition. Setting aside for a little while the pain of the insult, I must return with the reverence proper to debate to the exalted head.

Our head is Christ Jesus, whom, as the Apostle says, God “set forth as an expiation through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness because of the remission of preceding sins, in the forbearance of God and the demonstration of his righteousness at the present time, so that he himself might be just and the one who justifies the person who has faith in Jesus” (Rom. III, 25–26).

Therefore, established as an expiator through faith in his blood for the demonstration and form of righteousness, he himself is “the mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. II, 5).

Concerning him John, led almost into that inaccessible light itself, cries out: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him” (John I, 1–3).

A little later, having explained the truth of the divine work, he adds: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; and we saw his honor, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of glory and truth” (ibid. 14).

He “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. II, 22). He was “like a lamb before the one who shears it, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7). When he was scourged, crucified, and killed, he conquered the sting of death, rose from the dead, led captivity captive (Ps. LXVII, 19; Eph. IV, 8), and ascended into heaven.

He is the only-begotten in the Father and the firstborn among many brothers (Rom. VIII, 29), in whom “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II, 9).

This, then, is the Lord Christ; this, I say, is the Son of God, in the power and glory of the Father. The one who created all things in the beginning, redeemed them in the middle, will also judge them at the end.

### 26

Therefore, after the creation of the whole universe, which came into existence according to his will, he imposed upon things a mode of arrangement so that what had been made rational might subsist through reason. What he had endowed with free choice he restrained by the law of a commandment, lest it run headlong into the license of destruction.

Thus, when the creature recognized its Creator, the gift of its Lord, and the firmness of the commandment, foreseeing freedom in the subjection brought by the Fall, it would wish to use that freedom only to choose the service by which it would be governed.

It was fittingly established by judgment that, just as it should receive protection from prudent service, so it should receive a reward from free will. The Apostle confirms this when he says: “For if I do this willingly, I have a reward” (1 Cor. IX, 17).

Almighty God said, and the two great lights came into being; he commanded them to divide day and night and to be for signs, seasons, days, and years (Gen. I, 14). Does this distinction, once established, not continue to the present day?

And yet the Creator possessed the power to change these very things, which are carried along in such ordered motion, whenever he wished, if reason did not restrain him; for in all things the reason of God is joined to his power.

If there were a change of works in the Creator, how could obedience to commandments be expected from creation?

God commanded the earth to bring forth vegetation, grass, and fruit-bearing trees (ibid. 11); even now it preserves this through annual cycles and unceasing fertility. Yet God, very often angered against the earth, diminishes its fruits by denying the abundance of rain. What he could have taken away entirely, he preferred to chastise, so that the blow might display correction while nature preserved its order.

God made the human being from the clay of the earth and, by the breathing-in of the life-giving spirit, placed him alive in the paradise of delights (ibid. 17). He also granted him free choice, surrounding him with a commandment concerning immortality and death.

Your followers, who have drawn more abundant poisons from your breast, assert that he was made mortal and that no harm came to him from transgressing the commandment.
