But when the human being transgressed, the earth was cursed, and the human being himself was burdened with labors and pains; he was commanded to acquire bread by the sweat of his face. The mark of death was set upon him until he returned to the earth from which he had been taken (Gen. III, 17–19).

Adam was expelled from paradise (ibid. 23), and he fathered children who dragged along with them the original sin of an unbelieving seed. The human race sinned, and God also repented that he had made the human being on the earth (Gen. VI, 6).

### 27

O Lord, endure my foolishness for a little while, until the one who seems wise and prudent blushes and recognizes his imprudence!

When one human being sinned, from whom dire contagions passed into the whole succession of humanity and the kingdom of death prevailed over all, you repented, became angry, and grieved; and you were moved to the point that the Word became flesh and required passion, the cross, and death.

Perhaps it would have been better for the one sinner to be immediately destroyed, so that another might soon be substituted through a second creation, from whom a lineage free of every stain and blemish might descend.

But because we recognize that you, almighty God, did not do this, do we believe that you were unable to do it?

O Peter, upon what rock Christ founded his Church (Matt. XVI, 18); and O Paul, who laid the foundation, besides which no one can lay another, which is Christ Jesus (1 Cor. III, 11); blessed apostles, pillars and foundations of truth, at least answer this man, who makes himself God’s counselor and mediator, with sacred words!

Peter says: “Blessed is God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom you have been called to an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance, preserved in heaven for you, who are guarded by the power of God through faith for the salvation ready to be revealed in the last time” (1 Pet. I, 3–5).

Then Paul, the vessel of election, brings forth saving treasures and says: “Blessed is God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and immaculate in his presence in love, [Note: [Col. 1195D] Gallandius corrects the reading to *qui* and adds in a footnote: “Schottus has *quia*; Havercamp has *qua*. We restore the reading of the Vulgate, *qui*, which agrees with the Greek text, where we read προορίσας. Shortly afterward read *in laudem gloriae gratiae suae*, according to the Greek, εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ. The context of Paul requires that this word, which was omitted by the copyist in Orosius, be supplied.”] having predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ into himself, according to the purpose of his will, for the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he favored us in his beloved Son. In him we have redemption through his blood, the remission of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he made abound in us in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, which he established in him for the administration of the fullness of times: to restore all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth” (Eph. I, 3–10).

### 28.

Peter says: “for salvation ready to be revealed in the last time”; and Paul also testifies that God “purposed in him, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ.” And now some man—I do not know who—like a frog emerging from the mud, croaks out: “Why should I wait for the time, why await the judgment? If God can do something, he can always do it; if he can always do it, he is not a respecter of persons.”

Therefore he can—and even now he can—and you must prove that he is a respecter of persons in your case, if he were to do beforehand, in you alone, what he can do in everyone and will certainly do in his own time, although he did not do it even in Moses, to whom he reproached only one sin in this life and yet forgave it before his death: the one whom he ordered to die for this fault, so that he would not enter the promised land.

Let him therefore hear Solomon, bearing witness concerning the ordering of times and God’s decree:

> “Everything has its time, and all things pass in their appointed seasons under heaven:  
> a time to be born, and a time to die;  
> a time to plant, and a time to uproot what has been planted;  
> a time to kill, and a time to heal” (Eccles. III, 1–3).

Then elsewhere he says:

> “I saw under the sun, in the place of judgment, wickedness, and in the place of justice, iniquity; and I said in my heart: God will judge the righteous and the wicked, and then there will be a time for every matter” (ibid., 16–17).

Therefore, empty man, if you have any confidence, patiently await God’s order, which the Lord himself, who made all things, also deigned to await—he who was made subject to the law (Gal. IV, 4), though he had made the law.

Hear him saying to you: “It is not for you to know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts I, 7). Or, if you wish to receive a clearer testimony that, although God certainly can, he nevertheless does not act on account of his own ordering, he says to Peter:

> “Do you think that I cannot now ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? But how then will the Scriptures be fulfilled, that this must happen?” (Matt. XXVI, 53–54).

You see, then, that the one who governs time restrains his powers, and that the order of his plan mingles patience with power.

Then the Lord says: “Put the sword back into its sheath. For it cannot be that I should not drink the cup which the Father has given me” (John XVIII, 11). And yet God can do everything; nor is there anything he does not do, except perhaps what he does not wish, what ought not to be done, or what he has not purposed.

Paul speaks to the Thessalonians, signifying the coming of Antichrist:

> “Do you not remember that, when I was still with you, I used to tell you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time” (II Thess. I, 5–6).

So great is the force of God’s decree, and so immovable is the stability of the times established for their respective purposes, that the Lord said that, for the sake of his elect, the days of the world would be shortened (Matt. XXIV, 22), not abolished. Thus he would give the appointed times fullness in accordance with his majesty, and brevity in accordance with his mercy; at once mercy would embrace a shortened course, and the world would complete its appointed number.

And you want it now?—Behold, I speak with the grief of mercy—yes, you, a man like me, want people in this present time, of which nothing similar has ever before been found stated in the sacred books, to answer you that anyone is without sin; and, if they should happen to agree with you in this, to subscribe to the day and moment. You are constructing a new engine of accusation, so that, when we say that something does not happen, we may appear to have said that it cannot happen; and in that matter in which we especially proclaim the Almighty at work according to the arrangement he has established, you seek to prevent us from being judged to have impatiently slandered his inability.

I beg you, cast away this empty madness, since it itself contributes to the sin concerning whose removal you have thought of the opportunity afforded by time, rather than the Judge’s clemency.

Let this much suffice concerning the power of God, which we proclaim and worship, and concerning the determination of the times, which have been established by his deepest counsel. Even if there were no other writings of the saints concerning this matter, the single response of the demons would be enough; condemned by the testimony of their own conscience, they cry out to the Lord:

> “What have you to do with us, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to destroy us?” (Matt. VIII, 29).

Since you understand that they are confident in the appointment of judgment, take the most certain example of it against yourself.

> [Note: [Col. 1197D] “Confessing . . . . . wretched man.” We have restored the text in this way, following Cotelerius in *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. III, p. 526. The printed editions incorrectly read “confident . . . . . he has sent men.” We have also corrected the faulty punctuation. Formerly the passage read: “If he should have sent men seized in oppression: then you understand them to have been condemned in the last judgment. Receive, etc.” GALLAND.]

“If he has sent them, men seized in oppression”—then you understand them to have been condemned at the last judgment.

Receive also yourself here for purification through undisturbed correction.

> [Note: [Col. 1198D] “Purification.” Thus Schottus, and the following word *purgandum* supports this reading. Havercamp, however, preferred *emendatione* (“amendment”). GALLAND.]

But if, as the text reads, God’s patience still grants them freedom of choice, believe that you too are still being tested.

### 29.

Now I pass briefly to another question, which you are said repeatedly to hurl against all Catholics. For even in that very laboriously composed letter of yours we could scarcely understand this point.

Thus, I say, you did not blush to write in this manner to Demetrias, a girl—as I hear—holy and consecrated: teaching, I suppose, reverence for chastity through the story of Joseph and his lustful mistress, where you said:

> “The mistress, despised, more frequently lays snares for the young man; she reaches out her shameless hand and seizes him secretly and without witnesses,”

weaving an inappropriate story in the most obscene language. Yet we ought not to charge you with what is said neither appropriately nor decently, since neither your birth gave you the opportunity to be educated in more honorable studies, nor did it arise naturally in you to understand; rather, it came from those dictators of yours who write down a miserable sense in the most miserable language and expose you to be read with laughter, as though you were a title of disgrace.

Among other things, therefore, you vomited forth in the same letter, in disordered language, the following idea:

> “That many of our people say that God created an evil nature for human beings.”

Your own Phinehas also gradually attempted to insinuate this to us. Therefore I shall first state my position briefly, and then answer.

May he who says that God created some evil nature, whether of a human being or of anything else, or who takes away free choice in any respect, not be worthy to stand before Christ’s tribunal among the lambs at his right hand, nor deserve to see the Lord in the land of the living, nor have the life of Jesus manifested in his mortal body (II Cor. IV, 11)—since he has read that “everything that God made was very good” (Gen. I, 31).

And concerning human free choice it is written: “God created man imperishable” (Wis. II, 23), “and left him in the hand of his own counsel” (Ecclus. XV, 14).

Blind and malicious man—for I cannot speak to you otherwise—you possess neither a sense of the Lord’s authority, nor a sense of your own weakness, nor a sense of common understanding. We say that human nature is weak, not evil. For if it were evil, it would not grasp the good at all. But now, since by its innate inclination it desires the good and clings to the good, while wholly fleeing evil, where in it should its substance be called evil?

The Lord cries out: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI, 43).

Abraham cries out: “But I am earth and ashes” (Gen. XVIII, 27).

Job cries out: “Man is rottenness, and the son of man a worm” (Job XXV, 6).

Isaiah cries out: “Woe is me, for I am pierced through, because, though I am a man and have unclean lips, I dwell among a people also having unclean lips” (Isa. VI, 5).

Jeremiah cries out: “A soul in distress and an anxious spirit cries out to you: See, Lord, and have mercy” (Baruch III, 1–2).

Habakkuk cries out: “I kept watch, and my belly trembled; my condition was disturbed by the voice of the prayers within me” (Hab. III, 1 according to the Septuagint).

David cries out: “Hear me in your righteousness, and do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLIII, 1–2).

All the apostles, shaken by fear of weakness, cry out: “Lord, save us; we are perishing” (Matt. VIII, 23).

John cries out: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8).

James cries out: “For we all offend in many things” (James III, 2).

Paul cries out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 24–25).

And, so that the weakness of all may cry out generally, the Holy Spirit cries out in the saints:

> “All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, the flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. XI, 6–8).

### 30.

Against these clouds of divine testimonies, so splendid and so clear, let the whole world, laboring in its groaning, hear Pelagius protesting—and resisting humble truth not only with the shamelessness of words but also with cauteries.

For in the letter mentioned above he says:

> “But, on the contrary, with a careless and disdainful spirit and a wicked mouth, we protest against the Lord and say: ‘It is hard; it is difficult; we cannot; we are human beings, surrounded by fragile flesh.’ And, O blind madness! O profane presumption! We accuse the Lord of knowledge of a double ignorance, so that he appears not to know what he made and not to know what he commanded. And, as though he had forgotten human weakness, of which he himself is the author, he has imposed upon man something that he cannot bear.”

What, I ask, is more savage than this presumption? What more perverse than this reproach?

You reproach the Catholic Church, whose members we are, because she seems, as though in despair, to say that God, the author of humanity, has imposed upon human beings something they cannot bear. Yet her most faithful confession, both in word and in humility, is that God first commanded everything possible, but that, since no one fulfilled what was possible, the whole world was thereby made subject to God; afterward, by the indulgence of grace substituted for the burden of the commandment, he lightened that burden.

But you, wicked and malicious servant, who try to demand from your fellow servants what your master forgave you (Matt. XVIII, 29–32), I shall first examine your meaning and afterward, if you wish, explain mine.

You accuse certain people of saying that they cannot bear the burden of the law. Therefore, do you yourself claim that you can bear it? Wretched man, who, according to what is written, say in your heart: “I am rich and have grown wealthy, and I need nothing,” yet do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked (Rev. III, 17).

Did Christ speak to you: “Truly I say to you, flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 17)? Did he say to you: “You shall be called Cephas” (John I, 42)? Did he promise you: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18)?

Consider what the apostle Peter, taught by the Holy Spirit, reminds us when he says:

> “Now therefore, why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? But we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they were” (Acts XV, 10–11).

The apostle Peter says that the person who now attempts to impose the burden of the law upon humanity is truly testing God. But you, on the contrary, object and threaten that the person who, by confessing his own weakness, flees from the killing letter to the grace of the Spirit is accusing God of injustice.

Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Zechariah—all the saints, whether judges, kings, or prophets—are certainly our fathers. Yet Peter affirms that none of these fathers, nor even themselves—that is, the apostles, while they were Jews—could bear the burden of the law; rather, they were saved by faith in Christ according to the hope of grace.

### 31.

Or do you perhaps think that all these holy fathers of God had no divine assistance?

Behold, Peter rebukes those who were attempting to place a heavy yoke upon the necks of the disciples. You, on the contrary, to the scandal of Peter, rebuke those who flee to the faithful mercy of God and distrust their ability to bear the burden of the law by their own strength.

But perhaps you have a special confidence in your ability to carry the burden because, nourished by baths and banquets, you bear broad shoulders and a powerful neck, even displaying fatness on your forehead, as it is written:

> “For he stretched out his hand against God and strengthened himself against the Almighty. He ran against him with an erect neck and was armed with a thick neck. Fatness covered his face, and lard hung from his sides” (Job XV, 25–27).

But those who always hear Christ speaking in their hearts cannot be such people:

> “Strive to enter by the narrow way, for broad is the way that leads to destruction” (Matt. VII, 13; Luke XIII, 24).

And the apostle Paul admonishes: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII, 14).

The truth of Christ is in me (II Cor. XI, 10; Rom. IX, 1–2), because I grieve greatly for you. According to the saying of my blessed father Augustine, “Confidence is not the mark of a sane person, but of an insane one.”

Concerning one commandment, and the very first, I ask you, if you are willing. In the Law the Lord commands through Moses, and Christ confirms the same in the Gospels:

> “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength”; and similarly: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. VI, 5; Matt. XXII, 37–39).

I ask you: answer not me but God—not with your voice but with your conscience. Do you love God with all your heart in such a way that you admit no thought of him that could exist without fear and love of God? Do you follow him with your whole soul in such a way that, once you have taken up the cross, you turn entirely toward no pleasure of the happiness experienced for a time? Do you burn with the heat of love in all your inward being in such a way that, even as need increases, you yield absolutely to no weakness of desire or longing?

Furthermore, since it is written, “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV, 23), whether you see bishops of noble rank, powerful men of the world, or wealthy men professing religion, do you indulge absolutely nothing through being caught by flattery, fear, hope, or respect for persons? Is there nothing in which your heart accuses you and your conscience reproaches you? Or do you perhaps give no answer suited more to the times than to the truth?

I also ask whether you love all Christians as yourself. For under one head, which is Christ, and under one Church, which is Christ, we are all brothers and one body in Christ. Do you therefore love, as yourself, all who hope in God’s mercy, whom you nevertheless know and acknowledge?

I am not asking about strangers, whom you suppose you love because, since you do not know them, you do not hate them. But why should I demand these things from your confession, when the common people recognize your conduct?

You are perfect, without weakness; you are able to bear the entire burden of the law—you, I say, inflated yet empty man. Hear, if you are willing, the Lord and Savior calling you back to holiness, if you are capable of it:

> “Truly I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it” (Mark X, 15).

A child possesses nothing in himself except that he loves the one who caresses him; and, hoping for the nourishment of life, he obtains his bread not through his own sweat but through prayers, by a simple petition, which he does not earn through any confident work. Warned by this comparison, turn back to childhood, so that you may return to life.

### 32.

Since I said above that I would examine your first argument concerning the possibility of bearing the burden, and afterward, if you wish, explain my own, my position is this: we also sin in this matter when, although we are weak, we complain about our weakness.

> [Note: [Col. 1201C] The material that follows, enclosed in brackets up to the middle of number 46, is omitted by Gallandius. He explains the omission as follows: “Here, after the words ‘we complain about our weakness,’ a long excerpt from St. Augustine’s book *On Nature and Grace*, against Pelagius, had been inserted, as Schottus observed—namely, from the words in chapter 12, ‘this is the intention of the law that accuses,’ up to those in chapter 19, ‘How could what lacks substance have corrupted your soul?’ To these are again appended the words found at the beginning of chapter 3, ‘He needs a physician, because he is not healthy,’ up to ‘not observing, of course, the Scriptures of the New Testament, where we say’—perhaps ‘we have said’—‘this is the intention of the law that accuses,’ as quoted above. I certainly would not think that Orosius inserted these Augustinian passages into his own work while suppressing the holy Father’s name; rather, a copyist probably inserted them, perhaps reversing the order of the Doctor’s statements so that the fraud would not be detected. Whatever the case, following Schottus, we have taken the Augustinian excerpts out of Orosius’s work and placed them below, comparing them with the edition of the Benedictines, vol. X, p. 129 and following. Havercamp acted differently: recognizing none of the Augustinian material, he published everything as Orosian.” Thus he. After extracting the long passage, as he calls it, he places it in an appendix to the treatise. In our view, it is enough to warn the reader of the circumstance; for the rest, we will not omit Gallandius’s notes.]

This is the intention of the accusing law: that, because of the things wrongly done, one should flee to the grace of the merciful Lord, as though a tutor were enclosing us within the same faith that was afterward revealed.

> [Note: [Col. 1202C] The Benedictine edition of Augustine’s works, vol. X, *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 13, reads “in the same faith.” But the Orosian reading comes closer to Paul’s text, Gal. III, 23. GALLAND.]

There, the things wrongly done are forgiven, and, with the assistance of that same grace, they are not done again.

> [Note: [Col. 1202D] “Of those who are progressing . . . progressing.” We read it thus with the Benedictines. Schottus, followed by Havercamp, has *proficiscentium . . . proficiscientes*, apparently incorrectly. GALLAND.]

The way belongs to those who are progressing, although those who progress well may be called perfect travelers. The highest perfection, however, is that to which nothing can be added once what one is striving toward has begun to be possessed.

### 33.

Now the statement made to them, “Are you yourself without sin?”, does not really pertain to the matter under discussion. But when he says that “it should rather be attributed to his negligence that he is not without sin,” he speaks well—provided that he also deigns to pray to the Lord that this wicked negligence not dominate him.

> [Note: [Col. 1202D] “To God.” Thus the Benedictines. Schottus, together with Havercamp, reads “to the Lord.” Immediately afterward these same editors incorrectly have “which he was asking . . . and that it should not dominate.” GALLAND.]

A certain man prayed against it when he said:

> “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity dominate me” (Ps. CXVIII, 135).

Otherwise, while he trusts in his own diligence as though it were his own strength, he will arrive neither here at true righteousness nor there, where perfect righteousness must undoubtedly be desired and hoped for.

### 34.

The statement made to them by certain people—that it is nowhere written in these exact words that a person can be without sin—is easily refuted, because the question for you is not in what words a given opinion is expressed.

> [Note: [Col. 1202D] “There . . . whatever.” We follow the Benedictines. Schottus also correctly has “there.” Havercamp incorrectly has “to you.” Both editors, however, have “each thing.” GALLAND.]

Nevertheless, perhaps it is not without reason that, although Scripture sometimes says that people are “without complaint” (Luke I, 6), it does not say that anyone is without sin—except the one alone of whom it was clearly said that he “did not know sin” (II Cor. V, 20).

And where the holy priests were being discussed:

> “For he has been tested in every respect, according to likeness, without sin” (Heb. IV, 15),

namely, in that flesh which had the likeness of sinful flesh, although it was not sinful flesh.

Now how should we understand the statement, “Everyone who is born of God does not sin, and cannot sin, because his seed remains in him” (I John III, 9), when the apostle John himself, as though he were not born of God, or were speaking to people who had not yet been born of God, plainly says:

> “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8)?

In the books I wrote to Marcellinus on this subject, I took care to explain this as best I could.

> [Note: [Col. 1202D] “To Marcellinus.” Book II of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 8. Schottus incorrectly has “to Marcellus.” Havercamp could easily have corrected the error and at the same time noticed that it is not Orosius speaking here but Augustine. GALLAND.]

And the statement “cannot sin” means the same as if it had said “ought not to sin.” This interpretation does not seem to me objectionable. For what madman would say that one ought to sin, since sin is precisely called sin because it ought not to be done?

### 35.

Indeed, when the apostle James says, “No human being can tame the tongue” (James III, 8), I do not think it should be understood.

> [Note: [Col. 1203D] Thus Schottus. Gallandius adds, from the Benedictine edition, “as he wished to explain.”]

as though it had been said reproachfully, as if the meaning were:

> “So no human being can tame the tongue? You can tame wild beasts, but you cannot tame the tongue?”

—as though taming the tongue were easier than taming wild beasts.

I do not think that this is the meaning of the passage. For if he intended to speak of the ease of taming the tongue, what follows would have continued the comparison with beasts. But what follows is:

> “An unruly evil, full of deadly poison,”

and certainly more harmful than beasts and serpents. The latter kills the flesh; the former kills the soul. “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I, 11).

Therefore holy James did not pronounce that statement, nor intend it to be pronounced, as though taming the tongue were easier than taming wild beasts. Rather, he was showing how great the evil of the tongue is in human beings, so that no human being can tame it, even though human beings tame beasts.

Nor did he say this so that we might negligently allow the domination of this evil to remain over us, but so that we might ask for the help of divine grace in taming the tongue. For he did not say, “No one can tame the tongue,” but “No human being.” Thus, when it is tamed, we should confess that it happens through God’s mercy, God’s help, and God’s grace.

Let the soul therefore strive to tame the tongue; and while striving, let it ask for help. Let the tongue pray that the tongue may be tamed, through the gift of the one who said to his disciples:

> “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 20).

Thus we are urged to carry out the commandment; and, while striving and unable to do so by our own strength, we must pray for divine assistance.

### 36.

Accordingly, after he had magnified the evil of the tongue, saying among other things, “My brothers, these things ought not to happen” (James III, 10), he immediately taught, once he had completed what he was saying here, by what assistance the things he declared ought not to happen could be prevented.

> “Who is wise and disciplined among you?” he says. “Let him show his work from good conduct, in the gentleness of wisdom. But if you have bitter zeal and contention in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth. This is not the wisdom descending from above, but earthly, natural, demonic. For where there is zeal and contention, there is instability and every evil work. But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, modest, persuadable, full of mercy and good fruits, not judging, without hypocrisy” (ibid., 13–17).

> [Note: [Col. 1203D] The Benedictines and Gallandius have “without hypocrisy.”]

This is the wisdom that tames the tongue, descending from above, not springing forth from the human heart.

Or does anyone dare to deprive this wisdom also of the grace of God and, in such arrogant vanity, place it within human power?

> [Note: [Col. 1203D] “And place it in the most arrogant vanity.” The Benedictine edition reads this way. Both editors incorrectly have “and such arrogance.” GALLAND.]

Why, then, is it prayed for, so that it may be received, if it comes from human beings and is possessed by them?

Or is this prayer also contradicted, lest an injury be done to free choice?

> [Note: [Col. 1203D] The Benedictines, followed by Gallandius, wish the passage to be punctuated in this way: “lest an injury be done to free choice, which . . .”]

If free choice is sufficient to itself, by the capacity of nature, to fulfill all the commandments of righteousness, then let this also be contradicted—the apostle James, who admonishes and says:

> “If anyone among you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach them, and it will be given to him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing” (James I, 5–6).

This is the faith to which the commandments compel us: let the law command, and let faith obtain.

> [Note: [Col. 1203D] Here Gallandius, together with the Benedictines, adds the passage: “let faith obtain. For through the tongue, which no human being can tame, but through wisdom descending from above.” He adds the following note: “Schottus and Havercamp carelessly omit this. A little earlier in their editions, ‘let faith obtain’ is missing the conjunction ‘and,’ incorrectly.”]

“We all offend in many things” (James III, 2). For this apostle did not pronounce this in any other way than he pronounced the statement, “No human being can tame the tongue.”

### 37.

Nor should anyone similarly bring forward against these people, as proof of the impossibility of not sinning, the statement:

> “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God. For it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be; and those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. VIII, 7–8).

He said “the wisdom of the flesh,” not the wisdom descending from above. And it is clear that by “being in the flesh” he does not mean those who have not yet departed from the body, but those who live according to the flesh.

But that is not the question under discussion. This is what I await hearing from him:

> [Note: [Col. 1204D] The Benedictines and Gallandius have “if I can those who . . .”]

whether those who live according to the spirit—and who for that reason, although still living here, are already in some sense not in the flesh—live according to the spirit by God’s grace, or whether they are sufficient unto themselves, possessing, from the time they were created, the capacity of nature within their own will.

For the fullness of the law is love (Rom. VIII, 10), and the love of God has been poured into our hearts (Rom. V, 5), not by ourselves, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

This man also discusses sins of ignorance and says that “a person ought to watch beforehand so that he may not be ignorant; therefore ignorance is to be blamed, because through his own negligence a person does not know what he should have known had he applied diligence.” Yet he discusses everything rather than praying and saying:

> “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII, 75).

For one thing is failing to take care to know what one ought to know—sins of negligence that even seemed to be expiated through certain sacrifices of the law. Another is wishing to understand but being unable to do so, and acting against the law through not understanding what he wills to be done.

Therefore we are admonished to ask wisdom from God, who gives generously to all (James I, 5)—that is, to all who ask in this way and with the earnestness with which, and to the extent to which, so great a thing ought to be sought.

### 38.

He admits, nevertheless, “that committed sins must be expiated through divine means and that the Lord must be entreated on their behalf,” evidently in order to obtain forgiveness. For what has been done cannot be made undone by that power of nature and human will which he praises so highly, even by his own admission.

Therefore, since this necessity remains, one must pray for forgiveness. But he nowhere says—and I do not find it written here—that one should be helped so as not to sin.

There is a wholly astonishing silence concerning this matter, although the Lord’s Prayer teaches that both things must be requested:

> “That our debts may be forgiven us, and that we may not be led into temptation” (Matt. VI, 12–13).

The first petition concerns the expiation of past sins; the second, the avoidance of future sins.

Although this does not happen unless the will is present, the will alone is not sufficient for it to happen. Therefore prayer is offered to the Lord for this purpose—neither superfluous nor shameless.

For what could be more foolish than praying to do something that lies within one’s own power?

### 39.

Now observe what bears most directly on the matter: how he attempts to show human nature as though it were entirely without any defect, and how, against the clearest Scriptures of God, he struggles with the wisdom of words by which the cross of Christ is emptied of its force (I Cor. I, 17).

But the cross will certainly not be emptied; rather, this wisdom will be overturned. For when we have demonstrated this, perhaps God’s mercy will be present, so that he may even repent of having said these things.

“First,” he says, “one must discuss the claim that nature has been weakened and changed through sin. Therefore, above all, I think it must be asked what sin is.”

> “Is it some substance, or a name entirely lacking substance, by which not a thing, not an existence, not some body, but an act improperly performed is expressed?”

Then he adds:

> “I believe that this is so. And if it is so,” he says, “how could what lacks substance have weakened or changed human nature?”

Consider, I ask, how, in ignorance, he tries to overturn the saving words of the medicinal Scriptures:

> “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. XL, 5).

What is healed if nothing has been wounded, nothing injured, nothing weakened or corrupted? But if there is something to be healed, from where did its corruption come?

You hear a person confessing; what more do you want from the person who is arguing? “Heal my soul,” he says. Ask him from where that which he begs to be healed was corrupted, and hear what follows: “Because I have sinned against you.”

Let this man question him; let him ask him what he thinks ought to be asked, and say:

> “You who cry out, ‘Heal my soul, because I have sinned,’ what is sin? Is it some substance, or a name entirely lacking substance, by which not a thing, not an existence, not some body, but only an act improperly performed is expressed?”

He replied:

> “It is as you say. Sin is not some substance; rather, the act improperly performed is expressed by this name alone.”

And the other responds:

> “Why, then, do you cry out, ‘Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you’? How could your soul have been corrupted?”

> [Note: [Col. 1205D] These words are taken from the cited book of Augustine, chapter 3. In order to connect them with what precedes, the excerptor condensed Augustine’s wording. Thus the holy Doctor has, near the end of chapter 19: “How could what lacks substance have corrupted your soul?” GALLAND.]

“It needs a physician, because it is not healthy.”

Everything good that it possesses—in its formation, life, sensation, and mind—it has from the supreme God, its Creator and maker.

> [Note: [Col. 1206D] The Benedictines and Gallandius read “in its senses.”]

But the defect that darkens and weakens these natural goods, so that the soul needs illumination and healing, was not contracted from a blameless maker; it arose from original sin, which was committed through free choice. Consequently, the penal condition of nature belongs to the most just punishment.

> [Note: [Col. 1206D] The Benedictine edition should be read “although they conjecture” in this place. GALLAND.]

For although we are now a new creation in Christ (II Cor. V, 17), we were nevertheless by nature children of wrath, like the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ; by whose grace we have been saved (Eph. II, 2–5).

### 40.

> [Note: [Col. 1206D] Thus Schottus. The Benedictines and Gallandius read: “But this.”]

This grace of Christ, without which neither infants nor adults can be saved, is not bestowed according to merits but given freely. For this reason it is called grace:

> “Being justified freely through his blood” (Rom. III, 24).

Therefore those who are not liberated through it—whether because they have not yet been able to hear, because they have refused to obey, or even because, when they were unable to hear on account of their age, they did not receive the bath of regeneration, which they could have received and through which they would have been saved—are justly condemned.

For they are not without sin: either the sin they drew from their origin, or the sins they added through evil habits. For all have sinned, whether in Adam or in themselves, and they lack the glory of God (ibid., 23).

### 41

Therefore the whole mass owes punishment. And if the punishment of condemnation that was owed were repaid to everyone, [Col. 1206C] it would unquestionably be repaid justly. Those who are liberated from that mass by grace are therefore called not vessels of their own merits, but vessels of mercy. Whose mercy, if not that of the one who sent Christ Jesus into this world to save sinners (I Tim. 1:15)—those whom he foreknew and predestined, called, justified, and glorified (Rom. 8:29–30)?

Who, then, would be so utterly and madly insane as not to give ineffable thanks to the mercy that liberates those whom it wills, while rightly no one could in any way accuse the justice that condemns everyone without exception? If we understand this according to the Scriptures, we are not compelled to argue against Christian grace and to say things by which we try to demonstrate that human nature does not need a physician even in infants, because it is sound, [Col. 1206D] and that in adults it can, if it wishes, suffice for itself unto righteousness.

They seem to themselves to say these things acutely—but with a wisdom by which the cross of Christ is made void (I Cor. 1:17). This is not the wisdom that descends from above (Jas. 3:15). I do not wish to say what follows, lest I be thought to wrong our friends, whose very strong and very keen minds we want to run not perversely but straight.

**Editorial note:** BB. read *celerrima* (“swiftest”); this reading agrees with what follows, “to run.” Schottus and Havercampius read *acerrima* (“keenest”). —Gallandius.

### 42

[Col. 1207A] The greater the zeal, therefore, with which the author of the book you sent was inflamed against those who seek a defense for their sins from the weakness of human nature, the more and far more ardent ought our zeal to be, lest the cross of Christ be made void. It is made void if it is said that one can somehow attain righteousness and eternal life apart from the sacrament of Christ—which is what is done in this book. I do not wish to say that this was done knowingly, lest I judge the man who wrote it not even to be regarded as a Christian; rather, I believe it was done by someone who did not understand, with great strength indeed, but strength of the kind I wish to be sound, not like that which the insane customarily possess.

**Editorial note:** This is Schottus’s reading; BB. and Gallandius read *sed quod* (“but that”).

First he makes the distinction that “it is one thing to ask whether something can exist, which pertains only to possibility; another to ask whether it actually exists.” No one doubts that this distinction is true. [Col. 1207B] For it follows that what exists could have existed; but it does not follow that what can exist actually exists. Because the Lord raised Lazarus, he certainly could have done so; but because he did not raise Judas, should it therefore be said that he could not? He could, then, but he did not wish to. For if he had wished to, he would have done this also by the same power, since the Son gives life to those whom he wills (John 5:21).

**Editorial note:** BB. note that Peter Lombard cited and explained this passage in *Sentences*, book I, distinction 43, final chapter. —Gallandius.

But observe where this true and evident distinction leads, and what it tries to accomplish. “We,” he says, “are discussing possibility alone; unless something certain has been established about it, we say that it is extremely serious and out of order to pass on to something else.”

**Editorial note:** BB. and Gallandius read *ducimus* (“we consider”) in place of *dicimus* (“we say”).

He turns this over in many ways and at length, so that no one may think he is asking about anything other than the possibility of not sinning.

[Col. 1207C] Thus, among the many things by which he pursues this point, he also says:

> “I repeat again: I say that a human being can exist without sin. What do you say? That a human being cannot exist without sin? We are arguing about what can and cannot be, not about what is and is not.”

Then he recalls that certain passages commonly brought against them from Scripture do not pertain to this question, in which it is asked whether a human being can or cannot exist without sin:

> “For ‘no one is clean from defilement’ (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint), and ‘there is no human being who does not sin’ (III Kings 8:46), and ‘there is no righteous person on earth’ (Eccles. 7:21), and ‘there is no one who does good’ (Ps. 13:1), and the other statements of this kind,” he says, “pertain to nonexistence, not to inability. For by examples of this sort it is shown what certain people were at some time, not that they could not have been otherwise. [Col. 1207D] Hence they are rightly found to be culpable. For if they were such because they could not be otherwise, they would be free from blame.”

**Editorial note:** Some editions—BB. and Gallandius—omit *majore* (“greater”).

### 43

See what he has said. I, however, say that an infant born in a place where baptism could not aid him, [Col. 1208A] being forestalled by death, was such—that is, departed without the bath of regeneration—because he could not be otherwise. Let him therefore absolve that child and open to him the kingdom of heaven, contrary to the Lord’s sentence (John 3:1).

**Editorial note:** [Col. 1207D] BB. and Gallandius add the word *Christi* (“of Christ”) after “baptism”; Schottus agrees with our text.

But the Apostle does not absolve him, for he says:

> “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12).

Rightly, therefore, one is not admitted into the kingdom of heaven on account of that condemnation which runs through the whole mass, even though he was not only not a Christian but could not have been one.

### 44

“But,” they say, “he is not condemned, because it was said that all sinned in Adam not because of the sin drawn from their origin at birth, but because of imitation.”

[Col. 1208B] If Adam is therefore called the author of all the sins of those who followed him because he was the first sinner among human beings, why is Abel not placed at the head of righteous human beings rather than Christ, since he was the first righteous person among human beings?

But I am not speaking about an infant. A young man or an old man has died in a region where he could not hear the name of Christ. Could he have become righteous through nature and free choice, or could he not? If they say that he could, behold what it means to make the cross of Christ void: to contend that someone can be justified without it through natural law and the choice of the will (I Cor. 1:17).

**Editorial note:** The reading seems to require, “namely, to make it void without it,” and so forth. BB. and Gallandius have *evacuare sine illa* (“to make void without it”).

Let us say here also, then, that Christ died for nothing (Gal. 2:21). For all could have done this even if he had not died.

And if they were righteous, they would be so because they wished to be, not because they could not be righteous. [Col. 1208C] But if no one could be justified at all without Christ’s grace, let him, if he dares, absolve even a righteous person according to his own words: “Because he was such that he could not be otherwise, he was free from blame.”

**Editorial note:** BB. read *injusti* (“unrighteous”); Schottus and Havercampius read *justi* (“righteous”). Shortly afterward, BB. have *quia idcirco* (“because for this reason”), without *si* (“if”); and a little later they read *sed per Dei gratiam* (“but through God’s grace”), omitting *inquies* (“you will say”). These readings have been restored from the edition of BB. —Gallandius.

### 45

He raises an objection to himself as though made by someone else, and says:

> “He certainly can exist, but through God’s grace.”

Then, as though replying, he adds:

> “I thank your humanity for not merely being content not to attack or refuse to acknowledge my assertion, which you were previously attacking, but for not shrinking from approving it as well.

**Editorial note:** Amerbachius, Erasmus, and several manuscripts have this reading, as does Schottus; BB. and Gallandius read *aut non confiteri* (“or not to acknowledge”). For to say, ‘He certainly can exist, but through him or through it,’ what else is it than not only to agree that he could exist, but also to show how or in what manner he could exist? No one, therefore, approves the possibility of something more than the person [Col. 1208D] who also acknowledges its quality, because quality cannot exist without the thing itself.”

**Editorial note:** Schottus reads *sed per illum aut per illud* (“but through him or through it”); BB. and Gallandius read *sed per illud aut illud* (“but through this or that”). Later, those editions read *quod possit esse … vel qualiter possit* (“that he can exist … or in what manner he can”); a little later, *alicujus rei* (“of something”).

After saying this, he again raises an objection against himself:

> “But you will say: at this point, since you do not mention God’s grace, you appear to deny it.”

Then he replies:

> “Do I deny it, [Col. 1209A] when by confessing the thing I must confess also that through which the thing can be accomplished? Or do you deny it, when by denying the thing you undoubtedly deny whatever it is through which the thing is accomplished?”

He has now forgotten that he was replying to the man who does not deny the thing, whose objection he had shortly before presented as saying: “He certainly can exist, but through God’s grace.” How, then, does he deny the possibility for which he labors so much, when he himself also says: “He can exist, but through God’s grace”?

**Editorial note:** Schottus has the reading translated above; BB. and Gallandius read *ei jam* (“to him now”).

Nevertheless, setting aside the man who now acknowledges the thing, he continues to argue against those who deny that it is possible for a human being to exist without sin. What concern is that of ours? Let him argue against whomever he wishes, provided that he confesses what is denied with the most criminal impiety: that without God’s grace a human being cannot exist without sin.

He therefore says:

> “Whether through grace, assistance, [Col. 1209B] mercy, or whatever it is through which a human being can exist without sin, whoever acknowledges the thing itself acknowledges it.”

### 46

I confess to your Charity that, as I read these things, I was suddenly filled with joy because he did not deny God’s grace, through which alone a human being can be justified. This is precisely what I chiefly detest and abhor in the arguments of such people. But as I continued reading the rest, I first began to grow suspicious from the examples he supplied.

For he says:

**Editorial note:** Schottus has the reading in the text, *Nunc* (“now”); BB. and Gallandius read *Nam* (“for”).

> “Now, if I say that a human being can argue, a bird can fly, and a hare can run, and do not also mention through what these things can be accomplished—that is, the tongue, wings, and feet—have I denied the qualities of these functions, when I have confessed the functions themselves?”

Certainly he seems to have mentioned things that are effective by nature. [Col. 1209C] These members—the tongue, wings, and feet—were created for natures of this kind. He did not posit something like what we wish to understand by grace, without which a human being is not justified; for here the issue concerns natures that must be healed, not natures that must be established.

From this point I began anxiously to read what followed, and I discovered that my suspicion had not been mistaken.

**Editorial note:** Here too we agree with Schottus. Following BB., Gallandius reads *ergo … legere caetera* (“therefore … to read the rest”).

Before I come to that, however, observe what he said.

When discussing the difference between sins, he objected to himself:

> “Since certain sins frequently assail us and cannot all be avoided,”

and he denied that one ought to be reproved “even with a mild correction if they cannot be avoided at all.”

**Editorial note:** BB., Schottus, and Gallandius read: “what certain people say: that certain light sins, because they repeatedly assail us, cannot all be avoided.” Havercampius reads: “that certain [sins] repeatedly assail [us],” correcting *quaedam* to *quidam* and carelessly omitting the intervening words down to *saepe irruant*. —Gallandius.

He evidently failed to attend to the Scriptures of the New Testament, where we learned—as the Apostle says:

**Editorial note:** BB. read *dicimus* (“we say”), though they conjecture *discimus* (“we learn”); Schottus and Havercampius read *didicimus* (“we learned”). Gallandius notes that, after *dicimus*, Augustine immediately continues “that this is the intention,” etc.; these words appear at the beginning of this excerpt, as we noted there.

> “Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me thus?’” (Rom. 9:20).

The complaint of weakness is an ambition for one’s own strength, since the person who seeks a strength peculiar to himself secretly disdains [Col. 1209D] God’s help. Such a person is also the devil, who says, “I will accomplish it by my own powers.”

But I, in accordance with the Apostle, will always glory in my weaknesses (II Cor. 12:9), so that my heart may always say to God:

> “In the shelter of your wings I will rejoice; my soul has clung to you; your right hand has upheld me” (Ps. 62:8).

Thus it is also written:

> [Col. 1210A] “Let your requests be made known before God; and the peace of God, which surpasses every mind, will guard your hearts and bodies in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 4:6–7).

I therefore have weakness, and I rejoice in knowing my weakness. For when I am weak, then I am strong (II Cor. 12:10): strong because I invoke God, who hears me in my weakness and who has most faithfully promised us:

> “I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

It is the particular work of weakness to pray always and everywhere, so that almighty God, who promised not to abandon us, may also not cease to help us.

For Scripture cries out to the weak:

> “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. 104:4).

To this the true and devout confession responds:

> “Behold, as the eyes of servants [Col. 1210B] are upon the hands of their masters, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” (Ps. 122:2).

Great and certain is confidence concerning perfection when the Almighty does what the weak person desires. Again, great and certain is security concerning strengthening when the Almighty preserves the weak and does not destroy them, as it is written:

> “To him who is able to do far more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us, to him be glory in Christ Jesus” (Eph. 3:20–21).

Therefore the Apostle admonishes:

> “Set your minds on the things above, not on the things on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:2–4).

### 47

The fruit of life is holiness; holiness, however, [Col. 1210C] is being without sin. If, therefore, the glory of incorruption is hidden from all human beings at the present time, how do you boast that at this same time you can be clothed in incorruption itself?

For just as the beginning of corruption for a human being was turning aside into sin, so the beginning of incorruption will be not having sin. Who, then, has hidden it before God’s judgment, or taken it from Christ’s bosom and handed it over to you? Or perhaps you understand that because you do not deserve it now, you will receive it from the Lord in the future?

Paul, who instructs us beforehand, says:

> “When this mortal has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?’ The sting of death is sin” (I Cor. 15:54–56).

[Col. 1210D] By this the Apostle shows that no one can in any way insult death and sin until immortality succeeds mortality and incorruption succeeds corruption—when strength, perfected after weakness has been destroyed, takes its place; when there will be neither male nor female, but all will be like the angels of God.

If, however, someone already grows to such a height of holiness that, while living in this flesh, he no longer knows [Col. 1211A] whether he is male or female; if, having received the fullest purity of himself, he has no filthy garments and is like the angels of God; and if he is already surrounded by that brightness promised to the saints, like the radiance of the sun, then he may worthily profess this perfection not merely by his words but by his way of life.

Nevertheless, such presumption is destruction. Rather, it is beneficial for such a person not to listen to and follow his own heart, but Paul, the teacher of the nations, and to pray together with him, so that the Lord may answer him when he prays:

> “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (II Cor. 12:9).

### 48

Therefore, since free choice is effective only in this one matter, let each of us offer himself to God as willing soil:

> “We are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (I Cor. 3:9).

[Col. 1211B] Let him cast into his field the seed, the Word; let him believe in his heart. Let the true farmer himself plant, himself water, himself make fertile, and himself grant growth. What voluntary devotion alone can do in us is to supply faithfully whatever is needed to retain the seed’s root within itself and nourish its abundant fruits; and let it continually awaken its farmer through prayers, lest the enemy be able to sow weeds over it.

Let this be its cooperation in God’s work, with undoubting hope and sincere love. For the Lord Jesus says:

> “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15:5).

Whatever the branch possesses, it possesses from the vine. For the Apostle says:

> “You do not bear the root; the root bears you” (Rom. 11:18).

Why, then, does the branch exalt itself over fruits that appear in it, [Col. 1212A] when everything belongs to the vine—not only that the branch may be able, but also that it may exist at all? Otherwise it will be cut off and thrown into the fire (Matt. 3:10). For it is not the branch but the vine that has power; and what the vine can do, the branch displays.

It is therefore enough for each person to possess something. But let him humbly acknowledge and patiently await from where and where he possesses it, lest, while he does not possess it and believes that he does, the very thing he possesses be taken away from him.

God first expelled the sinning human being from paradise; then, on the cross, Christ first brought the believer into paradise. Rightly, therefore, as long as I am not in paradise and remain in Adam’s land of exile, I do not believe that I am without sin. But if I am transferred into paradise by God’s grace, there—in my perfection, with death overcome and sin destroyed—I will proclaim before God’s presence the eternal glory of his power.

[Col. 1212B] Thus, most blessed priests, I have set forth this matter of faith and simplicity as I was able. Let those who have done harm not be angry with me if, in some respect, they are marked by comparisons of names.

**Editorial note:** The reading may perhaps be *titillantur* (“are teased” or “are pricked”) rather than *titulantur* (“are marked”).

As for the questions, let them bear them calmly; indeed, if they have the fear of God, let them rejoice that the answer given is the true one.

I confess, with Jesus Christ as my witness, that I hate heresy, not the heretic. But, as is just, I avoid the heretic for the time being because of the heresy, since I have both prohibited and rebuked it. Let him detest and condemn it, by word and deed alike, and let him cling to the whole bond of brotherhood, for it is written:

> “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Matt. 13:12).

## Orosius’s Consultation with Augustine, or Memorandum on the Error of the Priscillianists and Origenists

This Consultation is not included in Havercamp’s edition; we have excerpted it, together with the notes, from Gallandius’s *Bibliotheca*, vol. IX. (C)

[Col. 1211C]

### Orosius to the Most Blessed Father Augustine, Bishop

### 1

I had already made a suggestion to Your Holiness, but I was intending to present a memorandum concerning the matter suggested when I perceived that your mind was free from the other necessities of dictation.

But since my lords, your sons, the bishops Eutropius and Paulus, moved by the same concern for the salvation of all as I, your servant [Note: [Col. 1211D] Perhaps read *presbyter*, “priest.”], have already submitted a memorandum concerning several heresies, though they did not indicate them all, it was necessary for me to hasten to set forth and gather together in one place all the trees of destruction, with their roots and branches, and offer them to your fiery spirit, so that, when you have seen the host and examined the wickedness, you may consider what ordering of your strength you can apply.

**Editorial note:** Perhaps the text should read “that you may be able, with whatever arrangement you can, to apply your zeal to virtue.” The Vatican manuscripts read: “that you may be able to apply, with whatever arrangement you can, a zeal for virtue.”

[Col. 1212C] You, most blessed father, must simply tear out and cut down the evil plantings or grafts of others, and scatter the true seed, which we will water from your springs.

I call God as witness and hope for the growth of your work, because that land which now, being cultivated insincerely, produces thankless fruits will eventually advance more freely in abundance unto a hundredfold yield, if you visit it by sending me and filling me with that manna stored up in you.

**Editorial note:** The printed editions read *in sincera cultura exhibet, si eamdem anno illo recondito apud te mandando*: “displays [fruits] in sincere cultivation, if the same … in that year … stored with you … by entrusting.” The printed alternative is corrupt. This has been corrected with the aid of the manuscript of Sigiramnus, or Saint Cigirannus.

Through you may our Lord God—through you, I say, blessed Father—correct by his word those whom he chastised with the sword. I have been sent to you by God; from you, through him, I hope for the outcome, when I consider how it came about that I should come here.

I recognize why I came: I left my homeland without intention, necessity, or consent, [Col. 1212D] driven by some hidden force, [Col. 1213A] until I was brought to the shore of this land. Only then did I recover the understanding that I had been commanded to come to you.

Do not judge me insolent if you receive me as one who confesses. Make me a capable negotiator for my beloved lady, having found the pearl (Matt. 13:46), and let me return—not as a runaway slave whose property has been destroyed.

**Editorial note:** The printed editions read “my beloved lord”; the manuscripts read “my beloved lady,” namely the homeland to which he wishes to return.

We have been torn apart more grievously by wicked teachers than by the bloodiest enemies. We confess the offense; you see the wound. Grant us the medicine, which is the one thing remaining, with the Lord’s help.

Briefly, therefore, I will show both what, having been badly planted before, has grown strong, and what, having later been grafted in still worse, has prevailed.

### 2

Priscillian was more wretched than the Manichaeans in this respect above all: he confirmed his heresy even from the Old Testament. He taught that the soul, which was born from God, [Col. 1213B] proceeded from a certain storehouse; that it declared before God that it would fight; and that it was equipped by the exhortation of angels.

**Editorial note:** The printed editions read *adoratu* (“by worship”); the Vatican manuscripts read *adhortatu* (“by exhortation”).

Then, descending through certain circles, it was seized by evil principalities, forced into various bodies according to the will of the victorious prince, and assigned a written bond.

Hence he also maintained the supremacy of astrology, asserting that Christ had dissolved this bond and fastened it to the cross through his passion. Priscillian himself says in one of his letters:

> “This is the first wisdom: to understand, in the patterns of souls, the natures of divine powers and the arrangement of the body. In this arrangement heaven and earth appear bound, and all the principalities of the world appear constrained to surpass the arrangements of the saints. For the patriarchs possess the first circle of God and the divine bond of [Col. 1213C] souls destined to be sent into flesh, fashioned with the agreement of angels, God, and all souls; they possess it in opposition to the work of the formal army.”

[Note: [Col. 1213D] The Louvain edition alone reads *quae* (“which,” neuter plural) instead of *qui* (“who,” masculine plural).]

And so forth.

He also taught that the names of the patriarchs were members of the soul, because Reuben was in the head, Judah in the breast, Levi in the heart, Benjamin in the thighs, and similarly for the rest.

Conversely, he arranged the signs of the heavens in the members of the body: the ram in the head, the bull in the neck, the twins in the arms, the crab in the breast, and so on. He wished it to be understood that there were eternal darknesses, and that the prince of the world had proceeded from them.

He also confirmed this from a certain book entitled *The Memoranda of the Apostles*, in which the Savior appears to be questioned secretly by the disciples and to show that, in the evangelical parable which says, [Col. 1213D] “A sower went out to sow his seed” (Matt. 13:46), the sower had not been good. He asserted that if he had been good, he would not have been negligent; [Col. 1214A] the seed would not have lain either beside the road, or on rocky ground, or in uncultivated places. He wished it to be understood that this was the sower who scattered captured souls into whatever different bodies he wished.

That book also contains many statements about the prince of moist things and the prince of fire. Priscillian wished it to be understood that all good things in this world are accomplished by art, not by God’s power.

For he says that there is a certain virginal light which God shows to the prince of moist things when he wishes to give rain to human beings. When the prince tries to seize it, he is agitated and sweats, producing rain; and when deprived of it, he arouses thunder with his bellowing.

He spoke of the Trinity in words alone. For, asserting a unity without any existence or property, he removed the “and” and said that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one Christ.

**Editorial note:** The Vatican manuscripts read: “having removed the ‘and,’ he said, ‘the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one Christ.’”

### 3

[Col. 1214B] Then two fellow citizens of mine, Avitus and another Avitus, when truth alone had already exposed such shameful confusion by itself, sought foreign lands. One went to Jerusalem, the other to Rome.

When they returned, one brought back Origen, the other Victorinus. Of these two, one yielded to the other: both, however, condemned Priscillian.

We know little of Victorinus, because, still almost before his works had been published, Victorinus’s follower yielded to Origen. Thus many magnificent doctrines began to be put forward from Origen, which truth itself would surpass on the basis of a slight occasion.

For we learned from him a sufficiently sound doctrine concerning the Trinity: that everything that had been made was made by God, that everything was very good, and that everything was made from nothing; and then sufficiently sober explanations of the Scriptures.

**Editorial note:** The same manuscripts read: “then, with a sufficiently sober explanation of the Scriptures, all these things…”

[Col. 1214C] All these teachings were immediately accepted by wise men after a faithful purification of the earlier errors. Only the offense concerning “from nothing” remained.

They had been persuaded to believe that the soul exists, but they could not be persuaded that it had been made from nothing. They argued that the will could not be “from nothing.”

**Editorial note:** The learned Franciscus Florius, in *Dissertation 1 on Bachiarius*, §3, p. 24, conjectures that the text should read: “because the will of God cannot be nothing.” To confirm this restoration, the same scholar observes that Saint Augustine, examining the question proposed to him by Orosius, sharply and clearly proves that from the soul’s being said to have been made from nothing it by no means follows that God’s will, by which it was made, is nothing. The holy Doctor’s words are these, in *Against the Priscillianists and Origenists*, chapter 3: “For it is said to him, ‘You have power whenever you will’ (Wis. 12:18), whether there is something from which it may be made or whether there is not; the will is sufficient where power is supreme. How, then, is it asserted that, in what is created from nothing, the will of the creator is nothing, when something can therefore be created from nothing because the creator’s will is sufficient for itself even without matter?”

[Col. 1214D] This point remains almost to the present day.

**Editorial note:** The Vatican manuscripts read “remains until now.”

These two Aviti, together with the Greek Saint Basil, who taught these matters in a most blessed manner, nevertheless transmitted certain teachings from Origen’s books incorrectly, as I now understand.

**Editorial note:** This is the manuscript reading; the printed editions read *ut nunc per intelligunt* (“as they now understand through …”), an evidently defective alternative.

First, they said that everything, before it appeared as created, had always remained made in God’s wisdom, using these words: “For God did not begin to make whatever he made by making it.”

Then they said that angels, principalities, powers, souls, and demons have one origin and one substance, and that a place was assigned to an archangel, soul, or demon according to the quality of its merits, using these words: “A lesser fault earned a greater place.”

Finally, they said that the world was made for this reason: [Col. 1215A] so that the souls that had sinned previously might be purified in it.

They also taught that the eternal fire in which sinners are punished is neither true fire nor eternal, saying that “fire” means the punishment of one’s own conscience. As for “eternal,” according to the Greek etymology, they said that it does not mean everlasting. They added testimony from the Latin, because Scripture says “forever and unto the age of the age” (Ps. 9:6; 10:16), placing “unto the age of the age” after “eternal.” In this way, they taught that all souls of sinners would, after the purification of conscience, return to the unity of Christ’s body.

They also wished to make the same assertion about the devil, but they did not prevail: since the good substance created in him could not perish, they said that, once his wickedness had been entirely burned away, the devil’s substance would eventually be saved.

Concerning the Lord’s body they taught as follows: since the Son of God, coming even to us [Col. 1215B] after so many thousands of years, had not been idle until then but had preached remission to angels, powers, and all higher beings, and since, when he visited them, he assumed the quality of their form, he passed through to the tangibility of flesh in the appearance of assuming it. He brought this to an end through his passion and resurrection, and then, [Col. 1216A] until he came to the Father, made it thin again by ascending.

**Editorial note:** The editions of Amerbachius and Erasmus read: “in the appearance of flesh, he passed through this passion more thickly,” and so forth.

Thus, they taught, the body had never truly been deposited, nor could God, reigning in any body, be circumscribed.

**Editorial note:** The Vatican manuscripts, together with Ar. and Er., read *usquam fuisse* (“had existed anywhere”) instead of *umquam fuisse* (“had ever existed”).

They also said that the creature subjected to corruption (Rom. 8:20), understood as unwilling, was the sun, moon, and stars; and that these are not elemental lights but rational powers. They serve corruption because of the one who subjected them in hope (ibid.).

**Editorial note:** Amerbachius and Erasmus read “understood to mean.”

### 4

This has been briefly set forth, insofar as I have been able to retain it, so that, once all the diseases have been surveyed, you may hasten to apply the medicine.

The truth of Christ is in me (II Cor. 11:10). Out of the venerable reverence I have for your holiness, I would not dare to be insolent unless I recognized, through the evident judgment and ordering of God, that you had been chosen to offer remedies to that great and extraordinary people, [Col. 1216B] to whom, just as a wound has been inflicted because of their sin, so a cure is owed after the wound; and that I had been sent.

Remember me, most blessed Father, and the many who, with me, await your word as dew descending upon them. Be willing to remember us.

## A.D. 426. Leporius, Monk and Priest

(From Gallandius’s *Bibliotheca of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. IX.)

## Prolegomena

### 1

[Col. 1215C] Leporius, a Gaul by nationality, appears first to have lived as a monk at Massilia. Since he excelled the others in that monastic way of life through integrity of conduct and innocence of character, he later supposed that he had achieved this by his own choice and effort alone, not by God’s help, and began to profess the Pelagian doctrine. Gennadius gives this testimony about him.

**Bibliographic note:** Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 59.

Cassianus gives a similar account.

**Bibliographic note:** Cassianus, book I of *On the Incarnation*, chapter 4, p. 908, Paris edition, 1642.

Leporius did not merely present himself as a follower of Pelagius; advancing further, he fell into the impiety that Nestorius later spread more widely in the East. Thus, according to Cassianus’s testimony [Note: [Col. 1215D] The same author, in the same place.], he was counted among the first or among the most important proponents of this later heresy in Gaul.

[Col. 1216C] Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, also committed the same account to memory.

**Bibliographic note:** Facundus, book I, chapter 4, p. 422, Paris edition, vol. II of Sirmondus’s works.

The author of the *Collations*, whom we have just cited, writes that this poisonous pestilence arose in his own time, especially in the city of Beligara—or, according to another reading, “from the great city of Veligara.” It is therefore uncertain whether he intended Belica on the Rhône in Bresse or Augusta Treverorum.

**Bibliographic note:** Cassianus, cited work, chapter 2, p. 902.

Sirmondus and Garnerius, adhering to the latter reading, understand the city of Trier; Tillemont does not disagree.

**Bibliographic notes:** Sirmondus, works, vol. I, p. 345, note a; Garnerius, *Dissertation 2 on Marius Mercator*, in the *Appendix to Augustine*, p. 145; Tillemont, vol. XIII, p. 1040, note 86 on Saint Augustine.

It was in that city, then, that Leporius first absorbed or taught his errors. [Col. 1217A] Afterward, when he had returned to Provence, he published them in a certain letter, which produced grave scandal and an offense against charity, as he himself admits in his *Book of Correction*.

**Bibliographic note:** Leporius, *Book of Correction*, §2, below.

Although Cassianus and other Gallic teachers admonished him to renounce his impiety, he disregarded their salutary counsel, and he was finally and deservedly expelled from the Church by Proculus and Cyllinius, Gallic bishops, because of his presumptuous error. This is clear from the letter of the African fathers to those same bishops, which is appended to Leporius’s book.

### 2

Exiled from his native soil, he crossed over to Africa with several followers of his depravity. There, by the favor of God and through the efforts of certain African bishops—especially Augustine—[Col. 1217B] he recognized and abandoned his error and professed sound doctrine.

But because he had caused scandal to many in Gaul, he sent a letter bearing witness to his faith to Proculus, Cyllinius, and the other bishops of Gaul, and confirmed it with this subscription:

> “I, Leporius, wishing to express from the depths of my heart the booklet dictated according to my understanding, in which, God willing, I shall maintain my faith to the end, have subscribed to it after it was presented before the holy bishops in the church of Carthage.”

**Bibliographic note:** The same work is meant.

Concerning this book of Leporius, Cassianus writes:

> “Thus he magnificently condemned the persuasion he had wrongly conceived, so that his correction is almost no less admirable than the unimpaired faith of many—for the first thing is never to fall wholly into error; the second is to renounce it properly.”

**Bibliographic note:** Cassianus, cited work, chapter 4, p. 908.

He adds:

> “Having therefore come to his senses, he confessed his error with grief and without shame, not only in Africa, where he then was and still is, [Col. 1217C] but also sent letters of tearful confession and lamentation to all the cities of Gaul, so that where his deviation had first become known, his correction might also become known; and those who had previously been witnesses of his error might afterward be witnesses of his correction.”

### 3

Furthermore, certain learned men—Garnerius [Note: Garnerius, in the cited Appendix, p. 145, note 2], Quesnellius [Note: Quesnellius, on Epistle 134 of Saint Leo, vol. II, p. 508, Lyon edition, 1700], Tillemontius [Note: Tillemont, vol. XIII, p. 884], and the editors of the works of Norisius [Note: Ballerini, on the works of Norisius, vol. IV, p. 889]—have judged that this kind of booklet of Leporius was composed by Augustine, both on the basis of its style and because of its modes of expression. They were especially influenced by the fact that, among the testimonies attached to Saint Leo’s Epistle 165 [Note: Works of Leo, vol. I, p. 1392, Ballerini edition], the booklet of Leporius is inscribed under Augustine’s name. They say that the same thing was done in the second session of the Council of Chalcedon [Note: Councils, vol. IV, p. 1234]. Nor is it read otherwise in Theodoret [Note: Theodoret, Dialogue II, Works, vol. IV, p. 108, no. 2].

But here it must be observed that the passage extracted from Leporius’s booklet is one and the same passage wherever it occurs in the authors just mentioned [Note: Leporius, Booklet of Correction, § 3, below]. Consequently, the statement concerning Augustine as the author of Leporius’s booklet must be said to have proceeded from a single epistle of Leo. As for the Council of Chalcedon, that same Leonine epistle is recited there. Theodoret, moreover, when he brings forward the same words, is understood to have copied them from that same epistle of Leo.

In any case, perhaps the great pontiff attributed that little work to Augustine for no other reason than that he knew it had been approved by him and endorsed by his subscription. For it is established that the booklet was signed by four African bishops, among whom Augustine is prominent. On that occasion, moreover, when they wrote a common letter to Proculus and Cyllinius, bishops of Gaul, they included, among other things, the following words, which deserve particular attention [Note: Letter of the African Bishops, below, col. 1231]:

> “Just as he [Leporius] was received by us through his personal presence, so let him be received by you through his letter. We have thought it right to subscribe to this letter also with our own hand, TESTIFYING THAT IT IS HIS.”

But, says Sirmondus [Note: Sirmondus, on Leporius, in his works, vol. I, p. 357, note a, Paris edition, 1696], although this letter of the African fathers is written in the name of four bishops, it nevertheless so strongly bears the style and character of Augustine that there seems to be no doubt that it was dictated by him. It has indeed been listed among Augustine’s letters [Note: Augustine, Epistle 219, Works, vol. II, p. 810]. On this matter, however, it will be useful to consult the learned writers of the *Literary History of France* [Note: *Literary History of France*, vol. II, pp. 173 ff.], who vigorously maintain that the little work inscribed under his name is the offspring of Leporius.

### 4
