We learn that this booklet enjoyed great authority among the ancients, and that its author, Leporius, was counted among the defenders of the Catholic faith against Nestorius. This is established above all by Cassian, who, after excerpting several passages from the same booklet, concludes his judgment in these words [Note: Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, book I, chapter 6, p. 912]:

> “All the African bishops from whom he was writing, and all the Gallican bishops to whom he was writing, approved this confession of his [Leporius]—that is, the faith of all Catholics. Nor has there yet been anyone at all to whom this faith was displeasing without the charge of unbelief; for it is a profession of impiety to deny an approved faith.”

Moreover, Pope John II took from the same Leporian booklet a testimony by which he confirmed the dogma of the faith, while also asserting that the booklet had been approved by the African synod. For it had evidently been reread in the presence of the holy bishops in the church of Carthage, as Leporius himself writes [Note: Leporius, *Booklet of Correction*, § 10, below]. Hear the words of the distinguished Roman pontiff [Note: John II, Epistle III, in the collection of the Councils, vol. V, p. 898, Labbé edition, Venice]:

> “Leporius, in the letter which Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, and blessed Augustine, and the African synod confirmed,” and so forth.

To this may be added that, in the petition of Basil the deacon and archimandrite and of the other monks, presented to the emperor Theodosius in the year 430 and preserved among the acts of the Council of Ephesus [Note: Council of Ephesus, part I, chapter 30, in the collection of the Councils, vol. III, p. 974], Leporius is numbered among the holy Fathers of the Church who, in explaining the mystery of the Incarnation, taught that Christ is truly God. (Nor should Quesnellius be heeded when he vainly persuades himself [Note: Quesnellius, cited work, p. 508] that the Leporius praised there by Basil was someone other than our Leporius—namely, a bishop of some see—on the grounds that he is listed among the bishops who defended Christ’s divinity.)

Facundus likewise praises the booklet of the same Leporius in such a way that he uses its testimony to establish orthodox faith [Note: Facundus, cited work, p. 422]. Finally, as we saw above, Gennadius lists its author among the illustrious men who became famous through ecclesiastical writings [Note: Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 59].

### 5

Thus, after Leporius—who had formerly taught corrupt errors against the faith as a monk in Gaul—had given so distinguished an example of his doctrine and piety in Africa, he was eventually ordained a presbyter of the Church of Hippo after taking up residence in that region. This is sufficiently clear from Cassian and Gennadius. The former says [Note: Cassian, cited work, chapter 4, p. 908]:

> “Leporius, then a monk, now a presbyter.”

The latter says [Note: Gennadius, cited work]:

> “Leporius, still a monk, afterward a presbyter.”

Among learned men, however, there is a dispute as to whether our Leporius, already a presbyter, is the same man who is named among the presbyters of the Church of Hippo in the ecclesiastical acts by which Saint Augustine designated Heraclius as his successor [Note: Augustine, Epistle 213, Works, vol. II, p. 788].

Those published acts are said to have been issued during the twelfth consulship of Theodosius and the second consulship of the emperor Valentinian, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October—that is, in the course of the year 426. At approximately the same time, the holy doctor delivered a second sermon on the life and conduct of clergy, in which he praises this same Leporius at greater length in the following words [Note: Augustine, Sermon 356, no. 10, Works, vol. V, p. 1388]:

> “I speak to you who perhaps do not know; for many of you do know: the presbyter Leporius, although distinguished by birth in the world and born among his own people in a most honorable station, yet, already serving God and having abandoned everything he possessed, I received as a poor man,” and so forth.

By these words Augustine plainly represents this presbyter of Hippo as having been both a monk and—what is the central point—as a foreigner. Norisius properly noticed this [Note: Norisius, *History of Pelagianism*, book I, chapter 23, Works, vol. I, p. 235]. Consequently, it seems reasonable to think that he is the same Leporius who had earlier gone from Gaul to Africa as a monk, where the holy father received him as a poor man.

It is preferable, however, to consult the learned men whom we mentioned shortly before, who, after examining the Augustinian passage just quoted more carefully, reached this very conclusion [Note: *Literary History of France*, vol. II, pp. 168 ff.]. Sirmondus likewise held this opinion [Note: Sirmondus, on Leporius, in his works, vol. I, p. 345, note a, near the end]. The distinguished scholars Baronius [Note: Baronius, under the year 420, § 14], Garnerius [Note: Garnerius, in the cited Appendix, p. 141], Tillemontius [Note: Tillemont, vol. XIII, p. 1039, note 85 on Saint Augustine], and the Ballerini [Note: Ballerini, on the works of Norisius, vol. IV, p. 889], however, held the contrary view.

### 6

Now, Leporius was still living in Africa in the year 430. For Cassian, speaking of him, says [Note: Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, book I, chapter 4, p. 908]:

> “Thus, having come to his senses, not only in Africa, where he was then—and NOW IS,” and so forth.

That is what he says in his books *On the Incarnation*. This work, written against Nestorius while Nestorius was still occupying the see of Constantinople, is known to have been composed before the Council of Ephesus, held in 431, and therefore around the year 430, as Norisius [Note: Baronius, under the year 430, § 90; Norisius, *History of Pelagianism*, book I, chapter 23, p. 235, and book II, chapter 12, p. 212, Works, vol. I] and Tillemontius [Note: Tillemont, vol. XIV, pp. 189 ff.] judged after Baronius.

If the evidence discussed thus far is now carefully weighed, it will nearly be possible to determine the time when Leporius published his booklet. Learned men have circulated differing opinions on this matter. Norisius places Leporius’s conversion, and therefore his confession, no later than the year 410, and indeed places it before that year [Note: Norisius, *History of Pelagianism*, book I, chapter 23, p. 234, and book II, chapter 3, p. 278]. Sirmondus thinks that it occurred around the year 425 [Note: Sirmondus, on Leporius, p. 345, note a, Works, vol. I], and Garnerius in the preceding year, 424 [Note: Garnerius, in the cited Appendix, p. 141]. Pagius assigns it to the year 427 [Note: Pagius, under the year 420, § 13], after Saint Augustine had published his book *On Correction and Grace*. Tillemontius [Note: Tillemont, vol. XIII, pp. 879 and 1039, note 85] and the Ballerini [Note: Ballerini, on Norisius, Works, vol. IV, p. 889] held the same view.

But setting aside these opinions, the very learned men whom we mentioned earlier say [Note: *Literary History of France*, vol. II, pp. 167 ff.] that the *Booklet of Correction* was composed by Leporius in the year 418, or at the latest in 419. For, they say [Note: Ibid., p. 93], the death of Proculus, bishop of Marseilles, should not be postponed beyond those years, as Tillemontius himself acknowledges [Note: Tillemont, vol. X, p. 699]. The booklet of Leporius and the letter of the African Fathers concerning Leporius’s conversion are addressed to this bishop; nor can another bishop Proculus be invented in place of the bishop of Marseilles in order to weaken the force of this argument and introduce another method of calculation.

We pass over the other arguments, none of them insignificant, by which these learned men confirm the proposed date. They also answer an objection drawn from the time when Saint Augustine published his book [Col. 1221A] *On Correction and Grace*, and at the same time show that Leporius’s errors were already well known to that holy doctor by the year 421, when he published his *Enchiridion*, in which work he also openly touched upon them [Note: Augustine, *Enchiridion*, no. 10, p. 210].

After duly considering these matters, we confidently adopt this last opinion. We know that it was later approved by Sirmondus for the reason that, as we reported above, Pope John II asserted that Leporius’s letter had been confirmed by the African synod. “If,” he says [Note: Sirmondus, on Leporius’s letter, Works, vol. I, p. 345, note a], “he called it African—the letter we possess being after the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, in the year of Christ 419—it must accordingly be concluded that Leporius’s correction occurred in that same year.”

### 7

As for what remains, only fragments of Leporius’s booklet, copied from Cassian’s books *On the Incarnation* and preceded by the letter of the bishops of Africa, were first published by Sirmondus in 1629 among the Councils of Gaul [Note: Sirmondus, *Councils of Gaul*, vol. I, p. 52]. In the following year, 1630, he published the complete work among five dogmatic treatises of the ancients, from a manuscript of the monastery of Hérivaux.

It subsequently appeared in the royal Luparensian edition of the Councils [Note: Royal Councils, vol. IV, pp. 669–671], as well as in the edition of Labbé [Note: Labbé, Councils, vol. II, p. 1678, Paris edition] and that of Hardouin [Note: Hardouin, Councils, vol. I, p. 1263]. Garnerius also attached the same work, purged of numerous errors, together with the letter of the African bishops, to his edition of Marius Mercator [Note: Garnerius, Marius Mercator, vol. I, p. 224, and in the Appendix to Augustine, pp. 142 ff.]. It was likewise inserted into the Lyon Library of the Fathers [Note: Library of the Fathers, Lyon, vol. VII, p. 14]. Finally, with Garnerius’s corrections, it appears in the collection of Sirmondian works [Note: Sirmondus, Works, vol. I, p. 345, Paris edition]. We have commissioned this edition to be set in type because it is much more carefully presented than the others.

---

# Booklet of Correction, or Satisfaction, of Leporius the Presbyter

Containing a confession of the Catholic faith concerning the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, together with abhorrence of his former error, addressed to the bishops of Gaul. (C)

To the most blessed and most venerable lords, priests of God, Proculus and Quillenus:

Leporius, the insignificant.

### 1

I do not know what I should first accuse in myself, my revered and most blessed lords and priests; I find nothing in myself that I can excuse. Thus ignorance joined with pride, foolish simplicity with harmful persuasion, fervor with intemperance, and—in more accurate terms—weak faith diminished by itself all took root and grew together in me, so that, after having obeyed so many and such great influences at once, I am both confounded by it and filled with amazement that I have been able to reject those same things from my mind.

I therefore acknowledge my offense, and willingly become my own accuser. But I hope for mercy, because I acted in ignorance. For my sin would be without excuse if, knowing perfectly, I had deliberately undertaken some course of action.

I call God as witness to my soul: I believed my error to be the truth, and I counted obscure darkness as the clearest light. Zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, deceived me in my heedlessness. But now, as we believed would be pleasing to Your Beatitude, His mercy has recalled me from deviation—walking through harsh places and thickets—to the straight road.

Thus crooked things have become straight for me, and rough places paths made level. And, instructed by all my fellow priests and your brothers, now that the mist has been wiped away, I understand in what respect I had been blind. Therefore recognition itself makes me a suppliant for the truth. I confess: I erred in ignorance, and in certain matters I exceeded the rule of truth while I thought that I was holding it completely.

My ignorance has been exposed, and this weighs upon me all the more because I tried, amid the scandal of many, to defend what—as is now clearer than daylight—I had presumed to defend more from the error of human judgment than from the reasoning of faith.

[Note: Garnerius reads, “But what else could have been done?” Baun.]

But since nothing else could happen except that my own foolishness should remain alive in me, when I had made myself my own teacher and pupil—would that humility had broken the presumption which ignorance had nourished! But alas for me, for I have been found both rash and proud.

Yet now, with your pardon, I pass over these matters, and I will not delay in dealing with what is now pressing. I will hasten to heal the wounds that I inflicted while I was whole. There will be no shame in accepting medicine, since there was no cautious care in preserving health. From where discord arose, let peace be born.

### 2

Accordingly, I ask, by the profession of this letter and by the authority of your holiness, that the letter which I once wrote simply, but which, as I acknowledge, was arranged unfaithfully in certain respects—the source of scandal and an offense against charity—be treated as something to be trampled underfoot and abolished in that part or respect in which it is shown to have been issued against the truth through ignorance. Thus it may become known and evident to everyone that, by a just judgment, what was hostile to the faith and contrary to the truth has been cut away from the body of that same letter together with its condemnation.

[Note: Garnerius reads, “Certain brothers cried out, I confess, my lords,” and so forth. The editor.]

I cry out, and truly confess, my lords: certain brothers saw the inner matters more clearly, while we groped at things far more external; and, standing in our own darkness, we attributed blindness to those who were looking more closely.

But now, with the Lord’s favor, our eyes at last opened, we behold the true light together with them. In that same grace of light, with the clay of healing placed upon our eyes by the true physician, we recover our sight. We look upon Jesus Christ the Lord—not as we were previously deceived, but as He truly is—with the most sincere gaze.

In accordance with the truth of the Creed, what under our former definition we were afraid to say—that God was born of Mary, although we were not led by any impiety but were being misled by error—we now confess with complete steadfastness.

[Note: Garnerius reads: “Although we did not then deny that Christ, the Son of God, was also born of holy Mary, as you yourselves remember; but we did not at all,” and so forth. The editor.]

Yet we denied that Christ, the Son of God, was then also born of holy Mary; and, as you yourselves remember, because we paid insufficient attention to the mystery of faith, we said that not God Himself was born as man, but a perfect man was born with God. We were afraid, of course, that we might assign a human condition to divinity.

O foolish wisdom! As though, if God did not disdain to be born with man, man would, because of the prejudice of his condition, disdain to be born! Or as though the former were possible but the latter perhaps impossible.

### 3

[Note: Garnerius reads, “I plainly believe that God cannot do this one thing,” and so forth. The editor.]

I plainly believe that God cannot do what He does not will. If He willed to be born, I most certainly believe that He could do what God willed, since the condition of God can suffer no danger.

Nor did the man made for us consider it unworthy to be born from a human being, since He did not consider it unworthy even to make the woman from whom the man would be born.

[Note: Cassian copied this passage as far as the words “He was mercifully mingled with human nature.” The following variant readings are noted: “as though God seemed to act upon lower things”; “and, instead of the one Son who is God, who was born from the Father before the ages, for us in time”; “always on behalf of the faith”; “as He knows how to pour Himself out wholly”; “in a kind of fused mode.” Garnerius.]

If, therefore, failing to perceive this power of God, we become wise according to our own judgment and reasoning, and, so that God may not seem to act upon lower things, say that man was born with God in such a way that we assign separately what belongs to God to God alone and separately what belongs to man to man alone, then we unmistakably introduce a fourth person into the Trinity and begin to make two Christs out of the one Son of God—not one.

May the Lord and God Christ Himself avert this from us. Therefore we confess our Lord and God Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, who was born from the Father before the ages, and who in the last time was made man, God born of the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-virgin.

Confessing both substances, God and man, we receive them with the devout credulity of faith as inseparable. From the time when the flesh was assumed, we say that everything belonging to God passed into man in such a way that everything belonging to man came into God.

By this understanding, the Word became flesh—not because through any conversion or change He began to be what He was not, but because, by the power of the divine dispensation, the Word of the Father, never departing from the Father, graciously deigned properly to become man. The Only-begotten was incarnate in that secret mystery which He alone knows. It is ours to believe; it is His to know.

Thus God the Word Himself, assuming everything that belongs to man, is man; and the man assumed, receiving everything that belongs to God, cannot be anything other than God. Yet, because He is said to be incarnate and mingled, this must not be understood as a diminution of His substance. God knows how to mingle without corruption of Himself, and yet to mingle truly. He knows how to assume in Himself in such a way that no increase accrues to Him, who knows how to pour Himself out wholly without suffering any loss.

### 4

Let us not, therefore, in order to accommodate our weak understanding, infer from visible examples and experiments involving created things entering into one another that God and man were mixed together and that some body was formed by such a confusion of flesh and Word.

Far be it from us to believe this: we must not imagine that, by some fused process, the two natures were reduced to one substance. Such a mixture is the corruption of both parts.

For God—who is capable of what cannot contain Him, penetrating what cannot be penetrated, filling what cannot be filled, everywhere wholly present and everywhere spread out through the infusion of His power—was mercifully mingled with human nature; human nature was not mingled with divine nature.

The flesh therefore advances into the Word; the Word does not advance into the flesh. Yet most truly the Word became flesh. But, as we have said, this occurred properly and personally, not naturally together with the Father or the Holy Spirit. For the Only-begotten God, true God, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one in nature, is another in person.

We do not say that the Father Himself is the Son, nor again do we say that the Son is the Father; nor do we call the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son. Rather, distinguishing the persons according to their properties, we properly call God the Father “Father,” and properly call God the Son “Son,” and properly confess God the Holy Spirit as “the Holy Spirit.” Although three times we say “God, and God, and God,” we do not believe in three Gods, but in one God made perfect in the Trinity of His omnipotence.

### 5

[Note: Cassian, John II in his Letter to Avienus, and Facundus of Hermiane, book I, chapter 4, praised this passage, though not all at equal length. John II quoted only the first sentence; Cassian quoted through the words “fullness and power”; Facundus only through “let Him be named, and truly be so.” The editor.]

Therefore Jesus Christ, God-man, the Son of God, is properly born for us from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-virgin. Thus the Word and the flesh become one with one another, while each substance remains naturally in its perfection, without prejudice to itself; the divine communicates with humanity, and the human participates in divinity.

He is not one God and another man, but the very same God who is also man; and conversely, the man who is also God, Jesus Christ, is one Son of God, both named and truly existing as such.

Therefore we must always act and believe in such a way that we do not deny that the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the true God whom we confess to have been eternally equal to the Father and equal to the Father before the ages, became God-man from the time when He assumed flesh.

Nor should we believe that He progressed into God by stages and times, being of one condition before the resurrection and another after the resurrection, but that He always possessed the same fullness and power.

### 6

And because He bore all our weaknesses—that is, the weaknesses of our nature—and truly assumed our affections in Himself according to the flesh, to prove that He was truly man, while nevertheless following the same course of our mortality, by power, certainly, and not by necessity, the Evangelist says (Luke 2:52): He advanced in age and wisdom; He was hungry; He was thirsty; He was wearied; He was scourged; He was crucified; He died; He rose again.

For this reason He was not changed from the nature of divinity. We have already professed above that the nature of divinity is unconvertible, unchangeable, and impassible.

[Note: This passage too was quoted by Cassian through the words “by the power of God.” Garnerius.]

But because God the Word graciously descended into man by assuming man, and through the assumption of God man ascended into God the Word, the whole Word of God became wholly man.

For God the Father did not become man, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Only-begotten of the Father. Therefore one person of flesh and Word must be understood, so that we may faithfully and without any doubt believe that the one and same inseparable Son of God, always of a twofold substance, was also called a giant of twofold substance in the days of His flesh, and that He truly always bore everything belonging to man and truly always possessed everything belonging to God.

For although He was crucified in weakness, He lives by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4). Therefore we are no longer afraid to say: God born according to God and born from man according to man; God suffered; God died; and so forth.

[Note: Garnerius reads, “We are afraid to say God born from man and, according to man, God,” and so forth. Baun.]

Rather, we glory in saying that God was born, and that the same God, according to man, suffered. “I am not ashamed of the gospel,” says the Apostle, “for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (Romans 1:16).

Indeed, it is the power of God for salvation to believe that God suffered according to man. But for one who does not believe, it is regarded as the weakness of God, leading to destruction, not to believe that God was crucified according to the flesh.

Again the same Apostle says: “But we preach Christ, and Him crucified”—truly, the power of God and the wisdom of God—“because what is foolish of God is wiser than men, and what is weak of God is stronger than men” (1 Corinthians 1:23–25).

For what seems so foolish and so weak to unbelieving men as hearing that God, the Son of God, was crucified? Yet it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe (ibid., 21).

For this above all constitutes our faith: that we believe the only Son of God— not adopted, but proper; not imaginary, but true; not temporary, but eternal—endured all things for us according to the flesh; that He did not struggle for Himself but for us; not for His own sake but for ours, because we lay fallen; and that He mercifully came down from on high to the depths, because, as the Apostle says:

> “Although He was in the form of God, He did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,” and so forth (Philippians 2:6 ff.).

### 7

What could be clearer than to recognize from this testimony the mystery of so great a dispensation? In the form of God, who is there except God? And let us see how the fountain of fullness emptied Himself.

Was it not when the form of God took the form of a servant? When the supreme Lord graciously assumed the things belonging to a servant? And when, for the sake of our forgiveness and mercy, by bearing and doing what is lower than Himself, the Word made flesh emptied in person what He possesses in nature, and, having become obedient in man in the true condition of humanity, restored in Himself through humility and obedience to our nature what had perished in Adam through disobedience?

Though dead in the flesh, He always lives, giving life in the spirit together with the Father in all things; and, having been raised in the flesh by the Father, He will never again die.

He becomes for us the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), who is the Only-begotten of the living God and living before the ages. Poor for us in time, and needy in man, He received for us what He always possesses abundantly in the Father.

“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are His judgments and unsearchable His ways!” (Romans 11:33).

For us He received the name that was given to Him.

[Note: Perhaps one should read, “everything that He received.” Baun. I would rather read, “the name that He received.” The retention of “name” is sufficiently suggested by the Apostle’s immediately following passage.]

But He bestows on everyone, because God, the giver of all things, recognizes Himself as God in giving and knows Himself as man in receiving, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11).

This is our faith, and this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High (Psalm 76:11), in the betterment of correction. Thus we believe; thus we hold fast. And this is not from ourselves (Ephesians 2:8), for it is God’s gift—not from the merit of our own wisdom, so that we may not glory in ourselves.

For we are His workmanship, having long ago been created in Christ (ibid., 10); but now again, through the apostolic men laboring to give us birth, we have been restored in the same Christ. To Him, therefore, be honor and glory forever.

### 8

But concerning what we most foolishly advanced in that letter, though in ignorance, and now confess to be detestable—namely, in ascribing to Christ labor, devotion, merit, and faith—we judge these things so unfitting for the Son of God that, recalling what we said, we regard it as the extreme blindness of our folly. We see plainly how truly certain persons were moved against us on rational grounds: although we never held this in our heart, we almost made Christ like each one of the saints and, assigning to Him who is God over all (Romans 9:5) those things which belong to bare and simple mortality, in some way placed Him among the rest in their number.

Although He is called the head of the body (Ephesians 5:23; Colossians 1:18), and truly is the head of the body of the Church, and is known according to the flesh to have come, without sin, from the same mass from which the whole human race descends, yet He who is unique must not be counted among the rest. Nor must those things that can have measure be referred to Him, because it was said of Him: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 2:34). For where there is fullness of divinity, there is neither measure nor limit. He who accomplishes all things by infinite and boundless power does not know how to attain an end of merits through labor, devotion, faith, or merit.

[Note: No plausible sense can be extracted; therefore one must undoubtedly read, “He indeed becomes man,” as Garnerius observed. Baun.]

He indeed becomes man, and is truly born man according to the flesh; but He does not cease to be God. He is nourished, advances, grows, matures, and, like a lamb silent before its shearer (Isaiah 53:7), endures insults and is scourged; and the author of life, coming in the flesh, does not refuse the accursed death. Yet He undergoes all these things not by necessity, as one of us does, but willingly deigns to assume them, having power to lay down His life and power to take it up again (John 10:18).

### 9.

I consider it also absolutely necessary not to suppress the following point.

[Note: [Col. 1227D] On account of this assertion, and another preceding it, Leporius was accused of denying divine grace [Col. 1228D], of excessive praise of free will, and of association with the Pelagians. GARN.]

In the same letter, straying into a similar error, I added that our Lord Christ had fulfilled everything that belonged to the sufferings in such a way that, as a perfect man, he was in no respect assisted by the help of the divinity. For I wished to designate in Christ a perfect man in such a way that I might assert the Word of the Father to be foreign to these sufferings, and tried to prove that the man alone, by himself, had done all these things through the capacity of mortal nature, without any assistance from the divinity. I was truly blind: I confessed that the man had been assumed by God, yet I did not wish those things that belonged to the man himself to have been assumed by God.

[Col. 1228B] In this respect, God had undoubtedly assumed the whole man into himself so that those things which we think unworthy of God might not be performed by the man alone, through a natural judgment, but that God, through the man and in the man—he himself having become man for us—might fulfill them by the power and mystery of the divine dispensation. Thereafter, so that nothing might be lacking to my folly, I, a most learned scribe confirming things not understood on the basis of things not understood, thought that the words I had set down above ought to be understood in this way: I tried to apply to this very matter the testimony in which it is written, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. XXI, 1). And for that reason I maintained that the Lord of glory had uttered this cry on the cross because the perfect endurance of the man, with the divinity providing no assistance whatever, was being tested amid such great sufferings.

Therefore, if he uttered this voice while suffering for the sake of proving human endurance, then, for the testing of that same endurance, he ought also to have cried out in the same words when he was scourged. He ought likewise to have spoken the same words when he bore that many-spined crown of wounds, where there were as many punishments as thorns he received in mockery. Or perhaps these things were lighter for Christ, while those were heavier. I think that he who deigned to possess one will for undergoing all these things had one and the same strength for suffering them all.

He therefore cried out, as it is written, and, hanging upon the wood of the cross, first sent this utterance forth to death—not in order to demonstrate in himself a human and perfect endurance, which was proved by the circumstances themselves and by evident facts without any testimony of the voice, but in order truly and manifestly to show that, according to the flesh, he, the Son of God, was about to die. And, as though using the voice of the flesh itself, putting the past in place of the future—because, through the death of the cross, the earthly body necessarily had to be abandoned by God for a time—he testified to us beforehand, before it happened, that it was to be abandoned not only by God but also by his own soul, which was united with God.

[Note: [Col. 1228D] This passage must be read cautiously, although several Fathers—and indeed three of very great renown—have thought that the body, abandoned by the divinity, lay in the tomb for the three days during which it remained there: Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 20 and 60; Hilary, canon 53 on Matthew; Ambrose, *Treatise on the Creed*, chapter 13. GARN.]

For after the spirit had been handed over, the dead flesh could not have cried out this; otherwise, who would believe Christ to have truly died? God did not abandon in the sufferings the man whom he had deigned to suffer in the man according to the flesh. Rather, in death, and in accordance with the law governing human departure, the divinity, together with the soul united to it, did not leave the crucified man to punishment, but abandoned the lifeless flesh for a time. Thus Christ, the Son of God, then lay dead in the tomb, just as that same Christ, the Son of God, descended to the underworld; as the blessed Apostle says: “But that he ascended, what does it mean except that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens” (Eph. IV, 9–10).

That same Lord and our God Jesus Christ, the only-begotten of God, descended with his soul to the underworld; he himself ascended with soul and body into heaven. Thus, both here and in the age to come, may we venerate him as perfect God and perfect man, and as the same Son of God, true God, forever and ever.

### 10.

I therefore believe and confess this Lord, my God, in accordance with the great mystery of piety: that he was born in the flesh, suffered in the flesh, died in the flesh, was raised in the flesh, taken up in the flesh, and glorified in the flesh. Likewise, I properly believe that he himself, in that same flesh, will come to pass judgment upon the living and the dead, and that from him each person will receive an everlasting reward according to his own deserts.

And so that I should leave no room here for anyone’s suspicion, I then said—or rather, I responded to the objections—that our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the man, was ignorant. But now I do not merely presume to say this; I even anathematize the earlier opinion expressed on this point, because it is not permissible to say that the Lord of the prophets was ignorant even according to the man.

As for the remaining questions concerning these matters, we put them forward either as an intention, or as an exhortation, or in a fraternal discussion.

[Note: [Col. 1229C] Garnerius reads, “either in an inquiry or in an exhortation.” BAUN.]

If perhaps we differed more in understanding than in faith, since it would take too long to examine each point individually, we testify that, in accordance with the faith of this letter, we either accept or reject all of them as the order of the Catholic Church maintains. We most sincerely confess the Lord Christ, not professing one thing while holding another in our heart.

Indeed, to condemn the infamy of every heresy among us—for we have always known ourselves, according to a pure conscience, to be Catholics from Catholics—we pronounce anathema upon all heretics: Photinus, Arius, Sabellius, Eunomius, Valentinus, Apollinaris, Manichaeus, and all who oppose sound doctrine. For although we have fallen through tongue or understanding, we have not fallen through will or heart, as it is written: “He who slips with his tongue but not from the heart—for who is there who does not sin with his tongue?” (Ecclus. XIX, 16–17).

Indeed, my most venerable and blessed lords and priests, insofar as I was able, as a son of peace, according to the Apostle’s saying, “Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. II, 10)—offending not in minor matters but in great ones—I made myself guilty of everything with all my heart.

But in this I proved the perfect charity of those who persecuted me—not, however, without cause: I was received and corrected with such swift and complete love as was the perfection of their purpose and zeal in pursuing me when I had gone astray.

For my part, I speak with God as my witness: peace is desired and coveted by me above all things. For the rest, we now ask again and again: grant us pardon by forgiving us, and obtain it for us by praying on our behalf. Fathers, I wish you to live for God.

I, Leporius, have subscribed, before the holy bishops in the Church of Carthage, to this little book dictated according to my understanding and reread there, in which I desire to express my faith from the depths of my being—a faith which, God willing, I shall hold to the end.

I, Domninus, hold and confess this faith, and have subscribed to it.

[Note: [Col. 1229C] This subscription, which was the last of all in Sirmond’s edition, seems more correctly placed here in the *Supplement to the Councils of Gaul*. ID.]

I, Bonus, hold and confess this faith, and have subscribed to it.

Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, having received and reread the little book presented by Leporius, have subscribed.

Augustine, bishop of the region of Hippo Regius, having received and reread the little book presented to us by Leporius, have subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 1229C] Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, book I, chapter 3, calls this city Hippo Regius. Hence Wesseling, in his notes on the *Ancient Roman Itinerary*, p. 20, suspects that “Hipporegiensis” should be read here.]

Florentius, bishop of the people of Hippo Diarrhitus, having received and reread the little book presented to us by Leporius, have subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 1230C] Solinus, *Polyhistor*, chapter 30: “Greek horsemen founded the most celebrated towns: Hippo, later called Regius, and another Hippo, named Diarrhitus, from the strait flowing between them.” Ruinart makes further learned observations about this city in his notes on the *African Provincial Register*, p. 219. [Col. 1230D] GARN.]

Secundus, bishop of the Church of Aquae, or of Megarmitanae,

[Note: [Col. 1230D] Garn. reads “of Magarmitanae.”]

having received and reread the little book presented to us by Leporius, have subscribed.

## APPENDIX

[Col. 1231]

[Note: [Col. 1231C] Although it was written in the name of four bishops, it nevertheless so strongly bears the style and character of Augustine that there seems no doubt that it was dictated by him. Perhaps it was also composed by others, or certainly at the direction and in the name of others. SIRMOND.]

## LETTER OF THE AFRICAN BISHOPS

[Note: [Col. 1231C] In the Liège manuscript this letter bears the following prefixed title: “Letter of Aurelius, Augustine, Florentius, and Secundinus to their fellow bishops Proculus and Cylinnius concerning Leporius, who, because he held certain unsound opinions and did not think rightly concerning the faith, was rebuked by the holy fathers mentioned, Proculus and Cylinnius, and expelled from his place on account of this presumption of his flesh; he came to Saint Augustine and the other men named above by the grace of refuge. Having then been beneficially corrected by them and restored to sound doctrine, he was reconciled to his bishop, together with his companions, by his own letter expressing Catholic belief.”]

which they sent to the bishops of Gaul together with the aforementioned little book of Leporius.

To our most beloved and honorable brothers and fellow priests Proculus and Cylinnius, Aurelius, Augustine, Florentius, and Secundinus send greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 1231A] When our son Leporius, having been deservedly and suitably corrected by your holiness for the presumption of his error, came to us after he had been driven out from there, we received him in salutary agitation, so that he might be corrected and healed. For just as you obeyed the Apostle by admonishing the unruly, so we obeyed him by consoling the fainthearted and supporting the weak (1 Thess. V, 14).

For since he had been overtaken, as a human being, in some offense (Gal. VI, 1)—and not a small one—in that he did not think rightly or hold the truth concerning the only-begotten Son of God, who was the Word in the beginning, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word (John I, 1), and concerning the fact that, when the fullness of time came (Gal. IV, 4), the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John I, 14), he denied that God had become man, lest an unworthy change or corruption should affect the divine substance, which is equal to the Father. He also failed to see that he was introducing a fourth person into the Trinity, something wholly alien to the soundness of the Creed and to Catholic truth.

We instructed him as best we could, with the Lord’s assistance, in a spirit of gentleness. For when the chosen vessel gave this admonition, he added: “Pay attention to yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI, 1)—lest certain people should rejoice that they had attained spiritual progress to such a degree that they thought they could no longer be tempted as human beings. He also added the salutary and peaceful command that we should bear one another’s burdens, for thus we shall fulfill the law of Christ. “For whoever thinks he is something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” (ibid., 2–3), most beloved and honorable brothers.

Yet perhaps we could not have completed his correction at all if you had not first condemned the faults that were in him. [Col. 1232A] Thus the same Lord and physician of ours, using his vessels and ministers, who said, “I will strike, and I will heal” (Deut. XXXII, 39), struck the swollen man through you and healed the suffering man through us. The same administrator and provider of his household, through you, destroyed what had been badly built, and through us restored what had been properly arranged. The same diligent cultivator of his estate, through you, uprooted the barren and harmful growth, and through us planted what was useful and fruitful.

Let us therefore give the glory not to ourselves but to his mercy, in whose hand both we and our words are. And just as our humility praised your ministry in the case of the son mentioned above, so may your holiness also rejoice in our ministry.

Receive him, therefore, whom our paternal and fraternal heart has corrected with merciful severity. For although one thing was done through us and another through you, one and the same charity made both necessary for fraternal salvation. One God therefore did it, since “God is love” (1 John IV, 8).

Accordingly, just as he was received by us through his presence, so let him be received by you through his letter. We have thought it proper to subscribe to this letter also with our own hands, testifying that it belongs to him.

We do not doubt that your love will both gladly receive this correction of his and make it known to those for whom his error was a scandal. For those who came with him to us were corrected and healed along with him, as is clearly demonstrated by their subscriptions, which were made in our presence.

It remains that, rejoicing in our brother’s salvation, you may deign in turn to make us rejoice through a reply expressing your blessedness. We wish you, our most beloved and honorable brothers, good health in the Lord, mindful of us.

## In the Year of Our Lord 428. Evodius, Bishop of Upsala.

[Col. 1233]

# BOOK ON FAITH, AGAINST THE MANICHAEANS

Although this book has often been attributed to St. Augustine, and although the closeness of its style and subject seems to demand that it be placed near his works, we must assign it among the appendices to the works of the holy Father mentioned above. See volume XLII of our *Patrologia*, column 139.

## In the Years of Our Lord 400–430. Several Fathers Contemporary with St. Augustine and in Literary Correspondence with the Illustrious Doctor.

[Col. 1233]

### [LETTERS]

During the first thirty years of the fifth century, several holy men flourished. Their writings, like those of Evodius, have been mixed with or appended to the works of St. Augustine, and not without reason, since they are nothing other than letters addressed to the bishop of Hippo, which ought to be read together with his replies.

Here, therefore, only the names of the authors will be indicated, together with the places either assigned to their writings or pertaining to them. They are found in volume XXXIII of the *Patrologia*, while Augustine’s works are in volume II:

Nebridius, letters 5, 6, 8. Augustine, 3, 4, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14.

Maximus of Madaura, letter 16; Augustine, 17.

Nectarius, letters 90, 103; Augustine, 91, 104.

Severus, letter 109; Augustine, 62, 63, 110.

Dioscorus, letter 117; Augustine, 118.

Consentius, letter 119; Augustine, 120.

Volusianus, letter 135; Augustine, 132, 137.

Marcellinus, letter 136; Augustine, 128, 129, 133, 138, 139, 143; Jerome, 165.

Macedonius, letters 152, 154; Augustine, 153, 155.

Hilary of Syracuse, letter 156; Augustine, 157.

Evodius, letters 158, 160, 161, 163; Augustine, 159, 162, 164, 169.

Timasius, letter 168.

Hesychius, letter 98; Augustine, 197, 199.

Valentinus, letter 226; Augustine, 224, 225.

Quodvultdeus, letters 221, 223; Augustine, 222, 224.

Prosper, letter 225.

Darius, letter 230; Augustine, 229, 231.

Longinianus, letter 234; Augustine, 233, 235.

Pascentius, letter 240; Augustine, 238, 239, 241.

Audax, letter 260; Augustine, 261.

**Martyrs of Ágreda, whose field is venerated.** Com. A. C. 300, no. 40. Two of their bodies are in the convent of the Virgins of Huelgas near Burgos. One of them was called St. Ibineus.

**The four factions of the charioteers:** the Albana, Veneta, Prasina, and Russata factions. Com. A. C. 120.

**The Alans, together with the Vandals and Suevi: when did they come into Spain?** Dex. A. C. 424. They are the first of the four beasts shown to Daniel in chapter VII. See the Appendix to A. C. 430, at the end of this book.

**Alba, a city near Acci—what city was it?** Com. A. C. 300, no. 55. Its martyrs. Ibid.

**Whence comes whiteness in monks’ clothing?** Com. A. C. 419, no. 3.

**The municipality of Alba—what was it?** Com. A. C. 300, no. 5. Its presbyter Eucharius took part in the Council of Illiberis. Ibid.

**Alexander, martyr of Pydna, or of Pyocium.** Dex. A. C. 95.

**Alexander, martyr and companion of Antonina.** Dex. A. C. 100; Com. no. 14, where you will find their acts; and Dex. A. C. 285.

**Alexander, son of Simon of Cyrene.** His deeds. Dex. and Com. A. C. 112, no. 10. He suffers at Carthage. Ibid.

**Alexander, martyr and companion of Victor and Martin, who were killed at Flaviobriga.** Com. A. C. 182, no. 3.

**Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem.** Com. and Dex. A. C. 206.

**Alexander, emperor.** Dex. A. C. 234. He is killed in A. C. 237.

**Alexander, bishop of Alexandria.** Dex. A. C. 317.

**Alone, what city was it?** Com. A. C. 52, no. 1. Its evangelist preacher. Ibid.

**Alotus, Nero’s judge.** See Halotus.

**An altar erected over the body of St. James by his disciples.** Dex. A. C. 42; Com. no. 4.

**Ambratia, what city?** Com. A. C. 268, no. 7. Ambratianus, bishop and martyr. Ibid. The Ambratians build Placentia in Cantabria. Dex. A. C. 384. They expel the Priscillianists. Dex. A. C. 424. Concerning their bishop Splendonius.

**Ambrose becomes bishop of Milan.** Dex. A. C. 369. In what year? The matter is discussed at length there in the Commentary. He writes to Justus, bishop of Vicus. Dex. A. C. 382, and against the Arians. Dex. A. C. 384. See Dex. and Com., A. C. 388, no. 3.

**Ammonius, lector of St. Theodore, bishop of Caesaraugusta, suffers martyrdom.** Dex. A. C. 71.

**Ammonius, martyr of Rhodes, with his companion.** Dex. A. C. 300; Com. no. 44.

**Amphilochia, a city, the same as Amphilochium.** See under that word.

**Amphilochium: what city and of what kind?** Com. A. C. 138, nos. 5, 6, and 7. Its virgins and martyrs. There and in Dexter.

**The Church of Amphilochium, erected by St. Peter of Braga.** Com. A. C. 36, no. 2.

**Amphilochius, commander and martyr of Barcelona.** Com. A. C. 138, no. 2.

**The amphitheater at Rome burned.** Dex. A. C. 220 and A. C. 252.

**Amphitria, what city?** Com. A. C. 66, no. 21. See Dex. A. C. 366.

**Anacletus and Cletus, one and the same Roman pontiff.** Dex. and Com. A. C. 86, no. 1.

**Ananias, disciple of Christ: where and when did he suffer martyrdom?** Dex. A. C. 70; Com. no. 5.

**Ananias, martyr of Juliobriga, with his companions.** Dex. A. C. 308; Com. no. 20.

**Anastasia, a Spanish virgin, cares for the bodies of the holy apostles together with her sister Basilissa.** Dex. A. C. 66; Com. no. 3.

**Anastasius, a Mantuan presbyter, flourishes at Lisbon with his companions.** Dex. A. C. 308, no. 12. He suffers martyrdom. Dex. A. C. 353.

**Pope Anastasius.** Dex. A. C. 398 and 401.

**Anatolia, Roman virgin and martyr: where was she killed?** Com. A. C. 255, no. 4.

**Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea.** Dex. A. C. 280.

[Col. 1236] **The Council of Ancyra: in what year was it convened?** Dex. and Com. A. C. 316.

**Andeolus, martyr of Nivaria.** Dex. A. C. 208. He suffers in Spain. Ibid.

**Andrew the Apostle sets out to preach.** Dex. A. C. 41; Com. no. 5. His female disciples. See Polyxena and Maximilla.

**England visited by St. James the Apostle.** Dex. A. C. 41; Com. no. 4.

**Anicetus, Roman pontiff: how many years did he sit?** Com. A. C. 156, no. 1.

**The Year of the City in which Christ was born.** Com. A. C. 1, no. 2. From what day and month is it to be reckoned? Ibid.

**Ansanus, martyr, led to the faith by St. Maxima of Caurium.** Com. A. C. 360, no. 5.

**Antigonius, martyr of Ebura, with his companions.** Com. A. C. 300, no. 20.

**Antima Maximilla.** See Antonia Maximilla.

**Antonia Maximilla, disciple of Blessed Andrew the Apostle.** Dex. A. C. 100; Com. no. 23. She suffers martyrdom. Dex. ibid. and in the Commentary.

**Antonina, companion of Alexander, suffers among the Olcades.** Dex. A. C. 100; Com. no. 14; and Dex. A. C. 285.

**Antonina, virgin, killed near Caea in Gallaecia.** Dex. and Com. A. C. 300, no. 16.

**Antoninus Pius, emperor.** Dex. A. C. 139. He dies. Dex. A. C. 162. He obtains victory through the prayers of Christians. Dex. A. C. 175.

**Antoninus Caracalla, emperor.** Dex. A. C. 217, 218, 219. He is killed. Dex. A. C. 224.

**Antoninus, martyr of Juliobriga, with his companions.** Com. A. C. 300, no. 19.

**Antoninus, martyr of Pamea.** Dex. A. C. 308; Com. no. 21. It is proved that he died in Spain. There in the Commentary.

**Marcus Antonius Verus and Marcus Aurelius, emperors.** Dex. A. C. 162.

**Antony the abbot is born.** Dex. A. C. 252.

**Antonius, martyr of Iturissa, with his companions.** Dex. A. C. 300; Com. no. 61. Elsewhere Antoninus. See “Ring” in the Commentary.

**The ring and scarf (*orarium*) of the saints Emeterius and Chelidonius flew up to heaven.** Com. A. C. 299.

**Apamea, what city?** Com. A. C. 382, no. 9. See Pamea and Tela.

**Apamus, martyr of Juliobriga, with his companions.** Com. A. C. 300, no. 19.

**Apellius, martyr of Seville, with his companions.** Dex. A. C. 308; Com. no. 16.

**Apodemius, martyr of Caesaraugusta, one of the eighteen companions.** Com. A. C. 300, no. 50.

**Apollinaris, bishop of Ravenna.** Com. A. C. 37. He comes to Spain. Dex. A. C. 50.

**Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis.** Dex. A. C. 174.

**Apollo, martyr of Alba, with his companions.** Dex. A. C. 300; Com. no. 55.

**Apollonius the Stoic.** Dex. A. C. 150.

**Apollonius, senator, writer, and martyr.** Dex. A. C. 190.

**Apollonius, martyr of Juliobriga, with his companions.** Com. A. C. 300, no. 19.

**The first part of the Apology for Dexter’s Chronicle.** See after the Author’s Life.

**The second part of the same Apology.** See at the end of this work.

**In what year and on what day did the Apostles divide the provinces of the world among themselves by lot?** Dex. A. C. 34; Com. no. 10. Which province fell to each? Ibid. and at length in Com. no. 15. When were they separated from one another? Ibid. no. 12.

**They appoint seven deacons from among the Greeks.** Ibid. How long did they remain in Jerusalem and Judaea? Ibid. no. 10, and Com. A. C. 41, no. 5.

[Col. 1237] **In what year did the martyrdom of the Apostles Peter and Paul occur?** Dex. and Com. A. C. 68.

**Apuleius Diocles.** See Diocles.

**Aquae, a city near Toledo.** Dex. A. C. 130. Which city? Com. ibid. It was elevated to an episcopal see. Ibid.

**Martyrs of Aquae.** Dex. A. C. 352.

**Aquae-Calidae: what city was it, and who were its martyrs?** Dex. A. C. 300; Com. no. 25.

**Aquae-Quintianae: what city was it, and who were its martyrs?** Dex. and Com. A. C. 95, no. 2.

**Aquila Ponticus preaches in Spain.** Dex. A. C. 70. His deeds. In the Commentary. He suffers martyrdom. Dex. A. C. 95.

**Aquilina, martyr of Pax Augusta, with her husband and son.** Com. A. C. 308, no. 24.

**Aquilius Severus, to whom Lactantius wrote, flourishes.** Dex. A. C. 370. Another of the same name, his kinsman. Ibid.

**Araducta, what city?** Com. A. C. 95.

**Arcadius, disciple of St. James, appointed by him the first bishop of Juliobriga.** Com. A. C. 37. He consecrates an altar to his master. Dex. A. C. 42; Com. no. 4. He suffers martyrdom. Dex. A. C. 60.

**Arcadius, martyr of Ursaon.** Dex. A. C. 110.

**Arcadius, martyr of Iturissa, with his companions.** Dex. A. C. 300; Com. no. 45.

**Arcadius, emperor, son of Theodosius.** Com. A. C. 388, no. 9.

**Archisynagogus Crispus—who was he?** See Crispus.

**Augustalis of Arles was not bishop of Arles but of Illiberis.** Com. A. C. 382, no. 7, and Dex. A. C. 388.

**Argenteola, what city?** Com. A. C. 300, no. 36. Its martyrs. There in Dexter.

**Arguments proving that Dexter’s work is genuine.** In Apol. I p., § 1. Namely, the purity and excellence of the style, the copyists’ errors, the defects in the history, the dedication, and so forth. Ibid.

**Arguments to the contrary have no force.** Ibid. § 2.

**Aristides of Athens, defender of the faith.** Dex. A. C. 128.

**Arlanco, a river of Spain.** Dex. A. C. 308; Com. no. 21. Its martyr. Ibid.

**Armentarius of Rome, writer of the Acts of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria.** Dex. A. C. 285.

**Arnobius, African rhetorician.** Dex. A. C. 330.

**Arrianus, distinguished philosopher.** Dex. A. C. 149.

**Arsa-Mariana, what city?** Com. A. C. 95, no. 4.

**Artemidorus Baeticus, martyr with his companions.** Dex. A. C. 308; Com. no. 15.

**Artemisia, a Spanish Jewess, wonderfully converted to Christ.** Com. A. C. 424, no. 11.

**Asclepiades, bishop of Antioch.** Dex. A. C. 214.

**Asianus, bishop of Sardica, defends the faith in his writings.** Dex. A. C. 173.

**Asion-Gaber was a seaport on the Mediterranean.** Com. A. C. 66, no. 22, where Tarsis is discussed.

**The Assumption of the Mother of God to the Son: in what year did it occur?** Discussed at length in Com. A. C. 48, no. 1.

**Asta, what city in Spain?** Com. A. C. 112, no. 3, and Com. A. C. 208, no. 8. There is also discussion of Asta in Italy.

**Martyrs of Asta.** Dex. in both years and numbers, and A. C. 300; Com. no. 31.

**The city of Astigi, or Astiagi, where was it?** Com. A. C. 66, no. 5. Its bishop was Crispinus the martyr. Ibid. Its presbyter Eumentianus took part in the Council of Illiberis. Com. A. C. 300, no. 5.

**Astorgius, bishop and martyr.** Dex. A. C. 91.

**Martyrs of the Astures.** Dex. A. C. 300; Com. nos. 34 and 36.

**The Church of Asturica, erected by St. James, with St. Ephraem appointed its first bishop.** Dex. and Com. A. C. 37.

**Asturius Serranus, a young man, flourishes at Toledo.** Dex. A. C. 370. He becomes a lector. Dex. A. C. 380. He becomes bishop of Toledo. Dex. A. C. 396. He attends the Council of Toledo. Com. A. C. 386, no. 1. Concerning the same man, Dex. A. C. 407. In what sense is he called by St. Ildephonsus the ninth bishop of Toledo? Com. A. C. 423, at the end. He discovers the tombs of the holy martyrs of Complutum and founds the church and see of Complutum. Dex. A. C. 423. He writes their ecclesiastical office. Ibid. He dies. Dex. A. C. 424. Where is his body? Com. there.

**Ataulphus, first king of the Goths in Spain, husband of Placidia Augusta.** Dex. A. C. 407. Concerning him in the Appendix to Dexter’s Chronicle. His death and epitaph. Dex. A. C. 430, at the end.

**Athanasius, disciple of St. James and first bishop of Caesaraugusta.** He was sent by the Spaniards to Peter, and for what reason? Com. A. C. 35, no. 7. Concerning the same man, Dex. and Com. A. C. 37. He consecrates an altar to his master. Dex. A. C. 42; Com. no. 4. He preaches in Celtiberia and Carpetania. Dex. and Com. A. C. 50, no. 7. He suffers martyrdom. Com. A. C. 60, no. 1.

**Athanasius’ judgment concerning Hosius, already dead.** See Hosius. Hosius is acquitted in the Council of Corduba. Dex. A. C. 356. He comes to Spain. Com. A. C. 352, no. 1.

**The Athenians receive laws from the emperor Hadrian, a Spaniard.** Dex. A. C. 125.

**The Athenian Library founded by the same emperor.** Dex. A. C. 134.

**Atocha, the image of the Mother of God at Madrid: how ancient is it?** Com. A. C. 50, no. 1.

**Attuvi and Aruci, what cities?** Com. A. C. 95, no. 5.

**Atubi, what city?** Com. A. C. 300, no. 5. Its presbyter Felicissimus took part in the Council of Illiberis. Ibid.

**Audentius, deacon of Toledo.** Dex. A. C. 360. He becomes bishop of Toledo. Dex. A. C. 366. His books against the heretics. Dex. A. C. 368. He builds colleges for young men. Dex. A. C. 370. He attends the Council of Caesaraugusta. Dex. A. C. 384. He writes against the heretics. Dex. A. C. 385.

**Auditus, martyr of Blitabrum near Segovia.** Dex. A. C. 208.

**Augurius, martyr of Tarragona, with his companions.** Dex. and Com. A. C. 268, no. 5.

**Augusta-Valeria, what city?** See Setabis.

**Augustalis, bishop of Illiberis, died at Arles in Gaul.** Dex. and Com. A. C. 382, no. 7. See also Dex. A. C. 388.

**Augustine institutes monasteries.** Dex. and Com. A. C. 406, no. 1. To what extent did Abbot Joachim foretell the restoration of the Augustinian monks? See the Apology at the end of this work. Concerning the same monks, see Dex. and Com. A. C. 429, no. 3. Concerning Augustine, Com. A. C. 400, no. 2.

**Aulus Altimus Paternus.** See Paternus.

[Col. 1238] **Aulus Cornelius Palma, nobleman of Toledo.** Dex. A. C. 91. He held the consulship at Rome with Gaius Sosius Senecio. Com. ibid. Concerning Cornelius Palma, his kinsman.

**Aulus Victor, bishop of Barcelona.** Dex. A. C. 139.

**Aurelian, emperor.** Dex. A. C. 273, 276, and 277.

**Ausonius of Bordeaux, uncle of St. Paulinus: what did he write to him while Paulinus was detained in Spain?** Com. A. C. 396, no. 1.

**The most ancient anonymous author: what did he say about the dwelling places of Noah’s sons?** Com. A. C. 66, no. 22.

**How many authors and of what kind does the Illustrator examine?** Apol. I p., § 3.

**The Author’s life.** See at the beginning of the work and in the Eulogies.

**Auxentius, heretical bishop of Milan.** Com. A. C. 369, no. 2. There were two men of this name. Ibid.

**Avitus, martyr in the Fortunate Isles.** Dex. and Com. A. C. 105, no. 6.

**Avitus, bishop of Barcelona.** Dex. A. C. 299.

**Avitus of Braga.** Com. A. C. 400, no. 2.

**Avitus of Tarragona:** two men bore this name and came from the same country. Com. A. C. 400, no. 2, and Dex. A. C. 429.

**Aza, martyr of Tuy, with 150 companions.** Dex. and Com. A. C. 300, no. 25. His marvelous acts. In the Commentary.

## B
## B

Bachillus, a distinguished bishop of Asia. Dex. A.C. 198.

Baetis, a city—also called Utriculum—which one? Com. A.C. 180, no. 2; and Dex. A.C. 308, Com. no. 15.

Martyrs of Baetica under Nero. Dex. A.C. 60.

The bishops of the province of Baetica attended the Council of Nicaea. Dex. A.C. 324.

Baetyrus, which city? See Berela.

Baga, which city? Com. A.C. 353, no. 2. Gracianus, bishop of Carthage, was born there. Ibid.

Balbinus, emperor, Spanish by descent. Dex. and Com. A.C. 268, no. 5.

Balcagia, which city? Com. A.C. 138, no. 6.

Balconius, bishop of Braga. Com. A.C. 386.

In what year did the baptism of Christ occur? Com. A.C. 31.

When did the baptism of the centurion Cornelius occur? Dex. A.C. 40.

Barbatus, a presbyter, attended the Council of Iliberis. Com. A.C. 300, no. 5.

The savage incursion of the barbarians into the Spains. Dex. and Com. A.C. 423, no. 6, and 424, no. 1.

Barbesola, which city? Com. A.C. 300, no. 5. Its presbyter Januarius attended the Council of Iliberis. Ibid.

Barca, which city? Com. A.C. 300, no. 5. Its presbyter Emeritus attended the Council of Iliberis. Ibid.

The praises of the city of Barcelona. Seek them in the Life of the Author.

Its church was founded by St. James. Dex. and Com. A.C. 37, no. 8.

Which bishops? I, first part of the Apology, § 2.

See also under the entries Theodosius, Lucius, Fulta, Severus, the other Severus (both martyrs), Avitus, Mademarius, Pacianus, Lampadius, Etherius, and Sedis, its founder.

The people of Barcelona entered into friendship with the people of Toledo. Dex. A.C. 100.

Martyrs of Barcelona. Dex. A.C. 138; and under the entries Etherius, bishop; Severus; Cucuphas; Eulalia; Philetus; and Laeda.

A bishop of Barcelona attended the Council of Nicaea. Dex. A.C. 324.

[Col. 1239] Bareas was a Christian. Dex. and Com. A.C. 89, no. 9.

The apostle Barnabas came to Spain. Dex. A.C. 50. He suffered martyrdom. Dex. A.C. 61.

Baronius incorrectly assigns the year of the City in which Christ was born. Com. A.C. 1, no. 2.

He is not to be followed when he denies that St. Petronilla was truly the daughter of St. Peter. Com. A.C. 34, no. 4.

Nor does he hold a correct view concerning St. James’s arrival in Spain for the sake of preaching. Com. A.C. 36.

Nor concerning the antiquity of the Epistle of St. James. Com. A.C. 37, no. 7.

Nor concerning the year of Paul’s ascent to Jerusalem after his conversion. Com. A.C. 38, no. 1.

Nor concerning the consecration of St. James’s church. Com. A.C. 42, no. 4.

He contradicts himself when he discusses the year of the Apostles’ death. Com. A.C. 68.

He is not to be followed when he criticizes Jerome’s letters to Chromatius and Heliodorus concerning the publication of the Martyrology. Com. A.C. 384, no. 3.

Nor when he speaks of the mission of Paul Orosius. Com. A.C. 400, no. 2.

The apostle Bartholomew set out to preach: in what year? Dex. A.C. 41, Com. 2.

Basilides, heresiarch. Dex. A.C. 136.

Basilides, philosopher. Dex. A.C. 150.

Basilides, bishop of Astorga, deposed. Dex. and Com. A.C. 255, no. 2.

Basileus, a disciple of St. James, became the second bishop of Braga. Dex. and Com. A.C. 37, and Dex. A.C. 110, no. 2.

Basil, the first bishop of Carthage in Spain, a disciple of St. James, consecrated by him. Dex. and Com. A.C. 37, no. 8.

He consecrated an altar to his teacher. Dex. A.C. 42, Com. 2, no. 4.

He suffered martyrdom. Dex. A.C. 60.

Basil the Great wrote to Audentius, bishop of Toledo. Dex. A.C. 368.

Basiliscus, martyr of Évora, with his companions. Com. A.C. 300, no. 20.

Basilissa, also called Basilla, a Spanish virgin and martyr, and her deeds. Com. A.C. 138, no. 5.

Bassa, virgin and martyr of Carthage, with her female companions. Com. A.C. 308, no. 5.

Bastetana, which city? Also called Bassetana. Com. A.C. 300, no. 5. Its bishop Eutychianus attended the Council of Iliberis. Ibid.

Baudelius, martyr of Cénticium. Dex. A.C. 356.

The war of Jerusalem. Dex. A.C. 66. The Jewish and Samaritan war is resumed. Dex. A.C. 200.

Belsinia, a city of Carpetania. Dex. and Com. A.C. 255, no. 3.

Benedictus, a Spanish bishop to whom St. Melchiades wrote. Com. A.C. 299, no. 3.

Benignus, deacon and martyr, brother of St. Vincent, bishop of Mevania. Com. A.C. 100, no. 21.

Berela, where was the city? Dex. and Com. A.C. 105, no. 4, and Com. A.C. 50, no. 5.

Berillus, a bishop of distinction. Dex. A.C. 230.

Who reduced the fragments of Berossus to five books? Dex. A.C. 300, Com. no. 13.

Besulcum, which city of Lusitania? Dex. A.C. 145.

Betulo, a city. There are two cities of this name in Spain. Com. A.C. 66, no. 7.

Which different libraries were examined by the Elucidator? I, first part of the Apology, § 3.

[Col. 1239] By whom was the library of the Church of Toledo supplied? Dex. A.C. 424.

St. Paternus, apostle of the Bilbilitani. Dex. A.C. 94.

The praises of the city of Bilbilis. Com. ibid.

Blanda, which city? Com. A.C. 156, no. 2. Its martyrs. Dex. ibid.

Blitabrum, which city? Com. A.C. 208, no. 3.

Bolanus. See Florentius of Seville.

Bolanus Rusticus, a Spanish consular official, father of Bolanus Florentius the martyr. Dex. A.C. 116.

Bonifacius of Caldeaqua: was he a member of the Augustinian order? Dex. and Com. A.C. 429, no. 3.

Bonosus, martyr who suffered at Blanda, with his companion Maximianus. Dex. A.C. 156.

Bonosus, Spanish emperor. Com. A.C. 285, no. 1.

Bonosus, martyr of Urgavo, with his companion. Dex. A.C. 308, Com. no. 4.

What is the Bosphorus in Abdias? Com. A.C. 37, no. 5.

A small shrine at Braga, erected by St. James in honor of the Mother of God. Hugo of Portugal, in the Author’s Eulogies.

The Church of Braga, founded by St. James, with St. Peter appointed there as its first bishop. Dex. and Com. A.C. 37, no. 8.

Bishops of Braga. See under the entries Peter, Basil, Ovidius, Caledonius, Senagris, Pancratianus, Balconius, and Paternus.

Martyrs of Braga. See under the entries Sylvester, Susanna, and Victor the Catechumen.

The Council of Braga under Pancratianus, and its complete acts. Com. A.C. 423, no. 6. When was it held? There, at the end.

The proper breviaries of many churches: what light did they shed on this work? I, first part of the Apology, § 3.

Bricius, bishop of Évora, a most illustrious martyr. Dex. A.C. 308, Com. no. 1. Where did he suffer? Ibid. His acts. Ibid.

Briena, virgin and martyr of Segura. Dex. A.C. 308, Com. no. 13.

Briga, an ancient Spanish word meaning “city.” Com. A.C. 54.

Britain traversed by St. James. Dex. A.C. 41. And by the apostle St. Peter. Com. A.C. 66, no. 21.

The synod of Bordeaux against Priscillian. Dex. A.C. 388.

Victoria, martyr of Burgos: who was she? Com. A.C. 300, no. 4. The martyrs Centolla and Helena. Ibid., no. 13.

## C

Caea, which city of Gallaecia? Com. A.C. 139, no. 4.

Martyrs of Caea. Ibid., and Com. A.C. 300, no. 3, together with Dex.

Caecilianus, martyr of Zaragoza, with eighteen companions. Com. A.C. 300, no. 40.

Caecilius, a disciple and lector of St. James. Com. A.C. 37, no. 8.

He was ordained bishop at Rome by St. Peter and sent to Spain. Dex. A.C. 43 and 44.

Where did he preach? Dex. A.C. 54.

His books were found again. Com. ibid. There concerning his book composed in the Spanish language.

He suffered martyrdom. Dex. A.C. 57.

The Caepori, a people of Nearer Spain: who were they? Com. A.C. 308, no. 2.

The Church of Zaragoza, founded by St. James, with St. Athanasius I appointed there as its bishop. Dex. and Com. A.C. 37, no. 8.

It was the first of all churches dedicated to the Mother of God. Dex. A.C. 38.

Bishops of Zaragoza. See under the entries [Col. 1240] Athanasius, Theodorus, Valerius, and Valerianus.

Martyrs of Zaragoza under Nero. Dex. A.C. 60.

Innumerable martyrs under the Deacon. Dex. A.C. 300, Com. no. 49.

Engratia and her eighteen companions. Ibid., no. 50.

Lambertus. Ibid., no. 51.

Two others. Ibid., in Com. no. 52.

The Council of Zaragoza against Priscillian. Dex. A.C. 384.

Prudentius the poet was born at Zaragoza, his mother being from Calahorra: and in what year? Dex. and Com. A.C. 580.

Caesarius, martyr of Iturissa, with his companions. Dex. A.C. 300, Com. no. 45.

Caesarobriga, which city? Dex. and Com. A.C. 407. Juvencus the poet came from there. Ibid.

Caesonius Maximus. Dex. A.C. 66, Com. no. 15. He was Seneca’s companion in exile on Corsica. Ibid., in Com.

Gaius Oppius was a Spanish centurion. Dex. A.C. 34, Com. no. 3. He was bishop of Milan. Ibid., and A.C. 34, Com. no. 12, where much is said about him; and A.C. 66, Com. nos. 2; and A.C. 70, Com. nos. 11 and 12.

Gaius Cornelius, the centurion of Capernaum, was from Málaga. Com. A.C. 34, nos. 3 and 8, and A.C. 52.

## E
## E

**Ebora.** See Ebura, or Elbora.

**Church of Eborensis** in Lusitania, erected by Saint Mancius, bishop and disciple of Christ. Commentary, A.C. 90.

**Ebura**, a city in Carpetania, the same as Talabera. Commentary, A.C. 130, no. 6, and Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 54.

**Eburenses**, martyrs in Carpetania. Dexter, A.C. 300; Commentary, nos. 20 and 54; and Dexter, A.C. 352.

**Eburenses**, Hebrews of Carpetania, converted to the faith on the island of Minorca. Dexter and Commentary, A.C. 424, no. 11.

**Martyrs of Ebredunum.** Dexter, A.C. 308; Commentary, no. 24.

**Churches erected by Saint James:** Caesaraugustana, Bracarensis, Carthaginensis, Hispalensis, Valentina, Tarraconensis, Toletana, Barcinonensis, Lucensis, Asturicensis, Palentina, and Juliobrigensis. Dexter and Commentary, A.C. 37, no. 8.

**Churches erected by Saint Peter of Braga, a disciple of Saint James:** Iriensis, Amphilocensis, Eminiensis, and Portuensis. Commentary, A.C. 36, no. 2. Likewise Conimbricensis, Ulyssipponensis, and others beyond Cape Nerium. See Hugh of Portugal, among the Author’s Eulogies. Likewise Emeritensis and Egitanensis. Ibid.

**Churches erected by Saint Basil, a disciple of Saint James:** Tudensis and Placentina, or Ambraciensis. Commentary, A.C. 36, no. 2.

**Churches erected by Saint Mancius, a disciple of Christ:** Eborensis in Lusitania, [Col. 1245] and Cathalaunensis in Gaul. Commentary, A.C. 90.

**All churches purchase peace from the pagans.** Dexter, A.C. 180. Especially the Spanish churches. Ibid.

**Tranquility of the churches throughout the world under Sylvester and Constantine.** Dexter, A.C. 312.

**Ega** brought relics of Saint Catherine to Spain. Dexter, A.C. 308; Commentary, no. 23.

**Egabrum**, a city whose presbyter Victorius took part in the Council of Illiberis—which city was it? Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 5.

**Church of Egitania**, erected by Saint Peter of Braga. Hugh of Portugal, among the Author’s Eulogies.

**Quinctianus**, bishop of Elbora, took part in the Council of Illiberis. Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 5.

**Saint Bricius**, bishop of Elbora. See Bricius.

**Elbora**, a city, elsewhere called Ebura, in Carpetania. See Ebura.

**Elepel**, a city called Ilipula, whose presbyter Saint Restitutus took part in the Council of Illiberis. Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 5.

**Eliocrota**, which city was it? Valladolid, perhaps? Commentary, A.C. 54. Its bishop Successus and its presbyter Liberatus took part in the Council of Illiberis. Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 5.

**The Author’s Eulogies.** Seek them after the Author’s life.

**Elpidius**, a disciple of Saint James, appointed by him as the first bishop of Toledo. Dexter and Commentary, A.C. 37, no. 8. He consecrates an altar to his teacher. Dexter, A.C. 42; Commentary, no. 4. He suffers martyrdom. Dexter, A.C. 60. See concerning him Dexter, A.C. 419.

**Church of Emerita**, erected by Saint Peter of Braga. Hugh of Portugal, among the Author’s Eulogies.

**Martyrs.** Commentary, A.C. 298.

**Bishop Liberius** took part in the Council of Illiberis. Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 5.

**Martyrs and virgins, Eulalia and Julia.** Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 52. And Lucretia. Dexter, A.C. 308; Commentary, no. 22.

**Idacius**, bishop, a most vehement persecutor of Priscillianus. Dexter, A.C. 384. **A council against Priscillianus.** Ibid. **Martialis**, bishop, deposed. Commentary, A.C. 255, no. 2. **Letter of Saint Cyprian to the Emeritans concerning the same matter.** Ibid.

**Emeritus**, presbyter of Barea, took part in the Council of Illiberis. Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 5.

**Emila**, bishop of Barcelona, took part in the Council of Caesaraugusta. Dexter, A.C. 384. He was deposed. Ibid.; in the Commentary, A.C. 388, no. 11, and Commentary, A.C. 396, no. 1.

**Church of Eminiensis**, erected by Saint Peter of Braga. Commentary, A.C. 36, no. 2.

**Emeterius and Celedonius**, martyrs of Calagurris. Commentary, A.C. 298.

**Emeterius**, a farmer and martyr, companion of Saint Severus, bishop of Barcelona. Commentary, A.C. 285, no. 10.

**Encratis**, the same as Engratia. See Engratia.

**Engratia**, a virgin, killed at Caesaraugusta together with her companions. Dexter, A.C. 300; Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 13. Her Acts are in the Commentary.

**Epaphroditus** was made bishop of Tarragona—not Tarracina—by the Apostle Saint Peter. Commentary, A.C. 50.

**Eparchius**, a martyr of Tarragona with his companions. Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 26.

**Epenetus** was made bishop in Spain by the Apostle Saint Peter. Dexter and Commentary, A.C. 50. He died. Dexter, A.C. 64.

**Ephrem**, a disciple of Saint James, appointed by him as the first bishop of Astorga. Dexter and Commentary, A.C. 37, no. 8. He suffers martyrdom. Dexter, A.C. 60.

**Epictetus**, a disciple of Saint Peter of Braga, [Col. 1246] and the first bishop of Tui, and of Ambracia, or Placentia, in Spain. Commentary, A.C. 36, no. 2; Commentary, A.C. 37, no. 8; and Dexter, A.C. 268, Commentary, no. 7. He becomes a martyr. Ibid. Elsewhere he is called Epitatius.

**Epictetus, or Epitatius**, bishop of Caesaraugusta, takes part in the Council of Toledo. Dexter, A.C. 105. See concerning him the hymn of M. Maximus. Commentary, A.C. 71, no. 5.

**The bishops created by Saint James in Spain**—with the single exception of Peter of Braga—were all faithful refugees from Jerusalem, driven out in the persecution that arose after the killing of Stephen; James had found them in Spain. Dexter, A.C. 37; Commentary, no. 8.

**Episcopal sees** throughout Spain are better distributed by Saint Eugenius. See Eugenius of Toledo. They are organized again under Bishop Natalis at the Council of Toledo. Dexter, A.C. 324.

**Bishops who took part in the nineteenth Council of Toledo.** Commentary, A.C. 405.

**Dedication-letter of Dexter to Orosius.** Seek it at the beginning of the Chronicle.

**Letters of Saint Eugenius of Toledo to Saints Nereus and Achilleus, martyrs.** Commentary, A.C. 34, no. 4. Another, their reply. Commentary, A.C. 91, no. 3. Another likewise from Eugenius to them. Ibid.

**The Canonical Epistle of Saint James**, defended at length as having been written not by James the Less but by James the Greater. Commentary, A.C. 37, no. 6. And that it was the first writing of the New Testament. Ibid., no. 7, with Dexter.

**The Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews**, written to the Spaniards. Dexter, A.C. 66; this is proved at length in the Commentary.

**The Epistle of John to Gaius:** to which Gaius was it written? Dexter, A.C. 70; Commentary, no. 4.

**Letters of Ignatius to the Blessed Virgin.** Dexter, A.C. 116, and Commentary, A.C. 430.

**Letter of the Blessed Virgin to Ignatius.** Ibid.

**Letter of the Blessed Virgin to the people of Messana.** Dexter and Commentary, A.C. 86, no. 11, and A.C. 430.

**Letter of the Blessed Virgin to the Florentines.** Commentary, A.C. 86, no. 11.

**Letters to M. Marcellus, or Eugenius of Toledo**, written under the name of Timothy as a memorial. Dexter, A.C. 220.

**Letter of Cyprian to Caledonius of Braga.** Commentary, A.C. 268, no. 1.

**His letter to the churches of Emerita, León, and Astorga**, and the passage corrected by him. Commentary, A.C. 255, no. 2.

**Letter of King Silo of Spain to Cyxillanus, bishop of Toledo.** Commentary, A.C. 286, no. 2, in Saint Thyrsus.

**The letters of Jerome, Chromatius, and Heliodorus concerning the publication of the Martyrology** are genuine. Commentary, A.C. 384, no. 3.

**Epitatius.** See Epictetus.

**The equuleus** is often called a cross. Commentary, A.C. 138, no. 6, in the case of the virgin Liberata.

**Errors in Dexter’s codex** lend authority to the codex itself; and which errors in particular? Part I of the Apology, § 1.

**Estuciana**, which city was it? Commentary, A.C. 138, no. 6. Its martyrs. Ibid.

**Etherius**, a disciple of Saint James, appointed by him as the first bishop of Barcelona. Dexter and Commentary, A.C. 37, no. 8. He suffers martyrdom. Dexter, A.C. 60.

**Etherius**, bishop of Ossonoba, takes part in the Council of Caesaraugusta. Dexter, A.C. 384.

**Eucharius**, presbyter of the municipality of Alba, [Col. 1247] took part in the Council of Illiberis. Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 5.

**Eucharius**, a Toletan presbyter, in Africa. Dexter, A.C. 384. Augustine on him. Commentary, ibid.

**Eucherius**, son of Stilicho: what sort of man was he? Commentary, A.C. 417, no. 1.

**Eugenius**, a disciple of Saint James, appointed by him as the first bishop of Valencia. Dexter and Commentary, A.C. 37, no. 8. He suffers martyrdom. Dexter, A.C. 60.

**Eugenius of Toledo**, first called M. Marcellus: who was he? Commentary, A.C. 34, no. 4. He writes to Saints Nereus and Achilleus. Ibid., and Commentary, A.C. 91. He came to Spain with Peter, whose disciple he was. Dexter, A.C. 50. He makes the Church of Toledo primatial and arranges the other sees of Spain more effectively. Dexter, A.C. 91. Much is said about him. Dexter, A.C. 100; Commentary, nos. 1, 3, 7, and 8. There is discussion there of his poems and his art of oratory. Dionysius the Areopagite dedicates his books to him. Commentary, A.C. 100, nos. 11 and 12. He celebrates a council at Toledo. Dexter, A.C. 105. What sort of man was his nephew through his brother? Dexter, A.C. 110. His mother and sisters. See under Xantippe and Polyxena. He convenes another council. Dexter, A.C. 112. He writes the martyrdom of Saint Dionysius in an outstanding poem. Dexter, A.C. 130. He sets out for Gaul, preaches at Toulouse, and suffers martyrdom near Paris. Ibid., and in the Commentary.

**Eulalia**, virgin and martyr of Barcelona, and her Acts. Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 52. Her tomb. Ibid., no. 53. Her church. Commentary, A.C. 312.

**Eulalia of Emerita.** Dexter, A.C. 300; Commentary, no. 54. Her Acts. Ibid. How similar were the two Eulalias to one another? Ibid.

**Eulogius**, a citizen and martyr of Tarragona, with his companions. Dexter, A.C. 268; Commentary, no. 4.

**Eumantius**, presbyter of Solia, took part in the Council of Illiberis. Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 5.

**Eumelia**, the same as Euphemia. See Euphemia.

**Eumentianus**, presbyter of Ossigi, took part in the Council of Illiberis. Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 5.

**Euphemia**, virgin and martyr, sister of eight other women in Gallaecia. Dexter and Commentary, A.C. 138, no. 7.

**Euphrasius**, a disciple and doorkeeper of Saint James, but made a bishop by Saint Peter and sent back to Spain. Dexter and Commentary, A.C. 37, 43, and 44. Where did he preach? Dexter, A.C. 54, no. 8. He suffers martyrdom. Commentary, ibid. Where is he buried? Ibid. He was formerly sent by the Spaniards to Peter, and for what reason? Commentary, A.C. 35, no. 1.

**Eusebius Palatinus and his companions**, martyrs of Medellín. Dexter, A.C. 134.

**Eusebius of Ebura and of Laodicea.** See below.

**Euthrandus**, continuator of Dexter’s Chronicle: who was he? Part I of the Apology, § 1; and in the Author’s Eulogies; also Part II of the Apology.

**Eutropius**, bishop of Xanthus: was he one of those Gentiles who came to Philip in order to speak with Jesus? Commentary, A.C. 35, no. 9.

**Eutropius**, martyr of Ebura, with his companions. Commentary, A.C. 300, no. 20.

**Eusebius**, bishop of Laodicea. Dexter, A.C. 276.

**Eusebius**, martyr of Ebura in Carpetania, with his companions. Dexter, A.C. 300; Commentary, no. 20.

**Epitaph of Eutyches the Charioteer**, a Spaniard. Commentary, A.C. 120.
